**Status:** Brand-new (created 2026-09-29, 5 commits, v1.0.0 release with prebuilt archives, CI green on all 5 runs). It is MIT OR Unlicense and small enough to vendor, but unofficial and pinned to upstream v2.18.

[repo](https://github.com/aplghl/stb-image-resize-opt) · [benchmark](https://github.com/aplghl/stb-image-resize-opt)

##### GraphicsMagick  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

ImageMagick-derived C image-processing library and gm CLI; about 2.2x faster than ImageMagick 7 on libvips's crop-shrink-sharpen test.

**Beats:** ImageMagick 7.1.1 (convert) — In the libvips maintainers' vips-bench run (Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04 distribution packages, 16 OpenMP threads, quickest of five runs, 12 Aug 2025), gm took 2.05 s against 4.44 s for ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert (about 2.2x) and 2.49 s against 4.38 s with JPEG input (about 1.76x), while using about 32% more peak memory (derived from page data). The 'gm 1.4' label is the Debian package string '1.4+really1.3.x', so the tested build was a 1.3.4x release (Ubuntu 24.04 shipped 1.3.42 and 25.10 ships 1.3.45+hg17696; the 25.04 build is no longer listed). GraphicsMagick's own benchmarks page (www/benchmarks.rst) gives only first-party hyperfine examples (rotate 92 degrees on a 3500x2300 PNM: gm 178.0 ms vs magick 785.3 ms, no CPU named).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the libvips maintainers' vips-bench (gm.sh and im.sh public; Threadripper PRO 3955WX, 12 August 2025): gm 2.05 s vs ImageMagick convert 4.44 s, Ubuntu packages with no flags. gm crops after load while ImageMagick crops on load, so the work differs. Hosted on SourceForge (hg), last commit 2026-10-03.

**Known shortcoming:** The libvips table's 'gm 1.4' label is Debian's '1.4+really1.3.x' version string (1.4 is unreleased; the 25.04 build is probably 1.3.45), and the 1.98 GB peak fits a Q16 build (derived from the INSTALL formula). ConvolveImage normalises the sharpen kernel by its sum of 8 and the bench compares no outputs. The project's own benchmarks.rst declines GraphicsMagick-versus-ImageMagick numbers, offering only a hyperfine rotate of 178.0 against 785.3 ms with no CPU. Coder heap overflows were still being fixed in 2026, so sandbox untrusted input.

**How:** Pixel loops are parallelised across rows or columns with OpenMP, and the pixel cache was rewritten so several threads can work on one image. Resize is a classic two-pass separable filter (HorizontalFilter then VerticalFilter in magick/resize.c), with per-thread contribution tables and the pass order chosen to minimise work. Convolution (magick/effect.c) uses a float kernel normalised by its sum, with a fixed-size inner loop per channel. There are no hand-written SIMD intrinsics in these paths; speed depends on the compiler's auto-vectorisation and on the build's quantum depth.

**Use it when:**
- Batch command-line or server image pipelines (decode, resize, sharpen, encode) that use ImageMagick today and want lower latency on a multi-core machine.
- C or C++ programs that need ImageMagick-style format coverage with an MIT-style licence and a conservative, stable API (core C API, Wand or Magick++).
- Scripts written for ImageMagick 6 convert syntax that can be pointed at gm convert, or at the compatibility links from --enable-magick-compat, after checking each command.
- Q8 builds for 8-bit-only workloads where speed matters more than precision; the project's install guide says Q16 runs 15% to 50% slower and uses twice the memory.

**Skip it when:**
- Large-image or memory-limited jobs: on the libvips test gm peaked at about 1.98 GB against about 94 MB for libvips, which was also about 3.6x faster.
- When you need ImageMagick 7 features or exact ImageMagick 7 command semantics: the two projects have diverged, and GraphicsMagick's own benchmarks page says the same filter arguments now do different amounts of work in each.
- Processing untrusted uploads without sandboxing: the 2025-2026 releases still fix heap overflows in coders (MIFF, PCX, TIFF EXIF, MNG and others), and the project's security page tells users to run it in a container and keep up with releases rather than trust distribution packages.
- Single-image latency work dominated by file I/O or start-up: the project's OpenMP notes say decode and encode usually do not speed up with threads, and start-up can outweigh the operation itself.

**Integration:** shared lib · none required for the core; optional delegate libraries per format (libjpeg or libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libtiff, zlib, bzip2, lcms2, FreeType, libwebp, JasPer, Ghostscript and others); optional tcmalloc · C99 compiler with stdint.h and inttypes.h (required since 2025-06-17); C++ compiler for Magick++; OpenMP-capable compiler (GCC or Clang) for multi-threading · Linux, BSD, macOS, Cygwin, MinGW/MSYS2 and Windows (Visual Studio); portable C, any CPU architecture

**Vs siblings:** Pick GraphicsMagick over libvips when you need ImageMagick-style command syntax, a broad set of formats and a whole-image API, and can accept far higher memory (2.05 s and about 1.98 GB against libvips's 0.57 s and 94 MB on the same test); pick it over OpenImageIO (3.46 s) or ImageMagick itself when the job is ImageMagick-style batch conversion. FFmpeg (2.06 s) is about equal on this test but is not a general still-image toolkit.

**Gotchas:**
- Quantum depth is fixed at build time and defaults to 8 bits; distribution packages appear to use 16 bits (the measured 1.98 GB peak matches two 10000x10000 images at about 1 GB each under the install guide's QuantumDepth*Rows*Columns*5/8 formula; derived, package flags not read). Q8 and Q16 builds differ in both speed and output precision.
- ConvolveImage divides a user kernel by its sum, so -convolve with the benchmark's sharpen kernel (sum 8) gives a mild sharpen; output can differ from an ImageMagick command that does not normalise. The libvips benchmark does not compare output images.
- Distribution version strings are misleading: Debian and Ubuntu package 1.3.x releases as '1.4+really1.3.x'. GraphicsMagick 1.4 is still an unreleased development branch (version.sh on the default branch: PACKAGE_VERSION '1.4', release date 'unreleased'); the latest release is 1.3.48 (2026-07-23).
- glibc malloc can limit OpenMP scaling on many cores; the install guide recommends --with-tcmalloc and reports up to 2x on some algorithms.

**Status:** Actively maintained by one lead developer (Bob Friesenhahn; release 1.3.48 on 2026-07-23, Mercurial commits on 2026-10-03) and MIT-licensed, so it can be copied or linked freely; use the latest release because nearly every release carries security fixes.

[repo](https://sourceforge.net/projects/graphicsmagick/) · [benchmark](https://github.com/libvips/libvips/wiki/Speed-and-memory-use)

##### OpenCV  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Computer-vision library whose cv::resize upscaling and cv::GaussianBlur ran 3-17x faster than ImageMagick 6.9, single-threaded.

**Beats:** ImageMagick (6.9 via the Wand binding, single-threaded, in pillow-perf; magick and convert 7.1.1 in the libvips Speed-and-memory-use table) — pillow-perf (run by the Pillow-SIMD authors) timed the opencv-python 4.1 binary wheel against ImageMagick 6.9 through Wand on one Core i5-4430 core (Ubuntu 18.04.3, both libraries forced single-threaded, compiler and flags not stated) on a 2560x1600 RGB image: like-for-like upscale to 5478x3424 is 17.5x faster bilinear and 10.9x faster bicubic, and Gaussian blur is 9.7x, 4.0x and 2.9x faster at sigma 1, 10 and 30. Reading the 4.1.2 source shows the sigma 10 and 30 blur rows ran a kernel whose 8-bit fixed-point taps summed to 254/256 and 243/256 per pass (computed from getFixedpointGaussianKernel, matching issue #9863's 10 percent darkening at ksize 151, sigma 30), a bug fixed in 4.2.0 by error-diffusion quantisation; the fix changes coefficients, not the code path, so the timings are probably still representative, but the measured output was wrong. Separately, the libvips wiki pipeline (crop, 0.9x resize, sharpen, TIFF load and save on a 16-core Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04 packages) has OpenCV 4.10 at 3.15 s against multi-threaded ImageMagick 7.1.1 at 4.41 s (1.4x).

**Known shortcoming:** Claim overstated: the pillow-perf 'bic' downscale cells (16.5x, 4.6x) are really INTER_AREA supersampling (the raw i5-4430.txt labels them 'sup') against ImageMagick's Catmull-Rom, not like for like. Like-for-like single-threaded rows: upscale 17.5x bilinear and 10.9x bicubic, blur 9.7x/4.0x/2.9x vs ImageMagick 6.9; the libvips wiki run gives 3.15 vs 4.41 s (1.4x). The speedtest-resize OpenCV row uses nearest neighbour (interpolation 0) and is not comparable, and OpenCV is slower than ImageMagick at JPEG load and save.

**Known shortcoming:** The Pillow-comparison blur rows were measured on OpenCV 4.1.x whose 8-bit GaussianBlur rounded each fixed-point tap without renormalisation (getFixedpointGaussianKernel, 8 fraction bits): at the 30 px case (151 taps, sigma 30) the taps sum to 243/256 per pass, about 10% darker (issue #9863), fixed in 4.2.0; the timing is probably unchanged since the code path is the same. In 4.1.2 cv::resize tries Intel IPP first and IPP accepts 8-bit INTER_CUBIC and LANCZOS4, so those rows may be IPP code rather than OpenCV's own. Large-sigma blur is O(window): Pillow 7.0 stays near 0.19 s at every radius against OpenCV's 1.40 s at 30 px, and Pillow-SIMD AVX2 bicubic upscale (76.6 ms) beats OpenCV (115.3 ms).

**How:** 8-bit INTER_LINEAR resize is a separable two-pass filter with precomputed integer coefficient tables (INTER_RESIZE_COEF_BITS = 11), a horizontal pass into an int row buffer and a SIMD vertical pass (VResizeLinearVec_32s8u), and it always reads only 2x2 source pixels, which is also why it does not antialias on shrinking. INTER_AREA has a SIMD box-average fast path for integer factors (ResizeAreaFastVec_SIMD_8u) and precomputed overlap weights otherwise. 8-bit GaussianBlur runs a bit-exact separable fixed-point filter (ufixedpoint16, 8 fractional bits) with symmetric-kernel folding and special 3- and 5-tap kernels, split over rows with parallel_for_ and compiled for several ISAs with runtime CPU dispatch (CV_CPU_DISPATCH). In the measured 4.1.2 build, cv::resize first tried Intel IPP's iwiResize when OpenCV was built with IPP (WITH_IPP defaults to ON on x86), which IPP accepts for 8-bit INTER_CUBIC and INTER_LANCZOS4 but not for 8-bit bilinear, area or nearest, so the bicubic and Lanczos rows may be IPP code rather than OpenCV's own kernels. Current 4.x routes this through hal/ipp (ipp_hal_resize).

**Use it when:**
- Upscaling 8-bit RGB images in-process where bilinear or bicubic quality is enough: pillow-perf measured 57.7 ms (bilinear) and 115.3 ms (bicubic) for 2560x1600 to 5478x3424 on one Haswell core, versus 1007.6 and 1256.1 ms for ImageMagick 6.9.
- Small-sigma Gaussian blur on 8-bit images (sigma about 1, 7-tap window): 69 ms vs 675 ms for ImageMagick on a 4 MP frame, single-threaded.
- Integer-factor downscales with INTER_AREA (box averaging), e.g. 2560x1600 to 320x200 in 5.4 ms, when a box filter is an acceptable shrink filter.
- Pipelines that already link OpenCV for vision work, where adding ImageMagick only for resize or blur would add a second heavy dependency.
- Multi-core servers: resize and GaussianBlur split rows across threads with parallel_for_ (pthreads by default); the catalogued numbers were taken with cv2.setNumThreads(1), so default runs can be faster.

**Skip it when:**
- Quality downscaling with bilinear or bicubic: cv::resize does no antialiasing, and the OpenCV docs advise INTER_AREA for shrinking; an antialiased resize is still an open feature request (#25620). Convolution resamplers such as Pillow-SIMD, libvips or fast_image_resize are the like-for-like choice.
- Large-sigma Gaussian blur: the separable filter costs O(window) per pixel, so sigma 30 (151 taps) took 1.40 s, while Pillow 7.0.0 in the same pillow-perf file stays at about 0.19 s at every radius and Pillow-SIMD AVX2 bicubic upscale (76.6 ms) also beats OpenCV's 115.3 ms.
- OpenCV builds older than 4.2.0 for 8-bit GaussianBlur with large windows: the fixed-point kernel was rounded tap by tap without renormalising, so output came out darker (issue #9863: ksize 151, sigma 30, about 10 percent darker).
- JPEG-heavy pipelines judged on codec speed: pillow-perf shows OpenCV slower than ImageMagick at JPEG load (47.9 vs 27.4 ms) and save (56.7 vs 48.0 ms).
- Projects that need a small dependency, colour management, or the format breadth of ImageMagick.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake build of opencv_core + opencv_imgproc; prebuilt opencv-python wheels and distro packages) · imgproc needs only opencv_core; optional Intel IPP ICV on x86 (WITH_IPP on by default except MinGW), TBB or OpenMP (off by default; pthreads parallel_for is on), Carotene and KleidiCV HALs on ARM, image codec libraries for imgcodecs · C++11 for the 4.x line, C++17 for the 5.x line (default branch); CMake 3.7+ for 4.x · x86-64 with runtime dispatch up to AVX2/AVX-512, AArch64 (NEON, Carotene, KleidiCV), RISC-V and others

**Vs siblings:** Pick OpenCV over Pillow-SIMD, libvips or fast_image_resize when you already depend on it or need fast bilinear upscaling and small-kernel blurs inside a vision pipeline; pick those convolution resamplers when downscale quality matters, and pick a box-blur approximation (FastBoxBlur, LibGaussianBlur, Pillow) for large-radius blurs. For a whole load-resize-save pipeline, libvips (0.57 s) is far ahead of OpenCV (3.15 s) in the same libvips wiki table.

**Gotchas:**
- Different filters under the same names: OpenCV INTER_CUBIC uses a = -0.75 (and the 4.1.2 IPP path is configured to match), while ImageMagick's catrom is a = -0.5; INTER_LANCZOS4 is an 8x8 Lanczos-4 kernel, not ImageMagick's Lanczos-3; INTER_AREA acts like nearest neighbour when enlarging.
- 8-bit results come from fixed-point arithmetic (11-bit resize coefficients, 8-bit-fraction Gaussian taps): at large sigma each Gaussian tap is only a few 1/256 steps, and plain INTER_LINEAR is not the bit-exact mode (INTER_LINEAR_EXACT is).
- When ksize is 0, GaussianBlur derives it from sigma with 3 sigma per side for 8-bit images but 4 sigma for float images, so 8-bit and float blurs of the same sigma use different windows.
- imread returns BGR channel order, and resize with interpolation code 0 is nearest neighbour; third-party benchmarks that pass 0 (as the speedtest-resize go-opencv row does) are not measuring bilinear.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-02 on 4.x, default branch 5.x, 91.1k stars) and Apache-2.0; usable directly from wheels or distro packages, but the catalogued pillow-perf numbers come from a 2019-2020 opencv-python 4.1 wheel.

[repo](https://github.com/opencv/opencv) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python-pillow/pillow-perf/HEAD/docs/src/data/i5-4430.json)

##### OpenImageIO  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

VFX-industry image I/O and processing library; its oiiotool ran a crop, resize and convolve job 1.3x faster than ImageMagick 7.

**Beats:** ImageMagick 7.1.1 (magick, convert) — In the libvips maintainer's vips-bench run (12 Aug 2025, Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16 cores, Ubuntu 25.04 packages, flags not stated), oiiotool 2.5.18 took 3.46 s, best wall time of five, to load a 10000x10000 8-bit tiled TIFF, crop, triangle-resize to 90%, 3x3-convolve and save, against 4.41 s for ImageMagick 7.1.1 magick and 4.44 s for convert, about 1.3x (derived from page data). The oiio script's broken crop made it process a mostly black 10000x10000 frame (about 4% more output pixels than ImageMagick) with a gaussian instead of a sharpen kernel, so the work is comparable but the output is not the intended image.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the libvips maintainers' wiki run (12 August 2025, Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04 packages, no flags): oiio 2.5.18 3.46 s vs ImageMagick magick 4.41 s and convert 4.44 s (1.27-1.28x derived), both triangle-filter resizes. Harness bug: oiio.sh's crop geometry uses an undefined $widthx (since 2014), so oiiotool treats it as an offset and processes a mostly black 10000x10000 frame, about 4% more pixels with wrong output; the timing is comparable but the output is not.

**How:** The measured path has no special algorithm. Every ImageBufAlgo call is split by parallel_image across all cores by default, and oiiotool converts 8-bit input to float once at read time. In 2.5.18, and unchanged on main, IBA::resize evaluates the triangle filter as a direct 2D gather of xtaps x ytaps source pixels per output pixel (5x5 at 90%), with separable tap weights precomputed per column and per row, and IBA::convolve is a plain 3x3 gather; both are scalar loops over ImageBuf iterators. Google Highway SIMD exists in 3.2 only for resample (nearest/bilinear) and some per-pixel arithmetic, so the margin over ImageMagick comes from whole-pipeline threading and lower per-operation overhead (inferred from the code, not profiled), not from a faster resampler.

**Use it when:**
- Pipelines built around OpenEXR (multi-part, deep), DPX/Cineon, tiled or MIP-mapped TIFF and OCIO colour management, where you need one C++/Python API across formats more than peak resize speed.
- Batch jobs that shell out to ImageMagick convert/magick for crop, resize and convolution of large images on a many-core box: oiiotool 2.5.18 was 1.27x to 1.28x faster in the libvips table.
- Applications that must read huge texture or plate sets with bounded memory: ImageCache keeps a capped working set and is documented as fully thread-safe.
- Renderers and texture tools needing filtered MIP-map lookups (TextureSystem, maketx / oiiotool -otex).

**Skip it when:**
- Throughput-first thumbnailing or web resizing: in the same libvips table libvips (0.57 s), GraphicsMagick (2.05 s), FFmpeg (2.06 s) and OpenCV (3.15 s) all beat oiio (3.46 s).
- Memory-constrained hosts: oiiotool promotes 8-bit input to float unless --native is given, and peaked at 2236.57 MB against 1500.52 MB for magick and 94.28 MB for libvips.
- Strong downscales with IBA::resize: the 2D gather reads (2*ceil(r/scale)+1)^2 source pixels per output pixel, so a 10% shrink costs 441 taps with the triangle filter and 3721 with the default lanczos3, against 42 and 122 for a two-pass separable resampler; use a dedicated resizer there (IBA::resample is cheap but does not filter, so it aliases).
- Untrusted input on old or distro builds: SECURITY.md says 2.5.x and earlier get no patches, and the 3.2 changelog lists dozens of reader hardening fixes including CVE-2026-59181 (Cineon), CVE-2026-59156 (FITS), CVE-2026-63422 (OpenEXR out-of-bounds write) and CVE-2026-63420 (PSD).
- Projects that want a small dependency: the required set alone is Imath, OpenEXR, libTIFF, OpenColorIO, libjpeg, zlib, fmt and robin-map, plus CMake 3.23.

**Integration:** shared lib · Required: Imath >= 3.1, OpenEXR >= 3.1, libTIFF >= 4.1, OpenColorIO >= 2.3, libjpeg >= 9 or libjpeg-turbo >= 2.1, zlib >= 1.2.7, fmt >= 9 and robin-map >= 1.3 (the last two auto-downloaded if missing). Optional per format or feature: libpng, LibRaw, FFmpeg, OpenJPEG, OpenJPH, libheif, libwebp, libjxl, giflib, DCMTK, OpenVDB, Ptex, Freetype, libultrahdr, TBB, OpenCV, Qt (iv viewer), Python with nanobind or pybind11, Google Highway (OIIO_USE_HWY). · C++17 (also C++20/23/26); gcc 9.3-16, clang 10-22, MSVC 2017-2026 (v19.14+), Intel oneAPI 2022+; CMake >= 3.23 for the 3.2 line · Linux, macOS, Windows; x86-64 builds default to an SSE4.2 baseline in 3.2 (x86-64-v2 on main), with NEON paths on aarch64

**Vs siblings:** Pick OpenImageIO over libvips, GraphicsMagick or FFmpeg only when you need its VFX format coverage (deep and multi-part EXR, DPX, MIP-mapped textures), OCIO colour management or ImageCache/TextureSystem; for batch resize and convolution throughput libvips was 6x faster and used about 24x less memory in the same table, and fast_image_resize or zimg are better single-kernel resizers.

**Gotchas:**
- The libvips oiio.sh bug survives on current main: the script passes '--crop 9800+100+100' (undefined $widthx), and scan_offset on main still parses the leading '9800+100' as an offset and ignores the rest, so a re-run on OIIO 3.2 again processes a mostly black 10000x10000 frame.
- oiiotool works in float by default; use --native (or read with the native type in the C++ API) to keep 8-bit data, at your own speed and accuracy trade-off (not benchmarked).
- The docs say Highway SIMD is enabled by default, but the OIIO_USE_HWY CMake option is OFF ('experimental'), so check how your build was configured before expecting those speedups; the filtered resize and convolve paths have no Highway code either way.
- IBA::resize takes filter options through KWArgs (filtername, filterwidth); with no name it picks lanczos3 when shrinking and blackman-harris when enlarging, and widens the filter by the enlargement ratio, so pin the filter for reproducible output and cost.

**Status:** Very active Academy Software Foundation project (3.2.1.0 released 1 Oct 2026, commits on 3 Oct 2026, monthly patch releases) under Apache-2.0; the benchmarked 2.5 line no longer gets security fixes, so use 3.2.x.

[repo](https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/OpenImageIO) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/libvips/libvips/Speed-and-memory-use.md)

##### Pillow-SIMD  `C (Python extension)`  `MIT-CMU (HPND-family; LICENSE file)`  `active`  `Tier B`

SSE4/AVX2 fork of Python's Pillow; resizes 8-bit RGB images 11-23x faster than ImageMagick 6 via Wand, single core.

**Beats:** ImageMagick 6.9 (via Wand) in the pillow-perf results; ImageMagick 7.1.1 in the libvips wiki table. pillow-perf also compares Pillow, OpenCV, Skia, libvips and Intel IPP. — On an AWS c5.large, one core, a 2560x1600 RGB image resized with Pillow-SIMD 7.0.0.post3 built with -mavx2 took 0.00523 s to 320x200 (Lanczos) versus 0.10633 s for ImageMagick 6.9 through Wand with MAGICK_THREAD_LIMIT=1 (about 20x), and 11-23x across all 12 size and filter cases; compiler, exact CPU and Python overhead in the Wand path are not controlled, and ImageMagick works in 16-bit quantum. The independent libvips crop, 10% bilinear shrink, sharpen and save pipeline on a Threadripper PRO 3955WX timed pillow-simd 9.5.0 (installed with plain pip, so the default SSE4 build) at 1.51 s against ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert at 4.44 s (about 2.9x).

**Known shortcoming:** Python extension in C (fork of python-pillow/Pillow, MIT-CMU). Tier B on the independent libvips vips-bench (pillow-simd 9.5.0 1.51 s vs ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert 4.44 s, Threadripper PRO 3955WX). Its own c5.large.txt shows 11-23x vs Wand, not the README's 16-40x; results are the median of 11 runs (5 for Wand). ImageMagick runs Q16 while Pillow-SIMD uses 8-bit fixed point.

**Known shortcoming:** Only 4-byte UINT8 resampling is vectorised (L, I;16 and F modes stay scalar); INT16 coefficients hold at most 15 bits against upstream Pillow's 22-bit INT32, so output is not bit-identical to Pillow. setup.py hard-codes -msse4 with no runtime dispatch and the ARM build fails (#116, #143); sdist only, no wheels; open PR #149 (ImageMath.eval hardening). The libvips wiki row is probably the SSE4 build (plain pip install); in the same c5.large pillow-perf file cv2 beats it on bilinear upscale (0.052 against 0.076 s).

**How:** Resampling is Pillow's separable two-pass convolution, but coefficients are quantised to INT16 with an adaptive precision (at most 15 bits) so each tap pair can go through _mm_madd_epi16/_mm256_madd_epi16 after a pshufb that interleaves RGBA bytes into 16-bit lanes. The horizontal pass processes four output rows at once (ImagingResampleHorizontalConvolution8u4x) with 4-tap unrolling, and the vertical pass works on 8 (AVX2) or 4 (SSE4) pixels per iteration. Other kernels use the same fixed-point integer SIMD pattern.

**Use it when:**
- Python services that already use Pillow for thumbnails or resizing of 8-bit RGB/RGBA images on x86 and can build from source.
- Downscaling large photos with bilinear, bicubic or Lanczos filters: the pillow-perf c5.large file shows 4.5-7.8x over Pillow 7.0.0 for downscales with the AVX2 build.
- Pipelines that also lean on Pillow's filter(), box/Gaussian blur, alpha_composite or mode conversion, which have SIMD paths too.
- Fleets where you control the CPU (AVX2 everywhere) and can compile per target, as Uploadcare does in production since 2015.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything outside Python, including C++ code: the SIMD kernels are not exposed as a standalone library.
- ARM (Apple Silicon, Graviton) or other non-x86 hosts: setup.py adds -msse4 unconditionally and the build fails there (issues #116, #143); a RISC-V Vector PR (#158) is still open.
- Grayscale (mode L), 16-bit (I;16) or float (I, F) images: in Resample.c only the 4-byte-per-pixel UINT8 path is vectorised; image8 and 16bpc paths stay scalar.
- End-to-end pipelines dominated by decode and encode: in the same c5.large file, load+resize+save is only about 4.5x faster than Wand (0.039 s vs 0.176 s), and in the libvips wiki pipeline libvips is 2.6x faster than pillow-simd (0.57 s vs 1.51 s) because it threads and streams.
- Binary-wheel deployments: PyPI carries only sdists, so every install needs a compiler and Pillow's native dependencies (zlib, libjpeg); issues #157 and #120 are zlib-not-found build failures.

**Integration:** module · CPython (or PyPy) >=3.10 for the 12.x line; build needs setuptools>=77, pybind11, a C compiler, and Pillow's native libraries (zlib and libjpeg required; libtiff, libwebp, freetype, lcms2 optional) · C compiler accepting -msse4 (GCC or Clang); AVX2 build via CC="cc -mavx2"; MSVC x64 gets the SSE4 path through a macro in ImagingSIMD.h · x86 and x86-64 only (SSE4.1 required; AVX2 optional at build time, no runtime dispatch)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libvips or OpenCV when the code base is already PIL-based Python and you want a speedup without rewriting calls; pick libvips for whole pipelines (2.6x faster than pillow-simd and far less memory in the libvips table), fast_image_resize for Rust, and OpenCV when bilinear upscaling dominates (cv2 single-threaded 0.052 s vs Pillow-SIMD AVX2 0.076 s to 5478x3424 in the same c5.large file).

**Gotchas:**
- The instruction set is fixed at compile time: an AVX2 build (CC="cc -mavx2") on a build host will crash with an illegal instruction on a CPU without AVX2, and the default build needs SSE4.1. There is no CPU check at import.
- Output is not bit-identical to upstream Pillow: Pillow-SIMD normalises filter coefficients to INT16 with at most 15 bits of precision, while upstream Pillow uses INT32 coefficients with 22 bits (PRECISION_BITS), so some pixels can differ by rounding.
- Installing it next to Pillow is unsupported; both provide the PIL package, so a later dependency that pulls in Pillow will silently overwrite the SIMD build.
- Older pillow-simd releases lag upstream security fixes: PR #149 (ImageMath.eval environment restriction) has been open since 2024-10-08, and the libvips benchmark used 9.5.0; prefer a .post release of a current Pillow (12.1.1.post0 is on PyPI, the repo is at 12.3.0.post0).

**Status:** Active: SIMD kernels were re-landed on Pillow 12.3.0 on 2026-09-17 and sdists up to 12.1.1.post0 were uploaded to PyPI on 2026-09-15 after a two-year gap at 9.5.0, but there are still no wheels; MIT-CMU licensed and maintained mainly by one Uploadcare developer (homm).

[repo](https://github.com/uploadcare/pillow-simd) · [benchmark](https://github.com/python-pillow/pillow-perf/blob/master/docs/src/data/c5.large.txt)

##### Skia  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

Google's 2D graphics library; its 2016 convolution scaler (Skia 53) resized 4.2x to 9.7x faster than single-threaded ImageMagick 6.8.

**Beats:** ImageMagick 6.8.9-9 — pillow-perf (python-pillow) timed Skia 53's SSE2 SkBitmapScaler in a C++ nanobench loop on a white 2560x1600 N32 bitmap against ImageMagick 6.8.9-9 through Python Wand with MAGICK_THREAD_LIMIT=1 on an RGB image, on a Xeon E5-2666 v3 (c4.large, Ubuntu 16.04.1) and a Core i5-4258U; Skia was 6.4x to 9.5x and 4.2x to 9.7x faster across 12 size/filter cases (derived from page data), with no compiler or flags recorded. The harnesses are not symmetric: the Skia loop reuses a destination preallocated outside the timed loop, while each ImageMagick run includes a clone, a fresh result image and Python call overhead.

**Known shortcoming:** Skia 53 resize at B on the pillow-perf data (c4.large.json, Xeon E5-2666 v3; macbook.json, i5-4258U; rows added by the Pillow-SIMD author on 2016-11-02 via a nanobench BitmapScaleBench.cpp gist, white N32 2560x1600 source) against ImageMagick 6.8.9-9 through Wand with MAGICK_THREAD_LIMIT=1: 6.4-9.5x and 4.2-9.7x (derived), same sizes and filter families (bicubic Mitchell vs Catmull-Rom). The Skia section is commented out of the pillow-perf docs/index.html, SkBitmapScaler.h no longer exists on Skia main, and no flags are recorded; 2016 numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Stale evidence (retier-11 corrects the caveats): the gist times SkBitmapScaler from Skia m53, deleted on 2017-07-20; current scalePixels is raster-pipeline linear or 4x4 cubic with no Lanczos, so the numbers describe no Skia since 2017. The harness preallocates Skia's destination outside the timed loop on a white source while ImageMagick pays clone, new-image and Python Wand overhead per call; Pillow-SIMD 4.3 AVX2 needed 0.32-0.54x of Skia's time on the same data. Skia now requires C++20 and strongly prefers Clang.

**How:** The measured Skia 53 scaler is a two-pass separable convolution over 8-bit BGRA pixels with precomputed per-output-pixel filter taps stored as int16 fixed point (kShiftBits = 14), with SSE2 (x86) and NEON kernels for the horizontal, four-rows-at-once horizontal and vertical passes; that matches the 'Skia 53 SSE2' label in pillow-perf. Current Skia instead resamples by drawing through its raster pipeline: bilinear (2x2 taps) or cubic B/C (fixed 4x4 taps, bicubic_n3x..p3x stages) per output pixel, optional mipmaps for linear filtering, plus a dedicated bicubic_clamp_8888 fast stage.

**Use it when:**
- You already link Skia (Chrome-, Android- or Flutter-style apps, PDF/vector renderers) and need decent-quality thumbnails without adding another imaging library.
- Moderate downscales or upscales of 8-bit RGBA/BGRA images where bilinear or Mitchell/Catmull-Rom cubic quality is enough.
- Workloads that already draw images to a canvas or GPU surface, where scaling is fused into the draw instead of being a separate pass.
- Large-ratio downscales on the CPU using mipmapped linear sampling or SkImage::asyncRescaleAndReadPixels with RescaleMode::kRepeatedLinear / kRepeatedCubic.

**Skip it when:**
- You want the speed measured here: the SkBitmapScaler code that produced the 4.2x to 9.7x numbers no longer exists in Skia, and no benchmark of current scalePixels against ImageMagick was found.
- You need Lanczos or other scale-adaptive convolution filters: current SkSamplingOptions offers only nearest, linear (plus mipmaps) and cubic B/C, and cubic cannot be combined with mipmaps.
- You only need a resize kernel: in the same pillow-perf data Pillow-SIMD 4.3 AVX2 needs 0.32x to 0.54x of Skia 53's time (Lanczos 320x200: 6.23 ms vs 18.1 ms on c4.large), so dedicated resizers are faster and much smaller to integrate.
- 16-bit, float or high-precision resizing pipelines (the measured scaler worked on 8-bit pixels with 14-bit fixed-point weights).
- Projects that cannot take a GN/Ninja build with Python-driven dependency sync, Clang and C++20.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (GN + Ninja; is_component_build for shared) · Python 3 for tools/git-sync-deps and bin/fetch-gn; GN and Ninja; third-party codecs and fonts (libpng, libjpeg-turbo, libwebp, FreeType, ICU, etc.) are optional per skia_use_* flags; Bazel for some Rust third-party code; CMake 3.30+ only for Dawn · C++20 (site/docs/user/build.md); Clang strongly preferred, since software-rasterizer and color-conversion paths are documented to be 'dramatically' slower with GCC or MSVC · Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS, ChromeOS; x86-64 and arm64 CPU paths, plus GPU backends

**Vs siblings:** Pick Skia when it is already in the binary and you also need drawing or GPU compositing; for a standalone fast resizer, Pillow-SIMD's resample code (faster than Skia 53 in the same dataset), libvips or OpenCV are better choices, and stb-image-resize-opt is the lightweight single-header option.

**Gotchas:**
- The measured API (SkBitmapScaler, SkConvolver, SkResizeFilter) was removed on 2017-07-20; nanobench numbers for Skia 53 do not describe any Skia release after that.
- Current cubic sampling uses a fixed 4x4 footprint per output pixel, so very large downscales with cubic alias unless you downscale in steps (asyncRescaleAndReadPixels kRepeatedCubic) or use mipmapped linear sampling.
- Skia has no stable API: RELEASE_NOTES.md lists removals and signature changes almost every milestone, so pin a milestone branch (chrome/mNNN).
- Chromium still carries the old convolution resizer (skia::ImageOperations::Resize in skia/ext, Lanczos-3/box/Hamming with SSE2, NEON and LSX), but it lives in the Chromium tree, not in Skia.

**Status:** Very actively developed (last commit 2026-10-03; RELEASE_NOTES.md already has a Milestone 156 section) and BSD-3-Clause, so copyable, but the benchmarked scaler was deleted in 2017 and today's equivalent is an unbenchmarked raster-pipeline path.

[repo](https://github.com/google/skia) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python-pillow/pillow-perf/HEAD/docs/src/data/c4.large.json)

#### font-shaping-text-layout

##### Fontations (skrifa / read-fonts)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Google's memory-safe Rust OpenType stack (read-fonts, skrifa); mostly 1.1-1.6x slower than HarfBuzz's own OT font functions.

**Beats:** HarfBuzz OT font backend (hb-ot font functions: cmap lookup, advances, extents, outline drawing) — HarfBuzz maintainer behdad's issue #2196 runs HarfBuzz's perf/benchmark-font with the 'fontations' and 'ot' backends doing the same hb_font calls on eight test fonts (default and wght=500), Clang 21.1.7 -O3 LTO and Rust 1.94.0-nightly fat LTO, pinned to one core of a Ryzen 9 5900X, CPU medians of seven runs. The page was revised on 2026-10-04 and now cites HarfBuzz 692a0aa30e and Fontations 08bfef45 rather than the eff2d6b9/ec902bd2 commits in the record; its numbers give Fontations/OT geometric means of 1.52x nominal glyphs, 1.39x horizontal advances, 1.10x vertical advances, 1.62x vertical origins, 1.33x extents, 1.56x drawing, 1.16x paint and 1.06x load-and-shape (derived from page data; above 1 means slower).

**Known shortcoming:** Mostly slower than HarfBuzz's OT font functions on HarfBuzz's own perf/benchmark-font.cc (Clang 21.1.7, meson release -O3 with LTO, Ryzen 9 5900X pinned to CPU 6): geometric means 1.29-1.58x slower and paint 1.26x slower, faster only on varied Roboto Flex origins (0.64x) and extents (0.63x), Adobe CFF2 extents (0.87x and 0.89x) and a few rows at 0.97-0.99x (derived from page data). The measured commit ec902bd2 is the head of the open, unmerged HarfBuzz PR #2197 plus local Cargo patches.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e107, 2026-10-05): A stands, no correctness bug. Issue #2196's body was revised 2026-10-04 (HarfBuzz 692a0aa30e vs Fontations 08bfef45; geomeans now nominal 1.52x, h-adv 1.39x, v-adv 1.10x, v-orig 1.62x, extents 1.33x, draw 1.56x, paint 1.16x, load+shape 1.06x; 10 of 96 rows faster; worst row Adobe VF nominal 3.50x). PR #2197 was closed and split into #2199-#2206, four merged 2026-10-04 and four still open, so the measured code is partly unreleased. Harness skews against Fontations: Rust std built optimize_for_size with forced frame pointers, no cross-language LTO; load_face_and_shape shapes a single space, so it measures setup cost; metric rows run HarfBuzz's src/rust/font.rs over read_fonts::model, not skrifa. Issue #1551: skrifa about 4x slower than ttf-parser on CFF outlining. Corrections in retier-31.

**Independent measurement:** HarfBuzz maintainer benchmark (issue #2196)

**How:** Tables are newtype wrappers over the font's byte slice with codegen'd accessors: minimal validation at parse time, big-endian records cast in place, and no allocation or copying. The current optimisation round (PR #2197, split into #2199-#2206) adds HarfBuzz-style lazily filled per-instance scalar caches for HVAR, VVAR and gvar (128 entries), skips scalar evaluation for zero deltas, reuses supplied gvar scalars for outlines and drawing, inlines cmap dispatch and CFF charstring opcode decoding, and skips unused Private DICT entries for unhinted CFF. None of this makes it faster than HarfBuzz OT except on a few varied-instance rows.

**Use it when:**
- Rendering untrusted or web fonts where memory safety matters more than the last 30-60% of font-funcs speed: both read-fonts and skrifa use #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and are fuzzed on OSS-Fuzz.
- Rust programs that need FreeType-equivalent outlines and hinting (TrueType, CFF, CFF2, autohinter) and full variable-font support without linking FreeType.
- Heavily varied instances of glyf/gvar fonts queried for extents or vertical origins: on varied Roboto Flex (wght=500) the issue measures 0.63-0.64x HarfBuzz OT's time.
- Glyph extents on CFF2 variable fonts (Adobe VF Prototype 0.92-0.93x of OT time) or nominal-glyph lookup on simple cmaps (about 0.98-0.99x).
- Projects that already pull the Rust font stack in through HarfBuzz -Dfontations, Skia or Chromium and want one implementation for shaping metrics and rasterisation.

**Skip it when:**
- As a speed upgrade over HarfBuzz's built-in OT font functions: across the 96 benchmark rows only 10 are faster; unvaried glyf extents and vertical origins are about 1.7-1.8x slower, unhinted drawing 1.17-1.94x slower, and Adobe VF Prototype nominal glyphs 3.5x slower.
- Fast CFF outline extraction in Rust: issue #1551 (July 2025) reports skrifa about 4x slower than ttf-parser on CFF outlining, about half of it from reparsing the Private DICT per glyph; only part of that has been fixed (PR #2204).
- C or C++ projects without a Rust toolchain: there is no C API, and HarfBuzz's meson rules for the backend use bindgen and cargo with -Z flags, so a nightly Rust is needed.
- Code that needs a stable API: all crates are pre-1.0 and bump the minor version for breaking changes roughly monthly (read-fonts 0.43.0 Aug 12, 0.44.0 Sep 8, 0.45.0 Oct 3, 2026).

**Integration:** crate (read-fonts, skrifa, font-types, write-fonts); from C/C++ via HarfBuzz built with -Dfontations=enabled, which links a Rust staticlib · read-fonts: font-types, yoke, bytemuck, once_cell (core_maths with the libm feature, serde optional); skrifa: read-fonts, bytemuck; HarfBuzz backend: cargo, bindgen, meson's unstable-rust module · Rust 1.85 (workspace rust-version, edition 2021); HarfBuzz's backend needs a nightly cargo for its -Z build-std and -Z unstable-options arguments · any Rust target; std is a default feature and the libm feature exists for builds without std

**Vs siblings:** Pick Fontations over ttf-parser when you need hinting, an autohinter, COLRv1 painting and FreeType-matching output (the repo's fauntlet tool compares against FreeType), and accept slower CFF outlining; ttf-parser is the faster parser for raw outline extraction. For rasterising, ab_glyph or fontdue are complete small rasterisers, while skrifa only produces outlines for a separate rasteriser such as Skia.

**Gotchas:**
- read-fonts returns a default value (0, None or an empty array) when a field of malformed table data cannot be read, instead of an error, so corrupt fonts degrade silently.
- Unhinted CFF drawing without a reusable HintingInstance reparses the Private DICT for every glyph (issue #1551); keep one instance per size if you draw many CFF glyphs.
- Through HarfBuzz, metric calls (cmap, advances, extents, origins) run HarfBuzz's own Rust glue (src/rust/font.rs, about 1,570 lines) over read_fonts::model; skrifa is used only for drawing, painting and bitmaps, so the benchmark is as much a test of that glue as of skrifa.
- HarfBuzz's backend build compiles Rust std with -Z build-std-features=optimize_for_size and -C force-frame-pointers=yes, and links it as a staticlib with no cross-language LTO, while the C++ side gets -O3 and LTO; the comparison is somewhat tilted against Fontations.

**Status:** Very active: read-fonts 0.45.0 and skrifa 0.48.0 shipped 2026-10-03, four of the eight split optimisation PRs merged 2026-10-04 (#2199, #2203, #2204, #2205) while #2200, #2201, #2202 and #2206 were still open on 2026-10-05, so the measured code is not all released; dual Apache-2.0/MIT, and skrifa has about 31 million crates.io downloads.

[repo](https://github.com/googlefonts/fontations) · [benchmark](https://github.com/googlefonts/fontations/issues/2196)

##### Parley  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Pure-Rust rich-text layout (fallback, bidi, shaping, line breaking); 2.4-9x faster than cosmic-text on paragraph-per-layout workloads.

**Beats:** cosmic-text 0.19.0 (pop-os/cosmic-text), the established Rust rich-text shaping and layout library (bevy_text, iced, COSMIC); both shape with HarfRust, but different versions: cosmic-text 0.19.0 pulls harfrust 0.5.2 while parley 0.11.1 pulls harfrust 0.12.0 (flui spike Cargo.lock). Not a C/C++ incumbent such as HarfBuzz with FreeType or Pango. — An independent downstream project (flui PR 1276) ran a public harness: parley 0.11.1 vs cosmic-text 0.19.0, release build, macOS on Apple Silicon (chip and rustc not stated), system SansSerif at 16 px, no wrapping, 5 runs each. On 10,000-line documents (one Layout per paragraph, cold) parley was 2.4x-9.0x faster (latin 781 vs 4255 ms, cjk 566 vs 5120 ms); recomputing from the checked-in measurements.jsonl shows warm runs are within 3% of cold (2.5x-8.9x), and each large run is about 10,000 times a warm single paragraph. Separately, massive's criterion bench (M-series Mac, JetBrains Mono 13 px) found parley ahead on mixed lines (4.8x), full screens (2x) and fallback stress (2.7x), behind by 16% on a single cluster, and about 600x faster at cold start.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust text layout (language-filter mismatch) measured against cosmic-text 0.19.0, a Rust-ecosystem incumbent rather than a C/C++ one. Tier B on an independent public harness (flui tools/text-spike at e30ab7194 plus raw measurements.jsonl; medians 2.4x-9.0x) with no rustc version or exact Apple Silicon chip. No line wrapping (unbounded width); harfrust 0.12.0 vs 0.5.2; Parley is 24x slower when given one whole-document Layout (78,782 vs 3,265 ms). The record had misread the massive ADR 0005 cold-start comparison: Parley wins there (61 us vs 36 ms).

**Known shortcoming:** The large-corpus run is one paragraph repeated 10,000 times, so it is about 10,000 warm per-paragraph layouts (warm within 3% of cold, 2.5-8.9x). Released 0.11.1 has a quadratic single-Layout path (fixed on main by PR 801, merged 2026-09-09, unreleased), and main carried a 20x GlyphRunIter regression (issue 763) before release; the complex-scripts feature is off by default, so CJK and Thai break per character.

**How:** Shaping goes through HarfRust with per-Shaper LRU caches (16 entries each) for shaper data, variation instances and shape plans, plus a reused UnicodeBuffer, so repeated runs in the same font skip plan construction. Text is itemised by script, bidi level and style, and each item is split into runs only where grapheme clusters change font, so a uniform paragraph is shaped in a few large calls. LayoutContext keeps allocations across layouts. Nobody has profiled where the gap to cosmic-text 0.19.0 comes from, and the two used different HarfRust versions (0.12.0 vs 0.5.2) in the flui test, so part of the gap may be the shaper itself.

**Use it when:**
- A Rust UI or document renderer that lays out many independent paragraphs: in flui's spike (Apple Silicon, parley 0.11.1 vs cosmic-text 0.19.0) one Layout per paragraph was 2.4x (Arabic) to 9.0x (CJK) faster over 10,000 lines.
- Repeated warm layout of short UI strings: a single warm paragraph took 0.07-0.14 ms against cosmic-text's 0.32-0.48 ms in the same data, 2.3-6.8x faster (derived from page data).
- Mixed-script or fallback-heavy text such as Latin with embedded Arabic, CJK or emoji, where massive's criterion bench shows parley about 4.8x faster on a full mixed line and 2.7x on fallback stress.
- Apps that create a font database often or need a fast cold start: massive measured parley 61 us vs cosmic-text 36 ms for a fresh font database, because cosmic-text's FontSystem construction dominates.
- Projects already on the Linebender or Bevy stack (Vello, Xilem/Masonry, Blitz; bevy_text moved from cosmic-text to parley in PR 22879, merged 2026-02-11).

**Skip it when:**
- Handing one Layout a whole multi-paragraph document of a single script on released 0.11.1: shaping is quadratic in item length (devanagari 10,000 lines took 78,782 ms vs cosmic-text 3,265 ms in flui's scaling study). Split on newlines yourself, or wait for a release that includes PR 801 (merged 2026-09-09 to main, not in 0.11.1).
- Terminal-style glyph-at-a-time work: cosmic-text was about 16% faster on a single ASCII cluster in massive's criterion bench.
- C or C++ code bases: there is no C API, so HarfBuzz with FreeType, ICU or Pango stay the native choice.
- Teams that need API stability: four minor releases (0.8 to 0.11, each semver-breaking for a 0.x crate) shipped in 2026, and main queues more breaking changes (Cluster now spans a grapheme cluster, LineMetrics ascent/descent/leading removed).
- Long Arabic paragraphs with wrapping, until someone checks it: flui issue 931 relays an unaudited floem report of parley being 93% slower on Arabic wrap, and the flui spike never exercised wrapping.

**Integration:** crate · fontique (font enumeration and fallback; CoreText via objc2 on Apple, fontconfig on Linux/FreeBSD, platform backends on Windows and Android), parley_engine, parlance, HarfRust 0.12, Skrifa/read-fonts, ICU4X 2.x (segmenter, properties, normalizer), hashbrown, smallvec, linebender_resource_handle · Rust 1.88 (edition 2024) · macOS/iOS, Windows, Linux, FreeBSD and Android with system fonts (default 'system' feature); no_std plus alloc with the 'libm' feature and caller-supplied fonts

**Vs siblings:** The other catalogued font entries are shapers (sigilbuzz, rustybuzz-wasm, text-shaper, SixLabors.Fonts), rasterizers (fontdue, font-rs, TiTanF) or a typesetter (Typst). Pick Parley when you need full paragraph layout in Rust: fallback, bidi, line breaking, alignment and editing. Draw the glyphs with a separate renderer; the repo's examples use swash, tiny-skia and Vello CPU.

**Gotchas:**
- Dictionary-based line breaking for CJK, Thai, Khmer, Lao and Myanmar is behind the off-by-default 'complex-scripts' feature; without it those scripts break at every character.
- Layout.break_all_lines(None) means unbounded width, and align() takes no width (since 0.9 it aligns to max_advance or to the longest line), so code ported from older versions can silently misalign.
- Main is churning: issue 763 recorded a 20x regression in GlyphRunIter::next on unreleased main (fixed by PR 764 before any release), so benchmark a pinned version, not a git dependency.
- The catalogued speedups compare against cosmic-text only, at unbounded width, using a single paragraph repeated 10,000 times; glyph counts differ by 3.2% on the emoji ZWJ corpus, and no one checked whether the system-font fallback produced tofu on either side.

**Status:** Actively developed by Linebender (last commit 2026-10-02; latest crates.io release 0.11.1 on 2026-08-16, about 3.5M all-time downloads), Apache-2.0 OR MIT, pre-1.0 with breaking changes in most releases.

[repo](https://github.com/linebender/parley) · [benchmark](https://github.com/vanyastaff/flui/pull/1276)

##### Typst  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Rust typesetting system (markup language, compiler, CLI) that built mail-merge PDFs 3-5x faster than pdfLaTeX in one shootout.

**Beats:** pdfLaTeX (pdfTeX 1.40.24, TeX Live 2022) and LuaLaTeX (LuaHBTeX 1.15.0); the same shootout also ran WeasyPrint 68.1, Apache FOP 2.11 and speedata Publisher 5.3.18 Pro — speedata's hyperfine runs on a MacBook Air M4 (Typst 0.14.2 against pdfTeX 1.40.24 and LuaHBTeX 1.15.0 from TeX Live 2022) put Typst at 105.7 ms for a one-page letter (3.1x faster than pdflatex, 4.9x than LuaLaTeX, derived from page data) and 156.6 ms for 500 identical letters (4.55x and 15.0x), with the LaTeX times including a Python and Jinja2 templating step. Typst's 500-page run used several cores (pagebreak() between letters enables parallel page-run layout) while pdflatex is single-threaded: on total CPU time (user plus system) the 500-page gap is 308 ms against 716 ms, about 2.3x, and the marginal cost per extra page is about 1.9x lower (both derived from page data), so roughly half of the 4.55x wall-clock win comes from parallelism and lower start-up. Zerodha's production report (blog blocked, search snippet only) gives about 3-4x faster than LaTeX overall and about 1 min against about 18 min with lualatex for 2000+ page table documents.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust typesetting system (language-filter mismatch) measured by an independent run (pgundlach/speedata typesetting-benchmark, hyperfine, MacBook Air M4, versions stated) against pdflatex and LuaLaTeX, typesetting engines rather than shaping libraries. Setups are not equal: the LaTeX timings include Python plus Jinja2, fonts differ, the 500 pages are 500 identical records (memoisation favours Typst), TeX Live 2022.

**Known shortcoming:** The 4.55x is wall clock with Typst 0.12+ laying out page runs in parallel against single-threaded pdflatex (retier-23): total CPU time is 308 against 716 ms, about 2.3x, and the marginal per-page CPU about 1.9x. Speed is version-sensitive: open regressions #7102 (0.13 at 200 ms against 0.14-rc1 at 1.5 s), #8611 (0.15.0 at 14 minutes and 41 GB against 0.14.2 at 1 min 17 s and 32 GB) and #8561 (50 s font scan).

**Independent measurement:** Zerodha contract-note pipeline (blog blocked; search snippet only): Typst 3-4x faster than LaTeX, 2000+ pages in about 1 minute against 18 minutes with LuaLaTeX.

**How:** Incremental compilation through comemo, constrained memoization: layout and evaluation functions are #[comemo::memoize]d over Tracked inputs that record which parts of the World or introspector a call actually read, so a cached result is reused whenever those parts are unchanged, across edits in watch mode and across identical content within one run. Since 0.12 the layout engine splits the document at explicit page breaks into page runs and lays them out in parallel (engine.parallelize over Item::Run in typst-layout pages/mod.rs; changelog: 'typical speedups are 2-3x for larger documents'). Justified paragraphs use Knuth-Plass optimal line breaking with a two-pass scheme: a cheap pass with approximate metrics yields an upper bound on cost that prunes the exact pass (linebreak_optimized_approximate then linebreak_optimized_bounded). Hyphenation comes from hypher's embedded automata, and the CLI is one native binary with no format files to load: the whole one-page benchmark compile took 105.7 ms.

**Use it when:**
- Batch generation of many similar documents from structured data (letters, invoices, contract notes) where templates can be written in Typst: the speedata shootout and Zerodha's contract-note pipeline (search snippet) both report several-fold speedups over LaTeX.
- Interactive or watch-mode editing of long documents, where memoized relayout recompiles only what changed.
- Multi-page output on multi-core machines: page runs separated by explicit page breaks are laid out in parallel (tune with --jobs).
- Containers and CI where a single static binary is simpler than a TeX Live installation.

**Skip it when:**
- Existing LaTeX documents, classes or journal templates: there is no TeX compatibility, so every template must be ported and many CTAN packages have no Typst equivalent.
- When you need a stable performance profile across upgrades: open regressions include #7102 (10,000 identical list items: about 200 ms on 0.13, 1.5 s on 0.14-rc1) and #8611 (a 300-page document with a glossary: 1 min 17 s and 32 GB on 0.14.2, 14 min and 41 GB on 0.15.0), and, per the verifier's notes, texlode/luatex-benchmark measured 0.14+ incremental edits 1.6-2.2x slower than 0.12/0.13 on x86.
- Table-heavy or introspection-heavy documents without testing first: #4560 (slow PDF compilation with many tables) is open, and memory can grow very large (#8611 reports 32-41 GB; #3150 and #8628 request limits and graceful out-of-memory handling).
- Hosts with very many installed fonts: the CLI scans every system font file at start-up (#8561 reports about 50 s on one Linux machine); use --ignore-system-fonts with --font-path.
- C or C++ embedding: there is no C API; drive the CLI as a subprocess or write a Rust wrapper.

**Integration:** CLI binary (typst-cli) or Rust crate (typst plus typst-layout, typst-pdf and related workspace crates) · Pure Rust; notable crates include comemo, rayon, hypher, rustybuzz, ttf-parser, fontdb, icu_segmenter/icu_properties, wasmi for plugins and krilla (pinned git revision) for PDF export · Rust 1.92 (workspace rust-version for 0.15.x; 0.14.2 required 1.89) · Any platform Rust targets; the speedata numbers are from macOS on Apple M4

**Vs siblings:** It is the only full typesetting system in this category: pick it when you need finished paged PDFs from markup or data, and pick Parley (rich-text layout) or hypher (hyphenation only, which Typst itself uses) when you are building your own layout or rendering stack.

**Gotchas:**
- Parallel layout only kicks in at explicit page breaks (pagebreak() or separate page runs); a single long flowing document gets less benefit.
- Performance is version-sensitive (see the open regression issues), so pin the version you benchmarked; 0.14.0 and 0.14.1 also shipped a wasmi use-after-free fixed in 0.14.2.
- Hyphenation uses hypher, which ignores the TeX \hyphenation{} exception lists, so line breaks can differ from LaTeX on exception words.
- Tagged (accessible) PDF output arrived in 0.14; the --no-pdf-tags opt-out is hidden and marked deprecated in the current CLI source (removal planned for the 0.17 cycle).

**Status:** Very active (0.15.1 released 2026-07-17, commits through 2026-09-30, 2.9M crates.io downloads, Apache-2.0); copyable as a Rust crate or used as a CLI, not as a C/C++ library.

[repo](https://github.com/typst/typst) · [benchmark](https://github.com/speedata/typesetting-benchmark)

#### image-codecs

##### ffpng  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Single-header C PNG decoder for x86-64-v3 (AVX2) that decodes 1.12-1.20x faster than image-png, the Rust png crate.

**Beats:** image-rs/image-png v0.18.1 (commit 4ab5484; the Rust png crate, already listed) built with --features=unstable at target-cpu=x86-64-v3. The same harness also times libpng + zlib, libspng, stb_image and ldpng (ffpng's front end with libdeflate inflate), but the README publishes no libpng, libspng or stb_image numbers — bench.c times ffpng and unmodified image-png v0.18.1 (commit 4ab5484, nightly, unstable feature, x86-64-v3, LTO) in one process on the 2848-image QOI benchmark suite, on one isolated core with boost off, taking the per-image median and checking every output with memcmp. Geomean results are 356.3 vs 319.5 MP/s (1.115x) on a Ryzen 9 7950X with gcc 16.1, and 352.6 vs 292.8 MP/s (1.204x) on a Ryzen 9 9950X3D with gcc 16.2.1; the README ties only the 9950X3D run to the current header (2026-09-25). The timed region is not symmetric: image-png's shim zero-fills its output buffer (vec![0u8; size]) on every decode, while ffpng mallocs its output uninitialized and reuses a thread-local raw buffer (it does pay for copying all IDAT data). That cost is not measured separately, but it could be a sizeable part of the 2-4% margin on the dense photo sets; it is too small to account for the 1.115x/1.204x overall result.

**Known shortcoming:** The baseline is image-png (the Rust png crate), not libpng: no libpng numbers are published, so the 1.115x and 1.204x (7950X and 9950X3D, gcc 16.1 and 16.2.1, image-png shim at x86-64-v3) say nothing about the category incumbent. No LICENSE file, only SPDX MIT headers in sources; weeks-old single-author repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e124, 2026-10-05): A stands, no correctness bug behind the numbers. The timed region is uneven: the image-png shim zero-fills its output (vec![0u8; size]) on every decode while ffpng mallocs the output uninitialised and reuses a thread-local raw scratch buffer (though it copies all IDAT), which could be a sizeable part of the 2-4% photo margins but not of the 1.115x/1.204x overall. Only the 9950X3D table is tied to the current header. Security bug: the palette index is not checked against the PLTE length, so an out-of-range index copies uninitialised stack bytes (plte[768]) into the output; no fuzzing, no memory or dimension limit, x86-64-v3 only, no MSVC. Clang builds are about 10% slower per the README, so the 7950X margin is about 1.01x (derived). No LICENSE file.

**Independent measurement:** first-party harness, public flags and CPU

**How:** A custom inflate modeled on fdeflate (image-png's backend): a 64-bit refill bit reader, a 12-bit combined Huffman table where one load yields one or two literals or a length, and a four-deep speculative literal cascade in which each lookup already carries the next shift (one shrx plus one L1 load per symbol); streams under 4 KB get a separate compact-table path, and match copies use 32-byte AVX2, 16-byte SSE or overlap-propagating stores over padded buffers. CRC-32 folds four PCLMULQDQ accumulators, unfiltering is SSE/AVX2 (Up as a flat 32-byte add, Sub/Average in 8-bit lanes, Paeth in 16-bit lanes), and for filtered data above 16 MB inflate, unfilter and pixel expansion are fused so each row is processed while still in cache once it is 32 KB behind the inflate frontier. The large intermediate buffer is a thread-local scratch reused across calls.

**Use it when:**
- C or C++ code on x86-64-v3 machines (Intel Haswell and later, AMD Zen and later) that decodes many PNGs and is bound by decode throughput.
- Screenshot, UI, icon and texture-heavy workloads: the README shows 1.57-1.83x over image-png on screenshot_web, 1.14x on screenshot_game and 1.10-1.31x on texture sets.
- You want one vendorable header with no zlib or libpng dependency and pluggable FFPNG_MALLOC/REALLOC/FREE allocator hooks.
- Long-lived worker threads decoding batches, where the thread-local scratch buffer is reused instead of reallocated.
- You build with gcc, which is what the published numbers use.

**Skip it when:**
- ARM, RISC-V or pre-AVX2 x86: the header targets x86-64-v3 with AVX2, BMI2 and PCLMUL intrinsics and has no runtime CPU detection or scalar fallback.
- MSVC builds (it relies on __builtin_add_overflow, __builtin_expect, __attribute__ and _Thread_local), or clang builds, which the README says run about 10% slower; that would cut the 7950X margin to roughly 1.01x (derived from page data).
- Untrusted input without sandboxing: no fuzzing or malformed-file test suite is documented, there is no caller-set memory or dimension limit (IHDR sizes up to 2^31-1 per side drive the output and raw allocations before any inflate), and palette indices are not checked against the PLTE length.
- You need 16-bit output, color management, metadata, APNG frames, progressive row-by-row display, or an encoder.
- Memory-tight decoding of very large images: it holds a copy of all IDAT data, the whole filtered raw image and the output at once, and the raw scratch buffer stays allocated per thread until pd_free_thread_cache.

**Integration:** header-only · none (libc and immintrin.h); the benchmark suite additionally needs libpng, zlib, libdeflate, libspng and nightly Rust · C99 plus GCC/Clang extensions (gcc 16.1 and 16.2 tested); compile with -march=x86-64-v3 and -mpclmul · x86-64 only, x86-64-v3 required (AVX2, BMI2, PCLMUL)

**Vs siblings:** Pick ffpng over image-png only when you are in C/C++ on x86-64-v3 and the extra 12-20% decode throughput matters; image-png stays the better choice for Rust, ARM, memory safety, streaming and metadata. Over libspng or libpng it trades portability and features for speed (its libpng numbers are unpublished), and ptpng is the pick when you also need an encoder or ARM support.

**Gotchas:**
- Security bug: in 8-bit palette images, pal32 is filled from all 256 entries of an uninitialized 768-byte stack array (plte[256*3]), and the sub-8-bit path indexes plte directly, so a pixel index at or beyond the PLTE entry count copies uninitialized stack bytes into the output instead of failing. It is not an out-of-bounds read, and it cannot occur on conforming files such as the benchmark corpus.
- Output layout varies with color type (1-4 channels, read pd_image.channels), and 16-bit samples are truncated, not rounded; there is no option for RGBA-always or 16-bit output.
- Validation is image-png-like but partial: critical-chunk CRCs are checked, ancillary CRC failures are ignored, Adler-32 is not verified, non-consecutive IDAT chunks are concatenated, and a truncated stream fails outright with no partial image.
- Public symbols are pd_decode/pd_free/pd_free_thread_cache (not ffpng_-prefixed). The benchmarked build turns off stack protector, _FORTIFY_SOURCE and CET (-fcf-protection=none), so a distro-hardened build is unmeasured.

**Status:** Active single-author project (27 commits from 2026-06-23 to 2026-09-25, 0 stars, no releases or tags); every file carries an SPDX MIT tag but there is no LICENSE file. It is one easily vendored header, but it is young and unfuzzed.

[repo](https://github.com/vtlmks/ffpng) · [benchmark](https://github.com/vtlmks/ffpng)

##### fpng  `C++`  `Unlicense`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Single-file C++ PNG writer/reader for 24/32bpp: about 35x libpng's default encode speed, files about 29% larger.

**Beats:** libpng — Nigel Tao's QOIR harness (gcc 10.2.1, -O3 -march=native, i5-10210U, single thread, QOI benchmark image set, Debian Bullseye libpng through its simplified API with default flags) measured fpng encoding at 192.16 vs 5.49 MPixels/s (about 35x). It measured decoding at 148.19 vs 56.18 MPixels/s (about 2.6x), with files 1.29x larger (CmpRatio 0.3115 vs 0.2423). Each codec decodes its own encoder's output. Wuffs, decoding the original PNGs, reached 140.79 MPixels/s, so fpng's decode lead over a modern general PNG decoder is about 5% (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on nigeltao/qoir full_benchmarks.txt rows 63/65 (192.16 vs 5.49 MB/s encode, 148.19 vs 56.18 decode; gcc 10.2.1, i5-10210U, Debian Bullseye libpng at default compression). Trade-off: files about 29% larger than libpng's, and the fast decode applies only to fpng's own output. The harness runs 5 repetitions with gettimeofday and never checks round-trip pixels. Vendored fpng.cpp equals upstream except the August 2024 bounds fix.

**Known shortcoming:** Decode asymmetry: fpng skips the IDAT CRC-32 and the zlib Adler-32 while libpng checks both by default; the encode baseline is libpng with flags 0 (PNG_IMAGE_FLAG_FAST never tried); per category encode is 21-45x faster with files 1.16-1.68x larger. Encoder bugs outside the benchmark: IHDR writes 16-bit width and height but the encoder accepts up to 2^24, so a side above 65535 yields a corrupt PNG with a success return (open #31); the (bpl+1)*h buffer size wraps in 32-bit arithmetic, a heap overflow above 4 GiB of filtered data (code reading, untested).

**How:** The encoder fixes every choice libpng searches over. The first row uses filter 0 and every later row uses filter 2 (Up), applied with SSE4.1 byte subtraction. A pixel-wise Deflate 'parser' emits literals in groups of 3 or 4 bytes and only RLE matches at distance 3 or 4 (whole pixels), all in one dynamic Huffman block. In the default one-pass mode the Huffman tables are precomputed (trained), so there is no frequency pass at all. CRC-32 uses PCLMULQDQ folding and Adler-32 uses SSE4.1, both chosen at run time after fpng_init(). The decoder relies on the same constraints: matches of distance 3 or 4 let it inflate straight into the output image with no window or temporary zlib buffer. A 12-bit lookup table packs two literals per entry when both codes fit, and it verifies neither the IDAT CRC-32 nor the zlib Adler-32.

**Use it when:**
- Writing many PNGs where encode time dominates: screenshots, frame dumps, texture-pipeline intermediates or debug images. QOIR's run measured 192 vs 5.5 MPixels/s against libpng's default settings, 21x to 45x per image category.
- Round-tripping your own files: fpng writes and fpng reads back at 148 MPixels/s (2.6x libpng decoding libpng's own files), with only the output buffer allocated during decode.
- Producing files other tools must open: the output is conformant PNG, which the author reports loads in libpng, Wuffs, lodepng, stb_image and pngcheck.
- Dropping two files into a C++ project with no zlib or libpng dependency, on x86-64 with SSE4.1/PCLMUL or with scalar fallbacks elsewhere.

**Skip it when:**
- File size matters. In QOIR's run fpng's files were 16% to 68% larger than libpng's, depending on category (icons worst), and fpnge was both 1.6x faster and 10% smaller overall in the same run.
- Decoding arbitrary or untrusted PNGs. The fast decoder rejects anything fpng did not write, and the author recommends Wuffs for decoding. Past reports include a heap-buffer-overflow read in fpng_get_info_internal (#26, fixed in the August 2024 bounds-check commit) and SIGILL crashes in fpng_adler32 on macOS CI runners (#24).
- Images wider or taller than 65,535 pixels. The encoder writes only the low 16 bits of width and height into IHDR but accepts sizes up to 2^24, so it returns success with a corrupt file (open issue #31).
- Grayscale, paletted, 16-bit, interlaced PNGs or PNGs with metadata: only 8-bit RGB/RGBA is supported, and issue #16 (asking for ICC/resolution tags and 8-bit support) is still open.
- Needing an active upstream: the last commit was 2024-08-26 and 17 issues are open.

**Integration:** source-drop (fpng.cpp + fpng.h; can be #included as a single translation unit) · none (C++ standard library std::vector; the test app adds lodepng, stb_image, qoi, wuffs) · C++11 (the CMake file sets -std=c++11); tested by the author with MSVC 2019/2022, gcc 7.5 and clang 6/10 · any little-endian CPU (big-endian code paths exist but are untested); SSE4.1+PCLMUL fast paths on x86/x64 only, and gcc/clang need -msse4.1 -mpclmul (or -DFPNG_NO_SSE=1) for the file to compile on x86; unaligned 32/64-bit loads are enabled by default only on x86

**Vs siblings:** Pick fpng over fpnge when you also want a fast reader for your own PNGs (fpnge is encoder-only) or need a scalar build. In QOIR's run fpnge encodes 1.6x faster into 10% smaller files, so pick fpnge for pure write speed. Pick QOI or QOIR instead when the files never leave your pipeline: QOIR decodes faster with smaller files than fpng. Pick libspng or Wuffs for reading arbitrary PNGs.

**Gotchas:**
- Call fpng::fpng_init() first. Without it the SSE4.1/PCLMUL paths never activate; fpng_cpu_supports_sse41() asserts and returns false.
- Building the whole file with -msse4.1 -mpclmul lets the compiler emit SSE4.1 anywhere in it, so the run-time CPU check is not a full guard on older CPUs. The code also uses type-punned unaligned loads (READ_LE32/WRITE_LE64 via reinterpret_cast) and the README says it was tested only with -fno-strict-aliasing.
- num_chans=4 always writes a 32bpp file: there is no automatic detection of opaque images. The one-pass Huffman tables were trained on the author's corpus; FPNG_ENCODE_SLOWER builds per-image tables, giving about 6% smaller files at about 40% slower encode.
- The scratch buffer size (bpl + 1) * h uses 32-bit arithmetic (int bpl, uint32_t h). The input check allows w*h up to 2^32 pixels, so an image above 4 GiB of filtered data (e.g. 32768x32768 RGBA) wraps the allocation, and the filter loop would write past it. Found by code reading, not run.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-08-26 (last commit: a chunk bounds-check fix), Unlicense public-domain dedication and two files to vendor; the 16-bit IHDR dimension bug (#31) is still open.

[repo](https://github.com/richgel999/fpng) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nigeltao/qoir/HEAD/doc/full_benchmarks.txt)

##### fpnge  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Two-file AVX2/SSE4.1 PNG encoder; about 57x libpng's default encode speed on the QOI corpus, files about 15% larger.

**Beats:** libpng — In Nigel Tao's QOIR harness (gcc 10.2.1, -O3 -march=native, Intel i5-10210U, one thread, 5 repetitions per image, totals over the QOI benchmark corpus), a 2022 fpnge snapshot at its default level encoded 312.59 MP/s against 5.49 MP/s for Debian Bullseye's libpng through png_image_write_to_memory at default zlib settings (about 57x), with CmpRatio 0.2798 vs 0.2423 (about 15% larger files). The harness has no fpnge decoder, so it never checks fpnge's output; correctness rests on upstream's round-trip test.sh.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on qoir full_benchmarks.txt rows 64/65 (312.59 vs 5.49 MB/s, 57x; same harness, 2022 snapshot). Encoder only; files about 15% larger than libpng's. The baseline libpng is the Debian package build, so the ratio sits above the 50x unstated-baseline-flags threshold; kept A because the encoder flags and the distro baseline are reproducible. Open issues #25 and #31 report memory bugs.

**Known shortcoming:** FPNGEEncode takes no output capacity and FPNGEOutputAllocSize ignores additional_chunks, so large custom chunks can overflow the heap (API hazard outside the benchmark path); #31 (heap corruption) was closed without a documented fix; output is a single IDAT with a 32-bit length. Size penalty is 7-10% on photos but 33-59% on screenshot_web and icon_512, and on icon_64 fpnge (82.45 MP/s) is 2.3x slower than fpng; x86 only (#error without SSE4.1). QOIR never decodes fpnge's output (upstream test.sh round-trips libjxl PNGs through ImageMagick compare, -march=native build only).

**How:** It replaces zlib's general LZ77 search with a single dynamic-Huffman deflate block whose only matches are distance-1 runs over whole SIMD vectors of zero filter residuals. The Huffman code is built from symbol counts of a few centre rows and constrained so residual bytes 16-239 share one code length, letting pshufb lookups on 16-entry tables (first16/last16/mid) produce code lengths and bits for 32 bytes at a time, with BMI2 PEXT (skipped when tuning for Zen 1/2) to pack them. Per-row PNG filter choice is made by costing all four predictors with those same SIMD tables (exact at the default level, approximate at level 3), Adler-32 is accumulated with psadbw, and the chunk CRC uses PCLMULQDQ folding.

**Use it when:**
- Screenshot, screen-recording, game-capture or render-output pipelines on x86 where PNG encode time is the bottleneck and files 7-60% larger than libpng's are acceptable.
- Photographic or textured RGB/RGBA images: in the QOIR data the speedup over libpng is largest there (84x on Kodak, 95x on Tecnick) and the size penalty smallest (7-10%).
- Large frames encoded on one core per image, where it stayed around 280-360 MP/s across the QOIR subsets on an i5-10210U.
- When you need real .png output (unlike QOI, QOIR or Zpng), including 16-bit or HDR (cICP PQ) PNGs.

**Skip it when:**
- ARM or any non-x86 target: fpnge.cc stops with '#error Requires SSE4.1 support minium' (Apple Silicon request #29 closed with no port).
- Size-sensitive storage or web delivery: on flat synthetic content its LZ77 finds only zero-residual runs, so files were 59% larger than libpng's on icon_512 and 33% larger on screenshot_web; run an optimiser such as oxipng afterwards or use libpng/zlib-ng at a higher level.
- Many tiny images: on 64x64 icons it fell to 82.45 MP/s, 2.3x slower than fpng (193.31 MP/s) and with larger files than fpng, because table construction and buffer setup are per call.
- Indexed-colour, 1/2/4-bit, interlaced or palette PNGs: only 8/16-bit gray, gray+alpha, RGB and RGBA are written.
- Decoding: it is encoder only; pair it with libspng, Wuffs or image-png for reads.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (the fpnge CLI in fpnge_main.cc uses lodepng only to read input) · C++14 (std::index_sequence, constexpr lookup tables); GCC, Clang, or MSVC since the November 2023 forceinline fix; must be compiled with at least -msse4.1, and -mavx2 -mbmi2 -mpclmul (or -march=native as build.sh does) for the fast path · x86 and x86-64 only; SSE4.1 required, AVX2 for full speed; instruction set fixed at compile time, no runtime dispatch

**Vs siblings:** Pick fpnge over fpng when you only encode and run on AVX2 machines: in the same QOIR run it encoded 1.63x faster (312.59 vs 192.16 MP/s) with 10% smaller output, though fpng is portable C++ with a decoder and wins on tiny images. Pick it over QOI, QOIR or Zpng when the output must be a standard .png; pick libjxl's fast_lossless (106.48 MP/s, 22% smaller files) when JPEG XL output is acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- No output capacity is passed to FPNGEEncode; it trusts the caller's buffer. FPNGEOutputAllocSize (1024 + (2*bytes*width*channels + 1)*height) ignores additional_chunks, so adding an ICC or EXIF chunk larger than the slack can overflow the heap unless you add the chunk sizes yourself. Issue #25 (fixed 2023-05-22) was an underestimate of this kind, and issue #31 (heap corruption on one 4-channel image, 2024) was closed without a documented cause.
- The whole image goes into one IDAT chunk and one deflate block, and the chunk length is written as 32 bits, so outputs above PNG's 2^31-1 chunk limit (multi-gigapixel 16-bit images) would be invalid.
- A binary built with -march=native or -mavx2 dies with an illegal instruction on CPUs without AVX2/BMI2; the default x86-64 target (SSE2 only) does not compile at all. Upstream CI (test.sh) round-trips the libjxl test PNGs through ImageMagick compare for all four speed levels, but only for the -march=native build on a GitHub runner, so the SSE4.1 and MSVC paths are untested.
- fpnge.h defines FPNGEOutputAllocSize and FPNGEFillOptions as plain inline functions inside extern "C"; a C caller built without optimisation may get an undefined reference to FPNGEOutputAllocSize, since under C99 inline rules no external definition is emitted.

**Status:** Maintained at low intensity by its author (last commit 2025-10-09, a simpler Paeth predictor in February 2025, BGR input and custom chunks in March 2024); Apache-2.0, two source files, easy to vendor, but the README still calls it a proof of concept and there is no NEON port.

[repo](https://github.com/veluca93/fpnge) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nigeltao/qoir/HEAD/doc/full_benchmarks.txt)

##### image-png (Rust png crate)  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-safe-Rust PNG/APNG decoder and encoder that decodes faster than libpng on most images; Chromium's default PNG decoder.

**Beats:** libpng 1.6.37 (Debian Bullseye) — Third-party Wuffs mimic benchmark, September 2022: png 0.17.5 (Rust 1.48, `cargo --release`, miniz_oxide 0.5.3 inflate with Adler-32 and CRC checked) vs Debian Bullseye libpng 1.6.37 through the simplified API (harness built with gcc 10.2.1 / clang 11.0.1 -O3), decoding five test images to BGRA (gray stays gray) on an Intel Core i5-10210U: 1.53x, 1.77x, 0.89x, 1.03x and 1.23x libpng's MB/s. The Rust side's timed loop also includes a scalar RGB/RGBA-to-BGRA swizzle that libpng does internally, so the comparison slightly handicaps Rust; current 0.18.x has not been re-measured on that page.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust crate (language-filter mismatch; C++ use needs FFI). Tier A on Wuffs doc/benchmarks.md (script/bench-rust-png and test/c/std/png.c at -O3, i5-10210U) against libpng 1.6.37: faster on 4 of 5 images, 0.89x on the 77k image; the measured png 0.17.5 dates from 2022 (now 0.18.1), and Wuffs's own C decoder is faster on every image.

**Known shortcoming:** The 2022 Wuffs rows are sound (png 0.17.5 with miniz_oxide 0.5.3 checked Adler-32 and CRC), but bench-rust-png has no Cargo.lock (png = "0.17"), so a rerun resolves 0.17.16, and current 0.18 ignores Adler-32 by default; the Rust side also times an RGB-to-BGRA swizzle that libpng does internally, slightly handicapping Rust. Newer first-party evidence (image-rs blog 2026-06-18, harness fintelia/corpus-bench@png-0.18.0, 2848 QOI images: geomean 339.9 versus libpng plus zlib-ng 180.4 MP/s on a 7950X; M4 310.5 versus 177.6) skews toward image-png (libpng forced to RGBA8 output, one decode per image without warm-up, no output check, libpng version unstated), so it is an upper bound at C. Chromium data: discussion #562 (M136 trial: desktop decode 15% faster in total, Android 9% slower) and issue #567 (79% of libpng runtime on Linux, 101% on Windows).

**Independent measurement:** image-rs blog 2026-06-18 (fintelia/corpus-bench at png-0.18.0, 2848 QOI-suite images, upper bound: libpng forced to RGBA8, no warm-up, no output check): geomean 339.9 MP/s versus libpng plus zlib-ng 180.4 MP/s on a Ryzen 9 7950X; Apple M4 310.5 versus 177.6 MP/s. Chromium M136 field trial (discussion #562): desktop decode 15% faster in total, Android 9% slower.

**How:** Since 0.17.8 (after the Wuffs measurement) decompression always uses fdeflate, a custom safe DEFLATE decoder, and the zlib Adler-32 check is skipped by default while chunk CRC32 is still verified (crc32fast, simd-adler32 when checking). Unfiltering is written as component-wise unrolled byte-array loops that LLVM auto-vectorizes (src/filter/optimization-notes.md, PR #382), with explicit `std::simd` Paeth paths only behind the nightly `unstable` feature. 0.18 unfilters in place and shrinks internal buffers so data stays in cache between inflate and unfilter (image-rs blog, 2026-06-18).

**Use it when:**
- Rust or mixed Rust/C++ codebases that decode untrusted PNG/APNG and want memory safety without giving up speed (it is Chromium's default PNG decoder since M139 and backs GNOME's glycin).
- Throughput-bound batch decoding of typical web/screenshot/photo PNGs: the maintainers' QOI-corpus run (2,848 images) reports 339.9 vs 180.4 MP/s geomean against libpng+zlib-ng on a Ryzen 9 7950X.
- APNG decoding or encoding, which upstream libpng does not support.
- Fast lossless PNG writing where a lighter compression ratio is acceptable: the fdeflate-based fast mode (fpnge-inspired) trades ratio for an order-of-magnitude encode speedup per the blog.

**Skip it when:**
- Plain C++ projects that cannot add a Rust toolchain and an FFI layer: the crate exposes only a Rust API (Chromium wrote its own integration).
- Android/ARM64 latency-sensitive decoding: Chromium's M136 field trial showed decode-time regressions of +2% to +9% across percentiles on Android while desktop improved about 15% in total (discussion #562).
- Windows builds where unfiltering dominates: issue #567 (Jan 2025) measured total decode time at 101% of libpng on Windows vs 79% on Linux, and 114-151% on one Paeth-heavy RGBA image, from different auto-vectorized code.
- When you need libpng's full transform set (gamma correction, rgb-to-gray, background compositing, custom row callbacks): only EXPAND, STRIP_16 and ALPHA exist; colour handling is left to the caller.
