- Small-image workloads where the 2022 Wuffs numbers apply: on the 77k 8bpp paletted image png 0.17.5 was 0.89x libpng.

**Integration:** crate · bitflags, crc32fast, fdeflate, flate2 (miniz_oxide backend by default; optional zlib-rs feature) · Rust 1.81 (rust-version in Cargo.toml for 0.18.1); `unstable` feature needs nightly · any Rust target; SIMD comes from compiler auto-vectorization at the target's baseline (SSE2 on x86-64 unless you raise target-cpu); wasm32 builds

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libspng when you can host Rust: in the 2026 QOI-corpus run it decodes about 1.46x spng's geomean on the 7950X (339.9 vs 233.1 MP/s, derived), while libspng stays the C option. Pick it over zune-png for broader adoption, APNG, encoding and a slight decode lead in the same run (339.9 vs 313.2 MP/s), and over Wuffs when you want a conventional Rust crate rather than generated C (Wuffs' C decoder was 1.55x-3.16x libpng and faster than png 0.17.5 on every image in 2022).

**Gotchas:**
- Adler-32 is ignored by default (zlib.rs: `ignore_adler32: true`); call `Decoder::ignore_checksums(false)` or the StreamingDecoder setter if you need libpng-equivalent zlib integrity checking. Chunk CRCs are still verified.
- Default output is the IDENTITY transform: paletted, low-bit-depth and 16-bit images come back in their stored layout unless you set EXPAND / STRIP_16 (`Transformations::normalize_to_color8()`); there is no BGRA or filler output.
- 0.18 changed the API: `Decoder` needs `BufRead + Seek`, `output_buffer_size()` returns `Option<usize>`, and the `Decoded` event enum was reworked; code written for 0.17 does not compile unchanged.
- The nightly `unstable` (std::simd) feature can make decoding slower: Chromium disabled it after Windows regressions (issue #567), and the blog says it regresses ARM performance cores.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23, 0.18.1 current, about 245 million crates.io downloads), MIT OR Apache-2.0, shipped to all Chrome users since M139 (August 2025) and used by GNOME 49 through glycin; only one open bug-labelled issue (#286, zlib decompression may exceed allocation limits, 2021).

[repo](https://github.com/image-rs/image-png) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/wuffs/HEAD/doc/benchmarks.md)

##### intel-tex-rs-2 (intel_tex_2)  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust bindings over a maintained fork of Intel's ISPC texture compressor; BC6H/BC7/ETC1 encode 2-6x faster than Intel's kernels on Apple Silicon.

**Beats:** Intel's upstream ISPCTextureCompressor (ispc_texcomp) kernels as vendored on the crate's main branch (GameTechDev submodule, built with ISPC 1.20), plus the same upstream kernels rebuilt with ISPC 1.31 (PR #49 column) to isolate the compiler change; all through the same Rust binding and criterion harness, not a separately built Intel ispc_texcomp library — Criterion (benches/compress.rs on the tests-and-benches and arm64-perf branches), Apple M5 Max, 1 thread, synthetic 256x256 'natural' image, kernels prebuilt with ISPC opt_level 2 and neon-i32x8. The cleanest baseline is the PR #49 column: Intel's unmodified kernels rebuilt with the same ISPC 1.31 and apple-a14 pin. Against it, PR #50 is 1.99-6.08x faster on BC7 (opaque basic 49.37 to 20.14 ms) and 5.91x on ETC1 (60.40 to 10.21 ms); BC1-BC5 are unchanged. Quality matches, checked with independent decoders (texture2ddecoder, bcdec_rs): BC7 within 0.0001 dB. The 'main' column (ISPC 1.20, built on CI via Rosetta without CPU pinning, and with the NaN-prone ETC1 kernel) overstates the ratios slightly. The 4K and bc7e numbers have no runner in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** The Criterion harness (benches/compress.rs) lives only on the tests-and-benches and arm64-perf branches (open PR #48), not on main or in the crates.io 0.5.0 release of 2025-07-02; measured on one thread of an Apple M5 Max (ISPC 1.31 against 1.20, build.rs opt_level 2, neon-i32x8, apple-a14) against the unmodified Intel upstream kernels, with x86 unmeasured, the rustc version unstated, and the 4K and bc7e numbers lacking a runner.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e123, 2026-10-05): no bug behind the fork numbers; output quality was checked with independent decoders. The 'main' column is confounded (ISPC 1.20, a Rosetta CI build, no CPU pin, and the ETC1 kernel reads uninitialised colors[q][7..10]); the clean baseline is the PR #49 column (same upstream kernels on ISPC 1.31): BC7 1.99-6.08x, ETC1 5.91x. Tier A holds when the #49 ratios are cited. Gotchas: a width not a multiple of 4 skews the block layout (store_data; an ignored test); BC6H decodes negative input as 65504.0; crates.io 0.5.0 still ships the old kernels; bc7_alpha's 5-6x is on a synthetic all-alpha image, about 2.3x on opaque.

**Independent measurement:** first-party criterion runs (PR #50)

**How:** The fork's 27 kernel commits remove per-lane gathers from the BC6H/BC7 hot loops. NEON has no gather, so each gather had become 8 scalar loads; the fork computes unquantization weights arithmetically and picks subsets with vector selects. It also inlines every helper, hoists per-subset setup out of the pixel loop, shares PCA work between modes 1/3 and 4/5, and skips the RGB-only modes 0-3 on blocks with alpha. ETC1 builds its 165-candidate list once per (flip, half) instead of 8 times, scores candidates with prefix sums and sorting networks, and uses exact integer lower bounds to skip candidates and tables that cannot win (branch and bound). PR #51 adds bc7e-style bounding-box partition ranking for modes 0-3.

**Use it when:**
- Offline or build-time texture baking on Apple Silicon (or other aarch64) that needs BC7, BC6H or ETC1 at ispc_texcomp quality in a fraction of the time.
- Rust asset pipelines already on intel_tex_2 that want the speedup without changing calling code.
- One dependency covering desktop BCn (including HDR BC6H from half-float RGBA) and mobile ETC1, with prebuilt kernels so neither ISPC nor libclang is needed at build time.
- Pipelines that parallelize by splitting the image into horizontal strips on threads: each call is single-threaded over caller-owned buffers, and the repo's own threaded_strips benchmark does exactly this.
- C/C++ projects that today vendor Intel's ispc_texcomp: the Traverse-Research kernel fork is the drop-in upgrade with the same entry points.

**Skip it when:**
- You need the speedup from a crates.io release: 0.5.0 (2025-07-02, latest as of 2026-10-05) ships Intel's old kernels. The faster code sits on the arm64-perf branch behind open PR #48 (opened 2026-09-24), so you must use a git dependency.
- x86-64 is your main build host: only an Apple M5 Max was benchmarked. The PR says removing gathers 'matters less on AVX2/AVX-512', so the x86 gain is unmeasured and may be much smaller.
- Real-time or very high-volume ETC1/BC1 encoding: etcpak, Goofy or Basis Universal's etc1f/bc7f trade quality for far higher throughput.
- Byte-reproducible output against Intel's ispc_texcomp, for example asset caches keyed on encoder output: ETC1 tie-breaking changed (about 10% of blocks differ), PR #51 retuned BC7 presets under the same names, and BC6H moved slightly with the ISPC version.
- ASTC: the README lists it as pending, and the PR #48 tests mark ASTC compression unimplemented.

**Integration:** crate (static ISPC kernel libraries prebuilt and checked into src/ispc; the kernel fork is also usable from C/C++) · ispc_rt 2; ISPC 1.31 + libclang + cc only with --features ispc to regenerate kernels · Rust 2021 edition; rust-version not declared (library code uses usize::div_ceil, stable since Rust 1.73); ISPC 1.31 (LLVM 23) to rebuild kernels · x86/x86-64 (ISPC multi-target SSE2, SSE4, AVX1, AVX2, AVX-512 SKX); aarch64 NEON (neon-i32x8; macOS pinned to apple-a14, so M1 or later; iOS apple-a7); prebuilt for macOS, iOS, Linux, Windows, Android; only Apple M5 Max benchmarked

**Vs siblings:** Against bc7e (catalogued, B): pick this for one Rust dependency covering BC6H, ETC1 and BC1-BC5 as well as BC7. On Apple Silicon, PR #51's first-party numbers have it beating bc7e on a 4K texture (very_fast 1.05 s vs 2.38 s at 51.27 dB), but on x86 bc7e's independent lead over ispc_texcomp has not been re-checked against this fork. Against etcpak, Goofy and Basis Universal etc1f/bc7f: pick this when quality matters more than raw throughput.

**Gotchas:**
- Widths that are not a multiple of 4 give a skewed block layout. The kernels' store_data advances output rows by width*block_words bytes, not by (width/4) blocks, and edge blocks are dropped. calc_output_size sizes the buffer from the texel count, not a padded block grid. The bug is inherited from Intel and recorded as an ignored test (unaligned_width_encodes_full_blocks). Pad images to multiples of 4 yourself.
- BC6H encodes unsigned half floats, so negative inputs decode as 65504.0 instead of 0.0. This is a known bug, also recorded as an ignored test (bc6h_negative_values_clamp_to_zero); clamp HDR input to non-negative values before encoding.
- Intel's upstream ETC1 kernel, which crates.io 0.5.0 still ships, reads uninitialized colors[q][7..10] for empty clusters; the resulting NaNs can abort encoding. The fork fixes it in commit 6ddb057, which on its own is a reason to switch.
- bc7_alpha speedups (5.2-6.2x) come from a test image whose alpha varies in every block, where skipping the RGB-only modes pays off most. On a fully opaque 4K texture the PR reports about 2.3x for the alpha presets.

**Status:** Actively developed by Traverse Research (MIT OR Apache-2.0, kernels MIT); the speedups were merged 2026-09-28 into a stacked branch chain waiting on open PR #48, and the kernel commits are AI-co-authored, so pin a commit and keep the round-trip quality tests on.

[repo](https://github.com/Traverse-Research/intel-tex-rs-2) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Traverse-Research/intel-tex-rs-2/pull/50)

##### libspng  `C`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `stale: last code release v0.7.4 on 2023-05-08; 69 issues and 18 pull requests open`  `Tier A`

Small C PNG decoder/encoder with a simpler API than libpng; decodes 1.02-1.07x faster on most images, 1.36x on 32bpp.

**Beats:** libpng 1.6.37 (Debian Bullseye) — Wuffs' doc/benchmarks.md (the benchmark_url; Debian Bullseye, Intel Core i5-10210U, clang 11.0.1 and gcc 10.2.1 at -O3, Wuffs commit 315b2e52, September 2022) measures libspng 0.7.3 against Debian's libpng 1.6.37 at 1.02x, 1.05x, 1.04x and 1.05x on the 19k, 40k, 77k and 4002k images and 1.36x on 552k_32bpp with checksums verified (1.60x when libspng skips checksums, which libpng's simplified API cannot do); the earlier Wuffs blog run on an Intel Core m3-6Y30 gives 1.02-1.07x and 1.33-1.39x. In that harness libspng still skips the final IDAT CRC-32 but also pays a scalar RGBA-to-BGRA swap that libpng does not, while mango's 1.28-1.52x decode figures come from a single cold run with libspng's CRC-32 and Adler-32 checks off.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the Wuffs benchmark blog (Intel Core m3-6Y30, gcc -O3, harness test/c/mimiclib/png.c at wuffs v0.3.0-beta.1). Not A: the libspng commit is unpinned and libspng 0.6.2 skipped Adler-32 through an inverted-flag bug (fixed 9c35dc3), so the 1.62x row has libspng skipping checksums while libpng verifies; checksum-verified rows are 1.02-1.39x. In mango's png_benchmark.cpp, spng ignores CRC, encodes at level 3 and writes files 14-21% larger.

**Known shortcoming:** libspng skips the final IDAT CRC-32 (decode_image stops at SPNG_STATE_EOI); the mango rows are first-party single cold runs where SPNG_CRC_USE also disables Adler-32, libpng runs defaults in native layout and milliseconds are printed as us%10. Encode is slower than libpng per its own issues (#224 confirmed: 740 ms vs 510 ms at level 6 with zlib-ng; #274: 64-bit encode 3x slower). Maintenance is stale (last code release v0.7.4 on 2023-05-08, 69 issues and 18 PRs open), not active as recorded. Retier-19 raises the tier to A on the reproducible doc/benchmarks.md run (i5-10210U, clang 11.0.1 and gcc 10.2.1 -O3).

**How:** It inflates the IDAT stream one scanline at a time into a two-row buffer using whole IDAT chunks per read, then defilters with SSE2 (x86) or NEON (arm64) Sub/Avg/Paeth kernels derived from libpng's own intrinsics, with optional target_clones (AVX2) for the Up filter. Row-level fast paths (memcpy when the output layout matches, a dedicated RGB8 to RGBA8 widening, NEON palette expansion) replace per-pixel transform chains. Inflate itself is whatever zlib it links, so on large images the gain over libpng is small; the biggest win in third-party data is on 32bpp images.

**Use it when:**
- You want a small, embeddable PNG reader/writer (two C files plus zlib or miniz) with a simpler API than libpng and slightly faster decoding.
- Decoding 32bpp RGBA PNGs to RGBA8: 1.36x libpng 1.6.37 with checksum verification in Wuffs' September 2022 run (392 vs 289 MB/s, libspng 0.7.3).
- Untrusted input where you want explicit limits: spng_set_image_limits() and spng_set_chunk_limits() cap dimensions and chunk memory to guard against decompression bombs, and the code is fuzzed on OSS-Fuzz.
- Progressive or row-by-row decoding and encoding of large images with a fixed small working set (two rows, three if interlaced).
- arm64 targets with indexed-colour or truecolour images, where the NEON defilter and palette-expansion paths apply.

**Skip it when:**
- Maximum decode speed: on the same Wuffs harness Wuffs decodes at 1.55-3.16x libpng (1.5-2.6x libspng, derived from page data), and image-png and fpng are also faster; libspng is only 1.02-1.07x libpng on 8bpp and 24bpp images.
- Fast encoding at libpng-equivalent settings: open issue #224 (labelled bug, confirmed) shows libspng at 740 ms vs libpng 510 ms with zlib-ng at level 6 on a 2708x2160 RGB image, and #274 reports 64-bit encode 3x slower than 32-bit; fpng, fpnge or mtpng are the fast encoders.
- Animated PNG (APNG): still listed as planned in the README.
- Code that is written against libpng's API or needs libpng's transform set: the APIs are incompatible, and gamma correction is not implemented for SPNG_FMT_PNG, G8, GA8 and GA16 outputs.
- Projects that need an actively developed library: the last code change was v0.7.4 (2023-05-08); 2026 commits only bump the copyright year, with 69 open issues and 18 open PRs.

**Integration:** source-drop · zlib (>= 1.2.11 for inflateValidate and Adler-32 control) or miniz via SPNG_USE_MINIZ; libm · C99 (meson c_std=c99); CMake or Meson builds, or compile spng.c directly; SSE2 enabled by default on x86 without extra flags · any platform with 32-bit int and size_t, CHAR_BIT 8 and two's complement (16-bit targets unsupported); SIMD on x86 (SSE2 tested, SSSE3/SSE4.1 selectable) and arm64 NEON (only arm64 builds are tested)

**Vs siblings:** Pick libspng over image-png or Wuffs when you need a C library that both decodes and encodes, handles every standard chunk and is a two-file drop-in; pick Wuffs for raw decode speed (1.5-2.6x libspng in Wuffs' own run, derived from page data) and fpng, fpnge or mtpng when encode speed matters.

**Gotchas:**
- spng_decode_image() returns at end-of-image without reading the rest of the last IDAT chunk, so that chunk's CRC-32 is only checked if you then call spng_decode_chunks() (Wuffs' harness flags this as WUFFS_MIMICLIB_PNG_DOES_NOT_VERIFY_FINAL_IDAT_CHECKSUMS, still defined at Wuffs HEAD).
- spng_set_crc_action(ctx, SPNG_CRC_USE, ...) also turns off Adler-32 checking of the zlib stream, not only chunk CRCs; SPNG_CTX_IGNORE_ADLER32 is silently ignored with miniz or zlib older than 1.2.11.
- Use v0.7.4 or later: older releases do a wild read on a zero-length eXIf chunk (fixed in #248, reported as security notice #285, no CVE), and v0.7.2 fixed an encoder heap overflow.
- The README's 'outperforms the reference implementation' is backed only by a chart image on libspng.org; the repository has no benchmark numbers of its own.

**Status:** BSD-2-Clause and easy to vendor, but in maintenance mode: last release v0.7.4 (2023-05-08), no code changes since December 2023, issues and PRs unanswered.

[repo](https://github.com/randy408/libspng) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/wuffs/HEAD/doc/benchmarks.md)

##### meshoptimizer (vertex codec used as a lossless float-image compressor)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Mesh library whose lossless vertex codec, misused on float pixels, beat OpenEXR ZIP: 1.4x encode, 3.1x decode, 7% smaller.

**Beats:** OpenEXR 3.4.0 ZIP compression at level 4 (deflate through OpenEXR's bundled libdeflate, OPENEXR_FORCE_INTERNAL_DEFLATE ON); the same harness also runs EXR RLE, PIZ, HTJ2K_32/HTJ2K_256 (OpenJPH inside OpenEXR) and libjxl lossless at efforts 1/3/4/7/8. No standalone zstd, fpzip or zfp baseline in this harness. — Aras Pranckevicius's public harness (aras-p/test_exr_htj2k_jxl) round-tripped ten float EXR images (3122 MB raw) in memory with a bit-exact check, best of 3 runs, 16 threads on both sides, Release builds with MSVC 2022 17.14 on a Ryzen 9 5950X and Xcode clang 16 on an M4 Max. meshoptimizer v0.25 level 2 reached ratio 2.011 at 1.600 GB/s encode and 7.861 GB/s decode versus OpenEXR 3.4.0 ZIP level 4 at 1.873, 1.172 and 2.526 GB/s on the Ryzen (1.37x and 3.1x, derived), and 3.104/14.808 versus 1.723/5.993 GB/s on the M4 Max (1.80x and 2.47x, derived).

**Known shortcoming:** Off-label use: meshoptimizer's vertex codec (meshopt_encodeVertexBufferLevel levels 0-3, version 1, no filters, optional zstd stage) in a custom container as a lossless float-image compressor. Tier A on checked-in result files (img/win-ryzen5950x-20250908.html, img/mac-m4max-20250908.html; Ryzen 9 5950X, 16 threads, VS 2022 v17.14, CMake Release): ratio 2.011 at 1.600/7.861 GB/s vs OpenEXR ZIP4 1.873 at 1.172/2.526 GB/s (1.37x compress, 3.1x decompress, derived); baselines OpenEXR RLE/PIZ/ZIP/HTJ2K and libjxl. The fpzip, zfp and zstd comparisons live in aras-p/float_compr_tester with numbers only in the blocked blog.

**Known shortcoming:** The vertex codec's only predictor is the previous pixel (left neighbour); records are at most 256 bytes and must be a multiple of 4, and the channel mode is chosen per 4-byte lane so misaligned half or float layouts compress worse; format v1 is not readable by EXT_meshopt_compression decoders. fp32 round-trip is compared by value, not bits; the encoder is scalar and the decoder SIMD; the numbers are from v0.25 and the v1.2 notes claim an SSSE3 decode 20-45% faster. The harness is not fully independent of the author: zeux sent harness PR #3 (per-thread padding buffers, about doubling decode performance on Windows) and the owner rewrote the same fix.

**How:** Records are processed in blocks of up to 256 (8 KB / record size). Each block is transposed into one byte stream per byte position and delta-coded against the previous record (byte delta, 16-bit delta or, at level 3, 32-bit XOR with a rotation, chosen once per 4-byte lane at levels 2-3) with zigzag mapping. Each 16-byte group of deltas is then bit-packed at 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits with a sentinel-plus-literal escape for outliers, chosen per group with 2-bit headers. There is no entropy coder or match search, so decoding is table-driven shuffles: SSSE3 (picked by cpuid on MSVC x64), NEON on arm64, Wasm SIMD and an opt-in AVX-512 path, about 8 GB/s on a 16-thread Ryzen 9 5950X and 14.8 GB/s on an M4 Max in the measured run. Encoding is scalar C++.

**Use it when:**
- Internal caches or intermediate files of half/float render buffers, AOVs, lightmaps or simulation fields where you control both writer and reader and do not need interop (the harness author's own recommendation).
- Decode-bound pipelines: the decode stayed at 7.9-8.1 GB/s (Ryzen 9 5950X) and 14.7-14.8 GB/s (M4 Max) across levels 0-3, versus 2.5 and 6.0 GB/s for EXR ZIP level 4.
- Layered images with many interleaved channels (the test set had up to 37 channels per pixel), as long as one pixel fits in 256 bytes.
- When you want a better ratio and can afford a bit more encode time: stacking zstd level 1 on level 2 raised the ratio from 2.011 to 2.248 at 1.53 GB/s encode and 6.7 GB/s decode on the Ryzen.
- Code-size-sensitive builds: the harness measured +26 KB of executable for the codec (+431 KB with zstd) versus +308 KB for EXR HTJ2K and +6017 KB for libjxl.

**Skip it when:**
- Files other tools must read: there is no image format, and the 'MOP' container exists only in the benchmark repository. Use OpenEXR (ZIP, or HTJ2K via OpenJPH) for interchange.
- Maximum lossless ratio: libjxl effort 7 reached 2.180 and effort 8 2.434 on the same files (at 0.05 and 0.007 GB/s encode), and plain Mop2 stops at 2.011.
- Data without left-to-right correlation: the only predictor is the previous record in memory order (no vertical or 2D prediction), and the README warns that unordered input compresses poorly.
- Records over 256 bytes or not a multiple of 4: the API asserts on both, so callers must pad (the harness zero-pads, which costs a copy per chunk) or split wide pixels into several streams.
- Data that must stay readable by glTF EXT_meshopt_compression decoders or meshoptimizer older than v0.23: the benchmark used vertex format version 1, which those cannot decode; pin version 0 if needed (levels then have no effect).

**Integration:** static lib by default (CMake, MESHOPT_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS option) or source-drop: the codec is src/vertexcodec.cpp plus the C-compatible header src/meshoptimizer.h · none (zstd only if you add the optional second pass yourself) · any mainstream C++ compiler; CMake 3.5+ if using CMake; the README says the sources build without special options or warnings; the benchmark used MSVC 2022 17.14 and Xcode clang 16 · any; SIMD decode on x86/x64 (SSSE3+POPCNT, runtime cpuid fallback on MSVC and GCC/clang), AVX-512 VBMI2 only when compiled in, NEON on ARM/AArch64, Wasm SIMD; scalar fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Among the catalogued image codecs only OpenJPH (as OpenEXR HTJ2K) and LERC target float or raster data; pick meshoptimizer over HTJ2K when you do not need a standard file and want speed (HTJ2K_256 in the same run: ratio 1.947 at 0.709/1.045 GB/s on the Ryzen versus Mop2 2.011 at 1.600/7.861 GB/s). The 8-bit lossless codecs (QOI, fpng, fpnge, QOIR) do not handle half/float pixels at all.

**Gotchas:**
- Channel modes are chosen per 4-byte lane of the record, so a float channel straddling a 4-byte boundary (possible in mixed half/float layouts) or an odd count of half channels gets a worse delta mode; reorder channels so each 4-byte lane holds one float or two halves.
- The decoder does not store the record count or size: the caller must keep vertex_count and vertex_size next to the payload (the harness keeps them in its own header).
- The decoder is safe on untrusted input but 'may produce garbage data' on malformed streams; check the return code and add your own checksum if integrity matters.
- The measured build was v0.25. The v1.2 release notes say a new mostly branchless SSSE3 decoder is about 20-45% faster on Intel/AMD and AVX-512 adds about 10%, so the current v1.3 should decode faster on x86 than measured; this has not been re-benchmarked in the harness.

**Status:** Very actively maintained (v1.3 released September 2026, last commit 2026-09-28, about 8.5k stars, 4 open issues), MIT-licensed and packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, FreeBSD, Nix, vcpkg and Conan; copyable, but the image use is off-label and the container format is yours to write.

[repo](https://github.com/zeux/meshoptimizer) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aras-p/test_exr_htj2k_jxl/HEAD/README.md)

##### oxipng  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Multithreaded Rust lossless PNG/APNG optimizer; 2.2x (default) to 5x (-o4) faster than OptiPNG 0.7.7 wall-clock on one test image.

**Beats:** OptiPNG — The v9.0.0 to v10.0.0 README timed a pre-release oxipng 9.0.0 (commit c16519b, rustc 1.74.0-nightly 2023-09-28, release profile lto = "thin", default features with rayon) against Debian's OptiPNG 0.7.7 with hyperfine on an Intel Core i7-12700 (20 threads): 59.6 ms versus 132.4 ms at the default level (2.22x) and 88.7 ms versus 444.9 ms at -o4 (5.01x), both in dry-run mode. The input is one 500x400 16-bit RGB PNG (116 KB) that both tools can losslessly reduce to 8-bit grayscale; output sizes were not reported, and at that commit -o4 meant four filter strategies (None, Bigrams, BigEnt, Brute) fully compressed with libdeflate level 12 in parallel, a different trial set from OptiPNG's -o 4, so the 5x is time-at-named-preset, not the same work done faster.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). Upgraded to A on the tagged v9.0.0 to v10.0.0 README hyperfine runs vs OptiPNG 0.7.7 (2.22x default, 5.01x at -o4; i7-12700, rustc 1.74.0-nightly, Cargo.toml lto thin at c16519b). The gain is mostly threads (user CPU about 1.65x at -o4), one test image, and a different trial set from OptiPNG's; the op111.net post is snippet-only.

**Known shortcoming:** The measured file is one 500x400 16-bit RGB image that losslessly reduces to 8-bit grey, so both tools reduce it; no output sizes are given, and at c16519b -o4 runs 4 filters at libdeflate level 12 in parallel, different trials from OptiPNG's, so the CPU-time gain is only 1.71x/1.65x. README library snippet asks for the filetime feature removed in 10.1.0 (so '10.0' resolves to 10.2.1 and fails to build); the README MSRV says 1.85.1 but 10.2.x needs 1.88.0; benchmark commands use -P, renamed -d in 10.0.0; the libdeflater crate seeks a new maintainer (#702).

**How:** Three things, not one faster algorithm: (1) trials run in parallel on rayon, each reduction candidate and filter strategy in its own task, with a shared atomic best size (AtomicMin) passed to the deflater as an output cap so losing trials abort early; (2) compression uses libdeflate (levels 10-12 are its near-optimal parser) instead of zlib; (3) in the default fast-evaluation mode (levels 0-4) reductions and filter strategies are ranked with a cheap libdeflate level (5, 7 or 8 per optimize_raw) and only the winner is compressed once at the main level (11 at -o2, 12 at -o4). Filter strategies include the five PNG filters plus heuristic MinSum, Entropy, Bigrams, BigEnt and a Brute strategy that test-compresses a few lines per row choice.

**Use it when:**
- Build, CI or pre-commit steps that losslessly shrink PNG assets; the project ships a pre-commit hook and a ghcr.io Docker image for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.
- Interactive or few-file runs on a multi-core machine where wall-clock time matters: one image's trials spread across cores, giving 2.22x at the default level and 5.01x at -o4 against single-threaded OptiPNG on a 20-thread i7-12700 in the README run.
- Replacing OptiPNG in image pipelines where the default level should also compress better: the op111.net comparison (search snippet only) reports 29.14% versus 25.42% size reduction on d3js.org.png at about 3.5x the speed.
- Rust programs that produce or post-process PNGs in memory: optimize_from_memory() or RawImage plus Options::from_preset(level), with --max-raw-size and timeout controls available.
- Web or WASM image tools: Squoosh and jSquash use it per the README, and a freestanding feature forwards to libdeflater for targets without a full libc.

**Skip it when:**
- Batch jobs that already run one OptiPNG process per core: then the parallel trials add little and the gain falls toward the CPU-time ratio, which was only 1.71x (default) and 1.65x (-o4) in the README run (derived from page data).
- Maximum compression at any cost: oxipng is not a brute-force optimizer, so a higher level can occasionally give a larger file and --zopfli is not guaranteed to help; op111 (snippet only) shows --opt max --zopfli taking 28.9 s for 30.25% versus 0.764 s for 29.14% at the default on the same image. ECT or other zopfli-based tools trade more time for bytes.
- Animated PNGs: APNG support is limited to alpha optimization, refiltering and recompression with all reductions disabled; the README recommends running apngopt first, and issue 'Feature-complete APNG optimization' is still open.
- C or C++ applications that want an in-process library: there is only a Rust API and no C ABI, so use the CLI as a subprocess or write your own FFI shim.
- Services processing untrusted or very large images under a hard deadline: --timeout is checked only between trials and does not stop a running compression, so set --max-raw-size; the libdeflater crate it depends on is looking for a new maintainer (issue #702, open, no decision).

**Integration:** crate (library) and CLI binary; also distro packages, Windows release binaries and a Docker image · libdeflater (Rust binding to the C libdeflate library; feature system-libdeflate links the system copy), indexmap, rgb, rustc-hash, log; optional rayon (parallel, default), zopfli (default), clap, env_logger, parse-size and glob (binary feature, default), image (sanity-checks) · Rust 1.88.0 for 10.2.x (Cargo.toml rust-version, crates.io metadata; 1.85.1 for 10.0.0 to 10.1.1), edition 2024; the README still says 1.85.1 · any target Rust and libdeflate support; Docker images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64; WASM used downstream (Squoosh, jSquash) but WASM tests in CI are an open issue

**Vs siblings:** Pick oxipng when you already have PNG files and want them smaller with identical pixels; fpng, fpnge and mtpng are fast encoders from raw pixels whose files are larger (fpnge's catalogued ratio is about 15% worse than libpng's), and libspng, image-png and zune-png are decoders. ECT (catalogued under general-lossless) squeezes harder with its zopfli-derived deflate at a much higher run time.

**Gotchas:**
- Version 10.0.0 renamed flags: -P/--pretend became -d/--dry-run, -Z became -z and --interlace takes on/off, so the README benchmark commands (oxipng -P) do not run on 10.x as written; the library API also changed (optimize() now returns original and optimized sizes, Deflaters became Deflater).
- --alpha alters the color of fully transparent pixels (the README calls it technically lossy), and --scale16 forcibly scales 16-bit to 8-bit; both are off by default, but pipeline scripts copied from the web often include --alpha.
- Default output removes interlacing (since 9.0.0); use -i keep to retain it, and interlacing is only applied when smaller unless --force is given.
- The README's library snippet (version "10.0", features ["parallel", "zopfli", "filetime"], default-features = false) no longer builds: the filetime feature was dropped in 10.1.0 (crates.io feature lists for 10.1.0 to 10.2.1) without a changelog entry, and "10.0" resolves to 10.2.1; list only parallel and zopfli.

**Status:** Actively developed (v10.2.1, last commit 2026-09-02, 4.3k stars), MIT and widely packaged; usable from C++ projects as a CLI build step rather than a linked library.

[repo](https://github.com/oxipng/oxipng) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oxipng/oxipng/v10.0.0/README.md)

##### PNG XL (PXL)  `C`  `libpng-2.0 AND BSD-3-Clause (files under ffmpeg/ are FFmpeg patch material under LGPL-2.1-or-later)`  `active`  `Tier A`

Lossless PNG-replacement format (.pxl) and C library: PNG row filters plus zstd, decoding about 2x faster than libpng.

**Beats:** libpng (decode into raw RGBA pixels) — bench/rawdec.c over the 24 Kodak photographs (median of 15 runs per file, single thread, Pentium B960, gcc 16.x -O3) times PXL decoding an in-memory level-12 .pxl at 143.2 ms total against 333.6 ms for system libpng 1.6.x decoding a default-settings PNG of the same pixels through pxl_load_png, about 2.3x, with PXL output memcmp-checked every repetition. bench/formatdec.c, with every decoder producing RGBA8888 in process, gives 199.6-275.8 MB/s for PXL levels 12 and 1 against 98.6 MB/s for libpng on photographs (about 2.0-2.8x), 449.8-536.7 against 308.7 MB/s on 30 synthetic stills, and on a real PSP-3008 none/delta are 2.8-3.5x libpng while adaptive ties and BCIF loses (0.54x) at 512x512.

**Known shortcoming:** Format-versus-format comparison, not a faster PNG decoder: PXL is its own PXL1 container (delta and BCIF filters ported from Zpng plus zstd), so beating libpng decode is different work. BCIF wins all 24 Kodak files, so the photo path is the Zpng transform plus zstd. The libpng side is timed with the file read from page cache plus a metadata scan (small bias against libpng); the BCIF path loses 0.54x at texture sizes (PSP). Single machine (Pentium B960, gcc 16.x -O3).

**Known shortcoming:** Pre-release format whose spec is not frozen (ROADMAP); no integrity check (ZSTD_compress default with no checksum or CRC) while libpng verifies CRC-32 and Adler-32, so libpng does extra work in the comparison; formatdec.c has no pixel check (rawdec does); the BCIF path needs a full-image buffer and cannot stream; an earlier heap overflow and two out-of-bounds reads were fixed; Linux-only CI.

**How:** Pixels go through one of four exactly reversible filters (none, Zpng's left-delta, Zpng's BCIF colour transform y=b, u=g-b, v=g-r with a planar split, or PNG-style adaptive per-row None/Sub/Up/Average/Paeth), and the result is one Zstandard frame instead of DEFLATE. The encoder keeps whichever filter compresses smallest. zstd decompression is much cheaper than inflate, so for none/delta/BCIF decode time is mostly zstd, and the unfilter adds 2-12% (bench/stages.c measurements). The unfilter loops are specialised per filter type, and Paeth is branchless. LTO was measured to undo that specialisation and is deliberately off.

**Use it when:**
- You control both ends of the pipeline (game assets, texture packs, thumbnail caches) and want lossless images that decode about 2x faster than libpng into RGBA on photographs and about 1.5x on synthetic stills, in files 12-15% smaller than default-settings PNG.
- Single-core or memory-tight targets (the design floor is a 32 MB PSP): the decode-only library is 174 KB of .text including zstd, and with -p the row-window streaming path decodes in about the memory of the output image.
- Progressive or row-at-a-time decode straight into GPU texture formats (RGB565, RGBA5551, RGBA4444, RGBA8888) without a separate conversion pass.
- Lossless photographs where QOI's files (about 103.5% of PNG) are too big but you still want decode speed close to QOI's (QOI is about 16% faster on the Kodak set).

**Skip it when:**
- You must read or serve existing .png files or deliver to browsers: nothing outside this repo (plus its own Qt/KDE plugins and FFmpeg patch) reads .pxl.
- Smallest files matter: JPEG XL (65.8% of PNG) and WebP (73.6%) beat PXL (85.6-88.6%) on photographs. On synthetic stills WebP is both smaller (44.6% vs 50.3%) and faster (570 vs 485-537 MB/s).
- Grayscale 8-bit content (100.3% of PNG, slightly worse) or texture-sized photographs on PSP-class CPUs: the BCIF filter the encoder picks for photos decoded at 0.54x libpng at 512x512 on a real PSP-3008. Encode with -s there.
- You need a frozen, interoperable format: the ROADMAP says the format is pre-release with no outside users and the spec can still change without a version bump until a freeze decision is made.
- You want encode speed at high levels or decode speed at high levels on photos: level 19 makes zstd decompression about 3x slower than level 1 on a Kodak photograph, and levels 6 and 12 can produce larger BCIF files than level 1.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (CMake; libpxlcore is PNG-free and needs only zstd, libpxl adds the libpng front end) · zstd (core); libpng and zlib for PNG/APNG interop; optional vendored submodules pinning libpng 1.6.59 and zstd 1.5.7 · C99 compiler, CMake 3.10+; benchmarks used gcc 16.1.1/16.2.1 at -O3 · Linux x86-64 (only platform in CI, ubuntu-latest); decoder also cross-compiled with psp-gcc and run on a real PSP-3008 (MIPS Allegrex); no SIMD required. Windows/macOS not documented as tested.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PXL over Zpng, which it descends from, when you need a real container with palettes, 1- to 16-bit depths, metadata pass-through, streaming, animation and a written SPEC.md; pick it over QOI or QOIR when you want zstd-level compression (about 85-88% of PNG) at near-QOI decode speed. If you must keep standard .png files, use a faster PNG decoder instead (libspng, image-png, ptpng, or fpng for fpng-written PNGs).

**Gotchas:**
- No integrity check: pxl_encode calls ZSTD_compress with default parameters (no zstd content checksum) and the container has no CRC, whereas libpng verifies chunk CRC-32 and zlib's Adler-32 on every decode. Part of the measured gap is libpng doing integrity work PXL skips, and a corrupted .pxl can decode to wrong pixels without an error.
- BCIF (picked for all 24 Kodak photographs) has no row window: it materialises the whole filtered image, roughly doubles decode memory, cannot stream, and delivers all rows only at pxl_stream_finish. -p excludes it at a 4-6.6% size cost on large images; -s keeps only none/delta.
- tRNS, bKGD, hIST and PLTE are not carried as chunks: transparency is canonicalised to a real alpha channel, so a PNG round-trip is pixel-exact but not always type-identical.
- Hard decode limits: width and height at most 1,000,000 and width x height at most 2^28 pixels. A 2026-09-15 heap overflow in the streaming DELTA path for sub-8-bit indexed images (fixed in cab6ccf) and two 32-bit integer-overflow out-of-bounds reads (fixed after the 2026-09-16 audit) show the decoders are young; CI runs an ASan/UBSan fuzz soak.

**Status:** Very active single-author project (81 commits, last 2026-09-29, 7 stars, no open issues) with unusually candid append-only benchmark logs, but the format is pre-release and not yet frozen; libpng-2.0 AND BSD-3-Clause, small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/LicaRedMoth/PNG-XL) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LicaRedMoth/PNG-XL/HEAD/README.md)

##### QLIC (Quick Lossless Image Codec)  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Lossless image codec reaching JPEG XL effort-9 file sizes at about one-ninth of cjxl's single-thread encode time.

**Beats:** JPEG XL lossless via stock cjxl (-d 0 -e 9 --num_threads=0) and WebP lossless via stock cwebp (-lossless -exact -z 6), per benchmark/run-large-matrix.ps1; the page also lists JPEG XL efforts 1-8, WebP presets 1-9 and an OxiPNG level 6 row. No PNG or QOI decoder is a baseline — First-party run on a Ryzen 9 9950X3D under Windows 11, one pinned logical processor, wall time including process start and file I/O, 3,167 images (1.96 Gpx), byte-exact round trip on every file. The QLIC 1.0 portable Clang 22.1.4 build took 618.7 s for 1,160,913,984 bytes, against cjxl -d 0 -e 9 at 5,674.2 s for 1,164,424,898 bytes (about 9.2x faster and 0.30% smaller) and cwebp -lossless -z 6 at 586.0 s for 1,289,518,274 bytes. Decode took 236.9 s for QLIC, 307.6 s for djxl and 117.9 s for dwebp. Baseline versions are not on the current page (the 0.5 run used cjxl 0.12.0 and cwebp 1.6.0), and per-file rows stay in a private workspace.

**Known shortcoming:** Borderline A: the public harness (benchmark/run-large-matrix.ps1) runs cjxl -e 9 and cwebp -z 6 on a single pinned core with ImageMagick checking pixels exactly (Clang 22.1.4, 9950X3D), but the current page names no baseline versions (the 0.5 record said cwebp 1.6.0 and cjxl 0.12.0), no script runs OxiPNG, decode times include process start-up and each tool's PNG writer, and WebP decodes about 2x faster than QLIC; the 9.2x win is against JPEG XL effort 9 while QLIC encodes at only 3.2 MP/s. Language is C, not C++. Weeks-old single-author repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e117, 2026-10-05): no correctness bug behind the totals (AE=0 on every file), but the headline uses the development corpus the encoder was built against; on the wider 10,628-image set in docs/architecture.md QLIC is 0.45% larger than JPEG XL effort 9, about level with effort 8, and still 8.99x faster to encode than effort 9. Decode is whole-process wall time including startup and PNG writing (QLIC writes PNG via WIC); the project's own docs put its core entropy decode 6.75x slower than WebP and 11.7x slower than WIC PNG, so the 1.30x lead over djxl is not a core-decoder ratio. Only QLIC, effort 9 and WebP z6 were re-timed in the final campaign. A is borderline but defensible for the encode matrix.

**Independent measurement:** first-party campaign, public scripts

**How:** The encoder runs a bounded tournament instead of an exhaustive search. Cheap image facts (palette cardinality, block repetition, transform score, alpha shape) produce an early candidate and gate specialist representations such as palettes, filtered bytes with LZMS and horizontal bands; each specialist gets the current size as a cutoff, and the smallest completed file wins. The native QST1 stream applies reversible integer colour transforms, per-plane spatial prediction with predictor maps scored by AVX2 kernels, and adaptive binary range coding of residuals with context models (mode 52 is the main photographic path). Decode is a serial scalar range-decoding chain; the project's own architecture guide puts about 98% of hot decode time in plane entropy decoding.

**Use it when:**
- Archiving lossless images you would otherwise compress with cjxl -e 8 or -e 9, when single-thread encode CPU matters: similar total size for about 9x less encode time on the author's corpus.
- Mixed asset sets of UI screenshots, game textures, icons and structured graphics, where the author reports QLIC is often smaller than both JPEG XL and WebP.
- Closed pipelines where you control both ends (game assets, internal datasets, a desktop app) and can ship the C, Rust or Wasm decoder.
- Exact storage of 9-24-bit integer samples or PQ/HLG code values together with their metadata, without wrapping another image format.

**Skip it when:**
- Decode-latency-bound serving: WebP lossless decoded this corpus about 2x faster in wall time, and the architecture guide says QLIC's entropy decode is about 6.75x slower than WebP and 11.7x slower than WIC PNG.
- Interchange with browsers, operating systems or other tools: the format is not standardised and only QLIC's own WIC plugin and Wasm package read it.
- Fast encoding: about 3.2 MP/s single-threaded; JPEG XL efforts 1-4, WebP presets 1-6, fjxl or fpnge encode much faster at 10-33% larger output.
- Photographic and alpha-heavy content where JPEG XL e9 stays smaller, and corpora unlike the author's: on the wider 10,628-image qualification set QLIC's total is 0.45% larger than e9.
- Platforms outside Windows x64 and Linux x86-64 (untested), float/half HDR (unsupported), or needs for true streaming or cheap region decode (region decode still pays the full entropy decode).

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (C17, CMake targets qlic::qlic_static and qlic::qlic, pkg-config) plus CLI; separate safe-Rust decoder crate and Wasm build · none for the codec core (LZMS is a bundled clean-room decoder); the CLI's input loaders use libpng, libwebp, libjxl, libavif and libtiff on Linux (libwim-dev also listed) and WIC on Windows · C17, CMake 3.25+, Visual Studio 2022+ or Clang on Windows (published binary built with Clang 22.1.4), GCC or Clang on Ubuntu 24.04; Rust 1.85 for the Rust decoder · Windows x64 and Linux x86-64 tested; portable x86-64 build with one AVX2 encoder-analysis source (map_avx2.c); wasm32 decoder; other architectures untested

**Vs siblings:** Pick QLIC over HALIC or fNBLI when JPEG XL e9-level density matters more than raw speed and you want a maintained C library with Rust and Wasm decoders plus alpha, animation, wide-integer and metadata support. Pick libjxl fast_lossless, QOIR or fpnge when encode or decode throughput comes first and 15-30% larger files are acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline size win is measured on the 3,167-image development corpus that the encoder's routes were built against; the architecture guide calls it 'a development gate, not a universal ranking'. On the wider 10,628-image qualification line QLIC totals 4,606,862,554 bytes vs JPEG XL e9 4,586,294,329 (0.45% larger, derived) and e8 4,607,544,830, while still encoding about 9x faster than e9.
- Decode figures are per-process wall time including start-up and writing a PNG. QLIC's CLI writes that PNG through the Windows WIC encoder at default settings, while djxl and dwebp use their own writers, so the published 1.30x lead over djxl is a whole-tool number and may not hold for in-process decode.
- QLIC 1.0.0 could write an invalid 32-byte file and report success for some large images with small, noisy palettes. Version 1.0.1 (2026-09-12) fixed it, so re-encode affected files and run qlic verify on stored archives.
- For untrusted files, set limits tighter than the 512 MiB / 67,108,864-pixel defaults and add an external time budget: the docs say limits cap allocation, not CPU time.

**Status:** Active single-author project (first commit 2026-07-29, 1.0.1 on 2026-09-12, last commit 2026-10-02, 23 stars). The Apache-2.0 C library is vendorable, but the format is new and non-standard, so pin the decoder and keep a PNG or JPEG XL fallback.

[repo](https://github.com/OzzyMitchell/QLIC) · [benchmark](https://github.com/OzzyMitchell/QLIC/blob/main/docs/benchmark-current.md)

##### QOI (Quite OK Image format)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Reference C header for the QOI lossless RGB/RGBA format: about 27x faster encode and 3.4x faster decode than libpng, with files about 17% larger.

**Beats:** libpng — In Nigel Tao's QOIR harness (test/benchmarks.c, gettimeofday around repeated in-memory encode and decode calls with allocation included, single-threaded, gcc 10.2.1 with -O3 -march=native for the QOI adapter, Intel i5-10210U), on the qoiformat.org benchmark image suite, qoi.h encoded at 146.87 MPixels/s and decoded at 193.53 against Debian Bullseye's libpng simplified API at default compression (5.49 and 56.18), about 27x and 3.4x (derived from page data), with CmpRatio 0.2823 vs 0.2423. QOI's decode lead shrinks to about 1.4x against the Wuffs PNG decoder in the same run (140.79). The record's caveat that QOI compresses worse than libpng on every subset needs one correction: on textures_pk QOI is smaller (0.5645 vs 0.5991).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on qoir full_benchmarks.txt rows 65 and 68 (146.87 vs 5.49 MB/s encode, 193.53 vs 56.18 decode; gcc 10.2.1, i5-10210U, Debian libpng default level). Compression ratio 0.2823 vs libpng 0.2423 (about 17% larger, derived from page data) and worse than libpng on every subset. No round-trip pixel check in the harness.

**Known shortcoming:** In the QOIR run fpnge is faster and smaller overall (312.59 MP/s, CmpRatio 0.2798) and Wuffs decodes at 140.79 MP/s, cutting QOI's decode lead to about 1.4x; the record's caveat that QOI never compresses better than libpng is wrong for textures_pk (0.5645 versus 0.5991). qoi_decode accepts truncated streams and a 22-byte file allocates 80 MB (#340 open); signed-char narrowing issues (#254, #328); the encoder returns an unshrunk worst-case buffer; no tags; qoi.h unchanged since April 2025.

**How:** QOI has no entropy coder and no match search: each pixel is emitted as one of six byte-aligned chunks chosen by a fixed priority. These are a run of the previous pixel (up to 62), a 6-bit index into a 64-entry cache of recently seen colours hashed as (r*3 + g*5 + b*7 + a*11) & 63, a 1-byte delta of -2..1 per channel, a 2-byte 'luma' delta (green -32..31, red and blue relative to green -8..7), or a literal RGB or RGBA chunk. Encode and decode are one linear pass with a small branch tree per pixel and a 256-byte state table on the stack. libpng instead tries PNG row filters and then runs zlib deflate (LZ77 match search plus Huffman coding), and the match search is what costs it most of its encode time. The reference code is deliberately plain scalar C (no SIMD, one pixel per loop iteration even inside runs); the README says performance pull requests will probably not be accepted.

**Use it when:**
- Writing lossless 8-bit RGB/RGBA frames where encode time dominates and you control the reader: screenshot capture, game or renderer frame dumps, intermediate pipeline images, asset caches. In the QOIR run it encoded 146.87 MPixels/s against libpng's 5.49 on one i5-10210U thread.
- UI screenshots, icons and flat-colour art, where runs and the colour cache work best: screenshot_web 271.61 MPixels/s encode and 358.64 decode at CmpRatio 0.0835 (libpng 0.0757), icon_512 277.20 / 341.29.
- Embedded, bootloader or freestanding code that needs a tiny auditable decoder: under 400 lines of C89-compatible implementation with only malloc/free/memset, endian-neutral byte I/O (the hash uses the r, g, b, a fields, not the packed word), and a frozen format with no version field.
- When a non-PNG format is acceptable but tool support matters: the README lists QOI support in ImageMagick 7.1.0-20+, ffmpeg 5.1+, GIMP 3.0, KDE KImageFormats, Microsoft PowerToys, IrfanView and XnView MP, plus Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora and AUR packages.

**Skip it when:**
- When the output must be PNG: the catalogued fpnge encodes real PNG at 312.59 MPixels/s with CmpRatio 0.2798 in the same QOIR run, which is both faster than and slightly smaller than QOI overall (146.87, 0.2823), and fpng also decodes its own PNGs at 148.19. On photo subsets, though, fpnge files are larger than QOI's (photo_kodak 0.6218 vs 0.5829).
- Photographs or anything where file size matters: QOI's ratio is about 17% worse than libpng's defaults overall and worse on photos (photo_wikipedia 0.6618 vs 0.5663, photo_tecnick 0.5992 vs 0.5011); Zpng gets 0.5190 on photo_wikipedia at similar speed, and WebP lossless reaches 0.1651 overall if encode time is not a concern.
- Decoding untrusted files without your own limits: the header alone decides the allocation, so a 22-byte file can make qoi_decode allocate 80 MB (issue #340, open since June 2026), and up to 1.6 GB for a 400-megapixel RGBA header. Truncated or chunk-less streams decode 'successfully' instead of returning NULL. Check width*height against your own cap before calling it.
- Grayscale, palette, 16-bit, HDR/float, premultiplied alpha, animation, ICC/EXIF metadata, or images over 400 million pixels: none of these is supported. The colorspace byte is informative only, and the reference loads the whole file into RAM (the README points to streaming implementations for huge images).
- When you need the fastest QOI codec rather than the reference: the README says this implementation 'is not extensively optimized'. The catalogued qoixx (C++) and qoi-rust (Rust) produce the same format faster, and qoi-asm (x86-64 assembly, listed in the README in September 2026) claims 1.07x to 2.16x over qoi.h.

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond libc (malloc/free/memset; stdio for qoi_read/qoi_write unless QOI_NO_STDIO is defined). The qoibench tool also needs libpng, stb_image.h and stb_image_write.h, and qoiconv needs the two stb headers. · C89 (commits 'make qoi.h build using c89 compilers' and 'Remove single line comments to conform to c89 -pedantic', Dec 2021) or any C++ compiler; the Makefile builds qoiconv with -std=c99 -O3 and qoibench with -std=gnu99 -O3 · any; portable scalar C with no SIMD or intrinsics, and byte-wise big-endian header I/O, so endianness does not matter

**Vs siblings:** Pick reference QOI when you want the most widely supported fast lossless format with a frozen spec and a vendorable header that reads like documentation. Use qoixx or qoi-rust for faster coding of the same files, fpnge or fpng when the output has to stay PNG, and QOIR or Zpng (custom formats too) when you want smaller files and faster decoding: QOIR_Lossless beat QOI on all three axes in the same run (0.2525, 168.90, 276.45).

**Gotchas:**
- qoi_encode mallocs a worst-case buffer of width*height*(channels+1)+22 bytes and returns it without shrinking (about 10 MB for a 1080p RGBA frame, whatever the output size). There is no way to pass a preallocated buffer (issue #285, open); allocation can only be swapped globally at compile time with QOI_MALLOC/QOI_FREE, and results must be freed with the matching function.
- qoi_decode never checks the 8-byte end marker or whether the chunks covered every pixel: when data runs out it fills the rest of the image with the last decoded colour and returns success (issue #340). Requesting channels=3 from an RGBA file silently drops alpha, and channels=4 from an RGB file yields alpha 255.
- Sizes are int: qoi_decode takes int size and qoi_encode writes int *out_len, which is why the reference caps images at 400 million pixels (QOI_PIXELS_MAX) to stay under 2 GB.
- Delta computation stores channel differences in signed char, which depends on implementation-defined narrowing (issues #254 and #328, both open). The qoi_rgba_t union is read through its packed .v member, which C allows but ISO C++ does not sanction. Both behave as intended on mainstream two's-complement compilers, but strict-UB checkers will flag them. There are no tags or releases (issue #261 'Tag a release?' open since 2023), so pin a commit hash.

**Status:** The format is final and qoi.h code last changed in April 2025 (the modulo-to-mask hash, merged May 2025; before that, stricter qoi_read/qoi_write error checks in June 2023). Commits since then, up to 2026-09-27, only add README links, so it is stable rather than actively developed. It is MIT-licensed, about 650 lines including the spec, and packaged by Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora, but has no tagged releases.

[repo](https://github.com/phoboslab/qoi) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nigeltao/qoir/HEAD/doc/full_benchmarks.txt)

##### qoi-asm  `x86-64 assembly (GNU as, Intel syntax) with a C test and benchmark harness`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Hand-written x86-64 assembly QOI codec, bit-identical to qoi.h and 1.07x-2.16x faster than its gcc -O3 build.

**Beats:** QOI reference implementation qoi.h (phoboslab/qoi) compiled with gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 — tests/bench.c links qoi.h (byte-identical to upstream, sha256 checked in CI) at gcc -O2 and at -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 into one binary with the assembly, checks every output bit for bit, then reports median TSC ticks over 11 or 31 single-call reps after 3 warm-ups. On an i7-14700F under WSL2 (gcc 13.3.0, taskset -c 3) the ASM was 1.07x-2.16x faster than -O3 on all 18 rows of 7 synthetic 512x512 and 1080p inputs; against -O2 the range is 0.88x-2.92x (derived from page data). The unchanged C rows agree within about 1-2% (worst about 7%) across the three committed result files, bench_after_M1, E2 and D1 (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Synthetic inputs only, and the assembly is slower than the -O2 C build on the 1080p_rgba_runs decode4 row (0.88x, derived from page data); the baseline qoi.h is the QOI reference, not a category incumbent; single commit, 0 stars. Harness tests/bench.c, Makefile flags, tests/bench_after_D1.txt, gcc 13.3.0 and i7-14700F all public.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e97, 2026-10-04): numbers hold (bit-identical gate before timing, hash constant checked by algebra, committed runs agree within 1-2%, worst 7%); against -O2 the range is 0.88x-2.92x (derived from page data). Photo-like decode gains only 1.07x-1.22x; the top ratios all come from random-pixel rows. Doc errors: README claims x86-64-v3 but the assembly uses nothing above SSE4.1 and has no CPUID check; the README snippet keeps QOI_IMPLEMENTATION defined, so libqoi.a silently keeps the C code; no QOI_MALLOC or QOI_NO_STDIO support; no CET note, so linking strips IBT/SHSTK marking.

**Independent measurement:** first-party harness, bit-identical output

**How:** The loops keep px, px_prev, run and the input/output cursors in registers instead of stack slots, and dispatch once on channels==3 or channels==4 into two specialised loops, removing qoi.h's per-pixel channel test. The QOI index hash (r*3+g*5+b*7+a*11)&63 becomes one 64-bit multiply of the byte-spread pixel by 0x0C001C0014002C00 and a shift by 58, which is exact because lower partial products stay below 2^58. Encode computes the three channel deltas with SSE4.1 psubb/pmovsxbd and folds the three DIFF range tests into one unsigned compare; decode applies DIFF/LUMA deltas with pinsrb/paddb; the trailing-run flush is moved out of the hot run loop.

**Use it when:**
- You already use qoi.h on x86-64 Linux and want faster encode/decode without changing a line of calling code or the output bytes.
- Encode-heavy pipelines (screenshots, frame dumps, texture caches): the published encode gains are 1.10x-1.99x over gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3, with 1.83x on the 1080p photo-like RGBA row.
- High-entropy or RGBA-op-heavy content, where gains are largest (about 2x encode and decode on the random rows).
- Projects that need a single reviewed object file with no dependencies beyond libc and an exact behavioural match to qoi.h, verified by in-process differential tests.

**Skip it when:**
- Non-x86 targets (ARM, RISC-V, WebAssembly), Windows x64 calling convention, or MSVC/MASM/NASM toolchains: there is only a GNU as, System V object.
- You rely on qoi.h compile-time options: QOI_MALLOC/QOI_FREE overrides and QOI_NO_STDIO cannot apply to the prebuilt object, which always calls libc malloc and stdio.
- Photo-like decode is the bottleneck: the gain there is only 1.07x-1.22x over gcc -O3, and on the run-heavy 1080p RGBA decode the ASM is slower than the plain -O2 C build (0.88x).
- You want independent or real-image evidence: all inputs are synthetic, the numbers come from one WSL2 host, and the repo is a single LLM-generated commit with no users yet.
- You need CET-hardened binaries: the object carries no GNU property note or endbr64, so linking it strips IBT/shadow-stack marking from the final executable.

**Integration:** static lib (build/libqoi.a) or a single object (build/qoi_asm.o) used with the unmodified qoi.h header · none beyond libc (malloc, memset, free, fopen, fread, fwrite, fseek, ftell, fflush, ferror, fclose); building needs GNU binutils as · GNU as (binutils) with Intel-syntax support; any C compiler for the consumer; tested with gcc 13.3.0 on Ubuntu 24.04 · x86-64 Linux/System V only. Documented requirement is x86-64-v3 (Haswell or newer), but the file uses no AVX, AVX2, BMI or FMA instructions; the highest ISA extension it uses is SSE4.1 (pinsrb, pextrd, pmovsxbd)

**Vs siblings:** Pick qoi-asm over the reference QOI (qoi.h) when you are on x86-64 Linux and want the same symbols and bytes, only faster. Pick qoixx (C++), rapid-qoi or the qoi Rust crate when you need ARM or Windows support or a source-level library; none of those was measured against qoi-asm, so no ranking among them exists.

**Gotchas:**
- If any translation unit still defines QOI_IMPLEMENTATION, linking qoi_asm.o gives duplicate symbols, while linking libqoi.a silently keeps the C code because the archive member is never pulled in. The README's first snippet still shows #define QOI_IMPLEMENTATION.
- The ISA baseline is overstated: the README says x86-64-v3 and warns of SIGILL on older CPUs, but only SSE4.1 is actually needed. There is no CPUID check, so a CPU without SSE4.1 faults at the first SIMD instruction.
- Like qoi.h, qoi_decode can read a few bytes past size on a truncated stream; the port reproduces this exactly, so validate or pad untrusted input.
- The bench's 'cycles/op' are invariant-TSC ticks (about 2.07 GHz on the host), not core cycles; use the ratios or ns/op.

**Status:** Published 2026-09-26 as a single commit with 0 stars and no issues, produced by a multi-agent LLM workflow (the same author also publishes stb-image-opt and stb-image-write-opt). It is MIT-licensed, one roughly 1,000-line assembly file, and CI runs the differential, ASan/UBSan and benchmark-correctness suites on ubuntu-latest.

[repo](https://github.com/aplghl/qoi-asm) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aplghl/qoi-asm/HEAD/docs/BENCHMARKS.md)

##### QOIR  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Single-header C codec for a new lossless image format; encodes about 30x and decodes about 4.9x faster than libpng.

**Beats:** libpng (Debian Bullseye build); also libwebp lossless — Author-run and reproducible: on the qoiformat.org benchmark suite (December 2022 run, Intel i5-10210U, gcc 10.2.1, QOIR built -Wall -O3 without -march, single-threaded, 5 timed repetitions per image with allocation included), QOIR lossless encodes 168.90 and decodes 276.45 MPixels/s against Debian Bullseye's libpng through the simplified API at default zlib settings at 5.49 and 56.18 (30.8x and 4.9x) and libwebp lossless at 2.49 and 89.94, at ratio 0.2525 against 0.2423 and 0.1651. The benchmark harness does not compare decoded pixels, but a separate round_trip_tests.c checks pixel equality; the published run shows no encode or decode failures.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on its own full_benchmarks.txt rows 65, 70, 73 (168.90/276.45 MB/s vs libpng 5.49/56.18 and WebP 2.49/89.94; README 30x/4.9x confirmed). QOIR was built in test/benchmarks.c with -Wall -O3 only (adapters get -march=native). Ratio 0.2525 vs libpng 0.2423 and larger than libpng on 4 subsets. The 2026-07-07 fix ce7b583 only relaxes an over-strict length check. 134 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** QOIR was built without -march and decoded RGB as 4-byte RGBA against libpng's 3-byte RGB (handicapping QOIR); the bench harness skips the pixel check (a separate round_trip_tests.c does check). ZPNG beats QOIR on all three columns for textures_photo. The format is still experimental with no release listed and no fuzz target; issue #4 (valid tiny files rejected) was fixed in ce7b583 without affecting the numbers.

**How:** The image is cut into independent 64x64 tiles. Each tile is coded with QOI-style byte opcodes (colour-index hash, small RGB and luma deltas, runs), helped by a 64 KiB luma look-up table and SSE2 on x86-64, and the encoder keeps the smallest of four tile formats: raw literals, opcodes, or either one compressed with the bundled LZ4 block codec. There is no Huffman/deflate stage and no per-row filter search, which is where libpng's default zlib encode spends its time. Because tiles are independent, a caller can decode them on several threads into one pre-allocated buffer (the qoirview commit 913011d reports 2.56x on a 1165x859 image and 3.56x on 3600x2085, and a slowdown on a 160x120 one).

**Use it when:**
- Lossless 8-bit RGB/RGBA images that your own code both writes and reads (game or app asset pipelines, thumbnail and texture caches, screenshot or frame dumps) where encode and decode time matter more than PNG compatibility.
- Decode-heavy paths that still want a PNG-like ratio: 276 MPixels/s single-threaded decode at ratio 0.2525 against libpng's 56 MPixels/s at 0.2423 in the author's suite, and 582 against 77 MPixels/s on web screenshots.
- You need premultiplied-alpha output, decoding into an existing buffer, region (clip) decoding, or tile-parallel decoding of large images.
- You want no dependencies: one header with its own LZ4 and a permissive licence.

**Skip it when:**
- Files leave your system (browsers, editors, other tools): use PNG, WebP or JPEG XL. QOIR is marked 'experimental and subject to incompatible changes' and no release is listed on the repository page.
- Smallest files matter: lossless WebP (0.1651) and JPEG XL at effort 7 (0.1548) are much smaller than QOIR (0.2525), and libpng is about 4% smaller overall and smaller on the photo_tecnick, photo_wikipedia, textures_photo and pngimg subsets.
- Mostly photographic content: ZPNG (zstd plus PNG filters) makes 15-31% smaller files and decodes 1.3-1.5x faster on the photo subsets, and on textures_photo it beats QOIR on ratio, encode and decode at once (derived from page data).
- Images beyond 8-bit RGB/RGBA: no 16-bit, grayscale-only, palette or float/HDR support (the lossy mode only quantizes 8-bit channels).
- Parsing untrusted files in a security-sensitive service: the repository has no fuzz target, and a 2026 report (issue #4) showed the decoder's length checks were wrong for tiny files (it rejected valid ones).

**Integration:** header-only (single-file C library: #define QOIR_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit) · none (bundled LZ4; QOIR_CONFIG__USE_OFFICIAL_LZ4_LIBRARY switches to liblz4) · C99 compiler (uses stdbool.h/stdint.h); also compiles as C++; benchmarked with gcc 10.2.1; MSVC gets a memcpy-based little-endian peek/poke path · any; SSE2 fast paths on x86-64 (gcc/clang/MSVC) can be turned off with QOIR_CONFIG__DISABLE_SIMD; published numbers are x86-64 only

**Vs siblings:** Choose QOIR over QOI when you want about 11% smaller files (0.2525 vs 0.2823) and 1.4x faster decode plus metadata, premultiplied alpha and tiling, and over fpng/fpnge when decode speed matters more than PNG output (fpng decodes 148 MPixels/s and only its own PNGs; fpnge has no decoder). Choose ZPNG instead for smaller files on photos if a zstd dependency is acceptable, and stay with PNG (libspng, the Wuffs decoder, fpnge) whenever other software must read the files.

**Gotchas:**
- Decoding with default options yields RGBA_NONPREMUL even for RGB images; set qoir_decode_options.pixfmt or pass a pixbuf to get 3-byte RGB. (The benchmark used the default, so QOIR wrote 4 bytes per pixel where libpng wrote 3, which slightly handicaps QOIR.)
- The scratch structs are large (about 32 KiB for decode, about 37 KiB for encode); pass preallocated decbuf/encbuf to avoid a malloc per call (the benchmark reuses static ones), and do not put them on small thread stacks.
- Use a copy at or after commit ce7b583 (2026-07-07): earlier versions reject valid tiny images whose QPIX payload is under 8 bytes (issue #4, up to about 282 pixels).
- qoir_lz4_block_encode fails when dst_len is below the worst-case bound even if the output would fit; the default build also carries a 64 KiB luma table (QOIR_CONFIG__DISABLE_LARGE_LOOK_UP_TABLES removes it).

**Status:** Mostly dormant (140 commits, 134 stars; one bug fix on 2026-07-07 after a gap since 2023-03-19, and one 2022 suggestions issue still open without a reply), but Apache-2.0 and a single dependency-free header that is easy to vendor; the file format itself is still labelled experimental.

[repo](https://github.com/nigeltao/qoir) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nigeltao/qoir/HEAD/doc/full_benchmarks.txt)

##### qoixx  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Single-header C++20 QOI codec with an AVX2/NEON/SVE encoder, 1.4-1.8x faster than the reference qoi.h.

**Beats:** qoi.h (reference QOI implementation, phoboslab/qoi) — The README runs src/qoibench.cpp, which compiles qoi.h and qoixx into one binary with the same -std=c++2a -O3 -march=native flags and checks round trips with memcmp before timing (20 runs plus a warm-up). On the public QOI benchmark suite qoixx was 1.37-1.66x faster at decoding and 1.47-1.76x faster at encoding on seven CPUs, for example i9-10900 with g++ 11.1.0: 344 vs 207 Mpx/s decode and 304 vs 183 Mpx/s encode. The 'ms' and 'size kb' columns are per-image means, not suite totals (issue #10, wontfix). The numbers date from 2022, before the 2024 encoder and decoder speed-ups (PRs #19 and #25) and before the fix for a decoder bug when the first opcode is QOI_OP_RUN (PR #23). The harness's memcmp check passed, so the timed decodes were correct for those inputs.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on src/qoibench.cpp with Makefile -O3 -march=native (unchanged since February 2022), g++ version and CPU stated per machine; the numbers date from 2022. Baseline is qoi.h, not a listed incumbent (baseline_in_list false); an independent C++20 re-implementation of QOI, not a port, so kept beside phoboslab/qoi.

**Known shortcoming:** README numbers are from 2022 code, older than the 2024 speedups (PRs #19 and #25) and the decoder fix for a first-op QOI_OP_RUN (PR #23); the benchmark's memcmp verification passed on its inputs, so the timed decodes were correct and the tier stands. A decoder read overrun on truncated input was fixed only on 2026-09-29 (PR #32; the size counter included the 14-byte header). Likely bug from code reading (not run): an RGBA file decoded with channels=3 hashes without alpha, giving wrong INDEX pixels when alpha is not 255, a path untested by CI. The ms/kb columns are per-image means (issue #10).

**How:** The encoder processes 32 pixels per AVX2 iteration (or one NEON/SVE vector). It computes channel deltas against the shifted previous pixels in one pass, skips whole runs of identical pixels with a single test, and builds candidate DIFF and LUMA opcodes plus colour hashes for all lanes before a short serial emit step. The scalar paths avoid qoi.h's per-pixel branching: the hash is a single 64-bit multiply, and 3-byte copies are split into 2+1-byte memcpy calls. On x86 the decoder updates the colour-index hash incrementally from constexpr lookup tables (QOIXX_DECODE_WITH_TABLES), and on AArch64 it writes long runs with 8-pixel NEON stores.

**Use it when:**
- You already store or stream QOI and encoding is the bottleneck, for example screen capture, game frame dumps or webcam streams on x86-64 with AVX2 or on ARMv8 servers and phones
- C++20 code bases that want a dependency-free single header that writes into std::vector or unique_ptr buffers without a malloc/free C API
- AArch64 targets with SVE (for example AWS Graviton3), which get a dedicated SVE encoder that qoi.h lacks
- Batch conversion where output must stay readable by any QOI decoder: CI diffs its decodes against the reference qoiconv on the official test images

**Skip it when:**
- If compression ratio or format reach matters more than speed: QOI stores the benchmark suite at 28.2% of raw size with no effort levels, and few tools read it; siblings fpnge (PNG output) or QOIR (better ratio options) fit that case
- Decode-dominated workloads: the README says the decoder is scalar and 'with some input, original implementation is faster', and the MSVC-built decoder is slow (FAQ: use MinGW-w64)
- Toolchains older than C++20, builds with -fno-exceptions (errors are thrown as std::runtime_error/std::invalid_argument), or 32-bit ARM, where SIMD is disabled (issue #26 open)
- Untrusted input on any commit before 2026-09-29: until PR #32 the decoder's remaining-byte counter included the 14-byte header, so truncated files could read past the end of the input buffer

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library plus immintrin.h, arm_neon.h or arm_sve.h when SIMD is enabled; QOIXX_NO_SIMD removes them) · C++20 (concepts, <bit>, std::endian); CI builds with GCC and Clang on Ubuntu x86-64 and arm64, plus MSYS2 on Windows · x86-64 (AVX2 encoder when compiled with -mavx2 or -march=native, otherwise scalar), AArch64 (NEON, or SVE at any vector length from 128 to 2048 bits), any other target via the scalar paths; SIMD is chosen at compile time with no runtime dispatch

**Vs siblings:** Pick qoixx over the reference qoi.h (phoboslab/qoi) whenever you can compile C++20 and want the same files faster, especially encode on AVX2, NEON or SVE. Pick qoi-rust instead in Rust code (its M1 decode gain over qoi.h, about 1.5x, is similar). Pick fpnge or QOIR when compression ratio or PNG compatibility matters more than staying on QOI.

**Gotchas:**
- Likely bug (from reading the code, not run): decoding a 4-channel file with channels = 3 drops alpha before computing the colour-index hash, while the QOI spec hashes r*3+g*5+b*7+a*11. Images with any alpha other than 255 can then fetch the wrong colour on QOI_OP_INDEX. CI only decodes at the file's own channel count, so this path is untested. Decode at native channels and strip alpha yourself.
- The SIMD encoder runs only when both input and output containers are contiguous (vector, unique_ptr pair or pointer pair). A custom non-contiguous container silently falls back to the scalar encoder.
- Output bytes differ from qoi.h even though sizes match: a 1-pixel run is written as QOI_OP_INDEX of the previous pixel instead of QOI_OP_RUN. Both are valid and decode identically, but byte-for-byte comparisons against qoi.h output fail.
- Images are capped at 400,000,000 pixels, and width or height 0 throws, the same limits as qoi.h.

**Status:** Actively maintained by a single author (last commits 2026-09-29: buffer-overrun fix and CI update), MIT and small enough to vendor; use a commit from 2026-09-29 or later.

[repo](https://github.com/wx257osn2/qoixx) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wx257osn2/qoixx/HEAD/README.md)

##### stb-image-opt  `C`  `MIT OR Unlicense`  `active`  `Tier A`

Drop-in stb_image.h v2.30 fork with AVX2 JPEG kernels and leaner PNG decode; about 1.10x upstream, partly from flags and PGO.

**Beats:** upstream stb_image.h v2.30 (nothings/stb at 2c980bb), compiled the way consumers compile it (-O2) — On an Intel i7-14700F under WSL2 with clang 23.1.2, the fork built at -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 -ffp-contract=off with PGO decoded a 14-file, mostly small synthetic suite 1.101x faster (geomean) than upstream stb_image v2.30 at -O2 (0.986x HDR to 1.289x palette PNG; JPEG rows 1.139x, PNG rows 1.097x), and 1.090x at req_comp=4. Unchanged decoders gain too (GIF 1.21x, 1.35x at req_comp=4), so flags and PGO carry a large share; the same-flag source-only gains (PNG +8.6%, IDCT +7.7% and +13.7%) exist only as NOTES.md text.

**Known shortcoming:** The baseline is upstream stb_image, not libjpeg-turbo or libpng, and the flags are asymmetric (fork at -O3 plus PGO against upstream -O2): the PSD and HDR decoders are unchanged in the header diff yet still gain (geomean 1.060x, derived from page data), so part of the 1.101x geomean is flags and PGO; the source-only A/B numbers are NOTES.md prose with no CSV.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): the 1.101x geomean mixes source changes with -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 and PGO against upstream at -O2; unchanged decoders gain too (GIF 1.21x, 1.35x at req_comp=4), so flags and PGO carry a large share, and the same-flag source-only gains (PNG +8.6%, IDCT +7.7%/+13.7%) exist only as NOTES.md text. The 'held-out' PGO set is near-identical content (same plasma_512 and grad_640_480 images at other settings; static.gif is frame 0 of the timed anim.gif). PNG gains apply only when img_n == out_n (req_comp=4 can be slower: 0.992x, 0.937x). STBI_FORCE_AVX2 skips the CPUID check and crashes on CPUs without AVX2; the rejected AVX2 PNG unfilter (0.44x-0.99x) is still in the header. Kernel figures (1.63x, 1.68x) are against the fork's own SSE2 path, not end-to-end. One author, 18 commits all on 2026-09-28, 0 stars; unofficial fork.

**Independent measurement:** first-party harness

**How:** For JPEG it adds a 16-pixel AVX2 YCbCr-to-RGBA kernel and a two-block AVX2 integer IDCT (two 8x8 blocks, one per 128-bit lane, a lane-wise widening of stb's SSE2 IDCT), picked at runtime with CPUID plus XGETBV; the non-interleaved, interleaved and progressive finish loops pair adjacent or same-stride blocks to feed it. For PNG, 8-bit rows with img_n == out_n are unfiltered directly into the output buffer (no scratch row and copy), and the inflate LZ77 copy uses memset for dist 1 and memcpy chunks for dist >= 8 instead of a byte loop. A large part of the headline comes from building the fork at -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 with profile-guided optimization against upstream at -O2: the unchanged GIF decoder gains 1.21x at req_comp=0 and 1.35x at req_comp=4 (derived from up4.csv and fork4.csv).

**Use it when:**
- You already vendor stb_image.h and decode JPEG on x86-64 CPUs with AVX2, especially to RGBA (req_comp=4; JPEG rows geomean 1.128x) or progressive JPEG (1.19x row at req_comp=0).
- You need byte-identical output to upstream so existing goldens stay valid: the repo's differential harness compares about 12,300 decodes against the pristine upstream oracle on every dispatch path with clang, gcc and zig cc.
- You decode palette or 8-bit PNGs at their native channel count (req_comp=0), where the direct-to-output unfilter and chunked LZ77 copy apply (palette PNG row 1.29x, which also includes flags and PGO).
- You are willing to build the library yourself with -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 and PGO (scripts/build_opt.sh with PGO=1), which is the configuration that was measured.

**Skip it when:**
- Raw decode speed is the goal: the baseline is stb_image, and no source compares this fork with libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libspng or Wuffs, so the 10% says nothing about those decoders.
- You only swap the header and keep -O2, or use the prebuilt release tarballs: release.yml builds them with zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dtarget=<triple>, with no PGO and no -march=x86-64-v2, so the roughly 6% PGO share and the flag share are absent.
- Your build uses -march=x86-64-v3 or native: NOTES.md measured that flag slowing JPEG decode (2.53 vs 2.37 ns/px), and the recommended -march=x86-64-v2 itself needs SSE4.2-class CPUs.
- MSVC or non-x86 targets: the AVX2 path is compiled only for GCC or Clang on x86 (STBI_AVX2 guard), so MSVC and aarch64 builds get only the portable PNG changes.
- Untrusted input: outside the JPEG IDCT/color and PNG row code it runs upstream's v2.30 loaders unchanged, and the GHSL reports CVE-2023-45661..45667 (filed against v2.28, GIF and other loaders) are partly still open; the Debian tracker lists CVE-2023-45664 (GIF double free) as unfixed (search snippet only).

**Integration:** header-only (single-header drop-in), or static lib via scripts/build_opt.sh or build.zig · none beyond libc and libm; the AVX2 path includes immintrin.h and cpuid.h · Same C dialect as upstream stb_image (compiles as C and C++ per README); AVX2 path needs GCC or Clang target attributes; tested with clang 23.1.2, gcc 13.3 and zig 0.16 zig cc · x86-64 with AVX2 runtime dispatch and SSE2 or scalar fallback; aarch64 Linux and macOS and x86_64 Windows (MinGW) cross-compile without new SIMD

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over libspng, zune-png, ffpng or libjpeg-turbo only when you are tied to the stb_image API, a single-header build and upstream-identical output; those siblings are measured against libpng, image-png or libjpeg-turbo and none is compared with this fork, so benchmark them first if decode speed is what matters. Its encode-side counterpart from the same author is stb-image-write-opt.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'held-out' PGO set excludes only the measured file names: corpus/gen_corpus.py also emits the same plasma_512 and grad_640_480 images at other JPEG quality and subsampling settings plus RGBA, gray, BMP and TGA variants, and static.gif is frame 0 of the timed anim.gif, so the profile was trained on near-identical content (NOTES.md: in-sample +7% vs held-out +6.3%).
- The PNG gains apply only when img_n == out_n; asking for RGBA from RGB or 16-bit PNGs can be slower (req_comp=4: plasma_512.png 0.992x, basn0g16.png 0.937x).
- STBI_FORCE_AVX2 makes stbi__avx2_available() return 1 without a CPUID check, so a build with it crashes on CPUs without AVX2; keep it for testing only. The rejected AVX2 PNG unfilter is still in the header behind STBI_AVX2_PNG_FILTER and measured 0.44x-0.99x.
- Kernel figures (AVX2 YCbCr 1.63x, IDCT pair 1.68x in kernels.csv, rounded to 1.70x in the README) are against the fork's own SSE2 path built at -march=x86-64-v3, not end-to-end decode.

**Status:** Active but brand new: one author, 18 commits all on 2026-09-28, releases v1.0.0 to v1.3.0, 0 stars and no issues or PRs; MIT OR Unlicense like upstream, so the single header is easy to vendor, but it is an unofficial fork not endorsed by the stb author.

[repo](https://github.com/aplghl/stb-image-opt) · [benchmark](https://github.com/aplghl/stb-image-opt)

##### stb-image-write-opt  `C`  `MIT OR Unlicense`  `active`  `Tier A`

Byte-identical stb_image_write.h v1.16 fork with an SSE2 deflate match scan; PNG encode about 1.7-1.9x upstream -O2.
