**Beats:** upstream stb_image_write.h v1.16 (nothings/stb at 2c980bb), compiled the way consumers compile it (-O2) — On an Intel i7-14700F under WSL2 with clang 23.1.2, the fork at -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 -ffp-contract=off with held-out PGO encoded 17 synthetic rows 1.627x faster (geomean) than upstream stb_image_write v1.16 at -O2. The 9 PNG rows, the only ones that touch changed code, give 1.725x (1.07x on random data, up to 2.15x on gradients), the 8 JPEG, BMP, TGA and HDR rows give 1.524x from flags and PGO alone, and a separate consumer program linking the PGO library measured PNG 1.90x and JPEG 1.17x.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim overstated: the fork changes only the DEFLATE and PNG code, yet 8 of 17 rows (JPEG, BMP, TGA, HDR) with byte-identical source still gain a 1.524x geomean from -O3, -march and PGO against upstream's -O2; the PNG rows run 1.07-2.15x (geomean 1.725x), not 1.62-2.15x; the countm microbenchmark's about 3.3x is invalid (a flat 1.41 ns from L3 to L258 points to a hoisted call); the 3.4x deflate same-flag figure is on synthetic data. Baseline is upstream stb_image_write, not libpng.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): the 1.627x headline mixes source and flags; only the 9 PNG rows touch changed code (1.725x, 1.07x on random data to 2.15x on gradients), the JPEG/BMP/TGA/HDR rows (1.524x) come from flags and PGO alone, and the JPEG rows are probably inflated by the writer, a no-op sink callback and the timing loop being compiled in one -O3 PGO translation unit (1.80x there vs 1.17x in results/consumer.csv with a separately built library). The countm 3.3x is not evidence (inlinable kernel on constant static buffers, flat SSE2 time from 3- to 258-byte matches). The deflate kernel 3.4x is a valid same-flag comparison but on input compressing 82:1. The 'held-out' PGO set overlaps the measured corpus (grad_640_480 variants). BMP/TGA/HDR rows are layout-sensitive noise (0.948x-1.74x) yet stay in the geomean. One author, 2 commits on 2026-09-29, 0 stars; unofficial fork.

**Independent measurement:** first-party harness

**How:** The DEFLATE match-length scan (stbiw__zlib_countm), which the author profiled at about 30% of PNG encode time, compares 16 bytes per step with baseline SSE2 and finds the first mismatch with movemask plus count-trailing-zeros. Fixed-Huffman codes come from precomputed, already bit-reversed tables instead of a per-symbol bit-reverse loop, and length and distance codes are found by binary search instead of linear scans. Nothing else in the writer changes, so the JPEG, BMP, TGA and HDR gains in the headline come only from building at -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 with PGO against upstream at -O2 (docs/REJECTED.md: -march=x86-64-v3 alone takes plasma_512 JPEG from 5.47 to 4.06 ns/px).

**Use it when:**
- You vendor stb_image_write and write PNGs with its builtin compressor (screenshots, debug dumps, tools) and want faster encodes with unchanged files: PNG rows 1.62x-2.15x, and 1.90x in the downstream consumer test.
- Smooth or highly compressible images such as gradients, UI captures and flat regions, where long matches make the SSE2 scan pay off (gradient PNG rows 1.89x-2.15x against 1.07x on incompressible random data).
- You rely on byte-for-byte identical output with upstream, for golden-file tests or content hashes: the differential matrix runs about 9,600 checks, and a non-vacuous test confirms that corrupted output fails it.
- x86-64 builds with GCC or Clang, where the SSE2 kernel is on by default with no runtime dispatch.

**Skip it when:**
- You need fast or small PNGs in absolute terms: the fork still spends about 50-70 ns per pixel on plasma_512 PNG (results/fork.csv), and upstream says its PNGs are 20-50% larger than an optimizing encoder's; fpng, fpnge or a better compressor plugged in through STBIW_ZLIB_COMPRESS are the tools for that (none is compared here).
- You already define STBIW_ZLIB_COMPRESS: every source change is in the builtin compressor, so only compiler flags would differ.
- JPEG, BMP, TGA or HDR output: that code is byte-identical to upstream; the bench's 1.63x-2.04x JPEG rows dropped to 1.17x in the downstream consumer test, and compiling upstream with the same flags would give the same effect.
- MSVC or non-x86 targets: the SSE2 kernel needs __SSE2__ with GCC or Clang, so MSVC and aarch64 builds use the scalar loop and get only the table changes, which docs/REJECTED.md measured as roughly neutral overall.
- Prebuilt release tarballs on older x86 CPUs: build.zig hard-codes -march=x86-64-v2 for x86-64, so they need SSE4.2-class CPUs, and release.yml builds them without PGO.

**Integration:** header-only (single-header drop-in), or static lib via scripts/build_opt.sh or build.zig · none beyond libc and libm (emmintrin.h on x86-64) · Same C dialect as upstream stb_image_write (compiles as C and C++ per README); the SSE2 kernel needs GCC or Clang (__builtin_ctz); verified with clang 23.1.2, gcc 13.3 and zig cc · x86-64 with baseline SSE2 and no runtime dispatch; aarch64 and other targets use the scalar fallback; cross-compiles to aarch64-linux-musl, x86_64-windows-gnu and aarch64-macos

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you need stb_image_write's API and upstream-identical bytes; for PNG encode speed, fpnge (QOIR: 312.59 MPixels/s) and fpng are in another class from this fork's 16.78 MPixels/s on plasma_512 (results/fork.csv; different machines and images, so only indicative), at the cost of different output bytes. Pair it with stb-image-opt, the decode-side fork by the same author.

**Gotchas:**
- The 1.627x headline mixes source and flags, and the JPEG rows probably overstate real use: the bench compiles the writer, a no-op sink callback and the timing loop into one translation unit at -O3 with PGO, and the JPEG writer emits every byte through the s->func callback (stbiw__putc), which that setup can devirtualize or inline. JPEG rows reach 1.80x geomean there (derived from page data) but only 1.17x in results/consumer.csv, where the encoder is a separately built PGO library; no committed run isolates the cause.
- The countm ~3.3x (1.41 vs 4.6 ns/call) is not evidence: kernbench calls the inlinable kernel on constant static buffers with limit 2048, the SSE2 time is flat from a 3-byte to a 258-byte match, and the scalar 258-byte call (3.54 ns) beats its own 3-byte call. The deflate kernel 3.4x (0.43 vs 1.47 ns/byte) is a valid same-flag comparison, but on a synthetic input that compresses 82:1 (3192 bytes from 256 KiB), a best case for long matches.
- The 'held-out' PGO set is not fully disjoint: HELDOUT trains on corpus/grad_640_480.png and grad_640_480_gray.png, which are also measured (with other channel counts or formats), and docs/MEASUREMENT.md reports held-out +62.7% above in-sample +58.5%, so the PGO share is within run-to-run noise.
- BMP, TGA and HDR rows are plumbing-bound and layout-sensitive (the same build measured 1.19 and 1.76 ns/px for BMP), so their 0.948x-1.74x ratios are noise, yet they stay in the geomean.

**Status:** Active but new: one author, 2 commits on 2026-09-29, release v1.0.0, 0 stars and no issues or PRs; MIT OR Unlicense and a single header, so easy to vendor, but an unofficial fork not endorsed by the stb author.

[repo](https://github.com/aplghl/stb-image-write-opt) · [benchmark](https://github.com/aplghl/stb-image-write-opt)

##### Zpng  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Zstd-backed lossless RGB/RGBA image format that encodes about 23x and decodes 4.6x faster than libpng, with smaller files.

**Beats:** libpng — Nigel Tao's QOIR harness ran single-threaded on an Intel i5-10210U with gcc 10.2.1 (-O3 -march=native for the adapter), 5 repetitions per image, over the whole QOI benchmark suite. Zpng (the vendored zpng.cpp with the system libzstd at level 1) encoded 126.21 MPixels/s and decoded 256.32 MPixels/s, against 5.49 and 56.18 for Debian Bullseye's libpng at default settings (about 23x and 4.6x, derived from page data), at CmpRatio 0.2182 vs 0.2423. The WangXuan95 CLIC2021 shootout used a lightly modified catid build (PNM output and a level switch; g++ -static -O3, vendored zstd 1.3.4) against Pillow's PNG, with process startup included in the times.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on qoir full_benchmarks.txt row 76 (126.21/256.32 MB/s, ratio 0.2182: smaller than libpng on all subsets, WebP 0.1651 smaller still), with zstd level 1 from the Debian libzstd package. Last commit 2018-06-17 (unmaintained); the vendored zpng.cpp equals catid HEAD plus a noFilter flag. The benchmark covers the full QOI suite, not photographic images only.

**Known shortcoming:** Security bugs from code reading (not run): a 32-bit byteCount overflow lets a crafted 32768x32768 RGBA header plus an empty zstd frame cause heap out-of-bounds reads and writes, and the decoder ignores the ZSTD_decompress output size so truncated files decode silently; width and height are truncated to uint16, the input StrideBytes is ignored and 16-bit StrideBytes is wrong. The README '6% time, 66% size' claim is against stb_image_write with the disk write included, not libpng; the QOIR run is not smaller than libpng on icon_512 (0.0534 vs 0.0499) and links Debian's system libzstd rather than the vendored zstd 1.3.4; the WangXuan95 shootout used a modified build (retier-05 corrects the record).

**How:** Filtering is one pass per row: each byte is replaced by its difference from the same channel of the pixel to the left (PNG's Sub filter only, with no Up or Paeth filters and no per-row filter search). For 8-bit RGB and RGBA it then applies the reversible GB-RG colour transform from BCIF (Y=B, U=G-B, V=G-R on the residuals) and writes Y, U, V and alpha as separate planes. In the author's README experiments the plane split made output about 1.8% smaller and compression faster than interleaved data. The planar residual buffer then goes through one ZSTD_compress call at level 1 (zstd's fast match finder with Huffman and FSE entropy coding). libpng at its defaults instead tries every filter on each row and runs zlib deflate at the default level. Decoding is ZSTD_decompress followed by the inverse transform. There are no SIMD intrinsics; the loops rely on compiler auto-vectorization (its CMake Release flags are -O3 -march=native).

**Use it when:**
- Caching, storing or moving 8-bit RGB or RGBA frames between programs you control (capture tools, asset caches, dataset shards), where a private format is acceptable: 126 MPixels/s encode and 256 MPixels/s decode on one i5-10210U thread across the QOI suite.
- Photographs and photo textures, where it gives the smallest files among the fast codecs in the QOIR table: photo_kodak CmpRatio 0.4776 (libpng 0.5630, QOIR 0.5345, QOI 0.5829) and textures_photo 0.4156 (libpng 0.5977, QOIR 0.6052).
- Read-heavy pipelines: decoding (256 MPixels/s) runs about twice as fast as encoding and beats QOI (193.5) and libjxl's fast-lossless path (33.2 decode) in the same harness.
- Projects that already link zstd and want a lossless image codec of roughly 600 lines under BSD-3-Clause that they can vendor and adapt.

**Skip it when:**
- Interchange or long-term archives: .zpng is not PNG, no viewer or browser reads it, the header has no version field and is written in host byte order.
- Untrusted files: the decoder trusts the header and never checks that zstd filled the output (see gotchas). Treat it as unsafe on hostile input unless you add those checks.
- Images wider or taller than 65535 px: width and height are stored as uint16_t, and ZPNG_Compress truncates them with no error. The QOIR adapter adds the missing guard itself.
- 16-bit data: deltas are taken per byte, not per 16-bit sample, and the colour transform runs only on 8-bit RGB/RGBA. ZPNG_Decompress also reports StrideBytes as width x channels, half the real stride. The CLI loads with stbi_load, which converts 16-bit PNGs to 8-bit (issue #6, closed with no fix in the code).
- Flat graphics and icons, or when you need the smallest output: on QOIR's icon_512 set Zpng is larger than libpng (CmpRatio 0.0534 vs 0.0499), and on textures_pk it is larger than QOIR (0.5384 vs 0.4929). WebP lossless (0.1651) and slower JPEG XL settings are much smaller overall. Encoding small icons is also slower (icon_64: 80.8 MPixels/s).

**Integration:** source-drop (zpng.cpp + zpng.h), or the CMake zpnglib static library, which also compiles the vendored zstd · zstd (a copy of zstd 1.3.4 is vendored in zstd/; the QOIR harness links the system libzstd instead, so newer versions work); the CLI and test app also use stb_image and stb_image_write · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake 3.5; the API is extern "C", but zpng.cpp uses templates and must be compiled as C++ · Any (portable scalar C++, no intrinsics); the CMake Release flags hard-code -O3 -march=native on non-MSVC compilers, which ties binaries to the build machine's CPU; files are not portable between little- and big-endian hosts because the header is written as a raw struct

**Vs siblings:** Pick Zpng over QOI or QOIR when file size matters more than the last bit of speed: on the QOI suite its output is about 14% smaller than QOIR's (0.2182 vs 0.2525) and 23% smaller than QOI's (0.2823), at about 75% of QOIR's encode speed (126 vs 169 MPixels/s) and similar decode speed (256 vs 276). Pick fpng or fpnge when you need real PNG files. libjxl fast_lossless matches Zpng's size (0.2171) in a standard format but decodes about 7.7x slower (33.16 vs 256.32 MPixels/s).

**Gotchas:**
- Possible memory-safety bug on crafted input (found by reading the code; not run): ZPNG_Decompress computes byteCount = width x height x bytesPerPixel in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic with no overflow check. A header of 32768 x 32768 RGBA wraps the product to 0, and with an empty zstd frame UnpackAndUnfilter then reads and writes about 4 GiB past two zero-byte allocations. The decoder also ignores how many bytes ZSTD_decompress actually produced, and level-1 frames carry no checksum, so truncated or corrupted files decode silently to zero-filled pixels.
- ZPNG_Compress ignores the input StrideBytes and assumes tightly packed rows; padded or sub-image buffers come out scrambled with no error.
- Memory per call is about 2-3x the image: compression allocates a filtered copy plus a ZSTD_compressBound output buffer, and decompression allocates the packed buffer plus the output. Results come back in malloc'd buffers that you must release with ZPNG_Free.
- The README's 'less than 6% of the time of a PNG compressor and 66% of the size' compares against stb_image_write's stbi_write_png, not libpng (apps/zpng_app.cpp times the stbi_write_png call, which also writes the 41.9 MB file to disk), against an in-memory Zpng compress of one JPEG-derived photo. The independent QOIR numbers are the ones to rely on.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2018-06-17 (one PR, #4 from 2018, now closed; issue #5 on integer-type portability is still open), but BSD-3-Clause and about 600 lines, so it is easy to vendor; add header and decompressed-size checks before you feed it files you did not write.

[repo](https://github.com/catid/Zpng) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nigeltao/qoir/HEAD/doc/full_benchmarks.txt)

##### bc7e (Binomial BC7 encoder, ISPC)  `ISPC (C-callable object code)`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

ISPC SIMD BC7 encoder; independent tests show its profiles 3-10x faster than ispc_texcomp's like-named profiles at higher PSNR.

**Beats:** Intel ispc_texcomp (Fast ISPC Texture Compressor) — The README alone (first-party, no data) claims 2-3x over ispc_texcomp at equal quality and about 8x over its slow profile. Independent support comes from Aras Pranckevicius's 'Texture Compression in 2020' (December 2020). He ran 20 Unity textures on a 2018 MacBook Pro (Core i9 2.9 GHz, 6 cores/12 threads) built with Xcode 11.7 (Apple clang 11.0.3) and ISPC 1.14, up to AVX2, multi-threaded, in perceptual mode, scoring Luma-PSNR. Average Mpix/s and dB were: bc7e fast 30.97 at 46.18 vs ISPC fast 10.10 at 45.36 and ISPC basic 4.53 at 46.07; bc7e basic 20.65 at 46.75; bc7e slow 13.04 at 47.40 vs ISPC slow 1.29 at 46.28. That makes bc7e about 3.0x, 4.0x and 10.1x faster than ispc_texcomp's like-named fast, basic and slow profiles, at 0.7-1.1 dB higher PSNR (derived from page data, harmonic means over the 20 images).

**Known shortcoming:** Texture encoder (BC7) whose baseline ispc_texcomp is not a listed incumbent. README claims 2-3x at matched PSNR/SSIM and about 8x against the slow profile with no table, machine or harness; the independent aras-p blog is blocked (snippet directional only). Repo archived 2026-01-28; the encoder ships inside bc7enc_rdo (used by todds) and as a scalar C++ port in basis_universal.

**Known shortcoming:** Archived; the shipped bc7e.ispc has a SIMD-width-dependent all() early-out in estimate_partition_list (issue #2), fixed only in bc7enc_rdo (BC7E_NON_DETERMINISTIC 0), and open issue #3 reports alpha 254 in opaque areas. The example tool's clock() timing over OpenMP measures CPU time, not wall time. The independent ratios (retier-03) hold against upstream ispc_texcomp only: Traverse-Research/intel-tex-rs-2 PR #50 (2026-09-28) makes ispc_texcomp BC7 2.1-6.2x faster; ultrafast is slower than ispc_texcomp (0.88x).

**How:** Each SIMD lane encodes one block through ISPC's SPMD model; the build line targets SSE2, SSE4, AVX and AVX2 in one object. Partitions for modes 0/1/2/3/7 are ranked with a cheap per-subset error estimate (estimate_partition_list), and only the best 1-4 go on to full encoding. Endpoints come from least-squares fits refined over a profile-set number of passes, plus optional p-bit search and 'uber' selector perturbation. Precomputed optimal-endpoint tables handle single-colour subsets. The profiles turn whole modes, rotations and partition counts on or off, which is where most of the speed difference comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Offline or build-time BC7 baking on x86-64 with AVX2, where you want more PSNR per second than ispc_texcomp gives. In Aras's tests every bc7e profile from fast upwards beat every ispc_texcomp profile.
- High-quality BC7 at moderate speed: the slow profile averaged 13.0 Mpix/s at 47.40 dB Luma-PSNR, against ispc_texcomp slow at 1.29 Mpix/s and 46.28 dB on the same 12-thread machine.
- Pipelines that already batch blocks and run their own thread pool (bc7e expects 32-64 or more blocks per call).
- sRGB colour textures where its perceptual (scaled YCbCr) metric can let you drop to a faster profile.

**Skip it when:**
- Bit-exact reproducible output across machines or builds from this archived copy. Its estimate_partition_list early-out uses all() across SIMD lanes, so results depend on SIMD width and on which blocks share a gang (issue #2). The fixed version is richgel999/bc7enc_rdo's bc7e.ispc (BC7E_NON_DETERMINISTIC 0).
- Your toolchain cannot run the ISPC compiler, or you need the best speed on ARM. bc7e is tuned for wide AVX2 lanes: single-threaded, Aras found a 2019 Intel MacBook Pro 1.5x faster than an M1 (4-wide NEON) for ISPC compressors including bc7e. Use bc7e_scalar or bc7f in basis_universal instead.
- Real-time or runtime encoding: ultrafast is mode 6 only and was 0.88x the speed of ispc_texcomp ultrafast (harmonic mean, derived), though 2.2 dB better. bc7f claims to be faster still.
- Opaque textures that must decode to alpha exactly 255: open issue #3 reports scattered alpha 254 in fully opaque areas.
- You need maintenance: the repo was archived on 2026-01-28 and bugs are fixed only in bc7enc_rdo.

**Integration:** source-drop (bc7e.ispc compiled by ISPC to an object file plus a generated C/C++ header) · ISPC compiler at build time; the example tool also uses lodepng, bc7decomp (detex) and OpenMP · ISPC 1.8.2 or 1.10.0 (README: tested mostly with 'v1.82', bundled ispc.exe 1.10.0); Aras built with ISPC 1.14; example project for Visual Studio 2015-2019 · x86/x86-64 via the sse2/sse4/avx/avx2 multi-target build; ISPC NEON builds run on ARM (Aras ran it on Apple M1); tested on Windows, Linux and macOS per README

**Vs siblings:** Pick bc7e over bc7enc (bc7enc16): in the same independent run, bc7enc's best preset reached 3.8 Mpix/s at 45.48 dB, while bc7e basic reached 20.6 Mpix/s at 46.75 dB. Pick basis_universal's bc7f instead when you need portable scalar real-time BC7 and can accept lower PSNR, or bc7e_scalar there when ISPC is not available.

**Gotchas:**
- Forgetting bc7e_compress_block_init() gives all-zero BC7 blocks in release builds (only an assert in debug).
- Results depend on SIMD width in this archived copy (issue #2, closed 2021-01-08 with the fix landing only in bc7enc_rdo). The README also says to restrict targets to SSE and drop --opt=fast-math if you need identical output on Intel and AMD.
- In perceptual mode the opaque path skips mode 5 and alpha blocks skip mode 4/5 rotations. The archived copy also has no solid-colour shortcut, which bc7enc_rdo added (exact mode 5 encode).
- The bundled bc7enc example times encoding with clock() around an OpenMP loop. On Linux and macOS that is CPU time summed over all threads, not wall time, so its 'Total time' overstates elapsed time when threaded.

**Status:** Archived on 2026-01-28 (182 stars, Apache-2.0) and copyable, but the maintained bc7e.ispc with the determinism fix lives in richgel999/bc7enc_rdo, with C++ (bc7e_scalar) and successor (bc7f) versions in basis_universal.

[repo](https://github.com/BinomialLLC/bc7e) · [benchmark](https://github.com/aras-p/aras-p.hugo/blob/master/content/blog/2020/12-texcompr.md)

##### CharLS  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

C++17 JPEG-LS (ISO 14495-1) lossless/near-lossless codec; encodes about 10x faster than libwebp lossless, decodes slower.

**Beats:** WebP lossless via Pillow 10.1.0 (libwebp, quality=100, method 1 and 5), Pillow PNG plugin (zlib, not libpng) and Pillow JPEG 2000 plugin (OpenJPEG), all run in-process in Image-Compression-Benchmark; the CharLS README separately cites the original HP JPEG-LS code, JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000 — In WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark (CLIC2021, 585 RGB images, 4.1 GB, single thread, Intel i7-12700H, Windows 10), CharLS 2.4.2 via the pillow-jpls 1.3.2 wheel took 72.2 s to encode and 66.6 s to decode versus 720.2 s / 37.0 s for libwebp lossless m1 and 334.8 s / 33.7 s for Pillow's zlib PNG, so it wins on encode only. The times include Python Image.open/save and PNM file I/O per image, the wheel's compiler flags are unstated, and RunBenchmark.py ships with CHECK_DISTORTION = False, so lossless round-trips are not checked by default.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the independent Image-Compression-Benchmark (RunBenchmark.py, i7-12700H, Python wheels with unstated flags; pillow-jpls 1.3.2 bundles CharLS 2.4.2). Against Pillow WebP (libwebp): encode 10x faster (720.160 vs 72.237 s total), decode 1.8x slower, files 29% larger. JPEG-LS is a different format from WebP or PNG.

**Known shortcoming:** The measured pillow-jpls 1.3.2 (still the latest on PyPI) links CharLS 2.4.2, affected by GHSA-mqrg-gfc8-73ff (CVSS 5.3, pixel_stride wrap, out-of-bounds; fixed in 2.4.4); the harness RunBenchmark.py ships CHECK_DISTORTION = False so the lossless round trip is unchecked by default, and times include Python and PNM I/O. Unreleased main carries encoder and decoder speedups (#361: 4.4% on x86, 13.6% on ARM).

**How:** The algorithm itself is light: per-pixel median edge detector (MED) prediction, gradient-quantized context modeling with bias correction, adaptive Golomb-Rice coding of residuals and a run mode for flat regions. CharLS compiles specialized codecs per sample type through C++ templates and traits (lossless_traits for 8/16-bit pair/triplet/quad pixels in sample-interleaved mode), uses precomputed gradient-quantization LUTs and per-k Golomb decode LUTs for codes of 8 bits or less, a 64-bit bit cache read with big-endian unaligned loads plus memchr to skip ahead to the next 0xFF stuffing byte, and countl_zero for unary prefixes. There is no SIMD; unreleased main-branch PRs by cl445 add more (#361 skips sample reconstruction in the lossless encoder: 473 to 452 ms on Ryzen 9 9950X/GCC 14, 428 to 370 ms on Apple Silicon for a 7680x4320 12-bit image; #376 PGO-derived branch hints and cold-path outlining: decode 8.5% and encode 3.6% faster on x86-64 Clang 20 for one 7216x5412 8-bit image), none of which the catalogued 2.4.2 numbers include.

**Use it when:**
- You must read or write JPEG-LS: DICOM transfer syntaxes 1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.80/.81, remote sensing or archives that mandate an ISO standard lossless codec.
- Lossless encoding of 8-bit RGB or grayscale at high volume where encode time matters more than file size: about 10x faster encode than libwebp lossless (quality=100) and 4.6x faster than Pillow's zlib PNG on CLIC2021.
- 12- to 16-bit medical, scientific or camera-raw-like single-channel images, which PNG handles poorly and QOI-family codecs do not support.
- Near-lossless coding with a hard per-pixel error bound (NEAR parameter), which the PNG/QOI siblings cannot do.
- You want a mature, standards-conformant library with a stable C ABI, vcpkg/Conan packages and .NET, WebAssembly and Python adapters.

**Skip it when:**
- Decode-heavy workloads of 8-bit RGB: in the CLIC2021 run CharLS decoded about 1.8x slower than libwebp lossless m1 and about 2x slower than Pillow's zlib PNG decoder.
- When ratio is the goal: its CLIC2021 output was 29% larger than WebP lossless m1 and larger than JPEG XL -e1, which also encoded faster (43.0 s vs 72.2 s).
- When raw speed with any format is acceptable: QOI, QOIR, fNBLI and HALIC beat it on both encode and decode in the same table.
- Web delivery: browsers do not decode JPEG-LS.
- Files using JPEG-LS Part 2 extensions, encoded restart markers, subsampled scans or point transform: the README lists these as unsupported (restart markers decode only, with no recovery for corrupted streams).

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake, vcpkg, Conan; source-only, no binary releases) · none · main branch: C++17, CMake 3.22, GCC 9.1, Clang 7, MSVC 2019, Apple Clang 12; 2.x LTS branch: C++14 · Windows, Linux, macOS on x86, x64, arm, arm64, mips, s390x, ppc64le (big-endian fixed in 2.3.3); portable C++, no SIMD

**Vs siblings:** Pick CharLS over QOI, QOIR, fNBLI or HALIC when you need an ISO/ITU standard format (DICOM) or more than 8 bits per sample; pick fpng/fpnge or libjxl fast_lossless instead when you need browser-readable output, and OpenJPH when the format is HTJ2K rather than JPEG-LS.

**Gotchas:**
- Releases 2.3.0 through 2.4.3 have GHSA-mqrg-gfc8-73ff (CVSS 5.3): a crafted oversize-dimension LSE marker wraps pixel_stride and causes out-of-bounds access; fixed in 2.4.4, which caps width and height at 100000. pillow-jpls 1.3.2, still the latest wheel on PyPI and the one benchmarked, statically links vulnerable CharLS 2.4.2.
- main is the unreleased 3.0 with breaking API changes (charls.h split into charls.h/charls.hpp, legacy 1.x API removed, include_pc_parameters_jai no longer default); 2.4.4 is the latest tagged release.
- Hewlett Packard claims JPEG-LS patents, licensed free for conformant implementations; the README tells commercial users to check hpl.hp.com/loco.
- The fast specialized paths cover lossless 8-bit and 16-bit data (sample-interleaved pairs, triplets and quads); near-lossless and other bit depths go through the generic default_traits path.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-02; 2.4.4 security release in June 2026, 3.0 encoder speedups merged on main), BSD-3-Clause and copyable, with libFuzzer/AFL harness options in the build.

[repo](https://github.com/team-charls/charls) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark/HEAD/README.md)

##### etcpak  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

SIMD multithreaded ETC1/ETC2/EAC/BC encoder: 500-1400x faster than Etc2Comp/ETCPACK multithreaded, 9-21x single-thread scalar, at lower quality.

**Beats:** Etc2Comp (effort=0, error metric rgba) and ETCPACK 4.0.1 (reference ETC2 encoder in Arm Mali Texture Compression Tool 4.3.0), as measured in the QuickETC2 paper (ACM TOG 2020); the current README only cites the NVIDIA in-driver ETC2 decoder (42.5 Mpx/s) for decompression, and the 2016-2018 README (etcpak 0.5) timed PVRTexToolCLI 3.5, Mali etcpack 4.2, etc2comp and crunch (rg-etc1) 1.04. — The independent QuickETC2 paper (ACM TOG 39(6), 2020; Ryzen 7 3700X, Ubuntu 20.04, compiler and flags not stated) timed etcpak 0.7 on 55 RGB textures. ETC2 planar-only ran at 1931 Mpx/s with 16 threads and SIMD (28.9 Mpx/s single-threaded scalar) against Etc2Comp effort 0 at 3.8 (3.1) and single-threaded ETCPACK 4.0.1 at 1.4 Mpx/s, at 36.82 dB vs 37.89/38.09 dB PSNR. Today's etcpak (1.0 and later) ships the paper's QuickETC2 T/H-mode and early mode-decision code, whose row in the same table is 2577 Mpx/s (40.6 single-threaded scalar) at 37.17 dB. The README's own Ryzen 9 7950X numbers (for example ETC2 356 Mpx/s single-threaded) time no competitor.

**Known shortcoming:** Upgraded C to B on the peer-reviewed QuickETC2 paper (ACM TOG 39(6) 2020, Ryzen 7 3700X; PDF reached via raw.githubusercontent.com/nahjaeho/nahjaeho.github.io): ETC2 planar 1931 Mpx/s vs Etc2Comp 3.8 and ETCPACK 1.4, single-thread scalar 28.9 vs 3.1/1.4 (9.3x/20.6x derived). Planar-only ETC2 at about 1.1-1.3 dB lower PSNR; no compiler or flags. Baselines are texture-compression tools, not the category's image codecs.

**Known shortcoming:** The current ETC2 encoder is the merged QuickETC2 (release 1.0; thresholds 0.03/0.09/0.38 match the paper), so the paper's 2577 Mpx/s at 37.17 dB row fits today's code better than the 0.7 planar-only row. CLI only with no library target; -march=native with no runtime dispatch (issue #39 SIGILL); --disable-heuristics turns off the T and H modes; BC1 uses bounding-box endpoints without PCA; BC7 is the vendored bc7enc; multiple-of-4 dimensions are checked only by assert; ETCPACK code carries Ericsson all-rights-reserved snippets and the LICENSE has placeholders (#24); open quality issues #48 and #40.

**How:** The ETC1 path does no endpoint search. It averages the block's colour for both 2x4/4x2 sub-block splits, keeps the split with the lowest error, then picks the best intensity-modifier table and selectors with SSE4.1/AVX2/NEON error arithmetic. Solid blocks exit early. ETC2 adds the QuickETC2 scheme (Nah, ACM TOG 2020; shipped in etcpak 1.0 as 'heuristics'): a luma-range test sends very-low-contrast blocks straight to planar mode (thresholds 0.03/0.09/0.38 in ProcessRGB.cpp). Only high-contrast blocks go to a luma-ordered T/H-mode search. BC1 takes per-channel bounding-box min/max endpoints with an inset and assigns selectors by projecting the summed channel offsets, all in SSE/AVX/NEON registers. BC7 is a SIMD-rewritten copy of Rich Geldreich's bc7enc (AVX2/AVX-512 paths). Images are cut into 32-block-row slices on a thread pool.

**Use it when:**
- Development or iteration builds that have to re-encode many or very large textures (8K-16K atlases) to ETC1/ETC2 in seconds rather than hours
- Runtime or on-device texture encoding where a few ms per 4K texture matters more than about 1 dB of PSNR (Godot uses it for its in-engine ETC/BC compression)
- Producing ETC2 for OpenGL ES 3 / Android targets when Etc2Comp at effort 0 or ETCPACK is the current bottleneck
- Fast BC1/BC3/BC4/BC5 encoding on x86-64 or AArch64 when quality is checked by eye rather than by a PSNR target

**Skip it when:**
- Final shipping assets where quality matters: in the QuickETC2 paper the etcpak-derived ETC2 is 0.72-1.47 dB PSNR below Etc2Comp and ETCPACK, and the paper names etcpak's ETC1 logic as the cause. Open issues report artefacts on subtle blue/white shades (#48) and over-brightened output (#40)
- Colour gradients whose channels move in opposite directions (for example red to green) in BC1: endpoints are the bounding-box min/max corners, with no PCA or cluster fit, so the encoder cannot represent that axis (from reading ProcessDxtc.cpp)
- Needs it does not cover: ETC2 RGB with punch-through alpha (open issue #21), ASTC, KTX/KTX2 output, or input formats other than PNG
- Portable binaries: SIMD is chosen at compile time and CMake defaults to -march=native with no runtime dispatch, so a binary built on a new CPU can crash with an illegal instruction on an older one (issue #39, SSSE3 shuffle on an Athlon II)
- High-quality BC7: the BC7 encoder is bc7enc limited to modes 1/6 (RGB) and 5/6/7 (RGBA), and the README's BC7 speed (12.1 Mpx/s single-threaded on a 7950X) has no competitor timing

**Integration:** source-drop (the repo builds only a CLI executable; copy ProcessRGB/ProcessDxtc, Tables, Dither, Math, Vector, ForceInline and ProcessCommon, plus bc7enc.cpp for BC7) · Encoder files: none beyond the C++ standard library. CLI: libpng via pkg-config, and Tracy fetched from its master branch by CPM at configure time (network needed). BC7 decode uses the bundled bcdec.h (MIT) · CMake 3.29 and C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20; bc7enc.cpp includes <bit>); GCC/Clang/MSVC paths are present, but SIMD on MSVC depends on __SSE4_1__/__AVX2__ being defined (since July 2026 __AVX__ implies SSE4.1) · x86-64 (SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512 paths), AArch64 NEON (ARMv7 NEON fixed per issue #25), scalar fallback; SIMD level fixed at compile time

**Vs siblings:** Pick etcpak over Goofy (ETC1/DXT1 only) when you need full ETC2 (planar, T and H modes, EAC alpha), BC3-BC5 or mipmapped PVR/DDS output from one tool. Pick bc7enc or bc7e directly for BC7 quality control, and ICBC for higher-quality BC1. Basis Universal's etc1f only claims, with no numbers, to be faster than etcpak.

**Gotchas:**
- --disable-heuristics does more than turn off the mode shortcut: in ProcessRGB_ETC2 the T/H-mode search runs only inside the heuristics branch. Without it, ETC2 output is limited to ETC1, planar and solid blocks.
- Width and height must be multiples of 4. This is checked only by assert() in BlockData and Bitmap, so release builds do not reject other sizes. The CLI's PNG loader also ignores setjmp's return value, so a libpng error does not abort cleanly.
- Licence hygiene: LICENSE.txt is BSD-3 but keeps template placeholders ('<organization>', '<COPYRIGHT HOLDER>'; open issue #24). ProcessRGB.cpp holds T/H helper functions marked '(C) Ericsson AB 2005-2013. All Rights Reserved' from ETCPACK v2.74, which point to an Ericsson statement the file does not include.
- Channel order is easy to get wrong: ETC paths expect BGRA-ordered input while BC paths expect RGBA (Application.cpp sets bgr only for ETC codecs; issues #32 and #34 complain about the naming).

**Status:** Actively maintained by Tracy's author (release 2.1 in February 2026, last commit 2026-09-13), BSD-3 and vendored by Godot; its 11 open issues are mostly quality and API complaints with no maintainer replies.

[repo](https://github.com/wolfpld/etcpak) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nahjaeho/nahjaeho.github.io/master/papers/SA20/QUICKETC2_SA20.pdf)

##### OpenJPH (HTJ2K encoder and decoder)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

BSD-2 C++ HTJ2K (JPEG 2000 Part 15) codec; its lossless decode ran 6-16x faster than OpenJPEG's Part 1 decode.

**Beats:** OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000 Part 1) — dicom-codecs (a third-party, WIP DICOM wrapper; tests/main.cpp and tests/benchmark.cpp) was run on an Apple M1 Pro with an unnamed compiler: each codec encoded four raw images losslessly with its own encoder, then one warm-up and one timed decode. OpenJPH took 4.09/1.43/1.53/89.20 ms against OpenJPEG's 24.73/15.65/22.27/1447.63 ms (about 6x-16x, derived). OpenJPEG was decoding a Part 1 EBCOT stream while OpenJPH decoded its own HTJ2K stream, so the ratio measures format plus library together. OpenJPH ran its generic non-SIMD path on arm64, OpenJPEG was built single-threaded with -ffast-math, and OpenJPEG's own HTJ2K decoder was not timed.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the dicom-codecs shootout (README plus tests/main.cpp, MacBook Pro M1 Pro, compiler unstated, 1 iteration) against OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000 Part 1): decode 6.0x/10.9x/14.6x/16.2x faster (derived), both reversible lossless; Kakadu is faster and CharLS slower, lossy not benchmarked. HTJ2K and Part 1 are different codestreams, so the gap is mostly the format; decomposition levels and colour transform differ slightly and compressed sizes are not reported.

**How:** The HT block coder replaces JPEG 2000's bit-plane-by-bit-plane MQ arithmetic coding (EBCOT) with a single cleanup pass. That pass codes 2x2 quads through three byte streams: an adaptive run-length MEL coder, table-driven VLC codewords (table0.h/table1.h) and raw MagSgn bits, plus optional SigProp/MagRef refinement passes. Decoding is mostly table lookups and bit extraction instead of one context-modelled binary decision per bit. The wavelet and colour transforms work line by line, which keeps memory small, and on x86-64 the block coder and transforms dispatch at runtime to SSE/SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512 kernels. There are also VSX (POWER8/9) and WebAssembly SIMD paths.

**Use it when:**
- Lossless storage of medical images under the DICOM HTJ2K transfer syntaxes (1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.201/202/203), where you control the encoder and decode latency matters (1.4-1.5 ms per 512x512 12/16-bit slice on an M1 Pro in the measured run).
- You need an open-source (BSD-2-Clause) HTJ2K encoder as well as a decoder, and Kakadu's licence is not an option.
- Streaming or low-memory pipelines that can feed or consume one image row at a time through exchange()/pull().
- Decoding in browsers or Node.js through the provided WebAssembly SIMD build.
- OpenEXR HTJ2K compression, which builds on OpenJPH (it appears as HTJ2K_32/HTJ2K_256 in the catalogued meshoptimizer harness, and issue #273 comes from an OpenEXR 3.4.11 user).

**Skip it when:**
- Existing JPEG 2000 Part 1 archives or third-party .jp2/.j2k files: OpenJPH implements only the HT block coder. Use OpenJPEG or Grok, or transcode first.
- Raw speed above all: in the same dicom-codecs run, Kakadu's HTJ2K decode was 2.4x to 3.6x faster (derived) than OpenJPH (for example 29.36 vs 89.20 ms on the 3064x4664 mammogram).
- Multi-core decoding of one large image: OpenJPH has no internal threading (no thread options in the API or in ojph_compress/ojph_expand), while OpenJPEG, Grok and Kakadu can parallelise across code blocks. The benchmark ran every codec single-threaded and compiled OpenJPEG's threading out.
- ARM targets that need SIMD: the CMake ARM section is empty and src/core/coding has no NEON kernels, so aarch64 (including Apple Silicon) runs the generic C++ path. Open issue #273 also reports a SIGSEGV in the scalar encoder's mem_elastic_allocator on arm64.
- Rate-controlled lossy encoding to a byte or bitrate target: docs/status.md says only quantisation-step lossy is implemented, with no rate control.

**Integration:** static or shared lib (CMake; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults to ON) · none for the library; libtiff for TIFF I/O in the command-line tools (OJPH_ENABLE_TIFF_SUPPORT defaults to ON, can be turned off); emscripten for the wasm build · CMake 3.12; C++14 by default (the CMake comment says C++11 suffices for the library, C++14 is for gtest); C11 for aligned_alloc · x86-64 (runtime dispatch over SSE through AVX-512), ppc64le (VSX kernels, POWER8+), WebAssembly SIMD, aarch64 and other targets generic C++ only; little- and big-endian handled

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over CharLS when you want a wavelet codec with resolution scalability and faster lossless decode: CharLS decoded 1.8-2.4x slower in the same run, although CharLS reads standard JPEG-LS data that OpenJPH cannot. Pick Grok or OpenJPEG instead when you must read Part 1 JPEG 2000 files or want multi-threaded decoding of large images.

**Gotchas:**
- Decoded line_buf samples are not clamped to the component bit depth; callers must clamp them, as the dicom-codecs wrapper does (OpenJPH issue #35). For colour without a colour transform, set_planar(true) takes a faster path (issue #34).
- Release 0.31.0 broke API and ABI compatibility, so pin a version. Issues #303 and #304 report a broken openjph-config-version.cmake in 0.30.0 and unusual shared-library names.
- Strict-aliasing type punning in the block decoders made GCC 15/16 (MinGW, -O2/-O3) produce silently wrong multipass irreversible decodes (issue #279, fixed in 0.30.0). Avoid older releases with recent GCC. The open crash issues are #273 (arm64 scalar encoder) and #374 (segfault with very small qstep values).
- '.raw' files are read as little-endian, unlike Kakadu and OpenJPEG ('.rawl'), and docs/usage_examples.md says this convention is planned to change.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-01, release 0.32.0, 296 stars, 91 forks, 31 open issues, packaged in several distributions per repology) under BSD-2-Clause. It is copyable, but the measured numbers come from a December 2023 snapshot (pinned commit 5aab43f) in a third-party harness that is itself marked WIP and has been dormant since 2023-12-14.

[repo](https://github.com/aous72/OpenJPH) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dicom-codecs/dicom-codecs)

##### PngEncoder (Java)  `Java`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Pure-Java PNG encoder that beats javax.imageio's PNG writer by compressing image segments in parallel on a thread pool.

**Beats:** javax.imageio PNG writer (ImageIO, JDK built-in encoder) — First-party JMH (1 fork, one 5 s measurement iteration, one benchmark thread, CPU and JDK not stated, '8 logical cores'): PngEncoder at level 9, unfiltered, compressing on an 8-thread pool encoded 5.1x to 7.1x more images per second than single-threaded ImageIO.write with defaults (random 1024x1024 ARGB, a 2121x350 logo, a 4900x6000 photo). An independent JMH suite in manticore-projects/FPNG-Java (JDK 21.0.1 GraalVM CE, -XX:+UseSerialGC, 10 iterations, CPU not stated) ran pngencoder 0.14.0 with multithreading disabled: at level 2 it took 0.70 to 0.88 of ImageIO's time (1.13x to 1.44x faster; 1120 vs 1270 ms on the same 4900x6000 photo) and at level 1 it was 2.26x to 3.53x faster (derived from page data), with output sizes not shown in the README.

**Known shortcoming:** The gain is multithreading (a pool of availableProcessors threads) against single-threaded ImageIO, with no CPU or JDK stated and one 5 s JMH iteration. PngEncoder writes rows unfiltered while ImageIO picks a filter per row and deflates at level 9 on JDK 8 (4 on JDK 9+), so compressed sizes differ and are not recorded; the ImageIO side keeps its default temp-file cache.

**Known shortcoming:** The random 1024x1024 case is incompressible noise, so ImageIO's five-filter trial there is pure overhead. Code bugs not behind the numbers: the toStream and toFile return values omit the sRGB, gAMA, cHRM, pHYs, iCCP, PLTE and tRNS bytes; the test helper assertThatPixelIs derives alphaExpected from the actual value; getProfileName's UTF-16 branch reads data[endIdx] twice. Multithreaded peak memory is about 0.75x the raw scanlines (about 90 MB at 4900x6000). Retier-29 raises the tier to B on the FPNG-Java measurement.

**Independent measurement:** Independent JMH run in manticore-projects/FPNG-Java's README (JDK 21.0.1 GraalVM, SerialGC, CPU unstated): pngencoder 0.14.0 single-threaded at level 2 encodes the 4900x6000 looklet image in 1120 ms against javax.imageio's 1270 ms (1.13x), 1.29x, 1.44x and 1.36x on the other cases, and 2.26-3.53x at level 1 (derived from page data).

**How:** The speedup is mostly parallel DEFLATE: scanlines are cut into segments of at least 128 KiB (raw size / (9 x availableProcessors)), each segment is compressed by a thread-local raw java.util.zip.Deflater with SYNC_FLUSH on a shared fixed pool of availableProcessors daemon threads, and the byte-aligned outputs are concatenated with a combined Adler-32, in the style of pigz. Each segment starts with an empty dictionary, which costs about 2% in size. By default it also skips PNG row filtering (filter type 0 on every row), whereas ImageIO tries all five filters per row; scanlines are pulled straight from the raster's int/byte buffer for the common BufferedImage types, and Deflater objects are reused per thread.

**Use it when:**
- A JVM service or batch job that writes large PNGs (multi-megapixel photos, renders, screenshots) on a machine with several idle cores and no JNI allowed.
- Latency of a single large encode matters more than total CPU spent, e.g. one request thread producing one big image while other cores are free.
- You want a dependency-free, Java 8 compatible ImageIO replacement with a tunable compression level (level 1 trades about 2.5x larger files for about 2.3x more speed per the README table).
- Images known to have at most 256 colors, where withTryIndexedEncoding(true) plus withPredictorEncoding(true) gives smaller files than ImageIO (at extra time).

**Skip it when:**
- Servers already encoding many images concurrently: the pool is one static fixed pool of availableProcessors threads shared by all callers, so the parallel gain mostly disappears (the project's own 8-thread JMH runner commit is titled 'ImageIO gains more :(' and publishes no numbers).
- Single-core or CPU-limited containers: the README says the speedup will not be significant there, and an independent single-threaded JMH run (FPNG-Java suite, JDK 21) measured only 1.13x to 1.44x over ImageIO even at compression level 2.
- Small images: when the raw scanline data is at most one segment (128 KiB, about 181x181 RGBA, derived from code) it always encodes on the calling thread with a plain Deflater.
- When smallest output matters at default settings: unfiltered rows compress worse than ImageIO's adaptive filtering on photographic content, so you must enable predictor encoding and give back much of the speed.
- When you need much higher throughput and JNI is acceptable: native fpng (SSE2) and fpnge (AVX2) through the FPNG-Java wrapper took about 4x to 20x less time than PngEncoder at level 2 in that same JDK 21 suite (derived from page data).

**Integration:** module (Maven Central jar, com.pngencoder:pngencoder) · none (JDK java.awt and java.util.zip only; JUnit, Hamcrest and JMH are test-scope) · Java 8 (maven.compiler.source/target 8); no module-info (issue #59 open; PR #124 for Automatic-Module-Name is unmerged) · any JVM with java.desktop/AWT image classes

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you must stay pure Java on the JVM; mtpng and pngenc use the same parallel-deflate idea natively (Rust with a C API, and C), and fpng/fpnge are far faster but need native code and give larger files on big photos.

**Gotchas:**
- Default output is unfiltered and split into independent deflate segments, so files are not byte-identical to ImageIO and are typically somewhat larger; the 'about the same size as ImageIO' claim was never measured by the benchmark, and ImageIO itself uses deflate level 9 on JDK 8 but level 4 on JDK 9+.
- Peak transient memory in multithreaded mode is roughly 0.75x the raw scanline size on top of the image: up to 3 x availableProcessors queued segments, each holding two pool buffers of 1.125x the segment size (derived from PngEncoderDeflaterOutputStream and PngEncoderDeflaterBufferPool). That is about 90 MB for a 4900x6000 RGBA image.
- toStream()/toFile() return a byte count that omits the sRGB, gAMA, cHRM, pHYs, iCCP, PLTE and tRNS chunks, because PngEncoderLogic.encode writes those to the raw stream instead of its counting wrapper; do not use the return value as the file size when those chunks are present.
- The test helper PngEncoderTestUtil.assertThatPixelIs computes alphaExpected from the actual pixel, so round-trip tests accept any pixel whose decoded alpha is 0; an earlier indexed-encoding corruption bug (issue #34) was fixed in 2022.

**Status:** Active but in maintenance mode (last commit 2025-11-25, release 0.16.0 of 2025-05-19, later commits are dependency bumps); MIT licensed, Java 8, no dependencies and small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/pngencoder/pngencoder) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pngencoder/pngencoder/HEAD/README.md)

#### rasterizers-2d

##### tiny-skia  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Rust port of Skia's CPU raster pipeline; about 1.7-2.3x faster than cairo on x86 overall, slower on solid rect fills.

**Beats:** Cairo (and raqote); slower than Skia — These are the project's own nightly cargo bench numbers. The x86 run (July 2021) used an AMD 3700X on Gentoo with tiny-skia built for SSE2 and for AVX2 (haswell), Skia built with clang and a forced raster-pipeline blitter, and cairo 1.16.0 from the system package (gcc -march=native). The ARM run (Aug 2022) used an Apple M1. Recounted from the gh-pages data, AVX2 beat cairo in 37 of 46 tests (geometric mean 2.24x). Dropping two unfair tests leaves 36 of 44 at 2.32x: 'Fill All' compares tiny-skia's overwrite (Pixmap::fill) with cairo's alpha-blended paint(), and 'Destination' is a no-op. On M1 the figure is 41 of 44 at 2.69x, but cairo's M1 times are 4.9-8.3x worse than its own 3700X times on basic fills while Skia's are unchanged, which points to an M1 cairo/pixman build without SIMD fast paths (the build is not documented).

**Known shortcoming:** Rust library (language-filter mismatch; C++ use via tiny-skia-cpp port or FFI). Tier A on its benches/ harness with stated compilers, flags and CPUs (AMD 3700X, Apple M1; gh-pages x86_64.html 2021 and arm.html 2022): beats Cairo in 41 of 49 x86 AVX2 tests (geomean 2.27x) and 46 of 49 ARM tests (2.7x), derived from page data; Cairo wins solid rectangle fills and nearest-neighbour patterns. Slower than Skia throughout; the Cairo baseline is a system gcc -march=native build, so a strict reading caps the Cairo comparison at B.

**Known shortcoming:** Harness flaws (retier-16 corrects the claim): the Fill All test compares tiny-skia's Pixmap::fill overwrite with cairo's paint() alpha blend and Skia's draw_color blend, so its 5.1x x86 and 62x ARM wins are invalid; the Destination operator is a no-op; the bicubic row compares cairo Filter::Best with tiny-skia bicubic. Recount against cairo on x86: 36 of 44 valid tests at a 2.32x geometric mean with AVX2, 34 of 44 at 1.71x on the default SSE2 build. The M1 cairo build appears to lack NEON (its basic fills are 4.9-8.3x slower than on the 3700X while Skia is unchanged; undocumented). Skia was handicapped with SK_FORCE_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLITTER, and the 2021 benches README says Skia v85 while the build steps check out m90.

**How:** It ports SkRasterPipeline: each draw is compiled into a list of stage function pointers (load, shade, blend, store) that run over 8 or 16 pixels at a time with no branching inside stages. If every stage has a low-precision version, it runs the u16x16 'lowp' pipeline; otherwise it falls back to the f32 'highp' pipeline. On x86 the lowp path is scalar u16x16 code that LLVM auto-vectorises, with SSE2 by default and AVX2 only with -Ctarget-cpu=haswell; AArch64 uses explicit NEON. Coverage comes from Skia's scanline rasteriser, including dedicated anti-aliased hairline code for thin strokes, which is where it beats cairo's general stroker most (4.4x on AA hairlines).

**Use it when:**
- Pure-Rust CPU rendering of SVG-like content (paths, gradients, patterns, blend modes) without a C/C++ toolchain. It is the renderer behind resvg and has about 490 reverse dependencies on crates.io (iced_tiny_skia, typst-render, i-slint-core, cosmic-text among them).
- Work heavy in non-separable or exotic blend modes, bilinear or bicubic patterns, AA clipping or hairlines. On the 3700X AVX2 run it was faster than cairo on Screen (9.1x), bilinear patterns (3.9x), AA hairlines (4.4x), spirals (2.0x), AA clip (1.65x) and linear gradients (1.55x) (derived from page data).
- Small binaries and fast builds: the README cites about 14 KLOC, about 200 KiB added to the binary and builds in under 5 s, against multi-MiB Skia builds that need clang and gn.
- no_std or WebAssembly targets: the crate builds without std (no-std-float feature) and has SIMD128 and relaxed-SIMD code paths for wasm.

**Skip it when:**
- UI-style drawing dominated by solid rect fills and plain source-over blending. In tiny-skia's own x86 data cairo was 2.5-2.7x faster on Rect and Rect AA, 1.7x on Source Over, 3.2x on Plus and 2.6x on nearest-neighbour patterns (derived from page data); the default SSE2 build loses by more (Rect 0.31x).
- When you need the fastest CPU renderer. tiny-skia is slower than Skia in 41 of 45 x86 AVX2 tests (geometric mean 0.68x) and 41 of 45 M1 tests (0.51x), and that Skia was built with SK_FORCE_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLITTER, so stock Skia may be faster still. Blend2D was faster in 870 of 870 thesis cells (about 7.5x), and Vello CPU is faster in most cells (derived from page data).
- Text, GPU rendering, PDF, non-RGBA8888 pixel formats, conic segments or path effects beyond dashing. All are out of scope per the README, which also calls the project 'more of a research project', not a Skia replacement.
- C or C++ code bases: there is no C API in the repository. The catalogued tiny-skia-cpp port claims up to 1.9x faster than the Rust original.
- Performance-sensitive ARM use: issue 55 (open since 2022) reports 2-4x slower than Skia on M1, with rect fills up to 6x slower and gradients 2-3x slower.

**Integration:** crate · arrayvec, bytemuck, cfg-if, log, tiny-skia-path; png optional (default feature png-format) · Rust stable (README says 'MSRV: stable'; no rust-version in Cargo.toml; edition 2021). Benchmarks need nightly. · any Rust target; SIMD on x86-64 (SSE2 by default, AVX2 only at compile time with -Ctarget-cpu=haswell, no runtime dispatch), AArch64 NEON, wasm32 SIMD128/relaxed SIMD; scalar elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over raqote, the other pure-Rust option, almost always: tiny-skia was faster in 40 of 41 comparable x86 tests (geometric mean about 5.8x, derived from page data) and has proper AA hairlines. Pick Vello CPU or Blend2D when speed matters more than a small, stable, dependency-light pure-Rust crate.

**Gotchas:**
- There is no runtime CPU detection, so the headline AVX2 numbers need a non-portable -Ctarget-cpu=haswell build. A default x86-64 build matches the SSE2 column: faster than cairo in 34 of 44 comparable tests, geometric mean 1.71x, against 2.32x for AVX2 (derived from page data).
- There is no global alpha (only Pattern has opacity), clipping goes through a full alpha Mask (README: Skia's method is 'way faster'; issue 10 on faster rectangular clips is open since 2020), and Pixmap has no stride (issue 168).
- Open panic and assertion reports: issue 100 (non-anti-aliased hairline stroke of a full-width rectangle), 51 (ClipMask debug_assert) and 167 (assertion in path.rs). Recent rendering bugs: 189 (hairline curve just outside the canvas is offset) and 179 (rounded-rect corner artefact at small sizes).
- Stroke cost jumps once a stroke stops being a hairline: issue 158 reports width 2.0 as 'considerably slower' than width 1.0, because thin strokes take the hairline fast path.

**Status:** Maintained but quiet under Linebender: last release 0.12.0 (2026-02-02), and commits since September 2024 are features and maintenance, not performance work; the published benchmarks date from 2021/2022. BSD-3-Clause, about 51.7M crates.io downloads, easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/linebender/tiny-skia) · [benchmark](https://github.com/linebender/tiny-skia/tree/main/benches)

##### Blend2D  `C++`  `Zlib`  `active`  `Tier B`

Zlib-licensed C/C++ CPU 2D vector renderer with JIT-compiled pipelines; about 4x Skia's and 7x Cairo's raster throughput.

**Beats:** Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also AGG, JUCE, Qt6, CoreGraphics — Laurenz Stampfl's ETH Zurich master's thesis (Vello CPU author, advised by Raph Levien) ran Blend2D 0.12.0, Skia (vcpkg unofficial-skia, version unstated) and Cairo 1.18.4 in Blend2D's own bl_bench harness on an Apple M1 Pro. Rendering 1000 unaligned 256x256 solid rectangles took 10.8 ms for Blend2D single-threaded, 50.3 ms for Skia and 21.9 ms for Cairo (about 4.7x and 2.0x). Across the published result JSON it was faster than Skia in 1032 of 1044 cells and Cairo in 863 of 870 (derived from page data). The compiler and the Skia/Cairo build flags are not stated, and Blend2D used its CMake release flags (-O2).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the independent ETH master thesis (LaurenzV/master-thesis main.pdf, Fig. 40: 10.8/50.3/21.9 ms, Apple M1 Pro, Blend2D 0.12.0) and its vello_chart data (data/arm/2025-09-24.json); compiler and Skia/Cairo build flags are unstated, so not A. The thesis author is the Vello CPU author, so the comparison is independent of Blend2D but first-party for Vello. Blend2D is also a listed baseline of this category; it is kept because it beats the other incumbents (Skia, Cairo).

**Known shortcoming:** The bl_bench harness (LaurenzV/blend2d-apps) is fair (same RNG sequence, anti-aliasing on, Blend2D timed including flush SYNC, best of 10), but the measured version is 0.12.0 and the API was renamed to snake_case by 0.21.3; no GitHub releases or tags. Blend2D loses to Vello CPU on tiny curved paths (up to 2.9x) and to Cairo on StrokeRectA Solid (1.35x on M1, 3.0x on i9, derived from page data); the 8-thread mode is slower than single-threaded in 24 of 174 8x8 cells; open issues #252, #255, #256, #265; JIT only on x86 and AArch64.

**How:** Fill and composition pipelines are generated at runtime with AsmJit, so each combination of pixel format, composition operator, fill type and fetch type gets specialised SIMD machine code for the host CPU. The analytic rasterizer is AGG-derived but renders strictly top to bottom so it can work in bands. It uses a dense cell buffer plus a per-scanline bit vector in which one bit covers N cells, which lets the compositor skip empty pixels in large steps. The thesis also points to fixed-point math where possible and a dedicated filler for unaligned rectangles. Multi-threaded mode queues commands and gives each worker horizontal bands, with the calling thread acting as one of the workers.

**Use it when:**
- Server-side or headless CPU rendering in C or C++ (charts, maps, thumbnails, PDF-to-image style rasterisation) where Skia's or Cairo's raster backend is the bottleneck. In the thesis data it was faster than Skia in 1032 of 1044 test cells (geometric mean about 4.1x) and faster than Cairo in 863 of 870 (about 7.2x) on an Apple M1 Pro (derived from page data).
- Large shapes with gradient or pattern paints where you can spare cores. With 8 threads the geometric-mean speedup over its own single-threaded mode at 256x256 was 3.95x on the M1 Pro and 4.65x on an i9-14900K (derived from page data).
- Replacing AGG, JUCE's software renderer or tiny-skia in a CPU-only stack. Single-threaded it was faster than AGG in 513 of 522 cells (about 3.3x), JUCE 8.0.8 in 838 of 870 (about 2.4x) and tiny-skia in 870 of 870 (about 7.5x) on the same M1 Pro run (derived from page data).
- x86-64 or AArch64 targets where runtime code generation is allowed, so the JIT pipelines that produced these numbers are actually used.

**Skip it when:**
- You need GPU rendering or GPU compositing for an interactive UI. Blend2D rasterises every frame on the CPU, and open issue #264 asks exactly this question with no answer yet. Look at Skia's GPU backends, ThorVG or vkvg.
- Mostly tiny, curve-heavy paths. At 8x8-32x32 on the Fish, Butterfly and Dragon shapes, Vello CPU single-threaded was up to 2.9x faster in the 2026-06-08 M1 Pro run, and Skia beat it by up to 1.13x on 8x8 Butterfly and Dragon (derived from page data).
- Workloads dominated by large axis-aligned solid rectangle strokes. Cairo was faster on StrokeRectA Solid at 32x32-256x256, by up to 1.35x on the M1 Pro and 3.0x on the i9-14900K (derived from page data).
- Targets without the JIT (32-bit ARM, RISC-V and other non-x86/AArch64 targets, BLEND2D_NO_JIT builds, sandboxes that forbid executable memory). These fall back to the reference pipelines, and none of the published numbers covers that configuration.
- Projects that need PDF, SVG or print output surfaces, SVG/Lottie parsing, or a frozen API. The source tree contains only the raster (CPU image) rendering context, and the library is still pre-1.0 (0.21.3) with recent renames.

**Integration:** shared lib by default, static lib with BLEND2D_STATIC=ON (CMake) · AsmJit, cloned into 3rdparty/asmjit and embedded (required unless BLEND2D_NO_JIT=ON); nothing else for the library. The shared build avoids linking the C++ standard library by default (BLEND2D_NO_STDCXX). Qt and the comparison libraries are needed only for demos and bl_bench backends. · C++20 compiler (cxx_std_20 is a PUBLIC compile feature on the CMake target), CMake 3.24; the C API is usable from C (the repo builds .c samples) · x86 and x86-64 (runtime dispatch from SSE2 to AVX2/AVX-512 plus JIT), AArch64 (JIT plus ASIMD), AArch32 (ASIMD, no JIT); other CPUs use the reference pipelines; Windows, Linux and macOS (Windows threads or POSIX threads)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Blend2D over Vello CPU, AGG, JUCE, tiny-skia or raqote when you want the fastest single-threaded CPU rasteriser in C or C++. In the same harness it beat all of them in most cells, and Vello CPU wins mainly on tiny curved shapes and in some 4-8 thread configurations. Pick ThorVG instead if you need SVG or Lottie loading, or Vello CPU if you want a Rust-native library.

**Gotchas:**
- The API was renamed between the measured version and HEAD. The thesis harness (Blend2D 0.12.0) calls setCompOp, threadCount and BLRuntime::queryBuildInfo, while 0.21.3 headers use snake_case (set_comp_op, thread_count, bl_context_* C functions). The GitHub repo publishes no releases or tags, and the vcpkg port lags (issue #249 asks for 0.21.2), so pin a commit.
- There are no exceptions (built with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti). Errors come back as BLResult, and convenience constructors such as BLContext(BLImage&) swallow errors, so use begin() and check its result.
- Threads hurt very small shapes. In the M1 Pro data, 8-thread mode was slower than single-threaded in 24 of 174 cells at 8x8 (derived from page data), and the thesis notes a slowdown 'for very small sizes' in Fill-Linear-RectA. Use the threaded context for large or numerous shapes, not for UI glyph-sized work.
- Open robustness issues: #252 (ASan READ in the edge builder when stroking a path with a subnormal move_to and a huge control point), #255 and #256 (integer overflow in BLString and BLPath reserve, fixes staged), and #265 (stroke coverage gap when a segment is shorter than the pen width). Separately, the CMake error for a missing AsmJit uses message(FATAL ...), which CMake does not treat as an error, so the build fails later at add_subdirectory.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-05, version 0.21.3 in core/api.h, about 2.0k stars, 37 open issues) under the Zlib licence, so it is copyable. It is pre-1.0 with API renames between versions and no GitHub releases, so vendor a pinned commit together with its AsmJit checkout.

[repo](https://github.com/blend2d/blend2d) · [benchmark](https://github.com/LaurenzV/master-thesis/blob/main/main.pdf)

##### raqote  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Small pure-Rust CPU 2D rasterizer built on Skia-style 4x4 supersampling. Its path fills beat Cairo's image surface on an M1 Pro; overall it does not beat Skia.

**Beats:** Cairo (image surface; 1.18.4 on the M1 Pro run, 1.18.2 on the Windows x86 run); not faster than Skia once the broken rotated tests are excluded — An independent run by the Vello CPU author of Blend2D's bl_bench (29 tests x 6 paint styles x 6 sizes, SrcOver, 512x600 target, single thread), calling raqote 0.8.5 through the unofficial raqote_c FFI shim on an Apple M1 Pro (2026-06-08) and an Intel i9-14900K on Windows (2026-01-22); compiler versions and the Skia and Cairo build flags are unrecorded. As published, raqote is 1.08x Skia and 1.84x Cairo 1.18.4. The four rotated tests are inflated by the backend's transform-order bug, and without them raqote is 0.93x Skia and 1.48x Cairo on the M1 Pro and 0.89x Cairo 1.18.2 on x86 (all derived). Its wins are path fills; its losses are strokes and rectangle fills.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch; reached only through the unofficial raqote_c shim). Claim overstated: backend_raqote.cpp in the harness multiplies transforms in the wrong order, rotating shapes about the canvas origin so most are clipped, which made raqote's rotated tests 3-4.8x faster than its own unrotated ones. Without those rows raqote 0.8.5 is 0.93x Skia (not faster), 1.48x Cairo on the Apple M1 Pro and 0.89x Cairo on x86; the baseline is cut to Cairo. The runner (Vello CPU author) is independent of raqote but wrote the buggy backend; compiler and flags unrecorded.

**Known shortcoming:** The transform-order bug is confirmed in raqote_c (rq_transform_multiply uses euclid's then order). crates.io 0.8.5 dates from 2024-09-11 (release commit 2024-07-24); the README's user list is stale (Servo canvas now uses vello_cpu, resvg dropped raqote, #214). DrawTarget is not Send or Sync (#185); BlendMode::Src has a row-overwrite bug (#193); non-separable blend modes are about 10x slower than Skia (#156).

**How:** DESIGN.md calls the design 'very conservative' and says it 'borrows heavily from Skia'. The rasterizer is an active-edge-list scanline rasterizer with 4x4 supersampling and 30.2 fixed-point coordinates. Edges are kept sorted with a bubble sort, because the list is almost always nearly sorted. Quadratic curves are split into y-monotonic pieces and stepped directly as curve edges, and cubics are first approximated by quadratics (lyon_geom, tolerance 0.01). Coverage goes into an 8-bit mask over the path's bounding box, which is then composited one scanline at a time through sw-composite shaders. Those shaders use SWAR arithmetic (two 8-bit channels per u32 with 0xff00ff masks) and gradient lookup tables, with no SIMD intrinsics and no threads. An integer-aligned fill_rect with an identity transform and no clip skips the mask entirely.

**Use it when:**
- A Rust program needs a small CPU canvas (UI widgets, charts, thumbnails, generated images) with pure-Rust dependencies. With default-features = false, no C toolchain or system library is needed.
- Path-fill-heavy scenes such as maps, complex polygons and outlines. In the 2026-06-08 M1 Pro run those were raqote's wins over Skia (FillWorld 1.77x, FillPolyEOi40 1.44x, FillFish 1.43x), and fills were 1.86x Cairo 1.18.4 by geometric mean (derived).
- Replacing Cairo's image surface in a Rust codebase on ARM: 1.48x Cairo overall on the M1 Pro with the broken rotated tests excluded (derived).
- You need the full Porter-Duff set plus separable and non-separable blend modes, layers and clips in a code base small enough to read and patch.

**Skip it when:**
- Stroke-heavy or rectangle-heavy work. Strokes were 0.77x Skia and 1.11x Cairo on the M1 Pro and 0.61x Cairo on the i9-14900K, and FillRectA was 0.68x Skia (rotated tests excluded, derived). The stroker emits separate overlapping subpaths for each segment, join and cap and then fills them.
- x86-64 desktops, or whenever peak throughput matters: raqote was 0.89x Cairo 1.18.2 on the i9-14900K, and Blend2D 0.12 was about 3.8x faster single-threaded (raqote 0.26x as published). tiny-skia and Vello CPU are maintained Rust alternatives.
- Anti-aliasing quality close to analytic coverage. 4x4 supersampling gives at most 17 coverage levels per pixel, and the only modes are Gray and None.
- Multi-threaded rendering: DrawTarget is neither Send nor Sync (issue #185), and there is no internal parallelism (issue #155). Non-separable blend modes are about 10x slower than Skia (issue #156: Hue and Saturation about 13.7 ms versus 1.4 ms).
- Projects that need an active upstream or a C/C++ API. The last commit was 2025-02-11, with 60 open issues and 10 open PRs. Servo's canvas crate now uses vello_cpu, resvg dropped its raqote backend (#214), and C++ access is only through unofficial shims.

**Integration:** crate · euclid 0.22, lyon_geom 1.0, typed-arena 2.0, sw-composite 0.7.15. Default features add font-kit 0.14 and pathfinder_geometry 0.5 (text, which uses platform font libraries; see build-failure issue #176) and png 0.17. · Rust 2018 edition; Cargo.toml declares no rust-version (MSRV) · Any target with Rust std (the rasterizer and compositor are portable scalar Rust, so speed depends on autovectorization and target features). Benchmarked on aarch64 macOS (Apple M1 Pro) and x86-64 Windows built with +avx2.

**Vs siblings:** Pick raqote over tiny-skia only if you need its wider blend-mode set or already depend on it: tiny-skia's README says it is faster than raqote in many cases, and tiny-skia is maintained under linebender. For throughput, Blend2D (C++) and Vello CPU (Rust) beat it in the same bl_bench runs. raqote's remaining advantage is a small, readable pure-Rust code base with Cairo-beating path fills on ARM.

**Gotchas:**
- Default features pull in font-kit and png. Set default-features = false for the pure-Rust core. Text rendering has open panics on a missing glyph (#150) and on '\n' (#196), and transform bugs (#145, #179).
- BlendMode::Src overwrites pixels across the whole canvas row outside the drawn rectangle, because the temporary row buffer is canvas-wide (#193; open, with a proposed fix unmerged). Clips ignore the current transform (#187).
- Validate untrusted geometry: arc() loops forever on NaN or inf (#177), drawing an image with alpha can panic (#202), and the rasterizer uses 30.2 fixed-point endpoints with 16.16 intermediates, which the source comments say limits coordinates to a 16.16 space.
- Each fill allocates a coverage mask the size of the path's clipped bounding box and shades all of it, including zero-coverage pixels. DESIGN.md and #158 describe the run-length alternative as future work. Large sparse paths such as long diagonals or big outlines therefore cost their whole bounding-box area. Only integer-aligned fill_rect with an identity transform and no clip avoids the mask.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit was 2025-02-11 ('Allow writing png to memory'), the last release is 0.8.5 (release commit 2024-07-24, published on crates.io 2024-09-11), and there are 60 open issues and 10 open PRs. It is BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor, with 711k all-time crates.io downloads and 32 reverse dependencies, but two of the three 'notable users' in the README (Servo, resvg) no longer use it.

[repo](https://github.com/jrmuizel/raqote) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LaurenzV/vello_chart/HEAD/data/arm/2026-06-08.json)

#### video-audio

##### gopus (pure-Go Opus codec)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Go (no cgo) Opus encoder/decoder whose SIMD build roughly matches, and in most tested encode cases beats, SIMD libopus 1.6.1.

**Beats:** libopus 1.6.1 (C reference encoder and decoder, SIMD build) — On a GitHub Actions AMD EPYC 7763 runner at revision 4b660d668, Go 1.27.1 (GOAMD64=v3, GOEXPERIMENT=simd, PGO) was timed against a libopus 1.6.1 static build (GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -march=x86-64-v3, RTCD + intrinsics, AVX2/FMA lane) on identical PCM and controls (complexity 10, CBR): Go SIMD took 2.5-28.7% less time in four 20 ms encode cases, 14.6% more for 5 ms CELT, and 7.7% / 3.1% less for float32 / int16 decoding of the 12 RFC test vectors. Scalar Go against scalar C was slower in 6 of 7 rows; each row is the median of three runs of at least 250 ms with one codec instance per side, while the repo's own interleaved harness notes buffer placement alone can move a config's speed by up to about 15%.

**Known shortcoming:** Mixed result: Go SIMD is faster than libopus 1.6.1 (built with intrinsics and RTCD at -O3 -march=x86-64-v3, same flags as the Go side; complexity 10, CBR, matched bitrate, bandwidth, application and frame size) in 4 of 5 encode cases but 14.6% slower on 5 ms CELT frames, and decode is only 3.1-7.7% faster. The Go build uses PGO while the C side has none; the run is on a GitHub Actions EPYC 7763 runner; the decode bench checks sample counts only (bit-exactness is covered by separate final-range and PCM parity suites).

**Known shortcoming:** The PGO profile is trained on benchmarks mirroring the timed workloads (Restricted CELT, CELT 5 ms, SILK CBR) and Go applies default.pgo only from the main package, so importers lose it and no no-PGO numbers are published; one instance per side with 3 runs while the repo's own interleaved harness says buffer placement shifts speed up to about 15%, so the 2.5-7.7% margins sit within noise. The default build (without GOEXPERIMENT=simd) is 18-66% slower than SIMD libopus (derived); the repo's 56-configuration scoreboard (Intel Xeon, 6c0b0640b) shows SIMD decode up to 1.253x libopus. 142 unsafe references were removed after the measured revision (#519, #523) with many correctness fixes on 2026-10-01 and 02.

**How:** It ports the libopus algorithms source-for-source, then replaces all 53 former assembly routines (41 .s files) with Go kernels written against Go 1.27's experimental simd/archsimd package (AVX2/FMA on amd64, NEON on arm64), chosen by runtime CPU checks with scalar fallbacks. Hot paths are allocation-free after warmup (caller-owned buffers), the 256-bit SILK kernels are arranged to avoid legacy-SSE/AVX transition penalties (table-loaded NSQ constants, paired stores), and the published builds use PGO from a profile of the repo's own encode/decode benchmarks.

**Use it when:**
- Go services (WebRTC SFUs, voice bots, transcoders) that need Opus without cgo, a C toolchain, or shipping libopus binaries.
- Cross-compiled or static Go binaries where cgo is off, e.g. scratch containers or CGO_ENABLED=0 builds for several OS/arch targets.
- amd64 (AVX2/FMA) or arm64 hosts where you can build with GOEXPERIMENT=simd and GOAMD64=v3: 20 ms SILK/Hybrid/CELT encode measured 2.5-28.7% less time than SIMD libopus, decode 3.1-7.7% less.
- Real-time paths that are sensitive to GC pressure: the packet APIs report zero allocations per encode/decode after warmup.

**Skip it when:**
- Default builds without GOEXPERIMENT=simd: scalar Go takes 18-66% more time than SIMD libopus on every row of the published table (e.g. Hybrid fullband mono encode 420.99 vs 253.40 ns/sample; float decode 42.29 vs 35.90) (derived from page data).
- Low-delay CELT with short frames: 5 ms CELT encode takes 14.6% more time than libopus, and the repo's own 56-config interleaved scoreboard (Intel Xeon, revision 6c0b0640b) has 2.5 ms CELT decodes at 1.22-1.25x libopus time even with SIMD.
- C/C++ codebases: there is no C ABI, so libopus or a C/C++ port is the natural choice; calling Go from C++ adds cgo export and runtime overhead.
- Toolchains older than Go 1.27, or builds where an experimental compiler feature is unacceptable: the SIMD path depends on GOEXPERIMENT=simd, and the validation report lists several open Go compiler SIMD bugs the code has to work around.
- Production use that needs a stable API or long track record: pre-v1 (v0.1.2, v0.1.0 retracted), 27 stars, and a stream of correctness fixes merged on 2026-10-01/02 (FEC, Ogg granules, soft clipping on NaN, codec boundaries).

**Integration:** module · none (go.mod lists no requirements); optional DRED, OSCE, QEXT, custom-modes and fixed-point features behind build tags; libopus and a C compiler are needed only to run the parity tests and benchmarks · Go 1.27 for master (go.mod 'go 1.27.0'); GOEXPERIMENT=simd for SIMD kernels; v0.1.2 is the published release · any Go target with scalar kernels; SIMD kernels on amd64 (runtime AVX2/FMA checks, GOAMD64=v3 recommended) and arm64 (NEON); CI parity on Linux, macOS and Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick gopus when the host language is Go and cgo is off; the other catalogued Opus reimplementations (opus-rs, ropus, ruopus, rusty-opus, opus-pure for Rust; opuspp for C++; libopus-rs's tuned libopus) target Rust or C/C++ callers. Of these, gopus has the most detailed matched-ISA parity and benchmark evidence, but its speed margin over libopus is smaller and less uniform than the larger claims some siblings make.

**Gotchas:**
- The fast numbers need three opt-ins: GOEXPERIMENT=simd, GOAMD64=v3 and PGO. Go applies a default.pgo only from the main package's directory (or an explicit -pgo path), so an application importing gopus does not inherit the repo's profile; the published Go SIMD rows have no no-PGO counterpart, while the C side had no PGO or LTO.
- The PGO profile is generated from benchmarks (EncoderEncode_Restricted CELT, CELT5ms and SILK CBR after reset, CELT/stereo decode) that mirror the timed workloads, so the table may be a best case for those shapes.
- Parity with libopus is scoped, not universal: the CBR contract (19 cases, 2,175 packets/ranges) is packet- and range-exact on the recorded lanes, but floating-point paths allow narrow documented differences and the README states universal packet or float-bit identity is not a release requirement.
- The default bitrate is 64 kbps while libopus defaults to automatic; set bitrate explicitly when comparing outputs, and note DTX makes Encode return zero bytes with a nil error.

**Status:** Very actively developed (3,296 commits, last merges 2026-10-02, branch names such as codex/correctness-edges suggest agent-assisted development) and BSD-3-Clause, but pre-v1 with a fast-moving master that requires Go 1.27; pin a commit and rerun tools/encoderbenchcmp on your own hardware before relying on the speed claim.

[repo](https://github.com/thesyncim/gopus) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thesyncim/gopus/HEAD/README.md)

##### opuspp  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++23 port of the libopus 1.6.1 decoder for one CELT stream type, bit-exact and 1.27-1.48x faster.

**Beats:** libopus 1.6.1 decoder (opus_decode_float), built with identical compiler and flags — tests/bench.cpp decodes the same libopus-encoded packets (60 s of tones, noise, transients and orchestral music; 320 kb/s, complexity 4, 10 ms fullband stereo) with opus_decode_float and with opuspp, best of 7 passes on one pinned Ryzen 5 9600X core with the packet arena clflushed before each pass; libopus 1.6.1 is built statically with the same GCC 16.2 or Clang 22.1 flags per profile (-Os, -O2, or -O3 -march=native -ffast-math with FLOAT_APPROX in both) and keeps its run-time AVX2 dispatch. opuspp is 1.27-1.48x faster like for like and 1.09-1.50x across 128/510 kb/s, 10% loss and complexities 0 and 2; libopus is not built with -flto, so part of the gain is the header-only inlining the project argues for, and only the rendered tables (not results.json) are committed.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on its own bench.cpp and profile_report.py (GCC 16.2 and Clang 22.1, same flags, Ryzen 5 9600X) against libopus 1.6.1 with the same packets, bitrate, complexity and frame size. Output is bit-exact only in the Size and Balanced profiles; the Fast profile is about 137 dB SNR against the reference, not bit-exact. The raw results.json is not committed.

**Known shortcoming:** The static libopus baseline is built without -flto while opuspp inlines header-only by design; only an x86-64 Ryzen 5 9600X is measured (NEON unmeasured); results.json is not committed; the bench sinks one sample per call (bit-exactness is checked separately across 47 configurations and 300k fuzz cases); a GCC -Os build runs at 0.88x of the fastest libopus.
