**Known shortcoming:** Idle-latency bug: after more than 5 ms idle, requests are falsely retransmitted (timing-wheel reap walks slot by slot, stale timestamp in enqueue_request; #104, #116); fix PR #123 unmerged, workaround is to keep polling. ~10M RPC/s per core needs ~10 nodes all-to-all (8 outstanding per session); users saw 1.5 Mrps on two machines (#35) and 3.1 vs 5 Mrps on 10 nodes (#121). Compile-time limits: ~128 sessions per Rpc endpoint by default, DPDK MTU hard-coded 1024 B. x86-64 Linux only (rdtsc, -march=native; aarch64 #111), needs hugepages/root/DPDK 21.11 or rdma-core; Nexus segfaults with offline CPUs (#31). Go-back-N with 5 ms RTO: usable only up to ~0.01% loss. Not an HTTP server (no HTTP/TLS). Faster claims compare against numbers from other papers; up to 18% slower per thread than FaSST. Last commit 2024-05; authors point to microsoft/machnet.

**How:** Each user thread polls its own NIC queue from userspace and runs short handlers to completion inside the event loop. Longer handlers can go to up to 8 eRPC background threads. The paper's common-case optimizations are zero-copy, single-DMA msgbufs (packet 1's header sits before the data and later headers go at the end), request handlers that read directly from the RX ring, preallocated MTU-sized responses, multi-packet RQ, and unsignaled, batched TX. The wire protocol is client-driven: a session's packet credits are capped near one bandwidth-delay product, and eRPC relies on large dynamic switch buffers so that loss stays rare. Congestion control is Timely plus a Carousel-style timing-wheel rate limiter. When a session is uncongested it skips the Timely update and the wheel and reads rdtsc once per batch, which cuts congestion-control overhead from 20% to 9%. The transports are picked at compile time through a template parameter (static polymorphism), so there are no virtual calls.

**Use it when:**
- Service-to-service or storage RPC where you own both ends and run on bare-metal Mellanox CX3–CX5 or other DPDK-capable 10 GbE+ NICs, and you want a few microseconds of median latency (paper: 2.3 µs on 40 GbE CX5, 3.7 µs on 25 GbE CX4)
- Small, fixed-size requests (32 B class) at high rate: in the paper one core handles ~10M RPCs/s when it is both client and server in an all-to-all cluster of about 10 or more nodes
- Replication or key-value work that would otherwise need RDMA or PFC: the paper runs a stock Raft port at 5.5 µs 3-way replication and Masstree at 2.7 µs median GET on lossy Ethernet
- Bulk transfers up to 8 MB per message on a fast link: up to 75 Gbps on one core over 100 Gbps InfiniBand (raise the 1024 B DPDK MTU constant for bandwidth on Ethernet)
- Research baselines where you need a general RPC layer within ~18% of FaSST's small-RPC rate and within 800 ns of RDMA-read latency

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that must speak HTTP or TLS, or talk to clients that are not eRPC: the UDP/IB wire protocol is custom, so it does not replace any of the HTTP servers in this category
- Public-cloud VMs, containers, dev laptops, or setups without root: it needs hugepages (at least 1024 per NUMA node), DPDK owning the NIC port or ibverbs, and NIC flow steering. Only Azure accelerated networking is documented, and the author notes that cloud guests often lack flow steering (issue #44)
- Low-rate or bursty callers that sleep between RPCs: latency grows with idle time (issues #104/#116), and the fix PR #123 is still unmerged
- Non-x86 hosts: timing uses the rdtsc instruction via inline asm and the build uses -march=native. An aarch64 port needs patches and trips the TSC-frequency assert (issue #111, open)
- Long-lived production dependencies: the last commit was 2024-05-09 and the authors now point new users to microsoft/machnet. Networks with more than ~0.01% loss or with packet reordering also hurt it: reordered packets are dropped and handled with go-back-N and a 5 ms RTO, and 8 MB throughput falls to 18 Gbps at 1e-4 loss

**Integration:** static lib · DPDK 21.11 (dpdk transport; README says other versions are unsupported) or rdma-core/ibverbs (infiniband/RoCE transport); libnuma, pthread, rt; bundled gflags, HdrHistogram_c, googletest and asio headers; 2 MB hugepages; optional libpmem for some apps · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake with pkg-config for DPDK; author reports GCC 7.4 works (issue #33); builds with -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic, so newer compilers may fail (issue #65 open) · Linux x86-64 only in practice (rdtsc inline asm, -march=native); NICs: Mellanox CX3–CX5 tested, any DPDK NIC with flow steering, Azure DPDK VMs; a WIN32 DPDK path exists in CMakeLists but is not documented; aarch64 unsupported

**Vs siblings:** Pick eRPC over Demikernel, Shenango, or FlexTOE when both ends are your own C++ code and you want finished RPC semantics (at-most-once execution, loss recovery, congestion control, nested and background handlers) at millions of small RPCs per core. Pick those siblings when you need a TCP or sockets-style path that other software can talk to, such as Demikernel's DPDK TCP stack or Shenango serving memcached. The HTTP servers here (Drogon, H2O, Lwan, Crow) solve a different problem and are not alternatives.

**Gotchas:**
- Idle gaps inflate latency. TimingWheel::reap() advances one slot at a time with no fast-forward, and enqueue_request stamps a stale event-loop TSC, so a request after more than 5 ms idle is falsely retransmitted. The workaround is to keep calling run_event_loop_once() instead of sleeping. The fix is PR #123, open since 2026-08-06.
- Most tuning is compile-time. kSessionReqWindow = 8 outstanding requests per session, kSessionCredits = 32, kNumRxRingEntries = 4096 (so about 128 sessions per Rpc before create_session returns -ENOMEM), kRpcRTOUs = 5000, and kMTU = 1024 B on DPDK. Two-machine tests do not reach the 10M RPC/s figure (issue #35: ~1.5 Mrps; issue #121: 3.1 vs 5 Mrps on 10 xl170 nodes).
- Buffer ownership is strict. With kZeroCopyRX, a single-packet request buffer is valid only during the handler. A response must use the ReqHandle's pre_resp_msgbuf_ or dyn_resp_msgbuf_, not your own buffer, and eRPC owns request and response msgbufs until the continuation runs. Message size is capped at 8 MB.
- Session setup goes over kernel UDP on the management network (ports 31850+n, reachable by hostname), not over the DPDK port. By default only one process can use a DPDK port; the multi-process daemon has been seen stuck in rte_eth_tx_burst (#118). The Nexus segfaults when CPUs are offline, for example with HT disabled (#31; the fix PR #36 has been open since 2019).

**Status:** Stale since the last commit on 2024-05-09 (last release v0.2, 2021), with 19 open issues and 5 open PRs, including the unmerged idle-latency fix. The authors point new users to microsoft/machnet. It is Apache-2.0 (per LICENSE and README; GitHub shows NOASSERTION) and about 6,200 lines of C++ per the paper, so it can be vendored, but expect to own DPDK and rdma-core version pinning yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/erpc-io/eRPC) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi19-kalia.pdf)

##### Homa (HomaModule) — Linux kernel implementation of the Homa RPC transport protocol  `C`  `BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+ (per-file SPDX headers on the module and benchmark sources; a few test/tool files are BSD-1-Clause or GPL-2.0; no top-level LICENSE file)`  `active`  `Tier B`

Linux kernel module for Homa, a message-based datacenter RPC transport with far lower short-message tail latency than TCP.

**Beats:** TCP (and DCTCP) — The USENIX ATC'21 paper compared this module (2021 code, Linux 5.4.80, MTU 3000) with Linux kernel TCP (TCP_NODELAY, per issue #51 and cp_node.cc) and DCTCP (ECN threshold 70 KB) on 40 CloudLab xl170 nodes (Xeon E5-2640v4, ConnectX-4 25 Gbps, one Mellanox 2410 switch). Under high load on workloads W2-W5, short-message P99 was 19-72x lower than TCP and 7-83x lower than DCTCP, and P50 was 3.5-7.5x and 2.7-3.8x lower. Best-case 100-byte RTT was 15.1 vs 23.4/24.1 us, and RPC rate was 1.6 vs 1.0 Mops/s. No compiler version or flags are stated. The author's unreviewed perf.txt log (Jan 2026, current code, 100 Gbps c6620, W4 at 80 Gbps) still shows short-message P99 of about 91-99 us for Homa versus 833-1272 us for TCP.

**Known shortcoming:** A transport protocol, not a gRPC/Thrift library: compared against Linux TCP and DCTCP. The 7-83x P99 gains apply to short messages only (P50 3.5-7.5x). Paper numbers are from 2021 code on Linux 5.4.80; the module has since been heavily reworked for kernel upstreaming. Needs a kernel module and Homa-capable peers. No compiler or flags stated.

**Known shortcoming:** The fast version exists only out of tree: the upstream netdev series (v20, 2026-09-14) is stripped to ~8k lines and its cover letter says performance is about the same as TCP; mainline has no net/homa. Needs jumbo frames, interrupt coalescing off, RPS on, RFS off, homa_qdisc on every tx queue, DSCP priority queues and TSO; software GSO is 'temporarily broken' and the TCP-hijacking fallback can be dropped by switch filters. Bulk throughput loses (10.0 vs 20.3 Gbps single-client 500 KB); messages capped at 1 MB. CPU cost high (~0.1 M req/s/core in the paper; polling costs 2-3 extra cores). Sharing hosts with TCP raises short-message P99 ~4x without homa_qdisc, ~30% with it. No encryption. Author notes grants get stranded at very high load (~60-70% of link bandwidth). The homa_send/recv/reply API in the record was removed in 2025 (now sendmsg/recvmsg with SO_HOMA_RCVBUF). No compiler/flags; latest data is the repo's perf.txt (2026-01: P99 ~91-99 us vs 833-1272 us for TCP).

**How:** Receiver-driven flow control: a sender sends the first rtt_bytes of a message without asking, then sends more only when the receiver grants it. Receivers approximate SRPT (shortest remaining processing time first) with a bounded degree of overcommitment. Priorities are set through 8 switch priority queues keyed on DSCP bits, and a homa_prio daemon sets unscheduled-priority cutoffs from observed message sizes. A sender-side pacer/homa_qdisc keeps NIC queues short so small messages never wait behind large ones, and message framing removes TCP's head-of-line blocking. On the host side the ATC'21 paper credits most of the 100-byte RTT gain to busy-polling in recvmsg (~4 us) and SoftIRQ core selection (3-4 us), and higher RPC rate to GRO batching across RPCs.

**Use it when:**
- Datacenter request/response traffic where P99 latency of short messages (hundreds of bytes to a few KB) under 50-80% network load is what hurts, e.g. fan-out services and storage/cache RPC.
- Mixed workloads with both short and long messages (the Montazeri W3-W5 shapes), where TCP's per-stream head-of-line blocking and switch queue buildup inflate tail latency.
- Highly connected clusters: one Homa socket reaches every peer, and the paper puts per-peer state at about 200 bytes versus about 2000 bytes per open TCP socket.
- You control the whole stack: Linux 6.17.8 (main) or RHEL 8/9.5 (branches) hosts, Mellanox ConnectX-4/5/6 or Intel E810 NICs, and top-of-rack switches you can configure for DSCP strict-priority queues.
- Transport research or benchmarking: the repo ships the cp_node/cp_vs_tcp/cp_bench harness, timetrace tools and /proc/net/homa_metrics used to produce its published numbers.

**Skip it when:**
- Bulk or single-stream throughput. In the paper's Table 2, one client doing 500 KB RPCs gets 10.0 Gbps versus 20.3 Gbps for TCP. Messages are capped at HOMA_MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH = 1,000,000 bytes, so large transfers must be chunked.
- WAN or cross-datacenter links. The homa(7) man page says Homa is for RTTs of a few tens of microseconds and is not suitable for wide-area use.
- Anywhere you cannot load an out-of-tree kernel module or configure switches: managed cloud VMs, unprivileged containers, macOS and Windows. Upstream Linux does not include it (no net/homa in mainline as of v7.3-rc4).
- CPU-bound small-RPC servers. In the paper, 1.6 Mops/s used about 18 of 20 hyperthreads (~0.1 M req/s/core, versus ~10 M for kernel-bypass eRPC), and perf.txt (Sep 2025) says receive polling costs an extra 2-3 cores.
- Hosts carrying heavy TCP traffic at the same time, or needing encryption. perf.txt (Jan 2026) shows Homa's short-message P99 rising about 4x when it shares hosts with TCP, and still about 30% worse with homa_qdisc. There is no TLS layer (grpc_homa supports only insecure channels).

**Integration:** module · Kernel build tree/headers that match the running kernel (main: Linux 6.17.8; rhel8 and rhel9.5 branches; older linux_x.y branches are stale), a kernel built with IPv6 (Kconfig depends on IPV6), and root for insmod. The homa_prio user-space daemon (util/) is recommended. Full performance also needs switch priority queues, jumbo frames, and NIC TSO for Homa packets (Mellanox) or TCP hijacking. The optional C++ homa::receiver helper and homa.h UAPI header ship in the repo. · Module is built with kbuild and the kernel's own compiler/flags (no GCC version documented). util/ tools and homa_receiver.cc need g++ with -std=c++17. · Linux only. Tested on x86-64 (Intel xl170/c6620 and AMD c6525 CloudLab nodes per perf.txt); other architectures not documented. Verified NICs: Mellanox ConnectX-4/5/6 and Intel E810.

**Vs siblings:** Pick HomaModule when tail latency of short RPCs under heavy network load is the problem and you can change host kernels and switch config. brpc, Kitex and rpcx win on QPS in user space but still run over TCP, so they keep its head-of-line blocking and congestion tails. grpc_homa is only a gRPC shim on top of this module, and its README says it has been unmaintained since late 2023 (gRPC 1.57, insecure channels only). Use it only if you must keep gRPC's API.

**Gotchas:**
- Out of the box, performance is poor until the host and network are tuned. That means jumbo frames, NIC interrupt coalescing off, RPS on and RFS off, homa_qdisc configured on each tx queue, switch DSCP priority mapping, and TSO. INSTALL.md says software GSO is 'temporarily broken', so on NICs that won't segment Homa packets the fallback is TCP hijacking. Hijacked packets masquerade as TCP and can be dropped by datacenter switch filters.
- The API has changed repeatedly. Homa 2.0 (Dec 2022) moved to sendmsg/recvmsg with an app-supplied mmap'd buffer pool. homa_send/homa_recv/homa_reply were removed in May 2025, private-RPC flags changed in Mar 2025, and since Feb 2025 unbound sockets reject incoming requests. Netdev review is expected to change the API again.
- Receive buffers are registered up front (page-aligned region, 'tens of MB'). recvmsg returns ENOMEM when the pool is exhausted, and bpages are only returned to Homa on the next recvmsg. Raising the 1 MB message cap means editing a static_assert and recompiling every app (issue #48).
- The upstream series (v20, posted 2026-09-14) is stripped to about 8,000 of 20,000 lines, and its cover letter says its performance is 'about the same as TCP'. The fast paths (grant scheduling, qdisc, hijack, GRO offload) exist only in this out-of-tree repo. notes.txt also records grant 'stranding' under very high load in large clusters, capping throughput at about 60-70% of link bandwidth. One rtt_bytes value is used for all peers, and the SIGCOMM incast optimization is not implemented.

**Status:** Actively maintained by John Ousterhout (last commit 2026-09-25, upstreaming in progress on netdev). BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+ via per-file SPDX headers, so it is copyable, but it is an out-of-tree kernel module that must be rebuilt and ported for each kernel version it runs on.

[repo](https://github.com/PlatformLab/HomaModule) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc21-ousterhout.pdf)

### numerics-and-science

#### autodiff-and-ml-kernels

##### fast.cu (H100 BF16 matmul and sum-reduction kernels)  `C++ (CUDA)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

From-scratch Hopper BF16 GEMM (TMA + WGMMA) beating cuBLAS by 2-7% on square H100 matmuls, plus a CUB-level reduction.

**Beats:** cuBLAS (cublasGemmEx, BF16 inputs, FP32 compute, CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT) for matmul; CUB for sum reduction — On one H100 (SXM 80GB and CUDA 12.6 per a worklog search snippet), the same binary timed the custom BF16 GEMM against cublasGemmEx (BF16 in and out, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F, CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT): 763 vs 716 TFLOPS at N=4096 and 808 vs 795 at N=8192 (about 1.07x and 1.02x, derived from page data); the README does not say which of kernels 1-12 produced them. An independent run in issue #13 (H100 variant unstated, CUDA 12.4, N=8192) measured cuBLAS at 518.6 TFLOPS and kernels 10/12 at 533.4/530.8 TFLOPS, about 1.02-1.03x (derived from page data), so the small margin held there though absolute numbers were far lower. The int32 sum of 2^30 elements ran at 3240.11 GB/s vs CUB's 3193.36 GB/s.

**Known shortcoming:** Margins over cuBLAS are only 2-7%; CUDA 12.6 and H100 SXM known from a search snippet (blog blocked here).

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #13 'Unable to reproduce reported numbers': another H100 (variant unstated, CUDA 12.4, N=8192) measured cuBLAS 518.6 TFLOPS vs kernel12 530.8 and kernel10 533.4, so the margin holds at ~1.02-1.03x (derived) but absolute numbers are far lower. Open #4: matmul_3 returns wrong, row-shuffled results at 128x128x64 (H800). -DNDEBUG compiles out the shape asserts (M,N must be multiples of 256, K of 64). TMA maps are cached on M only, so a new N/K with the same M reuses stale maps. The sum kernel zeroes *d_out inside the kernel while other blocks atomicAdd (formal race). It is 12 kernels plus cuBLAS as kernel 0, not 13.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The final kernels (11/12) are persistent, warp-specialized Hopper GEMMs: one producer warpgroup issues TMA bulk-tensor loads (cp.async.bulk.tensor with 128B swizzle, multicast across a 2-CTA thread-block cluster) into a 3-stage mbarrier-synchronized shared-memory ring, while two consumer warpgroups run wgmma.mma_async m64n256k16 BF16 instructions with FP32 accumulators, and setmaxnreg moves registers from producer to consumers. Output tiles (128 x 256, BK=64) are assigned to 128 persistent CTAs along a Hilbert curve for L2 reuse, and kernel 12 writes C through stmatrix into padded shared memory followed by a TMA store. The sum kernels use int4 vector loads (16 per thread), redux.sync warp reductions, one shared-memory atomic per warp and one global atomicAdd per block.

**Use it when:**
- Large square or near-square BF16 GEMMs (the published sizes are 4096 and 8192) on an H100 SXM, with M and N multiples of 256 and K a multiple of 64.
- Learning or prototyping Hopper GEMM design: the 12-kernel ladder goes from a naive kernel to TMA, WGMMA, warp specialization, clusters and Hilbert scheduling in plain CUDA plus inline PTX, without CUTLASS/CuTe templates.
- A starting point for a custom fused epilogue on Hopper when you control shapes and want a single-file kernel you can edit.
- Studying Blackwell (GB300/B300, sm_103a) NVFP4 GEMM: the gb300/nvfp4 ladder documents each optimization rung and a paired, cooldown-gated benchmark protocol against cuBLASLt.

**Skip it when:**
- Arbitrary shapes: nothing checks divisibility at runtime (the Makefile's -DNDEBUG compiles out every assert), and issue #4 (open) reports row-shuffled wrong results from matmul_3 at 128x128x64 on an H800.
- Any GPU other than an H100-class sm_90a part: kernels are compiled only for sm_90a, NUM_SM is hard-coded to 128 persistent CTAs, and nothing is tuned for H100 PCIe/H800/H200.
- When a 2-7% gain does not justify owning a kernel: the margin is about 1.07x at N=4096 and 1.02x at N=8192 (derived from page data), and issue #13 (open, 'Unable to reproduce reported numbers') reports much lower absolute throughput on another H100 (cuBLAS 518.6 TFLOPS at N=8192).
- FP16, FP8, transposed, batched or alpha/beta GEMMs, or multi-threaded host code: none are supported, and runKernelN keeps TMA descriptors and the schedule buffer in host globals.
- General reductions: the sum kernels handle int32 only, require N divisible by 4, and win by about 1.5% over CUB.

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA toolkit with the Driver API (cuTensorMapEncodeTiled, -lcuda); cuBLAS only for the reference/verification path; CUB for the sum comparison · C++17 nvcc with sm_90a support (Makefile: -gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a); CUDA 12.6 named only in a search snippet of the worklog, and issue #13 built it with CUDA 12.4; the GB300 NVFP4 kernels need CUDA 13.1 and sm_103a · NVIDIA H100 (sm_90a) for matmul and sum; GB300/B300 (sm_103a) for gb300/nvfp4; Linux build via GNU Make

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ThunderKittens when you want one readable, dependency-free Hopper GEMM file to fork rather than a tile-abstraction framework that matches cuBLAS more generally; pick it over bare-metal when the target is an H100 instead of an sm_86 laptop GPU, where bare-metal's margin is about 1.02x under a clock lock. For quantized or GEMV work, BitBLAS or FastGEMV fit better.

**Gotchas:**
- Kernel 12 needs M and N multiples of 256 (BM 128 x 2-CTA cluster, BN 256) and K a multiple of 64 (num_blocks_k = K / BK drops any tail); with -DNDEBUG the device and host asserts that guard this are compiled out, so bad shapes fail silently.
- runKernel11/12 rebuild their cached TMA maps only when M changes (keyed on _prev_m), so calling with the same M but a different N or K reuses stale descriptors; each rebuild also cudaMallocs a new schedule buffer without freeing the old one.
- The matmul harness hard-codes 8192 x 8192 (max_size), times 8 back-to-back launches after one verification run, uses a 0.1 absolute tolerance on BF16 outputs, and keeps benchmarking after a failed check; reproducing the N=4096 row means editing the source.
- The sum kernels zero *d_out from inside the kernel (thread i == 0) while other blocks atomicAdd to it, a formal race; the benchmark's own int32 total (2^30 values of rand() % 100, about 5.3e10, derived) wraps, identically in CUB.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-08-15, 625 stars, MIT, 17 commits) and small enough to vendor, but it is a demonstration repo: open issues #4 (small-shape wrong results) and #13 (reproducibility) have no maintainer replies.

[repo](https://github.com/pranjalssh/fast.cu) · [benchmark](https://github.com/pranjalssh/fast.cu)

##### FastGEMV (fp16/int8/int4 GEMV CUDA kernels)  `C++ (CUDA)`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Three small CUDA GEMV kernels (fp16, int8, int4 weights x fp16 vector) beating 2023 PyTorch fp16 matmul by 1.1-2.7x.

**Beats:** PyTorch fp16 matrix-vector product (torch.matmul on a size x size fp16 matrix and size x 1 vector, baseline.py, kernel time via Nsight Systems) — Nsight Systems kernel-time averages (10,000 iterations) for an n x n fp16 matrix times an n x 1 fp16 vector, against torch.matmul of mid-2023 (PyTorch version not stated; nvcc -O3, CUDA 11.7): 1.44-2.70x faster on a P100 (peak at n=8192, where PyTorch dropped to 202 GB/s) and 1.02-1.40x faster on an RTX 3090 (4372.4 vs 6106.2 ns at n=1024, 609235 vs 691660.6 ns at n=16384). One independent user report (issue #3, A30, CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.1) found the fp16 kernel slower than PyTorch at n=16384.

**Known shortcoming:** On RTX 3090 the gain is only 1.02x at n=8192; PyTorch version not stated; abandoned since 2023-06-06.

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #3: an A30 run (CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.1, n=16384) had the fp16 kernel slower than PyTorch (8550.95 vs 6031.96 ms for 10k iterations, ~0.71x, derived). Makefile emits SASS only for sm_60/70/75/86, no PTX. The harness correctness check only prints mismatches and never fails the run.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** GEMV is memory-bound, so the kernels aim at DRAM bandwidth: p = blockDim.x threads share one row, each loading 16 bytes at a time (float4 holding 8 halves; half4 holding 8 int8 values; two 4-byte packs of 8 int4 values each), and multiply in fp32 registers. Partial sums are combined with a __shfl_down_sync warp reduction (CUTLASS-style), plus one shared-memory pass when a row uses more than 32 threads. Block shape is hand-tuned per size and GPU; on the 3090 at n=16384 the fp16 kernel reaches an estimated 881.8 GB/s of 936 GB/s versus 776.3 GB/s for PyTorch.

**Use it when:**
- Batch-1 matrix-vector products on fp16 weights (LLM-decode-style GEMV) on Pascal or consumer Ampere GPUs, where you can hand-pick blockDim per matrix size.
- Weight-only int8 or int4 GEMV with a single per-tensor scale/zero point, when you want the bandwidth saving of quantized weights in a kernel small enough to read in a few minutes.
- Power-of-two sizes from 512 to 16384, the only range the authors measured.
- As a teaching example of vectorized loads plus warp-shuffle reduction for memory-bound kernels.

**Skip it when:**
- Modern data-center GPUs without re-measuring: issue #3 (open) reports the fp16 kernel slower than PyTorch on an A30 (8550.95 ms vs 6031.96 ms for 10,000 iterations at n=16384, about 0.71x, derived from page data).
- Real quantized LLM weights: only one per-tensor scale and zero point is supported (no per-channel or group-wise scales), and int4 values are unsigned 0..15.
- Batch sizes above 1 (GEMM), non-power-of-two or non-square shapes: the README and harness assume square power-of-two sizes, and issue #6 asking about rectangular matrices has no answer.
- Small fp16 matrices on newer cards when the gain matters: on the 3090 the fp16 speedup is 1.02x at n=8192 and 1.13x at n=2048 (derived from page data).
- Long-lived production use: no commits since 2023-06-06 and no releases.

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA runtime and cuda_fp16; curand only for the test data generator; PyTorch only for baseline.py; Nsight Systems for the published timings · C++17 nvcc; README lists CUDA 11.7 and Nsight Systems 2023.1.2; Makefile builds SASS for sm_60, sm_70, sm_75 and sm_86 only · NVIDIA GPUs; measured on P100 and RTX 3090 (README says 3090 Ti); other architectures such as sm_80/sm_89/sm_90 need a Makefile -gencode edit because no PTX fallback is emitted

**Vs siblings:** Pick FastGEMV over Marlin or BitBLAS when you want a tiny fp16 or per-tensor int8/int4 GEMV you can read and adapt; Marlin and BitBLAS support group-wise quantization, batch sizes above 1 and newer GPUs, and are measured against current baselines. fast.cu and bare-metal target compute-bound GEMM, not matrix-vector work.

**Gotchas:**
- Launch geometry is the caller's job and is not bounds-checked: rows are not guarded, so n must be divisible by blockDim.y; n / blockDim.x must be at least 8 (fp16/int8) or 16 (int4); blockDim.y must be at most 64 (shared-memory array size); and n must be a multiple of 8 for the 16-byte loads.
- Best blockDim differs by size and GPU (for example n=4096 uses 128x8 on the P100 but 256x1 on the 3090), so the published speedups need the same per-size tuning.
- The harness's correctness kernels only print mismatches and never fail the run; the fp16 tolerance is an absolute 0.125 * n / 512 (4.0 at n=16384).
- The int8/int4 timings move 2x/4x fewer matrix bytes than the fp16 PyTorch baseline, so their 'speedups' are not like-for-like; PyTorch had no direct quantized GEMV to compare against.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2023-06-06 (130 stars, MIT, four open issues without maintainer replies), but the kernels are a few hundred lines and easy to vendor and retune.

[repo](https://github.com/wangsiping97/FastGEMV) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangsiping97/FastGEMV/HEAD/method_and_result.md)

##### Fastor  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++ fixed-size tensor library whose small-GEMM kernels match MKL JIT and beat padded Blaze.

**Beats:** Eigen 3.3.7 / Blaze 3.7 / MKL JIT 2021.01 / LIBXSMM (small fixed-size GEMM, single-threaded) — The wiki's small-GEMM benchmarks (cbrt(MNK) <= 128, single-threaded, float/double/complex) against Eigen 3.3.7, Blaze 3.7, LIBXSMM (Apr 2020 devel) and MKL JIT 2021.01, built with GCC 9.2 -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx2 -mfma on i5-8259U and Xeon E3-1240 v6 and GCC 7.4 with AVX-512 flags on Xeon Gold 6128, show Fastor at parity with MKL JIT and padded Blaze roughly 50% slower (up to 2x in some cases). Results are plots only, and the Eigen gap is not quantified in text.

**Known shortcoming:** Results only as plots, no numbers in text; headline claim is only parity with MKL JIT; padded Blaze is 'in general about 50% slower'.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked library versions date from 2020; issue #42: ~2x slower than Eigen at 128x128 (~2x faster at 8x8); open issue #141: einsum ~2.3x slower than hand-written SIMD on 100k dot products; sparse commits (2 in 2025, 2 in 2024); built-in SIMD x86 only.

**How:** All sizes are template parameters, so SIMD kernels (SSE2 to AVX-512, FMA) for matmul and contractions are statically dispatched and fully unrolled for the exact shape, with no runtime dispatch or heap allocation. 'Smart' expression templates rewrite expressions at compile time (e.g. trace(A^T B) to inner(A,B), det(inv(A)) to 1/det(A), matrix-chain reordering) and a compile-time cost model picks a FLOP-minimal contraction order for tensor networks. Optional LIBXSMM or MKL-JIT backends can take over matmul.

**Use it when:**
- Many repeated small dense ops (roughly 2x2 to 64x64, sizes known at compile time), e.g. per-element or per-quadrature-point kernels in finite-element / continuum mechanics codes.
- Higher-order tensor contractions and einsum with fixed dimensions, where compile-time contraction-order optimisation cuts FLOPs.
- Embedded / FPGA / no-heap environments: no dynamic allocation and no RTTI.
- When you want small-GEMM speed near MKL JIT/LIBXSMM without linking a vendor library.

**Skip it when:**
- Medium or large matrices: issue #42 reports Fastor ~2x slower than Eigen at 128x128 (fine at 8x8, equal at 64x64); matmul is a register-blocked loop nest without the cache tiling/packing/threading of a BLAS.
- Runtime-sized data: there is no dynamic-size tensor type.
- Non-x86 SIMD: the built-in SIMDVector layer covers SSE2..AVX-512 only; other architectures fall back to scalar unless you configure the Vc or std::experimental::simd backend.
- Large dot products/reductions over long vectors: open issue #141 shows einsum ~2.3x slower than hand-written OpenMP-SIMD/AVX2 at 100k elements (while far faster on small ones).
- Projects that need a broad, actively developed library: commits are sparse (two in 2025, two in 2024).

**Integration:** header-only · none (optional: LIBXSMM, MKL JIT, sleef, Vc) · C++14 (config.h #errors below it); tested GCC 5.1-10.1, Clang 3.6-10, ICC 16-19, MSVC 2019 · x86 / x86-64 with SSE2-AVX-512 kernels; other CPUs via scalar fallback or Vc/std::experimental::simd backend

**Vs siblings:** Pick Fastor over LIBXSMM when you want a header-only, high-level tensor API (einsum, views, small LU/QR/inverse) for fixed shapes rather than a JIT GEMM library; LIBXSMM is the better choice for runtime-shaped small GEMM or DL primitives. Pick it over TCL when tensor shapes are compile-time and small; TCL targets larger runtime-shaped contractions.

**Gotchas:**
- Performance depends on -march/-mavx2 -mfma/-mavx512* flags and -DNDEBUG; without them it compiles to SSE2 or scalar code.
- auto on an expression or view holds an unevaluated expression/reference; assign to a Tensor to materialise it.
- matmul(A, transpose(B)) creates a temporary transpose (per maintainer in issue #42).
- Large fixed sizes live on the stack and inflate compile time and binary size.

**Status:** MIT-licensed, not archived, but low activity (last commits July 2025, previous ones 2024); v0.6.4 is the latest release and the benchmark library versions date from 2020.

[repo](https://github.com/romeric/Fastor) · [benchmark](https://github.com/romeric/Fastor/wiki/Benchmarks)

##### FlashAttention-3 (flash-attention)  `CUDA/C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Fused exact-attention CUDA kernels (FA2/FA3); FA3 on H100 is 1.5-2x faster than FA2 and beats cuDNN at sequence lengths of 1k and up.

**Beats:** NVIDIA cuDNN attention — The NeurIPS 2024 FA3 paper benchmarks attention forward and backward on an H100 SXM5 against FA2, a Triton implementation and cuDNN: FP16 forward is 1.5-2.0x faster than FA2, reaching up to 740 TFLOPs/s (75% utilization), backward is 1.5-1.75x faster, and it beats cuDNN at sequence lengths of 1k and up. FP8 reaches close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s but trails cuDNN for causal hdim 128/256. Toolchain versions differ between paper versions (CUDA 12.1-12.3, cuDNN 9.x, CUTLASS 3.x), and the comparison harness is hopper/benchmark_attn.py in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Search record's 'up to 1.5x faster than cuDNN' not found; paper: faster than cuDNN for seq len >= 1k, FP8 slower than cuDNN with causal masking at head dims 128/256; toolchain versions differ between paper versions.

**Known shortcoming:** README still calls FA3 beta; H100/H800 only; PyTorch-only interface, no standalone C++ API; open issue #2244: deterministic=True backward reportedly non-deterministic dQ (not reproduced by others).

**How:** IO-aware tiling with online softmax keeps Q/K/V blocks in shared memory and registers, so the score matrix never goes to HBM. FA3 adds Hopper features: warp specialization with TMA producer warps and WGMMA consumer warps, ping-pong scheduling so one warpgroup's softmax exponentials overlap another's GEMMs, and an intra-warpgroup two-stage pipeline overlapping softmax with the next GEMM. The FP8 path uses block quantization plus incoherent processing (a random orthogonal transform) to tame outliers, which the paper reports gives 2.6x lower error than baseline per-tensor FP8 attention.

**Use it when:**
- Training or prefill of transformers on H100/H800 with FP16/BF16 and sequence lengths of 1k or more, where the paper shows FA3 ahead of cuDNN.
- Ampere/Ada/Hopper GPUs (A100, RTX 3090/4090, H100) via FA2 when you need exact attention with linear memory instead of PyTorch's materialized attention.
- Autoregressive decoding with KV cache: flash_attn_with_kvcache does append-to-cache, rotary embedding and split-KV attention in one kernel, with paged-KV support.
- Models needing sliding-window, ALiBi, softcapping, or GQA/MQA attention in a single fused kernel.
- AMD MI200/MI300/MI355 and RDNA3/4 via the Composable Kernel or Triton backends (FA2 only).

**Skip it when:**
- FP8 causal attention with head dim 128 or 256 on H100: the paper shows cuDNN ahead there.
- Short sequences (under about 1k), where the paper does not show a win over cuDNN; recent cuDNN and PyTorch SDPA ship their own flash-style kernels, so check current versions.
- Turing and older GPUs (only a separate third-party flash-attention-turing repo), CPUs, or Windows builds, which the README calls under-tested.
- Pure C++ inference engines without PyTorch: the shipped interface is a Torch extension, so you would have to lift kernels out of csrc/ and hopper/ yourself.
- Builds on small machines: the README warns that compiling can take about 2 hours without ninja and that ninja can exhaust RAM under 96 GB unless MAX_JOBS is set.

**Integration:** module (PyTorch CUDA extension; pip wheels flash-attn, flash-attn-3 from hopper/, flash-attn-4) · PyTorch 2.2+, CUDA 12.0+ (FA3: CUDA 12.3+, 12.8 recommended) or ROCm 6.0+, CUTLASS (git submodule), packaging, psutil, ninja · nvcc compiling C++17 (-O3 --use_fast_math, -gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a for FA3) · Linux; NVIDIA sm80/sm86/sm89/sm90 (FA2), sm90 H100/H800 only for FA3, Hopper/Blackwell for FA4; AMD CDNA/RDNA via CK or Triton

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlashAttention over ThunderKittens when you want a maintained, pip-installable attention module with KV-cache, varlen, GQA and AMD support; ThunderKittens reports 10-40% faster attention backward than FA3 and is the choice for writing custom Hopper kernels. The CPU siblings (LIBXSMM, MNN, T-MAC, llamafile) do not target GPU attention.

**Gotchas:**
- Since v2.1 the causal mask is aligned to the bottom-right corner when seqlen_q != seqlen_k; rows that are fully masked return zeros.
- deterministic=False is the default for backward; an open FA3 issue (#2244) reports dQ still differing between runs with deterministic=True, which others could not reproduce.
- flash_attn_with_kvcache has no backward pass and updates k_cache/v_cache in place; paged blocks must be a multiple of 256.
- FA3 wheels compile a large instantiation matrix (head dims x dtypes x paged/split/softcap); use the FLASH_ATTENTION_DISABLE_* environment flags to cut build time.

**Status:** Actively maintained, very widely used (about 24.8k stars), BSD-3-Clause; FA3 is still labelled a beta release in the README, and new work has moved to the CuTeDSL FA4 package.

[repo](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08608)

##### FlashAttention-4 (CuTeDSL, Hopper/Blackwell)  `Python (CuTe-DSL, kernels JIT-compiled; flash_attn/cute)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Blackwell/Hopper exact attention kernels in CuTe-DSL; beat cuDNN 9.13 by 1.04-1.29x on B200, roughly tie cuDNN 9.19.

**Beats:** cuDNN 9.13.0 fused attention (also benchmarked: cuDNN 9.19.1.2, Triton 3.6.0, Gluon 3.6.0, FlashAttention 2.8.3) — The paper PDF in the repo times FA4 against cuDNN 9.13.0 and 9.19.1.2, Triton 3.6 and FA 2.8.3 on a B200 in BF16 (CUDA 13.1, CuTe-DSL 4.4.1, PyTorch 2.10.0; 5 warmup runs, mean of 10), with total tokens fixed at 32K and head dim 64, 128 or (192,128): FA4 is 1.04-1.24x faster than cuDNN 9.13 forward and 1.09-1.29x backward, peaking at 1613 TFLOPs/s (1654 at head dim 192/128). Against cuDNN 9.19.1.2 the forward is at parity (0.91-1.06x) and only the backward keeps a lead of up to about 1.14x at long sequences (ratios derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Upgraded B to A under the FlashAttention-3 precedent (public harness benchmarks/benchmark_attn.py, stated toolchain, named B200). The 1.3x headline is against cuDNN 9.13; against cuDNN 9.19.1.2 the lead is forward parity and backward up to 1.14x only.

**Known shortcoming:** PyPI is still alpha (4.0.0b33, weekly betas). Python-only, no C++ API; JIT compile on first use per shape (#2635: slow B300 training). Tied to nvidia-cutlass-dsl versions (#2797 open: backward never returns on cutlass-dsl 4.6.0/4.6.1, sm_103); #2860 open: SM120 illegal memory access with 4+ varlen segments. FP8 is forward-only and SM100-only; the default backward is nondeterministic. The interface also accepts SM80/SM120, for which the paper gives no numbers. A search snippet puts cuDNN ahead at 1K-2K causal (about 315 vs 208 TFLOPs/s), source unverified.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** On B200 the tensor cores doubled while shared-memory bandwidth and the MUFU exponential unit did not, so the paper attacks the non-matmul bottlenecks: a ping-pong pipeline over fully asynchronous Blackwell MMAs that write to tensor memory (TMEM), with a separate correction warpgroup for output rescaling. For 10-25% of each softmax row, exp2 runs as a polynomial on FMA units after Cody-Waite range reduction, in parallel with the hardware MUFU unit, and online-softmax rescaling is skipped unless the running max grows by more than a threshold (log2 256 = 8). The backward pass keeps more intermediates in TMEM and uses the 2-CTA MMA mode so each CTA stages only half of operand B, which cuts shared-memory traffic and halves the dQ global atomic adds; longest-processing-time-first tile scheduling helps causal and varlen workloads.

**Use it when:**
- Training or prefill on B200/GB200-class GPUs (SM100) in BF16/FP16 with head dim 64, 128 or (192,128), especially sequences of 4K tokens and longer where it leads every baseline in the paper.
- Backward-heavy training at long sequence lengths: the backward pass still leads current cuDNN 9.19.1.2 by up to about 1.14x at 8K-32K tokens (derived from page data).
- You need attention variants (custom score_mod/mask_mod, block sparsity, learnable sinks, MLA head dims 512, softcap) without writing CUDA C++; the paper reports 2.5 s / 1.4 s JIT compile per kernel versus 55 s / 45 s for FA3's C++ templates.
- Reproducible RL or debugging runs that need a deterministic backward (deterministic=True) at a moderate cost on SM90/SM100.
- A Hopper (SM90) codebase that wants one Python-level attention library spanning H100 and B200.

**Skip it when:**
- Short causal sequences (1K-2K) on B200 when cuDNN 9.19+ is available: cuDNN is ahead there (e.g. 822 vs 744 TFLOPs/s at 1K causal, head dim 128), and the paper's own Figure 4 caption says newer cuDNN reaches similar performance.
- A C or C++ application with no Python runtime: there is no C++ API; kernels are generated through Python, PyTorch and nvidia-cutlass-dsl at run time.
- Pre-Hopper or non-NVIDIA hardware: the README targets Hopper and Blackwell, the interface has SM80/SM120 paths but the paper reports no numbers for them, and AMD needs a different library.
- FP8 training: FP8 is forward-only and only on SM100 (the interface raises NotImplementedError for an FP8 backward).
- Shops that need a stable release: PyPI still ships weekly betas (4.0.0b33 on 2026-09-30) with the classifier 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha', and several FA4 correctness issues are open.

**Integration:** module · PyTorch, nvidia-cutlass-dsl>=4.6.2 (cu13 extra for CUDA 13), apache-tvm-ffi>=0.1.11,<0.2, torch-c-dlpack-ext, quack-kernels>=0.5.3, einops, typing_extensions · Python 3.10+; CUDA 12.x (CUDA 13 recommended for B200 via the cu13 extra); nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.6.2+ at HEAD (the paper used CuTe-DSL 4.4.1 with CUDA 13.1 and PyTorch 2.10.0) · Linux, NVIDIA GPUs: SM90 (H100/H200) and SM100/SM103/SM110 (B200/B300) are the documented targets; the interface also accepts SM80 and SM120 with reduced features (no block-sparse, score_mod or deterministic backward on SM120)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FlashAttention-3 when you are on Blackwell (FA3 does not run on B200 per the paper) or want Python-level attention variants with fast JIT builds; pick it over ThunderKittens when you want a maintained pip package with varlen, paged KV and GQA rather than a kernel-authoring framework. Choose SageAttention or SpargeAttn instead only if you accept quantized or sparse approximate attention on consumer GPUs.

**Gotchas:**
- Each new shape or option set JIT-compiles on first call; issue #2635 (closed) reported very slow Qwen3.5-35B-A3B training on 8x B300 caused by CUTLASS JIT compilation during the backward pass, so warm up shapes before timing or serving.
- The default backward is nondeterministic (inter-CTA atomic dQ reductions, and dK/dV for GQA); deterministic=True serializes them with a semaphore and reaches up to 75% of the 1-CTA nondeterministic backward speed per the paper.
- Softmax uses a polynomial exp2 for part of the elements: the degree-3 version has a max FP32 relative error of 8.8e-5 (about 600x the hardware MUFU.EX2) but matches hardware within 1 BF16 ULP; check against a reference softmax if you consume FP32 intermediates or the LSE.
- Version coupling to nvidia-cutlass-dsl matters: issue #2797 (open) reports the FA4 backward never returning with cutlass-dsl 4.6.0/4.6.1 on B300 (sm_103), #2860 (open) an illegal memory access on SM120 with 4+ varlen segments, and #2665/#2886 were hd256 non-contiguous Q/K correctness bugs on SM100 (fixed).

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-02, weekly PyPI betas, 25.1k-star repository shared with FA2/FA3) and BSD-3-Clause, but still labelled Alpha and tied to fast-moving nvidia-cutlass-dsl releases, so pin both versions.

[repo](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/HEAD/assets/fa4_paper.pdf)

##### HipKittens (AMD) / ThunderKittens sibling  `C++ (HIP)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

C++ tile-primitive kernel DSL for AMD Instinct GPUs; its GQA attention backward runs about 3x faster than AITER on MI355X.

**Beats:** AITER (AMD hand-tuned assembly attention kernels); also Composable Kernel, PyTorch SDPA, Triton and hipBLASLt in other plots — On one AMD Instinct MI355X with BF16 inputs, the repo's committed results for GQA attention backward (batch 16, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128) give HipKittens 881 to 1176 TFLOPS for sequence length 1024 to 16384 against AITER's 300 to 389 TFLOPS (about 2.9-3.0x; causal 3.0-4.3x), timed with torch.cuda events over 100 iterations after 500 warmups, kernels built with hipcc in the ROCm 7.0 preview image (-ffast-math, C++20, gfx950). AITER is timed through a PyTorch autograd backward call while HK times its three kernels directly, and on MHA shapes HK falls 3-9% behind AITER at longer sequences.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~3x win over AITER is GQA-only; on MHA backward HipKittens is 0.91-0.97x of AITER from N=2048-4096 up. Timing is asymmetric: AITER is timed through torch autograd .backward() while HipKittens times its kernels directly. PyTorch SDPA bars in the GQA plots copy the MHA values.

**Known shortcoming:** Open #74: ragged/unaligned shapes silently drop partial edge tiles (wrong results, no error). dQ is accumulated with BF16 atomics, so gradients are not deterministic. Open #42: possible vmcnt race in the 4-wave FP8 GEMM (same bug fixed in the 8-wave kernel, commit 20cd6bb). Shapes are compile-time -D constants; docs link is empty.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Tiles are sized to the CDNA matrix-core (MFMA) shapes and loaded with coalesced, bank-conflict-free layouts and direct buffer loads into shared memory to hide address computation. Kernels overlap compute and memory with two schedules the authors name 8-wave ping-pong and 4-wave interleave, and order thread blocks for the chiplet (XCD) layout; the inner loops use explicit s_waitcnt lgkmcnt/vmcnt counts and sched_barrier hints instead of relying on the compiler. The GQA backward kernel launches one block per (KV head, 256-row KV block, batch), loops over all query heads in the group and accumulates dQ with packed BF16 atomic adds.

**Use it when:**
- Training or fine-tuning with grouped-query attention (e.g. 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128) on MI350X/MI355X, where the backward pass is about 3x AITER's in the committed results
- Writing your own fused AMD kernel and wanting MFMA-shaped tile abstractions instead of raw HIP intrinsics or Composable Kernel templates
- Fixed, known shapes (batch, heads, sequence a multiple of the 256-row block) that you can bake into a build
- Studying how to schedule compute and memory on CDNA3/CDNA4 (the analysis/ directory has the sweep scripts, plots and baseline recipes from the paper)
- Consuming the HK kernels indirectly: AITER merged an HK-based 128-head MLA decode kernel (ROCm/aiter PR 2039, March 2026) and the README says AMD Transformer Engine has an HK backend

**Skip it when:**
- MHA (H_KV = H) attention backward at sequence length 2048-4096 and above: the same harness shows HK 3-9% slower than AITER
- NVIDIA or RDNA GPUs: CDNA3/CDNA4 (and initial CDNA5/gfx1250) only; RDNA4 support is an open question (issue 13)
- Ragged or unaligned shapes (MoE experts, variable-length batches): grids are computed with integer division, so partial edge tiles are silently dropped and results are wrong without padding (open issue 74)
- When you need deterministic gradients: dQ is accumulated with BF16 atomics
- When you want a stable, documented API: docs/README.md has an empty HipKittens documentation link, and kernels are research code tuned per shape

**Integration:** header-only · ROCm with hipcc (README uses the rocm/7.0-preview PyTorch Docker images), pybind11 and Python for the shipped kernels; PyTorch and AITER for the tests and benchmarks · C++20 (common.mk sets -std=c++20), hipcc from ROCm 7.0 preview images · AMD CDNA4 gfx950 (MI350X/MI355X) on main; CDNA3 gfx942 (MI300X/MI325X) via the cdna3 branch per README (include/cdna3 also exists on main); CDNA5 gfx1250 unit tests on main

**Vs siblings:** Pick HipKittens when the target is AMD Instinct hardware; ThunderKittens, FlashAttention-3, SageAttention and FFPA in this category are NVIDIA-only, and HK is the same tile-DSL idea as ThunderKittens ported to CDNA. On NVIDIA use ThunderKittens or FlashAttention-3 instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Batch, query heads, KV heads and sequence length are -D compile-time constants (ATTN_B, ATTN_H, ATTN_H_KV, ATTN_N); a new shape means a rebuild, and the backward grid uses ATTN_N / 256
- The backward pass is three launches (prep, combined dK/dV/dQ, dQ shuffle) and expects pre-zeroed output buffers in specific layouts
- Hand-tuned s_waitcnt counts are fragile: a race in the 8-wave FP8 GEMM epilogue was fixed in commit 20cd6bb and issue 42 asks whether the 4-wave FP8 kernel has the same bug (open, unverified)
- Gradients match AITER only to BF16 rounding (the verifier saw max abs error 0.0039 at N=1024), and -ffast-math is on for the attention builds

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-22, MLSys 2026 paper, CDNA5 support landing) and MIT-licensed, but it is research code with per-shape kernels and no API docs, so expect to read and adapt kernels rather than link a library.

[repo](https://github.com/HazyResearch/HipKittens) · [benchmark](https://github.com/HazyResearch/HipKittens/tree/main/analysis/attn/bkwd)

##### HyperJet (hyper-dual number automatic differentiation)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++23 hyper-dual numbers giving value, gradient and dense Hessian in one pass; 1.2-3.3x faster than Eigen AutoDiffScalar/autodiff.

**Beats:** Eigen AutoDiffScalar (nested), autodiff (dual2nd) and ceres::Jet — The author's Google Benchmark harness (benchmark/compare/compare.cpp, Apple clang 21.0.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG on an Apple M1 Pro, Eigen 3.4.0, autodiff v1.1.2, Ceres 2.2.0) times value, gradient and dense Hessian of a cable strain-energy sum: static HyperJet takes 15/101/921/12,214 ns at n=3/6/12/24 against 18/328/2,888/22,105 ns for nested Eigen AutoDiffScalar and 127/375/2,425/17,679 ns for autodiff dual2nd, after checking all contenders agree bit-for-bit. For gradients alone it ties Eigen AutoDiffScalar and is about 1.25x faster than ceres::Jet at n=24.

**Known shortcoming:** No gain for gradient-only work (the win is in second derivatives).

**Known shortcoming:** 'pip install hyperjet' gives 1.5.0 (2023), not the benchmarked C++23 code; README's CPM pin @2.0.0 points at a tag that does not exist (latest v1.5.0), and the rewrite is untagged on main; single-machine author benchmark.

**How:** Hyper-dual (truncated second-order Taylor) arithmetic propagates the gradient and Hessian through each operation via the chain rule, so the Hessian comes from one evaluation rather than nested first-order duals (Eigen AutoDiffScalar of AutoDiffScalar) or n(n+1)/2 re-evaluations (autodiff dual2nd's hessian()). The Hessian is stored as a packed upper triangle in a fixed-size std::array, all operators are force-inlined, and constant partials (zero, one, minus one) are compile-time tags that fold away. Above 8 variables the gradient and Hessian are updated in one fused pass over the data array, a threshold the source comments say was measured on an M1 Pro (n=16 35% faster fused, n=6 14% slower).

**Use it when:**
- Element-level Hessians in nonlinear finite-element, isogeometric or cable/shell mechanics codes, where each element has a small, compile-time-known number of DOFs (roughly 3-24).
- Newton-type solvers that need exact local Hessians of small dense functions evaluated many times (strain energies, constitutive laws).
- Python prototyping of second-derivative code: static types back a NumPy dtype, which the README measured at 52x-246x faster than dtype=object arrays for elementwise ops.
- Assembly code that wants derivatives keyed by variable name and projected onto a caller-chosen global ordering (SSScalar g(names)/hm(names)).

**Skip it when:**
- Gradient-only work: the README's own first-order table shows no gain over Eigen AutoDiffScalar (244 vs 245 ns at n=24), and Ceres Jet comes with a solver.
- Variable counts unknown at compile time: the dynamic variant allocates per operation and was 43x slower than static at n=3, and slower than both Eigen AutoDiffScalar nested and autodiff dual2nd at every tested size in the second-order table.
- Many inputs or large n: forward-mode cost and the dense Hessian grow quadratically, and the speedup already narrows to 1.5x at n=24; reverse-mode tools (Adept, XAD) suit scalar functions of hundreds of inputs.
- Toolchains older than GCC 14 / Clang 18 / MSVC 19.38: the header uses C++23 explicit object parameters ('deducing this').
- Projects needing third derivatives or sparse Hessians within a set of variables: only first and second order are provided, and SSScalar's Hessian is dense over the names it carries.

**Integration:** header-only · none for C++ (standard library only); Python bindings need pybind11, scikit-build-core and NumPy >= 2.0 · C++23; GCC 14+, Clang 18+, MSVC 19.38+ (README); CMake 3.14+ for the provided target · any (portable C++; benchmarks only on Apple M1 Pro)

**Vs siblings:** Pick HyperJet over Adept-2, XAD or FastAD when you need exact dense Hessians of small fixed-size functions, since those tape-based tools target first-order reverse mode over many inputs (Adept has no higher-order mode). Sleipnir bundles its own AD with an NLP solver and Enzyme needs an LLVM plugin; neither is a lightweight per-element Hessian scalar.

**Gotchas:**
- pip install hyperjet installs 1.5.0 from August 2023, not the benchmarked C++23 code; the README's CPM line pins HyperJet@2.0.0, but the tags page shows no 2.0.0 tag (latest v1.5.0), so pin a commit on main to get the rewrite (C++23 switch landed May 2026, benchmark July 2026).
- C++ accessors g(i), h(i), h(i,j) are only checked by assert in debug builds; constructors and resize/eval paths throw std::runtime_error unless HYPERJET_NO_EXCEPTIONS is defined.
- References returned by data() from a temporary expression are valid only within the full expression, as with std::vector::operator[].
- Performance depends on inlining: the README measured a 1.56x penalty for HyperJet (similar for Eigen and Ceres) when the enclosing expression is not inlined, and writing acc += term instead of acc = acc + term saved 8% at n=24.

**Status:** Actively developed by a single author (C++23 rewrite in May 2026, last commit 2026-07-28, 17 stars) under MIT, small enough to vendor as one header, but the rewritten version has no tagged release or PyPI package yet.

[repo](https://github.com/oberbichler/HyperJet) · [benchmark](https://github.com/oberbichler/HyperJet#performance)

##### Mooncake.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Julia source-to-source AD compiler (forward, reverse, Hessians) that roughly halves warm gradient time versus Zygote on CPU Flux models.

**Beats:** Zygote.jl (default reverse-mode AD behind Flux) — The repository's auto-generated Flux benchmark (Julia 1.12.7, Flux 0.16.11, Mooncake 0.5.51 at a dirty commit, 1 Julia thread, 1 BLAS thread, inputs enlarged 32x, median of at least 10 warm samples in a 2 s budget, first gradient in a fresh process) on an Arm GB10 machine (Cortex-X925 + Cortex-A725, NVIDIA GB10 GPU) found Mooncake's warm gradients 2.03x faster than Zygote by geometric mean over 19 small Flux models on CPU and 1.05x on GPU, with first gradients 10.57x (CPU) and 3.26x (GPU) slower. The baseline is Zygote, not a vendor kernel library, and the run is first-party on one machine.

**Known shortcoming:** Julia only, not callable from C++; first gradient 3-10x slower (compilation); benchmarks run from a '-dirty' tree.

**Known shortcoming:** Docs list silent wrong-gradient cases: global/NoTangent aliasing (#1295), type-parameter data, explicit invoke (#1300), args_to_zero=false corrupting gradients (#1238). No thread-safety guarantee. Julia only, not callable from C++.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It runs AD on Julia's type-inferred, optimised IRCode instead of tracing at run time: each primal statement becomes a forward fragment and a pullback fragment, these are assembled into separate forward and pullback CFGs (with block stacks and edge-specific reverse blocks for phi nodes), lowered back to IRCode, optimised by the Julia compiler and wrapped in opaque closures. The prepared cache owns all gradient buffers and reuses them in place on every call, so warm calls avoid most allocation. The cost is compile time: the first gradient includes building and compiling the derived rule.

**Use it when:**
- Julia training or inference loops that call the gradient of the same function on same-shaped inputs many times, so the one-off cache preparation is amortised
- Small, recurrent or allocation-heavy CPU models where Zygote spends time on run-time overhead: in the Flux benchmark RNN gradients were about 5x faster (1.62 ms vs 313 us) and Maxout about 12x (136 us vs 11.4 us)
- Numerical Julia code that mutates arrays in place, which the README names as the main coverage gain over Zygote, ReverseDiff and ForwardDiff
- Projects that need forward mode, reverse mode and Hessians (forward-over-reverse) from one package

**Skip it when:**
- Short-lived scripts or one-shot gradients: first gradients were about 10x slower than Zygote on CPU by geometric mean (Dense(2 => 4): 12.5 s vs 693 ms) and about 3x slower on GPU
- GPU-bound models: warm GPU gradients were only 1.05x faster by geometric mean, and about half the GPU rows were slightly slower than Zygote
- Normalisation and attention layers on CPU: LayerNorm (1.38x slower), MultiHeadAttention (1.37x slower) and Flux.Scale (1.26x slower) lost to Zygote warm
- Code using try/catch in reverse mode, mutation of globals, threads/tasks, KernelAbstractions-style foreign-call CUDA kernels, or self-referential types; the known-limitations page lists these, some as silent wrong-gradient cases
- Anything outside Julia: it cannot be called from C++; C/C++ projects should look at Enzyme or the C++ tape libraries instead

**Integration:** module · ADTypes, ChainRulesCore, DispatchDoctor, ExprTools, MistyClosures, PrecompileTools, plus stdlib LinearAlgebra, Random, Test; optional package extensions for CUDA, cuDNN, Flux, NNlib, LuxLib, Distributions, SpecialFunctions and others · Julia 1.10.8 (compat '~1.10.8, ~1.11.6, ~1.12.1, ~1.13.0'); only the current LTS (1.10) and latest stable (1.13) are officially supported and CI-tested · any platform Julia runs on; GPU through the CUDA/cuDNN extensions (benchmark run on aarch64 with an NVIDIA GB10)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Mooncake when your model is in Julia and you want a pure-Julia reverse-mode backend that handles mutation and beats Zygote warm; for C/C++ code it is not an option, and Enzyme (LLVM-level AD, also usable from Julia) or the C++ tape libraries XAD, FastAD and Adept-2 are the catalogued choices.

**Gotchas:**
- The returned gradient aliases the cache's own buffers; the next value_and_gradient!! call overwrites it, so copy it if you keep it
- A cache is tied to its input types and sizes; a differently sized input raises an error, so variable batch sizes need one cache per shape
- args_to_zero = false skips cotangent zeroing and can silently corrupt gradients of other arguments (issue #1238) unless the argument has no differentiable data
- Reverse mode can stop LLVM from vectorising loops that vectorise in the primal; the docs recommend hand-written rrule!! rules for hot SIMD loops (as done for kron)

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-30, version 0.5.61 in Project.toml, 409 stars, no open bug-labelled issues), MIT-licensed, installable through the Julia package manager; the maintainers state a conservative, correctness-first scope and plan to move rules for non-Base packages out of the repository.

[repo](https://github.com/chalk-lab/Mooncake.jl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/chalk-lab/Mooncake.jl/blob/HEAD/test/integration_testing/flux/README.md)

##### sgemm.cu (hand-tuned FP32 GEMM for NVIDIA GA102/Ampere GPUs)  `CUDA C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Hand-tuned row-major FP32 SGEMM kernels for Ampere; about 4-7% above cuBLAS SGEMM at large square sizes on an RTX 3090.

**Beats:** cuBLAS SGEMM (CUDA 12.6) — Two README plots, with no numbers in text: RTX 3090 at 350 W, CUDA 12.6 (driver 550.120), square row-major NN SGEMM at m=n=k 1024 to 12800 in steps of 128, sgemm.cu vs cublasSgemm in the same harness. By eye, sgemm.cu sits at about 25,000-25,500 GFLOP/s against cuBLAS at about 24,000-24,500 at large sizes (about 4-5%), and at about 23,000-23,500 vs 21,600-22,000 with clocks locked at 1395 MHz (about 6-7%). Each point is the mean of the second half of the timed calls (CUDA events, L2 flushed between calls) after 500 warm-up runs at 4096.

**Known shortcoming:** Gain over cuBLAS is about 4-7% at large sizes and it is slower at some small sizes; the HN title's '24% on 4090' is not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** All three kernels step C rows by n rather than ldc, so any ldc != n gives wrong output (tests always use ldc = n). sgemm.cuh puts non-inline functions in a header (single translation unit only). benchmark.sh defaults to CUBLAS=0: cuBLAS is a separate -DCUBLAS=1 build, not the same binary. Plot readings confirmed at about 4-5% over cuBLAS unlocked and 6-7% locked at large sizes.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Register-blocked SGEMM. On sm_80+, m or n above 2500 selects a 128x256x8 CTA tile with 256 threads, 64x64 warp tiles and a 16x8 accumulator per thread. Global-to-shared copies use cp.async into double-buffered shared memory, A is stored transposed with padding (ld 132), fragments are double-buffered in registers and read with 128-bit shared loads, and the hot paths are inline PTX. Smaller sizes use a 128x128x8 kernel (2 blocks per SM) with predicated LDG staging; pre-Ampere GPUs use a texture-fetch variant when operands are 16-byte aligned. The epilogue goes through shared memory and edges are handled with predicated loads and stores.

**Use it when:**
- Large FP32 GEMMs (m or n above about 4,000) on GA102-class Ampere (RTX 3080/3090, A10, A40, A6000) where results must stay strict FP32 rather than TF32.
- Power-limited or clock-locked GPUs: the margin over cuBLAS grew from about 4-5% to about 6-7% with clocks locked at 1395 MHz.
- When you want a small, readable, MIT-licensed SGEMM to vendor or study instead of linking cuBLAS, with row-major operands and ldc == n.
- As a starting point for tuning SGEMM on Ada or Turing, which the README expects to perform well but which are untested.

**Skip it when:**
- Small and mid-size GEMMs (below about 2,500): the curves cross, and cuBLAS wins at several sizes (near m=n=k=1280, about 17,000 vs 19,300 GFLOP/s).
- Calls that need transposes, batched or strided-batched GEMM, a non-default stream, error reporting, or a C stride different from n.
- When TF32, FP16 or BF16 tensor cores are acceptable: this is an FFMA kernel with single-digit gains, and tensor-core GEMMs are a different performance class.
- Hopper, Blackwell or non-NVIDIA hardware: the only published results are from one RTX 3090, and the tile choice is tuned for GA102.
- Long-lived production use: 10 commits, last on 2025-01-21, and an issue about the benchmark methodology left unanswered.

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA runtime only for the kernels (src/sgemm.cuh, src/kernels/*.cuh, common/'helper_cuda ptx.h'); cuBLAS and CMake 3.18+ only for the bundled benchmark and test · C++17; CUDA 11.5+ for sm_80+ (static_assert in sgemm.cuh); published results used nvcc V12.6.85, g++ 13.3 and CMake 3.28.3 · NVIDIA GPUs; the arch is a build-time macro (GPUCC, CUDA_ARCHITECTURES). sm_80+ uses the cp.async kernels and sm_7x uses the texture-load kernel; only the RTX 3090 (sm_86) is benchmarked; the README advises native Linux rather than WSL for measurements

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over fast.cu (BF16 tensor-core matmul for H100) and bare-metal (FP16 HGEMM tuned for an RTX 3070 Ti Laptop) when the GEMM must stay in FP32 on an Ampere or Ada consumer or workstation card. For int8 use nanoinfer; for CPUs, the AVX-512 DGEMM tutorial.

**Gotchas:**
- C-stride bug: all three kernels set the C pointer with m_idx * ldc but step between rows with n (stg_c_ptr + (i*16+p)*n), so any ldc != n writes to the wrong addresses. test.cu and benchmark.cu always pass ldc = n, so the tests never catch it.
- sgemm.cuh defines non-inline functions (and, for sm<80, global cudaResourceDesc/texture handles) in a header. Include it from only one translation unit or you get duplicate-symbol link errors.
- Reproducing the plots takes edits: benchmark.sh defaults to CUBLAS=0 and lock_clocks=0, and cuBLAS is a separate -DCUBLAS=1 build of benchmark.cu (default handle, no cublasSetMathMode call). benchmark.sh and test.sh also run sudo (rm -rf build).
- Correctness coverage is narrow: test.sh checks square sizes 2-3072 against a naive 16x16 kernel at 1e-4 tolerance, with no non-square shapes, strides or nonzero-offset submatrices.

**Status:** Stale since 2025-01-21 (10 commits, one unanswered issue, one unmerged Docker PR), but MIT-licensed and small enough (three kernel headers plus a PTX helper) to vendor. Fix or avoid the ldc != n bug first.

[repo](https://github.com/salykova/sgemm.cu) · [benchmark](https://github.com/salykova/sgemm.cu)

##### Sleipnir  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

C++23 reverse-mode autodiff plus Newton/SQP/interior-point NLP solver DSL; sets up and solves small optimal-control problems faster than CasADi+Ipopt.

**Beats:** CasADi 3.8.0 (autodiff and NLP frontend) with Ipopt 3.14.20 and MUMPS 5.8.1 — The project's own scalability benchmark (g++ 16.2.1, CMake default RelWithDebInfo, AMD Ryzen 7 7840U) compares Sleipnir with default options against CasADi 3.8.0 + Ipopt 3.14.20 + MUMPS 5.8.1 with tuned options: on the flywheel problem, solve is about 5.3x faster at 1000 samples (11.1 vs 59.0 ms) and 4.5x at 5000 (75.1 vs 339.4 ms) with setup 40-50x faster, but on cart-pole only setup wins and the solve is about 2x slower at 300 samples (2683 vs 1251 ms). This times a whole modelling+AD+solver stack, not AD alone.

**Known shortcoming:** Cart-pole solve is slower than CasADi from 150 samples up; flags come from the CMake RelWithDebInfo default (-O2 -g); baseline CasADi is not a category incumbent.

**Known shortcoming:** Heap corruption in RegularizedLDLT::compute_sparse (issue #1193, May 2026, fixed in PR #1198); AD speed is not isolated and open issue #660 says the AD is too slow for embedded use; cart-pole solve about 2x slower than CasADi; measured workload is a full NLP solve.

**How:** The autodiff graph records the linearity of every node (constant, linear, quadratic, nonlinear), so constant first and second derivatives are computed once at initialization and only nonlinear subgraphs are re-evaluated each iteration; quadratic problems get their Lagrangian Hessian and constraint Jacobians once without user hints. Expression nodes come from a thread-local pool allocator and are freed through intrusive reference counts with an iterative (non-recursive) teardown. Equality and inequality constraints are distinct types so setup dispatch happens at compile time, and Eigen's sparse matrices and a regularized LDLT factorization handle the KKT systems.

**Use it when:**
- Small to medium trajectory-optimization or model-predictive-control NLPs (hundreds to a few thousand stages) where problem setup time matters, e.g. re-building and solving each control cycle; flywheel setup was 0.37 ms vs 19.2 ms for CasADi at 1000 samples.
- Robotics code (the project comes out of the FRC robotics community) that wants a permissively licensed, dependency-light solver that cross-compiles via CMake toolchain files, since Eigen is the only heavy dependency.
- Problems with many linear or quadratic constraints, where cached constant derivatives remove most per-iteration AD work.
- When you want one modelling-plus-solver API in both C++ and Python, or need a non-double scalar type (the C++ API is templated for higher-precision types).

**Skip it when:**
- Harder nonlinear problems where solver robustness dominates: on cart-pole Sleipnir's solve time was slower than CasADi+Ipopt+MUMPS from 150 samples up (3065 vs 974 ms at 250 samples; 2683 vs 1251 ms at 300).
- If you need fast standalone derivatives: the AD is tree-based with dynamic dispatch and an open issue (#660) calls it too slow for embedded use; the benchmark never isolates AD speed.
- Large-scale NLPs that benefit from commercial sparse linear solvers (HSL MA27/MA57) in Ipopt; the benchmark README notes those may make Ipopt much faster than with MUMPS.
- Toolchains older than GCC 14 / Apple Clang 16 / Visual Studio 2022 17.13: the library requires C++23.
- Projects that need a stable versioned API: the README's FetchContent snippet tracks GIT_TAG main and PyPI is on 0.6.x with frequent dev builds.

**Integration:** shared lib (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults ON; static possible) via CMake FetchContent · Eigen (fetched at a pinned commit unless SLEIPNIR_USE_SYSTEM_EIGEN), gharveymn/small_vector; nanobind for Python bindings; Catch2 for tests · C++23; GCC 14 libstdc++ (Ubuntu 24.04), Apple Clang 16.0.0 (Xcode 16.2), MSVC from Visual Studio 2022 17.13; CMake 3.21+ · Windows 11, Ubuntu 24.04, macOS 14.5 (universal arm64/x86_64); PyPI wheels for Linux x86_64/aarch64, macOS universal2, Windows amd64/arm64

**Vs siblings:** Pick Sleipnir when the job is solving a constrained NLP end to end; Adept-2, XAD, FastAD and Enzyme only give you derivatives and leave the solver to you, and HyperJet gives dense small Hessians. If you only need gradients inside your own code, those siblings are the better fit.

**Gotchas:**
- The default CMake build type is RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g), which is also what the published benchmark used; set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release explicitly if you want -O3.
- solve() returns an ExitStatus (e.g. LOCALLY_INFEASIBLE, FACTORIZATION_FAILED, LINE_SEARCH_FAILED, DIVERGING_ITERATES, MAX_ITERATIONS_EXCEEDED, TIMEOUT) instead of throwing; check it. Defaults are tolerance 1e-8 and 5000 max iterations.
- Memory-safety history: issue #1193 (May 2026) found heap corruption in RegularizedLDLT::compute_sparse when two KKT matrices had the same nnz but different sparsity patterns (symbolic factorization cached by nnz only), fixed in PR #1198; aarch64-only test failures ('factorization failed', 'diverging iterates', issues #803/#804) were closed in March 2026.
- The benchmark README tells you to run ./tools/generate-scalability-results.sh, but the script lives at benchmarks/generate-scalability-results.sh.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-09-27, dev wheels weekly, 80 stars, BSD-3-Clause), with a pre-1.0 API and tracking of main recommended by the README, so pin a commit when vendoring.

[repo](https://github.com/SleipnirGroup/Sleipnir) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SleipnirGroup/Sleipnir/HEAD/benchmarks/README.md)

##### Adept-2  `C++`  `Apache-2.0 (library); GNU all-permissive license for test and benchmark code`  `active`  `Tier B`

Expression-template reverse/forward-mode C++ AD library with Fortran-like arrays; tapes faster than ADOL-C, CppAD and Ceres in third-party benchmarks.

**Beats:** CppAD (measured in the benchmark); autodiff (autodiff/autodiff, measured); ADOL-C and Sacado (named in the user guide, qualitative) — The ADBench paper (Microsoft, AD2016 / Optimization Methods and Software 2018) timed Adept 1.1-era code on a Xeon E5-1620 under Windows 10 with no compiler flags stated: bundle-adjustment Jacobians were about 12.5x faster than ADOL-C and 3.3x faster than Ceres at the smallest size (10.7x vs ADOL-C at the largest, where Ceres crashed), and split GMM gradients about 16x faster than ADOL-C, but unsplit GMM only about 1.8x and ADOL-C won at several sizes. Separately, Xcelerit's ad-benchmarks (GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma, Xeon Platinum 8488C) show Adept 2 faster than CppAD on Heston MC (91 vs 268 ms), SABR (19 vs 32 ms), XVA CVA (7.1 vs 8.0 s) and LIBOR swaption (1.15 vs 4.57 s), but slower than XAD on all four.

**Known shortcoming:** ADBench (OMS 2018) tested Adept 1.1 (2015), not Adept-2; Ceres crashed rather than 'did not finish'; unsplit GMM gain only 1.8x vs ADOL-C (the 16x is split-vs-split); ADOL-C is faster at some GMM sizes; baseline not in the category list.

**Known shortcoming:** Record mixed two sources: workload, benchmark_url, compiler and hardware describe Xcelerit ad-benchmarks (GCC 13.3, Xeon 8488C, run by the XAD vendor) while claimed_speedup came from ADBench (Adept 1.1 era); in ad-benchmarks Adept 2 beats CppAD on all 4 rows (Heston 91 vs 268 ms) and loses to XAD on all 4. Issues #36/#37 (wrong gradients, 2025) closed with no fix shown; unsplit GMM crashed at 429k parameters.

**How:** Expression templates collapse each right-hand-side statement into a single compile-time expression, so the tape stores one statement plus its precomputed partial derivatives instead of one node per elementary operation (Hogan 2014, ACM TOMS 40:26). Taping is cheap enough to redo on every call, which is why the ADBench paper found Adept's per-call ('split') taping barely slower than one large tape while ADOL-C slowed down markedly. The Stack uses raw dynamically allocated arrays (the base.h comment says these are faster than STL containers), passive array expressions are vectorized with SSE2/AVX/AVX-512/ARM NEON packets, and Jacobians are computed in OpenMP-parallel strips.

**Use it when:**
- Reverse-mode gradients of scalar objectives written in plain C++ with many inputs, where you want one-line taping per call and no separate tape-replay step (e.g. variational data assimilation, retrieval schemes, model calibration).
- Code that already thinks in Fortran-style arrays: Adept arrays let you differentiate whole-array expressions and exchange arrays with Fortran (array_fortran.h).
- Small dense Jacobians per residual, as in bundle adjustment, where ADBench measured Adept about 3.3x faster than Ceres and 10-12x faster than ADOL-C (derived from page data).
- Quant-style Monte Carlo or calibration sensitivities when you need an Apache-2.0 tape library and XAD is not an option: in Xcelerit's ad-benchmarks Adept 2 beat CppAD on all four workloads.
- Projects that need old toolchains: the ChangeLog keeps C++98 compatibility, with C++11 features (thread_local, move semantics, initializer lists) used when available.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need maximum tape speed: XAD's open-source tape mode was 1.1x (LIBOR) to 2.3x (Heston) faster than Adept 2 in ad-benchmarks, and the FastAD paper claims 2-10x over Adept.
- Higher-order derivatives: ad-benchmarks lists Adept as forward and reverse only, while CppAD and XAD are listed as higher-order; the Adept minimizers use first derivatives or a user-supplied Hessian.
- Very large single recordings: in ADBench unsplit Adept crashed on GMM at 429k parameters (and from the second size up on the 1k-point GMM), so large problems must be split into per-term recordings.
- Matrix-heavy code without an optimized BLAS: configure warns that without BLAS matrix multiplication is unavailable and without LAPACK linear-algebra routines are unavailable.
- When a hand-written adjoint or a source-transformation tool is feasible: ADBench found hand-written C++ about 3.5x faster than Adept on BA and Tapenade faster on GMM and BA.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (autotools build); a library-free single-translation-unit mode (adept_source.h) also exists · none for scalar AD; BLAS and LAPACK (detected via a Fortran compiler at configure time) for matrix multiply and linear algebra; OpenMP optional for parallel Jacobians · C++98 (C++11 required for ADEPT_STORAGE_THREAD_SAFE; thread_local used when available); autotools needed to build from a git snapshot (autoreconf -i) · any; vectorization on x86 SSE2/AVX/AVX-512 and 64-bit ARM NEON, disabled on 32-bit ARM

**Vs siblings:** Pick Adept over XAD or FastAD when you want Apache-2.0 AD with built-in multidimensional arrays, Fortran interop and minimizers more than peak tape speed (both siblings measure faster than Adept), and over Enzyme when you cannot depend on an LLVM/Clang plugin. HyperJet is for small dense second-order derivatives and Sleipnir is an AD-plus-NLP-solver stack, so neither replaces a general reverse-mode library.

**Gotchas:**
- Call stack.new_recording() after initializing independent variables and before any active arithmetic; the old Stack::start(), clear() and clear_statements() now throw feature_not_available.
- Errors are reported by throwing adept::exception subclasses (gradient_out_of_range, gradients_not_initialized, stack_already_active, wrong_gradient, non_finite_gradient, array exceptions).
- Compiling with -ffast-math silently turns on ADEPT_FAST_EXPONENTIAL, which changes exp results; ADEPT_FAST also disables dimension and alias checking, so aliased array statements need eval().
- Correctness history: 2020-2021 releases fixed wrong derivatives of Active<double>/int and product, wrong maxval/minval and norm2, and unaligned AVX crashes; two 2025 reports of wrong gradients on extreme-magnitude or redundant expressions (issues #36, #37) were closed with no maintainer fix shown on the issue pages.

**Status:** Maintained by Robin Hogan at ECMWF (last commit 2025-10-05, version 2.1.4 in progress, 189 stars); the Apache-2.0 library and all-permissive tests make it safe to vendor, though the official site and user guide (met.reading.ac.uk) were unreachable from here and open issues include a Mac install problem and out-of-tree build failure.

[repo](https://github.com/rjhogan/Adept-2) · [benchmark](https://github.com/auto-differentiation/ad-benchmarks)

##### BitBLAS  `Python (TVM/TileLang code generation) with CUDA kernels`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Auto-tuned mixed-precision GPU GEMV/GEMM (FP16/INT8 activations x INT4/INT2/INT1/NF4/FP4/FP8 weights) that beats FP16 cuBLAS by moving fewer bytes.

**Beats:** cuBLAS (W_FP16 A_FP16 GEMV/GEMM); also CUTLASS, bitsandbytes, FasterTransformer, TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and Marlin — First-party plots on an RTX 3090 and an A100-80GB with CUDA 12.1 (third-party baselines pinned by commit: bitsandbytes 0.43.0, vLLM, FasterTransformer, TensorRT-LLM, CUTLASS and Marlin, reproduced via the separate mlc-benchmark repo) show FP16/INT8 tensor-core GEMM matching cuBLAS/CUTLASS, FP16 x NF4 at 2x bitsandbytes and 4x FP16, and W_INT2 A_INT8 GEMV/GEMM at 8x/2x over FP16 cuBLAS on A100 for BLOOM/OPT/LLaMA layer shapes. The peer-reviewed Ladder paper (OSDI'24) covers the TVM-based artifact branch, not the later TileLang release, and all numbers are in images, not text.

**Known shortcoming:** At equal FP16 it is roughly even with cuBLAS (gains come from low-bit weights); tier B rests on the Ladder OSDI'24 artifact branch; archived 2026-02-24.

**Known shortcoming:** Archived with open wrong-result bugs in the headline formats, unanswered: #316 W2A8 6.2% mismatched on first call, #313 W4A8 Linear wrong values, #296 illegal memory access with scaling; no Hopper row in the support matrix.

**How:** It implements Ladder (OSDI'24): low-bit weights are stored packed and dequantized on the fly inside the tensor-core GEMM, so a memory-bound GEMV reads 4-16x fewer bytes than FP16. Weights are pre-permuted offline ('ladder permutate' into ldmatrix-friendly layouts, and 'lop3 permutate' so dequantization uses LOP3 bit tricks, fast_decoding), which removes layout shuffles and cheapens unpacking.
