Kernels are generated by TVM TIR or TileLang schedulers and tuned per shape and GPU, with dynamic-M kernels built for an opt_M list such as [1, 16, 32, 64, 128].

**Use it when:**
- Memory-bound LLM decode (batch 1 to small batches) with weight-only quantization (INT4/NF4/INT2) on Ampere or Ada NVIDIA GPUs (A100, A6000, RTX 3090/4090 are the tested platforms).
- Unusual format pairs that hand-written kernels lack: INT8 x INT2/INT1 (BitNet b1.58), INT4 x INT4, FP16 x FP4/FP8, BF16 x NF4.
- Research on new quantization formats, where you need a kernel for a dtype combination without writing CUDA (TIR/TileLang DSL customization).
- A frozen deployment where you can pre-tune kernels once and load them from BitBLAS's on-disk operator database.

**Skip it when:**
- New production work: the repo was archived on 2026-02-24 (last commit 2025-05-05) and open wrong-result bug reports will not be fixed.
- FP16 x FP16 or INT8 x INT8 GEMM alone: the benchmark README only claims to match cuBLAS/CUTLASS there.
- Hopper or Blackwell GPUs: the README support matrix has no sm_90 or newer row (tested platforms are V100, A100, A6000 and RTX 4090), so performance there is not documented.
- Latency-sensitive startup: the QuickStart says bitblas.Matmul initialization 'will take minutes' for a one-time kernel library build per configuration.
- Non-Linux hosts or Python-free C++ use: wheels are Ubuntu 20.04+ only, and the kernels are reached through a Python/TVM runtime.

**Integration:** module · PyTorch, a bundled TVM fork and TileLang (3rdparty, built with CMake against a downloaded LLVM 10.0.1 when building from source), CUDA toolkit >= 11.0, plus numpy, scipy, tornado, cloudpickle, ml_dtypes and others from requirements.txt · Python >= 3.8 and CUDA >= 11.0 for the PyPI wheel (Ubuntu 20.04+); source build needs CMake, gcc and LLVM · Linux x86-64 with NVIDIA GPUs; tested on V100 (sm_70), A100 (sm_80), A6000 (sm_86), RTX 4090 (sm_89); FP8 and INT4xINT4 only on sm_89. The OSDI artifact branch also lists an AMD MI250, and an install_amd.sh script exists (issue #298), but the main README support matrix is NVIDIA-only

**Vs siblings:** Pick BitBLAS over Marlin when you need weight formats other than FP16 x INT4 (INT2/INT1/NF4/FP4/FP8, or INT8 activations), or shape coverage beyond small batches; for plain GPTQ INT4 inference Marlin is a smaller, single-purpose kernel that is not archived. T-MAC and BitNet (bitnet.cpp) are the CPU counterparts for the same low-bit LLM workloads.

**Gotchas:**
- Open, unanswered correctness bugs in the formats the headline claim is about: #316 (W_INT2 A_INT8 Matmul, 0.1.0.post1) gives 6.2% mismatched elements (max abs diff 19,645) on the first call but correct results later, which the reporter attributes to a different kernel being selected; #313 reports wrong values from a W_INT4 A_INT8 Linear on an RTX 4090.
- #296 (open): bitblas.Linear with uint4 weights and with_scaling=True leads to a CUDA illegal memory access.
- Inputs whose M is not in opt_M run the next-larger tuned kernel (an M of 15 uses the M=16 kernel), so performance between tuned points is not what the plots show.
- The 8x/2x A100 claim compares W_INT2 A_INT8 against W_FP16 A_FP16 cuBLAS, so most of the gain comes from moving fewer bytes and depends on the model tolerating 2-bit weights; the PyPI release (0.1.0.post1, 2025-02-16) lags the repo, and the OSDI artifact lives on a separate TVM-based branch.

**Status:** Archived by Microsoft on 2026-02-24 (last commit 2025-05-05, PyPI 0.1.0.post1 from 2025-02-16); MIT-licensed and usable as a frozen dependency or reference for Ladder-style layout transforms, but bugs will not be fixed.

[repo](https://github.com/microsoft/BitBLAS) · [benchmark](https://github.com/microsoft/BitBLAS/blob/HEAD/benchmark/README.md)

##### Enzyme  `C++`  `Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception`  `active`  `Tier B`

LLVM/MLIR compiler plugin that generates gradients of optimized IR; matched or beat Tapenade and Adept in its NeurIPS 2020 study.

**Beats:** Adept and Tapenade (and AD on unoptimized IR) — The NeurIPS 2020 paper measures reverse-mode AD on ADBench (BA, LSTM, GMM) plus Euler/RK4 integrators, FFT and a 2D Brusselator on an AWS c4.8xlarge with hyperthreading and Turbo Boost disabled, taking geometric means over inputs: differentiating after optimization gives a 4.5x geomean speedup over differentiating unoptimized IR, and results vs Tapenade and Adept are given per benchmark only. LLVM version and flags are not stated in the evaluation, and the paper does not say where the benchmark code lives.

**Known shortcoming:** The 4.5x is Enzyme vs its own AD on unoptimized code; vs Tapenade and Adept only per-benchmark results, no overall ratio; no compiler flags or benchmark code location stated.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Outperforms Tapenade and Adept across tested benchmarks' overstates the paper (GMM/Bruss differences attributed to tape structure; ~0.8x Tapenade on GMM per Fig. 9 summary, unchecked); plugin needs LLVM 15+ while docs say 11-16; exceptions must be off and every differentiated function needs its IR.

**How:** It differentiates after the normal LLVM optimization pipeline has run, so loop-invariant code motion, inlining and dead-code elimination have already simplified the primal; the paper's norm example drops from O(N^2) to O(N) gradient work this way. Interprocedural type analysis (seeded from TBAA metadata) and activity analysis skip adjoints for values that cannot affect the output. Shadow memory mirrors active allocations, and cache minimization stores only the forward values the reverse pass needs. Being source-transformation AD, it avoids the runtime tape that operator-overloading tools such as Adept record.

**Use it when:**
- You need reverse-mode gradients of an existing C/C++/Fortran/Rust numerical kernel (simulations, integrators, bundle adjustment, LSTMs) without rewriting it in an AD type.
- Loop-heavy code where compiler optimizations shrink the primal before differentiation (the paper reports a 4.5x geomean gain from optimizing first).
- Mixed-language or GPU/parallel code: the authors' later SC'21/SC'22 papers add CUDA/ROCm kernels, OpenMP, MPI and Julia tasks.
- You already build with Clang/LLVM 15+ and can add a compiler plugin to the build.

**Skip it when:**
- Code that relies on C++ exceptions, runtime-loaded or self-modifying code, or shared libraries without IR: the paper requires IR for every differentiated function and exceptions disabled.
- Code with type punning (unions of differing types, copies of undefined memory) that defeats type analysis; you get errors or must use loose-type flags.
- Toolchains that are not LLVM-based (MSVC, stock GCC) or builds where loading an LLVM plugin is impractical.
- Quick prototyping where a header-only operator-overloading library (XAD, FastAD, Adept) is easier to set up and debug.
- When you need per-benchmark proof that it beats Tapenade: the paper attributes GMM and Bruss differences to tape structure and does not give a uniform win ratio.

**Integration:** shared lib (LLVM pass plugin: LLVMEnzyme-<ver>.so, ClangEnzyme-<ver>.so, LLDEnzyme-<ver>.so) · LLVM 15+ built with plugin support (CMake aborts below 15); CMake 3.13+; Ninja or Make. Packages on Homebrew, Spack and Nix. · C++17 to build the plugin; Clang/LLVM 15 or newer (CI matrix tests LLVM 15 and 16) · Linux and macOS in CI; any target LLVM supports in principle; GPU (CUDA/ROCm) per the SC'21 paper

**Vs siblings:** Pick Enzyme over XAD or FastAD when you cannot or will not rewrite code into an active scalar type, when the code spans languages or runs on GPU, or when compiler optimization of the primal matters; pick XAD or FastAD for a header-only C++ library with no compiler-plugin build step.

**Gotchas:**
- ClangEnzyme works on one translation unit only; if the differentiated function calls code in other files you need LLDEnzyme with LTO.
- Requires TBAA metadata and statically deducible types for active memory; enzyme-loose-types and enzyme-emptyfn-inactive exist to paper over ambiguous cases, at your own risk.
- The docs warn that LLVM's plugin infrastructure can be flaky or not built by default, and recommend building LLVM from source when loading segfaults.
- Indirect calls into code Enzyme cannot analyze need user-supplied custom gradients.

**Status:** Actively developed (1.7k stars, about 209 open issues) under Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions; usable today through Homebrew/Spack/Nix packages or a source build against LLVM 15+, with Julia, Rust and Fortran front ends.

[repo](https://github.com/EnzymeAD/Enzyme) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01709)

##### fbfft / fbcunn (FFT-based convolution for Torch7)  `Lua/CUDA C++ (Torch7 extension)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Archived Torch7 CUDA module set whose FFT spatial convolution ran about 4x faster than cuDNN R2 on large-kernel layers in 2015.

**Beats:** NVIDIA cuDNN R2 (layer-wise table); cuDNN R4 appears in the full-network tables where fbfft is slower — soumith/convnet-benchmarks (independent; Torch7 harness, 10 timed steps after dry runs with cutorch.synchronize) layer-wise table, last updated April 2015 on a Core i7-5930K + Titan X, gives fbfft 256 ms (101 forward, 155 backward) for five stride-1 layers (kernels 11x11, 9x9, 9x9, 7x7, 3x3, batch 128) vs 1019 ms (269 / 750) for cuDNN R2, about 4x. The same suite's whole-network tables show it ahead of cuDNN R2 but behind cuDNN R4 fp32 by 1.3x to 2.1x; compiler, flags and CUDA/cuDNN builds are not given.

**Known shortcoming:** Loses to cuDNN R4; repo moved to facebookarchive; BSD plus PATENTS rider; Torch7-era.

**Known shortcoming:** convnet-benchmarks 'fbfft' rows link to SpatialConvolutionCuFFT, whose current source uses cuFFT, so the page does not show whether fbfft kernels produced the 2015 numbers. Stride 1 only, float32 only, fbfft sizes power of 2 up to 256; needs CUDA 7.5/sm_35 plus Folly/fbthrift. Lost first-layer forward to cuda-convnet2 (57 vs 36 ms). Archived.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Convolution is done in the frequency domain: inputs, weights and gradients are zero-padded to a power-of-two size, transformed with batched FFTs, combined with batched complex matrix products (a transposed cuBLAS GEMM path, fbTransposeMM, is the default strategy) and transformed back, so cost depends little on kernel size. fbfft itself is a hand-written decimation-in-frequency FFT that keeps each transform in registers and exchanges data with warp shuffles, packing several small FFTs into one warp; it supports power-of-two sizes 2 to 256. The FFT path can also pad implicitly inside the transform instead of materialising padded copies, which the cuFFT path cannot.

**Use it when:**
- Reproducing or studying 2015-era FFT convolution results; the code is a readable reference for warp-shuffle FFTs and frequency-domain convolution (BSD-3-Clause)
- Stride-1 convolutions with large kernels (7x7 to 11x11) and many feature maps, which is where it won: in the layer-wise table its backward pass for the 9x9 layer took 45 ms vs 401 ms for cuDNN R2
- Mining the fbfft kernels for a small-size batched GPU FFT (sizes up to 256) in a new project, if you are willing to port them off Torch7 and old CUDA

**Skip it when:**
- Any current training or inference stack: it is a Torch7/Lua extension pinned to CUDA 7.5, sm_35, Folly, fbthrift, thpp and fblualib, and the repository was archived in 2022
- Modern cuDNN baselines: in the same benchmark suite whole networks were slower than cuDNN R4 fp32 (AlexNet 104 vs 81 ms, Overfeat-fast 342 vs 268 ms, OxfordNet 1092 vs 529 ms) and slower than Nervana neon
- Strided convolutions: both FFT modules assert stride 1 ('fft only supports stride-1 convolutions atm')
- Layers with few input planes or memory-tight GPUs: on the first layer (3 -> 96 planes, 11x11) its forward pass took 57 ms vs 36 ms for cuda-convnet2 and 56 ms for cuDNN R2, and padding every plane to a power of two inflates buffer memory
- fp16 or fp64 models: the module code assumes 4-byte float elements

**Integration:** module · Torch7 (with a patched nn branch), cutorch, cudnn.torch, fbtorch, fbnn, Folly, fbthrift, thpp, fblualib, glog, cuFFT, cuBLAS; fbfft kernels from fbcuda · CUDA 7.5 (CMake requires it), nvcc -arch=sm_35, C++11, Ubuntu 14.04-era toolchain; installed with luarocks · Linux x86-64 with an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 3.5 or higher

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only for historical or reference use: among GPU convolution siblings, Nervana neon beat both fbfft and cuDNN R4 in the same suite, and modern work should start from current cuDNN-backed frameworks; on CPU, NNPACK is the catalogued FFT/Winograd convolution library.

**Gotchas:**
- The rows labelled fbfft in convnet-benchmarks link to the SpatialConvolutionCuFFT class, whose current source sets fftImplementation = 'cufft'; which FFT backend produced the April 2015 numbers is not stated on the page
- fbfft returns UnsupportedSize for transform sizes other than powers of two up to 256 (asserts size <= 256), so very large feature maps fall back to cuFFT or fail
- SpatialConvolutionCuFFT rejects implicit padding ('cufft does not support implicit padding!'); pad the input explicitly or use the FBFFT module
- License is BSD-3-Clause plus Facebook's Additional Grant of Patent Rights Version 2, whose patent grant has a termination clause

**Status:** Abandoned: last code commit 2017-07-21, moved to facebookarchive/fbcunn and archived 2022-01-13; BSD-3-Clause with a patent grant, usable only as reference code since it does not build against current CUDA, Torch or PyTorch.

[repo](https://github.com/facebook/fbcunn) · [benchmark](https://github.com/soumith/convnet-benchmarks)

##### FlashInfer  `CUDA/C++ with Python`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

CUDA kernel library for LLM serving (paged/ragged attention, MLA, GEMM, MoE, sampling); beat vLLM 0.2.6 PageAttention and FlashAttention 2.4.2 kernels.

**Beats:** vLLM 0.2.6 PageAttention kernels and FlashAttention 2.4.2 (kernel-level, 2024 launch blog); Triton-based compiler attention backends in LLM serving (MLSys 2025 paper) — The project's 2024 posts timed FlashInfer 0.0.1 kernels (built with NVCC from CUDA 12.3.1, nvbench cold-L2) against FlashAttention 2.4.2 and vLLM 0.2.6 PageAttention on H100 SXM, A100 PCIe, RTX 6000 Ada and RTX 4090 with Llama-2-7B/70B head shapes: prefill and decode were best on all four GPUs (plots only), batch GQA decode was 3x vLLM at batch 64, and cascade attention reached up to 31x vLLM on H100 for a 32k shared prefix. The MLSys 2025 paper (abstract seen via search; PDF blocked here) reports 29-69% lower inter-token latency than compiler (Triton) backends in end-to-end serving. These numbers are first-party and were not re-measured for current versions.

**Known shortcoming:** 31x vs vLLM 0.2.6 PageAttention is a best case from the 2024 launch blog (2-3x for GQA, CUDA 12.3.1); MLSys 2025 venue from search results (paper unreadable here); numbers are 2024-vintage and FlashInfer now also dispatches to third-party backends.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bugs: #1419 SM90 ragged prefill illegal memory access at total seqlen >= 16384 (fixed PR #2801); #2883 MLA decode NaNs in CUDA-graph padding (0.6.4/0.6.6, closed not planned); v0.2 post admits v0.1.6 prefill was slower than v0.1.1; all numbers first-party from 2024.

**How:** It treats paged and ragged KV caches as block-sparse matrices (down to page_size=1 'vector sparsity'), so one FlashAttention-2/3-style tiled online-softmax kernel serves every cache layout. Page indices are prefetched into shared memory, so page size does not slow the kernel. Decode uses split-KV (Flash-Decoding style) with a plan-time load-balanced scheduler, and GQA decode reuses the tensor-core prefill kernel, which the 2024 post measured at 3x vLLM at batch 64. Cascade inference computes shared-prefix attention once with a multi-query kernel and merges it with per-request suffix attention via the log-sum-exp 'attention state' merge operator. Kernels are specialized at JIT time from Jinja/CUDA templates, and calls can be dispatched to FlashAttention-3, cuDNN, CUTLASS, TensorRT-LLM or CuTe-DSL backends.

**Use it when:**
- Building or tuning an LLM serving engine that needs batched decode and prefill over a paged KV cache, with CUDA graphs and torch.compile
- Many requests share a long prompt (document QA, self-consistency or tree search sampling): cascade attention was up to 31x vLLM 0.2.6 PageAttention at a 32k shared prefix, batch >= 128 and short unique suffixes on H100
- GQA models (Llama-2-70B-style 8:1 head ratio and up) in batched decode, where the tensor-core decode path gives the 2-3x over vLLM's kernel
- DeepSeek-style MLA, FP8/FP4 attention, GEMM or MoE on Hopper or Blackwell, where it exposes the TensorRT-LLM and CUTLASS kernels behind one API
- Custom attention variants (logit soft-cap, sliding window, sinks, custom logits/query transforms) without writing a new kernel

**Skip it when:**
- Training or plain dense attention with fixed shapes: FlashAttention-2/3 or cuDNN SDPA are simpler, and FlashInfer itself dispatches to them in many configurations
- Non-NVIDIA GPUs (AMD, Intel, Apple) or pre-Turing NVIDIA (below SM 7.5); many features exist only on Hopper or Blackwell
- Environments that cannot JIT-compile or download kernels at first use (no nvcc, no network) unless you also install the flashinfer-cubin and flashinfer-jit-cache wheels
- Teams that need a stable API and behaviour: pre-1.0 releases ship every few days (0.6.18, then 0.7.0 on 2026-09-22, 0.7.1rc1 on 2026-09-30) with about 426 open issues, and per-backend bugs keep showing up (see gotchas)

**Integration:** module (pip flashinfer-python, with JIT-compiled or downloaded cubins and optional precompiled flashinfer-cubin / flashinfer-jit-cache wheels); header-only CUDA C++ templates in include/flashinfer for direct C++ use · PyTorch, CUDA toolkit (nvcc and ninja for JIT), apache-tvm-ffi, cuda-python, nvidia-cudnn-frontend, nvidia-cutlass-dsl, nccl4py/nccl-extensions, numpy, einops; submodules CUTLASS, CCCL, spdlog and nixl · Python 3.10+; CUDA 12.9 or 13.0 per the README's supported list (13.4 preview); setuptools 77+ for source builds · NVIDIA GPUs SM 7.5 (Turing) through SM 12.x (Blackwell RTX 50, DGX Spark, Jetson Thor); Linux x86-64 and aarch64 wheels; feature coverage varies by compute capability

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlashInfer when you need serving-specific attention (paged or ragged KV, mixed prefill and decode, shared prefixes, MLA) behind one API; use FlashAttention-3 for training or dense Hopper attention, SageAttention for quantized approximate attention, and Bruce-Lee-LY's Decoding Attention only for short-sequence batch-1 decode, where its README beats FlashInfer 0.1.6.

**Gotchas:**
- Wrappers need a zero-initialized, 16-byte-aligned workspace buffer (128 MB recommended); with use_cuda_graph=True the batch size is fixed for the wrapper's lifetime and index buffers must be preallocated
- backend='auto' picks fa2, fa3, cudnn, trtllm-gen or cute-dsl by GPU and shape, and features differ per backend (for example the cudnn decode backend lacks RoPE, soft-cap and FP8 KV), so speed and supported options change across GPUs and versions
- Correctness bugs have hit specific backends: ragged prefill on SM90 hit illegal memory accesses at total sequence length >= 16384 (issue #1419, fixed via PR #2801), and trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla wrote NaNs into CUDA-graph padded rows in 0.6.4/0.6.6 (issue #2883, closed as not planned)
- Performance moves between releases: the project's own v0.2 post says v0.1.6 prefill was slower than v0.1.1; allow_fp16_qk_reduction buys about 50% on RTX 4090 at reduced accumulation precision

**Status:** Very active (commits daily, 0.7.0.post1 on PyPI 2026-09-29, 6.5k stars), Apache-2.0, and the default attention backend in several major serving engines, so it is safe to adopt, though the published speedups date from 2024 and the API is still pre-1.0.

[repo](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer-ai.github.io/blob/main/_posts/2024-01-03-introduce-flashinfer.md)

##### FlashTP (SNU-ARC)  `C++/CUDA (PyTorch extension)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Fused, sparsity-aware CUDA kernels for e3nn's channelwise (uvu) tensor product; paper reports up to 41.6x over e3nn.

**Beats:** e3nn o3.TensorProduct (uvu, with torch_scatter) and NVIDIA cuEquivariance — The ICML 2025 paper (read here only through search-result snippets of its abstract) reports up to 41.6x and 60.8x kernel speedups over e3nn and NVIDIA cuEquivariance on the uvu tensor product, and 4.2x inference and 3.5x training speedups with 6.3x and 6.2x lower peak memory for SevenNet-l3i5; snippets mention an A100, but GPU model, precision and the configurations behind the maxima were not confirmed from the paper itself. SevenNet's own docs say FlashTP gives 'up to ~4x' speedup and lose to cuEquivariance above about 10^3 atoms.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the ICML 2025 paper, whose 41.6x/60.8x kernel and SevenNet 4.2x/3.5x figures were seen only in abstract snippets (openreview, mlanthology, arXiv blocked); GPU and flags unverified. OpenEquivariance issue #171 confirms FlashTP did not benchmark against OpenEquivariance.

**Known shortcoming:** Input-1 multiplicities must be multiples of 32 (asserted; issue #4 closed without answer). SevenNet's own accelerator docs say cuEquivariance is faster above about 10^3 atoms. Shared memory is chosen by matching 'A100' or 'H100' in the GPU name, with a 48 KiB fallback for anything else; scatter uses atomicAdd, so results are not bitwise deterministic; example/test.sh checks correctness only with no timing code; no pip release (issue #5 open); DDP illegal-memory-access issue #1 closed with no visible fix.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It fuses gather, tensor product, per-edge weighting and scatter-add into one kernel per pass, so the large per-edge intermediate tensor that e3nn materializes is never written to memory; that is where the reported 6x peak-memory reduction comes from. The Clebsch-Gordan coefficients are stored sparsely (only nonzero 'fibers', with values deduplicated into a uint8-indexed table of up to 256 unique values, or an extended-CG kernel above that), skipping the zero entries a dense e3nn contraction multiplies. Paths are grouped per input irrep and per 32-channel warp, inputs are staged in shared memory sized to the GPU (163 KiB on A100, 227 KiB on H100), and outputs are accumulated with atomicAdd.

**Use it when:**
- Training or running an equivariant MLIP (NequIP, SevenNet-style) on NVIDIA A100/H100 where the uvu tensor product dominates step time or GPU memory limits system size (the paper reports 28,000 atoms on one A100).
- Force training that needs double-backward through the tensor product, which FlashTP implements natively in fp32 and fp64.
- SevenNet users: it is wired in via --enable_flash, and SevenNet's docs say FlashTP with LAMMPS: Torch beats cuEquivariance with LAMMPS: ML-IAP for small systems (below about 10^3 atoms).
- Irreps whose input-1 multiplicities are all multiples of 32 (e.g. 32x0e, 64x1o) with e3nn's default component/element normalization and per-edge (non-shared, non-internal) weights.

**Skip it when:**
- Multiplicities that are not multiples of 32 (e.g. 10x1o, 40x0e): the module asserts mul % 32 == 0 and fails; issue #4 asking for a workaround was closed without an answer.
- Large systems: SevenNet's accelerator docs (citing the SevenNet-Omni paper) report a crossover around 10^3 atoms beyond which cuEquivariance is more efficient.
- Tensor products other than channelwise uvu (fully connected uvw, shared or internal weights), fp16/bf16, or non-NVIDIA GPUs: none are supported.
- GPUs other than A100/H100 without manual tuning: the shared-memory budget is chosen by matching 'A100' or 'H100' in the device name, and any other GPU drops to a 48 KiB 'safe mode' unless you pass smem_size.
- Projects that need a pip wheel or a version policy: install is from source with a CUDA build of up to 10 minutes (issue #5 asking for a pip release is open), version 0.1.1.

**Integration:** module · PyTorch >= 2.4.1, e3nn, CUDA toolkit 12+, ninja; torch_scatter only for the e3nn reference benchmark · Python >= 3.10 (setup.py), CUDA 12, PyTorch 2.4.1; nvcc built with -O2 · NVIDIA GPUs only; built for the detected compute capability, or sm_80 and sm_90 with PTX fallback when no GPU is present at build time (Blackwell runs via PTX JIT)

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlashTP over cuEquivariance for uvu-based models on small-to-medium systems (below about 10^3 atoms per SevenNet's docs) or when peak memory is the limit; pick cuEquivariance or OpenEquivariance for larger systems, multiplicities not divisible by 32, or non-uvu products, and Sobek if you want streaming convolutions that its authors report beat OpenEquivariance.

**Gotchas:**
- Output accumulation uses atomicAdd in the scatter step, so results are not bitwise deterministic run to run; the bundled correctness check compares against e3nn with a 1e-4 absolute tolerance.
- Unique Clebsch-Gordan values are deduplicated after rounding through fp32 even in fp64 mode, which picks the kernel variant (uint8-indexed vs extended CG above 256 unique values).
- The example/test.sh 'microbenchmark' runs one forward, backward and double-backward pass and checks correctness; it has no timing code, so reproducing the paper's speedups needs an external profiler (e.g. Nsight).
- Building can be killed by out-of-memory in ninja (exit 137); SevenNet's docs recommend MAX_JOBS=1.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-05-27, adding GPU auto-detection and PTX fallback), MIT-licensed, 23 commits and integrated into SevenNet main via --enable_flash, but still a 0.1.1 source-only research release with a TODO for further performance work and a JIT path.

[repo](https://github.com/SNU-ARC/flashTP) · [benchmark](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=wiQe95BPaB)

##### LIBXSMM  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

JIT-generated small GEMM, batch-reduce GEMM and element-wise kernels; DL layers built on it beat MKL-DNN by 1.1-1.7x.

**Beats:** MKL-DNN (oneDNN) — In Georganas et al. (IPDPS 2020, arXiv 1906.06440), Intel authors built LSTM, fully-connected and ResNet-50 convolution layers on LIBXSMM's batch-reduce GEMM and measured them against 2019 MKL-DNN on a 28-core Xeon Platinum 8180 with Intel compiler 18.0.0: LSTM 1.2-1.3x faster forward and 1.1-1.7x backward/update, FC 1.09-1.36x, ResNet-50 conv efficiency 83% vs 81%. Flags were not stated and the paper notes the gains shrink for large matrices.

**Known shortcoming:** Authors are from Intel, same vendor as the MKL-DNN baseline; paper gives no code link; flags not stated (Intel compiler 18.0.0).

**Known shortcoming:** Since 2.0 the paper's DL layers (LSTM, FC, conv) live in libxsmm/libxsmm-dnn; core covers small matrices only ((MNK)^(1/3) <= 64), larger shapes silently fall back to a slow reference kernel; JIT GEMM only alpha=1, beta 0/1, no transpose of A; Windows JIT limited to matmul.

**How:** Runtime code specialization: for each (M,N,K,ld,datatype,flags) it emits machine code fully unrolled for that shape, using the best ISA found via CPUID (AVX-512/VNNI/BF16, AMX, NEON/SVE/SME, RVV, POWER10 MMA), with operand prefetch hints for batches. The batch-reduce GEMM kernel (C = beta*C + sum_i A_i*B_i) keeps the output block in registers across a whole sequence of A/B block pairs, so higher-level layers become loops around one tuned microkernel instead of separate GEMM calls with C round-trips through memory.

**Use it when:**
- Many repeated multiplications of small matrices, roughly (M*N*K)^(1/3) <= 64, e.g. block-sparse or spectral-element/DG codes (CP2K/DBCSR, SeisSol, Nek5000, PETSc block kernels).
- Writing custom CPU DL operators (conv, FC, RNN, attention blocks) as blocked loops around BRGEMM plus fused element-wise TPPs.
- Low-precision CPU kernels (BF16, FP16, FP8 variants, int8/int4, MX formats) on AVX-512 VNNI/AMX, Arm SVE/SME or POWER10 without hand-writing assembly.
- Shipping one binary that should pick the right ISA at runtime ('build once, deploy everywhere') without -march flags.

**Skip it when:**
- Large GEMMs: there is no multi-level M/N/K cache blocking; large sizes generate excessive unrolled code and miss cache tiling, so use MKL/OpenBLAS/BLIS.
- You want ready-made DL layers: in 2.0 they moved to libxsmm-dnn and the PyTorch integration to tpp-pytorch-extension; the core repo only gives primitives.
- Full BLAS semantics: JIT GEMM kernels are limited to alpha=1, beta in {0,1}, transA='N' (BLAS-style wrapper falls back otherwise).
- Windows deployments needing more than the MM domain: the Compatibility wiki lists Windows JIT as MM-only without prefetch kernels.
- GPU workloads: CPU-only.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (GNU Make or CMake 3.13+), or header-only via libxsmm_source.h · none for the core; libxsmmext and the Fortran module need an OpenMP runtime; Fortran compiler optional (FORTRAN=0) · C compiler; GCC 5.1+ recommended (older GCC degrades CPUID-dispatched code); Clang, Intel; Fortran 2003 for the module · x86-64 (SSE through AVX-512/AMX), AArch64 (NEON/SVE/SME), RISC-V RVV, POWER10 ppc64le; Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, Windows (limited JIT)

**Vs siblings:** Pick LIBXSMM over Fastor when shapes are runtime values or you need low-precision/AMX/SVE kernels rather than compile-time fixed-size C++ tensors (Fastor can even use LIBXSMM as its JIT backend); pick it over the AVX512 DGEMM tutorial kernels or llamafile tinyBLAS when you need a maintained, multi-ISA library of small/batched GEMMs rather than large-GEMM or LLM-specific kernels.

**Gotchas:**
- Shapes over the JIT limits (operand >2 GiB, or >2 MB stack scratch for VNNI reformatting) silently fall back to a slow reference kernel; check libxsmm_get_kernel_info or run with LIBXSMM_VERBOSE=2.
- The public header is generated at build time (not in the repo); header-only use exposes internals and compiles your settings (e.g. NDEBUG) into LIBXSMM.
- No error returns from the frontend: failures are reported only via verbose mode, so a NULL kernel pointer must be checked by the caller.
- With verbosity on it installs SIGABRT/SIGSEGV handlers; set LIBXSMM_SIGNAL=0 if the host application owns signals.

**Status:** Actively developed (commits in late Sept 2026, 2.0 release restructured the repo) and BSD-3-Clause, packaged in Debian/Fedora/Ubuntu/Spack/Conda; note the benchmarked DL operators now live in libxsmm-dnn.

[repo](https://github.com/libxsmm/libxsmm) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.06440)

##### MNN  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Alibaba's on-device inference/training engine with hand-written ARM/x86 assembly and GPU backends; beat TF-Lite, NCNN, MACE on 2020 phones.

**Beats:** TensorFlow Lite, NCNN, MACE, CoreML (MLSys 2020 paper) — The MLSys 2020 paper (by the MNN team) ran MobileNet-v1, SqueezeNet-v1.1 and ResNet-18 at 224x224, batch 1, averaged over 10 runs, on iPhone 8/X, Xiaomi MI6 and Huawei Mate 20, and reports MNN about 20-40% faster than CoreML, TF-Lite, NCNN and MACE in almost all settings (4-thread CPU: ~30% on iOS, ~34% on Mate 20); on Metal it is comparable to CoreML. No compiler flags or benchmark harness are given in the paper.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper written by MNN's own team; 2020-era phones; never compared against XNNPACK or oneDNN.

**Known shortcoming:** Leaves out XNNPACK-backed TFLite, ONNX Runtime and LiteRT; only 3.4.x gets security support (model-file parsing in scope); global Executor not thread-safe, one Module per thread.

**How:** A 'pre-inference' pass, run once per input shape, scores candidate algorithms and backends (C_total = C_algorithm + C_backend) and picks, for example, sliding-window vs Winograd convolution per layer, then preallocates memory. Kernels are hand-optimized SIMD/assembly on an NC4HW4 blocked layout, with a generic Winograd generator for any kernel size and Strassen matrix multiply for large 1x1 convolutions (7.5-13.5% gain per the paper). On ARMv8.2 it uses FP16 arithmetic and SDOT int8 dot products, and on x86 AVX2/AVX512/VNNI paths.

**Use it when:**
- Shipping CNN or transformer inference inside an Android/iOS app where binary size matters (paper: 400-600 KB added; README: ~800 KB core .so on armv7a)
- Batch-1 mobile CNNs (MobileNet, SqueezeNet, ResNet-class) on ARM CPUs, especially ARMv8.2+ with FP16 or int8 SDOT
- One codebase that must target CPU plus Metal/OpenCL/Vulkan GPUs across a fragmented Android fleet
- Running quantized LLMs or diffusion models on-device through MNN-LLM / MNN-Diffusion
- x86 AVX2/AVX512 servers or desktops that need a light, dependency-free C++ runtime

**Skip it when:**
- You need an independently benchmarked winner today: the published comparison is first-party, 2020-era phones and engine versions, and omits XNNPACK-backed TFLite, ONNX Runtime and LiteRT
- Your model uses ops outside the converter's coverage (178 TF, 158 ONNX, 163 TorchScript ops listed); unsupported ops mean custom op work
- Datacenter GPU serving at scale: CUDA backend is rated 'A' (works, not deeply optimized) for FP32 and int8; TensorRT or vendor stacks fit better
- Backends rated 'B' in the README table (native CPU without SIMD, NNAPI, QNN FP16) are documented as buggy or unoptimized
- Teams that need English-first support: the README says community discussion is mostly in Chinese (DingTalk groups)

**Integration:** shared lib (default MNN_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON) or static lib; Python wheel · none at runtime for the core ('no dependencies' per README); converters need protobuf/flatbuffers; GPU backends need the platform's Metal/OpenCL/Vulkan/CUDA · CMake 3.6+; C++11 by default (C++17/20 for some options such as CUDA transformer fuse) · iOS 8.0+, Android 4.3+, Linux/macOS/Windows, POSIX embedded; ARMv7a/ARMv8 (FP16/SDOT on v8.2, BF16 on v8.6), x86-64 SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX512

**Vs siblings:** Pick MNN when you need a whole deployable runtime for mobile CNNs or LLMs across CPU and mobile GPUs; llamafile tinyBLAS and T-MAC are matmul/low-bit kernels for llama.cpp-style LLM inference on desktop CPUs, and nanoinfer is an educational engine that does not beat ONNX Runtime.

**Gotchas:**
- The first run per input shape triggers pre-inference (algorithm selection and memory planning); resizing inputs repeats it, so dynamic shapes cost latency
- Interpreter/Session APIs are marked deprecated in the Python docs; new code should use the Module API
- Security policy supports only the 3.4.x line and lists model-file parsing and converters as in scope; treat untrusted .mnn files as an attack surface
- README speedups for FP16 ('twice') and SDOT/VNNI ('2.5x') compare MNN's own paths, not competitors

**Status:** Very active (3.6.1 released 2026-07-22, commits in late September 2026), Apache-2.0, 16k stars and used in 30+ Alibaba apps; safe to adopt, but the speed claims date from 2020.

[repo](https://github.com/alibaba/MNN) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12418)

##### Nervana neon (GPU convolution kernels)  `Python`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Archived Python deep learning framework whose hand-assembled Maxwell GPU convolution kernels beat cuDNN R4 by 1.2-2x on 2016 ConvNet benchmarks.

**Beats:** cuDNN R4 (fp16 and fp32, via Torch bindings) — soumith/convnet-benchmarks (independent; i7-5930K + Titan X, Ubuntu 14.04, full forward+backward, averaged over 10 runs) lists Nervana-neon beside cuDNN R4 via Torch: OxfordNet model A 320 vs 529 ms fp32 and 254 vs 471 ms fp16, GoogleNet V1 270 vs 470 ms fp32 and 230 vs 462 ms fp16, Overfeat 211 vs 268 ms fp32 and 176 vs 242 ms fp16, while cuDNN R4 wins AlexNet. No compiler, driver or CUDA versions are stated, and the kernels benchmarked were the nervanagpu beta release rather than a tagged neon build.

**Known shortcoming:** convnet-benchmarks imports the standalone nervanagpu beta kernels (maxas SASS), not the neon repo itself; same lineage but identical kernels not confirmed; archived.

**Known shortcoming:** maxas is a Maxwell-only assembler, nothing past Pascal; open #461: GPU backend 90.2% MNIST error on GTX 1050/CUDA 10, no reply; Python/SASS, not C++.

**How:** The kernels are written directly in NVIDIA SASS (shader assembly) and assembled with maxas, Scott Gray's Maxwell assembler, so register allocation, instruction scheduling and control codes are hand-tuned rather than left to nvcc. For 3x3 stride-1 convolutions the backend uses Winograd minimal filtering, F(2x2,3x3) and F(4x4,3x3) variants for fprop, bprop and weight update, which cuts the multiplies per output. fp16 storage halves memory traffic, and the convnet-benchmarks script passes hand-picked per-layer tile shapes (grid_P, grid_Q, update_size) to each ConvLayer.

**Use it when:**
- Reproducing or studying the 2016 convnet-benchmarks results on Maxwell (GTX 9xx, Titan X) or Pascal GPUs, where the SASS kernels were tuned.
- Learning hand-written SASS GEMM and Winograd convolution techniques: the .sass sources, maxas and the Python kernel wrappers are Apache-2.0 (maxas is MIT).
- Legacy neon models that already run on a Maxwell/Pascal box with CUDA 7.x-8.0 and Python 2.7/3 environments of that era.

**Skip it when:**
- Any new project: the repository was archived on 2023-01-03 with an Intel discontinuation notice, and the last release is v2.6.0 (January 2018).
- Volta, Turing, Ampere, Hopper or later GPUs: maxas is described as an 'Assembler for NVIDIA Maxwell architecture' and nothing in the repo documents support beyond Maxwell/Pascal; pre-Maxwell GPUs fall back to slower CUDA C kernels.
- C++ codebases: the kernels are driven from Python through PyCUDA, with no supported native API.
- Comparisons against current cuDNN: the measured baseline is cuDNN R4, and cuDNN R4 still won AlexNet (71 vs 78 ms fp16, 81 vs 87 ms fp32).
- Modern Python stacks: requirements pin 2016-2018 packages (numpy 1.13.1, Pillow 3.3.2, PyYAML 4.2b1, pycuda >= 2015.1, scikit-cuda 0.5.1).

**Integration:** module (Python package nervananeon; SASS kernels JIT-assembled into cubins on first use) · PyCUDA, scikit-cuda, numpy, h5py, aeon data loader (separate install), CUDA toolkit with ptxas on PATH, Perl for maxas; MKLML for the CPU backend · Python 2.7 or 3 (setup.py classifiers), CUDA 7.0-8.0 era toolkit (Makefile searches cuda-8.0, cuda-7.5, cuda-7.0) · Linux and macOS; NVIDIA compute capability 5.0+ for SASS kernels (5.2+ for fp16), 3.0+ via CUDA C fallback kernels; x86 CPUs via MKL

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings is a GPU convolution library: NNPACK is the CPU Winograd/FFT convolution counterpart, and LIBXSMM, FeatherCNN and MNN target CPUs. Pick neon only to study or reuse its SASS Winograd/GEMM kernels on Maxwell/Pascal; for current NVIDIA GPUs the cuDNN baseline itself has since added Winograd and is the practical choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Kernels are assembled at runtime by running ptxas and maxas.pl and cached under ~/.cache/neon/kernels; issue #416 shows ptxas failing with a floating-point exception for sm_61 under CUDA 9.0, closed without a documented fix.
- Open issue #461 (2019, GTX 1050 Mobile, CUDA 10.0) reports 90.2% misclassification on the MNIST MLP example with the GPU backend while other backends train normally; it never got a reply.
- The suite's fp16/fp32 rows were produced with the separate nervanagpu package (convnew branch) and Nervana's limited-release beta kernels; neon ships a descendant script, neon/backends/convnet-benchmarks.py, that runs the same nets through neon's own NervanaGPU backend (fp16 and AlexNet/BN variants by default).
- The convnet-benchmarks script hard-codes per-layer tile parameters (grid_P, grid_Q, update_size) tuned for the benchmarked shapes, so other layer shapes may not see the same speedup.

**Status:** Abandoned: archived 2023-01-03, last commit 2019-05-22, Intel accepts no patches; Apache-2.0, so the SASS kernels and Winograd wrappers can be copied for study, but they will not run unchanged on GPUs newer than Pascal according to anything the repo documents.

[repo](https://github.com/NervanaSystems/neon) · [benchmark](https://github.com/soumith/convnet-benchmarks)

##### PowerInfer  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

llama.cpp-derived CPU/GPU hybrid LLM engine that exploits ReLU activation sparsity; up to 11.69x llama.cpp on one RTX 4090.

**Beats:** llama.cpp — Per the README and the SOSP '24 paper, PowerInfer vs llama.cpp (late-2023 version) on one RTX 4090 with FP16 ReLU models (input length 64) reaches up to 11x on Falcon(ReLU)-40B and up to 3x on Llama(ReLU)-2-70B, averaging 13.20 tokens/s (peak 29.08) and up to 11.69x across models including OPT-175B; on an RTX 2080Ti with INT4 models (input length 8) it reaches up to 8x on Falcon-40B and 3x on Llama-2-70B. WebSearch snippets of the paper give the host as an Intel i9-13900K with 192 GB RAM (paper PDF not opened); compiler and flags are not stated, and the per-configuration numbers are only in README images.

**Known shortcoming:** Speedup (11.69x vs llama.cpp) needs ReLU-sparsified models: stock llama.cpp weights get no gain and the README FAQ admits the ReLU 70B model loses accuracy; OPT and predictor-training code unreleased; SOSP '24 venue (DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695964) seen only in search results; repo moved to Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer.

**Known shortcoming:** OPT model code was released 2025-02-19 (#245) though the README TODO still lists it; engine code last changed 2025-07 (2026 commits are README-only), so 'active' overstates it; builds with -march=native by default; FFN split quietly falls back to a slow mode (issue #131).

**How:** Neuron activations in ReLU LLMs follow a power law: a few 'hot' FFN neurons fire for most inputs while most 'cold' neurons fire rarely. PowerInfer profiles activations offline, solves an integer linear program (cvxopt GLPK, in powerinfer-py/solver.py) to place hot neurons in VRAM and leave cold ones in host RAM, then at runtime uses small per-layer MLP predictors to guess which neurons will fire and computes only those, hot ones on the GPU and cold ones on the CPU, so weights never cross PCIe per token. ggml gains neuron-aware sparse operators for this (GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_SPARSE, GGML_OP_AXPY, ggml_mul_mat_idx with sparse and GPU index tensors). The baseline loses because llama.cpp offloads whole layers and must run every remaining dense layer on the CPU.

**Use it when:**
- Single-user, batch-1 local generation on one consumer GPU (RTX 4090 24 GB, RTX 2080Ti 11 GB) with a model 2-6x larger than VRAM, such as a 40B or 70B model in FP16 or INT4.
- You can use or create a ReLU-sparse model variant (ReluLLaMA, ReluFalcon, ProSparse-Llama-2, Bamboo-7B, TurboSparse) and accept its accuracy.
- x86-64 hosts with AVX2 plus an NVIDIA (CUDA) or AMD (ROCm/HIP) GPU, on Linux or Windows.
- Research on activation-sparsity offloading: the predictor, the ILP placement and the sparse ggml operators are all in the tree.

**Skip it when:**
- Mainstream dense models (Llama 3, Qwen, Mistral and other SiLU/GELU models): the FAQ says only ReLU-family activations are supported, and llama.cpp weights give no gain.
- Accuracy-sensitive use of the 70B ReLU models: the FAQ says the ReLU fine-tune used only 5B tokens and shows a noticeable drop, worst for 70B.
- Multi-GPU boxes, multi-tenant serving or high-batch throughput: multi-GPU is an open TODO and the published speedups are for single-request generation.
- Apple Silicon: CPU-only on macOS, where the README says the improvement 'is not significant', and the Metal backend is still a TODO.
- Projects that need upstream llama.cpp features: the ggml/llama.cpp base is a late-2023 snapshot and the engine code has seen little change since 2024 (recent commits are README edits plus the 2025 SmallThinker drop).

**Integration:** static lib + CLI binaries (CMake build of a llama.cpp-style tree: main, server, quantize, batched, perplexity) · CUDA toolkit with cuBLAS (-DLLAMA_CUBLAS=ON) or ROCm hipBLAS (-DLLAMA_HIPBLAS=ON) for GPU builds; Python 3.8+ with the powerinfer helper package (torch>=2, cvxopt 1.3.2) for GPU-split solving, plus numpy, sentencepiece, transformers and gguf-py for weight conversion; the smallthinker/ engine needs clang-21 and mold · C11 / C++11, CMake 3.17+ (README; the top-level CMakeLists declares 3.13 and raises it to 3.17 for CUDA) · x86-64 with AVX2 on Linux and Windows, with or without NVIDIA or AMD GPUs; Apple M-series CPU-only on macOS without significant gains

**Vs siblings:** Pick PowerInfer over ik_llama.cpp, llamafile tinyBLAS, T-MAC or BitNet when the bottleneck is a model larger than your GPU's VRAM and you can run a ReLU-sparse variant: those siblings speed up dense or low-bit matmuls on the CPU, while PowerInfer avoids computing most FFN neurons at all. For standard dense models, or CPU-only machines, ik_llama.cpp or llamafile are the better choice.

**Gotchas:**
- FFN splitting fails quietly: if the powerinfer Python module or the model's activation/ directory is missing, no GPU index is generated and generation falls back to slow mode (see issue #131, 'Activation_32 Not Found (Very slow inference)'); check the log for 'offloaded ... MiB of FFN weights to GPU'.
- The generated .gpuidx placement is cached next to the model; after changing VRAM budget or hardware, a stale cache can cause CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY, fixed with --reset-gpu-index, a lower --vram-budget or --disable-gpu-index (FAQ).
- LLAMA_NATIVE defaults to ON (-march=native), so binaries built on one CPU may not run on another.
- Dense GGUFs from convert-dense.py may not work in llama.cpp because the activations (ReluLLaMA, ProSparse) or the architecture (Bamboo) were changed.

**Status:** MIT-licensed with about 9.8k stars, but now owned by Tiiny-AI, which sells hardware built on it; engine code last changed in 2025 (OPT model code on 2025-02-19, SmallThinker on 2025-07-27) with only README commits since, so 'active' overstates the core's maintenance.

[repo](https://github.com/Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SJTU-IPADS/PowerInfer)

##### SageAttention (SageAttention, SageAttention2, SageAttention2++)  `CUDA/C++ and Triton with Python API`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Quantized (INT8 QK, FP8/FP16 PV) forward attention kernels for NVIDIA GPUs that outrun FlashAttention2 and match FlashAttention3-FP8.

**Beats:** FlashAttention2 (also FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention3-FP8) — First-party kernel benchmarks (bench/ scripts using the flash-attn benchmark API, head_dim 64/128) on RTX 5090/4090/3090, L20, A100/A800/A6000, H100/H20/H800 show the INT8/FP8 kernels above FlashAttention2, for example 560 TOPS on RTX 5090 (2.7x FlashAttention2), and level with FlashAttention3-FP8 on Hopper; CogVideoX1.5-5B end-to-end on an H20 takes 12'07'' vs 25'34'' (FA2) and 17'32'' (FA3). The results are backed by ICLR 2025 and ICML 2025 papers, but CUDA version and flags for the plots are not stated, and the kernel figures leave out quantization time.

**Known shortcoming:** Kernel TOPS exclude quantize/smooth time; lossy INT8/FP8 attention; README's pip 2.2.0 is absent from PyPI (only 1.0.6); PyPI license string says BSD-3 while the repo says Apache-2.0; ICLR/ICML papers unreadable here (venue from README and search listings).

**Known shortcoming:** Open silent-corruption bugs without maintainer reply: #386 int32 offset overflow in Triton kernels (~100k tokens, non-contiguous QKV), #388 FP8 PV noise beyond ~160k tokens on sm120, #392 wrong output under CUDA graph replay; forward-only, head_dim <=128; the sageattn() dispatcher has no sm100 (B200) branch and raises there; last code commit 2025-12-22.

**How:** Q and K are quantized to INT8 (per-block, per-warp or per-thread granularity) after 'smoothing' K by subtracting its mean over the sequence, which removes channel outliers so the INT8 error stays small. QK^T then runs on INT8 tensor cores (mma / Hopper WGMMA), and PV runs in FP8 (sm89/sm90/sm120) or FP16 with an FP16 accumulator. A two-level accumulation strategy for FP8 PV (SageAttention2++, pv_accum_dtype='fp32+fp16') recovers accuracy lost to the FP8 MMA accumulator. The kernels keep the FlashAttention-style tiled online softmax, so the gain over FlashAttention2 comes from faster low-precision tensor-core throughput, not a different algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Inference of video and image diffusion transformers (CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, Mochi examples in the repo) where attention dominates runtime on long token sequences.
- Consumer and workstation GPUs (RTX 3090/4090/5090, L20, A6000) where FlashAttention3 is not available and FlashAttention2 is the realistic baseline.
- Hopper (H100/H20/H800) inference where you would otherwise use FlashAttention3-FP8 and want similar speed with less quantization error.
- Head dimension 64 or 128 with FP16/BF16 inputs, including GQA, varlen batches (sageattn_varlen) and causal masks with qo_len == kv_len.

**Skip it when:**
- Training or anything needing gradients: the SageAttention2 API in sageattention/core.py has no backward pass.
- Head dimension above 128: the wrappers raise 'Unsupported head_dim'; sizes below 64 or between 64 and 128 are zero-padded, which wastes work.
- Numerically strict workloads that need results close to exact FP16 attention: outputs are approximate, and open issues report black/NaN outputs with some models (#273, #221, #164 on RTX 50xx).
- Very long sequences (above roughly 100k-160k tokens) until the open int32 overflow and FP8 PV corruption issues (#386, #388) are fixed.
- Pre-Ampere GPUs (compute capability below 8.0), AMD or CPU: setup.py only builds sm80, 86, 89, 90, 100, 120 and 121, and the sageattn() dispatcher has no branch for sm100 (B200), so it raises 'Unsupported CUDA architecture' there; SageAttention3 for Blackwell is a separate package in sageattention3_blackwell/.

**Integration:** module · Python >=3.9, PyTorch >=2.3.0, Triton >=3.0.0, CUDA toolkit (nvcc) for the source build; flash-attn only for benchmarking · CUDA 12.0 (Ampere), 12.3 (Hopper FP8), 12.4 (Ada FP8), 12.8 (Blackwell or SageAttention2++); C++17 (setup.py passes -std=c++17 to g++ and nvcc) · Linux with NVIDIA GPUs sm80/86/89/90/100/120/121 (Ampere, Ada, Hopper, Blackwell); other OSes not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick SageAttention over FlashAttention-3 for inference on Ada/Ampere/Blackwell consumer GPUs or when lossy INT8/FP8 attention is acceptable; keep FlashAttention-3 for training and exact attention on Hopper. Use FFPA instead when head_dim exceeds 128 (SageAttention stops at 128), and FlashInfer for paged-KV LLM decode serving.

**Gotchas:**
- Kernel TOPS plots exclude the quantization and K-smoothing passes (README note), so end-to-end speedup is smaller than the kernel charts suggest.
- Open issue #392 (2026-08-18): output silently diverges about 90% from eager when replayed inside a captured CUDA graph on sm120; the README only claims torch.compile support in non-cudagraphs mode.
- Open issue #386 (2026-08-11): Triton kernels compute offsets in int32, so non-contiguous views (fused QKV buffers) at about 100k tokens silently corrupt output or crash; #388 reports FP8 PV noise above about 160k tokens on sm120.
- Packaging mismatch: the README says 'pip install sageattention==2.2.0', but PyPI only has up to 1.0.6 (the Triton-only SageAttention1, 2024-11-20), whose metadata says BSD 3-Clause while the repo LICENSE is Apache-2.0; build from source to get SageAttention2/2++.

**Status:** Apache-2.0 research code from Tsinghua (4,000 stars); last code commit 2025-12-22 and README edit 2026-01-17, with silent-corruption bug reports from August 2026 still unanswered, so it is maintained but slowing down; usable if you build from source.

[repo](https://github.com/thu-ml/SageAttention) · [benchmark](https://github.com/thu-ml/SageAttention)

##### SpargeAttn (SpargeAttention)  `C++ (CUDA) with Python bindings; Triton example`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Training-free block-sparse, INT8/FP8-quantized attention kernels; 1.8-4.5x per-layer over full attention in model runs, approximate.

**Beats:** FlashAttention2 (Figure 2 legend 'FlashAttn'; Table 1 'Full-Attention' does not name the implementation) — README Figure 2 (RTX 4090, sequence 22K, head dim 128) plots kernel TOPS against sparsity: FlashAttention2 about 165, SageAttention about 300, SpargeAttn+Sage2 about 410 at sparsity 0.1 rising to about 875 at 0.6 (about 2.5-5.3x, chart readings, derived from page data). Table 1 (assets/exp_table.png, GPU not stated, older SageAttention1-based version) gives per-layer attention speed in real model runs of 1.8x (Flux, SD3.5 at 4.5K) to 4.5x (Llama3.1 at 128K) over full attention with near-dense accuracy; no compiler flags or kernel benchmark script are published.

**Known shortcoming:** Most of the headline gain over FlashAttention2 comes from SageAttention's INT8 quantization (SageAttn alone is about 1.8x FlashAttn in Figure 2); sparsity adds the rest, and at sparsity 0.1 the FA2-based variant is only about 1.1x. No kernel benchmark script in the repo (Triton_SpargeAttn holds one example file).

**Known shortcoming:** Possible correctness bug read in source (not tested, no issue filed): spas_sage2_attn_meansim_topk_cuda and the other Sage2 APIs launch the kernel with is_causal hard-coded False, and the causal mask is applied only at block level, so a query can see up to 127 later tokens; the Sage1 API passes the flag through. Forward only; attn_mask, dropout_p and output_dtype are ignored; BF16 V is cast to FP16. setup.py archs stop at 9.0 so the RTX 5090 build fails (#109); CUDA 13, GCC 13 and Python 3.14 build failures (#115, #122, #114); open wrong-output issues #110, #106, #124. Last commit 2026-02-25 with 62 open issues, so 'active' overstates it; setup.py says BSD-3 while LICENSE is Apache-2.0.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Two multipliers stack: sparsity and SageAttention-style quantization. A Triton pre-pass mean-pools each Q and K block, keeps blocks whose tokens are not self-similar, scores the pooled blocks with a softmax and keeps the top-k fraction (or a CDF threshold) of key blocks, producing a lookup table the kernel walks. The CUDA kernels quantize Q and K to INT8 (K mean-smoothed) and, on sm89/sm90, V to FP8 with FP16 or FP32 accumulation (SageAttention2/2++), and a pv_threshold variant skips further P·V work inside the kernel.

**Use it when:**
- Inference of video and image diffusion transformers (CogVideoX, Mochi, Wan, Flux, SD3.5) at long token counts (17K-22K and up), where Table 1 shows 3.1-3.5x per-layer attention speedups with near-dense quality metrics.
- Long-context LLM prefill (Llama3.1 at 128K in Table 1, about 4.5x per layer) when a small accuracy loss is acceptable and you use non-causal attention or the SageAttention1-based API (see gotchas).
- Ampere, Ada or Hopper GPUs (A100, RTX 4090, H100/H20) with head dim 64 or 128 and FP16/BF16 activations.
- You already have a per-head block-sparse pattern (sliding tiles, video-locality masks) and want a fast INT8/FP8 kernel that executes it via block_sparse_sage2_attn_cuda.

**Skip it when:**
- Training or fine-tuning: there is no backward pass or autograd function.
- Workloads that need exact attention, or causal attention through the recommended SageAttention2-based APIs (see gotchas).
- Short sequences: at 4.5K tokens (Flux, SD3.5) the gain is only about 1.8x, sequences under 128 tokens are rejected, and at low sparsity the FlashAttention2-based variant is only about 1.1x over FlashAttention2 in Figure 2.
- Blackwell GPUs or new toolchains: setup.py lists only compute capabilities 8.0, 8.6, 8.7, 8.9 and 9.0, issue #109 (open, no reply) reports the build rejecting TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0 on an RTX 5090, and issues #115/#122/#114 report build failures with CUDA 13.0, GCC 13+ and Python 3.14.
- Head dims other than 64 or 128 (you must pad and pass the softmax scale yourself).

**Integration:** module · PyTorch>=2.3, Triton (block-map kernels), einops; ninja for the build; CUDA toolkit with nvcc · C++17 and CUDA 12.0+ (12.4+ for sm89/sm90, 12.8+ for the SageAttention2++ FP16-accumulate path), Python 3.9+; built from source with setup.py (no wheel documented) · Linux, NVIDIA sm80/sm86/sm87 (INT8 QK, FP16 PV), sm89 and sm90a (INT8 QK, FP8 PV); Blackwell not in setup.py's supported list; Windows source builds reported failing at link time (issue #103)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over SageAttention when sequences are long and attention maps are sparse: it reuses the same INT8/FP8 kernels and adds block skipping (SageAttention alone is about 300 vs FlashAttention2's 165 TOPS in Figure 2, SpargeAttn+Sage2 up to about 875). Prefer FlashAttention-3/4 when you need exact attention, a backward pass, or causal LLM training, and Chipmunk if you specifically want column-sparse attention for diffusion transformers measured against FlashAttention-3.

**Gotchas:**
- Causal masking in the recommended APIs: spas_sage2_attn_meansim_topk_cuda (and the other SageAttention2-based entry points) builds a causal block map but launches the kernel with the causal flag hard-coded to False, so the diagonal blocks run unmasked and a query can see up to 127 later tokens in its block (from reading spas_sage_attn/core.py and utils.py, not tested). The SageAttention1-based spas_sage_attn_meansim_topk_cuda passes is_causal through to the kernel.
- Silent dtype changes: output_dtype is ignored (the output takes the input dtype), and for BF16 inputs V is cast to FP16, which overflows for |v| above 65504.
- Open correctness reports against the recommended API: random black output (#110), garbled results (#106), and undefined values in masked tail loads of the block-pooling kernels when the sequence is not a multiple of the block size (#124, fix proposed in PR #125).
- The entry points are decorated with @torch.compiler.disable, so torch.compile graphs break around every attention call; the published Table 1 numbers came from the older SageAttention1-based version, and the README says the SageAttention2-based one is about 30% faster.

**Status:** Apache-2.0 (LICENSE and source headers; setup.py metadata says BSD 3-Clause) and copyable, but the last commit was 2026-02-25 and 62 issues are open, including unanswered build failures on CUDA 13, GCC 13 and Blackwell, so treat it as research code with slowing maintenance.

[repo](https://github.com/thu-ml/SpargeAttn) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thu-ml/SpargeAttn/HEAD/assets/speed_comparison.png)

##### T-MAC  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Lookup-table CPU kernels for 1-4-bit LLM weights; 2-6x faster token generation than llama.cpp Q2_K/Q4_0 at low thread counts.

**Beats:** llama.cpp low-bit dequantization kernels (Q2_K, Q4_0) — Authors measured end-to-end token generation with T-MAC 2-bit vs llama.cpp Q2_K and T-MAC 4-bit vs llama.cpp Q4_0 (llama.cpp b2794) on Surface Laptop 7, M2-Ultra, AGX Orin, Raspberry Pi 5 and Surface Book 3; BitNet-3B on Surface Laptop 7 reached 20 tok/s on 1 core and 48 on 4 (README '4~5x'), while the EuroSys'25 paper states 'up to 4x' throughput and 70% less energy. Per-run compiler flags are not given.

**Known shortcoming:** Peer-reviewed paper (EuroSys 2025) is by the project's own authors; baseline llama.cpp b2794 (May 2024) was thermally unstable in default mode; flags for published runs not stated; old x86 may see little speedup.

**Known shortcoming:** At full thread count 4-bit beats llama.cpp Q4_0 by only 1.09x (AGX Orin) and 1.13x (M2 Ultra); 4-5x applies to 1-2-bit models at low thread counts. Not drop-in: needs TVM from source, per-model kernel compile, a 2024 llama.cpp fork; 46 open issues incl. segfault #98.

**How:** Instead of dequantizing weights and doing multiply-add, it groups weight bits (e.g. 4 one-bit weights), precomputes all partial sums of the activations into a lookup table, and replaces MACs with table lookups (ARM tbl / x86 pshufb) plus shift-and-accumulate across bit planes. The table is halved (2^n to 2^(n-1)) using a sign bit. Cost scales linearly with weight bit-width, so 2-bit and 1.58-bit models gain far more than 4-bit ones.

**Use it when:**
- Token generation (batch 1 GEMV) for 1-2-bit models such as BitNet b1.58 or W2 GPTQ/EfficientQAT models on ARM CPUs (Apple M-series, Snapdragon X, Jetson Orin, Raspberry Pi 5)
- Edge deployments where you want the same tokens/s with fewer cores or less energy (README: 40 tok/s with 2 cores vs 8 for llama.cpp on Surface Laptop 7)
- Low-thread-count inference: the gap is largest single-threaded (e.g. Raspberry Pi 5 BitNet-3B 8.03 vs 1.37 tok/s)
- Prefill of W2 models on CPU without AMX (Surface Laptop 7 Llama-2-7B W2, 8 threads: 94.4 vs 21.3 tok/s llama.cpp, 37.7 with OpenBLAS)

**Skip it when:**
- 4-bit models at full thread count: the authors' own data shows only 1.09x (AGX Orin, 12 threads) and 1.13x (M2-Ultra, 8 threads) over llama.cpp Q4_0
- Old-generation x86: the README warns it cannot guarantee meaningful speedup there, especially for 4-bit token generation
- You need current upstream llama.cpp: integration is via a fork rebased to a 2024 llama.cpp; some models are unsupported by its convert script
- Multi-batch GEMM on Apple M2-Ultra, where AMX-backed BLAS is comparable or faster
- Simple builds: requires Python 3.8, building TVM from source (downloads clang+LLVM) and a per-model kernel compile step

**Integration:** static lib · TVM (built from source), Python 3.8 + virtualenv/conda, CMake >= 3.22, clang/LLVM (17.0.6 on Windows), patched llama.cpp submodule · C++17 (CMakeLists), CMake 3.22, Clang 17.0.6 on Windows · aarch64 (macOS, Linux, Windows on ARM, Android cross-compile), x86-64 (Linux, Windows); T-MAN variant targets Qualcomm NPU

**Vs siblings:** Pick T-MAC over llamafile tinyBLAS when weights are 1-3 bit (tinyBLAS targets F16/Q8_0 prompt eval); pick MNN for general mobile model inference rather than low-bit LLM GEMV.

**Gotchas:**
- Kernels are tuned per model shape and quantization config (kcfg.ini); a new model means re-running the compile step (prebuilt ARM kernels via -u)
- Published end-to-end numbers were measured on llama.cpp b2794 (May 2024) and without fast-aggregation; -fa adds 10-20% speed at some accuracy risk
- llama.cpp throughput on Surface Laptop 7 was thermally unstable in 'Better Performance' mode, so some comparisons depend on the power profile
- Open issues include a segfault (#98) and several build failures (missing t-mac-envs.sh, Windows CMake errors)

**Status:** MIT-licensed Microsoft Research project, stale since mid-2025 (last commit 2025-06-03) with 46 open issues; its ideas live on in microsoft/BitNet (bitnet.cpp), which the README says is powered by T-MAC.

[repo](https://github.com/microsoft/T-MAC) · [benchmark](https://github.com/microsoft/T-MAC)

##### ThunderKittens  `CUDA/C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only CUDA tile DSL for writing GEMM/attention/SSM kernels that match cuBLAS and FA3 and beat FA3 backward.

**Beats:** cuBLAS GEMM and FlashAttention-3 / cuDNN attention — On an H100 80GB SXM with CUDA 12.6, the ICLR 2025 paper by the project team shows TK GEMM competitive with cuBLAS, non-causal attention forward matching FlashAttention-3, and attention backward 10-40% faster than FA3 (largest gain at short sequences). It also shows 14x/6.5x over FLA linear attention and 4.7-7.9x over FlashFFTConv. The README's ~855 TFLOPs (86% of peak) H100 bf16 GEMM figure is first-party, and nvcc flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** No cuDNN attention comparison found in the paper; wins are on backward passes and non-standard baselines; flags not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Kernel-writing API, not a drop-in for cuBLAS or FA3; needs CUDA 12.8+ and C++20; Hopper and Blackwell only (no Ampere; Windows issue #174); no Python package since v2.0; B200 'match or beat cuBLAS' claim is chart-only.

**How:** Everything is expressed as tensor-core-sized tiles whose shared-memory layouts are chosen at compile time to avoid bank conflicts. A Load-Compute-Store-Finish (LCSF) template splits warps into producers (issuing asynchronous TMA loads) and consumers (issuing asynchronous WGMMA on Hopper, tcgen05 on Blackwell) with register reallocation between them, so memory movement overlaps compute. Persistent grids and supergrouped tile ordering improve L2 reuse; later versions add distributed shared memory and NVLink/NVSwitch multi-GPU primitives.

**Use it when:**
- You write custom fused kernels (attention variants, linear attention, long convolutions, Mamba-style SSMs) on H100/H200 or B200 and want near-cuBLAS/FA3 throughput without hand-writing PTX.
- Attention training workloads where the backward pass dominates: the ICLR 2025 paper reports 10-40% faster backward than FlashAttention-3 at head dim 64/128.
- Non-standard attention or SSM operators where the incumbent is Triton or a research kernel (FLA, FlashFFTConv): the paper reports 6.5-14x over FLA and 4.7-7.9x over FlashFFTConv.
- Low-precision Blackwell GEMMs (MXFP8, NVFP4) in TK 2.0, where the authors report matching or surpassing cuBLAS on B200.

**Skip it when:**
- You just need a GEMM or standard attention call: cuBLAS and FlashAttention already deliver matching forward performance with a stable API.
- Ampere or older GPUs (Ampere no longer actively supported), AMD (use HipKittens), or Windows builds (open issue #174).
- Toolchains older than CUDA 12.8 or compilers without C++20 concepts.
- You need a packaged, versioned library: since 2.0 there is no Python package, and each kernel under kernels/ is built separately by its own Makefile.

**Integration:** header-only · CUDA toolkit 12.8+; PyTorch 2.8+ and pybind11 only for the prebuilt kernels/ and demos · C++20, CUDA 12.8+ (README suggests gcc-11 / clang-11 or newer) · NVIDIA Hopper (SM90) and Blackwell (SM100/103/120), Vera Rubin added Sept 2026; Ampere (SM80) builds but is unsupported

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over FlashAttention-3 when you need custom attention/SSM variants or faster backward passes and can write CUDA; stay with FlashAttention-3 for a maintained drop-in attention API with forward performance that TK only matches. Unlike CPU siblings such as LIBXSMM or Fastor, it targets NVIDIA datacenter GPUs only.

**Gotchas:**
- Default operation scope is a single warp; assigning multiple warps to the same op is undefined behavior and can corrupt memory. WGMMA ops live in kittens::warpgroup / group<N>.
- Some ops alias-fail silently: transpose_sep must not be given the same registers as source and destination.
- Layouts are checked at compile time; a 'missing' operation is usually a layout mismatch (e.g. mma B operand needs column layout).
- The README says mma unit tests occasionally fail by a single element due to tensor-core floating-point rounding.

**Status:** Actively maintained by Stanford Hazy Research (TK 2.0 in Jan 2026, Vera Rubin support Sept 2026, last commit 2026-09-12), MIT-licensed and header-only, so easy to vendor; expect API churn between major versions.

[repo](https://github.com/HazyResearch/ThunderKittens) · [benchmark](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/05dc08730e32441edff52b0fa6caab5f-Abstract-Conference.html)

#### big-integer-arbitrary-precision

##### ctbignum  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only constexpr C++20 fixed-width big integers and Z/qZ arithmetic; beats GMP mpn_mul at 2-4 limbs.

**Beats:** GMP (mpn/mpz) — The 2018 arXiv paper times schoolbook multiplication against GMP mpn_mul on a 2.3 GHz Kaby Lake i5 (Turbo off) with Apple LLVM 9.0.0 -O3 -march=native and forced inlining: 4 vs 14 ns at 2 limbs (3.5x), 18 vs 29 ns at 4 limbs (1.6x), and 85 vs 67 ns at 8 limbs, where GMP wins. The public benchmark source is benchmarks/src/bench-mul.cpp.

**Known shortcoming:** Headline numbers need -march=native plus forced inlining; GMP is faster from ~5-6 limbs up, and up to 1.8x faster at 8 limbs without -march=native.

**Known shortcoming:** GCC/Clang only (__uint128_t, gnu::always_inline; MSVC issue #44); open bug #55 (shifts wider than one limb fail); not every function constant-time; O(n^2) schoolbook multiply only.

**Independent measurement:** paper Table 4: 4-limb Montgomery mult 39 ns vs libff hand-written asm 66 ns (forced inlining)

**How:** Because the limb count is a template parameter, the schoolbook loops (using unsigned __int128 for 64-bit limbs) have fixed trip counts that the compiler fully unrolls and, with [[gnu::always_inline]], inlines into the caller, avoiding GMP's call overhead and length dispatch. Arguments are passed by value so limbs can live in registers. Modulus-dependent constants for Barrett/Montgomery reduction and invariant division are precomputed at compile time.

**Use it when:**
- Cryptographic field/ring arithmetic on 2-4 64-bit limbs (128-256 bits), e.g. elliptic-curve or pairing fields, where the modulus is known at compile time.
- Tight inner loops of many small multiplications or Montgomery multiplications where GMP's per-call overhead dominates (paper: 4-limb Montgomery mul 39 ns vs libff assembly 66 ns, with forced inlining).
- You want big-integer constants or precomputation evaluated at compile time (constexpr, static_assert on big-integer results).
- Embedded or allocation-free code that needs fixed-size stack integers and only the C++ standard library.

**Skip it when:**
- Operands of about 5-6 limbs or more: GMP's mpn_mul is faster (8 limbs: 85 vs 67 ns with -march=native, 125 vs 69 ns without).
- Sizes not known at compile time or numbers that grow; there is no arbitrary-precision type (fixed vs expanding separation is an open issue).
- Side-channel-sensitive code that assumes every function is constant-time: the README says only explicitly marked functions are (add, mul and comparison are ct-verif checked).
- MSVC builds: the code relies on __uint128_t and [[gnu::always_inline]], and MSVC support is an open issue (#44).
- Large-number algorithms: multiplication is O(n^2) schoolbook only, with no Karatsuba/FFT.

**Integration:** header-only · none (C++ standard library); benchmarks need GMP, NTL 10.5+, libff and Google Benchmark · C++20 (releases up to v0.3 were C++17 on Clang 5 / Apple LLVM 9); needs GCC/Clang extensions __uint128_t and gnu::always_inline · 64-bit targets where the compiler provides __uint128_t (GCC/Clang on x86-64, aarch64); MSVC not supported

**Vs siblings:** Pick ctbignum over mp++ or FLINT when the width is fixed at compile time and small (2-4 limbs), or when you need constexpr evaluation; mp++/FLINT handle arbitrary sizes and grow dynamically. The AVX-512 batched Montgomery entry targets 1024-4096-bit operands in batches of 8, a different regime from ctbignum's 100-500-bit scalar operations.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline wins assume forced inlining and -march=native; without -march=native the 2-limb gain shrinks (5 vs 13 ns) and GMP is 1.8x faster at 8 limbs.
- mul returns big_int<M+N>, so result width grows by type; use partial_mul or Montgomery/Barrett reduction to stay at a fixed width.
- Open bug #55: bit shifts larger than the limb bit width do not work.
- ZqElement's skip_reduction constructor assumes input < modulus and does not check it.

**Status:** Small, Apache-2.0 header-only library marked 'work in progress' in its README, with commits as recent as 2026-08-07 and 12 open issues; easy to vendor, though the published benchmarks date from 2018.

[repo](https://github.com/niekbouman/ctbignum) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.07236)

##### dashu (dashu-int)  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Rust, no_std big-integer crate (an ibig fork) that beats GMP via rug on one- and two-word values.

**Beats:** GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate; gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 pinned in Cargo.lock) — DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks ran Criterion microbenchmarks (rustc 1.92.0, default bench profile, 2 s measurements) on an Apple M2 Max comparing dashu-int 0.4.2 with rug 1.30.0 (GMP via gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1) and other Rust crates: dashu was faster than rug in 98 of 153 small-value cases (e.g. 100-bit add 3.7 vs 21.9 ns), but rug won most cases from about 1000 bits upward. The report calls its numbers quick, machine-specific and not authoritative.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins only on small operands (rug pays a heap allocation per result); benchmarked 0.4.2 while crates.io is at 0.6.1; hard fork of ibig (is_fork_of set); Rust only.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked 0.4.2 had crash bugs fixed later (modpow scratch under-allocation and gcd_ext panic fixed in 0.4.3, large gcd abort in 0.5.1); 0.4.3 added NTT and Montgomery, so large-operand numbers are stale against 0.6.1; issue #54 asks for a GMP comparison, no reply.

**How:** The internal Repr is a union that stores one- or two-word magnitudes inline (up to 128 bits on 64-bit targets) and only spills to the heap above that, so small values never allocate, while GMP via rug pays a heap allocation per value; 0.6.1 also copies inline values directly on clone and compares them as single words. Larger operands use schoolbook multiplication with a double-word addmul kernel (BMI2 mulx on x86-64 with std), Karatsuba, Toom-3 from 96 words and, since 0.4.3, Proth-prime NTT with Garner CRT above about 4,000 words; division is schoolbook plus divide-and-conquer, and gcd is Lehmer's algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code where most integers fit in 128 bits but must not overflow (checked accumulators, parsers, symbolic or property-testing workloads): at 100 bits the report shows add 3.7 vs 21.9 ns and div 5.7 vs 32.4 ns against rug/GMP.
- no_std or WebAssembly targets, or projects that cannot link LGPL GMP: it is pure Rust under MIT OR Apache-2.0.
- Hex parsing and gcd around 1000 bits, where dashu matched or beat rug in the report (gcd 2.87 vs 3.05 us; from_hex at 10^4 bits 2.56 vs 6.60 us).
- When you need integers, rationals, decimals and binary floats from one consistent pure-Rust family.

**Skip it when:**
- Operands of about 1000 bits and up: rug/GMP wins add, sub, mul, div, pow and modular arithmetic there (mul at 10^4 bits 4.52 vs 12.76 us; modular pow at 1000 bits 305 vs 771 us).
- Large-number workloads such as computing many digits of a constant: in tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, 10M digits of e take 19.9 s with dashu 0.4.2 vs 2.8 s with rug, and Fibonacci(100M) 26.2 s vs 2.9 s.
- C++ projects: there is no C API, so using it from C++ means writing and maintaining Rust FFI shims; a C++ small-value library such as mp++ or Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int is simpler.
- Constant-time cryptography: no constant-time guarantees are documented (an optional zeroize feature exists, but that only clears memory).

**Integration:** crate · dashu-base, cfg-if, static_assertions, num-modular; optional num-order (default), num-traits, num-integer, rand, serde, zeroize, rkyv · Rust 1.68 (MSRV for the default build; some optional features such as rkyv_v08 need Rust 1.81+) · any Rust target (16-, 32- and 64-bit words); BMI2 mulx kernel on x86-64 with std; NTT multiplication compiled out on smaller-word targets

**Vs siblings:** Pick dashu over ibig (its ancestor) because it keeps two words inline and has a much faster gcd (10^4 bits: 64 us vs 851 us), and over Malachite when you need a permissive license instead of LGPL or want the float, decimal and rational crates; pick Malachite for better large-operand speed, and blip_mp or ctbignum only outside Rust.

**Gotchas:**
- The benchmark measured dashu-int 0.4.2, but the current release is 0.6.1; 0.4.3 added NTT multiplication, Montgomery arithmetic and lower Toom-3 thresholds, so large-operand gaps to GMP may now be smaller, and the small-value numbers have not been re-measured.
- Versions before 0.4.3 could exhaust the scratch allocator in modular exponentiation for Karatsuba-sized moduli and panic in gcd_ext when one operand divides the other; before 0.5.1, gcd of two large similar-sized integers could abort with 'not enough memory allocated'. Use 0.5.1 or later.
- 0.5.0 changed IBig's serde binary format to two's-complement little-endian bytes, so data serialized by earlier versions does not deserialize.
- The small-value win is mostly about allocation: each benchmarked op returns a new value, so rug pays a heap allocation while dashu stays inline; the 100-bit div bench divides operands of equal bit length, so it measures overhead rather than long division.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-30, 0.6.1 released 2026-09-25, about 3.9 million crates.io downloads), dual MIT/Apache-2.0, pre-1.0 with occasional breaking changes between minor versions.

[repo](https://github.com/cmpute/dashu) · [benchmark](https://github.com/DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks/blob/main/benchmark-report.md)

##### ibig  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Rust big integers that beat GMP (via rug) only on one-word (<=64-bit) values and on string parsing.

**Beats:** GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate; gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 pinned in Cargo.lock) — In DRMacIver's third-party Criterion suite (rustc 1.92.0, default bench profile, Apple M2 Max), ibig 0.3.6 beat rug 1.30.0/GMP on 10-bit add/sub/mul/div (1.5-2.1 ns vs 17.7-28.3 ns) and on hex/decimal parsing at all sizes, but lost to rug from 100 bits up on add/sub/div and at 10^4 bits on mul, gcd, pow, modular ops and formatting. The small-value win comes from avoiding a per-result heap allocation, not from faster limb kernels.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins only on 1-word values and parsing; rug is ahead from 100 bits; gcd 16x slower at 1e4 bits; last crate release 0.3.6 (2022); Rust only.

**Known shortcoming:** GitHub HEAD is an unreleased 0.4.0 rewrite ('early development'); the benchmarked code is 0.3.6 (2022, kept in ibig-old/) with binary (quadratic) gcd and multiplication capped at Toom-3 (explains large-operand losses); issue #18 (modular inverse of 0) closed after the last release; dashu beats it nearly everywhere.

**How:** UBig is an enum: Small(Word) holds a value that fits in one machine word inline, and only longer values allocate a Buffer, so one-word arithmetic avoids the heap allocation that rug/mpz pays per result. Multiplication switches from schoolbook (<=24 words) to Karatsuba (<=192 words) to Toom-3; division is schoolbook below 32 words and recursive divide-and-conquer above; non-power-of-two parsing works in 256-word chunks combined with precomputed radix powers. On x86-64 limb add/sub use the _addcarry_u64/_subborrow_u64 intrinsics; there is no hand-written assembly.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code where most values fit in 64 bits but must not overflow (counters, exact rationals with small parts, property-test shrinkers): one-word add/sub/mul/div measured 1.5-2.1 ns vs 17.7-28.3 ns for rug
- Parsing many decimal or hex strings into big integers: ubig_from_hex and ubig_from_dec beat rug at every size up to 10^4 bits
- Targets where linking GMP is impractical or LGPL is unacceptable: pure Rust, no_std, MIT OR Apache-2.0
- Embedded or wasm builds that need big integers without a C toolchain

**Skip it when:**
- Operands of two words or more: rug/GMP is already ahead at 100 bits on add, sub and div, and about 2.8x faster on 10^4-bit multiplication (4.52 us vs 12.69 us)
- gcd-heavy or modular-inverse-heavy code: gcd is a binary (quadratic) algorithm, 16x slower than rug at 10^4 bits (850.52 us vs 53.05 us) and 111x slower on extended gcd (7.82 ms vs 70.31 us)
- Large computations (millions of digits): multiplication stops at Toom-3 with no FFT/NTT path in the released code; ibig's own suite has 10M digits of e at 20.673 s vs rug 2.788 s
