- Converting big values to strings: ubig_to_hex at 10^4 bits is 7.34 us vs rug 2.47 us
- C or C++ projects: there is no C API; use dashu or malachite only if you are in Rust anyway, otherwise GMP itself

**Integration:** crate · ibig 0.3.6: cfg-if, static_assertions, num-traits (no_std); optional rand 0.8, serde 1.0 · Rust 1.49 for the crates.io 0.3.6 release (crates.io rust_version); the repo's ibig-old copy now declares 1.93 and the unreleased 0.4.0 rewrite needs 1.95 (edition 2024) · any Rust target; x86 and x86-64 get carry intrinsics, other targets use generic 16/32/64-bit word code

**Vs siblings:** Prefer dashu (a hard fork of ibig) in almost every case: it also inlines two-word values, has a subquadratic gcd (13x faster than ibig at 10^4 bits) and is within a few percent of ibig on add, mul and parsing at 1,000-10^4 bits in the same report. Pick ibig only for its smaller, frozen, permissively licensed 0.3.6 codebase; pick malachite or rug when operands exceed about 1,000 bits, and Boost.Multiprecision fixed cpp_int or ctbignum from C++.

**Gotchas:**
- The repository's main code (ibig 0.4.0 on ibig-core) is a from-scratch rewrite its README calls 'in early development'; the benchmarked and published code is 0.3.6 (2022-09-17), kept in ibig-old/, so the GitHub HEAD and the crate differ
- Only one word is stored inline: 65-128-bit values (u128, i128) already allocate, e.g. ubig_from_u128 21.4 ns vs dashu 1.8 ns
- UBig is capped at UBig::MAX_BIT_LEN (close to usize::MAX bits) and panics if exceeded; gcd(0, 0) panics
- Issue #18 ('0 shouldn't have a modular inverse') was closed in November 2022, after the last release; whether 0.3.6 is affected is not documented

**Status:** The repo is active (commits in July 2026) but on an unreleased rewrite; the crate has had no release since 0.3.6 in September 2022, still draws about 118k recent downloads, and is MIT OR Apache-2.0, small and pure Rust, so the old version is easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/tczajka/ibig-rs) · [benchmark](https://github.com/DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks/blob/main/benchmark-report.md)

##### libzahl  `C`  `ISC`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Small ISC-licensed C bignum library that beats GMP on cheap integer operations (assign, sign, compare, add/sub) but loses on multiply.

**Beats:** GMP (also TomsFastMath and LibTomMath) — The repo's STATUS file ranks libzahl per function against GMP, TomsFastMath and LibTomMath on 1 to 4097-bit operands, on an Intel Core 2 Quad Q9300 under Linux with one pinned CPU, no CPU extensions, libzahl built with gcc+glibc, gcc+musl and clang+glibc and the others with gcc+glibc, -O3 (-std=c99 -O3 -flto in config.mk). It reports rankings and crossover sizes, not times: libzahl is fastest for assignment, sign, comparison, bit test, save/load and add/sub at larger sizes, and slowest for multiply, square and decimal output. GMP and compiler versions are not stated, and some wins go through the bench/ translation layer: the GMP side of zsave/zload calls mpz_out_raw/mpz_inp_raw through an fmemopen stdio stream, so those rows are not like-for-like.

**Known shortcoming:** Rankings only, no timing tables; no compiler or GMP version; GMP wins mul/sqr/zstr/zrsh; 'zgcd 21 % of gmp' sits in an out-of-date legacy section (likely means slower); archived 2024-10-06.

**Known shortcoming:** The GMP translation layer runs zsave/zload through fmemopen stdio (mpz_out_raw), so the 'always fastest' save/load rows are not like-for-like; the library does have inline asm (record said none); zmul is plain Karatsuba down to 1 limb and division is bit-serial; global state, not thread-safe; header says not for crypto; won't compile as C++ (#4).

**How:** Allocations are never freed while the library is set up: limb arrays are rounded up to a power of two (plus 4 'fluff' limbs) and returned to per-size pools for reuse, and internal temporaries are preallocated globals. Error checks happen only where an error can first arise (longjmp out), and -DZAHL_UNSAFE removes them. Hot paths are header inlines; small copies use a computed-jump switch over 1-20 limbs, and x86-64 add/sub and copy loops use inline assembly (adcq in groups of four limbs). Multiplication is plain recursive Karatsuba down to a single 64-bit limb with no schoolbook base case, division is bit-by-bit shift-and-subtract, and gcd is binary gcd, which is why the arithmetic-heavy rows lose.

**Use it when:**
- Programs dominated by cheap bignum bookkeeping (set, swap, negate, abs, compare, bit test, truncate, save/load) on operands up to a few thousand bits, where STATUS ranks libzahl fastest against GMP, TomsFastMath and LibTomMath.
- Addition and subtraction of operands above roughly 100-850 bits (crossover depends on compiler and libc; clang+glibc ~90 bits, gcc+glibc ~840) on x86-64.
- Single-threaded C programs that want a permissively licensed (ISC) bignum without GMP's LGPL/GPL terms and are willing to vendor a small, frozen code base.
- Code that prefers longjmp-style error handling over checking every return value, or that wants allocation caching without writing its own pool.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything multiplication-, squaring-, division- or exponentiation-heavy: STATUS lists zmul, zsqr and zstr as 'slowest', and the legacy table lists zmodmul, zpow, zmodpow, zptest and small-divisor division as slowest; use GMP or FLINT.
- Multi-threaded programs: the header says libzahl is not thread-safe (global temporaries, a global jmp_buf and global memory pools in zsetup.c).
- Cryptography: zahl.h says 'Do not use libzahl for cryptographic applications'; nothing is constant-time.
- C++ code bases that include zahl.h directly: open issue #4 reports it does not compile as C++ because of register and restrict.
- Long-lived maintained dependencies: the repository was archived on 2024-10-06 and open issues have no maintainer replies.

**Integration:** static lib · none (libc only; POSIX /dev/urandom and /dev/random paths for zrand, configurable via CPPFLAGS) · C99 compiler; config.mk builds with -std=c99 -O3 -flto; GCC or Clang needed for the inline-assembly and builtin paths (-DZAHL_NO_ASM for others) · x86-64 tested (inline assembly for add/sub/copy); other targets through portable C fallbacks with -DZAHL_NO_ASM; big-endian listed as untested in TODO

**Vs siblings:** Pick libzahl over Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int, mp++ or ctbignum only when you need plain C, an ISC license and no GMP dependency, and your workload is mostly assignment, comparison and add/sub at hundreds to thousands of bits; for fixed small widths in C++ cpp_int or ctbignum fit better, and for multiplication-heavy work GMP-backed mp++ or FLINT win clearly.

**Gotchas:**
- Errors longjmp to the point registered by setjmp + zsetup(env); code between that point and the failing call is skipped, so resources must be cleaned up there. -DZAHL_UNSAFE turns checks off entirely and must be set both when building libzahl and before including zahl.h.
- Memory is pooled and only released by zunsetup(); peak memory stays allocated, and allocations round up to the next power of two.
- INSTALL says libzahl contains some inline assembly and asks for -DZAHL_NO_ASM on unsupported CPUs or compilers, and -DZAHL_ISA_MISSING_INDIRECT_JUMP on ISAs without computed jumps.
- znot is not GMP's NOT (GMP computes -x - 1); zstr writes decimal only, and zsets_radix/zstr_radix are TODO items.

**Status:** Abandoned: archived 2024-10-06, last commit 2022-07-20, three open issues unanswered; ISC-licensed and small enough to vendor, but treat it as frozen code.

[repo](https://github.com/maandree/libzahl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/maandree/libzahl/blob/master/STATUS)

##### VROOM (vectorized RNS modular multiplication, BoringSSL fork)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Research BoringSSL fork that swaps Montgomery multiplication for AVX-512 IFMA residue-number-system arithmetic to speed up RSA modexp.

**Beats:** BoringSSL BN_mod_mul_montgomery / BN modular exponentiation and RSA (same binary, multiplication backend swapped), OpenSSL at commit 7a53925 including its AVX-512 IFMA almost-Montgomery routines ossl_rsaz_amm52x{20,30,40} (separate harness kevin-he-01/vroom-openssl), FLINT 3.2.1 (GMP-based mpn_mod_mul / fmpz_mod_mul), and Arkworks (Rust, modmul only) — The repository prints no figures; it says the relative speedup over each baseline is the paper's claim and provides ./reproduce.sh, which runs bssl_bench pinned with taskset to core 0 (Clang 21.1.8, CMake Release -O3 plus -mavx512f -mavx512ifma, Xeon Platinum 8488C) for VROOM, BoringSSL BN_mod_mul_montgomery and FLINT 3.2.1, with OpenSSL and Arkworks in separate harnesses. Search summaries of the paper abstract (eprint 2026/393, not opened because the host is blocked) report 4.0x faster RSA-4096 verification over OpenSSL and, from the verifier's earlier search, 1.3x faster signing; two summaries disagree on the BLS figure (3.43x versus 4.05x), and BLS is not in this repository.

**Known shortcoming:** Security: README calls it a research prototype that may have memory and security bugs, and commit 616817a 'Fix buffer overflow in several files' confirms such bugs; not for production RSA. Repo has no numbers; the 4.0x verify / 1.3x sign for RSA-4096 vs OpenSSL is from the paper (ePrint 2026/393), seen only via search summary.

**Known shortcoming:** README says no GMP but install_deps.sh links GMP for radix<->RNS helpers; CMake fails without FLINT; Release adds -mavx512f -mavx512ifma to all flags; RNS only for exactly 1024/1536/2048/3072/4096-bit moduli; precompute BigInt uses a non-constant-time ossl_wrapper (consttime include commented out), a possible side channel on RSA-CRT p,q (unconfirmed).

**How:** Operands are held in two RNS bases of 52-bit residues and multiplied lane-wise with the AVX-512 IFMA instructions vpmadd52lo/hi (_mm512_madd52lo/hi_epu64), so the per-residue products are independent and fill 8-lane vectors. Modular reduction is an RNS Montgomery reduction: a per-residue Montgomery step followed by two base-extension ('CRNS') matrix products that move the value between the bases, described in rns/vector/batching_vs_no_batching_call_graph.md. Modulus size is a compile-time template parameter, so loops over limbs are fully unrolled, and exponentiation uses fixed-window tables with constant-time selection.

**Use it when:**
- Measuring or prototyping faster RSA verification and modular exponentiation latency on a single core of a CPU with AVX-512 IFMA (tested on Xeon Platinum 8488C, Sapphire Rapids, AWS c7i).
- Moduli of exactly 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072 or 4096 bits (the sizes instantiated in BN_MONT_CTX_set_use_rns), for example RSA-4096 verify or RSA-CRT with 2048-bit primes.
- Single-operation latency where you cannot batch independent multiplications: VROOM vectorizes inside one modular multiply rather than across eight.
- Reproducing the paper's Sections 6.1-6.3 tables with ./reproduce.sh against BoringSSL, FLINT 3.2.1 and the separate OpenSSL and Arkworks harnesses.

**Skip it when:**
- Production or any security-sensitive use: the README says it is not production-ready, was tested only on random inputs to select functions, and may contain memory errors and security bugs; commit 616817a (2026-05-22) fixed buffer over-reads in rns/vector/changebase.hpp and conversion.hpp.
- CPUs without AVX-512 IFMA: the Release build adds -mavx512f -mavx512ifma to all C and C++ flags, so treat the whole libcrypto build as AVX-512-only.
- Other modulus sizes: BN_MONT_CTX_set_use_rns prints a warning and leaves the ordinary Montgomery path in place for any bit length other than the five instantiated sizes.
- General big-integer arithmetic (arbitrary-size add, multiply, division, string conversion): it is a modular-multiplication backend for crypto, not a GMP replacement.
- Builds that cannot pull in GMP and FLINT: CMakeLists.txt stops with FATAL_ERROR without FLINT and includes GMP/FLINT headers into bcm.cc ('TODO: REMOVE GMP DEPENDENCY'), and install_deps.sh says 'The RNS code links GMP for radix<->RNS helpers', although the README says the VROOM code calls only BoringSSL BN_* routines.

**Integration:** static lib (BoringSSL fork; RNS core is header-only C++ templates under rns/) · BoringSSL build tooling (CMake, Ninja); GMP and FLINT 3.x found at configure time; Google Benchmark for bssl_bench and the OpenSSL harness; Rust 1.86 only for the Arkworks baseline · C++17 and C11 per CMakeLists.txt; tested only with Clang 21.1.8 (official LLVM prebuilt) · x86-64 with AVX-512F and AVX-512 IFMA; tested on Linux (Amazon Linux 2023) on Xeon Platinum 8488C, README says c7i-flex.large also reproduces relative speedups

**Vs siblings:** Pick VROOM over the truncated batch AVX-512 Montgomery code (lea-gl) when you need one RSA-size modexp faster rather than eight independent ones at once, and over FLINT or GMP-based code when the modulus is one of the five RSA sizes and the CPU has AVX-512 IFMA; for BLS12-381 or non-RSA moduli the authors' separate standalone repository (SimonLangowski/VROOM, MIT) is the better starting point, and CGBN only wins if a GPU is available.

**Gotchas:**
- The BigInt wrapper used to build RNS contexts (rns/precompute/gmp_wrapper.hpp) includes the plain ossl_wrapper.hpp; the constant-time ossl_wrapper_consttime.hpp include is commented out, so precomputation on secret moduli (the p and q contexts in RSA-CRT) may not be constant-time. Not checked further this session.
- Ring<modulus_bits> fixes the size at compile time; a modulus longer than the template size makes the constructor print to stderr and abort().
- AVXVector::load reads whole 8-lane vectors, which caused the out-of-bounds reads fixed in 616817a by copying into padded buffers; other call sites that load unpadded data could have the same problem.
- CMakeLists.txt carries a TODO about large stack frames in the RNS Montgomery code and has the -Wframe-larger-than check commented out.

**Status:** Active research artifact (last commit 2026-06-18, 11 commits, 8 stars), Apache-2.0 like upstream BoringSSL; usable for benchmarking and study, but the authors themselves say not to use it in production.

[repo](https://github.com/kevin-he-01/vroomssl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/kevin-he-01/vroomssl)

##### avxbls  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

AVX-512 IFMA BLS12-381 optimal ate pairing built on blst; about 1.9x lower single-pairing latency than blst's x64 assembly.

**Beats:** blst (non-vectorized x64 assembly BLS12-381 pairing) — The TCHES 2025(4) paper by Cheng, Fotiadis, Grossschaedl and Page (read only through search-result abstracts; tches.iacr.org and eprint.iacr.org are blocked here) reports a full BLS12-381 optimal ate pairing in 1,265,314 cycles (Granger-Scott) or 1,195,236 cycles (compressed cyclotomic squaring) versus 2,351,615 cycles for blst's scalar x64 assembly, 1.86x and 1.97x, on an Intel Core i3-1005G1 (Ice Lake). Both sides are built with the same gcc -O3 -march=native flags in the repo (Makefile and baseline/Makefile) and timed with rdtsc; the gcc version and turbo settings were not readable here.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on TCHES 2025(4), but the cycle counts (1,265,314 and 1,195,236 vs blst 2,351,615 on an i3-1005G1) were seen only in a search snippet (tches.iacr.org 403, ePrint 2025/1283 blocked). Bench code is public (src/main.c, baseline/ blst build, same gcc flags) but the gcc version is unconfirmed, so not A. Last commit 2025-09-27.

**Known shortcoming:** Code bug outside the measured n=1 numbers: add_n_dbl_n_vector reads only T[0]/Q[0]/Px2[0] and ignores n, so miller_loop_n and optimal_ate_pairing with n > 1 give a silently wrong multi-pairing result. Limbs are radix 2^48 (8x48 bits) in IFMA 52-bit lanes, not 52-bit limbs. The default build is the Granger-Scott variant (1,265,314 cycles); the 1,195,236 figure needs COMPRESSED_CYCLOTOMIC_SQR=1. The test checks bilinearity only, not output against blst; no library target.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Fp elements are held in radix 2^48 (8 limbs x 48 bits = 384 bits) inside 64-bit lanes so that AVX-512 IFMA's 52x52-bit multiply-accumulate (vpmadd52lo/hi) leaves 4 bits of headroom for lazy carry propagation; Montgomery multiplication and reduction run 8 lanes wide. The paper's contribution is choosing vectorization granularities per tower level (layouts named 8x1w, 4x2w, 2x2x2w, 1x4x2w in fp12_avx.h) so that independent Fp/Fp2 operations inside line doubling/addition, Fp12 squaring and cyclotomic squaring fill the 8 lanes, with values converted between blst's 64-bit radix and the 48-bit radix at step boundaries. Final exponentiation uses Granger-Scott cyclotomic squaring by default or Karabina-style compressed cyclotomic squaring via the COMPRESSED_CYCLOTOMIC_SQR compile-time switch.

**Use it when:**
- Latency of a single BLS12-381 pairing matters (one signature verification, one pairing check) on a CPU with AVX-512 IFMA: Intel Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, Sapphire Rapids or later Xeons, or AMD Zen 4/Zen 5.
- You already build on blst and can vendor its field code, swapping in the vectorized Miller loop and final exponentiation.
- As a reference for how to map extension-field tower arithmetic onto 8-lane IFMA when writing your own pairing or BN254 code.
- Research or benchmarking where reproducing the TCHES 2025 numbers against blst on the same machine is the goal (both sides ship with identical gcc flags).

**Skip it when:**
- Multi-pairing products (n > 1, e.g. aggregate BLS verification): the default vectorized Miller-loop step add_n_dbl_n_vector reads only T[0], Q[0] and Px2[0] and ignores n, so miller_loop_n with n > 1 does not compute the product of pairings.
- CPUs without AVX-512 IFMA (Intel client cores from Alder Lake on, older Xeons, Arm): there is no fallback path, and the build uses -march=native so binaries are not portable.
- Production signing/verification stacks: no library build, no hash-to-curve, signature API or subgroup/input validation in the pairing entry points, no side-channel claims, 9 stars and last commit 2025-09-27.
- Throughput-bound batch verification: it is latency-optimized for one pairing; a batch-oriented design such as VROOM's RNS approach may fit better.

**Integration:** source-drop · none beyond the bundled blst-derived sources (src/assembly.S, fields, points, recip) and src/rdtsc64.S for timing · gcc with AVX-512 IFMA intrinsics (Makefile: gcc -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -m64 -mbmi2 -march=native -fwrapv -mtune=native); C99 for VLAs in miller_loop_n; gcc version not stated · x86-64 with AVX-512F and AVX-512 IFMA plus BMI2/ADX (Linux/ELF toolchain assumed by the -z noexecstack flag)

**Vs siblings:** Against VROOM (also AVX-512 IFMA BLS12-381 versus blst), pick avxbls when you want plain Montgomery arithmetic in radix 2^48 tuned for single-pairing latency and a peer-reviewed TCHES result; pick VROOM for its RNS formulation or broader curve coverage (BN254). The GMP-oriented siblings (ctbignum, intx, mp++) do not implement pairings.

**Gotchas:**
- miller_loop_n/optimal_ate_pairing accept n but the vectorized Miller loop only processes the first (P, Q) pair; start_dbl_n loops over n, so results for n > 1 are silently wrong rather than rejected.
- The faster 1,195,236-cycle variant needs COMPRESSED_CYCLOTOMIC_SQR set to 1 in src/pairing.h; the default build is the Granger-Scott path (1,265,314 cycles in the paper).
- The bundled test checks bilinearity identities (e(P,[k]Q) == e([k]P,Q) and two variants) with a fixed scalar inside the same implementation; it does not compare output against blst or known-answer vectors.
- Cycle counts come from rdtsc over 10000 iterations after 1000 warm-up calls; on CPUs where rdtsc ticks at a fixed reference rate, turbo and AVX-512 frequency licensing affect the reading.

**Status:** Apache-2.0 research artifact (230 commits, last 2025-09-27, 9 stars) with no releases or library target; small enough to vendor for single-pairing latency work, but fix or avoid the n > 1 path and validate against blst before relying on it.

[repo](https://github.com/hchengv/avxbls) · [benchmark](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1283)

##### MultiFloats.hpp (dzhang314/MultiprecisionBenchmarks)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Paper harness with an AVX-512 header of branch-free double- to quad-double add/multiply that outruns MPFR, QD and CAMPARY.

**Beats:** MPFR (also GMP mpf, CLN, FLINT, Boost.Multiprecision, QD, CAMPARY, libquadmath in the same harness) — The SC '25 paper abstract (seen only as search snippets; the paper hosts are blocked here) reports peak throughput up to 11.7x QD, 34.4x CAMPARY, 35.6x MPFR and 41.4x FLINT across axpy, dot, gemv and gemm at 2 to 4 doubles, with search snippets naming AMD Zen 5 (Ryzen 9 9950X) and Apple M3 Pro; the public harness builds with g++-14/clang++-20 at -O3 -march=native -flto and runs MPFR at 53, 103, 156 and 208 bits. Which kernel, precision and thread count produce each peak ratio is not documented in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** SC25 abstract claims up to 35.6x vs MPFR, but it compares peak against peak and MultiFloats is not correctly rounded like MPFR; CPUs (Ryzen 9 9950X, M3 Pro) known from a snippet only.

**Known shortcoming:** The C++ header provides only + and * (no sub/div/sqrt/compare/IO) and needs AVX-512F/DQ/VL unconditionally. Inf inputs turn into NaN. The MPFR baseline ran with MPFR_RNDF (faithful rounding), not correctly rounded. Paper unopened here.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Numbers are unevaluated sums of 2 to 4 doubles (floating-point expansions), and each add or multiply is a fixed straight-line network of TwoSum, FastTwoSum and FMA-based TwoProd steps with no branches or renormalization loops (the paper calls these floating-point accumulation networks). With no data-dependent control flow, the same code instantiates on 2-, 4- and 8-wide SIMD registers; the dot and gemv kernels load 8 doubles per limb with _mm512_loadu_pd from split-array (one array per limb) storage, and axpy/gemm rely on '#pragma omp simd simdlen(8)'. The baselines (for example MPFR) are scalar per-element library calls on heap-allocated mpfr_t objects.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk elementwise or BLAS-style kernels (axpy, dot, gemv, small gemm) where double is not accurate enough and roughly 106, 159 or 212 significand bits suffice.
- You can lay out data as one double array per limb (structure of arrays) so the add/multiply networks vectorize.
- x86-64 with AVX-512 (the harness hardware per the paper abstract snippet was an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X); a scalar ARM header exists for Apple Silicon.
- As a reference implementation of the paper's add and multiply networks to port into your own SIMD code, or to reproduce the paper's library comparison (MIT license).

**Skip it when:**
- You need arbitrary or runtime-selectable precision, correct rounding, or MPFR's exponent range: these types have the exponent range of double and are capped at 4 limbs.
- You need anything beyond + and *: the C++ header has no subtraction, division, sqrt, transcendental functions, comparisons or string conversion (the full operation set is in the Julia package MultiFloats.jl).
- Your code must handle infinities or NaN-free overflow: TwoSum on an infinite input produces NaN error terms, and the Julia sibling documents that ±Inf inputs return NaN.
- Your target CPU lacks AVX-512: the x86 header defines __m512d overloads and uses _mm256_extractf64x2_pd (AVX-512DQ/VL) unconditionally, and the benchmark kernels call _mm512_loadu_pd directly.
- You want a maintained library: this is a 2-star benchmark repo with a one-line README and no tests beyond assert checks in the benchmarks.

**Integration:** header-only · none for MultiFloats.hpp (x86 intrinsics headers only); the harness needs Google Benchmark, OpenMP, GMP, MPFR, CLN, FLINT, Boost.Multiprecision, QD and CAMPARY (fetched by download_campary.sh) · C++17; the scripts use g++-14 and clang++-20 on Linux and Homebrew LLVM clang++ on macOS · x86-64 with FMA and AVX-512F/DQ/VL for multifloats/MultiFloats.hpp; multifloats-arm/MultiFloats.hpp is a scalar-only variant (no NEON intrinsics) for aarch64

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over DoubleFloats.jl or MPLAPACK's double-double/quad-double backends when you want C++ SIMD kernels at 2 to 4 doubles and can live with only + and *; pick MultiFloats.jl if you work in Julia and need the full operation set, and MPFR-based tools (or LibBF, FLINT) when you need arbitrary precision or correct rounding.

**Gotchas:**
- The error-free transformations depend on exact IEEE evaluation order: the harness builds with -ffp-contract=off and never enables fast-math; reassociation would cancel the error terms.
- Results are not normalized or rounded like MPFR; equality operator== only compares against a scalar double (leading limb equal, lower limbs zero).
- The baseline MPFR runs use MPFR_RNDF (faithful rounding) with separate mpfr_mul and mpfr_add calls, so MPFR was not in correctly rounded mode in this harness either.
- The repo commits no benchmark output; bench_linux.sh writes Google Benchmark JSON per library at OMP_NUM_THREADS 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 for you to generate.

**Status:** Stale research harness (last commit 2025-08-27, 46 commits, 2 stars) under MIT, so the 373-line header is easy to vendor, but it is a paper artifact rather than a supported library.

[repo](https://github.com/dzhang314/MultiprecisionBenchmarks) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3712285.3759876)

#### blas-lapack

##### blackwell-tensorcore-kernels  `CUDA C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Teaching repo: raw mma.sync FP16 GEMM that edges past cuBLAS's tensor-core kernel at 4096-8192 on Blackwell sm_120.

**Beats:** cuBLAS FP16-in/FP32-accumulate tensor-core GEMM (cublasGemmEx, which dispatches cutlass_80_tensorop_s16816gemm_f16_128x64 on sm_120) — On an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (sm_120, 300 W cap, CUDA 12.8, CMake build with no extra nvcc flags), FP16-in/FP32-acc M=N=K=8192 GEMM ran at 243.2 TFLOP/s against 229.0 for cublasGemmEx in the README's five-run session, and at 238.47 against 225.75 (about 1.056x, derived from page data) in the canonical results/bench.csv re-run after the cuBLAS handle-caching fix; nsys per-kernel times were 4.52 ms against 4.79 ms. The kernel is ahead only at 4096 (241.40 vs 235.13) and 8192, and behind cuBLAS at 2048 and smaller.

**Known shortcoming:** cuBLAS harness created a handle per timed call until the 2026-06-02 fix (win holds after the fix: 238.47 vs 225.75); workload is a 2-stage pipeline, not 3.

**Known shortcoming:** Win holds only at 4096 and 8192 (bench.csv loses at 2048: 200.96 vs 213.61, and at 1024 and 512); the launcher caches the FP16 cast by pointer, so new data in the same buffer gives stale results; K remainder past a multiple of 32 is silently dropped; not thread-safe (static globals).

**How:** The kernel issues PTX mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16 directly, loads fragments with ldmatrix.x4 (and .trans for B) from an XOR-swizzled, bank-conflict-free shared-memory layout, and fills shared memory with 16-byte cp.async copies in a 2-stage pipeline. Its decisive step is warptiling: a 128x128x32 CTA tile split into four 64x64 per-warp register tiles, which issues 32 mma.sync per 8 ldmatrix (a 4:1 ratio) and removes the MIO-queue-full stall that held the WMMA version at about 45% of cuBLAS. ncu at 8192^3 shows 85.0% tensor-pipe utilization against 74.0% for the cutlass_80_tensorop_s16816gemm kernel that cuBLAS picks on this card.

**Use it when:**
- Learning how a tensor-core GEMM is built on Ampere-style PTX (mma.sync, ldmatrix, cp.async, swizzling, warptiling), with measured TFLOP/s and ncu profiles for each step
- Large square FP16-in/FP32-out GEMMs (about 4096 and up) on an sm_120 workstation Blackwell card such as the RTX PRO 6000, where cuBLAS 12.8 dispatches an sm_80 CUTLASS kernel and this tile shape is 3-6% faster
- A starting point for your own fixed-shape FP16 kernel on sm_120 that you can fuse or modify, since the whole mainloop is about 150 lines in one file
- Reference numbers for FP8, unpacked FP4 and MXFP4 mma throughput on sm_120 (no cuBLAS FP4 GEMM exists there), keeping in mind the MXFP4 row uses unit block scales

**Skip it when:**
- Small and medium sizes: the fixed 128x128 tile loses to cuBLAS-TC at 2048 (200.96 vs 213.61 TFLOP/s), 1024 (69.45 vs 133.76) and 512 (14.59 vs 33.66) in results/bench.csv
- Hopper, datacenter Blackwell (sm_100) or any GPU other than sm_120: the mma.sync path caps well below wgmma/tcgen05, and on H100 the repo's best kernel (CUTLASS wgmma) reaches 85.5% of cuBLAS-TC, not more
- Production GEMM calls with arbitrary shapes, strides, transposes, alpha/beta, batching, BF16 or FP16 output: none of these exist; use cuBLAS/cuBLASLt or CUTLASS
- Workloads where a newer cuBLAS might pick a Blackwell-native kernel: the 6% win is over cuBLAS 12.8's heuristic choice of an Ampere kernel on this card, measured at one size on a power-capped 300 W Max-Q part

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA toolkit (cuBLAS and cuBLASLt for the benchmark driver, NVML for the rate probe); CUTLASS >= 3.4 only for the optional Hopper wgmma row · CUDA 12.8 nvcc (H100 rows used CUDA 13.1), C++17, CMake 3.24; FP4/MXFP4 kernels need the sm_120a target · NVIDIA GPUs; builds for sm_90 and sm_120 only and is tuned and measured as a winner only on sm_120 (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q). The FP16 kernel's PTX (mma.sync m16n8k16, ldmatrix, cp.async) is Ampere-level, but other architectures were not benchmarked

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over CUDA-L2 when you want a small, readable FP16 tensor-core kernel tuned for sm_120 rather than a large set of searched kernels for A100/H100 shapes; gpu-compute targets true-FP32 SGEMM on an RTX 5080 against pedantic cuBLAS and suits small FP32 problems, while for anything shipped cuBLAS or CUTLASS remains the safer default.

**Gotchas:**
- The FP32-to-FP16 cast is cached by pointer identity (if (A != g_cA)), so calling the launcher again on the same buffer after changing its contents silently multiplies the stale FP16 copy; this is how the benchmark keeps the cast out of the timed loop
- Shape assumptions are unchecked: K is processed as K/32 slabs (a remainder is silently dropped), and the 16-byte cp.async loads need N and K to be multiples of 8 with 16-byte-aligned rows; the code comment says M and N should be multiples of 128
- The tuned kernel uses about 186-196 registers per thread (ncu and ptxas figures differ) and runs 2 CTAs per SM, so it does not co-schedule well with other kernels
- The MXFP4 988 TFLOP/s figure feeds every block scale as 1.0, so it measures throughput only, not real per-block MXFP4 numerics (the README says so)

**Status:** Active personal learning project (1 star, 46 commits, last commit 2026-06-04, recent commits co-authored with an AI assistant); MIT-licensed, so the kernel and PTX helpers can be copied, but treat them as a tuned example for one GPU rather than a maintained library.

[repo](https://github.com/waynehacking8/blackwell-tensorcore-kernels) · [benchmark](https://github.com/waynehacking8/blackwell-tensorcore-kernels)

##### cpu_gemm_opt  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Single-core AVX2 SGEMM study (BLIS-style 6x16 asm kernel, per-size tuned blocking) about 4-9% ahead of OpenBLAS 0.3.4.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS 0.3.4 sgemm (README: 'most of the size exceed openblas(0.3.4)'; the driver times cblas_sgemm from the OpenBLAS it links) — On one 2.6 GHz core of an Intel Xeon Gold 6142 (hyperthreading off), built with clang++ 7.0.0 -O3 -mfma, the README's row-major SGEMM sweep shows the tuned 6x16 kernel at about 77-79 GFLOPS from 960^3 to 9120^3 against 72-75 GFLOPS for single-threaded OpenBLAS 0.3.4 cblas_sgemm (78.31 vs 75.11 at 960^3, 78.62 vs 72.70 at 9120^3), about 4-9% faster; it also leads at most small sizes (60.13 vs 43.05 at 48^3) but loses at 144^3. The OpenBLAS build target was not stated, and its column stays below the 81.25 AVX2 figure the driver uses as peak, so it was probably not running AVX-512 kernels (inference from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** 4-9% over OpenBLAS 0.3.4 from 960 up but slower at 144; old OpenBLAS; abandoned 2019.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness traps: only RowMajor/NoTrans/NoTrans is implemented (the other 7 branches return with C untouched); the 6x16 asm kernel ignores edge tiles, so M%6 or N%16 != 0 reads/writes out of bounds; aligned stores need C 32B-aligned and ldc%8==0; % of peak inflated (divides by 1024); blocking autotuned per size against untuned OpenBLAS.

**How:** It follows the Goto/van de Geijn loop nest: A is packed into mr x kc column panels (with alpha folded in) and B into kc x nr row panels in page-aligned buffers, C is scaled by beta once, and a 6x16 AT&T inline-assembly micro-kernel keeps 12 YMM accumulators, broadcasts A with vbroadcastss, issues vfmadd231ps, unrolls k by 4 and prefetches the next A and B panels. Blocking sizes are chosen so the panels fit L1, L2, L3 and the L1D TLB (the driver prints these checks), and a tuner stores the best mc/nc/kc per problem size in sgemm_tuned.db, which the benchmark then loads.

**Use it when:**
- Learning how a cache- and TLB-aware SGEMM is built on AVX2/FMA, with the derivation of the blocking constraints written out in a PDF
- Single-threaded row-major SGEMM experiments on an Intel Skylake-SP-class core (the author used a Xeon Gold 6142 at 2.6 GHz with hyperthreading off) for square sizes from about 192 to 9120, where the README table shows it ahead of OpenBLAS 0.3.4
- A starting point for your own per-machine tuned micro-kernel, since the tuner and the parameter database format are included

**Skip it when:**
- Any general BLAS use: column-major input and every transpose combination are unimplemented stubs, and there is no DGEMM or complex type
- Matrices whose M is not a multiple of 6 or N not a multiple of 16: the 6x16 assembly kernel ignores the edge-tile sizes passed to it (its assert is commented out), so edge tiles read and write past the matrix
- Multi-threaded workloads: it is single-core only, and the README states it beats OpenBLAS with OpenBLAS also limited to one thread
- AVX-512 machines where peak matters: the kernel uses 256-bit AVX2 even on the AVX-512-capable Gold 6142, so a library with AVX-512 kernels can be faster
- Small sizes such as 144^3, where OpenBLAS was faster in the README table (55.85 vs 64.26 GFLOPS), or sizes not in the tuned database, which fall back to default blocking

**Integration:** source-drop · A CBLAS header (gemm_driver.h includes <cblas.h>); OpenBLAS for the reference and benchmark driver; pthreads; Linux CPU-affinity calls in util.cc · C++11 with GCC-style AT&T inline assembly; the author built with clang++ 7.0.0 and -O3 -m64 -mfma -msse -msse2 via src/build.sh (paths are hard-coded to /opt) · x86-64 with AVX2 and FMA3; Linux; tested only on an Intel Xeon Gold 6142

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over sgemm.c (salykova) or matmul-cpu when you want the blocking derivation (cache and TLB constraints) spelled out and a per-size tuner; GEMM_AVX2_FMA3 targets multi-threaded AVX2 and is measured against MKL, and BLASFEO is the better choice for small matrices.

**Gotchas:**
- Non-row-major or transposed calls return silently with C unchanged, rather than failing
- The micro-kernel stores C with aligned vmovaps, so C must be 32-byte aligned with ldc a multiple of 8 floats, and M and N must be multiples of 6 and 16; the benchmark only uses multiples of 48, which hides this
- Packing buffers are malloc'd and freed on every call, which costs time at small sizes
- The % of peak column divides by 1024 instead of 1000 (81.25 rather than 83.2 GFLOPS at 2.6 GHz) and counts 2*M*N*(K+1) flops, so the 96% figures overstate efficiency by a few points; the GFLOPS comparison with OpenBLAS uses the same formula and is unaffected

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-04-15 (31 commits, 75 stars, one unanswered issue asking for an MKL comparison) but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as a study kernel; it is unsafe as a general SGEMM because of the stubbed paths and unchecked edge tiles.

[repo](https://github.com/carlushuang/cpu_gemm_opt) · [benchmark](https://github.com/carlushuang/cpu_gemm_opt)

##### MaxMulSK  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Single-threaded FP32 SME/SME2 GEMM for Apple M4; published v3 beats an SME-enabled OpenBLAS build, trails Accelerate.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS (tuned build reaching its own SME kernels, one thread) and Apple Accelerate — The reproducible claim is the 9 September 2026 session of bench/bench_headline.cpp: Homebrew Clang 22.1.8, -mcpu=apple-m4 and -march=armv8.7-a+sme+sme2, Apple M4 on macOS 26.6.2, one thread, FP32, allocation and packing inside the timed call. There the published v3 reached 1396-1768 GFLOP/s on squares 256^3-4096^3, which is 1.01-1.31x an OpenBLAS develop build reaching its SME kernels and 1.36-2.23x on LLM shapes, but only 0.83-1.05x of Accelerate. The 29 September table (v5.1: 1.86x OpenBLAS and 1.16x Accelerate, geometric mean over 35 shapes) comes from unpublished code.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A covers only the published v3 claim (bench/bench_headline.cpp, Clang 22.1.8, M4); the v5.1 headline code is unpublished.

**Known shortcoming:** Published v3 trails Accelerate on most shapes (0.83x at 256^3, 0.92-0.95x on LLM shapes); allocates ~8.5 MB per call with std::aligned_alloc and no null check; MAXMULSK_BLOCKING env override read every call without checking N_tile is a multiple of N_step; other kernels in the repo had silent wrong-result bugs and one is still latent in v1; Apple M4 only (pack_A hard-coded for 512-bit vectors).

**How:** It runs a BLIS-style blocked GEMM on Arm SME. A 1x4 geometry (a 16x64 FP32 output tile spread over four 16x16 ZA tiles) does four FMOPA outer products per A vector. A is packed through a ZA-tile transpose and B through SVE stores. The v2/v3 change keeps ZA live across the whole K panel, with K innermost: ZA is zeroed once per C tile and drained once with one svst1_f32_x4 per row, and the first K panel stores without a read-modify-write. That cut per-call fixed cost from 357 ns to 52 ns. v3 adds an outer Kc panel so the packed buffers scale with Kc rather than K. Blocking comes from a small per-shape table (gemm_tuning) whose entries are kept only if they won in three separate runs.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded FP32 row-major GEMM on an Apple M4 where Accelerate is not an option and OpenBLAS is the alternative. The published v3 is 1.01-1.31x an SME-enabled OpenBLAS develop build on squares 256^3-4096^3 and 1.36-2.23x on M=64/128 LLM shapes.
- Replacing Homebrew's OpenBLAS on M4. That build cannot reach its own SME kernels and falls off above 1024^3, per the README.
- Large squares (1024^3, 4096^3), where the published v3 edged Accelerate by 1.05x and 1.02x in the 9 September session.
- Learning SME kernel design. The repo documents every generation, the ablations and the failed experiments (bdirect, pack-once) with dated raw data.

**Skip it when:**
- You can call Accelerate. The published v3 trails it on most shapes: 0.83x at 256^3, 0.93x at 512^3, 0.97x at 2048^3 and 0.92-0.95x on the LLM shapes. v4c also trails it by 3-5% on the LLaMA shapes.
- You want the headline numbers (1.86x OpenBLAS, 1.16x Accelerate, 1.06x MpGEMM). Those come from the v5.1 kernel, whose code is not in the repository, measured with a separate harness.
- You need multithreading, FP64, transposed or strided (lda) operands, column-major data, or C = alpha*A*B + beta*C. None of these are supported, and SME multi-threading is listed as future work.
- Any chip other than Apple M4. M1-M3 lack SME. pack_A's transpose is hard-coded for a 512-bit streaming vector length (TODO.md: 'Not portable').
- Production use that needs a stable API. It is a 0-star single-student project with no library target, and the namespace-level entry point changes from generation to generation.

**Integration:** source-drop (copy sme/v3/sme-1x4-acc-kcout.{hpp,cpp} and sme/support/gemm_tuning.{hpp,cpp}; the CMake project builds only executables) · The kernel needs only the ACLE headers arm_sme.h and arm_sve.h. The repo build also needs Homebrew libomp and CMake 3.30+. OpenBLAS (dlopen), KleidiAI (fetched at v1.30.0, can be turned off), llama.cpp/ggml, NumPy and PyTorch are needed only for benchmarks. · C++20; Homebrew LLVM/Clang (README: Apple's bundled Clang lacks the SME/SME2 intrinsics; results used Clang 22.1.8); kernel sources compiled with -march=armv8.7-a+sme+sme2 · Apple M4 only (SME/SME2, 512-bit streaming vector length), macOS

**Vs siblings:** MTGEMM-A (MIT, all code public) covers the same M4 SME niche with FP64, alpha/beta, leading dimensions, both storage orders and two-SME-unit threading, and MPGEMM's code is now public too, so prefer those for real use. Pick MaxMulSK only for single-threaded FP32 row-major work on an M4 where you want its documented kernel history, or once v5.1 (reported 1.06x MpGEMM on the same M4) is published.

**Gotchas:**
- The v3 KcOut kernel overwrites C (C = A*B). Its header says every other MaxMulSK SME kernel accumulates (C += A*B), so swapping kernels changes semantics.
- Each call std::aligned_alloc's about 8.5 MB of packing buffers (1024x2048 floats for A plus 64x2048 for B at the default blocking) and does not check for a null return.
- MAXMULSK_BLOCKING='M_tile,N_tile,Kc,ir_outer' overrides the blocking on every call. The parser rejects only zero values, while the header requires N_tile to be a multiple of the kernel's N_step.
- Sibling kernels in the repo returned silently wrong results before fixes (4x1 pack_A when M_tile > 64; the same latent bug 'still sits in the v1 kernel', per gemm_tuning.cpp). Use only the v3 1x4 path the README documents. Timings of short calls such as 256^3 depend on the work that ran just before.

**Status:** Active (39 commits, last 2026-09-29) and Apache-2.0, so it is copyable. It is a 0-star single-maintainer student project with no releases, and its best kernel (v5.1) is not yet published.

[repo](https://github.com/UlasSertan/MaxMulSK) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UlasSertan/MaxMulSK/HEAD/README.md)

##### MTGEMM-A  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

SME2 FP32/FP64 GEMM for Apple M4 Pro, rebuilt from the MpGEMM paper: 1.18-1.26x Apple Accelerate on the paper's workloads.

**Beats:** Apple Accelerate sgemm/dgemm (also OpenBLAS develop and 0.3.34, Eigen master, LIBXSMM, KleidiAI) — Setup: Apple M4 Pro (8 P-cores, two SME units, SVL 512, macOS 27.0), Apple clang 21 with -O3 -march=armv8.6-a+sme2+sme-f64f64, minimum of five 50 ms trials on a shared machine (load 1.5-5.6). FP32 geometric mean over the paper's 24 workloads: 1421 vs 1196 GFLOPS for Accelerate on one thread column-major (1.19x), 1416 vs 1124 row-major (1.26x) and 2777 vs 2363 at default threading (1.18x); squares 512-4096 on one thread gain only 1.04-1.06x. In the same harness it is 2.20x LIBXSMM, 1.67x KleidiAI and 3.70x Homebrew OpenBLAS 0.3.34, which falls back to NEON at M=4096.

**Known shortcoming:** Run on a shared machine (minimum of 5 trials); slower below 64^3; independent reimplementation of the MpGEMM (ARM SME) design, not a duplicate.

**Known shortcoming:** README says no MpGEMM code exists, now false (github.com/mpgemm/MPGEMM, MIT); opt=nullptr runs one thread (the 'default threading' figures need threads=0); macOS only (pthread QoS, sysctl).

**How:** It uses Goto/BLIS six-loop blocking, with mc/nc/kc chosen by the paper's analytical model: an 8 MB L2 budget, a TLB bound and the best compute-to-memory ratio. Under it sits a 16x64 FP32 (8x64 FP64) micro-kernel that issues four FMOPA outer products into four ZA tiles per A vector. A is transposed while packing through the ZA array, and B is packed online during the first pass. All full-width loads and stores use SME2 four-register (x4) forms. The project's additions over the paper are core-side prfm pldl2keep prefetch of A, B and C into the L2 that the SME unit reads (1.12x row-major, 1.20x column-major) and four-row MOVA vg4 moves for C tiles and A packing. An optional second thread drives the second P-cluster's SME unit (1.95x scaling).

**Use it when:**
- FP32 or FP64 GEMM on an Apple M4/M4 Pro where you want to beat Accelerate. On one thread over the paper's 24 workloads it is 1.19x column-major and 1.26x row-major; at default threading it is 1.18x. FP64 row-major on one thread is 1.29x.
- Skinny and irregular shapes. With K=4096, one side 4-32 and the other two at 4096 it is 1.2-2.4x Accelerate on one thread. At K=25600 with M=N=80-200 it is 1.18-1.63x.
- Mid-size problems from 192^3 to 512^3 with threads=0. It brings in the second SME unit from 2^22 multiply-adds, where Accelerate waits until about 512^3 (1.2-2.0x).
- You need a BLAS-like alpha/beta/leading-dimension interface and one binary that dispatches across M2-M4 (SME, AMX or reference loop).
- A readable SME GEMM reference: the core is about 740 lines, with an ablation table per design element. It was used to port SME GEMM into Eigen and OpenBLAS.

**Skip it when:**
- Tiny problems. Squares below 64^3 run at 0.16-0.9x Accelerate and the 4x4 corner at 0.5x. Matrix-vector cases (one side = 1) run at 0.4x.
- K=512 with one side of 32 or less and the other of 512 or more, where it is at 0.6-0.9x on one thread.
- Transposed operands, complex types, mixed precision (FP16/BF16/INT8) or other BLAS/LAPACK routines. Only no-transpose real GEMM is implemented.
- Non-Apple SME2 hardware or another vector length. The code uses macOS APIs (pthread QoS, sysctl) and SVL-512 constants, and the AMX backend does not run on M1.
- Large squares on one thread only. The gain there is 1.04-1.06x, inside the few-percent noise of a shared machine.

**Integration:** static lib · None for the library (macOS system headers). Accelerate is used by the tests and benchmarks. LIBXSMM, KleidiAI, Eigen, OpenBLAS and Google Benchmark are fetched only for the comparison targets. · C++17; Apple clang with SME2 support (results with Apple clang 21) and -march=armv8.6-a+sme2+sme-f64f64 · macOS on Apple M4 family (SME2, SVL 512, FEAT_SME_F64F64); AMX backend for M2/M3 (incl. Vision Pro), not M1; portable reference loop elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over MaxMulSK when you need FP64, alpha/beta, leading dimensions, column-major input or both M4 Pro SME units, all from published code: MaxMulSK is FP32, single-threaded and row-major, and its fastest kernel is unpublished. Against MPGEMM (github.com/mpgemm/MPGEMM, MIT), the README says no MpGEMM code was found and compares only with the paper's chart numbers (1.06x/1.10x on one thread). That repository is now public, so run a side-by-side test before choosing.

**Gotchas:**
- The default mt_options has threads=1, so a call with opt=nullptr runs on one SME unit. The README's 'default threading' figures need threads=0 (two threads from 2^22 multiply-adds) or threads=2.
- Two-thread mode starts a persistent worker that is never joined and spins for 200 us after each call while the caller busy-waits. macOS cannot pin threads, so both threads can land on one SME unit, and threads=2 has no small-size fallback.
- Dimensions and leading dimensions are int (32-bit). The thread_local packing buffer stays allocated between calls in every thread that calls the library.
- The mt_options.prof setting gives wrong results by design (profiling only). The AMX backend relies on undocumented instructions (corsix/amx encodings), which a future OS or chip could remove.

**Status:** Active (51 commits, last 2026-09-29), MIT and small enough to vendor, but a 0-star single-author reproduction measured on one machine. Its tests run 2304 option combinations and 900 random cases against a double-precision reference.

[repo](https://github.com/tesch1/MTGEMM-A) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tesch1/MTGEMM-A)

##### Octavian.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Julia multithreaded GEMM built on LoopVectorization; median 1816 GFLOPS at 1000^3 vs OpenBLAS 1254 and MKL 1348.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS and Intel MKL (also BLIS) — One 2021 run of BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl (sizes 10-1000, 2h25m sweep) on an 18-core Intel Core i9-10980XE (Cascade Lake-X, AVX-512) with Julia 1.7.0-DEV.1124, LLVM 11.0.1 and 36 threads. At 1000x1000x1000 the median GFLOPS were Octavian 1816, MKL 1348, OpenBLAS 1254 and BLIS 1051, i.e. 1.35x MKL and 1.45x OpenBLAS (derived from page data). The README does not state the baseline library versions or the element type, and other sizes appear only in a plot.

**Known shortcoming:** Single 2021 36-thread run; the last year's commits are CI bumps only; depends on LoopVectorization (grant-funded upkeep); Julia.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: open issue #193 (Oct 2024, no maintainer reply) reports wrong results and segfaults from matmul! on 10x3000 by 3000x10 inputs (Julia 1.10/1.11, single thread); also open #191 (ReadOnlyMemoryError with 30 threads) and #109 (no dimension check); the B-buffer spin lock has no try/finally, so later calls can hang after an error.

**How:** It runs a Goto/BLIS-style blocked GEMM. Block sizes Mc/Kc/Nc are solved in closed form from L1/L2 cache sizes reported by CPUSummary (hwloc), with weights tuned per architecture: AVX-512, Zen1-3, a generic fallback and Apple aarch64. Depending on size and alignment it packs nothing, only A, or both A and B into page-aligned buffers preallocated at load time. LoopVectorization's @turbo generates the register-blocked micro-kernels. Threads are dispatched through PolyesterWeave/ThreadingUtilities spinning workers rather than Base.Threads tasks, which keeps per-call threading overhead low at small and mid sizes.

**Use it when:**
- Julia code doing dense real matmul on a many-core x86 CPU, where you call matmul! explicitly. At 1000^3 on 18 cores / 36 threads it was 1.45x OpenBLAS and 1.35x MKL by median (derived from page data).
- Element types a binary BLAS cannot take, such as integer matrices or ForwardDiff/HyperDualNumbers duals (through package extensions), while keeping a blocked, vectorized kernel.
- Inside your own Polyester- or LoopVectorization-threaded code, using matmul_serial! (Octavian does not start threads when nested in threaded code).
- Pure-Julia stacks that want to avoid OpenBLAS/MKL threading overhead on small and medium sizes.

**Skip it when:**
- C++ projects: there is no C/BLAS ABI, so you would have to embed the Julia runtime. Use a native sibling instead.
- Correctness-critical work on current Julia without your own tests. Open issue #193 (October 2024, no maintainer reply) reports wrong results and segfaults for matmul!(c, a, b) with 10x3000 by 3000x10 inputs on Julia 1.10.5/1.11, single-threaded, on Intel and AMD. Issue #191 reports a ReadOnlyMemoryError with 30 threads on a 271x24 product.
- Code that also uses Base.Threads @spawn/@threads. The docs warn that Octavian's tasks interfere with them and make execution much slower.
- More than 64 threads (#153), dual-socket machines (#151), or large unbalanced problems (#104; #152 reports the wrong strategy for large matrices on Zen3). All four issues are open.
- Long-term dependency risk. Commits in the last year are CI and dependency bumps only, LoopVectorization's upkeep depends on the SciML Small Grants program, and 32-bit Julia support was dropped.

**Integration:** module (registered Julia package, v0.3.29) · LoopVectorization, VectorizationBase, PolyesterWeave, ThreadingUtilities, CPUSummary, StaticArrayInterface, Static, ManualMemory, IfElse, PrecompileTools; ForwardDiff and HyperDualNumbers as weak dependencies · Julia 1.6 (Project.toml compat), 64-bit only · 64-bit x86-64 (tuned constants for AVX-512, Zen1-3, generic) and aarch64 (tuned constants for Apple)

**Vs siblings:** Choose Octavian over PureBLAS.jl, the other pure-Julia BLAS in the catalog, for multithreaded GEMM and generic element types. PureBLAS.jl's comparisons against OpenBLAS/AOCL are single-threaded. For C++ users, Eigen or a native BLIS-style sibling is the practical choice, since Octavian is not callable from C++.

**Gotchas:**
- matmul! does not check dimensions (#109, open). Mismatched sizes proceed silently where LinearAlgebra.mul! throws DimensionMismatch, and LoopVectorization's @turbo kernels do no bounds checking.
- The B-buffer lock is taken without try/finally. If a matmul throws, later calls can spin until you call Octavian.reset_bcache_lock!() (per its docstring).
- The thread count is min(Threads.nthreads(), physical cores), optionally lowered by OCTAVIAN_NUM_TASKS. It is read in __init__ along with the size of the preallocated pack buffers, so start Julia with -t before loading.
- Block sizes depend on correct cache sizes. The README asks for CPUSummary.use_hwloc(true), the default, for accurate hardware information.

**Status:** MIT, 255 stars and registered, but effectively in maintenance mode: the last commit (2025-10-21) was a CI bump, and correctness issue #193 has gone unanswered since October 2024.

[repo](https://github.com/JuliaLinearAlgebra/Octavian.jl) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JuliaLinearAlgebra/Octavian.jl/HEAD/README.md)

##### PureBLAS.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Julia BLAS 1-3 plus LAPACK that matches or beats single-threaded OpenBLAS and AOCL on AMD Zen3/4/5.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS (Julia's bundled build) and AOCL-BLIS (AMD's BLIS fork); the repo's gate is max(OpenBLAS, AOCL) — The author's harness (bench/plots.jl, single thread, frequency-locked, ABBA-interleaved rounds, median ratio) on a Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen3), Ryzen 5 7640U (Zen4) and Ryzen AI 5 340 (Zen5) laptop under Julia 1.13 against Julia's bundled OpenBLAS and AOCL_jll shows per-op median ratios such as gemm 1.17/1.08/1.23 and geqrf 1.55/1.79/1.66 vs OpenBLAS, with about 87% of 2619 cells at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL); worst cells lose (gemm 0.94 on Zen4, 0.90 on Zen5) and about 30% of cells sit within +-5% of parity.

**Known shortcoming:** gemm switches to Strassen-Winograd from n>=256, so it is not like-for-like with classical BLAS; notes.md 'gemm gates every size' contradicts the table's worst 0.90/0.94; Julia 1.13 patch unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Large gemm uses Strassen-Winograd and zgemm uses Karatsuba 3M (not like-for-like numerics); Apple Silicon gemm runs about 0.68x OpenBLAS (ROADMAP); correctness bug fixed in v0.1.2: complex gemv trans T/C threw MethodError for A larger than L2, breaking complex eigen() (live 2026-08-08 to 2026-08-29); the shared library cannot thread (juliac handle-signals=no); unregistered package.

**How:** Block sizes (MC/NC/KC, panel widths, crossovers) are derived at load time from detected cache sizes, vector width and register count instead of per-CPU hand-tuned tables, feeding a GotoBLAS-style packed GEMM engine with SIMD.jl microkernels. Above about min(m,n,k) >= 256, real gemm switches to Strassen-Winograd and complex gemm to Karatsuba 3M (three real products, 25% fewer flops), which is where much of the large-n BLAS-3 lead comes from. LAPACK routines are blocked ports (dlatrd/syr2k reduction, compact-WY back-transform, divide-and-conquer stedc, blocked dlaqps, dlasyf/zlahef) with fixes for power-of-two leading-dimension cache-set aliasing, and nrm2 scales only on overflow/underflow rather than always (hence 7-11x over OpenBLAS there).

**Use it when:**
- Julia code on AMD Zen3/Zen4/Zen5 that is dominated by single-threaded dense factorizations: the project's own tables show median 1.1-1.8x over OpenBLAS for potrf, geqrf, getrf, gesvd and syev
- Forward-mode AD through linear algebra in Julia: ForwardDiff duals run through the generic kernels, 1.1-50x faster than LinearAlgebra's generic fallback in the dual tables
- Large real or complex gemm (n >= 256) where Strassen-Winograd or 3M rounding behaviour is acceptable
- Swapping BLAS backends in an existing Julia program with one activate() call to A/B test against OpenBLAS

**Skip it when:**
- Production C/C++ code: the libpureblas.so path depends on experimental juliac --trim, embeds a Julia runtime, exports only ILP64 Fortran symbols (no CBLAS header documented), and the shared library is single-threaded because juliac builds with handle-signals=no
- Apple Silicon: the roadmap measures PureBLAS gemm at about 0.68x OpenBLAS at n=2048 on an M-series part, and Accelerate's SME path is about 7x faster than any NEON code; SME work is still a campaign
- Intel or Arm servers in general: every published gate number is from three AMD Ryzen machines; no Intel results exist
- Code that needs classical O(n^3) gemm error bounds or bitwise agreement with reference BLAS: large gemm/zgemm use fast algorithms
- Multi-threaded throughput against threaded vendor BLAS: threading is opt-in and recent, and the threaded-gate plots for Zen4 are flagged as not yet adjudicable

**Integration:** module · Julia packages CPUSummary, CpuId, SIMD, PrecompileTools, Preferences, StrictMode, TypeContracts (LinearAlgebra stdlib); ForwardDiff optional extension. Not registered in the General registry; install from the git URL. · Julia 1.13 (the only supported and CI-tested release) · x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512 (benchmarked only on AMD Zen3/4/5); runs on Apple Silicon/aarch64 via NEON but slower than OpenBLAS there; shared library built on Linux in CI, macOS .dylib path exists

**Vs siblings:** Pick PureBLAS over Octavian.jl when you need full BLAS plus LAPACK in Julia rerouted through libblastrampoline rather than a threaded gemm alone, and over RecursiveFactorization.jl when you want every factorization, not just LU, replaced. For small cache-resident matrices in C, BLASFEO is the mature choice; for C++ code that just needs a faster BLAS, Eigen or a vendor BLAS is far less risky than PureBLAS's experimental shared library.

**Gotchas:**
- Do not load libpureblas.so into a running Julia process (or lbt_forward to it): the embedded libjulia double-initializes and aborts; use activate() instead
- Calls routed through activate() go through the C ABI, so Dual numbers cannot pass; call PureBLAS.* directly for AD (reverse mode is not supported at all)
- Singular vectors are only available for Float64 and complex; the generic path raises an error rather than returning less
- v0.1.2 fixed a MethodError in complex gemv trans='T'/'C' for any A larger than L2 (which could make eigen() on complex Hermitian matrices throw); live 2026-08-08 to 2026-08-29, so pin to v0.1.2 or later

**Status:** Very active (1,368 commits, last 2026-09-30) but weeks-to-months old, 9 stars, tagged v0.1.2 and deliberately unregistered; MIT-licensed, so it is easy to try inside Julia, while the C-callable library is experimental.

[repo](https://github.com/el-oso/PureBLAS.jl) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/el-oso/PureBLAS.jl/HEAD/bench/gen_table.md)

##### RecursiveFactorization.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Julia recursive LU (Toledo's algorithm) that beats OpenBLAS and often MKL getrf on dense matrices up to about 500x500.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS (Julia LUFactorization default) and Intel MKL (MKLLUFactorization) — On SciML's CI runner (128-thread AMD EPYC 7502, Julia 1.12.7, RecursiveFactorization v0.2.26 via LinearSolve 5.5.0, OpenBLAS_jll 0.3.29, MKL_jll 2025.2.0, BLAS threads set to min(cores, nthreads)), RFLUFactorization reached roughly 33 GFLOPS at N=500 against about 18 for OpenBLAS and 23 for MKL, and about 2x OpenBLAS near N=200-240; values are read off a plot, and MKL beats it at a few noisy sizes.

**Known shortcoming:** Not independent (SciML runs both sides of SciMLBenchmarks); many-thread BLAS at N<=500 inflates the gap; Julia.

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #48: nested threading with thread=Val(true) makes Julia exit silently on Windows; a 2026-08-08 fix (pivot-free lu! returned the user's ipiv uninitialized) may postdate the benchmarked v0.2.26; LinearSolve picks it only for small N (<=100, <=500 on OpenBLAS, <=200 on MKL).

**How:** Sivan Toledo's recursive left-looking LU (SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl., DOI 10.1137/S0895479896297744) splits the column panel in two, factors the left half recursively, applies the pivots, does a unit-lower triangular solve (TriangularSolve.jl) and a Schur-complement update, then recurses on the right half; this keeps working sets cache-sized without hand-picked block sizes. The Schur update and the base-case kernels are LoopVectorization @turbo loops that JIT-compile SIMD micro-kernels for the host CPU, so there is no BLAS call and none of the threading or dispatch overhead that dominates OpenBLAS at small N. Threading (Polyester @batch / @tturbo) only switches on when the matrix exceeds about 92% of L2 cache.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated dense LU solves of square Float64/Float32 matrices from roughly 10x10 to 500x500 in Julia (ODE/DAE Jacobians, Newton steps, small FEM blocks).
- On x86-64 with OpenBLAS as Julia's default BLAS, where SciMLBenchmarks shows about 2x OpenBLAS around N=100-250 on an EPYC 7502.
- Inside LinearSolve.jl: load the package and the default algorithm already routes small square systems to RFLUFactorization.
- When you want pure-Julia code that also handles ComplexF32/ComplexF64 and non-BLAS element types through the same API (tested in runtests.jl, via the generic recursion path).

**Skip it when:**
- Large matrices (well above N=500): the only benchmark stops at 500 and LinearSolve itself hands larger sizes back to BLAS/MKL.
- From C or C++: it is a Julia package with no C ABI; use a LAPACK getrf (or ReLAPACK) instead.
- On Apple Silicon, where LinearSolve's own default prefers Apple Accelerate LU over RFLU.
- When you need other factorizations: only LU is implemented (Cholesky and QR are not; issue #74 asks about QR).
- Inside an outer Threads.@threads loop with thread=Val(true): issue #48 reports Julia exiting silently on Windows 10; pass Val(false) for the thread argument.

**Integration:** module · LinearAlgebra, LoopVectorization, Polyester, PrecompileTools, SparseBandedMatrices, StrideArraysCore, TriangularSolve, VectorizedRNG · Julia 1.10 (Project.toml compat) · any platform LoopVectorization supports; recursion threshold is tuned for AVX2 vs AVX-512 (40 vs 48 columns)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Octavian.jl or PureBLAS.jl when your bottleneck is solving small dense systems (LU) rather than GEMM, and over ReLAPACK or BLASFEO when you are already in Julia and want a recursive getrf without linking a C/Fortran LAPACK; from C++ those two are the relevant choices.

**Gotchas:**
- Direct calls default to single-threaded (thread = Val(false)) while LinearSolve's RFLUFactorization defaults to thread = Val(true); timings differ accordingly, and threading only engages above about 0.92x the L2 cache size.
- Fast path needs a StridedArray of Float32/Float64; other array types or element types fall back to a generic (slower) recursion, and pivoted matrices with min(m,n) < 10 go straight to LinearAlgebra.generic_lufact!.
- pivot = Val(false) (and the butterfly path) trades stability for speed; LinearSolve's docs say the butterfly variant is less robust for matrices that need pivoting.
- A commit of 2026-08-08 ('Initialize a user-supplied ipiv in pivot-free lu!') fixed no-pivot mode returning a user-supplied ipiv full of uninitialized memory; the benchmarked v0.2.26 may predate it (HEAD Project.toml is v0.2.30; which release first carries the fix is not documented). First calls also pay JIT/precompile latency.

**Status:** Actively maintained by the SciML/JuliaLinearAlgebra maintainers (v0.2.30, last commit 2026-08-09) and MIT-licensed; usable from Julia only, and it depends on LoopVectorization, which is kept alive through SciML small grants.

[repo](https://github.com/JuliaLinearAlgebra/RecursiveFactorization.jl) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SciML/SciMLBenchmarksOutput/main/markdown/LinearSolve/LUFactorization.md)

##### BLASFEO  `C`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

C BLAS/LAPACK subset tuned for cache-resident small matrices; 2-3x faster than OpenBLAS/BLIS at sizes in the tens.

**Beats:** Intel MKL and OpenBLAS (level-3 BLAS and LAPACK routines on small matrices) — The authors' BLAS API paper (arXiv 1902.08115) times single-threaded BLASFEO against OpenBLAS 0.3.4-dev, BLIS 0.5.0 and MKL 2019.1 on a Haswell Core i7 4810MQ, Cortex-A57 (Tegra TX1) and Cortex-A53: factor 2-3 over OpenBLAS/BLIS for level-3 BLAS at sizes in the tens on Haswell, about 2x for LAPACK factorizations up to ~100, on par with MKL dgemm and faster on other routines; compiler and flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper: 2-3x faster than OpenBLAS/BLIS at sizes in the tens (not '1.5-3x up to 100'); level with MKL on dgemm; no compiler or flags given.

**Known shortcoming:** arXiv abstract (TOMS paper 1704.02457) gives 20-30% over comparable libraries up to ~100, 2-3x only vs LAPACK; not a default drop-in (dgemm_/cblas_ exported only with FORTRAN_BLAS_API=1, only some routines optimized); single-threaded only; denormals in matrix memory or padding can slow it 10x+.

**How:** Hand-written assembly kernels per microarchitecture (Haswell AVX2/FMA, Skylake-X AVX-512, Cortex-A53/A57/A76, Apple M1, etc.) with a custom internal calling convention so kernels chain without function-call overhead. The native API stores matrices in panel-major format (fixed-height row panels, column-major inside), which is the layout GEMM kernels want, so no packing is done at all; the BLAS API packs on the fly with strategies tuned for small sizes. LAPACK factorizations are written directly on these kernels instead of the blocked LAPACK reference algorithms.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded dense linear algebra on matrices of roughly 10-250 per side that fit in cache (MPC, embedded optimization, Kalman filters, robotics)
- Cholesky/LU/QR on small matrices, where the BLAS API paper shows about 2x over OpenBLAS/BLIS LAPACK up to size ~100
- Low-power ARM (Cortex-A53/A57) boards, where the margin over OpenBLAS and BLIS is largest
- Code you control end to end and can move to the native panel-major API for another 10-15% over BLASFEO's own BLAS API

**Skip it when:**
- Large matrices or multithreaded throughput: routines are single-threaded and optimized for cache-resident sizes; use OpenBLAS/MKL/BLIS
- Needing full BLAS/LAPACK coverage: only a subset of routines and variants is optimized, others fall back to reference code or need Netlib complementing
- dgemm alone on Intel: the paper finds it only competitive with MKL there, not faster
- Complex-number routines: not listed among optimized routines

**Integration:** static lib · none (optional external BLAS/LAPACK for the wrapper backend, fallback or Netlib complement; Python 3.6 + jinja2 only for the test suite) · C compiler with GNU-style assembler (gcc default); Make or CMake; exact minimum not documented · x86-64 (SSE3/AVX/AVX2+FMA/AVX-512 targets), 32-bit x86, ARMv8-A (A53/A55/A57/A73/A76, Apple M1), ARMv7-A, plus a GENERIC C target; high-performance backend on Linux, Windows x86-64 and macOS

**Vs siblings:** Pick BLASFEO over Eigen or a general BLAS (FT-BLAS, BLIS forks) when your matrices are small and you also need fast factorizations (potrf/getrf/geqrf), not just GEMM; LibShalom reports 2x over BLASFEO at M=N=K=8 on Phytium, so for tiny GEMM-only work on ARM servers check LibShalom or IAAT first.

**Gotchas:**
- Target is chosen at build time (TARGET=...); a binary built for X64_INTEL_HASWELL will not adapt to other CPUs (CMake has X64_AUTOMATIC detection for the host only)
- Denormals in matrix memory, including padding, can slow routines 10x or more; the docs recommend zeroing memory passed to blasfeo_create_dmat and BLAS-API arrays
- Align memory to 64-byte cache lines and use leading dimensions that are multiples of the kernel size (typically 4 in double) for best speed
- Stack buffers sized by K_MAX_STACK (default 300) can exceed small thread stacks; lower it if the stack overflows

**Status:** Actively developed (commits through Sept 2026), BSD-2-Clause, and used as the linear algebra layer of embedded optimization toolchains, so it is safe to build from source or vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/giaf/blasfeo) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.02457)

##### CLBlast  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Auto-tuned OpenCL BLAS (levels 1-3, FP16, batched) for GPUs and accelerators; beats clBLAS GEMM, trails cuBLAS on NVIDIA.

**Beats:** clBLAS 2.12 (cuBLAS also tested; it is faster) — The peer-reviewed IWOCL '18 paper benchmarks CLBlast 1.3.0 GEMM against clBLAS 2.12 (and cuBLAS on NVIDIA) on seven devices (GTX 750 Ti, Titan X, Radeon HD 7970, Radeon M370X, Intel Skylake GT2, Core i5-6200U CPU, Mali T628) and reports better overall GEMM throughput than clBLAS, most visibly at irregular sizes (multiples of 129) and on Skylake and NVIDIA, shown in graphs without a numeric ratio; cuBLAS remained faster. The ~2x FP16 and up-to-10x batched figures compare CLBlast with its own FP32 and non-batched calls, not with another library.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper says cuBLAS is still faster; ~2x FP16 figure is vs CLBlast's own FP32; 10x batched figure is vs non-batched calls; win over clBLAS 2.12 only in graphs.

**Known shortcoming:** Open correctness issues: #669 CGEMM wrong on AMD RX 5700, #668 SSYRK/SSYR2K error on Apple M1, #561 FP16 GEMV wrong; installation.md says CMake 2.8.10 but CMakeLists needs 3.14.

**How:** Every kernel is parameterised (the GEMM kernel has 14 parameters: work-group tile sizes MWG/NWG, 2D register tiling MWI/NWI, vector widths VWM/VWN, unroll factor KWI, local-memory use) and auto-tuned per device in the style of CLTune, with a shipped database of best values for many NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Arm Mali, Qualcomm Adreno and Apple GPUs. GEMM has two paths: an indirect path that pads/transposes inputs with pre- and post-processing kernels so a fast main kernel can assume tile-multiple sizes, and a single 'direct' kernel for small matrices; a routine-level tuner picks the size at which to switch. FP16 routines and batched GEMM give further gains on hardware with fast half precision or many small problems.

**Use it when:**
- You need GEMM or other BLAS on non-NVIDIA GPUs (AMD, Intel integrated or Arc, Arm Mali, Qualcomm Adreno, Apple M-series) through OpenCL, and clBLAS is the alternative.
- Irregular or rectangular matrix sizes where clBLAS loses badly; you can tune for your exact shapes with the tuners or the tuning API and OverrideParameters.
- Mobile and embedded GPUs where half precision (cl_khr_fp16) is accelerated, e.g. deep-learning inference on Mali or Intel GPUs.
- Many small matrices at once: GEMMBATCHED or the faster GEMMSTRIDEDBATCHED instead of a loop of single GEMM calls.
- Portable code that must run across vendors, or OpenCL 1.1-era hardware.

**Skip it when:**
- NVIDIA-only deployments: the README itself says to use cuBLAS there, and the IWOCL '18 paper shows cuBLAS still faster.
- CPU BLAS work (it is not a replacement for OpenBLAS, MKL, BLIS or Eigen); Intel CPUs are only reachable through an OpenCL CPU runtime.
- You need LAPACK (factorisations, solvers, eigenvalues): only BLAS is implemented, and xROTG, xROTMG, xROT, xROTM, xTBSV and xTPSV are missing.
- Untuned devices where you cannot run the tuners: the README warns out-of-the-box performance can be poor and falls back to family defaults.
- Correctness-critical work on devices with open accuracy reports (e.g. CGEMM errors on AMD RX 5700 in issue #669, SSYRK/SSYR2K error on Apple M1 in #668, FP16 GEMV in #561) unless you run the bundled correctness tests on your device first.

**Integration:** shared lib (static via -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF); packages in Debian/Ubuntu (libclblast-dev), Homebrew, Windows release zips; Python binding pyclblast · OpenCL 1.1+ runtime and headers (or CUDA 7.5+ with NVRTC for the CUDA build); nothing else · C++11 (GCC 4.7+, Clang 3.3+, MSVC 2013+ per docs); CMakeLists now requires CMake 3.14 although installation.md still says 2.8.10 · Any OpenCL 1.1+ device: NVIDIA, AMD, Intel GPUs and CPUs, Arm Mali, Qualcomm Adreno, Apple M1/M2, Intel MIC; Linux, macOS, Windows, Android (cross-compile)

**Vs siblings:** It is the only GPU/OpenCL library among the catalogued blas-lapack siblings: pick it when the matrices live on a GPU or mobile accelerator; pick BLASFEO, LibShalom or Eigen for small or medium matrices on CPUs, and FT-BLAS or GEMMFIP when you need a CPU BLAS replacement for OpenBLAS/MKL.

**Gotchas:**
- First call of each routine compiles its OpenCL kernel at run time, so first-call latency is high; use FillCache(device) to precompile, and ClearCache to free the binaries.
- Indirect GEMM may allocate a temporary device buffer (error -4 on memory-tight devices); query GemmTempBufferSize and pass your own buffer, or raise the direct/indirect switch point with OverrideParameters.
- Versions 1.6.2 and older give wrong results on Intel Arc A770 and some other devices (GEMMK=1 kernel bug when MWG!=NWG, fixed in 1.6.3); distro packages may ship an older version.
- GemmStridedBatched with a C stride of 0 does not accumulate into one matrix (open issue #578); FP16 tests can fail on operation order, and integer-returning half routines (IHAMAX etc.) are not properly tested.

**Status:** Actively maintained (1.7.0 is the latest release, commits into September 2026, tuning results still being added), Apache-2.0 and packaged by major distros, so it is usable as-is; plan to run the tuners and correctness tests on devices outside its tuned list.

[repo](https://github.com/CNugteren/CLBlast) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.05249)

##### COSMA  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

Communication-optimal distributed (MPI) matrix multiply with a ScaLAPACK p?gemm drop-in; beats MKL ScaLAPACK and Cray LibSci pdgemm.

**Beats:** Intel MKL ScaLAPACK pdgemm (also Cray LibSci, Cray LibSci_acc, CARMA, CTF) — On Piz Daint (Cray XC50 nodes with Xeon E5-2690 v3 and Tesla P100, 2019), CP2K's 128-water RPA benchmark spent 75.3 s in pdgemm with GPU COSMA vs 139.8 s with Cray LibSci_acc 19.10.1 on 1024 nodes; on 128 nodes CPU COSMA took 1723.6 s vs 1836.9 s for MKL 19.0.1.144 ScaLAPACK and 5896.5 s for Cray LibSci. The SC19 paper (abstract via search snippet) reports up to 12.8x and 2.2x average over ScaLAPACK, CARMA and CTF; compiler and flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Against MKL in CP2K small the win is about 7% (pdgemm 1723.62 vs 1836.85 s); the 2x is vs LibSci_acc; paper unread here (arXiv blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug fixed in v2.8.3 (COSTA 2.3.1): pdgemm read C even when beta=0; open issue #118 memory blow-up (CP2K needed about 3x the nodes ScaLAPACK did); open issue #171 CMake BLAS auto-detect broken; README says CMake 3.17 but CMakeLists needs 3.24.

**How:** It derives a near-optimal sequential schedule from a red-blue pebble game I/O lower bound and then parallelizes it, choosing the processor decomposition from m, n, k, p and memory instead of fixing a 2D (SUMMA) or 2.5D grid upfront; it may idle some ranks to get a better grid. The paper reports up to sqrt(3) less communication than 2D/3D algorithms, which matters most for tall-and-skinny shapes. Buffers are preallocated and reused, local reshuffling is minimized via the COSTA layout-transform library, communication can overlap computation, and GPU runs pipeline tiles through Tiled-MM (cuBLAS/rocBLAS) with optional NCCL/RCCL or GPU-aware MPI.

**Use it when:**
- Distributed dense GEMM on clusters, especially tall-and-skinny or otherwise non-square shapes where 2D ScaLAPACK grids waste communication (CP2K RPA: 46 tall-and-skinny pdgemm calls)
- Fortran or C codes already calling ScaLAPACK pdgemm that want a speedup by relinking only
- GPU-accelerated nodes where matrices start in host memory: GPU COSMA was about 1.86x Cray LibSci_acc on 1024 Piz Daint nodes and 1.31x on 128
- Square multiplications at moderate node counts on CPU, where the README plot shows about 2x over MKL ScaLAPACK at n=20000 narrowing to about 1.3x at n=120000

**Skip it when:**
- Single-node or shared-memory GEMM: it is an MPI algorithm that calls a local BLAS (MKL, OpenBLAS, BLIS, cuBLAS, rocBLAS) for the actual work
- Memory-tight runs: open issue #118 reports CP2K gradient pdgemm calls (m=n=17,408, k=3,473,408) running out of CPU/GPU memory where ScaLAPACK fit, needing about 3x the nodes
- Anything beyond GEMM: no factorizations or other PBLAS/ScaLAPACK routines are provided
- Expecting large wins over Intel MKL ScaLAPACK in production on CPU: the CP2K 128-node pdgemm time improved only about 7% (1723.6 s vs 1836.9 s)
- Build environments with AMD or other non-MKL/OpenBLAS BLAS and COSMA_BLAS=auto: open issue #171 reports the CMake search stopping early

**Integration:** static lib · MPI 3, a BLAS backend (MKL, OpenBLAS, BLIS, ATLAS, Cray LibSci, NVPL, custom, or CUDA/ROCm), optional ScaLAPACK (MKL, Cray LibSci, NVPL, custom) for the p?gemm wrappers, optional NCCL/RCCL; bundled submodules COSTA, Tiled-MM, semiprof, gtest_mpi · C++14 (cxx_std_14), CMake 3.24 per CMakeLists.txt (the README still says 3.17) · Linux clusters with MPI; CPU any architecture with a BLAS, NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA, AMD GPUs via ROCm; Spack and Docker recipes provided

**Vs siblings:** Pick COSMA over SPLA (also eth-cscs, pdgemm-compatible) when you want the more general, peer-reviewed algorithm with native-layout and multi-GPU (NCCL/RCCL) options; SPLA's own README claims parity with COSMA on CPU and a lead on GPU, so benchmark both on GPU nodes. Tiled-MM is the single-node GPU engine COSMA itself uses, and node-local BLAS siblings (Eigen, BLASFEO, OpenBLAS forks) solve a different problem.

**Gotchas:**
- Link order matters: libcosma_pxgemm must come before any other library providing p?gemm, otherwise the ScaLAPACK version is silently used
- Releases before v2.8.3 (April 2024) read the user's C matrix even when beta=0, so uninitialized or NaN-filled C could corrupt results; the fix shipped in COSTA 2.3.1, so use COSMA 2.8.4 or later
- COSMA_CPU_MAX_MEMORY caps per-rank memory but throws runtime_error if the multiplication cannot fit, and the README marks it as still in testing
- Clone with --recursive: COSTA and Tiled-MM are submodules, and COSMA_BLAS must be set explicitly (the CMake default OFF is a fatal error, despite the README calling MKL the default)

**Status:** Maintained by ETH Zurich/CSCS (last commit 2026-07-29, latest release v2.8.4 from April 2024, 219 stars, used in CP2K), BSD-3-Clause, with 7 open issues including memory blow-up and CMake BLAS-detection bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/eth-cscs/COSMA) · [benchmark](https://github.com/eth-cscs/COSMA)

##### faer  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Pure-Rust dense (and sparse) linear algebra whose multithreaded QR and mid-size eigensolvers outrun OpenBLAS and Eigen; MKL still leads.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS, LAPACK and Eigen (paper text); Intel MKL not claimed as beaten — The JOSS 2023 paper (peer-reviewed software paper, DOI 10.21105/joss.06099) plots n^3/time for f64 matmul, QR and EVD on an Intel Core i5-11400 with 12 threads against OpenBLAS, BLIS, MKL and Eigen (built with -fopenmp); readings show about 3x OpenBLAS on QR at n=10^4, parity on large matmul, and a mid-size EVD win, while MKL stays ahead. No Rust toolchain, flags, library versions or benchmark code are given, and the plots date from November 2023, before the current 0.24 code.

**Known shortcoming:** Plots from 2023 (QR ~3x OpenBLAS, matmul level, large EVD loses to OpenBLAS/BLIS/MKL); tier B rests on JOSS acceptance (review #6099); Rust.
