**Known shortcoming:** Open correctness bugs: NaN from qr().solve_lstsq on an ill-conditioned 3x3 (#265), NaN determinant for a singular 3x3 on 0.23.2 (#260), full_piv_lu solve (#238), hang in partial_self_adjoint_eigen (#262). Checked-in faer-ffi/faer.h declares libfaer_v0_23_* while faer.hpp calls v0_24_*; faer-ffi is not on crates.io. Crate bundles MPL-2.0 Eigen-derived code (COPYING.EIGEN.MPL2). JOSS plots predate 0.24.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Matrix multiplication follows the BLIS approach (packing plus register-blocked micro-kernels), with runtime CPU-feature dispatch to precompiled SIMD variants through the pulp crate, the gemm crate, nano-gemm for small products and, on x86-64 with std, the author's private-gemm-x86 backend (0.22 changelog: 'accelerated matrix multiply backend on x86_64'). Decompositions are blocked so most flops land in that GEMM; memory-bound phases (column-pivoted QR, full-pivot LU, reduction to bidiagonal/tridiagonal/Hessenberg form) use fused kernels that do A x and A^T y in one pass over A. Threading is Rayon (plus the spindle crate); SIMD for user scalar types deinterleaves AoS data to SoA in registers.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code that needs dense factorizations (QR, LU, Cholesky, SVD, EVD) on medium-to-large matrices without linking a C/Fortran BLAS/LAPACK.
- Multithreaded QR of large f64 matrices: the JOSS plots (i5-11400, 12 threads) put faer about 3x OpenBLAS and about 5x Eigen at n=10^4.
- Eigendecomposition around n=1000, where the plots show faer ahead of OpenBLAS (about 2.2e9 vs 1.2e9 n^3/s).
- Extended precision: faer ships a SIMD double-double type (fx128/cx128) and the plots show it several times faster than Eigen on f128 matmul and QR.
- Projects that want one portable static binary (x86-64 and AArch64 NEON SIMD, no_std-capable core) instead of distributing OpenBLAS or MKL.

**Skip it when:**
- When Intel MKL is available on Intel hardware and only speed matters: the paper's plots show MKL ahead on QR and EVD and level on matmul.
- Large eigendecompositions (n=10^4): the plots show faer behind OpenBLAS, BLIS and MKL (about 2.9e9 vs 3.7e9, 4.0e9 and 4.6e9 n^3/s).
- Small fixed-size matrices (graphics, robotics, 3x3/4x4): the crate docs say its design is not well suited to that and point to nalgebra or cgmath.
- Existing C/C++ or Fortran code that calls BLAS/LAPACK symbols: there is no drop-in ABI, and the C/C++ binding (faer-ffi) is not published on crates.io.
- Ill-conditioned or singular inputs without your own checks: open bug reports show NaN from qr().solve_lstsq on a 1e16-conditioned 3x3 system (#265) and NaN instead of 0 from a singular 3x3 determinant on 0.23.2 (#260).

**Integration:** crate (faer on crates.io); optional cdylib with C and C++ headers built from faer-ffi in the repo · pure Rust crates: pulp, gemm, nano-gemm, private-gemm-x86 (x86-64, std), dyn-stack, bytemuck, generativity, reborrow, equator, num-complex, num-traits, libm; optional rayon + spindle (default on), rand, npyz · Rust 1.84.0 (MSRV); nightly needed only for the AVX-512 'nightly' feature; faer.hpp needs C++17 · any Rust target; explicit SIMD on x86-64 (AVX2/FMA, AVX-512 with nightly) and AArch64 NEON; no SVE/SME/RVV kernels yet; an open issue (#255) reports matmul compile failure on i686-unknown-linux-gnu

**Vs siblings:** Pick faer over Eigen when you are in Rust or need fast multithreaded large QR or mid-size eigensolvers (Eigen trails both faer and OpenBLAS in the paper's QR plot), and over OxiBLAS when you need full LAPACK-style decompositions rather than BLAS kernels; for matrices in the tens BLASFEO is the better fit.

**Gotchas:**
- Development moved to codeberg.org/sarah-quinones/faer; the GitHub repo is a mirror, so file issues and track releases there (crate repository field points to Codeberg).
- Pre-1.0 with frequent breaking changes: 0.20-0.21 was a full project refactor, 0.24 removed serde support, and the docs warn that eigenvalue order from Mat::eigen is unspecified and may change.
- The checked-in faer-ffi/faer.h declares libfaer_v0_23_* functions while faer.hpp calls libfaer_v0_24_*; build.rs only regenerates the header when FAER_FFI is set, so build it yourself rather than copying the header.
- The MIT crate carries ported code under other licences (COPYING.EIGEN.MPL2, COPYING.LAPACK.BSD and two SuiteSparse BSD notices in faer/), so keep those notices when vendoring.

**Status:** Actively developed (crate 0.24.4 released 2026-06-24, about 4.8M crates.io downloads, last mirror commit 2026-09-04), MIT-licensed and used widely in the Rust ecosystem, but still pre-1.0 with open correctness bugs on ill-conditioned inputs.

[repo](https://github.com/sarah-quinones/faer-rs) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sarah-quinones/faer-rs/HEAD/paper.md)

##### fast-matmul (Benson and Ballard)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Code-generated Strassen-like matrix multiplication in C++ that beat sequential Intel MKL dgemm by 1.1-1.2x on large matrices.

**Beats:** Intel MKL dgemm — Sequential median-of-five timings checked into data/all_sequential_algs/square.all.big (NERSC Edison, icpc -O3, MKL from composer_xe 2013) show two-level Strassen at 4836 ms vs MKL dgemm 5361 ms for N=4000 (1.11x) and 15790 vs 18075 ms at N=6000 (1.14x), with the best exact algorithms reaching 1.17-1.19x; approximate Bini reaches 1.21x. The PPoPP 2015 paper itself could not be opened here (arxiv.org and dl.acm.org blocked); its abstract, seen only in a search snippet, says novel fast algorithms 'can significantly outperform vendor implementations of the classical algorithm and Strassen's fast algorithm on modest problem sizes and shapes'.

**Known shortcoming:** int dimensions and allocation sizes overflow past 2^31 elements; parallel mode changes global OpenMP nesting and MKL thread settings.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each recursion level splits A, B and C into blocks and forms fewer block products than the classical algorithm (Strassen: 7 instead of 8 for 2x2 blocks; <4,2,3>: 20 instead of 24), paying with extra matrix additions; at the leaves it calls the vendor dgemm/sgemm (MKL). The generator applies common-subexpression elimination and offers three addition schemes (write-once, streaming, pairwise), and odd sizes are handled by dynamic peeling. Shared-memory parallel builds choose DFS, BFS or hybrid task scheduling at compile time through OpenMP.

**Use it when:**
- Large dense float/double products (N of about 2000 and above) where 10-20% off the GEMM time matters and you control the call site.
- Rectangular shapes that match a specific fast algorithm's base case (for example <4,2,3> or <3,2,3>); the paper's point is that the best algorithm depends on shape as well as size.
- Research or teaching on fast matrix multiplication: comparing dozens of algorithms, recursion depths and addition schemes with ready-made benchmarks and stability tests.
- Workloads that tolerate approximate products (for example neural-network training), using the APA/Bini algorithms added in 2021 (ICPP-W 2021).

**Skip it when:**
- Small or medium matrices: in the checked-in sequential data, exact algorithms beat MKL in only 329 of 756 points, mostly at N of about 2000 and above, and the extra additions dominate below that.
- Code that needs tight error bounds: exact algorithms give relative errors around 1e-14 to 1e-15 (README), errors grow with each recursion level, and the approximate algorithms are lossier still.
- As a general BLAS: FastMatmul has no transpose options, there are no complex types, no batched or level-2 routines, and you must pick algorithm and depth by hand.
- When you need a measured win on current hardware: the evidence is a 2013 MKL on NERSC Edison, and a modern MKL or OpenBLAS may move the crossover or erase the gain.
- Production use expecting maintenance: core code dates from 2014-2017, the last commit was 2021-07-06, and there is no CMake, packaging or CI.

**Integration:** header-only (generated .hpp in algorithms/ plus linalg/ and util/ headers); Python generator for new algorithms · a Fortran-ABI BLAS providing dgemm/sgemm (README requires Intel MKL; parallel builds call mkl_set_num_threads_local and mkl_set_dynamic); OpenMP for parallel modes · C++11 with OpenMP; tested mainly with Intel icpc (Edison config: composer_xe 2013, gcc/4.8.0 module); README warns g++ OpenMP task handling can crash the hybrid parallel mode · x86-64 Linux with Intel MKL as tested; other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick fast-matmul over fmm-gen when you want fast algorithms layered on a tuned vendor dgemm (MKL) with checked-in timings against that dgemm; fmm-gen fuses the additions into BLIS-style packing with its own AVX kernel instead. For tensor contractions tblis-strassen is the analogue, and for ordinary GEMM speed any tuned BLAS sibling is the simpler choice.

**Gotchas:**
- FastMatmul takes non-const references, sets a multiplier on A as a side effect, and returns its own elapsed time in milliseconds.
- Dimensions, strides and the allocation size m*n are plain int, so very large matrices (more than 2^31 elements) overflow.
- The parallel scheme (DFS, BFS, hybrid) is a compile-time define (_PARALLEL_=1/2/3), and sequential versus parallel is chosen in the make include file, not at run time.
- The x argument (default 1e-8) is the approximation parameter used by the approximate algorithms (for example Bini's); exact algorithms ignore it.

**Status:** Abandoned research code (last commit 2021-07-06, core from 2014-2017) under BSD-2-Clause (Sandia); header-only and small enough to vendor, but re-benchmark the crossover against your BLAS before relying on it.

[repo](https://github.com/arbenson/fast-matmul) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arbenson/fast-matmul/HEAD/data/all_sequential_algs/square.all.big)

##### GEMMFIP (BLIS fork)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Research BLIS fork whose DGEMM fuses packing into the first compute pass; paper plots show it ahead of OpenBLAS/ArmPL on medium sizes.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS, AMD BLIS/AOCL, ArmPL, Intel MKL — The authors' paper (arXiv 2302.08417, later published as 'Towards a Unified Implementation of GEMM in BLIS', ICS '23, pp. 111-121) compares single-core DGEMM against OpenBLAS, AMD BLIS/AOCL, ArmPL and MKL on Xeon E5-2690, Epyc 7R32, Graviton 2/3 and Apple M2 (GCC 10.2/11.3, Clang 14, Apple Clang 14; other flags unstated), and its plots show it beating OpenBLAS and conventional BLIS on Epyc, matching AOCL, leading on Graviton 3, and trailing MKL on Xeon. No numeric ratios are given; I could not open the paper itself in this session (arXiv and ACM blocked) and relied on the verified record plus search-result metadata.

**Known shortcoming:** Only source is an arXiv preprint by the fork's author (not peer reviewed); flags unstated; results plots only, no numbers; MKL still beats it on Xeon; fork of BLIS.

**Known shortcoming:** Double precision only; threading is JR-loop only (non-master JC/IC threads exit and the master does their share); x86 edge kernels for n=7 and n=3 read one double past the unpacked B row (out-of-bounds read, result masked off); release-build dispatch default silently skips the tile; fork stale and not merged upstream.

**How:** Fused-in packing (FIP): the GEMMSUP-style millikernel reads A and B directly from the caller's unpacked memory and, while computing the first micro-tile pass, writes the panels it touched into BLIS's packing buffers, so later passes over the same block reuse packed data without a separate memcpy-like packing stage. Whether A and B are packed at all is decided by size thresholds (BLIS_MT/NT/KT block sizes), so small problems never pay for packing and large ones still get contiguous, prefetch-friendly panels. Kernels are hand-written inline assembly: a 6x8 AVX2/FMA millikernel (reusing BLIS's Haswell 6x8 microkernel for fully packed large-k cases) and 8x6 NEON millikernels for ARMv8-A with explicit prefetch; small-m problems are transposed into small-n ones.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded DGEMM at medium sizes (roughly m=n=k 100-400) where neither the small-matrix nor the large-matrix path of a stock BLAS is at its best
- AWS Graviton 2/3 or other ARMv8-A NEON servers where the paper reports it ahead of ArmPL and OpenBLAS in single-core DGEMM
- AMD Epyc (Zen 2 class) single-core DGEMM, where the paper reports it beating OpenBLAS and conventional BLIS and matching AMD's BLIS/AOCL
- Research or prototyping of fused packing / unified small-large GEMM strategies inside the BLIS framework

**Skip it when:**
- Single precision, complex, or mixed-datatype GEMM: the sandbox handles only dgemm and falls back to stock BLIS for everything else
- Multithreaded GEMM: only the JR loop is parallelised; threads assigned to the JC/PC/IC/packing loops return immediately and the master thread does their work (source comment: 'Limited threading capability')
- Intel Xeon with MKL available: the paper reports MKL ahead of it on the Xeon E5-2690
- Production use: research fork with 1 star, no releases, last commit 2023-04-26, based on pre-1.0 BLIS; the gemmfip sandbox does not appear in upstream flame/blis's sandbox directory
- General-stride operands (neither A column-stored nor B row-stored): the fused path is skipped and stock BLIS runs

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (a BLIS build with the gemmfip sandbox compiled in) · none beyond a C99 compiler and BLIS's configure/make build; optional OpenMP/pthreads for threading · C99 with GNU extensions (sandbox uses typeof and GNU inline asm), i.e. GCC or Clang; paper used GCC 10.2/11.3, Clang 14 and Apple Clang 14 · x86-64 with AVX2+FMA (Haswell kernel set) and AArch64 NEON (ARMv8-A kernels, incl. Apple M-series and Graviton); other ISAs get a plain-C reference millikernel

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over BLASFEO or LibShalom when you want a standard BLAS dgemm interface that stays fast across small, medium and large sizes on Arm or AMD rather than a small-matrix specialist; for very small matrices BLASFEO/LibShalom/IAAT report larger gains, and for anything beyond single-thread double precision a maintained BLAS (or Eigen) is the safer choice.

**Gotchas:**
- GEMMFIP is off unless you configure with -s gemmfip; the README is the stock BLIS README and never mentions the sandbox (only sandbox/gemmfip/README.md does)
- Setting BLIS_JC_NT/BLIS_IC_NT (or letting BLIS auto-factor threads into those loops) wastes threads: non-master workers in those loops exit and the master computes their share
- Source reading: the x86 edge kernels for n=7 and n=3 load a full 8- or 4-wide row of unpacked B, reading one double past the row end (results are masked off, but it can touch memory past the last row of B), and an in-code TODO notes packed-B padding columns are left undefined
- In non-DEBUG builds the millikernel dispatch silently does nothing for an unexpected (pack_a, n) combination instead of failing; correctness depends on caller invariants in bls_dgemm

**Status:** Stale research fork (last commit 2023-04-26, 1 star) under BSD-3-Clause; the sandbox is a few C/asm files that could be ported to current BLIS, but expect to own the maintenance yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/xrq-phys/blis) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.08417)

##### HPTT (High-Performance Tensor Transposition)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Multi-threaded, AVX-vectorized out-of-place tensor transposition (B = alpha*perm(A) + beta*B); paper reports large wins over Eigen's tensor shuffle.

**Beats:** numpy.transpose (np.transpose(A, perm).copy(order=order) in pythonAPI/benchmark/benchmark.py) is the only baseline seen with numbers. The ARRAY 2017 paper reportedly compares against Eigen's tensor transposition (Eigen::Tensor shuffle), but that is known only from its abstract as quoted by search results; the paper was not opened. — The headline is from the peer-reviewed ARRAY 2017 paper, seen only through search-result abstracts: bandwidth comparable to SAXPY across Ivy Bridge, ARMv7 and Power7, 'remarkable speedups' over Eigen's tensor transposition (up to 27.4x per the verifier's search quote; the snippet seen here gave no number), and up to 3.1x faster CTF contractions; the CPU, compiler and thread counts behind the Eigen figure were not visible. The repo's own figure compares HPTT with 24 threads on 2x Xeon E5-2680 v3 against numpy.transpose(...).copy() (thread count and compiler not stated; numpy's copy is normally single-threaded) over 57 cases, about 5.1x to 19.7x read by eye, so much of that gap is parallel bandwidth; the C++ benchmark harness compares only with a naive reference and the original TTC.

**Known shortcoming:** Up to 27.4x vs Eigen tensor shuffle known from the ARRAY 2017 paper snippet only; the numpy comparison script uses float64, not float32 as the record said.

**Known shortcoming:** AArch64 build broken: src/transpose.cpp:247 NEON specialization drops the conjA template argument and the flags use ARMv7-only -mfpu=neon (fix in open PR #35). Open PR #33 reports a wrong innermost index for sub-tensors (outerSize > size, leading dim 1). verifyParameter writes found[perm[i]] before range-checking it, so a bad permutation is an out-of-bounds write; invalid input calls exit(-1) (#17). Makefile silently builds single-threaded when CXX is a full path (#36); CMake leaks PUBLIC -march=native into consumers. 7 PRs open without maintainer replies. The 27.4x vs Eigen figure was not seen by the enricher (snippet gave no number), so the B tier rests on the peer-reviewed ARRAY 2017 paper as reported by the verifier.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Size-1 indices are dropped and indices that stay adjacent under the permutation are fused, which lowers the effective rank. The remaining loop nest is cut into blocks that a register-level micro-kernel transposes in-register (8x8 for float and 4x4 for double with AVX unpack/shuffle, 4x4 float on NEON), with software prefetch of the next A and B blocks and non-temporal streaming stores (_mm256_stream_ps/pd) when beta is 0 and B is 32-byte aligned, which avoids write-allocate traffic. A cost model picks a loop order and an OpenMP parallelization strategy (prime-factor split of the loops for load balance); hptt::MEASURE, PATIENT and CRAZY instead time candidate plans for up to 10 s, 60 s or 1 h, FFTW-style.

**Use it when:**
- You need a materialized permuted copy of a rank-3 to rank-6 dense tensor (for example before a GEMM in a TTGT tensor contraction, or for layout conversion between libraries) and the copy is memory-bandwidth-bound
- Repeated transpositions of the same shape and permutation: build the plan once (optionally autotuned with MEASURE) and reuse it with setInputPtr/setOutputPtr
- Multi-core x86 machines with AVX, where the paper reports bandwidth close to SAXPY and the README figure shows 5x to 20x over numpy.transpose(...).copy() with 24 threads
- Fused scale-and-accumulate transposes (B = alpha*perm(A) + beta*B), including complex conjugation through setConjA, which Eigen's shuffle() and numpy need extra passes for
- Python code that copies large non-contiguous numpy views (np.ascontiguousarray after a transpose) and can tolerate a ctypes wrapper that needs HPTT_ROOT and psutil

**Skip it when:**
- In-place transposition, or plain 2-D matrix transposes where an in-place or BLAS-extension routine (mkl_simatcopy, the transpose-scale sibling) avoids the second buffer: HPTT is out-of-place only
- AArch64 or Apple Silicon: the NEON kernel's partial specialization in src/transpose.cpp (around line 247) names micro_kernel<float, betaIsZero> without the conjA argument, and the build files pass the ARMv7-only -mfpu=neon; open PR #35 fixes both, and also turns off GCC auto-vectorization of transpose_int on Apple Silicon. The paper's ARM results are ARMv7
- MSVC or strict ISO C++ builds: the code uses variable-length arrays, __restrict__, GCC attributes and float _Complex in C++ (open issue #26; Clang 13 also rejects the _Complex casts in src/hptt.cpp, issue #21)
- Libraries that must not terminate the host process: invalid sizes, permutations or outer sizes print to stderr and call exit(-1), not throw (issue #17, open since 2019)
- Sub-tensor transposes with outerSize > size where an innermost dimension is 1: open PR #33 reports that transpose_int then picks the wrong innermost index; check results for that shape class or apply the PR

**Integration:** static lib · OpenMP (optional in the code, but the build files add -fopenmp/-qopenmp only for compilers they recognize); Python interface needs numpy and psutil · C++11 with GNU extensions (VLAs, __restrict__, float _Complex); README says tested with icpc 15-17, g++ 5.4-6.3 and clang++ 3.8/3.9; CMake 3.7+. Makefile also builds libhptt.so · x86-64 with AVX (make avx / -DENABLE_AVX=ON; no AVX2 or AVX-512 kernels), ARMv7 NEON (AArch64 needs PR #35), scalar fallback elsewhere; IBM POWER kernel is commented out

**Vs siblings:** Pick HPTT when you need the permuted tensor itself (any rank, out-of-place, with alpha/beta); transpose-scale (hpit) covers in-place 2-D transpose with scaling against mkl_simatcopy, and TBLIS avoids explicit transposition altogether when the end goal is a contraction. TCCG builds on HPTT for its TTGT path, so HPTT is the piece to take if you only need the transposition.

**Gotchas:**
- Autotuning (MEASURE/PATIENT/CRAZY) runs candidate plans on your real A and B during create_plan; the header says the data is restored afterwards unless A holds NaN or inf
- execute() always requests streaming stores; they are used when beta is 0 and B is suitably aligned, which pushes B out of cache. If you read B right away (small tensors, packing for GEMM), call execute_expert<false, ...>() as the header advises
- CMake attaches -fopenmp -march=native -mtune=native as PUBLIC compile options, so they propagate to targets that link hptt and make the binary host-specific; the Makefile adds OpenMP only when CXX is exactly icpc, g++ or clang++, so CXX=/usr/bin/g++ or g++-13 silently builds a single-threaded library (issue #36)
- verifyParameter writes found[perm[i]] before checking that perm[i] is in range, and the row-major conversion runs before it, so an out-of-range permutation entry is an out-of-bounds access rather than a clean error; per-dimension sizes are int

**Status:** Unmaintained: last commit 2022-02-15, with 15 open issues and 7 open PRs (including the AArch64 fix #35 and the sub-tensor correctness fix #33) and no maintainer replies; BSD-3-Clause and only four source files, so it is easy to vendor with those patches applied.

[repo](https://github.com/springer13/hptt) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.04374)

##### LibShalom  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

ARMv8 assembly GEMM library for small and irregular-shaped SGEMM/DGEMM; beats OpenBLAS, BLIS, ARMPL, LIBXSMM and BLASFEO there.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS, BLIS, ARMPL, LIBXSMM, BLASFEO — The LibShalom paper (ACM, 2021) measured with GCC 8.2.1 -O3 on Phytium 2000+, Kunpeng 920 and ThunderX2: single-thread small GEMM reaches 2x BLASFEO at 8x8x8 and 5-10% over the best other library at 32-128, and multithreaded irregular GEMM with M=32 reaches 2.6x BLIS on Phytium 2000+ (averages 1.8x over BLIS on Kunpeng 920, 1.4x on ThunderX2). The repo's own benchmark times LibShalom only, so baseline numbers come from the paper.

**Known shortcoming:** Record overstated: 2x is vs BLASFEO and 2.6x vs BLIS, not OpenBLAS; repo benchmarks time LibShalom only, not the baselines.

**Known shortcoming:** Two repos by the same author carry identical LibShalom READMEs (MYLIB and LibShalom); repo_url set to the one named LibShalom.

**How:** It skips packing when operands fit in L1 or are read sequentially, and where packing is needed it interleaves the pack loads/stores with the FMA stream of the micro-kernel instead of running it as a separate pass. Micro-kernel tile sizes (7x12 for FP32) come from an analytical model that maximizes the compute-to-memory ratio, and edge cases get dedicated scheduled kernels. Multithreading partitions both M and N, with the N split chosen as ceil(sqrt(T*N/M)), so skinny shapes still feed all cores.

**Use it when:**
- Many tiny GEMMs (8..128 per side) on ARMv8 servers such as Kunpeng 920, Phytium 2000+ or ThunderX2, single-threaded
- Skinny multithreaded GEMMs such as conv-layer-as-GEMM (M of 16-64, N in the tens of thousands, large K) on many-core ARM
- Row-major C = A*B or C = A*B^T where you control the call site and can adopt a non-BLAS API
- Research baselines for small/irregular GEMM on ARM

**Skip it when:**
- x86 or any non-ARMv8 target: kernels are AArch64 inline assembly
- Code that needs a BLAS/CBLAS drop-in, alpha/beta scaling, strided (leading-dimension) operands or column-major layout
- Large square GEMMs: the paper defers those to existing libraries
- DGEMM beyond the small NN path, or complex types: the API covers only SGEMM variants and one DGEMM entry point
- Production use needing maintenance: anonymous-account repo, last commit 2022-04-08, new issues restricted

**Integration:** static lib (libsmm.a) or shared lib (libsmm.so) built by a plain Makefile · OpenMP · GCC 8.2+ (README); built as C++ with g++ because the header includes <vector> · aarch64 (ARMv8 NEON) only; tested on Phytium 2000+, Kunpeng 920, ThunderX2

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over BLASFEO when you need multithreaded skinny GEMMs on ARM (BLASFEO is single-threaded and was left out of that comparison), and over OpenBLAS/BLIS for tiny or irregular shapes on ARMv8; on x86 use BLASFEO or LIBXSMM-class code instead, and for Graviton 3 / medium sizes the GEMMFIP BLIS fork is the comparable option with a BLAS interface.

**Gotchas:**
- Despite being listed as C, LibShalom.h includes <vector> and has 'using namespace std', so it compiles only as C++
- NN_LIB/Makefile compiles object files without -O flags (-O3 appears only on the link line); the inline-assembly kernels are unaffected but the C driver code builds at -O0 unless you edit it
- Row-major only; the README example passes B as transposed (NT), so check the transb convention before use
- Header hard-codes blocking constants (GEMM_K 320, GEMM_N 4096, GEMM_M 256) tuned for the tested CPUs

**Status:** Stale since April 2022 with new issues restricted, but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as a source drop for AArch64 builds.

[repo](https://github.com/AnonymousYWL/LibShalom) · [benchmark](https://zwang4.github.io/publications/tpds21-1.pdf)

##### TBLIS (Tensor-Based Library Instantiation Software)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

Native tensor-contraction library on BLIS kernels; beats transpose-plus-GEMM (NumPy/MKL einsum) on strided and permuted contractions.

**Beats:** BLAS-based tensor contraction (TTGT: transpose plus GEMM). In the independent tblis-rs benchmark this is NumPy einsum backed by Intel MKL, alongside PyTorch (CPU). — In the independent tblis-rs README (AMD Ryzen 7945HX, 16 cores, FP64 tensors of shape 96^4, compiler and threads unstated), TBLIS beat NumPy einsum on MKL by about 1.1x on contiguous GEMM-shaped contractions and up to 5.8x on strided ones, and beat PyTorch CPU by 1.0-1.8x where it won; it lost 2x to MKL/PyTorch on plain contiguous GEMM shapes and 2.6x to PyTorch on a SYRK shape.

**Known shortcoming:** Independent tblis-rs numbers (Ryzen 7945HX) show wins only on strided/transpose-heavy contractions (1.1-5.8x vs MKL, derived); loses ~2x on plain GEMM-shaped contiguous cases and 2.6x vs PyTorch on SYRK; tensor contraction, an edge case for blas-lapack.

**Known shortcoming:** Open 2026 wrong-result issues #86/#87/#88 (conjugated tensor_add, tblis_scalar abs/conj/sqrt); #76: 2.0 code is 4x slower on M3 Pro and 1.3x on i7-4770K vs a 2023 commit (tblis-rs benchmarked a 2.0-era commit); #80 oversubscription collapse; crashes #81 (mixed-sign strides abort), #82; stale 1.x build docs.

**How:** It applies the BLIS GEMM structure (cache-blocked loops, packing into contiguous panels, register-blocked micro-kernels) directly to tensors: the packing step gathers tensor elements through their native strides, so no transposed copy of the whole operand is formed as in transpose-transpose-GEMM-transpose (TTGT). This is the algorithm of Matthews, 'High-Performance Tensor Contraction without Transposition' (SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 40(1) C1-C24, 2018); GETT/TCCG from Springer and Bientinesi is the concurrent related approach. Version 2.0 is rebuilt as a BLIS 2.0 plugin, so it uses BLIS's micro-kernels and architecture configurations, with its own TCI threading layer.

**Use it when:**
- Contractions whose index order would force large transposes before a GEMM, such as axyz,ybzx->ab or batched axby,yacx->abc (about 1.7x and 1.4x faster than PyTorch CPU in the tblis-rs table).
- Tensors that live in strided, non-contiguous memory (sub-blocks of larger arrays): 2.0 s vs 7.3 s for NumPy/MKL on a strided 96^4 GEMM-shaped contraction.
- Quantum chemistry and tensor-network codes (coupled cluster and similar) that need many differently-permuted contractions without extra workspace for transposed copies.
- Projects that want a C ABI usable from C++, Python (pytblis) or Rust (tblis-rs).

**Skip it when:**
- Contractions that already map to a contiguous GEMM: in tblis-rs, axyz,xyzb->ab took 132 ms vs 63 ms for MKL and PyTorch, and the SYRK-shaped axyz,bxyz->ab took 97 ms vs 37 ms for PyTorch.
- Apple Silicon/ARM with the 2.0 code line: issue #76 reports a 4x slowdown on an M3 Pro (0.73 s to 2.93 s) and 1.3x on an i7-4770K between an April 2023 commit and the August 2025 one.
- Applications that already run their own thread pool or a second OpenMP runtime: issue #80 reports 2.0 beta's performance collapsing under oversubscription (time spent in a BLIS barrier), and issue #47 covers multiple OpenMP runtimes in one process.
- Code relying on conjugated operands in tblis_tensor_add or on tblis_scalar abs/conj/sqrt: open issues #86, #87 and #88 (2026) report wrong results.
- Windows (not supported per the wiki; Cygwin only 'probably') or GPUs (CPU only).

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib · BLIS 2.0 (found via find_package/pkg-config or fetched at a pinned commit), bundled git submodules TCI, MArray and stl_ext; optional hwloc and memkind · C++20 compiler and CMake 3.23 for the 2.0 code on master (the wiki's GCC 4.8+/autotools notes describe 1.x); GCC 15/16 builds need a newer BLIS (issue #90) · Linux and macOS; x86-64 and other architectures BLIS supports (BLIS_CONFIG_FAMILY auto); no Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick TBLIS over Eigen's Tensor module or a hand-written reshape plus BLAS/MKL GEMM when contractions are permuted or strided, since it skips the transposed copies. tblis-strassen is a research code built on TBLIS that adds Strassen (up to 1.3x per its README); TBLIS is the maintained base library.

**Gotchas:**
- The 2.0 line on master (BLIS plugin) and the wiki's build instructions (1.x autotools, --enable-config=haswell etc.) disagree; clone with git submodule update --init --recursive and build with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (tblis-rs warns about this).
- Issue #85: BLIS headers cannot be included alongside TBLIS headers, which bites projects that also call BLIS directly.
- Mixed-sign strides can abort tblis_tensor_mult with an are_compatible assertion (issue #81); a std::bad_array_new_length crash is also open (#82).
- The project publishes no benchmark numbers of its own; the only table found is a third-party wrapper's laptop run with no compiler or thread settings, using a 2.0-era commit (9b95712).

**Status:** Active but slow to respond (last commit 2025-11-21; 2.0 is still a beta pre-release next to stable v1.3.0, with 18 open issues including several 2026 wrong-result reports); BSD-3-Clause and a C library, so straightforward to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/MatthewsResearchGroup/tblis) · [benchmark](https://github.com/restgroup/tblis-rs)

##### tblis-strassen (Strassen's Algorithm for Tensor Contraction)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research code on 2016-era TBLIS: tensor contractions via one- or two-level Strassen, up to 1.3x over regular TBLIS.

**Beats:** TBLIS regular tensor-contraction routine (Strassen level L=0 in the same code); TBLIS is itself the state-of-the-art non-BLAS contraction library — The authors' peer-reviewed SISC 2018 paper (README abstract) reports up to 1.3x effective GFLOPS over the same code's regular TBLIS contraction (L=0), measured on synthetic contractions and the TCCG benchmark on single-core, multicore and distributed runs. Those runs used icc 15.0.3, the Sandy Bridge AVX double-precision kernels and TACC Maverick (CPU model not stated). Per-case numbers are in the paper, which was not opened, so only the 'up to' figure is confirmed.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Up to 1.3x' is vs TBLIS L=0 (its own base); built on a 2016-era TBLIS snapshot with a Sandy Bridge config only; abandoned 2017.

**Known shortcoming:** Does not build on GCC 10.3 (issue #1 open since 2023-11); optimized Strassen micro-kernels exist only for double on Sandy Bridge AVX; bench scripts use tee without -a, so result files get overwritten.

**How:** It uses the Block-Scatter-Matrix layout to treat a tensor contraction as a GEMM on general-stride storage, so Strassen's 7-multiply recursion runs on the tensors in place, with no explicit permutation and no extra workspace (README). It adapts the authors' earlier BLIS-based Strassen-for-GEMM implementation (linked in the README): operand sums are folded into packing, and the default 'ABC' variant uses dedicated AVX micro-kernels (bli_dstra_asm_8x4 plus 'two' and 'four' variants) that write several C sub-blocks in one pass. 'AB' and 'Naive' variants are included for comparison. Each Strassen level does 7 block multiplies instead of 8, which is where the up-to-1.3x gain at large sizes comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Research or reproduction of the SISC 2018 Strassen-for-tensor-contraction results on an x86 machine with AVX.
- Very large double-precision contractions with big free and contracted dimensions (the square sweep runs 256 to 20480), where 1-2 Strassen levels can beat a conventional GEMM-based contraction.
- As a reference implementation of the Block-Scatter-Matrix plus fused-Strassen-packing technique for porting into a modern TBLIS or BLIS build.
- Distributed-memory contraction experiments on a SLURM cluster, using the bundled dist/ scripts as a starting point.

**Skip it when:**
- Production code: no commits since 2017-07-07, and it fails to compile with GCC 10.3 (open issue #1, 'B is not a constant expression' in stra_matrify.hpp).
- Single precision or complex data: optimized Strassen micro-kernels exist only for double (bli_dstra_asm_8x4 and its two- and four-output variants) in the sandybridge config. The float and complex Strassen slots are left empty.
- Modern CPUs with AVX2/AVX-512: the documented build is --enable-config=sandybridge (AVX, 8x4 double kernel), so FMA hardware is not used by the Strassen path.
- Small or skinny contractions: Strassen's extra additions only pay off at large sizes. The paper reports gains of at most 1.3x.
- Code that needs bit-for-bit agreement with a conventional contraction: Strassen reorders the floating-point arithmetic, and the driver reports a norm-2 error against the regular TBLIS result.

**Integration:** static lib · A 2016-era TBLIS with BLIS-derived kernels in the tree, and TCI threading (tci.h). Build needs autotools (autoreconf). OpenMP runtime for the driver (omp_get_wtime, OMP_NUM_THREADS/KMP_AFFINITY). Optional BLAS, hwloc and memkind are detected by configure. mvapich2 2.1 and SLURM for the distributed experiments. · C99 and C++11. Authors used icc/icpc 15.0.3 with the GCC 4.9.3 standard library. GCC 10.3 is reported to fail (issue #1). · x86-64 with AVX (artifact: 'x86-64 processor that supports AVX instructions'), Linux or macOS. Strassen kernels only in the sandybridge config.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over TBLIS (MatthewsResearchGroup/tblis) only when you are studying or porting Strassen for tensor contraction: TBLIS is the maintained, multi-architecture code base but has no Strassen path. For plain matrices, fmm-gen (also from the FLAME group) and fast-matmul (Benson and Ballard) cover a wider family of fast algorithms against a conventional GEMM or MKL.

**Gotchas:**
- Only 1 or 2 Strassen levels: stra_mult and stra_mult_2level. The driver prints 'More than 2-level is not supported' for L>2.
- Variant selection is a global setting (tblis::internal::impl = BLIS_BASED / STRA_AB / STRA_NAIVE), not a function argument.
- The bin/*_run_*.sh scripts write results with plain 'tee', not 'tee -a', so each line overwrites the .m result file. Capture stdout instead.
- The timing harness allocates two 100M-double cache-flush buffers (about 1.7 GB) on every timed call and reports best-of-niter (default 3) effective GFLOPS = 2mnk/time.

**Status:** Abandoned research artifact (last commit 2017-07-07, one open build-failure issue). BSD-3-Clause (TBLIS's license, copyright Devin Matthews), so copyable, but expect to patch it for modern compilers.

[repo](https://github.com/flame/tblis-strassen) · [benchmark](https://github.com/flame/tblis-strassen)

#### fft

##### go-fft  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Go (no cgo) float64 FFT for any length; fastest pure-Go option, behind FFTW on most single-core 1-D sizes.

**Beats:** FFTW 3.3.11 (native C, FFTW_MEASURE, threads=1); also numpy.fft, scipy.fft (pocketfft) and gonum/dsp/fourier — The author's public harness (benchmarks/run.sh plus a C FFTW driver) times steady-state float64 transforms with reused plans against FFTW 3.3.11 (Homebrew NEON, FFTW_MEASURE, one thread) on an Apple M4 Max and FFTW 3.3.10 built from source on an EPYC 7773X (Zen 3) and Neoverse-N1, with go1.26.4. In the June snapshot go-fft beat FFTW only on the 512x512 and 1024x1024 2-D rows, where it used all cores against single-threaded FFTW; the 2026-09-30 runs add single-threaded wins at complex 2^20 (0.81x on M4 Max, 0.67x on N1), prime 1009 on all three hosts (0.53x-0.75x) and RFFT 2^20 on N1 (0.92x), with most other 1-D rows 1.07x-2.92x slower than FFTW.

**Known shortcoming:** 2-D wins are multicore against single-thread baselines; 1-D single-thread wins only at a few sizes (runs dated 2026-09-30); Go, not callable from C++.

**Known shortcoming:** README's 'wins outright' at small N holds only vs pocketfft through Python; FFTW is faster there (N=256: 0.42 vs 0.72 us); float64 only.

**How:** Lengths whose prime factors are all <= 13 run an iterative Stockham autosort engine modelled on pocketfft's passes (radix 8/4/2/3/5/7 straight-line passes, a general pass for 11 and 13, unit-stride inner loops, no bit-reversal, bounds-check-free loops). Large powers of two use an iterative radix-4 kernel; primes whose N-1 is 7-smooth use Rader's algorithm, and other lengths use Bluestein's chirp-z at a cost-model-chosen smooth convolution length. On amd64 the butterfly, Stockham pass and real-FFT untangle kernels are generated AVX2/SSE2 assembly (via go-asmgen) picked at run time; on arm64 the gc autovectorizer is used. Real transforms pack N reals into an N/2-point complex FFT, and 2-D/N-D transforms fan rows and columns across goroutines.

**Use it when:**
- Go programs that need FFTs with CGO_ENABLED=0 (static or cross-compiled binaries on amd64, arm64, riscv64, ppc64le, loong64 or s390x) and cannot link FFTW
- Replacing gonum/dsp/fourier: faster at every size measured, typically 3-5x on composite N and 30x-200x on primes, where gonum uses a naive Bluestein
- Large 2-D double-precision transforms (512x512 and up) on a multicore host, where its goroutine fan-out beat single-threaded FFTW (0.43-0.51x FFTW's time on M4 Max, 0.25x at 1024x1024 on Neoverse-N1)
- Workloads that create many plans or use many distinct lengths: NewPlan at N=1,024 cost 14,808 ns vs 3,434,000 ns for an FFTW_MEASURE plan
- Code that needs bit-reproducible results across amd64 builds: the SIMD kernels avoid FMA and are tested bit-identical to the scalar Go path

**Skip it when:**
- C++ projects: it is a Go module, so FFTW, PocketFFT, KFR or Admiral are the native choices
- Single-core 1-D throughput against FFTW: in the fresh 2026-09-30 runs most 1-D rows still take 1.07x-2.92x FFTW's time, especially on Zen 3, where FFTW uses AVX2+FMA codelets and go-fft deliberately skips FMA
- Single precision: only complex128/float64 is supported
- Small 2-D shapes (64x64, 128x128): they ran 1.39x-3.20x slower than FFTW in the June snapshot, and on 64-128-thread hosts the GC cost of FFT2/FFTN's freshly allocated result slice dominates
- Teams that need a stable API: there is no tagged release, the repo started in June 2026, and an allocation-free N-D entry point is still an open design decision

**Integration:** module · none (the library module has no dependencies; gonum is isolated in the separate benchmarks/ module) · Go 1.26.4 (go.mod) · any Go 64-bit target; SIMD on amd64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX2 when CPU and OS allow, chosen at run time); arm64 relies on autovectorized Go; riscv64/s390x have only a SIMD complex-multiply kernel; ppc64le/loong64 run scalar code

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you are writing Go and must stay cgo-free; among the catalogued FFTs, PocketFFT, KFR and Admiral are the C++ choices, and RustFFT/PhastFT play the same role for Rust that go-fft plays for Go.

**Gotchas:**
- Plan.FFT/IFFT require dst and src to be exactly Len() long (behaviour on a wrong length is not documented), and FFT2/FFTN panic when the shape product does not equal len(data)
- The package-level FFT, RFFT, FFT2 and FFTN allocate a new output slice on every call; use NewPlan/NewRealPlan for zero-allocation steady state (only 1-D has a dst-taking API)
- On amd64 the AVX2 path keeps separately rounded multiply and add (no FMA) to stay bit-identical to the scalar code, which costs speed against FMA-using libraries
- The README status paragraph still describes 'radix-2 Cooley-Tukey plus Bluestein', while its Performance section and BENCHMARKS.md describe the newer Stockham/Rader engines; the README tables are the June snapshot

**Status:** Very active single-org project (48 commits from 2026-06-20 to 2026-10-01, 1 star, no releases); BSD-3-Clause, so easy to vendor in Go, but young and with no external users visible.

[repo](https://github.com/go-fft/fft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/go-fft/fft/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)

##### meow_fft  `C`  `0BSD`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Single-header C99 float FFT (0BSD), scalar radix-8 mixed-radix, 1.1-1.5x faster than KissFFT on power-of-two sizes.

**Beats:** KissFFT — gemmi's independent single-precision shootout (1d.cpp, GCC 8 -O3, Intel i7-5600U) timed meow_fft complex FFTs at 2120/4718/5745/4342 ns against KissFFT's 2536/4929/6030/6553 ns for n=256/384/480/512 (1.04-1.51x, derived from page data). In the same run its real FFT was slower at n=480 (3591 against 3140 ns) and faster at n=512 (2660 against 2985 ns). The author's own table (i7-4790, GCC 6.3.1 -O2 -g, benchmark code not published) shows N=1024 at 8.89 against 13.12 us and N=8192 at 84.72 against 119.38 us; accuracy after a round trip was about the same as KissFFT's.

**Known shortcoming:** Slower than KissFFT at N=64 and on real-to-complex n=480; author says his FFTW column is wrong; stale (2024-07-01).

**Known shortcoming:** Robustness bug: N with a prime factor >2048 (e.g. 4099) is not rejected at plan time and the transform calls abort(); slower than KissFFT at N=64, R2C n=480 and some non-power-of-two sizes; header comment on real-FFT output size stale (#14 open); README example does not compile; plain C99 inline helpers may fail to link at -O0 (code reading).

**How:** It is a recursive decimation-in-time mixed-radix FFT that factors N greedily by 8, 5, 4, 3 and 2. Each stage's twiddles are precomputed in the order they are read. The author says the radix-8 butterfly, generated with FFTW's codelet generator, is the only reason it beats KissFFT. The real-input transform runs a half-length complex FFT and then a symmetric post-processing mix (the two-for-one trick). The code uses no explicit SIMD.

**Use it when:**
- You want a GPL-free FFT as one 0BSD file with no build system, and KissFFT is what you would use otherwise
- Power-of-two float transforms from about 256 to 32768 points (for example audio frames): the author's i7-4790 table shows 1.07-1.50x over KissFFT, and gemmi measured 1.2-1.5x at n=256 and 512
- Targets where SIMD code is unavailable or unwanted (scalar builds, WebAssembly without SIMD, ARMv7): on a 1 GHz ARMv7 the author measured 1.1-1.75x over KissFFT for N=64-32768
- Reading a compact, commented mixed-radix FFT to learn how one is put together (one of the author's stated goals)

**Skip it when:**
- Whenever a SIMD FFT is allowed: pffft ran N=1024 in 2.19 us against meow's 8.89 us (i7-4790), and muFFT, FFTW and vDSP are also faster according to the author
- When a scalar FFT faster than KissFFT is enough: in gemmi's C2C run, PocketFFT (scalar, double precision) and pffft or FFTW with SIMD disabled all beat meow at every size tested (for example n=256: 1690-1826 ns against 2120 ns)
- Very small or non-power-of-two sizes: KissFFT is faster at N=64 (0.58 against 0.73 us), level or faster at N=100 and 500, and faster for gemmi's real FFT at n=480 (3140 against 3591 ns)
- Sizes with prime factors other than 2, 3 and 5: radix 7 and larger primes go through an O(p^2) generic DFT, and a prime factor above 2048 aborts the process
- Double precision, 2D/3D transforms, odd-length real FFTs or in-place transforms: none is supported

**Integration:** header-only · none (libc and libm only) · C99 (also compiles as C++ via extern "C" guards); MSVC before VS2022 (_MSC_VER < 1930) gets a volatile work-around for optimiser bugs · any (portable scalar C); author benchmarked x86-64 (i7-4790, Core2 Duo P8400) and ARMv7

**Vs siblings:** Against the catalogued siblings, muFFT and PFFFT are 3.5-6.5x faster with SIMD in gemmi's run, and PocketFFT (C++ branch) is faster even in scalar code while adding double precision, any size via Bluestein, and 2D/3D. Pick meow_fft only when the constraints are a single 0BSD C99 file and arbitrary 1D float sizes (PFFFT's SIMD path needs multiples of 16 complex or 32 real), and your sizes are mostly powers of two.

**Gotchas:**
- The real FFT writes N/2 complex values and stores the Nyquist bin's real part in out[0].j. The header comment still says countof(out) == countof(in), which predates the July 2024 change, and issue #14 (open) asks how to read the output. Inverse transforms are not scaled, so divide by N yourself.
- The plan generator accepts any N >= 2 (complex), or any even N >= 4 (real), and returns 0 otherwise. A prime factor above 2048 is not rejected at plan time: meow_dft_n_dit calls abort() during the transform (for example N = 4099). meow_fft_is_slow() reports when the slow generic DFT will be used.
- The plan is one caller-allocated block holding absolute pointers into itself, so do not memcpy or realloc it; allocate it where it will live. The internal helpers (meow_radix_2_dit, meow_add and others) have external linkage, and several are plain C99 `inline`, so define MEOW_FFT_IMPLEMENTATION in exactly one translation unit. Per C99 inline rules, an unoptimised C build may fail to link (from reading the code, not tested).
- Compiler flags can move performance either way: the author saw -march=native speed up sizes above 2048 but run sizes below 2048 twice as slow, and got mixed results with -ffast-math. The README example (void main(char** argv, int argv), <malloc.h>) does not compile as written.

**Status:** Stale: 15 commits, the last in July 2024 (real-FFT buffers halved), with two open PRs unmerged, including a 2025 sign-type fix. It is 0BSD and a single header, so it is easy to vendor and patch.

[repo](https://github.com/JodiTheTigger/meow_fft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/project-gemmi/benchmarking-fft)

##### muFFT  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Small MIT C99 single-precision power-of-two FFT with runtime SSE/SSE3/AVX dispatch; 5-9x faster than KissFFT, near FFTW.

**Beats:** KissFFT — The independent gemmi benchmark (public 1d.cpp/2d.cpp, GCC 8 -O3, i7-5600U, Ubuntu 18.04 FFTW packages, single precision) measured muFFT at 719 ns vs KissFFT 6553 ns for 1D C2C n=512, 4024 ns with SIMD disabled (1.6x like-for-like). In 2D 256x256 it took 259 us vs KissFFT 1583 us and FFTW measured-plan 306 us. 1D R2C n=512 took 511 ns vs FFTW meas. 681 ns and pffft 597 ns.

**Known shortcoming:** 1D speedup compares SIMD muFFT with scalar KissFFT (fair scalar: 4024 vs 6553 ns); power-of-two sizes only; loses to FFTW at n=512; abandoned (2019-02-15).

**Known shortcoming:** Power-of-two and single precision only, no 3D; no NEON (ARM gets scalar); SIMD-aligned out-of-place buffers only; one plan cannot run from several threads; measured FFTW faster for 1D C2C n=512 (588 vs 719 ns).

**Independent measurement:** gemmi shootout: 1D R2C n=512 511 vs FFTW 681 ns; 2D 256x256 259 vs 306 us

**How:** The Stockham autosort formulation removes the bit-reversal permutation pass. Hand-vectorised radix-2, radix-4 and radix-8 butterflies come in separate no-SIMD, SSE, SSE3 and AVX translation units, and the widest set the CPU supports is picked at runtime. Decompositions are chosen statically, so there is no FFTW-style measuring planner. Real transforms run as an N/2 complex FFT plus a final butterfly pass.

**Use it when:**
- Single-precision power-of-two FFTs of moderate size (hundreds to a few thousand points) on x86-64 where FFTW's GPL is not acceptable
- Block-based overlap-add FIR convolution for audio, including interleaved stereo signals and zero-padded inputs, via the built-in conv API
- Replacing KissFFT on x86: in the gemmi shootout (i7-5600U, GCC 8 -O3) 1D C2C n=512 took 719 ns against KissFFT's 6553 ns, and the 2D 256x256 transform took 259 us against 1583 us
- One portable binary that should use AVX where present and fall back to SSE or scalar code otherwise

**Skip it when:**
- Non-power-of-two sizes (n=384, 480 or primes): not supported; PocketFFT, pffft or FFTW cover them
- Double precision or 3D transforms: not implemented
- ARM/NEON targets: NEON was still listed as 'expected soon' when the last commit landed in 2019, so ARM gets the scalar path only
- Peak 1D throughput: FFTW with a measured plan was faster at n=512 (588 vs 719 ns) on the same machine
- Very large out-of-cache FFTs or tiny N=2/4/8 transforms: the README says neither is specially optimised

**Integration:** static lib · none for the library (libm); FFTW3f via pkg-config only for the optional bench/test binaries · C99; CMake 3.5+; GCC, Clang or MSVC · any (scalar C); SIMD paths on x86/x86-64 only (SSE, SSE3, AVX)

**Vs siblings:** Pick muFFT over PFFFT when you need 2D transforms or an AVX path (pffft is SSE/NEON-only and was ~1.7x slower at n=512 C2C SIMD), or a ready-made convolution API. Pick PocketFFT for arbitrary lengths, double precision, 3D or ARM, and VkFFT for GPUs.

**Gotchas:**
- Input and output buffers must be SIMD-aligned (use mufft_alloc/mufft_calloc/mufft_free), and execute declares them restrict, so in-place transforms are not supported
- Transforms are unnormalised, so forward followed by inverse scales by N; the convolution output, by contrast, is normalised
- Do not build with -ffast-math: the CMake file warns that the code relies on -0.0f behaviour
- The 2D R2C/C2R output uses a padded row stride for alignment, not the plain Nx/2+1 layout

**Status:** Abandoned since February 2019 (no NEON, no new sizes), but MIT-licensed, about 2.5 KLOC of C99 and easy to vendor; only the optional bench/test binaries fall under the GPL because they link FFTW.

[repo](https://github.com/Themaister/muFFT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/project-gemmi/benchmarking-fft)

##### Notorious-FFT  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C FFT with an FFTW-shaped API and minfft-style split-radix core; 8-13% faster than minfft on ARM, far behind FFTW.

**Beats:** minfft (aimukhin/minfft, small power-of-two FFT library; not one of the listed incumbents) — The repository's bench.c times notoriousfft against minfft in one binary (CLOCK_MONOTONIC, two warm-up calls, one timed batch of 500-100,000 repetitions per size, minfft run first), built with GCC 11.4.0 -O3 for armv8.2-a on a Jetson Orin Cortex-A78AE in double precision. v1.0.0 was 1.08-1.13x faster on forward complex DFT for N >= 256 (N=4096: 68.95 us vs 77.59 us), up to 1.18x on inverse, 1.01-1.07x on real DFT, and slightly slower at N=16 for real DFT and DCT-2; with a single timed batch, margins under ~5% are within run-to-run noise.

**Known shortcoming:** Only baseline is minfft, and its core is minfft-compatible without crediting minfft; the FAF README shows it slower than KissFFT on x86 AVX2 (0.57-0.76x), faster only on aarch64.

**Known shortcoming:** bench.c times one batch per library with minfft always first and no interleaving, so the 1-13% margins are fragile; minfft fetched at unpinned master; the author's FastAndFourier x86 table shows it 10-30x slower than FFTW_MEASURE (older build).

**How:** Powers of two use a recursive split-radix 2/4 decimation-in-frequency kernel with unrolled terminals for N <= 32 and no bit-reversal pass; header comments say it uses the same structure and twiddle layout as minfft's rs_dft_1d. Under MEASURE planning it may instead pick a DIT combine or iterative Cooley-Tukey, and it switches to a four-step algorithm at N >= 2^20. Factors 3/5/7 are peeled by mixed-radix passes, primes with 7-smooth N-1 use Rader, and other lengths use Bluestein. Compile-time NEON, AVX2 and AVX-512 paths exist (the README's summary lists NEON for f64 and f32, AVX2 for the inverse and AVX-512 for the forward transform), and each plan's memory is one 64-byte-aligned slab.

**Use it when:**
- You already use minfft and want a near drop-in with more transform types and arbitrary lengths: same aux-object calling style, 1.08-1.13x faster complex DFTs at N >= 256 on a Cortex-A78AE
- Embedded or edge aarch64 (Jetson-class) code that wants one MIT header with no dependencies beyond libc and libm
- Prototyping against an FFTW-like API with a permissive license, for a subset of FFTW calls, when FFTW-level speed is not required
- Small DCT-2/3/4 or DST-2/3/4 transforms where a header-only implementation is more convenient than linking a library

**Skip it when:**
- As an FFTW replacement for speed: in the author's FastAndFourier benchmarks on an x86 AVX2 Mac (Feb 2026, older build, one run, -ffast-math) it ran at 0.57-0.76x of KissFFT's throughput and 10x-30x slower than FFTW_MEASURE (e.g. N=1024 45.7 us vs 1.79 us; ratios derived from page data)
- x86 users who need published numbers: only an ARM Cortex-A78AE table exists for this repository; the AVX2/AVX-512 paths have no results
- Small real transforms and DCT-2 at N=16-64, where it was 0.83-0.97x of minfft's speed
- Projects needing a mature dependency: 7 commits, 0 stars, no releases on GitHub, and a Bluestein AVX inverse bug fixed only on 2026-08-22, after v1.0.0
- Calling one plan from several threads at once: plans own scratch buffers, so concurrent execute on the same plan is unsupported

**Integration:** header-only · none at runtime (libc, libm); OpenMP optional and switched on by default in the CMake build; the bundled tests and benchmarks fetch minfft (master) via FetchContent; Python 3 is needed by CMake to regenerate the amalgamated header · C11 (C++17 for the C++ wrapper and tests), CMake 3.14+ · any C11 target with a scalar path; NEON on aarch64/ARMv7, AVX2+FMA or AVX-512F/DQ on x86-64, all chosen at compile time from compiler flags (no runtime dispatch)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over minfft when you want the same small-library style plus non-power-of-two sizes, DCT/DST variants and an FFTW-like planner; for speed, PocketFFT, PFFFT or muFFT are better-measured permissive choices, and FFTW was 10x-30x faster on x86 in the author's own sibling benchmark.

**Gotchas:**
- Precision is a build-wide switch: in the FFTW compatibility header fftwf_complex is typedef'd to the same type as fftw_complex, so float and double FFTW code cannot coexist in one build
- NOTORIOUS_FFT_FAST_MATH swaps in Bhaskara I sin/cos approximations with ~0.1% twiddle error that grows with N; the README also warns against -ffast-math
- Multi-dimensional c2r / invrealdft may overwrite its input
- CMake regenerates include/notorious_fft.h in the source tree from the src/ modules whenever they change, and the published minfft comparison builds against minfft master without a pinned commit

**Status:** Young single-author project (7 commits, 2026-02-20 to 2026-08-22, 0 stars, MIT); small enough to vendor as one header, but treat it as experimental and expect FFTW-class libraries to be much faster on x86.

[repo](https://github.com/NotoriousLOB/Notorious-FFT) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NotoriousLOB/Notorious-FFT/HEAD/README.md)

##### PFFFT (marton78 fork)  `C`  `FFTPACK/NCAR (UCAR) BSD-style license (no SPDX id; terms equivalent to BSD-3-Clause)`  `active`  `Tier A`

Small BSD-licensed SIMD 1D FFT (float/double) plus fast convolution, about 5x faster than KissFFT, about half FFTW's speed.

**Beats:** KissFFT — In project-gemmi's benchmarking-fft (GCC 8 -O3, i7-5600U, single precision), Pommier's original pffft ran a 512-point complex FFT in 1255 ns with SSE vs KissFFT's 6553 ns (5.2x, derived), and 3792 ns with SIMD disabled. Real 512-point took 597 ns vs KissFFT 2985 ns. FFTW was faster at every size (588 ns measured at n=512). The fork's own additions were not measured there.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark measured Pommier's original bitbucket code, not this fork; FFTPACK/UCAR BSD-style license has no SPDX id; slower than FFTW.

**Known shortcoming:** Lengths must be 2^a*3^b*5^c, no Bluestein fallback; 1D only; double-precision SIMD only on AVX and WASM; issue #55 powerpc64le build failure; GCC much slower on 32-bit ARM (README recommends Clang).

**How:** It is FFTPACK v4 (Swarztrauber) translated to C and rewritten so every butterfly works on 4-wide SIMD vectors (SSE1, AltiVec, NEON, WASM SIMD; AVX for double), using radix 2/3/4/5 codelets. Skipping the final reorder ('unordered' output) saves a pass when you only need to multiply spectra for convolution. Transforms do no allocation: the caller passes a work buffer, or stack is used.

**Use it when:**
- Real-time audio/DSP on CPUs, where you need 1D float FFTs with no allocation in the transform call
- FIR filtering or convolution: the unordered transform plus pffft_zconvolve_accumulate skips the reorder pass
- Sizes of the form 2^a*3^b*5^c, best between 128 and 8192 points (per pffft.h)
- Proprietary products that cannot take FFTW's GPL and want a small library to vendor
- ARM NEON, PowerPC AltiVec or WebAssembly targets where KissFFT's scalar code is too slow

**Skip it when:**
- You need the fastest x86 FFT: FFTW measured 274-321 ns vs pffft 585 ns at n=256 complex in the gemmi benchmark; the README says the goal is only at least 50% of the fastest
- Lengths with prime factors above 5, or lengths below the SIMD minimum: there is no Bluestein fallback
- 2D/3D transforms, DCT/DST, or batched strided data: 1D only
- Double precision on NEON or SSE-only CPUs: the double SIMD paths are AVX and WASM only (scalar otherwise, per CMakeLists)
- 32-bit ARM built with GCC: the README measures much worse code and recommends Clang

**Integration:** static lib · none (CMake build; FFTW/MKL/KissFFT/PocketFFT only for optional benchmarks) · C compiler (C99-era) + CMake; C++ wrapper needs C++ with <complex>; exact minimum not documented · x86/x86-64 (SSE1, AVX for double; FMA opt-in via -DTARGET_C_ARCH=haswell), ARM/AArch64 NEON incl. Apple Silicon, PowerPC AltiVec, WASM SIMD, scalar fallback elsewhere; open issue #55 reports a powerpc64le build failure

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over muFFT when you need a mature, allocation-free 1D real/complex FFT with built-in convolution and ARM/PowerPC/WASM SIMD. Pick it over PocketFFT for SIMD 1D transforms (PocketFFT's 1D path is scalar) when your lengths are 5-smooth. Use PocketFFT for multi-D, arbitrary lengths or DCT/DST.

**Gotchas:**
- All float buffers must be SIMD-aligned (16 bytes on x86/PowerPC); use pffft_aligned_malloc
- Transforms are unscaled: backward(forward(x)) = N*x
- Real forward output packs DC and Nyquist into the first complex slot; pffft_transform output is in an internal order unless you use the _ordered variant or pffft_zreorder
- With work=NULL the transform uses the stack; large N on small thread stacks can overflow, so pass a heap work buffer

**Status:** Actively maintained (commits in 2026, upstream fixes cherry-picked and logged in the README); FFTPACK/UCAR BSD-style license allows vendoring into closed-source code.

[repo](https://github.com/marton78/pffft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/project-gemmi/benchmarking-fft)

##### PocketFFT (C++ branch)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++11 FFT (multi-D, any length, DCT/DST) behind NumPy and SciPy; about 4.5x faster than KissFFT on 3D transforms.

**Beats:** KissFFT — In project-gemmi's benchmarking-fft (GCC 8 -O3, i7-5600U, float, KissFFT scalar), the PocketFFT cpp branch with AVX did a 256^3 R2C in 97 ms vs KissFFT 436 ms (4.5x, derived) and 416x256x416 in 311 ms vs 2078 ms, matching FFTW measured from Ubuntu binaries (98 ms). The 3D C2C 256^3 run (SSE) took 264 ms vs KissFFT 785 ms but FFTW measured 162 ms.

**Known shortcoming:** GitHub repo is a fork of gitlab.mpcdf.mpg.de/mtr/pocketfft and the benchmark ran the gitlab cpp branch; 1D rows used the old C version (double, not vectorized); MKL is faster; FFTW from Ubuntu binaries.

**Known shortcoming:** 1D transforms not vectorized; SIMD only with GCC or Clang 5+ (MSVC/ICC scalar); multithreading via pthreads (issue #2); no versioned releases (issue #24); Android/Termux clang build fails on aligned_alloc (issue #23).

**How:** The core is a heavily reworked FFTPACK with radix codelets for 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 11 (complex) and 2, 3, 4, 5 (real), plus Bluestein's algorithm so large-prime lengths stay O(N log N). For multi-D or batched transforms it runs several 1D lines at once using GCC/Clang vector_size types (SSE2, AVX, AVX-512, NEON, VSX, RISC-V V), and it splits the work across an internal pthread thread pool. Twiddle factors take only about 2*sqrt(n) sin/cos calls, so plan setup is cheap (1274 ns vs FFTW's 25610 ns at n=512 in the gemmi benchmark).

**Use it when:**
- 2D/3D real or complex FFTs on strided or non-contiguous arrays, e.g. crystallography grids or image volumes
- Arbitrary lengths, including large primes, where FFTW's GPL or KissFFT's speed is a problem
- Workloads with many different sizes, where FFTW's plan time dominates (very fast setup)
- Projects that want one BSD header with DCT/DST and float/double/long double support
- Matching NumPy/SciPy FFT results in C++ code

**Skip it when:**
- Single short 1D transforms: the 1D path is not vectorized (4009 ns vs FFTW 588 ns and pffft 1255 ns at n=512 complex in gemmi's run, though that row used the older C version)
- Peak 3D throughput on Intel: MKL 2019 measured 61 ms vs 97 ms for 256^3 R2C
- Compilers other than GCC/Clang >= 5: MSVC and ICC get no SIMD (vectorization is gated on GCC/Clang)
- Windows multithreading: it uses pthreads (open issue #2 asks for a Windows pool)
- You need versioned releases: none are tagged (open issue #24)

**Integration:** header-only · none (pthreads for multithreading unless POCKETFFT_NO_MULTITHREADING) · C++11; SIMD needs GCC >= 5 or Clang >= 5 (AppleClang >= 9.1) · any C++11 platform; SIMD on x86 SSE2/AVX/AVX-512, ARM NEON, POWER VSX, RISC-V V via compile-time flags such as -march=native

**Vs siblings:** Pick PocketFFT over pffft and muFFT for multi-dimensional data, arbitrary lengths, double/long double, or DCT/DST. Pick pffft or muFFT for SIMD-accelerated short 1D transforms of 5-smooth or power-of-two sizes.

**Gotchas:**
- Strides are in bytes, not elements; r2c/c2r cannot be done in place
- Transforms are unnormalized: pass the scale via fct
- The plan cache is off by default (POCKETFFT_CACHE_SIZE=0); turn it on for repeated short 1D transforms, but it can use a lot of memory for large lengths
- Errors throw C++ exceptions (std::runtime_error, invalid_argument, bad_alloc); there is a reported aligned_alloc build failure on Android/Termux clang (issue #23)

**Status:** Active (commits through mid-2026); this GitHub fork mirrors the canonical gitlab.mpcdf.mpg.de/mtr/pocketfft cpp branch; BSD-3-Clause single header, easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/mreineck/pocketfft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/project-gemmi/benchmarking-fft)

##### TurboFFT  `CUDA/C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Code-generated batched 1D FP32/FP64 GPU FFT kernels with fused ABFT fault tolerance; matches or beats cuFFT, beats VkFFT.

**Beats:** NVIDIA cuFFT (also VkFFT) — The PPoPP 2025 paper (arXiv 2412.05824) reports that TurboFFT without fault tolerance is comparable to, or on certain sizes up to 300% faster than, cuFFT and faster than VkFFT, and that its fault tolerance costs 7-15% even under hundreds of injected errors per minute, for FP32 and FP64 batched 1D C2C FFTs. The artifact README gives the setup: A100-SXM4-40GB with AMD EPYC 7713, GCC 12.3.0, CUDA 12.0; and Tesla T4 with Xeon Silver 4216, GCC 11.2.0, CUDA 11.6; nvcc -O3 -lineinfo with sm_80/sm_75; timings are cudaEvent averages over 10 runs.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Up to 300%' only for some small sizes, otherwise on par with cuFFT; 7-15% overhead with fault tolerance; Apache-2.0 license added only in June 2026.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark tilt: TurboFFT gets one warm-up launch, cuFFT none, and both average only 10 runs; this favours TurboFFT exactly at the small sizes behind the 'up to 300%' claim.

**Known shortcoming:** At HEAD the A100 script (run_A100.sh) has its build and benchmark steps commented out, so the paper's A100 figures need the Zenodo artifact; run_T4.sh still works.

**Known shortcoming:** Last code commit Feb 2025 (Jun 2026 commit only added the license), so 'active' overstates it; benchmark driver only, no library API; tuned for A100/T4 only.

**How:** Each size gets its own generated kernel chain (one launch up to 2^12 or 2^13 depending on the tuning table, two for mid sizes, three for 2^23-2^25): every thread runs an 8-, 16- or 32-point radix-2 sub-FFT in registers with twiddles emitted as compile-time constants, threads exchange data through shared memory, and the large sizes split into multiple kernels with table twiddles between passes. The paper calls the design architecture-aware, padding-free and template-based, with tile sizes and batch-per-block chosen per GPU from a CSV. Fault tolerance is fused into the same kernels: DFT-matrix checksums are reduced with warp shuffles (two-side ABFT with location encoding), so detection and correction add no extra pass over memory.

**Use it when:**
- Batched small 1D power-of-two C2C FFTs (the paper's best case is problems under about 2 MB) on an A100 or T4, where cuFFT kernel choice is weak and launch-bound sizes dominate.
- Long-running HPC or ML jobs on GPUs where silent data corruption matters and you want error detection and correction inside the FFT at the 7-15% overhead the paper reports, instead of offline recomputation.
- As a starting point for your own fused FFT kernels (the code generator is about 780 lines of Python and the later commits fuse FFT with GEMM for Fourier neural operators).
- Reproducing or extending the PPoPP 2025 TurboFFT experiments against cuFFT and VkFFT.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a drop-in cuFFT replacement: there is no plan/exec API, no inverse or real-to-complex transform, no 2D/3D, no strides, and only power-of-two lengths up to 2^25 ('We currently only support radix-2').
- GPUs other than A100 and T4 or architectures other than sm_75/sm_80: CMake rejects any other ARCH_SM value and tuning tables exist only for those two GPUs.
- Large transforms where cuFFT is already bandwidth-bound: the claim is 'comparable to or up to 300% faster', with the big gains limited to certain small sizes.
- Production use without a maintainer: 9 stars, no releases, no issues filed; the last code commit is from February 2025 (TurboFNO work) and the June 2026 commit only added the Apache-2.0 LICENSE.
- Builds without Python: kernels must be generated with Python >= 3.9 and PyTorch before compiling.

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA toolkit (cudart; the driver also links cuFFT and cuBLAS), NVIDIA cuda-samples Common helpers via the CUDA_SAMPLES_COMMON environment variable, Python >= 3.9 with PyTorch >= 2.4 and NumPy for code generation; Matplotlib/Seaborn only for plots · GCC >= 11.2.0, CMake >= 3.24.3 (README; CMakeLists asks for 3.17), CUDA 12.0 for A100 or 11.6 for T4 · NVIDIA GPUs, sm_80 (A100) or sm_75 (T4) only; Linux shell scripts

**Vs siblings:** Pick TurboFFT over VkFFT when you need FP32/FP64 power-of-two batched FFTs on A100/T4 with built-in fault tolerance or the last bit of small-size throughput; pick VkFFT for arbitrary sizes, R2C, inverse, multi-dimensional transforms or non-NVIDIA GPUs, and tcFFT only for FP16 tensor-core work.

**Gotchas:**
- Benchmark asymmetry: test_turbofft launches the kernel chain once as a warm-up before the timed loop, but test_cufft starts timing on the first cufftExecC2C/Z2Z with no warm-up, and both average over only ntest = 10 runs; any first-call cost lands in cuFFT's number, which matters most for the small sizes where the up-to-300% gains are claimed.
- Both timing loops call cudaDeviceSynchronize after every launch inside the event-timed region, and TurboFFT does so after each of its 1-3 kernels, so per-launch host latency is included in all reported times.
- At HEAD, run_A100.sh has the codegen, build, 24 benchmark runs, VkFFT build and plotting all commented out (only the newer fft_codegen_stride scripts run); reproducing the paper's A100 figures needs the PPoPP artifact archive (Zenodo record 14220293) or manual uncommenting. run_T4.sh is still complete.
- Correctness check in the driver compares against cuFFT with a 1e-4 bound on |diff| / (1 + |ref|), so small-magnitude outputs are effectively checked in absolute rather than relative error.

**Status:** Dormant research artifact (last code commit February 2025, Apache-2.0 LICENSE added June 2026); permissively licensed and copyable, but expect to adapt the generator and driver yourself rather than link a library.

[repo](https://github.com/shixun404/TurboFFT) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.05824v1)

##### VectorFFT  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Double-precision x86 AVX2/AVX-512 FFT library in C, with generated codelets and a wisdom planner; median 1.29x Intel MKL on 1D c2c.

**Beats:** Intel oneMKL 2025.3 FFT (DFTI, sequential) — The author's gauntlet harness (public code and raw CSVs) on an Intel Core i9-14900KF P-core with AVX2 and GCC 15.2 at -O3 -march=native -mno-avx512f timed single-thread out-of-place interleaved FP64 c2c at every N from 2 to 4,096 against oneMKL 2025.3 sequential DFTI. It reports a 1.29x median speedup (89% of lengths at or above parity), 1.34x over 159 power-of-two 2D planes and 1.55x over 1,288 3D volumes, each ratio taking the worse of two engine orders. FFTW 3.3.10 (FFTW_MEASURE, vcpkg DLL) comparisons cover only real r2c/c2r and r2r transforms, with medians of 1.15-1.23x on powers of two and a few small-N losses.

**Known shortcoming:** Single machine (first-party, reproducible); on powers of two only 1.13x median over MKL with 25% of cases below parity; some odd lengths trade accuracy for speed (33 lengths error >1e-16), no accuracy mode; FFTW 3.3.10 comparison only for real transforms, loses small cases (N=15 at 0.70x); 5 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** FFTW comparisons cover only r2c/c2r/r2r, not the headline c2c; 33 lengths trade accuracy for speed.

**Known shortcoming:** vfft_set_num_threads pins the calling thread to core 0; build flags suppress implicit-function-declaration and incompatible-pointer-type warnings (-fpermissive).

**Known shortcoming:** Packaging gaps: no install target; examples/CMakeLists.txt links a vfft target defined only by an orphaned src/CMakeLists.txt; quickstart demo segfaults intermittently under MinGW GCC; FFTW binding targets Windows (POSIX path untested).

**Independent measurement:** Mid-size powers of two (32-512) run 0.94-1.03x MKL (enrichment reading of the repo's results).

**How:** Kernels are straight-line, register-allocated C codelets emitted per instruction set by the project's own DAG FFT compiler (OCaml-based, per the repo page), including Winograd-style odd radices, large conjugate-pair radix stages up to 47, Rader and Bluestein for primes, and a cache-tiled four-step path for large powers of two. The planner races every candidate route on the host CPU and keeps the winner as wisdom, so the first create of a size measures (milliseconds to seconds) and later creates replay the banked plan. Some odd composite lengths derive most twiddle factors from one loaded value instead of loading them all, trading a small accuracy loss for speed.

**Use it when:**
- Many FP64 complex transforms of modest length (N up to a few thousand) on AVX2 or AVX-512 x86, where MKL's sequential DFTI is the incumbent
- Awkward lengths (primes, large-prime composites, odd smooth sizes), where the README reports median 1.18x over MKL on primes and up to 7.04x at N=89
- Small 2D and 3D power-of-two grids (median 4.5x over MKL below 256 or 4,096 points) and batched DCT/DST work, where its tables show 2-4x over FFTW
- Projects that need an MIT-licensed alternative to MKL or GPL FFTW and can recalibrate wisdom on their target CPU

**Skip it when:**
- Single-precision, ARM/Apple Silicon or other non-x86 targets: it is FP64 only and ships only AVX2 and AVX-512 codelet trees
- Mid-size powers of two (32..512): it is at or slightly below MKL there (0.94-1.03x), and the power-of-two median lead is only 1.13x
- Workloads that need full double accuracy on every length: 33 large-odd-radix lengths exceed the README's 10e-16 error line and there is no accuracy mode
- Production code that needs a mature, packaged library: 5 stars, one author, very new, no install target; the root CMake builds only a codelet static lib and the benchmark tools
- Linux or POSIX-first deployments where you want tested comparisons: the harness targets Windows (its FFTW binding says the POSIX path is untested)

**Integration:** source-drop (header-only core in src/core plus src/core/vfft.c, linked with a static lib of generated codelets; no install or package target) · none at runtime beyond libm and the platform thread library; MKL and FFTW only for the optional benchmark comparators · C11; CMake 3.16; GCC, Clang, Intel ICX or MSVC-style front ends (README benchmarks used GCC 15.2); CPU with AVX2+FMA or AVX-512F/DQ · x86-64 only (AVX2+FMA default build, AVX-512 optional); ISA fixed at build time, with no runtime dispatch; developed and benchmarked on Windows, Linux builds supported by CMake

**Vs siblings:** Pick VectorFFT over KFR, PocketFFT or PFFFT when the workload is FP64 on modern x86, an MIT license matters, and you can benchmark and recalibrate on your own CPU; pick KFR or PocketFFT for portability (ARM, float), maturity or a C++ API, and VkFFT for GPUs.

**Gotchas:**
- vfft_set_num_threads(n>1) pins the calling thread to core 0 and the workers to the following cores; reset your own affinity afterwards
- The default layout is SPLIT, and for SPLIT at 2D and above the default output order is SCRAMBLED (only a roundtrip through the same plan decodes it); request VFFT_ORDER_NATURAL or the interleaved layout explicitly
- Errors are printed, not returned: vfft_create returns NULL, and vfft_execute with a pointer signature that does not match the plan computes nothing and returns void
- Shipped wisdom was calibrated on an i9-14900KF; on other CPUs the first create of each size races candidates unless you recalibrate. The build suppresses implicit-function-declaration and incompatible-pointer-type warnings (-fpermissive), and examples/CMakeLists.txt notes an intermittent MinGW GCC segfault in the quickstart demo

**Status:** Very active (2,449 commits, results dated up to 2026-10-01) but a 5-star single-author project with no tagged release; MIT-licensed, so it can be vendored if you also take on the build.

[repo](https://github.com/Tugbars/VectorFFT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Tugbars/VectorFFT)

##### Auto-MPFT  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Research code (KDD 2024) computing only a low-frequency block of 2-D Fourier coefficients faster than a full FFTW/MKL FFT.

**Beats:** FFTW 3.3.5 (planning excluded from run time), Intel MKL (version not stated), PFT (snudatalab/PFT, KDD 2021) and FFTW's pruned FFT (fftw.org/pruned.html); all single precision, with tolerances set so every method keeps relative l2 error below 1e-6. — Peer-reviewed KDD 2024 paper (pp. 2328-2339) whose abstract claims up to 7.6x over partial-FT methods (PFT, pruned FFT) and optimized FFT libraries (FFTW, MKL) at equal accuracy; a WebSearch summary of the paper PDF (not opened, host blocked) places the experiments on an Intel Core i7-10700KF at 3.80 GHz with 32 GB RAM and says PFT is weakest on the smaller images (Cityscapes, ADE20K, DF2K). The 7.6x is a maximum over datasets and baselines; compiler, flags, library versions and per-baseline ratios were not available, and the repository contains no harness to reproduce them.

**Known shortcoming:** Repo has no timing code (Auto-MPFT.cpp, FFTW.cpp and PFT.cpp only print coefficients), so the 7.6x claim cannot be reproduced from it; correctness bug: post-processing offsets only the first DS term per segment and every segment writes the same TEMP buffer, so M > p^2 gives wrong output (the shipped M=128, p=128 demo is fine); FFTW baseline hard-codes 32 threads.

**Known shortcoming:** KDD 2024 paper opened (author gh-pages PDF): i7-10700KF 3.80 GHz, 32 GB, single precision, relative L2 below 1e-6, FFTW 3.3.5 with planning excluded; 7.6x is the Cityscapes maximum, the other datasets give 5.7x, 6.9x, 2.8x, 2.6x and synthetic 4.7x, 3.3x. No compiler, flags, thread count or MKL version, so B not A.

**Independent measurement:** retier check 14 read the KDD 2024 paper

**How:** Partial Fourier transform: the input is split into p1 x p2 blocks of size q1 x q2, the twiddle factors inside each block are replaced by a truncated multivariate polynomial approximation (precomputed weights for tolerances 1e-1 to 1e-7 in src/precomputed/e-*.csv), so the block sums become two batched SGEMMs (cblas_sgemm_batch) against small r x q matrices. That leaves r1*r2 small p1 x p2 real FFTs (one batched MKL DFTI call) plus an elementwise post-processing pass with Intel IPP (ippsMul/ippsAddProduct) and a twiddle multiply, so the cost scales with the output size and the approximation order r rather than with a full N1 x N2 FFT. The 'Auto' part picks p (and hence r) by solving a convex cost model with Newton's method instead of a grid search.

**Use it when:**
- You only need a small low-frequency window of the 2-D spectrum of large real images (the paper's sets range from 2048 x 1024 Cityscapes frames to 6000 x 4000 Bird photos) and currently run a full FFTW or MKL FFT and discard most of it.
- Single-precision accuracy targets between 1e-1 and 1e-7 are acceptable (those are the only precomputed tolerance tables).
