- You are already on x86-64 with Intel oneMKL and IPP installed and can adapt a research kernel into your own code.
- You want a reference implementation of partial-FT by polynomial twiddle approximation to compare against pruned FFTs or sparse FFTs.

**Skip it when:**
- You need the full spectrum, complex input, double precision, or 1-D/3-D transforms: the shipped code handles 2-D real float input with a zero-centered target range only (its header says other cases need 'a slight modification', with details only in the paper).
- You need a reusable API: there is no function interface, no build files (no Makefile or CMake), sizes are compile-time constants, and the demo also runs a full MKL FFT before the partial one.
- Non-Intel platforms (Arm, Apple Silicon) or a dependency-free build: the core routines call proprietary Intel MKL and IPP.
- Production use: a 3-star research repository with no tests, no releases and no commits since 2025-08-19.
- Your coefficients of interest are not a contiguous low-frequency block (for a spectrum with a few large coefficients anywhere, a sparse FFT is the better fit).

**Integration:** source-drop · Intel oneMKL (DFTI, cblas_sgemm_batch, mkl_somatcopy, mkl_malloc) and Intel IPP (ipps complex vector ops); FFTW3 only for the baseline program; the precomputed/e-*.csv tables must sit at the relative path precomputed/ from the working directory · not documented; plain C++ (uses the 'and'/'or' alternative tokens); the FFTW baseline includes the Windows-only <tchar.h> and the code defines _USE_MATH_DEFINES, which points to a Visual Studio build · x86-64 only in practice (MKL and IPP); tested CPU not stated in the repo

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over a full-spectrum library such as FFTW, Admiral or VectorFFT only when you need a small zero-centered block of a large 2-D real spectrum and can live with MKL/IPP and research-grade code. Pick MPSFT instead when the 1-D spectrum is sparse with coefficients at unknown positions; Auto-MPFT targets a known contiguous range.

**Gotchas:**
- The repository has no timing code at all: Auto-MPFT.cpp, PFT.cpp and FFTW.cpp only compute and print a few coefficients, so the paper's speedups cannot be re-measured from what is committed, and the FFTW baseline hard-codes fftwf_plan_with_nthreads(32), FFTW_MEASURE and a 6000 x 4000 r2c size.
- In the 2-D post-processing loop only the first ippsMul_32fc term is offset to the current (s1, s2) segment of DS; the ippsAddProduct_32fc terms read segment 0, and every segment writes into the same TEMP buffer. With the shipped M = 128, p1 = p2 = 128 there is exactly one segment, so the demo is unaffected, but a larger target range (M > p2 or M > 2*p1) would give wrong or overwritten output as written (the 1-D PFT.cpp does offset every term).
- Arithmetic is float32 while the tightest table targets 1e-7, close to single-precision epsilon; tolerances below that are not offered.
- The precomputed tables are read with a relative path and stod() without error checks, so running from another directory throws or reads garbage; the demo also keeps about 0.8 MB of pointer arrays on the stack (six arrays of p1*p2 = 16,384 pointers).

**Status:** Stale research artifact (last commit 2025-08-19, 3 stars) under Apache-2.0, small enough to lift into your own code, but it needs proprietary Intel MKL and IPP and has no build system.

[repo](https://github.com/snudatalab/Auto-MPFT) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yongchanpark/yongchanpark.github.io/gh-pages/resources/2024/KDD/ParkKK24.pdf)

##### FINUFFT (with cuFINUFFT)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

CPU (and CUDA) nonuniform FFT library, types 1-3 in 1-3 dimensions, several times faster than NFFT3 and CMCL NUFFT.

**Beats:** NFFT3 (Chemnitz NUFFT library, built on FFTW); docs also name CMCL NUFFT — docs/nfft_migr.rst times a 2-D type-1 transform of 500,000 random points to 300 x 200 modes at tol 1e-13, single thread on an AMD 5700U laptop: NFFT3 3.5.4alpha 0.589 s versus FINUFFT 0.0787 s (7.5x), with the same output to all printed digits (compiler and flags not stated; the timing uses clock()). The peer-reviewed 2019 SIAM J. Sci. Comput. paper, seen only through a WebSearch summary because arxiv.org is blocked here, reports NFFT 3.3.2 as 3-5x slower without precomputation and 2-4x slower with it, FINUFFT at least 2x faster than every other code tested on random points except MIRT at 1-digit accuracy, and CMCL NUFFT up to 50x slower even on one thread (docs/related.rst).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B rests on the paper abstract seen via search (arXiv blocked here).

**Known shortcoming:** v2.5.0 had a thread-safety bug in parallel plan creation (fixed 2.5.1); open #839 (rare heap corruption during parallel plan creation) and #869 (50-80x slower at 96 threads); NUFFT, a loose fit for the fft category.

**Independent measurement:** nfft_migr: 7.5x over NFFT3 3.5.4alpha (0.589 s vs 0.0787 s, 1 thread, AMD 5700U, flags unstated).

**How:** Standard spread / FFT / deconvolve NUFFT, but with a cheap compactly supported kernel evaluated on the fly by Horner piecewise polynomials and SIMD (xsimd) instead of precomputed kernel tables, so no point-dependent precomputation or large RAM is needed. Points are bin-sorted for cache locality and type-1 spreading is split into load-balanced subproblems across OpenMP threads; the inner FFT is FFTW (default) or DUCC0, which exploits the block sparsity of the upsampled 2D/3D grids. The 2019 paper introduced the 'exponential of semicircle' kernel; since v2.5.0 the default is a PSWF (prolate) kernel, and upsampfac=0 picks the oversampling factor (for example 2 or 1.25) from a density-aware cost model.

**Use it when:**
- MRI, cryo-EM, radio-astronomy imaging, spectral analysis of unevenly sampled data or PDE solvers that need sums of exponentials at nonuniform points, where a direct O(NM) sum or NFFT3 is too slow.
- 2-D and 3-D problems with up to millions of points at tolerances from about 1e-2 to 1e-12 in double precision (about 1e-5 in single), on multicore CPUs.
- Repeated transforms with the same points: the guru or 'many' interface reuses the bin-sort and FFT plan, which the troubleshooting page says can be 10-100x faster than repeated simple calls on small problems.
- NVIDIA GPU workloads through cuFINUFFT in the same repository, whose legacy README claims up to 10x over CPU FINUFFT and up to 100x over other established GPU NUFFT codes.
- Projects that need one library with C, C++, Python, MATLAB/Octave, Fortran and Julia front ends under Apache-2.0.

**Skip it when:**
- Data on a regular grid: a plain FFT is faster and exact, and type 1 and type 2 are adjoints, not inverses, so you cannot undo one with the other; NFFT3 has inverse NUFFTs, sphere and rotation-group transforms that FINUFFT lacks.
- Very many tiny transforms through the simple interface, or very high thread counts: FFTW wisdom lookup costs about 0.1 ms per thread, and open issue #869 reports a 3-D grid running 50-80x slower at 96 threads than at 64 or fewer on a dual EPYC 9474F.
- Tolerances near machine precision or large 1-D N in single precision: errors cannot beat roughly N_max times machine epsilon, and requests the library judges unreachable return error 26 unless opts.allow_eps_too_small is set.
- Every regime against DUCC's own NUFFT: the project's docs say DUCC 'in some regimes is faster than ours', and NonuniformFFTs.jl is close on CPU and faster for real-valued data.
- Bitwise reproducibility across thread counts: results vary at rounding level, by up to about 1e-11 relative in double with upsampfac=1.25 at tol 1e-7 to 1e-9.

**Integration:** static lib · FFTW3 >= 3.3.6 single and double (default) or DUCC0 (fetched and bundled by CMake), xsimd and POET header-only (fetched), OpenMP (optional, ON by default); CUDA 11.8+ for cuFINUFFT · C++17, CMake 3.25; GCC 9+ recommended on x86-64 (GCC 8.5 can fail in xsimd with AVX-512); MSVC works on Windows · Linux, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), Windows (MSVC or MinGW; Windows CI builds DUCC0 only), PowerPC64/64le cross-builds; NVIDIA GPUs via cuFINUFFT; builds default to -march=native

**Vs siblings:** It is the general-purpose NUFFT among the catalogued FFT entries: pick it over TRON when you need all three transform types, CPU support and arbitrary sampling rather than a GPU MRI gridding pipeline compared against gpuNUFFT. Uniform-grid FFT entries (Admiral, PocketFFT, VkFFT) and FFTW++'s padded convolutions solve a different problem and are only relevant as its inner FFT or for regularly sampled data.

**Gotchas:**
- setpts keeps pointers to your nonuniform point arrays rather than copying them, so they must stay unchanged until the last execute that uses them.
- The default FFTW plan mode is FFTW_ESTIMATE; FFTW_MEASURE gives faster repeated transforms but can spend many seconds planning on the first call.
- v2.5.0 switched the default kernel to PSWF, which changes results at the tolerance level, and its kernel setup was not thread safe when plans are created concurrently (fixed in v2.5.1, #835/#838); open issue #839 reports a rare heap-corruption abort in that code path during parallel plan creation, not yet diagnosed.
- Unreleased master (v2.6.0-dev) fixes a Windows fine-grid size wraparound that silently ran transforms on a tiny grid, a clang -fassociative-math build that folded points wrongly and segfaulted, and an icpx bin-sort miscompile; build from master or a later release if you hit these configurations.

**Status:** Very active (3,747 commits, last commit 2026-09-30, release v2.5.1 of 2026-04-08 with v2.6.0 in preparation, CI across GCC, Clang, MSVC and CUDA 11.8-13.0) and Apache-2.0, maintained by the Flatiron Institute.

[repo](https://github.com/flatironinstitute/finufft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/flatironinstitute/finufft/blob/master/docs/nfft_migr.rst)

##### FlashFFTConv  `CUDA/C++ with PyTorch (Python) interface`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

CUDA tensor-core FFT convolution for PyTorch; 1.3x to 7.9x faster than torch.fft (cuFFT) convolution on H100.

**Beats:** PyTorch FFT convolution (torch.fft, backed by cuFFT) — On one H100-SXM, the README's gated-convolution table (fp16, times in ms per the benchmark script's torch.utils.benchmark mean x 1000, scaled to batch 64 x hidden 768) shows FlashFFTConv at 0.29 vs 2.30 at 1K (7.93x) and 10,049 vs 13,031 at 4M (1.30x) against a PyTorch reference that upcasts to fp32 and uses complex torch.fft.fft/ifft (not rfft). Rows from 16K up were measured at smaller batch/hidden sizes and rescaled, so the comparison favours FlashFFTConv on precision (fp16 vs fp32) and on the baseline's choice of complex rather than real FFT.

**Known shortcoming:** PyTorch baseline runs fp32 while FlashFFTConv runs fp16; rows of 16K and longer are scaled from a smaller batch; README's 8.21x memory claim exceeds its own table's 6.65x max.

**Known shortcoming:** PyTorch baseline upcasts to fp32 and uses complex fft/ifft, not rfft; open crash bugs: misaligned address with odd L under implicit padding (#20), illegal memory access at bf16 batch ~140k (#27); only compute_80 PTX is built (Hopper JIT-compiles); 18 of 25 issues open.

**How:** It writes the FFT as a Monarch decomposition: a length-N DFT becomes small 16x16 or 32x32 DFT matrix multiplies plus twiddle multiplies, which run on tensor cores in fp16/bf16 (separate kernels for 256/1K, 512/2K real-to-real, 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, and 16x/32x/64x/128x butterfly stages for 64K to 4M). FFT, pointwise multiply by the kernel spectrum and inverse FFT are fused in one kernel, so the intermediate spectra never go to HBM. Causal zero-padding and input/output gating are done inside the kernel (implicit padding), which removes the extra pad and gate passes a PyTorch implementation makes.

**Use it when:**
- Training or running long-convolution sequence models (Hyena, H3, HyenaDNA, Monarch Mixer) in PyTorch on Ampere or Hopper GPUs.
- Sequence lengths of 256 to 32K, where the README table shows the largest wins (5.4x to 7.9x at 256 to 8K, 2.5x to 3.2x at 16K to 32K).
- Gated and causally padded convolutions, where fusing the gates and padding saves several memory passes and about 6x activation memory.
- fp16/bf16 mixed-precision training where a 1e-2 absolute tolerance against an fp32 reference is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a general FFT (spectra, non-convolution transforms, real-valued output spectra): use cuFFT, VkFFT or tcFFT instead.
- fp32/fp64 accuracy is needed: only fp16 and bf16 inputs are supported, and the tests only assert allclose with atol=1e-2.
- Non-power-of-two FFT sizes, sizes below 256 or above 4,194,304, odd L, or H not a multiple of 16 for FFT sizes above 32K: the module raises NotImplementedError or fails.
- AMD GPUs, pre-Ampere NVIDIA GPUs or C++-only code bases: CUDA-only PyTorch extension (ROCm support is an open request, issue #34).
- Very long sequences (1M to 4M), where the gain falls to 1.3x to 1.7x and memory savings to about 2.8x.

**Integration:** module (PyTorch CUDA extension monarch_cuda built with setup.py, plus the pure-Python flashfftconv package) · PyTorch 2.0, CUDA toolkit (tested 12.1), einops; the README recommends the NVIDIA PyTorch container 23.05 · nvcc with C++17 (-std=c++17); CUDA 12.1 tested; build emits compute_80 PTX only · NVIDIA Ampere/Hopper GPUs (tested on A100 and H100; README says 3090/4090 should work); Linux with CUDA

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over tcFFT, TurboFFT or VkFFT when the job is a fused FFT convolution inside a PyTorch training loop (with gating or causal padding) rather than a standalone FFT; those siblings give a general FFT API and compare against cuFFT on the transform alone.

**Gotchas:**
- The kernel spectrum is still computed with torch.fft in fp32 on every forward call (the code says 'replace this with a kernel'), so precomputing FFT(k) is not supported.
- Input-size rules are enforced by crashes rather than checks: an odd L with implicit padding gives a CUDA 'misaligned address' error (issue #20, open), and a bf16 batch of about 140,000 x 4 x 4096 gives an illegal memory access (issue #27, open).
- Gated variants at 131K and above raise NotImplementedError when use_32_butterfly=False; the FlashDepthWiseConv1d bf16 backward pass has a known bug per the README.
- setup.py hard-codes --generate-code=arch=compute_80,code=compute_80, so Hopper runs JIT-compiled sm_80 PTX rather than sm_90 code; several open issues report build or cudaFuncSetAttribute errors (#6, #19, #29).

**Status:** Stale since December 2024, with 18 of the 25 listed issues open and no maintainer replies on the bug reports checked (#14, #20, #27), but Apache-2.0 and usable as a pinned PyTorch extension on Ampere/Hopper.

[repo](https://github.com/HazyResearch/flash-fft-conv) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HazyResearch/flash-fft-conv/HEAD/README.md)

##### heFFTe (Highly Efficient FFT for Exascale)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

MPI-distributed 2-D/3-D FFT layer over FFTW, MKL, cuFFT and rocFFT; on GPUs about 2x fftMPI and SWFFT, at parity on CPU.

**Beats:** Distributed 3-D FFT libraries fftMPI, SWFFT, AccFFT and P3DFFT (FFTW-MPI-class); FFTW is heFFTe's own CPU backend — Per search-result summaries of the peer-reviewed ICCS 2020 paper (the paper itself was not opened), on Summit (POWER9 plus V100, 6 ranks per node, one GPU per rank) heFFTe on GPUs is about 2x faster than the CPU-only fftMPI and SWFFT, more than 2x faster than FFTE with better scaling, and reaches about 90% of roofline peak for a 1024^3 FFT; its GPU local kernels are more than 40x faster than CPU kernels. Compiler, flags and competitor configurations were not seen. The repo's speed3d benchmark only prints heFFTe's own GFlops/s (5 N log2 N per run) for one backend, while the separate ICL hpfft harness wraps heFFTe, fftMPI, AccFFT, P3DFFT, FFTE, SWFFT, 2DECOMP&FFT, nb3dFFT, FFTW and FFTW++ without publishing results in its README.

**Known shortcoming:** The 2x over fftMPI/SWFFT compares GPU heFFTe against CPU-only libraries, so it is mostly a hardware gain; the CPU path is at parity. ICCS 2020 paper known from snippets only (publisher blocked here).

**Known shortcoming:** Open #88: the FFTW backend plans with FFTW_ESTIMATE on nullptr arrays, and r2c/c2r allocate a hidden buffer on each call (+65.9 MB at 200^3, +217 MB at 300^3). Open #90: MaxRSS grows per call in 2.4.1, no maintainer reply. ICL's harness github.com/icl-utk-edu/hpfft has no published results.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** A 3-D FFT is split into batches of local 1-D FFTs (or 2-D FFTs in slab mode), run by a backend (stock, FFTW, MKL, oneMKL, cuFFT or rocFFT), with global reshapes between pencil orientations. Reshapes pack, exchange and unpack with MPI_Alltoallv (the default), padded MPI_Alltoall or pipelined point-to-point Isend/Irecv. use_reorder transposes during unpacking so 1-D FFTs run on contiguous data, use_pencils switches between pencil and slab decomposition, and use_num_subranks/use_subcomm limit how many ranks take part in the reshapes. On GPUs, packing runs on the device and GPU-aware MPI sends device buffers directly, so data stays on the GPU. Batched calls merge communication buffers to cut latency for small signals. Since GPU local FFTs are reported >40x faster than CPU kernels, the remaining cost is mostly communication, which the paper puts at about 90% of roofline peak for 1024^3 on Summit.

**Use it when:**
- 3-D (or 2-D) FFTs too large for one node or one GPU, e.g. 512^3 to 1024^3+ grids in spectral/pseudo-spectral PDE, MD (PME/P3M) or cosmology codes on multi-GPU clusters
- Codes that must run on NVIDIA (cuFFT), AMD (rocFFT) and Intel (oneMKL) GPUs and on CPUs (FFTW, MKL, built-in stock) from one templated API
- Distributed jobs whose input layout (bricks) differs from the output layout (pencils or slabs): arbitrary non-overlapping per-rank boxes are reshaped for you
- Many same-shaped transforms per step: the batch overloads merge communication buffers to cut latency
- Applications that need distributed DCT/DST (types I and II) next to the FFT, available since 2.4

**Skip it when:**
- Single-process or single-GPU FFTs: heFFTe is only a communication and decomposition layer, so call FFTW, MKL, cuFFT or VkFFT directly
- CPU-only clusters where you expect a speedup over fftMPI, SWFFT or FFTW-MPI: the paper only claims its CPU path is 'at least as good' as those (parity); the 2x headline compares heFFTe on V100s with CPU-only libraries
- Long-running jobs with repeated r2c/c2r calls on the FFTW backend: open issue #88 shows FFTW plans made on nullptr arrays (in-place) but run out of place, allocating a hidden buffer on every call (+65.9 MB at 200^3, +217.4 MB at 300^3) that size_workspace() does not report; open issue #90 reports MaxRSS growing per forward/backward call in 2.4.1
- Builds without MPI, or a distributed 1-D FFT: MPI is mandatory, and the transforms are 2-D and 3-D only (2-D is a 3-D box of size 1 in one direction)
- One build that targets several GPU vendors: only one of CUDA, ROCm or oneAPI can be enabled per build, and the rocFFT backend has open issues (#82, #78; titles only seen)

**Integration:** shared lib (or static; CMake BUILD_SHARED_LIBS) with a header API (heffte.h) and CMake target Heffte::Heffte · MPI plus at least one backend: the built-in stock backend, FFTW3 (both fftw3 and fftw3f needed), MKL, oneMKL, cuFFT or rocFFT; optional MAGMA, SWIG/Fortran, Python · C++11 (cxx_std_11), CMake 3.19+; CI-tested with GCC 11-13, Clang 14-18, dpcpp 2024.2, OpenMPI 4.1.6, FFTW 3.3.7-3.3.10, MKL/oneMKL 2024.2, CUDA 11-12.6, ROCm 5.6-6.2 · Linux HPC systems: x86-64 and POWER9 CPUs (stock backend with optional AVX/AVX512), NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs; one GPU backend per build

**Vs siblings:** heFFTe is the only catalogued FFT sibling built for distributed-memory 3-D FFTs across many GPUs and nodes; use it when the grid does not fit one device. Use VkFFT, TurboFFT or tcFFT for single-GPU transforms, and FFTW++ for dealiased convolutions on CPU clusters.

**Gotchas:**
- The FFTW backend plans every local transform with FFTW_ESTIMATE on nullptr arrays (heffte_backend_fftw.h), so local kernels are untuned and r2c/c2r break FFTW's new-array execute contract (issue #88)
- No scaling by default (scale::none, like FFTW): pass scale::full to backward() (or scale::symmetric to both) to get the input back
- With a GPU backend, GPU-aware MPI is assumed ON at build time (Heffte_ENABLE_GPU_AWARE_MPI); on an MPI without GPU support, turn it off at build time or with plan_options::use_gpu_aware
- The stock backend has no vectorization unless built with -DHeffte_ENABLE_AVX or AVX512 (docs: up to an order of magnitude faster with them), and prime factors below HEFFTE_STOCK_RADER_MIN (100000) fall back to a direct O(p^2) DFT

**Status:** Maintained (DOE ECP, ICL UTK/ORNL): last commit 2025-11-19, CMake project version 2.4.1, BSD-3-Clause and copyable; 7 open issues include memory growth (#90) and the FFTW nullptr-plan problem (#88), and the README's 'Getting Help' link points to the SLATE issue tracker rather than heFFTe's.

[repo](https://github.com/icl-utk-edu/heffte) · [benchmark](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-50371-0_19)

##### PFT (Partial Fourier Transform)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Research C++ code computing only M of N Fourier coefficients with polynomial-approximated twiddles; up to 19x over FFTW/MKL.

**Beats:** FFTW (real-to-complex 1D, FFTW_ESTIMATE), Intel MKL DFTI, FFTW pruned FFT, Goertzel algorithm — The KDD 2021 paper (read from the author's GitHub Pages repository) times PFT on an Intel Core i7-6700HQ @ 2.60 GHz with 8 GB RAM, in single precision at relative L2 error below 1e-6, averaged over 100 runs of 1000 random vectors: up to 19x faster than FFTW 3.3.5 (planning excluded), MKL and pruned FFTW for the target range R_{0,2^9} as N grows to 2^22, with the best setting at N = 2^22 taking 1.273 ms for M = 2^9 and 11.924 ms for M = 2^18 (Table 3). The compiler, flags, MKL version and thread count are not stated, and the repository has no timing harness.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: README bibtex confirms KDD 2021, but the paper could not be opened and the snippet could not be tied to the abstract. No timing harness; the FFTW baseline uses FFTW_ESTIMATE; needs proprietary MKL/IPP.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered C to B on the KDD 2021 paper (opened via the author's gh-pages PDF). The repo's FFTW.cpp baseline (FFTW_ESTIMATE, 4 threads, N=2^20, timer never read) is not the paper's baseline. Reads precomputed/<tol>.csv by relative path with no check, does not check that p divides N, and needs MKL plus IPP.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher opened the KDD 2021 paper

**How:** The input is viewed as a p x q matrix (N = p*q) and the q-dependent twiddle factors are replaced by a degree-r minimax polynomial approximation of e^(pi*i*x), whose coefficients are precomputed per tolerance in src/precomputed/e-*.csv. The inner sums then collapse into one r x q by q x p SGEMM (O(rN)), r batched real FFTs of size p (O(r p log p)) and an elementwise post-processing pass over powers of the output index and twiddles (IPP ippsMul/ippsAddProduct, cblas_saxpy). The paper gives O((N + M log M) log(1/eps)) versus O(N log N), with r growing as M/p grows or the tolerance tightens; the heavy steps run in MKL BLAS and DFTI.

**Use it when:**
- You need only a small contiguous band (e.g. the lowest frequencies) of the spectrum of a long real series: the paper reports PFT beating the full FFT for M < 2^19 at N = 2^22, with the largest gains when the output is under about 10% of the input.
- Many transforms with the same N, M and tolerance, so the precomputed B, D, twiddle tables and DFTI descriptors amortize (batch feature extraction, sliding windows, the paper's anomaly detection at about 8x over FFT).
- Single-precision results at a stated tolerance such as 1e-6 relative L2 error, or looser: relaxing to 1e-4 or 1e-2 cut a further 17% or 27% in the paper.
- Intel x86 machines where MKL and IPP are already part of the build.
- Lengths with a convenient divisor p, including non-powers of two (the paper runs N = 32000).

**Skip it when:**
- M close to N or the full spectrum: the O(N) pre-processing and post-processing overhead makes it slower than a plain FFT (Table 3 omits settings that lost to FFT).
- Exact or double-precision coefficients: it is an approximation, and the sample is float-only.
- N prime or with only awkward divisors: the paper's N = 19735 = 5 x 3947 forced p = 3947.
- ARM, non-Intel or fully open-source builds: it depends on proprietary Intel MKL and IPP.
- Sparse spectra at unknown positions (use a sparse FFT), or production code needing an API, tests or maintenance: this is a 2021 research sample with hard-coded parameters and no timing harness.

**Integration:** source-drop · Intel MKL (cblas_sgemm, cblas_saxpy, DFTI), Intel IPP (ipps), the precomputed CSV tables in src/precomputed; FFTW 3 only for the baseline programs · not documented; any C++ compiler supported by MKL and IPP (the code is C++98-style); the FFTW.cpp baseline includes the Windows-only tchar.h · x86-64 with Intel MKL and IPP (paper machine: Intel Core i7-6700HQ); others not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick PFT over full-spectrum libraries (FFTW, Admiral, VectorFFT, PocketFFT) only when you need a small contiguous band of a long 1-D real series; for 2-D blocks use Auto-MPFT, the same group's KDD 2024 successor with automatic choice of p, and for sparse spectra at unknown positions use MPSFT or SFFT.

**Gotchas:**
- The tolerance table is read from the relative path precomputed/<tol>.csv with no open or parse check, so running outside src/ ends in a std::stod exception.
- q = N / p uses integer division with no check that p divides N, and r is capped at 27 by the 26-entry threshold table (M/p up to about 3.9 at 1e-7).
- The sample assumes real input and a target range centered at zero; another center needs the modulation step from the paper, which makes the input complex.
- The repo's FFTW.cpp (FFTW_ESTIMATE, 4 threads, N = 2^20, no timer read) is not the paper's baseline ('optimized FFTW 3.3.5' with planning excluded), so do not reuse it as a fair comparison.

**Status:** Stale research code (last source change 2021-06-03, README edits through 2025-08-19); Apache-2.0 and small enough to copy, but it needs proprietary MKL and IPP and must be refactored out of main() before use.

[repo](https://github.com/snudatalab/PFT) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yongchanpark/yongchanpark.github.io/gh-pages/resources/2021/KDD/ParkJK21.pdf)

##### TRON (TRajectory Optimized NUFFT)  `CUDA`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

CUDA NUFFT gridding/degridding hard-wired for 2D radial MRI trajectories; paper reports 6-30x over gpuNUFFT, BART and IRT.

**Beats:** gpuNUFFT (GPU NUFFT gridding library), Fessler's Image Reconstruction Toolbox (IRT, MATLAB) and BART (the reproduction steps also build BART) — The README claims 30x over gpuNUFFT and 75x over Fessler's CPU MATLAB IRT for radial gridding; the peer-reviewed MRM 2019 abstract (seen only via search summaries) gives 6-30x over the closest competitor depending on data set and calls TRON the most accurate code tested. Built with nvcc -O3 --use_fast_math against cuFFT; the GPU model and CUDA version are not stated on any page opened.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper abstract says 6-30x by data set, so the README's 30x is the best case; GPU model unknown.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: only 6 channels fit (MAXCHAN 6) and nothing checks nc*nt against it, so more coils overflow a per-thread array; the iterative CGNR path (-i) is marked 'NOT WORKING CORRECTLY YET'; cudaFreeHost(&ptr) is wrong; the built-in timer is clock() (CPU time) and includes plan creation; square 2D radial only; never compared against cuFINUFFT; dormant since 2021.

**How:** The trajectory is computed analytically inside the kernels (angle = pe*pi/npe or the golden-angle increment), so no trajectory array, presorting or atomic scatter is needed: in gridding each thread owns one Cartesian point (4x4 tiled thread mapping) and gathers, over every spoke, only the radial samples inside a circular band of +/- kernel width around its radius. Density compensation is an analytic ramp (precompensate kernel) instead of an iterative DCF, the Kaiser-Bessel kernel is evaluated on the fly with a polynomial I0 approximation, and float32 math is built with --use_fast_math; cuFFT does the oversampled (2x default) FFT.

**Use it when:**
- Offline or real-time reconstruction of 2D radial MRI (uniform-angle or golden-angle), including stack-of-stars and sliding-window golden-angle series on one Nvidia GPU.
- As a reference design for trajectory-specialised gridding: the 995-line tron.cu shows the gather-with-analytic-trajectory approach that beat general GPU gridders in the MRM 2019 paper.
- Reproducing or extending the MRM 2019 comparison against gpuNUFFT, BART and Fessler's IRT (scripts RUNME1-4 plus git-lfs data).
- Square-image adjoint NUFFT where single precision and a fixed Kaiser-Bessel kernel are acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Arbitrary, spiral or 3D trajectories: only 2D radial is implemented (a -3 'koosh' flag exists but the kernels are 2D); issue #7 asking how to add other trajectories is unanswered since Nov 2024. Use a general NUFFT (cuFINUFFT, gpuNUFFT, BART) instead.
- More than 6 coil channels times repetitions: per-thread accumulators are float2 utmp[MAXCHAN] with MAXCHAN hard-coded to 6, and nothing checks nc*nt against it.
- Iterative reconstruction: the CGNR path (-i) is commented 'NOT WORKING CORRECTLY YET' in tron.cu.
- Non-square images, double precision, multi-GPU (MULTI_GPU is compiled to 0) or use as an in-process library with several concurrent plans (global static state).
- Production builds on current toolchains without porting: the Makefile pins nvcc -ccbin gcc-6 and the CUDA code dates from 2018-2021.

**Integration:** source-drop (CUDA command-line program built with a Makefile) · CUDA toolkit with cuFFT and cuBLAS; reproduction also needs MATLAB, gpuNUFFT, BART and git-lfs data · nvcc with gcc-6 host compiler as written in src/Makefile; minimum CUDA version not documented · Linux/Unix with an Nvidia CUDA GPU (single GPU); POSIX headers (unistd.h, err.h) used

**Vs siblings:** FINUFFT/cuFINUFFT is the general-purpose choice (any trajectory, 1-3D, double precision, maintained library API); pick TRON only when data are strictly 2D radial on an Nvidia GPU and you want the trajectory-specialised, presort-free gather approach, noting that TRON's paper (2019) predates cuFINUFFT and never compared against it. The other FFT siblings (cuFFT alternatives such as VkFFT, tcFFT, TurboFFT) are uniform FFTs and do not address non-Cartesian gridding.

**Gotchas:**
- Channel count is capped silently: gridradial2d accumulates into a fixed 6-element per-thread array while looping over nc*nt channels, so larger coil arrays overflow it; compress coils to <=6 first.
- The built-in 'Elapsed time' uses clock() (process CPU time) around the whole recon including cuFFT plan creation, allocation and host transfers, not CUDA events; do not compare it directly with kernel-only timings.
- Image size is derived from the readout (nx = ny = nro/2) and images must be square; the pad kernel's '> 0' bounds test drops source row/column 0 in the forward (degridding) path.
- cudaFreeHost(&h_outdata) passes the address of the pointer instead of the pointer at exit, so the pinned buffer is not freed correctly (harmless for the CLI, wrong if reused as library code).

**Status:** Effectively dormant: the CUDA code was last changed 2018-2021 and the January 2026 commits only zip MATLAB files; MIT-licensed and small (one ~1000-line .cu file), so it is easy to vendor or study but expect to port the build.

[repo](https://github.com/davidssmith/TRON) · [benchmark](https://github.com/davidssmith/TRON)

##### VkFFT  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only, cross-vendor GPU FFT library; matches cuFFT on smooth lengths and is ~1.5-3x faster on prime/Bluestein lengths.

**Beats:** NVIDIA cuFFT (CUDA 11.7) and AMD rocFFT (ROCm 5.2) — The author's VkFFT_TestSuite (-vkfft 1001) batched 1D C2C FP64 transforms of every length 2-4096 into 500MB-1GB systems and reported achieved bandwidth on an A100 40GB vs cuFFT (CUDA 11.7) and an MI250 vs rocFFT (ROCm 5.2). Radix 2-13 lengths were at parity with cuFFT; Rader-prime and Bluestein lengths were roughly 1.5-3x faster (derived from page data). These are first-party numbers published in a peer-reviewed IEEE Access 2023 paper, with compiler and flags unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline cuFFT/rocFFT is a GPU library outside the category list; no gain on lengths that factor into radix 2-13 (level at ~1260 GB/s on A100); gains (~1.5-3x, derived from plot) only on Rader/Bluestein lengths; author's own numbers; compiler and flags not stated; stale (last commit 2024-02-05).

**Known shortcoming:** Master (v1.3.4) is Feb 2024 but the develop branch has unreleased fixes until 2026-04-04 (leaks #197, 2D zero-padding #201, conv kernel #222). Open correctness bugs: #228 Level Zero non-deterministic wrong results on Intel iGPU (v1.2.31-1.3.4), #206 Y-dim zero-padding wrong (CUDA), #226 Metal double free.

**How:** At plan time it generates GPU source specialised to the exact length, layout and device (shared-memory size, coalescing width, register file), with constants inlined and loops unrolled, then compiles it with the backend's runtime compiler (NVRTC, HIPRTC, glslang, OpenCL, clang+llvm-spirv). The core is a mixed-radix Stockham autosort FFT with radix 2-13 kernels that keeps whole sequences in shared memory, using the register file as extra storage ('register overutilization') so more sizes fit in a single upload; longer sequences use a Four-Step FFT. Primes from 17 up to the shared-memory limit are done in-kernel with Rader's algorithm (direct-multiplication or FFT-convolution variant), other lengths with Bluestein's algorithm using merged convolution and zero-padding to cut memory passes, which is where it beats cuFFT/rocFFT.

**Use it when:**
- Batched FP64 or FP32 GPU FFTs whose lengths contain primes above 13 or are not smooth: on A100 cuFFT's Bluestein path falls to ~100-180 GB/s above length 2048 while VkFFT stays far higher
- One FFT dependency for Nvidia, AMD, Intel and Apple GPUs (and Raspberry Pi 4) on Windows, Linux and macOS, or for Vulkan/Metal apps that have no cuFFT
- Vulkan or Metal rendering/compute pipelines that want FFT dispatches appended straight into their own command buffer without extra synchronisation
- FFT-based convolution or cross-correlation and zero-padded open-boundary systems: the last FFT pass, kernel multiply and first iFFT pass are fused, and padded zeros are skipped (README: up to 2x faster than padding the array)
- GPU DCT I-IV, or FP64 transforms that need better-than-cuFFT accuracy (FP128-precomputed twiddles) or double-double precision

**Skip it when:**
- Power-of-two or 2-13-smooth lengths on Nvidia/AMD datacenter GPUs: the author's own A100 plot shows parity with cuFFT (~1250-1280 GB/s), so you add a runtime compiler dependency for no speedup
- CPU-side FFTs: GPU only; use FFTW, PocketFFT or pffft
- Programs that create many short-lived plans of different sizes: every initializeVkFFT generates and runtime-compiles kernels unless you cache binaries with saveApplicationToString/loadApplicationFromString (not available on Metal)
- Intel iGPUs via Level Zero, Metal with NSAutoreleasePool, or Y-axis zero-padding on CUDA: open issues report non-deterministic wrong results (#228, v1.2.31-v1.3.4), a double free (#226) and wrong Y-padded results (#206)
- Multi-GPU split transforms: listed only as a future plan

**Integration:** header-only · backend runtime plus its runtime compiler: Vulkan + glslang/SPIRV, CUDA driver/runtime + NVRTC, HIP + HIPRTC, OpenCL, Level Zero + clang + llvm-spirv, or Metal + metal-cpp; quadmath for double-double; FFTW/cuFFT/rocFFT only for the benchmark suite · C99-style C (also compiles as C++); Vulkan 1.0 (1.1 for half precision); ROCm 4.5+ unless VKFFT_OLD_ROCM is defined; CMake 3.11 for the test suite · Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Apple and Raspberry Pi 4 GPUs; Windows, Linux, macOS

**Vs siblings:** Pick VkFFT over tcFFT and TurboFFT when you need a maintained, general library: non-Nvidia GPUs, double precision, arbitrary or prime lengths, multidimensional, DCT or convolution. tcFFT (half precision on tensor cores) and TurboFFT (small sizes, fault tolerance) are CUDA research codes that can beat cuFFT in their narrow niches; for CPU FFTs use PocketFFT or pffft instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Structs must be zero-initialised (C API); initializeVkFFT on a non-zero app returns VKFFT_ERROR_NONZERO_APP_INITIALIZATION
- Inverse transforms are unnormalised by default (set normalize=1); multidimensional sizes are given fastest axis first (XYZ), opposite to FFTW/cuFFT
- Sequences beyond one shared-memory upload (e.g. ~4096 FP64 with 64KB shared memory, less for strided axes) switch to Four-Step FFT and need a tempBuffer the size of the main buffer; Bluestein needs extra buffers too
- Bug fixes since v1.3.4 (memory leaks #197, 2D zero-padding #201, convolution kernel compile failure #222) exist only on the develop branch; master/releases still carry them

**Status:** The last release (v1.3.4) and the last master commit are from Feb 2024, but the single author kept pushing bug fixes to the develop branch until 2026-04-04 and issues are still being filed, so it is slow-moving rather than abandoned. MIT-licensed and header-only, so it is easy to vendor; take develop if you hit the zero-padding or memory-leak bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/DTolm/VkFFT) · [benchmark](https://scispace.com/pdf/vkfft-a-performant-cross-platform-and-open-source-gpu-fft-sr243p64.pdf)

#### geometry-spatial

##### geo-utils-cpp  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++17 port of Google Maps' spherical geometry utils; beats Boost.Geometry's spherical strategies on area and point-in-polygon.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry 1.90 (spherical_equatorial strategy: bg::within and bg::area); also S2 Geometry 0.14.0 and GeographicLib 2.7 — The author's Google Benchmark runs (Apple M1, Apple clang 17, -std=c++17 -O2 -DNDEBUG, Boost 1.90.0, s2geometry 0.14.0, GeographicLib 2.7, median of 5 repetitions) show area at 67-70 M polygons/s vs Boost.Geometry 36-45 M/s, and contains at about 8.5-14x Boost's spherical bg::within on a regular 5-degree n-gon of 10-1000 vertices with 1000 jittered query points. The contains gap is partly an algorithm difference (rhumb ray cast vs great-circle winding), and distance, heading and path_length are within noise of Boost.

**Known shortcoming:** The contains win compares rhumb-line with great-circle tests, not like-for-like; port of android-maps-utils (Java).

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark compares a rhumb-line ray cast (default geodesic=false) against Boost great-circle winding, so the two compute different predicates; geodesic=true is not benchmarked. Bench polygon is a regular 5-degree n-gon, not random lat/lng as the record says. Port of android-maps-utils (Java).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** area uses the polar-triangle accumulation from PolyUtil (Todhunter's two-sides-and-included-angle formula, one tan and one atan2 per vertex) in a tight loop with no allocation, against Boost's strategy machinery. contains is an O(N) ray cast to the South Pole that by default treats edges as rhumb lines (a Mercator-latitude comparison per edge) with cheap linear-latitude early exits, while Boost's bg::within with spherical_equatorial picks a great-circle winding strategy that costs more per edge. distance uses haversine with cached degree-to-radian factors, which ties Boost and hand-written haversine rather than beating them.

**Use it when:**
- Polygon area on lat/lng data is a hot path: about 1.5-1.9x Boost.Geometry and about 5x S2's S2Loop::GetArea in the author's M1 runs.
- Point-in-polygon for GPS/geofencing on small to medium polygons (10-1000 vertices) where rhumb-line edges are acceptable and S2 is too heavy a dependency.
- You want zero dependencies and a single header (amalgamated geo.hpp) instead of pulling in Boost, S2 plus Abseil, or GeographicLib.
- Mobile/backend code that must give the same answers as Google Maps Android Utils (same spherical model and conventions).
- Route utilities on lat/lng (point_at_distance, polyline6 encode/decode for OSRM, Valhalla or Mapbox).

**Skip it when:**
- Sub-meter or survey-grade work: it is spherical, not WGS84 ellipsoidal (use GeographicLib), and precision degrades near the poles and for antipodal pairs.
- contains on large polygons or many queries: S2 measured 18-21 M queries/s at N=100-1000 vs 2.87 and 0.33 M/s here, because the scan is linear with no built-in index or bounding-box prefilter.
- You need great-circle containment semantics that match Boost's bg::within: the default contains uses rhumb-line edges, so answers differ on long edges and at high latitude; geodesic=true exists but was not benchmarked.
- Planar/projected geometry, polygon booleans, validity repair or spatial indexing are needed; the feature set is far smaller than Boost.Geometry, GEOS or TG.
- Very young codebase (first release in 2026, 56 stars), so there is little production track record.

**Integration:** header-only · none (Google Test only for the test suite; Google Benchmark, Boost, S2 and GeographicLib only for the opt-in benchmarks) · C++17; CMake 3.14+ for the optional CMake package; CI covers GCC and Clang on Linux, AppleClang on macOS and MSVC on Windows · any (portable scalar code, no SIMD or intrinsics)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over TG when your data is raw lat/lng and you want spherical (rhumb or great-circle) area and containment without projecting; TG is planar but has indexed point-in-polygon (ystripes/natural) that scales far better on big polygons. Pair it with an index such as nanoflann or tidwall/rtree.c when you have many polygons, since it ships no spatial index of its own.

**Gotchas:**
- contains defaults to rhumb-line edges (geodesic=false) while on_edge and on_path default to great-circle edges; pass geodesic explicitly. The South Pole is always outside a polygon.
- LatLng is never validated: out-of-range coordinates give unspecified (memory-safe, no-throw) results; call is_valid() or normalized() on untrusted input.
- LatLng::operator== is approximate (1e-12 degree epsilon, longitude modulo 360), not bitwise.
- Polygons are implicitly closed (last vertex connects to the first); encode, decode and simplify allocate and can throw std::bad_alloc. decode had signed-overflow UB on malformed input before v1.2.0 (fixed, found by fuzzing).

**Status:** Active (v1.2.2, last commit 2026-09-20, CI with ASan/UBSan and a libFuzzer target on decode), Apache-2.0 with Google's original notices kept, and small enough (about 50 KB of headers) to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/gistrec/geo-utils-cpp) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gistrec/geo-utils-cpp/HEAD/docs/benchmarks.md)

##### jc_voronoi  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Single-header C99 Fortune-sweep 2D Voronoi/Delaunay generator, 1.4-3.7x faster than Boost.Polygon voronoi on random points.

**Beats:** Boost.Polygon voronoi_diagram (Boost 1.92.0); also jc_voronoi 0.9.0, and in older README prose Fastjet/Fortune C, O'Sullivan C++, voronoi++ — The author's test/release-0.10.0-performance.md (Apple M5 Max, Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG, medians with diagram destruction included) times jc_voronoi 0.10 against Boost.Polygon from Boost 1.92.0 at 178.00 us vs 649.83 us (1k random sites), 4.87 vs 6.82 ms (10k), 53.95 vs 80.21 ms (100k) and 18.63 vs 39.25 ms (100k pathological), with similar peak memory. The committed harness differs slightly from the published method: test/perftest.cpp seeds with srand(0) on a 4096-unit integer grid (the doc says seed 4), and compile_perftest.sh builds with -O2 -g, so reproducing the published numbers needs those settings changed.

**Known shortcoming:** README's '2.5x Boost memory' claim is not borne out (peak memory within ~5%); compile_perftest.sh uses -O2 -g, not the -O3 the performance doc states.

**Known shortcoming:** Committed harness differs from the published method: perftest.cpp uses srand(0) on a 4096 integer grid while the doc says seed 4; compile_perftest.sh uses -O2 -g while the doc says -O3 (seed 4 chosen to avoid a 0.9.0 bug). Own BENCHMARKS.md shows d3-delaunay ~3x faster than the JCV wasm build at JS generation (31.54 vs 98.21 ms, 100k). Header comment on site order contradicts README; 0.10 broke the API.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It is Fortune's sweep-line algorithm with: an introsort specialized for jcv_site (y-then-x order; already-sorted input returns at once, reversed input is reversed in place); a binary-heap event queue specialized for half-edges; and, since 0.10, a rank-balanced relaxed AVL (RAVL) tree that indexes the beachline, replacing a linked scan that went quadratic on adversarial input (the 100k issue48 case fell from 9.15 s to 18.63 ms). Memory comes from a few large blocks (one up-front block for sites and events, then 16 KiB arenas), so a 100k diagram makes 1,187 allocations against Boost's 557,371. Per-site edge topology is built after the sweep from shared edges rather than per-site copies, and edges are sorted around each site by an overflow-safe pseudo-angle (0.10 changelog).

**Use it when:**
- Games, procedural maps, stippling or Lloyd relaxation that need clipped Voronoi cells with ordered edge loops from thousands to a few hundred thousand points, in C or C++.
- Replacing Boost.Polygon voronoi_diagram when the sites are points and you want edges already clipped to a box or convex polygon, without Boost headers (0.17 s vs 0.97 s clean build and a 33.7 KB vs 150.6 KB minimal executable in the author's table).
- Allocation-sensitive or embedded code: jcv_diagram_generate_useralloc takes custom alloc/free callbacks, and generation does about a thousand allocations rather than hundreds of thousands.
- Inputs with heavy symmetry or collinear structure, where 0.10's RAVL beachline keeps O(n log n) behaviour (100k pathological case 18.63 ms vs Boost 39.25 ms).
- Browser or Node use via the npm jc-voronoi WebAssembly package when you need per-cell edge access.

**Skip it when:**
- Segment sites, medial axes or exact predicates: Boost.Polygon handles segment input with robust integer predicates; jc_voronoi is float-based Fortune on points and prunes duplicates and out-of-bounds points.
- Raw Delaunay or Voronoi speed in JavaScript: the repo's own BENCHMARKS.md has d3-delaunay generating 100k random diagrams in 31.54 ms against JCV-wasm's 98.21 ms, with lower memory.
- Upgrading from 0.9 just for speed on ordinary random input: at 100k random sites 0.9.0 (51.22 ms) is slightly faster than 0.10.0 (53.95 ms); 0.10 fixes worst-case scaling and memory instead.
- Clipping to non-convex boundaries: only box and convex-polygon clippers ship (open issue #50 asks for non-convex).
- Code that relied on the 0.9 API: 0.10 broke the edge API (jcv_graphedge, jcv_site.edges and jcv_diagram_get_next_edge removed) and changed struct layouts; see MIGRATION_GUIDE.md.

**Integration:** header-only (stb-style: define JC_VORONOI_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit); optional jc_voronoi_clip.h; CMake target jc_voronoi::jc_voronoi, Homebrew tap, npm WebAssembly package · none (libc math and stdlib only) · C99 (C11, C17 and C23 supported); includable from C++; the benchmark harness is C++11 · any; CI builds on macOS, Linux and Windows (MSVC build script provided); WebAssembly via Emscripten

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over Delaunay32 or detria when you need Voronoi cells with clipped, ordered edge loops in plain C, not a triangulation; Delaunay32 (multithreaded, beats delaunator-cpp and Triangle) and detria (constrained Delaunay) are faster or stronger when the Delaunay triangulation itself is the output. Against CGAL-based Voronoi, it trades exact predicates for a dependency-free single header.

**Gotchas:**
- Sites come back sorted for the sweep, not in input order; use site->index to map back. The header comment on jcv_diagram_get_sites still says 'each index is the same as the original input point array', which contradicts the README and the 0.10 changelog.
- Duplicate points, points outside the rect, and points rejected by the clipper are silently dropped, so diagram.numsites can be lower than num_points; with a NULL rect the bounds are computed automatically with 10 units of padding.
- Default precision is float (JCV_REAL_TYPE); for large coordinate ranges or near-collinear input, switch to double by overriding JCV_REAL_TYPE, JCV_ATAN2, JCV_SQRT, JCV_FLT_MAX, JCV_REAL_TYPE_EPSILON and JCV_PI identically in every translation unit.
- Allocation failures are not checked (the context block is memset straight after allocfn returns), and the fixed-size event-queue bound is guarded only by assert; several crash, infinite-loop and memory-blowup issues (#83, #85, #91) were closed during the July 2026 0.10 work.

**Status:** Active (0.10.0 released 2026-07-22, last commit 2026-07-25, 733 stars, 129 commits on dev) and MIT-licensed, so copyable; the 0.10 rewrite is recent and broke the API, so pin a version.

[repo](https://github.com/JCash/voronoi) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JCash/voronoi/dev/test/release-0.10.0-performance.md)

##### kigumi  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only, exact, multithreaded mesh Booleans for open, closed and non-manifold meshes; beats CGAL corefinement.

**Beats:** CGAL Polygon_mesh_processing corefinement ('coref.'); also libigl igl::copyleft::cgal::mesh_boolean (CGAL exact), geogram, Manifold, MCUT — Intersection of two generated mesh pairs on a 16-core MacBook Pro 14-inch M4 (2024, M4 Max-class), built with Homebrew Clang 22.1.1 in CMake Release, excluding I/O. kigumi took 4.6 s single-threaded and 1.1 s parallel on the closed case vs 27.2 s for CGAL PMP corefinement with EPECK and 39.3 s for libigl's CGAL-exact mesh_boolean. On the open case it took 2.4 s vs 3.2 s. These are first-party numbers from a single machine.

**Known shortcoming:** MIT code but needs LGPL/GPL CGAL (GPL obligation applies); benchmark table predates the Jul 2026 autorefinement change.

**Known shortcoming:** Needs C++20 plus Boost, CGAL and fast_float, so header-only still pulls heavy dependencies; CGAL parts are GPL (licence question #35 closed without reply). Corefine.h prints progress to std::cout unconditionally. Open unanswered issue #33: wrong union with a partial-intersection warning; #28: 273 s run, closed with no visible fix.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It implements an optimized version of Barki, Guennebaud and Foufou (2015), 'Exact, robust, and efficient regularized Booleans on general 3D meshes'. An AABB tree finds candidate face pairs. Intersections are found symbolically (which triangle features cross) before any exact point is built, intersected faces are re-triangulated with a CGAL constrained Delaunay triangulation, and faces are classified locally and then by propagating tags across connected components, so only one exact point-in-soup test is needed per component. Every stage (pair finding, symbolic intersection, exact-point evaluation, triangulation, global classification) runs on std::threads that pull work items from a shared atomic index; the README shows 4.6 s sequential vs 1.1 s parallel on the closed case.

**Use it when:**
- You need exact (EPECK) Booleans and CGAL's corefinement is too slow: closed case 27.2 s (CGAL) vs 4.6 s sequential and 1.1 s parallel in the author's run.
- Inputs are open surfaces (terrain, water surface) or non-manifold meshes, where CGAL corefinement, libigl, Manifold and MCUT all FAILED in the README table and kigumi finished in 0.1-2.4 s.
- You want many Boolean results from the same pair: the builder does the expensive mixing once and each operator call only extracts faces.
- Per-face attributes (material IDs, labels) must survive the operation.
- Multi-core desktops or servers: the code scales by thread count (KIGUMI_NUM_THREADS or a Threading_context).

**Skip it when:**
- Closed, manifold meshes where approximate results are acceptable: Manifold was faster (1.3 s sequential, 0.2 s parallel vs 4.6 s and 1.1 s) in the same table.
- Inputs with degenerate faces or self-intersections: the README says the result is undefined and may crash or produce broken meshes; Corefine throws 'mesh has self-intersections'.
- Proprietary binaries without a CGAL commercial licence: it needs CGAL's 2D Triangulations package (GPL or commercial) as well as the LGPL kernel, so the MIT label does not make the whole stack permissive.
- Projects that cannot take C++20 plus Boost, CGAL and fast_float as dependencies.
- You need a mature, widely deployed engine: 54 stars, version 0.1.0 in vcpkg.json, one maintainer; issue #33 reports a wrong union fixed by nudging the meshes, and issue #28 reports a 273 s run with no visible resolution.

**Integration:** header-only · CGAL (2D and 3D Linear Geometry Kernel, 2D Triangulations), Boost (container, container_hash, endian, iterator, range, unordered), fast_float; the repo pins all of them through a vcpkg submodule · C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20, designated initializers); CMake 3.18+; build docs exist for Windows, macOS (Xcode 16 plus Homebrew LLVM) and Ubuntu · any platform CGAL and Boost support; documented builds for Windows, macOS and Ubuntu

**Vs siblings:** Pick kigumi over Manifold, MeshLib or trueform when you need exact results or have open or non-manifold inputs. Manifold is several times faster on closed manifold meshes but approximate and fails on the other cases. Hob3l is narrower: it targets OpenSCAD CSG export.

**Gotchas:**
- Corefine.h prints progress lines ('Finding face pairs...', 'Triangulating...') to std::cout unconditionally, so a library user gets stdout noise.
- Open meshes must be clipped by a common convex region; otherwise you get the FIRST/SECOND_MESH_PARTIALLY_INTERSECTS warning and results can be wrong (see issue #33). Check builder.warnings().
- Inconsistently oriented inputs make the builder throw std::runtime_error, and faces with more than three vertices are read as triangle fans.
- The README table predates the 2026-07-20 Autorefinement change, and it gives no mesh sizes or CGAL version; the input meshes are generated by tools/gen_bench_meshes.sh.

**Status:** Maintained by one author (MIT, 54 stars, last commit 2026-08-31, Autorefinement added 2026-07-20). It is copyable, but any shipped binary carries CGAL's GPL obligations unless CGAL is licensed commercially.

[repo](https://github.com/unageek/kigumi) · [benchmark](https://github.com/unageek/kigumi)

##### pgl (Pangolin plane geometry library)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only, exact 2D geometry library (MIT) that beats CGAL on segment intersection, arrangements and unions, loses on Delaunay.

**Beats:** CGAL 6.1.2 (Delaunay_triangulation_2, convex_hull_2, Kd_tree, AABB_tree, Arrangement_2, General_polygon_set_2, minkowski_sum_2; EPECK and EPICK kernels) — doc/cgal.md times 18 2D problems on identical integer inputs (random data plus the Salzburg polygon database, about 32 sizes), pgl ERational vs CGAL 6.1.2 EPECK and pgl int vs EPICK, built with g++ 16.2.1 -std=c++23 -O2 -DNDEBUG on an AMD Ryzen 9 9900X and an Intel Xeon w5-3433, one run each, ratios averaged over the two machines. Medians range from CGAL 2.6x faster (Delaunay) to pgl about 4.4x faster (union of many triangles, 0.23x) with ERational, and from CGAL 1.8x faster to pgl about 4.8x faster (count in Triangle, 0.21x) with int.

**Known shortcoming:** Tuned against its own benchmark, and some rows favour pgl by construction; CGAL wins Delaunay, Minkowski and integer kNN.

**Known shortcoming:** Floating-point coordinates are untested ('at your own risk' per docs); some integer constructions truncate (smallestEnclosingDisk needs even coordinates).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Predicates on integer coordinates run in plain integer arithmetic with width promotion (int32 to int64, int64 to __int128, int128 to its own BigInt), so no filter or lazy-exact layer is needed on integer input; lines through integer points stay integral because they are stored as two points. Its own Rational<T> defers gcd reduction, and its BigInt stays inline below 2^127; types.md measures Rational<BigInt> at about 38 ns per segment-crossing test vs 1,062 ns for GMP mpq and 1,804 ns for boost::rational<cpp_int>. For arbitrary-precision types the orientation/incircle predicates first try a floating-point evaluation with an error bound. Algorithms are chosen adaptively, e.g. findIntersections prices a bounding-box scan against a Bentley-Ottmann sweep from a sample and switches once the scan exceeds the sweep's cost.

**Use it when:**
- 2D problems on integer-coordinate input (GIS rasters, lattice/polyomino work, competitive-programming-style geometry) where you want exact answers without paying for CGAL's EPECK lazy-exact machinery
- Segment intersection, arrangement point location, unions of many triangles/polygons and range counting in a Rectangle, the rows where doc/cgal.md shows pgl at 0.2x-0.7x of CGAL's time
- Projects that cannot take CGAL's GPL/LGPL licence or its Boost/GMP/MPFR dependencies: pgl is MIT, header-only and dependency-free on GCC/Clang
- Teaching, prototyping and research code where a readable predicate API (polygon.contains(segment)) matters more than CGAL's breadth; built-in Canvas exports SVG/PDF/Ipe for figures
- Exact Voronoi/power diagrams of order k or farthest-point diagrams, visibility graphs and Minkowski erosion, which CGAL does not offer directly

**Skip it when:**
- Delaunay triangulation throughput: CGAL is 2.6x faster (ERational vs EPECK) and 1.7x faster (int vs EPICK); also slower for Minkowski sum (1.7x), convex hull with ERational (1.8x) and, with int, kd-tree build and nearest-neighbour queries (1.7-1.8x)
- Anything beyond the plane: no 3D, curved geometry, alpha shapes, straight skeletons/offsets, snap rounding, polygon repair, mesh processing or file formats (WKT, DXF, OFF, STL)
- Floating-point input: types.md says double coordinates are accepted 'at your own risk' and robustness to rounding is untested; use int or rationals
- Production code that needs a long track record: v1.0.0 was tagged 2026-09-20, the repo has 6 stars and 0 forks, and its own README rates maturity 'Very low'
- Huge or adversarial integer coordinates without checking types.md's overflow table: plain int32 predicates are exact only up to about 1.5e9 with promotion (23,170 without), and Rational<int64_t> can overflow on long construction chains

**Integration:** header-only · none on GCC/Clang; on MSVC the Boost.Multiprecision headers (no native __int128). Bundled doctest, PDFGen and plf_nanotimer are for tests, PDF export and benchmarks only. · C++20 (C++23 and C++26 also work); CI runs GCC 13, Clang 18 and MSVC · any platform with a C++20 compiler; 128-bit integers native on GCC/Clang, emulated via Boost on MSVC

**Vs siblings:** Pick pgl over detria or Delaunay32 when you need a whole exact 2D toolkit (sweeps, arrangements, booleans, visibility) rather than only a fast triangulator, since those siblings beat CGAL-class triangulation and pgl does not; pick it over GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or nanoflann only when queries are arbitrary shapes (triangles, polygons) on integer data rather than point kNN.

**Gotchas:**
- Constructions from integral shapes return ERational (Rational<BigInt>) by default, which types.md puts at about 8x the cost of int; pick a smaller result type explicitly when bounds allow
- Some integer-typed constructions truncate: smallestEnclosingDisk divides by two, so integral coordinates should be even, and requesting an integral ResultNumber from Arrangement::halfplaneIntersection can truncate split coordinates
- ShapeTree::insert does no rebalancing, so repeated inserts can drive height to Theta(n) until rebuild(); Triangulation point-location indices are not updated after modification
- The benchmark page says pgl is tuned against this very benchmark and some rows (count in Triangle) race a CGAL query the benchmark authors wrote themselves; Range_tree_2 is deliberately not run

**Status:** Very actively developed (916 commits, last commit 2026-10-01, v1.0.0 tagged 2026-09-20, no issues filed) by one academic author with a student contributor and AI-assisted code; MIT-licensed and header-only, so easy to vendor, but young and unproven outside its own benchmarks.

[repo](https://github.com/gfonsecabr/pgl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/gfonsecabr/pgl/blob/main/doc/cgal.md#speed)

##### TG (tidwall geometry library)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Single-file C11 planar geometry library whose indexed point-in-polygon and intersects tests beat GEOS PreparedGeometry by about 1.1-2.7x.

**Beats:** GEOS (PreparedGeometry and plain geometry) — The author's tests/bench.c (GEOS_BENCH=1) times 10K random points within each polygon's MBR plus 10%, best of 10 runs, on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X with gcc 11.4.0 -O3 against GEOS 3.12.0 built from source. On Brazil (39,914 points), TG YStripes reaches 15.17M ops/s and Natural 10.14M against GEOS prepared at 7.89M and unprepared at 29.7K; on Texas, YStripes reaches 22.45M against 9.87M. Across all 13 PIP polygons Natural is 1.08-2.5x and YStripes 1.35-2.7x GEOS prepared (derived from page data), with identical hit counts. The GEOS loop calls the generic GEOSPreparedIntersects_r on prebuilt point geometries, while TG calls its point-specialised tg_poly_intersects_point, so part of the gap is per-call overhead rather than the index.

**Known shortcoming:** Open correctness issues #29 (covers on multi-component input) and #30 (multilinestring mod-2 boundary rule); #20 and #24 fixed only Sep 2026; #26 wasm32 struct-layout bug closed 2026-09-24.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark asymmetry: the GEOS loop calls generic GEOSPreparedIntersects_r on prebuilt points while TG calls point-specific tg_poly_intersects_point, so part of the gap is call overhead; planar only, no robust predicates.

**How:** Point-in-polygon is ray casting, accelerated by two segment indexes built at ring construction. Natural indexing is a flat, multi-level R-tree-like array of branch MBRs whose leaf level is the ring's own segment array in its original order (default spread 16), so the index adds about 7% memory and builds in one pass; by default its rectangles are 32-bit floats rounded outward. YStripes splits the y-range into hash-bucket-like stripes (count from a Polsby-Popper compactness score times segment count, minimum 32), each listing the segments it crosses, which gives O(1) lookup of the segments a horizontal ray can hit. Multi-geometries get a Hilbert-curve-ordered index over their members, clones are O(1) via atomic reference counting, and min/max use single minsd/maxsd instructions on x86-64 to avoid branches.

**Use it when:**
- Geofencing or stream filtering: many points tested against a fixed set of large polygons (10^3-10^5 vertices), where TG Natural gave 10-22M ops/s on one core for the real-world state and country outlines in the author's runs
- Polygons that are created or reloaded often: Natural index builds in tens of microseconds (Brazil, 39,914 points: 53 us vs 2,060 us for a GEOS prepared geometry) and uses about 4.5x less memory
- Peak point-in-polygon throughput on a long-lived polygon: index it with TG_YSTRIPES (about 1.5-2.7x GEOS prepared on the larger shapes) and keep Natural for other predicates
- Fast WKB/GeoJSON/WKT ingestion in C or C++ (Brazil WKB read 28,320 vs GEOS 3,150 ops/s in the same run)
- Embedding a small, dependency-free geometry core in C/C++ services or WebAssembly builds

**Skip it when:**
- You need overlay (union/intersection/difference), buffering, simplification, convex hull, Voronoi, DE-9IM relate matrices or validity repair: TG does not implement them; use GEOS
- Geographic (lon/lat on the sphere) semantics: TG is planar Cartesian only, so polygons crossing the antimeridian or spanning large areas need your own handling
- Edge-case OGC semantics on collections and multilinestrings: as of 2026-10-01, issues #29 (covers over multiple components) and #30 (mod-2 boundary rule) are open, and #20 and #24 were only fixed in September 2026
- Input that may be invalid: rings are defined as closed and non-self-intersecting, but tg.c does not check self-intersection, so bad input gives undefined predicate answers
- Highly irregular random-shaped polygons where you want YStripes: on the Random-100 and Random-1000 tests it was slower than Natural, and it costs about 20x Natural's build time

**Integration:** source-drop · none (tg.c and tg.h; C standard library, stdatomic.h unless TG_NOATOMICS is defined) · C11 compiler; MSVC builds were fixed in September 2026 (issue #15, GCC builtins) · Portable C: x86-64 (inline minsd/maxsd asm under GCC/Clang), aarch64, WebAssembly via Emscripten; big-endian WKB (#18) and ARMv7 alignment (#12) fixed in 2025, wasm32/ILP32 struct-layout bug (#26) closed 2026-09-24

**Vs siblings:** Pick TG when the job is polygon predicates (point-in-polygon, segment/geometry intersects) against a few large polygons. nanoflann, tidwall/rtree.c and GeoToolbox KdBoxTree index many separate points or boxes and pair well with TG as a first-stage filter, while Manifold, MeshLib and trueform are 3D mesh libraries for a different problem.

**Gotchas:**
- tg_geom_contains/within return false for a point on the polygon edge; use tg_geom_covers or tg_geom_intersects when boundary points must count
- Arithmetic is plain double with a precision-loss nudge (nexttoward) inside the collinear and raycast tests, not exact or extended-precision predicates; index rectangles are float32 rounded outward unless you build with TG_IXFLOAT64
- Constructors clone their inputs by reference count: every tg_*_new/parse/clone/copy needs exactly one free. Upcasting tg_line/tg_ring/tg_poly to tg_geom is free, but downcasting is unsafe
- Parsers return an error geometry rather than NULL on bad input; check tg_geom_error() and handle NULL for out-of-memory

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26, about 676 stars, MIT), with a stream of predicate-correctness fixes from an outside contributor in September 2026; the library is one tg.c plus tg.h, so vendoring a current commit is easy.

[repo](https://github.com/tidwall/tg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/HEAD/docs/BENCHMARKS.md)

##### ArborX  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

Kokkos linear BVH for batched kNN/radius search on CPUs and GPUs; single-threaded kNN beats Boost R-tree at 10^7 points.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry.Index R-tree (packing/bulk-load algorithm, Boost 1.67.0) and nanoflann kd-tree (hash 3b2065e) — The ACM TOMS 2020 paper ran single-threaded Google Benchmark medians on one core of an Intel Xeon E5-2695 v4 (2.1 GHz, CADES) for m = n from 10^4 to 10^7 points, comparing ArborX against Boost.Geometry.Index 1.67.0 (packed R-tree) and nanoflann 3b2065e. Its bar charts (relative to nanoflann) show similar construction times and k=10 nearest search about 1.6x (filled) and 2.1x (hollow) faster than Boost at 10^7 points, but slower than nanoflann below 10^6 in the filled case (bars read by eye, derived from page data). The paper states no compiler, flags or Kokkos version. The repo's bvh_driver still has a Boost R-tree backend (linear<16>, bulk-loaded) but no nanoflann backend.

**Known shortcoming:** Modest win: ~1.6-2.1x over Boost only for nearest search at 10^7; Boost builds faster in the hollow case; single thread on Xeon E5-2695 v4 with no compiler/flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins are single-thread kNN at 10^7 only; slower than nanoflann at <=10^6. Nearest traversal uses a fixed 64-entry stack with no bounds check (source reading, no issue filed). aarch64 test failures (#1241).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Construction is a linear BVH: object boxes are reduced to a scene box, centroids are mapped to 64-bit Morton codes (the curve is pluggable), sorted, and the hierarchy plus internal boxes are built in one parallel bottom-up pass using Apetrei's agglomerative variant of Karras's 2012 LBVH (one atomic compare-exchange per internal node). The 2020 paper used plain Karras; the current source uses Apetrei. Spatial queries walk the tree stacklessly through 'ropes' (skip links stored at build time), and nearest queries use a short stack that visits the closer child first (after Patwary et al.) and a k-sized max-heap in a preallocated per-query buffer that shrinks the search radius once k hits are found. Queries are pre-sorted by Morton code so neighbouring threads traverse similar nodes, and spatial results use a count-then-fill two-pass scheme or a one-pass scheme when the caller supplies a per-query buffer size.

**Use it when:**
- Batched neighbour search over 10^6-10^7+ points where all queries are known up front (particle neighbour lists, contact detection, mesh-to-mesh data transfer). In the paper's single-thread runs, kNN (k=10) at 10^7 points was about 1.6x (filled) and 2.1x (hollow) faster than Boost's packed R-tree (bars read by the verifier, derived from page data)
- Codes already on Kokkos (Trilinos, exascale applications) that need one search code path for OpenMP, CUDA, HIP and SYCL. The paper found one V100 beat a full two-socket POWER9 node except on small problems
- Multicore CPU batches: OpenMP strong scaling at n=10^7 (filled case, Table 1) reached 10.5x for construction, 12.2x for spatial search and 12.1x for nearest search on 16 threads
- Search over non-point primitives (boxes, triangles, segments, spheres, tetrahedra, rays) in arbitrary dimension, or distributed-memory search through DistributedTree with MPI

**Skip it when:**
- Small or medium single-threaded problems: in the filled case the paper shows ArborX slower than nanoflann for nearest search from 10^4 to 10^6 points (about 0.58-0.78x of nanoflann). Thread scaling is also poor below roughly 1000 objects per thread, because the Morton sort is the bottleneck (paper section 3.3)
- Data that changes by a few inserts or deletes at a time: there is no incremental update API, so every change means rebuilding the tree
- Projects that cannot take on Kokkos 4.5+, C++20 and CMake 3.22. ArborX is header-only, but Kokkos must be built and configured for your backend
- Construction-dominated workloads on surface-like (hollow) data: Boost's packed R-tree built faster in the paper's hollow case (about 1.02-1.40x of nanoflann vs 0.87-1.12x for ArborX)
- One-off queries from host code in a hot loop: each batched query() call sorts the predicates and launches Kokkos kernels, so the fixed cost per call is high. The PerThread overload helps only inside your own kernel

**Integration:** header-only (CMake INTERFACE target; configuring generates ArborX_Config.hpp and a version header, so install through CMake rather than copying src/) · Kokkos 4.5+ (required). Optional: MPI (DistributedTree), rocThrust (HIP, on by default), oneDPL (SYCL), Trilinos 16+. Tests and benchmarks only: Boost 1.67+ and Google Benchmark 1.5.4+ (auto-fetched) · C++20, CMake 3.22, Kokkos 4.5.00; compiler minimums follow Kokkos, and NVCC must be 11.5+ · any Kokkos backend: Serial, OpenMP, Threads, CUDA, HIP, SYCL. Test failures were reported on aarch64/ppc64le (issue #1196 hang, closed; issue #1241, stack smashing and wrong neighbour lists in v2.0 tests on aarch64)

**Vs siblings:** Pick ArborX over nanoflann or the single-threaded tree siblings (THST, PH-tree, tidwall rtree.c) when you need GPU or multithreaded batched queries, non-point geometry, or kNN at 10^7 scale. nanoflann is lighter (header-only, no Kokkos) and faster single-threaded up to about 10^6 points. Pick Pkd-tree instead when the point set changes through large parallel batch inserts and deletes on a CPU.

**Gotchas:**
- Spatial queries default to two traversals (count, then fill). TraversalPolicy::setBufferSize(n) enables one pass: a positive n falls back to two passes when exceeded, a negative n throws. An oversized estimate costs memory; the paper could not run the one-pass variant above 10^6 points in the hollow case
- Predicates are Morton-sorted before traversal by default. The paper found this hurt serial hollow-case spatial search at 10^7 points; turn it off with TraversalPolicy::setPredicateSorting(false)
- Nearest traversal keeps a fixed 64-entry stack with no bounds check (ArborX_TreeTraversal.hpp). Trees deeper than that, possible in principle with extreme clustering or duplicate Morton codes, are not guarded. This comes from reading the source; I found no issue reporting it
- API churn: v2.0 (2025-04-16) removed the APIv1 index interfaces and moved to C++20 and Kokkos 4.5. Several geometries and helpers (Segment, Ellipsoid, MST, attach_indices, DefaultIndexableGetter) still sit in the Experimental namespace. Within one query, the order of spatial results is unspecified

**Status:** Actively developed by an ORNL-led team (v2.1.0 on 2026-04-28, last commit 2026-09-16, a second TOMS paper for v2.0 in 2025) under BSD-3-Clause; easy to vendor as headers, but practical only if you can adopt Kokkos.

[repo](https://github.com/arborx/ArborX) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dalg24/dalg24.github.io/HEAD/files/2020-paper-toms-arborx.pdf)

##### gDel3D  `C++ (CUDA)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

CUDA GPU+CPU 3D Delaunay triangulator from NUS (I3D 2014), 6-9x faster than single-threaded CGAL 4.2 on scanned models.

**Beats:** CGAL 3D Delaunay triangulation (CGAL 4.2, sequential) — The peer-reviewed I3D 2014 paper (shipped in the repo) times gDel3D on an NVIDIA GTX 580 with an Intel i7-2600K (3.4 GHz, 16 GB) against sequential CGAL 4.2 on the same PC; the only build detail given is 'compiled with optimization enabled'. On uniform, Gaussian, thin-sphere, grid and cospherical sets up to 1.5M points the speedup starts at 4-6x and rises to 8-10x; on seven scanned models (173K-3.6M points) it is 6.1-9.2x, for example 3.61M-point Asian Dragon in 5.4 s. This compares one GPU against one CPU core, with a CGAL release that is now more than ten years old.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper gives no compiler or flags ('compiled with optimization enabled'); GPU vs sequential CPU CGAL 4.2; no commits since 2018.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug (third-party DelaunayBench, omarbesbes/Delaunay via the pyGDel3D binding; same 5-tet cube on upstream issue #14): small inputs silently return an unflipped (non-Delaunay) result at 8-12 points, hang at 32 and abort at 48 and 200; cause is the last-round rule at GpuDelaunay.cu line 834; 505+ points match CGAL.

**Known shortcoming:** Degenerate input: raw 100K photogrammetry clouds give +14,980 / +48,889 flat tets over CGAL and run 5-12x slower than jittered input (derived from page data); build rot (CMake hard-codes sm_30/35, newer Thrust needs an extra include); baseline is single-core CGAL 4.2 vs a GTX 580.

**How:** Phase 1 runs on the GPU and alternates massively parallel point insertion (each tetrahedron inserts the uninserted point nearest its circumcenter) with parallel bilateral 2-3/3-2 flipping, which leaves fewer than 0.05% of facets locally non-Delaunay. Phase 2 repairs those few on the CPU with an adaptive version of Shewchuk's star splaying that rebuilds only the stars of failed vertices. Robustness comes from Shewchuk's adaptive exact orientation/insphere predicates ported to CUDA plus simulation of simplicity; fast and exact checks run in separate kernels with shared-memory compaction so that the rare exact cases do not cause warp divergence. Points are Hilbert-curve sorted for coalesced access, and a flip-history DAG is used to relocate uninserted points after flipping.

**Use it when:**
- One-shot Delaunay tetrahedralization of 10^5 to a few 10^6 points on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU, where the paper reports 6.1-9.2x over sequential CGAL 4.2 on 173K-3.6M point scanned models
- Point sets in general position, or ones you can jitter: on two raw 100K-point photogrammetry clouds a 1e-6 jitter cut gDel3D's A100 time from 0.47 s and 1.08 s to about 0.09 s (5-12x, derived from DelaunayBench page data) and removed all flat tetrahedra
- Research or offline meshing pipelines where you can vendor and patch CUDA code and run the bundled DelaunayChecker on every output
- Python workflows through the third-party pyGDel3D binding (half-potato/pyGDel3D), which DelaunayBench built with CUDA 12.8 on an A100

**Skip it when:**
- Small inputs (up to a few hundred points) on unpatched upstream code: DelaunayBench found that it silently returns the unflipped insertion result (8-12 points), hangs (32 points) or aborts on an assertion (48 and 200 points); counts matched CGAL from 505 points up
- No NVIDIA GPU, or a current GPU without editing the build: CMakeLists.txt hard-codes sm_30/sm_35 and issue #11 reports 'no kernel image is available for execution on the device' on an RTX 2060
- Very large clouds on modest VRAM: the code preallocates arrays for 8.5 tetrahedra per input point, and issue #6 reports an illegal memory access at 10M points on an 8 GB GPU
- Strongly degenerate input (coplanar LiDAR/photogrammetry, grids) where downstream code cannot tolerate zero-volume tetrahedra: DelaunayBench counted 14,980 and 48,889 extra flat tetrahedra over CGAL on two raw 100K-point clouds
- Production code that needs maintenance or a multi-core CPU baseline: last commit 2018-03-26, open issues unanswered, and the published speedups are against one CPU core

**Integration:** source-drop · NVIDIA CUDA toolkit with Thrust; Shewchuk's predicates are bundled (CPU/predicates.cpp). CMake 2.8+ (FindCUDA) on Linux or the Visual Studio 2012 project on Windows · CUDA 7.5 (commit 'Compiles with CUDA 7.5 now'), CUDA 9.1 fixed in 2018; newer Thrust needs #include <thrust/device_malloc.h> added (issue #10, user workaround) · NVIDIA GPUs only (README: compute capability 1.1+, best on Fermi or later; tested on GTX 450-580 under Windows and GTX Titan under Linux). Default build targets only sm_30/sm_35, so newer architectures need the gencode lines changed

**Vs siblings:** Use HXT (in Gmsh) when you only have CPUs, need more than a few million points or want maintained code: it is about 3x sequential CGAL on one core and scales across cores (10M points in 4.48 s vs CGAL's 20.15 s on a 64-core Xeon Phi). Pick gDel3D only when an NVIDIA GPU is available, the point set fits in VRAM, the input is reasonably non-degenerate, and you can patch an unmaintained CUDA codebase. The other geometry siblings (TG, nanoflann, rtree.c, mesh-boolean libraries) solve different problems.

**Gotchas:**
- Small-input correctness bug in upstream GpuDelaunay.cu: active sets under 64 tetrahedra are deferred to a 'last round' of flipping that only runs once an insertion round inserts fewer than 10% of the points. DelaunayBench's patch_pygdel3d_final_flip.py runs that round unconditionally, and upstream issue #14 (2023, unanswered) shows the same 5-tetrahedra cube
- The output contains an extra 'kernel' vertex appended at index N (the input size; coordinates in output.ptInfty), and tetVec contains dead slots. Discard tetrahedra that reference it and check the alive flag in tetInfoVec before using the mesh
