- Degenerate input is handled by symbolic perturbation, so coplanar or cospherical points yield valid but zero-volume tetrahedra and much slower runs (the exact-arithmetic and star-splaying share grows; the paper's sphere distribution is dominated by splaying)
- Double precision is the default; defining REAL_TYPE_FP32 switches all coordinates to float

**Status:** Abandoned (6 commits, last 2018-03-26, maintainer silent on issues since 2019) but BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor; expect to patch the CUDA arch flags, a Thrust include and the small-input flipping bug before use on a current toolkit.

[repo](https://github.com/ashwin/gDel3D) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ashwin/gDel3D/blob/master/gdel3d_paper.pdf)

##### GeometryOps.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Pure-Julia 2D/spherical geometry ops; beats GEOS-through-GeoPandas/R on simple point tasks, but trails GEOS called directly.

**Beats:** GEOS (through GeoPandas/Shapely in Python and the 'geos' package in R) — Third-party kadyb/vector-benchmark (Ryzen 9 5900X, Ubuntu 22.04, median of runs; no Julia/R/Python versions) shows GeometryOps ahead of GEOS-through-wrappers on three point tasks: distance on a 5,000 x 5,000 point matrix 0.11 s vs 0.9 s (GeoPandas) and 5.37 s (R geos, row-wise sapply), 500,000 points-in-polygon intersects 0.04 s vs 0.12 s / 0.08 s, and sampling 0.04 s vs 0.9 s. The project's own direct comparison against LibGEOS (GEOS 3.14.1, Apple M4 Pro) shows it slower than GEOS on predicates and overlays except points x area unions.

**Known shortcoming:** Julia, not callable from C++. In kadyb/vector-benchmark, buffer uses GEOS via LibGEOS inside GeometryOps, transform uses PROJ on both sides and load/write uses GDAL, so real GEOS-vs-native comparisons are only distance, intersects and sample. Distance uses 5,000 points, not 500k. Julia is timed warm (Chairmarks) while R/Python are timed cold.

**Known shortcoming:** The win holds only against GEOS called through Python/R wrappers. Its own benchmarks (overlayng_realdata.jl, relateng_realdata.jl; M4 Pro, Julia 1.12.6, GEOS 3.14.1) show it slower than LibGEOS called directly: overlay 2-4x slower, river x country intersection 30x, pairwise intersects 14x, prepared point-in-polygon ~2x; the only win is points x area union (8.6x). The default Foster-Hormann union/difference on MultiPolygons raises MethodError.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Julia compiles each call specialised to the concrete geometry and coordinate types (plain tuples after GO.tuples), so tight loops such as point-to-point distance or point-in-polygon have no per-row interpreter or wrapper marshalling cost. Clipping uses Foster-Hormann with selectable edge-intersection accelerators (NestedLoop, single/dual STRtree, natural-index trees, AutoAccelerator), and the newer OverlayNG/RelateNG ports of the JTS algorithms use exact adaptive predicates plus a prepared, indexed point-in-area locator (GO.prepare). There is no GEOS-beating kernel algorithm: the third-party wins come from avoiding Python/R per-row overhead on simple point tasks.

**Use it when:**
- You already work in Julia and want generic geometry operations over GeoInterface types (GeoDataFrames, Shapefile, GeoJSON, ArchGDAL objects) without converting to GEOS.
- Bulk simple point workloads (pairwise point distances, many points against one polygon, rejection sampling inside a polygon) where kadyb/vector-benchmark measured 0.11 s vs 0.9 s (GeoPandas) and 0.04 s vs 0.12 s / 0.08 s (GeoPandas / R geos).
- Many repeated point-in-polygon queries against one large polygon, using GO.prepare (1.2 us per query on Canada vs 62.6 us unprepared in its own benchmark).
- Spherical-manifold predicates and overlays (great-circle edges) that GEOS does not offer, accepting about 5-11x the planar cost.
- Points x area overlays (union/symdifference of a MultiPoint with a polygon), the one case its own benchmark shows ahead of LibGEOS (2.4 ms vs 20.6 ms).

**Skip it when:**
- From C++: it is Julia-only and needs an embedded Julia runtime, so for a C++ project call GEOS, TG or Boost.Geometry directly.
- Polygon overlay throughput: its own benchmark (Apple M4 Pro, Julia 1.12.6, GEOS 3.14.1) has OverlayNG 2-4x slower than LibGEOS on country pairs and about 30x slower on river x country intersection; issue #129 reports Foster-Hormann clipping more than 10x slower than LibGEOS above about 100 vertices.
- Pairwise predicate filtering of mostly disjoint polygons: RelateNG takes 1.6 us per pair vs 115.7 ns for LibGEOS (about 14x behind).
- Union/difference on MultiPolygon inputs with the default Foster-Hormann engine, which raises MethodError per the project's benchmark notes; the OverlayNG alternative is marked experimental and has a known ring-assembly defect cluster.
- Production code that needs a stable API: the README warns it is 'still under heavy development', the version is 0.1.x, and open bug issues cover clipping on barely touching or coverage-like polygons (#281, #337), difference (#335) and touches (#155).

**Integration:** module (Julia package, registered as GeometryOps; core types in the GeometryOpsCore subpackage) · GeoInterface, GeometryOpsCore, ExactPredicates, AdaptivePredicates, DelaunayTriangulation, SortTileRecursiveTree, StaticArrays, Tables, DataAPI, Extents, GeoFormatTypes, CoordinateTransformations, AbstractTrees, PrecompileTools; optional extensions for LibGEOS (buffer and GEOS backend), Proj (reprojection), TGGeometry (libtg predicates), DataFrames, DimensionalData, FlexiJoins, Makie · Julia 1.10 (Project.toml compat) · any platform Julia supports (pure Julia); buffer needs LibGEOS.jl and reprojection needs Proj.jl, both binary artifacts

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over TG or qdgeo only when you are in Julia and want GeoInterface-generic, planar plus spherical operations in one package; for raw predicate speed TG is faster than GEOS prepared, and GeometryOps can even call it through GO.TG(). Arctern and qdgeo target the same GeoPandas/Shapely baseline from C++/GPU or Rust/WASM and are the better fit outside Julia.

**Gotchas:**
- GO.buffer always delegates to GEOS (LibGEOS must be loaded), so its vector-benchmark buffer time (5.75 s vs 4.07 s GeoPandas) is GEOS against GEOS.
- The third-party wins compare different strategies: GeoPandas distance runs a Python-level apply loop over 5,000 rows and GeoPandas intersects uses a cached STRtree sindex query, while GeometryOps brute-forces a Julia comprehension/broadcast after JIT warm-up.
- Unprepared predicates recompute extents on every call; GO.tuples(x; calc_extent = true) or GO.prepare change point-in-area cost from 62.6 us to 21.9 us or 1.2 us per query.
- Foster-Hormann returns a list of geometries, while OverlayNG returns a single most-specific geometry (possibly mixed-dimension), so switching engines changes result shapes.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-20, 488 commits, about 135 open issues and 44 open PRs) and MIT-licensed, but explicitly in-development 0.1.x software usable only from Julia.

[repo](https://github.com/JuliaGeo/GeometryOps.jl) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kadyb/vector-benchmark/HEAD/timings.csv)

##### Manifold  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Apache-2.0 C++ mesh-boolean kernel with guaranteed manifold output; 2.5-6.9x faster than CGAL corefinement on 1.3M-triangle spheres.

**Beats:** CGAL Nef/PMP mesh booleans (and OpenSCAD's CGAL backend) — The third-party axiolid/benchmarks harness (a Rust driver over a C++ shim) times Manifold v3.5.1 against CGAL Polygon_mesh_processing corefine_and_compute_* with the Exact_predicates_exact_constructions_kernel on two overlapping icospheres. At 1,310,720 triangles per operand: union 3,462.5 vs 23,922.9 ms, intersection 2,248.7 vs 5,602.2 ms, A-B 2,816.2 vs 13,368.2 ms (2.5-6.9x, derived from page data); results are checked by the volume identity |A u B| + |A n B| = |A| + |B|. The timed call includes building each library's mesh and computing the volume, on a '20-core host' with the compiler unstated and best of 1 rep. Manifold was built with default CMake flags, which leave MANIFOLD_PAR off, so it most likely ran single-threaded.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence from a competitor's 0-star unlicensed repo (axiolid); CPU and compiler not stated; single run; parallel Manifold vs serial CGAL.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark setup: MANIFOLD_PAR defaults OFF and the axiolid comparison was built with default flags, so Manifold most likely ran serial (the 'TBB-parallel vs serial CGAL' caveat looks wrong); CGAL side used EPECK and the timed call includes mesh build + Volume. CUDA backend removed, TBB only.

**Known shortcoming:** Open bugs: #1870 intermittent access violation 0xC0000005 constructing from a small non-manifold MeshGL64 (3.5.4, Windows; possible out-of-bounds/uninitialized read, memory safety); #1857 boolean regression on master since PR #1790 (584-triangle union 0.01 s to 17 s); #1706 sliver triangles.

**How:** It follows Julian Smith's dissertation: double-precision geometry with symbolic perturbation (the 'shadow' tests in boolean3.cpp) breaks exact ties, so each topological question is answered once and reused. The output is manifold by construction without the exact-constructions arithmetic that CGAL's robust path pays for. A BVH broad phase (a collider over Morton-sorted face boxes) cuts Smith's O(n^2) triangle-pair test to O(n log n). Boolean operators build a lazy CSG tree that is flattened into batched booleans when the result is requested. With MANIFOLD_PAR=ON the kernels run on TBB parallel for/scan/merge-sort above a 10^4-element threshold and fall back to serial code below it.

**Use it when:**
- Booleans on closed triangle meshes of 10^3 to a few 10^6 triangles where exact-kernel CGAL corefinement takes seconds: a 1.31M-triangle sphere pair union took 3.46 s vs 23.9 s for CGAL in the axiolid harness
- Many chained or many-cutter booleans (Menger sponges, walls with thousands of openings): in axiolid's Menger test CGAL corefinement failed past depth 1, while Manifold finished depth 4 (58,947 cutters) in 25.8 s
- Code-CAD, 3D-printing, game-engine or web tools that need watertight output, a permissive Apache-2.0 licence and Python/JS/WASM bindings
- Pipelines that must carry UVs, normals, colours or material IDs through booleans

**Skip it when:**
- Results that need exact rational coordinates or proven geometric validity: only manifold topology is guaranteed, and the wiki calls geometric validity a goal without a formal proof. CGAL with an exact kernel stays the reference.
- Non-manifold, open or self-overlapping input such as raw scans or STL soups: construction returns NotManifold, and the wiki says self-overlaps within one mesh cannot be removed yet. Repair the input first, or use MeshLib's voxel mode.
- Current master on coincident surfaces with different triangulations: open issue #1857 reports a 584-triangle union going from 0.01 s to 17 s after PR #1790 (RecursiveEdgeSwap churn in RemoveDegenerates). Pin a release and benchmark your own models.
- Maximum boolean speed on large scans when the licence allows it: in MeshLib's own benchmark Manifold was about 3x slower than MeshLib on a 2M-triangle union
- Curved B-rep/NURBS CAD: the boolean works only on flat triangles, so OpenCascade remains the tool for B-rep

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib · none required; optional oneTBB (MANIFOLD_PAR=ON) for parallelism, nanobind (Python), Emscripten (WASM), GTest, Assimp, Tracy. Also packaged via vcpkg, PyPI manifold3d and npm manifold-3d. · C++17, CMake 3.18+; tested with GCC, LLVM/Clang and MSVC · Linux, macOS, Windows (static build recommended; issue #1859 says the Windows ARM64 package is missing in 3.5.4), WebAssembly (serial only; MANIFOLD_PAR under Emscripten is not recommended because of possible memory corruption)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Manifold over MeshLib (faster in its vendor's benchmark, but under a non-commercial licence) when you need a permissive, embeddable boolean kernel with guaranteed manifold output and broad language bindings. Pick MeshLib for messy scans if its licence fits, and look at trueform for its wider CGAL-beating mesh ops. HXT, gDel3D and the spatial indexes (nanoflann, rtree.c, KdBoxTree, THST, TG) solve different problems.

**Gotchas:**
- MANIFOLD_PAR defaults to OFF, so a plain CMake build is single-threaded; turn on TBB yourself, and avoid MANIFOLD_USE_BUILTIN_TBB next to another TBB copy (the README warns it 'may cause performance issues or crash')
- Booleans are lazy and report errors through Status() (NotManifold, NonFiniteVertex, ResultTooLarge, Cancelled and others), not through exceptions unless MANIFOLD_DEBUG is set, so the cost and any failure surface at GetMeshGL()/Volume()/Status()
- Open issue #1870 (3.5.4, Windows): constructing from small non-manifold MeshGL64 input crashes intermittently with an access violation (0xC0000005), suspected to be an uninitialised or out-of-bounds read during validation. Treat untrusted meshes with care.
- Exporting to STL loses manifoldness on re-import; the README recommends 3MF or glTF with EXT_mesh_manifold. Issue #1706 also reports sliver triangles from booleans on near-coincident inputs.

**Status:** Very active (about 2.3k stars, 3.5.x releases, used by OpenSCAD and Blender) and copyable under Apache-2.0. The CUDA/GPU backend cited in older material is gone; TBB is now the only parallel backend.

[repo](https://github.com/elalish/manifold) · [benchmark](https://github.com/axiolid/benchmarks)

##### Pkd-tree (parallel kd-tree with batch updates)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Parallel ParlayLib kd-tree with batch insert/delete; builds 80-277x faster than CGAL's kd-tree on 10^9 points.

**Beats:** CGAL kd-tree (Spatial_searching) and Boost.Geometry R-tree (also BHL-tree and Log-tree) — First-party raw CSVs in script/data compare parallel Pkd-tree with CGAL's kd-tree, which was built with Parallel_tag and queried inside tbb::parallel_for. The CSVs give no units, hardware or date; times are presumably seconds. On 10^9 3-D points, build took 3.91 vs 1082.4 (uniform) and 4.77 vs 381.3 (Varden), and kNN (k=10) was only 1.4-1.8x faster. The batch insert and delete ratios are huge mainly because CGAL rebuilds after inserts and removes points one at a time. The SIGMOD 2025 paper was not opened; search snippets put its runs on a 96-core four-way Xeon Gold 6252 with 1.5 TB RAM. The code is built with -O3 -mcx16 -march=native, and the repo's Boost baseline is a sequentially built 2-D bgi::rtree<quadratic<2>>, a very small node capacity, so the Boost ratios flatter Pkd-tree.

**Known shortcoming:** Boost baseline is a 2-D bgi::rtree quadratic<2> run sequentially vs 96 cores; CGAL update wins come from CGAL's missing batch insert; repo no longer updated (successor ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib).

**Known shortcoming:** Claim inflation: the Boost baseline is a sequential 2-D bgi::rtree<quadratic<2>>; the repo kNN harness queries the tree's own points in tree order; kNN is only 1.4-1.8x over CGAL (paper snippet says kNN similar). Repo frozen; successor is PSI-Lib (ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib). CMake needs CGAL+Boost by default although the README says CGAL is off.

**Known shortcoming:** Per notes in Kiddo's benches/profile_cpp_competitors.rs, Pkd-tree's f32 build aborts on a box-containment assertion from 2^22 points up.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**Independent measurement:** enrichment (third-party bench notes)

**How:** Instead of one median split per level, the build samples about 32x64 points (hash-indexed) to choose splitters for 6 levels at once (63 pivots, 64 buckets). It then distributes the points into the buckets with a blocked, cache-friendly parallel 'sieve' (per-block counts plus prefix sums), and recurses in parallel with ParlayLib fork-join; the split axis is the dimension with the widest extent. Leaves hold up to 32 points, and subtrees below 1024 points are built serially. Batch updates sieve the whole batch down the same multi-level skeleton and rebuild only subtrees whose children leave weight balance (imbalance ratio 30%, alpha 0.3). An update therefore costs about the size of the batch, not a full rebuild (CGAL rebuilds on insert). Queries are classic kd-tree searches with bounding-box pruning and a bounded priority queue for kNN.

**Use it when:**
- Building kd-trees over 10^8-10^9 low-dimensional points on a many-core server: build.csv for 10^9 3-D points shows 3.91 vs CGAL 1082.4 (uniform, about 277x) and 4.77 vs 381.3 (Varden, about 80x), derived from page data
- Point sets that change through large batches (sliding windows, simulation steps, streaming scans): 10% batch insert into 10^8 12-D points took 0.115 vs CGAL's 171.2 (CGAL inserts and rebuilds), and deleting 0.1M points took 0.0054 vs 0.347 (uniform)
- Range report and range count on large static sets: the 12-D uniform range query took 17.4 vs 109.1 for CGAL (about 6.3x, derived from page data)
- Heavily skewed inputs (the Varden distribution), where the sampled multi-level build still stays balanced

**Skip it when:**
- kNN-dominated workloads: kNN was only 1.4-1.8x faster than parallel CGAL on 10^9 3-D points, and CGAL was slightly faster on one 12-D Varden row. Search snippets of the paper (not opened) say Pkd-tree, BHL-tree and CGAL have similar kNN performance
- Few cores or single-threaded use: every win comes from parallel build and update; a SERIAL build mode exists, but no single-thread comparison was found
- Production code that needs a maintained dependency: the README says 'This repository will no longer be updated'. The successor, PSI-Lib, notes it was later refactored with AI assistance and that some indexes' performance is 'slightly affected'
- Boxes, polygons, segments, non-Euclidean metrics or approximate NN: points only
- Windows, MSVC or non-x86 targets: only Linux with clang 17 and g++ 13 is documented, and the Release flags include the x86-only -mcx16 -march=native

**Integration:** header-only (include/cpdd) plus ParlayLib as a git submodule · ParlayLib (submodule). Optional: jemalloc, numactl. CGAL with TBB, Boost and ParGeo/Zdtree are only for the benchmark harnesses · C++20; CMake 3.15+; tested with clang 17 (recommended for speed), compiles with g++ 13 · Linux x86-64 documented (Release build uses -O3 -mcx16 -march=native); other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick Pkd-tree over nanoflann when you have many cores and need parallel build or large batch updates at 10^8-10^9 scale. nanoflann is single-threaded by default, but it is header-only with no ParlayLib dependency, maintained and widely packaged. Pick ArborX instead for GPU or Kokkos batched queries over arbitrary geometry with rebuild-only updates. For new projects, consider the successor PSI-Lib, which adds orth-trees and space-filling-curve trees.

**Gotchas:**
- The default batchDelete overload assumes every point to delete is in the tree (FullCoveredTag, per the header comment). Use the PartialCoverTag overload when some points may be absent
- The build files disagree with the README: the README lists the CGAL option as default OFF, but CMakeLists.txt sets option(CGAL ON) and calls find_package(Boost REQUIRED) unconditionally. A plain 'cmake ..' therefore fails without CGAL and Boost; pass -DCGAL=OFF or just include the headers
- Tuning knobs (BUILD_DEPTH_ONCE=6, LEAVE_WRAP=32, INBALANCE_RATIO=30) are static constexpr members. The README warns that different values 'on different machine may influence the performance dramatically'
- Benchmark reading: by default the repo's kNN harness (queryKNN in tests/testFramework.h) flattens the tree's own points into the query array inside the timed loop. Queries are therefore the indexed points in tree order, a locality-friendly workload

**Status:** Frozen research artifact (the README says it will no longer be updated; last commit 2026-08-20) under MIT; the maintained code is PSI-Lib (ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib, MIT, PPoPP 2026).

[repo](https://github.com/ucrparlay/Pkd-tree) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ucrparlay/Pkd-tree/tree/main/script/data)

##### PSI-Lib / SpaceTreeLib (P-Orth tree, SPaC-tree; also contains the Pkd-tree)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only parallel kd-, orth- and space-filling-curve trees with batch updates; 2-3x faster batch updates than a Zd-tree.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry bgi::rtree (quadratic, sequential); the repo also benchmarks CPAM and Zd-tree, and has a CGAL kd-tree harness (tests/cgal.cpp) — The repo's PPoPP '26 real_world.csv (times presumably seconds; CPU model and compiler not stated, -march=native -mcx16, many-core machine) compares parallel PSI trees with a Zd-tree implementation, pristine CPAM and a quadratic<32> bgi::rtree. The fairest comparisons are the Zd-tree and CPAM rows, with two limits: the Zd-tree is the authors' own in-repo implementation built on PSI's base_tree (THIRD_PARTY.md), not the original ParGeo code, and the pristine CPAM copy differs from PSI's fork on the k-NN path. SPaC-Z batch updates at 0.01% are about 2-3x faster than that Zd-tree and about 2-3.4x faster than pristine CPAM-Z (derived from page data), and P-Orth matches the Zd-tree on updates while winning k-NN and large range reports. The 134-495x 'build' ratios over Boost compare a parallel build with n single-threaded single-point inserts (Boost's packing bulk-load was timed but dropped from the CSV), the Boost '0.0001' rows do half the work of PSI's, and the Boost k-NN columns use the wrong query points, so only the Boost range-query columns are like-for-like (both parallel; PSI 7-18x faster on large ranges, slower on small).

**Known shortcoming:** Boost harness bugs: kNN queries the wrong points (ignores the query set; 3-D uses only x,y); the merge script mislabels Boost's n/2 single-point inserts/deletes as 0.01% batches; the 218-495x 'build' figures compare against one-at-a-time inserts (the Boost bulk loader is timed but dropped). Boost queries run in parallel and win small ranges. Against the fair rival Zd-tree, SPaC-Z is 2.1-3.2x faster on batch updates. Contains the archived Pkd-tree (catalogued separately).

**Known shortcoming:** The Zd-tree it is compared against is the authors' own in-repo rewrite on PSI's base_tree (THIRD_PARTY.md), not ParGeo's code, so the 2-3x over Zd-tree is weaker than a third-party comparison. Boost also wins small range queries.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Build and batch updates are fork-join parallel on ParlayLib. kd_tree and orth_tree build a multi-level skeleton at once (default skeleton height 6, so 64 buckets per round), sieve points into the buckets in parallel blocks, recurse in parallel (serial below 1024 points, 32-point leaves) and rebuild only subtrees whose weight balance passes an imbalance ratio of 30%. The orth tree splits at spatial midpoints in every dimension per level (2^d children), so a batch update never has to re-pick splitters. p_tree sorts points by Morton (libmorton) or Hilbert code with a sample sort and stores them in a heavily modified fork of CPAM (a parallel augmented, blocked balanced tree with bounding-box augmentation), so batch insert and delete are CPAM multi_insert/multi_delete on a 1-D key.

**Use it when:**
- Update-heavy 2-D or 3-D point sets on a many-core server where whole batches arrive at once: in the repo's real-world CSV, SPaC-Z inserts all of Cosmo50 in 10^4 batches in 5.6 s vs 13.8 s for the Zd-tree implementation and 19.0 s for pristine CPAM-Z (derived from page data)
- Mixed workloads that need both batch updates and fast k-NN: P-Orth k=10 uniform k-NN on Cosmo50 is 0.244 vs Zd-tree 0.301, while its 0.01% batch deletes total 17.9 s vs 800 s for the Pkd-tree in the same CSV
- Query-heavy or higher-dimensional data (the generator covers 2-16 D): use kd_tree, which the library's own guide recommends for queries and higher dimensions
- Replacing a bgi::rtree that is fed one point at a time from a single thread: the repo's Boost harness shows 134-495x faster whole-set loads, though against Boost's slowest construction path (see verified_claims_summary)
- Research or benchmarking of parallel spatial indexes: it ships baselines (pristine CPAM, a Zd-tree implementation, Boost R-tree and CGAL drivers), a data generator and the PPoPP '26 and SIGMOD '25 scripts

**Skip it when:**
- Small queries or few cores: Boost's R-tree wins small range reports on all three real-world sets (Cosmo50 0.00044 vs P-Orth 0.00082), and single queries are sequential by design; every win comes from parallel batches
- k-NN-heavy work on SPaC trees: SPaC-Z k=10 k-NN on Cosmo50 takes 11.5 vs 0.24 for P-Orth (about 47x slower), so pick the tree type per workload
- Point-at-a-time updates: the manual calls a loop over insert/erase 'the wrong shape'; orth_tree also does not grow its bounding box, so inserting outside bounds() is an error
- Boxes, polygons, segments, non-Euclidean metrics or approximate search: points only, Euclidean k-NN and axis-aligned box queries
- Old toolchains, MSVC or a need for stable releases: CMake rejects g++ below 14 and clang below 19, only Linux/x86-64 builds are documented, and issue #1 asked for versioned releases; pin a commit

**Integration:** header-only (include/psi) with ParlayLib and libmorton as git submodules; CMake target PSI::PSI or find_package(PSI) · ParlayLib and libmorton (submodules, MIT); vendored CPAM fork (MIT) and a Rice University Hilbert-curve file that requires an attribution notice. Boost (bgi R-tree driver), CGAL+TBB (correctness oracles, CGAL=OFF by default) and jemalloc are only for benchmarks · C++20; CMake 3.15+; g++ 14+ or clang 19+ (enforced by CMakeLists.txt) · Linux x86-64 documented; PSI_NATIVE_ARCH=ON by default adds -march=native and -mcx16 (x86 only, and the binary will not run on other CPUs; turn it off for portable builds). Other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick PSI over its predecessor Pkd-tree (ucrparlay/Pkd-tree, frozen) for new work: it contains the same kd-tree plus orth and SPaC trees, which handle small-batch updates far better. Pick nanoflann or PicoTree for single-threaded, static k-NN with no ParlayLib or C++20 requirement, and ArborX for GPU or Kokkos batched queries over boxes and other geometry.

**Gotchas:**
- batch_delete requires every point to be present; use batch_diff when some may be absent. In p_tree, points are identified by their id field, so every point needs a distinct id
- Results from knn(point, queue) are references into tree-owned storage and dangle after any update; knn(point, k) returns copies. range_query into a too-small buffer silently truncates and returns the written count
- PSI's -O3 and -march=native apply only to PSI's own targets: the manual warns that an unoptimised consumer build makes the index 'look broken rather than slow'. The orth tree's skeleton height must be a multiple of the dimension (static_assert)
- The README says the code was refactored with AI help after the papers and some indexes are 'slightly affected'; commit af67b82 is the original design. bounds() is a loose bound after batch deletes (except in p_tree)

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-09; 734 commits, 10 stars) MIT research library with CI, docs and a Docker artifact, but no documented release versioning; ship the THIRD_PARTY.md Rice University Hilbert-curve notice with any product.

[repo](https://github.com/ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib/HEAD/script/data/real_world/real_world.csv)

##### SPRK-tree (Sorted Projection Radius KD-tree)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Rust SIMD kd-tree for fixed-radius queries with sorted LUT leaves; ESA 2026 paper reports fastest queries across 2-960 dimensions.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry R-tree (named among the paper's competitors in search snippets) plus KD-trees in several languages (Kiddo, nabo, Neighbourhood), a Rust VP-tree, scikit-learn BallTree, SNN and brute force. nanoflann and CGAL kd-tree are feature-gated backends in the rembed harness, but I could not confirm they appear in the paper. — No numbers were verified. The ESA 2026 paper (LIPIcs ESA.2026.22, arXiv 2607.07367) could not be opened because arxiv.org, drops.dagstuhl.de and docs.rs are egress-blocked. Search snippets of its abstract say the SPRK-tree had the fastest query time in almost all benchmarks (graph embeddings plus real-world sets, up to 10M points, 2-960 dimensions), was second to SNN or brute force in the rest, and beat the Kiddo and Neighbourhood kd-trees. The public harness (wembed-pdf/rembed, a reproducibility CLI with Zenodo data and a nix flake) has feature-gated nanoflann, Boost R-tree and CGAL kd-tree backends, but which C++ baselines appear in the paper's figures, the CPU and the compiler were not seen.

**Known shortcoming:** ESA 2026 venue and abstract seen only in search snippets (paper unreadable here); no numbers seen; nanoflann/CGAL comparison in the paper unconfirmed (retier candidate).

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: for D>=6, IdDist.dist holds half the squared distance though documented as squared; the radius test is r^2/2 plus an absolute 1e-4 slack (f32) with no exact recheck. FFI dynamic path frees/queries DynSprk<f32,u64> but creates <f32,u32> (unreachable now because sprk_create rejects dim>16, though the FFI README advertises 18-24). Default features drop svd and parallel, which the paper harness enabled. Paper unopened here; no numbers verified. Rust.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The tree is an implicit, pointer-free balanced kd-tree: median splits on cycling axes are stored in a heap-indexed array, and leaves hold about 500-1000 points (LEAFSIZE 500, depth floor(log2(n/500))). During descent, it carries per-axis squared offsets so the radius left for a far subtree shrinks as planes are crossed. The paper calls this radius reduction; it prunes harder than a plain distance-to-plane test. Each leaf is sorted along one axis and indexed by a histogram lookup table (LUT), so two LUT reads turn the reduced radius into a contiguous slice of the leaf, in the style of SNN sorted buckets. Points are stored in W-wide (default 8) structure-of-arrays blocks. Distances are computed with SIMD FMAs (for D >= 6 via precomputed half-norms minus a dot product), and hits are written out with AVX-512 vcompressps/vpcompressd when the CPU has them (runtime check) or with `wide` shuffle tables otherwise. With the svd feature enabled and D > 16, the tree is built in SVD-rotated coordinates.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated fixed-radius neighbour queries on points that move every iteration, with a full rebuild each step (graph-embedding force layouts, particle or agent simulations): update() reuses the buffers
- Moderate to high-dimensional Euclidean data (the paper covers 2-960 dimensions and up to 10M points). Search snippets of the abstract say it was fastest in almost all benchmarks, second only to SNN or brute force in a few high-dimensional cases, and an order of magnitude faster than brute force at 16 dimensions (paper not opened)
- Rust code bases (crate sprk 0.2.0), or C/C++ callers through sprk-ffi when f32 coordinates and 2-16 dimensions are enough
- x86-64 servers with AVX-512, built with -Ctarget-cpu=native as the README advises

**Skip it when:**
- k-nearest-neighbour search, box or range queries, or non-point geometry: it only does radius queries
- A few inserts or deletes at a time: update() rebuilds the whole tree
- Code that relies on the IdDist distance or on exact behaviour at the radius boundary when D >= 6 (see gotchas), or that needs f64 through the C API (f32 only)
- Teams that cannot add a Rust toolchain (1.88+, edition 2024) to a C++ build
- Risk-averse production use: the project has 18 commits made between 2026-03-08 and 2026-04-07, 3 stars, no GitHub releases and no independent measurements, and the paper's numbers were not seen here

**Integration:** crate (Rust); C/C++ through the sprk-ffi static or shared library with sprk.h and the header-only sprk.hpp wrapper · num-traits. The default feature simd-compress adds wide and simd-lookup. Optional: rayon and sharded-vec-writer (feature parallel); faer-svd, faer-core and dyn-stack (feature svd) · Rust 1.88, edition 2024 · any Rust target: an AVX-512 compress path on x86-64 (runtime-detected) and a portable `wide`/scalar fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick SPRK over nanoflann when the workload is purely fixed-radius search in moderate or high dimensions and you can link Rust. nanoflann is the safer C++ choice for kNN, f64, mature packaging and no extra toolchain. ArborX fits GPU batched queries, and Pkd-tree fits many-core batch inserts and deletes.

**Gotchas:**
- IdDist.dist is documented as the squared distance, but for D >= 6 the leaf scan computes |p|^2/2 + |q|^2/2 - p.q (half the squared distance) and stores that value unchanged (src/query.rs snn, src/simd.rs dist_half_squared, src/output.rs); D < 6 gets the true squared distance. The D >= 6 test also compares against r^2/2 + DIST_EPS (an absolute 1e-4 for f32, 1e-8 for f64) with no exact recheck. Points near the boundary can therefore be wrongly included, or lost to cancellation when coordinates are large relative to r. This comes from reading the source; no issue has been filed
- Default features exclude svd and parallel (commit 2026-04-07, 'Disable svd and parallel construction features by default'), while the rembed benchmark builds sprk with svd, parallel and simd-compress. A plain `cargo add sprk` therefore gets neither the SVD projection for D > 16 nor the parallel build the paper used
- C API limits: sprk_create returns NULL for any dimension outside 2-16, even though the FFI README advertises 18-24; every query heap-allocates its result array (free it with sprk_free_results), and the C++ wrapper then copies it into a new std::vector and only assert()s that creation succeeded; there is no update() and no batch query. The FFI's dynamic-dimension path builds DynSprk<f32,u32> but queries and frees it as DynSprk<f32,u64>. That path is unreachable today because of the dimension check, but it becomes a type-confusion bug if the check is relaxed
- Each leaf's LUT range is rounded to whole units (floor of the minimum, ceil of the maximum). Data whose per-leaf extent is far below 1 gets coarse buckets and scans more of each leaf, so rescale tiny coordinates (from the source)

**Status:** A young research crate under MIT (crate 0.2.0, no commits since 2026-04-07) and small enough (about 3k lines of core Rust) to vendor; treat it as a paper artifact rather than a maintained library.

[repo](https://github.com/wembed-pdf/sprk) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07367)

#### random-and-quasi-random

##### EigenRand  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only SIMD random distributions for Eigen matrices; roughly 1.6-60x faster than std <random> plus NullaryExpr or Eigen::Random.

**Beats:** C++ <random> distributions (std::normal_distribution, std::uniform_real_distribution, std::uniform_int_distribution, etc.) and Eigen::DenseBase::Random — The repo's benchmark generates 1000x1000 Eigen arrays 20 times per distribution. It compares EigenRand against std::mt19937_64 plus the matching std distribution through Eigen NullaryExpr, and against Eigen::Random for 'balanced'. The README bar charts (Eigen 3.4.0; GCC 7.5 AVX2 on Xeon Platinum 8370C, MSVC 19.29 AVX2 on Xeon Platinum 8171M, Apple clang 13.1.6 NEON on M1 Pro) show speed-ups of about 1.6x-32x on Ubuntu, 3x-61x on Windows and 0.6x-15x on M1. All values are read by eye from images, and the runs were on shared CI machines.

**Known shortcoming:** macOS NEON chart shows binomial(100,0.75) ~0.6x and weibull ~0.75x, slower than std; the ~61x figure is from the MSVC chart.

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #29: access violation in uniformReal for a 5x3 matrix on Eigen 3.3.9. Integer distributions support only int32_t. On NEON, binomial and weibull are slower than std.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Every distribution has an Eigen packetOp, so a whole SSE2/AVX/AVX2/AVX512/NEON register of samples is produced per step and fused into Eigen's expression evaluation. Uniform reals use the mantissa trick: random bits are placed under a [1,2) exponent and 1 is subtracted. Normal uses vectorized Box-Muller with packet log/sincos and caches the second output. Rejection samplers (uniformInt bitmask rejection, gamma, binomial) pack the accepted lanes into a per-generator cache with a SIMD compress-append, so no lane is wasted. Discrete distributions use the alias method. Vmt19937_64 runs 2 (SSE2/NEON) or 4 (AVX2) Mersenne Twister 64 states in parallel lanes.

**Use it when:**
- You already use Eigen and generate large random matrices or arrays (e.g. 1000x1000 per call) for Monte Carlo, ML initialization or simulation.
- You need non-uniform distributions in bulk (normal, Cauchy, binomial, discrete, uniformReal). The Ubuntu AVX2 chart shows about 8x-32x for these.
- You want reproducible streams across SSE/AVX2/NEON builds (use P8_mt19937_64), or per-element parameters through vectorization over parameters (uniformReal, normal, binomial and others).
- You want to replace Eigen::Random (rand()-based, unseedable) with a seedable, higher-quality generator.

**Skip it when:**
- You draw a few scalars at a time outside Eigen expressions. The speed-up comes from bulk packet generation, and the library is tied to Eigen 3.3.4-3.4.x or 5.0.x.
- You need bit-identical streams to std::normal_distribution or other std distributions. The algorithms differ, and outputs only match statistically (checked by Earth Mover's Distance).
- chiSquared, gamma with large shape, fisherF, uniformInt over wide ranges (0~100k): only about 1.6-1.7x on the Ubuntu AVX2 chart. On Apple M1 NEON, binomial(100,0.75) and weibull are slower than std.
- You need integer distributions for types other than int32_t. UniformIntGen and DiscreteGen static_assert on int32_t, and issue #58 requesting other integral types is open.
- You need a library with many maintainers. It is a single-author project (105 stars), and issue #29 (an access violation in uniformReal for a 5x3 matrix on Eigen 3.3.9) is still open.

**Integration:** header-only · Eigen 3.3.4-3.4.0 or Eigen 5.0.x (googletest only for the tests) · C++11 (C++14 with Eigen 5.0.x); CMake 3.9+ only for building tests and benchmarks · x86 and x86-64 (SSE2, AVX, AVX2, AVX512), ARM64 NEON; scalar fallback when Eigen vectorization is off (Vmt19937_64 becomes std::mt19937_64)

**Vs siblings:** Pick EigenRand when your data already lives in Eigen and you need many distributions (including multivariate and vectorization over parameters) behind one API. Zest or normaldist-benchmark's Ziggurat are lighter for scalar normal/gamma sampling without Eigen. Randompack covers C-callable bulk U(0,1)/N(0,1) with paper numbers, and simdrng/VMT19937 are better if you only need a fast vectorized bit engine.

**Gotchas:**
- The -Like and generator functions return lazy expressions. Rand::balancedLike(mat, urng) alone does nothing until assigned, and each evaluation draws new numbers from the engine held by reference.
- Vmt19937_64 is a different type and stream depending on the compile-time ISA (Packet8i under AVX2, Packet4i under SSE2/NEON, std::mt19937_64 when unvectorized). Use P8_mt19937_64 when results must match across machines.
- Uniform reals are built by the mantissa trick, so float outputs have 2^-23 granularity and never hit tiny nonzero values (to_nzur adds epsilon/8 where log(0) must be avoided).
- Rejection loops have only a debug-mode assert after 100 iterations (EIGENRAND_CHECK_INFINITY_LOOP). Past bugs include a non-terminating normal (#27, fixed in 0.3.5) and out-of-range uniformInt (#42, fixed in 0.4.1), so pin to 0.6.0 or later.

**Status:** Active, with release 0.6.0 (2026-01-31) adding Eigen 5.0.x and AVX512 support and the last commit on 2026-03-17. MIT-licensed and header-only, so it is easy to vendor alongside Eigen.

[repo](https://github.com/bab2min/EigenRand) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bab2min/EigenRand)

##### normaldist-benchmark (Ziggurat and AVX/SSE2 Box-Muller)  `C++`  `MIT (src/ziggurat.cpp is Jochen Voss's GPL-2.0-or-later code)`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

2015 benchmark of normal-sample generators; Ziggurat and AVX Box-Muller run 2.8-8x faster than std::normal_distribution with minstd_rand.

**Beats:** std::normal_distribution with std::minstd_rand (the 'cpp11random' row) — On an iMac Core i5-3330S (2.7 GHz) with clang 6.1 and libc++, best of 10 runs of 1M samples: double cpp11random (std::normal_distribution + std::minstd_rand) 32.2 ns/sample vs Ziggurat 7.1 ns (4.55x); float 18.6 ns vs Ziggurat 6.7 ns (about 2.8x) and boxmuller_avx 2.25 ns (about 8.3x, derived from page data). Against the same-LCG polar method, Ziggurat's own algorithmic gain is about 1.6-1.8x (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** src/ziggurat.cpp is GPL-2.0+ inside an MIT repo; the std side pays minstd_rand's cost while the others use a bare LCG.

**Known shortcoming:** clt_avx steps the index by 4 but stores 8 floats: double work plus a 16-byte write past the buffer end on the last iteration. Ziggurat takes layer index and sign from the low 8 bits of a power-of-2 LCG (period 128/256); lanes seeded 1..8, so they are correlated. libc++ normal_distribution is itself the polar method and the repo's polar with a cheap LCG is already 2.5x faster than cpp11random in double, so the ziggurat's algorithmic gain is only 1.6-1.8x (derived from page data). Abandoned 2015.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Ziggurat (Marsaglia-Tsang 2000) covers the density with 128 equal-area layers, so about 99% of samples cost one 32-bit draw, a table lookup, a multiply and a compare; log/exp are needed only in the rare wedge and tail cases. The SSE2/AVX Box-Muller variants run 4 or 8 lanes of a 32-bit LCG and use vectorized log and sincos approximations from sse_mathfun/avx_mathfun, producing 8 or 16 floats per loop iteration. Every non-std variant uses a one-multiply LCG (Numerical Recipes constants for 32-bit, a 64-bit LCG for double) as the uniform source, which is far cheaper than minstd_rand plus uniform_real_distribution.

**Use it when:**
- Choosing a normal-sampling algorithm: the table shows how Box-Muller, polar, inverse CDF, CLT and Ziggurat compare under the same cheap uniform source
- Bulk float fills (Monte Carlo noise, procedural generation) on x86 with AVX where approximate log/sincos accuracy is acceptable: boxmuller_avx reached 2.25 ns/sample
- A scalar Ziggurat for float or double when you can accept GPL-2.0-or-later code or will rewrite it
- As a starting harness to benchmark your own normal sampler against std::normal_distribution

**Skip it when:**
- Statistically sensitive work: the uniform source is a power-of-two LCG, and the Ziggurat takes its layer index and sign from the LCG's lowest 8 bits, which cycle with period 128/256
- Projects that cannot take copyleft code: src/ziggurat.cpp is GPL-2.0-or-later even though the repo is MIT
- Code that needs a reusable sampler object: each call re-creates the generator at a fixed seed, so every call returns the same sequence and there is no seeding API
- The CLT variants: they fail the repo's own kurtosis check, and clt*_avx has a buffer-overrun bug (see gotchas)
- Non-x86 targets or modern CPUs without retesting: SIMD paths are SSE2/AVX intrinsics only, and the only published numbers are from a 2012 Core i5 with clang 6.1

**Integration:** source-drop · none for scalar variants; sse_mathfun.h / avx_mathfun.h (zlib license, vendored in src/) for SSE2/AVX variants; premake4 to build the harness · C++11 (premake gmake build passes -std=c++11 -mavx) · x86/x86-64; the AVX variants need AVX (the 8-lane LCG emulates 256-bit integer multiply with SSE4.1 _mm_mullo_epi32); scalar code is portable

**Vs siblings:** Use it to compare algorithms or to borrow a minimal Ziggurat or SIMD Box-Muller kernel; for production sampling, Zest (generalized Ziggurat, reported 3.6x over STL normal) or EigenRand (vectorized std-like distributions) give a maintained API with a proper engine. An open issue (#3, 2020) posts a faster single-table Ziggurat (about 4.0 ns vs 7.3-7.8 ns for the repo's version).

**Gotchas:**
- Alignment and size: boxmuller_sse2 needs 16-byte-aligned data and n % 8 == 0; boxmuller_avx needs 32-byte alignment and n % 16 == 0 (the code asserts 16, not 8); scalar boxmuller and polar need even n
- clt_avx steps the index by 4 while storing 8 floats per iteration, so it does twice the work and the last store writes 16 bytes past the end of the buffer; the harness's 32-byte slack may not cover it
- Not like-for-like with std: libc++'s normal_distribution is itself the Marsaglia polar method, and the repo's own polar method with the cheap LCG is already 2.5x faster than cpp11random in double, so most of the headline gap is the uniform source, not the algorithm (derived from page data)
- The SIMD lanes are seeded 1..4 or 1..8 with the same LCG constants, so lanes are linearly related; output is not suitable where independence between samples matters

**Status:** Abandoned since July 2015 (one open PR and two open issues from 2019-2020); the MIT harness and SIMD kernels are small enough to copy, but the Ziggurat file is GPL-2.0-or-later and needs a better uniform generator before reuse.

[repo](https://github.com/miloyip/normaldist-benchmark) · [benchmark](https://github.com/miloyip/normaldist-benchmark)

##### OpenRAND (Philox, Threefry, Squares, Tyche counter-based generators)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++17 counter-based RNGs (Philox, Threefry, Squares, Tyche) for CPU and CUDA/HIP; beats stateful cuRAND in a Brownian dynamics run and std::mt19937 on short streams.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 (libstdc++) on CPU and NVIDIA cuRAND on GPU — The authors' SoftwareX paper timed a 2D Brownian dynamics simulation (1M particles, 10,000 steps, Philox in every library, whole-process wall time, nvcc -O3 -std=c++17 -arch=sm_80) at 1.78 s with OpenRAND versus 3.20 s with cuRAND and 1.81 s with Random123 on an A100 SXM, and 2.48 s versus 4.23 s and 2.46 s on a Tesla V100 PCIe. Their CPU micro-benchmark on a Xeon Platinum 8260 against libstdc++ std::mt19937 (constructing a fresh engine per iteration; compiler and flags unstated) is only a log-scale chart: all four generators win on 10-100 draws, while at 10K draws only Tyche and Squares stay ahead.

**Known shortcoming:** Gain comes from the stateless API, not the algorithm (Random123 is on par); on CPU at 10K draws only Tyche/Squares beat mt19937, while Philox and Threefry are slower.

**Known shortcoming:** rand<float>() returns exactly 1.0f for the top 128 uint32 inputs (~1 in 33.5M draws) against the documented [0,1); double returns 1.0 for the top 1024 uint64 inputs (derived from base_state.h u01 code, not filed upstream). Open #25: 64-bit Squares output differs from Widynski's paper. Philox draw<uint32_t> computes a 4x32 block and returns one word, which explains the CPU loss to mt19937. squares.h leaks #define K globally. Stream period per (seed, counter) is 2^32.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Counter-based generation: each output is a keyed bijection of (seed, counter) computed in registers (Philox-4x32-10 multiply/xor rounds, Threefry-2x32-20 add-rotate-xor, Widynski's Squares middle-square rounds, or the Tyche ARX mix), so construction is a few register moves instead of mt19937's 624-word seeding or a cuRAND state load/store. On the GPU the win in the paper comes from skipping curand_init and the per-thread state round trip to global memory (about 64 MB saved per million particles), not from a faster Philox; on the CPU it comes from cheap construction for short streams.

**Use it when:**
- CUDA or HIP kernels where each thread or particle needs a few random numbers per launch and you want to stop storing curandState arrays; the paper measured 1.8x over cuRAND Philox on an A100 and 1.7x on a V100 in a RNG-bound Brownian dynamics kernel.
- Simulations that must be bitwise reproducible regardless of thread count or scheduling (seed = particle id, counter = timestep).
- CPU code that constructs many short-lived generators (10 to 1,000 draws each), where std::mt19937's seeding cost dominates.
- Code that must compile unchanged for host, CUDA and HIP from one header set with no intrinsics or platform-specific code.

**Skip it when:**
- Long single streams on the CPU: at 10K draws only Tyche and Squares beat std::mt19937 (roughly 3.5-4x); Philox is slightly slower and Threefry about 6x slower, and SIMD or small-state generators (xoshiro, PCG, Romu) are faster still.
- Already on Random123: the paper shows OpenRAND Philox on par with Random123 (1.78 s versus 1.81 s on A100), so the gain is API simplicity, not speed.
- More than 2^32 draws from one (seed, counter) pair: the paper states each stream has period 2^32 and the internal counter is a uint32_t.
- You need the published Squares64 output: open issue #25 reports the 64-bit Squares path differs from Widynski's paper.
- Cryptographic use: these are reduced-round statistical generators, not CSPRNGs.

**Integration:** header-only (include/openrand/*.h; CMake INTERFACE target OpenRAND::OpenRAND, FetchContent or make install) · none (Google Test, Google Benchmark, TestU01 and PractRand only for optional tests/benchmarks) · C++17 (if constexpr, std::void_t); CMake 3.18 if using the CMake target; nvcc for CUDA, hipcc for HIP · any C++17 host; NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA (__host__ __device__ through the OPENRAND_DEVICE macro) and AMD GPUs via HIP; no architecture-specific intrinsics

**Vs siblings:** Pick OpenRAND for portable GPU and CPU code that wants stateless per-work-unit streams with a two-line API; vphilox and benchmark-rngs PhiloxSIMD are faster for bulk Philox output on CPUs with AVX, and the standalone Squares generator or Random123 give the same algorithms with lower-level APIs. For CPU throughput or attack resistance, Randen, Randompack or a SIMD xoshiro fit better.

**Gotchas:**
- Philox::draw<uint32_t>() (used by operator() and rand<float>()) computes a full 4x32 Philox block and returns only one word, discarding three; use draw_int4()/draw_float4() to get all four, which is why scalar Philox loses to mt19937 on long CPU streams.
- rand<float>() and rand<double>() are documented as [0,1) but the u01 conversion (x * 2^-32 + 2^-33 in float) rounds to exactly 1.0f for the top 128 uint32 inputs (about 1 in 33.5 million draws), and to 1.0 for the top 1,024 uint64 inputs in double (derived from the base_state.h code, not documented upstream); clamp before using the value as an index.
- range<T>(N) defaults to the biased multiply-shift (biased=true); pass range<false>(N) for unbiased Lemire rejection. randn() discards the second Box-Muller value; use randn2().
- squares.h does #define K 0xc58efd154ce32f6d at global scope, which breaks any including code that uses K as an identifier; Philox, Threefry and Squares have const members, so they are copy-constructible but not copy-assignable.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-12-11 (37 stars, CMake project version 1.0, release issue #9 still open) but MIT-licensed and small (the paper counts 470 source lines of core headers at publication), so it is easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/msu-sparta/OpenRAND) · [benchmark](https://github.com/msu-sparta/OpenRAND/blob/main/docs/OpenRAND.pdf)

##### pure-rand (fast-check PRNG library for JavaScript/TypeScript)  `TypeScript`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Seeded JavaScript/TypeScript PRNGs (xoroshiro128+, Mersenne Twister, LCG) with unbiased ranges; author's shuffle benchmark beats Math.random 1.4x.

**Beats:** JavaScript native Math.random() (Xorshift128+ in Node 16.19.1) and the seedrandom, random-js, chance and faker Mersenne Twister libraries — The author's COMPARISON.md times a Fisher-Yates shuffle of a 1,000,000-element array (tinybench, 1,000 iterations) on Node 16.19.1 on a 2-vCPU Xeon Platinum 8272CL GitHub Actions runner. With biased float scaling, pure-rand 6.0.0 xoroshiro128+ took 24.5 ms against 33.3 ms for Math.random (V8's xorshift128+), 28.1-33.5 ms for seedrandom and 109-143 ms for the faker and chance Mersenne Twisters. With unbiased ranges it took 53.5 ms against random-js MT19937 at 119.6 ms (2.2x). The figures are for pure-rand 6.0.0 (January 2023); 8.4.2 has not been re-measured in that document.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on COMPARISON.md (perf/compare.cjs, Node 16.19.1, Xeon Platinum 8272CL), but the non-uniform rows use the mutating unsafeNext() path, not the pure API the library is named for.

**Known shortcoming:** The 'pure functional API' is stale: 8.0.0 (2026-03) made mutation the default, with pure semantics only via a purify() clone. The benchmark is pure-rand 6.0.0 on Node 16; perf/compare.cjs uses removed 6.x names and 8.4.2 was never re-measured. xoroshiro128plus next() returns the low 32 bits of the 64-bit sum (weak linear low bits per the xoroshiro128+ literature, snippet only); a 32-bit seed reaches only 2^32 states; uniformInt uses modulo rejection, not nearly-divisionless. fast-check 4.10.2 depends on pure-rand ^8.0.0.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Each 64-bit state word is kept as two 32-bit JavaScript numbers and advanced with |0, >>> and ^ so V8 stays in int32 arithmetic with no BigInt or allocation per draw (xoroshiro128plus.ts). congruential32 advances three LCG steps in parallel with Math.imul using precomputed a^2 and a^3 constants (8.4.1), and the 8.x releases also trimmed Mersenne Twister twisting, initialisation and allocations. uniformInt uses rejection sampling on one 32-bit draw followed by a modulo for ranges up to 2^32, with module-level scratch objects for wider ranges; it does not use Lemire's nearly divisionless method.

**Use it when:**
- JS/TS code that needs seeded, replayable randomness: property-based tests, simulations, procedural generation, games with replays.
- You need unbiased integer ranges (uniformInt) or 53-bit doubles (uniformFloat64) without writing your own rejection sampling, which Math.random-based Math.floor(r * n) code gets wrong.
- You need independent parallel streams (jump() moves xoroshiro128plus 2^64 steps ahead) or need to serialize and restore generator state (getState / *FromState).
- Functional or immutable codebases that want pure generator calls via purify() and accept a clone per call.
- You already depend on fast-check: fast-check 4.10.2 lists pure-rand ^8.0.0 as its only dependency, so it adds no extra package.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: it is TypeScript compiled to JS and cannot be called from C++. Use a C++ generator from this category instead.
- Anything security-sensitive (tokens, keys, shuffles with money at stake): none of the four generators is a CSPRNG; use crypto.getRandomValues.
- Statistically demanding work that reads low bits: xoroshiro128plus next() returns the low 32 bits of the 64-bit s0+s1 sum, the bits the xoroshiro128+ literature reports as failing linearity tests.
- Seeding many independent runs from random seeds: the xoroshiro128plus(seed) factory takes a 32-bit seed, so only 2^32 of its 2^128 states are reachable that way (use jump() for streams).
- Bulk throughput: there is no typed-array fill; generateN returns a plain number[], and purify() allocates a clone on every call.

**Integration:** module (npm package pure-rand, CommonJS and ESM builds, subpath exports only since 8.0.0, TypeScript types included) · none (no runtime dependencies in package.json 8.4.2) · No engines field; CI checks the bundle on Node 12.17.0 (test-legacy-bundle script). ES module subpath imports need a bundler or Node with exports-map support. · any JavaScript runtime (Node, browsers, Deno/Bun not documented)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when the code is JavaScript or TypeScript; the catalogued language-specific siblings fill the same role elsewhere (fastrand for Python, vpxyz/xorshift and pgregory.net/rand for Go, xrandom for Dart). For C++ use testingRNG's lehmer64 or aesctr, or SIMD generators such as simdrng or SHISHUA, plus FastShuffleExperiments for bounded integers, which use a nearly divisionless method where pure-rand uses a modulo.

**Gotchas:**
- 8.0.0 is a breaking release: no main entry point (import from pure-rand/generator/... and pure-rand/distribution/...), rng moved to the first argument, mutation became the default, unsafeUniformIntDistribution became uniformInt, and fromState moved to xoroshiro128plusFromState and similar exports. The benchmark code (perf/compare.cjs at 556ec331) uses the 6.x names and will not run on 8.x.
- next() returns a signed int32 in [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]; use >>> 0 for an unsigned value. uniformFloat64 consumes two next() calls per double.
- The README's 'non-uniform' recipe ((rng.next() >>> 0) / 2^32 scaled by the range) is the variant that won the 1.4x benchmark and is biased; the README itself recommends against it.
- Historic issues #1 (infinite loop when the range exceeded the generator) and #63 (non-uniform for gaps beyond 32 bits) are closed; no open bug or quality issues were listed on 2026-10-03.

**Status:** Active (8.4.2 released 2026-07-10, frequent performance commits), MIT, zero dependencies and the PRNG under fast-check, but JavaScript-only, so for this C++-first catalog it is a reference entry for JS projects.

[repo](https://github.com/dubzzz/pure-rand) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dubzzz/pure-rand/HEAD/COMPARISON.md)

##### pXart  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++17 SSE/AVX2 MT19937, Xoroshiro128+ and MSWS; AVX2 MT19937 matches std::mt19937 output and generates it about 8x faster.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 (libstdc++, GCC 9.2.0); also Boost.Random mt19937 — In the author's 2019 master's thesis (Jena), GCC 9.2.0 -O3 -march=native on a Core i7-7700K at 4.51 GHz, generating 16 GiB through a 16 KiB buffer took 9.29 s with libstdc++ std::mt19937, 5.79 s with Boost mt19937 and 1.15 s with pXart's AVX2 MT19937 (about 8.1x and 5.0x, derived from page data); scalar pXart MT19937 (7.61 s) beat STL but not Boost. In a 10^8-sample Monte Carlo pi run, using the AVX2 MT19937 through a buffer in scalar code took 0.15 s vs 0.53 s for STL with pXart's uniform conversion (about 3.5x, derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** The 0.07 s Monte Carlo figure vectorizes the whole pi loop; as an RNG-only drop-in ('AVX cache') it is 0.15 vs 0.53 s, ~3.5x.

**Known shortcoming:** simd256::xoroshiro128plus default constructor leaves state uninitialized; its seeding constructor calls rng() 8 times inside one _mm256_set_epi32, so evaluation order is unspecified and seeds differ across compilers. Templated RNG&& constructor hijacks copies from non-const lvalues. AVX2 MT19937 is bit-identical to std::mt19937 (repo test checks 10M outputs).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** For MT19937 it vectorizes the state twist of a single generator (Agner Fog's technique): 8 consecutive state words are updated per AVX2 instruction, and a copy of the first new block stored past the end of the state array handles the wrap-around, so output order is unchanged. Xoroshiro128+ and MSWS instead run several independent instances side by side in the vector lanes (multi-stream), so their SIMD output differs from the scalar sequence. Uniform floats are made by OR-ing the top 23 (float) or 52 (double) random bits into the exponent of 1.0 and subtracting 1, and bounded integers use a multiply-shift instead of a division.

**Use it when:**
- Code bound to the std::mt19937 sequence (reproducible simulations, saved seeds) that needs much higher throughput on x86 with AVX2 or SSE2
- Bulk fills of 32-bit randoms or floats, e.g. Monte Carlo inner loops where you can consume 8 values per call or buffer them
- SIMD kernels already written with AVX2 intrinsics that want random vectors directly in registers
- Projects that want a tiny MIT header-only dependency, usable via build2, CMake or by copying the pxart/ folder

**Skip it when:**
- Non-x86 targets: SIMD paths are SSE/AVX2 intrinsics only; ARM or other platforms fall back to the scalar engines
- When you need std <random> distributions on the vector engines: there are no normal, exponential or other non-uniform distributions
- When you are free to change the generator and want maximum speed: pXart's own AVX2 Xoroshiro128+ beats its AVX2 MT19937 (0.74 s vs 1.15 s for 16 GiB in the thesis), and other siblings are faster still
- Production code that needs maintenance or support: 3 stars, alpha build2 package, last commit January 2021
- Exact unbiased bounded integers: the multiply-shift range reduction has a small bias the code itself calls an approximation

**Integration:** header-only · none (doctest for tests, perfevent for benchmarks) · C++17; README lists GCC, Clang, Intel, MinGW and MSVC as tested; SIMD headers compile only when __AVX2__ / __SSE2__ are defined (e.g. -march=native) · any for scalar engines; x86-64 with SSE2 (simd128 MT19937) or AVX2 (simd256) for the vectorized engines

**Vs siblings:** Pick pXart when you must keep the exact 32-bit std::mt19937 sequence and want a small C++17 header with AVX2/SSE paths; VMT19937 also covers mt19937_64 and AVX-512, and if the generator can change, SIMD xoshiro siblings (simdrng, Xoroshiro-style engines) or SHISHUA are faster.

**Gotchas:**
- pxart::simd256::xoroshiro128plus's default constructor leaves its state uninitialized, and its seeding constructor calls rng() eight times inside one _mm256_set_epi32 argument list, whose evaluation order is unspecified, so seeded streams can differ between compilers
- The templated RNG&& seeding constructor of pxart::mt19937 is a better match than the copy constructor for a non-const lvalue, so 'pxart::mt19937 b{a};' seeds b from a's outputs instead of copying a
- uniform<double> from a 32-bit engine only has 32 random bits (low mantissa bits are zero); uniform<float> uses 23 bits and returns [0,1)
- The SIMD headers silently define nothing if compiled without AVX2/SSE2 flags; check the PXART_SUPPORT_SIMD256_* macros

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2021 (3 stars, alpha cppget.org package), but MIT-licensed, header-only and small enough to vendor; the AVX2 MT19937 is tested bit-for-bit against std::mt19937.

[repo](https://github.com/lyrahgames/pxart) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lyrahgames/pxart/HEAD/docs/thesis/main.pdf)

##### Randen  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

AES-based backtracking-resistant PRNG (C++11 URBG) at roughly std::mt19937_64 speed; reference code for absl::BitGen's engine.

**Beats:** std::mt19937_64 / pcg64_c32 (also Philox, ISAAC, ChaCha8) — On an Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 (Haswell) with Clang -O3, Google's paper reports Randen about 1.1x faster than std::mt19937_64 (geomean over shuffle, reservoir sampling and Monte Carlo, also on POWER8), while pcg64_c32 is fastest on x86; the README's tight-loop microbenchmark shows 1.54 cpb vs 1.79 for mt19937_64 and 0.78 for pcg64_c32. The standard library implementation for mt19937_64 is not named.

**Known shortcoming:** Google preprint, not peer reviewed; only ~1.1x faster than mt19937 (geomean) and slower than PCG in the microbenchmark and most paper tasks; README and paper reservoir-sampling tables disagree; standard library not stated; archived (last commit 2018-10-05).

**Known shortcoming:** No software fallback: will not compile without hardware AES (vector128.h #error "Port"); README says algorithm 'still under review and subject to change'; speed depends on loop unrolling (GCC 7.3 up to 1.6x more cycles/byte); maintained version is Abseil's absl::BitGen.

**How:** It plugs a 2048-bit Simpira-v2-style permutation (a 16-branch generalized Feistel network with improved block shuffle, 17 rounds of 2-round AES-128 functions) into the Reverie sponge construction, so one permutation call refills a 240-byte output buffer while keeping a 128-bit hidden capacity for backtracking resistance. The AES rounds run on hardware AES instructions (AES-NI, POWER8 VSX crypto, ARMv8 crypto), and operator() is just a buffer read with a rare refill branch.

**Use it when:**
- You want a default generator that is safe if outputs or state might be attacker-observable (shuffles, sampling, randomized algorithms in services) without paying CTR-DRBG or /dev/urandom costs (~10x slower in the README table).
- Applied workloads (shuffle, reservoir sampling, Monte Carlo) on x86 with AES-NI where std::mt19937_64 is the incumbent: about 1.1x faster geomean per the paper, with 256 bytes of state versus mt19937_64's ~2.5 KB.
- Already on Abseil: use absl::BitGen, which is this algorithm with runtime AES dispatch and a portable fallback.
- x86-64 with AES-NI, POWER8+ with VSX, or ARMv8 with crypto extensions.

**Skip it when:**
- Raw throughput is the goal: pcg64_c32 is ~2x faster in the tight-loop microbenchmark (0.78 vs 1.54 cpb) and the paper's shuffle tables show PCG ahead; non-crypto generators like Romu or xoshiro are faster still.
- Targets without hardware AES: the standalone repo has no software fallback (vector128.h hits #error "Port"); only Abseil ships a slow portable path.
- You need a vetted CSPRNG for keys/tokens: the README says the algorithm is 'still under review and subject to change' and the paper is not peer reviewed.
- You need a maintained standalone library: archived 2023-06-12, last commit 2018-10-05, no versioned releases or build system beyond a Makefile.
- Performance depends heavily on compiler unrolling: README reports up to 1.6x more cycles/byte with GCC 7.3 and 1.3x with Clang 4.0.1.

**Integration:** source-drop (randen.h, randen.cc, vector128.h) · none (compiler intrinsics only) · C++11; Makefile uses clang++ -O3 -mavx2 -maes; Clang recommended for loop unrolling · x86 with SSE2+AES-NI, POWER8 with VSX, ARMv8 with NEON+crypto; build fails elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick Randen when you need attack resistance (indistinguishability plus backtracking resistance) at near-Mersenne-Twister cost; Romu, SIMDxorshift and Randompack are faster but non-cryptographic, and Squares/Philox-style counter-based RNGs suit parallel stream splitting rather than state-compromise resistance.

**Gotchas:**
- Must be compiled with AES enabled (-maes or equivalent); there is no runtime CPU dispatch in this repo.
- Object is alignas(32) with 256 bytes of state; heap allocation of the engine relies on aligned new (C++17) or a custom allocator under C++11.
- Backtracking resistance only covers outputs before the last Generate call; prediction resistance needs periodic reseed() with fresh entropy.
- Output stream may change if the algorithm is revised (README: 'subject to change'); Abseil's absl::BitGen deliberately offers no seed stability across runs.

**Status:** Archived since 2023-06-12 (last commit 2018-10-05) but Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor; for production prefer the maintained Abseil absl::BitGen implementation.

[repo](https://github.com/google/randen) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02227)

##### Randompack  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

C11 bulk random-variate library (xoshiro/PCG/Philox/ChaCha, 20+ distributions); ~10-15x faster than C++ <random> for U(0,1)/N(0,1) fills.

**Beats:** C++ std <random> (std::mt19937_64 + std::uniform_real_distribution / std::normal_distribution), NumPy, Base-R, Julia, oneMKL — On an Intel Core i5-1335U with clang, the author's paper (Table 8) reports bulk U(0,1) at 0.42 ns/value vs 6.3 for C++ std::mt19937_64 + uniform_real_distribution (~15x) and N(0,1) at 1.4 vs 14.3 ns/value for std::normal_distribution (~10x); NumPy, Julia and MKL are also listed, with Julia and MKL close. The C++ comparison code (benchmark/TimeDistCpp.cpp) is public; the C++ standard library and clang version are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper only submitted to ACM TOMS, not yet peer reviewed; standard library and clang version not stated; the C++ std baseline is weak (Julia and MKL come close); 3 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** Speedup only in bulk array fills; oneMKL faster for U(0,1) (~1.3x) and beta/gamma, Julia matches on normals and wins on permutations/sampling; meson.build defaults to a debug build; source build needs a Fortran compiler; single author.

**How:** Bulk generation through an internal 144-word (1152-byte) buffer and tight inlined loops instead of one virtual-ish call per sample. The default engine x256++simd runs eight xoshiro256++ streams in parallel on AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON (unrolled scalar fallback elsewhere). Normals use a 256-strip ziggurat (Marsaglia-Tsang with McFarland's 2016 refinements), uniforms use a 52-bit mantissa bit trick, and vectorized log/exp come from Sleef.

**Use it when:**
- Filling large arrays (thousands+) of U(0,1), normal, exponential or gamma variates in Monte Carlo or simulation code where std::mt19937_64 + <random> distributions dominate the profile.
- Projects that need the same stream across C, C++, Fortran, Python, R and Julia, or across x86-64, ARM and Windows/macOS/Linux (bit-identical for the core distributions, optional bitexact mode for the rest).
- Parallel simulations needing reproducible independent substreams (spawn keys, jumps, Philox/squares keys) and checkpoint/restart via state serialization.
- Code that wants a choice of engines behind one API, including ChaCha20 when a cryptographically secure generator is required.

**Skip it when:**
- One-at-a-time draws inside a hot loop: the speed comes from bulk fills, and per-call use (n=1) does not get the buffered/SIMD benefit (only bulk timings are published).
- If you already have oneMKL: the paper reports MKL faster for U(0,1) (about 1.3x) and for some distributions such as beta and gamma; Julia is on par for normals and faster for permutations/sampling.
- If you need a header-only or std::-compatible URBG to plug into existing <random> code or templates.
- If you need a mature, widely used dependency: young project (0.1.x, first release 2026), 3 stars, single author, paper submitted to ACM TOMS but not yet peer reviewed.
- Non-bitexact mode gives tolerance (about 2 ulp) rather than bit reproducibility for secondary distributions; bitexact mode costs 2-4x on some distributions.

**Integration:** shared lib (Meson/Ninja build, default_library=shared; also conda-forge librandompack) · Meson >= 1.3, Ninja, pkg-config; BLAS/LAPACK for multivariate normal (Accelerate/OpenBLAS/MKL auto-detected, bundled reference fallback); README says a Fortran compiler is required for the source build; uses OpenLibm-derived transcendental code and Sleef vector math per the paper · C11 compiler (clang, gcc, icx, MSVC, nvc tested); C++17 for the C++ benchmark · x86-64 (AVX2/AVX-512 paths), aarch64/NEON (Apple M, Linux ARM), Windows; scalar fallback without SIMD or 128-bit multiply; requires 32-bit int and 64-bit long long

**Vs siblings:** Pick Randompack when you need full distributions (normal, gamma, beta, etc.) in bulk with cross-language reproducibility; SIMDxorshift and Randen only give raw bits, and cxx-ziggurat covers only the normal distribution as a header-only C++ piece. Use Randen when you need backtracking-resistant output with an std-compatible C++ engine.

**Gotchas:**
- meson.build defaults to buildtype=debug; pass --buildtype=release (as the README and scripts/meson-setup.sh do) or the benchmarked speed will not appear.
- The default engine is x256++simd (eight interleaved xoshiro256++ streams), so its output is not the same sequence as a scalar xoshiro256++ with the same seed.
- For Philox and squares, do not change the counter via randompack_set_state while in use; the library advances counters internally as it fills buffers.
- Multivariate normal is double precision only and pulls in BLAS/LAPACK.

**Status:** Actively maintained (0.1.11 on 2026-08-27, frequent releases with PyPI, CRAN, Julia and conda-forge packaging); MIT-licensed and copyable, but young and single-author.

[repo](https://github.com/jonasson2/randompack) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.05099)

##### Sirius64  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Six-line 64-bit-state PRNG, a SplitMix64-style Weyl counter with a stronger output mix; ~1.25x faster than xoshiro256++.

**Beats:** xoshiro256++, xoshiro256**, PCG64 (RXS-M-XS and DXSM), xoroshiro128++, RomuTrio — With the author's benchmark.c (gcc 13.3, -O3 -march=native, 1e8 calls, best of 10) on a Core Ultra 7 265H under WSL2, Sirius64 took 5.007 cycles per 64-bit value vs xoshiro256++ 6.331, xoshiro256** 6.158, RomuTrio 5.842 and PCG64 DXSM 8.623, essentially tied with SplitMix64 at 4.985. lemire/testingRNG independently measured 4.29 GB/s on a Xeon Gold 6548N with GCC 14, vs pcg64 2.53, wyrand 4.22 and splitmix64 4.35. That makes it a tie with wyrand and splitmix64, not a clear win.

**Known shortcoming:** 2 stars; statistical quality self-reported; timed under WSL2; only ~1.25x faster than xoshiro256++.

**Known shortcoming:** 5.0 vs 6.3 cycles/value vs xoshiro256++; ties wyrand and splitmix64 in testingRNG (4.29 vs 4.22/4.35 GB/s); benchmark via function pointer counting rdtscp ticks; testingRNG issue 30: output function not proven a bijection; design weeks old.

**Independent measurement:** lemire/testingRNG independently: 4.29 vs pcg64 2.53 on Xeon Gold 6548N

**How:** The state update is one add of the golden-ratio constant 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 (a Weyl sequence, as in SplitMix64). The output function is xorshift-17, a multiply, a 32-bit rotate, then a multiply of state ^ z ^ (z >> 17), all with the same constant. The state carries only an add dependency from call to call, and the multiplies are off that chain, so the cost is close to SplitMix64 (2.38 instructions/byte in testingRNG vs 2.75 for splitmix64).

**Use it when:**
- Scalar 64-bit random streams in simulations, games or procedural generation, where you want SplitMix64 speed but a generator that passes a 64-bit collision test
- Replacing xoshiro256++/** or PCG64 in a hot loop that draws one value at a time (README: 5.0 vs 6.2-8.6 cycles per value)
- When 8 bytes of state per stream matters, e.g. one generator per object or per thread
- When you need a trivially portable generator: pure C99 with 64-bit multiply, no 128-bit arithmetic (unlike wyrand and PCG64)

**Skip it when:**
- Anything security-related: it is explicitly non-cryptographic
- When you need jump-ahead, provably independent parallel streams or a period above 2^64 (xoshiro256 offers 2^256 and jump functions)
- When you need a widely reviewed design: it was published in 2026, has 2 stars and a single author, and all its quality testing (PractRand to 64 TB, BigCrush x300, HWD to 15 PB) is self-reported
- When the output must be a bijection of the state: the output function is not one, so not every 64-bit value is guaranteed to appear in a period
- Bulk generation, where SIMD generators (SHISHUA, 8-way xoshiro256++) are several times faster

**Integration:** source-drop · none · C99 (needs uint64_t); the benchmark tool needs GCC/Clang with x86intrin.h · any platform with 64-bit integer multiply; benchmarked only on x86-64

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Romu/RomuTrio or xoshiro256++ when you want the smallest state and the fastest scalar draw with no 128-bit multiply. Prefer testingRNG's wyrand or lehmer64 for similar speed and a longer public track record, and SHISHUA or the 8-way xoshiro256++ gist for bulk SIMD throughput.

**Gotchas:**
- The README's 'Collision 64: Yes' column means the generator passes a 64-bit collision test: it produces about as many repeated outputs as a random function (6.8 observed vs 6.94 expected per 16e9 values). SplitMix64 is marked 'No' because its output is a bijection and never repeats within a period. In testingRNG issue 30 a SmokeRand author points out that 64-bit bijectivity is not proven.
- Its benchmark calls each generator through a function pointer, XORs into a volatile sink and counts rdtscp TSC ticks, not core cycles. Call overhead is included, which compresses the gaps between generators, and the author says rankings changed on other machines.
- Seeds of 0 and UINT64_MAX are documented as fine; with a Weyl counter, nearby seeds give overlapping, shifted streams.
- The README's 'pgc64' labels mean PCG64.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-29) under Apache-2.0. The algorithm is six lines and easy to vendor, but the design is weeks old and has had no third-party cryptanalysis-style review.

[repo](https://github.com/matteo65/Sirius64) · [benchmark](https://github.com/matteo65/Sirius64)

##### testingRNG (aesctr, lehmer64 winners)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Benchmark-plus-quality shootout of C/C++ PRNGs; its winners (aesctr, lehmer64) beat MT19937, PCG and xoroshiro128+ on throughput.

**Beats:** mersennetwister (reference Nishimura/Matsumoto MT19937 C code adapted in source/mersennetwister.h, not std::mt19937), C library rand(), pcg32, pcg64, xoroshiro128+ — On an Intel Xeon Gold 6548N with GCC 14 (CMake Release -O3 plus -march=native), filling a 4 KB buffer, aesctr produced 5.35 GB/s and lehmer64 3.10 GB/s, versus 1.68 GB/s for reference MT19937 C code, 1.55 GB/s pcg32, 2.53 GB/s pcg64, 2.50 GB/s xoroshiro128+ and 0.28 GB/s glibc rand(); splitmix64 (4.35) and wyrand (4.22) also beat lehmer64.

**Known shortcoming:** 'mersennetwister' baseline is the reference MT19937 C code, not std::mt19937; only C-library baseline is rand().

**Known shortcoming:** No std:: generator timed; speed run fills only a 4 KB buffer through a function pointer with -march=native (in-cache throughput); headers keep static global state, not thread-safe (aesctr has aesctr_r); lehmer64 needs __uint128_t; aesctr compiles to nothing without __AES__.

**How:** lehmer64 is a 128-bit multiplicative LCG (one 64x64->128 multiply per output, returning the high 64 bits; about 1.75 instructions per byte). aesctr runs AES-128 rounds (AES-NI _mm_aesenc_si128) in counter mode over 4 interleaved counters, buffering 64 bytes per refill so the AES latency is hidden by instruction-level parallelism. Both pass BigCrush and PractRand 512 GB in the repo's runs, unlike the faster-looking xorshift/xoroshiro variants.

**Use it when:**
- Choosing a fast non-cryptographic 64-bit generator for simulation, sampling or randomized algorithms, with statistical-test results to back the choice
- Bulk generation on x86-64 with AES-NI where aesctr's ~5.35 GB/s (vs ~1.68 GB/s for MT19937) matters
- Portable fast 64-bit output on GCC/Clang targets with __uint128_t: lehmer64 is ~10 lines and passes BigCrush and PractRand
- Replacing MT19937 or rand() in hot loops: MT fails PractRand (BRank) in this repo and is ~1.8x slower than lehmer64
- Benchmarking your own generator: the harness gives a ready speed + TestU01 + PractRand pipeline

**Skip it when:**
- Cryptographic or adversarial settings: these are non-cryptographic generators; aesctr uses the seed as the AES key with a zero high half, and the repo makes no security claim
- Multithreaded code using the headers as-is: every generator keeps static global state (aesctr has a reentrant aesctr_r(state*) variant; lehmer64 does not)
- MSVC or 32-bit targets: lehmer64 needs __uint128_t; aesctr compiles to nothing unless __AES__ is defined
- Latency-bound single-draw code: the README says the benchmark stresses throughput, and aesctr's 64-byte refill makes per-call cost uneven
- Where you need a std::uniform_random_bit_generator class with distributions, jump-ahead or streams: the headers are bare C functions
