**Integration:** source-drop · none for the generator headers (each includes splitmix64.h for seeding); the harness needs CMake 3.20+, C++20, lemire/counters via CPM, TestU01 (bundled zip) and PractRand · Headers: C99 with GCC/Clang extensions (__uint128_t, __builtin_expect, immintrin.h); harness: C++20, GCC 14+ or Clang 17+ recommended · lehmer64: any 64-bit GCC/Clang target; aesctr: x86-64 with AES-NI only; README assumes Linux or macOS on x64

**Vs siblings:** Pick testingRNG's headers when you want a scalar generator with published BigCrush and PractRand results side by side with speed; SHISHUA and xoshiro8x256pp are much faster for bulk SIMD fills, and Randen is the choice if you need attack-resistant output, while simdpcg/SIMDxorshift only accelerate a single family.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'mersennetwister' baseline is the reference Nishimura/Matsumoto C code, not libstdc++ std::mt19937; no std:: generator is timed. The only C library baseline is rand() (0.28 GB/s)
- The speed binary is built with -march=native and fills a 4 KB buffer through a function pointer, so numbers measure in-cache throughput and may not carry to other CPUs or ARM (README warns)
- aesctr.h is wrapped in #ifdef __AES__; without -maes/-march=native it silently defines nothing
- lehmer64 is an LCG: low bits of the 128-bit state are weak, which is why it returns only the high 64 bits; do not change it to return the low half

**Status:** Actively maintained (speed table refreshed 2026-09-21), Apache-2.0, and each generator is a small standalone header that is easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/lemire/testingRNG) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lemire/testingRNG)

##### VectorizedRNG.jl (SIMD Xoshiro256++ for Julia)  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Julia SIMD xoshiro-style RNG with vectorized Box-Muller; about 2x Julia's old dSFMT MersenneTwister for randn! (1.5-3.4x for rand!).

**Beats:** Julia Base default RNG of the time (dSFMT-based MersenneTwister, a SIMD-oriented Mersenne Twister variant) — The README's BenchmarkTools minimum times for filling a 1024-element Vector{Float64} compare Base's then-default dSFMT MersenneTwister with local_rng(): randn! 7.235 us vs 3.744 us and rand! 791 ns vs 513 ns on an unspecified AVX2 Haswell, and randn! 1.676 us vs 854 ns and rand! 549.9 ns vs 159.9 ns on an Intel i7-1165G7 (AVX-512) under Julia 1.6.0-DEV.1581 with LLVM 11. No C++ std:: baseline is involved, and Julia's current Xoshiro-based default was not measured.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: not true Xoshiro256++ (output rotr23 missing +s0; state rotr45 = rotl19), so the standard jump constants are invalid and stream separation/period are unproven; claim kept because the baseline is MT, not xoshiro; Julia.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug (src/api.jl line 266): in samplevector!, when alpha is an ordinary number (anything except StaticInt(0)), the main loop reuses z1 for the second W-chunk, so adjacent chunks get identical draws; tests check only the mean. Nonstandard xoshiro; NEON randn! 69% slower (#20); dependency VectorizationBase deprecated for Julia 1.11 unless maintained; baseline is old dSFMT, never compared with current Julia Xoshiro. Julia, not callable from C++.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each thread owns XREGISTERS = 2 SIMD registers of independent xoshiro-style states, so 8 streams on AVX2 or 16 on AVX-512, spaced by the xoshiro256 2^128 jump polynomial. A bulk fill advances all lanes at once with integer shift/xor/rotate vector ops, converts bits to floats with mask tricks (vpternlog on AVX-512), and writes two vectors per loop iteration with masked tail stores. Normals come from a SIMD Box-Muller transform using Remez-fitted polynomial sin/cos and log approximations, whereas Julia's MersenneTwister randn uses a scalar ziggurat; the README credits most of the randn! gain to this.

**Use it when:**
- Julia code filling medium Float64 arrays (around 1024 elements, the size benchmarked) with normals, where the README shows 7.235 us to 3.744 us on AVX2 Haswell and 1.676 us to 854 ns on an AVX-512 i7-1165G7
- AVX-512 x86 machines, where uniform rand! went from 549.9 ns to 159.9 ns (about 3.4x, derived from page data)
- Monte Carlo kernels that need in-place scaled noise via randn!(rng, x, StaticInt(0), β, γ), i.e. x = γ·z + β without a temporary
- Statistical work where per-thread streams are enough and bit reproducibility across machines is not needed

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs a C or C++ library: this is a Julia package built on VectorizationBase.jl and SLEEFPirates.jl
- Code that relies on the documented xoshiro256++ algorithm, its period or its 2^128 stream spacing: src/xoshiro.jl drops the '+ s0' output term and rotates s3 right by 45 (a left rotation by 19, not 45), so it is a nonstandard variant and the reused xoshiro256 jump constants do not establish stream separation
- Current Julia (1.7+): the README's baseline is the old dSFMT MersenneTwister; Julia's default RNG is now a per-task Xoshiro256++ with its own SIMD bulk path (Julia Random docs, seen only via search snippets), and no comparison against it is published
- Apple M1/NEON: open issue #20 reports randn! at about 2.85 us vs 1.69 us for the default RNG (about 69% slower) and no faster rand!
- Large arrays that spill out of cache, or long-term maintenance: issue #4 argues the gain fades beyond about 2048 elements, and VectorizationBase.jl's README says it is 'looking for new maintainers, otherwise deprecated in Julia 1.11'

**Integration:** module (Julia package, registered; version 0.2.26) · VectorizationBase.jl (0.19.38, 0.20.1 or 0.21), SLEEFPirates.jl 0.6.29+, UnPack.jl, Random, Distributed, Requires; optional StaticArraysCore extension · Julia 1.6 (Project.toml compat) · x86-64 best (AVX2, AVX-512 where it shines); aarch64 NEON runs but is slower than Base for randn! per issue #20; vector width picked by VectorizationBase at load

**Vs siblings:** Pick this only inside Julia, where it is the ready-made SIMD normal and uniform filler. From C++, simdrng gives verified lane-correct xoshiro256++ with SIMD bulk fill, and EigenRand or the normaldist-benchmark Box-Muller code cover vectorized normals; simd-rand is the Rust equivalent.

**Gotchas:**
- Bug in the scaled in-place path: when α is passed as an ordinary number (anything other than StaticInt(0)), the main loop of samplevector! in src/api.jl line 266 uses z₁ for the second vector, so each pair of adjacent W-element chunks gets identical random draws; only the tail block uses z₂. The default rand!/randn! (α = StaticInt(0)) path is correct, and the test only checks the mean, so it does not catch this.
- Seeding is separate from Base: the generator is seeded from Base's global RNG at load time, Random.seed! has no effect, and VectorizedRNG.seed!(n) reseeds every thread's streams at once.
- Results depend on SIMD width and thread count: streams are interleaved across 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX-512) lanes per thread, so the same seed gives different sequences on different machines.
- The README itself reports that its BigCrush run on a 10980XE was slower than MersenneTwister's (511.5 s vs 481.8 s) and warns 'Watch out when mixing vectorized and non-vectorized code' (AVX-512 downclocking).

**Status:** MIT-licensed and registered, but effectively in maintenance mode: the only 2026 commits (May 27) fix compat entries, the previous code change was October 2023, 8 issues are open, and its VectorizationBase.jl dependency is seeking maintainers; 36 stars.

[repo](https://github.com/JuliaSIMD/VectorizedRNG.jl) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JuliaSIMD/VectorizedRNG.jl/HEAD/README.md)

##### VMT19937 (V-family and X-family vectorized Mersenne Twister)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only SIMD Mersenne Twister (MT19937, MT19937-64, SFMT); bulk fills 3.7-4.9x std::mt19937_64 on AVX2/AVX-512, X-family bit-identical.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (STL-MT19937 / STL-MT19937-64 rows); also the original reference MT19937 / MT19937-64 / SFMT19937 and Intel MKL MT/SFMT — The author's perf.cpp harness (GCC 16; -O3 -std=c++20 with -march=native or explicit ISA flags; volatile traps against dead-code elimination) measured millions of samples per second on five CPUs: Celeron J4125 (SSE4.2), Xeon E5-2686 v4 (AVX2), Xeon Platinum 8375C (AVX-512), Neoverse-N1 (NEON) and Neoverse-V1 (SVE256). In block mode (10,240 values per call) V-MT19937-64 reached 1161 and 2865 M/s against 317 and 590 for libstdc++ std::mt19937_64 on the AVX2 and AVX-512 Xeons. The STL 'vectorial' figures are copied from its per-call loop, since std::mt19937 has no block API (doc/main.tex footnote).

**Known shortcoming:** README leaves out the std::mt19937 32-bit row present in doc/main.tex (V-MT 7.8-9.8x faster, derived); README and tex AVX-512 numbers differ; MKL beats V-MT on AVX-512.

**Known shortcoming:** README parallel-streams example yields 10 identical generators (same seed, same jump). On NEON/SVE 64-bit, std::mt19937_64 ties or wins. The STL 'vectorial' figures are copied from its scalar loop. ISA is compile-time only (#error on SSE2-only builds). No URBG interface.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The V-family is inter-state vectorization: SIMD lane i holds its own MT19937 state jumped ahead by roughly P/N steps (x^J mod the characteristic polynomial, Haramoto et al.'s polynomial jump), so the twist and tempering run at full register width with no remainder iterations or misaligned word groups. The X-family vectorizes the single-state recurrence with shifts and blends, which caps its gain. Both families regenerate and temper the whole state in bulk and serve values from a cache-aligned buffer, which is why even one-value-per-call use beats the reference code by 1.5-3.5x (doc/main.tex).

**Use it when:**
- You must keep Mersenne Twister output: XMT19937_64 matches std::mt19937_64 for the same seed and ran 1095 vs 590 M/s per call (AVX-512) and 2525 vs 590 M/s in bulk (about 4.3x, derived from page data)
- Bulk generation on x86 with AVX2 or AVX-512 where a different MT-quality stream is acceptable: V-MT19937-64 reached 1161 (AVX2) and 2865 (AVX-512) M/s vs 317 and 590 for std::mt19937_64
- Many independent MT streams for Monte Carlo (finance is the author's target), using the shipped jump-polynomial files or the jump_generator tool to space instances
- 32-bit output on AVX2: V-MT19937 vectorial 2392 M/s vs 305.7 for std::mt19937 (about 7.8x, derived from doc/main.tex)
- Faster SFMT: V-SFMT19937 10943 M/s vs 4445 for the reference SFMT at AVX-512

**Skip it when:**
- ARM NEON or SVE for 64-bit output: std::mt19937_64 matched or beat it (NEON vectorial STL 285 vs X 255 and V 290 M/s; SVE256 scalar STL 573 vs V 513)
- AVX-512 bulk 32-bit MT where MKL is available: MKL-MT was faster than V-MT19937 (6479 vs 5742 M/s README, 6578.9 vs 5841.4 in doc/main.tex), and X-MT19937 also beat V-MT19937 there because the 16-state V-MT19937 needs about 40 KB of state and overflows L1
- Portable binaries for baseline x86-64: the ISA is fixed at compile time (no runtime dispatch), and simd_config.h stops with '#error SSE4.2 is needed' for SSE2-only flags or 'AVX2 is needed' for AVX-only flags
- Code that wants a drop-in engine for <random> distributions: there is no operator()/result_type/min/max, so you need a small adapter
- Teams that want an established dependency: single author, 3 stars, no tagged releases, and one open issue (MKL comparison request)

**Integration:** header-only (include/ directory; RandGen.h plus polynomial_jump.h); V-family also needs the ~4 KB dat/poly/*.bits jump files at runtime · none for the library; Intel MKL and TestU01 optional for the benchmark and test executables · C++20; README lists GCC 13+, Clang 16+ or MSVC 2022 (/std:c++20); bundled executables need GNU make · x86-64 with SSE4.2, AVX2 or AVX-512 (F/VL/BW/DQ plus PCLMUL in the Makefile), aarch64 NEON and SVE (256-bit vector length); chosen at compile time via SIMD_N_BITS/SIMD_ISA or compiler flags

**Vs siblings:** Pick VMT19937 over pXart, SFMT or cslarsen/mersenne-twister when you need Mersenne Twister specifically and want AVX-512, NEON and SVE paths, a bit-identical X-family, plus jump-ahead tooling for parallel streams. If you are free to change algorithm, simdrng (xoshiro256++/Philox) or SHISHUA give more throughput per core with far smaller state.

**Gotchas:**
- The README's 'Multiple Independent Generators' example builds 10 generators with the same seed and the same 2^100 commonJump, so all ten emit identical streams; the code comment admits you would need commonJump^i. Pre-compute distinct jumps per instance.
- V-family output depends on VRegBitLen, not the ISA: fix the template width (e.g. VMT19937<512>) to get the same stream on AVX2 and AVX-512 hosts, and load the jump file that matches it (J19934 for 256-bit MT32, etc.). Polynomial::fromBinFile does not check the generator type (loadWithCheck does).
- Constructing a V-family generator without a sequential jump throws std::logic_error ('Having multiple states and no sequential jump provided does not make sense'); missing files also fail through MYASSERT exceptions, so plan for exceptions at init.
- QryBlk16 switches the API at compile time: with it, genrand_uint32() fails a static_assert and you must use genrand_uint32_blk16(dst) (dst ideally 64-byte aligned); without it, only per-value and anySize calls exist.

**Status:** Active (393 commits, last commit 2026-05-29) and MIT-licensed, so easy to vendor, but single-author with 3 stars and no releases; the paper source is in doc/main.tex.

[repo](https://github.com/fabiocannizzo/VMT19937) · [benchmark](https://github.com/fabiocannizzo/VMT19937)

##### vphilox  `C++`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++20 SIMD Philox4x32-10 engine; bulk fill runs 1.3-4.6x std::mt19937 throughput, seekable and reproducible.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 (also compared with xoshiro256++ and PCG64) — With the project's Google Benchmark harness (GCC 13.3 on x86, GCC 12.2 on the Pi, CMake Release plus per-kernel ISA flags, pinned to one CPU), bulk generate_n (AVX-512 kernel on the x86 matrix runs, NEON on the Pi) cost 0.22-0.75x the cycles per byte of libstdc++ std::mt19937 on the same machine across a Raspberry Pi 5 (NEON), Sapphire Rapids, Skylake-SP and two Cascade Lake hosts, i.e. 1.3x to 4.6x the throughput; per-value operator() ranged from 0.51x to 1.15x. All numbers are first-party, and cycles/byte is only compared within one machine.

**Known shortcoming:** Loses to xoshiro256++ on 4 of 5 machines (wins are vs other counter-based engines); 0 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party only; untagged, 0 stars, one author. xoshiro256++ is cheaper per byte on 4 of 5 CPUs; operator() on a Raspberry Pi 5 is 0.87x mt19937. Copying include/ alone does not compile because vphilox.hpp needs the CMake-generated version.hpp.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Philox blocks are independent, so the kernels run many counters in parallel in a structure-of-arrays lane layout: 8 counters per iteration under AVX2, 16 under AVX-512 (native unsigned compare and mask registers for the counter carry) and 8 under NEON as two groups of four; each 32x32->64 multiply is done with _mm*_mul_epu32 on even and odd lanes plus a repack. The kernel is picked once at first use by CPUID/XGETBV runtime dispatch, with [[gnu::target]] attributes so one binary runs on any x86-64. generate_n writes straight into the caller's buffer and skips the 64-word refill buffer that operator() drains, which the project measures as 1.5-2.4x faster than the per-value path.

**Use it when:**
- Parallel Monte Carlo or simulation where each thread or task needs its own independent stream with no locks, and results must not change with thread count.
- Jobs that checkpoint and resume, possibly on another machine or standard library, where std::mt19937's library-specific stream format is a problem.
- Filling large buffers (a few hundred values per call or more) of u32 or float on x86-64 with AVX2/AVX-512 or on aarch64 with NEON.
- Replacing std::mt19937 behind std::shuffle or <random> distributions when you also want O(1) skip-ahead (discard) for stream partitioning.
- Cross-checking a CPU simulation against GPU code that uses Philox (the repo documents a seeding mapping to NVIDIA cuRAND).

**Skip it when:**
- Raw bits per byte with no need for seeking or reproducibility: xoshiro256++ is cheaper per byte on four of the five benchmarked CPUs (vphilox wins only on Skylake-SP).
- Hot loops that draw one value at a time on ARM: per-value operator() is 0.87x the speed of std::mt19937 on a Raspberry Pi 5, and the per-value path is 1.5-2.4x slower than generate_n everywhere.
- Projects that need a released, packaged dependency: no tag yet (API may still change), no vcpkg/Conan package (open issue #65), single author, 0 stars.
- Pre-C++20 toolchains, or GPU kernels (CPU only; no CUDA/HIP backend).
- Small bulk calls: an 8-word generate_n costs 1.4-1.9x the raw kernel per byte; the overhead fades only by about 256 words.

**Integration:** header-only · none at runtime; CMake configure generates vphilox/version.hpp; GoogleTest and Google Benchmark are fetched only for tests/benchmarks · C++20; CMake 3.24+ for the build/install; CI covers GCC and Clang on Linux, Apple Clang on macOS arm64, and MSVC on Windows · x86-64 (AVX2 or AVX-512F+DQ selected at runtime, scalar fallback), aarch64 (NEON), any other target via the scalar kernel

**Vs siblings:** Pick vphilox over OpenRAND or the benchmark-rngs PhiloxSIMD prototype when you need a CPU-only Philox with runtime-dispatched AVX2/AVX-512/NEON, bit-identical output across backends and a portable checkpoint format; pick OpenRAND if you need the same generator on GPUs, and simdrng or a SIMD xoshiro when raw throughput matters more than seekability.

**Gotchas:**
- vphilox.hpp includes vphilox/version.hpp, which CMake generates from version.hpp.in, so copying include/ alone without configuring or installing will not compile.
- counter() returns where the next refill starts, not the stream position; rebuilding an engine from key() and counter() silently skips up to 64 buffered outputs. Use state()/set_state() or the serialize.hpp stream operators.
- Size thread pools by physical cores: the kernel is execution-port-bound, and two workers on hyperthread siblings each lose about a third of their throughput.
- The VPHILOX_BACKEND environment variable (scalar/avx2/avx512/neon) is read once per process at first use; next_double() consumes two 32-bit words.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-08-31), MIT OR Apache-2.0 and header-only so it is easy to vendor, but untagged with a CalVer 2026.08.1 version, 0 stars and one author; the bit stream is declared frozen even though the API may change.

[repo](https://github.com/sinhaparth5/vphilox) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sinhaparth5/vphilox/HEAD/docs/benchmarks/README.md)

##### FastShuffleExperiments (nearly divisionless bounded random integers)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Benchmark and reference code for Lemire's nearly divisionless bounded random integers; Fisher-Yates shuffles about 8-10x faster than std::shuffle.

**Beats:** std::shuffle (same underlying PRNG), plus OpenBSD-style and Java-style bounded-integer generation — On the repo's own sample run (g++/clang++ -std=c++11 -O3, CPU and compiler version not stated), shuffling 1000-element uint32_t arrays with lehmer64 took 1.88 ns/element (32-bit words) and 1.86 ns/element (64-bit) with the nearly divisionless method versus 18.66 and 15.28 ns/element for std::shuffle driven by the same generator, about 10x and 8x. A WebSearch summary of the paper (not opened) says its figures were measured on an Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.4 GHz) with GCC 5.4 -O3 -march=native, where std::shuffle performed close to the OpenBSD-like method.

**Known shortcoming:** Sample output has no CPU or compiler version; current libstdc++ already uses this technique, so the gain over today's std::shuffle is smaller.

**Known shortcoming:** Experiment code, not a library: global lehmer64 state, uint32_t arrays only, needs __uint128_t (no MSVC). Float variants are biased. The precomputed column leaves index generation out of the timing.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Instead of x % n, it multiplies the random word by n into a double-width product (64-bit for 32-bit words, __uint128_t for 64-bit words) and takes the high half as the result; the low half tells whether the draw falls in the biased region, and only then (probability below n/2^L) does it compute -n % n and possibly redraw. So almost every bounded integer costs one multiply and one compare instead of one or two hardware divisions, while staying exactly unbiased. The benchmark pairs it with lehmer64, a 128-bit multiplicative generator that is itself one multiply per output.

**Use it when:**
- You need unbiased random integers in [0, n) or a Fisher-Yates shuffle in a hot loop and your toolchain's std::uniform_int_distribution / std::shuffle still uses division-based rejection (MSVC STL, libc++ or an older libstdc++; check yours).
- Writing your own shuffle, reservoir sampler or random index picker in C/C++ and want a short Apache-2.0 reference for the correct multiply-and-reject code (32-bit and 64-bit variants).
- Arrays from a few elements up to about 10^6 that fit in cache, where range reduction dominates: the sample run shows 1.8-1.9 ns/element versus 15-19 ns for std::shuffle.
- Reproducing or extending the TOMACS paper's figures (make benchmark / make plot in TOMACS_RCR).

**Skip it when:**
- As a library dependency: it is experiment code with global generator state, uint32_t-only arrays and no packaging or tests beyond a permutation check; copy the bounded-integer function instead.
- When your standard library already uses this method: the README says GNU libstdc++ adopted it for std::uniform_int_distribution, so the gap against a current libstdc++ std::shuffle is smaller than the sample output shows.
- MSVC or 32-bit targets without __uint128_t: the 64-bit variants and the lehmer64 generator need 128-bit integer support.
- Very large arrays (10^7 to 10^9 elements), where cache misses dominate and every method slows to roughly 6-47 ns/element; the nearly divisionless shuffle is still fastest of the unbuffered methods but by a smaller factor (about 3.6-3.8x vs std::shuffle at 10^9 in the sample run).
- When you need batched or SIMD generation of many bounded integers: Lemire's later batched technique is a separate project.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (C++ standard library only; gnuplot 5.2 only for the RCR figures) · C++11 (-std=c++11 in the Makefile); GCC or Clang for __uint128_t; README assumes a Linux-like system · 64-bit targets whose compiler provides __uint128_t (e.g. x86-64, aarch64 with GCC/Clang); not MSVC

**Vs siblings:** Pick this as the C++ reference for the range-reduction step (unbiased integers in [0, n) and shuffling), which fastrand ports to Python; generator siblings such as testingRNG (lehmer64, aesctr) or simdrng speed up the raw random bits instead, so they combine with this method rather than compete with it.

**Gotchas:**
- The generator is passed as a template parameter that must be a function pointer to a global-state function; a std:: engine object cannot be plugged in without a wrapper, so std::shuffle's column uses a small URBG wrapper around the same lehmer64 function.
- The float/double-multiplication variants use only 24 or 53 random bits and are not exactly unbiased; use only the nearly divisionless variant if fairness matters.
- The 'precomputed random indexes' column (about 0.9 ns/element) excludes index generation from the timing, so it is a lower bound, not a usable shuffle.
- The RCR README's sample numbers carry no CPU or compiler and say 'the exact numbers will vary'; the RCR gnuplot script plots the 32-bit Figure 3a std::shuffle series from the 64-bit rows.

**Status:** Stale research code (last commit 2024-03-12, no issues filed) under Apache-2.0; the technique matters more than the repo, which is small enough to copy from and is already absorbed into libstdc++, Abseil, Go, Swift, Julia, Zig and NumPy per the README.

[repo](https://github.com/lemire/FastShuffleExperiments) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lemire/FastShuffleExperiments/master/TOMACS_RCR/README.md)

##### SFMT (SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Saito and Matsumoto's 128-bit SIMD variant of the Mersenne Twister; about 2.3-2.8x faster than MT19937-64 for bulk 64-bit output.

**Beats:** MT19937-64 reference implementation (mt19937-64.c from the MT homepage; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64) — In the README of Harase and Kimoto's ACM TOMS 2018 companion repo (melg-64), generating 1e9 64-bit integers with SIMD SFMT19937 took 1.8457 s vs 5.1002 s for the reference mt19937-64.c on a Core i7-3770, and 2.8806 s vs 6.6490 s on a Phenom II X6 1045T: about 2.8x and 2.3x (derived from page data). Both were built with gcc -O3 on Linux, gcc version not stated. Without SIMD, SFMT was only about 1.2x faster. The baseline is the original C reference, not libstdc++ std::mt19937_64.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B rests on the MELG-64 TOMS table (SFMT homepage blocked here); check.sh diffs SIMD builds against scalar output, so the SIMD path is the same generator.

**Known shortcoming:** SIMD is off unless -DHAVE_SSE2/NEON is passed; avx2-check covers M19937 only. SFMT19937 reportedly fails 4/106 BigCrush tests (MatrixRank/LinearComp; search snippet only). howto-compile sample3 uses the removed pre-1.4 API. Abandoned 2021; NEON PR #10 (2026-01) unmerged.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The recursion works on 128-bit words (four 32-bit lanes) using only shifts, ANDs with a mask and XORs, so one SIMD instruction sequence produces 128 bits per step. The pick-up position (POS1=122 for 19937) and the lag-1/lag-2 feedback words (r1, r2) are chosen to keep dependency chains short. The block functions (sfmt_fill_array32/64) generate directly into the output array without copying the state. Since 1.5.2 an AVX2 path (SFMT-avx256.h, contributed by Masaki Ota) does two 128-bit steps per 256-bit operation and uses vpternlog under AVX-512VL. This relies on SL1 >= 16, so the dependent half-word term shifts out. A NEON path (SFMT-neon.h, optional SHA3 EOR3/BCAX) covers AArch64.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk generation of 32-bit integers or doubles from an MT-family generator (Monte Carlo, simulation) where you can call sfmt_fill_array32/64 into a 16-byte-aligned buffer
- Codebases that want a peer-reviewed, long-period (2^19937-1 or larger) F2-linear generator with jump-ahead for parallel streams (jump/ directory)
- x86-64 with SSE2/AVX2 or AArch64 with NEON, where the SIMD path is enabled explicitly at build time
- Replacing std::mt19937 when the exact MT19937 sequence does not matter but MT-style period and equidistribution analysis do

**Skip it when:**
- You need std::mt19937 / std::mt19937_64 bit-identical output (use a vectorized MT19937 such as VMT19937 instead)
- 64-bit integer output where high-dimensional equidistribution matters: Harase and Kimoto give SFMT19937-64 Delta=14095 vs 7820 for MT19937-64 and 0 for MELG19937-64. SFMT is tuned for 32-bit output, and dSFMT is the variant meant for doubles
- Small-state or many-instance uses (per-thread or per-object generators): the 19937 state is SFMT_N = 156 128-bit words (about 2.5 KB), versus 256 bits for xoshiro256-class generators
- Applications that care about TestU01 linearity tests: like all F2-linear generators, SFMT fails MatrixRank/LinearComp (per a search snippet, 4 of 106 BigCrush tests; source page not opened)
- Big-endian or AltiVec targets: the README says these 'ARE NOT TESTED AT ALL'

**Integration:** source-drop (SFMT.c + headers; CMakeLists.txt builds a static libSFMT.a) · none for the generator; the jump-ahead polynomial calculator (jump/calc-jump) needs NTL · C99 (Makefile uses -std=c99); gcc 3.4+ for SSE2 per howto-compile.html; MSVC supported via SFMT-sse2-msc.h; callable from C++ via extern "C" · any (portable C path); SIMD paths for x86 SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512VL (256-bit), ARM NEON (AArch64 and ARMv7 Makefiles), PowerPC AltiVec (untested)

**Vs siblings:** Pick SFMT over VMT19937 or pXart when you do not need the std::mt19937 sequence and want the original authors' peer-reviewed SIMD design with jump-ahead and many period choices. Pick MELG-64 instead for 64-bit output with full equidistribution, and xoshiro-family SIMD generators (simdrng, Xoshiro256PlusSIMD) for small state and no linearity-test failures.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD is off by default: you must pass -DHAVE_SSE2 (or HAVE_NEON / HAVE_ALTIVEC) plus the ISA flag, otherwise the plain C recursion is compiled even on x86-64. The AVX2 path is chosen automatically when __AVX2__ is defined together with HAVE_SSE2. CMake's USE_SSE2 passes -msse rather than -msse2.
- SFMT_MEXP must be identical in every translation unit because it changes sizeof(sfmt_t); if it is missing, gcc warns and assumes 19937.
- sfmt_fill_array32/64 require a 16-byte-aligned buffer on SIMD builds, a size that is a multiple of 4 (or 2) and at least SFMT_N32 (624) or SFMT_N64 (312) elements, and a freshly initialized or fully consumed state. They cannot be mixed with sequential calls without re-initializing, and gen_rand64 must not follow gen_rand32 (enforced only by assert).
- howto-compile.html sample3 still uses the pre-1.4 global API (init_gen_rand, genrand_res53) that no longer exists; follow sample1/2 and SFMT.h instead.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2021-05-18 (an open NEON update PR #10 from January 2026 is unmerged), but the 3-clause BSD code is small, stable since 2006 and easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/MersenneTwister-Lab/SFMT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/sharase/melg-64)

#### sparse-and-solvers

##### Kokkos Kernels SpGEMM (KKSPGEMM / KKMEM)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception`  `active`  `Tier A`

Portable Kokkos SpGEMM (hash-accumulator KKSPGEMM) that beat CUDA 8 cuSPARSE and MKL 18 sparse multiply in 2018 tests.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE SpGEMM (CUDA 8.0.44) on P100; Intel MKL sparse-sparse multiply (MKL-INS, MKL7, MKL8 variants; intel-18.0.128) on Knights Landing — 2018 wiki data (Kokkos 2.50 / Kokkos Kernels 2.60, symbolic plus numeric, 81-83 SuiteSparse products, best time over thread counts). On a Tesla P100 with CUDA 8.0.44 and gcc 5.4, KKSPGEMM beat cuSPARSE by a 3.61x geomean (faster on 75 of 81) but lost to Nsparse (0.92x). On 68-core KNL with icpc and MKL 18.0.128 it beat MKL by 1.19-1.25x (inspector-executor) and 1.79-3.75x (two-phase variants), and on Power8 it beat ViennaCL OpenMP by 2.79x; all ratios were derived from the linked xlsx tables.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A rests on the 2018-era P100 vs cuSPARSE (CUDA 8.0.44) SpGEMM tables; the MKL 18.0.128 KNL rows state no CPU SKU, and the P100 comparison with Nsparse is 0.92x overall (28 of 77 matrices won). Compiler on the configure page is Intel 18.0.128, not 18.2.199 as the record said (corrected).

**Known shortcoming:** The handle default SPGEMM_DEFAULT dispatches to cuSPARSE, rocSPARSE or MKL when the TPL is enabled, so a default build may run the baseline; SPGEMM_KK must be requested explicitly. Open issues #1542 (OpenMP hang with GCC 10 and ARMPL 21), #1668 (SYCL hang on a tiny matrix), #2291 (segfault on uk-2005, OpenMP aarch64). Needs C++20 via Kokkos 5.1.1+. The spECK PPoPP '20 paper (snippet only, tugraz.at blocked) found KokkosKernels best on only 3 of 2,263 matrices at 2730% of the best time on average: an independent counter-benchmark.

**Independent measurement:** verifier re-derived every ratio in claimed_speedup from the four SpGEMM_Benchmarks xlsx tables

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Row-wise (Gustavson) two-phase SpGEMM. The symbolic phase compresses B's column indices into bit sets so structure counting touches fewer words. The numeric phase accumulates each output row in a two-level hash map: level 1 in team scratch (GPU shared) memory, level 2 in chunks from a pre-allocated uniform memory pool in global memory. On CPUs it switches to dense accumulators when the problem looks dense. Team and vector sizes are chosen from a flop estimate per row, and one templated source covers the CPU and GPU backends (the Deveci et al. 'Multi-threaded Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication for Many-Core and GPU Architectures' design).

**Use it when:**
- You need one SpGEMM code path across OpenMP CPUs and NVIDIA, AMD (HIP) or Intel (SYCL) GPUs instead of maintaining cuSPARSE, rocSPARSE and MKL calls separately.
- Repeated products with fixed sparsity and changing values, such as algebraic multigrid setup (A*P, R*AP): run symbolic once and reuse the handle for numeric.
- Your code already uses Kokkos or Trilinos (Tpetra builds on Kokkos Kernels), so the dependency is already paid for.
- Many-core CPUs where vendor sparse-sparse multiply is weak: in the 2018 KNL runs it beat MKL 18's two-phase variants by 1.8-3.75x geomean.
- You also want the graph kernels that share the machinery (graph coloring, triangle counting, Gauss-Seidel with coloring).

**Skip it when:**
- Peak CUDA-only SpGEMM throughput: the repo's own 2018 P100 tables put Nsparse ahead (KKSPGEMM 0.92x geomean, faster on 28 of 77), and the spECK paper (PPoPP '20, search snippet only) found KokkosKernels best on 3 of 2,263 matrices, at 2730% of the best method's time on average; GPU-specific codes like spECK or OpSparse are faster.
- You need current numbers: the only published comparison is from 2018 (CUDA 8 cuSPARSE, MKL 18.0, P100, KNL), and today's perf_test driver no longer runs the vendor baselines.
- Small or one-off products in a code without Kokkos: you must build Kokkos plus Kokkos Kernels with explicit template instantiation, which takes a long time and now requires C++20.
- Distributed-memory SpGEMM: the kernels are local to one process; MPI distribution has to come from a layer such as Tpetra.
- Very large graphs on some CPU backends: issue #2291 reports a numeric-phase segfault on uk-2005 (39.5M rows, OpenMP, aarch64), and issue #1542 (open) reports openmp.sparse_spgemm hanging with GCC 10 and ARMPL 21.

**Integration:** static or shared lib (CMake or Spack), with explicit template instantiation (ETI) for the scalar, ordinal, offset and device types chosen at configure time · Kokkos core (current develop requires Kokkos 5.1.1+); optional TPLs cuSPARSE, rocSPARSE, MKL, cuBLAS, BLAS/LAPACK, MAGMA · C++20, inherited from Kokkos 5 (Kokkos changelog: GCC 10.4+ for C++20; CMake 3.25.2 for CUDA C++20); Kokkos Kernels' own CMake minimum is 3.16 · any Kokkos backend: Serial, OpenMP, Threads, CUDA, HIP, SYCL; x86-64, aarch64, Power, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs

**Vs siblings:** Pick Kokkos Kernels over spECK, OpSparse or TileSpGEMM when you need a maintained, vendor-portable library that also runs on CPUs and AMD or Intel GPUs and supports symbolic reuse. Pick those CUDA-only research codes when raw NVIDIA SpGEMM speed is the only goal; their papers report wins over cuSPARSE and nsparse, which Kokkos Kernels does not beat.

**Gotchas:**
- The handle's default SPGEMM_DEFAULT dispatches to the vendor TPL (cuSPARSE on CUDA, rocSPARSE on HIP, MKL) when that TPL is enabled at build time, so the default path can be the baseline itself. Request SPGEMM_KK to get the native kernel that was benchmarked; the README says KKMEM is outdated and KKSPGEMM is the default native algorithm. Issue #3153 (closed July 2026) was a regression in this routing.
- A handle cannot be reused for a product with a different sparsity pattern; spgemm_symbolic throws if the rowptrs or entries of A or B differ from the first call.
- On GPUs the level-2 hash pool is capped at half of the free device memory and rounded down to a power-of-two number of chunks, so on a nearly full device teams share chunks and contend.
- Correctness reports exist on less-tested backends: wrong entries with HIP at -O0 on MI50 (#2083, closed), a hang on tiny matrices with SYCL (#1668, open), and a float unit-test failure on serial and OpenMP (#2232, closed).

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-01; release 5.2.0, which needs Kokkos 5.1.1+), Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, 403 stars, used under Trilinos; the SpGEMM benchmark wiki is deprecated and reproducing it needs the 2.6.00-era tag.

[repo](https://github.com/kokkos/kokkos-kernels) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/kokkos/kokkos-kernels/SpGEMM_Benchmarks.md)

##### merge-spmv (merge-based CsrMV)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Merge-path load-balanced CSR SpMV (SC'16) for CPU and GPU; about 1.2x over MKL on average, wins big on skewed rows.

**Beats:** Intel MKL CSR SpMV; NVIDIA cuSPARSE csrmv — SC'16 paper over 4,201 SuiteSparse matrices, fp64. CPU, built with icpc 16 -O3 -xHost on dual Xeon E5-2690/2695 v2: harmonic-mean 1.21x vs MKL CsrMV (range 0.51-15.8x), 1.26x for the NUMA variant. GPU on a Tesla K40 with CUDA 7.5: 0.84x vs cuSPARSE CsrMV overall (1.13x on matrices above 300K nnz) and 1.29x vs cuSPARSE HybMV.

**Known shortcoming:** On GPU it averages 0.84x of cuSPARSE CsrMV (a loss); CPU average 1.21x over MKL; last commit 2017 (abandoned); paper and README name different Xeon models.

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #5 (Dec 2025): 4x slower than row-parallel SpMV inside a CG solver on 6 threads; GPU path uses cub::DeviceSpmv, deprecated in CCCL 2.8 and removed in 3.0; fixed 256-entry carry arrays overflow above 256 threads; int coordinates (rows+nnz < 2^31).

**Independent measurement:** SC'16 paper appendix: icc 16.0.1, -O3 -xHost -fno-alias -mkl

**How:** It treats the parallel split as a logical merge of the CSR row-end offsets with the nonzero indices 0..nnz-1. That merge path is cut into equal-length diagonals, one per thread, and each thread binary-searches its start coordinate (MergePathSearch). Every thread gets the same rows+nonzeros work no matter how skewed the row lengths are. Rows that span threads are patched in a carry-out fix-up pass. The gain comes from load balance, not from better memory access per nonzero, so it shows most on power-law or very irregular matrices.

**Use it when:**
- fp64/fp32 CSR SpMV on multicore CPUs where row lengths are highly skewed (circuit, web and graph matrices); the README circuit5M run is 53.6 ms with MKL vs 12.6 ms merge on 48 threads
- You need a short, permissively licensed (BSD-3) SpMV kernel to vendor into your own code, with no inspector or format-conversion step
- Matrices change every call, so per-matrix preprocessing (HYB, CSR5 tiles, plan-based libraries) would not amortize
- As a teaching or reference implementation of merge-path decomposition for other segmented reductions

**Skip it when:**
- Regular, well-balanced matrices (FEM stencils): the paper's minimum is 0.51x vs MKL, and open issue #5 (Dec 2025) reports it 4x slower than plain row-parallel SpMV inside a CG solver on 6 threads
- Small matrices on GPU: harmonic mean 0.79x vs cuSPARSE CsrMV for matrices with 300K nnz or fewer on the K40
- Modern CUDA: the GPU path relies on cub::DeviceSpmv, which CCCL 2.8 deprecates ('Use the cuSPARSE library instead') and which is gone from CCCL 3.0
- If you need a maintained library: no commits since 2017, and the build expects icpc 16 + MKL and CUDA 7.5-era nvcc (open build issues #2 and #3)

**Integration:** source-drop · CPU kernel: OpenMP only (the harness also links MKL and libnuma for comparison); GPU: bundled CUB snapshot, CUDA runtime, cuSPARSE for the comparison · Tested with icpc 16.0.1 and nvcc 7.5 + gcc 4.4.7; the CPU kernel is plain C++ plus OpenMP · CPU: x86-64 as tested (Intel AVX Xeon); GPU: NVIDIA compute capability 3.5+

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over CSR5 when you want to keep plain CSR with zero preprocessing and need a tiny vendorable kernel; CSR5 needs a format transform but reported higher averages on its irregular set. Pick it over ISpMV when you need open source or commercial use, or when the matrix changes too often to amortize a plan.

**Gotchas:**
- The CPU kernel uses fixed row_carry_out[256] and value_carry_out[256] stack arrays, so more than 256 OpenMP threads overflows them
- Merge coordinates and diagonals are int/int2, so rows+nnz must stay below 2^31
- The kernel computes y = A*x only (no alpha/beta), and the cross-thread fix-up is a serial loop after the parallel region
- The paper names the CPU as Xeon E5-2690 v2 while the README and artifact appendix say E5-2695 v2

**Status:** Abandoned since February 2017 but BSD-3 licensed. The CPU kernel is small enough to copy; the GPU path is better taken from its CUB lineage (deprecated in CCCL 2.8, removed in 3.0) or replaced by current cuSPARSE.

[repo](https://github.com/dumerrill/merge-spmv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dumerrill/merge-spmv/raw/master/merge-based-spmv-sc16-preprint.pdf)

##### ParAMD (parallel approximate minimum degree ordering)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

OpenMP parallel approximate minimum degree ordering, 2.9-8.5x faster than sequential SuiteSparse AMD on 64 cores.

**Beats:** SuiteSparse AMD (single-threaded approximate minimum degree fill-reducing ordering) — On a 64-core AMD EPYC 7763 (GCC 13.2.1, OpenMP, CMake Release), ParAMD at 64 threads computed AMD orderings of nine SuiteSparse matrices 2.85x (nd24k) to 8.51x (nlpkkt240) faster than single-threaded SuiteSparse AMD v7.10.1, taking the median of five random symmetric permutations, with fill-in 0.98x to 1.16x of SuiteSparse's; at one thread it was 0.44x to 1.01x as fast. These are the authors' committed exemplar results (plots/scaling.csv), reproducible with scripts/build.sh and scripts/scaling.sh.

**Known shortcoming:** Win is parallel scaling only: single-threaded ParAMD is slower than SuiteSparse AMD on 8 of 9 matrices, and fill-in grows up to 1.16x.

**Known shortcoming:** Possible memory bug: the quotient-graph buffer is allocated once at (1+mem) x nnz and new data is appended with no capacity check or compaction, so a large enough matrix could write past the buffer. All offsets are int32 (no 64-bit variant). Library code calls exit(1) on reader errors. Venue (SIAM PP26 proceedings) seen only in search snippets.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It keeps SuiteSparse AMD's quotient-graph machinery (approximate external degrees, supervariables, element absorption with aggressive absorption, dense rows above 10*sqrt(n) set aside) but replaces one-pivot-at-a-time elimination with multiple elimination. Each round it gathers candidates whose approximate degree is within a relaxation factor (mult, default 1.1) of the current minimum, capped at lim/threads (default 8192/threads), and picks a distance-2 independent set among them with Luby-style random priorities, so the chosen pivots share no neighbours and different threads can eliminate them concurrently. Degree lists are per-thread with thread affinity, new element lists are appended to a shared buffer through an atomic fetch-and-add, and the A+A^T symmetrization step is parallel too.

**Use it when:**
- Large sparse matrices (tens to hundreds of millions of nonzeros) where the AMD ordering itself takes seconds to minutes: stokes 79 s to 10 s and nlpkkt240 296 s to 35 s at 64 threads in the committed table.
- Many-core shared-memory nodes (the benchmarks assume 64 physical cores, for example an AMD EPYC 7763) whose cores otherwise sit idle during the symbolic/analysis phase of a direct solver.
- Workflows that reorder many different sparsity patterns, such as changing meshes or repeated analyse-factor cycles, where ordering time adds up.
- When a few percent more fill (0.98x to 1.16x SuiteSparse's in the published runs) is an acceptable price for a faster ordering.

**Skip it when:**
- Few cores or serial use: at one thread it ran at 0.44x to 1.01x the speed of SuiteSparse AMD, slower on 8 of 9 matrices.
- One-shot factorizations of huge matrices where factor cost dwarfs ordering cost: nlpkkt240's predicted fill rises from 1.60e12 to 1.85e12 (1.16x), which can cost more in factorization time and memory than the 260 s saved on ordering (judgement derived from page data).
- You need COLAMD, CAMD, constrained or column orderings, or SuiteSparse's Control/Info options: only symmetric AMD is provided (issue #1, January 2026, asks for COLAMD and is unanswered).
- Matrices beyond 32-bit index range: vtype and etype are both int32_t and there is no 64-bit variant like SuiteSparse's amd_l_order.
- Non-GCC or non-Linux toolchains without checking: the reader uses POSIX mmap and libstdc++ parallel mode (__gnu_parallel::sort), and the core needs OpenMP '#pragma omp atomic compare' support (GCC 13.2.1 was used).

**Integration:** shared lib · OpenMP (5.1 'atomic compare' support); optional SuiteSparse AMD (v7.10.1 in the scripts) only for the comparison mode of the CLI · C++17, CMake 3.22+, a GCC that supports '#pragma omp atomic compare' (GCC 13.2.1 used); Python 3.13 environment only for the benchmark plots · Linux shared-memory multicore (tested on x86-64 AMD EPYC 7763, 64 cores); no SIMD or ISA requirement in the code

**Vs siblings:** It is the only fill-reducing ordering among the catalogued sparse-and-solvers entries, so it complements rather than competes with them: put it in front of a direct solver such as CHOLMOD (or the task-based A64FX CHOLMOD entry), BaSpaCho or PanguLU when a sequential AMD step shows up in the analysis-phase profile.

**Gotchas:**
- The quotient-graph buffer is malloc'd once at (1 + mem) times the symmetrized nonzero count (mem defaults to 1.5), and new element lists are appended at an atomically advanced offset with no capacity check and no compaction, unlike SuiteSparse AMD's garbage collection; if a matrix needs more elbow room the code would write past the buffer, so raise --mem for unusual inputs.
- All offsets are int32 (etype): the reader checks that the file's nonzero count fits, but symmetric expansion roughly doubles it and the elbow room multiplies it by 2.5 at default settings, so inputs above roughly 850 million symmetrized off-diagonal entries would overflow 32-bit offsets (derived from the code).
- Library code calls exit(1) on reader errors, malloc results are not checked, and the mmap failure test compares against NULL rather than MAP_FAILED; config::print() reports 'Symmetry enabled' from the stat flag instead of sym (cosmetic).
- Orderings depend on the thread count (per-thread mt19937 seeded by thread id and per-thread candidate lists), so 1-thread and 64-thread fill-ins differ; the CLI randomly permutes the input first (--seed, default 1) to break ties, but a bare paramd() library call does not.

**Status:** Young Berkeley Lab project (v1.0.0, 4 commits April to November 2025, 9 stars, one open issue) under BSD-3-Clause with a Zenodo DOI; the arXiv paper 2504.17097 appears, per WebSearch snippets only, in the SIAM PP26 proceedings, which could not be confirmed because the publisher site is blocked here.

[repo](https://github.com/PASSIONLab/ParAMD) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PASSIONLab/ParAMD/HEAD/plots/scaling.csv)

##### sparsam  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

From-scratch C++20 SLAM/pose-graph backend whose own block-sparse Cholesky beats GTSAM 4.2 on M3500, not Ceres on BA.

**Beats:** GTSAM 4.2.1 (PyPI wheel driven through its Python bindings) on 2D pose graphs; Ceres 2.2 on BAL bundle adjustment — Author-run on an AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX laptop, single-threaded, GCC 13.3 -O3, median of 5: on M3500 both stacks converge to chi2 137.9 and sparsam's GN takes 0.078 s in-sweep (0.066 s standalone) against 0.133 s (0.141 s) for GTSAM 4.2.1's GN called through its prebuilt PyPI wheel, about 1.7-2.1x end to end with matched stopping criteria and a fresh backend per rep. Against Ceres 2.2 on BAL Ladybug it reaches the same final cost but is slower in wall clock on all four problems, though faster per iteration on ladybug-318 (552 vs 1091 ms).

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline GTSAM was the 4.2.1 pip wheel; SLAM/pose-graph solver, a loose fit for sparse-and-solvers.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins on 2D pose graphs only (1.7-2.1x vs GTSAM on M3500, partly from 7 vs 8 iterations). Ceres is faster on bundle adjustment and GTSAM is 3-5x faster per iteration on 3D graphs. Single-threaded, v0.1.0.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The normal equations H = J^T Sigma^-1 J are assembled into its own CSR-of-blocks storage and factored by a left-looking simplicial block Cholesky with dense per-block kernels; symbolic analysis, ordering and all storage are built once per problem and reused across iterations and LM retries with no reallocation (lambda is folded into the numeric pass). The fill-reducing ordering is a self-written quotient-graph approximate minimum degree (AMD, Amestoy-Davis-Duff degree bound), which takes M3500 factor+solve from 1623 ms (natural order) to 4.45 ms. The M3500 end-to-end win also comes from needing 7 GN iterations to GTSAM's 8.

**Use it when:**
- 2D pose-graph SLAM on Manhattan-style datasets (M3500-like, thousands of poses) where a single-threaded GN solve under 0.1 s matters and you can avoid GTSAM.
- You want a dependency-light estimation backend (C++20 + Eigen 3.4 only, no SuiteSparse, no Boost) to vendor and read.
- Teaching, auditing or extending a SLAM backend: each component has a committed derivation doc and analytic-vs-numeric Jacobian tests.
- Large 2D TORO graphs (M10000) from odometry initialization, where its GN reached chi2/dof about 1.2 in about 1 s and GTSAM 4.2's LM stalled in the author's runs.

**Skip it when:**
- Bundle adjustment where wall clock matters: Ceres 2.2 was 1.1-3.3x faster on BAL Ladybug (e.g. 1.74 s vs 0.67 s on ladybug-49), because its trust-region damping needs 2.2-3.5x fewer iterations.
- Fill-heavy 3D pose graphs: the README says GTSAM's per-iteration linear algebra is about 3-5x faster there; there are no supernodes yet.
- Problems where you rely on LM: its LM plateaus on M3500 (2.8e3 after 60 iterations, where GN and GTSAM's LM reach 137.9) and hits the 200-iteration cap on several hard sets.
- Multi-core or GPU solving: everything is single-threaded; use BaSpaCho, CHOLMOD or GTSAM with TBB instead.
- Production use: project created July 2026, version 0.1.0, 1 star, one author; the README architecture lists batch GN/LM/GNC only, with no incremental smoothing (iSAM2-style).

**Integration:** static lib (CMake target sparsam; the code lives in headers under src/sparsam and the library compiles only version.cpp) · Eigen 3.4 (dense types only); GoogleTest fetched for tests; Ceres and GTSAM (Python wheel) only for the off-by-default SPARSAM_BUILD_BENCH oracles · C++20, CMake 3.22; benchmarks built with GCC 13.3 · Linux x86-64 is the only platform the benchmarks name; no SIMD intrinsics in the linear-algebra headers read, other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick sparsam over BaSpaCho or Sympiler only when you want the whole nonlinear SLAM loop (factors, Lie groups, GN/LM/GNC) in one small dependency-free C++20 codebase for 2D pose graphs; for raw sparse Cholesky speed on large or fill-heavy systems, BaSpaCho's supernodal CPU/GPU factorization (benchmarked against CHOLMOD) is the stronger choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Fail-closed I/O and numerics: unknown g2o/TORO tags, non-PSD information matrices and gapped key sets throw instead of being skipped, so some datasets other tools ingest are rejected.
- Its Pose2 error uses the true SE(2) log, while GTSAM's default Pose2 local chart is first-order; chi2 values differ by 2.6% (M3500) up to 27-61% on rotation-heavy sets before convergence, so unconverged chi2 is not comparable across the two.
- BlockCholesky keeps a pointer to its BlockPattern (the rvalue constructor is deleted); the pattern must outlive the factorization, and one SparseBackend instance serves one fixed graph structure (adding factors after the first linearize throws).
- Each block is a separately allocated Eigen::MatrixXd, so very small blocks pay allocation and indirection costs that a supernodal solver avoids.

**Status:** Active one-author project (latest commit 2026-08-08, created July 2026) under MIT with careful, reproducible benchmark records; copyable, but young and SLAM-specific rather than a general sparse solver.

[repo](https://github.com/Manas-arumalla/sparsam) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Manas-arumalla/sparsam/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/m5.md)

##### TACO (Tensor Algebra Compiler)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Compiler that generates fused C/CUDA kernels for any sparse/dense tensor expression; matches Eigen and MKL, beats uBLAS, Gmm++ and MATLAB Tensor Toolbox.

**Beats:** Eigen (sparse), Intel MKL, OSKI and pOSKI, uBLAS and Gmm++ for sparse linear algebra; SPLATT and the MATLAB Tensor Toolbox for sparse 3rd-order tensor kernels — The peer-reviewed OOPSLA 2017 paper ran serial and 12-thread kernels on a two-socket Xeon E5-2695 v2 with GCC 5.4 (the taco-bench harness builds with -O3 -ffast-math): taco's SpMV matched Eigen within about 0-10% and was close to MKL across six SuiteSparse matrices, fused compound kernels ran up to about 1.4x faster than Eigen, MKL and OSKI on webbase-1M, uBLAS and Gmm++ were 5x to 73,000x slower on some kernels for algorithmic reasons, and SPLATT's MTTKRP was faster on two of three tensors. Overall the result is parity with hand-tuned libraries plus far wider coverage, not a broad speedup.

**Known shortcoming:** Mostly parity with Eigen/MKL (Eigen takes about 0.93x-1.4x of taco's time); huge wins only over uBLAS (SDDMM 2,412x-73,405x); SPLATT up to 1.53x faster and OSKI faster on blocked SpMV; taco-bench disabled validation for MKL SpMV, Gmm++ PLUS3 and uBLAS SDDMM/PLUS3.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: open bug #297 (since 2020) says taco generates incorrect code for sparse outputs of products (A*B, A^T*A, A*B*C); #514 heap-buffer-overflow and misaligned access on int insert(); #519 segfault with a workspace kernel; 25 open bug-labelled issues. JIT shells out to cc with -O3 -ffast-math by default.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The OOPSLA 2017 paper combines three ideas: per-dimension storage formats, iteration graphs that order the loop nest to follow each operand's storage tree, and merge lattices that generalise the two-way sparse merge loop so co-iteration over several sparse operands runs as specialised while-loops that drop exhausted operands. Compound expressions (e.g. y = alpha A^T x + beta z, or SDDMM) become one fused loop nest with no temporaries, which is where it beats Eigen, uBLAS and Gmm++. At HEAD a scheduling language (split, divide, reorder, fuse, pos, precompute into a workspace, parallelize with output-race strategies, unroll) lets you tile, add workspaces and target OpenMP or CUDA; generated C is compiled with -O3 -ffast-math by default.

**Use it when:**
- Compound or unusual sparse kernels (SDDMM, A^T x residuals, B + C + D, sparse tensor contractions) that no fixed library API offers as one fused call
- Sparse 3rd-order and higher tensor kernels (TTV, TTM, MTTKRP, inner products) in CSF or mixed formats, where the MATLAB Tensor Toolbox was 9x to 1856x slower in the paper
- Generating a standalone C or CUDA kernel offline with the taco CLI (e.g. -f=B:ds for CSR SpMV) and vendoring the emitted code with no runtime dependency
- Exploring format choices (CSR vs DCSR vs blocked vs dense) for a kernel before hand-tuning it
- Research prototypes that need a correct-by-construction baseline for new sparse formats or schedules

**Skip it when:**
- Plain SpMV, where it only matches Eigen and MKL (MKL was slightly faster on rma10 and cant in the paper) and tuned register-blocked OSKI beat it in almost all blocked cases
- MTTKRP on large tensors where SPLATT is available: SPLATT was up to about 1.5x faster on NELL-1 and NELL-2 in the paper
- Sparse outputs of products (A*B, A^T*A, A*B*C): the umbrella bug issue #297 (open since 2020) says taco does not currently generate correct code for such sparse outputs
- Deployments where invoking a C compiler at run time is unacceptable (the library JIT path shells out to cc/nvcc and dlopens the result from a temp dir)
- Projects that need active maintenance: last commit 2025-04-14, 25 open bug-labelled issues including crashes and wrong-result reports

**Integration:** shared lib by default (TACO_SHARED_LIBRARY=ON) plus taco CLI; generated kernels can be used as source-drop C/CUDA · none for the core library; a C compiler at run time for JIT; optional OpenMP (-DOPENMP=ON), CUDA toolkit (-DCUDA=ON, generated CUDA needs compute capability 6.1+), Python 3 with NumPy/SciPy and the pybind11 submodule for pytaco · C++14 (CMake sets -std=c++14), GCC 5.0+ or Clang 3.9+, CMake 3.4+; generated C is C99 · CPUs targeted by the host C compiler; build docs cover Linux (Debian/Ubuntu packages), and the JIT relies on system() and dlopen, so Windows is not documented; NVIDIA GPUs via generated CUDA (compute capability 6.1+)

**Vs siblings:** Pick taco over Sympiler when you need arbitrary fused tensor or matrix expressions rather than sparse Cholesky or triangular solves, and over the fixed SpMV kernels (CSR5, merge-spmv, SPC5, CVR) when the operation is not SpMV or the operands are higher-order tensors; for raw SpMV throughput those specialised kernels are the better pick.

**Gotchas:**
- Default JIT flags are -O3 -ffast-math -std=c99 (override with TACO_CFLAGS, compiler with the target's env var, TACO_NVCC/TACO_NVCCFLAGS for CUDA), so results can differ from strict-IEEE Eigen or MKL in the last bits
- Operands whose formats point opposite ways (CSR + CSC, transposes) form a cycle in the iteration graph, which the code generator does not support; convert formats first
- The paper's automatic parallelisation only parallelises outer for-loops with a fully dense output and no scatter; other cases need an explicit parallelize() schedule with an output race strategy
- Open bugs include a heap-buffer-overflow and misaligned access when inserting int values into a dense tensor (#514), a segfault for a kernel with a workspace (#519), and invalid COO pack/unpack code from the CUDA generator (#438)

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-04-14; the paper's taco-bench harness last changed 2017) but MIT-licensed, and kernels emitted by the CLI are plain C that can be vendored without the compiler.

[repo](https://github.com/tensor-compiler/taco) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tensor-compiler/tensor-compiler.github.io/HEAD/files/kjolstad-oopsla17-tensor-compiler.pdf)

##### ALBUS  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research OpenMP+AVX2 double-precision CSR SpMV kernel with nonzero-balanced thread split; paper reports beating MKL, CSR5 and Merge.

**Beats:** Intel MKL SpMV (oneAPI 2021); also CSR5 and merge-based SpMV — The FGCS 2021 paper abstract (quoted in the README) reports, on a dual-socket Xeon E5-2670 v3 with 20 regular and 20 irregular UF matrices, average speedups of 1.48x over MKL on regular and 2.44x on irregular matrices (up to 2.31x and 5.37x), plus 1.32-1.59x over CSR5 and Merge; the README's own table, on a dual Xeon Gold 6242 with icpc -O3 -xCORE-AVX2, gives ALBUS vs CSR5 vs CVR GFlops only (e.g. rma10 94.5 vs 42.1 vs 65.8) with empty MKL and Merge columns. Timing excludes the partition step and comes from repeated cache-warm iterations; the comparison harnesses for MKL, CSR5 and Merge are not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Preprocessing excluded from timing; real Makefile flags differ from the README example; paper unreachable here (sciencedirect blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** Record corrected: ALBUS uses plain CSR with no format conversion; preprocessing is only a thread partition. Correctness: rows of length 3 or 3 mod 4 read one double past the row (out of bounds on the last row; a neighbouring Inf/NaN turns the row into NaN); aligned SIMD loads at unaligned row starts. Check accepts 1% error. Bench ignores the iterations argument and runs cache-warm (README dense example works out to ~457 GB/s, derived from page data).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The nonzeros are split into equal contiguous chunks per OpenMP thread (binary search over row_ptr finds each chunk's start row and offset), so a thread may start and end mid-row; the partial sums of the boundary rows go to a small per-thread buffer and are added serially after the parallel region. This is nonzero-based load balancing in the spirit of CSR5 and merge-based SpMV, but it keeps plain CSR and the partition costs only O(threads log rows). Inside each row the AVX2 variant gathers x values with _mm256_set_pd and accumulates with FMA, with specialized paths for rows of 1-4 nonzeros, software prefetch and Intel unroll pragmas.

**Use it when:**
- Multi-threaded double-precision SpMV on x86 CPUs with AVX2/FMA where the matrix is already in CSR and you cannot afford a format conversion (CSR5, CVR and SPC5 all need one).
- Matrices with skewed row lengths (web, social and circuit graphs such as webbase-1M, web-Stanford, scircuit) where row-split OpenMP CSR loses to load imbalance.
- Iterative solvers that reuse one matrix and thread count for many products, so the one-off partition is amortized (it is cheap anyway).
- As a short, readable reference for nonzero-balanced CSR SpMV to port into your own code.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a library: there is no build target, versioning, tests beyond a printout check, or API beyond two inline functions; MKL's CSR SpMV or merge-spmv are better-supported options.
- Single precision, complex values, transposed products, y = alpha*A*x + beta*y or SpMM: only real double y = A*x is implemented.
- Non-x86 targets or CPUs without AVX2/FMA (use the OpenMP-only variant, which loses the SIMD part), and matrices with 2^31 or more nonzeros (int indices).
- Inputs that may contain Inf or NaN: the 3-remainder SIMD paths load one value past the row and multiply it by zero, so a non-finite neighbor value turns the row into NaN (see gotchas).
- Production use without your own testing: abandoned since April 2022, no issues filed, and the MKL and Merge speedups are only in the paper abstract.

**Integration:** source-drop · OpenMP; AVX2 and FMA intrinsics for the AVX2 variant · not documented; Makefiles target Intel icpc (version not stated) with a commented-out g++ line (-march=native -mavx -mavx2 -fopenmp -O3); code uses the register keyword (removed in C++17) and Intel-specific pragmas · x86-64 with AVX2+FMA for the SIMD variant; the OpenMP-only variant is portable C++

**Vs siblings:** Pick ALBUS over CSR5, CVR or SPC5 when you must keep plain CSR with no format conversion and target AVX2 CPUs; its README table shows it ahead of CSR5 on all 28 matrices and ahead of CVR on 25 of 28 on a dual Xeon Gold 6242. merge-spmv also keeps CSR (merge-path partition) and has an SC'16 evaluation over 4,201 matrices, and SPC5 is the catalogued choice for AVX-512 or SVE.

**Gotchas:**
- Memory-safety and NaN edge case: for rows whose length is 3 or leaves remainder 3 mod 4, the kernel does a full _mm_load_pd/_mm256_load_pd that reads one double past the row (past the end of mtx_val for the last row) and multiplies it by a zero lane; the over-read is out of bounds for the last row, and a neighboring Inf/NaN value yields NaN.
- The _mm256_load_pd/_mm_load_pd calls are aligned loads at row starts that are not generally 32-byte aligned; this only works when the compiler folds them into VEX memory operands (as at -O3), so a -O0 or different-compiler build can fault.
- The benchmark ignores the iterations argument: ReadFile sets it to 4*min(200000, max(100, 2^34/nnz)) for both warm-up and timed loops on the same matrix and vector, so mid-size matrices run cache-warm; the README's dense 2048x2048 example implies about 457 GB/s of matrix traffic (derived from page data: 4,194,304 nonzeros x 12 bytes in 0.110 ms).
- The built-in correctness check accepts up to 1% relative error per row against serial CSR, and the Matrix Market reader keeps only the real part of complex files and treats anything but 'symmetric' (e.g. hermitian, skew-symmetric) as general.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-04-04 (README edits) but MIT-licensed and a few hundred lines, so it is easy to vendor as a reference kernel after fixing the tail over-read and aligned loads.

[repo](https://github.com/nulidangxueshen/ALBUS) · [benchmark](https://github.com/nulidangxueshen/ALBUS)

##### ALP/GraphBLAS (nonblocking backend)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

C++ GraphBLAS framework whose nonblocking backend fuses chained sparse ops at run time; paper reports beating SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS and Eigen.

**Beats:** SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS and Eigen — Per the peer-reviewed ACM TACO 20(1) 2023 paper's abstract as quoted in search results (paper not opened), the nonblocking backend reaches up to 16.1x over SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS and up to 12.2x over Eigen, with PageRank on ten matrices as the headline and CG and sparse DNN inference also evaluated, and up to 4.11x over ALP's own blocking mode. A search snippet places the experiments on a dual-socket Xeon Gold 6238T (44 cores, 1.9 GHz, hyper-threading and turbo off), but compiler, flags and baseline versions remain undocumented here.

**Known shortcoming:** Up to 16.1x over SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS and 12.2x over Eigen for PageRank only (TACO paper abstract via search; paper blocked); paper year 2023, not 2022.

**Known shortcoming:** Open bugs: std::swap broken for nonblocking vectors; grb::dot aliasing; bad dense-descriptor use not always caught. Level-3 ops are not nonblocking. Paper unopened here (dl.acm.org blocked); search snippet gives dual Xeon Gold 6238T, 44 cores.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** In the nonblocking backend each level-1/level-2 call is recorded as a lambda stage instead of running immediately (lazy evaluation); dynamic data-dependence analysis groups stages that share containers into one pipeline, which is then executed with loop fusion and loop tiling so a tile of every vector stays in cache across the fused operations. An analytic model picks the thread count and tile size per pipeline from vector count, element size, L1 size (98% target, 512-element minimum tile) and core count. Sparse-vector bookkeeping uses lock-free per-tile local coordinate stacks merged by prefix sum, and is skipped entirely when vectors are known dense (dense descriptor or run-time analysis).

**Use it when:**
- Iterative sparse algorithms written as long chains of vector operations around SpMV, such as PageRank, conjugate gradient or sparse DNN inference, on a multi-core Linux CPU, where fusing the vector ops between SpMVs cuts memory traffic.
- You want one algorithm source that runs sequential, OpenMP, nonblocking or distributed-memory (LPF bsp1d/hybrid) by switching a compiler-wrapper flag.
- Algorithm work in C++ under an Apache-2.0 license, or quick prototyping through the alp-graphblas Python wheels (0.8.43, x86-64 Linux, CPython 3.9-3.12).
- NUMA machines: libnuma is a hard dependency and shared data defaults to interleaved allocation.

**Skip it when:**
- Level-3 workloads (mxm/SpGEMM, triangle counting): blas3 and some blas2 primitives are not natively nonblocking, run blocking and print a warning, so the fusion advantage disappears.
- A single isolated kernel such as one SpMV: the speedup comes from fusing several operations, and no single-kernel numbers are published in the repo.
- Code that must use the GraphBLAS C API or the SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS ecosystem (LAGraph, python-graphblas): ALP exposes a C++ API and only a subset of Sparse BLAS.
- macOS or Windows targets: Mac OS X support is an open enhancement issue, and the build requires libnuma and POSIX threads.
- Decisions that need verified numbers: the 16.1x and 12.2x figures are 'up to' maxima from the TACO paper abstract, and its hardware, compiler and baseline versions could not be checked here.

**Integration:** static lib (headers plus per-backend libraries installed via CMake; programs link statically, through the grbcxx/grbrun wrappers or find_package(ALPGraphBLAS)) · OpenMP, libnuma, POSIX threads, libm; optional LPF 1.0+ for distributed/hybrid backends; doxygen/graphviz/pdflatex only for docs · C++11 compiler with OpenMP (README: GCC 4.8.2 or higher), CMake 3.13+ · Linux (libnuma required); x86-64 Python wheels on PyPI; SIMD width must be set per target in include/graphblas/base/config.hpp; experimental RISC-V Snitch (Banshee simulator) backend

**Vs siblings:** Pick ALP over the GPU GraphBLAS siblings (GraphBLAST, spla, cuBool) when you run on CPUs, possibly across nodes via LPF, and your algorithm is iteration-heavy level-1/level-2 work that benefits from fusion; stay with SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS when you need the C API, its ecosystem or mxm-heavy workloads.

**Gotchas:**
- Lazy evaluation moves work and error checks: pipelines run on reads through iterators, container construction or destruction, scalar-returning ops like grb::dot, or grb::wait, so timings and failures appear there; the docs say an illegal dense descriptor on a vector that becomes dense inside the pipeline cannot be caught (also an open issue).
- Configuration is compile-time constexpr (SIMD_SIZE, cache line, L1 size, index types); objects compiled with different configurations are undefined behaviour when linked, so keep one install per target architecture.
- Run-time knobs: OMP_NUM_THREADS is an upper bound for the analytic model, GRB_NONBLOCKING_TILE_SIZE forces a fixed tile size, and the README asks for OMP_PROC_BIND; pipelines beyond 4 concurrent, 16 containers or 16 stages print capacity warnings.
- Open bugs at the time of reading include 'std::swap for nonblocking vectors is broken', reference/reference_omp grb::dot mishandling aliasing, a masked set overwriting values outside the mask (question label) and a constexpr build error on some compilers.

**Status:** Actively developed (latest commit 2026-02-24, PyPI alp-graphblas 0.8.43), Apache-2.0 and Huawei-backed with 179 issues filed; copyable as a library, though the nonblocking backend still covers only level-1/level-2 natively.

[repo](https://github.com/Algebraic-Programming/ALP) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3561652)

##### AmgT (tensor-core AMG)  `C (CUDA; HYPRE-based)`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Modified HYPRE 2.31 whose BoomerAMG SpGEMM and SpMV run on tensor cores; beats stock GPU HYPRE with cuSPARSE.

**Beats:** HYPRE (GPU build calling cuSPARSE) — Per a search-engine snippet of the SC '24 abstract (paper not opened: dl.acm.org and ieeexplore are blocked here), AmgT beats the original GPU HYPRE by geomean 1.46x on A100, 1.32x on H100 and 2.24x on MI210 (maximums 2.10x, 2.06x, 3.67x). The snippet does not say whether these are setup, solve or total times, or whether they are FP64 or mixed precision. The repo reproduces only the NVIDIA comparison: it builds stock HYPRE 2.31 with cuSPARSE SpGEMM/SpMV (HYPRE's default vendor path) against the AmgT builds and times setup and the 50-cycle solve separately with gettimeofday; it holds no result tables, and host CPU and matrix list are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B rests on the SC '24 proceedings record (DOI 10.1109/SC41406.2024.00058), which the verifier could not open; the numbers are from a search snippet and unverified. The repo harness (AmgT_test/test_new.c, compile.sh) builds the HYPRE+cuSPARSE baseline but names no host CPU or full flags. Last commit 2024-11-11, stale.

**Known shortcoming:** The verifier's harness description was wrong: test_new.c creates a PCG but never uses it; the timed run is a standalone BoomerAMGSetup plus Solve with tol 1e-20 and max 50 iterations, so a fixed 50 V-cycles. compile.sh ships execuative=cuSPARSE, which builds the baseline. AmgT's SpMV ignores the transpose flag (safe only because HYPRE's GPU default is keepT=1). The mixed build runs level 1 in TF32 and coarser levels in FP16 against HYPRE's FP64. No HIP path, so the MI210 2.24x is not reproducible from the repo. Issues #1-#3 (build and run failures) unanswered.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Matrices are converted lazily, on first use, from CSR to an 'mBSR' format: 4x4 dense blocks, each with a 16-bit occupancy bitmap, stored in the hypre_CSRMatrix struct next to the CSR arrays. SpGEMM uses binned, shared-memory hash-table symbolic passes over block columns. Its numeric pass issues FP64 mma.sync m8n8k4 tensor-core instructions for A-blocks with at least 10 of 16 entries filled, and CUDA-core bitmap arithmetic for sparser blocks. SpMV picks among four kernels by average nonzeros per block (tensor cores at 10 or more) and the standard deviation of blocks per block-row (warp-balanced row splitting at 12 or more). The mixed-precision build runs level-0 products in FP64, level-1 products through TF32 tensor cores (cvt.rna.tf32, mma m16n8k4) and all coarser levels in FP16. Because SpGEMM outputs mBSR directly, the format is reused across levels, which cuts CSR/BSR conversion cost.

**Use it when:**
- You already solve with HYPRE BoomerAMG on NVIDIA A100 (sm_80) or H100 (sm_90) and want faster setup and solve without retuning AMG parameters.
- Matrices whose nonzeros cluster into dense 4x4 blocks (FEM/PDE stencils, multi-DOF problems). The tensor-core paths only fire when blocks average 10 or more of 16 entries.
- Experiments with mixed-precision AMG where coarse levels can tolerate TF32/FP16 operators, inside an outer FP64 iteration that restores accuracy.
- Research baselines: reproducing or extending the SC '24 paper's tensor-core AMG kernels inside a known solver framework.

**Skip it when:**
- Production code that needs a maintained library: 7 commits, last on 2024-11-11, three open build/run issues (config file not found, missing HYPRE_krylov.h, cudaErrorInvalidDevice on H100 with CUDA 12.6), none answered.
- AMD or other GPUs: compile.sh builds only CUDA sm_80 or sm_90, and there is no HIP path, though the paper reports MI210 results.
- Very sparse or irregular matrices with little 4x4 block fill: these fall back to CUDA-core bitmap kernels and also pay a 4x4 padding memory cost.
- Accuracy-sensitive solves with the mixed build: level 1 runs in TF32 (10-bit mantissa) and levels 2 and coarser in FP16, which can change convergence.
- Multi-GPU runs: the driver calls cudaSetDevice(0) on every MPI rank, and multi-GPU behaviour is not documented.

**Integration:** source-drop · Its own embedded HYPRE 2.31.0 (configured --with-cuda --enable-unified-memory), CUDA toolkit (cuSPARSE, cuBLAS, cuRAND, Thrust), MPI (README asks for OpenMPI 4.0+) · CUDA 12.2+ recommended in the README (compile.sh defaults to /usr/local/cuda-12.0); mpicc; NVIDIA compute capability 8.0+ · Linux, NVIDIA A100 (sm_80) or H100 (sm_90) only as built by compile.sh

**Vs siblings:** Pick AmgT over Ginkgo or AMGCL only if you are committed to HYPRE BoomerAMG on A100/H100 and can carry a research fork; Ginkgo and AMGCL are maintained libraries with their own AMG. For a standalone tensor-core SpMV or SpGEMM kernel, use DASP or TileSpGEMM from the same lab. apxchol is the catalogued option that beats BoomerAMG with a different (approximate-Cholesky) method on Laplacian/SDDM systems.

**Gotchas:**
- The test driver builds and configures a PCG solver (tol 1e-5, 300 iterations) but never uses it. The timed run is standalone BoomerAMGSetup plus BoomerAMGSolve with tol 1e-20 and max 50 iterations, i.e. a fixed 50 V-cycles, PMIS coarsening, Jacobi (relax 18) and extended+i interpolation. This corrects the verifier's 'PCG with BoomerAMG preconditioner' reading.
- compile.sh ships with execuative=cuSPARSE, so running it unchanged builds the baseline, not AmgT. It also contains a broken 'chmod -R *' line and an unquoted CUDA_ARCH export.
- The AmgT SpMV entry (spmv_amgT_fp64/fp32/fp16) takes HYPRE's trans flag but never branches on it. It is correct inside BoomerAMG only because HYPRE's GPU default keeps explicit transposes (keepT = 1 in par_amg.c). Disabling KeepTranspose, or calling ParCSRMatrixMatvecT on a matrix without a stored transpose, would route a transposed product into a kernel that computes A*x.
- The mBSR copy is built once (bsr_tag set on first SpMV or SpGEMM) and I found no code that invalidates it, so changing a matrix's values in place after first use is risky. Every kernel launch is followed by cudaDeviceSynchronize.

**Status:** Stale research code (7 commits, last 2024-11-11, 9 stars, issues unanswered). It is Apache-2.0 at the top level, with HYPRE's own Apache-2.0/MIT files embedded, so the kernels are copyable, but expect build fixes before it runs.

[repo](https://github.com/SuperScientificSoftwareLaboratory/AmgT) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/SC41406.2024.00058)

##### Basker (ShyLU threaded sparse LU, in Trilinos)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

Threaded sparse LU (Trilinos ShyLU-Basker) for low-fill circuit matrices; paper reports 5.9x geomean over sequential KLU on 16 cores.

**Beats:** KLU (SuiteSparse) and Intel MKL PARDISO — The Basker paper (Booth, Rajamanickam, Thornquist; ASHES/IPDPS 2016 workshop, arXiv 1601.05725; journal version Parallel Computing 2017) reports, per its abstract seen only in search results, a geometric-mean 5.91x speedup on a 16-core CPU and 7.4x on a 32-core Xeon Phi over sequential KLU on circuit-type matrices, and up to 53x / 13.3x over MKL PARDISO on low-fill matrices. CPU models, compiler and flags, and the matrix list were not visible (the paper hosts are blocked), and the repo carries no benchmark code.

**Known shortcoming:** Only the ShyLU Basker component of Trilinos. Evidence is the Parallel Computing 2017 paper abstract (5.91x geomean vs KLU, up to 53x vs PARDISO); no numbers in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Basker's speedups come only from the 2016-17 paper abstract (search snippet); the repo has no harness. It builds only inside Trilinos (17.x needs C++20 and CMake 3.27). The thread count is rounded down to a power of 2; the Amesos2 adapter defaults replace_zero_pivot=true, so zero pivots are silently replaced; under MPI it factors on the root rank only; factorization errors when btf_nblks == 0. Sibling GPU solver Tacho (ShyLU) is not catalogued.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It parallelizes the left-looking Gilbert-Peierls LU kernel that KLU runs serially. A block triangular form (BTF) permutation splits the matrix into many small diagonal blocks, which are factored independently, and one large block. The large block is reordered by nested dissection (METIS or Scotch) into a hierarchical 2D block layout, so threads factor separate subtrees with no communication and then cooperate on separators using point-to-point synchronization instead of global barriers (the paper's 'hierarchical parallelism and data layouts'). Diagonal blocks get AMD ordering and optional max-weight matching.

**Use it when:**
- SPICE-style circuit simulation: low-fill, BTF-reducible Jacobians that are refactored many times with the same pattern on one 8-32 core node.
- You already build on Trilinos (Tpetra/Amesos2) and want a threaded replacement for KLU2 without leaving the stack.
- You need an open-source, BSD-3-licensed threaded KLU-class solver; the circuit-LU siblings NICSLU and CKTSO need license files.
- Real or complex scalars (the Entry template parameter; complex-build fixes landed in March 2025).

**Skip it when:**
