- High-fill matrices from 3D PDE/FEM discretizations: the code is designed for low fill-in, and the large PARDISO margins in the paper apply only to low-fill circuit matrices where supernodal PARDISO is a weak fit; use a supernodal or multifrontal solver there.
- You want to run on a GPU: factorization runs in the Kokkos host execution space; GPU builds since August 2025 only let it coexist with CUDA-enabled Kokkos.
- Distributed memory: through Amesos2 the matrix is gathered to the root MPI rank and factored there, so it does not scale across nodes.
- You need a standalone library: it builds only as a Trilinos subpackage (TriBITS, Kokkos, Teuchos, TrilinosSS); Trilinos 17 requires CMake 3.27 and a C++20 compiler.
- You need reproducible, current numbers: the only speedups are 2016-17 paper figures; the repo has no benchmark harness ('Compiler Option Flags: NA').

**Integration:** static or shared lib (Trilinos subpackage ShyLU_NodeBasker: template headers plus shylubasker.cpp, library shylu_nodebasker) · Kokkos (OpenMP backend for threads), Teuchos, TrilinosSS (bundled SuiteSparse AMD/BTF/COLAMD); optional METIS or Scotch for nested dissection, MKL, VTune; Amesos2 and Tpetra for the high-level interface · Trilinos 17.x: C++20 compiler and CMake 3.27+ (release notes); the original 2015 README said C++11 · shared-memory CPUs through Kokkos OpenMP; README lists Intel Sandy Bridge, Xeon Phi and IBM Power8 as tested

**Vs siblings:** Pick Basker over NICSLU and CKTSO, which target the same circuit-matrix niche and claim larger speedups, when you need source code under BSD-3 inside Trilinos; NICSLU is unmaintained and needs a nicslu.lic file. Pick it over GLU or CKTSO-GPU when there is no NVIDIA GPU, or the matrices are too sparse for a GPU to pay off.

**Gotchas:**
- SetThreads rounds the thread count down to a power of two and caps it at Kokkos OpenMP concurrency. Inside Amesos2 the default is every hardware thread when OpenMP is enabled.
- The Amesos2 adapter defaults replace_zero_pivot to true, so a zero pivot is silently replaced rather than reported as singular; check residuals. The parameter 'pivot' defaults to false in the valid-parameter list, and passing that list through disables pivoting.
- Symbolic cannot be rerun on the same object ('YOU CANNOT RERUN SYMBOLIC'), so a new sparsity pattern needs a new instance. Factor returns an error when BTF yields no blocks ('Case for btf_nbkls = 0 is not implemented'), so keep btf=true.
- Building with CUDA-enabled Kokkos plus Basker failed with an extended-lambda error (issue #14227, closed December 2025); use a recent Trilinos if you mix backends.

**Status:** Actively maintained inside Trilinos (Basker commits through 2026-08-06, adding threaded solve, worker threads and partial factorization in 2025-26) and BSD-3-Clause, but usable only as part of a Trilinos build.

[repo](https://github.com/trilinos/Trilinos) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.05725)

##### CapelliniSpTRSV (thread-level synchronization-free GPU sparse triangular solve)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

GPU sparse lower-triangular solve (CSR) using one thread per row; ICPP '20 reports 4.00x over cuSPARSE csrsv2.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE SpTRSV (CUSPARSE_SOLVE_POLICY_NO_LEVEL / USE_LEVEL) and the SyncFree SpTRSV of bhSPARSE — The ICPP '20 paper abstract (reproduced in the README) reports a 3.41 GFLOPS/s average for SpTRSV over 245 SuiteSparse matrices on three NVIDIA GPUs (GTX 1080, V100, RTX 2080 Ti; CUDA 8.0-10.2; nvcc -O3, sm_61 in the shipped Makefile). That is 5.26x over warp-level SyncFree SpTRSV and 4.00x over cuSPARSE csrsv2. The README does not say which GPU or aggregation the headline ratios come from, and the paper itself was not opened.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is the ICPP'20 paper abstract quoted in the README; host CPU not stated, so not A.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**How:** Synchronization-free SpTRSV (Liu et al.) gives each row a whole warp and waits on per-row ready flags. Capellini gives each row a single thread. Rows are handed out in order through an atomicAdd counter. Each thread walks its row in column order, adds up the entries whose x[col] flag is already set and spins on the next one; when it reaches the diagonal it writes x[i], calls __threadfence and sets its own flag. This removes the warp-per-row waste on matrices with many independent rows per level and few nonzeros per row. The 'mix' variant has a host pass that gives a 32-row group to a warp-per-row kernel when its average nnz/row is 10 or more, and to the thread-per-row path otherwise.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated triangular solves on NVIDIA GPUs where the matrix changes often enough that cuSPARSE's analysis phase or a level-set preprocessing step is a real cost
- Lower-triangular factors with short rows (few nonzeros per row) and many rows per dependency level, the case the paper targets
- As a reference implementation or starting point for your own thread-level sync-free SpTRSV kernel (MIT, about 100 lines of kernel code)
- OpenCL/AMD GPUs, using the openCL/WrtFst and openCL/mix variants (tested on a Radeon Vega 11 APU with ROCm)

**Skip it when:**
- Matrices with long rows or few rows per level: the README says the thread-level kernels target short-row, wide-level matrices, so use 'mix' or a warp-level solver there
- You need a maintained library API: there is no header, CMake target, error handling or upper-triangular/transposed solve, and the last commit was in 2021
- Comparisons against current cuSPARSE: the cuSP baseline calls the legacy cusparseDcsrsv2 routines on CUDA 8-10.2, not the generic cusparseSpSV API of later CUDA versions
- Modern toolchains without edits: Makefiles hard-code sm_61 and /usr/local/cuda, and open issue #2 reports a build failure in SyncFree_csc with CUDA 11.5 + GCC 11.4 (workaround: GCC 10.5 as host compiler)

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA toolkit (cudart, cuSPARSE for the baseline folders, Thrust headers included); OpenCL/ROCm for the OpenCL variant · Tested with CUDA 8.0, 9.0 and 10.2; Makefile targets compute_61/sm_61 (edit for other GPUs) · NVIDIA GPUs (GTX 1080, V100, RTX 2080 Ti tested); AMD Radeon Vega 11 via OpenCL

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Sympiler when the triangular solve has to run on a GPU and you have no time for symbolic preprocessing. Pick it over CSR5/merge-spmv/ISpMV only for triangular solves; those siblings are SpMV kernels and solve a different problem.

**Gotchas:**
- The kernel assumes column indices sorted ascending within each row and the diagonal stored as the last entry of every row (it divides by csrVal[rowPtr[i+1]-1]); a row without a stored diagonal never sets its ready flag, so dependent rows spin forever
- Ready flags are a plain int array (not volatile or atomic); visibility relies on __threadfence plus the -Xptxas -dlcm=cg flag in the Makefile that keeps global loads out of L1. Keep that flag if you vendor the kernel
- The benchmark harness does not solve with your matrix's values: change2tran keeps A's strictly-lower sparsity pattern, sets every value to 1 (unit lower-triangular), and checks the result against x = 1 with a loose 1% relative tolerance
- Precision, repeat count (BENCH_REPEAT 100) and warps per block are compile-time macros in common.h (default double precision); timings use gettimeofday around launch + cudaDeviceSynchronize

**Status:** Abandoned: last commit 2021-03-19, with one unanswered build issue from 2024. It is MIT-licensed and the kernel is small enough to vendor, but expect to update Makefiles for current CUDA/GCC versions and GPU architectures.

[repo](https://github.com/JiyaSu/CapelliniSpTRSV) · [benchmark](https://github.com/JiyaSu/CapelliniSpTRSV)

##### CB-SpMV / CB-Sparse (xing-cong)  `CUDA/C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

FP64 GPU SpMV on a 16x16 compressed-block format; about 3x faster than cuSPARSE BSR SpMV on SuiteSparse matrices.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE BSR SpMV (cusparse_bsrmv, cuSPARSE v12.4); also TileSpMV and DASP — The ICS '25 paper measures FP64 SpMV Gflop/s over 2,843 SuiteSparse matrices on an A100 and an RTX 4090 with CUDA 12.4: averages of per-matrix speedups are 2.99x and 2.95x over cuSPARSE v12.4 BSR SpMV (best of block sizes 2, 4, 8, 16), 3.95x and 3.06x over TileSpMV, and 1.21x and 2.76x over DASP. The repo ships only the cuSPARSE-BSR harness, not cuSPARSE CSR, TileSpMV or DASP runners, and the host CPU is not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B: the ICS '25 paper (read via raw.githubusercontent.com/hpcrl/ICS2025-webpage) carries every claimed number and the repo has a cuSPARSE-BSR harness with nvcc -O3 flags, but the host CPU is unstated and the TileSpMV and DASP harnesses are not in the repo, so not A.

**Known shortcoming:** No library API: cb_spmv() is a benchmark driver that reallocates, copies and frees the matrix on every call. FP64 hard-coded, int32 indices, atomicAdd into y so results are nondeterministic; the repo times ITER=10 launches where the paper says 1000; the self-check tolerance is loose (abs 1e-3, rel 1e-4). The edge over DASP on A100 is only 1.21x.

**Independent measurement:** verifier read the ICS '25 PDF

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Intra-block data aggregation: each sub-block's 4-bit row and column indices are packed into one uint8 and stored next to its FP64 values in one contiguous region, which raises L1/L2 hit rates (the paper measures this with Nsight Compute). Adaptive sub-block formats (COO under 32 nonzeros, dense above 128, CSR between, thresholds taken from TileSpMV) avoid BSR's padded zeros. Block-aware column aggregation packs the non-empty columns of super-sparse sub-blocks together so warps stay busy, and an inter-thread-block load-balancing pass redistributes blocks across SMs; partial sums are combined with warp shuffles and atomicAdd into y.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated FP64 SpMV with the same matrix (iterative solvers, power iterations) on an NVIDIA GPU, where the CPU-side conversion is paid once.
- Irregular matrices with many very sparse 16x16 blocks, where cuSPARSE BSR wastes bandwidth on padded zeros (the paper's largest wins, 37.54x and 54.27x, are such cases).
- Consumer or FP64-weak GPUs such as the RTX 4090, where it beat tensor-core DASP by 2.76x on average in the paper.
- As a reference implementation for a block-based SpMV kernel you will adapt into your own code.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a library API: there is none, the code is a benchmark driver that reallocates and copies the matrix on every cb_spmv() call.
- A100/H100-class GPUs with strong FP64 tensor cores, where the paper's average edge over DASP is only 1.21x.
- FP32 or mixed precision, or AMD/Intel GPUs or CPUs: ValType is hard-coded to double and the code is CUDA only.
- Matrices that change every call, since the COO-to-block conversion runs on the CPU and the paper reports it as comparable to TileSpMV and BSR conversion for matrices above 1 million nonzeros.
- Matrices beyond 32-bit indexing: nnz, rows and columns are int.

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA Toolkit (nvcc, CUDA runtime; cuSPARSE only for the baseline harness), host C++ compiler with OpenMP · Tested with CUDA 12.4 and driver 550.144.03; minimum version not documented · NVIDIA GPUs only; Makefiles default to -arch=sm_89 (RTX 4090), change to sm_80 for A100

**Vs siblings:** Pick CB-SpMV over DASP when the GPU has weak FP64 tensor cores (RTX-class) and over TileSpMV for the same 16x16 tiling with better cache locality; prefer merge-spmv, CSR5 or ISpMV when you need to stay in CSR without a conversion step, and DASP on A100-class hardware where the gap is small and DASP has more history.

**Gotchas:**
- Results are accumulated into y with FP64 atomicAdd, so y must be zeroed before each call and the summation order (and last bits of the result) is nondeterministic run to run.
- The built-in correctness check uses loose tolerances for FP64 (absolute 1e-3, relative 1e-4).
- The repo harness averages over ITER = 10 timed launches after one untimed launch, while the paper says each kernel ran 1000 times, so repo numbers will be noisier than the paper's.
- The program accepts only an absolute path to the .mtx file and uses GPU 0.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-02, a bug fix and preprocessing change that postdates the paper) and Apache-2.0, but small (six commits, no issues filed) and research-grade; CB-SpMM and CB-SpGEMM are announced but not released.

[repo](https://github.com/xing-cong/CB-Sparse) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hpcrl/ICS2025-webpage/HEAD/program/Proceedings_ICS25/ics25-7.pdf)

##### CSR5 (Benchmark_SpMV_using_CSR5)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Reference code for CSR5, a tiled CSR variant for SpMV that beat MKL, cuSPARSE, CUSP and pOSKI on irregular matrices in 2015.

**Beats:** Intel MKL 11.2, cuSPARSE v6.5, CUSP, ViennaCL, BiCSB, pOSKI — Peer-reviewed ICS 2015 paper: in double-precision SpMV on 10 irregular matrices, CSR5 averaged 17.6% over the best prior method on dual Xeon E5-2667 v3 (pOSKI there, not MKL), 28.5% on GTX 980, 173.0% on R9 290X and 293.3% on Xeon Phi 5110p, with peaks of 213.3/153.6/405.1/943.3%. On 14 regular matrices it was 'comparable or better', but MKL had the best CPU average. Compilers were Intel C/C++ 15.0.1, g++ 4.8.2 and CUDA 6.5; the paper gives no flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper compares against the best other method per platform (pOSKI on CPU), not MKL; no compiler flags; repo benchmark runs only CSR5 with no baseline; abandoned (last commit 2020-12-26).

**Known shortcoming:** CSR5 conversion rearranges the caller's CSR arrays in place; AVX2/Phi/KNL versions double precision only; on regular matrices MKL had the best CPU average and CSR5 lost to ESB and MKL on Xeon Phi; bug fixes in 2016 postdate the ICS 2015 measurements.

**How:** Nonzeros are cut into fixed-size 2D tiles of omega columns (the SIMD or warp width) by sigma rows (chosen from the matrix's average nonzeros per row and the cache). Each tile gets a bit-flag descriptor of row starts, so every SIMD lane does the same amount of work no matter how uneven the row lengths are. Partial row sums are combined with a redesigned segmented sum that is mostly a prefix-sum scan, and a calibrator array fixes rows that span tiles. Load balance comes from the nonzero count, not the row count, so power-law and other irregular matrices do not leave lanes idle.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated double-precision SpMV on irregular matrices (power-law graphs, web, circuit) where row-length skew hurts CSR kernels
- Iterative solvers with tens or more iterations: the paper says conversion costs about as much as a few SpMVs and that CSR5 was the only format beating CSR at 50 iterations
- GPU SpMV (CUDA or OpenCL) where you want one format that copes with both regular and irregular sparsity
- As a reference design to port into your own sparse kernel library under MIT terms

**Skip it when:**
- Regular, well-balanced matrices on Intel CPUs: the paper says MKL had the best CPU average on the regular set, and on Xeon Phi CSR5 lost to ESB and MKL there
- Single-shot SpMV, where the CSR->CSR5 conversion is not amortized
- When you need a maintained, packaged library: no commits since Dec 2020, the code is per-platform folders built from Makefiles, and the 2015-era baselines (MKL 11.2, cuSPARSE 6.5) have been improved since
- Single precision on CPU or Phi: the AVX2, KNC and KNL versions support only double; float exists only in the CUDA and OpenCL versions
- Other kernels (SpMM, SpGEMM, transpose-multiply): this repo does SpMV only

**Integration:** source-drop · OpenMP and AVX2 intrinsics (CPU); CUDA toolkit (CUDA version); OpenCL 1.2 runtime (OpenCL versions); Intel compiler suggested for Phi/KNL · C++ compiler with OpenMP and AVX2 (Makefile: -O3 -mavx -mavx2 -march=native -fopenmp); README tested Intel C/C++ 2015; CUDA 6.5-era · x86-64 with AVX2; Xeon Phi KNC; KNL AVX-512; NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA/OpenCL); AMD GPUs (OpenCL)

**Vs siblings:** Ginkgo is a maintained solver library with its own SpMV formats, so prefer it for production; pick CSR5 when you need to study or port a load-balanced SpMV kernel for irregular matrices. Sympiler and the A64FX CHOLMOD work target direct factorization, not SpMV.

**Gotchas:**
- asCSR5() transposes the caller's col_idx and values arrays in place; they are not valid CSR again until you call asCSR() or destroy().
- spmv() returns ANONYMOUSLIB_UNSUPPORTED_CSR_SPMV if the handle has not been converted to CSR5 first.
- The bundled main.cpp times only CSR5 against a single-thread naive loop and checks results with a 1% relative tolerance; it does not rerun the MKL/cuSPARSE comparisons from the paper.
- The README's change log records later fixes to the AVX2 and Phi versions (a small-matrix bug and y-update performance, Jul 2016) and a CUDA timing bug (Apr 2016), all after the ICS 2015 numbers.

**Status:** Abandoned since Dec 2020, but MIT-licensed, header-only per platform, and small enough to vendor or port; expect to modernize the CUDA and OpenCL build files and to re-benchmark against current MKL and cuSPARSE before adopting.

[repo](https://github.com/bhSPARSE/Benchmark_SpMV_using_CSR5) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1503.05032)

##### cuBool (sparse Boolean linear algebra on CUDA)  `C++ (CUDA)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

CUDA library of sparse Boolean-semiring matrix and vector operations; Boolean SpGEMM runs 1.3-16x faster than CPU SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS.

**Beats:** SuiteSparse on CPU (README does not say which package; GraphBLAS likely) — The authors' SpBench harness, also used for their IPDPS Workshops 2021 (GrAPL) paper, times only the operation, with data already resident and an average of 10 runs. It compares cuBool on a GTX 1070 with SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS on the host's 4-core i7-6700 (SuiteSparse version and thread count not stated; GCC and CUDA versions not stated). Boolean M*M was 11x faster on amazon0312, 16x on web-Google, 3.7x on roadNet-PA and 1.3x on luxembourg_osm, and M+M^2 addition about 3x faster on web graphs (ratios derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** The peer-reviewed IPDPSW 2021 (GrAPL) paper calls its own comparison 'not entirely fair': GTX 1070 GPU vs SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS on a 4-core CPU, thread count not stated; on road matrices CUSP and cuSPARSE beat cuBool for element-wise add; GCC and CUDA versions not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Commits since 2021 are CI/docs/format only; pycubool last released 1.2.0 (2021-06-11). Open #13: prebuilt .so lacks cuBool_Matrix_EWiseMult and source build fails with CUB/limits errors. Open #14: pycubool loads its own log as a library. Global backend with no lock. Boolean SpGEMM only, no solver.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Matrices are stored as value-less CSR (row offsets plus uint32 column indices only), so a matrix takes (m + nnz) x 4 bytes of GPU memory. Multiplication uses nsparse, a Boolean adaptation of the Nagasaka, Nukada and Matsuoka (ICPP 2017) hash-table SpGEMM, which bins rows by work and keeps memory use low. Element-wise addition uses GPU Merge Path (Green, McColl, Bader) with dynamic load balancing and a two-pass size-then-fill scheme. The baseline is a 4-core CPU, so most of the gap is GPU versus CPU; the paper shows a smaller gain over generic GPU libraries that treat floats as truth values.

**Use it when:**
- Graph reachability, transitive closure, RPQ/CFPQ or parsing algorithms that reduce to repeated Boolean SpGEMM on an NVIDIA GPU
- Web and co-purchase graphs of about 0.4-0.9M rows with 5-8 non-zeros per row (amazon0312, amazon-2008, web-Google), where M*M produces 14-30M non-zeros; there cuBool's mxm beat SuiteSparse by 11-16x and also beat cuSPARSE and CUSP
- Memory-tight GPU work: without stored values cuBool used 165-241 MB on the large mxm cases, against 897-1717 MB for CUSP
- Prototyping in Python (pycubool) on a laptop with the CPU fallback, then running the same code on a CUDA server

**Skip it when:**
- Anything beyond the Boolean semiring (numeric SpGEMM, min-plus, masks, user-defined monoids); use full GraphBLAS (SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS, GraphBLAST, or the authors' successor spla)
- Road-network or very sparse, low-degree matrices: there clBool's mxm was faster, and for element-wise add CUSP and cuSPARSE beat cuBool on every road matrix (roadNet-PA 16.9 ms vs CUSP 11.2 ms)
- Small matrices: on luxembourg_osm (115K rows) mxm was 2.4 ms vs 3.1 ms for SuiteSparse and 1.7 ms for cuSPARSE, and GPU memory never went below about 91 MB while SuiteSparse used 22 MB on wing
- Non-NVIDIA or non-Linux platforms: only Ubuntu 20.04 is tested, and Windows and macOS are still listed as 'coming soon'
- Linear-system solving: despite its category, it has no factorization or iterative solver

**Integration:** shared lib · CUDA toolkit with Thrust/CUB and the vendored nsparse-um SpGEMM (header-only, under deps/); googletest only for tests; Python 3 for pycubool · C++17 host code, CUDA standard 14, CMake 3.15+, GCC; the README's tested path is CUDA 10.1 with GCC 8 (newer combinations not documented) · Linux x86-64 with an NVIDIA GPU (tested Ubuntu 20.04, GTX 1070); CPU sequential fallback anywhere it builds

**Vs siblings:** Pick cuBool over GraphBLAST or ALP/GraphBLAS when the whole algorithm is Boolean and runs on one NVIDIA GPU, so value-less CSR and a Boolean-specialised SpGEMM pay off. For other semirings or for AMD and Intel GPUs, prefer the same group's spla (OpenCL) or GraphBLAST.

**Gotchas:**
- Indices are uint32 (cuBool_Index), so dimensions and nnz must stay below 2^32
- The pycubool PyPI wheel (1.2.0, last upload 2021-06-11) ships a prebuilt .so; open issue #13 (2022, labelled bug) reports that this .so lacks cuBool_Matrix_EWiseMult and that source builds fail with 'limits and CUB' errors on newer toolchains; open issue #14 says pycubool tries to load its own log file as the shared library
- The README advises replacing the system gcc/g++ symlinks with GCC 8 to match CUDA 10; on a modern system, set CC, CXX and CUDAHOSTCXX instead
- cuBool_Finalize fails if objects are still alive unless you initialised with CUBOOL_HINT_RELAXED_FINALIZE (the Python wrapper relies on that hint)

**Status:** MIT-licensed and listed as active (last commit 2025-11-17), but every commit since mid-2021 touches CI, docs or formatting, and the last PyPI release is 1.2.0 from June 2021, so treat it as a finished research library that you may need to patch for current CUDA.

[repo](https://github.com/SparseLinearAlgebra/cuBool) · [benchmark](https://github.com/EgorOrachyov/SpBench)

##### CVR (Compressed Vectorization-oriented sparse Row)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

CGO 2018 AVX-512 SpMV format for Xeon Phi Knights Landing that beats MKL CSR SpMV, especially on scale-free graphs.

**Beats:** Intel MKL CSR SpMV; also MKL CSR(I) inspector-executor, ESB, VHCC and CSR5 — On a Xeon Phi 7250 (68 cores, MCDRAM flat mode, icpc 17.04 -O3, 1000 iterations, best SMT thread count per method), double-precision CVR SpMV averaged 2.84x MKL CSR (up to 39.53x on wiki-talk) on 30 scale-free matrices and 1.22-1.24x MKL (up to 17.58x on ins2) on 28 HPC matrices, and 1.33x / 1.10x over the best of CSR(I), ESB, VHCC and CSR5; these are the authors' own peer-reviewed numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** MKL/CSR-I/ESB comparison harness ships as binaries only (sources withheld); needs KNL hardware; paper is inconsistent (intro: HPC avg 1.22x over MKL, Section 7.1: 1.24x).

**Known shortcoming:** Paper appendix says it 'only supports Xeon Phi currently'; needs the discontinued icpc compiler (Intel-only intrinsics). Printed GFlops count 1 flop per nonzero, half the usual 2. MKL, CSR(I) and ESB baselines ship as binaries only.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each SIMD lane owns one row at a time (8 lanes for double on AVX-512), so a single 512-bit fused multiply-add advances 8 rows at once and the per-row reduction disappears; when a lane's row ends, a 'tracker' is fed the next non-empty row, and once rows run out, empty trackers steal nonzeros from longer ones to keep lanes balanced. Conversion records (position, write-back row) pairs in a rec vector so results are written to y at the right point during the streaming kernel. Processing many rows together improves reuse of x; the paper reports an order-of-magnitude lower L2 miss ratio than the other formats and the cheapest conversion (median 2.14 MKL-iterations to amortize on scale-free matrices, versus 5.36 for CSR5 and 49-2,653 for CSR(I), ESB and VHCC).

**Use it when:**
- You still run Xeon Phi Knights Landing (AVX-512 MIC, MCDRAM in flat mode) and need double-precision SpMV on power-law matrices: web graphs, social, wiki, routing and FSM matrices, where the paper's domain averages were 2.5-6.3x MKL.
- Iterative solvers or graph kernels running tens to thousands of SpMVs on the same matrix, where CVR's low conversion cost (often under ten iterations to amortize, per the paper) matters.
- Matrices with many very short rows (for example ins2 at 4 nnz/row, 17.58x over MKL), where row-per-lane packing keeps all 8 lanes busy.
- As a reference design for row-per-SIMD-lane SpMV with feeding and stealing, to port to current AVX-512 Xeons, ARM SVE or GPUs (the authors planned a CUDA/OpenCL port that never appeared in the repo).

**Skip it when:**
- Any non-KNL machine: the artifact appendix says CVR 'only supports Xeon Phi currently', the Makefile hard-codes icpc -xMIC-AVX512, and Intel has discontinued both KNL and the classic icpc compiler.
- Wide, short-and-fat matrices with hundreds or thousands of nonzeros per row (connectus, 12month1, rail4284 in the paper), where VHCC's 2D jagged partition beat CVR.
- Regular FEM/HPC matrices where you already use MKL or CSR5: the paper's HPC average is only 1.24x over MKL and 1.10x over the next best format.
- Single precision, complex values, transposed products or multi-vector SpMM: the build is double-only (FLOAT_TYPE fixed to double) and only y = A*x is implemented.
- Production use: research code with leftover debug printing, a single 2018 code drop, no tests beyond the built-in result check, and no issues or maintainer activity since then.

**Integration:** source-drop · OpenMP; Intel C/C++ compiler 17 with AVX-512; numactl to place data in MCDRAM; Intel MKL only for the prebuilt comparison binaries · icpc 17.04 (-O3 -xMIC-AVX512 -qopenmp); building with GCC or Clang is not documented · x86-64 Xeon Phi Knights Landing only (AVX-512F/PF/ER, MCDRAM flat mode); Linux (CentOS 7.3 tested)

**Vs siblings:** Choose CVR over CSR5 or merge-spmv only on Knights Landing with scale-free matrices, where the paper measured 1.33x average over the best competitor (usually CSR5); on current AVX-512 or ARM SVE CPUs, SPC5 (maintained, block-based, MKL baseline) or CSR5/merge-spmv (portable, CPU and GPU) are the practical picks, and ALBUS targets MKL on regular matrices on Haswell-era Xeons.

**Gotchas:**
- Conversion allocates a second copy of values and int32 column indices (nnz entries each) plus a rec array of about 2 x numRows ints, so memory is roughly double the CSR footprint while both exist; all indices are 32-bit, and a kernel comment notes the padded tail uses column 0 with value 0.
- The kernel uses _mm512_permute4f128_epi32 and _mm512_i32logather_pd and the Intel-specific '#pragma noprefetch', which tie it to the Intel classic compiler; expect porting work before it compiles elsewhere.
- The printed throughput is nnz divided by time, i.e. one flop per nonzero rather than the usual 2*nnz, so its GFlop/s figures are half what most SpMV papers would report for the same time.
- The MKL, CSR(I) and ESB comparison programs ship only as binaries (sources withheld over licensing), and every method's SMT thread count was tuned separately, so the baseline side cannot be audited or rebuilt.

**Status:** Dormant since 2018 apart from a 2024 README edit (24 stars, MIT), so it is copyable but effectively frozen to discontinued Knights Landing hardware and the Intel classic compiler.

[repo](https://github.com/puckbee/CVR) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/puckbee/CVR/HEAD/CVR-%20Efficient%20Vectorization%20of%20SpMV%20on%20X86%20Processors.pdf)

##### Ginkgo  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

C++17 sparse linear algebra library with portable CUDA/HIP/SYCL/OpenMP kernels; beat AmgX AMG and MAGMA batched solves in DOE apps.

**Beats:** NVIDIA AmgX; MAGMA batched dense; MA57; LAPACK dgbsv — The IJHPCA 2024 ECP paper reports: Ginkgo AMG with 20-40% faster per-iteration preconditioner application than NVIDIA AmgX on a V100 (MFEM), and mixed-precision AMG 1.5x faster on one L-shape case; batched BiCGStab about 2x over MAGMA's batched dense direct solve in PeleLM (MI250X, Frontier); about 90% less linear-solver time than LAPACK dgbsv in XGC (Perlmutter A100, Crusher MI250X); and 1.8-2.4x end-to-end over a CPU MA57 baseline on MI250X for ACOPF (1.05-1.3x on V100). That last result compares GPU against CPU. Compiler flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** 1.8-2.4x over MA57 compares a GPU against a CPU; no flags given.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper says sparse direct solvers lack supernodal acceleration, AMG only graph-matching coarsening, communication limits strong scaling; headline numbers from application integrations (MFEM, PeleLM, XGC, ExaSGD), not a kernel shootout; no CPU comparison against SuiteSparse.

**Independent measurement:** first-party OpenFOAM integration (hpsim/OGL, OGL_DATA boxTurb16 v0.1-108): OpenFOAM native CG on one Xeon Gold 6230 process 36.04 s vs Ginkgo CUDA on a V100 21.93 s at resolution 64 (about 1.64x, derived from page data), BiCGStab 2.0x, GPU slower at resolution 32; Meccanica paper claims up to 8x / about 15x (snippet only)

**How:** Each backend gets hand-written kernels for its hardware (CUDA, HIP, SYCL), so nothing goes through a generic translation layer. The speedups in the measured cases come from mixed-precision AMG (coarse levels in lower precision, fine level in full precision, parallel graph-matching coarsening), batched iterative solvers that solve many small independent sparse systems inside one GPU kernel, and GPU-resident sparse direct factorization and triangular solves. Half and bfloat16 value types, plus adaptive-precision block-Jacobi, cut memory traffic in these memory-bound kernels.

**Use it when:**
- Iterative solves of large sparse systems on NVIDIA, AMD or Intel GPUs where you want one codebase across vendors
- Many small independent sparse systems per step (chemistry or combustion kinetics, per-cell plasma solves) through the batched BiCGStab/GMRES solvers
- Replacing NVIDIA AmgX with a vendor-neutral AMG preconditioner, especially in mixed precision
- Moving a CPU sparse direct solve (MA57- or LAPACK-banded-style) onto GPUs to remove host-device round trips
- Distributed solves via the MPI module (GPU-aware MPI recommended)

**Skip it when:**
- Small or one-off CPU-only sparse solves: Eigen/SuiteSparse are simpler, and no CPU-vs-SuiteSparse benchmark is cited
- Sparse direct factorization of hard 3D problems: the IJHPCA paper says the direct solvers lack supernodal techniques, so CHOLMOD/MUMPS-class solvers are likely stronger
- AMG needing aggressive or alternative coarsening: only parallel graph-matching coarsening is supported per the paper
- Strong scaling on many nodes: the paper names communication as the bottleneck
- Builds with limited compile time or memory: full GPU builds are heavy (INSTALL.md warns of >20 min and high memory for the Jacobi kernels with full optimizations)

**Integration:** shared lib (static optional via BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF); CMake find_package(Ginkgo), target Ginkgo::ginkgo · none for the core/reference build; optional CUDA 11+, ROCm 6.2+ (hipBLAS, hipSPARSE, rocRAND, rocThrust), oneAPI 2024.1+ (oneMKL, oneDPL), OpenMP, MPI 3.1+, METIS, PAPI · C++17; CMake 3.16+; GCC 7+, Clang 5+, Intel 2019+, MSVC 2019+, NVHPC 22.7+ · Linux, macOS, Windows; x86-64/aarch64 CPUs (OpenMP); NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (HIP), Intel (SYCL) GPUs

**Vs siblings:** Choose Ginkgo over AMGCL when you need full solver stacks on AMD or Intel GPUs, batched small-system solvers, or mixed-precision AMG. Choose it over CSR5, merge-spmv or ISpMV when you need complete solvers and preconditioners rather than one SpMV kernel, and over BaSpaCho or Sympiler when an iterative or batched method fits better than a supernodal Cholesky.

**Gotchas:**
- Half precision needs CUDA compute capability 5.3+ and bfloat16 needs 8.0+ unless built with CUDA 12.2+
- GINKGO_JACOBI_FULL_OPTIMIZATIONS gives the best adaptive block-Jacobi but greatly increases compile time and memory
- Windows builds can hit 'export ordinal too large' (needs -O1) and cc1plus out-of-memory errors
- The headline numbers come from application integrations (MFEM, PeleLM, XGC, ExaSGD), not from a standalone kernel shootout

**Status:** Actively developed (612 stars, commits through 2026-09) under BSD-3-Clause with an OpenSSF best-practices badge and CI on GitLab, so it is safe to adopt as a dependency, but it is too large to vendor as source.

[repo](https://github.com/ginkgo-project/ginkgo) · [benchmark](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10943420241268323)

##### GLU (GPU-accelerated sparse LU solver for circuit simulation)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

CUDA sparse LU numeric factorization for circuit matrices; papers report 19.56x over KLU (numeric phase only, float32).

**Beats:** KLU and UMFPACK (SuiteSparse) — TVLSI 2016 (GLU 1.0, PDF in docs/): numeric factorization time only, excluding preprocessing and symbolic analysis, on a Tesla K40 (CUDA 5.0) against CPU solvers on two 8-core Xeon E5-2670: 19.56x over KLU 1.2.0 and 47.13x over UMFPACK 5.6.2 on typical UFL circuit matrices, 39.39x and 24.04x on general matrices. GLU3.0 (IEEE D&T 2020, GTX TITAN X, -O3, float32): numeric factorization including memory copies averages 2.81x geometric mean (3.51x arithmetic) faster than 32-thread NICSLU on 15 circuit matrices, with the larger CPU preprocessing and symbolic times reported separately; neither paper measured the current repo code.

**Known shortcoming:** The TVLSI 2016 paper (docs/He_TVLSI_15.pdf in the repo) times numeric factorization only and measured GLU 1.0, not the GLU 3.0 code now in the repo (float32, 2.81x geomean vs NICSLU). Feb 2026 fixes addressed a __syncthreads deadlock. The repo bundles NICSLU under LGPL.

**Known shortcoming:** float32 only (REAL is float, CPU triangular solve in float, no refinement). The CPU preprocess plus symbolic phase is far slower than the GPU numeric phase (G3_circuit 9,729 ms vs 878 ms; Raj1 7,241 ms vs 845 ms; D&T Table I); Raj1 0.98x and rajat20 1.02x vs 32-thread NICSLU. No refactorization API; pyglu redoes symbolic analysis on every splu; tmpMem takes all free GPU memory minus 4 GB; the NaN check is compiled out under nvcc. Open issues #3 (nnz is 32-bit) and #6 (CSR .mtx gives wrong results).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** A hybrid right-looking column algorithm: symbolic analysis predicts the L+U pattern and groups columns into dependency-free levels (with GLU2.0's double-U dependency check, relaxed in 3.0), so all columns of a level are factorized at once and their submatrix updates are applied with atomicAdd. GLU3.0 adapts the kernel shape to each level: more than 896 columns use 2 warps per block, more than 448 use 4, more than 16 use 32, and the last 16 or fewer columns run as single-column kernels across 16 CUDA streams with 1024 threads each. Values are float32 because the Maxwell GPU used for the paper had no FP64 atomics; the paper expects FP64 to be about 30 percent slower. The TVLSI paper notes part of its large speedups (up to 530x over KLU on mc2depi) comes from denormal numbers that slow the CPU solvers down.

**Use it when:**
- Large, low-fill circuit-simulation matrices (tens of thousands to millions of rows) on an NVIDIA GPU where numeric factorization dominates: the GLU3.0 paper measured 2.9x to 10.5x over 32-thread NICSLU on ASIC_320ks, ASIC_680ks and G3_circuit.
- Research or prototyping of GPU LU where you will edit the C++/CUDA to reuse one symbolic analysis across many Newton-iteration refactorizations, since the shipped CLI and pyglu redo it every call.
- Python code that wants a GPU splu/spsolve with a SciPy-like call and can live with float32 accuracy.
- Matrices whose CPU factorization is slowed by denormal values (barrier2-11 in the TVLSI paper).
- When you need modifiable source under a permissive license: the GLU code is BSD-3-Clause (the bundled NICSLU is LGPL-2.1).

**Skip it when:**
- When you need double precision: REAL is typedef float, inputs are cast to float32, the CPU triangular solves run in float32 with no iterative refinement, and issue #2 reported a log-determinant differing from MATLAB at about 1e-9 relative on the 4,960-row add32 example.
- One-shot solves: CPU preprocessing and symbolic time dwarfs the GPU numeric time (9,729 ms vs 878 ms on G3_circuit, 7,241 ms vs 845 ms on Raj1 in the GLU3.0 paper's Table I), and pyglu repeats it on every splu call.
- Small circuits such as circuit_2 and rajat15, where the TVLSI paper says GLU is slower than the CPU solvers; on Raj1 and rajat20 the GLU3.0 numeric time only ties 32-thread NICSLU (0.98x, 1.02x), and on general matrices GLU 1.0 was only 1.12x over 16-thread PARDISO.
- Matrices that need dynamic partial pivoting: the GPU phase does no pivoting and relies on the static MC64-style permutation, plus optional perturbation of tiny pivots to 3.45e-4 times the 1-norm of A (-p / perturb=True).
- Matrices whose nnz approaches 2^32 or whose L+U factors exceed GPU memory (32-bit unsigned indices, issue #3 open), complex-valued systems (issue #5 open), and non-NVIDIA GPUs or non-x86 hosts (NICSLU is built with -msse2).

**Integration:** source-drop: src/Makefile builds the lu_cmd executable against bundled NICSLU static libraries; setup.py builds the pyglu Python extension · CUDA toolkit (nvcc, cudart), bundled NICSLU (LGPL-2.1), pthread, libm, librt; pyglu adds Python >= 3.9, pybind11 >= 2.11, NumPy >= 1.22 and optional SciPy >= 1.9 · C++11 (g++ -std=c++11 -O3, nvcc -O3 -std=c++11); minimum CUDA version not documented (the TVLSI work used CUDA 5.0) · Linux x86-64 with one NVIDIA GPU; the build passes no -arch flag, so nvcc's default target applies; LUonDevice always uses device 0

**Vs siblings:** NICSLU (1.87x over KLU, CPU) is the stronger choice for one-off solves: the GLU3.0 paper puts GLU's numeric phase at 2.81x geometric mean over 32-thread NICSLU, but GLU's CPU preprocessing and symbolic time alone often exceeds NICSLU's whole numeric factorization (7,241 ms vs 825 ms on Raj1). CKTSO-GPU claims 13.29x geometric mean refactorization over KLU 1.3.9 on the same circuit workload. Pick GLU when you want BSD-3-Clause GPU source to modify or a SciPy-style Python entry point, and float32 accuracy is acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- LUonDevice sizes its dense scratch buffer (tmpMem, one n-length float column per in-flight column) to fit all free GPU memory except 4 GB, or half the free memory when less than 4 GB is free, so a second process or factorization on the same GPU can fail (inferred from numeric.cu).
- Numerical failures can pass silently: pyglu scans the factors for NaN/Inf only when a CUDA error message was produced, and the NaN check in numeric.cu sits behind GLU_DEBUG, which the Makefile passes only to g++, not to nvcc (inferred from the source). Submatrix updates use float atomicAdd, so results are not bit-reproducible run to run.
- Issue #6 (open since May 2023): a matrix written row-wise (CSR) to .mtx gave wrong solutions, while the same matrix in CSC matched SciPy; feed CSC data.
- The February 2026 fixes (a __syncthreads() on a divergent path that could deadlock, unchecked CUDA calls, unsafe scratch sizing) mean pre-2026 checkouts, which the papers measured, can hang or mis-size memory; use current master.

**Status:** UC Riverside research code that sat dormant from 2020 to 2026, then got Codex-assisted bug fixes (Feb 2026), pyglu bindings (Mar 2026) and a GitHub Pages site (Jul 2026); 12 commits, no CI tests (the only workflow publishes Pages), 5 open issues, BSD-3-Clause GLU code bundling LGPL-2.1 NICSLU.

[repo](https://github.com/sheldonucr/GLU_public) · [benchmark](https://github.com/sheldonucr/GLU_public/blob/master/docs/He_TVLSI_15.pdf)

##### GraphBLAST (GraphBLAS on the GPU)  `C++ (CUDA)`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

CUDA implementation of the GraphBLAS API for graph algorithms; paper reports 43.51x geomean over multi-threaded SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS.

**Beats:** SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS through LAGraph (CPU) — The TOMS paper (Yang, Buluc, Owens, doi 10.1145/3466795), known here only from its abstract as quoted in search results, reports a 43.51x geometric-mean and 1268x peak speedup of one NVIDIA GPU over multi-threaded CPU SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (and 31.83x over GBTL) across its algorithm and graph mix, with the GPU, CPU and versions unverified. The independent spla README chart (GTX 1070 vs LAGraph on a 4-core i7-6700, read by eye) shows big wins for PageRank and triangle counting but mixed BFS and SSSP results, including losses; neither source compares like-for-like hardware.

**Known shortcoming:** GPU vs CPU comparison (43.51x geomean over SuiteSparse GraphBLAS per the ACM TOMS abstract, doi 10.1145/3466795); paper unreadable here.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: unmasked float mxm goes to cuSPARSE csrgemm2 and ignores the semiring, so MinPlus returns the PlusTimes result (open #20; fix PR #26 never merged). #9 hangs on sm_70+; #28 CUB build error on CUDA 11.5; csrgemm2 was removed in CUDA 12. Many ops print 'not implemented yet'.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Direction optimisation (push-pull) borrowed from Ligra and Gunrock: vxm/mxv switches between a push SpMSpV over CSC when the frontier is sparse and a pull masked SpMV over CSR when it is dense, keeping both formats on the GPU. Masked pull SpMV fuses the mask and can exit early per row for the Boolean semiring (spmvDenseMaskedOrKernel), and descriptor flags add structure-only mode (ignore edge values) and operand reuse. Load balancing for the general SpMV comes from moderngpu's merge-based SpmvCsrBinary, and sparse vectors are compacted with prefix scans.

**Use it when:**
- Traversal-style or iterative graph analytics (BFS, SSSP, PageRank, triangle counting) on a single NVIDIA GPU where the whole graph, in both CSR and CSC unless symmetric, fits in device memory.
- Large power-law or social graphs where PageRank and triangle counting are compute-heavy: the third-party spla chart puts GraphBLAST roughly 13-75x ahead of LAGraph for PageRank and 5-13x for triangle counting on a GTX 1070 against a 4-core i7.
- Research or prototyping where you want algorithms expressed as semiring linear algebra and are willing to work in C++ templates against an older CUDA toolchain.
- Older Pascal-generation (sm_6x) or earlier NVIDIA GPUs, which match the toolchain the README lists (CUDA 9.1/9.2, g++ 4.9.3/5.4.0).

**Skip it when:**
- Volta, Turing, Ampere or Hopper GPUs (sm_70+) without testing: open issue #9 reports hangs in BFS on medium matrices after patching the bundled moderngpu for SM >= 70, and the build defaults to compute_35 PTX (common.mk, CMake -arch=sm_35).
- Current CUDA toolkits: issue #28 reports a CUB namespace compile error with CUDA 11.5, and unmasked mxm calls cuSPARSE csrgemm/csrgemm2, which search results say NVIDIA removed in cuSPARSE 12.0; expect porting work.
- Code that relies on non-arithmetic semirings in unmasked mxm: it routes float SpGEMM to cuSPARSE csrgemm2, which only multiplies and adds, so MinimumPlus returns the PlusMultiplies result (open issue #20); the fix (draft PR #26, GALATIC) was never merged.
- Workloads needing the full GraphBLAS feature set: many paths print 'not implemented yet' and return GrB_NOT_IMPLEMENTED (sparse-sparse eWiseAdd per issue #5, unmasked non-float SpGEMM, SpMM/GEMM, masked reduce, several assign/extract variants), and the shipped BFS ('use float for now for both v and A') and README SSSP work in float.
- BFS or SSSP on road-like or small graphs, or graphs larger than GPU memory: the spla chart shows GraphBLAST slower than CPU LAGraph on several BFS/SSSP inputs and missing results on its larger graphs; indices are 32-bit int.

**Integration:** header-only templates (copy graphblas/ into the include path) plus two moderngpu sources to compile with your program (ext/moderngpu/src/mgpucontext.cu, mgpuutil.cpp); Makefile and CMake builds for the examples · CUDA with cuSPARSE, cuBLAS and cuRAND; Boost program_options (the Descriptor parses command-line options); git submodules ctcyang/moderngpu (a fork) and a standalone NVlabs CUB · Tested on CUDA 9.1/9.2, Boost 1.58, g++ 4.9.3/5.4.0, CMake 3.11.1 optional; compiled as -std=c++11 with -O3 -use_fast_math · NVIDIA GPUs only; build targets compute_35 by default; Linux toolchain paths in common.mk (Boost path hard-coded to the author's machine)

**Vs siblings:** Pick GraphBLAST over spla when you are on NVIDIA hardware and want direction-optimised BFS/SSSP and the fastest PageRank in the spla comparison; pick spla for AMD or Intel GPUs through OpenCL, cuBool when only Boolean semiring operations are needed and you want a maintained CUDA library, and ALP/GraphBLAS for a CPU GraphBLAS that beats SuiteSparse without a GPU.

**Gotchas:**
- Edit common.mk before building: BOOST_DIR and BOOST_DEPS point to /data/ctcyang/boost_1_58_0, and CUDA_ARCH is 35; the CMake build hard-codes -arch=sm_35.
- Builds use -use_fast_math, which relaxes float accuracy for PageRank-style numeric kernels; BFS and the README SSSP example use float for both vectors and matrix values.
- The benchmark scripts time only GPU kernels with a GpuTimer (not graph loading or host-device transfer) and run PageRank with --max_niter 10, so match iteration counts and what is timed before comparing with a CPU library.
- Directed graphs keep both CSR and CSC copies in device memory for push-pull; only symmetric structure lets it free the CSC index arrays.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2021-06-18 (10 open issues, including a correctness bug and Volta+ hangs, without maintainer replies); Apache-2.0 and readable as a reference design, but treat it as research code that needs porting to current CUDA and GPUs before use.

[repo](https://github.com/gunrock/graphblast) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3466795)

##### OpSparse (optimized GPU SpGEMM framework)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research CUDA hash-based SpGEMM (C = A*B, CSR, FP64) for V100; paper reports 7.35x average over cuSPARSE.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE SpGEMM, nsparse and spECK — Per the IEEE Access 2022 abstract (search snippets; the paper was not opened), on 26 common SuiteSparse matrices on a Tesla V100 with CUDA 11.2, OpSparse averages 7.35x (up to 27.8x) over cuSPARSE SpGEMM, 1.43x (up to 1.81x) over nsparse and 1.52x (up to 2.04x) over spECK, in FP64. The repo holds the harness (reg_opsparse, reg_cusparse, nvcc -O3 sm_70) but no result files, and later third-party studies find smaller margins or spECK ahead.

**Known shortcoming:** Peer-reviewed IEEE Access maxima only; one MIT LICENSE covers bundled nsparse/spECK code.

**Known shortcoming:** The drivers have the cuSPARSE result check commented out, and the cuSPARSE timed loop includes cusparseCreate/Destroy and the buffer malloc on every call, inflating the baseline. Meta::release frees malloc memory with delete[] (undefined behaviour). The Makefile builds sm_70 SASS only with no PTX, so no A100/H100 run without edits; the 96 KB shared-memory kernels fail on Turing; the timer is x86 rdtsc plus CPUID 0x16.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** independent: Ocean (ICS 2026, arXiv 2604.19004, CornellHPC/Ocean-SpGEMM) on A100 over 337 matrices is 1.4x over spECK and 2.6x over OpSparse, so spECK is ahead of OpSparse there (snippet confirms averages 7.35x / 1.43x / 1.52x)

**How:** Rows are binned by an upper bound on their output size (8 bins, ranges sized for about 1.2x hash-table headroom). Each bin then runs a kernel sized to it: a partial warp of 4 threads per row with a 32-slot table for tiny rows, thread-block shared-memory hash tables of 512 to 8192 slots, a 96 KB dynamic-shared-memory kernel, and a global-memory hash fallback for rows that overflow. The hash tables use linear probing with atomicCAS and a multiplicative hash (column * 107), and each row's output is put in column order by an in-block counting sort. Per the paper abstract, the other gains come from fewer hash-table accesses, packing all metadata into one combined allocation, and overlapping cudaMalloc of C with kernel execution across 8 streams.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated SpGEMM (A*A, A*P, Galerkin products in AMG setup, graph algorithms) on a Volta-class GPU, where cuSPARSE SpGEMM time dominates
- FP64 CSR matrices with 32-bit indices and up to about 2^31 nonzeros in C
- As a reference implementation or starting point when writing your own binned hash SpGEMM, since the kernels are short and readable
- Benchmark studies: the repo already wires cuSPARSE, nsparse and spECK drivers to the same matrix loader

**Skip it when:**
- On A100/H100-class GPUs, where independent results put it behind spECK: Ocean (ICS 2026, 337 matrices on A100) reports 2.6x over OpSparse but only 1.4x over spECK
- When you need FP32, complex, 64-bit indices, or a C = alpha*A*B + beta*C API: values are hard-wired to double and indices to int
- Production code that needs a maintained library: 9 commits, last one 2022-08-23, no tests, and the result check against cuSPARSE is commented out in the drivers
- Non-NVIDIA hardware or non-x86 hosts: CUDA only, and the timer reads rdtsc and the CPUID leaf 0x16 base frequency
- Turing-class GPUs (64 KB shared-memory limit per block): the large-row kernels request 98,304 bytes of dynamic shared memory

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA toolkit (tested 11.2) with cuSPARSE and CUB, OpenMP (host flop count), CUDA samples headers on the include path · nvcc from CUDA 11.x (tested 11.2) with g++; Makefile hard-codes -arch=compute_70 -code=sm_70 · NVIDIA GPUs, sm_70 (V100) as shipped; x86-64 host for the rdtsc-based timer

**Vs siblings:** Pick spECK (GPUPeople/spECK) by default: on the third-party sets found (Ocean on A100; the ACM study cited in the record's caveats, which puts OpSparse at 4.91x and spECK at 5.67x average over cuSPARSE) it is as fast or faster. OpSparse is the more compact code to adapt. TileSpGEMM reports beating spECK on 94 of 142 matrices, and Kokkos Kernels SpGEMM is the maintained, portable choice.

**Gotchas:**
- The Makefile embeds only sm_70 SASS (no PTX), so the binaries will not run on Ampere or Hopper until you change GENCODE
- Meta::release frees host memory from malloc with delete[] (combined_mem), which is undefined behaviour; fix it before embedding
- CUDA errors throw std::exception after printing; there is no error-code API
- The cuSPARSE driver times cusparseCreate/cusparseDestroy and buffer allocation inside every call (the OpSparse timing also includes its own allocations), which can inflate the cuSPARSE baseline on small matrices

**Status:** Abandoned since August 2022 (9 commits, no issues filed); MIT-licensed, including the bundled nsparse and spECK copies, and small enough to vendor, but last known to work only with CUDA 11.2 on V100.

[repo](https://github.com/lorentzbf/OpSparse) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07244)

##### PIQP  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only C++14/Eigen proximal interior-point convex QP solver; fastest and most robust on Maros-Meszaros, well ahead of OSQP.

**Beats:** OSQP — The independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0 (2024-09-07, i7-6500U laptop, prebuilt wheels through qpsolvers 4.3.3: piqp 0.4.1, osqp 0.6.7.post0) ran 138 Maros-Meszaros problems and ranked PIQP first at every setting. OSQP's shifted geometric mean runtime was 12.7x (default), 16.1x (high accuracy), 52.8x (low) and 51.9x (mid) PIQP's, with failures counted at the 1000 s limit, so the ratios mix speed with OSQP's 21-44% success rate. PIQP's own piqp_benchmarks on a Threadripper 3990X give OSQP 7.55x (low accuracy) and 42.66x (high accuracy).

**Known shortcoming:** QP solver measured against OSQP, which is off the sparse-and-solvers baseline list (no optimization category in wave 8).

**Known shortcoming:** Bug #42: out-of-bounds read in dual recovery, fixed only in 0.6.4 (2026-08-28). Open #37: false PRIMAL_INFEASIBLE with preconditioner_scale_cost. Sparse LDL is derived from SuiteSparse LDL; an LGPL-2.1+ notice ships beside the BSD-2 header. qpbenchmark ratios count failures at 1000 s, so they mix speed with robustness (OSQP 21-44% success).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It combines an infeasible primal-dual interior-point method with the proximal method of multipliers (an adaptation of Pougkakiotis and Gondzio), so it converges in a few dozen Newton steps to tight tolerances and tolerates rank-deficient constraints and ill-conditioning, where the ADMM in OSQP needs many cheap iterations and stalls at high accuracy. Each step solves a regularized KKT system with a modified SuiteSparse LDL (sparse, AMD ordering), a dense Cholesky, or a Blasfeo-based multistage backend for MPC-structured problems, with Ruiz equilibration and iterative refinement. Most of the speed ratio comes from far fewer failed or stalled solves rather than from cheaper iterations.

**Use it when:**
- Small-to-medium convex QPs that must be solved to 1e-6 to 1e-9 accuracy, where OSQP often stalls (qpbenchmark high accuracy: PIQP solved 73% of Maros-Meszaros vs OSQP 26%)
- Hard or ill-conditioned problems with degenerate or dependent constraints: PIQP solved 94-97% of the 138 problems at low, mid and default accuracy
- Model predictive control and other repeated solves with fixed sparsity: update() re-solves without allocating, and the sparse_multistage backend exploits stage structure
- Embedding in C++ code that already uses Eigen (header-only, BSD-2 core), or in Python, Matlab, Octave or R through prebuilt packages

**Skip it when:**
- Very large sparse QPs where one KKT factorization is too costly in memory or time; first-order methods such as OSQP or SCS only need matrix-vector products and a cheaper factorization
- Fast warm-started low-accuracy MPC loops are OSQP's home ground; this catalog has no matched warm-start comparison
- Nonconvex QPs, mixed-integer or conic (SOCP/SDP) problems are out of scope; use Clarabel, MOSEK or Gurobi
- Code paths that enable preconditioner_scale_cost with bounds near zero: open issue #37 (v0.6.1-0.6.2) reports false PRIMAL_INFEASIBLE results on feasible problems
- Strict BSD-only licensing needs: the sparse backend is derived from SuiteSparse LDL, whose LGPL-2.1+ notice ships next to it

**Integration:** header-only · Eigen >= 3.3 (Eigen 5 supported since 0.6.3); optional Blasfeo for the sparse_multistage backend; optional OpenMP; pybind11 and cpu_features for the Python bindings · C++14 (C++17 if built with std::optional or std::filesystem), CMake 3.21+ for the CMake build · any platform Eigen supports; PyPI wheels for Linux x86-64/aarch64/i686 (glibc and musl), macOS x86-64/arm64 and Windows x64

**Vs siblings:** Against ProxQP (ProxSuite) and QPALM, the other OSQP-beaters here, PIQP leads both runtime and success rate on Maros-Meszaros in the independent qpbenchmark (ProxQP 5.9-53x and QPALM 2.2-4.8x slower by shifted geometric mean). Choose ProxQP for dense, robotics-style QPs, where its own benchmark is strongest.

**Gotchas:**
- Default tolerances are tight (eps_abs 1e-8, eps_rel 1e-9, duality-gap check on) against OSQP's 1e-3, so comparisons at default settings compare different accuracy targets
- Versions before 0.6.4 (released 2026-08-28) have an out-of-bounds read in inequality dual recovery (#42) that caused intermittent PIQP_MAX_ITER_REACHED on identical inputs; 0.6.0 also brought a segfault report (#31) and new PRIMAL_INFEASIBLE results (#33), both closed, so pin 0.6.4 or later
- The default KKT solver is dense_cholesky; sparse problems need SparseSolver or one of the sparse_ldlt* backends
- BUILD_WITH_EIGEN_MAX_ALIGN_BYTES and template-instantiation options affect Eigen ABI compatibility when you link the prebuilt library into code built with different Eigen alignment

**Status:** Actively maintained (0.6.4 released 2026-08-28, 580 commits, 149 stars, on PyPI and conda-forge) and BSD-2-licensed, so it is safe to adopt; pin 0.6.4 or later for the memory-safety fix.

[repo](https://github.com/PREDICT-EPFL/piqp) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qpsolvers/maros_meszaros_qpbenchmark/main/results/maros_meszaros.md)

##### ProxQP (ProxSuite)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only C++ QP solver (ProxQP) on Eigen; 3.5-18x lower shifted-geomean solve time than OSQP on random QPs.

**Beats:** OSQP (also compared against Gurobi, MOSEK, qpOASES, quadprog) — The project's own proxqp_benchmark (dense backend, i7-11850H, compiler, flags and solver versions unstated) reports shifted geometric means at 1e-9 accuracy with ProxQP = 1.0: OSQP 18.2 on dense random QPs, 3.5 on random QPs of about 15% density, and 14.2 on Maros-Meszaros (108.5 at 1e-3). The independent qpbenchmark run (i7-6500U, proxqp 0.6.6 vs osqp 0.6.7.post0 called through qpsolvers) has ProxQP ahead of OSQP at high, mid and low accuracy (5.9 vs 16.1, 19.2 vs 51.9, 36.0 vs 52.8) but behind at default settings (53.3 vs 12.7).

**Known shortcoming:** QP solver whose baseline (OSQP) is not a category incumbent; independent qpbenchmark Maros-Meszaros shows it faster than OSQP at high/mid/low accuracy but slower at default settings (53.3 vs 12.7); RSS 2022 paper unreadable here.

**Known shortcoming:** Independent qpbenchmark has PIQP faster than ProxQP at every accuracy (1.0 vs 5.9-53.3) and QPALM faster too. User issue #227: OSQP 1.7x faster on a larger sparse MPC. Open termination bug #63. QP solver, a loose fit for the sparse-and-solvers category.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** ProxQP is a proximal method of multipliers. Each outer step minimizes a primal-dual augmented Lagrangian merit function with a semismooth Newton method, and penalty parameters follow a BCL (bound-constrained Lagrangian) update rule. When penalties or the active set change, the dense backend updates its LDL^T factorization with rank-r updates instead of refactorizing. It factors either the regularized KKT matrix (PrimalDualLDLT) or H + rho I + A'A/mu_eq (PrimalLDLT, quicker when constraints far outnumber variables), after Ruiz equilibration. Warm starts keep the factorization between solves, and the linear algebra is vectorized through SIMDe (AVX2/AVX-512) when built with -march=native; the paper benchmarks used AVX2.

**Use it when:**
- Small to medium dense QPs, solved repeatedly. The docs recommend the dense backend below a few thousand variables or above 0.1 matrix density; robotics MPC and inverse dynamics (TSID) are typical.
- High-accuracy solutions (1e-6 to 1e-9). In the independent qpbenchmark Maros-Meszaros run, ProxQP scored 5.9 vs OSQP's 16.1 runtime shifted geomean at 1e-9, with a 52.9% vs 26.1% success rate.
- Sequences of closely related QPs (MPC, control loops): the default WARM_START_WITH_PREVIOUS_RESULT mode reuses the previous iterates and factorization.
- Problems that may be infeasible, where the closest feasible solution is useful, and QP layers in PyTorch that need derivatives (QPLayer).
- C++ code already built on Eigen, or Python users who want `pip`/`conda` installs and CVXPY/CasADi integration.

**Skip it when:**
- Hard sparse QPs when PIQP or QPALM is available. On qpbenchmark Maros-Meszaros, PIQP is fastest at every accuracy (1.0 vs ProxQP's 5.9-53.3) with a higher success rate, and QPALM's runtime shifted geomean (2.2-4.8) also beats ProxQP's.
- Loose default-tolerance runs: on qpbenchmark default settings ProxQP's runtime shifted geomean is 53.3 vs OSQP's 12.7.
- Larger sparse MPC. One user (issue #227, 9 states per stage) found OSQP about 1.7x faster at horizon 70+, although ProxQP was faster at horizon 25 (1.1 vs 1.6 ms).
- Sparse problems whose sparsity pattern changes between solves: a sparse `update` only works for an identical pattern, otherwise you must build a new QP object.
- Hard real-time loops that need a guaranteed allocation-free solve: issues #103 and #200 about memory allocations are still open, and which calls allocate is not documented.

**Integration:** header-only · Eigen >= 3.0.5; optional SIMDe (vectorization, on by default in the CMake build), OpenMP (parallel batch solves), nanobind and cereal (Python bindings), Matio (tests) · C++14 minimum (CMake enforces 14, README says C++14/17/20); defaults to C++17, which the install doc lists as required; CMake build · Linux, macOS and Windows (CI plus pip, conda-forge and Homebrew packages); x86 AVX2/AVX-512 through SIMDe when compiled with -march=native; vectorization can be switched off for other CPUs

**Vs siblings:** PIQP and QPALM also beat OSQP in qpbenchmark, and PIQP is faster and more robust on hard sparse Maros-Meszaros problems at every accuracy, so prefer PIQP there. Pick ProxQP for small dense QPs re-solved with warm starts (robotics MPC, whole-body control), or when you need its box-constraint handling, closest-feasible solving, nonconvex regularization or QPLayer differentiation.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD speed needs the vectorized build (CMake target proxsuite::proxsuite-vectorized or -DPROXSUITE_VECTORIZE) plus -march=native in your own compile flags. The docs name the CMake switch inconsistently: BUILD_WITH_VECTORIZATION_SUPPORT in the install guide, BUILD_WITH_SIMD_SUPPORT in the API doc.
- The default initial guess is WARM_START_WITH_PREVIOUS_RESULT, so a re-solve on the same object starts from the previous iterates, proximal parameters and factorization unless you change `settings.initial_guess`.
- The dense backend picks PrimalDualLDLT or PrimalLDLT by a complexity heuristic, and PrimalLDLT is documented as less accurate. For very ill-conditioned problems at tight tolerances, undoing the Ruiz scaling can lose precision.
- Issue #63, a termination problem on the Maros-Meszaros problem QGFRDXPN, is still open.

**Status:** Actively maintained by Inria and LAAS-CNRS (594 stars, release 0.7.3 on 2026-05-11, commits through 2026-09-14). BSD-2-Clause and packaged for pip, conda-forge, Homebrew and vcpkg.

[repo](https://github.com/Simple-Robotics/proxsuite) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Simple-Robotics/proxqp_benchmark)

##### SPC5 (block-based SpMV kernels for AVX-512 and ARM SVE)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Single-header block-based SpMV kernels for AVX-512 and 512-bit SVE; median 1.2-1.5x over sequential MKL CSR SpMV.

**Beats:** Intel MKL CSR SpMV (sequential column of the results CSV) — On PlaFRIM Cascade Lake nodes (exact CPU model not given), g++ 11.2.0 with MKL 2022.0.2 sequential, the best of SPC5's four sequential kernels per matrix beat MKL's legacy mkl_cspblas_?csrgemv CSR SpMV by a median 1.23x in double and 1.49x in float over 23 SuiteSparse matrices, up to 1.90x and 3.00x, but lost on 7 and 6 matrices respectively (derived from page data, results-avx-2.csv). The baseline is MKL's deprecated legacy CSR routine, not the inspector-executor mkl_sparse_?_mv with mkl_sparse_optimize, and the A64FX CSV has no Arm Performance Libraries column, only a scalar CSR loop.

**Known shortcoming:** No CPU model; conversion to the SPC5 format costs about 40-55 SpMVs.

**Known shortcoming:** MKL baseline is the legacy mkl_cspblas_?csrgemv, not inspector-executor. Header defines non-inline kernels, so including it in 2+ translation units gives link errors. Scalar multi-row path indexes rowsSize by row instead of block-row (bug). Asserts on mat->format compile only with NDEBUG. Hard-coded 512-bit vectors, likely wrong on 128/256-bit SVE. A64FX CSV has no ARMPL column, scalar CSR only.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each block stores one starting column (int) plus a per-row bitmask (8 bits for double, 16 for float) of which of the next vector-width columns are nonzero, and the values are stored packed without zero padding. The AVX-512 kernel does an unaligned load of 8 (double) or 16 (float) x values at the block's column and a masked expand-load (_mm512_maskz_expandloadu_pd) that scatters the packed values into the lanes the mask names, then one FMA per row per block and popcount(mask) to advance the value pointer; the SVE kernel instead compacts x with svcompact to line up with the packed values. Multi-row blocks reuse the same x load across rows. Optional MHSUM does hand-written horizontal reductions of the 2/4/8 row accumulators, and FACTOLOAD (SVE) loads x once for the whole block.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated SpMV with the same matrix (iterative solvers, power iterations) on AVX-512 x86 (Skylake-SP/Cascade Lake class) where the CSR-to-SPC5 conversion, about 40-55 SpMVs' worth of time on one measured matrix, is amortised.
- Matrices whose nonzeros cluster in short column runs within rows or neighbouring rows (FEM, structured or banded patterns), where blocks hold several values each; the shipped CSV shows the 2rVc and 4rVc kernels winning on 19 of 23 matrices in double.
- A64FX (512-bit SVE) machines with no tuned vendor SpMV at hand: on the 23-matrix A64FX run the best SPC5 kernel is a median 2.9x (double) and 3.45x (float) over a plain scalar CSR loop (derived from page data, results-arm-8.csv).
- Projects that want to vendor a small MIT kernel rather than link MKL: one header plus farm_sve.h for the SVE-on-x86 emulation path.

**Skip it when:**
- One-shot or few-shot SpMV: conversion costs tens of multiplies, and MKL beat the best SPC5 kernel on some matrices outright (worst ratios 0.45x double, 0.41x float in the shipped CSV).
- Matrices with scattered single nonzeros per row (graph-like, power-law), where each block carries one value and the per-block header and x load dominate.
- CPUs without AVX-512 (AVX2-only x86, AMD before Zen 4, Apple and other NEON-only ARM) or SVE vectors narrower than 512 bits: the code hard-codes 512-bit vectors (ValPerVec = 512/(8*sizeof(T)); SVE kernels build 8-lane double masks), so 128/256-bit SVE cores such as Graviton or Neoverse are not a documented target and would likely need code changes.
- Matrices with more than 2^31 nonzeros or rows: all indices and counts are int.
- Codebases needing a maintained library with tests, CI or an issue tracker: the GitHub mirror's last commit is 2023-07-25 and it has 6 stars.

**Integration:** header-only (src/spc5.hpp, plus src/farm_sve.h for the x86 SVE emulation path); not a true multi-TU header, see gotchas · none for the kernels; OpenMP optional for the parallel kernels; Intel MKL or Arm Performance Libraries only for the comparison example · C++17 (CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17); the published runs used g++ 11.2.0 on x86 and gcc 10.3.0 on A64FX; AVX-512 flags -mavx512f -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512bw -mavx512dq (plus vbmi/ifma for CPU=CNL); SVE needs -march=armv8.2-a+sve · x86-64 with AVX-512 (define USE_AVX512); aarch64 with 512-bit SVE (A64FX); on x86 without USE_AVX512 it builds the SVE code through FARM emulation, which is for testing, not speed

**Vs siblings:** Pick SPC5 over CSR5 or merge-spmv when the target is AVX-512 or A64FX, the matrix has locally clustered nonzeros, and you want an MIT header you can vendor; pick merge-spmv or CVR for irregular, scale-free matrices where load balance, not vectorisation of short runs, is the bottleneck, and ALBUS or CSR5 if you also need GPU or non-AVX-512 targets.

**Gotchas:**
- Conversion is in place: CSR_to_SPC5_*(&mat) overwrites the CSR's values and row pointer, so keep a copy if you still need CSR.
- The kernels are defined in the header as non-inline functions (core_SPC5_*_Spmv_double/float, hsum_stor_*, SPC5_opti_merge_*), so including spc5.hpp in more than one translation unit should give duplicate-symbol link errors; include it in one .cpp and expose your own wrapper.
- The scalar reference path for multi-row formats indexes the block row pointer with the row number (core_SPC5_rVc_Spmv_scalar uses mat.rowsSize[idxRow] while conversion fills rowsSize per block row), and several asserts use mat->format on a reference, which only compiles when NDEBUG removes them; use the vector kernels, which the example checks against CSR.
- The OpenMP split copies each thread's slice of values and block headers into per-thread buffers, so the parallel path holds roughly a second copy of the matrix; SPC5_find_best's cubic predictor only considers 1rVc, 2rVc and 4rVc and uses one fixed set of fitted coefficients for every CPU.

**Status:** GitHub mirror of gitlab.inria.fr/bramas/spc5 with its last commit on 2023-07-25 (the GitLab original could not be checked), so treat it as research code that is finished rather than maintained; MIT-licensed and compact enough to copy.

[repo](https://github.com/berenger-eu/spc5) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/berenger-eu/spc5/HEAD/results/results-avx-2.csv)

##### spECK (lightweight-analysis GPU SpGEMM)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

CUDA SpGEMM (C = A*B in CSR) with adaptive hash/dense accumulators; PPoPP '20 reports wins over cuSPARSE and other GPU SpGEMM libraries.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE SpGEMM — Per the PPoPP '20 abstract as seen in search snippets (paper blocked here): over thousands of matrices spECK beat all compared GPU SpGEMM codes (snippets name CUSP, nsparse, RMerge, AC-SpGEMM and bhSPARSE) in 85% of cases and was second in 12%, about 2x the second-best on average and up to 25x; restricted to matrices with more than 15k products, the figures are 79%, 15% and 83% faster. GPU model, CUDA version and how cuSPARSE ranked were not seen, and third-party runs in the OpSparse paper (V100 per its README) put spECK 1.52x behind OpSparse on average.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is the PPoPP'20 abstract (83% average over second best, up to 25x); a third-party 5.67x figure was not re-verified.

**Known shortcoming:** Closed issues report wrong values (#4, a 4x7 by 7x4 product), a row-index mismatch on webbase-1M (#6) and an illegal memory access on an 80%-dense 2048x2048 (#10), with no visible maintainer reply; not bit-stable against cuSPARSE. master's harness uses cusparseDcsrgemm, which CUDA 11 removed; no CUDA 12 support stated; the cuda11 branch's last commit is 2023-07-18 (master 2022-07-29). The paper's averages and CUDA versions were not seen (tugraz.at blocked); OpSparse's README says its spECK runs used a V100 with CUDA 11.2.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** A lightweight, multi-level analysis: a cheap first kernel counts products per row of C (max and total), and finer per-row analysis and block load balancing run only when those statistics say the cost pays off (hard-coded thresholds in Multiply.cu). Rows are binned into six kernel variants that scale shared memory and threads per block, with up to 32 short rows packed into one block. Each row group gets the cheapest accumulator that fits: direct array indexing when the column range fits the map, a shared-memory hash map with linear probing and atomicCAS, dense accumulation for long rows, or a global-memory hash map fallback. It runs a symbolic (count) pass, then a numeric pass, then CUB segmented sort or in-place sorting of column indices.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated CSR SpGEMM on an NVIDIA GPU where cuSPARSE SpGEMM/csrgemm is the bottleneck, e.g. Galerkin products in algebraic multigrid setup or matrix powers in graph analytics.
- Input sets whose row-length distribution varies widely (power-law and regular matrices mixed), the case the per-call analysis and accumulator choice are designed for.
- float or double data with 32-bit indices and nnz(C) below 2^32.
- As a strong, MIT-licensed baseline when benchmarking a new GPU SpGEMM; OpSparse and TileSpGEMM both measure against it.

**Skip it when:**
- If you can use OpSparse: its IEEE Access 2022 paper reports OpSparse 1.52x faster than spECK on average, up to 2.04x (per its catalog entry; the OpSparse README gives a V100 with CUDA 11.2), and the OpSparse repo vendors spECK for that comparison.
- AMD, Intel or CPU targets: CUDA only.
- Production code that needs a supported library: master was last touched 2022-07-29 and the cuda11 branch 2023-07-18, CUDA 12 is not mentioned anywhere, and 64-bit index support was added and then removed on the cuda11 branch in January 2022. CornellHPC/Ocean-SpGEMM, partly adapted from spECK per its README, targets CUDA 12.4+ on compute capability 8.0+ (tested on A100 and H100); its speedups were not seen here.
- Workloads that need bitwise reproducible values or proven correctness on unusual inputs: closed issues report wrong values on a small 4x7 by 7x4 product (#4, labelled bug), row-index mismatches against cuSPARSE on webbase-1M on a 1080 Ti (#6), and an illegal memory access on a 2048x2048 matrix with 80% nonzeros (#10, RTX 3060, CUDA 11.6); the issue pages show no maintainer reply, though later commits fix related kernel bugs.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake target spECKLib) plus the runspECK benchmark executable; source-drop in practice · CUDA toolkit (Thrust, CUB); cuSPARSE is linked only by the runspECK driver for transposes and result comparison · master: CUDA 10.1 or 10.2, g++ > 7 (C++17) or Visual Studio, CMake 3.15.5 per README; CUDA 11+ needs the cuda11 branch (master's harness calls cusparseDcsrgemm, which CUDA 11 removed; cuda11 uses cusparseSpGEMM) · NVIDIA GPUs; CMake options for compute capability 5.0 through 8.6, a 2022 commit restores launch bounds so all kernels run on Pascal; Linux and Windows; a 2020 commit fixes PowerPC builds

**Vs siblings:** Over cuSPARSE, use it when you can vendor and tune research code for a fixed NVIDIA GPU. Over OpSparse (faster on V100 per its paper) and TileSpGEMM (faster on 94 of 142 large matrices, but no license), pick spECK when you need an MIT-licensed standalone library with float and double, or a reference baseline. Kokkos Kernels SpGEMM is the maintained, portable choice when support matters more than peak speed.

**Gotchas:**
- Per-GPU shared-memory limits are compile-time constants in include/Multiply.h (49152 static; dynamic 49152 pre-Volta, 65536 Turing, 98304 Volta, 101376 RTX 30xx, 166912 A100 per the cuda11 README); wrong values give runtime errors or warnings telling you to recompile.
- Results are not bit-stable: config.ini says values differ from cuSPARSE, so CompareResult checks only row lengths and column indices; a 2023 cuda11 commit restores the value-correctness check.
- CMake builds with -use_fast_math, and master also with -DVERBOSE and -keep/-lineinfo (CUDA_BUILD_INFO on by default).
- Multi-row hash keys pack a 5-bit local row and a 27-bit column into one uint32 (HashMap.cuh masks columns with 0x7FFFFFF), so B with more than 2^27 columns looks unsafe in that path (inferred from code, not documented).

**Status:** Abandoned (master 2022-07-29, cuda11 branch 2023-07-18, all issues closed) but MIT-licensed and compact enough to vendor; expect to port it yourself for CUDA 12 and newer GPUs.

[repo](https://github.com/GPUPeople/spECK) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3332466.3374521)

##### Sputnik (sparse GPU kernels for deep learning: SpMM and SDDMM)  `C++ (CUDA)`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

CUDA SpMM and SDDMM kernels tuned for the moderate sparsity of pruned neural networks; several times faster than cuSPARSE SpMM.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE SpMM — A third-party PyTorch binding (Torch-Sputnik) times fp32 SpMM on an A100 at M=N=K=4096: Sputnik 2.52 vs cuSPARSE 10.97 at density 0.05 (about 4.4x) up to 13.05 vs 107.38 at density 0.5 (8.2x), with no time unit, CUDA version or timing method stated; at 64^3 Sputnik is about 0.005 vs 0.09. The peer-reviewed SC'20 paper is the primary evidence (3.58x geometric mean over cuSPARSE on a V100 per a search snippet; this session's search snippet adds 27% of single-precision peak and 1.2-2.1x end-to-end speedups on sparse Transformer and MobileNet), but its PDF was not opened.

**Known shortcoming:** SC'20 3.58x geomean SpMM over cuSPARSE (V100) seen only in a search snippet (paper blocked); Torch-Sputnik tables give no time unit; slower than dense cuBLAS at density 0.25 or more; archived.

**Known shortcoming:** Archived; last commit 2020. Open #15: CMake errors unless -DCUDA_ARCHS is set. fp16 path uses 16-bit (short2) column indices. Hand-tuned kernel table covers MobileNetV1 shapes only. SC'20 paper not opened here.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The SpMM kernel uses a 1-D tiling scheme where a configurable number of threads (subwarp tiling) cooperate on an output tile, and it loads the sparse values, column indices and dense rows with vector instructions (float4/float2, half8/half4). To make vector loads legal on unaligned CSR rows, memory_aligner.h rounds each row's start offset down to the vector width and masks the extra leading values. Rows are processed in the caller-supplied row_indices order so that rows of similar length are scheduled together across warps and SMs, and a small heuristic (plus a lookup table of hand-picked configs for exact MobileNetV1 layer shapes) chooses tile sizes by n; the code comment says the heuristic reaches about 96% of an oracle on its synthetic RNN data.

**Use it when:**
- Pruned DNN layers (weights 50-95% zero, i.e. density 0.05-0.5) on NVIDIA Volta or newer, where cuSPARSE SpMM is far slower than the dense GEMM
- Sparse fully connected or 1x1 conv layers in inference where the fused SpMM + bias + ReLU kernel saves a pass over the output
- Sparse attention or masked products that need SDDMM in fp32 with the same CSR topology as the SpMM
- fp16 SpMM with fp32 accumulation when n and every row's nonzero count are even
- Research baselines: Sputnik is the standard reference kernel cited by later DNN SpMM papers

**Skip it when:**
- Density above about 0.2 at large sizes: in the Torch-Sputnik A100 table Sputnik (13.05 at density 0.5, 7.87 at 0.25) is slower than dense cuBLAS (7.29), so use dense GEMM there
- AMD, Intel or pre-Volta NVIDIA GPUs (README requires SM70+ and CUDA 10.1+), and any CPU target
- Scientific SpMV or highly irregular graph matrices: the kernels and heuristics are tuned on DNN weight matrices, not SuiteSparse or power-law graphs
- fp16 SDDMM, fp64, or tensor-core sparse formats such as 2:4 structured sparsity: none are provided
- Projects that need a maintained dependency: archived on 2026-04-19, last commit 2020-11-04, open build issue with no answer

**Integration:** static lib (CMake, CUDA sources) · CUDA toolkit 10.1+, glog; the library CMake also links cudart, cuBLAS, cuBLASLt and cuSPARSE static libs (a TODO says these should be test-only); tests and benchmarks add abseil, googletest and google/benchmark submodules · C++11, CUDA 10.1+, CMake 3.13+ · NVIDIA GPUs SM70+ (Volta, Turing, Ampere and later), Linux; a Dockerfile is provided

**Vs siblings:** Pick Sputnik over HP-SpMM-SDDMM when the sparse operand is a pruned DNN weight matrix at moderate density and you want fp16 or the fused bias+ReLU epilogue; pick HP-SpMM-SDDMM for very sparse power-law GNN graphs on recent GPUs (it is measured against cuSPARSE 12.2 on an H800). For SpMV on scientific matrices, ISpMV or the cache-aware SpMV entry fit better.

**Gotchas:**
