- key/value types that are not swappable or not copy/move constructible, or where you rely on std::unordered_map's bucket-inspection API (bucket(), bucket_size(), etc.), which robin_map omits

**Integration:** header-only · none for the library; Boost Test only needed to build the test suite · C++17 (README: "should work with any C++17 standard-compliant compiler") · portable C++17, no SIMD or arch-specific intrinsics in the source; CI covers Linux and macOS (GCC and Clang) and Windows (MSVC via Visual Studio 2025, x64 and x86)

**Vs siblings:** Prefer tsl::robin_map over ska::flat_hash_map/bytell_hash_map or sparsepp when you want an actively maintained, documented library with heterogeneous lookup, binary serialization, and a built-in prime-growth fallback (robin_pg_map) for weak hashes. Prefer tsl::hopscotch_map instead when erase-heavy iteration or memory density at high load factor matters more than raw lookup/insert throughput, since hopscotch avoids robin-map's backward-shift erase cost and identity-hash growth pathology.

**Gotchas:**
- Any insert, erase, or rehash invalidates all iterators, pointers, and references into the table (stricter than std::unordered_map).
- Default power-of-two growth policy + a poor/identity hash (common for std::hash<integral>) can make a linear insertion sequence blow up storage exponentially; use robin_pg_map/robin_pg_set or a stronger hash.
- erase(iterator) walks forward to the next nonempty bucket to return a valid iterator, which is O(expensive) at low load factor; use void erase_fast(iterator) when you don't need the returned iterator.
- Iterating while erasing can visit one element twice due to backward-shift deletion wrap-around; open upstream issue (#20) since 2019, maintainer's stance is 'that's the way it is'.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-06-13, 1508 stars, CI green across GCC/Clang/MSVC), MIT-licensed and header-only, so it is trivially vendorable even if upstream development ever stopped.

[repo](https://github.com/Tessil/robin-map) · [benchmark](https://tessil.github.io/2016/08/29/benchmark-hopscotch-map.html)

##### Verstable  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Single-header C hash table beating std::unordered_map on lookups, erasures, and iteration; insertion only average.

**Beats:** std::unordered_map — On the author's own interactive benchmark (GCC 13.2.0 via MinGW-w64, -O3 -DNDEBUG, AMD Ryzen 7 5800H at 90% locked frequency, libstdc++'s std::unordered_map as baseline, across 32-bit int, 64-bit-int/large-value, and string-key workloads), the page states std::unordered_map is far slower than most open-addressing tables except at looking up existing keys, and at least an order of magnitude slower at iteration; Verstable is described as having extremely fast lookups and erasures of nonexisting keys, iteration beaten only by boost::unordered_flat_map, emilib2, and contiguous-storage tables (and faster than absl::flat_hash_map on iteration), but 'only average' insertion speed. Results are shown as interactive charts rather than a numeric table.

**How:** It's open addressing with quadratic probing, but colliding keys that hash to the same 'home bucket' are linked into a chain via an 11-bit displacement value; a 1-bit flag keeps each chain rooted at its home bucket by evicting non-belonging occupants on insert. This chain metadata, plus a 4-bit hash-code fragment per bucket, lives in a separate uint16_t array instead of alongside the key/value, so lookups can skip most non-matching keys without touching the buckets array or calling the comparison function, and iteration walks a compact metadata array rather than sparse, cache-missing buckets. Deletion and insertion move at most one existing key and require no tombstones. The author describes it as a hybrid of open addressing and separate chaining, related to Malte Skarupke's Bytell table and classic coalesced hashing.

**Use it when:**
- C code that needs a generic, type-safe hash map/set without hand-rolling one, or C++ code that can call a C API via extern "C"
- Lookup- and iteration-heavy workloads, including lookups of nonexisting keys, where std::unordered_map's node-based layout causes cache misses
- Large keys/values or expensive hash/compare functions, since insert/delete move at most one existing key instead of shifting many (unlike Robin Hood schemes)
- High load factors, since the design is described as largely impervious to load factor for lookup speed
- Willing to vendor a single header and accept a non-STL API in exchange for speed

**Skip it when:**
- Need a true drop-in std::unordered_map replacement with C++ container semantics, allocator/exception conventions, or STL iterator guarantees
- Insertion throughput is the dominant cost: the benchmark author calls Verstable's insertion 'only average', and it sits behind absl/boost on raw speed generally
- Keys with a weak, low-entropy, or attacker-influenced hash function: a bucket's collision chain is capped at ~2,048 keys, and hitting that repeatedly makes the table grow until it exhausts memory instead of degrading to a linear scan
- Targeting an FPU-less embedded platform: the default max-load-factor check uses floating point (open issue #23 asks for an integer-only option)
- Need active upstream maintenance guarantees: last commit 2025-05-06, tagged 'stale' by the catalog

**Integration:** header-only · none (C standard library only; malloc/free by default, both overridable) · C99 (with explicit HASH_FN/CMPR_FN); full vt_*-generic macro API requires C11 _Generic; tested under GCC, Clang, MinGW, and MSVC; usable from C++ via extern "C" · not documented as architecture-restricted (portable C, no SIMD intrinsics in the header); an open issue notes the floating-point load-factor check is awkward on FPU-less embedded hardware

**Vs siblings:** Pick Verstable when the code is C (or C++ that can bind to a C ABI) and you want a single-header, type-safe table with tombstone-free deletion and strong lookup/iteration speed; the sibling C++-only tables (ska::flat_hash_map/bytell_hash_map, tsl::robin_map, tsl::hopscotch_map) use similar open-addressing ideas but require a C++ compiler, and emhash/emilib2/google::dense_hash_map generally edge it out on raw insertion or peak throughput if a C-only API isn't a requirement.

**Gotchas:**
- Insert, get_or_insert, erase, erase_itr, reserve, and shrink invalidate all existing iterators; use erase_itr's return value to keep iterating while deleting
- No RAII: forgetting to call NAME_cleanup leaks the table's memory (a reported 'stuck insert' bug turned out to be missing cleanup across repeated runs, per issue #22)
- A degenerate hash function (near-constant output) can make a bucket chain exceed its ~2,048-key limit, causing the table to keep doubling until allocation fails rather than falling back to a slow linear scan
- Custom allocators need CTX_TY plus matching MALLOC_FN/FREE_FN signatures that take a size and context pointer, not a drop-in std::allocator interface

**Status:** Maintenance status is 'stale' (last commit 2025-05-06), but it's MIT-licensed and a single vendorable header, so freezing at the current commit carries little risk; the bigger adoption cost is its non-STL API rather than staleness.

[repo](https://github.com/JacksonAllan/Verstable) · [benchmark](https://jacksonallan.github.io/c_cpp_hash_tables_benchmark/)

##### libcuckoo (cuckoohash_map, efficient/libcuckoo)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only concurrent cuckoo hash map with per-bucket locks; beats std::unordered_map only under real multi-core contention.

**Beats:** std::unordered_map — On a 16-core machine the EuroSys'14 paper reports ~40M inserts/sec and ~70M lookups/sec; Figure 1 (4-core Intel i7-4770 Haswell, 120M 8-byte-key/8-byte-value pairs, 1:1 read:write) places libcuckoo well above C++11 std::unordered_map, but the only explicit numeric multiplier given in text is 'up to 2.5x' vs Intel TBB concurrent_hash_map — the std::unordered_map comparison is visual-only in the figure, and the paper treats std::unordered_map as a single-writer table (run under a global or TSX lock), so the measured win is multi-core scalability, not single-threaded op speed.

**How:** Uses cuckoo hashing: each key maps to 2 candidate buckets of SLOT_PER_BUCKET=4 slots, so a lookup touches at most 2 cache lines and displacement chains stay short. Concurrency comes from fine-grained per-bucket spinlocks combined with a resize counter/versioning scheme (the EuroSys'14 optimistic-locking design), letting many writers and readers operate on different buckets simultaneously instead of serializing on one table-wide lock the way std::unordered_map does under concurrent access.

**Use it when:**
- Multi-threaded workloads with genuine concurrent inserts and lookups across several cores (paper measures gains at 4-16 cores, 1:1 read:write and mixed operation mixes).
- Fixed-shape, trivially hashable keys/values (paper benchmark uses 8-byte key/8-byte value, ~120M entries) where the 2-cache-line cuckoo probe pays off.
- Code that can adopt a non-STL API (out-parameter find, functor-based update/upsert) instead of std::unordered_map's interface.
- Workloads that need occasional safe bulk iteration via locked_table(), not concurrent iteration.
- C++11-capable toolchain on Linux/macOS; header-only, so easy to vendor into a build with no link step.

**Skip it when:**
- Single-threaded or low-contention use: the per-bucket spinlock/version machinery is pure overhead with no payoff.
- Memory-constrained settings: users report roughly 3x higher RSS than std::unordered_map for long-key/int-value maps at ~42M entries (issues #134, #136).
- Many reader threads hammering the same hot keys: open issue #159 reports spinlock contention degrading badly past ~16-64 threads, since even find() takes the bucket spinlock (no shared/exclusive mode).
- Code relying on std::unordered_map's free iterators or erase-while-iterating: normal access has no standalone iterators, only locked_table() does, and that locks the entire table.
- Scaling requirements beyond what's measured: the peer-reviewed numbers stop at 16 cores, and at least one independent report (issue #152) found scalability collapsing beyond ~16 threads in their own workload.

**Integration:** header-only · none (self-contained headers: cuckoohash_map.hh, bucket_container.hh, cuckoohash_config.hh, cuckoohash_util.hh; optional C wrapper in libcuckoo-c/) · C++11; clang++ >= 3.3 or g++ >= 4.8 per README (latest versions recommended for atomics support); CMake >= 3.1.0 needed only to build tests/examples · Tested on macOS >= 10.8 and Ubuntu >= 12.04 (README); no stated architecture restriction, plain std::atomic used, no SIMD/intrinsics observed in the header; Windows build status is an open/unclear question (issue #62)

**Vs siblings:** All catalogued siblings (emhash, dense_hash_map, rigtorp/HashMap, Verstable, sparsepp, hopscotch/ordered/robin-map, ska::flat_hash_map/bytell_hash_map) are single-threaded tables tuned for single-core cache behavior and are not safe for concurrent access without an external lock. Pick libcuckoo over any of them only when multiple threads genuinely insert into and look up the same map concurrently.

**Gotchas:**
- find(key, val) (bool-returning, out-parameter) and find(key) (returns mapped_type or throws std::out_of_range) are different overloads; there is no iterator/end() sentinel on the normal concurrent path.
- Automatic expansion throws load_factor_too_low if load factor falls below minimum_load_factor() (default 0.05) — a weak hash function or adversarial key set can trigger this.
- Bulk/STL-style iteration requires locked_table(), which takes an exclusive lock over the whole table for as long as it's held, blocking every other thread.
- Reported ~3x memory overhead vs std::unordered_map for 8-byte-key/4-byte-value workloads at scale (issues #134, #136); size capacity planning accordingly.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-07-31, 1747 stars); Apache-2.0, header-only, and small enough to vendor directly into a project (usability: copyable).

[repo](https://github.com/efficient/libcuckoo) · [benchmark](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~mfreed/docs/cuckoo-eurosys14.pdf)

#### io-and-filesystem

##### reckless  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Asynchronous C++ logging library, drastically lower caller-side latency than std::fstream/fprintf and other async loggers.

**Beats:** std::fstream, fprintf (stdio) — First-party benchmarks (doc/performance.md, gcc 7.3.0, AMD Ryzen 7 2700X @3.7GHz, libstdc++) show reckless's caller-side latency far below std::fstream (flushed per line) and fprintf (fflush per call): about 41-44x lower under light periodic load, and up to ~5720x lower than fstream in the disk-I/O scenario, though this compares an async design against baselines that synchronously flush every line, not raw I/O throughput.

**How:** Call site only pushes args onto a lockless MPSC ring buffer (mpsc_ring_buffer.hpp) shared with the writer thread, so the common case costs about one function call with no kernel transition, no lock, and no formatting or I/O on the caller's thread. Formatting and writing happen entirely on the background thread, and bursts of queued entries are batched into fewer I/O operations. Uses a home-grown float-to-string routine (template_formatter) instead of the standard library's, trading some accuracy for speed.

**Use it when:**
- Latency-sensitive hot paths that log frequently but can tolerate async/eventual persistence
- Single-threaded or lightly-threaded workloads where formatting cost on a shared background thread won't bottleneck
- Windows or Linux targets on x86-family hardware; C++11-only codebases
- Willing to vendor/pin an unmaintained MIT library instead of using an actively developed logger
- Need low overhead specifically vs. synchronous std::fstream/fprintf-with-flush logging

**Skip it when:**
- Need macOS/BSD support (README: OS X unsupported, BSD only 'on the roadmap')
- High log-argument volume from many parallel threads, since all formatting funnels through one background thread (README calls this out as a scalability limit)
- Passing pointers/references to short-lived data without ensuring they outlive the flush (dangling-pointer risk by design)
- Need guaranteed-precise float formatting: custom float-to-string algorithm mismatches the exact/shortest round-trip representation for roughly 0.6% of values per the manual's own stats
- Want an actively maintained project: last commit 2021-04-10, open ThreadSanitizer data-race report (#35) unresolved

**Integration:** static lib (built via Make/CMake/Visual Studio; not header-only) · pthread (POSIX threads) on Linux; no other third-party deps for core library · C++11 (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); GCC-compatible compiler or MSVC/Visual Studio · Windows and Linux only; no macOS/OS X, BSD listed as roadmap-only; no stated architecture restriction beyond x86 cache-line-size assumptions in the buffer sizing docs

**Vs siblings:** No siblings catalogued yet in this category target std::fstream/fprintf directly the way reckless does; CPath and FastReader address filesystem traversal and file reads, not logging, so they aren't substitutes for this use case.

**Gotchas:**
- Passing log arguments by pointer/reference requires the referenced data to stay valid until the log is flushed or closed; prefer std::string/shared_ptr/unique_ptr for dynamic data
- Crash safety requires explicit handling (panic_flush/crash_handler) since unflushed async data can be lost on crash, same class of issue as buffered fprintf but easier to overlook
- Custom float-to-string formatter is not always the shortest round-trip representation: manual reports 98.5% exact match and 99.4% correct-but-sometimes-longer over 100M random values
- worker_thread() exposes the internal std::thread for OS-level tuning (priority/affinity) but destructive operations on it (move/detach) will break the logger

**Status:** Abandoned: last commit on master 2021-04-10, no newer maintenance activity found; MIT licensed and small enough to vendor, but an unresolved ThreadSanitizer data-race report (#35) and a still-open VS2019 compile-error issue (#45) are unpatched.

[repo](https://github.com/mattiasflodin/reckless) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mattiasflodin/reckless/blob/master/doc/performance.md)

#### k-mer-dictionaries

##### RSHash  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Static compressed k-mer dictionary that swaps SSHash's MPHF for rank/select bitvectors; 1.4x faster streaming lookups than current SSHash.

**Beats:** SSHash — The authors' Bioinformatics 2026 paper ran k = 31 on one core of an AMD EPYC 9454 with GCC 12.2 in release mode (the repo sets -O3 -march=native), using the Pibiri 2022 genomes and read sets. Streaming lookups were on average 1.4x (up to 2x) faster than SSHash5 (commit e65dcb2) and 4.5x faster than SSHash3 (5a13d6a) at similar bits/k-mer. Random negative lookups were about 50% faster and positive lookups about 10% slower, and builds were 60% faster with 40% less memory. No standard-library or MPHF baseline was measured.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked only against SSHash (SSHash3/SSHash5); positive single lookups are ~10% slower than SSHash5. It does not use an MPHF.

**How:** Like SSHash, it buckets k-mers by random (XOR-seeded) minimizers over a 2-bit-packed copy of the input text. Where SSHash uses a PTHash MPHF, RSHash marks minimizers in an Elias-Fano bitvector R (from Vigna's sux) and ranks into it, then uses a select-indexed bitvector S to find that minimizer's run of text offsets. A negative lookup usually ends after one bit test in R plus a probe of a small hash table for frequent k-mers, with no MPHF evaluation and no text check. Streaming lookups load all text k-mers for the current minimizer into a buffer that is reused for the expected (k-m+2)/2 following k-mers, and extend hits one base at a time along the text. Minimizers that occur more than threshold t times go to up to three further levels with other minimizer lengths and seeds, and the last level is a gtl flat hash set or an Elias-Fano set.

**Use it when:**
- Streaming membership queries of sequencing reads against a static k-mer set with k <= 32 on one x86-64 core. The paper reports 21-142 ns/k-mer, on average 1.4x faster than SSHash5 at about the same bits/k-mer.
- Workloads where most k-mers are absent (screening, low-hit read sets). This is where the gap is largest: kestrel low-hit streaming takes 20 vs 40 ns/k-mer, and random negative lookups on human take 360 vs 464 ns.
- Indexing raw genome assemblies directly, without first building a compacted de Bruijn graph with BCALM2/UST or GGCAT, when you need text positions (locate) rather than k-mer IDs.
- Pipelines that rebuild indexes often. In the paper, builds from preprocessed inputs are on average 60% faster than SSHash5 and use 40% less memory (human: 3:23 and 10.4 GB vs 6:03 and 14.4 GB).
- Research or benchmarking where you can tune minimizer lengths, thresholds and levels per dataset. Use the single-level fast setup for speed, or two or three levels to reach about 8 bits/k-mer on human.

**Skip it when:**
- Random single lookups where most k-mers are present. These are about 10% slower than SSHash5 (human: 701 vs 626 ns). On human high-hit reads, streaming is a tie (83 vs 84 ns/k-mer) and the fast index is larger (10.7 vs 10.1 bits/k-mer).
- k > 32, k-mer IDs to index satellite data, weights/abundances, or navigational queries. The minimizer views throw for windows over 32, and k up to 63 is only listed as future work. SSHash offers all of these.
- Non-x86 targets or CPUs without BMI2, and macOS or Windows. shape.hpp includes <immintrin.h> and calls _pext_u64/_pdep_u64 with no fallback, CMake hard-codes -march=native, and only Linux/GCC builds are shown.
- Projects that need a packaged, stable library. There is no library target, no install rules, no releases or tags, and no API documentation. The project is one author's research code with 8 stars.
- Untuned or small inputs, and raw collections of many genomes. Parameters (m, t, levels) are tuned by hand for each dataset, and automatic selection is future work. Building the raw bacterial collection took 73.3 GB, against 29.7 GB for SSHash5 on the preprocessed input.

**Integration:** source-drop · seqan3 3.x, sharg-parser and sux (git submodules); gtl v1.2.0 (CMake FetchContent); cereal, which seqan3 pulls in through CPM; vendored kxsort.h and a modified copy of sux's EliasFano.hpp · C++20 and CMake 3.20+. The README builds with g++-14 and the paper used GCC 12.2. The GCC-specific -Wno-interference-size flag is set, and Clang is not documented. · x86-64 with BMI2 only (PEXT/PDEP intrinsics are unconditional and -march=native is hard-coded). Linux is the only documented OS.

**Vs siblings:** Pick RSHash over SSHash for single-threaded streaming read queries against a static k <= 32 set on x86-64. This is strongest for low-hit workloads, faster and leaner builds, text-position locate, or indexing raw genomes with no de Bruijn graph step. Stay with SSHash if you need k up to 63, k-mer IDs, weights or navigational queries, mostly-positive random lookups, or a packaged library that builds on macOS. Against BLight (AGPL-3.0, multi-threaded, needs a de Bruijn graph), RSHash is MIT-licensed and reports 8.0-10.7 bits/k-mer on human against BLight's 22.3, but the two have never been run head to head.

**Gotchas:**
- With CLI defaults (--level 2), building a small genome segfaults: when level 1 has no frequent minimizers, filter_freq_minimizers indexes an empty vector (open issue #5). Pass --level 1. The author says the defaults were changed, but main still has level{2} (last main commit 2026-07-31).
- Input is parsed as seqan3 dna4 with dna15 as the legal alphabet. N and other IUPAC codes are silently turned into bases (N becomes A), so N runs in raw genomes or reads become poly-A k-mers instead of being skipped.
- lookup() and streaming_lookup() return only the number of hits in the batch or read, not a result for each k-mer. Each call heap-allocates scratch buffers. locate needs an index built with --loc. build() and load() print progress to stdout, and the CLI exits with -1 and no message on bad arguments.
- Index files are raw cereal binary archives with no version field. The sux submodule and the vendored EliasFano.hpp carry LGPL-3.0+/GPL-3.0 headers (with the GCC Runtime Library Exception), not MIT, so check the licensing before you vendor the code.

**Status:** Active single-author research code: the last main commit was 2026-07-31, gapped-k-mer work landed on the multishapes branch in September 2026, and open crash issue #5 was answered within days. It is MIT-licensed with 8 stars and no releases, and you use it by building the CLI or copying source/ into a C++20 x86-64 Linux project.

[repo](https://github.com/jonsmcode/rshash) · [benchmark](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13501323/)

##### SSHash  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Compressed static DNA k-mer dictionary: ~5x smaller than Pufferfish, 1.6-2.4x faster streaming lookups, but slower random lookups.

**Beats:** Pufferfish (and dBG-FM, BLight k-mer dictionaries) — In the 2022 Bioinformatics paper (gcc 11.2.0 -O3 -march=native, Intel i9-9940X, one thread, human genome with 2.5 billion 31-mers), canonical SSHash answered streaming membership in 253/183 ns per k-mer (high/low hit rate), against 402/435 ns for Pufferfish dense and 440/1,088 ns for BLight. It used 9.39 bits/k-mer (vs 45.04 and 20.17) and built in 16.2 min (vs 70.7 and 25.0), but its random lookups (990/854 ns) were slower than Pufferfish dense (720/519 ns); no standard-library baseline was involved, and only the SSHash side of that harness is public.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked only against other k-mer dictionaries (Pufferfish, BLight, SBWT, FMSI), never against std::unordered_map or a standalone MPHF. Pufferfish (dense) is faster on random lookup; SSHash's wins are streaming queries, space and build time.

**How:** Sparse and skew hashing: consecutive k-mers of the input strings are grouped into super-k-mers by their minimizer, and a PTHash minimal perfect hash is built over the distinct minimizers only (about 6.5x fewer keys than k-mers at k=31, m=20 in the 2022 paper), so a lookup hashes the minimizer to a small bucket of offsets into the 2-bit-packed strings and verifies the k-mer against the text instead of storing k-mers. Singleton buckets resolve with one text comparison, buckets with fewer than 2^6 super-k-mers are scanned, and the rare heavy buckets go to a 'skew index' of per-size-class PTHash functions over the k-mers themselves, which caps string accesses. Streaming queries skip hashing while a read follows a stored string: after a hit the next query k-mer is compared with the next k-mer of the same unitig ('extension'), and v6 memoizes the last minimizer's bucket to shortcut negatives. Since v6 a forward minimizer scheme with a centre-closest tie-break puts a k-mer and its reverse complement in the same bucket, so every lookup is a single probe.

**Use it when:**
- Static sets of 10^8 to 10^10 DNA k-mers (bacterial pangenomes, human, HPRC) built from unitigs/eulertigs, where you need k-mer-to-ID and ID-to-k-mer, e.g. as the k-mer index inside a read mapper (the repo carries merged PRs for submodule integration into COMBINE-lab's piscem).
- Streaming membership over FASTQ reads, where consecutive k-mers overlap: v6 measures 76 ns/k-mer on Human k=31 (high-hit), against 266 ns for SBWT and 1,176 ns for FMSI on the same hardware in jermp/kmer_sets_benchmark.
- Memory-constrained indexing: 7.4-10.6 bits/k-mer at k=31 and 3.8-7.6 at k=63 in the current benchmarks (2.75 GB for human k=31), with an --mmap option to query the index from disk.
- Workloads that need Access (rank to k-mer) or navigational queries: Access takes 0.35 us/k-mer on Human k=31, against 10.81 us for SBWT and 18.62 us for FMSI.
- Pipelines that rebuild often: human k=31 builds in 2:35 with 64 threads under a 16 GB RAM cap, using an external-memory builder with a RAM limit (-g) and a temp directory (-d).

**Skip it when:**
- Isolated random point lookups with RAM to spare: in the 2022 paper Pufferfish dense answered them faster (720/519 ns positive/negative vs 990/854 ns) while using about 5x the space (45.04 vs 9.39 bits/k-mer).
- When the smallest index matters most: FMSI takes 3.2-4.4 bits/k-mer at k=31, against 7.4-10.6 for SSHash, though its lookups and streaming queries are more than 10x slower.
- Dynamic sets: the index is immutable, so any insert or delete means a full rebuild.
- Raw reads or sequences with duplicate or non-ACGT k-mers: the README requires deduplicated, N-free, one-sequence-per-line input, so you must run GGCAT/BCALM2 first. For membership-only use on inputs with duplicate k-mers (e.g. matchtigs), the author points to SSHash-Lite.
- General keys or tiny sets: it is not a general hash map or MPHF (use PTHash directly for that), and the author says the smallest input worth indexing is a single bacterial genome (issue #33).

**Integration:** static lib · PTHash (git submodule, which brings bits, essentials, fastmod, xxHash and mm_file), zlib; CityHash vendored in external/ · C++17, CMake 3.5+; CI builds with GCC 11-14 and Clang 16-18 on Ubuntu; k up to 63 needs __uint128_t (GCC/Clang) · x86-64 (CMake always adds -mavx2 -mbmi2, so AVX2/BMI2 CPUs are required) and aarch64 (builds since the Sep 2025 fix for issue #77); tested on Linux with gcc and macOS with clang; Windows not documented

**Vs siblings:** Over RSHash, which claims 1.4x faster streaming on average, pick SSHash for maturity and features: Bioconda packaging, a Rust port, releases since 2022, navigational queries, compressed weights and k up to 63 (RSHash has 8 stars, and its README builds with g++-14 and seqan3). Over BLight, pick SSHash when space and query speed matter: in the 2022 paper it used 9.39 vs 20.17 bits/k-mer and was faster on both streaming and random lookups, though BLight's build peaked at less RAM (7.5 vs 17.3 GB).

**Gotchas:**
- The builder does not screen its input: build with the same k that produced the unitigs, and supply deduplicated, ACGT-only sequences with one per line. Use --check to verify the built index.
- The default 2-bit nucleotide encoding is non-standard (A=00, C=01, T=10, G=11), so passing packed-integer k-mers from other tools needs -DSSHASH_USE_TRADITIONAL_NUCLEOTIDE_ENCODING=On. Max k (31 or 63) is also fixed at compile time.
- Performance and size depend on the minimizer length m, which you must choose. The builder prints a warning only in --verbose mode when m < ceil(log4(N))+1, and the benchmarks tune m per dataset (19-21 for k=31, 23-31 for k=63).
- The index format is versioned: v6.0.0 (Aug 2026) removed the canonical/regular modes, and loading an index with a different major version throws 'SSHash index needs rebuilding'.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v6.0.0 shipped 2026-08-29 with a breaking index-format change; last commit 2026-09-03), MIT-licensed, on Bioconda with a Rust port, and consumed as a CMake static-library target with submodules rather than a header-only drop.

[repo](https://github.com/jermp/sshash) · [benchmark](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9235479/)

#### math-simd-linear-algebra

##### FastMath C++ Library (fast_math_cpp)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only float math library beating glibc's <cmath> on composed functions (sinh, tanh, atan2, integer pow), not raw trig or exp/log.

**Beats:** <cmath> single-precision (float) overloads (std::sinh, std::tanh, std::atanh, std::atan2, std::pow, std::acos, std::log10, std::tan, std::exp, std::log, etc.), backed by glibc libm (sinhf, tanhf, ...) — Scalar float calls, both sides built with identical flags (-O3 -march=native -funroll-loops), best of 25 interleaved runs of 1,000,000 calls, on WSL2 x86_64 GCC 11.4 (no CPU model stated) and Raspberry Pi 4 GCC 12.2 against glibc's float <cmath>: composed functions like sinh (2.96x/3.94x), tanh (2.94x/3.91x) and integer pow (2.02x/4.54x) win; exp/log/log2/sqrt sit at parity (0.94x-1.01x) because they forward to std::; scalar sin/cos/sincos on wide angle ranges lose on ARM (0.63x-0.82x). A separate batch/array API for sin/cos/sincos/atan2 reached up to 6.16x (atan2) over a std:: loop on x86 and 3.48x on the Pi.

**How:** The scalar wins come from composing sinh/tanh/atanh/asinh/acosh/log10 directly out of std::exp/std::log rather than calling glibc's own (non-table-based) composed routines, plus binary exponentiation for pow(base,int). An FP-register rounding trick (add/subtract 1.5*2^23 to a float) gets the integer part needed for exp's and the angle reduction's range folding without crossing to the general-purpose register file. Where glibc already uses lookup tables (exp, log, log2, sqrt), the library forwards to std:: instead of trying to beat it with a polynomial. The batch API's speed comes from SIMD (GCC vector extensions compiling to SSE on x86 / NEON on aarch64) processing 4 floats per iteration, amortizing the call overhead and branches that dominate scalar timings.

**Use it when:**
- Scalar composed functions on floats: sinh/cosh/tanh/asinh/acosh/atanh/log10 -- 1.2x-4.5x over glibc, wider margin on ARM than x86
- Squared or small-integer-power distances: pow(base, int) is 1.5x-4.5x faster than std::pow via the explicit int overload
- Array workloads (lidar scans, particle sets): batch sin/cos/sincos/atan2, 2x-6.2x over a std:: loop depending on platform and function
- Scalar sin/cos/sincos on angles already normalized to [-pi, pi], where this ties or slightly beats std on both platforms
- Header/robotics C++17 codebases already tolerant of float precision that want one namespace instead of mixing FastMath:: and std::

**Skip it when:**
- exp, log, log2, sqrt, or pow with a fractional exponent -- these are thin std:: forwarders, switching buys nothing
- Scalar sin/cos/sincos on angles still needing range reduction ([-2pi,2pi]) on ARM -- measured slower than std (0.63x-0.82x on Pi)
- Anywhere double precision is needed -- the API is float-only, no double overloads exist
- Builds that require -ffast-math -- the library's rounding trick and inf/NaN/signed-zero contracts break under -ffinite-math-only, so it errors out rather than compiling silently wrong
- Dependencies where maintainer bus-factor matters -- 2 GitHub stars, single author, no issues or PRs filed to gauge responsiveness

**Integration:** static lib (default) or shared lib (CMake FAST_MATH_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS option) -- despite the README's 'Header-Only Design' claim, include/fast_math.hpp only declares functions; definitions live in src/fast_math.cpp and src/fast_math_batch.cpp and must be built/linked via CMake add_subdirectory + target_link_libraries · none for the library itself; GoogleTest required only to build the test target (BUILD_TESTS=ON by default, disable with -DBUILD_TESTS=OFF to skip the GTest dependency) · C++17, CMake 3.16+; CI builds with GCC 11 and Clang 15 · x86_64 and aarch64 (Raspberry Pi 4 / Cortex-A72) directly benchmarked; README badge also claims macOS/Windows but GitHub Actions CI only runs ubuntu-latest, so those are untested claims

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over VDT, SLEEF, fmath, or trigno_simd_cpp when the workload is scalar, float-only composed math (sinh/tanh/atan2/integer pow) rather than raw vectorized double trig or bulk elementwise arrays -- those siblings post larger, more consistent multiples (VDT 4.7x-12.8x on double exp/sin, SLEEF/fmath on vectorized batches), but fast_math_cpp is the only one of this set that documents where it loses (exp/log/sqrt/fractional pow at parity, ARM scalar sin/cos regressing on wide angles) rather than only showing wins.

**Gotchas:**
- CMakeLists.txt has a stray add_library(mcl::map ALIAS fast_math_cpp) -- looks like a leftover from a robotics 'MCL' (Monte Carlo Localization) template this was extracted from; harmless but a sign of how small/informal the project is
- -ffast-math is deliberately rejected by the build -- it silently breaks the FP-register rounding trick (folds (v+magic)-magic back to v), so the library errors out at compile time rather than returning wrong answers under it
- log, log2, asinh-family etc. return a sentinel (-1e38f) for out-of-domain input instead of -inf/NaN like std:: -- a behavioral difference from the baseline being replaced
- sqrt() returns 0 for non-positive input instead of NaN/domain-error like std::sqrt -- another silent semantic deviation

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-07-28), MIT-licensed, small enough to vendor -- but a very small personal project (2 stars, no issues or PRs filed, single named author), so verify it still builds against your toolchain before depending on it.

[repo](https://github.com/hijimasa/fast_math_cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/hijimasa/fast_math_cpp/blob/main/README.md)

##### trigno_simd_cpp (SIMD trigonometric approximations, Goyal & Arora)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Piecewise rational sin/cos/tan approximation using AVX2 FMA plus a fast inverse-sqrt hack; beats scalar libm sin/cos/tan.

**Beats:** <cmath> std::sin, std::cos, std::tan — arXiv 2502.10831 (Goyal & Arora) measured mean speed-up vs 'inbuilt' std::sin/cos/tan of 5.49x/5.52x/4.44x over 1000 random angles in [-1e6, 1e6] (seed 2024873), each called 1e5 times through a function pointer, built with g++ -std=c++17 -mavx2 -mfma -O3 -march=native on an AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX under Windows/MinGW-w64. This is scalar per-call latency against the MinGW CRT libm, not glibc, and not array/batch throughput.

**How:** Replaces libm's accurate but branchy range reduction and polynomial/CORDIC evaluation with a cheap piecewise rational fit: angle reduction picks 1 of 7 precomputed coefficient sets (SinHelperParams/CosHelperParams/TanHelperParams), then computes (linear numerator) * fastInverseSqrt(quadratic denominator) via AVX2 FMA (_mm256_fmadd_pd). The reciprocal-sqrt step uses a Quake III-style fast inverse square root (magic constant 0x5fe6eb50c7b537a9 plus one Newton-Raphson refinement) instead of hardware division or sqrt, trading accuracy for fewer cycles.

**Use it when:**
- Scalar sin/cos/tan calls where ~3-4 significant digits (max rel error ~0.004; tan max abs error 0.27 near asymptotes) is acceptable, e.g. graphics, audio, game logic, DSP.
- x86-64 targets with AVX2+FMA, or FPGA/HLS synthesis (vitis_hls_code/ ships Vitis HLS variants of the same algorithm).
- Call sites currently latency-bound on libm sin/cos/tan, willing to trade IEEE correctness for ~4.4-5.5x fewer cycles per call.
- OK vendoring a handful of .h/.cpp files directly, since there is no packaged library to link.

**Skip it when:**
- Need IEEE-correctly-rounded or tightly error-bounded trig (scientific/numeric code checked against std::sin/cos/tan).
- Need real batch/vector throughput over arrays of independent angles: the public API is one angle in, one double out, with no array entry point despite internal AVX2 use.
- Angles very near odd multiples of pi/2 for tan: the function returns +infinity via explicit masking rather than a precise blow-up value.
- Non-x86 targets or CPUs without AVX2/FMA: no scalar or portable fallback is present in the source.
- Need a mature, widely-used dependency: 7 stars, single first-party arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed), no CI/tests, no install target.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (only <immintrin.h> AVX2/FMA compiler intrinsics) · C++17; g++ (developed/tested with MinGW-w64 g++ on Windows; CMakeLists.txt requires CMake >=3.10) · x86-64 with AVX2 and FMA (uses __m256d/_mm256_* intrinsics); separate Vitis HLS C++ sources exist for FPGA synthesis in vitis_hls_code/

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over SLEEF or VDT only if you specifically want this piecewise-rational-plus-fast-inverse-sqrt technique or its FPGA/HLS variant; SLEEF gives true 4-wide vectorized libm replacements with selectable ulp accuracy, and VDT is an older, better-documented scalar libm-vs-SIMD comparison with wider function coverage — both are more mature (more usage, tests) than this 7-star single-paper repo.

**Gotchas:**
- Each call broadcasts the single scalar angle into all 4 AVX2 lanes and reads back only lane 0 — SIMD width is not used to batch multiple angles, so the reported per-call speedup may not translate into per-element throughput on arrays.
- tan() near odd multiples of pi/2 is special-cased to return +infinity via an AVX2 compare/blend, not computed from the rational approximation.
- Uses a Quake-style fast inverse square root (bit-hack + 1 Newton-Raphson step) in place of sqrt/division, an extra approximation layer on top of the rational fit.
- No CMake install or library target — the build only produces a benchmark executable (bin/trigno_benchmark.exe), so consumers copy the include/ and relevant src/ files into their own project.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-01-29 added tan asymptote masking) and Apache-2.0 licensed, but only 7 stars, no CI/tests, and no packaged library target — usability is 'copyable' source, not a dependency to pull in.

[repo](https://github.com/Nikhil0250/trigno_simd_cpp) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.10831)

##### SLEEF (SIMD Library for Evaluating Elementary Functions)  `C`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Vectorized C library of libm math functions (sin, cos, exp, log, pow); beats scalar <cmath>/libm when call sites are SIMD-batched.

**Beats:** <cmath> (scalar libm, represented in the paper by FDLIBM as the reference scalar implementation) — A peer-reviewed paper (Shibata & Petrogalli, IEEE TPDS vol. 31 no. 6, 2020; arXiv 2001.09258) Table 2 measured reciprocal throughput (ns/call) of SLEEF 3.4's 256-bit AVX2 double-precision vector functions (4 lanes/call, 1-ULP tier) against scalar FDLIBM 5.3, both built with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma, on an Intel Core i7-6700 with Turbo off: wide-domain sin/cos/tan ran ~3.2-3.6x faster per call, log ~2.0x, exp ~1.6x, pow ~1.25x; on narrow argument domains and for acos/atan, scalar FDLIBM was faster per call than vector SLEEF. This is a SIMD-vs-scalar comparison, not a like-for-like scalar replacement of std::sin/std::exp.

**How:** Processes multiple lanes per call (4/8 doubles, 8/16 floats depending on ISA) instead of looping scalar libm calls, and uses a modified Payne-Hanek argument-reduction algorithm redesigned to minimize the data-dependent branching that otherwise forces every SIMD lane onto the slow path if any single lane needs it (paper: 'SLEEF: A Portable Vectorized Library of C Standard Mathematical Functions', Shibata & Petrogalli). It offers a 1-ULP tier (compensated double-double arithmetic) and a faster ~3.5-ULP tier with a shorter polynomial, trading accuracy for speed. Portability comes from wrapping each ISA's intrinsics behind common inline-function/macro helper headers (helperavx2.h, helperadvsimd.h, helpersve.h, ...) compiled per-target.

**Use it when:**
- Hot loops that already batch scalar math across arrays and can call the Sleef_*dN_u10/u35 vector entry points directly instead of std::sin/std::exp per element
- Wide-domain or branchy transcendental workloads (large-magnitude arguments needing full range reduction) where scalar libm's branches hurt SIMD throughput — Table 2 shows ~3.2-3.6x per-call wins for wide-domain sin/cos/tan, ~2.0x log, ~1.6x exp, ~1.25x pow (SLEEF 4-wide AVX2 vs scalar FDLIBM)
- Need one source portable across AVX2, AVX512F, AdvSIMD (and experimentally SSE2/RISC-V) via runtime dispatch
- Can tolerate the 3.5-ULP accuracy tier for extra speed on non-critical paths
- Also need DFT or quad-precision elementary functions bundled with the math kernels

**Skip it when:**
- Scalar call sites (one value at a time): the benchmarked win is SIMD-vs-scalar, and on narrow argument domains or for acos/atan, scalar FDLIBM was faster per call than vector SLEEF in the same table
- Want a drop-in <cmath> replacement without restructuring loops to load SIMD vectors — API is a different symbol/type surface, not operator/name-compatible with std::sin
- SSE2-only x86 targets (experimental, 'seeking sponsorship') or RISC-V RVV targets (unmaintained, may be removed without notice)
- Code that compiles the inline-header path without -O3: open issue #436 reports wrong results in that configuration
- Need guaranteed-correct cos() when any vector lane's argument may reach >=1e14: open issue #444 reports inconsistent per-lane results there, and the benchmarked domain here goes up to 1e100

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (CMake build; not header-only, though inline-header build path also exists) · none at runtime for the library itself; build needs CMake 3.18+ and matching C/C++ compiler versions; TLFloat is auto-fetched if not present; tests additionally need libssl/libcrypto, libgmp, libmpfr, libfftw · CMake 3.18+; GCC/Clang/MSVC (README requires the C and C++ compilers to be the same version) · x86-64 (SSE2 experimental, AVX2 and AVX512F mainline-supported), AArch64 AdvSIMD (mainline), RISC-V RVVM1/RVVM2 (unmaintained); toolchain files also exist for POWER (ppc64el) and s390x; CI-tested on Linux/Windows/macOS per the README support matrix

**Vs siblings:** Pick SLEEF over VDT, fmath, or trigno_simd_cpp when you need multiple ISAs (AVX2/AVX512F/AdvSIMD/RISC-V) behind one API with runtime dispatch, plus quad-precision or DFT routines, or want a tunable 1-ULP/3.5-ULP accuracy knob; those siblings target a single ISA/precision and a narrower function set.

**Gotchas:**
- Inline-header build path gives wrong results if the including translation unit is compiled without -O3 (open issue #436, since 2021)
- Vectorized cos() can give inconsistent per-lane results once any lane's argument is >=1e14 (open issue #444) — relevant since the benchmarked domain in this record runs up to 1e100
- exp and pow can return infinity earlier than correct (open issue #600, 2024)
- Runtime CPU-extension dispatch is not thread-safe on first call, per an open maintainer-acknowledged issue (#560)

**Status:** Actively maintained — last commit 2025-12-25, latest tagged release 3.9.0 (March 2025); this session found five open issues touching accuracy and thread-safety dating back to 2021. BSL-1.0 licensed and small enough to vendor or build as a static/shared lib; the cited benchmark used the older 3.4 branch, several major releases behind current master.

[repo](https://github.com/shibatch/sleef) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.09258)

#### minimal-perfect-hash-functions

##### emphf  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Hypergraph-peeling (MWHC) minimal perfect hash builder that constructs 5-63x faster than CMPH's CHD, using ~0.5 more bits/key.

**Beats:** CMPH — In the PTHash authors' mphf_benchmark (Table 5 of the SIGIR'21 paper), single-threaded on an Intel i9-9900K with gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native, emphf's in-memory seq builder built an MPHF over 1 billion random 64-bit keys in 374 s at 2.61 bits/key with 199 ns/key average lookup, versus 1972-23746 s, 2.01-2.17 bits/key and 416-419 ns/key for CMPH's CHD at lambda 4-6. At 100 million keys the same table gives 24 s and 147 ns for emphf versus 121-1418 s and 197-204 ns for CHD; the comparison uses the benchmark authors' harness, not emphf's own.

**How:** It uses the Majewski-Wormald-Havas-Czech (MWHC) scheme: one Jenkins 64-bit hash pass gives each key three vertices of a random 3-partite 3-hypergraph with 1.23n vertices, the graph is peeled in linear time, and 2-bit vertex values are assigned in reverse peeling order; a rank over nonzero pairs (one 64-bit count per 512 pairs) makes the result minimal, which is where 1.23 x 2 + ~0.15 = 2.61 bits/key comes from. The in-memory peeler (seq) uses the 'xor trick': each vertex stores only its degree and the XOR of the other endpoints of its edges, so adjacency is a flat array of fixed-size records, not lists. There is no per-bucket displacement search as in CHD, whose build time in the same benchmark grows from 1972 s to 23746 s as lambda goes from 4 to 6. For inputs that exceed RAM, scan_mmap implements the paper's cache-oblivious peeling (sequential scans and sorts, O(sort(n)) I/Os), and HEM splits keys into ~256-key buckets (Botelho-Pagh-Ziviani) that are each peeled in memory.

**Use it when:**
- Static sets of 10^8-10^9+ keys where single-threaded build time matters and ~2.6 bits/key is acceptable: in PTHash's Table 5 it is the fastest-building row under 2.9 bits/key at both 100M keys (24 s) and 1B keys (374 s).
- Replacing CMPH's CHD in an offline build step: 24 s vs 121-1418 s at 100M keys and 374 s vs 1972-23746 s at 1B keys, with lookups also 1.4-2.1x faster.
- Key sets whose peeling working set does not fit in RAM: compute_mphf_scan_mmap builds the same structure from mmapped temporary files; the DCC 2014 paper reports 7.6 billion keys in under 21 hours on one machine.
- Variable-length string or binary keys: any key type works through an adaptor that returns a byte range, hashed once per lookup.
- Projects that can vendor and patch 17 small headers and do not need a maintained upstream.

**Skip it when:**
- Lookup-heavy paths: 199 ns/key at 1B keys (147 ns at 100M) versus 37-101 ns for PTHash configurations and 170 ns for BBHash gamma=1 in the same table; each lookup reads three random 2-bit slots plus a rank block that popcounts up to 16 words.
- Space-critical uses: 2.61 bits/key versus 1.80 for RecSplit l=8,b=100 and 2.01-2.17 for CHD itself.
- Multi-core machines where you want a parallel build: every construction path in the source is single-threaded.
- Dynamic sets or membership tests: the structure is static, and lookup() does no check, so a key outside the build set returns an arbitrary index.
- Code that needs an active upstream or portability: no commits since 2013-12-06, an open 2015 issue about an endless 'Hypergraph is not peelable' loop on a small set, an unmerged 2024 modernization PR, a Python 2 test script, and no Windows or non-x86 build as written.

**Integration:** source-drop · none beyond the C++ standard library and POSIX (sys/mman.h, sys/time.h, mkstemp for the mmap/HEM paths); build via CMake only for the CLI tools · C++11 (-std=c++11) with GCC or Clang; uses the GNU '?:' extension, __builtin_clzll/__builtin_ctzll and inline asm, so MSVC is out; CMakeLists declares cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 2.8), which CMake 4.0+ rejects unless CMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5 is set; the PTHash benchmark compiled the headers with gcc 9.2.1 in C++17 mode · Unix only (CMake stops with 'Unsupported platform' otherwise); x86/x86-64 as written because bitpair_vector.hpp includes <xmmintrin.h> (unused); little-endian assumed per a XXX note in base_hash.hpp; optional SSE4.2 hardware popcount via EMPHF_USE_POPCOUNT

**Vs siblings:** Pick emphf over RecSplit (Sux) only when build time outweighs space (374 s vs 936 s at 1B keys, but 2.61 vs 1.80 bits/key at similar ~200 ns lookups), and pick PTHash instead whenever lookup speed matters (37-101 ns vs 199 ns). Its remaining niche is external-memory peeling (scan_mmap) for key sets larger than RAM; none of the sources read here compare it with SicHash, SimdRecSplit, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit.

**Gotchas:**
- common.hpp defines non-inline functions (logger(), nonzero_pairs()) at namespace scope in a header, so including emphf from more than one .cpp gives multiple-definition link errors; mark them inline or keep emphf in one translation unit.
- Duplicate keys are not detected on the seq path and the retry loop in mphf.hpp is unbounded, so duplicates (or an input that never peels, see issue #1) retry forever; HEM restarts on duplicate hashes with the same result. Deduplicate first. The benchmphf README also reports HEM crashing with std::length_error on sets of ~1000 keys or fewer.
- Build and lookup must use the same adaptor: stl_string_adaptor hashes the trailing NUL byte, so hashing (s.data(), s.size()) at lookup time returns wrong indices.
- Construction logs timestamps to stderr unconditionally; seq and HEM need on the order of 30 bytes/key while building (benchmphf README); scan_mmap/HEM create 'mphf.temp.XXXXXX' files in the current working directory; save/load write raw host-endian binaries with no version or checksum.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2013-12-06 (one open issue from 2015, one unmerged PR from 2024), but Apache-2.0 per the LICENSE file and only 17 headers, so it is easy to vendor and patch; last known-good compiler in the sources read is gcc 9.2.1 (C++17 mode, via mphf_benchmark).

[repo](https://github.com/ot/emphf) · [benchmark](https://github.com/roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark/blob/main/README.md)

##### LPHash  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Locality-preserving MPHF for DNA k-mer sets: 0.53-0.87 bits/k-mer at k=63, versus 3.06-3.71 for BBHash and 2.04-2.76 for PTHash.

**Beats:** BBHash (also PTHash) — In the Bioinformatics 2023 paper, five whole-genome SPSS k-mer sets were tested (Yeast 11.6M to Human 2.77G k-mers). At k=63, partitioned LPHash took 0.53-0.87 bits/k-mer, against 3.06-3.71 for BBHash (gamma 1 and 2) and 2.04-2.76 for PTHash, and streaming queries over about 100M Human chr13 k-mers on one core took 22-53 ns/k-mer, against 42-190 ns for BBHash. All code was compiled with gcc 11.2.0 -O3 -march=native and run on an Intel i9-9900K with 64 GB RAM. No C++ standard library container was part of the comparison.

**How:** Each k-mer is keyed by its random minimizer. A run of consecutive k-mers that share a minimizer (a super-k-mer) is stored once, and a k-mer's code is the super-k-mer's prefix-sum offset plus a local rank computed from where the minimizer sits inside the k-mer. As a result, the stored parts are only a PTHash MPHF over the distinct minimizers (about 2/(w+1) of the k-mers, with w = k-m+1) and the offsets and positions, coded with Elias-Fano. The partitioned variant labels each super-k-mer as left-right-max, left-max, right-max or non-max in a 2-bit wavelet tree with Rank9, and skips the offsets or positions that each label already implies. Ambiguous minimizers (1-4% in the paper's datasets) go to a fallback PTHash over their k-mers. In streaming queries the minimizer usually stays the same from one k-mer to the next, so the next code is the previous code plus or minus 1, with no hash-table lookup.

**Use it when:**
- You need an MPHF, or a k-mer-to-slot index for counts, colors or unitig IDs, over the distinct k-mers of a genome or de Bruijn graph, and memory is the limit. At k=47-63 the paper measured 0.53-1.14 bits/k-mer, below the 1.44 bits/key lower bound for general MPHFs.
- Lookups arrive as consecutive k-mers from reads or sequences (streaming). At k=63 the paper measured 22-53 ns/k-mer on one core, against 24-72 ns for PTHash-v1 and 42-190 ns for BBHash.
- You want satellite values to compress well. Consecutive k-mers get consecutive codes, so a value array indexed by the code forms runs of similar values.
- Sets of millions to a few billion k-mers (11.6M-2.77G tested) on Linux or macOS. The build can spill to disk through --max-memory and -d.
- Your pipeline already produces SPSS input (BCALM2 + UST or a similar tool), so the preprocessing costs you nothing extra.

**Skip it when:**
- The keys are not k-mers from a spectrum-preserving string set. LPHash cannot hash arbitrary keys, and the paper itself calls BBHash and PTHash the general-purpose options.
- Most lookups are in random order. LPHash random lookups measured 110-188 ns/k-mer, against 24-72 ns for PTHash-v1.
- k is around 31 and lookups are streaming. At k=31, LPHash streaming was slower than PTHash-v1 on 4 of 5 datasets (for example 107 vs 72 ns on Human), and space was 1.18-1.74 bits/k-mer. The maintainer says k < 31 was never tested.
- You need canonical k-mers, where a k-mer and its reverse complement get the same code. LPHash treats them as different keys (issue #22), and BCALM2/UST output contains only one orientation of each k-mer, so reads from the other strand get arbitrary codes.
- You need a maintained library with a stable API, or Windows/MSVC support. There has been no main-branch commit since July 2023, there is no library target, and the code depends on __uint128_t and GCC/Clang flags.

**Integration:** source-drop · PTHash (git submodule, which brings its essentials and cmd_line_parser headers) and zlib; kseq.h is vendored. BBHash (external/BooPHF.hpp) is vendored only for the benchmark tools. · C++17 and CMake 3.5+, with GCC or Clang (__uint128_t required). The paper used GCC 11.2.0. With Clang, CMake adds -stdlib=libc++. · The README says it is tested on Linux with GCC and on macOS with Clang, on Intel and ARM (Apple M1). On x86-64, CMake forces -march=native -mbmi2 -msse4.2, so binaries need BMI2 and POPCNT and may not run on other CPUs (issue #21: 'Illegal instruction' on a Xeon E5-2470). Windows is not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick LPHash over PTHash, SicHash, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit only when the keys are DNA k-mers from a spectrum-preserving string set and k is about 47 or more. In that case it goes below the ~1.44 bits/key floor that general MPHFs approach (for example ShockHash at about 1.56 bits/key), and it beats PTHash on streaming lookups. For arbitrary keys, random-order lookups, or k near 31 (1.18-1.74 bits/k-mer), PTHash (which LPHash uses internally) or the RecSplit family is the better choice.

**Gotchas:**
- The k-mer width is a compile-time typedef in include/compile_constants.tpd (default __uint128_t, k <= 63). In issue #21, a k=25 build with the default type aborted with PTHash's 'seed did not work', and switching to uint64_t fixed it. The fallback hasher gives different results for the two typedefs, so query with a binary built with the same typedef as the one that built the .lph file.
- The query tool crashes on any sequence shorter than k (reported in issue #21 and acknowledged). The random-lookup loop is still unguarded on both main and dev. Non-ACGT bases are not supported: streaming mode skips k-mers that contain them, but random mode does not, so the two modes can return different counts.
- Construction uses external memory: --max-memory defaults to 8 GB, and temp files go to -d (default: current directory). A 955M-k-mer fallback build in issue #21 logged a peak of 28 GB of disk. With 4 threads, the build is slower than BBHash-v1 (Cod 05:30 vs 00:48, Human 07:25 vs 04:13) but faster than PTHash on the three largest sets.
- Like any MPHF, it returns a valid-looking code for a k-mer that was never indexed (maintainer, issue #22). Add a membership check (for example SSHash) if query reads can contain unseen k-mers.

**Status:** Abandoned by the catalog rule: the last commit on main is 2023-07-19, a restructured dev branch stops at 2023-11-18, and the short-input crash reported in 2023 is still unfixed. It is MIT-licensed, has about 20 source files plus the PTHash submodule, and builds with a C++17 GCC or Clang toolchain, so you can vendor it.

[repo](https://github.com/jermp/lphash) · [benchmark](https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/39/Supplement_1/i534/7210438)

##### PHast / PHast+ (bsuccinct-rs "ph" crate)  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust minimal perfect hash (PHast/PHast+) giving ~10 ns queries at under 2 bits/key; about 5x faster queries than PTHash.

**Beats:** PTHash — The authors' ALENEX26 paper ran the MPHF-Experiments harness on 50M random 10-50-byte string keys (AMD Ryzen 5600G, 6C/12T; rustc 1.84.1 and gcc 12.2.0 at third-level optimization with native CPU flags; GxHash for the Rust methods). PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3, Elias-Fano) used 1.94 bits/key with 10 ns queries vs PTHash (lambda=5, EF) at 2.11 bits/key and 54 ns. Its single-thread build was about 5% slower (606 vs 577 ns/key) but 3.3x faster on 12 threads (69 vs 231 ns/key). At 500M keys the query gap vs PTHash grows (25 vs 135 ns), and PHast+ builds in 61-140 ns/key at 50M keys; there is no comparison against std or CMPH.

**How:** PHast is a simplified bucket-placement scheme (the CHD/PTHash family). A 64-bit key hash picks a bucket through a plain linear map, and each bucket stores one fixed-width seed, usually one byte. The value is a linear offset floor(alpha*h) plus p(seed, h) inside a small slice of L values (e.g. 1024), so a query is one hash, one byte load, a multiply and a mask, with no nonlinear bucket function, variable-length seed decoding or rank. Buckets with no feasible seed are 'bumped' (seed 0, about 1% of keys) to further levels whose outputs are remapped through an Elias-Fano array. Construction sorts hashes, seeds buckets from a 256-bucket sliding window with a cyclic used/free bitmap, picks the seed that minimizes the values it occupies, and runs in parallel over chunks separated by small gaps. PHast+ switches to additive placement p = (c + s) mod L, so 64 candidate seeds are tested at once by OR-ing bitmap words; this makes construction about an order of magnitude faster.

**Use it when:**
- Static key sets from millions to hundreds of millions of keys where query latency dominates: at 50M random 10-50-byte string keys PHast answers in 9-12 ns vs 40-54 ns for PTHash and 33-66 ns for PHOBIC.
- You need about 1.9-2.1 bits/key and fast (re)builds: PHast+ builds at 61-140 ns/key on one thread and 15-26 ns/key on 12 threads at 50M keys.
- Multi-core construction of the smallest fast variant: regular PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3) goes from 606 to 69 ns/key on 12 threads, and parallel construction adds no query-time partitioning step.
- Rust code that replaces a read-only HashMap with MPHF + value array (e.g. k-mer or ID indexes). In an informal third-party test (issue #12, u64 keys) PHast + array lookups took 12/20/36 ns at 1M/10M/100M keys, vs 54/80/87 ns for std HashMap and 19/28/30 ns for a GxHash HashMap.

**Skip it when:**
- The key set changes, or you must reject foreign keys: there is no insert/delete, and `get` has no membership check. A key outside the build set returns an arbitrary index or can panic (open issue #18, no `try_get` yet). Store keys or fingerprints yourself.
- C++ projects without a Rust toolchain: the API is Rust-only with no C/C++ bindings. The MPHF-Experiments harness had to write its own `extern "C"` shim to call it.
- Key sets that do not fit in RAM: construction takes a Vec or slice and allocates a 64-bit hash per key. Iterator-based construction is only planned (issue #19), and the external-memory algorithm in the paper is not implemented.
- Space below about 1.8 bits/key: recursive-splitting methods go lower. PHast needs S=12 and 5,322 ns/key single-thread construction to reach 1.82 bits/key.
- Hard worst-case query bounds: bumped keys (about 1%) walk extra levels plus an Elias-Fano lookup, and the default configuration has no constant-level guarantee.

**Integration:** crate · bitm, binout, dyn_size_of, seedable_hash (all from the same repo), rayon, voracious_radix_sort, arrayvec; default features add sux, epserde and mem_dbg (aligned-vec on 32-bit targets); optional hash backends: gxhash, wyhash, rapidhash, xxhash-rust, fnv, sip13 (nightly) · Rust edition 2021. `ph` declares no rust-version, but the default `sux` feature pulls sux/epserde releases that require Rust 1.85; `sip13` needs nightly · Optimized for 64-bit CPUs; CI builds only on x86-64 Linux with target-cpu=native. The README says it also compiles on 32-bit targets such as wasm32, but slower. The recommended gxhash backend needs x86 AES-NI+SSE2 or ARM AES+NEON and has no fallback

**Vs siblings:** Pick PHast over PTHash or PHOBIC when query time matters: at 50M keys it answers in ~10 ns vs 33-66 ns at equal or smaller size (1.94 vs 2.11 bits/key for PTHash with EF). Against PtrHash (the closest rival, also Rust), PHast+ at 50M keys is smaller and at least as fast (2.07 bits/key, 12 ns query, 80 ns/key build vs PtrHash 2.12 bits/key, 14 ns, 192 ns/key cubic), but at 500M keys PtrHash matches its queries; choose SIMDRecSplit, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit only when space under ~1.8 bits/key matters more than 100+ ns queries.

**Gotchas:**
- The default hasher is slow unless you pick one. `ph` depends on seedable_hash with default-features off, so without a hash feature `BuildDefaultSeededHasher` is std's SipHash `DefaultHasher`. A user reported PHast as 'strangely slow' in issue #12 because of this. The paper's numbers use the `gxhash` feature, which needs RUSTFLAGS such as `-C target-cpu=native`.
- `write`/`read` serialization requires the same hasher at load time. std's DefaultHasher algorithm is explicitly unspecified across Rust releases, and gxhash output is stable only within a major version, so pin the hasher before persisting functions.
- Keys must be distinct (every constructor says so), and construction runs no dedup check. The author warned in issue #2 that duplicate keys make ph (FMPH) construction never finish, so dedupe first.
- The API is still 0.x and the released crate lags git. crates.io 0.11.0 (Feb 2026) uses `Params` and `with_slice_p_threads_hash_sc`, while git HEAD uses `Conf` and `with_slice_conf_threads_sc`. PHast docs have no examples. Issue #20 reported that 0.11.0's dependency tree would break on a future rustc.

**Status:** Very active: the author commits almost daily as of 2026-09-25, and PHast research (k-perfect, a new paper) is ongoing. It is MIT OR Apache-2.0 and on crates.io (ph 0.11.0, ~878k downloads), but the released crate trails git and the API is still changing.

[repo](https://github.com/beling/bsuccinct-rs) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17918)

##### PTHash  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++17 minimal perfect hash library (PTHash/PHOBIC) with 3.1-4.6x faster lookups than BBHash at ~3 bits/key.

**Beats:** BBHash — On the authors' mphf_benchmark harness (1 billion uniformly random 64-bit keys, single core, gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native, Intel i9-9900K with 64 GB DDR3), PTHash looked up keys in 37 ns/key (C-C, 3.23 bits/key) and 55 ns/key (D-D, 2.99 bits/key), versus 170 ns/key for single-threaded BBHash gamma=1 (3.06 bits/key), about 3.1-4.6x faster. BBHash built the set faster (253 s versus 689-1042 s), and these numbers come from a 2022 PTHash commit, not the current lambda-based code.

**How:** It revisits the FCH (Fox-Chen-Heath) scheme: keys are hashed once into buckets (skewed so 60% of keys land in 30% of buckets, or with PHOBIC's 'optimal' bucket function), and the builder processes buckets largest-first, searching for a small integer 'pilot' per bucket that sends all its keys to free slots via a multiply-high reduction of mix(h(x) XOR mix(pilot)). A lookup is therefore one key hash, one random access into a compressed pilot array and a multiply, whereas BBHash can hash the key several times per lookup (once per level). The pilots compress well because small ones are tried first; encodings include compact, dictionary, Elias-Fano, Rice, front/back 'dual' and PHOBIC's interleaved codes. Building with a load factor alpha < 1 makes the pilot search much faster, and minimality is restored by an Elias-Fano 'free slots' array consulted only for keys that land at a position >= n.

**Use it when:**
- Static sets of millions to billions of keys (64-bit integers, strings, URLs, n-grams) where lookup latency matters most. On 1B random 64-bit keys, a single core looks up in 37-55 ns/key at 3.0-3.2 bits/key.
- Build-once/query-many deployments. You build offline, serialize with essentials::save, and load or mmap the function at query time.
- Long variable-length keys. PTHash hashes each key only once per lookup; the paper reports only a 6-26 ns/key increase for q-grams and URLs relative to 64-bit keys.
- Key sets larger than RAM. single_phf and partitioned_phf have external-memory builders capped by config.ram, and construction can be multi-threaded with config.num_threads.
- Space/speed tuning. The author's current recommended default is PHOBIC (dense partitioned, C-int encoder, opt bucketer, lambda=7). On 100M keys with 8 threads on a Xeon W-2245, it gave 2.51 bits/key and 33.5 ns/key lookup in an 8.3 s build (author's own benchmark, with no BBHash comparison).

**Skip it when:**
- Dynamic key sets. The function is static by design, so any insert or delete means a full rebuild.
- When single-threaded build time matters more than lookup speed. At similar space on 1B keys, BBHash gamma=1 built in 253 s versus 689-1042 s for the fast-lookup PTHash configurations.
- Tiny key sets (tens to thousands of keys). Fixed metadata dominates: 469 bits/key for 6 keys was reported in issue #88. Several pathological small inputs made the pilot search hang (#14, #67, #87; the maintainer reports these as fixed). The author says MPHFs are meant for at least hundreds of thousands of keys.
- When you need order preservation or membership tests. Output slots come in arbitrary order, and a key outside the build set still returns a valid-looking slot in [0, n), so you must store and compare keys yourself.
- 32-bit, embedded or MSVC/Windows targets. The author says it is meant for 64-bit architectures, and the code relies on __uint128_t and POSIX sysconf. Also, PHOBIC's dense_partitioned_phf cannot yet be built in external memory (open issue #90).

**Integration:** header-only · Header-only git submodules: jermp/bits (which pulls in jermp/essentials), jermp/mm_file and xxHash (included inline via xxh3.h). Also pthreads via CMake Threads::Threads. cmd_line_parser is used only by the bundled build/example tools. · C++17 (C++14 is explicitly unsupported, per issue #8) and CMake >= 3.5. CI builds with GCC 11-14 and Clang 16-18 on Ubuntu 24.04; the paper used GCC 9.2.1. · 64-bit only. Tested on Linux/GCC and macOS/Clang, on both x86-64 and Apple ARM (the author reports faster queries on M1 than on the x86 box). On x86-64 Unix, the CMake target adds -march=native -mbmi2 -msse4.2. Windows/MSVC support is not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PTHash when lookup latency dominates. In the same 1B-key table it answers in 37-101 ns/key, versus 199 ns for emphf and 197-220 ns for RecSplit, at a cost of roughly 0.4-1.4 bits/key more than RecSplit's 1.80. Prefer RecSplit, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit when you need to get down near 1.5-1.8 bits/key, and LPHash for k-mer sets (the PTHash author himself points k-mer users there).

**Gotchas:**
- build_configuration defaults to verbose=true, and seed-retry messages go to std::cout regardless, so set config.verbose=false in library code. The default seed is random (up to 10 retries), so builds are not reproducible unless you set config.seed. With a fixed seed, a failed search throws seed_runtime_error instead of retrying.
- Duplicate keys, or colliding 64-bit hashes, make construction throw 'seed did not work'. The xxhash_64 hasher throws outright above 2^30 keys; use xxhash_128 for large sets.
- The exported PTHASH CMake target injects -march=native into every consumer target on x86-64 Unix. Binaries built this way may not run on older CPUs; override the flags if you ship binaries.
- The API and parameters changed after the benchmarked version. mphf_benchmark pins a Dec-2022 commit (b9a0c37) that uses the old 'c' parameter and MurmurHash2, while current master uses 'lambda', xxHash and a Bucketer template argument. Use release v2.0.0 to get 'c' semantics, and re-tune rather than copying the paper's configurations.

**Status:** Actively maintained: the last commit on 2026-07-27 added string_view keys and key mappers, and only one issue is open. It is MIT-licensed and header-only, and adding it as a git submodule is the documented integration path.

[repo](https://github.com/jermp/pthash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark/blob/main/README.md)

##### PtrHash  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust minimal perfect hash with 8-bit pilots (PTHash descendant); queries 2.7-3.8x faster than BBHash, ~7.6x faster than CMPH CHD.

**Beats:** BBHash and CMPH (CHD) in the arXiv 2506.06536 survey; PTHash and PHOBIC (plus CMPH CHD) in the SEA 2025 paper arXiv 2502.15539 — The survey (arXiv 2506.06536v3, Table 6) linked ptr_hash 1.1.0 as a Rust staticlib (Rust 1.85, target-cpu=native) and ran it against C++ BBHash and CMPH CHD (GCC 14.2, -O3 -march=native). The run used 100M random 10-50-byte strings, single-threaded, on an i7-11700 pinned at 2.5 GHz. PtrHash queried in 45-47 ns vs 127-173 ns for BBHash and 356 ns for CHD, and built in 141-358 ns/key vs 157-273 and 1,522 ns/key. The author's SEA 2025 paper (300M strings, 6 threads, i7-10750H at 2.6 GHz, compiler not stated) reports 37 ns (23 ns streaming) vs 77 ns for the fastest PTHash config; no source compares against std::unordered_map.

**How:** It is a PTHash/PHOBIC-style bucket-placement MPHF. Keys hash into buckets, and each bucket stores a 'pilot' whose hash is XORed into the key hash to choose a slot. PtrHash limits pilots to 0..255 and stores them as a plain `Vec<u8>`, with no compact, dictionary or Elias-Fano decoding. When no pilot fits, construction uses cuckoo-style hash-and-evict. The result is that most queries cost one cache-line read plus a few multiply-high range reductions (Lemire's fastrange). With alpha=0.99, the ~1% of slots at or above n are remapped through a plain vector or CacheLineEF, which packs 44 Elias-Fano values into one cache line. `index_stream` hashes keys ahead and software-prefetches pilots 32 iterations early, which the paper shows saturates per-core memory bandwidth. Construction radix-sorts hashes and fills cache-sized parts.

**Use it when:**
- Static key sets from ~1M to 10^9+ keys (the docs say it was tested up to 10^11) that are queried far more often than rebuilt, e.g. k-mer indexes, string-to-id dictionaries, or dense value arrays indexed by key.
- Throughput-bound bulk lookups you can stream: on 1e9 integer keys, `index_stream` reaches 8.6-9.7 ns/key, vs 12.5-21.7 ns/key for a plain for-loop (SEA paper Table 1).
- Tables much larger than L3, where cache misses dominate: the survey measured 1.0 L1 miss per query, vs 4.0-7.4 for BBHash and 11.4 for CHD.
- You want fast construction without giving up query speed: 141 ns/key single-threaded at 2.99 bits/key (survey Table 6), or 27 ns/key on 6 threads (SEA Table 2).
- Rust codebases, or C++ projects willing to link a Rust staticlib behind a small extern "C" shim, as MPHF-Experiments does.

**Skip it when:**
- Space is the priority: at 2.1-3.0 bits/key it is well above Consensus-RecSplit (1.58), SIMDRecSplit (1.81) and PHast (1.85-2.0) in survey Table 6.
- You need membership tests or a mutable set: it has no insert/delete and no key storage. Any change means a full rebuild, and rejecting non-members needs a separate key or fingerprint array.
- Pure C++ builds that cannot take a Rust toolchain. There is no C/C++ API. The only C++ port (bassiounix/PtrHash-cc, 3 stars) is an 'as is' rewrite for an LLVM libc RFC; its README says GPLv2 but GitHub detects no license file, and it has no benchmarks.
- Small sets with the compact config: at 10,000 keys, survey Table 7 shows the cubic/EF config taking 44,300 ns/key to build (the linear/vec config takes 147 ns/key). The README warns that small inputs carry relatively large constant space overhead.
- You need reproducible builds: construction is not deterministic (issue #36 is open; `build_part` uses an unseeded `fastrand::Rng`), so rebuilding the same keys reassigns indices.

**Integration:** crate · bitvec, itertools, rand 0.10, rand_chacha, rayon, rdst (radix sort), fastrand, tempfile, mem_dbg, colored, log, fxhash, xxhash-rust, prefetch-index; default features add sucds (Elias-Fano) and cacheline-ef; optional: gxhash (StringHash), epserde (zero-copy/mmap serialization), extra hashers · Stable Rust. No MSRV is declared (crates.io rust_version is unset), but the rand 0.10 dependency needs Rust 1.85 (edition 2024). There is no C/C++ API. · x86-64 and aarch64 are built and tested in CI. i686 and armv7 are cross-built only, with --no-default-features (sucds is 64-bit-only and gxhash needs AES). The repo's .cargo/config.toml sets target-cpu=native. Prefetch uses SSE on x86 or PRFM on aarch64 and is a no-op elsewhere. The paper's CacheLineEF lookup uses BMI2 PDEP, which it calls very slow on AMD Zen 2.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PtrHash over PTHash when query latency and build speed matter and Rust is acceptable: 45 vs 76 ns/query and 141 vs 516 ns/key build in survey Table 6, or 37 vs 77 ns in SEA Table 2. Prefer PHast/PHast+ (also Rust) for slightly faster queries at ~2 bits/key (38-44 ns, 1.85-2.07 bits/key), and SIMDRecSplit or Consensus-RecSplit when getting below 2 bits/key justifies 5x+ slower queries.

**Gotchas:**
- `index_stream` returns an Iterator whose `next()` is `unimplemented!()`. Only fold-based consumers work (`sum`, `for_each`, `fold`); a plain `for` loop over it panics.
- `new()` panics after 10 failed global seeds; use `try_new()` to get an `Option`. Duplicate keys always fail because duplicate hashes are rejected. `new_from_par_iter` discards the build result, so a failed build is not reported. Regular integer keys broke earlier FxHash-based versions (#19, #21): use `StrongerIntHash` for structured integers, and `StringHash128` for more than 10^9 string keys.
- The paper's 'Default' config (lambda=3.5, cubic, CacheLineEF, 2.40 bits/key) is now `default_balanced()`, and the crate's `PtrHashParams::default()` is the paper's 'fast' config (~3.0 bits/key). Sharding requires SINGLE_PART=false (`CompactPtrHash`). Setting `params.sharding` on the default single-part types panics in `init`, and the repo's own examples/string_keys.rs does exactly that.
- Before 2.1.0, safe `index()` could read past the remap array for a key outside the build set (#35). `Packed::index` impls still use `get_unchecked` inside safe fns, and epserde deserialization is `unsafe`. The maintainer says zero-copy CacheLineEF deserialization has alignment issues.

**Status:** Actively maintained by a responsive single author: v2.1.1 shipped 2026-08-27 and the last commit is 2026-08-28. It is MIT-licensed with ~62k crates.io downloads. The 1.x to 2.x break changed type aliases and parameter names and invalidated old on-disk structures, and the benchmarked 1.1.0 predates 2.x. Issue #40 reports 2.x's default_compact building 1.6-1.9x slower at 1M keys because it uses fewer parts.

[repo](https://github.com/RagnarGrootKoerkamp/PtrHash) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06536)

##### Sphinx  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Dynamic succinct perfect hash index (~4 bits/key) for log-structured KV stores; paper reports ~2x lower latency than DHT/Aleph Filter.

**Beats:** DHT (Delta Hash Table, a dynamic perfect hash table) / RSQF / Aleph Filter / Adaptive Aleph Filter (state-of-the-art fingerprint and perfect-hash indexes for log-structured hash tables / key-value stores) — The PVLDB 18(11) paper measures Sphinx against the authors' own C++ DHT and DHT-expandable and against RSQF, Aleph Filter and Adaptive Aleph Filter (Memento Filter codebase), using ~1.2x10^8 xxhash-hashed int64 keys and uniform queries to existing keys, built with GCC 11.4.0+ -O3 -march=native -mbmi2 on a Xeon W7-2495X (in memory and on a Samsung 980 PRO SSD) and on dual Xeon Silver 4314 with Optane PMem 200. The results are figures only: Sphinx has the lowest in-memory average and p99 query/update latency (average insert is slightly slower unless 4 Reserve Bits are used), a slight edge over DHT-expandable on SSD with uniform keys, and 10-35% speedup at 90-99% cache hit rates; std::unordered_map and static MPHFs were never measured.

**How:** Each 64-slot block is a 256-bit Trie Store: an occupancy bitmap, 1-delimited unary slot sizes, and DHT-style delta tries with one extra delimiter bit, so the number of 1s before any slot's trie is known and the slot is reached with rank (POPCNT) and select (PDEP+TZCNT) over four 64-bit words instead of DHT's bit-by-bit scan, at a cost of about 0.3 bits/entry. A 4 KB L1-resident Decoder, a collision-free 512-bucket table of the 128 most probable trie shapes hashed with shifts and XOR, turns trie decoding into one PEXT of the fingerprint plus a packed-offset lookup; only about 1% of lookups fall back to walking the trie. Overflowing slots go to 4 shared extension blocks per 64-block group instead of chains. Growth splits one block group at a time through an extendible-hashing directory and reuses hash bits already in the tries and the optional Reserve Bits, so expansion rarely rereads keys from storage.

**Use it when:**
- In-memory key-to-log-address index for an index+log / Bitcask-style KV store on SSD or Optane, where index memory per key limits scale.
- Queries, updates and deletes of existing keys that must cost exactly one storage read with stable p99 latency (no fingerprint false positives, unlike RSQF/Aleph-style fingerprint indexes).
- Datasets that grow over time: the index expands one 64-block group at a time rather than being preallocated like DHT or fully rehashed.
- Skewed workloads with a hot block cache where index CPU cost dominates: the paper measures 10-35% speedup over DHT-expandable at 90-99% cache hit rates.
- x86-64 Linux servers with fast BMI2 (Intel Haswell or newer, AMD Zen 3 or newer).

**Skip it when:**
- As a general in-memory hash map: it stores no keys, so every hit reads the backing log to get the key and value, and you must provide the log and its garbage collection yourself.
- Static key sets: the catalogued static MPHFs use about 2-3 bits/key and need no backing log. Sphinx's Trie Store alone is about 4 bits/key before payloads, and with uncompressed 32-bit pointers the payloads dominate. The paper's ~20 bits/key total depends on DHT-style pointer compression.
