- Most of the headline miss-ratio results ignore object size (the paper assumes slab-style caches). Byte miss ratio is shown only for the CDN traces, and the paper's mean ARC-over-LRU reduction appears as both 6.7% and 6.3%.

**Status:** libCacheSim is actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26, Apache-2.0, 347 stars), but Sieve.c has had only cosmetic edits since January 2024, and the CacheLib throughput prototype (Apache-2.0, 11 stars) has not been pushed since 2023-12-13. The algorithm is small enough to copy into your own cache, which is how the listed adopters (TiDB, Ceph, DragonFly, PostgREST, DNSCrypt-proxy, Immudb and others) use it.

[repo](https://github.com/1a1a11a/libCacheSim) · [benchmark](https://junchengyang.com/publication/nsdi24-SIEVE.pdf)

#### columnar-analytics

##### ALP (Adaptive Lossless Floating-Point Compression)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Reference C++ primitives for ALP, a lossless double/float column encoding that decodes 17-66x faster than Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp and Patas.

**Beats:** Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas (existing lightweight and general-purpose floating-point compressors) — In the authors' SIGMOD 2024 micro-benchmark (Ice Lake Xeon 8375C on AWS i4i.4xlarge, clang -O3, one L1-resident 1,024-value vector timed 300K times, Zstd level 3 given about 1 MB), ALP averaged 0.487 values/cycle compressing and 2.609 decompressing: 8-251x faster compression and 7-66x faster decompression than Zstd (0.035/0.101), Gorilla (0.052/0.047), Chimp (0.042/0.039), Patas (0.060/0.157) and PDE (0.002/0.387), at 21.7 bits/value against Zstd's 20.6 (ratios computed from a size formula, not written bytes). Inside DuckDB 0.10 the gain shrank to 2-4x faster decompression than Patas, and a query over ALP data (0.020 s) was still slower than over uncompressed data (0.012 s).

**Known shortcoming:** Zstd compresses slightly better (20.6 vs 21.7 bits/value); the 14x/26x vs Zstd and 55x decode vs Gorilla are from Table 5 on a Xeon 8375C; clang-only build.

**Known shortcoming:** Primitives only: no byte-level API, stream format, spec or releases (compressor.hpp was deleted in 2024-09). The library ships only the scalar kernels; the SIMD kernels live in publication/ and fail to link from the library. CMake is Clang-only, needs clang-tidy on Linux and exports -march=native/-mavx512dq publicly, so binaries are not portable.

**Known shortcoming:** Loses on POI lat/lon (ALP_rd) and many-repeat columns (NYC/29 40.4 vs 20.5 bits/value). In DuckDB 0.10 it was only 2-4x faster than Patas and an ALP query took 0.020 s vs 0.012 s uncompressed. Zen 4 VPCOMPRESSPD slowdown open (#45); an encoder race was fixed only in 2025-10; an unchecked int64 cast is UB (as in duckdb#24634).

**How:** Most real-world doubles began as decimals. ALP multiplies each value by 10^e and 10^-f and rounds with the branch-free magic-number add/subtract trick (2^52+2^51 for double). It keeps the integer only if decoding reproduces the exact bits; values that fail are stored as exceptions and patched in afterwards. The int64s are frame-of-reference bit-packed in FastLanes' interleaved layout and decoded by a generated, branch-free, auto-vectorized kernel per bit width that fuses unpacking with the multiply (a median 40% gain from fusing in the paper). A two-level sample keeps the (e,f) search off the hot path: 8 vectors × 32 values per 102,400-value row group shortlist at most 5 pairs, and each vector tries only those, stopping after two worse ones; non-decimal data switches to ALP_rd, which dictionary-encodes the top 1-16 bits of each value into at most 8 entries and bit-packs the rest.

**Use it when:**
- You are building a columnar format, database or time-series store and need a float codec whose unit is one 1,024-value vector, so scans can skip or decode single vectors. Zstd, by contrast, must decompress a whole block. The paper's example is 32 vectors of 8 KB inside a 256 KB block.
- Doubles that originate as fixed- or low-precision decimals, such as prices, sensor readings, temperatures and stock ticks. Examples: City-Temp takes 10.7 bits/value against 16.2 for Zstd and 59.7 for Gorilla. Averaged over the 13 time-series datasets, ALP takes 16.4 bits/value against 17.2 for Zstd.
- Scan- or aggregate-heavy analytics where decode CPU dominates. In the authors' Tectorwise run on City-Temp (Ice Lake), single-threaded SCAN over ALP ran at 1.337 tuples/cycle against 0.565 uncompressed and 0.044 for Zstd, and SUM at 0.233 against 0.197 uncompressed.
- Replacing Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128 or Patas in an existing lightweight float slot. ALP beat Chimp128 and PDE on compression ratio on 27 of 30 datasets and is faster in both directions. DuckDB made exactly this swap in v0.10.
- Mixed hardware fleets: the decoder is plain C++ that auto-vectorizes. The paper measured it on Ice Lake (AVX-512), Zen3 (AVX2), Apple M1 and Graviton2/3 (NEON), and Ice Lake was fastest.

**Skip it when:**
- You want a compress(buf)/decompress(buf) library like zstd. There is no container or stream format, no bitstream specification (issue #32, left to contributors), and no tags or releases (issue #43). Use FastLanes, or an engine that already ships ALP: DuckDB picks it automatically for FLOAT/DOUBLE at checkpoint since 0.10, and ClickHouse has it as a beta codec behind enable_alp_codec since 26.9.
- High-precision 'real' doubles with no decimal structure, such as radians, simulation output or ML values. POI-lat and POI-lon fall back to ALP_rd at 55.5 and 56.4 bits/value (about 1.15x), worse than Zstd's 48.1 and 53.1. ALP_rd is also about 3x slower to compress and 4x slower to decompress than regular ALP.
- Columns full of exact repeats. On CMS/1, Medicare/1 and NYC/29 ALP needs 35.7, 39.4 and 40.4 bits/value, against 24.5, 28.7 and 20.5 for Zstd and 28.2, 32.3 and 28.7 for Chimp128. You need your own dictionary or RLE stage in front; the paper's cascade reaches 33.1, 35.7 and 24.7.
- Cold storage where ratio beats speed. Across all 30 datasets Zstd level 3 averages 20.6 bits/value against 21.7 for ALP alone. ALP only wins (18.8) when cascaded with dictionary or RLE, which this repo does not provide.
- float16, bfloat16 or fp8 data, or GPU decoding. Reduced-precision types are unsupported (issue #38), and the GPU kernel PR #23 has been open and WIP since October 2024.

**Integration:** shared lib (the CMake target ALP is built SHARED from headers in include/ plus generated FastLanes sources in src/); in practice teams vendor or port the source · none for the library (C++17 standard library only). Tests and benchmarks fetch googletest v1.13.0. The paper-reproduction harness also needs Boost, bzip2, OpenSSL, libcurl, g++ (for PDE), Java 8 with Maven (for Elf), and pandas/seaborn for plots. · C++17; Clang only (CMake stops with 'Only Clang is supported!' and no minimum Clang version is stated); CMake 3.22+; on Linux, clang-tidy must also be installed unless -DALP_ENABLE_CLANG_TIDY=OFF · x86-64 (explicit AVX-512 exception compaction when built with AVX-512F; otherwise scalar or auto-vectorized code) and aarch64 (tested on Graviton2/3 and Apple M1). CI runs on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest. Windows is not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick this repo when you want only the float/double codec to embed in your own engine or format. Choose FastLanes (same CWI group) if you want ALP packaged with integer and string encodings and a file reader/writer, and Vortex if you want a Rust columnar format that ships its own ALP encoding. Over BtrBlocks, whose float scheme is PseudoDecimals (PDE), ALP measured about 7x faster decompression, 251x faster compression and a 31% better average ratio in the paper's benchmark.

**Gotchas:**
- src/CMakeLists.txt reads the build host's /proc/cpuinfo and adds -mavx512dq, or -march=native on other x86 hosts, as PUBLIC compile options. The flags reach your targets, and the binaries only run on CPUs like the build machine. Issue #33 was a macOS runtime failure the maintainer put down to AVX-512 support that the CPU did not actually have.
- Vector and row-group geometry is compiled into config.hpp: 1,024 values per vector and 100 vectors (102,400 values) per row group. You must pad the last partial vector yourself; PRIMITIVES.md suggests the first non-exception value. In issue #24, a 307,200-value column crashed on the last row group (vector subscript out of range); the maintainer's workaround was to re-init every 100 vectors or edit ROWGROUP_SIZE.
- Only the scalar fused falp kernel (one 1.6 MB generated file) is built into the library. The SSE, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, SVE and WASM falp variants declared in falp.hpp live in publication/source_code/generated and are not part of the ALP target, so calling them fails to link unless you add those sources. PRIMITIVES.md is also stale: it calls fused falp double-only, though a float overload now exists.
- On AMD Zen 4, the AVX-512 path's _mm512_mask_compressstoreu_pd (VPCOMPRESSPD) is microcoded and slower than scalar code (open issue #45, August 2026, no reply). encode_simdized also casts large finite doubles to int64 without a range check (encode_value<false>). That is the same undefined behaviour UBSan flagged in DuckDB's port (duckdb#24634).

**Status:** Quiet reference repo: the last commit was the thread_local fix on 2025-10-16, with no tags or releases, 234 stars, and 9 open issues including an unanswered Zen 4 slowdown. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but DuckDB and ClickHouse each maintain their own implementations rather than depending on it.

[repo](https://github.com/cwida/ALP) · [benchmark](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/33334/33334.pdf)

##### Bespoke OLAP  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

LLM agent that writes an in-memory C++ OLAP engine per fixed SQL workload; beats DuckDB and Umbra.

**Beats:** DuckDB — With every system single-threaded, pinned to the same core and holding data in memory (the DuckDB harness sets PRAGMA threads=1 and pins core 3), the paper reports TPC-H SF20 at 4.4s vs 49.2s for DuckDB 1.4.1 (11.17x) and CEB SF2 at 0.4s vs 19.5s (45.33x, with Q8a excluded), plus 7.24x and 9.56x over Umbra 26.02. These are on an AMD EPYC 9654P with 768 GB RAM, built with g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -flto (version unstated). With 1-64 threads the gaps shrink to 7.65x and 23.97x over DuckDB. The repo's harness scripts only the Bespoke and DuckDB runs, not Umbra.

**Known shortcoming:** The 11.17x/45.33x are single-threaded; multi-threaded it is 7.65x/23.97x vs DuckDB. Engines are synthesized per workload, not a general-purpose library.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo is archived and deprecated; its successor SynnoDB is PolyForm Noncommercial (not Apache-2.0). One engine per fixed workload, no SQL front end, in-memory only, Linux x86-64; the multi-threaded Q1 artifact uses AVX-512 without a CPU check. Correctness is checked only on sampled parameters and accepts results within 1% of DuckDB; ingest time is excluded.

**Known shortcoming:** The agent prompt bans indexes/precomputation, yet the paper reports hash indexes in 47% of queries. Numbers shift between paper versions (v1 11.78x/9.76x/~$120; v2 11.17x/45.33x/$276-303) while the text still says 'a few dollars'. The published single-threaded Q1 is the pre-final scalar version, not the paper's AVX-512 one; open assertion crash with W&B logging (#3).

**How:** Most of the gain comes from a workload-specific physical layout. Examples: lineitem sorted by l_shipdate then l_orderkey, with zone maps that skip 64K-row blocks; dictionary codes; 16-bit date offsets; scaled-integer decimals; an 8-byte AoS pack of the four hottest aggregate columns; a precomputed discounted_price column; string arenas carrying per-row letter and bigram bitmasks for LIKE filters. In the paper's ablation (Table 1), optimized code over flat struct-of-arrays storage reaches only 5.18x (TPC-H) and 8.09x (CEB) over DuckDB. With bespoke storage it reaches 12.35x and 51.40x. The per-query code is fused and abstraction-free: inline aggregation (97% of queries), bitmap semi-joins (74%), O(1) hash-index joins, __restrict, branch hints, software prefetch and, in the multi-threaded artifacts, AVX-512 kernels. Join orders are picked by benchmarking candidates on sampled parameter values, not by a cost model.

**Use it when:**
- A stable set of parameterized query templates, such as a dashboard or reporting suite, that runs repeatedly over data you can reload from Parquet.
- The whole dataset fits in RAM. The engines are in-memory only; the paper's runs were TPC-H SF20-100 and CEB SF2-10 on a 768 GB box.
- You can pay for synthesis: the paper reports $276 (TPC-H) and $303 (CEB) in LLM API costs and 10-30 hours of wall-clock time per engine.
- Research, or as a reference: studying what workload-specific storage and per-query C++ look like. The Apache-2.0 generated TPC-H and CEB engines are published in BespokeOLAP_Artifacts.
- Linux x86-64 with GCC or Clang, Apache Arrow/Parquet C++ libraries and an LLM API key.

**Skip it when:**
- Ad-hoc or evolving SQL. Anything outside the query templates it was synthesized for needs a separate engine (DuckDB), and substantial workload drift means re-running the paid synthesis.
- Data larger than memory. The paper says its disk-based mode does not yet reach the in-memory speedups.
- Workloads with inserts or updates. Data enters only through a Parquet ingest step, and incremental updates are not documented.
- Production use. The repo is archived and deprecated. The maintainer calls it 'a research prototype published for inspirational purposes only' (issue #3), and that issue, an assertion failure in run_gen_base_impl.py when W&B logging is on, is still open.
- Workloads that need exact decimal results. Validation accepts answers within 1% of DuckDB's, and the multi-threaded TPC-H Q1 accumulates money sums in doubles.

**Integration:** source-drop · Apache Arrow and Parquet C++ libraries (the generated engines). The generator needs Python >=3.10 per pyproject (the README badge says 3.12+), uv, openai 2.11.0, openai-agents[litellm], duckdb>=1.4.3 as the correctness reference, landlock, an LLM API key, and optionally W&B/weave. · C++20. Builds use $CXX (default g++) with -std=c++20 -O3 -flto; no minimum compiler version is documented. · Linux x86-64 per the README. The multi-threaded TPC-H Q1 artifact calls an AVX-512 kernel ([[gnu::target("avx512f,...")]]) with no runtime CPU check, so it needs an AVX-512-capable CPU.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over GenDB (also an LLM-generated engine; about 2.8x over DuckDB on 5 TPC-H SF10 queries) when you want all 22 TPC-H queries plus CEB with the generated source published, and over JetStream when you need code you can actually get. Stay with Umbra, DuckDB or Sirius (GPU) whenever queries are ad hoc: in the paper's multi-threaded runs on CEB, Bespoke's lead over Umbra shrinks to 1.87x.

**Gotchas:**
- Correctness means matching DuckDB on sampled parameter values at small scale factors, with atol=rtol=1e-2 on float columns (run_and_check_queries.py). Parameter values outside the tested samples are not validated.
- The benchmark times cover query execution only. Building the custom layout (sorts, dictionaries, zone maps, derived columns, hash indexes) is timed separately as 'Ingest ms' and is not reported in the paper. The agent's prompt (optim_constraints.txt) forbids indexes and query-specific precomputation, yet the paper reports hash indexes in 47% of queries, precomputed derived columns in 37%, and denormalized columns in Q5.
- The numbers depend on which synthesis run you look at. The April 2026 ADRS blog post (paper v1) reported 11.78x on TPC-H, 9.76x on CEB and about $120. Paper v2 reports 11.17x, 45.33x and $276/$303, and its text still says synthesis costs 'a few dollars'.
- The published artifacts do not match the paper's description of the final Q1. The single-threaded bespoke_tpch Q1 is the 4-way unrolled scalar scan with branch hints that the paper attributes to earlier stages. The artifacts' run.py hardcodes /mnt/labstore/bespoke_olap as the Parquet path and runs only the single-threaded variants.

**Status:** The repo was archived and deprecated after its last push on 2026-07-22, and the README points to SynnoDB, which is PolyForm Noncommercial rather than Apache-2.0. The Apache-2.0 generator and generated engines can still be copied as a reference, but they are fixed to TPC-H and CEB and need the Arrow/Parquet toolchain plus LLM API access to regenerate.

[repo](https://github.com/DataManagementLab/BespokeOLAP) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02001)

##### GenDB  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

LLM-agent pipeline that writes a custom C++ executable per SQL query; 2.8x faster than DuckDB on 5 TPC-H queries.

**Beats:** DuckDB — On the paper's setup (2x Xeon Gold 5218, 64 threads, 384 GB RAM, hot in-memory runs, mean of 3 runs after a warm-up), Sonnet 4.6-generated C++ built with g++ -O3 -march=native -fopenmp ran 5 TPC-H SF10 queries in 214 ms. That compares with 594 ms for DuckDB v1.4.4 and 590 ms for Umbra (2.8x). Per query versus DuckDB: Q1 40 vs 84 ms, Q3 55 vs 83, Q6 14 vs 19, Q9 38 vs 231, Q18 68 vs 177. On SEC-EDGAR (6 queries) it took 328 ms, versus 1,549 ms for DuckDB and 1,280 ms for Umbra. The later template-native version (VLDB 2026 demo paper) reports smaller gains: 249 ms, 2.4x versus DuckDB and 2.7x versus Umbra on TPC-H, and 403 ms, 3.8x versus DuckDB on SEC-EDGAR.

**Known shortcoming:** The 163x is GenDB's own iteration gain on Q18 (12,147 to 74 ms), not vs DuckDB; on SEC-EDGAR it is 5.0x. Engines are LLM-synthesized per query set, not a general-purpose library.

**Known shortcoming:** Not an engine: an LLM writes a C++ binary per query, so ad-hoc SQL is impossible; generation costs $14-62 and 1.5-4 h per 5-6 queries. Timing is unequal (GenDB uses an in-binary timer minus output; baselines use a Python client including fetchall) and ingest-time derived files are not counted. Large run-to-run swings (a rerun gave 285 vs 214 ms on TPC-H, 830 vs 328 on SEC-EDGAR); the template-native demo paper shows only 2.4x vs DuckDB.

**Known shortcoming:** SF10 sizes and 64 threads hard-coded, -march=native, Linux only. hash_utils.h CompactHashMap::operator[] returns the wrong slot after a Robin Hood swap; correctness is checked only by matching DuckDB. Last code 2026-03-27; package.json says ISC while LICENSE says Apache.

**How:** Five agents (workload analyzer, storage/index designer, query planner, code generator, query optimizer) write code specialized to the exact data statistics and machine. The generated code narrows columns to fit the data (for example, lineitem price stored as int32 cents and discount and quantity as uint8). It picks aggregation by cache fit: a direct per-thread array for Q1's 6 groups, and for Q3's roughly 4M groups a shared open-addressing table with keys and values in separate arrays, updated with lock-free CAS. It also uses zone-map pruning with branchless scans, and query-specific derived structures built at ingest, such as Q9's nibble-packed orderkey-to-year file. Everything runs over mmap'd columns with OpenMP and is compiled with g++ -O3 -march=native. A profiling feedback loop then rewrites slow queries; Q18 went from 12,147 ms to 74 ms when a cache-thrashing hash aggregation was replaced with an index-aware sequential scan.

**Use it when:**
- A fixed set of recurring, templated OLAP queries (scheduled reports, dashboards) where a one-off generation run pays for itself. The demo paper puts it at about $14 and 91 minutes for 5 TPC-H queries, and $23 and 140 minutes for 6 SEC-EDGAR queries, with Sonnet 4.6.
- Read-mostly analytical data that fits in RAM on a many-core Linux x86-64 server, where hot latency in the tens of milliseconds at the ~10 GB scale matters.
- A hybrid setup, which the authors themselves recommend: DuckDB or Umbra keep serving ad-hoc SQL while the hottest query templates are routed to GenDB binaries.
- A readable starting point for hand-tuning a critical query. The generated C++ is plain, self-contained code, and the repo's language comparison got a further 1.30x on TPC-H with a human-directed refinement pass.
- Research on LLM-synthesized query processing: the full pipeline is open, and ablation, model-comparison and iteration-history data are checked in.

**Skip it when:**
- Ad-hoc or exploratory SQL. Every new query shape needs an LLM generation run (minutes to hours, and paid API use), and nothing at runtime can answer a query that was not generated in advance.
- Data that changes or grows. Storage is a custom format produced by a generated ingest program, and the binaries hard-code SF10 key ranges and thread counts. Inserts, updates and transactions are not documented.
- Workloads that need guaranteed correct answers. Validation only matches results against DuckDB ground truth, plus fuzzing across template parameters in the newer version, and the authors say this does not prove semantic equivalence. The paper documents LLM bugs: dropped DECIMAL scale divisions that gave wrong results, and open-addressing tables with no resize or probe bound that looped forever.
- Non-Linux, non-x86 or mixed hardware fleets. The pipeline reads /proc/cpuinfo, lscpu and lsblk, the binaries are built with -march=native, and every published number comes from one 2x Xeon Gold 5218 server.
- Anything production-critical. Results vary a lot between generation runs: a later Sonnet 4.6 run got 285 ms on TPC-H (paper: 214 ms) and 830 ms on SEC-EDGAR (paper: 328 ms). The README warns that Sonnet 4.6 agents now hang, and baselines were compared on only 5 TPC-H queries and 6 SEC-EDGAR queries.

**Integration:** source-drop · Generator: Node.js 18+ with npm packages @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk, @anthropic-ai/claude-code, @openai/codex-sdk and openai; an Anthropic or OpenAI API key or subscription; Python 3 for result comparison and benchmarks; DuckDB for ground truth. Generated binaries: g++ with OpenMP, pthreads and POSIX mmap only. · C++17 (g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17 -fopenmp); the GCC version is not documented; Node.js 18+ · Linux x86-64 in practice (tested only on 2x Xeon Gold 5218 with AVX-512 and 64 threads). The hardware probe recognizes NEON, but aarch64 is not documented or tested.

**Vs siblings:** Pick GenDB over Bespoke OLAP (also LLM-synthesized per workload, headline numbers single-threaded) and JetStream (generates accelerators that sit beside an existing DBMS) when you want standalone, multi-threaded C++ executables per query template from an Apache-2.0 pipeline that can use either Claude or Codex agents. Pick Umbra, Sirius or plain DuckDB whenever you need a real SQL engine that handles arbitrary queries without a generation step.

**Gotchas:**
- The query times are not measured the same way for GenDB and the baselines. GenDB's number is the binary's own [TIMING] total minus its output phase. DuckDB, Umbra and the others are timed from the Python client and include fetchall(). Work done at ingest time (indexes, derived files like Q9's orderkey-to-year nibble file) is not counted at all.
- Generated code is sized for the data it was generated against. Examples: Q9 declares part_bitset[2000001] and suppkey_nk[100001] with N_THREADS = 64, and the latest Q3 uses BITMAP_MAX = 1500001, all SF10 key ranges. A larger dataset or a different machine needs regeneration; the orchestrator re-benchmarks on a hardware-fingerprint change.
- Bug in the shared helper src/gendb/utils/hash_utils.h: when CompactHashMap::operator[] displaces an entry (Robin Hood), it overwrites `key` with the displaced key before its final lookup. It then returns the displaced key's value slot, so `m[k] += v` can update the wrong group. The generated files checked use find() plus insert(), which avoids this path.
- The checked-in runs cannot execute from a fresh clone. The storage folders (12 GB for TPC-H, 3.3 GB for SEC-EDGAR) must be downloaded from Google Drive. The stable paper version is on branch arxiv-03-02-2026, and main has since moved to template-native generation.

**Status:** A Cornell research prototype (arXiv 2603.02081 plus a VLDB 2026 demo paper), licensed Apache-2.0 although package.json still says ISC, with 75 stars. The last code change was 2026-03-27 and the 2026-06-08 commit only touched the README, so 'active' is generous. You can run the generator if you have LLM API access and a Linux server; the reusable output is generated C++ per query, not a library to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/SolidLao/GenDB) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02081)

##### Minarrow  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Lean Rust Apache Arrow implementation with enum-dispatched typed arrays; about 1.7x faster than arrow-rs on a 1,000-element sum microbenchmark.

**Beats:** Apache Arrow — The benchmark summed 1,000 i64 values, with array construction inside the timed region, and averaged 1,000 Instant-timed runs on an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H under Ubuntu 24.04 (release build; the footnote says Rust 1.97-nightly). Minarrow IntegerArray took 88 ns (124 ns through the Array enum), against 147 ns for arrow-rs Int64Array as a struct, 181 ns through an ArrayRef downcast, and 85 ns for a raw Vec. The same five figures have been in src/lib.rs since v0.1.0 (2025-08-13, built against arrow 55.2.0), so they were probably not re-measured on the stated toolchain or against the current arrow 59.2 dependency.

**Known shortcoming:** The arrow-rs side sums via value(i) rather than slices, so the comparison favors Minarrow; a micro-benchmark of one hot loop.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark numbers are stale: the same five figures have sat in src/lib.rs since v0.1.0 (2025-08, arrow 55.2) and were not re-measured against the current arrow 59.2 dependency; its own SIMD table shows parity (170 vs 173 ns). Nightly only; no List/Struct; Interval/Null FFI import panics; zero-copy import needs 64 B-aligned buffers (pandas/Polars columns get copied, #57); .num()/.i64() convert and allocate on variant mismatch and panic on failure. An unsound out-of-bounds bug in string kernels (#200) was fixed in 0.18.2; vmap64 with FFI is UB; pre-1.0 churn; single maintainer with a CLA assigning copyright.

**How:** Type dispatch goes through nested enums (Array -> NumericArray -> Arc<IntegerArray<T>>) instead of arrow-rs's Arc<dyn Array> plus as_any().downcast_ref, so the compiler can inline the match and hand back a concrete typed array. Every owned buffer is a Vec64 (the author's 64-byte-aligned Vec, built on the nightly allocator_api), so values are read as a plain aligned slice and fed to std::simd (portable_simd) kernels whose lane counts build.rs fixes from the target's features (SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON). There is no new algorithm, and in the published benchmark part of the gap comes from the access pattern: the Minarrow paths iterate a slice, while the arrow-rs paths call the bounds-asserting value(i) once per element.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code that keeps Arrow-layout columns in memory and wants typed access (arr.num().i64()) without dyn Array downcasting, especially in latency-sensitive loops over primitive i64/f64 columns.
- Rust-to-Python handoff of tables to PyArrow/Polars through PyCapsule or the C Data Interface. Export is zero-copy, and the README reports 165 ns Rust->Python and 2.5 us Python->Rust for 1M rows x 2 columns. Import is zero-copy only for 64-byte-aligned buffers.
- Projects that want a small dependency tree and fast builds. The base build pulls in only num-traits, vec64 and log, and the README claims compiles under 2 s.
- Custom SIMD kernels that need every owned buffer guaranteed 64-byte aligned.
- Passing numeric data to PyTorch, JAX or NumPy through DLPack (the ndarray and dlpack features).

**Skip it when:**
- You need nested Arrow types (List, Struct). They are not implemented, and Interval and Null arrays panic on C Data Interface import.
- You must build on stable Rust. The crate requires nightly for allocator_api and portable_simd; CONTRIBUTING asks for 1.89.0-nightly or later, and CI runs only on nightly.
- You need broad compute kernels, SQL, or Parquet/IPC file I/O in the same crate. arrow-rs plus DataFusion covers far more; Minarrow ships a small kernel set and leaves IPC streaming to the separate lightstream crate.
- Your arrow-rs code already sums over values() slices or uses arrow compute kernels. The headline gap was measured against per-index value(i) calls, and the crate's own SIMD table in src/lib.rs shows Minarrow via enum at 170 ns vs arrow-rs dyn at 173 ns (parity).
- You need API stability or an open contribution model. Pre-1.0 releases break often (0.17.0 switched integer division to floor semantics, 0.18.0 added enum variants), there is effectively one maintainer, and contributors must sign a CLA that assigns copyright to him.

**Integration:** crate · Base: num-traits, vec64 (the author's 64-byte-aligned Vec crate) and log (a default feature). Optional, behind feature flags: arrow/arrow-schema 59.2, polars-core/polars-arrow 0.55.2, rayon, time, phf, ahash, hashbrown, parking_lot, regex, ryu, memchr and libc. · Rust nightly, edition 2024 (CONTRIBUTING says 1.89.0-nightly or later). Needs the allocator_api and portable_simd features. · x86-64, with SIMD width picked at build time from target features (SSE2, AVX2 or AVX-512); aarch64 (NEON); wasm32 (simd128); scalar fallback elsewhere. CI runs tests on Linux, macOS and Windows but only compile-checks aarch64 and armv7 Linux. The memfd and vmap64 features are Linux-only.

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings is an in-memory Arrow array library. Pick Apache DataFusion (built on arrow-rs) when you need SQL or query execution, and Vortex or Lance when the problem is on-disk columnar encoding. Pick Minarrow when you want a lean, typed in-memory Arrow container in Rust with a fast Python handoff and can accept nightly Rust and no nested types.

**Gotchas:**
- Accessors such as Array::num() and NumericArray::i64() return a shared Arc handle only when the variant matches. Otherwise they allocate and convert (for example Int32 or Float64 to i64), and they panic on Null or a failed cast. Use the try_ variants in library code.
- Zero-copy import requires 64-byte-aligned buffers. Data from pandas and Polars is typically not aligned that way, so each such column is copied into a Vec64 and a log warning is emitted (issue #57). String offsets, categorical dictionaries and Utf8View arrays are always copied on import.
- build.rs bakes SIMD lane counts in from compile-time target features. The repo's .cargo/config.toml forces x86-64-v3 only for builds run inside the repository, so a downstream x86-64 build without -C target-cpu gets 128-bit SSE2 lanes.
- Hot paths use unchecked access. Issue #200 (fixed in 0.18.2) showed out-of-bounds reads reachable from safe code in the string kernels and in Buffer::from_shared_column. Cargo.toml also warns that vmap64 combined with any FFI export (cast_arrow, cast_polars, memfd) is undefined behaviour.

**Status:** Actively developed under Apache-2.0 by essentially one maintainer (0.18.2 released 2026-09-19, with frequent minor releases since v0.1.0 in August 2025); it installs from crates.io (about 7.8k downloads, 9 reverse dependencies including the author's lightstream, simd-kernels and minarrow-pyo3) but is nightly-only and pre-1.0.

[repo](https://github.com/SpaceCell/minarrow) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SpaceCell/minarrow#benchmarks)

##### Apache DataFusion  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Embeddable Rust/Arrow SQL query engine; on ClickBench hot runs over Parquet on a 192-vCPU box, 1.56x faster than DuckDB.

**Beats:** DuckDB — ClickBench ran its 43 queries over the 100M-row hits table as a single Parquet file on AWS c7a.metal-48xl (AMD EPYC 9R14, 192 vCPU, implied by the instance type), comparing datafusion-cli 54.0.0 (built with LTO, codegen-units=1 and an unpinned stable rustc; run 2026-08-20) with DuckDB's prebuilt CLI (version not recorded; run 2026-05-11). Summed best-of-3 hot times were 9.78s for DataFusion against 15.28s for DuckDB on the same file (1.56x; geometric mean per query 1.78x) and 15.70s for DuckDB's native format. That result reverses on cold runs and on the 16-vCPU c6a.4xlarge. Per ClickBench's harness, datafusion-cli is single-user only, so the concurrency test was skipped, and DataFusion's own 55.0 release notes say ClickBench files have no page index and only integer and string columns.

**Known shortcoming:** The 9.78 s vs 15.70 s holds on c7a only; vs DuckDB on the same Parquet file it is 15.28 s (~1.56x). DuckDB wins on c6a.4xlarge (26.3 s vs 45.6 s) and on cold runs.

**Known shortcoming:** On ClickBench c6a.4xlarge (16 vCPU) it loses: 45.57 s vs DuckDB 32.48 s on the same Parquet (26.25 s native), winning 13/43 and 5/43 queries; cold runs lose even on c7a (173.8 s vs 122.4 s). Q23 is pathological because late materialization is off by default (#3463; 9.65 s vs 0.43 s). Open wrong-result bugs for correlated NOT IN/EXISTS subqueries (2026-09; 393 open bugs); API breaks every major (~2-3 months); no default memory limit; Windows CI off.

**How:** Execution is vectorized over Arrow columnar batches (8,192 rows by default) using arrow-rs kernels. Each plan is split into target_partitions streams (one per core by default), connected by Volcano-style exchange operators (RepartitionExec) and run on Tokio's work-stealing thread pool with cooperative yielding. The Parquet reader pushes projections and limits down, prunes with row-group statistics, the page index and bloom filters, and answers COUNT(*)/MIN/MAX from exact file statistics without scanning (the AggregateStatistics rule). This is why ClickBench Q0 and Q6 take 1 ms hot. Strings use Arrow StringView (German-style strings) to avoid copies, and hash aggregation is two-phase with a runtime switch that skips the partial phase once groups exceed 80% of input rows. Multi-column GROUP BY keys are stored column-wise (GroupValuesColumn), so each value is copied once, and TopK, join and aggregate operators push dynamic filters down into the scan.

**Use it when:**
- You are building a database, query service, SQL front end or data pipeline in Rust and want a complete planner, optimizer and executor that you extend through traits (TableProvider, UDFs, optimizer rules, custom ExecutionPlans) instead of writing your own.
- Repeated analytical queries over Parquet files in place on machines with many cores. On c7a.metal-48xl (192 vCPU), the ClickBench hot-run total was 9.78s against 15.28s for DuckDB on the same file, DataFusion won 36 of 43 queries, and on the 100-file partitioned layout it was 7.42s against 14.72s.
- Aggregation-heavy dashboards with high-cardinality or multi-column GROUP BY, and ORDER BY ... LIMIT (TopK) queries. Its largest ClickBench gains are on these: Q32 (GROUP BY WatchID, ClientIP) took 0.54s against 1.42s for DuckDB.
- Arrow-native systems that want to pass RecordBatches in and out without conversion, including Python via datafusion-python, or Spark offload via Comet.

**Skip it when:**
- Small or mid-size machines. On c6a.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32 GB) the hot total is 45.57s, against 32.48s for DuckDB on the same Parquet file and 26.25s for DuckDB native storage. DataFusion wins 13 of 43 queries against the first and 5 of 43 against the second, and the partitioned layout is also slower (41.87s vs 30.95s).
- Cold or one-shot queries over files that are not in cache. Even on c7a.metal-48xl the first-run sum is 173.8s, against 122.4s for DuckDB on Parquet, and 55.9s of it is Q23 alone.
- You want a self-contained database file with its own storage, like DuckDB's .duckdb. DataFusion only reads files or whatever your TableProvider supplies (ClickBench tags it 'stateless').
- Correlated subqueries you cannot test yourself. September 2026 brought a batch of open wrong-result bugs: NOT IN ignoring NULLs (#25347, #25473, #25474), EXISTS with OFFSET (#25283), and correlation lost or misplaced (#25480, #25507, #24960).
- Teams that need a stable library API. A major release ships every 2-3 months (52 in January, 53 in March, 54 in June, 55 in August 2026), each with breaking changes (the 55.0.0 upgrade guide lists about 28), and 55.0.0 raised the MSRV from 1.88 to 1.94.

**Integration:** crate (datafusion on crates.io, a workspace of about 40 sub-crates); also the datafusion-cli binary and Python/Java bindings · arrow-rs and parquet 60.x, object_store 0.14, sqlparser 0.63, tokio 1.52 (an async runtime is required), futures. Default features pull in compression codecs (xz2, bzip2, flate2, zstd), crypto, regex and unicode function crates; optional features add avro, backtrace, parquet_encryption and serde. · Rust 1.94.0 for 55.x (rust-version in Cargo.toml); 54.x, the version benchmarked, needs 1.88.0 · Pure Rust. CI runs the full suite only on Linux x86-64; macOS aarch64 CI covers only the FFI crate, and Windows CI has been commented out since issue #13726 because builds were too slow. wasm32-unknown-unknown builds are tested with wasm-pack. ClickBench's harness also lists an ARM64 instance (c8g.4xlarge).

**Vs siblings:** Databend is essentially tied on the same c7a.metal-48xl ClickBench run (9.91s vs 9.78s) but is a full warehouse server with its own storage. Velox is a C++ execution library with no SQL parser or optimizer, and chDB is embedded ClickHouse for Python. Pick DataFusion when you want to embed and customize a complete SQL engine (parser, optimizer and executor) in a Rust or Arrow-native system.

**Gotchas:**
- Parquet late materialization (pushdown_filters) is still off by default; issue #3463 has been open since 2022. A 'SELECT * ... WHERE URL LIKE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10' query therefore decodes all 105 columns: issue #23263 measured 97M rows and 137.8 GB decoded. That query (ClickBench Q23) takes 9.65s hot on c6a.4xlarge against 0.43s for DuckDB. Turning pushdown on can also slow other queries (#22883), so benchmark both settings.
- Unquoted identifiers are lowercased, so mixed-case Parquet columns must be double-quoted. Some legacy Parquet writers do not flag strings as UTF-8, and those columns come back as Binary unless binary_as_string is set. ClickBench's harness sets it and also casts the UInt16 EventDate column to DATE through a view.
- Memory is unbounded by default (runtime.memory_limit is NULL), and operators spill only once you configure a limit. With FairSpillPool the memory is split evenly across partitions, so a high target_partitions makes spilling more frequent.
- Q0 and Q6 run in 1 ms because they are answered from Parquet metadata and statistics. That shortcut accounts for 2 of the 36 per-query wins but almost none of the total time.

**Status:** Very active Apache-2.0 project: commits daily (last 2026-09-26), 55.1.0 published 2026-09-11, about 9.4k stars, 175 contributors to 55.0, about 2,300 open issues and PRs (393 open bugs), and no published security advisories. It is easy to adopt through cargo, Homebrew or pip, but pin the major version, because each one ships breaking API changes.

[repo](https://github.com/apache/datafusion) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench (data.generated.js: datafusion/results/20260820/c7a.metal-48xl.json vs duckdb/results/20260511/c7a.metal-48xl.json))

##### BtrBlocks  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

C++ columnar compression library: sampled cascades of lightweight encodings; authors measured 2.6-3.8x faster decompression than Parquet.

**Beats:** Apache Parquet (generated/read via the Apache Arrow C++ library) and Apache ORC — The authors' SIGMOD'23 runs used a c5n.18xlarge (Skylake-SP, 36 cores, GCC 10.3.1, no optimization flags stated). Multi-threaded in-memory decompression of a 43-table, 2,451-column Public BI subset was 2.6x, 3.6x and 3.8x faster than uncompressed, Snappy and Zstd Parquet (written by pyarrow 9.0.0, read with the low-level Arrow C++ Parquet API), and 2.6x, 3.9x and 4.2x faster on TPC-H, although the Zstd variants compressed better. The Parquet/ORC harness is not public. The competing FastLanes paper (i4i.4xlarge Ice Lake, DuckDB 1.2 Parquet) broadly corroborates faster decoding: 115 ms total versus 713 ms (Snappy) and 731 ms (Zstd). It also found BtrBlocks' encoding much slower.

**Known shortcoming:** The Parquet/ORC comparison harness is not in the repo; no flags, CPU family only (c5n.18xlarge). The FastLanes paper measures BtrBlocks encoding 1.37x (not 7x) and its ratio well below Parquet+Zstd.

**Known shortcoming:** A compression layer, not a file format: no Parquet interop, metadata or statistics; int32/double/string only. Encoding is slow (FastLanes paper: 111 s vs 5.9 s Snappy / 6.9 s Zstd for DuckDB Parquet) though decoding is ~6x faster; no row-level random access (whole 64K blocks decode); Parquet+Zstd compresses smaller. The 9x/20x S3 win is mostly metadata layout (the paper admits); full-dataset loads are 1.8x cheaper.

**Known shortcoming:** Fragile build: -march=native forced, AVX2 the main target, ARM via SIMDe, macOS clang 16 build failure open (#11). Output buffers are unchecked and SIMD writes up to 128 B past the end. Stale since 2025-04; benchmark data deleted (#13), benchmark segfault (#14); the maintainer points to Vortex.

**How:** It drops Parquet's general-purpose codec layer (Snappy/Zstd) and uses only lightweight encodings: RLE, One Value, dictionary, frequency, SIMD-FastPFOR/FastBP128 bit-packing, FSST for strings, the new Pseudodecimal encoding for doubles, and Roaring bitmaps for NULLs. It applies these recursively (cascading compression, default max depth 3). At each level of each block it picks the scheme by collecting min/max/unique/run-length stats, pruning schemes that cannot help, and trial-compressing a sample of 10 runs x 64 values (about 1%) with every remaining scheme. The paper says this selection takes about 1.2% of compression time. The decompression kernels are AVX2-vectorized: RLE writes past the buffer end instead of branching, dictionary decoding uses gathers, RLE and dictionary decoding are fused, and string dictionaries decode to (offset, length) pairs instead of copying strings. In the authors' ablation, scalar kernels were only 17% slower and still 2.3x faster than the fastest Parquet variant, so most of the win comes from avoiding the heavyweight codecs.

**Use it when:**
- Scan-heavy analytics that decompress whole columns or blocks, where decode CPU rather than stored bytes sets the cost. An example is pulling data from S3 over 100 Gbit links, where the paper found no Parquet variant could keep up with the network.
- Real-world, denormalized BI-style tables with low-cardinality or prefix-heavy strings, long runs and decimal-like doubles (Public BI-style data), where dictionary/RLE/FSST cascades pay off.
- Building your own C++ engine or storage format on x86-64 Linux, when you want a compression layer with explicit caller-owned block buffers and a configurable scheme pool (enable or disable schemes, cascade depth, block and sample size).
- Research and benchmarking, as the reference implementation of sampling-based cascaded scheme selection to compare against, extend or fork.

**Skip it when:**
- You need interoperability. Nothing else reads BtrBlocks blocks, and there is no Arrow, Spark, DuckDB or Trino integration and no file-level metadata or statistics.
- Point lookups or row-level random access. A whole 64K-value block must be decoded, and the FastLanes paper found first-row retrieval about 800x slower than FastLanes because BtrBlocks has no API for decoding a single value.
- Ingest-bound or write-heavy pipelines. In the FastLanes paper's Table 4, BtrBlocks' total encoding time was 111 s, against 5.9 s for DuckDB's Parquet+Snappy and 6.9 s for Parquet+Zstd.
- Minimizing storage bytes. Parquet+Zstd compresses better in the authors' own Figure 8. FastLanes' Table 3 puts BtrBlocks 18% larger than FastLanes on Public BI, against 2% larger for Parquet+Zstd.
- Column types other than int32, double and string. int64, float32, small ints, decimals, dates/timestamps and nested types are marked out of scope in Units.hpp. Also avoid it for Windows builds, which CMake rejects, and for production macOS builds.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake; shared with -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBRARY=ON) · Core library: FastPFor, FSST, CRoaring and Boost.dynamic_bitset, all fetched by CMake at pinned commits; SIMDe on ARM; spdlog only with WITH_LOGGING. The tools, tests and benchmarks also pull oneTBB, gflags, yaml-cpp, csv-parser, the AWS SDK, googletest, Google Benchmark and lz4. · C++17, CMake 3.12+. The paper used GCC 10.3.1. GCC 14 build breakage in the vendored TBB was addressed by the 2025 dependency bump. An Apple clang 16 build failure is still open (issue #11). · Linux x86-64 with AVX2. The FastLanes paper could not run it in an SSE-only build. aarch64 is supported through SIMDe since May 2024, and the README claims Linux/macOS ARM were tested, but a 2025 macOS arm64 build report is unresolved. CMake refuses non-UNIX platforms.

**Vs siblings:** For new C++ work, FastLanes is usually the better pick: its authors measured about 7x faster decoding than BtrBlocks, better compression, zero dependencies and real random access. If Rust fits, pick Vortex: the BtrBlocks maintainer points users there, and it adopts the same sampled cascading selection with FastLanes, ALP and FSST. Choose BtrBlocks when you want the original, compact C++ reference of the SIGMOD'23 sampling-plus-cascade design to study, benchmark against or fork, or specifically its Pseudodecimal double encoding, for which ALP is the newer alternative.

**Gotchas:**
- Output buffers are not bounds-checked. The shipped example warns that an undersized compression buffer causes a crash or undefined behavior. The SIMD kernels also deliberately write up to 128 bytes (SIMD_EXTRA_BYTES) past logical ends, so allocate slack.
- The top-level CMakeLists adds -march=native and -g to every build. Binaries are tied to the build machine's ISA unless you override the flags.
- The headline 9x/20x cheaper S3 column scans come mostly from metadata layout, and the paper says so itself: Parquet needs three dependent S3 requests per column, while BtrBlocks stores one file per column. When whole datasets were loaded, BtrBlocks was 1.8x cheaper than Parquet+Snappy/Zstd and 2.6x cheaper than uncompressed Parquet.
- The authors' S3-hosted benchmark datasets were deleted (issue #13, open), and the regression benchmark segfaults on user-supplied data (issue #14, open). btrblocks.com is a separate TUM cloud-storage spin-off (BtrBlocks GmbH), not documentation for this library.

**Status:** Stale research code: the last commit (2025-04-07) was a dependency bump, 3 issues and 4 PRs are still open, the maintainer calls the build setup "terrible" and points Rust users to Vortex. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but expect to fix the build and add your own metadata layer.

[repo](https://github.com/maxi-k/btrblocks) · [benchmark](https://www.cs.cit.tum.de/fileadmin/w00cfj/dis/papers/btrblocks.pdf)

##### chDB  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

In-process ClickHouse SQL engine for Python that queries pandas DataFrames directly; median ~166x faster than pandas on ClickBench.

**Beats:** pandas — In ClickBench's DataFrame mode (43 queries against the hits data preloaded into an ~82 GB pandas DataFrame, the same FastAPI harness for every system, AWS c6a.metal, prebuilt pip wheels, no compiler flags stated), chDB's hot total (best of runs 2-3) was 6.00 s on 2026-08-16, against 2,430 s for pandas and 11.92 s for Polars on 2026-08-24. Per query, chDB's median speedup is ~166x over pandas (range 2.9x to 5,058x; three lambda-heavy pandas queries make up ~71% of the pandas total) and 1.77x over Polars; cold runs include reloading the DataFrame (~71 s per query for chDB), and the README's Oct-2024 chart (x1.35 vs pandas x71.18) is out of date.

**Known shortcoming:** The 7.4x over Polars comes from an Oct 2024 ClickBench snapshot; the live Aug 2026 raw results give chDB 6.00 s vs Polars 11.92 s (~2x) and pandas 2430 s (~405x). ClickBench is ClickHouse Inc's suite and chDB is a ClickHouse derivative (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** Repo split in 2026-01: chdb-io/chdb is now pure Python and the C++ engine lives in chdb-io/chdb-core (22 stars). The ~405x over pandas is skewed by three lambda-heavy pandas queries (~71% of pandas time); per query the median is ~166x (range 2.9-5058x). Against Polars the median is only 1.77x and Polars wins 9 of 43 queries. The DuckDB comparison is stale/broken in current ClickBench runs. Tiny queries take >1 ms (#442); no Windows; 104-175 MB wheels; an engine bug gave silently wrong Parquet counts until 4.1.9 (#587); forked child processes hang (#355). Not a pandas drop-in (the benchmark path is SQL over Python dataframes; DataStore lacks category/timedelta and has dtype/timezone gaps).

**How:** The speed comes from ClickHouse's vectorized, block-at-a-time columnar execution: typed column vectors run through tight batch loops in a multi-threaded pipeline that uses every core. pandas is mostly single-threaded, and the ClickBench pandas versions of several queries depend on Python lambdas. chDB's Python() table source (PythonSource.cpp) maps contiguous numpy numeric buffers without copying them, splits the frame into blocks that N parallel streams read round-robin, and applies filters before it builds the other columns (at 1/8 selectivity or lower it copies out only the selected rows), and some string predicates run directly on Arrow string buffers. A per-session PythonTableCache keeps schema inference, column sizes and Arrow chunk tables between queries, which cuts the fixed per-query overhead on repeated runs.

**Use it when:**
- Analytical SQL (group-by, top-N, count distinct, string LIKE filters) over multi-GB pandas DataFrames or Parquet files on one many-core Linux or macOS machine, where pandas runs single-threaded.
- Replacing lambda-heavy pandas pipelines: the ClickBench pandas queries built on groupby().filter(lambda ...) took 536 s and 1,005 s hot, against 0.11 s and 0.31 s in chDB on the same DataFrame.
- Notebooks or ETL scripts that want ClickHouse's SQL dialect and functions, plus file, S3, MySQL and Postgres table functions, without running a ClickHouse server.
- Embedding an OLAP engine in C, C++, Go, Rust or Node through the libchdb C ABI (shared or static tarballs are published with each chdb-core release) when your team already standardizes on ClickHouse SQL.
- ARM servers: on Graviton c8g.metal-48xl the chDB DataFrame hot total was 3.53 s, against 4.96 s for Polars and 1,418 s for pandas (Aug 2026 ClickBench).

**Skip it when:**
- Tiny DataFrames or tight per-call loops. Open issue #442 measures over 1 ms per simple query on a 1,000-row frame (pandas 0.1 ms, DuckDB 0.6 ms), mostly from building the query plan and pipeline. Open issue #254 reports short ClickBench queries running slower on c6a.metal than on the smaller c6a.4xlarge.
- If you already use Polars, the gain is modest. On c6a.metal the median per-query speedup is 1.77x (geomean 1.52x), and Polars is faster on 9 of 43 queries, mostly the cheap ones.
- Windows has no native build (ClickHouse does not compile there, per issue #368), so it runs only through WSL.
- Size-constrained deployments: the chdb-core wheel that holds the engine is 104-175 MB, against 2 MB for the pure-Python chdb wheel.
- Code that needs exact pandas semantics. The engine does not support category or timedelta dtypes, the Python() source adds the local timezone offset to dates (an open xfail as of Jan 2026), and DataStore returns nullable integer dtypes where pandas returns float64 or object.

**Integration:** module (Python abi3 wheels: chdb on top of chdb-core); the engine also ships as a prebuilt shared lib and a static lib (libchdb, C header chdb.h) · chdb needs chdb-core>=26.7.0, pandas>=2.1.0 and pyarrow>=13.0.0. chdb-core bundles the whole ClickHouse engine in one binary wheel. · Python 3.9+ with prebuilt wheels. Building from source needs Clang 21+ and C++23 (the ClickHouse toolchain; GCC is rejected). · Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux2014), macOS x86-64 (10.15+) and arm64 (11+). No Windows. Separate WebAssembly and Cloudflare builds exist, and a free-threaded Python 3.14t build is published as a GitHub release asset.

**Vs siblings:** Pick chDB over Bodo DataFrames when you want SQL over DataFrames already in memory, inside one pip-installed process, with no JIT compilation step (Bodo's catalogued win comes from its JIT path, not its pandas API). Pick it over Umbra when you need something open-source and embeddable: Umbra has no public repo in the catalog, and its 7.41 s ClickBench total comes from its own loaded tables, not DataFrame mode, so it cannot be compared directly with chDB's 6.00 s.

**Gotchas:**
- The repo was split. The catalogued chdb-io/chdb is now pure Python (DataStore, agents, durable storage), and the C++ engine lives in chdb-io/chdb-core (a GitHub fork with 22 stars). Engine bugs and releases are tracked there, and ClickBench installs the chdb-core release wheel directly.
- Python(df) finds the DataFrame by variable name at query time (ClickBench's server.py depends on a module-level global named hits). Numeric numpy columns are mapped without copying, but object-dtype string columns are converted element by element from Python str objects on every scan, and they exclude the frame from the session metadata cache. Arrow-backed strings avoid that conversion.
- The embedded ClickHouse version trails upstream, and engine bugs can return silently wrong results. In issue #587, chDB 4.1.8 (ClickHouse 26.3) undercounted = filters on Parquet files with Bloom filters and many row groups. The fix was bumping to ClickHouse 26.5 in chDB 4.1.9, so pin and upgrade chdb-core deliberately.
- If chdb is imported in a parent process, queries in forked child processes hang (issue #355). Use the multiprocessing 'spawn' start method.

**Status:** Actively developed (chdb 4.4.0 and chdb-core 26.7.3 were both released on 2026-09-11, last commit 2026-09-23), Apache-2.0 and maintained by ClickHouse Inc. since chDB joined ClickHouse in 2024; it installs with pip, but engine issues and source are in the separate chdb-io/chdb-core repo.

[repo](https://github.com/chdb-io/chdb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/tree/main/chdb-dataframe (current raw results: chdb-dataframe/results/20260816/c6a.metal.json vs pandas/results/20260824/c6a.metal.json and polars-dataframe/results/20260824/c6a.metal.json; the README image https://github.com/chdb-io/chdb/raw/main/docs/_static/df_bench.png is an Oct-2024 snapshot))

##### Crystal (GPU query-processing library)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Header-only CUDA library of block-wide device functions for hand-writing fused SQL query kernels; about 16x faster than OmniSci on SSB.

**Beats:** OmniSci (commercial GPU OLAP DBMS, formerly MapD, now HEAVY.AI) on the same GPU. Also the authors' own equivalent CPU implementation, which is itself compared against Hyper and MonetDB. — The SIGMOD 2020 paper (Section 5.2, Figure 14) ran the 13 SSB queries at SF20: a 120M-row lineorder table of about 13 GB, dictionary-encoded to 4-byte ints, with queries hand-rewritten and data preloaded into device memory, averaged over 3 runs. The Crystal-based GPU kernels averaged about 16x faster than OmniSci on the same V100 (32 GB, 880 GB/s, CUDA 10.0). They also averaged about 25x faster than the authors' own CPU implementation on an 8-core i7-6900 with 53 GB/s memory bandwidth (compiler and flags not stated); in the q2.1 case study this was 3.86 ms vs 125 ms. The 1.17x (vs Hyper) and 2.5x (vs MonetDB) figures belong to that CPU implementation, not to Crystal. On AWS pricing (p3.2xlarge at $3.06/h vs r5.2xlarge at $0.504/h), the paper concludes the GPU is about 4x more cost-effective, provided the dataset fits in GPU memory.

**Known shortcoming:** The 2.5x/1.17x vs MonetDB/Hyper is the authors' CPU code, not the GPU library; the GPU result is about 16x vs OmniSci on the same V100 and 25x vs their own CPU code. Abandoned (last commit 2020-08).

**Known shortcoming:** The repo's SSB kernels run 128 threads x 4 items while the paper used 256 x 8, and the Makefile targets sm_52 (V100 is sm_70), so paper numbers are not reproducible as shipped. Hash-join tables have no collision handling (colliding keys silently dropped, key 0 reserved): dense unique integer keys only.

**Known shortcoming:** The paper's BlockScan/BlockShuffle/BlockLoadSel/BlockLookup and the CPU implementation are missing from the repo (issues #8, #12). Pinned to CUB 1.6.4 with a hard-coded BASE_PATH; newer-CUDA include fixes unmerged (PRs #10, #11); no live fork.

**How:** It uses the paper's 'tile-based execution model'. The unit of work is the thread block, not the thread. Each block loads a tile of BLOCK_THREADS x ITEMS_PER_THREAD values with coalesced, striped loads into registers and tracks selections as per-item flags. A whole query (filters, then a probe of every dimension hash table, then aggregation) is fused into one kernel, so intermediate results never go to global memory. Aggregates are reduced in two steps, first with warp shuffles (__shfl_down_sync) and then through shared memory, which leaves one global atomicAdd per block; in the paper's selection microbenchmark this cut runtime from 19 ms to 2.1 ms. Joins use 'perfect hash' tables: direct-mapped arrays indexed by (key - min) % len over dense integer keys, so a probe is a single random read and the small dimension tables stay in GPU L2. The paper credits the larger-than-bandwidth-ratio gain over CPU to GPU warp switching hiding latency on irregular join probes. The Makefile also builds with -Xptxas -dlcm=cg, which caches global loads in L2 only.

**Use it when:**
- You have an Nvidia GPU and a fixed set of star-schema analytic queries (SSB-like: filter the fact table, join 1-4 small dimensions, aggregate) that you are willing to hand-code as one CUDA kernel each.
- All columns are, or can be dictionary-encoded to, 4-byte integers, and the working set fits in device memory. The paper's SF20 run was about 13 GB on a 32 GB V100.
- Dimension join keys are dense surrogate integers (for example 1..N part/supplier keys or yyyymmdd date keys), so a direct-mapped array can act as the hash table.
- You are doing GPU database research or teaching and want a small, readable reference: the SSB kernels are the baseline many GPU-DB papers cite.
- Data is loaded once and many queries run over it. The paper measures PCIe at 12.8 GB/s, versus 880 GB/s of HBM bandwidth, so repeated transfers would erase the gain.

**Skip it when:**
- You need ad-hoc SQL, strings, NULLs, 64-bit or decimal columns, or general GROUP BY. The library only offers integer comparison predicates, perfect-hash joins and a sum reduction. Each SSB kernel hard-codes its group-by as a fixed arithmetic index into a result array.
- The data does not fit in GPU memory or lives on the host. There is no out-of-core, multi-GPU or transfer pipelining, and the paper's own analysis shows GPU-as-coprocessor loses to a good CPU engine once PCIe is involved.
- Join keys are sparse, skewed or duplicated. Build ignores the atomicCAS result and does no collision handling, so colliding keys are silently dropped and 0 is reserved as the empty-slot marker.
- You want the full API described in the paper. BlockLoadSel, BlockScan, BlockShuffle, BlockLookup and BlockAggregate (paper Table 1) are not in the repo (open issue #8), so selection with compacted output (the paper's Q0) cannot be built from the published headers.
- You need a maintained dependency. The last commit was Aug 2020. The build pins CUB 1.6.4, targets sm_52 by default, and uses 32-bit int row counts. Two 2024 PRs that fix include paths for CCCL-era CUDA are still unmerged.

**Integration:** header-only · The crystal/*.cuh headers need only the CUDA toolkit (nvcc). The bundled SSB and ops programs also need CUB 1.6.4, fetched by `make setup` for CachingDeviceAllocator and test_util.h, plus cuRAND. SSB data generation needs the bundled dbgen/loader (C) and Python. · Not stated. __shfl_down_sync implies CUDA 9+, and the code uses --std=c++11. The paper used CUDA 10.0, and issue #1 reports a working build on CUDA 10.2 with GCC 7.5 after a template fix. On newer CUDA with bundled CCCL, the cub/test include paths need editing (PRs #10, #11). · Nvidia GPUs only (CUDA). The Makefile defaults to sm_52, with the sm_70/V100 lines commented out. Linux: the paper used Ubuntu 16.04, and the scripts assume a POSIX shell.

**Vs siblings:** Sirius (benchmarked against DuckDB at SF100-SF1000) and cuDF (cudf.pandas, a pandas accelerator) are engines you point at data. Crystal is a kit for hand-writing fused GPU kernels, so pick it only when you control the exact queries and want minimal, inspectable primitives, for example for research or a fixed dashboard query set. Compared with Velox, StarRocks or Umbra, it makes sense only when the data fits in GPU memory and integer-only columns are acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- The repo's SSB kernels launch with 128 threads x 4 items per thread, but paper Section 5.2 says the SSB runs used 256 threads x 8 items. The Makefile also targets sm_52, not the V100's sm_70. To reproduce Figure 14, both need editing.
- src/ssb/ssb_utils.h hard-codes SF 1 and BASE_PATH /home/ubuntu/dbops/..., and loadColumn returns NULL silently when a file is missing. A wrong path therefore shows up as 'CUDA error 11 invalid argument' at cudaMemcpy (issue #3).
- The bundled SSB dbgen segfaults on some systems (issue #4). The reported workaround is raising MAXAGG_LEN or using eyalroz/ssb-dbgen instead.
- The published BlockLoad is a plain striped load loop that keeps the tile in registers. The paper's vectorized full-tile loads and shared-memory staging are not in the headers, so performance on other GPUs depends on the tile-size template parameters you choose.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last commit on master was 2020-08-29 (13 commits in total), with 8 open issues, unmerged 2024 CUB/CCCL build-fix PRs and no active fork (every fork found has 0 stars). It is MIT-licensed, though, and the core is about five small .cuh headers that are easy to vendor; the last toolchain reported to work is CUDA 10.x.

[repo](https://github.com/anilshanbhag/crystal) · [benchmark](http://anilshanbhag.in/static/papers/crystal_sigmod20.pdf)

##### Cylon  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

C++/Arrow distributed-memory dataframe engine on MPI/UCX/Gloo that scales join, groupby and aggregation past serial pandas.

**Beats:** pandas — PPAM 2022 (arXiv 2209.06146), Fig. 3: strong scaling on 10^9 rows of two uniform-random int64 columns (C=0.9) on 15 Xeon Platinum 8160 nodes (up to 40 cores each, 40 Gbps InfiniBand). Cylon (GCC 9.4, OpenMPI 4.1, Arrow 5.0; optimization flags not stated) is plotted against serial pandas 1.4, Dask 2022.1 and Modin 0.12, with speedup over pandas drawn only as log-scale dotted lines. The gains come from 1-512 ranks versus one pandas process, time rises again at 512, and at one rank Cylon is described only as 'on par or better than pandas'.

**Known shortcoming:** The big gains are up to 512 cores vs serial pandas; compiler flags unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** The speedup comes from MPI ranks (1-512 over 15 nodes) vs serial pandas; at one rank it is only 'on par or better' and time rises again at 512. ~25% pandas API coverage at publication (no window/transpose), no fault tolerance, needs dedicated resources. Default join is sort-based (hash must be requested); multi-column hash join rejects chunked arrays; groupby reads only chunk(0); distributed sort crashes when any rank is empty (#664, #611 open).

**Known shortcoming:** The conda package is stale (0.4.0, 2021, linux-64 only), so build from source against Arrow 16.1 + MPI; docs say C++14 while CMake needs C++17; release 2.0 (2026-03) is mostly experimental features.

**How:** Operators are built from BSP patterns. Shuffle-Compute hash-partitions rows (MurmurHash3 mod P), runs an all-to-all shuffle and then a local operator; Combine-Shuffle-Reduce pre-aggregates first, MapReduce-style; sort uses sample sort with regular sampling. The local operators are single-threaded C++ over Arrow columns: ska::bytell_hash_map row-index groupby, hash (std::unordered_multimap) or sort joins, and Arrow Compute where it fits. The speedup over pandas comes mainly from spreading work over hundreds of MPI ranks; at parallelism 1 the paper claims only 'on par or better than pandas'.

**Use it when:**
- Joins or groupbys over roughly 10^8-10^9+ rows that don't fit comfortably in one pandas process, and you have a multi-node Linux/HPC cluster with MPI (ideally InfiniBand) already allocated to you
- BSP/mpirun batch pipelines where pandas-like data prep feeds MPI-based ML (e.g. PyTorch distributed) in the same processes, without a Spark/Dask scheduler
- High-cardinality key-based operations (the paper's C=0.9 worst case), where hash shuffle-compute scaled up to 256 ranks in the paper
- Low-cardinality groupby, where the combine-shuffle-reduce (mapred) groupby shrinks the shuffle a lot. The variant is chosen by the caller (pycylon groupby_type), not automatically.
- C++ codebases already on Arrow that want distributed relational operators with a pluggable transport (MPI, Gloo, UCX/UCC)

**Skip it when:**
- Single machine, or only a few cores: at parallelism 1 the paper claims only parity-or-better with pandas, and a single-node engine will usually do better
- Workloads that need broad pandas API coverage: coverage was about 25% at publication, and window and transpose operators were not implemented then
- Multi-tenant, elastic or fault-tolerant environments: the paper says execution needs dedicated resources and has no fault tolerance, and Release 2.0 checkpointing is labelled experimental
- Very small per-rank partitions: in the paper, wall time went back up from 256 to 512 ranks once communication dominated
- Teams that need prebuilt binaries: the only conda package (cylondata/pycylon 0.4.0) is linux-64 from 2021, so current code (Arrow 16.1, Release 2.0) has to be built from source

**Integration:** shared lib · Apache Arrow C++ (CMake pins 16.1.0; conda env pins pyarrow/libarrow 16.1.0), MPI (required even for other transports), glog; optional UCX/UCC, Gloo, Redis (hiredis, redis++), CUDA/cuDF for GCylon; Python bindings need Cython, NumPy <2.0 and pandas >=2.0,<2.2.3 · C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17), CMake 3.17+; CI uses GCC 11 on Ubuntu 22.04; the docs still say C++14 and CMake 3.16.5 (stale) · Linux x86-64 is the primary target (README: 'only works on Linux'). There is a macOS conda env pinned to Arrow 9 and a Windows env file, but no current CI for either. SIMD level is set at build time: SSE4.2 by default, AVX2/AVX512 optional.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Cylon over cuDF (cudf.pandas), data.table or chDB when the data and compute must span many CPU nodes under MPI rather than one GPU or one machine. Pick it over Bodo DataFrames when you want an Apache-2.0 C++ library of explicit Arrow operators with swappable transports, not a pandas-API/JIT layer.

**Gotchas:**
- The default join algorithm is SORT, both in the C++ JoinConfig and in pycylon merge/join (algorithm="sort"). Request the hash join explicitly (JoinAlgorithm::HASH / algorithm="hash"). The multi-column hash join also returns Invalid on chunked arrays.
- hash_groupby.cpp is marked 'todo handle chunked arrays', and its aggregation loop reads only chunk(0) of each value column. Combine chunks (arrow::Table::CombineChunks) before grouping.
- Distributed sort throws 'empty vector passed onto merge' when any rank's partition is empty, which is common after a filter (open issues #664 and #611).
- Errors come back as Status, except that JoinConfig's constructor throws a raw string literal. That size check runs after std::move of the shadowed parameters, so it never fires, and mismatched key lists are reported later by Join().

**Status:** Active but research-driven: Release 2.0 (2026-03-12) added mostly experimental features (Rust port, checkpointing, WASM, SIMD), and CI still runs on feature branches in 2026-09. However, docs, conda packages (0.4.0) and many 2021-2023 issues are stale; Apache-2.0 and buildable from source with CMake, but not small enough to vendor casually.

[repo](https://github.com/cylondata/cylon) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06146)

##### FastLanes  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

CWI's columnar file format with SIMD-friendly lightweight encodings; decodes 7-44x faster than Parquet, DuckDB and BtrBlocks in its paper.

**Beats:** Apache Parquet (Snappy and Zstd variants, written and read with DuckDB v1.2's Parquet implementation) and DuckDB v1.2's native storage format; also BtrBlocks — The paper (VLDB 2025) ran everything on one AWS i4i.4xlarge (Ice Lake, compiler not named, AVX-512 build) over 36 Public BI tables. Total decode time was 16.32 ms for FastLanes against 483 ms for DuckDB v1.2's native format, 713 ms and 731 ms for Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd (written and read through DuckDB v1.2), and 115 ms for BtrBlocks. First-value access took 0.14 ms (6x to 814x faster), while encoding was 4-14x slower than DuckDB and Parquet. Caveat: the artifact's FastLanes timers cover only get_chunk() on a first rowgroup that is already opened and read into memory, whereas Parquet and DuckDB random access was timed as a full DuckDB 'LIMIT 1' query. The paper's own Parquet+Snappy decode total also differs about 3x between Table 4 (712 ms) and Table 6 (2,071 ms), so treat the multipliers as upper bounds.

**Known shortcoming:** The 29/43/44/7x figures are decode only; encoding is 4-14x slower than DuckDB/Parquet. Compiler unnamed and CPU given only as 'Xeon (Ice Lake)'; Parquet was read through DuckDB 1.2.

**Known shortcoming:** The speed comparison is not like-for-like: FastLanes times only get_chunk() on a row group already in memory, while Parquet/DuckDB are timed as a full DuckDB LIMIT 1 query. The paper disagrees with itself (Parquet+Snappy decode 712 ms in Table 4 vs 2,071 ms in Table 6), so the multipliers are upper bounds. The whole table is held in RAM before writing.

**Known shortcoming:** No interop (no Arrow/Parquet/DuckDB reader; Python exports only CSV; no HTTP range reads). list<bigint> columns abort (#67, open); the footer is a separate file by default; CMake adds -march=native. Pre-1.0 format (v0.1.4), no GitHub releases, PyPI last updated 2025-05.

**How:** Every encoding works on 1024-value vectors in the authors' Unified Transposed / 1024-bit interleaved layout (VLDB 2023 'FastLanes Compression Layout'), which removes data dependencies so decode kernels, delta included, are plain scalar loops the compiler auto-vectorizes (no intrinsics; the paper measured AVX-512 builds about 40% faster than SSE). 'Expression encoding' cascades these light operators (e.g. dictionary codes then FFOR bit-packing) and adds multi-column compression that reuses codes or dictionaries across correlated columns, reaching Zstd-class ratios without a heavyweight decompressor. Decoding is vector-at-a-time into L1-sized buffers, and the writer picks each column's expression by trying a fixed pool on a few sampled vectors per rowgroup (paper: 'three-way' sampling; code default 7 vectors).

**Use it when:**
- Write-once, scan-many analytics on flat tables (integers, decimals, doubles, strings, dates) where decode CPU dominates and much slower writes are acceptable.
- Your own C++ vectorized engine or research prototype that can consume 1024-value vectors, including still-compressed ones such as dictionary codes in transposed order, to try compressed execution.
- Denormalized data with correlated columns, like the Public BI corpus: FastLanes stored 172 MB, Parquet+Snappy was 41% larger, BtrBlocks 18% larger and Parquet+Zstd 2% larger.
- Point reads of one vector from a rowgroup that is already loaded, where decompressing a whole Parquet page with Snappy/Zstd is the bottleneck.
- Builds that must stay portable across x86-64 and ARM without hand-written SIMD while still gaining from wider vector units.

**Skip it when:**
- Write-heavy or ETL ingestion. v0.1 encoding took 81.3 s against 5.9 s for Parquet+Snappy and 20.3 s for DuckDB in the paper. The writer also loads the whole table into memory before encoding.
- When you need interop. There is no Arrow, Parquet, DuckDB, Spark or Polars reader or writer. The Python API only exports CSV. In July 2025 the maintainer said HTTP range reads and a DuckDB extension were on the roadmap, not implemented.
- Nested or ML-style data. LIST, STRUCT and MAP appear in the type list, but a list<bigint> column aborts with UNREACHABLE (issue #67, open). The paper lists nested types and schema evolution as future work.
- Normalized or synthetic data such as TPC-H, where Parquet+Zstd compressed 15.3% smaller than FastLanes in the paper.
- Long-term archival or production storage. The format is pre-1.0 (the code's version tag is v0.1.4), the GitHub repo has no releases or tags, and readers accept only a whitelist of five version tags. Crashes on real datasets were reported in 2025 (issue #55, since fixed).

**Integration:** static lib by default, built with CMake (FetchContent from the dev branch); shared lib via FLS_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS. Bindings: pyfastlanes on PyPI, fls-rs for Rust. · none external. FlatBuffers is vendored in-tree, and the ALP and FSST codecs are in-tree. GoogleTest is fetched only for tests. · C++20 and CMake 3.22+. Clang 13+ is the default on Linux and macOS. GCC 11+ and MSVC have been accepted since April 2026 (PR #69), but the maintainer has said Clang is preferred for predictable auto-vectorization (issue #61). · Portable C++ with no intrinsics. CI builds on Linux x86-64 and aarch64, macOS 15 and Windows x64 (Clang and MSVC); the Windows-on-ARM job is disabled. The paper benchmarked only x86 (Ice Lake).

**Vs siblings:** Pick FastLanes over BtrBlocks when you want vector-granular decoding, a better compression ratio, or non-x86 targets; the paper says BtrBlocks needs AVX2/AVX-512. Prefer Vortex (which has DuckDB and DataFusion integrations, per its maintainer on HN) or Lance when ecosystem support matters more than peak decode speed. Use ALP, from the same authors and embedded in FastLanes, if you only need a float codec inside your own format.

**Gotchas:**
- At configure time CMake reads /proc/cpuinfo and adds -march=native (x86 without AVX-512DQ) or -mavx512dq to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS. A binary built on one host can therefore crash with an illegal instruction on an older CPU. FastLanes also compiles its own sources with -Wall -Werror -Wpedantic, so a newer compiler that adds warnings can break the build.
- The footer is not inlined by default (CFG::Footer::IS_INLINED = false). The reader then looks for a sidecar table_descriptor.fbb in the same directory. Call inline_footer() to get a single self-contained file; the README's Python and Rust examples do this, but the C++ example does not.
- read_csv() takes a directory, not a file. The directory must contain a .csv file and a schema.json, and the default delimiter is '|'. to_fls() throws if the output path already exists.
- Decoded vectors stay in the transposed (UTL) order. To get the original row order you must apply the 1024-entry selection vector, or ask the decoder to restore the order with a gather step.

**Status:** This is MIT-licensed CWI research code that moves slowly: the last commit was 2026-04-22 (GCC/MSVC support), there are no GitHub releases, and pyfastlanes was last published on 2025-05-30. It is easy to vendor via FetchContent, but the format is pre-1.0 and has no ecosystem readers.

[repo](https://github.com/cwida/FastLanes) · [benchmark](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p4629-afroozeh.pdf)

##### Velox  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Meta's C++ vectorized execution-engine library; as Presto's C++ worker it ran 3TB TPC-H queries 2-9x faster than Presto Java.

**Beats:** Presto Java execution engine (stock Presto vs Prestissimo, i.e. Presto with Velox C++ workers) — Meta's own VLDB 2022 paper ran Prestissimo (Java coordinator with Velox C++ workers) against stock Presto Java on an 80-node cluster (64 GB RAM and 2x2TB SSD per node; CPU model and compiler not stated), using 3TB TPC-H in uncompressed ORC with a warm cache and hand-written join orders, and reports wall times of 5s vs 42s (Q1), 1s vs 9s (Q6), 15s vs 31s (Q13) and 6s vs 13s (Q19), with 2.1-6.5x less CPU time; a production-traffic replay averaged 6-7x, and the same shadowed workload ran on 3x fewer servers. Only 4 of the 22 TPC-H queries are reported and no harness is public, Meta's 2023 blog claims 3-6x on shuffle-bound queries against the paper's 2.0-2.1x, and the earlier claim that it beats ClickHouse fails on ClickBench (214.09s vs 124.35s).

**Known shortcoming:** Loses to ClickHouse (a listed baseline) on ClickBench (214.09 s vs 124.35 s, wins 4 of 43 queries); the headline is now vs Presto Java per the VLDB'22 paper (TPC-H 3 TB 2-9x wall time, production average 6-7x). The record's 2.27x is Q32, not Q33 (1.67x) (verifier downgrade from A).

**Known shortcoming:** The Presto Java claim is first-party (Meta VLDB'22): 4 of 22 TPC-H queries, harness not public, CPU and compiler unnamed (Q1/Q6 8-9x, Q13/Q19 ~2x; Meta's 2023 blog says 3-6x on shuffle queries while the paper table says 2.0-2.1x). On ClickBench it has a fixed ~0.7 s per-query cost and Q29 is 126x slower than ClickHouse. A library only (no parser, optimizer or catalog); Presto C++ replaces only Presto Java workers, with gaps (no Java plugins/UDFs, missing CHAR/TIME/QDIGEST/GEOMETRY types, no hard memory caps). Source-only build: C++20, GCC 11+/Clang 15+, heavy dependencies (folly, fbthrift, boost, arrow), ~4 GB RAM per compile unit, AVX2 by default, no Windows. Open wrong-result bugs: GROUP BY on TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (#10338), CASE (#17115); strict-aliasing UB (#19100).

**How:** Execution is vectorized and works on encoded data directly: dictionary 'peeling' runs a function once per distinct value, results are memoized across batches that share a dictionary, and Lazy Vectors defer loading columns until they are used. Expressions get common-subexpression elimination and constant folding at compile time, and at run time conjuncts and pushed-down scan filters are reordered adaptively by time/(1 + rows_in - rows_out); simple filters use SIMD through xsimd (the paper cites about one integer hit per clock on AVX2). Joins and aggregations share an F14-style hash table (128-byte buckets of 16 slots with 7-bit tags, vectorized inserts and lookups, interleaved probes that keep several cache misses in flight), and a VectorHasher maps keys to a flat array or a single 64-bit normalized key where it can. There is no JVM or GC, a mmap/madvise allocator keeps large buffers unfragmented, and a RAM+SSD cache with coalesced reads and adaptive prefetch keeps remote IO off the critical path.

**Use it when:**
- You run prestodb with Java workers on Hive or Iceberg tables in ORC, DWRF or Parquet and want to cut worker CPU and server count. Presto C++ swaps the workers and keeps the Java coordinator; Meta's paper reports 8-9x lower wall time on CPU-bound TPC-H Q1 and Q6, about 2x on shuffle-heavy Q13 and Q19, and the same production load served with 3x fewer servers.
- Spark SQL batch or ETL jobs, through Apache Gluten's Velox backend. Gluten's README reports a 2.71x overall speedup over vanilla Spark on its 22-query TPC-H-style suite, and notes that the figure does not reflect the latest performance.
