Reads get back to LSM speed through per-sstable bloom filters (about one sstable read per level), seek-triggered forced compaction, optional parallel seeks within a guard, and larger sstables that miss the table cache less often.

**Use it when:**
- Write-heavy ingest of random (hashed or UUID-like) keys into an on-SSD store much larger than RAM, where compaction write IO or SSD wear is the bottleneck. The paper measured 2.4-3x less write IO than RocksDB and 2.5x lower write amplification at 500M keys.
- Update-heavy workloads: in the paper, PebblesDB kept 75% of its initial insert throughput across two full update rounds, while the other stores fell to about 50%. Its update throughput was 2.15x HyperLevelDB's.
- Existing LevelDB or HyperLevelDB code that needs more random-write throughput with no API changes. Point-read throughput stayed equal or slightly higher in the paper's runs.
- Mixed YCSB-like workloads whose range scans do many next() calls after each seek, or that interleave writes. The paper measured only 6% overhead on YCSB workload E.
- Research or reproduction of FLSM ideas: the repo ships db_bench and YCSB bindings, and there are companion JNI and MongoDB (mongo-pebbles) layers.

**Skip it when:**
- Sequential or append-ordered key inserts: 3x lower throughput than HyperLevelDB, because guards force sstables to be split and rewritten where LSM stores just move files. The paper itself recommends RocksDB for this case.
- Short seek-heavy range queries on a fully compacted store: 30% slower than HyperLevelDB, 40% on an aged file system or with scarce RAM, and 47% on seeks for fully cached small datasets.
- Large values or tiny KV pairs: only 1 KB values were tested. Open issue #29 reports crashes with values over a few tens of KB, and issue #24 documents a memory leak with many small key-value pairs.
- Durability-critical deployments: open issue #28 shows torn log writes after a simulated power failure leaving partially persisted values after RepairDB. LevelDB fixed the same bug in 1.23.
- When you need RocksDB features or a maintained engine: there are no column families, transactions or compression other than Snappy. Median CPU was 171% vs 98-110% for the others, memory was about 300 MB above HyperLevelDB at 100M keys, and the code has been untouched since 2019.

**Integration:** shared lib (autotools/libtool builds libpebblesdb shared and static; a CMake target is also provided) · Snappy (optional, auto-detected) and pthreads; autotools with libtool, or CMake 3.9+, to build · C++11 (-std=c++11). The README says it was tested with g++-4.7, 4.9 and 5 and 'may not work' with other compilers. A 2019 commit fixed a g++-7 build error, and PR #18 for a g++-6 test build error was never merged. · POSIX only (LEVELDB_PLATFORM_POSIX). The old Travis CI built on Linux and macOS. atomic_pointer.h has x86, ARM-Linux and PPC paths and falls back to <atomic> elsewhere. No Windows port.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PebblesDB only if you already code against the LevelDB/HyperLevelDB API and want a no-code-change boost in random-write throughput with less write IO. For new designs that start from RocksDB, SplinterDB (maintained, 6-10x RocksDB inserts while matching it on small range queries) or Titan (a RocksDB plugin for large values) are safer, and KVell reports beating PebblesDB itself on both read- and write-dominated workloads.

**Gotchas:**
- Almost all tuning happens at compile time, not through Options. kMaxFilesPerGuardSentinel (default 2) is in db/dbformat.h, and the FILE_LEVEL_FILTER, SEEK_PARALLEL and DISABLE_SEEK_BASED_COMPACTION macros are in db/version_set.h. The guard-density constants top_level_bits=27 and bit_decrement=2 are hard-coded in db/write_batch.cc, and the paper says to raise top_level_bits above about 100M keys or guards become skewed.
- The per-sstable bloom filters live only in memory (a std::map). DB::Open rebuilds them by scanning every sstable: the paper measured about 1.2 s per GB, or 62 s for 52 GB. They are built only if Options.filter_policy is set, and it defaults to NULL, so without NewBloomFilterPolicy the main read optimization is off.
- Guard deletion is not implemented, so deleted key ranges leave empty guards behind. The paper saw no read slowdown with 9,000 empty guards, but they are never reclaimed.
- Everything is declared in namespace leveldb with LevelDB's class names, so linking it into one binary with LevelDB would likely clash (not documented). It is also unrelated to CockroachDB's Go 'Pebble' despite the similar name.

**Status:** Abandoned since the last commit on 2019-08-03, with 13 issues and PRs open (including crash-consistency and thread-safety bugs) and a CockroachDB Pebble author calling it 'a research project and ... dead' on HN in 2020; it is BSD-3-Clause and about 9.1k changed lines on top of HyperLevelDB, so it can be vendored, but you own the fixes.

[repo](https://github.com/utsaslab/pebblesdb) · [benchmark](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~vijay/papers/sosp17-pebblesdb.pdf)

##### SplinterDB  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Embedded C key-value store for NVMe SSDs; paper reports 6-10x RocksDB insert throughput and 2-2.6x point-query throughput.

**Beats:** RocksDB — The USENIX ATC'20 paper replayed YCSB-derived traces (load and A-F, 24B keys, 100B and 1KiB values) against an unnamed version of RocksDB (and PebblesDB) on a Dell R720 with a 32-core 2.0 GHz Xeon and an Optane 905p SSD, memory capped at 4GiB by a cgroup: SplinterDB was 6-10x faster on inserts, 2-2.6x on point queries, roughly equal on short scans, with half the write amplification. Compiler and flags were not reported; the repo's tests/functional/ycsb_test.c is a SplinterDB trace replayer, but the traces and the RocksDB side of the harness are not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** No crash recovery: log replay is 'not wired yet' in src/core.c, an uncleanly closed DB refuses to mount, WAL off by default, no fsync API. ~15% slower than RocksDB on YCSB E short scans; the paper names no RocksDB version, CPU model, compiler or flags; traces and the RocksDB harness are not public. Linux-only (libaio), x86-64 CI only, Release uses -march=native -ffast-math. Open critical assert on small-pair inserts (#560) and segfault on YCSB-C (#585) since 2023. No releases; 'not for production before 1.0'.

**How:** The core structure is the STBε-tree (size-tiered Bε-tree): a trunk tree of fanout 8-16 whose nodes point to immutable B-tree 'branches', each paired with a quotient filter instead of a Bloom filter. Size-tiering plus a flush-then-compact policy rewrite each key fewer times than leveled LSM compaction (about half RocksDB's write amplification in the paper) and let many small, local compactions run in parallel. A concurrent memtable (hand-over-hand locking) and a user-level clock cache with distributed reader-writer locks and O_DIRECT I/O remove the CPU and lock contention that, per the paper, holds RocksDB to about 30% of an Optane SSD's bandwidth.

**Use it when:**
- Write-heavy ingest of small pairs (paper: 24B keys, 100B values) on fast NVMe, where RocksDB is CPU-bound rather than device-bound
- Datasets far larger than RAM (paper caps memory at about 10% of the dataset, 4GiB) that still need fast point lookups
- Many-threaded clients: the paper reports point reads at 18.5x single-thread throughput with 24 threads (YCSB C)
- Workloads that can express changes as blind updates (append, increment) through a custom data_config, skipping read-modify-write
- Research systems or prototypes on Linux that can accept an unstable API and unversioned on-disk format

**Skip it when:**
- Data that must survive a crash: the write-ahead log is off unless use_log is set, there is no fsync/commit API, and core_mount still says crash recovery (log replay + allocator rebuild) is not wired, so a database that was not cleanly closed refuses to mount
- Short range scans on small values: the paper measured YCSB E about 15% slower than RocksDB with 100B values (about 15% faster with 1KiB values)
- Anything needing transactions/atomic multi-put, range delete, a stable API, or an on-disk format that survives upgrades (all listed in docs/limitations.md)
- Non-Linux targets: macOS and Windows are unsupported because the I/O layer is built on libaio
- Long-running production ingest before re-testing: open issues #560 (critical assert in routing_filter_add on large small-pair insert runs, 2023) and #585 (segfault in routing_filter_lookup under YCSB-C) have no recorded resolution

**Integration:** shared lib · libaio, libxxhash, pthread, libm (build docs also install libconfig-dev) · C with GNU extensions; minimum version not documented; CI uses GCC 13 and Clang 19; public headers are C++-compatible (extern "C") · Linux only; CI runs on x86-64 Ubuntu; the Makefile adds -march=native on x86-64 and skips it elsewhere, but aarch64 support is not documented or tested

**Vs siblings:** Pick SplinterDB for write-heavy, small-pair ordered workloads on NVMe when you can accept an experimental engine with weak crash safety; choose TerarkDB or Titan to stay RocksDB-compatible (Titan for large values), libmdbx for read-mostly ACID transactions, and NuDB for append-only insert/fetch with no ordering.

**Gotchas:**
- The default release build uses -O3 -ffast-math -flto and, on x86-64, -march=native, so a library built on one machine can fault on an older CPU
- cache_size and data_config (key compare, merge functions) are not stored in the database and must be supplied identically on every open; disk size is fixed at create time
- Iterators must be deinitialized; the header warns a live iterator can block inserts, deletes and close from the same thread
- docs/limitations.md lags the code: it still says keys and values must be smaller than the 4KiB page, but PR #674 (May 2026) added values larger than a page

**Status:** Actively developed by VMware Research (values larger than a page, async scans and checkpointing all landed in 2026) under Apache-2.0, but there are no releases and the maintainers say it is not for production before 1.0.

[repo](https://github.com/vmware/splinterdb) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc20/presentation/conway)

##### TreeLine  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Update-in-place key-value store for NVMe SSDs with record caching and page grouping; beats RocksDB on read-heavy, skewed, scan YCSB.

**Beats:** RocksDB — In the authors' own PVLDB 16(1) paper (their C++ YCSB runner; 20-core Xeon Gold 6230, 128 GiB RAM, 1 TB Intel DC P4510 NVMe, Linux 5.12.5/ext4; memory for 33% of the data; compiler not named, build uses -march=native), TreeLine averaged 2.20x RocksDB's throughput (geometric mean) on 1024 B point workloads, up to 10.95x, but only 1.45x on uniform point workloads. RocksDB 6.14.6 ran with block compression and checksums off and Bloom filters on, and write-ahead logging was disabled on every system.

**Known shortcoming:** The original record misattributed its numbers: 2.20x is the 1024 B point-read average, 2.50x is uniform YCSB-E scans (not Zipfian), 1.62x is Zipfian 64 B; up to 10.95x in the best case. No compiler named.

**Known shortcoming:** pg_treeline has no WAL or recovery (dirty writes live only in cache and are lost on crash), and the paper benchmarked with WAL off everywhere. API: uint64 keys only, no Delete, must BulkLoad before any Put, fixed-size records; not a RocksDB drop-in. Loses to RocksDB on pure writes (the paper says so); needs NVMe with high I/O parallelism.

**Known shortcoming:** Linux only (O_DIRECT/fallocate), -march=native, one DB per process, and the header says no concurrency although the paper used 16 threads. Stale since 2024-01 with build issues (#112); the old 'treeline' target is unsupported and segfaults (#113).

**How:** Each record lives in exactly one 4 KiB on-disk page, so a point read that misses the cache costs at most two page reads (base page plus at most one overflow page), whereas RocksDB may probe SSTables on several levels and spends reads on compaction. A Masstree-indexed record cache with clock-style priority eviction buffers every write, keeps hot records rather than hot pages, and batches dirty records bound for the same page when one is evicted. Page grouping runs the PGM-index's optimal piecewise linear regression during reorganization, writes key-adjacent pages as contiguous 1-16 page segments, and indexes only segment boundaries plus a linear model in an in-memory TLX B+tree, so scans become long sequential reads. Insert forecasting uses a per-epoch equi-depth histogram of inserts to decide how much free space each page keeps, cutting reorganizations.

**Use it when:**
- Larger-than-memory datasets on NVMe SSDs with skewed (Zipfian) read/update point traffic: the paper averages 1.62x (64 B records) and 2.99x (1024 B) over RocksDB on YCSB A/B/C/D/F.
- Short range-scan-heavy workloads (YCSB E: 95% scans of up to 100 records) with many request threads: 2.21x (64 B) and 2.50x (1024 B) over RocksDB on uniform scans, because it reads at least 1.9x less data from disk.
- Hot records scattered across the key space (for example user IDs whose activity has nothing to do with their key order): caching records instead of pages kept TreeLine's writes at 3.09 GiB against LeanStore's 23.1 GiB on YCSB A with 64 B records.
- Fixed-size records with 64-bit integer keys whose distribution is locally near-linear: page grouping cut index entries 1.8-4.8x on the Amazon, OSM and synthetic datasets, which leaves more memory for the cache.
- As a reference implementation or starting point for research on update-in-place engines versus LSMs, not as a production store.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs durability: the primary pg_treeline path has no write-ahead log, dirty writes reach disk only on eviction or clean shutdown, and the paper only sketches crash recovery and leaves it for future work (the code still has TODOs for logging reorganizations).
- Pure write or insert-heavy workloads: the paper says TreeLine 'currently cannot compete with RocksDB on pure write workloads', because every insert still needs a page read-modify-write.
- String or variable-length keys, deletes, or variable-size values: the pg API takes only uint64 keys, has no Delete (the code carries 'TODO: Support deletes'), and the page-grouping models assume fixed-size records.
- HDDs, SATA SSDs, or setups with little I/O parallelism: the design depends on random writes approaching sequential throughput on NVMe, which the paper shows only as concurrent writer threads increase. Scans also get no help from the record cache, whereas RocksDB's block cache can serve hot scan ranges.
- Production use in general: stale since January 2024, Linux-only I/O, one DB instance per process, and users have hit build problems (issue #112: Masstree config.h not generated, dl not linked).

**Integration:** static lib (pg_treeline CMake target; shared lib with TL_BUILD_SHARED=ON) · System packages libtbb-dev, libjemalloc-dev and autoconf (for Masstree's configure). CMake FetchContent pulls google/crc32c 1.1.1 and libcuckoo. Masstree, TLX and PGM are vendored in third_party. Benchmarks additionally fetch gflags, Google Benchmark, RocksDB 6.14.6, ycsbr, libaio and LeanStore. · C++17 (needs std::filesystem), CMake 3.17+. Compiler versions are not documented. CI builds Debug on ubuntu-latest. · Linux only in practice: storage I/O uses O_DIRECT|O_SYNC with pread/pwrite and fallocate(). Built with -march=native, so binaries are tied to the build CPU. Only Ubuntu x86-64 appears in CI and the paper.

**Vs siblings:** Pick TreeLine over KVell when you need range scans and a small in-memory index (the paper notes KVell indexes every key and does random I/O on scans), and over F2/FASTER when ordered range scans matter, since the paper says FASTER does not support them efficiently. Prefer SplinterDB or RocksDB itself for insert-heavy or durability-critical workloads.

**Gotchas:**
- No WAL on the pg_treeline path: Put only marks a record dirty in the in-memory record cache. The RecordCache destructor writes dirty entries out on clean close, so a crash loses every unflushed write. The paper's benchmarks disabled write-ahead logging on all three systems, RocksDB included.
- You must BulkLoad a non-empty, sorted, distinct record set into a fresh DB before any write; Put on an unloaded DB returns NotSupported. Keys 0 and 2^64-1 are reserved.
- Only one DB per process: the record cache keeps its entries in a static vector and the page manager uses a static thread_local workspace. PutBatchParallel (used by the optional parallel final flush) has a known deadlock TODO if a reorganization is needed.
- The repo contains two engines. pg_treeline (pg_db.h) is the primary, supported artifact. The older treeline target (db.h, which takes Slice keys and has Delete) is no longer supported, and a user hit a 2-thread segfault in it (issue #113). The default options also write debug CSVs (write_debug_info=true) and start 16 background I/O threads.

**Status:** A stale research prototype (last commit 2024-01-02, a README tweak; the 8 open issues are mostly unfinished cleanup) that is MIT-licensed and copyable, but expect to fix the build and add durability and deletes yourself before relying on it.

[repo](https://github.com/mitdbg/treeline) · [benchmark](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p99-yu.pdf)

#### filters-bloom-cuckoo-xor

##### FastPLBF (fast PLBF / fast PLBF++)  `Python`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Python reference code for fast PLBF and PLBF++, which cut partitioned learned Bloom filter construction time 34x-761x versus PLBF.

**Beats:** PLBF (Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter) — The NeurIPS 2023 paper times Python construction (including LightGBM training and key insertion) of fast PLBF and fast PLBF++ against the authors' own reimplementation of PLBF, on the Malicious URLs and EMBER datasets, in the memory-budget framework. At N=1000, k=5, fast PLBF is 50.8x (URLs) and 34.3x (EMBER) faster and fast PLBF++ is 63.1x and 39.3x faster; at N=1000, k=50 with a 500 Kb backup-filter budget the figures are 233x/199x and 761x/500x. Fast PLBF gives identical FPR and fast PLBF++ is at most 1.0019x (URLs) and 1.000083x (EMBER) worse; no CPU, Python version or hardware is stated.

**Known shortcoming:** The 233x/761x construction speedups are the k=50 ablation; at the default N=1000, k=5 it is 34-63x faster than PLBF; no hardware stated.

**Known shortcoming:** The speedup is build time only, in a pure-Python reference with pure-Python Bloom backups (source drop, no package; the caller must pass a model score per query). The baseline is the authors' own O(N^3 k) complete PLBF; the original PLBF code appears to run a relaxed single DP about as fast as fast PLBF (App. F). fast PLBF++ is not guaranteed optimal (FPR up to 1.85x PLBF on synthetic non-monotone data). A 2025-06 counting fix means the code differs from the paper-era code; *_M report the last loop's memory, not the best; asserts used for validation; stale, no releases (also vendored in the learnedbf PyPI package).

**How:** PLBF solves a separate O(j^2 k) DP for each j = k..N, which is O(N^3 k) in total. Fast PLBF observes that every one of those subproblems is a prefix of the single j = N table, so it builds that table once and traces back each j in O(k). That gives O(N^2 k) with an identical result. Fast PLBF++ also treats each DP layer as a row-maxima 'matrix problem' on a monotone matrix (Aggarwal et al. 1987) and solves it by divide-and-conquer: exhaustively search the middle row, then recurse on the narrowed ranges (matrix_problem_on_monotone_matrix.py). That gives O(Nk log N + Nk^2). Monotonicity is proven only for an 'ideal' score distribution where g_i/h_i is non-decreasing; otherwise the result can be suboptimal.

**Use it when:**
- You use or plan to use a PLBF, and the parameter search dominates build time at N around 1000. The paper reports PLBF spending over 3 minutes finding t and f, while fast PLBF and fast PLBF++ finish the whole build in under 2 seconds.
- The filter is rebuilt often (model retraining, changing key sets), so construction latency matters more than query speed.
- You want to raise N and k to lower FPR without cubic build cost. The authors suggest N ~1000 and k ~100, with builds of a few tens of seconds.
- Pick fast PLBF when you need exactly PLBF's thresholds and FPRs. Pick fast PLBF++ when classifier scores are close to monotone and an FPR penalty of about 0.2% (URLs) is acceptable.
- You want a compact reference for porting the DP into your own C++ or Rust learned filter. The core is about 100 lines across calc_DPKL.py, fast_calc_DPKL.py and matrix_problem_on_monotone_matrix.py.

**Skip it when:**
- On a production query path. Backup filters use the pure-Python bloom-filter 1.3.3 package, contains() does a Python bisect plus Python hashing, and the paper reports no query-throughput numbers. The speedup is build-time only.
- When you have no classifier that produces [0,1] scores at query time. Every lookup needs s(x), so model inference cost and model size (312 Kb and 1.19 Mb LightGBM models in the paper) add to each query and to total memory.
- When scores are weakly correlated with membership, use fast PLBF++ with care. It is not guaranteed optimal, and on synthetic data with almost no monotonicity (10^8 swaps) its FPR reached 1.85x PLBF's (paper Appendix G). Use fast PLBF there.
- When the baseline you actually run is the original public PLBF code (kapilvaidya24/plbf). That code appears to run one DP over at most 100 quantile chunks, which is the 'relaxed' method. Appendix F shows the relaxed method builds about as fast as fast PLBF, although its FPR is up to 1.48x worse on EMBER. The 34x-761x figures are against the O(N^3 k) complete method.
- When you need dynamic inserts or deletes. Keys go in once at construction, into fixed-size backup Bloom filters, and there is no update or serialization API.

**Integration:** source-drop. There is no setup.py or pyproject and it is not on PyPI; the scripts prepend the parent directory to sys.path. The MIT code is also vendored in the pip package learnedbf (SLIMlaboratory, Apache-2.0). · bloom-filter==1.3.3 (pure Python), pandas==2.3.0, scikit-learn==1.6.1. PLBF.py imports pandas and scikit-learn at module top level even though only the CLI uses them. · Python 3.9+ (inferred: signatures use list[float] annotations, and the pinned pandas 2.3.0 and scikit-learn 1.6.1 require >=3.9); not otherwise documented · any (pure Python)

**Vs siblings:** No siblings catalogued yet. Compared with the baseline PLBF code, pick this when you need the complete, fi <= 1-constrained optimum at large N or k in seconds. If you want a pip-installable wrapper with scikit-learn-style classifiers, learnedbf vendors this code.

**Gotchas:**
- Inputs are validated with assert statements, one per score. Running under python -O strips them, and when they are active they add an O(n) Python loop to construction.
- A June 2025 commit ('fix counting method') switched to add-one smoothing: segment and region counts now start at 1 and totals include the pseudo-counts. The current code is therefore not identical to the code behind the 2023 paper numbers.
- In PLBF_M and FastPLBF_M, memory_usage_of_backup_bf is computed from the last loop iteration's t and f, not from t_best and f_best, so the reported figure may not match the configuration chosen. The filters themselves are built with the best values.
- Segments are equal-width score intervals (i/N), not quantiles as in the original plbf code, so heavily skewed score distributions leave many segments nearly empty.

**Status:** Stale research code: 13 stars, no releases or tags, and only four small commits since 2023 (June 2025: import fix, counting fix, eval scripts, dependency bump). It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor or port, and it is already vendored in the learnedbf PyPI package.

[repo](https://github.com/atsukisato/FastPLBF) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02846)

#### indexes

##### Cuckoo Trie  `C`  `Unlicense`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Research C ordered index storing a trie in a cuckoo hash table; faster DRAM-bound lookups than HOT, ARTOLC, STX B-tree.

**Beats:** B-tree (STX B-Tree), ART, HOT, Wormhole — In the SOSP'21 paper (arXiv 2201.09331, Sec. 6.2), single-threaded YCSB-C with uniform lookups on 200M osm keys ran up to 35%, 20%, 50% and 360% faster than HOT, ARTOLC, Wormhole and the TLX STX B+-tree respectively (not std::map), on a dual-socket Xeon Gold 6132 (Skylake, 2.6 GHz, Turbo and hyper-threading off, NUMA-interleaved) with GCC 7.5.0, jemalloc and 2 MB huge pages. Growing from 10M to 640M random 8-byte keys slowed HOT, ARTOLC and STX lookups by about 1.7x but the Cuckoo Trie by only 1.23x.

**Known shortcoming:** Slower than ARTOLC on the az dataset, on scans and on inserts. Abandoned (last main commit 2021-10).

**Known shortcoming:** Research code (the README says it is not robust enough for real programs); abandoned since 2021-10 with only student forks. No delete and no resize: fixed capacity, and after S_OVERFLOW every later operation is undefined. Stores the caller's record by pointer (no copy); max key 256 B.

**Known shortcoming:** Linux x86-64 Haswell+ only (BEXTR/PDEP/BZHI), GCC 5.4+; needs reserved 2 MB huge pages (ct_alloc returns NULL when short). Slowest of all tested on scan-heavy YCSB-E; loses on long-common-prefix keys; up to 156% more memory than HOT/STX. The 360% win is vs the TLX STX B+-tree.

**How:** It stores the nodes of a path-compressed trie in a bucketized cuckoo hash table keyed by key prefix, so every node on a search path can be located from the key alone, with no pointer-chasing. A lookup therefore computes the prefix hashes up front and prefetches both candidate buckets for the next D=5 levels, keeping several DRAM misses in flight at once (memory-level parallelism). Each bucket is one 64-byte cache line holding four 15-byte entries that store no keys: a small tag, a 'color' and the parent's color identify each node, using peelable hashing. Keys are split into 5-bit symbols with BMI2 PDEP, and sorted iteration walks a linked list of leaves, prefetching the next leaf.

**Use it when:**
- Read-heavy point lookups (YCSB-B/C style) on a large in-memory ordered index that is far bigger than the LLC. The paper's datasets were 1 GB or more, and the lead over HOT, ARTOLC and STX grows with index size.
- Keys that diverge early, i.e. short unique prefixes: random 8- or 16-byte keys, 64-bit encoded integers like the osm dataset, or short strings like the reddit usernames.
- Linux x86-64 servers (Haswell or newer) where you can reserve 2 MB huge pages, run jemalloc with THP, and size the table ahead of time from a known key count.
- Multi-threaded lookup-heavy services (lookups take no locks and scaled almost linearly on 28 cores), or systems like a Redis sorted set whose per-element work hides the leaf-list latency during scans.
- As an MLP-aware research baseline or a design to port, not as a production dependency.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys with long common prefixes, such as composite IDs or URLs. On az (average unique prefix 138 bits) it is slower than HOT and ARTOLC, because jump nodes save memory but not DRAM round trips.
- Scan-heavy standalone workloads. On YCSB-E its scan throughput was the lowest of all indexes tested.
- Workloads that need deletes, automatic growth, or top insert speed. Deletion and resizing are not implemented. ARTOLC inserts faster, and ARTOLC also wins YCSB-D, where recently inserted keys are served from cache.
- Memory-constrained deployments. It uses up to 156% more memory than HOT and STX, although up to 28% less than ARTOLC and Wormhole.
- Production use, non-Linux or non-x86 platforms, pre-Haswell CPUs, or keys over 256 bytes. The README says the code 'is not robust enough to be used as an index in your program'.

**Integration:** shared lib (libcuckoo_trie.so from a plain Makefile; about 25 C files, small enough to vendor as a source-drop) · pthreads and Linux MAP_HUGETLB with 2 MB huge pages reserved in advance via nr_hugepages. jemalloc with MALLOC_CONF=thp:always is recommended for the caller's key/value memory (it is not linked by the library). · GCC 5.4+ (the authors tested GCC 5.4.0 and 7.5.0; GCC 4.8.5 fails because it lacks -march=haswell). Needs GNU C extensions (__uint128_t, x86 BMI builtins). Clang support is not documented. · Linux x86-64 only, Haswell or newer (uses BEXTR, PDEP and BZHI via -march=haswell).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over HOT or ART Synchronized (OLC) for DRAM-resident, lookup-dominated work on keys with short unique prefixes (the paper measured +35% over HOT and +20% over ARTOLC on osm YCSB-C), and over the learned-index siblings (ALEX, LIPP, PGM, RMI), which were benchmarked on numeric keys, when you need variable-length byte keys. Stay with HOT for lower memory, long-common-prefix keys or scans, and with ART OLC for insert-heavy work or deletes.

**Gotchas:**
- Capacity is fixed at ct_alloc and there is no resize. After an insert returns S_OVERFLOW, the result of every later operation except ct_free is undefined. Size the table up front: the API suggests 1.5N to 2N cells, the benchmark defaults to 2.5N, and the paper ran at 85% load.
- ct_insert stores a pointer to your ct_kv without copying it. The record must not be freed or modified while it is in the trie, and ct_free does not free records. There is also no ct_iter_free; iterators are plain malloc'd.
- ct_alloc returns NULL (and prints a message) if not enough 2 MB huge pages are reserved. Separately, jemalloc's THP silently falls back to 4 KB pages, costing throughput. Watch thp_fault_fallback in /proc/vmstat.
- API.md says ct_insert aborts on a duplicate key, but the code returns S_ALREADYIN. The bucket-mix table uses a fixed seed (rand_seed(1)), so the table layout is not keyed per instance.

**Status:** Abandoned research code. There are three commits, all from the October 2021 public release, no maintained fork (only 0-star student forks from 2024-2026, whose epoch/resize PRs were closed unmerged), and the authors warn it is not production-robust; it is Unlicense (public domain) and small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/cuckoo-trie/cuckoo-trie-code) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.09331)

##### indexset  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust two-level B-tree (sorted Vec leaves) with positional indexing; beats std BTreeMap/BTreeSet on scans and Mutex-wrapped std under contention.

**Beats:** std::collections::BTreeMap / BTreeSet (Rust) — The author's Criterion suite at master commit 7e3ac23 (rustc 1.97.0-nightly, default bench profile, 12-core Apple M2 Pro, macOS) measured 100k-entry trees. Against std::collections::BTreeSet/BTreeMap, full traversal was 1.5-2.5x faster and small-entry inserts and map updates were slightly faster at cap 256, but std won get/contains/remove. With 12 threads, the concurrent tree at cap 256 beat a Mutex-wrapped std tree by about 3.2x (map, 0.722 vs 2.314 ms) and about 3.5x (set, 0.728 vs 2.545 ms) at 50/50 read/write with 64-byte values. No one has reproduced this independently.

**Known shortcoming:** Inserts are only 1.08-1.17x faster (1.5x holds only for map updates); mixed single-thread results; license stated only in Cargo.toml.

**Known shortcoming:** The headline wins need node capacity 256; at the default 1024, 64 B inserts/removes lose to std and concurrent 50/50 loses to Mutex<std> (4.0 vs 2.5 ms). Correctness bugs: range() wrong on absent bounds (#56), multimap range bug (#68), set get() skips the equality check (from source). 100M reverse-order inserts take 34-61 s vs std ~2 s (#39). crates.io 0.16.0 lacks the split-panic (#57) and UB (#55) fixes; the bench ran unreleased commit 7e3ac23. Concurrent iteration uses unsafe transmute and rescans per leaf (quadratic); monotonic inserts take a global write lock; only a Mutex-wrapped std baseline.

**How:** The tree is flat. A Vec holds sorted Vec leaves, 1024 slots each by default and set with with_maximum_node_size. A lookup is one binary search over the leaves' max elements and one unchecked binary search inside a leaf. Iteration is plain slice iteration over contiguous memory, which is why full scans are 1.5-2.5x faster. A Fenwick tree (the ftree crate) over the leaf lengths gives positional select/rank in O(log(n/B)). The concurrent variants index their leaves in a crossbeam lock-free SkipMap keyed by each leaf's max, and each leaf sits behind its own parking_lot Mutex. Ordinary operations take only a read guard on a global ShardedLock plus one leaf mutex. Splits, leaf-max changes and leaf removals take the global write lock, so threads that touch different leaves run in parallel instead of queuing on one Mutex<std::BTreeMap>.

**Use it when:**
- Scan-heavy ordered data in Rust: full traversal of 100k entries was 1.5-2.5x faster than std, and 128-entry range scans were 1.1-1.4x faster.
- You need order statistics: the k-th element (get_index ran in about 11-13 ns at 100k), rank of a key, or slicing by position with range_idx. std BTreeMap cannot do these without an O(n) walk.
- A shared ordered set or map hit by many threads with random-position keys. At cap 256 and 12 threads the concurrent tree was about 3.2-3.5x faster than Mutex<std BTree> at 50/50 read/write, and about 2.8-3.2x faster at 90/10.
- Small keys and entries (u64, 16-byte map entries) inserted at random positions with node capacity near 256 (1.08-1.17x faster inserts), or maps that often overwrite existing keys (1.17-1.53x faster updates).

**Skip it when:**
- Workloads dominated by point lookups and deletes. std is faster on contains/get (map get 24.7 ns vs 38.7-46.5 ns) and on remove (1.9-2.6x faster at cap 256, about 5-6x faster for 64-byte records at cap 1024), because a remove shifts up to B elements.
- Large sets filled in descending or low-locality order. In issue #39, 100M reverse-order inserts took 34-61 s vs about 2 s for std, and the author agreed the flat design is less general than a normal B+tree.
- Code that calls range() with bounds that are absent from the collection. Open issue #56 (still in master's source) returns elements outside the range and drops elements inside it, and the concurrent BTreeMultiMap has an open wrong-keys-in-range bug (#68).
- 64-byte records at the default node capacity of 1024. Inserts are 1.9-2.5x slower than std, and the concurrent set at 50/50 (4.0 ms) loses to a plain Mutex<std::BTreeSet> (2.5 ms).
- You need serde or order statistics on the concurrent types (neither is supported), or evidence against real concurrent ordered maps. The only published concurrent baseline is a Mutex-wrapped std tree, and the comparison bench against congee, arctic and WorkTablesIndex has no results in the README.

**Integration:** crate · ftree (always); optional: serde (serde feature); crossbeam-skiplist, crossbeam-utils, parking_lot (concurrent/cdc); fastrand (multimap) · Not documented: no rust-version field, edition 2021 (so at least Rust 1.56). The benchmarks used rustc 1.97.0-nightly, and a migration to edition 2024 is an open PR (#62). · Any (pure Rust, no arch-specific or SIMD code seen)

**Vs siblings:** Pick indexset when you need an in-process, in-memory ordered set/map in Rust with std-style ergonomics, positional indexing, or a simple multi-threaded replacement for Mutex<BTreeMap>. Bf-Tree, the other Rust sibling, is benchmarked as a storage engine against RocksDB and LeanStore. ALEX, PGM-index and the rafaelkallis ART are C++ indexes you would reach through FFI, and they are benchmarked against STX B+Tree or std::map rather than Rust's std.

**Gotchas:**
- The default node capacity is 1024, but most headline wins were measured at 256. At 1024, 64-byte inserts, removes and concurrent 50/50 runs lose badly to std, so call with_maximum_node_size and tune it for your record size and n.
- crates.io 0.16.0 (2026-04-14) is behind master: master's Cargo.toml still says 0.15.0 and the changelog lists the fixes as Unreleased. That release lacks the fix for the node-split panic at small node sizes (#57), the fix for replacing a key during a concurrent split, and the fix for immediate UB from an uninitialized sentinel in BTreeMultiMap::get (#55). The benchmarks ran on unreleased master (7e3ac23).
- From reading src/lib.rs: BTreeSet::get returns the element at the lower-bound position with no equality check, so a missing key that falls between two stored keys appears to return the next larger element. This is the same bug shape as the since-fixed BTreeMap::get/get_mut bugs (#25, #47), so prefer contains() plus a check.
- Concurrent internals, from reading src/concurrent/set.rs: get() returns a Ref that holds the leaf's exclusive mutex (up to B elements), blocking every other thread on that leaf while you hold it. Iterators extend slice lifetimes with unsafe transmute and drop the leaf guard when they move to the next leaf. Each leaf-to-leaf step rescans the skip list from the front, so a full concurrent iteration is quadratic in leaf count. len() locks every leaf. Inserts past the current maximum (monotonic keys) take the global write lock every time.

**Status:** Actively maintained: master's last commit is 2026-08-27, and correctness fixes and a benchmark rework landed in July-August 2026. The newest crates.io release (0.16.0, April 2026, about 196k total downloads) predates those fixes, several range/multimap bugs are still open, and the Apache-2.0 OR MIT license is declared only in Cargo.toml with no LICENSE file in the repo.

[repo](https://github.com/lucidarium-systems/indexset) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lucidarium-systems/indexset#benchmarks)

##### ALEX (Adaptive Learned indEX)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Header-only C++ learned ordered index for numeric keys; beats STX B+Tree up to 4x on in-memory lookups and inserts.

**Beats:** STX B+Tree (std::map-like ordered index); also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), a 2-stage RMI ("Learned Index"), and a Model-enhanced B+Tree — In the SIGMOD'20 paper (single-threaded, Intel Core i9-9900K, 64 GB RAM), ALEX reached up to 4.1x read-only and 4.0x read-write throughput over an STX B+Tree whose page size was grid-searched per dataset and workload, and up to 2.2x over a 2-level RMI Learned Index. The tests used 8-byte keys: 1B longitudes, 200M longlat, 190M lognormal and 200M YCSB keys with 80-byte payloads. The paper names no compiler or flags, does not compare against std::map, and the repo's benchmark runs ALEX alone. GRE (PVLDB'22, gcc 8.3.0 -O3, Xeon Platinum 8268) independently ranked ALEX among the top single-threaded indexes against STX B+Tree, ART and HOT, except on hard data with 50% or more writes.

**Known shortcoming:** Not thread-safe; lookups write stats counters, so even concurrent readers race (the ALEX+ port in GRE declares no license). x86-64 only (x86intrin, cpuid, lzcnt/tzcnt; needs BMI).

**Known shortcoming:** Iterators and payload references dangle after inserts; payload destructors never run, so non-trivial payloads leak. On hard data with 50%+ writes it loses to traditional indexes (GRE); easy-to-hard distribution shift costs up to 52% throughput. Stale since 2024-03 with unanswered memory-blowup and null-child issues; baseline was a page-tuned STX B+Tree, no compiler flags stated.

**How:** ALEX is an updatable Recursive Model Index (RMI). Each internal node holds a linear regression that computes the child slot directly, so no key comparisons happen above the leaves. Leaves are Gapped Arrays filled by model-based inserts, so most keys sit at or near their predicted slot and an exponential search from the prediction finishes in a few steps; a per-leaf bitmap marks gaps, and popcnt/lzcnt/tzcnt find the nearest gap for an insert. Cost models (expected search iterations and key shifts) plus a 'fanout tree' decide the node layout at bulk load and whether a full leaf expands and retrains, splits sideways or splits downward.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded (or externally locked) in-memory ordered map with 8-byte integer or double keys and small fixed-size payloads, where point lookups dominate: the paper reports up to 4.1x read-only throughput over a page-size-tuned STX B+Tree.
- Read-only to read-intensive mixes with inserts (for example 95% reads / 5% inserts): the independent GRE study found single-core learned indexes such as ALEX beat traditional indexes there regardless of how hard the key distribution is.
- Short range scans (up to about 1000 keys) mixed with lookups and inserts: the paper shows up to 2.27x over B+Tree on its 95% scan / 5% insert workload, helped by large leaves (median 161 KB on longitudes).
- Append-heavy keys such as timestamps or sequence IDs: leaves detect append-mostly behavior, and the paper shows up to 3.6x over B+Tree when the remaining keys are inserted in ascending order.
- Memory-constrained cases where you would otherwise pick LIPP: GRE measured ALEX as the most space-efficient of its three top performers, with LIPP using 4-5x more memory.

**Skip it when:**
- Concurrent access: the public code has no locking, and even lookups write per-node statistics. GRE's concurrent port (ALEX+, based on the APEX protocol) lives in a research repo (gre4index/GRE) that declares no license.
- String, composite or custom-ordered keys: a static_assert requires an arithmetic key type and the default AlexCompare comparator.
- Hard, locally nonlinear key distributions with 50% or more writes: GRE found learned indexes lose to traditional indexes there. ALEX's key shifts per insert grow with hardness (42.6 on genome versus 8.1 on covid), and its 99.9th-percentile insert latency is high on osm and genome. The README also warns that extreme outlier keys inflate the key domain and tree depth.
- Workloads whose distribution shifts from easy to hard after bulk load (GRE measured up to a 52% throughput drop), large payloads under heavy writes (payloads are stored inline and copied on every expansion or split; ART matched ALEX on write-only YCSB with 80-byte payloads), and long scans past about 1000 keys, where a B+Tree tuned for scans wins.
- Non-x86 targets: the code includes x86intrin.h, runs inline cpuid assembly and calls _lzcnt_u64/_tzcnt_u64/_mm_popcnt_u64 unconditionally, so aarch64 (Apple Silicon, Graviton) needs porting.

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond the C++ standard library and x86 intrinsics headers (doctest is downloaded by CMake only for the unit tests) · C++14 (README and CMakeLists). The shipped CMake uses -O3 -march=native for GCC/Clang and /O2 /arch:AVX2 for MSVC. The CPU and flags must enable POPCNT and LZCNT/TZCNT (BMI, Haswell or later), or builds fail with 'target specific option mismatch' (issues #13, #31). C++20 against libc++ will probably not compile: ALEX uses std::allocator::rebind and destroy, which the libc++ headers declare only for C++17 and earlier (inferred from the headers, not built). · x86-64 only (Linux, Intel macOS, Windows/MSVC); no aarch64 code path

**Vs siblings:** Pick ALEX over LIPP when memory or a path to concurrency matters: GRE measured LIPP at 4-5x ALEX's memory and found LIPP scales poorly when parallelized, while ALEX+ scales well. Pick LIPP or CARMI when raw single-threaded lookup speed is all that counts (their catalog entries claim up to 2.8x and on average 1.9x over ALEX), PGM-index for write-only or static data (GRE saw PGM with the best insert throughput at 100% writes but lookups dominated by ALEX), and ART Synchronized when you need a concurrent index today.

**Gotchas:**
- Inserts shift keys inside a leaf, and expansions or splits allocate new slot arrays and free the old ones. Iterators and payload references (from operator[], at() or iterator payload()) can therefore dangle after any insert, unlike std::map. The repo does not document these invalidation rules.
- Payload slots are default-constructed with placement new and freed with deallocate(); neither resize nor the leaf destructor calls payload destructors. Use trivially destructible payloads (integers, POD structs, raw pointers); a std::string payload would leak.
- Gap slots after a leaf's largest key hold std::numeric_limits<T>::max() as an end sentinel, and find_key compares slot contents without checking the gap bitmap. Treat max() as a reserved key value (inferred from the source, not documented).
- bulk_load() expects sorted input and silently does nothing if the index is not empty or num_keys <= 0. Key counts are int, so one index cannot exceed about 2.1 billion keys. The paper's '800x-2000x smaller index' counts inner nodes only; leaves start 70% full, and GRE found that no learned index saves more than 3.2x end to end versus traditional indexes.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit is 2024-03-12 (bug-fix PR #29), and issues about runaway memory on insert (#30) and unassigned child pointers in expand_root (#26) have no maintainer reply. It is MIT-licensed and six headers, so it is easy to vendor on x86-64 with C++14/17.

[repo](https://github.com/microsoft/ALEX) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08898)

##### APEX (learned index on persistent memory)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Persistent, concurrent learned index for Intel Optane PM; up to 3.8x faster inserts than FAST+FAIR and other PM B+-trees.

**Beats:** FAST+FAIR (also compared against LB+-Tree, DPTree, uTree, FPTree, BzTree) — These are the authors' single-thread microbenchmarks on a 24-core Xeon Gold 6252 with 768 GB Optane DCPMM in App Direct mode, compiled with GCC 10.2: 100M bulk-loaded 8-byte keys followed by 100M operations. APEX inserts are up to 3.8x faster than FAST+FAIR (up to 15x vs BzTree) and lookups up to 4.1x faster, but on FB inserts beat FAST+FAIR by only 1.18x and lose to LB+-Tree and DPTree. Every baseline is another PM tree, not a stdlib container, and the authors' modified competitor code is not in the repo, so the comparison cannot be rerun from public code.

**Known shortcoming:** The public harness runs only APEX (competitor code is linked upstream only). The 15x is vs BzTree on inserts; vs FAST+FAIR it is 3.8x. Requires Intel Optane persistent memory.

**Known shortcoming:** Requires Intel Optane in App Direct/DAX mode (Optane discontinued in 2022); the pool path/size/address are hard-coded in allocator.h and globals in headers limit it to one translation unit. On hard (FB-like) keys its inserts lose to LB+-Tree (1.3x faster at 24 threads) and DPTree.

**Known shortcoming:** Open bugs: persist race (#7, unanswered), empty-index hang (#1; fix PR #9 unmerged), Count-error exit (#3); bulk_load segfault (#5) closed without a fix. No merge/shrink on erase; range_scan_by_key is a stub; numeric keys of <=8 B only. Code inactive since 2021-09.

**How:** Each data node's linear model predicts a slot (ALEX-style model-based search). ALEX's gapped arrays shift elements on insert; APEX instead uses probe-and-stash, which probes at most 16 slots (two 256-byte Optane XPLines) and then falls back to a stash array, so most inserts cost one PM write. DRAM-resident accelerators hold 1-byte fingerprints and overflow-bucket pointers for every 16 slots and compare them with SSE, which skips useless PM reads. Data nodes are capped at 256 KB (inner nodes at 16 MB) to keep structural changes cheap, and reads are lock-free, validated by one optimistic version lock per 256 records. Lazy recovery compares a global version number with per-node version numbers and defers repair work to the first access of each node.

**Use it when:**
- You already run Intel Optane DCPMM in App Direct mode and need a persistent, concurrent ordered index on 8-byte integer or double keys with 8-byte payloads (inline or pointer).
- Point lookups, updates, deletes and short scans dominate, on keys that fit piecewise-linear models (geo coordinates, lognormal, YCSB-style IDs). In the paper, lookups scale almost linearly up to 24 physical cores.
- Restart time matters: the paper measures about 42 ms recovery whether the index holds 50M or 150M keys, then under 0.35 s of warm-up with 24 threads (up to 5.2 s single-threaded).
- You want a reference design or research baseline for persistent learned indexes (probe-and-stash, rebuildable DRAM accelerators, crash-consistent structural changes).

**Skip it when:**
- You have no Optane: 3D XPoint/Optane was discontinued in July 2022. On DRAM or a RAM disk APEX runs but its persistence buys nothing, so ALEX or LIPP is the simpler choice.
- Your keys are hard to fit, like the FB user-ID set: there APEX inserts are 5.77% slower than LB+-Tree and 42% slower than DPTree, trees get deeper (3.13 levels on average) and scans slow down on long overflow buckets.
- Your insert bursts split nodes heavily at high thread counts: with nearly full nodes at 24 threads, LB+-Tree beat APEX by 1.3x.
- You need string or variable-length keys, duplicate keys, or payloads larger than 8 bytes. A static_assert limits keys to arithmetic types, and duplicates need a pointer to a linked list as the payload.
- You need production-grade crash consistency: open issue #7 (2024) reports that searches can return inserts and updates that are not yet persisted. Also still open: inserting into an empty index hangs (#1) and an out-of-range insert pattern hits a 'Count error' exit (#3). A 2024 comment on issue #5 reports a bulk_load segfault; the issue was closed by its reporter with no fix.

**Integration:** source-drop · PMDK libpmemobj/libpmem from a pinned fork (HaoPatrick/pmdk, addr-patch branch; the allocator calls pmemobj_create_addr/pmemobj_open_addr) and XiangpengHao/epoch-reclaimer (headers, master branch), both fetched from GitHub at CMake configure time. The benchmark also links TBB, PAPI, tcmalloc_minimal and libnuma. · C++14 and CMake 3.12+. Tested only with GCC 10.2 on Linux 5.10.11; the README requires kernel >= 4.17 and glibc >= 2.29. · x86-64 Linux only: needs the CLWB instruction (inline asm) and SSE/AVX2 intrinsics, and builds with -march=native. Persistence needs Optane DCPMM in App Direct mode on a DAX-mounted filesystem; the author suggests a RAM disk for functional testing without PM.

**Vs siblings:** Choose APEX over DPTree on PM when you need double keys, deletes, instant recovery and faster lookups and scans: per the APEX paper, DPTree's code lacks double keys, delete and recovery. DPTree still inserts about 42% faster on hard-to-fit data like FB. Without Optane persistence, use ALEX (the DRAM index APEX is built on) or LIPP instead.

**Gotchas:**
- The PM pool path (/mnt/pmem0/baotong/template.data), its 40 GB size and its fixed mapping address are constants in src/util/allocator.h, so you must edit them. There is one static pool per process, and if the pool file already exists the benchmark takes the recovery path, so delete it before a fresh run.
- The headers define non-inline global variables and static data members (allocator.h, apex_base.h, apex.h), so include them from exactly one translation unit or expect duplicate-symbol link errors.
- API semantics: insert does not overwrite an existing key (it returns false). range_scan_by_key is a stub that returns 0. range_scan_by_size allocates its result with new[] if you pass nullptr. Every call's epoch flag defaults to false, which skips the reclamation guard, so pass true under concurrency.
- Erase never shrinks or merges nodes (merge() prints FATAL and exits), so deleted space is not reclaimed. size() is approximate because each thread batches its key-count updates in chunks of 2^19. Internal consistency checks call exit(-1) instead of returning an error.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last code change was in September 2021 (only README edits in 2023), a 2024 crash-consistency bug report is unanswered and a 2026 fix PR is unmerged. It is MIT-licensed but targets hardware discontinued in 2022, so treat it as a research reference rather than a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/baotonglu/apex) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.00683)

##### ART Synchronized (Optimistic Lock Coupling / ROWEX for Adaptive Radix Tree)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

In-memory concurrent Adaptive Radix Tree (OLC and ROWEX variants); roughly 1.5-3x Masstree's throughput on 8-byte integer keys.

**Beats:** Masstree (concurrent B-tree/trie hybrid key-value index) -- not one of the assignment's named baselines, recorded honestly as the incumbent the paper actually benchmarks against — The DaMoN 2016 paper benchmarked the ART variants against Masstree (masstree-beta), all using jemalloc, on a single-socket Xeon E5-2687W v3 (10 cores/20 threads, 25 MB L3). It does not state the compiler or flags, publishes no harness, and calls the comparison not apples-to-apples. On 50M random 8-byte integers at 20 threads, OLC and ROWEX reached about 82-86M lookups/s vs about 29M, 56M inserts/s vs 24M, and 38M removes/s vs 26M (read off Figure 5). On string keys at 20 threads, Masstree won on Wikipedia titles and URLs, genome lookups were roughly even, and ART won clearly only on genome inserts (about 29M vs 7M).

**Known shortcoming:** The '2x on genome and URL keys' claim is wrong: Masstree wins on URL and Wikipedia keys and genome lookups roughly tie; the real win is 50M integer keys at 20 threads (~3x lookups, ~2.3x inserts, Fig. 5). A memory-corruption fix landed 2026-05-25 (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** Keys aren't stored: callers must supply a loadKey(TID) callback; TIDs are 63-bit with 0 meaning not found; no upsert, and a duplicate insert reads past the key end. Open author-confirmed infinite loop in OLC lookupRange under concurrent writes (#6); inserted keys not found on the FB dataset (#5). x86-64 only (SSE2, no fallback); needs TBB and jemalloc; an idle ThreadInfo pins the epoch so no nodes are freed; OLC restarts have no backoff or cap, so hot writes can starve lookups. The GRE 24-thread winner was a modified fork, not this repo. Research code, mostly dormant.

**How:** ART keeps the tree shallow for fewer cache misses. It uses adaptive node sizes (Node4/16/48/256, with an SSE2 compare in Node16), path compression and lazy leaf expansion. Optimistic Lock Coupling puts a 64-bit version/lock/obsolete word in each node. Readers never write shared memory: they re-validate versions and restart from the root on conflict. That avoids the cache-line ping-pong that ruins classic lock coupling, which in the paper's table goes from 418 to 2787 cycles per lookup between 1 and 20 threads. ROWEX (Read-Optimized Write EXclusion) takes locks only for writers and makes every node change atomic for readers (Node4/16 append unsorted, child pointers are atomic, prefix and length are updated in one store), so lookups never block or restart. Epoch-based reclamation frees replaced nodes. Against Masstree, the paper attributes the integer-key gap to 4.8x fewer instructions and 3.6x fewer L3 misses per lookup.

**Use it when:**
- A multi-threaded in-memory ordered index inside a database or storage engine that already has row IDs or record pointers, so loadKey can rebuild the key from the TID.
- Short fixed-length keys (for example 8-byte integers stored big-endian) with many threads running lookups, inserts and removes. At 20 threads on 50M random keys, the paper measured about 82-86M lookups/s and 56M inserts/s, 2-3x Masstree.
- Read-heavy workloads with writers on hot keys: use the ROWEX variant. Its lookups never block and stayed around 15-18M ops/s under extreme Zipf skew, where OLC lookups dropped to about 10M (Figure 6).
- Low-contention workloads where simpler code matters: use OLC. It has slightly faster lookups (about 7%, per the paper) and less code than ROWEX (148 vs 200 lines for insert).
- Single-socket x86-64 Linux deployments that can take on TBB and jemalloc.

**Skip it when:**
- Longer string keys such as Wikipedia titles (22 bytes on average) or URLs (63 bytes): in the paper's own Figure 7 at 20 threads, Masstree beat it on both lookups and inserts.
- When you need a self-contained key-value map. Keys are not stored, there is no update or upsert API, values are limited to 63-bit TIDs, and lookup() returns 0 for 'not found'.
- Variable-length keys where one key can be a prefix of another (strings without a terminator). The README and issue #8 say this is unsupported by design, and such inserts crash.
- Range scans on the OLC tree running alongside inserts and removes: open issue #6, confirmed by the author in 2021, shows lookupRange (getChildren, findStart, findEnd) can loop forever on obsolete nodes. The single-threaded ART's lookupRange is commented out (issue #9).
- Non-x86 targets, MSVC, multi-socket scaling, or memory-constrained sparse key sets. Node16 uses SSE2 intrinsics with no fallback. The GRE study (PVLDB'22) found ART the least space-efficient traditional index on sparse keys, and saw ART-OLC struggle to scale across sockets on dense-key datasets.

**Integration:** static lib: the CMake target ARTSynchronized builds all three Tree.cpp files. Each Tree.cpp #includes its node .cpp files and Epoche.cpp, so projects such as GRE vendor it as a source drop by #including Tree.cpp directly. · Intel TBB (Epoche.h uses tbb::enumerable_thread_specific; the example uses tbb::parallel_for), jemalloc (linked by CMake and used for the paper's numbers), and pthreads · C++14 (CMake sets -std=c++14 -march=native) with GCC or Clang, since the code uses __builtin_ctz and __builtin_bswap64; CMake 2.8+. The README warns that some g++ versions fail to link jemalloc (check with ldd or LD_PRELOAD it). A g++ build error was fixed in December 2019 (PR #3). · x86-64 only in practice: Node16 includes <emmintrin.h> with no scalar fallback, and leaf tagging assumes 64-bit pointers and TIDs. Install instructions cover only Debian/Ubuntu Linux. The paper's benchmarks ran on a single-socket Haswell-EP.

**Vs siblings:** Pick this when several threads must insert, remove and look up in one ordered index at the same time. The rafaelkallis ART sibling is a single-threaded std::map-like container. GRE notes that, as published, updatable learned indexes such as ALEX and LIPP lacked concurrency (it built its own ALEX+ and LIPP+). In GRE's 24-thread heatmap, ART-OLC (from a modified fork of this repo) was one of three winners and led write-heavy workloads on easy datasets, while the learned indexes kept the edge on read-only and single-threaded numeric workloads.

**Gotchas:**
- The leaf is the TID with bit 63 set as a tag, so TIDs must fit in 63 bits (a comment in example.cpp notes that random keys lose their top bit). TID 0 cannot be told apart from 'not found'. remove(key, tid) deletes only when the stored TID matches.
- Integer keys must be byte-swapped to big-endian for correct order (the example uses __builtin_bswap64). Inserting a key that already exists is not handled: the leaf-split loop compares bytes past the end of the key, and ROWEX guards this only with a debug-build assert.
- ThreadInfo binds to the creating thread's TBB thread-local deletion list, so do not share one across threads. A thread that holds a ThreadInfo but goes idle keeps its old epoch published, which blocks freeing of replaced nodes for every thread until it runs another operation or destroys the ThreadInfo.
- OLC readers restart from the root whenever they see a locked node, with no backoff and no restart limit. The paper suggests capping restarts and falling back to write locks, but the repo does not do this, so writes to hot keys can starve OLC lookups.

**Status:** Research code that has been dormant apart from occasional merges: since 2016 it received a g++ build fix (2019), a README note (2020), a no-upper-bound range scan (2022) and a May 2026 fix for a new/delete type mismatch that affects only the unsynchronized ART. Issues #5 (inserted keys not found on the FB dataset) and #6 (OLC range-scan infinite loop) remain open. The code is Apache-2.0 (per the LICENSE file; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) and small enough to vendor, as GRE did through a fork.

[repo](https://github.com/flode/ARTSynchronized) · [benchmark](https://db.in.tum.de/~leis/papers/artsync.pdf)

##### Bf-Tree  `Rust (prototype, code not released)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Microsoft Research's larger-than-memory concurrent B-Tree for small records, with record-level caching; beats RocksDB and page-cached B-Trees.

**Beats:** RocksDB (commit 54d6286); the authors' own conventional B-Tree and Bδ-Tree in Rust; Leanstore (commit 677126c); TwoTree — In the peer-reviewed VLDB 2024 paper, run with 31 threads on a CloudLab sm110p node (32 hyper-threads at 2.4 GHz, CPU model not named; 128 GB RAM; PCIe 4.0 NVMe; Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15), with 200M 32-byte records, Zipf 0.9 and a 2 GB cache, Bf-Tree was about 2.5x RocksDB (commit 54d6286, direct I/O, WAL and fsync off) on scans, about 6x the authors' own Rust B-Tree (Bf-Tree minus mini-pages) on writes, and about 2x both on point lookups. Its p99 read latency was 70 us against RocksDB's 131 us. On scans all the B-Tree variants performed about the same, and in memory it roughly matched Leanstore. The Rust version was not stated, logging was disabled for every system, and the released benchmark crate has not been shown to reproduce these figures.

**Known shortcoming:** The 6x write gain is vs the authors' own B-tree; code is now public at microsoft/bf-tree (MIT).

**Known shortcoming:** The 2.5x scan gain is vs RocksDB only (WAL and fsync off); B-tree variants tie on scans. Keys over 16 B are rejected by default; read() panics if the buffer is too small; the default backend is std::fs, not the paper's io_uring. Open bugs: scan stack overflow on tombstones (#39), panic after snapshot recovery (PR #38), deadlocks reported with WAL on. Durable only via explicit snapshots; tested on Linux only; needs Rust >=1.87.

**How:** The core idea is 'mini-pages': variable-size in-memory buffers of 64 B to 4 KB that sit in front of each 4 KB on-disk leaf. Each one holds only the hot records for that leaf plus buffered dirty writes, and it grows, shrinks and is merged back in a batch on eviction. This gives record-level caching and write buffering in one structure, so a buffer pool of whole pages holding a few hot rows each is not needed. The mini-pages live in a circular-buffer allocator inspired by FASTER's hybrid log, which approximates LRU with a 10% 'second-chance' copy-on-access region. Other techniques are phantom records that cache negative lookups, inner nodes pinned in memory with optimistic latch coupling, prefix compression and look-ahead bytes, and, in the paper's setup, io_uring kernel-polling direct I/O with zero syscalls.

**Use it when:**
- Skewed (Zipf-like) point-lookup plus update workloads on small records (the paper uses 16 B keys and 16 B values; the README targets about 100 B) where the dataset is several times larger than the RAM you can give the cache.
- Mixed read/write/scan workloads where an LSM (RocksDB) hurts scans and a page-cached B-Tree hurts random small writes. The paper shows it as the only system strong on all three.
- Linux servers with modern NVMe SSDs whose parallel random 4 KB writes run close to sequential throughput, where you can opt into the IoUringPolling/IoUringBlocking or StdDirect backends.
- High-thread-count embedded use from Rust: BfTree is Send + Sync, all operations take &self, and throughput scaled up to 31 threads until the SSD saturated.
- Secondary-index-style data with keys of 16 bytes or less by default (configurable up to 2020 B) where record-level caching beats caching whole 4 KB pages.

**Skip it when:**
- Large records: the authors' own README says large records perform like ordinary B-Trees or LSM-Trees, so the advantage disappears.
- Uniformly random access: in the paper every system does poorly because caching cannot help, and the gap narrows when most of the data fits in memory.
- When you need a production-grade durable store with transactions or crash-safe reopen: the WAL is off by default, and state survives restarts only through explicit snapshots (issue #9). An HN tester reported deadlocks with the WAL enabled (Jan 2026), and an open PR (#38, Aug 2026) fixes a panic when inserting after recovering from a CPR snapshot.
- Deletion-heavy workloads with long range scans: open issue #39 (v0.5.6) says ScanIter::next recurses once per tombstone or empty leaf and can overflow the stack. The fix (PR #40) is not merged.
- Older or consumer SSDs where random 4 KB writes are much slower than sequential ones. Leaf pages are written in place, and the docs flag possible SSD garbage-collection burden as future work.

**Integration:** crate · rand, serde, serde_json, toml, thread_local, cfg-if; Linux adds io-uring and libc; Windows adds windows-sys; optional tracing, hdrhistogram, chrono, auto_ops and variant_count behind the metrics/tracing features · Stable Rust, edition 2021. No rust-version is declared and rust-toolchain.toml says only channel=stable. The source uses usize::is_multiple_of, which was stabilized in Rust 1.87. · Linux is the only platform the README calls rigorously tested (CI runs only on ubuntu-22.04 x86-64). Windows and macOS are said to be supported, but the io_uring and direct-I/O backends are Linux-only and the benchmarks run only on Linux. CPU architecture support is not documented (issue #6 is open). SPDK support is experimental and for developers only.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over redb when the working set is much larger than RAM, records are small and access is skewed, and you can live without redb's ACID transactions and crash-safe reopen. Pick it over in-memory ordered indexes like indexset or the ART variants when the data does not fit in memory. Stay with RocksDB-derived siblings (TerarkDB, MountDB) if you need RocksDB's API and operational tooling.

**Gotchas:**
- By default keys over 16 bytes are rejected: cb_max_key_len defaults to 16 and insert returns LeafInsertResult::InvalidKV. Records must also be between cb_min_record_size (default 4 B) and cb_max_record_size (default 1952 B), with hard caps of 2020 B per key and 16332 B per value. Raise these limits in Config before loading data.
- read() copies into a caller buffer and, per its own doc comment, panics if the buffer is too small. Invalid Config values also trigger assert! panics while the tree is built, not only Result errors.
- The default storage backend is plain std::fs::File (StorageBackend::Std) with a 32 MB circular buffer. The paper's numbers used io_uring kernel polling with direct I/O and a 2 GB cache, so you must pick the backend and size explicitly to get comparable results.
- Snapshot files write BfTreeMeta as a raw repr(C) struct with no serialization, so portability across architectures or versions is not documented. Only one snapshot can run at a time, and scan_mut_* is refused in cache-only mode.

**Status:** The code at microsoft/bf-tree (MIT, crate bf-tree 0.5.6, about 313k downloads, about 1.07k stars) has been actively maintained since its public release in December 2025, with the last commit on 2026-08-19. It is usable as a crate but still research-grade: open bugs cover scan stack overflow and panics after snapshot recovery, and the record's repo_url points at the docs-only repo, which still calls the code internal.

[repo](https://github.com/microsoft/bf-tree) · [benchmark](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p3442-hao.pdf)

##### Bourbon (learned index for LSM-trees, OSDI'20 artifact)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

LevelDB/WiscKey-based LSM key-value store that swaps SSTable index search for per-file linear models; 1.23-1.78x faster lookups than WiscKey.

**Beats:** WiscKey (the authors' LevelDB-derived LSM with key-value separation; no direct stock-LevelDB or RocksDB comparison) — The OSDI'20 paper ran 10M in-memory read-only lookups with 16 B integer keys and 64 B values on six datasets (four synthetic 64M-key sets, Amazon Reviews 33.5M, NY OSM 21.9M). Bourbon's file models (delta = 8) averaged about 2.65-3.64 us per lookup, 1.23-1.78x lower latency than WiscKey, the authors' LevelDB-derived key-value-separated LSM built from the same codebase. The machine was a 20-core Xeon E5-2660 with 160 GB RAM and a SATA SSD (an Optane SSD for the fast-storage runs); the compiler is not stated, and there is no RocksDB or stock-LevelDB head-to-head.

**Known shortcoming:** The only baseline is WiscKey (LevelDB-derived), never RocksDB or stock LevelDB; no compiler stated. github.com/edydfang/bourbon is a third-party course-project copy; the authors' original code is bitbucket.org/daiyifandanny/learned-leveldb.

**Known shortcoming:** Wrong-result bug in the OSDI snapshot: a duplicate user key within one SSTable gives a NaN PLR slope and over 3% bad Gets on a real trace (PR #7; fixed only in a fork in 2023). Value-log GC was never ported, so overwrites and deletes never free space.

**Known shortcoming:** Keys must be fixed-width ASCII-decimal integers; x86 only (rdtscp); mode is set by process globals (one DB per process). From code reading, iterators return raw value-log pointers and Put/Get touch the value-log buffer outside the DB mutex, so concurrent use looks unsafe. Hard to reproduce: segfault issue #6 open and datasets never published.

**How:** Each SSTable gets a greedy piecewise linear regression model (GreedyPLR, adapted from RyanMarcus/plr) with error bound delta = 8. A lookup binary-searches the model's segments, predicts the key's position plus or minus delta, and reads only that byte range of the data block. Because entries are fixed-size, this replaces the index-block and data-block binary searches and also cuts the bytes loaded. A cost-benefit analyzer waits T_wait = 50 ms after a file is created, then learns the file only if the estimated lookup-time savings (per-level stats for positive and negative lookups) outweigh the training cost, so short-lived files under writes are skipped. The paper prefers file models to whole-level models because levels change constantly under writes; level learning only pays off when read-only.

**Use it when:**
- Read-dominated LSM workloads where the working set is in the page cache or on Optane-class storage, so indexing dominates lookup time: about 1.6x on YCSB-C and 1.23-1.78x on in-memory read-only lookups vs WiscKey.
- Fixed-width integer keys (zero-padded decimal strings such as the paper's 16 B keys) with smooth distributions. Fewer PLR segments means bigger gains: the linear dataset, at one segment per file, got 1.78x.
- Point lookups and very short scans: 1.90x at range length 1 on the Amazon Reviews data, falling to 1.15x at 100 items.
- Skewed (zipfian) reads on a memory-limited SATA-SSD machine where the hot set stays cached: 1.25x lower latency.
- Reproducing or extending learned-index-in-LSM research. The repo ships the WiscKey baseline mode (-m 8), the read_cold driver and the scripts/run_*.sh experiment scripts.

**Skip it when:**
- Production storage. It is an abandoned research artifact configured through global variables. Value-log garbage collection was never ported (Vlog.h: 'Bourbon doesn't test on deletion'), so overwrites and deletes never reclaim space.
- String or variable-length keys, or key compression. The paper says these are unsupported, and the code turns keys into integers by parsing ASCII decimal digits (SliceToInteger).
- Write-heavy workloads. Writes are not sped up, and YCSB-A/F gain only 1.06-1.18x. Always re-learning at 50% writes did more total work than plain WiscKey, and level learning ran slower than baseline (0.87x).
- Uniform random reads over data much larger than RAM on a SATA SSD. I/O dominates and the gain is only 1.04x.
- If you need proof it beats RocksDB or stock LevelDB. The paper and repo compare only against their own WiscKey port, whatever the abstract's 'production LSMs' wording says.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake target 'leveldb', a modified LevelDB 1.22; shared build via BUILD_SHARED_LIBS) plus the read_cold benchmark driver · Threads (required). snappy, crc32c and tcmalloc are auto-detected and optional. cxxopts is bundled (mod/cxxopts.hpp) for read_cold. · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake >= 3.7. Compiler and version not documented. · x86-64 Linux in practice. mod/util.h includes <x86intrin.h> and uses __rdtscp, and the experiment scripts drop caches with sudo via /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches. Windows and non-x86 builds not documented.

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued learned indexes (PGM-index, RMI, RadixSpline, ALEX, LIPP) are in-memory structures over sorted arrays. Pick Bourbon only when you want learned indexing inside a persistent LSM store with write-aware re-learning, mainly as a research base. To embed an index, use PGM-index or ALEX. For a production LSM that measurably beats RocksDB, TerarkDB is the catalogued choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Wrong-result bug in the OSDI snapshot. If the same user key is written twice before a flush, both versions land in one SSTable, the PLR computes a NaN slope, and Get can fail. PR #7 (merged 2023-09-06) reported more than 3% bad Gets on a real-world trace. Only this fork's main branch has the fix (commit 0cd4715). The 'original bourbon' commit ad6abcb and the Bitbucket artifact (last updated 2020-10-05) predate it.
- Fixed-size keys are assumed. generate_key zero-pads decimal keys to key_size, and block entry count and entry size are recorded once in globals, so the byte-range read assumes every entry has the same size.
- Experiment config is fiddly. Mixed read-write runs need a rebuild with -DLEVEL_SWITCH=ON -DINTERNAL_TIMER_SWITCH=ON (CS736_README). The reported numbers use file models (--change_level_load, called 'Sazerac-File' in the README). The CPU frequency used to turn rdtscp cycles into time for the learning timers is hardcoded (reference_frequency = 2.6).
- Hard to reproduce. Issue #6 reports segfaults in scripts/run_load_order.sh with no fix. The datasets are not published (issues #5, #8). The artifact's ready-made CloudLab machine was only for OSDI reviewers and UW-Madison students (issues #2, #3).

**Status:** Abandoned: the fork's last commit is 2023-09-06 (a bug-fix PR) and the authors' Bitbucket original was last updated 2020-10-05; the code is BSD-3-Clause and about 5K LOC on top of a WiscKey port, fine for research but not production-ready (no value-log GC, global config).

[repo](https://bitbucket.org/daiyifandanny/learned-leveldb) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/dai)

##### CARMI (Cache-Aware RMI)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Header-only, updatable learned index (a cost-model-built RMI) for numeric keys that beats STX B+ Tree and ALEX on in-memory lookups.

**Beats:** STX B+Tree and ALEX; also beats RMI on the SOSD benchmark platform — In the authors' own single-threaded runs on an AMD Ryzen 3700X (Ubuntu; compiler and flags not stated, the repo's CMake builds Release), over seven ~67M-key datasets and five 100K-operation workloads, CARMI averaged 2.2x (up to 4.2x) the throughput of STX B+ Tree with 512-byte nodes and 1.9x (up to 7.2x) that of ALEX, using about 0.77x the B+ Tree's memory. Ported to SOSD (200M-key amzn/face/wiki/osmc, 10M uniform lookups), it averaged about 1.2x faster than a tuned RMI, but ART was faster on face32 and RMI/RS came within about 1-5 ns on face64 and wiki; no std:: container was benchmarked.

**Known shortcoming:** Real datasets have 67,108,864 records, not ~10^8 keys; 'beats all on SOSD' is overstated (ART wins face32); no compiler stated.

**Known shortcoming:** No thread safety; numeric keys only; DBL_MAX cast as the empty-slot sentinel is UB for integer keys. insert() has no duplicate-key check (stores a second entry and returns true, unlike std::map). In SOSD it uses among the most memory (3918/5481 MB vs RMI 2472/3143, B+Tree 2657/3541); the '0.77x B+Tree memory' comes only from the authors' harness. Build takes 0.3-3.2 min vs ~10 s for a B+Tree; knobs are constexpr and repo defaults differ from the paper. README references a missing header; the public harness runs CARMI only and the SOSD port isn't published, so comparisons can't be reproduced. Abandoned since 2022-01, no CI, unit tests commented out.

**How:** Every node that holds a model is exactly 64 bytes, so each inner step costs at most one cache miss, and each leaf is a 'cache-friendly array' (a 64-byte header of block minimum keys over a few 256-byte sorted data blocks), so the last-mile search scans one block instead of doing RMI/ALEX-style error-bounded binary search. A cost model (measured per-node latency + lambda × space, with the entropy of child partition sizes as the measure of how well a node splits the data) drives a hybrid dynamic-programming/greedy construction that picks each subtree's node type and fanout. The result is a flat tree: average depth 2.1 in the paper, against 2.5 for ALEX and 7.3 for the B+ Tree. The piecewise-linear root also has a prefetch model, which issues __builtin_prefetch for the predicted data block while the leaf is being fetched.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded, in-memory ordered index over 64-bit numeric keys (double or uint64) with small fixed-size numeric values, at roughly 10^7-10^8 keys, where point lookups and short range scans dominate.
- Real-world key sets whose CDF is locally non-linear (OSM coordinates, user IDs, timestamps), where RMI and ALEX degrade. The paper reports about 1.5x over ALEX on OSMC/Facebook read-only, and about 1.2x over a hand-tuned RMI on SOSD.
- Mixed read/insert workloads (50/50, 95/5, inserts clustered in one key range) where you can bulk-load first and supply representative sample insert keys. The paper reports 2.2x over the B+ Tree and 3.0x over ALEX on write-heavy workloads.
- Indexes that are rebuilt rarely (the authors suggest off-peak rebuilds), so a construction step of several minutes is acceptable in exchange for faster lookups.
- Learned-index research or prototyping where you want an explicit time/space knob (lambda) and swappable node types.

**Skip it when:**
- Any concurrent access. The headers contain no locks or atomics, and the paper describes read/write-lock concurrency only as a possible extension.
- String, composite or other non-arithmetic keys or values. The paper states that only numeric key types are supported, and the code relies on DBL_MAX sentinels and key+1 arithmetic.
- Memory-tight deployments. SOSD Table 4 shows CARMI at 3918/5481 MB (uint32/uint64) against 2472/3143 MB for RMI and 2657/3541 MB for the B+ Tree, over 2289/3052 MB of raw data. The headline '0.77x the B+ Tree's memory' comes only from the authors' own harness.
- Fast startup or frequent rebuilds. Construction took 0.3-3.2 minutes on the 67M-key datasets, against about 10 s for STX B+ Tree and 20 s for ALEX.
- Production code that needs a maintained dependency. The repo has had no commits since Jan 2022, has 10 stars, no releases, no CI, and its unit tests are commented out in CMakeLists.txt.

**Integration:** header-only · none (C++ standard library only; the bundled STX B+ Tree and the ALEX/RadixSpline pointers exist only for the experiments) · C++17 (CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 and a Release build); no compiler versions documented · Linux/macOS with GCC or Clang (__builtin_prefetch). A Windows branch uses _mm_prefetch, so x86 only there. No SIMD is required. The per-node latency constants in params.h are the authors' measurements; the repo tells you to re-run src/profiler on your own machine.

**Vs siblings:** Pick CARMI over PGM-index when you need an updatable, std::map-like container with values stored inline, tuned for skewed real-world keys, and you can accept more memory and minutes-long builds; PGM-index is maintained, orders of magnitude smaller and the better fit for static or space-critical use.
