Choose an ART (such as rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree) instead when keys are byte strings or dense 32-bit IDs: SOSD's ART beat CARMI on face32 (182 vs 187 ns).

**Gotchas:**
- Empty slots are marked with static_cast<KeyType>(DBL_MAX), and values with static_cast<ValueType>(DBL_MAX). During construction, a value equal to that sentinel is treated as an insert placeholder. For integer types the cast is out of range (undefined behaviour), so keep keys and values away from the type's maximum and check what your compiler produces.
- insert() has no existing-key check. It stores a second entry and returns true, where std::map would return false; erase(key) is documented as removing all entries with that key.
- Block size, the DP/greedy switch threshold, external leaf capacity and the latency constants are all constexpr in params.h, which also has a global '#define DEBUG'. Tuning means editing the header. The repo defaults also differ from the paper's appendix (kAlgorithmThreshold 60000 vs kDPThreshold 512; external leaf capacity 1024 vs 512). The two-iterator constructor derives lambda from the data size, while the paper tuned lambda per dataset.
- The README says to include ./include/carmi_common.h, but that file does not exist. Include carmi_map.h or carmi_external_map.h instead. The public experiment harness runs only CARMI (no B+ Tree/ALEX drivers), and the SOSD port is in neither this repo nor upstream learnedsystems/SOSD, so the comparisons cannot be reproduced out of the box.

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2022 (a single author, 10 stars, no issues filed), but it is MIT-licensed, header-only C++17 and small enough to vendor as research code: numeric keys only, single-threaded, parameters compiled in.

[repo](https://github.com/embryo-labs/CARMI) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00858)

##### CHT (Compact Hist-Tree)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Header-only C++ compact Hist-Tree: a flattened radix-histogram table over sorted integer keys, beating RMI/PGM/RadixSpline lookup latency.

**Beats:** RMI, PGM-index, RadixSpline (learned index baselines) — The 1.1-1.8x (RMI), 1.7-2.5x (PGM-index) and 1.2-2.7x (RadixSpline) lookup-latency wins come from Crotty's CIDR 2021 paper. They compare each index's fastest configuration on SOSD's 200M-key amzn/face/osm/wiki sets, compiled with gcc/g++ 9.3.0 (flags unstated) on an AWS c5.4xlarge (Xeon Platinum 8124M), using Crotty's own C implementation rather than this repo. Separately, Maltry & Dittrich (PVLDB 15(5), 2022) benchmarked this exact repo with clang 12.0.1 -O2 on a single thread of a Xeon E5-2620 v4 and found it the fastest index on books, fb and osmc once its index reaches about 100 MiB (graph-only; wiki excluded because of duplicates).

**Known shortcoming:** The paper's numbers are for Crotty's C implementation; this repo is Stoian's C++ port (from PLEX) with no public paper benchmark code or flags, and it does not support duplicate keys.

**Known shortcoming:** An independent check of this exact repo (Maltry & Dittrich, PVLDB 15(5) 2022, clang 12 -O2) finds it fastest on books/fb/osmc only when the index is ~100 MiB or larger (graph only). Duplicate keys give wrong bounds (#4 open); read-only; assert-only input checks; 31-bit positions/node ids cap it at ~2.1B keys; GCC/Clang builtins (no MSVC); builder.h is missing includes; abandoned since 2021-07.

**How:** Each node is an equal-width histogram over a power-of-two key range, so picking a bin is one right shift of (key - min) instead of a comparison or a model evaluation. Bins holding more than max_error keys get a child node, and the rest are terminal. The compact layout flattens all nodes into one array of 32-bit cells. A terminal bin stores the prefix-sum position, flagged in bit 31, and an inner bin stores its child's row, so each level of a lookup is a shift, a load and a flag test. The configurations that tune best use high bin counts, which keeps the tree to a few levels. An optional cache-oblivious (van Emde Boas-style recursive) node order is provided for deep trees, meaning small bin counts or small errors.

**Use it when:**
- Read-only, sorted, duplicate-free 32- or 64-bit unsigned integer keys (SOSD-style books, fb or osm distributions) where lowest lookup latency matters and you can rebuild when the data changes.
- You can afford a large index. In an independent evaluation it was the fastest index on books, fb and osmc at 200M keys, but only from about 100 MiB of index upward.
- Skewed or clustered key distributions where RadixSpline's single radix table degenerates. The PLEX authors' auto-tuner picked CHT over a radix table on the face dataset for exactly this outlier problem.
- You want a tiny, dependency-free header drop with two knobs. SOSD's tuned fastest configurations are a starting point: 1024 bins with error 16 on books and osm, and 256 bins with error 32 on fb.
- You need a secondary radix layer over a small sorted key set, such as spline knots, which is how PLEX uses it.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys with duplicates. Open issue #4 reports wrong search ranges on SOSD's wiki dataset, and the returned bound can silently miss the key. Both the PLEX and Maltry/Dittrich papers had to exclude wiki.
- Any inserts or deletes. The compact layout is build-once. The paper's updatable Hist-Tree is 2-3x slower and is not in this repo.
- Tight memory budgets. At smaller index sizes, RMI, PGM-index and RadixSpline beat it in Maltry & Dittrich's evaluation. The table costs nodes x num_bins x 4 bytes, and a small max_error multiplies the node count.
- Strings, floats or signed keys. Only uint32_t and uint64_t are tested, and binning relies on unsigned subtraction and shifts.
- MSVC/Windows, or when you need a maintained dependency. It uses __builtin_clz/__builtin_clzl, has no releases, has 9 stars and has had no commits since July 2021.

**Integration:** header-only · none (STL only; CMake fetches GoogleTest 1.10.0 only to build the tests) · C++17 (structured bindings, std::optional); GCC or Clang builtins required. Known to build with gcc 9.3 (paper) and clang 12.0.1 (Maltry & Dittrich). · LP64 targets with GCC/Clang (Linux; macOS/AppleClang since the May 2021 ambiguity fix). The headers have no ISA-specific code, though the repo's CMake adds -march=native. MSVC is not supported.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over RadixSpline, RMI and PGM-index when the data is static and duplicate-free and you can spend a 100 MiB-class index for the lowest probe latency, with builds far cheaper than RMI's optimizer. Pick PLEX instead when you want one hyperparameter, a small index or duplicate keys: it embeds this CHT under a spline and auto-tunes it. For updates, use PGM-index, ALEX or LIPP.

**Gotchas:**
- Input validation is assert-only. Release builds do not catch unsorted keys, min/max that don't equal the first/last key, a num_bins that is not a power of two, or a key range smaller than num_bins, and any of these yields wrong bounds.
- Positions and node ids are 31-bit, because bit 31 of each unsigned cell is the leaf flag. That caps the index at about 2.1 billion keys or nodes. A fork (jakubpawlewicz/CHT) adds Builder::CheckFeasible() because some parameter/data combinations make the tree too large.
- builder.h uses std::cerr and std::function but includes neither <iostream> nor <functional>. Include both before it or it may fail to compile.
- The default two-pass Builder copies every key into its own vector and also keeps per-node bin vectors, so peak build memory is well above the final index size. single_pass=true avoids the key copy, but it is ignored, with only a stderr warning, when use_cache (the cache-oblivious layout) is set.

**Status:** Abandoned since July 2021 with the duplicate-key bug (#4) still open, but it is MIT-licensed, under 18 KB of headers and still pinned as a SOSD competitor submodule, so vendoring and patching it is realistic.

[repo](https://github.com/stoianmihail/CHT) · [benchmark](https://cs.brown.edu/people/acrotty/pubs/cidr2021_paper20.pdf)

##### DPTree (Differential Indexing for Persistent Memory)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research persistent-memory index that buffers writes in DRAM; up to 1.82x faster point lookups than FAST+FAIR on Optane.

**Beats:** FAST+FAIR (also FPTree, WORT) — These numbers come from the authors' own PVLDB 13(4) paper: 2x Xeon Platinum 8263C with 512 GB Optane DC PMM (App Direct, ext4-DAX), g++ 6.4 -O3, threads pinned to one socket. With 25M-100M random 64-bit keys and 16-byte entries, single-threaded DPTree had 1.27-1.43x lower insert latency and up to 1.82x faster point lookups than FAST+FAIR, while scans were up to 1.1x slower. At 50M keys and up to 32 threads it reached up to 1.36x InsertOnly and 1.32-1.58x ReadOnly throughput over FAST+FAIR. FPTree was the authors' own reimplementation, the baseline harness is not public, and no stdlib comparison was made.

**Known shortcoming:** The 1.82/1.85/2.19x are point-lookup gains vs FAST+FAIR/FPTree/WORT respectively; scans are up to 1.1x slower than FAST+FAIR. Baseline code not public; requires Intel Optane persistent memory.

**Known shortcoming:** No recovery code (issue #4 open; confirmed by the APEX paper), and its 'PM' allocations are posix_memalign DRAM. uint64 keys only (double keys segfault, #3); the concurrent version has no erase; lookups return the internally encoded (<<1) value and the upsert base-tree path writes raw values, which is inconsistent. Header non-inline functions cause multi-TU link errors; static thread_local epochs allow one instance per type. ~34% more memory; APEX beats it on most operations.

**How:** It spreads the cost of persistence over a batch of writes: each write costs one cache-line log append (clwb+sfence) plus a DRAM insert. The batch is then merged into PM leaves in place using coarse-grained versioning. Each leaf keeps two metadata copies, and one persisted global-version flip makes a whole merge visible, so the flushes inside the merge need no fences. That comes to 2.26 flushes per insert, against 4.35 for FAST+FAIR and 3.64 for FPTree (paper Table 1). Base-tree leaves are 256-slot hash tables using linear probing plus 1-byte fingerprints, with an order array for sorted scans. A lookup is usually a bloom-filter check on the buffer plus about 2 PM accesses. The concurrent version adds a hash-partitioned PM log with lock-free fetch-and-add appends, an Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC) B+-tree buffer, RCU-style thread-local epoch words and a parallel background merge.

**Use it when:**
- Research or prototyping on Intel Optane DC PMem (App Direct / DAX) when you need a strong buffered-index baseline to compare against FAST+FAIR, FPTree or WORT.
- Workloads dominated by point lookups, or by 50/50 read-update, on uniformly random 64-bit integer keys with 8-byte values. The paper shows 1.32-1.58x ReadOnly throughput over FAST+FAIR and 1.7-5.07x on ReadUpdate at 50M keys.
- Insert-heavy workloads where the limit is PM write bandwidth or endurance rather than CPU: DPTree issues the fewest flushes and fences per insert of the indexes the paper measured.
- As a readable, MIT-licensed reference for buffered/differential PM indexing (in-place merge, coarse-grained versioning, partitioned PM log) that you port into your own engine.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs real crash recovery. The public code has no recovery routine (issue #4, open since 2021 with no reply). It allocates its 'PM' with posix_memalign in ordinary DRAM and has no PM pool or allocator. The paper's validity-bit log, restart counters and pending-leaf list are also missing.
- Scan-heavy workloads: scans are up to 1.1x slower than FAST+FAIR single-threaded, FAST+FAIR keeps the highest scan throughput in ScanInsert, and DPTree's scan throughput levels off after about 20 threads.
- Keys that are not uint64: the code hard-codes 8-byte big-endian conversion (__builtin_bswap64). Issue #3 reports very low throughput and segfaults with double keys, and there is no string or variable-length key support.
- Workloads with deletes under concurrency: concur_dptree exposes no erase, and the APEX authors likewise report that DPTree's code does not support delete, recovery or double keys.
- Memory-constrained deployments or non-Optane hardware: 1.7 GB versus 1.26 GB for FAST+FAIR after 50M inserts (about 34% more, from the two metadata copies). Optane is discontinued, so the claimed advantage has no current target hardware.

**Integration:** source-drop · stx-btree (headers), Intel TBB (used by the bundled ARTOLC epoch code), tcmalloc_minimal, pthreads; you must also compile the bundled src/*.cpp, src/bloom.c and misc/ARTOLC/*.cpp. The paper's PM allocator (nvm_malloc) is not included. · C++11 with GCC (paper used g++ 6.4; CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11 and -fpermissive); CMake 2.8+; README targets Ubuntu 18.04. The CMake default build type is RelWithDebInfo, not the paper's -O3. · Linux x86-64 only. It needs CLWB (Skylake-SP or newer), SSE/AVX and -mrtm, and enables AVX2/AVX-512 flags by reading /proc/cpuinfo. The published numbers need Optane DC PMM in App Direct mode; without it everything runs in DRAM.

**Vs siblings:** APEX is the only persistent-memory sibling. The APEX paper measured it beating DPTree (inserts up to 1.66x, lookups up to 3.2x, scans up to 1.83x), and APEX supports recovery, deletes and double keys, so default to APEX. Pick DPTree only if you want a non-learned design that does not depend on the key distribution (on the hard-to-fit FB dataset APEX's insert throughput was 42% below DPTree's) or you are studying buffered in-place PM merging. The DRAM-only siblings (ALEX, LIPP, HOT, ART) provide no persistence.

**Gotchas:**
- Stored values are shifted left one bit (the low bit is the tombstone flag), and lookup returns them still encoded, so callers must shift right by 1 (the test drivers call strip_upsert_value). Values are therefore limited to 63 bits. Also, concur_dptree::upsert's in-place base-tree update (update_if_found) writes the raw, unshifted value, which is inconsistent with the other paths.
- dpftree::lookup does not check the tombstone bit in the DRAM buffer, so a key that was erased but not yet merged is still reported as found.
- concur_dptree.hpp defines the non-inline function spin_until_no_ref in the header, so including it in more than one translation unit causes duplicate-symbol link errors. Its thread-local epoch words are static per template instantiation and register with only the first instance's managers, so do not run two instances of the same <K,V> in one process. The embedding program must also define the global int parallel_merge_worker_num.
- The benchmark drivers default to dense keys 0..n-1; pass sparseKey=1 to get the random 64-bit keys the paper used. The public drivers cover only insert and search (plus single-thread scans); the YCSB mixes and the baseline harness are not published.

**Status:** Abandoned: the code was published in Sep 2020 and last touched 2021-07-28 (a build fix), and two 2021 issues (missing recovery code, crashes with double keys) are unanswered. It is MIT-licensed and about 6K lines, so treat it as a research reference for discontinued Optane hardware rather than a library to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/zxjcarrot/DPTree-code) · [benchmark](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p421-zhou.pdf)

##### HOT (Height Optimized Trie)  `C++`  `ISC`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Header-only C++14 order-preserving trie for in-memory indexes. Beats STX B+-tree, ART and Masstree on string-key lookups, scans and memory.

**Beats:** B-tree (STX B+-Tree), ART, Masstree — In the SIGMOD'18 paper, 50M keys (url, email, yago, random 63-bit integers) were loaded and then 100M uniform YCSB-style operations were run single-threaded on an Intel i7-6700 with GCC 7.2 (no flags stated). Workload C lookups ran 1.3/1.5/4.1/5.3 Mops/s against the best rival's 0.9 (Masstree), 1.2 (Masstree), 2.4 (ART) and 5.0 (ART), per the Figure 8 labels. So the text's 'at least 25% higher' holds for url, email and yago but not for integers (~6%). The '200% higher' is workload E on URLs (0.6 vs 0.2 Mops/s for the STX B+-tree and ART). The STX B+-tree baseline uses 256-byte nodes and resolves string keys through tuple ids, which helps explain its low string throughput.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo benchmarks only HOT (no public head-to-head harness); ART inserts about 50% faster on the integer set.

**Known shortcoming:** The paper's '>=25% on all' for workload C does not hold for integers: its own Fig. 8 gives 5.3 vs ART 5.0 Mops (~6%). The string and memory wins are real (url C 1.3 vs 0.9 Mops, E 3x, 11-14 B/key). The STX B-tree baseline resolves string keys through tuple ids, which handicaps it.

**Known shortcoming:** Single-threaded version uses a shared static unsynchronised MemoryPool, so separate instances race across threads; the ROWEX variant has no delete and needs TBB. Keys capped at 255 B with silent truncation; values <=63 bits; keys are re-derived from values. x86 AVX2/BMI2 only (pext is slow on Zen 1/2). The build is broken (submodule, Boost download 403, GCC 8+ with Hana); frozen since 2018 with 9 unanswered issues; the TODS'22 code is unreleased.

**How:** It is a binary Patricia trie whose nodes are grouped into compound nodes of at most k=32 entries. Each node's span, meaning how many key bits it looks at, is chosen from the data so that the overall tree height is as small as possible, which keeps fanout high even for sparse string keys. Inside a node, the discriminative bit positions are stored as a single or multi byte mask, and the matching bits of the search key are gathered with one BMI2 PEXT. The result is compared against all of the node's 8/16/32-bit 'sparse partial keys' at once with AVX2 and/cmpeq/movemask, and the last match wins. Inserts rebuild partial keys with PDEP into copy-on-write nodes. Nodes come in 9 physical layouts, the node type is encoded in the low bits of each child pointer, and the first 4 cache lines of each node are prefetched. On the paper's string data sets the mean leaf depth is up to 68% lower than ART's.

**Use it when:**
- Read-mostly in-memory ordered indexes on variable-length string keys of 255 bytes or less, such as URLs or emails. Paper workload C (50M keys): 1.3 vs 0.9 Mops/s for Masstree on URLs, and 1.5 vs 1.2 on emails.
- Short range scans over string keys. On workload E (95% scans of up to 100 entries) over URLs, HOT ran 0.6 Mops/s against 0.2 for the STX B+-tree and ART and 0.1 for Masstree.
- Memory-bound indexes. For 50M keys the paper measured 11.4-14.4 bytes/key: 0.53-0.67 GB against 1.26 GB for the STX B+-tree, 1.09-1.64 GB for ART and 1.53-5.05 GB for Masstree (all figures include 0.37 GB of raw tuple ids). HOT was also smaller than the raw URL and email key bytes.
- Skewed or compound 8-byte keys, such as the yago triples: lookups ran 4.1 vs 2.4 Mops/s for ART.
- Concurrent insert and lookup without deletes on Intel x86-64 Linux. HOTRowex readers never take locks, and the paper shows near-linear scaling to 10 cores (mean lookup speedup 9.96x, insert 9.00x).

**Skip it when:**
- Uniformly random 64-bit integer keys. Figure 8 shows lookups only ~6% ahead of ART (5.3 vs 5.0 Mops/s), and ART inserts 50% faster (3.9 vs 2.6 Mops/s).
- Point lookups where you don't need key order. In issue #3, one user measured HOT at 82 ns/find and 236 ns/insert against Folly F14 at 27/31 ns, on ~570K short strings on a Xeon E-2278G.
- Workloads that need concurrent deletes (HOTRowex has no remove), keys longer than 255 bytes, binary keys with zero bytes, or an index that owns its keys and values the way std::map does.
- CPUs other than Intel Haswell or newer. AVX2, BMI2 and LZCNT are required. PEXT is slow on AMD Zen 1/2 (issue #8), and an ARM port using SIMDe ran 'very poor' (issue #10). MSVC and Windows are not supported as written.
- Anything that needs upkeep. The code has been frozen since March 2018, nine issues from 2019-2024 have no maintainer reply, and the bundled build breaks on current toolchains.

**Integration:** header-only (copy libs/idx/content-helpers, libs/hot/commons, libs/hot/single-threaded and/or libs/hot/rowex; CMake INTERFACE targets are also provided) · HOTSingleThreaded needs nothing outside the repo headers. HOTRowex needs Intel TBB (enumerable_thread_specific for epoch reclamation), and the README recommends tcmalloc. The repo's own build also pulls TBB 2018, boost-cmake 1.66 and Boost.Hana (for benchmarks and tests) as git submodules. · C++14, CMake 2.8+. The paper used GCC 7.2. On GCC 8+ the bundled benchmark framework fails to compile under -std=c++14 because of Boost.Hana constexpr lambdas (issues #1, #7). The code uses GCC attributes and glibc's __bswap_64. · x86-64 with AVX2, BMI2 and LZCNT (Haswell or newer); build with -march=haswell or native. Only Linux is documented. There is an optional USEAVX512 CMake flag. No ARM or other non-x86 support.

**Vs siblings:** Pick HOT over ART (ARTSynchronized or rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree) when keys are strings or skewed and index memory matters. Stay with ART for uniformly random integer keys and insert-heavy loads, where HOT's own paper has ART inserting 50% faster at near-equal lookup speed. The learned-index siblings (RadixSpline, RMI, PLEX, fast64, PGM-index) report results on fixed-width integer key sets, while HOT needs no training and has its largest wins on variable-length strings.

**Gotchas:**
- The trie stores only your 63-bit value (tid or pointer), not the key. Every lookup ends by dereferencing the value through KeyExtractor and running a full compare (strcmp for strings), so the key memory must stay alive and unchanged while it is indexed.
- C-string keys are capped at 255 bytes because bit offsets are uint8 (issue #6). KeyUtilities.hpp silently truncates longer keys to 255 bytes with strncpy/std::min instead of rejecting them, and every operation copies the key into a 255-byte fixed array.
- There is no allocator hook. Nodes are allocated with posix_memalign (the single-threaded version adds a static free-list pool), a failed allocation throws std::bad_alloc, and inserts and deletes use an unchecked fixed 64-entry std::array traversal stack. The paper says HOT's worst-case height has not yet been proven.
- Builds break out of the box. The pinned boost-cmake submodule commit can't be checked out (issue #2) and its Boost download URL returns 403 (issue #3). Without BMI/LZCNT target flags, GCC fails with 'inlining failed ... _tzcnt_u32' (issue #4).

**Status:** Abandoned since 2018-03-26 with no active fork, and the code for the extended TODS 2022 'Height Optimized Tries' version (DOI 10.1145/3506692) was never released (issue #9). It is ISC-licensed and header-only, so vendoring the core headers is feasible, but expect to fix the build yourself; GCC 7.2 on Linux x86-64 is the last toolchain documented to work.

[repo](https://github.com/speedskater/hot) · [benchmark](https://15721.courses.cs.cmu.edu/spring2019/papers/08-oltpindexes2/p521-binna.pdf)

##### LIPP (Updatable Learned Index with Precise Positions)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Header-only, single-threaded learned index for numeric keys; beats STX B+Tree, ART and ALEX on point-lookup and insert throughput.

**Beats:** STX B+Tree; also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), ALEX, PGM-index, BwTree, and a 2-level RMI ("Learned Index") — The PVLDB 14(8) 2021 paper ran single-threaded on an unnamed 4.0 GHz Intel Core i7 (4C/8T, 32 GB) with GCC 9.0.1 -O3 on four datasets (Longitudes 1B doubles, Longlat 200M, Lognormal 190M, YCSB 200M int64), and its harness was never published. It reports up to 9.8x STX B+Tree throughput read-only (100M-key bulk-loaded index, lookups of existing keys only) and up to 5.4x on insert/lookup mixes from an empty index, but only 1.47x over ALEX on Longlat, while the independent GRE study (Xeon Platinum 8268, gcc 8.3 -O3) also ranks LIPP and ALEX the top single-threaded indexes, with LIPP slightly below the paper's numbers after its bug fixes and using 4-5x ALEX's memory.

**Known shortcoming:** No CPU model ('i7 4.0GHz') and no public harness against the baselines (repo is core + examples); the GRE benchmark (VLDB'22) found 2 bugs whose fixes slightly lower performance (verifier downgrade from A).

**Known shortcoming:** Single-threaded; in GRE the concurrent LIPP+ stops scaling once writes appear. Memory is 4-5x ALEX's (highest in GRE), and ALEX given the same memory wins lookups.

**Known shortcoming:** The main branch has no erase/update/range scan (only on the range branch or GRE's fork). RT_ASSERT calls exit(0), so a duplicate insert, unsorted bulk_load, NaN model or depth >128 kills the process with a success code; at() on a missing key returns garbage. The constructor pre-pools ~1e7 nodes (~1.6-2.3 GB, estimated from struct layout); paper harness unpublished.

**How:** Each node holds a linear model and a sparse slot array whose predicted slot is exact, so each level of a lookup costs one model evaluation plus a bitmap check, with none of the last-mile binary or exponential search that ALEX, PGM and RMI need. When two keys land on the same slot, LIPP swaps the entry for a pointer to a new small child node ('node chaining') instead of shifting elements. The FMCD (Fastest Minimum Conflict Degree) algorithm picks each node's model in linear time to keep conflicts rare. A subtree is rebuilt with FMCD once it has grown 4x since its last build and conflicts reach 10% of its inserts, which bounds tree height at an amortized O(log^2 N) insert cost; two-key nodes are recycled through a preallocated pool.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded, lookup-heavy point queries on 64-bit integer or double keys that mostly exist in the index. The paper reports up to 9.8x STX B+Tree throughput read-only, but it only looked up keys that were present.
- Mixed insert/lookup streams (33-67% inserts) with unique keys and a single writer. The paper reports up to 5.4x STX B+Tree and 3.7x ART, and the GRE study also ranks LIPP among the top single-threaded indexes on easy real datasets.
- Machines where index memory is cheap relative to the data: plan for roughly 4-5x ALEX's footprint, plus a large fixed pool allocated at construction.
- As a compact (~880-line, MIT) starting point or baseline for research on exact-position learned indexes.

**Skip it when:**
- Any multi-threaded access. There is no concurrency control, and GRE's concurrent rewrite (LIPP+, item-level optimistic locks) stopped scaling once writes were involved, because every insert updates per-node statistics all the way up to the root.
- Memory-constrained deployments. GRE measured LIPP's memory at 4-5x ALEX's, the highest of all indexes it tested, and ALEX tuned to use the same memory beat LIPP on lookups. In issue #1, bulk-loading 200M SOSD keys ran out of memory on a 32 GB machine where ALEX, STX B+Tree and Dynamic PGM fit.
- Workloads that need erase, upsert, ordered iteration or range scans: main has none of them. Even on the range branch the paper reports at most 1.5x on scans, and GRE found the mixed data/child node layout branch-heavy for scans.
- String or composite keys, possible duplicate keys, or untrusted input: keys must be arithmetic, and inserting an existing key kills the process.
- Hard, highly non-uniform key distributions or tail-latency-sensitive writes. The gain over ALEX falls to 1.47x on Longlat. GRE saw high p99.9 insert latency on its osm and genome datasets and found learned indexes losing to traditional ones on hard data with 50% or more writes.

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only; src/core/lipp.h + lipp_base.h) · C++11 per CMakeLists, using GCC/Clang extensions (__builtin_ctz, compound literals). The range branch and the GRE fork need C++17 (if constexpr). Tested with GCC 9.0.1 (paper) and gcc 8.3.0 (GRE). · Only x86-64 Linux is tested. The GCC/Clang builtins mean MSVC is not supported as written. The 64-bit-key precision fix relies on long double being wider than double.

**Vs siblings:** Pick LIPP over ALEX only for single-threaded, point-lookup-heavy work on numeric keys when memory is plentiful and you can do without erase and range scans. ALEX uses 4-5x less memory, beats LIPP on lookups when given the same memory, and has a scalable concurrent variant (ALEX+ in GRE). Prefer PGM-index for static or space-critical data, or insert-only streams (its LSM-style inserts were the fastest at 100% writes in GRE), and rafaelkallis ART for non-numeric keys.

**Gotchas:**
- Every internal failure goes through RT_ASSERT, which prints to stderr and then calls exit(0). The triggers are: inserting a key that already exists (insert is not an upsert, issue #8), unsorted or duplicate bulk_load input, a model parameter going non-finite, and an insert path deeper than MAX_DEPTH=128. Each one ends the process with a success exit code.
- at(key) defaults to skip_existence_check=true and, for a missing key, returns whatever the predicted slot holds (garbage). Call exists() first. Passing false does not help, because a miss then triggers RT_ASSERT and exit(0).
- The constructor eagerly builds and pools 10 million two-key nodes, so even an empty LIPP is slow to construct and holds a lot of heap. From the struct layout I estimate about 1.6 GB for int/int up to about 2.3 GB for 64-bit key/value, before malloc overhead. Issue #14 (./example killed) may be this, but it was never diagnosed.
- Precision and depth edge cases. Models convert keys to long double; PR #11 (from the GRE authors) fixed segfaults and non-finite-model asserts on SOSD 64-bit datasets (issues #2, #10), and it may not hold where long double is only 64-bit, which is untested. Nodes built from more than 1e6 keys are marked fixed and never rebuilt. Inserting 100M sequential ints into an empty index hit MAX_DEPTH (issue #13); the maintainer's fix is to raise the constant by hand.

**Status:** Abandoned since the Feb 2022 commit that merged the GRE bug fixes (in issue #3 the authors said they had moved to other work, though they still answered an issue in 2025), but it is MIT-licensed and a single ~880-line header that is easy to vendor, and for remove/update/range scans the GRE fork pohchaichon/lipp@a1189c3 is the better copy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/Jiacheng-WU/lipp) · [benchmark](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1276-wu.pdf)

##### PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model index)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Header-only learned index over sorted integer arrays that matches B+-tree lookup latency with an index orders of magnitude smaller.

**Beats:** STX B+-tree (v0.9) and cache-efficient CSS-tree (authors' implementation), plus a 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index) — In the authors' own PVLDB'20 experiments (2.3 GHz Xeon Gold with no model stated, compiler and flags not given, no stdlib baseline), on 715M 8-byte Web-log keys with 128-byte payloads and 10M random queries, PGM matched the fastest STX B+-tree v0.9 latency with an 87 KiB index against 874 MiB and matched the fastest CSS-tree with 4 MiB against 341 MiB. The Dynamic PGM (epsilon 64, 1B keys, 10M mixed operations) was 13-71% faster than the STX B+-tree except at 0.8 and 0.9 query fractions. The independent SOSD benchmark (Xeon Gold 6230) confirms PGM beats a B-tree (326 vs 482 ns, 14 vs 166 MB) but contradicts the paper's claim that it dominates RMI, blaming the paper's weaker RMI implementation.

**Known shortcoming:** The paper's own dynamic test has it 1-15% slower than a B+-tree at 0.8/0.9 query fractions; in GRE its lookups are beaten by ALEX and LIPP. The max key value is reserved as a sentinel (throws), and DynamicPGM uses the max value as a delete tombstone. Default float slopes miss keys on some datasets (#30, #45; use double). uint32 intercept throws above ~4.29B keys; MSVC breaks (__int128); no -fno-exceptions build; DynamicPGM has no locking. Stale since 2024-11, 12 open issues.

**Independent measurement:** SOSD benchmark (independent): PGM-index 326 ns vs B-tree 482 ns lookups with 14 vs 166 MB, but behind RMI (181 ns) and RadixSpline (267 ns), contradicting the paper's 'dominates RMI'.

**How:** It computes an optimal piecewise linear epsilon-approximation (a convex-hull streaming algorithm) of the key-to-rank function, so each segment of (first key, float slope, uint32 intercept) predicts a position within +/-Epsilon. It then indexes the segment keys recursively with the same method (EpsilonRecursive defaults to 4), which gives a short tree with a linear scan over a few segments at each level instead of storing every key in inner nodes the way a B+-tree does. Because the index has m segments with m often 2-5 orders of magnitude below n, it stays in cache, and construction is one linear pass per level, parallelised with OpenMP when available.

**Use it when:**
- Read-mostly sorted arrays of 32/64-bit integer (or float/double) keys that need point, predecessor/lower_bound or range queries at B+-tree-like latency, with the index taking KiB-MiB instead of hundreds of MiB (paper: 87 KiB vs 874 MiB on 715M keys).
- Keys with a smooth or locally linear distribution, such as timestamps, log offsets or mostly sequential IDs, where few segments are needed and the index fits in L2/L3.
- Memory-constrained services or large mmap'd sorted key files (MappedPGMIndex), where a per-key index structure would not fit in RAM.
- You need a guaranteed worst-case search window (a fixed epsilon bound) rather than the data-dependent error of an RMI.
- Write-heavy integer key/value workloads on a single thread, where DynamicPGMIndex's LSM-style merging gave the highest insert throughput in the independent GRE benchmark at 100% writes.

**Skip it when:**
- Point-lookup latency matters more than memory: in the independent SOSD benchmark (200M 32-bit amzn keys) PGM took 326 ns, against 181 ns for RMI, 267 ns for RadixSpline and about 94-115 ns for hash tables that use far more memory.
- Read-heavy dynamic workloads: in the authors' own paper the Dynamic PGM was 1.0% and 15.2% slower than the best B+-tree at 0.8 and 0.9 query fractions, and GRE found its lookups dominated by ALEX and LIPP.
- String, composite or wider-than-word keys: the author says it is made for integers that fit in a machine word (issue #8), and key differences are converted to double for prediction.
- Builds with MSVC (the __int128 use breaks it, issue #19 still open), with -fno-exceptions (issue #56 open), or with concurrent writers (DynamicPGMIndex has no synchronisation).
- Hard-to-learn distributions, such as SOSD's Hilbert-projected osm cell IDs, where learned indexes lost to a simple radix lookup table and gave little gain over binary search.

**Integration:** header-only · None required. OpenMP is optional and parallelises construction (without it you get a '#pragma message' warning). A BSD-licensed SDSL subset (sdsl.hpp) is bundled for the compressed and Elias-Fano variants. MultidimensionalPGMIndex needs BMI2/AVX2, and MappedPGMIndex uses POSIX mmap. · C++17 (CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17; README uses g++ -std=c++17); GCC or Clang, because it uses __int128, __builtin_clzll and __builtin_prefetch. CI builds gcc and clang on ubuntu-22.04 and macos-12, with a gcc 13.2 fix in 2024. MSVC is not supported. · Linux and macOS on x86-64 and arm64 (an Apple arm64 compile issue was fixed in 2021). On Windows only MinGW-w64 is reported to work. The multidimensional variant is x86-only (BMI2 _pdep/_pext). The bundled CMake adds -march=native.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PGM over CARMI when index footprint and a provable epsilon-bounded search window matter more than raw lookup speed: CARMI claims an average 2.2x over the STX B+Tree but still uses about 0.77x the B+Tree's memory, while PGM's index is KiB-MiB. Pick rafaelkallis ART instead for a general mutable ordered map with byte-string keys; libmdbx, redb and TerarkDB are persistent transactional stores, not in-memory search indexes, so they do not substitute.

**Gotchas:**
- Sentinel values: std::numeric_limits<K>::max() (or infinity for floating-point keys) is reserved. Building on data that contains it throws, and querying it in DynamicPGMIndex segfaulted (issue #36); the GRE benchmark had to shift Facebook keys by -1. In DynamicPGMIndex with an arithmetic value type, numeric_limits<V>::max() is the delete tombstone and cannot be stored.
- Floating-point precision: slopes default to float (the paper used double). Users saw keys fall outside the returned [lo, hi) window on the SOSD books and GRE eth datasets (issues #30 and #45), and the author's fix was Floating=double or a wider search window. Results can differ across CPUs and compilers.
- Segment intercepts are uint32_t, so indexing more than about 4.29 billion positions throws overflow_error('Change the type of Segment::intercept to uint64'), which means editing the header.
- Errors are reported by throwing exceptions (unsorted input, the sentinel value, the tombstone value). DynamicPGMIndex::lower_bound tracks tombstoned keys in a std::set while scanning levels, so delete-heavy data slows it. An untriaged 2025 comment on issue #63 reports a wrong lookup for a duplicate-heavy uint64 array built on 2 cores.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit was 2024-11-28 (edge-case fixes for float and one-element inputs), and 12 issues are open, including MSVC and noexcept requests. It is Apache-2.0 and header-only, and the core static index is two headers of about 630 lines, so it is easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/gvinciguerra/PGM-index) · [benchmark](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p1162-ferragina.pdf)

##### PLEX / TrieSpline  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Read-only learned index for sorted integer keys: error-bounded spline plus auto-tuned radix tree; ~2x faster lookups than B-tree.

**Beats:** B-tree (and ART, PGM-index) — Fig. 3 of the AIDB@VLDB'21 extended abstract plots lookup time against index size for 200M-key 64-bit SOSD datasets (amzn, face, osm, wiki), run on an AWS m5zn.metal (48 vCPUs, 4.5 GHz turbo, 192 GiB). Read off the plot, PLEX's best points (about 190-255 ns) sit roughly 2-2.7x below SOSD's BTree baseline at its best (about 505-515 ns) and below ART (about 360-450 ns; ART is not plotted on wiki). RMI stays about 25 ns faster on amzn and face, and the paper states no exact numbers, compiler or flags (the repo's CMake uses C++17 with -march=native).

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is a plot only (read off Fig. 3: PLEX ~200-300 ns vs B-tree ~500-900 ns, approximate); RMI is about 25 ns faster. AWS m5zn instance with no CPU model named.

**Known shortcoming:** Read-only, uint32/uint64 keys only; returns a search window into the caller's sorted array (not a container). Abandoned since 2022 with an open out-of-bounds crash on sequential keys (#4) and an unmerged off-by-one fix (PR #3); the README example passes keys.size() as the max-error argument. Input checks are assert-only (release builds return wrong bounds); SOSD's copy predates the 2022 radix-table fix; GCC/Clang builtins (no MSVC); no serializer. CHT is faster on osm.

**How:** A greedy error-bounded linear spline (GreedySplineCorridor, Neumann & Michel, BNCOD'08) is fitted in one O(N) pass, so every prediction lands within epsilon positions of the true slot. The spline points are indexed either by a flat radix table (as in RadixSpline) or by a Compact Hist-Tree (CHT, Crotty CIDR'21), a flat-array radix tree that keeps splitting dense bins. The choice is automatic: cost models built from an lcp histogram of adjacent spline keys estimate the average lookup depth and exact size of every (radix bits, bin error) configuration without building any of them, then pick the cheapest one whose size does not exceed the spline itself. A lookup is a few shift/mask table hops, a short linear search (under 32 points) or binary search over spline points, one FMA interpolation, and a last-mile binary search over the epsilon window, which is far fewer cache misses than walking B-tree nodes.

**Use it when:**
- Static or bulk-loaded sorted arrays of 32/64-bit unsigned integer keys (IDs, timestamps, cell IDs) in the 10^6 to 10^8+ range, where you rebuild rather than update
- You want roughly half of a B-tree's lookup latency over the same sorted array (best points about 190-255 ns vs about 505-515 ns for BTree on 200M-key SOSD data, read from the plot) with an index that can be KBs to MBs
- You want one knob (max error epsilon) and a fast rebuild: about 1-2 s for 200M keys including auto-tuning, against about 10-20 s for RMI plus its offline grid search (Fig. 2)
- Distributions with outliers or long shared key prefixes that defeat RadixSpline's flat radix table (the paper's 'face' dataset), since PLEX switches to a CHT there
- Keys with duplicates: the spline only records distinct keys, so duplicate-heavy data (e.g. 'wiki') works, unlike the paper's standalone CHT

**Skip it when:**
- Any workload with inserts, deletes or in-place updates: the structure is read-only and a change means a full rebuild (the Fenwick-tree update extension was only proposed as future work)
- Non-integer or signed keys (strings, floats, composite keys): only uint32_t and uint64_t overloads of the bit helpers exist
- When peak lookup latency matters more than build cost: RMI sits about 25 ns lower on amzn and face, and the standalone CHT is lower on osm in the paper's own Fig. 3
- Production code that needs a maintained dependency: abandoned since mid-2022, 16 stars, a reported out-of-bounds crash on sequential keys (issue #4, Feb 2024) and a radix-layer off-by-one patch (PR #3, June 2022), both unresolved
- MSVC/Windows builds: it relies on GCC/Clang __builtin_clz/__builtin_clzl, and the 64-bit path assumes a 64-bit 'long'

**Integration:** header-only · none (C++ standard library only; the CMake Threads requirement is for the bundled example/benchmark) · C++17 (std::optional; CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17), GCC or Clang for __builtin_clz/clzl; specific compiler versions not documented · 64-bit LP64 targets (Linux/macOS, x86-64 or aarch64) by construction; the repo CMake adds -march=native; no SIMD or ISA-specific code; Windows/MSVC not supported as written

**Vs siblings:** Over RadixSpline: pick PLEX when your key distribution has outliers or long common prefixes (RS's flat radix table stalls there), or when you do not want to tune radix bits; you pay a slightly longer build. Over RMI and PGM-index: pick it when you want a single-knob static index that builds in seconds; RMI is still about 25 ns faster at lookup but needs offline tuning, and PGM-index is maintained and supports updates. LIPP and ALEX are the choice once you need writes.

**Gotchas:**
- The README snippet calls ts::Builder tsb(min, max, keys.size()), but the third argument is spline_max_error, not a key count, so copying it gives an error bound equal to the dataset size. example.cc correctly passes a small epsilon (32).
- The input contract is checked only by assert(): keys must arrive in non-decreasing order, and the first and last keys must equal the min/max passed to the constructor. A release (NDEBUG) build silently returns wrong bounds if you violate it, and min == max hits __builtin_clz(0), which is undefined behaviour.
- SOSD's competitors/ts submodule pins commit 862e3c5 (June 2021), which predates the March 2022 fix to the single-node radix-table fallback (it read past the bin array). Vendor PLEX HEAD, and consider applying the open PR #3 fix too.
- The radix/CHT layer stores 32-bit offsets, with the top bit used as a leaf flag, so the spline must stay under about 2^31 points. There is no serializer for TrieSpline (only the bundled RadixSpline has one), so you rebuild after every load.

**Status:** Abandoned research code (last commit June 2022; the author acknowledged a 2024 crash report but no fix landed); MIT-licensed, about 1.1k lines of headers, and easy to vendor, as long as you pin HEAD and add your own input validation.

[repo](https://github.com/stoianmihail/PLEX) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.05117)

##### RadixSpline  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Single-pass, read-only learned index (spline + radix table) for sorted uint32/uint64 arrays; beats STX B+Tree lookups at ~1/40th the size.

**Beats:** B-tree (STX B-Tree) — SOSD paper (PVLDB 14(1), Table 2): 32-bit version of the 200M-key amzn dataset, 10M random lookups, single-threaded, Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz, fastest variant of each index. RS averaged 266.58 ns/lookup with a 4.0 MB index vs 482.11 ns and 166.0 MB for the STX B+Tree (about 1.8x lower latency, about 41x smaller), with the last-mile binary search included. No compiler is named (the SOSD build is CMake Release with -march=native), and no std:: container was measured.

**Known shortcoming:** Read-only (no insert/erase; full rebuild). On the face dataset (outliers) the radix table is nearly useless and the best config exceeds 600 MiB; hash tables and RMI are faster on point lookups (Table 2). uint32/uint64 keys only; clz(0) UB when all keys are equal; builder preconditions are assert-only, so NDEBUG builds can write past the radix table. The serializer is raw native-endian with no checks; abandoned since 2021-05 with 3 unmerged PRs.

**How:** It first fits an error-bounded linear spline to the key->position CDF using GreedySplineCorridor (Neumann & Michel, BNCOD'08). This runs in one pass with constant work per key and guarantees that interpolating between two knots lands within max_error positions of the true one. A flat radix table (a uint32 array indexed by the top r bits of key - min_key, with common prefix bits removed, similar to one ART Node256 level) narrows the search to a few spline points, which are scanned linearly (<32) or binary-searched. An FMA interpolation then gives the estimate, followed by a short binary search over about 2*max_error+2 elements. A lookup is therefore a shift, one table load, a short knot search and a tiny last-mile search, instead of a walk down several B-tree levels.

**Use it when:**
- Immutable or write-once sorted arrays of uint32/uint64 keys that get rebuilt in bulk, such as LSM-tree runs or SSTables at compaction time. The paper's preliminary RocksDB swap on osmc (50/50 reads/writes) cut total time from 712 s to 521 s and memory use by about 45%.
- Point or lower_bound lookups where both latency and index memory matter. On SOSD 32-bit amzn the best RS was about 1.8x faster than the best STX B+Tree with a 4 MB vs 166 MB index.
- When a learned index must build fast. SOSD measured 20 s for RS vs 38 s for PGM and 80 s for RMI on the largest (800M-key) dataset, with constant work per key.
- Range and predecessor queries over sorted data, which hash tables cannot serve.
- Smooth real-world key distributions (amzn/wiki-like CDFs) where tuning just two knobs (radix bits, spline error) to hit a memory budget is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Any inserts, updates or deletes. It is strictly read-only and needs a full rebuild; use a B-tree or an updatable learned index (ALEX, LIPP, dynamic PGM).
- Key sets with a few extreme outliers or empty high-bit ranges. On SOSD face, about 100 keys in (2^59, 2^64-1) against a bulk below 2^50 made the radix table nearly useless. The aiDM paper's fastest face config needed over 600 MiB (39% of the key data).
- Pure point lookups with memory to spare. In the same Table 2, RobinHash (93.69 ns) and CuckooMap (114.50 ns) beat RS (266.58 ns), and RMI (180.90 ns at 48 MB) was also faster.
- Non-uint keys (strings, floats, signed or composite keys) are not supported. 32-bit keys give essentially no gain over 64-bit, because RS converts keys to 64-bit floats.
- Production use needing support. There have been no commits since May 2021, no releases or packages, and GCC/Clang builtins with no Windows/MSVC build. A 2023 PR arguing that the spline-cut condition is stricter than the paper (more knots than needed) was closed unmerged.

**Integration:** header-only · none (GoogleTest only for the repo's own tests, pulled by CMake) · C++14 per CMakeLists.txt (CMake 3.10+). Needs GCC or Clang for __builtin_clz/__builtin_clzl; no minimum compiler version documented. · Not documented. The code is plain C++ apart from the GCC/Clang builtins; __builtin_clzl on 64-bit keys assumes a 64-bit long (LP64 Linux/macOS). The repo's CMake adds -march=native, but only for its own example/bench/test targets. CI runs on an unspecified self-hosted runner.

**Vs siblings:** Choose RS over PGM-index or RMI when the data is immutable, rebuilt often, and build time matters. It built 800M keys in 20 s vs 38 s for PGM and 80 s for RMI, and on 32-bit amzn it beat PGM's lookup (266.58 vs 326.48 ns) with a smaller index, though RMI was faster (180.90 ns at 48 MB). Choose ALEX or LIPP instead when you need inserts.

**Gotchas:**
- Builder preconditions are checked only by assert(): keys added in sorted order, min/max known up front, and the last key equal to max_key. In NDEBUG builds a violation silently yields wrong bounds, and a key above max_key can write past the end of the radix table.
- The radix table is a flat uint32 array of up to 2^r+2 entries, whatever the data size. The default r=18 costs about 1 MiB even for tiny inputs, and bench.cc's tuned configs go up to r=28 (up to about 1 GiB).
- Only uint32_t/uint64_t compile, because GetNumShiftBits overloads only those. When all keys are equal (min==max), 0 is passed to __builtin_clz, which is formally undefined, although the SingleKey/AllMinKeys tests pass.
- Serializer writes raw native-endian size_t/key/double fields with no header, version or length checks. The bytes are not portable across architectures and are unsafe to load from untrusted input.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last commit on master is 2021-05-13 (tuning configs only; the last functional change, a serializer, landed 2021-03-03), and three outside PRs were closed unmerged. Still, it is MIT-licensed and five small dependency-free headers, so vendoring and patching it yourself is easy.

[repo](https://github.com/learnedsystems/RadixSpline) · [benchmark](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

##### RMI (Recursive Model Index, reference implementation)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Rust generator emitting a C++ two-stage learned index for static sorted arrays; beats STX B+Tree latency and size.

**Beats:** B-tree (STX B-Tree) — The claim comes from the SOSD paper (PVLDB 14(1), Table 2): 200M 32-bit amzn keys, 10M random lookups, Xeon Gold 6230. There, the fastest CDFShop-tuned RMI took 180.90 ns per lookup at 48 MB, against 482.11 ns at 166 MB for the STX B+Tree, about 2.7x lower latency at about 3.5x less space. The SOSD harness is a CMake Release build with -ffast-math -march=native, but the paper names no compiler, and both hash tables beat RMI on point lookups.

**Known shortcoming:** Read-only and not a container: it returns a position guess and error bound and the user does the last-mile search; any data change needs retrain, regenerate and recompile. Only the 2-layer implementation works (3-layer panics #5; radix root with branch 1-3 panics #3; ~100-key inputs assert #8). Open PR #14: duplicate runs can make the error bound too small; PR #15: cargo tests do not compile.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Active' is misleading: no code changes from 2020-08 to 2026-05. Loses to hash tables on point lookups, poor on the osm dataset, slowest learned-index build (80 s vs PGM 38 s, RadixSpline 20 s). Little-endian, tested on x86 only.

**How:** It uses a two-stage Recursive Model Index (Kraska et al. 2018). A root model (linear, cubic spline, radix, normal-CDF, etc.) picks one of B leaf models, and that leaf's linear model predicts the key's position in the array. Each leaf's stored maximum error bounds a short binary search. Inference is a few `std::fma` evaluations with at most two cache misses, while a B-tree takes roughly one cache miss per level. The generator packs each leaf's error next to its parameters to save a cache miss, and hard-codes small layers as constants. The CDFShop optimizer (`--optimize`) searches model types and branching factors along the size/error Pareto front.

**Use it when:**
- Immutable or bulk-rebuilt sorted arrays of 32/64-bit unsigned integers or doubles, such as read-only segments, lookup tables or analytics columns, where you look up the same data many times.
- Point or lower-bound lookups where you want lower latency than a B+Tree at a fraction of the memory: in SOSD, 181 ns at 48 MB vs 482 ns at 166 MB for STX B+Tree on 200M 32-bit amzn keys.
- Key sets with a learnable CDF (SOSD amzn, face, wiki), where the SOSD paper found learned indexes Pareto-optimal up to about 100 MB of index size.
- Read-heavy multithreaded lookup: in SOSD's 40-thread test with 50 MB models, RMI was the only learned index to out-throughput the radix lookup table (RBS).
- Build pipelines that can absorb an offline train, codegen and recompile step, and can ship the rmi_data/ parameter files with the binary.

**Skip it when:**
- Any inserts, deletes or updates. Each change means retrain, regenerate and recompile. Use ALEX or LIPP instead.
- Pure point lookups with memory to spare: in the same Table 2, CuckooMap (114.5 ns, 1.5 GB) and RobinHash (93.7 ns, 6.1 GB) are faster.
- Hard-to-learn key distributions such as OSM Hilbert-curve cell IDs. On osm, no learned index beat a plain radix table, and small RMIs were slower than binary search over the whole array.
- String or variable-length keys. Only u32, u64 and f64 inputs are supported, and 32-bit keys gain nothing because model math runs in 64-bit doubles.
- Frequent rebuilds or when you need a maintained, tested library. Build was the slowest of the learned indexes (80 s vs 38 s for PGM and 20 s for RS on the largest amzn size), and substantive development stopped in Aug 2020.

**Integration:** source-drop · Generator: Rust/cargo plus crates rayon, memmap 0.7, byteorder, clap 2.33, json, indicatif, env_logger, log, bytesize, approx, superslice, tabular. Generated code: C++ standard library only, plus the rmi_data/ parameter files at runtime. · Generated code needs C++17 (it uses std::filesystem). The repo's tests build with g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -ffast-math -march=native, add -lstdc++fs for older GCC, and CI installs g++-8. The generator is Rust edition 2018; the minimum Rust version is not documented and CI uses rust:latest. · Tested only on x86-64 Linux (Xeon Gold 6230 in SOSD, Docker CI). Parameter files are written little-endian and read back with raw ifstream reads, so a little-endian host is assumed. Bounded (--bounded) mode emits __attribute__((packed)), which ties it to GCC/Clang.

**Vs siblings:** Pick RMI over RadixSpline (266.58 ns at 4 MB) or PGM-index (326.48 ns at 14 MB) when the lowest static lookup latency matters more than memory, build time and tuning effort; those two are tuned with two knobs and build faster. If you need inserts, use ALEX or LIPP. CARMI reports beating RMI on the SOSD platform, so benchmark it too.

**Gotchas:**
- Only two-layer RMIs are implemented. A three-layer spec such as `linear,linear,linear` hits a bare panic!() (issue #5, not in the README). A radix root with branching factor 1-3 panics (issue #3, open), and very small inputs (~100 keys) can trip an assertion in train_two_layer (issue #8, open).
- Correctness of the error bound on duplicate keys is in question. Open PR #14 (Jun 2026) says longest_run never records the final run of duplicates, so the per-leaf error bound can come out too small. Open PR #15 says the cargo unit tests no longer compile and that FixDupsIter feeds every model one phantom duplicate row. Neither is merged.
- Each generated index is a C++ namespace with global state and is tied to one dataset. Changing the data means regenerating code and recompiling. load() returns false if rmi_data/ is missing, and lookup() before load() reads unset parameters.
- Tuning decides performance. The README calls it critical, and poorly sized RMIs can lose to plain binary search. Inference is std::fma-based, and the repo builds with -march=native -ffast-math.

**Status:** Listed as active, but the commit log shows no code changes from Aug 2020 until May 2026, when a 2020 cleanup PR (#7, header guards) was merged. Fix PRs #14 and #15 are open. It is MIT-licensed, and the generated C++ is small and dependency-free to vendor, but regenerating needs the Rust toolchain.

[repo](https://github.com/learnedsystems/RMI) · [benchmark](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

#### message-queues-logs

##### Monocoque  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Rust, ZeroMQ wire-compatible (ZMTP 3.x) async messaging library; about 3x lower REQ/REP latency than libzmq.

**Beats:** ZeroMQ (libzmq) — In zmq-arena's 2026-08-26 run on a bare-metal i5-13400 (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, turbo off), monocoque 0.4.1 (rustc 1.96, fat LTO, x86-64-v3) had REQ/REP p50 round trips 2.69x-3.12x lower than Ubuntu's libzmq 4.3.5 package. libzmq was driven from an -O3 C++ wrapper with one I/O thread; example cells are 13.79 vs 42.16 us over IPC at 1 KiB and 15.48 vs 42.99 us over TCP at 1 KiB. Monocoque's author wrote the harness and published both run files, and no third party has reproduced them.

**Known shortcoming:** The zmq-arena harness is by Monocoque's own author; the tokio backend gain is ~4.3x (the 2.75-3.12x p50 figure is the fastest backend).

**Known shortcoming:** The speedup comes from skipping libzmq's I/O-thread hop; the tokio/epoll backend beats the io_uring default on IPC REQ/REP (9.36 vs 13.08 us p50). Its CURVE cipher was not real CurveZMQ before 0.4.0 (2026-07-31), which also fixed pre-auth DoS holes. Young (crate from 2026-06, 312 downloads, author filed 49 of 50 issues), pre-1.0 with breaking changes; async Rust only (no C ABI/zmq_poll/blocking API), sockets are !Send, CI Linux only.

**Known shortcoming:** Fan-in with 16 B messages on compio is 0.94x libzmq and fan-in at 1 KiB uses 85.6 vs 38.5 MB RSS. A cancelled send poisons the socket (clashes with select! advice); coalescing needs a manual flush() (deadlock/loss risk). Author-run benchmark pinned to cpuset 0-3 on a hybrid SMT i5, which the arena README itself warns about.

**How:** The main latency lever is that there is no background I/O thread. send() and recv() do the I/O inline on the caller's single-threaded runtime (thread-per-core, and sockets are !Send). libzmq instead passes every message through a lock-free queue to a separate I/O thread. The arena data backs this up: the epoll-based tokio backend matches or beats the io_uring default on REQ/REP (IPC 16 B: 9.36 vs 13.08 us p50), so the win comes from removing the thread hop, not from io_uring. For bulk traffic it uses refcounted Bytes (PUB fan-out clones references and never copies payloads), a reused 64 KiB read slab, allocation-free recv_into, writev for bodies of 32 KB and up, and opt-in write coalescing that packs many small frames into one 64 KB write. The arena's throughput cells turn coalescing on; its REQ/REP cells do not.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services on Linux that must talk to existing libzmq/pyzmq peers and want lower request/reply latency: in the arena run, REQ/REP p50 was about 13-22 us against 40-61 us for libzmq across 16 B-16 KiB payloads.
- Same-host request/reply over IPC: with the tokio backend, p50 was 9.36-9.70 us at 16 B-1 KiB against 40.17-42.16 us for libzmq.
- Small-message PUSH/PULL pipelines where you can call flush() at batch boundaries: coalesced PUSH/PULL reached 13.3 M msg/s at 64 B over IPC against 2.84 M msg/s for libzmq, and 7.6 M vs 3.1 M over TCP.
- PUB/SUB fan-out to many subscribers: at 32 subscribers it delivered 1.7x-4.5x libzmq's message rate, with lower peak RSS (35 MB vs 162 MB at 16 KiB).
- Async Rust codebases already on tokio or smol: pick the matching backend feature and run the sockets on a current-thread runtime.

**Skip it when:**
- Non-Rust callers, or code that depends on libzmq's C ABI, blocking send/recv, zmq_poll or libzmq's many language bindings. This is an async Rust library only.
- Deployments that need transports or features beyond TCP/IPC: PGM/EPGM, TIPC, draft sockets and GSSAPI are listed as skipped in the CHANGELOG, and inproc is a channel bridge that the migration guide says is not the same as libzmq inproc.
- Security-critical CURVE setups that need a track record. Before 0.4.0 (2026-07-31) the CURVE message cipher was not the real CurveZMQ construction, so encrypted interop with libzmq never worked. That same release also closed several pre-auth DoS holes (slow-loris recv timeout, unbounded handshake, unbounded multipart).
- Fan-in of many tiny messages from many producers: at 4-peer fan-in with 16 B messages, the default compio backend reached only 0.94x libzmq's rate. At 1 KiB its peak RSS was 85.6 MB against 38.5 MB for libzmq.
- Teams that need a mature dependency. The crate was first published on 2026-06-22 and has 312 total downloads and 46 stars. It is essentially single-maintainer (49 of 50 issues were filed by the author) and pre-1.0, with breaking changes in 0.3.0 and 0.4.0.

**Integration:** crate (monocoque-rs; library name `monocoque`; the ZeroMQ API sits behind the opt-in `zmq` feature) · No libzmq or C library. Requires exactly one runtime: compio 0.19 (default, io_uring), tokio or smol. Also pulls bytes, compio-io/compio-buf, tracing and flume, plus dashmap, parking_lot, hashbrown, smallvec, socket2 and zeroize in the core crate. The workspace declares RustCrypto x25519-dalek, crypto_box, chacha20poly1305 and sha2 for PLAIN/CURVE. · Rust 1.95 (edition 2024) for every backend, as checked in CI. The manifest notes that the tokio/smol backends can compile as far back as 1.93. · Linux first: the io_uring default needs kernel 5.11+ for the full benefit and falls back to thread-pool I/O on older kernels. The docs offer the tokio/smol backends for macOS, Windows and older kernels, but CI runs only on ubuntu-latest. IPC is Unix-only.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Monocoque over TCPSHM when the other side must stay a stock ZeroMQ peer: TCPSHM uses its own protocol and wins on raw same-host RTT, especially in shared-memory mode. Pick it over NanoMsg when you need ZMTP wire compatibility and CURVE rather than nanomsg's own SP protocols.

**Gotchas:**
- Write coalescing is off by default, so each eager send() is one syscall (about 0.44-0.52 M msg/s at 64 B in the project's local bench). Turning coalescing on makes you own flush(): in request/reply, forgetting flush() before recv() deadlocks, and messages still in the buffer are lost if the process crashes.
- Cancelling a send future mid-write (a timeout, or a losing select! branch) poisons the socket, and later I/O fails with BrokenPipe, 'reconnect required'. This matters because the migration guide suggests futures::select! as the replacement for zmq_poll.
- On the tokio backend, the worker-pool PubSocket's writes depend on the runtime that accepted the subscriber. A short-lived publisher that lets that runtime shut down right after sending can drop the tail of its broadcast.
- Benchmark caveat: the run kept the default cgroup cpuset 0-3. The arena's own README says that setting is only correct on four distinct physical performance cores. The i5-13400 is a hybrid SMT part, and libzmq's extra I/O thread per process competes for those four logical CPUs, so the gap may be different on other hardware.

**Status:** Actively maintained (0.4.2 released 2026-09-22 after roughly monthly releases since June 2026) and MIT-licensed, but it is pre-1.0, single-maintainer and lightly used, so pin the version and expect API breaks between minor releases.

[repo](https://github.com/vorjdux/monocoque) · [benchmark](https://vorjdux.github.io/zmq-arena/history/2026-08-26-run.json)

##### NATS JetStream  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

CNCF Go messaging server whose built-in JetStream persistence showed ~14x lower median latency than Kafka at light load.

**Beats:** Apache Kafka — A personal benchmark (nipunnair/streaming-showdown) ran single-node, unreplicated nats:2.10-alpine JetStream (default file storage, R1) against Kafka 3.6 (cp-kafka 7.6.1, KRaft) in Docker under OrbStack on an Apple M4. Go 1.25 clients (nats.go PublishAsync plus an explicit-ack pull consumer, vs franz-go v1.21.4 at defaults) sent small JSON at 500 msg/s for 20 s after a 5 s warm-up, and HdrHistogram end-to-end latency came out at NATS p50 0.5 / p99 0.9 / p999 2.8 ms vs Kafka 7.2-7.8 / 12.7-13.5 / 14.0-19.1 ms; much of Kafka's median is plausibly franz-go's default 10 ms producer linger, which the bench never lowered, and NATS acked without fsync, so treat this as a light-load, client-default-sensitive result rather than a broker ceiling.

**Known shortcoming:** Kafka's p50 in this benchmark is likely inflated by franz-go's default 10 ms linger, so the ~14x p50 gap overstates the difference; single Apple M4 machine.

**Known shortcoming:** Default JetStream acks before fsync (2-minute sync interval): Jepsen (2025-12, NATS 2.12.1) lost 131k of 930k acknowledged writes on correlated power loss, and issues #7549/#7556/#7564/#7567 remain open. Burst mode shows no throughput win; replication and multi-partition were not tested; the bench ran 2.10 (current 2.15.0). Not a Kafka drop-in; pull consumers have no partitions (ordering lost across parallel workers); subject/dedup indexes stay in RAM (#8485 OOM when memory is capped).

**How:** In this test the gap is mostly per-message path length and client defaults, not a storage algorithm: nats.go flushes each publish as soon as its flusher goroutine is kicked (no linger timer), while franz-go defaults to a 10 ms producer linger. On the server, the file store appends each record with a HighwayHash-64 checksum into a write-through cache of the current message block and, for unreplicated streams, writes it straight to the OS ("flush in place"), with fsync only every 2 minutes by default. A signal goroutine then matches the subject against the stream's consumer sublist and wakes the consumer loop, which serves the waiting pull request from that cache. Per-subject state is kept in an adaptive radix trie (server/stree).

**Use it when:**
- Internal service-to-service events, fan-out and request/reply where you want replayable persistence and sub-millisecond p50 at modest rates (the test: 0.5 ms p50 at 500 msg/s with small JSON messages).
- Edge, IoT or small deployments that want one static binary with no JVM and no separate controller quorum. Release builds cover Linux on many architectures, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD.
- Workloads that need both queue semantics (work-queue retention, per-message ack and redelivery, shared pull consumers) and log-style replay in one system, plus KV or object storage.
- Many fine-grained or hierarchical subjects consumed with wildcard filters (for example per-entity subjects), instead of a fixed set of partitioned topics.

**Skip it when:**
- You depend on Kafka's wire protocol or ecosystem (Connect, Kafka Streams, ksqlDB, schema registry, key-based log compaction). NATS offers a Kafka bridge connector, not API compatibility.
- You need acknowledged writes to survive power loss and plan to run the defaults. JetStream acks before fsync (sync_interval 2 min). Jepsen (NATS 2.12.1, Dec 2025) lost 131,418 of 930,005 acked writes under coordinated power failure, and issues #7549, #7556, #7564 and #7567 (loss from .blk bit-flips, stream deletion from corrupt snapshots, deferred fsync, split-brain) were still open on 2026-09-26.
- High-throughput partitioned ingestion: the same benchmark's burst mode showed no clear throughput win (NATS ~269-339K vs Kafka ~252-333K msg/s producer-side), and replicated or multi-partition setups were not measured at all.
- Very high subject or dedup-ID cardinality on file-backed streams: per-subject and dedup indexes stay in RAM, and open issue #8485 reports OOMs or GC-driven latency when memory is capped.

**Integration:** standalone server binary (tar.gz/zip/deb/rpm and the official `nats` Docker image); JetStream enabled with `-js` or a `jetstream {}` config block; the source is the Go module github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 · None at runtime (single Go binary). Go module deps: klauspost/compress (S2), minio/highwayhash, nats-io jwt/nkeys/nuid/nats.go, golang.org/x/crypto, x/sys, x/time, google/go-tpm, antithesis-sdk-go (no-op build). Apps need a NATS client with JetStream support (the benchmark used nats.go v1.52.0). · Prebuilt binaries need nothing. Building from source needs Go 1.26.0 (go.mod declares toolchain go1.26.8). The benchmark client was built with Go 1.25. · v2.15.0 release binaries: Linux amd64/386/arm64/arm6/arm7/loong64/mips64le/ppc64le/riscv64/s390x, macOS amd64/arm64, Windows amd64/386/arm64, FreeBSD amd64. The benchmark ran linux/arm64 containers under OrbStack on an Apple M4.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Redpanda (Kafka-API compatible, but it trailed Kafka in this same single-core, 500 msg/s test) when you don't need Kafka clients and care about small-message latency in one lightweight binary. Wisp beats NATS core pub/sub throughput but has no persistence, JetStream or clustering, so pick JetStream whenever you need durable, replayable streams.

**Gotchas:**
- Durability is opt-in. `sync_interval` defaults to 2 minutes, so an R1 stream can lose acknowledged messages on an OS crash or power loss, and the docs say even R3 can lose them under correlated failures. `sync_interval: always` fsyncs before every ack, which the docs call the slowest setting.
- Shared pull consumers are partition-less, so two sequential messages on the same subject can go to different subscribers and ordering across parallel workers is lost. Use `partition()` subject mapping if you need per-key ordering.
- JetStream publish is at-least-once. Exactly-once needs the `Nats-Msg-Id` header deduplicated within the stream's DuplicateWindow, plus consumer-side double ack. Messages are capped at 1 MB by default; the Object Store chunks larger objects.
- nats.go PublishAsync allows 4000 in-flight acks by default and then stalls, waiting up to 200 ms by default. The docs also say Replicas=2 brings no benefit, so use R1, R3 or R5.

**Status:** Actively maintained CNCF project (v2.15.0 released 2026-09-17, commits through 2026-09-25, ~20.8k stars, Apache-2.0, Trail of Bits audit April 2025), though the benchmark used the older 2.10 line and the four Jepsen durability issues filed in Nov 2025 remain open.

[repo](https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server) · [benchmark](https://github.com/nipunnair/streaming-showdown/blob/main/COMPARISON.md)

##### NanoMsg  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

C library of brokerless messaging patterns (PUB/SUB, REQ/REP, etc.) with lower small-message latency than ZeroMQ on one host.

**Beats:** ZeroMQ — An independent Hitachi Energy study (IEEE SRDS 2025) compared nanomsg 1.1.5 with ZeroMQ (libzmq 4.3.4 + CZMQ 4.2.1) and NNG 1.9.0, using a gcc -O2 C harness against prebuilt distro packages (NNG built from source). The test was one-host PUB/SUB on a Xeon w3-2435 (8 cores, 64 GB), 5000 messages x 4 runs. With 1 subscriber at a 1000 us publish interval, nanomsg's mean latency at 1 KB was 7.5 vs 10.3 us in-process and 16.2 vs 25.8 us over IPC (about 1.4-1.6x, derived from the published CSV). The gap narrowed to about 1.1-1.2x at 32 KB and reversed at larger sizes, and ZeroMQ kept the best peak throughput and worst-case latency.

**Known shortcoming:** The win is modest (~1.1-1.6x latency, derived from the paper's CSV) and TCP at 16-32 KB is much worse than ZeroMQ; the library is in sustaining mode (successor: nng). GCC version and flags of the distro-built libraries unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: CVE-2026-97152 (WebSocket handshake overflow) is fixed only in 1.2.3; the benchmarked 1.1.5 distro package predates the fix. TCP has a 16-64 KB latency spike (~560 vs 40 us) because Nagle is on by default (won't-fix, #674) and the harness never disabled it. ZeroMQ wins peak throughput (4.8 vs 3.8 GB/s inproc), large payloads and many subscribers; PUB/SUB silently drops (#390); 512-socket cap; sustaining mode (upstream recommends NNG).

**How:** It is plain C that uses intrusive containers to keep allocations per message low. nn_chunkref stores payloads of 32 bytes or less (usually protocol headers) inline. PUB fan-out (nn_dist_send) shares one reference-counted chunk across all subscriber pipes instead of copying the body for each subscriber. SUB sockets match subscriptions against a memory-compact Patricia trie with sparse and dense child nodes, and the library avoids ZeroMQ's double buffering (a user-space queue plus the kernel buffer) by relying on the transport's own buffers. It is not zero-copy, though: the inproc transport still memcpys each message once, and all async I/O runs on a single internal epoll/kqueue worker thread (src/aio/pool.c). That keeps CPU and memory low for small messages but limits how far it scales with large payloads and many subscribers.

**Use it when:**
- Same-host PUB/SUB or request/reply with small-to-medium messages (about 1-64 KB in-process, up to 128 KB over IPC), where mean latency and CPU matter more than peak throughput. The SRDS 2025 study measured a 1 KB mean of 7.5 vs 10.3 us in-process and 16.2 vs 25.8 us over IPC against ZeroMQ.
- CPU- or memory-constrained hosts. It is ANSI C89 with no C++ runtime, and the study found it had the lowest CPU at every IPC message size and the lowest memory use of ZeroMQ, nanomsg and NNG.
- Designs that want SURVEY (surveyor/respondent) or BUS as built-in socket types, or REQ sockets with built-in request retry, rather than building these on top of ZeroMQ primitives.
- Existing nanomsg deployments, or peers that must speak the SP wire protocol, including NNG, which upstream says is wire-compatible.

**Skip it when:**
- New projects. Upstream says the library is in 'sustaining' mode: new features have stopped and only severe defects are fixed. It points users to NNG, which it says is API-compatible for about 99% of apps.
- TCP with 16-64 KB messages at default settings. In the study, mean latency at 16-32 KB was about 560 us vs ZeroMQ's 40 us. NN_TCP_NODELAY defaults to 0 (Nagle on), and upstream closed the request to change that default (#674) as will-not-fix, whereas libzmq always sets TCP_NODELAY. The benchmark harness never set it. If you must use TCP, set NN_TCP_NODELAY=1 and re-measure.
- Large payloads, peak throughput or many subscribers. ZeroMQ won these in the study: peak throughput was about 4.8 vs 3.8 GB/s in-process and 2.9 vs 1.7 GB/s over IPC, and 512 KB in-process latency was 86 vs 118 us. nanomsg funnels all async I/O through one worker thread.
- Workloads that need delivery guarantees, backpressure or persistence on PUB/SUB. Delivery is best-effort, and messages are silently dropped when a subscriber or the TCP stack falls behind (#390). There is no broker and no shared-memory transport (#902).
- Streaming many tiny messages through one inproc pipe as fast as possible. A 2014 report (#300) found PAIR inproc throughput about 4.5x slower than ZeroMQ (2.45 s vs 0.55 s), which contributors attributed to an eventfd signal per message.

**Integration:** shared lib (default) or static lib (-DNN_STATIC_LIB=ON; Windows callers must also define NN_STATIC_LIB) · none beyond libc, POSIX pthreads and BSD sockets (Windows: ws2_32, mswsock, advapi32); CMake to build; asciidoctor optional for docs; also packaged in vcpkg and distro repos · ANSI C89 compiler; CMake 2.8.12+ (CMake 4.x supported since 1.2.2); Windows Vista+ with MSVC 2010+ (mingw-w64 untested) · Linux, macOS, FreeBSD/NetBSD/OpenBSD, Solaris, HP-UX, QNX, Android and Windows per CMakeLists; CI covers Linux, Windows and macOS; architecture-independent C

**Vs siblings:** Pick nanomsg over TCPSHM, a Linux-only, header-only, point-to-point channel with acked in-memory resend, when you need one-to-many PUB/SUB fan-out or Windows/macOS. Pick it over Mino, an IDL-typed zero-copy shared-memory framework, when you want a small, stable C library that sends untyped byte messages through a socket-style API. For raw same-host latency, TCPSHM's SHM mode (0.34 us RTT vs ZeroMQ IPC's 30.7 us) is in a different class.

**Gotchas:**
- Filtering happens on the subscriber side. PUB sends every message to every connected SUB and the SUB's trie discards non-matches, so traffic nobody subscribed to still costs transport bandwidth and CPU.
- NN_RCVMAXSIZE defaults to 1024 kB, so larger messages are refused on receive unless you raise it (-1 removes the limit). NN_MAX_SOCKETS is a build-time cap of 512 sockets per process, and inproc ignores NN_SNDBUF (the receiver's NN_RCVBUF sets the buffer).
- Versions before 1.2.3 have a remotely exploitable buffer overflow in the WebSocket handshake (CVE-2026-97152, CVSS 4.0 score 8.6). 1.2.5 (2026-09) stopped malformed IPC headers from aborting the process. Distro packages such as the benchmarked 1.1.5 predate both fixes.
- The 'nanomsg' name is a trademark, separate from the MIT code license. COPYING names Martin Sustrik as the owner and nanomsg.org names Garrett D'Amore.

**Status:** Active by commit date (1.2.5 released 2026-09-06), but officially in sustaining mode: only severe fixes are made and NNG is recommended for new work. It is MIT-licensed pure C that is easy to build via CMake or vcpkg, or to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/nanomsg/nanomsg) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07934)

##### NNG (nanomsg-next-generation)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Maintained C rewrite of nanomsg (Scalability Protocols). It beats nanomsg's pub/sub throughput only for very large messages.

**Beats:** NanoMsg — An independent Hitachi Energy study (IEEE SRDS 2025, arXiv 2508.07934) benchmarked PUB/SUB on one Xeon w3-2435 host (8 cores, 64 GB). It compared NNG 1.9.0 (built from source with CMake and no build type) against distro-packaged libnanomsg 1.1.5 and libzmq 4.3.4, using 1-512 KB messages over inproc, IPC and TCP loopback. NNG out-threw nanomsg only at the two largest IPC sizes, and above ~128 KB on TCP, where it reached ~2 GB/s against nanomsg's ~1.5 GB/s peak. ZeroMQ led overall at ~2.9 GB/s. The paper gives no compiler flags; the C harness is built with gcc -O2.

**Known shortcoming:** Mostly loses to ZeroMQ and nanomsg in the SRDS 2025 study; its real win is narrow (large-payload throughput vs nanomsg); NNG was likely built unoptimized (cmake with no build type).

**Known shortcoming:** Beats nanomsg only on large payloads (256/512 KB over IPC, >128 KB over TCP loopback, ~2 vs ~1.5 GB/s); ZeroMQ is fastest overall (~2.9 GB/s) and nanomsg best on latency and CPU; NNG has higher jitter, spiking at 512 KB. Pub/sub silently drops messages by default (16-message per-pipe PUB queue, drop-oldest). The main branch is 2.0 beta with a breaking API (nn_* compat removed). SECURITY: remote-abort bug GHSA-8rrv (nni_msg_alloc overflow) fixed in 1.12.3; set RECVMAXSZ for untrusted peers.

**How:** NNG replaces nanomsg's design, where each socket ran on a single worker thread driven by state machines, with an asynchronous I/O framework (nng_aio). Completion callbacks run on a task-thread pool, and platform pollers (epoll, kqueue, event ports) do the I/O. Contexts let one socket run many concurrent state machines. The PUB fan-out does not copy the message: it bumps a refcount per pipe and uses a small bounded queue per pipe. The TCP/IPC transports send an 8-byte length, the header and the body as one scatter-gather write, and on receive they allocate an exact-size message and read the body straight into it. Neither the paper nor the project says which of these mechanisms produces the large-payload win over nanomsg.

**Use it when:**
