- You use tweetnacl-js only for Ed25519 signatures and must support runtimes without native Web Crypto Ed25519 (Chrome before 137, Firefox before 129, Safari before 17)
- Cold-start-sensitive pages that sign or verify once right after load (e.g. an auth token): the README shows first-call sign/verify of 1.3-3 ms vs 8-44 ms for tweetnacl-js
- Verifying signatures over large payloads (tens of KB) in the browser, where native SHA-512 helps: ~5.6-5.9x vs tweetnacl-js on an ~80 KB message
- Bundle-size-sensitive front ends that need only signing: 7.4 kB min+gz vs 10.6 kB for tweetnacl-js (which also includes box/secretbox)
- You want TweetNaCl's constant-time design (no secret-dependent branches or memory access), not the BigInt field arithmetic of noble-ed25519 v1

**Skip it when:**
- Modern targets with native Web Crypto Ed25519 sign/verify (Chrome 137+, Firefox 129+, Safari 17+, Node 16.17+, Deno 1.26+); watsign was never benchmarked against these native paths
- Strict-CSP pages or Chrome MV3 extensions: the watever-js-wrapper glue calls indirect eval on the JS import strings, and issue #4 (open) reports it failing in MV3
- Synchronous code paths, X25519/box/secretbox, batch verification or other curves: none are provided
- Choosing between it and today's @noble/ed25519 (3.2.0): the noble comparison used noble-ed25519 1.2.6 from 2021, so the '1.2-3x faster than noble' claim is outdated
- Consensus-critical or compliance-driven use: there is one maintainer, the project has been stale since 2024-04, it has no audit, it gets ~154 npm downloads/month, and verification inherits TweetNaCl's non-strict rules

**Integration:** module (ESM-only npm package; Wasm embedded as base64 in the JS; Deno can import mod.js from raw.githubusercontent.com or use npm:watsign) · watever-js-wrapper ^0.3.2 at runtime, plus the platform's Web Crypto (crypto.subtle SHA-512, getRandomValues) or node:crypto · Node >= 16 (package engines); ESM ('type': 'module'); browsers need WebAssembly and Web Crypto SHA-512; rebuilding needs the author's watever WAT bundler (0.5.2) · Any JS runtime with WebAssembly: modern browsers, Node >= 16, Deno

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings (ENG25519 AVX-512IFMA, SUPERCOP amd64-64-24k Ed25519, libsecp256k1, UltrafastSecp256k1) are native C or assembly and cannot run inside a browser or Deno sandbox. Pick watsign only when Ed25519 must run in JS or Wasm; on servers, use those native libraries or the runtime's built-in crypto.

**Gotchas:**
- sign() does not check the secret-key length: the 64-byte check exists only as a comment in sign.wat. Passing the wrong value (e.g. the whole key pair) gives 'RuntimeError: memory access out of bounds' (issue #3) instead of tweetnacl's 'bad secret key size'. verify and the keyPair functions do validate sizes.
- verify ports TweetNaCl's check (unpack A, reduce H, compute [H](-A) + [S]B, compare with R) without rejecting non-canonical S >= L, so it is not a strict RFC 8032 verifier and accepts malleated signatures just as tweetnacl-js does.
- Tests only cover two fixed identities cross-checked against tweetnacl-js; there are no RFC 8032 or Wycheproof vectors. Version 0.1.6 fixed a byte-widening bug in i8_to_i64 that had corrupted the hash reduction, so avoid anything older than 0.1.6 (latest is 0.1.9).
- Timing uses performance.now() around awaited calls, so the async hop through the Web Crypto promise is included; cold-start numbers are single samples that the README itself says vary between runs.

**Status:** Stale: the WAT core last changed in October 2021 (v0.1.6), and the latest release, v0.1.9 (2024-04-15), only fixed TypeScript exports. Two issues are open, including the CSP/MV3 breakage. It is MIT-licensed and small, but edits require the author's watever toolchain, and native Web Crypto Ed25519 now covers most of its use case.

[repo](https://github.com/mitschabaude/watsign) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mitschabaude/watsign/blob/main/README.md)

### media-and-graphics

#### color-and-resampling

##### Albumentations  `Python`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Python image-augmentation library on OpenCV and LUT kernels; 1.2-13x the throughput of torchvision, Kornia, imgaug and AugLy per transform.

**Beats:** torchvision, Kornia, imgaug and AugLy (CPU image-augmentation transforms) — The project's own harness (albumentations-team/benchmark at ab6e84d) times each transform alone over 2000 ImageNet-style images on one thread on macOS 15.1 arm64 (16 cores, chip not named), median of 5 passes: for example Brightness 11985 img/s vs AugLy 2108, Hue 1944 vs Kornia 150, Resize 3532 vs imgaug 2995; Albumentations 2.0.4 ran on 2025-02-18 and the competitors in separate January 2025 sessions with different Python and NumPy builds. Reading the harness shows two quoted rows compare unequal work beyond the verifier's notes: Albumentations' Contrast is a pure LUT gain while AugLy's ImageEnhance.Contrast computes the image mean and blends, and AugLy's Grayscale converts back to 3-channel RGB while Albumentations outputs 1 channel (the like-for-like 1-channel comparator, torchvision at 2600 img/s, gives about 12.4x, derived from page data). The harness's requirements/albumentations.txt installs Albumentations from a local '../albumentations' checkout rather than the PyPI release, so the reported 2.0.4 is the checkout's version string and the exact code measured is not pinned.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-baseline (torchvision, Kornia, imgaug, AugLy) and archived 2025-07-10. CPU stated only as 'arm, 16 cores'. Rows do unequal work: torchvision Resize keeps aspect ratio with antialias on, Kornia receives float32 input and its Grayscale outputs 3 channels, AugLy ColorJitter has no hue; Albumentations and competitor runs used different Python builds on different dates.

**Known shortcoming:** Further harness flaws: the Contrast row is unequal work (Albumentations applies a pure LUT gain of 1.2 with no mean while AugLy's ImageEnhance.Contrast computes the mean and blends); AugLy's Grayscale converts back to 3-channel RGB, so the like-for-like 1-channel comparison is torchvision at 2600 (12.4x, derived); imgaug's 'Contrast' row is really AddToHueAndSaturation (mislabelled). requirements/albumentations.txt installs a local checkout rather than PyPI 2.0.4, so the measured code is not pinned; uint8 HSV quantises hue to 0-179; import performs a PyPI version check unless NO_ALBUMENTATIONS_UPDATE=1.

**How:** Almost every op is a single call into an OpenCV kernel on the uint8 HWC array (cv2.resize, cv2.cvtColor for gray and HSV, cv2.addWeighted, cv2.LUT-style point ops), with no float conversion or tensor layout change. Point operations on uint8 (brightness/contrast gain, gamma, hue shift, posterize) go through the albucore helper package, which builds a 256-entry lookup table and applies it with StringZilla's SIMD byte translate (sz.translate), or uses SimSIMD for weighted sums. The competitors in its benchmark pay for float32 tensor math (Kornia), per-op Python and tensor overhead (torchvision), or PIL ImageEnhance blends (AugLy).

**Use it when:**
- CPU data-loading pipelines for image classification, detection or segmentation in Python where per-sample augmentation time limits GPU utilisation.
- Augmenting uint8 RGB images together with masks, boxes or keypoints so the geometry stays consistent across targets.
- Colour point ops (brightness, contrast gain, gamma, hue/saturation shift) on uint8 images, where the LUT path gave 3-13x over the other libraries in the first-party table.
- Projects that need a permissive (MIT) licence and can pin the final 2.0.8 release without further fixes.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ code: it is a Python package; call OpenCV (also catalogued) directly, which is what Albumentations uses for resize and colour conversion.
- High-quality downscaling: Resize and RandomResizedCrop default to cv2 INTER_LINEAR with no antialiasing, so large reductions alias; use INTER_AREA, Pillow-SIMD or a dedicated resampler instead.
- Colour-accurate work: uint8 HSV goes through OpenCV's 8-bit HSV (hue 0-179), so hue shifts move in 2-degree steps and the RGB-HSV-RGB round trip is lossy; results do not match torchvision or Kornia float math.
- Elastic distortions and some illumination effects: imgaug was faster on Elastic (395 vs 374 img/s) and Kornia on LinearIllumination (708 vs 479) and PlasmaShadow (216 vs 183).
- Long-lived projects that need bug fixes: the repo is archived and fixes land only in AlbumentationsX, which is AGPL-3.0 or commercial.

**Integration:** module · numpy>=1.24.4, scipy>=1.10.0, PyYAML, pydantic>=2.9.2, albucore==0.0.28 (which pulls stringzilla>=3.10.4 and simsimd>=5.9.2), and an OpenCV wheel >=4.9.0.80 (opencv-python-headless if none is installed) · Python 3.9+ (classifiers list 3.9 to 3.13); binary wheels only, no compiler needed · any platform with OpenCV, StringZilla and SimSIMD wheels (x86-64 and arm64 Linux, macOS, Windows); the benchmark ran on macOS 15.1 arm64

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over calling OpenCV directly only when you want ready-made random augmentation policies with mask/box/keypoint bookkeeping in Python; for plain resizing its Resize is cv2.resize plus wrapper overhead (only 1.18x over imgaug, which calls the same kernel), and Pillow-SIMD or Lycon are the catalogued choices for antialiased Python resizing.

**Gotchas:**
- Importing the package performs a PyPI version check (urllib request to pypi.org/pypi/albumentations/json, 2 s timeout, in albumentations/check_version.py) unless NO_ALBUMENTATIONS_UPDATE=1 is set; this adds start-up latency and outbound traffic in air-gapped or sandboxed jobs.
- RandomBrightnessContrast's 'contrast' is a gain about zero (x*alpha + beta through a LUT, with beta from brightness only), not the mean-centred blend that torchvision, Kornia and PIL use, so the same parameter gives a different image and does less work.
- OpenCV threads multiply inside multi-worker DataLoaders and can saturate shared CPUs (issue #1246); call cv2.setNumThreads(0) in workers, as the benchmark harness does.
- Inputs are NumPy HWC arrays in the channel order you load; feeding cv2.imread BGR data where torchvision saw RGB produced large output differences in issue #2484, and HueSaturationValue left whites tinted under saturation increases in issue #2353.

**Status:** Archived on 2025-07-10 after the 2.0.8 release (15.3k stars, all issues closed); the MIT code is usable as-is but receives no fixes, and the maintained successor AlbumentationsX is AGPL-3.0 or commercial.

[repo](https://github.com/albumentations-team/albumentations) · [benchmark](https://github.com/albumentations-team/benchmark/tree/ab6e84d4c88485dd3ea1e045c03373a6bf4f488a)

##### CUDARGB2Y  `C++ (CUDA)`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

20-line CUDA kernel converting packed BGR8 already on the GPU to 8-bit gray; claims 5-30x over OpenCV's CPU cvtColor.

**Beats:** OpenCV cv::cvtColor(image, out, CV_BGR2GRAY) on a host cv::Mat (CPU), as called in main.cpp; OpenCV version and build (SIMD, threading backend) unstated, though the CV_BGR2GRAY and CV_WINDOW_NORMAL C-API constants point to OpenCV 2.x/3.x — The only performance figure is the README and source-header sentence 'Roughly 5x to 30x faster than OpenCV's implementation, depending on your card'; no run output, GPU, CPU or OpenCV version is recorded. main.cpp times the kernel launch plus cudaDeviceSynchronize with a host clock, averaging 2000 calls after 100 warm-ups, on the repo's test.jpg (1920x1080, decoded in this session), with the input already resident as a texture and the output left on the device. It compares this with cv::cvtColor(CV_BGR2GRAY) on the CPU over the same number of calls; OpenCV's own CUDA path (cv::cuda::cvtColor) is never measured, so the ratio is GPU against CPU without transfers. The harness then requires every pixel to be within 1 of OpenCV. An enricher brute force over all 16.7 million BGR colours shows the kernel's 6-bit weights (7, 38, 19 over 64, truncated) differ from OpenCV 4.x's 15-bit rounded coefficients (3735, 19235, 9798 over 32768) by up to 3: 49.9% of colours by 1, 7.5% by 2 and 1,438 by 3. On test.jpg the maximum difference is 1 (44% of pixels off by one), so the harness passes on its own image. Its claim that the default weights 'match OpenCV's default' holds only to about 1/64 precision.

**Known shortcoming:** GPU against CPU: main.cpp times kernel launch plus cudaDeviceSynchronize against CPU cv::cvtColor with uploads and downloads untimed; no recorded output, GPU or CPU model, or OpenCV version (2.x/3.x constants); built for sm_30.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e111, 2026-10-05): the 6-bit truncated weights differ from OpenCV's conversion by up to 3 grey levels (7.5% of 24-bit colours off by 2 or more, e.g. BGR 218,0,243 gives 95 vs 98); the README's 'match OpenCV' holds only to 1/64 precision, and the 1920x1080 test.jpg has a max difference of 1 so the harness passes. Timing excludes the 6.2 MB upload and 2.1 MB download; there is no cv::cuda::cvtColor baseline; no CUDA error checks, and a check failure still prints timings. Tier C stays.

**Independent measurement:** first-party timing

**How:** There is no algorithmic trick; the gain is GPU memory bandwidth against a CPU. One thread handles one pixel (256-thread blocks). It reads its three bytes with three tex1Dfetch calls through the texture cache, computes a 6-bit fixed-point sum ((7*B + 38*G + 19*R) >> 6, clamped to 255) and writes one byte. The kernel is memory-bound, moving 3 bytes in and 1 byte out per pixel, so newer cards with more bandwidth give the larger end of the claimed range.

**Use it when:**
- BGR8 frames that already sit in contiguous (unpitched) CUDA device memory and must stay there, where you need 8-bit luma as one step of a GPU pipeline.
- Batch or video workloads that already pay the host-to-device copy for other GPU stages, so the conversion adds only a sub-millisecond kernel per 1080p frame (no measured figure is recorded).
- Applications that tolerate small luma differences from OpenCV (display, thresholding, feature detection) rather than needing bit-exact cvtColor output.
- As a minimal, MIT-licensed template for a per-pixel CUDA kernel driven by texture objects, small enough to paste and adapt.

**Skip it when:**
- Images that live in host memory: the harness times the kernel with the input already uploaded and the result left on the device. A host caller also pays the copy of 3 bytes per pixel up (6.2 MB for the repo's 1920x1080 test.jpg) and 1 byte per pixel down, which is likely to cost more than OpenCV's whole CPU conversion; this end-to-end case is not measured.
- Pipelines that need OpenCV-identical gray values. The 6-bit truncated weights differ from OpenCV's 15-bit rounded coefficients by up to 3 levels: 7.5% of all 24-bit colours differ by 2 or more (enricher brute force), e.g. BGR (218, 0, 243) gives 95 against OpenCV's 98.
- Pitched GPU buffers (cudaMallocPitch, cv::cuda::GpuMat with row padding), RGB-ordered data or 4-channel BGRA input: it assumes tightly packed BGR rows, and RGB input swaps the R and B weights.
- Multi-stream or latency-sensitive GPU code: every call launches on the default stream and then runs cudaDeviceSynchronize, which waits for all device work, not just this kernel, and no CUDA error is checked or returned.
- Current toolchains without edits: the Makefile targets sm_30, which current CUDA toolkits cannot build for (per the verification record), and main.cpp uses OpenCV 2.x/3.x C-API constants (CV_BGR2GRAY, CV_WINDOW_NORMAL). The code has not changed since October 2016.

**Integration:** source-drop (CUDARGB2Y.h plus CUDARGB2Y.cu; main.cpp is only the demo and harness) · CUDA runtime (texture objects). OpenCV (core, imgproc, imgcodecs, highgui, features2d) only for the demo harness. · nvcc with -std=c++11 for the .cu file; the Makefile's ARCH=sm_30 must be raised for current CUDA. The harness needs a C++17 host compiler (-std=gnu++17) and OpenCV 2.x/3.x-era constants. · NVIDIA GPUs only (CUDA texture objects, so compute capability 3.0 or newer).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when the BGR frame is already on an NVIDIA GPU and you want a tiny standalone kernel to paste. If the image is on the CPU, the author's own RGB2Y (AVX2), CompV (about 7x over OpenCV for RGB24 to gray in its result file) or OpenCV itself avoid the PCIe round trip. If you chain OpenCV-CUDA operations, fusing the conversion into neighbouring steps, as cvGPUSpeedup does, saves more than a faster standalone kernel.

**Gotchas:**
- The README says custom weights are set in CUDARGB2Y.h, but the B_WEIGHT/G_WEIGHT/R_WEIGHT constants live in CUDARGB2Y.cu. Any weight is rounded to a multiple of 1/64 (0.114 becomes 7/64 = 0.109) and the sum is truncated, not rounded.
- The input must be bound as a single linear 1D texture, so it is bounded by the device's maxTexture1DLinear limit. main.cpp never checks cudaCreateTextureObject, cudaMalloc or the kernel launch, so a failed setup would time an empty synchronize loop, and only the later pixel check would notice.
- The harness's pixel check only prints an error and breaks out of the comparison loop. It still prints both timings, so a run with wrong output can still report a speedup.
- main.cpp sets display_image = true and blocks on cv::waitKey(0) after opening HighGUI windows, so it hangs or fails on a headless machine unless that flag is changed.

**Status:** Abandoned: three commits, code last changed 2016-10-30 and an MIT LICENSE added 2021-03-23, 16 stars and 6 forks. Small enough to vendor, but it needs the sm_30 target and the OpenCV 2.x/3.x constants in the demo updated.

[repo](https://github.com/komrad36/CUDARGB2Y) · [benchmark](https://github.com/komrad36/CUDARGB2Y)

##### cvGPUSpeedup (OpenCV-style wrapper on the Fused Kernel Library)  `C++ (CUDA)`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only CUDA C++20 wrapper that fuses chains of OpenCV-CUDA-style preprocessing calls into one kernel; first-party 38x over OpenCV-CUDA.

**Beats:** OpenCV-CUDA calls launched as separate kernels on one stream (per crop cv::cuda::GpuMat::convertTo and cv::cuda::resize INTER_LINEAR, then cv::cuda::multiply, cvtColor RGB2BGR, subtract, divide and split), against one fused cvGS::executeOperations kernel — First-party only: the README states 38x kernel execution for 50 crops on an RTX A2000 12GB, 1/167th of the time in a user's Nsight timeline, and 2x to 10000x from unit tests run as benchmarks; no result files are committed, and the host CPU, OS/driver model, OpenCV build and build type are unstated. The public harness (tests/batchresize/test_batchresize_x_split3D.cu) times OpenCV-CUDA's per-crop chain (seven launches per crop, or a partly batched variant) against one fused kernel with cudaEvents on the same stream over 100 iterations, BATCH 10 to 300, with inputs already on the GPU. Because the OpenCV side is dominated by host launch rate, the ratio depends heavily on the unstated CPU and driver, and the CSV's first block is corrupted by the warm-up rows described above. The README's OpenCV and cvGS snippets are illustrative and not identical (different divide values; alpha folded into convertTo on one side and a separate multiply on the other).

**Known shortcoming:** Same-GPU comparison (RTX A2000) of an OpenCV-CUDA kernel chain against one fused kernel using cudaEvent stream time with transfers excluded (harness tests/batchresize/test_batchresize_x_split3D.cu); no result CSVs back the 38x, 167x or 2x-10000x figures and the host CPU is unstated; the arXiv 2508.07071 20931x is snippet-only. The repo moved to Libraries-Openly-Fused/cvGPUSpeedup-FastOpenCV.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e115, 2026-10-05): C stands. Measurement flaw in tests/testsCommon.cuh: the warmup pass still calls processExecution, so each benchmark CSV starts with rows whose mean is one cold iteration divided by 100 and whose variance and 'Mean Speedup' average 99 uninitialised slots; whether the README's 2x-10000x used them is unknown since no CSV is committed. The batchresize input is constant-filled, so the OpenCV check cannot catch resize-coordinate errors; variable-batch resize was broken until PR #184 (2025-11-11); the wrapper covers only INTER_LINEAR resize plus channel-swap/grey cvtColor; the OpenCV side is launch-bound; host CPU and OS unstated.

**Independent measurement:** first-party CSV harness

**How:** Vertical kernel fusion: the whole operation list becomes one templated CUDA kernel, so intermediates stay in registers, the input is read once and the output written once, and there is one launch instead of one per operation and per crop. Horizontal fusion batches all crops of a std::array<GpuMat, BATCH> into the same grid (batch resize with a usedPlanes count), and executeOperations enables 'thread fusion' by default, where each thread processes several elements. The gain therefore comes mostly from removing launch overhead, idle GPU gaps and global-memory round trips between many tiny OpenCV-CUDA kernels, not from a faster resize algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Images already live in cv::cuda::GpuMat on an NVIDIA GPU and an Nsight Systems trace shows long chains of tiny OpenCV-CUDA kernels (convertTo, resize, arithmetic, cvtColor, split) before a neural network.
- Crop-and-resize of many small detections per frame (tens to hundreds of crops of about 60x120 into 64x128, as in the batchresize test) followed by normalisation and channel split into a planar float tensor.
- Latency-bound real-time video pipelines where launch overhead and intermediate GpuMat allocations dominate preprocessing, including updating a temporal tensor of recent frames in one kernel.
- Projects already compiling .cu files with nvcc in C++20 that can accept template-heavy headers.

**Skip it when:**
- One large, bandwidth-bound operation (a single 4K resize or colour conversion): there is little launch overhead to remove, and the README itself says the speedup grows with the number and smallness of fused kernels.
- Interpolations other than bilinear or colour conversions beyond channel reorders and to-gray: cvGS restricts resize to cv::INTER_LINEAR and cvtColor to RGB/BGR/RGBA/BGRA swaps and *2GRAY at compile time (no cubic, area, Lanczos, YUV or HSV in the wrapper).
- CPU-only, AMD, Intel or Apple GPUs: it is CUDA-only.
- Toolchains on CUDA 12.4 to 12.6, which the README says cannot compile it (an nvcc template-deduction bug), or codebases limited to C++17.
- Teams that need documentation or a stable API: the README says there is no documentation (read the tests) and that FKL is 'less than 1% complete'; the API is still changing (e.g. resize and warp overloads without an input GpuMat added in August 2026).

**Integration:** header-only (include/*.cuh plus the FKL headers in the fkl submodule), compiled into your own .cu translation units by nvcc · CUDA toolkit; OpenCV 4.x built with the CUDA modules (the tests link core, cudaarithm, imgproc, cudafilters, cudaimgproc, cudawarping, imgcodecs); Fused Kernel Library submodule (header-only; the repo's CMake asks find_package(FKL 0.1.8)) · C++20 with nvcc from CUDA 11.8, 12.1, 12.3 or 12.8 (12.4 to 12.6 unsupported); MSVC v14.39 to v14.43 on Windows; CMake 3.24 for the repo's tests and benchmarks; OpenCV 4.8, 4.9 or 4.11 tested (CI moved to OpenCV 4.14.0 in 2026) · NVIDIA GPUs (tested on compute capability 7.5, 8.6 and 8.9) on x86-64 and ARM64 (Jetson Orin), Windows 11 and Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 including WSL2

**Vs siblings:** The other color-and-resampling entries are mostly CPU libraries (fast_image_resize, libvips, CompV, kornia-rs, stb-image-resize-opt) or a stand-alone GPU kernel (CUDARGB2Y). Pick cvGPUSpeedup when your frames are already on an NVIDIA GPU in OpenCV-CUDA and the cost is a chain of small calls. Pick those CPU libraries when there is no NVIDIA GPU or the job is one large resize, where cvGPUSpeedup's fusion has little to remove.

**Gotchas:**
- Benchmark CSV flaw: in ENABLE_BENCHMARK builds the warm-up pass (warmup = true, loop breaks after one iteration) still calls processExecution, so each CSV starts with rows whose means are one cold iteration divided by 100 and whose variance and 'Mean Speedup' are averaged over 99 uninitialised std::array slots. Only the second block of rows (the real 100-iteration run) is meaningful; discard the first when reading your own results.
- The batch-resize tests that double as benchmarks fill the 3840x2160 input with a constant value, so the check against OpenCV-CUDA (absolute tolerance 1e-4 for float) validates the arithmetic chain but cannot catch wrong resize sampling coordinates; validate on your own images.
- Variable batch sizes were broken until PR #184 (merged 2025-11-11): cvGS::resize on a std::array of GpuMats did not forward usedPlanes and backgroundValue to fk::Resize, so code like the README's activeDetections example needs a version from after that fix.
- Batch size, OpenCV types and interpolation are compile-time template arguments, and thread fusion is on by default (executeOperations<true>); every new combination instantiates a new kernel, so expect long nvcc compile times and code growth.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-08-27; CI moving to CUDA 13.4, CMake 4.4 and OpenCV 4.14), Apache-2.0 and header-only, so it is copyable. It is undocumented, its authors call it a demonstration platform, and the repo moved to Libraries-Openly-Fused/cvGPUSpeedup-FastOpenCV (the old morousg URL redirects).

[repo](https://github.com/morousg/cvGPUSpeedup) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Libraries-Openly-Fused/cvGPUSpeedup-FastOpenCV)

##### DeltaCV  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Four hand-written SSE/AVX2 kernels that fuse colour conversion and threshold masking; first-party 3.4-7.6x over OpenCV call chains.

**Beats:** OpenCV (cv::cvtColor RGB2GRAY and RGB2HSV on CPU, and OpenCV chains for fused colour-space plus threshold operations) — The README's same-machine CPU table (1024x1280 BGR, unnamed CPU and compiler, OpenCV version not stated, -O3 -mavx2 -march=haswell) reports the fused kernels at 3.4-7.6x OpenCV call chains, e.g. ycrcbWithSeg 0.88-0.90 ms vs cvtColor plus inRange 6.68-6.75 ms. The repo has no timing code to reproduce this, and the ycrcbWithSeg output does not match the OpenCV chain it was timed against. The GPU table (GTX 1070 kernel-only vs OpenCV on an i5-7500 CPU) is not a like-for-like comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim overstated and abandoned (2019): the headline rows are GPU (GTX 1070, kernel-only) against CPU OpenCV on an i5-7500, a different machine class; the GPU RGB2HSV does different work (masks RGB) and is buggy ('_h = (_h<0)*(_h + 360)' zeroes the hue), and the example timing code is missing or does not compile. The valid part is the same-machine CPU SIMD rows at 3.4-7.6x, CPU model unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug behind the headline ycrcbWithSeg row (7.4-7.6x): channel order is mixed (Y treats channel 0 as B, Cr treats it as R, Cb is 0.564*(ch0 - Y_rgb), Cb in neither order), so BGR(120,150,220) gives (168,107,112) against OpenCV's (168,165,101), and the timed example calls COLOR_RGB2YCrCb on BGR data; the mask is not OpenCV-equivalent (retier-07 drops the row). grayBRWithSeg has color_mode swapped against the header, a 0.144 grey-weight typo, tail loops that skip trailing pixels, a 1-channel inRange tail that reads 2 bytes past the buffer (asserts in debug), no row stride, and the weightedGray baseline is a naive split plus MatExpr chain. CPU model unknown (the author's blog on zhihu is blocked here).

**How:** Kernel fusion: the colour transform and the range test run in registers on the same 16 or 32 pixels, so no intermediate YCrCb, grey or split-plane image is written to memory. BGR de-interleaving uses pshufb (_mm_shuffle_epi8) byte shuffles. The weighted sums are Q15 fixed-point dot products via pmaddwd (_mm_madd_epi16), packed back with saturation, and compared with unsigned max/min-plus-cmpeq tricks. ycrcbWithSeg and 3-channel inRange are 128-bit SSSE3/SSE4.1. weightedGrayWithSeg, both grayBR functions and 1-channel inRange use 256-bit AVX2, with the two 128-bit lanes split so the in-lane packus keeps pixel order.

**Use it when:**
- Per-frame colour segmentation (robot vision, coloured-marker or light-bar detection) on x86 CPUs with AVX2, where the only output you need is a binary mask from a fixed BGR, grey-weight or channel-difference threshold.
- Hot loops that today run cv::split plus scaled Mat adds plus cv::threshold (weightedGrayWithSeg) or a channel difference plus threshold (grayBRWithSegStandard). The fused pass avoids several full-image temporaries.
- Plain 3-channel cv::inRange on contiguous 8-bit BGR images whose pixel count is a multiple of 16 (README: 0.29-0.30 ms vs 1.06-1.18 ms on 1024x1280).
- As a reference or starting point for writing your own pshufb + pmaddwd fused kernels; each function is about 150 lines of intrinsics.

**Skip it when:**
- When the mask must match OpenCV's YCrCb: ycrcbWithSeg's colour math is wrong (see gotchas). Its Cr and Cb channels match neither BGR2YCrCb nor RGB2YCrCb, so thresholds tuned on cv::cvtColor output select different pixels.
- Images whose pixel count is not a multiple of 16 (3-channel inRange, ycrcbWithSeg) or 32 (AVX2 functions): the scalar tail loop starts at a byte offset instead of a pixel index, so the trailing pixels are never written. For 1-channel inRange the tail reads two bytes past the buffer and trips an assert in debug builds.
- Strided or ROI images (cv::Mat with padding or submatrices): there is no row-stride parameter, and every function assumes width*height*3 contiguous bytes.
- Non-x86 targets or CPUs without AVX2: there is no scalar fallback, NEON path or runtime dispatch, and the build hard-codes -mavx2 -march=haswell.
- The GPU part: the README's RGB2HSV speed-up compares an RGB mask kernel (it zeroes every non-negative hue) with a real OpenCV HSV conversion. GPU times exclude transfers and are set against a CPU, not OpenCV CUDA or NPP.

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the SIMD kernels (raw pointers; core.hpp and DataTypes.hpp only include the intrinsics headers). OpenCV for the examples; Boost (system, atomic, interprocess) for shm.hpp and the CMake targets; CUDA plus OpenCV for the GPU part. · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); compiler not stated; built with -O3 -msse4.1 -mavx2 -march=haswell · x86-64 with SSSE3/SSE4.1 for ycrcbWithSeg and 3-channel inRange and AVX2 for the rest (effectively Haswell or newer); GPU kernels need CUDA (tested on a GTX 1070)

**Vs siblings:** Pick DeltaCV only when you want a fused threshold mask in one pass and will fix and test the kernels yourself. For colour conversion that matches OpenCV, CompV (RGB to grey, YUV and HSV, 6-7x OpenCV in its own result file) or FlyCV are maintained libraries, and RGB2Y covers plain BGR-to-grey at 2-3x OpenCV.

**Gotchas:**
- Correctness bug behind the headline 7.4-7.6x row: ycrcbWithSeg mixes channel orders. The Y row treats channel 0 as blue (0.114, 0.587, 0.299). The Cr row (0.499, -0.419, -0.081) is RGB-order Cr, so channel 0 is treated as red. The Cb row (0.395, -0.331, -0.064) equals 0.564*(ch0 - Y_rgb), which is not Cb in either order. For a skin-tone BGR pixel (120,150,220) it yields (Y,Cr,Cb) = (168,107,112), where cv::cvtColor BGR2YCrCb gives (168,165,101) (derived by evaluating both formulas). The timed example also runs cv::COLOR_RGB2YCrCb on an imread (BGR) image, so neither side is the conversion the header documents.
- grayBRWithSeg's color_mode is swapped against its header comment ('0 -> red, 1 -> blue'): mode 0 computes B-G and mode 1 computes R-G. The header and example suggest gray weights scalar_d(0.144,0.587,0.299), a typo for 0.114 that brightens grey by 3% and no longer matches the cv::COLOR_BGR2GRAY output it is compared with.
- The SIMD and scalar-tail paths disagree. The SIMD path uses saturating unsigned subtraction and truncating Q15 shifts; the tail uses signed differences. Grey and weighted-grey values are truncated, not rounded, so they can be 1 below OpenCV's. ycrcbWithSeg is declared bool but returns nothing, which is undefined behaviour if the result is used.
- There are no tests and no timing harness. Every example compares outputs by imshow; ycrcbWithSeg.cpp and grayBRWithSegStandard.cpp declare timers that are never used, and the former references an undeclared loop variable i, so it does not compile.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-04-27 (58 commits, one open issue from 2018 that says the interface is awkward to use). MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but treat it as unreviewed sample code: fix the YCrCb coefficients and the tail loops before shipping it.

[repo](https://github.com/DasudaRunner/DeltaCV) · [benchmark](https://github.com/DasudaRunner/DeltaCV)

##### fast-srgb8  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0, MIT, CC0-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Tiny no_std Rust crate: table-based linear-f32 to sRGB-u8 and back, several times faster than per-call powf.

**Beats:** naive powf-based sRGB transfer function (reference implementation inside the crate's own benchmark) — The README shows the crate's own nightly libtest #[bench] output: 51 linear-to-sRGB conversions in 144 ns versus 971 ns for a naive powf reference written in the same file (about 6.7x), 51 four-wide conversions in 440 ns versus 3,625 ns for four naive calls (about 8.2x) and 482 ns for four scalar fast calls, and 256 sRGB-to-linear lookups in 81 ns versus 4,026 ns (about 50x), all derived from page data. No CPU, rustc version or flags are given, and the baseline is a straw-man reference, not an incumbent library; the README prose itself claims only about 5x and 20x.

**Known shortcoming:** The baseline is the crate's own naive powf transfer function, not an incumbent; the 104-entry table is byte-identical to stb_image_resize2.h's fp32_to_srgb8_tab4, so the incumbent stb already ships the same trick. f32_to_srgb8 is not bitwise exact to the rounded reference (max error 0.544, within the D3D 0.6 bound); srgb8_to_f32 is exact for all 256 inputs.

**Known shortcoming:** The 104-entry table is confirmed identical to stb_image_resize2.h's fp32_to_srgb8_tab4 (104 of 104) and stb also ships a SIMD path, so the incumbent already carries the trick; the bench inputs are loop constants with a division in both arms (hot-L1 best case, no CPU or rustc stated); the SSE2 x4 path is only 1.1x over scalar and there is no NEON. Issue #2 (test_from_srgb8 fails on Debian i386 with Rust 1.66; table and runtime powf differ in the last digit) has no maintainer reply; downloads came mostly through palette 0.7.6, and palette 0.7.7 dropped the dependency.

**How:** Linear to sRGB uses Fabien Giesen's (ryg) public-domain trick: clamp the float to [2^-13, 1-eps], use its exponent and top mantissa bits as an index into a 104-entry u32 table of packed (bias, scale) pairs, and linearly interpolate with the next 8 mantissa bits in integer arithmetic, so no powf, no division and no libm. The SSE2 version does the clamp, shifts and the multiply-add (_mm_madd_epi16) four-wide, but the four table loads stay scalar because SSE2 has no gather. sRGB to linear is a plain 256-entry f32 lookup table.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code (including no_std, embedded or WASM) that converts individual colour components or small batches between linear float and 8-bit sRGB, e.g. writing a linear-light framebuffer to RGBA8.
- Replacing per-pixel powf calls in a hand-written loop: the crate's own benchmark shows about 6.7x for f32 to u8 and about 50x for u8 to f32 against a powf reference (derived from page data).
- Graphics output where the D3D11 FLOAT-to-SRGB rule (error under 0.6 on the integer side, monotonic, round-trips with the inverse) is the accuracy you need.
- Building colour constants at compile time: srgb8_to_f32 is a const fn.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: there is no C API, and stb_image_resize2.h already contains the identical 104-entry table (fp32_to_srgb8_tab4, stbir__linear_to_srgb_uchar) plus a 256-entry inverse table, with SIMD paths in stb itself.
- When output must match a correctly rounded powf result bit for bit: f32_to_srgb8 is approximate (max error 0.544 against the exact value), so some inputs round to a neighbouring u8 compared with the reference; the source comment itself flags this for scientific or medical imaging.
- Bulk image conversion on aarch64 or other non-x86 targets: f32x4_to_srgb8 falls back to four scalar calls (no NEON), and even on x86 the SSE2 path is only about 1.1x faster than four scalar calls (440 vs 482 ns/iter, derived from page data).
- Anything beyond 8-bit sRGB: no 16-bit, no other transfer functions (gamma 2.2, PQ, HLG), no colour-space conversion; a request for general gamma routines (issue #1, 2022) and a portable-SIMD port (issue #3, 2024) are open without response.
- Projects that need an active maintainer: last commit 2021-05-09, version 1.0.0, and the Debian i386 test failure (issue #2, 2023) has no reply.

**Integration:** crate · none (no libm either) · Rust 1.46 (MSRV badge; CI matrix includes 1.46.0); benchmarks need nightly with --cfg unstable_bench · any Rust target (no_std); SSE2 four-wide path on x86/x86_64 selected at compile time when target_feature sse2 is enabled, scalar elsewhere and under Miri

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings (fast_image_resize, stb-image-resize-opt, tir, colortwist, yuv2rgb, ImageSharp) exposes a standalone sRGB transfer function; pick fast-srgb8 in Rust when you only need the per-component conversion without a resize library. In C or C++, take the same routine from stb_image_resize2.h (or the stb-image-resize-opt fork) instead.

**Gotchas:**
- The crate's srgb8_to_f32 table equals the x86-64 powf reference for all 256 inputs, but on Debian i386 (i686, Rust 1.66) test_from_srgb8 fails because the runtime powf reference there differs in the last digit for several entries (issue #2); the shipped table is constant, so outputs do not change, but the 'exact' claim is relative to one platform's powf.
- The README benchmark loops use compile-time loop counters as inputs and include an int-to-float conversion and a division in both arms, on an unstated CPU and rustc; treat the ratios as hot-L1 best cases for 51 or 256 values per iteration, not image-pipeline throughput.
- The SIMD dispatch is compile-time only: an x86 build without target_feature sse2 (for example i586 targets) silently uses the scalar path; there is no runtime CPU detection and no AVX2 or gather path.
- The table index relies on get_unchecked (unsafe) after clamping; the bounds argument is documented in the source and the exhaustive all-2^32-input tests (run in CI on stable in release mode) check error bound, monotonicity and SIMD-equals-scalar.

**Status:** Unmaintained since 2021-05-09 (v1.0.0) but tiny, dependency-free and available under CC0-1.0, MIT or Apache-2.0, so it is easy to vendor; its 18.3M crates.io downloads came largely through palette 0.7.6, which depended on it, while palette 0.7.7 replaced it with its own palette_math crate.

[repo](https://github.com/thomcc/fast-srgb8) · [benchmark](https://github.com/thomcc/fast-srgb8)

##### FastBoxBlur  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++ sliding-sum box blur with reflect-101 borders; claims 2-3x over OpenCV cv::blur on huge kernels.

**Beats:** OpenCV cv::blur (box filter) — The README claims 2-3x over cv::blur on an i7-10750H. The hard-coded notebook timings (45 RGB 8-bit images, 1500x1000 to 11400x7600, ksize = 2*width-1) give 1.27x to 2.92x for 1 pass and 1.49x to 3.36x for 2 passes (derived from page data), rising with size. The cv::blur driver, OpenCV version and build (IPP or HAL), and thread settings are not in the repo, and FastBoxBlur most likely ran OpenMP on 12 threads against single-threaded FilterEngine code, so per-core it may not be faster.

**Known shortcoming:** Borderline category (box blur, a convolution, not resampling). Timings live in py/performance.ipynb (1-pass 1.27-2.92x, 2-pass 1.49-3.36x vs cv::blur, derived from page data); the cv::blur driver is not in the repo, OpenCV version, build and thread count unstated, and FastBoxBlur runs OpenMP on every pass while OpenCV 4.x's CPU boxFilter has no parallel_for_, so likely 12 threads against 1. Kernel width 2*width-1 is extreme; radius clamped per axis. MIT stated only in the README.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug in horizontal_blur_kernel_reflect: when 2r+2 exceeds the row width the middle loop is skipped and the tail loop restarts at w-r-1 with wrong sums, and the mirror index (max_end - ri % max_end) uses absolute indices so rows after the first read the previous row's last pixel (Python transliteration: up to 59/255 off at ksize 151 on a 150x100 image). At the chart's ksize of 2*width-1 (radius clamped to dim-1) the error is at most 1 level and the bug path does about 2w steps per row, so the chart is not inflated. The only published cv::blur-versus-fastboxblur driver (Blur_algorithms Source.cpp, same 45 sizes) gives fastboxblur ksize 1500 against cv::blur 1444 with 2 passes, radius 749 on 1000-wide rows inside the bug range; the chart driver is undocumented. No SIMD, OpenMP; header not self-contained; even ksize rounded down.

**How:** Each 1D pass is a running-sum (sliding accumulator) box filter, O(1) per pixel regardless of kernel size, with the mirrored border folded into the initial sum instead of padding the row. Vertical passes are run as horizontal passes on a transposed image, with a cache-blocked transpose (flip_block, blocks sized for 256 KB). Every row loop and the transpose are '#pragma omp parallel for', so with -fopenmp (the repo Makefile's flag) it uses all cores; there is no SIMD.

**Use it when:**
- You need a cv::blur-like box filter with reflect-101 borders and want no OpenCV dependency (one ~250-line header).
- Large odd kernels that stay below the image's smaller dimension (ksize <= min(w,h) - 1), where the O(1)-per-pixel sliding sum pays off.
- Repeated box passes (passes = 2-3) as a cheap Gaussian approximation on 8-bit, 16-bit or float buffers with 1-4 channels.
- Multi-core x86 or ARM builds with OpenMP, where the parallel row loops supply the speed (the code is scalar).

**Skip it when:**
- Kernels wider than about half an image dimension: the large-radius path in horizontal_blur_kernel_reflect computes wrong sums (see gotchas); up to 59/255 off in a transliteration test.
- Small kernels (3x3, 5x5) or single-threaded builds: no SIMD, and the only published numbers use kernels thousands of pixels wide.
- Even ksize, non-square kernels, an anchor, or border modes other than reflect-101: r = (ksize-1)/2 is truncated, so ksize 4 becomes a 3-tap box.
- More than 4 channels, strided or ROI buffers, or images above about 715 MP RGB: other channel counts only print a message and leave garbage, and w*h*channels is computed in int.

**Integration:** header-only · none (stb_image only in the demo); OpenMP optional · C++17 (std::is_integral_v, if constexpr per commit history); repo Makefile uses g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17 · any (portable scalar C++)

**Vs siblings:** Among catalogued entries only go-images/images also does box blur, in Go, and loses to OpenCV there. Pick FastBoxBlur when you want a dependency-free C++ header and can keep kernels below the image size. For SIMD-tuned general image kernels, FlyCV or OpenCV itself (with IPP) is the safer choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Correctness bug for big kernels: when 2r+2 exceeds the row length (ksize above about the dimension minus 1), the middle loop is skipped and the tail loop restarts at position w-r-1 <= r, so the running sum is out of step with the output position. The mirror index 'max_end - ri % max_end' uses absolute buffer indices, so later rows can read the previous row's last pixel and row 0 mirrors differently. A Python transliteration of the loop gave wrong sums at every pixel for w=20, r=10..19, and up to 59/255 error on a 150x100 test image at ksize 151. At the benchmark's own setting (ksize 2*width-1, radius clamped to dimension-1 on both axes) the 2D error was at most 1 level.
- The radius is clamped per axis (r = min(r, w-1)), so ksize larger than the smaller side silently gives a non-square kernel that cv::blur would not use.
- The header includes only <vector> but calls sqrt, std::min, printf and std::conditional_t, so add <cmath>, <algorithm>, <cstdio> and <type_traits> before including it on stricter toolchains. The demo driver parses ksize as 'sigma', defaults passes to 3 (README says 1), and its USE_FLOAT path writes back a buffer that is never filled.
- Benchmark provenance is unclear. The only published cv::blur-vs-fastboxblur driver is in the same author's Blur_algorithms Source.cpp (Test flag 4 and -Dboxblur, commented-out loop over the same 45 sizes, which are actually 1000 wide by 1500 tall via cv::Size(y, x)). It passes ksize = x (the image height, e.g. 1500) to fastboxblur but (int)sqrt(x)^2 (e.g. 1444) to cv::blur, with 2 passes each. That is not the chart's '2*width-1', and on 1000-wide rows radius 749 falls in the wrong-output range above. Which driver produced the chart is not documented.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-11-01 (5 stars, no issues or PRs); MIT is stated in the README only (no LICENSE file). The header is small enough to vendor, but fix or guard the large-kernel path first. The chart was last updated on 2022-09-28, before the 2022-10-11 flip_block block-size change, so HEAD differs slightly from the timed code.

[repo](https://github.com/michelerenzullo/FastBoxBlur) · [benchmark](https://github.com/michelerenzullo/FastBoxBlur#performance)

##### FastOpenCV (fastcv kernels)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Threaded cv::Mat kernels that replace OpenCV 4.14 resize (cubic downscale, integer INTER_AREA), transform and general-exponent pow.

**Beats:** OpenCV 4.14.0 cv::resize (INTER_CUBIC, INTER_AREA), cv::transform and cv::pow, built from source by the repo's scripts with IPP disabled (WITH_IPP=OFF in every variant) and TBB threading at the default thread count; libfastcv is compiled against the linux-dispatch install, so the cv:: column is most likely that build, not a distribution build. — The author measured on a Ryzen 9 9950X3D (32 threads, Arch Linux) against OpenCV 4.14.0 built from source with IPP off and TBB at default threads, using 1080p random images and 20-50 timed runs: cubic downscale 1.5-1.9x bit-exact (upscale 0.7-0.9x, slower), INTER_AREA x4 18.7x C1 and 3.5x C3, transform 32FC3 with a 4x4 matrix 10.7x, pow 19-22x on inputs in [0.01, 10]. No result files back these numbers, and every baseline except upscale cubic runs on far fewer threads than fastcv.

**Known shortcoming:** Headline 4.1x INTER_CUBIC resize is overstated: the 3.4 ms OpenCV time was taken under setNumThreads(0), the trap the repo's own PLAN.md 5e calls a 4x artefact; re-measured OpenCV takes 0.88 ms, and the author's fastcv.hpp states downscale 1.5-1.9x and upscale 0.7-0.9x (slower), which the README never reflects. Own universal-intrinsics plus AVX-512 code (no Qualcomm FastCV), same resize algorithm (A=-0.75, 11-bit fixed point, clamped borders); area x4 18.7x on C1 and 3.5x on C3, integer factors only. Every build has WITH_IPP=OFF, TBB with 32 threads; the transform bench's 10.7x is threading only (OpenCV's generic single-thread scalar loop), pow32f's x<=0 mask is dead code so zero or negative inputs give garbage. Ryzen 9 9950X3D per PLAN.md, g++ version unstated; no result files for the 1080p numbers; 6 commits, 0 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** Verifier caveat corrected by the enricher: OpenCV 4.14.0 cv::pow with a general exponent runs SIMD hal::log32f/exp32f single-threaded, not scalar powf, so the 19-22x is 32 threads plus cheaper polynomials, and pow32f skips cv::pow's zero and negative fix-up (zero input gives garbage). OpenCV resize uses parallel_for_ with nstripes = dst.total()/65536 (about 2 stripes for area x4 at 480x270, 8 for cubic to 960x540, 32 for the 1080p upscale) while fastcv uses all threads, so the wins are mostly threading policy, matching the upscale loss; transform 10.7x is the 3-to-4-channel scalar path only (OpenCV has its own SIMD 3x3 path). Accuracy: area x4 rounds ties up where OpenCV rounds half-even, predicting about 3% of values off by one, not the README's 0.2%; the test bound is 62,208 of 388,800 values despite the '<1% px' label; no tests for resizeCubic8u or transform32f; the area kernel's header comment promises SIMD but the code is scalar.

**How:** Mostly parallelism: every kernel runs a plain cv::parallel_for_ over rows with no stripe hint, while OpenCV 4.14.0 runs cv::transform and the general cv::pow single-threaded (NAryMatIterator) and runs resize with nstripes = dst.total()/65536. That OpenCV heuristic gives about 2 stripes for a 480x270 INTER_AREA x4 output, about 8 for a 960x540 cubic downscale and about 32 for a 1920x1080 upscale (derived from OpenCV's resize.cpp), which fits fastcv winning on downscale and losing on upscale. resizeCubic8u also does a two-phase separable pass (horizontal 11-bit fixed-point into an int buffer, with an AVX-512 32-bit gather of 4 taps for C1 interior pixels, then a float SIMD vertical pass), so each source row is filtered once. pow32f replaces OpenCV's SIMD log32f/exp32f plus its zero/negative fix-up loop with fused exp2(p*log2(x)) polynomials (atanh series for log2, degree-6 Taylor for exp2).

**Use it when:**
- You already link OpenCV and do 8UC1/8UC3 INTER_CUBIC downscaling of 1080p-class frames on a many-core x86 box: the author's corrected figure is 1.5-1.9x with bit-exact output.
- Integer-factor INTER_AREA decimation by 4 (or 3, 5, ...) on 8UC1/8UC3 where OpenCV's area-fast path only gets a couple of threads; x4 measured 18.7x (C1) and 3.5x (C3) with +/-1 differences.
- Per-pixel 3-in/4-out float colour transforms (cv::transform with a 4x4 matrix on 32FC3), where OpenCV falls back to a single-threaded scalar loop.
- Gamma curves on strictly positive CV_32FC1 data (for example after adding an epsilon), when about 1e-5 relative error is acceptable.
- As a reference for how much of OpenCV's latency on a 32-thread CPU is threading policy rather than arithmetic.

**Skip it when:**
- Upscaling with INTER_CUBIC: the author's own log measures fastcv at 0.7-0.9x of OpenCV (slower) and says to keep cv::resize there.
- INTER_AREA by 2: OpenCV's SIMD 2x2 path is faster (README and header both say use cv::resize for x2).
- pow on data that can contain 0, negative values, NaN/Inf or results outside the float exponent range: pow32f returns garbage there, while cv::pow returns 0/inf/NaN.
- Single-core, latency-bound or already-parallel pipelines (or calls from inside another cv::parallel_for_, where the nested loop runs serially): the speedups come largely from using all 32 threads of a Ryzen 9 9950X3D.
- Production use that needs maintenance or review: 0 stars, no issues or third-party reports, one v1.0.0 release, comments and logs in Russian, and the README's headline cubic 4.1x is stale.

**Integration:** static lib (libfastcv.a via scripts/build-fastcv.sh); single kernels can also be copied as one .cpp each · OpenCV core headers and library (built and tested against the repo's OpenCV 4.14.0 linux-dispatch install); the library build also passes -I/usr/include/openblas, and other kernels need OpenBLAS and FFTW (-lopenblas -lfftw3f -lfftw3f_threads); the four resampling/colour kernels need only opencv_core · C++17 (README badge); g++ with -O3 -march=native (version not documented); OpenCV 4.x function-style universal intrinsics (v_add/v_mul/v_muladd) · Linux x86-64 tested (Zen 5, AVX-512 + VBMI); resizeCubic8u's gather path needs AVX-512F at compile time and otherwise falls back to scalar; Windows MinGW and aarch64 builds are documented but not verified

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over KLERP, CompV or FlyCV when you want to keep cv::Mat and OpenCV's exact cubic coefficients and only fix the specific OpenCV calls that leave cores idle (cubic downscale, area x4, 3-to-4-channel transform); pick fast_image_resize or stb-image-resize-opt for a standalone, maintained resizer with many filters and published per-case results.

**Gotchas:**
- pow32f's x <= 0 mask is computed and discarded, and exp2 has no range clamp: zero inputs (black pixels in a gamma curve) give garbage instead of 0, and the repo's own test adds +0.001 to the image to avoid it.
- cv::pow's general-exponent baseline in OpenCV 4.14.0 is vectorized (hal::log32f/exp32f in blocks, single-threaded), not scalar powf as the fastcv source comment says; the 19-22x is 32 threads plus cheaper polynomials, against a baseline that also does the zero/negative handling fastcv skips.
- resizeAreaInt8u rounds ties up with (sum+8)>>4, while OpenCV's area-fast loop for x4 does saturate_cast(sum*(1/16.f)), which rounds half to even; by code reading about 1 in 32 output values should differ by 1 on uniform random input, more than the README's 0.2%, and the regression test's bound (img3.total()*3/100 = 62,208 of 388,800 output values) is far looser than its '<1% px' label. Its header comment promises SIMD, but the code is plain scalar loops left to the compiler.
- The resize kernels call dst.create() before reading src and keep no copy of the src header, so passing the same Mat as src and dst breaks; resizeCubic8u also allocates a fresh sh x dw*cn int32 buffer every call (about 12 MB for 1080p C3 to 960x540). resizeCubic8u and transform32f have no regression tests, and transform32f's SIMD 3x3 path (FMA chain in a different order from OpenCV's v_matmuladd) was never benchmarked or checked for bit-exactness.

**Status:** Created September 2026 (6 commits, v1.0.0 on 2026-09-08, last commit 2026-09-10, 0 stars, no issues); Apache-2.0 and the resampling kernels are single files depending only on opencv_core, so they are easy to vendor, but treat them as unreviewed.

[repo](https://github.com/devpilgrin/FastOpenCV) · [benchmark](https://github.com/devpilgrin/FastOpenCV)

##### FlyCV  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

ARM NEON-tuned C++ image library (colour conversion, resize, warps) with an OpenCV-like API; first-party phone demos beat OpenCV 1.16-2.19x.

**Beats:** OpenCV (per-operator average speedup; operator list is in image charts, not text) — The only readable comparisons are first-party screen recordings of an Android demo app at 1920x1080: NV12 to BGR 6.49 vs 7.55 ms (1.16x), BGR to RGBA with mask 9.69 vs 14.87 ms (1.53x) and a cvt_color + warp_affine + resize pipeline 29.6 vs 64.91 ms (2.19x), with OpenCV version, build, thread counts and compiler flags unstated; Paddle's launch post (search snippet only) puts the pipeline run on a Snapdragon 636 and quotes average speedups of 1.36x (Snapdragon 888), 1.77x (835) and 4.38x (625). The public Android sample links only flycv_static and the benchmark/ code times FlyCV alone, so the OpenCV side cannot be reproduced from the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Upgraded D to C on on-screen millisecond labels in the repo's docs/assets GIFs: NV12 to BGR 6.49 vs 7.55 ms (1.16x), BGR2RGBA with mask 9.69 vs 14.87 (1.53x), cvt_color plus warp_affine plus resize 29.6 vs 64.91 (2.19x), all derived; phone model, OpenCV build and flags unstated, and benchmark/ times FlyCV only. Six-phone charts on user-images.githubusercontent.com are unread (blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** The OpenCV side is not reproducible: the public Android sample links only flycv_static and benchmark/ times FlyCV alone; the Paddle blog snippet names a Snapdragon 636 for the 29.6 versus 64.91 ms pipeline and averages of 1.36x, 1.77x and 4.38x on Snapdragon 888, 835 and 625. NV12-to-BGR NEON uses 6-bit fixed-point coefficients (not bit-exact with OpenCV); default 2-thread global pool; built -Ofast -ffast-math. Correctness bugs by code reading (not behind the numbers): the NEON YUV-to-RGB assembly loops lack an nn > 0 guard so widths under 16 wrap the count (out of bounds); resize_cubic_neon skips RGBA/BGRA (call commented out) yet returns 0; cvt_color_neon returns 0 on unsupported codes and odd NV12 sizes; issue #190 (thread-pool crash with concurrent callers) closed with no visible fix.

**How:** The hot kernels are hand-written NEON inline assembly for aarch64 and armv7: NV12 to BGR, for example, converts 16 pixels on two rows per loop iteration with ld2/st3 (de)interleaving and 6-bit fixed-point BT.601 coefficients (Y 74.5, V 102, 52, U 25, 129, truncating shift by 6), trading some precision for fewer instructions. Resize has dedicated exact 2x and 4x downscale kernels and separable fixed-point horizontal/vertical passes. Rows are split across a built-in spin-then-block thread pool (default 2 threads on multi-core CPUs, changeable with set_thread_num), and fused APIs remove intermediate buffers and passes; Android builds use -Ofast -ffast-math.

**Use it when:**
- Android, iOS or ARM Linux camera pipelines that turn NV12/NV21 frames into BGR/RGB, resize and warp them before a neural-network runtime, especially on mid- and low-end SoCs where the first-party averages show the largest gains.
- Apps where OpenCV's binary size is the problem: per-operator CMake switches (WITH_FCV_RESIZE, WITH_FCV_COLOR_CONVERT, ...) build only what you use, and Paddle's launch post claims 1.3 MB versus 15.9 MB for OpenCV for common operators (search snippet only).
- Projects that already vendor another image library and need a custom namespace (-DFLYCV_NAMESPACE=...) to avoid symbol clashes.
- Preprocessing chains that match one of the fusion_api functions (BGR plus mask to RGBA, NV12 resize to BGR, normalize plus mean-subtract plus HWC-to-CHW reorder).

**Skip it when:**
- x86 servers and desktops: the Linux x86 build is plain C unless you pass -DENABLE_AVX=ON (which then adds -march=native), SIMD selection is compile-time with no runtime CPU detection, and no x86 comparison with OpenCV is published.
- When output must match OpenCV bit for bit: the README only promises essentially the same result, and kernels such as NV12 to BGR use 6-bit fixed-point coefficients with truncation.
- Workloads needing operators FlyCV lacks: no smoothing filters (issue #208), no drawContour (#213), limited copy_make_border modes (#207), no video I/O (#177); resize rejects INTER_NEAREST although the enum defines it.
- Several application threads calling FlyCV at once: issue #190 reports reproducible crashes inside the thread pool when multiple inference threads call it without a lock (closed without a visible fix).
- Long-lived products needing support: last commit 2023-06-02, recent issues unanswered, and release download links reported broken (#214, #216).

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake, BUILD_SHARED_LIBS); prebuilt release packages exist but their links are reported broken · none for core and img_transform; libjpeg-turbo, libpng and zlib for the media_io imgcodecs module (on by default, can be switched off); googletest, Google Benchmark and gflags are downloaded only for tests, benchmarks and samples · C++11; CMake 3.10 (3.12 with Xcode); Android NDK for Android builds · Android armeabi-v7a/arm64-v8a and ARM Linux (NEON, optional SVE2 path), iOS, macOS (NEON on arm64, SSE/AVX on x86_64), Windows (SSE through AVX enabled by default), x86 Linux (scalar unless ENABLE_AVX), Emscripten/JS; Rockchip RV1109 code paths

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlyCV over CompV or DeltaCV when the target is an ARM phone and you need a broad OpenCV-style preprocessing set (YUV conversion, resize, warps, normalize) in a small binary; for YUV conversion alone, sparkyuv or xxYUV have reproducible numbers against libyuv, and on x86 OpenCV itself or fast_image_resize are safer choices.

**Gotchas:**
- Silent failures: cvt_color_neon logs and still returns 0 for unsupported conversion codes and for odd NV12 sizes (CHECK_CVT_SIZE returns from a void helper), and resize_cubic_neon leaves 4-channel RGBA/BGRA images untouched (the call is commented out) while returning 0, so INTER_CUBIC on RGBA on ARM yields an unwritten dst.
- Code reading (not tested): the NEON YUV-to-RGB assembly loops (NV12/NV21/I420 to BGR/RGB/BGRA/RGBA) decrement the 16-pixel block count only after running the loop body and have no nn > 0 guard, unlike the BGR-to-YUV kernels; for widths under 16 the 32-bit count wraps and the loop runs far out of bounds.
- Colour order lives in the Mat type, so in-place swaps such as cvt_color(src, src, CVT_PA_BGR2PA_RGB) fail the destination type check (issue #205 reported no effect); Mat is constructed as (width, height), the reverse of OpenCV's (rows, cols).
- The Android toolchain file compiles the whole library with -Ofast -ffast-math, which can change float results (normalize, warp) and NaN handling.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2023-06-02 with unanswered issues, but Apache-2.0 and modular enough to vendor selected operators; audit the NEON kernels for small-width and unsupported-type paths before shipping.

[repo](https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/FlyCV) · [benchmark](https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/FlyCV/tree/develop/docs/assets)

##### go-gfx (resample package)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go (CGO=0) RGBA resizer whose multicore Bicubic/Lanczos beat single-thread Pillow 12.2 1.7-4.9x; its serial Box loses.

**Beats:** Pillow 12.2.0 Image.resize (BICUBIC, LANCZOS, BOX) — On an unnamed Apple Silicon Mac (16 logical CPUs), Go 1.26.4 `go test -bench` resizing random opaque RGBA images beat Pillow 12.2.0 Image.resize (best of 30) 1.66x (Bicubic) and 1.72x (Lanczos) for 1024x1024 to 256x256, and 4.9x and 3.2x for 256x256 to 1024x1024. Box lost 0.65x and 0.77x. go-gfx tiled the filtered modes across all cores against single-thread Pillow; Box was serial on both sides. The Pillow timing script is not committed.

**Known shortcoming:** The bicubic and Lanczos wins (docs/perf.md) run multicore (GOMAXPROCS) against single-threaded Pillow 12.2.0 while the serial Box path loses (0.65x, 0.77x); no Pillow timing script is committed (generate.py only writes parity fixtures) and the Apple Silicon chip is unnamed.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): the Pillow comparison (1.66x/1.72x downscale, 4.9x/3.2x upscale; Box loses 0.65x/0.77x) tiles the filtered modes across all 16 logical cores of an unnamed Apple Silicon Mac against single-threaded Pillow 12.2.0; the Pillow timing script is not committed. Work is unequal: Resize filters four straight-alpha channels while Pillow converts RGBA to premultiplied and back for every non-NEAREST filter (ResizePremultiplied is the equivalent call), and the uncommitted harness does not say whether Pillow paid both passes. docs/perf.md calls Pillow's resampler 'single-threaded C with SIMD' and BOX 'hand-tuned SIMD C', but stock Pillow Resample.c has no SIMD intrinsics (scalar fixed-point convolution); Pillow-SIMD was not tested. The amd64 kernel is SSE2 multiply-then-add (no FMA, no AVX2). Brand new (first commit 2026-08-28, 0 stars, no releases). Tier C stands.

**Independent measurement:** first-party Go benchmark vs uncommitted Pillow script

**How:** Bicubic and Lanczos are separable: a horizontal gather pass writes a float64 scratch plane, then the vertical pass builds each output row as one axpy (dst += w*src) per filter tap over a whole contiguous RGBA row, run by go-asmgen assembly kernels (arm64 NEON VFMLA, amd64 SSE2 MULPD+ADDPD, s390x vector). Both passes split their rows into contiguous bands, one goroutine per band up to GOMAXPROCS, once rows x output width reaches ParThreshold (16384). Most of the measured win is that fan-out: Box, which runs a serial scalar float64 weighted span sum with no SIMD and no tiling, is 0.65-0.77x Pillow.

**Use it when:**
- Go services built with CGO disabled that need Pillow-quality Bicubic or Lanczos thumbnails or enlargements without linking libvips or Pillow.
- Multi-core machines with spare cores per request: the 1.66-4.9x wins come from tiling both passes across GOMAXPROCS goroutines (16 logical CPUs in the published run).
- Images large enough to cross ParThreshold (16384 output elements per pass, about a 128x128 output), e.g. 1024x1024 to 256x256 or 256x256 to 1024x1024.
- Pipelines that must stay numerically close to an existing Python/Pillow pipeline: parity_test.go checks 42.7-61.2 dB premultiplied-space PSNR against Pillow 12 references.
- Cut-out images with transparency, via ResizePremultiplied, which removes the colour fringe that straight-alpha filtering leaves.

**Skip it when:**
- Box/area downscaling or enlargement: serial and unvectorised, 0.65x (1024 to 256) and 0.77x (256 to 1024) of Pillow's speed.
- Single-core containers, GOMAXPROCS=1, or servers already running one resize per core: no single-thread numbers are published. Rough estimate (not measured): Bicubic 1024 to 256 does about 4x the multiply-adds of Box (16 taps per axis versus 4), and serial Box already takes 3.53 ms, so a single-thread Bicubic run is likely behind Pillow's 3.14 ms. `go test -bench Resize -cpu 1` would settle it.
- Small thumbnails: a pass below ParThreshold (e.g. a 64x64 output's vertical pass) runs serially.
- Bit-exact Pillow output: go-gfx stays in float64 while Pillow uses 22-bit fixed-point integers with an 8-bit intermediate, and Box has no Pillow parity test at all (only a self-consistency test).
- Memory-tight or mature-dependency settings: the scratch plane is srcH x dstW x 4 float64 (8 MiB in both benchmark cases), allocated per call; the repo dates from 2026-08-28 with 0 stars and no tagged releases.

**Integration:** module · resample imports only go-gfx's own color and raster packages; the module's go.mod also requires golang.org/x/image, sergeymakinen/go-ico, go-images/jpeg2000 and tannevaled/gobig2 (for the codec package), despite the README's 'no third-party dependencies' · Go 1.26.4 (go.mod 'go 1.26.4'); CI also runs Go stable · any Go target; SIMD axpy kernel on amd64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and s390x (vector); scalar loop plus multicore tiling on loong64, ppc64le, riscv64, 386 and arm (CI runs these under qemu)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over rez (bamiaux/rez, the other pure-Go SIMD resizer, measured only against ImageMagick and Go resizers) when you want Pillow-matching Bicubic/Lanczos output and multicore tiling built in. Pick fast_image_resize (Rust, single-thread AVX2/NEON wins over libvips) or stb-image-resize-opt and tir (C) when you are not on Go or need a single-thread speed win that has been measured.

**Gotchas:**
- Resize filters all four channels independently (straight alpha), while Pillow's Image.resize converts RGBA to RGBa (premultiplied) and back for every non-NEAREST filter; ResizePremultiplied is the Pillow-equivalent call. The benchmark times Resize, and the uncommitted Pillow harness does not say whether Pillow got RGBA (and so paid both conversion passes, the second over the full 1024x1024 output on enlargement).
- docs/perf.md calls Pillow's resampler 'single-threaded C with SIMD' and its BOX 'hand-tuned SIMD C'. Stock Pillow's src/libImaging/Resample.c (main branch) has no SIMD intrinsics: it is a scalar fixed-point convolution (PRECISION_BITS 22), and BOX goes through the same generic convolution as BICUBIC with support 0.5. Pillow-SIMD, the SIMD fork, was not tested.
- raster.Image is straight-alpha with stride 4*W, unlike the standard library's premultiplied image.RGBA, so going through FromImage and ToRGBA adds a conversion pass that the benchmark does not time.
- The amd64 kernel is SSE2 multiply-then-add (no FMA, no AVX2); TestAxpyMatchesScalar allows a small tolerance for GOAMD64=v3 builds, where the scalar fallback uses fused multiply-add.

**Status:** Active (57 commits from 2026-08-28 to 2026-10-01, CI on six 64-bit architectures plus 32-bit, 2 open issues, neither about resample) and BSD-3-Clause, but brand new, with 0 stars and no releases. Its stated consumers are the same author's go-images, go-widgets and go-webengine.

[repo](https://github.com/go-gfx/gfx) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-gfx/gfx/HEAD/docs/perf.md)

##### go-images/images (RGB to HSV and box-blur kernels)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go (CGO=0) scikit-image-style image library; first-party table shows RGB to HSV and box blur 2-5x faster than float64 scikit-image, far slower than OpenCV.

**Beats:** scikit-image 0.26.0 (rgb2hsv, scipy.ndimage.uniform_filter); OpenCV 4.13.0 also measured and is faster — Author-run parity table on an Apple M4 Max (macOS 26.5), go1.26.4 with go test -cpu=1 -count=5 against scikit-image 0.26.0/scipy 1.18.0 and OpenCV 4.13.0 pinned to one thread: RGB to HSV 65 vs 13.7 Mpix/s (4.7-4.8x) and box blur r=2 1.8-2.6x over scikit-image, but the scikit-image side runs float64 in and float64 out while go-images and OpenCV run uint8, and OpenCV is 15-30x faster than go-images on those same rows. The code review adds measurement caveats in both directions: morphology rows, labelled '(gray)' by aggregate.py, time go-images on three RGB channels of a random colour image against scikit-image and OpenCV on one uint8 gray plane (so its losses there are overstated), Gaussian is 3-sigma vs 4-sigma, and the HSV numbers (BENCHMARKS.md last edited 2026-07-02) predate the 2026-08-15 move of the HSV kernel onto go-gfx/color, which was not re-timed in the published table.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded A to C: the scikit-image side times float64 in and out (img_as_float in run.py) while go-images runs uint8 with byte-quantised HSV, and benchmarks/verify.py has no HSV check, so the compared work differs; the Gaussian upper ratio is 1.30x, not as claimed. Off the category baselines, and OpenCV in the same table is about 24x faster on HSV and 15-30x on box blur.

**Known shortcoming:** The headline wins come from algorithm, not SIMD: RGBToHSV is scalar Go on one goroutine and BoxBlur a scalar running sum (only the Gaussian axpy is SIMD). benchmarks/verify/main.go writes hsv.bin but verify.py never reads it, and the gate tolerances (BoxBlur 2, Gaussian 4) contradict the README's 'exact' and 'within 1 LSB'. The morphology rows run 3 RGB channels against 1 uint8 grey plane in skimage and OpenCV, overstating the losses and the OpenCV 165-186x gap. BENCHMARKS.md (2026-07-02) predates the HSV kernel's move to go-gfx/color (2026-08-15) and was not re-timed; transient memory at 4096x4096 is about 400 MB (BoxBlur) to 800 MB (Gaussian) of float64.

**How:** The wins come from algorithm and data layout, not vector code: RGBToHSV is one fused scalar per-pixel pass (via go-gfx/gfx/color.SRGBToHSV) instead of scikit-image's chain of float64 numpy temporaries, and BoxBlur is a separable running-window sum (O(1) per pixel in the radius) with a float64 intermediate plane. The only go-asmgen SIMD kernel the current code calls is a float64 axpy (SSE2 on amd64, NEON FMLA on arm64, z/vector on s390x) used by the separable Gaussian; morphology is a scalar van Herk / Gil-Werman running min/max on bytes. Separable passes fan rows or columns out over GOMAXPROCS goroutines above 16,384 pixels; RGBToHSV has no such tiling.

**Use it when:**
- Go services or CLIs that must build with CGO_ENABLED=0 (static binaries, cross-compiling to arm64, s390x, riscv64, loong64 or ppc64le) and need blur, edge, morphology or HSV ops without libvips, ImageMagick or OpenCV.
- Batch filtering of large images (1024x1024 and up) on many-core machines, where the goroutine tiling gave 4.2-10.3x over single-threaded scikit-image in the author's 16-core table for box blur, Gaussian, Sobel and morphology.
- Porting a scikit-image pipeline to Go when matching its semantics matters: box blur, morphology, Otsu and Rotate/Warp are written and tested against scipy/skimage references.
- Byte-quantized HSV for thresholding or colour keying inside an RGBA pipeline, where 1.4-degree hue steps are acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Raw throughput: in the same single-thread table OpenCV (uint8 in, uint8 out) is about 24x faster on RGB to HSV, 15-30x on box blur, 6-8x on Gaussian and 7-8x on Sobel (derived from page data). If cgo is acceptable, OpenCV (or libvips) wins every row.
- Small-radius morphology, Rotate90, Crop or Otsu on one thread, where the table shows go-images at 0.24-0.93x of scikit-image.
- Memory-constrained 4096x4096 work: every call allocates a new RGBA output, BoxBlur allocates a width*height*3 float64 plane (about 400 MB at 4096x4096) and GaussianBlur six width*height float64 planes (about 800 MB), derived from the code.
- Code that needs float or 16-bit images, or HSV in OpenCV's 0-180 or skimage's float convention: everything is 8-bit RGBA and RGBToHSV packs hue into 0-255.
- Resizing benchmarks or resize-heavy workloads chosen on these numbers: the parity table has no resize rows and Resize lives in go-gfx/gfx.

**Integration:** module · github.com/go-gfx/gfx v0.34.0, go-images/gif v0.1.0, go-images/jpeg v0.2.0, go-images/png v0.1.0, sergeymakinen/go-ico v1.0.0, golang.org/x/image v0.46.0 (indirect: ajroetker/go-highway, go-images/jpeg2000, sergeymakinen/go-bmp, tannevaled/gobig2, golang.org/x/sys); no cgo · Go 1.26.4 (go.mod) · any Go target; README targets amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x. Gaussian axpy is SIMD on amd64 (SSE2), arm64 (NEON) and s390x; other ops are scalar Go everywhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over OpenCV, CompV or DeltaCV (all faster C/C++ RGB to HSV) and FastBoxBlur only when the hard requirement is a cgo-free Go build; on speed alone those win, OpenCV by 15-30x on the measured ops. Against rez, the other pure-Go entry, it is complementary: rez is a SIMD resizer, go-images covers filters, colour and morphology and leaves resizing to go-gfx.

**Gotchas:**
- RGBToHSV stores H as round(hue*255/360) in the R byte (about 1.41 degrees per step), S and V as bytes; this is neither skimage's float [0,1] nor OpenCV's 0-180 hue. The correctness gate never checks it: benchmarks/verify/main.go writes hsv.bin but benchmarks/verify.py never reads it (only the internal hsv_parity_test.go compares against the previous Go kernel).
- GaussianBlur truncates at ceil(3*sigma) (13 taps at sigma 2 vs scipy's 17) and rounds the horizontal pass to bytes before the vertical pass; verify.py allows 4 levels of difference from skimage although BENCHMARKS.md and the README say within one level.
- Erode/Dilate/Open/Close work per channel on RGB, so on a colour image they are not luminance morphology; a grayscale result needs Grayscale first.
- Setting GOMAXPROCS (or go test -cpu) changes the internal fan-out; the single-thread numbers in BENCHMARKS.md depend on -cpu=1 collapsing the tiling to one goroutine.

**Status:** Active (37 commits from 2026-06-15 to 2026-09-27, mostly feature work and go-gfx dependency bumps), BSD-3-Clause and pure Go so it is easy to vendor, but it has one star, no releases and no outside users or issue reports yet.

[repo](https://github.com/go-images/images) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-images/images/HEAD/BENCHMARKS.md)

##### H264Sharp (native SIMD color converter)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

AVX2/SSE4.1/NEON RGB<->I420 converters inside a .NET OpenH264 wrapper; about 2.4x OpenCV cvtColor single-threaded, 3x multithreaded.

**Beats:** OpenCV cv::cvtColor (RGB <-> YUV) — README tables, measured on 1080p with 5000 iterations; each iteration is one YUV420-to-RGB plus one RGB-to-YUV420 call from C#, with matched thread counts. The OpenCV side is 4.10 through the OpenCvSharp4 4.10.0.20241108 Windows runtime; the H264Sharp side is a prebuilt native DLL whose compiler and flags are not stated. Ryzen 7 3700X: 4899 vs 11919 ms on one thread (2.43x) and 822 vs 2543 ms on 8 threads (3.09x). i7-10600U: 6010 vs 11719 ms (1.95x). Both libraries point-sample chroma, so they do the same work. H264Sharp computes in truncating 16-bit lanes where OpenCV uses rounded 32-bit lanes (outputs within 1-2 code values, derived from the source formulas), and its 16-thread row used at most 8 workers.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark is a C# harness (Examples/H264SharpBenchmark/Program.cs, OpenCvSharp4 4.10, matched Cv2.SetNumThreads) timing a prebuilt native DLL whose compiler and flags are not stated. 8-bit fixed-point coefficients, so output is not bit-identical to OpenCV cvtColor.

**Known shortcoming:** Chroma is point-sampled in every path (the 2x2 averaging routine is unused), which matches OpenCV 4.10's RGB2YUV_I420, so the comparison is like-for-like (verifier note corrected); exhaustive formula check: RGB to YUV at most 1 code lower (about 50% of inputs, bias -0.5), YUV to RGB within 2. The custom pool caps 1080p at 8 workers (minimum chunk 245,760 px), so the 16-thread row is 8 against 16 threads. Odd heights make the SIMD loops touch row y+1 (out-of-bounds read and write); RGBX2YUV420 ignores the U and V pointers and strides; needs Clang (VLAs, target attributes); LICENSE.txt is an unfilled MIT template; v1.6.0 fixed a YUV luminance overflow and the README does not name the measured version.

**How:** It does BT.601 limited-range conversion in 16-bit fixed point with 8-bit coefficients: 66/129/25 >> 8 for Y, the halved chroma weights 56/47/9 and 19/37/56 >> 7, and 149/128 plus x/64 terms for the inverse. One 256-bit AVX2 register therefore holds 16 pixels, while OpenCV 4.10's universal-intrinsics path widens to 32-bit lanes with 20-bit coefficients and rounding. Interleaved pixels are split with byte shuffles and blends, two rows are processed per iteration, and chroma is point-sampled from the top-left pixel of each 2x2 block (as OpenCV does) using wrap-around 16-bit arithmetic and an unsaturated pack. YUV to RGB duplicates each chroma sample with one byte shuffle and packs with saturation. Row bands go to a custom spin-wait thread pool (or PPL on Windows), with runtime dispatch on x86 (AVX2, then SSE4.1, then scalar) and NEON on arm64.

**Use it when:**
- .NET apps (WPF, Unity, MAUI) that already use H264Sharp and OpenH264 and convert camera or screen frames between RGB and I420 every frame.
- Real-time 720p/1080p capture-and-encode pipelines on x86-64 with AVX2, where frame widths are multiples of 32 (16 for the SSE and NEON paths) and heights are even.
- C++ projects that want a small MIT-licensed BT.601 RGB<->I420 kernel to vendor: Rgb2YuvAVX2.cpp, Yuv2RgbAVX2.cpp and AVX2Common.h (plus the SSE/NEON variants and ThreadPool.h), built with Clang.
- Video-encoder input or preview display, where values that differ from OpenCV by 1-2 code values do not matter.

**Skip it when:**
- BT.709/BT.2020 matrices, full-range (JPEG) YUV, 10-bit, or 4:2:2/4:4:4 layouts: only 8-bit BT.601 limited-range 4:2:0 (plus NV12 input) is implemented.
- Bit-exact parity with OpenCV or libyuv, or best chroma quality. The arithmetic truncates instead of rounding, so computed from the source formulas, RGB to YUV lands 1 code value below OpenCV for about half of all inputs (mean bias about -0.5) and YUV to RGB is within +/-2. Chroma is point-sampled rather than averaged, so thin coloured edges alias.
- MSVC-only or GCC-only builds without changes: the code uses Clang/GCC extensions (__attribute__((target("avx2"))), a variable-length array in ThreadPool::ForRange, #pragma clang loop), and the CMake files hard-code clang/clang++ paths.
- Projects that need a maintained dependency: last commit 2025-03-14, 37 stars, open decoder-offset bugs (#20, #21), a reported AVX2 YUV-to-RGB crash on a QEMU Debian guest (#19, closed with no fix visible), and no macOS/iOS binaries (#17).
