**Integration:** shared lib (H264SharpNative DLL/.so with an extern "C" API, called from C# by P/Invoke; NuGet package H264Sharp); source-drop for C++ use of the converters · Cisco OpenH264 shared library for the codec part (loaded by name at runtime); the converter files need only the repo's ThreadPool.h, Logger and pch headers; the Windows build links 'synchronization' and can use PPL (concurrency::parallel_for) · C++17 with Clang (CMakeLists hard-codes clang/clang++, CMakePresets uses LLVM clang++ on Windows, the vcxproj uses ClangCL); the C# wrapper targets .NET Standard and the benchmark targets net6.0 · x86/x86-64 (runtime dispatch: AVX2, SSE4.1, scalar), arm64 NEON, other ARM scalar; prebuilt binaries for Windows, Linux and Android, none for macOS/iOS

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you are already in .NET with OpenH264 and want RGB<->I420 at about 2.4-3x OpenCV with matched threads. For C++ code, libyuv (the incumbent, with many more formats and matrices) or the smaller xxYUV and descampsa/yuv2rgb are easier to adopt, and sparkyuv or yuvutils-rs cover more matrices and bit depths.

**Gotchas:**
- RGBX2YUV420 writes one contiguous I420 buffer starting at to->Y, with Y stride equal to the width and U then V directly after it; it ignores the U/V pointers and strides in YuvNative. YUV420ToRGB does honour strides.
- Width decides the path without telling you: AVX2 needs width % 32 == 0 and SSE/NEON need % 16, otherwise the scalar code runs. Images under 640x480 always run on one thread. With the custom pool, each worker needs at least 245,760 pixels (128 rows at 1080p), so 1080p uses at most 8 workers however many threads you request.
- The SIMD loops step two rows at a time and always touch row y+1, with no tail handling, so an odd height reads and writes one row past the planes (found in the source, not reported in any issue).
- Rgb2Yuv.cpp contains a 2x2-averaging chroma routine, but nothing calls it: the scalar, SSE, AVX2 and NEON paths all point-sample chroma. Release v1.6.0 notes a 'YUV luminance overflow' fix, and the README does not say which version produced its benchmark tables.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-03-14, 37 stars) but MIT: LICENSE.txt is the MIT template with '[year] [fullname]' left unfilled, and the repo page reports MIT. The converter is about ten C++ files that can be vendored if you build with Clang.

[repo](https://github.com/ReferenceType/H264Sharp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ReferenceType/H264Sharp)

##### hsvbench (branchless HSV to RGB)  `C`  `Unlicense`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Branchless, expression-only HSV-to-RGB float function in a public-domain C header, about 5.7x faster than the textbook 6-way switch on random input.

**Beats:** the repo's own hsv_to_rgb in hsv.h: the common 6-way switch formula seen in StackOverflow answers (calls double-precision floor() and branches on the hue sector); a naive in-repo baseline, not an incumbent library — On the author's unnamed CPU, with clang-10 -O2 (no -march), 300 passes over 1,048,576 random float HSV pixels took 3.745 s for the switch formula, 0.655 s for the branchless expression and 1.865 s for the lookup table, measured as whole-process wall time (about 5.7x and 2.0x, derived from page data). The baseline is the repo's own textbook switch, not a library, and no CPU model or repeat count is given.

**Known shortcoming:** The baseline is the repo's own 6-way switch hsv_to_rgb (double floor(), random hues), not an incumbent library; 3.745 s against 0.655 s is whole-process time with clang-10 -O2 and no CPU; 396 of 65536 pixels differ by 1 LSB.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e122, 2026-10-05): no correctness bug, only a 1-LSB output drift (the switch variant scales hue by 5.9999). Measurement flaws: the switch baseline calls double floor() per pixel (likely a libm call at -O2 without -march); uniformly random hues are the worst case for branches; the fast run moves about 7.5 GB in 0.655 s (about 11.5 GB/s, derived), so it is likely near single-core memory bandwidth. Gotchas: hsv.h needs <math.h> included first; GNU __inline__; an unprefixed multiple-evaluation CLAMP01 macro; no hue wrap; the table function in hsvbench.c is non-static C99 inline, so it likely fails to link at -O0. Tier C stands.

**Independent measurement:** first-party micro-benchmark

**How:** Each channel is a piecewise-linear 'tent' of the hue: r = |6h-3|-1, g = 2-|6h-2|, b = 2-|6h-4|, each clamped to [0,1] and blended with saturation and value, so there is no sector index, no floor() and no switch. fabsf and the ternary clamp compile to andps and min/max instructions, so the loop body is straight-line float code with no data-dependent branches and is a candidate for compiler auto-vectorisation (not confirmed by disassembly in the repo). The baseline it beats branches six ways on the hue sector and calls double-precision floor() per pixel, which at -O2 without -march (no SSE4.1 round instruction on baseline x86-64) is typically a libm call (inference from the Makefile flags, not measured).

**Use it when:**
- Per-pixel or per-vertex HSV-to-RGB in C or C++ code (colour pickers, procedural palettes, particle and heat-map colouring) where pulling in OpenCV or a colour library is overkill.
- Hot loops over float HSV data whose hues vary unpredictably from one element to the next, where the switch version mispredicts most.
- Code you want to auto-vectorise or port to SIMD intrinsics or shaders: the function is branch-free and uses only abs, min/max, multiply and add.
- Projects that need public-domain (Unlicense) code to paste in without attribution.

**Skip it when:**
- Whole-image 8-bit conversions: OpenCV cvtColor (COLOR_HSV2RGB) or a SIMD colour converter works on packed u8 buffers and threads; hsvbench never compares against any library.
- When you need bit-identical output with an existing switch implementation: 396 of 65,536 test pixels differ by 1 LSB in 8-bit (README ppmhist), partly because the bundled switch version scales hue by 5.9999 rather than 6.
- Hue values outside [0,1] or in degrees: the expression does not wrap (h = 1.2 clamps to pure red instead of hue 0.2), so wrap and normalise before calling.
- Spatially coherent real images, where the switch's branches predict well; the 5.7x was measured on uniformly random hues, the worst case for the baseline, so expect a smaller gain.
- Anyone wanting a maintained library: 7 commits on one day (2020-12-08), no tests, no issues or releases.

**Integration:** header-only · libm (<math.h> must be included before hsv.h; the header uses fabsf, floor and powf without including it) · C99 with the GNU __inline__ keyword (GCC or Clang); the Makefile uses clang-10 -std=c99 -O2. MSVC needs a #define for __inline__ (not documented). · any (portable scalar float code; no intrinsics)

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over OpenCV, CompV or DeltaCV when you need a single-pixel float HSV-to-RGB function to paste into C code rather than an image-wide cvtColor call; like fast-srgb8 it is a scalar per-value transform measured only against a naive reference, so for bulk 8-bit image conversion the library siblings remain the better-evidenced choice.

**Gotchas:**
- CLAMP01 is an unprefixed function-like macro that evaluates its argument up to three times and does not parenthesise the second use of x; it can collide with or misbehave beside other macros.
- hsv.h is not self-contained: include <math.h> first, and it defines generic names (hsv_to_rgb, hsl_to_rgb, linear_to_srgb) that may clash with other colour code.
- The benchmark times whole processes with time(1), including identical setup (3M rand() calls and table init) in each run; the fast run moves about 7.5 GB of array traffic in 0.655 s (about 11.5 GB/s, derived from page data), so it may be near single-core memory bandwidth and the compute-only ratio is not isolated.
- Building hsvbench.c at -O0 is likely to fail to link: hue_sat_val_lookup is a non-static C99 inline definition with no external definition; the -O2 Makefile build inlines it. The table benchmark also maps byte hue to h/256 while the reference uses h/255, so part of the table's visible error is a mapping mismatch.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2020-12-08 (all 7 commits on one day, no issues or PRs), but Unlicense and only a 20-line function, so it is trivial to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/stolk/hsvbench) · [benchmark](https://github.com/stolk/hsvbench)

##### imgdiff (n7olkachev)  `Go`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Multi-threaded Go pixel-diff CLI and package with pixelmatch-style YIQ threshold; README says 3-4.5x faster than 2020 odiff, but odiff v2 matched it.

**Beats:** odiff v1 (2020); PR #5 re-measured against odiff v2 — The README's hyperfine runs on a Linux Core i7-4700HQ (4 cores, 8 threads) time multi-threaded imgdiff against an unversioned late-2020 odiff (v1). On the 3446x10728 cypress pair imgdiff took 1.442 s against odiff's 6.475 s (4.49x); on the 8400x4725 water pair, 1.908 s against 6.016 s (3.15x). The Go version, flags and harness are not given, the two tools did different output work, and the benchmark-era binary wrote truncated PNGs. All four odiff test PNGs are 8-bit RGBA and fully opaque (alpha channels decoded during enrichment: minimum alpha 255), so the color bug does not change these counts. The gap did not last: odiff's author re-ran the cypress pair in PR #5 after odiff v2 removed a dependency's 'massive data copying' and measured odiff 1.194 s against imgdiff 1.146 s, with imgdiff at 2.616 s when single-threaded.

**Known shortcoming:** Multi-core (NumCPU goroutines on an i7-4700HQ, 4 cores and 8 threads; the README says 8 cores) against single-threaded odiff, with a different default output (transparent mask, png.BestSpeed); the benchmark-era main.go (1be7ce7) skipped the deferred Flush through os.Exit(1), so the diff PNG was truncated until the 2021-03-25 fix; the odiff compared is old and unversioned (6.475 s against odiff's own 1.168 s on the same pair). Image diffing is a weak fit for colour-and-resampling.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e116, 2026-10-05): speed claim obsolete. The README's 4.49x/3.15x was against odiff v1 (whose dependency did 'massive data copying'); imgdiff PR #5 by the odiff author (January 2021) shows odiff v2 1.194 s vs imgdiff 1.146 s on the cypress pair (parity, imgdiff multi-threaded) and imgdiff single-thread 2.616 s (odiff 2.19x faster). Correctness bug: pkg/yiq/delta.go applies uint8(r) to 16-bit RGBA() values, keeping the low byte, wrong for JPEG, 16-bit and semi-transparent pixels (the four benchmark PNGs are 8-bit RGBA with alpha 255, so the README numbers are unaffected). A larger compare image with a matching overlap reports equal (#13); --diff-image leaves holes; the README download link points to the buggy v1.0.0 (truncated or zero-byte output, #8; fixed in v1.0.2). Corrections in retier-35; C stands.

**Independent measurement:** first-party README; PR #5 by odiff author

**How:** Mostly by using all cores. cmd/main.go decodes both images in parallel goroutines with Go's standard image/png and image/jpeg. Diff() then interleaves rows over runtime.NumCPU() goroutines (row y goes to goroutine y mod NumCPU) and counts with an atomic add. Per pixel it compares the two color.Color interface values and runs the pixelmatch YIQ delta (0.5053 y^2 + 0.299 i^2 + 0.1957 q^2 against 35215 * threshold^2) only when they differ. The mostly transparent mask is written with png.BestSpeed. Nothing is SIMD: pixels go through the generic image.At interface, and the author writes that it 'isn't as fast as a tool like this should be' and that image decoding and encoding take most of the time.

**Use it when:**
- Go test suites that want a small MIT, pure-Go image comparison (about 70 lines in pkg/imgdiff plus a 40-line YIQ helper) instead of shelling out to a native binary.
- Opaque 8-bit PNG screenshots of identical size (the case it handles correctly), when you need only a differing-pixel count and a red mask.
- Multi-core CI runners diffing very large screenshots, where spreading rows across cores lowers wall time compared with a one-thread tool.

**Skip it when:**
- Picking it as faster than odiff: in imgdiff PR #5 (January 2021), odiff's author timed odiff v2 at 1.194 s and imgdiff at 1.146 s on the same cypress pair (parity). With imgdiff limited to one thread, it took 2.616 s, so odiff was 2.19x faster per core. odiff has since been rewritten in Zig with SSE2/AVX2/AVX512/NEON.
- JPEG, 16-bit PNG or semi-transparent images: the color delta reads the wrong byte of Go's 16-bit RGBA() values (see gotchas), so differences there are miscounted.
- Images that can differ in size: it only iterates image1's bounds. A larger compare image with an identical overlap reports 'equal' unless --fail-on-layout is passed (issue #13, open since 2024-12-06).
- Anti-aliasing-tolerant comparisons, ignore regions, or diffs rendered over the base image the way odiff and pixelmatch do: none of these are implemented.
- Single-core containers or anything needing a maintained dependency: the speed comes from goroutines, and the project has been dormant since 2021-03-25 with 2024 bug reports unanswered.

**Integration:** module (Go package github.com/n7olkachev/imgdiff/pkg/imgdiff) plus a CLI binary (prebuilt binaries on GitHub releases) · Go standard library (image, image/png, image/jpeg) for the package; the CLI adds alexflint/go-arg v1.3.0 and logrusorgru/aurora v2.0.3 · Go 1.14 per go.mod; the Go toolchain used for the README benchmark is not stated · any Go target; scripts/build.sh cross-compiles windows, linux and darwin for amd64 and 386 only (no arm64 builds)

**Vs siblings:** Against odiff, the only catalogued sibling doing the same job, pick imgdiff only if you need an in-process pure-Go call on opaque 8-bit PNGs and can use several cores. odiff matched it in v2, has anti-aliasing detection, ignore regions and cross-format input, and is maintained, so it is the default choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Color bug: pkg/yiq/delta.go normalize() turns color.RGBA()'s 16-bit channels into bytes with uint8(r), which keeps the low byte instead of r >> 8. The result is right only for opaque 8-bit pixels, where RGBA() returns v*0x101. It is wrong for JPEG: Go's own ycbcr.go comment shows YCbCr{0x7f,0x7f,0x7f}.RGBA() = 0x7e18 0x808d 0x7db9, so imgdiff sees 0x18, 0x8d, 0xb9 instead of 0x7e, 0x80, 0x7d. It is also wrong for 16-bit PNGs and for partially transparent pixels, whose values come back premultiplied.
- The README's Download link points to v1.0.0. In that build main.go defers writer.Flush() and f.Close() and then calls os.Exit(1), which skips deferred calls. Diff PNGs therefore came out truncated, or zero bytes when the whole file fit in bufio's buffer (issue #8: about 1-2 in 100 diffs). The fix is in v1.0.2 (commit 3eef05c, 2021-03-25). os.Create and png.Encode errors are still ignored, so a bad output path gives exit 1 and no file.
- --diff-image copies base pixels only where the two pixel values are exactly equal. Pixels that differ but fall under the threshold stay transparent, so the 'diff image' has holes.
- The loops use <= on Bounds().Max, so they run one row and one column past the image (issue #12, open). It is harmless today because image.At returns zero outside the bounds, but it adds an extra out-of-range row of work to every goroutine pass.

**Status:** Abandoned: 7 commits, last release v1.0.2 on 2021-03-25, and 2024 bug reports (#12, #13) unanswered. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but fix the low-byte color conversion, the size check and the loop bounds first, and do not rely on its speed claim.

[repo](https://github.com/n7olkachev/imgdiff) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/n7olkachev/imgdiff/master/readme.md)

##### KLERP / KNERP  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Header-only AVX2 bilinear and nearest-neighbour resize for 8-bit grayscale; author claims 25-100% faster than OpenCV cv::resize.

**Beats:** OpenCV resize (bilinear and nearest-neighbor interpolation) — The only claim is the author's bare '25-100% faster than OpenCV' range with no per-case numbers, CPU, compiler, OpenCV version or thread settings; main.cpp times KLERP alone (2x2 input upscaled to 800x2000, multithreaded, 2000 runs) and never calls cv::resize. The code dates from December 2016, and OpenCV 4.x's resize.cpp still performs the same fixed-point vertical pass with universal intrinsics, so any lead now rests on row reuse and threading and has not been re-measured.

**Known shortcoming:** Bare '25-100% faster than OpenCV' claim (grayscale bilinear/nearest resize): main.cpp times KLERP only, with no OpenCV side, machine, flags or OpenCV build; both sides likely multithreaded. Code from 2016, last commit 2021-03-23 (LICENSE only), MIT, 23 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug in the multithreaded row split (KLERP and KNERP): stride = ceil(dst_h/hw) with hw-1 full chunks launched, so writes run past dst when (hw-1)*stride exceeds dst_h (simulated: 2000x10 on 8 threads, 1000x100 on 16; on 64 threads 640x480 overruns by 15360 bytes and main.cpp's own 800x2000 by 12800), a heap overflow on modern many-core machines (the author's box was probably 16 threads or fewer, so the numbers are likely unaffected). Helpers are non-inline in the header (ODR link errors across two translation units); a static std::future array is not reentrant; std::async spawns a thread per task per call; main.cpp never runs OpenCV, so the claim is untestable from the repo.

**How:** Separable fixed-point bilinear: per-call tables of source columns and 11-bit weights, a scalar horizontal pass into 32-bit row buffers, then an AVX2 vertical pass (shift right 4, packs, _mm256_mulhi_epi16 by the row weights, rounding shift, packus) that writes 32 pixels per iteration; this is the same arithmetic as OpenCV's VResizeLinearVec_32s8u. Horizontally filtered source rows are cached and reused when consecutive output rows map to the same source rows, which skips most of the horizontal work when upscaling. Outputs of 20000 pixels or more are split by rows across std::thread::hardware_concurrency() std::async tasks; KNERP is a scalar table-driven gather threaded the same way.

**Use it when:**
- Upscaling 8-bit grayscale frames or ROIs on x86-64 with AVX2 where row reuse removes most of the horizontal pass.
- Computer-vision code that already relies on OpenCV INTER_LINEAR fixed-point output but wants a dependency-free kernel for this one operation.
- Single-threaded use (KLERP<false>), which avoids the threading defects below and is small enough (about 260 lines) to vendor and audit.
- As a readable reference for OpenCV-compatible fixed-point bilinear resizing with AVX2.

**Skip it when:**
- Multithreaded calls on machines with many hardware threads unless the row split is patched: it writes past the end of dst for common heights (see gotchas).
- Colour or multi-channel images, 16-bit or float data, or strided ROIs: only packed 8-bit single-channel buffers are supported.
- CPUs without AVX2 or non-x86 targets: there is no SSE, NEON or scalar fallback for KLERP.
- Area, bicubic or Lanczos filtering, or any case needing published, reproducible speed numbers: the repo has no OpenCV timing code.
- Calling KLERP<true> or KNERP<true> from several threads at once: the calls share one function-static std::future array.

**Integration:** header-only (KLERP.h), but its helper functions are not marked inline · none beyond the C++ standard library, <immintrin.h> and pthreads (Makefile links -lpthread) · C++14 (Makefile uses g++ -std=gnu++14 -mavx2 -mfma -march=native -Ofast); compiler version not documented · x86-64 with AVX2 (also uses the SSE4.1 _mm_round_ps); no other architectures

**Vs siblings:** Pick KLERP only when a tiny dependency-free header for OpenCV-compatible bilinear on 8-bit grayscale matters more than evidence; CompV publishes measured speedups over cv::resize bilinear, and fast_image_resize, tir and stb-image-resize-opt cover multi-channel data and better filters with published benchmark tables.

**Gotchas:**
- Heap overflow in the multithreaded row split (KLERP and KNERP): stride = ceil(dst_h / hardware_concurrency()) and hardware_concurrency()-1 full chunks are launched before the remainder, so whenever (threads-1)*stride > dst_h the tasks write rows past the end of dst (and read past the end of the weight table). A simulation of the split shows it for a 2000x10 output on 8 threads (4 extra rows), 1000x100 on 16 threads, and on 64 threads 1891 of the heights 2-4096, including 640x480 (15360 bytes past the buffer), 1280x720 and main.cpp's own 800x2000 (12800 bytes). Fix by launching only ceil(dst_h / stride) chunks.
- _KNERP, pass1, pass2 and _KLERP are non-inline functions defined in the header, so including KLERP.h from two translation units gives duplicate-symbol link errors; add inline or include it in one .cpp.
- Each multithreaded call starts its tasks with std::async(std::launch::async); libstdc++ and libc++ create a new thread per task (MSVC uses a pool), so outputs just above the 20000-pixel cutoff pay thread start-up on every call. A hardware_concurrency() of 0 would divide by zero.
- The demo builds with -Ofast -mfma, which lets the compiler contract the double-precision coordinate maths into FMAs; bit-exact agreement with a given OpenCV build is plausible from the arithmetic but is not tested anywhere in the repo.

**Status:** Abandoned: the code is a single 26 Dec 2016 commit and the only later commit (23 Mar 2021) added the MIT license; no issues or pull requests exist. Small enough to vendor, but patch the row split and mark the helpers inline first.

[repo](https://github.com/komrad36/KLERP) · [benchmark](https://github.com/komrad36/KLERP)

##### kornia-rs (Image.resize and imgproc kernels, kornia-py)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust/Python (PyO3) vision library whose NEON u8 resize and colour kernels beat OpenCV bilinear resize on aarch64 Jetson.

**Beats:** OpenCV 4.13.0 cv2.resize (INTER_LINEAR, INTER_CUBIC, INTER_LANCZOS4) and cv2.cvtColor; Pillow 12.2.0 Image.resize (LANCZOS) — These are first-party numbers from kornia-py/benchmarks.md on a Jetson Orin (Cortex-A78AE, 6 cores, Rust 1.93.0 at opt-level=2, OpenCV 4.13.0 at default threads, Pillow 12.2.0), best-of-N minimum on random 1080p RGB u8, run at commit 07e52d7, which is not on GitHub. The like-for-like bilinear comparison against cv2 INTER_LINEAR shows 1.55-1.97x at 1080p to 540p, 1.33x (derived from page data) to 2.84x at 1080p to 224x224, 3.09x to 4.1x (derived from page data) at 640 to 320, and 5.52x on the exact-2x upscale. Each range spans the matrix's aa=True and aa=False columns, which run identical code because antialias does not affect bilinear, so the spread is run-to-run noise. The 2x-upscale output carries a +0.74 LSB rounding bias that the page does not disclose.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded A to C: bake_off_pil_cv2.py calls k_img.resize(1280, 720) with Image.resize's default interpolation bilinear (at HEAD and 9e040c4), so the 'Lanczos 4.4x' pits bilinear against cv2 INTER_LANCZOS4 and PIL LANCZOS; kornia's Lanczos is 3-lobe against cv2's 4-lobe, and with antialias on its Lanczos downscale is slower than cv2 (0.79x, 0.64x, 0.87x, derived from page data). The matrix aa and PIL columns are not produced by the committed scripts, the run commit 07e52d7 is a 404, cv2.setNumThreads is never set and the OpenCV build is unstated. The like-for-like bilinear wins (5.52x, 2.84x, 1.97x, 3.09x) stand.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e112, 2026-10-05): numeric flaw behind the 5.52x 2x-upscale row: pyrup_2x_rgb_u8 double-rounds rhadd(a, rhadd(a, b)) in both passes, a +0.74 LSB mean bias with 71% of pixels 1 LSB high (Python replay of the scalar reference); the test checks corners only and the fidelity script lacks the 2x-up case. The bilinear matrix's aa=True and aa=False columns run identical code yet differ 2.2x (224^2: 1.33x vs 2.84x), so the bilinear ratios are noise-bound. Image.resize on 1- or 4-channel images silently falls back to nearest; bicubic uses a=-0.5 vs OpenCV's A=-0.75; the general bilinear row is scalar on all architectures, x86 pyrdown/pyrup rows are scalar and CIE colour AVX2 falls back to scalar; cv2.imencode('.webp') defaults to lossless, so the page note is wrong; the u16 column LUT wraps above 65535 px (debug_assert only). Issue #667 user report: resize 1.7-4.9x slower than OpenCV (2026-01, hardware unstated). C stands.

**Independent measurement:** first-party benchmark vs OpenCV

**How:** A dispatch cascade sends special cases to dedicated kernels. An exact 2x bilinear downscale becomes a 2x2 box average (NEON vpaddlq_u8 plus vrshrn), and an exact 2x upscale uses fixed {0.25, 0.75} weights computed with vrhaddq_u8 pairs. General bilinear precomputes Q14 tap LUTs per column and spreads 16-row chunks across rayon threads; the per-row loop itself is scalar. Bicubic and Lanczos3 follow the Pillow-style separable two-pass Q14 convolution: an i16 intermediate, u16 column LUTs, a 4-row NEON horizontal kernel that shares coefficient loads, and an L2-aware strip-fused H-then-V plan. antialias=False fixes the taps at 4 or 6 instead of widening them with the scale. The f32 colour kernels deinterleave with vld3q, apply the 3x3 matrix in registers, and use a degree-4 log2 / degree-3 exp2 pow and a one-iteration Halley cbrt (about 4e-4 and 2.3e-5 relative error).

**Use it when:**
- Python or Rust pipelines on aarch64 edge boards (Jetson Orin, Raspberry Pi 5, Apple silicon) that call cv2.resize INTER_LINEAR on u8 RGB frames. The Orin page shows 1.55-1.97x at 1080p to 540p and 3.09x at 640 to 320, plus 5.52x on an exact 2x upscale, where the output is slightly biased (see gotchas).
- Model-input preprocessing: resize_normalize_to_tensor fuses resize, /255, mean/std and HWC-to-CHW into one pass to f32, replacing a cv2-plus-numpy chain; a CUDA Preprocessor does the same on device.
- Replacing Pillow LANCZOS or BICUBIC with the same antialiased semantics on ARM, where Pillow-SIMD has no NEON path: kornia's antialiased Lanczos is 3.1-5.3x faster than Pillow 12.2.0 on the Orin (derived from page data).
- RGB to Lab in f32 where colour-grade precision is enough: 1.35-1.55x faster than cv2.cvtColor, and closer to true Lab than OpenCV's LUT-interpolated f32 path, according to the page.
- Free-threaded CPython (3.13t/3.14t) or GIL-free Rust services that want thread-safe image ops with numpy and DLPack zero-copy.

**Skip it when:**
- Antialiased (default) bicubic or Lanczos downscaling as a cv2 replacement: it is slower than OpenCV on the page's own matrix, Lanczos at 0.64-0.87x and bicubic AA at 0.55-0.85x. Its antialias=False Lanczos is 3-lobe (6 taps) against OpenCV's 8-tap INTER_LANCZOS4, so even those wins do less work.
- x86-64: there are no published x86 numbers. The general bilinear row kernel is scalar on every architecture, the exact-2x downscale and upscale row kernels are scalar off aarch64, and the CIE colour kernels fall back to scalar under AVX2. Issue #667 (January 2026, open, hardware unstated, predates the April-June 2026 tuning) reported bilinear resize 1.7-4.9x slower than OpenCV.
- Pipelines that need byte-for-byte OpenCV output: bicubic uses a = -0.5 (Pillow) while OpenCV INTER_CUBIC uses A = -0.75, Lanczos has 3 lobes against OpenCV's 4, Lab and Luv differ by up to 0.67, and the exact-2x upscale is biased.
- Non-u8 resizing (f32/u16 fast resize is the open issue #862), and HSV, HLS, Luv or YCbCr conversions, where kornia is at parity or slower than cv2 (0.61-1.08x across the page's two colour tables).
- Codec speed claims from the same bake-off: JPEG is a tie (libjpeg-turbo on all sides). In the 23x WebP row, cv2.imencode('.webp') with no parameters actually runs lossless libwebp (OpenCV grfmt_webp.cpp falls back to lossless when no quality is given), which contradicts the page's 'lossy' note; PIL's is lossy. File sizes are not reported, and PNG level 1 is set against PIL's default level.

**Integration:** crate (kornia or kornia-imgproc), plus a PyO3 wheel (kornia-rs on PyPI) and C++ bindings (kornia-cpp) · kornia-imgproc: rayon, wide, num-traits, thiserror, kornia-image/-tensor/-algebra; optional cudarc and half (cuda feature). Python wheel: numpy; turbojpeg (needs nasm to build) on by default in kornia-py · Rust 1.89 (workspace rust-version); Python 3.8-3.14 including free-threaded builds; maturin >= 1.9 to build the wheel · aarch64 NEON first (Linux incl. Jetson, macOS, Windows arm64); x86-64 with AVX2 for some resize kernels (blend, separable H/V passes) chosen at run time, scalar elsewhere; wheels for manylinux x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64, win_amd64/arm64; optional CUDA path loaded lazily

**Vs siblings:** Pick kornia-rs on aarch64 (Python or Rust) when you want numpy-in, numpy-out, multi-threaded bilinear resize and colour conversion that beats cv2 there, with optional CUDA dispatch. Pick fast_image_resize for antialiased convolution resizing in Rust on x86-64 AVX2 (single-thread, beats libvips), Pillow-SIMD for antialiased resizing in Python on x86, and OpenCV itself for bicubic/Lanczos downscales or byte-exact cv2 output.

**Gotchas:**
- The exact-2x bilinear upscale fast path (the 5.52x row) computes 0.75a+0.25b as rhadd(a, rhadd(a, b)) in both passes and requantizes to u8 between them. The code comment says this equals round(0.75a+0.25b), but double rounding always rounds up: a pure-Python replay of the scalar reference on random u8 input gave a +0.74 LSB mean bias against float64 bilinear, with 71% of pixels 1 LSB above the correctly rounded value (max 1 LSB). The unit test checks only the four corner pixels, and bench_resize_vs_libs.py has no 2x-upscale case, so a 1920x1080 to 3840x2160 resize comes out slightly brighter than a 3838-wide one, which takes the general Q14 path.
- Image.resize on 1- or 4-channel images silently ignores the interpolation argument and runs a floor-convention nearest-neighbour resize. Only 3-channel input reaches the bilinear, bicubic and Lanczos kernels.
- Image.resize defaults to interpolation="bilinear", antialias=True. The page's '1080p->720p (Lanczos)' bake-off row actually ran this bilinear default against cv2 INTER_LANCZOS4 and PIL LANCZOS, so it says nothing about Lanczos speed.
- The rust doc of xyz_from_rgb says it gamma-decodes, but the kernel is matrix-only (to match cv2 COLOR_RGB2XYZ), so it is not colorimetric sRGB-to-XYZ; use linear_rgb_from_rgb first if you need that. The bicubic/Lanczos column LUT is u16, guarded only by a debug_assert, so release builds would silently wrap source columns for images wider than 65,535 px.

**Status:** Actively developed: 1,001 commits, v0.2.0 released 2026-09-26, last commit 2026-09-27, 720 stars, kornia-imgproc at about 47.6k crates.io downloads. Apache-2.0 and usable as a crate or a wheel, but the speed work targets aarch64 first.

[repo](https://github.com/kornia/kornia-rs) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kornia/kornia-rs/HEAD/kornia-py/benchmarks.md)

##### libblur  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust SIMD blur crate (Gaussian, stack, box, median); exact large-kernel Gaussian about 4x faster than multithreaded OpenCV GaussianBlur.

**Beats:** OpenCV (Gaussian blur, stack blur and median blur) — First-party criterion runs (app/benches/gauss/main.rs) on two unnamed machines labelled NEON and AVX, against OpenCV 4.x through the opencv crate (version, build and thread count unstated), both multithreaded: the Exact Gaussian on a 3000x4000 RGB 8-bit image with kernel 155 and sigma 25.83 (README says 151) took 49.40/43.41 ms against OpenCV's 180.56/182.44 ms (about 3.7x/4.2x, derived from page data), and on a single 3000x4000 plane 17.59/15.51 ms against 74.73/64.20 ms (about 4.2x/4.1x, derived). OpenCV's 8-bit ALGO_HINT_ACCURATE path here is GaussianBlurFixedPoint, which quantizes kernel weights to 8 fractional bits (ufixedpoint16), so it is bit-exact across platforms but not more precise in its weights than libblur's f32 Exact mode. The README's RGBA Gaussian, stack-blur, box and median rows are not backed by matching harness code, and the tables were last edited in May 2025, before the 2026 kernel rewrites.

**Known shortcoming:** Only the Gaussian RGB exact rows (about 3.7-4.2x; app/benches/gauss/main.rs with kernel 155 and sigma 25.83 on both sides, labelled 151; OpenCV on its threaded bit-exact SIMD path without IPP or HAL, border Clamp against reflect-101, OpenCV's destination allocated inside the timed loop) survive scrutiny. Harness bugs invalidate the rest: cvt_color is passed CV_8UC3 (16, which is COLOR_BGRA2BGR565) as the code, so OpenCV's 'RGBA' and stack-blur inputs are 2-channel; the OpenCV stack-blur radius is 38 against libblur's 77; the RGB stack run uses 2828x4242 dimensions on a 3000x4000 buffer; the median harness runs single-threaded at radius 1-4 on different images and cannot produce the README's radius-35 table. No CPU, OpenCV build or flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e100, 2026-10-05): the Exact-mode Gaussian win of about 4x holds for RGB and single plane, but OpenCV's 8U ALGO_HINT_ACCURATE path (GaussianBlurFixedPoint) quantizes weights to 8 fractional bits, so the 'approximation vs bit-exact' caveat overstates the precision gap. The box-blur README rows are also unbacked: OpenCV box_filter is called with normalize=false, the 'RGBA' OpenCV input is 3-channel BGR, the RGB row uses kernel 35 rather than the stated 77 radius, and libblur's RGB source is the RGBA test_image_4 buffer read as 3 channels. No C API (cbindgen.toml empty, no FFI in lib.rs). README tables last edited 2025-05-09, before the 2026 kernel rewrites (v0.24.0); the 0.23.0 skipped-rows regression (#86, fixed in 0.23.1) postdates the tables. novtb spawns and core-pins fresh threads on every parallel stage of every call.

**Independent measurement:** first-party README tables

**How:** The Gaussian is a separable two-pass convolution that folds the symmetric kernel (adds mirrored taps before one multiply, halving multiplies) in hand-written intrinsics for AVX2+FMA and SSE4.1 (chosen at runtime with is_x86_feature_detected), NEON with RDM, SVE and AVX-512 (opt-in) and wasm simd128. Exact mode uses f32 weights with FMA accumulation; FixedPoint mode scales weights to Q15 integers with i32 accumulators. The vertical pass computes 2 output rows (x86) or 3 (NEON) per iteration to reuse loaded rows, kernels of 61 taps or fewer use a sliding row buffer instead of a full transient image, and rows are split into static zones across threads from the author's novtb crate. Stack and box blurs are O(1)-per-pixel running sums; median is a Huang-style sliding 256-bin histogram per channel.

**Use it when:**
- Rust pipelines that need a true Gaussian with large kernels (tens to ~150+ taps) on 8-bit RGB, RGBA or grayscale frames in the 10-12 MP range, run multithreaded, without linking OpenCV.
- Code that must run the same SIMD-accelerated blur on x86-64 and aarch64 (Apple silicon, ARM servers), including u16 and f32 images or arbitrary separable kernels.
- UI, thumbnail or background-blur work where an approximation is acceptable: stack_blur, fast_gaussian_next and box_blur are the crate's fastest paths (author's speed order: box, stack, fast_gaussian_next, fast_gaussian, ..., gaussian, bilateral, median).
- Builds that want pure Rust (no C/C++ toolchain); wasm32 with simd128 is partially covered.

**Skip it when:**
- When output must match OpenCV bit for bit: weights, intermediate rounding and borders differ (libblur benches use Clamp; OpenCV defaults to reflect-101), and the default ConvolutionMode is the approximate FixedPoint.
- From C or C++ without writing your own FFI shim and adding a Rust toolchain; no C header or extern "C" API ships.
- Median blur as a speed play: the README shows only 3-16% over OpenCV (derived) and no public harness produces those rows; the per-pixel cost grows with radius (sliding histogram, not Perreault O(1)).
- Small kernels or small images: the README publishes no numbers below kernel 151 (the gauss harness has 3- and 13-tap cases but no results), and each multithreaded call spawns fresh threads.
- Analysis that needs an analytic Gaussian: the approximations are flagged by the author as unsuitable for advanced analysis, and FixedPoint adds a stated 1-3% error.

**Integration:** crate · num-traits, rayon, num-complex, novtb (author's scoped thread-pool crate, which uses core_affinity); optional image 0.25 (feature image) and zaft (feature fft) · Rust 1.89 for 0.24.0 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, edition 2024); nightly for the sve, nightly_f16 and nightly_fcma features (avx512 needs nightly before 1.89). The repo's own rust-toolchain.toml pins an unversioned nightly. · x86-64 (SSE4.1 and AVX2+FMA selected at runtime; AVX-512 opt-in feature), aarch64 NEON (RDM on by default; SVE on nightly), wasm32 simd128 partial, scalar fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick libblur over the C++ Gaussian siblings (LibGaussianBlur, archived in 2024; zanazakaryaie/fastGaussianBlur, a tutorial; bfraboni/FastGaussianBlur, an approximation with no OpenCV comparison) when you can take a Rust dependency and want a maintained exact Gaussian plus fast approximations, u16/f32 support and NEON/AVX kernels in one crate. Pick FastBoxBlur or bfraboni's header-only code when you need a C++ source drop and a box or approximate blur is enough.

**Gotchas:**
- ConvolutionMode::FixedPoint is the default (doc comment: estimated error not less than 1-2%); pass ConvolutionMode::Exact for f32 weights. In both modes the horizontal pass is stored in the image's own type (u8 for 8-bit) before the vertical pass, so 'Exact' means f32 weights and accumulation, not a float intermediate.
- Kernel sizes must be odd: GaussianBlurParams::new with an even size returns BlurError::OddKernel, while new_from_kernel rounds to the nearest odd size and derives sigma.
- Every parallel stage of every call spawns new scoped OS threads through novtb and pins them to cores round-robin with core_affinity; this adds spawn cost per call and can collide with other pinned workloads or thread pools.
- Kernels are rewritten often: 0.23.0 (2026-02-13) skipped rows in the single-plane FixedPoint Gaussian (issue #86, fixed in 0.23.1 by PR #87 'Fix skipped rows'), and earlier f32 Gaussian artifacts were reported in issues #21 and #38. Pin the version and compare output after upgrades.

**Status:** Active: v0.24.0 on crates.io 2026-05-09 (about 101k downloads), last commit 2026-05-08, 685 commits and 0 open issues; dual Apache-2.0/BSD-3-Clause, so copyable, but Rust-only with no C API.

[repo](https://github.com/awxkee/libblur) · [benchmark](https://github.com/awxkee/libblur)

##### LibGaussianBlur (FFT Gaussian blur, from Blur_algorithms)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

C++20 FFT (pffft) separable Gaussian blur for 8-bit RGB/RGBA; 9-20x faster than cv::GaussianBlur at very large sigma.

**Beats:** OpenCV cv::GaussianBlur — Blur_algorithms' notebook (hard-coded single runs, Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores) shows the pffft path taking 9.0x to 20.0x less time than cv::GaussianBlur(img, img, Size(0,0), sigma=sqrt(x)) at 45 of 46 sizes, and 0.78x at 1500x1000 (derived from page data). The timed pffft_ includes deinterleave, kernel FFT and setup, so it is end-to-end. Current OpenCV 4.x runs 8-bit GaussianBlur as a bit-exact fixed-point direct convolution (233 taps at sigma 38.7) under parallel_for_, so both sides were probably multi-threaded, but the OpenCV version, build, compiler and thread settings are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug behind the numbers: pffft_sorted_optimized_convolution scales the packed Nyquist element by the kernel DC instead of the kernel Nyquist (same code in the benchmarked Blur_algorithms pffft_ path), so 1-pixel stripes give 243.8/11.2 instead of 127.5, noise is off by plus or minus 11.9 and a half-stripe row by plus or minus 58 in its black half; with the index fixed the output matches direct convolution exactly, so the README's 'indistinguishable from direct convolution' is false while the timing (same operation count) stands. Heap out-of-bounds read when the kernel is clamped to the long side and the pad exceeds the short side minus 1 (aspect over 2 with sigma above about short/3.33; the benchmark pads of 128-514 are safe); float to uint8 without clamping; ENABLE_MULTITHREADING off by default; the OpenCV version is unknown and its 8U GaussianBlur is fixed-point with parallel_for_.

**How:** Separable FFT convolution: each row is reflect-101 padded and zero-padded to a 2^a*3^b*5^c length, transformed with pffft (Pommier's SIMD real FFT), multiplied by the precomputed spectrum of a centred, symmetric Gaussian (real-valued, so only real parts are used), and inverse transformed. Columns get the same treatment after a cache-blocked transpose. Cost per pixel grows with log(FFT length) instead of with the kernel width, which is what beats direct convolution once sigma reaches tens of pixels. Rows and columns are split across std::thread workers (hybrid_loop) when built with ENABLE_MULTITHREADING.

**Use it when:**
- Very large sigma (roughly 30 px and up) on multi-megapixel photos, where direct separable convolution needs hundreds of taps per pixel.
- 8-bit RGB/RGBA in apps that cannot ship OpenCV: mobile (Android/iOS), browser (WASM with threads and SIMD), or a small native dependency.
- Python 3.11 on macOS arm64 or Linux x86-64 where a pip wheel without OpenCV is convenient.
- Smooth photographic content, where the Nyquist-bin defect below stays under about 1 level.

**Skip it when:**
- Small or moderate sigma: OpenCV was faster at the smallest benchmark size (1500x1000, sigma 38.7: 24.97 ms vs 32.05 ms), and FFT padding overhead dominates small kernels.
- Content with pixel-level texture, noise, dithering or halftones: the highest-frequency component is not blurred (gotcha 1), so stripes survive and leak across whole rows.
- Elongated images with sigma above about one third of the short side: the reflect padding then overruns the row buffer (gotcha 2).
- Grayscale, 16-bit, float or planar data (only 3- or 4-channel uint8 is accepted; other channel counts print an error and return unchanged), or when bit-exact parity with cv::GaussianBlur is needed.

**Integration:** static lib · pffft (Pommier, git submodule, built as an object library); pybind11 for the Python module; googletest for tests · C++20 (std::numbers), CMake 3.14+ · Linux, macOS, Android, iOS, WebAssembly (Emscripten, -msimd128); pffft SIMD on SSE/NEON/WASM; Windows not supported yet (on roadmap)

**Vs siblings:** No other catalogued color-and-resampling entry does large-sigma Gaussian blur; FastBoxBlur (same author) is the cheaper option when a box-blur approximation is acceptable. Use LibGaussianBlur when you need a true Gaussian at huge sigma without OpenCV, and stay with OpenCV for small kernels or bit-exact output.

**Gotchas:**
- Nyquist-bin bug (in LibGaussianBlur's src/gaussianblur.cpp and in the benchmarked Blur_algorithms pffft_ path): pffft_transform_ordered packs F(0) and F(N/2) into elements 0 and 1, but pffft_sorted_optimized_convolution scales element 1 by the kernel's DC gain (1) instead of its Nyquist response (about 1e-4). The alternating component therefore passes unblurred across the whole row. In a Python transliteration (n=200, sigma=sqrt(n)), 1-px stripes came out 243.8/11.2 instead of 127.5, uniform noise was off by up to 11.9 levels, and a half-striped/half-black row gave +-58 in the black half. With the index fixed, the output matched direct convolution exactly. The fix costs nothing, so timings are unaffected.
- The kernel width is clamped to the larger image side, but the reflect-pad copy needs pad <= tile length - 1. For aspect ratio above 2 and sigma above about short side/3.33 (e.g. 500x2000 at sigma 200: pad 665 vs 499), std::copy_n reads outside the column buffer (heap over- and under-read). The benchmark's pads (128-514) were well inside, and the tests use only 3x3 and 10240x10240 square images.
- Float to uint8 conversion adds 0.5 with no clamp, so negative or >255.5 results (which the Nyquist leak can produce) are undefined conversions in C++.
- Performance knobs are hard-coded for the author's Apple M3 Pro: L2_CACHE_SIZE is 16 MB (2048x2048-float transpose blocks, far larger than typical x86 L2), threads are created per stage rather than pooled, and every row and column task copies three aligned buffers.

**Status:** Stale: 23 commits, 5 stars, no issues or PRs, PyPI 1.1.2 on 2025-03-29, and the last commit is a coverage-badge update. It is Apache-2.0 with a LICENSE file, so it is copyable, but fix the Nyquist index and guard the pad length before production use. The benchmark itself lives in the archived Blur_algorithms repo, which has no LICENSE file.

[repo](https://github.com/michelerenzullo/LibGaussianBlur) · [benchmark](https://github.com/michelerenzullo/Blur_algorithms)

##### libyuv  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Google's SIMD YUV/RGB conversion, scaling and rotation library; snippet-only reports put it 4-10x ahead of libswscale.

**Beats:** FFmpeg libswscale — No reproducible libyuv-versus-libswscale benchmark exists in reach: the 4-5x (1088x1920 BGR24 to 480x854 YUV420P, 500 runs, about 4.19 s vs 0.93 s, MacBook Pro 2016) and about 10x (RGBA to YUV420P on Apple M1) figures come from search snippets of blocked ffmpeg-devel threads, where FFmpeg developers answered that swscale's defaults run a higher-quality scaler. The one page with numbers, libheif issue #1215 (no hardware, compiler or code), times a whole HEVC multi-tile decode-to-RGB step at 42 ms with libheif's own converter and 30 ms with a 'hacky' libyuv hookup, which is about 1.4x and does not involve libswscale.

**Known shortcoming:** Upgraded D to C on libheif issue #1215 (42 ms vs 30 ms whole conversion step against libheif's own yuv2rgb, hardware unstated). The libswscale comparison exists only in search snippets (4.19 s vs 0.93 s on a 2016 MacBook Pro, about 10x on Apple M1; ffmpeg.org archives blocked here), and FFmpeg developers replied that swscale defaults to a higher-quality scaler, so it is not like-for-like. No public libyuv-vs-swscale benchmark code; libyuv's unit tests time only its SIMD paths against its own C. Record points at the unofficial GitHub mirror (lemenkov/libyuv); upstream is chromium.googlesource.com/libyuv/libyuv (blocked here). BSD-3-Clause plus Google PATENTS grant.

**Known shortcoming:** The libheif #1215 comparison (42 versus 30 ms) is likely unequal work: libheif defaults to bilinear chroma upsampling plus a 4:4:4 intermediate pass (heif_color.cc) while plain I420ToRGB24/RAW does nearest chroma in one pass, and the reporter names no function or matrix. libyuv's own unittest prints one cold C call against the mean of N SIMD calls, overstating SIMD-versus-C ratios (outputs are asserted bit-exact).

**How:** Every operation is a loop over rows that calls one row function chosen once per call by runtime CPU detection (TestCpuFlag): hand-written GCC/Clang inline assembly for SSE2/SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512 (row_gcc.cc), Neon, SVE2 and SME on Arm, RVV, LSX/LASX and MSA, with C fallbacks and '_Any_' wrappers for widths that are not a multiple of the vector size. YUV to RGB uses 6-bit fixed-point coefficients: pmaddubsw on bias-shifted UV, pmulhuw for the Y gain, saturating adds, then shift and pack, all in 16-bit lanes. The scaler has dedicated 2x, 4x, 3/4 and 3/8 down paths, a box filter, 16.16 fixed-point bilinear, and ScaleFilterReduce drops to a cheaper filter when the scale factor allows it.

**Use it when:**
- Real-time camera, WebRTC or video pipelines converting between I420/NV12/NV21/YUY2 and ARGB/RGB24/RAW at 8 bits, where per-frame latency matters more than resampling quality.
- Decoders and image libraries (the libheif report) that need a fast final YUV 4:2:0 to interleaved RGB step on x86 or Arm.
- Downscaling video frames by 2x, 4x, 3/4 or 3/8 with box or bilinear filtering, or rotating mobile camera frames by 90/180/270 degrees.
- Projects that want a permissive (BSD-3-Clause plus Google patent grant), widely shipped library with a C fallback on every platform and bit-exact SIMD versus C output in its unit tests.

**Skip it when:**
- High-quality resampling or colour-space work (Lanczos, correct chroma siting, dithering): libyuv offers only point, linear, bilinear and box, its bilinear upsampler is described in docs/filtering.md as 'not technically correct' (the image is slightly magnified), and zimg or libswscale with quality flags fit better.
- Chroma upsampling quality: the plain I420ToARGB/I420ToRGB24 paths replicate each chroma sample over a 2x2 block (nearest neighbour); you must call the *MatrixFilter variants with kFilterBilinear for interpolated chroma.
- Workloads that want the absolute fastest 8-bit kernels on a given path: catalogued siblings yuvutils-rs (NV12 to RGBA 377.59 vs 621.11 us), xxYUV and sparkyuv (8-bit 4:2:0 decode on Apple M3) beat it on some paths, though sparkyuv loses to libyuv on encode.
- Plain MSVC (cl.exe) builds: x86 kernels then come from row_win.cc, a smaller set, and the CMake Arm/SVE/SME/RVV objects are only built when not MSVC; Chromium compiles Windows x64 libyuv with clang to get the inline assembly.
- Multi-core scaling of one large frame: the library spawns no threads, so callers must split the image across threads themselves.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake builds both; GN for Chromium; also Makefile and Bazel files) · none required; optional libjpeg for MJPG decode (HAVE_JPEG, on by default when found); gtest and pthread only for the unit tests · CMake 3.16; a C++ compiler (no C++ standard pinned in CMakeLists.txt); GCC or Clang for the x86 inline-assembly kernels; Arm SVE2/SME kernels need a compiler accepting -march=armv8.5-a+i8mm+sve2/+sme · x86/x86-64 (SSE2 to AVX-512, runtime dispatch), 32- and 64-bit Arm Neon, SVE2, SME, RISC-V RVV, LoongArch LSX/LASX, MIPS MSA, portable C elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick libyuv over yuvutils-rs, xxYUV, sparkyuv or the old descampsa/yuv2rgb when you need one maintained, permissively licensed C/C++ library covering nearly every 8/10/12-bit YUV and RGB layout plus scaling and rotation on every major ISA; pick zimg or FFmpeg's libswscale with quality flags when resampling and colour accuracy matter more than speed, and yuvutils-rs if you are in Rust and want its faster NV12/RGBA paths.

**Gotchas:**
- Format names follow register order, not memory order: ARGB is B,G,R,A in memory, RGB24 is B,G,R and RAW is R,G,B, so 'interleaved RGB' output means I420ToRAW, not I420ToRGB24.
- The plain I420ToARGB/I420ToRGB24 entry points assume BT.601 limited range (kYuvI601Constants); full-range or BT.709 content needs the J/H/F-prefixed functions or a *Matrix call, or colours shift silently.
- 10/12-bit inputs converted to ARGB are reduced to 8 bits per channel; use the AR30/AB30 or 16-bit paths to keep precision.
- The GitHub repo is an unofficial mirror: issues and patches go to chromium.googlesource.com/libyuv/libyuv, there is no ABI promise (CMake sets no SOVERSION) and the version is a single integer (1974 here) that consumers pin.

**Status:** Active (mirror last commit 2026-10-02, version 1974, shipped and marked security-critical in Chromium); BSD-3-Clause with a separate patent grant, so copyable, but track upstream on googlesource rather than the mirror.

[repo](https://github.com/lemenkov/libyuv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/strukturag/libheif/issues/1215)

##### Lycon  `Python with C++ core`  `BSD-3-Clause (OpenCV-derived code) and MIT (Lycon changes)`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Small OpenCV-derived resize and JPEG/PNG I/O extension for NumPy; beats Pillow 4.0 and scikit-image, ties OpenCV.

**Beats:** Pillow (PIL) 4.0.0 and scikit-image 0.12.3 via their Python APIs; OpenCV 3.2+ cv2 (whose code Lycon reuses) runs at parity — First-party 2017 table (perf/benchmark.py, mean of 10 runs after one warm-up, 15360x8640 RGB image, Ubuntu 14.04 on an unnamed Skylake Core i7, compiler not named): Lycon's resize ties OpenCV 3.2+ to within 1-3% and beats single-threaded Pillow 4.0.0 by 2.3x-51x and float64 scikit-image 0.12.3 by 66x-200x, but it runs OpenCV's multi-threaded, non-antialiased kernels against Pillow's wider filters. Its only gains over OpenCV are JPEG read (1.5x) and JPEG write (1.3x), with no explanation of the libjpeg builds.

**Known shortcoming:** Python with a C++ (OpenCV-derived) core (language-filter mismatch). perf/benchmark.py with -O3 -march=native, compiler unnamed, CPU only 'Core i7 Skylake'. Measured work differs: Lycon's resize is multithreaded (pthreads parallel_for_) against single-threaded Pillow 4.0, the 2x bilinear downsample becomes a 2x2 area average with no anti-aliasing versus Pillow's widened convolution, PIL times include fromarray/asarray copies and skimage outputs float64. Same speed as OpenCV, whose code it reuses.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug (not behind the timings): save and the resize failure path return Py_None without Py_INCREF, so CPython before 3.12 aborts with 'deallocating None' after about 10k saves (issue #26). The 4.2x PNG-write win partly buys bigger files: default zlib level 1 with SUB filter and Z_RLE against Pillow 4.0's compress_level -1 (level 6). Build broken on arm64 macOS (#29) and PowerPC -march=native (#21); sdist only, last release 0.2.0 on 2019-01-21; JPEG pixels differ from Pillow (#19).

**How:** Speed comes from OpenCV's separable fixed-tap resize kernels (SSE2/SSE4.1 on x86 with runtime CPUID checks, NEON for the cubic, Lanczos and area paths only), split across all cores by a pthreads parallel_for_, with the GIL released during load, save and resize. An exact 2x INTER_LINEAR downscale is rewritten to a 2x2 box average (area fast path), and the PNG writer defaults to zlib level 1 with the SUB filter and Z_RLE strategy. The CMake build compiles everything with -O3 -march=native.

**Use it when:**
- Python data loaders on x86-64 Linux that need OpenCV-equivalent resize speed and JPEG/PNG I/O in RGB order without pulling in all of OpenCV.
- Bulk upscaling or downscaling of large 8-bit or float32 RGB arrays where OpenCV's interpolation (no antialiasing on downscale) is acceptable.
- Replacing Pillow 4-era or scikit-image resize calls in old pipelines where the multi-threaded OpenCV kernels give 2.3x-51x on a 15360x8640 image (README table).

**Skip it when:**
- Anywhere opencv-python(-headless) is already installed: the README itself says the advantages are minimal, and the table shows resize at 1x OpenCV.
- Quality-sensitive downscaling: bilinear, bicubic and Lanczos use fixed 2/4/8-tap kernels with no antialiasing, unlike Pillow's support-widened filters, so Pillow output differs and aliases less.
- Apple Silicon, PowerPC, Windows or modern Python: issue #29 (cv_vrndq_u32_f32 undefined on arm64 macOS), #21 (-march=native rejected on PowerPC), #15 (no Windows support) and install failures #22/#23/#30 are open; PyPI has only source tarballs, the last being 0.2.0 from 2019-01-21.
- Long-running processes on CPython older than 3.12 that call lycon.save many times: the binding returns Py_None without a new reference and crashes with 'Fatal Python error: deallocating None' (issue #26, about 10,000 calls).
- Formats beyond JPEG and PNG, alpha-aware or EXIF-orientation control, or decoding from memory buffers (issues #12, #13, #24 open).

**Integration:** Python extension module built from source by CMake through setup.py (pip sdist); static C++ library 'lycon' with no install rules · libjpeg, libpng, NumPy, CMake 2.8.11+, make, a C++11 compiler · C++11 (GCC or Clang); tested in 2017 with Python 2.7 and 3.5 · Linux and macOS on x86-64 as tested in 2017; arm64 macOS build fails (issue #29); no Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick Lycon over OpenCV only when you need cv2.resize behavior in a tiny source-built extension with RGB order and can build on x86-64; otherwise opencv-python-headless gives the same kernels, maintained. Pick Pillow-SIMD when you need antialiased downscaling in a Pillow-compatible API, and fast_image_resize (Rust) for a maintained SIMD resizer with convolution filters.

**Gotchas:**
- lycon.save ends with 'return Py_None;' and the resize failure path does the same, with no Py_INCREF, so every save call drops a reference to None; CPython below 3.12 eventually aborts (issue #26). On 3.12+ None is immortal, which hides it.
- The PNG writer defaults to zlib level 1, SUB filter and Z_RLE (OpenCV's speed setting), while Pillow 4.0 defaults to compress_level -1 (zlib level 6): the 4.2x PNG-write win over PIL partly buys larger files. Pass Encode options for a fair comparison.
- -march=native is hard-coded in CMakeLists.txt, so a build is tied to the build machine's CPU (issue #28: prebuilt wheel fails on another CPU) and breaks on compilers that reject the flag.
- JPEG decoding can differ from Pillow's: issue #19 reports about 11% of pixels off by an average of 1.46 on one JPEG, from whichever libjpeg the build linked.

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2019 (37 commits, 16 open issues including build failures on arm64 and an interpreter-crashing refcount bug); BSD-3-Clause plus MIT, so the resize code can still be vendored, but upstream OpenCV is the maintained source of the same kernels.

[repo](https://github.com/ethereon/lycon) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ethereon/lycon/HEAD/README.md)

##### MagicScaler (PhotoSauce)  `C#`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

.NET image resizing pipeline (MagicScaler) that makes JPEG thumbnails 5-9x faster than Magick.NET in its author's runs.

**Beats:** ImageMagick via Magick.NET-Q8-AnyCPU 12.2.0 (also System.Drawing, ImageSharp, SkiaSharp, NetVips/libvips 8.13.2) — The author ran a locally modified copy of bleroy/core-imaging-playground in Nov 2022 (BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun, .NET 6.0.10, MagicScaler 0.13.2 with libjpeg-turbo, Magick.NET-Q8 12.2.0): loading, resizing to 150 px and saving 12 JPEGs of about 1 MP took 46.85 ms against 345.99 ms for ImageMagick on a Xeon W-11855M under Windows 10, about 7.4x, and 65.72 against 588.63 ms on a Snapdragon ARM64 dev kit. The 'Linux x64' table (99.8 against 522.6 ms) is labelled WSL2, so it ran in a VM on the same Windows laptop, not on bare-metal Linux.

**Known shortcoming:** C# library (language-filter mismatch). README timings (7.4x/5.2x/9.0x vs ImageMagick, derived) come from the author's locally modified copy of bleroy/core-imaging-playground; the measured work differs: MagicScaler uses hybrid decoder pre-shrink, linear-light processing with sharpening and the libjpeg-turbo codec, while ImageMagick decodes the full image in gamma space. NetVips's margin is larger on Linux.

**Known shortcoming:** The work done differs from the baseline: hybrid mode decodes at half scale through libjpeg-turbo's scale_denom and then applies Catmull-Rom (SettingUtil), while Magick.NET does a full decode plus its default Lanczos (resize.c), roughly 17 against 51 taps per axis (derived from code). The 'Linux x64' table ran in WSL2 (a VM), not bare metal. Planar mode linearises only luma (sRGB curve forced) and sharpens only luma; no hand-written intrinsics on ARM64 (Sse2 gate); issue #180 reports 360 ms against GDI+'s 130 ms on small images; last NuGet release 0.15.0 (December 2024).

**How:** Hybrid scaling: for large reductions it asks libjpeg-turbo for a DCT-domain scaled decode (scale_denom) or box-averages by a power of two (HybridScaleTransform), then runs the high-quality filter only for the remaining ratio. JPEGs are processed planar: Y is resampled (in approximate linear light) and Cb/Cr at chroma resolution, then handed straight to the encoder, so no full-size YCbCr-to-RGB conversion happens. Resampling is a separable convolution with precomputed kernel maps, hand-written SSE/AVX2/FMA convolvers on x86 (System.Numerics.Vector fallbacks elsewhere), fixed-point UQ15 or float paths, and lookup-table gamma conversion. The pipeline streams lines through sliding and windowed buffers from a pool instead of materialising whole images, which keeps peak memory low.

**Use it when:**
- .NET server code (CMS, e-commerce, upload handlers) that turns large JPEGs into thumbnails or web-size renditions at high throughput on Windows or Linux.
- You want good-quality defaults (linear-light blending, automatic filter choice, post-resize unsharp mask, colour-profile normalisation) without writing filter or ICC code.
- Memory-constrained parallel batch resizing: in the author's 351-image Bee Heads run MagicScaler peaked at 420 MB and 37,153 ms CPU against ImageMagick's 878 MB and 277,780 ms.
- Strong reductions (roughly 3x and up) of JPEG input, where decode-time DCT scaling and planar processing give the biggest gains.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: it is C# only; libvips, fast_image_resize or Skia are the native options in this category.
- macOS: the README says it runs on Windows and Linux, and the native codec packages ship Windows and glibc Linux binaries only.
- Many small images through an encode step: issue #180 (2025) reports 144 images of 256x256 resized to about 144x144 taking 360 ms against 130 ms with GDI+, even with nearest-neighbour; no maintainer reply was visible.
- BMP or TIFF input on Linux: the README lists them as the notable formats the cross-platform codec plugins do not support.
- Bit-exact or reference-filter output: hybrid mode trades a little quality for speed, and the defaults pick filter, sharpening and JPEG quality for you; set HybridMode=Off and explicit Interpolation and Sharpen values if you need control.

**Integration:** module · None on Windows (WIC codecs); on Linux one or more PhotoSauce.NativeCodecs.* NuGet plugins with bundled native libraries (libjpeg-turbo built from a custom psjpeg vcpkg port, libpng, libwebp, libheif, libjxl, giflib). · Library targets net8.0 and net472, with net462, netstandard2.0 and netstandard2.1 added in the Dist build (MagicScaler.csproj); hardware-intrinsic paths only on .NET Core 3.0+ targets. · Windows x86, x64 and ARM64; Linux glibc x64 and ARM64. Hand-written intrinsics on x86 SSE2/AVX/AVX2 only; other architectures use Vector<T> or scalar paths.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ImageSharp when you are on .NET for Windows or Linux and want the fastest JPEG thumbnailing (46.85 ms against ImageSharp's 115.90 ms in the same Windows x64 run). Pick ImageSharp for pure-managed portability including macOS, and libvips (NetVips) or Skia when you need native, cross-language or macOS support; NetVips was 2.2x slower here on Windows x64 and 3.8x on WSL2 Linux (derived from page data).

**Gotchas:**
- Default HybridMode=FavorQuality changes the work done: for about 1 MP to 150 px it decodes at half size and then uses Catmull-Rom on the rest (SettingUtil.GetDefaultInterpolation), while the Magick.NET harness decodes full size and applies ImageMagick's default Lanczos (MagickCore/resize.c), roughly 17 against 51 filter taps per output pixel per axis (derived from code).
- In planar JPEG mode only luma is linearised, with the sRGB curve forced when the source profile is not sRGB (MagicTransforms.AddInternalFormatConverter); chroma is resampled gamma-encoded and only luma is sharpened.
- Gamma lookup tables are 256 entries (to linear) and 1024 entries (from linear, interpolated), which issue #183 says is too coarse for float or 16-bit HDR pipelines.
- The 1.0 version has not shipped: the latest NuGet release is 0.15.0 (Dec 2024), and the README says APIs are not yet stable.

**Status:** Active: dependency and native-codec updates landed in Sep-Oct 2026 after a gap since Apr 2025, but the last NuGet release is 0.15.0 (Dec 2024); MIT licensed, so the code can be copied, but it is C# and of no direct use to C++ code.

[repo](https://github.com/saucecontrol/PhotoSauce) · [benchmark](https://github.com/saucecontrol/PhotoSauce/blob/master/readme.md)

##### moxcms  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust ICC colour-management crate; the author's README showed 8-bit transforms 3.7-7.4x faster than stock Little CMS 2.

**Beats:** Little CMS 2 (lcms2); also qcms — The moxcms 0.7.4 README (Aug 2025) times 8-bit transforms of a 1997x1331 JPEG with Criterion against the lcms2 6.1 crate and qcms 0.3, in unnamed NEON and AVX2 columns with no CPU, rustc version or flags. For example, RGB to RGB took 2.68/4.52 ms against lcms2's 13.1/27.73 ms, about 3.7-7.4x across rows (derived from page data). The lcms2 side is stock: lcms2-sys either links the system library or builds only the core src/*.c files, and the bench registers no fast_float plugin. Precision is roughly comparable on matrix-shaper rows (moxcms Q2.13 fixed point vs lcms2's 1.14 fixed-point MatShaper8 path), and both use Perceptual intent. The rows still do not do the same work: moxcms converts to its built-in sRGB while lcms2/qcms convert to assets/bt_2020.icc, the lcms2 CMYK row is fed the RGBA buffer, the qcms 'CMYK' row is built with DataType::RGBA8 (which in qcms 0.3 builds a 33^3 RGB CLUT, not the 4D CMYK path), and the LUT variant behind each moxcms LUT/CMYK row is not stated. The table is not reproducible from the repo: the lcms2/qcms rows were never re-measured after Mar 2025, and the app/Cargo.toml checked in with the last table (commit 178e732) enables no moxcms features, so SIMD is off and the options-gated LUT bench cannot compile.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). 0.7.4 table matches public bench code (app/benches/icc, lut) with no CPU, rustc version or flags; same Perceptual intent and 8-bit on both sides, moxcms in Q2.13 fixed point. Destinations differ (moxcms to built-in sRGB, lcms2 and qcms to bt_2020.icc) and the lcms2 CMYK row was fed the RGBA buffer instead of CMYK data. lcms2 rows were never re-measured after March 2025; the last table before their removal (April 2026) showed moxcms slower, 2.8-3.8x, on LUT and CMYK. Lead: imazen/cms-bench harness, no published results.

**Known shortcoming:** The Little-CMS side is stock lcms2 (lcms2-sys builds the core sources or links the system library; no fast_float plugin, no cmsPlugin call), both sides Perceptual; matrix-shaper precision is comparable (moxcms Q2.13 versus lcms2 MatShaper8 1.14 fixed point) but destinations differ (built-in sRGB versus bt_2020.icc). The qcms 'CMYK' row is built with DataType::RGBA8, so qcms times a 33^3 RGB CLUT, not CMYK. app/Cargo.toml at 178e732 (the last table) enables no moxcms features, so SIMD is off and the options-gated LUT bench cannot compile: the table is not reproducible. Colour bugs after the 0.7.4 numbers: CMYK yellow axis up to 8/255 (#144, fixed PR #147, 2025-12-29), default path up to 12/255 off versus float tetrahedral (#162, fixed PR #181), x86-64 and aarch64 outputs differ (#192 open).

**How:** When both profiles are matrix/TRC (matrix-shaper) profiles, the transform becomes 256-entry linearisation tables, a 3x3 matrix in Q2.13 fixed point and a 4096-entry output gamma table, run with SSE4.1, AVX2, NEON or opt-in AVX-512 intrinsics. Stock lcms2's equivalent 8-bit path (MatShaperEval16 in cmsopt.c, 1.14 fixed point) is scalar C. LUT-based and CMYK profiles are pre-sampled into a 3D/4D grid and evaluated with trilinear (the default), tetrahedral, pyramid or prism interpolation, in Q0.15 fixed point or float, with SIMD variants. So most of the gain is SIMD over a precomputed pipeline at similar fixed-point precision, not a different colour model.

**Use it when:**
- Rust image pipelines that convert embedded ICC profiles to sRGB. The image crate, jxl-oxide and typst already depend on it (about 89.7M crates.io downloads).
- Bulk 8-bit RGB/RGBA conversion on x86-64 with AVX2 or aarch64 with NEON, where stock lcms2 is the current cost.
- CMYK JPEG/TIFF to RGB(A) in Rust without linking C.
- Parsing untrusted ICC data in a memory-safe language: unsafe code is confined to SIMD paths, the crate forbids unsafe when all SIMD features are off, and a fuzz target ships in the repo.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects without a Rust toolchain: there is no C API, so stock lcms2 with its fast_float plugin is the in-language option.
- Pipelines that need bit-identical output across platforms. Issue #192 (Sep 2026) reports x86-64 vs aarch64 differences on about 1.7 % of pixels (up to 3/255) on the fixed-point path and about 91 % (1/255) on the float path, traced to per-architecture SIMD and FMA.
- Work that needs a user-facing black-point-compensation flag (commented out in TransformOptions) or other lcms2 features such as proofing or device links, which the README does not document.
- Precision-critical 8-bit conversions under default options (trilinear, low barycentric weights, fixed point). Issue #162 reported up to 12/255 divergence from the float/tetrahedral/high-weight path before PR #181 (May 2026), and the tetrahedral/pyramid/prism and High-weight choices need the non-default options feature.
- Deciding against an already-tuned lcms2: the published comparison used stock lcms2 without the fast_float plugin, so the gap to a tuned lcms2 is unmeasured.

**Integration:** crate · num-traits, pxfm · Rust 1.89 for 0.9.x (1.85 for 0.8.x); the opt-in sve feature on aarch64 needs nightly (feature(stdarch_aarch64_sve)) · any Rust target; SIMD paths for x86-64 (SSE4.1 and AVX2 by default, AVX-512 opt-in) and aarch64 (NEON by default, SVE opt-in), scalar elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick moxcms over the Little-CMS fast_float plugin when the code base is Rust and memory-safe profile parsing matters. Stay with lcms2 plus fast_float in C/C++, or when you need lcms2's wider feature set. jsColorEngine fills the same role only for JavaScript/WASM, and babl is GIMP's pixel-format engine rather than a general ICC transform library.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD and the faster matrix-shaper variants are separate cargo features. The default set omits avx512, the *_shaper_optimized_paths features, options and in_place, all of which the benchmark app enables, so a default build (for example through the image crate) may not run the code paths that were timed.
- allow_use_cicp_transfer defaults to true. Issue #155 reported wrong PQ/HLG output with that default and #154 reported setters not clearing CICP (both closed Feb 2026), so check HDR profiles against a reference.
- CMYK output had a real colour error: issue #144 (Dec 2025) found green 2-8/255 low on the pure-yellow axis of US Web Coated SWOP against lcms2 and skcms, fixed in PR #147 ('Remove invalid gamut clipping', 2025-12-29). That is after the 0.7.4 README numbers.
- Issue #122 (Dec 2025) flagged unsound safe wrappers around get_unchecked in the SIMD interpolation code; keep up with releases if you feed untrusted LUT profiles.

**Status:** Very active (0.9.1 on 2026-09-15, last commit 2026-09-29, one open issue) and dual BSD-3-Clause/Apache-2.0. Most of its 89.7M downloads come through the image crate. The README benchmark table was removed in Apr 2026, so the project currently publishes no speed numbers.

[repo](https://github.com/awxkee/moxcms) · [benchmark](https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/moxcms/0.7.4/readme)

##### odiff  `Zig`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zig (formerly OCaml) CLI and Node tool that diffs screenshots pixel by pixel with a YIQ threshold; README times it 4.8-7.6x faster than ImageMagick compare and pixelmatch.

**Beats:** ImageMagick compare (and pixelmatch) — Only first-party hyperfine wall-clock runs exist (MacBook Pro 16 on macOS 11 beta, CPU and tool versions unstated; images/README.md invokes the OCaml-era binary 'ODiffBin'), timing whole processes including PNG decode and encode: on the cypress.io screenshot pair 1.168 s vs ImageMagick compare -compose src 8.881 s (7.6x) and pixelmatch 7.712 s (6.6x), and on the water pair 1.951 s vs 9.326 s (4.8x) and 10.614 s (5.4x), with ratios derived from the means. The tools do different work (pixelmatch runs anti-aliasing detection by default, and odiff does not), so the README's claim that all three produce the same difference is wrong.

**Known shortcoming:** Tables last changed 2021-01-27 (OCaml era) on a MacBook Pro 16 with no CPU model, versions or flags; the relative column mismatches the stated means (water 4.78/5.44 against 5.24/5.50); outputs differ (ImageMagick has no YIQ threshold, pixelmatch does anti-aliasing detection; discussion #82 shows 1.07% against 0.75%); bench.sh compares odiff commits only. Image diffing is a weak fit for colour-and-resampling.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e103, 2026-10-04): the README comparison does unequal work: pixelmatch runs with anti-aliasing detection on by default while odiff runs with it off; the AVX-512 path is opt-in only (--enable-asm, threshold 0.1, no diff image) and release binaries target a baseline CPU; JPEG decode uses TJFLAG_FASTDCT unless -t 0. A vendor blog (Vizzly, which sells the rival Honeydiff) reports the opposite ordering, pixelmatch faster (80 vs 240 ms at 2.1-2.5 MP; 450 vs 710 ms at 18 MP), seen in search snippets only. The images/README.md harness runs ODiffBin, confirming the OCaml build was measured.

**Independent measurement:** first-party hyperfine comparison; contrary vendor blog (snippet)

**How:** compareSameLayouts loads std.simd.suggestVectorLength(u32) packed RGBA pixels at a time and tests base != comp as whole vectors; the YIQ NTSC color delta (the Kotsarenko-Ramos metric pixelmatch also uses) is computed only for lanes that differ, so mostly identical screenshots cost little more than a memory compare. The delta itself uses 12-bit fixed-point integer arithmetic (calculatePixelColorDeltaSimd) instead of doubles. The two input images are decoded in parallel on two threads with bundled libspng, libjpeg-turbo (TJFLAG_FASTDCT unless threshold is 0), libtiff and libwebp. Optional extras: a hand-written AVX-512 NASM kernel (vxdiff.asm) for count-only runs and an RVV C kernel on riscv64; server mode removes process spawn cost.

**Use it when:**
- Screenshot-based visual regression in CI (Playwright via playwright-odiff, Cypress via cypress-odiff; Argos, Lost Pixel and Visual Regression Tracker use it) where most pixels are identical between baseline and candidate.
- Large full-page captures (tens of megapixels) where a JavaScript pixelmatch run takes seconds and you want a native single binary.
- High comparison counts from Node: keep one ODiffServer alive to avoid per-call process start-up and initialization.
- Pipelines that compare across formats (PNG baseline vs JPEG or WebP capture) or need ignore regions and the bounding rows/columns of the change.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need ImageMagick compare's metrics (AE with fuzz, RMSE, PSNR, SSIM) or a perceptual metric such as SSIM or CIEDE2000: odiff only reports a count and percentage over a YIQ threshold.
- When diff counts must match pixelmatch: anti-aliasing detection is off by default in odiff (--antialiasing to enable) but on by default in pixelmatch, JPEGs decode with libjpeg-turbo's fast DCT, and the delta is fixed-point (discussion #82 reports 1.07% vs pixelmatch's 0.75% at threshold 0.1).
- Small images compared in-process from JavaScript: a third-party benchmark by Vizzly (vendor of the competing Honeydiff; blog read from a search snippet only, method unknown) timed odiff at 240 ms vs pixelmatch 80 ms on 2.1-2.5 MP images and 710 ms vs 450 ms at 18 MP, so process and decode overhead can erase the advantage.
- Saturating many cores on one huge image pair: the per-pixel loop is single-threaded; only the two image decodes run in parallel.
- Relying on the README's 6x figure for the current Zig build: it was measured in 2021 on the OCaml version and has not been re-run against ImageMagick or pixelmatch since.

**Integration:** CLI executable plus npm package (odiff-bin) and server mode; the Zig sources build a static odiff_lib library · libspng, libjpeg-turbo, libtiff, libwebp (fetched and built through the imgz Zig package, or system libspng/libjpeg/libtiff with -Ddynamic=true outside Windows); nasm for x86_64 Linux and macOS builds; Node.js for the npm API · Zig 0.16.0 (build.zig.zon minimum_zig_version) plus nasm on x86_64 Linux/macOS; prebuilt binaries need no toolchain · Prebuilt for macOS, Linux and Windows on x86_64 and aarch64, plus Linux riscv64 (generic and RVA23 builds); SIMD width is fixed at compile time (SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON/RVV); the AVX-512 asm kernel is x86_64 Linux/macOS only

**Vs siblings:** Pick odiff over imgdiff (Go), which its own README times at 1.442 s vs 6.475 s for an older odiff on the same cypress pair, when you want the Node, Playwright and Cypress integrations, server mode, ignore regions and anti-aliasing detection; pick libvips or OpenCV only if you are scripting a custom absdiff-and-threshold pipeline rather than running a turnkey visual-regression comparator.

**Gotchas:**
- The fast AVX-512 kernel almost never runs: it needs a build targeting AVX-512BW/VL (the release targets in build.zig set only arch and OS, so they get Zig's baseline CPU), the --enable-asm flag, threshold exactly 0.1, no diff image, no anti-aliasing, no ignore regions and identical dimensions.
- Any threshold other than 0 switches JPEG decoding to libjpeg-turbo TJFLAG_FASTDCT, so JPEG inputs can show small decode-dependent differences that other tools would not report; use -t 0 for the accurate DCT.
- Correctness fixes to know about: before PR #185 (merged 2026-08-24, after v4.5.0) the fixed-point YIQ constants were truncated, which under-counted near the threshold (3 extra pixels out of 2.27 million on a test image after the fix); versions 4.1.1-4.1.2 could write incomplete diff PNGs for large files (issue #153, fixed in PR #155).
- The diff PNG is written only when pixels differ; with --fail-on-layout (CLI, off by default) or failOnLayoutDiff (Node), images of different sizes return reason 'layout-diff' without being compared, and otherwise extra non-transparent pixels count as differences.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v4.5.0 released in July 2026, fixes merged 2026-08-24), MIT-licensed, 3.2k stars and used by several visual-testing services; the speed claim is first-party, five years old and was measured on the OCaml version.

[repo](https://github.com/dmtrKovalenko/odiff) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmtrKovalenko/odiff/HEAD/README.md)

##### Photon (photon-rs)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust image-effects library that also ships as WebAssembly for browsers and Node; one mixed first-party result against the libvips CLI.

**Beats:** libvips (vips CLI, Windows vips.exe) — One first-party wiki page (2020-06-04, photon-rs 0.2.0 with image 0.21.1) timed open, invert and save inside a criterion loop (10 samples) against libvips's Windows vips.exe under hyperfine, which includes process start-up. Photon won the PNG case (244.87 ms vs 915.1 ms) and lost the JPG case (117.26 ms vs 84.2 ms). No CPU, OS, image size or encoder settings are given, and the PNG bench code was never committed. Reading the code adds that the timed work is dominated by image-crate decode and encode: Photon's own step is a scalar invert loop, and save_image always writes RGBA8 with image-crate defaults, while vips used its own encoder defaults. So the PNG gap most likely reflects codecs, settings and process start-up rather than Photon's pixel code.
