**Known shortcoming:** Mixed result: PNG invert 244.87 ms against vips.exe 915.1 ms (about 3.7x) but JPG 117.26 against 84.2 ms (libvips about 1.39x faster); an in-process criterion run against the vips CLI including process start-up, with no CPU, OS or versions; the committed bench (b802192, 2020-06-04, photon 0.2.0) covers only input.jpg and the PNG bench was never committed. The operation is invert, not resampling.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e121, 2026-10-05): no SIMD, threads or unsafe code; invert is a scalar step_by(4) loop. The wiki-timed work is mostly image-crate decode and encode (save_image always writes RGBA8 at image-crate defaults), so the PNG win is likely codecs plus vips.exe start-up rather than Photon pixel code. Stays C; no independent numbers found. Bugs not behind the numbers: blend() reads the second image by linear offset so rows misalign when it is wider; the blend-mode string is lowercased per pixel; LinSrgba into_linear is a no-op so blends operate on gamma values; open #119 last-pixel skip remains in primary, inc_brightness and dec_brightness. The current adjustments bench mutates one cloned image every iteration (unpublished numbers).

**Independent measurement:** first-party wiki timings

**How:** There is no special technique: the effects are scalar, single-threaded loops over the RGBA byte buffer (for example, invert is a step_by(4) loop computing 255 - v), with no SIMD intrinsics, no threading (no rayon) and no unsafe code. Decoding, encoding, resize (image::imageops::resize, a separable filter) and the 90-degree rotation steps come from the image crate 0.24.8, and gaussian_blur is a three-pass box-blur approximation. In the browser the gain is compiling these loops to WebAssembly rather than running them in JavaScript; the README says it 'run[s] at near-native speed' but publishes no WASM numbers.

**Use it when:**
- Browser or Node.js apps that need client-side photo filters, tints, channel edits or simple resizes without a native addon (no libvips or sharp binary to install).
- Rust apps that want a large catalogue of ready-made Instagram-style effects and colour adjustments on 8-bit RGBA images, where the code to write matters more than raw throughput.
- Serverless or edge runtimes that accept WASM but not native modules (issue #138 discusses Cloudflare Workers).
- Single-image, interactive edits where per-call cost is tens to hundreds of milliseconds and a lazy streaming pipeline is not needed.

**Skip it when:**
- High-throughput server pipelines (thumbnails, batch conversion): libvips is threaded and streams; Photon decodes the whole image to RGBA8 in memory and runs one thread. Its own wiki shows libvips faster on the JPG case (84.2 ms vs 117.26 ms).
- Quality or speed-critical resampling: resize is the image crate's generic imageops::resize. fast_image_resize (catalogued) uses SIMD and beats libvips on Lanczos3.
- 16-bit, HDR, float or colour-managed work: everything is converted to 8-bit RGBA on load (issue #155 asks for 16-bit grayscale and is open), there is no ICC handling, and blend() treats sRGB bytes as linear (it calls LinSrgba::new(...).into_linear(), which is a no-op), so blending happens on gamma-encoded values.
- Code that must not panic on bad input: many public functions unwrap() decode and encode results (new_from_byteslice, get_bytes, get_bytes_jpeg), and in WASM a panic shows up as 'RuntimeError: unreachable' (issues #45, #134 and #175 are open).
- Projects that need fixes on a release: crates.io's latest is 0.3.3 (2025-05-10), and the 2026 adjustments module and memory-copy fixes are only on master.

**Integration:** crate · image 0.24.8 (gif, jpeg, png, tiff, webp, bmp and other codecs), palette 0.6.1, imageproc 0.23, rusttype 0.9.2, rand 0.7, base64 0.13, serde, thiserror, time, perlin2d, instant; the default enable_wasm feature also pulls in wasm-bindgen, web-sys, js-sys, node-sys and console_error_panic_hook (turn it off with default-features = false for native builds) · Rust 2021 edition (Rust 1.56 or later); no rust-version is declared, and CI runs on stable · any Rust target (pure Rust, scalar code), plus wasm32 builds for browsers and Node

**Vs siblings:** Pick Photon when you need a ready-made effects catalogue that runs unchanged in the browser, Node and native Rust. For resizing, pick fast_image_resize (SIMD, measured faster than libvips). For OpenCV-style kernels, pick kornia-rs. For server throughput, use libvips itself.

**Gotchas:**
- The native get_raw_pixels_slice() (no copy) exists only when enable_wasm is off. With the default features you get get_raw_pixels(), which clones the whole buffer.
- blend() panics unless the first image is no larger than the second, but it then indexes the second image at the same linear byte offset. If the second image is wider, rows misalign and the wrong pixels are blended. It also lowercases the blend-mode string inside the per-pixel loop, which allocates once per pixel.
- Open issue #119: some filters skip the last pixel. The loop bound 'len() - 4' is still present in primary, inc_brightness and dec_brightness in effects.rs (monochrome.rs has been fixed). rotate() truncates the angle to an integer, and issues #170 and #198 report noise and bugs on rotation.
- In JavaScript, PhotonImage objects live in WASM linear memory. Issue #175 hit an out-of-memory error after about 174 new_from_base64 calls in Node 20. PR #227 (2026-09) reduced copies, but callers should still free images explicitly.

**Status:** Actively maintained (Apache-2.0, 3.9k stars, last commit 2026-09-18, with community bug and memory fixes through 2026), but releases lag master and no benchmark has been published since 2020.

[repo](https://github.com/silvia-odwyer/photon) · [benchmark](https://github.com/silvia-odwyer/photon/wiki/Benchmarks)

##### Pillow  `Python with C core`  `MIT-CMU`  `active`  `Tier C`

Python's standard imaging library (C core): 3-4x faster resizing and 10-30x faster grayscale/3D-LUT than single-threaded ImageMagick 6.9.

**Beats:** ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 (via Wand) — In pillow-perf on an Intel Core i5-4430 under Ubuntu 18.04.3, Pillow 7.0.0 was built from source with default CFLAGS and no -march (the compiler is not recorded); run.sh checks out the upstream 7.0.0 tag, whose README is plain Pillow, from a pillow-simd clone. It was compared with ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 through Wand with MAGICK_THREAD_LIMIT=1 on a 2560x1600 RGB image, taking the median of 5 runs (3 for ImageMagick blur and LUT, 11 for convert and load). Results: Lanczos to 320x200 40.5 vs 134.4 ms (3.3x); Lanczos upscale to 5478x3424 374.8 vs 1495.6 ms (4.0x); RGB to L 5.3 vs 51.5 ms (9.8x); 4^3 3D LUT 111 vs 3354 ms (30x); JPEG load 21.4 vs 27.4 ms (1.3x). All ratios are derived from page data. The resize and LUT rows are like for like; the blur and grayscale rows are not.

**Known shortcoming:** Python library with a C core (language-filter mismatch). First-party pillow-perf run (i5-4430.json: Pillow 7.0.0 vs ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 through Wand, both single-thread; harness public, compiler unrecorded). Resize and LUT are equivalent work; the blur row is not (box approximation vs true Gaussian).

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers are stale: the pillow-perf run used upstream Pillow 7.0.0 (run.sh checks out the 7.0.0 tag inside the pillow-simd clone) and the 12.3.0 release notes claim up to 5.6x on resample and filter since; the blur and greyscale rows are not like-for-like, and in the same file OpenCV 4.1.2 upscales 3.9x (bilinear) and 2.6x (bicubic) faster than Pillow and blurs 1 px in 69 ms against 186 ms. Pillow's kernels have no SIMD. 12.3.0 fixed about a dozen 2026 CVEs.

**How:** Resampling is a separable two-pass convolution. The filter coefficients are precomputed once per output column and row, with support widened by the downscale factor so the result is properly antialiased. 8-bit images are accumulated in 32-bit fixed point (22 fractional bits) and clipped through a lookup table, and the horizontal pass only processes the source rows the vertical pass will read. GaussianBlur is three passes of an extended box filter (Gwosdek et al., SSVM 2011) using running sums, with a transpose for the vertical pass, so its cost does not depend on the radius. Color3DLUT does trilinear interpolation in 16-bit fixed point, and RGB-to-L is a single fixed-point multiply-add per channel (ITU-R 601-2 weights). None of these kernels uses SIMD intrinsics (that is the Pillow-SIMD fork); each releases the GIL while it runs.

**Use it when:**
- Python services that thumbnail or resize 8-bit RGB/RGBA images and currently call ImageMagick through Wand or a subprocess: Lanczos and bilinear downscales ran about 3x faster, and 2.14x upscales about 4x faster, with the same filter families.
- Large-radius blurs: Pillow's GaussianBlur took 186-188 ms on a 4-megapixel frame at radius 1, 10 and 30, while ImageMagick grew from 0.68 s to 4.1 s; accept that it is a box approximation.
- Colour grading with 3D LUTs (Color3DLUT, 4^3 to 36^3 tables): about 111 ms per 2560x1600 frame against 3.1-3.4 s for ImageMagick's HaldClut on an i5-4430.
- You want broad format I/O plus basic processing in one permissively licensed (MIT-CMU) dependency, with wheels for Linux, macOS and Windows; JPEG save also ran 2.2x faster than ImageMagick (21.8 vs 48.0 ms).

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ code: there is no public C API, so embedding CPython is the only route; use libvips, OpenCV or a dedicated resizer instead.
- Maximum single-core resize speed: in the same data files, Pillow-SIMD 7.0 AVX2 is about 4-7x faster at resizing with the same API, and single-threaded OpenCV 4.1.2 upscaled to 5478x3424 3.9x faster bilinear (57.7 vs 222.9 ms) and 2.6x faster bicubic (115.3 vs 298.3 ms).
- Small blur radii or an exact Gaussian: OpenCV blurred at radius 1 in 69 ms against Pillow's 186 ms, and Pillow's result is a three-box approximation, not a true Gaussian kernel.
- Using all cores on one large image: each kernel runs on one thread, so parallelism means tiling or processing different images on different threads; libvips threads automatically.
- Parsing untrusted images in a privileged process without staying current: 12.3.0 alone fixed about a dozen CVEs (out-of-bounds writes in Image.paste() and RankFilter, PDF and font decompression bombs, a McIdas out-of-bounds read).

**Integration:** module · CPython; zlib and libjpeg are required for source builds by default (they can be disabled), and libtiff, libwebp, FreeType, LittleCMS, OpenJPEG, libavif and libraqm are optional; binary wheels bundle them · Python 3.11+ on main (13.0.0 drops 3.10; 12.0.0 dropped 3.9); a C compiler only for source builds · CI on Linux x86-64 (Alpine, Amazon Linux, Arch, CentOS Stream, Debian, Fedora, Gentoo, Ubuntu), Ubuntu 26.04 arm64v8/ppc64le/s390x, macOS arm64 and x86-64, Windows x86 and x86-64, and PyPy3

**Vs siblings:** Pick plain Pillow over Pillow-SIMD when you need the official wheels on every platform (ARM, ppc64le, s390x, PyPy) and prompt security releases, and accept giving up roughly 4-7x of resize speed. Pick it over OpenCV when you need correctly antialiased convolution downscaling, large-radius blurs or 3D LUTs together with broad format I/O from Python. For multi-threaded or out-of-core pipelines, libvips is the better choice.

**Gotchas:**
- GaussianBlur(radius) treats radius as the standard deviation and computes three extended box passes, so its output differs from ImageMagick's -blur/-gaussian-blur; pillow-perf's 3.6-21.9x blur ratios compare these two different algorithms.
- convert('L') applies ITU-R 601-2 luma weights (fixed point 19595/38470/7471) to gamma-encoded values, so it will not match ImageMagick's grayscale type conversion.
- Image.thumbnail() defaults to reducing_gap=2.0 (a fast integer box reduce, plus JPEG draft decoding, before the final filter), while Image.resize() defaults to reducing_gap=None, so the two calls trade speed and accuracy differently.
- Decompression-bomb guard: Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89,478,485 pixels) raises a warning above the limit and DecompressionBombError above twice the limit; very large legitimate images need the limit raised.

**Status:** Very active (quarterly releases on Jan 2, Apr 1, Jul 1 and Oct 15; 12.3.0 is current and 13.0.0 is on main) and MIT-CMU licensed. The catalogued numbers are from the old 7.0.0, and the 12.3.0 release notes claim up to 5.6x speedups for resample, filter, matrix and other operations, so current Pillow is probably at least as fast (not re-measured).

[repo](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python-pillow/pillow-perf/HEAD/docs/src/data/i5-4430.json)

##### quantette  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust palette quantizer (Wu and Oklab k-means); author's 4-thread runs show 3-14x faster than libimagequant on large opaque photos.

**Beats:** libimagequant (imagequant crate 4.4.1, the engine behind pngquant); also color_quant 1.1.0 (NeuQuant) and exoquant 0.2.0 — Author's harness (examples/cli.rs, 30 runs averaged, quantize+remap timed, rustc -C target-feature=+avx2, CPU and rustc version unstated), 256 colours, 4 threads for quantette and imagequant 4.4.1 at defaults. Without dithering, k-means took 53-97 ms vs 253-1044 ms on eleven 17-30 MP photos (3.3-14.1x) and 28-32 vs 93-266 ms at 1920 px wide (2.9-8.6x) with DSSIM close to imagequant's (worse on some 1920 px images, e.g. Futuristic 0.000846 vs 0.000545); with dithering 1.13-5.1x and 3.3-8.4x, with lower DSSIM than imagequant in 21 of 22 rows (derived from page data). imazen/zenquant's approximate, competitor-run table puts quantette at about 1.2x imagequant speed 4.

**Known shortcoming:** Doc numbers match examples/cli.rs (+avx2, no CPU or rustc): k-means is 3.3-14.1x faster than imagequant without dither and 1.13-5.1x with dither on large photos, but the Wu sRGB ratio is quality-mismatched (DSSIM 0.0072 against 0.0044) and imagequant runs on RGBA while quantette runs RGB; the zenquant competitor run (about 1.2-2.1x) marks its own timings approximate, so it does not lift the tier.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e108, 2026-10-05): no bug behind the numbers. The large-photo gap comes from automatic radix deduplication (only at 2048x2048 pixels and above, dither off) plus the k-means sample cap of 262,144; the pipeline defaults (Wu, dither on, serial) differ from the benchmarked configuration; AVX2 is compile-time only (wide crate with cfg(target_feature)); the timer's as_millis truncates; the harness lacks imagequant's speed option. Parallel dither bands depend on thread count; no alpha support (#28 unanswered); no C API; the benchmark document predates v0.6.0. Tier C holds.

**Independent measurement:** first-party harness vs imagequant

**How:** Pixels are converted to Oklab with wide-crate f32x8 SIMD. Wu's greedy orthogonal bipartitioning builds the palette, optionally refined by k-means: online (MacQueen) k-means when serial and mini-batch k-means (batch 4096) on rayon when parallel, sampling at most 262,144 pixels by default, so k-means cost is nearly flat in image size. For images of 2048x2048 pixels or more with dithering off, the pipeline automatically radix-deduplicates pixels into an indexed image with counts, so colour conversion, Wu and nearest-palette mapping run on unique colours only. That explains why the gap to imagequant is largest on the 17-30 MP photos and smallest with dithering.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services or tools making PNG8/GIF palettes from large opaque photos: no-dither k-means took 53-97 ms against imagequant's 253-1044 ms on 17-30 MP photos (4 threads) at similar DSSIM.
- Palette extraction only (output_srgb8_palette), e.g. theme or LUT generation and terminal image display; crates.io reverse dependencies include okolors, lutgen-cli, icy_sixel and yazi-adapter.
- Projects that cannot take libimagequant's GPL-3.0-or-later or commercial terms: quantette is MIT OR Apache-2.0.
- no_std (alloc) or wasm32 builds: with the threads and image features off the crate is no_std, and CI runs clippy for wasm32-unknown-unknown.
- Quick previews where palette quality matters less: Wu in sRGB took 21-34 ms on the large photos, but its DSSIM was 1.6-3.1x imagequant's (derived from page data).

**Skip it when:**
- Images with transparency: there is no alpha support (README benchmark doc; issue #28, opened 2025-12-18, still open without a reply).
- C or C++ codebases without Rust in the build: there is no C API or header, so you would write your own FFI shim; libimagequant ships a C API.
- Dithered output on images where imagequant is already quick: with dithering, auto-dedup is off and the gap falls to 1.13x on Futuristic (318 vs 360 ms).
- When you need dithered output that is identical across machines: parallel Floyd-Steinberg splits the image into min(rayon threads, ceil(height/256)) bands, so results depend on thread count.
- When perceived quality or file size matters more than DSSIM: zenquant's README finds quantette best on DSSIM and SSIMULACRA2 but says imagequant 'consistently looks best to the human eye', and its own PNG/GIF outputs are smaller.

**Integration:** crate (quantette on crates.io, v0.6.0) · palette, wide, bytemuck, bitvec, num-traits, libm, ordered-float, ref-cast; optional (all on by default) rayon for threads, image 0.25 for image integration, rand + rand_xoshiro for kmeans · Rust 1.90 (rust-version), edition 2024 · any Rust target; no_std with alloc when threads and image are disabled; SIMD through the wide crate, with AVX2 used only when enabled at compile time

**Vs siblings:** Against pngquant/libimagequant, the only quantizer among the siblings: pick quantette for opaque RGB images in Rust when you want MIT/Apache licensing instead of GPL-3.0-or-later/commercial and k-means quality in a fraction of imagequant's default-speed time on large photos. Keep libimagequant for alpha, a C API or its speed and quality knobs. The other siblings (fast_image_resize, libvips, moxcms, libyuv) are resizers and colour converters, not quantizers.

**Gotchas:**
- The published times used rustc -C target-feature=+avx2. The code relies on wide's f32x8 and has cfg(target_feature = "avx2") branches (for example the dedup threshold for custom palettes), so a default x86-64 build without AVX2 is a different, unbenchmarked configuration.
- Pipeline::new() defaults to Wu (not k-means), Floyd-Steinberg dithering on (7/8 error diffusion) and parallel off. To get the benchmarked k-means no-dither numbers you must set quantize_method(QuantizeMethod::kmeans()), ditherer(None) and parallel(true) yourself.
- The speedups depend on two size-dependent shortcuts: auto-dedup only at 2048x2048 pixels or more and only without dithering, and k-means sampling capped at 262,144 pixels (max_samples). Smaller images, dithered runs or dedup(false) lose part of the advantage.
- The benchmark doc was last edited 2025-12-23, before v0.6.0 (2026-05-15). The harness times one quantize+remap per process with Instant::elapsed().as_millis(), which truncates to whole milliseconds, so the 3 ms Wu figures at 1920 px are coarse. Its imagequant runs use only the library defaults (speed 4, quality target 100) because the harness has no speed option.

**Status:** Active single-maintainer crate (v0.6.0 on 2026-05-15; since then dependency and lint maintenance, last commit 2026-08-02), MIT OR Apache-2.0, about 1.42M crates.io downloads and 16 reverse dependencies.

[repo](https://github.com/IanManske/quantette) · [benchmark](https://github.com/IanManske/quantette)

##### rez (pure Go and SIMD image resizer)  `Go`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go image resizer with SSE2 assembly kernels for YCbCr, RGBA and Gray planes; faster than other pure-Go resizers.

**Beats:** ImageMagick convert -resize; also nfnt/resize, disintegration/imaging, gift, bild and golang.org/x/image/draw — In fawick/speedtest-resize (third-party, MIT; run by contributor nono on a 3.4GHz Core i7 with Ubuntu 16.10, one pass over the first ten 5616x3744 JPEGs, decode plus resize plus encode timed together), rez_bilinear averaged 0.349 s per file against 0.568 s for ImageMagick `convert -resize 150x150>` and 0.370-0.515 s for the other pure-Go resizers, while ImageMagick's -thumbnail path took 0.057 s. Reading the harness adds three points to the verifier's notes: rez runs on all cores by default (GOMAXPROCS goroutines) and the harness sets no thread limits for any contender; its bilinear kernel widens to about 76 taps at this 37x reduction, so the resize itself is a real antialiased filter, and every pure-Go row also pays for a full Go image/jpeg decode; and the harness ignores decode and convert errors but still counts the file and its time, although rez's 0.140% average output size (other pure-Go rows: 0.146-0.160%) shows no sign that files were skipped.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: speedtest-resize (co-authored by the rez author) compares rez bilinear on YCbCr at Go default quality with a spawned ImageMagick convert -resize using its default filter and quality (output 3.9x larger), so the filters differ; ImageMagick's -thumbnail path is about 6x faster than rez; no Go or ImageMagick version or CPU model. Repository archived 2024-05-19.

**Known shortcoming:** Bilinear widens to about 76 taps on downscale (real antialiased work); the harness has no thread control (rez uses GOMAXPROCS goroutines by default) and ignores errors while counting the file; SSE2 only (no AVX2 or NEON); int16 kernel offsets overflow above 32767 px wide (from source, untested); open issue #8 (gamma-space filtering) unanswered; the Converter is not safe for concurrent use.

**How:** It filters the decoded YCbCr planes directly instead of converting to RGBA first (imaging and gift convert), with a separable two-pass resize (vertical, then horizontal) driven by precomputed 14-bit fixed-point int16 kernels. Hot loops are generated SSE2 assembly per tap count (2 to 12, plus a generic N-tap path) built on PMADDWD multiply-accumulate with PUNPCKLBW/PACKUSWB widening and packing; the tests check that the assembly output is bit-identical to the pure-Go loops. Each plane is split into GOMAXPROCS horizontal slices run as goroutines, and a reusable Converter avoids rebuilding kernels and buffers for repeated geometry.

**Use it when:**
- Go services that make thumbnails or scaled copies from JPEGs decoded with image/jpeg and must stay free of cgo; staying in YCbCr skips a full-resolution RGBA conversion.
- Video or frame pipelines in Go that resize many frames of the same size (reuse one Converter per goroutine), including interlaced material and chroma-subsampling changes.
- amd64 servers, where the SSE2 kernels are used; the filter widens on downscale (support divided by the scale factor), so even the bilinear setting is antialiased rather than point-sampled.
- Vendoring a small, dependency-free MIT resizer into a Go codebase that cannot take new upstream maintenance.

**Skip it when:**
- Whenever cgo or an external process is acceptable: in the same i7 table ImageMagick -thumbnail with jpeg:size (0.057 s), the libvips binding (0.070 s), epeg (0.079 s), fastjpeg (0.082 s), OpenCV (0.110 s) and vipsthumbnail (0.115 s) all beat rez (0.349 s).
- Large-reduction JPEG thumbnails: rez needs the full-resolution decode, while DCT-domain downscaling on load (jpeg:size, epeg, fastjpeg) skips most of the decode work.
- arm64 and other non-amd64 targets: only SSE2 amd64 assembly exists (no AVX2, no NEON), so other architectures run the scalar Go loops.
- Colour-accurate work: filtering runs on gamma-encoded 8-bit values (issue #8, open since 2015, unanswered), NRGBA is filtered as packed bytes without premultiplying alpha, and there is no 16-bit or float path.
- Paletted, CMYK, RGBA64 or Gray16 images: anything other than YCbCr, RGBA, NRGBA or Gray returns 'unknown image format' (issue #12 hit this with a PNG).

**Integration:** module · none (Go standard library only) · CI was Go 1.5 to 1.8 (issue #9, 'Cannot build with Go >1.7', closed 2016); no go.mod, so modules use a pseudo-version. fawick/speedtest-resize's go.mod (go 1.26.0) still pins rez at the 2017-07-31 commit, which suggests it builds on current Go; not verified here · amd64 with SSE2 assembly; any other Go target through the pure-Go fallback (scalers_gen.go)

**Vs siblings:** Pick rez only when the program must stay pure Go: if cgo or an external process is allowed, libvips, epeg and OpenCV were 3-6x faster in the same shootout, and fast_image_resize is the stronger SIMD choice in Rust (AVX2 and NEON).

**Gotchas:**
- The destination must be pre-allocated at the target size with the same type and plane layout as the source; YCbCr-to-RGBA or other pack/plane mismatches return an error even though the docs say Convert applies 'any necessary colorspace conversion'.
- One-shot rez.Convert rebuilds kernels and buffers on every call and defaults to GOMAXPROCS goroutines per call; under concurrent request load set ConverterConfig.Threads to 1 and reuse Converters to avoid oversubscription and repeated setup.
- From kernels.go: horizontal kernel offsets are stored as int16 absolute pixel positions, so inputs wider than 32767 px would overflow (slice panic in Go, out-of-range reads in assembly); this was read from the source, not tested.
- Planes smaller than 2 px in either dimension are rejected, and the assembly is disabled for outputs narrower than 16 px (pure-Go path used).

**Status:** Abandoned: last commit 2017-07-31 and archived 2024-05-19 (214 stars, one open issue). It is MIT-licensed with no dependencies, and small enough to vendor (a dozen Go files plus two generated assembly files), but it will get no fixes and has no SIMD outside amd64.

[repo](https://github.com/bamiaux/rez) · [benchmark](https://github.com/fawick/speedtest-resize)

##### sparkyuv  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Archived C++20 Highway-SIMD YUV/RGB converter; ties or beats libyuv on 8-bit decode on Apple M3, loses on encode.

**Beats:** libyuv — Only valid on Apple M3 Pro, as Google Benchmark output from the author against a prebuilt libyuv.a of unknown version and flags, on one JPEG (filirovska.jpeg, not in the repo, size unstated) with no compiler named. 8-bit 4:2:0/4:2:2 decode to RGBA is about 1.32x libyuv (347.9 vs 458.8 us), 4:4:4 is 1.10x, NV12/NV21 tie, and libyuv is 1.37-2.0x faster at encode and 1.21x faster at premultiply. Three claims are not like-for-like: the 1.92-2.12x 10-bit decode lead (different output depth, and byte strides passed as element counts so sparkyuv reads overlapping half-size planes while libyuv reads full ones), and the 1.54x unpremultiply lead, where libyuv has no NEON ARGBUnattenuate row ('TODO(fbarchard): Neon version' in libyuv 1974 planar_functions.cc), so it races libyuv's C fallback.

**Known shortcoming:** README numbers (Apple M3 Pro) match, but the 1.9-2.1x 10-bit wins compare sparkyuv's 10-bit RGBA output against libyuv's 8-bit ARGB path; libyuv is faster on 8-bit encode (2.0x at 4:2:0) and premultiply. The prebuilt libyuv.a version and the test image size are unknown.

**Known shortcoming:** Headline 10-bit decode wins (1.92-2.12x) are a harness bug: the benchmark passes element counts as byte strides on uint16 planes, so sparkyuv reads overlapping half-size planes while libyuv reads full planes, and the output depth differs; unpremultiply 1.54x is NEON against libyuv's C fallback. Valid wins are the 8-bit decodes only (4:2:0 and 4:2:2 1.32x, 4:4:4 1.10x, NV ties); libyuv wins the encodes. Correctness bug in src/YCbCr420-inl.h: the 8-bit 4:2:0 SIMD encoder reloads mSrc instead of the next row, so vertical chroma averaging is a no-op and disagrees with the scalar tail. No tests (CI runs ctest with none defined), no libyuv equality check, NV12/NV21 libyuv calls swapped, libyuv 4:2:2 decode fed 4:2:0 chroma, J422 full range against TV range; depends on the author's Highway fork (widen_mul). Retier-02 corrects the record.

**How:** The kernels are written once against Google Highway (pinned to the author's fork, branch widen_mul) and compiled per SIMD target. 8-bit decode follows libyuv's approach: 6-bit fixed-point coefficients, 16-bit saturating multiply-add, interleaved RGBA stores. 8-bit encode uses 8-bit fixed point with 32-bit WidenMulAccumulate and averages chroma pairs in registers (SumsOf2). The 10/12-bit paths widen to 32-bit lanes and narrow back to 16-bit RGBA, so they skip libyuv's reduction to 8-bit ARGB.

**Use it when:**
- C++ code that needs YUV matrices libyuv lacks (YCgCo-Re/Ro, YIQ, YDbDr, YDzDx, BT.2020 CL) or 10/12-bit YUV to 16-bit-per-channel RGBA.
- 8-bit YCbCr 4:2:0/4:2:2 to RGBA decode on arm64 (NEON), where the README shows about 1.3x over libyuv I420/I422ToABGR on an M3 Pro.
- Targets Highway covers (SVE/SVE2, RVV, POWER, Z, WASM) where you want one portable SIMD codebase rather than per-ISA assembly.
- Projects that will vendor and freeze the code, since upstream is archived.

**Skip it when:**
- 8-bit RGBA to YUV encode: libyuv is 2.0x faster to 4:2:0 and 1.37x faster to 4:2:2 in the project's own table, and libyuv also wins premultiply (1.21x).
- x86: there are no x86 numbers, and the README says 8-bit decode 'should be considered same' as libyuv off arm64.
- When you need output that matches libyuv bit for bit or a tested library: the repo has no tests (CI runs ctest, but CMakeLists.txt defines none), and nothing compares output with libyuv.
- When chroma downsampling quality or siting matters: the subsampling filter is fixed and cannot be turned off, and the 8-bit 4:2:0 SIMD encoder skips vertical averaging (see gotchas).
- When you need maintenance or bug fixes: archived 10 Feb 2025, last commit 14 Jul 2024, 0 issues ever filed.

**Integration:** static lib · Google Highway, cloned by deps.sh from the author's fork (github.com/awxkee/highway, branch widen_mul) into ./highway; the benchmark/tools targets also need libjpeg, Google Benchmark and a prebuilt libyuv.a placed in the repo root (not shipped) · C++20, CMake 3.22 · Highway targets: x86 SSE2 to AVX-512 (AVX3/AVX3_DL/ZEN4/SPR), Arm NEON/SVE/SVE2, POWER8-10, IBM Z14/Z15, RISC-V RVV, WASM. HWY_SCALAR is disabled. Apple builds use static dispatch only (HWY_COMPILE_ONLY_STATIC); other platforms use runtime dispatch.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over yuvutils-rs (same author, Rust, active, with Fast/Balanced/Professional precision modes) only if you must stay in C++ and want its unusual matrices or 16-bit RGBA output. For plain 8-bit BT.601/709 conversion, libyuv (faster encode, maintained) or the tiny xxYUV are safer choices.

**Gotchas:**
- Strides are in bytes even for uint16_t planes: the YCbCrP16 kernels advance a uint8_t pointer by yStride/uStride/vStride. The project's own 10-bit benchmark passes element counts (yPlaneStride = inWidth), so it runs on overlapping rows.
- Correctness bug in the 8-bit 4:2:0 SIMD encoder (src/YCbCr420-inl.h): its 'next row' load calls LoadRGBA(du8, mSrc, ...) on the same row, so vertical chroma averaging does nothing and chroma comes from even rows only. The scalar tail does average 2x2, so the two paths disagree. This contradicts the README's 'bi-linear scaling is automatically applied'.
- The Release-only -O3 is the sole optimisation flag. The Dockerfile runs plain 'cmake -G Ninja .' with no build type, which gives an unoptimised build, and it does not run deps.sh.
- YCgCo-Re/Ro 8-bit needs 16-bit storage and is always full range. 4:2:0/4:2:2/NV inputs reject null U/V planes.

**Status:** Abandoned: archived 10 Feb 2025, last commit 14 Jul 2024, 9 stars. Apache-2.0 (BSD-3-Clause file from the same author also present), so it is copyable, but vendoring also means carrying the author's Highway fork and fixing the 4:2:0 encoder bug yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/awxkee/sparkyuv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/awxkee/sparkyuv)

##### TinyScaler  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Python/Cython float32 RGBA image downscaler with SSE C kernels; beats Pillow by skipping antialiasing, loses to OpenCV bilinear.

**Beats:** Pillow resize (bilinear) and OpenCV cv2.resize (area filter); scikit-image also timed — The project's scripts (examples/benchmark_bilinear.py and benchmark_area.py, reachable in the author's original 222464/TinyScaler repo, whose scaler.c matches the 1.2.8 sdist) convert the NASA 4928x3279 PNG to float32 RGBA and resize it to 852x567 100 times with OpenCV set to one thread, on an AMD 1950X. Bilinear: TinyScaler 0.797 s vs OpenCV INTER_LINEAR 0.487 s (OpenCV 1.64x faster). Area: TinyScaler 4.35 s vs OpenCV INTER_AREA 8.12 s (1.87x, derived from page data), but on a mis-weighted kernel. Pillow (12.67 s) did antialiased resizing of uint8 RGBA, skimage (164.45 s) produced a transposed, Gaussian-prefiltered output, and compiler, flags and library versions are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Repository gone from github.com (page and raw 404; deprecated 2025-08-11 per a search snippet), so the numbers come from the PyPI 1.2.8 description and the C source from the sdist. The 15.9x against Pillow is not equal work (2x2-tap bilinear, no antialiasing); OpenCV bilinear is 1.6x faster; the area kernel uses approximate weights.

**Known shortcoming:** Corrections (retier-28): the author's original repo 222464/TinyScaler holds the benchmark scripts, so the harness is reachable. The 206x against scikit-image is invalid (skimage was called as resize(img, (852, 567)), a transposed output with default Gaussian anti-aliasing) and Pillow got uint8 RGBA; the fair float32 RGBA pair shows OpenCV bilinear 1.64x faster. The area kernel is mis-weighted (second weight term always 1, so a 2x downscale is an overlapping 3x3 mean) and its 1.87x win runs that kernel; bilinear reads out of bounds for 1-pixel sources; SIMD only on GCC or Clang x86_64 or 32-bit arm (aarch64, Apple Silicon and MSVC wheels scalar); the GIL is held.

**How:** Each output pixel is one 128-bit SSE vector (NEON on 32-bit ARM) holding all four RGBA float channels. Bilinear is a 2x2 point-sampled lerp with no antialiasing, so its filter support does not grow with the scale factor. 'area' sums a box of source pixels with approximate edge weights. The speedup over Pillow comes from doing far fewer taps than Pillow's support-scaled convolution. There is no separable pass, no precomputed coefficient table and no threading, and the plain C file is built with Python's default extension flags.

**Use it when:**
- RL observation preprocessing (Gymnasium/PettingZoo style) where frames are already float32 RGBA and you want to avoid an opencv-python dependency.
- Large non-integer downscale ratios (the benchmark used about 5.8x) where aliasing is acceptable and you need nearest or bilinear speed within about 1.6x of OpenCV.
- Tight loops that reuse a preallocated float32 (h, w, 4) dst buffer; that only avoids allocations when the input is also float32 RGBA.
- Linux or Intel macOS x86_64 builds with GCC or Clang, the only 64-bit targets where the SSE path is compiled.

**Skip it when:**
- Quality-sensitive downscaling: bilinear has no antialiasing, and 'area' mis-weights pixels (at exactly 2x it averages a 3x3 block that overlaps the next output's block).
- Raw speed when OpenCV is acceptable: cv2.resize INTER_LINEAR was 1.64x faster in the project's own run. Sibling fast_image_resize reports 3.53 ms (AVX2, u8 RGB, antialiased convolution, different machine) for the same NASA 4928x3279 to 852x567 job, against TinyScaler's 7.97 ms per call.
- uint8 RGB pipelines: every call expands to float32 RGBA (16 bytes per pixel instead of 3) and converts back by truncation.
- Apple Silicon, Linux aarch64 and Windows: the SIMD code is guarded by `__x86_64__` (GCC/Clang only, not MSVC) or `__arm__` (32-bit ARM only), so the arm64 macOS slice, aarch64 builds and win_amd64 wheels run the scalar fallback.
- Anything needing a maintained dependency: it was deprecated on 2025-08-11, the Farama GitHub repo now returns 404, and wheels stop at CPython 3.12.

**Integration:** Python extension module (Cython wrapper over one C file, src/scaler.c plus scaler.h); the C file can be dropped into a C or C++ project · numpy>=1.21.0 for the Python package; the C core needs only libc and libm · Python >= 3.8 (wheels for CPython 3.8 to 3.12); building from the sdist needs Cython, setuptools and a C compiler · Wheels for Linux x86_64 (manylinux2014), macOS (universal2 and x86_64) and Windows amd64. SSE path only with GCC/Clang on x86_64, NEON path only on 32-bit ARM (setup.py adds -mfpu=neon there); everything else uses scalar C.

**Vs siblings:** Pick TinyScaler only when you need a dependency-light Python wheel on float32 RGBA frames and can accept aliasing. OpenCV is faster for bilinear and has a correct INTER_AREA, and Pillow-SIMD and Lycon give antialiased or OpenCV-grade resizing from Python. From C, C++ or Rust, stb-image-resize-opt or fast_image_resize are faster and filter correctly.

**Gotchas:**
- Area weights are wrong. In scale_area_4f32 the second weight term tests area_y == src_upper_y, which the loop never reaches, so it is always 1. Every pixel therefore gets weight 1 to 2 instead of its 0 to 1 coverage, and the upper bound includes the pixel at floor(upper)+1. A 1-D simulation of the code gives a uniform 3-tap average per output at 8 to 4 (exact: 2 taps). At the benchmark's 4928 to 852 ratio, an edge pixel with 3.7% coverage gets 9.2% of the weight.
- Bilinear always loads the right and lower neighbours (p01, p10) even when their weight is zero, so a source 1 pixel wide or 1 pixel high is read past the row or the buffer. Since 0 x NaN = NaN, garbage can reach the output. 'area' falls back to this bilinear path whenever either axis is upscaled.
- `size` is (width, height) while arrays are (height, width, channels). uint8 results are truncated by astype rather than rounded. For uint8 input with 1 or 3 channels the wrapper returns a sliced, non-contiguous view, which scale() rejects ('Input image must be contiguous') if you feed it back in.
- Benchmark harness flaws on the baseline side: Pillow received uint8 RGBA and ran its antialiased BILINEAR, and skimage was called as resize(img, (852, 567)). skimage reads that as (rows, cols), so it produced a transposed 852x567x4 output, and its default anti_aliasing (True when downsampling, per the v0.19.3 source) adds a Gaussian prefilter. The 206x skimage ratio is not a valid comparison.

**Status:** Deprecated by Farama on 2025-08-11 (search snippet) and gone from the Farama GitHub org. The last release is 1.2.8 (2024-08-02); the code is MIT and a single 448-line C file that is easy to vendor, but fix the area weights and the edge reads first.

[repo](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/TinyScaler) · [benchmark](https://github.com/222464/TinyScaler/tree/master/examples)

##### tir (tiny image resize, in tinyexr)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-C11 separable float resizer in tinyexr's tools/resize; 2.2-3.6x tinyexr's own resizer, roughly level with SSE2-built stb_image_resize2.

**Beats:** stb_image_resize2 (successor of stb_image_resize, matched filter, float32 path); also tinyexr's own exr_resize_float — Author-run make resize-bench on one Zen 2 core (Ryzen 9 3950X), compiler unnamed (system cc, -O2 -g), Mitchell 4-tap, f32 random data, clamp edges, straight alpha: tir AVX2 reached 295/78/7.6 MP/s on 4-channel 2x up/2x down/7.3x down versus 266/73/6.4 for stb_image_resize2 built at SSE2 and 135/30/2.2 for tinyexr's exr_resize_float; on 1-channel stb2 led the two 2x cases (1279 vs 1218, 365 vs 334) and tir led 7.3x down (27.3 vs 25.4). The stb2 comparison is ISA-mismatched, so the solid result is the 2.2-3.6x gain over exr_resize_float; the win over stb2 is unproven against an AVX2 build of stb2.

**Known shortcoming:** tir (tiny image resize inside tinyexr) downgraded A to C: the resize-bench recipe builds stb_image_resize2 at SSE2 (-O2 -g, no -mavx2/-mfma) while tir dispatches AVX2+FMA at runtime, so the 7-19% lead is smaller than the 10-40% plus about 12% that stb2's own docs attribute to AVX2; compiler unstated ($(CC)) and the stb2 header version unpinned. Work matches (Mitchell B=C=1/3, clamped edges, straight alpha, f32); the 1-channel 2x downscale is 0.92x, not within 5%.

**Known shortcoming:** The lead over stb_image_resize2 is unproven: resize-bench builds stb2 at -O2 -g with SSE2 only (CFLAGS ignored) while the stb2 header says its AVX2 build is 20-50% faster, more than tir's 7-19% lead; the solid result is 2.2-3.6x over tinyexr's own exr_resize_float. Fuzz-found WRAP heap overflow (94405e1) and a threaded-band deadlock (8c631a7) were fixed on 2026-07-02; the lazy global kernel table is set up without atomics, undocumented.

**How:** Two-pass separable convolution over precomputed, edge-folded, zero-padded coefficient tables, so inner loops have no edge branches; pass order (horizontal-first or vertical-first) is chosen by a multiply-count cost model. The AVX2+FMA kernels use independent accumulator chains: the 1-channel horizontal pass computes 4 outputs at once and reduces them with one 4x4 transpose, and the 4-channel pass packs two RGBA output pixels per 256-bit register for narrow windows (commit fdf7b0d took 4-channel 2x up from 275 to 295 MP/s). Kernels are compiled with __attribute__((target)) and selected by CPUID at run time, so a baseline-ISA build still runs AVX2 on capable CPUs.

**Use it when:**
- HDR / float32 or half-float texture pipelines in C or C++ that need resampling without clamping, with optional anti-ringing plus clamp_min = 0 for a hard no-negative-pixel guarantee
- Normal-map or height-map mip and LOD generation, where renormalization after filtering and endpoint-exact grid-vertex registration matter
- Distributing one portable x86-64 binary: tir dispatches AVX2+FMA at run time, while stb_image_resize2 only uses AVX/AVX2 when the including TU is compiled with -mavx2 (or STBIR_AVX2), so in a default -O2 build tir is 1.07-1.19x faster on 4-channel Mitchell (Ryzen 9 3950X, page data)
- Streaming or memory-bounded resizing (tiles, scanline EXR decode) through push_row/pull_row with a single arena allocation
- Replacing tinyexr's own exr_resize_float, which tir beats 2.2-3.6x on every measured Mitchell shape

**Skip it when:**
- If you can build stb_image_resize2 with -mavx2 -mfma: no published run compares against an AVX2 build of stb2, and stb2's header says AVX is 10-40% faster than SSE2 plus about 12% more for AVX2, which exceeds tir's 7-19% 4-channel lead
- 1-channel 2x Mitchell resizes, where the SSE2 stb2 build is already faster in the README table (0.95x up, 0.92x down)
- 8-bit sRGB photo thumbnailing at scale: tir always filters in f32, has no gamma-aware/linear-light conversion option in the header, and was only benchmarked on f32 random data; libvips, Pillow-SIMD or fast_image_resize target that workload
- Projects that need a stable, separately versioned dependency: tir is version 0.1.0, about three months old, lives inside the tinyexr tree rather than its own repository, and its tools/resize code last changed 2026-07-05
- MSVC-only or non-x86/non-ARM targets that want SIMD: x86 kernels rely on GCC/Clang target attributes (MSVC compiles intrinsics without them), NEON is compile-time on AArch64, and other ISAs get the scalar path

**Integration:** source-drop (tools/resize/src: about 12 .c files plus include/tir.h; make resize-lib builds build/libtir.a) · none for the library (libm); the CLI and benchmark link libtinyexr3.a for EXR I/O; optional C11 <threads.h> or pthreads for -DTIR_ENABLE_THREADS · C11 compiler (tested gcc/clang; header is C++-safe via extern "C"); AVX2 kernels need GCC/Clang target attributes for runtime dispatch · x86-64 (SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2+FMA+F16C runtime dispatch), AArch64 NEON, SVE behind an HWCAP gate on Linux, scalar fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick tir over stb_image_resize2 (and the stb-image-resize-opt fork) when you need HDR, normal-map or height-map aware float resizing, streaming rows, or runtime AVX2 dispatch in a portable binary; pick zimg for C++ float resizing with colorspace conversion, and fast_image_resize or libvips for 8-bit photo resizing, where tir has no published numbers.

**Gotchas:**
- The README's stb2 column comes from make resize-bench STB=1, which compiles stb_image_resize2.h at -O2 -g with no -m flags (the recipe ignores CFLAGS), so stb2 ran its SSE2 kernels while tir ran AVX2+FMA; the stb header is not vendored or version-pinned.
- SIMD kernels reassociate sums (multiple accumulators, FMA), so output differs from the scalar path by a few ULP; set deterministic = 1 for bit-identical output across ISAs and thread counts, at scalar speed.
- Defaults differ from stb2: premultiplied-alpha filtering for 4 channels and no clamping (Mitchell can undershoot below 0 on HDR edges unless antiring/clamp_min are set).
- EDGE_WRAP on the y axis buffers the whole image; a heap overflow on WRAP/REFLECT axes with trimmed windows (found by fuzzing, repro 28x10 to 26x2 heightmap) was fixed in 94405e1 on 2026-07-02, along with a threaded-band deadlock (8c631a7).

**Status:** Active (tinyexr last commit 2026-09-07, tools/resize last changed 2026-07-05), BSD-3-Clause and copyable; tir itself is 0.1.0, written July 2026 with an AI co-author, with unit tests against an independent double-precision reference, ASan/UBSan/TSan targets and a libFuzzer corpus.

[repo](https://github.com/syoyo/tinyexr) · [benchmark](https://github.com/syoyo/tinyexr/blob/release/tools/resize/README.md)

##### xxYUV  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Small MIT C++ BT.709 RGB/YUV 4:2:0 converter (SSE2/SSSE3/AVX2/NEON) whose README claims to beat libyuv and Accelerate.

**Beats:** libyuv (version not stated) and Apple Accelerate — First-party README tables give microseconds per conversion for xxYUV against libyuv (version and matrix not stated) and Apple Accelerate on an Apple M1 (NEON, plus x86 rows presumably under Rosetta) and an i7-8700B (AVX2): about 1.2-1.55x faster encode and 1.3x (AVX2) to 3.2x (M1 NEON) faster decode than libyuv. Compiler, flags, image size and pixel layout are not stated and the harness is not public; because only the 4-channel paths are vectorised, the SIMD rows must be RGBA/BGRA, and the microsecond scale implies a small cache-resident image (inference).

**Known shortcoming:** First-party README tables only (Apple M1 and i7-8700B; decode up to 3.2x derived from page data); the linked xxImGui harness has no YUV code at head, so nothing reproduces the numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Output bugs by code reading (not proven behind the README numbers): the RGBA and YUVA SIMD loops continue past the scalar tail, so columns after the last 16-pixel (NEON, SSE2) or 32-pixel (AVX2) block are never written (24 columns on a 1080-wide AVX2 frame); the NEON video-range decode uses a non-saturating vshrn_n_u16 so luma 236-255 wraps to 0-22; scalar rgb2yuv applies the R coefficient to byte 2, so the RGB24 encode swaps R and B against the SIMD path; strideV is ignored (strideU passed twice). SIMD exists only for 4-channel data, so the README's SIMD rows must be RGBA; the target attributes are Clang-only, so GCC CPUID dispatch is broken; BT.709 8-bit 4:2:0 only; the AVX-512 code is never instantiated; the benchmark harness was still not found.

**How:** Each converter is one template instantiated per (channels, swizzle, interleaved, U-first, range) combination and compiled several times from the same .inl file with HAVE_NEON/SSE2/SSSE3/AVX2 defined, then picked once by CPUID into a function-local static pointer. Kernels process two rows at a time with 8-bit fixed-point coefficients: decode uses 16-bit mulhi (x86) or 8-bit widening multiplies (NEON_FAST, always on for ARM), encode uses maddubs+hadd (SSSE3/AVX2) or widening multiply-accumulate with pairwise adds for 2x2 chroma averaging (NEON), and results are interleaved with unpack transposes or vld4/vst4. Precision is traded for fewer, narrower multiplies.

**Use it when:**
- Converting RGBA/BGRA frames to or from I420/NV12/NV21 with BT.709 coefficients when the width is a multiple of 32 (AVX2) or 16 (SSE2/NEON).
- Apple Silicon or AVX2 desktops where you want a few-file MIT source drop instead of building libyuv.
- Preview, thumbnail or GPU-upload paths where a 1-3 code-value difference from a reference converter is acceptable.
- Projects built with Clang or MSVC, where the per-function target attributes (Clang) or MSVC's intrinsic rules let the runtime dispatch work as written.

**Skip it when:**
- RGB24 (3-channel) data: every SIMD loop runs only for 4 channels, so 3-channel conversion is the scalar loop on all CPUs, and the scalar encoder applies the R coefficient to byte 2 (the SIMD encoders and the decoder treat byte 0 as R), so RGB24 encode swaps R and B unless the swizzle flag is inverted.
- Widths that are not a multiple of the SIMD block: for 4-channel and YUVA conversions the code skips the scalar tail ('if (componentRGB == 4) continue;' after the SIMD loop), leaving the rightmost (halfWidth mod 8, or mod 16 on AVX2) x2 columns unwritten, e.g. 24 columns of a 1080-wide frame on AVX2.
- Video-range content with super-whites on ARM: the NEON decode narrows (Y-16)*149>>7 with a non-saturating vshrn_n_u16, so luma 236-255 wraps to 0-22 (near black); the x86 paths keep 16 bits and do not wrap.
- Anything beyond 8-bit 4:2:0 BT.709: no BT.601 or BT.2020, no 4:2:2/4:4:4, no 10-bit, no scaling or rotation.
- Code that needs maintenance or tests: last commit 20 Oct 2021, no tests in the repository, and the linked benchmark harness cannot be found.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (Apple Accelerate is only a benchmark comparison; the AMX path uses undocumented Apple instructions taken from dougallj's reverse-engineering gists) · C++20 for the designated-initializer convenience wrappers in yuv2rgb.h, rgb2yuv.h and yuv.h (define xxYUV_DEPRECATED to drop them); Clang or MSVC for working runtime dispatch; no build files are provided · x86/x86-64 (SSE2 baseline, SSSE3 and AVX2 chosen at run time by CPUID), 32/64-bit ARM with NEON, Apple M1 AMX for YU12 decode; other targets get the scalar loop. AVX-512 kernels exist in yuv2rgb.inl but are never instantiated.

**Vs siblings:** Pick xxYUV over libyuv, sparkyuv or yuvutils-rs only when you need a tiny MIT C++ drop for BT.709 RGBA/NV12 on M1 or AVX2 with 32-pixel-aligned widths; sparkyuv covers 4:4:4 to 4:1:0, NV16/NV24 and many matrices, yuvutils-rs is the Rust option with like-for-like rows against libyuv, and libyuv stays the safe default for odd sizes, RGB24 and other matrices.

**Gotchas:**
- The planar entry points pass strideU twice (converter(..., strideY, strideU, strideU, ...)), so a caller-supplied strideV is ignored in yuv2rgb_yu12/yv12 and rgb2yuv_yu12/yv12.
- Under GCC the target-attribute macro expands to nothing (it is defined only for __llvm__), so the AVX2/SSSE3 kernels need -mavx2/-mssse3 on the whole file, which also lets the compiler use AVX2 in the fallback paths and defeats the CPUID dispatch (inference from the macro).
- Outputs differ by platform: NEON_FAST uses 6-7 bit chroma coefficients (full-range B gain 1.844 vs 1.863), x86 decode scales by coefficient*255/256, and the SSSE3/AVX2 encoders halve the luma weights so full-range white encodes to Y=253 (254 on NEON and scalar, both truncating).
- Odd widths or heights lose the last column or row (loops run over width>>1 and height>>1).

**Status:** Abandoned since October 2021 (64 commits, 2 closed questions, no PRs, no tests) but MIT-licensed and about fifteen small files, so it is easy to vendor if you first fix the tail, strideV, video-range wrap and RGB24 channel-order bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/metarutaiga/xxYUV) · [benchmark](https://github.com/metarutaiga/xxYUV/blob/master/README.md)

##### yuv2rgb (descampsa)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Two-file C99 SSE2 converter between planar YUV420 (also NV12/NV21) and RGB24 that roughly doubles old libswscale's speed.

**Beats:** FFmpeg libswscale 3.0.0 (MMX path) — Author's run of the public test_yuv_rgb harness (clock() over 100 conversions of one 4096x2160 BT.601 frame, CMake Release build with GCC 4.9.2, Core i7-5500U): yuv2rgb SSE2 0.607 s with streaming stores and 0.704 s with plain stores vs libswscale 3.0.0 about 1.22 s (about 2x) and IPP 9.0.1 0.636 s. rgb2yuv SSE2 0.641/0.677 s vs swscale 3.39 s (about 5.3x, probably swscale's generic filtered-chroma path, not an equivalent converter) and IPP 0.579-0.594 s. Each frame touches about 40 MB (13.3 MB of YUV plus 26.5 MB of RGB, derived from page data), so the loop streams from DRAM rather than running cache-warm, and outputs are never compared across methods.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on the repo's own test_yuv_rgb.c (gcc 4.9.2, i7-5500U, CMake Release -O3 -DNDEBUG, 2015-era). The 5.3x rgb2yuv figure is likely against swscale's generic RGB24 path (filtered chroma, no unscaled fast path), not like-for-like; the yuv2rgb 2x is the fairer number. Outputs were never compared against swscale's.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered A to C (retier-08): README timings are from 2017 code whose SSE2 yuv2rgb path overflowed int16 for luma 236 and above (pixels decoded black, issue #12, fixed 2022-02-09 with a same-cost instruction swap) and were never re-run. The 'aligned' path's edge is _mm_stream_si128 non-temporal stores without an sfence, not alignment; the plain-store SSE2 path is slower than IPP 9.0.1; the test streams about 40 MB per frame from DRAM. Width below 31 wraps the uint32 loop (out-of-bounds); rgb32_yuv420_std still uses cb_factor for V at HEAD (issue #15 fix missed the RGBA path); unconditional emmintrin.h so no ARM build; swscale 3.0.0 is likely Libav 11 (Debian 8).

**How:** The SSE2 kernels process 32 pixels across two rows per step. Chroma is handled once per 2x2 block (nearest-sample replication when decoding, a plain 2x2 sum then >>2 when encoding), and all arithmetic is 16-bit fixed point (_mm_mullo_epi16 with 6-8 fractional bits) instead of swscale's higher-precision filter path. RGB24 is interleaved and de-interleaved with chains of byte unpack/pack shuffles (rgb.txt in the repo explains the scheme). The aligned (_sse) variants write with _mm_stream_si128 non-temporal stores, and the unaligned (_sseu) variants use ordinary _mm_storeu_si128.

**Use it when:**
- You decode or capture planar I420, NV12 or NV21 frames on x86 and need RGB24 output with no FFmpeg or libyuv dependency.
- Large frames (HD to 4K) streamed straight to a file, encoder or GPU upload, where the _sse variant's non-temporal stores avoid read-for-ownership traffic on a destination far larger than the CPU cache.
- RGB24 or RGBA to I420 for an encoder input path when box-filtered chroma (2x2 average) is acceptable.
- Codebases that want a small BSD-3-Clause source drop they can read and modify in an afternoon.

**Skip it when:**
- ARM/aarch64 or any non-x86 target: yuv_rgb.c includes <emmintrin.h> unconditionally and there is no NEON path, so it does not compile there without editing.
- You need AVX2/AVX-512 speed: the code is SSE2 only, and Intel IPP 9.0.1 already beat it on rgb2yuv (0.579-0.594 s vs 0.641-0.677 s) and matched it on yuv2rgb in the author's own run.
- Quality-sensitive work: chroma is nearest-sample upsampled and box-downsampled, and the fixed-point math truncates instead of rounding, so output is not bit-exact with libswscale or IPP.
- High bit depth, 4:2:2/4:4:4, BGR/ARGB output or scaling: only 8-bit 4:2:0 to or from RGB24 (plus RGBA input) is implemented.
- Images narrower than 32 pixels with the SSE functions (see gotchas), or anything that needs an actively maintained dependency (last commit 2022-02-15).

**Integration:** source-drop · none (SSE2 intrinsics; the test program optionally links libswscale and Intel IPP) · C99 compiler with SSE2 intrinsics (GCC, Clang; MSVC since the Feb 2022 commit); the README numbers used GCC 4.9.2 · x86 and x86-64 with SSE2; the _std functions are portable C, but the unconditional <emmintrin.h> include must be removed for other architectures

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libyuv, xxYUV or sparkyuv only when a two-file SSE2 C source drop matters more than speed or coverage, since those carry AVX2/NEON paths and many more formats. Against FFmpeg's libswscale it wins on same-size I420<->RGB24 on old x86 at the cost of precision and features.

**Gotchas:**
- The SSE functions leave the last width%32 columns unconverted and the C and SSE functions leave the last row and column untouched for odd sizes (documented in yuv_rgb.h; open issue #13); the caller must convert the tail itself. The SSE loops use uint32_t `x < width-31`, which wraps for widths below 31 and runs past the buffers.
- The _sse variants use non-temporal stores and never issue _mm_sfence: hand the buffer to another thread only after a fence, and expect a cold cache when you read the RGB right after converting. Much of the README's aligned vs unaligned gap (0.607 vs 0.704 s) comes from these stores, not from alignment. At 4096 width the harness's malloc'd 'unaligned' buffers are 16-byte aligned too, and swscale and IPP time the same on both buffer sets.
- Bugs: the SSE2 yuv2rgb code timed in the README (commit 1fc2be8, Sept 2017; the timings have not changed since) overflowed 16 bits for BT.601/709 input with Y >= 236, so those pixels came out black (issue #12). It was fixed on 2022-02-09 (e805bf2: srai to srli and sub_epi8 to subs_epu8). rgb32_yuv420_std still scales V with cb_factor at HEAD, the same bug issue #15 fixed only in the RGB24 path, so RGBA-input chroma from the C path is desaturated.
- yuv_rgb.c defines a global non-static `uint8_t clamp(int16_t)`, which can collide with other `clamp` symbols at link time. CMakeLists.txt adds -Werror globally and builds only the test program, so vendor yuv_rgb.c/.h rather than add_subdirectory.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-02-15 (191 stars, 62 forks, not archived) but BSD-3-Clause and about 1,300 lines of C, so easy to vendor and patch. The README's libswscale 3.0.0 is a 2014-era build (version number consistent with the Libav 11 packages in Debian 8, and the README uses avconv), and modern swscale has newer SIMD paths that would narrow the gap.

[repo](https://github.com/descampsa/yuv2rgb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/descampsa/yuv2rgb)

##### yuvutils-rs  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust SIMD YUV/RGB conversion crate (yuv) that matches or beats libyuv by 1.1-2x on NEON and Linux x86.

**Beats:** libyuv built from source by the yuv-sys 0.3.x crate (livekit/rust-sdks, required as 0.3.7 in app/Cargo.toml); libyuv commit not stated — These are first-party Criterion runs (500 samples, 7 s) on one 1997x1331 JPEG against libyuv built by the yuv-sys crate's cc build (0.3.7 vendors libyuv 1886). On an M3 (NEON), 8-bit decode to RGB/RGBA is 1.64-1.95x libyuv and RGB to 4:2:0 encode is 1.20x. On Linux AVX2 (m4.large) and AVX-512 (c5.large), CPU models unstated, the lead is 1.07-1.89x and libyuv wins several rows. The Windows i9-14900HX column and the NEON 10-bit rows are not fair comparisons: libyuv there runs C or SSSE3 row code, as the measurement notes explain.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). Downgraded to C: the headline NV12 2.3x is not like-for-like (the libyuv row rs_NV21ToABGR writes 4 bytes per pixel against 3-byte RGB); like-for-like rows are 1.07-1.64x on NV12 and 1.1-2x elsewhere (derived), libyuv wins several x86 rows, and the Windows libyuv build was likely a partial-SIMD build. Issue #144 open.

**Known shortcoming:** README tables (Nov 2024 to Jan 2025, yuv-sys 0.3.7 = libyuv 1886): the Windows column is invalid because cc builds libyuv with cl.exe and libyuv 1886 on x64 MSVC has SSSE3 rows only for I422/I444ToARGB (everything else C); the NEON 10-bit 2x is SIMD against C (no I210ToARGBRow_NEON in 1886); the RGB to YUV 4:2:0 benches behind the 1.20x encode headline are commented out at HEAD (app/benches/yuv8/main.rs lines 128-344). No output comparison against libyuv; open #144 (SIMD versus scalar off by 2); fuzz crate skips sse and avx paths; undated nightly toolchain. Valid wins: 8-bit NEON and Linux x86 rows at 1.07-1.95x. Retier-02 corrects the record.

**How:** Each format has hand-written row kernels for NEON (with RDM vqrdmulh and optional i8mm), SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512BW/VBMI (nightly) and WASM simd128. x86 picks a kernel at runtime with is_x86_feature_detected; aarch64 checks for RDM at runtime. Planar decoding runs 13-bit fixed-point arithmetic with rounding shifts, which is more precise than libyuv's 6-bit coefficients, and 4:2:0/4:2:2 decoding uses dedicated 422 kernels that reuse each chroma sample for two pixels. Encoding offers a libyuv-precision Fast mode, a default higher-precision Balanced mode and a Professional mode.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code (AVIF/HEIF/video pipelines) that wants libyuv-class speed without linking C. It is a pure crate with no build script, and at 4.27M downloads it is widely used.
- 8-bit YUV 4:2:0/4:2:2/NV12 to RGB/RGBA on Apple silicon or other aarch64, where the README shows 1.6-1.95x over libyuv's NEON rows.
- 10/12/14/16-bit formats (I010/I210/I410, P010/P210/P016) to 16-bit or F16/AR30 RGB, which libyuv covers only partly.
- Sharp YUV encoding, YCgCo-R, or a choice between libyuv-equivalent and higher-precision encoding.

**Skip it when:**
- C++ projects that cannot add a Rust FFI layer: the crate has no C header or C ABI.
- x86 workloads dominated by 4:4:4 or 4:0:0 decode, or by RGBA to 4:2:0/4:2:2 encode on AVX-512: libyuv wins or ties several of these rows in the README.
- Pipelines that need bit-identical output across platforms: issue #144 (open, 2 Oct 2026) reports the AVX2/SSE kernels differing from the scalar path by up to 2 levels on 29-35% of samples, so wasm and x86 builds decode the same AVIF differently.
- When you must reproduce the published numbers exactly: the tables are from Nov 2024 to Jan 2025 (git blame), the crate has since moved to 0.8.19, and the harness no longer runs some rows.

**Integration:** crate · num-traits; optional rayon (feature rayon) and fast_transpose (feature geometry). The benchmarks also use yuv-sys (libyuv built from source), image and criterion. · Rust 1.82 (rust-version). The nightly_avx512, nightly_i8mm and nightly_f16 features need a nightly compiler, and the repo's rust-toolchain.toml selects an undated nightly. · x86/x86-64 (SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512BW/VBMI with nightly; runtime dispatch), aarch64 NEON (RDM runtime-detected, i8mm opt-in), wasm32 with simd128 enabled at compile time; scalar fallback elsewhere. Big-endian YUV via the big_endian feature.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over sparkyuv (same author's archived C++ predecessor) for anything new: it is maintained, has more formats and has a precision knob. Pick xxYUV or libyuv itself when you need a C/C++ library without a Rust toolchain or FFI glue.

**Gotchas:**
- The x86 SIMD kernels have shipped wrong output before. #92 (yuyv422_to_yuv420 broken with SSE/AVX), #97 (AVX rgba_to_yuv400 black vertical lines) and #130 (SSE 16-bit bilinear wrong chroma, i414 panics) are all fixed. The fuzz crate builds yuv with default-features = false and without sse/avx/rdm, so those kernels are not fuzzed by default; the fuzzers check only for panics and the alpha value, not against a reference.
- The default YuvConversionMode is Balanced, not libyuv-equivalent. Fast (libyuv precision) and Professional exist only when the fast_mode/professional_mode features are enabled.
- AVX-512 needs both the nightly_avx512 feature and a nightly compiler. Without them, x86 tops out at AVX2 even on AVX-512 hardware.
- Unit tests check round trips within a per-mode tolerance (for example max_diff of 3 levels); nothing in the repo compares output with libyuv.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 17 Sep 2026, 1,062 commits, 126 stars, 21 forks; crate yuv 0.8.19 with 4.27M downloads), dual BSD-3-Clause OR Apache-2.0, so it is copyable, but only from Rust or through an FFI shim you write.

[repo](https://github.com/awxkee/yuvutils-rs) · [benchmark](https://github.com/awxkee/yuvutils-rs/blob/master/README.md)

##### zimg  `C++`  `WTFPL`  `active`  `Tier C`

C++ library for scaling, colourspace and bit-depth conversion of video frames; its 2018 README shows about 2x FFmpeg 4.0.2's filters.

**Beats:** FFmpeg 4.0.2 filters (README column label 'swscale 4.0.2'): the swscale scale filter for the Lanczos resize and the libavfilter colorspace filter for the BT.709 to BT.2020 conversion — The README table (added 22 Sep 2018, z.lib 2.8) times an FHD-to-UHD Lanczos resize at 7.7 against 15.2 ms (i7-8565U) and 10.8 against 22.2 ms (Xeon Platinum 8176) against FFmpeg 4.0.2's scale filter, and a BT.709-to-BT.2020 conversion at 8.3 against 17.5 and 11.5 against 25.6 ms against libavfilter's colorspace filter, about 2x, with no compiler, flags, pixel formats, thread counts or zimg command given. The repo's timing tools cannot reproduce the FFmpeg side's formats as given: resizeapp handles only greyscale or 4:4:4 (float by default), colorspaceapp only 4:4:4 float, and graphapp times zero-filled frames, against the FFmpeg commands' yuv420p and yuv420p10 (derived from code).

**Known shortcoming:** README numbers date from 2018 (z.lib 2.8 vs FFmpeg 4.0.2); the second row's baseline is FFmpeg's colorspace filter, not swscale; the testapp timing tools exist but no compiler, flags or command lines are published. The swscale comparison exists only in a forum.doom9.org search snippet (blocked here). WTFPL licence, treated as public-domain-equivalent (copyable).

**Known shortcoming:** The in-repo timing apps cannot reproduce the FFmpeg-side formats: resizeapp runs grey or 4:4:4 float by default, colorspaceapp 4:4:4 float and graphapp times zero-filled frames, while the FFmpeg side is yuv420p and yuv420p10; AVX-512 engages only with ZIMG_CPU_AUTO_64B and the chroma filter defaults to bilinear. Independent evidence from issue #238 (July 2026; FFmpeg 6.1.1 with zimg 3.0.5 zscale, i5-12400F) shows upscale 184 against 169 fps (about 1.09x) and downscale 462 against 466 fps (parity), so the README's 2x is stale. The benchmarked 2.8 introduced an AVX-512 sRGB/709 negative-input bug fixed in 3.0.6; resize coordinate rounding was fixed in 3.0; July 2026 master fixes are unreleased (last release 3.0.6, August 2025).

**Independent measurement:** Independent run in zimg issue #238 (July 2026; FFmpeg 6.1.1 with zimg 3.0.5 zscale against libswscale, i5-12400F): upscale 184 versus 169 fps (about 1.09x, derived from page data), downscale 462 versus 466 fps (parity).

**How:** Resizing is separable. Filter rows are precomputed per output pixel as float and as Q14 int16 coefficients, with the rounding error diffused so each row sums to exactly 1<<14, and they run in runtime-dispatched SIMD kernels: AVX2, AVX-512 and AVX-512 VNNI on x86, NEON on ARM since 3.0. The graphengine scheduler runs the whole conversion chain in tiles whose width comes from the detected per-thread cache size (CPUID leaf 4 on Intel), so intermediate scanlines stay in cache and no full-frame intermediates are built. Colourspace conversion plans a minimal chain of matrix, transfer and primaries steps and has SSE2/AVX2 lookup-table and AVX-512 paths for common transfer functions.

**Use it when:**
- Video and frameserver pipelines that need standards-exact conversion: chroma siting, limited and full range, BT.709, BT.2020 (including constant luminance), PQ or HLG transfer functions, and interlaced fields.
- High-bit-depth or float workflows (16-bit, half, float) that need good dithering (ordered, blue-noise random, error diffusion) when going back to 8 or 10 bits.
- Batch conversion of many frames with the same formats: build one graph and process frames in parallel, one temp buffer per thread, as the repo's graphapp benchmark does.
- Lanczos or spline resizing of planar YUV on AVX2 or AVX-512 x86, where it is at least on par with current swscale.

**Skip it when:**
- Expecting the README's 2x over current FFmpeg: issue #238 (Jul 2026; FFmpeg 6.1.1 built from source, zimg 3.0.5 via zscale, i5-12400F, 9000 raw yuv420p FHD frames) measured upscaling to UHD at 184 against 169 fps (48.6 s against 52.8 s user time, about 1.09x) and a downscale to 1796x1010 at 462 against 466 fps, so parity.
- Packed RGB or RGBA photo resizing or ICC colour management: buffers are planar (packed needs callbacks), and the README warns it is not a colour management system and should not be used for drastic gamut or contrast reduction such as BT.2020 to BT.709.
- x86 CPUs without AVX2: the current resize dispatcher (resize_impl_x86.cpp) only has AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels, so older CPUs fall back to plain C++.
- Builds that need CMake or Meson: GNU autotools is the only supported build system, the README calls the Visual Studio projects unstable, and the Meson request (#228) is open.
- Shipping only tagged releases: 3.0.6 (Aug 2025) lacks the Jul 2026 master fixes for integer weight rounding compensation, an out-of-bounds load in the AVX2 u16 permute resizer and an out-of-bounds read in SIMD error diffusion; the new-release request (#239) is open.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (autotools build; graphengine is a git submodule compiled in) · none at runtime; graphengine submodule (WTFPL) at build time · C++17 compiler (configure.ac fails without -std=c++17); byte-addressable machine with two's-complement integers and a word of 32 bits or more · Windows and POSIX; x86 SIMD (AVX2, AVX-512, AVX-512 VNNI for resize; SSE2/AVX2 elsewhere) and ARM NEON since 3.0; scalar C++ on other CPUs

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FFmpeg's libswscale when you need standards-exact video conversion (siting, HDR transfer functions, float and half formats, quality dithering) from a small library at equal or slightly better speed. Pick libyuv or xxYUV for the fastest 8-bit packed YUV-to-RGB conversion, and fast_image_resize (Rust) or libvips for packed 8-bit RGB(A) photo resizing.

**Gotchas:**
- AVX-512 kernels run only when cpu_type is ZIMG_CPU_AUTO_64B (added in 2.6). The default ZIMG_CPU_AUTO stays on AVX2 even on AVX-512 CPUs, so the README does not say whether the Xeon Platinum 8176 rows used AVX-512.
- C API defaults: luma bicubic (Catmull-Rom since 2.9, Mitchell-Netravali before), chroma bilinear, no dithering, and exact transfer functions (allow_approximate_gamma off). A like-for-like comparison with swscale's lanczos flag must set resample_filter_uv too, as FFmpeg's zscale does; the README does not say what its zimg run used.
- The SIMD paths have a long fix history. The ChangeLog includes an AVX-512 sRGB/709 negative-input bug introduced in 2.8 (the benchmarked version) and fixed in 3.0.6, and a resize pixel-coordinate rounding fix in 3.0. Issues report a colourspace segfault on AVX-without-AVX2 CPUs (#226) and Lanczos 5- and 7-tap float artifacts on the SIMD path of git builds on an Apple M2 Pro (#223), both closed.
- Colour defaults changed recently: master disabled chromatic adaptation by default in Aug 2026, so output can differ between 3.0.6 and master when white points change.

**Status:** Maintained by one author with commits on master through 4 Sep 2026, but the last release is 3.0.6 (Aug 2025) and later fixes are unreleased; WTFPL v2 (a public-domain-equivalent grant, not OSI-approved, no patent clause), so it can be vendored freely.

[repo](https://github.com/sekrit-twc/zimg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/sekrit-twc/zimg)

##### AVIR / LANCIR (Aleksey Vaneev)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier D`

Header-only C++ image resizers: AVIR, quality-first sinc resampling, plus LANCIR, a SIMD Lanczos-3. No speed comparison against other libraries exists.

**Beats:** No third-party incumbent timed; LANCIR is compared only with the project's own AVIR algorithm — Nothing is compared against another resizer. The README times only AVIR itself (245 ms single-threaded, 74 ms with 8 threads, for an 8-bit RGB 5184x3456 to 1920x1280 downscale on an i7-7700K, Intel C++ 18.2 with AVX2, harness not published) and calls LANCIR 'up to three times faster' than AVIR with no numbers. The README's comparison plots are quality-only (frequency response and dynamic range), and their 'Lanczos-3' is the project's own CLancIR per other/frtest.cpp.

**Known shortcoming:** No comparison against stb_image_resize or ImageMagick anywhere in the README, lancir.h or other/ (frtest.cpp measures quality against Lanczos-3): the only numbers are LANCIR 'up to 3x' faster than AVIR itself and bare AVIR timings of 245 and 74 ms on an i7-7700K with ICC 18.2, so tier D.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): nothing is compared against another resizer; the README times only AVIR itself (245 ms single-threaded, 74 ms with 8 threads, 5184x3456 to 1920x1280 on an i7-7700K, Intel C++ 18.2 with AVX2, harness not published, AVIR version unstated and predating the 3.0 upsizing speedup) and calls LANCIR 'up to three times faster' than AVIR without numbers. No timing code exists in the repo: other/frtest.cpp is a quality test that includes a private header and uses CLancIR itself as the 'Lanczos-3' baseline; bin/ holds prebuilt binaries whose sources are not published (issue #26). Floating-point output is not clamped (issue #12 green/pink pixels); k=1 is not an identity copy; version 3.1 removed the 2.8 'unbiasing' as a compiler-dependent statistical error, so 2.x and 3.1 output differ. Tier D stands.

**Independent measurement:** none (self-timings only)

**How:** LANCIR precomputes a filter bank at 1000 fractional offsets (enough for its 8-bit precision), replicates taps per channel to fit SIMD width, and runs the multiply-accumulate loops with SSE2, AVX, NEON or WASM SIMD128 intrinsics chosen at compile time. It resizes vertically first in batches of output rows sized to a roughly 5.5 MB cache budget, then horizontally per row, and keeps its buffers between calls so batches of same-sized frames skip reallocation and filter regeneration. AVIR relies mostly on compiler auto-vectorization of plain float code, with optional SSE float4 and de-interleaved AVX float8 types; the README says the AVX de-interleaved path gives up to 50% over non-SIMD code for 1-2 channel images.

**Use it when:**
- You want a dependency-free, header-only C++ resizer you can vendor (MIT), with an 8-bit Lanczos-3 path that has NEON and WASM SIMD128 kernels as well as SSE2/AVX.
- Batch-resizing many same-sized frames (video pipelines, asset baking): one CLancIR object per thread reuses its filters and buffers between calls.
- Quality-critical downscaling or upscaling of photos where frequency response and low ringing matter more than time: AVIR's sinc and Peaked Cosine design, with selectable low-ringing parameter sets.
- 16-bit or float pipelines that need high-precision resampling (AVIR), accepting that it is slower than LANCIR.
- Fractional-offset sub-pixel shifts or non-uniform x/y scale factors (kx, ky, ox, oy parameters).

**Skip it when:**
- Choosing the fastest CPU resizer: the repo has no timing against stb_image_resize2, OpenCV, libvips, Pillow-SIMD or IPP, and issue #18 (2020) says of AVIR 'I just tried to use it for real-time processing and, well, it's not fast'. Benchmark against fast_image_resize or zimg first.
- 16-bit-accurate fast resizing: LANCIR accepts uint16 and float buffers, but its precision is limited to 8-bit.
- Built-in parallelism: neither resizer threads by default. AVIR needs your own CImageResizerThreadPool implementation, and LANCIR offers no slicing helper.
- Rotation, affine warps or EWA/radial filtering: only orthogonal (separable) resizing is provided, and the README warns about diagonal aliasing.
- One binary that adapts to the CPU: LANCIR picks SSE2, AVX or NEON from compiler macros, so a default x86-64 build gets SSE2 only unless you compile with AVX enabled.

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard C/C++ library only) · C++98 (both headers carry pre-C++11 fallbacks for nullptr and cstdint); tested with GCC, MSVC, Clang and Intel C++ · any CPU with IEEE float; LANCIR SIMD on x86 SSE2/AVX, ARM NEON (32- and 64-bit), WASM SIMD128, scalar elsewhere; AVIR optional SSE (avir_float4_sse.h) and AVX (avir_float8_avx.h) types

**Vs siblings:** Pick LANCIR over stb_image_resize2-based siblings (stb-image-resize-opt, tir) when you need a C++ header with NEON and WASM SIMD Lanczos kernels and will measure speed yourself, and pick AVIR when resampling quality matters more than time. For documented speed wins, zimg (Lanczos about 2x faster than FFmpeg swscale) and fast_image_resize (faster than libvips) have measured numbers that this entry lacks.

**Gotchas:**
- Floating-point output is not clamped in either resizer, so sinc and Lanczos overshoot can leave values outside [0,1]. Issue #12 reported green and pink pixels when resizing float buffers while uint8 was fine. Clamp before converting.
- AVIR at k=1 is not an identity copy: it always low-pass filters first and applies a correction filter at the end. Its default parameters may change between releases, so save the parameter set if you need reproducible output.
- AVIR's sRGB gamma correction is off by default, and when enabled it also applies to alpha unless Vars.AlphaIndex is set. The README warns it can produce 'greenish/reddish/bluish haze' near edges.
- Version 3.1 removed the scanline 'unbiasing' added in 2.8, which the author now calls a compiler-dependent statistical error, and fixed a 16-bit to 8-bit conversion bug. Output from 2.x and 3.1 differs.

**Status:** Maintained by its single author (AVIR 3.1, LANCIR 3.1.1, last commit 2026-08-22, no open issues or PRs), MIT-licensed, header-only with no dependencies, so easy to vendor; the README asks for the credit line 'AVIR image resizing algorithm designed by Aleksey Vaneev'.

[repo](https://github.com/avaneev/avir) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avaneev/avir/HEAD/README.md)

##### FastGaussianBlur  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier D`

Header-only C++17 template approximating Gaussian blur with repeated box passes and blocked transposes; beats only a naive 2D convolution.

**Beats:** author's own naive non-separable 2D Gaussian convolution ((2k+1)^2 taps, k = ceil(2.57 sigma), gaussian_blur in the 2021 fast_gaussian_blur.h at commit 84e5f2d, since removed); no OpenCV or ImageMagick comparison — The only numbers are the project's own absolute times for 8-bit RGB, 3 passes, all cores of a Ryzen 7 2700X with OpenMP (Makefile: g++ -O3 -fopenmp): about 7 ms for FHD (2 MP), about 50 ms at 4K and about 200 ms at 8K, from a plot last updated 2021-02-09 (commit 84e5f2d). That plot predates the 2023-2024 rewrites (v1.0 to v1.2), the README's own TODO says 'redo timings', and its harness and sigma are not in the repo. The plot's 'true Gaussian blur' baseline, as it existed in the repo's 2021 header (gaussian_blur in fast_gaussian_blur.h, since removed), is a naive non-separable 2D convolution with (2k+1)^2 taps per pixel (k = ceil(2.57 sigma)) and a bounds check per tap, so the roughly 100x gap is against a straw man, not against a separable or library Gaussian such as OpenCV's.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: only its own timings (FHD about 7 ms, 4K about 50 ms, 8K about 200 ms on time.png) against an unpublished in-house true Gaussian with sigma unstated; no incumbent compared.
