**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e101, 2026-10-05): the plot's 'true Gaussian' baseline is the author's own naive non-separable 2D convolution ((2k+1)^2 taps, k = ceil(2.57 sigma); gaussian_blur in the 2021 header at 84e5f2d, since removed), so the roughly 100x gap is against a straw man; data/time.png dates from 2021-02-09, before the v1.0-v1.2 rewrites, and harness and sigma are absent (README TODO 'redo timings'). Current code (49f0128) edge-case bugs, not behind the numbers: mirror border with box radius == w-1 reads one element past the row (past the allocation on the last row); mirror on a 1-px-wide or 1-px-tall image divides by zero in remap_index; unsupported c>4 or n>10 silently no-op; sigma below about 0.58 gives zero-radius boxes (output = input); the header has no #includes. Open PR #12 (AVX2, claims 1.5-2x, CPU unstated) is broken (int16 row sums overflow at radius >= 64, main reads the second-pass buffer, t.sh runs sigma 0) and is not evidence. Tier D stands.

**Independent measurement:** none (self-plot against own naive convolution)

**How:** Sigma is converted to box widths with Kovesi's 'Fast Almost-Gaussian Filtering' formula (sigma_to_box_radius). Each 1D box pass is a sliding running sum (one add, one subtract and one multiply per sample), so the cost is O(1) per pixel whatever the radius. Vertical passes run as horizontal passes over a transposed copy: N row passes, a cache-blocked transpose (flip_block, 256/C-element tiles), N more row passes and a transpose back, so every filter loop walks memory row-major. Rows and tiles are split across cores with OpenMP parallel for; channel count, pass count, border policy and kernel-size regime are template parameters so the inner loops are specialised; integer images accumulate in int (issue #5 measured int about 15% faster than float on a 6000x8000 horizontal pass). There is no explicit SIMD, and the README says an ISPC port did not beat it.

**Use it when:**
- Medium to large sigma (roughly 5 and up) on 8-bit RGB or RGBA frames where the cost must not grow with radius: UI backdrop blur, bloom, depth-of-field previews, video at FHD to 4K.
- You want one dependency-free header and can accept an approximate Gaussian (box passes, approximate sigma, inexact borders).
- Multi-core CPUs with OpenMP available: every pass is an embarrassingly parallel loop over rows.
- As a readable starting point to fork; michelerenzullo/FastBoxBlur was derived from this code.

**Skip it when:**
- Small sigma: the README says a separable Gaussian is as fast and more accurate at sigma <= 2, and with 3 passes any sigma below about 0.58 yields zero-radius boxes, so the output equals the input.
- You need a true Gaussian (scale-space features, scientific or medical imaging, golden-image tests): the sigma oscillates around the target and the borders lose signal because no padding is added between passes.
- You already link OpenCV or a SIMD library: nothing in the repo measures this against cv::GaussianBlur, cv::blur or IPP, and the only published baseline is a naive O(sigma^2) 2D convolution.
- More than 4 channels, more than 10 passes, planar or strided layouts, const or in-place input (it needs two full-size scratch-able buffers), or buffers above 2^31-1 elements (all indexing is int).
- Tiny images, or sigma comparable to the image size, with the mirror border: see the edge-case memory bugs under gotchas.

**Integration:** header-only · none at run time; OpenMP is optional (without -fopenmp the pragmas are ignored and it runs on one core). The header has no #include lines of its own, so the includer must first include <algorithm>, <cmath>, <cstdio>, <cstdint>, <cstdlib> and <type_traits> (the demo gets them through <iostream> and the bundled stb_image/stb_image_write). · C++17 (if constexpr, std::is_integral_v, std::conditional_t); the Makefile builds with g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17. Clang and MSVC are not documented; issue #9 says OpenMP linking is awkward on WebAssembly, Android and macOS. · any (portable scalar C++, no intrinsics); timings exist only for a Ryzen 7 2700X

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you want a single dependency-free C++ header with four border policies and a cost that stays flat as sigma grows, and an approximate Gaussian is acceptable. libblur has published multithreaded numbers against OpenCV's Gaussian blur, zanazakaryaie/fastGaussianBlur and LibGaussianBlur (FFT) aim at an exact Gaussian, and FastBoxBlur (derived from this code) is the better fit when you want an accurate mirrored box blur with a cv::blur comparison.

**Gotchas:**
- Both buffers are overwritten and the pointer variables are swapped: after the call, `out` may point at the memory you passed as `in`. Pass pointer variables, not array names or pointers you must keep. The 8-argument overload defaults to kExtend, while the README demo defaults to mirror.
- Unsupported arguments do not fail: c > 4 or n = 0 or n > 10 only printf a message and return, leaving `out` as the untouched input (the 3-pass path still swaps pointers) or as whatever the buffer held before.
- Edge-case memory bugs in the current code (commit 49f0128, read and checked with a Python port of the index arithmetic): with the mirror border, a box radius of exactly w-1 takes the kMid branch, which reads one element past the row, and past the allocation on the last row of the buffer. The value is added and then subtracted, so integer results are unaffected, but a NaN or Inf in that garbage would poison a float row. Also with the mirror border, a 1-pixel-wide or 1-pixel-tall image divides by zero in remap_index (slength = 0). Issue #3 (2022, before the 2023 rework) reported an access violation at sigma 250.
- Type handling: every integral T accumulates in int (uint32 or int64 data can overflow; negative signed results are truncated toward zero after the +0.5 rounding), and double data accumulates in float. Float running sums drift slightly along long rows.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-08-18 (v1.2), with 3 open issues; MIT, a single 865-line header that is easy to vendor. The open AVX2 PR #12 (April 2026, unreviewed, claiming 1.5x to 2x on an unstated CPU) should not be merged as is: its int16 row sums overflow for box radius 64 and up on 8-bit data, its 3-pass loop leaves main.cpp reading the second-pass buffer, and its t.sh test runs at sigma 0.

[repo](https://github.com/bfraboni/FastGaussianBlur) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bfraboni/FastGaussianBlur)

##### pic-scale  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

Rust SIMD image-resampling crate with 30+ filters and colour-space-aware scaling; no valid speed comparison against fast_image_resize exists.

**Beats:** fast_image_resize (the baseline series of the repo's speedtest harness; no published result) — Nothing valid is measured. Up to v0.6.11 the README showed a Lanczos3 4x-downscale table against fast_image_resize (for example RGB 10.47 vs 15.62 with AVX2; units and rustc version not given). Those runs used a kernel at half the correct Lanczos3 support, so pic-scale did about half the work, and commit 30b40e5 (v0.6.12) fixed the kernel and deleted the table. The current speedtest harness (4928x3279 RGBA8, single thread on both sides, geometric mean after 10 warm-ups) publishes no results.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the old README table (v0.6.11 at 927a4fa; Lanczos3 RGB 4x downscale 6.97 against fast_image_resize 21.74 ms on NEON, 10.47 against 15.62 on AVX2) was measured on pre-0.6.12 code whose Lanczos3 kernel was half width (radius 1.5x the scale instead of 3x, about half the taps), and the same commit 30b40e5 'Filter generation fix' (2025-10-16) fixed the kernel and deleted the table; the current speedtest runner.rs allocates the fast_image_resize destination at width x width. 1.45M crates.io downloads.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): beyond the half-support Lanczos3 kernel and the width x width destination bug, the speedtest crate enables rdm and nightly_i8mm with the default WorkloadStrategy::PreferSpeed, so on aarch64 it picks Q0.7 int8 weights with vusdot (i8mm, scale below 10) or the RDM i16 path ('slightly lower precision') against fast_image_resize's i16 weights with i32 accumulation: any ARM chart from that harness compares a lower-precision kernel against a higher-precision one. Issue #161 (2026-08-23) documented correctness bugs in released SIMD paths (SSE f32-to-f16 fallback dropped the sign bit, NEON f16 row kernel read out of bounds, Miri misaligned NEON loads and out-of-bounds reads in vertical_f32, SVE2 dot kernel hard-coded 128-bit offsets), fixed in PR #164 (0.7.12, 2026-09-10). SIMD is a cargo feature: default-features = false leaves scalar code only; Fixed/Adaptive threading builds a new novtb pool per filter pass; README example needs the non-default 'colorspaces' feature. Nothing valid is measured; D stands.

**Independent measurement:** none valid

**How:** It does separable convolution with per-output weight tables computed once at plan time and quantised to fixed point. On x86 the u8 paths use Q15 i16 weights with _mm256_madd_epi16 into i32 (SSE4.1 and AVX2 runtime-dispatched; AVX-VNNI under the avx512 feature). On aarch64 the default WorkloadStrategy::PreferSpeed switches to cheaper arithmetic: with RDM (scale below 8) pixels are shifted left 6 bits into i16 and multiplied with vqrdmulh, and with the nightly_i8mm feature on an i8mm CPU (scale below 10) both passes use Q0.7 int8 weights and vusdot dot products. Rows are processed four at a time, and an optional novtb thread pool splits rows when ThreadingPolicy is Fixed or Adaptive. Optional supersampling pre-shrinks large downscales (3x or more) with Box or Nearest before the quality filter.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code that needs gamma-correct or perceptual resizing (linear light, Oklab, Lab, sigmoidal) without writing the conversion passes yourself.
- Pipelines with formats most resizers lack: f16 (nightly), AR30/RA30 10-bit packed, 10/12/16-bit u16 with an explicit bit depth, signed i16 planes, or YUV chroma (CbCr) planes.
- Repeated resizes of the same geometry (video frames, tiles), where one plan plus a reused scratch buffer avoids recomputing weights and allocating per call.
- Apple Silicon or other ARMv8.2+/v8.6 hosts where a lower-precision fast path is acceptable for thumbnails (RDM by default, i8mm with nightly_i8mm).
- Projects that already pull it in transitively: its largest crates.io dependent is the hayro PDF renderer (hayro 0.7.1 alone has about 1.26 million downloads).

**Skip it when:**
- When you need a measured speed advantage: no valid published comparison exists. The old README table was taken on a Lanczos3 kernel at half the correct support (fixed in v0.6.12), and the current speedtest commits no results.
- When output must be bit-exact across CPUs or match a reference: the default PreferSpeed mode picks different arithmetic per ISA (Q0.7 int8 weights on i8mm ARM, RDM i16 on ARMv8.1+, Q15 i16 on x86), and issue #161 (Aug 2026) found SIMD and scalar results diverging; set WorkloadStrategy::PreferQuality if this matters.
- Releases before 0.7.12: issue #161 listed a sign-bit loss in the SSE f32-to-f16 fallback that corrupted Lanczos output with negative taps, an out-of-bounds read in a NEON f16 row kernel, Miri-flagged misaligned NEON loads and an SVE2 kernel that assumed 128-bit vectors. These were fixed in PR #164 (merged 2026-09-10, the day 0.7.12 was published). Issue #150 (an all-zero last row on a 1x5 to 2x5 CatmullRom resize) was fixed in PR #151 in May 2026.
- C or C++ code bases that want a stable, documented library: the C++ header needs a nightly Rust build with -Z build-std, and covers six filters only. zimg (C++) or libvips are more natural there.
- Stable-Rust users who need f16, i8mm or SVE paths: those sit behind nightly-only features.

**Integration:** crate (plus an optional static library with a C++ header from the picscale/ subcrate) · num-traits, pxfm; optional novtb (threading, on by default) and colorutils-rs (colorspaces feature) · Rust 1.89 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, edition 2024); nightly for nightly_f16, nightly_i8mm, nightly_avx512fp16, sve and for building the C bindings · x86-64 and i686 (SSE4.1 and AVX2 detected at run time; AVX-512/AVX-VNNI with the avx512 feature), aarch64 NEON (RDM, i8mm, fp16 detected at run time; SVE2 partial), wasm32 with simd128 enabled at compile time, scalar fallback elsewhere (CI builds powerpc and riscv64)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over fast_image_resize when you need colour-space-aware scaling, f16/AR30/CbCr formats, built-in threading or the exotic EWA/Jinc filters. fast_image_resize is the safer choice for plain 8-bit resizing, because it has reproducible numbers against libvips, the image crate and the resize crate, while pic-scale has none. In C++ projects, zimg or stb-image-resize-opt avoid a nightly Rust build.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD is a cargo feature, not automatic: default-features = false (for example to drop the novtb threading dependency) turns off neon, rdm, sse and avx and leaves scalar code only. zenresize's paired_bench documents this ('by default pic-scale builds scalar-only') because it depends on pic-scale with default features off.
- WorkloadStrategy::PreferSpeed is the default. On ARM it trades precision for speed (RDM i16 path, or Q0.7 int8 weights when nightly_i8mm is on), and the source comments warn that the RDM path 'won't work really well on huge kernel'. On x86, PreferSpeed turns the AVX-VNNI horizontal u8 kernel off.
- With ThreadingPolicy::Fixed or Adaptive, a new novtb pool is constructed for each filter pass of every call rather than reused. Adaptive uses one thread per 65,536 output pixels, capped at available_parallelism.
- The README example still uses LinearScaler, which needs the non-default 'colorspaces' feature. It also mentions a 'nightly_avx512' feature that Cargo.toml names 'avx512'.

**Status:** Actively maintained by one author (last commit and 0.7.12 release 2026-09-10, 803 commits, 0 open issues) and dual BSD-3-Clause/Apache-2.0, so copyable; it has only 41 stars, and its crates.io volume comes largely from dependents such as hayro. Treat any speed claim as unmeasured until someone publishes a like-for-like run.

[repo](https://github.com/awxkee/pic-scale)

##### RGB2Y  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Header-only AVX2 BGR-to-grayscale for 8-bit images; README claims roughly 3x faster than OpenCV cv::cvtColor.

**Beats:** OpenCV cv::cvtColor (CV_BGR2GRAY) — The only claim is the README's 'roughly 3x faster than OpenCV with AVX2, or 2x with SSE only', with no CPU, timings or OpenCV version; that sentence was already in the README at commit e67dffa (Feb 2017), when the kernel used 6-bit weights with truncation (up to 3 grey levels off OpenCV, 57.4% of colours different), and it was not re-measured after the 30 Sep 2018 rewrite to the current Q15 kernel, which also dropped the SSE path. main.cpp times both sides (50 warm-ups, 100 runs, RGB2Y multithreaded, OpenCV with its own parallel_for_) on the repo's test.jpg, but publishes no output; the only posted run (issue #1, OpenCV 3.4.3, a Debug build) had RGB2Y at 15139.5 us against OpenCV's 2592.71 us.

**Known shortcoming:** README states a ratio with no measurement behind it (no result table, machine or baseline version); Makefile builds g++ -Ofast -march=native. The SSE claim has no code behind it (NO_AVX_PLEASE is unused). Per-term rounding can differ from cv::cvtColor by 1 grey level and is checked only against its own reference. The last block reads at least 1 byte past the end of the input buffer (out-of-bounds read).

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered C to D (retier-15): the README's 3x AVX2 / 2x SSE line dates from the February 2017 kernel (6-bit weights, 57.4% of colours differing from OpenCV) and was never re-measured after the 2018 Q15 rewrite; the SSE path was removed (issue #5); the only public run (issue #1, Debug build) shows RGB2Y slower than OpenCV. Exhaustive check against OpenCV 4.x: 33.2% of outputs off by 1; the multithreaded row split overruns the destination at 18 or more threads; tail over-read of 1-28 bytes; the g++ -Werror Makefile breaks on __forceinline and an unannotated fallthrough; the function is really BGR2Y (issue #4).

**How:** Each step converts 10 pixels (30 bytes): two overlapping 16-byte loads widened to 16 bits, one _mm256_mulhrs_epi16 against a repeating B,G,R Q15 weight vector, packus back to bytes, then three pshufb masks gather each pixel's three products and saturating byte adds sum them, so no 32-bit dot products are needed. Rows are split across up to min(height/16, hardware_concurrency()) std::async tasks. The unweighted path sums channels in 16 bits and divides by 3 with mulhrs by 10923, which equals round(sum/3) for every possible sum.

**Use it when:**
- BGR8 frames in OpenCV layout converted to gray on x86-64 with AVX2, where a 1-level difference from OpenCV on some colours is acceptable and an OpenCV dependency is not wanted.
- Large frames processed multithreaded on machines with 16 or fewer hardware threads, where thread start-up is amortised and the row-split bug cannot trigger.
- Equal-weight channel averaging (weighted=false), which is exact for all inputs.
- As a compact example of pshufb-based deinterleaving of 3-channel pixels with AVX2.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need OpenCV's exact output: an exhaustive check of all 16,777,216 BGR triples against OpenCV 4.x's 15-bit BGR2GRAY formula gives 33.2% differing by one grey level (16.4% lower, 16.8% higher), never by more.
- RGB-ordered, 4-channel, 16-bit or float input: weights are global constants in the header (swap B_WEIGHT and R_WEIGHT for RGB), and only 3-byte pixels are handled.
- CPUs without AVX2 or non-x86 targets: the SSE path the README advertises was removed on 30 Sep 2018 (commit 6a822b7, open issue #5), and NO_AVX_PLEASE now does nothing.
- Unpadded input buffers: the final 10-pixel block of the last row loads 31 bytes and reads 1 to 28 bytes past the end, depending on width mod 10.
- Multithreaded calls on machines with 24 or more hardware threads: the row split overruns the image for some heights (see gotchas).

**Integration:** header-only (RGB2Y.h, all functions are templates) · none for RGB2Y.h beyond the C++ standard library and <immintrin.h> (it uses std::vector and std::thread without including <vector> or <thread>); the main.cpp demo needs OpenCV 3.x for the CV_BGR2GRAY constant · Written for MSVC: it uses __forceinline, which g++ and clang++ on Linux do not predefine (checked with g++ 13.3 macro dump), and an unannotated switch fallthrough that -Wextra flags (-Wimplicit-fallthrough since GCC 7) under the Makefile's -Werror; Makefile otherwise asks for g++ -std=gnu++17 -mavx2 -march=native -Ofast · x86-64 with AVX2 (also SSE4.1 _mm_extract_epi8); no SSE-only, NEON or scalar fast path

**Vs siblings:** CompV (RGB24 to gray 449 ms vs OpenCV 3086 ms) and DeltaCV publish measured BGR/RGB-to-gray results against OpenCV, and H264Sharp measures cvtColor-style conversion by thread count; choose RGB2Y only when a single dependency-free AVX2 header for BGR8 to gray matters more than evidence, bit-exactness or maintenance.

**Gotchas:**
- Out-of-bounds rows in the multithreaded split: thread_stride = ceil(height / threads) and threads-1 full chunks are launched before the remainder, and the final call always processes at least one row, so whenever (threads-1)*thread_stride > height the tasks read past the input and write past the output. Because threads is capped at height/16 this needs 18 or more hardware threads: a simulation finds 49 affected heights up to 4096 on 24 threads (for example 385 rows, 7 rows out of bounds), 225 on 32 threads (520 rows) and 1713 on 64 threads (721 rows: 28 out of bounds; 1000 rows: 38).
- The input stride is in pixels (row i starts at data + 3*i*stride) while the output is written packed at out + i*width; RGB2Y_ref instead writes out[i*stride + j], so with padded rows the fast path and the reference disagree on output layout. Divide cv::Mat::step by 3, and only if it is a multiple of 3.
- main.cpp's 'N pixels disagree' line compares RGB2Y with its own RGB2Y_ref, which reproduces the per-term rounding exactly (0 mismatches over all colours), not with OpenCV's output.
- Each multithreaded call starts new tasks with std::async(std::launch::async); libstdc++ and libc++ create a thread per task (MSVC pools them), so small images pay thread start-up on every call.

**Status:** Abandoned: the kernel last changed on 30 Sep 2018 and the only later commit (23 Mar 2021) added the MIT license; four open issues (missing SSE path, BGR naming, an unexplained 'A bug?' report with an error image) have no replies. Vendorable after fixing the row split and padding the input.

[repo](https://github.com/komrad36/RGB2Y) · [benchmark](https://github.com/komrad36/RGB2Y)

##### skcms  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier D`

Skia's small ICC colour-management library (parse profiles, SIMD pixel transforms); no published speed comparison against Little CMS.

**Beats:** Little CMS (lcms2) — Nothing comparative has been measured: neither README makes a speed claim, and bench.c (mirror branch) only prints skcms's own ns per pixel for 255-pixel batches of sRGB to a Display P3 matrix, which its header calls 'mostly to run in a profiler'. imazen/cms-bench has a zenbench harness timing moxcms, skcms and lcms2 on 8-bit, 16-bit, float and LUT profiles but commits no results; in its identity group skcms gets the same profile pointer twice (no colour math), and only the skcms rows include per-call setup.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: bench.c on the GitHub mirror times skcms alone, there is no lcms2 number anywhere reachable, imazen/cms-bench commits no results, and the mirror's last commit is 2025-09-16 with the upstream (skia.googlesource.com) unverifiable here.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e107, 2026-10-05): stays D, no catalogued numbers. bench.c times all-zero static buffers and rotates formats; skcms_Transform has no transform object and re-plans every call; passing the same source and destination profile pointer skips the colour math, which is exactly what the imazen/cms-bench identity group does (only the skcms rows include setup; no results committed). GitHub mirror last synced 2025-09-16.

**Independent measurement:** none

**How:** Each skcms_Transform call compiles a short program of at most 32 ops (load, curves, matrix or CLUT, clamp, premul, store) and runs it over float vectors of 4 (SSE/NEON/LSX/WASM), 8 (AVX2+F16C, 'hsw') or 16 (AVX-512, 'skx') lanes, picked by a one-time cpuid/xgetbv check. Stages are chained with [[clang::musttail]] tail calls where the compiler supports it, transfer functions use approximate log2/exp2 (approx_pow) instead of powf, the source and destination gamut matrices are concatenated into one 3x3, an identical gamut skips the matrix, and LUT/CLUT lookups use AVX2/AVX-512 gathers and hardware half-float conversion.

**Use it when:**
- You already build Skia or Chromium-style code and want the same colour conversions they ship, with no new dependency.
- Decoding images (JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL) whose embedded ICC or CICP profile must be converted to sRGB or a display profile, row by row.
- HDR pipelines that need PQ and HLG transfer functions, including the HLG OOTF, plus half-float and 10-bit XR output formats.
- Many pixel formats in one library without writing per-format packing code; 255-pixel or larger batches, so the per-call planning cost is amortised.
- Untrusted ICC input: the repo carries libFuzzer targets (fuzz/fuzz_iccprofile_info.c, fuzz/fuzz_iccprofile_transform.c), and skcms.cc never calls malloc, so parsing does not allocate or copy.

**Skip it when:**
- You need lcms2 features: rendering intents beyond the A2B0/A2B1 preference, black point compensation, proofing, device links, named colours or multi-profile chains.
- Destination profiles with tabulated TRCs: they must be rewritten by skcms_MakeUsableAsDestination(), which fits a parametric curve and fails or approximates badly on some profiles (tests.c lists several).
- You need bit-exact or lcms2-identical output: transfer functions run through approx_pow, and the repo's own A2B round-trip test tolerates 1/255 error (9/255 at zero).
- You picked it for speed: no benchmark against Little CMS, its fast_float plugin, qcms or moxcms is published, and bench.c only times skcms itself.
- General CMYK workflows: CMYK is handled as Photoshop-style inverted CMYK only (the code says those are the only CMYK profiles it has seen).

**Integration:** source-drop (skcms.cc plus src/*.cc and headers); ninja and Bazel builds produce a static library · none (C standard library only) · C++ with lambdas and constexpr (C++11 level; the exact standard is not documented); Clang or GCC vector extensions for the SIMD paths, otherwise SKCMS_PORTABLE scalar code (for example MSVC without clang-cl) · x86-64 with runtime dispatch to SSE baseline, AVX2+F16C or AVX-512 (AVX2/AVX-512 paths disabled on Android); aarch64 and armv7 NEON; LoongArch LSX; WebAssembly SIMD via Emscripten; ppc64le and RISC-V without musttail; Windows without musttail

**Vs siblings:** Pick skcms over the Little-CMS fast_float plugin when you want a small, dependency-free, fuzzed C/C++ library matching Skia and Chromium output and can live without lcms2's intents and device links; pick moxcms instead in Rust code, where it at least publishes timings against lcms2. Keep lcms2 plus fast_float when you need the full ICC feature set or measured speed.

**Gotchas:**
- skcms_Transform has no cached transform object: every call re-plans the pipeline (including inverting the destination transfer functions), so very small calls pay setup each time.
- Passing the same profile pointer as source and destination skips the colour conversion entirely (only format conversion runs); any benchmark against lcms2 that does this is not like for like.
- skcms_ICCProfile points into the ICC buffer passed to skcms_Parse(); the buffer must outlive the profile.
- bench.c times skcms on static float buffers that are never filled (all-zero pixels) and rotates pixel formats each iteration, so its ns-per-pixel figure is a profiling aid, not a throughput number for real images.

**Status:** The GitHub repo is a read-only mirror whose last sync is 2025-09-16 ('Disable must_tail on GCC when compiling for RISC-V'), so it reads as stale even though upstream on skia.googlesource.com is likely still used by Skia and Chromium; BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/google/skcms)

##### Smolscale  `C`  `LGPL-3.0-only OR BSD-4-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Embeddable C bilinear/box RGBA scaler (SWAR, AVX2, row-batch threading); no published speed ratio against Pixman, libswscale or stb.

**Beats:** libswscale (FFmpeg), Pixman, stb_image_resize, GDK-Pixbuf, SDL_gfx and Skia (as wired into the project's own benchmark harness) — No comparative number is reachable. The repo's harness (test.c run_benchmark_proportional via bench.sh) times one-shot calls including setup: smol_scale_simple; sws_getContext + sws_scale + sws_freeContext per call (SWS_FAST_BILINEAR up to 2x reduction, SWS_AREA beyond); Pixman separable box convolution or bilinear into a calloc'd buffer; GDK-Pixbuf bilinear; and the bundled stb_image_resize v0.97 (the old v1) box filter. It reports the mean of (input + output pixels) per second with 5th and 95th percentiles, and no results are committed. Search-result text of the blocked 2019 post says it ran on an i7-4770K at 3.5 GHz with a 2000x2000 RGBA input, taking the fastest of 50 runs at each of 500 sizes, and compared GDK-Pixbuf, Pixman 0.36.0, SDL, Skia and Smolscale; libswscale and stb are not named there. Its qualitative findings put Pixman fastest single-threaded at 0.5-1.0x and Skia among the fastest below 0.5x. Its one number, 8-thread Smolscale at about 5.3 Gpx/s on a 16383x16383 input, measured 2019 code that was largely rewritten in 2023 (premultiplication overhaul, AVX2 lerp).

**Known shortcoming:** Repo carries no results; the numbers (16383x16383 in about 50 ms on 8 threads, i7-4770K) are snippet-only from the blocked hpjansson.org post and give no ratio against a baseline. Smolscale's multi-threaded path gets all cores while libswscale, Pixman and stb ran single-threaded, each with its own filter. Code is maintained inside chafa/internal/smolscale (Chafa, 5.3k stars, commit 2026-09-25).

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered C to D (retier-13): no ratio against any baseline is reachable; the blog snippets give absolute throughput and directional claims only (Pixman 0.5-1.0x, Skia under 0.5x), for the 2019 code before the 2023 rewrite, and libswscale and stb_image_resize are not in the published comparison. README stale (build needs smolscale-generic.c); no allocation or argument checks (dimension 0 divides by zero); the harness times sws_getContext per call and bundles stb_image_resize v0.97; the Chafa copy is maintained but API-incompatible.

**How:** SWAR: each 32-bit pixel is unpacked into a uint64 with four 16-bit lanes (mask 0x00ff00ff00ff00ff), so one 64-bit multiply, shift and add interpolates all four channels with an 8-bit fraction. A 128bpp layout (two words, 24-bit lanes) is used for linear sRGB or reductions beyond 255x. The filter is picked per axis: copy at 1:1; plain bilinear for upscaling and reductions down to 1/2; bilinear with one or two built-in 'halvings' (2 or 4 bilinear taps accumulated per output, then shifted) for 1/2 to 1/8; and box (area) averaging, with precomputed spans and a fixed-point reciprocal multiplier, beyond 1/8. Scaling is separable: offsets are precomputed once per context, and each horizontally scaled input row is kept in a 4-row ring for the vertical pass. The AVX2 file is chosen at run time with __builtin_cpu_supports, and threading is done by splitting output rows into batches.

**Use it when:**
- Large-factor downscaling or thumbnailing of big RGBA buffers in-process on x86-64, with output rows split across threads. Per a search snippet of the author's post, 8 threads scaled a 16383x16383 image down in about 50 ms, roughly 5.3 Gpx/s of input.
- Pipelines that need scaling fused with pixel-order and alpha-mode conversion, for example unassociated RGBA in and premultiplied BGRA out for a compositor, without a separate conversion pass.
- C or C++ projects that want a dependency-free source drop (libc only) where 'no jaggies' bilinear or box quality is enough, as in Chafa's terminal image renderer.
- Streaming or tiled output: the batch API produces any range of output rows on demand, and the post-row callback can process each row.

**Skip it when:**
- High-quality resampling (Lanczos, Mitchell, bicubic): it offers only automatically chosen bilinear and box filters with 8-bit interpolation fractions.
- Single-threaded scaling at 0.5x-1.0x: according to search-result text of the author's own 2019 post (snippet only), Pixman's SIMD code was the fastest single-threaded implementation in that range and Skia was among the fastest below 0.5x.
- YUV or planar input, 16-bit or float channels, or images wider or taller than 65535 px.
- Long-term use of the standalone repo. It has been frozen since 2023-04-12 with 19 open issues, and later fixes (allocation checks, a premul16 AVX2 alpha-extraction fix, argument validation) went only into Chafa's copy, which has an incompatible API.
- MSVC builds: the code relies on GNU C extensions (statement expressions in smol_alloc_aligned, __attribute__((always_inline)), __builtin_assume_aligned, __builtin_cpu_supports).

**Integration:** source-drop · none beyond libc (the test.c benchmark needs glib, libpng, pixman, gdk-pixbuf, SDL_gfx and libswscale) · GCC or Clang with GNU C extensions; a shim covers GCC < 8 missing _mm256_set_m128i; no C standard is stated · any 64-bit-capable C target through the generic SWAR path; an optional x86-64 AVX2 path (compile smolscale-avx2.c with -mavx2 and everything with -DSMOL_WITH_AVX2) is picked at run time; no NEON or SSE-only path

**Vs siblings:** Pick Smolscale for a dependency-free C drop-in that fuses channel reordering and premultiplication with scaling and lets you thread by output-row batches. For measured speed with quality filters, fast_image_resize (Rust, AVX2, beats libvips single-threaded) or stb-image-resize-opt and zimg (C/C++, published ratios) are better-evidenced choices.

**Gotchas:**
- The README is stale. It says to copy three files, but smolscale.c calls _smol_get_generic_implementation() from smolscale-generic.c, so four files are needed (five with AVX2). It also says the AVX2 file is 'mostly just a straight copy of the generic code', yet the current smolscale-avx2.c has about 278 _mm256 intrinsic uses in pack/unpack and the 64bpp horizontal lerp, added in the March-April 2023 rework.
- There is no argument validation and no allocation-failure handling: smol_scale_new's calloc and do_rows' mallocs are unchecked and every entry point returns void. An output dimension of 0 divides by zero in precalc_boxes_array (test.c clamps sizes to at least 1), and the uint16 precalc offsets cap dimensions at 65535 with no check. Chafa's copy rejects dimensions outside [1, 65535] and returns 0 on failure.
- The defaults differ between copies: here with_srgb is an explicit argument and switches to the 128bpp path, and issue #2 ('Check if linearization works above 1:8191') is still open; Chafa's copy linearizes by default unless SMOL_DISABLE_SRGB_LINEARIZATION is passed.
- The last standalone commit (2023-04-12) fixed a potential over-read in box precalc, so older vendored copies carry that bug. The code itself comments that box filtering is only precise enough when the input dimension exceeds five times the output.

**Status:** The standalone repo has been abandoned since 2023-04-12 (278 commits, 19 open issues, almost all the author's own TODOs). The maintained copy is chafa/internal/smolscale in Chafa (commits through 2026-09-25: AVX2 linearization, compositing, nearest mode, argument and allocation checks), but its API is incompatible, so vendor from Chafa under the same LGPLv3-or-BSD-4-Clause choice.

[repo](https://github.com/hpjansson/smolscale) · [benchmark](https://github.com/hpjansson/smolscale/blob/master/bench.sh)

#### font-shaping-text-layout

##### ab_glyph  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust glyph loading, scaling, positioning and rasterization crate; rewrite of rusttype with cheaper per-glyph layout, especially for CFF fonts.

**Beats:** rusttype 0.9 (Rust OpenType/TrueType glyph layout and rasterization crate, which describes itself as a pure Rust alternative to FreeType) — First-party Criterion runs from May 2020 (ab_glyph 0.1 against rusttype 0.9; rustc version, flags and CPU not stated) laid out one 225-character sentence with Exo2 Light at 25 px: 11.1 us vs 17.3 us for .ttf (1.56x) and 11.1 us vs 98.1 us for .otf (8.85x); the first README version (2020-05-08) also showed an OpenSans-Italic .ttf row at 19.3 vs 25.3 us (1.31x) that was removed three days later in 'Simplify bench comparison'. The two harnesses do different work: rusttype's layout computes a pixel bounding box per glyph (a stored glyf bbox read for .ttf, a full CFF outline pass for .otf in ttf-parser 0.5/0.6) while ab_glyph defers it and additionally wraps lines at 600 px, so the ratio measures work avoided by ab_glyph's API rather than the same computation done faster.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-baseline (rusttype, not FreeType or HarfBuzz); the README critcmp table (1.56x TTF, 8.85x OTF) dates from May 2020 with no rustc, CPU or machine stated, the current dev/benches/layout.rs no longer includes rusttype, and the rusttype bench does single-line layout while ab-glyph also wraps.

**How:** Mostly API design: layout yields lightweight `Glyph` values and defers outlining and bounding boxes until `outline_glyph`/`glyph_bounds`, whereas rusttype 0.9's `positioned()` computed a pixel bounding box for every glyph during layout via ttf-parser `glyph_bounding_box`, which for CFF fonts runs the full charstring outliner (ttf-parser 0.5/0.6 read the stored glyf bbox for .ttf but outlined CFF glyphs) - this is where the large .otf gap comes from. Since 0.2.12 it also pre-parses the Unicode cmap and horizontal kern subtables once at font load (owned_ttf_parser `PreParsedSubtables`), which the changelog credits with 25-30% faster layout benchmarks. The rasterizer is a font-rs-derived signed-area accumulation rasterizer: line segments add signed coverage deltas into a float buffer and one running-sum pass (`for_each_pixel`) produces coverage; quadratics are flattened by a deviation-based segment count and cubics by stb_truetype-style recursive midpoint subdivision. Line drawing is the same scalar code compiled with `#[target_feature(enable = "avx2")]` and `sse4.2` and chosen once at runtime (compiler auto-vectorization, no hand-written intrinsics).

**Use it when:**
- Rust code that needs char-to-glyph mapping, advances, simple kerning and coverage rasterization of individual glyphs (game UIs, GPU text atlases via glyph_brush, plotting and image libraries such as plotters and imageproc already depend on it).
- Migrating from rusttype 0.9, especially with CFF .otf fonts: layout cost no longer depends on outline complexity (the 2020 table shows ab_glyph at 11.1 us for both the Exo2 .ttf and .otf, rusttype at 17.3 us and 98.1 us).
- no_std or wasm targets: CI builds both crates for thumbv6m-none-eabi (no default features, libm) and wasm32-unknown-unknown; FontArc works on no_std targets with pointer atomics since 0.2.32.
- Left-to-right scripts without contextual shaping, where per-pair kerning from a legacy 'kern' table (or none) is acceptable.
- When you want a widely deployed, small-dependency crate: about 45.2 million crates.io downloads and 269 reverse dependencies.

**Skip it when:**
- Complex scripts, ligatures, mark positioning or any OpenType feature: there is no GSUB/GPOS support (issue #74 'OTF feature tags' open since 2023-02); use HarfBuzz/HarfRust or a layout stack such as Parley or cosmic-text.
- Fonts that kern only through GPOS (common in modern OpenType fonts): `kern` reads only the legacy 'kern' table subtables, so those pairs come back unkerned.
- Raw rasterization throughput is the bottleneck: sibling entries report faster pure-Rust rasterizers (fontdue's own plots versus ab_glyph 0.2.3; TiTanF's README medians put Fontdue ahead of ab_glyph at 10-160 px). There is no hinting, so small-size output will not match FreeType hinted rendering.
- Supply-chain policies that block unmaintained dependencies: ttf-parser, its parsing backend, is flagged RUSTSEC-2026-0192 (informational, unmaintained, 2026-06-28); the Skrifa port (PR #122) is a draft, needs a breaking release, and its author measured it slower (about 70 us TrueType and 90 us CFF vs about 55 us with ttf-parser on the layout-and-outline benchmark).
- C or C++ projects: it is a Rust crate with no C API; calling it from C++ requires your own FFI layer.

**Integration:** crate (ab_glyph plus the separately published ab_glyph_rasterizer) · owned_ttf_parser 0.25 (wraps ttf-parser), ab_glyph_rasterizer 0.1 (no dependencies); optional libm for no_std · Latest stable Rust only (README policy; no rust-version field in Cargo.toml); edition 2021 · any Rust target; CI tests on ubuntu-latest (x86-64) and builds thumbv6m-none-eabi (no_std + libm) and wasm32-unknown-unknown; runtime AVX2/SSE4.2 dispatch for line drawing on x86/x86_64 with the std feature

**Vs siblings:** Pick ab_glyph over fontdue or TiTanF when you need CFF .otf and variable-font support, no_std, and compatibility with the glyph_brush/imageproc/plotters ecosystem, accepting a slower rasterizer by those projects' own measurements; it is a higher-level glyph API than Fontations' skrifa or ttf-parser (which it builds on), and it does no shaping, so Parley or a HarfBuzz port is the choice once text needs real OpenType layout.

**Gotchas:**
- Coverage values are not clamped: since ab_glyph_rasterizer 0.1.5 a value of 1.0 or more means fully covered. Open issue #121 (2025-08-20) reports tiny non-zero coverage (about 1.6e-7) outside glyphs from floating-point cancellation in draw_line_scalar, visible as shadows when glyphs are drawn repeatedly; the reporter's workaround rounds coverage.
- Out-of-bounds panics in draw_line_scalar were fixed in three rounds (rasterizer 0.1.3, 0.1.9 in 2025-06, 0.1.10 in 2025-08); make sure the lockfile has ab_glyph_rasterizer 0.1.10 or later.
- `OutlinedGlyph::draw` allocates a fresh width x height float buffer for every call; cache rasterized glyphs (as glyph_brush does) rather than redrawing per frame.
- Missing characters map silently to GlyphId(0) (.notdef) rather than returning None; some `Font` default methods return None or 0.0 where fonts lack data (issue #99 open).

**Status:** Apache-2.0 and copyable; last release ab_glyph 0.2.32 on 2025-09-28 with only lint, CI and test-hash commits since (latest 2026-08-30), so effectively in maintenance mode while the unmaintained ttf-parser backend awaits the draft Skrifa port.

[repo](https://github.com/alexheretic/ab-glyph) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexheretic/ab-glyph/main/glyph/README.md)

##### canvas-hypertxt  `JavaScript`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Zero-dependency JavaScript line breaker for HTML5 canvas text; up to 9.8x faster than canvas-txt 3.x (19x with HyperWrapping).

**Beats:** canvas-txt (JavaScript canvas multi-line text library) — First-party Storybook benchmark in an unnamed browser and machine: 5000 iterations of wrapping a song-lyric string (iteration number prepended, so results are not memo hits) into a 450 px box at 20px sans-serif and drawing it, 1000 chars 11.19 s for canvas-txt 3.x vs 1.43 s for canvas-hypertxt and 0.77 s with HyperWrapping (about 7.8x and 14.5x, derived from page data). The canvas-txt timing includes setting ctx.font on every call, canvas-hypertxt stops drawing below 500 px, and HyperWrapping trains and is measured on the same text.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-baseline (JavaScript canvas text layout). The harness benchmark.stories.tsx is public but states no browser or machine, and the timing is asymmetric: canvas-txt sets ctx.font inside the timed loop and draws overflow lines while hypertxt keeps warm metrics (the win is still real because canvas-txt calls measureText per character). Stale since 2023-11-25.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e105, 2026-10-05): correctness bug, not behind the numbers: an empty line, or a width below about 2/3 of a glyph, gives a NaN font average, after which split() for that font key returns lines unwrapped (open issues #12 and #11; reproduced in node with a mock canvas: 1 line instead of about 15). Lines of narrow glyphs overflow unwrapped because only the first 1.5 average line lengths are measured (reproduced). Harness order effects and HyperWrapping training on the same text it measures noted. Tier C stands; the baseline is superseded. Lead: canvas-txt v5 benchmarks 51.3 vs 566.2 us/op against canvas-hypertxt standard mode on never-repeating 600-char strings (about 11x, node-canvas, Apple Silicon).

**Independent measurement:** first-party benchmark

**How:** canvas-txt 3.x finds wrap points by calling ctx.measureText once per added character (and sets ctx.font inside every drawText call); canvas-hypertxt guesses the split point from a running per-font average character width, measures only a window of about 1.5 average line lengths, then steps the guess forward or jumps back to the previous space, so it needs a handful of measureText calls per line. Results are memoised in a 500-entry map keyed by text, font key and width. Optional HyperWrapping learns a per-character width table by gradient-style back-propagation against real measureText results (after 20,000 measured characters for that font key) and, once 500,000 characters have been seen, estimates widths with a 1% safety margin without calling measureText at all.

**Use it when:**
- Canvas-rendered UIs (data grids, charts, canvas editors) that wrap many short-to-medium Latin strings per frame and draw them themselves, as glide-data-grid does (its core package 6.0.4-alpha25 still depends on canvas-hypertxt ^1.0.3).
- Re-layout of the same strings at the same width (scrolling, redraws): repeated calls return the memoised line array.
- Long-running pages with a large volume of text in one font where HyperWrapping can train, and an occasional line that wraps one word early is acceptable.
- Wrapping at non-space break points (CJK, hyphens) when you can supply break opportunities from a UAX #14 implementation through the optional callback.

**Skip it when:**
- Text that contains blank lines (consecutive, leading or trailing newlines) or calls with a width narrower than about two thirds of one glyph: open issues #12 and #11, reproduced here with a mock canvas, show the per-font average width becoming NaN, after which every later split() for that font key returns lines unwrapped until clearCache().
- Lines whose characters are much narrower than the font key's learned average (below about two thirds of it, e.g. runs of 'i', 'l', '.' after training on ordinary prose): split() measures only the first 1.5 average line lengths, so such lines are returned unwrapped and overflow (code reading plus mock-canvas reproduction).
- Never-repeating text without HyperWrapping against current alternatives: the canvas-txt maintainer's node-canvas benchmark (issue #13) gives 566.2 µs/op for canvas-hypertxt standard mode vs 51.3 µs/op for canvas-txt v5 on 600-char strings (about 11x slower, derived from page data), and uWrap reports 770 ms for canvas-hypertxt vs 82 ms for itself in Chrome 135.
- Layouts that need justify, vertical alignment, managed line heights or preserved leading spaces (every wrapped line after the first is trimmed; issue #7).
- Projects that need a maintained dependency: last commit and npm release 1.0.3 on 2023-11-25, six open issues with no maintainer replies.

**Integration:** module (npm package canvas-hypertxt 1.0.3, ESM and CommonJS builds with TypeScript types; the logic is one ~240-line source file that is easy to vendor) · none · Any JavaScript runtime with Map, for...of and a CanvasRenderingContext2D (browsers; node-canvas works per the canvas-txt maintainer's benchmark); not documented beyond that · any JavaScript environment with a 2D canvas context

**Vs siblings:** uWrap, the only like-for-like sibling, reports about 9x lower time than canvas-hypertxt in Chrome 135 (about 18x in Firefox 137, derived from page data) and better accuracy but documents Latin-only accuracy, no \r\n handling and only pre-line wrapping; pick canvas-hypertxt only when you need its pluggable break-opportunity callback or you already depend on glide-data-grid. Pretext targets DOM-free measurement in general and Parley or text-shaper do real shaping, so none of them replace a canvas line splitter directly.

**Gotchas:**
- fontStyle is only a cache key: the caller must set ctx.font to the matching font before calling split(), use a distinct key per font, and call clearCache() once web fonts finish loading (document.fonts.ready), or the learned widths belong to the fallback font.
- The result memo key is text, font key and width but not hyperWrappingAllowed, and eviction past 500 entries drops the oldest inserted key rather than the least recently used one.
- HyperWrapping estimates are deliberately inflated by 1%, so a minority of lines wrap one word early, and the model is only as good as the text it trained on for that font key.
- Width <= 0 returns an empty array; first lines are right-trimmed and later lines fully trimmed.

**Status:** Stale since 2023-11-25 (npm 1.0.3) with an open NaN bug that silently disables wrapping, though MIT, dependency-free and small enough to vendor and patch (skip measureText for empty strings); the baseline it beat has since been rewritten (canvas-txt v5).

[repo](https://github.com/glideapps/canvas-hypertxt) · [benchmark](https://github.com/glideapps/canvas-hypertxt)

##### displaywidth  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Go monospace display-width and truncation library; 1.6-3.3x faster than go-runewidth v0.0.23 in its own benchmarks, zero allocations.

**Beats:** mattn/go-runewidth (the common Go terminal display-width library) and rivo/uniseg; ICU, HarfBuzz and FreeType are not involved — go test -bench in comparison/ on an Apple M2 (darwin/arm64), Go version unstated, numbers refreshed in the 2026-04-18 'update versions & benches' commit, against go-runewidth v0.0.23 and rivo/uniseg v0.4.7 in their default configurations. Results: about 1.7 KB of mixed test strings 6085 vs 9970 vs 19060 ns/op; the same with East Asian Ambiguous wide 6118 vs 13917 vs 19263; East Asian runes 3454 vs 11432; truncation 2495 vs 4569 (with tail) and 2456 vs 5182 (without). Reading the harness: both sides do equivalent default work, but go-runewidth's opt-in CreateLUT fast path was not enabled; its default condition follows the runner's locale; its Truncate scans the string twice; and on the emoji set (flags, VS16 emoji) the libraries return different widths. The numbers predate PR #24 (2026-05-17, VS16 rewrite, about 1% per the PR) and go-runewidth v0.0.24-v0.0.30. Record correction: go-runewidth v0.0.23's go.mod declares go 1.20; go 1.23 is its current HEAD.

**Known shortcoming:** Go library (language-filter mismatch); display-width primitive, not shaping. README numbers match the public comparison/benchmark_test.go (Apple M2), Go toolchain version unstated; baseline go-runewidth is the Go-ecosystem incumbent and now uses the same author's uax29 segmenter.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarks are stale: the baseline is pinned to go-runewidth v0.0.23 (2026-04-08) and v0.0.24 to v0.0.30 (May to September 2026) added a precomputed East Asian table, a lazy full lookup table and rune fast paths, so the 2.3-3.3x gaps may have shrunk; runewidth's opt-in CreateLUT is unused and its default follows the locale. The emoji row returns different widths (flags, VS16) and the numbers predate PR #24's VS16 fix (2026-05-17, about 1%). Open issue #25: Thai SARA AM clusters measure 1 instead of 2. The go-runewidth v0.0.23 go.mod says go 1.20 (1.23 is HEAD).

**How:** Width properties live in a generated multi-stage trie indexed directly by UTF-8 bytes, in the style of x/text/internal/triegen (trie.go: about 16 KB of values plus a 1.9 KB index). It returns a one-byte bitmap (zero-width, wide, ambiguous, VS16-eligible) without decoding runes. Runs of printable ASCII are counted by a plain byte loop that skips grapheme segmentation entirely; the changelog says 2-10x faster on ASCII than v0.7.0. Other text goes through the clipperhouse/uax29 grapheme iterator, and each cluster costs one trie lookup on its leading rune, plus an IndexByte scan for VS16. The code is generic over string and []byte and allocates nothing. The go-runewidth v0.0.23 baseline instead binary-searches interval tables per rune (up to three tables in East Asian mode), and its Truncate measures the whole string before a second cutting pass.

**Use it when:**
- Go TUIs and CLI tables that measure or truncate many short cells per frame. lipgloss v2, charmbracelet/x/ansi (v0.11.0) and olekukonko/tablewriter (v0.10.0) already depend on it in their go.mod files.
- ASCII-heavy text: 54.5 ns vs 125.5 ns for 128 bytes over five strings against go-runewidth v0.0.23 (2.3x), and 27x faster than rivo/uniseg.
- Strings carrying ANSI SGR colour codes: Options.ControlSequences counts escape sequences as zero width, and TruncateString keeps trailing escapes so colours do not bleed.
- Emoji-heavy output where flags, keycaps and VS16 emoji should take 2 cells, matching Ghostty, iTerm and VS Code per the author's compatibility notes.
- Allocation-sensitive hot paths: String, Bytes, Rune and TruncateString without a tail report 0 allocs/op.

**Skip it when:**
- Before re-benchmarking against a current go-runewidth. The comparison pins v0.0.23 (2026-04-08). v0.0.24 (2026-05-29) added a precomputed East Asian width table, v0.0.28 a lazily built full-range lookup table, and v0.0.30 (2026-09-10) a rune fast path in StringWidth and Truncate. The README numbers have not been re-run, so the 2.3-3.3x East Asian gaps may have shrunk.
- Code that uses go-runewidth's Wrap, FillLeft, FillRight or TruncateLeft helpers, which have no displaywidth equivalent.
- Thai and similar text: a cluster's width comes from its leading rune, so Thai clusters ending in SARA AM (U+0E33) measure 1 where terminals draw 2 (issue #25, open since 2026-10-01).
- Layouts that must match macOS Terminal or existing go-runewidth output exactly. Here flags and keycaps are 2 cells and VS16 forces 2, while go-runewidth gives 1, and the author notes Mac Terminal draws flags as 1.
- Proportional-font text layout or shaping. It counts monospace cells only: no bidi, no line breaking, no font metrics.

**Integration:** module (pure-Go package) · github.com/clipperhouse/uax29/v2 v2.7.0 (grapheme segmentation, same author) · Go 1.18 per go.mod (generics); CI tests Go 1.20-1.25 with -race. The comparison module needs Go 1.20+, because the pinned go-runewidth v0.0.23 declares go 1.20. · any GOOS/GOARCH (no assembly; the published benchmark ran on darwin/arm64)

**Vs siblings:** Among the catalog's terminal-width siblings, pick displaywidth for Go code that wants grapheme-aware widths, ANSI-aware truncation and the library the Charm stack (lipgloss v2, x/ansi) and tablewriter already pull in. uniwidth's numbers are against the older go-runewidth v0.0.19 on an EPYC in CI, so the two cannot be ranked from catalog data. uwcwidth is the Python counterpart and not an alternative for Go.

**Gotchas:**
- EastAsianWidth defaults to false and is never set from the environment. Code moved from go-runewidth on a CJK locale silently changes ambiguous characters from 2 to 1 cells unless you set Options.EastAsianWidth yourself.
- Invalid UTF-8 is not validated and its results are undefined; the code is fuzzed only against panics and infinite loops. ControlSequences8Bit treats C1 bytes 0x80-0x9F, which are also UTF-8 continuation bytes, as escapes, and Truncate ignores that option.
- Width is taken per grapheme cluster from the leading rune, so measuring rune by rune (Rune) gives different and usually wrong totals for combining sequences, ZWJ emoji and flags. The README itself warns against it.
- Unicode 17 tables are compiled in (v0.9.0). Width changes arrive with library upgrades, as with v0.5.0's VS15 change and PR #24's narrower VS16 rule in May 2026, so pin the version if column layout must stay stable.

**Status:** Active: v0.11.0 is the latest changelog release, the last commit is 2026-05-17 and one issue is open. MIT, small and pure Go with a single dependency, and already used by lipgloss v2, charmbracelet/x/ansi and tablewriter.

[repo](https://github.com/clipperhouse/displaywidth) · [benchmark](https://github.com/clipperhouse/displaywidth)

##### font-rs  `Rust (optional C SSE3 intrinsics module)`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Small Rust TrueType glyph rasterizer (dense accumulation buffer plus prefix sum); 2016 author numbers claim 4-7.6x over FreeType 2.6.5.

**Beats:** FreeType 2.6.5 (glyph rasterization), per search snippets of the author's post; freetype-go is mentioned qualitatively in the README — Snippet only: the author's 2016 post timed rendering the glyph 'g' from Roboto Regular at 1-200 px/em on a 2.9 GHz Xeon E5-2690 against FreeType 2.6.5 and reports about 7.6x faster at larger sizes with the SIMD accumulate, over 4x at 12 px/em and over 6x at 12 px/em on a CJK face. FreeType's load flags and hinting mode, the compilers and the harness could not be checked (the post and the freetype-devel threads are blocked), and the repo's benches time font-rs alone; the measured code was the 2016 C SSE3 accumulate, which master replaced with a Rust std::arch port in 2018.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust library (language-filter mismatch). The only numbers (7.6x vs FreeType 2.6.5 at larger sizes, over 4x at 12 px/em, Xeon E5-2690) come from a 2016 Medium post seen only in search snippets (blocked here); the repo's benches time font-rs alone.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers remain snippet-only (Medium and lists.gnu.org blocked) and describe the 2016 C SSE3 accumulate module; master swapped to Rust std::arch in 2018 and crates.io 0.1.3 (2018-07-09) predates the Rust SIMD port, the metrics API and the 2020 out-of-bounds fix. The SSE accumulate loads up to 3 floats past the slice end (safe only through the Raster +4 padding; the crate's own tests read past the allocation, undefined behaviour); parse() panics on malformed fonts (#12, #44 open); prints to stdout; unbounded compound-glyph recursion; cmap format 4 only; integer pixel sizes; uses SSSE3 _mm_shuffle_epi8 without runtime detection (#29).

**How:** It is an accumulation-buffer (signed-area) scanline rasterizer in the libart/FreeType-smooth family, but instead of sorting cells into a sparse structure it writes exact-area coverage deltas for every line segment straight into a dense f32 array (Raster::draw_line, about 100 lines in src/raster.rs), which avoids branch mispredictions. Quadratic Beziers are flattened into n evenly spaced line segments with n derived from the curve's deviation (not recursive subdivision). One prefix-sum pass then turns the deltas into 8-bit coverage; the optional 'sse' feature does that four floats at a time with shift-and-add, min, truncating convert and a byte shuffle. Glyph parsing is pull-style iterators over the raw glyf data, so no point or curve arrays are allocated.

**Use it when:**
- Learning, porting or vendoring the original dense accumulation rasterizer: src/raster.rs plus src/accumulate.rs are about 230 lines of Apache-2.0 Rust excluding tests, and fontdue, ab_glyph_rasterizer and golang.org/x/image/vector follow the same design.
- Rasterizing grayscale coverage masks for a glyph atlas from trusted TrueType (glyf) fonts at integer pixel sizes, in Rust, with zero crate dependencies.
- Larger glyph sizes, where the author's snippet-only 2016 numbers show the widest gap to FreeType (about 7.6x with the SIMD accumulate).
- As a reference implementation when writing a C++ rasterizer: the algorithm is short enough to port directly, and FreeType's own GSoC 2022 'dense' module (branch gsoc-anurag-2022-final, src/dense) is a C port of it.

**Skip it when:**
- Untrusted or user-supplied fonts: parse() unwraps missing head/maxp tables and slices table offsets without range checks, so malformed files panic (issues #12 'Out-of-bounds path nodes shouldn't panic' and #44 'Potential wrapping add' are still open).
- CFF/CFF2 OpenType, variable fonts, colour or bitmap glyphs, or code points above U+FFFF (only cmap format 4 is read; lookup_glyph_id returns None above 0xFFFF).
- Small UI text that needs hinting or LCD subpixel rendering, or text that needs fractional sizes or subpixel x positions (size is a u32 and the glyph origin is snapped to whole pixels).
- Projects that need a maintained dependency: last commit 2020-09-05, 9 open issues, 3 open PRs, and the crates.io release (0.1.3, 2018-07-09, 8,212 downloads, one reverse dependency) predates the Rust SIMD port, the metrics API and the out-of-bounds fixes on master.
- Expecting the 2016 gap against current FreeType: FreeType's smooth rasterizer was sped up afterwards (2.11, 2021, per search snippets), and no current head-to-head numbers are public.

**Integration:** crate · none (Cargo.toml lists no dependencies; the 'sse' feature uses std::arch on master, while the crates.io 0.1.3 release still builds the C SSE module through build.rs) · Stable Rust for the library (CI built and tested on stable, beta and nightly; Cargo.toml has no edition, so edition 2015); nightly Rust for the benches (#![feature(test)]). No rust-version is declared. · any for the scalar build; the 'sse' feature is x86/x86-64 only, chosen at compile time with no runtime CPU detection (issue #29 open), and uses _mm_shuffle_epi8, an SSSE3 instruction despite the feature name

**Vs siblings:** Pick font-rs only to study or vendor the original ~230-line rasterizer core; for an application, fontdue (same accumulation design, maintained, TrueType and OpenType, its own latency plots against FreeType) is the better choice, and ttf-parser is the better choice if you only need outlines to feed your own rasterizer.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'sse' accumulate does unaligned 4-float loads up to 3 floats past the end of its input slice; it stays inside the allocation only because Raster::new pads its buffer by 4 floats. accumulate() is public, and its own unit tests call it on unpadded Vecs of length 1-7, so those tests read past the allocation (undefined behaviour in Rust; not behind the published numbers).
- The library prints to stdout: render_glyph prints 'glyph N error' and returns None for empty glyphs such as the space, and 'unhandled glyph case' for empty compound components.
- Compound glyphs are rendered recursively with no depth limit, and only the ARGS_ARE_XY_VALUES component form is handled (a TODO in src/font.rs); a font with cyclic components would recurse until the stack overflows.
- Coverage is scaled by 255 and truncated (issue #13 suggests 256-epsilon), and the SIMD and scalar prefix sums add in a different order, so 'sse' and non-'sse' builds are not guaranteed bit-identical; the unit tests only check hand-picked inputs.

**Status:** Abandoned (last commit 2020-09-05, crates.io release from 2018) and self-described as not production-ready, but Apache-2.0, dependency-free and small enough to vendor or port.

[repo](https://github.com/raphlinus/font-rs) · [benchmark](https://medium.com/@raphlinus/inside-the-fastest-font-renderer-in-the-world-75ae5270c445)

##### fontdue  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR Zlib`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust, no_std TrueType/OpenType glyph rasterizer and simple layout; first-party plots show 2.3x-11x lower per-glyph latency than FreeType.

**Beats:** FreeType 2 (glyph rasterization, via freetype-rs); also rusttype 0.9.2 and ab_glyph 0.2.3 for rasterization, glyph_brush_layout 0.2.0 for layout — First-party criterion plots last regenerated in September 2020 (CPU, rustc, flags and FreeType version unstated) time 37 glyphs of a pangram in Exo 2 at 10-200 px: roughly 3x faster than FreeType 2 (via freetype-rs) for TrueType and 11x for CFF at 10 px, 2.3x and 2.8x at 200 px, and 5.8x faster layout than glyph_brush_layout at 1000 characters (chart readings). The comparison favours fontdue: its parsing and flattening run at load outside the timed loop, while every FreeType iteration calls set_char_size and then parses, hints and renders each glyph. In current FreeType source that size request resets the auto-hinter and TrueType size state, and this TTF (no fpgm, 7-byte prep, maxSizeOfInstructions 0) meets ftobjs.c's rule for the auto-hinter. In the layout benchmark glyph_brush_layout does a kerning lookup per glyph pair and returns a new Vec per call, while fontdue reuses its Layout and applies no kerning.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust library (language-filter mismatch). Plots are dated 2020-09-05 and the harness is not like-for-like: the FreeType side renders hinted (LoadFlag::RENDER) and calls set_char_size inside the timed loop, while fontdue's Font::from_bytes parses and flattens every outline outside the timed loop at the exact benchmark size.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark asymmetry is larger than the record states: the FreeType loop calls set_char_size on every iteration (resetting the TrueType size state and autohint metrics), and the Exo2 test font has no fpgm, a 7-byte prep and maxSizeOfInstructions 0, so current FreeType routes it to the auto-hinter, meaning the TrueType rows include auto-hinting too (the 2020 FreeType version is unknown); the bench builds a separate Font per size with scale=size; the end-to-end dev/benches/load.rs results were never published; the layout bench pits glyph_brush_layout's per-pair kerning against fontdue's no-kerning layout that reuses its Layout. Soundness, not behind the numbers: unicode::decode_utf16 (name table, reached from Font::from_bytes) still uses from_u32_unchecked, so a leading lone low surrogate yields a code point of 0x110000 or more (undefined behaviour, same class as #172, unfixed in 0.9.4); #169 wrong glyphs for U+0080-U+00FF (cmap subtables merged without an is_unicode check); #164 170 MB for a 28,987-glyph CJK font.

**How:** Most work is moved to load time: every glyph reachable from cmap (and GSUB when load_substitutions is on) is outlined through ttf-parser, curves are flattened by midpoint subdivision with a triangle-area tolerance tied to FontSettings.scale, lines are re-based to the glyph bounding box with orientation fixed and reciprocal slopes precomputed. Per call it only scales those lines and runs a font-rs style signed-area accumulation rasterizer: each line walks the pixels it crosses (a separate path for vertical lines) and adds coverage deltas into an f32 buffer with unchecked indexing, then one prefix-sum pass converts the buffer to 8-bit coverage, four lanes at a time with SSE shift-adds, truncating converts and saturating packs into an output vector that is not zero-initialised. There is no hinting and no per-call table parsing; char-to-glyph lookup is a hashbrown HashMap.

**Use it when:**
- Rust games, immediate-mode GUIs or wasm apps that rasterize Latin-like glyphs on demand into a glyph atlas, load a font once, and care about per-glyph latency.
- no_std + alloc targets (embedded, wasm) that need TTF/OTF grayscale coverage without linking FreeType or another C library.
- Replacing rusttype or ab_glyph plus glyph_brush_layout where simple left-to-right wrapping without kerning or shaping is acceptable.
- Rendering at one or a few known sizes: building a Font with FontSettings.scale equal to that size reproduces the setup behind the README plots.

**Skip it when:**
- Complex scripts, running-text ligatures or bidi: there is no shaping (the README points to Cosmic Text) and the layout is self-described as naive.
- Crisp small UI text: no hinting of any kind, and open issues #162 and #168 report blurry text at small sizes.
- Large CJK fonts or tight memory: every mapped glyph is parsed and flattened at load (fast load is a stated non-goal); #164 links a Slint report of a 170 MB memory difference with a 28,987-glyph Chinese font.
- Untrusted font files in a hardened process: a transmute-to-char UB on crafted cmap data (#172) was fixed only in 0.9.4 (2026-07-29), the rasterizer relies on unchecked writes over sanitised geometry, and a fuzzing-harness PR (#17) has been open since April 2020.
- Colour emoji, embedded bitmap strikes, variable-font axes (#121, no API) or a C/C++ codebase: unsupported, and the API is Rust-only with no C ABI.

**Integration:** crate · ttf-parser 0.25 (opentype-layout, no-std-float); hashbrown 0.15 by default (or the std feature for std::HashMap); optional rayon 1.10 for the parallel feature (threaded font loading) · Not documented: no rust-version in Cargo.toml (edition 2018); the default hashbrown 0.15 dependency declares Rust 1.63 · Any target with alloc (no_std); SSE/SSE2 intrinsics on x86 and x86-64 with the default simd feature, scalar fallback elsewhere (aarch64, wasm)

**Vs siblings:** Pick fontdue over TiTanF when you want the more widely used pure-Rust rasterizer (TiTanF's own README measures fontdue faster at 10-160 px) and over raw ttf-parser when you need bitmaps, not just outlines; font-rs is the project it was forked from and then rewritten. Pick Parley (or cosmic-text) instead whenever text needs shaping, bidi or real paragraph layout.

**Gotchas:**
- FontSettings.scale (default 40 px) fixes the curve-flattening tolerance at load: per the doc comment, smaller sizes render slightly slower and larger sizes look worse. The README plots built a separate Font per benchmarked size with scale equal to that size, so a single default Font will not match them at 10 px or 200 px.
- rasterize allocates a new f32 accumulation buffer and a new Vec<u8> on every call; cache results (layout's GlyphRasterConfig is the documented hashable key).
- Kerning is read only from the legacy kern table (GPOS pair kerning is ignored, #161), and the Layout type applies no kerning at all.
- Open #169 reports wrong glyphs for U+0080-U+00FF with Courier, Monaco and Menlo; from_bytes merges codepoints from every cmap subtable without checking whether the subtable is Unicode, which would let a Mac Roman subtable overwrite Latin-1 entries (my reading of src/font.rs; not confirmed by the maintainer). Separately, the name-table decoder (unicode::decode_utf16, called from from_bytes) still builds chars with from_u32_unchecked without validating surrogates: a name string that starts with a low surrogate yields a code point of 0x110000 or more, the same class of UB as #172.

**Status:** Active but solo and slow-moving (Cargo badge 'experimental'): 0.9.4 on 2026-07-29 only fixed soundness issue #172, with 30 open issues and 7 open PRs; 9.2M crates.io downloads (2.3M recent) and an MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR Zlib licence make it easy to adopt in Rust, but it is not copyable into C++ without an FFI layer.

[repo](https://github.com/mooman219/fontdue) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mooman219/fontdue)

##### hypher  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Allocation-free Rust Knuth-Liang hyphenator with patterns embedded as automata; about 2x faster per word than the hyphenation crate.

**Beats:** hyphenation crate 0.8 (embedded Liang/Knuth patterns, the common Rust hyphenation library) — A first-party Criterion 0.3 run on an Apple M1 (rustc version and flags unstated) timed one word per call: 'extensive' with English patterns 356 ns vs 698 ns for hyphenation 0.8 (about 1.96x) and 'διαμερίσματα' with monotonic Greek 503 ns vs 1121 ns (about 2.23x, derived from page data); the 0 us load rows are a design property, not a timed run. The table dates from the first README commit (2022-03-06, before 0.1.0) and has not been re-run since the tries were pre-generated (October 2022) or the Bytes buffer changed (PR #20, 2025), and the baseline also does exception lookup, soft-hyphen handling and case realignment that hypher skips, so part of the gap is less work rather than a faster equivalent.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust hyphenation crate (language-filter mismatch); text-layout primitive, not shaping. bench/bench.rs criterion run against the hyphenation 0.8 crate (Apple M1; rustc and flags unstated): 1.96x English, 2.23x Greek (derived); the '0 us load' is a design property, never timed. Baseline is the Rust-ecosystem incumbent (1.15M downloads).

**Known shortcoming:** The README table dates from the first README commit (2022-03-06, before 0.1.0) and was never re-run after the tries were pre-generated (October 2022) or the Bytes change (PR #20). Not like-for-like: the hyphenation crate also scans soft hyphens, refolds case, looks up an exception HashMap and returns a Vec. hypher's generate.rs parses only \patterns{} and drops \hyphenation{} exceptions (issues #24 and #17 open; 15 en-us exceptions such as 'project' and 'present'), though hyph-de and hyph-el have none so the benchmark words agree. MAX_INLINE_SIZE is 45 in lib.rs while the README says 41.

**How:** Liang's pattern algorithm run over a byte-level (UTF-8) trie that tests/generate.rs builds from each .tex file, suffix-compresses into a minimal acyclic automaton (identical subtrees merged) and encodes with variable-width (i8/i16/i24) relative target offsets and shared level slices packed as dist*10+level in one byte. The encoded tries/*.bin are include_bytes!'d and decoded lazily state by state during the walk, so nothing is deserialized at start-up; the level array lives in a 47-byte stack buffer for words up to 45 bytes, so the hot path allocates nothing. The baseline does more per call: it scans for soft hyphens, case-folds into a new string with realignment shifts, looks the word up in an exception HashMap and returns a Vec of breaks.

**Use it when:**
- Rust text layout or typesetting that hyphenates many short words with a language that can change per word: no dictionary handle to keep alive or cache (the reason it was written for Typst, per the author's 2022 post).
- Binaries that must embed patterns: English alone adds 27 KiB and all 48 languages about 1.1 MiB, against about 2.8 MB for hyphenation's embed_all (author's figures).
- no_std, WASM or start-up-sensitive tools where hyphenation's Standard::from_embedded cost (151 us for English in the README table) matters more than the per-word time.
- Permissive-licence products: only patterns under LPPL, MPL, MIT or BSD-3 style licences are included, and the crate itself is MIT OR Apache-2.0.

**Skip it when:**
- When TeX-exact output matters: the generator parses only \patterns{} and drops every \hyphenation{} exception block (open issues #24 and #17), so the 15 exceptions in hyph-en-us.tex (for example 'project' and 'present', which TeX leaves unbroken, and 'ta-ble') get pattern breaks instead; the hyphenation crate consults them.
- Languages or variants not compiled in: no de-1901, en-gb, Welsh, Irish, Kazakh, Romanian or GPL-only pattern sets (issues #22, #25, closed PR #7), and no way to load a pattern file at runtime (issue #11).
- C or C++ projects: there is no C API, so this needs a Rust toolchain plus your own extern "C" shim.
- Non-standard hyphenation (spelling changes at the break, as in hyphenation's Extended dictionaries for Hungarian and Catalan) or soft-hyphen-aware input: neither is supported.

**Integration:** crate · none (no_std; optional alloc feature on by default) · Rust 1.64 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, checked by the CI min-version job); CI tests on 1.88 · any (pure safe Rust, no SIMD or platform code, #![forbid(unsafe_code)])

**Vs siblings:** It is the only hyphenation library in this category; the layout siblings solve other steps (Parley shapes and lays out text, Typst is a full typesetter that depends on hypher through typst-layout per crates.io reverse dependencies), so use it alongside them when your own line breaker needs hyphenation points.

**Gotchas:**
- Without the alloc feature, words longer than MAX_INLINE_SIZE (45 bytes in src/lib.rs; the README still says 41 and the 2022 post 39) panic instead of allocating.
- Lowercasing keeps a character unchanged when its lowercase form has a different UTF-8 length or expands to several chars (for example U+0130 or U+1E9E), so patterns stop matching around it; there is no Unicode normalization either, so NFD input with combining accents misses NFC patterns. The hyphenation crate refolds and realigns these cases and offers nfc/nfd features.
- Output is hyphenation segments under each language's left/right minima, not linguistic syllables: short words come back as one segment (issue #5), and French words with apostrophes can break right after the apostrophe (issue #13, open).
- Each language is a Cargo feature; the default 'full' feature embeds all 48, so pick features explicitly to keep binaries small.

**Status:** Active (0.1.8 released 2026-09-17, 3.29M crates.io downloads, used by typst-layout and nine other crates), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 code with permissively licensed embedded patterns; copyable as a Rust crate, not from C++.

[repo](https://github.com/typst/hypher) · [benchmark](https://github.com/typst/hypher)

##### kb_text_shape  `C`  `Zlib`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-header C library for Unicode segmentation and OpenType shaping; claimed faster than HarfBuzz, measured 2-160x slower independently.

**Beats:** HarfBuzz — The one opened independent comparison (HarfBuzz maintainer Behdad Esfahbod, discussion #5375, 2025-07-23, HarfBuzz's benchmark-shape and benchmark-font through its kbts backend; CPU, compiler, flags and kb version not stated) found kb slower everywhere: Roboto paragraph 26.5 vs 9.11 ms, Roboto words 38.4 vs 11.3 ms, Amiri 48.3 vs 40.6 ms, Gulzar Urdu 5198 vs 782 ms, Gulzar Latin 4021 vs 24.9 ms, Noto Devanagari 50.5 vs 25.3 ms, and font load 40x to 760x slower; that path converts HarfBuzz buffers and allocates kb glyph storage on every call (src/hb-kbts.cc), which taxes kb somewhat but cannot account for 6.6x to 160x gaps. The author's claim of 4.5x faster on average (HarfBuzz's test suite plus own tests, Ryzen 9 5900HX, clang 20, Linux) exists only in a search snippet with no harness, and no re-measurement of v2.06 ('Faster GSUB and GPOS feature culling'), v2.07 ('Performance improvements') or later versions was found.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster than HarfBuzz: the author's 4.5x claim exists only in a search snippet of a blocked post, while HarfBuzz discussion #5375 has the HarfBuzz maintainer measuring kb_text_shape 2.9x to 160x slower at shaping and 40x to 760x slower at font load (harness perf/benchmark-shape.cc plus src/hb-kbts.cc; no CPU, compiler, flags or kb version), and kb issue #21 reports a third party seeing about 2x slower. Kept as a flagged entry (the author's number is unverified, not shown fabricated); kb is now v2.28e.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e110, 2026-10-05): not-faster flag stands at C. HarfBuzz main pins kb v2.07 (ca6c962) while the header is v2.28e; the kb version in the July 2025 run is unknown and the 2.06/2.07 changelog performance work was never re-measured. hb-kbts.cc allocates glyph storage per call, a small tax that cannot explain 6.6-160x gaps; font load builds glyph x lookup bit matrices, matching the 40-760x slower load. Record caveats were outdated: variable fonts added in v2.28, SourceSerifVariable crash fixed (issue #44 closed), crash issues #43, #61, #63 fixed; no fuzzing. Nothing new found on the author's 4.5x claim.

**Independent measurement:** HarfBuzz maintainer run (discussion #5375)

**How:** Font loading copies the font's tables into a private blob, byte-swaps them in place to native endianness, and precomputes bit matrices of glyph x lookup and glyph x lookup-subtable coverage, so during shaping one bit test decides whether a lookup or subtable can touch a glyph instead of walking coverage tables; each shape_config also builds a glyph x enabled-lookup matrix for the active feature set. Transient shaping state lives in contexts and scratchpads that the caller can size, place in its own memory (fixed-memory placement is supported) and reuse across calls. The cost is paid up front: building those matrices scales with glyphs x lookups, which fits the independent measurement of font loading 40x to 760x slower than HarfBuzz. kbts_LoadFont also accepts a prebuilt kbts blob, so that work can be done once and shipped.

**Use it when:**
- Games, editors-for-display, tools and embedded targets that want shaping plus segmentation from one Zlib-licensed header with no ICU, FriBidi, FreeType or HarfBuzz build, and are willing to give up speed for that.
- Programs that must control every allocation: contexts and scratchpads can be placed in caller memory, a custom allocator can be supplied, and KB_TEXT_SHAPE_NO_CRT drops the C runtime.
- Display-only rendering of complex scripts (Arabic, Indic v2 fonts, Khmer, Myanmar, Hangul and others) with a small, bundled and trusted font set loaded once at startup or shipped as prebuilt blobs.
- Prototyping a text pipeline where the README's model (segment, shape, then hand glyph IDs to stb_truetype or another rasterizer) is enough.

**Skip it when:**
