- Throughput-critical shaping: the only reachable measurements put it behind HarfBuzz on every font tested (2.9x on a Roboto paragraph, 6.6x on Urdu Nastaliq, 160x on Latin text in Gulzar) and about 2x behind raqm/HarfBuzz in a user's test (kb issue #21).
- Untrusted or user-supplied fonts: the header says it provides no security guarantee, crash reports on real fonts were fixed during 2025-2026 (issues #43 NotoNastaliqUrdu, #44 SourceSerifVariable-Roman, #61 and #63 glyph insertion), and there is no fuzzing in the repository, unlike HarfBuzz's oss-fuzz coverage.
- Text editing, selection, cursor movement or text-extractable PDF: glyphs carry a source codepoint index, but there is no documented HarfBuzz-style cluster merging, explicit bidi control characters (embeddings, overrides, isolates) are not supported, hinting is unsupported, and there is no vertical layout (HarfBuzz's kbts backend rejects vertical directions; issue #64 asking how to do vertical text is open).
- Apps that open many fonts or large fonts on demand: each load copies the whole font into dirty memory and builds per-glyph-per-lookup bit matrices (Gulzar load plus one-character shape 235.9 ms against HarfBuzz's 0.31 ms).
- Dictionary-based word breaking (CJK), Indic1 fonts (e.g. 'beng' rather than 'bng2'), Zawgyi, the Syriac abbreviation mark, Windows 3.1 Arabic or Thai/Lao PUA fonts, which the header lists as unsupported.

**Integration:** header-only (stb-style: define KB_TEXT_SHAPE_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit; KB_TEXT_SHAPE_STATIC for static linkage) · none (C runtime optional via KB_TEXT_SHAPE_NO_CRT with user KBTS_MALLOC, KBTS_FREE, KBTS_MEMSET, KBTS_MEMCPY) · C99 or C++ (uses declare-anywhere, so not C89/VC6); GCC 15.2 reports unused-variable and enum-conditional warnings in the current header (issue #91, 2026-10-02), so -Werror builds need flags adjusted · any: portable scalar C, with SSE2 used only for float rounding when available; MSVC, GCC and clang paths in the header

**Vs siblings:** It is the only C/C++ shaper in the category; the catalogued shaping siblings are Rust (Fontations, sigilbuzz, Parley), .NET (SixLabors.Fonts) or JavaScript (text-shaper, rustybuzz-wasm) and all measure against HarfBuzz or its ports. Pick kb over HarfBuzz only for a dependency-free single header with built-in segmentation and trusted fonts, not for speed.

**Gotchas:**
- The font stack prefers the most recently pushed font, so fallbacks must be pushed first unless KBTS_SHAPE_CONTEXT_FLAG_FONT_PRIORITY_BOTTOM_TO_TOP is set.
- In the context API, kbts_glyph.UserIdOrCodepointIndex is always a codepoint index; your own user ID has to be read back through kbts_ShapeGetShapeCodepoint.
- With KB_TEXT_SHAPE_NO_CRT and no custom allocator, the default allocator returns 0; a custom KBTS_MALLOC must also return non-null for zero-size requests (open issue #73).
- The API has churned: v2.0 replaced the 1.x API, v2.07 changed kbts_ShapeDirect and struct layouts, and v2.28 added variation-aware *2 entry points; HarfBuzz still pins v2.07 (commit ca6c962) while the header is at v2.28e.

**Status:** Actively developed (v2.28e, last commit 2026-10-02, 80 commits, about 1.2k stars, 13 open issues, frequent bug-fix releases) and Zlib-licensed, so easy to vendor, but it is a young, single-author shaper whose speed advantage is unproven.

[repo](https://github.com/JimmyLefevre/kb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/harfbuzz/harfbuzz/discussions/5375)

##### msdfgl  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

OpenGL shader port of Chlumsky's MSDF glyph generator; first-party chart shows 60x-132x faster than single-threaded msdfgen on one laptop.

**Beats:** msdfgen (Chlumsky's CPU multi-channel signed distance field generator, single-threaded and OpenMP builds); incumbent for MSDF font atlas generation, not one of HarfBuzz or FreeType — The only evidence is the first-party README chart; there is no benchmark code, no compiler or flags, and no msdfgen version. Setup: ASCII 0-127 of DejaVu Sans, mean of 100 runs, Core i7 '8550m' with Intel UHD Graphics 620 on Debian. msdfgl takes 0.0081 s to 0.2345 s across scales 1 to 8, against 0.4890 s to 31 s for msdfgen (60x to 132x) and 0.1334 s to 8 s for OpenMP msdfgen (16x to 34x); both msdfgen values at scale 8 are extrapolated. The comparison is not like-for-like in three ways. msdfgl's time includes having the result in a texture while msdfgen's excludes the upload. msdfgl skips the roughly one-second shader compile. In msdfgen v1.6 (April 2019), generateMSDF also runs msdfErrorCorrection by default, a step msdfgl lacks; whether the benchmark called generateMSDF is not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** README chart labels only, no benchmark code or flags; a GPU (Intel UHD 620) against CPU msdfgen (i7) on one laptop SoC, so a different machine class. No cubic segments supported; the msdfgen 8.0 points are extrapolated. Baseline msdfgen is not a listed incumbent.

**Known shortcoming:** Not like-for-like with msdfgen: msdfgen 1.6's generateMSDF runs msdfErrorCorrection by default while msdfgl skips it, generate has no glFinish, and the benchmark code is unpublished. Likely edge-colouring off-by-one in msdfgl_serializer.c (prev_npoints indexed at nsegments-2 with the pointer on the last segment), affecting quality rather than timings; crashes on CFF and cubic fonts (cubic_to NULL, unchecked FreeType calls); a corners[30] stack overflow is unchecked; glyphs with more than 127 segments break on x86.

**How:** msdfgen's per-pixel stage runs as a fragment shader, one fragment per atlas texel, with one two-triangle draw call per glyph. That stage covers true and pseudo distance to every edge, the overlapping-contour inner/outer combine, and the median. Outlines are serialized on the CPU into an R8UI metadata buffer and an R32F point buffer that the shader reads with texelFetch. The CPU only decomposes outlines with FreeType, computes contour winding and runs msdfgen-style corner-based edge coloring. The shader also does less work than the baseline: it computes in 32-bit float rather than msdfgen's double, and it has no error-correction pass.

**Use it when:**
- An application already rendering with OpenGL 3.3 core or OpenGL ES 3.2 that wants MSDF text built at runtime, including on-demand glyphs through msdfgl_set_missing_glyph_callback, instead of shipping a prebaked atlas.
- Large glyph scales or big glyph sets, where CPU msdfgen takes seconds (README: 7.74 s at scale 4 against 0.0645 s for msdfgl).
- TrueType fonts with quadratic outlines for Latin-like scripts (the benchmark font is DejaVu Sans).
- C code bases that want a small MIT library whose only external dependency is FreeType (glad is vendored).

**Skip it when:**
- OpenType/CFF fonts with cubic outlines are unsupported, and the failure is unsafe. From the code: msdfgl_serialize_glyph sets FreeType's cubic_to callback to NULL, and FT_Outline_Decompose calls it without a check, so generating a cubic glyph should crash. The size pass's error is ignored first, so serialization also writes into a zero-size buffer slot. Convert fonts to quadratic first (cu2qu is suggested in issue #8).
- Real text layout: there is no shaping (no HarfBuzz), only optional FreeType kerning, so no ligatures, bidi or complex scripts. Multiline printf is only an open PR (#15).
- Offline atlas baking, headless or CPU-only pipelines, WebGL, Metal or Vulkan-only renderers. A GL context is required, and the text renderer uses a geometry shader (issue #3, open).
- Ornamental, symbol or CJK glyphs with long contours. From the code: corner indices go into a fixed int corners[30] stack array with no bounds check, and per-contour segment and contour counts are stored in a char. char is signed on x86, so counts over 127 skip CPU coloring, while the GPU reads the same bytes as unsigned 8-bit.
- When output must match msdfgen quality. There is no error-correction pass. Teardrop contours with 1 or 2 segments print 'Non-supported shape' and are left uncoloured, and wrong-winding detection is a README TODO. The shader math is declared precision mediump float, which GLES drivers that honour it may run at reduced precision.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (CMake, BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults to ON) · FreeType 2.9.1+ (CMake downloads 2.10.1 if none is found), glad (vendored), an OpenGL 3.3 core or OpenGL ES 3.2 context; glfw only for the example · C11 (c_std_11), CMake 3.11; README reports a 32-bit MSVC 2019 build on Windows · Linux (Wayland EGL with GLES 3.2, or GL 3.3 core with glfw3), macOS Mojave (deprecated OpenGL), Windows 10; README says it was tested only on Intel GPUs

**Vs siblings:** fontdue, font-rs and TiTanF rasterize coverage bitmaps on the CPU at a fixed pixel size, and Pathfinder 3 is a general Rust GPU vector rasterizer. Pick msdfgl for a C program on OpenGL 3.3 or ES 3.2 that wants one runtime-built atlas that stays sharp at any text size.

**Gotchas:**
- Shader compilation takes close to a second (README) and happens in msdfgl_create_context. Create the context once; the benchmark excludes this time.
- msdfgl_generate_* only queues GL commands; there is no glFinish. A CPU timer around the call measures submission rather than GPU completion. The README says it averaged 100 runs and subtracted context creation and destruction time, but the benchmark code is not published.
- Likely edge-colouring bug (found by reading msdfgl_serializer.c, not tested): when detecting corners, the start-of-contour tangent takes its point count from the second-to-last segment (meta_index + 2 * (nsegments - 2) + 1) while the pointer sits on the last segment. When those two segments differ in type (line and quad), the tangent is wrong, and it can read the next contour's first point. That can misplace a colour switch and produce corner artifacts. It affects output quality, not the timings.
- The atlas texture is GL_RGBA32F (16 bytes per texel), and its height doubles as glyphs are added. Generation fails once the height passes GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit is 2024-10-13 (a warning fix), the core code dates from 2019-2020, and 5 issues are open. It is MIT-licensed and small (about 1,550 lines of C plus shaders), so it can be vendored, but it needs fixes before it is safe on untrusted or CFF fonts.

[repo](https://github.com/nyyManni/msdfgl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/nyyManni/msdfgl)

##### sigilbuzz  `Rust (C ABI)`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust, no_std HarfBuzz-API text shaper with an hb_* C library; faster than rustybuzz on Latin/Hebrew only, slower on complex scripts.

**Beats:** rustybuzz 0.20 (archived Rust port of HarfBuzz) only; HarfBuzz itself and FreeType are never measured, and the sigilbuzz-capi hb_* C library is never benchmarked against libharfbuzz — First-party Criterion medians from the 0.6.0 release on the maintainer's unnamed macOS arm64 machine (rustc version not stated) shape one fixed string per script against rustybuzz 0.20 with default features: sigilbuzz is faster on Latin (11.39 vs 15.03 us) and Hebrew (10.99 vs 17.28 us) and slower on Arabic (290 vs 108 us), Devanagari (419 vs 85.8 us) and Khmer (91.6 vs 49.0 us). Reading the bench sources shows only the Latin corpus is the 200 codepoints PERFORMANCE.md claims (compile-time asserted); Arabic is 183, Devanagari 188, Hebrew 179 and Khmer 147 codepoints (same string for both engines, so ratios are unaffected). The CHANGELOG says the Indic shaper matched HarfBuzz 14.5.0 on only 4,826 of 7,656 test strings and the Khmer shaper on 281 of the first 510 before the 0.22.0 rewrites, so the Devanagari and Khmer timings were taken on shapers later replaced for correctness, and no run shows output parity on the bench strings.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust with a C ABI via sigilbuzz-capi (exports hb_* symbols; language-filter mismatch). Compared only against rustybuzz 0.20, never HarfBuzz, so no HarfBuzz win is shown: Latin 1.32x and Hebrew 1.57x faster, Arabic 2.70x, Devanagari 4.89x and Khmer 1.87x slower; numbers from 0.6.0 (2026-04-24, current 0.23.0) on an unnamed macOS arm64 machine. rustybuzz itself is 1.5-2x slower than HarfBuzz.

**Known shortcoming:** PERFORMANCE.md dates from 0.6.0 and was never re-run after 0.22.0 rewrote GSUB (previously quadratic) and the Indic, Khmer and USE shapers; before 0.22.0 the Indic shaper matched HarfBuzz on only 4,826 of 7,656 strings and Khmer on 281 of 510, so the Devanagari and Khmer timings come from shapers later replaced for correctness. Only the Latin corpus has the claimed 200 code points (Arabic 183, Devanagari 188, Hebrew 179, Khmer 147; the same string on both sides, so ratios hold). No shape-plan cache (pipeline.rs); no HarfBuzz timing anywhere; 0 stars; releases 0.1.0 to 0.21.0 were all cut on 2026-04-24/25; ROADMAP lists known bugs (CFF2 FDSelect, morx).

**How:** There is no special fast-path technique; the documented gains are removal of algorithmic waste in the GSUB driver. Per docs/PERFORMANCE.md (0.6.0, #74-#76) it keeps one glyph-ID snapshot per lookup instead of rebuilding a Vec at every cursor step, parses each lookup's subtables once per lookup walk (ParsedGsubSubtable in src/shape/gsub_parsed.rs) instead of at every position, and pre-checks coverage so positions whose glyph is in no subtable's coverage skip dispatch, mirroring HarfBuzz's skip-iterator digest check. In 0.22.0 GSUB moved to HarfBuzz's out-buffer model (out_info/next_glyph/replace_glyphs), making ligature and multiple substitution linear instead of quadratic in run length. src/shape/pipeline.rs states there is no shape-plan cache, so every shape() call re-selects features and re-parses lookup subtables, which is a likely reason it trails rustybuzz on complex scripts.

**Use it when:**
- Rust projects that need a dependency-free, no_std (alloc-only) shaper, e.g. wasm32-unknown-unknown or embedded targets, where linking C HarfBuzz is not an option.
- Byte-for-byte deterministic shaping output for golden-file tests, replays or lockstep networking (no random hashers, integer design-unit output).
- Mostly Latin or Hebrew text where the first-party Criterion run showed it 1.32x (Latin, Open Sans) and 1.57x (Hebrew, Noto Sans Hebrew) faster than rustybuzz 0.20 on an unnamed Apple arm64 machine.
- C or C++ builds that want to drop the C/C++ toolchain dependency of HarfBuzz and can live with the hb_* subset declared in sigilbuzz-capi's include/hb.h.
- Projects that also want subsetting, WOFF2, COLRv1 paint and a GPU outline encoder from one pure-Rust workspace.

**Skip it when:**
- Arabic, Indic (Devanagari etc.) or Khmer heavy workloads: the only published numbers show it 2.70x, 4.89x and 1.87x slower than rustybuzz, which rustybuzz's own README puts at 1.5-2x slower than HarfBuzz; there is no measurement against HarfBuzz at all.
- When you want a speedup over libharfbuzz from C/C++: the hb_* drop-in library has never been benchmarked against HarfBuzz, and every shape() call rebuilds its plan (no shape-plan cache), unlike hb_shape_plan caching in HarfBuzz.
- Production stacks that need maturity: 0 stars and 0 forks, crates.io publication only since 2026-10-02, releases 0.1.0 to 0.21.0 all cut on 2026-04-24/25, pre-1.0 API that may change in any minor release, and a ROADMAP 'Known bugs' list (CFF2 FDSelect format 4 truncation, morx ligature action bug, VARC axis inheritance, CFF hint-mask sizing).
- Code that relies on the full HarfBuzz C API: sigilbuzz-capi exports only what include/hb.h declares (e.g. no hb_font_draw_glyph, no hb_paint_funcs_get_empty, the paint image callback never fires) and targets the 8.2 API surface.
- Text that needs HarfBuzz's automatic fraction features or rand, or relies on Script-property lookups outside the older UnicodeScript block ranges (ROADMAP lists these as gaps).

**Integration:** crate (sigilbuzz); C library via sigilbuzz-capi built as cdylib + staticlib with cargo-c (cargo cinstall installs libsigilbuzz, include/sigilbuzz/hb.h, sigilbuzz.pc and a CMake package) · none for the core crate; companion crates add miniz_oxide (WOFF1/PNG), brotli (WOFF2) and clap (CLI); sigilbuzz-capi build needs cargo-c 0.10.0+ for the install step · Rust 1.81 (MSRV, edition 2021); cargo-c 0.10.0+ for the C library install · any target stable Rust builds, including wasm32-unknown-unknown and no_std + alloc; benchmarks only reported for macOS arm64

**Vs siblings:** Among shaping siblings, SixLabors.Fonts is the pick for .NET and text-shaper or rustybuzz-wasm for JavaScript, and those at least compare against a HarfBuzz build; pick sigilbuzz only when you need a pure-Rust, no_std or C-toolchain-free shaper (or an hb_*-compatible C library built from Rust) and can accept that no HarfBuzz parity in speed has been shown. For full paragraph layout in Rust, Parley (on HarfRust) is the more established choice.

**Gotchas:**
- An unset direction shapes as LTR even for Arabic or Hebrew (no automatic direction detection in shape()); set Direction::Rtl yourself, as the benches do for Arabic and Hebrew.
- With no script set, shape() splits mixed text into script runs and shapes each with its own shaper, which differs from HarfBuzz; call buffer.guess_segment_properties() first to get HarfBuzz's one-shaper behavior.
- sigilbuzz-capi returns a fresh empty object where HarfBuzz returns its inert singleton, and earlier capi releases had different reference/destroy rules for subset sets: code written for capi before 0.3.0 can double-free now.
- The published PERFORMANCE.md numbers come from 0.6.0 (2026-04-24) and were never re-run after the 0.22.0 rewrite of GSUB and the Indic, Khmer, Myanmar and USE shapers, despite the file's own rule to update it whenever a hot path changes; current speed relative to rustybuzz is unknown in either direction.

**Status:** Very active (0.23.0 on 2026-10-03, 546 commits, Apache-2.0) but young and unadopted: 0 stars, crates.io since 2026-10-02, pre-1.0 API, and a speed table that predates the current shaping engine by 16 minor releases.

[repo](https://github.com/Oneiriq/sigilbuzz) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Oneiriq/sigilbuzz/HEAD/docs/PERFORMANCE.md)

##### text-shaper  `TypeScript`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-TypeScript OpenType shaper and rasterizer; about 1.2-1.5x harfbuzzjs (WASM) on simple-script shaping under Bun.

**Beats:** harfbuzzjs ^0.4.13 (HarfBuzz compiled to WebAssembly, called from JavaScript), not native HarfBuzz; opentype.js also compared; the rasterization rows compare with FreeType through the freetype2 (node-freetype2) Node native binding — Under Bun 1.3.4 on an M1 Pro (one run, 2025-12-16, 10 warmup calls then 3 batches of 100), shapeInto with reused buffers beat harfbuzzjs ^0.4.13 by about 1.2-1.5x on Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and CJK text. These are the only comparable rows, and output was never compared. The Hindi 3.25x, Khmer 2.25x, Thai 1.58x and Myanmar 10.6x rows time shaping that applies no script-specific GSUB features (only content-detected reordering), so they are not comparable. The path-extraction (50x) and text-to-SVG (5.3-7.1x) rows time WeakMap cache hits for getGlyphPath and pathToSVG against harfbuzzjs regenerating path strings, plus a buffer.json() serialization in the pipeline case.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded to C: TypeScript library whose baseline is harfbuzzjs (WASM), not native HarfBuzz. Several README rows are not valid comparisons: the path-extraction row times a WeakMap cache hit, and the complex-script rows call shapeInto with no script or direction (Zyyy, LTR), so default features only and no RTL shaping. README ratios differ from the committed benchmarks.json (Apple M1 Pro, Bun 1.3.4); the no-features row is 0.91x (slower). Only the Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and CJK rows are like-for-like, at about 1.2-1.5x.

**Known shortcoming:** The complex-script rows (Hindi 3.6x, Myanmar 10.5x, Thai, Khmer) compare incomplete shaping: by code reading there are no Indic, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar or USE default features, GSUB lookups never read the per-glyph masks set by the Arabic and Indic setup, and the complex-script tests check glyph counts only (retier-25 limits the claim to the Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, CJK, Hebrew and Arabic rows at 1.04-1.48x). pathToSVG is WeakMap-cached, so the text-to-SVG 5.3-7.1x rows time cache hits while the harfbuzzjs side pays buffer.json(); shape() ignores buffer direction and the README's bidi auto-reorder claim is not implemented.

**How:** It is plain JIT-friendly TypeScript with no JS-to-WASM boundary. Shape plans are cached per font, script, language, features and axis coordinates, and shapeInto reuses caller-owned buffers. Each lookup carries a SetDigest filter, so lookups whose coverage cannot match any glyph in the buffer are skipped, and single-subtable delta substitutions take a fast path. In the benchmark, each harfbuzzjs call instead pays for buffer creation, a text copy into WASM memory, segment-property guessing and destroy. Glyph outlines and default SVG strings are memoized in WeakMaps (getGlyphPath, pathToSVG), and optional embedded WASM kernels accelerate some raster paths. Much of the measured lead on complex scripts comes from doing less shaping work, not from faster code.

**Use it when:**
- Browser, Bun or Node apps that need shaping plus rendering in JavaScript without shipping a HarfBuzz WASM binary: Canvas or WebGL text, glyph atlases, SDF/MSDF, hinted grayscale or LCD bitmaps.
- Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and CJK text with standard features (ccmp, locl, liga, calt, kern, mark). These are the only like-for-like rows, at about 1.2-1.5x harfbuzzjs ops/s on an M1 Pro under Bun.
- Hot loops that shape many short strings with the same font and options, where shapeInto with reused buffers and cached plans avoids per-call allocation.
- Repeated SVG or path output for the same glyphs (icons, labels), where the WeakMap path and SVG caches turn repeated requests into lookups.

**Skip it when:**
- Arabic, Indic, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar or other complex scripts where output must match HarfBuzz. getDefaultGsubFeatures enables Arabic, Syriac, Mongolian, Tibetan, Ethiopic and Georgian extras but no Indic, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar or USE features. GSUB lookups run in lookup-index order over the whole buffer, and no code in shaper.ts reads the per-glyph masks that setupArabicMasks or setupIndicMasks write. The complex-script tests check glyph counts and mask arrays, not glyph output.
- RTL or mixed-direction text through shape() alone: reversal happens only when options.direction is 'rtl'. UnicodeBuffer.setDirection does not trigger it, and shapeInto does no bidi, despite the README's 'automatically reordered' example. Use processBidi and reorderGlyphs yourself.
- C, C++ or native code: it is TypeScript only, and native HarfBuzz was never measured. The baseline is harfbuzzjs, the WASM build.
- Decisions based on the README table: it does not match the committed results file. The results come from one 2025-12-16 run, and on mixed text with features turned off text-shaper is slower (0.91x).
- CommonJS-only consumers: the package is ESM-only ("type": "module", import-only exports), built for a browser target.

**Integration:** module (npm package text-shaper, ESM, 0.1.28 at HEAD) · none at runtime (harfbuzzjs, opentype.js and freetype2 are dev-only, for the benchmarks) · an ES-module JavaScript runtime (modern browser, Bun or Node.js); no minimum versions documented; built with Bun and TypeScript 7.0.2 · any JavaScript runtime; optional embedded WebAssembly kernels for some raster paths

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Typr.js (a parser vs opentype.js) when you need GSUB/GPOS shaping plus hinted rasterization in pure JavaScript. Pick it over rustybuzz-wasm (parity with harfbuzzjs) when you want no WASM and your text is Latin, Cyrillic, Greek or CJK. For correct complex-script output in JavaScript, harfbuzzjs or rustybuzz-wasm remains the safer choice. fontdue, font-rs and TiTanF are Rust rasterizers and do not compete in JS.

**Gotchas:**
- shape() returns a GlyphBuffer from a shared pool. Call releaseBuffer() when done, and do not keep using a buffer after releasing it, or the next shape() call will overwrite it.
- Without options.script, the buffer's default script 'Zyyy' selects the font's DFLT (then latn) lookups with only the default feature set. Content-based detection then sets masks that lookups never consult, so pass script and features explicitly.
- getGlyphPath and pathToSVG return cached objects and strings for default options. Mutating a returned GlyphPath corrupts later calls for that glyph.
- Cluster values from addStr are code-point indices starting at startCluster, not UTF-8 or UTF-16 offsets.

**Status:** Active (version 0.1.28, last commit 2026-07-17, MIT, 51 stars, 2 closed issues and 0 open). It is a young solo project, fine to vendor for JavaScript rendering of simple scripts, but not a verified HarfBuzz substitute for complex scripts.

[repo](https://github.com/wiedymi/text-shaper) · [benchmark](https://github.com/wiedymi/text-shaper/blob/main/docs/.vitepress/data/benchmarks.json)

##### TiTanF  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zero-dependency no_std Rust TrueType rasterizer; 1.5-3.5x faster than RustType and ab_glyph, slower than Fontdue below 200px.

**Beats:** RustType and ab_glyph (long-standing, widely used pure-Rust glyph rasterizers); Fontdue, another pure-Rust rasterizer, also measured and faster at 10-160px; FreeType and HarfBuzz are not measured — These are first-party criterion medians (cargo bench, default bench profile, no RUSTFLAGS, so a baseline SSE2 x86-64 build; CPU and rustc unstated) for rasterizing a 106-character string (30 CJK, 76 ASCII; the README says 84) from NotoSansSC-Medium.ttf, which is not in the repo, at seven sizes with the cache off and every library's font load outside the timed loop. TiTanF is 1.5-3.5x faster than RustType 0.9.3 and 1.7-3.1x faster than ab_glyph 0.2.32. Against fontdue 0.9.3, with FontSettings.scale set to each size, it is 1.06-1.47x slower up to 160 px and 1.10x and 1.28x faster at 200 and 320 px (derived from page data). The table was committed in 0c4078c (2026-07-08), together with the string change and after the restructuring commit, so it matches current code. The README's quality argument that 'Fontdue reuses geometry tessellated for 40px' describes Fontdue's default scale of 40, not the benchmarked setup. No output-equivalence or quality check is run, and TiTanF skips zeroing its output buffer while RustType and ab_glyph allocate zeroed ones.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust font rasterizer (language-filter mismatch) with no FreeType baseline: its own criterion bench (benches/rasterize_bench.rs) against RustType, ab_glyph and Fontdue gives 1.5x-3.5x and 1.7x-3.1x (derived), no CPU or rustc stated; the bench font NotoSansSC-Medium.ttf is gitignored and absent, the string is 106 characters not 84, the whole-font preprocessing runs outside the timed loop, and Fontdue is faster from 10 to 160 px.

**Known shortcoming:** README table is from commit 0c4078c (2026-07-08) and matches the current bench, but the string is 106 characters (not 84); the README's claim that Fontdue reuses a 40 px tessellation is wrong for the bench (scale is set per size); the README says AVX2 and NEON but the code has SSE only with scalar elsewhere, and i686 probably does not compile. Library bugs from code reading (not run, not behind the simple bench glyphs): nested composites drop the outer offset and scale (points.rs load_from_parent); contours starting with three or more off-curve points lose the curve through the second point (lines.rs preprocess); GSUB-only glyph ids render .notdef; a single cmap subtable can drop non-BMP; integer metrics; Vec::set_len on uninitialised memory.

**How:** load_font converts every cmap-mapped glyph once into raster-ready primitives: vertical lines, sloped lines with precomputed reciprocals, and quadratic Beziers split at their extrema into monotonic pieces with precomputed polynomial coefficients. Per call, scaling to pixel space is one SSE multiply-add per primitive. A grid-walk (DDA) cell traversal deposits exact signed-area coverage into a float accumulation buffer, solving the quadratic with one sqrtss at each pixel-boundary crossing instead of flattening curves. A span-limited SSE prefix sum per row then turns the coverage into alpha bytes and re-zeroes only the touched spans, so the buffer never needs a separate clear. The README advertises SSE2/AVX2 and NEON, but the code has only SSE intrinsics on x86 and scalar fallbacks elsewhere.

**Use it when:**
- Kernels, bootloaders and other no_std + alloc targets that need anti-aliased TrueType text with zero crate dependencies (Fontdue pulls in ttf-parser 0.25).
- Large glyphs: at 200 px and 320 px it beats Fontdue (configured for each size) by 1.10x and 1.28x, and RustType or ab_glyph by 2.1-2.3x (derived from page data).
- Replacing RustType or ab_glyph for per-glyph bitmap rasterization when a one-off whole-font load cost is acceptable: 1.5-3.5x faster per call in the first-party bench.
- Fixed character sets mapped by cmap, such as consoles, terminals and UI labels, where the built-in (glyph id, size) cache of up to 4096 bitmaps absorbs repeats.

**Skip it when:**
- Body text at 10-160 px: Fontdue is 1.06-1.47x faster in the same bench (54.3 vs 71.0 us at 10 px, 83.7 vs 123.2 us at 20 px).
- CFF/CFF2 .otf fonts, variable fonts, colour or bitmap glyphs, or font collections: only glyf outlines are parsed, and load_font returns TableNotFound("glyf") without that table.
- Shaped or complex-script text: there is no GSUB, and only cmap-reachable glyphs are preprocessed, so get_indexed returns the .notdef glyph for ligature and contextual-form ids that a shaper produces, despite its doc comment suggesting shaper use.
- Supplementary-plane characters (emoji, CJK Extension B) in fonts whose cmap lists a Unicode-platform BMP format 4 subtable before the format 12 one: load_cmap_subtables keeps only one subtable, ranks every platform-0 entry first and sorts stably, so non-BMP code points can fall back to .notdef.
- Fast startup or tight memory with large CJK fonts: every mapped glyph is preprocessed at load (tens of thousands for NotoSansSC), and neither load time nor memory is reported. It is a single-author project with 3 stars and no issues ever filed.

**Integration:** crate · none (fontdue 0.9.3, ab_glyph 0.2.32, rusttype 0.9.3 and criterion 0.7 are dev-dependencies for the bench only); optional std feature switches BTreeMap to HashMap and uses std float methods · Rust edition 2024 with if-let chains (fastmap.rs), which implies rustc 1.88+; no rust-version is declared · x86-64 with SSE intrinsics compiled in unconditionally (no AVX2 code and no runtime dispatch); aarch64 and other targets use scalar fallbacks (including a three-step Newton sqrt), with no NEON code; 32-bit x86 appears not to compile, because geometry/simd.rs imports core::arch::x86_64 under cfg(target_arch = "x86")

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over fontdue only for zero dependencies, mostly large sizes (200 px and up), or exact curves at sizes far from one preset scale. Fontdue is faster from 10 to 160 px, also no_std, and far more used. font-rs has no benchmark numbers in its repo, and ttf-parser only parses outlines, so neither replaces a rasterizer the way this does.

**Gotchas:**
- Outline bugs found by reading the code (not run): (a) a composite glyph whose component is itself a composite loses the outer component's offset and scale, because load_from_parent recurses without passing the transform, and point-matched components (ARGS_ARE_XY_VALUES clear) get no offset at all; (b) a contour that starts with three or more off-curve points drops the curve through its second point, because preprocess() stores it in last_off_curve but the off-curve branch never reads it. The tests use only a synthetic square-glyph font, with no reference-image comparison.
- Metrics are integers: advance_width is truncated to usize and left_side_bearing to isize, so layouts built on them accumulate rounding error, and the baseline comes from the glyf header's yMax rather than the computed bounds.
- The cache (get_char::<true>) keys on the glyph id and the exact f32 bit pattern of the size, flushes completely at 4096 entries, and returns a cloned Vec on every hit. The default dpi is 72, so size is in pixels, and set_dpi flushes the cache.
- Beyond the SIMD intrinsics, the code has other unsafe: to_bitmap calls Vec::set_len on uninitialized bytes (clippy::uninit_vec is silenced), and the rasterizer's coverage writes use get_unchecked_mut, protected only by debug_assert and coordinate clamping.

**Status:** Active single-author crate (115 commits, last 2026-07-08, v3.0.0 on crates.io with about 2.6k downloads), MIT and small enough to vendor, but no issues filed and no CI visible; treat the composite-glyph and off-curve-start parsing bugs as open.

[repo](https://github.com/Hoteira/titanf) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Hoteira/titanf)

##### ttf-parser  `Rust (with a basic C API)`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Safe, zero-allocation Rust font parser with a C API; extracts unscaled glyph outlines 1.3-5x faster than FreeType's FT_Load_Glyph path.

**Beats:** FreeType (FT_Load_Glyph with FT_LOAD_NO_SCALE, glyph outlining); stb_truetype also compared — The author's Google Benchmark 1.4.1 harness (benches/outline/outline.cc) outlined every glyph of Source Sans Pro (TTF and OTF) and Source Sans Variable (TTF with gvar, OTF with CFF2, wght 500) through the ttf-parser C API, FreeType (FT_LOAD_NO_SCALE + FT_Outline_Decompose) and stb_truetype, on an AMD 3700X and an Apple M1; ttf-parser was 1.30x/1.55x faster on glyf, 1.39x/2.02x on gvar, 4.72x/4.96x on CFF and 3.25x/3.40x on CFF2 (x86/M1, derived from page data). The table first appeared in the v0.14.0 README (2021-12-28), when the feature table's 'Tested version' row read ttf-parser 0.14.0, FreeType 2.10.4, stb_truetype 1.24; that row was later bumped to 0.17.0/2.12.0 without the numbers changing, so the benchmark's FreeType version is likely 2.10.4 but never stated, and no compiler or rustc version is given. The harness ignores ttfp_outline_glyph's return value and never compares segment counts between libraries (ttf-parser's counter also counts close_path, which FreeType has no callback for), so it does not prove that ttf-parser outlined every glyph it was timed on.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust crate with a basic C API (language-filter mismatch). The FreeType comparison table (1.3x to 5x on AMD 3700X and Apple M1; benches/outline/outline.cc) lives only in the v0.25.1 tagged README: it was cut from the current README on 2026-08-06 as stale (unchanged since v0.15.0), compiler and FreeType versions are unstated, and stb_truetype is faster on x86 glyf outlines. README now says maintenance mode.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark table first appeared in the v0.14.0 README (2021-12-28) with FreeType 2.10.4 as the tested version, later relabelled 2.12.0 with the numbers unchanged, so the measured FreeType is probably 2.10.4 and never stated. The harness ignores ttfp_outline_glyph's return value and never compares segment counts (ttf-parser's counter includes close_path), so the record's 'same segment counts' caveat is unsupported. crates.io 0.25.1 (2024-11-29) lacks main-branch fixes: a CFF subroutine hang (a 255-byte table takes over 30 s), a GSUB/GPOS extension infinite loop, wrong scale on a non-default FontMatrix, and static CFF2 without vstore yielding no outlines; gvar with more than 32 tuples fails without gvar-alloc; the C API crate is MIT only; maintenance mode, fontations recommended.

**How:** Everything is zero-copy over the font bytes (lazy arrays and a big-endian Stream reader) and nothing is allocated or copied into a glyph slot: the glyf path walks the flag/x/y streams with iterators, synthesises implied on-curve midpoints on the fly (Builder::push_point) and calls the user's callbacks directly while accumulating the bbox. CFF and CFF2 use a Type 2 charstring interpreter with a fixed 48-entry operand stack and a 10-deep subroutine limit that skips all hint operators ('We are ignoring the hint operators'). gvar deltas are applied while streaming, holding up to 32 tuple iterators on the stack and re-parsing a contour when it has to infer untouched-point (IUP) deltas. The FreeType side of the benchmark instead loads each glyph into the face's glyph slot with FT_Load_Glyph(FT_LOAD_NO_SCALE) and then walks it a second time with FT_Outline_Decompose.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code that needs unscaled glyph outlines to feed its own rasterizer, SDF/MSDF generator, path tessellator or PDF/SVG writer, especially from CFF/CFF2 (OTF) fonts, where the measured gap to FreeType was largest (3.3x-5.0x).
- Parsing untrusted fonts in a memory-safe way: no unsafe code in the core crate, no heap allocation by default, depth limits on recursion and panics treated as bugs (use the main branch to get the 2026 work-budget fixes, see below).
- no_std or WASM targets that need metrics, cmap lookup and outlines with zero dependencies (core_maths only for no_std float).
- Projects that already pull it in through fontdue, rustybuzz or Typst (all depend on ttf-parser 0.25) and want direct outline or table access without a second font stack.
- C or C++ programs that only need outlines, metrics and cmap and are willing to ship a Rust-built shared library to replace FreeType's parsing layer.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs hinting, scaled or hinted bitmaps, LCD filtering or rasterization, which is FreeType's main job; ttf-parser stops at font-unit outlines.
- Plain static TrueType (glyf) outlining from C or C++: in the same harness stb_truetype beat it on x86 (0.675 vs 0.901 ms) and was only 1.28x slower on M1 (0.703 vs 0.550 ms), as one header with no Rust toolchain.
- New projects: the README (2026-08-06) puts the crate in maintenance mode (bug fixes only, no performance work) and recommends fontations (read-fonts and skrifa); issue #230 (2026-08-05) called it unmaintained and announced a fork.
- Shipping the crates.io release 0.25.1 (2024-11-29, 112.7M downloads) against untrusted fonts: the unreleased main branch fixes a CFF subroutine fan-out where a 255-byte CFF table hung for over 30 s, an infinite loop on self-referential GSUB/GPOS extension lookups in release builds, unbounded composite-glyph and COLRv1 fan-out, and a C API panic in ttfp_get_glyph_name that aborts across the extern "C" boundary.
- Fonts that hit 0.25.1 correctness gaps fixed only on main: CFF fonts with a non-default FontMatrix outlined at the wrong scale, static CFF2 fonts without a vstore returned no outline for any glyph, glyphs using the deprecated dotsection operator produced no outline, and 65536-glyph loca tables dropped glyf entirely. Composite point matching and cmap format 8 remain unsupported.

**Integration:** crate (Rust); C API is a separate crate (ttf-parser-capi) built as a cdylib, or a static lib via cargo-c, with the hand-written header ttfparser.h · none (optional core_maths for no_std float); the C API needs a Rust toolchain to build · crates.io 0.25.1: Rust 1.63 (manifest rust-version); main branch: Rust 1.88, edition 2024. Header is plain C (stdbool/stdint); the benchmark compiles it as C++14 · any Rust target, including no_std and WASM; scalar code, no SIMD or platform-specific paths

**Vs siblings:** fontdue and Typst already use ttf-parser for parsing; pick it directly when you need the outlines or tables themselves rather than fontdue's rasterized bitmaps or Typst's layout. Pick fontdue (or FreeType) when you need pixels, and a HarfBuzz-family shaper (rustybuzz, SixLabors.Fonts, text-shaper) when you need shaping, which ttf-parser does not do.

**Gotchas:**
- ttfp_outline_glyph may already have emitted segments when it returns false on a partially malformed outline; the header says to check the return value before using the builder's output.
- gvar glyphs with more than 32 variation tuples fail unless the gvar-alloc feature is enabled (it then heap-allocates), so 'zero allocation' and full gvar support are mutually exclusive.
- C API: the caller mallocs ttfp_face_size_of() bytes and passes them to ttfp_face_init, the font buffer must outlive the face, and the C API omits GSUB/GPOS/morx and other layout tables. The c-api crate is licensed MIT only, not MIT OR Apache-2.0 like the core crate.
- Every C API call wraps the Rust code in catch_unwind; the core crate forbids unsafe, but the FFI layer necessarily uses it.

**Status:** Maintenance mode since 2026-08-06 (bug fixes only) with active security hardening on main, but the last crates.io release is 0.25.1 from November 2024, so pin a main-branch commit for the hang and correctness fixes; MIT OR Apache-2.0 core, MIT C API.

[repo](https://github.com/harfbuzz/ttf-parser) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harfbuzz/ttf-parser/v0.25.1/README.md)

##### Typr.js  `JavaScript`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Small browser JavaScript font parser (TTF/OTF/TTC/WOFF) that claims 2x-5x faster parsing than opentype.js, largely by parsing less up front.

**Beats:** opentype.js (the widely used JavaScript OpenType font parser, a recognisable incumbent in JavaScript); HarfBuzz and FreeType are not measured — Nothing measurable is published. The README has said 'ultra fast (2x to 5x faster parsing than opentype.js)' since at least May 2020 (when it also gave the size as 70 kB), with no benchmark code, font set, opentype.js version, JavaScript engine or machine. Reading both parsers shows the comparison is not like-for-like: Typr defers glyph decoding, skips GPOS and GDEF and keeps only GSUB feature tags, whereas current opentype.js parses GDEF, GPOS and GSUB eagerly.

**Known shortcoming:** JavaScript (language-filter mismatch). Only a README line ('2x to 5x faster parsing than opentype.js') with no benchmark code, corpus or machine; Typr.parse is lazy on glyf and skips GPOS and GDEF, so the parsing work is not equal. Last commit 2025-08-28.

**Known shortcoming:** The speed claim is unchanged since at least May 2020 with no benchmark, and the comparison is not like-for-like: Typr skips GPOS and GDEF, reads only GSUB tags and parses glyf lazily while opentype.js master parses GDEF, GPOS and GSUB eagerly. The record's trade-off text is wrong: Typr.U.shape has no GSUB ligatures and no GPOS, only legacy kern pairs, and ignores fts and ltr. console.log(out) runs on every parse; the module reads window at load so breaks in Node and Workers; WOFF2 is sent down the WOFF1 path and WOFF needs a global pako; a variable font with 0 named instances returns []; the npm typr.js package is a third-party 2018 snapshot.

**How:** The parser is a set of hand-written table readers over one Uint8Array with manual big-endian byte reads. It also does much less work at load time. The glyf table becomes an array of nulls, and each glyph is decoded on the first glyphToPath call and memoised in font.glyf. CFF CharStrings and subroutines become zero-copy Uint8Array views that are interpreted only when a path is requested. GPOS and GDEF are not parsed at all, and GSUB is reduced to a set of feature tags. By contrast, current opentype.js master parses GDEF, GPOS and GSUB and builds its kerning pairs inside its parse routine. Tables shared between TTC members are parsed once (keyed by offset). With no benchmark in the repo, it is unknown how much of the claimed gap comes from leaner code and how much from skipped tables.

**Use it when:**
- Browser apps that need glyph outlines from user-supplied fonts to draw on Canvas or export as SVG paths: text-as-paths in an image or vector editor (the README says it is Photopea's main text engine), font previews and thumbnails.
- Opening many fonts quickly just to read metadata or cmap coverage (font pickers, family/instance lists from fvar, glyph-coverage checks), where lazy outlines and the skipped layout tables keep load cheap.
- Variable and colour fonts in the browser without a native dependency: outlines interpolated through gvar, avar and HVAR, COLR/CPAL layers, SVG glyphs, and CBDT/sbix PNG glyphs (with UPNG.js loaded).
- Pages where script size matters: three plain script files (README: 110 kB unminified, 4x smaller than opentype.js) with no build step. You can pair it with a HarfBuzz WASM build via Typr.U.initHB when complex scripts need real shaping.

**Skip it when:**
- Shaping text with the library alone: in the current code, Typr.U.shape maps each code point to one glyph and adds only legacy 'kern' table pairs (found by linear indexOf) and HVAR advances. It applies no GSUB ligatures, no GPOS kerning or mark positioning, and ignores the fts and ltr parameters, so fonts that keep kerning only in GPOS get none. This also contradicts the catalogue record's tradeoff that shape covers ligatures. For real shaping use shapeHB with a HarfBuzz WASM file (the README links one hosted on photopea.com; it is not in the repo) or a dedicated JavaScript shaper.
- Node.js, Deno or Web Workers without shims: src/Typr.js reads window['TextDecoder'] when it loads (Typr.B._tdec) and has no module export, so it throws a ReferenceError where window is undefined. The npm package named typr.js is a third-party snapshot from January 2018 (version 1.0.0), not this repository.
- WOFF2 fonts, or WOFF 1.0 without pako: WOFF tables are inflated through a global pako object that the repo does not ship. WOFF2 is unsupported, and because its 'wOF2' signature starts with the same 0x77 byte as WOFF, it is routed into the WOFF 1.0 converter and fails (inferred from the source).
- Untrusted or malformed fonts where you need clean failures: the byte readers have their bounds checks commented out, so out-of-range reads yield undefined/NaN instead of errors, failures are thrown as bare strings (for example 'unknown cmap table format'), and issue #55 (October 2024, no reply) reports browser crashes when loading the genseki-font TTC files.
- When you need a measured speed advantage or a font writer: the 2x-5x figure has no benchmark behind it, and opentype.js can also write fonts.

**Integration:** source-drop · none for TTF/OTF/TTC; global pako for WOFF 1.0; global UPNG (UPNG.js) for CBDT/sbix PNG glyphs; a HarfBuzz WASM build plus fetch and WebAssembly for Typr.U.shapeHB · Not documented. The code needs an ES2015 engine (typed arrays, String.codePointAt) and a global window object; the variable-font naming path calls String.replaceAll (ES2021); shapeHB needs fetch, WebAssembly and TextEncoder. · Web browsers (main thread). Node.js, Deno and Workers work only with a window shim. readUint/readInt reassemble bytes through a shared typed-array scratch buffer, which assumes a little-endian host (true of all mainstream JS engines).

**Vs siblings:** Pick Typr.js for in-browser font loading and glyph outlines (including variable and colour fonts) from a tiny dependency-free script. For shaping in JavaScript, the catalogued text-shaper and rustybuzz-wasm were actually measured against harfbuzzjs and opentype.js; in native or Rust code, ttf-parser covers outline parsing with published numbers against FreeType.

**Gotchas:**
- Typr.parse ends with an uncommented console.log(out) (src/Typr.js line 126 on gh-pages), so every parse logs the parsed fonts; while DevTools is open those objects, each holding the whole font buffer, stay reachable. The name-table parser also logs when it meets unknown encodings.
- For a variable font, Typr.parse returns one object per fvar named instance, not one per file, and a font whose fvar lists zero named instances yields an empty array (inferred from readFONT), so Typr.parse(buf)[0] is undefined.
- Typr.U.shape sets the cluster index cl to the glyph's position in the glyph list, not its UTF-16 offset, so cl drifts from the string index after any astral character such as an emoji. shapeHB caches its HarfBuzz face by postScriptName, so two different font files that share a PostScript name reuse the first one's face.
- Lazy glyph decoding re-scans the table directory (findTable) for each glyph and re-parses empty glyphs on every call. Memory grows as glyphs are drawn because parsed glyphs are cached in font.glyf and never evicted.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit is 2025-08-28 ('Add files via upload' on the gh-pages default branch), there are no tags, releases or package.json, and none of the 8 open issues has a maintainer reply. It is MIT-licensed, three files to vendor, and per the README still Photopea's main text engine.

[repo](https://github.com/photopea/Typr.js) · [benchmark](https://github.com/photopea/Typr.js/)

##### uniwidth  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go terminal cell-width library; CI shows 1.1-52x faster StringWidth than go-runewidth v0.0.19, with width bugs on symbols.

**Beats:** mattn/go-runewidth v0.0.19 (the de facto Go terminal display-width library) and rivo/uniseg v0.4.7 StringWidth, both pinned in bench/go.mod; HarfBuzz, FreeType and ICU are not involved — The 'Library Comparison' comment on PR #5 (2026-08-25) ran on a GitHub-hosted AMD EPYC 7763 (linux/amd64) with Go 1.25, -count=3 -benchtime=100ms, taking medians, against go-runewidth v0.0.19 and uniseg v0.4.7 in default configuration. Against go-runewidth: StringWidth 12-52x faster on ASCII, 2.1-2.2x on CJK, 1.7-2.0x on mixed, emoji and flags, 1.1x on ZWJ and 1.2x on the table header; RuneWidth 8.7x on CJK. The workflow itself warns of 10-20% runner variance. Reading the code: the ASCII gap comes mostly from skipping go-runewidth's per-string UAX #29 segmentation. The TUI Prompt row (156.0 vs 270.7 vs 389.7 ns) times a wrong result: uniwidth returns 17 for '❯ Enter command:', where go-runewidth's Neutral classification gives 16, and the harness never cross-checks outputs.

**Known shortcoming:** Go library (language-filter mismatch); display-width primitive, not shaping. Tier A on the CI Library Comparison in PR #5 (public bench/comparison_test.go, Go 1.25, go test -bench with -benchmem -count=3, AMD EPYC 7763 shared runner): ASCII 12-52x, non-ASCII StringWidth 1.1-2.2x, RuneWidth CJK 8.7x over go-runewidth v0.0.19, which does full UAX #29 segmentation while uniwidth does not; Unicode 16.0 vs 15.1.0, no output cross-check, bench/README Windows table stale, and the headline 3-46x overstates the low end.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered A to C (retier-24): RuneWidth's hot path returns width 2 for all of U+2600-27BF and the U+1F300-1F5FF, U+1F680-1F6FF and U+1F900-1F9FF blocks although 402 of 448 code points in U+2600-27BF and 259 in those SMP blocks are not East Asian Wide per go-runewidth's Unicode 15.1 tables (check mark, cross, right arrowhead, star, heart), the generator filters these ranges out and the tests repeat them, so the CI 'TUI Prompt' row times a wrong answer (17 against go-runewidth's 16); the catalogued rows' inputs are unaffected. The *WithOptions path lacks ZWJ, variation-selector and flag handling (family emoji measures 8) and returns len(s) for ASCII; WithEmojiPresentation is never read; no Truncate, Wrap or Fill.

**How:** ASCII strings go through SWAR: 8-byte words are tested against a 0x8080... mask, and control bytes are found with the subtract-and-mask zero-byte trick (Lemire), while strings under 8 bytes use one fused loop. RuneWidth answers from hard-coded range checks for CJK ideographs, Hangul, kana and Bopomofo, four SMP emoji blocks and U+2600-27BF, and otherwise from a 3-stage table (ROOT[256], MIDDLE[17x64], LEAVES[78x32], 2 bits per code point, about 3.8 KB). Non-ASCII strings are converted to []rune and scanned once with a 3-state ZWJ/modifier state machine. go-runewidth v0.0.19's StringWidth instead runs clipperhouse/uax29 grapheme segmentation on every string, ASCII included, and binary-searches interval tables per rune; that difference explains the 12-52x ASCII gap.

**Use it when:**
- Go TUIs and CLI tables whose cells are mostly ASCII. In CI on an EPYC 7763: 6.06 vs 73.18 ns for 5 characters and 64.08 vs 3,327 ns for 228 characters against go-runewidth, with 0 allocations.
- CJK, Hangul or kana text where per-code-point width is all you need: StringWidth is about 2.1-2.2x faster, and RuneWidth('世') takes 2.50 vs 21.97 ns.
- Modules that must stay dependency-free. The library module imports only the standard library; the competitors are confined to the separate bench/ module.
- Emoji-heavy status lines where ZWJ families, skin tones and flags should count as 2 cells, without pulling in a grapheme segmenter.

**Skip it when:**
- Text with dingbats or miscellaneous symbols such as ❯ ✓ ✗ ➜ ★ ♥ ☀ ❤ (without VS16). RuneWidth returns 2 for every code point in U+2600-27BF and in U+1F300-1F5FF, U+1F680-1F6FF and U+1F900-1F9FF. Per the Unicode 15.1 tables in go-runewidth v0.0.19, 402 of the 448 code points in U+2600-27BF are not East Asian Wide (✓ U+2713, ❯ U+276F and ➜ U+279C are Neutral and not even emoji), nor are 259 in those SMP blocks. Prompts and check-mark columns come out misaligned.
- CJK-locale terminals that draw ambiguous characters wide. StringWidthWithOptions drops the ZWJ, VS and flag handling (a family emoji measures 8), returns len(s) for ASCII input so control characters count 1, and ambiguous symbols inside the hard-coded ranges (★ ♥ ♠) stay 2 whatever the option says.
- Code that needs truncation, wrapping, padding or grapheme iteration; none of these exist in the package.
- Layouts that must match uniseg or terminals exactly. Widths come from heuristics rather than segmentation: any character followed by U+FE0F counts 2, and Extended_Pictographic is approximated by whole blocks, including arrows, geometric shapes and Misc Technical.
- Toolchains older than Go 1.25. The project is also young (v0.2.0, 18 commits, 8 stars).

**Integration:** module (pure-Go package) · none (bench/ is a separate module that pins go-runewidth v0.0.19 and rivo/uniseg v0.4.7) · Go 1.25.1 per go.mod (README says Go 1.25+) · any GOOS/GOARCH (no assembly; the SWAR helpers do unaligned 8-byte loads through unsafe); benchmarked on linux/amd64 and windows/amd64

**Vs siblings:** displaywidth is the safer Go choice: it measures grapheme clusters with clipperhouse/uax29, has ANSI-aware truncation and ships in lipgloss v2 and tablewriter. Choose uniwidth only when almost all your strings are ASCII and you can avoid or patch the U+2600-27BF over-width. The two were benchmarked against different go-runewidth versions on different machines, so catalog data cannot rank them. uwcwidth is the Python counterpart and not an option in Go.

**Gotchas:**
- The tests cannot catch range mistakes. cmd/generate-tables filters U+2600-27BF and the other hot ranges out of the generated tables, and the test reference function runeWidthViaBinarySearch repeats the same hard-coded ranges, so the tests compare the code with itself. The conformance test even expects ☀ U+2600 and ❤ U+2764 to be 2.
- RuneWidth/StringWidth and the *WithOptions variants disagree: the options path has no ZWJ/VS/flag state machine, counts ASCII control characters, and uses a narrower kana range (0x3040-0x30FF, so Bopomofo is excluded). WithEmojiPresentation is accepted but never read.
- The README's truncate example adds up RuneWidth per rune. That miscounts ZWJ sequences and flags, which only StringWidth handles.
- Non-ASCII StringWidth builds a []rune copy for lookahead. The CHANGELOG lists this as one allocation; the verifier observed it only for medium and long strings.

**Status:** Active but small: v0.2.0 (2026-02-05), last commit 2026-08-25, 8 stars, 18 commits, no open issues. MIT and dependency-free, so easy to vendor, but patch the U+2600-27BF hot path before relying on it for symbol-heavy TUIs.

[repo](https://github.com/unilibs/uniwidth) · [benchmark](https://github.com/unilibs/uniwidth/pull/5)

##### uwcwidth  `Cython (Python)`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Cython wcwidth/wcswidth for Python with Unicode 16 emoji rules; beats pure-Python wcwidth 0.2.13 by 18-42x on short strings.

**Beats:** jquast/wcwidth, the standard Python terminal-width package, which was pure Python when measured (most likely 0.2.13, the only wcwidth release between January 2024 and September 2025 per PyPI); cwcwidth, a Cython binding to the C library's wcwidth/wcswidth, was also measured; neither version is stated — The README times wcswidth on one 11-code-point katakana and ASCII string with IPython %%timeit: wcwidth 1.73 us, cwcwidth 211 ns, uwcwidth 41 ns. No CPU, OS or versions are given, but the wcwidth timing fits the pure-Python 0.2.13 of 2024. Re-run in this session on an Intel Xeon 2.1 GHz cloud VM (Linux, glibc 2.39, CPython 3.11.15, best of 7), the numbers were uwcwidth 1.0.0 87-89 ns, wcwidth 0.2.13 1,623 ns (18x, not 42x), wcwidth 0.9.1 183-186 ns (2.1x), and cwcwidth 0.1.9 49-52 ns and 0.1.12 63-67 ns. So on Linux, uwcwidth is about 1.7x slower than cwcwidth, not 5x faster, though cwcwidth gets ZWJ sequences wrong; the README's cwcwidth ratio is presumably specific to the libc of its unstated platform.

**Known shortcoming:** Cython (language-filter mismatch); display-width primitive, not shaping. One IPython %%timeit string: wcwidth 1.73 us vs uwcwidth 41 ns (about 42x) and cwcwidth 211 ns (5.1x, derived), with no CPU, Python or wcwidth version and no bench script; the gain is mostly Cython -O3 against the pure-Python wcwidth of 2024, and wcwidth 0.9.1 now ships a C11 core with abi3 wheels, unmeasured. Last commit 2024-10-28.

**Known shortcoming:** README ratios are stale and platform-specific (retier-26): re-measured on Linux, uwcwidth is 18x faster than pure-Python wcwidth 0.2.13 (not 42x), 1.7x slower than cwcwidth 0.1.9 (not 5x faster; cwcwidth is wrong on ZWJ sequences), and only 2.1x faster than the current wcwidth 0.9.1 C extension, which beats uwcwidth 4.5x on ASCII text. Widths differ from wcwidth on 730 (0.2.13) or 5,541 (0.9.1) code points; VS16 widens any narrow character. The author of issue #1 ported uwcwidth to Node.js (duplicate if found).

**How:** Width comes from musl libc's two-level sparse bitmaps (a 256-entry page index, then 32-byte bit pages) for zero-width and wide code points, recomputed for Unicode 16.0, plus a dense bitmap for Emoji_Modifier_Base; the tables total about 4 KB. Code points below U+00FF take one arithmetic test, and planes 2-3 return 2 without a lookup. The whole loop is a typed Cython function that reads code points straight from the str with no per-character Python objects, while wcwidth 0.2.13 runs a Python while-loop that binary-searches its tables per character behind an lru_cache.

**Use it when:**
- Python TUIs, table printers and log formatters that measure many short, emoji-heavy or CJK strings and still depend on pure-Python wcwidth 0.2.x.
- When ZWJ sequences, flags, keycaps and skin-tone modifiers must count as 2 cells: in this session cwcwidth on glibc 2.39 returned 11 and 6 for the README's edge-case strings, against 8 and 5 from uwcwidth.
- Cython code that can cimport wcswidth and call it without Python-call overhead (ugrapheme does this for ljust, rjust and center).
- Projects that want a tiny, dependency-free MIT module whose widths do not depend on the platform libc or locale.

**Skip it when:**
- You already run wcwidth 0.3 or later: 0.9.1 ships a C extension, and in this session it was only 2.1x slower on the README string, 1.9x slower on 1,750 characters of mixed text, and 4.5x faster on 2,250 ASCII characters (about 1.1 us against 5.0 us).
- Plain ASCII or Latin text measured in long strings: the per-character loop runs at about 2.2 ns per character, slower than wcwidth 0.9.1 and cwcwidth.
- Unicode 17 text, or output that must match wcwidth exactly: it has had no commits since 2024-10-28, and widths differ from wcwidth 0.2.13 on 730 single code points and from 0.9.1 on 5,541 (spacing marks such as U+0903 are 1 here and 0 there; wide code points added in Unicode 17, such as Tangut ideographs and new emoji, and lone regional indicators are 1 here and 2 in 0.9.1).
- C or C++ callers: it is a CPython/PyPy extension. Its musl-derived tables and loop are short enough to port, and the catalogued Go siblings displaywidth and uniwidth do the same job in Go.
- Platforms without wheels (CPython 3.14+, Linux aarch64): pip falls back to building the sdist with Cython and a C compiler.

**Integration:** module · none at runtime; Cython, setuptools and a C compiler only when building from source · CPython 3.8+ or PyPy 3.7-3.10 (1.0.0 wheels cp38-cp313 and pp37-pp310 for x86-64/i686 manylinux and musllinux, Windows and macOS arm64); built with -O3 on non-MSVC compilers · any platform with a C compiler; prebuilt wheels as listed, none for Linux aarch64

**Vs siblings:** displaywidth and uniwidth are the catalogued Go terminal-width libraries and beat go-runewidth there. uwcwidth is the Python counterpart, worth taking when a CPython or Cython codebase needs emoji-sequence-aware widths without the jquast wcwidth package or a libc-dependent binding such as cwcwidth.

**Gotchas:**
- Any narrow character followed by VS16 (U+FE0F) becomes width 2, even when it has no emoji presentation: wcswidth('a\ufe0f') is 2 here and 1 in wcwidth.
- A ZWJ (U+200D) swallows the next code point and one trailing skin-tone modifier or VS16 whatever they are, so '\u200dabc' measures 2; wcwidth 0.2.13 behaves the same.
- Tabs, newlines, ESC and other controls make wcswidth return -1 for the whole string (closed issue #1), so strip ANSI escapes and expand tabs first. Unicode noncharacters such as U+FFFE also return -1, where wcwidth returns 1.
- wcswidth(s, n) with n greater than len(s) raises IndexError, as wcwidth 0.2.13 did; wcwidth 0.9.1 clamps and returns the width.

**Status:** Stale since its 1.0.0 release on 2024-10-28 (4 stars, 4 commits, no open issues) and still at Unicode 16.0, but it is about 80 lines of MIT-licensed Cython plus musl-derived tables, so it is easy to vendor or port; its speed advantage now holds mainly against pure-Python wcwidth 0.2.x.

[repo](https://github.com/Z4JC/uwcwidth) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Z4JC/uwcwidth)

##### uWrap  `TypeScript`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Sub-2KB TypeScript Canvas2D line-wrap counter for virtualized lists; 7.7-18x faster than canvas-hypertxt in the author's browser runs.

**Beats:** canvas-hypertxt (JavaScript canvas text-wrapping library) — First-party README numbers: 100k random txtgen sentences at random widths of 50-250px, 14px Inter with 0.15px letterSpacing. uWrap setup plus count() took 82, 90 and 185 ms, against 770, 1660 and 1430 ms for canvas-hypertxt split(hyper=true), in Chrome 135, Firefox 137 and Safari 18.1 (9.4x, 18.4x, 7.7x, derived from page data), one console.time run each, machine unstated. The enricher reran the same loops in Node 22 with a synthetic measureText (4-vCPU Xeon 2.80GHz container, 3 reps, identical inputs for both libraries): uWrap count 122-133 ms, uWrap split 139-142 ms, canvas-hypertxt 909-989 ms. Timing count() instead of split() therefore flatters uWrap by only 7-14%, and the gap stays 6.4-7.1x like for like, mostly algorithmic. No flaw was found in the timed code beyond the count-vs-split mismatch and the single unrepeated runs.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-baseline (JavaScript canvas text wrapping, not HarfBuzz or FreeType) and the harness times different calls: uWrap's count() (a counter with no strings) against canvas-hypertxt's split(..., true), which slices and trims line strings and builds a cache key; each library draws its own random widths; both are approximations (character LUT plus uppercase kerning versus a trained estimate); the accuracy and memory claims carry no numbers; single console.time runs with no machine named. Last commit 2025-08-01.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e112, 2026-10-05): a Node 22 re-run with synthetic measureText gives count 122-133 ms, split 139-142 ms, canvas-hypertxt 909-989 ms, a 6.4-7.1x like-for-like gap that is mostly algorithmic (hypertxt's quadratic prefix re-measure); the count-vs-split asymmetry is only 7-14%. C stands. Accuracy bugs, not timing: the faux letterSpacing path (Safari before 18.4, including the README's Safari 18.1 run) drops spacing on uppercase plus ASCII pairs ('ABCDEF' 10 px short at 2 px); no CJK or tab wraps; '\r' kept; a trailing '\n' adds an empty line. Synthetic accuracy: uWrap 99.5% match to exact greedy, hypertxt hyper mode 65.7%.

**Independent measurement:** first-party benchmark; enricher re-run

**How:** Setup measures each of the ~95 printable ASCII characters, plus every uppercase-led pair (26x95), with ctx.measureText once, filling a width table and a kerning table; that was 2,594 calls in the enricher's run. After that, wrapping is one linear pass over charCodeAt with table lookups and greedy tracking of break points. The hot loop calls measureText only for unseen non-ASCII characters (then cached), and count/test allocate no strings. canvas-hypertxt does far more per call: it builds a string cache key and re-measures growing prefixes one character at a time in getSplitPoint, which is quadratic in line length. In hyper mode it switches to trained per-character estimates times 1.01 after 500k measured characters.

**Use it when:**
- Virtualized lists and data grids in the browser that need row heights for thousands to hundreds of thousands of Latin-text cells without DOM reflow.
- UI text in one font and size per context (for example 14px Inter) with letterSpacing or wordSpacing and pre-line semantics: explicit newlines plus wrapping at spaces and hyphens.
- Only a line count or a 'does it wrap' test is needed: count() and test() allocate nothing per call, and test() stops after the second line.
- Bundle-size-sensitive front ends: under 2KB minified, no runtime dependencies, ESM and IIFE builds.

**Skip it when:**
- Text without spaces between words, such as CJK or Thai: a 32-character Chinese string came back as one overflowing line in the enricher's test. Breaks happen only at the ASCII space and after '-'. There is no UAX #14 line breaking and no shaping or ligature handling, and characters outside the BMP are measured one UTF-16 code unit at a time.
- Text with tabs or Windows line endings: tabs are not break points (CSS pre-line turns them into spaces, so browsers wrap there), and '\r' stays inside the line ('first line\r\nsecond line' gave 'line\r' as a line). The README says \r\n is not handled.
- Long words or URLs that need overflow-wrap or word-break: they are not split and overflow one line (issue #1 is the open TODO).
- white-space normal, pre-wrap or break-spaces, mixed fonts or rich text: only the pre-line strategy exists, with one font per context.
- Node or server-side use without a Canvas2D implementation: it needs a CanvasRenderingContext2D (the tests use skia-canvas).

**Integration:** module (npm uwrap: ESM dist/uWrap.mjs, IIFE dist/uWrap.iife.min.js, TypeScript .d.ts) · none at run time; needs a CanvasRenderingContext2D (browser canvas, or skia-canvas in Node as the tests do) · Any JS runtime with ES modules or a script tag and Canvas2D measureText; Canvas letterSpacing is optional (a faux fallback adds it manually) · Browsers (README timings for Chrome 135, Firefox 137, Safari 18.1); Node with a canvas implementation

**Vs siblings:** Pick uWrap over canvas-hypertxt for predicting Latin pre-line row heights. Its pass is linear, needs no per-call cache key, and in the enricher's synthetic-font test it matched an exact greedy wrap on 99.5% of 100k inputs (the rest were hyphen breaks the reference ignored), against 65.7% for hyper-mode canvas-hypertxt, which over-counted lines on 34%. Pretext is the broader DOM-free measurement and layout sibling; look at it when you need more than Latin pre-line line counting.

**Gotchas:**
- The width tables are built from ctx.font when varPreLine() runs. Changing ctx.font afterwards, or building before a web font has loaded, leaves stale widths, so rebuild after the font is ready.
- Accuracy bug in the faux letter-spacing path, used when the canvas ignores letterSpacing (Safari before 18.4 per the source comment, which includes the README's Safari 18.1 run): an uppercase letter followed by an ASCII character loses its letter spacing, because the pair width subtracts the next character's spacing and adds back only one. In a Node test with 2px spacing, 'ABCDEF' came out 10px (5 x 2px) narrower than expected and 'Hello World' 4px narrower. This affects predicted widths, not timing.
- Widths are sums of per-character advances measured in isolation, with kerning only for uppercase-plus-ASCII pairs. The README's accuracy claim is backed only by the visual overlays on the demo page.
- A trailing newline produces an extra empty line: split('abc\n') returns ['abc', ''] and count gives 2, so check this case against how your renderer sizes rows.

**Status:** Stale since 2025-08-01: 17 commits, npm uwrap 0.1.2 published 2025-07-28, MIT, 319 stars, 5 forks, one open issue (word-break TODO). It is small enough to vendor and patch.

[repo](https://github.com/leeoniya/uWrap) · [benchmark](https://github.com/leeoniya/uWrap)

##### libmsdf  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

Rust/wgpu SDF and MSDF text renderer whose WGSL compute shader generates MSDF glyphs at runtime; no speed data versus msdfgen.

**Beats:** msdfgen (CPU MSDF generator; the lead's msdfgl was not compared either); neither is in the listed HarfBuzz/FreeType baselines — No speed was measured. The only comparison is the output-parity test compute_matches_cpu_baseline: Roboto 'A', 'o', 'g', '5' and '#' at 48 px cells with a 6.0 px range, compute shader versus msdfgen via the msdfgen crate, scored on channel medians in the near-outline band. Recorded mean deviations are 0.0009 ('o'), 0.030 ('g'), 0.033 ('5'), 0.066 ('A') and 0.114 ('#'); pass thresholds are mean at most 0.13, at most 35% of texels beyond 0.125 and coverage IoU at least 0.98, on headless Metal with no GPU model given.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: an output-parity claim against msdfgen with no timings anywhere; PLAN.md is a 404 and the README names wgpu 29 while Cargo.toml pins 30.0.1. Kept under the keep-and-document rule.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e128, 2026-10-05): tier D stands, no timings anywhere. The parity claim is loose: tests/compute_msdf.rs allows a mean median deviation of 0.13 with 35% of texels beyond 0.125 ('#' at 0.114). Brute-force per-texel edge loop with no batching; the fragment shader loops over all draw commands per pixel; publish = false in Cargo.toml; GPU tests skip-pass when no adapter is present.

**Independent measurement:** none

**How:** No performance claim is made, so there is no speedup technique to credit. The runtime generator extracts and colours edges on the CPU (msdfgen edgeColoringSimple scheme, 3.0 angle threshold), then a WGSL kernel runs one thread per texel in 8x8 workgroups and loops over every edge: quadratics are flattened into 8 segments and cubics into 16, each channel takes the pseudo-distance of its nearest edge by true distance, and the sign comes from a nonzero-winding ray test. That is brute force, O(texels x edges x segments), with no spatial acceleration and no error-correction pass. Its value is where it runs (on the GPU, including wasm32/WebGPU where the msdfgen C++ FFI cannot build), not a measured speed advantage.

**Use it when:**
- Rust apps on wgpu that target wasm32/WebGPU and want MSDF text, where the msdfgen C++ FFI cannot be built.
- Generating glyph cells on demand in a browser instead of downloading baked atlases (a code comment puts a style's baked cells at about 290 KiB gzipped against a 13 KiB face).
- Small UI scenes, such as highbay's node graph, that mix SDF shapes and text and fit in one full-screen pass.
- As a reference: the 221-line, MIT/Apache-licensed msdf_compute.wgsl is self-contained enough to port to another engine.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need a measured speedup over msdfgen: none exists; msdfgl publishes numbers, this crate does not.
- Corner-heavy glyphs that need fields close to msdfgen's: the parity test allows a mean channel-median deviation up to 0.13 and up to 35% of near-outline texels off by more than 0.125, and the code comments record 0.114 for '#'.
- Large scenes: the fragment shader loops over every draw command (MAX_DRAW_CMDS 4096) for every pixel, with only a vertical-band reject for text and no tiling or binning.
- Production dependencies: Cargo.toml has publish = false (git dependency only), the repo has 0 stars and first commits from August 2026, the public API carries highbay-specific items (HIGHBAY_ICONS, PHASE_STATUS), and the README still says wgpu 29 although Cargo.toml uses 30.0.1.
- Shaping-heavy text: TextShaper wraps rustybuzz 0.20 (the archived HarfBuzz port, per the sigilbuzz sibling entry) and re-parses the face with rustybuzz::Face::from_slice on every shape call.

**Integration:** crate (unpublished; Cargo git dependency) · wgpu 30.0.1, bytemuck, log, rustybuzz 0.20, ttf-parser 0.25, unicode-segmentation 1.13; build-time naga 30.0.1 (validates the three WGSL shaders); optional cpu-bake adds msdfgen 0.2 (C++ FFI) and ttf-parser 0.18 · Rust edition 2024 (rustc 1.85 or newer); cpu-bake needs a C++ toolchain, and on macOS the LLVM codegen backend because the Cranelift dev profile fails to link msdfgen symbols · native wgpu backends (GPU tests documented only on headless Metal) and wasm32 WebGPU; the CPU msdfgen bake is native only

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over msdfgl (OpenGL compute MSDF, with published timings against msdfgen) only when you are on wgpu or WebGPU in Rust and need runtime MSDF on wasm32. Pick fontdue or ab_glyph instead for CPU coverage rasterisation, where this crate offers nothing measured.

**Gotchas:**
- 'Matches the CPU msdfgen baseline' means median-of-channels within loose tolerances on five Roboto glyphs at 48 px. Edge colouring differs from msdfgen, so individual channels are not comparable, and corners diverge because the compute path extrapolates pseudo-distance from a flattened polyline.
- A plain cargo test does not exercise the compute path: GPU tests need --features gpu-tests (plus cpu-bake for the msdfgen comparison) and the LLVM backend, and they print 'SKIP: no GPU adapter' and pass when no adapter is found.
- Each generate_cell or generate_into_texture call creates three new buffers and a bind group and submits its own command buffer, so bulk atlas generation is not batched.
- Fixed caps: 4096 draw commands, 4096 glyph-table entries and 8 texture layers per renderer; glyph ids are u16, and styled faces are addressed through a prefixed glyph id.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-26, 60 commits since August 2026) and MIT OR Apache-2.0, but unpublished, single-author and tied to highbay, so vendoring the WGSL shader is safer than depending on the crate.

[repo](https://github.com/tmzt/libmsdf)

##### Pretext  `TypeScript`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier D`

TypeScript library that predicts the browser's line breaks and paragraph heights from cached Canvas widths, so apps skip DOM reflow reads.

**Beats:** Browser DOM text measurement (getBoundingClientRect, offsetHeight and the layout reflow they trigger) — No Pretext-versus-DOM measurement exists in the repo: bun harness bench times Pretext builds against each other in Chrome 154, Firefox 156.0.1 and Safari 27 on an M5 Max, and the only absolute figures are Pretext's own (chat demo on a stand-in Canvas: 46-100 us per first prepare, 0.4-0.7 us per layout; Chrome 153 prepared the corpora in 115 ms and Safari 26.5.2 in 350 ms on 2026-09-15; early npm READMEs: prepare about 19 ms and layout about 0.09 ms for 500 texts). The 300-600x, 500x and 540x figures come from third-party pages (one snippet: about 380 ms DOM versus 0.7 ms on 1,000 paragraphs), and per a search snippet the author called that comparison unfair because it sets a cached layout() against a cold DOM measurement.

**Known shortcoming:** TypeScript library (language-filter mismatch) that measures and breaks lines without glyph shaping. Tier D: no DOM head-to-head anywhere; the bun bench compares Pretext builds only, early npm READMEs give its own timings only (prepare 17-19 ms, layout 0.09-0.10 ms per 500 texts), and the 500x claim exists only in third-party snippets. Kept as notable (50.7k stars).

**Known shortcoming:** No Pretext-versus-DOM number in the repo (tier D); its own RESEARCH.md figures are against a stand-in Canvas (46-100 us first prepare, 0.4-0.7 us layout, 43-59 ms per 100k-message resize), and the third-party 540x snippet (380 ms versus 0.7 ms on 1,000 paragraphs) sets a cached layout() against cold DOM measurement, which the author called unfair. npm 0.0.9 lags main (main bundle 38 KB gzipped versus 16 KB); a JSON-copied handle hangs the line APIs; the width cache is unbounded until clearCache(); open issues #334 (undercount) and #421 (kerned-word break); no SSR; licence notices for ported engine code and data not yet written (TODO.md).

**How:** A two-phase cache. prepare() runs ports of each engine's own line-break scan and grapheme rules (Blink, WebKit and Gecko tables pinned to browser builds, src/line-breaks.ts and src/gecko-line-breaks.ts), splits the text into break-delimited segments and measures each with Canvas measureText on an OffscreenCanvas, caching widths per (font, segment) in a shared Map. layout() is a greedy first-fit line walk over parallel arrays (widths as number[], segment kinds as a Uint8Array) with no Canvas calls, string work or per-line allocation; for plain prose a single numeric loop counts lines (the #338 fast path the CHANGELOG credits with a 2-3x faster layout() in Chrome and Safari). The range APIs return cursors instead of line strings, because the project found that most of the cost of getting lines was allocating strings and the GC that followed.

**Use it when:**
- Virtualized lists, chat histories and feeds with thousands of text rows whose exact heights must be known before render and recomputed on every resize: prepare each message once, then call layout() per width (RESEARCH.md, before #338 and on a stand-in Canvas: 0.4-0.7 us per layout, 43-59 ms median to re-lay out 100,000 messages).
- Userland layout that needs line geometry: masonry grids, chat bubbles shrink-wrapped to the widest line (walkLineRanges), text flowing around images (layoutNextLineRange), or drawing wrapped text into Canvas or SVG.
- Code that would otherwise interleave DOM writes and reads across components and has to batch them to avoid layout thrashing.
- Pre-sizing textarea-like pre-wrap text, or checking in development that labels do not wrap, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari 27 with named fonts and px sizes, including CJK, Arabic, Thai and emoji.

**Skip it when:**
- Measuring a text once: prepare() still calls Canvas measureText for every new segment, and nothing in the repo compares that cold cost with one DOM read; the gain comes from repeated layout() calls on cached widths.
- Server-side rendering, Node or Bun without a Canvas, and React Native: it throws 'Text measurement requires OffscreenCanvas or a DOM canvas context.' (SSR #123 and React Native #131/#157 are open, server-side measurement is punted).
- Pagination, print or any place where an undercount breaks the page: open #334 reports Songti SC 16px at 120 and 135 px giving 2 lines where Chrome gives 3, and #421 (2026-10-04) reports kerned overlong words ('AV', 'WAVE', 'To.') broken one letter off in Firefox 156, Chromium 147 and WebKit 26.4.
