- CSS outside its subset: system-ui or -apple-system on macOS, rem/em sizes, font-feature-settings or font-variation-settings, non-default font-kerning or word-spacing, hyphens: auto, word-break: break-all (#402), overflow-wrap: normal, bidi visual order, or per-span font sizes beyond what rich-inline models.
- C or C++ code, or native apps: it is browser JavaScript tied to the host's Canvas text engine; for native shaping and layout see HarfBuzz-based stacks or Parley.

**Integration:** module (npm @chenglou/pretext, ESM only, ships dist JS and TypeScript source; subpath export @chenglou/pretext/rich-inline) · none at runtime (devDependencies only); needs Canvas 2D measureText via OffscreenCanvas or a DOM canvas, Unicode property escapes, and Intl.Segmenter for Thai, Lao, Khmer, Myanmar and other Southeast Asian scripts · ES2018+ JavaScript engine with Unicode property escapes (a SyntaxError at load without them); built with TypeScript 6.0.2, developed with Bun; the WebKit profile follows Safari 27 · Browsers: Chrome/Edge (Blink), Firefox (Gecko), Safari 27 (WebKit); unrecognized engines get Blink's rules; works in Web Workers through OffscreenCanvas (emoji correction off there). Harness runs are on macOS (M5 Max) and an iOS simulator; Windows and Android are untested.

**Vs siblings:** The other browser-JavaScript siblings (text-shaper, rustybuzz-wasm, Typr.js) parse fonts and shape glyphs themselves; Pretext does no shaping and instead predicts where the browser will wrap text it paints with its own font engine. Pick Pretext when the browser renders and app code needs heights or line breaks ahead of time; pick text-shaper or a HarfBuzz/Parley stack when you draw glyphs yourself or work outside a browser.

**Gotchas:**
- On main a JSON copy of a handle hangs: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(prepared)) turns the Uint8Array segmentFlags into an object with no length, and the line APIs never return (CHANGELOG, #340); 0.0.9 tolerated it. Use structuredClone() or postMessage().
- The shared per-font width cache grows with every new segment until clearCache() (TODO.md lists bounding it as open). After a web font finishes loading, call clearCache() and prepare again, or the cached widths stay those of the fallback font; the emoji correction also goes stale when zoom or devicePixelRatio crosses 1.25/1.5, leaving 4-5 px per emoji (#418).
- Overlong words break between graphemes like overflow-wrap: break-word, which is not CSS's default, so set that property on the painted text; an empty string gives lineCount 0 where browsers size one line; a maxWidth that is NaN or undefined lays out as unbounded.
- npm 'latest' is 0.0.9 (2026-09-07). Main carries a large unreleased section (engine ports #340, layout fast path #338, main bundle about 38 KB gzipped against 16 KB in 0.0.9), the maintainer holds releases until an API review, and license notices for the ported browser line-breaking code and engine data are not written yet (TODO.md), so check licensing before vendoring main.

**Status:** Very active (1,511 commits on main, last commit 2026-10-03, 50.7k stars, 38 open issues) and MIT-licensed, but pre-1.0: the published 0.0.9 lags main by a month of engine rewrites, and the maintainer will not release before an API review.

[repo](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext) · [benchmark](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext)

#### image-codecs

##### @napi-rs/image  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust napi-rs addon for Node.js image resize and WebP/AVIF/JPEG/PNG encoding; edges out sharp on small-thumbnail throughput.

**Beats:** sharp (Node.js binding over libvips with libwebp and libavif) — bench/bench.mjs, run in April 2022 on an Apple M1 Max (macOS 12.3.1) with @napi-rs/image 1.1.0 and sharp 0.30.3, rotated, Lanczos3-resized and encoded one small JPEG: WebP 202 vs 169 ops/s and AVIF 26 vs 24 ops/s with the default libuv pool, and 431 vs 238 and 36 vs 32 ops/s with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=10 (1.08x to 1.81x, derived from page data). Node version, compiler and flags were not recorded; both sides encode with libwebp and libaom, so the gap is decode, resize and job scheduling, not a faster encoder.

**Known shortcoming:** Node binding over the image crate (zune-jpeg decode, Lanczos3 resize), libwebp and libavif/libaom, the same encoders sharp uses, so the gain is pipeline and concurrency rather than codec speed. Historical M1 Max run with Node and sharp versions unknown; prebuilt binary with no compiler or flags.

**Known shortcoming:** The README table is from commit a09b74d (April 2022): @napi-rs/image 1.1.0 (image 0.24 with jpeg-decoder 0.2 jpeg_rayon, libwebp-sys 0.6, a libavif-rs 0.10 fork) against sharp 0.30.3 per yarn.lock, so the verifier's zune-jpeg caveat describes current code, not the measured build; the input is one 600x450 JPEG resized to 225x300 (overhead-dominated) and the run was never repeated. ThreadsafeDynamicImage is Send and Sync with no lock (concurrent async encodes on one Transformer are unsafe); x86_64 libwebp is built -mavx2 -msse4.1 (issue #165 SIGILL, closed); open leak #128; old releases linked the GPL imagequant 4.0.0.

**How:** There is no new codec: each job is one libuv task that decodes with the Rust image crate, runs the image crate's separable Lanczos3 resize, then calls libwebp's simple API (WebPEncodeRGB/RGBA, default method) or libavif with libaom (speed 5, libaom threads set to the core count). The measured edge over sharp comes from low per-call overhead on tiny images and from running many independent jobs side by side when UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is raised, while sharp runs each job as its own multi-threaded libvips pipeline. Release builds use fat LTO with codegen-units=1, CI enables mozjpeg's NASM SIMD (`with_simd`), libwebp is compiled with its SSE4.1/AVX2/NEON paths, and a separate `fastResize` method uses the SIMD fast_image_resize crate, which the benchmark does not call.

**Use it when:**
- Node.js servers or build scripts that turn many small JPEGs into WebP or AVIF thumbnails and can raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to the core count (the recorded 1.8x is WebP at UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=10).
- You want one npm package with prebuilt binaries for macOS, Windows (x64, arm64, ia32), Linux glibc and musl, Android arm64 and FreeBSD, with no system libvips.
- In-browser processing through @napi-rs/image-wasm32-wasi when you can serve COOP/COEP headers for cross-origin isolation.
- Combined resize plus PNG/JPEG size optimization in one dependency (oxipng, palette quantization, mozjpeg re-encode).
- HEIC decode or encode on macOS or Windows through the OS codecs (ImageIO, WIC).

**Skip it when:**
- Large images or memory-tight services: every job decodes the whole image into memory and clones it before transforms, with no tiled streaming or JPEG shrink-on-load in the binding's decode path.
- Animated images (no animation pipeline; GIF, OpenEXR and farbfeld are disabled in the published build) or HEIC on Linux, Android, FreeBSD or WASM.
- With the default libuv pool of 4 threads the recorded edge is only 1.20x for WebP and 1.08x for AVIF (derived from page data), within what different encoder settings or images could erase.
- Long-running processes that call `Transformer.fromRgbaPixels(...).png()` in a loop: open issue #128 (v1.4.0, macOS 15.4.1, Node 23.11.0) reports about 16.8 MB retained per call even after GC.
- Migrations that need sharp's exact output: equal numeric quality does not give equal visual quality, and the defaults differ (here WebP quality 90, AVIF quality 80 at 4:4:4).

**Integration:** Prebuilt Node-API native addon on npm (Rust cdylib, one optional-dependency package per platform) plus a separate WASM package · None at runtime beyond Node.js; statically bundles the image crate 0.25, libwebp (libwebp-sys 0.14), libavif 0.14 with libaom, mozjpeg-sys 2, oxipng 10, fast_image_resize 6, resvg 0.48 and lodepng 3; HEIC needs the OS codec (ImageIO on macOS, HEIF/HEVC extensions for WIC on Windows) · Node-API 3 (package.json engines: node >= 10; the README asks for a current Node.js LTS); building from source needs Rust with edition 2024 and @napi-rs/cli 3 · macOS x64/arm64; Windows x64/arm64/ia32; Linux glibc x64/arm64/armv7; Linux musl x64/arm64; Android arm64; FreeBSD x64; wasm32-wasip1-threads

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings are codecs (libjpeg-turbo, zenjpeg, wpd, fpng, oxipng, mozjpeg-rs); pick @napi-rs/image when you are in Node.js and want one prebuilt package for resize plus WebP/AVIF encode plus PNG/JPEG optimization. Pick the codec siblings when you own a native pipeline and need codec-level speed, since this package reuses libwebp, libaom, mozjpeg and oxipng rather than beating them.

**Gotchas:**
- The README table is from commit a09b74d (April 2022): @napi-rs/image 1.1.0 built on image 0.24 with jpeg-decoder 0.2 (jpeg_rayon), libwebp-sys 0.6 and a libavif-rs 0.10 fork, against sharp 0.30.3 per that commit's yarn.lock. The current 1.15.0 decodes JPEG with zune-jpeg through image 0.25 and has not been re-measured.
- The benchmark input is a single 600x450 4:2:0 JPEG with EXIF orientation 5, resized to 225x300, so per-call overhead and scheduling dominate; output sizes and quality are not compared, and AVIF also oversubscribes the CPU (up to core-count parallel jobs, each with libaom threads set to the core count).
- x86_64 Linux and Windows builds enable libwebp-sys's avx2 and sse41 features, which compile the vendored libwebp with -mavx2 -msse4.1 (libwebp-sys build.rs). Issue #165 reported 'Illegal instruction' on older Xeons from v1.10.0; it is closed and .cargo/config.toml now drops +avx2 rustflags for the quantizer, but whether the libwebp path is safe on pre-AVX2 CPUs is not documented.
- Releases around 1.1.0 linked imagequant 4.0.0, which is GPL-3.0-or-later; the current Cargo.toml no longer depends on imagequant, so pin a recent version if license matters.

**Status:** Actively maintained (release 1.15.0, last commit 2026-09-30, 417 stars, 4 open issues) and MIT-licensed with prebuilt binaries, but the performance table has not been re-run since 2022.

[repo](https://github.com/Brooooooklyn/Image) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Brooooooklyn/Image/HEAD/README.md)

##### astc-encoder (astcenc)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Arm's reference ASTC texture compressor (CLI plus C/C++ library); 2.x and later are 2-3.5x faster than its own 1.7 series.

**Beats:** astcenc 1.7 (earlier major series of the same encoder; no third-party baseline opened) — Arm's changelog charts (i5-9600K at 4.2 GHz, 6 threads) show astcenc-avx2 2.0 coding about 2-3x faster than astcenc 1.7 at -thorough and mostly 2-3.5x at -medium and -fast, with PSNR mostly within 0.2 dB and one -3.6 dB -fast grayscale outlier; 4.0 is about 1.17-1.74x over 3.7 at -thorough. The baseline is the project's own 1.7: its stock Makefile builds scalar code with -O3 -msse2, against 2.0's -O3 -flto -mavx2 -mpopcnt, so part of the gain is ISA and LTO. No compiler is stated for either side, and no rival encoder is timed.

**Known shortcoming:** A self-comparison of astcenc 2.0 against the project's own 1.7 (chart images on an i5-9600K with 6 threads, compiler unstated; 2.1-3.1x thorough, 1.7-3.8x medium, 1.3-4.0x fast) with no third-party incumbent; one -fast case loses 3.6 dB PSNR. The SPEC CPU2026 731.astcenc_r workload is snippet-only (spec.org blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): the changelog charts compare against the project's own 1.7, whose stock Makefile builds scalar -O3 -msse2 code, against 2.0's -O3 -flto -mavx2 -mpopcnt, so part of the 2-3.5x is ISA and LTO; no compiler is stated and no rival encoder is timed. The 2.0 harness runs a 1.7 binary from an untracked Binaries/1.7 directory (build unrecorded) and parses different timer output lines; the 3.7 wrapper implies a locally modified 1.7 binary; every harness keeps the best of N repeats; Docs/Testing.md says 4.3 GHz where the changelogs say 4.2 GHz. No correctness bug behind the timings. No runtime ISA check in the core library (AVX2/SVE builds fault on other CPUs); invariance on by default costs 5-20% speed; preset effort changed across 4.2, 4.6 and 5.7 (removed -repeats), so re-measure when upgrading. Tier C stands.

**Independent measurement:** first-party charts

**How:** The 2.0 rewrite added a SIMD abstraction (vfloat4/vint4/vfloat8) with SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX2 and later NEON, SVE and RISC-V V backends, replacing 1.7's scalar code. Partition search runs k-means on the block's texels, ranks all 1024 hash-generated partitionings by how many texels disagree with that clustering, and gives the detailed endpoint and weight search only the top N candidates. Per-preset tuning tables (astcenc_entry.cpp) cap block modes, partition indices and refinement passes, and dB-target and correlation early-outs skip 2-plane and 3/4-partition trials once a good enough encoding is found. 4.x added in-register SIMD permutes for small tables, deferred weight and color packing, and a narrower search for later trials.

**Use it when:**
- Offline asset pipelines that must produce ASTC for mobile or Apple GPUs, especially block sizes above 8x8, HDR (-ch/-cH) or 3D textures, which narrower ASTC encoders do not cover.
- Quality-sensitive content (normal maps, mask maps, UI) where -medium or -thorough quality matters more than encode time.
- Many-core build machines: one image can be split across N caller threads, and since 5.4.0 several contexts with the same config can share read-only tables when you run one image per thread.
- Builds that need identical output on every platform: invariant builds (the default) give bit-exact results across compilers and ISAs.
- Arm64 build hosts: NEON and SVE 128/256 backends are first-class, with prebuilt Linux Arm64 binaries since 5.2.0.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency-bound runtime encoding of 2D LDR photos: Arm's own astcenc 3.1 blog (search snippet only, page blocked) says ISPC TexComp can be up to 3x faster at quality similar to -fast, though worse on normal and mask maps. A Chalmers thesis snippet claims up to 44x for Intel's encoder at the same quality, against an unstated, probably older astcenc.
- Non-ASTC targets (BC1-BC7, ETC1/ETC2): astcenc encodes ASTC only.
- Distributing one binary for unknown x86 CPUs: the core library does no runtime ISA dispatch (issue #672, open, asks for it), so you ship SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2 variants and choose one yourself. macOS gets a universal binary.
- Data that needs 1-bit punch-through alpha, signed values (as in BC6H signed) or two-plane .rg sampling like BC5: Encoding.md says ASTC has no direct equivalent.
- Choosing a speed winner over rival encoders: the only measured speedup is against astcenc's own 1.7 release, so this entry gives no evidence against ISPC, GPU or other ASTC encoders.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake core codec library, optional shared lib via ASTCENC_SHAREDLIB) plus CLI tool · none for the core codec; the CLI bundles stb_image, Wuffs and TinyEXR; unit tests use a googletest submodule · C++14 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14), CMake 3.15+; tested with Clang 9+, Visual Studio 2019+ (ClangCL recommended) and Xcode 14+; astcenc.h is C-compatible since 5.4.0 · x86-64 (SSE2; SSE4.1+POPCNT; AVX2+POPCNT+F16C), aarch64 (NEON, SVE 128-bit, SVE 256-bit), RISC-V V at VLEN=256 through the NONE/NATIVE build, portable reference C (big-endian with ASTCENC_BIG_ENDIAN=ON); Windows, Linux, macOS, Android unofficial

**Vs siblings:** Pick astcenc over refreshed-astc-encoder, a fork of the 2015-era code measured only against old Arm binaries, for anything current. Pick it over the ISPC kernels behind intel-tex-rs-2 when you need HDR, 3D, block sizes above 8x8 or the highest-quality presets; bc7e, bc7enc, etcpak, Goofy and ICBC target BCn/ETC, not ASTC.

**Gotchas:**
- No runtime ISA check in the core library: an AVX2 or SVE-256 build on a CPU without that ISA faults, so the caller must check, as astcenccli_entry.cpp does. SVE builds must match the host vector length.
- Invariance is on by default and costs speed. ASTCENC_INVARIANCE=OFF enables -ffp-contract=fast (and -mfma on AVX2) for up to 5-20% more speed at up to 0.2 dB lower quality, but output then differs across compilers and platforms. Building.md also says Clang builds are about 15% faster than GCC builds.
- If textures are sampled with the decode_unorm8 extension, compress with -decode_unorm8 or ASTCENC_FLG_USE_DECODE_UNORM8 to get the right rounding. Contexts made with ASTCENC_FLG_SELF_DECOMPRESS_ONLY can return magenta error blocks when decoding images from other encoders or configurations.
- Preset names do not mean equal effort across major versions (4.2 retuned -exhaustive to 3x slower and added -verythorough; 4.6 pruned -medium and -thorough again), and 5.7.0 removed the -repeats benchmarking option. Re-measure on your content when upgrading.

**Status:** Actively maintained by Arm (5.7.0 in August 2026, last commit 2026-08-29), Apache-2.0, fuzzed in OSS-Fuzz; main is the development branch, so production users should pin a release tag.

[repo](https://github.com/ARM-software/astc-encoder) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ARM-software/astc-encoder/3.7/Docs/ChangeLog-2x.md)

##### bc7enc (rgbcx BC1 and bc7enc16 BC7 encoders)  `C++ (BC7 encoder in C)`  `MIT OR Unlicense`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Scalar single-file BC1-5 (rgbcx.h) and modes-1/6 BC7 encoders; first-party tables beat ispc_texcomp, independent tests mostly do not.

**Beats:** libsquish (BC1 cluster fit); Intel ispc_texcomp (BC7); also AMD Compressonator and DirectXTex CPU BC7 — The README's BC7 table is first-party: 31 images (Kodak plus others), encode time only, OpenMP on an unnamed dual Xeon, compiler unstated, ispc_texcomp at AVX. Its largest wins are against ispc_texcomp slow (9.3x at +1.0 dB Luma-PSNR in perceptual mode) and a locally patched DirectXTex (263x). At matched RGB PSNR it shows parity with ispc_texcomp fast. Independent per-image data from Aras Pranckevicius (December 2020; i9-8950HK, 12 threads, Apple clang 11.0.3 up to AVX2; 20 Unity textures; bc7enc and rgbcx built from April 2020 code) reproduce the speed lead only against ISPC slow (bc7enc 64.4: 2.62x geomean, faster on 20/20, at 0.79 dB lower mean Luma-PSNR). Against ISPC fast, basic and vfast at similar quality, bc7enc is slower or tied. The BC1 claims against libsquish and Compressonator have no numbers anywhere.

**Known shortcoming:** Texture encoder (BC7) whose baseline ispc_texcomp is not a listed incumbent. README claims 2-3x at matched PSNR/SSIM and about 8x against the slow profile with no table, machine or harness; the independent aras-p blog is blocked (snippet directional only). Repo archived 2026-01-28; the encoder ships inside bc7enc_rdo (used by todds) and as a scalar C++ port in basis_universal.

**Known shortcoming:** Texture encoder (BC1 and BC7) whose baselines ispc_texcomp and DirectXTex are not listed incumbents; ispc_texcomp is faster in the ultrafast rows, and the matched-RGB-PSNR update shows parity (41.42 s vs 41.45 s); perceptual rows are scored on luma PSNR, which favours bc7enc16. Only BC7 modes 1 and 6, so different work from ispc_texcomp; the 263x over DirectXTex is against a slow baseline. Dual Xeon unnamed, no flags. Licence MIT OR Unlicense.

**Known shortcoming:** Independent data contradicts the BC7 headline (retier-21 narrows the claim): in Aras Pranckevicius's 2020 run (i9-8950HK, clang 11.0.3, 20 Unity textures) bc7enc level 64.4 runs at 0.34x the speed of ispc_texcomp fast and level 16.0 at 0.99x of vfast at -0.35 dB, winning only against ispc_texcomp slow at lower quality (2.62x at -0.79 dB, 10.6x at -1.45 dB); it leads on opaque photo crops and loses up to 4-5 dB on normal maps and alpha. The repo's test.cpp is single-threaded without OpenMP, so the README's harness is absent; the BC1 claim against libsquish and Compressonator is measured nowhere (Aras: rgbcx 0 is 1.07x stb_dxt at -0.17 dB; ispc_texcomp 2.1x faster than rgbcx 0); issue #3's solid-block bug is not confirmed in rgbcx v1.12.

**How:** rgbcx's 'prioritized cluster fit' replaces cluster fit's walk over all orderings with precomputed tables. There are 969 unique 4-colour selector histograms (g_unique_total_orders4) with precomputed least-squares factors, plus, for each ordering, a ranked list of up to 128 other orderings likely to help (g_best_total_orderings4). Higher levels simply try more of them (level 10 tries 20, level 17 tries 128); low levels use bounding-box, 2D least-squares or PCA endpoint fits like stb_dxt. bc7enc's speed comes from searching only two BC7 modes. Mode-1 partitions are scanned in usage-frequency order with a cheap per-subset error estimate, and an optional 'filterbank' skips lesser-used partitions unless the best of the first 14 predicts them (about 11% faster for about 0.08 dB). Single-colour subsets use precomputed optimal-endpoint tables, and 'uber' levels 1-4 add selector perturbation passes.

**Use it when:**
- You need a dependency-free, portable scalar BC1/BC3/BC4/BC5 encoder with a single quality knob, e.g. in an asset pipeline that cannot run the ISPC compiler or on ARM/WASM, where SIMD-only encoders lose their edge.
- Highest-quality BC1 when encode time does not matter. In Aras Pranckevicius's 2020 test (20 Unity textures, i9-8950HK, 12 threads) rgbcx level 18 had the best DXTC Luma-PSNR of any library (38.47 dB) at 4.7 Mpix/s.
- Fast BC1 near stb_dxt quality: level 0 was 1.07x stb_dxt's speed at 0.17 dB lower PSNR (per-image geomean, derived from Aras's chart data). Goofy's README measured rgbcx 1.08 level 0 at 60 MP/s and 40.85 dB, against stb_dxt at 43 MP/s and 40.82 dB, on one thread.
- Opaque, photographic BC7 content scored on luma, where bc7enc's perceptual YCbCr metric pays off: on kodim23crop it was 6.9x faster than ISPC slow at +1.40 dB Luma-PSNR in Aras's data.
- Learning or prototyping BC7: about 2,200 lines of readable C covering endpoint fitting, p-bits, partition estimation and block packing.

**Skip it when:**
- Production BC7. In the same independent run, bc7e fast was about 9x faster than bc7enc's best preset (per-image geomean) at 0.70 dB higher mean Luma-PSNR. The author's own README points to bc7e.ispc in bc7enc_rdo, and basis_universal carries bc7e_scalar and bc7f.
- Whenever ispc_texcomp's fast or veryfast presets are available. At matched Luma-PSNR on Aras's 20 textures, ISPC fast (10.10 Mpix/s, 45.36 dB) was 2.6x faster than bc7enc 64.4 (3.82 Mpix/s, 45.48 dB), and bc7enc 16.0 tied ISPC vfast on speed at 0.35 dB lower.
- BC7 normal maps, alpha gradients or mixed content. bc7enc lost up to 4-5 dB to ISPC on normal maps, sprites and frymire in Aras's data, and open issue #2 reports blocky, sawtooth alpha on translucent gradients, with no maintainer reply.
- Throughput-critical BC1 on x86 with SIMD. ISPC BC1 was 2.1x faster than rgbcx level 0 at equal mean PSNR, and icbc level 8 (AVX2) was 3.2x faster than rgbcx level 10 at 0.11 dB lower (per-image geomeans, derived).
- You need upstream maintenance: archived on 2026-01-28 with the last code change in February 2021; issues #2, #3 and #5 and PR #6 (missing abs/memcpy/memset includes) were never answered.

**Integration:** source-drop (rgbcx.h single header with RGBCX_IMPLEMENTATION; bc7enc.c/.h and bc7decomp.cpp/.h as separate files) · none for the encoders (libc/libm and <algorithm>); the test app adds lodepng and dds_defs.h · C++11 for rgbcx.h (enum class, static_assert); C99 for bc7enc.c (inline functions in the header); CMake 2.8 file builds the test app with -fno-strict-aliasing · any: portable scalar C/C++, no SIMD or intrinsics; tested by the author with MSVC, and clang warnings fixed in 2020

**Vs siblings:** Pick rgbcx over ICBC when you need BC3/BC4/BC5 as well as BC1, or a scalar build (scalar ICBC is slower than RGBCX at most levels in its own chart). Pick Goofy only for real-time BC1, where it is far faster at about 4 dB lower PSNR. For BC7, prefer bc7e (or bc7e_scalar/bc7f in Basis Universal); bc7enc is only worth picking for its tiny plain-C footprint.

**Gotchas:**
- Skipping the init call does not fail in release builds. bc7enc only asserts, and its header warns you will 'get artifacts'; rgbcx needs init() before any encode or decode.
- bc7enc_compress_block_params_init() selects the perceptual YCbCr metric by default. Call bc7enc_compress_block_params_init_linear_weights() if you judge output by RGB PSNR, which is the metric under which the README shows ispc_texcomp ahead.
- BC1 at level 5 and above with use_transparent_texels_for_black codes dark texels with the 3-colour transparent index, so your shader must ignore sampled alpha. An unknown level silently falls back to level 5, and level 19 is a hidden, extremely slow training mode.
- The default rgbcx build carries a 969x128 uint16_t ordering table (about 248 KB). Define RGBCX_USE_SMALLER_TABLES 1 for the 969x32 table, which caps BC1 levels at 32 orderings.

**Status:** Archived on 2026-01-28, with the last code commit on 2021-02-03; MIT or Unlicense and trivially vendorable, but the maintained rgbcx and BC7 code (with RDO) lives in richgel999/bc7enc_rdo.

[repo](https://github.com/richgel999/bc7enc) · [benchmark](https://github.com/richgel999/bc7enc)

##### bcdec  `C`  `MIT OR Unlicense`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-header C BC1-BC7 block decoder; 1.3-11x DirectXTex's single-thread throughput in aras-p's 2022 decoder comparison.

**Beats:** DirectXTex BCn decoders (also Compressonator and bc7enc_rdo decoders) — aras-p's 'Comparing BCn texture decoders' (2022-06-23) is a third-party, single-threaded Mpix/s comparison; the post's source and chart PNGs are readable in the public aras-p/aras-p.hugo repo. The harness is public (aras-p/bcn_decoder_tester: 20 runs per DDS file, pinned submodules, test_images in the repo; Windows preset RelWithDebInfo plus /Ob2 with cl or clang-cl). Against DirectXTex (679538e), bcdec (e3ca0) measured BC1 1319 vs 272 (4.85x), BC3 704 vs 254 (2.77x), BC6H unsigned 85 vs 25 (3.40x) and BC7 142 vs 93 (1.53x) on a Ryzen 9 5950X with VS2022. With clang 14 on the same CPU: BC1 1449 vs 223 (6.50x), BC3 621 vs 207 (3.00x), BC7 169 vs 127 (1.33x). On an M1 Max with clang 13: BC1 2088 vs 183 (11.4x), BC3 1093 vs 185 (5.91x), BC7 220 vs 140 (1.57x). All ratios are derived from page data. Two caveats: the harness only warns on output-hash mismatch, and the measured bcdec had small rounding differences (BC1 off by up to 1 per channel; alpha bias +1) that were fixed in 2024 with integer operations of the same cost. The Mac build flags are not given in the presets.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the only numbers are a before-and-after of its own code in PR #1; the cross-decoder chart there sits on user-images.githubusercontent.com (blocked) and aras-p/bcn_decoder_tester has a harness (src/main.cpp) but no committed results, with search snippets conflicting on which decoder is fastest. Retier candidate when aras-p.info is reachable.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e109, 2026-10-05): aras-p's independent 2022 comparison is readable through the aras-p.hugo repo and its harness is public (bcn_decoder_tester, pinned submodules, RelWithDebInfo plus /Ob2, Ryzen 9 5950X VS2022/clang 14, M1 Max clang 13): bcdec 1.33-11.4x faster than DirectXTex, but bc7enc_rdo's decoder is 2.3-4.4x faster on BC7, etcpak 1.16-1.7x faster on BC1/BC3, and BC6H on the M1 is behind ConvectionKernels, SwiftShader and Mesa. The measured e3ca0 had rounding bugs fixed in 2024 with same-cost operations (BC1 off by up to 1 per channel, #15; alpha +1 bias, #12) and the harness only warns on hash mismatch, so the tier is capped at C by the measured-on-later-fixed-code rule (retier-32, D to C).

**Independent measurement:** independent harness (aras-p)

**How:** It is plain scalar C with no SIMD. The speed comes from doing the work at word level instead of byte level (aras-p's PR #1): each block is loaded as 16/32/64-bit little-endian words, BC1 builds a 4-entry 32-bit RGBA palette and writes each pixel with one 32-bit store, and BC4/BC5 alpha indices are pulled from a 64-bit word 3 bits at a time. BC6H and BC7 use a two-word (128-bit) bitstream reader instead of per-bit extraction, plus hard-coded partition and fix-up tables. BC6H endpoint unquantization was moved out of the per-pixel loop (PR #8). BC1 palette interpolation uses multiply-shift 'magic' constants on the 5/6-bit endpoints instead of division (issue #15). DirectXTex, by contrast, decodes every texel through float XMVECTOR math and then packs back to 8-bit.

**Use it when:**
- CPU-side decoding of BCn textures (asset pipelines, texture viewers, compression-quality evaluation, software fallbacks for GPUs without BCn support) where you want every format, including BC6H signed and unsigned, from one 1,500-line header.
- Replacing DirectXTex's decoders outside Windows: no DirectXMath, DirectX-Headers or sal.h stubs needed, and it ran 4.85-11.4x faster on BC1 and 1.3-1.6x faster on BC7 in the 2022 single-thread comparison.
- Embedding in C or C++ projects with strict dependency or licence rules: one header, no runtime library calls, MIT or Unlicense.
- Multi-threaded decoding where you split the image into block ranges yourself: the functions keep no state between calls.

**Skip it when:**
- BC7-heavy workloads where decode speed matters: bc7enc_rdo's bc7decomp was 2.3-4.4x faster than bcdec on BC7 in the same 2022 charts (517 vs 220 Mpix/s on M1 Max, 621 vs 142 on a 5950X with VS2022).
- Maximum BC1/BC3 throughput: etcpak's decoder was 1.16-1.7x faster on BC1 and BC3 in the same charts. It is harder to extract, though.
- BC6H on Apple Silicon: in the 2022 M1 Max chart, bcdec (79 Mpix/s) trailed ConvectionKernels (149), SwiftShader (143) and Mesa (84). PR #8 (Sep 2022) sped BC6H up after those charts, and that change was not re-measured.
- When you need bit-exact agreement with an older bcdec build or with a float reference. BC1 interpolation was off by up to 1 per channel until the June 2024 fix (issue #15). BC3/BC4/BC5 alpha rounding was changed in November 2024 (issue #12): BC3 alpha now truncates, and float-matching rounding needs BCDEC_BC4BC5_PRECISE.
- Big-endian hosts, or when you need whole-image or DDS handling: the output stores pack 0xAABBGGRR as native 32-bit words, and edge blocks and padding are the caller's job.

**Integration:** header-only (stb style: define BCDEC_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit; BCDEC_STATIC or BCDECDEF control linkage) · none (no C runtime calls) · C with 64-bit unsigned long long (C99 or C++11 era compilers); built by MSVC 2022, clang 13/14 and GCC in the public harnesses · any little-endian target; scalar code, no SIMD or intrinsics; since 2026-09-02 input blocks may be unaligned

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued image-codecs siblings (ffpng, fpng, QOI, libspng and others) decodes GPU block formats. Among block-texture entries, pick bcdec over etcpak or bc7enc_rdo's decoders when you want every BCn format, including BC2, BC4/BC5 signed and BC6H, in one header, and use those two only for peak BC1/BC3 (etcpak) or BC7 (bc7decomp) speed.

**Gotchas:**
- Pitch units differ by function: bytes for the 8-bit formats, but float or half elements for bcdec_bc6h_float and bcdec_bc6h_half (and for the BC4/BC5 float variants). The bcn_decoder_tester call passes width * 3 for BC6H float.
- BCDEC_*_COMPRESSED_SIZE(w, h) computes (w>>2)*(h>>2) blocks, so it returns 0 for a 256x1 image and undercounts any size that is not a multiple of 4. Round dimensions up yourself. Issues #7 (tiny images) and #18 (256x1 BC3 crash) were in this area.
- Output pixels are written through unsigned int, unsigned short and float pointers, so destination rows should be naturally aligned. Unaligned input reads were only fixed on 2026-09-02 (commit 80859ed, prompted by PR #23): DX10-header DDS payloads start at byte 148 and are never 8-byte aligned. Older copies are formally undefined behaviour there and fault on strict-alignment CPUs.
- The maintainer rejects LLM-generated contributions (README; PR #23 was declined for that reason), so plan to carry local patches yourself if needed.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-02, alignment fix); single-header and MIT OR Unlicense, so it is trivially vendorable. Pin a version, because decoded values changed slightly in the 2024 rounding fixes.

[repo](https://github.com/iOrange/bcdec) · [benchmark](https://github.com/aras-p/bcn_decoder_tester)

##### gif_load  `C (ANSI C single header)`  `Unlicense`  `active`  `Tier C`

Public-domain single-header C animated-GIF decoder; with the file cached it decodes 1.3-1.7x faster than giflib 5.2.2.

**Beats:** giflib 5.2.2 (also stb_image) — First-party README only: on an unnamed Linux 6.4 machine (GCC 11.5 -O2), wall time including reading the file, best of two runs, to decode all frames of six synthetic non-interlaced GIFs (320x240 x100, 640x480 x200, 1920x1080 x150; flat shapes and noise). With a warm cache gif_load beat giflib 5.2.2 by 1.28x-1.72x and stb_image by 1.39x-2.42x on the compositing +RGBA rows. Cold, it won 1.42x-1.51x on shapes but lost on noise; the prose figure of 0.83x-0.85x matches neither the read() row (0.89x-0.91x) nor the mmap() row (0.75x-0.79x) but roughly their average (about 0.83x-0.84x, derived from page data). The timed code (commit 5a961ff) differs from HEAD only by the 2026-10-01 one-byte bounds check, but the harness and CPU are not published, and stb_image's figure includes its known O(N^2) realloc-and-copy of the whole animation buffer (open stb issue #1883), so the stb gap partly measures that rather than LZW speed.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers only in the README Performance section (commit 2026-09-27; GCC 11.5 -O2, Linux 6.4, no CPU model) with the harness unpublished (tests/ checks accuracy only). README prose (cold-noise 0.83x-0.85x) contradicts its own table (0.89x-0.91x read, 0.75x-0.79x mmap). A 1-byte out-of-bounds read was fixed on 2026-10-01, after the numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** The prose cold-noise figure of 0.83-0.85x is roughly the average of the read and mmap rows, and part of the stb_image gap is stb's O(N^2) realloc of the whole animation (stb issue #1883). From code reading: a frame without a leading clear code is rejected (line 104, return -2), an extra sub-block after EOI is refused, a mid-animation decode failure returns a positive smaller count despite the README, uint16_t loads are unaligned type-punned, and the 2019 vendored copies carry the issue #14 overflow and NULL bugs.

**How:** Each LZW code-table entry is packed into one uint32_t (prefix code in bits 0-11, string length in bits 12-23, last byte in bits 24-31). Because the string length is known up front, the decoder writes each string straight into the frame buffer back to front by following prefix links, with no temporary stack and no per-row copy. Codes are pulled from the sub-blocks 16 bits at a time into a bit accumulator. A first pass only skips sub-blocks to count frames and find the largest one; then one allocation holds the 16 KB code table directly in front of a frame buffer that is reused for every frame. Output stays as palette indices, and there is no I/O layer in the decode loop because the whole GIF is one in-memory buffer.

**Use it when:**
- Animated GIFs already in memory (asset packs, network buffers, mmap'd files) where you want per-frame palette indices and do your own compositing or GPU palette lookup: warm-cache wall time was 1.28x-1.72x better than giflib's line-by-line API on the author's six test GIFs.
- Long or high-resolution animations where stb_image's whole-animation RGBA buffer is too big: at 1080p x150 frames stb_image peaked at 1254 MB (shapes) and 1611 MB (noise) versus 52-60 MB and 409-418 MB for gif_load, most of which is the GIF file itself.
- Embedded, freestanding or no-libc builds: under 300 lines of C89 plus stdint.h, the only external call is realloc (replaceable with GIF_MGET), and a call makes exactly one allocation (largest frame + 16 KB + 2 bytes).
- Projects that need to vendor a decoder with no licence obligations: Unlicense public-domain dedication in the header.
- Progressive display of a GIF still downloading, at whole-frame granularity, by calling again with skip set to the frames already shown.

**Skip it when:**
- Cold reads of large or poorly compressible GIFs from disk: the whole file must be in memory before the first pixel, so giflib, which overlaps reading with decoding, won on the three noise GIFs (gif_load at 0.89x-0.91x with read() and 0.75x-0.79x with mmap(), derived from page data).
- Minimal-memory streaming: giflib's line API holds a single row, while gif_load holds the whole file (twice with read(): page cache plus copy) and a full-frame buffer.
- When you want ready-to-use RGBA frames: deinterlacing, disposal modes, transparency and frames that extend past the logical screen are all the caller's job (the README's own C example carries a TODO for out-of-bounds frames).
- Lenient decoding of oddly encoded files: a frame whose LZW data does not begin with a clear code is rejected (gif_load.h line 104 returns -2, though GIF89a only says encoders 'should' emit one), and a frame with another sub-block after the end-of-information code is refused (tests/extradata.gif returns 0); either one stops loading at that frame. Found by code reading; the first case has no test.
- Old vendored copies (the 2019 header, before 2026-09-27): issue #14 integer overflow of the frame-buffer size where long is 32 bits (all Windows, all 32-bit targets) giving an undersized buffer and heap out-of-bounds access, NULL dereference on failed allocation, uninitialised pixels on short streams and rejected palette-less GIFs; issue #15 (1-byte over-read at a trailing 0x21) was fixed on 2026-10-01.

**Integration:** header-only (gif_load.h; can also be built as a shared library with GIF_EXTR) · none beyond stdint.h; realloc from stdlib.h by default, replaceable through the GIF_MGET macro · ANSI C / C89 plus stdint.h (the test suite builds it with -std=c89 -pedantic -Wall -Wextra -Wno-long-long without warnings); usable from C++ via extern "C"; MSVC build line given in the README · any; little-endian by default, big-endian targets must define GIF_BIGE=1; relies on unaligned 16-bit loads

**Vs siblings:** Among the catalogued GIF entries, giflib-turbo patches giflib's own LZW decoder, so it keeps the giflib API, but its 2.5x-30x claim comes with no harness, machine or images; pick gif_load when you can hold the file in memory and want a dependency-free public-domain header with published, if unreproducible, timings. msf_gif is an encoder and does not compete here.

**Gotchas:**
- A positive return value is documented as the total frame count of a properly terminated GIF, but if a frame fails to decode in such a file, loading stops and the return value is the number of frames delivered so far, still positive; compare it with whdr->nfrm from the callback to detect truncation (traced in GIF_Load, lines 260-264 and 292).
- LZW codes are read as *(uint16_t*) at arbitrary byte offsets (lines 104 and 112): unaligned, type-punned loads that work on x86 and ARM but are undefined behaviour in C and trip -fsanitize=alignment or strict-alignment CPUs.
- whdr->bptr is one buffer reused for every frame, and cpal is NULL with clrs 0 when the file has no palette; copy what you need inside the callback.
- The default GIF_MGET frees with realloc(m, 0), which the header itself warns does not free on some systems; define GIF_MGET with malloc/free there, as the README shows.

**Status:** Revived after seven idle years by a hardening burst (2026-09-27 to 2026-10-01: overflow, NULL and over-read fixes plus a valgrind-checked accuracy suite); Unlicense and under 300 lines, so vendor the current header rather than any 2019 copy.

[repo](https://github.com/hidefromkgb/gif_load) · [benchmark](https://github.com/hidefromkgb/gif_load)

##### giflib-turbo  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Single-file C rewrite of giflib's slurp-style API whose LZW decoder uses the output image as its dictionary; speed unmeasured.

**Beats:** giflib — Nothing has been measured. The only numbers are first-party prose: the DecodeLZW comment in gif_lib.c claims about 2.5x over giflib on poorly compressed images and up to 30x on well-compressed ones, and a search summary of the blocked 2021 blog post gives 2x/5x/20x. None of them names a CPU, compiler, giflib version or image set. The repo's A/B Makefile (gif_test_old against Homebrew -lgif vs gif_test_new, gcc -O3) builds a test.c that has no timer and only writes a generated wedge image.

**Known shortcoming:** No reachable number: the README, repo page and AnimatedGIF wiki carry none; the 5x to 20x versus giflib exists only in search snippets of the author's blocked blogspot post. The Makefile builds old (Homebrew -lgif) and new (gcc -O3) targets, but test.c has no timer and its decode loop never runs (main returns after DoGifWedge), and no machine or test images are stated. Tier D on the keep-and-document rule.

**Known shortcoming:** Security bugs from code reading (not run): the frame buffer is W*H+8 rounded up to 64 KiB but 256 root-dictionary bytes are written after W*H, so valid GIFs with W*H mod 65536 in 65281-65528 (for example 300x218, 120 bytes past) overflow the heap; DecodeLZW ignores iLZWSize and reads past the file buffer; sub-block and extension parsing is unbounded; LZW code size unchecked; a descriptor closed twice; mallocs unchecked. Partial drop-in only: DGifOpen stub returns NULL, DGifGet* absent, six declared functions undefined (GCB helpers, EGifPutExtension, GifFreeSavedImages). The only number is a 2.5x to 30x comment in gif_lib.c DecodeLZW with no harness or machine (retier-04, D to C).

**How:** The LZW decoder stores each dictionary entry as an (offset, length) pair pointing into pixels already written to the frame buffer. Emitting a code is then a forward copy, done 8 bytes at a time with unaligned 64-bit loads and stores on 64-bit targets, instead of walking a prefix linked list backwards and reversing the result. The compressed data is first 'de-chunked' in place, with the 255-byte sub-block headers removed, so the inner loop refills a 64-bit bit buffer without checking block boundaries. The file is read with a single read() call, and there are no per-byte input bounds checks in the hot loop (see gotchas).

**Use it when:**
- Trusted GIF files on Linux or macOS x86-64/arm64 when the code already uses only DGifOpenFileName/DGifOpenFileHandle + DGifSlurp + DGifCloseFile and you want to try a faster decoder without changing source.
- Batch or offline jobs (thumbnailing your own assets, tests) where you can confirm the output matches giflib's pixel for pixel on your own corpus, and where buffering the whole file plus each frame in memory is acceptable.
- Studying the output-as-dictionary LZW technique; the same author's maintained AnimatedGIF library uses it as its 'Turbo' mode.

**Skip it when:**
- Any untrusted input (browsers, upload services, chat clients). The decoder does not validate the LZW minimum code size, ignores the compressed-data length, does not bounds-check sub-block parsing, and leaves malloc results unchecked. Valid images can also overflow the heap (see gotchas). The README itself lists security vulnerabilities as an open risk.
- Code that uses DGifOpen with a read callback or in-memory buffer, the DGifGetRecordType/DGifGetImageDesc/DGifGetLine low-level decoder, the GraphicsControlBlock helpers (DGifSavedExtensionToGCB and others) or GifFreeSavedImages. These fail at runtime or at link time.
- Big-endian 64-bit CPUs, or 64-bit CPUs that trap on unaligned access. INTELLONG reads a native-endian uint64_t, and LZWCopyBytes does unaligned 8-byte stores.
- Windows or non-seekable input. The code includes unistd.h and sys/fcntl.h and uses open/read/lseek/close. On a pipe, lseek fails, no file buffer is allocated, and GIFPreprocess then dereferences a NULL file pointer.
- Production use where you need a maintained, measured option. There are 10 commits, the last core change was on 2023-01-16, there are no tests, and there is no benchmark. gif_load is the measured alternative.

**Integration:** source-drop (gif_lib.c + gif_lib.h), or a CMake library installed as 'gif' with giflib.pc and SOVERSION 7 · none beyond libc and POSIX file I/O · C99 (Makefile uses -std=c99 -O3); CMake 3.11 for the CMake build · POSIX (Linux, macOS, BSD); the fast path assumes a little-endian 64-bit CPU with cheap unaligned access (x86-64, arm64); 32-bit builds fall back to byte-by-byte copies; no Windows support in the source

**Vs siblings:** Only when you need giflib's exact SavedImage structures from a recompile and the input is trusted. Otherwise use gif_load (C tier, measured 1.28x-1.78x over giflib 5.2.2 in its own README tables, different callback API), or msf_gif if what you need is fast GIF encoding.

**Gotchas:**
- Heap overflow on valid files. Each frame buffer is malloc'd as Width*Height+8 rounded up to 64 KiB, but DecodeLZW writes the 2^codesize root dictionary bytes just past Width*Height. With 8-bit LZW codes, any frame where Width*Height mod 65536 falls in 65281-65528 overruns the buffer; for example, a 300x218 frame writes 120 bytes past it (derived from reading gif_lib.c). Separately, the 8-byte copy overshoot near the end of a frame can overwrite those root bytes before the last few pixels are decoded.
- Out-of-bounds reads on malformed or truncated files. The sub-block de-chunk loop and extension parsing never compare iOff with the file size. DecodeLZW never uses its iLZWSize argument, so a stream with no EOI keeps reading past the file buffer until the frame is full. The LZW code-size byte is never range-checked: a value of 13 or more gives memset a negative length, and 14 or more writes past the 12,288-entry symbol table. The decoder always returns GIF_OK, so pixels a short stream never writes stay as uninitialized heap memory.
- Ownership differs from giflib. Local ColorMap->Colors and every ExtensionBlock.Bytes point into the slurped file buffer, which DGifCloseFile frees. Copying decoded frames with GifMakeSavedImage and then calling EGifSpew/EGifCloseFile passes those pointers to free() in GifFreeExtensions, which is an invalid free. This is the decode-and-re-encode loop in test.c that is never reached.
- Each handle is closed twice: DGifSlurp and EGifSpew close the file descriptor, then DGifCloseFile and EGifCloseFile close the same number again. In a multithreaded program that fd number may already belong to another file. EGifSpew writes the LZW code-size byte from SColorResolution and dereferences SColorMap without a NULL check.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2024-03-22, a BSD build fix; last code change 2023-01-16; 39 stars, no releases, no tests, no open issues). It is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, but it is not safe for untrusted input without substantial hardening.

[repo](https://github.com/bitbank2/giflib-turbo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bitbank2/giflib-turbo/blob/master/gif_lib.c)

##### Goofy (realtime DXT1/ETC1 encoder)  `C++ (header-only, SSE2)`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only SSE2 BC1/ETC1 encoder, about 1.4 GP/s per core, trading about 4 dB PSNR for 24-400x speed.

**Beats:** stb_dxt (ryg DXT1, STB_DXT_NORMAL); also rgbcx 1.08, icbc 1.0 and rg_etc1 1.04 — The author's 2020 README table (Src/main.cpp harness, i7-7820HQ single thread, best of 128 runs, 42 images; compiler and flags not stated, likely the repo's VS2017 Win64 build) gives Goofy DXT1 1429 MP/s at 37.02 dB against stb_dxt 43 MP/s at 40.82 dB (about 33x), rgbcx 1.08 level 0 60 MP/s (about 24x), icbc 1.0 fast 24 MP/s (about 60x), and Goofy ETC1 1221 MP/s against rg_etc1 1.04 low quality 3 MP/s (about 407x), all ratios derived from page data. Reading the harness narrows the init-in-loop concern: rgbcx's init returns at once after its first call and rg_etc1's is under 1% of its time, so only the icbc ratio is inflated (see measurement_notes), and the README's 'RGB-PSNR' sits about 4.8 dB above conventional RGB PSNR for every encoder alike.

**Known shortcoming:** Real-time DXT1/ETC1 encoder: Src/main.cpp public, i7-7820HQ, compiler and flags unstated; competitors reach 3.8-4.6 dB higher PSNR and Goofy's ETC1 is ETC1S only. The harness calls icbc, rgbcx and rg_etc1 initialisation inside the timed loop, inflating those ratios; the stb_dxt 33x row is the cleanest. test-results/ is empty. Baselines are texture encoders, not the category's image codecs.

**Known shortcoming:** Only icbc::init_dxt1 is unguarded in the harness (a 1,310,720-iteration table rebuild inside each timed call), so the 60x against ICBC is probably 10-25% high (code estimate); rgbcx and rg_etc1 inits are guarded, so the 24x stands. The README's 'RGB-PSNR' is 10*log10(768^2 / summed MSE), 4.805 dB above standard RGB PSNR for every encoder, so gaps are valid but absolute dB values are not comparable. Aligned _mm_load_si128 on unaligned input (crashes with NDEBUG), width must be a multiple of 16, the header forces GOOFYTC_IMPLEMENTATION (multi-translation-unit link errors), SSE2 hard-coded with no NEON, bounding-box endpoints fail on anti-correlated chroma; issues #4 and #5 (2025) unanswered.

**How:** Each call encodes four 4x4 blocks (a 16x4 pixel strip, one 64-byte cache line per row) entirely in 8-bit SSE2 lanes. Per-channel min/max via _mm_min_epu8/_mm_max_epu8 plus 4x4 transposes give bounding-box endpoints (quantised to RGB555 with shifts done as repeated _mm_avg_epu8). Luma is computed as YCoCg Y = avg(avg(R,B),G), and each pixel is classified against the block's luma midpoint and a 0.375*range threshold. The two resulting byte masks are packed into 2-bit selectors with movemask. There is no endpoint search, least-squares refinement, floating point or error evaluation; for ETC1 the base colour is the block average and the intensity-table control byte comes from a 256-entry lookup on the luma range.

**Use it when:**
- On-the-fly BC1 compression of runtime-generated or downloaded RGBA8 textures on x86-64, when encode time matters more than about 4 dB of PSNR (README: 1429 MP/s per thread on an i7-7820HQ).
- Fast 'preview' content builds with thousands of textures, re-encoding later with rgbcx, ICBC or bc7e for shipping.
- Live-sync editor tools: show a Goofy encode immediately, then replace it with a slow high-quality encode in the background.
- ETC1 targets where ETC1S-level quality is already acceptable: the README puts Goofy ETC1 (36.30 dB) level with Basis Universal ETC1S output (36.27 dB) on its image set, with no supercompression.

**Skip it when:**
- Shipping assets: on the README image set it scores 3.8-4.6 dB lower RGB-PSNR than stb_dxt, rgbcx level 0, icbc fast and rg_etc1 low quality, the fastest settings of those encoders.
- Normal maps (the README warns quality is much worse), alpha or punch-through textures, and any format other than BC1 and ETC1 (no BC3/BC4/BC5/BC7, ETC2 or ASTC; the README's DXT5/ETC2 alpha plan never landed and issue #5 asking about ETC2 is unanswered).
- ARM devices, where ETC1 is mostly used: GOOFY_SSE2 is hard-coded to 1, there is no NEON path, and the scalar emulation path needs a header edit and has no published speed numbers.
- Arbitrary image sizes or unaligned buffers without padding or copying first (width must be a multiple of 16, height of 4, and rows 16-byte aligned).
- Projects that need an active upstream: last commit 2024-01-29 (README and contributor WASM/CI work), and issues #4 and #5 from 2025 have no reply.

**Integration:** header-only · none (SSE2 intrinsics from <emmintrin.h>) · not documented; the header uses C++11 features and the repo's CMake builds it as C++17, with CI Release builds on MSVC, GCC and Clang · x86/x86-64 with SSE2; WebAssembly via Emscripten SSE2 emulation (-msimd128 -msse2, used by the in-repo test page); no NEON

**Vs siblings:** Pick Goofy over bc7enc/rgbcx or ICBC only when raw single-thread encode speed dominates and about 4 dB lower PSNR is acceptable; those encoders are the ones to use for shipping BC1. For ETC1, etcpak is the quality-and-speed incumbent (QuickETC2 paper: 3250 Mpx/s with 16 threads on a Ryzen 7 3700X, about 200 per thread, derived); Goofy's 1221 MP/s on one i7-7820HQ thread is a different machine and harness and a simpler ETC1S-only search, so prefer Goofy only for x86 previews where ETC1S quality is enough.

**Gotchas:**
- Loads use _mm_load_si128, so the input pointer and every row (stride) must be 16-byte aligned (the code asserts 64-byte). With NDEBUG the assert is compiled out and misaligned input crashes instead of failing cleanly. The Jan 2024 Linux port of the test harness hit exactly this ('compilation on linux (crashes though)', then 'fix alignment').
- The header #defines GOOFYTC_IMPLEMENTATION itself and has no include guard, so the non-inline compressDXT1/compressETC1 are compiled into every translation unit that includes it. Include it from exactly one .cpp and declare the two functions elsewhere, or you get duplicate-symbol link errors.
- Endpoints are the per-channel bounding-box min and max, with no choice of box diagonal, and selectors come from luma alone. Blocks whose channels move in opposite directions (red-to-green or blue-to-yellow edges) or change only in chroma at equal luma are badly encoded, beyond the normal-map warning in the README.
- DXT1 output is always 4-colour opaque (colour0's green LSB is forced to 1 so colour0 > colour1), and endpoints are effectively RGB555, so smooth green gradients lose a bit of precision against encoders that use full 565.

**Status:** Stale: code essentially unchanged since 2020, last commit 2024-01-29 (README edits and a contributor's WASM/CI port), and two 2025 issues are unanswered. It is MIT and a single 1,500-line header, easy to vendor on x86 if you accept the size, alignment and quality limits.

[repo](https://github.com/SergeyMakeev/Goofy) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SergeyMakeev/Goofy)

##### ICBC (high quality SIMD BC1 encoder)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Single-header SIMD BC1 (DXT1) block encoder from NVTT; at the highest quality levels it is faster than RGBCX only when built with AVX2 or AVX-512.

**Beats:** RGBCX 1.12 (levels 0-18), squish 1.15, stb_dxt 1.09 with improvements proposed by Rich Geldreich and Ignacio Castano (not stock), and AMD CMP_Core V4.0.4855 — The only comparison is the author's chart of average PSNR on the Kodim and Waterloo sets against encode time, with an unlabelled time unit, made with ICBC 1.03 (current header 1.05), RGBCX 1.12, a modified stb_dxt 1.09, squish 1.15 and AMD CMP_Core. At the top quality (about 30.9 dB), ICBC-AVX512 takes about 5.5 units against about 20.6 for scalar RGBCX; ICBC-Scalar is slower than RGBCX at most levels, so the lead is SIMD rather than the algorithm. The repo's harness (icbc_test.cpp) times only ICBC, on the 24 Kodak images alone, multithreaded through ic_pfor, so the chart's baseline timings, threading and machine cannot be reproduced from public code. Since v1.03, commits from September 2022 changed low-quality inset handling and added level 0, so the chart's curve no longer describes the current code. Third-party data in Goofy's README (i7-7820HQ, one thread) measured the older icbc v1.0 SSE2 at 24 MP/s and 41.00 dB, against rgbcx 1.08 level 0 at 60 MP/s and 40.85 dB and stb_dxt at 43 MP/s and 40.82 dB. No correctness bug was found behind the BC1 numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Only a chart: doc/results.txt holds ICBC-only timings, icbc_test.cpp times ICBC alone, and the chart's machine is unnamed. The lead is AVX-512 against scalar RGBCX; ICBC-Scalar is slower than RGBCX almost everywhere, and the stb_dxt 1.09 baseline was modified. Texture encoder with baselines outside the category list.

**Known shortcoming:** The chart was made with v1.03 and the September 2022 commits changed the low quality levels, so it is stale for v1.05; the harness times ICBC only on the 24 Kodak images (no Waterloo set), multithreaded via ic_pfor. Scalar ICBC is slower than RGBCX, and RGBCX beats ICBC-AVX512 at about 30.4-30.6 dB; ICBC wins only above about 30.7 dB. compress_bc3 is a public stub that returns 0 and writes nothing; the VMX backend never compiled (open PR #10); no runtime SIMD dispatch (NEON auto-select checks only __ARM_NEON__).

**Independent measurement:** Third-party single-thread run in the Goofy README (i7-7820HQ): icbc v1.0 24 MP/s at 41.00 dB versus rgbcx 1.08 60 MP/s and stb_dxt 43 MP/s.

**How:** The quality ladder runs from bounding-box fit (level 0) through box fit plus least-squares endpoints (level 1) to squish-style cluster fit over every order-preserving 4-cluster partition (968 combinations) and 3-cluster partition (152), with 3-colour mode at levels 8 and 9 and iterative endpoint refinement at level 9. Near-duplicate colours are merged first, under a per-level threshold, to cut the combination count. Each partition's least-squares error comes from summed-area tables, as in rgbcx, and the cluster-fit loop is vectorised over 4/8/16 lanes. The SIMD back end (SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, AltiVec) is chosen at compile time, and the AVX2 and AVX-512 paths use permute instructions for table lookups. The SIMD path does most of the work: in doc/results.txt the AVX-512 build is about 9x faster than the scalar build on Sky Lake (0.166 s vs 1.519 s), with identical PSNR.

**Use it when:**
- Offline or build-pipeline BC1 compression where you want the top quality band (above about 30.7 dB average on the author's Kodim+Waterloo chart). There the AVX-512 build reaches RGBCX's best quality in roughly a quarter of the time.
- x86-64 build machines where you can compile a dedicated AVX2 or AVX-512 binary. The scalar build is slower than RGBCX at almost every quality level on the same chart.
- Texture tools that already use NVTT, or that need BC1 tuned to a specific GPU vendor's decoder rounding (D3D10, NVIDIA, AMD/Apple M1, Intel).
- Embedding with no build system: one MIT header with no dependencies beyond the C/C++ standard headers and SIMD intrinsics.

**Skip it when:**
- Low and mid quality BC1. In the chart, stb_dxt and RGBCX's lowest levels match ICBC below about 30.1 dB, and RGBCX (about 30.52 dB at about 0.5 time units) beats the AVX-512 ICBC points at about 30.38 and 30.57 dB (about 0.75 each). For real-time encoding, Goofy is far faster at much lower quality.
- Anything beyond BC1 (BC3/4/5/7): compress_bc3 returns 0 and writes nothing, and the alpha/BC4/BC5 encoders are open issue #3. The README itself recommends RGBCX as the better-supported library.
- Shipping one portable x86 binary: there is no runtime CPU dispatch, so an AVX-512 or AVX2 build faults on CPUs without those instructions, and a portable build falls back to the slow SSE2 or scalar path.
- PowerPC: according to open PR #10 (August 2026), the AltiVec/VMX back end never compiled, with typos, missing mask/any/all functions and a wrong vec_div.
- Teams that need maintenance: the last commit was 2022-11-09, and PR #10 and 6 issues are open with no maintainer response.

**Integration:** header-only (define ICBC_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit) · none (standard C headers plus x86/ARM/PowerPC intrinsics headers); the test harness adds stb_image, stb_image_write and ic_pfor.h · C++11 (icbc_test.cpp's compile comment reads 'g++ icbc_test.cpp -O3 -mavx2 -lpthread -std=c+=11', a typo for c++11; build.bat uses MSVC 2019 'cl /O2 /arch:AVX512'; results.txt runs used MSVC 2017/2019, clang 11/13 and gcc 8.3/10) · x86/x86-64 (SSE2 to AVX-512, selected at compile time from __AVX512F__/__AVX2__/__AVX__/__SSE4_1__ or ICBC_SIMD), ARM NEON, scalar fallback; the PowerPC VMX path is broken

**Vs siblings:** Pick ICBC over rgbcx in bc7enc only when you need the highest-quality BC1 on AVX2/AVX-512 build machines and can live with an unmaintained, BC1-only header. Otherwise rgbcx (also BC3-5, faster in the mid-quality range) is the default, and Goofy is the choice for real-time speed at a large quality loss.

**Gotchas:**
- Encoding before icbc::init() leaves the single-colour and cluster tables zeroed. The decoder passed to init changes the produced blocks, so encode for the decoder you ship on.
- Automatic NEON selection checks only __ARM_NEON__. Compilers that define only the ACLE macro __ARM_NEON (GCC for AArch64, for example) may silently fall back to scalar unless ICBC_SIMD is set to -1.
- three_color_black=true (used in the chart for ICBC and RGBCX) stores black texels with the transparent-black index. That raises PSNR but makes those texels alpha 0 when the texture is sampled as RGBA.
- Input is 16 float RGBA texels per block, not 8-bit pixels. Conversion, edge padding and block layout are the caller's job, and the test harness rounds image sizes down to multiples of 4.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-11-09 (157 commits, 131 stars, MIT), though it remains NVTT's BC1 encoder. It is small and dependency-free enough to vendor; build per-ISA binaries and do not rely on the VMX or BC3 entry points.

[repo](https://github.com/castano/icbc) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/castano/icbc/HEAD/README.md)

##### ImageZero  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Tiny one-pass lossless codec for 24-bit RGB photos; README claims 20x faster compression than PNG, with no benchmark to back it.

**Beats:** PNG (format only; the README never names the PNG implementation, tool or compression level, so libpng/zlib is inferred) — Nothing has been measured reproducibly. The README states, with no method, that compared with PNG (implementation and level unnamed) it compresses 24-bit PPM files about 20x faster and decompresses about 2x faster at a nearly equal ratio on natural photos; the repository has no timing code. The one third-party observation is a 2018 ROS gist on an i7-6700HQ (640x320 at 30 fps), where the imagezero transport used 82-84% CPU against 108% for PNG levels 3 and 9, a CPU-load reading, not a codec throughput benchmark; the swri ROS plugin also routes every frame through an OpenCV PPM encode and decode.

**Known shortcoming:** README-only claim (about 20x compress, 2x decompress vs 'PNG' with the implementation unnamed); main.cpp is a converter, no benchmark code. Archived 2022-09-14. The only independent data is an informal 2018 gist (CPU time 82-84% vs PNG 108%); LWN and ROS discourse pages blocked here.

**Known shortcoming:** No benchmark code in the repo and no third-party run in QOIR or WangXuan95; the only outside data is a 2018 ROS gist (CPU 82-84% versus PNG 108%). The code relies on undefined behaviour (out-of-bounds predictor loads that only inlining removes; -O0 and debug builds crash); the decoder can over-read 4 bytes past a valid stream; skipping the init tables gives silently corrupt output; padded rows overrun; no magic, version or checksum; host-endian; RGB only.

**How:** Every pixel costs the same, fixed amount of work in a single pass. ImageZero predicts each channel with a blend of planar and average prediction, (3*left + 3*up - 2*upleft + 2) >> 2; the first row and first column use the left or upper neighbour instead. Green's residual is then subtracted from the red and blue residuals, and each residual is zigzag-mapped to an unsigned value. The coder finds how many bits the largest of the three residuals needs (0-8). It writes that length with a static prefix code chosen by the previous pixel's length (9 contexts, codes up to 6 bits long), then writes all three residuals as fixed-length fields of that size. There is no LZ matching, no filter search, no Huffman table construction and no arithmetic coding. The bit I/O uses a 64-bit cache flushed in 32-bit words, and decoding is one 64-entry table lookup per pixel plus shifts. Branch-free bit tricks (intmacros.h) do the clamping and sign handling.

**Use it when:**
- Real-time lossless capture or streaming of 8-bit RGB camera frames where encode CPU per frame matters more than file size, especially in ROS, where swri-robotics/imagezero_transport already wraps it as an image_transport plugin (ROS Indigo to Lunar).
- Noisy natural photographs or camera video, which is the content the README says compresses nearly as well as PNG. The per-pixel prefix code cannot exploit long flat runs anyway.
- Embedded or legacy builds that need a dependency-free codec of about 930 lines of library code under BSD-2-Clause, and can accept a private, unversioned file format.
- Studying a minimal context-coded predictive image coder; the design is small enough to read in one sitting.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need measured performance: the 20x/2x figures are one README sentence with no benchmark program, test images, PNG implementation, compiler or CPU. nigeltao/qoir left it out because it cannot represent alpha, and the WangXuan95 shootout does not include it. The only third-party data point is an informal 2018 ROS gist (i7-6700HQ, 640x320 at 30 fps) showing 82-84% CPU for the imagezero transport against 108% for PNG levels 3 and 9 (with frame lag at level 9) and 36-40% for JPEG.
- Images with alpha, grayscale, palettes or 16-bit samples: the Pixel class is hard-coded to three 8-bit channels, and the CLI rejects anything other than 24-bit PPM.
- Flat computer-generated graphics, screenshots and UI captures (the README excludes them): with no run-length or LZ stage, every pixel costs at least one bit, so it cannot approach PNG or QOI ratios on such content.
- Untrusted or archival data: there is no magic number, version, checksum or input-length parameter, the bitstream is written in host byte order (byte swapping is commented out), and the author calls both the format and the API 'early work in progress'.
- Anything that needs upkeep: last commit 2013-11-06, archived 2022-09-14; issues #3 (2018) and #5 (2022) are still open, and the only PR (#2, 0.2.4) was closed unmerged.

**Integration:** source-drop (libiz.cpp + table.cpp + headers); autotools builds libiz as a library, while the CMake and qmake files build only the iz CLI · none for the library; the CLI's file.cpp uses POSIX mmap when HAVE_MMAP is defined and falls back to stdio otherwise · GCC or Clang (uses __attribute__((always_inline)) and __builtin_clz, C++98-era code); must be built with optimization (shipped flags -O2 -mmmx -mtune=atom -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions); MSVC support not documented · 64-bit LP64/LLP64 targets use a 64-bit integer bit cache, and 32-bit x86 uses MMX; macOS needs MAP_POPULATE removed from file.cpp (patch in issue #1, never merged); the swri-robotics fork drops the Intel-only flags off x86 (CHANGELOG 0.2.2); .iz files are tied to the host's byte order

**Vs siblings:** Rarely. For 24-bit photos, QOI, QOIR and Zpng have independent, reproducible numbers against libpng on the QOI suite (for example Zpng encodes 126 MPixels/s at CmpRatio 0.2182 vs libpng's 5.49 at 0.2423) and also handle alpha. Choose ImageZero only when you already run its ROS image_transport plugin or need a dependency-free RGB-only coder you can read in an afternoon.

**Gotchas:**
- Relies on undefined behaviour being optimized away: on the first row and first column the predictor call still evaluates p[-bpp], p[-bpr] and p[-bpp-bpr], memory before the image start, as arguments that the chosen predictor ignores. Only inlining removes those loads, which is why the WARNING file says non-inlined predictors 'cause an access violation'. The autotools --enable-debug build (-O0) and sanitizer builds hit this.
- Forgetting initEncodeTable() fails silently: the encoder copies the zero-filled global staticdBits table and writes a corrupt stream with no error. Decoding likewise needs initDecodeTable().
- Buffer contracts are on the caller. The encoder needs up to width*height*4 + 33 bytes (the CLI's sizing). Rows must be tightly packed (samplesPerLine == 3*width): with padded rows the encoder's end-of-image test never matches and it reads past the buffer. From reading the code, the decoder has no input-length argument and can fetch one 32-bit word past the end of even a valid stream, so pad input buffers by at least 4 bytes.
- Dimensions are limited by the 4-bit field width to 32768 per side (the CLI rejects anything above 16384x16384), and the decoder always assumes 3*width bytes per row.

**Status:** Abandoned (last commit 2013-11-06, archived 2022-09-14). It is BSD-2-Clause and small enough to vendor, but treat it as experimental: unversioned host-endian format, optimization-dependent memory safety, no tests.

[repo](https://github.com/cfeck/imagezero) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cfeck/imagezero/HEAD/README)

##### jpeg-nitro (nitrojpeg and nitropng parallel decoders)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Parallel single-image baseline JPEG and 8-bit PNG decoders in C; one-thread speed equals libjpeg-turbo, all-core latency ~9x lower.

**Beats:** libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (TurboJPEG 3 API, SIMD, one thread) for JPEG; Wuffs (unpinned wuffs-unsupported-snapshot.c, decoding to BGRA) for PNG; libpng is not measured — On the author's macOS 'Intel i9 13th gen' (16 threads, SKU and clang version not stated) with 50 private 24 MP camera JPEGs, bench/bench (one timed pass per decoder, from memory) measured nitrojpeg 103.0 ms on one thread vs libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 107.4 ms to YUV planes (parity) and 11.7 ms on 16 threads (9.2x); on an M1 Air 153.8 vs 168.1 ms and 30.4 ms on 8 threads; for 34 PNGs nitropng took 45.5 ms in parallel vs Wuffs to BGRA 180.1 ms, but 222.6 ms on one thread. The '5.0x to BGRX' row (24.7 ms) is not the shipped decoder: nj_decode_bgrx exists only under -DNJ_REFERENCE and calls the old engine in which libjpeg-turbo decodes re-emitted bands and does the upsampling and colour conversion; also, bench/pngbench divides nitropng's total by every file, including any it rejects as unsupported (palette, 16-bit, interlaced) in near-zero time while Wuffs decodes them, so such a file in the private PNG set would flatter nitropng's average.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded A to C: the i9 SKU and clang version are unstated and the 50 test photos are private. Single-thread like-for-like decode is only 1.04x libjpeg-turbo (103.0 vs 107.4 ms; 1.09x on Apple M1); the 9.2x (to YUV) and 5.0x (to BGRX) are parallel decode against one-thread libjpeg-turbo (built with get-deps.sh -O3 -march=x86-64-v3). nitropng's baseline is Wuffs, not libpng, and single-thread nitropng is 1.24x slower than Wuffs.

**Known shortcoming:** The '5.0x to BGRX' row times an unshipped path: nj_decode_bgrx exists only under -DNJ_REFERENCE, calls the old libjpeg-turbo-based engine and is not exported in libnitro.map; the public API outputs YUV planes only, so the valid figures are 1.04x on one thread and 9.2x on 16 threads (retier-11). bench/pngbench divides by all files, so unsupported PNGs (palette, 16-bit, interlaced) count near 0 ms for nitropng while Wuffs decodes them. SIMD is compile-time only with undocumented scalar fallback speed; the global buffer pool is never freed (about 100-200 MB resident after a 24 MP image, estimate); needs clang -fblocks; the Linux pthread pool makes concurrent calls take turns; no CRC-32 check; issue #3 (progressive JPEG, GCC) closed as not planned.

**How:** nitrojpeg strips byte stuffing in parallel, cuts the entropy-coded data into about 32 x CPU chunks and decodes each speculatively from an arbitrary bit offset; Huffman codes self-synchronise (2.4 garbage MCUs on average over the author's 10,240 measured sync points), and an in-order stitching pass finds where each chunk meets the true decoding path, which fixes its MCU index and DC predictors. Coefficients are Huffman-decoded once, and each stitched chunk is dequantised and run through libjpeg's ISLOW IDCT (AVX2 or NEON, same constants and rounding as jidctint.c) by the thread that decoded it while it is still in cache; restart-marker files are decoded per interval in parallel. nitropng is a pugz-style speculative parallel inflate (each thread finds a valid dynamic-block header in its chunk, writes 16-bit placeholders for back-references into the unknown 32 KB window, resolves them after chaining, and combines per-chunk Adler-32 sums) followed by a wavefront filter reversal where row r trails row r-1 in 1 KB segments. Per-core speed is about libjpeg-turbo's (single 11-bit lookup Huffman decoder), so the whole gain is intra-image parallelism.

**Use it when:**
- Image viewers, editors or on-demand previews where the latency of one large (12-50 MP) camera JPEG matters and cores are idle: about 11.7 ms instead of 107 ms per 24 MP photo on the author's 16-thread i9.
- Pipelines that consume planar YCbCr directly (GPU shader colour conversion, video or ML preprocessing that does its own conversion), since that is the library's native output.
- Camera and phone JPEGs without restart markers (the common case), which libjpeg-turbo cannot split across threads at all.
- Large 8-bit truecolour PNGs (screenshots, scans, AI-generated images) when raw unfiltered rows are enough: about 4x lower latency than Wuffs to BGRA on all 16 threads of the author's i9.
- Parallel inflate of one big zlib stream of known output size (np_zlib_decompress), as the repo does for PSD ZIP data.

**Skip it when:**
- Batch or server workloads that decode many images at once: on one thread nitrojpeg is at parity with libjpeg-turbo (1.04x i9, 1.09x M1) and nitropng is about 1.24x slower than Wuffs, so decoding images in parallel with libjpeg-turbo gives the same or better total throughput; on Linux the shared pthread pool makes concurrent calls take turns.
- Progressive, arithmetic-coded, 12-bit, lossless, CMYK, RGB-coded or multi-scan JPEGs and images over 16384 px; palette, 16-bit, sub-8-bit and interlaced PNGs (palette PNGs are common on the web). All return 'unsupported'; issue #3 (the reporter's first JPEG was progressive) was closed as not planned.
- When you need RGB/RGBA pixels or a libjpeg/TurboJPEG/libpng-compatible API: the shipped library outputs planar YCbCr or filtered-byte-prefixed rows only; the BGRX path exists only in the -DNJ_REFERENCE test build and uses libjpeg-turbo.
- GCC- or MSVC-only toolchains: the loop bodies are clang blocks, so it needs clang with -fblocks (issue #3 also reports no MSYS GCC build).
- Code that needs a mature dependency: single-author repository first committed 2026-09-27, 0 stars, no releases, README numbers revised daily, and a nitropng bug (incomplete fixed-Huffman distance table, so every fixed block with a match failed and fell back) was only fixed on 2026-09-30.

**Integration:** source-drop (src/nitrojpeg.c/.h, src/nitropng.c/.h, src/nitropsd.c/.h, src/nitro_os.h); on Linux `make linux` also builds libnitro.so / libnitro.a · none at runtime beyond pthreads (Grand Central Dispatch on macOS); libjpeg-turbo 3 (TurboJPEG 3 API), Wuffs, stb_image and zlib only for the benchmarks, verify tools and the viewer's fallback · clang with -fblocks (GCC unsupported; no blocks runtime library needed); C standard not documented; Windows via llvm-mingw or MSYS2 CLANG64 · x86-64 (AVX2 IDCT and Adler-32 when compiled with -march=x86-64-v3 or native, otherwise scalar), aarch64 (NEON); macOS, Linux, Windows (MinGW)

**Vs siblings:** libjpeg-turbo-rs and zenjpeg compete with libjpeg-turbo on single-thread speed and give RGB output; pick nitrojpeg only when wall-clock latency of one image on many idle cores matters and planar YCbCr is acceptable. For PNG, libspng, zune-png and ptpng give complete pixel output, checksum handling and wider format coverage; nitropng wins only on latency for a large 8-bit truecolour PNG with spare cores.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD is chosen at compile time (#ifdef __AVX2__ / __ARM_NEON), with no runtime dispatch: a generic x86-64 build silently uses the scalar IDCT, whose speed is not documented.
- Large internal buffers (unstuffed bit stream, per-chunk coefficient buffers sized at about twice the image's coefficient count) go into a process-global pool of up to 4096 buffers that is never freed and has no release API, so after one 24 MP decode on the order of 100-200 MB stays resident (estimated from the pool_take sizes in nitrojpeg.c).
- The 'nthreads' argument is the number of work pieces, not threads (<= 0 means 4 x CPUs; 1 means truly single-threaded); the thread count is set globally with nj_set_max_workers.
- Output planes are padded to whole MCUs and the padding differs from libjpeg-turbo (the verify tool compares only the visible region); EXIF orientation is parsed but not applied; nitropng verifies the zlib Adler-32 but not PNG chunk CRC-32s.

**Status:** Very active (82 commits between 2026-09-27 and 2026-10-01, two merged PRs from a second contributor adding the GNOME viewer and the Linux shared library) and MIT-licensed C that is small enough to vendor, but it is a weeks-old single-author project with 0 stars, no releases and commits co-authored with an AI coding assistant; treat it as experimental.

[repo](https://github.com/gereoffy/jpeg-nitro) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gereoffy/jpeg-nitro/HEAD/README.md)

##### jpeg-rusturbo  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust SIMD JPEG encoder and decoder with libjpeg-turbo-derived kernels; encodes about 5x faster than the image crate's encoder.

**Beats:** Rust image crate 0.25: its own built-in scalar JPEG encoder (4:2:0 only) and its zune-jpeg-backed decoder. libjpeg-turbo is never measured. — The first-party harness benches/vs_image.rs (release profile with fat LTO and codegen-units=1, unstated rustc, mean of one 50-iteration batch) encodes a synthetic 4K RGB pattern at q=80 4:2:0 in 13.41 ms against 67.61 ms for the image 0.25 crate's own scalar encoder on an unnamed Apple M-series laptop (5.04x), and 57.27 against 320.93 ms on a 4-vCPU Xeon Platinum 8272CL (5.60x); threads=auto raises that to 10.02x and 6.86x against single-threaded image. Decoding its own q=80 output, it runs 0.97x to 1.22x of image's zune-jpeg path, and libjpeg-turbo is never measured.

**Known shortcoming:** No number against libjpeg-turbo anywhere; the baseline is the image crate's own scalar JPEG encoder (not jpeg-encoder) and zune-jpeg. Encode is compared on a synthetic XOR pattern only and the decode baseline pays an extra to_rgb8 copy; rustc version unstated. Kernels are translated from libjpeg-turbo (NOTICE.md), so it is a partial port (libjpeg-turbo-rs precedent kept).

**Known shortcoming:** Decode flaw: the image-crate side times decode().to_rgb8() (an extra copy of about 24.9 MB at 4K) while jpeg-rusturbo writes into an uninitialised Vec, so the 1.18-1.22x 4K lead may be mostly that copy; encode against image uses an XOR pattern only with no size or quality check and no Cargo.lock (image and zune-jpeg versions unrecorded). decode/mod.rs uses Vec::set_len on uninitialised u8 (clippy::uninit_vec allowed) with no Miri or fuzzing in CI; set_threads(n) above 1 builds a new rayon pool per encode; before 0.9.1 the encoder returned Ok with a corrupt JPEG above 65535 px.

**How:** The encoder front end (RGB to YCbCr, 4:2:0/4:2:2 downsample, integer LL&M forward DCT, reciprocal-multiply quantize) is a translation of libjpeg-turbo's NEON and AVX2 kernels, selected at compile time on aarch64 and by runtime AVX2 detection on x86_64. The Huffman AC emit walks a SIMD-built 64-bit nonzero bitmap with trailing_zeros jumps, and set_threads splits quantize and bitmap work across MCU rows on rayon. Its profile puts about 65% of single-thread encode in the scalar Huffman emitter, so further front-end SIMD buys little. The decoder ports libjpeg-turbo's jidctint IDCT (with DC-only and sparse-row fast paths), fancy upsample and YCC-to-RGB, and adds a SWAR bit-reader refill.

**Use it when:**
