- Rust services that encode many JPEGs and currently use the image crate's encoder: about 5x (Apple M) to 5.6x (Xeon 8272CL) faster single-threaded at 4:2:0 q=80, and more with threads on many-core hosts.
- You need encoder features image's encoder lacks: 4:4:4/4:2:2, progressive output, optimized Huffman (about 5% smaller), restart markers, EXIF/ICC pass-through, CMYK.
- You want a pure-Rust build with no C toolchain or nasm on x86_64 (AVX2) or aarch64 (NEON); CI covers Linux, macOS, Windows x64 and Windows on Arm, with a bit-exact scalar fallback elsewhere.
- Decode, operate and re-encode pipelines that must preserve EXIF and ICC on both sides.

**Skip it when:**
- You can link C: libjpeg-turbo (catalogued, whose kernels these are) or the libjpeg-turbo-rs and zenjpeg ports were benchmarked against libjpeg-turbo itself, while this crate never was. Its speed relative to libjpeg-turbo is unknown.
- Decode-heavy workloads: the decoder is at parity with image's zune-jpeg backend (0.97x to 1.22x), and the 4K lead is partly harness overhead (see gotchas). Use zune-jpeg or libjpeg-turbo for decode speed.
- You need arithmetic-coded, lossless, hierarchical or 12-bit JPEG, CMYK-to-RGB conversion, or progressive grayscale/CMYK encode: all return Unsupported.
- Many-core scaling on small VMs: on the 4-vCPU Xeon, threads=auto adds only 1.06x at 1080p and 1.22x at 4K over one thread.
- Smallest files at a given quality: there is no trellis quantization (mozjpeg-rs and mozjpeg do that), and no output-size or quality comparison against any other encoder is published.

**Integration:** crate · rayon (image and minifb are dev-dependencies only) · Rust 1.85 (edition 2024) · x86_64 (AVX2 runtime-detected, SSE2 baseline, scalar fallback), aarch64 (NEON), any other target via the scalar path; CI on ubuntu-latest, macos-14, windows-latest, windows-11-arm

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libjpeg-turbo when you must stay pure Rust with no C or nasm in the build and encode is the bottleneck. Pick it over mozjpeg-rs when encode speed matters more than the last few percent of file size. libjpeg-turbo-rs and zenjpeg are the Rust alternatives with published numbers against libjpeg-turbo itself, so prefer them when you need that assurance.

**Gotchas:**
- The decode comparison is not like for like: benches/vs_image.rs times image's ImageReader::decode().to_rgb8(), which converts into a second full-frame buffer (about 24.9 MB at 4K RGB), while jpeg-rusturbo decodes straight into an uninitialised output Vec. The 1.18-1.22x 4K natural-content lead may be mostly that copy. Encode was compared only on a synthetic XOR full-AC pattern, with one 50-iteration mean, no Cargo.lock (image 0.25.x and zune-jpeg versions unrecorded) and no size or quality check.
- decode/mod.rs compose_output calls Vec::set_len on uninitialised u8 memory (clippy::uninit_vec allowed) to skip zero-fill. This rests on every byte being written before it is read, and the code comment's claim that u8 makes it sound contradicts set_len's documented precondition. CI runs no Miri or fuzzing, so treat the decoder as unhardened for untrusted input.
- set_threads(n) for n>1 spawns a new thread pool per encode, which hurts small images. Benchmarks used threads=auto (0), which reuses the global pool.
- Before 0.9.1 the encoder returned Ok with a corrupt JPEG for dimensions above 65535 and accepted zero quant-table entries; pin 0.9.1 or later.

**Status:** Single-author pre-1.0 crate (0.9.2, 197 commits, last commit 2026-06-08, 0 stars, about 7.8k crates.io downloads) under MIT OR Apache-2.0, with libjpeg-turbo's BSD-3 notice kept in NOTICE.md for the translated kernels.

[repo](https://github.com/naoto256/jpeg-rusturbo) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/naoto256/jpeg-rusturbo/HEAD/BENCH.md)

##### jxl-rs  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Memory-safe pure-Rust JPEG XL decoder (Chrome, Firefox); roughly libjxl parity single-threaded, faster on lossless, slower on lossy VarDCT.

**Beats:** libjxl (C++ JPEG XL reference decoder, djxl) — One first-party single-threaded table from PR #705 (closed unmerged 2026-09-03; description targets libjxl 0.12, but libjxl's build, thread setting and repetitions are not stated) on an AMD EPYC 9645 with a PGO + AVX-512 jxl-rs build: 0.81x to 1.27x libjxl per image, with a 1.04x total that equals the geometric mean of the per-image ratios, while the arithmetic mean of MP/s gives 0.98x (derived from page data). The same PR's CI run on a GitHub x86-64 runner measured patches_lossless at 3.313 MP/s against 14.30 MP/s in the EPYC table, a 4.3x gap where the other seven images differ by 1.14x to 1.51x (derived from page data), so that row may not be the same file or setting; no number has been published for current main against libjxl.

**Known shortcoming:** Raised D to C on the PR #705 comment (repeated in issue #724): single-threaded AMD EPYC 9645 AVX-512, PGO build, total 15.74 versus libjxl 16.35 MP/s (0.96x), VarDCT slower (0.93x, 0.94x), bicycles 0.81x; the PR was closed unmerged and the libjxl build is not stated. The older PR #506 measured 2.23x slower on average. Not faster than libjxl.

**Known shortcoming:** PR #705's TOTAL 1.04x is a geometric mean of ratios; the arithmetic mean of MP/s gives 0.98x. patches_lossless shows 14.30 MP/s on the EPYC against 3.313 in the same PR's CI run (a 4.3x gap where other rows differ 1.14-1.51x), likely a different file or setting. PGO is not in the repo profile (#723 merged thin LTO only); #966 (AVX-512 path not reliably CI-tested) and #950 (EPF slow) open; a Chromium-era snippet puts jxl-rs 24-35% slower than libjxl.

**How:** SIMD kernels are written once against a SimdDescriptor trait and the simd_function! macro picks AVX-512F+BW, AVX2+FMA+F16C, SSE4.2 or scalar at runtime on x86-64 (NEON on aarch64, simd128 on wasm32). The March 2026 speed-up work re-landed from the closed PR #705 through PRs #707-#723 (tracked in issue #724) added bounds-check elimination, inlining changes, a faster BitReader, allocation removal and specialised modular predictor and MA-tree paths. Rows can be processed in parallel through the runner interface; jxl_cli drives it with a rayon pool.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services, browsers or tools that must decode untrusted JPEG XL input and want to avoid linking the C++ libjxl: the jxl crate denies unsafe code at its root and confines unsafe to SIMD and reviewed hot spots
- Lossless or modular JPEG XL images: in the PR #705 single-thread table jxl-rs was 1.04x to 1.27x libjxl on five of eight images (sunset_logo, green_queen_modular, delta_palette, lz77_flower, patches_lossless)
- Progressive or incremental display where lower memory use and partial rendering matter more than peak MP/s
- Targets libjxl is awkward to build for, such as wasm32 (simd128) or pure-Cargo builds, or projects already using the image crate (register_image_decoding_hook)

**Skip it when:**
- You need an encoder: jxl-rs only decodes (encoder support for the image integration is an open request, issue #959)
- Throughput-critical decoding of lossy VarDCT photos, the common web case: 0.93x and 0.94x libjxl in the PR #705 table, and the edge-preserving filter is called 'very slow' in open issue #950; a WebSearch snippet (page not opened) from the Chromium integration period cites 24-35% slower decode times than libjxl
- Weighted-predictor-heavy modular images such as bicycles (0.81x libjxl in the same table)
- C or C++ code bases that want a drop-in for libjxl's JxlDecoder C API; no C ABI crate ships in the workspace
- You need cropped decoding, LF-only (reduced resolution) decoding, some progressive modes or EXIF/XMP extraction: open issues #933, #857, #730 and #674

**Integration:** crate (jxl 0.7.4 on crates.io, plus jxl-image-rs-integration and the jxl_cli binary) · thiserror, byteorder, num-derive, num-traits, array-init and internal jxl_transforms/jxl_simd/jxl_macros; optional brotli-decompressor (brotli feature) and tracing; jxl_cli adds rayon · Rust 1.89.0 (edition 2024) · any Rust target with scalar fallback; runtime-dispatched SIMD on x86-64 (SSE4.2, AVX2+FMA+F16C, AVX-512F+BW), aarch64 NEON and wasm32 simd128

**Vs siblings:** No other JPEG XL decoder is catalogued: the libjxl fast_lossless (fjxl) entry is an encoder, so the two pair up (fjxl to write, jxl-rs to read in Rust); pick jxl-rs over the PNG/WebP/JPEG siblings (image-png, zune-png, wpd, zenjpeg) only when the format itself is JPEG XL.

**Gotchas:**
- The 1.04x total in PR #705 came from a PGO build on an AVX-512 EPYC 9645; the repository's release profile is only lto = "thin", panic = "abort", debug = true, so a plain cargo build is not that build
- -Ctarget-cpu=native halved modular decode speed in issue #803 (i5-12400, 14.757 to 7.895 MP/s, weighted predictor worst; closed), so test target-cpu flags before shipping them
- jxl_cli --speedtest uses all cores by default (--num-threads 0 means automatic); pass --num-threads 1 and a single-threaded djxl run to compare like for like
- The AVX-512 path the headline numbers ran on is not reliably exercised by CI: open issue #966 shows the 'avx512' job silently falls back to AVX2 on GitHub runners without AVX-512 (AMD EPYC 7763)

**Status:** Very active (commits to 2026-10-03, jxl 0.7.0-0.7.4 released in September 2026, 317k crates.io downloads) and BSD-3-Clause; shipped in Chrome and Firefox, but performance parity with libjxl rests on one first-party PGO measurement.

[repo](https://github.com/libjxl/jxl-rs) · [benchmark](https://github.com/libjxl/jxl-rs/pull/705#issuecomment-4063790496)

##### LERC (Limited Error Raster Compression)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Esri's raster codec with a per-pixel error bound for 8- to 64-bit integer and float tiles; encodes far faster than zlib level 9.

**Beats:** zlib deflate level 9 (labelled 'LZW' in the benchmark document; called through compress2) — Esri's own 2016 PDF, which predates LERC 1.0 and runs zlib compress2 level 9 on raw samples without a predictor (mislabelled 'LZW'), reports lossless LERC encodes 16-bit DTED and multispectral tiles about 11-13x faster and decodes them about 2.3-2.6x faster (derived from page data), at a slightly better average ratio. The float rows are lossy only (MaxZError 0.01 and up). No CPU, OS, compiler or flags are given, and the driver and test rasters are not published.

**Known shortcoming:** The numbers come from the first-party doc/LercBenchmarks_Feb_2016.pdf with no CPU, compiler or flags; the benchmark driver and ZLibAccess.h are not published and the data is not in testData/. Only the MaxZError 0 integer rows are like-for-like with lossless zlib-9 (encode 10.8-12.7x, decode 2.3-2.6x, derived from page data); the float rows are lossy-by-tolerance, different work, and zlib-9 compresses better on 2 tiles.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark's zlib baseline is level 9 with no predictor and is mislabelled LZW in the PDF; encode and decode fail on big-endian hosts; 4.1.1 fixed two unpublished security issues.

**Independent measurement:** Independent GDAL test (gpxz.io/blog/lerc-benchmarks, search snippet only; page blocked here), Copernicus DEM float32: LERC at 1e-5 tolerance writes 315 MB/s and reads 473 MB/s at ratio 1.9; DEFLATE 33/253 MB/s at ratio 1.6; zstd 519/957 MB/s at ratio 1.5, so zstd is faster than LERC on that data.

**How:** Lerc2 splits the tile into 8x8 micro-blocks (retrying at 16x16 when that is smaller). For each block it stores min/max, quantizes n = (x - min)/(2*MaxZError) + 0.5 to unsigned ints, and bit-stuffs them with ceil(log2(range+1)) bits, optionally through a lookup table of distinct values; constant and empty blocks cost only a header. That is one scalar pass with no match search, which is why encode is much faster than deflate's level-9 lazy matching. Lossless 8-bit data can switch to delta plus Huffman coding, and lossless float/double (since 4.0) to a delta-delta Huffman path kept only when it is at least 10% smaller. The encoder also detects floats that sit on a decimal grid (multiples of 0.1, 0.01 and so on) and raises MaxZError to half that step for free. There is no SIMD and no threading in the code.

**Use it when:**
- Elevation models, scientific float grids and 11-16-bit multispectral imagery where you can name a tolerable absolute error (e.g. 0.01 m), so lossy encoding gives several times the ratio of lossless deflate at a known bound.
- Tile servers and caches that encode on the fly: the 2016 PDF shows about 10-13x faster encode than zlib level 9 on lossless 16-bit tiles (231 vs 2484 ms per 3601x3601 DTED-2 tile).
- Rasters with void areas: the valid-pixel mask is RLE-coded and masked pixels cost nothing, and lerc_getDataRanges reads per-band min/max without decoding.
- GDAL GeoTIFF/COG or MRF pipelines (COMPRESS=LERC with MAX_Z_ERROR) and ArcGIS-compatible services, where readers already exist in C++, Python, JS and C#.

**Skip it when:**
- 8-bit RGB or photographic imagery: the README itself says PNG compresses 8-bit lossless better and recommends JPEG where it is good enough.
- Plain lossless speed against a modern compressor: one third-party GDAL test (gpxz.io, 3600x3600 float32 Copernicus DEM, 512x512 blocks; search snippet only, page blocked) measured zstd at 519 MB/s write and 957 MB/s read, against 315 and 473 for LERC at MAX_Z_ERROR 1e-5 (lossy) and 33 and 253 for DEFLATE. LERC's ratio there was 1.9, zstd's 1.5.
- Low-entropy integer tiles with small value ranges: zlib out-compressed lossless LERC on the flat Georgia DTED tiles in the vendor's own PDF (4.9 vs 4.6 and 7.1 vs 5.3).
- Big-endian hosts: Lerc2 encode, decode, header and range calls return failure unless the machine is little-endian with 4-byte int.
- Whole large images in one blob: since 4.2 a blob is capped at 2 GB per band and 4 GB overall, and the API notes say LERC is meant for tiles.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults to ON); vcpkg and Conan packages exist · none · C++17, CMake 3.12 (Visual Studio, Code::Blocks and Xcode project files also provided) · little-endian only (Windows, Linux, macOS; WASM decoder via Emscripten); no SIMD, so any little-endian CPU

**Vs siblings:** Pick LERC when the data is float, double or 32-bit integer, or when you need a hard per-pixel error bound with masks. CharLS (JPEG-LS NEAR mode) bounds error only for integer samples up to 16 bits, and OpenJPH or Grok (JPEG 2000) fit 8-16-bit imagery that needs JPEG 2000 interoperability. For exact float storage, meshoptimizer's vertex codec is the catalogued lossless alternative.

**Gotchas:**
- MaxZError is a bound before the float cast: decode computes zMin + n*2*MaxZError in double and casts to T, and the sample program subtracts a 0.0001 'safety margin ... to account for finite floating point accuracy' from the wanted error.
- For integer types MaxZError is floored and clamped to at least 0.5, so 0 means exact and 0.7 behaves like 0.5. A negative MaxZError on integers switches to bit-plane noise compression, and the undocumented value 777 maps to -0.01.
- lerc_encode always runs a full sizing pass first (tiling, Huffman tries and a 16x16 retry) and then writes, so calling lerc_computeCompressedSize beforehand repeats that work; closed issue #197 notes lerc_encode can return fewer bytes than that estimate.
- NaNs are never returned: they are moved into the mask, or in the mixed nDepth case replaced by the noData value (encode fails if none is set). Release 4.1.1 (2026-07-02) 'fixed two security issues' with no published advisory, and 4.2.0 added size and overflow checks, so use 4.2.0 or later on untrusted blobs.

**Status:** Actively maintained (4.2.0 released 2026-07-23, last commit 2026-09-17), Apache-2.0 and dependency-free, so it is easy to vendor; it ships in Esri ArcGIS and GDAL.

[repo](https://github.com/Esri/lerc) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Esri/lerc/master/doc/LercBenchmarks_Feb_2016.pdf)

##### libjpeg-turbo  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause AND IJG AND Zlib`  `active`  `Tier C`

SIMD-accelerated, ABI-compatible replacement for IJG libjpeg; the vendor says 2-6x faster JPEG encode and decode.

**Beats:** IJG libjpeg (libjpeg 6b reference) — First-party only: the README says 'generally 2-6x as fast as libjpeg, all else being equal' with no machine, compiler or libjpeg version; the per-platform tables (libjpeg v6b and v8d baselines, tjbench Mpixels/s) live on libjpeg-turbo.org, which was not reachable, and tjbench itself times a 1 s warm-up and then at least 5 s of repeated compress/decompress calls and reports Mpixels/s. Third-party runs do not use IJG libjpeg as baseline: jpeg-nitro's README (Intel i9 13th gen) puts libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 at parity with its own one-thread decoder, and google/decoder-benchmarks-for-rust (2.6 GHz 6-core Core i7, macOS) has turbojpeg at 84.25 ms versus 126.2 ms for the Rust jpeg-decoder crate on a 2000x3000 JPEG.

**Known shortcoming:** The category's own incumbent, kept against IJG libjpeg (zlib-ng precedent): the README's '2-6x as fast as libjpeg' and ChangeLog AltiVec notes (3-4x and 2-2.5x vs v6b) are first-party, and the libjpeg-turbo.org performance page (3.47-6.00x compression, 2.08-3.43x decompression vs v6b) is blocked here, so C. Independent confirmation exists in jpeg-nitro's and Google's decoder benchmarks. IJG licence OSI status unchecked.

**Known shortcoming:** The 2-6x claim is first-party and from the libjpeg v6b/v8 era. Restart markers force the slow Huffman decoder for the whole image (the #910 fix, 1.08x, was declined); the fast FDCT is up to 40% slower at quality 98-100; the 12-bit, lossless and arithmetic paths are C only (#199); no AVX-512, SVE2 or WebAssembly SIMD.

**How:** Hand-written SIMD modules (NASM for x86 SSE2/AVX2, intrinsics for Arm Neon, PowerPC AltiVec, Loongson MMI and RISC-V Vector) replace the libjpeg C paths for color conversion, chroma down/upsampling (including merged upsampling plus color conversion), integer sample conversion and quantization, accurate-integer forward and inverse DCT, and the baseline and progressive Huffman encoders. A runtime dispatcher picks the best instruction set per instance. Huffman decoding is not SIMD but uses an optimized table-lookup fast path in C, which is where most of the gain on non-SIMD systems comes from. Only 8-bit-per-sample lossy paths are vectorized (simd/README.md).

**Use it when:**
- Any C or C++ program that links IJG libjpeg (v6b, or v7/v8 through ABI emulation) and wants faster JPEG encode/decode with no code changes.
- Server-side thumbnailing, image proxies and photo pipelines that decode or encode many 8-bit baseline or progressive JPEGs, one image per thread.
- Decoding straight into RGBX/BGRA/XRGB buffers or planar YUV (TurboJPEG tj3DecompressToYUV8), or decoding at 1/2 and 1/4 scale (SIMD-accelerated IDCT scaling) for previews.
- Lossless JPEG transforms (rotate, flip, crop, drop) through jpegtran or tj3Transform without re-encoding.
- Portable deployments across x86-64, Arm64, PowerPC, Loongson and RISC-V, where one codebase gets SIMD on each.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency of a single large image on an idle many-core machine: libjpeg-turbo decodes one image on one thread; the catalogued jpeg-nitro decodes one baseline JPEG on all cores (about 9x lower wall time on 16 threads in its README).
- Smallest files per quality: it has no trellis quantization (mozjpeg, a libjpeg-turbo fork, adds it) and no adaptive quantization (google/jpegli, also libjpeg62 API/ABI-compatible, advertises it); when bytes matter more than encode speed, evaluate those instead.
- 12-bit lossy or 2-16-bit lossless JPEG and arithmetic-coded JPEG throughput: those paths run in C only (issue #199, 'Performance improvements (SIMD extensions) for 12-bit JPEGs', is open with 'funding needed').
- Code that needs the libjpeg v9 ABI, SmartScale, DCT scaling in the compressor or lossless RGB JPEG from IJG v9: not supported, and cinfo.scale_num/scale_denom and cinfo.block_size are silently ignored.
- Targets that need AVX-512, Arm SVE2 or WebAssembly SIMD paths: all are open 'funding needed' issues (#732, #860, #250), so wasm builds fall back to C.

**Integration:** shared lib or static lib (libjpeg API library libjpeg.so/jpeg-static and TurboJPEG API library libturbojpeg.so/turbojpeg-static); built with CMake · none at runtime; build needs CMake 3.15+ and NASM 2.13+ or Yasm 1.2.0+ for the x86 SIMD code (libspng and zlib are bundled for cjpeg/djpeg and tj3LoadImage/tj3SaveImage PNG support) · C compiler: GCC 4.1+ or Clang on Un*x, Visual C++ 2005+ or MinGW on Windows; Arm builds need GCC 12+ or Clang for full Neon performance since 3.2 (the GAS Neon code was removed) · x86 and x86-64 (SSE2, AVX2), Arm 32/64 (Neon), PowerPC (AltiVec), Loongson MIPS64 (MMI), RISC-V 64 (RVV); any other CPU through the C code

**Vs siblings:** Pick libjpeg-turbo when you need the standard C libjpeg/TurboJPEG ABI, the widest set of SIMD architectures and full format coverage (progressive, arithmetic, 12-bit, lossless, transforms); libjpeg-turbo-rs and zenjpeg are Rust re-implementations that report slightly faster decode on their own x86 tests, and jpeg-nitro beats it only on single-image multi-core latency for baseline JPEGs to YCbCr planes.

**Gotchas:**
- Restart markers switch the decoder to the slow Huffman path for the whole image (README: up to 20% slower). Issue #910 showed a 1.08x decode gain on 25 restart-marker camera JPEGs (Ryzen 7 5800X) by limiting the slow path to restart boundaries; it was closed 'won't implement'.
- The fast integer forward DCT at quality 98-100 cannot use the SIMD quantizer and runs up to 40% slower; the ChangeLog (3.0 beta2) also says the fast DCT/IDCT fail the ISO compliance tests and are no faster than the accurate ones on modern x86, so TurboJPEG 3 defaults to the accurate algorithms.
- Valgrind and MemorySanitizer report false uninitialized reads in the SIMD code; set JSIMD_FORCENONE=1 at run time or build with -DZERO_BUFFERS=1 when running memory checkers.
- When decompressing to RGBX/BGRX/XBGR/XRGB the X byte is left undefined for speed; use the RGBA/BGRA/ABGR/ARGB colorspaces if you need 0xFF alpha. Decompressing 4:4:0 and the float IDCT can differ slightly from libjpeg v6b output.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-25, release 3.2.0 on 2026-06-30 with 3.2.1 fixes in the ChangeLog, CVE fixes such as CVE-2026-75466 handled promptly) and permissively licensed (IJG plus Modified BSD, SIMD code under Zlib); it is the ISO/ITU-T JPEG reference implementation and the default system libjpeg on most platforms, so usability is copyable with no caveats beyond the usual BSD/IJG attribution.

[repo](https://github.com/libjpeg-turbo/libjpeg-turbo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/libjpeg-turbo/libjpeg-turbo)

##### libjpeg-turbo-rs  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust port of libjpeg-turbo with AVX2/NEON kernels that decodes a few percent faster than C on x86_64 and encodes at about C speed.

**Beats:** libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (decode) and 3.2.0 (encode) — Decode, first party: on an Intel i5-10400 (turbo off) a stock `cargo build --release` (fat LTO) decoded q75 fixtures in 0.87-0.97x of C libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2's time from 640x480 4:2:2 up to 3840x2160 and 0.77x at 320x240, but was slower at 64x64 (1.23x) and on the 640x480 gradient (1.05x). Both sides used the accurate integer IDCT and fancy upsampling (TurboJPEG FASTDCT=0, FASTUPSAMPLE=0; Rust defaults IsLow, merged upsampling off). The C loop reuses its output buffer while Rust's Criterion loop allocates one per decode. Encode is the only table with full methodology (rustc 1.98.1, official libjpeg-turbo 3.2.0 .deb, cc -O2 harness, AMD EPYC 7763), and there Rust is slower at 1.00-1.08x of C.

**Known shortcoming:** Pure-Rust port of libjpeg-turbo (not an FFI wrapper), so a port of the category's incumbent; kept because libjpeg-turbo itself is a baseline, not a catalogued entry. README x86 decode 3-23% faster on most sizes (i5-10400, libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2) with rustc and the C build unstated; the portable encode build is slower (1.05-1.10x at 1080p), and only that table is fully specified (rustc 1.98.1, cc -O2, official 3.2.0 deb, EPYC 7763). Rust (language-filter mismatch).

**Known shortcoming:** Settings are like-for-like (islow plus fancy upsampling on both sides; Rust allocates per decode), but the 320x240 0.77x best case looks like a C outlier (13.0 versus 10.8-11.3 ns per pixel, derived from page data; the same CPU's 2026-04-12 report gave 1.00x), so the realistic x86 decode win is about 2-17%. rustc and the C build are unstated for the decode table (the encode harness comment links a conda libjpeg). Open issue #610: Encoder::scan_script with Se above 63 writes out of bounds on the stack from safe Rust on x86_64. crates.io 0.8.0 (2026-07-28) predates the measured main; about 40k downloads with 9 stars. A port of the listed libjpeg-turbo (zlib-rs precedent would fold it; kept per the libjpeg-turbo-rs decision).

**How:** It reimplements libjpeg-turbo's pipeline (Huffman decode, accurate integer IDCT, fancy upsampling, colour conversion) with hand-written AVX2/SSE2 intrinsics chosen by runtime CPUID dispatch and NEON on aarch64. Its own fused kernels go beyond C's, such as an AVX2 fancy H2V2 upsampler that does the vertical and horizontal triangle filters in one pass over 16 samples and a fused FDCT, quantize, colour and downsample encode path. The Huffman encoder skips zero coefficients with a bitmap using TZCNT/BLSR/LZCNT (BMI1/LZCNT) and has a runtime-dispatched BMI2 tier. The release profile uses fat LTO for cross-module inlining.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services that decode many photo JPEGs of 320x240 and up on x86_64 with AVX2: the repo's own runs put decode at 0.83-0.98x of C libjpeg-turbo's time on an i5-10400.
- You want libjpeg-turbo-identical output without a C toolchain: cross-compiling, wasm32 with SIMD128, or no_std + alloc firmware (thumbv7em is CI-built).
- Replacing zune-jpeg in `image`-crate pipelines: the README reports 31 wins and 3 losses out of 34 decode cases on aarch64 and 1.31x faster through the image bridge at 1080p.
- You need libjpeg features that lighter Rust decoders lack: progressive or arithmetic encode, lossless JPEG, 12/16-bit, DCT-coefficient access, lossless rotate/flip with marker copying.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ code that already links libjpeg-turbo: speed is at parity (M1 Pro decode 0.99-1.07x and encode 1.03-1.07x of C), and the C library is far more mature.
- Encode-heavy x86_64 work on a portable (distro-style) build: 1.00-1.08x of C 3.2.0's time on a Zen 3 runner and 1.09-1.10x on Zen 4 at 1080p. The float DCT path trails C by 1.4-1.9x (issue #600).
- Untrusted input where memory safety is the reason to choose Rust: the README makes no memory-safety guarantee while the unsafe SIMD boundary is audited, and issue #610 (open) is an out-of-bounds stack write reachable from safe Rust.
- Tiny images (64x64 decodes 1.23x slower than C; 16x16 cases lose on fixed cost) and 32-bit ARM or RISC-V Vector hardware, where there is no SIMD backend and the README estimates 2-5x (armv7) and roughly 1.5-4x decode (RVV) slower than C.
- As a system libjpeg.so.62 (v6b) or v7 replacement: the README says struct layouts differ and substitution corrupts memory; the v8 ABI is experimental.

**Integration:** crate (plus cdylib C ABI shims: libturbojpeg.so.0 for TurboJPEG 3, experimental libjpeg.so.8) · thiserror; optional png crate behind the `png` feature; no C libraries · Rust 1.87 (MSRV, CI-enforced); the image-bridge crate needs 1.88 · x86_64 (AVX2/SSE2 runtime dispatch, Linux/macOS/Windows), aarch64 (NEON), wasm32 (SIMD128); scalar on RISC-V, POWER, s390x, armv7 and thumbv7em (no_std)

**Vs siblings:** It is a port of libjpeg-turbo, so for C/C++ the original stays the default. Pick this one when a Rust or C-toolchain-free build needs libjpeg-turbo's exact output and full feature set at roughly equal speed. Compared with zenjpeg (faster Rust decode with different upsampling defaults) or the jpeg-nitro parallel decoders, it trades peak decode speed for bit-exact libjpeg-turbo compatibility and a TurboJPEG C ABI.

**Gotchas:**
- Issue #610 (open, 2026-09-08): Encoder::scan_script accepts a spectral end Se > 63. On x86_64 the SSE2 prepare_ac_first_sse2 path then writes about 272 bytes past two [u16; 64] stack arrays and returns Ok with corrupt output; aarch64 panics instead. Validate custom scan scripts yourself until it is fixed.
- The newest crates.io release is 0.8.0 (2026-07-28), but the README's performance tables and the runtime BMI2/FMA dispatch come from main in September 2026. Pin a git revision if you need the measured code. Compile-time -C target-feature=+bmi2,+fma binaries fault on CPUs without those features.
- The x86_64 decode table (i5-10400, C 3.1.2) does not state the rustc version or how the C library was built (the encode harness's build comment links a conda $CONDA_PREFIX libjpeg). Its best case, 0.77x at 320x240, looks like a C-side outlier: C's time there is 13.0 ns per pixel vs 10.8-11.3 ns at 1280x720 4:2:0 and 640x480 4:2:2 (derived from page data), and the repo's 2026-04-12 report on the same CPU measured 1.00x for that case.
- The repo root carries committed benchmark binaries (bench_c_decode_matrix is a Mach-O arm64 build linked to Homebrew's libjpeg.8.dylib; bench_c_encode_linux is an x86-64 ELF). The C sides of the aarch64 tables used the classic libjpeg API, while the x86 decode harness (benches/c_baseline.c) used TurboJPEG tj3Decompress8.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-09-22, 1,759 commits, most recent ones co-authored with Claude), 9 GitHub stars but about 40k crates.io downloads (38.5k in the last 90 days), MIT OR Apache-2.0. 44 open issues, mostly C-ABI parity and unsafe-audit items, so treat the C ABI shims as pre-1.0.

[repo](https://github.com/developer0hye/libjpeg-turbo-rs) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/developer0hye/libjpeg-turbo-rs/HEAD/README.md)

##### libjxl fast_lossless (fjxl) encoder  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

libjxl effort-1 lossless JPEG XL encoder (fjxl): about 19x faster than libpng, 43x faster than libwebp lossless.

**Beats:** libpng and libwebp (lossless encoders) — Third-party run (nigeltao/qoir doc/full_benchmarks.txt, about 2022): the then-experimental fast_lossless.cc, compiled into the harness with gcc 10.2.1 -O3 -march=native and AVX2 intrinsics on one core of an Intel i5-10210U, encoded the QOI benchmark images at 106.48 MP/s versus 5.49 for Debian Bullseye libpng and 2.49 for libwebp lossless, at compression ratio 0.2171 versus 0.2423 and 0.1651. Measurement caveats: the harness never compares decoded pixels with the source, and the measured snapshot predates the PR #4291 palette fix (the same check-then-insert code is in v0.7.0 of July 2022 and was still reported in v0.11.1), so a few RGBA images with few colors may have been encoded lossily. That could flatter the ratio slightly but should not change the speed. The JXL decode rows also carry the adapter's inverted channel count. WangXuan95's single-threaded CLIC2021 run (i7-12700H, Windows 10, cjxl v0.9.0 -q 100 -e 1 launched once per image, so process start and PNM I/O are included) took 42.993 s versus 334.791 s for in-process Pillow PNG (zlib, optimize=False), with 18% smaller output.

**Known shortcoming:** FJXL (lib/jxl/enc_fast_lossless.cc, effort 1; experimental/fast_lossless is gone) writes JPEG XL, not PNG: qoir full_benchmarks.txt rows 55/65/73 give 106.48 vs 5.49 MB/s libpng and 2.49 WebP lossless on encode, while its decode (33.16 MB/s) is slower than libpng's 56.18. Harness bug in adapter/jxl_adapter.cpp: decode num_channels is inverted (alpha_bits==0 ? 4 : 3), affecting the JXL decode rows only; the harness never checks round-trip pixels.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered A to C (retier-15): the 2022 QOIR run timed fast_lossless effort 1 whose palette detection could emit lossy output on RGBA few-colour images (issue #4287, present from v0.7.0 to v0.11.1, fixed PR #4291 in June 2025), and QOIR never round-trip checks, so the 0.2171 ratio may be slightly flattered. Default CMake disables the fjxl AVX-512 path; x86 SIMD is gated on !_MSC_VER so MSVC and clang-cl Windows builds are probably scalar; the fast path falls back on animation, crop and extra channels; the WangXuan95 timing includes cjxl.exe process start against in-process Pillow.

**How:** It runs a fixed pipeline with no search (doc/encode_effort.md, e1 row): fixed YCoCg color transform, fixed ClampedGradient predictor, one entropy context with no MA tree, Huffman prefix codes instead of ANS, run-length-only LZ77 for zero runs, and a simple palette path (up to 512 colors found through a 64K-entry hash, 8-bit one-shot input only). Huffman tables come from a histogram sampled from only 2 x effort rows per 256-row group. The hot loop tokenizes and bit-packs 16 residuals at a time with SIMD (AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON: pshufb nibble lookups compute tokens, then bit fields merge from 16- to 32- to 64-bit lanes before one scalar flush). 256x256 groups are encoded independently, so a parallel runner can spread them across threads.

**Use it when:**
- Lossless archiving or export of 8-bit RGB/RGBA screenshots, renders and photos when encoder time dominates and readers support JPEG XL: about 106 MP/s on one i5-10210U core with AVX2, versus 5.49 MP/s for default libpng, with smaller files.
- High-bit-depth lossless capture (up to 16-bit integer, or float16 input through libjxl) where PNG encoders are slow; the fast path handles 1-4 channels, alpha included.
- Large single images on many cores: groups are independent, so libjxl's thread pool (or your own FJxlParallelRunner in standalone mode) parallelizes the encode.
- A quick first-pass lossless JXL that a background job can later re-encode at effort 7+ (0.1548 versus 0.2171 compression ratio in the same QOIR run) without leaving the format.
- Embedding a JXL writer without libjxl: the standalone build of enc_fast_lossless.cc needs no libjxl, highway or brotli.

**Skip it when:**
- Consumers that need PNG or WebP, or that lack a JPEG XL decoder: the output is JXL only.
- Read-heavy workloads: in the same QOIR run libjxl decoded fjxl files at 33.16 MP/s versus 56.18 for libpng and 89.94 for WebP lossless (single-threaded), and in WangXuan95's CLIC2021 run djxl -e 1 output took 57.650 s to decode versus 33.677 s for Pillow PNG.
- Best ratio: WebP lossless (0.1651) and libjxl at effort 7 (0.1548) are 24-29% smaller than fjxl's 0.2171, if encode time allows.
- Raw encode speed whatever the format: in the same run fpnge (312.59 MP/s, PNG), fpng (192.16), QOIR (168.90), QOI (146.87) and Zpng (126.21) all encoded faster; fpnge and fpng still emit ordinary PNG.
- Frames that miss the fast path: CanDoFastLossless in lib/jxl/encode.cc rejects animation, cropped layers, frame names, frame-index boxes, extra channels other than one alpha, more than 16 bits, stripped alpha and LSB-padded bit depths, and those inputs silently fall back to the much slower general modular encoder at effort 1.

**Integration:** shared or static lib (libjxl via CMake), or source-drop of lib/jxl/enc_fast_lossless.cc built with -DFJXL_STANDALONE · libjxl: brotli, highway, and skcms or lcms2 (git submodules or system packages); standalone fjxl: none beyond the C++ standard library · CMake 3.16+; C++17 when available (CMake falls back to C++14/11); Clang 7+ recommended; fjxl's AVX-512 path needs GCC 11+ or Clang 8+ · Any; fjxl SIMD on x86-64 (AVX2, AVX-512 with runtime CPUID dispatch) only with compilers that do not define _MSC_VER (GCC, Clang; not MSVC or clang-cl), NEON on aarch64, scalar elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick fjxl over fpnge, fpng, QOI, QOIR or Zpng when you want a standardized, widely packaged format (JPEG XL) with files smaller than libpng's and can afford slower decode; pick fpnge or fpng when the output must stay PNG, and QOIR or Zpng when you control both ends and need faster decode.

**Gotchas:**
- Correctness bugs in this path were fixed late: before 0.12.0, palette detection checked all 8 pixels of an unrolled block before inserting any, so two colors in one block with the same hash slot could slip through and produce lossy output from 'lossless' -e 1 (issue #4287 on an emoji PNG, fixed by PR #4291 in June 2025); PR #4027 (December 2024) fixed a shift-by-64 in BitWriter::WriteMultiple behind issue #4026, 'Lossless images are not actually lossless'. Use 0.12.0 or later (the README also urges 0.12 for security fixes) and round-trip check critical archives.
- Default CMake builds compile out fjxl's AVX-512 code: the AVX3 highway target is off by default, and CMakeLists.txt then adds -DFJXL_ENABLE_AVX512=0. Pass -DJPEGXL_ENABLE_HWY_AVX3=ON to get it. The x86 SIMD block is enabled only when _MSC_VER is undefined, which rules out MSVC and also clang-cl (it defines _MSC_VER), the compiler of the official Windows release builds since 0.12, so Windows builds likely run fjxl's scalar path (inferred from the preprocessor guards, not measured).
- Effort numbers do not line up: libjxl e1 calls fjxl with effort=2, while the standalone API takes 0-127 (more rows sampled for the Huffman histogram, slower). Below effort 2, with streaming input, or above 8 bits, palette detection is skipped.
- Decode is the weak side: there is no fast decoder for the fast encoder (libjxl 0.12 notes a fix to its 'specialized decoding path for fast lossless', #4836), so measure decode on your target before switching an image store.

**Status:** Actively maintained under the libjxl/Google JPEG XL project (0.12.0 released 2026-07-01, last commit 2026-09-29), BSD-3-Clause with a patent grant, packaged by major Linux distributions and Homebrew; copyable as part of libjxl or as one standalone .cc file, but use 0.12.0+ because of the e1 lossless corruption fixes.

[repo](https://github.com/libjxl/libjxl) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nigeltao/qoir/HEAD/doc/full_benchmarks.txt)

##### lowzag  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Progressive-JPEG decoder in C99 that decodes at 1/2-1/8 scale in a fraction of libjpeg-turbo's coefficient memory.

**Beats:** libjpeg-turbo (progressive coefficient array memory); also ROM TJpgDec for decode time on ESP32 — On a generated 12 MP 4:2:0 progressive file, lowzag 2.3.0's own peak_alloc is 36.2 / 19.6 / 6.8 / 3.4 MB at 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 (pinned in CI by test/check_docs.py), against 36.1 MB computed for libjpeg-turbo's coefficient array (282,000 blocks x 128-byte JBLOCK); a separate process-RSS table (lowzag CLI vs djpeg -nosmooth, libjpeg-turbo 3.0.4, unnamed aarch64 machine) was measured on the first release (pjpeg 1.0.0, peak_alloc 36.2 / 23.0 / 8.9 / 3.6 MB) and never re-run, so it understates the current gap at 1/2 and 1/4. The ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz times (lowzag on a progressive file vs the ROM TJpgDec, which is fixed at JD_FASTDECODE=0, on a jpegtran baseline copy) are single 1.0.0-era runs: lowzag slower at 800x480 1/1 (0.63 vs 0.46 s) and faster at 4000x3000 1/4 (5.7 vs 9.1 s).

**Known shortcoming:** A memory metric rather than speed: peak_alloc is pinned by CI (test/check_docs.py) and the libjpeg 36.1 MB figure is computed, not measured; the measured RSS table (4,636 against 36,536 KiB at 1/8 scale, 7.9x derived) names no CPU or script. The ESP32 timing pits a progressive-file lowzag against the ROM TJpgDec on the baseline file in single runs and is slower at 800x480. Weak fit for a speed list.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e114, 2026-10-05): no correctness bug; the AC refinement loop matches libjpeg-turbo's logic. Two stale tables, neither inflating the claim: the RSS table (36,580 / 23,648 / 9,916 / 4,636 KiB) is identical to the first commit e4d11e4 (pjpeg 1.0.0, peak_alloc 36.2 / 23.0 / 8.9 / 3.6 MB) and was never re-run after 2.3.0 (19.6 / 6.8 / 3.4 MB), so the record's '7.9x RSS at 1/8' pairs a 1.0.0 measurement with the 2.3.0 table and understates the current gap; ESP32 times are also unchanged since e4d11e4. The ROM TJpgDec baseline is fixed at JD_FASTDECODE=0 (esp_jpeg README; level 2 is only about 12% faster). The GitHub description still says 3.6 MB. C stands.

**Independent measurement:** first-party tables

**How:** The win is memory, not speed. A reduced-scale IDCT reads only the low-frequency bs x bs corner of each 8x8 block, so lowzag stores just that corner (64, 16, 4 or 1 coefficients, row-major since 2.3.0, written through a 64-entry zigzag-to-slot map) plus an 8-byte nonzero bitmap per block. The bitmap carries the T.81 G.1.2.3 nonzero history that AC successive-approximation refinement scans need to consume the right number of correction bits for the discarded coefficients, so every scan is still entropy-decoded in full. Dequantization, the 1/2/4/8-point Loeffler IDCT (Q13, int32 only), upsampling and color conversion run only on the kept corner, which is also why it overtakes ROM TJpgDec at 1/4 on large files.

**Use it when:**
- Showing camera-size progressive JPEGs (several MP) on an ESP32-S3 or similar MCU with PSRAM, at 1/2 to 1/8 scale for a small panel
- Host-side thumbnailing of large progressive JPEGs where peak memory per decode matters more than throughput (at 1/4, 6.8 MB against libjpeg-turbo's 36.1 MB coefficient array for 12 MP 4:2:0)
- When you must refuse or size a decode before allocating: lowzag_estimate() returns the exact peak_alloc from the header alone, and mem_limit degrades instead of failing
- Streaming input (socket, SD card) that cannot be seeked or held in RAM, including partial files via cfg.allow_partial
- Cropping a region out of a big progressive frame: an 800x480 window of 12 MP costs 3.4 MB at 1/1

**Skip it when:**
- Baseline JPEG, arithmetic coding, 12-bit, CMYK/Adobe, lossless JPEG or 4:1:1 sampling: all refused
- Throughput on a host: no speed comparison against libjpeg-turbo exists, there is no SIMD, and progressive input costs a full entropy decode of every scan
- Full-scale (1/1) decodes: lowzag stores exactly what libjpeg stores (128.5 vs 128 bytes per block), so there is no memory saving
- Memory budgets in the tens of kilobytes: storage is still proportional to the source (8-byte map per source block, 2.26 MB floor at 12 MP); bitbank2/JPEGDEC decodes progressive at 1/8 in about 18 KB constant, per the lowzag README
- Byte-identical thumbnails to libjpeg's scaled IDCT or fancy upsampling: reduced scales use coefficient truncation and chroma replication

**Integration:** source-drop (two files: src/lowzag.c and include/lowzag.h, plus optional src/lowzag_mem.c), or static/shared lib via CMake, or ESP-IDF component defensiblelogic/lowzag · none (the core object references only memcpy and memset; lowzag_decode_mem() adds malloc/free) · C99; CMake 3.15+ for the CMake build; ESP-IDF 5.4.1 tested for the component · any (portable C99, no SIMD, no 64-bit multiply); tested on x86-64 and aarch64 hosts and an ESP32-S3 board

**Vs siblings:** Pick lowzag over libjpeg-turbo (or jpeg-nitro and zenjpeg, which target host decode speed) only when the input is progressive and peak memory at reduced scale is the binding constraint, typically on an MCU with PSRAM; for decode speed on a host, libjpeg-turbo remains the choice and lowzag publishes no comparison against it.

**Gotchas:**
- Every public struct needs struct_size set (use LOWZAG_CFG_INIT / LOWZAG_INFO_INIT / LOWZAG_ESTIMATE_INIT); a zero or stack-garbage value returns LOWZAG_ERR_VERSION or worse
- mem_limit is opt-in (0 means unlimited) and under automatic scale selection a tight limit silently lowers chroma resolution and then scale; check info.chroma_steps as well as info.scale
- Memory follows the source dimensions, not the output: a 48 MP source decoded to 1000x750 costs 13.5 MB against 6.8 MB from 12 MP
- A crop covering more than about 93% of a 12 MP frame costs more than no crop at 1/1, because it forces the 2.26 MB nonzero map

**Status:** Active (31 commits, 2.3.0 on 2026-08-11, every commit co-authored with Claude, 1 star, developed on a self-hosted GitLab with GitHub as mirror and no issues or PRs yet); MIT, two files, unusually thorough tests (differential vs djpeg, ASan/UBSan/TSan/MSan, libFuzzer) and an explicit SECURITY.md threat model.

[repo](https://github.com/lowzag/lowzag) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lowzag/lowzag)

##### MANGO image codecs  `C++`  `Zlib`  `active`  `Tier C`

C++20 graphics library whose multi-threaded PNG/JPEG codecs beat single-threaded libpng and libjpeg, mostly on mango-encoded files.

**Beats:** libpng (via find_module(PNG), version and zlib build not stated); 'libjpeg' is whatever jpeglib.h find_module(JPEG) linked, used through the libjpeg API one scanline at a time. Every current install path in docs/installation/setup.md and vcpkg.json installs libjpeg-turbo, but the library used for the i9-8950HK table run is not recorded. — These are first-party README tables, present by October 2023 and never re-measured, with compiler and flags unstated. PNG on an i7-11800H: on 2560x1600, mango decoded in 3.2 ms against 57.3 ms for libpng, 37.7 for spng and 23.9 for wuffs, and encoded in 57.2 ms against 820.5 for libpng and 46.0 for fpng; on 4833x5875, decode 53.7 vs 379.5 ms and encode 287.0 vs 14051.3 ms. JPEG on an i9-8950HK: on 5184x3456, decode 23.3 vs 197.8 ms for 'libjpeg' (wuffs 185.9) and encode 18.5 vs 70.1 ms. Mango ran multi-threaded against single-threaded baselines, each library was timed once, and both PNG test files are byte-for-byte the size of mango's own output, which means they carry pLLD. The author's own 2023 README text said the JPEG decoder is 'up to three times the speed of jpeglib-turbo' in the best case and about equal in the worst, so the 8.5x table result implies either restart markers in the test file or a baseline other than libjpeg-turbo (not recorded).

**Known shortcoming:** Table numbers come from examples/image/{png,jpeg}_benchmark/*.cpp with the CPU named but compiler unstated; mango runs multithreaded by default against single-threaded baselines. The PNG test files are likely mango-encoded (pLLD parallel segments; input size equals mango output size), so the 18x decode is not general, and mango's PNG output is 19-24% larger. JPEG encode quality differs (95 vs 0.70) and the baseline 'libjpeg' is most likely libjpeg-turbo per the build docs, version unrecorded. An iDCT wrong-output bug was fixed 2026-09-29 (2a974fb).

**Known shortcoming:** The README JPEG and PNG tables are about three years stale and predate the iDCT bug (b1061f2 of 2023-10-06 dropped 'r_xmm2 = row5', copied into the AVX2 and AVX-512 paths by c655646, fixed by 2a974fb on 2026-09-29; issue #48: 254 decoded as 126, up to 122-128 levels wrong on 9-29% of pixels), so the published numbers are from pre-bug code and were never re-measured. --nomt cannot disable pLLD parallel decode or parallel encode, so no single-thread mango number exists; the PNG parser skips chunk CRCs, the ISA-L and pLLD paths skip Adler-32 and per-segment decompress errors are ignored; JPEG encode is 4:4:4 at about libjpeg quality 93 (derived) against libjpeg q95 4:2:0; parallel Huffman decode needs a Mango1 APP14 marker or DRI equal to one MCU row. The author's 2023 README said 'up to three times' libjpeg-turbo while the table shows 8.5x, so the baseline or test file is unclear; fpng single-thread encode (46.0 ms) beats mango multithreaded (57.2 ms) in mango's own table.

**How:** Most of the gap comes from splitting one image across cores. The PNG encoder (ImageEncodeOptions::parallel = true by default) writes a private pLLD chunk and up to 128 independently deflated segments, filtered with SUB only and compressed with ISA-L on x86; the decoder sees pLLD and inflates the segments in parallel on a ConcurrentQueue. The JPEG encoder emits a restart marker per MCU row plus a private APP14 'Mango1' offset table, so its own files, or standard files whose DRI equals one MCU row, get parallel Huffman decoding; other JPEGs decode Huffman serially and only hand iDCT and colour conversion to worker threads. Kernels are SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON iDCT, PNG unfilter and colour conversion, chosen at compile time (the default CMake build enables SSE4 only).

**Use it when:**
- You control both ends of the pipeline (game or app assets, caches, screenshots) and can store PNGs and JPEGs written by mango, so later decodes take the parallel pLLD / Mango1 paths
- Interactive single-image latency on a many-core desktop, such as opening one large photo or texture, where using every core for one image matters more than total throughput
- Camera JPEGs that carry a DRI restart interval of exactly one MCU row, which mango's decoder splits across threads
- Projects already on mango (or wanting one C++ API for PNG, JPEG, DDS/KTX, EXR, HEIF, WebP and more) that need fast encode of RGB/RGBA PNGs and accept slightly larger files

**Skip it when:**
- Decoding arbitrary third-party PNGs: they lack the pLLD chunk, take the single-stream inflate path, and have no published mango numbers, so the 18x decode lead does not carry over
- Throughput servers that already decode many images at once on separate threads: the gain comes from per-image threading, not faster single-core code, and no single-threaded mango numbers exist
- Untrusted or integrity-sensitive input: the PNG parser skips every chunk CRC, the ISA-L and parallel paths inflate raw deflate after skipping the zlib header (no Adler-32 check), and decode_plld ignores per-segment decompression errors, so corrupt data can decode silently
- Smallest files: mango's PNGs were 24% and 19% larger than libpng's in its own tables (SUB filter only, zlib level 4, parallel segments), and its JPEG encoder always writes 4:4:4 with fixed standard Huffman tables
- Any build from before commit 2a974fb (2026-09-29) on x86, or before 17c019c on ARM: the default SIMD JPEG decode produced wrong pixels (issue #48), so pin to a fixed commit

**Integration:** shared lib (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS ON by default) or static lib, built with CMake · fmt, zlib, libdeflate, zstd, lcms2, ISA-L, LZ4, bzip2 and simdjson per the vcpkg 'base' feature and the apt/brew lines; optional codec libraries (libjxl, OpenJPEG, libwebp, libavif, libheif, LibRaw, jxrlib) and Vulkan/FreeType/HarfBuzz; the benchmark examples also need libjpeg-turbo, libpng and blend2d · C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20), CMake 3.19+; documented builds use g++ (apt/pacman), Xcode command-line tools (macOS) and MSVC with vcpkg (Windows); libjxl 0.9+ if JPEG XL is enabled · x86-64 (default build compiles with SSE4.1/4.2; AVX, AVX2, AVX-512 opt-in), ARM/AArch64 NEON, Linux, macOS, Windows, Emscripten/wasm

**Vs siblings:** For single-threaded PNG encode, pick fpng or fpnge: in mango's own table fpng (46.0 ms) beat multi-threaded mango (57.2 ms) on the 2560x1600 image. For arbitrary PNGs, pick wuffs, libspng or image-png; for parallel JPEG decode measured against a pinned libjpeg-turbo, pick jpeg-nitro. Pick mango when you write the files yourself and want one image decoded on many cores, or when you already use its C++20 framework.

**Gotchas:**
- x86 SIMD JPEG iDCT bug: commit b1061f2 ('Optimize SSE2 iDCT', 2023-10-06) dropped 'r_xmm2 = row5', so the column pass subtracted from a leftover register. The 2026-08-15 refactor copied it into the AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels, and it was fixed in 2a974fb on 2026-09-29 (NEON in 17c019c). Issue #48 reports 254 decoding as 126, with up to 122-128 levels of error on 9-29% of pixels. The README JPEG tables were already in README.md before b1061f2, so the published timings predate the bug.
- In png_benchmark, --nomt only clears ImageDecodeOptions::multithread. decode_plld runs whenever a pLLD chunk is present, whatever that flag says, and the mango encode path always uses parallel = true, so the harness cannot produce a single-threaded mango row for its own files.
- The JPEG encode rows differ in settings, not only in speed: mango ran at quality 0.70, which scales its quant tables to about 14% of base (roughly libjpeg quality 93, derived from jpeg_encode.cpp), with 4:4:4 sampling. libjpeg ran at quality 95 with jpeg_set_defaults' 4:2:0 sampling and was fed one scanline per call.
- Mango's PNGs stay valid for other decoders (segment Adler-32s are combined), but pLLD is a private chunk. Its JPEGs carry RST markers every MCU row and an APP14 'Mango1' table; other decoders ignore both.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-29, vcpkg version 3.8.2) under the zlib license, so copyable, but it is a large framework with many package-manager dependencies rather than a vendorable codec, and its benchmark tables are about three years older than the current code.

[repo](https://github.com/t0rakka/mango) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/t0rakka/mango/HEAD/README.md)

##### mozjpeg-rs  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Safe-Rust port of the mozjpeg JPEG encoder; its trellis mode timed 6% faster than C mozjpeg on one synthetic image.

**Beats:** mozjpeg (C encoder, libjpeg-turbo fork with trellis quantization) — tests/bench_2k.rs encodes one synthetic 2048x2048 gradient-plus-periodic-noise RGB image at Q85 4:2:0, sequential and single-threaded, 3 warmups then 30 timed runs per side, in the same process as C mozjpeg built by mozjpeg-sys 2.2.3 (default features include nasm_simd). The README reports 197 vs 210 ms with Huffman optimization plus AC/DC trellis and no deringing, and 42 vs 9 ms with no optimizations; CPU, rustc and RUSTFLAGS are not stated, and output sizes for the timed image are discarded. The trellis comparison sets the same encoder parameters on both sides but pits Rust's reduced trellis search (standard-table rates, adaptive lookback and candidate caps added in 0.6.0, when the changelog first claimed 7% faster) against C's full search with gather and requantize passes, so the gain is less work, not a faster implementation of the same search.

**Known shortcoming:** Single synthetic 2048x2048 image at Q85 4:2:0 (tests/bench_2k.rs), AC and DC trellis on, deringing off on both sides: trellis 197 ms versus mozjpeg 210 ms. The Rust side uses TrellisMode::Optimized, so output is not byte-identical and the bench reports no sizes; the README labels the 4.6x-slower row 'huffman opt' but the code runs it with Huffman optimisation off; no CPU or rustc version. The older Kodak CSV shows about 36% less time but files 0.9-3.9% larger.

**Known shortcoming:** The '6% faster' trellis claim is not like-for-like (retier-28): Rust times TrellisMode::Optimized with the Adaptive limiter (lookback 8/16, 3/4 candidates, blocks over 48/55 non-zero coefficients) against the C full quantize_trellis search with no speed limiter, so it does less work, and the timed image's sizes were never checked; the adaptive limiting landed in 0.6.0, the same release that first claimed 7% faster. Open issue #9 (greyscale plus progressive preset panics); Encoder::default() is progressive; simd-intrinsics is off by default; crates.io latest 0.9.2 (0.10.0 unreleased).

**How:** The trellis-mode win comes mainly from doing less trellis work than C mozjpeg. The default TrellisMode::Optimized runs trellis inline in the single forward-DCT pass and estimates rates from the standard Huffman tables. C mozjpeg instead gathers statistics, builds optimal tables and then runs extra trellis and Huffman passes per component. TrellisSpeedMode::Adaptive also caps the O(n^2) predecessor search at lookback 8 with 3 candidates for blocks with more than 55 nonzero AC coefficients, and at 16 with 4 above 48; upstream quantize_trellis in jcdctmgr.c searches every predecessor. DCT and colour conversion use safe SIMD (archmage, runtime AVX2/NEON dispatch, autovectorised fallback), but the non-trellis entropy coder is much slower than C's hand-tuned SIMD path.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services that want mozjpeg-style trellis-quantized JPEGs without a C toolchain, cmake or nasm, and with forbid(unsafe_code) across the whole encoder
- Encoding untrusted images on a server: Limits rejects oversized dimensions, allocations and metadata before any pixel work, and *_with_stop variants accept a cancellation or deadline token
- Replacing the C mozjpeg crate while keeping output bytes for non-trellis baseline and progressive configs (byte-exact parity on CID22 at Q75-95)
- Photo encoding at roughly Q75-95 with trellis on, where its measured speed is on par with or slightly ahead of C mozjpeg
- aarch64 or wasm32 targets: CI covers 15 platform configurations, including NEON and wasm32-wasip1 with SIMD128

**Skip it when:**
- Fast encoding without trellis: the no-optimization config timed 42 ms against 9 ms for C mozjpeg at 2048x2048 (4.6x slower), so for speed-first baseline JPEG use libjpeg-turbo or C mozjpeg
- You need decoding: it is encoder-only. The author recommends zenjpeg (encode and decode) for new projects
- Grayscale progressive output: open issue #9 (2026-08-29) reports an index-out-of-bounds panic in the SOS writer for Subsampling::Gray with ProgressiveBalanced or ProgressiveSmallest
- You need byte-identical trellis output to stock C mozjpeg: the default Optimized trellis gives different (usually slightly smaller) files, and TrellisMode::MozjpegExact is slower and is validated against imazen's patched mozjpeg fork
- Arithmetic coding, multipass trellis, a C ABI, or code that has had a human audit: the README says much of the code is AI-generated and not fully human-reviewed

**Integration:** crate · archmage, safe_unaligned_simd, wide, bytemuck, enough; default features add zenyuv (fast-yuv), imgref and rgb; optional png, zencodec/zenpixels/garb, and mozjpeg-sys + libc (mozjpeg-sys-config, which lifts forbid(unsafe_code) and builds C) · Rust 1.89 (edition 2024) · x86-64 (AVX2 dispatched at runtime), aarch64 (NEON), wasm32 (SIMD128); other targets use an autovectorised fallback. CI also covers armv7 and i686 under QEMU

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over zenjpeg (same author, encoder and decoder, beats libjpeg-turbo) only when you need mozjpeg-compatible settings and output bytes rather than the best size/quality. Pick it over libjpeg-turbo or jpeg-rusturbo when smaller trellis-quantized files from memory-safe Rust matter more than raw baseline encode speed.

**Gotchas:**
- Encoder::default() is Preset::ProgressiveBalanced (progressive, trellis, deringing), not a baseline JPEG; use Encoder::baseline_optimized() or Preset::BaselineBalanced for sequential output
- The README speed table does not use the shipped defaults: the 6% trellis row has deringing off and runs Adaptive search limiting, and the row labelled 'Baseline (huffman opt)' actually times TestEncoderConfig::baseline() with Huffman optimization off
- Hand-written SIMD intrinsics sit behind the non-default simd-intrinsics feature; default builds use autovectorised DCT/colour code, which Cargo.toml puts at about 87% of the intrinsics speed
- fast_color(true) (zenyuv) is about 40% faster at RGB to YCbCr but changes output bytes by ±1 rounding, so it breaks C parity

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-29; 0.10.0 prepared but unreleased, crates.io latest 0.9.2 from 2026-04-17 with about 120k downloads), BSD-3-Clause and easy to add with cargo, but a single-maintainer project with 3 stars whose author now steers new users to zenjpeg.

[repo](https://github.com/imazen/mozjpeg-rs) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/imazen/mozjpeg-rs/HEAD/README.md)

##### msf_gif  `C (single header, compiles as C99 or C++98)`  `Dual: MIT or Unlicense-style public-domain dedication (text at the bottom of msf_gif.h)`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Single-header C animated-GIF encoder with SSE2 frame quantization; first-party timings 5x to 30x faster than gif.h and jo_gif.

**Beats:** gif.h (Charlie Tangora's single-header encoder, named gif_h in the timings file) and jo_gif — The comparison rests on first-party, undated timings.txt totals with no CPU, compiler or input set given: scalar msf_gif ~14 s and SSE ~8 s against gif_h ~75 s (undithered) or ~315 s (dithered) and jo_gif ~425 s. The code that timed gif_h and jo_gif is not published, though .gitignore lists gif-h/, gif-h2/, gif-h3/, jo_gif/, jo_gif2/ and alt/ output folders, so such a harness existed. The public test.cpp times only msf_gif (clang -march=native -Os, profiling trace compiled in, 13 clips, quality 16, alpha threshold 128). If the totals cover the 11 clips whose sizes notes.txt logs (about 2.0 GB of RGBA), that works out to roughly 136 MiB/s scalar and 239 MiB/s SSE (derived; the input set behind timings.txt is not stated).

**Known shortcoming:** timings.txt (9 lines): single-thread 14 s vs gif_h 75 s (5.4x) and vs gif_h dithered 315 s (22.5x); threaded rows are not in the shipped single-thread v2.4, the gif_h and jo_gif timing code is not public, and there are no giflib, gifski or ffmpeg numbers nor any size or PSNR comparison. Licence MIT or public domain. The msfgif.handmade.network post (about 500 MB/s, no baseline) is blocked here.

**Known shortcoming:** The baseline harness is unpublished (though .gitignore lists gif-h, gif-h2, gif-h3, jo_gif and jo_gif2 output dirs, so it existed); timings.txt is undated and was carried in a February 2025 history-rewrite commit after the history was wiped in January 2025. If the totals cover the 11 clips in notes.txt (about 2.0 GB RGBA) the throughput is about 136 MiB/s scalar and 239 MiB/s SSE (derived, assumed input). test.cpp calls encode inside assert(), so an NDEBUG build would time nothing (the shipped build.sh is fine). Colourful frames fall to 128 colours (issue #8); _mm_srli_epi32 with a runtime count breaks SIMDe and ARM builds (issue #11 open); msf_gif_begin skips the NULL check on the tlb and used allocations; the LZW reset memsets up to 2 MB; a pre-2.4 heap overflow was fixed in f56d744.

**How:** There is no palette search: each frame is quantized to a fixed RGB bit split (up to 5-6-5 bits at quality 16) with a 4x4 ordered (Bayer-style) dither, done four pixels at a time with SSE2 integer intrinsics. If 256 or more colors end up in use, it drops one bit of depth and quantizes the frame again. The LZW coder uses a dense 4096 x palette-size int16 child table indexed directly by (prefix code, color) instead of a hash table. Pixels whose quantized value matches the previous frame are emitted as the transparent index 0, which gives long runs for LZW.

**Use it when:**
- Recording GIFs inside a game or tool at interactive speed, where encode time matters more than palette quality.
- Flat-shaded or pixel-art content with mostly static backgrounds, where inter-frame delta coding and ordered dither work well (the author's test set includes clips named diwide and flip, matching the README's examples from his games DIWide and Escher).
- Projects that want a vendorable single header with no dependencies, under public domain or MIT, that compiles as C99 or C++98.
- Memory-limited targets: allocation is bounded by a documented formula, malloc/realloc/free can be replaced through macros, and the to-file API keeps memory to about one frame.

**Skip it when:**
- Photographic or gradient-heavy video where palette quality matters: colorful frames often end up with 128 colors (issue #8) at a coarse 2-3-2 bit split, with a visible dither pattern. An adaptive quantizer such as gifski produces better-looking output.
- When you need the smallest file: every frame is written full-size (no sub-rectangle cropping), and delta coding turns off for any frame with transparent pixels or a palette bit-depth change.
- Non-x86 targets that need SIMD speed: there is only an SSE2 path (NEON is a TODO), and SIMDe ports to ARM fail to compile because _mm_srli_epi32 is called with a runtime shift count (issue #11, open since February 2025).
- Multithreaded encoding of one GIF: the shipped v2.4 is single-threaded; the threaded rows in timings.txt come from a variant that was never released (notes.txt).
- High-entropy frames with many colors: from reading the code (not measured), each time the 4096-code LZW table fills it is reset with a memset of 4096 x palette-size x 2 bytes (up to 2 MB), so noisy content pays that cost often.

**Integration:** header-only · none (C standard library; emmintrin.h when SSE2 is available) · C99 or C++98 (README); MSVC, GCC and clang paths in the source · any; SSE2 fast path on x86/x86-64 (enabled automatically by __SSE2__ or _M_X64, disabled with MSF_GIF_NO_SSE2); scalar code elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** It is the only GIF encoder in this category. gif_load and giflib-turbo are GIF decoders and pair with it rather than compete, while fpng, fpnge and QOI encode still lossless frames. Pick msf_gif when the output has to be an animated GIF and capture speed matters more than palette quality.

**Gotchas:**
- Use v2.4 (commit f56d744, May 2025) or later. It fixed a potential heap buffer overflow on small images and added dimension checks (1 to 65535 per side, 1 GB of RGBA at most). The repository history was rewritten in January 2025 ('fresh initial commit'; tag v2.2 deleted, issue #14).
- msf_gif_begin checks only the lzw, frame and header allocations for failure. A failed 64 KB tlb or used allocation is not caught, despite the header's promise that allocation failures come back as return values (found by reading the v2.4 source).
- BGRA input and 1-bit transparency are switched on through the globals msf_gif_bgra_flag and msf_gif_alpha_threshold, not per handle. Set them before msf_gif_frame and do not change them while another thread is encoding.
- The in-memory API holds the whole GIF until msf_gif_end and then copies it into one buffer, so peak memory is about twice the output size. msf_gif_*_to_file avoids this.

**Status:** Small and dual MIT / public-domain licensed, so it is easy to vendor. The last commit was 2025-09-10 (a compiler-compatibility PR), issues #8 and #11 are open with no maintainer reply, and the README still says 'actively maintained'; treat it as stable but slow-moving.

[repo](https://github.com/notnullnotvoid/msf_gif) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/notnullnotvoid/msf_gif-testing/HEAD/timings.txt)

##### mtpng (parallel PNG encoder with C API)  `Rust (C API)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Multithreaded Rust PNG encoder with a C API; chunked zlib deflate gives libpng-like file sizes, several times faster on many cores.

**Beats:** libpng — The author re-encoded one 7680x2160 RGBA screenshot (samples/dual4k.png, 1.69 MB) with mtpngenc --repeat=10, keeping the fastest run. In 2018 on a 2015 MacBook Pro (Linux), one thread took 555 ms against 850 ms for libpng built with gcc (1.53x), and 4 threads took 248 ms (3.4x vs single-threaded libpng). On a Xeon E5520, 8 threads took 165 ms against libpng's 1695 ms. The libpng timings have no published harness, version or zlib build ('@fixme how did I measure those libpng times?'), no output sizes are reported for either side, and the 2026 reruns time mtpng only. Code read this session shows a like-for-like zlib configuration (level 6, Z_FILTERED, 32 KiB window), but mtpng skips None-filter scoring and the timed 2018 builds predate the 0.3.5 heuristic change. No correctness bug affects the timed image: its 30,720-byte rows are far below the 256 KiB chunk size involved in issue #30.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust core with a C API (language-filter mismatch). Single-thread 1.53x/1.51x vs libpng with gcc, slower on armhf (0.88x); multi-thread rows (up to 10.9x derived) run against single-thread libpng. The libpng harness is unknown (@fixme in the repo) and the filter heuristics differ (mtpng skips the None filter, libpng 1.6 scores it; mtpng's heuristic changed in 0.3.5 in 2021, after the 2018 timings). Repo moved to bvibber/mtpng.

**Known shortcoming:** The libpng side of the harness is missing and the 2026 reruns time mtpng only; no output sizes are published although the adaptive filter skips None (zlib config matches libpng: level 6, Z_FILTERED, 32 KiB window). Speed depends on the linked zlib (open PR #29 moves to zlib-rs: 128 ms to 55 ms). crates.io 0.4.1 (2024-04-26) predates the fix for issue #30 ('Incomplete image input' on rows wider than a chunk, PR #31); building from the repo needs Rust 1.88+ (edition 2024, if-let chains). The C API has no streaming toggle and reports OK or ERR only.

**How:** The pigz scheme applied to PNG. Rows are grouped into chunks of at least 256 KiB. Each chunk is filtered on its own thread, then deflated by stock zlib (through libz-sys) as an independent stream: a raw stream after the first chunk, primed with the previous chunk's last 32 KiB of filtered bytes through deflateSetDictionary, ended with Z_SYNC_FLUSH so the pieces concatenate into one valid IDAT stream. The Adler-32 values are merged with adler32_combine. Filtering runs all four predictive filters (Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) over each whole row and keeps the one with the smallest sum of absolute signed bytes. The loops are plain iterator code compiled several times under target_feature (AVX2, AVX, SSE4.2, SSE4.1) and picked at run time, so LLVM auto-vectorises them. That is where the single-thread gain over libpng comes from; deflate itself is the same zlib.

**Use it when:**
- Saving large images (screenshots, renders, frames of tens of megapixels) on a multi-core machine where PNG encode latency matters and output should stay close to libpng's default size (zlib level 6, adaptive filters, Z_FILTERED strategy).
- Many-core boxes: the author's 2026 runs on the 7680x2160 RGBA screenshot take 23 ms on 16 threads (Apple M3 Max) and 25 ms on 32 threads (Ryzen 9 5950X), against 237 ms and 301 ms on one thread.
- Rust or C/C++ programs that need palette, greyscale, 1/2/4-bit or 16-bit output, which fpng (24/32bpp only) does not cover.
- Streaming a big PNG to a socket or file as it is produced: Rust Options::set_streaming emits one IDAT per chunk so bytes leave before the image is finished (not exposed in the C API).

**Skip it when:**
- Small images: below 128 KiB of uncompressed data there is no threading gain (README), and the project says small-file support 'needs work'.
- Raw single-core speed: one-thread mtpng on the dual-4K screenshot runs at about 30 Mpx/s on a 2015 i7 and 55 Mpx/s on a Ryzen 9 5950X (derived from page data). fpnge and fpng are far faster per core if larger files are acceptable.
- 32-bit ARM single-threaded: on a Raspberry Pi 3B+ under armhf, mtpng took 6068 ms against libpng's 5368 ms.
- Projects that need a stable API or a current crates.io release: both APIs are documented as unstable before 1.0, and crates.io's latest is 0.4.1 (2024-04-26). That release predates the February 2026 fix (PR #31, issue #30) for rows wider than the chunk size, which failed with 'Incomplete image input'.
- Decoding, Adam7 interlacing, or writing gamma, ICC or text metadata without hand-building chunks.

**Integration:** crate (rlib), plus cdylib/staticlib with the C header c/mtpng.h when built with the 'capi' feature · rayon, crc, itertools, libz-sys (system zlib, or builds C zlib where none ships, e.g. Windows); libc for the C API; png, clap and time only for the mtpngenc CLI · Rust 1.88 or newer for the repo's 0.5.0 (edition 2024, and encoder.rs uses an if-let chain; Cargo.toml declares no rust-version); the C header needs a C99 compiler (stdint.h, stdbool.h) · any Rust target with zlib; README lists Linux x86/x86-64/arm/arm64, macOS x86-64, iOS arm64, Windows x86/x86-64/arm64; runtime-dispatched x86 SIMD paths, scalar elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick mtpng over fpng or fpnge when you need libpng-like compression ratios or non-RGB formats (palette, greyscale, 16-bit), and over pngenc when you want a Rust crate or a maintained C API that reuses stock zlib. If single-core speed matters more than file size, fpnge (about 57x libpng encode in the QOIR benchmark, about 15% larger files) wins outright.

**Gotchas:**
- Adaptive filtering never scores the None filter (libpng's default PNG_ALL_FILTERS does), so screenshot-style truecolor images, where None often wins, can come out larger. The README says the heuristic 'fails to correctly predict good performance of the none filter'. Palette images are forced to None.
- Speed depends on which zlib libz-sys links. Open PR #29 (zlib-rs backend) reports 128 ms down to 55 ms on one image, and open PR #17 adds zlib-ng, so the C zlib in use matters as much as the threading.
- Without streaming mode the whole compressed IDAT is buffered in memory and written at finish(); the C API offers no streaming toggle.
- The C API returns only OK or ERR, with no message. The Rust code still has internal panics (chunk bookkeeping), and a panic in a rayon::spawn job or across the extern "C" boundary aborts the process.

**Status:** Active again in 2026 (last commit 2026-06-08: edition 2024, clippy cleanup, C-API build rework; chunk-row fix merged in February), MIT-licensed, 228 stars, about 95k crates.io downloads and 3 reverse dependencies. crates.io still ships 0.4.1 from 2024, and the README's CLI example link still points to src/bin/mtpng.rs, which was renamed to mtpngenc.rs.

[repo](https://github.com/bvibber/mtpng) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bvibber/mtpng/HEAD/docs/perf.md)

##### nativewebp  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go lossless WebP (VP8L) encoder; README shows it 1.2-2.3x faster than Go's image/png at BestCompression with 14-26% smaller files.

**Beats:** Go standard library image/png encoder at png.BestCompression — A first-party 'quick benchmark' in the README encodes five images from Google's WebP lossless-and-alpha gallery with nativewebp.BestCompression vs Go's image/png at png.BestCompression: 1.21-2.31x less time per image (412.2 ms vs 222.5 ms in total, 1.85x) and 80.5% of the PNG bytes in total, derived from page data. No benchmark code (no Benchmark functions), Go version or CPU is published, the comparison is across formats (VP8L vs PNG/flate-9) rather than two encoders of one format, and a third-party report from March 2026 (issue #18) found the encoder slower than png.BestCompression on its images.

**Known shortcoming:** Different format from the baseline: lossless WebP (VP8L) against Go image/png at BestCompression (DEFLATE level 9), so the 1.85x total (1.21-2.31x per image, derived from page data) and the 80.5% output size compare different codecs. No Benchmark functions in the repo, no Go version or CPU, no comparison against libwebp.

**Known shortcoming:** A third-party run in issue #18 (i5-13600KF, Go 1.26.1, 2026-03-30) puts the default encoder at 400 ms against 150 ms for png.BestCompression on a large image (9 vs 7 ms small), predating the May 2026 README revision. CompressionLevel only changes the predictor tile size, and default and BestCompression give identical output for images of about 204x204 to 816x816 px, so the README's 'both at max compression' is probably the default. Latent bug by code reading: the 15-bit Huffman limit is a weight-floor heuristic, and Fibonacci-shaped histograms yield 16-18-bit codes that would be written as repeat symbols and corrupt the stream (not seen on real images); Encode ignores w.Write errors; never compared with libwebp.

**How:** It is a deliberately simple VP8L encoder: subtract-green, then a predictor transform that picks one of the 14 VP8L predictors per tile by a Gini-style histogram score, then pixel-granular LZ77 (3-pixel hash, chain depth 128, matches up to 4,096 pixels, VP8L 2-D distance codes) with an 11-bit colour cache, entropy-coded with one set of five Huffman codes for the whole image. Working on 32-bit pixels instead of bytes, with no meta-Huffman image and no cross-colour transform (it is hard-coded off), keeps the work per pixel low compared with Go's compress/flate at level 9 behind png.BestCompression. Paletted inputs (*image.Paletted) take the colour-indexing transform with pixel bundling instead.

**Use it when:**
- Go services that must stay CGO_ENABLED=0 and want lossless WebP output (thumbnails, UI assets, screenshots, LED-matrix frames) without linking libwebp.
- Replacing image/png at png.BestCompression when WebP is an acceptable output format and smaller lossless files matter; the README's five gallery images came out 14-26% smaller.
- Lossless animated WebP from Go (EncodeAll), where image/gif's 256-colour limit is the alternative.
- Small to mid-size images; the published numbers are all on Google's lossless-and-alpha gallery images.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need lossy WebP, or the best lossless ratio: there is no lossy mode, no meta-Huffman codes and no cross-colour transform, and nothing in the repo compares it with libwebp (cwebp -lossless) on speed or size.
- When the alternative is image/png at its default level or BestSpeed: only png.BestCompression (flate level 9) was compared, and a third-party report (issue #18, i5-13600KF, Go 1.26.1, March 2026, before the May 2026 revision) measured the default encoder at 400 ms vs 150 ms for png.BestCompression on a large image and 9 vs 7 ms on a small one.
- Images above 16,384 pixels on either side: Encode returns 'invalid image size'.
- Large batches needing parallel encode inside one image: the encoder is single-goroutine and allocates several full-image buffers (an NRGBA copy, a pixel slice, a deltas slice and an int slice of 4 entries per pixel).

**Integration:** module · golang.org/x/image v0.24.0 (decoder only); no cgo · Go 1.22.2 (go.mod) · any Go target (pure Go, no assembly)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when the output must be WebP from a cgo-free Go build; no other catalogued image-codecs entry is a Go WebP encoder. If PNG output is fine and native code is acceptable, fpnge and fpng (C/C++) encode PNG one to two orders of magnitude faster than libpng, and libjxl's fast_lossless or QOI give much faster lossless encodes in other formats.

**Gotchas:**
- CompressionLevel only changes the predictor tile size (transBits); the LZ77 search, colour cache and Huffman coding are identical at every level. From getHistoBits/getTransformBits, Default and BestCompression produce the same tile size, and so the same output, for images between about 204x204 and 816x816 pixels, so 'both at maximum compression' in the README may mean the default encoder for its gallery images (their sizes are not stated).
- Encode and EncodeAll ignore errors from w.Write and return nil on a failed write, despite the doc comment; internal failures surface as panics rather than errors (bitWriter.writeBits panics on overflow; issues #3, #15 and #16 were encoder panics, all closed).
- The 15-bit Huffman depth limit is a weight floor (counts raised to total>>13), not a guaranteed length-limiting algorithm: a simulation of the same rule gives 16-18-bit codes for Fibonacci-shaped histograms of 17-19 symbols, which the writer would emit as code-length symbols 16-18 (repeat codes) and corrupt the stream. Derived from the code; not observed on a real image.
- Tests compare against stored golden bytes and round-trip only through golang.org/x/image/webp; nothing checks output against libwebp's decoder.

**Status:** Maintained by one author (MIT, 462 stars; last commits 2026-05-10 added compression levels, the revised README numbers and a 256 MiB decode read limit); feature request #17 is open and issue #18's resolution is not visible on the page, but the code is small (about 1,350 lines of non-test Go) and easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/HugoSmits86/nativewebp) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HugoSmits86/nativewebp/HEAD/README.md)

##### opencodecs  `Python (Cython and C/C++ extensions)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Python imaging-codec package over libdeflate, libspng, libjpeg-turbo, OpenJPEG and libjxl, with its own TIFF LZW decoder about 2x faster than imagecodecs'.
