**Beats:** none in the README; the only comparison found is against NVIDIA nvJPEG in two user issues (not libjpeg-turbo) — Only absolute first-party times exist: gpujpegtool -n 100 on a 16K DCI frame scaled to HD-16K at quality 75, encode 4K 1.65 ms (RTX 4080) and 1.71 ms (RTX 3080), decode 4K 1.46 ms (RTX 4080), including PCIe copies and excluding the first iteration, with CUDA, driver and host CPU unstated and some rows built without Release flags; there is no CPU or nvJPEG baseline, hence tier D. One table cell looks wrong: RTX 2080 Ti decode is 1.02 ms at HD and 1.07 ms at 4K (four times the pixels) but 11.29 ms at 8K, and that 4K cell beats the RTX 4080's 1.46 ms.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: README numbers are GPU timings with no CPU or nvJPEG baseline on the page; issues #47 and #48 (same post) report a mixed result against nvJPEG (1.8x faster and 1.4x slower) with no GPU named; the FGCS 2013 paper is blocked here.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e103, 2026-10-04): still no CPU (libjpeg-turbo) or nvJPEG baseline, so D stands. README timing table has an inconsistent cell (RTX 2080 Ti 4K decode 1.07 ms vs HD 1.02 ms and 8K 11.29 ms, and faster than the RTX 4080's 1.46 ms), likely a typo. Benchmark input sits in cudaMallocHost pinned memory, so pageable user buffers transfer slower than shown. License caveat: src/gpujpeg_dct_gpu.cu carries a 1993-2010 NVIDIA EULA header ('strictly prohibited' outside the EULA), so the tree is not cleanly BSD-2-Clause. Open bug #108: wrong colors when a decoder instance is reused.

**Independent measurement:** first-party GPU timings only

**How:** Every stage except stream parsing and formatting runs on the GPU: color conversion, a fixed-point 8x8 forward/inverse DCT with quantization (the DCT file carries NVIDIA CUDA SDK sample code), and Huffman coding. Restart markers split the bitstream into thousands of independent segments: the library default is 8 MCUs, and gpujpegtool asks for RESTART_AUTO, which picks 4 to 12 MCUs by megapixel count, times the component count for non-interleaved streams (the README's 24-36); gpujpeg_huffman_encoder_encode_kernel_warp codes one segment per warp, using __ballot_sync bitmaps of nonzero coefficients and constant-memory codeword LUTs with in-kernel byte stuffing. The decoder parses segment offsets on the CPU (faster when the encoder wrote its APP13 segment-info header) and decodes segments in parallel with a 10-bit quick lookup table plus a JPEG-spec slow path.

**Use it when:**
- Real-time capture or streaming pipelines that encode many equal-sized HD to 16K frames per second on an NVIDIA GPU (README: about 1.7 ms per 4K frame and 6.2-6.3 ms per 8K frame on RTX 3080/4080 including PCIe copies).
- Frames already in CUDA or OpenGL memory, where skipping host transfers matters (8K q70 encode 2.28 ms without PCIe copies vs 6.21 ms with them on RTX 3080).
- Closed systems where GPUJPEG both writes and reads the JPEGs, so the restart markers and segment-info header that enable GPU Huffman decoding are always present (the UltraGrid-style use case).
- Batch tools that can keep one encoder or decoder alive across images to amortize the 28.6 ms (8K) to 87.1 ms (16K) first-frame initialization measured on RTX 3080.

**Skip it when:**
- Decoding arbitrary camera or web JPEGs: progressive and arithmetic-coded files are unsupported, and files without restart markers fall back to the CPU Huffman decoder (the FAQ shows a 600 ms foreign-JPEG decode dominated by a 543 ms stream reader).
- Choosing it as 'faster than libjpeg-turbo' or 'faster than nvJPEG' on the catalog's evidence: no such comparison exists in the repo, and the only cross-codec numbers (2020 issues #47/#48) are mixed (1.8x faster on a noise texture, 1.4x slower on a portrait) with unknown GPU and method.
- Single small images or one-shot command-line conversions: initialization and PCIe transfers dominate, and the README timings exclude the first iteration.
- Machines without an NVIDIA GPU (AMD only through ZLUDA), or very large images on small GPUs: about 20 bytes of GPU memory per pixel per component (1901 MiB for 8K 4:4:4).
- Needs beyond baseline 8-bit: no 12-bit (issue #13 open since 2018), no progressive, no lossless JPEG.

**Integration:** shared lib (static via BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF) · CUDA toolkit and runtime (cudart); optional OpenGL/GLEW/GLFW/GLUT for texture interop; optional fpnge (C++, SSE4.1) for PNG output in the tool · CMake 3.10 (3.18 for CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES), C compiler plus nvcc; GPU compute capability 2.0 or newer per README · Linux and Windows (MSW tool support since 2020) with an NVIDIA CUDA GPU; AMD Radeon via ZLUDA; host CPU architectures and macOS not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libjpeg-turbo, jpeg-nitro or zenjpeg when you control both ends and have an NVIDIA GPU with frames in GPU memory and need millisecond 4K/8K encode; pick oss-nvjpg only on Tegra/Switch hardware decoders, and look at the Weissenberger-Schmidt GPU decoder (catalogued as a paper) when you must decode JPEGs that lack restart markers, which GPUJPEG cannot parallelize.

**Gotchas:**
- License: COPYING is BSD-2-Clause, but src/gpujpeg_dct_gpu.cu carries a 'Copyright 1993-2010 NVIDIA Corporation' header that refers to the NVIDIA end-user license agreement and says use outside that EULA 'is strictly prohibited'; check this before vendoring.
- Encoder defaults favour speed over compatibility: non-interleaved scans, restart markers, and SPIFF or Adobe headers when the internal color space is not full-range BT.601 (some third-party decoders ignore SPIFF color information).
- The README timings feed the encoder from cudaMallocHost pinned memory (gpujpeg_image_load_from_file); pageable user buffers will make the PCIe part slower. Reported numbers are gpujpegtool's 'Avg w/o 1st Iter' wall time from encode start to formatted stream, which includes host-device copies and CPU stream formatting.
- Open decoder bugs as of 2026-10-04: issue #108 (bug label, open) reports wrong colors on the second image when one decoder instance is reused; issue #107 (rows of odd-width images misaligned for OpenCV, width_padding always 0) got only an alignment option, GPUJPEG_DEC_OPT_ALIGNMENT_BYTES_INT, in 0.27.13.

**Status:** Actively maintained by CESNET (release 0.27.13 in March 2026, commits into October 2026) and BSD-2-Clause apart from the NVIDIA-EULA header on the DCT file; usable as a library today, but its speed advantage over CPU or nvJPEG codecs is unmeasured.

[repo](https://github.com/CESNET/GPUJPEG) · [benchmark](https://github.com/CESNET/GPUJPEG)

##### jpeg-encoder  `Rust`  `(MIT OR Apache-2.0) AND IJG`  `active`  `Tier D`

Pure-Rust baseline/progressive JPEG encoder with optional AVX2 DCT and color conversion; informally about 2x the image crate's encoder on x86.

**Beats:** image crate JPEG encoder (informal); libjpeg-turbo and mozjpeg not compared — No measured speedup exists: the only comparison is issue #35, where a user said that inside their own app the crate is 'like twice as fast as image' on an unnamed x86 CPU and slower than the image crate at higher qualities on a Raspberry Pi 5, with no harness, flags or figures. The repo's criterion benches compare its scalar and AVX2 paths only (PR #22 reported 0.1-4.5% end-to-end gains on Zen 4 from AVX2 color-conversion changes), so the D tier stands.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the only comparison is issue #35's informal in-app test ('like twice as fast' as the image crate on x86, slower at higher qualities on a Raspberry Pi 5 A76) with no harness, CPU or flags; the criterion benches time only its own code; the simd feature is AVX2-only. Widely used (8.0M crates.io downloads, 83 reverse dependencies including zune-image and kornia-io).

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e124, 2026-10-05): D stands, no numbers. crates.io 0.7.1 has no NEON; the wide-crate DCT for ARM, WASM and SSE2 (PR #25, feature flag use_wide, not in the README) exists only on the unreleased 0.8.0 HEAD (MSRV 1.89). Progressive mode does spectral selection only; width and height are capped at u16; the optimised-Huffman and progressive paths buffer the whole image. criterion/benches/fdct.rs has not been touched since 2024-10 and still passes [i16; 64] to fdct(&mut AlignedBlock), which has been crate-private since PR #28, so the bench no longer builds (code read, not built).

**Independent measurement:** none

**How:** The forward DCT is a Rust port of the libjpeg/mozjpeg jpeg_fdct_islow integer DCT (Loeffler-Ligtenberg-Moschytz, 12 multiplies, 13-bit fixed point), and with the 'simd' feature a port of libjpeg-turbo's jfdctint-avx2.asm plus an AVX2 RGB/BGR(A) to YCbCr converter, both chosen at run time with is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2"). Coefficient blocks are 32-byte aligned (PR #28) so loads vectorize, and the default interleaved baseline path streams one MCU row at a time instead of buffering the image. At HEAD only, an unreleased 'use_wide' feature (PR #25) computes the DCT with the portable wide crate (SSE2, NEON, WASM SIMD); its author reported about 50% faster DCT on SSE2 and about 20% slower than the hand-written AVX2 path.

**Use it when:**
- You need a JPEG encoder in pure Rust (no C toolchain, no libjpeg-turbo/mozjpeg linking), including no_std + alloc targets.
- x86-64 servers or desktops with AVX2, where the 'simd' feature enables the AVX2 DCT and color conversion and the issue #35 reporter saw roughly twice the image crate's encode speed.
- Default build must contain no unsafe code: without 'simd' the crate is #![forbid(unsafe_code)].
- You need CMYK/YCCK output, ICC or EXIF embedding, restart markers or custom quantization tables, which the image crate's encoder does not all expose.
- Streaming encode of large baseline images: the interleaved path keeps only one MCU row of samples in memory.

**Skip it when:**
- ARM (Raspberry Pi 5, Apple silicon, Graviton) with the released crate: 0.7.1 has no NEON path at all, and issue #35 (open) reports it slower than the image crate's encoder at higher qualities on a Cortex-A76; the wide-based DCT is only on unreleased HEAD and does not cover color conversion.
- You want smallest files at a given quality: no trellis quantization, and progressive mode does only spectral selection (no successive approximation), so mozjpeg-rs, mozjpeg or zenjpeg/jpegli produce smaller output.
- You need a published speed claim to rely on: there is no benchmark against libjpeg-turbo, mozjpeg or the image crate anywhere in the repo; the only outside comparison is one informal issue comment with no figures.
- Images wider or taller than 65,535 pixels (width and height are u16), or input with 12-bit samples (extended JPEG is open request #32).
- Multi-core throughput on a single image: encoding is single-threaded with no rayon option, unlike zenjpeg's rayon-based parallel feature.

**Integration:** crate · none by default; optional wide 1.0 + bytemuck 1.24 for the HEAD-only 'use_wide' feature; jpeg-decoder 0.3 as a dev-dependency for tests · Rust 1.87 for crates.io 0.7.1 (edition 2024); Rust 1.89 at HEAD (0.8.0) · any (scalar, no_std + alloc); AVX2 acceleration on x86/x86-64 with the 'simd' feature (runtime-detected, scalar fallback); wide-crate DCT for SSE2/NEON/WASM only on unreleased HEAD

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over jpeg-rusturbo when you need progressive mode, 4:4:4/4:2:2 and other sampling factors, CMYK or no_std, since jpeg-rusturbo's measured 5x win over the image crate covers only its 4:2:0 path; pick mozjpeg-rs or zenjpeg instead when file size per quality matters more than encode speed, and libjpeg-turbo when a C dependency is acceptable and you need fast encoding on ARM too.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'simd' feature only accelerates x86 AVX2; on other CPUs, or x86 without AVX2, it silently runs the scalar code, and it switches off the forbid(unsafe_code) guarantee.
- use_wide (portable SIMD DCT for ARM64/WASM/SSE2) is merged on main but missing from crates.io 0.7.1, which was published from the commit just before PR #25 merged; the README does not document it either.
- Turning on optimized Huffman tables, progressive mode or a sampling factor that cannot be interleaved switches to a path that buffers every component plane plus every quantized 8x8 block (roughly 3 bytes of samples plus 6 bytes of coefficients per pixel for RGB) before writing anything.
- The repo's criterion/benches/fdct.rs was last changed in October 2024 and still passes a [i16; 64] to fdct(), which PR #28 changed to take the crate-private AlignedBlock; reading the source, that bench no longer compiles at HEAD (not built here). The encode and ycbcr benches only time jpeg-encoder against itself.
- The forward-DCT code is IJG-licensed: binary distributions must state they are based in part on the work of the Independent JPEG Group (LICENSE-IJG, added July 2026).

**Status:** Actively maintained (several PRs merged 2026-07-27, crates.io 0.7.1 the same day, 8.0M downloads and 83 reverse dependencies); dual MIT/Apache-2.0 plus IJG for the DCT, small, dependency-free and easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/vstroebel/jpeg-encoder) · [benchmark](https://github.com/vstroebel/jpeg-encoder/issues/35)

##### jpegli  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier D`

Google's libjpeg62-compatible JPEG encoder/decoder tuned for quality per byte; not faster than libjpeg-turbo, and slower at decode.

**Beats:** libjpeg-turbo — The repository publishes no speed numbers, and its benchmark doc is a leftover libjxl text about density metrics. The only measured numbers are third-party: oximg issue #61 (Zen 4, 512 px, q80, single-thread encode time on 1 logical CPU) kept libjpeg-turbo as its decoder because jpegli decoded 1.6-2.0x slower. It timed jpegli encodes at 1812-1912 us (jpegli-sys 0.10.2, progressive 4:4:4, AQ on), 960-976 us (baseline 4:4:4, AQ off), 615-630 us (baseline 4:2:0, AQ off) and 534-546 us (upstream 031a0077 with clang, baseline 4:2:0, AQ off), against mozjpeg trellis at 10316 us, with no libjpeg-turbo encode timing. A search snippet attributed to a libjpeg-turbo-users thread ('Jpegli', groups.google.com blocked here) says libjpeg-turbo was 2-8x faster than jpegli at baseline compression; this is unverified.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the repo publishes no speed numbers although tools/benchmark/benchmark_codec_jpeg.cc can time jpegli against libjpeg; the third-party oximg issue #61 puts jpegli decode 1.6-2.0x slower than libjpeg-turbo and gives only a mozjpeg trellis encode comparison (10316 us against 1812-1912 us) with no libjpeg-turbo encode timing; Google's blog says speed is comparable (snippet only).

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e106, 2026-10-05): no first-party speed numbers, D stands. The oximg issue #61 figures are single-thread encode times on 1 logical CPU; the record misses configuration N (jpegli 0.10.2 baseline 4:2:0 with adaptive quantization off, 615-630 us), and settings alone move encode time 2.9-3.1x on the same build; decode is 1.6-2.0x slower than libjpeg-turbo there with no methodology. A libjpeg-turbo-users thread (snippet only, groups.google.com blocked) says libjpeg-turbo is 2-8x faster at baseline encode. Harness traps in benchmark_codec_jpeg.cc: p0 means progressive (jpeg_simple_progression) for the libjpeg codec but sequential for enc-jpegli; the cjpeg/mozjpeg path times subprocess start plus file I/O; the Q option adds an extra libjpeg encode and distance search; defaults split (libjpeg API sequential fixed-Huffman since eca9351, cjpegli progressive 2 plus AQ plus 4:4:4). Compatibility: decoder accepts only SOF0/1/2 8-bit; no TurboJPEG API; libjpeg.so not built on Apple, Windows or Emscripten; output not bit-exact; issue #248 rejects empty DHT files; no releases (#44). Open unreviewed PRs fix library out-of-bounds accesses (#242 crop_scanline OOB read, #241 add_quant_table off-by-one OOB write).

**Independent measurement:** third-party issue figures (oximg #61)

**How:** It is not built for speed: the design spends extra work on quality. The encoder does color conversion, subsampling and DCT in float (Highway SIMD, kernels capped at 8 float lanes) and adds adaptive dead-zone quantization driven by a masking field (fuzzy erosion over a pre-erosion image). The decoder gathers per-coefficient nonzero and abs-sum statistics and applies Price-Rabbani Laplacian dequantization biases, then runs float IDCT, upsampling and color conversion. Speed comes only from Highway runtime dispatch (SSE2 to AVX-512, NEON, SVE, RVV, WASM) and a streaming single-pass path for sequential fixed-Huffman encodes.

**Use it when:**
- New web or archive JPEGs where bytes at a given visual quality matter more than encode CPU, and the output must stay plain JPEG for every decoder.
- Linux services already linked against libjpeg62 that want jpegli's quality by swapping libjpeg.so.62 without code changes (libjpeg API only, not TurboJPEG).
- Replacing mozjpeg trellis encodes on a CPU budget: oximg issue #61 timed jpegli at 534-1912 us against mozjpeg trellis at 10316 us per 512 px q80 encode, about 5.4x to 19x faster depending on jpegli settings (derived from page data).
- Pipelines that need 16-bit or float input to the encoder or 16-bit/float output from the decoder, or XYB-ICC JPEGs.

**Skip it when:**
- Decode-throughput-bound workloads (thumbnailing, ML data loading): the only third-party number (oximg #61) puts jpegli decode 1.6-2.0x slower than libjpeg-turbo, with no methodology shown.
- Encode-throughput-bound workloads that are fine with libjpeg-turbo quality: no source shows jpegli encoding faster than libjpeg-turbo, and its default tool settings (progressive level 2, optimized Huffman, adaptive quantization, 4:4:4) do the most work.
- Code that uses the TurboJPEG API (tj*), arithmetic-coded, 12-bit, lossless or hierarchical JPEGs: the decoder accepts only SOF0/SOF1/SOF2 at 8-bit precision and the encoder errors on arithmetic coding and CCIR601 sampling.
- Ingesting messy real-world files: issue #248 (open) reports djpegli rejecting progressive JPEGs with empty DHT segments ('DHT marker: no Huffman table found'), including 276 WhatsApp images from FODB that libjpeg-turbo-based decoders accept.
- Projects that need versioned releases or a drop-in shared library on macOS or Windows: there are no tags or releases (issue #44 unanswered), and lib/jpegli.cmake builds libjpeg.so only when not APPLE, WIN32 or EMSCRIPTEN.

**Integration:** static lib (jpegli-static, jpegli_* API) plus shared lib (libjpeg.so.62.3.0 drop-in on non-Apple, non-Windows targets) and CLI tools · Highway (third_party submodule or system libhwy), threads; libjpeg-turbo headers vendored for jpeglib.h/jmorecfg.h; tools add lcms2 or skcms, libpng, optional giflib, OpenEXR, sjpeg; tests need gtest and a system libjpeg · CMake 3.16+; C++17 when the compiler offers it (CMake falls back to C++14 or C++11); build breakages reported on macOS Sonoma (#55) and Fedora 42 (#133) · any Highway target with runtime dispatch: x86-64 SSE2 to AVX-512, aarch64 NEON/SVE, PPC8-10, RVV, s390x Z14/Z15, WASM, scalar fallback

**Vs siblings:** Pick jpegli over libjpeg-turbo only when smaller files at equal perceived quality matter more than CPU; keep libjpeg-turbo (or jpeg-nitro and zenjpeg for decode) when speed is the goal. Pick it over mozjpeg when you want a density-focused encoder at a fraction of trellis cost (oximg #61: 534-1912 us vs 10316 us), accepting that the density comparison rests on Google's own study ('Users prefer Jpegli over same-sized libjpeg-turbo or MozJPEG', not opened here).

**Gotchas:**
- Defaults depend on the entry point: through the libjpeg API, jpeg_set_defaults gives sequential mode with fixed Huffman codes (kDefaultProgressiveLevel = 0 since commit eca9351, April 2023), which takes the streaming single-pass path; cjpegli and the extras EncodeJpeg API default to progressive level 2, optimized codes, adaptive quantization and no chroma subsampling, which buffer the whole image's coefficients and tokens. In oximg #61, settings alone on the same jpegli-sys 0.10.2 build move encode time 2.9-3.1x (progressive 4:4:4 AQ on 1812-1912 us vs baseline 4:2:0 AQ off 615-630 us, derived from page data).
- Decoded pixels are not bit-exact with libjpeg-turbo: dequantization biases are computed from running statistics of the image's own coefficients and the pipeline is float, so golden-image tests written against libjpeg-turbo will fail.
- The in-repo harness (tools/benchmark/benchmark_codec_jpeg.cc) has comparison traps: the pN parameter means jpeg_simple_progression for the libjpeg codec at p0 but sequential mode for enc-jpegli at p0; the cjpeg/mozjpeg path times a subprocess including process start and file I/O while jpegli is timed in process; and the Q (libjpeg_quality) option times an extra libjpeg encode plus a distance search inside the jpegli measurement.
- Open, unreviewed PRs fix out-of-bounds bugs reachable through the library API with bad caller arguments: #242 (jpegli_crop_scanline 32-bit overflow leading to an out-of-bounds read) and #241 (jpegli_add_quant_table accepts which_tbl == 4 and writes 64 coefficients through a bogus pointer).

**Status:** Active but thinly maintained: the last merged change is a Dependabot bump (2026-06-01, #236) while about ten bug-fix PRs from May-October 2026 sit unreviewed; BSD-3-Clause with a Google patent grant and no tagged release, so it is copyable but should be treated as a quality tool, not a speed win.

[repo](https://github.com/google/jpegli)

##### libqoi  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Small C++14 port of the QOI reference codec; a single informal user report says faster than qoixx, which the code does not support.

**Beats:** qoixx (wx257osn2/qoixx) — The only number is a third-party issue comment (2022-07-24): 'about 20% faster to encode and about 30% faster to decode' than qoixx on a 640x480 30 fps webcam stream inside ROS on an i7-10875H, with no harness, qoixx version, build type or flags. The same user's ROS PRs report QOI at 28%/13% CPU against PNG over 100% CPU (30 vs 3 fps), which is a property of the format. Read against the code, the qoixx claim is implausible: libqoi is a scalar qoi.h port with extra allocation and zero-fill work, while qoixx publishes 1.4-1.7x over qoi.h, so the gap more likely comes from how each library was wired into the ROS node than from the codec.

**Known shortcoming:** The only speed numbers are issue #1's informal 20% encode and 30% decode over qoixx on an i7-10875H with no harness; the ROS PRs #103 and #104 name libqoi (30 against 3 fps versus PNG, 28% against 13% CPU) but #103 closed unmerged and #104 is open. Abandoned since 2022-09.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e120, 2026-10-05): the repo's tests/benchmark.cpp is commented out of the build, uses a Fibonacci placeholder template and feeds dice.png (a PNG) to qoi::decode (parses as 218,765,834 x 13 x 73 channels, about 207.6 GB), so nothing was ever timed with it; the code is a scalar qoi.h port with a zero-filled worst-case buffer and a shrink_to_fit copy, so the issue #1 '20-30% faster than qoixx' remark is implausible (qoixx itself reports 1.4-1.7x over qoi.h). Retiered C to D (retier-36). Security: no run-length bound check in decode (heap overflow up to 61 pixels on crafted input), 1- or 2-channel overrun by 2 bytes, get_header out-of-bounds read under 14 bytes, 32-bit size math with no pixel cap, QOI_HEADER_ONLY apparently broken, fuzz target covers get_header only with ASAN off.

**Independent measurement:** informal third-party remark (issue #1)

**How:** There is no speed technique beyond QOI itself: it is a line-by-line scalar port of phoboslab's qoi.h (64-entry colour hash, run, diff, luma and literal ops). It adds overhead the reference avoids: encode zero-fills a worst-case (channels+1) bytes-per-pixel std::vector, then calls shrink_to_fit (a second allocation and copy), and both loops branch on the channel count for every pixel. Nothing in it compares with qoixx's AVX2/NEON/SVE encoder or table-driven decoder.

**Use it when:**
- Practically never over the alternatives: the reference qoi.h is equally simple, works from C++ and is maintained; qoixx is measurably faster.
- Only if you need a std::vector-based QOI API under C++14 (qoixx requires C++20) and will vendor and harden the two source files yourself.
- Trusted, in-process image data of normal size (well under about 859 million pixels), where malformed input cannot occur.

**Skip it when:**
- Decoding untrusted input (network streams, as in the ROS transport it was proposed for): decode() does not check run length against the output size, so a crafted run chunk writes up to 61 pixels past the heap buffer, and headers with 1 or 2 channels overrun it by up to 2 bytes.
- Anything speed-critical: no benchmark in the repository backs a speed claim, and qoixx's README shows qoixx 1.4-1.7x faster than qoi.h on the QOI benchmark suite, while this library is a slower-than-reference port of qoi.h.
- Huge images: width*height is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic with no pixel limit (qoi.h caps at 400 million pixels), so sizes wrap and the encode output buffer is undersized for RGBA images above about 859 million pixels.
- Projects that need a maintained dependency: README says work in progress with API breaks expected; 5 commits, last 2022-09-07.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake) or source-drop of include/qoi/qoi.hpp and src/qoi.cpp · none for the two library files; the CMake project requires Conan packages fmt 8.0.1, libpng 1.6.37, catch2 2.13.7 and stb at configure time for its tests · C++14 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14); CMake 3.4+ for the project build · any (portable scalar C++)

**Vs siblings:** Hard to justify: pick qoixx (C++20, SIMD encoder, published 1.4-1.7x over qoi.h) for speed, phoboslab/qoi (qoi.h) for portability, maintenance and input validation, or qoi-rust/rapid-qoi in Rust; libqoi only if C++14 plus a std::vector API is a hard requirement and inputs are trusted.

**Gotchas:**
- decode() does not call is_valid() and does not check the header: inputs shorter than 14 bytes are read out of bounds in get_header, and inputs shorter than 8 bytes make size() - 8 wrap and read past the buffer. Call is_valid() first, but it checks only the magic and the 8-byte end marker, not channels or dimensions.
- The QOI_HEADER_ONLY switch includes qoi.cpp inside namespace qoi, and qoi.cpp reopens namespace qoi and includes <iostream> there, so the header-only mode looks unusable as written (definitions land in qoi::qoi); compile src/qoi.cpp as a normal source (from code reading, not built).
- The only fuzz target (tests/qoi_fuzz.cpp) fuzzes get_header alone, accepting inputs from 4 bytes, and ASAN is off in Config.cmake; decode() has never been fuzzed.
- tests/benchmark.cpp, commented out of the build, is a Catch2 template (Fibonacci cases) whose only codec case passes dice.png, a PNG file, to qoi::decode; its PNG signature parses as width 218,765,834, height 13 and 73 channels, so it would request about 207.6 GB and throw. No working benchmark exists in the repo.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-09-07 (5 commits, README says work in progress); MIT and tiny enough to vendor, but the decoder needs bounds checks before it can be used on untrusted data.

[repo](https://github.com/ShadowMitia/libqoi) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ShadowMitia/libqoi/issues/1)

##### lodepng-turbo  `C++`  `Zlib`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

2019 lodepng hack with libdeflate inflate and SSE2 PNG unfiltering; claims 2x libpng decode, unmeasured, and HEAD has decode bugs.

**Beats:** libpng — Nothing was measured. The single README sentence, 'twice as fast as libpng' on x86/x86-64/ARM, has no CPU, compiler, libpng/zlib version, images or harness behind it, and nothing in the repository links libpng. The ARM part of the claim cannot have been measured on this tree, which has no ARM-capable unfilter.

**Known shortcoming:** README names libpng and says 'twice as fast' with no data; lodepng_benchmark.cpp is the stock lodepng benchmark and never links libpng. Output-correctness fixes of 2019-01-21/22 may postdate the claim. Fork of lvandeve/lodepng.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered C to D (retier-15): the only evidence is the README's 'twice as fast as libpng' with no measurement, and HEAD has correctness bugs by code reading: sub-8-bit grey and palette PNGs are never unfiltered after commit 61f9f24 (bytewidth = bpp/8, no case 0 in depng), Adam7 images with a dimension of 4 or less wrap the row loop out of bounds, the encoder passes a NULL output buffer to libdeflate_zlib_compress, two libdeflate objects leak per state, invalid filter bytes are not rejected. README MMX, AVX2, NEON and TurboPNG API claims match nothing in the tree (SSE2 only); the Linux Makefile hard-codes libdeflatestatic.lib.

**How:** Two swaps. IDAT data is inflated by libdeflate_zlib_decompress straight into a buffer sized from the IHDR prediction, replacing lodepng's bit-by-bit inflater. Then depng_filter_sse2 reverses Sub, Up, Avg and Paeth per row in place with 16-byte SSE2 vectors: Sub uses a log-step prefix sum (shift-and-PADDB), Up is a plain vector add, and Paeth is computed branch-free in 16-bit lanes with a divide-by-3 reciprocal trick, specialized by template for 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 bytes per pixel. Rows are then memcpy'd out of the filtered buffer. There is no MMX, AVX2 or NEON code in the build, despite the README.

**Use it when:**
- Only for experiments: a quick check of how much libdeflate plus SIMD unfiltering speeds up a lodepng-based tool on x86-64, with trusted, non-interlaced 8-bit or 16-bit-per-channel PNGs, where you compare the output pixel for pixel against stock lodepng first.
- As reading material on combining libdeflate with Kobalicek's depng SIMD reverse filter. For production, take the idea, not this code.

**Skip it when:**
- 1-, 2- or 4-bit greyscale or palette PNGs (icons, scans, many small UI assets). The final code commit (61f9f24, 2019-01-22) changed bytewidth to bpp/8, which is 0 for these formats, and depng_filter_sse2 has no case for 0. The rows are never unfiltered: output is all zeros, or still-filtered bytes when the row has padding bits (derived from reading lodepng-turbo.cpp and depng_sse2.cpp; not run).
- Adam7-interlaced PNGs with width or height of 4 pixels or less. These have an empty Adam7 pass, and depng's do { } while (--y != 0) loop called with h = 0 wraps to about 4 billion rows, with heap reads and writes far out of bounds. Original lodepng's for-loop handled h = 0 (derived from code reading).
- Untrusted input. An invalid filter-type byte (>4) is silently ignored instead of returning lodepng's error 36. The row pointer is then not advanced, so later rows are misaligned; if the first row is the bad one, the next 'previous row' pointer lands before the buffer start. Interlaced decoding also memcpys between overlapping regions of the same buffer.
- Encoding. With LODEPNG_TURBO_COMPILE, addChunk_IDAT passes a NULL output buffer to libdeflate_zlib_compress, which writes the zlib header through it. The wrapper also never sets *outsize and treats the returned byte count as an error enum, so lodepng_encode* should crash (derived from code reading, including libdeflate cb7ee82's zlib_compress.c).
- ARM, 32-bit x86 without -msse2, or any non-x86 target. depng_sse2.cpp (SSE2 intrinsics via emmintrin.h) is the only unfilter compiled, and it is called unconditionally, so the README's 'ARM' and 'NEON' claims do not hold for this tree.

**Integration:** static lib (liblodepngturbo.a plus libdeflate's static lib) or shared lib; git submodules libdeflate (cb7ee82) and kanryu/simdtests (1b8e25d) · libdeflate (2019 snapshot, submodule); kanryu/simdtests depng (public domain, submodule) · C++11 (-std=c++11), GCC or Clang with GNU make; MSVC only through the vstudio project linking a libdeflate built with MSYS2 g++ · x86-64 in practice (SSE2 intrinsics, no runtime dispatch); no NEON/AVX2/MMX code despite the README

**Vs siblings:** Practically never. libspng (third-party measured 1.02x-1.07x over libpng, maintained, fuzzed) and ptpng (1.80x geometric mean over libpng with zlib-ng on Linux x64, published harness) are faster-than-libpng decoders with evidence. image-png or Wuffs-based decoders cover the safe-decoder case, and fpng only wins on its own files.

**Gotchas:**
- Every lodepng_state_init (and so every lodepng_decode32/decode_memory call, which makes a temporary state) allocates a libdeflate decompressor and a level-6 libdeflate compressor, even for decode-only use. lodepng_state_cleanup frees neither, so each decode leaks both.
- The LodePNGState layout differs from stock lodepng: it adds an 'inspected' field and libdeflate pointers. After lodepng_inspect, decode skips re-reading the header and trusts the caller's w and h, so reusing a state for another file decodes it with the stale header unless you re-init the state.
- The default 'make' on Linux likely fails at the shared-library step. The Makefile hard-codes ./libdeflate/libdeflatestatic.lib, MinGW's name, while libdeflate's Makefile builds libdeflate.a on Linux. The static library target does not depend on it (derived from both Makefiles; not built).
- No turbo-specific tests exist. lodepng_unittest.cpp and lodepng_benchmark.cpp are upstream's files: the unit test uses the lodepng:: C++ API that the Makefile compiles out, and the benchmark needs SDL, round-trips through the broken encoder, and never links libpng.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-01-22 (35 commits over 11 days, 21 stars, 2 forks, no issues or releases). The zlib licence is copyable, but at HEAD sub-byte PNGs decode wrongly and small interlaced PNGs and encoding hit memory errors, so it needs fixes before any use.

[repo](https://github.com/kanryu/lodepng-turbo) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kanryu/lodepng-turbo/HEAD/README.md)

##### mozjpeg  `C`  `IJG AND BSD-3-Clause AND Zlib`  `stale`  `Tier D`

libjpeg-turbo fork that trades much slower JPEG encoding for smaller files; it is not faster than libjpeg-turbo at anything.

**Beats:** libjpeg-turbo — Nothing here measures a speed win. The project itself says it compresses considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo with default settings. Third-party figures agree but lack full methodology: the 2014-era sergejmueller gist has jpegtran -progressive about 2.3x slower; oximg issue #61 (Zen 4, 512 px, q80) has trellis at 10316 us per image. mozjpeg-rs's README (2048x2048, 30 iterations, AVX2, CPU not stated) shows C mozjpeg at 210 ms with trellis against 9 ms Huffman-optimized baseline. Search-result snippets, apparently from libjpeg-turbo.org/About/Mozjpeg (page blocked, not opened, source not certain), put jpgcrush plus trellis at about 4-7x the encoding time of plain progressive for 4-15% better compression.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster: tier D with the project's own README-mozilla.txt saying compression is considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo; a sergejmueller gist puts mozjpeg 2.0 jpegtran about 2.3x slower for 1.18% smaller files with no hardware. Stale (last commit 2025-06-23).

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e116, 2026-10-05): D stands, no speed win. The default profile runs 64 candidate scans (each a Huffman-optimisation pass plus output pass) plus two trellis passes per component; mozjpeg-rs's README puts C mozjpeg at 210 ms with trellis vs 9 ms baseline Huffman-opt for a 2048x2048 image (about 23x slower, CPU unstated). The TurboJPEG API forces JCP_FASTEST, so tj callers get plain libjpeg-turbo behaviour. Correctness bug in the default path: overshoot deringing plus the 16-bit wrapping SIMD islow FDCT overflows (8 x 5056 = 40448), flipping DC/low-AC signs and inverting 8x8 blocks (issue #444; fix PR #453 open, 2 of 639 test encodes changed); not behind any catalogued speed number. Latest tag v4.1.1 (libjpeg-turbo 2.1.3) while master carries an untagged 3.0.x merge; cjpeg PNG input broken (#450); libjpeg name clash with libjpeg-turbo (#382); jpegtran size regression (#433).

**Independent measurement:** none (slower by design)

**How:** It is not; the work goes into file size. For 3-component YCbCr, jpeg_search_progression() sets up 64 candidate scans (23 for grayscale). Each candidate gets a Huffman-statistics pass and an output pass into an in-memory buffer, and select_scans() then keeps the smallest combination (jpgcrush-style). That makes at least 128 entropy passes before trellis. Trellis quantization (quantize_trellis in jcdctmgr.c) is a scalar float rate-distortion search per 8x8 block, with lambda = 2^14.75 / ((2^16.5 + n) * q^2) by default. It runs 2 passes per component per trellis loop over the saved unquantized coefficients of the whole image. The speed it does have is libjpeg-turbo's: SIMD color conversion, downsampling, forward DCT and baseline Huffman.

**Use it when:**
- Offline or build-time compression of web images (static-site pipelines, CDN pre-processing, image optimizers), where encoding runs once and the smaller file is downloaded many times.
- Lossless recompression of existing JPEGs with jpegtran (progressive plus scan search), when you cannot re-encode from pixels.
- Programs already on the libjpeg API that want smaller output without code changes: relink and jpeg_set_defaults() turns on the max-compression profile.
- As the reference encoder when you evaluate size-for-quality JPEG encoders such as mozjpeg-rs, zenjpeg or jpegli, all of which benchmark against it.

**Skip it when:**
- Real-time or per-request encoding (thumbnail proxies, camera or video frames, screenshots). Its own README-mozilla.txt says it is considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo, and even than libjpeg, at default settings. In mozjpeg-rs's README, C mozjpeg needs 210 ms with trellis against 9 ms for Huffman-optimized baseline on a 2048x2048 image (about 23x, derived from page data; hardware not stated).
- As a speed upgrade for decoding: decoding is libjpeg-turbo's code. Its default progressive output also decodes slower than baseline in libjpeg-turbo: zenjpeg's README (Ryzen 9 7950X) lists 34 MiB/s for progressive against 78.1 MiB/s for baseline 4:2:0, possibly on different files.
- Memory-constrained encoding of large images: trellis keeps quantized and unquantized whole-image coefficient arrays (whole_image and whole_image_uq in jccoefct.c), and scan optimization buffers every candidate scan in memory.
- Processes or distro packages that also need stock libjpeg-turbo: both ship libjpeg/libturbojpeg with the same names and symbols. Issue #382, open since 2020, asks for a separately named libmozjpeg, and PR #383 has been open since then.
- Projects that track upstream security fixes through tagged releases: the latest tag is v4.1.1, built on libjpeg-turbo 2.1.3. The libjpeg-turbo 3.0.x merge on master (January 2025, CMake VERSION 5.0.0) is untagged.

**Integration:** static lib and shared lib (libjpeg API library plus TurboJPEG library), CMake build; cjpeg, djpeg and jpegtran tools · none for the library; NASM 2.13+ or Yasm 1.2.0+ for x86 SIMD; cjpeg PNG input needs libpng 1.6 and zlib (PNG_SUPPORTED defaults to TRUE; turn it off if libpng is absent) · C89-era C compiler (GCC 4.1+ or Clang recommended, Visual C++ 2005+), CMake 2.8.12+ · Same as libjpeg-turbo: x86, x86-64, Arm/aarch64 (Neon), PowerPC (AltiVec), MIPS (MMI) SIMD, plus a C fallback anywhere; Linux, macOS, Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick C mozjpeg over libjpeg-turbo only when file size matters more than encode time; over mozjpeg-rs when you need the C libjpeg ABI, jpegtran's lossless recompression or the fastest Huffman-only path (mozjpeg-rs's README has C at 9 ms vs Rust 42 ms for baseline); prefer mozjpeg-rs for memory-safe Rust or slightly faster trellis (197 vs 210 ms in its README), and look at jpegli or zenjpeg when you want better quality per byte at much lower encode cost.

**Gotchas:**
- Default output can be corrupted by a SIMD FDCT overflow, open as of 2026-10-05. Overshoot deringing (on by default) can push level-shifted samples to +/-158. The 16-bit wrapping adds in the SIMD islow forward DCT (SSE2, AVX2, MMX, Neon, MMI, AltiVec) then overflow (8 x 5056 = 40448), which flips the sign of DC/low-AC coefficients and leaves inverted-brightness 8x8 blocks (issue #444). PR #453 switches these to saturating adds and reports 2 of 639 test encodes changed. The C DCT path is not affected; -noovershoot avoids the bug.
- TurboJPEG API callers (tjCompress2/tj3Compress8, and tjbench) get libjpeg-turbo behavior, because turbojpeg.c sets JCP_FASTEST before jpeg_set_defaults(). To get mozjpeg's gains, use the libjpeg API or set the extension parameters yourself.
- jpeg_set_defaults() resets every mozjpeg parameter from JINT_COMPRESS_PROFILE. Set the profile first, then quality and the extensions. mozjpeg-rs's README warns that the Rust mozjpeg crate's setters silently undo earlier settings for the same reason.
- Output size is not monotonic across releases: issue #433 (open) shows jpegtran in 4.1.1 producing larger files than 3.1 on some inputs (402,438 vs 400,769 bytes on lab.jpg). PNG input in cjpeg is broken in the current CMake build (issue #450, fix PR #455 unmerged).

**Status:** Stale: the last commit is 2025-06-23 and the last tag is v4.1.1 (libjpeg-turbo 2.1.3), and six PRs sit unreviewed or in review, including the FDCT overflow fix. Licensed IJG, BSD-3-Clause and zlib, and safe to use as an offline size optimizer, but not a performance pick.

[repo](https://github.com/mozilla/mozjpeg)

##### PNGenc  `C (Arduino-style C++ class wrapper; can be built as C)`  `Apache-2.0 (src/ also vendors zlib 1.2.11 deflate.c, trees.c, crc32.c, adler32.c and zutil.c under the zlib license)`  `active`  `Tier D`

Line-by-line, no-malloc PNG encoder for microcontrollers; a low-RAM libpng substitute with no speed claim or measurement.

**Beats:** libpng — No speed claim and no measurement exist: the README's 'How fast is it?' only points to examples/PNGenc_Test, which times one generated 128x128 8-bpp indexed image at compression level 3 with micros(), by default including the SD-card open and writes, and prints a single time with no baseline. linux/main.cpp prints only the output size. Because the compressor is stock zlib 1.2.11 deflate driven row by row, with libpng-style adaptive filtering, it should not beat libpng on throughput, and the reduced MCU window (4 KB, memLevel 5) probably costs compression ratio (not measured).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: no numbers and no baseline; PNGenc_Test times one 128x128 image with micros() including SD-card writes and function_test checks sizes only. It vendors zlib 1.2.11's deflate, the same deflate libpng uses, so no speed edge is expected. Apache-2.0 plus the vendored zlib licence.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): no speed claim and no measurement exist; examples/PNGenc_Test times one generated 128x128 8-bpp indexed image at level 3 with micros(), including SD-card I/O by default, with no baseline, and linux/main.cpp prints only the output size. The compressor is stock zlib 1.2.11 deflate driven row by row with libpng-style adaptive filtering, so it should not beat libpng on throughput; the reduced MCU window (4 KB, memLevel 5) likely costs ratio. Bugs: the bpp argument is not checked against the pixel type (TRUECOLOR_ALPHA with bpp 8 writes malformed PNGs and the function test passes anyway); palettes read in B,G,R order (issue #19); addRGB565Line issues Z_PARTIAL_FLUSH after every row; issue history is mostly corrupt output (#2, #14, #16, #18), all closed without a decoding regression test. Tier D stands.

**Independent measurement:** none

**How:** It is not built for speed: compression is a vendored copy of zlib 1.2.11 deflate (the same codec libpng normally calls) fed from a static pool, so throughput should track libpng at the same level. Each row gets a per-line adaptive filter chosen by minimum sum of absolute differences across None/Sub/Up/Average/Paeth (libpng's classic heuristic); 1/2/4-bpp rows are left unfiltered. On MCUs the deflate window and hash memory are cut eightfold (windowBits 12, memLevel 5) to fit RAM, and output is batched into a 2 KB buffer to reduce write() calls.

**Use it when:**
- Saving screenshots or sensor images to PNG on an ESP32, RP2040, Teensy or similar board with no heap and roughly 45K of RAM to spare.
- Streaming a frame buffer straight to an SD card line by line, including RGB565 display buffers via addRGB565Line.
- Small images (the default line buffer holds 2,560 bytes: 640 RGBA, 853 RGB or 2,560 8-bit pixels) where encoding speed is irrelevant next to SD-card write time.
- Projects that already use the author's PNGdec and want a matching, dependency-free encoder (the 2025 'simultaneous use with PNGdec' change).

**Skip it when:**
- Any desktop or server workload that needs speed: nothing shows it beating libpng, and fpnge, fpng or mtpng are measured to be many times faster.
- Lines wider than 2,560 bytes unless you raise PNG_MAX_BUFFERED_PIXELS: encodeBegin accepts widths up to 32,767, and nothing checks row size against the fixed line buffers (PNG_TOO_BIG is defined but never returned), so wide rows overflow into the live deflate output buffer and past the encoder struct.
- Grayscale or truecolor images that need a transparent color: setTransparentColor() returns success, but the tRNS chunk is only written inside the indexed-palette branch of PNGStartFile, so the transparency is silently dropped.
- 16-bit-per-channel images, gray+alpha, interlacing or metadata chunks: encodeBegin rejects 16 bpp, so gray+alpha cannot be encoded correctly, and only IHDR/PLTE/tRNS/IDAT/IEND are written.
- Code that needs strong memory safety: header and trailer writes are not bounds-checked against the caller's RAM output buffer, and the vendored zlib 1.2.11 deflate predates the CVE-2018-25032 fix (its trigger is mostly Z_FIXED, which PNGenc does not use).

**Integration:** source-drop · none external; vendors zlib 1.2.11 deflate.c, trees.c, crc32.c, adler32.c and zutil.c (zlib license) in src/. Arduino.h is included unless __LINUX__, __MACH__ or __MCUXPRESSO is defined. · C++ compiler for the class (GCC/Clang, since addRGB565Line uses __builtin_bswap16); linux/Makefile builds libpngenc.a at -O2. The README says it can be built as plain C, but the header's C prototypes name an undefined PNGIMAGE type and give PNG_addRGB565Line the wrong arity, so a C build likely needs header fixes. · Any 32-bit MCU with about 45K free RAM (Arduino architectures=*), plus Linux and macOS, where MEM_SHRINK 0 makes each PNGENC object about 270 KB. Windows needs -D__LINUX__ and a compiler with __builtin_bswap16.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PNGenc only when RAM and no-malloc constraints decide the choice. For any throughput goal, fpnge (about 57x libpng encode in the QOIR benchmark), fpng (about 23x per its README) or the multi-threaded GregorBudweiser pngenc are the encoders with measured wins over libpng.

**Gotchas:**
- The bpp argument to encodeBegin is bits per pixel and is not checked against the pixel type: TRUECOLOR_ALPHA with bpp 8 is accepted and writes width-byte rows under an RGBA IHDR (a malformed PNG). examples/function_test Test 1 does exactly this and still passes, because it checks only the output size (127 bytes) and the magic bytes.
- Palettes are read in B,G,R order (PNGStartFile writes ucPalette[i*3+2] as red); see closed issue #19.
- addRGB565Line issues Z_PARTIAL_FLUSH after every row, which costs compression ratio and time compared with addLine's Z_NO_FLUSH.
- The issue history is mostly about corrupt output (#2 IDAT CRC errors at 256x256, #14 missing data, #16 addLine corruption, #18 wrong IDAT length on about 25% of files with getLastError() returning 0). All are closed, but no regression test decodes the output.

**Status:** Maintained at low intensity (last commit 2025-11-17, v1.4.0, NLnet NGI Zero Core funded, 18 issues all closed); Apache-2.0 plus zlib-licensed vendored files, small enough to vendor, but treat it as a convenience encoder for small embedded images and validate its output.

[repo](https://github.com/bitbank2/PNGenc)

#### rasterizers-2d

##### Arduino_GFX (GFX Library for Arduino)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Arduino display library for about 40 panel controllers and many buses; 1.2x-5.2x faster than Adafruit_GFX on an ESP32 SPI ILI9341.

**Beats:** Adafruit_GFX (Adafruit-GFX-Library) with the Adafruit_ILI9341 driver — The author's single-pass Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ run (2021-06-16; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6, TTGO T8 v1.8 ESP32, PSRAM off, ILI9341 over 4-wire SPI at 40 MHz, no DMA; compiler flags, CPU clock and library versions not recorded) timed identical test bodies in four libraries: Arduino_GFX beat Adafruit_GFX with Adafruit_ILI9341 by 5.2x on text, 2.9x on outline circles, 2.6x on lines, 2.5x on outline triangles, 1.5x on pixels and 1.2x on fills. Timings stop after the last call returns, and Arduino_ESP32SPI blocks until each SPI transfer completes, so no queued work escapes the timer; the 2020-10-15 run of the same suite gave nearly identical Arduino_GFX numbers (Text 18,933, Pixels 903,550, Lines 433,864 us).

**Known shortcoming:** Embedded SPI display driver (ILI9341 240x320 RGB565 at 40 MHz on a TTGO T8 v1.8 ESP32, arduino-esp32 1.0.6, no DMA), a weak fit for 2D rasterizers; baseline Adafruit_GFX plus Adafruit_ILI9341 is not a listed incumbent. First-party single-pass microsecond timings (moononournation/Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ result.txt, 2021-06-16, commit 8798d61) with flags and board settings unstated. Faster than Adafruit_GFX on every row but slower than LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI on every row except Text; screen fill sits at the 153,600 us SPI wire limit (derived).

**Known shortcoming:** Slower than LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI on every row but Text (up to 1.65x) in its own result.txt; fills reach 95.9% of the SPI link against 98.5-99.5% for the others. The 2021 sketch will not build against 1.6.8 (WHITE and BLACK gone, only RGB565_* names); the bench used the default is_shared_interface=true plus a MISO pin; Arduino IDE only; open #754 (9-bit SPI garbage).

**How:** The display layer is split from the bus layer, and each bus class writes the MCU's peripheral directly. On ESP32, Arduino_ESP32SPI programs the SPI registers itself, packs bytes into a 64-byte DMA-capable buffer and polls cmd.usr until each transfer ends; fills preload the hardware data buffer with the colour and re-trigger 32-pixel transfers, and DC and CS are toggled with single GPIO set/clear register writes. Arduino_ILI9341::writeAddrWindow caches the last column and row windows and skips CASET or PASET when unchanged. Arduino_TFT::writeSlashLine splits Bresenham lines into horizontal or vertical runs sent as one window each, and opaque built-in or GFXfont characters go out as one address window per character with a row buffer (writePixels) instead of per-pixel writes, which is why it posted the fastest Text row. Like the other non-Adafruit libraries, it never reads back display memory.

**Use it when:**
- Arduino IDE projects on ESP32-family boards (ESP32, S2, S3, C3, C5, C6, H2, P4), RP2040/RP2350, ESP8266, AVR, nRF52, RTL872x, STM32 or SAMD21 that use a panel or bus few other libraries cover: 9-bit SPI panels (HX8357B), ESP32-S3 RGB panels, ESP32-P4 DSI, AMOLED dev boards from LilyGo, Waveshare, Makerfabs and others.
- Replacing Adafruit_GFX plus a controller driver when text, outline shapes and lines are slow: the 2021 run measured 5.2x on text, 2.9x on outline circles and 2.6x on lines against Adafruit_GFX with Adafruit_ILI9341.
- Text-heavy screens with opaque (background-coloured) built-in or GFXfont text, where it had the fastest Text row of the four libraries (18,960 us vs 21,752 for TFT_eSPI and 22,473 for LovyanGFX).
- Projects that want the panel and pins chosen in the sketch (or from the bundled dev-device declarations) instead of editing a header inside the library folder, or that need CJK text from U8g2 fonts.
- LVGL front ends on supported dev boards; the library ships LVGL benchmark, hello-world and widgets examples.

**Skip it when:**
- Maximum drawing speed on ESP32 SPI: in the same 2021 run LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI beat it on every row except Text, by up to 1.65x (Lines 412,026 vs 264,950 us; Rounded rects outline 21,562 vs 13,089 us; derived from page data). Its own README says speed is not its first priority.
- Fill-dominated screens: fills are bound by the 40 MHz SPI link, so it is only 1.2x faster than Adafruit_GFX there; the blocking poll per 32-pixel chunk reached 95.9% of the link rate versus 98.5-99.5% for TFT_eSPI and LovyanGFX (derived from page data).
- PlatformIO or ESP-IDF-first projects: the README says only the Arduino IDE is supported and points PlatformIO problems to PlatformIO; ESP32LCD8, ESP32LCD16 and ESP32RGBPanel buses work only on arduino-esp32 2.x, not 3.x.
- Projects needing support or new features on request: the author estimates sponsorship at under one man-hour per month, closes non-issue issues and routes feature requests to Discussions.
- Desktop, anti-aliased or vector-path rendering: it is an integer RGB565 embedded display stack, not a path rasterizer like the Blend2D, Skia or AGG entries in this category.

**Integration:** Arduino library compiled from source (src/*.cpp: core classes plus per-bus and per-display classes) · Arduino core for the target board; optional U8g2 (include U8g2lib.h before Arduino_GFX_Library.h for U8g2 fonts); LVGL only for the LVGL examples · Arduino IDE (the only supported IDE per README); C++ standard not documented; ESP32 RGB/LCD parallel buses need arduino-esp32 2.x, and v1.6.5 added compatibility with arduino-esp32 3.3.6 · ESP32, ESP32-S2/S3/C2/C3/C5/C6/H2/P4, ESP8266, RP2040/RP2350, AVR (Uno, Nano, Mega), Arduino UNO R4, nRF52 (Nano 33 BLE), RTL8720/8722, STM32 (BlackPill F411), SAMD21, Sony Spresense; generic boards through the Arduino SPI class

**Vs siblings:** Pick Arduino_GFX over TFT_eSPI or LovyanGFX when you need its panel and bus breadth (9-bit SPI, RGB and DSI panels, many ready-made dev-board declarations), sketch-level configuration, U8g2 CJK fonts or the fastest opaque text; pick LovyanGFX or TFT_eSPI when SPI drawing speed for lines, shapes and pixels dominates, since both were faster on every other row of the same run.

**Gotchas:**
- The published numbers are from a mid-2021 release on arduino-esp32 1.0.6 and are not reproducible as-is today: the PDQ sketch uses WHITE, BLACK, RED and similar names, while the 1.6.8 headers read here define only RGB565_* constants, and the bus and text code has changed since (v1.6.5 fixed drawChar crashes, v1.6.7 clips built-in font pixels before preclipped writes).
- Arduino_ESP32SPI defaults to is_shared_interface = true, which runs spiTransaction on every startWrite; pass false to hold the bus from begin() when no other SPI device shares it. The benchmark sketch kept the default and also passed a MISO pin, which makes writeRepeat reload the SPI data registers for every 32-pixel chunk.
- Plain drawLine with diagonal slopes still costs one address-window update per run, and drawPixel costs a CASET (or PASET), RAMWR and a blocking transfer per pixel; batch pixels into a Canvas or draw16bitRGBBitmap when you can.
- Open bug #754 (January 2026): 9-bit SPI on ESP32-family chips pads partial bytes with garbage in flush_data_buf, corrupting 9-bit panels; the 8-bit DC/SPI path used in the benchmark is not affected.

**Status:** Active, single maintainer: release v1.6.8 (September 2026, mostly new boards and DSI fixes), 1,539 commits, 1.1k stars, 249 forks and only 2 open issues because non-bug issues are closed; the Adafruit-derived two-clause BSD licence (license.txt; GitHub detects none) makes it copyable, but support is explicitly minimal.

[repo](https://github.com/moononournation/Arduino_GFX) · [benchmark](https://github.com/moononournation/Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ/blob/master/result.txt)

##### Blaze (aurimasg/blaze)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Research-grade multi-threaded CPU rasterizer for solid-color path fills; the author reports 2.6x faster than multi-threaded Blend2D (2023 version) on an M1 Max.

**Beats:** Blend2D, Skia (CPU), Apple CoreGraphics — The claim exists only in search snippets of the author's blocked article. On an Apple M1 Max (10 cores), Paris-30k (50,681 paths, drawn at 2x scale to 4222x3474) takes 18 ms with Blaze, 47 ms with Blend2D (2023-era, multi-threaded with threadCount = hardware threads), 190 ms with Skia and 390 ms with CoreGraphics. The harness renders 500 times and averages the middle 490 whole-millisecond system_clock readings. The repo's adapters show that Skia (SkCanvas::MakeRasterDirect) and CoreGraphics (CGBitmapContext) run single-threaded, so the 10.6x and about 20x figures mostly reflect 10 cores against 1. Blend2D is the only like-for-like (multi-threaded) baseline, and its BLContext is created and ended inside every timed frame. Anti-aliasing is the same class for Blaze and Blend2D (analytic area coverage), but no image comparison is published. The harness also has three output-equivalence flaws. The Skia adapter passes Blaze's premultiplied colors to SkPaint::setColor, which expects unpremultiplied ARGB, so Skia draws Paris-30k's 33,171 translucent paths (of 50,681) with wrong colors. All three baseline adapters ignore each path's fill rule, so they draw Tiger's 235 even-odd paths as nonzero (Paris-30k is all nonzero). The CoreGraphics adapter leaves path and color pointers uninitialized for fully transparent paths (none in Paris-30k). None of these changes the work much, but the outputs are not identical. No compiler, flags, library versions or result files are published, and the Benchmarks/ files have no build file.

**Known shortcoming:** Snippet-only numbers (gasiulis.name article blocked): Paris-30k 18 ms vs Blend2D 47, Skia 190, CoreGraphics 390 on an M1 Max; Benchmarks/Benchmark.cpp matches the 500-run method but publishes no results. Skia ran single-threaded while Blend2D ran multi-threaded, so the Blend2D comparison is not like-for-like.

**Known shortcoming:** The Paris-30k comparison is not configuration-matched: the Skia and CoreGraphics adapters run single-threaded against Blaze's 10 workers, and Blend2D is multi-threaded but has its BLContext created inside each timed frame. The Skia adapter passes premultiplied colours as unpremultiplied (33,171 of 50,681 Paris-30k paths are translucent, so Skia's output colours are wrong); every baseline adapter ignores the fill rule (Tiger: 235 of 301 paths even-odd); no image diff is done. Open issues #8 (Paris-30k output differs from Inkscape, unanswered) and #4 (broken Tiger render); Threads.cpp calls the Darwin-only pthread_set_qos_class_self_np so a Linux build needs a patch; Benchmarks/ has no build file; the demo Release build uses -Ofast. An HN snippet reports Blend2D beating Blaze in some x86_64 tests.

**How:** Rendering runs in three parallel phases on a pthread worker pool sized to the online CPU count. (1) Paths are transformed, curves flattened in 24.8 fixed point, and the resulting lines binned per path into 16-pixel-tall tile rows, with start-of-row cover values, all in parallel across paths. (2) Per-row lists of contributing paths are built in parallel bands. (3) Each 16-row band is rasterized independently in paint order. Rasterization uses exact-area cover/area accumulation into a dense per-band int32 table, plus a bit vector of touched cells that is walked with popcount and count-trailing-zeros to emit spans. Fully covered runs are filled from the carried cover, and spans are composited with 64-bit SWAR source-over, with a store-only fast path for opaque spans and for zero destination pixels. Per-thread bump allocators avoid malloc during a frame.

**Use it when:**
- Rendering very large, static, fill-only vector scenes (maps, CAD or GIS layers, pre-flattened text) at high resolution on a many-core Apple Silicon Mac, where one frame has tens of thousands of paths.
- WebAssembly apps that can enable SharedArrayBuffer (cross-origin isolation headers) and want a multi-threaded software rasterizer; the repo ships an Emscripten build script and demo.
- As a reference design for band-parallel scanline rasterization (sparse cell accumulation with bit vectors) when building your own renderer.
- When geometry is already converted to fills with premultiplied solid colors, and you need throughput rather than a full 2D API.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a general 2D API (strokes, dashes, gradients, images, clipping, text, blend modes): use Blend2D, Skia or another full library.
- Windows, which is unsupported per the README. Linux builds also need a patch, because Threads.cpp calls the Darwin-only pthread_set_qos_class_self_np on every non-Emscripten build.
- Single-core or low-core targets, or small scenes: the design relies on parallelism, the README makes no single-thread claim, and a search snippet of a Hacker News comment says Blend2D beats Blaze in some tests on x86_64.
- Production use that needs support: code is essentially unchanged since June 2023, and correctness reports go unanswered. Issue #8 (open) says the Paris-30k output differs from Inkscape's, issue #4 (open since 2023-10) reports a broken Tiger render with suspected threading problems, and issue #7 (radiation symbol defect) was closed with no fix commit.

**Integration:** source-drop (Blaze/ directory: header templates plus 9 .cpp files; no CMake or library target) · none beyond POSIX threads and the C11 <stdatomic.h> header used from C++ · C++20 with Clang: the Xcode demo uses gnu++20 with Release at -Ofast and SIMD_NEON=1, and the WebAssembly build uses em++ -O3 -std=c++20 -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions. GCC builds are not shown. · macOS (arm64 NEON path or generic C++) and WebAssembly with pthreads; other POSIX systems after patching the QoS call; no Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick Blaze over Blend2D only for fill-only scenes on many-core macOS or WebAssembly where you can feed pre-converted geometry, and only after benchmarking against a current Blend2D. Blend2D is maintained, full-featured, cross-platform and has its own multi-threaded context. Over Vello CPU, AGG or tiny-skia, Blaze's case is solely parallel fill throughput in C++. Those siblings offer strokes, paints and active maintenance.

**Gotchas:**
- Colors must be premultiplied RGBA8, and the destination must be cleared by the caller. Call Threads::ResetFrameMemory after each frame (the benchmark does), or per-frame bump memory keeps growing.
- There is no SVG importer: issue #6 asks for the converter that produced the .vectorimage files, and it is not published, so you build Geometry arrays yourself.
- Matrix::PreMultiply computed the wrong translation component until the 2024-09-30 fix (issue #5). The benchmark is unaffected because per-path transforms are identity and the frame matrix is scale plus translate, but older copies are wrong under rotation or skew.
- Curve flattening uses fixed tolerances: quadratics are split until the control point lies within 0.125 px (L1) of the chord midpoint, and cubics until each second difference is at most 0.5 px. That bounds the deviation at roughly 0.18 px (derived from LinearizerUtils.h). Coordinates are quantized to 1/256 px.

**Status:** Stale (feature work ended June 2023; the last commits on 2024-09-30 are a matrix fix and cleanup; three open issues without replies). It is MIT and small enough to vendor, but treat it as a research codebase, not a maintained library.

[repo](https://github.com/aurimasg/blaze) · [benchmark](https://gasiulis.name/parallel-rasterization-on-cpu/)

##### GPU scanline path rendering (Li, Hou, Zhou 2016)  `C++ (CUDA, OpenGL)`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Research code for the SIGGRAPH Asia 2016 CUDA and OpenGL scanline path renderer; the abstract claims about 2.5x over prior GPU path renderers.

**Beats:** state-of-the-art GPU path renderers (exact baselines not confirmed from an opened source) — The only numbers come from search-result text of the abstract (ACM TOG 35(6), 2016): a consistent 2.5x speedup over 'state-of-the-art alternatives' for high-quality rendering at Ultra HD, more than 30x in extreme cases, and 10x on animated input. The compared systems and the GPU were not readable here; search snippets only associate NVpr and MPVG with the paper. The repo can reproduce this renderer's own frame times but contains no baseline to compare against.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C on snippet-only numbers: the ACM TOG 35(6) 2016 paper (DOI 10.1145/2980179.2982434) is blocked here, so the 2.5x / >30x / 10x figures come from search snippets of the abstract; the repo's run.rb driver times only this renderer with no baseline. Code last touched 2017-07-03 (research prototype). Retier to B once the paper's comparison tables (and whether Skia or Cairo appear in them) are read.

**Known shortcoming:** Windows plus NVIDIA demo application with no library API. The repo harness runs 16 warm-up and 256 timed frames (min and mean wall clock with glFinish) with the scene resident on the GPU and no baseline; a fixed 256 MB CUDA pool throws when exhausted. The TOG paper remains unreachable here, so its baselines are unconfirmed.

**Independent measurement:** paper tables (blocked)

**How:** The work runs over boundary fragments (pixels the path outline crosses), not over all covered pixels. Curves are cut into monotonic pieces at pixel rows, and each piece emits fragments with per-sample coverage masks (k_make_intersection_0/1, k_gen_fragment_and_stencil_mask). A segmented sort orders the fragments by (y, x) within each path (Modern GPU segmented sort), and a scan gives winding numbers. Fragments are then merged, and the interior runs between them become horizontal spans, as in a CPU scanline rasterizer. OpenGL finally draws the merged fragments, using gl_SampleMask from a precomputed mask table, and the spans as quads into a 32-sample multisample target. Interior pixels therefore need no per-pixel winding computation, which is where the abstract's speedup at Ultra HD resolution comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or porting a GPU path-filling algorithm. The kernels are a readable reference for the boundary-fragment plus span approach that linebender/vello's sparse-strip work (issue #670) cites as 'boundary fragment merge'.
- Reproducing the paper's GPU timings on the 13 MPVG scenes (boston, car, contour, embrace, hawaii, paper-1/2, paris-30k/50k/70k, tiger, reschart, chord) with working_directory/run.rb on an NVIDIA GPU under Windows.
- High-quality anti-aliasing (32 samples per pixel) of large static vector scenes at high resolution, where per-pixel winding work dominates other GPU methods.
- Scenes animated on the GPU: an --animation mode re-renders perturbed input every frame, the case behind the abstract's 10x claim for animated input.

**Skip it when:**
- Any production use. The code is a 4-commit research prototype last changed 2017-07-03, with no tests, no releases and no issue or PR activity.
- Non-NVIDIA, non-Windows or headless targets. It needs CUDA, OpenGL 4.5 and a 32-sample multisample texture, and it times with QueryPerformanceCounter/LARGE_INTEGER. The only build files are a Visual Studio 2013/2015 project importing the CUDA 7.5 build customization.
- General SVG. The README says only a subset of SVG features works (see the paper). The scene model in svg.cpp covers path fills with nonzero/evenodd rules, solid colours, linear and radial gradients, and strokes (with a --stroke-to-fill option).
- As a drop-in for Skia, Cairo or Blend2D. It has no drawing-context API, and none of those CPU renderers is compared in any source opened here.
- Very large scenes or resolutions without tuning. A fixed 256 MB CUDA scratch pool throws 'cuda_cached_allocator: reserved memory exhausted' when it overflows, and the fragment texture is a compile-time 4096x4096.

**Integration:** source-drop (Visual Studio solution building gpu-scanline.exe; a pre-built x64 binary is described in the README) · CUDA 7.5/8.0 with Thrust, Modern GPU (vendored), SDL 2.0.3 and Boost 1.60 (the README says to download them with test data from the project site), glm, stb, rapidxml, glLoadGen-generated GL loader · Visual Studio 2013 (v120 toolset; v140 in one configuration), CUDA 7.5 build customization; device code is generated for compute_20/sm_20 and sm_52 · 64-bit Windows 10 with an NVIDIA GPU (README: CUDA sm_50 and OpenGL 4.5; tested on driver 368.81)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over NV_path_rendering (driver extension, hardware MSAA) or vkvg only to study or port the scanline boundary-fragment algorithm on NVIDIA hardware. For shipping code, Vello (which builds its sparse-strip design on this paper) or a CPU renderer such as Blend2D is the practical choice.

**Gotchas:**
- The README warns that the behaviour of gl_SampleMask changed around NVIDIA driver 368.22, so drivers on the other side of that change may render incorrectly. Output correctness depends on the driver version.
- The repo's benchmark (vg_main.cpp benchmark()) renders 16 warm-up frames, then reports the minimum and the mean wall-clock time over 256 frames of rasterize(), which ends in glFinish(). Scene data is already resident on the GPU, so parsing and upload are excluded and only the per-frame transform and rasterization are timed. No baseline renderer and no results are committed.
- Shader files are loaded at runtime from ./shader/R_cut_A_stencil/ relative to the working directory, so the exe must run from working_directory.
- Building with a current CUDA toolkit means editing the project's Code Generation setting (compute_20/sm_20 and sm_52); the README itself tells users to match it to their device.

**Status:** Abandoned research code (4 commits, last 2017-07-03) under the MIT licence (Zhejiang University). It is copyable, but it is tied to Windows, NVIDIA and a 2016 CUDA/Visual Studio toolchain, and its value now is mainly as a reference implementation of the algorithm.

[repo](https://github.com/Mochimazui/gpu-scanline-path-rendering) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2980179.2982434)

##### LovyanGFX  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Embedded display driver and drawing library for ESP32-class MCUs; 1.3x to 4.6x faster than Adafruit_GFX on an ILI9341 at 40 MHz SPI.

**Beats:** Adafruit_GFX (Adafruit-GFX-Library) with the Adafruit_ILI9341 driver; TFT_eSPI is roughly equal in the same table — One single-pass run of moononournation's Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ (2021-06-16; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6, TTGO T8 v1.8 ESP32, PSRAM off, ILI9341 over 4-wire SPI at 40 MHz, no DMA; compiler flags, CPU clock and LovyanGFX version not recorded) timed the same test body per library: LovyanGFX beat Adafruit_GFX with Adafruit_ILI9341 by 4.6x on outline circles, 4.3x on text, 3.9x on lines, 3.7x on outline triangles, 1.6x on pixels and 1.27-1.3x on fills. The v0 code waits for the SPI busy flag in dc_h() before releasing the bus, so each timing includes the last transfer; the earlier 2020-10-15 run of the same suite gave LovyanGFX numbers up to 6.6% different (Pixels 814,232 vs 867,702 us).

**Known shortcoming:** Embedded SPI display driver, a weak fit for 2D rasterizers; the only numbers are a competitor's run (Arduino_GFX author's result.txt, TTGO T8 ESP32, ILI9341 at 40 MHz, 2021-06-16) against Adafruit_GFX, not a listed incumbent. Fastest of the four libraries on 11 of 15 rows. Not a well-known suite, so C rather than B.

**Known shortcoming:** The PDQ sketch uses the v0 API (Panel_ILI9341 freq_write and spi_cs, setPanel, init(sclk, miso, mosi)), probably tag 0.3.12; the v1 rewrite removed it, so the sketch does not compile on 1.2.32 and the current code was never re-measured. The 2020 and 2021 runs differ by up to 6.6% (Pixels), and TFT_eSPI is 12% faster on Pixels. Bus_SPI defaults freq_write to 16 MHz (the bench used 40); issue #940 (firmware +575 KB in 1.2.30) fixed in 1.2.32 on 2026-10-02; #491 (ESP32-S3 shared-bus SPI mode break) and #851 (P4 DMA) open.

**How:** On ESP32 the Bus_SPI layer drives the SPI peripheral registers directly (MOSI_DLEN, W0-W15, CMD) and toggles D/C with one GPIO set/clear register write, skipping the Arduino SPI and ESP-IDF driver calls per transfer. Solid fills (writeDataRepeat) preload the 64-byte W0-W15 buffer with the colour and, on the original ESP32, retrigger 2048-bit transfers that reuse that buffer as a ring, so a fill runs at the link rate (Screen fill 154,341 us against a 153,600 us floor for five 240x320 RGB565 frames at 40 MHz, derived from page data). Pixel streams (writePixels) ping-pong between the W0-W7 and W8-W15 halves with SPI_USR_MOSI_HIGHPART so colour conversion overlaps the previous transfer. Panel_LCD caches the CASET/RASET window and skips resending it when unchanged; drawLine is Bresenham emitted as horizontal or vertical runs (writeFillRectPreclipped per run, with off-screen segments skipped before the bus is touched), and drawCircle is the midpoint algorithm emitted as eight H/V spans per step inside one held transaction.

**Use it when:**
- Arduino or ESP-IDF firmware on ESP32, ESP32-S2/S3/C3/C6/P4 driving a supported SPI, I2C or parallel panel where Adafruit_GFX plus a controller driver is too slow: in the 2021 run it was 4.3x faster on text, 3.9x on lines and 3.3x to 4.6x on outline circles, triangles and rounded rectangles.
- Shape-heavy screens (gauges, outlines, arcs): it was the fastest of the four libraries on 11 of 15 rows, and the only one besides Arduino_GFX with arc primitives (Arcs filled 21,546 us vs Arduino_GFX 33,381 us).
- Products that must pick the board or panel at run time (LGFX_AUTODETECT for M5Stack, ODROID-GO, Wio Terminal and others), drive several displays at once, or use 24-bit colour, EPD panels or rotated and zoomed sprites (pushRotateZoom).
- UI development on a desktop first: the same code renders through SDL2 or OpenCV on Windows, Linux or macOS (examples_for_PC) before flashing.
- Moving an existing TFT_eSPI sketch onto a newer ESP32 core, via the LGFX_TFT_eSPI.hpp alias header.

**Skip it when:**
- Fill-dominated screens on SPI: fills are bound by the bus clock, so the gain over Adafruit_GFX is only 1.27x on Screen fill and 1.27-1.28x on filled rectangles and rounded rectangles at 40 MHz (derived from page data); a parallel bus or partial redraws matter more than the library.
- Per-pixel plotting through drawPixel or text-heavy screens where every few percent counts: TFT_eSPI was 1.12x faster on Pixels (775,781 vs 867,702 us) and Arduino_GFX 1.19x faster on Text (18,960 vs 22,473 us) in the same run (derived from page data).
- MCUs outside the README table: AVR, STM32 and nRF52 are not listed; RP2040 is SPI only with no touch support, and ESP8266 I2C is a software implementation.
- Flash-tight targets on 1.2.30 or 1.2.31: merging the implementation into one translation unit kept unused panel and touch code and grew an ESP32-C3 build by about 575 KB (#940); 1.2.32 brings it back to 346 KB (1.2.29: 329 KB), so pin 1.2.32 or later and check the map file.
- An SPI bus shared with devices in a different SPI mode on ESP32-S3: pinned open issue #491 reports a DAC in mode 2 stops responding after a display update, with no maintainer workaround posted.

**Integration:** Arduino / PlatformIO library compiled from source (include LovyanGFX.hpp; v1 implementation in a few .cpp translation units since 1.2.32); ESP-IDF component and pico-sdk builds through CMakeLists.txt and boards.cmake · None outside the platform SDK for drawing; bundles TJpgDec, Pngle, QRCode and bitwizeshift/result; on ESP-IDF requires the nvs_flash, efuse, esp_lcd, driver and related components, and links an arduino-esp32 component automatically when present; SDL2 or OpenCV for PC builds · No language standard or core version is documented; CI badges cover Arduino IDE, PlatformIO and ESP-IDF builds, and the 1.2.32 release notes mention arduino-esp32 2.0.x and 3.0.x (ESP-IDF 5.1); PC builds use CMake 3.8+ with Clang or GCC · ESP32, ESP32-S2, ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 per the README table (SPI with DMA, I2C, parallel; RGB on S3; composite video on ESP32), plus ESP32-C6 and ESP32-P4 per recent commits (open issue #851: SPI DMA not working on ESP32-P4); ESP8266 (SPI), SAMD51/SAMD21 (SPI, I2C), RP2040 (SPI); Windows, Linux and macOS through SDL2 or OpenCV

**Vs siblings:** Pick LovyanGFX over TFT_eSPI for the fastest shapes, fills and arcs on ESP32 SPI, run-time panel setup, ESP-IDF builds and current ESP32 chips (C6, P4, S3 RGB); TFT_eSPI kept a 12% lead on single pixels and a 1.5% lead on lines (the latter within the 7% spread between LovyanGFX's 2020 and 2021 runs) and has the STM32 and RP2040 PIO paths. Pick Arduino_GFX when you need its wider data-bus range or the fastest text; neither is comparable to Blend2D, Skia or AGG, which are desktop anti-aliased path rasterizers.

**Gotchas:**
- The catalogued numbers were measured with the v0 API (lgfx::Panel_ILI9341 with public freq_write/spi_cs fields, setPanel, init(sclk, miso, mosi)); the run date points to tag 0.3.12 (2021-05-30), but the version was not recorded. v1 removed that API, so the benchmark sketch does not compile against current 1.2.x and the rewritten v1 code has not been re-measured.
- Bus_SPI::config_t defaults freq_write to 16 MHz, not the 40 MHz the benchmark used; set it explicitly for ILI9341-class panels.
- Colour arguments are typed by C++ type: uint32_t means RGB888, uint16_t and int32_t mean RGB565, uint8_t means RGB332. A bare literal like 0xFF0000 is an int and is read as RGB565; write 0xFF0000U for 24-bit colours.
- draw* calls acquire and release the bus on every call (that is how the benchmark ran), while write* calls require an explicit startWrite(); holding startWrite() across a frame is faster but blocks other devices such as an SD card on the same SPI bus until endWrite() or endTransaction(). Before 1.2.32, pushImageDMA() with a source in PSRAM or flash sent garbage on ESP32 (#949).

**Status:** Actively maintained: 2,008 commits, release 1.2.32 on 2026-10-02 fixing firmware size, ESP32-C6 builds and DMA from PSRAM, 16 open issues and no open pull requests; the main code is FreeBSD two-clause with MIT, BSD and IPA Font licences for bundled parts, so it is copyable.

[repo](https://github.com/lovyan03/LovyanGFX) · [benchmark](https://github.com/moononournation/Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ/blob/master/result.txt)

##### LunaSVG  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Small C++17 SVG 1.1/Tiny 1.2 renderer on the plutovg rasterizer; converts icons to PNG about 2x faster than cairosvg through Python.

**Beats:** cairosvg 2.9.1 (Python, renders through Cairo 1.18.4) and resvg-py 0.5.0 — On an Apple M4 (macOS 26.5.1), pillow-lunasvg 0.1.0 (LunaSVG 3.5.0; built by scikit-build-core, whose default CMake build type is Release, compiler not stated) converted 3,460 simple-icons SVGs to PNG at a median 1.00 ms versus 2.17 ms for cairosvg 2.9.1 (Cairo 1.18.4) and 2.84 ms for resvg-py 0.5.0 at 256 px, and 12.56 versus 23.63 and 34.85 ms at 1024 px. LunaSVG's own parse plus render was only 0.11 ms and 0.88 ms of those times (about 89% and 93% of the pillow-lunasvg time is Pillow PNG encoding and Python overhead, derived from page data), and no render-only time is given for the baselines, so this is an end-to-end SVG-to-PNG comparison dominated by Python front-ends and PNG encoders, not a rasterizer comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on pillow-lunasvg results.md (public bench.py, Apple M4, no compiler or flags) against cairosvg and resvg-py, neither a listed baseline. The measurer is the Python wrapper's author (README PR #273), so a strict vendor reading gives C. Much of the gap is the Python front-end and PNG encoders, not the rasterizer.
