**Known shortcoming:** The comparison is end to end rather than rasteriser speed: render-only time is 0.11 of 1.00 ms at 256 px and 0.88 of 12.56 ms at 1024 px, so 89-93% of LunaSVG's measured time is Pillow PNG encoding plus Python, and the baselines have no render-only rows. The wheel was an optimised Release build (scikit-build-core default), correcting the verifier, but the compiler is still unstated. CVEs 2024-33763 and 33764 (2.3.9) and 2024-57720, 57721 and 57722 (3.0.0) per search snippets; fuzzer issue #223 open; open #248 (pattern canvas allocating 16,000x16,000); the wrapper guards deep nesting, exponential use elements and a plutovg dash infinite loop; external file loading is on by default.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e113, 2026-10-05, via resvg): the pillow-lunasvg benchmark's resvg baseline is resvg-py 0.5.0, whose Cargo.toml builds resvg 0.48.0 with opt-level 'z' (size-optimised), so the 2.8x over resvg-py measures a handicapped build; cairosvg parses SVG in Python. Retiered B to C (retier-34).

**Independent measurement:** pillow-lunasvg benchmark (handicapped baselines)

**How:** Rendering goes through plutovg, a small C library whose scan converter is FreeType's ftgrays (exact-area coverage per pixel cell, emitted as coverage spans) and whose strokes come from the FreeType stroker; spans are composited with Qt-style per-span blend functions on premultiplied 32-bit pixels (scalar code; SSE2 is used only for the 32-bit fill helper). LunaSVG itself is a compact C++ DOM and layout tree with no Cairo context, no external XML or CSS library and no Python in the loop, which is where most of the measured advantage over cairosvg (a Python SVG parser driving Cairo) comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Rendering SVG icons, UI assets or emoji glyphs to bitmaps inside a C++ application or game (it is used by Dear ImGui, RmlUi, OpenSiv3D and node-canvas) where pulling in Cairo, librsvg or Skia is too heavy.
- Python thumbnail or icon pipelines that currently call cairosvg: pillow-lunasvg ships self-contained wheels (259-467 KB, no system cairo) and was measured at about half cairosvg's per-file time.
- Static SVG content that sticks to SVG 1.1 basics: paths, shapes, gradients, patterns, clip paths, masks, markers, <use>, <text> with registered fonts.
- Applications that need to restyle or hit-test a loaded document (applyStyleSheet, setAttribute, elementFromPoint) and re-render without reparsing.

**Skip it when:**
- SVGs with filters (blur, drop shadows, lighting), mix-blend-mode, CSS transform properties, transform-origin, context-fill, or SVG/WebP inside <image>: none are implemented, and only 59% of resvg's feature tests match resvg's output at loose tolerance.
- Untrusted input without hardening: CVE-2024-33763 and CVE-2024-33764 (lunasvg 2.3.9) and CVE-2024-57720, -57721 and -57722 (lunasvg 3.0.0) are stack, segfault and allocation bugs, a fuzzer is still only requested (issue #223), and the pillow-lunasvg author had to add his own guards against deep-nesting stack overflow, exponential <use> expansion and a plutovg dashing loop that never terminates.
- Throughput-critical rendering of large scenes on many cores: plutovg's compositing is scalar, and engines such as Blend2D or ThorVG are built for that workload.
- Animated content (no SMIL; LunaSVG says animation is unlikely ever to be supported) or Lottie, where ThorVG is the fit.
- Patterns in documents with large user-space coordinates: open issue #248 reports the pattern tile canvas being allocated at user-space size (16,000 x 16,000 px in the report) before downscaling.

**Integration:** static lib · plutovg (C, bundled as a git submodule or found as plutovg >= 1.3.0 via USE_SYSTEM_PLUTOVG), which itself bundles FreeType's ftgrays/stroker (FTL license) and stb_image/stb_truetype · C++17, CMake 3.15 or Meson · any (portable C/C++; SSE2 used only for a fill helper when available)

**Vs siblings:** Pick LunaSVG over NanoSVG2 when you need real SVG documents (clipping, masks, patterns, CSS, <use>, text) rather than flat fills, and over ThorVG when you only need static SVG to bitmap with a smaller codebase and a DOM API; pick ThorVG for Lottie or animation, and Blend2D when you are drawing your own vector content at high throughput rather than rendering SVG files.

**Gotchas:**
- Bitmaps are ARGB32 premultiplied (BGRA bytes on little-endian); call Bitmap::convertToRGBA() in place before handing pixels to code that expects straight RGBA.
- By default <image href="/path"> may load local files; build with LUNASVG_DISABLE_EXTERNAL_RESOURCES=ON (as pillow-lunasvg does) when rendering untrusted SVGs, and consider LUNASVG_DISABLE_LOAD_SYSTEM_FONTS for reproducible text.
- <use> is expanded by deep copy, so a short chain of nested <use> grows exponentially in memory and time; cap input size or element counts yourself.
- Text needs fonts registered through lunasvg_add_font_face_from_file/_data or system font loading, so the same file can render differently on different machines.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-17, release 3.5.0), MIT-licensed, 1.2k stars and embedded in Dear ImGui, RmlUi, node-canvas and others; safe to adopt for trusted static SVG, but harden it before rendering untrusted files.

[repo](https://github.com/sammycage/lunasvg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Maksim-Burtsev/pillow-lunasvg/blob/main/benchmarks/results.md)

##### NanoSVG2 (RudjiGames fork)  `C`  `Zlib`  `active`  `Tier C`

Copy of the two-header NanoSVG parser and rasterizer with SSE2 blending and span-delta coverage, 2.5-3.7x faster than its own previous rasterizer.

**Beats:** The fork's own pre-PR master, not a category incumbent: a 2024-08-15 copy of memononen/nanosvg whose rasterizer matches upstream nanosvgrast.h apart from later upstream fixes (paint order, NaN clamping, dash stroke preparation). Skia, Cairo and Blend2D are not measured, and upstream nanosvg HEAD is not measured either. — The fork's own PRs time its rasterizer against its pre-PR master (essentially upstream NanoSVG's 2024 rasterizer) on example/23.svg, drawing.svg, nano.svg and a gradient test at 1x and 3x scale, -O2 on x86-64 with no CPU or compiler version: PR #2 reports 2.5-3.7x (mean of 40 runs) and PR #3 adds 1.34-1.98x with SSE2 (best of 11, callgrind counts); no harness is committed, and the two PRs' absolute times are not comparable, so the gains should not be multiplied. Reading the diffs found no correctness bug behind these numbers: the SSE2 blend, coverage prefix sum and reciprocal unpremultiply match the scalar arithmetic (the reciprocal identity holds for all 8-bit inputs when rechecked).

**Known shortcoming:** Fork of memononen/nanosvg whose 2.5x-3.7x (PR #2) and 1.34x-1.98x (PR #3) rasterizer gains are measured against the fork's own pre-PR master (an upstream NanoSVG 2024 snapshot), not a category incumbent; Skia, Cairo and Blend2D were never run. No harness in the repo, no CPU, -O2 x86-64 only; the commits are by an account named claude.

**Known shortcoming:** No harness, no CPU and the compiler is unknown; the NSVG_NO_SIMD column is only about 1.0-1.1x, so non-x86 targets get only the PR #2 gain. The fork lacks upstream's paint-order support, nanosvg.h now needs C99 (mixed declarations in CDATA), and output differs from upstream only through the defringe fix and the hex-colour parser rejecting malformed colours. 0 stars, AI-authored pull requests, and the README still says 'not actively maintained'.

**How:** The rasterizer is NanoSVG's 5-subsample scanline converter with exact horizontal fixed-point coverage; the fork stores fully covered spans as start/end deltas in an int array and prefix-sums them once per pixel row instead of adding 51 to every byte five times per row. The blend loop fuses that prefix sum with SSE2 4-pixel source-over blending (div255 as _mm_mulhi_epu16(x+1, 257)), skips zero-coverage pixels, writes fully opaque runs directly, evaluates gradient colors only for covered pixels, starts at the first edge's row and stops when edges run out, and limits the unpremultiply/defringe pass to the drawn bounding box using 24-bit reciprocals instead of divisions. It also stops zero-length cubics from recursing 2047 times in the flattener, and the parser replaces strtoll/pow/sscanf/strchr with hand-written digit loops and power-of-ten tables.

**Use it when:**
- Baking SVG icons or UI glyphs into textures at load time in a game or tool, where a two-header, dependency-free C library is worth more than full SVG conformance.
- You already ship upstream NanoSVG and want a faster drop-in rasterizer on x86-64 without changing call sites.
- Small to medium images (tens to a few hundred pixels per side) with simple fills and gradients, rendered on one thread per rasterizer object.
- Builds that cannot pull in C++ or a large dependency tree (Cairo, Skia, Blend2D).

**Skip it when:**
- You need correct rendering of real-world SVG: no clip paths, masks, filters, patterns, text, <use> handling beyond the parser's support, or embedded images; the inherited README still calls the rasterizer 'not particular fast or accurate'.
- Quality matters: anti-aliasing uses only 5 vertical subsamples per pixel, so near-horizontal edges show visible banding compared with analytic-coverage renderers.
- Non-x86 targets expect the full gain: the SSE2 path is x86 only, and PR #3's own NSVG_NO_SIMD column runs about 1.0-1.1x the post-PR #2 code, so ARM gets roughly the PR #2 algorithmic speedup only.
- You need upstream NanoSVG's newer features: this copy lacks upstream's paint-order support (shape->paintOrder) and uses its own 2024 CSS style handling rather than upstream's class-based one.
- You want a maintained, reviewed library: 0 stars, 12 commits, all speed work landed on 2026-09-24 from an AI-agent branch, and no tests or fuzzing harness are in the repo.

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond libc and libm (stdio.h, string.h, stdlib.h, math.h); emmintrin.h for the SSE2 path · C99 for nanosvg.h (the CDATA skip in nsvg__parseXML declares a variable after a statement); nanosvgrast.h is stated to build with -std=c89 -pedantic; CMake 3.10 for the optional package · any; SSE2 fast path on x86-64 (GCC, Clang, MSVC) and 32-bit MSVC with /arch:SSE2, scalar elsewhere or with NSVG_NO_SIMD

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over LunaSVG or ThorVG when you want two C headers with no build step and only need flat fills, gradients and strokes for icon baking; pick LunaSVG for a C++ renderer with much broader SVG support, and Blend2D or ThorVG when rendering quality, clipping or throughput on large scenes matter.

**Gotchas:**
- Output is not byte-identical to the pre-PR code or to upstream: PR #2 fixes the defringe check (x-1 > 0 became x > 0), which changes the color of fully transparent pixels in column 1 and row 1, and the hex color parser now rejects malformed colors (spaces, signs, 0x prefixes) that the sscanf version accepted.
- nsvgRasterize still clears the whole destination buffer each call, so it cannot composite onto existing pixels; the unpremultiply pass then runs only over the drawn bounding box plus a one-pixel border.
- Coverage still wraps modulo 256 like the original unsigned char sums, so heavily overlapping sub-paths under the nonzero rule keep NanoSVG's existing artifacts.
- The repository is a standalone copy of a 2024 NanoSVG snapshot with local parser changes (title capture, CDATA skipping, rgba alpha), not a GitHub fork, so upstream fixes do not flow in automatically.

**Status:** Active only in the sense that the owner merged three AI-authored PRs on 2026-09-24 (0 stars, README still says 'not actively maintained'); zlib-licensed and two headers, so it is easy to vendor, but treat it as a lightly tested patch set over NanoSVG.

[repo](https://github.com/RudjiGames/nanosvg2) · [benchmark](https://github.com/RudjiGames/nanosvg2/pull/2)

##### ragg  `R (C++ core on AGG 2.4)`  `MIT; bundled AGG 2.4 sources under a BSD-style license (LICENSE.note)`  `active`  `Tier C`

R raster graphics devices (PNG/JPEG/TIFF/WebP) on AGG 2.4; about 1.3x faster than R's anti-aliased cairo png() on a composite ggplot2.

**Beats:** Cairo (R grDevices png(type = 'cairo') anti-aliased raster device) — First-party bench::mark runs (min 10 iterations) in the pkgdown-rendered vignette, built 2026-04-08 on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 x86_64 runner with R 4.5.3 and ragg 1.5.2 (CPU model and compiler flags not stated), timing agg_png() against png(type = 'cairo') with antialias none, gray and subpixel: the layered ggplot2 composite takes about 245 ms with ragg vs about 320-325 ms with anti-aliased cairo and about 265 ms with non-anti-aliased cairo, where a void_dev() run of the same plot (about 130 ms, single system.time call) marks the non-rendering share, so ragg's rendering part is roughly 1.6x faster (derived from page data, plot readings). R's cairo device turns anti-aliasing off for every solid fill (cairoFill sets CAIRO_ANTIALIAS_NONE), so the anti-aliased cairo settings only anti-alias strokes and text; ragg does more work on fills, not less.

**Known shortcoming:** R graphics device with a C++ core on AGG 2.4 (language-filter mismatch; the C++ needs Rinternals and the R graphics engine). Benchmark is the R script vignettes/ragg_performance.Rmd run on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 runner (rendered 2026-04-08; no CPU or flags): composite about 245 vs 320 ms against the anti-aliased cairo device (about 1.3x); the README's 40% has no backing figure, the vignette says about 33%.

**Known shortcoming:** The rendered 2026-04-08 plots contradict the vignette prose: on clip paths cairo is about 1.6x faster (ragg about 87 ms vs about 55 ms, because drawShape re-rasterises the whole clip path per primitive via sbool_intersect_shapes_aa); text is about 4x faster in ragg (about 19 vs 81 ms), gradients about 140 vs 167 ms (not on par), masks about 8 vs 37 ms, patterns about 94 vs 410 ms, device open/close about 7.3 vs 3 ms. R's cairoFns.c confirms CAIRO_ANTIALIAS_NONE on fills for the non-anti-aliased cairo rows. The void_dev baseline is a single system.time run and the raster baseline draws 100 rasters against the 1 benchmarked; the composite advantage with the baseline removed is about 1.6x (derived from page data).

**How:** Every primitive goes through AGG's scanline anti-aliasing rasterizer (rasterizer_scanline_aa: exact-area coverage cells, sorted and swept per scanline) and is blended as spans straight into a premultiplied RGB/RGBA buffer by renderer_scanline_aa_solid; fills use packed scanlines (scanline_p8), strokes and dashes are turned into polygons by conv_stroke/conv_dash and rasterized the same way. Text goes through FreeType with a process-wide static agg::font_cache_manager, so repeated glyphs come from a cache; shaping is done by the textshaping package (HarfBuzz/FriBidi). Masks are applied at scanline level through masked-scanline adaptors over an alpha or luminance buffer, whereas R's cairo device pushes and pops a cairo group and calls cairo_mask for every masked primitive (cairoBegin/cairoEnd in grDevices cairoFns.c), which is why the mask and pattern tests show the largest gaps.

**Use it when:**
- You render R plots to raster files (PNG/JPEG/TIFF/WebP) with anti-aliasing and want them faster than png(type = 'cairo'): about 245 ms vs about 320 ms for the vignette's layered ggplot2 composite.
- Text-heavy plots: in the 2026-04-08 build 1000 text strings took about 19 ms with ragg vs about 81 ms with every cairo setting (about 4x, read from the plot).
- Plots using grid masks or pattern fills (R >= 4.1): about 8 ms vs 37 ms for the mask test and about 94 ms vs 410 ms for the pattern test against anti-aliased cairo (read from the plots).
- Headless servers, CI and knitr/pkgdown builds that need system fonts, right-to-left text, emoji and identical output across Linux, macOS and Windows without X11.
- RStudio (>= 1.4) or Positron users who want the AGG backend as the interactive graphics device.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a 2D rasterizer callable from C++: ragg's C++ core needs R's graphics engine and Rinternals; use AGG 2.6 or Blend2D directly.
- Plots that clip many primitives with a complex grid clipping path: in the 2026-04-08 build ragg took about 87 ms vs about 55 ms for cairo on the vignette's clip-path test (cairo about 1.6x faster), because ragg re-rasterizes the whole clip path for every primitive.
- Many small, nearly empty images: opening and closing a device costs about 7.3 ms vs about 3 ms for png(type = 'cairo') (mostly PNG encoding and file size, per the vignette).
- Fill-only output where non-anti-aliased edges are acceptable: cairo skips anti-aliasing on fills and wins on filled rectangles (about 0.85 ms vs 1.1 ms per 1000) and other single fill-heavy primitives.
- Vector output (PDF, SVG): ragg is raster-only; use cairo_pdf, svglite or the pdf device.

**Integration:** module · R with the systemfonts and textshaping packages (HarfBuzz, FriBidi via textshaping); system FreeType, libpng, libtiff, libjpeg, libwebp and libwebpmux; AGG 2.4 sources are bundled and built as a static library inside the package · Built by R CMD INSTALL with R's configured C/C++ compiler; src/Makevars.in sets no CXX_STD, so R's default C++ standard applies (code uses C++11 features such as unique_ptr and unordered_map). pkg-config is used to find system libraries; Windows builds use Rtools. · Linux, macOS, Windows (Rtools, Arm Windows prepared in 1.2.6); big-endian handled through separate raster pixel formats (WORDS_BIGENDIAN)

**Vs siblings:** Pick ragg when the caller is R code and you want a faster anti-aliased replacement for png(type = 'cairo'); from C++ use the rasterizer underneath it (Anti-Grain Geometry, catalogued as AGG 2.6) or Blend2D, which beats AGG and Cairo in the catalogued third-party thesis and has a JIT pipeline that ragg does not.

**Gotchas:**
- Fills are always anti-aliased, so adjacent filled shapes can show faint seams; open issue #103 (geom_tile banding on Windows) and #131 (striping between spplot polygons) report this, and 1.3.0 added rectangle snapping to the pixel grid (on by default) for fill-only rectangles.
- The vignette prose is older than its plots: it calls ragg 'much better' on clipping paths and only 'slightly faster' on text, while the 2026-04-08 rendered plots show ragg slower on clipping paths and about 4x faster on text.
- Loading the package can be slow when the user's local font directory is large, because systemfonts rescans it on every load (issue #210, open as of 2026-10).
- Gradient stops placed very close together (e.g. 0.0001 apart) lose the flanking colours, while cairo renders them (issue #154, open).

**Status:** Actively maintained by Posit (ragg 1.5.2 on CRAN, last commit 2026-05-13, 184 stars), MIT-licensed with AGG 2.4 under a BSD licence, and safe to adopt for R graphics; its C++ is not reusable outside R.

[repo](https://github.com/r-lib/ragg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/r-lib/ragg/blob/main/vignettes/ragg_performance.Rmd)

##### resvg  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust static-SVG renderer with a C API; benchmarks faster than librsvg on icon sets, much slower on clip-path-heavy files.

**Beats:** librsvg (2.45.5 in the resvg 0.8.0 README charts; 2.50 in the MediaWiki snippet) and QtSvg 5.12.3; Inkscape 1.0 and Batik only in the snippet-only MediaWiki table — Only first-party numbers are reachable: the resvg 0.8.0 README (2019, no hardware, compiler or harness stated; that tag's testing-tools folder holds only regression and test-runner scripts) rendered the Elementary icon theme in 19 s against librsvg 2.45.5's 24 s (about 1.26x), but the Oxygen theme in 175-205 s against librsvg's 163 s (slower), using cairo, raqote, Skia and Qt backends that current resvg no longer has. The independent Wikimedia 2021 comparison (resvg 0.14.0 at 1m04s CPU time against librsvg 2.50 at 1m47s over W3C test files) is search-snippet only, and an open third-party issue (#1146) measures current resvg 23-59x slower than librsvg on a clip-path-heavy file.

**Known shortcoming:** Mixed result against librsvg in the reachable first-party v0.8.0 README charts: Elementary 19 s against librsvg 2.45.5's 24 s (1.26x) but Oxygen 175-205 s against 163 s (7-26% slower); the Wikimedia 1.66x and 7.4x figures are snippet-only (mediawiki, phabricator and gitlab.gnome.org blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e113, 2026-10-05): the only first-party numbers are the 0.8.0 README figures against backends that no longer exist, with no harness. Open issue #1146 (2026-10-01): a clip-path-heavy file renders in 960 ms vs librsvg's 42 ms at 1000 px and 31.7 s vs 537 ms at 4000 px because each clip allocates a layer-sized pixmap; #1147: <use> re-decodes images; #857 (filters performance) closed as not planned. C stands, usability mixed. The pillow-lunasvg benchmark's resvg-py baseline builds resvg at opt-level 'z', so its resvg numbers are handicapped (recorded against LunaSVG).

**Independent measurement:** first-party 0.8.0 README; issue #1146 user numbers

**How:** usvg resolves CSS, units, use/symbol references and shapes into plain paths and groups before rendering, so the renderer is a simple tree walk over pre-resolved paths. Rasterization goes through tiny-skia, a Rust port of a subset of Skia's CPU raster pipeline with SSE/AVX and AArch64 NEON paths. Since 0.33 each isolated group gets a layer sized to its computed bounding box instead of the whole canvas (the changelog reports paris-30k going from about 33.8 s to 0.29 s on an M1 Pro). Gaussian blur uses a 5-pass box blur for sigma of 2 or more and an Alvarez-Mazorra IIR cascade below that. Rendering is single-threaded.

**Use it when:**
- Batch SVG-to-PNG of icon sets, maps and other static artwork where you want one self-contained binary with no cairo, pango or GLib dependency.
- Rendering untrusted SVG: the resvg crate forbids unsafe code, and the project guards against endless loops and deep recursion.
- Output that must be pixel-identical across platforms (x86 Windows and ARM macOS give the same bytes per the README), e.g. golden-image tests or reproducible thumbnails.
- C or C++ programs that want an SVG renderer through a small C API with static linking.
- WASM or embedded targets where Rust compiles but system graphics libraries are unavailable.

**Skip it when:**
- Files with many clip paths, such as Illustrator exports: issue #1146 (2026-10-01, open) measured upstream resvg at 960 ms versus librsvg 42 ms at 1000 px and 31.7 s versus 537 ms at 4000 px; each clip path allocates and masks a full layer-sized pixmap.
- Documents that reuse large raster images through <use>: issue #1147 (open) shows the image decoded again for every use (30 uses of one 4000x3000 JPEG: 1374 ms, 257 ms with a proposed patch).
- Filter-heavy documents: issue #857 reports over 4 s for a document with 10 filters and was closed as not planned; the 0.8.0 README also notes librsvg's faster blur on the Oxygen theme.
- Animated or scripted SVG, SVG Tiny 1.2, or GPU rendering: none are supported.
- Text that must match the platform's native hinting: text is shaped and filled as paths, and needs fonts loaded explicitly.

**Integration:** crate (resvg, usvg) plus C API as shared or static library (resvg.h), and CLI · pure Rust crates only (tiny-skia, usvg, svgtypes; optional zune-jpeg, gif, image-webp, fontdb/skrifa/harfrust for text); no system libraries · Rust 1.85 (MSRV of 0.48.1, edition 2024); any C/C++ compiler for the C API · anywhere Rust compiles, including WASM; SIMD in tiny-skia on x86-64 and AArch64

**Vs siblings:** Pick resvg over LunaSVG when SVG coverage and memory safety on untrusted input matter more than raw speed: LunaSVG wins the pillow-lunasvg end-to-end timing, but resvg-py in that harness builds resvg with opt-level 'z', and resvg passes more of the resvg test suite. Use ThorVG for Lottie or animation, and tiny-skia directly (resvg's backend) when you draw your own vector content rather than SVG files.

**Gotchas:**
- resvg_render expects a width*height*4 buffer of premultiplied RGBA8888; convert before handing pixels to straight-alpha code.
- Text renders only if fonts are loaded (for example resvg_options_load_system_fonts or the system-fonts feature); 0.48 moved text to skrifa and harfrust, so glyph output can differ slightly from 0.47.
- Cost scales with layer and clip area, not with element count: large output sizes with clip paths, masks or filters can be tens of times slower than small ones.
- Release builds should use the repository's production profile (opt-level 3, LTO, one codegen unit); bindings built otherwise (resvg-py 0.5.0 builds resvg with opt-level 'z') will be slower.

**Status:** Actively maintained by Linebender (0.48.1 released 2026-08-02, commits to 2026-10-03), Apache-2.0 OR MIT, about 28.4 million crates.io downloads, so safe to depend on; the C API is versioned with the crate and has no stable ABI promise documented.

[repo](https://github.com/linebender/resvg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/linebender/resvg/blob/v0.8.0/README.md)

##### Rive Renderer (rive-runtime)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rive's C++ runtime and GPU vector renderer (Metal, Vulkan, D3D, GL); vendor claims 66x Skia on animated tiles.

**Beats:** Skia (and Flutter Impeller, per the same post); Skia backend and configuration unstated — The only speed number is Rive's own LinkedIn post (dated 2023-05-05, derived from its activity ID, so about ten months before the renderer was open-sourced): on an 'iPhone 12 Max', Skia drew 9 animated Rive tiles in about 100 ms while the Rive Renderer drew 100 tiles in about 16 ms (and 36 tiles in about 5 ms), stated as 66x or 6000 vs 90 tiles/sec. The Skia backend and settings, the measured code version and the harness are not published (the post is snippet-only here), and no third-party measurement was found.

**Known shortcoming:** Only numbers are a vendor marketing claim seen in search snippets (LinkedIn post and Rive announcement: Skia 9 tiles at about 100 ms vs Rive 100 tiles at about 16 ms on an iPhone, '66x faster, 6000 vs 90 tiles/sec'); tests/bench holds internal micro-benchmarks with no Skia or Impeller baseline. Tier C.

**Known shortcoming:** The only number remains a vendor LinkedIn snippet from a post dated 2023-05-05 (about 10 months before the open-source release), so the measured code, Skia configuration and harness are unpublished. iPhone is the best case (Metal raster order groups); WebGL and GL fall back to atomics or MSAA depth-stencil (issue #83 unanswered). tests/bench uses RenderContextNULL (CPU side only, no Skia). The build fetches dependencies from GitHub at configure time; open issues #99 (D3D11 crash), #57 (DX init) and #92 (Linux GL).

**How:** Paths are not stenciled or CPU-rasterized: curves are tessellated on the GPU (Wang's formula picks segment counts; TessVertexSpan rows are rendered into a tessellation texture) and drawn as 'midpoint fan' triangle patches with analytic anti-aliased coverage, or, for large filled paths, through a cached interior triangulation (a Skia-derived GrInnerFanTriangulator) gated by a TriangulationController. Coverage and per-path 16-bit IDs live in pixel local storage, so many paths batch into one pass without clearing a coverage buffer; overlapping fragments are synchronized per platform by an InterlockMode (rasterOrdering via Metal raster order groups or GL framebuffer fetch / EXT/ANGLE PLS, atomics, clockwise, clockwiseAtomic, or an MSAA depthStencil fallback). A SIMD IntersectionBoard (255x255 tiles, int16x8 lanes) groups non-overlapping draws so they can share a batch, and GPU buffers are ring-allocated (3 frames) so CPU preparation overlaps GPU rendering.

**Use it when:**
- Shipping Rive (.riv) animations in a C++ app, game engine or embedded UI: this is the reference renderer behind Rive's Apple, Android, Flutter, Unity, Unreal and web runtimes.
- Many animated, path-heavy vector layers per frame on Apple GPUs (iOS and Apple Silicon Macs), where Metal raster order groups give the fully featured rasterOrdering mode.
- GPU vector rendering on Android GL ES devices exposing EXT_shader_pixel_local_storage or framebuffer fetch, or on Vulkan/D3D12 desktops, when CPU rasterization (Blend2D, Skia CPU) is the frame-time bottleneck.
- You already render through Rive's abstract Renderer and want to swap a Skia or CoreGraphics backend for the native GPU one without changing scene code.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a drop-in SkCanvas replacement, PDF/SVG output, text shaping APIs outside Rive's text system, or CPU-only/headless rendering: there is no CPU rasterizer backend (RenderContextNULL only counts work for benchmarks).
- Hardware without PLS-class features: WebGL and many GL drivers fall back to atomics or the MSAA depthStencil mode, and open issue #83 (Feb 2026, unanswered) asks how to get PLS on WebGL at all; the 66x claim came from an iPhone, the best case.
- Build-system constraints: it builds with premake via build/build_rive.sh, which clones a pinned premake and fetches Vulkan-Headers, VulkanMemoryAllocator, DirectX-Headers, harfbuzz (Rive fork) and python ply from GitHub at configure time, then compiles shaders with a make + Python minifier step; there is no CMake package and issue #69 asks for prebuilt libraries.
- Mature D3D11 or Linux GL deployments without testing: open issues include #99 (D3D11 access violation in makeImageTexture), #57 (invalid DX resource flags fail renderer init) and #92 (OpenGL context fails on Linux).
- Many identical sprites: issue #81 (open) notes each Rive instance is its own draw, with no GPU instancing across artboards.

**Integration:** static lib (librive.a plus librive_pls_renderer.a, built with premake) · Platform GPU SDK (Metal/Xcode, Vulkan SDK, Windows SDK for D3D, GL/WebGL); configure-time GitHub downloads of Vulkan-Headers, VulkanMemoryAllocator, DirectX-Headers, python ply (shader minifier) and Rive's forks or pins of harfbuzz (rive-app/harfbuzz rive_13.1.1), SheenBidi, yoga and miniaudio for text, layout and audio; optional rive decoders for images · C++17; clang (Xcode CLI tools on macOS, distro clang on Linux), clang-cl or MSVC with Visual Studio 2022 on Windows; bash, git and Python 3 for the build · iOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS (Metal), Android (GL ES, Vulkan), Windows (D3D11, D3D12, GL, Vulkan), Linux (GL, Vulkan), WebAssembly (WebGL2, WebGPU)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ThorVG or TGFX when your content is Rive animation or you want a renderer whose hot path is GPU PLS coverage rather than a CPU raster backend; pick vkvg or vger only for simpler Vulkan/Metal UI drawing, and Blend2D when you need fast, portable CPU rendering with an independent benchmark behind it.

**Gotchas:**
- Feature set depends on InterlockMode: atomics mode masks out nested clipping and modulated images, and clockwise/clockwiseAtomic modes override every path's fill rule (no even-odd), per ShaderFeaturesMaskFor in gpu.hpp.
- Per-device quirks are handled in code: pre-Apple-Silicon iOS PowerVR GPUs drop the low 3 bits of path IDs for fp16 precision, the iOS simulator has no framebuffer reads and falls back to atomics, and ANGLE devices run a runtime test before trusting KHR_blend_equation_advanced.
- The build fetches pinned third-party repos from GitHub and runs a shader make step during premake configuration, so offline or hermetic builds need those mirrored.
- tests/bench micro-benchmarks run against RenderContextNULL (CPU-side draw preparation only) and print the minimum time over a 5 s loop; they measure no GPU time and no Skia baseline.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-10-03, about 3,300 commits) and MIT-licensed, so copyable, but it is a large engine with its own build system rather than a vendorable library, and the speed claim is first-party marketing.

[repo](https://github.com/rive-app/rive-runtime) · [benchmark](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/guidorosso_the-rive-renderer-is-66x-faster-here-activity-7060336385030819841-QkSZ)

##### stilus  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go sparse 2D rasterizer; 2.0x x/image/vector on 20k short strokes (first-party); 477x hatch figure is harness-inflated.

**Beats:** golang.org/x/image/vector (the Go project's rasterizer) and gogpu/gg v0.52.5 CPU rasterizer — First-party README table produced by bench/compare_test.go (go test -bench, one goroutine, bench module on Go 1.26 with x/image v0.46.0 and gogpu/gg v0.52.5) on an unnamed 'cloud Xeon @ 2.1 GHz', A3 page at 150 dpi: 20,000 short 0.35 mm strokes take 55 ms with stilus versus 111 ms with x/image/vector (2.0x, derived from page data) and 2,090 ms with gg; 2,000 page-spanning hairline hatch lines take 70 ms versus 33,400 ms (477x) and 14,800 ms. The x/image/vector side uses stilus's own stroker and a separate box-sized rasterizer for each outline.

**Known shortcoming:** Go (language-filter mismatch). The 477x on hatch lines is unfair: the baseline builds one golang.org/x/image/vector rasterizer per 45-degree page-spanning line sized to its bounding box; short strokes at 2.0x are roughly fair. Bench module uses Go 1.26.0 on a 'cloud Xeon @ 2.1 GHz' only. Baseline is not a listed incumbent.

**Known shortcoming:** The 477x hatch figure is a harness artefact (retier-22 removes it): the x/image/vector side re-creates a page-spanning rasteriser per 45-degree line, paying about 3.6e9 bounding-box pixels in total, whereas one page-sized pass would take about 40 ms against stilus's 70 ms (derived, unmeasured). stilus clips a 10 mm page margin the others do not, skipping about 9% of the short strokes; comparison times are go test means while the Numbers table is a minimum of 15. Open issue #28 (conflation seams, 24.9% of pixels off by more than 16/255 on hatch; fix in PR #29); tags v0.4.0 to v0.7.0 were all cut on 1-2 October 2026, some commits by an AI agent account.

**How:** Cost follows edge length plus covered spans, not bounding-box area: edges are accumulated as FreeType/AGG-style area/cover cells into a 32-row band (24.8 fixed point) instead of a page-sized buffer, and the sweep integrates only the touched cells of narrow rows, or walks a dirty bitset and emits constant runs on wide rows, zeroing cells as it reads them. Stroked polyline segments take an analytic path in which each pixel's coverage is the difference of two closed-form half-plane areas; only the rows around joins and caps go through the accumulator. Rectangle clips cost nothing per pixel, compositing is SWAR on premultiplied RGBA8 (AVX2/AVX-512 kernels under GOEXPERIMENT=simd), destination rows are pre-touched so cache misses overlap, prepared Shapes let band-parallel workers reuse stroking, and drawing allocates nothing after warm-up.

**Use it when:**
- Go programs that render technical drawings, CAD- or PDF-like pages, maps or plots with many long thin strokes (hatching, contours) on the CPU, where x/image/vector's cost per path grows with the path's bounding-box area.
- Builds that must stay pure Go with no cgo, for cross-compiling or js/wasm.
- Large pages rendered in bands on several cores: the README Numbers table gives 67 ms on 1 core and 19 ms on 4 cores for 2,000 hatch lines at 0.35 mm, and 41 ms vs 12 ms for 20,000 short strokes.
- Custom compositors or GPU upload paths that want spans rather than pixels, by implementing Blitter or Shader.
- Render loops sensitive to GC pressure, since the README and alloc-gate tests claim zero allocations per scene after warm-up.

**Skip it when:**
- Production code that needs a stable, proven library: the repository is days old (0 stars, tags v0.4.0 to v0.7.0 all on 1-2 October 2026, one maintainer, some commits authored by an AI coding agent account), and the API is still moving.
- Text layout, font loading, colour management, or SVG/PDF parsing or output: the README lists these as out of scope.
- Dense overlapping fills or strokes of one colour that must look seamless: separately drawn paths conflate at anti-aliased edges. Open issue #28 reports 24.9% of pixels off by more than 16/255 on the 2,000-line hatch at 150 dpi against an exact union (Ghostscript 0.06%), and the proposed union fill is in open PR #29.
- Glyph-sized or short shapes where x/image/vector is already box-efficient: the gain there is about 2x (55 vs 111 ms on 20,000 short strokes), and the SIMD kernels stay scalar below 16 px spans.
- Picking a renderer across languages: only Go baselines (x/image/vector, gogpu/gg) were measured, with no comparison against C/C++ engines such as Blend2D, Skia or AGG.

**Integration:** Go module (github.com/timzifer/stilus); comparison benchmarks live in a separate bench module · none (standard library only); the bench module adds golang.org/x/image v0.46.0, gogpu/gg v0.52.5 and timzifer/figure · Go 1.24 (go.mod); Go 1.26 or 1.27 with GOEXPERIMENT=simd for the AVX2/AVX-512 compositing kernels · all GOOS/GOARCH including js/wasm with scalar kernels; SIMD kernels only on amd64 with GOEXPERIMENT=simd, chosen at run time

**Vs siblings:** The closest catalogued sibling is tdewolff/canvas (Go): pick stilus when you only need a fast, allocation-free rasterizer core for stroke-heavy pages and will build the rest yourself, and tdewolff/canvas when you want a complete Go vector library with text and file output. For C or C++ code, Blend2D or Vello CPU have far stronger evidence.

**Gotchas:**
- Strokes thinner than one device pixel are drawn one pixel wide (PDFium-style hairlines), so very thin lines come out wider and darker than their exact geometry.
- Dash patterns past the subdivision budget skip or truncate the affected subpath and set ErrDashBudget, and patterns finer than a quarter pixel are drawn as a solid stroke at the pattern's mean coverage; the Canvas never panics, so check Err() after drawing.
- The SIMD kernels exist only with GOEXPERIMENT=simd on amd64, and the experiment's API changed between Go 1.26 and 1.27 (handled by build-tagged wrappers); STILUS_SIMD=0 or 256 forces scalar or AVX2-only at run time.
- Drawing many paths of one paint one by one gives conflation seams on touching anti-aliased edges (issue #28); until a union fill lands, merge such geometry into one path yourself.

**Status:** Very active but brand new (95 commits, last commit 2026-10-02, latest tag v0.7.0 on 2026-10-02, 0 stars, one open issue and one open PR); MIT and dependency-free, so copyable, but treat it as experimental.

[repo](https://github.com/timzifer/stilus) · [benchmark](https://github.com/timzifer/stilus)

##### TFT_eSPI  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Arduino TFT driver plus drawing library for ESP32, RP2040, ESP8266 and STM32; 1.3x to 4.7x faster than Adafruit_GFX on an ILI9341 at 40 MHz.

**Beats:** Adafruit_GFX (Adafruit-GFX-Library) with the Adafruit_ILI9341 driver — One single-pass run of moononournation's Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ (2021-06-16; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6, TTGO T8 v1.8 ESP32, PSRAM off, ILI9341 over SPI at 40 MHz, no DMA; compiler flags, CPU clock and TFT_eSPI version not recorded) timed the same test body in each library: TFT_eSPI beat Adafruit_GFX with Adafruit_ILI9341 by 4.7x on outline circles, 4.5x on text, 4.0x on lines, 1.8x on pixels and 1.26-1.3x on fills. Timings stop after end_tft_write's SPI-busy wait, so they include the final transfer; the 2020 run of the same suite gave noticeably different TFT_eSPI numbers, and the README's own '3 to 10 times faster' claim has no benchmark behind it.

**Known shortcoming:** Embedded SPI display driver, a weak fit for 2D rasterizers; the only numbers are a competitor's run (Arduino_GFX author's result.txt, TTGO T8 ESP32, ILI9341 at 40 MHz, 2021-06-16) against Adafruit_GFX, not a listed incumbent. The README's 'typically 3 to 10 times faster' has no benchmark behind it. February 2026 commits include a DMA code fix.

**Known shortcoming:** Fills are bound by the SPI link: TFT_eSPI reaches 98% of the 40 MHz limit against Adafruit_GFX's 78% (derived from page data), so the fill gain is only 1.26x, and LovyanGFX is faster on 9 of 13 shared rows of the same result.txt. Configuration lives in the library folder with a shipped default of 27 MHz SPI; no RTOS mutex (plain bool flags); DMA only for image pushes; open issues #3329 (ESP32-S3 crash on cores newer than 2.0.14) and #3438 (C6/H2 need edits); last release V2.5.43 predates the February 2026 fixes on master (2.5.44) after a gap from July 2024.

**How:** On ESP32 it bypasses the Arduino SPI library and writes the SPI peripheral registers directly (TFT_WRITE_BITS sets the length register, the W0 data register and the SPI_USR start bit), and toggles DC and CS with single GPIO set/clear register writes. Solid fills (pushBlock) load the 64-byte W0-W15 buffer with the colour once and re-trigger 512-bit transfers, so a fill streams at the SPI link rate; fillScreen reached 98% of the 40 MHz link limit in the benchmark versus 78% for Adafruit_GFX (derived from page data). drawPixel caches the last column and row address and skips re-sending CASET or PASET when they are unchanged. drawLine splits Bresenham's line into horizontal or vertical runs drawn with drawFastHLine/drawFastVLine, circles are drawn as runs too, and one bus transaction is held across a whole primitive (inTransaction) instead of one per pixel.

**Use it when:**
- Arduino or PlatformIO firmware on ESP32, ESP32-S2/S3/C3, RP2040, ESP8266 or STM32F/L4 driving a supported SPI panel, where Adafruit_GFX plus a controller driver is too slow for pixel-, line- and text-heavy screens.
- Per-pixel or line-heavy drawing (plots, gauges, wireframes): it had the fastest Pixels (775,781 us) and Lines (264,950 us) rows of the four libraries measured.
- RP2040 with 8- or 16-bit parallel panels driven by PIO, with DMA, which the README reports at 4 ms to clear a 320x480 screen.
- Projects that want a large example set and ecosystem: Sprites for flicker-free updates, vlw smooth fonts from flash arrays or LittleFS, OpenFontRender TrueType add-on, TFT_eWidget GUI widgets, XPT2046 touch.
- Porting an existing Adafruit_GFX sketch with minimal source changes.

**Skip it when:**
- Recent ESP32 Arduino cores and new chips: open issues report ESP32-S3 boot crashes on cores newer than 2.0.14 (#3329) and that ESP32-C6/H2 on core 3.0.x need local modifications (#3438). The Feb 2026 commits fix DMA on C3/S3 for 3.x board packages, but the last tagged release, V2.5.43 (6 March), predates them.
- When raw speed on ESP32 SPI is the only criterion: LovyanGFX beat it on 9 of the 13 rows both ran in the same 2021 run (TFT_eSPI won only Text, Pixels, Lines and outline Circles), by up to 17% (Rounded rects outline 13,089 vs 15,371 us), and also ran the Arcs rows that TFT_eSPI lacked then (derived from page data).
- Fill-dominated screens: fills are bound by the SPI clock, so at 40 MHz the gain over Adafruit_GFX is only 1.25x to 1.3x (Screen fill 1.26x, Rectangles filled 1.26x, Rounded rects filled 1.26x); a faster bus, a parallel panel or partial redraws matter more.
- Generic Arduino boards outside the optimised list: the README says they fall back to the slower Arduino SPI calls, and only SPI panels are supported there.
- Projects needing runtime display selection or several different panels in one build: the configuration is compile-time and global to the library folder.
- Desktop or vector-graphics work: it is an embedded panel driver with integer primitives, not a general path rasterizer like the Blend2D, Skia or AGG entries in this category.

**Integration:** Arduino library compiled from source (TFT_eSPI.cpp plus a per-processor file); also usable as an ESP-IDF component that requires the arduino component · Arduino core for the target (SPI; FS/SPIFFS or LittleFS for smooth fonts loaded from flash); ESP-IDF spi_master driver for ESP32 DMA; Earle Philhower's arduino-pico core for RP2040 PIO features · Arduino IDE or PlatformIO; ESP32 Arduino board package 2.x.x or later for the ESP32 family (README); arduino-pico core for RP2040 PIO · Optimised: RP2040, ESP32, ESP32-S2/S3/C3, ESP8266, STM32F1/F2/F4/F7 (DMA on ESP32, RP2040 and STM32 SPI); other 32-bit Arduino boards through generic Arduino SPI calls

**Vs siblings:** Pick TFT_eSPI over LovyanGFX when per-pixel and line drawing dominate, you are on RP2040 parallel/PIO panels, or you rely on its Sprite, smooth-font and widget ecosystem; pick LovyanGFX for the fastest fills, shapes and arcs on ESP32 SPI, runtime panel configuration and better tracking of new ESP32 cores. Pick Arduino_GFX when you need its wider range of data-bus classes and panels; it was slower than both on lines, shapes and pixels but fastest on text in the same run.

**Gotchas:**
- Configuration lives inside the library folder (User_Setup.h / User_Setup_Select.h); updating the library overwrites it unless you keep setups in a sibling folder as the README's Tips describe. The shipped default User_Setup.h sets SPI_FREQUENCY to 27 MHz, not the 40 MHz used in the benchmark.
- On ESP32, pushBlock and drawPixel return before the last SPI transfer finishes (the 'Do not wait here' comment and tft_Write_16N); end_tft_write waits, but code that toggles the shared bus inside startWrite()/endWrite() must account for it. Sharing the bus with an SD card requires TFT_MISO/MOSI/SCLK to be defined explicitly (README).
- DMA is used only by pushImageDMA/pushPixelsDMA; fillRect, lines and text always use the blocking register path, and DMA is unavailable for ILI9481/ILI9486/ILI9488 over SPI.
- Smooth (vlw) fonts cannot be scaled with setTextSize, and a later change added the smooth-font background-rendering flag as a new setTextColor parameter, which the README calls breaking for some sketches.

**Status:** Active but slow-moving: after a gap from July 2024 to February 2026, a burst of commits (DMA fix for ESP32 C3/S3 on 3.x board packages, STM32L4 DMA, new setups) ends with a README update on 2026-04-03; master reports version 2.5.44 while the latest tagged release is V2.5.43, with 278 open issues and 75 open pull requests. The licence (FreeBSD two-clause for Bodmer's code plus Adafruit BSD and MIT notices) makes it copyable, and a June 2025 issue (#3770) calling it abandoned recommended LovyanGFX.

[repo](https://github.com/Bodmer/TFT_eSPI) · [benchmark](https://github.com/moononournation/Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ/blob/master/result.txt)

##### ThorVG  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

MIT C++ SVG/Lottie vector engine; its CPU renderer averaged 2.9x Skia raster fps on 5k-shape scenes (4 threads vs 1).

**Beats:** Skia (CPU raster backend, Skia v148) — First-party chart from ThorVG's own public harness (thorvg/thorvg.benchmark): 5,000 shapes per frame at 2560x1440 on an Apple M2 Pro (macOS 26), ThorVG v1.1 with 4 worker threads against Skia v148 from vcpkg drawing single-threaded into a raster surface, frame time including clear and SDL_UpdateWindowSurface; per-test ratios run from 1.0x (rotated images) to 5.6x (rotated rects plus stroke), and the headline 2.9x is their arithmetic mean. No compiler or Skia build flags are named, and no independent measurement exists.

**Known shortcoming:** README chart (2.9x mean of 10 per-test ratios vs Skia v148, Apple M2 Pro) runs ThorVG with 4 worker threads (default since commit 2f87860, 2026-08-31, the day the chart was updated) against single-threaded Skia raster, which the README does not say; compiler unnamed. Image and gradient cases are only about 1.0-1.2x. Maintainer discussion #1815: no Blend2D comparison exists.

**Known shortcoming:** Beyond the 4-thread versus 1-thread asymmetry, the compared work differs: every Skia paint has setAntiAlias(true) while ThorVG fills axis-aligned rectangles as pixel-rounded boxes without anti-aliasing (_axisAlignedRect, utilBBox, _rasterRect) and skips AA on fills under opaque strokes of 2 px or more (SwShapeTask::antialiasing), so the 4.4x Rects, 4.0x Rects+Stroke and 5.6x Rotated Rects+Stroke rows render less work; the like-for-like anti-aliased rows are Rotated Rects 3.6x and Circles 3.7x, still on 4 threads, and the default meson extra=openmp also row-parallelises the scaled-image loops. tvgSwRle.cpp carries FreeType License text (credit needed beyond MIT); open bug #4751 (CPU partial rendering); --help says threads default to the maximum while the code says 4.

**How:** Per-shape preparation (outline transform, stroking and scan conversion into RLE coverage spans, using a rasterizer derived from FreeType's anti-aliased 'gray' rasterizer) runs as tasks on a worker pool sized by tvg::Initializer::init(n), while the calling thread composites the spans with NEON or AVX2 span blenders. Retained shapes are re-prepared only when their path, transform or colour flags change. Two quality shortcuts save work: axis-aligned unclipped rectangles take a 'fast track' that skips scan conversion and fills a pixel-rounded box without anti-aliasing, and fills under an opaque stroke at least 2 px wide are scan-converted without anti-aliasing. Optional OpenMP row-parallel loops (image scaling, premultiply) and dirty-region partial rendering (SmartRender) add further gains in some scenes.

**Use it when:**
- Lottie playback or SVG icon/UI rendering on the CPU in a C++ app on embedded, mobile or desktop targets, where a core of about 170KB and no mandatory dependencies matter (README lists LVGL, an Espressif ESP-IDF component, Godot, Tizen and Canva iOS as users).
- Frames with thousands of retained geometric shapes that move every frame and spare cores to run the worker pool: the README chart gives 3.6x on rotated rectangles and 3.7x on circles over single-threaded Skia v148 raster on an Apple M2 Pro, both anti-aliased on both sides, with ThorVG on 4 worker threads.
- Mostly static UIs where only small regions change, since SmartRender partial rendering repaints only dirty regions (the benchmark turns it off, so this gain is not in the chart).
- Projects that want one scene-graph API across CPU, OpenGL/ES, WebGL and WebGPU backends, including WebAssembly builds.

**Skip it when:**
- Image- or gradient-heavy content: the chart shows parity with Skia for PNG images (6.4 vs 6.0 fps), rotated images (4.4 vs 4.4) and linear/radial gradients (1.1x and 1.2x), so switching buys little there.
- Single-core or core-limited deployments: the published 2.9x mean pits ThorVG with 4 worker threads (and OpenMP if linked) against single-threaded Skia raster, and no single-threaded ThorVG figure is published.
- When you need exact anti-aliased edges on axis-aligned rectangles at fractional coordinates or on fills under thick opaque strokes: the fast track snaps such rectangles to whole pixels, and a TODO in _axisAlignedRect admits it hurts smooth rectangle movement.
- When you want the fastest CPU rasterizer: Blend2D and Vello CPU have independent thesis measurements against Skia, ThorVG has none, and in discussion #1815 (December 2023) the maintainer said accurate data including Blend2D was still needed.
- Full SVG 1.1/2 documents (only the SVG Tiny subset; no SVG animation, interactivity or multimedia), PDF output, or Skia's breadth in text shaping and colour management.

**Integration:** shared lib by default via meson (static with -Ddefault_library=static); packaged in vcpkg, Conan, Homebrew, Debian, Fedora, MSYS2 and others · none required; optional OpenMP for the CPU engine (meson option extra=openmp is on by default), libpng/libjpeg-turbo/libwebp for external image loaders (built-in static loaders exist), OpenGL 3.3/ES 3.0 or wgpu-native v29 for the GPU backends · C++14 (meson default cpp_std=c++14), meson and ninja; GCC/Clang builds use -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti · Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, web (WASM), Tizen and RTOS/ESP32 per README; CPU SIMD is AVX2 on x86/x86-64 and NEON on ARM/AArch64 (meson simd option, on by default), with a scalar C fallback

**Vs siblings:** Pick ThorVG over Blend2D, Vello CPU or AGG when you need SVG and Lottie loading, text, a retained scene graph and optional GPU backends in one small C++14 library for embedded or mobile targets; pick Blend2D when raw single-threaded CPU fill speed is the goal (independent thesis data, about 4x Skia), and LunaSVG when you only rasterize static SVG files.

**Gotchas:**
- Axis-aligned, unclipped rectangles are filled as pixel-rounded boxes without anti-aliasing (tvgSwShape.cpp _axisAlignedRect, tvgSwUtil.cpp utilBBox, tvgSwRaster.cpp _rasterRect), and fills under an opaque stroke of 2 px or more are scan-converted aliased (SwShapeTask::antialiasing). Output therefore differs from Skia or Blend2D on such shapes, and slowly moving rectangles step in whole pixels.
- SwCanvas::gen() with the default option turns on SmartRender partial rendering, which has an open 'cpu: partial rendering bug' (#4751) and, per the README, can add overhead when nearly everything changes each frame; pass EngineOption::None for full redraws, as the benchmark does. EngineOption::Aliased (turn AA off everywhere) is marked experimental.
- With OpenMP built in (the default meson option), the first SwRenderer calls omp_set_num_threads(threads), which also changes the default team size for the host program's own OpenMP regions on that thread.
- The scan converter is derived from FreeType code and tvgSwRle.cpp carries the FreeType Project License text, which asks for a FreeType credit in your documentation in addition to the MIT notice.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-03, release v1.1.2 on 18 September 2026, about 1.9k stars, dev version 1.2.0 in meson.build) under MIT with FreeType-licensed portions, so it is copyable and widely packaged.

[repo](https://github.com/thorvg/thorvg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/thorvg/thorvg)

##### tiny-skia-cpp  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

C++20 port of Rust tiny-skia (Skia-subset CPU rasterizer) with AVX2/NEON backends; first-party 1.2-1.9x faster than the Rust original.

**Beats:** Rust tiny-skia (linebender/tiny-skia, a Skia subset) — First-party Google Benchmark runs (RenderPerfBench.cpp, 5 repetitions, mean real time) of one 512x512 anti-aliased FillRect and one FillPath, C++ AVX2+FMA or NEON build against Rust tiny-skia 0.12.0 called through FFI, on unnamed Apple Silicon and Intel/AMD machines with an unstated compiler: README 1.9x/1.3x (FillRect, ARM/x86) and 1.4x/1.2x (FillPath). The README chart matches the 2026-03-03 calibration in run_render_perf_regression_test.sh (arm64 1.42 FillPath, 1.91 FillRect; x86 1.18 and 1.29) and was never updated; later arm64 calibrations rose to 2.00/2.80 (2026-03-05) and 2.90/3.50 (2026-04-02), so the ARM numbers are stale rather than contradicted, while the x86 side still compares AVX2+FMA C++ with SSE2-only Rust.

**Known shortcoming:** Port of linebender/tiny-skia (catalogued at A in this wave), so a possible duplicate; its baseline is the Rust original, not a listed incumbent. The x86 comparison is unfair: the C++ build uses -mavx2 -mfma while the Rust tiny-skia was built without AVX, and FillPath runs analytic anti-aliasing against the Rust path. README ARM figures (1.9x/1.4x) conflict with the committed regression baselines (3.50/2.90).

**Known shortcoming:** A C++ port of the listed linebender/tiny-skia (duplicate rule would apply; kept because it adds analytic anti-aliasing and SVG filters). The README chart is stale: it matches the 2026-03-03 calibration (arm64 1.42/1.91, x86 1.18/1.29) while later arm64 calibrations read 2.00/2.80 and 2.90/3.50 (2026-04-02). Flaws: the timed loop clears the pixmap (memset in C++, a per-pixel store loop in Rust); FillPath since April 2 is analytic AA against Rust supersampling; the regression guard is skipped in CI (no -c option); x86 compares AVX2 against SSE2. The native target needs AVX2 plus FMA with no runtime dispatch (illegal instruction elsewhere). PR #30 (2026-07-04) fixed a one-pixel out-of-bounds write in blitAntiH2/V2 (benchmark shapes never touch the edge).

**How:** Rendering goes through a port of Skia's raster pipeline (high-precision float and low-precision 16-bit stage paths) whose vector types (F32x8T, U16x16T and friends in src/tiny_skia/wide/) are hand-written for AVX2+FMA on x86-64 and NEON on ARM64, selected at compile time, with a scalar fallback. Since 2026-04-02 anti-aliased path fills use a port of Skia's Analytic Anti-Aliasing rasterizer (SkScan_AAAPath, src/tiny_skia/scan/PathAa.cpp), which computes exact edge coverage instead of the supersampled scanlines Rust tiny-skia uses. Axis-aligned anti-aliased rectangles take a dedicated fillRectAa path with no edge building.

**Use it when:**
- A C++ program needs a small, dependency-free, BSD-licensed CPU rasterizer with Skia-style semantics (SVG-like paths, strokes, gradients, patterns, masks), for example SVG rendering, thumbnails or offscreen chart output.
- You are porting Rust tiny-skia or resvg-style rendering code to C++ and want output that matches the Rust crate within a golden-image tolerance.
- ARM64 / Apple Silicon targets, where the project's own numbers show the largest gain over Rust tiny-skia (README 1.4-1.9x; later calibrated baselines 2.9-3.5x).
- You need SVG filter primitives (blur, colour matrix, lighting, displacement, turbulence) in C++ without pulling in a browser engine or Skia.

**Skip it when:**
- Maximum CPU rendering throughput: it is measured only against Rust tiny-skia, which its own README puts 20-100% slower than Skia on x86-64 and 100-300% slower on ARM; on the independent bl_bench M1 Pro run, Blend2D, Vello CPU and the JUCE renderer (3.09x Rust tiny-skia, derived from page data) are far ahead of Rust tiny-skia, and none of them has been compared with this port.
- Portable x86-64 binaries: the native target is compiled with -mavx2 -mfma (CMake and Bazel) with no runtime dispatch, so it faults on CPUs without AVX2 and FMA (the author's Donner issue #1286 says this of the vendored copy); ship the tiny_skia_scalar target or per-ISA builds instead.
- Text rendering: like Rust tiny-skia (whose README lists text as the main missing feature), the drawing API is fillRect, fillPath, strokePath, drawPixmap and applyMask only.
- You need bit-exact Rust tiny-skia output: analytic AA and other changes make it near-pixel-accurate only.
- Low risk tolerance: 9 stars, one maintainer with many commits co-authored by an AI assistant, no tagged releases seen, and an out-of-bounds pixel write in the anti-aliased blitter fixed only on 2026-07-04 (PR #30).

**Integration:** static lib · none at runtime; the tests and benchmarks use GoogleTest, Google Benchmark and a Rust toolchain (rules_rust) for the tiny-skia FFI cross-checks · C++20; GCC 11+, Clang 14+ or MSVC 19.30+ (CONTRIBUTING); Bazel 7+ or CMake 3.16+ · x86-64 (native target requires AVX2+FMA), ARM64 (NEON), any other target via the scalar library; CI builds Bazel on Ubuntu and CMake on Ubuntu and macOS, with no Windows CI

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Rust tiny-skia when the host program is C++ and you want the same rendering model with native SIMD and SVG filters; pick Blend2D or AGG instead when raw speed or a long track record matters, since this port has never been measured against them, Skia or Cairo.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD backend is chosen at compile time: link tiny_skia (native) or tiny_skia_scalar deliberately, and on x86 the native build assumes AVX2+FMA on every target machine.
- Versions before PR #30 (merged 2026-07-04) could read or write one pixel past the pixmap in RasterPipelineBlitter::blitAntiH2/blitAntiV2 when an anti-aliased edge touched the right or bottom edge; use a later commit.
- Anti-aliased fillPath uses Skia's analytic AA, not Rust tiny-skia's supersampling, so edge pixels differ slightly from the Rust crate; the golden-image tests compare with a tolerance.
- The library compiles with -ffp-contract=off; if you vendor the sources into a build without it (or with -ffast-math), float rounding may drift from the golden images (inference from the build files).

**Status:** Active but small (156 commits, 9 stars, last author commit 2026-07-04, then only renovate[bot] dependency PRs); BSD-3-Clause and dependency-free so easy to vendor, and the author also vendors it as the default CPU renderer in jwmcglynn/donner (third_party/tiny-skia-cpp), whose copy already adds a wasm simd128 backend the standalone repo lacks.

[repo](https://github.com/jwmcglynn/tiny-skia-cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/jwmcglynn/tiny-skia-cpp)

##### Vello CPU (sparse strips renderer)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust CPU 2D vector renderer (sparse strips, SIMD, optional threads); about 2.4x Skia and 4x Cairo raster speed on M1.

**Beats:** Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also Rust tiny-skia, raqote, AGG, JUCE — In the author's ETH Zurich master's thesis (first-party, not independently reproduced), a Blend2D bl_bench fork on an Apple M1 Pro rendered 1000 unaligned 256x256 solid rectangles in 14.2 ms with vello-cpu ST, against 50.3 ms for Skia (CPU, version unstated), 21.9 ms for Cairo 1.18.4 and 10.8 ms for Blend2D 0.12.0. Rust crates were built with target-feature=+avx2 on x86 and no extra flags on ARM, and the C++ compilers and flags are not stated. Across the published result JSON it was faster than Skia in 954 of 1044 cells and Cairo in 822 of 870 (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: the ETH thesis is by the Vello CPU author (first-party, no peer review), and the vello-cpu harness backend is not in the public fork LaurenzV/blend2d-apps. Rust library (language-filter mismatch; C++ use needs FFI). Multi-thread gain is up to 5.3x, not about 4x. Newer 2026-06-08 chart data has Vello CPU at 9.26 ms vs Blend2D 10.8 ms on RectU 256.

**Known shortcoming:** The vello-cpu backend used in the thesis harness is not public code, only the vello_cpu_c bindings (OptimizeSpeed u8 pipeline; strokes use bevel joins while the other backends keep their default joins). On the x86 i9-14900K run Cairo 1.18.2 wins 16 tests at 256x256 (StrokeRectA Solid 8.2x, FillRectA Pattern_NN 3.7x, FillRectU Solid 1.2x); on the 2026-06-08 M1 run 8-thread scaling fell from 3.96x to 3.02x and image-pattern rectangles are up to 37% slower; Blend2D with 8 threads wins all 174 cells at 256x256. Complex filters panic.

**How:** Paths are flattened (kurbo's analytic quadratic subdivision, with an early exit that emits one line when a curve cannot exceed the 0.25 px tolerance and a lookup table instead of powf when estimating quad counts) and binned into 4x4 tiles. The tiles become sparse strips, a run-length encoding that keeps per-pixel coverage only along path edges and marks interior spans as cheap solid fills, so cost grows with edge length more than with area. A coarse rasterizer then builds per-wide-tile command lists, and fine rasterization composites them with SIMD code written once over the fearless_simd abstraction and dispatched at runtime (NEON, SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512, WASM SIMD128, scalar fallback), by default on a u8 pipeline. With the multithreading feature, path rendering and fine rasterization run on a rayon pool while the main thread does coarse rasterization.

**Use it when:**
- Pure-Rust CPU rendering of GUI, document or SVG content where tiny-skia or raqote is the bottleneck. In the author's Blend2D-harness data on an Apple M1 Pro (2025-09-24) vello-cpu ST was faster than tiny-skia in 843 of 870 cells (geometric mean about 4.2x) and raqote in 881 of 1044 (about 2.2x) (derived from page data).
- Medium to large shapes (32x32 and up) on AArch64, especially many-edge polygons and curve-heavy paths. On the M1 Pro its geometric-mean lead over Skia grows from about 1.5x at 8x8 to 3.3x at 256x256, and over Cairo from 3.2x to 4.5x (derived from page data).
- Curve-heavy small shapes: on 8x8 FillFish Solid it was 2.2x faster than Blend2D in 2025-09 and 2.9x in the 2026-06-08 run (derived from page data), thanks to the curve-flattening shortcut.
- Software rendering that must scale across cores: the 8-thread mode gave a geometric mean of about 4.0x over its own single-thread time on the M1 Pro (2025-09-24) and 5.3x on an i9-14900K (2026-01-22) (derived from page data).
- no_std/WASM targets that need a safe, dependency-light rasteriser: the crate is #![no_std] (with alloc) and #![forbid(unsafe_code)], with a libm feature and WASM SIMD paths.

**Skip it when:**
- You want the fastest CPU rasteriser regardless of language: Blend2D was faster in about 95% of cells (vello-cpu ST geometric mean about 0.57x of Blend2D on M1, 0.43x on i9-14900K), and Blend2D 8T beat vello-cpu 8T in 174 of 174 cells at 256x256 in the 2026-06-08 run (derived from page data).
- x86 workloads dominated by rectangles or image patterns. In the i9-14900K run Cairo 1.18.2 beat it at 256x256 on 16 tests, for example StrokeRectA Solid by about 8x, FillRectA Pattern_NN by about 3.7x and FillRectU Solid by about 1.2x (derived from page data). The README itself says x86 still has 'more room for performance improvements'.
- Very small simple shapes such as icons and UI glyph-sized rectangles: the fixed 4x4 tile adds overhead, and at 8x8 AGG and JUCE beat it on aligned solid rectangles in the thesis (Figure 39).
- C or C++ projects that need a supported API: the only C bindings (vello_cpu_c) say they are 'not meant for production' and exist only for the benchmark harness.
- Scenes with complex filter graphs (they panic) or any filter in multi-threaded mode (unsupported), per the crate docs.

**Integration:** crate (vello_cpu 0.3.0 on crates.io; Rust library, no official C API) · vello_common (kurbo/peniko geometry and paint types, fearless_simd, smallvec, guillotiere), bytemuck, hashbrown; optional png, glifo (text, default on), and rayon, crossbeam-channel, ordered-channel, thread_local for the multithreading feature · Rust 1.89 (MSRV), edition 2024 · Any Rust target with alloc; runtime SIMD dispatch for x86/x86-64 (SSE2 baseline, SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512) and AArch64 NEON; WASM SIMD128 (and relaxed SIMD) chosen at compile time; scalar fallback elsewhere; big-endian rendering fixed in 0.3.0

**Vs siblings:** Pick Vello CPU over tiny-skia or raqote when you want the fastest maintained pure-Rust CPU renderer: it beat both in most cells, tiny-skia by about 4x. Pick Blend2D instead when C/C++ is fine and peak single-thread or 8-thread speed matters, and AGG or JUCE only for very small shapes.

**Gotchas:**
- The API is pre-1.0 and churns: 0.3.0 (2026-10-02) replaced CompositeMode with TargetInit, renamed pop_clip_path to pop_clip and changed glyph-run return types, and 0.1.0 replaced render_to_pixmap with render/render_with. The C bindings still call render_to_pixmap and pin a git revision (35a4279).
- Turning on the multithreading feature changes the default: RenderContext::new then uses up to 8 worker threads. Create contexts with RenderSettings { num_threads: 0, .. } for single-threaded rendering, and do not create many contexts, because each one owns a thread pool.
- Default rendering uses the u8 pipeline (RenderMode::OptimizeSpeed). Enable the f32_pipeline feature and OptimizeQuality when you need accuracy, for example for snapshot tests. Canvas width and height are u16, so the maximum is 65535 px.
- Open sparse-strips issues include FunkyPathsScene rendering incorrectly (#1240), zero-length paths with round caps not following the SVG spec (#1450), image quality loss when downscaling more than 2x (#1289), and slow image-heavy scenes (#1427 bunnymark: 70 ms ST, 26 ms MT, versus 273 ms for Skia CPU and 8.3 ms for Skia Ganesh). Version 0.0.9 widened a winding histogram from i8 to i16 after high winding counts overflowed (PR #1673).

**Status:** Very active (vello_cpu 0.3.0 released 2026-10-02, about 5.1M crates.io downloads, 3.8M of them recent) and dual-licensed Apache-2.0 OR MIT, so it is copyable. It is still 0.x with breaking releases every few weeks, so pin the version.

[repo](https://github.com/linebender/vello) · [benchmark](https://github.com/LaurenzV/master-thesis/blob/main/main.pdf)

##### vger (Audulus)  `Objective-C++ and Metal (C API)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Small Metal GPU renderer for immediate-mode UIs (Apple only); its author reports 120 fps where nanovg managed 30 fps.

**Beats:** nanovg — The only number is the author's README anecdote: in the Audulus UI on an unnamed 120 Hz iPad, vger holds 120 fps while nanovg (which nanovg build, presumably Metal, is not stated) drops to 30 fps. The author attributes this to CPU-side tessellation in nanovg. 120 fps is the display cap, so vger's real headroom and the GPU cost are unknown, and there is no scene description, compiler or frame-time data. The commented-out testNanovgPerf in Tests/vgerTests/vgerTests.mm would not be a like-for-like check either. It calls a stale API that no longer exists (vgerColorPaint without a context, a vgerPrim aggregate), strokes 5.12 px wide where testBezierPerf strokes 1 px, and does not wait for nanovg's GPU work, while the vger test waits with waitUntilCompleted and also times its rand() calls.

**Known shortcoming:** The '120fps vs 30fps' claim against nanovg appears only in the README's 'Why?' section: unnamed 120 Hz iPad, Metal only, no scene or frame times; testNanovgPerf in Tests/vgerTests/vgerTests.mm is commented out and no results are published. Implementation is Objective-C++ plus Metal with a C API (Apple-only).

**Known shortcoming:** Metal GPU UI renderer, Apple only (macOS 11+, iOS 14+): comparable to GPU renderers (nanovg Metal, Rive, TGFX, vkvg, Vello), not to CPU rasterizers. Even-odd fill only; cubics approximated by two quadratics; no joins, dashes or scissor. vgerQuadTo silently drops segments past 1024 and GPUVec drops primitives past 256 MB; single-buffered by default; swift build fails (issue #15). The commented-out testNanovgPerf is itself flawed (stale API, 5.12 px versus 1 px strokes, no GPU wait on the nanovg side, rand() inside the vger timing), so the README anecdote stays the sole evidence.

**How:** Each primitive becomes one instanced quad, and the fragment shader evaluates the shape's signed distance analytically (SDF, anti-aliased with smoothstep over fwidth), so the CPU does no path tessellation. The CPU only appends primitive records into shared-storage MTLBuffers. A compute pass then computes bounds, and a single instanced draw per layer covers everything, split only when the texture changes. Path fills are cut on the CPU into horizontal slabs (vgerPathScanner), and each slab's quad tests a pixel against only the segments active in that band. The inside test is even-odd: it counts crossings with each segment's chord and flips again inside the region between the curve and its chord, a 'reverse Loop-Blinn' that avoids solving quadratics. Text layouts are cached per string and glyphs go into a CoreGraphics-rasterized atlas.

**Use it when:**
- iOS 14+ or macOS 11+ app whose UI redraws every frame (audio and synth UIs, node editors, plotting) and is CPU-bound in nanovg or CoreGraphics because of path tessellation.
- Scenes made mostly of simple shapes (knobs, rounded rects, wires, short quadratic strokes, short text labels), where one instanced draw replaces thousands of tessellated meshes.
- You want a small, vendorable MIT renderer with a C drawing API that you can call from C++ or Swift, and you can write a little Objective-C++ or Swift glue for context creation and command-buffer encoding.
- Prototyping a GPU UI on Apple hardware that you may later port with the same design via the Rust/wgpu port audulus/vger-rs.

**Skip it when:**
- Any non-Apple target or headless CPU rendering: it needs Metal, and text depends on CoreText and CoreGraphics; use vger-rs or a CPU rasterizer instead.
- SVG or PDF-grade vector output: cubics are approximated by two quadratics ('crude approximation' per vger.h, 'lousy method' per the README), fills are even-odd only, and there are no path strokes with joins, caps or dashes, and vger.h has no clipping, scissor or blend-mode API.
- Large or complex paths: vgerQuadTo silently drops segments beyond 1024 per path, and vgerFill gives up (returns false) after 2048 slabs. Per-pixel cost grows with the number of segments active in a slab.
- Pixel-exact anti-aliasing: coverage is an SDF smoothstep across about one pixel, not exact area coverage. Open issues report different stroke widths for line and Bezier segments (#7) and propose better AA (#18).
- Workloads that need a measured advantage: the only comparison with nanovg is an anecdote, and nothing compares vger with Skia, Rive, Vello or other GPU renderers.

**Integration:** Swift Package (Objective-C++ and Metal sources, built as a library; also source-drop into an Xcode project) · Apple frameworks only (Metal, MetalKit, CoreText, CoreGraphics); bundles stb_rect_pack; the test target alone depends on wtholliday/MetalNanoVG (branch spm) · Swift tools 5.9 and C++20 (Package.swift); Xcode with the Metal compiler. Command-line `swift build` fails ('Bundle has no member module', missing default.metallib), open issue #15. · macOS 11+ and iOS 14+ on Metal GPUs only

**Vs siblings:** Pick vger over the Rive Renderer, TGFX or vkvg when the app is Apple-only, the scene uses vger's simple primitive set, and you want a few thousand lines of MIT code with a C API rather than a full engine. Pick those siblings (or Vello) when you need cross-platform GPUs, full path semantics or published comparative numbers. It is not comparable to the CPU rasterizers in this category (Blend2D, AGG, Blaze, tiny-skia), which produce exact-coverage pixels without a GPU.

**Gotchas:**
- Default is single-buffered: unless you pass VGER_DOUBLE_BUFFER or VGER_TRIPLE_BUFFER to vgerNew, vgerBegin reuses the same shared MTLBuffers the GPU may still be reading (vger.mm), so wait for the previous command buffer to finish or turn buffering on.
- Overflow can go unreported: vgerQuadTo ignores segments beyond 1024 per path, and GPUVec::append stops adding primitives once a buffer would exceed 256 MB (vgerScene.h). Check vgerFill's return value and vgerPrimCount.
- Lines are stored as degenerate quadratics, and cubics are split into two quadratics with no error control, so SVG-style cubic art can visibly deviate. Text is not affected because glyphs are rasterized into an atlas by CoreGraphics.
- Paints are per frame: paint indices from vgerColorPaint and the gradient calls become invalid after the next vgerBegin, and invalid indices make vgerFill return false.

**Status:** Active (commits through 2026-06-08, including a layer-specific encode API, clipped stroke prims and pixel-diff tests) and MIT-licensed (the header carries a zlib-style notice). It ships in the Audulus app, so it is copyable for Apple-only projects, but it is a single-maintainer library with 10 open issues.

[repo](https://github.com/audulus/vger) · [benchmark](https://github.com/audulus/vger)

##### vkvg  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Cairo-style 2D vector library in C on Vulkan; the author's chart shows it beating Cairo's GL ES3 backend on lines, circles and stars.

**Beats:** Cairo (GL ES3 backend) and Skia (Vulkan backend) — The only evidence is the author's vgperf chart from 2022-01. It shows median wall-clock seconds per iteration of 100 random shapes on a 512x512 window for vkvg, Cairo's GL ES3 backend and a patched Skia Vulkan build, with GPU, CPU, versions and options unstated. Derived readings: vkvg about 24x faster than Cairo ES3 on lines, 5x on circles and 3x on stars, tied on rectangles; against Skia about 3x faster on lines, tied on stars, slightly slower on rectangles and about 4x slower on circles. With the harness defaults the anti-aliasing is unequal (Cairo anti-aliases, vkvg and Skia do not), Skia's rectangle test uses different placement, and the harness no longer builds against current vkvg.

**Known shortcoming:** Chart dated 2022-01-19 (vgperf main.c, median seconds per iteration); the Cairo baseline is Cairo's GL ES3 backend, not its image backend; the stars test against Skia is a near tie, not a win. Ratios derived from chart readings.

**Known shortcoming:** The vgperf harness is not like-for-like at its defaults: with -a vkvg runs at 1 sample (non-antialiased per vkvg.h) and Skia has sk_paint_set_antialias(false) while Cairo uses CAIRO_ANTIALIAS_DEFAULT (antialiased), and the chart's options are unstated, so the 24x lines and 5x circles against Cairo are probably aliased against anti-aliased; the Skia rectangles are placed in [0, 0.2w) against [0, w) for the others; the chart omits Cairo's default image (CPU) backend. The harness calls vkvg_device_create_from_vk*, which no longer exists in include/vkvg.h, so the chart is not reproducible against current vkvg. logicOp is required (MoltenVK fails, #141); the MSVC Release flags are '/O2 /TC /W0 /Od' (probably unoptimised); only 4 compositing operators; open segfault #165; vkvg_flush blocks on a fence (#163).

**How:** Path geometry is tessellated on the CPU and appended to per-context vertex and index caches, which are drawn as batched indexed draws in one command buffer per flush, so many shapes share a pipeline and a submit. Strokes become triangle geometry with joins and caps, and curves are flattened with AGG's recursive Bezier subdivision (README credit). Non-zero fills are triangulated with the bundled GLU tessellator (VKVG_USE_GLUTESS, on by default) or ear clipping. Even-odd fills and clips use the stencil buffer: the path is drawn into the stencil, then a quad over the path bounds is covered. Anti-aliasing comes only from hardware MSAA chosen at device creation, and destroyed contexts are cached per thread so that recreating one is cheap.

**Use it when:**
- A Vulkan application on Linux or Windows (engine, tool UI, HUD, plotting overlay) that needs Cairo-style 2D drawing rendered into a VkImage on its own VkDevice and queue, with no CPU raster and upload step.
- Porting existing Cairo drawing code to the GPU: call names and semantics (paths, line caps and joins, dashes, gradients, save/restore) mostly map one to one.
- Frames with many thin strokes or simple polygons, batched in one context per frame. Lines were vkvg's largest margin in the author's chart: about 0.00013 s versus about 0.0031 s for Cairo GL ES3 per 100 random 1 px lines.
- You can accept MSAA anti-aliasing (2x to 8x samples) instead of exact-coverage anti-aliasing.

**Skip it when:**
- You need exact-coverage anti-aliasing or output that matches Cairo pixel for pixel. A 1-sample device (the default) draws aliased edges, and higher quality costs MSAA memory and bandwidth.
- macOS or iOS through MoltenVK: vkvg enables the logicOp device feature (vkvg_device.c), and device creation fails on an Apple M2 with VK_ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_PRESENT (issue #141, open since 2023-07).
- You need Cairo's full compositing model: only CLEAR, SOURCE, OVER and DIFFERENCE are enabled, the other operators are commented out of vkvg.h, and 'Operators' is still unchecked in the README to-do list.
- Production use where robustness matters. The README calls the project alpha, and open bugs include a save/restore segfault (#165), test crashes and validation errors (#121), first dashes with an offset not drawn (#50), and premultiplied-alpha problems on image load and save (#115, #156) and on unclipped paint (#157).
- Circle- or arc-heavy scenes, or targets without a Vulkan 1.1 GPU. In the author's own chart Skia's Vulkan backend was about 4x faster on circles, because vkvg tessellates every arc on the CPU. A CPU fallback exists only as an open idea (#149).
