**Integration:** static or shared lib (CMake, BUILD_SHARED_LIBS); AUR and MPR packages exist · Vulkan 1.1 loader and driver; git submodules vkh (jpbruyere/vkhelpers), glutess and vkvg-svg; bundled vk_mem_alloc; optional FontConfig, FreeType (stb_truetype otherwise) and HarfBuzz; GLFW for tests; glslc and xxd only to rebuild the shaders (precompiled SPIR-V headers are in the tree) · C11 (C_STANDARD 11 required), CMake 3.16+, Vulkan 1.1+ · Linux and Windows with a Vulkan 1.1 GPU driver. CI builds on Windows, Ubuntu and macOS, and CMake has an Android branch, but MoltenVK on Apple M2 fails at device creation (logicOp, #141).

**Vs siblings:** Pick vkvg over Blend2D, AGG or tiny-skia when the frame is already on a Vulkan GPU and you want Cairo-style calls that render straight into a VkImage. Pick vger for Apple-only Metal UIs, and the Rive Renderer or TGFX for a more mature GPU renderer with more backends. For exact anti-aliased output or CPU-only targets, Blend2D is the better-measured choice in this category.

**Gotchas:**
- Anti-aliasing is fixed when the device is created. vkvg.h says a 1-sample device is non-antialiased, so set info.samples above 1 for smooth edges. With deferredResolve the multisampled image is resolved only on vkvg_surface_get_vk_image or an explicit resolve call.
- vkvg_flush submits and then blocks the CPU on the context's fence until the GPU finishes (_flush_cmd_buff then _wait_ctx_flush_end). A full vertex buffer also forces a submit-and-wait in the middle of a path (_poly_fill). Flush once per frame, not per shape. Issue #163 (2026-06) reports long CPU waits in this function.
- The MSVC branch of the stock CMakeLists adds '/O2 /TC /W0 /Od' to non-Debug builds. cl lets the later /Od override /O2, so Windows builds are probably unoptimized unless you edit the flags. Unix Release builds use CMake's defaults.
- Clone with --recursive (forks need the submodule fallback URLs given in the README). The older entry points vkvg_device_create_from_vk and vkvg_device_create_from_vk_multisample are gone from include/vkvg.h (only vkvg_device_create(info) remains), so older code, including the vgperf harness, must be ported. With VKVG_USE_GLUTESS=OFF, ear clipping puts a stack VLA sized by the path's point count, so very large paths risk stack overflow.

**Status:** Actively developed by a single maintainer (639 commits, last 2026-10-01, version 0.3.0, self-described alpha, 35 open issues). MIT-licensed and copyable, but its only performance evidence is a 2022 chart made against an older API.

[repo](https://github.com/jpbruyere/vkvg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/jpbruyere/vgperf)

##### Pathfinder 3  `Rust (with C bindings via cargo-c)`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

Rust GPU rasterizer for glyphs and vector paths (OpenGL, Metal, WebGL 2); claims to match or beat CPU rasterizers, with no numbers.

**Beats:** Unnamed 'best CPU rasterizers' (README). FreeType, stb_truetype and font-rs are named as comparison points only in the 2017 Pathfinder 1 blog post (pcwalton.github.io), which is blocked here and is known only from a search snippet. — There is no measurement against any baseline. The README claims Pathfinder 'often matches or exceeds' unnamed 'best CPU rasterizers', with 'multi-factor speedups' at large sizes. doc/architecture.md quotes only absolute Pathfinder 3 stage times for the Ghostscript tiger at 1600x1600 on an i7-7920HQ with Intel HD Graphics 630 (about 2.2 ms CPU tile/cull/pack, 2.6 ms GPU fill, 2.3 ms GPU shade). An independent 2019 write-up by Mozilla's Nicolas Silva says only that it is 'a good deal faster at rendering very large and complex SVG drawings than using a CPU rasterizer and uploading the result to a texture', also without numbers, so tier D stands.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: README is qualitative, no named baseline or number in the repo; the 2017 blog post is blocked here and its source repo is 404. Rust library (language-filter mismatch). Kept as notable (3.9k stars, Servo).

**Known shortcoming:** No number against any baseline (tier D): doc/architecture.md gives absolute tiger 1600x1600 timings (2.2, 2.6 and 2.3 ms on an i7-7920HQ with HD 630) with no comparison, and the nical 2019 post is qualitative. crates.io renderer, canvas and text crates are stuck at 0.5.0 (2020-04-17) without the D3D11 compute mode; recent activity is pathfinder_simd 0.5.6 upkeep; open SSE4.1 undefined-behaviour issues #502 and #588. Category moved to rasterizers-2d.

**How:** Paths are cut into 16x16 tiles. Tiles that are entirely one solid colour are flagged, and tiles hidden behind them are culled before any GPU work, which avoids the overdraw of painter's-algorithm software renderers. Edges are rasterized into a 16-bit float coverage mask with exact trapezoidal area coverage (described as effectively 256xAA), and tiles are then shaded back to front from that mask. At the 'D3D9' level (OpenGL 3/WebGL 2) binning and tiling run on the CPU with SIMD (pathfinder_simd) and Rayon, pipelined with the GPU. At the 'D3D11' level (OpenGL 4.3, Metal) bin, fill and composite all run in GPU compute shaders. Because GPU fill parallelises across pixels while CPU rasterizer cost grows with pixel area, the claimed advantage is largest at large glyph sizes.

**Use it when:**
- Rust apps, or C/C++ apps willing to link a Rust static library, that already render with OpenGL or Metal and draw large, zoomed or per-frame-transformed text and vector paths, where CPU rasterize-and-upload is the bottleneck.
- Complex SVG- or PDF-like scenes with heavy overlap, where tile occlusion culling skips hidden geometry.
- Text placed in 3D or VR scenes, or animated in size, where a glyph-atlas cache from a CPU rasterizer keeps getting invalidated.
- As a readable reference design for tiled GPU vector rendering with exact area coverage.

**Skip it when:**
- You need CPU bitmaps or a glyph atlas (headless servers, no GPU, software fallback): use FreeType, fontdue or font-rs. Reading pixels back from the GPU gives up the advantage.
- You need shaping or line layout: Pathfinder delegates that to skribo/HarfBuzz, and the record's category fit is approximate.
- You want a stable, versioned dependency: the crates.io releases of pathfinder_canvas, pathfinder_renderer and pathfinder_text are still 0.5.0 from 2020-04-17, and that pathfinder_renderer has no D3D11 compute mode at all (checked in the 0.5.0 crate source), so the compute path the README highlights needs a git dependency on main. The README itself says 'under heavy development and is incomplete'.
- C or C++ projects that want a native library: the C bindings are 'less complete' (README), produce a static library only, need a Rust toolchain plus cargo-c, and pin old dependencies (font-kit 0.6, usvg 0.9).
- Small UI text on low-end hardware, where the README itself only claims to 'often match' CPU rasterizers, or CPUs without SSE4.1 (see gotchas).

**Integration:** crate (modular pathfinder_* Rust crates); static lib with a C API via cargo-c · rayon, font-kit, skribo (HarfBuzz), usvg/resvg for SVG, gl or metal bindings, half, hashbrown and others; C build needs cargo-c · not documented; Rust 2018 edition, CI builds on stable Rust; no rust-version declared on crates.io · Needs a GPU: OpenGL 3.0+/ES 3.0+, WebGL 2 or Metal ('D3D9' level, CPU binning); compute 'D3D11' level needs OpenGL 4.3 or Metal. CPU side: x86-64 (SIMD paths assume SSE4.1) and aarch64 (CI cross-builds the simd and geometry crates)

**Vs siblings:** The other entries in this category are CPU glyph rasterizers (font-rs, fontdue, TiTanF) or, in msdfgl's case, GPU atlas generators. Pick Pathfinder only when glyphs are drawn directly on the GPU at large or changing sizes and transforms. Pick fontdue or font-rs for CPU bitmaps and atlases at UI sizes, and msdfgl for scalable atlas-based text. For general GPU vector rendering, Vello (rasterizers-2d) is the actively developed compute renderer with third-party measurements.

**Gotchas:**
- pathfinder_simd calls SSE4.1 intrinsics (_mm_floor_ps, _mm_ceil_ps, _mm_min_epi32, _mm_max_epi32, _mm_mullo_epi32) from safe APIs without a target-feature check, so pre-SSE4.1 x86 CPUs hit undefined behaviour or illegal-instruction crashes. Issues #502 (2022) and #588 (May 2026) are open with no fix.
- Which level you get is decided per device (RendererLevel::default_for_device): on WebGL 2 and other GL 3.x devices, tiling stays on the CPU, so very complex scenes can be CPU-bound (issue #228, 'High CPU overhead on very complex scenes').
- crates.io 0.5.0 (2020) and git main differ substantially (no compute mode in 0.5.0), so examples and docs on main may not match the published crates.
- Font hinting is limited to 'slight' hinting, and stem darkening is optional, so small-size output will not match FreeType's full hinting.

**Status:** The repo is technically active (last commit 2026-04-23), but the activity is SIMD and build upkeep: the renderer has had no release since 0.5.0 in 2020, and the README still says it is under heavy development. MIT OR Apache-2.0 makes it easy to adopt from git main, but plan to own your fork.

[repo](https://github.com/servo/pathfinder)

##### TGFX (Tencent Graphics)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier D`

Tencent's GPU-only C++17 2D renderer (PAG's engine), claimed 10-16x more animated rectangles per frame than Skia Ganesh m136.

**Beats:** Skia (m136) — The only number is first-party: discussion #567 (2025-04-24) reports 510,308 vs 34,721 animated 4-14 px anti-aliased rects held at 60 FPS (about 14.7x) for TGFX vs Skia chrome/m136 Ganesh, from the online WebGL benchmark built from libpag/tgfx-benchmark (TGFX main commit a56652e) and libpag/skia-benchmark. Device, GPU and browser are not stated. Reading the April 2025 harness code shows the two sides were not timed alike: Skia's frame time includes flushAndSubmit with GrSyncCpu::kYes (a blocking wait for the GPU), TGFX's flushAndSubmit() used syncCpu=false, and the ramp-and-stop rule keys on that frame time, so the 14.7x is inflated by an unknown amount.

**Known shortcoming:** GPU-vs-GPU comparison (TGFX GPU backend vs Skia Ganesh, WebGL/WASM or native) from discussion #567: 510,308 vs 34,721 rectangles at 60 FPS (14.7x derived) with public bench code (libpag/tgfx-benchmark and libpag/skia-benchmark, src/benchmark/ParticleBench.cpp) but the device, GPU and browser for the posted numbers are never stated, so C. Skia benchmark moved to m136 on 2025-04-08 and m142 on 2025-10-15; screenshots sit behind private-user-images tokens. tgfx.org/benchmark blocked here.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered C to D (retier-22): the April 2025 harnesses time Skia with flushAndSubmit(GrSyncCpu::kYes), waiting for the GPU, and TGFX with flushAndSubmit() without a CPU sync (one-frame deferred submit since November 2025), and the ramp-and-stop rule keys on that draw time, so the 510,308 versus 34,721 rectangle counts (14.7x) are inflated by an unknown amount; only Skia is linked with -sASSERTIONS=2; the wasm-mt build runs TGFX vertex generation on worker threads while Skia records on one thread; a user test in issue #381 (TGFX 1.2.1) found Skia far faster; open bug #1172 (thin polygon strips).

**How:** OpsCompositor defers draws into pending lists and merges consecutive drawRect calls that share clip and brush (colour may differ and goes per vertex) into one RectDrawOp of up to RectDrawOp::MaxNumRects = 2048 rects, drawn with a cached shared index buffer (30 indices per coverage-AA quad). That turns the benchmark's 500k drawRect calls into a few hundred draw calls. With TGFX_USE_THREADS, which is on by default for native builds and the wasm-mt web build, vertex data is generated by async tasks on worker threads (RenderFlags::DisableAsyncTask turns this off for single-rect ops) into a shared, block-allocated vertex buffer. The rest of the speed is a small code base built for batching rather than Skia's general Ganesh op pipeline; V2.1 also added SIMD math (Highway is a dependency).

**Use it when:**
- Animated 2D scenes with very many small, simple primitives (rects, rounded rects, sprites, atlas text) drawn on a GPU, where per-draw CPU overhead is the bottleneck.
- Mobile or web apps that want a Skia-like API with a much smaller binary, especially on WebGL 2 or WebGPU via WebAssembly.
- Projects already in the PAG/libpag ecosystem, or ones that need the same renderer on iOS, Android, HarmonyOS, desktop and the browser.
- Layer-tree UIs with partial or tiled redraw (the V2.1 notes claim support for canvases of up to 200,000 layers).

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs a CPU or software rasterizer (headless servers, printing pipelines): TGFX is GPU-only, and Linux without a GPU needs SwiftShader. Blend2D, ThorVG's CPU backend or Skia's raster backend fit better there.
- Workloads dominated by complex anti-aliased paths, strokes, gradients or blend modes: the only published comparison is the rectangle test, and the announcement says the platform runs only basic rectangle rendering.
- When you need Skia's full feature set (SkSL runtime effects, Graphite, PDF/SVG fidelity, mature text shaping) or a drop-in Skia replacement.
- When you need stable APIs: the latest tag is v2.1.1 (2025-09-26) while main has kept moving, and the benchmark repo itself needed a fix in August 2026 to adapt to the current TGFX window API.
- Apple-only Metal deployments: the README still lists the Metal backend as in progress.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake; dependencies synced with depsync) · pathkit and skcms (libpag forks), zlib, libpng, libwebp, libjpeg-turbo, FreeType, HarfBuzz, Highway, concurrentqueue; expat/json for SVG and PDF; shaderc, SPIRV-Cross, Vulkan-Headers, volk and VMA for Vulkan; Tint and Abseil for WebGPU (most codecs toggled by TGFX_USE_* options) · C++17; Xcode 13+, GCC 9+, Visual Studio 2019+, CMake 3.13+, NDK 25 (25.2.9519653 recommended), Emscripten 4.0.15 pinned (4.0.11 rejected, 4.0.18+ breaks -sUSE_WEBGPU) · iOS 15+, Android 5+, HarmonyOS 5+, macOS 12+, Windows 7+, Linux, Chrome 69+/Safari 15+; backends OpenGL 3.2+, OpenGL ES 3.0+, WebGL 2, Vulkan 1.1+, WebGPU, plus CMake options for D3D12 and Metal (README: Metal in progress)

**Vs siblings:** Pick TGFX over vkvg, vger or the Rive Renderer when you want a broad Skia-like GPU API that ships on mobile, desktop and the web (WebGL 2 and WebGPU) from one code base. Pick Blend2D, ThorVG (CPU) or Vello CPU when no GPU can be assumed or when you need independently measured numbers.

**Gotchas:**
- Batching is the speed source: a change of draw type, clip or brush (shader, filters, blend) flushes the pending batch, and a batch holds at most 2048 rects, so interleaved heterogeneous draws lose most of the advantage the rectangle benchmark shows.
- The default web build is multithreaded wasm (pthreads with a worker pool of navigator.hardwareConcurrency); the README warns that renaming the generated .js breaks the worker bootstrap, and a single-threaded build (build:st) turns off async vertex generation.
- Open correctness issue #1172 (January 2026): thin polygon strips render incorrectly. Earlier anti-aliasing seam (#1068) and Src/SrcIn path blend (#544) bugs are closed.
- An independent user test in issue #381 (TGFX 1.2.1, Windows 11, December 2024) got about 30 FPS with 500 moving rects in TGFX versus about 100 FPS with 8,000+ in Skia. That predates the 2.0 rect batching and had no recorded maintainer resolution, but it is the only third-party data point found.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-09-24, 1.6k stars, BSD-3-Clause, copyable), but the latest tagged release, v2.1.1, is a year behind main, and the only performance evidence is a first-party rectangle test whose harness favours TGFX.

[repo](https://github.com/Tencent/tgfx) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Tencent/tgfx/discussions/567)

#### unicode-utf8

##### libutf  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Small malloc-free C11 library for NFC, DUCET collation and grapheme clusters on raw UTF-8; first-party numbers beat ICU on short strings.

**Beats:** ICU 78.3 (ICU4C: ubrk grapheme break iterator, unorm2 NFC, ucol DUCET collation) — Author-run microbenchmarks on an Apple M5 Max against ICU 78.3 (gcc -O2 build lines, compiler version unstated) report, with ICU paying u_strFromUTF8 conversion, NFC 2.1x, NFC check 3.8x, collation 1.3x and grapheme counting 1.4x faster; with ICU on pre-converted UTF-16 the margins are NFC 1.4x and graphemes 1.2x for libutf, and ICU wins collation by 1.4x. Each figure is a single wall-clock total, with no warmup or repeats, over 8 to 12 short strings; outputs are never cross-checked between the libraries; the check benchmark pits a quick check against ICU's definitive isNormalized; the grapheme rules omit GB9c; and the numbers (2026-07-30) predate later changes to every measured path, including a rewrite of the NFC segment-boundary scan on 2026-08-13.

**Known shortcoming:** Category moved to unicode-utf8 (ICU baseline), not font shaping. The NFC code changed after the numbers: commit c7537c0 (2026-08-13) rewrote the segment-boundary scan (HasBoundaryBefore, segment cap 128 to 1024) and the old code could drop text. The quick-check bench is not like-for-like: utf_nfc_is_nfc returns 0 on NFC_QC Maybe while ICU unorm2_isNormalized gives a definitive answer; the benches never cross-check outputs, and a Devanagari string yields 4 grapheme clusters against ICU's 3 (no GB9c). One wall-clock run, no warm-up. The article's single-pass DFA grapheme claim is false (a rule loop plus two DFA lookups per code point); sort-key truncation is unsignalled.

**How:** Unicode properties (CCC plus NFC_QC combined, decompositions, compositions, GCB, Extended_Pictographic, DUCET collation elements) are looked up through compressed byte-level DFAs generated from the UCD (state merging, column deduplication, RUN/COPY encoding), so UTF-8 is consumed directly with no UTF-16 conversion and no allocation. NFC copies already-normalized runs through and only decomposes, reorders and recomposes dirty segments, with an ASCII skip and algorithmic Hangul. Collation has a lazily built table for U+0000..U+017F that compares single-collation-element Latin characters inline, computed implicit weights for CJK, and bounded stack buffers for the general path. Grapheme segmentation is a hand-written UAX #29 rule loop that does two DFA property lookups per code point; it is not one fused DFA as the project article describes.

**Use it when:**
- C or C++ code that keeps text as UTF-8 and needs NFC normalization or an is-it-NFC check on short strings (identifiers, user names, keys, chat lines) without linking ICU.
- Root-order (DUCET) comparison or memcmp-able sort keys for short UTF-8 strings, including a case-insensitive comparison, when locale tailoring is not required.
- Footprint-constrained or dependency-free builds: about 702 KB static versus about 42 MB of ICU static libraries with full data (README), no malloc, no runtime dependencies.
- Terminal and MUD-style applications that need grapheme counting for Latin, CJK, Hangul and emoji, display width, and inline PUA color handling in one library.

**Skip it when:**
- Indic scripts or any text where grapheme clusters must follow Unicode 15.1+ rule GB9c: libutf has no InCB property, so a conjunct such as Devanagari 'स्ते' in the benchmark's 'नमस्ते' splits into two clusters where UAX #29 (and ICU 78) keeps one (by the rules; the benchmark never compares counts).
- Locale-sensitive sorting (tailorings such as Swedish or German phonebook), word, sentence or line breaking, bidi, NFD/NFKC/NFKD, case folding by locale, or Unicode 17 characters: use ICU.
- Long-document bulk throughput: all published numbers come from 8 to 12 short hand-written strings repeated 100,000 to 500,000 times, and the code is byte-at-a-time with no SIMD, so per-call overhead is what was measured.
- Projects that need a mature, widely reviewed dependency: single author, 0 stars, no CI, and the grapheme, NFC and collation code each received correctness fixes in August and September 2026 after the published numbers.
- Untrusted, possibly malformed UTF-8 for grapheme segmentation: utf_grapheme_next advances by the lead byte without validation, so malformed input is segmented arbitrarily.

**Integration:** static lib · none at runtime; ICU development headers only for the benchmarks and the tests/test_*_icu.c differential tests; C++, Perl and the UCD files only to regenerate tables; Ragel only to regenerate color_ops.c · C11 (Makefile: gcc -O2 -std=c11); <stdatomic.h> used unless __STDC_NO_ATOMICS__ or UTF_NO_ATOMICS is defined · any (portable C, no SIMD or platform intrinsics); results published only for Apple M5 Max (macOS); Windows dllexport/dllimport macros exist but there is no CI for any platform

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings in font-shaping-text-layout does this job: displaywidth, uniwidth (Go) and uwcwidth (Python) only compute terminal display width, and HarfBuzz-style shapers do not normalize or collate. Pick libutf when a C program needs NFC, root collation and grapheme clusters on UTF-8 without ICU; the category fit is Unicode processing (ICU baseline), not shaping.

**Gotchas:**
- utf_nfc_is_nfc is a quick check: it returns 0 for NFC_QC=Maybe characters, so some text that is already NFC (a base letter plus a combining mark with no precomposed form) reports 'not NFC'; ICU's unorm2_isNormalized, which the benchmark compares against, gives a definitive answer.
- utf_nfc_normalize can expand text up to 3x: size dst with utf_nfc_normalize_bound() and check the returned status (UTF_NFC_TRUNCATED, or UTF_NFC_SEGMENT_TOO_LONG past 1024 code points in one combining sequence, raised with -DUTF_NFC_SEG_MAX).
- utf_collate_sortkey returns at most nKeyMax and gives no required-size answer when the key does not fit; a 16-bit weight that straddles the end is skipped, so the last byte of a truncated key can be left unwritten. Size key buffers generously. The final NFC tiebreak only considers the first 256 input bytes unless rebuilt with -DUTF_NFC_TIEBREAK_MAX.
- Collation is raw DUCET (allkeys.txt, Unicode 16.0) with no variable-weighting (shifted) option; ICU's ucol_open("") is CLDR root, which tailors DUCET, so results match ICU only where the two agree (33 tested pairs do).

**Status:** Active single-author project (48 commits, last 2026-09-29, issues #1 to #3 all closed), MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but young and unreviewed outside its author, so treat it as a compact ICU subset for UTF-8 C code and re-measure on your own strings.

[repo](https://github.com/brazilofmux/utf) · [benchmark](https://github.com/brazilofmux/utf)

##### uax29 (graphemes and words)  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zero-allocation Go UAX #29 grapheme/word/sentence segmenter (Unicode 17); 14x rivo/uniseg graphemes, 3.6x blevesearch/segment words, first-party.

**Beats:** rivo/uniseg (graphemes); blevesearch/segment (words) — First-party go test -bench on an Apple M2 (darwin/arm64, GOMAXPROCS 8), Go version unstated, single runs, from the in-repo comparative modules (local replace, so they measure HEAD-era code from February 2026). Graphemes are 14.2x (multilingual 34,962-byte sample) and 41.5x (4,500-byte ASCII) faster than rivo/uniseg v0.4.7's NewGraphemes, which also computes word, sentence, line and width state, so those ratios overstate a graphemes-only comparison. Words are 3.6x and 6.2x faster than blevesearch/segment v0.9.1. That baseline ran in its default build, the table-driven Ragel -T1 machine its README says is not the fastest; the -tags prod goto machine (-G2) was not used. Its loop also copies the input to []byte on every iteration, so the word ratios are upper bounds as well.

**Known shortcoming:** The grapheme ratios (14.2x, 41.5x on ASCII) are inflated because uniseg's Graphemes.Next runs StepString, computing word, sentence, line and width boundaries per step; Unicode 17 with GB9c is compared against uniseg's 15.0.0 tables; the Bleve loop copies []byte on every iteration; Go version unstated. The ASCII fast path comparison is valid.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e127, 2026-10-05): no correctness bug; the ASCII fast paths (graphemes, words) are correct under UAX #29. New measurement flaw: the blevesearch/segment v0.9.1 baseline was built without -tags prod, so the slower table-driven Ragel -T1 machine ran instead of the documented fastest -G2 build, plus a []byte copy per iteration, so the word ratios 3.6x/6.2x are upper bounds. uniseg v0.4.7 is still the latest tag. Tier C stands.

**Independent measurement:** first-party go test -bench

**How:** Break properties come from generated tries indexed directly by UTF-8 bytes, so a lookup needs no rune decoding. The rules run as one forward pass that carries the last two non-ignored properties, a regional-indicator count and a three-state GB9c (Indic conjunct) tracker, so it never looks back. ASCII fast paths in Next() (PR #42, January 2026) skip the rule engine: an ASCII byte other than CR followed by another ASCII byte or end of text is a grapheme by itself, and a run of [A-Za-z0-9] followed by an ASCII space or end of text is a word. Both shortcuts are correct under UAX #29, since no ASCII character is Extend, SpacingMark, Prepend or regional indicator. Iterators are generic over string and []byte and report 0 allocs/op.

**Use it when:**
- Go search and NLP pipelines (inverted indexes, BM25, embedding chunking) that need standard UAX #29 word tokens: 212 MB/s multilingual and 282 MB/s ASCII prose on an Apple M2, with no allocations.
- Grapheme-correct cursor movement, truncation or counting in Go TUIs and CLIs; clipperhouse/displaywidth and the Charm stack build on it.
- ASCII-heavy or mostly-Latin text, where the fast paths apply on almost every byte (509 MB/s graphemes on a repeated ASCII pangram).
- Terminal output carrying colour codes: AnsiEscapeSequences keeps each escape sequence as one token, checked against charmbracelet/x/ansi's DecodeSequence in the comparative tests.
- Streaming input via FromReader/SplitFunc with bufio.Scanner, or text already in memory as string or []byte with no conversion.

**Skip it when:**
- When you also need line-break (UAX #14) opportunities or monospace width per cluster: rivo/uniseg's Step returns graphemes, words, sentences, line breaks and width in one pass. uax29 has no line breaking (issue #50 closed), and width lives in the separate displaywidth package.
- Language-tailored word segmentation (Thai, Lao, Khmer, Chinese and Japanese dictionary breaking): only the default UAX #29 rules are implemented, so ideographs and Southeast Asian scripts are not split into dictionary words.
- Untrusted input that may be invalid UTF-8: the README calls the result undefined (garbage in, garbage out); fuzzing guards only against panics and infinite loops, so validate with utf8.Valid first.
- Pipelines that rely on blevesearch/segment token types (Letter, Number, Kana, Ideo) or its exact boundaries: uax29 words returns untyped tokens, and the harness itself notes that counts can differ from blevesearch.
- Non-Go code: this is a pure Go module. The C# port (clipperhouse/uax29.net) is separate, and for C/C++ the catalogued alternatives are libgrapheme, uni-algo and ICU.

**Integration:** module (pure-Go packages: graphemes, words, phrases, sentences) · none (root go.mod has no require lines; the comparative benchmark modules pull rivo/uniseg v0.4.7, blevesearch/segment v0.9.1 and charmbracelet/x/ansi v0.11.6) · go.mod declares go 1.18 (generics); CI only tests Go 1.21-1.26 with -race -short. PR #42 described a bump to 1.20 that HEAD's go.mod does not show. · any GOOS/GOARCH (no assembly or unsafe in the iterator and split code read); the published benchmarks ran on darwin/arm64

**Vs siblings:** It is the only Go segmenter in the category. Pick it for Go code, and pick cometkim/fast-grapheme-segmenter (Rust), unicode-segmenter (JavaScript), ugrapheme (Python) or uni-algo, libgrapheme and ICU (C/C++) in those languages. Its multilingual grapheme rate (245 MB/s on an M2) is in the same range as those siblings' own first-party numbers, but no shared harness compares them.

**Gotchas:**
- v2.1.0 and v2.1.1 are retracted in go.mod (surprising allocations). v2.5.0 changed FromString/FromBytes to return a pointer iterator, and v2 removed the Filter, Transform and All helpers, so code written for v1 needs rework.
- words yields whitespace and punctuation tokens. Filtering to word-like tokens is now up to the caller, since the v1 Wordlike filter was removed.
- FromReader inherits bufio.Scanner's 64 KiB default token limit, so a pathological grapheme or word longer than that (for example stacked combining marks) stops the scan with an error unless you call Buffer to raise it.
- AnsiEscapeSequences8Bit reads C1 bytes 0x80-0x9F as controls. They are only checked at a token start, where valid UTF-8 never has a continuation byte, so valid text is unaffected, but mixed-encoding input will tokenize differently with it on.

**Status:** Active: v2.7.0 tagged 2026-02-16 with the last commit the same day, one open issue (#51, README link) and one open PR (#52, exporting the ANSI length functions). MIT-licensed, zero dependencies, conformance-tested against the Unicode 17 test files in CI and fuzzed.

[repo](https://github.com/clipperhouse/uax29) · [benchmark](https://github.com/clipperhouse/uax29/blob/master/graphemes/README.md)

##### libgrapheme  `C`  `ISC`  `active`  `Tier D`

Tiny freestanding C99 Unicode segmentation and case-mapping library; claims to beat libutf8proc, ICU and libunistring, with no published numbers.

**Beats:** libutf8proc (the only library the repo's benchmark/ programs compare against: grapheme cluster break and UTF-8 decode); the README also names ICU and GNU libunistring, but no benchmark against them exists — Nothing was measured on the record: the README says 'way smaller and much faster' than ICU, libunistring and libutf8proc with no numbers, and the repo's character and utf8-decode benchmarks (clock() CPU time, 100,000 passes over the GraphemeBreakTest codepoints, libgrapheme static at -Os against a dynamically linked libutf8proc) print run-time ratios that were never published. The benchmark's label that libutf8proc's decoder is 'unsafe (does not detect overlong encodings)' is stale: current utf8proc_iterate rejects overlong 2-, 3- and 4-byte forms and surrogates, and the generated input is valid UTF-8 anyway, so the decode comparison is like-for-like on validation.

**Known shortcoming:** Category moved to unicode-utf8. No number in the repo: benchmark/character.c (grapheme_is_character_break) and utf8-decode.c compare libutf8proc only, the word, sentence, line and case benchmarks time libgrapheme alone, and bidirectional.c is empty; the 'twice as fast' claim against libutf8proc exists only in a search snippet of a blocked May 2022 suckless dev-list post, so the baseline narrows to libutf8proc and the tier is D.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): nothing is measured on the record; the README's 'way smaller and much faster' than ICU, libunistring and libutf8proc has no numbers, and the repo's benchmarks (clock() CPU time, 100,000 passes over GraphemeBreakTest codepoints, libgrapheme static at -Os against a dynamically linked libutf8proc) print ratios that were never published. Its label that libutf8proc's decoder is 'unsafe' is stale (current utf8proc_iterate rejects overlong forms and surrogates). Gotchas: grapheme_is_character_break reuses the cached cp1 property once state is non-zero (reset state per string); grapheme_decode_utf8 returns more than len for a truncated trailing sequence; default config.mk builds -Os and strips; make test fails line and bidi on the shipped 17.0.0 data (half-finished gen2 generator); stray #include <stdio.h> ahead of the license header in src/character.c. Single-maintainer, 3.0.0 on 2025-12-24 after a year idle. Tier D stands.

**Independent measurement:** none

**How:** Property lookup is a two-stage table generated from the Unicode data (major[cp >> 8] + (cp & 0xFF) into a byte-sized minor table), and the UAX #29 pair rules are precomputed bitmask tables, so a break decision is a couple of loads and AND tests instead of utf8proc's branch chain over a larger property struct. The stateful break call caches the right-hand codepoint's property inside a 16-bit caller-held state, so a scan does one table lookup per codepoint where utf8proc_grapheme_break_stateful looks up both codepoints on every call. There is no SIMD and no ASCII fast path; the UTF-8 decoder is a scalar per-codepoint loop.

**Use it when:**
- C or C++ code that needs correct grapheme-cluster counting or cursor movement (terminals, text editors, TUI widgets) without pulling in ICU.
- Bare-metal or libc-free builds: the library is freestanding and the shared object links with -nostdlib.
- Word and sentence segmentation or Unicode case conversion of short strings where a small ISC-licensed dependency matters more than measured peak throughput.
- Replacing utf8proc only for grapheme breaking and UTF-8 decoding, where the bundled benchmarks give you a ready comparison to run on your own hardware.

**Skip it when:**
- Line breaking or bidirectional layout on Unicode 16/17 text: the author's own 17.0.0 data-update commit says line-segmentation and bidi conformance tests fail, and src/line.c has no LB15a-d, LB19a, LB20a or LB28a rules.
- You need normalization (NFC/NFD), case folding for comparison, collation or locale-tailored breaking: use ICU, utf8proc or a sibling with those features.
- You need demonstrated speed: no benchmark result has ever been published, so measure with make benchmark before relying on the 'much faster' claim.
- Bulk UTF-8 validation or transcoding throughput: the decoder is scalar per codepoint with no SIMD, so SIMD validators in this category are far faster for that job.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (one POSIX Makefile plus ./configure; installs grapheme.h, man pages and a pkg-config file) · none at run time (freestanding); benchmarks link -lutf8proc · any C99 compiler and POSIX make · any (portable C99, no architecture-specific code)

**Vs siblings:** Pick libgrapheme over uni-algo or libutf when you want plain C99, zero dependencies, an ISC license and grapheme, word and sentence segmentation plus case mapping in a few hundred KB; pick uni-algo (C++) or libutf when you need normalization or collation or want numbers measured against ICU, which libgrapheme lacks.

**Gotchas:**
- Once the state has been used, grapheme_is_character_break ignores cp0 and reuses the property cached from the previous call's cp1; reset the state to 0 for each new string or after skipping codepoints.
- grapheme_decode_utf8 maps invalid sequences to U+FFFD and returns the bytes consumed, but returns a value larger than len for a truncated trailing sequence; callers must check ret > len.
- The default config.mk builds with -Os and strips binaries (LDFLAGS -s); set CFLAGS to -O2 or -O3 for speed-sensitive builds, and expect make test to report failures for line and bidi on the shipped 17.0.0 data.
- src/character.c starts with a stray #include <stdio.h> ahead of the license header, which can break a truly libc-less freestanding toolchain despite the freestanding claim.

**Status:** Single-maintainer suckless project, version 3.0.0 released 2025-12-24 after a year without commits, ISC-licensed and small enough to vendor; the half-finished move to a new table generator (gen2, wired only into a generator and not into src/) leaves line breaking and bidi below Unicode 17.0.0 conformance.

[repo](https://github.com/FRIGN/libgrapheme) · [benchmark](https://github.com/FRIGN/libgrapheme)

#### video-audio

##### audioFlux  `C (with Python bindings)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

C audio feature-extraction library (mel, MFCC, CQT, CWT, pitch) with Python bindings; mel spectrograms faster than librosa, mostly torchaudio-competitive.

**Beats:** librosa 0.10.0 and torchaudio 0.11.0 (mel spectrogram); essentia 2.0.1 listed as a compared library — First-party benchmark (audioFlux 0.1.5, librosa 0.10.0, torchaudio 0.11.0; 2048-point FFT, hop 512, 128 mels, average per call reported as seconds per 1000 calls) on a Threadripper 3970X, i7-6850K, macOS Intel i7 and Apple M1, with build flags, BLAS backend and thread counts not recorded: against torchaudio audioFlux is 1.2x to 7.1x faster on the 3970X except at 100 frames (0.92x), slower on the i7-6850K from 10 frames up, and faster on the Macs only for long inputs. The 10x to 56x librosa ratios overstate the core's advantage: run_librosa.py times librosa.feature.melspectrogram, which in librosa 0.10.0 rebuilds the 128-band mel filter bank on every call (filters.mel cache is off unless LIBROSA_CACHE_DIR is set) and is called without sr (22050 Hz default instead of 32000), while audioFlux's and torchaudio's filter banks are built at object creation outside the timer; audioFlux also runs up to 32 OpenMP threads with no thread limits set for any library.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-baseline: compared only with librosa and torchaudio (Python), never with a C baseline; scripts are public but compiler, flags, BLAS and thread counts are unstated. Torchaudio is faster on Linux Intel at 10 or more steps and on macOS for short inputs.

**Known shortcoming:** The librosa ratios are inflated (retier-28): run_librosa.py times librosa.feature.melspectrogram, which in librosa 0.10.0 rebuilds the mel filter bank every call (cache off without LIBROSA_CACHE_DIR) at the 22050 Hz default (sr omitted), while audioFlux and torchaudio build banks at init outside the timer; audioFlux's STFT runs 32 OpenMP threads on the 3970X with no thread limits anywhere. Open issues #35 (mel output changes after importing torch), #46 (unreported vulnerability), #27 (1.4 GB allocation for a 3-minute track), #44 (arm64 unanswered); PyPI stuck at 0.1.9; run_benchmark.py's -r and -er are swapped against the README.

**How:** Per-frame FFTs go to a vendor FFT chosen at build time: Intel MKL DFTI on Linux, Apple Accelerate vDSP on macOS/iOS, FFTW3f on Android/Windows, or a built-in cached-twiddle radix-2 FFT. The STFT splits frames across omp_get_max_threads()/2 OpenMP worker FFT objects (32 threads on the 64-thread Threadripper 3970X used for the headline chart). The mel filter bank is built once when the object is created and applied as a matrix product, so repeated calls only pay for FFT, power and the dot product.

**Use it when:**
- Batch extraction of mel, MFCC, CQT or chroma features from long clips in Python on x86-64 Linux or macOS, where the C core's multi-threaded STFT pays off (500 to 3000 frames per call)
- Replacing librosa.feature.melspectrogram in a data pipeline that calls it many times, since audioFlux builds the filter bank once and keeps it in the object
- Mobile or embedded feature extraction from C (iOS Accelerate, Android FFTW3f builds) where pulling in PyTorch is not an option; the README reports 0.25 to 0.89 ms per 4096-sample mel frame on phones
- Research that needs less common transforms (NSGT, S-transform, synchrosqueezed CWT, reassigned STFT) in one library

**Skip it when:**
- You already depend on PyTorch: torchaudio was as fast or faster on the Intel i7-6850K Linux box at 10 frames and above, at 100 frames on the Threadripper, and for short inputs on both Macs
- You need outputs that match librosa or torchaudio numerically: the benchmark never compares outputs, defaults differ (Slaney scale without filter normalisation here), and open issue #35 reports different mel values when torch is imported in the same process
- Linux ARM64 or other platforms without a prebuilt library: issue #44 (arm64 Docker) is unanswered, and the PyPI package is a single 70.8 MB py3-none-any wheel carrying prebuilt binaries
- Very long inputs on memory-constrained devices: issue #27 reports 1.4 GB allocated for a 3-minute track (15 M samples, hop 512) on Android; the STFT stores full fftLength complex frames, not just the fftLength/2+1 non-redundant bins
- Projects that need a responsive upstream: most issues since 2023 have no maintainer reply, including #46, an unreported vulnerability (the reporter could not file it because GitHub security reporting is off)

**Integration:** shared lib (C core built with CMake) plus Python package (ctypes wrapper); static lib on iOS · Linux: optional Intel MKL (MKL_INCLUDE_PATH/MKL_LIB_PATH) and LLVM libomp; macOS: Accelerate and libomp (Homebrew llvm); Android/Windows/OHOS: FFTW3f; Python: numpy, scipy>=1.2.0, soundfile>=0.12.1, matplotlib · CMake 3.5; Linux CMakeLists hard-codes /usr/bin/clang with -O3 -fopenmp=libomp; macOS needs Homebrew llvm (C_COMPILER_PATH); Python >=3.6; setup.py refuses to build on Windows (cross-built from macOS/Linux) · Linux and macOS (x86-64, Apple M1), Windows, iOS, Android, OpenHarmony per the build scripts; Linux arm64 not documented

**Vs siblings:** No catalogued sibling does audio feature extraction: pedalboard covers effects and file I/O against pySoX and librosa.load, and libsoxr/r8brain cover resampling, so pick audioFlux when the job is mel/MFCC/CQT features and you cannot or do not want to depend on PyTorch.

**Gotchas:**
- The STFT calls omp_set_num_threads() on each call (timeLength threads for short inputs, omp_get_max_threads()/2 otherwise), changing the OpenMP thread count other code in the same runtime then inherits; the benchmark README also warns that mixing its libomp with MKL/PyTorch OpenMP runtimes can fail or slow down
- On Apple platforms the real-input FFT goes through the complex vDSP_fft_zop path because, per a source comment, 'real to complex fft has problem', so it does twice the FFT work there
- The PyPI release is still 0.1.9 (2024-05-24); the TuneTrack features (README 'v0.1.10', commits of 2026-02/03) are only in the source tree
- benchmark/run_benchmark.py treats -r as the number of subprocess launches and -er as calls per launch, the reverse of what benchmark/README.md says; the per-call average it prints is still correct

**Status:** MIT-licensed and usable from Python today, but maintenance is sporadic: no PyPI release since 0.1.9 (2024-05-24), a commit gap from May 2024 to February 2026, and most open issues (including an unreported vulnerability) without a maintainer reply.

[repo](https://github.com/libAudioFlux/audioFlux) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/libAudioFlux/audioFlux/master/benchmark/README.md)

##### av-denoise  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust GPU video denoiser (NLMeans, NLMeans-HQ, NL4D on CubeCL); first-party chart shows about 11x FFmpeg nlmeans_opencl at 1080p.

**Beats:** FFmpeg libavfilter nlmeans_opencl (OpenCL NLMeans filter) at its defaults s=1, p=7, r=15; not hqdn3d or the CPU nlmeans filter. V-BM3D (vsdenoise, HIP) is a second, VapourSynth-only reference. — One end-to-end run per arm (repeats = 1 after a warm-up; fps = probed frame count / wall time) on an unpublished 1080p 8-bit clip with an AMD GPU named RX9700. The chart shows av-denoise NLMeans at FFmpeg-matched geometry at about 116 fps against FFmpeg nlmeans_opencl at about 10.6 fps (about 11x, read from the chart), while the README text says about 2x; host CPU, FFmpeg version, driver and rustc are not published. Part of the gap comes from a weak baseline (FFmpeg's serial row and column prefix sums, about 500 launches and a clFinish per frame, single filter chain against two scene workers). KNLMeansCL, the established GPU NLMeans, is not measured, and the V-BM3D claim holds only CLI-to-plugin: through the plugin on both sides NL4D is about 29 fps against V-BM3D FAST at about 28 fps at 1080p, and slower at 4K.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). Public harness (scripts/src/benchmark_e2e.py, configs/benchmark_e2e.toml) against FFmpeg libavfilter's nlmeans_opencl at defaults (s=1 p=7 r=15; avd arm strength 1.0, patch 3, search 7) on a GPU known only as 'RX9700' from file names; host CPU, rustc, FFmpeg version and clips unpublished, no PSNR or SSIM. The README says about 2x while the chart shows about 11x (116 vs 10.6 fps), and the charts do not show the claimed 1.3x over V-BM3D (ties V-BM3D FAST at 1080p, trails it at 4K).

**Known shortcoming:** Weak baseline: FFmpeg's nlmeans_opencl does serial row and column prefix sums with about 500 kernel launches plus clFinish per frame. Strength is not matched (exp(-SSD/147) over 7x7 versus exp(-SSD/100) over 6x6); 2 workers against 1 chain, repeats=1, warm kernel cache; charts from 2026-09-06 (0.4.0) and not re-run. The README's 2x and the chart's about 11x are unreconciled; the 1.3x over V-BM3D is not shown like-for-like (plugin NL4D about 29 versus V-BM3D FAST about 28 fps); KNLMeansCL was not measured.

**How:** In the spatial pass one fused kernel launch covers the whole search window: patch distance, weight exp(-max(d - noise_offset, 0) * h2_inv_norm) and accumulation, all in f32 out of a 32x8 shared-memory tile with a halo. CubeCL compiles that kernel at runtime with the search window unrolled ((2r+1)^2 iterations, per the Denoiser::create docs), and the weight's symmetry (pixel p against p+q equals p+q against p) lets each offset's distance serve both pixels. Two scene-parallel workers and two in-flight readbacks keep the GPU busy. The baseline is weak by comparison, derived from FFmpeg's vf_nlmeans_opencl.c and nlmeans.cl: for each group of 4 offsets per plane it launches a horizontal prefix-sum kernel with one work-item per row scanning the row serially, a vertical one with one work-item per column, and a weight-accumulate kernel. That is 56 groups x 3 planes, about 500 kernel launches per frame at its defaults, followed by a clFinish on every frame.

**Use it when:**
- Cleaning video before an encode on a machine with a GPU, where FFmpeg's nlmeans_opencl, CPU nlmeans or hqdn3d is the throughput bottleneck; the first-party 1080p 8-bit chart shows about 105-116 fps for the NLMeans arms on an AMD GPU named RX9700.
- 10 or 12-bit sources: depth is detected and kept, while FFmpeg's nlmeans_opencl rejects the 10-bit formats its hwupload path offers (per the benchmark config).
- Temporal denoising with motion compensation and automatic per-scene noise estimation (NLMeans-HQ, NL4D), where you would otherwise hand-tune sigma per source in KNLMeansCL or run V-BM3D.
- Cross-vendor GPU fleets: the same build runs on AMD, Intel and NVIDIA through Vulkan and on Apple Silicon through Metal, with no ROCm or CUDA SDK needed on the vulkan backend.
- Rust programs that want an embeddable GPU denoiser with a push/receive frame API.

**Skip it when:**
- Machines without a usable GPU: there is no software backend (CubeCL's CPU runtime lacks the atomics the collaborative filter needs); a lavapipe-style software Vulkan device is the only CPU fallback.
- C or C++ code, or an FFmpeg filter graph: there is no C API and no libavfilter filter, so integration means a separate process and a y4m pipe.
- Output that must match FFmpeg's nlmeans: the 'matched' arm is not equivalent. av-denoise weights exp(-SSD/(3 s^2 x 49)) over a 7x7 patch while nlmeans_opencl uses exp(-SSD/(10s)^2) over the 6x6 window its integral-image corners cover (derived from both sources), and no PSNR or SSIM comparison is published.
- Search windows wider than radius 8 (17x17) or patches wider than radius 16 (MAX_SEARCH_RADIUS, MAX_PATCH_RADIUS); FFmpeg's r goes up to 99.
- Speed-critical VapourSynth graphs: through the plugin NLMeans-HQ drops from about 105 fps (CLI) to about 35 fps and NL4D from about 80 to about 29 fps at 1080p (chart readings), where NL4D only ties V-BM3D FAST (about 28 fps). It is also an alpha (0.5.0-alpha3, 14 stars, one maintainer) that has shipped backend bugs: green output and crashes on CUDA on an RTX 4080 under Windows (#13), and a motion-compensation alignment error unless frame height was a multiple of 512 (#4), both closed.

**Integration:** crate (av-denoise on crates.io: library plus the CLI behind the `binary` feature; av-denoise-core holds the kernels), VapourSynth plugin wheel vsavd on PyPI, GHCR container images per backend · cubecl 0.10 (GPU JIT) with one backend feature: vulkan (default), metal, cuda (needs CUDA headers and nvcc at runtime) or rocm (needs the HIP compiler and headers at runtime); the CLI needs FFMS2 and FFmpeg libraries (optional static build via vcpkg, `static-ffms2`); anyhow, thiserror, tracing, bon, strum, etcetera · Rust edition 2024 (Rust 1.85+); no rust-version declared; CUDA and ROCm backends need the vendor SDK present at runtime for kernel JIT · GPUs reachable through Vulkan (AMD, Intel, NVIDIA), Metal (Apple Silicon), CUDA or ROCm/HIP on Linux, macOS and Windows; published numbers cover one AMD GPU named RX9700 on the Vulkan backend

**Vs siblings:** No other denoiser is catalogued in video-audio; the siblings are codecs, resamplers, RTP stacks and a VAD. av-denoise belongs before an encoder such as SVT-AV1, x265 or VVenC as a pre-encode cleanup step. The comparisons that would matter, KNLMeansCL (which the README names as its inspiration) and the BM3DCUDA/HIP filters, are not catalogued or benchmarked here.

**Gotchas:**
- The first run JIT-compiles the kernels (about 10 s) and caches them on disk under a hash of the kernel source; set AV_DENOISE_COMPILATION_CACHE=off to measure the cold cost. The bundled e2e benchmark runs an untimed warm-up and leaves the cache on, so its timed pass excludes compilation, although the config comment says shader compilation counts.
- When embedding: the windowed NLM kernels unroll (2 x search_radius + 1)^2 times, and a search radius of about 5 or more can overflow the 2 MiB stack of CubeCL's codegen thread and abort the process. Call raise_codegen_stack_limit() at the top of main; the workspace sets RUST_MIN_STACK to 16 MiB for cargo runs.
- --strength is an absolute FFmpeg-style value only in the `fast` variant (preset veryfast). Every other preset picks `hq`, where it multiplies the measured noise level, and the default preset `base` also sets temporal radius 2, search radius 2 and patch radius 4, so the default run is not FFmpeg's geometry.
- The README's '~2x FFmpeg nlmeans_opencl' and '~1.3x V-BM3D' lines disagree with its own charts (about 11x and about 1.04x like-for-like through VapourSynth). The charts were committed 2026-09-06, the day 0.4.0 was released, and have not been re-run on later code.

**Status:** Active (0.5.0-alpha3 published 2026-10-03, last commit 2026-10-03, 403 crates.io downloads) and Apache-2.0, so it is copyable as a Rust crate, CLI or VapourSynth plugin. It is an alpha with a single maintainer and 14 stars, and has no C/C++ interface.

[repo](https://github.com/ChillFish8/av-denoise) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ChillFish8/av-denoise)

##### edge264  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Compact C H.264 (progressive High, MVC) decoder that beats single-threaded FFmpeg libavcodec by about 1.2x in its CI.

**Beats:** FFmpeg libavcodec H.264 decoder (README chart also shows LibAVC and OpenH264) — The repo's own workflow_dispatch CI (27 July 2026, GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest x86-64 and ubuntu-24.04-arm runners, CPU model not recorded, median of 5) decoded the 1080p 10 s Big Buck Bunny clip single-threaded: edge264 Clang 3.9 s and GCC 4.5 s versus apt FFmpeg (-threads 1) 4.6 s on x86-64, and 3.8/3.9 s versus 4.7 s on arm64, built with -march=native -std=gnu11 -O3 using the runner's apt compilers. Reading bench-decoders.py against edge264_test.c shows both native edge264 and FFmpeg figures are user CPU time of the whole process (edge264's 'CPU:' line from getrusage ru_utime, FFmpeg's -benchmark utime), so that pair is like for like; only the WASM bar (wall clock), LibAVC (wall clock around the process) and OpenH264 (self-reported) use other clocks, and the harness never checks that edge264 decoded every frame (-y turns off YUV comparison and the PASS/FAIL count is ignored), although this same clip failed to decode in 2022 (issue #5, since closed).

**Known shortcoming:** Own CI benchmark (.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml, misc-scripts/bench-decoders.py, median of 5, every decoder single-threaded with ffmpeg -threads 1): Clang build 3.9 vs FFmpeg 4.6 s on x86-64 (1.18x) and 3.8 vs 4.7 s on arm64 (1.24x); the GCC build ties on x86-64 (4.5 vs 4.6 s). Timing is like-for-like for the native rows (bench-decoders.py reads edge264's getrusage ru_utime 'CPU:' line and FFmpeg's utime; only the WASM, LibAVC and OpenH264 rows use wall or self-reported time); flags -march=native -O3 but runner CPU model and compiler versions unstated, so C. Decodes progressive High and MVC profiles only; the benchmark skips the output check (-y). The fork edge264-mvc adds multithreading, where FFmpeg with all cores wins.

**Known shortcoming:** The harness never checks decode success (-y, PASS/FAIL ignored), and the same clip failed to decode in 2022 (issue #5, closed). Open issues: #32 and #16 (output order), #30 (multithread segfault), #21 (hang), #28 (idct8x8 crash), #8 (no fuzzing); unmerged fix PRs #26 (scaling-matrix defaults) and #25 (single-thread hang). The README API is out of date against edge264.h (callback argument order); the FetchContent tag v1.0 is missing (only v0.1 exists).

**How:** It replaces hand-written assembly with GCC/Clang vector extensions and aliased SSE/NEON intrinsics (about 80% shared code across x86 and ARM, and WASM SIMD via Clang). The slice decoder is a forward pipeline of non-inlined code blocks joined by tail calls, with tree-shaped jump tables for intra prediction, to keep the hot code small enough for L1. Branches are removed with fake 'unavailable' neighbour macroblocks around each frame and relative neighbour offsets, the bitstream reader uses a register-wide cached reader with on-the-fly SIMD unescaping, and CABAC keeps its state in full-width registers so it renormalises less often and decodes bypass bins in batches.

**Use it when:**
- Decoding progressive 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 (High/Main/constrained Baseline without FMO) on one core per stream, for example many concurrent streams on a server
- Embedding a small, dependency-free BSD-3-Clause C decoder instead of linking all of libavcodec
- WebAssembly or browser decoding: the same source builds with emscripten (WASM SIMD, optional relaxed SIMD) and ran at 5.0-5.2 s on the benchmark clip versus 4.6-4.7 s for native FFmpeg
- MVC (stereo 3D) streams: both views come out of one decoder, the second in Edge264Frame.samples_mvc
- x86-64 or arm64 builds where you control the compiler; Clang builds measured faster than GCC builds on x86-64 (3.9 vs 4.5 s)

**Skip it when:**
- Interlaced (PAFF/MBAFF) broadcast or camera content, 10-bit, 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 streams: unsupported, decode returns ENOTSUP
- Latency-bound single-stream playback where FFmpeg's frame/slice threading counts: multithreading is labelled experimental in edge264_test, issue #30 reports a segfault in worker_loop with n_threads 1-2, and the edge264-mvc fork's chart shows multithreaded FFmpeg ahead
- Untrusted input without your own sandboxing: no fuzzing is set up (issue #8 open since 2024), and open issues report a hang (#21), a crash in add_idct8x8 on ESP32-P4 (#28) and decode failures on user samples (#19)
- Players that depend on exact output order: issues #16 (Main profile) and #32 (High profile, August 2026, a P frame emitted where FFmpeg emits a B frame) are open
- Projects that need a stable ABI or MSVC: pre-1.0 with API renames planned for 1.0 (2027), and only GCC and Clang are supported

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (Makefile; CMakeLists.txt wraps it as imported target edge264::edge264) · none beyond libc and pthreads; SDL2 is loaded at runtime only by the edge264_test display mode · C11 (gnu11) with GCC or Clang vector extensions; Clang 15+ for the generic backend on other ISAs; emscripten for WASM · x86/x64 (SSE; optional runtime dispatch to x86-64-v2/v3 builds via VARIANTS), ARM32/64 with NEON, WASM32/64 SIMD, other little-endian ISAs via Clang generic vectors; macOS, Linux, Windows (MinGW), Android, iOS

**Vs siblings:** Among catalogued video decoders, rivet-h26x claims gains over libavcodec mainly with all threads, on H.265 wavefront content; pick edge264 when you want a small embeddable C library for progressive H.264 with single-thread speed, a WASM build or MVC output, and stay with FFmpeg when you need the full H.264 feature set or multithreaded latency.

**Gotchas:**
- The README API reference is out of date against edge264.h: it documents the decode_NAL callback as free_cb(void *free_arg, int ret) while the header declares Edge264UnrefCb(int ret, void *unref_arg), and shows pixel_depth_Y where the header has bit_depth_Y; code to the header.
- The README's CMake FetchContent example pins GIT_TAG v1.0, but the only tag in the repository is v0.1 (2014), so pin a commit hash instead.
- With borrow = 0 a frame is valid only until the next edge264_decode_NAL call, and ENOBUFS means drain frames with edge264_get_frame and resubmit the same NAL; errors are detected late per NAL by clamping, so corrupt input yields frames plus an mb_errors probability map rather than a hard failure.
- Open correctness fixes are unmerged: PR #26 (High profile default scaling matrices per H.264 Table 7-2) and PR #25 (single-threaded decode hang when ready_tasks is zero), both from February 2026.

**Status:** Active solo project (971 commits, last commit 2026-07-28, 437 stars) under BSD-3-Clause and easy to vendor, but pre-1.0 with API freeze targeted for 2027 and several open crash, hang and output-order reports.

[repo](https://github.com/tvlabs/edge264) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tvlabs/edge264/HEAD/README-benchmark.svg)

##### Falcon audio codec  `Rust (with C and C++ API)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

New MIT-licensed MDCT audio codec in Rust, with a C API, whose decoder runs about 1.5x faster than libopus at equal file size.

**Beats:** libopus 1.6.1 (float and fixed point), opusfile 0.12, libvorbis 1.3.7, Tremor (decoders) — First-party, single-thread, library-level decode of an 18-file 48 kHz stereo corpus from memory in 20 ms reads (open, decode and close timed; best run over two passes): Falcon 2.0 through its C API at 1114x real time vs float libopus 1.6.1 at 731x on an Intel Core Ultra 9 185H P-core (Windows 11; Falcon built with the MSVC Rust toolchain for x86-64-v3, C decoders with GCC 15.1 MinGW-w64 -O3 -march=x86-64-v3), and 1551x vs 1056x on Apple M5 (Apple clang 17). Falcon decodes its own files, size-matched to libopus VBR files of 96-214 kbps, while raw libopus is fed pre-extracted packets; the C program that produced the table is not public, the 2.0.0 numbers it replaced were withdrawn the same day (FFmpeg's built-in decoders and cached reference times), and 11 of the 18 corpus files are not redistributed.

**Known shortcoming:** Different codec from libopus, matched only by file size, with quality parity resting on the project's own metrics; the C decoder harness behind the README table (1114x versus libopus 731x realtime, 0.66x time) is not published anywhere (tools/ holds only a Python quality script and an old ffmpeg-subprocess evaluation).

**Known shortcoming:** v2.0.1 fixed aarch64 builds that produced invalid output on the same day the M5 numbers appeared (the README says outputs are SNR-checked); the 2.0.0 numbers were withdrawn (FFmpeg built-in decoders, cached reference times); pulse counts use libm powf on both sides with cross-platform desync untested; panic = abort in release builds; the 'fuzz' tests are fixed truncation and byte-flip cases on one tone. The C comparison program is still unpublished.

**How:** The format moves every decision to the encoder: the decoder reads static canonical Huffman codes for 27 band energies, derives each band's pulse count from the transmitted energies (no allocation side info), decodes integer pulse vectors from static cell tables (stars-and-bars composition index plus Fischer pyramid enumeration or Golomb-Rice), scales each band in one autovectorized pass and runs one FFT-based inverse MDCT (rustdct/rustfft) per frame, or four short ones on transients. There is no decoder-side psychoacoustics, spreading rotation or anti-collapse logic, the per-band 10^(dB/20) uses a polynomial instead of libm powf, and x86-64 builds default to x86-64-v3 (AVX2, FMA) with fat LTO.

**Use it when:**
- Games or apps that ship their own audio assets, control both encoder and decoder, and want lower CPU per voice than libopus or libvorbis/Tremor at Opus-like file sizes.
- Mixing many simultaneous 48 kHz stereo streams on one thread, where decode CPU matters more than memory (README: 256 voices in 291 ms vs 365 ms for float libopus on x86-64).
- C or C++ engines that want an MIT-licensed codec with a small C ABI and a CMake target, and that can take a Rust-built static or shared library.
- Projects that prefer a codec whose design avoids four named patents (PATENTS.md), accepting that this is the author's own analysis, not legal advice.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that must interoperate: browsers, WebRTC, Ogg/Opus or Vorbis files, or third-party players cannot read .falcon, and 1.x files cannot be read by 2.x.
- Real-time voice or lossy networks: no packet-loss concealment, no low-delay mode, 20 ms frames plus encoder look-ahead.
- Memory-tight many-voice playback: about 318-345 KB of heap per stereo stream plus a full copy of the compressed file in the C API (libopus 27 KB), and about 629 KB of decoder code vs 130 KB for libopus.
- When stb_vorbis is an option: in Falcon's own table it is 4% faster on the x86-64 P-core and 1.28x faster on Apple M5, with less memory per stream and a standard format.
- Production use that needs an outside track record: two stars, five commits, first release July 2026, no independent measurement, and the cross-codec harness is not published.

**Integration:** Rust crates (falcon_decoder, falcon_encoder, falcon_core), plus static lib and shared lib via falcon_capi (C99 header falcon.h, C++17 falcon.hpp) · rustfft, rustdct, num-complex, thiserror, crc, byteorder, once_cell (Rust); the C library links the Rust standard library, plus ntdll on MSVC or pthread, dl and m on Linux/macOS · Rust 1.70 (declared MSRV), Cargo; C99 or C++17 compiler for the bindings; verified with MSVC and MinGW · Windows, Linux, macOS; x86-64 builds default to x86-64-v3 (AVX2, FMA, BMI) via .cargo/config.toml, aarch64 uses NEON; tuned for 48 kHz

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued Opus decoders (ruopus, opuspp, opus-pure) report decode gains over libopus 1.6.1 of a similar size (1.27x to 1.79x in their own first-party tests) while keeping the standard Opus bitstream, so take one of those when you need Opus compatibility. Pick Falcon only for a closed asset pipeline where you choose the codec and want an MIT-licensed format with a deliberately simple decoder.

**Gotchas:**
- Pulse counts come from f32 powf/exp/ln on both encoder and decoder (falcon_core::alloc), so a different libm can in principle change an integer pulse count and desynchronize the stream; the README says cross-platform agreement has not been tested systematically, and the CLI and C API encoders emit a random-access frame only at the start, so a desync would not recover.
- The release profile sets panic = "abort", so any panic that slips past the decoder's error paths aborts the host process; the corrupt-input coverage is deterministic truncation and byte-flip tests on one synthetic tone, not a coverage-guided fuzzer.
- The default x86-64 build requires AVX2/FMA (x86-64-v3); rebuild with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=x86-64" for older CPUs. Before 2.0.1 the same setting broke aarch64 builds, which produced invalid output.
- Seeking is linear: a backward seek re-decodes from the file start, and the decoder makes about seven heap allocations (about 8 KB) per 20 ms frame. A MinGW build of the Rust library decodes 1.45x slower (771x) because it links msvcrt pow/exp/log.

**Status:** Active but very new (five commits, v1.0.0 July 2026, v2.0.0 and v2.0.1 both on 2026-09-29, two stars); MIT-licensed and copyable, but the format is young and the speed claim is first-party with no public harness.

[repo](https://github.com/pbtechlab/Falcon) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pbtechlab/Falcon/HEAD/README.md)

##### fast-vad  `Rust (Python bindings via maturin)`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust/Python voice activity detector using a logistic regression over 8 FFT bands; first-party chart puts it 2-11x past webrtcvad.

**Beats:** webrtcvad (Google WebRTC voice activity detector, C) — One first-party bar chart (docs/assets/processing-speed.png, Ryzen 7700X, 8 cores and 16 threads) gives speed relative to Silero ONNX: fast_vad offline 721x, streaming 129x, webrtcvad 63x. That makes streaming about 2x webrtcvad and offline about 11.4x (derived from page data), but the offline figure uses all 16 threads against single-threaded webrtcvad. The Python harness that produced the chart is not in the repo (bench_py/ is absent and excluded from the sdist; notebooks/ is gitignored), so the webrtcvad frame size (10, 20 or 30 ms), whether the float-to-int16 PCM conversion webrtcvad needs was inside the timing, Silero's ONNX thread settings, the audio used, compiler and flags are all unknown. The public criterion benches (bench_rs) time fast_vad alone on synthetic noise.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). The 721x/129x/63x figures are against Silero (a neural VAD, a different model class) on a Ryzen 7700X with the comparison harness (bench_py/, notebooks/) gitignored; bench_rs/benches/vad_bench.rs times fast_vad alone on noise. Detectors differ (32 ms FFT plus logistic regression vs webrtcvad's own model on 10/20/30 ms frames) and the offline run uses 16 threads; the fair figure is streaming at about 2x webrtcvad. Baseline webrtcvad is not a listed incumbent.

**Known shortcoming:** Weak category fit: a voice-activity detector is audio classification, not a codec. The 721x offline figure is 16 threads against single-threaded webrtcvad; the 2x streaming figure is Python per-frame calls with webrtcvad frame size and int16 conversion placement unknown; bench_py/ is uncommitted (sdist-excluded, not gitignored) and notebooks/ is gitignored, so the harness is absent. Offline (look-ahead) and streaming (causal) smoothing differ, so labels can differ; the noise floor is seeded from the first frame; pyo3 and numpy are unconditional dependencies for Rust users; no C API. The blog's '721x realtime' misreads the chart, which is speedup versus Silero ONNX.

**How:** The model is tiny: per frame a SIMD Hann window, one realfft real-to-complex FFT, power summed into 8 log-energy bands (about 94-4000 Hz), then a 32-weight logistic regression (raw, noise-normalised, first- and second-delta features, weights compiled in as f32x8 constants from the portable `wide` crate) and a threshold. In the offline path the window/FFT/band stage runs over all frames in parallel with rayon; the classifier is then a sequential scan, because the per-band noise floor (an EMA with alpha 0.01) only updates on frames judged silent. The streaming path reuses preallocated window, FFT output and scratch buffers, so a frame does no allocation.

**Use it when:**
- Batch pre-segmentation of large 16 kHz or 8 kHz speech corpora (ASR or diarisation pipelines) where throughput matters more than best-in-class F1 and all cores are free for the offline rayon path.
- Python pipelines that already hold float32 numpy audio and want segment boundaries without loading ONNX Runtime or a neural model (the Silero ONNX comparison in the docs is 721x slower than the offline path and 129x slower than streaming).
- Clean or read speech close to LibriVAD, where the docs report F1 about 0.93-0.94 from 0 to 20 dB SNR with precision steady near 0.908.
- Rust services that need a cheap, allocation-free per-frame streaming detector with 32 ms decision granularity.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: it is a Rust crate plus a Python wheel with no C API, so it needs your own FFI layer. WebRTC VAD is C and easy to embed.
- Hard real-world audio where accuracy dominates: on AVA-Speech the docs report F1 0.680 against 0.738 for Silero (webrtcvad 0.669), and the presets were tuned on LibriVAD read speech.
- Sample rates other than 8 or 16 kHz (no 32/48 kHz as in WebRTC VAD), multichannel input, or decisions finer than 32 ms (WebRTC VAD takes 10, 20 or 30 ms frames).
- Latency-critical turn-taking: streaming onset needs min_speech frames (2 frames, 64 ms, in normal mode) on top of the 32 ms frame, and offset waits for min_silence plus hangover.
- Projects that need a stable or mature dependency: version 0.2.x, PyPI classifier 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha', 28 stars, one breaking API change already (0.2.0 return types).

**Integration:** crate (fast-vad on crates.io, cdylib + lib) and Python abi3 wheel (fast-vad on PyPI) · rayon, realfft, wide, thiserror, plus pyo3 0.28 (extension-module, abi3-py311), numpy and ndarray, which are unconditional even for pure-Rust users; Python package needs numpy >= 2.0 · Rust edition 2024 (Rust 1.85+); Python >= 3.11 · Wheels for Linux x86_64 and aarch64 (manylinux_2_28), macOS x86_64 and arm64, Windows x64; CI runs Rust tests on Ubuntu x64/arm64, macOS Intel/arm64 and Windows. SIMD is portable through `wide`, so no specific ISA is required.

**Vs siblings:** No other voice activity detector is catalogued. The video-audio siblings are codecs, resamplers, RTP stacks and denoisers, so none competes with it. A VAD classifies audio rather than encoding it, so it sits in this category only as audio analysis; judge it against webrtcvad and Silero, not against libopus or FFmpeg.

**Gotchas:**
- The offline VAD and streaming VadStateful smooth labels differently: offline applies hangover and then drops short speech and silence runs over the whole label array, which looks ahead; streaming uses a causal state machine. The same audio can therefore get different labels from the two paths.
- The noise floor is seeded from the first frame's band energies, and afterwards only moves on frames classified as silence (alpha 0.01, roughly a 3.2 s time constant at 32 ms frames, derived from the code). A stream that starts mid-speech begins with a speech-level floor. Call reset_state() between streams.
- Python input must be a contiguous float32 numpy array: float64 (the default dtype of soundfile.read), int16 or int32 raise TypeError. Trailing samples that do not fill a frame are ignored by detect_frames, and detect() copies the last frame's label onto them.
- Secondary write-ups describe the result as '721x realtime', but the docs chart's axis is a speedup factor relative to Silero ONNX, not a real-time factor; no absolute timings are published.

**Status:** Active (0.2.1 released 2026-03-25 on crates.io and PyPI, 83 commits, CI on Linux, macOS and Windows) and dual MIT/Apache-2.0, so it is easy to adopt from Rust or Python; it is still alpha-labelled, has a single author and its speed evidence is first-party only.

[repo](https://github.com/AtharvBhat/fast-vad) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AtharvBhat/fast-vad/HEAD/docs/README.md)

##### fcvvdp  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

C reimplementation of the CVVDP video-quality metric; first-party 1.28x (1 thread) and 3.22x (8 threads) faster than Python cvvdp.

**Beats:** cvvdp reference implementation (gfxdisp/ColorVideoVDP, Python, multithreaded) — One first-party poop run (3 runs each) on Linux with a Core i7-13700K scoring a 302-frame 360p clip against its x264 encode (fhd display): Python cvvdp (multithreaded, PyTorch version and device unstated, start-up and decoding included) took 19.1 s at 1.03 GB RSS, fcvvdp -t 1 14.9 s (1.28x) and -t 8 5.94 s (3.22x) at about 90 MB. The Zig/clang version and flags at the time are unstated, the clip is not shipped, and the measured commit predates the sRGB and PR #19 scoring fixes.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-baseline (a video-quality metric, not a codec). The README poop run on an i7-13700K matches the record but there is no benchmark script or clip, and the 2026-03-10 numbers predate PR #19 (2026-09-22), which fixed scoring bugs of up to 0.22 JOD against FFVship.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e108, 2026-10-05): the README numbers (6ce3696, 2026-03-10) ran code with a second scoring bug the verifier missed: plain gamma 2.4 instead of the piecewise sRGB transfer, fixed by e123ffe (2026-06-21, about 3-4% slower worst case), plus the PR #19 bugs; the measured code also predates the AVX2/NEON kernels (PR #14), runtime dispatch (PR #17) and the 'about 20% faster' CSF, so current speed against Python cvvdp is unmeasured. build.zig sets no -mavx2/-mfma or target attributes and relies on Zig's native target (portable build undocumented); -ffast-math with per-thread partial sums, so the score varies with -t; Windows unsupported (#6 not planned); memory grows with resolution x fps (about 3.4 GB at 4K60, derived), so the 91% memory saving is a 360p figure; scalar JOD only. Tier C holds (numbers from code later fixed for correctness).

**Independent measurement:** first-party README timings

**How:** It runs the whole CVVDP pipeline (display model, RGB to XYZ to DKL, FIR temporal filtering over a ring buffer of about 0.25 s of frames, Gaussian/Laplacian pyramid, CSF LUT weighting, cross-channel masking, Minkowski pooling) as float32 C instead of PyTorch, with preallocated, reused pyramid scratch buffers, which is where the roughly 90 MB vs 1.03 GB RSS comes from. A pthread pool splits each stage into chunks within a frame (intra-frame data parallelism; frames stay sequential). Current code adds hand-written AVX2+FMA kernels chosen at run time by cpuid and NEON kernels on aarch64, built with -O3 -ffast-math. The README benchmark (commit 6ce3696, 2026-03-10) predates those SIMD kernels (PR #14, merged 2026-05-22), so the published speedup came from the plain C pipeline plus task threading.

**Use it when:**
- Batch CVVDP scoring of encoder sweeps on CPU-only servers, where the Python reference's PyTorch dependency and about 1 GB RSS per process (at 360p in the README run) limit how many jobs fit on a machine.
- Embedding CVVDP in a C or C++ encoder, tuner or test harness: static libcvvdp.a plus cvvdp.h with extern "C", fed one frame pair at a time through cvvdp_process_frame.
- FFmpeg-based pipelines that can carry a patched FFmpeg n8.0 build (-lavfi fcvvdp, per-frame stats_file output).
- Still-image comparisons (PNG, QOI, PNM/PAM) across many display models, including HDR PQ/HLG presets and custom display parameters.
- Apple Silicon and other aarch64 machines, where the NEON kernels are always used (the PR #19 timings were taken on an Apple M5 Pro).

**Skip it when:**
- When your numbers must match the official Python ColorVideoVDP release: the repo validates score parity only against Vship/FFVship (PR #19: 0.000001-0.000002 JOD after the fix); no comparison against the Python package is published.
- Windows builds: README lists macOS, Linux and Unix-like systems, the code uses pthreads and sysconf, and issue #6 (Windows build fails) was closed as not planned.
- High-resolution, high-frame-rate video on memory-tight machines: each context keeps two float RGB ring buffers of 2*ceil(fps/8)+1 frames, roughly 3.4 GB at 4K60 versus about 50 MB at 360p30 (derived from cvvdp.c), so the 91% memory saving measured at 360p is not a general figure.
- When you need difference heatmaps or other per-pixel output: cvvdp.h returns only a scalar JOD and raw quality value.
- When GPU throughput matters: there is no GPU path; Vship (GPU CVVDP, SSIMULACRA2, Butteraugli, now moved from GitHub to Codeberg) is the project fcvvdp was derived from.

**Integration:** static lib (libcvvdp.a + cvvdp.h) plus fcvvdp CLI; optional FFmpeg n8.0 filter patch · library: libc and pthreads only; CLI: libspng and simpleimgio fetched as Zig packages (build.zig.zon) · Zig 0.16.0 (minimum_zig_version in build.zig.zon); C sources compiled -std=c23 -O3 -ffast-math by Zig's bundled clang. No CMake or Makefile is provided. · x86-64 (AVX2+FMA kernels selected at run time, portable C fallback), aarch64 (NEON); macOS, Linux and Unix-like systems; Windows unsupported

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued video-audio siblings is a quality metric: dav1d, Kvazaar, VVenC, SVT-AV1 and the resamplers are codecs and filters. Use fcvvdp to score their output on CPU (for example preset or bitrate sweeps) when CVVDP is the target metric and a Python/PyTorch stack is unwanted.

**Gotchas:**
- The README timings (commit 6ce3696, 2026-03-10) ran code with scoring bugs fixed later: plain gamma 2.4 instead of the piecewise sRGB curve (commit e123ffe, 2026-06-21, 'Incurs a small speed penalty (~3-4% worst-case)'), and PR #19 (2026-09-22) fixes for an inverse-RFFT bug that erased half of each temporal kernel, reversed CSF interpolation weights, an inaccurate log approximation, RGB-to-XYZ coefficients and Y4M range handling (errors of 0.155 and 0.221 JOD against FFVship before). The same commit also predates AVX2/NEON, runtime dispatch and the 2026-07-13 '~20% faster' CSF change, so the current speed against Python cvvdp has not been measured by anyone.
- build.zig passes no -mavx2/-mfma for cvvdp_avx2.c and cvvdp_avx2.h has no per-function target attributes, so the AVX2 kernels compile because Zig targets the native CPU by default; that also compiles the C fallback for the build host, so runtime cpuid dispatch does not by itself make a natively built binary portable, and a -Dcpu=baseline distribution build is not documented.
- Everything is built with -ffast-math, and cvvdp_compute_norm sums per-thread partials when a pool is active, so low-order digits of the score can differ between -t 1 and -t N or across compilers.
- The CLI decodes Y4M and converts YUV to RGB on the main thread between frames (threading covers only the metric stages), requires equal frame counts and dimensions, and reads no other video container; doc/cvvdp.md still describes the sRGB decode as 'approx. 2.4 power'.

**Status:** Active (82 commits, v0.4.0, last commit 2026-09-22) single-company project (Halide Compression) under Apache-2.0; the core is one 2,069-line cvvdp.c plus SIMD headers, small enough to vendor into a C/C++ build if you replace the Zig build.

[repo](https://github.com/halidecx/fcvvdp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/halidecx/fcvvdp)

##### flacenc-rs  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust embeddable FLAC encoder library and CLI; its multithreaded mode outruns single-threaded flac 1.4.3 at near -8 compression.

**Beats:** FLAC reference encoder: flac 1.4.3 command-line tool (-f -8, -f -8 --lax, -f -5), single-threaded (1.4.3 predates flac's -j threading) — The repository's own report (pytools/reporter.py: one wall-clock CLI run per file and setting on four Wikimedia recordings, start-up and file I/O included, on a GCP c2-standard-8 Xeon Cascade Lake VM, 4 cores/8 threads) gives nightly flacenc 331.5x real time single-threaded and 1309.5x with 8 workers against flac 1.4.3 (generic ./configure build, single-threaded) at 229.7x for -8 and 550.4x for -5, with output 0.4% larger than -8; the stable build reaches 126.5x and 575.3x. Every flacenc output was decoded with flac -d and matched the input byte for byte, so the numbers are for lossless streams, but no configuration is both faster and at least as small as a tested flac setting at equal thread count.

**Known shortcoming:** CLI-versus-CLI comparison with one timing run per file; the flac C compiler is not logged.
