**Integration:** crate (opus-rs on crates.io, 0.1.34) · none at runtime with default features (std, heap); libm (pure Rust) for no_std builds; criterion, proptest and the opus 0.3 bindings crate (audiopus_sys) are dev-dependencies only · Rust edition 2024 (Rust 1.85+); no rust-version is declared in Cargo.toml · x86-64 with runtime SSE/AVX/AVX2 dispatch (compile-time detection without std, so build with -C target-feature=+avx2), x86 32-bit (AVX import fix in PR #16), aarch64 with NEON, thumbv7em-none-eabi and wasm32-unknown-unknown in no_std mode

**Vs siblings:** Pick opus-rs over ropus, ruopus, rusty-opus or gopus when you need a pure-Rust Opus encoder and decoder that is already widely pulled from crates.io (about 182,000 downloads), has zero runtime dependencies and builds no_std without an allocator; the siblings' own first-party numbers are larger (ruopus 1.4-1.8x libopus decode, opus-pure 1.09-1.76x encode, rusty-opus 1.50x on CELT speech), so do not pick opus-rs for speed alone.

**Gotchas:**
- The README's command cargo bench --bench opus_vs_c_bench does not exist: Cargo.toml registers only opus_bench, whose opus_real group runs Rust encode plus decode at complexity 0, CBR, 20 or 64 kb/s, with 48 kHz input made by repeating each 16 kHz sample three times and 8 kHz input by dropping every other sample. libopus 1.6.1 skips tonality analysis below complexity 7, so if the private C bench matched complexity 0 the work was comparable; if it ran at the default complexity 9, libopus did analysis work opus-rs never does. The README does not say which.
- Byte-exact CELT output against libopus is claimed per architecture only: tests/oracle_celt.rs keeps separate x86_64 and aarch64 fixtures, and its impulse fixture diverges from libopus 1.6.1 after byte 7 because analysis.c is not ported. The PVQ cross-check against C (tests/verify_pvq_match.rs) uses n = 8, so it never reaches the batched n >= 32 search path.
- Without the heap feature (no_std) OpusEncoder and OpusDecoder are about 250 KB and 175 KB inline, so place them in a static; before 0.1.29 even the std build needed about 0.85 MiB of stack to construct an encoder (issue #12).
- pvq.rs (71 unsafe occurrences) and celt.rs use raw-pointer loops and intrinsics; the crate is not #![forbid(unsafe_code)], and issue #7 (closed) asked for decoder hardening against untrusted packets.

**Status:** Actively maintained (0.1.34 on 2026-09-22, 96 commits, outside contributors fixing CELT byte-exactness and SIMD bugs) and BSD-3-Clause, so it is easy to adopt from Rust, but nine issues were open on 2026-10-04, five of them encoder or decoder correctness bugs filed in late September 2026.

[repo](https://github.com/restsend/opus-rs) · [benchmark](https://github.com/restsend/opus-rs)

##### QOA (Quite OK Audio)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-header C codec for fixed 3.2-bit/sample lossy audio; author's run encodes 12x and decodes 7x faster than ffmpeg Opus.

**Beats:** Opus (libopus); also MP3 encoding — Seen only through search snippets of the author's April 2023 post (blocked here): qoaconv encoded a 2 h 43 min 44.1 kHz stereo WAV (Blade Runner 2049 soundtrack, 1650 MB) in 25.752 s and decoded it in 2.996 s on one thread of an i7-6700K, against 315.232 s / 20.410 s for Opus and 146.223 s / 9.631 s for MP3 through the ffmpeg CLI at default settings, about 12.2x/6.8x versus Opus and 5.7x/3.2x versus MP3 and about 3,270x real-time decode (derived from snippet data). The codecs ran at very different bitrates (QOA 333 MB vs Opus 116 MB), the ffmpeg runs carry CLI overhead, and neither QOA build flags nor the timing method were published; qoaconv only gained its own timing printout in Sep 2024, and it defines QOA_RECORD_TOTAL_ERROR and chooses output format by file extension, so it cannot have written to /dev/null as the ffmpeg runs did (both effects add work on QOA's side, not ffmpeg's).

**Known shortcoming:** Different work from Opus: a time-domain codec at about 280 kbit/s against Opus at about 96 kbit/s run through ffmpeg. The repo, qoa.h and issues carry no numbers; the blog table (Opus 315.232/20.410 s against QOA 25.752/2.996 s, 12.2x encode and 6.8x decode derived) is a search snippet of the blocked phoboslab.org post.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e118, 2026-10-05): no correctness bug behind the numbers; C stands. A snippet confirms the QOA side was timed with qoaconv (333 MB vs Opus 116 MB); timing method and build flags are unpublished and qoaconv's timing printout was only added in September 2024. The decoder was hardened in 2026 (#82 heap overflow, out-of-bounds slices, unchecked QOA_MAX_CHANNELS, PR #80 wrap-around). The encoder's size calculation is still unsigned int with the malloc result unchecked (wraps with 3 or more channels and very long input); crafted weights can overflow the int32 LMS predictor; open #69 encoder saturates samples 74-240 to -32768; open #56 weights stored as 16-bit.

**Independent measurement:** first-party timing

**How:** It is a pure time-domain coder: a 4-tap sign-sign LMS predictor in fixed point predicts each sample, and the residual is quantized to 3 bits against one of 16 per-slice scalefactors, with a lookup table for dequantization. Decoding is one 4-term dot product, one table lookup, one 16-bit clamp (with a rarely taken branch) and four weight updates per sample; there is no transform, psychoacoustic model, entropy coding or bit reservoir. The encoder brute-forces all 16 scalefactors per 20-sample slice, but starts with the previous slice's winner, abandons a candidate as soon as its accumulated squared error exceeds the best so far, and replaces the division by a .16 fixed-point reciprocal multiply. There is no SIMD and no threading; the speed comes from doing very little work per sample.

**Use it when:**
- Games and engines that play many sound effects or music streams and want near-zero decode CPU; Godot 4.3 (WAV-to-QOA import), raylib's raudio and SerenityOS already ship it.
- Microcontrollers or small embedded players where an Opus or MP3 decoder is too large or too slow: the decoder keeps 8 ints of LMS state per channel and needs one frame buffer (4136 bytes for a stereo frame by QOA_FRAME_SIZE).
- Assets that need cheap random access: frame size is fixed by the channel count, so seek offsets are computed rather than searched (qoaplay seeks this way).
- Fast batch conversion of 16-bit PCM where a fixed 5x size reduction is enough and the quality target is 'often not audible' rather than perceptually optimised.

**Skip it when:**
- Bandwidth- or storage-bound delivery: in the author's own run QOA produced 333 MB against 116 MB for Opus and 149 MB for MP3 at ffmpeg defaults, and the format has no bitrate control.
- Untrusted input: the README says the implementation has not been fuzzed; 2026 commits fixed a heap overflow from malformed frame lengths (issue #82), out-of-bounds reads on bad slices, an unchecked QOA_MAX_CHANNELS in decode and a buffer-size wrap-around, and crafted frame weights can still push the int32 LMS predictor into signed overflow (weights grow by up to 896 per sample with no clamp; read from source).
- Material where encoder artefacts are unacceptable without checking: open issue #69 (Aug 2025) reports a 5120-sample mono file whose samples 74-240 all encode to -32768, and the third-party brute-force encoder ETDAW (issue #79) exists because qoaconv's greedy per-slice choice leaves audible high-frequency noise on some audio.
- 24-bit, float or more-than-8-channel sources: input is 16-bit only, this implementation caps channels at QOA_MAX_CHANNELS 8 (the spec was clarified to 31 in Sep 2026), and it only handles files with a known total sample count, not the streaming header with samples = 0.

**Integration:** header-only (qoa.h, STB style: define QOA_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit) · none beyond libc: malloc/free (overridable through QOA_MALLOC/QOA_FREE) and stdio for qoa_read/qoa_write unless QOA_NO_STDIO; the qoaconv tool optionally uses dr_mp3.h/dr_flac.h and qoaplay uses sokol_audio.h · C99 (Makefile: -std=c99 -O3 for qoaconv, -std=gnu99 for qoaplay); callable from C++ through extern "C"; a GCC 15 build failure (issue #73) was closed in Dec 2025 · any: portable scalar C with byte-wise big-endian I/O, no SIMD or intrinsics; qoaplay is marked 'not yet tested on Windows/macOS' in the Makefile

**Vs siblings:** Pick QOA over minimp3, nanomp3, Falcon or the libopus ports (opus-rs, ruopus, opuspp) when decode cost, code size and instant seeking matter more than file size and you control both the encoder and the player; pick an Opus implementation for bandwidth-bound delivery and minimp3/nanomp3 when the files are already MP3.

**Gotchas:**
- qoa_decode allocates whole 5120-sample frames for the entire file and returns NULL when frames x 5120 x channels exceeds 0x7fffffff samples (about 6.7 h of 44.1 kHz stereo); qoa_read sizes the file with int/ftell, so files over 2 GB fail. Long material should go through qoa_decode_frame.
- qoa_encode computes the output size in unsigned int and does not check the malloc result: with 3 or more channels and more than about 1.07e10 total samples the size wraps and the encoder writes past the buffer. The decoder got the equivalent wrap-around guard in June 2026 (PR #80); the encoder did not.
- The encoder keeps 32-bit LMS weights but stores them in each frame header masked to 16 bits; if a weight leaves the int16 range at a frame boundary the decoder restarts from different weights than the encoder assumed. Open issue #56 asks whether this overflow is intended; the weights penalty in the encoder is what normally keeps them small.
- Driving qoa_encode_frame yourself (streaming encode) means initialising qoa->lms to weights {0, 0, -8192, 16384} and zero history as qoa_encode does, and only the last frame may be short (since the #82 fix the decoder stops at the first short frame). QOA_FREE is defined only inside the implementation, so callers cannot portably free qoa_decode's buffer with the matching allocator (open issue #64), and defining QOA_MALLOC without QOA_FREE breaks the stdio helpers.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-27; most 2026 commits harden the decoder against malformed files after outside reports), MIT-licensed and a single 759-line header that is trivial to vendor, but still unfuzzed by the author's own README.

[repo](https://github.com/phoboslab/qoa) · [benchmark](https://phoboslab.org/log/2023/04/qoa-specification)

##### remade_ffmpeg_rs  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust, Apache-2.0 FFmpeg rebuild whose MP3 decoder and frame-parallel AAC/Vorbis encoders beat FFmpeg's CLI on wall clock.

**Beats:** FFmpeg libavcodec native MP3 decoder and native AAC encoder; libvorbis — First-party, unnamed machine, Rust 1.95.0 thin-LTO builds. rusty_mp3's decode loop (the decprof example) against the FFmpeg CLI's native mp3float decoder (`-f null -`, FFmpeg version not stated) on one 27.5-minute stream, 15 alternated wall-clock pairs: 1,952 vs 2,431 ms on 1 physical core and 1,017 vs 1,455 ms on 2 with the two-thread pipeline; the serial build on 2 cores lost, 1,807 vs 1,445 ms. AAC-LC encode via the rff CLI was 3.2-7.9x faster than FFmpeg 8.1.2's native encoder (unpinned subprocesses, best-of-5, all cores against one), and Vorbis encode about 5.2x faster than libvorbis on 24 cores but about 1.45x slower single-threaded.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch); one repo holding rusty_mp3, rusty_aac and rusty_vorbis. Harnesses public (codec-bench.ps1, pinab.py, aac_vs_ffmpeg.py; Rust 1.95.0, thin LTO) but no CPU named for the audio rows and no FFmpeg flags. MP3 decode (rusty_mp3 vs FFmpeg's native decoder through the CLI) is 1.24x on one core, while the repo's own control row has FFmpeg 1.25x ahead of the serial build on two cores (derived). The AAC 5-6x (vs FFmpeg 8.1.2 native encoder) and Vorbis 5.3x (vs libvorbis) are multi-thread against single-thread; single-thread Vorbis is 1.45x slower with lower PEAQ quality.

**Known shortcoming:** The MP3 one-core 1.24x pits an in-process decprof loop against the whole ffmpeg CLI run with -f null -, which also performs an fltp-to-s16 filtergraph plus pcm_s16le encode (nullenc.c) with pipeline threads sharing one core; the project's own two-core control row bounds the libavcodec decoder at 1,455 ms against serial rusty_mp3's 1,807 ms, so decoder for decoder FFmpeg is about 1.25x faster (derived) and the per-core 1.39x is a thread-count effect. The MP3 table's command, CPU, FFmpeg version and affinity masks are unpublished; codec-bench.ps1 pins one logical CPU and is video-shaped. The AAC and Vorbis encoders are batch-only (no packets before finish); the AAC PEAQ downmixes to mono so stereo rows are blind; the AAC decoder uses a naive O(N^2) f64 IMDCT (open issue #16); the profiler is always on in rusty_mp3; the crate README's 1.30x control row is really 1.25x.

**How:** MP3 decode: five bit-identical changes (an 8-byte word-load bit reader for Huffman peeks, a circularly addressed synthesis V-FIFO instead of a 960-float memmove per pass, a half-work IMDCT that derives mirrored outputs from exact symmetries of the stored cosine tables, runtime-detected AVX matrixing and windowing kept bit-exact by using separate mul+add, and a division-free Huffman pair decode), plus `decode_pipelined`, which splits entropy decoding (bit reservoir) from the transform (IMDCT overlap, synthesis FIFO) across two threads joined by a bounded channel. AAC and Vorbis encode: frame parallelism. Window decisions are made up front, then contiguous frame ranges are encoded on `available_parallelism()` scoped threads. This works because the AAC encoder has no bit reservoir (fixed per-frame budget) and the Vorbis encoder codes independent 2048-sample long blocks. N/4-point FFT MDCTs, AVX2 quantize kernels and a Vorbis energy-bucket residue-class shortlist cut per-frame cost.

**Use it when:**
- You need MP3 decoding in a Rust or wasm program under a permissive licence with no C or FFI; the authors gate it bit-exact against FFmpeg, and it is bit-exact on wasm32-wasip1 and wasm32-unknown-unknown with zero host imports.
- Offline batch transcoding of whole files to AAC-LC or Vorbis on a many-core box, where wall-clock time matters more than CPU time and the whole input can sit in memory (AAC 3.2-7.9x and Vorbis about 5.2x faster than single-threaded FFmpeg/libvorbis, first-party).
- Embedding an AAC-LC or MP3 encoder in a Rust binary without FFmpeg's LGPL/GPL or FDK's licence; rusty_aac's PEAQ table has it ahead of FFmpeg's native AAC on real mono music at 128 kb/s and above.
- Decoding long MP3 files already in memory on a 2-core budget: `decode_pipelined` measured 1,017 ms against FFmpeg's 1,455 ms on two physical cores.

**Skip it when:**
- Live or low-latency encoding: the AAC and Vorbis encoders buffer the whole stream and return `Again` from `next_packet` until `finish()`, so the parallel speedup exists only in whole-file mode.
- CPU-bound single-threaded encoding or best quality per bit: single-thread Vorbis is about 1.45x slower than libvorbis and 0.6-0.7 PEAQ ODG behind on tonal music; rusty_aac has no bit reservoir or VBR and trails FFmpeg at 96 kb/s and below, on piano stereo and on noise-like content.
- AAC decoding at scale, HE-AAC or more than 6 channels: the decoder's IMDCT is a naive O(N^2) f64 cosine sum (open issue #16 measured 24.4 ms per 21.3 ms frame on an EPYC 7763), SBR is not reconstructed, and 7+ channels are rejected.
- Video work: VP9 decode runs at 0.16-0.21x of FFmpeg and H.264 decode about 2x behind.
- Anything needing an audited, settled codebase: pre-1.0, 'not yet independently audited', 6 stars, and open issue #14 reports `cargo test` red on all three CI runners (rusty_av2d overflow).

**Integration:** crate (standalone rusty_mp3 0.8.0, rusty_aac 0.5.0, rusty_vorbis 0.1.1; engine library remade-ffmpeg 0.2.0; rff-cli binaries) · none for the three codec crates (empty [dependencies]); examples, benches and the CLI use the in-house rusty_alloc global allocator · Rust 1.85 (crate rust-version); workspace pins 1.95.0 in rust-toolchain.toml; rusty_aac's opt-in AVX-512 tier needs Rust 1.89+ · Windows, macOS and Linux for the CLI; x86-64 gets runtime-detected AVX/AVX2 kernels with scalar fallbacks, and other targets run the scalar paths; rusty_mp3 verified bit-exact on wasm32-wasip1 and wasm32-unknown-unknown

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Symphonia when you also need encoders (AAC-LC, MP3, Vorbis) or FFmpeg-bit-exact MP3 output. Symphonia is the broader decode-only library, and its comparison against libavcodec runs in-process, which is stronger evidence than this repo's CLI timing. Pick glint instead for a C/C++ AAC encoder with a streaming per-frame C ABI. Pick rusty-opus (same organisation, separate repo) for Opus.

**Gotchas:**
- rusty_mp3's per-stage profiler ships in the library on every target except wasm32-unknown-unknown: each stage of each granule calls `Instant::now()` twice and does a global atomic `fetch_add` (about 26 scope pairs per frame, about 1% self-tax per decprof's comment), and those counters are shared across threads.
- `decode_pipelined(&[u8]) -> Vec<DecodedAudio>` takes the complete stream and returns all PCM at once (582 MB of f32 for the 27.5-minute benchmark stream), so the 2-core speedup is not available to the streaming `Mp3Decoder` API.
- The main README says '100% safe Rust on the core path', but rusty_mp3's synthesis uses `unsafe` AVX intrinsics (matrixing_avx, window_avx) and rusty_aac's SIMD is `unsafe` behind its default `simd` feature; build rusty_aac with `--no-default-features` for a fully safe scalar build.
- Main-README figures lag the crate READMEs: the MP3-encoder gap to LAME is still quoted as 0.72/1.08 ODG at 192/128 kb/s, while rusty_mp3's README re-measured 0.08/0.23 on a different corpus; MP3 VBR output was undecodable by FFmpeg through 0.4.1, so pin 0.5.0 or later.

**Status:** Active (394 commits; last code commit 2026-09-16, last commit a 2026-10-04 install-count banner edit), Apache-2.0, pre-1.0 with 2 open issues and 6 open dependency-bump PRs; the codec crates are small and dependency-free enough to vendor, but they were first split out and published only in July-August 2026.

[repo](https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/remade_ffmpeg_rs) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remade-With-Rust/remade_ffmpeg_rs/main/readme.md)

##### ropus (Rust port of libopus)  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE is the upstream Xiph libopus BSD text plus a 2026 copyright line for the Rust port additions; ropus/Cargo.toml declares BSD-3-Clause)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust, bit-exact port of fixed-point libopus 1.5.2; runs at about parity with the C reference, not faster.

**Beats:** libopus 1.5.2 C reference as built by the repo's own harness (harness/build.rs via the cc crate): fixed-point (FIXED_POINT=1 in harness/config.h), no DNN, x86 runtime dispatch limited to SSE/SSE2/SSE4.1 (no AVX2 sources); the Apple M1 Pro rows use upstream AArch64 NEON intrinsics. Not the stock float build most distributions ship. — The project's own tools/bench_sweep.sh (harness cmd_bench, 10 WAV vectors, CBR, complexity 10, 20 ms frames, C encode and decode timed before Rust in a fixed order, no output comparison) on an i7-14700KF under WSL2 gives Rust/C time ratios with a mean of 1.06x for encode and 1.01x for decode (medians of 5 sweeps; the sub-1.0 rows fall inside the 0.02-0.32 cross-sweep spread). On Apple M1 Pro against upstream NEON C the means are 1.16x and 1.22x. The baseline is the harness's fixed-point, SSE4.1-only libopus 1.5.2, compiler versions are unstated, and both tables predate the 2026-08-01 harness fixes.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster: a port of the listed libopus with mean encode 1.06x and decode 1.01x on an i7-14700KF (1.16x/1.22x on an M1 Pro); sub-1.0 rows sit inside the cross-sweep standard deviation. The C side is the harness build (fixed-point, SSE4.1-only dispatch, NSQ_del_dec_avx2.c not compiled) while the Rust side is built x86-64-v3, so the README's 'SSE4.1/AVX2' overstates the baseline; compiler versions unstated. Decode is sample-exact against C; encode is byte-exact except the analysis path (about 5% byte drift on music). The crates.io README still shows the stale pre-fix table.

**Known shortcoming:** Both README tables (x86 at 54fef85 of 2026-05-11; Apple of 2026-07-31) were measured with harness/Cargo.toml forcing trace-silk-encode (a Rust unbounded Mutex<Vec> trace, with C running a traced enc_API.c; tracked as ROP-BUG-FLUX-00026) and with the C timer covering one create/destroy per run (FLUX-00027); both were fixed on 2026-08-01 but the tables were never re-measured, so the size of the effect is unknown. The C build gets -msse4.1 on every file with no AVX2; x86-64-v3 lives only in the workspace .cargo/config.toml, so crates.io users get generic x86-64 (own generic run: encode 1.19x slower); crates.io 0.12.18 ships an empty DNN blob and lags the repo by four months.

**How:** It is a line-by-line port of libopus's fixed-point code, not a new algorithm; speed comes from compiler work. Hot kernels use the wide crate's portable SIMD types plus unchecked indexing in the SILK and CELT inner loops (NSQ, Burg, autocorrelation, FFT butterflies, MDCT rotations), and the workspace builds with ThinLTO, codegen-units = 1 and target-cpu x86-64-v3 (apple-a14 on macOS ARM), so LLVM auto-vectorises at 256-bit width. There are no hand-written intrinsics; the project's April journal credits the x86-64-v3 switch alone with moving mean encode from 1.19x to 1.02x of C.

**Use it when:**
- Rust projects (native or WebAssembly) that want Opus without linking C libopus or needing a C compiler; videocall.rs reports using it in production for encode and NetEQ decode, including WASM clients (issue #1).
- When output must match fixed-point libopus 1.5.2 byte for byte (decode, and encode outside the tonality-analysis path), for example to test against a C reference or to replace audiopus or opus-sys bindings without changing bitstreams.
- When you need features most other ports skip: multistream, ambisonics projection, the repacketizer, in-band FEC/DTX and neural PLC.
- Throughput similar to the C reference is enough: about 1.06x encode and 1.01x decode time on x86-64 with the workspace's x86-64-v3 build.

**Skip it when:**
- If the goal is more speed than libopus: it is at parity on x86-64 and 16-22% slower on Apple M1 Pro, and several sibling ports report real speed-ups.
- Default crates.io builds on x86-64: the x86-64-v3 flag lives in the workspace's .cargo/config.toml, which dependents do not inherit, so a plain cargo add build targets baseline x86-64; the project's own generic-target run was about 1.19x slower than C on encode (Ryzen 9 9950X3D, before the bench fix).
- When you need bit-exactness with the float libopus that distributions ship: ropus tracks the fixed-point build, so decoded PCM will not match a float build bit for bit.
- When you need DRED PCM reconstruction (opus_decoder_dred_decode*), OSCE, QEXT or custom modes: these are deferred or not ported.
- When maturity and outside review matter: one maintainer with AI agents doing most of the work (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, codex and claude co-authored commits); 9 stars; the latest crates.io release, 0.12.18 (2026-05-11), is four months behind the repository.

**Integration:** crate · wide 0.7 (runtime); cc (build script, only used when xiph reference sources are on disk) · Rust 1.88 (edition 2024) · Any Rust target via portable code; tuned for x86-64-v3 (AVX2, FMA, BMI2) and Apple M1 (apple-a14) in workspace builds; WebAssembly reported by a downstream user; no hand-written intrinsics on any platform

**Vs siblings:** Pick ropus over the faster Opus ports (opuspp, opus-pure, ruopus, rusty-opus, gopus) when you need a full libopus API surface (multistream, projection, repacketizer, PLC) and bit-exact agreement with fixed-point libopus 1.5.2, checked by a differential harness and the RFC 6716/8251 vectors, rather than extra speed. For lower CPU cost, those siblings, or libopus-rs's 1-5% gain, are better candidates.

**Gotchas:**
- The crates.io package ships an empty DNN weights blob (build.rs only embeds weights when the xiph reference tree is on disk), so neural PLC and DRED fall back to classical PLC unless you call set_dnn_blob; workspace builds instead embed an 8.78 MB blob that takes about 3.34 ms to load per decoder.
- Published numbers come from a harness with since-fixed measurement flaws. At commit 54fef85 (x86 table, 2026-05-11) and at the 2026-07-31 Apple run, harness/Cargo.toml always enabled trace-silk-encode, so Rust SILK encode pushed trace records into an unbounded Mutex<Vec>, while C ran a harness-modified traced enc_API.c (project bug ROP-BUG-FLUX-00026, severity High). The C timer also included one codec create and destroy per run (ROP-BUG-FLUX-00027). Both were fixed on 2026-08-01, but the README tables were not re-measured, and the size of either effect is unmeasured.
- The C baseline is the harness's own build: fixed-point, -msse4.1 applied to every C file, SSE4.1-only runtime dispatch (libopus 1.5.2's AVX2 NSQ_del_dec source is not compiled) and -ffp-contract=off. The Rust side gets x86-64-v3, so the 'C dispatches to hand-tuned SSE4.1/AVX2' wording overstates the baseline.
- The crates.io README still shows the stale April table (encode 1.02x, decode 0.95x, Ryzen 9 9950X3D), measured before the bench fix that took decoder construction and its weight load out of the timed loop.

**Status:** Very active (1,289 commits, last 2026-09-13; the 99 of 124 internal bug-ledger records fetched are all Closed) and BSD-3-Clause, so it can be copied freely, but it is a young, mostly AI-written port whose crates.io release lags the repository and which is no faster than the C library it replaces.

[repo](https://github.com/0x4D44/ropus) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0x4D44/ropus/HEAD/README.md)

##### ruopus  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust Opus encoder and decoder: SILK/hybrid decode 1.4-1.8x faster than libopus 1.6.1; encode at parity at matched complexity.

**Beats:** libopus 1.6.1 (SIMD-enabled C) — The author's in-process harness (benches/vs_libopus.rs, built with the release profile: opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1) ran on one pinned core against system libopus 1.6.1 through the opus 0.3 FFI crate. Decoding identical libopus-made packets, ruopus was 1.79x (SILK WB 16 kb/s) and 1.41x (hybrid FB 32 kb/s) faster and 0.89x on CELT FB 64 kb/s; encoding identical input, it was 0.99-1.00x at complexity 0 and 1.60-3.18x against libopus at complexity 10, which is unequal work. CPU model, OS, rustc version and libopus build flags are not stated, and the test signal is mostly clipped noise rather than the speech-like tones it is described as (see measurement_notes).

**Known shortcoming:** Rust with no C API (language-filter mismatch). Baseline is the real libopus 1.6.1 through the opus FFI crate (benches/vs_libopus.rs, in-process, same packets) with no CPU model, OS, rustc or libopus flags. Decode 1.41-1.79x on SILK and hybrid but 0.89x on CELT, like-for-like (RFC 8251 vectors pass, final ranges bit-exact, PCM not bit-exact). Encode is at parity at complexity 0; the 3.18x/2.20x/1.60x at complexity 10 compare unequal work (ruopus skips delayed-decision NSQ and noise shaping) with encoder quality checked by waveform SNR only.

**Known shortcoming:** The harness signal() has a noise-term bug ((seed >> 9)/65535 spans -0.5 to 127.5), so the test input carries a +1.27 DC offset and 0.74 RMS noise against 0.30 RMS tones with 61% of samples over full scale; the record's 'tones plus light noise' workload is wrong, although both sides receive the same input so the ratios stay like-for-like on it. encode_auto mode is simulated and its smoothed music probability peaks at 0.66 (below 0.7), so SILK/hybrid mode likely matches libopus; one timing pass with no variance; encoder SIMD is x86-64 only; with default-features=false decode runs about 10x realtime.

**How:** The decode path has no SIMD of its own. The README does not explain why SILK and hybrid decode beat libopus; it attributes the CELT deficit (0.89x) to libopus's SIMD MDCT. The default 'spectrograms' feature routes the CELT MDCT's inner FFT through realfft/rustfft plans, which Cargo.toml puts at about 10x faster decode than the built-in O(n^2) evaluation. Encode speed comes from profile-driven hot-loop work listed in the v0.1.2 CHANGELOG: AVX2+FMA/SSE2 dot products and a four-lag cross-correlation for SILK and CELT pitch analysis, an SSE2 PVQ pulse search, a port of silk_NSQ_sse4_1's rate-distortion lookup table, LPC filters specialised by prediction order, and stack-allocated scratch buffers; the 1.6-3.2x wins over libopus at complexity 10 come mainly from search that ruopus does not do (delayed-decision NSQ, warped noise shaping).

**Use it when:**
- Rust, wasm32 or no_std targets that need an Opus decoder without a C toolchain. Speech-mode streams decoded 1.79x (SILK wideband 16 kb/s) and 1.41x (hybrid fullband 32 kb/s) faster than libopus 1.6.1 in the author's in-process bench.
- Python pipelines that want Opus encode and decode from pip wheels. The bindings release the GIL around codec calls, and the CHANGELOG reports decode scaling from 810x to 2308x realtime across 1 to 4 threads.
- Pure-Rust speech or VoIP encoding where libopus would otherwise run at its default complexity 10 and the simpler ruopus search is good enough: 1.6-3.2x faster than libopus at complexity 10, and at parity with libopus at complexity 0.
- Projects that want a memory-safe codec whose decoder passes all twelve RFC 8251 vectors (99.2-100% on opus_compare, final ranges bit-exact), with unsafe code limited to Miri-checked SIMD kernels.

**Skip it when:**
- C++ code bases. There is no C API, so you would write and maintain a Rust FFI layer; for C++ the existing libopus or a C/C++ port is less work.
- Music- or CELT-heavy decoding (0.89x of libopus at 64 kb/s fullband), or pipelines that need PCM bit-identical to libopus.
- Encoders where quality at complexity 10 matters. ruopus lacks delayed-decision NSQ and warped noise shaping, and its encoder quality is checked only by waveform SNR (examples/encoder_quality.rs), not a perceptual metric such as PESQ, POLQA or ViSQOL.
- Encoding on ARM or wasm. The encoder's SIMD kernels exist only for x86-64 (AVX2+FMA detected at runtime, SSE2 baseline), and other targets fall back to scalar code; no non-x86 numbers are published.
- Teams that need a mature dependency. ruopus is at version 0.1.2 (first published 2026-06-29), has one author and 1 star, and has no surround or multistream encoder.

**Integration:** crate (ruopus 0.1.2 on crates.io; rlib + cdylib for the PyO3 module); Python wheels on PyPI; no C header · none required; default feature 'spectrograms' 2.0 (realfft) for the fast MDCT; optional libm for no_std; pyo3 0.29 + numpy 0.29 behind the 'python' feature · Rust 1.85 (edition 2024), stable · any Rust target; decoder also no_std + alloc (CI builds thumbv7em-none-eabihf) and wasm32; encoder SIMD AVX2+FMA (runtime-detected) or SSE2 on x86-64, scalar elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Among the Rust Opus siblings, pick ruopus when you need both a conformance-checked decoder that builds no_std and wasm32 and a feature-complete encoder (FEC, DTX, hybrid, Python bindings); ropus (a libopus 1.5.2 port at about 0.96-0.97x time against fixed-point libopus) and opus-rs (encoder within a few percent of libopus) report near-parity speed. A C++ project is better served by opuspp's decoder, which was compared with libopus under identical compiler and flags and needs no FFI layer.

**Gotchas:**
- default-features = false, the zero-dependency and no_std configuration, swaps the FFT-backed MDCT for an O(n^2) evaluation. The CHANGELOG puts that at about 10x realtime decode, against 410-730x with the default 'spectrograms' feature.
- decode_packet and encode_auto return a fresh Vec for every packet, and there is no decode-into-buffer call, so tight loops pay an allocation per packet (the bench includes this on the ruopus side).
- encode_auto picks SILK, hybrid or CELT itself, from a cheap energy, tilt and zero-crossing analysis with hysteresis (CELT once the smoothed music probability exceeds 0.7). The encoder defaults to application Audio and signal Auto; call set_application or set_signal if you need libopus-like VoIP behaviour.
- Decoded PCM differs from libopus in float rounding (only the final range is bit-exact), and encoded bitstreams differ from libopus's, so golden-file tests against libopus output will fail.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-07-07, crate 0.1.2), but very young, with one author and 1 star. It is MIT-licensed, so wrapping or vendoring it is unrestricted.

[repo](https://github.com/jmg049/ruopus) · [benchmark](https://github.com/jmg049/ruopus)

##### rusty-av1-toolkit  `Rust`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

rav1e fork whose default AV1 encode is byte-identical to stock rav1e and about 1.10x faster single-threaded; bundles a rav1d fork.

**Beats:** stock rav1e (AV1 encoder); decoder side is a fork of rav1d, itself a Rust port of dav1d — First-party, on an unnamed machine with about 5% thermal noise. The fork's rav1e CLI at 885a2887 against stock rav1e 564ae3b0 (an upstream xiph/rav1e master commit), built with the same unstated flags, encoded one synthetic 640x480, 60-frame ffmpeg testsrc2 clip at --speed 6 --quantizer 100 --tiles 1 --threads 1. Median 6.911 s vs 7.588 s (1.098x over 7 interleaved rounds, every round 1.072-1.117x), with identical 262,180-byte output; a single-binary racecar A/B reproduced 1.079x, and a QP sweep gave 1.058-1.126x. The 1.69x mode changes the bitstream (+60% bytes, -2.28 dB PSNR) and divides by a stock time from a different session; within one session it is 1.61x over the byte-identical mode.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). The numbers are its own encoder kernels against stock rav1e 564ae3b0 (not vendored numbers), 1.098x median over 7 rounds on one testsrc2 640x480 60-frame clip, machine unnamed, and the ab.sh script is not in the repo; the --racecar 1.69x costs 60% more bytes and 2.28 dB. No decoder claim.

**Known shortcoming:** All timings are one thread, one tile and one synthetic clip, 1.69x across sessions (1.61x same-session); the README's claim that the FNV gate is pinned in tests/profile_encode.rs is false (the test asserts determinism only) and byte identity has been unverified since 2026-07-02; no CI (PRs #3 and #4 open); the tier work is env-gated and off by default; no NEON twin of the AVX2 kernel; about 40 RAV1E_* environment variables change output.

**How:** Profiling put `write_coeffs_lv_map` (coefficient token coding) at 48.6% and quantize at 12.3% of a speed-6 single-thread encode, and three byte-identical changes were kept. B7a turns the per-scan-position non-zero-map context stencil into a full-area, column-contiguous kernel that can vectorize. B7a-SIMD is a hand-written AVX2 twin of that kernel (one ymm register per column of up to 32 rows, vpminub/vpaddb stencil, vpavgb for (mag+1)>>1). Q2 rewrites quantize's serial main loop branch-free, removing two data-dependent mispredicted branches. Per the ledger the stencil dropped from 878 to 96 ms and the quantize loop from 676-730 to 440-466 ms. `--racecar on` additionally switches on rav1e's existing `tx_domain_rate`/`tx_domain_distortion` options, which replace real token coding in RDO with a table-based rate estimate.

**Use it when:**
- You already ship rav1e and want shorter encodes with output that is byte-identical to the default stock bitstream: 1.058-1.126x single-threaded at speed 6 on the authors' clip, with the full gain on x86-64 CPUs that have AVX2.
- Dense, high-rate encodes (low QP), where entropy coding is a larger share of encode time: 1.126x at QP 60 against 1.058x at QP 160.
- A pure-Rust, BSD-2 AV1 encoder embedded in a Rust application (it backs AVIF/AV1 encoding in remade_ffmpeg_rs), where a C encoder is not an option.
- CPU-bound, bandwidth-insensitive encoding where 50-60% more bytes is acceptable: `--racecar on --tune Psnr` ran about 1.6x faster than the byte-identical mode on the same clip.

**Skip it when:**
- When encode speed per core is the main goal and a C encoder is acceptable: SVT-AV1 is the catalogued fast AV1 encoder, and a 1.10x gain does not change rav1e's position against it (no cross-encoder numbers here).
- Multi-threaded or tiled production encodes: every A/B is `--threads 1 --tiles 1` on one synthetic 640x480 clip, and the gain at default threading is not measured.
- aarch64: the AVX2 stencil has no NEON twin yet (ledger item 9), so ARM gets only the portable B7a and Q2 changes, and its speedup is unmeasured.
- Bandwidth-limited delivery in `--racecar on`: +60% bitstream and -2.28 dB PSNR at the default tune; a faster stock `--speed` preset may be the better trade, and none was compared.
- Long-term dependencies that need upstream fixes: the code is vendored rather than a GitHub fork, upstream tracking is an unchecked roadmap item, there is no CI (PRs #3 and #4 adding a check workflow are still open), and the repo has 0 stars.

**Integration:** crate (rusty_av1e 0.8.0 library plus `rav1e` CLI; rusty_av1d 1.2.0 library plus `dav1d` CLI); two separate Cargo projects, no top-level workspace · rusty_av1e defaults pull nasm (via nasm-rs and cc) for upstream asm, plus clap/y4m/ivf and the other CLI crates, and maybe-rayon for threading; `default-features = false` gives a no-asm build in which the AVX2 stencil still runs (std runtime detection). rusty_av1d needs nasm for x86 asm. · rusty_av1e rust-version 1.83.0; rusty_av1d rust-version 1.79 for a stable library build, though its directory pins nightly-2026-02-05 · any rav1e target; x86-64 with AVX2 gets the hand-written stencil (runtime-detected, scalar fallback); upstream x86 and ARM asm kept; Windows, macOS and Linux named in the README

**Vs siblings:** SVT-AV1 is the catalogued fast AV1 encoder (C); pick rusty_av1e only when you are tied to rav1e's Rust API or exact bitstream and want the same output sooner. For decoding, use the catalogued dav1d, or rav1d-safe if you need safe Rust; this repo's rusty_av1d makes no speed claim.

**Gotchas:**
- The process environment changes output. About 40 RAV1E_* variables (RAV1E_FAST, RAV1E_TRELLIS, RAV1E_LAMBDA_MULT, RAV1E_MODE_TOPK, RAV1E_WARP_FORCE and others) are latched into statics and alter encoder decisions. RAV1E_RACECAR=0 restores the stock kernels, and RAV1E_HARVEST=<path> appends CSV telemetry and panics if the file cannot be opened.
- The 'byte-identical gate' is not automated: tests/profile_encode.rs prints the bitstream FNV and only asserts run-to-run determinism, and the stock hash 688d5eeaee94d95e that the README says is pinned there is not in the file. Byte-identity at HEAD therefore rests on manual checks last ledgered on 2026-07-02, while later tier work landed behind environment gates.
- Naming is inverted between layers. On the CLI, `--racecar off` is the optimized default and `on` changes the bitstream, but racecar.rs and the toggle-site comments still describe the pre-remap meaning (racecar on = kernels = default). The dispatch comment says the AVX2 kernel honours RAV1E_CPU_TARGET, but the code calls `is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")` directly, so RAV1E_CPU_TARGET cannot turn it off.
- `--racecar on` uses stock rav1e's own tx-domain rate estimator (off at every stock speed preset), not new fork code. It also forces `tx_domain_distortion` on, working around an upstream assert that the fork's ledger documents: tx_domain_rate with the psychovisual tune panics in `distortion_scale`, reachable through the API or a config file.

**Status:** Last code change 2026-08-02 (113 commits; later commits through 2026-10-04 only edit an install-count banner), BSD-2-Clause plus the AOM patent licence, 0 stars, no issues, no CI. Reasonable to trial as a rav1e drop-in, but a thin, recently forked dependency to build on.

[repo](https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty-av1-toolkit) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty-av1-toolkit/HEAD/rusty_av1e/docs/entropy-bricks.md)

##### rusty-opus  `Rust`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust Opus codec (opus-rs performance fork) claiming 1.5-1.6x libopus single-core CELT encode speed; SILK 4% slower.

**Beats:** libopus (C reference encoder); also FFmpeg's native Opus encoder — First-party, i7-14650HX on Windows: each encoder runs as a process on looped 300 s and 150 s clips, the slope of process CPU time is taken, pinned to one core at High priority, ABBA order, 31-41 reps with a null arm: CELT 48 kHz speech at 32 kb/s 436x vs libopus 291x realtime (1.50x), CELT stereo music at 128 kb/s 213x vs 133x (1.60x), SILK 16 kHz VoIP at 16 kb/s 139x vs 145x (0.96x), with the coded path checked from TOC bytes; rustc and flags are unstated and the libopus arm is ffmpeg -c:a libopus from PATH (docs/benchmarks.md names FFmpeg 8.1.2 for its earlier run) with no libopus version or build flags. The slope cancels start-up but not FFmpeg's per-frame CLI work (WAV demux, PCM decode, filtergraph, Ogg mux and, since FFmpeg 7.0, thread hand-offs between those stages, here time-sliced on the one pinned core), speed is compared at nominal bitrate although the README says libopus's VBR overshoots by 15-20% on this corpus, and the complexity 9 vs 10 mismatch adds almost no libopus work (libopus 1.5.2 float gates nothing above complexity 8 except a fixed-point-only analysis switch); no correctness bug was found behind the numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust fork of restsend/opus-rs with its own 3-way harness (tools/bench_encode_3way.ps1, i7-14650HX), so not inherited numbers. Complexity mismatch: rusty-opus defaults to 9 while ffmpeg's libopus defaults to 10; libopus version and build and the rustc version are unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** The timing slope does not cancel ffmpeg's per-frame CLI work (demux, filter, Ogg mux, thread hand-offs); libopus VBR overshoots the nominal rate by 15-20%; complexity 9 against 10 costs almost nothing extra in libopus 1.5.2 float (nothing is gated above 8 except fixed-point-only analysis), so the verifier's complexity caveat is weak. The in-repo docs/benchmarks.md still says SILK 2.9x and Hybrid 2.7x slower and Hybrid was never re-timed; the CELT lead is inherited from opus-rs; the library reads environment variables that change the bitstream or write files (CELT_PF_OFF, NO_STEREO_TRIM, RUSTY_OPUS_GATE_HARVEST); last code change 0.9.1 on 2026-08-08; the README's 'Active Installs' banner is the crates.io total download count.

**How:** It is a structural port of libopus's float encoder (tonality analysis, CELT MDCT, band energy and PVQ, SILK NSQ) with hand-written SIMD kernels chosen at runtime and kept beside scalar twins: AVX/AVX+FMA CELT kernels and AVX2 pitch/PVQ/comb-filter code inherited from opus-rs, plus three byte-identical AVX2 SILK kernels the fork added (LPC short-term prediction, warped autocorrelation, cross-state NSQ noise-shaping filter), and NEON on aarch64. The CELT encoder allocates its per-frame work buffers once in CeltEncoder::new. docs/benchmarks.md says the single-thread CELT lead was already in upstream opus-rs (music 250x upstream vs 262x for the fork, with the fork's own gains on SILK/Hybrid) and warned then that the encoder's VBR was effectively CBR with less tonality/VBR analysis than libopus; the fork has since wired in the missing analysis signals, while libopus's tonality VBR boost is still opt-in (RUSTY_OPUS_TONAL_VBR). For wall-clock time, encode_parallel splits a stream into chunks on std::thread workers, each re-encoding 8 warm-up frames to prime its state (PEAQ delta-ODG <= 0.03, not byte-identical).

**Use it when:**
- Rust applications that need Opus encode and decode without a C toolchain, bindgen or cross-compiled libopus, under the same BSD-3-Clause licence as libopus.
- CELT-path encoding (48 kHz music, or speech the classifier routes to CELT, at about 32-128 kb/s) where the first-party table shows 1.50x and 1.60x libopus single-core throughput.
- Offline or batch transcoding of long files on multi-core machines, where encode_parallel trades a little extra CPU (warm-up frames per chunk) and byte-identity for wall-clock speed.
- Real-time voice or streaming stacks in Rust that need the libopus feature set (FEC, DTX, PLC, CNG, multistream surround) rather than a decode-only crate.

**Skip it when:**
- SILK and VoIP speech at low rates: libopus is 4% faster on the only SILK row (about 3 Windows timer quanta), Hybrid mode was not timed at all, and the README's own quality table puts the encoder behind libopus on VoIP-application speech (BD-ODG -0.200 to -0.416) and on stereo piano and guitar (-0.217, -0.162).
- C or C++ projects: there is no C API, so linking libopus directly is simpler and is the measured baseline anyway.
- When encoder output must match libopus byte for byte: decisions differ by design (zero-lookahead analysis with a 10-frame warm-up guard, opt-in tonality VBR boost, default complexity 9), and only the decoder claims bit-exact conformance on the 12 RFC vectors.
- Integer PCM pipelines or 44.1 kHz input without a resampler: the API takes f32 only and the encoder accepts 8, 12, 16, 24 or 48 kHz.
- Teams that need an engaged upstream: no issue has ever been filed, the last library change was 0.9.1 on 2026-08-08 (later commits are README install-count bumps and CI), and docs/benchmarks.md in the same repo still says SILK is 2.9x and Hybrid 2.7x slower than libopus, which the README later calls a mis-measurement and re-measures only for SILK.

**Integration:** crate · none at runtime; dev-dependencies criterion, proptest and rusty_alloc-api (benches and examples only) · Rust 1.85 (rust-version in Cargo.toml), edition 2024 · std targets; AVX/AVX2/FMA kernels on x86-64 and NEON on aarch64, runtime-detected with scalar fallbacks; benchmarked only on Windows x86-64 (i7-14650HX)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over upstream opus-rs for the same API plus AVX2 SILK kernels, frame-parallel encode and the later quality fixes, and over ruopus, opus-pure or ropus when you want the full libopus feature set (FEC, DTX, PLC, multistream, repacketizer) in a crate already shipped inside remade_ffmpeg_rs. If the decision rests on a controlled libopus comparison, ropus's in-process cc-built harness and the libopus 1.6.1 baselines named by opus-pure and ruopus are better documented than this README's FFmpeg-hosted libopus of unknown version.

**Gotchas:**
- Behaviour depends on environment variables read when an encoder is built or once per process: RUSTY_OPUS_FORCE_MODE, RUSTY_OPUS_SILENCE_FLAG=0, RUSTY_OPUS_TONAL_VBR, RUSTY_OPUS_ANALYSIS_WARMUP, RUSTY_OPUS_MODE_DWELL and RUSTY_OPUS_LSB_DEPTH change the bitstream, RUSTY_OPUS_GATE_HARVEST=<path> makes the library append a CSV row per encoded frame to that file, and the unprefixed names CELT_PF_OFF (turns off the CELT pitch prefilter) and NO_STEREO_TRIM also apply process-wide.
- lsb_depth defaults to 24 (libopus float-API default); the source says to set 16 for s16-sourced material to match opus_demo, since the analysis noise floor depends on it.
- encode_parallel output differs from serial encoding at chunk seams, and every chunk re-encodes 8 warm-up frames, so it spends more total CPU than one serial encoder.
- Benches and examples run under the org's rusty_alloc global allocator (a dev-dependency; the library itself sets none). CHANGELOG 0.9.1 reports no measurable encode-speed change from that switch because steady-state encode reuses its buffers.

**Status:** Code last changed with 0.9.1 on 2026-08-08 and later commits through 2026-10-04 only bump the README banner or CI; BSD-3-Clause, 5 stars, 4 forks, no issues ever filed, and the README's '35,223 Active Installs' equals the crates.io total download count (35,223), not a measured install base.

[repo](https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty-opus) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty-opus)

##### rusty_flac  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust FLAC encoder and decoder claiming 17% faster encode and 23% faster decode than FFmpeg 8.1.2's flac.

**Beats:** FFmpeg 8.1.2 native flac encoder and decoder (libavcodec) — First-party README numbers on an unnamed Windows x86-64 machine with an unstated rustc and flags: both binaries pinned to one core, process CPU time, 31 ABBA pairs on one 180 s 44.1 kHz stereo music clip, encode at -compression_level 8 672 ms vs 813 ms and decode of an FFmpeg-encoded stream 266 ms vs 344 ms against the prebuilt Gyan FFmpeg 8.1.2 full_build. The timing harness, the clip and the command lines are still not public (remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/bench holds only codec-bench.ps1, pinab.py and unrelated scripts on 2026-10-04), so it is unknown whether process start-up, WAV/file I/O and, for the FFmpeg arm, the per-frame hand-offs between the demux, decode, filter, encode and mux threads that FFmpeg 7.0+ runs (all time-sliced on the one pinned core) are cancelled, as the sister rusty-opus harness's 300 s minus 150 s slope does for start-up; the smaller-file claim mostly reflects FFmpeg's default padding block, and level 8 means different search work in the two encoders.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). Downgraded to C: README times (672/813 ms encode, 266/344 ms decode, single core each) have no CPU model, compiler or flags, the FLAC timing harness and clip are unpublished, and all four times are exact multiples of the 15.625 ms Windows tick. The 'smaller on 20/20' claim is inflated by FFmpeg's default 8,192-byte PADDING block (libavformat/flacenc.c in FFmpeg 8.1); pink noise, vocal and silence are not smaller once it is removed. Lossless interoperability is gated by the public flac_gate.ps1.

**Known shortcoming:** The FLAC timing harness is still unpublished (remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/bench as of 2026-10-04), so whether start-up, I/O and FFmpeg 7+ CLI thread hand-offs on the pinned core were cancelled is unknown, and the encoders do a different level-8 search (FFmpeg 4608-sample blocks with 4LEVEL order search). Security: issue #9 (a 42-byte stream causing an 80 GB allocation and abort) was closed on 2026-09-15 but decode() still does Vec::with_capacity(total_samples) at HEAD v0.2.0. 32-bit stereo (33-bit side channel) is not handled (read_bits n of 32 or less into i32; tests gate 8, 16 and 24 bits only); no resync on a bad frame; no ID3; MD5 is never checked; only STREAMINFO is written. The README's 'Active Installs' banner is the crates.io total download count.

**How:** The encoder does a two-phase, estimate-gated search per fixed 4,096-sample block: every stereo arm (left, right, mid, side) gets a cheap estimate (exact integer autocorrelation over Q15 Tukey windows 0.5 and 0.2, Levinson-Durbin, one-pass fixed-order |residual| sums), and only arms whose stereo mode is within a margin of the best estimate are realized with real residuals and an exact Rice plan. The Rice planner merges partition sums bottom-up so every partition order (to 8) and both Rice and Rice2 are costed in one pass instead of a per-parameter scan, and four runtime-detected AVX2 kernels (autocorrelation, Rice sums, fixed-order sums, FMA LPC residual) sit beside scalar twins; an accumulator bit writer, table CRCs and an unrolled MD5 cut the rest. The decoder uses a 64-bit left-aligned bit reader refilled a word at a time, leading_zeros Rice reads with one refill, and const-generic LPC restore loops for orders 1-12. FFmpeg's level 8, by contrast, uses 4,608-sample blocks at 44.1 kHz, Levinson LPC with its 4-level order search and an estimated stereo mode (libavcodec/flacenc.c), so the two encoders search different spaces.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services, desktop apps or WASM builds that need FLAC encode and decode with no C toolchain and no LGPL code (Apache-2.0); RAG Converter uses it in the browser.
- no_std microcontroller encoders: the README reports about 15-20 ms per 4,096-sample 16 kHz mono block on an ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz and a byte-gated peak heap of about 124 KB for an 8,192-sample stream (first-party).
- Whole-file encoding of 8/16/24-bit PCM (up to 8 channels) that libFLAC or FFmpeg will later decode; round trips are gated against claxon in tests and against FFmpeg in remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/flac_gate.ps1.
- Devices that close one file per chunk (for example one second of audio): Encoder::finish_and_reset keeps buffers and window tables and gives bytes identical to a fresh encoder.
- Decoding trusted 16- or 24-bit FLAC already in memory from Rust code that previously used claxon.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: there is no C API, so you would need an FFI shim, and the comparison was against FFmpeg's flac, not libFLAC, which was never timed.
- Untrusted input through decode(): it reserves Vec::with_capacity(total_samples) per channel straight from the 36-bit STREAMINFO field. Issue #9 (a 42-byte stream can request 80 GB and abort the process) was closed on 2026-09-15, but that line is still in src/decode.rs at HEAD (v0.2.0). Use Decoder::next_frame with your own bounded buffers, or check total_samples against the input length first.
- Real-world files with ID3v2 prefixes, trailing tags or damaged frames, or Ogg FLAC: the decoder requires fLaC at byte 0, a bad sync, CRC-8 or CRC-16 returns an error, and decode() gives up on the whole stream instead of resynchronising.
- 32-bit FLAC: the README says 4-32-bit decode, but 32-bit stereo side channels need 33 bits while BitReader::read_bits/read_signed are written for n <= 32 and samples are i32. The gate matrix tests only 8, 16 and 24 bits, and 32-bit encode is a roadmap item.
- Large or streaming jobs and tagging workflows: the encoder holds the whole input as i32 before finish(), the decoder needs the whole file in memory, there is no seeking, and no seek table, Vorbis comment, picture or padding block is written.

**Integration:** crate · none required; optional libm (pure Rust) for no_std; dev-dependencies claxon and rusty_alloc-api · Rust 1.85 (rust-version in Cargo.toml), edition 2021 · any Rust target; Windows, Linux and macOS build and test per the README; no_std checked in CI on riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf and thumbv7em-none-eabihf; runs on ESP32-S3; AVX2/FMA kernels only on x86-64 with the std feature (runtime-detected)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Symphonia (decode-only, multi-format, single-threaded tables against FFmpeg's native decoders) or flacenc-rs (encoder only, measured against the libFLAC flac 1.4.3 CLI) when you want one dependency-free Apache-2.0 crate that both encodes and decodes FLAC, including no_std encoding on a microcontroller. For decoding untrusted or messy real-world files, or when the comparison you care about is libFLAC rather than FFmpeg's flac, those siblings or libFLAC itself are the safer choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Output carries only STREAMINFO (no Vorbis comment, no padding), so tag editors must rewrite the whole file; that missing 8,192-byte PADDING block is most of the README's 'smaller on 20/20' headline against FFmpeg.
- Encoded bytes changed in 0.2.0 (integer autocorrelation); the CHANGELOG says to pin one version wherever two builds must agree byte for byte, and to enable the libm feature on the host for host-chip byte identity.
- The decoder parses the STREAMINFO MD5 but never computes it; only frame CRC-8 and CRC-16 are checked.
- unsafe is confined to four #[target_feature(enable = "avx2")] kernels, each with a bit-identity test against its scalar twin; the in-repo flacbench example hard-codes 44,100 Hz and runs under the org's rusty_alloc global allocator, which the project says is required for comparable numbers.

**Status:** Active but very young (49 commits, last commit 2026-10-04 bumping the README banner, v0.2.0 on 2026-09-30, a v0.2.1 release PR open); Apache-2.0 and dependency-free, so easy to vendor, but it has 1 star and the README's '1,358 Active Installs' banner equals the crates.io total download count (1,358), not a measured install base.

[repo](https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty_flac) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty_flac/HEAD/README.md)

##### rusty_h265  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust, memory-safe HEVC decoder: about 5% faster than FFmpeg's hevc decoder on one stream, 1.1-1.67x slower on three.

**Beats:** FFmpeg 8.1.2 native hevc decoder (libavcodec, hand-written assembly) — First-party run on an unnamed Windows machine, one pinned core, 21 ABBA-alternated pairs on four unpublished 720p-class streams: rusty_h265 0.6.0 (rusty_alloc build; portable or x86-64-v3 not stated) took 703 ms against 741 ms for FFmpeg 8.1.2's hevc decoder at -threads 1 on a weighted-prediction stream (1.05x), but took 1.10x, 1.45x and 1.67x as long on the deblocking-heavy, 10-bit and 8-bit mainstream streams. The two timers differ in scope: rusty_h265's decode_ms starts after the file is in memory, while ffmpeg's -benchmark rtime spans its whole transcode() with demuxer, decoder, filter and null-muxer threads sharing the one pinned core, so a 5% margin is within that bias.

**Known shortcoming:** Marginal mixed result: 1.05x over FFmpeg on the weighted-prediction stream only; FFmpeg is faster on the other three (1.10x, 1.45x, 1.67x). Timers differ (decode_ms versus FFmpeg -benchmark rtime, which includes the demux and mux pipeline); the bench binary uses rusty_alloc (1.133x per the CHANGELOG); streams unpublished; CPU, rustc and FFmpeg build unstated; frame counts only, no MD5 against FFmpeg on the bench streams (conformance from 147 of 147 JCT-VC MD5s).

**Known shortcoming:** The harness default RefArgs uses -v error without -benchmark while ffmpeg logs its bench rtime line at AV_LOG_INFO, so the published table needs unpublished arguments; the 0.992x null arm is wall clock ffmpeg against ffmpeg and cannot catch the decode_ms-versus-rtime scope bias. Issue #3: a debug_assert in the accel luma_edge path panics on every stream in debug builds (release falls back to scalar); the README quick start calls nonexistent decode_nal and annex_b_nal_units; planes are always u16; the README banner's 2,634 installs against crates.io's 520 downloads.

**How:** The pixel kernels (motion compensation, intra prediction, inverse DCT/DST, deblocking, SAO) live in a separate rusty_h265-accel crate with runtime-dispatched SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2 versions, each differential-tested bit-exact against a scalar twin; the CHANGELOG measures them at 2.81x over scalar, with AVX2 only 1.045x over SSE4.1. CABAC fuses the LPS-range and state-transition tables into one branchless step. Most of the remaining gains are removed allocations and copies, found with a stage profiler and an assembly-level memcpy census: a picture-buffer pool that zeroes only coding tree blocks no slice covered, per-4x4 maps reused without pre-filling, sequence-invariant scan tables cached, and short copies dispatched to constant widths so they inline. The non-kernel code (about 87% of the time) builds for baseline x86-64 SSE2 unless you build with -C target-cpu=x86-64-v3 (1.066x).

**Use it when:**
- A Rust program that must decode HEVC without C, FFI or libavcodec's LGPL/GPL licensing; the crate is Apache-2.0 with no required third-party dependencies.
- Untrusted HEVC input where memory safety matters more than speed: the decoder core is #![forbid(unsafe_code)], and --no-default-features builds with no unsafe code anywhere (at about 2.8x lower speed).
- Main or Main 10 4:2:0 content where single-threaded decoding at roughly 0.6x to 1.05x of FFmpeg's single-thread speed is enough, e.g. thumbnailing, inspection or offline 720p work.
- Content heavy in explicit weighted prediction (fades), the only stream class measured at or above FFmpeg's speed.

**Skip it when:**
- Throughput-bound decoding: the pipeline is single-threaded (tiles and wavefronts are parsed but not run in parallel), and even on one core it is 1.45x to 1.67x slower than FFmpeg on mainstream 8- and 10-bit inter content.
- Range Extensions (4:2:2, 4:4:4, 12-bit), screen content coding, or SHVC/MV-HEVC enhancement layers (only the base layer is decoded).
- Debug-profile builds: open issue #3 (2026-09-30) reports that a debug_assert in rusty_h265-accel's luma_edge fires on horizontal edges at x < 4, so every HEVC stream panics in a dev build; release builds stay correct by falling back to the scalar edge filter.
- 8-bit pipelines that are bound by memory bandwidth: every plane is stored as u16 (frame.rs calls an 8-bit u8 plane domain a future 'speed brick'), and converting to 8-bit output cost 5.4% of decode per the README.
- Production use that needs a track record: 0.1.0 to 0.6.0 were all published 2026-09-06 to 2026-09-08 by one organisation, with no independent users or measurements found.

**Integration:** crate (rusty_h265 on crates.io, with the companion rusty_h265-accel kernel crate) · rusty_h265-accel (default simd feature); rusty_alloc-api =1.1.6 only with the optional bench-alloc feature used by the bundled CLI · Rust 1.85 (MSRV), edition 2021 · any Rust target on the scalar path; SIMD kernels runtime-dispatched SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2 on x86-64 (the README also lists a NEON baseline rung); the optional x86-64-v3 build needs AVX2, BMI1/2 and FMA (Haswell or later)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FFmpeg's libavcodec only when a pure-Rust, Apache-2.0, memory-safe HEVC decoder matters more than speed. If you need multicore throughput, rivet-h26x (also pure Rust, with frame and wavefront threading and single-thread parity on wavefront streams) fits better, provided you accept its source-available attribution licence. remade_ffmpeg_rs ships this same decoder.

**Gotchas:**
- The top-level README's Quick start calls dec.decode_nal(nal) and annex_b_nal_units(), which do not exist in 0.6.0; use push_annexb/push_nal, flush and next_frame as shown in the crate README and lib.rs docs.
- The published numbers use the bench-alloc build (rusty_alloc, a pure-Rust mimalloc remake), which the harness notes was measured 1.133x apart from the system allocator; a library user gets whatever global allocator the application uses.
- Debug builds panic on every stream (issue #3); until it is fixed, set debug-assertions off for this dependency or build it with an optimized profile.
- Frames are u16 planes at the coded size with a separate crop rectangle, so callers must apply cropping and narrow 8-bit samples themselves.

**Status:** Active but very new: six releases between 2026-09-06 and 2026-09-08, and later commits only edit the README (its banner now claims 2,634 active installs against 520 total crates.io downloads); Apache-2.0 and copyable.

[repo](https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty_h265) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty_h265/HEAD/README.md)

##### SampleRateTap (async engine)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++20 near-unity ASRC for clock-drift bridging; its datapath beats libsamplerate MEDIUM/BEST at near-unity ratios.

**Beats:** libsamplerate 0.2.2 (Secret Rabbit Code, MEDIUM and BEST converters) — The author's Google Benchmark harness (bench_compare.cpp; GCC 13.3 -O3 for SampleRateTap, Ubuntu 24.04 distro builds of libsamplerate 0.2.2 and soxr 0.1.3, on an unnamed shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz) times only SampleRateTap's fractional_resampler at a fixed known ratio of 1 + 200 ppm in 128-frame blocks: 14.6 vs 4.8 M stereo frames/s against libsamplerate MEDIUM (3.04x, derived from page data), 20.3 vs 5.2 mono, 3.0 vs 1.9 at 8 channels, and 9.6 vs 1.6 stereo against BEST. Deterministic QEMU instruction counts on Cortex-M55, Cortex-M33 and Hexagon (arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2.1, hexagon-clang 19.1.5, -O3) show libsamplerate MEDIUM executing 2.7-3.3x the steady-state instructions per stereo frame; the speedup is real for the timed code but partly comes from a shorter filter with a narrower passband, and neither the servo nor the FIFO is timed.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party shootout (async/bench/compare/bench_compare.cpp, GCC 13.3 -O3, 'shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz' with no CPU model): tiers were matched on stop-band dB only, not equal work (Balanced: 48 taps with a 20-28 kHz transition whose edge sits above the 24 kHz Nyquist; libsamplerate MEDIUM: 120.61 dB, about 91 taps, 90% bandwidth; Transparent 80 taps vs BEST 154.67 dB, about 286 taps; tap counts derived from source data), and no THD+N is given for libsamplerate MEDIUM (Balanced -133.9 dB vs sinc_best -143.5 dB). The timed path is the fixed-ratio datapath with the servo quiescent, so clock recovery is not timed; the engine handles near-unity ratios only (+/-1000 ppm) against libsamplerate's general 1/256 to 256, a different problem. Slower than libsoxr HQ and r8brain on x86; embedded rows are QEMU instruction counts, not time.

**Known shortcoming:** bench_compare.cpp times only the fractional_resampler (servo and FIFO untimed); the mono and stereo float dot products are scalar double, so the speedup comes mostly from 48 taps against about 91 (the filter-pairing caveat stands); flags are not matched (SampleRateTap at -O3 against distro builds of libsamplerate and soxr). The README's full-pipeline table (2026-06-12, Xeon 2.80 GHz) gives 107.8 ns per stereo frame, slower than the datapath-only 14.6 M frames/s. Latent API bug: polyphase_filter.h blend_row() calls bank.numPhases(), which does not exist, and compiles only because it is never instantiated.

**How:** At near-unity the conversion degenerates into a creeping fractional delay, so each output frame needs only one short polyphase FIR: a Kaiser-windowed sinc prototype split into L phase rows of T taps (balanced: 256 x 48), with coefficients linearly interpolated between the two rows adjacent to the fractional position. The position is an unsigned Q0.64 accumulator that adds only the rate deviation per sample, so whole-sample slips are detected by integer wraparound and the per-sample path has no double arithmetic. For multichannel streams the blended coefficient row is computed once per frame and shared by all channels, and from 4 channels up on hosts the history is stored frame-major so the dot product vectorizes across channels (the float path keeps strict per-channel double accumulation, so mono and stereo float dots are scalar by design).

**Use it when:**
- Bridging two independently clocked devices at the same nominal rate (USB or network audio into a local DAC, AVB, ALSA device pairs) where you also need the clock recovery that libsamplerate, soxr and r8brain leave to the caller.
- Live monitoring or duplex paths with a 1-2 ms latency budget: 24-frame (0.5 ms) filter group delay for balanced, about 1.5 ms end to end with the default 48-frame FIFO setpoint.
- FPU-less or FP64-less embedded targets (Cortex-M33/RP2350 class, Hexagon, HiFi-style DSPs) via the Q15/Q31 datapaths, where the author's QEMU counts put the Q15 steady state at 879 (M33) and 457 (Hexagon) instructions per stereo frame.
- Multichannel streams that must stay phase-coherent: every channel of one instance is resampled at the same fractional position each frame.
- Fixed near-unity ratios where you would otherwise run libsamplerate MEDIUM/BEST block by block and can accept a 20 kHz passband instead of libsamplerate's wider one.

**Skip it when:**
- General sample-rate conversion (44.1 to 48 kHz, 2x, arbitrary ratios): the async engine only handles small deviations around a common nominal rate; use soxr, r8brain or libsamplerate (or this repo's separate bridge/rational engines).
- Maximum host throughput or offline/batch work: on the author's own x86 table soxr HQ (52.9 M stereo frames/s) and r8brain 120 dB (16.5) beat SampleRateTap balanced (14.6) when latency does not matter.
- When you need libsamplerate-equivalent filtering: balanced is 48 taps with a 20 kHz passband and a 28 kHz stopband edge above the 24 kHz Nyquist, so 20-24 kHz content can alias into 20-24 kHz, while libsamplerate MEDIUM/BEST use roughly 2x and 3.5x the taps with wider passbands; at the 24-bit interface it measures -133.9 dB THD+N against about -143.5 dB for the oracle-fed libraries.
- Devices that construct converters at boot on FP64-less cores: filter design runs in double at construction and costs about 870-884 M QEMU instructions on Cortex-M33 (seconds on a 150 MHz part), against 20.9 M for libsamplerate MEDIUM.
- Projects that need a stable, packaged dependency: pre-1.0 (v0.5.0 family version), API may still change, no install/package rules, 5 stars, single main author.

**Integration:** header-only · DspTap (tap::dsp, MIT, header-only C++20, standard library only; pulled as a git submodule, so clone with --recurse-submodules). GoogleTest for tests; Google Benchmark, libsamplerate, soxr and r8brain-free-src only for the optional comparison benchmarks. · C++20, CMake 3.24+, GCC 11+ / Clang 14+ / MSVC 19.30+ · any; CI covers Linux (GCC, Clang, ASan/UBSan, TSan), macOS, Windows MSVC, arm64, and Cortex-M33, Cortex-M55 and Hexagon under QEMU. Tensilica HiFi4/5 only as a commented self-hosted CI template.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libsoxr and r8brain-free-src when you need drift correction with clock recovery inside a 1-2 ms budget or a fixed-point embedded path; those two are faster on x86 but carry 8.8-37 ms of latency in the same table and have no servo. Pick zita-resampler with zita-ajbridge instead if you are on Linux/JACK and GPL is acceptable, and LibFResample or r8brain for genuine rate conversion.

**Gotchas:**
- The filter presets' band edges and servo bandwidths are absolute Hz for about 48 kHz; at other rates construct through config::for_sample_rate() or quality drops silently (the README measures about 32 dB lost at 16 kHz with unscaled defaults).
- The FIFO setpoint must exceed the pull block size; the converter raises it automatically and latency follows, and callbacks above about 340 frames also need fifo_frames set explicitly. With coarse blocks (32 frames and up) the servo stays in its Track stage and the README documents cent-scale low-rate FM (about 62 dB wideband at 32-frame blocks, 54 dB at 5 ms blocks).
- Q15 is format-limited to about 77 dB SNR; use float or Q31 when quality matters, Q15 when cycles do.
- polyphase_filter.h exposes a blend_row(bank, row, mu) helper that calls bank.numPhases(), which polyphase_filter_bank does not have (its accessor is num_phases()); it compiles only because the template is never instantiated, so calling it fails to build. The shipped datapath uses blend_row_phase and is unaffected.

**Status:** Active (225 commits, last activity 2026-10-03, v0.5.0 family version, 1 open PR, no issues filed) and MIT-licensed, but young, pre-1.0 and consumable only via add_subdirectory/FetchContent; the benchmarks are first-party.

[repo](https://github.com/tap/SampleRateTap) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tap/SampleRateTap/blob/main/async/docs/COMPARISON.md)

##### uvgRTP  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

C++ RTP/SRTP/ZRTP library with built-in H.264/HEVC/VVC packetization; its authors report 4.4x FFmpeg's RTP goodput.

**Beats:** FFmpeg (libavformat RTP) and Live555 as RTP senders/receivers for HEVC video — The only numbers are from the uvgRTP authors' MMSP 2020 abstract, seen as a search snippet: sending a Kvazaar-encoded 4K HEVC file from a Core i7-4770 over 10 GbE, uvgRTP reached 5.0 Gb/s, 4.4x FFmpeg libavformat's peak goodput with 92.1% lower round-trip latency, and over 2x Live555's goodput with 82.3% lower latency. The rtp-benchmarks harness (g++ -O2 -g) is public but has no result files, and the library versions and build flags are not stated. Reading that harness shows that FFmpeg's latency path was measured with its default HEVC parser buffering and with the intended low-latency options silently unset (see measurement_notes), so the latency gap mostly reflects configuration, not RTP stack speed.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded to C: the only numbers (4.4x goodput, 92.1% lower latency vs FFmpeg and Live555) come from a search snippet of the authors' own MMSP 2020 abstract; the paper is blocked (IEEE, tuni.fi, ultravideo.fi) with no copy on GitHub. The rtp-benchmarks repo has harness code (-O2 -g) but no results, and its README says the FFmpeg and Live555 code is untested lately.

**Known shortcoming:** The 92.1% lower-latency claim rests on a mis-set baseline: rtp-benchmarks (7151dba of 2020-06-10, before the paper, and HEAD) passes NULL to av_dict_set for 'nobuffer' and 'flush_packets', which deletes the keys, so FFmpeg's low-latency options were never applied, and FFmpeg's rtpdec_hevc uses AVSTREAM_PARSE_FULL so the HEVC parser holds each frame until the next access unit (about 33 ms per hop at the hard-coded 30 fps, two hops). FFmpeg latency is also matched FIFO per packet (598 against 602 counts) with an unlocked deque and unordered_map race and a duplicate-size skip that desyncs the file walk; both libraries floor latency to whole milliseconds; the 2020 uvgRTP used RCE_SYSTEM_CALL_DISPATCHER, since removed; HEAD-only harness bugs include a tid = thread_num/2 counter collision, a 604 against 602 frame mismatch and the SRTP salt written into the key. Transport only (no RTSP/SDP, ICE or congestion control); open issues #261 (marker bit), #246 (timestamp), #235 and #262 (RTCP crashes); use 4.0.1 or later for the out-of-bounds fix.

**How:** The NAL start-code lookup scans 8 bytes at a time with the SWAR 'has a zero byte' bit trick (haszero64/haszero32) instead of testing byte by byte. On the send side, RTP and FU headers sit in small separate buffers and are gathered with the caller's payload through iovecs into sendmmsg(2) (WSASendTo on Windows), so frame data is not copied unless RTP_COPY is set; RCE_SYSTEM_CALL_CLUSTERING batches up to 1024 packets per sendmmsg call. On the receive side a dedicated receiver thread (it requests SCHED_FIFO priority on Linux) fills a preallocated ring buffer and a separate processor thread reassembles fragments into frames allocated with the start code already in place. Each NAL unit reaches the callback as soon as it is complete, with no access-unit parser holding it back.

**Use it when:**
- Streaming pre-encoded H.264, HEVC or VVC (or V3C atlas) bitstreams between endpoints you control, with your own signalling.
- 4K/8K or high-frame-rate video over a 10 GbE LAN, where per-packet CPU cost and kernel buffering limit the frame rate (larger socket buffers and RCE_PACE_FRAGMENT_SENDING are documented for bursts).
- Low-latency links where the receiver should get each NAL unit through a callback without demuxer or parser buffering.
- Encrypted point-to-point media (SRTP with ZRTP or user-managed keys) without pulling in a WebRTC stack.
- C++17 projects on Linux or Windows that need a BSD-2-Clause RTP stack, with an ABI-stable C-style Core API in shared builds.

**Skip it when:**
- You need RTSP/SDP signalling, container demuxing or decoding: FFmpeg, Live555 or GStreamer cover the whole pipeline, and uvgRTP covers only the RTP transport.
- WebRTC interop (ICE, DTLS-SRTP, congestion control): not provided. RTCP report blocks are exposed, but congestion control is left to the application.
- Strict RFC interop with third-party receivers: open issues report that the H26x marker bit is set per NAL unit rather than per access unit (#261) and that the RTP timestamp is incremented incorrectly by default (#246); the 4.0.0 release notes list both as known issues.
- Heavy RTCP use: open issues report a crash in rtcp::update_session_statistics (#235, labelled critical) and a segfault during RTCP teardown (#262).
- macOS (community-supported only), 32-bit targets (a 64-bit compiler is required), or access units that hold several large NAL units needing fragmentation (the docs warn this may lead to undefined behaviour).

**Integration:** static lib (default; full Extended C++ API) or shared lib (UVGRTP_BUILD_SHARED, Core API only) · pthreads; Crypto++ optional (auto-detected with __has_include) for SRTP/ZRTP · C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17), CMake 3.14+, 64-bit GCC, MinGW or MSVC · Linux and Windows (x86-64 builds documented); macOS community-supported

**Vs siblings:** The only transport sibling is rustrtc (a Rust WebRTC stack measured against webrtc-rs and pion). Pick uvgRTP for plain RTP/SRTP in C++ with native HEVC/VVC/AVC packetization and no ICE/DTLS, and rustrtc when browsers must connect. Codec siblings such as Kvazaar (same group; the benchmark files are Kvazaar-encoded), dav1d or VVenC are complementary: uvgRTP carries their output.

**Gotchas:**
- push_frame() runs start-code lookup by default. Pass RTP_NO_H26X_SCL if your encoder hands over bare NAL units. The receiver prepends start codes unless RCE_H26X_DO_NOT_PREPEND_SC is set, and frames arrive per NAL unit, not per access unit.
- push_frame() does not take ownership and works in place: SRTP in-place encryption is the default, so the caller's buffer is modified unless RTP_COPY is passed. Every received frame must be released with uvgrtp::frame::dealloc_frame().
- Defaults are 4 MB socket and ring buffers. For bursty 4K60+ traffic the docs suggest 40-80 MB buffers and fragment pacing (RCE_PACE_FRAGMENT_SENDING, which sleeps inside push_frame), and the benchmark harness itself sets 40 MB. sendmmsg clustering is opt-in and the docs warn it can raise frame loss at high frame rates.
- Use 4.0.1 or later: that release adds protection against out-of-bounds memory access on invalid headers (extension header length checks), and 4.0.0 added checks for too-small payloads.

**Status:** Actively maintained (Release 4.0.1 on 2026-07-28, after the ABI-safe 4.0.0 in May 2026) and BSD-2-Clause, so it is copyable. The benchmark repository's last commit is 2024-01-23, and its README says the FFmpeg and Live555 harnesses may no longer work out of the box.

[repo](https://github.com/ultravideo/uvgRTP) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ultravideo/rtp-benchmarks)

##### video_reader-rs  `Rust (Python module over FFmpeg bindings)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust-built Python video reader over libavcodec for ML loading; its own table beats OpenCV VideoCapture and decord.

**Beats:** OpenCV VideoCapture and decord — First-party README table, decoding one 2004-frame 1472x1472 video to RGB uint8 on an i7-9750H laptop with 15 GB RAM under Ubuntu 22.04: decode_fast 6.2 s vs OpenCV VideoCapture 65 s and decord 18 s at full frame rate, and 3.8 s vs 7.16 s and 14.03 s at compression factor 0.25. FFmpeg, OpenCV and decord versions, the codec and the timing script are not published, decord ran on a different, larger machine, and the OpenCV and decord columns come from a single July 2024 run while the video_reader columns were re-measured at later commits.

**Known shortcoming:** Decoding is FFmpeg's libavcodec through ffmpeg-next 9.0.0 (Linux wheels ship FFmpeg 8.1.1; the table's FFmpeg version is unstated), and OpenCV and decord also decode with libavcodec, so the gain is pipeline (frame threading, a compression factor that converts only selected frames, the Rust yuv crate instead of swscale, tokio-parallel conversion), not codec speed. No script produces the table (scripts/bench_get_batch.py times get_batch only); the decord column ran on another machine; the table dates from 2024 code.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e105, 2026-10-05): no bug behind the timings; C stands.
