- Memory-bandwidth-bound token generation where weight size dominates, especially larger models (the report's gains grow with model size; 100B ternary model at 5-7 tok/s claimed).
- Energy-constrained edge inference on Apple Silicon or recent x86 (report: 55-82% less energy than llama.cpp FP16).
- CPU embedding workloads with the BitNet-embedding 0.6B/270M models on x86 (README: 1.3-2.3x prefill over F16).

**Skip it when:**
- Ordinary FP16/INT4 models: it gives no benefit unless weights were trained ternary; Microsoft itself points to T-MAC for general low-bit models.
- Comparing against quantized llama.cpp: the headline 6x is vs FP16 weights; against llama.cpp TQ1_0 the companion paper (arXiv 2502.11880) reports only up to 1.33x (x86) / 1.65x (M2).
- Prompt-heavy workloads: the system paper says prefilling is not addressed by its optimizations (later README updates add GEMM work, but the headline numbers are decode).
- Projects that need a stable embeddable C/C++ API or current upstream llama.cpp features: it pins an older llama.cpp fork.
- Kernel coverage gaps: TL1 is ARM-only, TL2 x86-only, and embedding models have no ARM kernels per the README support table.

**Integration:** built application (CMake) driven by Python scripts; vendored llama.cpp/ggml fork · Python 3.10+ (conversion scripts, requirements.txt), CMake 3.22+, Clang 18+, vendored llama.cpp submodule; Hugging Face models · Clang 18+ (Visual Studio 2022 with the LLVM toolset on Windows), CMake 3.22 · x86-64 and ARM64 (NEON, incl. Apple Silicon); separate CUDA GPU kernel in gpu/

**Vs siblings:** Pick bitnet.cpp over T-MAC when the model is ternary BitNet b1.58 (its TL2/I2_S kernels beat T-MAC by up to 2.32x on x86 per its paper and are lossless); pick T-MAC, llamafile tinyBLAS or Intel Neural Speed for general 2-8-bit or FP16 models where ternary weights are not available.

**Gotchas:**
- Builds of the vendored llama.cpp fail on newer compilers due to missing #include <chrono> (issue #334, README FAQ Q1); patch the four files or pin the compiler.
- A third-party test on a pre-AVX2 Xeon E3-1230 v2 hit garbled output (repeated '!' tokens) from a tokenization mismatch in the official pre-converted GGUF and a stack-overflow crash.
- Reported speedups take the best of 2-thread and unrestricted-thread runs; tune threads and gemm-config.h block sizes for your CPU.
- Kernel choice matters: I2_S suits many threads, TL1 limited threads with large models, TL2 memory/bandwidth-limited setups.

**Status:** Active (last commit July 2026, frequent model/kernel releases), MIT-licensed and widely used (40k+ stars), but first-party evidence only and tied to an older llama.cpp fork.

[repo](https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.16144v2)

##### ByteTransformer  `C++/CUDA`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Padding-free fp16 BERT encoder inference on NVIDIA GPUs; first-party A100 numbers show about 2x over PyTorch and 1.8x over FasterTransformer at long, variable lengths.

**Beats:** PyTorch 1.13.0, TensorFlow, FasterTransformer, DeepSpeed (BERT-base inference) — First-party README tables on an A100 (CUDA 11.6, PyTorch 1.13.0, fp16, 12-layer BERT-base, average length 0.6 of max): at batch 16 and max length 1024 ByteTransformer takes 24.70 ms vs 53.21 for PyTorch, 65.94 for TensorFlow, 45.22 for FasterTransformer with remove-padding and 59.96 for DeepSpeed (about 2.2x and 1.8x, derived from page data); at batch 1 it is 3.16 vs 4.2 ms (PyTorch) and 4.51 ms (FasterTransformer). Only the ByteTransformer column has a public script; the IPDPS 2023 paper (best paper award, per WebSearch snippets) reports 6.13x fused MHA over PyTorch and 55% over FasterTransformer end to end but was not opened.

**Known shortcoming:** bert_bench.sh times only ByteTransformer, so the baseline columns are not reproducible; FasterTransformer with padding removal wins at batch 16 seq 64 and at 256-384; IPDPS paper unopened (arXiv blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** Resource bug: bert_infer (src/bert_transformer.cu) calls cudaEventCreate twice per call and never destroys them, and the Torch op builds a new encoder per layer per call, so serving leaks (matches open issue #11, no reply); padding-free path off for batch<=2; fused/CUTLASS attention gated to sm70-86, so H100/Ada fall back to unfused attention; bench harness has no final torch.cuda.synchronize.

**How:** Padding-free execution: a single-block parallel prefix sum over the mask builds per-token offsets (batch_idx/word_idx), the input is packed to the valid tokens, and every GEMM and elementwise kernel runs on that packed row count; the last add-bias+LayerNorm kernel scatters results back to the padded layout. Attention is chosen by length: a single-kernel tensor-core (WMMA) fused MHA holding Q, K/V and the logits in shared memory for sequences up to 80, a split 'long' fused kernel up to about 384, and on A100 a CUTLASS-based attention for 384 < seq <= 1024 (the paper describes it as grouped-GEMM fused MHA). Other operators are fused too: GEMM with bias+GELU epilogue and add-bias+residual+LayerNorm in one pass.

**Use it when:**
- fp16 inference of BERT-base/large-style encoders (head size 64, GELU, post-LayerNorm) on an A100 with batches of 3 or more variable-length sequences, where padding waste is large.
- Batch 16 with max lengths of 448 to 1024 and average length around 60% of max: the README shows the biggest gap there (e.g. seq 512: 9.22 ms vs 13.79 for FasterTransformer with remove-padding, 21.0 for PyTorch).
- A C++/CUDA inference server that wants a small per-layer encoder API taking raw device pointers, a cuBLAS handle and a stream.
- Studying or vendoring a padding-free plus fused-MHA implementation under Apache-2.0.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything other than the BERT encoder: no decoder, GPT/LLM, T5 or training/backward pass (README: only the standard BERT encoder; issue #5 asking about training is unanswered).
- Hopper, Ada or other GPUs newer than sm86: the code turns fused attention off above seq 128 when arch > 86 and uses the CUTLASS long-sequence path only on sm80; the README lists only V100, T4 and A100 and tests CUDA 11.6.
- Batch size 1 or 2: padding removal is switched off when max_batch_size <= 2, and at batch 1 FasterTransformer is faster for seq 192-384 per the README.
- Batch 16 at seq 64 or 256-384, where the README shows FasterTransformer with remove-padding ahead (e.g. 5.49 vs 6.85 ms at 256).
- Sequences longer than 1024 tokens (the PyTorch op rejects them with 'Input seq_len too long').

**Integration:** shared lib (libbytetransformer.so, plus optional TorchScript op library libths_bytetransformer.so built with -DBUILD_THS=ON) · CUDA toolkit (README: 11.6), cuBLAS, cuBLASLt (Torch op), CUTLASS (git submodule 3rdparty/cutlass), PyTorch >= 1.8 for the Python plugin · C++17 with nvcc (CUDA 11.x; tested 11.6), CMake >= 3.13 · Linux, NVIDIA compute capability 7.0 (V100), 7.5 (T4), 8.0 (A100); data type fixed at build time (-DDataType=FP16 or FP32)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FasterTransformer for fp16 BERT-encoder serving on A100 with batches of 3+ variable-length inputs and max lengths of 448 and up, where its README beats FT's remove-padding mode by 1.5-2x; FasterTransformer also covers decoding and beam search for translation. LightSeq (also ByteDance) also accelerates training, and FlashAttention's varlen interface is the maintained choice if you only need padding-free attention rather than a whole encoder layer.

**Gotchas:**
- BertTransformer::bert_infer creates two cudaEvents on every call and never destroys them (src/bert_transformer.cu), and the Torch op constructs a new encoder per layer per call, so long-running services leak; open issue #11 (Sep 2023, 'memory leak' on an RTX 3090) has no maintainer reply.
- The padding-free path copies the valid-token count from device to pageable host memory every layer (cudaMemcpyAsync in build_sequence_length_padding_offset_kernelLauncher), which blocks the host once per layer.
- Fused attention needs fp16 and head size 64; FP32 builds and other head sizes fall back to the unfused attention, which allocates a batch x heads x seq x seq score buffer.
- The benchmark harness (unit_test/python_scripts/bert_transformer_test.py) times wall clock with timeit and no final torch.cuda.synchronize(), and bert_bench.sh only times ByteTransformer, so the README's baseline columns cannot be reproduced from the repo.

**Status:** Stale: 11 commits, last on 2024-03-15, no releases, and the open memory-leak issue is unanswered; Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, but expect to patch it (event leak, sm90 dispatch) before production use on current CUDA and GPUs.

[repo](https://github.com/bytedance/ByteTransformer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bytedance/ByteTransformer/blob/main/README.md)

##### Chipmunk (column-sparse attention and MLP kernels for diffusion transformers)  `CUDA / Python (Triton ports)`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Training-free dynamic column-sparse attention and MLP kernels for diffusion transformers; about 2.16x end-to-end on HunyuanVideo over torch.compile'd dense.

**Beats:** FlashAttention-3 (attention layer) and cuBLAS / torch.compile'd nn.Sequential (MLP layer); torch.compile'd reference repos for end-to-end — First-party README numbers on H100: HunyuanVideo 720x1280x129 at 50 steps drops from 1030 s (torch.compile'd reference repo) to 477 s with Chipmunk alone (2.16x) and to 277 s with step caching (3.72x, vs 3.69x for TeaCache alone); FLUX.1-dev 768x1280 goes from 6.60 s to 4.90 s (1.41x). The layer-level claims (attention 9.3x over FlashAttention-3, MLP 2.5x over torch-compiled nn.Sequential) come from a chart with no stated sparsity level, shapes or script, and the repo's only timing code is commented out and compares against torch SDPA.

**Known shortcoming:** Lossy (approximate sparse attention/MLP). The 3.7x headline is mostly step caching (TeaCache alone gives 3.69x); Chipmunk alone is 2.16x on HunyuanVideo and 1.41x on FLUX. No script for the 9.3x/2.5x per-layer numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** MLP path asserts batch size 1. Open unanswered issues: flicker (#4), OOM (#6). Stale since 2025-09-08.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Activations change slowly across diffusion steps and attention and MLP activations are sparse, so on a dense 'full step' it records each query group's top keys (column sums of attention, via dense_colsum_attn) and a cached output, and on later steps computes only the contribution of those keys/neurons as a delta added to the cache. The sparsity is laid out as [192, 1] column-sparse chunks for attention and [128, 1] for the MLP, so producer warps gather the needed K/V columns into dense shared-memory tiles and the tensor-core GEMMs stay dense; kernels are written in ThunderKittens for Hopper (TMA, cp.async.reduce.bulk for the cache scatter-add). Tokens are reordered into patches or 4x6x8 voxels so neighbouring queries share one sparsity pattern, and dense steps are injected on a schedule to limit drift.

**Use it when:**
- Batch-1 text-to-video or text-to-image DiT inference on H100 (Hopper) where attention dominates, e.g. HunyuanVideo 720x1280x129, where Chipmunk alone cut 1030 s to 477 s
- You already use one of the four integrated models (HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1, FLUX.1-dev, Mochi) and can run the shipped example scripts and configs
- You accept a small, measurable quality change (the README reports VBench, ImageReward, GenEval and CLIP scores per setting) in exchange for latency
- You want to stack sparsity with step caching (TeaCache-style) or sliding-tile attention (STA), which the README combines for 2.5-3.7x end-to-end
- Ampere GPUs, via the Triton ports, if you accept that the README gives no separate Ampere numbers beyond 'comparable E2E generation speedup'

**Skip it when:**
- You need exact attention or MLP outputs: this is lossy approximate computation, not a drop-in replacement for FlashAttention-3 or cuBLAS
- LLM serving, training, causal attention or head dims other than 128: dense_attn is non-causal with 128-dim heads, and the method relies on the multi-step denoising loop
- Batched generation: SparseDiffMLP asserts input shape (1, N, C) and the static masks are built for batch 1
- You only need the headline 3.7x on HunyuanVideo: step caching alone (TeaCache) reaches 3.69x, so most of that number is not Chipmunk
- Production use needing support: stale since 2025-09-08, open unanswered issues on flickering (Wan 14B I2V on A100) and OOM (Wan2.1-14B on A100 80GB with 120 GB host RAM)

**Integration:** module (Python package with a torch CUDAExtension built by pip install -e . --no-build-isolation) · PyTorch >= 2.5, ThunderKittens (git submodule), Triton, flash_attn, CUDA libraries (cuda, cublas, cudart, cudadevrt), plus diffusers, transformers, einops, ray and other packages in requirements.txt · CUDA Toolkit >= 12.4 (12.8 recommended), nvcc -std=c++20, Python 3.11 in the quickstart; built with -O3 --use_fast_math · NVIDIA Hopper (sm_90a) for the CUDA attention and MLP kernels; other generations (Ampere tested) fall back to Triton ports, with copy_indices, topk_indices and mask_to_indices compiled for all; Linux with conda in the docs

**Vs siblings:** Pick Chipmunk over FlashAttention-3 or SageAttention only for H100 diffusion-transformer inference where a small quality change is acceptable, since it skips work rather than computing exact (FA3) or quantized-but-dense (SageAttention) attention; for anything else, including LLMs, those two are drop-in and model-agnostic. It is built on ThunderKittens, which remains the choice for dense Hopper kernels.

**Gotchas:**
- The first one or two generations are slower because of torch.compile cold starts; the README says speedups appear from generation 3
- Pinned-CPU-memory offloading of caches and indices can take up to ~5 minutes at model initialization and can exhaust host RAM (issue #6 needed offloading disabled and a smaller LARGE_BUF_SIZE)
- SparseDiffMLP requires the activation to be a GELU module because the kernel fuses bias, GELU and cache subtraction
- Multi-GPU is supported only for HunyuanVideo, on a separate multigpu branch with its own Dockerfile

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-09-08) research code from Together AI, Hazy Research and Sandy Research; MIT-licensed so the kernels can be copied, but expect to own the integration and the open quality and memory issues yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/sandyresearch/chipmunk) · [benchmark](https://github.com/sandyresearch/chipmunk)

##### CTranslate2  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

C++ inference runtime for converted Transformer models; about 2.4-3.6x the CPU throughput of PyTorch-based translation.

**Beats:** PyTorch 1.13.1 (OpenNMT-py, Hugging Face Transformers), TensorFlow 2.11.0 (OpenNMT-tf), Marian 1.11.0, FasterTransformer 5.3 (GPU) — First-party README tables (CTranslate2 3.6.0, newstest2014 En-De, tokens/s excluding tokenization and model load) show 658.8 vs 275.8 tok/s against OpenNMT-py on PyTorch 1.13.1 and 525.0 vs 147.3 (Transformers) and 344.5 (Marian 1.11.0) on 4 threads of an AWS c5.2xlarge Xeon Platinum 8275CL; on an A10G (CUDA 11) float16 reaches 10990.7 vs FasterTransformer 5.3 float16 at 8592.5, while fp32 trails FasterTransformer. Docker-based scripts in tools/benchmark reproduce it, but no compiler flags are given and the table predates the current 4.8.x release.

**Known shortcoming:** Table measured on 3.6.0 while the current release is 4.8.x; int8-vs-int8 gains are smaller; FasterTransformer fp32 beats CTranslate2 fp32 on GPU; baselines are frameworks, not kernels.

**Known shortcoming:** Security: 4.8.1 fixed a model-load heap overflow (#2068) and 4.8.2 fixed StorageView out-of-bounds reads (#2073) plus allocation size checks (#2091, #2094), so untrusted models are unsafe before 4.8.2; open: Whisper encode ~4x slower than OpenAI PyTorch (#1699), numpy-import segfault (#1181).

**How:** A hand-written graph per architecture with layer fusion, padding removal, batch reordering (sorting inputs by length within max_batch_size), in-place ops and caching allocators on CPU and GPU. Weights can be stored and computed in int8 (per-row scale, Wu et al. 2016), int16, float16, bfloat16 or AWQ int4, which also cuts memory (721MB vs Marian's 7605MB on the CPU OPUS-MT run). Matrix math is delegated late to Intel MKL (packed GEMM on Intel by default since 4.8.0), oneDNN, OpenBLAS, Ruy, Apple Accelerate or cuBLAS, with runtime ISA dispatch (AVX/AVX2/AVX512); dynamic vocabulary reduction (vmap) shrinks the output softmax for translation.

**Use it when:**
- Serving a supported Transformer (MT models, Whisper speech recognition, small and mid-size LLMs) where PyTorch or TensorFlow inference is the incumbent and you want 2-4x more tokens/s on CPU.
- CPU-only translation on x86-64 or AArch64 with int8 weights: the README shows 860 tok/s int8 vs 324 tok/s for OpenNMT-py int8 on 4 Xeon threads.
- Embedding an inference engine in a C++ application without pulling in PyTorch (the project FAQ names this case), with control over intra/inter-op threads and memory.
- Batch or streaming jobs that can feed many batches concurrently: multiple replicas share weights on one device, and calls release the Python GIL.
- Memory-constrained deployments where int8/float16 quantization (4x smaller on disk) matters more than bit-exact output.

**Skip it when:**
- Training, fine-tuning or architectures not in the supported list: the FAQ says it only exports weights and re-implements the graph, so unsupported models cannot run.
- When you need a kernel-level win over oneDNN, cuBLAS or cuDNN: it calls those libraries, and the benchmarks compare whole frameworks, not kernels.
- GPU fp32 versus FasterTransformer: the README shows FasterTransformer 5.3 faster (6979 vs 6635 tok/s); open issues report Whisper encode about 4x slower than the OpenAI PyTorch reference (#1699) and bfloat16 GEMM slower than float16 (#2033).
- Large-scale LLM serving with paged KV cache and continuous batching: its features are batch reordering, async queues and tensor parallelism via MPI, not a serving scheduler.
- Loading untrusted model files on releases before 4.8.1/4.8.2, which fixed a model-load heap overflow and out-of-bounds reads.

**Integration:** shared lib (static optional via BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF); pip wheels and Docker images · One CPU BLAS backend: Intel MKL (default, >= 2019.5), oneDNN >= 3.0, OpenBLAS, Ruy or Apple Accelerate; optional CUDA >= 11.0 (wheels need CUDA 12.x), cuDNN >= 8 for convolutional models, ROCm/HIP, NCCL + MPI for tensor parallelism; pybind11 for the Python module · C++17, CMake 3.15+ (per the install docs); Python >= 3.9 for wheels · x86-64 with SSE4.1 or newer, AArch64/ARM64; Linux, macOS, Windows; NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability >= 3.5 (tensor cores need >= 7.0); AMD ROCm wheels on the releases page

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FasterTransformer or LightSeq when you need CPU inference, an actively maintained engine, or a single C++/Python API across MT, Whisper and LLMs; pick FasterTransformer or ByteTransformer only for NVIDIA-GPU BERT/GPT pipelines already tuned around them. Kernel libraries such as LIBXSMM or FBGEMM sit below it and do not replace it.

**Gotchas:**
- The runtime silently falls back to another compute type when the requested one is not optimized on the device (e.g. int16 runs as float16 on GPU, float16 runs as float32 on CPU); query get_supported_compute_types or set CT2_VERBOSE=1.
- Quantized outputs differ slightly from the original model (BLEU 26.77 to 26.64-26.85 in the README tables); int8 + vmap is the fastest CPU row but also the lowest BLEU.
- Keep inter_threads x intra_threads at or below the physical core count; the default intra_threads is 4 and async queues block once max_queued_batches is full.
- Open bug #1181: importing numpy after ctranslate2 can segfault; tensor-parallel Flan-T5 XXL gave unexpected output in #1691.

**Status:** Actively maintained (4.8.2 released 2026-08-31 on PyPI, MIT-licensed, 4.7k stars, backend of faster-whisper); security fixes go to the latest release series only, so stay current.

[repo](https://github.com/OpenNMT/CTranslate2) · [benchmark](https://github.com/OpenNMT/CTranslate2/blob/master/README.md)

##### Decoding Attention (Bruce-Lee-LY)  `CUDA/C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

CUDA-core decode-attention kernel for LLM inference; beats Flash-Decoding and FlashInfer only at short KV lengths.

**Beats:** Flash-Decoding (FlashAttention v2.6.3) and FlashInfer v0.1.6 decode attention — First-party plots from the public Python harness (1 warmup, 10 timed iterations, CUDA events) on an RTX 3090 with CUDA 12.1, FP16, 32 heads, head dim 128, compare against flash_attn_with_kvcache from FlashAttention v2.6.3 and FlashInfer v0.1.6 (the author's fork): faster at KV lengths below 1536 and across a batch sweep at KV length 128, about 2x slower than FlashInfer at 8192. In the batch sweep FlashInfer runs through its paged-KV wrapper with page size 1 while this kernel reads contiguous KV, so the baselines are not on equal footing; host CPU and host compiler are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** FlashMLA is 1.3x to ~70x faster than Decoding Attention on H20 MLA plots; the FlashInfer baseline is the author's own fork.

**Known shortcoming:** FlashInfer batch baseline uses paged KV with page_size=1 (not equal footing); context capped near 25k tokens on sm86/89 by the shared-memory score buffer; output rows for zero-length KV left uninitialized (torch::empty); softmax scale hard-coded to 1/sqrt(dim); tests only to seq 512.

**How:** Avoids tensor cores, which Flash-Decoding underuses when the query length is 1, and instead runs a plain CUDA-core kernel adapted from OpenPPL: one thread block per (sequence, query head), 128-bit vectorised K/V loads, warp-shuffle reductions for the Q.K dot products, all scores kept in shared memory, then a block-wide softmax and a P.V pass. Launch shape is picked per head dim and batch (e.g. 256 threads for batch <= 4, 128 otherwise at head dim 128), and kernels are built with --use_fast_math. With no split over the sequence and a three-pass softmax, it is cheapest when the KV length is short and the batch fills the GPU.

**Use it when:**
- Decode-stage MHA with short contexts (README: faster than Flash-Decoding and FlashInfer below KV length 1536 at batch 1, about 1.75x at 1024 on an RTX 3090 by plot reading).
- Large batches of short sequences: in the KV length 128 batch sweep it led both baselines at every batch size (about 1.4-1.6x at batch 16, roughly level with FlashInfer from batch 128).
- Ampere/Ada consumer or workstation GPUs (sm80, sm86, sm89 build targets) where you control the KV layout and want a small, readable kernel to fork.
- ALiBi models or GQA/MQA decode where a contiguous varlen KV buffer is already available.

**Skip it when:**
- KV lengths above about 1536: FlashInfer reached about 0.84 vs 0.43 TFLOPS at 8192 on the same plots, roughly 2x faster.
- MLA decoding: on an H20 the README's own plots show FlashMLA 1.3x to about 70x faster; each block re-reads its KV head, so MQA/MLA traffic grows with the number of query heads.
- Paged KV caches, prefill, speculative decoding with more than one query token, or FP8/INT8 KV caches (KV quantization is listed as TODO).
- Long contexts in general: the kernel needs max_seq_k x 4 bytes of shared memory per block, which caps KV length at about 25k tokens on sm86/sm89 and about 58k on sm90 (derived from the source and CUDA per-block shared-memory limits); tests only cover KV lengths up to 512.
- Production use needing maintenance: two commits, no releases or issues, last commit 2025-06-11.

**Integration:** source-drop (CUDA sources plus a PyTorch CUDAExtension; the CMake build produces only a benchmark executable) · CUDA >= 11.4; PyTorch, ninja and psutil for the Python extension; gflags and OpenMP for the C++ benchmark; pytest for tests · C++17 (nvcc -std=c++17), CMake 3.16+; README says GCC >= 5, but the kernel uses if constexpr and std::is_same_v, so a C++17-capable host compiler is required · Linux; NVIDIA sm80 (A100), sm86 (RTX 3090/A6000), sm89 (L20/L40S), sm90 (H20/H800)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FlashInfer only for short-context, large-batch MHA/GQA decode on Ampere/Ada with a contiguous KV buffer; for long contexts, paged KV caches or MLA, FlashInfer (or FlashMLA) wins, and FlashAttention-3 targets Hopper prefill and training rather than this niche.

**Gotchas:**
- Softmax scale is hard-coded to 1/sqrt(dim); models needing another scale (e.g. absorbed MLA with dim 576) must pre-scale Q themselves.
- Sequences with zero KV length return early without writing their output rows, and the PyTorch wrapper allocates the output with torch::empty, so those rows hold uninitialised memory.
- Strides are recomputed from head counts and dims; the wrapper checks only that the last dimension is contiguous, so a strided view (e.g. K sliced from a combined KV tensor) is read incorrectly. For MLA pass v=None, since the V row stride is computed from dim, not dim_v.
- The P.V partial sums are combined with shared-memory float atomicAdd across warps, so outputs are not bitwise reproducible run to run; setup.py also forces _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 regardless of how the installed PyTorch was built.

**Status:** Stale single-author research code (2 commits, last 2025-06-11, 48 stars, no issues filed), BSD-3-Clause and small (one kernel template), so it is easy to vendor and adapt but has no releases or maintenance.

[repo](https://github.com/Bruce-Lee-LY/decoding_attention) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Bruce-Lee-LY/decoding_attention)

##### Effort (bucketMul approximate matrix multiplication for LLM inference on Apple Silicon)  `Swift`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Swift/Metal LLM engine whose approximate bucketMul matrix-vector product trades quality for speed against Apple MPS on Apple Silicon.

**Beats:** Apple MPS default matrix-vector multiplication (benchmark.swift prints 'Default Apple MPS implementation (comparable to llama.cpp)'); the project page also plots a llama.cpp tokens/s line — First-party only: on the author's Apple Silicon Mac (M2 Pro per the setup notes; the charts name no chip), FP16 Mistral 7B matrix-vector products timed in benchmarks/benchmark.swift show bucketMul at about 15 tps-equivalent at 100% effort, about 26-27 at 50% (roughly MPS's 26) and about 47-49 at 25% (about 1.85x MPS, read from chart images); 2x is reached only near 22% effort, where the chart marks a quality breakdown on Mistral. No Xcode or compiler settings are given, and actual tokens/s reaches the llama.cpp line (about 25 tok/s) only near 30% effort.

**Known shortcoming:** Swift/Metal only, not C++. Claim overstated: the chart shows about 1.85x over Apple MPS at 25% effort and 2x only near 22%, which the chart itself marks as 'breakdown on Mistral'; slower than MPS at 100%. Approximate (lossy) matmul. The author's own pages say the implementation 'seems just broken' for Mixtral and does not beat quantization yet.

**Known shortcoming:** The startup benchmark charges MPS for about 14% more weights than bucketMul (3x wq 50.3M x 4/3 = 67.1M vs w1 58.7M, derived from benchmark.swift and timeit.swift). The 4 low bits of each FP16 weight store position, so precision is lost even at 100% effort; results are nondeterministic (atomic dispatch); machines with 16 GB or less silently load 11/16 of the weights; macOS-only; issue #5 unanswered and the HF weights repo 404'd once (issue #3).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Offline, each transposed weight row is cut into buckets of 16, sorted by absolute value, interleaved so that the largest-magnitude weights of every input dimension come first, and annotated with per-bucket mean-|w| statistics plus diagonal 'probe' weights; the 4 low bits of each FP16 weight store its output position. At decode time a GPU kernel estimates the cutoff for the chosen effort from probe x input products (top-k), a second kernel builds a dispatch list of only the bucket rows whose stat x input value clears the cutoff, and the bucketMul Metal kernel streams those rows, accumulating into 16 per-thread registers selected by the embedded position bits. The speedup comes from reading fewer weight bytes in a memory-bound GEMV; the author says the kernel reaches about 50-70% of memory bandwidth and is ALU-limited.

**Use it when:**
- Research on input-dependent (dynamic) weight skipping for batch-1 decode, where you want a working Metal reference of the bucket/dispatch idea to read or port.
- Experiments on Apple Silicon Macs with enough unified memory for FP16 Mistral 7B, where a 25-50% effort level and its quality loss are acceptable.
- Exploring 'ad hoc distillation' by loading only part of each matrix (percentLoad) to fit a model into less memory without retraining.
- Studying the speed/quality curve of approximate GEMV: the repo ships cosine-similarity, next-token agreement and multiple-choice quiz harnesses across effort levels.

**Skip it when:**
- Production or quality-sensitive inference: the author's own pages say the current implementation 'seems just broken' (Mistral worse than before, Mixtral 'barely works'), and early KL-divergence tests 'seem to not win against Quantization yet'.
- Anything outside macOS on Apple Silicon: Swift plus Metal only, Xcode project, no Linux/CUDA/CPU path (issue #5 asks for other platforms, unanswered).
- When you need exact results or full speed: at 100% effort bucketMul is slower than MPS (about 15 vs 26 matrix-only tps read from the project chart), and parity needs about 50-70% effort.
- Real end-to-end throughput: every generated token carries about 15 ms of overhead the author could not remove, attention is unoptimised and slows quickly with longer contexts, and only FP16 Mistral is wired up (Q8 incomplete, Q4 'extremely slow').
- Maintained dependencies: last commit 2024-07-01, one-person demo, and the weights repo has gone missing before (issue #3: huggingface kolinko/mistral-buckets returned 404, April 2024).

**Integration:** source-drop (Xcode macOS command-line app in Swift with Metal shaders; no library target) · Apple Metal and MetalPerformanceShaders (MPS used for the baseline multiply and top-k); Xcode; converted bucketed FP16 Mistral weights (huggingface-cli download kolinko/mistral-buckets, or the built-in convert mode from .safetensors) · not documented (Xcode project; Swift and Metal versions not stated) · macOS on Apple Silicon only (author's M2 Pro; notes M3 seems faster than M1/M2)

**Vs siblings:** Among catalogued siblings, PowerInfer also skips weights based on the input (predicted-active neurons, CUDA/CPU on llama.cpp) and FastGEMV is an exact fp16/int GEMV for CUDA; pick Effort only when you want an Apple-Silicon Metal implementation of magnitude-sorted dynamic weight skipping to study or port, and use PowerInfer or an exact quantised kernel when you need working inference.

**Gotchas:**
- Output is nondeterministic: the dispatch list is built with atomic counters, so token generation varies between runs at the same effort (author's GPU page).
- The 4 low bits of every FP16 weight hold the output position (kernel reads as_type<ushort>(w) & 15), so stored weights lose mantissa precision even at 100% effort.
- The startup benchmark compares different matrices: MPS times 3 x wq (3 x 4096x4096, 50.3M weights) scaled by 4/3, while bucketMul times one w1 (4096x14336, 58.7M weights); derived from code, that charges the MPS line for about 14% more weights than bucketMul at 100% effort, and the printed 'tps' is matmul-only, not generation speed.
- On machines with 16 GB RAM or less the loader silently loads only 11/16 of each matrix (the message says 75%, or 37% for 8 GB, but both branches set 0xB), which lowers quality before you touch effort; kernels are tuned for 4096x14336 and need per-shape hand-tuning.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-07-01 and self-described as a buggy demo looking for collaborators, but MIT-licensed; worth reading as a reference for the bucketMul idea rather than vendoring.

[repo](https://github.com/kolinko/effort) · [benchmark](https://github.com/kolinko/effort/blob/main/docs/index.html)

##### FastAD  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++17 expression-template AD library; author reports 2-10x over Adept and 2-19x over Stan Math gradients.

**Beats:** Adept, Stan Math, ADOL-C, CppAD, Sacado (C++ AD libraries) — In the author's unrefereed arXiv preprint (2102.03681), built with GCC 10, C++17, -O3 -march=native on an 8-core Google Cloud Xeon VM (model not stated), FastAD's gradient time beat Adept 2.0.8 and Stan Math 3.3.0 by about 10x/15x (sum), 2.5x/7.7x (log-sum-exp), 9x/19x (normal log-pdf), 10x/8.6x (Bayesian regression) and 2x/2.6x (stochastic volatility). Matrix product was roughly a tie with Adept. The harness is public (JamesYang007/ADBenchmark, tested only on macOS Catalina). The README's 'orders of magnitude' claim is not supported by these numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party arXiv preprint, no review venue; CPU model missing (unnamed GCP Xeon VM); README's 'orders of magnitude' overstates the paper's 2-19x.

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #110 (2026): GCC 16 -O3 miscompile (segfault / Eigen resize assertion in RcppFastAD), fix PR #111 unmerged; no commits since 2023-09; no higher-order derivatives, Jacobians, sparse matrices or checkpointing; ties Adept on matrix products.

**How:** There is no runtime tape. The computation graph is a compile-time expression template (no virtual calls, no per-node heap allocation), and the exact value/adjoint storage size is computed up front so one contiguous block is allocated ('lazy allocation'). Vector/matrix variables store 'a pair of pointers to a matrix of doubles' instead of a matrix of (value, adjoint) pairs, so Eigen can emit packed SIMD (the paper shows vaddpd vs Stan's scalar vaddsd). C++17 if constexpr/SFINAE detects constant arguments and precomputes things like sufficient statistics in normal log-pdf.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated gradient evaluation of a fixed-structure scalar objective (MCMC/HMC log-densities, MLE, regression likelihoods) where the graph is built once and re-evaluated with new inputs.
- Vectorized objectives over Eigen vectors/matrices (sums, log-sum-exp, normal log-pdf), where the paper shows the largest gaps (about 9-19x vs Stan, 9-10x vs Adept).
- Projects already using Eigen 3.3 and C++17 that want a small, MIT-licensed header-only AD dependency.
- First-order gradients only, on x86-64 with -O3 -march=native.

**Skip it when:**
- Data-dependent dynamic graphs (graph shape changes per call, arbitrary loops/branches on runtime values): you must restate them with if_else/for_each, which a tape-based library (Adept, XAD, CppAD) handles naturally.
- Higher-order derivatives, Jacobians of vector functions, sparse matrices or checkpointing: not supported (open issues #75, #101, #109, #28; the paper calls higher order 'a great challenge').
- Workloads dominated by dense matrix products: the paper shows FastAD only comparable to Adept and about 2x over Stan there.
- Production use needing a maintained library: last commit Sept 2023, and the paper says function/distribution/decomposition coverage is incomplete.
- Builds with GCC 16 at -O3 until PR #111 lands (see gotchas).

**Integration:** header-only · Eigen 3.3 (GoogleTest and Google Benchmark for dev builds only) · C++17; benchmarks used GCC 10; developed mainly with Clang; CMake package (FastAD::FastAD) or FetchContent of tag v3.2.1 · any platform Eigen supports; CI on Linux and macOS; benchmarked on x86-64 only

**Vs siblings:** Pick FastAD over XAD when the objective is a fixed, Eigen-vectorized statistical model and you want the smallest header-only dependency. Pick XAD when you need a maintained, tape-based library that handles arbitrary C++ control flow, higher-order modes and checkpointing.

**Gotchas:**
- Evaluating an expression that was never bound to storage segfaults (README warns explicitly); use ad::bind(...) unless you manage buffers yourself.
- Adjoints accumulate: call reset_adj() on every Var, placeholders included, before differentiating again or gradients are wrong.
- Open issue #110 (2026): with g++-16 at -O3, RcppFastAD examples segfault in memcpy or hit Eigen's 'DenseBase::resize() does not actually allow to resize' assertion; it goes away with -fno-inline or Clang. Unmerged PR #111 (Sept 2026) fixes Eigen::Map rebinding in ValueView::bind().
- && and || are undefined behavior on multi-dimensional non-boolean expressions; setting several forward-mode adjoints gives a scaled directional derivative.

**Status:** Stale since Sept 2023 (one community PR open for a GCC 16 miscompile), but MIT-licensed and header-only, so it can be vendored; the R package RcppFastAD still depends on it.

[repo](https://github.com/JamesYang007/FastAD) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.03681)

##### faster-enhancer.c  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Dependency-free C int8 runtime for the FastEnhancer-Medium speech denoiser; paper reports 3.3x lower RTF than fp32 ONNX Runtime on M2.

**Beats:** ONNX Runtime fp32 graph of the same FastEnhancer-Medium weights — The author's arXiv paper (2607.25350, seen only as a search snippet) reports 0.069 RTF for the int8 engine vs 0.230 for the fp32 ONNX Runtime graph on one Apple M2 core (3.3x); the README tables time only this engine (M2 and Galaxy S23+, 5569-frame clips, median of repeats) and give PESQ 3.054 vs 3.060 for fp32 ONNX over 824 VoiceBank-DEMAND utterances. The ORT version, threads and execution provider were not seen, the compiler is not named, and the ONNX benchmark artifacts the docs place under experiments/ are not in the public repo, so the comparison is int8 vs fp32 and cannot be reproduced from the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Docs say the ONNX benchmark artifacts are in experiments/, but that directory is a 404 in the public repo, so the 3.3x baseline timing cannot be reproduced; int8 compared against fp32.

**Known shortcoming:** The 0.069 vs 0.230 RTF (3.3x) figure comes only from a search snippet (arXiv blocked); x86 tiers are not timed; one global engine, not thread-safe; built with -ffinite-math-only, so NaN/Inf input is unsupported.

**How:** W8A8 post-training quantization (per-row symmetric int8 weights, per-tensor asymmetric uint8 activations recomputed every frame) feeding six hand-written int8 GEMM microkernel tiers chosen at init: NEON vmull/vmlal/vpadalq, DOTPROD vdotq_laneq_s32 with A row-quad pre-pack, I8MM vmmlaq_s32 with KleidiAI-style row-pair pre-pack, AVX2 vpmovsxbw+vpmaddwd, AVX-VNNI and AVX-512-VNNI vpdpbusd. The k=3 convolutions run as Winograd F(2,3) (2/3 of the multiplies), the GRU (both matmuls, gates and state update) is fused into one kernel per tier, dequantization, residual adds, bias and requantize-scale tracking are fused into GEMM epilogues, and recurrent/skip state is kept in fp16. All state lives in one 432,384-byte struct with no heap allocation after init, and init page-locks buffers and runs a 128-frame warmup.

**Use it when:**
- You need FastEnhancer-Medium noise suppression at 48 kHz in a native C/C++ app (voice chat, conferencing, recording) and want to drop the ONNX Runtime dependency.
- Hard real-time audio threads where allocation and allocator jitter are not acceptable: nothing is allocated after fe_init.
- ARMv8.2+ devices with DotProd or I8MM (Apple M-series, recent Snapdragon): README measures 0.069 RTF on one M2 core and 0.096 on a Galaxy S23+.
- Deployments that need bit-reproducible output across SIMD tiers of one architecture family (a SHA-256 regression gate enforces it).
- Small binary budgets: the static library is 162 KiB on macOS arm64 plus the 565 KB weight blob.

**Skip it when:**
- Any model other than FastEnhancer-Medium at 48 kHz: there is no graph loader, and the one open issue (#1) asks for GTCRN support.
- x86 deployments where you need measured latency: the README times ARM only, the x86 tiers were not re-measured under the current protocol, and the AVX-512 tier was checked only under Intel SDE.
- Older or non-mainstream CPUs: there is no scalar fallback, so fe_init fails on x86 hosts without AVX2+FMA3+F16C (SSE4.1-only parts are deliberately unsupported), and only arm64 and x86-64 build at all (no 32-bit ARM, RISC-V or MSVC).
- Plain ARMv8.0 NEON cores, where the floor tier is about 2.4x (M2) to 3.6x (S23+) slower than the I8MM tier (derived from the README table).
- Several independent streams in one process: the engine is a single global instance, so you cannot run two channels concurrently.

**Integration:** static lib · none at runtime; Python with ONNX tooling only to regenerate weights from the upstream export (the committed weights/fe.q8 blob avoids this) · C11, CMake 3.20+, GCC or Clang with GNU-style target attributes (MSVC and clang-cl rejected; MinGW or GNU-driver Clang on Windows) · arm64 (NEON baseline; DotProd/I8MM tiers) and x86-64 (AVX2+FMA3+F16C required; AVX-VNNI, AVX-512 VNNI tiers); macOS, Linux, Android, Windows via MinGW

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over RTNeural or a general engine such as MNN or OpenVINO only when the model is exactly FastEnhancer-Medium and you want an allocation-free, dependency-free C engine; RTNeural is the better choice for your own small LSTM/GRU/conv audio networks, and general runtimes cover arbitrary graphs.

**Gotchas:**
- Global state: one engine per process; a second fe_init without fe_free is a no-op, so switching weight blobs needs fe_free first, and the blob memory must outlive the engine (weights are referenced zero-copy).
- Built with -ffinite-math-only and documented as a finite-input contract: feeding NaN or Inf samples is unsupported.
- Benchmarks race the core; a paced real-time callback on an M2 P-core costs 4.2x more per frame (0.286 RTF), and docs show E-cores on hybrid Intel parts run a frame 3.6x slower, so set thread priority/QoS yourself (the library does not).
- Output is delayed by a fixed 704 samples; comparing against an offline centered-STFT reference measures framing phase, not quantization error (the docs' own earlier fidelity table had this error and was corrected).

**Status:** Active but young (4 commits, last 2026-07-29, single author, 25 stars); MIT-licensed C with no dependencies, so it is easy to vendor if your model matches.

[repo](https://github.com/kdrkdrkdr/faster-enhancer.c) · [benchmark](https://github.com/kdrkdrkdr/faster-enhancer.c)

##### FasterTransformer  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

NVIDIA's discontinued CUDA C++ transformer inference library; beats TensorFlow XLA and TorchScript FP16 BERT on T4, mostly via INT8.

**Beats:** TensorFlow XLA (FP16) and PyTorch TorchScript (FP16) for the BERT encoder; TensorFlow and PyTorch decoder and beam-search implementations for translation decoding — NVIDIA's own docs/bert_guide.md tables on a T4 (Xeon E5-2670 host) show BERT-base FP16 FT 1.28x to 3.04x faster than TensorFlow XLA FP16 and 1.52x to 6.41x faster than TorchScript FP16, rising to 5.53x over TF FP16 with padding removal plus INT8-v2 (batch 8, seq 384: 39.50 vs 7.14 ms). The numbers come from the public benchmark scripts, but the compiler and CUDA versions used are not stated and the comparison mixes INT8 FT with FP16 baselines.

**Known shortcoming:** The 5x headline is INT8 FasterTransformer vs FP16 baselines; same-precision gains are 1.28-3.04x; the TorchScript baseline is overhead-bound.

**Known shortcoming:** Discontinued (moved to TensorRT-LLM); FP32 FT vs TF on T4 only 1.03-1.44x; a TF FP16 baseline anomaly (b1/s32 at 5.84 ms slower than s128 at 3.30 ms) inflates small-batch ratios; open bugs #736 (BLOOM 0% accuracy) and #790 (position_encoding_table malloc); docs warn multithreaded op calls may deadlock.

**How:** Each BERT layer is reduced to 6 or 8 cuBLAS GEMMs plus 6 fused custom CUDA kernels (bias, activation, residual and layernorm fused), with an offline GEMM autotuner (bert_gemm writes gemm_config.in) choosing cuBLAS algorithms per shape. Effective FasterTransformer removes padding tokens before the encoder (the ByteDance Effective Transformer idea) and uses TensorRT's fused multi-head attention kernel; INT8 modes v1 (per-channel weights, int32 GEMM output) and v2 (per-tensor, int8 residual and GEMM output) run through cuBLASLt, and Ampere 2:4 sparse GEMM via cuSPARSELt is optional. Generation models use a fused masked multi-head attention kernel for the 1-token decode step, a preallocated key/value cache, buffer reuse across layers, and Megatron-style tensor parallelism with two all-reduces per block.

**Use it when:**
- Legacy deployments already pinned to FasterTransformer 5.x (TF1/PyTorch ops or the Triton FT backend) where the model is in its support matrix and you cannot move to TensorRT-LLM yet.
- BERT-style encoder inference on Turing/Ampere GPUs with variable-length batches, where padding removal plus INT8-v2 gives the largest gains (docs: up to 5.5x over TF FP16 at batch 32, seq 384 on T4).
- Studying or borrowing proven fused CUDA kernels (layernorm, fused MHA, beam search, top-k/top-p sampling) under Apache-2.0.
- Encoder-decoder translation decoding where FT-Decoding replaces a framework beam search loop (README: 4x to 18x over TensorFlow FP16 on T4).

**Skip it when:**
- New LLM serving: NVIDIA states development has moved to TensorRT-LLM and the repo will get no further development; serving engines and newer kernels (ByteTransformer, CTranslate2 per their own READMEs) beat it in several settings.
- Non-NVIDIA hardware or CPU inference: it is CUDA, cuBLAS and cuBLASLt only, verified for compute capability 7.0 and newer.
- Same-precision FP32 speedups: on T4, FP32 FT is only 1.03x to 1.44x faster than TensorFlow (bert_guide tables), so most of the headline gain needs FP16 or INT8 plus padding removal.
- Modern toolchains without patching: open bug-labelled issues report CUDA 12.2 incompatibility, clang CUDA build errors and a C++17 compile error, and the README's Known issues list TensorFlow 2.10 undefined symbols and C++ ABI mismatches when importing the PyTorch extension.
- Models outside the support matrix: each architecture is hand-written C++, so a new model means writing a new model class.

**Integration:** static lib · CUDA (10.2+ in CMake, 11.0+ in the BERT guide, 11.8+ for FP8), cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, optional cuDNN, CUTLASS submodule; MPI and NCCL for multi-GPU; cuSPARSELt for sparsity; TensorFlow 1.15 or PyTorch >= 1.5 for the framework ops · CMake 3.8 (3.13 for PyTorch), C++14 by default (CXX_STD cache variable; CXX flags also pass -std=c++17), nvcc with -DSM per target GPU; NGC 22.09 containers recommended · Linux x86-64 with NVIDIA GPUs (SM 52 to 90 in the build list; correctness verified on SM 70+; INT8 on Turing+, sparsity on Ampere+, FP8 on Hopper)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ByteTransformer or LightSeq only when you need its wider model zoo (GPT, T5, BLOOM, multi-GPU tensor/pipeline parallel) or an existing Triton FT backend; for BERT alone ByteTransformer reports 24.70 vs 50.28 ms at batch 16, seq 1024, and CTranslate2 is the better-maintained choice for translation models on CPU and GPU.

**Gotchas:**
- Run the GEMM autotuner (bert_gemm, gpt_gemm and similar) for your batch/sequence shapes; without gemm_config.in it falls back to default algorithms and the guide says inference may be slower.
- The TorchScript FP16 baseline sits near 10.4 to 11 ms for every small case and TF FP16 at batch 1 seq 32 is slower than at seq 128, so small-batch ratios reflect framework overhead, not kernel speed.
- Release builds compile CUDA with --use_fast_math by default (BUILD_FAST_MATH=ON), and decoding results differ from TensorFlow because of accumulated log probabilities (Known issues).
- TensorRT's fused MHA kernel is used only on Turing+ with size_per_head 64; other shapes fall back to FT's own slower attention, and INT8 mode 1 needs sequence length a multiple of 32 above 384.

**Status:** Discontinued: last commit 2023-10-19, last release 5.2 (Dec 2022), a notice moving development to TensorRT-LLM, and 250 open issues and 38 open PRs; Apache-2.0, so kernels can be copied, but treat it as a reference rather than a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/NVIDIA/FasterTransformer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/NVIDIA/FasterTransformer)

##### FBGEMM  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Meta's x86 low-precision GEMM, convolution and embedding kernel library behind PyTorch quantized CPU ops; INT8 reported 2x MKL FP32 at batch 1.

**Beats:** Intel MKL FP32 GEMM (via a cited Microsoft paper), caffe2/perfkernels (embedding SpMDM), a prior 64-bit GEMM implementation — The FBGEMM wiki (last edited 2020-01-18) cites a Microsoft/Marian NMT paper reporting FBGEMM INT8 at 2x MKL FP32 throughput at batch 1 (1.3x at batch 32), and reports first-party gains against caffe2 perfkernels (EmbeddingSpMDM about 2x) and FBGEMM's own earlier code (64-bit GEMM 10.5 vs 3 GOps/s on a Xeon Gold 6138 with turbo off; groupwise conv 4-10x and 60x). No compiler, flags or benchmark harness is named for these numbers, and the cited paper and the FBGEMM arXiv paper could not be opened here.

**Known shortcoming:** Wiki dates from 2020; most wins are against its own older code or INT8 vs FP32; the Marian WNGT 2019 paper is unreadable here (possible B on retier).

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #4679 reports incorrect SVE kernel results on arm64; fbgemmGroupwiseConv does nothing for thread_id>0; needs C++20 and AVX2; FP16/FP32 fall back to reference kernels on aarch64.

**How:** Inner GEMM kernels are generated at runtime with asmjit, specialized to the matrix shape and the detected instruction set (AVX2, AVX-512, AVX-512 VNNI, with cpuinfo for dispatch), and cached in a code cache shared across threads. Quantization bookkeeping is fused into packing (row offsets computed while packing A) and into a composable output pipeline (requantize, bias, ReLU, sparse outlier SpMDM on the int32 buffer), so bandwidth-bound low-precision GEMMs avoid extra passes. 16-bit-accumulation kernels (ACC16), specialized depthwise and groupwise convolution paths, and EmbeddingSpMDM kernels for embedding bags cover the shapes that dominate recommendation and NLP inference.

**Use it when:**
- INT8 quantized inference on x86 servers with AVX2 or AVX-512/VNNI, especially small-batch fully connected layers where packing and requantization overhead matter (cited Marian paper: 2x MKL FP32 throughput at batch 1, 1.3x at batch 32).
- Recommendation models with large embedding tables: EmbeddingSpMDM is about 2x the older caffe2 perfkernels per the wiki, with 18-25% lower average latency on production models.
- Groupwise or depthwise convolutions with few channels per group (2, 4, 8, 16), where the wiki reports 4-10x for stride 2 and 60x for 3D groupwise over FBGEMM's earlier im2col path.
- You already use PyTorch quantization (the fbgemm qengine) and want to call the same kernels directly from C++.
- Moderately sparse weights (around 90%) where the sparse INT8/FP32 kernels report 2x-4x.

**Skip it when:**
- ARM servers or Apple silicon: the docs require AVX2 or higher; aarch64 builds define reference-kernel fallbacks for FP16/FP32 GEMM, direct convolution is compiled out, and open issue #4679 reports build problems and incorrect SVE kernel results on arm64.
- Plain FP32 BLAS replacement: the API is pack-then-compute with quantization parameters, not sgemm, and the headline gains come from reduced precision versus FP32.
- When you need an independent, reproducible speed claim: the public numbers are 2019-2020 first-party wiki prose or a cited paper, and the large ratios (60x, 3.5x) are against FBGEMM's own earlier code.
- Accuracy-sensitive models that you cannot quantize or calibrate: INT8 and ACC16 paths need per-tensor or per-channel scales and zero points and may need outlier handling.
- Toolchains older than C++20 or CMake 3.21: the current build rejects anything below C++20.

**Integration:** static lib · asmjit and cpuinfo (bundled as submodules, overridable via ASMJIT_SRC_DIR / CPUINFO_SRC_DIR); OpenMP optional; GoogleTest only for tests; Python needed at configure time to read source lists from defs.bzl; KleidiAI on non-Apple aarch64; no MKL dependency · C++20, CMake 3.21; GCC or Clang (libc++/libomp for Clang), MSVC 2019+ on Windows; GCC 12+ needs -Wno-error workarounds per the build docs; SVE paths need GCC 14+ or Clang 17+ · x86-64 with AVX2 required (AVX-512 and AVX-512 VNNI kernels dispatched at runtime); aarch64 NEON/SVE builds exist but are partial; Linux, macOS, Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over LIBXSMM when the job is INT8 quantized inference with fused requantization or embedding-bag lookups on x86, especially inside PyTorch; LIBXSMM is the better fit for small dense FP32/BF16 GEMMs and convolutions on both x86 and ARM, and llamafile tinyBLAS or T-MAC target LLM weight formats instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Call fbgemmSupportedCPU() before use; on CPUs below AVX2 the optimized paths are unavailable.
- fbgemmGroupwiseConv does nothing for thread_id > 0, so splitting it across threads silently leaves work to thread 0.
- Row offsets from packing A and column offsets with zero points must be supplied correctly to ReQuantizeOutput; passing nullptr is only valid for symmetric weight quantization.
- Bug reports in the issue tracker are often for FBGEMM_GPU (for example #5326, zeroed embeddings above dim 1024), not the CPU library; check which package an issue applies to.

**Status:** Actively developed by Meta (last commit 2026-10-01, 5,473 commits, 66 open issues) and BSD-3-Clause, but the CPU library's public performance documentation dates from 2020 and most recent work is in the GPU packages.

[repo](https://github.com/pytorch/FBGEMM) · [benchmark](https://github.com/pytorch/FBGEMM/wiki/Recent-feature-additions-and-improvements-in-FBGEMM)

##### FeatherCNN  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Small dependency-free ARM CPU CNN inference library; 2017 wiki shows 2-13x lower latency than Caffe+OpenBLAS and Caffe2+Eigen.

**Beats:** Caffe2 with Eigen, Caffe with OpenBLAS, Caffe2 with NNPACK, TensorFlow Lite, ARM Compute Library, TVM — The first-party wiki reports whole-network fp32 inference time on ARM CPUs measured in late 2017. On a 64-core Huawei D05 (Cortex-A72), best time at any thread count gives VGG-16 102 ms vs 1108 ms for Caffe+OpenBLAS and 1310 ms for Caffe2+Eigen. On an iPhone 7 with 2 cores, VGG-16 runs in 284 ms vs 905 ms for TensorFlow Lite, and on an Nvidia TX2 in 706 ms vs 3569 ms for Caffe2+NNPACK. No compiler, flags or benchmark harness are published, and the wiki's own GoogleNet speedup column (13.7x) disagrees with its timing tables (about 6.6x, derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Wiki speedup column does not match its own tables (GoogleNet 13.7x listed vs ~6.6x from the timings); BSD-3-Clause only in file headers, no LICENSE file; TPDS 2020 paper unreadable here (possible B on retier).

**Known shortcoming:** Master was rewritten 2019-04-28; wiki numbers are from 2017 pre-rewrite code (the .feathermodel API the README still documents); master Net() hard-codes 1 thread with no setter, so the wiki's multithread tables cannot be reproduced through the public API; debug printf on every conv Forward; -Ofast -ffast-math global; build_android.sh enables OpenCL but src/booster/cl is missing; SqueezeNet segfault #33 unanswered.

**How:** 3x3 stride-1 convolutions use Winograd F(6x6,3x3) (F(2x2,3x3) also exists), with the transformed tiles multiplied by a batched GEMM the TPDS paper calls TensorGEMM. Other convolutions use im2col plus a hand-written NEON SGEMM (4x12 and 8x12 register-blocked micro-kernels using vfmaq_f32), and depthwise layers get a dedicated kernel. A ReLU that follows a convolution is fused into it, and activations come from a shared memory pool.

**Use it when:**
- Reading the Winograd F(6x6,3x3) and NEON GEMM kernels (src/booster/arm) as BSD-3 reference code for your own ARM convolution work.
- Float32 inference of a classic Caffe CNN built only from conv, depthwise conv, pooling, ReLU, BN/Scale, inner product, eltwise, concat and softmax on an ARMv8 phone or board, where you can accept an unmaintained library.
- VGG-style networks dominated by 3x3 stride-1 convolutions, where the Winograd path does most of the work (the largest gains on the wiki are for VGG-16).

**Skip it when:**
- Any new production deployment: there have been no commits since 2019-09-24, open issues (segfault on SqueezeNet, unregistered Deconvolution layer, build failures) have no maintainer replies, and MNN, ncnn or XNNPACK cover the same ground and are maintained.
- Models that need ops outside the 13 registered layers (no Deconvolution, Reshape, Permute, detection or SSD layers), partial group convolution, or anything other than fp32 (no int8 or fp16).
- Choosing on the wiki numbers: they were measured on the pre-April-2019 code (the .feathermodel / InitFromPath API the README still describes) against Caffe, Caffe2 and TFLite builds from late 2017, and the code was rewritten on master after that.
- Multi-core inference through the public API: on master Net() hard-codes one thread and exposes no setter, unlike the per-thread-count tables on the wiki.

**Integration:** static lib · none for the library (OpenMP optional, GCD on iOS); the Caffe model converter described in the README needs protobuf · C++11, CMake 2.8; Android NDK (android-21 for arm64-v8a, android-16 for armeabi-v7a) or the Xcode iOS SDK · aarch64 and armv7 with NEON (Android, iOS, Linux); x86-64 with AVX2 via the BOOSTER_AVX backend (built with -march=core-avx2)

**Vs siblings:** Pick MNN over this for any real ARM deployment: it is maintained, supports far more ops and has its own peer-reviewed (MLSys 2020) comparison against TFLite and ncnn. FeatherCNN is worth taking over NNPACK only as compact BSD-3 reference code for Winograd F(6x6,3x3) with a batched GEMM, not as a runtime.

**Gotchas:**
- The README is stale: it documents Net(num_threads), InitFromPath(.feathermodel) and Forward(float*), while master's net.h has Net(), LoadParam/LoadWeights and ncnn::Mat inputs (the param parser comes from bundled ncnn code).
- The top-level CMakeLists adds -Ofast and -ffast-math globally, so results may differ slightly from strict IEEE fp32.
- ConvLayer::Forward on master calls printf("thread num =%d") on every convolution, which is debug output left in the hot path.
- build_scripts/build_android.sh passes -DCOMPILE_OPENCL=1, which adds src/booster/cl, but that directory is not in master (its CMakeLists.txt returns 404), so expect to edit the script before the Android build works.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-09-24, and the README does not match the rewritten master code. BSD-3-Clause source headers make the ARM kernels copyable, but treat it as reference code rather than a runtime to adopt.

[repo](https://github.com/Tencent/FeatherCNN) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Tencent/FeatherCNN/wikis/Benchmarks)

##### FFPA (ffpa-attn, Faster Flash Prefill Attention for large head dimension)  `CUDA/Python (CUDA, Triton and CuTe-DSL backends)`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Exact GPU attention kernels for head dims 320-1024 (beyond FlashAttention-2's 256); 1.5x-15x faster than PyTorch SDPA.

**Beats:** PyTorch SDPA (F.scaled_dot_product_attention); FlashAttention-2 supports head dim only up to 256, FP8/FP4 variants also compared with SageAttention 2/3 — bench/README.md (first-party; PyTorch 2.11, CUDA 13.0, D=512, B=1, fp16/bf16) reports latency against torch SDPA, which cannot use its flash backend at D=512. Results: B200 CuTe-DSL forward 6.45-8.41x and backward 8.21-14.69x (up to 1517/763 TFLOPS); H200 CuTe-DSL forward 1.81-3.46x and backward 4.09-6.00x; L20 Triton forward 1.03-1.67x and backward 1.63-2.21x. No host CPU, driver or build flags are given, and the README's H200 peak (535 TFLOPS) does not match bench/README (427 TFLOPS, table max 426).

**Known shortcoming:** For head_dim > 256 SDPA falls back to slower backends, so the baseline is weak there; FP8/FP4 measured against BF16.

**Known shortcoming:** is_causal is bottom-right aligned when Nq != Nkv while SDPA is top-left, so the monkey-patch silently changes cross-causal output; varlen backward hang on H100 D=512 (#298) closed not-planned; silent SDPA fallback when Nkv<512 or D<=256; README H200 peak 535T vs bench README 427T.

**How:** It keeps FlashAttention's online-softmax tiling and adds two changes that stop SRAM and register use growing with D. Split-D tiles the head dimension, so Q, K and V shared-memory tiles stay a fixed Br x 16 instead of O(D). A TiledMMA M4N2 warp layout for the PV GEMM halves the per-thread O accumulator to O(D/4) registers, which avoids the register spilling the FA-2-style M8N1 layout hits at D=512 and keeps D=1024 feasible (README: 1.55x over M8N1 at D=1024 on RTX 5090, 154 vs 100 TFLOPS). There are three implementations: Triton with persistent autotune configs, CuTe-DSL kernels using TMA/WGMMA on sm_90a and tcgen05 2-CTA on sm_100a, and a forward-only CUDA extension with FP8/FP4 quantized variants.

**Use it when:**
- Training or prefill with head dim 320-1024 in fp16/bf16 on NVIDIA sm_80 or newer, where SDPA falls back to its slower efficient/math backends: about 1.5-1.7x forward on L20 (Triton) and 2.6-3.5x forward / 4-6x backward on H200 (CuTe-DSL) at D=512.
- B200 (sm_100a) with D=512 exactly, where the CuTe-DSL tcgen05 path reports 6.5-8.4x forward and 8-15x backward over SDPA.
- Models that mix a few large-D full-attention layers with ordinary layers (the README cites a NeMo Automodel PR reporting 1.4-1.5x end-to-end Gemma4-31B training throughput on 8xH200 with FFPA on the 10 of 60 D=512 layers; PR not opened).
- Long sequences only: each of Nq and Nkv must be at least 512 (Nq below 8 is also accepted, for decode); anything else goes to SDPA anyway.
- Diffusion inference on RTX 50 / RTX PRO Blackwell (sm_120) if you can accept FP8/FP4 accuracy loss and test quality yourself; the end-to-end FLUX.1-dev gain is about 7% at 1024x1024 and 12-17% at 2048x2048.

**Skip it when:**
- Head dim 256 or less in bf16/fp16: those shapes fall straight through to SDPA, so FlashAttention-2/3 or cuDNN are what actually run.
- Short sequences: if Nkv < 512, or 8 <= Nq < 512, the call falls back to SDPA. FP8/FP4 are also documented as not suitable for small models or short sequences.
- Production stability: the code changes several times a day (dozens of commits in Sept 2026 alone), the CuTe-DSL backend is described as 'early stage', a varlen backward hang on H100 with D=512 (#298) was closed as not planned, and a cross-causal misalignment issue (#311) lists CUDA, Triton and CuTe-DSL but links only a Triton fix (PR #300).
- fp32 inputs, non-NVIDIA hardware other than AMD through the Triton backend, or code that needs attn_mask or dropout on the CuTe-DSL backend (rejected with NotImplementedError).
- Expecting the largest speedups to carry over: on B200 they are measured against SDPA's non-flash fallback at D=512, a weak baseline.

**Integration:** module · torch>=2.10, Triton (via PyTorch), nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.6.2, quack-kernels==0.6.4, apache-tvm-ffi (>=0.1.11,<0.2), ray, numpy, ninja, packaging; the optional CUDA extension (ffpa_attn._C) is built from source with build.sh plus git submodules · Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.10+ (pyproject); the README says the PyPI wheel needs CUDA 13.0+ and PyTorch 2.11+ · NVIDIA sm_80+ for Triton and CuTe-DSL (fastest on sm_90a for D 320-512 and sm_100a for D=512); CUDA forward backend sm_80+; FP8 on sm_89 and sm_120; FP4 on sm_120 only; Triton backend also runs on AMD ROCm/HIP (PR #268)

**Vs siblings:** Pick FFPA over FlashAttention-3 or ThunderKittens only when head dim is above 256, which they do not target. At D<=256, FFPA just calls SDPA (bf16) or competes with SageAttention on FP8/FP4, where SageAttention-2 is the more established choice at D=128 and FFPA's edge is head dims Sage does not cover (README: Sage-2/3 support D<=128).

**Gotchas:**
- Silent semantic change when monkey-patching: with is_causal=True and Nq != Nkv, FFPA aligns the mask to the KV tail (FlashAttention convention), while SDPA aligns it top-left, so cross-causal outputs differ from what SDPA would have returned.
- Hardware or head-dim mismatches fall back to SDPA with only a warning_once log line, so you can believe FFPA is running when it is not. Set FFPA_FORCE_NO_SDPA_FALLBACK=1 when testing.
- Dtype, dropout and mask constraints raise exceptions instead of falling back, so a monkey-patched model with fp32 attention at D>256 will throw.
- The FP8/FP4 kernels quantize Q, K and V internally from bf16 inputs. Their 3.8-4.9x 'speedup over SDPA' compares low precision with BF16 SDPA; against SageAttention-2 (also FP8) the README says only 'comparable or slightly better'.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-09-26, several commits a day) and Apache-2.0, so it is copyable, but APIs and kernels are moving fast and parts (CuTe-DSL, FP8/FP4) are labelled experimental or early stage.

[repo](https://github.com/xlite-dev/ffpa-attn) · [benchmark](https://github.com/xlite-dev/ffpa-attn/blob/HEAD/bench/README.md)

##### Flash Attention PTX/CUDA (hand-written PTX prefill attention for RTX 5080)  `C++ (CUDA/PTX)`  `MIT (stated only in the README's License section; no LICENSE file in the repository, raw LICENSE returns 404)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Hand-written PTX flash-attention prefill and paged decode library for RTX 5080 (sm_120); edges out vLLM's FlashAttention-2 at small batch.

**Beats:** FlashAttention-2 as bundled in vLLM 0.23.0 (vllm.vllm_flash_attn.flash_attn_varlen_func, FA2 path) — In a same-process harness on an RTX 5080 (shared torch.randn fp16 inputs, interleaved rounds, outputs cross-checked to ~2e-4 nrmse), causal prefill latency against vLLM 0.23.0's bundled FA2 (flash_attn_varlen_func, driver-JIT from sm_80 PTX) was strictly lower at 17 of 34 shapes; the '23 of 34' headline also counts 6 losses under 2%. Wins concentrate at B=1 and short context (up to +31.9% at B=1, S=1024, D=64); losses reach -4.8% at the largest batch x context shapes; peak is ~202 vs ~212 TFLOPS. The vLLM harness script (fa_sweep2.py) is not in the repo, and the end-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B decode wins (4.70 vs 5.12 ms/token at B=1, 5.28 vs 5.43 ms at B=8) compare this repo's best-of-3 runs on a Windows desktop GPU (5-15% run-to-run spread) with vLLM's 5-iteration average, including its scheduler and sampler.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Wins 23 of 34' is 17 strict wins plus 6 losses under 2%. The FA2 baseline is sm_80 PTX JIT-compiled on sm_120, a handicapped baseline. The vLLM harness is not in the repo. MIT stated only in the README (no LICENSE file).

**Known shortcoming:** End-to-end Qwen numbers compare the author's best-of-3 on a Windows desktop GPU (5-15% spread) against vLLM's 5-iteration average including the scheduler. No cuDNN comparison. Forward only; errors abort the process.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It uses PTX mma.sync.m16n8k16 with ldmatrix and cp.async, the tensor-core path consumer Blackwell has (no WGMMA or TMA), and keeps the whole online softmax in registers. The saturated-grid 'fat-warp' kernel gives each of 4 warps one 16-row Q tile, so softmax needs only intra-warp shuffles, and feeds P straight from the QK accumulator fragment into the PV MMA without touching shared memory; K and V loads are software-pipelined behind the matmuls. An exp2 fold (scale times log2 e folded into the score multiply) makes every exponential a raw EX2, and a runtime dispatcher sends under-saturated grids (B=1, short S) to a 32-row split-N tile that doubles the CTA count, with optional per-shape autotuning cached in a wisdom file.

**Use it when:**
- Causal fp16/bf16 prefill on an RTX 5080-class consumer Blackwell GPU at batch 1 with S up to 2048, where it measured 9-32% lower latency than vLLM 0.23's FA2 at D=64 and 4-17% at D=128 (gains shrink to 0-16% at B=4-8 with S<=1024)
- Building a small custom inference loop in C++ or PyTorch on a GeForce card that needs varlen prefill, a paged KV cache and CUDA-graph-captured decode without pulling in vLLM or FlashInfer
- Long-context decode where VRAM is tight, using the FP8 KV cache (documented ~1.8x faster decode at D=128 long context, ~0.035 worst-case nrmse)
- Studying how to reach ~85% of tensor-pipe peak with mma.sync on sm_120; the docs record each optimization step and the failed experiments

**Skip it when:**
- Large batch times long context (B>=4 with S>=4096, or Llama-class H=32 at B>=4): it loses to vLLM FA2 by 2-5%
- Training: only forward prefill and decode kernels are documented, no backward pass
- Hopper or datacenter Blackwell GPUs, where FlashAttention-3 or cuDNN with WGMMA/TMA apply; it builds for sm_80 and up but was tuned and measured only on one RTX 5080
- Head dims other than 64 or 128, or quantized prefill: FP8/INT4 caches are decode-only, and INT4 KV collapsed generation quality on Qwen2.5-1.5B (30/64 teacher-forced argmax agreement)
- You need a cuDNN comparison or a license file for compliance review: neither exists in the repo (MIT is stated only in the README)

**Integration:** static lib (CMake target flash_attention) plus an optional PyTorch CUDAExtension (fa_ptx, pip install -e python/) · CUDA runtime only for the C++ library; PyTorch with CUDA and nvcc for the Python bindings · CUDA Toolkit 12.0+ (tested with 13.1), CMake 3.20+, C++17; Python >= 3.9 for fa_ptx · NVIDIA compute capability 8.0+ (CMake builds sm_80/86/89/90/120), tuned only for sm_120 RTX 5080; developed on Windows (MSVC flags in setup.py and docs) and benchmarked against vLLM under WSL2

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over learn-cuda's SM120 attention or Mini-Attention when you need a usable library rather than a teaching kernel: varlen, GQA, paged and quantized KV decode, and torch.compile/CUDA-graph-ready bindings. Pick SageAttention instead if quantized QK is acceptable and you want larger consumer-GPU speedups; learn-cuda's RTX 5090 data puts PyTorch's cuDNN SDPA backend ahead of both its own kernel and the flash-attn FA2 package, and this repo never measured cuDNN.

**Gotchas:**
- Errors terminate the process: bad arguments abort with an 'fa_*:' message and the header's CUDA_CHECK calls exit(EXIT_FAILURE), so wrap it if your host process must survive misuse
- Index arrays (cu_seqlens, block_table, seq_lens, slot_mapping) must be device memory; host pointers give garbage output without an abort, per the troubleshooting table
- FP8 caches need k_scale/v_scale > 0 set by you (zero-init default aborts); decode needs a scratch buffer sized by fa_cache_attention_scratch_bytes
- The default branch is dev/FlashAtt with no tags or releases, the README clone URL is a placeholder (yourusername/flash-attention-cuda), and docs/cutlass-comparison.md still calls the prefill kernel MHA-only while how-to-use.md documents GQA

**Status:** Active single-author project (76 commits, last 2026-07-03, 12 stars) with seven correctness-gate executables; MIT per the README but no LICENSE file, so confirm the license with the author before vendoring.

[repo](https://github.com/Tugbars/Flash-Attention-PTX-CUDA) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Tugbars/Flash-Attention-PTX-CUDA/HEAD/docs/vllm-comparison.md)

##### flash-attention-minimal (forward-only FlashAttention in about 100 lines of CUDA)  `CUDA C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Educational 100-line FP32 CUDA FlashAttention forward kernel; its 13x win over eager PyTorch attention is a cold-start profiling artifact.

**Beats:** naive PyTorch attention (eager matmul + softmax + matmul) — The README's sample output on an AWS T4 is a single profiled forward call at batch 16, 12 heads, seq_len 64, head_dim 64, FP32: manual attention 52.545 ms vs minimal flash attention 3.908 ms Self CUDA time (about 13x, derived from page data), built with nvcc -O2, with CUDA and PyTorch versions not stated. The verifier judged this a cold-start artifact of timing an unwarmed baseline; warmed or CUDA-event-timed runs reported in issues #11 and #13 show eager PyTorch attention is faster.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not reproducible: bench.py times one cold call with no warm-up, so the 52.5 ms 'manual' PyTorch figure is mostly initialisation; issues #11 and #13 report naive PyTorch is faster once warmed or timed with CUDA events. Educational code (~100 lines, forward only, tiny sizes).

**Known shortcoming:** The reported speedup is a cold-start profiler artifact (issues #11, #13, #16). No bounds check when N is not a multiple of 32 (16 on the tensorcore branch); on main head_dim above about 117 exceeds 48 KB shared memory with no opt-in and an unchecked launch; the tensorcore branch leaks cudaMalloc'd l/m every call; Faial race-freedom conditions are in issue #1. The leloykun fork's 94x over FA2 on an RTX 3060 (4.048 vs 377.542 ms) is likely the same artifact.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It applies FlashAttention-1 tiling with online softmax: K/V tiles of 32 rows and a Q tile go into shared memory, a running row max m and row sum l are kept, and partial outputs are rescaled, so the N x N score matrix is never written to global memory. The outer loop runs over K/V tiles and the inner loop over Q tiles (the FA1 order), so O, l and m are re-read and re-written in global memory for every K/V tile. There is one thread block of 32 threads per (batch, head), and each thread computes a whole query row's dot products serially on FP32 CUDA cores. That keeps the matmuls slow and occupancy low, so in practice it shows the I/O-aware idea rather than delivering speed. The tensorcore branch uses one warp per block with 16x16x8 TF32 WMMA fragments for QK^T and PV.

**Use it when:**
- Learning how FlashAttention's tiling and online-softmax rescaling work, by reading about 100 lines of CUDA next to the paper's Algorithm 1.
- A minimal starting point for your own attention-kernel experiments (many forks and open PRs add a backward pass, FA2 loop order, GQA or causal masking).
- Classroom or interview exercises at small shapes (for example seq_len 64, head_dim 64, FP32) where correctness against a manual reference matters more than speed.
- Checking a tensor-core rewrite step by step: the tensorcore branch keeps the naive kernel and a WMMA TF32 kernel side by side.

**Skip it when:**
- Any case where speed matters: measured with warm-up or CUDA events, eager PyTorch attention is faster (issues #11 and #13), and the README concedes it gets slower than the manual implementation for longer sequences and larger block sizes.
- As a substitute for PyTorch SDPA, flash-attn or cuDNN attention: it was never benchmarked against them and runs FP32 one-thread-per-row matmuls without tensor cores (main branch).
- Training, causal or masked attention, or FP16/BF16 models: forward only, no mask, FP32 inputs only (a BF16 request, issue #7, is open).
- Sequence lengths that are not a multiple of the block size (32 on main, 16 in the tensorcore branch) or head dimensions above about 117 on main (see gotchas).
- Code that relies on CUDA streams or multiple GPUs: kernels launch on the default stream, and the main branch queries shared memory on device 0 only.

**Integration:** module (PyTorch C++/CUDA extension JIT-built from flash.cu and main.cpp by torch.utils.cpp_extension.load; the kernel can also be copied as a source-drop) · PyTorch with CUDA, Ninja, nvcc · not documented (bench.py builds with nvcc -O2; the tensorcore branch sets TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.0 and -O3 -use_fast_math, and TF32 WMMA needs sm_80 or newer) · NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA (README sample on a T4); the tensorcore branch targets Ampere (sm_80) or newer

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to read the algorithm in its smallest form. For a from-scratch learning path that ends at competitive speed, use the catalogued learn-cuda attention (gau-nernst, beats the flash-attn package on SM120) or Mini-Attention (beats cuDNN SDPA at short sequences). For real workloads, use FlashAttention-3/4 or cuDNN through PyTorch SDPA.

**Gotchas:**
- The README speedup is not a speedup: bench.py profiles one cold call of each implementation (manual attention first) under torch.autograd.profiler with no warm-up, so the 52.5 ms baseline is mostly first-call initialisation; issue #16 adds that the old autograd profiler does not capture the custom op properly.
- No bounds checks on N (derived from code): tiles are read and written in full for ceil(N/Bc) iterations, so a seq_len that is not a multiple of the block size reads past the head's slice and writes O out of range. A Faial data-race analysis (issue #1) found the main kernel race-free only when Bc == Br == blockDim.x, Tr <= blockDim.x and N >= blockDim.x^2.
- Shared memory (derived from code, not tested): the main branch requests 3*Bc*d*4 + Bc*Br*4 bytes per block (28 KB at head_dim 64, 52 KB at 128) without the cudaFuncSetAttribute opt-in above the 48 KB default, and the launch is not error-checked, so head_dim above about 117 can fail without an error at the call and return the zero-initialised O. It also printf's the shared-memory line on every call.
- The tensorcore branch cudaMallocs the l and m buffers on every call and never frees them (a leak of B*nh*N*8 bytes per call), and computes in TF32, which has less precision than the FP32 main kernel.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-12-30 (9 commits on main), and open PRs that add a backward pass, FA2 and GQA are unmerged; it is Apache-2.0 with 1.2k stars and is good teaching code, but not something to depend on for performance.

[repo](https://github.com/tspeterkim/flash-attention-minimal) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tspeterkim/flash-attention-minimal)

##### FlashKDA  `C++/CUDA (CUTLASS) with Python bindings`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

CUTLASS CUDA forward kernel for Kimi Delta Attention; 1.7-3.3x lower latency than flash-linear-attention's Triton chunk_kda on H20/GB200.

**Beats:** flash-linear-attention (fla) Triton chunk_kda kernel, and fla chunk_gated_delta_rule (GDN) as a second reference — BENCHMARK_H20.md and BENCHMARK_GB200.md (first-party, generated by benchmarks/generate_benchmark_md.py using CUDA-event timing, warmup 30, 200 iters x 5 repeats) report KDA forward latency at T=8192, D=128, H=96 and 64. With FlashKDA run in fp32-state mode against fla's Triton chunk_kda, the speedup is 1.85-2.31x on H20 and 1.70-3.27x on GB200, largest for varlen batches. No fla, PyTorch or CUDA versions, driver or host CPU are recorded, and the numbers predate later correctness fixes.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers predate the TMA proxy-fence race fix (#25) and the fp32 solver precision change; GB200 H=64 is 0.96x vs GDN (slower).

**Known shortcoming:** test_fwd exact-match fails on B200 with CUDA 13.0 (#12, open); TMA fence UB (#24: hangs, stale data, silent corruption) fixed after the bench tables; lower_bound not validated; forward and inference_mode only.

**How:** It uses chunk size 16 instead of FLA's 64. With the gate lower_bound at -5 this keeps exp(cumsum(g)) within bf16 range without intra-chunk rescaling, and the 16x16 inverse becomes cheap: fp32 forward substitution on two 8x8 diagonal blocks, merged with bf16 HMMA GEMMs. The work is split into a token-parallel kernel (gate activation, L2 norm, decay, L/Mqk build, inversion) and a head-parallel kernel (chunked delta-rule recurrence, output, state), which the authors say is at least 15% faster than one fused kernel.
