Other tricks: the on-chip state is held in bf16 but updated with fp32 FMAs; base-2 ex2.approx and tanh.approx-based sigmoid; __launch_bounds__(256,8) with shared-memory unions for occupancy; register-file transposes (MOVM) instead of shared-memory round trips; and TMA loads.

**Use it when:**
- Serving or prefill for KDA-based models (Kimi Linear style) on Hopper or Blackwell, where fla's chunk_kda is on the critical path: about 1.85-2.3x on H20 and 1.7-3.3x on GB200 at T=8192, H=64/96.
- Varlen batches of mixed sequence lengths, where the gain over the Triton kernel is largest (2.3x on H20 and 3.2-3.3x on GB200 for 8x1024 packed sequences).
- Stacks already built on flash-linear-attention: install FlashKDA and chunk_kda picks it up with no code changes, as long as the call runs under torch.inference_mode().
- Inference where a bf16 recurrent state is acceptable (it halves the state's memory); fp32 state in and out is also supported and is what the published tables measure.

**Skip it when:**
- Training: there is no backward pass, and FLA only dispatches to FlashKDA in inference mode.
- Head dims other than K=V=128 (enforced by TORCH_CHECK; issue #4 asks about other sizes), non-bf16 activations, or pre-Hopper GPUs (setup.py builds only sm_90a, 100a, 103a and 120a).
- Scalar-gate gated delta rule (GDN) models: that is a different algorithm, and against fla's GDN kernel FlashKDA is only 0.96x (slower, GB200 H=64 fixed) to 1.80x.
- Anywhere you need a stable, released dependency: version 0.0.1, 10 commits, no PyPI wheel documented, 14 of 16 issues open, and an exact-match correctness test failing on B200 with CUDA 13.0 (#12, open).

**Integration:** module · PyTorch 2.4+ (C++/CUDA extension built with torch.utils.cpp_extension), CUTLASS (git submodule); flash-linear-attention >= 0.5.0 for auto-dispatch and for the tests and benchmarks · CUDA 12.9+, PyTorch 2.4+, nvcc targeting sm_90a or newer · NVIDIA sm_90a (H100/H20/H200), sm_100a/sm_103a (B200/GB200/B300), sm_120a (RTX 50 / RTX PRO Blackwell); benchmarked only on H20 and GB200

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlashKDA when the model uses KDA's per-channel gate and you only need inference. FlashQLA targets the scalar-gate gated delta rule (Qwen-style GDN) and also covers backward, so it is the better fit for GDN models or training. FlashInfer's GDN prefill kernel is the option if you are already inside FlashInfer.

**Gotchas:**
- The published H20 (2026-04-22) and GB200 (2026-05-26) tables predate the fix for missing TMA proxy and mbarrier-init fences (#24/#25, 2026-07-29), which issue #24 says could cause hangs, stale data or silent corruption. They also predate the 2026-09-01 switch from an fp16 Neumann inverse to fp32 forward substitution. No re-run has been published, and issue #34 asking about the performance effect is unanswered.
- lower_bound is documented as -5 to 0, but csrc/flash_kda.cpp does not check it. The chunk-16 bf16-range argument in the design doc assumes -5, so do not pass values below that without testing accuracy yourself.
- In varlen mode B must be 1 and cu_seqlens int64; initial_state and final_state must share a dtype.
- The default build compiles only for the GPU visible at install time and fails if none is visible; set FLASH_KDA_CUDA_ARCHS=all (or e.g. 90a,100a) for wheel or CI builds.

**Status:** Active but early (v0.0.1, last commit 2026-09-01, 10 commits). MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, though it builds against a CUTLASS submodule and needs CUDA 12.9+ on Hopper or Blackwell.

[repo](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/FlashKDA) · [benchmark](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/FlashKDA/blob/HEAD/BENCHMARK_H20.md)

##### FlashQLA  `Python (TileLang-generated CUDA kernels)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

TileLang-built fused CUDA kernels for Gated DeltaNet chunked prefill; about 2x faster forward and 2.5-3x faster backward than FLA Triton.

**Beats:** FLA Triton kernels (flash-linear-attention chunk_gated_delta_rule) and FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel — First-party per-shape CUDA-graph timings (10 warmup, 100 repeats, bf16, d=128) from the public benchmark/bench_gated_delta_rule.py on H200 (torch 2.8.0+cu128, FLA 0.5.1, FlashInfer 0.6.13, TileLang 0.1.12) and GB200: forward 1.18-3.32x vs FLA Triton on H200 (geometric mean about 2.1x) and 1.07-3.58x on GB200, but only roughly at parity with FlashInfer's GDN prefill (as low as 0.48x on GB200 small-batch varlen); backward 1.38-5.47x (H200) and 1.94-6.44x (GB200) vs FLA. Host CPU and compiler flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** On GB200 FlashInfer is faster in 85 of 171 forward rows; H200 stats check out.

**Known shortcoming:** Open #35: sm120 varlen forward tests fail with relative error 1e16-1e25 (RTX 5090); #15 (closed, no fix shown): max diff 0.047 vs FLA flipped greedy tokens on 2 of 3 prompts; #43: B200 packed varlen L<64 4.4-7.7x slower; import fails on GPUs other than sm90/100/103/120/121.

**How:** Instead of FLA's chain of separate Triton kernels, it fuses gate, decay and matmul stages into a few warp-specialized TileLang kernels that overlap TMA data movement, Tensor Core and CUDA Core work, with separate Hopper (sm90), Blackwell (sm100/103) and sm120 code paths. An algebraic reformulation of the GDN chunked forward/backward cuts Tensor Core, CUDA Core and SFU (exp) work. When heads per GPU are few (high TP) or sequences are long, it uses the exponential decay of the gate to split one sequence across SMs (gate-driven intra-card context parallelism), which is why the biggest gains are at TP8 with long single sequences.

**Use it when:**
- Training or prefill of GDN-based models (Qwen3.5/3.6, Qwen3-Next style linear-attention layers) at head dim 128 in bf16 on H100/H200, B200/GB200 or RTX 50-series
- Long single sequences with few heads per GPU (tensor parallel TP4-TP8): H200 1x32768 at TP8 forward 0.348 ms vs FLA 1.019 ms and FlashInfer 1.645 ms
- Backward pass / pretraining: 32 backward shapes on H200 run 1.38x to 5.47x faster than FLA (geometric mean about 2.6x); FlashInfer has no GDN backward to compare
- Already on FLA: switch via FLA's FlashQLA backend or the same-signature chunk_gated_delta_rule without changing model code

**Skip it when:**
- Inference serving with many short varlen sequences and FlashInfer available: FlashInfer's GDN prefill beats FlashQLA in 56 of 171 H200 forward rows and 85 of 171 GB200 rows (down to 0.48x), so FlashQLA is roughly at parity there
- Decode / token-by-token generation or MTP: only chunked prefill is implemented (decode and MTP kernels are an open feature request, issue #11)
- Ampere, Ada, AMD or Ascend hardware: import raises ValueError on anything other than sm90, sm100, sm103, sm120 or sm121
- Packed varlen batches whose segments are shorter than one 64-token chunk on B200: issue #43 measured L32 at 4.4x and L63 at 7.7x slower than padding to L64 (incomplete chunks fall back from TMA to guarded elementwise loads)
- RTX 5090 / sm120 varlen workloads in production: issue #35 (open) reports four forward tests on varlen/padding configs with relative errors of 1e16-1e25

**Integration:** module · PyTorch >= 2.8, TileLang >= 0.1.12 (kernels compiled through TileLang), CUDA 12.8+; FLA and FlashInfer only for benchmarks and tests · Python 3.10, CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.8 · NVIDIA sm90 (Hopper), sm100/sm103 (B200, GB200, B300), sm120/sm121 (RTX 50-series, DGX Spark GB10); Linux; no CPU or AMD path

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlashQLA for GDN (gated delta rule) layers, training or long-context prefill; pick FlashKDA for Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers, and FlashInfer's GDN prefill for batched short-sequence serving where it is as fast or faster. FlashAttention-3 and SageAttention cover softmax attention, not linear attention.

**Gotchas:**
- The kernel set is chosen at import time from tilelang's detected compute capability, so a process with mixed GPU generations or no supported GPU fails on import
- Numerics differ from FLA: tests check a 2% relative error against an fp64 reference; issue #15 (closed, no explanation shown) reported max abs diff 0.047 vs FLA Triton that flipped greedy tokens on 2 of 3 prompts. Validate end-to-end outputs before switching inference
- Issue #23 (B200 integrator) found heap-corruption risks from an id()-keyed tensor cache and from zero-length cu_seqlens segments; the current utils/index.py keys on object identity instead, but check zero-length segments on your version
- Benchmarks and tests use bf16 inputs; open issue #38 reports NaNs in fp16 forward beyond 32k tokens (reporter's H100/CUDA 12.4/PyTorch 2.4 setup is below the stated requirements, so unconfirmed). Prefer bf16

**Status:** Very active Qwen/Alibaba project (v0.1.3, last commit 2026-09-30, 716 stars), MIT-licensed and pip-installable as flash-qla; young (first release April 2026) with open correctness issues on sm120 varlen.

[repo](https://github.com/QwenLM/FlashQLA) · [benchmark](https://github.com/QwenLM/FlashQLA/blob/HEAD/benchmark/benchmark_results_H200.txt)

##### FlashRT  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Hand-built CUDA-graph inference pipelines for robot VLA models (Pi0/Pi0.5, GR00T) on Jetson Thor and RTX GPUs; beats TensorRT latency.

**Beats:** NVIDIA TensorRT, torch.compile, PyTorch eager, OpenPI reference implementation (numbers copied from NVIDIA Isaac GR00T and Jetson AI Lab pages, not re-measured in one harness) — FlashRT's own FP8 latencies for GR00T-N1.6-3B (Thor 45 ms end to end; RTX 5090 13.08 ms graph replay) are set against NVIDIA's published GR00T-N1.6 TensorRT, torch.compile and eager numbers (92/105/117 ms Thor, 31/37/58 ms RTX 5090), not re-measured in one harness; the only matched-harness rows (GR00T N1.7 LIBERO on Thor, JetPack 7.2 MAXN, 4 denoising steps, batch 1, medians of 20 runs) show 36.8 ms FP8 vs TensorRT FP8 ~44 ms and 23.7 ms NVFP4 vs TensorRT mixed NVFP4 ~40 ms (about 1.2x and 1.7x). Kernels are built with -O3 --use_fast_math; the CUDA toolkit used per row is not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** N1.6 baselines are copied NVIDIA numbers (4 denoising steps; FlashRT rows say T=50, precision unstated); matched-precision N1.7 Thor rows give only about 1.2x (FP8) and 1.7x (NVFP4) over TensorRT.

**Known shortcoming:** RTX 5090 rows (13.08 ms GR00T, 17.58 ms Pi0.5) are CUDA-graph replay only, excluding preprocessing, H2D/D2H and postprocess, yet are set against NVIDIA's end-to-end numbers; open reproduction disputes without maintainer reply (#188: 21.24 vs documented 16.61 ms; #153: 25.76 vs 42.8 tok/s); built with -O3 --use_fast_math; Qwen3-8B baseline is HF eager at 3.6 tok/s (weak). Correction: 'T=50' is the action horizon and FlashRT's DiT also runs 4 denoising steps, so the earlier step-count caveat was wrong.

**How:** Each model's whole forward pass (vision encoder, LLM backbone and the 4-step diffusion action head) is written out by hand and captured once as a static CUDA Graph over fixed buffers, so steady-state calls are a graph replay with no Python dispatch. Activations and weights run in static per-tensor FP8 (E4M3), or NVFP4 with AWQ pre-scaling on Blackwell, calibrated on the first call and cached as JSON. Hand-written CUDA kernels fuse the memory-bound steps (residual + RMSNorm + quantize, bias + GELU + quantize, RoPE/QKV split), while GEMMs and attention go to cuBLASLt FP8 with epilogue fusion, CUTLASS and a vendored FlashAttention-2 (FA4 or CUTLASS FMHA on Thor).

**Use it when:**
- Closed-loop robot control with Pi0/Pi0.5/GR00T on Jetson AGX Thor: Pi0.5 2-view 44 ms FP8 (27 ms NVFP4) vs 91-95 ms for NVIDIA's TensorRT baseline
- Batch-1 VLA inference on RTX 5090/4090 where per-decision latency matters more than throughput (GR00T N1.6 2-view about 13 ms graph replay)
- You want to skip TensorRT engine builds, per-driver/per-GPU rebuilds and ONNX export; a model change only needs a process restart
- Fixed-architecture realtime workloads it already supports (Qwen3.6-27B NVFP4 single-stream decode, Higgs Audio TTS, Wan2.2/Cosmos video) on Blackwell

**Skip it when:**
- Multi-user or high-batch serving: one process serves one captured graph, with no continuous batching (the docs point to vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM)
- Models it does not ship: each new architecture needs an 800-1500 line hand-written frontend and weight spec, not an automatic import
- When you need FP32/BF16-exact outputs: the fast tiers are FP8/NVFP4 with about 0.998-0.999 action cosine to the reference, and 1-view NVFP4 Pi0.5 misses the project's own 0.995 gate (worst sample 0.971)
- When you need a published number reproduced exactly: open issues report 21.24 ms vs a documented 16.61 ms (GR00T N1.7, RTX 5090, #188) and 25.76 vs 42.8 tok/s (Qwen3.6 on Thor, #153)
- GPUs older than SM80, or Hopper if you need FlashAttention (FA2 is not built for sm90, which falls back to cuBLAS-decomposed attention)

**Integration:** shared lib · CUDA 12.4+ (12.8+ for Blackwell), PyTorch or pinned JAX 0.5.3, pybind11, CUTLASS v4.4.2 (cloned into third_party), transformers<4.56, safetensors, numpy; vendored FlashAttention-2 v2.7.4.post1 built in; ROCm/hipBLASLt for the separate MI350X backend · C++17/CUDA C++17, GCC 11+, CMake 3.24+, Python 3.10-3.12; built with -O3 --use_fast_math · NVIDIA SM80+ Linux: Jetson AGX Thor (SM110), RTX 5090 (SM120), DGX Spark (SM121), RTX 4090 (SM89), A100/RTX 3090, Jetson Orin (community port); AMD MI350X (gfx950) via a separate HIP backend

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlashRT for batch-1 robot policy (VLA) inference on Jetson Thor or RTX Blackwell; for LLM serving pick FlashInfer- or ZhiLight-style engines (or vLLM/SGLang), and for general transformer encoders and translation pick FasterTransformer or CTranslate2, which cover many architectures without a hand-written pipeline per model.

**Gotchas:**
- The RTX 5090 figures (GR00T N1.6 13.08 ms, Pi0.5 17.58 ms) are CUDA-graph replay p50 that exclude image normalization, host-device copies and post-processing; Pi0.5 wall-clock p50 is 19.58 ms at 2 views
- GR00T 'T=50' is the action horizon, not the denoising step count; FlashRT's GR00T DiT also runs 4 steps, the same count as NVIDIA's table
- CUDA Graph instantiation on Thor varies by about 2 ms run to run; autotune=3 (default) recaptures, and Pi0.5 NVFP4 needs about 300 warmup calls to settle
- pip install flash-rt ships no compiled kernels; load_model needs an editable install plus a 6-25 minute CMake build with the same Python interpreter; the GR00T base checkpoint emits noise for untrained embodiment slots (use gr1 etc.)

**Status:** Very active, young (2026) Apache-2.0 project with frequent releases and community ports (Orin, L40, MI350X), but open, unanswered reproduction disputes (#188, #153) mean you should benchmark it yourself before relying on the headline numbers.

[repo](https://github.com/flashrt-project/FlashRT) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flashrt-project/FlashRT/HEAD/docs/benchmark_comparison.md)

##### ik_llama.cpp  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

llama.cpp fork with rewritten CPU quantized-matmul kernels; 1.1-7x faster CPU prompt processing than mainline on the same GGUF.

**Beats:** llama.cpp (mainline ggml CPU kernels) — The author's January 2025 llama-bench run (ik_llama.cpp 3c5f8722 vs llama.cpp 9f7add1c, same llama.cpp-quantized LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct GGUF, CPU only, no BLAS, no flash attention, -rtr on the fork) measured pp512 speedups of 1.78-5.18x on a Ryzen 7950X (Zen4/AVX-512), 1.52-5.13x on a Ryzen 5975WX (AVX2) and 1.09-7.03x on an M2-Max (NEON) across 15-17 quant types; it is first-party, compilers and flags are not stated, and only prompt processing was tabulated.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim overstated: Discussion 8's 'iqk' column compares new IQ2_K/IQ3_K quant types against llama.cpp IQ2_XS/IQ3_S, not same-quant kernels; same-quant gain is 3.43x pp and 1.12x tg; benchmark_url switched to the Jan 2025 wiki page (same GGUF in both: pp512 1.08-7.03x, geomeans 2.88x Zen4 and 3.35x NEON); fork of llama.cpp.

**Known shortcoming:** No SECURITY.md or advisories; RPC deserialize_tensor bounds crash open (#2164); last upstream sync Aug 2024; a Zen4 build without GGML_NATIVE/AVX512 flags silently uses AVX2; CMakeLists sets C++20 but docs say C++17; hardware: 7950X is the Zen4/AVX-512 path and the AVX2 box is a Ryzen 5975WX.

**How:** The CPU hot path is the iqk GEMM code (ggml/src/iqk/iqk_gemm_*.cpp), which multiplies several weight rows against several activation columns per kernel call, with activations quantized to 8-bit and integer dot products (AVX512-VNNI/AVX-VNNI vpdpbusd, NEON dot). Weights can be repacked at load time (-rtr) into row-interleaved layouts (4 or 8 rows), and quants that are slow to unpack (i-quants, k-quants) are expanded a few rows at a time to Q8_0_R8 and fed to one tuned Q8_0_R8 x Q8_2_X4 GEMM (PR 515: IQ2_XXS from about 107 to 288 t/s on a Ryzen 7950X). Its IQ*_K types use small non-linear lookup tables (4-32 int8 values) held in SIMD registers via pshufb/vqtbl1q, so dequantization costs about the same as a linear format.

**Use it when:**
- CPU-only or CPU-heavy LLM inference where prompt processing (prefill) dominates: same-GGUF pp512 on LLaMA-3.1-8B was 1.8-5.2x mainline on Zen4 (geometric mean 2.88x) and 1.1-7.0x on M2-Max NEON (3.35x)
- i-quant and k-quant models (IQ2_XXS-IQ4_XS, Q3_K-Q6_K), where the gap was largest (IQ3_S 5.2x Zen4, 7.0x NEON)
- AVX-512 CPUs (Zen4, Sapphire Rapids+), whose VNNI/VBMI paths mainline used little at the time of the comparison
- Large MoE models such as DeepSeek, GLM or Kimi with experts left in system RAM and attention on a CUDA GPU, using tensor overrides, FlashMLA and fused MoE ops
- You want lower-bpw-at-equal-quality IQ*_K / IQ*_KT quantizations that mainline does not have

**Skip it when:**
- Token generation bound by memory bandwidth: same-format TG gains in Discussion 8 were only about 1.08-1.12x
- GPU backends other than CUDA Turing+: the README says ROCm, Vulkan, Metal, older NVIDIA GPUs and AVX-only CPUs are not supported and related issues will not be fixed
- You need upstream llama.cpp's newest features, models or APIs exactly: the fork diverged in August 2024 and ports models itself
- Interoperability: GGUFs made with ik-only quant types do not load in mainline, and Unsloth _XL models containing f16 tensors are likely not to work
- Exposed or untrusted network deployments, especially the RPC backend: there is no SECURITY.md and no published advisories, and an RPC deserialize_tensor bounds-check crash (#2164) is open

**Integration:** shared lib · none for the CPU build (cmake + compiler; libcurl optional); CUDA toolkit for GPU; vendored cpp-httplib, nlohmann/json, stb-image, miniaudio for the server and multimodal tools · CMake 3.14; the top-level CMakeLists sets C++20 (docs/build.md says a C++17 compiler); GCC, Clang, or MSVC/clang-cl on Windows · x86-64 with AVX2 or better (AVX-512 path needs VNNI/VL/BW/DQ), aarch64 NEON (Linux, macOS, Android/termux), NVIDIA CUDA Turing or newer; Windows and Linux

**Vs siblings:** Pick ik_llama.cpp over llamafile's tinyBLAS when you run i-quants or k-quants (tinyBLAS mainly speeds up F16/Q8_0 prefill), and over T-MAC or BitNet unless the model is 1-2 bit or ternary, where their lookup-table kernels are built for it; PowerInfer targets sparse-activation GPU-CPU offload of specific models, while ik_llama.cpp is a general GGUF engine.

**Gotchas:**
- On Zen4 / Sapphire Rapids, a plain Release build without -DGGML_NATIVE=ON or the GGML_AVX512_* options silently falls back to the AVX2 kernels; HAVE_FANCY_SIMD needs AVX512F, VNNI, VL, BW and DQ all defined at compile time
- -rtr (run-time repacking) is needed for the published speedups, but with hybrid CPU/GPU MoE it forces matmuls on repacked RAM tensors onto the CPU (k-quants have no CUDA row-interleaved kernels), which lowers prompt speed
- Split mode 'graph' with partial GPU offload can produce gibberish; the README workaround is -cuda graphs=0
- The Jan 2025 comparison used mainline build 4517 and states mainline's ARM Q4_0/IQ4_NL repacking had already closed most of the gap for those types (1.09x and 1.24x); re-measure against current mainline before switching for those formats

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-01, 3.3k stars), MIT-licensed, single-maintainer-led fork with a large contributor community; it diverges further from mainline over time, so treat it as a separate engine rather than a patch set.

[repo](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp/wiki/Jan-2025:-prompt-processing-performance-comparison)

##### Intel Neural Speed / LLM Runtime  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Archived Intel llama.cpp-style CPU LLM runtime with low-bit weight-only GEMM kernels; ~1.2-1.4x faster INT4 next-token latency than ggml on Xeon.

**Beats:** ggml-based (llama.cpp) INT4 — The Intel NeurIPS 2023 workshop paper (arXiv 2311.00502) reports next-token latency for INT4 models on an unspecified 4th Gen Xeon Scalable cloud instance (input/output 32 tokens). At equal group size 32 it beats a ggml-based baseline: GPT-J-6B 22.99 vs 31.62 ms, Llama-2-7B 23.4 vs 27.71 ms, GPT-NeoX-20B 80.16 vs 92.36 ms. Group size 128 brings GPT-J to 19.98 ms. No compiler flags, core count or llama.cpp version are given.

**Known shortcoming:** 1.6x headline compares group size 128 against ggml group size 32; at equal group size ~1.2-1.4x; archived 2024-08-30; vendor numbers with no compiler flags.

**Known shortcoming:** README's 'up to 40x vs llama.cpp' links to an Oct 2023 Medium post that states only 'up to 7.27x' (Core i9-12900); AVX512, VNNI and AMX off by default in CMake options.

**How:** BesTLA is a CUTLASS-style template library (Launcher / Parallel / GemmCore / Prologue / Epilogue) whose micro-kernels are generated at runtime with Xbyak for AVX2, AVX_VNNI, AVX512F/BW/VNNI, AVX512_FP16, AMX_BF16 and AMX_INT8. Weights are group-wise quantized (int1-int8, fp4, nf4, fp8) and activations are dynamically quantized per batch/per K-group to int8 so the dot products run on VNNI/AMX integer units, with fused epilogues (GELU, SWISH etc.) and an L2-cache-blocked parallel split. At graph level it fuses QKV, FFN and multi-head attention and pre-allocates the KV cache instead of reallocating it per token.

**Use it when:**
- Single-stream INT4 LLM decoding on Intel Xeon (Sapphire/Emerald Rapids with AMX_INT8, or Ice Lake/Cascade Lake with AVX512_VNNI) where you control the build and pin threads with numactl.
- Reading or borrowing BesTLA's JIT weight-only-quantized GEMM kernels for your own x86 inference engine (Apache-2.0, header-only plus Xbyak).
- Experimenting with group size 128 or per-channel int4/int3 instead of llama.cpp Q4_0-style group 32, which the project recommends for speed with similar accuracy (validated on Llama-2-7B per its docs).
- Hybrid client CPUs (12th Gen and later) where its own thread pool is claimed to beat OpenMP.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything needing maintenance or security fixes: Intel archived the repo on 2024-08-30 and accepts no patches; it points users to Intel Extension for PyTorch.
- Non-Intel or non-x86 CPUs: kernels are x86-only (BesTLA is described as an x64 library); AMD support is not documented and ARM is not supported.
- Models or GGUF quant types released after mid-2024: model support is frozen at v1.0 (March 2024).
- Accuracy-sensitive int1-int3 RTN quantization: docs warn of accuracy loss; int7-asym and int8 can overflow on AVX2-without-VNNI or AVX512BW compute paths.
- If you need an independently reproduced speedup: all numbers are Intel's own, with no published compiler flags or exact CPU SKU in the paper.

**Integration:** shared lib (Python package neural-speed); BesTLA alone is header-only · Xbyak (fetched by CMake), OpenMP (default thread pool), Python toolchain for conversion/quantization scripts; optional Intel Extension for Transformers for HF-style API · GCC 10+ for Neural Speed (README); BesTLA: GCC 9+ / MSVC 1900+ / oneAPI 2024.0+, GCC 11+ recommended; CMake 3.12+ · x86-64 Intel CPUs (AVX2 minimum; AVX512/VNNI/AMX paths), Linux and Windows

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over llamafile's tinyBLAS when you're on AMX/VNNI Xeons and want integer-unit int4 kernels instead of F16/Q8_0 prompt-eval speedups. Choose it over T-MAC/BitNet when you run ordinary int4 group-quantized models rather than 1-2 bit lookup-table or ternary models. Because it is archived, BesTLA is mainly worth mining for kernel ideas; for a maintained runtime, prefer the siblings.

**Gotchas:**
- The paper's 1.6x headline compares Neural Speed at group size 128 with ggml at group size 32; like-for-like group 32 is 22.99 vs 31.62 ms on GPT-J (~1.38x) and 23.4 vs 27.71 ms on Llama-2-7B (~1.18x) (derived from page data).
- The README's 'up to 40x vs llama.cpp' links to an Oct 2023 Medium post whose text states only 'up to 7.27x' on a Core i9-12900 (input 1024, output 32); the 40x figure is not stated in that text.
- AVX512, VNNI and AMX are OFF by default in the CMake options (NS_AVX512, NS_AVX512_VNNI, NS_AMX); build flags determine which kernels you get.
- AMX_INT8 wants group sizes aligned to 128 for best efficiency.

**Status:** Abandoned: archived by Intel 2024-08-30 (last release v1.0, March 2024); Apache-2.0, so BesTLA can still be vendored, but nobody upstream will fix bugs or add models.

[repo](https://github.com/intel/neural-speed) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00502)

##### Kaoken (baked-weight C code generation for CPU transformer inference)  `C (generated by a Python tool)`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Python generator that emits GPT-2 layers as straight-line C with baked weights; first-party per-layer timings beat PyTorch CPU.

**Beats:** PyTorch CPU layers (transformers GPT-2 building blocks) — The README table times single PyTorch layer calls (time.time(), no warm-up) against single generated-C calls (clock()), averaged over five runs, on an unstated ARM64 machine (MacBook Air implied) with torch 2.0.1 pinned: LayerNorm [1,768] 0.052 vs 0.0052 ms, GELU 0.174 vs 0.084 ms, Linear [768,50257] 22.4 vs 2.378 ms, Attention 14.484 vs 9.386 ms, all with synthetic patterned weights rather than GPT-2's. The margin likely comes mostly from PyTorch cold-call overhead and constant folding over repeated weights.

**Known shortcoming:** PyTorch is timed as one cold first call with no warm-up (validation/*.py) while the C side uses clock(); weights are synthetic patterned values, not GPT-2. Ratios are likely overstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not reproducible: committed generated/*.c are toy shapes (10x10 Linear, 4-element LayerNorm), not the benchmarked [768,50257] code, which is not in the repo. Validation Linear weights repeat the same row for every output, so after unrolling clang -O3 can fold every output into one dot product; the 9.4x Linear ratio likely does not reflect real work. ARM64 only; nothing works end to end.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Ahead-of-time specialization: shapes and weights are known at generation time, so the generator (utils.unroll_loops plus MAT_MULTIPLY / MAT_MULTIPLY_TRANSPOSE macros) explodes every matrix multiply into one multiply-add expression per output element with constant weights, removing loops, framework dispatch and tensor allocation. LayerNorm uses hand-written ARM NEON intrinsics (vld1q_f32, vaddvq_f32, vdivq_f32). The measured gap also includes PyTorch's per-call Python and dispatch overhead, which dominates at batch 1 and [1,768].

**Use it when:**
- Studying how far constant-folding and full unrolling of a tiny, fixed-shape layer can go on an ARM64 (Apple Silicon) CPU with clang -O3.
- Prototyping a code-generation backend for a very small model whose weights fit comfortably in generated source.
- As a teaching example of turning a PyTorch module into specialized C, with the PyTorch validation scripts as reference outputs.

**Skip it when:**
- Real GPT-2 or any real model inference: the README says baked attention with actual GPT-2 weights (16k lines of C) could not be compiled on a MacBook Air, and no end-to-end model.generate() benchmark exists.
- x86-64 or any non-ARM target: the templates include arm_neon.h and the Makefile hard-codes clang -arch arm64.
- Large layers such as the lm_head Linear [768 x 50257]: fully unrolled, that is about 38.6 million literal multiply-adds in one function, so compile time, memory and code size are prohibitive.
- Models whose weights change or need quantization; every weight change means regenerating and recompiling the C.
- Anything that needs a maintained project: 17 commits over about one month in late 2024, no releases, no tests beyond the validation scripts.

**Integration:** source-drop (generated .c files) · Generation: Python with torch 2.0.1, transformers 4.34.1, numpy 1.26.1 (requirements.txt) and a local GPT-2 checkout; generated code: libc and libm only · clang with ARM NEON support (Makefile: clang -arch arm64 -O3); C standard not documented · aarch64 only (arm_neon.h, -arch arm64); Apple Silicon implied by the Makefile and the README's MacBook Air mention

**Vs siblings:** Pick Kaoken only to study baked-weight code generation on ARM; CodeJeNN is the closer working 'emit C++ from a trained model' tool, llm.c's train_gpt2.c is a readable, working plain-C GPT-2, and CTranslate2 or OpenVINO are what to deploy for real CPU transformer inference.

**Gotchas:**
- The committed generated/*.c files are toy shapes (10x10 Linear, 4-element LayerNorm, embedding size 8 attention), not the [1,768] and [768,50257] shapes in the benchmark table; the code that produced the table is not in the repo.
- The validation Linear weights repeat the same row for every output feature (every row is 0.1*(i+1)), and the committed 10x10 test bakes 0.1 everywhere, so after unrolling every output is the same expression and clang -O3 can fold them into a single dot product; the 22.4 ms vs 2.378 ms Linear ratio may not reflect real lm_head work.
- Weights are baked as double literals (e.g. input[0][1] * 0.1) and GELU calls pow/tanh/sqrt in double with pi approximated as 3.14159, so results drift slightly from PyTorch's float32 math.pi version.
- Generated code mallocs its buffers and never frees them, and attention needs gpt2_attention_0_initialize_heap_memory() called first.

**Status:** Stale prototype (last commit 2024-11-16, 17 commits, 4 stars), MIT-licensed so code is copyable, but nothing works end to end and it needs regeneration per model.

[repo](https://github.com/sushrut141/kaoken) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sushrut141/kaoken/HEAD/README.md)

##### KleidiAI (via the llama.cpp KleidiAI backend PR)  `C`  `Apache-2.0 (the LICENSES directory also carries BSD-3-Clause.txt for some files)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Arm's C micro-kernels for quantized/float matmul on NEON, SVE, SME; independent llama.cpp runs show wins only at 1-2 SME threads.

**Beats:** llama.cpp ggml CPU backend's own Arm Q4_0 kernels (master at the time: AArch64 i8mm/dotprod repacked kernels); not XNNPACK, oneDNN or Eigen — In llama.cpp PR #11390 (Arm-authored, merged 2025-02-20), reviewers outside Arm benchmarked llama 1B/7B Q4_0 with KleidiAI against llama.cpp's own AArch64 i8mm/dotprod repacked kernels, built with Apple Clang or LLVM Clang 19.1.7 and GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON. On an Apple M4 Pro, SME was about 1.3x faster at 1 thread but 2.7x slower at 10 threads, I8MM tied or trailed, and slaren's 12-thread M3 Max run was slower (pp128 192.93 vs 229.89 t/s); only Arm's Pixel 8 run showed 1.03-1.19x at 1-4 threads, and Arm's later SME2 F32 claim (PR #24414) has not been reproduced.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: the independent measurements in llama.cpp PR #11390 (M3 Max, M4 Pro, Galaxy S25, Galaxy A34) show KleidiAI mostly equal to or slower than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels; the only independent win is the SME path at 1-2 threads on M4 Pro (about 1.28-1.30x). The numbers showing a general win are Arm's own (Pixel 8 1.03-1.19x; PR #24414 SME2 F32 without test name or flags).

**Known shortcoming:** llama.cpp issue #26630 (gcc 13.3 on Cortex-X925): GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON built zero kai_run_matmul kernels while the banner said KLEIDIAI = 1, closed as not planned. Arm's PR #24414 SME2 table stops scaling past 2 threads (892 t/s at 2, 452-609 at 4-8; the M4 Pro has 2 SME units). The llama.cpp backend handles only Q4_0, Q8_0 and F32 and no MUL_MAT_ID; the API can change without notice. gitlab.arm.com (the official issue tracker) was blocked.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Hand-written kernels per Arm ISA feature: NEON SDOT (FEAT_DotProd), SMMLA (FEAT_I8MM), SVE/SVE2, and SME/SME2 outer-product (MOPA) accumulation into the ZA tile array. Operands are first packed into register-blocked panels (mr x kr for the LHS, nr x kr for the RHS, with scales and bias interleaved) so the inner loop streams contiguous memory. For the int4 paths, f32 activations are quantized to int8 per row or per 32-element block at run time (qai8dxp, qsi8d32p) and multiplied against int4 weights packed offline (qsi4cxp, qsi4c32p), with the output clamp fused. Separate GEMV (1xN) and GEMM (MxN) variants and several tile sizes let the framework pick per shape.

**Use it when:**
- You maintain an inference runtime for AArch64 (Android, Linux on Arm, Apple Silicon) that already has its own thread pool and allocator, and need int4/int8 x f32, bf16, fp16 or f32 matmul kernels you can vendor as plain .c/.h files with no dependencies and no dynamic allocation.
- Single-thread or 2-thread LLM decode/prefill on SME-capable CPUs: in PR #11390 an independent run on an Apple M4 Pro measured the SME kernels 1.28x (pp128) and 1.30x (tg64) faster than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels at 1 thread.
- F32 models in llama.cpp on SME2 hardware: Arm's own PR #24414 table shows 4.3x-23.6x over ggml's native F32 path on an M4 Pro (1B model, 1-8 threads), unreproduced but large enough to be worth a local test.
- Building llama.cpp for a phone-class Arm SoC with few big cores and Q4_0/Q8_0 models: try GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON and compare with llama-bench on your own device.

**Skip it when:**
- Any non-Arm target: the README FAQ says it does not compile for x86, including the packing and quantization kernels.
- Multi-threaded Q4_0 inference on many-core Arm chips: in PR #11390, M3 Max at 12 threads ran pp128 192.93 vs 229.89 t/s for llama.cpp master, and M4 Pro SME at 10 threads ran pp128 435 vs 1174 t/s; the I8MM kernels tied or trailed master on M4 Pro and Galaxy S25.
- You want complete operators with threading, memory management and fusion: Arm's own FAQ points those frameworks to the Compute Library (ACL) instead.
- llama.cpp with K-quant or IQ GGUF files, or MoE models: the backend only takes Q4_0, Q8_0 and F32 weights for MUL_MAT/GET_ROWS and has no MUL_MAT_ID path, so those ops fall back to ggml's kernels.
- You need a stable API: the README warns that API changes, including function renames, may occur without notice, with two releases a month.

**Integration:** source-drop (per-kernel .c/.h pairs plus kai_common.h) or static lib via the provided CMake build · none for the kernels; CMake for the build system (CMakeLists requires 3.16, README says 3.18); GoogleTest and Google Benchmark only for tests and benchmarks · C99 kernels (C++17 for tests and examples); GCC 11+ or Clang 11+ (CMake warns below that); SME/SME2 kernels need SME-ABI compiler support or KLEIDIAI_INTERNAL_EXTRA_ARCH=+sme; MSVC builds a subset of NEON dotprod/i8mm kernels since v1.29.0 · AArch64 only (Linux, Android, macOS; Windows on Arm via MSVC for some kernels); each variant needs the feature in its name (dotprod, i8mm, bf16, fp16, SVE, SVE2, SME, SME2) and runtime dispatch is the caller's job

**Vs siblings:** Pick KleidiAI when you are building or maintaining your own Arm inference runtime and want Arm-maintained, vendorable kernels with SME/SME2 coverage and many data types. If you just want faster llama.cpp-style CPU inference, T-MAC (catalogued at 4-5x over llama.cpp's low-bit kernels on a Surface Laptop 7) and ik_llama.cpp report larger gains over llama.cpp than KleidiAI's independent results, though ik_llama.cpp's catalogued numbers are from x86.

**Gotchas:**
- SME matrix units are shared per CPU cluster, so SME throughput stops scaling past the unit count: Arm's PR #24414 table on an M4 Pro (2 SME units) peaks at 2 threads (892 t/s) and drops to 452-609 t/s at 4-8 threads. Current llama.cpp caps SME threads at the detected unit count; GGML_KLEIDIAI_SME=N overrides it and 0 disables SME kernels.
- llama.cpp issue #26630 (2026-08, closed as not planned): with gcc 13.3 on Cortex-X925, the -mcpu=native feature probes fail, so GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON compiles zero kai_run_matmul kernels while the build banner still says KLEIDIAI = 1. The workaround is GGML_NATIVE=OFF with an explicit GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH; the reported 1.42x-4.57x loss covers all Arm feature kernels, not KleidiAI alone.
- Packed RHS buffers are tied to one variant's mr/nr/kr/sr layout, and the LHS is quantized and packed on every call, so end-to-end gains depend on how the framework handles packing; in PR #11390 Arm noted that early reviewer runs lacked commit f4eb1b3, which made LHS packing multithreaded.
- Precondition checks (KAI_ASSUME/KAI_ASSERT) call abort(), or __builtin_trap with KLEIDIAI_ERROR_TRAP; the _ALWAYS variants stay active under NDEBUG. SME kernels used inside a call chain that already uses ZA need a compiler with SME-ABI support.

**Status:** Actively developed by Arm (v1.32.0, two releases a month; the GitHub repo is a read-only mirror of gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidiai). It is Apache-2.0, with some files under BSD-3-Clause, and copyable as plain .c/.h files, but the API can change without notice.

[repo](https://github.com/ARM-software/kleidiai) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/11390)

##### Larq Compute Engine  `C++ (hand-written kernels with inline assembly and intrinsics) with Python converter`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

TensorFlow Lite custom ops for binarized neural networks on 64-bit ARM; reports lower Bi-RealNet latency than dabnn on a Pixel 1.

**Beats:** dabnn (its own published Bi-RealNet time on Pixel 1, cross-report, not a same-run measurement); the MLSys 2021 LCE paper (not opened) reportedly compares binary convolutions against full-precision TensorFlow Lite convolutions — The README reports first-party latencies from its TFLite benchmark tool with XNNPACK enabled and random inputs: Bi-RealNet runs in 41.6 ms on a Pixel 1, versus the 61.3 ms that dabnn published for the same model (about 1.47x, a cross-report comparison, not a same-run measurement); QuickNet runs in 25.5 ms single-threaded on a Pixel 1 and 45.0 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4B. The MLSys 2021 paper's 8.5-18.5x figure (known only from search snippets) compares binary convolutions with full-precision ones, which is not equal work; no compiler flags are stated.

**Known shortcoming:** dabnn number taken from dabnn's own report, not the same run; MLSys 2021 paper unreadable here (possible B on retier).

**Known shortcoming:** Optimized kernels are AArch64-only; x86 falls back to portable C++ (std::bitset popcount). Bug #421 (int8 ranges) open since 2020. Kernels over-read 16 bytes. Last release v0.16.0 (2024-06), pinned to TF 2.16.1. dabnn comparison is cross-report, not one harness.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Binary convolution becomes a binary GEMM: activations and weights are bit-packed into 32-bit words, and each multiply-accumulate is an XOR followed by a popcount. On AArch64 the indirect-BGEMM kernels (8x4x1, 8x4x2 and 8x4x4, picked at runtime from the packed input depth) do this in inline NEON assembly (eor, cnt, addp) with 16-bit accumulators, and the im2col path plugs custom kernels into Google's Ruy GEMM framework. The kernels apply a per-channel output transform (multiplier, bias, clamp) in the same pass, and since v0.7.0 the converter keeps activations bit-packed between binary layers by default.

**Use it when:**
- You are deploying a BNN (QuickNet, Bi-RealNet or your own Larq model) to an AArch64 phone or board such as Android or Raspberry Pi 4 in 64-bit mode.
- Your binary layers are standard 2D convolutions (grouped convolutions are supported since v0.5/v0.6) and the rest of the model can stay on built-in TFLite ops.
- You already train with Larq/Keras and want a converter path that keeps the training graph and the deployed graph consistent.
- You want per-layer latency numbers on device: the repo ships a TFLite benchmark tool with the LCE ops registered.

**Skip it when:**
- Full-precision or int8 models: LCE adds nothing; it only speeds up layers that are truly binarized, and binarization costs accuracy (QuickNet tops out at 66.9% ImageNet top-1).
- x86 or other non-AArch64 targets as an inference engine: the hand-written kernels are AArch64-only, and elsewhere the code falls back to portable C++ (Ruy kStandardCpp path, std::bitset popcount).
- GPUs, NPUs or LLM workloads: CPU only, convnet-oriented ops.
- Projects that cannot take a Bazel build pinned to a specific TensorFlow source tree (TF 2.16.1 in WORKSPACE, Bazel 6.5.0).
- Teams wanting fast upstream movement: the last tagged release is v0.16.0 (2024-06-21) and recent commits are mostly dependency bumps.

**Integration:** static lib (TFLite custom-op library built with Bazel against a pinned TensorFlow source tree) plus a Python converter wheel · TensorFlow Lite (TensorFlow 2.16.1 sources), Ruy, flatbuffers; the converter needs Python 3.10-3.12 and TensorFlow >= 2.8; Bazel 6.5.0 to build · Bazel 6.5.0; aarch64 builds use -march=armv8-a; Android NDK for Android; exact minimum compiler not documented · Optimized kernels: AArch64 (Android, 64-bit Raspberry Pi and other ARM boards, Apple M1 per the README benchmarks). Portable C++ fallback elsewhere. Converter wheels: Linux x86-64, macOS x86-64 and arm64, Windows x86-64.

**Vs siblings:** Pick LCE over MNN, OpenVINO or FeatherCNN only when your network is binarized end to end, since those engines target float/int8 models; pick BitNet (bitnet.cpp) or T-MAC instead for low-bit LLM inference, which is where LCE has no kernels.

**Gotchas:**
- Kernels may read (never write) up to 16 bytes past the end of an array (LCE_EXTRA_BYTES in core/types.h); custom tensor allocations need that padding.
- The AArch64 assembly kernels use 16-bit accumulators and are chosen only if the maximum accumulator value fits in uint16; otherwise the code falls back to the portable 4x2 C++ kernel, and bit-packed output is also portable-only.
- The benchmark tool defaults to use_indirect_bgemm=false (Ruy-based BGEMM); pass the flag to measure the indirect kernels.
- Open bug #421 (since 2020): int8 default ranges break when a binary conv is followed by a normal conv.

**Status:** Apache-2.0 and still receiving commits (mostly dependency bumps, plus a RISC-V build path in 2026), but the last PyPI release is v0.16.0 from June 2024 and the build is tied to TensorFlow 2.16.1, so expect to do your own porting.

[repo](https://github.com/larq/compute-engine) · [benchmark](https://github.com/larq/compute-engine)

##### Liger-Kernel  `Python (Triton kernels)`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Triton kernels that monkey-patch Hugging Face LLMs for training; mainly cut memory, with roughly 15-40% end-to-end throughput gains over eager PyTorch.

**Beats:** Hugging Face Transformers default PyTorch eager modeling code (RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, cross-entropy, fused linear cross-entropy) — End to end, the README charts show more than 20% higher throughput and 60% less memory than stock Hugging Face eager code for Llama 3-8B training (bf16, batch 8, AdamW, gradient checkpointing, FSDP1, 8x A100); the example scripts report 15-40% throughput gains. At kernel level, the repo's benchmark CSV (median timings of full forward+backward, versus the Hugging Face modules, on A100/H100/B200/RTX GPUs with the Liger version recorded but no Triton/PyTorch versions) gives cross-entropy 2.40-2.87x, RMSNorm 1.11-8.63x and RoPE 1.88-10.24x, with fused linear cross-entropy slower (0.46-0.89x) but 1.4-4.8x lighter on memory.

**Known shortcoming:** Its own CSV shows softmax at a median 0.33x of torch, fused linear cross-entropy at 0.46-0.89x of HF, and embedding slower than torch.compile; wins are mostly memory, not speed.

**Known shortcoming:** Open #272: the in-place cross-entropy gradient write skips autograd version tracking, so gradients come out silently wrong if logits are reused. FLCE accumulates grad_weight in bf16 by default (accum_dtype=None). Per the repo CSV, FLCE runs 0.46-0.89x the speed of HF, softmax median 0.33x of torch and megatron_rms_norm median 0.63x, so many kernels are slower than baseline.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Kernel fusion of memory-bound elementwise and row-reduction ops (one Triton program per row, with the forward pass caching per-row rstd for backward), so the gain comes from fewer HBM round trips and kernel launches. Cross-entropy computes the gradient during the forward pass and writes it in place over the logits tensor, so the backward pass only rescales it. Fused linear cross-entropy chunks the batch x tokens dimension so the full BT x V logits matrix is never materialized (by default transient logits are bounded at about BT x H elements), which is where most of the 60% memory saving comes from. Optional cuTile and CuTe-DSL backends (LIGER_KERNEL_IMPL) provide Hopper/Blackwell variants of some kernels.

**Use it when:**
- Fine-tuning or pretraining a supported Hugging Face causal LM (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, DeepSeek and others) where large vocabularies (128k+) make the logits plus cross-entropy step the activation-memory peak; fused linear cross-entropy lets you raise batch size or context (the README chart: Hugging Face OOMs at 4K context while Liger reaches 16K on 8 A100s).
- Eager-mode PyTorch training with FSDP, DeepSpeed or DDP where you cannot or do not want to rely on torch.compile.
- Alignment or distillation losses on large-vocabulary models, where the chunked fused-linear losses save memory (benchmark CSV, CPO/ORPO/SimPO/KTO versus the Hugging Face references: 1.04-1.31x faster and up to 3.9-8.9x less memory, though ORPO uses more memory on one shape, 0.86x).
- Mixed GPU fleets: the same Triton code is run in CI on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs and on Ascend NPUs.

**Skip it when:**
- When raw speed of the loss step is the goal: the repo's own CSV shows fused linear cross-entropy at 0.46-0.89x the speed of the Hugging Face baseline (it trades time for memory), and fused_linear_jsd at a median 0.54x.
- Standalone softmax, embedding or Megatron RMSNorm: Liger is slower than torch on most measured shapes (softmax median 0.33x, embedding 0.50-0.80x versus torch.compile, megatron_rms_norm median 0.63x), and layer_norm/group_norm drop to 0.30x/0.51x on some shapes.
- Inference serving: the kernels target training (forward plus backward); use FlashInfer, FasterTransformer or engine-native kernels instead.
- Models or Transformers versions outside the patching table: monkey-patching depends on Hugging Face module names and has broken on upstream changes (issues #543 and #723).
- Code that reuses the logits after passing them to LigerCrossEntropyLoss: the in-place gradient write can silently corrupt gradients (open issue #272).

**Integration:** module (pip package liger-kernel; pure Python plus Triton JIT, optional native liger-cute-kernels wheel) · torch >= 2.1.2 and triton >= 2.3.1 (CUDA); triton >= 3.0.0 with ROCm PyTorch; torch >= 2.6.0 for Intel XPU; torch/torch_npu 2.9.0 and triton-ascend 3.2.2 for Ascend; transformers for the patching APIs; optional cuda-tile, nvidia-cutlass-dsl >= 4.6.0, liger-cute-kernels with NVSHMEM · Python 3.10+; torch 2.1.2 and Triton 2.3.1 on CUDA; CUDA Toolkit 13.1+ for the optional cuTile backend; CUDA 12.9 for the native LCK wheel · Anything Triton supports: NVIDIA GPUs (benchmark CSV covers A100, H100, B200, RTX 3090/4090), AMD ROCm GPUs, Intel XPU, Ascend NPU; CuTe-DSL and native kernels only on Hopper/Blackwell

**Vs siblings:** Pick Liger over QuACK when you want a one-line patch for Hugging Face models that also runs on AMD, Intel and Ascend; QuACK's CuTe-DSL memory-bound kernels report higher throughput than Liger v0.5.10 on H100 but are NVIDIA-only. Pick it over LightSeq when your models come from current Hugging Face Transformers rather than LightSeq's own Transformer layers.

**Gotchas:**
- LigerCrossEntropy stores the gradient in the logits buffer during forward without bumping PyTorch's version counter, so autograd cannot detect a later reuse of those logits; issue #272 shows gradients differing from F.cross_entropy (open since 2024-09).
- With bf16 parameters and accum_dtype=None, fused linear cross-entropy accumulates grad_weight/grad_bias in bf16; pass accum_dtype=torch.float32 if you need fp32 accumulation.
- The fused linear cross-entropy forward calls .item() (a CUDA synchronization, noted as a TODO in the source), and an optional CuTe-DSL backend raises an error if it is selected on an unsupported device.
- The headline 20% throughput and 60% memory numbers are images measured against untuned eager Hugging Face code (no torch.compile, Llama 3-8B, FSDP1, 8 A100s); kernel-level gains vary from 0.3x to 10x by op and shape.

**Status:** Very active (v0.8.4 on PyPI 2026-09-30, commits through 2026-09-30, CI on NVIDIA/AMD/Intel/Ascend), BSD-2-Clause, and widely integrated, so it is safe to adopt; pin the Transformers version you patch against.

[repo](https://github.com/linkedin/Liger-Kernel) · [benchmark](https://github.com/linkedin/Liger-Kernel)

##### LightSeq  `C++/CUDA`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Fused CUDA Transformer layers for training and beam-search inference; 1.4-2.1x faster training than PyTorch fp16 AMP on A100.

**Beats:** PyTorch fp16 mixed precision (training and inference), PyTorch QAT — First-party README tables give speedup ratios over PyTorch fp16 mixed precision on one A100 (training) and eight A100s (inference): fp16 training 1.44-1.99x on Transformer and 1.59-2.12x on BERT, and inference 6.2-11.8x on Transformer and 1.8-10.6x on BERT, with no raw timings, compiler flags or host CPU; the headline 'up to 3x' training figure is not in the tables. docs/performance.md (T4, Transformer-base, beam 4) has raw milliseconds against FasterTransformer: slower at batch 1, up to 1.39x faster at batch 32-128 (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** 'Up to 3x' fp16 training is not in the README tables (max 2.12x); slower than FasterTransformer at batch 1; NAACL 2021 / SC22 papers unreadable here (possible B on retier); archived.

**Known shortcoming:** Training softmax throws above 1024 tokens (message says 512; #197); setup.py swallows inference-extension build failures and installs a training-only package; docs say CUDA <11 while CMakeLists requires 11; no sm_90; --use_fast_math; open bugs #256 (BART top-k wrong) and #263 (small vocab).

**How:** Coarse-grained kernel fusion: chains of element-wise ops (bias add, dropout, residual, layer norm, softmax with mask) run as one launch around cuBLAS GemmEx calls, cutting launch count and intermediate memory traffic. The inference engine adds Hierarchical Auto-Regressive Search (HARS) to remove redundant work in beam search, plus dynamic GPU memory reuse with buffers preallocated for the maximum batch and length. LightSeq2 (SC22) adds a mixed-precision trainer that links all parameters and gradients into one contiguous workspace so the optimizer update is a single fused pass, and int8 GEMM paths for quantised training and inference.

**Use it when:**
- Training Fairseq or Hugging Face Transformer/BERT/GPT-2/ViT models on V100/A100-class GPUs with small token batches (512-1024 tokens), where the README tables show the largest gains (1.78-1.99x Transformer, 1.92-2.12x BERT vs PyTorch fp16).
- Seq2seq translation serving with beam search at batch 8-128 on T4-class GPUs, where docs/performance.md shows it 1.0-1.39x faster than FasterTransformer (derived from page data).
- Int8 quantisation-aware training followed by int8 inference of the same Transformer, Bert or GPT-2 model in one toolchain.
- Legacy pipelines already pinned to Python 3.6-3.8, PyTorch 1.x and Fairseq 0.10.2.

**Skip it when:**
- Sequences longer than 1024 tokens: the training softmax kernel throws a runtime_error above to_len 1024 (issue #197 asks for longer sequences and is unanswered); attention is materialised, not FlashAttention-style.
- Hopper or newer GPUs: the CMake and JIT arch lists stop at sm_86/sm_87, and nothing has been updated since 2023.
- Batch-1 beam search latency: on T4 it is slower than FasterTransformer (29.66 vs 26.25 ms at seq 32, 63.04 vs 54.02 ms at seq 64).
- Large token batches: training speedup flattens to about 1.44x at 4096-15000 tokens, which torch.compile or fused-kernel PyTorch paths may already match (not measured here).
- Any project needing a maintained dependency: the repository was archived on 2025-07-21 and PyPI wheels cover only Python 3.6-3.8 on Linux.

**Integration:** Python package (pip wheel with prebuilt inference extension; training ops JIT-compiled through torch.utils.cpp_extension and ninja) or C++ static/shared lib built with CMake; Triton backend · CUDA toolkit (cuBLAS, Thrust, CUB submodule), pybind11, protobuf >= 3.13, HDF5; PyTorch for training; Fairseq 0.10.2, transformers or DeepSpeed for the integrations · C++14, CMake 3.18; docs/build.md says CUDA >= 10.1 and < 11, but the current CMakeLists requires find_package(CUDA 11) · Linux, NVIDIA GPUs (CMake arch lists 60-86 legacy or 70-87 new arch; training JIT defaults to 6.0/6.1/7.0 plus 8.0/8.6); the new-arch build has fp32-only x86 and arm device targets

**Vs siblings:** Pick LightSeq over FasterTransformer or ByteTransformer when you need training acceleration as well as inference (both siblings are inference-only, and ByteTransformer covers only the BERT encoder), or when you run Fairseq beam search at batch 8 and up. For new inference deployments prefer CTranslate2, which is maintained and also covers CPUs.

**Gotchas:**
- setup.py catches any build failure of the inference extension, logs a warning and installs the training-only package anyway, so a broken CUDA build can go unnoticed until lightseq.inference is imported.
- Training layers preallocate for max_batch_tokens and max_seq_len set in get_config; exceeding either raises ValueError at forward time.
- Training kernels are JIT-compiled with -O3 --use_fast_math, so results are not bit-identical to PyTorch; the user guide warns Hugging Face BERT fine-tuning 'is unstable and may not converge', and issue #138 reports non-convergence with fairseq --update_freq.
- Open bug reports include wrong BART top-k sampling results (#256), a bug with small decoder vocab sizes (#263) and failures at batch size 1 in the Hugging Face example (#191).

**Status:** Archived on 2025-07-21 with no commits since 2023-05-10, but Apache-2.0 and usable as a frozen dependency on CUDA 11-era stacks (Python 3.6-3.8 wheels, PyTorch 1.x, Ampere or older GPUs).

[repo](https://github.com/bytedance/lightseq) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bytedance/lightseq/blob/master/README.md)

##### llamafile tinyBLAS CPU matmul kernels  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

tinyBLAS: register-tiled CPU GEMM kernels from llamafile; 1.3-5x faster LLM prompt eval than March-2024 llama.cpp, upstreamed since.

**Beats:** llama.cpp CPU matmul (prior kernels); Intel MKL sgemm — The author's blog (justine.lol/matmul, March 2024) compares llamafile 0.7 to llama.cpp builds from 2024-03-26/29 on an i9-9900, i9-14900K, Raspberry Pi 4/5, M2 Ultra and Threadripper 7995WX. Prompt tok/s improved by up to 3.8x (14900K f16) and 2.5x (7995WX f16), and by about 1.1-1.6x on Q8_0, while generation tok/s was flat. A single 513x512x512 GEMM on the i9-14900K hit 810 vs MKL's 295 GFLOPS. PR #6414 reports about 2x on F16 and 40% on Q4_0/Q8_0. Flags for the tok/s runs are not stated; first-party only.

**Known shortcoming:** Gains are in prompt eval only (token generation barely changes); the March-2024 llama.cpp baseline has since merged these kernels.

**Known shortcoming:** Kernels now in llama.cpp upstream (ggml/src/ggml-cpu/llamafile/sgemm.cpp, on by default), so the gain over current llama.cpp is gone; MKL wins at 1024-size GEMMs; on M2 Ultra TinyLlama q8_0 slower (457 vs 564 prompt tok/s); repo moved to mozilla-ai/llamafile.

**How:** It unrolls both outer loops of the matmul into a fixed RM x RN tile of accumulator registers (outer-product register tiling, e.g. mnpack<4,6> with 32 vector registers, <4,3> with 16). Each loaded A vector is reused across several B columns, which cuts loads per FMA. It skips the cache-blocking/packing and malloc that MKL-style BLAS does, so it wins on cache-resident matrices. Threads take tile jobs from ggml's own threadpool and barrier, avoiding a second BLAS thread pool, and llamafile picks per-microarchitecture builds at runtime (AVX2, AVX-512F, Zen 4 AVX-512 BF16/VNNI, NEON).

**Use it when:**
- CPU-only LLM inference where prompt processing (prefill, batch n>1) dominates: long prompts, RAG, summarization, LLaVA image tokens.
- F16/BF16/F32 weights on x86 with AVX2 or AVX-512, where the blog shows the largest gains (e.g. i9-14900K Mistral 7B f16 50 vs 13 prompt tok/s; 7995WX 485 vs 197).
- Small to mid GEMMs that fit in L2 (author's best case: under ~1000 prompt tokens, 512-wide matrices) where MKL's packing overhead dominates.
- Shipping one binary that runs on many OSes and CPUs: llamafile dispatches the right kernel at runtime.
- Borrowing a compact, MIT-licensed register-tiled GEMM micro-kernel design for your own C++ code (ggml/src/ggml-cpu/llamafile/sgemm.cpp in llama.cpp).

**Skip it when:**
- Token generation (n=1 matvec): memory-bound, and the tables show eval tok/s unchanged (e.g. 17 vs 16 on 7995WX).
- Large GEMMs: the author says that at 1024 'MKL wins once more'; use MKL/OpenBLAS/BLIS for general dense linear algebra.
- Apple Silicon: off by default on M2 in the upstream PR; on M2 Ultra TinyLlama q8_0 it was slower (457 vs 564 prompt tok/s).
- K-quants and other formats outside its supported set: the kernel returns false and you get the regular ggml path.
- If you already run a current llama.cpp: the kernels were merged there (default on), so the 2024 speedup is no longer an advantage over upstream.

**Integration:** source-drop (one sgemm.cpp/sgemm.h inside ggml), or the whole llamafile executable · ggml internals (ggml_compute_params, threadpool, quant block types); llamafile builds also need Cosmopolitan Libc · C++17 (if constexpr); GCC or Clang with target intrinsics; the blog's example used -O3 -ffast-math -march=native; Clang takes about 45 s to compile the kernels (PR #6414) · x86-64 (AVX/AVX2/AVX-512F/AVX512-BF16), aarch64 NEON (fp16 arithmetic optional); upstream also has POWER (MMA/VSX), s390x VXE and RISC-V RVV variants

**Vs siblings:** Choose tinyBLAS for F16/BF16/Q8_0 prefill on x86 or ARM inside a ggml-based stack. Choose T-MAC for 2-4-bit weights or BitNet decoding, and the AVX512 DGEMM tutorial kernels or MKL for double-precision or large general GEMMs.

**Gotchas:**
- Silent fallback: it handles only shapes where k is a multiple of the vector width and m a multiple of 4 (n >= 2 except on POWER MMA), and only an F32 output; otherwise it returns false and the slower generic path runs.
- No bound on rounding error: the source says error 'grows along with k', and the blog warns ARMv8.2 fp16 accumulation without Kahan summation adds error.
- The repo now lives at github.com/mozilla-ai/llamafile; v0.10 rebuilt on a newer llama.cpp and dropped some features (pledge sandbox, localscore, stable diffusion).
- LLAMAFILE_DISABLE_SGEMM=1 turns the kernels off in llamafile; use it when you A/B test.

**Status:** Active (Mozilla.ai, 26.1k stars, commits in Sept 2026); llamafile is Apache-2.0, but the kernels are MIT and already live in llama.cpp, so copy them from there.

[repo](https://github.com/mozilla-ai/llamafile) · [benchmark](https://justine.lol/matmul/)

##### llm.c (GPT-2/GPT-3 training in C/CUDA)  `C (CUDA)`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

GPT-2/GPT-3 pretraining in plain C/CUDA with hand-written fused kernels; about 7% faster than PyTorch nightly on one A100.

**Beats:** PyTorch Nightly (parallel reference implementation train_gpt2.py) — Karpathy's May 3, 2024 'State of the Union' (Discussion #344) measured GPT-2 124M training on TinyStories, batch 32 x 1024 tokens, bf16, on one A100 40GB PCIe (CUDA 12.2, driver 535.129.03): llm.c about 167K tok/s (160K on master) against train_gpt2.py with torch.compile and flash attention at about 150K tok/s, or about 156K with the vocab padded to 50304, so about 7% ahead of PyTorch nightly. The nightly build and host CPU are not identified; the PyTorch script is described in #481 as lacking full feature parity.

**Known shortcoming:** The comparison (~167K tok/s vs PyTorch nightly ~156K with padded vocab, A100 40GB PCIe, CUDA 12.2; discussion #344) used an unmerged PR; host CPU and PyTorch nightly build not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Help text says -ge (GELU fusion) defaults to 2 on SM90+, but the code forces 0. Open issues: #263 inf loss at large batch, #321 dataloader bugs. Discussion #481 says train_gpt2.py lacks feature parity with llm.c's training loop, which weakens the PyTorch baseline.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** No framework or Python overhead, bf16 mixed precision, and kernel fusion: a fused classifier computes the cross-entropy loss without materializing the full softmax and starts the backward pass in the same kernel, a fused residual-plus-LayerNorm forward, optional GELU fused into cuBLASLt matmul epilogues, and Packed128 128-bit vectorized loads and stores. Attention uses cuDNN's flash attention (USE_CUDNN=1), matmuls go through cuBLASLt, the vocabulary is padded internally to 50304 for GPU-friendly shapes, and recomputing GELU in the backward pass saves activation memory so larger batches fit.

**Use it when:**
- Pretraining GPT-2 or GPT-3-style decoder-only models (124M up to the 1.6B reproduction target) on NVIDIA GPUs where you want a dependency-light binary and a few percent over torch.compile.
- Reproducing GPT-2 124M cheaply: Discussion #481 reports about 90 minutes and about $20 on an 8x A100 80GB SXM node at about 60% MFU.
- Learning or teaching how each transformer layer's forward and backward pass maps to CUDA, using dev/cuda's progression of kernels and the doc/layernorm tutorial.
- Borrowing specific fused kernels (fused classifier, fused residual+LayerNorm, bf16 AdamW) as reference code for your own engine.

**Skip it when:**
- Any architecture outside the GPT-2/GPT-3 family: there is no general autodiff, so a new layer means hand-writing its forward and backward kernels.
- Serving or production inference: it is a training loop whose only inference is sampling inside the binary (-g genT); use an inference engine instead.
- Non-NVIDIA hardware: mainline is CUDA only, cuDNN attention is not supported on macOS per the Makefile, and AMD, Metal, OpenCL support exist only as third-party forks.
- If you need an actively maintained stack: the last commit is from May 2025, with 93 open issues and 133 open pull requests on the repo page.
- Expecting a large margin over current PyTorch: the 7% was measured in May 2024 against a nightly build, and it shrinks to that only after padding PyTorch's vocab by hand (46% was against stable 2.3.0).

**Integration:** source-drop (single-file training program built with the repo Makefile; llmc/*.cuh headers) · CUDA toolkit with cuBLAS and cuBLASLt and NVML (-lnvidia-ml); optional cuDNN plus the header-only cudnn-frontend for flash attention (USE_CUDNN=1); optional NCCL and OpenMPI for multi-GPU; Python with PyTorch only to prepare data and the initial checkpoint; CPU build uses OpenMP if found · nvcc with -std=c++17 (CUDA 12.x in the published runs; the cuDNN path on Windows uses C++20); CPU reference builds with clang or gcc -Ofast · Linux x86-64 with NVIDIA GPUs (multi-GPU and multi-node via NCCL); Windows build path in the Makefile; CPU fp32 reference on any OS including Apple Silicon

**Vs siblings:** Pick llm.c when you want to own the whole GPT-2 training stack in C/CUDA; Liger-Kernel is the drop-in choice for speeding up existing Hugging Face PyTorch training, FlashAttention-3 or ThunderKittens give faster individual attention/GEMM kernels, and yalm is the from-scratch C++/CUDA counterpart for inference rather than training.

**Gotchas:**
- cuDNN flash attention is off by default (USE_CUDNN=0) because it raises compile time from seconds to about a minute; the published speed comparison was built with USE_CUDNN=1, and the FP32 test path does not support cuDNN.
- The usage text says GELU fusion (-ge) defaults to 2 on SM90+, but the code currently forces the default to 0 ('off for now'), so pass -ge explicitly if you want it.
- The build uses --use_fast_math for nvcc and -Ofast for the CPU reference, so results match PyTorch only within the tolerances test_gpt2 checks.
- Open issues include 'inf loss at big batch' (#263), 'Possible bugs in the data loading functions' (#321) and a multi-GPU dataloader shuffle_rng question (#792).

**Status:** Stale since the last commit on 2025-05-10 but MIT-licensed, widely studied (31.1k stars, 3.8k forks, many language ports) and easy to vendor as reference code.

[repo](https://github.com/karpathy/llm.c) · [benchmark](https://github.com/karpathy/llm.c/discussions/344)

##### Lucebox Megakernel (single-launch CUDA forward pass for Qwen 3.5-0.8B)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Model-specific CUDA decode megakernel for Qwen 3.5-0.8B at batch 1; 1.55x llama.cpp BF16 decode on an RTX 3090.

**Beats:** llama.cpp (BF16, CUDA backend) and PyTorch + HuggingFace Transformers (BF16) — On an RTX 3090 in BF16, the first-party RESULTS.md reports pp520 at 21,347 tok/s against 11,247 for llama.cpp BF16 (unversioned, 'default settings', run outside the harness) and 7,578 for eager Hugging Face Transformers; tg128 is 413 vs 267 vs 108 tok/s (1.55x and 3.8x). The repo's final_bench.py times only the megakernel and Hugging Face (10 warm-up plus 20 timed prefills, perf_counter around cuda.synchronize); the CUDA version and host CPU of the 3090 run are not stated, and the numbers predate the PR #761 and #804 correctness fixes.

**Known shortcoming:** 413 tok/s is the stock run (220 W power cap gives 411). Prefill on the RTX 3090 uses cuBLAS plus separate kernels, not the megakernel. llama.cpp is run separately with no version stated.

**Known shortcoming:** All published numbers predate two correctness fixes: PR #761 (merged 2026-09-24) fixed a cross-block attention race that gave non-repeatable output, and PR #804 (open 2026-10-01) fixes an in-place Q RoPE bug still in kernel.cu at HEAD (before the fix about 47% top-token agreement with HF, cosine 0.70, on an RTX 3050). bench_pp_tg.py's 'correctness' compares the megakernel with its own decode path, not HF. Not one dispatch (decode_kernel plus lm_head_kernel per token); the grid barrier is an atomic spin under a plain launch, not cooperative launch; greedy argmax only; the HF baseline is eager mode. Lucebox sells hardware.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Decode runs all 24 layers in one persistent kernel (decode_kernel in kernel.cu, 82 blocks x 512 threads on a 3090), so there are no per-layer launches or CPU round-trips. Blocks meet at a hand-rolled atomic grid barrier (AtomicGridSync) between phases. Each layer is a bandwidth-bound BF16 matrix-vector product with FP32 accumulation, the DeltaNet recurrence keeps its state in FP32, and attention uses online softmax with the KV cache written inside the kernel. A second kernel does the 248,320-row LM head and argmax. On the 3090, prefill (prefill.cu) is cuBLAS GEMMs plus standalone kernels and a chunk-parallel DeltaNet scan (chunk size 8); it is not a megakernel.

**Use it when:**
- Single-user, batch-1 local generation with Qwen 3.5-0.8B in BF16 on an Ampere or newer NVIDIA consumer GPU (RTX 3090 is the tuned target), where decode latency and tokens per joule matter.
- Power-capped deployments: the DVFS sweep keeps 411 tok/s at a 220 W limit against 433 tok/s at stock.
- As a reference implementation when writing your own persistent decode kernel for a hybrid linear-attention (DeltaNet) plus attention model.
- Turing (RTX 2080 Ti, FP16) or Blackwell (RTX 5090, DGX Spark via an NVFP4 decode path) when you need this model there and accept less-documented paths.

**Skip it when:**
- Any other model or size: the layer layout, head counts and vocabulary are compile-time constants, and the README says fusion gains shrink as models grow.
- Batched or multi-tenant serving (batch size 1 only; the README points to vLLM or SGLang), quantized weights (no GGUF, GPTQ or AWQ), or prompts longer than the default max_seq_len of 2048.
- Where output must match the reference model today: the in-place RoPE bug fixed by PR #804 (open on 2026-10-01) gave about 47% top-token agreement with Hugging Face before the fix.
- Sampling-based generation: decode does greedy argmax with an optional repetition penalty and has no temperature or top-p.
- A GPU shared with other work (other processes, MPS): the grid barrier needs every block to be resident at the same time.

**Integration:** module · PyTorch 2.0+ (torch.utils.cpp_extension build), cuBLAS (plus cuBLASLt on Blackwell), Hugging Face transformers and the Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B weights; built with pip install -e . --no-build-isolation or uv sync --extra megakernel · CUDA 12+ with nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 --use_fast_math; Blackwell sm_120/sm_121a needs CUDA 12.8+ (cuda_fp4.h); RESULTS.md's GB10 run used CUDA 13.2 · NVIDIA only, Linux: sm_86 (RTX 3090, BF16) is the benchmarked target; sm_75 (FP16), sm_80+ (BF16), Pascal sm_6x shims in the source, and Blackwell sm_120/121a via NVFP4; the arch is auto-detected at build time

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over yalm or ik_llama.cpp only when the model is exactly Qwen 3.5-0.8B at batch 1 on an NVIDIA GPU and decode tok/s or tok/J is what you are optimizing; those engines run many models. For batched or large-model Gated DeltaNet prefill on datacenter GPUs, FlashQLA's kernels are the closer fit.

**Gotchas:**
- Known correctness bugs after the published numbers: PR #761 (merged 2026-09-24) fixed attention blocks overwriting each other's partial results in full_attention_layer (non-repeatable output), and PR #804 (open on 2026-10-01) fixes Q RoPE rotating in place, so the second half of each rotary pair reads an already-rotated value. kernel.cu at HEAD still has this pattern.
- The built-in correctness check in bench_pp_tg.py compares the megakernel against its own step-by-step decode path, not against Hugging Face, so it cannot catch math errors both paths share. final_bench.py prints both completions but does not compare them.
- 'Single dispatch' means the 24 layers: each token still launches decode_kernel plus a separate lm_head_kernel, with three small memsets. The grid barrier is an atomic spin-wait under a normal <<<>>> launch, not cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel; the block count is clamped to the occupancy-reported resident limit, and the README warns that grid.sync inside loops deadlocks silently.
- Prefill speedups on the 3090 come from cuBLAS plus standalone kernels, not the megakernel. Only Blackwell has a single-dispatch prefill megakernel.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-01) in an Apache-2.0 repo with 2.9k stars from Lucebox, which sells a local-AI PC; the megakernel is a self-described research proof of concept for one model, copyable but with an open RoPE correctness fix at the time of reading.

[repo](https://github.com/Luce-Org/lucebox) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Luce-Org/lucebox/blob/main/optimizations/megakernel/RESULTS.md)

##### Marlin (FP16xINT4 LLM matmul kernel)  `CUDA`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

FP16 x INT4 weight-only GEMM for Ampere/Ada GPUs; near-ideal 3.9x over FP16 torch.matmul up to batch 16-32.

**Beats:** FP16 PyTorch matmul (calls CUTLASS) and other 4-bit kernels: torch-nightly, exllamav2, AWQ, bitsandbytes — First-party plots only: on an NVIDIA A10 with ECC disabled, a 72k x 18k group-128 matmul ran about 3.87-3.9x faster than FP16 torch.matmul at batch 1-16, 3.1x at 64 and 1.55x at 128 (about 1.0x at 128 with clocks locked to base), and the linear layers of Llama and Falcon models at batch 16 ran about 3.4-4.25x faster on A10, 3090 and A6000 and 2.2-3.65x on A100 (approximate plot readings, derived from page data); compiler flags and host CPU are not stated. One user report (#21, A6000 Ada) measured 1.16x at 1024 rows and 0.82x at 16384 rows.

**Known shortcoming:** Gain comes from 4-bit weight traffic and falls to 1.55x at batch 128; PPoPP '25 paper unreadable here (possible B on retier).

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: issue #45 (2026-09-29) reports wrong, nondeterministic outputs with groupsize 128 at Llama-7B shapes on sm_87 (rel err 1.3e-3 to 2e-2); possible async race #42; nondeterminism #27/#38; test.py test_llama_shapes starts with a bare return, so those shapes are never tested; #21: 0.82x of FP16 at 16384 rows on A6000 Ada; failures on RTX 5090 (#40); nvcc 13.1 sm_90 miscompile (#44).

**How:** It is built to stay memory-bound on weights up to larger batches: weights are streamed with cp.async and an L2 evict_first cache policy, activations stay in L2 and registers, and shared-memory tiles are double-buffered in a 4-stage pipeline so loads overlap compute. Weights and scales are permuted offline so int4 values dequantise (via LOP3 bit tricks) directly into mma.sync m16n8k16 tensor-core fragments loaded with conflict-free ldmatrix. A 'striped' partitioning gives each SM a contiguous run of tiles that may span several column slices, keeping all SMs busy on realistic shapes, and the cross-block reduction happens in the L2-resident output buffer guarded by global locks.

**Use it when:**
- Decode-phase LLM inference with 4-bit GPTQ-style weights on A10, A100, A6000, RTX 3090/4090-class GPUs at 1-32 tokens per step, where the weight read dominates.
- Batched serving, speculative decoding or multi-sample schemes that push the effective batch to 16-32, where older 4-bit kernels (exllamav2, AWQ, bitsandbytes) fall below FP16 speed.
- Embedding a dependency-free FP16xINT4 GEMM in a custom C++/CUDA inference engine (one .cu file, plain pointers plus a stream).
- Fitting larger models in GPU memory: 4-bit weights with group-128 scales use about 4.125 bits per weight instead of 16.

**Skip it when:**
- Prefill or large batches: the README plots fall to about 1.55x at batch 128 (about 1.0x at locked base clock), and issue #21 reports 0.82x of FP16 on an A6000 Ada at 16x1024 = 16384 rows.
- Hopper or Blackwell GPUs: the README says it is not optimised for Hopper; open issues report failures on RTX 5090 (#40) and an nvcc 13.1 ptxas miscompile of the cp.async cache hint on sm_90 (#44).
- Formats it does not cover: BF16 activations, asymmetric or zero-point quantisation (AWQ format), bias, group sizes other than 128 or per-channel, other bit widths; layer dims must have in_features % 128 == 0 and out_features % 256 == 0.
- Volta, Turing, AMD or CPU targets: it needs compute capability 8.0 or newer, and a ROCm port request (#43) is open.
- Correctness-critical group-128 inference on small GPUs until issue #45 is resolved (see gotchas).

**Integration:** PyTorch CUDA extension (pip install . from source, no wheel) or source-drop of marlin/marlin_cuda_kernel.cu · kernel: CUDA runtime only; Python wrapper: torch >= 2.0, numpy; GPTQ example: transformers, datasets, sentencepiece · CUDA >= 11.8 with nvcc matching torch's CUDA; C++ standard and flags are torch CUDAExtension defaults (not stated) · NVIDIA compute capability >= 8.0 (Ampere, Ada); Hopper works but is not optimised; Linux assumed (not stated)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Marlin over BitBLAS when you only need FP16xINT4 on Ampere/Ada and want one small kernel file with no TVM-based tuning stack; pick BitBLAS for INT2/INT1/FP4 or mixed formats. For CPU inference of low-bit models use T-MAC, BitNet or ik_llama.cpp instead; for production serving use vLLM's maintained Marlin fork (gptq_marlin, awq_marlin) rather than this frozen repo.

**Gotchas:**
- Issue #45 (2026-09-29, unanswered) reports wrong and non-deterministic outputs with groupsize 128 at Llama-2-7B shapes (m=300) on a Jetson Orin Nano (8 SMs), relative errors 1.3e-3 to 2e-2 with whole 64-row blocks corrupted, while per-channel scales stay correct; in test.py, test_llama_shapes starts with a bare return, so the repository's own tests never run those shapes.
- Issue #42 reports a possible async race where the per-channel scale load (cp_async4_stream) followed by thread_block_reduce leaves sh_s zeroed; #27 and #38 report slight non-determinism and batch-size-dependent results. None has a maintainer reply.
- Split-k reduction downcasts FP32 accumulators to FP16 in the output buffer, so results depend on how tiles are partitioned across SMs.
- The README benchmarks ran with ECC disabled on the A10 (10-15% more bandwidth), and bench.py times 10 launches with time.time without synchronising between them.

**Status:** Stale research code (14 commits, last 2024-09-04, 34 open issues mostly unanswered) under Apache-2.0; the kernel is easy to vendor, but the maintained descendants live in vLLM, and the open correctness reports (#45, #42) should be checked against your shapes before use.

[repo](https://github.com/IST-DASLab/marlin) · [benchmark](https://github.com/IST-DASLab/marlin#benchmarks)

##### metal-flash-attention  `Swift`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Swift/Metal port of FlashAttention for Apple GPUs; claims higher ALU utilization than FlashAttention-2/3 on NVIDIA, not wall-clock wins.

**Beats:** Dao-AILab FlashAttention-2 (A100) and FlashAttention-3 (H100), compared by utilization percentage, not wall time — First-party README figures only: FP16 ALU utilization on Apple GPUs (M1 architecture forward 85-86%, fwd+bwd 62-64%; M3 architecture forward 82-94%, fwd+bwd 61-71% at D = 64/128/256; 4400 gigainstructions/s, 83%, on M1 Max at large sizes), computed with the author's own work model, set beside A100 FlashAttention-2 and H100 FlashAttention-3 utilization derived from the papers' peak GFLOPS. No same-machine timing against MPS, MLX or PyTorch exists, and the 'faster than Nvidia' sentence refers to utilization normalized for GPU size, not wall time.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: the only comparison is ALU utilization against FlashAttention-2 (A100) and FlashAttention-3 (H100) figures taken from their papers, not a wall-clock run on the same machine; no MLX, MPS or PyTorch comparison exists. Last commit 2024-09-22, stale.

**Known shortcoming:** Single-head only, no masks, Swift/Metal only. Issue #8 FP16 overflow (scale applied after Q*K^T) looks unchanged in the current pseudocode. Users report its GEMM slower than MPS (issues #11 and #29: about 1 s vs 0.06 s at 4096^2 on an M2). Stale, recent issues unanswered.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It implements the FlashAttention tiling with online softmax, so the N x N attention matrix is never written to memory. Because Apple GPUs lack native FP32 atomics, the backward pass is split into separate dQ and dK/dV kernels (7 GEMMs instead of 5, (9D+15)N^2 work instead of (7D+10)N^2) that need no atomics or scratch space and parallelize fully across rows and columns.
