For large head dimensions it adds a third blocking dimension along D with deliberate, bandwidth-minimizing register spilling, and picks block sizes and register-cached operands from per-architecture parameter tables (M1/M2 vs M3/M4 'apple9' family, which also switches between async load and async cache paths).

**Use it when:**
- Native Swift/Metal apps on macOS 14+ or iOS 17+ that need attention on Apple silicon and can integrate Metal command encoding directly.
- Training-style workloads that need the backward pass on Apple GPUs; the README reports 62-64% (M1 architecture) and 61-71% (M3 architecture) fwd+bwd ALU utilization at D = 64, 128 and 256.
- Large or odd head dimensions (e.g. 256, or non-power-of-two values), where the D-blocking and register-spilling scheme is designed to keep utilization flat.
- As a reference implementation to port or extend (masks, multi-head, block sparsity) for an Apple-GPU inference engine.

**Skip it when:**
- You need multi-head attention, causal or padding masks, or a PyTorch/Python API out of the box: none are in this repo; the third-party fork imperatormk/metal-flash-attention and its mps-flash-attention bindings add causal masking, macOS 15 fixes and PyTorch MPS integration (issue #32, unanswered).
- You need a measured speedup against MPS, MLX or PyTorch SDPA on the same Mac: the README compares only utilization percentages against NVIDIA GPUs from the FlashAttention papers, so no wall-clock win is documented.
- Standalone GEMM: users reported its GEMM slower than MPS on M3 (issue #11) and a 4096x4096 GEMM taking about 1 s versus about 0.06 s for MPSMatrixMultiplication on M2 (issue #29, user measurement, cause not established); both issues were closed without a maintainer answer.
- Projects that need an actively maintained dependency: last author commit 2024-08-27, last commit 2024-09-22 (README PR), and recent issues get no replies.

**Integration:** module · none beyond Apple's Metal framework (Swift package with no package dependencies) · Swift tools 5.10; build with -Xswiftc -Ounchecked; macOS 14, iOS 17, tvOS 17, visionOS 1 · Apple silicon GPUs only (Metal); parameter tables tuned for M1/M2 and M3/M4 families

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ThunderMittens when you need a backward pass or large head dimensions on Apple GPUs from Swift, since ThunderMittens' evidence is a forward attention kernel compared with MLX; on NVIDIA use FlashAttention-3 or SageAttention instead, as this project only runs on Metal.

**Gotchas:**
- Every kernel is JIT-compiled at runtime from generated Metal source, so first use of each problem configuration pays shader compilation latency; the older precompiled-metallib version (Xcode 14.2) was replaced by this design.
- Default mixed precision keeps Q/K/V in FP16 and stores dO, D and the gradients dV/dK/dQ in BF16 (emulated on chips without native BF16); source comments report output errors around 5e-2 in typical mixed-precision runs and up to 4e-2 BF16 error when gradients are paged to memory.
- Issue #8 reported NaNs on SSD-1B because the softmax scale is applied after Q*K^T and the product overflows FP16; the current pseudocode still applies scaleFactor after S = Q*K^T, so test with large-magnitude activations.
- Performance needs -Ounchecked for the CPU-side Swift; the README says plain Release mode is impractical for development because it recompiles everything.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-09 with unanswered issues and a third-party fork carrying fixes, but MIT-licensed and small enough to copy into an Xcode project as the README intends.

[repo](https://github.com/philipturner/metal-flash-attention) · [benchmark](https://github.com/philipturner/metal-flash-attention)

##### nanoinfer (int8 GEMM vs cuBLAS)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Educational from-scratch C++ CNN inference engine plus CUDA int8 GEMM; beats cuBLAS only in its slow NN layout.

**Beats:** cuBLAS int8 GEMM; ONNX Runtime — On an RTX 4090 its best int8 WMMA kernel beat cuBLAS called in NN layout up to n=1024 (2.09x at 256) and lost from 2048 up, while cuBLAS in its proper TN layout is 1.6-4.5x faster at every size. On an Apple M4 Pro (CMake Release, -O3, Accelerate sgemm) the CPU engine measured 49/110/240 us vs ONNX Runtime's 48/67/184 us on the three MLPerf-Tiny-style models, so it is not faster on CPU.

**Known shortcoming:** Verifier rejected as not faster: beats cuBLAS only in slow row-major NN layout; README says cuBLAS TN is 1.6-4.5x faster at every size; CPU engine 0.60-0.99x of ONNX Runtime. Kept flagged: not faster than incumbent on its proper path.

**Known shortcoming:** int8 path slower than its own fp32 path on M4 Pro; fused fp32 conv beats cuDNN on 3 of 4 batch-1 edge-CNN shapes but loses 3x on 64-to-64 3x3 (host cost included, weak).

**How:** CPU: im2col lowering to a BLAS sgemm (Apple Accelerate, which reaches the AMX unit), bias+ReLU fusion, load-time pre-transposed Linear weights, and passing 1x1 convolutions straight to sgemm without im2col. GPU int8 GEMM: WMMA tensor-core fragments with shared-memory tile staging and a 32x32 output tile per warp (four accumulators). GPU conv: direct convolution with fused bias/ReLU epilogue and filters staged in shared memory.

**Use it when:**
- Learning or teaching how an inference engine is built: every fast path keeps a reference kernel, and the README documents each optimization step and three subtle correctness bugs
- Small batch-1 edge CNNs on Apple Silicon where you want a tiny dependency-free engine and accept 1.0-0.6x of ONNX Runtime speed
- Studying the int8 GEMM optimization ladder on Ada GPUs (dp4a, WMMA, staging, Triton tile/pipeline ablations)
- Tiny fp32 conv layers (3-channel stem, 1x1 pointwise, depthwise) at batch 1 on GPU, where its fused kernels timed faster than cuDNN back-to-back (not yet re-timed without host cost)

**Skip it when:**
- Any production int8 GEMM: cuBLAS in TN layout is 1.6x-4.5x faster than its best kernel at every size from 256 to 4096
- When you need speed over ONNX Runtime on CPU: it ties on the dense MNIST model and is 1.3-1.7x slower on depthwise models
- int8 for latency on Apple Silicon: its int8 path is 1.5-6x slower than its own fp32 path (74 vs 49 us MNIST, 1426 vs 240 us VWW)
- Models beyond the 11 supported ops (Conv2d, depthwise, Linear, ReLU, pooling, Add, Softmax, Flatten, quantize/dequantize) or anything not NCHW
- Mature dependencies: 3 commits, 0 stars, single author

**Integration:** static lib (CMake) built from source · a BLAS sgemm (Accelerate on Apple, else a blocked fallback) and pthreads; optional CUDA toolkit with cuBLAS and cuDNN for the GPU backend; uv/Python for export and benchmark tools · C++20, CMake 3.20; CUDA C++17 for the GPU backend (sm_89 default) · macOS/Apple Silicon is the measured target (NEON, SDOT probed at configure time); other platforms use a scalar/blocked fallback; CUDA on NVIDIA Ada

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to learn; for a real mobile CNN runtime use MNN, and for fast CPU matmul in LLM inference use llamafile tinyBLAS or T-MAC.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline 2.09x/1.26x/1.24x over cuBLAS is against cuBLAS called with row-major B (NN), a slow path; the author retracts it in the same README
- GPU timings in the first tables are back-to-back launches that include about 10 us of host cost per cuBLAS call at small n
- Tensor-core kernels require dimensions that are multiples of 16 (wmma) or 64 (staged); ragged shapes fall back to CUDA-core kernels
- Author states run-to-run noise of about +/-10% on an unpinned laptop; CPU differences under 15% are ties

**Status:** Active as of September 2026 but a single-author learning project (3 commits, 0 stars); MIT-licensed and small enough to read or vendor, not to depend on.

[repo](https://github.com/AshrithaG/nanoinfer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/AshrithaG/nanoinfer)

##### NNPACK (Winograd/FFT convolution)  `C`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

C99 CPU convolution primitives using Winograd and FFT tiles for stride-1 layers; fp32, AVX2/FMA3 or NEON.

**Beats:** XNNPACK (convolution_bench, 2020 version) — The only numbers are from one user's June 2020 XNNPACK issue (#689): on an unnamed 6-core 4.3 GHz x86 CPU, single-threaded, NNPACK's 8x8 Winograd took 31.9 ms and 76.2 ms on two large 3x3 layers (256 to 128 channels at 128x128, 192 to 96 at 256x256) against 1345.8 ms and 3060.0 ms for XNNPACK's convolution_bench, about 42x and 40x (derived from page data). XNNPACK was most likely built without -c opt (Bazel's unoptimised default), and Winograd's effective GFLOPS are not comparable with direct convolution, so the ratio overstates the gap; the reporter's own estimate for real networks was 3-5x, with no numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** 42x claim overstated: XNNPACK was run without '-c opt' (likely an unoptimized Bazel fastbuild).

**Known shortcoming:** nnp_initialize rejects VMs that hide L3 cache (#221, #207); SIGFPE divide-by-zero from misdetected cache sizes under nosmt (#218); silent PSIMD fallback when Python/PeachPy is missing at configure time; Winograd F(6x6,3x3) accuracy concern (#8).

**How:** Fast-convolution algorithms cut the multiply count: 3x3 stride-1 layers use tiled Winograd F(6x6,3x3) on 8x8 tiles, kernels up to 16x16 use 2D FFT on 8x8 or 16x16 tiles, 1x1 uses a direct GEMM, and everything else falls back to implicit GEMM. The transformed tiles are multiplied with register-blocked GEMM microkernels (s8gemm, c8gemm, s4c6gemm), generated on x86-64 as AVX2/FMA3 assembly through PeachPy, with L1/L2/L3 blocking sizes computed at init from cpuinfo's cache detection. Kernel transforms can be precomputed once and reused across inference calls.

**Use it when:**
- fp32 inference or training of stride-1 3x3 convolutions with many channels (VGG/ResNet-style layers) on AVX2+FMA3 x86-64 or NEON ARM CPUs, where Winograd F(6x6,3x3) does far fewer multiplies than direct convolution.
- Stride-1 convolutions with larger kernels (4x4 up to 16x16), which select the FFT 8x8 or 16x16 path.
- CPU training loops that need convolution backward passes (input and kernel gradients), not only inference.
- Repeated inference with fixed weights, using transform_strategy precompute/reuse to skip kernel transforms on every call.
- Maintaining an existing Caffe2, MXNet, TVM, tiny-dnn or darknet-nnpack deployment that already links it.

**Skip it when:**
- Depthwise, grouped or strided convolutions: these fall back to implicit GEMM, and mobile depthwise-separable networks are better served by XNNPACK (a 2019 PyTorch issue, #30622, proposed replacing NNPACK with XNNPACK on Android for this reason, without numbers).
- Quantised (int8) or fp16/bf16-activation inference: NNPACK is fp32, apart from an fp16 Winograd path on ARM with NEON-HP and fp16-weight fully-connected inference.
- x86 CPUs without AVX2/FMA3, or VMs and containers where cpuinfo cannot see a 3-level cache: nnp_initialize returns unsupported hardware (issues #221 on a Ryzen 9 7950X under Proxmox, #207 on a VM).
- Accuracy-sensitive layers: Winograd F(6x6,3x3) is less numerically stable than direct convolution; issue #8 proposes transforms said to be 100x more stable, and their adoption is not documented.
- New projects that need maintenance, Windows/MSVC or AVX-512 kernels: no commits since 2023-02-01, only an unofficial Windows port, and the x86-64 kernels are AVX2/FMA3 only.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (CMake; also a vcpkg port) · pthreadpool, cpuinfo, FXdiv, FP16 and psimd (downloaded by CMake at configure time unless *_SOURCE_DIR is set); x86-64 backend also needs Python with PeachPy, opcodes and six to generate assembly; googletest for tests · C99 (C++11 for tests), CMake 2.8.12+, Python for PeachPy on x86-64; clang required for Android arm64-v8a · x86-64 Linux/macOS (AVX2+FMA3 and a 3-level cache), ARM NEON and ARM64 on Linux/Android/iOS, Android x86/x86-64 (generic SSE2 PSIMD kernels), Emscripten asm.js/WebAssembly, scalar fallback; no mips, no official Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick NNPACK over FeatherCNN or MNN when you want standalone fp32 convolution primitives, including backward passes, for large stride-1 3x3 or bigger-kernel layers rather than a full inference engine; FeatherCNN reports beating Caffe2+NNPACK on ARM servers, and LIBXSMM is the better choice on AVX-512/AMX x86 for small-GEMM-based convolution.

**Gotchas:**
- On x86-64, if CMake cannot find a Python interpreter it silently falls back to the generic PSIMD backend instead of the AVX2 assembly kernels; Android x86-64 builds always use SSE2 PSIMD kernels.
- Cache-blocking sizes come from detected cache sizes: issue #218 reports a SIGFPE (input_channels_block_max rounding to 0, then a division) in convolution-inference.c on an AMD EPYC 7552 booted with nosmt, where cache sizes were misdetected.
- Workspace buffers must be 64-byte aligned; passing workspace_buffer NULL with a size pointer returns the required size and does not compute, and passing both NULL makes NNPACK allocate on every call.
- The CMake build downloads dependencies and PeachPy from the network at configure time; issues report a failed cpuinfo tag checkout (#213), a missing fp16/psimd.h (#222) and non-reproducible builds (#206).

**Status:** Abandoned (last commit 2023-02-01, many open build and hardware-detection issues) but BSD-2-Clause and still an optional backend in PyTorch and TVM builds; vendor it only for fp32 stride-1 convolution on AVX2 or NEON CPUs.

[repo](https://github.com/Maratyszcza/NNPACK) · [benchmark](https://github.com/google/XNNPACK/issues/689)

##### OneFlow  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Distributed deep learning training framework (C++/CUDA core, PyTorch-like Python API); vendor DLPerf shows 1.1-1.5x NGC PyTorch/MXNet on 32 V100s.

**Beats:** NVIDIA NGC 20.03 containers (MXNet 1.6.0, TensorFlow 1.15.2, PyTorch 1.5.0a0) running NVIDIA DeepLearningExamples, plus stock PyTorch 1.6.0, TensorFlow 2.3.0, MXNet 1.6.0 (gluon-cv/gluon-nlp), PaddlePaddle 1.8.3 and MindSpore official model scripts — OneFlow's own DLPerf report (Oct 2020) trains ResNet-50 v1.5 and BERT-base on 4 nodes x 8 V100-SXM2-16GB (Xeon Gold 5118 hosts, 100 Gb/s InfiniBand, CUDA 10.2) with each framework's official or NVIDIA DeepLearningExamples scripts, taking the median of repeated 100-step runs. OneFlow 0.2.0 reached 12411.97 img/s FP32 and 33141.02 img/s AMP on ResNet-50 vs 10917.09 and 22551.16 for NGC PyTorch 20.03 (about 1.14x and 1.47x) and 11331.93 and 30713.68 for NGC MXNet (about 1.10x and 1.08x), and 15724.70 vs 10349.12 sentences/s (about 1.52x) on BERT AMP against NGC PyTorch; ratios derived from page data, no compiler flags given for any framework.

**Known shortcoming:** Vendor-run (Oct 2020) with 2020-era baselines; only 1.10x FP32 / 1.08x AMP over NGC MXNet; README NGC MXNet 11233.92 vs report 11331.93 inconsistency; stale.

**Known shortcoming:** Speedup comes from multi-node scaling: on 1 V100 only ~1.4% over NGC MXNet (397.64 vs 392.24); on BERT AMP bsz64 at 32 GPUs MXNet without clip beats OneFlow without clip (11269.14 vs 11195.72); newest PyPI is 0.9.0 (2023) and v1.0.0 is a GitHub release only; softmax/layernorm fast-math on by default.

**How:** Per the OneFlow paper (arXiv 2110.15032; abstract read via WebSearch, PDF not opened), the speed comes from two ideas: the SBP abstraction, which lets the compiler insert the needed collective ('boxing') operations automatically, and an actor-model runtime where each op is an actor that runs when its inputs and its output buffers are ready, so compute, data movement and communication overlap without a central scheduler. The DLPerf numbers point to scaling rather than per-kernel speed: on one V100, ResNet-50 FP32 is 397.64 vs 392.24 img/s for NGC MXNet (about 1.4%, derived from page data), widening to 12411.97 vs 11331.93 at 32 GPUs. The build also enables fused/fast-math softmax and layer-norm kernels by default (OF_SOFTMAX_USE_FAST_MATH, OF_LAYER_NORM_USE_FAST_MATH).

**Use it when:**
- Multi-node, multi-GPU training on NVIDIA clusters where you want data, tensor (model) and pipeline parallelism expressed through placement/SBP annotations instead of hand-written NCCL calls.
- Large embedding or recommendation (Wide&Deep-style) training: DLPerf shows OneFlow 0.2.0 holding about 22.4 ms per iteration up to 819.2M-row vocabularies, while HugeCTR 2.2 ran out of memory above 25.6M rows.
- Teams that already write PyTorch-style code and want a static-graph compile step (nn.Graph) with ZeRO, gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing built in.
- Chinese accelerator targets: recent commits add Ascend NPU, Cambricon MLU and KunLunXin XPU device support.

**Skip it when:**
- As a kernel library to drop into an existing C++ or PyTorch codebase: it is a whole framework, and the C++ API is beta and off by default.
- Single-GPU training: the vendor's own numbers show near parity with NGC MXNet on one V100 (about 1.4% FP32), so the claimed gains appear only at multi-node scale.
- Projects that need current releases and fast bug turnaround: PyPI stops at 0.9.0 (2023-01-07), v1.0.0 exists only as a GitHub release, the last commit was 2025-08-20, and performance issues such as #10437 (slow elementwise template on RTX 3090) have no visible maintainer reply.
- Comparisons on modern hardware: every published framework-vs-framework number is from 2020 (OneFlow 0.2.0, V100, CUDA 10.2) against 2020 NGC containers; nothing shows the gap still holds against current PyTorch.
- Windows or macOS hosts: the README lists Linux only, with Python 3.7 to 3.11, and the PyPI wheels are x86-64 manylinux only.

**Integration:** module (Python package with a C++/CUDA shared-library core; pip wheels or CMake source build) · CUDA Toolkit 10.0+ and cuDNN for GPU builds, NCCL, oneDNN (WITH_ONEDNN on by default), OpenBLAS, nasm, protobuf/gRPC-era third-party libraries built by the CMake THIRD_PARTY step; optional MLIR, RDMA · C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17), CMake 3.18+, CUDA 10.0+ with driver 440.33+, Python 3.7-3.11 · Linux x86-64; NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 6.0+ (Pascal and newer); CPU-only builds; Ascend NPU, Cambricon MLU and KunLunXin XPU backends in recent commits

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings (LightSeq, ByteTransformer, FasterTransformer, oneDNN Graph Compiler) are kernel or inference libraries that plug into an existing framework; pick OneFlow only when you want to replace the training framework itself to get SBP-based multi-node parallelism. If you just need faster transformer layers inside PyTorch training, LightSeq is the smaller change.

**Gotchas:**
- Softmax and layer-norm kernels are compiled with fast-math variants by default (OF_SOFTMAX_USE_FAST_MATH and OF_LAYER_NORM_USE_FAST_MATH are ON), which can change low-order bits compared with PyTorch.
- The headline BERT comparison against MXNet is run without gradient clipping (gluon-nlp lacks clip_by_global_norm); at AMP batch 64 on 32 GPUs, MXNet without clipping (11269.14) is slightly ahead of OneFlow without clipping (11195.72).
- Sources in the DLPerf table disagree: the README summary lists NGC MXNet ResNet-50 FP32 at 11233.92 img/s, while the report's 4x8 row gives 11331.93.
- The CUDA build cache defaults to RelWithDebInfo and shared libraries; the README's source build expects CUDA_TOOLKIT_ROOT_DIR and CUDNN_ROOT_DIR to be set, and NCCL may fail under make -j$(nproc) (troubleshooting doc).

**Status:** Stale: last commit 2025-08-20 (NPU multinomial support), with the newest PyPI wheel 0.9.0 from 2023-01-07, though the repo is not archived, is Apache-2.0 and has about 9.4k stars; treat it as a framework to evaluate, not a library to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/Oneflow-Inc/oneflow) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf/blob/master/README.md)

##### OpenEquivariance  `Python/C++ (JIT-generated CUDA, HIP and SYCL kernels)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

JIT GPU kernel generator for e3nn-style Clebsch-Gordan tensor products and fused graph convolutions; claims up to 10x over e3nn.

**Beats:** e3nn (torch.compile max-autotune with CUDA graphs in the harness); also compared with NVIDIA cuEquivariance and FlashTP — All headline claims are first-party. The README claims up to 10x over e3nn, with the harness's e3nn baseline compiled by torch.compile max-autotune with CUDA graphs, and parity with cuEquivariance; the docs claim up to 2x over FlashTP's fused kernels, measured on an A100-SXM-80GB at LBNL/NERSC Perlmutter with no compiler or flags stated. The paper abstract (SIAM ACDA25, seen only as search snippets whose figures vary by version) gives up to 4.5-4.8x forward and 3x backward over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn and up to 5.3-5.4x MACE inference speedup. One outside data point: the Nequix maintainer reported 2.5x (1000 atoms) and 3.3x (1728 atoms) end-to-end gains from adding the oeq kernels to Nequix's PyTorch port, on an A100 per the thread.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: README gives order-of-magnitude over e3nn and docs 2x over FlashTP, first-party; the ACDA25 paper (arXiv 2501.13986: >10x e3nn, up to 4.5x forward over cuEquivariance) was blocked and seen only as snippets. B candidate once the paper is opened.

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #211: an AMD HIP warp-sync bug gave non-conservative forces on NequIP-OAM-L at l_max=3 (9.3-32.8 meV/A, +79.7 eV/ns NVE drift, OEQ 0.6.8), fixed in PR #217 on 2026-09-10 (v0.7.0). Paper abstract snippets give 4.5x or 4.8x forward over cuEquivariance depending on version; the paper is still unopened.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo holds a harness (tests/benchmark.py, docs name an A100-SXM-80GB) but no committed numbers, and e3nn/cuEquivariance versions are unpinned; a newer paper snippet claims only 1.3x over cuEquivariance and 6.2x on MACE (older: 4.5x).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** semi-independent: Nequix maintainer (discussion #5) measured oeq kernels 2.5x (1000 atoms) and 3.3x (1728 atoms) end-to-end on the Nequix PyTorch port, A100; he also contributed OEQ JAX lowerings

**Independent measurement:** retier check 14

**How:** It exploits the sparsity of the Clebsch-Gordan (Wigner 3j) coefficient tensor. At JIT time the generator enumerates the nonzeros and writes them as hex float literals into fully unrolled CUDA/HIP code from Jinja templates (ComputationSchedule.py, loop_unroll_tp.cuh), so no sparse indexing happens at run time. Each warp works out of its own shared-memory slice: the problem is split into segments whose irreps and weights fit per-warp shared memory, and 'uvw' paths use a warp-level, register-tiled matmul (wmm.cuh). The fused convolution never materializes per-edge messages; it reduces with atomics, or deterministically over receiver-sorted edges with a transpose permutation for the backward pass, with optional Kahan summation.

**Use it when:**
- Training or running MACE, NequIP, Nequix or SevenNet-style models on NVIDIA or AMD GPUs where e3nn tensor products dominate step time; NequIP documents an OpenEquivariance acceleration path.
- Large molecular graphs where unfused e3nn message passing runs out of memory: the docs say the MACE carbon.xyz benchmark (158K edges) needs an 80GB GPU with e3nn, while the fused oeq convolution is expected to fit.
- You need an open-source alternative to NVIDIA cuEquivariance (closed-source kernel package), or you need AMD (HIP), JAX or Intel XPU (beta SYCL) support.
- Models that need float64 tensor products or higher-order derivatives (forces, force-matching training, Hessian-like terms).

**Skip it when:**
- Tensor products outside pure 'uvu'/'uvw': mixed instruction types, other connection modes and non-trainable instructions are unsupported. Per a NequIP docs snippet seen in search, Allegro models cannot use it.
- CPU-only systems, or nodes with mixed GPU generations: there is no CPU path, and kernels are compiled for the compute capability of the first visible GPU only.
- You need an independent head-to-head against FlashTP at high angular momentum: issue #171 asked for one and got no answer, and the '2x over FlashTP' claim is first-party.
- MACE symmetric contraction: it is beta, needs e3nn, is not exposed at the package top level, and the docs note user reports of weak backward-pass performance.
- AMD GPUs with versions before 0.7.0: a HIP warp-sync bug produced non-conservative forces (issue #211).

**Integration:** module (pip package 'openequivariance' plus a C++ extension; kernels are JIT-compiled at first use, with NVRTC on CUDA per issue #162) · PyTorch >= 2.4 (>= 2.10 for the precompiled extension, AOTI, export and Intel XPU) or JAX > 0.5.0 with the separate openequivariance_extjax package; CUDA or HIP toolkit, or oneAPI icpx for SYCL; e3nn only for tests, benchmarks and symmetric contraction · GCC 9+ (c++ --version >= 9.0), Linux, Python with PyTorch or JAX · Linux GPUs only: NVIDIA (run-tested V100, A100-40/80GB, A5000, T4, H100), AMD (MI250x, MI300x), Intel Data Center GPU Max via beta SYCL; no CPU backend

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over cuEquivariance when you need open-source kernels, AMD/Intel GPUs, JAX, float64 or the memory-saving fused convolution. Pick cuEquivariance for NVIDIA-only, vendor-supported kernels that also cover Allegro. batmobile reports larger single-kernel gains over e3nn on an RTX 3090 but covers a much narrower set of operations and frameworks.

**Gotchas:**
- The first import builds a C++ extension, which can take minutes; issues #156 and #207 report import hangs on a stale build lock (PR #209 added a timeout), and #175 reports a compilation cache that did not persist on L40S/RTX 6000.
- Modules saved after torch.compile or torch.export load only on the same GPU architecture; uncompiled modules recompile kernels when loaded on another GPU.
- deterministic=True (the faster, atomics-free convolution) requires edges sorted by receiver, inputs permuted with receiver_perm, and a sender transpose permutation; deterministic=False accepts any order but uses atomics.
- Before v0.7.0 the HIP kernels used a block-level thread fence where CUDA used __syncwarp. On an MI300, NequIP-OAM-L (l_max = 3) gave non-conservative forces: 9.3-32.8 meV/A force differences and +79.7 eV/ns NVE energy drift (issue #211, OEQ 0.6.8). It was fixed in PR #217 on 2026-09-10, so upgrade on AMD.

**Status:** Actively maintained academic project (v0.7.0 on 2026-09-10, SYCL backend merged 2026-09-23), BSD-3-Clause (LBNL/UC Berkeley) and pip-installable; it ships frequent correctness fixes, so pin a recent version.

[repo](https://github.com/PASSIONLab/OpenEquivariance) · [benchmark](https://github.com/PASSIONLab/OpenEquivariance/blob/main/docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst)

##### OpenVINO (CPU inference runtime)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Intel's open-source inference runtime; on x86 CPUs it ran ResNet-50 about 2x faster than TFLite+XNNPACK, but did not win on MobileNet V2.

**Beats:** TensorFlow Lite with the XNNPACK delegate (XNNPACK) — A small third-party harness (yaysummeriscoming/xnnpack_benchmarks; 8-vCPU Google Cloud VM, CPU model not stated, Ubuntu 16.04, OpenVINO 2020.3.194 apt packages vs TFLite built from TensorFlow master with Bazel 3.0.0) measured batch-1 ResNet-50 at 62.55 ms vs 118.3 ms single-threaded and 16.70 vs 32.8 ms with 8 threads (about 1.9x and 2.0x, derived from page data). MobileNet V2 tied at 1 thread and lost at 8 threads; throughput mode reached 382.44 vs 316.46 FPS (MobileNet V2) and 67.73 vs 30.49 FPS (ResNet-50). No compiler flags or CPU model were stated, and the source is first-party-level evidence (tier C).

**Known shortcoming:** Source is a 1-star personal harness; engines ran different models (Caffe OMZ vs modified Keras with random weights); CPU model and flags unstated; first table is single-thread; loses MobileNet V2 at 8 threads.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is from 2020.3 with mismatched model graphs; 'throughput' rows are multi-stream async vs single-stream TFLite; automatic bf16/f16 on AMX/Arm changes f32 results; telemetry on by default (GA4); 2026 releases require AVX2.

**How:** The CPU plugin lowers the graph onto its own fork of oneDNN, whose kernels are JIT-generated with Xbyak for the host ISA (AVX2, AVX-512, AMX), and also vendors MLAS and LIBXSMM, plus Arm Compute Library and KleidiAI for Arm. Graph passes fuse convolution with activations, ScaleShift/PReLU and FakeQuantize, FullyConnected with activations, and convolution with a following depthwise convolution, which cuts memory round-trips. On hardware with native bf16/f16 it switches inference precision to half automatically (AMX on Xeon, armv8.2-a+fp16 on Arm). Throughput mode runs several 'streams', each with its own host thread pinned to a NUMA-aligned group of cores, so independent requests run in parallel.

**Use it when:**
- Batch-1 latency for mid-size CNNs such as ResNet-50 on Intel x86 CPUs, where the benchmark shows about 1.9x (1 thread) and 2.0x (8 threads) lower latency than TFLite+XNNPACK.
- Throughput serving of many independent requests on multi-core Xeons with the THROUGHPUT hint or ov::num_streams, letting the plugin pin streams to cores and NUMA nodes.
- INT8-quantized or bf16 models on recent Xeons (AMX) where the plugin's FakeQuantize fusion and automatic half precision apply.
- Teams that want one C++/Python runtime across Intel CPU, integrated or discrete Intel GPU and NPU, fed by models from several training frameworks.
- Hybrid Intel client CPUs (P-cores plus E-cores), where the plugin decides which core types each hint uses.

**Skip it when:**
- Small mobile-style networks such as MobileNet V2: TFLite+XNNPACK was faster at 8 threads (3.16 vs 3.56 ms) and tied single-threaded (11.48 vs 11.14 ms).
- x86 CPUs without AVX2: the 2026 release notes state the CPU plugin now requires AVX2 and SSE-only CPUs are no longer supported, although the repo's system-requirements page still lists SSE4.2 Atom parts.
- Arm deployments of quantized models: the docs say Arm executes them in simulation mode, entirely in floating point; CPU inference on Windows ARM64 is not supported.
- Size-constrained embedded builds: the source tree pulls in dozens of submodules (frontends, protobuf, ONNX, OpenCL, level-zero), so expect to use the selective-build option to trim it.
- Workloads that need bit-identical f32 results on AMX or Arm fp16 hardware unless you pin ov::hint::inference_precision to f32.

**Integration:** shared lib (OpenVINO Runtime core plus per-device plugin libraries); also pip, conda-forge, Homebrew and npm packages · bundled as git submodules: openvinotoolkit/oneDNN fork, Xbyak, MLAS, LIBXSMM, Arm Compute Library, KleidiAI, pugixml, zlib, protobuf, ONNX, flatbuffers, snappy, OpenCL and level-zero (for GPU/NPU), telemetry · C++17, CMake 3.26+, GCC 7.5+ on Linux (build docs); Python 3.9-3.12 for the Python API · x86-64 (AVX2 minimum for the CPU plugin in 2026 releases), Arm armv7a and arm64-v8a, Apple silicon; Windows 10/11, Ubuntu 22.04-26.04, RHEL 8/9, macOS 12.6+; Intel GPU and NPU via separate plugins

**Vs siblings:** Pick OpenVINO over MNN for whole-model inference on Intel x86 servers and desktops (AMX, INT8, multi-stream throughput, Intel GPU/NPU offload); MNN's own paper targets mobile CPUs, where it beats TFLite and NCNN. Over LIBXSMM or the oneDNN Graph Compiler, pick it when you want a complete runtime rather than kernels; OpenVINO's CPU plugin already vendors LIBXSMM and a oneDNN fork.

**Gotchas:**
- On CPUs with native bf16/f16 the plugin silently uses half precision instead of f32; the docs warn accuracy can differ (notably for LLMs) and say to set ov::hint::inference_precision to f32 or use the accuracy execution mode.
- The README says OpenVINO collects performance and usage telemetry, partly via Google Analytics 4; opt out with `opt_in_out --opt_out`.
- The benchmark's 'throughput optimized' rows come from benchmark_app -api async (several streams) and trade per-image latency for FPS (MobileNet V2: 10.40 ms latency at 382 FPS), while the TFLite rows ran one inference at a time, so compare like-for-like modes.
- The benchmark used OpenVINO 2020.3 with Caffe models converted to FP32 IR, while TFLite+XNNPACK ran Keras-built models with padding layers and the global-average-pool mean removed, so the two engines did not run identical graphs.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-01, release 2026.3 on 4 August 2026, about 10.9k stars, Apache-2.0); the comparison is from the 2020.3 release, so current OpenVINO and XNNPACK may differ in either direction.

[repo](https://github.com/openvinotoolkit/openvino) · [benchmark](https://github.com/yaysummeriscoming/xnnpack_benchmarks)

##### pytorch-qrnn (QRNN CUDA kernels)  `Python (CUDA kernels compiled at runtime via CuPy and pynvrtc)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Archived PyTorch QRNN layer with a runtime-compiled CUDA recurrence kernel; trained language models about 2x faster per epoch than cuDNN LSTM.

**Beats:** NVIDIA cuDNN LSTM — The README's 2-17x figure is Figure 4 of the ICLR 2017 QRNN paper, measured on an earlier (pre-PyTorch) implementation: a 320-unit QRNN layer is 1.3x (batch 256) to 16.9x (batch 8, sequence 512) faster than an equal-size cuDNN LSTM in inference, and a two-layer 640-unit PTB LM trains at roughly 150 vs 290 ms per batch (read off the bar chart). The only numbers on this PyTorch code are first-party from awd-lstm-lm on an NVIDIA Quadro GP100: Penn Treebank 28 vs 65 s/epoch and WikiText-2 90 vs 180 s/epoch for QRNN vs cuDNN LSTM, with differently shaped models and no PyTorch, CUDA or cuDNN versions given.

**Known shortcoming:** README figure comes from the Nov 2016 paper, which predates this code (first commit 2017-09-28); low end overstated (1.3x at batch 256, not 2x); measured numbers for this code are only about 2x per epoch on a Quadro GP100 (awd-lstm-lm README).

**Known shortcoming:** Does not run on current PyTorch (legacy non-static autograd.Function, #29). Kernel takes float pointers with no dtype check, so fp16/fp64 input is a correctness risk. CUDA stream cached per device. pynvrtc install breaks (#26, #17). Gate convention flipped vs the paper (#22).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** QRNN removes the hidden-to-hidden matrix product: the candidate, forget and output gates for all timesteps come from one large nn.Linear over the input (with a window of 1 or 2 previous inputs concatenated), which runs as a single big GEMM. The only sequential part is ForgetMult, a small CUDA kernel compiled at runtime with NVRTC and launched through CuPy, which assigns one thread per (batch, hidden unit) and walks the timesteps in a loop; the backward kernel walks them in reverse with a double-precision accumulator. The README says gains are largest at small batch sizes and long sequences, where cuDNN LSTM is limited by its step-by-step dependency.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or reproducing QRNN / AWD-QRNN language-model results from 2017-2018 on the PyTorch versions of that era
- Unidirectional sequence models on GPU with long sequences or small batches, where the paper figure shows the largest advantage over cuDNN LSTM (up to 16.9x at batch 8, sequence length 512)
- As a template for a fused gated linear recurrence: the 60-line ForgetMult kernel is easy to port to a modern torch.autograd.Function or a C++/CUDA extension

**Skip it when:**
- Current PyTorch: GPUForgetMult is a legacy autograd.Function with a non-static forward, which newer PyTorch rejects ('Legacy autograd function with non-static forward method is deprecated', issue #29, unanswered)
- Bidirectional models, batch_first inputs, bias=False or PackedSequence variable-length batches: the constructor asserts against the first three and the README lists PackedSequence as unsupported
- fp16, bf16 or fp64 training: the CUDA kernels are written for float pointers only and the Python wrapper does not check the dtype
- Large-batch workloads: the paper figure shows only 1.3x-1.4x at batch 256 for every sequence length, and the awd-lstm-lm README notes that most time then goes to softmax and optimizer overhead
- Cases needing an exact LSTM: QRNN gives 'similar accuracy' after retraining, not identical outputs or transferable weights

**Integration:** module · PyTorch (2017-era Variable API), CuPy, pynvrtc (NVIDIA NVRTC Python bindings), a CUDA toolkit with NVRTC · Python 3; PyTorch 0.2-0.4 era (awd-lstm-lm, its main user, requires PyTorch 0.4); exact upper bound not documented · Linux with an NVIDIA GPU for the fast path; CPU fallback is a Python loop over timesteps

**Vs siblings:** No catalogued sibling is a GPU recurrent-layer replacement for cuDNN LSTM; RTNeural is the pick for small real-time LSTM/GRU inference on CPU, while the transformer runtimes (CTranslate2, LightSeq, FasterTransformer) target attention models. Choose pytorch-qrnn only if you specifically want the QRNN architecture and are prepared to modernise its autograd code.

**Gotchas:**
- The CUDA stream is captured once per device when the kernel is first configured; later calls on a different stream still launch on the cached one
- Installation breaks with newer pynvrtc (issue #26: 'bytes' object has no attribute 'encode'; issue #17 on double encoding), and there are open reports of window=2 size mismatches (issue #19)
- The forget-gate convention is the reverse of the paper's equation (issue #22, unanswered); harmless when training from scratch but matters when porting weights between implementations
- With window=2 and save_prev_x=True you must call reset() between independent sequences, or the previous batch's last input leaks into the next one

**Status:** Abandoned: last code commit 2017-11-26, archived 2022-02-12, BSD-3-Clause; small enough to vendor and port, but it does not run unmodified on current PyTorch.

[repo](https://github.com/salesforce/pytorch-qrnn) · [benchmark](https://github.com/salesforce/awd-lstm-lm/blob/HEAD/README.md)

##### QuACK (CuTe-DSL memory-bound kernels)  `Python (CUTLASS CuTe-DSL)`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Python CuTe-DSL GPU kernels for RMSNorm, softmax and cross-entropy that reach about 3 TB/s on H100, beating torch.compile and Liger.

**Beats:** cuDNN v9.10.1 (RMSNorm only), torch.compile (PyTorch 2.7.1, default mode) and Liger Kernel v0.5.10 — The authors' July 2025 blog measures model memory throughput of RMSNorm, softmax and cross-entropy (forward and backward, FP32 and BF16, batch 8k-32k, reduction dim 256-262k) on one H100 80GB HBM3 (3.35 TB/s peak) with a Xeon Platinum 8468 host, against torch.compile (PyTorch 2.7.1, default mode), Liger Kernel v0.5.10 (up to 65k only) and cuDNN v9.10.1 (RMSNorm only). QuACK holds about 3 TB/s (about 90% of peak) above 4k and reaches 3.01 vs 1.89 TB/s for FP32 softmax at 262k (about 1.59x, derived from page data, which the blog calls 'nearly 50% more'); CuTe-DSL and CUDA versions are not stated and the per-size numbers are only in a figure.

**Known shortcoming:** CuTe-DSL version not stated (harness public).

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #9: the blog's Liger cross-entropy comparison is unfair (Liger forward also computes the gradient); the current harness benchmarks CE against torch.compile only; issue #77: rmsnorm_fwd 2.6x slower inside torch.compile on B200; softmax uses rcp_approx.

**How:** Each row is read from HBM once with 128-bit coalesced cp.async loads into shared memory and registers, then reduced hierarchically: thread, warp (butterfly shuffle), block (shared memory) and, on Hopper and newer, thread-block cluster reduction over distributed shared memory (DSMEM), where up to 16 SMs pool their shared memory. That lets a 3-pass softmax keep a 65k-262k element row on chip instead of re-reading it, whereas torch.compile's Triton softmax reads the input twice and Liger's softmax spills registers above 32k (blog NCU analysis). The reported metric is model memory throughput (minimum bytes over time), so most of the gain over torch.compile comes from moving fewer bytes, not from faster DRAM access.

**Use it when:**
- LLM training or inference on H100, B200/B300 or RTX 50 GPUs where RMSNorm, softmax or cross-entropy shows up in profiles, especially with very wide rows (vocab-size cross-entropy, reduction dim 65k and up), where the blog says QuACK beats every baseline.
- Replacing torch.compile-generated norm or softmax kernels in eager PyTorch code; at reduction dim 262k FP32 softmax it reports 3.01 vs 1.89 TB/s.
- Fused RMSNorm with residual add, prenorm output, per-head (B, S, H, D) weights or Gemma-style weight_offset in a single kernel.
- Teams that want readable kernel source to adapt: the blog walks through the TV-layout, load strategy and reduction helpers used in rmsnorm.py and softmax.py.
- JAX users needing a fast softmax on Hopper/Blackwell via the optional jax extra.

**Skip it when:**
- A100, Ada (RTX 40) or older GPUs, or AMD: the README lists only H100, B200/B300 and RTX 50 (issue #21 asks about Ada, and a ROCm backend is only an RFC, #178). Cluster reduction, the source of the long-row advantage, needs sm90+.
- C++ or non-Python inference engines: kernels are Python CuTe-DSL compiled at runtime through nvidia-cutlass-dsl, so there is nothing to link from C++.
- Small reduction dims (under about 4k), where the blog claims no advantage and the per-size results exist only in a figure.
- Inside a larger torch.compile graph: open issue #77 reports rmsnorm_fwd going from 0.0413 ms (4685 GB/s) to 0.1067 ms (1815 GB/s) on B200 when wrapped in torch.compile.
- Environments pinned to older toolchains: it needs CUDA 12.9+, a recent nvidia-cutlass-dsl (>=4.7) and Python 3.12 per the README, and several open issues (#187, #188) are crashes from API drift in cuda-bindings and CUTLASS.

**Integration:** module (pip package quack-kernels; Python CuTe-DSL kernels JIT-compiled at first call) · nvidia-cutlass-dsl>=4.7 (cu13 extra for CUDA 13), torch, apache-tvm-ffi>=0.1.6,<0.2, einops; optional nvidia-matmul-heuristics, jax + jax-tvm-ffi · CUDA toolkit 12.9+, Python 3.12 (README; pyproject declares >=3.10) · NVIDIA H100 (sm90), B200/B300 (sm100) and RTX 50 (sm120) per the README; OS not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick QuACK over Liger-Kernel when you are on H100/B200-class GPUs and need the fastest standalone norm, softmax or cross-entropy, especially with rows of 65k elements or more, where Liger spills registers or does not support the size. Liger-Kernel is the easier choice for patching Hugging Face models' RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU and cross-entropy in one step. FlashAttention-3 and ThunderKittens cover attention and GEMM, not these reductions.

**Gotchas:**
- Kernels are compiled per dtype and row length N on first call (jit_cache), so new hidden or vocab sizes pay a one-time compile; issue #166 asks to bucket N in the norm forward cache key.
- Softmax forward multiplies by an approximate reciprocal (rcp_approx) of the denominator, so outputs differ slightly from torch.softmax; layernorm requires 2D input and fp32 weight and bias.
- Importing quack monkey-patches CuTe's tensor classes process-wide (quack.dsl indexing sugar), which can surprise other CuTe-DSL code in the same process.
- The blog's cross-entropy comparison with Liger is disputed: issue #9 notes that Liger's CE forward also computes the gradient, so timing forward alone understates Liger, and the current benchmarks/benchmark_cross_entropy.py compares only quack against torch.compile.

**Status:** Actively developed (Apache-2.0, about 1.2k stars, 48 PyPI releases from 0.1.0 on 2025-06-20 to 0.6.5 on 2026-09-11, last commit 2026-09-13), but pre-1.0 and tracking fast-moving CUTLASS DSL releases, so pin versions.

[repo](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/HEAD/media/2025-07-10-membound-sol.md)

##### RTNeural  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Real-time-safe C++ inference for small Dense/GRU/LSTM/Conv nets; per-sample calls run 2x-190x faster than ONNX Runtime/libtorch/TFLite.

**Beats:** libtorch, ONNX Runtime 1.15.1, TensorFlow Lite 2.14.0 — In the author's RTNeural-compare harness on a 2018 Mac Mini (Intel Core i7-8700B), single layers process 10 s of 48 kHz signal one sample per call: LSTM size 4 runs at 268x real time (Eigen, compile-time API) vs 1.42x for ONNX Runtime 1.15.1 and 0.375x for libtorch, narrowing to 6.46x vs 1.13x and 0.262x at size 64; Dense size 64 is 76.8x vs TensorFlow Lite 2.14 at 40.7x. Release CMake build, compiler unstated; the libtorch loop runs without NoGradGuard/InferenceMode at default threads (ONNX Runtime is pinned to 1 thread), and baselines were timed only in the STL-backend run.

**Known shortcoming:** STL backend slower than ONNX Runtime (LSTM 64) and TFLite (Dense 64); baselines timed only in the STL run; compiler unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Biased baseline: RTNeural-compare's libtorch loop runs without NoGradGuard/InferenceMode at the default thread count while ONNX Runtime is pinned to 1 thread; open issue #157 reports a segfault with two 512-unit GRUs in the compile-time API (no reply).

**How:** It removes framework overhead rather than out-computing the frameworks: no tensor objects, graph dispatch, threading or allocation per call, just a matrix-vector product per layer on preallocated, aligned buffers. The compile-time API fixes every dimension at compile time (Eigen fixed-size matrices or xsimd arrays), so loops unroll and vectorize. The LSTM, for example, stacks W, U and bias into one [4*out x (in+out+1)] matrix and does a single GEMV per step, then applies sigmoid/tanh to the gate segments. Backends: Eigen (default, better for larger layers), xsimd (better for very small layers) or plain STL; an optional RTNEURAL_USE_AVX build adds -mavx2 -mfma with 32-byte alignment.

**Use it when:**
- Neural audio effects and amp/pedal models (GuitarML, AIDA-X, BYOD, NeuralNote-style plugins) that must process one sample or a short block per callback with no allocation.
- Small recurrent or dense networks, roughly 4-64 hidden units, where per-call overhead of a general runtime dominates; the author's logs show 6x-268x real time for LSTM at 48 kHz on one i7-8700B core.
- Architectures known at compile time: use ModelT with the Eigen or xsimd backend for the fastest path.
- Embedded or plugin targets (x86, ARM incl. armv7 and Raspberry Pi per downstream users) where you want a header-style dependency with BSD-3 licensing and no runtime library.

**Skip it when:**
- Batched or large-model inference: the benchmark gap shrinks fast with layer size (Dense 64: Eigen 76.8x vs TFLite 40.7x real time), and a reported crash with two 512-unit GRUs in the compile-time API (issue #157, open, no reply) suggests large static models are untested.
- Layers outside Dense, Conv1D/Conv2D, GRU, LSTM, BatchNorm1D/2D and the tanh/ReLU/sigmoid/softmax/ELU/PReLU activations: MaxPooling, vanilla RNN, attention/transformers and TCN-style blocks are open requests (#102, #147, #120).
- Training, GPU execution or importing ONNX/TorchScript graphs: inference only, CPU only, JSON weights only.
- The STL backend on anything but tiny layers: at size 64 it falls to 1.01x (LSTM) and 8.69x (Dense) real time, below ONNX Runtime and TFLite in the author's own logs.

**Integration:** header-style library; CMake add_subdirectory builds a small STATIC target, or include headers directly without CMake · nlohmann/json (bundled in modules/json) for model loading; Eigen or xsimd (bundled submodules) depending on backend; none for the STL backend · C++14 (CMake errors below 14; C++17 enables if constexpr); CMake 3.11+ · any C++14 target; armv7 uses 8-byte alignment; optional AVX2+FMA on x86 via RTNEURAL_USE_AVX

**Vs siblings:** Pick RTNeural over OpenVINO, MNN or ONNX-class runtimes when the network is tiny and called per audio sample under a hard real-time deadline; pick tiny-cuda-nn for small MLPs only when you are on an NVIDIA GPU with large batches, and LIBXSMM when you are writing your own CPU kernels rather than loading a trained model.

**Gotchas:**
- Without CMake you must define RTNEURAL_DEFAULT_ALIGNMENT (16 or 32) and a backend macro yourself; a missing alignment define only warns and falls back to 16, which mismatches an AVX build.
- Recurrent layers are stateful by default; call reset() before the first forward() and between independent sequences (issue #167 reports pops/clicks when reset() is called mid-stream).
- JSON parsing and model construction allocate and use iostreams: do them off the audio thread; only forward()/reset() are marked RTNEURAL_REALTIME (checked with RealtimeSanitizer in CI).
- Default sigmoid/tanh are exact Eigen/STL math; faster approximations require supplying your own MathsProvider template argument.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-20, 848 stars, used by more than a dozen shipping audio plugins) and BSD-3-Clause, so safe to vendor; note the reference paper (arXiv 2106.03037) is a preprint.

[repo](https://github.com/jatinchowdhury18/RTNeural) · [benchmark](https://github.com/jatinchowdhury18/RTNeural-compare/blob/main/README.md)

##### Sobek (streaming equivariant tensor-product convolutions)  `Python/CUDA (generated CUDA kernels, PyTorch extension)`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Generated-CUDA PyTorch backend for equivariant tensor-product graph convolutions; claims 1.2x-49.7x over OpenEquivariance with bounded memory.

**Beats:** OpenEquivariance (primary), also cuEquivariance and e3nn — The authors' preprint (arXiv 2607.18074, read only through search snippets) reports Sobek faster in all 75 OpenEquivariance-capacity-matched comparisons (UVW 16-profile and UVU 9-profile grids, forward, backward and double backward), 1.2x to 49.7x, with up to 99% lower peak allocated memory, on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 in fp32 per a search snippet. The repo's harness (sobek/benchmarks/measure.py, runners.py) times medians of CUDA-event samples after warmup, and by default times OpenEquivariance including the phi @ radial_linear weight expansion and receiver sort (an oe_preexpanded variant excludes the expansion); no result files are checked in and the nvcc flags are -O3 plus PyTorch arch flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: first-party arXiv 2607.18074 preprint (snippet only) with 1.2x-49.7x over OpenEquivariance across 75 comparisons; the repo has a benchmark CLI but no published results and the GPU is unknown. 12 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** v0.1.0 with 5 commits; float32 only; not a drop-in replacement (different call signature and ir_mul layout); no FlashTP comparison. The harness times OpenEquivariance including its phi @ radial_linear expansion and receiver sort (the oe_preexpanded variant leaves the expansion out); paper hardware per snippet is an RTX 5090 in fp32; no result files are checked in.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It fuses the last radial linear layer into the convolution and reassociates the computation so edge-local products are reduced straight into bounded receiver-side state, so the per-edge weight tensor, per-edge messages and their adjoints are never materialized. Per-problem CUDA kernels are code-generated from the irreps/instruction spec and JIT-compiled with nvcc -O3 via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline, combined with cuBLAS GEMMs; graph traversal is receiver-owned (CSR by receiver, with a source-ordered pass for gradients), deterministic and atomic-free. A receiver_scratch_bytes budget (default 128 MiB) drives node-chunking and a knapsack-style choice of which receiver aggregates to retain for the backward pass.

**Use it when:**
- Training equivariant GNN potentials in PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs where force training needs double backward and memory, not FLOPs, limits graph size.
- Large or dense graphs (many edges per node, wide irreps) where materializing [E, weight_numel] edge weights blows past GPU memory with OpenEquivariance or e3nn.
- Models whose last radial MLP layer can be handed to the convolution (phi plus projection weight), so the fusion boundary fits.
- Fixed-topology workloads (MD steps on one structure) that benefit from TPConvGraph reuse and CUDA Graph replay.
- Runs that need bitwise-deterministic results, since the kernels avoid atomics.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything other than float32: no fp64, fp16 or bf16 path (GEMMs can only switch between ieee and tf32).
- Problems that mix uvw and uvu paths in one instruction set, or uvu with unequal input/output multiplicities or spherical-harmonic multiplicity above one; only weighted fully connected uvw and homogeneous channel-wise uvu are supported.
- Non-NVIDIA hardware or environments without a CUDA toolkit for JIT compilation; every new problem shape pays a first-call nvcc compile.
- Production use that needs maturity: version 0.1.0, 5 commits (2026-07-20 to 2026-07-24), no releases, no issue history, single-company authorship.
- Pipelines already built around e3nn/OpenEquivariance's precomputed edge-weight interface and mul_ir layout; using mul_ir mode in Sobek adds transposes and emits an efficiency warning.

**Integration:** module · Python >= 3.11, PyTorch >= 2.12 with CUDA, cgen >= 2025.1, a CUDA toolkit usable by PyTorch's JIT extension builder (13.3 recommended); benchmarks extra adds e3nn, OpenEquivariance, torch-geometric 2.8.0, numpy, matplotlib · Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.12, CUDA Toolkit (13.3 recommended; 12.9 builds about 25% slower per README) · NVIDIA CUDA GPUs only (kernels compiled for the local arch via PyTorch's arch flags)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Sobek over OpenEquivariance, cuEquivariance or FlashTP when the per-edge weight tensor is what runs you out of memory or you need double backward at scale and can fuse the final radial layer; pick cuEquivariance or OpenEquivariance for drop-in e3nn compatibility, other dtypes, or a mature dependency, and FlashTP for its published SevenNet end-to-end results (Sobek reports no FlashTP comparison).

**Gotchas:**
- First call for each new tensor-product specification compiles CUDA; the extension is cached only when PyTorch, CUDA, GPU arch, problem and codegen settings all match.
- The CUDA toolkit is chosen from CUDA_HOME; the README reports identical kernels about 25% slower when built with CUDA 12.9 instead of 13.3.
- TPConvGraph tensors must not be modified in place, and a user-supplied sender_perm is only structurally checked, not validated as a permutation.
- phi_dim not divisible by four disables aligned float4 radial-embedding loads in receiver-side kernels.

**Status:** Apache-2.0, version 0.1.0 published in July 2026 by Cortex Discovery GmbH with 12 stars and no activity since 2026-07-24; usable as a pip-installable PyTorch module but young enough to pin and validate against e3nn before trusting it.

[repo](https://github.com/Cortex-Discovery/sobek) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18074)

##### SparseDNN  `C++/Python`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Python code generator emitting per-weight-matrix x86 assembly SpMM kernels for pruned networks; beats LIBXSMM sparse and dense BLAS above ~70% sparsity.

**Beats:** LIBXSMM, Intel MKL/OpenBLAS dense, OpenVINO — The author's own arXiv paper (2101.07948) measured generated FP32 SpMM kernels on an AWS Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (AVX-512) and AMD Epyc 7R32 (AVX2): 2.5x geomean over LIBXSMM single-threaded on Intel (1.3x on AMD), 1.7x on Intel and breakeven on AMD at 4 threads, about 4x over dense MKL/OpenBLAS at 95% sparsity, sparse conv 3.0x/4.8x (Intel) and 3.4x/6.3x (AMD) over dense oneDNN at 90/95% sparsity, and up to 5x pruneBERT throughput over OpenVINO; compiler and flags for the baselines are not given in the paper.

**Known shortcoming:** Single-author arXiv paper; no flags in repo; sparse-conv generator and inference engine not open source; abandoned (last commit 2022-09-28).

**Known shortcoming:** Correction: paper says 22% faster on Intel and 9% slower on AMD vs SkimCaffe single-threaded; at 4 threads only breaks even with LIBXSMM on AMD; each kernel works for one fixed sparsity pattern and shape; fastsparse.py runs test code on import; autotune script likely passes wrong -D CT value; driver built with icc -mkl -O3 -march=native (paper states no compiler).

**Independent measurement:** paper: sparse conv vs dense oneDNN on AMD 3.4x at 90%, 6.3x at 95% sparsity

**How:** The generator unrolls the whole sparse matrix into straight-line code: each nonzero is a vbroadcastss of the weight followed by vfmadd231ps against a row slice of B whose offset is baked into the instruction as an immediate, so there is no index decoding at run time. It adapts dense-GEMM register blocking (AT x CT microkernel tiles) plus split-K tiling over the reduction dimension, and stores values in a custom order matching the kernel's traversal. Tile sizes are autotuned per matrix by brute-force search over AT/CT/B_blocks.

**Use it when:**
- CPU inference of models pruned to 80-95% unstructured sparsity with weights fixed at deploy time (pruneBERT-style fully connected / 1x1 conv layers).
- x86-64 servers with AVX2 or AVX-512 where you can afford an offline code-generation and autotune step per weight matrix.
- Research or benchmarking of sparse FP32 SpMM kernels against LIBXSMM/MKL, since it exposes kernel-level timing.
- Single-threaded or low-core-count deployments, where its advantage over LIBXSMM is largest (2.5x geomean on Intel single-thread vs 1.7x at 4 threads).

**Skip it when:**
- Sparsity below about 70%: the paper puts the break-even with dense BLAS there, so dense MKL/oneDNN wins.
- Dynamic or activation sparsity: patterns must be known at code-generation time; the paper says it does not handle ReLU-induced activation sparsity.
- Production end-to-end inference: the sparse-convolution generator and the inference engine from the paper were never open-sourced; the README itself points end-to-end users to Neural Magic DeepSparse.
- Multi-threaded throughput on AMD (breakeven with LIBXSMM at 4 threads) or aarch64 (code paths for ARM exist in the generator but no ARM results are published).
- Anything needing maintenance or support: last commit 2022, single author who says he works on it sparingly.

**Integration:** source-drop · Python + NumPy for the generator; gcc to assemble the generated .s; C++ driver needs cnpy and the autotune script calls icc with -mkl and OpenMP · C++17 for driver_cpu.cpp (per autotune script); otherwise not documented · x86-64 with AVX2 (AVX-512 used when present); Linux assumed (reads /proc/cpuinfo)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over LIBXSMM when weights are highly sparse (90%+) and fixed, since LIBXSMM is the faster general choice for dense small GEMM and its sparse path lost 2.5x here single-threaded; for LLM inference with quantized rather than pruned weights, T-MAC or llamafile tinyBLAS fit better.

**Gotchas:**
- Each generated kernel is valid only for one weight sparsity pattern and one dense column count (C_dim); new weights or batch shapes require regeneration.
- fastsparse.py has module-level test code that loads matrix.npy and benchmarks on import, and compile() writes out.s/out.cpp to the current directory and shells out via os.system.
- The Python API adds noticeable ctypes overhead on small matrices; the paper's numbers come from the C++ driver.
- autotune_cpu_random.sh passes -D CT=$1 (the A dimension) to the driver instead of $CT, so the tuning script's driver build looks buggy; check before trusting its output.

**Status:** Abandoned since September 2022 but Apache-2.0 and only a handful of Python files, so the generator can be vendored; the parts needed for end-to-end inference were never released.

[repo](https://github.com/marsupialtail/sparsednn) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07948)

##### tiny-cuda-nn  `C++/CUDA`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

CUDA framework whose fully fused small-MLP kernels train and infer 2x-10x faster than TensorFlow 2.5 XLA (RTX 3090).

**Beats:** TensorFlow v2.5.0 with XLA (which uses cuDNN/cuBLAS) — The only external comparison is the author's chart: fully fused MLPs 64 and 128 neurons wide vs TensorFlow 2.5.0 with XLA (whose script also runs the matmuls in FP16) on an RTX 3090, learning an image at batch sizes 2^14-2^21; read approximately, 64-wide training is about 10x faster at 2^14 narrowing to about 2x at 2^21, and inference about 8x at 2^21. CUDA, driver and compiler versions are not stated; the 1.5x-2.5x JIT-fusion and 5x Instant NGP figures are against tiny-cuda-nn's own earlier path, not an external baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** TensorFlow 2.5+XLA comparison is a chart only (read from PNG: about 2x-10x training, 8x+ inference on RTX 3090); README bench paths 404 (real files benchmarks/image/bench_ours.cu and bench_tensorflow.py); no CPU or compiler given.

**Known shortcoming:** FullyFusedMLP accepts only widths 16/32/64/128 in FP16 and silently (log warning only) falls back to the slower CutlassMLP on older GPUs or FP32 builds; open issue #511 reports a shared-memory error on A100 at width 64.

**How:** The fully fused MLP evaluates every layer of a narrow network in one kernel: each thread block keeps its slice of the batch's activations in shared memory, loads weight tiles into registers and runs the matrix products on tensor cores via WMMA 16x16x16 FP16 fragments, so intermediate activations never go to global memory and there is one launch per pass instead of one per layer. Hidden widths are template parameters (16/32/64/128) and shared-memory rows are skewed by 8 halfs to avoid bank conflicts. Version 2.0 adds JIT fusion: the model is emitted as a CUDA device function and compiled with NVRTC, optionally fused with the caller's own kernel (Instant NGP fuses its whole NeRF ray marcher this way).

**Use it when:**
- Neural fields, NeRF/neural radiance caching, SDFs and other coordinate networks: millions of points per step through MLPs 16-128 neurons wide, often after a hash-grid or frequency encoding.
- Online training inside a renderer or simulator where both training and inference must run every frame on the GPU.
- Large batches (2^14 and up); the README says PyTorch-binding overhead roughly doubles runtime at 64k batch but is much smaller from 256k.
- Tensor-core NVIDIA GPUs (compute capability above 7.0, e.g. Turing and newer) with enough shared memory; the README names RTX 2080 Ti / RTX 3090 or higher for the default fully fused configuration.

**Skip it when:**
- Wide or general networks: FullyFusedMLP accepts only 16, 32, 64 or 128 neurons per hidden layer; anything else needs the slower CutlassMLP, and convolutions, attention or recurrent layers are not provided.
- Non-NVIDIA hardware, CPUs, or GPUs at or below compute capability 7.0: the fully fused path is not compiled there and falls back to CutlassMLP; FP32 builds also fall back.
- Lower-end or some data-center GPUs where the default shared-memory footprint does not fit (issue #511 reports the insufficient-shared-memory error on an A100 at 64 neurons, open with no reply).
- Teams without CUDA build expertise: about 240 open issues, dominated by pip/CMake/Windows/new-GPU build failures; there are no tagged releases after 2.0.
- Small batches or per-sample latency work: batch sizes must be multiples of 256 (BATCH_SIZE_GRANULARITY) and the kernels are tuned for throughput.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake add_subdirectory; builds the tiny-cuda-nn STATIC target) or PyTorch extension via pip from bindings/torch · CUDA toolkit; NVRTC for JIT fusion (TCNN_BUILD_WITH_RTC, on by default); bundled submodules CUTLASS, fmt and nlohmann/json; cuBLAS/cuSolver only for the Shampoo optimizer (off by default); PyTorch for the bindings · C++17, CMake 3.21+ per README (CMakeLists says 3.18), GCC 8+ or Visual Studio 2019/2022, CUDA 10.2+ on Linux or 11.5+ on Windows · Linux and Windows with an NVIDIA GPU; fully fused MLP needs compute capability > 7.0 and FP16 (TCNN_HALF_PRECISION, default on except sm_61 and <= sm_52); targets up to sm_120 with recent CUDA

**Vs siblings:** Pick tiny-cuda-nn over ThunderKittens or FlashAttention-3 when the workload is many tiny MLP evaluations (neural fields) rather than large GEMMs or attention, and over RTNeural when you have an NVIDIA GPU and huge batches instead of per-sample CPU inference; for CPU small-GEMM building blocks LIBXSMM is the closer fit.

**Gotchas:**
- The fully fused forward and backward passes throw unless network precision is __half, so outputs and gradients are FP16; mixed-precision accuracy is your problem to check.
- Unsupported widths, too-old GPUs or FP32 builds silently degrade to CutlassMLP (a log warning), which is much slower; check the logged network type.
- JIT fusion is opt-in (set_jit_fusion) and the README warns it can slow training for hash grids over ~20M parameters, MLPs wider than 128, or RTX 3000-series and older GPUs; measure both modes.
- The README benchmark caption still names benchmarks/bench_ours.cu and bench_tensorflow.py, which moved to benchmarks/image/.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-29, 4.5k stars, used by Instant NGP, Nerfstudio and NerfAcc) and BSD-3-Clause per LICENSE.txt, so copyable, but builds are fragile and the last tagged release is 2.0.

[repo](https://github.com/NVlabs/tiny-cuda-nn) · [benchmark](https://github.com/NVlabs/tiny-cuda-nn/blob/master/README.md)

##### tiny-ml-runtime  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Educational pure-C MLP inference loop; beats per-call Python PyTorch only on tiny nets, loses 5x on MNIST.

**Beats:** PyTorch 2.x (Python, batch size 1) — On an Apple M1 with gcc -O2 (version unstated), the C engine ran a 4-8-3 Iris MLP at 2,732,240 single-sample predictions/s versus 10,596/s for PyTorch 2.x driven from a single-threaded Python 3.11 loop (258x), but on a 784-128-10 MNIST MLP it managed 4,244/s versus PyTorch's 22,502/s, so PyTorch was about 5.3x faster. The timers differ between sides (CPU time vs wall clock) and no C/C++ runtime such as libtorch was compared.

**Known shortcoming:** The 258x is Python dispatch overhead; PyTorch is 5.3x faster on MNIST; C side timed with clock() and Python with time.time(); 0-star toy, flagged only.

**Known shortcoming:** Security bug: the standalone C load_weights() reads num_layers and the input size from the weight file with no bounds check into fixed arrays (layer_sizes[10], scaler_mean/std[784]), so a malformed file overflows the struct; malloc results in predict() are never checked; the Python binding rereads the weight file on every predict() and leaks memory on a failed load; README says the MNIST PyTorch row used 100K iterations but benchmark_mnist.py runs 10,000.

**How:** It does not have a fast kernel: linear() is a naive row-major double loop with no SIMD, tiling, threading or restrict qualifiers, compiled with gcc -O2. The Iris win comes purely from skipping the Python interpreter and PyTorch's per-op dispatch on a 4-8-3 network (about 56 multiply-adds), which the README states itself. Each predict() still mallocs and frees two scratch buffers, so even the overhead-bound path is not minimal.

**Use it when:**
- Reading or teaching how a dense forward pass, numerically stable softmax and a weight loader work in about 300 lines of C.
- Seeing the overhead-vs-compute crossover: tiny networks (tens of weights) called one sample at a time from code that would otherwise go through Python.
- A starting point you intend to rewrite (preallocated buffers, SIMD GEMV) for a microcontroller-style dense classifier, under MIT terms.

**Skip it when:**
- Any compute-bound network: on the 784-128-10 MNIST MLP the author's own numbers show PyTorch about 5.3x faster (22,502 vs 4,244 predictions/s).
- Production or untrusted model files: the standalone engine's load_weights() reads num_layers and the input width from the file without bounds checks into fixed arrays (layer_sizes[10], scaler_mean/std[784]), so a malformed file overflows the Network struct; malloc results in predict() are unchecked.
- Real-time or allocation-free contexts: predict() calls malloc/free twice per sample.
- Anything beyond dense + ReLU + softmax with at most 10 layers and 784 inputs (MAX_LAYERS, MAX_FEATURES): no convolutions, recurrent layers, other activations or batching.
- Through the Python binding: tinymlinference.predict() reopens and reparses the weight file on every call.

**Integration:** source-drop (src/c/inference.c + inference.h; Makefile builds a demo executable) or CPython extension via pip install . · none for the C core (libc, libm); PyTorch and NumPy only for training/export and the Python benchmark · C11 per README; built with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 · any C11 target; benchmarked only on Apple M1 (ARM64); weight file is raw native-endian int32/float32

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to learn; for real per-sample CPU inference of small networks RTNeural does the same job with compile-time-sized, allocation-free SIMD layers plus recurrent layers, and faster-enhancer.c is the catalogued example of a single-model C engine that beats ONNX Runtime on the same weights.

**Gotchas:**
- The 258x figure compares C CPU time (clock()) with wall-clock time (time.time()) of a Python loop that calls .item() per prediction; it measures interpreter plus dispatch overhead, not PyTorch kernels.
- The README's MNIST table header says 100K iterations, but src/python/benchmark_mnist.py runs 10,000 PyTorch iterations (10,000 / 0.444 s matches the 22,502/s shown); only the C side ran 100K.
- The CPython extension carries its own copy of the loader (with bounds checks) that leaks earlier layer buffers on a mid-file read failure; the two copies can drift.
- The weight format has no magic number, version or endianness marker.

**Status:** A 0-star student portfolio project (MIT, 47 commits, last commit 2026-03-25) with CI and tests; small enough to read and copy, but its own docs say it is not production-ready.

[repo](https://github.com/odeliyach/tiny-ml-runtime) · [benchmark](https://github.com/odeliyach/tiny-ml-runtime/blob/main/README.md)

##### ZhiLight  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zhihu/ModelBest C++/CUDA LLM serving engine tuned for PCIe multi-GPU boxes; cut TTFT versus vLLM and SGLang on 4x AD102.

**Beats:** vLLM and SGLang (versions not stated) — Zhihu's own serving benchmark (a closed-source Docker load generator that steps offered QPS, 3.7k-token prompts) on 4x AD102 PCIe shows Llama-3.1-70B GPTQ-INT4 at 1419.74 ms mean TTFT vs vLLM 4796.32 and SGLang 3962.99 ms, and TPOT 30.97 vs 41.54 and 63.22 ms; on A800 and for the 8B model SGLang or vLLM win. Engine versions, CPU, driver and compiler flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Mixed results: Llama-3.1-8B TPOT 66.24 ms vs vLLM 18.68 ms; SGLang beats it on A800 QPS; QPS values look like offered-load steps; bench tool ships as a Docker image only; a serving engine, not a kernel library, so the category is questionable.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not reproduced: open issue #59 measured 4017.89 ms mean TTFT on 4x RTX 4090 (72B GPTQ, 4k prompt, concurrency 1) vs README ~1112 ms, no reply; benchmark tool source never released (#17); wins rely on HIGH_PRECISION=0 and INT8 all-reduce; several SGLang baseline runs had --disable-radix-cache.

**How:** It targets tensor parallelism over PCIe, where all-reduce is the bottleneck: 'dual streams' overlap prefill (encode) compute with the all-reduce on a second CUDA stream (the CHANGELOG claims 20%+ on a '4090pro'), the all-reduce can be quantized to INT8 above a token threshold (REDUCE_TP_INT8_THRES), and an optional host-side all-reduce sums FP16/FP32 buffers on the CPU with AVX/F16C intrinsics. On the GPU it fuses QKV, feed-forward input, residual and layernorm kernels, uses a tensor-core fused batch attention for decode, flash-attention prefill and chunked prefill, and calls Marlin (GPTQ), TensorRT-LLM W4A16/W4A8/INT8 GEMMs and DeepGEMM/FlashMLA for DeepSeek.

**Use it when:**
- Serving dense 14B-110B INT4 (GPTQ/AWQ) models with tensor parallelism on 2-4 PCIe Ada-class GPUs without NVLink, where time to first token on ~4k-token prompts matters most
- Prefill-heavy traffic such as RAG or long-prompt chat: its clearest wins are TTFT (for example 1111.8 ms vs vLLM 3493.97 and SGLang 2276.1 ms for Qwen2-72B GPTQ on 4x AD102)
- DeepSeek-R1 AWQ or FP8 on 8x A800/H20 nodes where the published run sustained twice vLLM's offered QPS
- Teams that already run Llama, Qwen2 or DeepSeek models and want an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a self-built CUDA 12 wheel or Docker image

**Skip it when:**
- Small models or decode-heavy workloads: on 2x AD102 Llama-3.1-8B it lost to vLLM and SGLang on every metric (TPOT 66.24 vs 18.68 ms for vLLM), and its TPOT was also worse for MiniCPM-2B, Qwen1.5-110B on AD102 and DeepSeek-R1
- NVLink data-center GPUs: on 4x A800, SGLang sustained twice ZhiLight's QPS for Qwen2-72B and Qwen1.5-110B
- Non-NVIDIA hardware, pre-Ampere GPUs or aarch64 hosts: default CUDA architectures are 80, 89 and 90a, FP8 conversion needs sm_89+ (open issue #12), and DeepGEMM, FlashMLA and the AVX host all-reduce are x86-64 only
- You need independently reproduced numbers or an open benchmark: the load generator ships only as a Docker image (issue #17 asked for its source), and open issue #59 reports 4017.89 ms mean TTFT on 4x RTX 4090 with a 4k prompt at concurrency 1, about 3.6x the README's ~1112 ms, with no maintainer reply
- Broad model coverage and community support: a small Zhihu team (111 commits), many issues answered in Chinese or not at all, and no GitHub releases

**Integration:** module (Python package built by setup.py/CMake into a wheel with a C++/CUDA static backend and pybind11 extension); Docker image ghcr.io/zhihu/zhilight/zhilight · CUDA 12+ runtime, cuBLAS, NCCL; PyTorch >= 2.4.1; a flash-attn >= 2.7.0.post2 shared library (CMake stops if none is found); transformers, fastapi, uvicorn, pybind11 2.13.6; vendored bmengine, deep_gemm, flash_decoding, flash_mla and zmq; Boost.Serialization for multi-node inference · C++17 and CUDA C++17, CUDA 12.0+ (Dockerfile: CUDA 12.4.1, NCCL 2.21.5), CMake 3.20+, Python 3.9+; the C++ ABI flag is taken from the installed torch · Linux x86-64 with NVIDIA GPUs (Ampere sm_80, Ada sm_89, Hopper sm_90a by default); tested on AD102 PCIe, A800 and H20

**Vs siblings:** Pick ZhiLight when you need a whole multi-GPU serving engine for INT4 70B-class models on PCIe GPUs; FasterTransformer is archived in favor of TensorRT-LLM, PowerInfer targets a single consumer GPU with CPU offload and sparse activation, and Marlin is just the GPTQ matmul kernel that ZhiLight itself calls.

**Gotchas:**
- The fast published configurations depend on an --env string of knobs (HIGH_PRECISION=0, CPM_FUSE_QKV=1, CPM_FUSE_FF_IN=2, REDUCE_TP_INT8_THRES=100, DUAL_STREAM=1) shown in the benchmark launch lines; HIGH_PRECISION=0 and INT8 all-reduce trade numerical precision for speed, which the vLLM/SGLang baselines did not do
- In several baseline runs SGLang was launched with --disable-radix-cache, while ZhiLight's prefix-cache setting is not stated, so prefix reuse may differ between engines
- The benchmark doc's Qwen1.5-110B launch line misspells the module (api_sever), and the benchmark tool is pulled as image 1.0.1 but run as 1.0.0
- Reported QPS values are offered-load steps (many engines tie at exactly 0.09 or 0.18), so a 2x QPS is the next sustained step, not a measured 2x throughput

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-03-18, recent work on session generation and W4A8 caching; 908 stars), Apache-2.0, buildable from source or Docker (README tag 0.4.8-cu124), but the speed claims are first-party and one third-party report did not reproduce them.

[repo](https://github.com/zhihu/ZhiLight) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhihu/ZhiLight/HEAD/docs/benchmarks/benchmarks.md)

#### big-integer-arbitrary-precision

##### avx-ecm  `C`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

AVX-512 command-line ECM factoring program running 8 or 16 curves per thread; about 1.5-2.5x GMP-ECM curve throughput below ~1000 bits.

**Beats:** GMP-ECM (the ecm program, built on GMP) — The only checked claim is the README's first-party statement of about 1.5 to 2.5 times GMP-ECM's curves per second for inputs up to about 1000 bits on AVX-512 CPUs, with no table, CPU model, GMP-ECM version or flags. Forum numbers (about 2x with 1 thread on a Xeon Gold 5122; a search summary also quotes 900-bit t35 at 2.78 s versus GMP-ECM 7.0.4 at 10.04 s per curve) were seen only as search snippets from mersenneforum.org, which is blocked here, and are unverified.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: the README's '1.5 to 2.5x GMP-ECM' is first-party with no CPU stated; the Xeon Gold 5122 numbers live on mersenneforum (blocked). Last commit 2021-03-09, abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #1 (SIGSEGV in vecsqrmod52 on a YAFU build) closed with no visible reply. avx_ecm.h defines the globals MAXBITS, NWORDS, NBLOCKS and lcg_state without extern, so a GCC 10+ (-fno-common) link likely fails (inferred from source, not tested); the Makefile hard-codes the author's GMP paths; prebuilt .exe files sit in the repo. A mersenneforum post (blocked, snippet only) gives 2.78 s/curve vs GMP-ECM 7.0.4 at 10.04 s/curve on a 900-bit t35 (about 3.6x). The maintained copy lives in bbuhrow/yafu (factor/avx-ecm, commits through 2026-08-31).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Each AVX-512 lane carries a different curve over the same modulus, so Montgomery multiplication and squaring (vecmulmod52/vecsqrmod52) run 8 curves at once with 52-bit digits in 64-bit lanes (16 curves with DIGITBITS=32); ICELAKE/TIGERLAKE builds add -DIFMA for the 52-bit multiply-add instructions. Stage 1 uses Montgomery-form curves with Suyama sigma parametrization and Montgomery's PRAC Lucas chains; stage 2 is the standard continuation with pairing. Inputs of the form 2^n-1, 2^n+1 or 2^n-c switch to special Mersenne/pseudo-Mersenne reduction instead of REDC. Work is spread over threads with pthreads.

**Use it when:**
- Running many ECM curves (t30-t60 style work) on composites of roughly 200-1000 bits on Skylake-X, Cascade Lake, Ice Lake, Tiger Lake or later AVX-512 x86-64 CPUs.
- Batch stage 1 on AVX-512 hardware followed by GMP-ECM stage 2 from the savefile, when you want GMP-ECM's faster stage 2 but higher stage 1 throughput.
- Factoring Mersenne-like or 2^n+-c inputs, where the special reduction path applies.
- Choosing DIGITBITS=32 for sizes just above a 208-bit step, since the 32-bit build steps in 128 bits and can have higher throughput there.

**Skip it when:**
- CPUs without AVX-512 (all AVX2-only Intel and pre-Zen 4 AMD parts, and all ARM): the program targets AVX-512 intrinsics only.
- Inputs well above about 1000 bits: the README says GMP-ECM wins because this program has no sub-quadratic multiplication.
- Single-curve or latency-bound work: the speedup comes from running 8 or 16 curves together per thread.
- Production use that needs maintenance or bug fixes: the standalone repo's last commit is 2021-03-09; its one issue (a SIGSEGV in vecsqrmod52 reported from a YAFU build) was closed with no visible reply. The maintained copy lives inside YAFU (factor/avx-ecm).
- Embedding as a library: there is no documented API; the Makefile archives the objects (including main.c) into libavxecm.a only to link the program.

**Integration:** source-drop · GMP (-lgmp), pthreads, libm; Intel builds also link MKL (-mkl) · README: gcc 7.3.0 or icc (only these tested); MinGW64/MSYS2 supported via COMPILER=mingw · x86-64 with AVX-512 (SKYLAKEX=1, KNL=1 for Knights Landing, ICELAKE=1 or TIGERLAKE=1 for IFMA); Linux and Windows (MinGW)
