**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ECM-ELF when you need a complete ECM (stage 1 and stage 2, multi-threaded, savefiles for GMP-ECM) on generic inputs rather than a stage 1 IFMA backend benchmarked on one Mersenne number, and over primefactors when you have AVX-512 CPUs rather than an NVIDIA GPU. For general big-integer arithmetic (not factoring), the GMP-replacement siblings such as FLINT or mp++ are the relevant entries; this program only does ECM.

**Gotchas:**
- Run time is constant within 208-bit steps (128-bit with DIGITBITS=32): a 417-bit input costs the same as a 623-bit one, so the speedup over GMP-ECM depends strongly on where the input falls in a step.
- The Makefile hard-codes the author's GMP paths (/sppdg/scratch/..., ../../gmp-6.2.1) and a gcc-7.3.0 binary name; edit INC/LIBS before building. The IFMA build options (ICELAKE=1, TIGERLAKE=1) exist in the Makefile but not in the README.
- avx_ecm.h defines globals without extern (uint32_t MAXBITS; NWORDS; NBLOCKS; uint64_t *lcg_state) in a header shared by several .c files; GCC 10+ defaults to -fno-common, so a link with multiple-definition errors is likely unless -fcommon is added (inferred from the source, not tested).
- The repo ships prebuilt Windows binaries (avx-ecm-32.exe, avx-ecm-52.exe, avx-ecm-52-icc-static) of unstated build provenance; prefer building from source.

**Status:** Standalone repo abandoned since 2021-03-09 (34 commits, 8 stars) but BSD-2-Clause and small enough to vendor; active development continued inside bbuhrow/yafu under factor/avx-ecm (commits through 2026-08-31, with added Karatsuba and AVX-512 P-1 files), which is the better source today.

[repo](https://github.com/bbuhrow/avx-ecm) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bbuhrow/avx-ecm)

##### bigfft  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go Schonhage-Strassen multiplication for math/big integers: 3-25x faster than math/big from 1 Mbit, 1.2-3x slower than GMP.

**Beats:** Go math/big (README also benchmarks GMP, which is faster) — First-party Go benchmarks: on a Core 2 Quad Q8200 (Go version unstated), multiplication of equal-size random integers is 3.7x faster than math/big at 1 Mbit and 24.9x at 100 Mbit, but 1.85x-1.96x slower than GMP; a later Go 1.8 run on a Core i5-4590 (benchmarks/ directory) shows 3.0x-28.8x over math/big and 2.0x-2.6x slower than GMP 6.1.2 (gmpbench), all derived from page data. Decimal scanning is 12x faster than SetString at 1e6 digits on the i5-4590.

**Known shortcoming:** README calls it a 'toy proof-of-concept'; slower than GMP at every size and loses to Go math/big below ~1 Mbit; Go.

**Known shortcoming:** Below the threshold bigfft.Mul is up to 1.76x slower than math/big (allocates a new result each call); FromDecimalString ignores SetString's ok, so bad input gives a wrong number without error; relies on go:linkname into math/big internals; 2.0-2.6x slower than GMP 6.1.2 (benchmarks/ dir); abandoned 2023-01-29.

**How:** Schonhage-Strassen: operands are cut into 2^k chunks and transformed with a recursive radix-2 FFT over the ring Z/(2^n+1) (fermat.go), where roots of unity are powers of two, so twiddle multiplications are bit shifts (with a sqrt(2) half-shift trick). Pointwise products are a single level that calls math/big's Karatsuba, not a recursive FFT. Inner loops reuse math/big's assembly kernels (addVV, subVV, mulAddVWW and others) via go:linkname. FromDecimalString splits the string in halves and multiplies by precomputed powers of 10, so parsing cost follows multiplication cost instead of math/big's quadratic digit loop.

**Use it when:**
- A pure-Go program (no cgo) that multiplies integers of roughly 1 Mbit or more: README shows 3.7x at 1 Mbit and 24.9x at 100 Mbit over math/big on a Core 2 Quad (derived from page data).
- Parsing decimal strings of 100,000+ digits into big.Int: 12x faster at 1e6 digits and 56x at 1e7 digits than SetString on a Core i5-4590 (derived from benchmarks/scan.*), with about 53x less allocation at 1e6 digits.
- Number-theory or pi-digit experiments in Go where cgo bindings to GMP are not allowed.
- Already pulled in transitively (modernc.org/sqlite uses it, per issue #22) and you want FFT products for your own big multiplications too.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ code: GMP is faster at every size the README measured (1.2x to 3.1x; bigfft 1.85x slower at 1 Mbit and 1.96x slower at 100 Mbit, derived from page data), and FLINT is faster still.
- Operands below about 1 Mbit: math/big is equal or faster; in the Go 1.8 run, bigfft.Mul at 1 kbit took 525 ns vs math/big's 298 ns (1.76x slower, derived from benchmarks/bench and bench.big).
- Division, modular exponentiation, GCD or decimal output: only multiplication and decimal input are provided (division request issue #20 is open).
- Production code that needs a maintained dependency: the author's README calls it a toy proof of concept, the last commit is 2023-01-29, and 5 issues and 4 PRs (loong64, gccgo, wasm) sit unanswered.
- gccgo builds: the package reaches into math/big's internal kernels with go:linkname, and the 2021 gccgo build fix (PR #14) was never merged; gccgo support after the 2023 linkname switch is not documented.

**Integration:** module · none outside the Go standard library (math/big internals via go:linkname) · go.mod says go 1.12; CI was set up for Go 1.12, 1.17 and latest in January 2023 · any GOARCH of the standard gc toolchain since the January 2023 switch from per-arch assembly stubs to go:linkname (no .s files remain in the repo root); gccgo not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick bigfft only in pure Go with Mbit-scale operands; holiman/uint256 is the Go sibling for fixed 256-bit math, and for C/C++ FLINT or GMP itself beat bigfft at every size, as do the GPU/NTT multipliers (TzdLanguage) on huge operands.

**Gotchas:**
- Depends on go:linkname into math/big internals (addVV, subVV, addVW, subVW, shlVU, mulAddVWW, addMulVVW). Go master keeps these symbols explicitly for bigfft ('hall of shame' comments citing go.dev/issue/67401), so builds work today, but the package relies on Go not removing them.
- FromDecimalString ignores the ok result of big.Int.SetString on each chunk and expects digits only: no sign, no error return, so malformed input yields a wrong number rather than an error.
- The FFT path switches on at 1800 words (about 115 kbit on 64-bit), a hard-coded package variable; the README says 200 kbits. Below that, Mul just calls math/big and adds an allocation.
- Old releases (pseudo-version v0.0.0-20170806...) used assembly jump stubs and fail on some setups with 'missing function body' (issue #21); use the 2023 commit.

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2023 and self-described as a toy, but BSD-3-Clause, about 700 lines of Go (4 source files), used in production by modernc.org/sqlite (issue #22) and kept building because Go's math/big preserves its linkname targets.

[repo](https://github.com/remyoudompheng/bigfft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/remyoudompheng/bigfft)

##### Boost.Multiprecision (cpp_int fixed-precision)  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++ big-number types; fixed-width cpp_int (128-bit) beats GMP's mpz on basic arithmetic by 1.5-6x.

**Beats:** GMP (mpz_int via gmp_int backend) — Boost's own docs (GCC 10.3.0, GMP 6.2.0, Boost 1.78, run 2021-09-30; CPU and flags not stated) time 500,000 ops excluding allocation/copy: fixed 128-bit cpp_int beats gmp_int on * (4.80x), + (5.87x), / (1.70x), % (1.47x); at 256 bits it still wins + (1.45x) but loses *, / and %, and GMP wins all 512/1024-bit multiply and modulus rows.

**Known shortcoming:** Docs from 2021 (GCC 10.3, GMP 6.2.0, Boost 1.78), no flags, CPU model or benchmark-code link; win limited to small fixed widths (all 128-bit ops; at 256 bits only +, -, ^, construct; GMP wins 256-bit * 1.77x and +(int) 1.73x); on Miller-Rabin (perf/int_real_world.html) dynamic cpp_int is ~11x slower than GMP and fixed uint1024_t 9.3x slower (inputs were 128-bit).

**Known shortcoming:** At 256 bits fixed cpp_int also loses / (1.72x) and % (1.29x) to GMP; GMP wins every 512- and 1024-bit * and % row; dynamic cpp_int is slower than GMP at every size.

**Independent measurement:** int_real_world: Boost.Polygon Voronoi builder, int256_t 3.8x faster than mpz_int (derived from page data)

**How:** Fixed-width cpp_int stores its limbs inline with no heap allocation and no runtime size checks beyond the fixed limb count, so small-width operations avoid the allocation and dispatch overhead GMP's mpz layer pays per call. Expression templates (enabled by default) fuse compound expressions and cut temporaries. Fixed-precision types are also constexpr-capable, so constant arithmetic can be folded at compile time.

**Use it when:**
- 128-bit integer arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %, xor) in hot loops, where the docs measure fixed cpp_int 1.5-5.9x faster than gmp_int
- 256-bit-ish workloads dominated by add/sub/construct or many temporaries (Voronoi builder test: int256_t 3.8x faster than mpz_int)
- Projects that need a permissively licensed (BSL-1.0), header-only bigint with no GMP/LGPL dependency
- Compile-time (constexpr) big-integer constants with fixed-width types
- Code that wants one generic interface and may swap to the GMP backend later

**Skip it when:**
- Multiplication, division or modulus at 256 bits and above: gmp_int wins (256-bit * 1.77x, / 1.72x slower for fixed cpp_int; 512/1024-bit * ~1.5-1.6x slower)
- Modular exponentiation / primality testing on wide types: Miller-Rabin with uint1024_t and cpp_int runs ~9-11x slower than mpz_int
- Dynamic (arbitrary-precision) cpp_int in general: it is slower than GMP at every size in the integer_performance tables
- Very large numbers (thousands of bits and up) where GMP/FLINT's subquadratic algorithms matter

**Integration:** header-only · Boost.Config only in standalone mode (BOOST_MP_STANDALONE); otherwise other Boost headers; optional GMP/MPFR/MPIR/TomMath for those backends · C++14; constexpr cpp_int arithmetic needs C++2a or GCC 6+ in C++14 mode · any platform with a compliant C++14 compiler

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ctbignum or mp++ when you want a mature Boost-licensed header-only type with full operator coverage, signed types and Boost.Math interop rather than maximum small-limb speed; pick FLINT or mp++ for large operands and number-theory kernels where GMP-class algorithms dominate.

**Gotchas:**
- Fixed-width types use sign-magnitude, not two's complement: int128_t has 128 magnitude bits plus a sign bit and is one machine word larger than expected
- Unchecked fixed types wrap modulo 2^MaxBits silently; checked_* variants throw std::overflow_error instead
- Division by zero throws std::overflow_error; negative values cannot be printed in hex or octal
- Disabling expression templates can cost a lot (Miller-Rabin: cpp_int 16.2x vs 11.2x of GMP's time without/with them)

**Status:** Actively maintained Boost library (commits through Sept 2026), BSL-1.0 and header-only, so it is easy to vendor; the published performance tables are from 2021 and may not reflect current versions.

[repo](https://github.com/boostorg/multiprecision) · [benchmark](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/libs/multiprecision/doc/html/boost_multiprecision/perf/integer_performance.html)

##### CGBN (Cooperative Groups Big Numbers)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

NVIDIA's header-only CUDA library for fixed-size unsigned big integers; a V100 out-throughputs 20-core OpenMP GMP 4-77x on batches.

**Beats:** GMP 6.1.2 (OpenMP, 20-core Xeon) — NVIDIA's 2018 beta measured batch throughput on a Tesla V100 against GMP 6.1.2 running across all 20 cores of a 2.2 GHz Xeon E5-2698v4 with OpenMP, using the repo's perf_tests (nvcc -arch=sm_70; the GMP driver built with g++ -fopenmp and no -O flag): average speedups over 128-8192 bits of 77.4x (add) down to 4.1x (modular inverse). Compiler versions are not stated, and the comparison is GPU device throughput versus CPU, not a faster algorithm.

**Known shortcoming:** V100 vs 20-core Xeon measures hardware throughput, not the algorithm; the GMP harness is built without an -O flag (driver at -O0), handicapping the baseline; compiler versions unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Open bug #15: mont_sqr returns an unreduced result ((a^2 mod m)+m, 971-bit modulus, 2021, no reply); #23 div/div_rem do not compile above 512 bits; CONSTANT_TIME=true reports unsupported_operation; the README powm_odd table uses a 512-bit exponent at every size and a custom fixed-window Montgomery kernel (perf_tests/xmp_test_powm.cu), not the library's cgbn_modular_power.

**How:** Instead of one thread per bignum (which runs out of registers), each value's 32-bit limbs are distributed across TPI threads and kept in registers, and carries, comparisons and broadcasts move between the group's lanes with warp shuffles (__shfl_sync). Sizes and thread counts are template parameters, so loops over the per-thread limbs are fully unrolled, and the code picks multiply-add instruction sequences per architecture (IMAD/XMAD/WMAD paths selected by __CUDA_ARCH__). Throughput comes from running thousands of these groups concurrently on the GPU; the headline powm number uses a hand-written 5-bit fixed-window Montgomery kernel in the perf tests.

**Use it when:**
- Large batches (thousands or more) of independent fixed-width operations: RSA/DH-style modular exponentiation, Montgomery multiplication, primality testing or sieving, where each instance is 128-8192 bits.
- Workloads already on an NVIDIA GPU where you can write your own CUDA kernel around the arithmetic, e.g. GPU Miller-Rabin (the repo's sample 4) or prime-gap searches.
- Throughput-bound jobs where moving data to the GPU is amortized: the README's averages are 77x (add), 43.5x (low mul), 29.3x (Montgomery reduce) and 21.4x (odd powm) over 20-core OpenMP GMP on a V100.
- Building blocks for higher-level GPU multiprecision libraries (gnu-mpfr-cgbn and the steleman/nvidia-cgbn fork build on it).

**Skip it when:**
- Single values or small batches: it only pays off with many concurrent instances, and per-operation latency including transfer will lose to GMP on the CPU.
- Signed, variable-size or mixed-size integers, operands above 32K bits, or sizes not divisible by 32 (open issues #3 and #13); copying between environments of different sizes is described as very slow.
- Secret-key cryptography that needs constant time: CONSTANT_TIME exists as a parameter but a checked context reports cgbn_unsupported_operation when it is set, and the library cgbn_modular_power is plain binary square-and-multiply.
- Non-NVIDIA hardware, or Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs without testing: the Makefile targets stop at Ampere, and a third-party README (mr_blackwell) reports CGBN running orders of magnitude slower than expected there.
- gcd- and inverse-heavy workloads: the README says these are not optimal, and the docs call the number-theoretic functions 'a little bit slow'.

**Integration:** header-only · CUDA toolkit; GMP for the host-side mpz backend, samples and perf tests; Google Test for unit tests · CUDA 9.0+ for Kepler/Maxwell/Pascal, CUDA 10+ for Volta and newer (README); a CUDA 12.5 build problem (issue #31) was fixed in 2025 · NVIDIA GPUs; Makefile targets sm_35 (Kepler) through sm_80 (Ampere); no CPU fallback without GMP (cgbn_cpu.h is an #error stub)

**Vs siblings:** Pick CGBN over CPU libraries such as ctbignum, blip_mp or mp++ when you have thousands of independent fixed-width operations and an NVIDIA GPU; pick midint-arithmetic-division or TzdLanguage's NTT for a few very large operands, and gnu-mpfr-cgbn when you need MPFR-style floating point on top of CGBN.

**Gotchas:**
- The perf-table powm_odd uses a 512-bit exponent at every modulus size and a custom fixed-window Montgomery kernel (perf_tests/xmp_test_powm.cu), not the library's cgbn_modular_power; the README itself says the sample-3 odd-modulus powm is much faster than the library API.
- Open bug #15 (2021, no reply): cgbn_mont_sqr returned (a^2 mod m) + m for a 971-bit modulus, i.e. an unreduced result; reduce or compare before trusting mont_sqr output.
- Open issue #23: cgbn_div, cgbn_div_rem and cgbn_div_rem_wide fail to compile ('incomplete type is not allowed') above 512 bits in the reporter's setup; issue #33 reported multiple-definition link errors with several .cu files, which the 2026-03-31 'Mark non-templated functions inline' commit appears to address.
- Do not #define TPI before including cgbn/cgbn.h (the docs warn it breaks compilation), and the default context constructor uses cgbn_no_checks, so errors such as division by zero are silent unless you pass a monitor and report object.

**Status:** MIT-licensed NVIDIA Research code (252 stars) that has stayed at its 2018 'XMP 2.0 beta' feature level, with only small maintenance commits since (latest 2026-03-31) and several open correctness and compile issues; it is vendorable and still the common base for GPU bignum work, and the steleman/nvidia-cgbn fork adds signed integers and Ada/Blackwell support.

[repo](https://github.com/NVlabs/CGBN) · [benchmark](https://github.com/NVlabs/CGBN)

##### DoubleFloats.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Julia double-double floats (Double64, about 106-bit significand) running 6-25x faster than 128-bit BigFloat/MPFR on vector and matrix kernels.

**Beats:** MPFR (via Julia BigFloat at 128-bit precision, 'Big128') — The README's first-party table (BenchmarkTools on unnamed hardware, Julia version unstated) shows Double64 taking 6-25x less time than BigFloat at 128-bit precision and 2-12x less than Quadmath Float128 on 1000-element vectors and 50x50 matrices; the repo's own docs/reports/benchmarks.jl run (Julia 1.12.6, CPU not stated) adds scalar multiply 2 ns vs 41 ns and 64x64 matmul 136 us vs 15.8 ms against 256-bit BigFloat. Neither comparison is precision-matched or names the CPU.

**Known shortcoming:** Unequal precision: about 106-bit double-double vs correctly rounded 128-bit MPFR; no hardware or Julia version stated; Julia-only, not callable from C++.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: v1.8.0-1.9.1 inv loses accuracy (LU residual 1.8e-31 becomes 7.9e-19, #291); open #164 (cos near pi), #151 (overflow), #323 (loggamma exported but undefined); sin/cos on large arguments and asin/acos fall back to Float128 (~10x slower).

**How:** Each value is a non-overlapping (hi, lo) pair of hardware floats, and every operation is built from error-free transformations: two_sum (Knuth) and FMA-based two_prod (s = a*b; t = fma(a, b, -s)), so an add or multiply is a handful of native Float64 instructions with no heap allocation. Values are immutable bits types stored inline in arrays, which the project's benchmark notes name as the main advantage over BigFloat (each BigFloat is a heap-allocated MPFR object). Elementary functions use argument reduction plus fused Horner polynomial kernels, with Float128 (libquadmath) fallbacks for hard ranges.

**Use it when:**
- Julia code that needs roughly 30-32 significant digits for ill-conditioned sums, dot products, LU/QR solves or eigenproblems: README reports 6x (elementwise exp) to 25x (elementwise multiply) less time than BigFloat at 128 bits.
- Arrays and 50x50-to-64x64 matrices where BigFloat's per-element allocation dominates: the 2026 benchmark report shows 64x64 matmul at 136 us vs 15.8 ms for 256-bit BigFloat.
- Mixed-precision refinement: map Float64 inputs to Double64 for the numerically sensitive part, then convert back, as the README recommends.
- Replacing Quadmath.jl Float128 when 106 bits suffice: README shows 2-12x less time than Float128 on the same kernels.

**Skip it when:**
- You need more than about 106 bits, an exponent range wider than Float64, or MPFR-style correct rounding: use BigFloat/MPFR (or Float128 for the wider exponent).
- Dense linear algebra where Float64 accuracy is enough: Double64 runs pure-Julia generic algorithms, 9-32x slower than Float64 LAPACK/BLAS in the project's report (n = 32-64).
- Double32: the README itself says Float64 is better for most purposes, and 64x64 matrix exp is 1017x slower than Float32 in the report.
- C or C++ projects: this is a Julia package; a C++ double-double library or a quad-precision library such as TLFloat fits there.
- Hot loops calling sin/cos on large arguments, or asin/acos at all: those take Float128 paths at about 600-1,100 ns per call (input-timing report).

**Integration:** module · GenericLinearAlgebra, GenericSchur, Quadmath (GNU libquadmath), SpecialFunctions, plus stdlib LinearAlgebra, Printf, Random · Julia 1.10 (Project.toml compat) · not documented beyond Julia's own platforms; needs a working Quadmath.jl, which is a hard dependency

**Vs siblings:** Pick DoubleFloats over MultiFloats.jl when you want the broader function library (elementary, special, complex, matrix functions, generic eigen/SVD) and accept that MultiFloats claims to be 2x faster; pick BigFloat/MPFR or APFP-style accelerators when you need more than 106 bits, and TLFloat or MPLAPACK's double-double backend when the code is C++.

**Gotchas:**
- Float64 literals are converted exactly as binary doubles: Double64(0.2) is 0.2000000000000000111..., so use df64"0.2" or Double64(2)/10 for decimal constants (README).
- Large-argument trig and deep-negative exp leave the fast path: sin/cos for abs(x) >= 6.28125 go from 65 ns to about 630 ns, exp(-650) from 55 ns to 1,254 ns, and infinite inputs to sin/cos throw DomainError (docs/reports/input_timing_report.md).
- Versions 1.8.0-1.9.1 computed inv with only Float64-level accuracy for inputs whose low word is zero, degrading Double64 LU residuals from 1.8e-31 to 7.9e-19 (issue #291); a muladd allocation regression from v1.10 was fixed in July 2026. Use the current 1.11 line.
- Open accuracy and semantics issues: cos just below pi (#164), overflow behaviour that differs from Float64 (#151), subnormals (#181), and isapprox with tolerances beyond Float64 precision (#206).

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-28, version 1.11.2), MIT-licensed, and registered in Julia's General registry under JuliaMath; usable only from Julia.

[repo](https://github.com/JuliaMath/DoubleFloats.jl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/JuliaMath/DoubleFloats.jl)

##### LibBF (Fabrice Bellard)  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Fabrice Bellard's tiny MIT-licensed C arbitrary-precision float library; NTT multiplication edges MPFR only at very high precision.

**Beats:** GNU MPFR (mpfr_mul, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate: GMP 6.3 / MPFR 4.2) — A report by the author of libbeef, a competing Rust port, put libbf 2025-06-03's own bftest (clang -O2, modified to use clock_gettime, random-length run-length operands) next to MPFR 4.2 via rug 1.30.0 in a separate Rust harness on an Apple M4; libbf's mul was faster only at 300,000 bits (51.2 vs 78.9 ns/limb, about 1.5x) and slower on every other operation and size. The comparison is cross-harness with different operand generators, so even that one win is not like-for-like.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster in any like-for-like test: the only win (mul at 300k bits, 51.2 vs 78.9 ns/limb) compares libbf's C bftest with the rug Rust harness on different operands and an unstated rounding mode; public bftest.c uses x86 rdtsc, so the M4 harness was modified and the patch is unpublished; bftest's own same-operand MPFR column was not reported; slower than MPFR everywhere else; QuickJS dropped libbf in its 2025-04-26 release. Kept flagged per the keep-and-document rule.

**Known shortcoming:** Possible security bug: radare2 issue 23317 / PR 23318 (2024) report an unchecked size calculation before bf_malloc in __bf_div that could overflow into an out-of-bounds write; the 2025-06-03 mirror still lacks the check (likely theoretical given BF_PREC_MAX, enricher's reading). Schoolbook multiplication only below 100 limbs; libbf.h has no extern "C" guard; README admits no rigorous rounding-error proof for transcendentals and incomplete allocation-error reporting.

**How:** Above 100 limbs (6,400 bits) for the smaller operand, multiplication switches from schoolbook to a Number Theoretic Transform over up to five word-sized primes (50-51-bit moduli in the AVX2 build, 61-62-bit in the portable build) recombined by CRT; the AVX2 build uses an original SIMD NTT on 64-bit doubles that relies on FMA to get exact products, and the portable build uses 128-bit integers with modular reductions replaced by multiplications. Division, square root and radix conversion are built on that multiplication, giving near-linear running time for the basic operations. Below 100 limbs there is no Karatsuba or Toom stage, which is why it trails MPFR at ordinary precisions.

**Use it when:**
- Very high precision multiplication (hundreds of thousands of bits and up) where a permissive license matters more than peak speed: the one measured win is mul at 300,000 bits, 51.2 vs 78.9 ns/limb for MPFR on an Apple M4
- Embedding arbitrary-precision floats in a small C/C++ program, interpreter or calculator without linking GMP/MPFR (LGPL): a few C files, custom allocator hook, MIT license
- Exact emulation of IEEE 754 formats with a configurable exponent width and subnormals, e.g. checking hardware or soft-float results
- Needing integers, binary floats and decimal floats from one tiny library with a single number type

**Skip it when:**
- Ordinary precisions (53 bits to tens of thousands of bits): MPFR is faster on mul, add, div and sqrt in the same report (mul at 53 bits 43.4 vs 15.6 ns/limb, div at 30,000 bits 370.9 vs 64.9)
- Transcendental-heavy code: exp, log, sin, cos, tan are about 2-7x slower than MPFR at 53-256 bits (exp at 53 bits 2985 vs 518 ns/limb); the README says they use an O(n^(1/2) M(n)) method and lack a rigorous rounding-error proof
- Record-size constant computation: the README says it is about 4x slower than Bellard's TachusPI on pi
- Decimal floats at high precision: base-10 arithmetic, input and output are quadratic per the README
- 32-bit targets: the README says the code is not designed to be efficient there and numbers are limited to about 10 million digits

**Integration:** source-drop (libbf.c, libbf.h, cutils.c, cutils.h; Makefile builds examples only) · none for the library (libm); bftest needs MPFR, GMP and libmpdec · GCC or Clang with __int128 and GNU builtins/attributes on 64-bit (C99-era C); Windows via the Makefile's mingw cross-compile option; MSVC not documented · tested on 64-bit x86 per the README; portable C elsewhere (aarch64 used in the Apple M4 benchmark); optional AVX2+FMA build (-mavx2 -mfma -mbmi2) needs Haswell or later

**Vs siblings:** Pick libbf over MPFR-based options (FLINT, MPFR itself) only when you need an MIT-licensed, dependency-free arbitrary-precision float in a few C files; for speed at 53-256 bits, double-double/quad-double types (DoubleFloats.jl, MultiFloats.jl in Julia, TLFloat in C++) are far faster, and for huge-precision throughput FLINT (GMP-backed) is the stronger choice.

**Gotchas:**
- libbf.h has no extern "C" guard; C++ code must wrap the include itself
- The AVX2 and portable builds handle different maximum sizes (8*10^12 vs 4*10^16 digits per the README)
- A 2024 radare2 report (issue 23317, PR 23318) flagged an unchecked size computation (na + 1) * sizeof(limb_t) before bf_malloc in __bf_div that could overflow; the 2025-06-03 code in this mirror still lacks that check
- The README says memory allocation failures are not always reported correctly in the transcendental functions, and some unlikely overflow/underflow cases in exp and pow are not handled

**Status:** Stale mirror (last commit 2025-08-19, synced to Bellard's 2025-06-03 tarball plus warning fixes and CI); QuickJS dropped libbf in 2025, but the code is MIT, small and self-contained enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/rurban/libbf) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lifthrasiir/libbeef/blob/main/docs/benchmark-report.md)

##### libQD3 (double-double, triple-double, quad-double, extended-double)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Maintained fork of the Hida-Li-Bailey QD library adding triple-double and binary80/binary32 expansions; fixed 106-212-bit floats, much cheaper than MPFR.

**Beats:** MPFR (the MPLAPACK manual's Rgemm numbers for upstream QD against MPFR and GMP at their 512-bit default); libQD3's own docs/qd.tex also carries the original QD paper's per-operation timing table against Bailey's MPFUN — Nothing measures libQD3's current code. The inherited evidence is the original QD paper table in docs/qd.tex (Pentium II 400 MHz, g++ 2.95.2 -O3 -funroll-loops): quad-double add 0.583 us, mul 1.965 us, div 5.267 us vs Bailey's MPFUN 5.729, 7.624 and 10.102 us (about 9.8x, 3.9x, 1.9x, derived from page data), and the MPLAPACK manual's Rgemm peaks with upstream QD on a Threadripper 3970X (GCC 9.3.0, flags not stated): quad-double 33 MFlops vs 512-bit MPFR 11 MFlops single-threaded and 1.3 GFlops vs 390 MFlops with OpenMP, at unequal precision (212 vs 512 bits).

**Known shortcoming:** Raised D to C on lineage only: every number covers the inherited upstream QD library, not libQD3 itself (docs/qd.tex QD vs MPFUN on a Pentium II with g++ 2.95.2; the MPLAPACK manual's Rgemm figures of QD 33 vs GMP 19 vs MPFR 11 MFlops, 1.3 GFlops vs 693 vs 390 MFlops with OpenMP). MPFR ran at 512 bits against QD's 212. The manual PDF on master is titled version 1.0.0, not 2.0.1. Fork of BL-highprecision/QD, 2 stars. Kouya's arXiv 1510.08642 and 2603.14926 (QD/TD vs MPFR matmul) were blocked and seen only as snippets.

**Known shortcoming:** td.tex says accurate QD multiplication is the default, but CMake defaults QD_ENABLE_SLOPPY_MUL=ON. License mismatch: LICENSE is BSD-3, COPYING asks for LBNL commercial-use contact, td.tex says BSD 2-clause. -ffp-contract=off is not passed to consumers by default (QD_PROPAGATE_FP_CONTRACT_FLAG OFF) even though the arithmetic is inline in headers, so a consumer's FMA contraction can break the error-free transforms. Upstream BL-highprecision/QD merged td_real (PR #15, 2026-09-25), so the fork's main addition now exists upstream.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Each value is an unevaluated sum of non-overlapping hardware floats, and arithmetic is a short fixed sequence of error-free transformations (TwoSum, TwoProd via FMA or Dekker splitting) plus renormalization, all on the stack and inlinable, with no heap-allocated limb arrays or per-operation rounding-mode bookkeeping. The default build trades a few bits for speed: Cray-style sloppy addition, sloppy QD multiplication that computes the O(eps^3) terms in plain double arithmetic and skips the O(eps^4) terms, and sloppy division with fewer quotient corrections. FMA is auto-detected with a residual correctness probe (td.tex: TwoProd costs 2 flops with FMA vs 17 without, about 1.8x fewer flops for TD/QD multiplication), and optional branch-free add/multiply (Kouya and Zhang-Aiken algorithms, QD_ENABLE_BF*) target SIMD-friendly, branch-predictable dataflow.

**Use it when:**
- C, C++ or Fortran inner loops that need 30-64 significant digits (ill-conditioned linear algebra, SDP solvers, Newton refinement) where 106, 159 or 212 bits is enough and MPFR's per-operation overhead dominates; the lineage evidence is upstream QD at 1.3 GFlops Rgemm vs 512-bit MPFR at 390 MFlops in MPLAPACK on a Threadripper 3970X.
- About 40-50 digits are needed: td_real does a default add in 41 flops vs 84 for qd_real and a multiply in 116 vs 182 flops with FMA (docs/td.tex flop counts, not timings), so you stop paying for QD's 63 digits.
- You want a maintained QD with complex types, exact int64/uint64 constructors, IEEE special-value handling in division and sqrt (1.4.0), MPFR/MPC oracle tests and a CMake package, instead of the older upstream QD releases.
- You build MPLAPACK or other code that already uses the QD API (dd_real/qd_real, fpu_fix_start), since libQD3 keeps that API and is MPLAPACK's QD back end.

**Skip it when:**
- You need more than about 212 bits, or precision chosen at run time: use MPFR, FLINT or LibBF. The exponent range is binary64's (about 1e308) and the legacy README says the types do not extend it.
- You need correctly rounded or IEEE-style error-bounded results: the defaults are sloppy add/multiply/divide, the qd.tex paper says the basic routines lack a full correctness proof, and TODO.md still lists 'sane handling of overflow / underflow / NaNs' and wider signed-zero/NaN/Inf oracle coverage as open.
- You need published throughput for this fork: no benchmark of libQD3 itself exists; the only numbers are a circa-2000 QD vs MPFUN table and MPLAPACK's upstream-QD Rgemm at unequal precision, and the new td_real, edd_real, binary32 and branch-free paths are untimed.
- edd_real on MinGW under Wine (EDD trig tests fail per the README) or on targets without binary80 long double/_Float64x, where EDD is not built.
- Low-adoption risk matters: a 2-star single-maintainer fork; upstream BL-highprecision/QD merged the same author's td_real (PR #15) on 2026-09-25, so upstream may be the more conservative pick if you only need DD/TD/QD.

**Integration:** shared lib (a static library is also built by default; inline arithmetic lives in installed headers) · none at run time beyond libm (librt for clock_gettime where needed); a Fortran compiler for the optional Fortran modules; MPFR, GMP and MPC only for the optional oracle test suites · C++11 (cxx_std_11), CMake 3.20; Autotools removed in 1.2.0; the compiler must accept -ffp-contract=off or -fp-model strict or configuration fails · release gates on Linux amd64, macOS arm64 and amd64, Windows MinGW; Debian i386 x87 supported since 1.3.1; edd_real needs binary80 (x86); QD_ARCH can target generic, x86-64-v3 or native

**Vs siblings:** Pick libQD3 over MultiFloats.hpp (dzhang314/MultiprecisionBenchmarks) when you need a full transcendental and complex function set, triple-double, binary80 limbs or C/Fortran bindings rather than peak branch-free SIMD kernel throughput, which that sibling's SC '25 abstract claims at up to 11.7x QD; pick MPLAPACK on top of it when you need LAPACK routines, and MPFR, FLINT or LibBF when you need more than 212 bits.

**Gotchas:**
- Assigning a double literal gives only double accuracy: write qd_real a = "0.1" (string), not a = 0.1, as the qd.tex manual warns.
- On x87 (32-bit x86 without SSE2 math) call fpu_fix_start() before any DD/TD/QD arithmetic, or 80-bit registers break the error-free transformations; edd_real needs the opposite 80-bit mode (fpu_fix_start_80bit), which 1.3.1 had to separate.
- The library compiles itself with -ffp-contract=off (or -fp-model strict) but does not pass that flag to consumers unless QD_PROPAGATE_FP_CONTRACT_FLAG=ON, although QD_ENABLE_INLINE=ON puts the arithmetic in headers compiled with your flags; build your code without FP contraction or fast-math.
- The docs and build disagree on defaults: td.tex marks accurate QD multiplication as the default, but CMake defaults QD_ENABLE_SLOPPY_MUL=ON. The license files also differ: LICENSE is BSD-3-Clause, COPYING carries the LBNL notice asking commercial users to contact LBNL's Technology Transfer Department, and the td.tex abstract says BSD 2-clause.

**Status:** Actively developed (1.5.0 released 2026-09-18, last commit 2026-09-19, 158 commits, no GitHub issues filed) and BSD-3-Clause with an LBNL commercial-use contact notice; copyable, but a 2-star single-maintainer fork whose main consumer is MPLAPACK, and its td_real was merged into upstream BL-highprecision/QD on 2026-09-25.

[repo](https://github.com/nakatamaho/libQD3) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nakatamaho/mplapack/master/doc/manual/manual.pdf)

##### mpFFT (multiprecision FFT on MPFR)  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Research-grade MPFR-based split-radix FFT in C that runs faster than Mathematica and MATLAB/Advanpix multiprecision FFTs.

**Beats:** Mathematica 11.1 FFT with SetPrecision, and MATLAB 2019a with the Advanpix Multiprecision Toolbox (mp.Digits) — First-party plots on one Intel Core i5-6500 inside an Ubuntu 20.04 VMware Workstation VM (gcc 9.3.0 -O3, static MPFR 4.1.0 / GMP 6.2.1) time the kernel alone for a length-1024 random complex FFT: serially at 1,048,576 digits about 110 s versus about 250 s for Mathematica 11.1 and about 1,300 s for MATLAB 2019a with Advanpix, narrowing to about 2x over MATLAB at 16 digits; at fixed 1024 digits it is about 3x faster than both across lengths 16 to 1,048,576, and on 4 cores about 2-3x faster than MATLAB/Advanpix (all values read from log-scale plots, derived from page data). Baseline scripts are not in the repository, so the comparison cannot be rerun from it.

**Known shortcoming:** MATLAB gap only about 2x at low precision, 10x at high (read from plots); no Mathematica/MATLAB scripts in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarks ran inside a VMware VM; the shipped mpFFT.c is not configured as benchmarked (operation counters on, O(N^2) DFT check on, fixed input); a program, not a library (compile-time length/precision, global state, not thread-safe); timings exclude twiddle-table construction.

**How:** It cuts the number of multiprecision multiplications, which dominate cost at high precision: a recursive decimation-in-time conjugate-pair split-radix-2/4 FFT (Yavne / Duhamel-Hollmann family) with the 3-multiply/3-add complex product (3m3a) using precomputed cos, cos+sin and cos-sin twiddle tables, hard-coded n = 1, 2, 4 base cases and a special butterfly at k = n/8; at P = 1024 bits, N = 1024 the 3m3a scheme drops multiplications from 9,336 to 7,172 and time from 3.32 ms to 3.02 ms (lab OPTIONS.md). The recursive depth-first order removes the bit-reversal pass and keeps the working set local. The parallel version only splits the inner butterfly loop of each recursion level (n >= 16) across 4 OpenMP threads; all arithmetic is plain MPFR calls, so per-operation speed is MPFR's.

**Use it when:**
- You need a forward complex FFT at hundreds to about a million decimal digits in C and currently call Mathematica or MATLAB with the Advanpix toolbox for it.
- Power-of-two lengths from 16 to about 1M points at fixed high precision (the dP = 1024 plots show it about 3x ahead of both baselines across that whole range).
- You already hold data as mpfr_t and want a small, readable split-radix kernel to vendor and adapt (Apache-2.0).
- Studying multiprecision FFT design trade-offs: the lab/ tree keeps several kernel variants, complexity counters and an inverse-FFT error test.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a library API: there is no init/plan/execute interface, N and P are #defines, and state is global, so each size/precision is a recompile.
- Non-power-of-two lengths, real-input, inverse or multidimensional transforms: none are implemented (the README only describes how they could be derived).
- You need rigorous error bounds or arbitrary lengths: FLINT's acb_dft does ball arithmetic and supports any length (naive, CRT, cyclic, radix-2, Bluestein).
- Precision near double-double or quad-double (about 32-64 digits): at 16 digits mpFFT is only about 2x ahead of MATLAB/Advanpix in its own plot, and hardware-double-based formats are a better fit there.
- Production use: single 2021 commit, self-described as 'still in development and far from complete', no tests or CI, no open issues or releases.

**Integration:** source-drop · MPFR (4.1.0 used; mpfr_get_str_ndigits needs 4.1+), GMP (6.2.1 used), libm; OpenMP and pthread for the parallel kernel; MPFR must be built with --enable-thread-safe for parallel runs · C with GCC; only gcc 9.3.0 -O3 is documented · POSIX (uses clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)); tested only on an Intel Core i5-6500; others not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FLINT's acb_dft when you only need a plain power-of-two forward FFT on mpfr_t values and want MPFR semantics rather than ball arithmetic, accepting that no head-to-head with FLINT exists. Unlike MPLAPACK or APFP, which speed up multiprecision linear algebra, it is the only catalogued entry aimed at the FFT itself.

**Gotchas:**
- The shipped mpFFT.c defaults are not the benchmark configuration: CC = 1 turns on operation counters (inside '#pragma omp critical' in the parallel kernel), CH = 1 runs an O(N^2) double-precision DFT check, IN = 2 uses a fixed input rather than the random input in the plots, and M = 1; set CC 0 and CH 0 before timing.
- Benchmarks time the FFT kernel only; building the twiddle table (N/4 mpfr_cos and mpfr_sin calls at full precision) and allocation are excluded and can dominate a one-off transform at high precision.
- The parallel kernel hard-codes num_threads(4) and opens a new OpenMP region (with fresh mpfr_inits2 temporaries) at every recursion level with n >= 16; the author notes at best about 3x on 4 cores because only the inner loop is parallel.
- Conjugate-pair recursion indexes the input through negative offsets (inr - s, wrapped by s0 = N), so the input arrays must follow the exact layout the kernel expects.

**Status:** Abandoned after a single commit on 2021-10-10, but the code is Apache-2.0 (docs CC BY 4.0) and the kernel is small enough to vendor and adapt.

[repo](https://github.com/mfrewer/mpFFT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mfrewer/mpFFT)

##### MPLAPACK (multiple-precision BLAS/LAPACK with double-double, quad-double and CUDA backends)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Full BLAS/LAPACK in C++ at binary80/128, double-double, quad-double, GMP and MPFR; the dd/qd backends far outrun its 512-bit GMP/MPFR backends.

**Beats:** GMP (mpf) and MPFR backends of the same library, at their default 512-bit precision — First-party manual figures on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X (GCC 9.3.0 in Docker, optimization flags not stated, square matrices up to about n = 1000): Rgemm with OpenMP peaked at 11.2 GFlops for double-double and 1.3 GFlops for quad-double versus 693 MFlops for 512-bit GMP and 390 MFlops for 512-bit MPFR, about 16x and 29x for dd (derived from page data). The 2022 logs on the A100 box show OpenMP dd 8.16 GFlops versus GMP 667 and MPFR 403 MFlops, and the CUDA dd Rgemm at 487 GFlops kernel-only or 382 GFlops with transfers (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Compares its own double-double/quad-double backends with 512-bit GMP/MPFR (unequal precision); A100 486,829 MFLOPS is kernel-only (381,882 with transfers).

**Known shortcoming:** The 'optimized' CPU Rgemm is the reference triple loop with one OpenMP pragma; CUDA kernels use QD's less accurate fast-multiply/fast-add; 2022 benchmarks predate the 3.0.0 rewrite of the GMP/MPFR wrappers (ABI/API break); the GMP backend aborts with SIGFPE on division by exact zero and some helpers silently drop to 53-bit precision.

**How:** The speedup comes from the format, not from kernel tuning: double-double (about 32 digits) and quad-double (about 64 digits) are unevaluated sums of 2 or 4 hardware doubles using Dekker/Knuth error-free transformations (QD library), avoiding GMP/MPFR's heap-allocated limb arithmetic. The optimized CPU Rgemm is the reference triple loop with one '#pragma omp parallel for' over output columns (no blocking or SIMD). The CUDA double-double Rgemm/Rsyrk kernels (2010-2011 Fermi/Tesla code) use FMA-based dd multiply and add on the GPU.

**Use it when:**
- You need LAPACK-level algorithms (LU/Cholesky solves, eigenvalues, SVD, least squares) beyond binary64 in C/C++, for ill-conditioned systems or interior-point SDP solvers (it began as the backend of SDPA-GMP).
- About 32 digits is enough: the dd backend with OpenMP reached 11.2 GFlops Rgemm on a 32-core Threadripper 3970X versus 0.69 GFlops for 512-bit GMP and 0.39 GFlops for 512-bit MPFR.
- An NVIDIA GPU is available and dd precision suffices: the CUDA dd Rgemm logged about 380 GFlops including transfers (487 GFlops kernel-only) on an A100.
- You need precision chosen at run time (MPFR, e.g. 65,536 bits via MPLAPACK_MPFR_PRECISION) while keeping one LAPACK-style code path across backends.
- You want a heavily tested multiprecision LAPACK: 3.0.0 release QA ran over 126 million lin tests and 116 million eig tests across 11 platform/compiler triplets.

**Skip it when:**
- binary64 or fast high-precision BLAS: the manual says its double results 'are not competitive to OpenBLAS or Intel MKL' (15 GFlops OpenMP versus 1.46 TFlops OpenBLAS DGEMM on the same CPU); the multiprecision kernels have no blocking or vectorization ('Rgemm acceleration' issue #59 open since 2022).
- You need more than about 64 digits and high throughput: the GMP/MPFR paths ran at 0.4-0.7 GFlops at 512 bits on 32 cores.
- You need certified error bounds: results are rounded floating-point values, not interval or ball enclosures.
- GMP backend for CSD or transcendental-heavy paths: GMP's mpf lacks atan2, so Rorbdb/Cunbdb fail at entry, and the manual says GMP support will be dropped in favor of MPFR.
- Clang-only toolchains needing binary128 (unsupported), or users who need bit-identical results across platforms (the project warns last-digit differences are the default).

**Integration:** shared lib · Bundled and built by the autotools build: GMP, MPFR, MPC, QD (libQD3), gmpfrxx_mkII wrappers, OpenBLAS (benchmarks only); CUDA for the dd GPU flavor; the experimental CMake build uses system GMP/MPFR/MPC/QD instead · C++17 (C++17/20/23/26 selectable); GCC with gfortran for the autotools build, GCC 15 supported since 2.1.1; Intel oneAPI icx/icpx supported; Clang lacks binary128 · Tier 1: Linux and macOS on amd64 and arm64, Windows via MinGW-w64, Debian i386; binary80 x86 only; CUDA dd kernels on NVIDIA GPUs (V100, A100 and RTX 3080 results published)

**Vs siblings:** Pick MPLAPACK over FLINT or APFP when you need complete LAPACK factorizations, eigen and SVD solvers rather than only fast big-number or matrix-multiply kernels, and over DoubleFloats.jl or MultiFloats.jl when you are in C++ rather than Julia and want one API spanning double-double to arbitrary MPFR precision.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline speedups compare unequal precision: dd (106 bits) and qd (212 bits) against 512-bit GMP/MPFR; at equal precision there is no speedup claim, and benchmarks are from 2022 (v2.0, GCC 9.3.0, flags not stated), before the 3.0.0 move to expression-template MPFR/GMP wrappers.
- 3.0.0 broke the ABI and API: mpreal and mpcomplex became mpfr_class and mpc_class, the GMP complex type became mpfc_class, and since 2.3.0 the separate libmpblas_* libraries are gone, so the v2.0.1 manual's examples and link lines are out of date.
- GMP backend hazards documented by the project: exact division by zero aborts with SIGFPE instead of producing Inf, and any helper reached through mpf_class's implicit operator double() silently truncates to 53 bits.
- DD needs -ffp-contract=off (a DD miscompilation was fixed in 2.1.1 by forcing it); dd/qd do not implement full IEEE Inf/NaN/signed-zero semantics; the CUDA dd kernels compile with QD's SLOPPY_MUL and CRAY_ADD variants, and the 487 GFlops A100 figure excludes host-device transfers.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v3.0.1 released 2026-09-15, latest master commit 2026-09-19, 3,808 commits, 24 open issues), BSD-2-Clause, with a large tiered release test matrix; the performance data has not been refreshed since 2022.

[repo](https://github.com/nakatamaho/mplapack) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nakatamaho/mplapack/master/doc/manual/manual.pdf)

##### mr_blackwell (native Miller-Rabin GPU kernel)  `CUDA C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

CUDA base-2 Miller-Rabin kernel with PTX-carry Montgomery multiplication; replaces CGBN in prime-gap and runs about 9x faster than the CPU/GMP pipeline.

**Beats:** GMP (CPU Miller-Rabin probable-prime test with GMP modular exponentiation) — On an RTX 5070 (CUDA 12.9, nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_120) the standalone kernel tests 65,536 random odd 683-bit candidates at about 1.8 million base-2 PRP/sec (295,000 at 1240 bits). The '132x versus GMP' figure divides that by a hard-coded 13,700 PRP/sec from a single-threaded CPU run on a 'Ryzen 9 8800X3D' (as named in the README), with GMP version and flags not stated. The measured prime-gap run (P=503, 13K tests) takes 3.1 s on the GPU versus 28.0 s for CPU gap_test_simple, about 9x (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** mr_blackwell.cu prints 'vs CPU' by dividing by a hard-coded 13700 and never times GMP (close to the zokio precedent, but the constant matches a CPU run from prime-gap reported in the README, so kept); measured pipeline 28.0 s vs 3.1 s (about 9x); CPU baseline gap_test_simple looks single-threaded; README names a CPU 'Ryzen 9 8800X3D' that is not a known model.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark kernel is not the shipped kernel (the shipped header computes R^2 mod n on the GPU, the benchmark gets it from the host); only base 2 tested and the rounds argument is ignored; not constant-time (not for crypto); code uses a 5-bit window while the README describes 4-bit.

**How:** One GPU thread per candidate runs Montgomery CIOS multiplication written with inline PTX carry-chain instructions (mad.lo.cc, madc.hi, add.cc, addc), fixed-window modular exponentiation, and comparisons against 1 and n-1 done in Montgomery form to skip conversions. The limb count is a template parameter sized to the operand (22 limbs for 683 bits instead of 32, about 2x per the README). Version 2 computes R^2 mod n (by repeated doubling) and -n^-1 mod 2^32 (Newton iteration) on the device, so the host only exports limbs: per-candidate data drops from 268 to 136 bytes and the measured prime-gap run went from 92 s to 70 s.

**Use it when:**
- You run sethtroisi/prime-gap's gap_test_gpu on a Blackwell GPU (sm_120), where the author reports CGBN as orders of magnitude too slow.
- Bulk base-2 PRP screening of many independent, pre-sieved odd numbers of 512-2048 bits (prime-gap and primorial searches) on a consumer NVIDIA GPU.
- The CPU PRP stage is your bottleneck: paired with the included hunt_parallel.sh, which overlaps CPU sieving with GPU testing (85 s down to 52 s per range in the script's own example).
- You want a small Apache-2.0 reference for Montgomery multiplication with PTX carry chains to adapt to another fixed-size modular-exponentiation kernel.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a proof of primality or a multi-base or BPSW test: only base 2 is tested and the rounds argument of test_runner_t is ignored, so base-2 strong pseudoprimes pass; confirm survivors on the CPU.
- Secret exponents or any cryptographic use: the code declares CONSTANT_TIME = false and uses exponent-indexed window tables and early exits.
- General bignum arithmetic, arbitrary bases or moduli, operands above 2048 bits, AMD/Intel GPUs or CPU-only machines.
- Pre-Blackwell NVIDIA GPUs where CGBN works: other architectures are listed as 'should work (untested)', and no comparison with CGBN on a GPU where CGBN runs normally is published.
- Multi-GPU or library embedding: test_runner_t hard-codes cudaSetDevice(0) and calls exit(1) on CUDA errors or oversized candidates.

**Integration:** header-only · CUDA Toolkit (README: 11.0+, 12.x recommended; tested with 12.9), GMP on the host for mpz_export and the correctness check · nvcc from CUDA 11.0+ (README); built with nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_XXX · NVIDIA GPUs SM 3.5+ claimed; only SM 12.0 (RTX 5070) tested; Linux (Linux Mint) tested

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over CGBN on Blackwell (sm_120) when you only need base-2 PRP tests at fixed sizes; CGBN remains the general GPU bignum library with published V100 results for add, mul and powm. For CPU-only batches, the AVX-512 truncated batch Montgomery entry (about 4-5x GMP on batched 1024-4096-bit Montgomery multiplications) is the closer alternative.

**Gotchas:**
- The '132x vs CPU (GMP)' and '21x' figures divide GPU throughput by a hard-coded 13,700 PRP/sec ('%.1fx vs CPU@13700' in mr_blackwell.cu); GMP is only an untimed correctness check (mpz_probab_prime_p(n, 1)), and the 13,700 comes from a single-threaded CPU run. The measured end-to-end comparison is 28.0 s versus 3.1 s, about 9x.
- The standalone benchmark kernel takes R^2 mod n and n0inv precomputed on the host, while the shipped header computes them on the GPU (its comments estimate about 8% extra kernel time), so 'make bench' does not time the shipped kernel exactly; both time the kernel only, without host-device copies.
- The code defaults to a 5-bit window (MR_WINDOW_BITS 5), while the README describes a 4-bit window and says 5 bits gave only 2.3%; the 32-entry table per thread (about 2.8 KB at 22 limbs, 5 KB at 40) lives in local memory.
- In the header LIMBS = BITS / 32, so BITS must be a multiple of 32 that covers the candidate (e.g. BITS=704 for P=503), or from_mpz_native aborts the process. The carry flag is passed between separate asm volatile statements, which relies on the compiler not inserting flag-clobbering instructions; the only correctness evidence is the GMP cross-check in 'make test'.

**Status:** Recently active (18 commits, last 2026-05-05; 3 stars, no releases or open issues) and Apache-2.0 with a single header of about 19 KB, but tested on one RTX 5070 only and tied to prime-gap's interface.

[repo](https://github.com/pscamillo/mr_blackwell) · [benchmark](https://github.com/pscamillo/mr_blackwell)

##### MultiFloats.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Julia double/triple/quad-Float64 expansion arithmetic (about 106-212 bits) claimed 30x faster than BigFloat (MPFR) at 30 digits.

**Beats:** MPFR (via Julia BigFloat) — The only package-level evidence is a first-party README sentence: at 30-digit precision it is 30x faster than Julia BigFloat (MPFR), 6x faster than Quadmath.jl (libquadmath) and 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl. No table, hardware, Julia version or package version accompanies it, and the earlier QR/pseudoinverse benchmark gist has code but no recorded output. Search snippets say the peer-reviewed SC25 paper (not opened, host blocked) measures a C++ prototype of the same algorithms against GMP 6.3.0, MPFR 4.2.1 and FLINT 3.2.1, not this Julia package.

**Known shortcoming:** 30x/6x/2x claim in README with no method; correctness history: v2.0 Float64x5-x8 'fundamentally broken' (removed), v2.0 lost accuracy from denormalization, prevfloat/nextfloat skipped values before v3.0; Julia-only.

**Known shortcoming:** README says transcendentals go through MPFR, but sin/cos/atan raise an error unless use_bigfloat_transcendentals() is called (exp/log are native); open perf issues #85 (LinearAlgebra solver slower than DoubleFloats, 3.42 vs 2.95 s) and #34.

**How:** Each value is an unevaluated sum of 2-4 machine floats (a floating-point expansion, as in double-double and QD quad-double). Arithmetic is fixed, branch-free networks of two_sum, fast_two_sum and FMA-based two_prod error-free transformations, fully inlined. Per the README these are new algorithms found by computer search (Zhang and Aiken, CAV25 and SC25 papers). There is no heap allocation and no data-dependent branching, so the code vectorises through SIMD.jl and runs as-is in CUDA, AMDGPU and oneAPI kernels via package extensions. exp2 and log2 are native polynomial and table kernels with expansion coefficients, not MPFR calls.

**Use it when:**
- Julia numerical code (linear algebra, ODEs, SDP or least-squares refinement) that loses accuracy in Float64 but needs only 30-60 digits.
- Element-wise kernels over large arrays where BigFloat's per-value heap allocation dominates; MultiFloat values are isbits tuples that pack into plain arrays.
- GPU kernels in Julia that need more than double precision (Float64x2), or more than single precision on Float32-only hardware (Float32x2-x4).
- Explicit SIMD code through the MultiFloatVec types (Vec2-Vec32 lanes), for example batched dot products.
- As a reference design for a C++ port: the author's MultiprecisionBenchmarks repo has a 373-line header-only C++ MultiFloat<T,N> with + and * over double, __m128d, __m256d and __m512d.

**Skip it when:**
- You need more than about 212 bits, or a precision you choose at run time: Float64x5-Float64x8 were removed in v3.0 because the v2.0 algorithms for them were 'fundamentally broken', and no replacement exists yet.
- You need IEEE semantics for infinities: most operations treat +-Inf inputs as NaN (Float64x4(Inf) + 1.0 returns NaN), and the exponent range is only Float64's.
- Trigonometric, hyperbolic and inverse functions (sin, cos, atan, sinh and others) raise an error unless you call MultiFloats.use_bigfloat_transcendentals(), which converts to BigFloat on every call and loses the speed advantage. Open issues #90 (atan) and #74 (sin/cos) track this.
- Code in C++: the package is pure Julia. The C++ header in MultiprecisionBenchmarks covers only + and * and needs x86 SSE/AVX/AVX-512 intrinsics plus FMA.
- Non-IEEE hardware or rounding modes other than round-to-nearest; the README says obscure architectures may need extra setup.

**Integration:** module · Julia stdlib LinearAlgebra, Printf and Random; MPFR_jll 4 (conversions and the optional transcendental fallback); SIMD.jl 3. Weak dependencies: CUDA.jl, AMDGPU.jl and oneAPI.jl for GPU extensions. · Julia 1.6 (Project.toml compat), package version 3.3.2 · Any IEEE 754 CPU in round-to-nearest mode (x86 and ARM work out of the box per the README); FMA hardware needed for speed; NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs through extensions

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over DoubleFloats.jl when you need triple or quad-double (Float64x3/x4), SIMD vector types or GPU kernels, or the claimed 2x speedup at double-double. Pick TLFloat or simd-f128 instead when you need C or C++ code (TLFloat when you also need IEEE binary128 semantics), and MPLAPACK's dd/qd backends for C++ BLAS/LAPACK at this precision.

**Gotchas:**
- Rare non-unique representations: about 1 in 2^53 values has several normalized forms, so use MultiFloats.canonize before bitwise hashing or equality on limbs.
- Mixed-type promotion: multiplying Float64x4 by UInt8 or Float32 promotes to the full Float64x4 product (open issue #34: about 250 us vs 170 us for a Float64 scalar). Convert small scalars to Float64 first.
- Generic LinearAlgebra solver paths can be slower than with DoubleFloats.jl despite faster matmul (open issue #85: 20x20 SDP 3.42 s vs 2.95 s for Double64).
- v3.0 fixed correctness bugs from v2.0: denormalized results that caused spurious accuracy loss (issues #42 and #45), prevfloat and nextfloat skipping values, and non-commutative multiplication. Pin v3 or later.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v3.3.2, last commit 2026-09-16, 159 stars) and MIT-licensed, but usable only from Julia; C++ users would port the published networks or start from the benchmark header.

[repo](https://github.com/dzhang314/MultiFloats.jl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dzhang314/MultiFloats.jl)

##### primefactors (CPU GMP/GMP-ECM reference plus CGBN GPU factoring programs)  `C and CUDA`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Hobby integer-factoring programs: CPU GMP-ECM reference plus CGBN GPU variants that, by the author's own numbers, lose to CPU ECM.

**Beats:** GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (libecm, on GMP): the repo's own CPU reference path is GMP plus libecm, and the GPU programs are measured against it — These are first-party wall-clock figures, and they are not a speedup. On an RTX 4080 (CUDA 12.9, nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_89) the GPU Pollard's rho needs about 8.7 s for a 16-digit factor, versus about 2 s for the CPU GMP-ECM path on the same number. The CPU path (gcc -O3 -fopenmp, GMP-ECM 7.0.6) took about 10.5 s, 20.6 s and 5.7 min for 30-, 35- and 40-digit factors on an unnamed 32-core machine, and was never compared with the stock ecm binary or with single-threaded GMP-ECM.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster: the README's first-party figures put its GPU Pollard rho at 8.7 s against 2 s for CPU GMP-ECM, and the CPU path claims no win over stock GMP-ECM. Tier C, 1 star, last commit 2026-09-01.

**Known shortcoming:** GPU Miller-Rabin uses the fixed bases 2-37 only; cgbnprimefactors has no ECM fallback and prints unsplit composites after a warning; the Makefile puts -lecm -lgmp before the object file, so linkers defaulting to --as-needed reject it; the README dependency table does not match the Makefile.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It is not faster than its baseline; the design is about GPU parallelism. The CPU path runs one OpenMP task stream over a 12-level {B1, curves} ladder modelled on GMP-ECM's tables (15 to 70 digits), with no barrier between levels and a shared stop flag polled through libecm's stop_asap callback, so all cores stay busy and in-flight curves stop once one thread finds a factor. The GPU rho kernel runs about 8192 warps of independent Floyd walks (one constant c each), computes a double-width square then reduces it (cgbn_sqr_wide + cgbn_rem_wide), and sends each cofactor to the narrowest of nine CGBN widths (128 to 32768 bits). Per the design doc, those two changes cut the 16-digit case from about 37 s to 8.65 s on the GPU, which is still slower than CPU ECM.

**Use it when:**
- As readable example code for CGBN: width dispatch through an X-macro, the cooperative atomicCAS + __shfl_sync claim of a result, exact modular squaring, per-thread CUDA streams, and a design PDF that records three reverted 'optimizations' with measured slowdowns (Brent batched gcd about 2.6x slower, per-instance ILP 2-4x, __launch_bounds__ capping).
- Quick CPU factoring of 30-40 digit factors on a many-core Linux box that already has GMP and libecm: the author reports about 10.5 s (30 digits), 20.6 s (35) and 5.7 min (40) for balanced semiprimes on a 32-core machine.
- Throughput experiments that split many small factors (up to about 16 digits) across several GPUs with one MPI rank per GPU; the author has not tested multi-node runs.
- A starting point for MPI-distributed trial division against a table of primes you have already proven.

**Skip it when:**
- You want something faster than GMP-ECM: GPU rho took about 8.7 s on an RTX 4080 for a 16-digit factor vs about 2 s for CPU ECM (about 4x slower, derived from page data); factors of 19 or more digits are impractical on the GPU path; below 2^64 both GPU programs are 'much slower' because of CUDA and MPI start-up.
- Factors beyond about 45 digits: the README says single-machine ECM tops out there, and there is no quadratic or number field sieve.
- You need guaranteed factorizations: primality is Miller-Rabin (40 rounds on the CPU, 12 fixed bases 2-37 in the GPU kernel), and when the rho or ECM budget runs out the composite is printed as a 'factor' after a warning.
- You need a library or multiplicities: these are CLI programs with global state that print distinct primes only, sorted, on stderr.
- You need maturity: 7 commits (2026-08-28 to 2026-09-01), 1 star, no test suite, MPI scaling never measured on a real cluster.

**Integration:** source-drop · CPU program: GMP, GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (libecm), OpenMP. GPU programs: CUDA toolkit (12.9 or 13.2), the author's CGBN fork steleman/nvidia-cgbn installed in /usr/local/include/cgbn (adds signed arithmetic, Ada/Blackwell support and widths up to 256K bits), GMP, OpenMPI 5.0.5; ecmcgbnprimefactorsmpi also needs libecm and pthreads · GCC with C17 and OpenMP for the CPU program; nvcc from CUDA 12.9 (-arch=sm_89) or 13.2 (sm_120) for the GPU programs · Linux (tested on Fedora 41 and 44, x86-64 hosts); GPU programs on NVIDIA Ada (RTX 4080) and Blackwell (RTX PRO 4500), other GPUs by editing GPU_ARCH

**Vs siblings:** Do not pick it for speed. ECM-ELF is the sibling that beats GMP-ECM (about 3x per curve in stage 1 with AVX-512 IFMA), and CGBN itself or mr_blackwell are better places to get GPU big-integer or Miller-Rabin throughput. Use this repo only as worked example code for CGBN, MPI and libecm orchestration.

**Gotchas:**
- cgbnprimefactors has no ECM fallback: after 7 rho attempts (walk length starts at 200,000 iterations and triples each time) it records the unsplit composite with only a warning, and results go to stderr alongside the warnings.
- ecmcgbnprimefactorsmpi treats every number in the primes file as proven prime and never tests it, so a bad table silently yields wrong factors; whatever the table misses goes to a single-threaded GMP-ECM ladder on rank 0.
- The Makefile hard-codes /usr/bin/gcc, /usr/local/cuda-12.9, sm_89 and /usr/lib64/openmpi, and its CPU link rule puts -lecm -lgmp before primefactors.o, which linkers that default to --as-needed reject. The README's dependency table (GMP-ECM and CUDA rows) does not match the Makefile, and the design PDF's ecmcgbnprimefactorsmpi command line predates the current -f/-t options.
- The README says the author used Claude Opus 5.0 for the Pollard's rho code and for testing and bug finding.

**Status:** Hobby project, MIT, 7 commits ending 2026-09-01: copyable but unpackaged and untested beyond the author's two Fedora machines, catalogued only to record that it does not beat GMP-ECM.

[repo](https://github.com/steleman/primefactors) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steleman/primefactors/HEAD/README.md)

##### simd-f128  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C11/C++11 double-double (about 106-bit, 31-digit) type, claimed 1.5-3.4x lower latency than GCC __float128.

**Beats:** GCC __float128 (libquadmath) — First-party only. The project's bench_compare.c runs loop-carried add, mul and div 10M times each against GCC __float128 on an unnamed 12-thread, 3.27 GHz machine with no compiler version stated. The current console output reads __float128 153.37/193.23/325.37 ms vs simd-f128 (AVX2) 99.44/74.46/207.98 ms (1.54x, 2.59x, 1.56x). A second README table from a different run claims up to 3.38x on multiplication.

**Known shortcoming:** README has two inconsistent tables (mul 3.38x vs 2.59x; div 1.73x vs 1.56x) and the '1.7x-3.3x' headline uses the more favourable run; baseline is __float128 only (no GMP/MPFR numbers); double-double is not IEEE binary128; the Google Benchmark mul loop overflows to inf; no CPU or compiler version (flags inferred from CMakeLists); extended-precision float rather than big integers, an edge case for this category.

**Known shortcoming:** numeric_limits is_iec559=true on a non-IEEE type; add is the QD 'sloppy' add; the Google Benchmark table mixes latency (add/mul) and independent-op (div/sqrt) timings; bodies are static inline behind SIMD_F128_IMPLEMENTATION, so the README's one-TU rule breaks multi-TU builds (inferred); default CMake build is scalar without FMA.

**How:** Values are unevaluated sums of two hardware doubles, so each operation is a dozen or so native double operations instead of software-emulated 113-bit binary128. Addition is Knuth TwoSum on the high parts plus plain addition of the low parts (QD's 'sloppy' add); multiplication uses hardware FMA for the exact product error when FP_FAST_FMA is defined, otherwise the Dekker/Veltkamp split; division and sqrt take one hardware estimate plus one Newton-Raphson-style correction. The scalar API keeps the pair in a SIMD register but computes lane by lane, so the speedup over __float128 comes from hardware double arithmetic and FMA, not lane parallelism; only simd_f128x4 (AVX2) processes four values at once.

**Use it when:**
- Deep-zoom fractal rendering (the author's mandelbrot-c reaches 1e-28 coordinates) and other inner loops that need about 31 digits without heap allocation.
- Long-horizon integrators (RK4, n-body, orbital mechanics) where double rounding error accumulates and the range of double (about 1e308) is enough.
- Projects that must build on MSVC, ARM, RISC-V or WebAssembly where __float128 is unavailable or emulated slowly.
- Batch element-wise work on x86 with AVX2 and FMA, using simd_f128x4 or the SoA array helpers.
- Eigen or std::complex code that needs a higher-precision scalar through the provided traits.

**Skip it when:**
- You need IEEE binary128 semantics: correct rounding, the 15-bit exponent range, or bit-exact results matching other quad implementations. Use __float128 or TLFloat.
- Your code subtracts nearly equal values: the README warns of catastrophic cancellation, and the sloppy add has no small relative-error bound in that case.
- sin and cos of large arguments: math_theory.md says range reduction is simplified and Payne-Hanek reduction must be applied externally for |x| much larger than 2*pi.
- You need more than about 31 digits or arbitrary precision: use MPFR, or a triple/quad-double library such as MultiFloats.jl or QD.
- Mature production use: first commit 2026-08, one author, 2 stars, a small test suite (two ctest targets in the README run) and no external users besides the author's own projects.

**Integration:** header-only · none (libm on Linux/UNIX for fma); optional Google Benchmark for benchmarks; pybind11, Emscripten or cc/bindgen for the bindings · C11 (C99 for the scalar path) or C++11; README lists GCC 4.9+, Clang 3.5+, MSVC 2019+, Emscripten 3.0+, with CI on GCC 11+, Clang 14+ and MSVC 2022 · x86-64 (scalar, SSE2, AVX2), AArch64 NEON, ARMv7 (scalar, VFPv4 for FMA), RISC-V64 scalar, WebAssembly SIMD128 and scalar; backend chosen at compile time from compiler macros

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over TLFloat when you are in C or C++, can accept double-double semantics, and want the cheapest roughly 31-digit type on MSVC, ARM or WebAssembly; pick TLFloat when you need IEEE binary128. Pick it over MultiFloats.jl and DoubleFloats.jl only because those are Julia-only; they offer triple and quad-double, normalized algorithms and a longer track record.

**Gotchas:**
- Every function body is static inline but sits behind #ifdef SIMD_F128_IMPLEMENTATION. Contrary to the README's 'exactly one translation unit' instruction, any translation unit that calls the arithmetic must define the macro, or it sees only declarations (inferred from simd_f128.h).
- Speed depends on build flags: the default CMake build is the scalar backend, and exact products use FMA only when FP_FAST_FMA (or __FMA__ for the x4 path) is defined. Build with -mavx2 -mfma (SIMD_F128_AVX2=ON) or an AArch64 target, or multiplication falls back to the slower Dekker split.
- std::numeric_limits<f128::float128>::is_iec559 is set to true although the type is double-double and not IEEE binary128. Generic code that trusts this trait will assume IEEE behaviour.
- The README's Google Benchmark table mixes metrics: Add and Mul (11.7 and 10.1 ns) are loop-carried latency, while Div and Sqrt (2.87 and 6.05 ns) time independent operations (bench_math.cpp). In the Mul loop the value roughly doubles every iteration and soon overflows to infinity, hitting the early-return path.

**Status:** Brand-new (2026-08) single-author MIT project with 2 stars, active through 2026-08-17 (v1.6.0, PyPI 1.6.2), small enough to vendor but not yet proven in outside use.

[repo](https://github.com/tiw302/simd-f128) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tiw302/simd-f128)

##### Swift-BigInt (BInt)  `Swift`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Swift arbitrary-precision integers (BInt) and fractions (BDouble), claimed about 2x faster than mini-gmp, not full GMP.

**Beats:** mini-gmp (GMP's portable minimal subset without assembly kernels); the README says full GMP was not counted because it needs to be installed and is not portable — The only comparison is one first-party README sentence: BInt is about 2x faster than mini-gmp (GMP's portable C subset without assembly), adding via fib(100,000) in 272 ms vs 530 ms and multiplying more than twice as fast. No hardware, compiler, build mode, date or comparison harness is given; the repo's benchmarks time only BInt against its own saved baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline is really mini-gmp (README says full GMP is not counted; no GMP code in the repo), so the record's 'beats GMP' framing was wrong; Swift.

**Known shortcoming:** README fib numbers are stale (predate the PR #90 rewrite; Fib 100000 is now 70x faster); multi-limb divMod is bit-by-bit O(n^2); correctness history #78 (Int(5)+=BInt(10) gave 20) and #80 comparison bug, #83 nthroot infinite loop still open; not constant-time; needs Swift 5.5+ though manifests say 4.2.

**How:** Multiplication is Karatsuba above 48 limbs and schoolbook below, on 64-bit limbs using multipliedFullWidth. Decimal I/O works in base 10^18 chunks. Addition and multiplication skip zero limbs. The baseline, mini-gmp, is GMP's portable subset without assembly kernels, so the comparison measures portable code against portable code. A 2026-03 rewrite (PR #90) reported 70x on its own Fib 100000 benchmark, 6.5x on 270k-bit multiplication and 3.56x on factorial of 40,000 against the previous BInt, but division was unchanged (0.99x).

**Use it when:**
- Swift apps on iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS or Linux that need big integers or exact rationals without linking GMP, for licensing or packaging reasons.
- Moderate-size combinatorics, factorials, Fibonacci or exact-fraction arithmetic where multiplication and addition dominate.
- Teaching or prototyping, where a single readable source file you can vendor beats a C dependency.
- Generic Swift code over BinaryInteger that should also work with arbitrary-size integers.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything in C or C++: Swift only, with no C ABI. Use Boost.Multiprecision, mp++, FLINT or GMP instead.
- Division-heavy or modular work (mod_exp, gcd on large values, modulo loops): multi-limb divMod is a bit-at-a-time shift-subtract loop with a full remainder shift per bit, so it is quadratic with a large constant. There is no Knuth Algorithm D, Barrett/Montgomery or subquadratic division.
- Very large operands (millions of digits): no Toom-Cook or FFT multiplication beyond Karatsuba, and quadratic base-10^18 string conversion.
- Cryptography: arithmetic is not constant-time and mod_exp is plain square-and-multiply over the slow division.
- Workloads that need proven correctness: the tracker shows past wrong-result bugs (#78, Int(5) += BInt(10) gave 20; #80, a comparison returned the wrong answer for a variable Int vs a BInt, closed 2026-03-29), and #83 (BDouble nthroot(1024000, 2) loops forever) is still open.

**Integration:** module · none (Foundation; Glibc on Linux) · Swift 5.5+ in practice, since BInt and BDouble declare Sendable; Package.swift and the podspec still say Swift 4.2 and the README says Xcode 9+/Swift 4+. Podspec targets iOS 11, macOS 10.11, watchOS 4, tvOS 11. · Apple platforms and Linux; any CPU Swift targets (pure Swift, no assembly or SIMD)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only for Swift projects that cannot link GMP; every sibling in the catalog is C, C++ or Rust, and in C++ Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int or mp++ fill the same 'no external GMP' role with far better division and stronger evidence. Rust users have Malachite, ibig or dashu, which carry measured comparisons against real GMP.

**Gotchas:**
- Benchmark numbers in the README (fib(100,000): 272 ms vs 530 ms for mini-gmp) predate the 2026-03 performance rewrite and give no hardware or build mode. The README says debug builds are more than 10x slower than release, so measure in release (-O).
- In the README's performance paragraph 'GMP' means mini-gmp; full GMP was deliberately not compared and would likely win on large operands.
- BDouble is an exact rational that auto-reduces by gcd, so long chains of operations grow numerators and denominators, and every gcd uses the slow division. pow and nthroot on BDouble are only accurate to the precision setting (docs say to compare with nearlyEqual).
- Errors stop the program rather than being recoverable: division by zero, negative exponents and invalid bases trigger precondition or fatalError traps; String initialisers return nil on bad input.

**Status:** Maintained (v2.4.0 and a large performance rewrite merged 2026-03-29, 259 stars, MIT); one Swift file small enough to vendor, but irrelevant to C++ users and with a history of correctness bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/mkrd/Swift-BigInt) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mkrd/Swift-BigInt)

##### TLFloat  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Constexpr C++20 template library for IEEE half to octuple floats; inlined Quad beats libquadmath on add/mul/fma/sqrt/casts, loses on div/exp/log/pow.

**Beats:** GNU libquadmath (GCC __float128) — The project's own bench tool (src/util/bench.cpp, -DBUILD_BENCH=True) times 256-element loops of each operation for 10 s on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X at 4.5 GHz with gcc 12.3.0: TLFloat 1.11.0 Quad (inlined) beat GNU libquadmath / GCC __float128 on add (124 vs 88 Mops/s), mul (102 vs 78), compare, casts to/from double (168 vs 64), sqrt (15.9 vs 9.5), rint (191 vs 38), fma (68.5 vs 1.9) and sin (2.13 vs 1.77), and lost on div, atan, exp, log and pow. First-party, single machine, flags beyond the CMake defaults not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Loses to libquadmath on div/atan/exp/log/pow; run flags not stated; baseline libquadmath is not a category incumbent.

**Known shortcoming:** bench.cpp's 'libquadmath' add/mul/div/cmp/cast rows use GCC __float128 operators, not libquadmath calls (baseline mislabel); README numbers from v1.11.0 while the source is 1.17.1.

**How:** Each float is unpacked into sign, exponent and an integer mantissa held in a recursive BigUInt<N> template (two 2^(N-1)-bit halves), and arithmetic is done as fixed-width integer operations that use x86 intrinsics (_addcarry_u64, _umul128, inline-asm divq, __builtin_clzll) or __int128 when available, with Karatsuba only at 1024+ bits and Newton-style reciprocal approximations for division and sqrt. With TLFLOAT_ENABLE_INLINING every operation is marked always_inline, so the compiler can inline the whole soft-float path into the caller's loop instead of calling an out-of-line routine; the benchmark builds TLFloat this way (--inline-limit=1000000) while libquadmath functions remain shared-library calls.

**Use it when:**
- You need IEEE binary128 arithmetic on clang or MSVC, where GCC's __float128/libquadmath is unavailable, and want bit-identical results across Linux, Windows, wasm and CUDA device code.
- Inner loops heavy on quad add/mul/compare/rint/casts or fma: the README run shows 1.3-1.4x on add/mul, about 5x on rint and about 35x on fma versus libquadmath on a Ryzen 9 7950X.
- Compile-time evaluation of high-precision constants or tables (all C++20 functions are constexpr), or freestanding/microcontroller targets with no malloc.
- You need octuple (binary256) precision with correctly rounded basic operations and 1-ulp elementary functions, where no hardware or compiler type exists.

**Skip it when:**
- Division- or transcendental-heavy quad code on GCC/x86-64: libquadmath was faster on div (72.6 vs 50.8 Mops/s), atan (3.02 vs 1.30), exp, log and pow in the same run.
- Arbitrary or run-time-selected precision: widths are fixed by template parameters (BigUInt sizes are powers of two), so it does not replace MPFR/GMP.
- Code that relies on non-default rounding modes or floating-point exception flags: neither is documented for TLFloat.
- Throughput-oriented SIMD work: the project's wiki says it prioritizes accuracy and portability over throughput, unlike its sibling SLEEF.
- Projects that cannot use C++20 for the header API (the C++11 API is non-constexpr and requires linking the built library).
