**Integration:** header-only (C++20 API) or static/shared lib (C and C++11 API, -ltlfloat) · none for the library; MPFR optionally for testers and table generation; libquadmath only for the comparison benchmark · C++20 for tlmath.hpp/tlfloat.hpp (README example uses g++ -std=c++20); C++11 or C for tlfloat.h; CMake 3.16+ to build; CUDA 12+ for device use with --expt-relaxed-constexpr · Linux, Windows (MSVC, clang-cl), microcontrollers, wasm and CUDA per README; x86-64 intrinsics and __int128 paths used where available, portable C++ otherwise; big-endian supported since v1.8.0; a ppc64el build failure (issue #4) was closed in Feb 2026

**Vs siblings:** Pick TLFloat over simd-f128 (whose README tables against __float128 disagree with each other) when you want a full IEEE binary128/binary256 math library with correctly rounded basic operations and portability to MSVC/CUDA; pick DoubleFloats.jl or MultiFloats.jl instead for faster ~106-bit double-double arithmetic in Julia when non-IEEE semantics are acceptable, and MPFR-based entries (LibBF, FLINT) when precision must exceed 237 bits or vary at run time.

**Gotchas:**
- The published speedups come from the header-only C++ Quad built with forced inlining; the C/libquadmath-emulation API calls into libtlfloat and was not benchmarked against libquadmath in the README (the C-API bench target is only built when the compiler lacks __float128).
- In bench.cpp the 'libquadmath' add, mul, div, compare and cast rows apply plain operators to GCC __float128, so they time GCC's compiler-provided soft-float routines rather than libquadmath functions; only fma, sqrt, rint, sin, atan, exp, log and pow call libquadmath.
- The README numbers are from TLFloat 1.11.0, while the current CMakeLists.txt declares 1.17.1, and the optimization flags of the published run (e.g. -march=native) are not stated.
- Building the library or tests sets very high constexpr step limits (-fconstexpr-ops-limit=1000000000 on GCC, /constexpr:steps1000000000 on MSVC); heavy constexpr use in your own code may need the same flags.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-17, 223 commits, no open issues) by the author of SLEEF under BSL-1.0, with a README request that companies earning over US$1M from it fund maintenance; small but niche (38 stars), with releases on GitHub up to v1.15.0 and a source tree now at 1.17.1.

[repo](https://github.com/shibatch/tlfloat) · [benchmark](https://github.com/shibatch/tlfloat)

##### TzdLanguage NTT BigInt multiplier  `C++ (CUDA)`  `MIT (stated only in the README and badge; there is no LICENSE file in the repository: raw main/LICENSE and github.com blob/main/LICENSE both 404)`  `active`  `Tier C`

3-prime NTT big-integer multiply (AVX2 CPU, CUDA GPU) inside a Windows hobby language; beats single-core GMP only on GPU or decimal I/O.

**Beats:** GNU GMP 6.3.0 (single-core mpz_mul) — First-party README/wiki figures for one 4,741,006-digit multiplication on an Intel Core i7-4790 (4C/8T) and an NVIDIA P106-090: GPU NTT kernel 29.20 ms (42.01 ms with CRT, carry and copy) and CPU AVX2 NTT 54.02 ms (151.1 ms with CRT/carry) vs single-core GMP 6.3.0 mpz_mul 111.78 ms from a vcpkg MSVC build (cl /O2 /openmp), so only the GPU path beats GMP on the multiply itself (about 2.66x, derived from page data); end-to-end decimal-string-to-string times are 56.52 ms GPU and 175.41 ms CPU vs 2,549.30 ms for GMP.

**Known shortcoming:** Misleading CPU ratio: the 54.02 ms 'pure' multiply excludes 97.08 ms of CRT/carry; the full 8-thread CPU multiply (151.10 ms) is slower than single-core GMP (111.78 ms) (derived from page data). Only the GPU path (42.01 ms full) and decimal-I/O end-to-end win.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not reproducible: tables contradict each other (MT GMP end-to-end ~519 vs 2,522 ms; GPU page says 'over 10x' vs 3.83x measured); single runs; GMP built with vcpkg + MSVC, asm config unknown; code lives inside a Windows-only interpreter, not a library; no LICENSE file (MIT stated in README only).

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: the CPU NTT path never checks the 2^22 transform limit (P2=235*2^22+1), so inputs above ~4.19M combined limbs (~37.7M digits) use an invalid root and give a silently wrong product (the GPU path throws); race: the global twiddle cache checks size outside the mutex and sets size before the tables are built; the wiki's primes, carry scheme and fast_div_1e9 do not match the code; LICENSE still 404.

**How:** Numbers are stored as base-10^9 limbs, so parsing and printing decimal strings is linear chunking instead of GMP's binary/decimal radix conversion, which is where most of the 14.5x/45.1x end-to-end gains come from. The product is a cyclic convolution done as three 32-bit NTTs (primes 998244353, 985661441, 754974721 in the current source) with AVX2 Montgomery multiplication, Bailey's four-step decomposition into cache-sized row transforms with tiled transposes, OpenMP threads, and Garner CRT reconstruction. The GPU engine runs the same scheme as NVRTC-compiled Stockham kernels with shared-memory padding and a parallel carry scan.

**Use it when:**
- As reference code for a 3-prime 32-bit NTT multiplier with AVX2 Montgomery arithmetic and four-step cache blocking.
- Workloads that start and end as decimal strings of millions of digits (e.g. printing huge products), where avoiding binary/decimal conversion dominates: the wiki's end-to-end run is 175 ms CPU and 57 ms GPU vs 2,549 ms for single-core GMP at 4.74M digits.
- Windows x64 machines with an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 6.0+ when one multiplication of roughly 1M-38M digits must finish faster than single-core GMP (GPU kernel 29.2 ms vs 111.8 ms at 4.74M digits; complete GPU product 42.0 ms).

**Skip it when:**
- As a faster CPU multiplier than GMP: the complete CPU product (54.02 ms NTT + 97.08 ms CRT/carry = 151.1 ms on 8 threads) is slower than single-threaded GMP mpz_mul (111.78 ms) on the same i7-4790.
- Any project that needs a library: the code is embedded in an interpreter that also pulls in ANTLR-generated sources, LLVM, LibTorch and CUDA, and the repository has no LICENSE file (MIT appears only in the README and badge).
- Linux, macOS or non-AVX2 CPUs: the CPU engine uses AVX2 intrinsics unconditionally and the MSVC _umul128 intrinsic, and the README lists Windows 10/11 x64 with Visual Studio as the platform.
- Very large operands on the CPU path: nothing checks the 2^22-element transform limit (P2 = 235*2^22+1), so combined inputs above about 4.19M limbs (~37.7M digits) would compute with an invalid root of unity; the GPU path throws instead.
- Anything beyond multiplication of non-negative decimal strings with a sign: no division, modular arithmetic or binary-limb interface is exposed by this engine.

**Integration:** source-drop (two files inside an interpreter; no library target) · CPU engine: OpenMP, AVX2, MSVC intrinsics (_umul128); GPU engine: CUDA Toolkit 12+ with NVRTC, LibTorch (used to detect CUDA), compute capability 6.0+; the full build also wants LLVM and ANTLR4 · C++20 (CMakeLists.txt), Visual Studio 2022/2026 (MSVC v143/v145) or CMake 3.20+ · Windows 10/11 x64 only per README; AVX2 required for the CPU engine; NVIDIA Pascal or newer for the GPU engine

**Vs siblings:** Pick FLINT or mp++ for a maintained library that beats GMP on large multiplications with full arithmetic, and CGBN or the GMP-on-GPU entries for batched fixed-size GPU work; TzdLanguage is only worth opening as readable NTT/CRT example code or if your inputs and outputs are huge decimal strings on a Windows/CUDA box.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline CPU '2.07x faster than GMP' times only the NTT phase; the --bigTime breakdown shows a 97.08 ms serial CRT/carry step that is excluded, and the GMP side is a complete mpz_mul.
- The wiki and the code disagree: the wiki lists primes 469762049/167772161/754974721, a Kogge-Stone carry chain and a fast_div_1e9 helper for the CPU path, while TzdExperimentalCompute.cpp uses 998244353/985661441/754974721, a sequential carry loop and plain division. The wiki's fast_div_1e9 snippet also returns a wrong quotient for some inputs above about 1.23e19 (checked by script), though the current code does not call it.
- README and wiki give two different multi-threaded GMP end-to-end figures (~519 ms and 2,522.09 ms), and the 'multi-threaded GMP' rows are the author's own Karatsuba split over mpz_mul, not a GMP feature; all figures are single runs.
- GPU timings are taken after a warm-up multiplication at the same size with cached device buffers and twiddles (the sample output shows alloc=0.00 ms, twiddle=0.00 ms), and the kernels are NVRTC-compiled with --use_fast_math.

**Status:** Very young (first commit 2026-09-13, 81 commits, 10 stars, last commit 2026-09-30) and changing daily; no LICENSE file was present on 2026-10-01 (raw LICENSE 404) despite the README's MIT claim, so copying the code carries licence risk until one is added.

[repo](https://github.com/tzdwindows/TzdLanguage) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tzdwindows/TzdLanguage)

##### uint256 (holiman)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Allocation-free fixed 256-bit unsigned integer type for Go; 1.2-17x faster than math/big.Int on 256-bit arithmetic.

**Beats:** Go math/big (big.Int) — First-party `go test -bench` tables in the README compare uint256.Int with Go's math/big.Int on fixed 256-bit inputs and show uint256 faster on every listed row, from -18.6% (MulMod/mod64) to -94.2% (Exp/small, about 17x), e.g. Add 1.99 vs 18.11 ns, Mul 12.10 vs 57.69 ns, SDiv/large 94.64 vs 642.10 ns, with zero allocations on most rows; the README gives the commands but no CPU, OS or Go version, and the status line is dated 2020-03-18.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Orders of magnitude' not borne out: max ~17x (Exp/small), some rows only ~19%; baseline Go math/big; Go.

**Known shortcoming:** 2020 tables; big.Int Add baseline grows untruncated while Mul is truncated, so rows are not exactly like-for-like.

**How:** Values live in a fixed four-word array, so operations are straight-line code over 4 limbs using math/bits intrinsics (Add64, Sub64, Mul64) with no heap allocation, length checks or normalisation, unlike big.Int's variable-length slices. Division uses Knuth-style long division with a reciprocal-based 2-by-1 step ported from chfast/intx ('Improved division by invariant integers', Algorithm 4), and MulMod for 192-256-bit moduli reduces the 512-bit product with a precomputed 320-bit reciprocal refined by Newton-Raphson. There is no Go assembly; the README says assembly is deferred.

**Use it when:**
- EVM, blockchain or cryptographic Go code whose values are always at most 256 bits (balances, hashes as integers, gas math).
- Hot loops where big.Int allocations dominate: SDiv, Sqrt, Exp, MulMod and decimal parsing go from several allocations per op to zero.
- Simple 256-bit add/sub/mul/compare in Go, where the README shows about 2 ns vs 17-18 ns (add/sub) and 12.1 vs 57.7 ns (mul).
- Modular arithmetic with 256-bit moduli, e.g. MulMod/mod256 188.8 ns vs 489.2 ns, or about 77 ns when the reciprocal is reused (MulModWithReciprocal).

**Skip it when:**
- Values that can exceed 256 bits or need arbitrary precision: results silently wrap modulo 2^256 unless you use the *Overflow variants.
- C or C++ projects: it is a pure Go package with no C API; a C++ codebase would look at fixed-width C++ types instead.
- Code that relies on big.Int's divide-by-zero panic: Div, Mod, DivMod, AddMod and MulMod return 0 for a zero divisor.
- Decimal formatting-heavy workloads expecting large wins: ToDecimal is only 19% faster than big.Int and still allocates (248 allocs/op in the README table).
- Workloads dominated by 64-bit-modulus MulMod: only 18.6% faster (91.7 vs 112.6 ns).

**Integration:** module (Go package github.com/holiman/uint256) · none outside the Go standard library (math/bits, math/big, encoding/binary) · Go 1.19 (go.mod) · any Go target (pure Go, no assembly)

**Vs siblings:** Pick uint256 only when you are writing Go and need 256-bit words; for C++ the catalogued fixed-width options are ctbignum (constexpr, compile-time limb count), Boost.Multiprecision fixed cpp_int and Unsigned Bigint (ADX/BMI2), and the arbitrary-precision siblings (GMP-beating mp++, FLINT, ibig/malachite in Rust) solve a different, variable-width problem.

**Gotchas:**
- Division and modulo by zero return 0 instead of panicking (documented as 'OBS: differs from the big.Int').
- SetBytes with more than 32 bytes silently keeps the last 32 bytes; FromBig reports overflow through a bool, while MustFromBig panics.
- The README benchmark tables date from 2020 (no CPU, Go version or OS given), and v1.3.0 later changed Mul, Exp and DivMod, so current numbers may differ in either direction.
- The big.Int baselines differ slightly per benchmark: Add/single lets the big.Int grow without truncation, while Mul truncates to 256 bits with a helper, so per-row ratios are not perfectly like-for-like.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-23, 352 commits, latest tagged release v1.3.2 fixing an unmarshalling overflow) and BSD-3-Clause; production-hardened through go-ethereum and erigon, with 100% test coverage claimed since v1.0.0 and an OSS-Fuzz script in the repo.

[repo](https://github.com/holiman/uint256) · [benchmark](https://github.com/holiman/uint256)

##### Unsigned Bigint (fixed-width ADX/BMI2 big integer)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Fixed-width unsigned big integer for MSVC x64 with MASM MULX/ADX kernels; beats Boost.Multiprecision on add/sub/mul/modexp, loses on division.

**Beats:** Boost.Multiprecision (backend and version not stated) — The README table (author's own run; CPU, Boost version and backend, compiler flags and time units not stated; no benchmark source in the repo) times 500,000 add/sub/mul/div and 1,000 modular exponentiations at 256-4096 bits against Boost. Multiply is 1.75x to 4.32x and modexp 3.9x to 10.3x less time, add 1.4x to 2.6x and subtract 1.5x to 3.0x, while division is slower at every size (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** No benchmark source in the repo; single commit (2019-06-01), abandoned; division slower than Boost at every size.

**Known shortcoming:** Memory-safety bug (code read): mul_fft (used at 128+ limbs, also by multiply_mod/Miller-Rabin at 4096 bits) writes one complex<double> past its heap buffer when LEN is a power of 2; is_prime_number on even input trips an assert; modexp is variable-time and RDRAND failure is ignored; README says Haswell but ADX needs Broadwell; tests cover only unsigned_bigint<8>; MSVC/MASM x64 only.

**How:** The limb loops are hand-written MASM: addition and subtraction are 4-way unrolled ADC/SBB chains, and the schoolbook multiply-accumulate (mul_mix_add) uses BMI2 MULX with the two independent ADX carry chains (ADCX/ADOX), the same trick GMP and OpenSSL use on Broadwell and later. Multiplication only computes the low N limbs (truncated product). Modular exponentiation converts to Montgomery form and uses a sliding window (k = 1 to 6 by exponent length) over a word-by-word Montgomery reduction built on the same MULX/ADX kernel; division is HAC Algorithm 14.20 with a bit-by-bit quotient correction loop, which is why it is slower than Boost.

**Use it when:**
- Windows x64 projects built with Visual Studio (v141 toolset or a compatible later one) that need fixed-width 256-4096-bit unsigned arithmetic dominated by multiplication or modular exponentiation
- Non-secret modular exponentiation at 512-4096 bits, where the README table shows 6.3x to 10.3x less run time than Boost (derived from page data)
- Studying a compact MULX/ADCX/ADOX schoolbook multiply and Montgomery modexp written in MASM
- Code that already treats big integers as fixed-size values (no heap allocation per number) and can live with wraparound on overflow

**Skip it when:**
- Division- or remainder-heavy code: the README table shows division slower than Boost at every size, 4.0x to 5.3x at 256-1024 bits and 1.1x to 1.25x at 2048-4096 bits (derived from page data), and % uses the same algorithm
- Cryptography with secret exponents: fast_pow_mod uses a variable-time sliding window with data-dependent branches, randIntel() ignores RDRAND's failure flag, and Miller-Rabin witnesses come from std::rand()
- Linux, macOS, GCC or Clang builds, 32-bit targets, or non-x86 CPUs: the code uses MASM, __stdcall, <intrin.h>, the MSVC-only 1i64 literal suffix and unsigned __int8, and the assembly uses 64-bit registers
- Sizes of 128 limbs (8192 bits) or more, and is_prime_number()/multiply_mod() at 4096 bits: these route through an untested double-precision FFT multiply with an out-of-bounds write (see gotchas); the unit tests cover only unsigned_bigint<8>
- Anything needing signed values, arbitrary/dynamic precision, rationals or floats; use GMP, Boost.Multiprecision or mp++ instead

**Integration:** static lib · none at run time; builds need Visual Studio 2017 (v141 toolset) with MASM build customizations · Visual Studio 2017 (MSVC v141, default C++14 mode, std::complex_literals); other compilers not supported · Windows x64 only; CPU needs BMI2, ADX and RDRAND. The README says Haswell or newer, but Haswell lacks ADX (ADCX/ADOX arrived with Broadwell), so on Haswell the multiply kernels would fault

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Boost.Multiprecision's fixed cpp_int only on Windows/MSVC x64 when multiply and Montgomery modexp dominate and division is rare; ctbignum gives a portable compile-time fixed-width alternative with a peer-reviewed comparison against GMP, and mp++ or FLINT/GMP are the safer choices for general or variable-size work.

**Gotchas:**
- mul_fft (used by operator* whenever the type has 128 or more limbs, including the unsigned_bigint<2N> temporary inside multiply_mod and Miller-Rabin at 4096 bits) writes one std::complex<double> past its heap buffer when the limb count is a power of two (n == LEN*8, loop touches index LEN*8); it also uses a cyclic convolution, so an overflowing product is not reduced mod 2^(64*N) the way mul_classic is
- is_prime_number() on an even number above 2 trips assert(mod.bit(0) == 1) in fast_pow_mod (the pre-sieve starts at 3, not 2); with NDEBUG it runs Montgomery code with an even modulus, so the answer is not reliable
- multiply_mod_Montgomery ends with if (rlt > mod) instead of >=, so a result can come back equal to the modulus instead of 0; fast_pow_mod with a zero exponent scans exponent.bit() down to negative indices
- Octal input accepts the digit 8, and multiplication silently wraps on overflow (truncated N-limb product)

**Status:** Abandoned: a single commit from 2019-06-01, 2 stars, no issues or releases; Apache-2.0, so copyable, but the Windows/MSVC-only build and the memory-safety bug in the large-size FFT path make it reference material rather than something to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/nzh63/Unsigned-Bigint) · [benchmark](https://github.com/nzh63/Unsigned-Bigint)

##### VROOM (RNS Montgomery arithmetic with AVX-512 IFMA, BLS12-381 and BN254)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++20 RNS Montgomery arithmetic on AVX-512 IFMA; BLS12-381 pairing 3.9x faster than BLST on Sapphire Rapids.

**Beats:** BLST (supranational/blst at 8065152, a modified vendored copy in blst/ with benchmark wrappers); GMP is used only for parameter generation and validation, not timed — Single-threaded Google Benchmark on an AWS c7i.metal-24xl (Xeon Platinum 8488C, 3.79 GHz, CPU scaling off), VROOM built with clang 21.1.0 -O3 -march=native -mavx512ifma against the in-tree BLST fork at 8065152 (its own -O2 build with x86-64 assembly and ADX): full BLS12-381 pairing 128.1 us vs 500.0 us (3.9x), Miller loop 4.3x, final exponentiation 3.5x, single Fp multiply 1.33x. The repo's optional baseline log from the same CPU gives gnark-crypto 529 us, arkworks 1.02 ms and zkcrypto 1.07 ms per pairing, i.e. about 4.1x, 8.0x and 8.4x slower than VROOM (derived from page data); all numbers predate the August 2026 correctness fixes.

**Known shortcoming:** Capped at C: the methodology is A-grade (every ratio verified, raw JSON shows threads=1) but the correctness fixes 145f864 and 0131695 (August 2026) touched the runtime conversion headers after the published results/ (2026-06-17), so the numbers predate the fixed code. The IACR ePrint venue could not be confirmed (eprint.iacr.org blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #1 (2026-08-10): MatrixNoK ConvertTo could pick a negative CRT representative, breaking round-trip and multiply-by-one; fixed 2026-08-14 in PR #2, after results/ (2026-06-17). Micro-op rows are not like for like: BLST is called through gcc -O2 C glue while VROOM builds -O3 -march=native, and even the Fp12 conjugate shows 2.2x. The pairing still uses BLST's Fp inverter. Unaudited.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** same-host baselines in results/baselines_bls12_bench.log (Xeon 8488C), per pairing: gnark-crypto 529,187 ns, arkworks 1.0229 ms, zkcrypto 1.0743 ms, zksync 1.515 ms vs VROOM 128,146 ns, about 4.1x/8.0x/8.4x/11.8x (derived from page data)

**How:** A field element is stored as residues modulo a set of small moduli spread across zmm lanes, so one 381-bit multiply becomes lane-wise vpmadd52lo/hi products instead of a serial carry chain. RNS Montgomery reduction then needs a base extension (change-base) between two residue sets, which VROOM computes as small matrix products laid out to avoid cross-lane permutation overhead (paper abstract, via search snippet). The production MatrixNoK variant uses a cyclic r1 permutation found by an offline parameter search that removes the k-correction term, and delayed reduction lets Fp2/Fp12 formulas accumulate products before reducing, which is why compound operations gain far more (Fp12 mul 6.1x) than a single Fp multiply (1.33x).

**Use it when:**
- Latency-critical BLS12-381 pairings, Miller loops or G1/G2 scalar multiplications on one core of an AVX-512 IFMA x86 server: measured 3.9x full pairing, 2.5x G1 GLV and 3.6x G2 GLS scalar multiplication over BLST on a Xeon Platinum 8488C.
- Pairing-heavy verification code (BLS signature aggregation checks, SNARK verifiers) where you are willing to wire the field and curve templates into your own protocol layer.
- Extension-field-heavy work (Fp12 mul 6.1x, Fp12 squaring 5.0x, cyclotomic squaring 3.6x over BLST) where the delayed-reduction formulas pay off.
- Research on RNS/IFMA arithmetic for other fixed moduli of similar size, using the Python generator (scripts/rns_secp256k1.py) that emits parameter headers.

**Skip it when:**
- Production signing or any secret-dependent use: the README says the code is research-grade and 'has not been vetted or audited for security'; the constant-time claim comes only from the paper abstract (search snippet) and was not checked.
- CPUs without avx512ifma in /proc/cpuinfo: the integer fallback build (Makefile.fallback) is for correctness only, not performance.
- Builds with GCC or older clang: the README says they are 'significantly slower' than clang 21.x on the IFMA path, so the published ns/op will not reproduce with distro compilers.
- Inversion-heavy code: Fp12 inversion using BLST's Fp inverter is slower than BLST (7.60 us vs 5.56 us, 0.73x), and the pairing itself still calls BLST for the base-field inversion.
- Other curves or large moduli: only BLS12-381 and BN254 parameters ship, MatrixNoK parameter search is exponential in the number of radix words, and RSA-size moduli are covered by the sibling vroomssl fork instead.

**Integration:** header-only (C++20 templates in src/*.hpp and cpu/, no shared library), plus a vendored BLST static library (libblst_small.a) for the pairing's base-field inversion · GMP and gmpxx (BigInt conversion, parameter setup, tests); the BLST fork in blst/ (Apache-2.0) for the BLST-inverter pairing path; Google Benchmark for the benches; Python for parameter regeneration · C++20 (-std=c++20 with clang++, -std=c++2a with g++); clang 21.1.0 for paper-comparable speed, other compilers for correctness only · Linux x86-64 with AVX-512 IFMA (Amazon Linux 2023 and Ubuntu documented; measured on Xeon Platinum 8488C, Sapphire Rapids); optional CUDA kernels need a separate NVIDIA host

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over kevin-he-01/vroomssl (the same paper's BoringSSL/RSA fork, whose README carries no figures) when the target is BLS12-381 or BN254 pairing and curve arithmetic rather than RSA-size moduli, and over the Truncated batch SIMD AVX512 Montgomery code when you need low latency for one operation rather than throughput across 8 independent modexps; no other catalogued sibling covers pairing-friendly fields.

**Gotchas:**
- The production MatrixNoK path had a correctness bug: issue #1 (opened 2026-08-10) showed ConvertTo could select a negative CRT representative for a canonical BLS12-381 input, breaking import/export round-trip and multiply-by-one. Fixes landed 2026-08-14 (floor instead of ceiling rounding in generated constants, PR #2) and 2026-08-28, but results/ dates from 2026-06-17 and was not re-run.
- Per-operation ratios are not like-for-like: the BLST side is called through blst_fp_* wrappers in a C glue file built with gcc -O2, while VROOM's header templates are built at -O3 -march=native, and even trivial Fp12 conjugation shows 2.2x. Trust the pairing, Miller loop and scalar-multiplication rows over the micro-op rows.
- A lone Fp multiply gains little (1.33x MatrixNoK, 1.03x for the Matrix variant); amortized gains of 2.0-2.3x need batches of 5-10 multiplies through BatchModMul or delayed reduction.
- MatrixNoK uses 50-bit (not 52-bit) words for integer-to-RNS conversion; regenerating parameters for a new modulus means rerunning the Python generator, rebuilding src/ and running scripts/smoke_test.sh.

**Status:** Research artifact for IACR ePrint 2026/393 (commits mention a camera-ready version and artifact-evaluation feedback; venue not confirmed), last commit 2026-08-28; MIT-licensed headers are small enough to vendor, but the code is explicitly unaudited.

[repo](https://github.com/SimonLangowski/VROOM) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SimonLangowski/VROOM/HEAD/results/bench_bls12_381_vs_blst.txt)

##### intx (fixed-size 256/512-bit integers)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

Header-only C++20 fixed-width uint128-uint512 integers for EVM and crypto code; no published win over GMP yet.

**Beats:** GMP (low-level mpn_tdiv_qr and mpn_mul_n, called through the repo's own wrappers in test/utils/gmp.hpp) — Nothing has been measured against GMP in public: intx-bench registers uint256/uint512 udivrem against mpn_tdiv_qr and multiplication against mpn_mul_n (Google Benchmark, CMake Release, -falign-functions=32, no -march), but no results are committed or quoted. The only published numbers are intx versus earlier intx (PR #99: 256-bit division by 64- and 128-bit values up to 40% faster) and PR #367's CI medians across 13 CPU types, where intx's software reciprocal_2by1 is 2-3x slower than the x86 divq instruction on Ice Lake and Zen 5 (11.4 vs 4.0 ns; 8.9 vs 4.1 ns) but 4.7x faster on Coffee Lake (5.7 vs 26.4 ns).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: no published intx-vs-GMP numbers anywhere; kept because ethereum/evmone depends on it, so it is widely referenced. Last commit 2026-10-02.

**Known shortcoming:** from_string<uint256> silently wraps some 78-digit inputs (issue #343 open, fix PR #370 unmerged); division by zero is undefined behaviour in release builds (INTX_REQUIRE becomes unreachable). mikelik/int128-benchmark has intx::uint128 slower than __int128, absl and boost for add and mul. PR #367 (merged 2026-10-01) has CI medians on 13 CPUs for reciprocal_2by1 vs x86 divq (Ice Lake 11.4 vs 4.0 ns, Zen 5 8.9 vs 4.1 ns, Coffee Lake 5.7 vs 26.4 ns), still intx vs hardware, not GMP.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Everything is inline templates over a fixed word count, so there is no heap allocation, no size field and no dispatch; carries use compiler builtins (__builtin_addcll/__builtin_subcll or the x86 addcarryx/sbb intrinsics) and 64x64->128 products use unsigned __int128 or MSVC _umul128. Division follows Moller and Granlund's 'Improved division by invariant integers' (a table-seeded reciprocal_2by1/reciprocal_3by2 replaces the hardware divide), with dedicated 1-word and 2-word divisor paths and Knuth Algorithm D for longer divisors. addmod has a fast path for moduli of at least 2^192 with already-reduced operands (ported from holiman/uint256 PR #86).

**Use it when:**
- EVM, Solidity tooling or blockchain clients that need exact 256-bit wrapping arithmetic; evmone already depends on it.
- Hot loops over fixed 256- or 512-bit values where mpz allocation and size bookkeeping would dominate, e.g. small-operand division (256/64, 256/128) and full 256x256->512 products.
- Code that needs compile-time (constexpr/consteval) big-integer constants, including division at compile time.
- Projects that want a single header with no link dependency and can use C++20, on x86-64, arm64 or big-endian targets.

**Skip it when:**
- Operands that grow or vary in size (RSA, number theory, bignum factorials): there is no variable-size type, so use GMP, FLINT or Boost.Multiprecision.
- You need a measured speedup over GMP before adopting: the repo has a GMP benchmark harness but publishes no results, so the claim is unproven (tier D).
- Plain 128-bit math: a third-party harness (mikelik/int128-benchmark, 2023, GCC and Clang, 20-thread 4.6 GHz CPU) has intx::uint128 slower than unsigned __int128, absl::uint128 and even boost uint128_t for add (16.8 vs 1.74, 7.10, 13.2 ns with GCC); use the compiler builtin or _BitInt(128).
- Repeated modular multiplication with a fixed modulus (elliptic-curve fields): mulmod computes the full product and then runs Knuth division, with no Montgomery or Barrett form.
- Signed arithmetic as a type: there is no signed intN (issue #112 open); only sdivrem interprets the bits as two's complement.

**Integration:** header-only · none for the library (single include/intx/intx.hpp); the tests and intx-bench pull Google Benchmark via Hunter and need GMP · C++20 (required since 0.10.0); CMake 3.16+ if using its CMake package; MSVC x64 19.44+ / arm64 19.50+ to avoid a compiler miscompile of addc in constant evaluation (issue #369) · any 64-bit-word target; uses __int128 where available and _umul128 on MSVC x64, with portable fallbacks; CI covers non-x86 architectures and big-endian since 0.8.0; 32-bit Windows build fixed in 0.9.1

**Vs siblings:** Pick intx over ctbignum or Boost.Multiprecision's fixed cpp_int when you want a minimal, production-tested (evmone) uint256/uint512 value type with EVM helpers and byte-order I/O; pick ctbignum for fixed-modulus Montgomery arithmetic or Boost cpp_int when you need signed or checked types, since both publish measured wins over GMP and intx does not.

**Gotchas:**
- Division by zero is undefined behavior in release builds: INTX_REQUIRE is assert() with NDEBUG unset and __builtin_unreachable() otherwise.
- from_string<uint256>() silently wraps some out-of-range 78-digit decimal inputs (issue #343, e.g. a value just above 2^256-1 parses as 9); the fix, PR #370, was still unmerged when checked, so validate untrusted decimal input yourself.
- from_string/to_string throw std::invalid_argument or std::out_of_range; with -fno-exceptions they print to stderr and abort(). Arithmetic operators are noexcept.
- Xcode 14.3.1 on arm64 miscompiled __builtin_subcll; intx works around it from 0.9.3 and 0.10.1 (CHANGELOG, PR #294), so older intx versions built with that Xcode can give wrong subtraction results.

**Status:** Actively maintained by one maintainer (v0.15.0 released 2026-01-30; reciprocal benchmarks merged 2026-10-01), Apache-2.0, a single header that is easy to vendor, also on Conan Center.

[repo](https://github.com/chfast/intx)

#### blas-lapack

##### apple-bottom  `Objective-C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Double-float (FP32-pair) DGEMM/ZGEMM on Apple Silicon GPUs via Metal; about 1.1-1.2x Accelerate's AMX DGEMM for resident N>=2048 matrices.

**Beats:** Apple Accelerate DGEMM on AMX (and OpenBLAS 6-thread in a Quantum ESPRESSO run) — First-party, one Apple M2 Max (38-core GPU), clang -O3, compiler/Xcode version unstated: the README reports 552 vs 468 GFLOP/s (2048^2) and 643 vs 566 (4096^2) against Accelerate's AMX DGEMM, and the committed run shows 1.09-1.16x at N=2048-4096 but losses below N=2048. The 22% Quantum ESPRESSO Si64 wall-time gain was measured against 6-thread OpenBLAS, not Accelerate.

**Known shortcoming:** GPU timing excludes double-double conversion, upload and download; README numbers are not in the committed results CSV; its own results show the GPU losing to Accelerate on QE-shaped ZGEMM (0.38-0.88x); the 22% QE win is vs OpenBLAS, not Accelerate; max per-element relative error up to 2.3e-7.

**Known shortcoming:** Default AB_MODE=auto sends DGEMM >=50M FLOPs through the BLAS ABI to the GPU, and the repo's own end-to-end sweep shows 2-20 vs 250-690 GFLOP/s for Accelerate (28-200x slower); the header itself recommends AB_MODE=cpu, so the drop-in and QE 22% claims are weak; FP32 exponent range, denormals below ~1e-38 flushed; not thread-safe.

**How:** Each double is stored as an unevaluated sum of two floats (hi, lo), and products/sums use Dekker/Knuth error-free transformations (twoSum, twoProduct; the DWTimesDW2 algorithm by default, DWTimesDW3 optionally), giving about 48 mantissa bits on the GPU's FP32 ALUs. The Metal kernel uses 64x64 tiles with 4x4 register blocking, compiled with MTLMathModeSafe so the shader compiler cannot reassociate the FMAs. Complex GEMM uses Gauss's 3-multiplication trick (three real GEMMs instead of four). The win comes from the GPU's FP32 throughput exceeding the CPU AMX unit's FP64 throughput at large N, once data already sits on the GPU.

**Use it when:**
- Iterative codes on Apple Silicon (SCF, CG, GMRES, Lanczos) that keep square matrices of N >= 2048 resident on the GPU across many GEMMs; the repo's steady-state run shows 1.09-1.16x Accelerate at N=2048-4096 on an M2 Max.
- ZGEMM-heavy workloads with N >= 1024 kept in ABMatrix handles (the header's steady-state crossover).
- When you want to offload FP64-class GEMM from the CPU to free it for other work (the QE run reports 47% less CPU time).
- Applications that tolerate ~1e-15 relative error per element rather than bit-exact IEEE FP64, with values inside roughly 1e-30 to 1e30.

**Skip it when:**
- Through the drop-in BLAS ABI with raw pointers: the repo's own end-to-end sweep (commit 271a0f0) measures 2-20 GFLOP/s on the GPU path vs 250-690 for Accelerate at all shapes up to 2048^3 (roughly 28-200x slower), because FP64-to-double-float conversion runs at about 140 MB/s; the header itself recommends AB_MODE=cpu for Fortran hosts.
- Matrices below about N=1024-2048 or one-shot GEMMs: steady-state DGEMM is 0.18x Accelerate at 256 and 0.93x at 1024, with about 50-100 us dispatch overhead per call.
- Anything needing IEEE FP64 semantics: double-float has FP32 exponent range (validated 1e-30 to 1e30), flushes values below about 1e-38 to zero, and per-element errors reach 1e-11 to 1e-7 on some shapes; the README itself rules out pivoted LU and eigensolvers.
- Non-Apple platforms, or multi-threaded callers: Metal-only, and matrix operations are documented as not thread-safe.
- Production use that needs a track record: a single-author project (3 stars) measured on one M2 Max.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib · Metal and Foundation frameworks; Accelerate (re-exported by the dylib, used for CPU routing); OpenBLAS optional for the Fortran bridge · macOS 14+ with an Xcode 16+ SDK (needed for MTLMathModeSafe; older SDKs build but give about 1e-8 precision); clang, C11 and Objective-C++ (-std=c++11) sources · Apple Silicon (M1-M4) macOS only; benchmarked only on M2 Max

**Vs siblings:** Pick apple-bottom only when you need FP64-class GEMM on an Apple GPU with operands kept resident; for IEEE FP64 or FP32 on the CPU, MTGEMM-A (beats Accelerate sgemm/dgemm) or the SME kernels in sme-gemm and MaxMulSK are the safer choices, and they need no host-device conversion.

**Gotchas:**
- Default AB_MODE is auto with a 50M-FLOP real / 100M-FLOP complex crossover, so a 512^3 DGEMM through the BLAS ABI goes to the slow GPU path; set AB_MODE=cpu or raise AB_CROSSOVER_FLOPS_REAL unless you use resident handles.
- The README's headline numbers (552/643 GFLOP/s vs 468/566) do not match the committed result files (654/670 vs 563/586 in 2026-04-22-b9b0641/dgemm.csv), and the benchmark times the GPU kernel on already-uploaded matrices while timing Accelerate whole.
- Linking order matters: libapplebottom must precede Accelerate/OpenBLAS so its dgemm_/zgemm_ win, which silently redirects every BLAS GEMM in the process.
- Hard limits: maximum dimension 46,340, 128 pool entries (ab_pool_get_matrix returns NULL when full), 64 matrices per session; ZHERK is marked deprecated in the README (20x slower than CPU) although the header claims a later GPU win at N >= 1024.

**Status:** Recently active single-author project (v1.3.1-dev, last commit 2026-04-25, no open issues) under MIT; small enough to vendor, but treat it as experimental because the default drop-in path is slower than Accelerate.

[repo](https://github.com/grantdh/apple-bottom) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/grantdh/apple-bottom/HEAD/README.md)

##### cbk (Compact Batch Kernels)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Batched QR, Cholesky and unpivoted LDL^T solves for thousands of small matrices in interleaved layout; beats per-matrix LAPACKE and matches or beats MKL compact.

**Beats:** Intel MKL compact kernels (mkl_dgeqrf_compact, mkl_dpotrf_compact, mkl_dtrsm_compact pipeline) and per-matrix LAPACKE (LAPACKE_dgels, LAPACKE_dposv, LAPACKE_dgeqrf) — First-party, labelled 'indicative', on a '4-core AVX-512 container' (CPU model not named), gcc -O3 -march=native, sequential MKL for its compact kernels and LAPACKE, all paths given the same thread count, and pack/unpack not timed. One-call gels was 2.7x faster than LAPACKE_dgels (geomean over n=10..120, 1000 matrices, 1 RHS; 1.3x at 64 RHS), and the open three-step chain beat MKL's compact chain by 1.12-1.25x. The fused SPD solve ran 2-9x faster than LAPACKE_dposv at orders 8-48 and only matched MKL's compact pipeline (0.9-1.0x geomean).

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline LAPACKE is MKL's own (building.md); no CPU model; no lwork check, so a short workspace causes an out-of-bounds write (documented).

**Known shortcoming:** Docs disagree on the OpenMP gate (cbk.h 2e5 flops vs threading.md 5e4); clang AVX segfault #34 fixed by PR #35; tested against MKL 2020.4 only; no pack/unpack helpers in the portable API.

**How:** It uses SIMD across matrices instead of within one: V independent factorizations run in lockstep, one vector lane per matrix, so small n never starves the vector unit and no lane masks are needed. The kernels are vectorized unblocked LAPACK algorithms (geqr2 with a branch-free larfg, potf2, a square-root-free potf2 for LDL^T, a register-tiled blocked LDL^T update), written once with GNU vector types and lowered to SSE, AVX or AVX-512. The fused drivers (?posv, ?sysvnp, ?gels) factor and solve each group of V matrices while it is still in cache instead of streaming the pool through separate passes. OpenMP threads the loop over groups.

**Use it when:**
- Thousands of independent same-sized dense systems of order roughly 8-120 (per-element FEM/DG blocks, small least-squares fits, Kalman updates, batched local solves) on x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512
- You already use MKL's Compact API (mkl_?geqrf_compact, mkl_?potrf_compact) and need the missing pieces: apply/form Q, a Cholesky or LDL^T solve, or a one-call batched gels
- SPD or diagonally dominant / well-behaved symmetric indefinite systems, where unpivoted Cholesky or LDL^T is numerically safe
- One-RHS or few-RHS solves: the gels win over per-matrix LAPACKE_dgels is 2.7x geomean at nrhs=1 and narrows to 1.3x at nrhs=64
- You want a dependency-free library (only CMake >= 3.28 and a C++17 GCC/Clang) that you can build with -march=native

**Skip it when:**
- Matrices of order above about 128: per-matrix LAPACK pulls ahead from roughly n=128-168 (0.25x at n=256 for the SPD solve) because the compact kernels are unblocked
- Matrices that need pivoting: there is no column-pivoted QR, the LDL^T is unpivoted (no Bunch-Kaufman), and rank deficiency or a non-SPD input is not reported (that lane silently becomes Inf/NaN)
- Badly scaled or ill-conditioned inputs: there is no LAPACK dlarfg-style overflow/underflow rescaling (listed as a known limitation)
- Mixed sizes, complex numbers or GPUs: one size per call, real s/d only, CPU only
- Production code that needs a long track record: v0.2.0 (2026-09-15), 1 star, mostly written by Claude models with human review per the README, and the API is still changing (0.2.0 broke ?ormqr's signature)

**Integration:** static lib (shared with -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON); CMake package cbk::cbk · none for the library (OpenMP optional); tests need LAPACKE + CBLAS (OpenBLAS, Netlib, Accelerate via accelerate-lapacke, or MKL); benchmarks and the MKL-style API need Intel MKL · C++17 GCC or Clang (GNU vector extensions; icpx also handled), CMake >= 3.28; tested with GCC and Clang on x86-64 Linux, plus a macOS CI job · Any target GCC/Clang can lower vector types for (SSE, AVX, AVX-512, non-x86 extensions per the CHANGELOG); performance documented only on an unnamed AVX-512 x86-64 machine

**Vs siblings:** Pick cbk over BLASFEO when you have many independent small systems of one size to factor or solve at once; BLASFEO speeds up one small matrix at a time (panel-major, chained operations such as Riccati recursions) and offers more of BLAS/LAPACK. The small-GEMM siblings (LibShalom, IAAT) cover only matrix multiply, not factorizations.

**Gotchas:**
- Build with -march=native (or an explicit -m flag): the library sets no -march, so a default build emits baseline SSE2 while MKL dispatches AVX-512 at runtime. Building from your own build system also needs -fno-math-errno, or the vector square root turns into scalar libm calls.
- Workspace is not checked: an undersized lwork in the MKL-style compact routines is an out-of-bounds write, and under MKL's threaded layer MKL's own ?geqrf_compact sizes its workspace per thread.
- Align buffers to 64 bytes: unaligned bases still work but cost up to ~40% on small sizes. Issue #34 (clang 18 with AVX segfaulting on 16-byte-aligned buffers) was closed by PR #35, and cbk.h now says the loads and stores never fault.
- The upper-triangle LDL^T convention is A = U^T D U, the transpose of LAPACK ?sytrf's A = U D U^T. The docs also disagree on the OpenMP gate (cbk.h says about 2e5 flops, threading.md and building.md say 5e4).

**Status:** Actively developed (v0.2.0 released 2026-09-15, 316 commits, one open feature issue for rank-revealing QR) and Apache-2.0, so it is copyable. It is young, has a single maintainer, and the CHANGELOG lists testing only on x86-64 Linux against Intel MKL 2020.4.

[repo](https://github.com/ivan-pi/cbk) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ivan-pi/cbk/blob/main/examples/BENCHMARKS.md)

##### chgemm  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Symmetric int8 x int8 to int32 GEMM for ARMv8 (aarch64) NEON, hand-written assembly; reported above gemmlowp on RK3399.

**Beats:** gemmlowp (int8 GEMM); also reported against the fp32 single-core peak of the same CPU — chgemm's README reports up to 18.6 GFLOPS (counting int8 multiply-adds) on one RK3399 core with gcc -O3, plotted against the 14.3 GFLOPS fp32 single-core peak rather than another library, and about 23 GFLOPS on one AWS Cortex-A72 core. The gemmlowp comparison is an approximate, unsourced 'about 12-14 GFLOPS' in the separate how-to-optimize-gemm README, so the roughly 1.3x-1.55x lead over gemmlowp is derived from page data, not from a measured gemmlowp run.

**Known shortcoming:** The gemmlowp baseline ('about 12-14 GFLOPS') is an unsourced approximation; the repo's own graph shows only its fp32 peak. BSD-3 is declared by a README badge only (no LICENSE file). Built with gcc -O3 -g -Wall.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: inputs must stay in [-127,127] because two int8 products are summed in one int16 lane, so -128 overflows silently; the bundled test only fills inputs with val%3 (0, 1, 2), so negatives and overflow are never tested. lda/ldb are ignored. The default build looks multithreaded (omp parallel for num_threads(3) in MMult_4x8_22) but runs on one thread because the makefile has no -fopenmp. README's ncnn link (gemm_symm_int8.h) is now 404.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** GotoBLAS-style packing: reorder_a (assembly) and reorder_b (a C header in MMult_4x8_22; MMult_4x8_21 transposes B and reuses reorder_a) copy A and B into panel order, then int8kernel_m4 computes 4-row by 4-column tiles with 16 int32 accumulator registers (v8-v23), with int8kernel_m2/m1 for leftover rows and K split into 8/4/2/1 remainders. The inner loop uses the SMULL/SMLAL/SADALP pattern: SMULL multiplies int8 pairs into int16, SMLAL adds a second int8 product into the same int16 lane, and SADALP pairwise-widens into the int32 accumulators, which halves the widening work. It uses no SDOT dot-product instructions (the m4 kernel has only smull/smlal/saddlp/sadalp/addp arithmetic), so it runs on ARMv8.0 cores like the RK3399's.

**Use it when:**
- Int8 inference GEMM or 1x1 convolution on ARMv8.0 aarch64 cores without dot-product instructions (RK3399-class boards, Cortex-A72 servers such as the AWS A72 the README mentions)
- Symmetric quantisation is already in use, so weights and activations are in [-127, 127] and an int32 (or requantised int8) output is wanted
- Single-threaded row-major workloads where you can pre-pack the weight matrix once, since the pack step is exposed as a separate call
- As a compact, readable reference for the SMULL/SMLAL/SADALP int8 micro-kernel when writing your own

**Skip it when:**
- Cores with SDOT/I8MM (ARMv8.2 and later): these kernels do not use them, so kernels that do will be faster
- Asymmetric uint8 quantisation with zero points (the gemmlowp/TFLite convention) or data that contains -128
- Anything that needs a BLAS-style interface: no alpha/beta, transposes, leading dimensions, column-major input or float output; multi-threading is not provided (issue #6, 'can it support multi-core', open since July 2022 with no reply)
- x86, 32-bit ARM, Windows or Apple aarch64: the .S kernels are wrapped in '#if __aarch64__' and '#ifndef __APPLE__', and the C driver stops with '#error only support arm neon' without NEON
- Projects that need a maintained dependency or a clear license file: abandoned since June 2020 (13 commits), and BSD-3-Clause is stated only by a README badge

**Integration:** source-drop · none (C plus GNU-syntax aarch64 assembly); OpenMP only if you build MMult_4x8_22.c with -fopenmp · not documented; the makefile uses gcc -O3 with C99-style declarations in for loops and .S files assembled by gcc; an Android Studio sample (android/MyApplication) is included · aarch64 Linux and Android with NEON only; not Apple, not armv7, not x86

**Vs siblings:** It is the only int8 CPU kernel among the catalogued blas-lapack entries (LibShalom, IAAT and BLASFEO target fp32/fp64 small GEMM, MuBLIS and MTGEMM-A target Apple fp32), so pick it only for symmetric int8 to int32 on pre-dot-product aarch64; for floating point use those siblings or OpenBLAS.

**Gotchas:**
- The [-127, 127] limit is a correctness requirement, not a recommendation: two int8 products are summed in an int16 lane before widening, and (-128)*(-128)*2 = 32768 overflows int16 silently.
- The test driver's random_int8_matrix fills inputs with val % 3 (only 0, 1, 2), so the bundled correctness check never exercises negative values, extremes or the int16 overflow edge.
- MY_MMult ignores lda and ldb (it packs as if A is m x k and B is k x n contiguous), passes n as the output stride, and mallocs, packs and frees both A and B on every call; the published timings include that packing.
- The makefile's default NEW is MMult_4x8_22, which carries '#pragma omp parallel for num_threads(3)', but CFLAGS has no -fopenmp, so it runs single-threaded; adding -fopenmp silently switches it to exactly 3 threads. parameters.h defaults to a single 77x77x77 run with NREPEATS 1, so reproducing the README graph means editing it.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2020-06-07 (13 commits; the README's ncnn file link, src/layer/arm/gemm_symm_int8.h, now returns 404 on ncnn master), but it is a dozen small C and assembly files that are easy to vendor once you settle the license question (badge says BSD-3-Clause, no LICENSE file).

[repo](https://github.com/tpoisonooo/chgemm) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tpoisonooo/how-to-optimize-gemm)

##### COSTA (communication-optimal distributed matrix redistribution and transpose; ScaLAPACK pxgemr2d/pxtran replacement)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

MPI library for redistributing and transposing distributed matrices; link-time replacement for ScaLAPACK pdgemr2d/pdtran, 2-21x faster than MKL's.

**Beats:** Intel MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 pdgemr2d (matrix redistribution between block-cyclic layouts) — First-party README charts (from the public miniapps/pxgemr2d_miniapp.cpp, which times COSTA and ScaLAPACK in one binary) compare pdgemr2d on square double matrices against Intel MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1, on 8 Piz Daint (Cray XC40) nodes with 16 MPI ranks in a 4x4 grid, without rank relabelling or memory pools: with the same 128x128 block-cyclic layout on both sides, 14 vs 292 ms at n=20000 up to 324 vs 6702 ms at n=100000 (about 19-21x); with 36x36 to 128x128 blocks, 188 vs 406 ms up to 4557 vs 12737 ms (2.2-2.9x). Compiler, flags, MPI library, CPU model and which repetition is plotted are not stated. The peer-reviewed ISC 2021 paper (also compared against Cray LibSci, per search snippets; its abstract says COSTA 'outperforms the best available ScaLAPACK redistribute and transpose routines multiple times') could not be opened here.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: first-party pdgemr2d charts against MKL ScaLAPACK 19.1 on 8 Piz Daint nodes, with no compiler, flags or CPU model stated. The ISC21 paper (arXiv 2106.06601) could not be opened; paper-access retier candidate (likely B).

**Known shortcoming:** The about 20x figure appears only when source and target layouts are identical; a real reshuffle is 2.2-2.9x. Issue #10 (1.5 Gb/s on a 200000x600 transform) closed with no fix shown. The ScaLAPACK wrapper creates a union communicator per call with no MPI_Comm_free seen; a global per-type workspace singleton makes it not thread-safe. v2.3.1 is deprecated (beta == 0 bug). CMake minimum is 3.22 while INSTALL.md says 3.12.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It works out the exact block-to-block overlap between the source and target grids, packs everything bound for each rank into a single message with OpenMP-parallel packing (applying alpha/beta, cache-blocked transpose and conjugation during the copy), posts all MPI_Irecv/MPI_Isend nonblocking, copies rank-local blocks while messages are in flight, and unpacks each message as soon as MPI_Waitany returns it. Data already on the right rank never touches MPI. Optionally it suggests an MPI rank relabelling, computed from the communication-volume graph by a greedy pass over edges sorted by volume, so that layouts differing only by a rank permutation need no communication at all. The README benchmarks did not use relabelling.

**Use it when:**
- ScaLAPACK codes (CP2K-style quantum chemistry, dense eigen/linear-solver pipelines) that call pdgemr2d or pdtran/pztranc often enough to show up in profiles: relink against costa_scalapack and the calls switch over with no code changes.
- Changing block sizes or process grids between solver stages (for example 36x36 to 128x128 blocks), where the README shows 2.2x-2.9x over MKL ScaLAPACK pdgemr2d at n=20000-100000 on 16 ranks.
- Moving data between a custom or irregular distribution (FFT slabs, application-owned panels) and a block-cyclic layout, which ScaLAPACK's routines cannot express.
- Several matrices that must be redistributed at the same moment: transformer::schedule() plus one transform() sends them in one communication round.
- Codes that can pick their own target rank assignment and want the communication-volume-minimising relabelling.

**Skip it when:**
- Single-node or shared-memory transposes and copies: COSTA needs MPI 3 and runs the full message machinery; an in-place or tiled shared-memory transpose (transpose-scale, HPTT) fits better.
- Memory-tight runs: each call packs data into temporary send and receive buffers, and batching several layouts in one round makes those messages, and the memory they need, larger.
- Tall-skinny row-to-column reshuffles: issue #10 reported only about 1.5 Gb/s for costa::transform() on a 200000 x 600 matrix (2 Piz Daint nodes, 1 rank and 12 threads each); it was closed in January 2023 with no fix or explanation shown on the page.
- Expecting 'orders of magnitude' in general: the published charts show about 20x only when source and target layouts are identical (a case where nothing needs to move), and 2.2x-2.9x when block sizes actually change.
- Builds for Windows/MSVC or other non-GCC-compatible compilers: transform.cpp uses variable-length arrays (a GNU extension), and past issues show build breaks on Cray, Stampede2, nvc++ and in cross-compilation.

**Integration:** static lib · MPI 3 and OpenMP (required); a ScaLAPACK (MKL, Cray LibSci, NVPL or custom via SCALAPACK_ROOT) only for the wrapper libraries; cxxopts and semiprof are fetched by CMake only for the miniapps, tests and profiling. Search results list a conda-forge package (costa-scalapack); a request to add COSTA 2.1 to Spack (issue #11) is closed. · C++14 (target_compile_features cxx_std_14); CMake 3.22 per CMakeLists.txt (INSTALL.md still says 3.12); Release build by default plus -funroll-loops (or -Munroll for NVHPC). · Linux HPC systems with MPI (Cray XC/EX, NVHPC toolchains); CMake has macOS rpath handling; Windows not documented. The only published benchmark machine is Piz Daint (Cray XC40).

**Vs siblings:** COSTA is the layout-conversion layer under COSMA (the catalog's communication-optimal pdgemm replacement), so use COSMA or SPLA when the bottleneck is the multiply itself and COSTA when it is pdgemr2d/pdtran or moving data between custom and block-cyclic layouts. For transposes within one node, HPTT or transpose-scale are the right tools; COSTA only pays off across MPI ranks.

**Gotchas:**
- Link order is the whole switch: if ScaLAPACK appears before costa_scalapack on the link line, the vendor routine silently wins. Use costa_prefixed_scalapack if you want both versions side by side.
- Each wrapper call builds the union of A's and C's communicators with MPI_Comm_create_group on MPI_COMM_WORLD, and costa_pxgemr2d.cpp never frees it (no MPI_Comm_free in the files read). Programs that call pdgemr2d thousands of times should watch for communicator-handle exhaustion.
- The native transform() takes the layouts by non-const reference and temporarily transposes the initial layout object in place, undoing it afterwards. Do not share a layout object across threads during a call.
- Release v2.3.1 is marked deprecated: its beta==0 handling had a bug that v2.3.2 fixed (beta==0 or alpha==0 must overwrite the destination). Pin v2.3.2 or later.

**Status:** Actively maintained by ETH Zurich/CSCS (v2.3.3 released 2026-09-14 with an nvc++ build fix; one open issue, about empty install directories) and BSD-3-Clause, with production use through COSMA in CP2K, which makes it a low-risk relink for ScaLAPACK users.

[repo](https://github.com/eth-cscs/COSTA) · [benchmark](https://github.com/eth-cscs/COSTA)

##### CUDA-L2  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

1,000 per-shape fp16 GEMM CUDA kernels found by LLM-guided reinforcement learning; on average 7-12% faster than autotuned cuBLASLt on A100/3090/H100 (offline mode).

**Beats:** NVIDIA cuBLAS (also cuBLASLt heuristic, cuBLASLt AutoTuning, torch.matmul) — First-party harness on an A100, an RTX 3090 and an H100 (host and CUDA version not stated), with kernels built with nvcc -O3 --use_fast_math against CUTLASS 4.2.1. Each call is timed by host wall clock around one synchronized launch, with the cuBLAS layout (TN or NN) that is faster for each shape. Averaged over 1,000 shapes (64 to 16384 per dimension), the offline gain over autotuned cuBLASLt (20 GB workspace) is +12.2% on A100, +12.7% on RTX 3090 and +7.0% on H100 for fp32 accumulate. These are arithmetic means of per-shape ratios; geometric means are 1.11x (A100) and 1.056x (H100), and 300 and 338 shapes respectively are slower than cuBLASLt (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** README gains are arithmetic means; per its CSVs it is slower than cuBLASLt-AutoTuning on 300/1000 shapes on A100 and 338/1000 on H100 (worst 0.21x); for M, N, K all >= 4096 it is 0.986x on A100 and 0.928x on H100; builds with --use_fast_math; GEMM, so moved to blas-lapack; first published as deepreinforce-ai/CUDA-L2.

**Known shortcoming:** Kernels need inputs zero-padded to tile multiples (no K tail); launch on the legacy default stream; the H100 64x4096x64 file autotunes on first call into unsynchronized statics and uses SM80 mma.sync, not wgmma; correctness gate tests 0/1 inputs only; geomean vs cuBLASLt-AutoTuning 1.24x A100 / 1.13x H100 below 1e9 flops but 0.98x / 0.91-0.94x at 1e11+ (derived); harness bugs (#6) open.

**How:** An LLM proposes kernel code and an RL loop rewards measured speed, so each shape gets its own tile sizes, pipeline depth and variant choice. The kernels inspected use standard Ampere-style tensor-core techniques: CuTe tiled mma.sync (SM80 16x8x16) with cp.async multi-stage shared-memory pipelines, swizzled shared-memory layouts and ldmatrix loads (e.g. the A100 64x4096x64 kernel: BM=64, BN=128, BK=32, 3 stages). The H100 64x4096x64 file uses hand-written PTX mma.sync, not Hopper wgmma/TMA, and times three variants on its first call to pick one. The win comes from per-shape specialization on small and skinny problems where cuBLAS heuristics pick poor configurations.

**Use it when:**
- Fixed, known fp16 GEMM shapes in an inference service (projection layers at a few batch sizes) on exactly an A100, RTX 3090 or H100, where the shape (or a slightly larger padded one) is in the released set
- Small and skinny problems: from the per-shape CSVs (derived from page data), for 2MNK below 1e9 the geomean over cuBLASLt-AutoTuning is 1.24x on A100 and 1.13x on H100
- Latency-sensitive serving with idle gaps between calls: the 'server' mode, with Poisson-spaced calls, shows larger gains (+12.7% A100, +22.1% H100 over cuBLASLt-AutoTuning) than back-to-back offline runs
- As a reference for what per-shape CuTe/mma.sync tuning can recover over cuBLAS heuristics on Ampere

**Skip it when:**
- Large GEMMs: for 2MNK of 1e11 or more the per-shape CSVs give a geomean of about 0.98x (A100) and 0.91-0.94x (H100) against cuBLASLt-AutoTuning, and the worst shapes run at 0.545x (A100) and 0.209x (H100) (derived from page data)
- Arbitrary or dynamic shapes: no runtime dispatch, and padding to a larger released shape spends extra flops
- Other GPUs, or the same GPU family with different SM counts or clocks: the FAQ says A100 kernels are only expected to win on A100
- FP32, BF16, FP8, batched or strided GEMM, or epilogues with alpha/beta/bias: only plain fp16 C = A*B with fp16 output
- Projects that cannot take a PyTorch build-time dependency or need a C++ API without torch::Tensor

**Integration:** source-drop (one .cu per shape, built as a PyTorch C++/CUDA extension via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load) · PyTorch >= 2.6.0, NVIDIA CUTLASS/CuTe v4.2.1 headers, CUDA toolkit (cuBLAS/cuBLASLt only for the baselines) · nvcc with -std=c++17 (CUDA toolkit version not documented); TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST 8.0 or 9.0a · NVIDIA sm_80 (A100, RTX 3090 kernels) and sm_90a (H100 kernels) only

**Vs siblings:** Pick CUDA-L2 for fixed small or skinny fp16 shapes on A100, RTX 3090 or H100. Pick blackwell-tensorcore-kernels for large square fp16 GEMM on sm_120, and gpu-compute for true-FP32 tiny GEMMs on Blackwell. Unlike CUDA-L2, those two are general kernels rather than a per-shape lookup.

**Gotchas:**
- Callers must replicate the harness's input preparation: A, B and a pre-transposed B copy zero-padded to the kernel's BM/BN/BK multiples (the A100 kernel loops k/BK with no tail handling), and C allocated at the padded size and sliced afterwards.
- Kernels launch with <<<grid, block>>> on the legacy default stream, not PyTorch's current stream, so they can serialize with or race against other streams' work.
- Some H100 files time three variants with cudaEvents on the first call and cache the choice in a static, so the first call is slow and the choice is made once for the whole process.
- Built with --use_fast_math. The harness's correctness gate tests only 0/1-valued inputs against a CPU FP32 reference (exact match required), so it is a weak check for general rounding behaviour. Issue #6 (open) reports eval_one_file.sh bugs, such as a wrong unknown-option message and rm failing on a fresh directory.

**Status:** Research artifact from DeepReinforce (MIT, 482 stars, 21 commits; H100 kernels added 2026-03-30, the last commit) with open harness bugs. It is copyable kernel by kernel, but it is a per-shape snapshot rather than a maintained library, and no independent reproduction turned up in one web search.

[repo](https://github.com/ornith-ai/CUDA-L2) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ornith-ai/CUDA-L2/HEAD/README.md)

##### emugemm-cdna  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

FP32 GEMM emulated with bf16 matrix-core products on AMD MI250; 1.20-1.22x over per-shape-tuned rocBLAS sgemm at a lower accuracy tier.

**Beats:** rocBLAS native FP32 sgemm on AMD MI250 (per-shape tuned solutions) — On one MI250 GCD with ROCm 7.2.3 and hipcc -O3 --offload-arch=gfx90a, the author's emu_tuned harness measured bf16x3 at 45.33, 44.26 and 45.06 TFLOP/s against per-shape-tuned rocBLAS FP32 at 37.52, 37.03 and 37.02 (1.21x, 1.20x, 1.22x) on 8192x28672x8192, 16384x8192x8192 and 12288^3, and 325.1 vs 278.4 TFLOP/s (1.17x) with all 8 GCDs at 8192^3. These are first-party numbers from an unpublished harness, measured before the 2026-08-13 timing-error fixes, and they compare against FP32 that is about 2.8x more accurate at those K.

**Known shortcoming:** Harness behind the 1.20-1.22x (emu_tuned.cpp) is not in the repo and the public emugemm_test times untuned native; only 3 shapes; bf16x3 is about 2.8x less accurate than native FP32 at tested K (4.49e-6 vs 1.62e-6), so not like-for-like; timing fixes (2026-08-13) came after the Round 8 numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Code splits each input into 2 bf16 slices and runs 3 products (record said 'three slices'); public bench times emu vs untuned rocBLAS default with 3 back-to-back calls, no warm-up, not interleaved; globals unsynchronized (not thread-safe); kernels go on the null stream, not the handle stream; bf16x3 error up to 35x FP32 on cancelling data (Round 9).

**How:** Multiword (split-precision) GEMM emulation in the line of Markidis 2018, Ootomo and Yokota 2022, and Fasi-Higham et al. 2023: each FP32 value x becomes s0 = bf16(x) and s1 = bf16(x - s0), and C = A0*B0 + A0*B1 + A1*B0 (the small A1*B1 term is dropped). On MI250 the bf16 MFMA rate is 3.98x the FP32 MFMA rate (169.2 vs 42.5 TFLOP/s measured), so three bf16 products cost about 0.75 of one FP32 product, a ceiling of 1.33x; the repo reaches 1.20-1.22x of it. Solution tuning is what makes the bf16 side reach that rate: an offline table (data/tune_table.csv, 820 rows) maps shapes to rocBLAS solution indices via rocblas_gemm_algo_solution_index, because the default rocBLAS bf16 kernel choice ran as low as 83.9 TFLOP/s versus 137.8 for the best solution at the MLP shape.

**Use it when:**
- Large FP32 GEMMs (thousands per side, e.g. 8192x28672x8192 or 12288^3) on an MI250 / gfx90a GCD where about 4.5e-6 normwise relative error is acceptable.
- GEMM-bound pipelines; the repo's CholeskyQR2 randomized SVD got 1.19x end to end at a 1e-5 target, while a Householder-QR pipeline gained only 1.8% because GEMM was 300 of 6192 ms.
- Inputs with wide dynamic range where you want FP32's 8-bit exponent kept (bf16 path) rather than fp16 scaling tricks.
- All-positive or non-cancelling data (counts, histograms, convolutions): Round 9 measured bf16x3 4x more accurate than FP32 at K=65536 on U(0,1) inputs.
- As a template for tuning rocBLAS itself: the tuning-table and solution-index plumbing (and the ROCm/rocm-libraries#9985 evidence) show where the default rocBLAS heuristic leaves 1.3-4.5x on skinny or large-K shapes.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need bit-for-bit or better-than-native FP32 accuracy: bf16x3 has a hard floor of 4.4355e-6, worse than native FP32 at K=8192 (4.49e-6 vs 1.62e-6 in the repo's own table); below the floor the planner falls back to FP32 with FP64 chunk sums, which is slower than native.
- Strongly cancelling products (large rho = || |A||B| || / ||AB||): bf16x3 error grew to 1.65e-3 (35x FP32) in Round 9 and peaked at 31.5x FP32 near rho = 1.2e4 in Round 10; the planner probes rho with 64 Rademacher vectors (about 1.6% extra cost) and may then refuse or escalate.
- Any GPU other than gfx90a: every model constant and the tuning table were measured on MI250 with ROCm 7.2.3; the README says CDNA3/CDNA4 may invert the conclusions, and on CDNA2 FP64 emulation is a loss.
- Small shapes: scan and split passes (one read of A and B plus two low-precision copies) cost more than the GEMM saves; the planner then returns native FP32 (the doc cites 2048x2048x4096 at 1.39 ms vs 1.03 ms before that fix).
- Production code needing transposes, alpha/beta, batched calls, column-major layout or concurrency from several host threads: none of these is supported.

**Integration:** source-drop · ROCm (tested 7.2.3) with HIP and rocBLAS; rocSOLVER only for the randsvd2 example; a tuning table generated by bench/gen_tune_table.cpp for your GPU and ROCm version · hipcc from ROCm 7.2.3 (only version tested); C++ (std::vector, lambdas, so C++11 or later); C-compatible extern "C" API · AMD CDNA GPUs; only gfx90a (MI250) tested

**Vs siblings:** It is the only catalogued GEMM entry for AMD Instinct GPUs: pick it over the NVIDIA-only blackwell-tensorcore-kernels, gpu-compute and CUDA-L2 when you are on an MI250, have FP32 data, and can accept about 4.5e-6 error in exchange for about 1.2x.

**Gotchas:**
- Unless you pass a_absmax, b_absmax and rho in emu_hints_t, every call runs an absmax scan and a 64-probe rho estimate, each ending in a blocking hipMemcpy; reuse the hints struct (the call writes measured values back) to pay this once. The a_is_reused flag is declared but the code does not cache splits.
- Split, scan and accumulate kernels launch on the default (null) stream, not on the rocBLAS handle's stream, and kernel launch errors are not checked.
- emugemm_init reads the architecture of device 0, not the current device, and with no table file it runs untuned (the code warns up to 1.7x slower bf16); shapes farther than a log2 distance of 1 from any table row fall back to the rocBLAS default solution.
- The headline 1.20-1.22x came from emu_tuned.cpp, which is not in the repository; the published bench/emugemm_test.cpp times three back-to-back calls with no warm-up against an untuned rocblas_gemm_ex default, so it does not reproduce the headline table.

**Status:** Active single-author research repo (MIT, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-03, no issues filed), unusually candid about its own corrected numbers; small enough to vendor, but treat it as a measured prototype for gfx90a rather than a maintained library.

[repo](https://github.com/Mazukiri/emugemm-cdna) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Mazukiri/emugemm-cdna/blob/main/docs/RESULTS_ROUND8.md)

##### Laser (GEMM)  `Nim`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Nim BLAS-style GEMM with strided and int32/int64 support; roughly at parity with OpenBLAS, not reliably faster.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS — The README claims 97-102% of OpenBLAS speed (float32 and float64, single- and multi-threaded) without stating sizes or versions. Recorded runs in the bench files on an overclocked 18-core i9-9980XE (nim cpp -d:release -d:danger -d:openmp, OpenBLAS version unstated) give Laser 1874 vs OpenBLAS 1732 GFLOP/s by mean time at 1920^3 float32, but 442 vs 543 at 960^3 float64, and the author's later open issue #40 reports about 1011 vs 1499 GFLOP/s at 1920^3; this is parity at best, not a speedup.

**Known shortcoming:** README says parity but its bench files disagree (float32 1.08x faster than OpenBLAS, float64 0.81x); Nim.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster than OpenBLAS on current code: the author's own open issue #40 shows ~1011 vs ~1499 GFLOP/s at 1920^3 (unexplained regression), contradicting the README's 97-102% claim. Issue #10: dual Xeon 6154, MKL 4 TFLOPS vs Laser 600 GFLOPS. No NEON kernel; Clang build error (#22). Arraymancer vendors a maintained copy of the GEMM (src/arraymancer/laser).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It follows the Goto/BLIS blocking scheme: for each kc slice of K it packs a kc x N panel of B, each OpenMP thread packs its own mc x kc block of A, and a GEBP macro-kernel drives a register-blocked mr x nr micro-kernel over the packed data. The micro-kernels are emitted by a Nim macro (ukernel_generator) from SIMD intrinsic templates for SSE, SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX, AVX+FMA, AVX2 and AVX-512, and the kernel is picked at runtime with cpuinfo. Parallelism is OpenMP over the ic (M) loop, enabled only when M*N*K exceeds a per-kernel threshold. Blocking sizes are fixed constants (mc = 768 bytes / sizeof(T), kc = 2048 bytes / sizeof(T)), and N is not split at all (nc = N).

**Use it when:**
- Nim code, or Arraymancer users, who want a GEMM with no external BLAS dependency that lands within a few percent of OpenBLAS on large square float32/float64 matrices on x86-64.
- Strided or sliced operands (for example A[0::2, :] during cross-validation) that you want to multiply without materialising a contiguous copy first.
- Integer GEMM (int32, int64) with SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512 kernels on x86, which most BLAS libraries do not provide.
- As readable reference code for a macro-generated, BLIS-style micro-kernel design that is easy to extend to a new SIMD set.

**Skip it when:**
- You want a faster BLAS from C++: the README claims only 97-102% of OpenBLAS, the author's open issue #40 later measured about 1011 vs 1499 GFLOP/s for OpenBLAS at 1920^3, and there is no BLAS ABI, so using it means compiling Nim and exporting a C function.
- ARM/aarch64 or any non-x86 target: there is no NEON micro-kernel (marked TODO in gemm_tiling.nim), so other architectures get the generic scalar kernel.
- Small matrices or many repeated calls: there is no small-GEMM path or pre-packing (both listed as future work in the README), and every call allocates fresh pack buffers sized kc x N for B plus one mc x kc block per M tile for A.
- Multi-socket servers or CPUs whose caches differ from the author's desktop: block sizes are hard-coded and N is not partitioned per socket; issue #10 (December 2018, dual Xeon Gold 6154, 2304^3) recorded Intel MKL at 4 TFLOPS against Laser at 600 GFLOPS.
- Anything needing a stable, packaged dependency: the README calls the library unstable and in heavy development, it was never published on nimble, and the repository has been idle since January 2024.

**Integration:** source-drop (Nim modules; not published on nimble) · Nim compiler plus a C or C++ backend compiler; bundled Facebook cpuinfo (BSD-2-Clause) for x86 feature detection; OpenMP (enabled with -d:openmp) for multithreading · Nim >= 0.19.2 per laser.nimble; the benchmark was built with nim cpp -d:release -d:danger -d:openmp. Compatibility with current Nim releases is not documented. · x86 and x86-64 with SIMD kernels from SSE to AVX-512 chosen at runtime; other architectures fall back to a generic kernel

**Vs siblings:** Pick Laser only inside Nim or Arraymancer, or when you need integer or arbitrarily strided GEMM on x86. For raw speed from C or C++, use OpenBLAS itself, Eigen, or BLASFEO for small matrices; Octavian.jl is the closest pure-language GEMM sibling and publishes larger measured wins over OpenBLAS.

**Gotchas:**
- Multithreading only exists when built with -d:openmp; otherwise the OpenMP templates fall back to plain loops. In open issue #23 a user's 100 x 1000^3 run took 5.4 s wall at 99% CPU against 1.84 s for NumPy.
- Argument order is M, N, K followed by alpha, then each matrix as pointer, row stride, column stride; issue #23 asks for this to be documented, and the README does not spell it out.
- Open issue #22 reports a clang build error ('always_inline function _mm256_setzero_pd requires target feature xsave') when compiling gemm_strided, with no reply.
- The author notes 'strange OpenMP interferences' between Laser and OpenBLAS in one process (issue #40), and the recorded benchmark runs use 10 samples with a standard deviation as large as the mean time, so single-run comparisons swing either way.

**Status:** Stale since January 2024 and never released on nimble, but Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor; Arraymancer vendors this GEMM under src/arraymancer/laser, which still received commits from 2024 to January 2026.

[repo](https://github.com/mratsim/laser) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mratsim/laser/HEAD/benchmarks/gemm/gemm_bench_float32.nim)

##### LoopVectorization.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Julia @turbo macro that SIMD-vectorizes plain loops; its triple-loop gemm edges single-threaded MKL on small matrices.

**Beats:** Intel MKL dgemm (single-threaded, via Julia LinearAlgebra.mul!) — README example on an unnamed AVX-512 CPU, Julia version not stated: a @turbo triple-loop Float64 gemm at M=191, K=189, N=171 has a minimum of 111.7 us (110.5 GFLOPS) against 117.2 us (105.3 GFLOPS) for single-threaded MKL mul!, about 5% faster, and 44x faster than the same loop under @inbounds @fastmath. The project's own docs say the advantage disappears beyond roughly 70x70 for square C = A*B, so this is a narrow small-matrix win.

**Known shortcoming:** Julia, not callable from C++. Its own docs say it falls behind MKL gemm beyond about 70x70, so the win holds only for small matrices. CPU not named.

**Known shortcoming:** 116 open issues, several reporting wrong results (#542, #539, #512, #507); #510 reports intermittent heap corruption from a @turbo A'*A loop. Project.toml needs Julia 1.10 while the README says 1.1.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The macro builds a LoopSet model of the loop nest and runs a cost model (determinestrategy.jl, instruction latency/reciprocal-throughput/register-pressure tables mostly from Agner Fog's Skylake-X numbers) over loop orders, choosing which loop to vectorize and which one or two loops to unroll; this yields register-blocked micro-kernels with multiple independent accumulators. It handles loop remainders with masked SIMD instead of LLVM's slow scalar tails, uses FMA, and substitutes SIMD-able special functions. There is no cache blocking, packing or memory modelling, which is why it wins only at small sizes.

**Use it when:**
- Julia code with small dense Float64/Float32/Int matrix kernels (roughly up to 70x70 for C = A*B per the docs; the README's 191x189x171 example is about 5% ahead of 1-thread MKL) where BLAS call overhead dominates
- Custom fused loop kernels that BLAS cannot express, e.g. gemm plus an elementwise epilogue, tropical/max-plus products, or reductions with special functions (sincos_turbo 614 ns vs 3.9 us for the plain loop in the docs' 512-element example)
- Loops that LLVM vectorizes poorly because of remainders (README dot product: 12.2 ns vs 36.5 ns at length 255)
- As the kernel generator under a larger library: Octavian.jl, RecursiveFactorization.jl, Tullio.jl and TropicalGEMM.jl build on it

**Skip it when:**
- Matrix multiply beyond about 70x70: the project's own docs say it falls behind MKL gemm there, and for A'*B it is well behind MKL and OpenBLAS because it does not pack
- From C++: it is a Julia macro, so there is nothing to link; using it means embedding Julia
- Loops that depend on execution order (cumsum, loop-carried dependencies), triangular/ragged iteration spaces, multiple loops at the same nest level, or arrays of structs/Complex without StructArrays
- Code that must be bounds-checked or bit-reproducible: @turbo does no bounds checking, reorders operations and swaps in faster special functions (about 3 ULP per the docs)
- Projects needing a well-staffed dependency: 116 open issues including wrong-result reports (#542, #539, #512, #507) and a memory-corruption report (#510); maintenance runs through SciML Small Grants

**Integration:** module · Julia packages: VectorizationBase, SLEEFPirates, ArrayInterface, StaticArrayInterface, LayoutPointers, HostCPUFeatures, CPUSummary, PolyesterWeave, ThreadingUtilities, OffsetArrays, SpecialFunctions, ForwardDiff/ChainRulesCore and others (Project.toml); optional extensions for ForwardDiff, NNlib, SpecialFunctions · Julia 1.10 (Project.toml compat julia = "1.10"; the README's 'Julia 1.1 and later' is out of date); version 0.12.174 · CPUs supported by Julia/LLVM (x86-64, aarch64); performance depends on SIMD width, and the README benchmarks used an AVX-512 machine (Float64 vector width 8, CPU not named). Some tests are reported broken on macOS ARM (#564).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Octavian.jl when you need a custom or fused small kernel rather than a full gemm (Octavian builds on LoopVectorization and is the one that beats MKL at 1000x1000); in C or C++, BLASFEO or Eigen are the small-matrix equivalents, and LoopVectorization is only relevant if the code is already in Julia.

**Gotchas:**
- No bounds checking and iterating an empty collection is undefined behaviour; misuse can segfault or corrupt memory (README warning). Issue #510 reports intermittent heap corruption from a @turbo A'*A loop on Julia 1.10-beta.
- Broadcasting an Array whose size(A,1) == 1 is not supported unless known at compile time and will probably crash Julia (getting_started.md); use LowDimArray.
- Performance is much higher when matrix dimensions are multiples of the SIMD width (docs); padding columns (PaddedMatrices.jl) helps.
- Keyword arguments inside @turbo calls fail with a TypeError; wrap the call in a functor. Issue #540 reports the same TypeError for plain broadcasts on Julia 1.12 nightly (Dec 2024); a later commit fixes 1.12 precompile warnings, but whether #540 is fully resolved is not documented.

**Status:** Active but in maintenance mode (last commit 2026-05-31, version 0.12.174, Julia 1.10+ with CI on LTS/latest/pre/nightly), funded through SciML Small Grants with no original-author development; MIT-licensed and usable only from Julia.

[repo](https://github.com/JuliaSIMD/LoopVectorization.jl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/JuliaSIMD/LoopVectorization.jl)

##### Mir GLAS  `D`  `BSL-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

D-written single-threaded BLAS GEMM that beat OpenBLAS 0.2.18 by 10-15% in 2016; abandoned since 2018.
