**Beats:** OpenBLAS (also Eigen, Apple Accelerate; equal to Intel MKL on average) — The author's 2016 single-thread benchmark on a 2.2 GHz i7-4770HQ MacBook Pro (Mir GLAS 0.18.0 built with LDC, version and flags unstated) against OpenBLAS 0.2.18, Eigen 3.3-rc1, MKL 2017.0.098 and Accelerate for m=n=k from 10 to 2000 gives median Mir/OpenBLAS ratios of 1.15x sgemm, 1.13x dgemm, 1.12x cgemm and 1.10x zgemm; the margin is largest at n <= 100 (median about 1.4x for real types) and shrinks to about 1.03x for dgemm at n >= 500, and MKL is roughly equal (ratios derived from page data). The benchmark source (libmir/mir benchmarks/glas/gemm_report.d) is gone, and the numbers predate the LLVM 4 slowdown reported in issue #18.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not reproducible: open issue #18 reports about 2x slower with LLVM 4+; benchmark source 404; blog ratios derived from its chart data; D language.

**Known shortcoming:** Thread-safety bug: the pack buffer is a process-global __gshared buffer reused by every call, so concurrent GEMM calls race. C header bug: include/glas/ndslice.h declares glas_zaxpy alpha as float _Complex while the D code takes cdouble (ABI mismatch, wrong results for C callers). README ticks Netlib test CI but test.sh is commented out in .travis.yml. ISA fixed at compile time (-mcpu=native); build breakage in #22, #29. Gain over OpenBLAS 0.2.18 is mostly at n<=100 (~1.4x), only ~1.03x for dgemm at n>=500 (derived from page data).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It is a Goto-style packed GEMM: A and B are packed into contiguous panels, and a register-blocked micro-kernel accumulates an mr x nr tile of C using LLVM vector types, without assembler. One generic kernel serves float, double and both complex types; the register-blocking shape comes from a small per-ISA configuration (x87, SSE2, AVX/AVX2, AVX-512F) chosen at compile time with __traits(targetHasFeature). Block sizes kc and mc are computed at runtime from the L1 and last-level cache sizes reported by mir-cpuid. The author also argues that the kernels are not unrolled, so they put less pressure on the instruction cache.

**Use it when:**
- Reading or porting a compact, assembler-free generic GEMM design (one kernel for real and complex types, a per-ISA register-blocking table) as a reference.
- Single-threaded GEMM on small square matrices (n <= 100) on an Intel Haswell-class CPU, where the 2016 data show the largest margin over OpenBLAS 0.2.18 (median about 1.4x for sgemm and dgemm).
- Single-threaded complex GEMM where the alternative is Eigen 3.3 or Apple Accelerate: the 2016 data show about 1.9x over Eigen and about 3.3x over Accelerate for cgemm and zgemm.
- D projects already pinned to an old LDC and mir-algorithm 0.x that want a dependency-light BLAS with an ndslice interface.

**Skip it when:**
- Any multithreaded workload: multithreading is an unchecked item in the README, while OpenBLAS and MKL scale across cores.
- Current toolchains: the README warns of open issue #18, a 2x GEMM slowdown when built with LLVM 4.x-5.x versus 3.9.1, and the build prints a 'PERFORMANCE NOTE: LLVM >=4.0 has a bug in register renaming' and falls back to a smaller kernel. Issue #29 (open since June 2018) says a release is needed for mir-algorithm > 0.9.0, and issue #22 reports dub failing to build it with its dependencies.
- AMD CPUs: open issue #20 (April 2017) reports it slower than OpenBLAS and ACML for DGEMM on an AMD machine, with no maintainer reply.
- Large double-precision GEMM where Intel MKL is available: in the author's own data MKL is ahead on dgemm and zgemm at every size from about 500 to 2000.
- Code needing a full BLAS: TRSM, TRMM, SYRK, SYR2K, HERK and all Level 2 routines are missing, so LAPACK cannot sit on top of it alone.

**Integration:** static lib (built with dub and LDC; a dynamic configuration exists in dub.json but the README lists shared-library support as unfinished) · mir-cpuid (link order -lmir-glas -lmir-cpuid); mir-algorithm for the D headers; Netlib CBLAS if you want the CBLAS interface · LDC >= 1.1.0 beta 6 (README); built with ldmd2, -betterC and -mcpu=native for the target-native build; works with C99 callers via include/glas/*.h. Builds with current LDC releases are not documented. · x86 and x86-64 (register configurations for x87, SSE2, AVX/AVX2, AVX-512F); POSIX and Windows memory back-ends; other targets need a mir-cpuid port and a new configuration

**Vs siblings:** Rarely: Laser is the closest sibling (same era, also stale, but multithreaded and at parity with modern OpenBLAS), and BLASFEO is the maintained choice for small matrices. Pick Mir GLAS only to study a generic, assembler-free GEMM kernel design or for single-threaded complex GEMM in an old D toolchain.

**Gotchas:**
- The ISA kernel is fixed at compile time (__traits(targetHasFeature), -mcpu=native in the target-native build), so a library built on an AVX-512 machine is not safe to ship to older CPUs, and there is no runtime dispatch.
- The C header include/glas/ndslice.h declares glas_zaxpy and _glas_zaxpy with a float _Complex alpha, while the D implementation takes cdouble; C or C++ callers of zaxpy through that header pass alpha with the wrong type.
- The README ticks 'CI testing with Netlib's BLAS test suite', but in .travis.yml the test.sh step that runs the Netlib CBLAS tests is commented out; CI only builds the gemm and hemm examples.
- Call glas_release() to free the shared pack buffer; otherwise it stays allocated at its largest size for the life of the process.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last code change was in mid-2018 and the last commit a README edit in August 2022; Boost-licensed and small, but it needs an old LDC/LLVM to reproduce the published speed.

[repo](https://github.com/libmir/mir-glas) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/libmir/blog/HEAD/_posts/2016-09-23-glas-gemm-benchmark.md)

##### MuBLIS  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Small BLIS-style C framework for real L3 BLAS with NEON/AVX2 kernels; matches single-threaded OpenBLAS on Apple M4.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS (single-threaded, built for Apple Silicon) — The README chart for an Apple M4, single thread, f32, shows MuBLIS against an OpenBLAS built for that machine: GEMM 111.0 vs 109.9 GFLOP/s, SYMM 109.7 vs 109.5, SYRK 109.4 vs 108.8, SYR2K 109.4 vs 109.0, TRSM 100.9 vs 100.2, and TRMM 95.8 vs 110.3. That is parity on five routines and a loss on TRMM; matrix sizes, compiler, flags and OpenBLAS version are not given, and the AVX2 results on Xeon Gold 6248R, Ryzen 7 7700X and i5-7500 are described without numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Parity with OpenBLAS, not faster: GEMM 111.0 vs 109.9 GFLOP/s, TRMM 95.8 vs 110.3 (slower).

**Known shortcoming:** Parity only (TRMM 13% slower). linux_avx2 dispatch always returns the AVX2 context with no CPU check, so it faults on non-AVX2 x86. Kernels built with -ffast-math (NaN/Inf semantics). No complex types, no Level 1/2, no Fortran ABI, no internal threading.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It uses the BLIS/Goto layered loop nest: B is packed into kc x nc panels, A into mc x kc blocks, and a register-blocked micro-kernel computes one mr x nr tile of C (12x8 for f32 and 6x8 for f64 on the Apple 'firestorm' target) with NEON FMA intrinsics, full unrolling and a software prefetch of the next C tile. The out-of-place routines (GEMM, SYMM, SYRK, SYR2K) are thin shims over one L3 driver that skips or restricts blocks according to matrix structure; TRSM uses fused GEMM-TRSM micro-kernels, and TRMM sizes its triangular blocks from the cache block and the matrix size. Pack buffers are recycled from a pool rather than allocated on every call.

**Use it when:**
- You are bringing up a CBLAS Level-3 library on new or unusual hardware and want the packing and tiling framework done, so that you only write micro-kernels and block sizes.
- Single-threaded real f32/f64 GEMM, SYMM, SYRK, SYR2K or TRSM on Apple M-series or other NEON CPUs, where its README chart shows it within about 1% of single-threaded OpenBLAS.
- Multithreaded applications that call BLAS concurrently from many threads, each on its own small or medium problem: the library is reentrant and pools its pack buffers.
- Teaching or studying a compact, readable BLIS-style implementation in plain C with intrinsics rather than assembly.

**Skip it when:**
- You want more speed than OpenBLAS: the published gains are 0.2-1% (within noise), and TRMM is about 13% slower (95.8 vs 110.3 GFLOP/s on M4).
- Large matrices that should use every core: there is no internal multithreading, and all published numbers are single-threaded.
- Complex types, Level 1/2 routines, or Fortran BLAS symbols (dgemm_): none are implemented, so it cannot back LAPACK on its own.
- Apple Silicon throughput work: its kernels are NEON only; the catalogued Apple siblings (sme-gemm, MTGEMM-A) report Accelerate's SME/AMX path at about 2 TFLOP/s f32, against MuBLIS's 111 GFLOP/s on one core.
- Production use that needs maturity: the project started in July 2026, has 2 stars, and its own README calls its correctness tests non-comprehensive.

**Integration:** static lib and shared lib (make CONFIG=<config> builds build/<config>/lib/libmublis.a and libmublis.so/.dylib) · none beyond libc and pthreads · C17 compiler (CSTD=c17) and GNU make; clang gets a --target triple from the config, while GCC is used without one · Apple Silicon (firestorm NEON target, -mcpu=apple-m1), Linux aarch64 (NEON), Linux and macOS x86-64 with AVX2+FMA, plus a portable reference config

**Vs siblings:** Pick MuBLIS over GEMMFIP (the BLIS fork) or OxiBLAS when you need a small, readable C framework to port Level-3 BLAS to new hardware, or a reentrant single-threaded CBLAS on NEON. For raw speed, OpenBLAS itself, Accelerate, or the SME-based siblings sme-gemm and MTGEMM-A on Apple Silicon are faster or equal.

**Gotchas:**
- Every bundled micro-kernel target is compiled with -ffast-math, so IEEE NaN/Inf and signed-zero behaviour inside GEMM is not guaranteed to match OpenBLAS or reference BLAS.
- The bundled configs do not detect the CPU at runtime: linux_avx2's dispatch.c always returns the AVX2 context although the reference target is also linked in, so that build will fault on x86 CPUs without AVX2/FMA. The 'fat binary' support means you write your own dispatch function.
- test/performance/benchmark_cblas.py times only one library per run (switch with MUBLIS_LIB) on all-ones and identity inputs; there is no committed OpenBLAS harness, and the README's matrix sizes, compiler and OpenBLAS version are not stated.
- Cache block sizes are fixed constants per target, not read from the CPU, so a CPU with different cache sizes needs retuning in the target's context.c.

**Status:** Active (first commit July 2026, last 2026-09-01) and MIT-licensed, small enough to vendor, but a 2-star single-author project with limited tests.

[repo](https://github.com/NinjadenMu/MuBLIS) · [benchmark](https://github.com/NinjadenMu/MuBLIS)

##### NanoGEMM  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Tiny AVX2/NEON float32 GEMM C kernel behind a Python extension; beats NumPy/OpenBLAS call latency for matrices up to ~64x64.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS (through NumPy 2.2.x sgemm / matmul) — First-party README table, timed through Python on an unnamed AVX2+FMA x86-64 CPU (GCC -O3 -mavx2 -mfma, single thread) against NumPy 2.2.3 '@' backed by OpenBLAS: 1.71 vs 4.05 us at 16x16, 4.21 vs 7.14 us at 32x32, 13.89 vs 19.69 us at 64x64, and slower at 128x128 (115.90 vs 89.44 us). The shipped benchmark reports mean loop time (the notebook takes best of 3), not the median the README states, NanoGEMM writes into a preallocated buffer while NumPy allocates each result, and the 7.26x headline at 24x24 rests on an outlying NumPy timing.

**Known shortcoming:** README says median but the bench reports a mean (notebook: best of 3); only NumPy pays to allocate its output while NanoGEMM writes into a preallocated buffer; the 7.26x headline at 24x24 rests on a NumPy outlier; the INT8 table uses NumPy's int8 matmul, which skips BLAS and returns wrapping int8 (not like-for-like); no CPU model.

**Known shortcoming:** Possible memory-safety bug (code read): ng.matmul with no backend calls _ext.matmul_fast, which checks only ndim and K, not dtype, contiguity or out= shape, so float64 or strided input gives silently wrong results and an undersized out= is written past its end; every CI step ends in '|| true' and pytest collects only the ISA test; no CPUID check (faults without AVX2); -ffast-math.

**How:** Register-blocked outer-product micro-kernels: on x86 a 6x16 AVX2/FMA tile held in 12 ymm accumulators (broadcast an A element, two 8-wide B loads, two FMAs), with 4x16, 2x16 and 6/4/2x8 boundary kernels; on ARM a 4x8 NEON tile. Loops are cache-blocked (64x128x128) but nothing is packed, so there is no packing cost, no threading and no runtime dispatch; the Python wrapper calls the kernel through the buffer protocol with the GIL released. The speedup over NumPy at small sizes comes mostly from skipping per-call dispatch and output allocation rather than from faster arithmetic.

**Use it when:**
- Many tiny float32 matmuls (16x16 to ~64x64) called from Python in a loop, where NumPy's per-call overhead dominates and you can reuse a preallocated out= buffer.
- You need a few hundred lines of dependency-free C to vendor for small row-major float32 GEMM on AVX2+FMA or NEON, and can live with a non-BLAS API.
- Free-threaded or multi-threaded Python where you run independent small GEMMs in parallel threads (the kernel releases the GIL and is single-threaded per call).
- Reading material: a compact example of a 6x16 AVX2 micro-kernel with boundary tiles.

**Skip it when:**
- Matrices of 128x128 and up: the project's own table shows it slower than NumPy/OpenBLAS at 128x128 (0.77x), and with no packing or threading it falls further behind at larger sizes.
- Anything needing float64, complex, transposed or column-major operands, or the rest of BLAS/LAPACK.
- x86 machines without AVX2+FMA: the x86 build uses -mavx2 -mfma with no CPUID check, so the module will fault with an illegal instruction instead of falling back.
- Production code that needs a mature, tested library: 3 stars, 0 forks, released in 2026, and its CI cannot fail (every step ends in '|| true'); pytest collects only the ISA test from tests/test_correctness.py because the other checks are named run_* rather than test_*.
- Fast int8 inference: the int8 kernels widen to int32 and use _mm256_mullo_epi32 (no VNNI or vpmaddubsw path) and have no K blocking.

**Integration:** source-drop (two C files) or Python extension (pip/conda; PyPI 0.3.8 ships only a cp314 win_amd64 wheel plus an sdist, so other platforms compile from source) · none for the C kernel; NumPy for the Python package · C99-style C with GCC/Clang target attributes or MSVC /arch:AVX2; Python >= 3.8 for the extension (exact compiler versions not documented) · x86-64 with AVX2+FMA (required), aarch64/Apple Silicon NEON; scalar fallback only on other architectures

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over BLASFEO or Eigen only when the call site is Python and per-call overhead on tiny float32 matrices is the bottleneck; from C or C++, BLASFEO (small dense linear algebra with packed panel-major storage and LAPACK-style factorizations) or Eigen's fixed-size products are more complete and better tested.

**Gotchas:**
- Possible memory-safety bug (code read, not run): ng.matmul without a backend argument calls the C fast path first, and that path checks only ndim and the inner dimension, not dtype, contiguity or the out= shape. float64 or non-contiguous inputs are read as if contiguous float32 (silent wrong results), and an undersized out= array is written past its end; the wrapper's own validation runs only if the C call raises.
- Built with -ffast-math (/fp:fast on MSVC), so NaN/Inf propagation and summation order differ from IEEE-strict BLAS results.
- get_simd_isa() reports the compile-time macros, not the running CPU; on MSVC (which does not define __FMA__) it reports 'AVX2' even though the FMA kernels are used.
- Uses int for M, N, K and index arithmetic, so very large matrices can overflow (not an issue in the small-size range it targets).

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-28, 62 commits, 0 issues), MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but very young, single-author and marketing-heavy; treat it as a Python micro-optimization rather than a BLAS replacement.

[repo](https://github.com/eminsk/nanogemm) · [benchmark](https://github.com/eminsk/nanogemm)

##### optimize-gemm (Avafly)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Step-by-step ARM NEON SGEMM tutorial for Raspberry Pi 4 whose final kernel beats OpenBLAS 0.3.28 and Eigen 3.4.0 at one size.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS 0.3.28 and Eigen 3.4.0 (BLIS 0.9.0-156 and GSL 2.8 also measured) — On a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Cortex-A72, 4 cores, OpenMP 4 threads), one 1536x1152x1344 float32 row-major GEMM took 123.49 ms (38.52 GFLOPS) with mm_optimize versus 151.21 ms (31.45 GFLOPS) for OpenBLAS 0.3.28 cblas_sgemm and 238.22 ms (19.97 GFLOPS) for Eigen 3.4.0; BLIS 0.9.0 was slightly faster at 39.57 GFLOPS. Built with -O3 and an unnamed compiler; first-party, single cold run per library.

**Known shortcoming:** Each library timed with one cold call, no warm-up; sizes fixed at compile time and must divide the block sizes, so it is tutorial code, not a general GEMM; compiler not named.

**Known shortcoming:** Kernel adds into C (C += AB) rather than overwriting it; no edge handling.

**How:** Goto/BLIS-style GEMM: a 12x8 register-blocked micro-kernel holding 24 float32x4 accumulators and using vfmaq_laneq_f32 lane-broadcast FMAs, fed by A packed into transposed 12-row panels (NEON 4x4 transposes) and B packed into 8-column panels so both reach the kernel as sequential streams. Each matrix is packed once, outside the loop nest; one OpenMP parallel region with a static schedule gives every thread its own rows of C, so no barriers are needed after packing, and the kernel software-prefetches a few k steps ahead.

**Use it when:**
- Learning how a NEON SGEMM micro-kernel, packing and cache blocking fit together on an in-order-ish ARMv8 core; each optimization step is a separate file with its own measured GFLOPS.
- As a starting point for a fixed-shape float32 GEMM on Cortex-A72 class boards (Raspberry Pi 4) where you control M, N and K at compile time and they are multiples of the block sizes.
- Comparing your own kernel against OpenBLAS, BLIS, Eigen and GSL on a Pi with ready-made harnesses that print a checksum.

**Skip it when:**
- General-purpose GEMM: there is no edge handling, so M must be a multiple of 384 (and 12), N of 96 (and 16) and K of 192, and sizes are fixed by -DM_SIZE/-DN_SIZE/-DK_SIZE at build time.
- When BLIS is available: on the author's own table BLIS 0.9.0 is slightly faster (39.57 vs 38.52 GFLOPS).
- x86 or any non-NEON target: the kernel is written only with arm_neon.h intrinsics.
- Double precision, transposed or column-major inputs, alpha/beta scaling, or any other BLAS routine.
- Code that needs reentrancy: pack buffers and matrices are global arrays, so only one GEMM can run at a time.

**Integration:** source-drop (tutorial program; copy mm_optimize.cpp and utils.hpp) · OpenMP; OpenBLAS, BLIS, Eigen and GSL only for the comparison programs · C++11 and CMake 3.10 (CMakeLists.txt); GCC-style __attribute__ and __builtin_prefetch; compiler name and version not documented · AArch64 with NEON (tuned for Cortex-A72 / Raspberry Pi 4B); no other targets

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over salykova's sgemm.c or carlushuang's cpu_gemm_opt when you want the ARM NEON version of the same Goto-style tutorial on a Raspberry Pi; for a usable ARM library with edge handling, use LibShalom (small and irregular shapes on ARMv8) or plain BLIS instead.

**Gotchas:**
- The kernel loads C and accumulates (C += A*B); it relies on C being zero-initialized, so calling matmul twice on the same C doubles the result.
- Benchmarks time a single cold call per program (no warm-up, no repetitions), so thread start-up and first-touch costs land inside the timing for every library.
- CMakeLists.txt sets only -O3 (no -mcpu=cortex-a72), and the OpenBLAS/BLIS/Eigen builds and their thread counts are not described, so the baseline configuration cannot be reproduced exactly.
- Matrices are read from text files in ../data relative to the build directory; the program exits if they are missing.

**Status:** Small MIT-licensed tutorial (17 stars, 11 commits) that was revived in July-August 2026 with the layout/scheduling step and the BLIS comparison; fine to copy as teaching code, not maintained as a library.

[repo](https://github.com/Avafly/optimize-gemm) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Avafly/optimize-gemm)

##### sgemm.c (salykova)  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Compact pure-C, OpenMP, AVX2/FMA SGEMM in BLIS style that claims parity with OpenBLAS on two desktop CPUs.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS 0.3.26 (sgemm) — The author's plots (GCC 13.3, -O3 -march=native -mno-avx512f, Ryzen 7 9700X and Core Ultra 265 at 90 W, DDR5-7000) show multithreaded FP32 GEMM on square sizes roughly matching OpenBLAS 0.3.26; no numbers appear in the text, and the OpenBLAS harness is not in the repo. A third-party reproduction on a Xeon Silver 4310 found it consistently slower than OpenBLAS.

**Known shortcoming:** Claims only parity ('comparable') with OpenBLAS, graphs only; repo's benchmark.c times only its own kernel; matmul-cpu README reports it slower than OpenBLAS on a Xeon Silver 4310; stale (2025-04-21).

**Known shortcoming:** Not a BLAS API (no alpha/beta, transposes or leading dims; overwrites C); not reentrant (static global packing buffers); thread count and schedule fixed at compile time; -march=native with AVX-512 disabled.

**How:** It follows the BLIS/Goto loop nest: cache blocking with MC/NC/KC (KC=500; MC and NC scale with the compile-time thread count), packing A into 16-row panels and B into 6-column panels with zero padding, and a 16x6 register-blocked micro-kernel that does rank-1 updates with _mm256_broadcast_ss + _mm256_fmadd_ps into 12 YMM accumulators. Edge tiles use masked loads and stores. OpenMP parallelizes the packing loops and the jr loop around the micro-kernel.

**Use it when:**
- Learning or teaching how a Goto/BLIS-style GEMM reaches near-BLAS throughput, with readable C instead of assembly
- Vendoring a small, dependency-free FP32 GEMM into a C/C++ project on AVX2/FMA x86-64 desktops (Zen 5, Arrow Lake class) where you can tune MC/NC/KC and thread count
- Large square FP32 matrices in column-major layout where a ~2-file kernel is preferred over linking OpenBLAS
- Starting point for a custom fused kernel (e.g. adding an epilogue) that a BLAS library will not let you modify

**Skip it when:**
- When you need speed over OpenBLAS: the README only claims 'comparable', and an independent run (tianyuxbear/matmul-cpu on a Xeon Silver 4310) measured it below OpenBLAS
- On AVX-512 CPUs: AVX-512 is deliberately disabled (-mno-avx512f), and the tutorial says BLAS libraries may be notably faster there
- Many-core servers: the README says its threading strategy and tile sizes are tuned for the Ryzen 7 9700X / Core Ultra 265 and recommends nested parallelism elsewhere, which is not implemented
- Double precision, complex, strided/submatrix operands, transposes or C += alpha*A*B: none are supported
- Small matrices: the tutorial notes multithreading pays off only at large sizes; siblings aimed at small GEMM do better there

**Integration:** source-drop · OpenMP (libgomp/libomp); CMake for the bundled build · C compiler with AVX2/FMA intrinsics and OpenMP; tested with GCC 13.3 on Ubuntu 24.04; CMake 3.10+ · x86-64 with AVX2 + FMA3 only; no ARM or scalar fallback

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Eigen or BLASFEO only when you want a tiny, readable C kernel to study or modify; for production FP32 GEMM, Eigen or OpenBLAS itself is safer, and the catalogued tianyuxbear/matmul-cpu reports multi-core numbers that slightly exceed OpenBLAS. BLASFEO or LibShalom fit small matrices better.

**Gotchas:**
- NTHREADS and OMP_SCHEDULE are compile-time macros (CMake fails without NTHREADS) and MC/NC derive from them, so the binary is tied to one thread count
- matmul overwrites C (the first k-block zero-initialises the accumulators); it does not accumulate into existing C
- Static packing buffers of size MC*KC and NC*KC floats live in .bss and grow with NTHREADS
- Built with -march=native, so binaries are not portable across CPUs

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-04-21) but MIT-licensed, about two source files, and easy to vendor or study; treat it as a reference implementation, not a maintained library.

[repo](https://github.com/salykova/sgemm.c) · [benchmark](https://salykova.github.io/matmul-cpu)

##### sme-gemm  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust crate of hand-written Apple M4/M5 SME GEMM kernels; edges out Accelerate sgemm/dgemm at mid-to-large sizes.

**Beats:** Apple Accelerate (cblas_sgemm, which may use AMX); also candle and burn — First-party README tables from examples/vs_accelerate.rs on an Apple M5 (interleaved best-of-12 rounds, row-major no-transpose cblas_sgemm/cblas_dgemm writing preallocated C): f32 1.97 vs 1.61 TF/s at 512^3, 2.34 vs 2.03 at 1024^3, 2.14 vs 2.07 at 4096^3, but behind at 256^3 (1.50 vs 1.67) and 2048^3 (2.04 vs 2.14); f64 ahead at every shape (0.46-0.61 vs 0.44-0.52 TF/s). Kernels built with -mcpu=apple-m4 -ffp-contract=fast -O3 and Rust opt-level 3 with thin LTO; Apple clang and rustc versions not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-category baseline (Apple Accelerate); f32 wins are mixed and Accelerate has lower per-call latency up to 256^3; the large f16 margin is against an upcast path; no clang or rustc version stated; kernels are C with Rust bindings.

**Known shortcoming:** f64/i16 on M4 silently fall back to a scalar reference (~1 GFLOP/s); not on crates.io; wins only 1.03-1.22x on f32.

**How:** Kernels are C against arm_sme.h running in SME streaming mode with SVL=512: each output tile is accumulated in the 4 KB ZA array by outer-product MOPA instructions, two ZA tiles kept in lockstep so consecutive MOPAs do not collide. Because Apple has one SME unit per CPU cluster rather than per core, M-tile (or, for flat decode shapes, N-tile) chunks are spread over both the P- and E-cluster units with GCD dispatch_apply and work-stealing from an atomic cursor. Large problems use BLIS-style jc/ic blocking sized to the E-cluster L2, A is packed through ZA transposes while cache-resident, and small-B problems skip packing and load B directly.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code on Apple M4/M5 doing f32 GEMM in the 512^3 to 4096^3 range or tall-skinny shapes like 4096x512x512, where the README shows 1.03-1.22x over Accelerate cblas_sgemm on an M5.
- f16/bf16 inference on M4/M5 from Rust, where Accelerate has no half-precision GEMM: about 2.3-2.8x over an upcast-to-f32 Accelerate path at 1024^3-4096^3, and native 16-bit accumulate on M5.
- Inference layers that want GEMM plus bias/activation/dequant fused into one pass (README: fused bias+relu adds 5-27% to GEMM time, while the separate bias+relu row is 4-12x the GEMM time), int8/int16 GEMM, or 4-bit weights with a 4x smaller resident weight set.
- Single-row decode shapes (1x4096x4096) against resident pre-packed weights, where packed SME measured 634 us vs 836 us for Accelerate.
- f64 GEMM on an M5 specifically (0.46-0.61 vs 0.44-0.52 TF/s for Accelerate cblas_dgemm, ahead at every measured shape).

**Skip it when:**
- Small matrices or latency-bound calls: Accelerate cblas_sgemm has lower per-call time at every square size from 8^3 to 256^3 (e.g. 3.2 vs 7.9 us at 128^3), and below a flop floor (2^18, or 2^12 when m*n>=8) the crate runs its scalar reference at about 1 GFLOP/s.
- f64 or i16 on an M4: those kernels need M5 features (FEAT_SME_F64F64, FEAT_SME_I16I64), so on M4 matmul_f64 silently falls back to the scalar reference, far slower than Accelerate dgemm.
- Anything that is not macOS on Apple M4+ (Intel Macs, M1-M3, Linux/Windows aarch64, x86): no SME path, only the scalar fallback.
- C/C++/Fortran code expecting a BLAS ABI, or Rust projects needing a crates.io release: there is no CBLAS interface, the crate is not on crates.io (404), and it needs Rust 1.97 (edition 2024) plus Apple clang 16+.
- Production use needing maturity: first commit August 2026, 10 commits, 0 stars, no releases; the f32 win over Accelerate is small and mixed (Accelerate leads at 256^3 and 2048^3).

**Integration:** crate · half; build-time cc crate and an Apple clang 16+ (Xcode 16) that accepts -mcpu=apple-m4, linking clang_rt.osx from the same toolchain; optional candle-core 0.11, burn 0.21, ort 2.0.0-rc.13 for adapters/benchmarks · Rust 1.97 (MSRV, edition 2024); Apple clang 16 / Xcode 16 for the C kernels · macOS aarch64 on Apple M4+ for SME (f64, i16, native f16/bf16 accumulate and Q4 need M5); scalar reference fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick sme-gemm when you are in Rust on an M4/M5 and need half-precision, int8/int16 or 4-bit GEMM with fused epilogues; for f32/f64 against Accelerate, MTGEMM-A reports a larger 1.18x f32 geomean over 24 workloads and apple-bottom targets DGEMM, while MPGEMM reports 1.23x average over Accelerate on SME.

**Gotchas:**
- Native f16/bf16 accumulate (Accum::F16/Bf16, M5) is about 2x the widening rate but its error grows about sqrt(K); a mismatched or unsupported Accum silently falls back to F32.
- The fused relu/gelu/silu/tanh/sigmoid shortcuts share one in-register rational tanh with about 4e-2 error, visible on a bare .tanh() or .sigmoid(); scalar-divisor DIV is a reciprocal multiply about 1 ULP off (ARCHITECTURE.md section 6).
- Integer SMOPA accumulation wraps silently on overflow (the oracle uses wrapping adds to match).
- Benchmarks are best-of-N with constant-valued inputs (0.01/0.02), the f32 bench has no packed entry point, and some f16 cells in the comparison table come from the candle adapter or the inference_value example rather than vs_accelerate.

**Status:** Brand-new (first commit 2026-08-03, last 2026-09-30), single-author, active, 0 stars, not on crates.io; Apache-2.0 OR MIT, with a strict lint setup and 169 tests (oracle, proptest, guard-page, concurrency) that make it reasonable to vendor as a git dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/electricapp/sme-gemm) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electricapp/sme-gemm/HEAD/README.md)

##### SPLA  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

MPI(+CUDA/ROCm) library for tall-and-skinny distributed GEMM with stripe layouts; outscales MKL ScaLAPACK pzgemm and Cray LibSci_acc.

**Beats:** Intel MKL ScaLAPACK pdgemm (also COSMA and Cray LibSci_acc) — First-party README plots from Piz Daint (CPU: 2x18-core Xeon E5-2695 v4, two ranks per node; GPU: Xeon E5-2690 v3 + Tesla P100, one rank per node) for complex double M=N=10k, K=1M, block size 500: on CPU SPLA reaches parity with MKL ScaLAPACK at 36 sockets and about 1.6x at 484, and on GPU about 2.3x to 6x over LibSci_acc (values read from plots). Benchmark code exists in tests/programs/benchmark_scalapack.cpp, which times spla::pgemm_ssb and pzgemm/pdgemm on the same 1-D grid (100 repeats by default), but compiler, flags and library versions are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Read from plots: 1.6x vs MKL only at 484 sockets, parity at 36; COSMA is ahead up to 196 sockets.

**Known shortcoming:** Correction: benchmark code exists (tests/programs/benchmark_scalapack.cpp times pgemm_ssb vs pzgemm/pdgemm on the same 1-D grid, 100 repeats) but compiler/flags are missing; open build issues #35 #24 #17 #18; past 6x6-grid hang (#22) and a GPU deadlock fixed in 1.5.4.

**How:** pgemm_ssb is a distributed reduction (every rank contributes to every C element), and SPLA does it with a ring pattern after Del Ben et al.'s GW work (SC20): each rank computes a different block, passes the partial sum to its neighbour while computing the next one, and several block groups are interleaved so communication overlaps local zgemm calls. Internal block sizes are chosen independently of the output layout (with a final redistribution), and on GPUs each block runs on its own CUDA/HIP stream synchronized individually for MPI, which gives finer overlap than COSMA's grouped streams. Data can stay in device memory, avoiding host-to-GPU copies that otherwise limit scaling.

**Use it when:**
- Plane-wave / electronic-structure style products of two very tall stripe-distributed matrices (k in the millions, m and n in the thousands), e.g. wavefunction overlap A^H*B, where the README case is M=N=10k, K=1M complex double.
- Runs at higher node counts where communication dominates: the README CPU plot shows parity with MKL ScaLAPACK at 36 sockets but about 1.6x per socket at 484 sockets (values read from plot).
- GPU clusters with CUDA or ROCm, especially when A, B and C already live in device memory; the README GPU plot shows SPLA ahead of COSMA and Cray LibSci_acc at every node count from 36 to 484.
- Codes already using SIRIUS (its CMakeLists requires SPLA 1.4.0+) or needing a cuBLASXt-like local gemm that mixes host and device pointers.

**Skip it when:**
- General square or block-cyclic-by-block-cyclic distributed GEMM: SPLA only covers the stripe-stripe-block and stripe-block-stripe patterns; use ScaLAPACK p?gemm or COSMA.
- Small CPU runs: at low rank counts COSMA is faster because SPLA must assign at least one block per rank for the ring (README), and SPLA only matches MKL at 36 sockets.
- GPU runs with host-memory inputs at large node counts: blocks shrink, data is re-copied to the GPU more often and host-GPU bandwidth becomes the limit (README).
- Projects needing active maintenance: last commit 2024-06-25 (v1.6.1, a HIP 6.0 fix), with open build issues (#35 SPLA_BUILD_EXAMPLES configuration failure, #24 tests fail to link, #17/#18 CMake package config).
- Single-node or non-MPI applications: MPI is a hard requirement even for the library build.

**Integration:** shared lib · MPI (required), BLAS chosen via CMake BLA_VENDOR (MKL, OpenBLAS, BLIS, ArmPL, Cray LibSci), optional OpenMP, optional CUDA (cudart + cuBLAS) or ROCm (HIP + rocBLAS); tests download googletest and CLI11 · C++17 compiler, CMake 3.18+, CUDA 11.0+ for the CUDA backend (v1.6.0 release notes); Fortran compiler only for SPLA_FORTRAN=ON · Linux HPC clusters; x86-64 and aarch64 hosts (ArmPL support since 1.5.3), NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA, AMD GPUs via ROCm

**Vs siblings:** Pick SPLA over COSMA when the operands are tall-skinny stripes with C block-cyclic, particularly on GPUs or with device-resident data, where SPLA's plot shows it ahead at every node count; COSMA is the better choice for general shapes and for CPU runs below about 196 sockets. Tiled-MM (same group) covers only single-node GPU GEMM against cublasXt, not distributed products.

**Gotchas:**
- The Context must be destroyed before MPI_Finalize (README example comment), and it holds memory pools whose size can grow with use (allocated_memory_* accessors); custom allocators can be installed per host, pinned and GPU memory.
- Below a 2mnk operation threshold (op_threshold_gpu) a GPU context may compute on the host instead; tile sizes and the number of tiles are tunable and the README notes a performance jump at 256 nodes when MPI messages cross Piz Daint's protocol threshold, so fixed block sizes may need manual tuning per system.
- Errors are reported as C++ exceptions (GenericError hierarchy) in the C++ API and as SplaError codes in the C API.
- Past bugs: a hang on a 6x6 MPI grid (issue #22, closed) and a deadlock when GPU input memory locations differed across ranks (fixed in 1.5.4); 1.6.0 did not compile with rocBLAS 6.0.2 until 1.6.1.

**Status:** Stale since v1.6.1 (June 2024) but BSD-3-Clause, CMake-installable and used by SIRIUS; expect to fix CMake packaging issues yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/eth-cscs/spla) · [benchmark](https://github.com/eth-cscs/spla)

##### Tiled-MM  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Out-of-core GPU GEMM on host-memory matrices for CUDA/ROCm; 2-4.7x faster than default cublasXt, on par with tuned cublasXt at n>=12000.

**Beats:** NVIDIA cublasXt (vanilla and manually tuned with 4000 tile size and pinned memory) — First-party chart (docs/performance.svg) on one Piz Daint P100 node with CUDA 10.1: double-precision square column-major GEMM with alpha=beta=1 on host matrices. Against default cublasXt it is 83 vs 167 ms at n=4000 (2.0x) up to 4044 vs 852 GFlop/s at n=32000 (4.7x). Against cublasXt tuned to tile 4000 with pinned memory it is 1.5x at n=4000, 1.17x at n=8000, and within about 1% from n=12000 up. Compiler, flags and host CPU are not stated, and the measured 2019 code was later fixed for wrong-result bugs.

**Known shortcoming:** Two wrong-result bugs fixed in 2024 (Feb: some tile sizes; Jun: a sync issue), after the 2019 measurements; chart sizes do not match examples/compare.sh; vs tuned cublasXt only 1.5x at n=4000, 1.17x at n=8000 and about equal from n=12000 (tuned slightly faster at 20000 and 28000); compiler, flags and host CPU not stated; stale since 2024-12-06.

**Known shortcoming:** tiled_mm.cpp builds std::runtime_error for bad ld_a/ld_b/ld_c but never throws, so bad leading dimensions pass silently; open #19 (since 2024-06-21): wrong NN results at 46656x152x480 after 2.0 to 2.3, no reply; only float/double/complex instantiated despite 'arbitrary data types'.

**How:** It does tiled, multi-stream pipelining. Tiles of A and B (and of C on the first k-tile when beta != 0) are copied with async 2D memcpys into per-stream device buffers, and each stream runs cuBLAS or rocBLAS GEMM on its tile. Results are copied back on a separate result stream, ordered by events, so PCIe transfers overlap compute. Tile size (default 5000 per dimension) and stream count (default 2) are set per dimension, device buffers persist in the handle across calls, and copy_c_back=false keeps the full C on the device to skip the return copy.

**Use it when:**
- DGEMM/SGEMM/ZGEMM on matrices held in host memory that are too big for the GPU, or that you do not want to manage on the device yourself.
- Replacing a default (untuned) cublasXt setup: the published chart shows 2.0x at n=4000 up to 4.7x at n=32000 on a P100.
- Repeated large multiplies where a reusable context, pre-pinned host buffers and per-dimension tile sizes can be set up once.
- Code that must run on both NVIDIA (CUDA) and AMD (ROCm/rocBLAS) GPUs through one host-pointer GEMM interface.

**Skip it when:**
- Data already resident on the GPU: call cuBLAS or rocBLAS directly. Tiling and host transfers only add overhead.
- Against a well-tuned cublasXt (tile 4000, pinned memory) at n >= 12000: the chart shows parity, and tuned cublasXt is slightly faster at n=20000 and 28000.
- Half, bf16, int8 or tensor-core mixed precision: only float, double, complex<float> and complex<double> are instantiated, despite the README's 'arbitrary data types'.
- Multi-GPU in one call: multi-device use is not documented (each handle wraps one context; the cublasXt comparison also selected one device). For multi-node GEMM use COSMA.
- Code that cannot tolerate correctness risk without its own tests: wrong-result bugs were fixed in Feb and Jun 2024, and issue #19 (wrong NN results after 2.0 to 2.3) is still open.

**Integration:** static lib · CUDA toolkit (cuBLAS, cudart) or ROCm rocBLAS. cxxopts (fetched by CMake) only for tests and examples. · C++14 (cxx_std_14), CMake 3.17+. README build example uses gcc-8. · Hosts with an NVIDIA GPU (TILEDMM_GPU_BACKEND=CUDA) or an AMD GPU (ROCM).

**Vs siblings:** Pick Tiled-MM for one GPU with host-resident matrices. Pick COSMA (which uses Tiled-MM underneath) or SPLA when the GEMM is distributed across MPI ranks. For device-resident data, the GPU GEMM kernels in this category (cuBLAS or the hand-written kernels) are the comparison, not Tiled-MM.

**Gotchas:**
- The leading-dimension checks in tiled_mm.cpp build a std::runtime_error but never throw it, so ld_a/ld_b/ld_c smaller than the row count is accepted silently.
- pin_host_buffers defaults to true, so each call registers and unregisters A, B and C with the driver. Allocate with gpu::malloc_pinned and pass false for repeated calls: the benchmark miniapp does this, so published timings exclude pinning.
- The default context preallocates 2 streams x three 5000x5000 tiles, about 1.2 GB of device memory for double (derived from the defaults in mm_handle.hpp). The README's gpu::make_context() example omits the required template argument (make_context<double>()).
- Issue #19 (opened 2024-06-21, no reply) reports wrong results for trans N/N on tall-skinny 46656x152x480 after upgrading from 2.0 to 2.3. A synchronization fix ('incorrect result would sometimes be returned') landed four days later in v2.3.1, but whether it resolves #19 is not documented.

**Status:** Stale but not abandoned: last commit 2024-12-06 (CMake/FetchContent cleanup; issue #24 notes a v2.3.2 git tag), maintained mainly as COSMA's backend. BSD-3-Clause and small (about 20 source files), so it is easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/eth-cscs/Tiled-MM) · [benchmark](https://github.com/eth-cscs/Tiled-MM)

##### Blaze  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier D`

Header-only C++14 dense/sparse linear-algebra library with smart expression templates; claims Eigen/MKL-class speed, but no checkable numbers.

**Beats:** Eigen, Intel MKL/BLAS and other C++ linear-algebra libraries: the Blazemark suite's Configfile has switches for BLAS (MKL), Boost uBLAS, Blitz++, GMM++, Armadillo, FLENS, MTL and Eigen. The result pages (Bitbucket Benchmarks wiki) were unreachable, so the comparison set actually published is unconfirmed. — No Blaze-vs-baseline number could be checked: the Bitbucket Benchmarks wiki returned 404, and the repo has only the Blazemark harness (switches for MKL/BLAS, Eigen, Armadillo, uBLAS, Blitz++, GMM++, FLENS, MTL), no results. The one third-party measurement opened (Fastor wiki; Blaze 3.7, GCC 7.4 -O3 with AVX-512 flags, Xeon Gold 6128, double, M=1-32, N=7/13/21/31, K=31) puts Blaze with padding at parity to over 2x slower than Fastor, about 50% slower on average, and generally behind MKL JIT.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the Bitbucket wiki Benchmarks page is 404 and blazemark/ code has no published results here; the Fastor wiki shows Blaze ~50% slower than Fastor (up to 2x); stale (last commit 2024-12-30).

**Known shortcoming:** Docs say Blaze cannot run concurrent parallel operations (must use serial()); default CMake requires LAPACK; last release 3.8.2 (2020).

**How:** 'Smart expression templates': operators build expression objects that are dispatched at assignment to hand-written SIMD kernels (SSE through AVX-512/FMA, optional SLEEF or XSIMD), so it does not just fuse element-wise loops. Dense vectors and matrices are padded and aligned by default, so the kernels need no scalar remainder loops. Large dense products go through a blocked, packed mmm() kernel (blaze/math/dense/MMM.h copies K x N panels of A and B into temporaries) or, if BLAZE_BLAS_MODE is set, to cblas gemm. Shared-memory parallelism (OpenMP by default, or C++11/Boost threads or HPX) starts only above per-operation size thresholds in blaze/config/Thresholds.h.

**Use it when:**
- Code that mixes dense and sparse vectors and matrices in one expression syntax (for example sparse matrix times dense vector inside an iterative solver)
- Small and medium fixed-size or bounded-size algebra (StaticMatrix/HybridMatrix) where padding to the SIMD width is acceptable
- HPC codes already on HPX: Blaze has an HPX parallel backend, and STEllAR's blaze_tensor and blaze_cuda extend it
- Large dense products where you will link MKL or OpenBLAS anyway: BLAZE_BLAS_MODE routes gemm to the BLAS and keeps the expression syntax

**Skip it when:**
- If you need evidence that it beats Eigen or MKL: the Benchmarks wiki is unreachable, results quoted on HN date from 2016-17, and the one third-party benchmark found (Fastor wiki) has Blaze about 50% slower than Fastor and MKL JIT for small fixed-size products
- Projects that need an active upstream: the last release is 3.8.2 (August 2020), and the stated compiler testing stops at GCC 10.2, Clang 10 and VS2017
- Running several Blaze operations at once from different threads (OpenMP sections, task pools): the docs say Blaze 'does not support concurrent parallel computations', so you have to serialize them
- Memory-tight code with many tiny matrices: padding makes aligned StaticVector/StaticMatrix larger than their elements, and zeroing the padding costs time
- Builds without LAPACK: the CMake package does find_package(LAPACK REQUIRED) by default, and decompositions, inverse, eigen and svd fail to link without it

**Integration:** header-only · none for basic arithmetic; LAPACK for decompositions/inversion/eigen/svd (required by the default CMake config); optional BLAS (cblas.h), OpenMP, Boost.Thread, HPX, SLEEF, XSIMD · C++14 (cxx_std_14); README says it is tested with GCC 6.0-10.2, Clang 5.0-10.0 and Visual C++ 2017 (Win64 only) · Any C++14 target; SIMD kernels for x86 SSE through AVX-512/FMA and SVML; other ISAs only through the optional XSIMD/SLEEF paths or scalar code

**Vs siblings:** Choose Blaze over Eigen if you want one expression syntax over dense and sparse types and an HPX backend, and you can accept a stale upstream and no current evidence on speed; Eigen is the safer default and is the one with published, monitored numbers. For many tiny matrices, BLASFEO has measured wins over OpenBLAS and BLIS, which Blaze does not.

**Gotchas:**
- Aliasing like x = A * x is detected and fixed with a temporary; noalias() turns this check off, and the docs warn that misuse is undefined behavior
- Padding is on by default (BLAZE_USE_PADDING=1, blaze::padded); turning it off sends remainders to scalar code, which is what the Fastor benchmark saw
- Thread counts come from BLAZE_NUM_THREADS or OMP_NUM_THREADS, or setNumThreads(); OpenMP is the default backend in CMake and drops silently to one thread (with a CMake warning) if OpenMP is not found
- With BLAZE_BLAS_MODE, BLAZE_BLAS_IS_PARALLEL has to match the BLAS you link; otherwise Blaze threads and BLAS threads can oversubscribe the cores

**Status:** Stale: last commit 2024-12-30 and no release since 3.8.2 (2020-08-15). It is BSD-3-Clause and header-only, ships as vcpkg and Conan packages, and is fine to vendor, but plan to maintain it yourself.

[repo](https://bitbucket.org/blaze-lib/blaze)

##### fmm-gen (Generating Families of Practical Fast Matrix Multiplication Algorithms)  `Python (code generator emitting C)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Python generator for Strassen-like DGEMM variants that fuse the extra additions into BLIS-style packing and micro-kernels; claims wins over conventional GEMM.

**Beats:** Conventional GEMM. The public harness (the test driver emitted by meta/misc_gen.py) times the generated Strassen-like routine against the project's own BLIS-style dgemm (bl_dgemm in common/dgemm/my_dgemm.c, built on the same AVX 8x4 micro-kernel) and prints the effective GFLOPS of both. MKL is linked (-DUSE_BLAS, -mkl=parallel) only for bl_dgemm_ref. Whether the IPDPS 2017 paper also compared against BLIS or MKL dgemm could not be checked. — Only a qualitative claim was readable: the README and artifact say the generated FMM implementations 'demonstrate a performance benefit over conventional GEMM on single core and multi-core systems', and the public harness times the generated routine against the project's own BLISlab dgemm built on the same AVX 8x4 micro-kernel (icc 15.0.3, -O3 -mavx, TACC Maverick). A search-result snippet of the arXiv version (page not opened) gives the test machine as a dual-socket Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2 (Ivy Bridge) at 3.54 GHz on one core and 3.10 GHz on ten, and says the comparison included a BLIS-based DGEMM and Intel MKL DGEMM; no numbers were seen.

**Known shortcoming:** No number on any reachable page (IPDPS 2017 paper blocked here); the public harness times FMM against its own BLISlab dgemm (common/dgemm/my_dgemm.c), not MKL/BLIS; icc 15.0.3 -O3 -mavx on TACC Maverick, no CPU model; retier candidate once the paper is reachable.

**Known shortcoming:** Still no numbers reachable from this session. Kernels are AVX without FMA, 8x4, tuned for Ivy Bridge; build uses `source` via /bin/sh (fails on dash); Python 2.7. Follow-up: the paper (arXiv 1611.01120) names dual-socket Xeon E5-2680 v2 with BLIS and MKL DGEMM baselines, so a B/A retier is possible where arxiv.org is reachable.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each fast algorithm is a [U,V,W] coefficient triple, and multi-level algorithms (including mixed shapes such as <2,2,2> then <3,2,3>) are built with Kronecker products of those triples. Instead of forming the sums of submatrices in temporary buffers, the 'ABC' variant folds the A and B sums into the GEMM packing routines and the C updates into generated micro-kernels, so there is no extra workspace and less memory traffic; 'AB' and 'naive' variants are also generated for comparison. Parallelism reuses GEMM's own loop-level data parallelism instead of task parallelism, and a performance model predicts which algorithm suits a given size and shape.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or prototyping Strassen-like DGEMM inside a BLIS-style GEMM, including choosing among 20+ algorithms by size and shape with the included performance model.
- Large double-precision products on hardware close to the paper's (an AVX Ivy Bridge-class Xeon), where the authors report gains over conventional GEMM on one core and on ten cores.
- Non-square and rank-k-like shapes, where the paper argues that fusing additions into packing helps compared with buffer-based Strassen implementations.
- As a reference design when building fused FMM into your own GEMM (the sibling tblis-strassen applies the same idea to tensor contraction).

**Skip it when:**
- As a production BLAS: double precision only, no alpha/beta or transposes, generated per algorithm, and no packaging.
- On current CPUs without retuning: the micro-kernels are AVX inline assembly (vmulpd/vaddpd, no FMA) with an 8x4 register block and Ivy Bridge cache blocking (MC=96, KC=256, NC=4096), so today's BLIS, OpenBLAS or MKL kernels with FMA or AVX-512 have a higher peak than the in-repo baseline the generated code was compared with.
- When accuracy matters more than a modest speedup: Strassen-like algorithms have weaker error bounds than classical GEMM, and this repo documents no stability testing.
- When you need published numbers: none appear in the repo, and the paper (cs.utexas.edu, arxiv.org) was unreachable from this environment.
- When you need maintained code: the last commit was 2017-07-07, the scripts are Python 2.7, and paths for TACC Maverick and SLURM are hard-coded.

**Integration:** source-drop (Python 2.7 code generator emitting C99 plus AVX inline assembly; builds a static and shared library per generated algorithm) · Python 2.7; Intel icc/icpc 15+ by default (sourceme.sh sets BLISLAB_USE_INTEL=true; a GNU make include is also selectable); OpenMP; Intel MKL linked when BLISLAB_USE_BLAS=true (only for the bl_dgemm_ref reference path); SLURM optional · C99 compiler with AVX and OpenMP; artifact used icc/icpc 15.0.3 with GCC 4.9.3; Python 2.7 · x86-64 with AVX (artifact: 'x86-64 processor that supports AVX instructions'); Linux or macOS per the artifact description; no ARM or other kernels

**Vs siblings:** Pick fmm-gen over fast-matmul (Benson and Ballard) when you want the additions fused into GEMM packing with no extra workspace and plain data parallelism, and you are willing to own the GEMM kernel; fast-matmul layers fast algorithms on a vendor dgemm and ships measured timings against MKL. For tensor contractions use tblis-strassen, from the same group.

**Gotchas:**
- The in-repo GEMM requires C and ldc to be aligned (my_dgemm.c: 'C must be aligned', 'ldc must also be aligned'); the test driver pads ldc to a multiple of 8 and allocates n+4 columns, so pass C the same way.
- The test driver accumulates C += A*B over three timed repeats for both routines and reports min-time effective GFLOPS, with the FMM run first and the conventional run second on the same inputs.
- control.py builds with os.system('source sourceme.sh; make ...'), which runs under /bin/sh; where /bin/sh is dash (Debian, Ubuntu) `source` fails, and sourceme.sh hard-codes BLAS_DIR=/u/jianyu/blis and OMP_NUM_THREADS=10.
- The make include uses -openmp and -mkl=parallel, flags of the classic Intel compilers; current oneAPI icx and GCC need different flags.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2017-07-07 (12 stars, no open issues) and BSD-3-Clause; usable as a reference design or for generating kernels to retune, not as a library to link.

[repo](https://github.com/flame/fmm-gen) · [benchmark](https://github.com/flame/fmm-gen)

##### ReLAPACK  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Recursive C replacements for LAPACK compute kernels (LU, Cholesky, LDL, trtri, Sylvester) that beat reference LAPACK's blocked versions.

**Beats:** reference LAPACK, OpenBLAS LAPACK routines and Intel MKL LAPACK routines — The repo states only that ReLAPACK outperforms reference LAPACK and improves on OpenBLAS and MKL; no numbers, hardware or compiler details are in any repo file. The measurements are in Peise and Bientinesi, arXiv:1602.06763 (ACM TOMS Algorithm 979), which could not be opened here (arxiv.org blocked), so the claim stays directional (tier D).

**Known shortcoming:** No numbers on any reachable page; TOMS paper blocked here, so tier D for now (likely B with the paper); notable because OpenBLAS vendors relapack/.

**Known shortcoming:** Security/correctness bug: upstream xsytrf/xhetrf workspace query and malloc size n*(n/2) while the recursion can write n*REC_SPLIT(n), corrupting the heap; fixed only in OpenBLAS's copy (commit 4a4cd8f, 2026-08-08), upstream src/dsytrf.c unchanged; 32-bit int only (no ILP64); gbtrf/pbtrf workspace fixes also only in OpenBLAS (de63675). Use OpenBLAS's maintained relapack/ (BUILD_RELAPACK=1) instead of upstream.

**How:** Instead of LAPACK's fixed-block-size loops with BLAS-2 panel factorizations, each routine splits the matrix into two halves recursively (split point rounded so one half is a multiple of 8 or 16 elements for cache-line alignment) and does the trailing updates with large BLAS-3 calls (dtrsm, dgemm), so almost all FLOPs run in the tuned GEMM. Recursion stops at a crossover size (default 24) where LAPACK's unblocked xxxf2 kernel takes over, which removes the block-size tuning that blocked LAPACK needs. xsygst can use an n^2/2 scratch buffer to do about 30% fewer FLOPs than LAPACK (config.md).

**Use it when:**
- Code that calls reference LAPACK (or a LAPACK without tuned factorizations) for LU, Cholesky, LDL^T, triangular inversion or Sylvester solves and you want a faster drop-in without changing call sites.
- Matrix sizes where blocked LAPACK's panel factorization is BLAS-2 bound and a good BLAS-3 is available underneath (OpenBLAS, BLIS, MKL, Accelerate).
- Sylvester (xtrsyl, xtgsyl) and generalized symmetric-definite reduction (xsygst) workloads, which most tuned libraries leave as reference LAPACK code.
- Building OpenBLAS with BUILD_RELAPACK=1 (and RELAPACK_REPLACE=1 to override the LAPACK symbols), which uses OpenBLAS's maintained copy of this code.

**Skip it when:**
- QR, eigenvalue reductions (sytrd, gehrd, gebrd) and SVD: not covered, because recursive variants need extra FLOPs (coverage.md).
- ILP64 (64-bit integer) builds: the upstream code uses plain int for every dimension and pivot; only OpenBLAS's copy was converted to blasint/INTERFACE64 (OpenBLAS commits 9a19616, 798c448, 2019).
- Symmetric indefinite LDL^T (xsytrf/xhetrf) from upstream: the workspace size it reports and allocates (n*(n/2)) can be smaller than what the recursion writes when the split exceeds n/2; OpenBLAS fixed this on 2026-08-08 (commit 4a4cd8f, 'silently corrupting both the factorization and the heap'), upstream src/dsytrf.c still has the old formula.
- When the vendor library already has recursive or parallel factorizations (OpenBLAS's own getrf/potrf, MKL): the gain over them is claimed in the paper but no numbers are in the repo, and the code was last compared with 2016-2017 OpenBLAS and MKL versions.
- Projects needing an actively maintained upstream: the HPAC repo's last commit is a 2022 typo fix, its two issues are unanswered (issue #5 on XERBLA arguments is still open), and later bug fixes went only into OpenBLAS's copy.

**Integration:** static lib · a BLAS plus LAPACK (for unblocked kernels such as dgetf2, dlaswp, dsytf2); tests need LAPACK 3.5.0 or newer · C99 compiler (make.inc default: gcc -O3 -std=c99 -pedantic); plain Makefile, no CMake · any platform with a Fortran-convention BLAS/LAPACK; no architecture-specific code (speed comes from the BLAS underneath)

**Vs siblings:** Pick ReLAPACK when you want unchanged LAPACK call sites in C/C++/Fortran and need faster getrf/potrf/sytrf/trtri/trsyl on top of whatever BLAS you already use; BLASFEO is faster for matrices in the tens but uses its own panel-major API, and RecursiveFactorization.jl applies the same recursive-LU idea only to Julia and only to LU.

**Gotchas:**
- Complex-return calling convention: default is the gfortran struct-return style; with MKL set COMPLEX_FUNCTIONS_AS_ROUTINES=1 in config.h, otherwise ctrsyl/ztrsyl segfault or return errors of order 1 (config.md).
- Hidden allocations: xsygst and xsytrf malloc n^2/2-sized buffers by default (ALLOW_MALLOC), and xpbtrf/xgbtrf call malloc unconditionally without a NULL check; OpenBLAS disabled the xsytrf reallocation in 2019 after memory problems in the LAPACK tests (commit 2cd463e).
- Upstream lacks fixes that OpenBLAS's relapack/ copy carries: workspace sign errors and zero-size early returns in xgbtrf/xpbtrf (de63675, 2020), xGEMMT argument lists (2022, 2024) and the sytrf/hetrf workspace size (2026). Prefer OpenBLAS's copy if you can.
- Upstream xgetrf passes the shared info pointer to the second recursive half, whose dgetf2 leaf resets it, so a zero pivot found in the left half may not be reported (read from src/dgetrf.c, not tested); OpenBLAS's copy returns early when info is set. A guide written for OpenBLAS builders also advises against BUILD_RELAPACK=1 because 'make lapack-test' shows too many errors.

**Status:** Upstream abandoned (code from 2016-2017, last commit a 2022 typo fix) but MIT-licensed and small; the maintained copy with ILP64 support and bug fixes lives in OpenBLAS's relapack/ directory (optional BUILD_RELAPACK=1).

[repo](https://github.com/HPAC/ReLAPACK) · [benchmark](https://github.com/HPAC/ReLAPACK/blob/master/README.md)

#### fft

##### AppleSiliconFFT  `Metal Shading Language, Swift`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Research Metal GPU and SME2 FFT kernels for Apple Silicon; M1 GPU N=4096 batch beats one-thread vDSP by 29%.

**Beats:** Apple vDSP/Accelerate FFT (CPU) — On an Apple M1 (macOS and Xcode versions not stated), the radix-8 Metal kernel computed N=4096 complex FP32 FFTs in batches of 256 at a median 1.78 us per FFT of GPU-only time (138.45 GFLOPS by 5N log2 N), against 2.29 us (107 GF) for single-threaded vDSP_fft_zop timed by wall clock, so +29% is GPU vs one CPU core. On an Apple M6 (macOS 27.0, logs dated 2026-09-26), one-pass kernels beat MPSGraph about 2.3x at DRAM-resident N=8192 and lose about 3.7x at L2-resident N=16384. The SME2 FFT is 1.21-3.52x vDSP on contiguous batches before packing, 0.51-1.76x after, and 5.3x on N=512 x 256 column FFTs against vDSP transpose+fftm+transpose.

**Known shortcoming:** M1 +29% is the whole GPU against a single-threaded vDSP loop; the M6 '5.3x over vDSP' applies only to column FFTs of a matrix, and on contiguous batches the SME2 path (counting packing) is slower than vDSP from N=512 up; the one-pass kernels beat MPSGraph only on DRAM-resident batches (MPSGraph is 3.7x faster at L2-resident N=16384).

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not reproducible as shipped: fft_host.swift loads fft_4096_mma.metal, which is not in the repo; the 138 GFLOPS kernel (src/fft_4096_radix8.metal, function fft_4096_mma) claims simdgroup_matrix MMA in a comment but all four passes run the scalar radix8_butterfly, and the README calls it both 'Stockham' and 'split-radix DIT'; hosts use Metal fastMath; SME2 'up to 5.3x' compares against vDSP transpose+fftm+transpose (11.3x against strided fftm).

**How:** Each GPU threadgroup holds a whole N=4096 transform in registers and uses the 32 KiB of threadgroup memory only as an exchange buffer between passes. Four radix-8 passes use a split-radix 8-point butterfly with twiddles from sincos, and Stockham autosort keeps device-memory access coalesced. On M6, one-pass N=8192/16384 kernels keep the transform on chip, so large batches make a single trip through DRAM and run near the 150 GB/s limit. The SME2 path writes each radix-8 butterfly, twiddles included, as a 16x16 real matrix applied with FMOPA outer products to 16 FFTs at once in a ZA tile (constant-geometry Pease DIF, batch-minor layout).

**Use it when:**
- As a reference when writing your own Metal FFT for one fixed power-of-two size (N=4096 complex FP32), where a register-resident single-threadgroup design matters
- Large DRAM-resident batches of N=8192 or 16384 complex FP32 on an M-series GPU: on M6 the one-pass N=8192 kernel ran at 604 GF vs 257 GF for MPSGraph (batch 2048, hot)
- Column FFTs of a row-major split-complex matrix on an M4-or-later CPU (SAR azimuth pass, second pass of a 2-D FFT): the SME2 column kernel needs no transpose and logged 2.7-5.3x over vDSP transpose+fftm+transpose at N up to 4096
- Matched-filter style pipelines (FFT, pointwise multiply, IFFT) where fusing into one dispatch removes device-memory round trips: the fused SAR pipeline was 22x faster than the author's own unfused version on M1

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs a library: there is no packaged API, the GPU kernels are FP32 and powers of two only (the N=4096 kernels are hard-coded, multi-size covers 256-16384), and the SME2 path accepts only N = 64, 512, 4096 or 32768
- Comparisons against a multithreaded CPU: the +29% is GPU-only time against a single-threaded vDSP_fft_zop loop timed by wall clock
- L2-resident batches at N=16384 on M6: MPSGraph (805 GF) and the repo's own two-pass four-step kernel (708 GF) beat the one-pass kernel (220 GF)
- Contiguous batched FFTs on the CPU with data already in vDSP's split-complex layout: once packing into the SME layout is counted, SME2 runs at 0.51-0.89x of vDSP for N >= 512
- Non-Apple hardware, or Apple GPUs before M1: Metal and Apple Silicon only, macOS 13+; the SME2 code needs an M4 or later

**Integration:** source-drop · Metal and Accelerate frameworks; Xcode Command Line Tools (swiftc, xcrun metal, clang); M6 harness: Swift 5.9+; plots: Python 3 with pandas and matplotlib (MLX 0.29.3 and NumPy for the landscape script) · macOS 13.0+ and Swift via Xcode CLT for the M1 code; Swift 5.9+ and clang -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 for the M6/SME2 code; GPU matrix-unit modes need macOS 26+ and an M5-class GPU · Apple Silicon only (M1 or later for the GPU kernels, M4 or later for SME2)

**Vs siblings:** VkFFT is the catalogued choice for a real GPU FFT library on Apple hardware (it has a Metal backend and arbitrary sizes). Pick AppleSiliconFFT only as reference kernels for Apple-specific tricks: register-resident one-pass N=8192/16384 kernels, fused SAR pipelines, or SME2 column FFTs on M4+ CPUs. For portable CPU FFTs, Admiral or PocketFFT apply instead.

**Gotchas:**
- The M1 host fft_host.swift compiles Metal source at run time and looks for fft_4096_mma.metal, which is not in the repo. The 138 GFLOPS kernel is src/fft_4096_radix8.metal (kernel function fft_4096_mma), so you have to copy or rename it; the README's xcrun metal/metallib steps are not what the host loads
- The headline kernel is labeled inconsistently. Its header comment says stages 1-3 use simdgroup_matrix MMA, but all four passes call the scalar radix8_butterfly, and the README calls it both 'Radix-8 Stockham' and 'split-radix DIT'. The simdgroup_matrix kernel is the 128 GFLOPS fft_4096_ct_mma.metal
- The hosts enable Metal fastMathEnabled, and the pass criterion is an L2 relative error below 1e-5 against vDSP
- sme_fft_execute leaves output in base-8 digit-reversed order and batch-minor blocks of 16 FFTs (use sme_fft_unpack). Build with -mcpu=apple-m4, not -march=armv9, or the program dies with SIGILL. On M6, hot and cold runs differ by up to 3.7x

**Status:** Active as of 2026-09-26, with 5 commits and 6 stars. It is MIT-licensed research code tied to the author's preprints and is easy to copy kernels from, but it has no API, tests beyond the validation hosts, or packaging.

[repo](https://github.com/aminems/AppleSiliconFFT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/aminems/AppleSiliconFFT)

##### FastAndFourier (FAF, JIT-compiled DSP/FFT library)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

C11 DSP library (FFT, DCT/DST, DWT, CWT, STFT) with IR interpreter plus runtime gcc JIT; beats KissFFT only at some sizes.

**Beats:** KissFFT (and FFTW3 FFTW_ESTIMATE/FFTW_MEASURE, which beat it); also NotoriousFFT — First-party Google Benchmark runs, double-precision C2C: on an unnamed 2.3 GHz AVX2 x86_64 Mac (macOS Ventura, -O3 -march=native -ffast-math, 2026-02-22) FAF beat KissFFT only at N = 65,536 (907 vs 3,253 us, about 3.6x) and lost 2.5-4x at N = 64-16,384, with FFTW3 measure fastest everywhere; on an unnamed 6-core 1.73 GHz aarch64 Linux box (-O3 -march=native, frequency scaling on, 2026-09-03) it beat KissFFT by ~1.1-1.8x at N = 8 and N >= 32 and lost slightly at N = 16. Compiler names and CPU models are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark README contradicts itself (two x86 tables disagree; a February run 'pinned' to the August v1.0.1); beats KissFFT on x86 only at N=65536.

**Known shortcoming:** Security: the JIT writes .c/.so files to predictable /tmp/faf_jit_<pid>_<n> paths, runs gcc via system() and dlopens the result, and dlopens ~/.cache/fastandfourier/jit_<hash>.so with no integrity check (hash ignores library version, compiler and CPU); bug: faf_jit_destroy unlinks the cached .so after a cache hit; built with -ffast-math -march=native; benchmarks drive the slower interleaved path; x86 table predates v1.1.

**How:** Transforms are lowered to a 34-opcode IR that either runs on a direct-threaded interpreter (VM) or is emitted as C with AVX2/AVX-512/NEON intrinsics, compiled at runtime by invoking gcc through system(), and dlopen'ed; the AUTO backend switches to the JIT at N >= 128. Version 1.1 added hard-coded split-plane codelets for N = 2-12, recursive split-radix DIF for powers of two >= 16, radix-2/3/4/5 mixed radix for 5-smooth sizes, Rader for primes with 7-smooth N-1, and optional Bluestein. Fused R2C -> pointwise -> C2R pipelines run as one generated kernel.

**Use it when:**
- You want a scriptable or config-driven DSP chain (filter banks, wavelet denoisers, matched filters) where FFT, DWT, CWT and STFT share one API and can be fused, more than raw FFT speed.
- Replacing KissFFT on AArch64 for double-precision C2C at N = 8 or N >= 32 (author's run: 16.5 vs 21.7 us at N = 1024, 2238 vs 2735 us at N = 65536, ~1.1-1.8x).
- Large power-of-two transforms on x86 AVX2 where the JIT engages (author's Feb 2026 run: 907 vs 3253 us at N = 65536).
- Embedding into C projects that can tolerate a runtime C compiler, or builds with FASTANDFOURIER_SINGLE_HEADER=ON to stay VM-only.

**Skip it when:**
- Raw FFT speed: the README itself says FFTW3 FFTW_MEASURE wins at nearly every size (3-10x ahead on its x86 table), and the same author's Notorious-FFT is 1.2-2.15x faster than FAF on aarch64.
- Small and mid sizes on x86: the published x86 table has FAF 2.5-4x slower than KissFFT from N = 64 to 16,384 (e.g. 75.3 vs 27.1 us at N = 1024); it predates the 1.1 codelets and has not been re-run.
- Hardened, multi-user or sandboxed processes: the JIT writes generated C and .so files to predictable names in /tmp (faf_jit_<pid>_<counter>), shells out to gcc with system(), and dlopen()s the result and any jit_<hash>.so found in $HOME/.cache/fastandfourier without integrity checks.
- Transforms longer than 2^16 points (the VM register file is sized for N <= 65,536) or non-5-smooth lengths without opting into Bluestein (RFFT and DWT refuse it).
- Production dependencies needing maturity: 0 stars, no tagged releases on the repo page, and benchmark tables with internal inconsistencies.

**Integration:** static lib · none at build time beyond libm, libdl and pthread on Linux; a system gcc at runtime for the JIT (otherwise VM only); tests and benchmarks fetch Google Test and Google Benchmark · CMake 3.18+, C11 compiler (C++17 only for tests) · x86-64 (SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512) and AArch64 (NEON/SVE) on Linux, macOS and Windows per README; CUDA backend experimental

**Vs siblings:** For plain FFTs prefer Notorious-FFT (same author, faster on aarch64), PocketFFT or PFFFT, which beat KissFFT more consistently without a runtime compiler; pick FastAndFourier only when you need its breadth (DCT/DST, DWT, CWT/CQT, STFT, MDCT) behind one API and the Chirp scripting/fusion layer, and can accept the JIT's runtime-compiler and /tmp file model.

**Gotchas:**
- Release builds compile the library with -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops, and the JIT also compiles kernels with -ffast-math and -march=native (or -march=armv8.2-a+fp16 on AArch64 with the SIMD flag), so binaries and cached kernels are not portable to older CPUs and IEEE NaN/Inf semantics are not guaranteed.
- The disk cache key is an FNV-1a hash of the IR, size, precision and flags only, not of the library version, compiler or CPU; a stale or foreign jit_<hash>.so in $HOME/.cache/fastandfourier is loaded as-is. faf_jit_destroy also unlinks ctx->so_path, which after a cache hit is the cached file itself, so the cache entry is deleted after it is reused.
- The first JIT execution of each transform pays a full gcc invocation; non-power-of-two sizes and kernels that bake process pointers (FFT_STAGE, pipelines) are never disk-cached, so every process recompiles them.
- Benchmarks drive the interleaved faf_execute_f64 path, which the README calls the slower convenience path; split-plane buffers are the fast path and require explicit faf_deinterleave/faf_interleave conversion.

**Status:** Actively developed by a single author (last commit 2026-09-25, v1.2.0 commit on 2026-09-04) and MIT-licensed, but young, unstarred and with a security-sensitive JIT design, so treat it as experimental.

[repo](https://github.com/NotoriousLOB/FastAndFourier) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NotoriousLOB/FastAndFourier/HEAD/README.md)

##### fbcuda / fbfft (archived)  `CUDA C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Archived Facebook CUDA headers whose fbfft kernels batch tiny power-of-two FFTs; authors claim ~1.5x over cuFFT at CNN sizes.

**Beats:** cuFFT (NVIDIA GPU FFT library) — The only fbfft-vs-cuFFT numbers come from the authors' ICLR 2015 paper (arXiv 1412.7580), seen here only as search snippets: over 1.5x faster than cuFFT (mean 1.51x, geometric mean 1.49x) for the batched FFT sizes used in CNNs, with the convolution experiments on an NVIDIA K40m; the cuFFT version, compiler flags and per-size tables were not seen and the repo has no benchmark. The co-author-maintained convnet-benchmarks compares convolutions with cuDNN, not FFTs with cuFFT: fbfft beat cuDNN R2 in April 2015 (256 vs 1019 ms layer-wise) and lost to cuDNN R4 fp32 on Titan X.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: the fbfft paper (arXiv 1412.7580) could not be opened, so the ICLR venue and the 1.5x over cuFFT are snippet only; the repo has no cuFFT benchmark. The co-author's convnet-benchmarks compare fbfft convolution with cuDNN (not cuFFT): faster than cuDNN R2 (256 vs 1019 ms) but slower than cuDNN R4 on Titan X (104 vs 81 ms). Archived; Facebook PATENTS v2 grant attached.

**Known shortcoming:** Will not compile for sm_75 or newer: ComputeCapabilities.cuh has '#error Unknown __CUDA_ARCH__' above 700 and the code uses the non-_sync __shfl/__shfl_xor that NVIDIA removed for 7.x targets. Sizes are capped at 256 (1-D) and 128 (2-D), and the 2-D code says larger sizes are often slower than cuFFT. initTwiddles() has an unsynchronized static flag and copies twiddles only to the first current device. No tests (issue #2 open since 2017). On convnet-benchmarks' Titan X, fbfft is slower than cuDNN R4 fp32 (AlexNet 104 vs 81 ms, VGG-A 1092 vs 529 ms). Paper 1412.7580 not opened (ar5iv, mlanthology blocked); tier stays C.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Each transform lives in the registers of one warp: sizes up to 32 run a radix-2 decimation-in-frequency butterfly through warp shuffles (__shfl_xor), with 2 to 16 tiny FFTs packed into a single warp; sizes 64 to 256 keep several values per thread and do the butterflies across registers without shuffles, using shared memory only for bit reversal. The FFT size is a template parameter so every loop fully unrolls, twiddles come from a 128-entry precomputed single-precision table read through __ldg, and two real FFTs are packed into one complex FFT for R2C. The 2-D 32x32 path mixes Volkov-Kazian (2008) style hand-unrolled vertical FFTs with shuffle-based horizontal FFTs.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or porting warp-register FFT designs for very many tiny (2 to 256 point) single-precision transforms, e.g. tile-based FFT convolution.
- Keeping legacy Torch-7 fbcunn FFT convolutions running on Kepler, Maxwell or Pascal GPUs (compute capability 3.5 to 6.x) with an old CUDA toolkit.
- Batched R2C/C2R 1-D sizes 2 to 256, or 2-D up to 32x32, where the batch count is a multiple of the per-warp packing factor.
- As a reference design when benchmarking modern small-size GPU FFT kernels (VkFFT, TurboFFT, tcFFT) against an older warp-shuffle approach.

**Skip it when:**
- Any GPU newer than Volta: ComputeCapabilities.cuh stops with '#error Unknown __CUDA_ARCH__' above 700, and the code uses the non-_sync __shfl/__shfl_xor intrinsics, which NVIDIA deprecated in CUDA 9.0 and removed for compute capability 7.x targets.
- 1-D sizes above 256, 2-D sizes above 128, non-power-of-two lengths, double or half precision, complex 1-D input, or 3-D transforms: these assert or return UnsupportedSize, and the 2-D code itself says larger sizes 'are often slower than cufft'.
- Getting fast convolutions today: soumith/convnet-benchmarks (Titan X) shows fbfft convolutions slower than cuDNN R4 fp32 (AlexNet 104 vs 81 ms, OverFeat 342 vs 268 ms, VGG-A 1092 vs 529 ms).
- Production code that needs plans, a C ABI, tests or support: the repo is archived, ships no build files or fbfft tests (issue #2 asking for test files has been open since 2017), and the FFTIteratedConvolution.cuh prototypes are self-described as having 'bad performance'.
- Projects that cannot accept Facebook's 'Additional Grant of Patent Rights Version 2', which terminates on patent assertions against Facebook.

**Integration:** header-only · CUDA toolkit, glog (glog/logging.h), fbcuda's own DeviceTensor/Complex/CudaUtils headers under a cuda/ include prefix; the fbcunn consumer also needs Torch-7, Folly, fbthrift, thpp and fblualib · nvcc with C++11 (constexpr used); fbcunn's INSTALL targets CUDA 7.5 on Ubuntu 14.04; GPU compute capability 3.5 or above (__ldg) · NVIDIA GPUs sm_35 to sm_6x as written (sm_70 passes the arch check but loses the non-sync shuffles under CUDA 9+); Linux

**Vs siblings:** VkFFT (cuFFT parity on radix 2-13 lengths), TurboFFT and tcFFT (half precision) run on current GPUs and are the practical choices; pick fbfft only to study its warp-register design for tiny fp32 batches or to keep legacy fbcunn code alive, and use FlashFFTConv for FFT convolution on modern hardware.

**Gotchas:**
- A batch count that is not a multiple of the per-warp packing factor drops to one FFT per warp (a TODO in FBFFT-inl.cuh), and the 2-D warp kernels assert that the batch divides evenly.
- Padding is only on the left/top; the caller must choose a 2^(k+1) transform when the padded input no longer fits in 2^k.
- Size limits are enforced partly with assert(), which compiles out under NDEBUG; always check the returned ErrorCode.
- The twiddle table has 128 complex entries, so 256 is a hard ceiling for 1-D without regenerating Twiddles.cuh.

**Status:** Archived read-only since 2020-03-03 (last commit 2018-05-29); BSD-3-Clause plus a non-OSI patent grant, header-only and small enough to vendor, but it needs patches (sync shuffles, the __CUDA_ARCH__ check) before it compiles for any GPU from Turing onward.

[repo](https://github.com/facebookarchive/fbcuda) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7580)

##### FFTS (The Fastest Fourier Transform in the South)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

BSD-3 C library for single-precision FFTs that JIT-compiles a machine-code plan; beat FFTW on pre-AVX SSE CPUs, loses on AVX.

**Beats:** FFTW — A user-posted table in issue #28 (2014) compared FFTS with FFTW on power-of-two complex FFTs from N=4 to 262144. FFTS is single precision; the FFTW version, planner flags and compiler were not stated. On an i7-870 (SSE4.2, no AVX) FFTS was 1.11-1.88x faster at every size; on an i5-3340M (AVX) it won only for N <= 32 (1.17-1.81x) and ran at 0.64-0.91x of FFTW's speed for N >= 64. The issue page showed no comments this session, so the record's second-user report (i5-3470, VS2015, real N=2048, ~50% slower) could not be re-traced.

**Known shortcoming:** Faster only on pre-AVX CPUs, FFTW wins on AVX CPUs (issue #28); another user measured ~50% slower for real N=2048; author points to linkotec and ValveSoftware forks; stale (2024-05-15).

**Known shortcoming:** The record's 'second user (i5-3470, VS2015, real N=2048) ~50% slower' claim is untraceable: issue #28 has no comments. #28 table: on the AVX i5-3340M FFTS wins at N<=32 (1.17-1.81x) and loses at N>=64 (0.64-0.91x).

**Known shortcoming:** Open segfault #81 (forward 2D real, misaligned row pointer); SIGILL #66 on ARM32; float-only, no AVX, no AArch64 SIMD (JIT falls through to x86 SSE codegen on non-ARM32); ffts_execute only logs on misaligned buffers; chirp_z_init skips a malloc NULL check; code frozen since 2017, forks idle since 2019.

**How:** Plan creation fixes size and direction, precomputes twiddle lookup tables and input-offset tables, and on x86-64 (SSE) or 32-bit ARM (NEON/VFP) emits specialised machine code into an mmap'd buffer that is then flipped to read+execute. The generated code runs SIMD size-8 leaf transforms over the permuted input, then radix-4/radix-8 butterfly passes. The authors' IEEE TSP 2013 paper (Blake, Witten, Cree) calls this a cache-oblivious algorithm with run-time specialisation, without FFTW's large codelet library or time-consuming machine-specific calibration. A static (no-JIT) build uses the same SSE/NEON kernels through C macros.

**Use it when:**
- Power-of-two single-precision FFTs on SSE-only x86-64 CPUs (Nehalem-class and older): on an i7-870 FFTS was 1.11-1.88x faster than FFTW at every N from 4 to 262144
- Very small transforms (N <= 32): even on the AVX i5-3340M FFTS beat FFTW by 1.17-1.81x
- 32-bit ARMv7 targets (older Android/iOS) that want a BSD-licensed FFT with hand-written NEON or VFP assembly
- Replacing GPL FFTW with a permissively licensed library that has a similar plan/execute shape for 1D/2D/N-D real and complex transforms

**Skip it when:**
