- AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 CPUs at N >= 64: the only SIMD paths are SSE-SSE3 and NEON, and on the i5-3340M FFTW was ~1.1-1.56x faster (FFTS ran at 0.64-0.91x of FFTW's speed, derived from page data)
- Double precision: every kernel is float-only (_32f); only the linkotec fork added 'initial support for double precision' (2018)
- AArch64 (Apple Silicon, arm64 Android, ARM servers): no 64-bit ARM SIMD path, and the JIT falls through to the x86 SSE code generator, so dynamic code has to be disabled; open issues #73 and #75 ask about arm64/NDK builds
- Non-power-of-two lengths: they run Bluestein with a power-of-two FFT of size >= 2N-1 plus three extra buffers, so they cost several power-of-two transforms; PocketFFT or VectorFFT handle them natively
- Projects that need a maintained dependency: the library code last changed in 2017, and issues #81 (segfault in forward 2D real transforms) and #66 (SIGILL in neon_transpose8 on 32-bit ARM) are still open

**Integration:** static lib · none (libm); GNU assembler for the ARM .s files · C (standard not documented); CMake 2.8.12+ or autotools (./configure --enable-sse --enable-single); GCC, Clang or MSVC · x86-64 with SSE/SSE2/SSE3 (runtime code generation x86-64 only; 32-bit x86 falls back to the static path); 32-bit ARMv7 NEON/VFP; other targets need --disable-dynamic-code and get the scalar static path; no AVX

**Vs siblings:** Pick FFTS only for power-of-two single-precision work on SSE-only x86-64 or 32-bit ARM NEON, where it has hand-tuned code and a permissive license. On current hardware muFFT (runtime AVX dispatch), PocketFFT (any length, double precision, ARM) or KFR (beats FFTW on modern CPUs, GPL/commercial) are better and maintained.

**Gotchas:**
- Input and output buffers must be 16-byte aligned on SSE/NEON builds. ffts_execute only LOGs a warning on misalignment and then runs aligned SIMD code; issue #81 is a segfault from an internally misaligned row pointer in forward 2D real transforms
- The default build generates machine code at plan time and mprotects anonymous memory to read+execute. Where JIT memory is forbidden, build with --disable-dynamic-code (autotools) or DISABLE_DYNAMIC_CODE (CMake)
- On ARM the CMake build probes the host with -march=native and runs test programs to pick NEON hard/soft-float or VFP, so cross-compiles skip this detection
- ffts_chirp_z_init writes into its scratch buffer without checking the aligned malloc result, so an allocation failure on a large non-power-of-two plan dereferences NULL

**Status:** Abandoned: the code last changed in June 2017 (a merge of linkotec's Bluestein support), and the only later commit (May 2024) is a README note from the author pointing to the linkotec and ValveSoftware forks. Those forks are themselves idle since March 2019. The library is BSD-3 and small enough to vendor, but treat it as frozen legacy code for SSE/ARMv7 single precision.

[repo](https://github.com/anthonix/ffts) · [benchmark](https://github.com/anthonix/ffts/issues/28)

##### GPU_FFT (Raspberry Pi VideoCore IV, hello_fft in raspberrypi/userland)  `C with VideoCore QPU assembly kernels`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Andrew Holme's GPU_FFT: power-of-two complex FFTs on the Raspberry Pi VideoCore IV GPU, about 10x FFTW on the Pi 1 ARM.

**Beats:** FFTW (FFTW_MEASURE) running on the Raspberry Pi 1 ARM CPU — The library author's own gpu_fft.txt (release 3.0, 2015) gives per-transform times on a 700 MHz Pi 1 with VC4 L2 cache enabled: GPU_FFT at batch 1 takes 0.033 ms vs 0.092 ms for FFTW_MEASURE at 256 points, 0.25 vs 3.0 ms at 4K, 7.0 vs 83 ms at 64K and 786 vs 8800 ms at 4M (2.8x to 12x). The FFTW version, build flags and timing code are not published; hello_fft.c only times the GPU side with clock_gettime and reports rms error.

**Known shortcoming:** Only the hello_fft component of the archived (2025-08-27) raspberrypi/userland repo. FFTW harness, version and flags not published; the hello_fft makefile runs gcc with no -O flag. The doc says FFTW is 10x more accurate. Runs only on the VideoCore IV GPU (Pi 1-3/Zero) and needs root.

**Known shortcoming:** Needs root; only VideoCore IV Pis (Pi 4/5 support undocumented). The short-batch path busy-waits with no timeout. Repo archived and its README calls itself deprecated. The listed gpu_fftw is an LD_PRELOAD shim over this same GPU_FFT library.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Hand-written VideoCore IV QPU assembly (qasm/*.qasm, assembled to hex/*.hex and embedded) splits each transform into a few passes of radix-16, radix-32 or radix-64 butterflies (e.g. the 256-point kernel is two radix-16 passes, the 4M-point kernel two radix-64 passes plus radix-32 passes), loading the first pass bit-reversed and ping-ponging between two buffers, with writes through the VPM and VC4 L2 cache. Twiddles are advanced with a trig recurrence corrected by float-float (df64) subtraction to recover accuracy. For short batches the ARM pokes V3D registers directly and busy-waits instead of using the firmware mailbox, which removes about 100 us of overhead per call.

**Use it when:**
- Spectrum analysis, SDR or audio DSP on a Raspberry Pi 1, Zero or other VideoCore IV board where the ARM core is the bottleneck: the doc table shows 2.8x at 256 points and 8-12x from 4K to 4M points over FFTW_MEASURE on a 700 MHz Pi 1
- Many same-size power-of-two transforms that can be batched into one execute call (batch of 10 roughly halves per-transform time at 256-512 points)
- Applications that tolerate single precision with 0.33-1.5 ppm rms error
- Freeing the ARM CPU for other work while the GPU computes longer transforms (mailbox path for long jobs avoids 100% CPU busy-waiting)

**Skip it when:**
- Any non-VideoCore IV hardware: the kernels are QPU machine code and gpu_fft_base.c only has Pi 1 and 'Pi 2?' memory paths; support for Pi 4/5 is not documented
- Double precision, non-power-of-two lengths, real-input (r2c) transforms or lengths below 256 or above 4,194,304
- When accuracy matters: the doc says FFTW is still one order of magnitude more accurate
- Programs that cannot run as root: mailbox.c opens /dev/mem and /dev/vcio and maps the V3D registers
- New projects on current Raspberry Pi OS: the userland repo README calls itself ancient and deprecated, the repo is archived, and its code is no longer installed on Bookworm images

**Integration:** source-drop · Raspberry Pi firmware mailbox device (/dev/vcio), /dev/mem, libbcm_host.so (dlopen'd for SDRAM and peripheral addresses), librt, libm, libdl · Plain C (gcc, no flags in the makefile); prebuilt shader hex files included, the QPU assembler is only needed to change kernels · Raspberry Pi boards with the VideoCore IV GPU (BCM2835 Pi 1/Zero; gpu_fft_base.c also has a Pi 2 memory path); 32-bit Raspbian/Raspberry Pi OS era firmware

**Vs siblings:** Pick GPU_FFT itself when you can change the code and want the full speed, batching and the 2D transpose; gpu_fftw (already catalogued) is an LD_PRELOAD shim over this same library that keeps the FFTW API but copies arrays, falls back to FFTW and supports only 1-D 2^8-2^21. On anything other than a VideoCore IV Pi, the CPU libraries in the list (FFTW itself, PocketFFT, PFFFT, Ne10 on ARM) are the options.

**Gotchas:**
- Input is destroyed and the result is out of place for log2_N 12-16 (odd pass count) but in place otherwise; always read fft->out.
- GPU memory is permanently lost until reboot if gpu_fft_release() is not called (doc and hello_fft.c comment), so crash handling matters.
- The direct-register path (batches up to about 1 ms of work) busy-waits on V3D_SRQCS with no timeout; only the mailbox path has the 2000 ms timeout.
- Buffers are separated by fft->step, which is larger than N because of guard space; index batches with step, not N.

**Status:** Abandoned: last hello_fft commit 2022-06-16 and raspberrypi/userland archived on 2025-08-27 with a README telling users to rethink solutions built on it; BSD-3-Clause and only a handful of C files plus shader hex, so it is easy to vendor for legacy Pi 1/Zero projects.

[repo](https://github.com/raspberrypi/userland) · [benchmark](https://github.com/raspberrypi/userland/blob/master/host_applications/linux/apps/hello_pi/hello_fft/gpu_fft.txt)

##### gpu_fftw  `C/C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

LD_PRELOAD shim that reroutes FFTW3 1-D power-of-two complex float FFTs to the original Raspberry Pi's VideoCore IV GPU.

**Beats:** FFTW3 (running on the Raspberry Pi CPU) — The project's own self-test, on an unnamed Raspberry Pi (Makefile targets ARMv6, so Pi 1 class), timed 1,000 forward 1,024-point complex float FFTs: 11,523 FFT/s on the GPU versus 1,619 FFT/s for CPU fftw3f with an FFTW_ESTIMATE plan (7.1x); plan creation and the GPU path's one-time input copy are outside the timed loop, and the compiler/FFTW versions are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Security: needs sudo/root to reach the GPU mailbox (the 'drop root' TODO is open); FFTW baseline planned with FFTW_ESTIMATE and only N=1024 timed.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bugs: input is copied to the GPU only at plan creation, so re-running a plan after writing new data returns the FFT of the old data (the self-test timing leaves that copy out); destroying plans out of creation order lets the next plan overwrite a live one, and past 1024 live plans it dereferences NULL; bundled GPU_FFT 2.0 hard-codes the BCM2835 base (Pi 1/Zero only) and issue #1 on a Pi 3 suggests the GPU path never ran; creates /dev/gpu_mb with mknod.

**How:** The work is done by Andrew Holme's GPU_FFT 2.0 (bundled as hello_fft/): per-size hand-written QPU shader binaries that compute the transform in 2 to 4 passes of radix-16/32/64 butterflies (N=1,024 is two radix-32 passes) spread over the 8 VideoCore IV QPUs, with twiddles and ping-pong buffers in GPU-shared memory. For small batches (N*jobs <= 20480) it launches the shaders by poking V3D registers directly through /dev/mem and busy-waits; larger jobs go through the firmware mailbox. The speedup is simply that the Pi 1's ARM11 CPU running FFTW is much slower than the QPUs.

**Use it when:**
- Legacy Raspberry Pi 1 / Zero-class (BCM2835, ARMv6) systems running an existing FFTW3-linked program you cannot recompile, e.g. SDR or audio spectrum tools.
- 1-D complex single-precision FFTs of power-of-two length 2^8 to 2^21 where the plan is reused and the program fills the input before planning.
- Quick experiments to see whether GPU offload helps an FFT-bound Pi 1 workload before porting code to the GPU_FFT API directly.

**Skip it when:**
- Any program that plans once and then writes new data into the input array before each fftw_execute: the shim copies the input to GPU memory only at plan time, so later executes transform the stale plan-time data.
- Raspberry Pi 2/3/4/5 or any non-Pi hardware: the bundled GPU_FFT 2.0 hard-codes the BCM2835 peripheral base 0x20000000, and open issue #1 reports the self-test override check failing on a Pi 3 (GPU/FFTW difference 0 ppm, i.e. the GPU path apparently never ran).
- Double precision work: the -d 'double squashing' mode silently computes double requests in float.
- 2-D/3-D, real-to-complex, batched (plan_many), new-array execute (fftw_execute_dft) or threaded FFTW use: none are intercepted.
- Production or multi-user systems: requires root (/dev/mem mapping, mknod of /dev/gpu_mb), runs the target program as root with LD_PRELOAD, and the README calls it an early alpha.

**Integration:** shared lib · FFTW3 (libfftw3 and libfftw3f, called via dlsym RTLD_NEXT), libdl, bundled GPU_FFT 2.0 (hello_fft, BSD-3-Clause), root access to /dev/mem and the VideoCore mailbox · C99 + C++11 (gcc/g++; Makefile tunes for -march=armv6 -mfpu=vfp -mtune=arm1176jzf-s) · Raspberry Pi with BCM2835 / VideoCore IV (Pi 1, Zero); Linux only

**Vs siblings:** No catalogued sibling targets the Raspberry Pi GPU; on a Pi 1/Zero with an unmodifiable FFTW binary this is the only drop-in, while for new code or newer Pis a NEON CPU library such as Ne10, or PFFFT/muFFT, is the safer choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Plan slots are taken as mplan_arr[mplan_n++] and freed by decrementing mplan_n, so destroying plans out of LIFO order lets the next plan overwrite a live one; past 1024 live plans the fallback path dereferences a NULL metaplan.
- The input array is copied to GPU memory inside fftw_plan_dft_1d and never again; FFTW_MEASURE-style 'plan first, fill later' code gets wrong results with no error.
- Planner flags (FFTW_MEASURE, FFTW_PATIENT, wisdom) are ignored on the GPU path; each GPU plan allocates and maps its own VideoCore memory, so many concurrent plans can exhaust GPU memory (then it falls back to FFTW).
- The launcher passes child arguments poorly (open issue #2: the child's flags are parsed as gpu_fftw options unless separated with --).

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2015 (two open, unanswered issues) and alpha quality; MIT-licensed and small, but only of historical or Pi-1-specific interest given its stale-input and plan-slot bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/gpu-fftw/gpu_fftw) · [benchmark](https://github.com/gpu-fftw/gpu_fftw)

##### gpuNUFFT  `CUDA C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

CUDA gridding/NUFFT library for 2D/3D non-Cartesian MRI with MATLAB and Python front ends; GPU alternative to CPU NUFFTs.

**Beats:** cuFINUFFT (3D, single-coil and 32-coil MRI data, as measured in cufinufft issue #126, Jan 2022); CPU NUFFT libraries only directionally via the MRI-NUFFT benchmark statement — The repo publishes no speed numbers, and the MRI-NUFFT JOSS paper only says cufinufft and gpuNUFFT performed best in its benchmark, which commits no results; a gpuNUFFT Python-binding author co-wrote that paper. One concrete measurement is in cufinufft issue #126 (Jan 2022, GPU and tolerances unstated, gpuNUFFT timings include host-device copies): forward 73.42 ms vs 279.36 ms and adjoint 62.73 vs 132.27 ms on single-coil 128x128x160, and 1582.74 vs 8952.54 ms and 1739.30 vs 4159.96 ms with 32 coils, while the cuFINUFFT paper reports the opposite direction for general-purpose benchmarks.

**Known shortcoming:** No numbers; the MRI-NUFFT JOSS paper only says it ranks among the fastest. Upstream abandoned; the chaithyagr/gpuNUFFT fork is active and is what PyPI ships (0.10.8, 2026-07-08).

**Known shortcoming:** Uses the legacy texture-reference API that CUDA 12 removed; gencode stops at sm_75; device-global __constant__ state; single GPU only (#72); open crash/OOM issues #84, #68 and CUDA 10/11 build issues #89, #91. Double precision exists via the GPU_DOUBLE_PREC CMake option (the record said single only). The chaithyagr fork drops texture references and adds sm_80 to sm_120. The cuFINUFFT paper (arXiv 2102.08463, snippet only) reports cuFINUFFT 78x faster for type 1 and 5x for type 2.

**Known shortcoming:** Raised D to C (retier-14) on cufinufft issue #126 (closed, no replies): 3D single coil 3.8x forward / 2.1x adjoint and 32 coils 5.65x / 2.39x over cuFINUFFT, with GPU, eps and gpuNUFFT parameters unstated and host-device copies counted only on the gpuNUFFT side. The cuFINUFFT paper (arXiv 2102.08463, blocked) claims the opposite (78x type 1, 5x type 2; harness MelodyShih/cuFINUFFT-bench, CUDA 10.0, gcc 7.4.0).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** semi-independent: flatironinstitute/cufinufft issue #126 (Jan 2022, GPU and tolerance unstated) has gpuNUFFT 3D 128x128x160 forward 73.42 vs cuFINUFFT 279.36 ms and adjoint 62.73 vs 132.27 ms (32 coils: 1582.74 vs 8952.54 ms, 1739.30 vs 4159.96 ms), with the gpuNUFFT side including host-device copies and the reporter saying cuFINUFFT is faster in 2D

**Independent measurement:** semi-independent: cufinufft issue #126 (user paquiteau), 2022

**How:** Kaiser-Bessel gridding with Beatty et al.'s minimal-oversampling kernel, read from a precomputed radial lookup table held in constant memory or in GPU textures with linear interpolation. Samples are pre-sorted into fixed-size grid sectors (e.g. 8^3) so each thread block caches its sector's data in shared memory and scatters with atomicAdd. A 'balanced' operator precomputes a sector processing order to even out load on clustered trajectories such as radial or spiral centers, and cuFFT does the oversampled FFT.

**Use it when:**
- Iterative 3D non-Cartesian MRI reconstruction (CG-SENSE, compressed sensing) with a fixed trajectory, where the one-time sector precomputation is amortized over many forward/adjoint calls.
- Multi-coil 3D data with sensitivity maps and density compensation built into the operator; in a 2022 cufinufft issue (#126) gpuNUFFT ran 2.1x to 5.65x faster than cufinufft on 3D 128x128x160 data with 1 and 32 coils (tolerances not matched, GPU not stated).
- MATLAB-based MRI pipelines that want a drop-in GPU NUFFT operator object.
- Python MRI work through MRI-NUFFT or pysap-mri, installed from PyPI (the gpuNUFFT package built from the chaithyagr fork).

**Skip it when:**
- General-purpose or 2D NUFFTs with a target accuracy: cuFINUFFT takes an explicit tolerance and, per its paper (seen only as a search snippet), averages 78x faster than gpuNUFFT on type 1 and 5x faster on type 2; the issue #126 reporter also found cufinufft faster in 2D.
- Upstream on current CUDA: the code uses the legacy texture-reference API (texture<> globals, cudaBindTextureToArray), which NVIDIA removed in CUDA 12 (removal known from CUDA release notes, not opened here). Its gencode list stops at sm_75, and CUDA 10/11 build issues (#89, #91) are open. Use the chaithyagr fork, which drops that API and adds sm_80 to sm_120.
- Multi-GPU or concurrent use: one GPU per process (issue #72, open), and the operator state lives in device-global __constant__ symbols (GI, KERNEL[10000]) and global textures.
- Very large 3D problems: indices are 32-bit unsigned int; an overflow on large trajectories (#81) was fixed, while a crash on large 3D matrices (#84) and an out-of-memory report (#68) are still open.
- Codebases without CUDA: there is no CPU fallback; the CPU-side code covers only precomputation.

**Integration:** shared lib · CUDA Toolkit with cuFFT; MATLAB for the default mex build (GEN_MEX_FILES=ON); optional pybind11 Python bindings (GEN_PYTHON_FILES) and Google Test · C++11, CMake 3.12 (FindCUDA), CUDA 8 to 11 for upstream (README says it was tested with CUDA 5.0 and gcc 4.6); CUDA 12 needs the chaithyagr fork · NVIDIA GPUs only; upstream gencode sm_50 to sm_75 plus compute_52/compute_61 PTX for JIT on newer cards; Linux (gcc) and Windows (Visual Studio 2013 Win64) documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick gpuNUFFT (preferably the chaithyagr fork) for 3D multi-coil MRI operators with coil sensitivities and density compensation built in, where the one reported head-to-head (cufinufft issue #126) favours it. Pick cuFINUFFT (FINUFFT) for general or 2D NUFFTs with a guaranteed tolerance. TRON's README claims 30x over gpuNUFFT, but only for its own trajectory-optimized radial/spiral use.

**Gotchas:**
- Accuracy is set indirectly by kernel width and oversampling factor, not by a tolerance, so speed comparisons against FINUFFT or cuFINUFFT must match error levels; issue #101 ('How to determine the scaling?') is open.
- Single precision by default; double precision requires rebuilding with GPU_DOUBLE_PREC=ON.
- Operator construction sorts samples into sectors (CPU or GPU) and must be redone when the trajectory changes; loadPrecomputedGpuNUFFTOperator reuses saved mappings.
- Host-array calls copy data to and from the device each time and return arrays that must be freed manually; for iterative loops use the GpuArray overloads that keep data on the GPU.

**Status:** Upstream has been abandoned since 2022-02-06, with many open build and crash issues; it is MIT-licensed (with a request to cite Knoll et al., ISMRM 2014), and the maintained chaithyagr fork (PyPI gpuNUFFT, recommended by MRI-NUFFT) is the version to adopt.

[repo](https://github.com/andyschwarzl/gpuNUFFT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/flatironinstitute/cufinufft/issues/126)

##### JTransforms  `Java`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Java multithreaded FFT/DCT/DST/DHT library; beat a per-call-planned FFTW (via JNI) on smooth 2-D/3-D sizes, lost on primes.

**Beats:** FFTW 3 through the ezFFTW Java wrapper (single-threaded) — Third-party FFTBench (JMH 1.21, Oracle JDK 1.8.0_111, AMD Phenom II X4 955, Ubuntu 16.04, 2-3 iterations) ran a real-to-complex forward, DC-zero and inverse round trip with JTransforms 3.1 against FFTW through the ezFFTW 0.1.2 JNI wrapper, which plans FFTW_ESTIMATE inside every call. Single-threaded JTransforms won on smooth 2-D sizes (1.13x at 1280x720 up to 1.40x at 5000x5000) and on 256^3 (1.87x), but lost at 1,087x1,931, 100x120x140 and 400x300x200; threaded 1-D JTransforms won at 10,000,000 elements (1.42x) but lost at 98,304, 589,829 and 1,000,000 (ratios derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline crippled: ezFFTW plans and destroys an FFTW_ESTIMATE plan inside every timed call; 1-D wins are multithreaded JTransforms vs single-thread FFTW, and single-thread results split both ways; Java.

**Known shortcoming:** Open correctness issues: #21 realInverse gives 2x amplitude on non-power-of-two sizes, #15 FloatFFT_2D.realForwardFull hangs at 4098x4097, #14 non-daemon pool threads delay JVM exit; losses line up with prime sizes routed to Bluestein.

**How:** The constructor picks one of three algorithms: Ooura's split-radix FFT for powers of two, FFTPack-derived mixed-radix (factors 4, 2, 3, 5, plus generic odd factors) when what remains after those factors is below 211, and Bluestein's chirp-z algorithm (zero-padded to the next power of two at or above 2n-1) otherwise. Twiddle and bit-reversal tables are precomputed in the constructor. Above size thresholds (1-D: 8,192 elements for 2 threads, 65,536 for 4; 2-D/3-D: 65,536) the butterflies and row/column passes are split across a JLargeArrays ConcurrencyUtils thread pool. There is no explicit SIMD.

**Use it when:**
- JVM applications (Java, Kotlin, Scala) that need FFT, DCT, DST or DHT without JNI or native libraries, e.g. image processing (the companion paper is on large-scale image deblurring).
- Large 2-D or 3-D real/complex transforms on multi-core machines, where the built-in threading helps: in FFTBench, threaded JTransforms ran 1,920x1,080 in 0.125 s vs 0.360 s for single-threaded FFTW via ezFFTW.
- Power-of-two or 2/3/5-smooth sizes (image dimensions like 1280x720, 3000x2000), which use the split-radix or mixed-radix paths.
- 1-D arrays larger than 2^31 elements, through DoubleLargeArray/FloatLargeArray (changelog 3.0: sizes up to 2^63).

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ code: this is Java only; native projects should use FFTW, PocketFFT or a sibling C/C++ library.
- Sizes with large prime factors: they go to Bluestein; in FFTBench the prime 1-D size 589,829 (1.052 vs 0.815 s) and the prime-by-prime 1,087x1,931 2-D case (single-threaded 2.132 vs 0.998 s) lost to even a per-call FFTW_ESTIMATE baseline.
- Non-power-of-two DoubleFFT_1D.realInverse: open issue #21 (2020) reports output with twice the expected amplitude (example size 48).
- Workloads where you could use properly planned native FFTW: the only FFTW comparison found re-plans FFTW_ESTIMATE on every call through JNI, so JTransforms has not been shown to beat tuned FFTW.
- Allocation- or latency-sensitive loops: the mixed-radix and Bluestein paths allocate scratch arrays on every call (new double[...] in the source), adding GC pressure.

**Integration:** module (Maven Central JAR com.github.wendykierp:JTransforms:3.2) · JLargeArrays (org.visnow; 1.7 for release 3.2 per the changelog, 1.8-SNAPSHOT in the HEAD pom); Apache Commons Math was dropped in 3.2 · HEAD pom compiles with --release 11 and adds module-info.java; JTransforms 3.1 ran on Java 8 (JDK 1.8.0_111) in FFTBench · any JVM

**Vs siblings:** No catalogued sibling is a Java library; pick JTransforms when you must stay on the JVM without native code. For C/C++ code, PocketFFT or KFR cover the same transforms faster, and FFTW itself remains the reference.

**Gotchas:**
- The internal thread pool uses non-daemon threads, so main() can hang about 60 s before the JVM exits (open issue #14); call ConcurrencyUtils.shutdownThreadPoolAndAwaitTermination() or set the thread count to 1.
- realForward returns a packed half spectrum in place (for even n, a[1] holds Re[n/2]); realForwardFull needs an array of length 2n with only the first n filled, and its inverse is complexInverse.
- Inverse transforms take a boolean scale flag; pass true to get 1/n normalisation.
- Open issue #15 (2018): FloatFFT_2D.realForwardFull hangs at 4,098x4,097 right after a 4,096x4,096 call succeeds.

**Status:** Active again after ten quiet years (3.1 in 2015, 3.2 released November 2025, last commit 2025-12-05); BSD-2-Clause and on Maven Central, though several correctness and hang issues (#15, #21) are still open.

[repo](https://github.com/wendykierp/JTransforms) · [benchmark](https://github.com/hageldave/FFTBench)

##### juFFTe  `Fortran`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Fortran FFTE rewrite with Spiral-generated RISC-V Vector kernels; its authors report beating FFTW3 on RVV 1.0 chips, but the FFTW comparison is weak.

**Beats:** FFTW3 — The numbers are first-party only, from preprint arXiv 2608.28076 (accepted per search snippets to the RISC-V for HPC workshop at ISC26), seen only through search summaries. Against FFTW3, average multi-core speedups are 1.09x on SiFive X280, 1.91x on SpacemiT K3 and 3.03x on Sophon SG2044; single core, juFFTe is 1.53x faster on the X280 but slower on the K3's X100 and the SG2044. The K3 and SG2044 multi-core runs used FFTW_ESTIMATE, as does the repo's benchmark/fftw_m.F90, so the headline gains are against untuned FFTW plans. FFTW version, compilers, flags and sizes were not seen.

**Known shortcoming:** Repo FFTW harness uses FFTW_ESTIMATE, and per the paper snippet the headline K3/SG2044 runs (1.09x/1.91x/3.03x) also use ESTIMATE plans, a weak baseline. Fixes landed after the preprint (2-D work-array thread-privacy race, C sign constants), so the numbers predate correctness fixes.

**Known shortcoming:** Four open issues filed 2026-09-23: #9 2-D results silently wrong when ny has a factor of 3 or 5 (64x96, 96x96, 100x100); #7 only one live plan per module (a second init aborts or reuses stale twiddle tables); #8 FFTW shim broken (backward scaled by 1/n, multiple-definition link errors, missing functions); #10 CI tests only size 2. Not thread-safe. src/juffte.h does not compile as C++ (two closing braces for one extern "C"). Preprint reportedly accepted at the ISC26 RISC-V for HPC workshop, but its numbers use FFTW_ESTIMATE and predate correctness fixes, so the tier stays C.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The kernels follow FFTE: Stockham autosort passes with radix-8/5/4/3/2 butterflies (fft235). Long 1-D transforms (n > 174,762, i.e. L2SIZE/48) switch to a six-step decomposition n = nx*ny, with NBLK=16 cache-blocked transposes, a twiddle multiply and padding (NP=8) to avoid cache conflicts. The OpenMP loops run over those blocks. With -DWITHRVV=ON the butterflies are swapped for Spiral-generated C kernels using RVV 1.0 intrinsics (src/spiral/rvv: dft2 to dft16, double and single precision), and factor2() chooses radices from {3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12,15,16}. The claimed win comes from explicit RVV vectorization, which upstream FFTW lacks (per the verifier, only an open RVV pull request exists); on x86 and Arm the generic Fortran path relies on compiler autovectorization.

**Use it when:**
- Double-precision 1-D/2-D/3-D FFTs on RVV 1.0 hardware (SiFive X280, SpacemiT K3/X100, Sophon SG2044/C920v2), where FFTW has no vector kernels; per the preprint, juFFTe wins multi-core on all three and single-core on the X280
- Fortran HPC codes that already use FFTE's zfft1d/zfft2d/zfft3d calling convention and want a maintained, Apache-2.0 successor
- Single-plan workloads: one transform size per precision and module, initialized once and executed many times from one thread (with OpenMP inside)
- RISC-V porting and benchmarking work at HPC centers, where you can check correctness at your own sizes before relying on it

**Skip it when:**
- Any program that needs more than one live plan (e.g. a forward and an inverse plan at different sizes, or several sizes): the work and twiddle arrays are module-level statics, so a second init aborts with 'Attempting to allocate already allocated variable b' or silently reuses stale tables (open issue #7)
- 2-D transforms whose ny has a factor of 3 or 5 (e.g. 64x96, 96x96, 100x100, 120x120): they silently return wrong results (open issue #9, 2026-09-23); whether 3-D and r2c/c2r share the bug is unchecked, and CI only tests size 2 (issue #10)
- As an FFTW drop-in: the C shim is defined in the header (multiple-definition link errors with more than one TU), the backward transform is normalized by 1/n where FFTW's is not, fftw_destroy_plan and fftw_plan_with_nthreads are missing from C, and a second plan breaks the first (open issue #8)
- x86-64 or Arm: no SVE or AVX kernels exist (-DWITHSVE stops at configure time), and no x86 or Arm results are published, so there is no evidence it beats FFTW, MKL or KFR there
- Lengths that are not 2^p 3^q 5^r: factor() just stops at the first other prime and nothing checks this, so these sizes are not rejected (read from the source)

**Integration:** static lib · Fortran runtime (libgfortran or the vendor equivalent) and OpenMP; a C99 compiler for the Spiral/RVV kernels; FFTW3 only for the optional benchmark comparison · Fortran 2003 compiler (tested with gfortran, nvfortran, Flang and Intel ifx/ifort); CMake 3.15+ or the plain Makefile; a riscv64 cross toolchain with RVV 1.0 support for the vector kernels · Any target with a Fortran compiler (generic kernels); RISC-V RVV 1.0 for the Spiral vector kernels, which are the only accelerated backend

**Vs siblings:** Pick juFFTe only on RVV 1.0 RISC-V machines, where FFTW lacks vector kernels and none of the catalogued siblings publish RVV results; on x86 or Arm, KFR, PocketFFT or (on AMD) AOCL-FFTW have evidence and none of juFFTe's single-plan or correctness limits.

**Gotchas:**
- In C++, src/juffte.h does not compile at HEAD: it opens one extern "C" { block but closes two braces under __cplusplus, includes <complex.h> inside the extern "C" block and uses double _Complex. It also defines non-static globals (int juffte_init = 0, and FFTW_FORWARD etc. as ints, not macros) in the header (read from the header)
- Each OpenMP thread gets private copies of two fixed-size automatic arrays, about 16.8 MB for c((NDA2+NP)*NBLK) complex(real64) plus 1 MB for d, in the six-step path; this matches the README's known issue of segfaults unless OMP_STACKSIZE and ulimit -s are raised (size worked out from the source)
- Hard size caps from src/param.F90: 2-D transform length up to 65536 per dimension and 3-D up to 4096 per dimension
- The backward transform scales by 1/n (FFTE convention). Commit 1d91fc8 (2026-09-23) fixed inverted FFT sign constants in the C API and a thread-privacy race in the 2-D work arrays, so the preprint's numbers predate these fixes

**Status:** Active (initial release 2026-06-25, last commit 2026-09-24, Julich Supercomputing Centre, 3 stars). It is Apache-2.0 and copyable, but four open issues opened on 2026-09-23 (#7 single plan, #8 broken FFTW shim, #9 wrong 2-D results, #10 test suite) make it pre-production.

[repo](https://github.com/FZJ-JSC/juFFTe) · [benchmark](https://github.com/FZJ-JSC/juFFTe/tree/main/benchmark)

##### matchedfilter (formerly peak-fft)  `C core with Python bindings; GPU kernels in Slang (Vulkan/Metal)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Fused batched matched filter (spectral product, inverse FFT, peak scan) for data x template banks; peak-only mode beats FFTW's inverse-only time.

**Beats:** FFTW (inverse transform only, timed through pyFFTW); on GPU rocFFT / MLX FFT inverse-only references — First-party seven-machine run at revision eecb43c (2026-09-28): 16 data x 512 templates x 4096-point complex64 per call, one pinned thread, against a single batched FFTW_PATIENT backward plan (pyFFTW-bundled FFTW 3.3.5 sse2-avx built with gcc -O2 on x86, FFTW 3.3.10 NEON via the C API on M2). Peak-only took 34.27 vs 63.63 ms on a Ryzen 9 5950X and 20.68 vs 69.54 ms on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (1.86x and 3.36x), but the two sides do different work: FFTW does only the inverse FFT and writes every output, while matchedfilter adds the product and peak scan but never writes the correlation; the x86 FFTW build also lacks AVX2/FMA codelets.

**Known shortcoming:** Unequal work: FFTW times the inverse FFT only while matchedfilter fuses product + IFFT + peak scan, so it is not a drop-in FFT (closer to correlation than FFT). Weak FFTW baseline: x86 uses pyFFTW's FFTW 3.3.5 SSE2/AVX build (no AVX2/FMA); M2 FFTW at 252 ms vs 45-87 ms on x86 suggests the 4.37x M2 ratio is inflated. Full-output mode is slower than FFTW on i5-13500H and Haswell. Compiler not recorded.

**Known shortcoming:** The x86 FFTW baseline is FFTW 3.3.5 sse2-avx built with gcc -O2. Its CHANGELOG fixes a stage-B intermediate indexing bug, and an older benchmark note says correctness for that revision was not yet established. Alpha, 1 star.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each pair's inverse FFT uses a balanced (four-step style) split N = N1*N2 with both factors near sqrt(N) and multiples of the SIMD width, so SIMD lanes run independent small transforms with broadcast twiddles and no in-register shuffles; the one corner turn is fused into stage A's store through a WxW register transpose. The data*conj(template) product is fused into stage A's loads (both banks are rearranged once at ingest into the layout stage A walks), and in peak-only mode the binned maximum is computed in registers inside stage B, so the correlation is never written to memory. Google Highway compiles the kernel once per SIMD target (AVX2, AVX-512, NEON) with runtime dispatch; the hierarchical mode correlates only a low-frequency band on a coarse lag grid and runs the full filter only for pairs above a calibrated coarse threshold.

**Use it when:**
- Template-bank searches (gravitational-wave style, radar/sonar, pulse detection) where many data segments are correlated against many templates and only the loudest lag per window is needed
- Power-of-two segment lengths from 64 to 1,048,576 (peak-only CPU) in complex64, where the 1.3x-3.4x gain of peak-only over FFTW's bare inverse FFT on the measured x86 hosts matters
- Searches where most pairs are noise and a calibrated false-dismissal budget is acceptable: hierarchical mode ran 3.95 ms vs 34.27 ms for flat peaks on a Ryzen 9 5950X at SNR 5.5, fd=1e-2
- Python pipelines that want the same API on CPU, Vulkan GPUs (Linux/Windows) and Metal (macOS)

**Skip it when:**
- General FFT work: there is no standalone transform API, only fused correlation of pre-transformed spectra
- When you need every lag on CPU: full-output mode was slower than FFTW's inverse-only time on the Core i5-13500H (56.24 vs 44.96 ms) and the Haswell node
- Float64 or non-power-of-two lengths: complex64 only, power-of-two sizes only
- Multithreaded single filters: CPU filtering uses one thread and parallelism is left to the caller
- Production use that needs a stable API or reviewed code: alpha (0.1.0a5 on PyPI, 0.1.0a6 in the tree), 1 star, single author; the 0.1.0a6 changelog fixes a stage-B intermediate indexing bug and an earlier fleet benchmark note says correctness for that revision was not yet established

**Integration:** module · NumPy (>=1.20); Google Highway (vendored git submodule, or HIGHWAY_ROOT); optional pyFFTW / mkl-fft for reference timings; GPU path needs a Vulkan or Metal driver (SPIR-V and Metal kernels ship in the wheel) · Python 3.10+, setuptools 77+, a C++17 compiler (manylinux_2_28 toolchain needed for Highway's AVX-512 targets); no Makefile or CMake, pip install is the only build · Wheels for Linux x86-64 and macOS arm64; Linux arm64 builds from source and runs in CI; x86 baseline SSE4.2 with runtime dispatch to AVX2/AVX3; SVE and RVV targets disabled; macOS x86-64 untested

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FFTW, PocketFFT or VkFFT when the workload is many-data x many-template correlation and you only need peaks, since the gain comes from fusing the product and never writing the correlation; FlashFFTConv is the analogous fused-FFT-convolution choice for PyTorch/H100 sequence models, not for detection searches.

**Gotchas:**
- Correlation is circular and the inverse is unnormalised (a perfect match returns n * energy); zero-pad for linear correlation and check the threshold's normalisation.
- Results reuse internal storage; copy them before the next call. Series execution consumes the data slots, so a later run() needs set_data() again.
- Hierarchical mode can drop detections by design, refuses to run without a covering calibration file (or an explicit band plus threshold with no guarantee), and can be slower than flat filtering when many pairs survive (Iris Xe: 23.01 ms vs 9.75 ms flat).
- CPU and GPU results can differ slightly and near-equal maxima can select different lags; full output for large banks is huge (2^22 x 128 x 512 is 2 TiB) and automatic allocation is capped at 512 MiB.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-09-30, 638 commits) but alpha with an unstable API and a single maintainer; MIT-licensed, installable from PyPI, and usable from C/C++ only by building the C sources and Highway yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/ahnitz/matchedfilter) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ahnitz/matchedfilter/blob/main/docs/measurements/teaser-fleet-20260928.md)

##### minfft  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Two-file C89 power-of-two FFT/DCT/DST library, about 2x KissFFT's speed; still slower than PocketFFT and FFTW.

**Beats:** KissFFT (the README also plots PocketFFT and FFTW with SSE2 for reference) — The author's gnuplot chart (benchFFT harness; per the README's test-environment section, removed in April 2024: GCC 13.2.1 -O2, one isolated core of an Intel Pentium Gold G5420 at 3.8 GHz, FFTW 3.3.10 with configure-chosen flags, KissFFT 1.3.1, PocketFFT 1.0) plots double-precision 1-D complex forward DFT Mflops for N = 2^1 to 2^20. Digitised, minfft runs 1.36x to 4.83x KissFFT (median about 1.96x), about 0.74x to 0.96x PocketFFT at most mid sizes, and 0.34x to 0.89x SSE2 FFTW (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Beats KissFFT 1.36-4.83x but is ~0.92x PocketFFT and ~0.56x FFTW (sse2) per its own SVG plot; no bench code, CPU or flags; stale (2025-08-11).

**Known shortcoming:** A README test-environment section removed in commit 82917dd gives benchFFT, GCC 13.2.1 -O2, Pentium Gold G5420 isolated core, FFTW 3.3.10, KissFFT 1.3.1, PocketFFT 1.0, but minfft's benchFFT harness code is unpublished; one aux object is not safe to share across threads.

**How:** The complex DFT is an explicitly recursive split-radix (2/4) decimation-in-frequency FFT with hand-unrolled leaves for N = 1, 2, 4 and 8 and a precomputed chain of twiddle factors stored in the aux object. Each level touches mostly adjacent memory, which the author credits for cache-friendliness. Real transforms and DCT/DST reduce to a half-length complex transform, and multi-dimensional transforms apply a strided 1-D routine along each axis through a temporary buffer. There is no explicit SIMD; the speed comes from fewer operations than KissFFT's mixed-radix code plus simple, compiler-friendly scalar loops.

**Use it when:**
- You want a small, dependency-free, MIT-licensed FFT you can vendor as two files (minfft.c/minfft.h) into C or C++, and power-of-two sizes are enough.
- Replacing KissFFT for power-of-two transforms: the author's plot shows minfft above KissFFT at every size from 2^1 to 2^20 (about 2x at N=1,024).
- You need DCT/DST types 2-4 or multi-dimensional real transforms with no FFTW dependency (FFTW is GPL or commercially licensed).
- Mixed C and Fortran 2003 codebases that want the same library from both languages.
- Accuracy matters: the accuracy plot puts its relative L2 error near FFTW's and PocketFFT's (about 2.9e-16 at N=2^20, about half of KissFFT's 5.8e-16; derived from page data).

**Skip it when:**
- Non-power-of-two lengths: every aux maker returns NULL unless N is a positive power of two.
- Peak throughput: the same plot has PocketFFT faster at 2^7 to 2^16 and 2^19 to 2^20, and SSE2 FFTW about 1.1x to 2.9x faster at every size; SIMD libraries (PFFFT, muFFT, KFR) or Notorious-FFT, which reports 1.08-1.13x over minfft, are faster.
- Sharing one plan across threads: the aux object holds a scratch buffer that every transform writes, even though the API takes a const pointer.
- Memory-tight settings: the README says it 'does not try to save memory'; a 1-D complex DFT aux takes 2N complex values, type-4 transforms 6N reals, and multi-dimensional transforms add a buffer as large as the input.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (libm only) · C89 (C99 complex used if <complex.h> is included first); Fortran 2003 for the Fortran module; the author's benchmark build used GCC 13.2.1 · any (portable scalar C, no SIMD or architecture-specific code)

**Vs siblings:** Choose minfft over KissFFT or meow_fft when your sizes are powers of two and you want DCT/DST types 2-4 and multi-dimensional support in a tiny C89 drop-in. Choose PocketFFT for arbitrary lengths or more speed, PFFFT/muFFT for SIMD speed, and Notorious-FFT if you want a slightly faster derivative.

**Gotchas:**
- Multi-dimensional inverse real DFT overwrites its input (README note), unlike the 1-D routines, which preserve input when run out of place.
- minfft_cmpl is C99 double complex only if `complex` is defined (i.e. <complex.h> was included before minfft.h); otherwise, including in C++, it is a double[2] array, binary-compatible with std::complex<double> but needing a cast.
- Dimensions for the 2-D/3-D aux makers are given in C (row-major) order; Fortran callers must pass them reversed.
- Transforms are unnormalized like FFTW (no 1/N factor anywhere in minfft.c); scale the inverse yourself.

**Status:** Stale: code is mature and recent commits (to August 2025) are documentation only; MIT-licensed, two source files, one closed MSVC build issue, easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/aimukhin/minfft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/aimukhin/minfft)

##### Ne10 (NEON FFT)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

ARM's NEON-optimized C library whose FFTs (float, Q31, Q15) beat FFmpeg's assembly FFT on an Android phone.

**Beats:** FFmpeg libavcodec FFT (assembly); also tricl_fft and CkFft — A single third-party post (issue #165, 2017) reports cycles for a 1024-point complex FFT on a Samsung Galaxy S6: Ne10 (asm) 10125 vs FFmpeg libavcodec (asm) 14375, about 1.42x faster (derived from page data), also ahead of tricl_fft and CkFft but behind SuperpoweredFFT (7375). The post gives no compiler, flags, Ne10 version, timing method or code, and does not define 'cycles'.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Cycles' unit undefined; the issue poster (lieff) does not claim to be SuperpoweredFFT's author (record fixed).

**Known shortcoming:** Open correctness issues without fix: #237 FFT returns all zeros with NDK r20 clang, #241 -Ofast breaks real FFTs at N>=4096, #218 a plan cannot be shared across threads, #233 NEON and C fixed-point results differ; root CMake aborts unless CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR matches ^arm (blocks native aarch64 builds); still only one benchmark (#165), no FFTW or KissFFT comparison.

**How:** It runs a mixed-radix Cooley-Tukey FFT (radix 2/3/4/5, with a combined radix-8 first stage) over twiddle and factor tables precomputed in the config. For sizes divisible by 4 the NEON path splits the transform into four interleaved sub-FFTs processed across NEON lanes, then finishes with a 'super twiddle' last stage. Power-of-two kernels exist as NEON intrinsics and, on ARMv7 builds, as hand-written NEON assembly (*.neon.s); the issue #165 figure is for that '(asm)' path.

**Use it when:**
- 32-bit ARMv7-A Android or Linux targets with NEON where you need a small, permissively licensed FFT; the hand-written assembly path is enabled only on ARMv7.
- Audio and DSP on phones and embedded Cortex-A: power-of-two complex or real FFTs (e.g. 256-4096 points) reusing one config per size.
- Fixed-point pipelines that need Q15 or Q31 FFTs with optional per-stage scaling (scaled_flag), which most float-only libraries lack.
- Projects that already use other Ne10 DSP blocks (FIR, IIR) and want one consistent ARM library.

**Skip it when:**
- x86 or any non-ARM target: CMake refuses non-ARM Linux builds, and there is no SSE/AVX code.
- Double precision, multi-dimensional or batched transforms: not provided (issues #243, #234 and #251 ask for doubles and 2-D).
- Arbitrary lengths: float C2C needs 2^a*3^b*5^c (NEON also needs N % 4 == 0 above 2), and the int32, int16 and real transforms are powers of two only; alloc returns NULL otherwise.
- If you need the fastest NEON FFT: the only head-to-head (issue #165) has SuperpoweredFFT about 1.37x faster than Ne10 at N=1024 (derived from page data), and there is no comparison against FFTW, KissFFT or PFFFT on the repo pages read here.
- Toolchain-sensitive builds: reports of all-zero output with NDK r20 clang (#237), broken r2c/c2r at N >= 4096 under -Ofast (#241) and AArch64 NDK/iOS build failures (#239, #252), with no maintainer fixes since 2018.

**Integration:** static lib · none (shared library optional via -DNE10_BUILD_SHARED=ON) · CMake; GCC with GNU assembler syntax (C built as gnu99, some FFT files are C++); Android NDK with API level >= 21 and GCC >= 4.8 for AArch64; iOS 7.0+ · ARMv7-A with NEON and AArch64 on Linux, Android and iOS; math and physics modules are ARMv7-only; no non-ARM support

**Vs siblings:** Pick Ne10 over SYLT-FFT when the target is a NEON-capable Cortex-A rather than a Cortex-M4. Pick it over PFFFT or PocketFFT when you need Q15/Q31 fixed-point FFTs or ARMv7 hand-tuned assembly; prefer those for portable or x86 code or maintained sources.

**Gotchas:**
- Call ne10_init() before using the generic names (ne10_fft_c2c_1d_float32 and so on); they are function pointers that ne10_init() binds to the NEON or C variant.
- Scaling: by default only the inverse transform is scaled by 1/N; the fixed-point variants take a scaled_flag; sizes below 15 silently fall back to the C path.
- The root CMakeLists.txt aborts unless CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR starts with 'arm', so native builds on hosts that report 'aarch64' hit that check; the GAS-syntax assembly is also awkward for clang outside the iOS toolchain file.
- NEON and C fixed-point Q31 results differ slightly (#233), and the R2C example comment in NE10_dsp.h is reported wrong (#267).

**Status:** Abandoned since 2018-11-15 (no releases or maintainer replies to the FFT bug reports read here, about 100 open issues) but BSD-3-Clause (ARM Limited), 1.5k stars and small enough to vendor; pin your toolchain and test outputs.

[repo](https://github.com/projectNe10/Ne10) · [benchmark](https://github.com/projectNe10/Ne10/issues/165)

##### OFFT  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Scalar, BSL-licensed C++11 mixed-radix FFT for arbitrary lengths; beats FFTW_ESTIMATE at some awkward sizes, loses elsewhere.

**Beats:** FFTW 3.3.5 (FFTW_ESTIMATE, with and without SIMD) and Intel oneMKL — First-party table (doc/OfftSpeedComparison.md, v0.3.0): MSYS2 GCC 12.2.0 on Windows 10, Intel i5-2450M (SSE4 only), against the official FFTW 3.3.5 Windows DLLs with FFTW_ESTIMATE (with and without SIMD) and oneMKL limited to 1 or 2 threads, in ns per n ln n. OFFT wins 10 of 30 non-power-of-two sizes against SIMD FFTW (best 16777217: 8.7 vs 12.3, 1.41x) and 12 of 30 against 1-core MKL, but loses at every power of two and ten; optimization flags are not stated, and the FFTW/MKL comparison harness is not in the repo (examples/benchmark links only OFFT).

**Known shortcoming:** Beats 1-core MKL at only 12 of 30 awkward sizes; optimization flags not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Not reproducible: the FFTW/MKL comparison code is not in the repo (examples/benchmark links only OFFT); forward transform uses the opposite sign to FFTW by default; Transform() is const but writes a shared scratch buffer, so concurrent calls on one object race.

**Independent measurement:** Beats scalar FFTW_ESTIMATE at 25 of 30 awkward sizes (derived from page data).

**How:** It runs an out-of-place, decimation-in-time mixed-radix Cooley-Tukey driver over code-generated straight-line kernels for factors up to 32. Primes 3-31 use Rader's algorithm with Winograd cyclic convolutions, composites such as 6, 10, 12 and 15 use the Good-Thomas prime-factor decomposition, and 8, 16 and 32 use split-radix. Larger prime factors go through a general Rader algorithm with an FFT-based cyclic convolution, so run time stays O(n log n) for any n, and twiddles are precomputed in compact storage. There is no SIMD; its wins come at lengths with large or awkward prime factors, where FFTW_ESTIMATE plans are weak.

**Use it when:**
- Complex FFTs at awkward lengths with large prime factors (e.g. 1025, 4097, 16385, 262145, 16777217) where you cannot afford FFTW_MEASURE planning: OFFT beat FFTW_ESTIMATE with SIMD at 10 of 30 such sizes on the author's machine.
- Projects that need a permissive (Boost Software License), dependency-free FFT and cannot ship FFTW under GPL or install Intel MKL.
- Portable scalar code for any C++11 platform, including targets without SSE/AVX, where FFTW's SIMD advantage disappears (OFFT beat scalar FFTW_ESTIMATE at 25 of 30 awkward sizes, derived from page data).
- Multi-dimensional or strided transforms on interleaved data such as stereo audio or RGB planes, with a choice of DFT sign and scaling convention.

**Skip it when:**
- Powers of two or ten: SIMD FFTW_ESTIMATE and 1-core MKL are about 1.4-4.2x faster on the author's table (derived from page data; 1024: 2.1 vs 0.5 ns per n ln n for both).
- Throughput on modern AVX/AVX-512 hardware: OFFT has no SIMD, and the benchmark machine was an SSE4-only laptop the author calls 'pretty ancient'; he expects the SIMD gap to be larger on newer CPUs.
- Real-valued signals, in-place transforms or split real/imaginary arrays: none have a public API yet (README known limitations).
- Sizes with a prime factor that does not fit in 32 bits fail, even on 64-bit targets.
- When you need a stable API or active maintenance: version 0.3.0 (June 2023), the API may change between minor versions, 3 stars, last commit 2024-05-12 (.clang-format only).

**Integration:** static lib · none · C++11 (target_compile_features cxx_std_11; GCC builds force -std=c++11), CMake 3.10; Visual Studio 2017 solution, VS2013 via toolset v120; benchmarked with MSYS2 GCC 12.2.0 · any (platform-independent scalar C++11; no SIMD paths)

**Vs siblings:** Pick OFFT over FFTW when GPL or MKL licensing is a blocker and your sizes are prime-heavy. For speed on regular sizes, prefer SIMD libraries such as PocketFFT (C++ branch), pocketfft-tuned or VectorFFT; OFFT has no head-to-head numbers against them.

**Gotchas:**
- The default convention FourierParameters{1,1} computes the forward transform with e^(+2 pi j ik/N), the opposite sign to FFTW's forward transform; pass offt::FourierParameters::FFTW ({1,-1}) to match FFTW. Inverse is scaled by 1/N by default.
- Source and destination must differ (no in-place); data must be std::complex<float/double>, interleaved.
- Thread-safety trap: the transform methods are const yet mutate internal scratch memory (see thread_safety); ReleaseTemp() frees it and the next call reallocates.
- The constructor throws (std::invalid_argument for a bad sign parameter; the element-count product throws on overflow), so wrap construction if your code is exception-free.

**Status:** Stale one-person project (v0.3.0 June 2023, last commit May 2024, 3 stars, CI self-test on GitHub Actions) under the Boost Software License; small enough to vendor, but treat the API as unstable.

[repo](https://github.com/christian-volmer/OFFT) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/christian-volmer/OFFT/HEAD/doc/OfftSpeedComparison.md)

##### PhastFT  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Safe-Rust, in-place, power-of-two FFT with low memory and optional threads; beats RustFFT at mid sizes and a scalar FFTW build.

**Beats:** FFTW 3.3.8 (via the Rust fftw crate); also RustFFT — Third-party astral4/fft-benchmark (M1 MacBook Pro, single thread, phastft 0.2.1, plan built inside every timed call for all libraries) shows PhastFT ahead of FFTW 3.3.8 at every size (e.g. f32 2^10 4.75 us vs 7.29 us, 2^23 109 ms vs 193 ms), but that FFTW was planned with FFTW_ESTIMATE on each call and built by the fftw crate's default 'source' feature, whose configure line has no --enable-neon. PhastFT's own steady-state criterion plots (Apple M2, plans reused) put FFTW_MEASURE at about 2.3x to 3.4x RustFFT's time for f32 2^15 to 2^24 with the same scalar FFTW build (PhastFT's dev-dependency is fftw 0.8.0 with default features), so no comparison against a SIMD-enabled FFTW exists.

**Known shortcoming:** astral4 benchmark builds a new FFTW_ESTIMATE plan inside every timed iteration, so FFTW's 'slower' result comes from planning cost; PhastFT's own benchmarks are first-party with numbers only as plot labels; repo moved to smu160/PhastFT; Rust.

**Known shortcoming:** In its own M2 plots PhastFT single-threaded is 1.01-1.19x slower than RustFFT from about 2^17 points up (#120); its FFTW baseline is the fftw crate's default build without NEON/AVX, so there is no comparison against a SIMD FFTW; the default 'parallel' feature makes it multi-threaded.

**How:** Radix-2 decimation-in-time Cooley-Tukey written recursively (cache-oblivious, switching to a loop once a block fits in L1), with a separate bit-reversal pass using the cache-optimal CO-BRAVO algorithm with SIMD. Working in place on split real/imaginary arrays cuts memory traffic and peak memory compared with out-of-place or self-sorting FFTs. SIMD kernels for SSE4.2, AVX2, NEON and WASM come from fearless_simd with runtime dispatch, and the default 'parallel' feature uses rayon for the recursive FFT and two threads for bit reversal on large inputs.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code doing power-of-two FFTs of 2^6 to 2^14 points single-threaded, where its own M2 plots show it 0.70x to 0.93x of RustFFT's time at most sizes.
- Very large power-of-two FFTs (megabytes to gigabytes) on a multi-core machine, using the parallel feature that the README headline plots measure.
- Memory-limited jobs: in astral4's run it allocated about 5x less than RustFFT (8.39 MB vs 41.94 MB at 2^20 f32), and the README claims up to 2x lower memory.
- Projects that forbid unsafe code (the crate uses #![forbid(unsafe_code)]) and want runtime SIMD selection without -C target-cpu=native.

**Skip it when:**
- Non-power-of-two lengths: the planner asserts is_power_of_two and panics; use RustFFT, PocketFFT or FFTW.
- Single-threaded large FFTs: in its own M2 plots PhastFT takes 1.01x to 1.19x RustFFT's time from about 2^17 points up, and astral4 shows RustFFT faster at f32 N>=2^22 and f64 N>=2^21 (issue #120 raises the same point).
- Tiny transforms (N=16, 32), where RustFFT's hand-written butterflies win.
- C or C++ code bases: no C ABI, so you would need your own FFI layer.
- When you need FFTW's multi-dimensional or arbitrary-stride interfaces; the README documents only 1-D transforms.

**Integration:** crate · num-traits, fearless_simd; rayon (default 'parallel' feature); num-complex and bytemuck with the optional 'complex-nums' feature · Rust 1.88 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, crate v0.4.1); the 2024 v0.2.1 used in astral4's benchmark needed nightly for portable SIMD · any Rust target; SIMD on x86-64 (SSE4.2, AVX2), aarch64 (NEON) and wasm, picked at runtime

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over RustFFT when lengths are powers of two and memory or multi-core throughput on huge transforms matters; stay with RustFFT for arbitrary lengths and tiny sizes. For C++ projects, PocketFFT (C++ branch) or PFFFT are the native-language siblings with similar 'no FFTW dependency' appeal.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'parallel' feature is on by default, so a plain dependency is multi-threaded; set default-features = false for single-threaded or deterministic-latency use.
- The inverse FFT scales by 1/N (IFFT(FFT(x)) == x), unlike FFTW and RustFFT, which leave output unnormalized.
- The interleaved Complex API allocates temporary buffers and is slower than the split real/imag API; the convenience fft_* functions build a new planner on every call.
- Issue #73 (open) reports intermittent slowdowns at the largest sizes on x86, suspected cache-associativity or TLB effects of power-of-two strides.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-07-31, v0.4.1), MIT OR Apache-2.0 and pure safe Rust, so it is easy to depend on from Rust but not callable from C++ without a wrapper.

[repo](https://github.com/smu160/PhastFT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/astral4/fft-benchmark)

##### pocketfft-tuned (benchmark-driven PocketFFT fork)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only PocketFFT fork with AVX float 1-D codelets: 2.4x upstream, 1.35x FFTW_ESTIMATE on 1-D c2c; loses to FFTW_MEASURE.

**Beats:** FFTW3 FFTW_ESTIMATE, upstream PocketFFT (ref 32424d2) and KissFFT; the fork is slower than FFTW_MEASURE and KFR — The author's randomized, CPU-pinned (taskset -c 2) Google Benchmark sweep ran 90 iterations per scenario in single precision. Makefile defaults: g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++20 for the SIMD build, clang++ with vectorization off and FFTW_NO_SIMD for the no-SIMD build, FFTW 3.3.10 built from source; CPU model not stated, workstation not quiet. Median 1-D c2c times: 2.40x faster than upstream PocketFFT 32424d2 and 1.35x faster than FFTW_ESTIMATE, but 0.71x of FFTW_MEASURE and 0.49x of KFR; 2-D/3-D were about even with upstream.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark-driven fork of PocketFFT (listed separately); kept as its own entry because its tuning and numbers are its own, but it may fold under PocketFFT.

**Known shortcoming:** Fork of PocketFFT; the new AVX codelets handle float only and the benchmarks are float only, so double and NEON users get essentially upstream code. README and header guard claim C++11 but the header uses if constexpr in 15 places (C++17 in practice). Flags are stated in the benchmarking-fft Makefile (corrected); CPU model still not stated.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It adds hand-written AVX intrinsics codelets for complex<float> radix-2/3/4/8 passes and for the real radf4/radb4 passes, some with AVX2/FMA variants. Upstream PocketFFT vectorizes only across lines of multi-D arrays, so its 1-D path is scalar. Power-of-two c2c plans also get fused radix-4x4 middle stages and blocked/batched terminal stages. Selected mixed-radix lengths get measured factorization and dispatch choices, and float prime lengths choose between Rader (computed internally in double) and Bluestein. A change was promoted only after paired randomized benchmark runs, pass-level probes and correctness checks.

**Use it when:**
- You already call PocketFFT (or vendor its header) for single-precision 1-D c2c/r2c/c2r on x86 with AVX and want a median 2.4-2.75x speedup without changing the API
- You cannot use GPL FFTW and your alternative is FFTW_ESTIMATE-quality planning: the fork beat FFTW_ESTIMATE in 813 of 1260 1-D c2c pairs (median 1.35x) and 447 of 450 2-D c2c pairs (median 6.43x)
- Real-input float transforms at awkward lengths such as 131071 or 315392 points, where it was the fastest of all tested libraries in the 2026-06-26 snapshot
- Float 3-D r2c in a BSD header-only package: median 1.13x over FFTW_MEASURE and 1.99x over KFR in the snapshot

**Skip it when:**
- You can use FFTW with FFTW_MEASURE/PATIENT plans, or KFR: they won most 1-D cases (fork median 0.71x and 0.49x on 1-D c2c), and FFTW_MEASURE was 6.06x faster at N=4096
- Double or long double, ARM/NEON, or x86 builds without AVX: the new codelets handle only float and need AVX, so these builds run almost entirely upstream code. They were not benchmarked, except for the scalar no-SIMD float build (1.12x to 1.67x over upstream)
- 2-D and 3-D workloads: medians against upstream PocketFFT are 0.98x to 1.04x, so the fork adds risk for no measured gain
- 1-D lengths below 4096: the sweep's smallest size was 4096, so nothing smaller was measured
- Code that needs a supported library: one author, 0 stars, no releases or tags, and the README calls the numbers a local snapshot from a noisy workstation

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond the C++ standard library and threads (multi-threading can be disabled with POCKETFFT_NO_MULTITHREADING) · C++17 in practice: the header's guard checks only for C++11 and the README still says 'strictly C++11', but the header uses if constexpr in 15 places. The benchmarks build it with g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++20. · Any C++ platform. The tuned 1-D SIMD paths need x86 AVX (some AVX2/FMA) and float; other targets fall back to upstream PocketFFT code paths.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over upstream PocketFFT (mreineck/pocketfft) when the hot path is 1-D float on AVX x86 and you want the same API; for multi-D or double precision upstream is equivalent and better tested. Pick FFTW (MEASURE planning), KFR or Admiral when raw 1-D speed matters more than a BSD header-only drop-in.

**Gotchas:**
- The published SIMD run also defined about 15 opt-in macros (POCKETFFT_TUNED_DEFINES in the benchmarking-fft Makefile, e.g. POCKETFFT_C2C_POWER2_FUSED_PASS4X4 and ..._SPLIT8_TILE256_CACHED_BUFFER). A plain #include does not get them, and by default they only engage at N >= 1,048,576 (some at 32M+). Copy those defines to reproduce the published configuration.
- Codelets are chosen at compile time from __AVX__/__AVX2__/__FMA__, with no runtime CPU dispatch: build with -mavx2 (or at least -mavx) or -march=native, or you get scalar 1-D code, and a binary built that way will not run on CPUs without AVX
- Plan caching is off unless POCKETFFT_CACHE_SIZE is set (the benchmarks use 16); without it every 1-D call re-plans, which hurts repeated small transforms
- With POCKETFFT_C2C_POWER2_SPLIT8_TILE256_CACHED_BUFFER, each cached plan keeps a length-N complex<float> scratch array alive (256 MiB at N=32M)

**Status:** Active single-author fork (226 commits, last 2026-06-27, 0 stars, no releases). BSD-3-Clause and header-only, so easy to vendor, but treat it as experimental until its changes reach upstream.

[repo](https://github.com/Dimandragon/pocketfft-tuned) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dimandragon/benchmarking-fft/main/results/full-machine-bench-2026-06-26-randomized-90iter/summary.md)

##### RustFFT  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust SIMD FFT for any length, including primes; beats a scalar, per-call-planned FFTW 3.3.8 at tiny and huge sizes.

**Beats:** FFTW 3.3.8 (via the Rust fftw crate v0.8.0, built from source by fftw-src without any SIMD configure flag, FFTW_ESTIMATE plan created inside each timed call) — In the third-party astral4/fft-benchmark on an M1 MacBook Pro (rustfft 6.2.0, single thread, divan medians), RustFFT beat FFTW 3.3.8 at N=8 to 32 (about 124 ns vs 1.4 us) and at large sizes (f32 2^20 12.49 ms vs 14.20 ms; 2^23 103.9 ms vs 193.3 ms), but lost at f32 N=1,024 to 16,384 and f64 N=1,024, 2,048 and 524,288. Both libraries planned inside every timed call, and FFTW was planned with FFTW_ESTIMATE and built by the fftw crate's default 'source' feature with no --enable-neon, so the result does not show RustFFT beating a SIMD, pre-planned FFTW; a 2020 Rust-forum post claiming RustFFT 5.0 AVX matched or beat FFTW at every size could only be seen as a search snippet (forum host egress-blocked).

**Known shortcoming:** astral4/fft-benchmark handicaps the FFTW baseline: fftw-src builds FFTW 3.3.8 without SIMD (no --enable-neon), plans with FFTW_ESTIMATE and times plan creation on every call; a 5-star suite, not well known. Losses understated: RustFFT is slower at f32 N=1024-16384 and f64 N=1024, 2048 and 524288, so 'fftw consistently slower' is wrong. Pure Rust, no C ABI.

**Known shortcoming:** No C API; a C++ FFI attempt hit double-free and segfaults (#148, no reply); Rader multiply-overflow panic on 32-bit/wasm (#163) fixed in 6.4.1.

**How:** The planner factors N and builds a recipe tree from Radix4/RadixN, MixedRadix (Cooley-Tukey), the Good-Thomas prime-factor algorithm, Rader's algorithm for primes and Bluestein's algorithm for primes with large factors, with hand-written butterflies for sizes 2 to 32. Each algorithm has AVX+FMA, SSE4.1, NEON (optional FCMA on ARMv8.3) and WASM SIMD versions, and the planner picks one by runtime CPU detection. Twiddles are precomputed at plan time and callers can reuse scratch buffers to avoid allocation.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code needing FFTs of arbitrary or prime lengths without a C dependency; sizes of the form 2^n * 3^m are fastest under AVX per the crate docs.
- Very small transforms (N = 8 to 32), where it ran about 124 ns vs FFTW's 1.4 us in astral4's plan-included M1 run.
- One-shot transforms where planning cost counts, e.g. a few FFTs of many different sizes.
- WebAssembly targets (wasm_simd feature) and AArch64 with NEON, where it ships native SIMD paths.
- Large single-threaded power-of-two FFTs (2^21 and up) on Apple Silicon, where it beat both PhastFT and the scalar FFTW build in astral4.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: there is no C ABI, and a user report of a hand-written FFI layer hitting double-free and segfaults (issue #148) is unanswered.
- Mid-size power-of-two FFTs (1K to 16K) on Apple M1: even a scalar FFTW_ESTIMATE build planned per call was faster there (e.g. f32 N=2048 11.74 us vs 22.87 us).
- Multi-threaded large transforms: no built-in threading is documented, while PhastFT's parallel feature and FFTW threads exist.
- Memory-tight huge FFTs: astral4 measured about 5x the allocations of PhastFT (335.5 MB vs 67.1 MB at 2^23 f32).
- Real-to-complex or multi-dimensional transforms: the crate exposes only 1-D complex FFTs (a 2-D example is still an open request, issue #146).

**Integration:** crate · num-complex, num-traits, num-integer, strength_reduce, transpose, primal-check · Rust 1.86 (crate v6.4.1); the fcma feature needs nightly · any Rust target; runtime-detected AVX+FMA or SSE4.1 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64, opt-in WASM SIMD; scalar fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over PhastFT when lengths are not powers of two, when transforms are tiny, or for single-threaded power-of-two sizes of 2^21 and up; pick PhastFT for lower memory and multi-core large FFTs. C++ users should look at PocketFFT (C++ branch), PFFFT or KFR instead, since RustFFT has no C interface.

**Gotchas:**
- Building an algorithm directly (e.g. Radix4::new) bypasses the planner and disables all AVX, SSE, NEON and WASM SIMD paths.
- process() allocates a scratch Vec on every call; use process_with_scratch with get_inplace_scratch_len() to avoid it (Bluestein sizes may need scratch larger than N).
- wasm_simd cannot be runtime-detected: with the feature on, runtimes without fixed-width SIMD trap.
- Before 6.4.1, Rader's algorithm could panic with multiply overflow on 32-bit and wasm targets at sizes around 3.6M points (issue #163, fixed in 6.4.1 by using u64).

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-29, v6.4.1, about 30M crates.io downloads), MIT OR Apache-2.0 with a no-breaking-changes policy, but usable from C++ only through your own FFI wrapper.

[repo](https://github.com/ejmahler/RustFFT) · [benchmark](https://github.com/astral4/fft-benchmark)

##### OTFFT (OK Ojisan's Template FFT)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

MIT double-precision Stockham FFT library for x86 (SSE2/AVX/AVX2) whose upstream author claims it beats FFTW at 2^1 to 2^24.

**Beats:** FFTW — Nothing measured was opened. The upstream homepage (egress-blocked here; seen only through a search snippet) reports OTFFT 11.6 faster than multi-threaded FFTW 3.3.10 at every power of two from 2^1 to 2^24 on a Surface Laptop 5 (10 cores/12 threads, WSL2 Ubuntu 22.04, GCC 11.4.0). The snippet gives two ratios, 81% of FFTW's time at 2^10 and 89% at 2^11. The upstream benchmark sources (fftbench with an FFTW3 wrapper) exist, but their FFTW planner flags were not seen.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: upstream homepage (wwwa.pikara.ne.jp) unreachable here; a search snippet says faster than FFTW for 2^1-2^24 (Surface Laptop 5, GCC 11.4.0, FFTW 3.3.10); needs a retier from a host that can reach it; abandoned (2022-08-17).

**Known shortcoming:** Fork is at OTFFT 11.5; upstream homepage blocked here. Search snippet: OTFFT 11.6 vs multi-threaded FFTW 3.3.10 on a Surface Laptop 5, GCC 11.4.0, 81% of FFTW's time at 2^10 and 89% at 2^11. fwd() scales by 1/N, unlike FFTW. CPUID probe runs xgetbv before checking OSXSAVE, so it can crash on CPUs/VMs without XSAVE. Abandoned since 2022.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It uses the self-sorting Stockham algorithm (no bit-reversal pass) in radix-4, -8 and -16 decimation-in-frequency and decimation-in-time variants, written as C++ templates over SSE2 (__m128d) and AVX/AVX2 (__m256d) complex arithmetic. Large power-of-two sizes use a six-step/eight-step (cache-blocked, transpose-based) algorithm, and other lengths use a mixed-radix kernel. A hard-coded table, copied from upstream's ffttune-generated setup, picks one of these seven kernels for each power of two up to 2^24. Above 2^15 points it runs OpenMP loops automatically unless built with DO_SINGLE_THREAD.

**Use it when:**
- Double-precision 1-D complex or real FFTs on x86-64 desktops and servers where an MIT license matters and FFTW's GPL does not fit
- Power-of-two lengths from 2 to 2^24, the range the upstream benchmark covers
- Windows (MSVC) or Linux (GCC/Clang) products that need one binary for SSE2, AVX and AVX2 machines: the fork builds all three back-ends and picks one at run time with CPUID
- Applications that also need DCT-II or arbitrary-length (Bluestein) transforms from the same small library

**Skip it when:**
- When you need a verified win over FFTW: no repository has numbers, and the only comparison is the upstream homepage (search snippet, not opened: OTFFT 11.6 vs FFTW 3.3.10 multi-threaded on a Surface Laptop 5 under WSL2, GCC 11.4.0, OTFFT taking 81% of FFTW's time at 2^10 and 89% at 2^11; FFTW planner flags unknown). This fork is at 11.5, not 11.6
- Single precision, 2-D/3-D transforms, batched/strided (guru-style) plans, or wisdom: none exist
- ARM, Apple Silicon or other non-x86 targets: kernels are SSE2/AVX intrinsics and dispatch uses x86 cpuid/xgetbv inline assembly; kfrlib/fft-benchmark lists it as x86 only
- AVX-512 machines expecting 512-bit kernels: the build only compiles SSE2, AVX and AVX2 back-ends
- Projects that need upkeep: the fork's last commit is 2022-08-17, and the kernel-selection table was tuned on the upstream author's machine with no ffttune tool in the fork to retune it

**Integration:** static lib · OpenMP (find_package(OpenMP REQUIRED) in the standalone build); Boost.Test only for the unit tests · C++11; CMake 3.0+; GCC, Clang, Intel C++ or MSVC (CI badges: Ubuntu 14.04 and 20.04, VS2013; a 2018 commit fixed the VS2017 build) · x86 only; x86-64 gets SSE2, AVX and AVX2 back-ends chosen at run time by CPUID, 32-bit x86 builds only the SSE2 back-end

**Vs siblings:** Choose OTFFT over PocketFFT or PFFFT only if you want x86 double-precision 1-D transforms with run-time AVX2/AVX/SSE2 dispatch under MIT and accept an unmaintained codebase; PocketFFT (N-D, any length, any arch) and KFR or VectorFFT (published wins over FFTW/MKL) are the better-documented choices.

**Gotchas:**
- fwd() divides by N (forward normalization), unlike FFTW's unnormalized forward transform; use fwd0() for FFTW-style scaling. inv() is unnormalized, and the real inverse transforms destroy their input
- The factory comment says complex, real and DCT lengths must be even (up to 2^30); only the Bluestein transform takes any length (up to 2^28). Non-power-of-two and above-2^24 lengths fall through to the mixed-radix kernel
- Internal OpenMP parallelism above 2^15 points can oversubscribe cores when the caller already runs FFTs on several threads; define DO_SINGLE_THREAD to turn it off
- The README examples (OTFFT::FFT fft(N), OTFFT::FFT0) do not match the public header, which only exports the Factory functions. The CPUID probe also runs xgetbv before checking the OSXSAVE bit, so it can fault with an invalid-instruction error on CPUs or VMs without XSAVE

**Status:** Abandoned: the fork has 38 commits, the last a 2022-08-17 upstream sync to 11.5, and no open issues. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as a CMake static library, with unit tests and a GitHub Actions build.

[repo](https://github.com/DEWETRON/otfft)

##### SpFFT (sparse-input 3D FFT)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier D`

3D FFT layer for sparse (spherical-cutoff) frequency data that skips empty columns before calling FFTW/MKL/cuFFT/rocFFT; no published speedup.

**Beats:** FFTW / MKL and cuFFT / rocFFT dense 3D FFT (implied; no comparison is published; SpFFT itself calls these libraries for its 1D/2D sub-transforms) — Nothing measured: the repository, its docs and its benchmark program make no speed claim and contain no comparison against FFTW, MKL, cuFFT or rocFFT. The only third-party numbers found (cuSpFFT README, RTX 4090, single precision, 2D full-output use) show SpFFT slower than dense cuFFT, which is outside SpFFT's sparse 3D design point.

**Known shortcoming:** No speed claim at all; it wraps FFTW/cuFFT. Kept as a required SIRIUS dependency. Post-v1.1.1 fix #65 (array size mismatch for local transforms) not yet released.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo makes no speed claim; pruning covers the z-FFT over occupied columns and the y-FFT for occupied x only, while the GPU path runs a full 2D xy. The third-party cuSpFFT README (RTX 4090, single precision, 2D full output, off-design) puts SpFFT at 0.74x/0.41x/0.17x of dense cuFFT with 1.3-2.3x memory and OOM at 52,329^2. Issue #51: wrong results with 2 OpenMPI ranks (closed Jan 2022); ROCm Release builds carried debug syncs until 1.1.0; the post-v1.1.1 array fix (PR #65) is unreleased.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Pruned 3D FFT by dimension: on the host it runs the batched 1D z-transforms only over the z-columns that hold data (decompress, z-FFT, transpose), then the y-transforms only for x indices that own a column (Transform1DVerticalHost with uniqueXIndices), and full x-transforms last, so zero columns and empty y-lines are never touched. For R2C/C2R it exploits Hermitian symmetry so only half the columns (plus the non-redundant half of the x=0 plane) are needed. The z-to-xy redistribution is an MPI all-to-all (Alltoall, Alltoallv or Alltoallw variants, optionally exchanging doubles as floats to halve traffic), and Grid buffers are reused across transforms; all 1D/2D kernels are FFTW, MKL, ARMPL, NVPL, cuFFT or rocFFT plans, not SpFFT's own.

**Use it when:**
- Plane-wave DFT or similar codes where frequency data is a sphere inside a cube, so most z-columns are empty (this is what SIRIUS, and through it Quantum ESPRESSO and CP2K, use it for).
- Repeated transforms of the same sparsity pattern, where the cost of building the Grid/Transform (FFTW planning, index setup) is amortized over many calls.
- MPI-distributed 3D grids that already use z-column ownership per rank, on CPU or on NVIDIA (CUDA 11+) or AMD (ROCm 5+) GPUs, with optional GPU-aware MPI.
- Codes that need one interface for host and GPU execution and C/Fortran bindings.

**Skip it when:**
- Dense frequency data or 2D problems: there is nothing to prune, and a third-party test (cuSpFFT course project, RTX 4090, single precision, full R2C output set) measured SpFFT at 0.74x, 0.41x and 0.17x the speed of plain dense cuFFT with 1.3-2.3x more device memory; it ran out of memory on a 52,329^2 case.
- When you need evidence of a speedup: the repo publishes no timings against FFTW, MKL or cuFFT, and tests/programs/benchmark.cpp times only SpFFT itself.
- Sparsity in the space domain (sparse inputs to a forward transform) or arbitrary non-column patterns: only frequency-side sparsity grouped into complete z-columns is supported.
- 1D FFTs, non-uniform FFTs, or sizes with large prime factors: it only does 3D transforms and inherits the backend's speed on sizes not of the form 2^a 3^b 5^c 7^d.
- Projects that need a multi-GPU single transform: each Grid/Transform is tied to one GPU.

**Integration:** shared lib (static with SPFFT_STATIC=ON); CMake build, conda-forge package · a library with the FFTW 3.x interface (FFTW3, Intel MKL, ARM Performance Libraries or NVPL); optional MPI, OpenMP, CUDA 11+ (cuFFT) or ROCm 5+ (rocFFT/hipFFT) · C++17; GCC 7+, Clang 5+ or ICC 19+; CMake 3.18 (3.21 for ROCm) · Linux HPC targets: x86-64 and Arm CPUs, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs; other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick SpFFT over heFFTe (dense distributed 3D FFT) when your frequency data is a plane-wave cutoff sphere and you want the empty columns skipped for you. cuSpFFT solves a different problem (binary-sparse 2D inputs on one GPU) and beat SpFFT only in an off-design test where SpFFT was given a full output set.

**Gotchas:**
- Index layout rules: all elements of one z-column must be on the same rank, R2C inputs need x in [0, n/2], and the docs say the order and rank distribution of z-columns strongly affects speed (continuous in y for host, in x for GPU).
- Normalization is only applied on forward transforms (1/(Nx*Ny*Nz)); backward is never scaled.
- Bug history in released versions: wrong results with 2 OpenMPI ranks (issue #51, labelled Bug/Wrong Results, closed January 2022), ROCm Release builds left debug device_synchronize() on (fixed in 1.1.0), C/Fortran multi-transform segfault (fixed in 1.1.1), and an array size mismatch for local transforms fixed in PR #65 (2025-07-25) after the last release v1.1.1.
- Creating Grids/Transforms inside an OpenMP parallel region crashed in FFTW planning (issue #32); create them outside the region.

**Status:** Stale but maintained at a low rate: last release v1.1.1 (2025-01-19) and last commit 2025-07-25; BSD-3-Clause, packaged on conda-forge and a required dependency of SIRIUS, so it is exercised in production electronic-structure codes.

[repo](https://github.com/eth-cscs/SpFFT)

##### tinyfft  `C`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Two tiny C files for power-of-two complex FFT and real convolution; author says the AVX version beats FFTW_MEASURE at 2^17-2^20.

**Beats:** FFTW3 (FFTW_MEASURE planner) — There is only one claim, a single README sentence with no numbers: the AVX variant is 'faster than FFTW3 with FFTW_MEASURE' for lengths 2^17 to 2^20 and slower for all other lengths. No benchmark program, CPU, compiler version or FFTW version is published, and the comparison skips the bit-reversal permutation that FFTW performs.

**Known shortcoming:** Verifier rejected as not notable at tier D: README speed claim with no numbers and no benchmark code.

**Known shortcoming:** Output stays bit-reversed, so it is not like-for-like with FFTW. 15 stars; README claim has no numbers.
