- Large-k nearest-neighbour queries: nearest_neighbors(k) reruns a full single-nearest search k times while excluding already-picked IDs, so cost grows with k
- Polygons or exact geometry predicates: only points and axis-aligned boxes are indexed; use Shapely STRtree or GEOS for geometry-level tests

**Integration:** module · none at runtime (NumPy optional, for the *_np methods); Rust build dependencies: pyo3 0.28 (abi3-py39), numpy 0.28, smallvec, wincode, num-traits · Python 3.9+ (CPython, abi3 wheels); building from source needs Rust 1.89+ and maturin · Prebuilt wheels for Linux x86_64/aarch64/armv7l (manylinux_2_28), macOS x86_64/arm64, Windows amd64, Pyodide wasm32; no SIMD-specific code

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings are C++/Rust/JS libraries (nanoflann, PH-tree, KDBush, RBush, geo-index), none callable from Python as a drop-in; pick fastquadtree when you are in Python and need a mutable point/box index with NumPy I/O. Pick geo-index or a C++ kd-tree such as nanoflann for static data in compiled code.

**Gotchas:**
- The default dtype is f32, so large projected or geographic coordinates lose precision; pass dtype='f64' when you need it
- With dtype i32 or i64, squared distances in nearest-neighbour search are computed in the coordinate type itself. The release profile does not enable overflow checks, so i32 trees should return wrong neighbours once distances exceed about 46,340 units (from reading geom.rs and Cargo.toml, not tested)
- insert_many raises TypeError on NumPy input, so you must call insert_many_np explicitly. Containment is half-open (min inclusive, max exclusive), so points exactly on the max edge of the root bounds are rejected
- Serialized blobs are version-sensitive: data written by bincode-based releases (v2.2 and earlier) cannot be loaded by current wincode-based ones, and from_bytes enforces a 64 MiB preallocation limit unless you raise it

**Status:** Active single-maintainer project (v2.4.2 on PyPI 2026-06-22, 303 commits, 33 stars, 7 issues all closed), MIT-licensed, with 100% test coverage claimed; usable from Python only.

[repo](https://github.com/Elan456/fastquadtree) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Elan456/fastquadtree/blob/main/docs/benchmark.md)

##### geo-index (packed immutable R-tree and k-d tree)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Packed, immutable 2D R-tree and k-d tree crate (Rust port of flatbush/kdbush); builds about 2x faster than rstar bulk_load.

**Beats:** rstar (georust dynamic R-tree, bulk_load) — One first-party Criterion run (benches/rtree.rs) on a single bundled box dataset (benches/bounds.raw) shows Hilbert-packed construction at 80.9 ms vs 159.3 ms for rstar bulk_load (1.97x, derived from page data) and one fixed bounding-box query at 116.4 us vs 153.6 us (1.32x, derived from page data); CPU, rustc version and build profile are not stated. The rstar build closure also clones its input Vec inside the timed loop, and per GitHub's blame view the README timings date from a 2023 'Quick bench' commit, so they predate the v0.3.2 search optimization and do not name the rstar version used.

**Known shortcoming:** One query only; the rstar timed loop includes a Vec clone; Rust port of the flatbush/kdbush layout.

**Known shortcoming:** README bench numbers come from a 2023 'Quick bench' commit, before the v0.3.2 search optimization; rstar version then unstated. RTreeIndex::neighbors compares squared distance to an unsquared max_distance (flatbush squares it). README says safe Rust but search uses unsafe get_unchecked. Open #148: KDTree within loses precision for tiny values. Rust; no C ABI.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Construction is a bulk pack: item centers are mapped onto a 65,536 x 65,536 grid and sorted by Hilbert curve value (the threadlocalmutex bit-twiddling Hilbert function), or by sort-tile-recursive, and then parent boxes are computed bottom-up so every node is full except the last on each level. Sorting only has to order whole node-sized blocks (k_block_sort_by with select_nth_unstable_by), not the full array. Boxes and indices sit in flat contiguous arrays, so search is a breadth-first scan of 4-value box runs with no pointer chasing; the search loop skips bounds checks with get_unchecked, which a code comment credits with up to 30%. The optional rayon feature parallelizes the STR y-sort (STR construction 116.5 ms to 72.1 ms in the README).

**Use it when:**
- Static 2D box or point sets (map features, tile footprints, GeoArrow geometries) built once and queried many times from Rust or Python
- Bulk construction is on the critical path: the README run builds a Hilbert-packed tree in 80.9 ms vs 159.3 ms for rstar::RTree::bulk_load on the same boxes
- You need to persist an index or pass it across an FFI/process boundary without serialization: the single-buffer flatbush layout reopens zero-copy and is readable by flatbush/kdbush in JS
- Memory must be predictable: RTreeMetadata gives the exact byte size for a given item count and node size before you build
- Nearest-neighbor ranking with your own metric (Manhattan, spherical with valid bounds) via neighbors_with_callbacks, without pulling in the geo crate

**Skip it when:**
- Data that changes after build: there is no insert or delete, so every update means a full rebuild; rstar supports dynamic updates
- 3D or higher-dimensional data: only two dimensions are indexed
- Coordinates outside i8/u8/i16/u16/i32/u32/f32/f64 (no u64/i64), or data containing NaN, which the docs say may panic
- You want the tree to hold and return your objects: queries return insertion indexes and you keep the collection yourself
- You need k-nearest queries on the k-d tree: KDTree offers range and within (radius) only; kNN for the k-d tree is an open issue (#97)

**Integration:** crate · bytemuck, float_next_after, geo-traits 0.3, num-traits, thiserror, tinyvec; optional rayon (parallel STR sort) and geo 0.31 (use-geo_0_31 feature for geometry distance APIs) · Rust 1.75 (rust-version in Cargo.toml), edition 2021 · any platform Rust targets; no SIMD or architecture-specific code seen. Python bindings published on PyPI as geoindex-rs

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over KDBush or RBush when you are in Rust or Python rather than JavaScript but still want the flatbush/kdbush buffer format, and it adds a box R-tree that KDBush lacks. Pick GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or ArborX instead for 3D+ data or C++ code, and tidwall/rtree.c or Boost R*-tree when the data must be updated in place.

**Gotchas:**
- RTreeIndex::neighbors(x, y, max_results, max_distance) ranks by squared Euclidean distance and compares that against max_distance without squaring it (upstream flatbush squares maxDistance), so pass the squared radius there; neighbors_with_distance with EuclideanDistance takes a plain radius
- RTreeBuilder::new takes the exact item count up front and finish() asserts that exactly that many boxes were added
- The README calls it safe Rust, but the hot search loop uses unsafe get_unchecked, and RTreeRef::new_unchecked skips buffer validation; use try_new for untrusted buffers
- Open issue #148: KDTree::within uses x^2 + y^2 <= r^2, which loses precision for extremely small coordinates and radii (e.g. 1e-308)

**Status:** Active (v0.4.0 released 2026-09-09, last commit 2026-09-15, now under the georust org), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed and published on crates.io and PyPI, with recent fixes for stack overflows, empty-tree panics and kNN distance bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/georust/geo-index) · [benchmark](https://github.com/georust/geo-index)

##### GeoRepair (geo-repair)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust crate (with a C API) for OGC validity checks and ST_MakeValid-style repair; faster than GEOS on most invalid-input classes.

**Beats:** GEOS 3.14.1 (conda-forge libgeos, MSVC build) makeValid / UnaryUnion — First-party runs on an Intel i5-12400F under Windows 10 (Rust release profile with fat LTO, mimalloc, 12-thread Rayon batch; rustc version not stated) against conda-forge GEOS 3.14.1, MSVC build, serial per call but driven concurrently from Rayon in the same process. Validation of 1.58M production polygons was 1.4x faster than GEOS and the full repair pass was 0.83x. Synthetic rows range from 0.05x to over 9,000x, and BENCHMARKS.md counts 73 wins in 91 cases. The production dataset is not public.

**Known shortcoming:** No rustc version; the 1.58M-polygon GeoPackage is gitignored, so the real-world rows are not reproducible; README overlap/dense-grid 183-318x contradicts BENCHMARKS.md 4-14x, which calls ~200x a WKT round-trip artifact; the latest commit fixes repair output that shipped with crossings; Rust.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust crate; callable from C++ only through the ffi feature (include/geo_repair.h). Three docs give three different real-world speedups (README 1.4x, BENCHMARKS.md 1.40x on other timings, lib.rs 1.16x). Experimental 0.x; default features install mimalloc as the global allocator. Correctness fixes for shipped invalid output on 2026-09-26 and 09-27; nightly fuzzing keeps finding contract breaches. Described as a rewritten GEOS/JTS repair module with undocumented provenance (GEOS is LGPL).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The default Structure strategy follows GEOS makeValid's shape (planar graph extraction, face walking, winding-number assembly), but puts a cheap fast-path gate first: a fused duplicate/basic-form/envelope scan, a monotone-chain plus grid self-intersection test, and fast floating-point orientation that escalates to Shewchuk exact predicates only inside a 32-ulp collinear band. Inputs that pass the gate skip noding entirely. Noding uses a radix-sorted sweep and an R-tree (brute force only up to 128 edges). A CDT-based Arrange strategy (spade) is the fallback. Batches run in parallel over Rayon with mimalloc as the global allocator.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk cleaning of messy GIS polygons before overlay or loading into PostGIS/GeoPackage, where many inputs are invalid (bowties, collapsed rings, star or spoke shapes, overlapping MultiPolygon parts): the author measures 5-25x on bowtie/collapsed rows and hundreds of times on spoke and star-burst rows.
- Repairing self-intersecting linework (zigzag, dense self-overlap, spiral): 10-120x against GEOS UnaryUnion in the author's tables.
- Rust pipelines on geo/geoarrow/wkb data that need a validity gate without linking GEOS, including no_std and WASM builds.
- Validation-only passes over large mostly-valid datasets, where it measured about 1.4x GEOS (2.1 s vs 3.0 s on 1.58M polygons, 12 threads).

**Skip it when:**
- Mostly valid, large polygons or linestrings: GEOS is faster on valid polygons of 100 vertices or more (down to 0.31-0.37x at 10,000 vertices) and on valid linestrings of 10-500 vertices.
- Full validate-and-repair passes on mostly valid data: GEOS was faster on the 1.58M-polygon real-world full pass (3.0 s vs 3.6 s).
- Dense random-walk 'spaghetti' rings, self-intersecting linestrings of 100+ vertices and large-coordinate (1e12) rings, where GEOS wins by 1.5x to 20x in the README table.
- You need exact GEOS isValid parity: the eps-class tolerance (1e-12 x ring scale) rejects 213 GEOS-valid XML-suite cases, mostly orientation, and repair returns an empty GeometryCollection when it cannot certify the output.
- You want a stable dependency: the crate is labelled experimental, 0.x with breaking changes expected, 1 star, and correctness fixes for shipped invalid output landed as recently as 2026-09-27.

**Integration:** crate (also cdylib/staticlib with a C header via the ffi feature, and a PyPI wheel) · geo 0.33, robust, spade (CDT), rstar, rayon, mimalloc (default, C allocator), rusqlite with bundled SQLite (default io-gpkg feature), plus smaller crates; GEOS only for the opt-in benchmarks · Rust 1.88 (edition 2024); simd-portable needs nightly · x86-64 and aarch64 on Windows/Linux/macOS; WASM32 and no_std without parallelism or file I/O

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings does validity repair: TG speeds up GEOS predicates (intersects, point-in-polygon) and qdgeo speeds up GEOS overlay and buffer, but both assume valid input. Use GeoRepair as the cleaning step in front of them, or in place of GEOS makeValid when the batch has many invalid shapes.

**Gotchas:**
- The default features install mimalloc as the process-wide #[global_allocator] and pull in bundled SQLite; turn off default features if you embed it in a larger Rust binary or need the proj feature (sqlite3 link conflict).
- The README, docs/BENCHMARKS.md and the crate docs give different numbers for the same rows (for example overlap mp 186-318x in the README vs 6.85-10.34x in BENCHMARKS.md, which calls ~200x figures a WKT round-trip artifact; lib.rs still says 1.16x on the real-world set).
- The spade-based Arrange (CDT) path may panic on degenerate input (all-collinear exterior rings, coordinates near f64::MAX); the release profile keeps panic=unwind so panics are caught and the C API reports them as an error code.
- GeometryCollection cross-component intersections and Z/M consistency are not validated; Cargo's description calls the crate a 'rewritten GEOS/JTS repair module', and the provenance of any ported logic is not documented.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-09-27, nightly fuzzing that keeps finding contract breaches), Apache-2.0, but 1 star and self-described as experimental with breaking 0.x releases.

[repo](https://github.com/Wolren/GeoRepair) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Wolren/GeoRepair/blob/HEAD/docs/BENCHMARKS.md)

##### GeoToolbox KdBoxTree  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Static C++17 k-d tree that indexes boxes as well as points; out-queries Boost.Geometry's R*-tree on bulk-loaded data.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree (also GEOS 3.14.1 STR-tree, nanoflann 1.10.1, tidwall rtree.c) — The author's own harness compares KdBoxTree with Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree, nanoflann 1.10.1, GEOS 3.14.1 STR-tree and tidwall rtree.c on synthetic and real 2D/3D point and box sets of 10^2-10^6 elements. It was built with MSVC 2026 and Clang 22 on an ASUS ROG Strix G16 laptop under Windows 11 (CPU model not stated; the repo's CMake sets /arch:AVX2 plus /GL /LTCG on MSVC and -msse4.2 -flto on Clang). The README reports rankings, not a KdBoxTree-vs-Boost ratio: KdBoxTree builds fastest and wins range queries and box kNN, and Boost 'lags behind in query performance'; raw TSVs are in ikolev21/ikolev21.github.io.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party only; README gives no CPU model, flags or explicit ratio against Boost; 0 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** Tested only on Windows, no releases; index has no insert or erase; published results used StoreSpatialKeys=true while the template defaults to false. Flags are in CMakeLists (/arch:AVX2 /GL /LTCG on MSVC, -msse4.2 -flto otherwise); CPU still unstated.

**How:** It is a k-d tree built top-down by midpoint splits on the longest axis of each node's bounding box, with in-place partitioning of a flat element array and nodes kept in one contiguous vector (leaf size 32 by default). Boxes that straddle a split plane go into a third 'middle' child, which is then split only on the other axes, so a box index keeps cheap k-d descent instead of the overlapping MBRs an R-tree has. Each node stores the tight bound of its elements, so a query can return a whole subtree without per-element tests once the window contains the node. An optional StoreSpatialKeys template flag keeps a contiguous copy of the keys so scans need no pointer chasing (about 1.2x faster at the largest sizes, for more memory).

**Use it when:**
- Bulk-loaded static point or box sets (10^3 to 10^6 elements) queried many times: the README measures it as the fastest index to bulk-load and pays back its build cost within about 100 queries versus a linear scan
- Range/window queries on 2D or 3D box keys (GIS footprints, parcels, mesh triangle bounds), where it ranks first on average ahead of Boost R*-tree, GEOS and tidwall
- k-nearest queries on box keys: Boost R*-tree is the only other index in the comparison that supports them, and KdBoxTree is faster
- Point range queries from 10^4 elements upward, or point kNN at 10^6 elements and on strongly structured data, where it passes nanoflann
- Code that needs float or double keys, more than 2 dimensions, and a custom allocator (the template takes a TElementAllocator)

**Skip it when:**
- Data that changes: there is no insert or erase. Use Boost R*-tree or tidwall rtree.c for dynamic sets
- Point kNN below about 10^5 elements, or a minimal memory footprint: nanoflann wins both
- 2D box range queries on Polygon-like (ring-shaped) data, where GEOS STR-tree is faster, or 2D boxes around 10^4-10^5 elements, where tidwall is
- Fewer than about 100 queries on about 100 elements: the README says an index tops out at 1.2-2x over a plain std::vector scan at that size
- Production use where maturity matters: 0 stars, no releases or tags, a single author, and the README says it is tested only on Windows

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the index itself: KdBoxTree.hpp plus GeoToolbox's own GeometryTools/Span/SpatialTools headers and the standard library. Eigen is optional; Catch2, Shapelib and LodePNG are only for the tests and benchmarks · C++17; tested with MSVC 2026 and Clang 22 on Windows · Tested only on Windows x64 (README). The core code is plain portable C++, but the repo's CMake adds /arch:AVX2 (MSVC) or -msse4.2 (other compilers), so on non-x86 targets you build the header yourself

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over nanoflann when the keys are boxes, or when you have points at 10^6 scale or need range queries above 10^4 elements. Pick it over tidwall rtree.c when the data is static and large or unevenly spread and you need kNN or runtime-chosen dimensions/scalar types. tidwall, and Boost R*-tree for its versatility, remain the choice for dynamic data, and TG is for polygon predicates rather than indexing.

**Gotchas:**
- IndexType is int, so one tree holds fewer than 2^31 elements
- The constructor takes the element vector by value and reorders it during the build. Queries hand back elements by reference or as indices into the tree's own reordered copy, not into your original vector
- StoreSpatialKeys defaults to false, but the published benchmark results were measured with it on. Turning it on raises memory on box keys slightly above Boost R*-tree
- Splits are at the box midpoint, not the median. Coincident points or rounding make a split fail, which leaves that node an oversized leaf; heavily duplicated keys can therefore produce large leaves

**Status:** Active single-author project (last commit 2026-09-06, no releases, 0 stars) under BSL-1.0; the index is one roughly 1,300-line header plus a few helper headers, so vendoring it is straightforward.

[repo](https://github.com/ikolev21/GeoToolbox) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ikolev21/GeoToolbox)

##### Indexicon R-tree  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-header C++17 dynamic N-D R*-tree for points or boxes; matches or beats Boost.Geometry's R-tree, by up to about 35%.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry R-tree (boost::geometry::index::rtree) — Two first-party README charts compare Indexicon's R-tree with Boost.Geometry's R-tree on six real datasets (MARINE, MIAMI, OSM, TAXIS, TIGER, TORONTO; 3.5M-112.8M points or boxes, 2D and 3D) at node capacities 32-512. Indexicon is at or below Boost at every plotted point: insertion is about 20% lower at capacity 512 (MARINE about 25 s vs 31.8 s) and range queries about 34% lower at capacity 32 (MARINE about 280 ms vs 425 ms), all values read off the images (derived from page data). Neither the Boost balancing algorithm (linear, quadratic or rstar), compiler flags, CPU nor the query workload is stated, and the Boost harness is not in the repo; the companion arXiv paper 2606.04676 (same authors) could not be opened from this environment.

**Known shortcoming:** Boost harness not in the repo; paper (arXiv 2606.04676) unreadable here; gains 10-35% with several configs at parity.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bugs: RTree has no copy/move handling, so copying double-frees; knnQuery with k=0 calls front() on an empty vector (UB); kNN results come back unsorted. Headers put using namespace std and RTree/RPoint/RBox at global scope, so point and box headers cannot share one translation unit. R-tree reuses Boost rstar defaults and pack_create packing (reimplementation). Boost variant, hardware, flags and query workload unstated; no harness; issue #1 on nanoflann fairness closed without reply.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The R-tree follows the same design and defaults as Boost's rstar<MaxElements> parameters (min elements and forced-reinsert count 0.3 x capacity, overlap-cost threshold 32), and its bulk load is the same top-down packing scheme as Boost's pack_create (median counts by subtree size, nth_element along the longest edge of a hint box). The differences are in the layout and hot paths. Leaf and internal capacities are separate template parameters, and nodes keep entries in fixed inline arrays. The point tree stores raw points in leaves rather than degenerate boxes. R* splits score every split position with prefix/suffix bounding boxes in one pass per axis. A range query emits a whole subtree without per-entry tests when the query window contains the child's box.

**Use it when:**
- Dynamic in-memory workloads mixing bulk load, inserts, deletes, range and kNN queries over tens of millions of 2D or 3D points or boxes, which is what the README charts measure (3.5M to 112.8M records)
- You already use Boost's R*-tree and want the same algorithm with about 10-20% less insertion time at large capacities (256-512) and about 15-35% less range-query time at small capacities, without a Boost dependency
- Projects that want a single dependency-free header and compile-time dimension, coordinate type and node capacities, including more than 3 dimensions
- Research or teaching code that compares several index families (R-tree, quad-tree, MX-CIF, oct-tree, KD-tree) behind one API

**Skip it when:**
- You need Boost's query language (intersects/within/covered_by/nearest predicates and their combinations), query iterators, or adapting your own geometry types
- Static data queried far more than it changes: packed static indexes such as GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or a Hilbert-packed R-tree avoid insert machinery entirely
- Production code that needs maturity: 17 commits, a repo created in May 2026, no tests beyond usage examples, and no published benchmark harness
- Insertion-heavy workloads where the gap matters: the gain over Boost is small (parity at capacities 32-64 on OSM and MIAMI), while PH-tree reports about 5x faster inserts than Boost

**Integration:** header-only · none (C++ standard library only) · C++17 (the examples build with g++ -std=c++17 -O2/-O3) · any platform with a C++17 compiler; no SIMD or OS-specific code in the R-tree headers

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over PH-tree or tidwall/rtree.c when you want a classic R*-tree that behaves like Boost's (same parameters and packing) in arbitrary dimensions, as one dependency-free header. Pick PH-tree for much larger insert gains, tidwall/rtree.c for a plain C 2D dynamic tree, and GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or nanoflann for static data.

**Gotchas:**
- Both R-tree headers put `using namespace std;` at global scope and define RPoint, RBox, Node, RTree, contains and intersects in the global namespace, so rtree_point.hpp and rtree_mbr.hpp cannot be included in the same translation unit and may clash with your own names
- RTree owns raw node pointers and deletes them in its destructor but neither deletes nor defines copy or move operations, so copying a tree (for example, passing it by value) double-frees
- knnQuery writes the k results in heap order, not sorted by distance, and k = 0 calls front() on an empty vector (undefined behavior)
- Each node is a fixed std::array of capacity + 1 entries (default capacity 128), so sparse nodes still occupy full size. remove() needs an exact coordinate match plus Value ==

**Status:** New, active academic project (MIT, 25 stars, 17 commits, last commit 2026-08-17). Its one GitHub issue, which questioned the fairness of the paper's dynamic-tree vs nanoflann comparison, was closed with no reply shown. Small enough to vendor, but treat it as research-grade code.

[repo](https://github.com/psimatis/Indexicon-Spatial-Library) · [benchmark](https://github.com/psimatis/Indexicon-Spatial-Library)

##### iOverlay (Rust polygon boolean overlay engine)  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust 2D polygon boolean engine (union/intersect/difference/xor, offsetting) that outscales Clipper2 on very large, intersection-heavy inputs.

**Beats:** Clipper2 (C++ polygon clipping library, v1.4.0); also Boost.Geometry (Boost 1.86.0) — First-party comparison page: iOverlay Rust v1.9.0 versus Clipper2 C++ v1.4.0 (and Boost 1.86) on six synthetic grid tests, on a '3 GHz 6-Core Intel Core i5' with no compiler named; single-thread iOverlay is 16.7x faster on 8,384,513 checkerboard squares (38.6 s vs 644.3 s), 12.4x on Not Overlap, 17.1x on Windows, 6.1x on Lines Net 4096, 81x on Spiral 1M and 869x on Nested Squares 65,536 (ratios derived from page data), while Clipper2 wins or ties at small sizes. The numbers are for an old iOverlay release (current 9.0.0) and Boost's build type is unset.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: the performance page (verified from its source in iShape-Rust/iShape-js docs, github.io blocked) gives the CPU only as '3 GHz 6-Core Intel Core i5' and names no compiler; baselines are Clipper2 v1.4.0 and Boost 1.86. crates.io shows 9.0M downloads.

**Known shortcoming:** No C/C++ API: iShape-ffi is an undocumented 0-star staticlib bridge that builds from sibling paths. The measured version is v1.9.0 while the crate is now 9.0.0. Clipper2 ties or wins below about 1k elements. 2026 correctness issues, all closed: #87 Frag strategy dropped a filled region, #88 i16 overflow panic, #91 hole-binding panic, #37 buffer infinite loop. The integer APIs do not check coordinate range.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** All geometry runs on integer coordinates: segments are sorted (i_key_sort, parallel radix-style sort when allowed), coincident edges merged, then split at intersections by one of three solvers chosen by size: an all-pairs list below about 4,000 segments, a sweep over an interval tree of expiring segments (i_tree SegExpTree), or, above 16,000 segments, a grid of vertical strips where each strip is split independently (in parallel with rayon when the allow_multithreading feature is on). Intersections are snapped with a growing snap radius and the split repeats until stable, after which winding counts are filled and contours extracted from the graph. The comparison page's large factors over Clipper2 appear where Clipper2's run time grows much faster than linearly with intersection count.

**Use it when:**
- Rust (or WASM/Swift via the iShape bindings) code that needs polygon booleans on large inputs: hundreds of thousands to millions of edges with dense intersections, where the comparison page shows 2.5x (130k squares) to 17x (8.4M squares) over Clipper2 single-threaded.
- Deeply nested or spiral-like inputs, where Clipper2 degraded sharply on the comparison page (Nested Squares 65,536: 4.03 s vs 3502 s; Spiral 1M: 3.19 s vs 260 s).
- Unioning many shapes at once (simplify_shape) instead of chaining pairwise overlays.
- Pipelines that want deterministic integer-grid results or OGC-valid output (OverlayOptions::ogc()), or that already use georust/geo, whose boolean ops are built on it.
- no_std targets: the crate is #![no_std] with alloc.

**Skip it when:**
- Small inputs: on the comparison page Clipper2 is equal or faster at a few hundred to about a thousand elements (Checkerboard 481 squares 1.017 ms vs 1.117 ms; Lines Net 64: 0.75 ms vs 1.01 ms; Spiral 1024: 2.94 ms vs 3.57 ms).
- C++ codebases wanting a supported library: there is no C/C++ API; iShape-ffi is an undocumented staticlib bridge (0 stars, built against sibling-repo paths) aimed at the Swift binding.
- Workloads needing exact arithmetic or no snapping: results are rounded to an integer grid and intersections are snapped within a growing radius (Precision setting), so vertices can move slightly.
- Integer inputs outside -2^(N-2)..2^(N-2)-1 for the chosen engine: the integer APIs do not check the bound, and overflow gives wrong results.
- Risk-averse production use without your own tests: 2026 issues include panics (#88 i16 Frag overflow, #91 hole binding), a Frag strategy dropping a filled region (#87), an infinite loop in buffering (#37) and non-OGC union output (#57); all are closed, but they show the edge-case surface.

**Integration:** crate · i_float, i_shape, i_tree, i_key_sort (same author); rayon optional via allow_multithreading; optional glam and serde features · Rust 1.88 (edition 2024) for i_overlay 9.0.0 · any Rust target; #![no_std] + alloc; WASM via iShape-js; multithreading needs rayon (std)

**Vs siblings:** Pick iOverlay over clipper2next (a C++ Clipper2 fork with about 1.6x geometric-mean gain) when inputs are large and intersection-dense enough to hit Clipper2's super-linear growth and a Rust dependency is acceptable; stay with clipper2next or Clipper2 for C++ drop-in use and small polygons. For offsetting with true arcs pick CavalierContours, and for GEOS-compatible unions in Python/WASM pipelines qdgeo is the closer fit.

**Gotchas:**
- Multithreading is off by default; you must enable the allow_multithreading Cargo feature, and parallel sorting kicks in only above par_sort_min_size (32,768 by default). Issue #65 (closed) reported the feature not enabling parallel sort in i_key_sort.
- Default float conversion uses the i32 engine with a conservative coordinate budget; pick i64 (overlay_as::<i64> or FloatOverlay::<_, i64>) when bounds or precision demand it, and expect i64 to be about 30 percent slower (README chart).
- Polygon offsetting assumes valid input (no self-intersections, CCW outer and CW holes); run simplify_shape first otherwise. Integer-math miter joins clip corners sharper than 5 degrees.
- Infallible float APIs panic on non-finite or out-of-range coordinates; the fixed-scale APIs return errors instead.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-24, 940 commits, every listed issue closed), dual MIT/Apache-2.0, 9.0M crates.io downloads and the boolean engine inside georust/geo; usable from C++ only through your own FFI layer.

[repo](https://github.com/iShape-Rust/iOverlay) · [benchmark](https://ishape-rust.github.io/iShape-js/overlay/performance/performance.html)

##### KDBush  `JavaScript`  `ISC`  `active`  `Tier C`

JavaScript static 2D point index (flat kd-tree in one ArrayBuffer); its author says it indexes points 5-8x faster than RBush.

**Beats:** RBush (JavaScript R-tree) — The only number is a one-line first-party claim in the RBush README, by the author of both libraries, that kdbush 'performs point indexing 5-8x faster than RBush'. It gives no workload, Node version or hardware. kdbush's own bench.js builds an index of 1M Uint32 points and times 10,000 small box and 10,000 small radius queries, but it runs kdbush alone, never RBush, and publishes no results.

**Known shortcoming:** The 5-8x is one line in the RBush README and bench.js times kdbush only; JavaScript.

**Known shortcoming:** JavaScript library, not callable from C++; its C++ port mourner/kdbush.hpp was archived 2026-06. The 5-8x claim is one first-party line in the RBush README and bench.js never runs RBush. Minor bug: header stores raw nodeSize as Uint16 while build clamps to 65535, so KDBush.from with nodeSize >65535 gives a mismatched tree.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** finish() kd-sorts the coordinate and id arrays in place: it recursively places the median on alternating axes with Floyd-Rivest selection and stops at leaves of nodeSize points (default 64), which are scanned linearly. The tree is implicit (no node objects or pointers). Ids and coordinates live in typed arrays inside a single ArrayBuffer, with Uint16 ids under 65,536 points and a coordinate type you choose (Int32Array or Uint32Array is smaller and faster than the Float64 default). Queries walk the tree iteratively with a preallocated Uint32Array stack, and withinInto can write into a caller-supplied typed array so queries allocate nothing.

**Use it when:**
- Browser or Node code that indexes a large fixed set of 2D points (map markers, clustering input, hit-testing) and then runs many small box or radius queries.
- Integer or grid coordinates, where Int32Array or Uint32Array storage shrinks the index and speeds it up.
- Building the index in a Web Worker and handing it to the main thread without copying (postMessage with a transferable ArrayBuffer, KDBush.from on the other side), or sharing it through a SharedArrayBuffer.
- Saving a prebuilt index to a file and loading it back with KDBush.from, without rebuilding.
- Point-only datasets where Flatbush would also work: the README says KDBush uses about 2x less memory than Flatbush for points.

**Skip it when:**
- Data that changes after indexing: there is no insert or remove, so every change means a full rebuild. RBush is the dynamic option.
- Rectangles, polygons or other extents: use Flatbush (static) or RBush (dynamic).
- k-nearest-neighbour queries: the core library offers only box and radius queries. kNN with great-circle distances is in the separate mourner/geokdbush extension.
- 3D or higher-dimensional points: 2D only (3D support is an open feature request, issue #38).
- Native C++ code: this is JavaScript. The official C++11 port (mourner/kdbush.hpp) was archived in June 2026; nanoflann covers k-D point search in C++.

**Integration:** module · none (npm package kdbush; ES module, plus UMD bundles kdbush.js and kdbush.min.js that expose a KDBush global) · Any engine with ES modules and typed arrays; package.json declares no engines field. TypeScript types (index.d.ts) are generated from JSDoc at publish. · any JavaScript runtime (browsers, Node.js); SharedArrayBuffer sharing requires a runtime that exposes it

**Vs siblings:** Pick KDBush over RBush when the points are static and points-only, which is where the 5-8x indexing claim applies. Pick geo-index (its Rust port of this layout) or nanoflann in native code, and nanoflann or a C++ kd-tree if you need kNN or more than two dimensions.

**Gotchas:**
- finish() throws unless exactly numItems points were added, so the count must be known before you start.
- Queries return indices in the order the tree was traversed, not insertion order. Issue #42 (order changing after a rebuild) was closed without a fix.
- Range bounds are inclusive on all sides, and radius queries compare squared Euclidean distance on raw coordinates. For latitude and longitude that is planar distance, not geodesic (geokdbush handles geographic kNN).
- The serialized header stores the raw nodeSize argument as a Uint16, while the build clamps it to 2..65535. A nodeSize above 65535 would therefore serialize a different leaf size than the one used to build, and KDBush.from would rebuild a mismatched index. Keep nodeSize at the default 64 or another small value.

**Status:** Active (v4.1.0, last commit 2026-05-19, 713 stars), ISC-licensed and about 300 lines of dependency-free JavaScript, so easy to vendor; it is JavaScript, not C++, and the official C++ port is archived.

[repo](https://github.com/mourner/kdbush) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mourner/rbush)

##### Kiddo (Rust k-d tree)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust k-d tree for low-dimensional exact/approximate NN; 1.2-1.5x faster queries than nabo-rs; no C/C++ API.

**Beats:** pykdtree, scipy.spatial.KDTree and sklearn KDTree (Python), nabo-rs and FNNTW (Rust); no C++ baseline (nanoflann, PCL, CGAL) is benchmarked — The author's Criterion suite (sdd/kd-tree-comparison, Ryzen 5900X, 32 GB, rustc version and flags not stated) times 1,000 queries per iteration on uniform random points (not the unit sphere the README describes). For 1M 3-D f64 points, Kiddo v3/v5 nearest-1/10/100 is about 1.2-1.45x faster than nabo-rs and 1.5-3.2x faster than pykdtree, and construction is slower than pykdtree (derived from page data). The 18-38x over scipy and sklearn compares rayon-parallel queries with single-threaded ones. The repo has an FFI harness against nanoflann, ALGLIB and Pkd-tree, but no results from it were found on a reachable page (sdd.github.io is blocked), so there is no measured C++ comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust only with no C/C++ API, outside the C++ scope. Kiddo/nabo/FNNTW queries run rayon-parallel against single-threaded scipy/sklearn, so the 18-38x is mostly threading. Repo has a nanoflann FFI bench but no published results.

**Known shortcoming:** No published C++ comparison. #475 (MutableKdTree add panics when many points share one axis value) and #474 (unsound memory free converting to the rkyv type) were reported on 5.3.2 and closed with the fix unconfirmed.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Interior 'stem' nodes are stored implicitly in a cache-friendly array layout (Eytzinger order, and in v6 the alternative 'Donnelly' block ordering with configurable prefetch) and points live in fixed-size leaf buckets, so descent is index arithmetic rather than pointer chasing. Leaf scans and, in the Donnelly SIMD strategies, descent, pruning and backtracking use hand-written AVX2, AVX-512, NEON and wasm simd128 kernels (the 'simd' feature needs nightly Rust). The immutable tree is balanced at construction, and batch queries and construction are parallelised over the rayon thread pool by default.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services and pipelines doing many nearest-neighbour or radius queries on static 2-D to 4-D point sets (geocoding, star-catalogue cross-matching, colour-palette lookup, simulation neighbourhoods)
- Prebuilt trees loaded from disk at startup: ImmutableKdTree with rkyv 0.8 supports zero-copy loading from memory-mapped files
- Batched query workloads on multi-core machines, where query_batch spreads the queries over rayon
- Periodic-boundary simulations (cosmology, molecular boxes) that need wrapped distance queries built in
- Integer or fixed-point coordinates, which most C++ k-d trees do not support directly

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: there is no C API or header, so you must write and maintain an FFI layer (the crate is out of this catalog's C/C++ scope)
- High-dimensional vectors (tens to thousands of dimensions): the README says plain k-d trees are the wrong structure there
- Heavy insert/delete churn: MutableKdTree does no dynamic rebalancing, and the README suggests periodic rebuilds
- When construction time dominates: on 1M 3-D f64 points Kiddo builds in 125-161 ms vs pykdtree's 92 ms in the author's suite
- Stable-only toolchains that need the fastest path: the SIMD stem strategies require nightly Rust, and v6 needs Rust 1.89+

**Integration:** crate · Default features pull rayon (multi-threaded) and fixed; optional serde, rkyv 0.8, half (f16). The C++ competitor benches vendor nanoflann, ALGLIB and Pkd-tree behind a feature · Rust 1.89 (v6 MSRV; v5 needs 1.85); 'simd' feature needs nightly · any Rust target; SIMD kernels for x86-64 AVX2/AVX-512, aarch64 NEON and wasm32 simd128; disabling multi-threaded supports WASM, embedded and single-core targets

**Vs siblings:** Pick Kiddo only if your code is Rust (or you will maintain an FFI shim) and you query static low-dimensional data in batches. For C++ use nanoflann, PicoTree or libnabo (whose Rust port nabo-rs Kiddo beats by 1.2-1.5x on queries); none of these C++ libraries appears in Kiddo's published results.

**Gotchas:**
- v6 (2026-07-27) is a near rewrite with a builder query API: v5 calls such as nearest_one and within must be ported, rkyv 0.7 support is gone, and every published comparison number is for v1-v5
- Many points sharing one coordinate on an axis have broken trees before: issue #475 (v5.3.2) reports MutableKdTree add panicking when 33 points share an axis value with bucket size 32. It is closed, but no fix is shown; test with your data or raise the bucket size
- Issue #474 (v5.3.2, rkyv feature) reported an unsound conversion that freed a 128-byte-aligned allocation with 8-byte alignment through safe API; closed, fix not confirmed. v6.0.1 also fixed several fuzzer-found SIMD over-pruning and construction bugs, so stay on the latest 6.x
- Batch queries are multi-threaded by default; a benchmark against single-threaded code (as the published scipy/sklearn comparisons do) measures threading, not the tree

**Status:** Actively maintained (v6.3.0 on 2026-09-06, CI, fuzzing, 176 stars), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed; a strong choice in Rust, but outside the C/C++ scope with no C ABI.

[repo](https://github.com/sdd/kiddo) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sdd/kd-tree-comparison/HEAD/all-benchmarks.json)

##### libnabo  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Eigen-based C++ kd-tree for exact (or epsilon-approximate) k-NN in low dimensions; the README claims 5-20% faster than ANN.

**Beats:** ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor library, exact-search kd-tree); tests/knnbench.cpp benchmarks ANN (stack and priority search) when ANN is installed. A FLANN code path exists but is switched off in knnbench.cpp ('currently disable FLANN', #undef HAVE_FLANN). — The only speed claim is first-party: the README and the doxygen FAQ say libnabo is 'about 5% to 20% faster than ANN (both -O3 -NDEBUG), probably due to the smaller memory footprint', with no CPU, dataset or table. tests/knnbench.cpp compares against ANN only when ANN is installed, and publishes nothing. In its current form it times libnabo's matrix knn(), OpenMP-parallel when OpenMP is found, against ANN queried one point at a time on one thread, so today's 'make test' numbers would not be a like-for-like comparison. The JOSER 2012 paper (co-authored by the libnabo author) that should hold the measurements was unreachable here (stephane.magnenat.net and uni-wuerzburg.de are egress-blocked); search snippets confirm only that it compares 3DTK, ANN, CGAL, FLANN, libnabo, SpatialIndex and STANN for ICP.

**Known shortcoming:** FLANN path disabled in knnbench.cpp, so only ANN is raced; ethz-asl URL redirects to norlab-ulaval (transferred, not a fork); JOSER 2012 paper unreachable here, so B is possible if it can be read.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not like-for-like: knnbench.cpp times libnabo batched kNN with OpenMP (default ON) against single-threaded ANN. JOSER 2012 paper unreachable here. Default self-match exclusion drops any neighbour with dist2 <= machine epsilon, including true duplicates. Wrappers jefferis/nabor (R) and enlightware/nabo-rs (Rust) are ports, not separate entries.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It is ANN's sliding-midpoint kd-tree (ANN_KD_SL_MIDPT) with a more compact memory layout. Points sit in buckets at the leaves (default bucketSize 8). Nodes live in one contiguous array; the left child is implicitly the next node, and the split dimension and right-child index share one packed uint32. Cell bounds are not stored, and the search tracks incremental offsets as in ANN's paper. The authors credit the roughly 5-fold smaller memory footprint for the speed, since the search is memory-bound. Two heap variants exist: a linear vector heap for small k (up to about 30) and an STL tree heap for larger k. The matrix knn() overload runs queries in parallel with OpenMP, which is on by default in CMake.

**Use it when:**
- ICP or point-cloud registration in 2D or 3D on CPU, especially if your code already uses Eigen matrices. The ICP paper the README cites evaluates exactly this use, and the CHANGELOG muted Ubuntu jammy 'until libpointmatcher build pass on jammy', so the two projects are built together.
- Many queries at once: pass them as one matrix so the size checks run once and OpenMP spreads the queries across threads.
- Exact or bounded-error kNN with a per-query maximum radius to prune the search, for example outlier rejection in registration.
- Replacing ANN in old C++ code with a reentrant, BSD-licensed library templated on scalar type (float or double).
- Projects that also want Python (pynabo, via Boost.Python) or a pure-Rust port (nabo-rs) of the same algorithm.

**Skip it when:**
- High-dimensional data (descriptors, embeddings): it is built for low dimensions and offers only Euclidean distance, with no approximate high-dimensional index. Use FLANN or an ANN-graph library.
- Header-only or zero-dependency builds: it is a compiled CMake library that needs Eigen, plus Boost for the Python bindings. nanoflann is header-only.
- Dynamic point sets: the tree is built once over the given cloud, with no insert or delete. Pkd-tree supports batch updates.
- Fixed-radius searches that return every point within r: knn() returns at most k results, and the radius only prunes.
- New projects on recent toolchains: CI tests only Ubuntu 18.04 and 20.04, the project builds as C++11, and Eigen 5 compatibility (#147) and MSVC build failures (#124, #113) are open issues.

**Integration:** static lib · Eigen 2 or 3 (header-only); optional Boost.Python for pynabo; optional OpenMP (on by default, links gomp under GCC); optional OpenCL code paths are disabled by default ('not up-to-date with API') · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake 3.10.2+ · x86 and arm64 on Ubuntu 18.04 and 20.04 (tested in CI); macOS and Windows 'reportedly' work, per the README

**Vs siblings:** Pick libnabo over nanoflann, picoflann or PicoTree when you already store points as Eigen matrices in an ICP stack and want batched, OpenMP-parallel exact kNN with per-query radius limits. nanoflann (header-only, no Eigen requirement) and PicoTree (which publishes numbers against nanoflann) are easier to adopt and better documented on speed. SPRK-tree's harness benchmarks nabo, but no numbers were seen.

**Gotchas:**
- The point matrix is held by reference: 'M must stay alive throughout the use of libnabo, otherwise the results of knn are undefined.' create() returns a raw owning pointer you must delete.
- Self-matches are excluded by default. The check is squared distance > numeric_limits<T>::epsilon() (about 1.2e-7 for float), so exact duplicate points and any neighbour closer than about 3.5e-4 units in float are silently dropped unless you pass ALLOW_SELF_MATCH.
- Results are unsorted unless SORT_RESULTS is set. Missing neighbours (radius limit) come back as InvalidIndex and infinite distance. Asking for k >= cloud size (k > size - 1 without self-match) throws std::runtime_error.
- The node index shares a 32-bit field with the split dimension, so the constructor throws if cols/(bucketSize/2) could exceed 2^(32 - dimBits) - 1 nodes, and Index is a 32-bit int. Very large or higher-dimensional clouds need a larger bucketSize.

**Status:** Stale: last commit 2025-07-16, last release 1.1.2 (2024-05-23), recent changes mostly CI and Docker work under NorLab maintenance. It is BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor, but the build targets older Ubuntu and Eigen 3.

[repo](https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/libnabo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/libnabo)

##### madmann91/bvh  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++20 binary BVH builder and ray traverser; its chart shows it faster than nanort and Fast-BVH, but slower than Embree.

**Beats:** nanort and Fast-BVH (Embree 3.13 also compared and is faster) — One README chart (chart.png) compares build time and 1-spp 720p primary-ray render time on one unnamed .obj scene. Readings, approximate: v2 medium about 150 ms build and 275 ms render; nanort about 360 and 645; Fast-BVH about 460 and 1225; Embree 3.13 about 70 and 170. That makes v2 roughly 2.3x faster than nanort and 4.5x faster than Fast-BVH at rendering (derived from page data), but slower than Embree. No CPU, compiler, flags, thread count or scene is given. test/benchmark.cpp times only this library: it builds with a thread pool sized to hardware_concurrency and renders single-threaded. The harness used for Embree, nanort and Fast-BVH is not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Embree 3.13 beats it on build and render; competitor harness not in the repo; scene unnamed.

**Known shortcoming:** Embree is faster and TinyBVH claims to beat both. SmallStack overflow is checked only by assert, so it overflows silently in release (#108 open, unanswered). README CMake flag names differ from CMakeLists. Chart gives no thread count; the repo benchmark uses hardware_concurrency threads.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Low quality uses Wald's binned SAH builder. Medium and High use a full sweep SAH builder single-threaded, or, with a thread pool and at least 1,024 primitives, Ganestam et al.'s mini-tree builder with pruning. High then runs Meister and Bittner's parallel reinsertion optimizer to raise tree quality. Nodes are compact binary nodes with siblings stored next to each other and one packed index (first child or primitive plus primitive count). Traversal visits the nearer child first and orders box tests by ray octant, uses FMA-based slab tests (Ize's robust variant is optional) and a fixed-size stack; shadow rays can use SATO ordering.

**Use it when:**
- CPU ray tracers, path tracers or visibility queries that need a small dependency-free BVH (standard library only), and where Embree's size or license model is unwanted.
- Replacing nanort or Fast-BVH: the README chart shows faster build and roughly 2-4x faster primary-ray render than both.
- Choosing your own trade-off between build time and traversal quality per scene (Low, Medium, High), for example a quick rebuild for animated geometry and High for static scenes.
- Non-ray queries on a BVH (box overlap, custom culling, 2D or 4D bounding boxes, float or double), using traverse_top_down with your own inner-node and leaf callbacks.
- C projects that only need the high-level build and intersect functions, through the optional C API (BVH_BUILD_C_API).

**Skip it when:**
- Peak performance: Embree 3.13 beats every preset on the README chart (about 70 ms build and 170 ms render, against about 150 ms and 275 ms for v2 medium), and TinyBVH reports beating both.
- Packet or wide-BVH (BVH4 or BVH8) SIMD traversal and GPU traversal: the nodes are binary and the traversal is single-ray (the GPU question is issue #92).
- Toolchains without C++20 (it uses std::span and defaulted comparison operators) or with CMake older than 3.21.
- Packaging that needs versioned releases: there is no tagged v2 release, and issue #116 asks for one for Debian.
- Frequent incremental insert or remove: there is refit but no dynamic insertion, so topology changes mean a rebuild (asked in issues #94 and #85).

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond the C++ standard library (Threads::Threads linked for the std::thread-based pool); optional C API library · C++20 (CMake target sets CXX_STANDARD 20), CMake 3.21+ · any (portable C++; GCC, Clang and MSVC force-inline macros in platform.h)

**Vs siblings:** TinyBVH is the closer competitor and claims to beat both Embree and this library on build time, so prefer it for top speed or wide BVHs. Pick madmann91/bvh for a clean, modern-C++ API with multiple builders, arbitrary dimensions and scalar types, serialization and a C API. ArborX and Coal are for spatial queries and collision on a different scale.

**Gotchas:**
- SmallStack<Index, N> (the benchmark uses N = 64) checks overflow only with assert(), so a BVH deeper than N overflows silently in release builds. Issue #108 (December 2025) asks what depth is safe and has no visible answer; use GrowingStack or size the stack to the tree depth.
- Leaves hold ranges into bvh.prim_ids, not your primitive order. Either index through prim_ids or permute your primitives after building, which the benchmark's --permute_prims option does.
- The README is out of date in places: it says -DENABLE_TESTING=ON and -DBVH_STATIC_LINK_STDLIB_C_API=ON, but CMakeLists uses CTest's BUILD_TESTING and BVH_C_API_STATIC_LINK_STDLIB, and the snippet's target_link_library should be target_link_libraries.
- Past bugs fixed upstream: ReinsertionOptimizer could loop forever (#84), extract_bvh could use a stale pointer (#81), and a span went out of range below 3 dimensions (#106). Pin a commit that includes these fixes.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-21, 1.2k stars, 438 commits) and MIT-licensed. It is header-only and easy to vendor, but has no tagged v2 release, so pin a commit.

[repo](https://github.com/madmann91/bvh) · [benchmark](https://github.com/madmann91/bvh)

##### nanoflann  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++11 k-d tree for exact point kNN/radius search; about 2.4x faster point kNN than Boost.Geometry's R*-tree.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree (point k-nearest and range queries) — The independent GeoToolbox harness compared nanoflann 1.10.1 (pinned tag, compile-time DIM, L2_Simple, single-threaded build) with Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree on 2D/3D point sets of 10^2-10^6 elements. It was built with MSVC 2026 and clang-cl 22 (Release, /arch:AVX2 and LTO per its public CMakeLists) on an ASUS ROG Strix G16 laptop under Windows 11, CPU model not stated. Its result TSVs give point-kNN query times 2.40x (clang-cl) and 2.52x (MSVC) faster than Boost as a geomean, falling to about 1.85x at 10^6 points, and point range queries 1.14-1.23x faster. Bulk load was 1.4-1.7x slower, and the range queries used GeoToolbox's own traversal code rather than nanoflann's findWithinBox (all ratios derived from page data). The README's separate ~50% speedup over original FLANN comes from first-party charts with no stated CPU or compiler, and the perf-tests directory it links has moved to MRPT/nanoflann-benchmark.

**Known shortcoming:** ~50% gain over FLANN only in first-party charts, no CPU or compiler stated (code in perf-tests/); FLANN not in the category list; Boost comparison only in GeoToolbox's README.

**Known shortcoming:** GeoToolbox tested 1.10.1, not 1.14.0, and its range queries used GeoToolbox's own traversal, not findWithinBox; bulk load 1.4-1.7x slower than Boost; at 10^6 points Boost wins build+nearest total (0.68-0.72x); 2D Synthetic_Polygon 10^6 kNN 2.7x slower than Boost; unsigned ElementType crash/wrong results fixed only in 1.13.0; README perf-tests link stale (moved to MRPT/nanoflann-benchmark).

**Independent measurement:** kNN geomean 2.40x (clang-cl) / 2.52x (MSVC) vs Boost.Geometry (derived from GeoToolbox page data).

**How:** It is a code-level fork of FLANN's single k-d tree with the virtual-dispatch layers replaced by CRTP and inlined templates. An optional compile-time DIM lets the compiler unroll the distance loops. Splits use FLANN's sliding-midpoint rule: cut the widest-spread axis among those near the maximum bounding-box span at the box midpoint, clamped to the data's min/max, then partition three ways (Dutch national flag). Queries descend the nearer child first and prune the other with an incremental per-axis distance bound (mindist + cut_dist - old_dist, as in Arya-Mount ANN). Leaves hold up to leaf_max_size points (default 10) that are scanned linearly. Since 1.14.0, nodes sit in one contiguous depth-first array and the far child is prefetched (__builtin_prefetch) while the near one is searched.

**Use it when:**
- Static 2D/3D point clouds (LiDAR scans, ICP correspondences, particle neighbours) queried many times for k nearest or fixed-radius neighbours: point kNN was about 2.4-2.5x faster than Boost R*-tree (geomean over 49 GeoToolbox runs, derived from page data)
- Memory-constrained indexing: zero-copy adaptors over your existing array. In GeoToolbox, 10^6 2D points took about 8.8 MB of index versus about 43 MB for Boost R*-tree (derived from page data)
- Data already in Eigen matrices or std::vector<std::vector<T>>, using the bundled adaptors, or in custom containers via a three-method adaptor
- Many concurrent query threads against one immutable index: queries are const and documented thread-safe while nothing is building
- Sliding-window maps that need add/remove: KDTreeSingleIndexIncrementalAdaptor (single self-balancing tree with removeBox/removeOutsideBox) or the Bentley-Saxe KDTreeSingleIndexDynamicAdaptor forest

**Skip it when:**
- Box or polygon keys: points only. Encoding a box as a 2N-D point needs custom query code and was about 1.4-1.5x slower than Boost on box range queries (derived from page data). Use GeoToolbox KdBoxTree, tidwall rtree.c or Boost
- Build-dominated workloads: the single-threaded bulk load (n_thread_build=1 in GeoToolbox's adapter) was about 1.4-1.7x slower than Boost R*-tree packing. At 10^6 points the GeoToolbox nearest scenario's total time (build plus queries) favoured Boost (Boost/nanoflann 0.68-0.72, derived from page data); use n_thread_build or 1.13+'s faster concurrent build
- Strongly structured data such as points on concentric circles: on GeoToolbox's 2D Synthetic_Polygon set at 10^6 points, nanoflann kNN took 146 ms versus 53 ms for Boost and 15 ms for KdBoxTree
- Approximate NN in high dimensions: no randomized trees, no LSH and no auto-tuning. The only approximation knob is eps in SearchParameters, so use FLANN, FAISS or an HNSW library
- Metrics beyond L1/L2/SO(2)/SO(3), C or Python bindings from this repo, or SE(3): not supported (README 1.6)

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library; std::thread/std::async unless NANOFLANN_NO_THREADS is defined). Eigen is optional for the Eigen adaptors; GTest and Eigen only for the tests and examples · C++11 (uses if constexpr when C++17 is available); CI covers GCC/Clang on Linux, MSVC and clang-cl on Windows, and macOS 14/15 · any; no intrinsics apart from a GCC/Clang prefetch builtin. ROS 2 binaries are built for amd64 and arm64

**Vs siblings:** Pick nanoflann over GeoToolbox KdBoxTree for exact point kNN/radius search up to about 10^5 points, for the smallest memory footprint, or for a widely packaged dependency (apt, vcpkg, Conan, ROS). KdBoxTree wins on box keys, at 10^6 points and on structured data. Pick it over tidwall rtree.c or THST when keys are points and queries are proximity rather than box overlap.

**Gotchas:**
- With L2 metrics, the radius you pass and every distance returned are squared distances
- The index stores only indices into your adaptor's data, which must outlive the index. A static index does not see points appended or changed after the build, so call buildIndex() again or use the dynamic or incremental adaptors. removePoint does not touch your dataset (open issue #304)
- The default IndexType is uint32_t (about 4.29e9 points). Unsigned coordinate types need an explicitly signed, wide-enough DistanceType; before 1.13.0 this case crashed or returned wrong results
- saveIndex files are version-locked: loadIndex throws on any NANOFLANN_VERSION mismatch, so persisted indices must be rebuilt after an upgrade. Tie order between equidistant points is unspecified unless NANOFLANN_FIRST_MATCH is defined

**Status:** Actively maintained (1.14.0 released 2026-09-25, four releases since June 2026; 2.7k stars; packaged in Debian/Ubuntu, Homebrew, vcpkg, Conan and ROS 2) under BSD-2-Clause, and a single header you can vendor; the measured 1.10.1 predates the 1.13 build rewrite and the 1.14 contiguous-node layout.

[repo](https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ikolev21/GeoToolbox)

##### ParGeo (parallel 3D convex hull and kd-tree library)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Multicore C++17 computational-geometry library (3D convex hull, kd-tree, spatial graphs) that outruns sequential CGAL and Qhull hulls through parallelism.

**Beats:** CGAL (3D convex hull) and Qhull — Not reproduced, and the paper was not opened (arxiv.org, cs.ucr.edu, par.nsf.gov, dspace.mit.edu blocked). Search-result snippets of the ESA 2022 paper say the fastest parallel hulls on 36 cores with two-way hyper-threading are 10.5-124x (61.4x on average) faster than CGAL and 5.68-43.8x (19.9x on average) faster than Qhull for 3D hulls, while another snippet says pseudohull reaches up to 43.7x over Qhull and up to 5.05x over CGAL; the two statements conflict, and CPU model, compiler and CGAL/Qhull versions are unknown.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: the CGAL/Qhull speedups come from arXiv 2207.01834 and a PPoPP poster, both blocked here and unverified; benchmark/hull3d_bench.cpp times only ParGeo's own serial quickhull versus pseudohull. Last commit 2022-09-12, abandoned. Paper-access retier candidate (possible B).

**Known shortcoming:** Search snippets conflict on the paper's numbers (one says 10.5-124x, 61.4x average, over CGAL and 5.68-43.8x, 19.9x average, over Qhull on 36 cores; another says up to 5.05x over CGAL); the paper is still unopened. The hull visibility test uses a fixed absolute epsilon of 1e-5 (float and double) with no exact predicates. CMakeLists overwrites CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS and hard-codes -mcx16; the Clang build fails (issue #1, open since 2024-01). Pseudohull is instantiated only for fpoint<3>/point<3>.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** All modules run on parlaylib's work-stealing fork-join scheduler. The 3D pseudohull first prunes interior points in parallel: it builds an extreme-point simplex, partitions points by the facet they see (split_k), recurses on each facet's points in parallel, then runs a parallel quickhull on the survivors; per search snippets of the paper, its parallel hull uses a reservation technique so several facets can be inserted into the hull concurrently. The divide-and-conquer hull splits the input into one block per processor, hulls each block with sequential quickhull, and hulls the union of block-hull vertices. The kd-tree splits in parallel during construction and runs queries data-parallel.

**Use it when:**
- 3D convex hulls of millions of float or double points on a many-core machine (the paper used 36 cores with two-way hyper-threading), where single-threaded CGAL or Qhull is the bottleneck.
- Batch k-NN or radius/box range queries over a static 2D-7D point set, where a parallel kd-tree build plus data-parallel queries fit the workload.
- Building spatial graphs in parallel: k-NN graph, 2D Delaunay graph, beta-skeleton/Gabriel graph, WSPD-based t-spanner, Euclidean MST.
- Research or prototyping that wants several parallel geometry primitives (enclosing ball, closest pair, Morton sort) on one scheduler.

**Skip it when:**
- Inputs needing robust hulls: visibility tests compare against a fixed absolute epsilon of 1e-5 in float/double (pargeo point eps, pseudohull numericKnob); there are no exact predicates in the code read, so very small, very large or degenerate (coplanar, duplicate) coordinates are risky, and the README says nothing about robustness.
- Few cores or single-threaded builds: the claimed gains come from parallelism, and the repo's own benchmark compares only ParGeo's serial quickhull against its pseudohull, not CGAL or Qhull.
- Hulls above 3D, or callers who need a half-edge/polyhedron mesh: hulls are 2D and 3D only, and the 3D result is a flat list of triangle facets (vertex coordinates).
- Production code that needs maintenance: last commit 2022-09-12; the only issue (#1, January 2024, clang rejects a redefined default template argument in src/dataset/seedSpreader.cpp) is still open.
- Dynamic kd-tree workloads where a maintained alternative exists (see Pkd-tree under siblings).

**Integration:** static lib (each hull module builds its own CMake library, e.g. pseudoHull3dLib) plus header-only parts (kd-tree, point types) · parlaylib (ParAlg fork, pargeo branch, git submodule); batch-dynamic-kdtree submodule; Google Benchmark and Google Test for benchmarks/tests; pthreads · C++17, CMake 3.10; GCC-style flags; clang fails to build seedSpreader.cpp without the one-line fix in issue #1 · x86-64 as configured (CMakeLists hard-codes -mcx16 for 16-byte compare-and-swap); other architectures not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick ParGeo over DGtal QuickHull (sequential, about 2x CGAL convex_hull_3) when you have many cores and very large 3D point sets and can accept epsilon-based float predicates; prefer DGtal for single-threaded or integer-lattice work. For parallel kd-trees, the Pkd-tree from the same research lineage (ucrparlay) is newer and benchmarks against the CGAL kd-tree and Boost R-tree directly, so use ParGeo's kd-tree mainly when you also want its WSPD, EMST or spatial-graph routines.

**Gotchas:**
- The root CMakeLists.txt overwrites CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS with set(...) (-DHOMEGROWN -pthread -mcx16 -O3 -DNDEBUG -fPIC), so flags you pass on the command line are discarded unless you edit it; USE_PARALLEL=OFF switches to -DPARLAY_SEQUENTIAL.
- pseudo::compute is explicitly instantiated only for fpoint<3> and point<3>; other point types will not link without adding instantiations.
- By construction the pseudohull filter only discards interior points, so inputs with most points on the hull (the repo's onSphere set) get little benefit from the pruning step.
- The README's Multi-core Parallelism section is empty; thread control is only through parlaylib.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-09-12 (one open build issue from 2024) but MIT-licensed; modules are small enough to vendor together with the parlaylib fork, and the ESA 2022 paper documents the algorithms.

[repo](https://github.com/ParAlg/ParGeo) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01834)

##### PH-tree (phtree-cpp)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only PH-tree (bitwise Z-order quadtree) spatial map; about 5x faster inserts than Boost.Geometry's R-tree, slower kNN.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry R-tree (boost::geometry::index::rtree); libspatialindex R-tree also measured — In the author's separate phtree-cpp-perf repo (Google Benchmark, PH-tree 1.4.0 vendored, Feb-Mar 2023, GCC 12.1 and Clang 14, 8 x 4600 MHz CPU with 12 MiB L3, model unnamed), 3D inserts at 1M entries run at 2.79M/s vs 500k/s (points, CUBE) and 1.44M/s vs 406k/s (boxes) against Boost.Geometry's R-tree, about 3.5-5.6x; window queries are mixed and Boost wins box queries (about 4.7x) and 3D kNN (about 13-26x).

**Known shortcoming:** Insert ~5x over the Boost R-tree is real, but for 3D kNN Boost is ~13-26x faster (record understated this); the perf repo vendors PH-tree 1.4.0 with 2023 runs and an unnamed CPU.

**Known shortcoming:** Open bug #154: multimap emplace_hint after erase inserts at the wrong location; test crashes with NUM_DUPL=10. Heap use-after-free in multimap relocate (#153) fixed only in 1.6.2. No concurrency support per README; kNN for box keys not implemented (#36).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The PH-tree (Zaeschke et al., SIGMOD 2014) is a bitwise prefix-sharing 2^DIM-ary trie: each node is a binary hypercube addressed by one bit per dimension, so entries sit in Z-order (Morton) order and a lookup or insert walks at most one path with bit arithmetic, no rebalancing. Insert/erase modify only one node (plus possibly one created or deleted), which is why updates are cheap; relocate() reuses the shared path when an entry moves a short distance. Node entry storage switches by dimension (fixed array_map for DIM<=3, sparse sorted vector up to 8, B+tree beyond), and traversal relies on count-trailing-zeros (TZCNT/BMI2) and AVX, hence the recommended -O3 -mavx -mbmi2. Doubles are mapped to int64 losslessly via their IEEE bit pattern by default.

**Use it when:**
- Dynamic point sets with heavy insert/erase/move churn (simulations, game entities, moving objects) where an R-tree's rebalancing costs dominate; author's benchmark shows about 5x Boost R-tree insert throughput at 1M 3D points
- Small window queries returning roughly up to 100 results per query, especially on clustered data (PH-tree 1.36x faster than Boost on 1M CLUSTER points)
- Map semantics on exact coordinates (one value per key, find/count by point) with spatial queries on the same structure
- Moderate dimensionality: the README says it works very well up to about 30 (sometimes 50) dimensions, with a hard limit of 63
- Large datasets (millions of entries) built incrementally rather than bulk-loaded

**Skip it when:**
- kNN-heavy workloads: in the author's own 3D run Boost's R-tree answers k=1 queries about 13-26x faster at 1M points; there is no kNN for box keys at all (issue #36 open)
- Box (rectangle) data with window queries: Boost R-tree is about 4.7x faster on 1M CUBE boxes in the same benchmark
- Queries returning large result sets (the README says 1000+ results is inefficient; Boost already wins at about 100 results per query)
- Static datasets that can be bulk-loaded once (packed R-trees or kd-trees such as nanoflann build fast and query faster)
- Concurrent access: the README states the implementation does not support concurrency

**Integration:** header-only · none for the library (copy include/phtree); Bazel or CMake 3.14 only for tests, examples and benchmarks, which use GoogleTest and Google Benchmark · C++17; verified with GCC 12, Clang 14, Visual Studio 2022 (CMake) and AppleClang 14 (Bazel) · Linux, Windows, macOS; x86-64 recommended with -mavx -mbmi2 for TZCNT (works without, slower bit iteration); benchmarks do not build on Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick PH-tree over GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or nanoflann when the dataset changes constantly (insert, erase, relocate) rather than being bulk-loaded and queried, and over tidwall/rtree.c when you want a typed C++17 map API with up to 63 dimensions; pick nanoflann or Boost's R-tree instead when kNN or box queries dominate.

**Gotchas:**
- Map semantics: inserting a duplicate key silently does nothing (the FAQ calls this 'losing updates'); use PhTreeMultiMap or a set as value type
- Iteration order is Z-order on the unsigned bit pattern, so negative coordinates come after positive ones; iterators are invalid after modification except as a hint after exactly one erase()
- Correctness history: a heap-use-after-free in multimap relocate (vector reallocation in a node's sparse map, issue #153) was fixed in 1.6.2; issue #154 (bug, open since Aug 2023) reports a crash in the multimap test with NUM_DUPL=10 where emplace_hint after erase inserts at the wrong location
- Lossy ConverterMultiply can speed indexes up by 10%+ but truncates coordinates; the default IEEE converter is lossless. Values are stored inside nodes, so store pointers for large objects

**Status:** Maintained by the original PH-tree author as a fork of Improbable's abandoned repo; last commit 2026-03-19 but the last release is v1.7.0 (GitHub release dated March 2024; CHANGELOG header says 2025) with 14 open issues, so slow-moving; Apache-2.0 and header-only, easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/tzaeschke/phtree-cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tzaeschke/phtree-cpp-perf)

##### PicoTree  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++17 kd-tree for exact and approximate kNN, radius and box search; builds faster than nanoflann and OpenCV FLANN.

**Beats:** nanoflann v1.7.1 (also OpenCV FLANN 4.11.0, SciPy KDTree, scikit-learn KDTree, pykdtree) — The author's README table compares PicoTree v1.0.0 with nanoflann 1.7.1 and OpenCV FLANN 4.11.0 (C++), and with SciPy 1.15.2, scikit-learn 1.6.1 and pykdtree 1.3.7 (Python), on an Intel Core i9-14900HX: one thread, max_leaf_size=10, knn=1, a 7,733,372-point Bremen LiDAR cloud to build and a 7,200,863-point cloud to query. The compiler and flags are not stated. PicoTree is 1.2x faster than nanoflann at knn and 2.0x faster than OpenCV FLANN, and it builds 1.8x faster than OpenCV FLANN. The 2.6x build gap against nanoflann is inflated: since nanoflann 1.4 its KDTreeSingleIndexAdaptor constructor already calls buildIndex(), and examples/benchmark/bm_nanoflann.cpp then calls tree.buildIndex() again inside the timed loop, so nanoflann's 1.42 s covers two builds. That matches the '90% slower in nanoflann v1.5.0' note in docs/benchmark.md. Halving it suggests about a 1.3x real gap (derived estimate, not measured). In Python, pykdtree builds faster (0.43 s vs 0.54 s).

**Known shortcoming:** Compiler for the README table unstated (benchmark code in examples/benchmark).

**Known shortcoming:** README nanoflann build number counts two builds: bm_nanoflann.cpp constructs KDTreeSingleIndexAdaptor (whose constructor calls buildIndex() since nanoflann 1.4) and then calls buildIndex() again inside the timed loop, so the 2.6x faster build is inflated (real gap ~1.3x, derived estimate, not measured); the same bug explains the docs' 'nanoflann 1.5.0 regressed 90%' note. kNN numbers unaffected. Not on PyPI.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The default split rule is sliding midpoint (Maneewongvatana and Mount, 'It's okay to be skinny, if your friends are fat'): it cuts the longest box side at its middle with a linear std::partition and falls back to std::nth_element only when one side would be empty, which avoids median selection at every level. During construction each leaf's box is shrunk to the points it holds, and the parent stores the actual left-child max and right-child min on the split axis, so queries pick the nearer child from the real gap and prune with tighter bounds. Nearest-neighbour search uses Arya-Mount incremental distance calculation (only the split-axis term of the box distance is updated per step) with non-square-rooted metrics. Nodes come from a pool allocator in chunks of 256 rather than per-node new or std::deque, and fixing the dimension at compile time lets the distance loops unroll.

**Use it when:**
- Static 3D point clouds (LiDAR scans, ICP correspondence search) where the tree is rebuilt often: on the author's 7.7M-point scan a single-threaded build took 0.54 s vs 0.99 s for OpenCV FLANN and 1.42 s reported for nanoflann 1.7.1
- Single-nearest-neighbour or small-k queries over millions of query points in C++: knn=1 took 1.13 s vs 1.40 s (nanoflann) and 2.30 s (OpenCV FLANN) for 7.2M queries
- Python pipelines that need exact kNN on NumPy float arrays: knn=1 took 1.64 s vs 2.95 s for pykdtree, 11.9 s for scikit-learn and 212 s for SciPy KDTree in the README, and the bindings can parallelize queries with OpenMP
- Data already in Eigen matrices, cv::Mat or a flat float buffer, used without copying (pass a std::reference_wrapper or space_map)
- Robotics or planar problems with angular coordinates (SO(2), SE(2)) where the metric has to wrap around

**Skip it when:**
- Point sets that change: builds are static only, with no insert or remove. Use nanoflann's dynamic/incremental adaptors or Pkd-tree for batch updates
- Build-dominated workloads on multi-core machines: construction is single-threaded, while nanoflann 1.5+ has n_thread_build and Pkd-tree builds in parallel
- High-dimensional approximate search (descriptors, embeddings): only the (1+e) kd-tree approximation and an example KdForest exist, so FAISS or an HNSW library is a better fit
- pip-only Python environments: there is no PyPI package (pypi.org/pypi/pico_tree returns 404), so you build from source with scikit-build, pybind11 and OpenMP
- Projects that need an actively maintained dependency: the last commit is 2025-08-10, there are 49 stars, and the 7 issues ever filed are all closed

**Integration:** header-only · none for the C++ core; Eigen and OpenCV are optional (traits headers only); Python bindings need pybind11, NumPy, OpenMP and scikit-build (Python 3.10+); Google Benchmark, nanoflann and OpenCV only for the benchmarks; Google Test for the unit tests · C++17 (issue #32: does not compile with GCC 7.5 on Ubuntu 18.04); CMake 3.12+ if you use the CMake package rather than copying src/pico_tree · any; no SIMD intrinsics. CI builds on the latest macOS, Ubuntu and Windows runners

**Vs siblings:** Pick PicoTree over nanoflann when you rebuild static trees often on one thread, need box search or wrap-around metrics, or want NumPy bindings in the same package. Pick nanoflann when you need dynamic insert/remove, a multi-threaded build, distro/vcpkg/Conan packaging or active maintenance. picoflann, Janos95/kdtree and kd3 make similar nanoflann-beating claims but cover fewer query types.

**Gotchas:**
- With the default metric_l2_squared, radius inputs and all returned distances are squared, and approximate-search error ratios must be squared too (pass tree.metric()(1 + e))
- The tree takes the point set by value: pass std::move(points) or a std::reference_wrapper to avoid a copy. The tree holds pointers into its node pool, so it is move-only, and a referenced point set must outlive it and stay unchanged
- The default index type is int (32-bit signed). Query and tree scalar types must match exactly (a double query against a float tree fails to compile), and an empty input is caught only by assert
- save/load is a same-machine convenience: no endianness handling, no check that the stored tree matches the point set or template arguments, and the point set itself is not saved

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-08-10, v1.0.0 is the latest release, 49 stars) but MIT-licensed, header-only and small enough to vendor by copying src/pico_tree; the Python bindings must be built from source.

[repo](https://github.com/Jaybro/pico_tree) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Jaybro/pico_tree)

##### Polylidar3D  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

C++ concave-polygon (with holes) extraction from 2D points and 3D data; about 4.8x faster than CGAL 2D alpha shapes.

**Beats:** CGAL 2D Alpha Shapes (also PostGIS ST_ConcaveHull 2.5.2 and Spatialite ST_ConcaveHull, which the README treats as GEOS-based) — In the author's concavehull-evaluation repo, the 2D Polylidar (robust predicates on, Python bindings) was timed against CGAL 4.12 Alpha_shape_2 (C++, alpha shape plus unordered boundary edges), PostGIS 2.5.2 ST_ConcaveHull (via psycopg client, upload excluded) and in-memory Spatialite ST_ConcaveHull on points sampled inside the California outline. At about 64,000 points the chart shows Polylidar at about 30-40 ms versus about 200 ms for CGAL and 3-4 s for PostGIS. The 30-run subtimings on caholes_64000 give about 41 ms for Polylidar versus about 197 ms for CGAL (about 4.8x) and about 11.3 s for Spatialite (about 270x, derived from page data). No hardware, compiler or flags are stated. The RA-L 2020 paper (arXiv 2002.01886) reports 'more than four times speedup' per search snippets, but arxiv.org is blocked here and it was not opened.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked code is the old Polylidar2D (submodule 6e25d1f), not current Polylidar3D; RA-L paper unreadable here (possible B on retier); text sub-timings show ~4.8x vs CGAL.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked code is the polylidar2d branch, not master Polylidar3D. Robust predicates are off by default (the benchmark used them on). Boundary-trace failure prints to stderr and returns an empty shell. Abandoned 2023-03; wheels only up to cp310.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It Delaunay-triangulates the points with an in-tree port of Delaunator (mapbox/delaunator-cpp, a sweep-hull algorithm), drops triangles whose circumradius exceeds alpha or whose edges exceed lmax, and groups the remaining edge-connected triangles by breadth-first region growing over the half-edge structure.
