Each region becomes a polygon through boundary following: border half-edges (those whose twin is missing or filtered out) go into parallel-hashmap tables keyed by point, the shell is traced from the right-most extreme point, and the leftover border loops become holes. In the 64,000-point subtimings, about 36 ms of Polylidar's 41 ms is triangulation, with 4.4 ms for filtering and region growing and 1.0 ms for polygon extraction. CGAL spends 44 ms on triangulation and 153 ms building the alpha shape, including alpha intervals for every edge. In 3D mode, marl fibers and OpenMP parallelize over multiple dominant planes.

**Use it when:**
- Outlines with holes from dense 2D point sets (footprints, coverage areas, sampled regions) at 10^3-10^5 points, where CGAL alpha shapes took about 200 ms and PostGIS 2.5 ST_ConcaveHull about 3-4 s for 64,000 points versus Polylidar's 30-40 ms
- When you need a ready-made polygon (ordered shell plus holes) rather than unordered boundary edges you must stitch yourself
- Ground-plane or floor-region polygons from airborne LiDAR, RGB-D range images or meshes, in real-time robotics loops (RealSense and KITTI use-case repos exist)
- Python users who want a prebuilt wheel: PyPI polylidar 1.0.9 ships CPython 3.7-3.10 wheels for Linux x86-64, macOS (x86-64, arm64) and Windows x64

**Skip it when:**
- You need the exact CGAL alpha-shape definition, or many alpha levels from one build: Polylidar's circumradius/edge-length filter defines a different hull, and the benchmark itself notes that CGAL's per-edge alpha intervals give you a whole family of shapes
- Near-degenerate input (collinear or cocircular points) with default builds: Delaunator lacks robust predicates unless you compile with PL_USE_ROBUST_PREDICATES, which is OFF by default in CMake and is not set by setup.py
- Python 3.11+ or a maintained dependency: the last release (1.0.9) and last commit are from 2023-03-13, there are no wheels after cp310, and issues #16 (no polygons on airborne LiDAR) and #19 are open
- Precise geodesic or GIS-grade output: there is no snapping, validity repair or CRS handling, and polygons come back as point-index lists that you turn into geometries yourself (the Python helpers use Shapely)

**Integration:** static lib · Eigen, google/marl (task scheduler), greg7mdp parallel-hashmap and a fast-exp header, all bundled under thirdparty; optional OpenMP (disabled on Apple) and Shewchuk robust predicates (PL_Predicates); pybind11 for the Python module, with numpy, shapely and matplotlib in requirements.txt · C++14, CMake 3.14+ (the benchmark repo asks for a C++14 compiler) · Linux, Windows and macOS (x86-64 and arm64 wheels on PyPI); no SIMD-specific code found in the files read

**Vs siblings:** No sibling in this category extracts concave hulls. detria and Delaunay32 are fast 2D triangulators (benchmarked against CDT and Triangle, not Delaunator) but stop at the triangulation, the step that dominates Polylidar's runtime, and CGAL alpha shapes remain the reference when you need the exact alpha-complex definition or a family of alpha values.

**Gotchas:**
- The benchmarked code is the 2D Polylidar on the polylidar2d branch (the concavehull-evaluation submodule is at commit 6e25d1f). Master is Polylidar3D with a different API, and its 2D timings were not re-measured
- Defaults are tuned for 3D: lmax=1.0, min_triangles=20 and alpha=0.0 (off). For a 2D point set you must set alpha or lmax to your data's scale, or small regions are silently dropped
- When boundary tracing hits a broken edge (e.g. Delaunator mislabelling a hull edge), ConcaveSection prints to stderr and returns an empty shell instead of throwing, so check for empty polygons
- Robust predicates cost speed: the evaluation README says turning them off gives a further ~30%, so the headline numbers were taken with robust predicates on, while stock builds have them off

**Status:** Abandoned since 2023-03-13 (PyPI 1.0.9; 338 stars) but MIT-licensed. The 2D path is small enough to lift from the polylidar2d branch, while master pulls in marl, Eigen and parallel-hashmap.

[repo](https://github.com/JeremyBYU/polylidar) · [benchmark](https://github.com/JeremyBYU/concavehull-evaluation)

##### qdgeo  `Zig`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zig/WASM polygon booleans and rounded buffer for web GIS; 2.7-3.3x faster than native GEOS on a 4,040-parcel union.

**Beats:** GEOS 3.13.1 (via Shapely 2.1.2): union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and buffer — The author's comparison suite (tests/compare, Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseSafe, Node 22+) ran 26 union and buffer workloads on a 4,040-parcel, 135,080-coordinate public GeoMoose dataset. Each figure is the median of three suite runs of 11 repeats, on one unnamed idle machine. Against GEOS 3.13.1 via Shapely 2.1.2, the full union took 160 ms (WASM) and 130 ms (native) vs 426 ms (2.7x and 3.3x, derived from page data; the README rounds this to '3.1x native GEOS'). The geometric mean over all 26 workloads has native GEOS 1.5x slower than qdgeo WASM (1.36-1.62 across runs), and GEOS wins on the 19,208-coordinate single-parcel buffer. Boundaries differ: GEOS times the operation only on prebuilt GEOS objects, while qdgeo native includes a WKB parse and encode round trip. GEOS itself measured 417 ms and 356 ms an hour apart, so gaps under about 20% are unresolved.

**Known shortcoming:** No CPU model; the '3.1x' headline vs the table's 2.7x (wasm) / 3.3x (native); the GEOS boundary handling favours GEOS.

**Known shortcoming:** Zig, not C++: no C header; the native C ABI uses global state, is non-reentrant and meant for benchmarks. Not on npm (404); 0 stars, two weeks old. 4/3946 valid cluster unions error by design; GEOS is 4x faster on a 19k-coordinate buffer.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The overlay is a single Martinez-Rueda sweep line. It uses per-layer winding counts instead of in/out parity (no edge-type classification), orders events lexicographically by (x, y) as a symbolic shear so vertical edges need no special case, and calls exact adaptive orientation predicates at every sign decision. Events are stored structure-of-arrays with order-preserving u128 sort keys, bucketed by x and pdq-sorted within buckets, and the sweep processes all events at one point as a batch. The buffer follows the JTS/GEOS construction: one raw self-intersecting offset curve per ring, line or point, resolved in one overlay pass by keeping regions with winding depth at least 1. The result-vertex hash map is pre-sized to its upper bound with a cheap custom hash. There is no snap-rounding ladder: a failed labelling is retried once with a graph relabelling and once with re-noding, otherwise an error is returned. The WASM build enables simd128.

**Use it when:**
- Browser or Node web-GIS apps (OpenLayers, deck.gl, MapLibre, Leaflet) that need union/difference/buffer client-side: GEOS has no supported browser build, and qdgeo was 7-28x faster than JSTS, Turf and polyclip-ts on the author's parcel suite
- Unioning or buffering many adjacent cadastral parcels with hairline gaps and shared boundaries: the full 4,040-parcel union took 160 ms (WASM) or 130 ms (native) vs 426 ms for GEOS 3.13.1, and qdgeo was one of only two engines returning correct geometry there
- Pipelines that would rather get an error than snapped or approximated geometry: qdgeo's disputed vertices matched exact rational reconstruction (0 m error) where GEOS was off by up to 7.2e-5 m
- Small-download constraints: 50.8 KB gzipped vs about 778 KB for geos-wasm (which was not benchmarked)

**Skip it when:**
- Very large single polygons: on a 19,208-coordinate parcel GEOS buffered +2 m in 8.25 ms vs 33.2 ms (about 4x faster), and 13.0 vs 31.9 ms for -2 m
- Dirty or invalid input you expect the library to fix: qdgeo rejects zero-area or degenerate rings and failed noding instead of repairing them (6 of 161 JTS buffer assertions fail for this reason). Run make_valid/ST_MakeValid or GeoRepair first
- Workloads that need an answer for every valid input: 4 of 3,946 adjacent-parcel cluster unions return an error because f64 cannot hold the crossing. Smaller batches make this more likely (4 failures at 250-parcel batches, 0 at 500-1,000)
- C++ codebases wanting a native library: the core is Zig 0.16, no C header ships, and the native shared library's C ABI (global result block, single-threaded, non-reentrant, errors printed to stderr) is described as built for differential benchmarks
- Anything beyond five areal operations (predicates, line/point outputs, simplification, spatial indexes, CRS handling), or projects that need maturity: first commit 2026-09-14, 0 stars, not published to npm (registry returns 404)

**Integration:** module · none (pure Zig, no C or C++, WASM declares no imports); the comparison suite needs Python 3.13, Shapely/GEOS, Rust 1.88+ and npm engines · Zig 0.16.0 (minimum_zig_version); JS consumers need an ESM bundler or Node, and the harness used Node 22+ · wasm32-freestanding with simd128 (browsers, Node, workers; heap capped at 512 MiB), plus any native target Zig builds (static library, or shared libqdgeo_native with a C ABI)

**Vs siblings:** Pick qdgeo over clipper2next/Clipper2 or CavalierContours when the target is the browser or you need exact, unsnapped output on GIS parcels rather than integer-lattice C++ clipping. Pair it with GeoRepair, which handles the invalid-geometry repair qdgeo refuses, and use TG for fast point-in-polygon/intersects predicates, which qdgeo does not offer.

**Gotchas:**
- ABI status 5 means both 'malformed geometry' and 'valid but not representable in f64'. The failure is deterministic, so retrying does nothing, but nudging or rounding the input usually moves past it
- Coordinates are planar in input units and no CRS is read from WKB: reproject lon/lat to a metric CRS before asking for metre buffers
- Buffering several polygons buffers their union, and a zero-distance buffer still runs union and normalisation rather than returning a copy. Output limits are checked after construction, not enforced as an allocation budget
- The shipped WASM is ReleaseSafe (runtime safety checks on). ReleaseFast is 11% faster with bit-identical output if you build it yourself

**Status:** Brand-new (first commit 2026-09-14, last 2026-09-23, 15 commits, 0 stars) and actively developed by one author under MIT, with CI running unit tests, WASM checks and the JTS suite. The 'experimental' label was removed on 2026-09-16, but it has no npm release yet, so install it from git or vendor the WASM artifact.

[repo](https://github.com/theduckylittle/qdgeo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/theduckylittle/qdgeo)

##### RBush  `JavaScript`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

JavaScript 2D R-tree for rectangles and points with bulk loading; beats the older imbcmdth RTree JavaScript library.

**Beats:** imbcmdth RTree (older JavaScript R-tree library) — The README table is a first-party run on Node.js v6.2.2 on a mid-2012 Retina MacBook Pro (CPU model not given) with 1M random rectangles of ~0.01% area and maxEntries 16: one-by-one insert 3.18 s vs 7.83 s for imbcmdth's old RTree, 1000 searches at 0.01%/1%/10% area 0.03/0.35/2.18 s vs 0.93/2.27/9.53 s, removing 1000 items 0.02 s vs 1.18 s (about 59x, derived from page data, printed as 50x), and bulk insert of 1M items 1.25 s (the printed 6.7x does not follow from the table; 7.83/1.25 is about 6.3x, derived from page data). The script the README cites (debug/perf.js) is now bench/perf.js and times RBush alone, so the baseline column cannot be reproduced from the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Cited perf script is now bench/perf.js and runs RBush only, so the old-RTree column is not reproducible; Node 6.2.2 on a 2012 laptop; JavaScript.

**Known shortcoming:** JavaScript, not callable from C++. Current README recommends only kdbush, not Flatbush. Bulk-insert '6.7x' does not follow from the table (7.83/1.25 is ~6.3x, derived from page data). README fromJSON example still uses the old rbush(9) call.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Single inserts use a non-recursive R-tree insertion with the R*-tree split heuristics only (split axis by minimum total margin, split index by minimum overlap then area), skipping R*-tree forced reinsertion, which the author found too slow in JS. Bulk loading is OMT (Overlap Minimizing Top-down) packing: items are partitioned into roughly square tiles with a multi-select built on Floyd-Rivest quickselect, filling nodes to target height; bulk insertion into a non-empty tree uses Small-Tree-Large-Tree (the new batch is built as a subtree and grafted in). Search is iterative with an explicit stack and copies a whole subtree without per-item tests when the query box contains a node's box; deletion uses free-at-empty (no reinsertion on underflow).

**Use it when:**
- JavaScript/TypeScript maps, data visualisation, canvas or game code that needs bounding-box queries over 2D rectangles that are inserted and removed over time.
- Batch indexing of roughly 10^4 to 10^6 rectangles with load() (README: bulk insertion ~2-3x faster than one-by-one, and queries ~20-30% faster afterwards).
- Building an index on a Node.js server and sending it to browsers via toJSON()/fromJSON() with the same maxEntries.
- Incremental bulk updates where each batch is spatially clustered (STLT grafting works well for clustered data per the README).

**Skip it when:**
- Static point sets: the README itself points to kdbush, which indexes points 5-8x faster than RBush.
- C or C++ projects: this is a JavaScript library and its benchmark is JS versus JS; use a native sibling instead.
- 3D or higher-dimensional data, or nearest-neighbour queries without the extra rbush-knn package (RBush is 2D bounding-box search only).
- Bulk-inserting scattered data into an existing tree: the README warns this makes query performance worse.
- Rapidly moving objects: there is no update operation, only remove plus insert (issue #28, open since 2015); and CommonJS-only environments, since v4+ is ESM only.

**Integration:** module (npm ES module; also a UMD browser bundle rbush.min.js exposing a global RBush) · quickselect ^3.0.0 · An ES-module JavaScript environment (RBush v4+ dropped CommonJS); IE11 needs transpiling per the README · any JavaScript runtime (modern browsers, Node.js)

**Vs siblings:** Among catalogued siblings, pick RBush over KDBush only when you index rectangles or need insert/remove (KDBush is static points and, per RBush's own README, 5-8x faster at that); the native siblings (tidwall/rtree.c, PH-tree, GeoToolbox KdBoxTree) and the Rust geo-index are the choice outside JavaScript.

**Gotchas:**
- remove() matches by object reference by default; with a custom equals function the item you pass must still carry the original bounding box, because the traversal only descends into nodes whose box contains the item's box (index.js remove(); open issue #95).
- fromJSON() trusts its input and requires the same maxEntries as the exporting tree; the README's import example still uses the old rbush(9) factory call, while v4 is a class (new RBush(9)).
- maxEntries is clamped to at least 4 and minimum fill is 40%; higher maxEntries speeds insertion and slows search (README default 9, benchmark used 16).
- search() allocates and returns a fresh array per call, and load() copies the input array (data.slice()) before partitioning it.

**Status:** Maintained (last commit 2026-04-03, a dev-dependency update; last functional release v4.0.1 per package.json), MIT-licensed, a single ~500-line source file with one dependency, so easy to vendor; 8 open issues, all enhancements or questions.

[repo](https://github.com/mourner/rbush) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mourner/rbush)

##### SedonaDB (Apache Sedona DB)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust single-node spatial SQL/DataFrame engine on DataFusion; beats DuckDB Spatial and GeoPandas on spatial and KNN joins.

**Beats:** GeoPandas 1.1.1 and DuckDB 1.4.0 (SpatialBench single-node comparison); neither is one of the listed C++ baselines — Apache Sedona's own SpatialBench (v0.1.0 pre-release, run 2025-09-22) timed SedonaDB 0.1.0, DuckDB 1.4.0 and GeoPandas 1.1.1 with Shapely 2.1.1 on 12 queries at SF1 and SF10, on an AWS m7i.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GB; CPU model not named), from cold S3 Parquet reads, with default settings and no build flags stated. Against DuckDB, SedonaDB was 1.05-1.5x faster on most filter queries, 11x faster on SF1 q10 and 218x/2,480x faster on q9, finished q11-q12 where DuckDB timed out or errored, and was 2.8-3.5x slower on q5 (ratios derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Rust spatial SQL engine, not a C++ library (wrong language, arguably wrong category). First-party SpatialBench (m7i.2xlarge, no CPU model, v0.1.0, a year old); 2.8-3.5x slower than DuckDB on q5; the q9 218x/2,480x wins and ERROR/TIMEOUT cells reflect DuckDB/GeoPandas plans and missing KNN-join support.

**Known shortcoming:** A Rust SQL engine, not a C++ library: the only native entry point is the ADBC driver (AdbcSedonadbDriverInit). SpatialBench is first-party and was run on 0.1.0 only; q5 spatial aggregation is 2.8-3.5x slower than DuckDB. Releases are at 0.4.1 (2026-08-22) with main at 0.5.0. Internally it uses tidwall/tg as the default refiner and geo-index's Hilbert RTree, both already catalogued. The spatialists.ch 130-million-point join post (SedonaDB 0.3.0 6 s vs DuckDB 13 s / 1m30s on an M4) is by a Wherobots engineer and SedonaDB contributor, so not independent; the 0.4.0 GPU-join blog (Q11 7.51 s CPU vs 1.61 s on an RTX 3090) is first-party. Both seen only as snippets.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Spatial joins are two-phase: a filter phase on a packed Hilbert-sorted R-tree (geo-index RTree<f32> over bounding boxes) and a refine phase that checks exact predicates with tidwall's TG library (y-stripes index, the default), GEOS or the Rust geo crate. A speculative execution mode samples the first 1,000 geometries and then decides whether to build prepared geometries on the build side, the probe side or neither. KNN joins have their own operator. The engine is columnar and vectorized on Arrow and DataFusion, runs multi-threaded with probe-side repartitioning, and can spatially partition and spill the build side to disk for joins larger than memory.

**Use it when:**
- Spatial joins (point-in-polygon, intersects, ST_DWithin) and KNN joins over millions of rows in Parquet/GeoParquet on one machine: the largest wins on the page are q9-q12, where DuckDB 1.4.0 timed out or errored
- Replacing single-threaded GeoPandas pipelines: SF1 queries ran 1.2x to 82x faster than a hand-written GeoPandas mirror, and SedonaDB finished SF10 queries where GeoPandas errored or timed out
- Python or R analytics that already use Arrow, DuckDB or Polars and want a spatial engine with CRS tracking and zero-copy Arrow exchange
- Joins bigger than RAM: the spatial join can partition the build side and spill it to disk
- Optional GPU spatial joins (libgpuspatial, added in 0.4.0) for heavy joins, if you can build and run that path

**Skip it when:**
- Inside a C++ program that needs geometry predicates, overlays or an index: it is a Rust query engine, not a C++ library; use GEOS, TG or Boost.Geometry directly
- Spatial aggregation queries: SpatialBench q5 ran 2.8x (SF1) and 3.5x (SF10) slower than DuckDB, and the project calls this a known weakness
- Simple spatial filters where DuckDB Spatial is already in the stack: q1-q8 are roughly even (1.0-1.5x either way)
- Projects that need a stable API: the engine is pre-1.0 (0.1.0 in September 2025, 0.4.1 in August 2026, workspace at 0.5.0) and adds features each release
- Transactional or multi-node workloads: it is a single-node analytical engine; the project points to PostGIS-style databases and SedonaSpark/SedonaFlink for those

**Integration:** module · Python wheel (pip install "apache-sedona[db]" or sedonadb; conda-forge sedonadb); R package on R-multiverse; from source: Rust workspace on Apache Arrow 58 and DataFusion 54, with C libraries GEOS, TG, PROJ, s2geography, GDAL and an optional GPU library behind wrapper crates · Rust 1.88 (rust-version in Cargo.toml); Python >= 3.9 · PyPI wheels for Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux_2_28), macOS arm64 and x86-64 (macOS 12+), and Windows x86-64

**Vs siblings:** Pick SedonaDB when the job is a whole spatial query over tables (joins, KNN joins, filters on Parquet) and you are in Python, R or SQL. Use TG or geo-index directly from C or Rust when you only need predicates or an index; SedonaDB uses both inside its join. Arctern targets the same GeoPandas-replacement niche but publishes only its own 24x claim.

**Gotchas:**
- The join's R-tree stores f32 bounding boxes; exact predicates are evaluated in the refine phase, and which library does that (TG by default, then GEOS or geo) depends on sedona.spatial_join options. TG falls back to geo for predicates it does not support
- KNN joins drop tied-distance rows by default (knn_include_tie_breakers = false)
- The published SpatialBench numbers are for 0.1.0 with cold reads from S3 and DuckDB's external file cache turned off; later releases have no published re-run on the same hardware
- For C/C++ hosts the only native entry point is the ADBC driver (AdbcSedonadbDriverInit in rust/sedona-adbc), which you build from source

**Status:** Very active Apache project (509 stars, 1,084 commits, five PyPI releases from 0.1.0 in September 2025 to 0.4.1 on 2026-08-22, main at 0.5.0); Apache-2.0 and pip/conda installable, but it is a Rust engine and not something you vendor into C++.

[repo](https://github.com/apache/sedona-db) · [benchmark](https://github.com/apache/sedona-spatialbench/blob/main/docs/single-node-benchmarks.md)

##### small_gicp  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++17 point-cloud registration (ICP/GICP/VGICP) and voxel downsampling; beats PCL VoxelGrid, PCL GICP and fast_gicp.

**Beats:** PCL pcl::VoxelGrid (voxel downsampling) and pcl::GICP / fast_gicp::GICP (registration) — First-party KITTI 00 runs (BENCHMARK.md and README, plots only): single-thread voxel downsampling about 1.3x faster than pcl::VoxelGrid and 3.2x with 6 TBB threads; single-thread GICP odometry about 2.4x faster than pcl::GICP and 1.9x faster than fast_gicp::GICP with near-identical accuracy (APE 6.096 vs fast_gicp 6.118 vs pcl_gicp 6.451); parallel kd-tree build up to 4x (BENCHMARK.md) or 6x (README) over its own single-thread build, which is about nanoflann speed. CPU, compiler and flags are not stated (only a struck-through AMD 5995WX remark); scripts are public, the CMake default is Release without -march=native.

**Known shortcoming:** JOSS paper restates first-party bullets; kd-tree gain stated as 4x/6x/6x vs nanoflann; point-cloud registration, an edge case for geometry-spatial.

**Known shortcoming:** Open #134: unbounded nearest-neighbour search with rejection afterwards, measured slower than Open3D on ~10%-overlap data. #127 (non-orthogonal rotation then NaN after ~40 incremental clouds) fixed 2026-09-29. Threaded downsampling is nondeterministic (up to 10% more points); by code reading the OMP variant still outputs an out-of-range point when one starts a 1024-point block.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Voxel downsampling packs each point's three integer voxel coordinates (fast floor) into one 63-bit key (21 bits per axis), sorts (key, index) pairs (parallel quicksort in the OpenMP/TBB variants) and averages each run, so no hash map is needed. The kd-tree is a from-scratch nanoflann-style median-split tree (std::nth_element on the widest axis) whose recursive build runs as OpenMP or TBB tasks, with fixed-size compile-time kNN result buffers. Registration linearizes one GICP factor per source point (Mahalanobis weight from the inverse of the fused target and rotated source covariances) and sums the 6x6 normal equations with an OpenMP or TBB parallel reduction; a TBB flow-graph odometry pipeline scales to about 128 threads.

**Use it when:**
- LiDAR odometry or scan matching that already uses pcl::GeneralizedIterativeClosestPoint or fast_gicp on the CPU and wants a faster, mostly source-compatible replacement.
- Voxel downsampling of large scans, including fine resolutions where pcl::VoxelGrid fails (README: 0.5 mm voxels on a 1000 m-wide cloud) and you want exact per-voxel means rather than pcl::ApproximateVoxelGrid's spurious points.
- Multi-core machines: downsampling, kd-tree build, covariance estimation and the registration reduction are all parallel (OpenMP or TBB).
- Python pipelines that need GICP/VGICP without PCL (pip install small_gicp; works on NumPy and Open3D data).
- Scan-to-scan odometry that reuses preprocessed clouds and trees across successive alignments (swapSourceAndTarget, preprocess_points).

**Skip it when:**
- Low-overlap registration with a tight correspondence distance: it runs an unbounded nearest-neighbour search and only then rejects by max_dist_sq, and a user measured it slower than Open3D's radius-limited search on ~10% overlap data (issue #134, open).
- GPU pipelines: no GPU code is included (fast_gicp's CUDA VGICP/NDT have not been ported; issue #80).
- General computational geometry or spatial indexing: it is a registration toolkit, not a Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS replacement, and its kd-tree offers kNN only (no radius search in kdtree.hpp).
- Workflows needing bit-identical, deterministic downsampling with threads: the OpenMP/TBB voxel functions can return up to 10% more points than the single-thread one, varying run to run.
- ROS Noetic's stock PCL or any PCL older than 1.11 (boost::shared_ptr), which the PCL interface does not support (README; issue #33).

**Integration:** header-only (optional compiled helper library, shared by default, and a pybind11 Python module) · Eigen 3 (CMake downloads 3.4.0 if missing); bundled nanoflann-derived kd-tree and Sophus-derived Lie utilities; optional OpenMP, Intel TBB, PCL >= 1.11; fmt for tests, examples and benchmarks · C++17, CMake 3.16; Python >= 3.7 for the bindings · Linux, macOS and Windows (CI for all three); PyPI wheels for manylinux x86-64 and aarch64, macOS 14+, Windows 64-bit; SSE/SSE2 baseline unless BUILD_WITH_MARCH_NATIVE=ON

**Vs siblings:** It is the only catalogued sibling that does point-cloud registration and voxel downsampling; for plain kNN or radius search pick nanoflann (which its own single-thread kd-tree roughly matches) or PicoTree, and pick small_gicp when you need the whole parallel registration pipeline or a faster PCL GICP.

**Gotchas:**
- BUILD_WITH_MARCH_NATIVE gives about 1.1x but crashes unless every linked library (Eigen users, PCL) is built with -march=native; it is off by default for that reason (BENCHMARK.md). Open issue #108 reports an Eigen unaligned-array assertion in the basic example.
- Voxel coordinates must fit 21 bits per axis (for 1 cm voxels, coordinates within about ±10.5 km); out-of-range points are dropped with one std::cerr line per point. By my reading of downsampling_omp.hpp, an out-of-range point that starts a 1024-point block is still emitted in the parallel variant.
- align() re-orthonormalizes the rotation of init_T since the fix for issue #127 (incremental registration into a Gaussian voxel map drifted to non-orthogonal rotations and NaN after ~40 clouds; closed 2026-09-29); use a current commit for long incremental runs. It only warns, and still runs, when a cloud has 10 points or fewer.
- Input point types must expose homogeneous 4D coordinates with w = 1: downsampling divides each voxel sum by its w component to get the mean.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-29, version 1.0.1), MIT-licensed, on PyPI, with a JOSS 2024 paper; a single main author (Kenji Koide, AIST) and 24 open issues, several labelled bug (performance reports #89, #118, #134; build issues #90, #104).

[repo](https://github.com/koide3/small_gicp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/koide3/small_gicp/blob/master/BENCHMARK.md)

##### THST (Hierarchical spatial trees)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++03 R-tree and 2D quadtree that compile about 25x faster than Boost.Geometry rtree code; runtime is not faster overall.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry index (rtree) — The author reused Loskot and Wulkiewicz's spatial_index_benchmark: 1M small random boxes inserted iteratively, 100K intersection queries with boxes 10x larger, and a 200-run dynamic clear/query/insert loop, comparing THST quadtree/quadratic/quadratic-sphere (heap and custom allocator) with Boost.Geometry rtree linear/quadratic/R* (iterative and bulk, compile-time parameters) on an Intel Core i7-4870HQ under macOS Sierra, built as an Xcode Release (exact compiler and flags not stated). The only numeric claim is benchmark compile time, 35.3 s for Boost vs 1.4 s for THST; runtime results are PNG charts in which Boost bulk/R* leads queries and THST quadratic wins only the dynamic case above about 400 objects.

**Known shortcoming:** Only win is compile time (35.3 s vs 1.4 s); its own benchmark README says Boost.Geometry rtree has faster queries; wins only the dynamic case above ~400 objects.

**Known shortcoming:** Only win is compile time (35.3 s vs 1.4 s); Boost bulk/R* rtree has better query times; no bulk loading; open #23 assertion failure in choosePartition (bad node split); several failure cases checked only by assert; iterators use a fixed 16-level stack; nearest() 2D only; 'C++03' claim partial (k_nearest needs C++11).

**How:** The compile-time win comes from a small templated code base (Guttman's 1984 R-tree via the Greg Douglas / nushoin C++ ports) with none of Boost.Geometry's concept, variant-visitor and strategy machinery. At runtime it uses Guttman's quadratic split (pickSeeds/classify) with an optional spherical-volume measure, fixed-size nodes holding parallel arrays of values, boxes and child pointers, and a pluggable node allocator; the benchmark's fastest THST variant uses a test-only allocator that places all nodes in one pre-sized std::vector. There is no bulk loading (listed under 'Future improvements'), no R*-tree reinsertion and no SIMD.

**Use it when:**
- Projects where build time matters and Boost.Geometry's rtree headers dominate compile time: the README reports 1.4 s vs 35.3 s to compile the benchmark program
- Games, physics and editors that rebuild or heavily update a small index every frame: the project's dynamic benchmark shows THST quadratic ahead of bgi linear above about 400 objects
- Hierarchical scene partitioning where you want to store data on internal nodes, walk the tree level by level (dbegin/child iterators) or stop a query once a node is fully contained (hierachical_query)
- Ray casting against boxes (rayQuery with a filter predicate) without pulling in a BVH library
- Old toolchains: the core RTree/QuadTree is written for C++03 and needs no dependencies

**Skip it when:**
- Query-heavy static data: per the project's own charts, Boost.Geometry rtree with bulk loading or R* gives the best query times, ahead of THST's best (quadratic with custom allocator)
- Large static datasets that you can bulk-load: THST has only one-by-one insertion, while Boost's packing algorithm loads fastest
- Fewer than about 400 objects in a rebuild-every-frame loop: bgi linear was slightly faster there in the same benchmark
- QuadTree for 1M-box workloads: the benchmark README calls quadtree queries 'really slow' and building 'very slow' for capacities 256-1024
- Code that needs active maintenance or a package: last commit March 2024, issue #23 (assertion failure in RTree::choosePartition, Oct 2023) is still open, and there is no vcpkg port (issue #26 open)

**Integration:** header-only · none (the benchmark needs Boost headers, CMake and gnuplot; tests use doctest as a git submodule) · C++03 for the core trees; RTree::k_nearest (priority_queue::emplace) and QuadTree::clear (nullptr) need C++11; move constructors are enabled under C++11/MSVC 2013+ · any (portable scalar C++; benchmarked on macOS with Xcode, CMake files also handle MSVC, GCC and Clang)

**Vs siblings:** Pick THST over tidwall/rtree.c or GeoToolbox KdBoxTree when you want a templated, header-only C++ tree with hierarchical iteration, ray queries and low compile cost; pick those siblings (or nanoflann for point k-NN) when raw insert/query throughput against Boost is the goal, since THST's own benchmark does not show a runtime win over a bulk-loaded Boost rtree.

**Gotchas:**
- Several failure cases are checked only by assert, so release builds do not catch them: inserting a box outside a QuadTree's world box, more than 16 levels in the depth/leaf iterators' fixed stack (a write past the array), and the under-filled node split reported in open issue #23
- RTree::nearest(point, radius) is 2D only (static assert) and ranks by distance to box centre; k_nearest works in N dimensions and uses minimum distance to the box
- Node capacity and min fill are template parameters (defaults M=8, m=M/2); the benchmark sweeps M from small values up to 40x the base and results depend strongly on it
- The 'custom' allocator in the benchmark is test/custom_allocator.h, not part of include/; it must be pre-sized (nodeCount * 1.5) and only asserts on overflow

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2024-03-16, a CMake install-script PR) but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and small (RTree.h is about 1,800 lines, QuadTree.h about 800), so easy to vendor; treat it as a compile-time and feature pick, not a runtime-speed pick.

[repo](https://github.com/tuxalin/THST) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tuxalin/THST)

##### tidwall/rtree.c  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-file C dynamic R-tree with O(1) copy-on-write clones; inserts 20-40x faster than Boost.Geometry's R*-tree.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree — The independent GeoToolbox suite compared rtree.c v0.5.3 (compiled as C with RTREE_NOATOMICS, 2D, double) with Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree on 25 point and 44 box dataset/size combinations of 10^2-10^6 elements. It was built with MSVC 2026 and clang-cl 22 (Release, /arch:AVX2 and LTO per its public CMakeLists) on an ASUS ROG Strix G16 laptop under Windows 11, CPU model not stated. The result TSVs show dynamic insert/erase/reinsert far faster than Boost: insert 21-41x, erase 2.8-4.1x, reinsert 8-10x and the scenario total 4.8-6.4x (geomeans). Range queries were at parity (1.00-1.12x) after dynamic builds and slightly slower (0.80-0.92x) than Boost's bulk-loaded tree (all ratios derived from page data). The author's own README reports 151 ns/op insert and 242 ns/op item search on 1M random points (clang-17 -O3, Ryzen 9 5950X) with no Boost comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Range queries only on par with Boost.Geometry (1.06-1.08x, as low as 0.3x on some datasets); source is a small third-party suite (GeoToolbox) with no flags and no CPU model; highest memory of the indexes tested; no bulk-load, results depend on insertion order.

**Known shortcoming:** GeoToolbox pinned v0.5.3 (May 2024); v0.6.0 (2026-09-05) dropped 10% min fill, sort-on-split and default path hints, so current code is unbenchmarked. Measured 2D double only (record said 2D/3D). Range query vs a bulk-loaded Boost tree 0.80-0.92x, 0.3-0.7x at 10^2 elements; memory 58-70 MB vs Boost 43 MB at 10^6.

**Known shortcoming:** API: rtree_delete returns true when nothing was deleted; rtree.h hard-codes double/void* and rtree.c no longer includes it, so an RTREE_NUMTYPE override compiles silently mismatched (inferred from code).

**How:** Insertion is a cheap Guttman R-tree variant rather than R*: descending, it takes the first child whose rectangle already contains the new item, otherwise the child with least area enlargement. It never computes overlap and never does R*'s forced reinsertion, which is where Boost's insert cost goes. A full node is split in one linear pass ('edge snap'): each entry goes to whichever edge of the node's largest axis it is nearer, with no sorting since v0.6.0. Nodes are wide (64 entries) and keep their 64 rectangles in one contiguous array beside the child or payload array, so a search scans packed coordinates with branch-light intersect tests. Deletion only unlinks emptied nodes and never condenses or reinserts, which keeps erase cheap.

**Use it when:**
- Dynamic 2D sets with heavy churn (moving entities, live map features, geofences, editors): in GeoToolbox's insert/erase/reinsert/query scenario, insert was 21-41x, erase 2.8-4.1x and reinsert 8-10x faster than Boost R*-tree (geomeans), and the whole scenario 4.8-6.4x faster (11-13x at 10^6 elements). All ratios derived from page data
- Point or box keys with window (intersects) queries on 10^3-10^6 elements when the index is built and updated by insertion. Range queries afterwards were at parity with a dynamically built Boost tree (1.00-1.12x geomean) and up to about 2x faster at 10^4-10^5 elements (derived from page data)
- C code or FFI that wants one MIT-licensed .c/.h pair with no dependencies and a custom malloc/free hook
- Snapshot isolation: rtree_clone is O(1) and copies nodes lazily on write, so readers can keep an old version while a writer mutates a clone
- Input you can pre-sort along a Hilbert curve: the README's 1M-point run drops insert from 151 to 73 ns/op and item search from 242 to 83 ns/op compared with random order

**Skip it when:**
- Nearest-neighbour or kNN queries: there are none. Use nanoflann (points), GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or Boost R*-tree
- Static, query-heavy data: there is no bulk load (STR or Hilbert packing). After an insert-built load, range queries were 0.80-0.92x the speed of Boost's packed tree (geomean), and KdBoxTree is faster still. Insert-built loading itself was 1.3-1.5x faster than Boost's packing (derived from page data)
- Tiny sets of about 10^2 elements: range queries ran at 0.3-0.7x Boost's speed and the full insert/erase/query scenario at 0.33-0.79x (derived from page data)
- Tight memory: at 10^6 2D keys it used about 58-70 MB against Boost 43 MB, KdBoxTree 30-50 MB and nanoflann 8-17 MB (GeoToolbox memory deltas)
- Several dimensions or coordinate types in one program: one DIMS/NUMTYPE per compiled copy of rtree.c. GeoToolbox measured only 2D with double coordinates

**Integration:** source-drop · none (libc; <stdatomic.h> for copy-on-write reference counts unless RTREE_NOATOMICS is defined) · C11 (stdatomic.h, compound literals in the examples); MSVC needs RTREE_NOATOMICS or /experimental:c11atomics, which GeoToolbox handles that way. From C++, compile rtree.c as C · any; portable C with no SIMD or platform code

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over GeoToolbox KdBoxTree and nanoflann when the set changes continuously, since neither supports erase. Pick it over THST when you want a plain C, MIT-licensed dynamic tree with copy-on-write snapshots. For static data, or when you need nearest-neighbour queries, KdBoxTree (boxes) or nanoflann (points) are faster, and TG covers polygon predicates rather than indexing.

**Gotchas:**
- rtree.h has no extern "C" guard, so wrap the include from C++. Its prototypes hard-code double coordinates and a void* payload, and since v0.6.0 rtree.c no longer includes rtree.h. Changing RTREE_NUMTYPE/RTREE_DATATYPE without editing the header therefore compiles silently against mismatched types (inferred from code; the README says to edit the header to match)
- rtree_delete needs a bit-identical rectangle and the same payload pointer (memcmp, or a comparator via rtree_delete_with_comparator), and removes only the first match. It returns true even when nothing matched, so check rtree_count if you need to know
- The published numbers are for older code. GeoToolbox pinned v0.5.3 (May 2024), and the README's run dates from 2023. v0.6.0 (2026-09-05) removed the 10% minimum fill on splits (a node may hold one entry), removed sort-on-split and turned path hints off by default, and no benchmark of the current code is published
- The README's algorithm notes (ties go to the smallest area; an 'equal' bucket during splits) do not match the current code, which keeps the first least-enlargement child and sends ties to the left node. Deletes never refill underfull nodes, so heavy deletion can leave sparse nodes

**Status:** Maintained by a single author (v0.6.1 tagged 2026-09-06, last commit 2026-09-21, 149 stars, 2 open issues), MIT-licensed and about 800 lines of C, so easy to vendor. Pin a tag, because v0.6.0 changed the split rules after the published benchmarks.

[repo](https://github.com/tidwall/rtree.c) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ikolev21/GeoToolbox/blob/main/Readme.md)

##### TinyBVH  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++ BVH builder and ray tracer; author's benchmark shows faster SAH builds and single-ray traversal than Embree.

**Beats:** Intel Embree (also madmann91/bvh) — The author's preliminary chart, produced with the public tiny_bvh_benchmark.cpp (built per build.bat with g++ -std=c++20 -mavx2 -mfma -Ofast; Windows-only harness; CPU model not published), measures Crytek Sponza (263k triangles): a 'fast build' takes ~6.7 ms vs Embree 4 at ~17.5 ms and madmann91/bvh at ~13 ms (~2.6x vs Embree, derived from page data). Single-core single-ray traversal reaches ~16 vs ~6.2 (Embree) vs ~2.3 (madmann91) MRay/s for nearest hit and ~36 vs ~23.5 MRay/s for any hit. The harness tilts some comparisons: TinyBVH traces an SBVH BVH4 optimized for 100 iterations while Embree's build quality for the chart is not stated; Embree's timing loop resets tfar to 1e30 instead of each ray's tmax (this matters for the AO ray set, whose tmax is 5% of scene size); madmann91 creates a new thread pool inside every timed build. An earlier README, still in the wjakob fork, said Embree beat TinyBVH on any-hit rays.

**Known shortcoming:** Author calls results 'preliminary'; numbers read off a chart; only single-ray traversal compared, not Embree's packet/stream paths; Embree is not a listed category baseline; no CPU, compiler or flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark tilts against rivals: Embree's timing loop resets tfar to 1e30 instead of each ray's tmax (matters for the AO set, tmax = 5% of scene size); madmann91 builds create a new thread pool inside every timed build; TinyBVH traces an SBVH BVH4 optimized for 100 iterations while Embree's build quality is not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** An earlier README (still in the wjakob fork) said Embree beat TinyBVH on any-hit rays; the current chart shows TinyBVH ~36 vs Embree ~23.5 MRay/s. Flags are public in build.bat (g++ -std=c++20 -mavx2 -mfma -Ofast) but the harness is Windows-only and names no CPU, so it stays C.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: BVH_GPU::ConvertFrom ignores vertex indices (issue #301, open, still at HEAD), so indexed meshes get wrong GPU geometry.

**Known shortcoming:** Robustness: a NaN ray or any fatal error calls exit(1); traversal stacks are fixed-size with no bounds check (stack overflow on San Miguel reported in #300).

**Known shortcoming:** Possibly the wrong category: ray-tracing acceleration structure, not a Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS workload.

**How:** The default build is a binned SAH builder (8 bins) with AVX or NEON bin evaluation, run on a process-wide std::thread pool for meshes of 50k+ triangles. The fastest CPU layout, BVH4_CPU, follows the WiVe design (Fuetterling et al., HPG 2017): 128-byte 4-wide nodes with child bounds in SoA form and a precomputed per-octant child order, kernels templated on the ray-direction signs, FMA slab tests, and leaves of 4 triangles tested together with SIMD. Optional quality passes are SBVH spatial splits (Stich et al. 2009), pre-splitting and tree-rotation optimization (Bittner et al. 2013), which lower SAH cost at the price of build time. There is also a 64-ray bundle (packet) traversal path (WiVeC) for coherent rays.

**Use it when:**
- CPU ray casting against static or rigidly instanced triangle meshes (visibility, AO, baking, picking, path tracing) when you want one dependency-free header instead of linking Embree and TBB.
- Frequent rebuilds of meshes in the 100k-1M triangle range: the author measures a ~6.7 ms SAH build for the 263k-triangle Sponza. Refit is the cheaper option for small deformations with a fixed triangle count.
- Building BVHs on the CPU for your own GPU traversal (CWBVH, Aila-Laine BVH_GPU, BVH4_GPU) in OpenCL, compute shaders or WebGPU without vendor ray-tracing APIs.
- Targets where shipping one header is simpler than shipping Embree: WASM/Emscripten (SIMD128), Android/Apple NEON, plus double-precision BVHs (BVH_Double, BVH4_Double).

**Skip it when:**
- Spatial queries this category's baselines serve: point k-NN, box range queries, polygon predicates and GIS geometry. TinyBVH answers ray and sphere-overlap queries over triangles and AABBs only.
- Workloads that need Embree's wider primitive set (curves/hair, subdivision surfaces, motion blur), none of which is in TinyBVH's feature list.
- Code that must not be terminated by a library: fatal errors (NaN in a ray, empty mesh, rebuilding a non-rebuildable BVH) call exit(1) unless you install a handler that throws.
- x86 builds without -mavx2 -mfma, and 32-bit x86, RISC-V or PowerPC: the SIMD builder and the BVH4_CPU/BVH8_CPU kernels compile out, leaving scalar code.
- Projects that need a frozen API: in September 2026 alone the header was split into several files and ray directions stopped being normalized, and correctness issues remain open (#301, #291).

**Integration:** header-only · none (tiny_ocl.h and OpenCL are needed only for the GPU examples) · C++17 by default (threaded builds); C++14 with NO_THREADED_BUILDS; the repo's CMake and build.bat use C++20. GCC, clang, MSVC and Emscripten are supported. · x86-64 (SSE4.2/AVX/AVX2+FMA kernels, scalar fallback without them), aarch64 NEON, WASM SIMD128; scalar code on any other C++17 target

**Vs siblings:** Pick TinyBVH when the query is ray-triangle intersection (nearest or any hit) over large meshes, on the CPU or GPU. The catalogued siblings answer other questions: nanoflann, tidwall/rtree.c, THST and GeoToolbox for point k-NN and box range queries, TG for 2D polygon predicates, and Manifold, MeshLib or trueform for mesh booleans and mesh processing.

**Gotchas:**
- Every BVH::Intersect call runs VALIDATE_RAY, so one NaN in a ray's origin, direction or t ends the process with exit(1). Call tinybvh_set_fatal_error_handler with a handler that throws if you need to recover.
- On x86, compiling without -mavx2 -mfma only prints a warning and defines TINYBVH_NO_SIMD, so the program silently falls back to scalar code. The fast layouts need AVX2+FMA; CMake passes -march=native and build.bat passes -mavx2 -mfma.
- Since PR #296 (merged 2026-09-23), ray directions are used as given, so hit.t scales with |D|; define NORMALIZE_RAY_DIR for the old behaviour. Input vertices are float4, with w as padding that is sometimes reused (for example for triangle color).
- BVH_GPU::ConvertFrom ignores vertex indices (issue #301, open; still at tiny_bvh_base.h line 4650 at HEAD), so indexed meshes give wrong GPU geometry in that layout. Traversal kernels use fixed stacks (TINYBVH_STACK_SIZE 128, doubled for wide layouts) with no bounds check in the hot loop, and a stack overflow on the San Miguel scene in BVH4_CPU conversion was reported (#300).

**Status:** Very active (v1.9.0, last commit 2026-09-25, 1,753 commits, 34 contributors, 1.2k stars), MIT-licensed and used in Remedy Northlight, SideFX Houdini and EA SEED Gigi; it is easy to vendor, but pin a commit because layouts and semantics still change.

[repo](https://github.com/jbikker/tinybvh) · [benchmark](https://github.com/jbikker/tinybvh)

##### trees (balanced and left-balanced kd-trees)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++17 kd-trees (balanced and stackless left-balanced) for parallel kNN; builds faster than nanoflann, queries sometimes slower.

**Beats:** nanoflann (parallel construction and querying) — Author's issue #1 (Aug 2023, under the earlier name 'mapletrees') compares parallel construction and parallel all-points kNN for k = 10, 50 and 100 against nanoflann on z-curve-sorted random 3D points with 12-point leaves, on a 2022 MacBook Pro with Apple M1 Pro. The results are graphs only: build is faster, and combined build plus query is ahead until nanoflann catches up near k = 100. The flags are -O3 -ffast-math -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=fast, the compiler is not stated, and nanoflann is cloned at HEAD and built with hardware_concurrency threads in the wrapper.

**Known shortcoming:** Graphs only (plot images unreadable here); flags in CMake (-O3 -ffast-math) but compiler unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Likely concurrency bug (code reading plus a simulation of split sizes, not compiled or run): the parallel build is on by default and joins its threads only when exactly 2^ceil(log2(hw threads)) are spawned; some n spawn fewer (balanced tree, 8 threads: n 136-142; left-balanced with leaves, 8 threads: n 128-239), so the constructor returns while threads still write the tree, the left-balanced constructor frees index_ under them, and destroying the tree calls std::terminate. k=1 search or kIterative on the balanced tree calls exit(1). Max bounds start at numeric_limits::min() (perf only). README's radius search is not in the current kdtree.h.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Every internal node is itself a data point (the median from std::nth_element along the widest bounding-box extent), and the node stores the point index with the split axis packed into the low 3 bits, so balanced and bucketed left-balanced trees take 3 x sizeof(index_t) per point and the bucketless left-balanced tree only 1 x (README; nanoflann about 3-4 x). The left-balanced layout needs no child pointers and allows a stackless parent-index traversal (after Ingo Wald's work); the balanced query prunes with an incrementally updated point-to-cell box distance. Construction is parallelised by spawning one std::thread per subtree at depth ceil(log2(hardware threads)); the benchmark also pre-sorts points along a Morton (z-order) curve, timed separately and given to both libraries.

**Use it when:**
- All-points k-nearest-neighbour queries with small k (roughly 10-50) on millions of 3D points, e.g. Voronoi or Delaunay meshing via the radius-of-security theorem, where build time matters.
- Static point sets that are rebuilt often, so faster parallel construction outweighs slightly slower queries.
- Memory-tight cases: the bucketless left-balanced tree uses one index per point.
- Experiments with stackless, GPU-portable kd-tree traversal (the iterative left-balanced query).

**Skip it when:**
- Large k (about 100 or more): the author reports nanoflann catching up, and queries can be slower than nanoflann.
- Radius search, dynamic insert/remove or more than 6 dimensions: the README calls radius search experimental and not recommended, I found no radius function in the current kdtree.h, and dim <= 6 is a static_assert.
- Production code that needs support: 1 star, one author, no releases or unit tests (only a benchmark driver), stale since 2025-06-17.
- MSVC builds: the header uses GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_clz, __builtin_clzll, __builtin_expect).
- Single-nearest queries through NearestNeighborSearch with k = 1: its constructor calls exit(1) unless k > 1 (use the nearest() helper, which searches k = 2 internally).

**Integration:** header-only (single kdtree.h) · none for kdtree.h (standard library and std::thread); the benchmark build clones nanoflann, morton-nd and the author's stlext at HEAD · C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17) with GCC or Clang builtins; compiler versions not documented · not documented; author benchmarks on an Apple M1 Pro (aarch64) and runs a smaller benchmark in GitHub Actions

**Vs siblings:** Among catalogued kd-tree siblings, nanoflann is the safer general choice (radius search, dynamic indices, maintained), and PicoTree and Janos95/kdtree also report beating nanoflann. Pick trees only when you want a tiny dependency-free header with parallel construction and a 1-index-per-point layout for small-k all-points kNN, and you can set parallel = false or control input sizes.

**Gotchas:**
- Parallel build (options.parallel defaults to true) joins its threads only when the number spawned at depth ceil(log2(hardware_concurrency)) is exactly 2^depth. By my reading of kdtree.h plus a simulation of its split sizes, some inputs spawn fewer: balanced tree, leaf_size 16, 8 threads: n = 136-142; left-balanced with leaves, 8 threads: n = 128-239; bucketless left-balanced, 32 threads: n = 65-125. In those cases the constructor returns while threads still write the tree, the left-balanced constructor then frees its index_ buffer under them, and destroying the tree calls std::terminate on joinable threads. Set options.parallel = false for small or medium inputs.
- Maxima are initialised with std::numeric_limits<coord_t>::min() (the smallest positive value, not the lowest), so on an axis whose coordinates are all negative the split-axis choice and root bounding box are wrong. As far as I can tell this only loosens pruning (results stay correct), but shifting data to positive coordinates avoids it.
- The tree keeps a raw pointer to your coordinate array, which must outlive it and stay unchanged. The point index is stored shifted left by 3 bits (4 for leaf offsets), so uint32_t indices cap out near 2^29 points (2^28 leaf slots); the overflow check is an assert() removed under NDEBUG.
- The balanced KdTree supports only the recursive search: passing NearestNeighborApproach::kIterative hits KDTREE_ASSERT, which calls exit(1) even in release builds.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-06-17), 1 star, single author, Apache-2.0; a ~900-line header that is easy to vendor, but treat it as research code and turn off the parallel build for small inputs.

[repo](https://github.com/philipclaude/trees) · [benchmark](https://github.com/philipclaude/trees/issues/1)

##### VoronoiDelaunay.jl  `Julia`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Julia package for incremental 2D Delaunay/Voronoi tessellation; its author's 2014 benchmark had it about 20% faster than CGAL 4.4.

**Beats:** CGAL 4.4 2D Delaunay triangulation — In 2014 the package author inserted 10K to 10M uniform points (5 runs each) on an Intel Core i7-4800MQ under Windows 8, with Julia 0.3.0 against CGAL 4.4 built with VS2013 64-bit release, and reported about 20% faster construction at 2-3x CGAL's memory. The timings exist only as a graph image. CGAL's time includes memory allocation while Julia's storage was preallocated, so the margin is partly an allocation effect.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is a 2014 gist with code shown only as screenshots; Julia, off-scope for a C++ catalog; the record's 'used in Illustris' misread the README (it means Arepo's algorithms, not this package).

**Known shortcoming:** Julia, not callable from C++. Open correctness bugs: push! hang (#38), missing triangles or edges for 3-4 or collinear points (#55, #51), triangle union not matching the convex hull (#34). Bulk push! reorders the caller's array in place; out-of-range or duplicate points are not checked ((0,0) hung, #36). README recommends successor DelaunayTriangulation.jl.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It does incremental insertion with Lawson edge flips to restore the Delaunay property, following the Arepo paper (arXiv 0901.4107). Bulk push! shuffles the input and then applies a multiscale Hilbert sort (mssort!), so each point lands near the previous one and the walk to its triangle stays short. Predicates come from GeometricalPredicates.jl, which filters in Float64 with bounded error and falls back to exact BigInt arithmetic. The fixed [1,2) coordinate range gives a constant exponent, so each mantissa maps one-to-one onto an integer. Triangles are mutable structs in one preallocated vector (sizehint!), and they cache their predicate terms.

**Use it when:**
- You work in Julia and need a 2D Delaunay or Voronoi tessellation of thousands to millions of points without depending on CGAL.
- Points are roughly uniform and can be affinely rescaled into [1,2]^2 without any loss of meaning.
- You insert points incrementally and need point location plus neighbour walking on a live tessellation.
- You want Voronoi edges for plotting or mesh generation from images (from_image), and approximate results on degenerate inputs are acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Your project is C or C++. This is Julia-only, and the C++ siblings (pgl, Delaunay32, detria) can be linked directly.
- You need weighted (power) diagrams, constrained edges, 3D tessellations or Lloyd relaxation. The README lists all of these as unimplemented.
- Inputs are small or degenerate. Open issues report no triangles or edges for 3-4 points or collinear points (#55, #51), a triangle union that does not match the convex hull (#34), and an indefinite hang in push! on an 81-point set (#38).
- Memory is tight. The author's gist measured about 2-3x CGAL's memory use.
- You need an actively maintained library. The README itself recommends DelaunayTriangulation.jl instead.

**Integration:** module · GeometricalPredicates.jl (0.2-0.4), Colors.jl, Random (stdlib) · Julia 1.6 (Project.toml compat) · any platform Julia runs on (pure Julia, no native code)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only inside a Julia codebase. For C++, pgl (measured against CGAL 6.1.2 Delaunay_triangulation_2), Delaunay32 (multithreaded, beats Triangle and Fade2D) or detria (constrained) are callable directly and have more recent evidence, and jc_voronoi covers plain 2D Voronoi in C.

**Gotchas:**
- Coordinates outside [1.0+eps, 2.0-2eps] are not checked by push!. Out-of-range points break the predicates, and inserting (0.0, 0.0) hung forever in closed issue #36.
- push!(tess, array) shuffles and Hilbert-sorts the caller's array in place, so the input order is lost.
- Duplicate points are not handled. GeometricalPredicates assumes vertices never overlap, so callers must deduplicate.
- Iteration skips every triangle that touches the four auxiliary corner points. This is the likely reason small or collinear inputs yield no triangles or edges (issues #55, #51) and hull triangles can go missing (#34).

**Status:** In maintenance mode, with the last commit on 2023-06-28 and the README pointing users to DelaunayTriangulation.jl. It is MIT-licensed, about 760 lines and easy to read, but several correctness issues remain open.

[repo](https://github.com/JuliaGeometry/VoronoiDelaunay.jl) · [benchmark](https://gist.github.com/skariel/3d2018f9341a058e00fc)

##### chusitoo/flatbush (C++ port of Flatbush)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier D`

Header-only C++11 port of the Flatbush packed Hilbert R-tree for static 2D boxes; no measured head-to-head win over any baseline.

**Beats:** Flatbush JavaScript original (mourner/flatbush, Node v24) — The repo makes no speedup claim; its README table reports only its own Google Benchmark timings on an i7-1185G7 (clang 18.1.3 / gcc 13.3.0 / MSVC 19.29, CMake Release, SIMD level unstated): index 1M rectangles 55-72 ms, 1000 searches at 1% area 17-18 ms, 1 search of 1M neighbours 63-88 ms. Comparing with the JS original's README (M1 Pro, Node v24) gives only cross-machine directional ratios (about 2x on build, about 3.7x on 1% searches, none on the 1M-neighbour kNN).

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded C to D: bench.cpp runs no baseline, and the only comparison is two README tables on different CPUs (i7-1185G7 vs M1 Pro); the matching 1M-neighbour kNN row has C++ at 86/88 ms (gcc/clang) against JS 84 ms, so no win is shown. Kept as a separate C++ entry cross-referenced to mourner/flatbush (JS, not callable from C++).

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #9: the SIMD updateBounds stored only min values for integer coordinate types, so queries missed items (closed 2026-06-27; the README bench uses double, so its numbers are unaffected). Issues #2 (multiple definition) and #14 (32-bit compile) also closed.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Items are sorted by the Hilbert-curve value of their box centres (quantized to a 16-bit grid) and packed bottom-up into a fixed-fanout tree (default node size 16) stored in one flat array, so there are no per-node allocations or pointers. The build uses a custom partial quicksort that only orders items down to node granularity, plus a bucket pass, and computes Hilbert indices with SIMD (SSE2 up to AVX-512, chosen at compile time). Queries test node boxes with SIMD comparisons, prefetch child nodes, and kNN uses a priority queue over node distances.

**Use it when:**
- Read-mostly 2D datasets (map features, tiles, bounding boxes of shapes) that are built once and queried many times, from thousands to millions of items.
- Sharing or memory-mapping a prebuilt index, including indexes produced by the JavaScript Flatbush, without a copy (fromView on an aligned buffer).
- Projects that want a single header with no dependencies and C++11 support, installable from Conan Center or vcpkg.
- Range queries returning few hits (the README's 1000 searches at 0.01% area take 2 ms total on an i7-1185G7) and small-k nearest-neighbour lookups.

**Skip it when:**
- Data that changes after building: there is no insert or delete; any change means a full rebuild.
- 3D or higher-dimensional data, or non-box geometry predicates (polygons, segments): it indexes 2D axis-aligned boxes only.
- Choosing on proven speed over Boost.Geometry rtree, nanoflann or GEOS STRtree: the repo benchmarks only itself and publishes no comparison with any C++ or JS baseline.
- Very large single kNN result sets: the README's 1 search of 1,000,000 neighbours takes 86-88 ms with gcc/clang, no better than the JS original's 84 ms on a different machine.
- Inputs above uint32 item counts: numItems is stored as uint32_t and the builder throws std::length_error past the format limits.

**Integration:** header-only · none (Google Benchmark, GoogleTest and fuzztest are fetched by CMake only for benchmarks and tests) · C++11 (uses std::span automatically in C++20); README table built with clang 18.1.3, gcc 13.3.0 and MSVC 19.29 · any C++11 target; SIMD paths for x86/x86-64 (SSE2 default on x64, SSE3/SSSE3/SSE4/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 by compiler flags) with a scalar fallback elsewhere; a 32-bit compile failure was fixed in issue #14 (closed 2026-09-25)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over the JavaScript Flatbush when the consumer is C++ (the formats are interchangeable), and over nanoflann or tidwall/rtree.c when you need a static box index (not just points) with zero-copy loading of a prebuilt buffer. If you need updates, 3D or measured speed against Boost.Geometry, GeoToolbox KdBoxTree, PH-tree or nanoflann have published comparisons and this does not.

**Gotchas:**
- Errors are reported with exceptions (std::invalid_argument, std::length_error): wrong template type for a buffer, misaligned fromView buffer, empty builder, oversized index. Builds with -fno-exceptions need care.
- The SIMD level is fixed at compile time from compiler flags (#pragma message prints which one); the default on x64 is only SSE2, so pass -mavx2 or /arch:AVX2 for the faster paths, and keep the same flags and FLATBUSH_SPAN setting across translation units.
- Integer coordinate types had a SIMD bug: updateBounds stored only the minimum values (issue #9, closed 2026-06-27), corrupting node boxes so queries missed items; use a release after that fix if you index int types. Earlier issues: a multiple-definition link error (#2) and search/neighbors not compiling on 32-bit targets (#14), both closed.
- A custom distance callback must return a lower bound of the point-to-box distance, and it bypasses the SIMD path; fromView requires the buffer to outlive the index and stay unchanged.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-03, 161 commits, CI with unit, fuzz, CodeQL and benchmark jobs), MIT-licensed single header, packaged on Conan Center and vcpkg; evidence tier D because nothing is measured against a baseline.

[repo](https://github.com/chusitoo/flatbush) · [benchmark](https://github.com/chusitoo/flatbush/blob/HEAD/bench.cpp)

##### Clipper (Clipper1 / polyclipping 6.4.2)  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Clipper1: two-file C++ Vatti polygon clipper and offsetter on integer coordinates; reported faster than Boost.Geometry on simple Booleans.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry (polygon intersection/union) — The only comparison is a third-party .NET-wrapper benchmark of nine C/C++ clipping libraries (Clipper 5.1.2, Boost 1.53, GEOS 3.3.7, among others), seen only through search snippets: Clipper was fastest in one test, followed by Boost.Geometry, but Boost.Geometry won a longer test and scaled better with more intersections. No numbers, compiler, flags or hardware were visible, and every timing includes .NET marshalling.

**Known shortcoming:** Obsolete (last release 2017-02-27; superseded by Clipper2). The cited benchmark tested Clipper 5.1.2, not 6.4.2, through .NET wrappers; blog and svn.osgeo.org blocked here, so snippet only.

**Known shortcoming:** Code limits differ from the docs: use_int32 caps coordinates at 0x7FFF (32,767) while the docs say 46,340; the hard limit is 4.6e18 while the docs say 9.2e18. SourceForge lists 6.4.2 as 2024-01-09 but the changelog and header say 2017-02-27.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It implements Bala Vatti's scanline clipping algorithm: local minima are sorted once, a std::priority_queue of scanbeam Y values drives the sweep, and an active edge list is updated per scanbeam, with crossings found by bubble-sorting the active edges at the top of each beam. All coordinates are integers (64-bit by default), and 128-bit multiplication (an internal Int128 class) is used only when a coordinate exceeds +/-0x3FFFFFFF, so most inputs run on plain 64-bit math. The docs quote about 10% more speed for flat Paths output instead of PolyTree and 20-30% for the use_int32 build.

**Use it when:**
- Legacy C++ code (or C#/Delphi) already on ClipperLib 6.x, especially via the many third-party ports bundled in the zip (Python, Java, Go, Ruby, Lua, Matlab and others), where switching APIs is not worth it.
- Polygon Booleans with few edge crossings per scanline, such as clipping to tiles or windows and unioning modest shape sets, the case where the third-party wrapper benchmark had Clipper ahead of Boost.Geometry.
- Offsetting closed or open paths with square, round or miter joins and butt, square or round ends, using integer-scaled CAD, CNC, PCB or 2D game geometry.
- Projects that want a BSL-1.0 two-file source drop (clipper.hpp + clipper.cpp) with no dependencies beyond the C++ standard library.

**Skip it when:**
- New code: the SourceForge page marks Clipper1 obsolete and unmaintained, superseded by Clipper2 (same author, BSL-1.0); among catalogued siblings, clipper2next reports about 1.6x over Clipper2 on intersection and union.
- Inputs with many intersections, or long multi-stage tests: the same snippet-only benchmark says Boost.Geometry was fastest in a longer test and Boost.Geometry and GEOS scale better as intersection counts grow. The per-scanbeam bubble sort over active edges is consistent with that.
- Floating-point workflows that cannot accept snapping to an integer grid: rounding can leave tiny self-intersection artefacts that need CleanPolygons or StrictlySimple.
- You need validity repair, spatial predicates, buffering on a sphere or OGC semantics: it only clips and offsets planar paths; GEOS-class work fits qdgeo or GeoRepair better.
- You need a reproducible speed claim: no benchmark with numbers, compiler or hardware could be opened, so the evidence is tier D.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (C++ standard library only) · C++98-era code; CMake 2.6 build script (shared library by default, SOVERSION 22) · any

**Vs siblings:** Pick Clipper1 only when you are tied to its API or one of its language ports; for new work, Clipper2 or clipper2next are the maintained successors, and CavalierContours is faster for arc-aware offsetting (3.5x to 4x on its square and pathological profiles, though slower on others).

**Gotchas:**
- Coordinate limits in the 6.4.2 code differ from the docs: the fast range is +/-0x3FFFFFFF and the hard limit +/-0x3FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (about 4.6e18); with use_int32 the code limit is +/-0x7FFF (32,767), stricter than the documented +/-46,340. Out-of-range points make AddPath throw clipperException.
- Errors are reported by throwing clipperException (derived from std::exception), including internal errors such as 'ProcessIntersections error' and 'DoMaxima error'.
- Open paths must be added as subjects and need PolyTree output for line clipping; adding them as clip paths throws.
- The 6.x API renamed Polygon/Polygons to Path/Paths and replaced OffsetPolygons with ClipperOffset, so older 4.x/5.x snippets and benchmarks (the third-party one used 5.1.2) do not compile unchanged.

**Status:** Abandoned: last release 6.4.2 (27 Feb 2017, changelog and header date), marked obsolete in favour of Clipper2, but BSL-1.0, dependency-free and about 5,000 lines, so it is easy to vendor and still downloaded about 7,300 times a week.

[repo](https://sourceforge.net/projects/polyclipping/)

##### Flatbush  `JavaScript`  `ISC`  `active`  `Tier D`

Static packed Hilbert R-tree for 2D boxes in JavaScript, stored in one ArrayBuffer; billed as faster and leaner than RBush.

**Beats:** RBush (dynamic JavaScript R-tree; counts as an R-tree baseline) — The only numbers are Flatbush's own (node bench.js, MacBook Pro M1 Pro, Node v24, 1,000,000 seeded random boxes, nodeSize 16, 10 runs): index 109 ms, 1,000 searches of 1% area 66 ms, 10,000 1-NN queries 30 ms, and one 1,000,000-neighbour query 84 ms. bench.js never imports RBush, and RBush's own table (Node 6.2.2, 2012 laptop) is not comparable. The 'faster than RBush' claim is qualitative (tier D). The one third-party comparison found, Bokeh PR #7583 (2018), shows its 1k-500k point profiling only as a graph.

**Known shortcoming:** JavaScript, not callable from C++. The RBush comparison is qualitative and bench.js never runs RBush. C++ port: chusitoo/flatbush.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D stands: bench.js times only Flatbush itself; the Bokeh PR #7583 (2018) Flatbush vs RBush profiling is a graph with no numbers. JavaScript. Issue #67 (open): about 2 GB index cap. The old recursive sort overflowed the stack on duplicate boxes (#61, #69); 4.6.2 uses an explicit stack. Search rows were understated 4x before June 2026 (#62).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** finish() computes a Hilbert value for each box centre on a 65,536 x 65,536 grid (the bit-twiddling Hilbert function from rawrunprotected/hilbert_curves), sorts only as far as node boundaries with an iterative quicksort, and packs nodes bottom-up (a packed Hilbert R-tree, nodeSize 16 by default). Boxes and child indices sit in flat typed arrays (Float64Array by default, Uint16/Uint32 indices), so there are no per-node objects for the garbage collector and scans are sequential in memory. search() emits a whole subtree as one contiguous leaf range without further tests once a node lies fully inside the query box, and neighbors() is a best-first traversal on a FlatQueue binary heap with a tightened bound when k = 1.

**Use it when:**
- Static data sets of 10^5 to 10^8 boxes or points (map features, chart glyphs, mesh triangles) that are built once and queried many times
- Browser or Node code that needs to move an index between workers without copying, or share one read-only index via SharedArrayBuffer
- Shipping a precomputed index as a compact binary file; the same layout is readable from Rust (geo-index, ABI compatible) and C++ (chusitoo/flatbush accepts JS-encoded buffers)
- Hit-testing and viewport culling in visualization libraries; Bokeh adopted it in place of RBush for large scatter plots (PR #7583, 2018)
- As the reference design to port: the README lists C++, Rust, C#, Python and Dart ports

**Skip it when:**
- Data that changes: there is no insert or remove, so every change means a full rebuild; RBush is the dynamic option
- C++ code: this is JavaScript; use the C++ port chusitoo/flatbush or a native index (Boost.Geometry rtree, nanoflann, tidwall rtree.c)
- Indexes near 2 GB: issue #67 (open) reports a 100M-item Float32Array index at 1.9 GB and asks for a way past the 2 GB buffer limit
- Exact nearest geometry: neighbors() ranks by distance to bounding boxes, in coordinate units; for lon/lat data the README points to the geoflatbush extension
- When you need a measured speed-up over RBush: the repo's benchmark times Flatbush alone, so the 'faster' claim is unquantified

**Integration:** module · flatqueue ^3.1.0 (priority queue, same author) · ES module package ("type": "module") plus a UMD browser bundle and TypeScript typings; no engines field in package.json; README benchmark run on Node v24 · any JavaScript runtime with typed arrays (browsers, Node); SharedArrayBuffer sharing needs a runtime that allows it

**Vs siblings:** Pick Flatbush over RBush when the data is static and you want lower memory use and a transferable buffer; use KDBush instead for points only. In Rust, or for Python bindings, use geo-index (ABI-compatible port, ~2x faster construction than rstar on its own benchmark); in C++ use chusitoo/flatbush or nanoflann/GeoToolbox KdBoxTree, which have baseline numbers.

**Gotchas:**
- add() must be called exactly numItems times before finish(), which throws otherwise; search() and neighbors() throw until finish() has run
- A non-default ArrayType (Float32Array, Int32Array) stores coordinates by ordinary typed-array conversion with no outward rounding, so stored boxes can be slightly smaller than the originals and hits on box edges can be missed
- Many duplicate boxes overflowed the call stack in the old recursive sort (issues #61 and #69, the latter reported through Bokeh); the current code sorts with an explicit stack (package 4.6.2); older bundled copies may still crash
- Serialized data carries format version 3 and Flatbush.from() rejects other versions; byteOffset must be 8-byte aligned. Before June 2026 the README's search rows understated the query area by 4x (issue #62)

**Status:** Active: version 4.6.2, 196 commits, 1.6k stars, last commit 2026-07-08, 5 open issues. ISC-licensed, a single 519-line index.js with one small dependency, so it is easy to vendor or port.

[repo](https://github.com/mourner/flatbush) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mourner/flatbush)

#### random-and-quasi-random

##### AVX512-VAES2-PRNG (AVX-512/VAES/GFNI 8-way hybrid PRNG, proof of concept)  `C/C++ (header AVX512-VAES2-PRNG.h)`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-header AVX-512/VAES/GFNI bulk PRNG proof of concept; author claims 0.093 cycles/byte versus about 4-6 for mt19937.

**Beats:** Mersenne Twister (mt19937), PCG32 / XorShift128+, ChaCha8 and ChaCha20 AVX-512 (rows in the README table) — The author's README reports 0.0932 cycles per byte (5.964 cycles per 64 bytes) for bulk output with non-temporal stores on an unnamed AMD EPYC with AVX-512/VAES/GFNI in a shared server environment, with no compiler, flags or harness published. The 43-64x figure against mt19937 compares that to an unmeasured 4-6 cpb range listed in the same table, and against PCG32/XorShift128+ the derived gap is 6-11x.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline rows are unmeasured ranges and there is no harness; proof of concept.

**Known shortcoming:** Quality flaw: the 'VPSHUFB+VPTERNLOGD' step is ternlog 0xFE, a 3-input OR; from the header LUTs 256 byte inputs give only 56 outputs with 77% one-bits, so the b-lane update is many-to-one with no period guarantee, and output vectors 4-7 start from a biased value (v[7] = ~v[4]) hidden only by 2 AES rounds. Proof of concept. NT stores need an undocumented 64-byte-aligned buffer; C99 restrict blocks g++/MSVC builds without a shim; seed must be a pre-derived uniform 256-bit key.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The state is just two 512-bit vectors (a, b). Each block adds Weyl constants, applies a GFNI affine byte transform to a and a VPSHUFB nibble lookup combined with VPTERNLOGD to b, and expands the two vectors into eight via rotations and complements. The eight vectors then go through two VAESENC rounds with seed-derived round keys and a cross-vector rotate-XOR 'diagonal' between the rounds. The eight 64-byte vectors are written with non-temporal stores (_mm512_stream_si512), and a small add/rotate/XOR remix is placed between the sixth and seventh store. There are no multiplications in the generation loop, and eight independent vectors keep the VAES and store ports busy.

**Use it when:**
- Experiments and benchmarking on AVX-512 + VAES + GFNI hardware (the README names AMD Zen 4/Zen 5 and Intel Sapphire Rapids/Emerald Rapids as targets) where you want a very high-throughput bulk random stream
- Filling large buffers (many 512-byte blocks) that are not read back immediately, so the non-temporal stores help rather than hurt
- Non-cryptographic simulation or noise generation where you can validate the output quality yourself before relying on it

**Skip it when:**
- Anything security-sensitive: the author states it is not a proven CSPRNG, and its mixing is only two AES rounds per block; use ChaCha or AES-CTR based generators instead
- Production simulations that need well-tested statistical quality: the README shows only TestU01 SmallCrush and 0.962 GiB of PractRand plus home-grown statistics, and the state transition is not a bijection (see gotchas), so the period is unproven
- CPUs without all of AVX-512F, GFNI and VAES, and any non-x86 target: the header has no fallback path
- Small or immediately consumed outputs: generation is in 512-byte blocks with non-temporal stores, which evict the data from cache just before you read it
- C++ projects without a shim: the header uses the C99 'restrict' keyword and GCC attributes, so it needs '#define restrict __restrict' under g++/clang++ and does not build with MSVC as written

**Integration:** header-only (single C header) · none (immintrin.h; sys/mman.h or windows.h for the optional lock helpers) · C99 compiler with AVX-512F/GFNI/VAES intrinsics and GCC-style __attribute__ and inline asm (GCC or Clang with -mavx512f -mgfni -mvaes or a suitable -march); exact versions not documented · x86-64 only, requires AVX-512F + GFNI + VAES (the README tested an unnamed AMD EPYC in a shared server environment)

**Vs siblings:** Rarely. SHISHUA (52.93 GB/s per its catalog record), testingRNG's aesctr and Google's Randen cover the same bulk-throughput niche with more scrutiny and without an AVX-512+VAES+GFNI requirement. Pick this one only to experiment with VAES/GFNI-based generator design on Zen 4+ or recent Xeon hardware.

**Gotchas:**
- Output buffer must be 64-byte aligned and sized in 512-byte blocks (128 uint32 words per block): _mm512_stream_si512 faults on unaligned addresses, and the README does not mention this.
- The 'VPSHUFB + VPTERNLOGD' step uses ternlog immediate 0xFE, a three-input OR of two nibble-substituted values and the input. Computing it from the header's LUTs gives only 56 distinct outputs for the 256 byte inputs, with 77% one-bits. The b-lane update is therefore many-to-one and the output vectors 4-7 start from that biased value (v[7] is its bitwise complement), so the generator has no period guarantee and rests on two AES rounds to hide the bias.
