- Seeding takes a 32-byte key that the comment says must already be uniformly distributed ('KDF boundary'). Passing a small integer padded with zeros is not supported by the design.
- The README speed table mixes this generator's measured 0.0932 cpb with approximate '~' ranges for ChaCha8, VAES, PCG32/XorShift128+ and mt19937 that do not appear to come from the same run, and no harness, compiler or flags are published. By its own table, AVX-512 ChaCha8 (~0.08-0.18 cpb) is in the same range.

**Status:** A 0-star repo created on 2026-09-15 (all 11 commits that day), self-described as a preliminary proof of concept under a codename. MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but treat it as experimental.

[repo](https://github.com/Watney-0717/AVX512-VAES2-PRNG) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Watney-0717/AVX512-VAES2-PRNG/HEAD/README.md)

##### cauldron random.h (ziggurat normal distribution)  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Single-header C (C++-compatible) RNG library whose ziggurat standard-normal sampler measured 2.2x (float) and 4.2x (double) faster than std::normal_distribution.

**Beats:** std::normal_distribution (driven by std::minstd_rand in the benchmark's cpp11random entry) — In camel-cdr's issue #3 on miloyip/normaldist-benchmark (2020-12-19; 1M samples, minimum of 10 trials; CPU and compiler not stated), a template ziggurat that is the precursor of random.h's code took 4.018 ns per float and 4.081 ns per double, against 8.852 and 17.009 ns for std::normal_distribution driven by std::minstd_rand and 7.289 and 7.817 ns for the benchmark's existing ziggurat. That code fed the ziggurat from the Numerical Recipes 32-bit LCG, taking the box index from its low 7 bits, and built the double version's 64-bit draw from two identically seeded copies of that LCG, so both halves are equal; no output-quality result was reported, and the repo's own tools/random/bench.c times dist_normal(f)_zig but publishes no numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: the numbers come from the author's own issue #3 table; the baseline 'cpp11random' is std::normal_distribution driven by std::minstd_rand, and clt4 ties with it (4.064 vs 4.088 ns). The current random.h double default is 256 blocks, not the configuration timed in the issue.

**Known shortcoming:** The issue #3 benchmark took the box index from the low 7 bits of a 32-bit NR LCG (period 128), and the double draw concatenates two identically seeded LCGs so both halves are equal; no statistical quality result is reported. Sign and box index come from low bits although random.h recommends the +/* variants (weak low bits) for floats. test.sh ends with 'exit 0', so CI never fails. A custom ZIG_COUNT needs your own _R/_AREA tables.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It is the Marsaglia-Tsang ziggurat in Doornik's formulation, but with a single table of box x-coordinates (129 floats for the default 128 boxes, 257 doubles for the default 256); the source comment says dropping the second bound table halves memory and allows bigger tables. Each sample usually costs one RNG call, one multiply and one compare, because one 32- or 64-bit draw is split into the sign (bit 0), the box index (the next 7 or 8 bits) and the uniform (the top 24 or 53 bits). Only rejected draws reach the wedge test (two expf/exp calls) or Marsaglia's 1964 log-based tail method.

**Use it when:**
- C or C++ simulation and Monte Carlo code that draws many scalar standard normals and where std::normal_distribution shows up in profiles (about 9-17 ns per sample in the cited run versus about 4 ns).
- Projects that want a vendorable MIT single header with no dependency beyond libm that builds as C89 and as C++ (both are exercised by the repo's test script).
- Code that already controls its own fast PRNG (Romu, PCG, xoshiro**) and wants to plug it in per thread through the function-pointer interface.
- Float sampling where a small (516-byte, 129 floats) read-only table that stays in L1 is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Bulk or SIMD fills of large arrays: the routine is scalar, one sample per call; vectorized siblings such as EigenRand target that case.
- Code that needs the <random> distribution-object interface (URBG, param_type, mean/stddev) or other distributions such as gamma or Student t.
- Results that must be bit-identical to std::normal_distribution or another library: the sequence differs.
- Pairing it with a generator whose low bits are weak (the + and * scramblers, plain power-of-two LCGs): the sign and box index come from the lowest bits of each draw, while random.h's own notes say the xoshiro/xoroshiro + variants' lower bits fail linear tests yet recommend those variants for floating point.
- Decisions that need hard numbers: the only published comparison is a first-party 2020 run of precursor code with no CPU, compiler or flags; re-measure on your target.

**Integration:** header-only · libm (logf/expf/sqrtf and the double versions); the TRNG section uses OS APIs (getrandom, arc4random, RtlGenRandom or /dev/urandom), not needed by the ziggurat · C89 (test script builds with -std=c89 -Dinline=) or C++ via g++ -xc++; requires uint32_t/uint64_t and float/double formats with at least 7 spare bits beyond the mantissa (checked by #error) · any (portable C, no intrinsics in the ziggurat path); the test script also runs a big-endian MIPS build under qemu when that toolchain is installed

**Vs siblings:** Pick cauldron when you want plain C (even C89) and a scalar standard-normal function driven by your own PRNG; its precursor ran about 1.8x faster than the existing ziggurat in miloyip's normaldist-benchmark. Pick EigenRand for vectorized bulk fills on Eigen arrays, Zest for a C++ distribution-object API covering gamma, Student t and other ziggurat-able distributions, and cxx-ziggurat or zigg if you prefer a C++ class or R integration.

**Gotchas:**
- You must call dist_normalf_zig_init / dist_normal_zig_init before sampling. Table size is a compile-time macro: DIST_NORMALF_ZIG_COUNT defaults to 128 and cannot exceed 128; DIST_NORMAL_ZIG_COUNT defaults to 256 (power of two, at most 1024). The matching _R and _AREA constants are only defined when you leave COUNT at its default, so a custom COUNT needs its own constants from tools/random/ziggurat-constants.c.
- Because the sign and box index use the low bits of each draw, a generator with poor low bits biases the output; a related issue (#2, closed 2024-11-22) showed dist_uniform*_dense returning only 1.0 with the odd-only randu LCG.
- The repo's CI runs test/random/dist_normal.c (Jochen Voss's GPL-2 testgauss checks of mean and tail probabilities, with Romu generators) under gcc, sanitizers and g++, but test.sh ends with 'exit 0' and has no 'set -e', so a failing test would not fail CI. The GPL applies to that test file only; random.h itself is MIT.
- dist_normalf_fast is an approximation (sum of popcounts plus a linear nudge), not an exact normal sampler; do not confuse it with the ziggurat functions.

**Status:** Stale (random.h last changed 2025-02-01, 'small changes'; 0 open issues, 143 stars) but MIT-licensed, self-contained and easy to vendor; the ziggurat section can be copied on its own per the header's design notes.

[repo](https://github.com/camel-cdr/cauldron) · [benchmark](https://github.com/miloyip/normaldist-benchmark/issues/3)

##### cpp_prngs (QuarkBurst64, RomuDuoJr, Konadare192 engines)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only constexpr C++17 small-state PRNG engines (RomuDuoJr, QuarkBurst64, Konadare192 and others) with a game-oriented Random<E> API, faster than std::mt19937.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 (also std::minstd_rand, std::default_random_engine and C rand()) — The author's Quick Bench charts (August 2026) put raw next() at about 13,300 for std::mt19937 versus about 2,700 for RomuDuoJr and 2,600 for QuarkBurst64, in units of CPU time / no-op time, values read by eye. That is roughly 5x per call, but it compares 64-bit-output engines with the 32-bit-output std::mt19937. Compiler, flags, standard library and CPU are not stated (the Quick Bench links were unreachable). The harness is public (benchmarks/engine_comparison.cpp, Google Benchmark, 1024 values summed per iteration).

**Known shortcoming:** QuarkBurst64 has no PractRand/TestU01 evidence and upstream eightomic/quarkburst is 404 (KAT checked only against an archived reference). RomuDuoJr period unproven. float between(lo,hi) can round to hi; child() streams are not independent. Repo mostly curates third-party engines.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The gain comes from replacing the 624-word Mersenne Twister with register-sized nonlinear generators. RomuDuoJr is one multiply plus a rotate-subtract on two 64-bit words. QuarkBurst64 is rotate/XOR/add with a Weyl counter and no multiply. Konadare192 is add/rotate with a Weyl increment. The wrapper uses Lemire's nearly divisionless multiply-and-reject for bounded integers (division-free when the bound is a compile-time constant). Floats are built by writing random bits into the mantissa field (the 'IQ float hack') instead of dividing.

**Use it when:**
- Games and procedural generation that need fast, reproducible, cross-platform integer streams and replay checkpoints from a tiny state
- Many independent generator instances (per entity, per thread, per job) where std::mt19937's 2.5 KiB state is a cache cost
- Compile-time generation of tables or test data (engines and most of Random<E> are constexpr)
- Bounded integers and weighted picks in hot loops: Lemire's multiply-and-reject avoids most divisions (the README's bounded-integer chart compares it with std::uniform_int_distribution and rand() % n)
- 8/16-bit microcontrollers (AVR Arduino built as C++17) via the SmallFast8/16 and XorShift32Star8 engines

**Skip it when:**
- Security or anything adversarial: none of the engines is cryptographic, as the README states
- Scientific Monte Carlo that needs proven period, jump-ahead or guaranteed non-overlapping parallel streams: RomuDuoJr has no proven period (its seeding comment cites only empirical cycle checks), and child() explicitly 'does not promise independent or non-overlapping streams'
- Code that must reproduce std::mt19937 sequences or the exact output of std distributions
- Projects that need high-precision floats by default: normalized()/between() default to float with 23 random mantissa bits, and normal_approx() is an Irwin-Hall approximation clipped at about six standard deviations
- When you need audited statistical quality for QuarkBurst64: the repo has known-answer tests against an archived reference but no PractRand/TestU01 results, and the upstream eightomic/quarkburst repo returns 404

**Integration:** header-only (copy include/ or link the CMake INTERFACE target cpp_prngs::cpp_prngs) · none (GoogleTest is fetched only for the test build) · C++17 (CMake 3.21+ for the provided target); C++20 adds constexpr std::bit_cast floats and the rnd::RandomBitEngine concept; AVR needs -std=gnu++17 (CI uses Arduino AVR core 1.8.8) · any C++17 target (desktop, MSVC project included, AVR Arduino validated in CI)

**Vs siblings:** Pick cpp_prngs over libchaos or the bare Romu entry when you want ready-to-copy constexpr C++17 engines plus a convenience layer (bounded ints, weighted picks, snapshots) with portable, deterministic output, including on AVR. For SIMD bulk throughput (simdrng, SHISHUA) or scientific-grade streams with jump-ahead (Randen, xoshiro reference code, OpenRAND), look at those entries instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Default construction uses a fixed seed, so Random<E>() gives the same sequence every run. Seeding helpers live in a separate gist (seeding.hpp), not in the repo.
- Floating between(lo, hi) is computed as lo + (hi - lo) * normalized(), so rounding can return hi for some ranges despite the documented [lo, hi). In C++17 the float path is constexpr arithmetic unless RND_FAST_FLOAT is defined.
- from_state() bypasses seeding. All-zero states are invalid for most engines (PCG32's inc must be odd), and this is checked only by assert in debug builds.
- Third-party engine headers keep their own licenses (PCG32 and Konadare192 are Apache-2.0, QuarkBurst's upstream is BSD-3-Clause), so check the per-file headers when vendoring rather than assuming MIT throughout.

**Status:** Actively maintained by a single author (232 commits, last 2026-08-20, 1 star, CI on desktop and AVR). MIT for the wrappers, with third-party engines under their original permissive licenses; small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/ulfben/cpp_prngs) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ulfben/cpp_prngs)

##### Cromulent-PRNG (seanwevans/Cromulent-PRNG, cromulent128 with AVX2 variant)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Small MIT C library for a new 128-bit-state nonlinear PRNG; its own benchmark beats xoshiro256++ but loses to splitmix64.

**Beats:** xoshiro256++, a 64-bit-state PCG variant labelled pcg64, and splitmix64 (reference copies in src/reference/, timed by the repo's own apps/bench_micro.c) — The README's sample output from apps/bench_micro.c (10^10 calls per generator, seed 69420, each called through a function pointer on static global state in a separately compiled static library) gives xoshiro256++ 4.00, cromulent128 2.93, pcg64 1.76 and splitmix64 1.27 ns/sample on an unnamed 'modern CPU' with unstated compiler, flags and build type; cromulent128 is 1.37x faster than this xoshiro256++ harness (derived from page data) but slower than the other two. The AVX2 variant is not benchmarked, and the 128 TB PractRand log (2025-05-28, RNG_stdin64, all results 'normal') does not name the generator or seed, while PR #51 says those transcripts never covered the registry entry that the benchmark times.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: README numbers reproduce, but the repo's 'pcg64' is not real PCG64 (64-bit state), every generator is called through a function pointer with no LTO, and the build sets no default -O flag, so the comparison penalises all sides equally and says little about the generators.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo's 'pcg64' baseline is broken: it rotates a 37-bit value within 64 bits, so every output has at least 27 consecutive zero bits counting cyclically (checked by simulating the code), so it is not PCG64. The record's jump-ahead claim is stale (removed July 2026, PR #26, since the recurrence is nonlinear); the 'period about 2^128' is unproven; the PractRand 128 TB log (2025-05-28) names no generator and PR #51 says it never covered the registry generator the benchmark times. The public header leaks macros C1-C6/MH3 and global rotl/mix.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Each step is a few 64-bit operations on two registers: s0 = s0*C6 + s1, s1 = rotl(s1,31) + mix_fast(s0), with a single-multiply xor-shift finalizer (MH3) inside the recurrence and a multiply-xorshift output mix (s0 + rotl(s1,11), then xorshift-27, multiply by C3, xorshift-27). That is three 64-bit multiplies per output against none for xoshiro256++, so its 1.37x lead in the README comes from the harness (all generators called through function pointers on static global state, where xoshiro256++ must load and store four words per call) rather than from fewer instructions. cromulent_range uses Lemire's multiply-and-reject method with __uint128_t, and the AVX2 path runs four independent lanes using an emulated 64-bit multiply built from three _mm256_mul_epu32.

**Use it when:**
- You want a tiny MIT-licensed C generator with 16-byte state and a portable, endian-independent save/restore format.
- You need the same generator and stream in several languages: the repo ships bindings for 20 languages and the C++ binding is tested bit-for-bit against the C reference.
- Non-cryptographic simulation or game code where a 64-bit output generator that passed a 128 TB PractRand run (per the repo's log) is enough.
- As a std::mt19937_64 replacement in C++ via cromulent::engine when you also need its C or other-language twins.

**Skip it when:**
- When raw speed is the goal: the repo's own table shows splitmix64 (1.27 ns) and its 'pcg64' (1.76 ns) faster than cromulent128 (2.93 ns), and siblings such as Sirius64, DualMix128, RomuDuoJr or wyrand publish better numbers against proper references.
- Parallel streams that must not overlap: the jump-ahead was removed in July 2026 (PR #26) because the recurrence is nonlinear and no valid skip-ahead exists; per-thread seeds are the only option.
- When a proven period matters: the README states 'period approximately 2^128', but the step is nonlinear and the repo offers no proof that it is invertible or of a minimum cycle length.
- Cryptographic or adversarial use, including the 'strong' variant: nothing in the repo claims or analyses unpredictability.
- Production code wanting an established algorithm: 0 stars, no external review, and the design changed repeatedly in 2025-2026 (seeding of the registry entry fixed 2026-08-30).

**Integration:** static lib (C, CMake); header-only C++17 binding in bindings/cpp · none (C11 standard library; optional __uint128_t and AVX2) · C11, CMake 3.19+; C++17 for the C++ binding; CI builds Release with GCC and Clang on Ubuntu and Clang on macOS · any 64-bit target for the scalar code; AVX2 variant on x86-64 only, compiled with -mavx2 and with no runtime CPU dispatch

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Sirius64, DualMix128 or shioi128/seiran128 only when you value one MIT generator with identical streams across C, C++ and other language bindings more than speed or published analysis; for scalar speed those siblings, or splitmix64 and RomuDuoJr, are better documented, and for bulk throughput SHISHUA or the SIMD xoshiro variants are far ahead.

**Gotchas:**
- The public header cromulent.h includes internal.h, which defines macros C1-C6 and MH3 and static inline functions rotl, rotr, diffuse, mix and mix_fast in the global namespace, and pulls in <immintrin.h> on x86-64; these names can collide with user code.
- A plain 'cmake ..' as shown first in the README sets no build type and therefore no -O flag; use -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release before benchmarking.
- The AVX2 generator seeds four lanes from eight SplitMix64 outputs, so its output is four interleaved substreams that never match the scalar stream for the same seed, and its declarations are only visible when the including file is itself compiled with AVX2 enabled.
- The benchmark's 'pcg64' (src/reference/pcg64.c) is not PCG64: it is a 64-bit LCG whose 37-bit xorshifted value is rotated within 64 bits, so every output contains a run of at least 27 consecutive zero bits, counting cyclically (checked by simulating the code); comparisons against it say nothing about real PCG64.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-08-30, 122 commits, 0 stars), MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but young, single-author and without a proven period or valid stream-splitting.

[repo](https://github.com/seanwevans/Cromulent-PRNG) · [benchmark](https://github.com/seanwevans/Cromulent-PRNG)

##### cslarsen/mersenne-twister  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Loop-unrolled, batch-tempered MT19937 in one C++ file; same output as reference mt19937ar.c, 1.1-1.6x faster on Intel.

**Beats:** reference mt19937ar.c (Mersenne Twister) — Author's own test-mt run (best of 20 passes, both implementations built with the repo Makefile's -O2 -march=native flags) gave 351-355 M numbers/s vs 222-223 M/s for the reference mt19937ar code (1.59x) on an unnamed Intel Xeon with gcc 6.3, and only 1.12x on an older Core i7 with clang 4; no comparison with std::mt19937.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline is mt19937ar.c, not the std library; CPU models unstated; clang version hedged ('I think'); no LICENSE file, modified BSD only per README.

**Known shortcoming:** Not thread-safe (one static global state); exports unprefixed C symbols seed and rand_u32; never compared with std::mt19937; ~5 KB state, double the reference; older unrolled versions gave wrong output and had an out-of-bounds read (fixed).

**Independent measurement:** reference/mt19937ar.cpp built with same flags: 1.59x like-for-like

**How:** The state-update loop is split into two index ranges (0..226 and 227..622) so the wrap-around modulus disappears, the odd/even matrix select uses a branchless sign-extension trick ((int32_t(y) << 31) >> 31) & MAGIC instead of a table lookup, and tempering is done for all 624 words in one batch into a second array so rand_u32() is just an array read. The Makefile adds -O2 -march=native -funroll-loops -ftree-vectorize so the batch loops can vectorize.

**Use it when:**
- Legacy code that must keep the exact MT19937 sequence (reproducible simulations, saved seeds) but wants a faster scalar implementation than mt19937ar.c
- C or C++ projects on x86 that want a tiny vendorable MT19937 with no dependencies
- Single-threaded Monte Carlo code drawing many 32-bit values in a tight loop

**Skip it when:**
- Multithreaded code: state is one static global struct with no locking; you must edit the source to make it per-instance
- When you are free to change generator: modern generators (lehmer64, wyrand, splitmix64, pcg64) are faster and MT19937 fails PractRand binary-rank tests
- Non-Intel CPUs: the author says he only tested Intel and doubts the speedup holds elsewhere; the extra unrolling (MT_UNROLL_MORE) is slower on newer Xeons
- Code already using std::mt19937: no comparison against libstdc++/libc++ is published, and those implementations may already be competitive
- Need for 64-bit outputs, jump-ahead, or cryptographic unpredictability (624 outputs reveal the state, per the README)

**Integration:** source-drop · none · C++11 (Makefile uses --std=gnu++11; source uses default member initializers) · any in principle; only tested on Intel x86-64

**Vs siblings:** Pick this only when you must keep the MT19937 sequence; if the generator can change, testingRNG's lehmer64 or wyrand headers are about 2x faster than MT19937 in that repo's table, and SHISHUA or xoshiro8x256pp are far faster for bulk fills.

**Gotchas:**
- Exports unprefixed C symbols named seed and rand_u32, which can collide with other code; the README's namespace wrapper does not change the extern "C" linkage names
- Earlier unrolled versions produced wrong numbers and had an out-of-bounds read (both fixed per README); the srand/rand drop-ins were removed because the author believed they had errors
- State is ~5 KB (624 raw + 624 tempered words), double the reference's footprint
- No LICENSE file in the repo; the BSD license is stated only in the README and source headers

**Status:** Abandoned since December 2017, but it is two small BSD-licensed files (license stated in README only) that are easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/cslarsen/mersenne-twister) · [benchmark](https://github.com/cslarsen/mersenne-twister)

##### Culumi PRNG (SIMD CLMUL-based 128-bit-per-step generator)  `C (SSE4/PCLMUL/FMA) and C#`  `CC0-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

SIMD PRNG returning 128 bits per call via carry-less multiply; author's table puts it ahead of xoshiro256**, PCG64DXSM, MT19937.

**Beats:** MT19937_32 (also SFMT19937, PCG64DXSM, xoshiro256**, xoroshiro128++, SFC64 listed in the same table) — The README's comparison table lists Culumi at 58.68 ns per KiB against xoshiro256** 137.79, PCG64DXSM 308.30 and MT19937_32 547.58 (about 2.3x, 5.3x and 9.3x, derived from page data). It names no language, compiler, flags or CPU and ships no harness; its baseline links point at .NET, Java and Unity generators, SFMT comes out slower than MT, and Shishua is listed at 220.97 ns/KiB, far below SHISHUA's own figures, so the baselines look like scalar managed ports, not std::mt19937 or SIMD code. A separate BenchmarkDotNet run (.NET 8 preview, RyuJIT AVX2, i7-12700F, Windows 11) puts Culumi's Next() at 0.937 ns against System.Random's 1.619 ns (1.73x); its benchmark code is not published either.

**Known shortcoming:** ns/KiB table likely used managed non-SIMD baselines (SFMT slower than MT).

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug in the C port (code reading, not run): the nextDouble2/nextFloat4 retry path passes _mm_andnot arguments in the wrong order and nextDouble2 uses min2 where max2 belongs, so the valid lane is zeroed and the retried lane gets garbage (rare near zero, ~6% of draws per lane for [1e15, 1e15+1), derived). C# version is correct. README rates SHISHUA at 220.97 ns/KiB, far below SHISHUA's own ~19 ns/KiB, so the baselines look like scalar/managed ports. c/culumi.c holds the full library plus a test main().

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The state update is GF(2)-linear (an LFSR-type step): one PCLMULQDQ carry-less multiply of the low 64 bits by a constant, two XORs and a 64-bit lane swap, which is what makes the 2^256-1 period provable. The output scrambler is nonlinear and also cheap: a 64-bit-lane add of the two state halves, a pshufb byte shuffle, and another add. So each call yields 128 bits from a handful of SSE instructions. The helpers use the whole vector: four 32-bit or two 64-bit bounded integers per call (multiply-high with a rejection/carry fix-up, no division) and 4x float or 2x double conversions with FMA.

**Use it when:**
- .NET 7/8 code that wants a faster, richer System.Random replacement: the author's BenchmarkDotNet table (i7-12700F) has Next() at 0.94 ns vs 1.62 ns, NextDouble() 1.08 vs 1.85 ns and Shuffle(char[16]) 19 vs 55 ns.
- x86-64 C/C++ code that consumes random bits 128 at a time (bulk byte fills, SIMD Monte Carlo with 4x float or 2x double lanes) and wants a 32-byte state.
- Parallel simulations that need many non-overlapping streams via constant-time jumps (2^128 streams of length 2^128 per the README).
- Projects that want public-domain (CC0) code they can paste in without license tracking.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything security-sensitive: the README says the internal state was recovered from three consecutive 128-bit outputs with the Z3 solver in a few hours.
- Portable C/C++: the C version uses x86 intrinsics and needs SSE4.1, PCLMUL and FMA; there is no ARM or scalar path in C (only the C# version has ARM and software fallbacks).
- When you need a std::-compatible engine, a maintained library or independent numbers: 4 commits, all on 2023-05-25, no benchmark harness in the repo, and the ns/KiB table states no language, compiler or CPU.
- If you just need fast scalar 64-bit outputs: the same table has SFC64 at 97.80 and xoroshiro128++ at 113.53 ns/KiB against Culumi's 58.68, a gap small enough that a portable, better-studied generator may be the better trade.

**Integration:** source-drop (one C file with an embedded test main(); one C# file) · none (C: x86intrin.h or intrin.h, seeds from /dev/urandom or rand_s; C#: .NET base library only) · C: gcc/clang/MSVC with -msse4 -mpclmul -mfma (source comment); C#: README says .NET 7, the shipped Culumi.csproj targets net8.0 · C: x86-64 with SSE4.1 + PCLMULQDQ + FMA; C#: any .NET 7+ runtime, fast on x86 PCLMUL and ARM AES (PMULL), with a slow software carry-less multiply fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick Culumi over the same author's scalar Shioi and Seiran when you can rely on x86 PCLMUL (or .NET) and consume 128-bit vectors. For raw bulk throughput SHISHUA is the stronger sibling (its own README claims 52.93 GB/s, about 19 ns/KiB derived, against Culumi's 58.68 ns/KiB), and SIMD xoshiro ports such as simdrng suit you better if you want a well-analysed generator with C++ engine semantics.

**Gotchas:**
- Correctness bug in the C port (found by reading the code; not run): the retry path of nextDouble2 and nextFloat4, taken when min + u*(max-min) rounds up to max, passes _mm_andnot_pd/_ps arguments in the wrong order (Intel's andnot(a,b) is ~a & b, while the C# original's Vector128.AndNot(a,b) is a & ~b), and nextDouble2's retry multiplies by min2 where max2 belongs. A lane that already succeeded is zeroed and the retried lane gets garbage bits. The retry is rare for ranges near zero but common for narrow ranges at large magnitude (about 6% of draws per lane for [1e15, 1e15+1), derived). The C# version is correct.
- nextBytes stores through an __m128i* cast of the caller's byte buffer, which compilers may emit as aligned stores, so pass a 16-byte-aligned buffer.
- In C, next() is declared non-static 'inline' (DLLEXPORT inline), which under C99 inline rules can fail to link at -O0, and the exported names (init, next, prev, jump64) are generic enough to collide; rename or make them static inline when vendoring.
- initState() calls exit(-1) on an all-zero seed, and init() falls back to time()/clock() seeding, which the source comment says lacks entropy, if /dev/urandom cannot be read.

**Status:** Abandoned (4 commits, all on 2023-05-25; 4 stars, no issues filed) but CC0 and one file per language, so it is easy to vendor; prefer the C# file, or fix the C retry bug before using the C range helpers.

[repo](https://github.com/andanteyk/prng-culumi) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andanteyk/prng-culumi/HEAD/README.md)

##### DualMix128 (128-bit-state PRNG; superseded by LoopMix128)  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Tiny 128-bit-state add-rotate PRNG; author's gcc benchmark: 0.401 ns/call vs xoroshiro128++ 0.829, tied with wyrand.

**Beats:** xoroshiro128++ (also wyrand, Java xoroshiro128++ and java.util.Random) — benchmark.out (gcc 11.4.0 on Ubuntu 22.04, -O3 -march=native, CPU not stated) times 10^10 single-stream calls each storing to a volatile: DualMix128 0.401 ns/call, xoroshiro128++ 0.829 ns (about 2.07x, derived from page data), wyrand 0.401 ns. The xoroshiro128++ in benchmark.c is the standard algorithm, so the gap mostly reflects xoroshiro's longer dependency chain.

**Known shortcoming:** No CPU stated; the 0.401 ns tie with wyrand suggests a loop floor rather than generator cost; no period proof; superseded by LoopMix128.

**Known shortcoming:** All-zero state is a fixed point and the seed function does not check for it. Period unproven. Speed ties wyrand (both 0.401 ns, suggesting a loop/store floor). Repo has no Java code (language corrected to C).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each step is one add (mix = s0 + s1), two rotates and two adds for the new state, and one multiply of mix by the golden-ratio constant for the output. The loop-carried dependency is only about two adds deep and the multiply sits off the critical path, while xoroshiro128++'s update chains xor, rotate, shift and xor. The state update is a nonlinear add-rotate mix with a multiplicative output scrambler, so no linear-algebra structure and no jump function.

**Use it when:**
- Hot scalar loops (Monte Carlo, procedural generation, randomized testing) where a single 64-bit draw per call must be as cheap as possible and PractRand/BigCrush-level quality is enough.
- When a 16-byte, multiply-free state update is wanted, e.g. one generator embedded per object or per thread.
- As a reference for the design line that continued in LoopMix128 and biski64.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need a guaranteed period: injectivity is unproven (the README strikes its 'possibly injective' claim), so the period and the risk of short cycles are unknown; the author points to LoopMix128 instead.
- Parallel simulations that need non-overlapping streams: there is no jump or stream function.
- Anything security-sensitive: the README says it is for non-cryptographic use.
- When wyrand is already available: the author's own benchmark has wyrand at the same 0.401 ns/call.
- When you want a maintained, packaged library: 23 commits, 4 stars, no header or API, and the LoopMix128 link now redirects to the biski64 repository.

**Integration:** source-drop (copy the function from the README or benchmark.c) · none · C99 (stdint.h); the published benchmark was built with gcc 11.4.0 -O3 -march=native · any platform with 64-bit integers (portable C, no intrinsics; the benchmark harness uses POSIX clock_gettime)

**Vs siblings:** Rarely: wyrand ties it in its own benchmark with 8 bytes of state and a Weyl-sequence period of 2^64, biski64 (already catalogued; the LoopMix128 link now lands there) is the author's later design with a guaranteed minimum period, and Sirius64, Romu or the xoshiro family are better analysed. Choose DualMix128 only if you specifically want its multiply-free 16-byte state update and accept an unknown period.

**Gotchas:**
- The all-zero state is a fixed point (mix = 0 keeps both words 0 and the output stays 0 forever); benchmark.c's seed function does not check for it, so seed through SplitMix64 as test_practrand.c does.
- The reference code uses global state and non-static 'inline' functions, which under C99 inline rules can fail to link at -O0; wrap it as a static inline function over a state struct.
- The timing is single-stream latency with a volatile store per call, and the CPU is not stated; DualMix128 and wyrand land on the identical 0.401 ns, which suggests a loop or store floor rather than a measured difference between them.
- The README's Java claims (27% faster than Java xoroshiro128++, 8.82x java.util.Random) have no Java code or output in the repo.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-05-10) and superseded by its author, but MIT-licensed and five lines long, so copying is trivial; prefer the successor if you need a period guarantee.

[repo](https://github.com/the-othernet/DualMix128) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-othernet/DualMix128/HEAD/benchmark.out)

##### fast_prng (cd-mcfarland modified ziggurat)  `C`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only C modified-ziggurat normal and exponential samplers; reference code for the McFarland 2016 algorithm, faster than classic ziggurats.

**Beats:** Doornik ziggurat normal and Marsaglia-Tsang ziggurat exponential (other ziggurat generators profiled in the repo); not std::normal_distribution or Boost — The only number in the repo is a README sample run: 7.987 ns per standard normal over 1e9 draws with gcc -O2, clock()-timed, CPU not stated and no baseline row; profile_all.py names gcc-4.8 -O2 on an i7-3770K, but its timings.csv is missing. Outside the repo, the paper's snippet reports median runtimes cut to 53% (normal) and 58% (exponential) of other ziggurats on pre-fix code, and an independent C port in pedrobtz/zurand PR #45 (merged 2026-09-27) measured its McFarland method at 1.08-1.25x the speed of its NumPy-table ziggurat on EPYC 7763/9V74, about 1.04-1.10x on Neoverse N2 and 1.02-1.08x on Apple M1.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: README 7.987 ns per normal with no baseline timing in the repo (timings.csv 404); the paper's 58%/53% runtime vs other ziggurats is snippet-only, and the paper timed code later fixed for two bugs (Alex Herbert). Notable through its Commons RNG port and JDK 17's nextGaussian. Last commit 2025-05-21, stale.

**Known shortcoming:** PyPI fast_prng 1.1.2 (2015-06-10) predates the 2021 Herbert fixes (PR #1 convex-overhang bug that flattened the bell curve within +/-0.25, PR #2 off-by-one, a follow-up for about 4% of first-overhang values), so pip installs the biased sampler and the paper timings ran on pre-fix code. Global state, not thread-safe, x86 SSE2 only, seed only from pid/time/ppid; headers define non-static symbols (duplicate-symbol link errors across files); profile.c's omp pragma races on global state under -fopenmp.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** algorithm only, not this code: pedrobtz/zurand PR #45 (merged 2026-09-27) ports the McFarland method and measures 1.08-1.25x over its NumPy-table ziggurat on EPYC 7763/9V74, 1.04-1.10x on Neoverse N2, 1.02-1.08x on M1

**How:** McFarland's modified ziggurat (J. Stat. Comput. Simul. 86(7), 2016): 252/253 layers are built entirely under the density, so about 98.8% of draws exit after one 64-bit uniform, one table lookup and one multiply, with no rejection test. The low 8 bits of that same uniform, which the float multiply discards anyway, pick the layer. Draws that miss go to Walker alias sampling over the overhang/tail areas, and precomputed triangle bounds (min_iE/max_iE) accept or reject most overhang points without calling exp(). The uniform source is a pointer into a pre-filled SFMT block buffer, so the fast path is a pointer increment.

**Use it when:**
- Monte Carlo or simulation code in C that needs very large numbers of N(0,1) or Exp(1) doubles from a single thread and can live with a process-global generator.
- As a reference to port: the algorithm already powers Apache Commons RNG ZigguratSampler, and the pedrobtz/zurand R package re-derived its tables, so the C here is the canonical starting point for a new port.
- When a classic ziggurat (Marsaglia-Tsang, Doornik) is your hot spot and you want the same exactness with a shorter fast path.
- x86-64 Linux/macOS builds with SSE2 where you control the compile flags.

**Skip it when:**
- Multithreaded code: the generator state (sfmt array, iRandS buffer, global Rand pointer) is process-global with no locking or per-thread instances.
- Reproducible experiments: mt_init() seeds only from getpid(), time(NULL) and getppid() and ignores repeat calls, and there is no public seed function.
- Non-x86 targets or MSVC: MT19937.h uses __m128i/_mm_set_epi64 (MMX __m64) unconditionally and stores 64-bit values in 'signed long', which is 32-bit on Windows; unistd.h is required.
- Code that needs other distributions, float output, or a generic C++ engine/distribution interface; Zest or EigenRand fit better there.
- The PyPI package: fast_prng 1.1.2 dates from 2015-06-10, before the 2021 correctness fixes, so pip installs the biased sampler.

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond libm and POSIX unistd.h; bundled SFMT-derived MT19937.h (BSD) is required · C99 compiler with SSE2 intrinsics (README builds with gcc -O2 ... -lm; profile_all.py targets gcc-4.8) · x86-64 with SSE2, POSIX (Linux, macOS); Windows path partially stubbed but not workable as written

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over the miloyip/normaldist-benchmark and cauldron ziggurats when you want the McFarland layout (fewer rejection tests, exp() avoided on most overhang draws) as a C reference to port; pick Zest or EigenRand instead when you need a C++ distribution interface, more distributions, thread-local engines or SIMD batch output, and Randompack when you also need fast uniforms across languages.

**Gotchas:**
- Two correctness bugs found by Alex Herbert were fixed only in Aug-Sep 2021 (PR #1: convex-overhang resampling reused X and flattened the bell curve within +/-0.25; PR #2: off-by-one inflection index in both samplers; a follow-up commit fixed '~4% of sampled values in the 1st overhang'). The README says neither showed up in the first six moments, so the 2016 paper's timings ran on pre-fix code.
- The headers define non-static symbols (normal_setup, exponential_setup, global 'rand64_t *Rand'), so including them in more than one translation unit causes duplicate-symbol link errors; keep them in one .c file and wrap them.
- Rand is a raw cursor into the uniform buffer: if you mix in the helper uniforms (rand_long, wide_uniform) you must follow the README rule to call MT_FLUSH() at least every two increments, or you read past the buffer.
- benchmarks/profile.c has '#pragma omp parallel for' around the timing loop; compiled with -fopenmp it races on the global state, so time only single-threaded builds.

**Status:** Stale: the last code change was the Sept 2021 bug fixes and the 2025-05-21 commit only added an MIT LICENSE; the repo has 2 issues (both closed) and is small enough to vendor, but the 2015 PyPI release predates the fixes.

[repo](https://github.com/cd-mcfarland/fast_prng) · [benchmark](https://github.com/cd-mcfarland/fast_prng)

##### fastrand (PCG32 and xorshift128+ with nearly-divisionless bounded integers for Python)  `C (CPython extension)`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Tiny CPython C extension: PCG32/xorshift128+ bounded integers about 9x faster per call than random.randint.

**Beats:** CPython random.randint (Mersenne Twister) — The README's python3 -m timeit lines (also in scripts/runtests3.sh) show pcg32bounded(1001) at 23.6 ns and pcg32randint(100,1000) at 24.6 ns per call, against random.randint(0,1000) at 216 ns (about 9x, derived from page data) and legacy numpy.random.randint(0,1000) at 955 ns. No CPU, Python version, compiler or flags are given, and the comparison is per call to CPython's Mersenne Twister path, not against std::mt19937.

**Known shortcoming:** Bug (code read, not run): pcg32randint with a negative lower bound wraps via Py_BuildValue("I"), and error paths raise SystemError instead of ValueError; Python extension.

**Known shortcoming:** pcg32randint returns n1+r via Py_BuildValue("I"), so negative or >2**32 results wrap (code reading); error paths set ValueError then return None (SystemError). Fixed hard-coded default seed, never seeded from OS entropy, so every process gets the same stream. No tests in CI. README numbers give no CPU or Python version and the numpy baseline is per-call legacy randint. Issue #21: OverflowError on big ints. Python extension, not a C++ API.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each call is one METH_O or METH_FASTCALL C function, so it skips the several Python-level frames that random.randint goes through (randint -> randrange -> _randbelow). The generator is PCG32 (XSH-RR: one 64-bit multiply-add plus a xorshift and rotate), and the bounded draw uses Lemire's nearly-divisionless multiply-shift method (TOMACS 2019), which needs a modulo only on the rare rejection path. Most of the README's 9x gap is interpreter call overhead rather than generator speed.

**Use it when:**
- Pure-Python loops that draw one bounded integer at a time (simulations, randomized algorithms, sampling indices), where random.randint's ~200 ns per call dominates.
- Ranges that fit in 32 bits with a non-negative lower bound (pcg32bounded / pcg32randint), or unsigned 64-bit ranges via xorshift128plusbounded on Linux/macOS 64-bit builds.
- When you want a fixed, reproducible stream that you seed explicitly, and the global-state API is acceptable.
- As a reference for porting the PCG32 + nearly-divisionless bounded-integer code into C or C++: the core is about 30 lines.

**Skip it when:**
- Bulk generation of arrays: numpy's Generator (PCG64/SFC64) is vectorized and much cheaper per value; the README's numpy comparison times the legacy per-call numpy.random.randint, not batched draws.
- Negative lower bounds or results above 2**32-1 with pcg32randint: the result n1 + r is returned through Py_BuildValue("I"), an unsigned 32-bit format, so it should wrap or truncate (code reading, not executed). xorshift128plusrandint accepts only unsigned bounds.
- Anything security-related (tokens, keys, shuffling for gambling): PCG32 and xorshift128+ are not cryptographic; use the secrets module.
- Code that needs independent per-object or per-thread generators, getstate/setstate, or the random module's distributions and sequence helpers.
- Arbitrary-size integers: bounds must fit in a C long (issue #21 shows OverflowError for a 256-bit bound where random.randint succeeds).

**Integration:** module · none (CPython C API only; build needs setuptools>=77 and a C compiler, or a prebuilt wheel) · Python 3.9+ (pyproject requires-python); randint functions need 3.7+ METH_FASTCALL; wheels for CPython 3.9-3.14 and 3.14t · Wheels for Linux x86-64/aarch64 (glibc and musl), macOS x86-64/arm64/universal2, Windows AMD64. xorshift128+ bounded/randint functions exist only where __int128 is available on a 64-bit target (fastrand.SIXTYFOUR == 1); issue #26 reports a 32-bit Linux build failure.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over numpy's Generator or randomgen when you need single scalar draws inside Python code rather than arrays. If you are in C++, take the same nearly-divisionless method from FastShuffleExperiments, or use simdpcg when you need PCG32 throughput, instead of going through this Python wrapper.

**Gotchas:**
- Fixed default seed: both generators start from hard-coded constants and the module never seeds from OS entropy, so every new process produces the same sequence until you call pcg32_seed (and pcg32inc for distinct streams). Forked workers share the same state.
- Error paths set ValueError and then return None, which CPython reports as SystemError (returned a result with an exception set); a non-integer or out-of-range argument does not raise a clean ValueError.
- pcg32_uniform has only 32 bits of resolution (r * 2**-32); xorshift128plus_uniform uses the low 53 bits of xorshift128+, whose lowest bits are its weakest.
- Seeding xorshift128+ with both state words zero leaves it stuck at zero; there is no check. The repo has no unit tests: CI only builds wheels and scripts/runtests3.sh runs the timeit lines.

**Status:** Active: version 3.1.0 was released on 2026-05-15 with wheels for CPython 3.9-3.14. Apache-2.0, and the C core is small enough to copy, but the Python wrapper has the bound and error-handling bugs noted above.

[repo](https://github.com/lemire/fastrand) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lemire/fastrand/HEAD/README.md)

##### frand (lukechampine/frand, Go userspace CSPRNG)  `Go`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Go userspace CSPRNG: a sync.Pool of crypto/rand-seeded ChaCha8 generators, far faster than crypto/rand for bulk and parallel reads.

**Beats:** Go crypto/rand (and math/rand in parallel benchmarks) — The current README claims 20x faster than crypto/rand for large reads and over 100x in parallel, but gives no hardware, Go version or results. The only published numbers are in the pre-2024 README for the ChaCha12 fast-key-erasure version: Read of 512 KB 5094 vs 239 MB/s (about 21x, derived from page data), and with 64 goroutines 19665 vs 191 MB/s (about 103x, derived from page data); math/rand was faster for Intn and Perm. For the ChaCha8 generator frand now wraps, a 2025 Lemire benchmark (search snippet only; code in lemire/Code-used-on-Daniel-Lemire-s-blog 2025/10/15) reports 2.6 ns vs 51 ns per uint64 for ChaCha8 vs crypto/rand on an Apple M4. That supports the order of magnitude for the generator but does not measure frand itself.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C, Go only: frand_test.go does hold crypto/rand benchmarks, but the 21x and 103x figures (derived from page data) come from the old README table at 3f951cc for a previous implementation with no hardware stated.

**Known shortcoming:** The 20x and 100x figures come from the pre-2024 ChaCha12 build; no results are published for the current ChaCha8 wrapper (frand_test.go has benchmarks), and the speed now comes mostly from Go stdlib ChaCha8. NewCustom ignores bufsize and rounds, and its seeded output changed at the 2024-10-07 switch; Source.Uint64 never returns 2^64-1. Go only, 22 commits, stale.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** independent context: Lemire's 2025/10/15 Go post (snippet) has math/rand/v2 ChaCha8 at 2.6 ns vs crypto/rand 51 ns per uint64 on an Apple M4, measuring the generator frand wraps rather than frand itself

**How:** Random bytes come from the ChaCha8 stream cipher keystream in userspace (Go's math/rand/v2 ChaCha8, partly in assembly) instead of a getrandom syscall per call, so large reads run at keystream speed. The sync.Pool gives each concurrently running goroutine its own derived generator, so there is no shared lock and throughput scales with cores. Since the 2024-10-07 commit 'switch to stdlib ChaCha8 generator', the generator itself is Go's stdlib code; frand's own contribution is the seeding, pooling and helper API (before that it was a hand-written ChaCha12 fast-key-erasure design).

**Use it when:**
- Go services that need lots of unpredictable bytes (tokens, nonces, salts, test data) and are bottlenecked on crypto/rand.Read, especially from many goroutines at once.
- Replacing math/rand in Go code where predictability is a bug: hash-table salts, randomized test cases that must differ run to run, load-balancer jitter.
- Bulk fills of hundreds of KB per call, where the old README measured 5094 MB/s vs 239 MB/s for crypto/rand on 512 KB reads.
- Code that wants Intn/Perm/Shuffle helpers on a secure source without handling errors on every call.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: this is a pure Go module with no C ABI; for a C userspace random pool see randp or the aesctr generator in testingRNG.
- Long-lived key material where you want the kernel to hold the state: the generator state lives in process memory and no new entropy is mixed in after the one-time seed (README).
- Small-integer hot loops (Intn, Perm) where an insecure PRNG is acceptable: the old README table had math/rand faster (Intn 20 vs 45 ns/op, Perm(32) 789 vs 954 ns/op), and Uint64n still uses modulo with rejection rather than Lemire's nearly divisionless method (issue #3, open since 2020).
- Reproducible seeded streams across versions: NewCustom output changed when the backend moved from ChaCha12 to ChaCha8, and the bufsize and rounds arguments are now ignored.
- Go 1.22 and older toolchains: go.mod requires Go 1.23.1 because it depends on math/rand/v2.ChaCha8.

**Integration:** module · none (Go standard library only) · Go 1.23.1 (go.mod; needs math/rand/v2 ChaCha8) · any platform Go supports

**Vs siblings:** Pick frand when a Go program needs a secure source that is fast and scales across goroutines; valyala/fastrand and pgregory.net/rand (sfc64) report lower per-call times in their own benchmarks but are not cryptographic, and vpxyz/xorshift is a set of plain non-crypto generators. For C/C++, randp (AES-CTR pool beating glibc arc4random) is the closest catalogued analogue.

**Gotchas:**
- Since 2024-10-07 the package is a thin wrapper over Go's math/rand/v2 ChaCha8; on Go 1.23+ you get most of the speed by using rand.NewChaCha8 with a crypto/rand seed yourself, and frand adds the pool and helpers.
- NewCustom(seed, bufsize, rounds) silently ignores bufsize and rounds and panics unless the seed is exactly 32 bytes; the old README described the default as ChaCha12, the current code is ChaCha8.
- Source.Uint64 calls Uint64n(math.MaxUint64), so it can never return 2^64-1; Source.Seed makes the stream deterministic, which removes the security property for that Source.
- The README's 20x and 100x figures were measured on the pre-2024 implementation against the crypto/rand of that time; Linux's vDSO getrandom (LWN reports about 15x faster small reads than the syscall) narrows the gap on new kernels, so re-measure on your Go version and kernel.

**Status:** Stale since the 2024-10-07 ChaCha8 switch (22 commits, 1 open issue, 93 stars), but MIT-licensed, a single 270-line file using only the stdlib, so it is easy to vendor; usable from Go only.

[repo](https://github.com/lukechampine/frand) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lukechampine/frand)

##### libchaos (KISS, Xoroshiro128Plus, Xorshf96 and other PRNGs)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Abandoned C++11 grab-bag of small PRNGs (xorshift128+, xorshift1024*, KISS, xorshf96) about 2.6x faster per call than std::mt19937.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (also std::minstd_rand, ranlux24/48, knuth_b) — README Google Benchmark rows from a Travis CI VM (CPU not stated; g++-4.8, -O3 -flto -march=native per the build files) report the '128+' class at 178.4M items/s and xorshf96 at 185.1M, against std::mt19937 at 68.2M and mt19937_64 at 60.1M items/s (about 2.6x, derived from page data). The libchaos and STL rows are shown separately; the harness counts one item per four discarded next() calls and uses no DoNotOptimize, so the absolute rates are understated 4x and output tempering may be optimized away for every engine.

**Known shortcoming:** Mislabelled generators: XOROSHIRO128PLUS is actually xorshift128+ and XOROSHIRO1024STAR is xorshift1024*; the bench discards outputs (no DoNotOptimize) and counts 4 calls as 1 item (ratios still valid).

**Known shortcoming:** Misnamed generators: XOROSHIRO128PLUS is actually xorshift128+ and XOROSHIRO1024STAR is xorshift1024*. prng<> has no result_type, so it is not a URBG and std distributions should fail. seed() overwrites one word only (first 128+ output = seed + 0x121fd2155c472f96). truely<> reads uninitialized members (UB). README pitches chaos::password for hashing with no third-party cryptanalysis. CMake rejects MSVC; library built with -march=native; bench discards outputs. Abandoned 2017.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** There is no special technique: the speedup is what any small-state xorshift- or multiply-with-carry-family generator gets over MT19937's 624-word state and periodic twist. next() is an inline handful of shifts, xors and adds on 2-16 words of state (xorshift128+, xorshift1024* with a final multiply, Marsaglia's xorshf96 and KISS, and an MWC pair called 'abyssinian'). The benchmark builds everything with -O3 -flto -march=native.

**Use it when:**
- Reading or reproducing the chaos-machine research (XORRING32/64 machines and the ePrint paper), which is the library's actual focus.
- Needing a copy of Marsaglia's KISS or xorshf96 with the exact sequences pinned by the repo's signature tests.
- Quick non-critical C++11 simulations or games where a small generator about 2-3x faster per call than std::mt19937 is enough and BSD-2-Clause is acceptable.
- Otherwise, take the reference xoshiro/PCG code or a maintained sibling instead; nothing here is faster than those originals.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need xoroshiro128+ or xoroshiro1024*: the classes with those names implement the older xorshift128+ and xorshift1024* algorithms, so the output and quality do not match the names.
- With <random> distributions or any template that expects a UniformRandomBitGenerator: chaos::prng<> has min(), max() and operator() but no result_type typedef, so std::uniform_int_distribution and similar should not compile against it (code reading, not compiled).
- Anything security-related: the README offers chaos::password<CHAOS_MACHINE_XORRING64,...> for password hashing and calls the machines suitable for cryptographic primitives, but the repo cites no third-party cryptanalysis, only the author's ePrint paper.
- MSVC or portable binaries: CMake stops on any compiler other than GCC or Clang, Clang is forced to -stdlib=libc++, and the installed library is built with -march=native.
- Production use in general: the code was last committed on 2017-01-01, the CHANGELOG still reads 'Release 0.0.1 (in development)', the README warns 'early stage of development', and a 2017 link-error issue (#11) is unanswered.

**Integration:** header-only · none for the PRNG headers; the chaos machines link libchaos (src/, built with CMake); tests and benchmarks use Google Test and Google Benchmark submodules · C++11, g++ 4.7+ (CMake check); Travis CI used g++-4.8. Clang builds force libc++. MSVC is rejected by CMakeLists.txt. · Linux/macOS with GCC or Clang (Travis used Ubuntu trusty); no architecture-specific code in the PRNG headers

**Vs siblings:** Rarely. For a fast modern engine, cpp_prngs (RomuDuoJr, QuarkBurst64) is benchmarked directly against std::mt19937 and the other std engines, and testingRNG benchmarks the original lehmer64, xoroshiro128+ and PCG code. Pick libchaos only for its chaos-machine experiments or for its KISS/xorshf96 implementations with pinned test signatures.

**Gotchas:**
- Weak seeding: seed(n) on the '128+' and '1024*' classes overwrites only the first state word and leaves the rest as fixed constants, so the first CHAOS_PRNG_XOROSHIRO128PLUS output after seed(n) is just n + 0x121fd2155c472f96, and streams from nearby seeds start correlated. KISS.seed(x) never reseeds its two MWC words, and seed(0) zeroes its xorshift component.
- Every generator object carries two std::string members (name and authors, from CHAOS_META_DEFINE), so construction can allocate and copies are heavier than the state alone.
- chaos.h #defines and then #undefs short macro names (M, R, KISS, MWC, SHR3, CONG, znew, wnew), which clobbers user macros with those names.
- chaos::truely<> reads current_position and current_checkpoint in its constructor (via reseed()) before they are initialized, which is undefined behaviour.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2017-01-01 with 23 commits; BSD-2-Clause, and the PRNG headers are small enough to copy, but the mislabelled algorithms and missing result_type make it a poor dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/maciejczyzewski/libchaos) · [benchmark](https://github.com/maciejczyzewski/libchaos)

##### mir-random (libmir/mir-random, D random number generators)  `D`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

D random library: Lemire bounded integers, a faster Mersenne Twister (since merged into Phobos), xoshiro/PCG engines, ndslice distributions.

**Beats:** D Phobos std.random (Mt19937 generation and initialization, modulo-reduction bounded integers) — bench/Mt19937_bench.d (100 million outputs, LDC via ldmd2 with dub release-nobounds, CPU not stated) shows mir's 32-bit Mt19937 at 6.81 Gb/s vs the Phobos Mt19937 of that time at 4.42 Gb/s (1.54x), with matching checksums. Phobos has since adopted this implementation (D 2.074.0 changelog per a search snippet; dlang.org is blocked here, but current Phobos std/random.d credits it). bench/randindex_bench.d on an Intel Core i7-7920HQ compares Lemire multiply-shift with modulo-with-rejection, both written in the bench file, over 800 million calls with moduli 6 to 105: ulong from Xoroshiro128Plus 4.40 vs 1.02 x10^8 calls/s, ulong from Mt19937_64 1.87 vs 0.80 x10^8. Current Phobos uniform and _uniformIndex still use modulo-with-rejection, so that gap should still hold against Phobos, but Phobos itself was not timed.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: bench/Mt19937_bench.d gives mir 6.81 vs Phobos 4.42 Gb/s (1.54x) with no CPU listed; randindex_bench.d (i7-7920HQ) compares modulo vs Lemire within the same file, not Phobos. No benchmark backs the +100% init claim. No root LICENSE file; BSL-1.0 per dub.sdl and file headers.

**Known shortcoming:** The Mt19937 +54%/+100% claim no longer applies: current Phobos std/random.d credits Yaroshenko/mir-random for its Mersenne Twister (D 2.074.0 changelog, snippet only). randIndex 1.4-4.3x is measured against a modulo version written in the bench file, not Phobos, though Phobos uniform still uses modulo so that gap probably holds. 'Active' overstates it (2 compiler-fix commits since 2022-01); issue #133 (sign errors in flex unit-test expectations) open since 2021; rand!float returns (-1,1), not [0,1); the default Random is Mt19937_64.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** randIndex replaces modulo-with-rejection by Daniel Lemire's multiply-shift reduction (a double-width multiply; the rejection threshold, and its division, is computed only when the low half falls below m), with a branch hint on the rare path. The Mersenne Twister updates one state word per call over a reversed state array and interleaves tempering of the previous output with the state update so values stay in registers, instead of regenerating all 624 words in a block. Floating-point rand!T fills every mantissa bit (saturated values; README: rand!real can produce more than 2^78 distinct values).

**Use it when:**
- D programs doing many bounded integer draws (shuffles, sampling, random indexing), where randIndex measured 1.4x to 4.3x more calls per second than modulo reduction on the same engine.
- D code that needs a faster default generator than Phobos's 32-bit Mt19937: switch to Xoroshiro128Plus or Xoshiro256StarStar, which the bench runs much faster than Mt19937_64 under randIndex.
- Filling ndslice arrays with normal, exponential, gamma or multivariate-normal variates for simulation or Monte Carlo in D.
- -betterC or @nogc nothrow code that cannot use DRuntime; the engines and rand functions are @nogc and do not need the GC.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: generators are D templates with no C ABI; only the entropy functions (mir_random_genRandomNonBlocking and mir_random_genRandomBlocking) have C names. In C++ use the catalogued C++ entries instead.
- Mersenne Twister throughput alone: Phobos's MersenneTwisterEngine has used this implementation since it was merged (current std/random.d credits Ilya Yaroshenko and mir-random), so the +54% generation figure no longer applies to current Phobos.
- Cryptography, tokens or secrets: the README says not to use it for that.
- Projects that need an active upstream: only 2 commits since January 2022 (December 2024 and June 2026, both compiler fixes), and issue #133 (wrong signs in flex transformation unit-test expectations) has been open since 2021.
- Code built on Phobos's range-based RNG API: engines use opCall and forbid default construction and copying, so porting needs PhobosRandom or rewrites.

**Integration:** module · mir-core (>=0.2.0 <2.0.0); mir-linux-kernel on Linux; advapi32 on Windows; mir-algorithm optional ('default' configuration) or required ('extended') for ndslice and distribution features; the 'minimal' configuration omits it · not documented; code branches for LDC, GDC and DMD, and README figures used LDC 1.6.0; last commit (2026-06-10) adapted to recent compilers · Linux, Windows, macOS/iOS and the BSDs (seeding via getrandom, Windows APIs or arc4random); any architecture D compilers target

**Vs siblings:** Pick mir-random only for D code; for C++ the same ideas are catalogued directly: FastShuffleExperiments for Lemire's nearly divisionless bounded integers, cslarsen/mersenne-twister or VMT19937 for a faster Mersenne Twister, and dqrng or simdrng for xoshiro/PCG engines with fast distributions.

**Gotchas:**
- rand!float / rand!double / rand!real return values in (-1, 1), not [0, 1); apply fabs or use a uniform variable for [0, 1).
- The default Random is Mt19937_64 on 64-bit targets (Mt19937 on 32-bit), which is slower than the bundled xoshiro/xoroshiro engines; choose an engine explicitly when speed matters.
- Engines @disable default construction and postblit, so they must be passed by ref or pointer; seeding Mt19937 from a 64-bit unpredictableSeed requires masking to Mt19937.max (shown in the docs).
- Xoroshiro128Plus (xoroshiro128+) has weak low bits that fail binary-rank tests; the module docs recommend Xoshiro256StarStar as the all-purpose generator.

**Status:** Maintenance-only rather than active (2 commits since January 2022, both compiler fixes; 32 stars; dub package), but Boost-licensed (Apache-2.0 for PCG) and usable from D; out of language scope for C++.

[repo](https://github.com/libmir/mir-random) · [benchmark](https://github.com/libmir/mir-random/tree/master/bench)

##### miranda (coolbutuseless/miranda, R package with C PRNGs: romu trio, xoshiro256+, lehmer64, splitmix64)  `R`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Tiny R package exposing RomuTrio, xoshiro256+, lehmer64 and SplitMix64 as runif-style functions, about 20x faster than R's runif().

**Beats:** R base runif() — README bench::mark of 1e6 uniform doubles: R's runif(N) (default Mersenne-Twister) sits at about 30 ms, while non-GC iterations of runif_romutrio and runif_xoshiro256p cluster near 1.5 ms, lehmer64 near 1.7 ms and splitmix64 near 2.5 ms (about 12x-20x, values read off a log-axis beeswarm, derived from page data); iterations that triggered garbage collection took 5-13 ms. No CPU, R version, compiler or flags are given, and the gap measures R's runif call path against an inlined C loop, not generator against generator in C++.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: a README chart only (runif about 30 ms vs romutrio about 1.5 ms, roughly 20x, read by eye), no CPU or flags. Last commit 2022-05-10, abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** R glue only, with no value over the upstream generator sources for C++. romutrio.c carries an Apache-2.0 header, not MIT. lehmer64 is compiled out on Windows (runif_lehmer64 returns a single 0 there); one global state per generator, not thread-safe; issue #1 (Windows build failure) has no reply. On a chart re-read, GC iterations take 5-13 ms, so the 20x holds only on non-GC runs.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Each runif_* call runs one tight C loop that steps the generator inline and converts the top 53 bits to a double with (x >> 11) * 0x1.0p-53, writing straight into a freshly allocated REALSXP. The generators themselves are cheap: RomuTrio is a multiply plus two subtract-rotates, xoshiro256+ is xor/shift/rotate, lehmer64 is one 128-bit multiply (unsigned __int128), SplitMix64 is an add plus two xorshift-multiplies. The speedup is mostly avoided per-value overhead in R's runif path rather than a novel generator technique.

**Use it when:**
- R code that draws millions of plain U(min, max) doubles in a hot loop and does not need set.seed() reproducibility through R's own RNG machinery.
- You need to save and restore generator state exactly (get_state_*/set_state_* as raw vectors) or skip ahead 2^128/2^192 steps with jump_xoshiro256p/long_jump_xoshiro256p.
- You want a readable reference of how to bind a small C PRNG to R's .Call interface with state save/restore.
- Linux or macOS 64-bit R builds, where all four generators compile (lehmer64 needs unsigned __int128).

**Skip it when:**
- C++ projects: the files add only R glue (R.h/Rinternals.h, SEXP returns, global state); take the generators from their reference sources or a catalogued C++ library instead.
- You need normals, integers, sampling or other distributions: only uniform doubles are provided (dqrng covers rnorm and sample.int).
- Windows R builds that need lehmer64: it is compiled out under _WIN32 and runif_lehmer64 prints a message and returns a single 0 instead of n values.
- Production or packaged work: lifecycle badge says experimental, 11 commits, last code change September 2020, install is from GitHub only per the README, and issue #1 (Windows i386 build failure) has no maintainer reply.
- Parallel or multi-stream use: each generator has exactly one global stream per process, with no per-object state.

**Integration:** module · R (built via R CMD INSTALL / remotes::install_github); testthat suggested for tests · C compiler accepted by R's build tools; lehmer64 needs unsigned __int128 (64-bit GCC or Clang). R version minimum not documented. · Any 64-bit R build for xoshiro256+, RomuTrio and SplitMix64; lehmer64 disabled on Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick dqrng over this for almost any R use: it is a header-only C++ library and R package with xoshiro256++/PCG64, fast rnorm and sample.int, and active maintenance. miranda is only the better pick if you specifically want RomuTrio or lehmer64 behind a runif-like call; for C++ code use the reference generators directly (Romu, testingRNG's lehmer64) or a SIMD sibling such as simdrng.

**Gotchas:**
- Licensing is mixed despite the package's MIT label: romutrio.c carries Mark Overton's Apache-2.0 header and xoshiro256p.c/splitmix64.c carry Blackman/Vigna CC0 headers; vendoring romutrio.c brings Apache-2.0 obligations.
- Generators are seeded once in .onLoad from stats::runif, so results are reproducible only if you call the package's set_seed_* (or set.seed() before the package loads); forked workers such as parallel::mclapply would start from copies of the same state unless reseeded or jumped (inferred from the global state in the C code).
- The double conversion maps 53 bits to [0, 1), so an exact 0 (or min) is a possible output.
- romutrio.c does arithmetic on void* when copying state (pbytes + 8), a GNU extension; porting it to strict C or C++ needs a cast to unsigned char*.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022 (last code change September 2020, then a README typo fix); MIT package licence with Apache-2.0 and CC0 file headers, and the C cores are small enough to vendor, but they offer nothing over the upstream reference sources for C++ users.

[repo](https://github.com/coolbutuseless/miranda) · [benchmark](https://github.com/coolbutuseless/miranda)

##### MRG32k3a branchless implementation (Vigna)  `C (with Java version)`  `CC0-1.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Branchless 64-bit-integer MRG32k3a in C and Java, about 4x faster per double than L'Ecuyer's reference code, same stream.

**Beats:** L'Ecuyer's reference double-based MRG32k3a.c (also the equivalent 64-bit integer implementation) — The author's header comment reports, on an Intel Core i7-7700 @3.60GHz with gcc 9.2.1 and his own harness (prng.di.unimi.it/harness.c; flags not stated), about 17.5 ns per double for L'Ecuyer's double-based MRG32k3a.c, 7.9 ns for a straightforward 64-bit integer version and 4.1 ns for this code (about 4.3x and 1.9x, derived from page data). A Python re-implementation of both update rules run in this session produced identical outputs for 201 seeds x 2000 draws (first value 0.12701112204657714 for seed 12345 x6), which supports the identical-stream claim.

**Known shortcoming:** Flags unstated; harness host (prng.di.unimi.it) blocked here; no LICENSE file (CC0 in headers).

**Known shortcoming:** Code unchanged since 2019-11 (the 2026-06 commit is wording only), so 'active' overstates. Single global state, no streams. Header lacks extern "C"; Java constructors are package-private. Output matches the L'Ecuyer reference (independent re-implementation, 201 seeds x 2000 draws).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It works on int64_t instead of doubles and removes all three data-dependent branches of the reference code. The two negative-residual fixes go away by adding the constant m*a13 (m*a23) before the % so the operand is always nonnegative; modulo by a constant compiles to multiply-and-shift. The combination step's 'if p1 <= p2 add m1' becomes the mask m1 * ((r - 1) >> 63). The output is computed from the current state rather than the new one, so the CPU can overlap it with the next state update; this is why init6 discards one value to stay aligned with L'Ecuyer's stream.

**Use it when:**
- You need MRG32k3a specifically, for example to reproduce results from codes or papers that use L'Ecuyer's generator, and want its scalar draws about 4x cheaper than MRG32k3a.c (17.5 ns to 4.1 ns per double on the author's i7-7700).
- Monte Carlo or discrete-event simulation in C or C++ that draws one double at a time in (0,1) and must use L'Ecuyer's published generator.
- Java simulations that use SSJ's MRG32k3a and want a faster single-stream nextDouble (header Javadoc: 21.6 ns SSJ double-based, 13.6 ns SSJ long-based, 5.4 ns this, JMH on i7-7700).
- Code bases that need a public-domain (CC0) generator they can paste in: two C files or one Java file.

**Skip it when:**
- Multiple independent streams or substreams (jump-ahead): not implemented; the header points to SSJ's MRG32k3aL for that.
- Batch or vectorized generation: the README itself says Intel MKL's vectorized MRG32k3a is faster for batches.
- When you do not need MRG32k3a in particular: modern 64-bit generators in the same category (xoshiro, PCG, Philox) are cheaper per bit and produce 64 bits instead of one 32-bit-resolution double.
- Multithreaded C code: the C version keeps its state in six global variables with no per-thread instance.
- Integer or 64-bit output: the only output is a double with roughly 32 bits of resolution (multiples of 1/(m1+1)).

**Integration:** source-drop · none (C: stdint.h, inttypes.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h; Java: none) · Not documented; needs C with stdint.h/inttypes.h and 64-bit integers. The author timed gcc 9.2.1 (C) and Java 13 (Java). · any with 64-bit integer arithmetic; relies on arithmetic right shift of negative int64_t, which C leaves implementation-defined (gcc, clang and MSVC all shift arithmetically)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Randen, OpenRAND/Philox or the xoshiro/PCG siblings only when MRG32k3a itself is required for reproducibility or validation, since those siblings are faster general-purpose generators. Prefer OpenRAND or another counter-based generator when you need many parallel streams or GPU support.

**Gotchas:**
- Seeding by writing the state directly instead of calling MRG32k3a_init6/setSeed(long...) shifts the stream by one value: the generator emits from the current state, so you must discard one output to line up with the reference.
- MRG32k3a_init6 calls abort() on an all-zero or out-of-range seed instead of returning an error.
- The C header has no extern "C" guards, and its state uses reserved double-underscore names; from C++ either compile MRG32k3a.c as C++ or wrap the #include in extern "C".
- In the Java file the constructors have no access modifier (package-private) and the class is in the default package, so you must copy it into your own package or use setSeed on an instance made in that package.

**Status:** The code has not changed since November 2019; the June 2026 commit only renamed 'testless' to 'branchless' in the comments. It is CC0, has no open issues and is small enough to vendor as is.

[repo](https://github.com/vigna/MRG32k3a) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vigna/MRG32k3a/HEAD/MRG32k3a.h)

##### NumPy numpy.random Generator (PCG64, PCG64DXSM, SFC64 bit generators)  `Python/C (Cython)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

NumPy's Generator API with PCG64/PCG64DXSM/SFC64 bit generators and ziggurat samplers; about 1.6-2.5x faster than legacy MT19937 RandomState.

**Beats:** MT19937 (legacy RandomState and MT19937 under Generator) — NumPy's own timeit script (min of 3 runs, 1,000,000 values per call) on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X under Ubuntu 20.04 with GCC 9.3.0 gives uniforms in 3.1 ns (PCG64), 2.9 ns (PCG64DXSM) and 2.6 ns (SFC64) versus 5.9 ns for MT19937 under Generator and 6.0 ns for legacy RandomState, for overall geometric-mean speedups over RandomState of 2.19x, 2.25x and 2.51x. Optimization flags are not stated, the baseline is NumPy's own C MT19937 rather than std::mt19937, and 32-bit Windows reverses the result for the PCG generators.

**Known shortcoming:** Flags missing (GCC 9.3.0 / MSVC 19 on Ryzen 9 3900X; script doc/source/reference/random/performance.py); bulk draws (1e6 per call); the new generators lose on 32-bit Windows and Laplace is slower with PCG64DXSM; Python library, the C core is reachable only via numpy's C API.

**Known shortcoming:** Python-first, not a C++ API. Known PCG64 multi-stream weakness (#16313, addressed by PCG64DXSM). On 32-bit Windows PCG64 is slower than MT19937 (25 vs 100).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The bit generators are cheaper per 64-bit output than MT19937: PCG64 is a 128-bit LCG with an XSL-RR output permutation, PCG64DXSM uses a cheaper 64-bit multiplier on the LCG step plus a stronger xorshift-multiply (DXSM) output, and SFC64 (from PractRand) is a 256-bit add/xor/shift/rotate generator with no multiplications. Native __uint128_t is used where the compiler has it, with _umul128 emulation on MSVC. Much of the larger gain over RandomState comes from the samplers: ziggurat normals and exponentials instead of Box-Muller and log inversion, and Lemire's nearly divisionless method for bounded integers; draws are made in bulk loops in C with the GIL released.

**Use it when:**
- Python code still calling np.random.* or RandomState for bulk draws: switching to default_rng() gives about 2.2x geometric-mean speedup overall (5.3x for normals, 10.7x for exponentials) on the page's 64-bit Linux run.
- Large array draws (the benchmark uses 1,000,000 values per call) of uniforms, ints, normals, exponentials or gammas on 64-bit x86 Linux or Windows.
- Raw speed with no jump-ahead needed: SFC64 is the fastest NumPy bit generator (2.5 ns per uint64, 2.6 ns per uniform versus 5.6/5.9 for MT19937), including on 32-bit builds.
- Many parallel streams: SeedSequence.spawn or BitGenerator.spawn for independent streams; prefer PCG64DXSM over PCG64 when spawning millions of streams.
- C, Cython or Numba code that already ships with NumPy and wants its distribution samplers through the bitgen_t C API instead of writing its own.

**Skip it when:**
- Plain C++ projects: the measured path is the Python API, and using the C core means linking NumPy's npyrandom and npymath static libraries or copying sources; pcg-cpp or a header-only generator is simpler.
- 32-bit builds: on 32-bit Windows PCG64 scores 25 and PCG64DXSM 39 versus MT19937 at 100 overall; only SFC64 (77) comes close.
- One value at a time in a Python loop: per-call interpreter overhead dominates and the per-value nanosecond figures do not apply.
- Laplace, Poisson or binomial-heavy workloads: gains are small or negative (Laplace 76.1 ns with PCG64DXSM versus 73.2 ns with MT19937 under Generator).
- Security or cryptography: the docs say these generators are not suitable; use secrets.

**Integration:** module (Python package with Cython/C extension); C access via the npyrandom static library shipped in numpy/random/lib · Python and NumPy; the C API also needs npymath · not documented on the pages read; the C sources require C99 or later (pcg64.h errors on nonstandard GNU inline semantics) · any platform NumPy supports; fast path needs a 64-bit build (native __uint128_t where available, _umul128 emulation on MSVC)

**Vs siblings:** Pick NumPy's Generator when you are already in the Python/NumPy stack and need many distributions with sound parallel seeding at no integration cost. randomgen (the project this code came from) adds faster bit generators such as Romu and Xoshiro256 with the same interface, and Randompack's paper reports lower per-value times than NumPy (U(0,1) 0.42 versus 1.8 ns); in C++ use pcg-cpp, EigenRand or a SIMD generator instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Stream compatibility is only promised for the same seed, method calls, NumPy build and machine; Generator algorithms may change in X.Y releases, and default_rng may switch its default bit generator (PCG64DXSM is slated to replace PCG64).
- PCG64 (XSL-RR) has a known weakness with millions of randomly seeded streams: two streams sharing the low 58 state bits fail PractRand when interleaved (numpy issue #16313); use PCG64DXSM, SFC64 or Philox at that scale.
- SFC64 has no jumped() or advance(); parallel use must go through SeedSequence spawning.
- Calling rng.random() five times is not guaranteed to equal rng.random(5); NumPy reserves the right to use different algorithms for different block sizes.

**Status:** Actively maintained (32.9k stars, commits on 2026-10-01) and BSD-3-Clause; the Generator API has shipped since NumPy 1.17 and the C sources are small enough to copy if you need the generators without Python.

[repo](https://github.com/numpy/numpy) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/numpy/numpy/main/doc/source/reference/random/performance.rst)

##### randomgen (NumPy-compatible bit generators: SFC64, Romu, Xoshiro256, PCG64, SFMT)  `C (Cython/Python wrapper)`  `BSD-3-Clause OR NCSA`  `active`  `Tier C`

Python/C package of extra NumPy bit generators (Romu, SFC64, Xoshiro256, counter-based); about 2.3-2.8x faster overall than legacy RandomState.

**Beats:** MT19937 as used by NumPy's legacy RandomState (also compared against MT19937, MT64, DSFMT inside randomgen) — The project's doc script times numpy.random.Generator draws of 25,000 values per call (min of 10 repeats of 100 calls) on an Intel Cascade Lake at 3.1 GHz under Linux, compiler and flags unstated: uniform doubles take 2.4 ns (Romu trio), 2.5 (SFC64) and 2.9 (PCG64) versus 4.0 ns for MT19937 and 5.2 ns for NumPy's legacy RandomState, and the geometric mean across six distributions is 2.3-2.8x RandomState for the listed fast generators.
