**Known shortcoming:** On gammas MT19937 beats PCG64, PCG64DXSM and Xoshiro256; overlaps NumPy (NumPy's Generator was derived from it); dual-licensed BSD-3-Clause OR NCSA; Python package.

**Known shortcoming:** Latest PyPI release 2.3.0 fails to import with NumPy 2.4 (#426 open; fix on main, unreleased). randomgen/meson.build adds -mavx2 -maes -mrdrnd to every extension, so x86 builds appear to assume AVX2 CPUs (inferred from the build file). Gain over NumPy's own PCG64/SFC64 is at most ~1.2x. Python package; Romu C sources are Apache-2.0.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each generator is a small C state machine (randomgen/src/<gen>/) exposed through NumPy's bitgen function pointers (next_uint64, next_uint32, next_double), so Generator fills whole arrays in C. The fast cores are cheap per step: RomuTrio/RomuQuad are rotate-multiply generators with 3-4 words of state, SFC64 is add/xor/shift/rotate plus a Weyl counter with no multiply, Xoshiro256 (xoshiro256**) updates four words with xor/shift/rotate and scrambles with two multiplies, whereas MT19937 regenerates a 624-word state block and, per the docs, needs two 32-bit outputs per 64-bit value. 32-bit draws use the cached upper half of a 64-bit output. Most of the normal and exponential gap against RandomState comes from NumPy Generator's ziggurat samplers versus the legacy methods, not from the bit generator.

**Use it when:**
- Python/NumPy simulations that still use RandomState or MT19937 and draw arrays of thousands of values, where a faster bit generator under numpy.random.Generator is a one-line change
- You need a generator NumPy does not ship (Romu, Xoshiro256/512, JSF, LXM, SFMT, Squares, Tyche, EFIIX64, AESCounter, ChaCha, SPECK128, HC128), for example to reproduce a C/C++ simulation's stream from Python
- Thousands of parallel streams: SFC64 with distinct Weyl increments (weyl_increments(n)), keyed counter-based generators, or PCG64DXSM with SeedSequence.spawn, as the performance page recommends
- C/C++ developers who want tested C sources for many generators with Python bindings for cross-checking output

**Skip it when:**
- Pure C++ projects: this is a Python extension, and lifting a generator from randomgen/src means also taking common/randomgen_config.h and honoring that component's own license
- When NumPy's built-in PCG64 or SFC64 is enough: in the same table Romu(trio) draws uniforms in 2.4 ns versus 2.5 ns for SFC64 and 2.9 ns for PCG64 (about 1.2x at best, derived from page data), a small gain for an extra dependency
- Environments on NumPy 2.4 with the latest release (2.3.0): import fails (open issue #426)
- Scalar one-at-a-time draws from Python: the timings amortize 25,000 values per call, so per-call overhead dominates single draws
- Mersenne Twister variants (MT19937, MT64, SFMT, DSFMT) or RDRAND (about 880 ns per value): the docs advise against the MT family unless backward compatibility is needed

**Integration:** module (Python/Cython package on PyPI and conda-forge; the per-generator C files under randomgen/src can be used as a source-drop) · NumPy >=1.22.3 at runtime; building needs NumPy >=2.0, Cython >=3.0.10 and meson-python (meson >=1.9) · Python 3.9-3.13 per README (pyproject says >=3.8); C99 compiler (GCC, Clang or MSVC) · PyPI 2.3.0 wheels for Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux), musllinux x86-64, macOS x86-64 and arm64, Windows x86-64; README also lists FreeBSD and Linux ARM CI. RDRAND is x86-only and AESCounter is fast only with AES-NI

**Vs siblings:** Against the NumPy Generator entry, pick randomgen only for generators NumPy lacks (Romu, Xoshiro, JSF, AES, ChaCha, Squares, Tyche) or for SFC64's configurable Weyl increment; NumPy's own PCG64/SFC64 give nearly the same speed. For C or C++ code, Randompack (a C library) or EigenRand are the better catalogued choices, and dqrng fills the same role in R.

**Gotchas:**
- randomgen 2.3.0 (the latest PyPI release, 2025-10-22) fails to import with NumPy 2.4 because numpy.random.bit_generator.SeedlessSequence was removed (issue #426, open since 2025-12-22); main's common.pyx no longer references it, but no newer release was on PyPI as of 2026-10-01
- randomgen/meson.build adds -msse2 -mssse3 -maes -mrdrnd -mavx2 to every extension on GCC/Clang, so x86-64 builds appear to assume AVX2 and AES-NI CPUs (inferred from the build file; not stated in the docs)
- Component licenses differ from the package's BSD-3-Clause/NCSA: the Romu sources are Apache-2.0 and the SFC64 header is MIT (per file headers), which matters when lifting C code
- Past correctness fixes worth knowing if you pinned an old version: a non-deterministic Xoshiro256 jump (#336) and a wrong xoroshiro128 jump (#321), both closed 2023, and LCG128Mix ignoring its default inc (fixed in 2.1.0)

**Status:** Actively maintained (commits through 2026-09-28, mostly dependency bumps; last release 2.3.0 on 2025-10-22), dual BSD-3-Clause/NCSA with per-component licenses, and marked Production/Stable on PyPI.

[repo](https://github.com/bashtage/randomgen) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bashtage/randomgen/main/doc/source/performance.rst)

##### seiran (seiran128 PRNG)  `C`  `CC0-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Tiny CC0 128-bit-state LFSR PRNG in C with jump functions; author measured 3.75x reference mt19937-64.c throughput.

**Beats:** Reference mt19937-64.c (Matsumoto-Nishimura C code; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64, but std::mt19937_64 itself was not timed), pcg64_xsh_rr and xoshiro256** — The author ran Vigna's xoshiro harness.c with gcc 7.3.0 (flags not stated) on an Intel Core i7-7700HQ at 2.80 GHz: seiran128 produced 1.20 64-bit values/ns versus 0.32 for the reference mt19937-64.c (3.75x, derived from page data), 0.38 for pcg64_xsh_rr, 0.99 for xoshiro256** and 1.21 for sfc64; std::mt19937_64 itself was not timed.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline is the reference mt19937-64.c, not std::mt19937_64; flags unstated (self-test vectors reproduced).

**Known shortcoming:** Speed lead depends on the harness: the same author's later .NET table (Culumi README) puts Seiran at 97.26 ns/KiB, behind Shioi (81.97) and SplitMix (91.80) and level with SFC64 (97.80). seiran128.c includes a test main().

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The state update is an xorshift/rotate linear (F2) transform in the xoroshiro style (s0 ^ rotl(s1, 29) and s0 ^ (s1 << 9)), and the output scrambler is one add, one multiply by 9, one rotate and one add: rotl((s0 + s1) * 9, 29) + s0. With 16 bytes of state, no 128-bit multiply and no table, each value costs a handful of ALU ops, against MT19937-64's 2,500-byte state (README table).

**Use it when:**
- Games and simulations that want 64-bit outputs from a 16-byte state with no 128-bit multiply or SIMD (portable to any 64-bit integer target; C# and Motoko ports exist)
- Replacing mt19937_64 in single-threaded C or C++ code where the exact Mersenne Twister sequence does not matter
- Parallel or partitioned simulations that need jump-ahead: jump64() gives 2^64 disjoint streams of 2^64 values each
- Projects that need public-domain (CC0) code to paste without attribution

**Skip it when:**
- Anything security-relevant: the author recovered the full state from three consecutive outputs with the Z3 solver in minutes
- When you want a generator with outside scrutiny: all PractRand, BigCrush, gjrand and hwd results are the author's, and the README says it has not been investigated by others; xoroshiro128++/xoshiro256** or PCG64DXSM have far more analysis
- When raw speed is the only criterion: it ties sfc64 (1.20 vs 1.21 values/ns) in its own table, and in the same author's later .NET 8 table (Culumi README) Seiran at 97.26 ns/KiB trails Shioi (81.97) and SplitMix (91.80) and ties SFC64 (97.80); SIMD generators such as SHISHUA or 8-way xoshiro are much faster for bulk fills
- When you need a 32-bit-word variant, float/double helpers or a std::uniform_random_bit_generator class: none are provided
- Long-lived dependencies: last commit 2021-01-30 (5 commits), and CC0 gives no patent grant

**Integration:** source-drop (single C file) · none (inttypes.h only) · C99 (static inline, loop-scoped declarations, inttypes.h); timing used gcc 7.3.0 · any with 64-bit unsigned integers; no architecture-specific instructions

**Vs siblings:** Against Shioi (same author, same 16-byte state) and Culumi (same author, faster but needs SSE4/PCLMUL), pick seiran when you want the plainest portable scalar code with a jump function; SFC64 has no jump function (Stream column '-' in the Culumi table), and xoroshiro128++/xoshiro256** are the better-vetted alternatives at similar speed.

**Gotchas:**
- seiran128.c has a test main() and assertion macros below the generator and exports bare next, init, jump32, jump64 and jump96 symbols; strip the test code and rename or make them static before linking into a project
- The all-zero state {0, 0} is forbidden; init() cannot produce it, but custom seeding must avoid it
- Each jump runs 128 calls of next() (polynomial jump), so it is cheap but not free, and it overwrites the global state
- The speed table's harness (Vigna's harness.c) is not in the repo and its flags are not stated; splitmix at 0.68 values/ns, slower than seiran128 there, is unusual and suggests results are harness-specific

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2021 (the last commit only added a C# port link), but CC0 and a single 131-line C file including its self-test, so trivial to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/andanteyk/prng-seiran) · [benchmark](https://github.com/andanteyk/prng-seiran)

##### shioi128 (Shioi PRNG)  `C`  `CC0-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Public-domain 16-byte-state 64-bit PRNG with O(1) 2^64 jump; about 3x reference mt19937-64, parity with xoshiro256**.

**Beats:** Reference mt19937-64.c (Matsumoto-Nishimura C code; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64, but std::mt19937_64 itself was not timed), pcg64_xsh_rr and xoshiro256** — Author-run xoshiro harness.c on an i7-7700HQ with gcc 7.3.0 (flags not stated): shioi128 1.00 64-bit outputs/ns vs the reference mt19937-64.c at 0.32 (3.1x), pcg64_xsh_rr 0.38 and xoshiro256** 0.99; std::mt19937_64 itself was not timed. An independent casual C++ benchmark (t-mat gist, last updated 2022-11-24, -std=c++20 -O3, CPU not stated) measured Shioi128 at 10.15 GiB/s with GCC 11.2 vs xoroshiro128+ 8.02 and wyrand 8.85, and 10.86 GiB/s with MSVC 19.32 vs xoroshiro128+ 6.75 and wyrand 12.81.

**Known shortcoming:** About parity with xoshiro256** (1.00 vs 0.99), not a clear win; needs arithmetic right shift of negative int64_t (implementation-defined before C23/C++20).

**Known shortcoming:** shioi128.c has file-static state, bare next()/init() and a main() self-test in the same file. Only jump64 is O(1); jump32/jump96 cost 128 next() calls. Independent t-mat gist (GCC 11.2 / MSVC 19.32, -O3, CPU not stated): Shioi128 10.15 GiB/s vs xoroshiro128+ 8.02 and wyrand 8.85.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each step is one 64-bit constant multiply (by 0xD2B74407B1CE6E93), a rotate-left by 29 and an add for the output, plus a shift/xor update of the state (s1' = (s0 << 2) ^ (s0 >> 19, arithmetic) ^ s1). That is a two-word linear recurrence over GF(2) (the README calls it LFSR-based) with a multiply-rotate-add output scrambler, so everything stays in two registers. mt19937-64 instead keeps about 2.5 KB of state that it regenerates in blocks. Because the recurrence is linear, a 2^64-step jump reduces to a closed-form two-word update costing about one next().

**Use it when:**
- Games, simulations and Monte Carlo code on 64-bit CPUs that need a small non-cryptographic 64-bit generator faster than std::mt19937_64 and can vendor ~20 lines of CC0 code.
- Parallel or per-task streams: jump64() costs about one next() and splits the period into 2^64 non-overlapping subsequences of length 2^64.
- Many independent generator instances (per particle, per entity), where 16 bytes of state beats mt19937_64's ~2.5 KB.
- When you want a fast 128-bit-state generator that, per the author, passes PractRand to 32 TB, BigCrush (normal and bit-reversed), the Hamming-weight-dependency test to 1.5 PB and gjrand. In the same table xoroshiro128+ fails BRank and hwd.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything security-relevant (tokens, keys, adversarial inputs). It is not a CSPRNG, and the only attack the author reports is one day of Z3 that did not recover the state.
- When raw speed is the goal: in the author's own C table it is behind sfc64 (1.21), seiran128 (1.20) and xoroshiro128+ (1.13) and only ties xoshiro256** (1.00 vs 0.99 outputs/ns).
- 32-bit targets or cores without a fast 64x64-bit multiply: the README warns that speed may drop there, and the 32-bit-word variants are unfinished.
- When you need a widely analysed or standardized generator: the author says it 'has not been investigated by others', and no paper or third-party statistical analysis is linked.
- When you need a maintained, packaged library: there are four commits (the last on 2019-08-18) and no tests beyond the self-test main() in the source file.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (<inttypes.h>; <stdio.h> only for the bundled self-test main) · C99 (for-loop declarations, <inttypes.h>); needs a compiler whose >> on a negative int64_t is an arithmetic shift, which is guaranteed only from C23 / C++20 and implementation-defined before that · any target with 64-bit integers; benchmarked only on x86-64 (i7-7700HQ); slower where 64-bit multiply is slow

**Vs siblings:** Over seiran128 (same author, 1.20 vs 1.00 outputs/ns in the shared C table), pick shioi128 for the O(1) jump64. In the author's later Culumi table, Seiran's state is rated 'easy(Z3)' to predict and Shioi's 'unknown', and Shioi was faster there (81.97 vs 97.26 ns/KiB under .NET 8). Over xoshiro256**, it gives half the state and a constant-time 2^64 jump at equal measured speed; pick Culumi (needs SSE4/PCLMUL) or a SIMD generator such as simdrng or SHISHUA when bulk fill throughput matters more.

**Gotchas:**
- shioi128.c defines bare global symbols next(), init(), jump32/64/96() and a main() self-test in the same file. Strip main and rename or namespace the functions before linking into a real program.
- The update must use an arithmetic (sign-extending) right shift of (int64_t)s0 (the source says 'MUST use arithmetic right shift'). A port that uses a logical shift, such as Java's >>> or an unsigned >> in Rust or C#, silently produces a different, untested generator.
- State {0,0} is a fixed point. The shipped init() seeds both words through a 64-bit LCG, which never yields {0,0}, but custom seeding must avoid two zero words.
- Only jump64() is O(1). jump32() and jump96() run the generic polynomial jump, which is 128 next() calls plus XORs.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-08-18 (four commits, no issues), but CC0 and about 20 lines of logic, so vendoring and maintaining a wrapper yourself is trivial.

[repo](https://github.com/andanteyk/prng-shioi) · [benchmark](https://github.com/andanteyk/prng-shioi)

##### SHISHUA  `C`  `CC0-1.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Non-cryptographic SIMD PRNG for bulk byte streams; about 6.7x xoshiro256+ throughput on AVX2 Intel per first-party numbers.

**Beats:** xoshiro256+ (also RomuTrio, wyrand, ChaCha8) — The author's benchmark-perf script ran on a GCP N2 KVM guest reporting 'Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU' family 6 model 85 at 2.8 GHz, built with -O3 -march=native and an unstated compiler. It measured SHISHUA at 0.0527 cycles/byte (52.93 GB/s) against xoshiro256+ at 7.99 GB/s in the raw file (7.88 in the README), RomuTrio 8.62, wyrand 7.00, ChaCha8 6.28 and an 8-way vectorized xoshiro256+ at 40.18 GB/s. These are first-party numbers and were not compared with std::mt19937.

**Known shortcoming:** Compiler/version unstated (-O3 -march=native); CPU only generic 'Intel Xeon' (model 85, KVM); raw bench file says xoshiro256+ 7.99 GB/s where README says 7.88; CC0 gives no patent grant.

**Known shortcoming:** Correction: AVX2 not required (SSE2, NEON with Clang, scalar fallback); AVX2 only for the 52.93 GB/s figure. prng_init is non-static non-inline in the header (two TUs break the link); buffer must be a multiple of 128 bytes; README says 'cycles per byte' but table shows GB/s.

**How:** The state is four 256-bit vectors plus a 256-bit counter. Each 128-byte round uses only shift, 32-bit lane permute (_mm256_permutevar8x32_epi32) and 64-bit add, then XORs pairs of state parts to make the output. There is no multiplication and the dependency chain per round is short. Writing 128 bytes per iteration amortizes loop overhead, which is how it reaches roughly 0.05 cycles per byte on AVX2.

**Use it when:**
- Filling large buffers with random bytes (Monte Carlo inputs, test data, noise, hashing salts) where GB/s matters more than per-call latency
- x86-64 hosts with AVX2, which is where the 52.93 GB/s figure was measured
- You can consume output in 128-byte blocks, or wrap it in your own buffered next() function
- You want a CC0 source-drop with no dependencies and need PractRand quality (the author reports passing 32 TiB, plus BigCrush)

**Skip it when:**
- Any security use: the README says not to use it for cryptography and points to ChaCha20
- Code that needs one value at a time with low latency or a std::uniform_random_bit_generator engine: you must write the buffering layer yourself
- ARM: the author's Graviton figure is 8.78 GB/s, and GCC's NEON codegen is slow enough that the header falls back to scalar unless the compiler is Clang
- You need jump-ahead, independent substreams with guarantees, or reproducible streams across versions: none of these is documented
- Projects that need a maintained dependency: last commit August 2023, and a request for a shared-library build (issue #10) is still open

**Integration:** source-drop (C header shishua.h plus per-ISA headers shishua-avx2.h / -sse2.h / -neon.h) · none (libc, plus <immintrin.h>/<arm_neon.h> for the SIMD paths) · C99 compiler with AVX2 intrinsics for the fast path (the Makefile builds the AVX2 variant with -mavx2 -mtune=haswell); exact minimum not documented · x86-64 (AVX2 fast path, SSE2/SSSE3 fallback), aarch64/ARMv7 NEON (auto-selected only with Clang), portable scalar fallback elsewhere; RISC-V vector support requested (issue #9) but not implemented

**Vs siblings:** Pick SHISHUA over xoshiro8x256pp, Xoshiro256PlusSIMD or SIMDxorshift when you want the highest bulk throughput and better PractRand results than xoshiro256+-style generators (the author's table: xoshiro256+x8 fails at 1 KiB, SHISHUA passes 32 TiB). Pick simdpcg instead when you need a stream identical to the reference PCG32, and testingRNG's aesctr or Randen when you want an AES-based construction.

**Gotchas:**
- prng_gen asserts that size % 128 == 0, and the AVX2 path stores 32-byte chunks without alignment requirements (storeu). Tail handling is a TODO in the source.
- prng_init is defined in the header as a non-static, non-inline function, so including shishua.h in more than one translation unit causes duplicate-symbol link errors. Wrap it in one .c file.
- The SIMD, scalar and NEON paths are meant to produce the same bytes (the Makefile has per-target test vectors), but endianness handling is explicit only in the scalar path. Check on big-endian targets.
- README footnote 1 says 'cycles per byte' but the table shows GB/s, and the raw Intel file has xoshiro256+ at 7.99 GB/s while the README says 7.88.

**Status:** Stale (last commit August 2023, 4 open issues) but CC0 and a few hundred lines of header code, so it is easy to vendor; Rust, Node.js and Python ports exist.

[repo](https://github.com/espadrine/shishua) · [benchmark](https://github.com/espadrine/shishua)

##### simd-rand (SIMD Xoshiro256+ / Xoshiro256++ and frand generators for Rust)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust crate of 4- and 8-lane SIMD Xoshiro256+/++, frand and biski64 generators; about 4.5x scalar rand_xoshiro Xoshiro256+ on AVX-512.

**Beats:** Scalar Xoshiro256+ (benchmark label 'rand/Xoshiro256+', from the rand crate ecosystem) — The author's Criterion run on an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D (unpinned cargo nightly, target-cpu=native plus AVX-512 RUSTFLAGS, LTO, one pinned SMT pair) took 33.1 ns to generate and sum 64 u64 values with scalar rand_xoshiro Xoshiro256+, versus 7.51 ns for the portable Xoshiro256+X8 and 7.08 ns for the AVX-512 version (about 4.4x and 4.7x, derived from page data). For frand the gain over the compiler-autovectorized scalar crate is only about 1.26x (3.18 ns vs 2.53 ns).

**Known shortcoming:** rustc nightly unpinned; the 13x frand figure compares different generators (real FrandX8 vs scalar frand ~1.26x); correctness bug: FrandX8::seed_from_u64 gives 8 identical lanes (Xoshiro256+X8 and FrandX8 otherwise compute correct generators); Rust.

**Known shortcoming:** FrandX8/FrandX4::seed_from_u64 gives identical lanes. crates.io 0.1.0 (2026-02-01, 64 downloads) predates the frand fix PR #34 (2026-03-15). Rust only; nightly needed for the portable module.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each lane holds an independent copy of the generator state (multi-stream), so one vector step of xoshiro256+ (add, shift by 17, four XORs, rotate by 45) produces 4 or 8 outputs at once; the scalar xoshiro256+ has a serial state dependency that the compiler does not vectorize. frand (a Weyl increment followed by a multiply-xor-shift mix) is simple enough that the compiler already autovectorizes the scalar crate, so FrandX8 gains only from keeping eight lane states resident instead of broadcasting one state each call.

**Use it when:**
- Rust Monte Carlo or simulation kernels already written with std::simd or AVX2/AVX-512 intrinsics that consume random u64 or f64 vectors
- Bulk generation on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 (avx512f+avx512dq) or AVX2 where 8 independent streams are acceptable
- Throughput-bound code where the scalar rand_xoshiro Xoshiro256+ is a measured bottleneck
- Projects on nightly Rust that want a portable SIMD RNG that also compiles on non-x86 targets

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: it is a Rust crate with no C API, so it needs FFI work; use a C++ SIMD xoshiro sibling instead
- Code that needs the same sequence as a scalar generator, reproducible jump-ahead between lanes, or lane splitting (lane jumps are a README TODO)
- Stable Rust without x86 SIMD: the portable module needs nightly; the specific modules compile only with the matching target features
- Statistically critical work: the author says he is no expert and has only run PractRand; no TestU01 results are published
- Production use expecting a mature crate: one crates.io release (0.1.0, February 2026, 64 downloads), 7 stars

**Integration:** crate · rand_core 0.9 · Rust 1.89 (MSRV, edition 2024); nightly for the portable feature · portable: any target with nightly std::simd; specific::avx2: x86-64 with AVX2 (extra paths with avx512dq/avx512vl); specific::avx512: x86-64 with avx512f and avx512dq

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you are writing Rust and want SIMD xoshiro or frand vectors directly; for C++ the closest siblings are xoshiro8x256pp (8-way xoshiro256++ gist), Xoshiro256PlusSIMD and simdrng, and SHISHUA is faster still if you can switch generator. Romu and Squares are scalar designs, so they suit code that cannot batch.

**Gotchas:**
- FrandX8::seed_from_u64 (portable and AVX-512 versions, and FrandX4) copies one seed into every lane, so all lanes emit the same stream; the README's own benchmark rows use it. Seed with distinct from_seed bytes when you need independent lanes
- The crates.io 0.1.0 release (2026-02-01) predates the 2026-03-15 'fix frand implementation (#34)' commit that made FrandX8 match the upstream frand crate; use the git main branch for upstream-identical frand output
- The crate uses a fair amount of unsafe for the intrinsics paths, and the specific modules silently vanish if the target features are not enabled at compile time (.cargo/config.toml in the repo sets target-cpu=native)
- Results are vectors, not single values; consuming them one element at a time through a scalar API gives back much of the speedup

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-03-15) but young and lightly used: MIT, 7 stars, one 0.1.0 crates.io release that predates the frand fix; Rust-only, so C++ users would need to port the small generator kernels.

[repo](https://github.com/martinothamar/simd-rand) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/martinothamar/simd-rand/HEAD/README.md)

##### simdpcg  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Vectorized PCG32 (pcg32 XSH-RR) in AVX2 and AVX-512 C intrinsics; 1.8x to 3.7x faster than scalar PCG32 at filling arrays.

**Beats:** PCG32 (scalar reference by O'Neill) — The README sample, from benchmark/fillarray.c (RDTSC, best of 500 runs, 50,000 32-bit values in a 195 kB array, -O3 -march=native with an unstated compiler and CPU), shows scalar O'Neill pcg32_random_r at 4.25 cycles/value. The AVX-512 one-, two- and four-key variants run at 2.37, 1.21 and 1.14 cycles/value, which is 1.8x to 3.7x (derived from page data). The multi-key variants interleave independent streams, and nothing was compared with std::mt19937.

**Known shortcoming:** Flags from Makefile (-O3 -march=native) but no compiler or CPU model; needs AVX-512; baselines are scalar PCG32 only.

**Known shortcoming:** Correction: AVX-512 not required (AVX2 paths exist) and 2026 *_initialize helpers reproduce the scalar PCG32 stream; published numbers predate AVX2/avx512bis variants; 1.14 cycles/value interleaves 4 generators; two AVX2 helpers marked 'untested'.

**How:** It runs the scalar PCG32 step (an LCG multiply-add, then an xorshift and a data-dependent rotate) across 64-bit SIMD lanes. On AVX-512 it uses _mm512_mullo_epi64 (AVX512DQ) and _mm512_rorv_epi32. The AVX2 path builds the 64-bit multiply from 32-bit partial products (_mm256_mul_epu32) and emulates the rotate with variable shifts (code credited to Wenzel Jakob's pcg32_8.h). Leapfrog seeding (multiplier^k per lane) keeps the scalar sequence. The benchmark's 'two' and 'four' variants interleave 2 or 4 independent generator keys to hide multiply latency.

**Use it when:**
- You already depend on PCG32 output (seeds, reproducibility) and want the same stream generated 8 values at a time, e.g. filling arrays of 32-bit randoms
- AVX-512 servers (Skylake-X or newer with AVX512DQ), where the four-key variant reaches 1.14 cycles per value against 4.25 for scalar
- Throughput-bound Monte Carlo or simulation code that can consume values in 8- or 16-wide vectors
- C or C++ projects that want an Apache-2.0 header with no dependencies

**Skip it when:**
- Portable or ARM code: there are only x86 AVX2 and AVX-512 paths and no scalar fallback in simdpcg32.h, and the types disappear when __AVX2__ / __AVX512DQ__ are not defined
- Code that needs a std::uniform_random_bit_generator engine or one value per call: you must buffer the vector output yourself
- Peak bulk throughput regardless of algorithm: SHISHUA reports about 0.05 cycles per byte, against roughly 0.29 cycles per byte here (1.14 cycles per 4-byte value)
- Any cryptographic use (PCG32 is not a CSPRNG)
- Older AVX-512 chips where heavy 512-bit use can lower clocks: not measured in the repo, so benchmark on your own hardware

**Integration:** header-only (include/simdpcg32.h; include/pcg32.h holds the scalar reference) · none · C99 (Makefile uses -std=c99 -march=native); the compiler must support AVX2 or AVX512F+AVX512DQ intrinsics · x86-64 with AVX2 (avx2_/avx256_ paths) or AVX-512F+DQ (avx512_/avx512bis_ paths); no ARM or scalar fallback

**Vs siblings:** Pick simdpcg over SHISHUA, SIMDxorshift or xoshiro8x256pp when you need the exact PCG32 stream (reproducibility with existing scalar PCG32 code) rather than the fastest new generator. Pick testingRNG's lehmer64/aesctr or SHISHUA when raw throughput matters more than matching PCG32.

**Gotchas:**
- Each feature path is compiled only when its macro (AVX2PCG / AVX512PCG) is set by __AVX2__ or __AVX512F__ && __AVX512DQ__. Without -mavx2/-mavx512dq or -march=native the types are silently missing.
- If you fill the struct by hand (as the benchmark and older README code do) instead of calling *_initialize, every inc lane must be odd. That was a 2025 bug fix (PR #3). Hand-filled lanes also give independent streams, not the scalar sequence.
- Two helpers in the AVX2 path (hacked_mm256_rorv_epi32, hacked_mm256_mullo_epi64) are marked '// untested' in the source, although the 2026 check_identity unit test now exercises the avx256 path.
- The README 'Sample result' shows only the scalar and three AVX-512 variants. The current benchmark/fillarray.c also times AVX2, avx256 and avx512bis variants that have no published numbers.

**Status:** Small but active (merges in January 2026 for an AVX-512 packing speedup and August 2026 for scalar-identical initialize helpers), Apache-2.0, and easy to vendor as one header.

[repo](https://github.com/lemire/simdpcg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lemire/simdpcg)

##### tinyrand (obsidiandynamics/tinyrand, Rust no_std PRNGs)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Dependency-free no_std Rust crate with Wyrand, Xorshift and SplitMix-style PRNGs; README shows about 2x fastrand and 6x rand's ChaCha12.

**Beats:** Rust rand crate (ChaCha12 StdRng) and the fastrand crate (Wyrand) — The README table lists bandwidth in GB/s: rand ChaCha12 (thread_rng) 2.4, tinyrand SplitMix 6.5, Xorshift 6.7, fastrand Wyrand 7.5 and tinyrand Wyrand 14.6, with no CPU, toolchain, flags, date or formula for GB/s. The public criterion bench (cri_rand.rs; criterion 0.3.6, rand 0.8.5, fastrand 1.8.0) times single calls, but its fastrand row times a bounded u64(0..u64::MAX) call while the tinyrand rows time raw next_u64, and the rand row is a reseeding CSPRNG. The only same-algorithm comparison, Wyrand 14.6 versus 7.5 GB/s (about 1.9x, derived from page data), is therefore partly a call-shape difference rather than generator speed.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: README table from the public Criterion bench (tinyrand/benches/cri_rand.rs) with no CPU or toolchain; the fastrand row calls the bounded u64(0..u64::MAX) while tinyrand calls next_u64, so the comparison is not like for like.

**Known shortcoming:** Its Xorshift saves state before the <<17 step; the enricher's GF(2) check (Berlekamp-Massey plus factoring, confirmed by matrix power) gives period 2^48-1, not 2^64-1, and 65,535 seeds cycle at 51 or 255 steps (e.g. 0x1e250d05b6eea0). Its 'SplitMix' is not SplitMix64 (no Weyl increment, iterated bijection, period not guaranteed). No floats, no rand_core implementation, constant default seed; issue #1 'Always resulting in 0' closed with no reply. The only like-for-like benchmark row is Wyrand vs Wyrand (14.6 vs 7.5 GB/s); the fastrand row times the bounded u64(0..u64::MAX).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Each generator is a single u64 with an #[inline(always)] next_u64; the default Wyrand step is a Weyl increment (0xA0761D6478BD642F), one 64x64-to-128-bit multiply and an xor fold. Bounded integers up to 64 bits use Lemire's multiply-shift method with a rarely taken rejection loop (credited in the README); ranges wider than 64 bits fall back to modulo with rejection. There is no buffering, reseeding or cryptographic work, which is where most of the gap to rand's ChaCha12 thread_rng comes from.

**Use it when:**
- no_std or bare-metal Rust (microcontrollers, kernels) that needs fast non-cryptographic u64s or bounded integers without a heap.
- Unit tests that must force random branches: the tinyrand-alloc Mock lets a test script next_u128, next_bool and next_lim results and count invocations.
- Jitter, randomized backoff, games and simulations where a 64-bit Weyl-sequence generator (Wyrand) is good enough and you want one tiny dependency-free crate.
- Per-thread generators in std code via tinyrand-std's thread_rand, seeded from the system clock.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything security-sensitive: the README says none of the generators is cryptographically secure and points to rand for a CSPRNG.
- You need floats or distributions: the Rand trait has no f64 method and no normal, exponential or shuffle helpers (issue #2 asks how to make floats); signed-integer ranges are not implemented either.
- Code built on the rand ecosystem: it does not implement rand_core::RngCore, so rand's distributions, SliceRandom and seeding helpers cannot use it directly.
- Long or parallel simulations with Xorshift: its state recurrence has period 2^48-1, not 2^64-1 (see gotchas); use Wyrand or a larger-state generator.
- C++ projects: Rust only, with no C ABI.

**Integration:** crate · none (tinyrand); optional companion crates tinyrand-std and tinyrand-alloc · Rust 2021 edition; lib.rs uses inline format arguments (Rust 1.58+, inferred); no rust-version declared; CI pinned to Rust 1.66.0 · any (no_std, no architecture-specific code; next_usize is defined for 16/32/64/128-bit pointer widths; CI tests x86-64 and i686-unknown-linux-gnu via cross)

**Vs siblings:** Pick tinyrand over simd-rand when you draw one value at a time, need no_std or bounded integers and mocks; pick simd-rand for bulk u64 fills, where its portable Xoshiro256+X8 path reports 8.52 Gelem/s and the AVX-512 path is faster still. For C or C++ code the same Wyrand idea is available in lemire/testingRNG, which also benchmarks it against lehmer64 and PCG.

**Gotchas:**
- Default::default() uses a constant seed (0 for Wyrand, 1 for Xorshift and SplitMix), so every run repeats the same sequence unless you seed it (README warns); issue #1 (2023) reports the README examples always returning 0 and was closed with no visible reply.
- Xorshift is not textbook xorshift64: it saves the state after the <<13 and >>7 steps and applies <<17 only to the output. A GF(2) analysis run this session gives a characteristic polynomial with factors of degree 8, 8 and 48, so ordinary seeds cycle after 2^48-1 outputs (about 2.8e14, roughly 4 days at the README's 6.7 GB/s) instead of 2^64-1, and 65,535 nonzero seeds (for example 0x1e250d05b6eea0) cycle after 51 or 255 steps; no seed in 1..2^20 hits those short cycles.
- SplitMix is not Steele/Lea/Flood SplitMix64: it has no Weyl increment and iterates x -> (x ^ x>>32) * 0xff51afd7ed558ccd mod 2^64 (a bijection with 0 as a fixed point, which seed() avoids), so its period depends on the seed and is not guaranteed; constants and shifts differ from the splitmix64.c reference (0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 increment, shifts 30/27/31).
- next_u16 and next_u32 return the low bits of next_u64, and next_lim, next_range and Probability::new panic (assert!) on a zero limit, an empty range or p outside [0, 1]; there is no fallible API.

**Status:** Abandoned since late 2022 (crate 0.5.0 published 2022-09-12, about 92k total downloads per crates.io, CI pinned to Rust 1.66.0), but MIT, dependency-free and small enough to vendor; prefer Wyrand and avoid the Xorshift and SplitMix variants.

[repo](https://github.com/obsidiandynamics/tinyrand) · [benchmark](https://github.com/obsidiandynamics/tinyrand)

##### valyala/fastrand (Go scalable per-CPU pseudorandom generator)  `Go`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Tiny Go xorshift32 PRNG with a sync.Pool of generators; out-scaled the mutex-locked global math/rand under parallel load.

**Beats:** Go math/rand (global rand.Int31n and rand.New(...) instances) — The README's go test -bench output (goos linux, goarch amd64; CPU and Go version not stated; results committed in April 2017) uses b.RunParallel loops drawing bounded values below 1e6: fastrand.Uint32n took 29.7, 17.6 and 14.2 ns/op versus math/rand's global Int31n at 31.8, 51.2 and 145 ns/op at GOMAXPROCS=1, 2 and 4, and a per-goroutine RNG.Uint32n took 6.50, 3.36 and 3.30 ns/op versus a per-goroutine rand.New(rand.NewSource(42)).Int31n at 17.9, 11.0 and 8.35 ns/op. The global-function gap measured lock contention in pre-Go 1.21 math/rand, which Go 1.21 removed for unseeded programs.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: README numbers from the public fastrand_timing_test.go with no Go version or CPU stated. Since Go 1.20 the global math/rand uses a per-thread wyrand source without the mutex (seen as a search snippet; go.dev blocked), so the scaling gap it was built to avoid is likely gone. Last commit 2021-09-15, abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** Correction to the verifier's caveat: Go 1.20's math/rand global source is still a lockedSource (only auto-seeded); the lock-free per-M wyrand fastSource arrived in Go 1.21 (checked golang/go at go1.20 and go1.21.0), so the contention gap is gone on Go 1.21+ but was never re-measured. xorshift32 state; Uint32n is multiply-shift with no rejection, so biased; pool RNGs are seeded from the clock (issue #4 open since 2021, same seed possible) and Seed(0) falls back to a clock seed; uint32-only API; 4 PRs closed unmerged on 2024-04-04.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The generator is Marsaglia's 32-bit xorshift (shifts 13, 17, 5) on a 4-byte state, and bounded values use Lemire's multiply-shift reduction ((x * maxN) >> 32) with no division or rejection loop. The scaling comes from the sync.Pool: each P tends to reuse its own pooled RNG, avoiding the single mutex that guarded the global math/rand source in Go versions before 1.21. The per-goroutine RNG path (6.50 ns/op at GOMAXPROCS=1) is cheaper again because it skips the pool Get/Put.

**Use it when:**
- Legacy Go code pinned to Go 1.20 or older that calls top-level math/rand functions from many goroutines and spends measurable time contending on the global generator's lock.
- Hot loops needing cheap bounded uint32 values for non-security decisions: random load-balancer or shard selection, sampling, jitter, test data.
- Single-goroutine or per-worker code that can own a fastrand.RNG value, where a 4-byte xorshift state and a multiply-shift bound are good enough.
- As a reference for the pool-of-generators pattern if you must vendor something very small (about 80 lines, MIT).

**Skip it when:**
- Go 1.21 and later: unseeded top-level math/rand functions already use a lock-free fastSource that calls the runtime's per-M wyrand (fastrand64), so the multi-CPU contention this package fixes is gone; prefer the standard library or math/rand/v2 there. No benchmark of fastrand against Go 1.21+ math/rand exists.
- Anything security-related: the package doc says to use crypto/rand for cryptographically secure numbers, and seeds come from the wall clock.
- Simulation or statistics work: a 32-bit xorshift on 4 bytes of state has period at most 2^32-1, small next to the 64-bit and larger generators in this category; Uint32n's multiply-shift without rejection is slightly biased whenever maxN is not a power of two.
- Reproducible streams from the global functions: pooled generators are created and reseeded from the clock whenever the pool is empty (sync.Pool can drop objects at garbage collection), so sequences cannot be replayed.
- Code needing floats, 64-bit integers, shuffles or other distributions; only uint32 output is offered.

**Integration:** module · none (standard library sync and time only) · not documented; go.mod declares only the module path with no go directive (Go modules support was added in 2019) · any platform Go supports (pure Go, no assembly)

**Vs siblings:** Among Go siblings, pgregory.net/rand (flyingmutant/rand) is maintained, offers the full math/rand-style API on sfc64 and benchmarks against math/rand/v2, and vpxyz/xorshift offers stronger 64-bit xorshift/xoroshiro sources; pick valyala/fastrand only when you need a tiny vendored uint32 helper on an old Go toolchain, and lukechampine/frand when you need cryptographic strength.

**Gotchas:**
- Seeds come from time.Now().UnixNano() folded to 32 bits when a pooled RNG is first used; open issue #4 (2021) notes that many goroutines starting together can get identically seeded generators on systems with coarse clock resolution, and that the pool holds one RNG per concurrent caller rather than strictly one per CPU.
- RNG.Seed(0) does not give a fixed stream: a zero state is treated as unseeded and is replaced by a clock-derived seed on the next call.
- Uint32n has no argument check: Uint32n(0) silently returns 0.
- The README benchmark at GOMAXPROCS=1 shows only a small gain for the global function (29.7 vs 31.8 ns/op); most of the single-thread gain is from owning an RNG (6.50 ns/op), which you could equally get by owning a rand.New(...) source (17.9 ns/op) or a faster per-goroutine generator.

**Status:** Abandoned: last commit 2021-09-15 (RNG.Seed), issue #4 open since 2021 with no reply, and four contributor PRs (crypto/rand seeding, go.mod version, sync.Pool New, test fix) closed unmerged in April 2024; MIT and small enough to vendor, but on Go 1.21+ the standard library makes it largely unnecessary.

[repo](https://github.com/valyala/fastrand) · [benchmark](https://github.com/valyala/fastrand)

##### vpxyz/xorshift (Go xorshift*, xorshift+, xoroshiro and splitmix64 generators)  `Go`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go ports of Vigna's xorshift/xoroshiro/xoshiro and SplitMix64 generators; raw calls 2-3x faster than math/rand's default source.

**Beats:** Go math/rand (rand.NewSource Int63 source, and rand.New(source).ExpFloat64()) — The author's go test -bench run (Go 1.14, default flags, i7-3840QM, Fedora 31, 2020) measured raw Uint64 calls at 1.61 ns (SplitMix64) to 2.66 ns (128-bit-state generators) versus 4.93 ns for math/rand.NewSource(...).Int63 called through the Source interface, so about 2-3x, partly from static versus interface dispatch; wrapped in rand.Rand for ExpFloat64 the best variants are about 1.2x faster (8.10-8.66 ns versus 10.2 ns) and the 256/512-bit variants are slower. math/rand/v2 was not measured.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A on xorshift_test.go (Go 1.14, i7-3840QM), but once wrapped in rand.Rand, Xoroshiro256 (11.7 ns/op) and Xoroshiro512 (13.2/13.6 ns/op) are slower than math/rand (10.2 ns/op); the raw rows compare a concrete-type Uint64 call against Int63 through the rand.Source interface. Last commit 2020-05-02.

**Known shortcoming:** Capped A to C (retier-11): xoroshiro512starstar's update is 's6 ^ ^s7 ^ s3' (unary NOT complements s7; the package's own 512plus has 's6 ^ s7'), so it is not Vigna's xoshiro512** and its Jump is invalid; xoroshiro128plus (2016 parameters 55/14/36) Jump uses the xorshift128+ constants {0x8a5cd789635d2dff, 0x121fd2155c472f96} instead of {0xbeac0467eba5facb, 0xd86b048b86aa9922}. Packages named xoroshiro256/512 are actually xoshiro; most Int63 implementations keep the weak low bits; no reference-output tests (Vigna asked in issue #2); the README example does not compile.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The generators are linear xorshift / xor-rotate-shift-rotate recurrences over a few 64-bit words, costing a handful of shifts, xors and one add or multiply per output; the benchmark compares them with math/rand's default source called through the rand.Source interface (its internals were not inspected here). The 2020 rewrite switched to math/bits.RotateLeft64, which Vigna suggested in issue #3 because the standard function can be intrinsified by the compiler, and the 256/512-bit variants copy the state into locals because, per a source comment, the Go compiler generated slower code for array indexing.

**Use it when:**
- Go code (not C++) that calls Uint64() directly on a concrete generator in a hot loop, e.g. Monte Carlo or simulation inner loops, where the README shows 1.6-2.7 ns/op versus 4.93 ns/op for math/rand's source on an i7-3840QM.
- Go programs pinned to an older toolchain (go 1.9+ per go.mod) that lack math/rand/v2 and want a small MIT-licensed SplitMix64 or xoshiro256** source.
- Single-goroutine code, or one generator per goroutine, since nothing is locked.
- As readable reference code for porting Vigna's generators, after checking each one against the reference outputs (see gotchas).

**Skip it when:**
- From C or C++: it is a Go package; use Vigna's reference C code or a catalogued C/C++ generator instead.
- Through rand.Rand (rand.New(src).Float64/ExpFloat64 etc.): the README's wrapped rows gain only about 1.2x (8.1-8.7 ns versus 10.2 ns), and the 256- and 512-bit variants are slower than math/rand (11.7-13.6 ns).
- When you need Jump() to create non-overlapping parallel streams with xoroshiro128plus or xoroshiro512starstar: both have defects (see gotchas).
- Concurrent use of one generator: README says it is not concurrency-safe.
- Security-sensitive randomness: none of these generators is cryptographic.

**Integration:** module · none (Go standard library math/bits only) · Go 1.9 (go.mod 'go 1.9'; math/bits.RotateLeft64 needs 1.9); benchmarked on Go 1.14 · any platform Go supports (pure Go, no assembly)

**Vs siblings:** Among Go siblings, pick pgregory.net/rand (flyingmutant/rand, sfc64, maintained, measured against math/rand/v2) for a modern faster rand.Rand replacement and valyala/fastrand for many goroutines sharing an RNG; pick this only if you specifically want a Vigna generator family in pure Go on an old toolchain and can audit the variant you use. C++ users should take the C/C++ siblings (e.g. simdrng, Xoshiro256PlusSIMD, testingRNG's lehmer64/aesctr) instead.

**Gotchas:**
- xoroshiro512starstar's state update is written 's6 ^ ^s7 ^ s3'; in Go the second '^' is unary bitwise NOT, so it complements s7, unlike the repo's own xoroshiro512plus ('s6 ^ s7 ^ s3') which shares the same xoshiro512 engine. The 512** generator therefore does not reproduce Vigna's xoshiro512** sequence and its Jump polynomial no longer applies (read in source; not run).
- xoroshiro128plus uses the original 2016 parameters (rotl 55, shift 14, rotl 36, as in sysbench's copy of Vigna's code) but its Jump() uses internal.Jump128 = {0x8a5cd789635d2dff, 0x121fd2155c472f96}, the xorshift128+ jump constants that XorShift128Plus.Jump also uses; Vigna's jump for this xoroshiro128+ is {0xbeac0467eba5facb, 0xd86b048b86aa9922}, so Jump() is not the advertised 2^64-step jump. The repo's xoroshiro128starstar uses the newer 24/16/37 parameters and the matching jump constants.
- The packages are named 'xoroshiro256*' and 'xoroshiro512*' but implement Vigna's xoshiro256/xoshiro512 engines (the 256-bit update and jump constants match xoshiro256); look them up under xoshiro. Package docs also call 256++ a 'floating-point' generator although ++ and ** are Vigna's all-purpose scramblers.
- Int63() masks off the top bit (keeping the weak low bits) for most generators; only the + scramblers xoroshiro128plus/256plus/512plus were changed in 2020 to return the upper 63 bits after Vigna's issue #1. Vigna also reported a jump operator-precedence bug (issue #2, fixed 2020-02-27) and recommended reference-output unit tests, which the repo still lacks (xorshift_test.go has only benchmarks). The README example code does not compile as written (xorshift256plus.NewSource, unqualified XorShiftExt, rand not imported).

**Status:** Abandoned since 2020-05-02 (44 commits; the only three issues, filed by Vigna on 2020-01-30, were fixed 2020-02-27) but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and tiny; vendor only the generator you need and test it against Vigna's reference outputs first, avoiding xoroshiro512starstar and xoroshiro128plus.Jump as written.

[repo](https://github.com/vpxyz/xorshift) · [benchmark](https://github.com/vpxyz/xorshift)

##### Xoshiro256PlusSIMD  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++17 xoshiro256+ with an AVX2 four-stream next4() that roughly doubles throughput over the scalar reference.

**Beats:** scalar xoshiro256+ (Blackman/Vigna reference) — Catch2 benchmarks in the author's README, run in a 2-core Ubuntu 20.04 VM on a Ryzen 7 1700 (compiler and flags not stated): generating 1M uint64 values took 1.09 ms with the Blackman/Vigna C reference, 1.08 ms with the class's serial next(), and 526 us with AVX2 next4() discarding results. That is about 2.07x over the reference (derived from page data), falling to about 1.27x when the four lanes are summed into a uint64_t (860 us).

**Known shortcoming:** Compiler and flags not stated; measured in a 2-core VM; gain disappears if the four values are consumed one by one; abandoned (last commit 2021-08-21).

**Known shortcoming:** x86-only (includes immintrin.h even in scalar build); issue #1 (Jan 2023): does not build on MSVC 2022; double conversion type-puns through a union (UB in C++); bounded output uses weak low bits; 2.07x drops to ~1.27x when lanes are summed.

**How:** next4() runs four independent xoshiro256+ states in the four 64-bit lanes of AVX2 registers, coded with explicit intrinsics rather than relying on auto-vectorization. The four lane states are seeded 2^192 apart with xoshiro long_jump. Bounded integers use a 32x32 multiply-shift reduction (Lemire-style), not a modulus, and doubles are built by OR-ing the top 52 bits into the 1.0 exponent and subtracting 1.0.

**Use it when:**
- Monte Carlo or simulation kernels already written with AVX2 that can use a __m256i or __m256d of four randoms directly
- Filling large buffers of uint64 or double randoms on x86-64 with AVX2, where 4-wide generation measured about 2x the scalar reference (526 us vs 1.09 ms per 1M values)
- When you want xoshiro256+ quality for floating-point output (Vigna's recommended use) with jump-separated streams per instance

**Skip it when:**
- Single-value draws: the author says AVX2 brings no gain there, and extracting the four lanes one at a time loses the speedup
- Non-x86 targets: the header includes <immintrin.h> and uses __m256i types unconditionally, even in the serial build
- MSVC: issue #1 (Jan 2023, open) reports build errors with Visual Studio 2022
- Integer outputs where low-bit quality matters: xoshiro256+ has weak lowest 3 bits, and the bounded functions use the low 32 bits of the output
- Bounded integers wider than 32 bits: bounds are uint32_t only

**Integration:** header-only · none (Catch2 only for the unit tests and benchmarks) · C++17 (if constexpr); GCC on Linux is the only documented toolchain. Compile with -mavx2 and define __AVX2_AVAILABLE__ for the AVX2 variant. · x86-64 only; AVX2 required for the fast path

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over SIMDxorshift or simdpcg when you want a C++17 header with xoshiro256+ quality, bounded-int and double helpers, and serial and SIMD outputs that match. The 8-way xoshiro256++ gist or SHISHUA give more bulk throughput, and Sirius64 or wyrand are better for scalar one-at-a-time draws.

**Gotchas:**
- The AVX2 template instance cannot be created unless the __AVX2_AVAILABLE__ macro is defined before the include (static_assert).
- dnext() and dnext4() type-pun through a union, which is undefined behavior in ISO C++; it works on GCC and Clang.
- Serial next4() is 1.8x slower than four serial next() calls (1.93 ms vs 1.08 ms per 1M values); use next4() only with the AVX2 instance.
- Without -mavx2, serial dnext4() became much slower (6.39 ms vs 2.26 ms per 1M values) in the author's no-AVX benchmark.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2021-08-21, with an unanswered MSVC build issue. It is MIT-licensed (built on CC0 xoshiro code) and about 580 lines, so it is easy to vendor on GCC and Clang x86-64.

[repo](https://github.com/stephanfr/Xoshiro256PlusSIMD) · [benchmark](https://github.com/stephanfr/Xoshiro256PlusSIMD)

##### xrandom (rtmigo/xrandom_dart, Dart random number generators)  `Dart`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Pure-Dart PRNG classes (xorshift, xoshiro, splitmix64, mulberry32) implementing dart:math Random; Xrandom is 1.4-1.7x faster than Random on AOT.

**Beats:** Dart core dart:math Random — First-party README tables (AOT-compiled binaries on an AMD A9-9420e under Ubuntu 20.04, milliseconds, iteration count, Dart SDK version and benchmark harness not published) show Xrandom at 627 / 640 / 391 ms versus dart:math Random at 895 / 929 / 662 ms for nextInt / nextDouble / nextBool, about 1.43x, 1.45x and 1.69x (derived from page data); Xorshift64 has the fastest nextDouble at 569 ms. The nextInt figures predate the 0.7.1 uniformity fix.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: README tables (AMD A9-9420e, Ubuntu 20.04) with no benchmark code in lib, test or example. Last commit 2022-03-15, abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** The README timings predate the 0.7.1 nextInt uniformity fix (issue #3; commit 4367cf3 left the README unchanged), so the nextInt rows measured biased plain-modulo code; Drandom.nextInt still uses a loop that never fires, so it stays plain modulo and biased for large non-power-of-two max (code reading). The benchmark harness is not public (benchmark/ 404). Qrandom and Xoshiro256pp are slower than dart:math Random for nextInt/nextDouble. pub.dev 150/160 points, about 1,649 downloads per 30 days.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The default Xrandom is Marsaglia's xorshift32 (shifts 13, 17, 5), a few shifts and XORs per 32-bit output. nextBool draws one 32-bit word and hands out its bits one at a time, which is why the nextBool gain (391 vs 662 ms) is larger than the nextInt gain. nextInt masks for power-of-two bounds and otherwise uses modulo with a rejection loop; nextFloat converts a single 32-bit word with Doornik's method instead of the two words nextDouble uses.

**Use it when:**
- Dart or Flutter code that calls Random.nextInt, nextDouble or nextBool in hot loops (games, procedural generation, sampling) on native AOT targets.
- Code that needs the same random sequence on Dart VM, AOT and JavaScript builds, or across future SDK versions, from a fixed seed (use Xrandom, Qrandom or Xorshift128 when JavaScript is a target).
- Tests needing reproducible random input: Drandom or Qrandom.seeded() give fixed, reference-checked sequences.
- Cross-language reproducibility, where a Dart port must match numbers produced by the C reference xoshiro128++, xorshift or splitmix64 code with the same seed.

**Skip it when:**
- Cryptographic use: the classes are xorshift, xoshiro, splitmix64 and mulberry32 generators with clock-based default seeds, not cryptographic generators.
- When quality matters more than speed: the README itself points computational work at Qrandom (xoshiro128++), and Qrandom/Drandom (933 / 1219 ms) and Xoshiro256pp (1138 / 1182 ms) are slower than dart:math Random (895 / 929 ms) for nextInt and nextDouble; only nextBool is faster for them.
- Web targets with the 64-bit generators: Xorshift64, Xorshift128p, Splitmix64, Mulberry32 and the Xoshiro256 classes throw Unsupported64Error under JavaScript.
- Projects that need an actively maintained dependency: last release 0.7.2 on 2022-03-15 and no commits since.
- Measured speed on JavaScript or Flutter mobile targets: the README only benchmarks AOT binaries on one x86 laptop CPU.

**Integration:** module (Dart pub package xrandom) · meta ^1.3.0 · Dart SDK 2.12 (null safety); pubspec constraint is >=2.12.0 <3.0.0, and pub.dev tags the package dart3-compatible · Dart VM and AOT (pub.dev lists Android, iOS, Windows, Linux, macOS) and web; only Xrandom, Qrandom, Drandom and Xorshift128 work when compiled to JavaScript

**Vs siblings:** It is the only Dart entry in this category; pure-rand (JavaScript/TypeScript) and lemire/fastrand (Python) play the same role in their runtimes, and C++ projects should take the reference xoshiro or SIMD siblings such as simdrng instead. Pick xrandom when Dart or Flutter code needs a faster Random-compatible generator or bit-identical sequences across VM and web builds.

**Gotchas:**
- The README timing tables were last edited before release 0.7.1 (2022-03-14), which fixed issue #3: the old nextInt's 'debiased modulo once' check could never trigger with Dart's 64-bit ints, so the nextInt timings were taken on plain, biased modulo code. The current nextInt adds a power-of-two branch and a working rejection loop and has not been re-benchmarked.
- Drandom still overrides nextInt with the old loop (u - (r = u % max) + m < 0), which by the same reasoning never repeats, so Drandom.nextInt is plain modulo and is noticeably biased for large bounds that are not powers of two (finding from reading lib/src/80_drandom.dart; 0.7.1 only narrowed its max to 2^31).
- Unseeded constructors seed from DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch mixed with the object's hashCode; Xorshift32's clock path does not exclude a zero state, which would make it return 0 forever (explicit seeds are range-checked to 1..0xFFFFFFFF).
- nextInt accepts bounds only up to 2^32 (RangeError above), and sequences differ from dart:math Random for the same integer seed.

**Status:** Abandoned since the 0.7.2 release of 2022-03-15, but MIT, pure Dart with one small dependency, all four GitHub issues closed, 150 of 160 pub points and about 1,650 downloads in the last 30 days, so it is still usable and easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/rtmigo/xrandom_dart) · [benchmark](https://github.com/rtmigo/xrandom_dart)

##### cxx-ziggurat  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Single-header C++11 ziggurat sampler meant to replace std::normal_distribution; the repo publishes no speed numbers.

**Beats:** std::normal_distribution — No measurement is published. The repo includes a benchmark that times 10 million draws (ns/gen) of std::normal_distribution against the ziggurat for mt19937_64, mt19937 and JSF64 with double and float, built with C++11 -O2 -mtune=native -funsafe-math-optimizations, but it records no results, compiler or hardware.

**Known shortcoming:** Verifier rejected as not notable (tier D): 4 stars, no published numbers, last commit 2018-11-14. Kept per keep-and-document rule.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark exists but no recorded results; its Makefile uses -funsafe-math-optimizations; with 32-bit engines (std::mt19937) it draws only 31 bits and the same low bits pick layer, sign and part of the value; README's LICENSE.txt link 404s (Boost licence only in the header).

**How:** Marsaglia-Tsang style ziggurat with a precomputed 129-edge (128-layer) table. A single URNG draw supplies the uniform, the layer index (low 7 bits) and the sign (bit 7). Most samples are accepted with one multiply and compare, marked __builtin_expect-likely. Only rare wedge rejections call exp(), and only the base layer falls back to a log-based tail sampler (both noinline).

**Use it when:**
- Hot loops that draw many N(mu, sigma) doubles or floats from a 64-bit engine (mt19937_64 or a fast 64-bit PRNG) and are bound by std::normal_distribution's cost
- Projects that want a tiny, dependency-free, Boost-licensed header and an API identical to std::normal_distribution
- Monte Carlo, Brownian or Langevin dynamics, and noise injection, where sample-for-sample reproducibility against libstdc++ is not required

**Skip it when:**
- When you need published, verified speedups: the repo has a benchmark program (benchmark/bench_normal_distribution.cc) but no results anywhere
- With 32-bit engines (std::mt19937): it then draws only 31 bits, and the uniform's low bits are the same bits that pick the layer and sign, so samples have coarse resolution and correlation between layer and value
- When you need other distributions (exponential, gamma); only the normal is provided
- When you need sequences identical to std::normal_distribution, for example regression tests seeded against libstdc++ output
- When you need long-term maintenance: last commit 2018, 14 commits, 4 stars, CI on the defunct travis-ci.org

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only) · C++11 · any (portable C++; GCC-specific __builtin_expect/noinline guarded by __GNUC__)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Randompack when you want a single header that keeps your existing std URNG and std::normal_distribution call sites; Randompack is a larger library with its own engines but has published measurements. Randen, Romu, SIMDxorshift and Squares are uniform bit generators, not normal samplers, so they pair with this rather than compete with it.

**Gotchas:**
- Bit budget comes from log2(URNG::max()-URNG::min()), so a 64-bit engine yields 63 bits and std::mt19937 yields 31; with doubles from a 32-bit engine, canonicalize uses all 31 bits, including the 8 bits that also choose the layer and sign
- The benchmark Makefile builds with -funsafe-math-optimizations -mtune=native -O2, so any number you measure with it is not under default flags
- The license is stated in the header and README badge; the README's LICENSE.txt link returns 404, so keep the header notice when vendoring

**Status:** Abandoned since November 2018, but a single Boost-licensed header with no dependencies, so it is easy to vendor and audit; treat the speedup as unverified.

[repo](https://github.com/snsinfu/cxx-ziggurat)

##### stochastic-generation (Owen-scrambled Sobol', Halton, Faure and pmj02 sample sequences)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier D`

Reference code for EGSR 2021 stochastic generation: Owen-scrambled Sobol', Halton, Faure and pmj02(bn) sequences at O(1) per coordinate.

**Beats:** other published generators of Owen-scrambled Sobol', Halton, Faure and pmj02(bn) sequences (not named in the README) — There are no measurements to verify. The README claims the code is 'faster than any other published method' for these sequences, names no competitor, and says the paper's 2D-only Listing 2 is about 3x faster. The paper abstract (WebSearch snippet only; the paper itself is egress-blocked) puts Listing 2 at 200 million samples/s on one CPU thread, which would imply roughly 65 million 2D samples/s for this library (derived, unmeasured, hardware unknown). For context, the author's earlier pmj-cpp documents pmj02 at about 1.65 million samples/s on a 2017 MacBook Pro, but that is different code and hardware.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Faster than any published method' has no numbers or baseline in the repo; the EGSR paper (blocked here) gives ~200M samples/s per thread without a named baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** No measurements anywhere reachable; the paper is still blocked. Array generators take no seed (std::random_device), so output is not reproducible; the stateless Sobol' generator was broken until the 2022-09-01 fix; errors call std::terminate. Rough context only: the author's pmj-cpp documents pmj02 at about 1.65M samples/s on a 2017 MacBook Pro while the paper snippet gives 200M samples/s for Listing 2, on different code and hardware.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Stochastic generation (Helmer, Christensen, Kensler, EGSR 2021) builds the scrambled sequence directly instead of generating Sobol' points and then Owen-scrambling them digit by digit. For each new index prev_len+i, each dimension looks up an earlier sample at i XOR a precomputed per-dimension 'xor-value', takes that sample's stratum, flips its last digit (stratum ^ 1, or a base-b digit add for Faure and Halton), and draws one uniform offset inside the flipped stratum. So each coordinate costs one table lookup, one array read and one PCG32 draw, and the output is distributed as an Owen-scrambled sequence. The stateless variant recurses over the index bits instead, at O(log n) per coordinate.

**Use it when:**
- Monte Carlo or quasi-Monte Carlo integration (rendering, option pricing, uncertainty propagation) where you want Owen-scrambled Sobol', Faure or Halton points with fresh randomization per run.
- Precomputing sample tables (pmj02, pmj02bn, ssobol) in a renderer or tool, where the whole array is generated at once.
- Low-dimensional integrands of 3, 5, 7 or 11 dimensions at power-of-base sample counts: the sfaure (0,s)-sequences stratify on all elementary intervals.
- Learning or reimplementing the paper: the code favours readability, and the README says a specialised 2D version (paper Listing 2) is about 3x faster.

**Skip it when:**
- You need plain uniform random numbers: this produces stratified point sets, not a PRNG stream; use a PRNG (std::mt19937 replacement) instead.
- You need reproducible output: the array generators take no seed and seed PCG32 from std::random_device on each call; only the stateless Sobol' function takes a seed.
- Per-sample on-the-fly generation inside a renderer: the main generators need the whole n x nd array resident because each point reads an earlier one, so streaming needs the slower stateless path.
- More than 64 Sobol' or 10 Halton dimensions, or more than about 2^31 coordinates: dimensions are capped by compile-time tables, and indices and n*nd products are plain int.
- Production use that needs error handling: bad arguments call std::terminate via an ASSERT macro, and there are no tests, releases or packaging.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (C++ standard library only); xor_values.py (Python) is needed only to regenerate xor-value tables · C++14 (makefile: g++ -std=c++14 -O2, 'make release' adds -O3) · any; portable scalar C++ with no SIMD or intrinsics; 32-bit builds fixed by PR #1 (merged 2023-12-14)

**Vs siblings:** No quasi-random siblings are catalogued yet; every listed sibling (Randompack, OpenRAND, EigenRand, the xoshiro and PCG variants) is a pseudo-random generator for independent uniforms. Pick this when you need stratified, Owen-scrambled point sets for integration, and a sibling PRNG when you need a random stream.

**Gotchas:**
- Best-candidate mode (--bn2d, candidates > 1) evaluates kBestCandidateSamples = 100 candidates per point, with a grid nearest-neighbour query each, so pmj02bn-style output costs far more than plain pmj02 or ssobol.
- The stateless Sobol' functions were broken until the 2022-09-01 commit 'Fix bugs with the stateless Sobol' implementation'; use current HEAD.
- Progressive shuffling ASSERTs that the sample count is a constant multiple of a power of the base (otherwise std::terminate) and copies the full array. Halton cannot be shuffled, and passing owen=true to ssobol or pmj02 only prints a warning and is ignored.
- Strata of earlier points are recovered by multiplying stored doubles by the stratum count, so outputs must stay as double; do not narrow the buffer to float.

**Status:** Code has been stable since the 2023-12-14 32-bit fix (the 2026 commits only touch the README); MIT-licensed, about 1,700 lines of plain C++14 across sampling/, easy to vendor, with 55 stars and no open issues.

[repo](https://github.com/Andrew-Helmer/stochastic-generation) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Andrew-Helmer/stochastic-generation)

#### sparse-and-solvers

##### AMGCL  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++ algebraic multigrid solver library; sets up AMG preconditioners faster than Trilinos ML and PETSc GAMG on shared memory.

**Beats:** PETSc (GAMG); Trilinos ML; CUSP — On a dual Xeon E5-2640 v3 node, solving a 3D Poisson finite-difference system (3,375,000 unknowns, 23.5M nonzeros) with AMG-preconditioned CG, the author's docs report AMGCL (OpenMP) setup about 20-100% faster than Trilinos ML and 4-7x faster than PETSc (both via MPI), with overall CPU time on par with Trilinos; a Tesla K80 CUDA run cut solve time 3-4x but total time only about 30%. Compiler and flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Win is mostly solver setup time (metric 'build-time' means setup); overall CPU speed on par with Trilinos; distributed runs 2.5-3x worse than Trilinos.

**Known shortcoming:** Each library ran its default smoother; open issues: i386 build failure (#312), int overflow in CUDA backend (#287), memory growth when called repeatedly from pybind11 (#291).

**How:** The AMG hierarchy (e.g. smoothed aggregation coarsening) is built on the CPU with OpenMP using shared-memory data structures, avoiding the distributed-memory bookkeeping that the docs blame for PETSc's and Trilinos' slower setup. After setup the hierarchy is moved to a backend (builtin OpenMP, CUDA/cuSPARSE, VexCL/OpenCL, ViennaCL, HIP), so the solve phase runs on GPUs transparently. Cheap default smoothers (SPAI0) and static block value types (e.g. 4x4 blocks) cut setup cost and memory traffic; Schur pressure-correction field-split preconditioners handle coupled systems like Navier-Stokes.

**Use it when:**
- Single-node solves of large elliptic/PDE systems (millions of unknowns) where you rebuild the preconditioner often and setup time matters.
- C++ codes that want an AMG preconditioner without adopting PETSc or Trilinos data structures or build systems.
- Solve-heavy workloads on a GPU (CUDA, OpenCL, HIP) where solution phase alone was 3-4x faster than CPU on the docs' Poisson test.
- Block-structured systems (elasticity, Navier-Stokes) using static block value types or field-split Schur pressure correction.
- Mixed precision or custom value types via template specialization.

**Skip it when:**
- Large distributed-memory runs: the project's own weak-scaling test shows AMGCL about 3x slower than Trilinos AMG, and PETSc scales better than both on shared memory.
- You need a direct solver or robust black-box behaviour on hard indefinite or highly anisotropic problems; open issues report convergence trouble on a 3D structural problem (#300).
- Total time-to-solution on GPU for one-shot solves: setup always runs on the CPU, so CUDA total time was only about 30% better than OpenMP AMGCL.
- 32-bit targets (open i386 build failure, #312) or very large CUDA problems (int overflow, #287).
- Strict bitwise reproducibility across thread counts unless you define AMGCL_DETERMINISTIC_REDUCTIONS (may be slower on many cores).

**Integration:** header-only · OpenMP (recommended); Boost.property_tree only for the runtime interface (removable with AMGCL_NO_BOOST); per-backend extras: CUDA/cuSPARSE/Thrust, VexCL (Boost + OpenCL/CUDA), ViennaCL, ROCm hipSPARSE/rocSPARSE; MPI 3.0 for distributed solvers; optional Eigen, METIS/Scotch, PaStiX · C++ standard not documented for the core; CMake 3.10+ for the bundled build; HIP backend requires C++17 · any with a C++ compiler (GCC, Clang, Intel, MSVC configured in CMake); GPUs via CUDA, OpenCL or HIP; i386 build currently broken per open issue

**Vs siblings:** Pick AMGCL over Ginkgo when you want a small header-only AMG with fast CPU setup and runtime-configurable solvers; pick Ginkgo for GPU-first sparse work where its AMG beat NVIDIA AmgX. Unlike BaSpaCho or Sympiler (direct Cholesky), AMGCL is iterative and suits very large PDE systems where factorization fill-in is too costly.

**Gotchas:**
- Benchmarks compare each library on its default smoother (AMGCL SPAI0, Trilinos symmetric Gauss-Seidel, PETSc damped Jacobi), so iteration counts and solve time are not like-for-like.
- OpenMP reductions give last-bit differences with different thread counts by default; define AMGCL_DETERMINISTIC_REDUCTIONS to fix.
- Heavy template composition means long compile times and large binaries (MSVC needs /bigobj, set by the CMake target).
- Open issue #291 reports growing memory when called repeatedly from a pybind11 module.

**Status:** Actively maintained (release 1.4.9 in June 2026, 871 stars, 59 open issues), MIT-licensed and header-only, so easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/ddemidov/amgcl) · [benchmark](https://amgcl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/benchmarks.html)

##### BaSpaCho  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Supernodal sparse Cholesky for block-structured SPD systems with CPU and batched-CUDA backends; factors faster than CHOLMOD on its synthetic tests.

**Beats:** CHOLMOD (SuiteSparse) — The repo's bench tool timed factorization against CHOLMOD on synthetic FLAT, FLAT+SCHUR, GRID and MERI block graphs (5 random instances each) on a Xeon Silver 4214 with a Quadro RTX 5000. With OpenBLAS and 16 threads, CPU factor time was 4-17% lower on FLAT problems and 44-74% lower on Schur-heavy and larger grid problems. With MKL the result ran from about 20% slower to 88% faster. The CUDA backend was 77-95% faster than CPU CHOLMOD. Compiler and flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Compiler and flags not stated; with MKL it is 15-23% slower than CHOLMOD on some problem types; CUDA numbers compare GPU build against CPU CHOLMOD.

**Known shortcoming:** With OpenBLAS only 4-17% faster than CHOLMOD on FLAT; CPU single-RHS solve ~2.1-2.5x slower than CHOLMOD on FLAT 1000; symbolic analysis ~3.5-4x slower on sparse FLAT; no comparison with CHOLMOD's GPU path; supernodal only, no update/downdate or LDL^T; CUDA path nondeterministic with sparse-elimination ranges; issues page not reviewed.

**How:** Supernodal Cholesky groups columns into dense blocks so most of the work runs through BLAS/LAPACK potrf/trsm/syrk/gemm. A fitted computation model of BLAS timings chooses which supernodes to merge. Independent small diagonal blocks (the 'Schur-complement trick' from Ceres-style BA) go through a parallel 'sparse elimination' stage before the supernodal part, which gives the large wins on FLAT+SCHUR problems. On GPU it runs entirely in CUDA/cuBLAS and can batch several matrices that share a sparsity pattern.

**Use it when:**
- Bundle adjustment or SLAM normal equations with many small (1-12) parameter blocks and a large set of independently eliminable points (point/landmark Schur structure)
- Repeated factorizations of a fixed sparsity pattern in an LM/Gauss-Newton loop, where the analysis cost is paid once
- Batched solves of same-structure systems on an NVIDIA GPU, e.g. differentiable optimization in PyTorch/Theseus
- Moderately to strongly interconnected graphs (2D grids, mesh-like graphs) where supernodes are large enough for BLAS to pay off
- When you need partial factorization or marginal covariances, or a direct/PCG hybrid

**Skip it when:**
- Banded or very sparse matrices where simplicial Cholesky wins; the README says to use CHOLMOD or Eigen there
- Matrices that need update/downdate of the factor, or non-SPD/indefinite systems (no LDL^T or LU, and singularity reporting is listed as future work)
- Single-RHS CPU solves dominate your runtime: in the repo's own runs, CPU solve-1 was about 2.1-2.5x slower than CHOLMOD on FLAT 1000
- One-shot factorizations of very sparse FLAT problems: symbolic analysis was about 3.5-4x slower than CHOLMOD on FLAT size=4000 fill=0.01
- If you link Intel MKL: with MKL, BaSpaCho's CPU factor was 15-23% slower than CHOLMOD on two FLAT problem types

**Integration:** static lib (CMake build) · BLAS/LAPACK (OpenBLAS, ATLAS or MKL); Eigen 3.4, dispenso 1.4 (threads), gtest and Sophus are fetched by CMake; optional CUDA toolkit + cuBLAS/cuSPARSE, SuiteSparse AMD, and CHOLMOD (benchmarks only) · C++17, CMake 3.28+; CUDA tested with 10.2/11.7, compute capability >= 6.0 for double atomicAdd (else a workaround define) · x86-64 Linux documented (CPU via BLAS); NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA; other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick BaSpaCho over Sympiler when you need a GPU or batched backend and BA-style Schur elimination built in, rather than code generation specialised to one sparsity pattern on the CPU. Ginkgo and AMGCL are iterative solvers (Krylov/AMG); choose BaSpaCho when you want an exact direct factorization of a block SPD system and the fill is manageable.

**Gotchas:**
- Numeric data and vectors live in the solver's internal reordered layout; use the accessor/paramToSpan permutation to load values and map results back
- The CUDA path is not deterministic when sparse-elimination ranges exist (atomic adds in factor and solve); the CPU path is deterministic given deterministic BLAS
- Default Settings use 16 threads and an untuned computation model; the README advises re-fitting the model (bench -Z plus opt_comp_model) per CPU/BLAS/GPU
- Every entry is a block; matrices with no block structure become 1x1 blocks and run slightly slower, and very large parameter blocks fit the thread/kernel design poorly

**Status:** Maintained at low volume by Meta research (76 commits, last commit 2025-10-08, 112 stars) and MIT-licensed, so copyable, but the CMake/BLAS/CUDA build is not trivial to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/facebookresearch/baspacho) · [benchmark](https://github.com/facebookresearch/baspacho/blob/main/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md)

##### fast_matrix_market (parallel Matrix Market sparse matrix I/O)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Parallel, full-format Matrix Market (.mtx) reader/writer; about 10x single-thread and 30x on 8 threads over IOStreams loaders.

**Beats:** C++ IOStreams (std::istream/ostream) and scanf-based Matrix Market loaders; for the Python bindings, scipy.io.mmread/mmwrite before SciPy 1.12 — First-party Google Benchmark (benchmark/fmm_bench via run_benchmarks.sh, CMake Release, compiler not stated) on an 8-core Apple M1 Pro: coordinate reads 1578 MB/s on 8 threads vs 48.5 MB/s for a sequential IOStreams loader (about 32x; about 10x on one thread); coordinate writes 691 MB/s vs 60.9 MB/s (about 11x; 3.6x on one thread). The README's '>1 GB/s, about 25x' headline holds for reads and for array writes, not for coordinate writes.

**Known shortcoming:** Coordinate read ~32.5x over sequential IOStream at 8 threads but write only ~11.3x (691 MB/s); the '>1GB/s write' claim holds for array files only; compiler unstated; edge of the sparse category (I/O, not compute).

**Known shortcoming:** Presizes output from the header's nnz, so a bad or crafted header can force a huge allocation. Some paths run single-threaded (bool values, symmetric array files, coordinate files read into dense handlers). PyPI wheels stop at CPython 3.12.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Field conversion uses fast_float or C++17 std::from_chars for numbers and Dragonbox/Ryu or std::to_chars for writing, avoiding scanf/strtod/IOStreams, which also lock on the locale and get slower with threads. The main thread reads the stream in 2 MiB line-aligned chunks; a thread pool counts lines per chunk so each chunk's output offset (coordinate) or row/column start (array) is known, then parses chunks in parallel straight into presized output vectors. Bounded in-flight chunks give backpressure, and chunk buffers are reused to keep RSS down.

**Use it when:**
- Loading multi-GB SuiteSparse or graph .mtx files into C++ where the existing loader (Eigen's loadMarket, hand-written scanf/IOStreams code) is the bottleneck
- Coordinate files with real/integer/complex/pattern fields read into std::vector-like triplets or CSC/CSR; the example output shows about 500 MB/s on one thread and about 1.6 GB/s on 8 threads on an M1 Pro
- Writing large sparse or dense results to .mtx, including CSC/CSR directly without a COO intermediate
- Python on SciPy older than 1.12, or when you need vector files, longdouble or direct CSR/CSC writes, which scipy.io.mmread lacks (pip or conda fast_matrix_market)
- Files SuiteSparse ships that partial loaders reject: array format, vector objects, skew-symmetric/hermitian, 64-bit indices

**Skip it when:**
- Small files where load time is already negligible; the gain only matters at hundreds of MB and up
- Binary formats would be faster still: if you control both ends, a binary sparse format avoids text parsing altogether
- Some paths fall back to sequential: bool value types, symmetric array files, and coordinate files read into dense handlers do not parallelize
- Toolchains without float std::from_chars and with fast_float disabled fall back to strtod, which the author's parse-bench shows serializing on the locale lock
- If you need an actively maintained dependency: last commit June 2024, PyPI wheels stop at CPython 3.12 (1.7.6, December 2023)
