**Integration:** header-only (CMake INTERFACE target; header-only only when the optional fast_float, Dragonbox and Ryu dependencies are disabled) · C++11 threads; optional and on by default: fast_float, Dragonbox, Ryu (vendored under dependencies/); bundled task_thread_pool header. Eigen/GraphBLAS/CXSparse/Blaze/Armadillo only for their bindings · C++17, CMake 3.14+; CI tests GCC 8 and 13, LLVM/Clang 8, MSVC and MinGW 13 (CMake probes for std::from_chars/std::to_chars support) · any platform with C++17 and std::thread (CI: Linux, macOS, Windows; PyPI wheels for x86-64 and aarch64)

**Vs siblings:** No sibling does the same job: the other sparse-and-solvers entries (merge-spmv, CSR5, AMGCL, Ginkgo) are kernels and solvers that need their input loaded first. Use this as their I/O front end when .mtx parsing dominates benchmark or pipeline start-up time.

**Gotchas:**
- Open output streams in binary mode; text mode on Windows writes CRLF line endings that other loaders may reject
- Symmetric files are expanded to general by default (generalize_symmetry=true); a diagonal entry gets an extra explicit zero (ExtraZeroElement) unless the app binding generalizes, so nnz can differ from what other loaders produce
- Output vectors are resized from the header's nnz before parsing, so a corrupt or hostile header can force a very large allocation before any error is raised
- Uses all hardware threads by default; set num_threads (C++) or parallelism (Python) inside already-parallel programs

**Status:** Stale since June 2024 (C++ header version 1.7.7, PyPI 1.7.6) but feature-complete, BSD-2-Clause and shipped inside SciPy 1.12+, so it is safe to vendor; open issues are build and packaging requests, not bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/alugowski/fast_matrix_market) · [benchmark](https://github.com/alugowski/fast_matrix_market)

##### LAMG+ (lean algebraic multigrid for graph Laplacians)  `Julia`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Julia algebraic multigrid solver for graph-Laplacian systems; 6.6-13.6x faster than PETSc GAMG on social, web and optimization graphs.

**Beats:** PETSc GAMG; the same study also runs hypre BoomerAMG, pyAMG, CMG and approximate Cholesky (Laplacians.jl approxchol_lap) — Source: the author's arXiv preprint in the repo (doc/lamg_plus.tex). Setup plus solve to 1e-8 relative residual, run serially on an Apple M5 Pro and reported as mean microseconds per nonzero for each graph class over a class-stratified SuiteSparse/SNAP corpus plus synthetic families. LAMG+ beats PETSc GAMG on social/citation (0.47 vs 3.10), web (0.37 vs 2.76), optimization (0.15 vs 2.04) and the chimera families, ties on FE/structural (0.12), and loses on mesh/grid, 3D grid, road, SPE and star. PETSc, hypre and pyAMG were prebuilt binaries with unstated build flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Mixed vs PETSc GAMG: wins 7 of 13 classes and loses 5; PETSc/pyAMG run in subprocesses, not in the same process as the paper says; Claude is co-author on every commit.

**Known shortcoming:** Julia only, no C API (off-language). The paper says competitors run in the same Julia process, but run_class_comparison.jl runs PETSc GAMG/pyAMG/CMG in subprocesses from prebuilt binaries. Class-table defaults: nnz cap 5M, 6 graphs per class. Loses to PETSc GAMG on mesh/grid/3D/road/SPE classes.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It implements Lean Algebraic Multigrid (Livne and Brandt, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2012). Exact low-degree elimination, a Schur complement over an independent set of nodes with degree at most 4, alternates with caliber-1 (piecewise-constant) aggregation. Because of this, the Galerkin coarse operators stay as sparse as the graph and do not fill in around scale-free hubs the way classical AMG does. Nodes are grouped into aggregates by the affinity (squared cosine) of K=4 Gauss-Seidel-relaxed test vectors, subject to an energy-ratio guard. LAMG+ adds a strength-of-connection veto and a selective caliber-2 interpolation that fix stalls on grid-aligned anisotropy. The paper credits the low per-edge constants to a self-gated reverse Cuthill-McKee reordering, single-pass Gustavson-fused Schur extraction, allocation-free elimination and an in-place, residual-maintaining Gauss-Seidel kernel.

**Use it when:**
- Laplacian solves on large irregular graphs (social, citation, web, optimization/network-flow), where PETSc GAMG and BoomerAMG slow down by up to an order of magnitude. Class means: 0.47 vs 3.10 us/nnz on social, 0.15 vs 2.04 on optimization.
- Finite-element and structural graph Laplacians. Among the robust solvers it was fastest there (for example bmwcra_1 0.08 vs 0.28 us/nnz for approxchol_lap) and leanest in memory (21-30 bytes/nnz vs 33-55 for approximate Cholesky).
- Graphs with high mean degree: the paper's rule 'LAMG+ wins iff mean degree >= 30' picked the faster solver against approxChol 91% of the time.
- Many right-hand sides on one graph (the hierarchy is reused), or lower-accuracy solves: at 1e-4 its geometric-mean speedup over approxchol_lap rises from 0.99x to 1.20x.
- Julia pipelines (spectral clustering, electrical flow, interior-point network flow) that want a solver depending only on Julia standard libraries.

**Skip it when:**
- Meshes, grids, roads and reservoir models: PETSc GAMG is faster on mesh/grid (0.23 vs 0.84 us/nnz), 3D grid (0.25 vs 1.30), road (0.57 vs 0.68) and SPE (0.90 vs 1.09), and BoomerAMG is faster still on grids.
- Social, web, citation and chimera graphs when Laplacians.jl approxchol_lap is an option: it is faster there (social 0.25 vs 0.47, web 0.29 vs 0.37, chimera 0.14 vs 0.40 us/nnz).
- C or C++ codebases: the solver is Julia-only and no C API is documented.
- General SPD, SDDM or unsymmetric matrices, and disconnected graphs: `setup` asserts zero row sums, and the library handles several components by reducing to one connected component (`largest_component`) instead of solving them all.
- Multi-core or distributed runs, and memory-tight web/social workloads. All published timings are single-threaded, the paper calls distributed coarsening unresolved, and the hierarchy takes 62-80 bytes/nnz on web/social graphs vs 32-40 for approxChol.

**Integration:** module · none beyond Julia standard libraries (LinearAlgebra, SparseArrays, Random, Statistics, Printf); the comparison scripts also need Laplacians.jl, HYPRE.jl, PyCall/pyAMG and PETSc_jll in a separate environment · Julia 1.10+ · any platform Julia supports (no other restriction documented); the paper's timings are from an Apple M5 Pro

**Vs siblings:** Pick AMGCL (C++ header-only AMG with faster setup than PETSc GAMG) for PDE and mesh systems in C++. Pick apxchol for parallel approximate-Cholesky Laplacian/SDDM solves from C++. Pick LAMG+ for serial Julia work on graph Laplacians, especially FE/structural or high-degree graphs, where it beats approximate Cholesky.

**Gotchas:**
- The right-hand side must be compatible (zero mean), and the solution is returned orthogonal to the constant vector. The default `max_cycles` is 100, so check `info.cycles` and the residual on hard inputs.
- Setup is randomized (relaxed test vectors) but seeded with a fixed MersenneTwister seed (0xfa11), so runs repeat exactly unless you change `LAMGOptions.seed`.
- The class-comparison harness defaults to graphs with at most 5,000,000 nonzeros and 6 graphs per class. PETSc GAMG, pyAMG and CMG run in subprocesses (PETSc GAMG from the prebuilt PETSc_jll binary, timed inside the subprocess with startup excluded), and hypre runs through HYPRE.jl, which contradicts the paper's statement that every competitor runs in the same Julia process.
- Version 0.1.0 with no release tags. The package UUID is hand-written, and the README installs it from the cloned project, not from a package registry.

**Status:** Active single-author research code (49 commits, last commit 2026-07-06, 0 stars, no releases). Apache-2.0 and free of dependencies, but Julia-only and not packaged in a registry.

[repo](https://github.com/orenlivne/lamgplus) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/orenlivne/lamgplus/HEAD/doc/lamg_plus.tex)

##### RA-SpMM (regime-aware GPU SpMM router for GNN workloads)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rule-based GPU SpMM dispatcher (five CSR/tensor-core kernels) for GNN graphs, 1.70x warm geomean over FP32 cuSPARSE.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE SpMM (FP32, cusparseSpMM) — On an RTX 3090 with CUDA 11.8 (nvcc -O3 --use_fast_math -arch=sm_86), over 51 graphs x N in {64,128,256,512}, routed kernels ran 1.702x faster (warm geomean, 50 warmup + 200 timed CUDA-event iterations, preprocessing outside the timed region) than FP32 cusparseSpMM with CUSPARSE_SPMM_CSR_ALG2; the figure recomputes from the released CSV, but compares FP16/TF32 tensor-core paths against FP32 cuSPARSE, so the precision-matched figure is 1.222x (1.053x on an RTX 4090).

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers recomputed exactly from the released CSV (1.702x, 173 hits, 0.868), but the paper is still under review.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**How:** A single O(M) pass over the row-pointer array computes row count, mean degree and degree coefficient of variation; with feature width N, a seven-rule decision tree picks one of five kernels: subwarp-per-row CSR (CSR_DIRECT), degree-binned CSR (ZERO_OVERHEAD_CSR), and three tensor-core kernels on an 8x1 vector-block layout using mma.m16n8k8 (TC_DIRECT, COMMUNITY_TC with a leading-neighbour locality sort, SEGMENT_HYBRID with balanced window splits). Tile kernels run FP16 or TF32 inputs chosen by a precision rule, and a cuSPARSE guardrail covers the case where no specialist wins; most of the headline gain comes from tensor-core reduced precision (precision-matched speedup is 1.222x).

**Use it when:**
- GNN training or inference in PyTorch on Ampere/Ada GPUs (sm_86 RTX 3090, sm_89 RTX 4090 tested) where the same graph is multiplied many times, so the one-time tile build amortizes (median break-even 388 calls per RESULTS.md).
- Feature widths N of 64 to 512 on graphs resembling its 51-graph suite (citation, social, web, Reddit/ogbn-proteins-style dense rows, synthetic power-law and community graphs).
- Cold first-call SpMM where you cannot amortize setup: the cold path dispatches a zero-conversion CSR kernel (2.269x over cuSPARSE descriptor+workspace+first call on the 3090).
- When FP16/TF32 accumulation error (max deviation 0.125 observed under its tolerance gate) is acceptable for your model.

**Skip it when:**
- You need FP32 or bit-identical results to cuSPARSE: tile paths use FP16 or TF32 inputs and the build uses --use_fast_math; restricted to precision-matched comparison the gain drops to 1.222x on the 3090 and 1.053x on the 4090.
- Graphs unlike the tuning suite: rule thresholds are named after specific benchmark graphs (com-youtube, Reddit, amazon-photo, web-Google), and the frozen router on 9 unseen graphs reached only 1.197x with 11/34 oracle hits; wiki-Talk and cit-Patents at N=512 exhausted memory on every deployed kernel.
- If FlashSparse or MP-SpMM is an option: per RESULTS.md FlashSparse is 1.28x faster than the router over 190 configs on the 4090, and MP-SpMM beats it on aggregate at N=128 (router 0.84x; router wins only on real graphs, 1.15x).
- Non-NVIDIA hardware, CPU, int64 indices, double precision, or code outside PyTorch: none are supported.
- Production use: a research artifact for a paper under review, 1 star, 7 commits on one day; the model-based runtime router (ra_runtime_router.py) loads results/router/runtime_cost_model.json, which is not in the repository.

**Integration:** module (PyTorch CUDA extension built with python setup.py install; C++/CUDA sources compiled by nvcc) · CUDA 11.8+ toolkit, cuSPARSE, matching PyTorch (torch.utils.cpp_extension), OpenMP for host-side plan construction; numpy/scipy/scikit-learn only for the evaluation scripts · C++17 host code, nvcc from CUDA 11.8+; target arch set by RA_SM_ARCH (default 86) · NVIDIA GPUs with tensor cores; tested only on sm_86 (RTX 3090, CUDA 11.8) and sm_89 (RTX 4090, CUDA 12.1); Linux implied

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over HP-SpMM-SDDMM or Sputnik when your graphs vary in structure and you want one call that picks a CSR or tensor-core kernel per graph and accept FP16/TF32 precision; HP-SpMM-SDDMM is a single FP32 kernel tuned on an H800 and Sputnik targets deep-learning sparsity patterns rather than graph adjacency.

**Gotchas:**
- The one-shot run_router_plan helper rebuilds the plan and host-copies the CSR on every call; the binding's own docstring says to cache make_<kernel>_plan/run_<kernel>_plan pairs for real use.
- Tile kernels need a format build (1 ms to 36 ms geomean per kernel, worst 1.5 s) and are withheld when the estimated build (about 20 ms per 1e6 nnz) exceeds 20 s or N < 16; 9 configurations never amortize the tile build at all.
- Plan building copies rowptr/colind/vals to the host, so the cold path includes a device-to-host transfer.
- CUDA errors are thrown as std::runtime_error (surfacing as Python exceptions); setup.py compiles every ablation kernel too, so build time is long.

**Status:** Code dump from 2026-07-31 accompanying a paper under review at FGCS; MIT code with CC-BY-4.0 data and a full reproduce script, but no issues, releases or users yet, so treat it as a research artifact to study or vendor rather than a maintained library.

[repo](https://github.com/tariqaf/RA-SpMM) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tariqaf/RA-SpMM)

##### RSLAB (pure-Rust sparse LDL^T, LU and KLU solver)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust sparse LDL^T/LU/KLU direct solver; solve phase 2.3-3.3x faster than MKL PARDISO, factorization usually slower.

**Beats:** Intel MKL PARDISO — The README table gives wall time relative to MKL PARDISO (pardisoinit defaults, taking the faster of classic and two-level factorization) on 28 non-public production systems at 12 threads, as a geomean per class. Solve time is 0.30-0.43 of PARDISO's (2.3-3.3x faster), while factorization is 0.95-4.76 and one-shot 0.74-1.12, so RSLAB is ahead end-to-end only on MoM near field. Both solvers are timed from the same Python harness (benches/pardiso_corpus.py), PARDISO through ctypes against pip-installed MKL; CPU model, Rust version and flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Only the solve phase is faster than PARDISO; factorization is slower on 3 of 4 classes; the test corpus is private; Rust.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust only, no C API. Correctness issue #74: default LU matching gives 5e-5 accuracy on saddle matrices (1e-12 with matching off). Open perf issues: #88 KLU refactor 3-8x behind PARDISO, #87 peak memory 2.3x PARDISO, #82/#83 x86 scaling and analysis. The crates.io name rslab is an unrelated slab allocator. 31 PyPI releases in 3 months; benchmark corpus not public.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** LDL^T and LU are left-looking and supernodal, run in parallel over the elimination tree in a scoped rayon pool, and do their dense updates with the pure-Rust `gemm` crate (runtime AVX2/AVX-512 dispatch). Several fill-reducing orderings (AMD, AMF, RCM, parallel nested dissection) are tried and raced on the exact fill each produces, with MC64-style matching and scaling. The solve-phase advantage comes from supernodal, tree-parallel triangular solves over the factor's panels. The KLU path factors independent BTF blocks in parallel and refactors without a new pivot search.

**Use it when:**
- Many solves per factorization (multiple right-hand sides, iterative refinement, Krylov preconditioning), where the solve phase at 0.30-0.43x PARDISO's time dominates.
- Method-of-moments near-field systems (complex): the one class where factor (0.95), refactor (0.90) and one-shot (0.74) time also beat PARDISO.
- Rust or Python projects that want a PARDISO-style solver without an MKL, BLAS or LAPACK dependency, or that need factors bit-identical across thread counts.
- Embedded or scheduled solves that must check memory before factoring: `memory_plan` and `estimate_memory` predict the heap peak from the analysis alone.
- Circuit-simulation sweeps on a fixed pattern through KLU `refactor`, or GMRES/COCG with a factor of a nearby matrix that never fails thanks to static pivoting.

**Skip it when:**
- Workloads dominated by factorization or one-shot solves on FEM curl-curl (factor 1.35x PARDISO's time), power-grid (3.97x) or circuit (4.76x) matrices, where PARDISO is faster.
- Medium-size circuit matrices with frequent refactorization: open issue #88 reports KLU refactor 3-8x behind PARDISO.
- Large complex-symmetric factorizations under memory pressure (#87: peak memory 2.3x PARDISO's), or x86 machines with many cores (#82: factorization scales poorly; #83: symbolic analysis takes 2.8x PARDISO's time).
- Saddle-point matrices with zero diagonals on the LU path with the default `lu_matching = true`. Issue #74 reports 154-408 floored pivots and 5e-5 relative accuracy on a complex EM saddle matrix, vs 1e-12 with matching off.
- C or C++ codebases (no C API; FFI exists only in the Python bindings), or teams that need a mature solver: 12 stars, and 31 PyPI releases between 2026-06-29 and 2026-09-29.

**Integration:** crate · rayon, gemm 0.19, num-complex, serde/serde_json, plus in-workspace ordering crates (AMD, AMF, METIS-style nested dissection); optional ureq/flate2/tar (feature matgen-download) and sysinfo (feature tuning); Python wheels need numpy>=1.21 and scipy>=1.7 · Rust 2021 edition on current stable (rust-toolchain.toml tracks stable; no rust-version/MSRV declared); Python >= 3.9 for the bindings · pure Rust (runtime AVX2/AVX-512 dispatch on x86, wasm32 clock shim in source); PyPI abi3 wheels for Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux_2_28), macOS x86-64 and arm64, and Windows x86-64

**Vs siblings:** Against GSS (trial binaries only, also benchmarked against PARDISO), pick RSLAB when you need MIT source and fast repeated solves. Pick CKTSO for C/C++ circuit simulators that care most about parallel factorization speed against KLU, and BaSpaCho for SPD Cholesky in C++. RSLAB covers indefinite, complex-symmetric and unsymmetric matrices in Rust or Python.

**Gotchas:**
- The crates.io name `rslab` belongs to an unrelated slab-allocator crate (versions 0.1-0.2 from 2022). Depend on the git tag as the README shows; `cargo add rslab` pulls the wrong crate.
- The default Threads::Auto caps workers at 4. The README benchmark passed 12 threads explicitly, so pass `threads=0` (all cores) or `'auto'` to match it.
- The dense kernels allocate per product. The docs recommend a caching global allocator such as mimalloc, especially on Windows.
- Licensing: the code is MIT and forked from feral (MIT), with Hungarian/MC64 routines translated from SPRAL (BSD-3-Clause). Releases 0.20.0-0.23.0 contained METIS-derived Apache-2.0 code (see NOTICE).

**Status:** Very active but young: 624 commits, v1.1.0 released 2026-09-29, 12 stars, one listed author, and open performance issues against PARDISO (#82, #83, #87, #88). MIT-licensed, installed from git or from PyPI wheels.

[repo](https://github.com/milanofthe/rslab) · [benchmark](https://github.com/milanofthe/rslab)

##### sparse_dot_topn  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Python package with a C++17 OpenMP kernel for sparse A*B that keeps only the top-n values per row; multithreaded, so it beats single-threaded SciPy.

**Beats:** SciPy sparse CSR matrix multiplication (scipy.sparse A.dot(B), SciPy 1.12.0) — The project's richbench run (30 repeats, SciPy 1.12.0 vs sparse-dot-topn v1.0.0, two 20,000 x 193,190 TF-IDF matrices of SEC EDGAR company names) shows the plain product 5.1x faster on 8 threads of an Apple M2 Pro (0.032 s vs 0.165 s) and 3.4x on an 8-core 2.3 GHz Intel i9. top_n=10 reaches 6.9x (M2 Pro) and 12.7x (i9) at 8 threads. Single-thread plain product is about 1.0x, and top_n>=100 on one thread is slower than SciPy. The compiler and flags of the benchmarked build are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Speedup comes mostly from threads (1.0x single-thread); baseline SciPy; Python package.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug from source reading (not reproduced): threshold=None sets the floor to std::numeric_limits<eT>::min() (~1.2e-38 for float), so negative and zero top-n results are silently dropped, against the README claim that negatives work. Suspected second bug: plain sp_matmul sizes indptr symbolically but skips sums that are exactly 0, so cancelling values or stored zeros give misaligned rows or uninitialised memory. Tests use non-negative data only. MT top-n index maths can overflow int32 when nrows*top_n > 2^31.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The kernel is SciPy's own row-wise Gustavson SpGEMM (a modified csr_binop/csr_matmat: a dense accumulator plus a linked list of touched columns) parallelised over rows of A with OpenMP. Each thread has its own accumulator. With top-n, each row's candidates go through a fixed-size heap (std::push_heap/pop_heap, O(top_n) memory per row instead of O(n_columns)), so the full product row is never stored. In the multithreaded path each row writes into a preallocated nrows x top_n buffer, which is compacted at the end. On one thread the plain product is the same algorithm as SciPy, which is why single-thread speed is about 1.0x.

**Use it when:**
- Top-k similarity joins (cosine similarity of L2-normalised TF-IDF or other non-negative sparse vectors) where you need only the best 10-30 matches per row: 5.5-6.9x over SciPy on 8 M2 Pro threads in the project's benchmark.
- Large A x B^T products whose full result would not fit in memory, but whose top-n result does.
- Multi-core machines running Python where SciPy's single-threaded sparse matmul is the bottleneck: the plain sp_matmul scales to 5.1x at 8 threads.
- Matching jobs too large for one machine (O(10M+) rows): split A and B into row blocks, run each pair anywhere (the README mentions Spark), merge with zip_sp_matmul_topn and vstack.

**Skip it when:**
- Large top_n on few threads: top_n=1000 is 6.2x slower than SciPy on one M2 Pro thread and still 1.2x slower at 8 threads; top_n=100 on one thread is 1.9x slower.
- Single-threaded use of the plain product: about 1.0x on the M2 Pro and the i9, so there is nothing to gain.
- Signed data with the default threshold=None (see gotchas): from reading the source, float results at or below the smallest positive float are dropped.
- General C++ SpGEMM: the headers include nanobind through common.hpp and the API exists for Python; use a C++ sparse library instead.
- Very large top-n jobs on the multithreaded path: memory for the nrows x top_n buffers is allocated up front, whatever the real output size.

**Integration:** module (Python package with a nanobind C++ extension; the core kernels are header-only templates under src/sparse_dot_topn_core/include) · numpy>=1.18, scipy>=1.4.1, psutil; nanobind and scikit-build-core to build; OpenMP optional (bundled in the PyPI wheels per the README; non-bundled wheels on the releases page) · C++17 compiler for source builds; CMake 3.15+; CPython 3.9-3.14 wheels (stable-ABI cp312 wheels for 3.12+) · Wheels for Windows x86-64, Linux 64-bit, macOS x86-64 and arm64. Wheels are generic builds with arch flags off; source builds add -march=native on Apple arm64 and SSE/AVX flags on x86.

**Vs siblings:** Of the catalogued siblings, only VBCSR also targets SciPy sparse. Pick sparse_dot_topn for unstructured TF-IDF-style similarity search with a small top-n, and VBCSR for block-structured operators. For general multithreaded SpGEMM inside C++ code, TACO-generated kernels or ALP/GraphBLAS fit better, because this package's kernels are tied to its Python bindings.

**Gotchas:**
- Possible correctness bug, from reading the source and not reproduced: when threshold is None the bindings use std::numeric_limits<eT>::min() as the floor. For float/double that is the smallest positive normal (about 1.2e-38), not the lowest value, so negative and zero results never enter the top-n heap. This contradicts the README's claim that disabling threshold makes negative values work. Integer dtypes are unaffected.
- Possible correctness bug, from reading the source and not reproduced: plain sp_matmul sizes C_indptr with a symbolic pass that counts every touched column, but the numeric pass skips sums that are exactly 0. If values cancel, or the input stores explicit zeros, the single-thread path shifts later rows' entries against indptr and the multithreaded path leaves unwritten slots, so the output holds uninitialised memory. The tests use only non-negative sparse.random data.
- The multithreaded top-n path computes nrows*top_n and per-row offsets in the index type (int32 when indices fit) and sums row counts with an int accumulator. Very large nrows x top_n (above 2^31) can overflow.
- n_threads=None means one thread, and -1 means physical cores minus one. Without OpenMP the call warns and runs single-threaded. COO and CSC inputs are converted to CSR first, which costs time.

**Status:** Active (v1.2.0 adds CPython 3.14 wheels; last commit 2026-09-14), Apache-2.0, 425 stars and 3 open issues. Easy to pip install, but the kernels are coupled to nanobind, so vendoring them into a C++ project takes some unpicking.

[repo](https://github.com/ing-bank/sparse_dot_topn) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ing-bank/sparse_dot_topn/master/bench/README.md)

##### spla (generalized sparse linear algebra, vendor-agnostic GPU)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

OpenCL GraphBLAS-style sparse linear algebra for Intel, AMD and Nvidia GPUs; on a GTX 1070 it beats CPU LAGraph/SuiteSparse on PageRank and SSSP.

**Beats:** SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS through LAGraph (CPU) — First-party README charts compare spla on an Nvidia GTX 1070 against LAGraph (SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS) on the same machine's 4-core i7-6700, over 13 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graphs (Ubuntu 20.04). Read off the log axis: PageRank about 7.5-50x, SSSP about 1.4-23x, TC about 4-12x, BFS about 0.7-3.7x. On integrated GPUs (Intel HD 530, AMD GFX1036) spla wins only PageRank. Compiler, flags and baseline versions are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** PageRank top is about 50x, not 65x; the omitted chart rq3_int.png shows spla slower than LAGraph on most BFS/SSSP/TC runs on integrated GPUs; LAGraph/GraphBLAST/Gunrock harness not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** README says 'not ready for usage'; only PyPI release is pyspla 0.0.5 (2022); graphs must fit in VRAM (#211 open); the '1 billion edges' and 'faster than scipy/networkx' claims have no numbers. Name clash with eth-cscs/spla (a different, already catalogued project).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Graph algorithms are written as masked sparse matrix-vector products over semirings and run as OpenCL kernels. For a sparse frontier, vxm uses expand-sort-compress: it counts products per row, prefix-sums the offsets, collects products, then runs a GPU sort-by-key and reduce-by-key. Masked mxv has a scalar kernel with early exit, which pulls only until a hit. User operators are pasted into the OpenCL source as #defines and functions, compiled at runtime and cached by a key, so custom semirings get fused kernels. Most of the headline gain is GPU memory bandwidth and parallelism against a 4-core CPU baseline.

**Use it when:**
- PageRank-style iterative SpMV on a discrete GPU: the README chart shows about 7.5x to 50x over LAGraph on a 4-core i7-6700 on 12 graphs, and spla beats Gunrock on every one.
- SSSP on large high-diameter graphs (road networks), where the chart shows up to about 23x (road_central) on a GTX 1070.
- Code that must run on Intel, AMD and Nvidia GPUs, including integrated ones, from one OpenCL code base instead of CUDA-only GraphBLAST or cuBool.
- Prototyping GraphBLAS-style algorithms with custom semirings from Python or C++, where runtime-compiled user operators matter more than peak speed.

**Skip it when:**
- Production use: the README says 'project under heavy development! Not ready for usage.', the CHANGELOG has no release entries, and PyPI's only pyspla release is 0.0.5 from 2022-08-17.
- BFS: the chart shows about 0.7x to 3.7x, and spla is slower than LAGraph on coAuthorsCiteseer, belgium_osm, com-Orkut and indochina-2004.
- Integrated GPUs with the CPU baseline on the same chip: spla loses to LAGraph on every BFS run, on most SSSP runs, and on every triangle-counting run on the Ryzen 9 7900X/GFX1036, and wins only PageRank.
- Graphs larger than GPU memory: RAM-to-VRAM streaming is an open feature request (#211), so the matrix must fit on the device.
- Sparse linear solvers or numerical linear algebra (factorizations, Krylov methods): spla is graph-analytics oriented and has none.

**Integration:** shared lib (libspla_<arch> built with CMake; C and C++ headers; pyspla Python package) · OpenCL 1.2 runtime and drivers (Khronos headers and ICD loader vendored as submodules; Apple's OpenCL framework on macOS), robin_hood and svector (vendored, private); cxxopts and gtest only for examples and tests · C++17; CMake 3.15+; Ninja and Python 3.7+ for build.py; MSVC is the only supported compiler on Windows · Linux (x64, riscv), Windows x64, macOS x64 and arm64. GPU acceleration on Intel, AMD and Nvidia through OpenCL; a CPU-only mode is available via set_force_no_acceleration.

**Vs siblings:** Pick spla over GraphBLAST or cuBool when you need non-Nvidia or integrated GPUs, or PageRank-heavy work. GraphBLAST is CUDA-only, and cuBool is CUDA-only and Boolean-only (cuBool comes from the same SparseLinearAlgebra organisation). GraphBLAST beats spla's PageRank on several graphs (belgium_osm, roadNet-CA, cit-Patents). For CPU-only or production GraphBLAS work, ALP/GraphBLAS or SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS are far more mature.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline chart compares a GTX 1070 GPU with LAGraph on a 4-core CPU. Compiler flags, LAGraph and SuiteSparse versions and thread counts are not given, and the harness for LAGraph, GraphBLAST and Gunrock is not in the repo; only spla's examples/ (bfs, sssp, pr, tc) are.
- The README text claims '1 BILLION edges ... without memory issues' and 'much faster than scipy or networkx', but no published numbers back either. The largest benchmarked graph has 302M edges (indochina-2004).
- OpenCL programs are built at first use (with -cl-std=CL1.2), so the first call of each operation and type combination pays a compile cost before the cache helps; exclude warm-up from timing.
- Not the same project as eth-cscs/spla (distributed GEMM), which is also catalogued; check the repo owner.

**Status:** Some activity (last commit 2025-11-17, 35 stars, 10 open issues, mostly feature requests) but self-described as not ready for use, with no releases beyond a 2022 pyspla 0.0.5. MIT-licensed, so research code is free to borrow.

[repo](https://github.com/SparseLinearAlgebra/spla) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SparseLinearAlgebra/spla)

##### SparseX (CSX-format SpMV library with LLVM runtime code generation)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Multicore CPU SpMV library: CSX compressed format plus LLVM-JIT kernels per matrix; claims parity-or-better vs Intel MKL CSR.

**Beats:** Intel MKL CSR SpMV (and pOSKI, ViennaCL in the TOMS paper) — No SparseX-versus-MKL numbers could be read from an opened page. Per search snippets, the TOMS 2018 abstract claims superior performance on large-scale problems and performance comparable to Intel MKL and ViennaCL. A third-party ICS 2025 paper (DIV, snippet only) says SparseX reliably speeds up SpMV on large matrices by a 13% median and 7.7% geometric mean; its baseline is presumably MKL CSR but is not stated in the snippet, and no hardware or compiler is given.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded to D: the 19.5x/1.6x vs MKL came from a different paper (arXiv 1711.05487, a CSR optimizer), not SparseX; the SparseX TOMS abstract only says 'comparable to MKL'.

**Known shortcoming:** configure.ac accepts only LLVM 4.0.0-6.0.0 (Clang-internal JIT) while the User's Guide says LLVM 3.0; issues #2 (Boost.atomic) and #4 (LLVM install) unresolved; public headers lack extern "C". No opened page shows SparseX vs MKL numbers. The same lab's DIV (ICS 2025, snippet) beats SparseX by 87% (Intel) and 100% (AMD) and MKL by 77% / 115%, and the same snippet puts SparseX at a 13% median, 7.7% geomean gain on large matrices.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** SpMV on CPUs is limited by memory bandwidth, and CSR spends one column index per nonzero. CSX (Compressed Sparse eXtended, PPoPP'11 / TPDS'13) detects dense substructures: horizontal, vertical, diagonal and anti-diagonal runs, row- and column-aligned blocks, and delta-encoded leftovers. It stores one short descriptor per substructure instead of per-element indices, which shrinks the index stream. For each matrix, the library fills C kernel templates for the patterns it chose (src/templates/*_tmpl.c), compiles them at runtime with the Clang frontend and LLVM MCJIT, and runs them on a pinned thread pool with NUMA-aware allocation. A symmetric variant (CSX-sym) stores only half the matrix, and optional Reverse Cuthill-McKee reordering improves locality.

**Use it when:**
- Iterative solvers (CG, GMRES, eigen-solvers) on one large sparse matrix that run thousands of SpMVs, so the one-off tuning and JIT cost is amortized; spx_mat_save/spx_mat_restore can skip re-tuning in later runs
- Matrices with regular dense substructure (FEM and structural meshes with blocks, diagonals or long row runs), where index compression cuts memory traffic the most
- Large symmetric matrices, where CSX-sym (spx.matrix.symmetric) halves the storage that has to be streamed
- Multi-socket NUMA Linux servers, where the library's thread pinning and NUMA placement do the tuning for you
- As a historical baseline in SpMV research: later papers (DIV, ICS 2025) still benchmark against it

**Skip it when:**
- One-shot or few SpMVs: the user's guide calls CSX preprocessing (substructure detection plus JIT compile) 'non-negligible' even with sampling
- Any current toolchain: configure.ac accepts only LLVM 4.0.0 to 6.0.0, the JIT uses Clang's internal C++ API (which the README says breaks with almost every LLVM release), and the last commit is from 2018. The two open issues (#2 Boost.atomic not found with Boost 1.58, #4 cannot install LLVM) have no fix
- Matrices whose sparsity pattern changes: after tuning, nonzeros cannot be inserted or deleted, only existing values updated through spx_mat_set_entry
- GPUs, Windows or macOS: CPU only, Linux only (futex wrapper, libnuma required)
- When a large margin over MKL is the goal: the only third-party figures found (DIV, ICS 2025, search snippet) put SparseX at a 13% median and 7.7% geometric-mean speedup on large matrices, and DIV reports 1.87x (Intel) and 2.0x (AMD) over SparseX

**Integration:** shared lib · LLVM/Clang 4.0.0-6.0.0 (linked, used at runtime for the JIT), Boost >= 1.48 (atomic, regex, serialization, system), libnuma >= 2.0.7, pthreads; optional Intel MKL or pOSKI for the bundled benchmark driver · gcc/g++ >= 4.8 plus LLVM/Clang 4.0.0-6.0.0 exactly (configure rejects other versions); autotools (autoreconf -vi) to build from git; JIT kernels are compiled as C99 · Linux on SMP and NUMA multicore CPUs; the JIT targets the host triple, and CPU architectures beyond an x86_64-specific fix in the ChangeLog are not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick SparseX over merge-spmv, CSR5 or CVR only when the matrix has strong block, diagonal or run structure (or is symmetric and large) and you can pin an old LLVM 4-6 toolchain. For irregular or scale-free matrices, CVR and merge-spmv report clearer wins over MKL, and SPC5 is the maintained block-kernel option for AVX-512 and ARM SVE.

**Gotchas:**
- The public headers read (sparsex.h, matvec.h, common.h, types.h) have no extern "C" guards; C++ callers must wrap the #include themselves (the cslab-ntua SpMV-Research wrapper notes undefined references otherwise)
- The JIT compiles C at runtime and needs the system C headers: set SPX_JIT_INC_PATH if they are in a non-standard location, and LD_LIBRARY_PATH for a non-standard install prefix
- The default thread count and affinity grab all cores with a share-nothing pinning policy, which can clash with an OpenMP or MPI application's own pinning; set spx.rt.nr_threads and spx.rt.cpu_affinity explicitly
- The bundled User's Guide still lists LLVM == 3.0, the README says >= 4.0, and configure.ac accepts only 4.0.0-6.0.0; trust configure.ac. Explicit zeros in the input are kept as logical nonzeros

**Status:** Abandoned since 2018-06-10, when the last change added LLVM 6 support; BSD-3-Clause and copyable, but expect to port the Clang-based JIT before it builds against any LLVM newer than 6.

[repo](https://github.com/cslab-ntua/sparsex) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3134442)

##### SPRAL SSIDS  `Fortran (with C interface; GPU build via CUDA)`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier D`

BSD-licensed multicore/GPU sparse symmetric indefinite LDL^T solver (SSIDS); paper claims beat HSL and PARDISO, unverified here.

**Beats:** Not verified from an opened page. Per search snippets only: the ACM TOMS 2016 GPU paper compares against 'a state-of-the-art multifrontal solver on a multicore CPU' (not named in the snippet); the Duff-Hogg-Lopez a-posteriori-threshold-pivoting paper (RAL-TR-2016-017 / NLAFET Working Note 21) compares SSIDS v2 with HSL_MA86, HSL_MA97 and PARDISO on a multicore machine. MUMPS is not named in either snippet. — No benchmark could be opened: the repo has no performance numbers and the papers are on blocked hosts. Search snippets say the TOMS 2016 paper reports up to 4.6x for large indefinite problems against an unnamed state-of-the-art multifrontal solver on a multicore CPU (GPU version), and the SISC 2020 APTP paper (42(2) C23-C42) compares SSIDS v2 with HSL_MA86, HSL_MA97 and PARDISO with no ratio in the snippet; an independent power-grid study (snippet) found GPU mode slower than CPU-only and than one-thread MA57. Treat speed as unverified (tier D).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the repo publishes no numbers. The TOMS 2016 paper (up to 4.6x vs an unnamed multicore CPU multifrontal solver) and the APTP paper (vs HSL_MA86, HSL_MA97, PARDISO) were blocked (centaur.reading.ac.uk, nlafet.eu, osti.gov) and seen only as snippets; retier candidate to B. An independent study (Swirydowicz, Parallel Computing) found SSIDS's GPU mode slower than its CPU mode and than single-thread MA57.

**Known shortcoming:** The solve phase is serial and the docs say the positive-definite path may trail a dedicated Cholesky. The default meson build adds no -march flags, so the AVX kernels are probably not compiled in (inferred from source, undocumented); a mismatched gpu_arch can silently give wrong results (meson.build comment). Open issues #218 (segfault on a large Ipopt problem, no reply), #223 (GPU tests fail on CUDA 12.5), #259 (memory leaks), #258 (aarch64-darwin test failure); Ipopt PR #677 (2023) ranked MUMPS above SPRAL as the default.

**Known shortcoming:** Tasseff et al. (arXiv 1909.08104, snippet only) rank SPRAL's GPU solver worst among Ipopt linear solvers, with MA57 and MUMPS best.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The assembly tree is cut into leaf subtrees that are pre-assigned to NUMA regions or GPUs and factored in parallel, after which all CPU cores cooperate on the root subtree (OpenMP tasks); small leaf subtrees below small_subtree_threshold (4e6 flops) are merged into one task to cut scheduling overhead. On CPU the default pivoting is block a posteriori threshold pivoting (APTP, Duff-Hogg-Lopez): blocks are eliminated optimistically with a Cholesky-like communication pattern and pivots that fail the threshold test afterwards only force recomputation of their block column, which keeps the factorization task-parallel where classic threshold partial pivoting is serial. Dense kernels are blocked (cpu_block_size 256, inner block 32) with AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 intrinsics in SimdVec.hxx plus BLAS/LAPACK; the GPU path (TOMS 2016 paper) runs subtrees of at least min_gpu_work (5e9 flops) in CUDA with cuBLAS.

**Use it when:**
- Large sparse symmetric indefinite systems (KKT and saddle-point matrices from interior-point optimization, mixed finite elements) on a multicore node where you need LDL^T with 2x2 pivoting and the inertia, under a BSD licence instead of HSL MA57/MA97 or MKL PARDISO terms.
- Ipopt or other C/C++ optimizers that want an open-source parallel alternative to MUMPS or MA27: Ipopt ships an interface (linear_solver=spral; Ipopt 3.14.13 needs SPRAL v2023.03.29 or later).
- Sequences of factorizations with a fixed sparsity pattern: analyse once and reuse akeep for many ssids_factor calls.
- Workflows that need run-to-run bit-identical results: the docs promise bit-compatibility given bit-compatible BLAS and compiler options.
- Very large problems on NVIDIA GPU nodes, where subtrees above 5e9 flops are offloaded (the paper's up to 4.6x claim is for large indefinite problems).

**Skip it when:**
- Small or medium KKT systems such as power-grid optimal power flow: an independent study (Swirydowicz et al., Parallel Computing, seen only as a snippet) found SSIDS's GPU mode slower than its CPU mode and slower than one-thread MA57, and Ipopt merged PR #677 (2023) 'Linear solvers such as MUMPS should be prefered over SPRAL' when choosing its default.
- Positive definite problems: the docs warn that SSIDS is designed for indefinite systems and its Cholesky path may be slower than a dedicated Cholesky solver (CHOLMOD, BaSpaCho).
- Solve-dominated workloads (many right-hand sides or many repeated solves per factorization): the docs state the solve phase runs in serial.
- Unsymmetric, complex or single-precision matrices, or distributed-memory (MPI) runs: SSIDS is real double symmetric only and the build has no MPI dependency.
- Windows, or host applications that cannot set OMP_CANCELLATION=TRUE process-wide: Windows support is an open question (issue #137), and without that variable SSIDS fails with error -53.

**Integration:** shared lib · BLAS, LAPACK, METIS (4 or 5, optional 64-bit idx), OpenMP; hwloc optional (topology detection; needs CUDA support for GPU use); CUDA 10+ with cuBLAS optional · Fortran compiler (gfortran, Intel ifx/ifort, NAG, NVIDIA HPC or LLVM flang) plus C99 and C++11 compilers; Meson 0.63+ · Linux x86-64 primarily (AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 kernels when compiled with those flags, scalar fallback otherwise); macOS handled in the build but issue #258 reports a test failure on aarch64-darwin; NVIDIA GPUs optional

**Vs siblings:** Most catalogued sparse direct siblings are LU solvers (Basker, NICSLU, CKTSO, HYLU, PanguLU) or Cholesky-only (BaSpaCho, Sympiler); pick SPRAL SSIDS when the matrix is symmetric indefinite and you need 2x2 pivoting plus inertia under BSD with optional GPU offload. RSLAB (Rust LDL^T) has measured numbers against PARDISO but is Rust; for SPD problems BaSpaCho's measured wins over CHOLMOD are the better bet.

**Gotchas:**
- Set OMP_CANCELLATION=TRUE and OMP_PROC_BIND=TRUE in the environment before the OpenMP runtime starts, or factorization returns error -53 (cancellation) or warning +50 (binding); these are process-wide settings that also affect the host application.
- meson.build adds no -m flags, and SimdVec.hxx uses AVX intrinsics only under __AVX__/__AVX2__/__AVX512F__, so a default build runs the scalar kernels; pass e.g. -Dcpp_args=-march=native (inference from the source; not documented). For GPU builds set -Dgpu_arch to the card's sm_XX: meson.build warns a mismatched JIT-compiled arch can silently produce wrong results.
- ssids_free must be called explicitly (going out of scope leaks C++/CUDA memory, and akeep must outlive its fkeeps); open issues include memory leaks (#259), a segfault in assemble_expected_contrib on a large Ipopt problem with 5.7M Hessian nonzeros (#218, no maintainer reply) and GPU test failures with CUDA 12.5 (#223).
- Ipopt's ChangeLog records a use-after-free in its SPRAL interface when solving a second structurally singular system (fixed in Ipopt 3.14.20, 2026-08-27, PR #848), so use Ipopt 3.14.20 or later if you go through it.

**Status:** Active (version 2025.09.18 in meson.build, last commit 2026-08-14, 142 stars, 19 open issues including an unanswered large-problem segfault), BSD-3-Clause and maintained by STFC's numerical analysis group; a mixed Fortran/C++/CUDA build with external METIS and BLAS, so not something to vendor casually.

[repo](https://github.com/ralna/spral)

##### SyLVER (NLAFET)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Research StarPU task-based sparse Cholesky/LDL^T solver built on SPRAL SSIDS kernels; no published speedup in the repo.

**Beats:** SPRAL SSIDS / HSL MA87 / PARDISO (no comparison found in the repo) — The repo has no measured result: the README and doc pages only say the DAG algorithms 'enable an efficient exploitation of multicore CPU architectures and GPU-accelerated systems'. The related NLAFET papers (SpLLT vs HSL MA87 on 28 cores, reported only as 'comparable performance'; SSIDS v2 APTP vs MA86/MA97/PARDISO, 'performs favourably') were seen as search snippets only, because nlafet.eu, researchgate and epubs.stfc.ac.uk are blocked here, and they measure sibling codes, not SyLVER.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: no numbers anywhere (README, docs, drivers; nlafet.eu blocked); StarPU-based successor of SPRAL SSIDS, 13 stars, abandoned 2020-05-11.

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #2 (2020, unanswered): L and D cannot be extracted. Coupled to SPRAL internal headers through a submodule pinned at f71ab9e (branch gpufix); the splu path is undocumented. NLAFET working notes and RAL-TR-2016-017 (nlafet.eu, epubs.stfc.ac.uk blocked) unread.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The multifrontal factorization is written as a sequential task flow: fronts are split into blocks (block size nb), and each block operation is submitted as a task to StarPU, which builds the DAG and schedules it across CPU cores and, optionally, NVIDIA GPUs (lws or heteroprio schedulers). Indefinite factorization uses A Posteriori Threshold Pivoting (APTP), which factors blocks optimistically and checks stability afterwards, so pivoting does not serialise the column sweep; failed pivots are delayed or redone with TPP. This is the method of Duff-Hogg-Lopez (NLAFET Working Note 21 / SSIDS v2), which per search snippets performs favourably against HSL MA86, HSL MA97 and PARDISO on multicore, but those numbers are for SSIDS, not for this repo.

**Use it when:**
- Research on runtime-system (StarPU) scheduling of sparse direct solvers, as a worked example of an STF multifrontal Cholesky/LDL^T on CPU+GPU nodes.
- Studying or reproducing NLAFET-era APTP and heterogeneous-scheduling results where you need the StarPU variant of SSIDS rather than the OpenMP one.
- Large symmetric indefinite systems on one multicore node with optional NVIDIA GPUs, when you already run StarPU and SPRAL and can tolerate prototype code.

**Skip it when:**
- Production solves: the last commit was 2020-05-11, there are no releases, CI was Travis, and no benchmarks or regression results are published; use SPRAL SSIDS, MUMPS, PARDISO or CHOLMOD instead.
- When you need the factors: open issue #2 (March 2020, unanswered) reports that L and D cannot be obtained from spldlt_factorize().
- Unsymmetric systems: the splu path is commented out of the documentation and has no driver beyond splu_test.F90.
- Simple builds: it needs StarPU >= 1.3, a SPRAL submodule pinned to commit f71ab9e (branch 'gpufix'), MeTiS, hwloc, a sequential BLAS/LAPACK, and Fortran, C and C++ compilers, plus CUDA for GPU runs.
- Distributed-memory (MPI) runs: nothing in the README or CMake options offers them.

**Integration:** static lib · StarPU >= 1.3 (or sequential STF runtime), SPRAL (git submodule, built automatically), MeTiS, hwloc, sequential BLAS/LAPACK (MKL/ESSL/OpenBLAS); optional CUDA, CUTLASS, OpenMP · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), Fortran 2003 compiler, CMake; CUDA toolkit for GPU builds · Linux x86-64 and IBM POWER (ESSL recommended there) are implied by the README; NVIDIA GPUs optional; other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Choose SPRAL SSIDS, which carries the same APTP kernels in a maintained OpenMP/CUDA library with published comparisons, for real solves; pick SyLVER only to study or extend the StarPU task-based variant. For SPD-only problems with published speedups over CHOLMOD, BaSpaCho or Sympiler are better documented.

**Gotchas:**
- It must be linked against a sequential BLAS/LAPACK (README); a threaded BLAS oversubscribes cores under StarPU.
- It includes SPRAL's internal C++ headers (ssids/cpu/cpu_iface.hxx, ThreadStats.hxx), so it is coupled to the pinned SPRAL submodule commit; building against a current SPRAL release is not documented and may break.
- STARPU_DIR must be set in the environment for FindSTARPU.cmake, and the default runtime is StarPU, so a plain cmake without StarPU fails unless you pass -D SYLVER_RUNTIME=STF.
- The docs claim bit-compatible results, but no test evidence for that is in the repo.

**Status:** Abandoned since May 2020 (EU H2020 NLAFET project ended), with 844 commits, 13 stars and one unanswered issue; BSD-3-Clause so copyable, but a research prototype with heavy dependencies.

[repo](https://github.com/NLAFET/SyLVER) · [benchmark](https://github.com/NLAFET/SyLVER)

### parsing-and-text

#### csv-tabular

##### cisv  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

SIMD-accelerated C CSV parser/writer (AVX-512/AVX2) beating csvkit and PapaParse; monorepo now deprecated.

**Beats:** csvkit — Author's blog, built with -O3 -march=native -mavx512f -mavx512bw on an unspecified Intel Core i9, reports CLI row-counting of a 1M-row/98MB CSV: miller 0.004s, cisv 0.055s, wc -l 0.083s, rust-csv 0.664s, csvkit 9.788s (~178x over csvkit, but ~14x slower than miller in the same table). Separately, Node.js synchronous parsing measured cisv at 60.80 MB/s vs PapaParse 25.12 MB/s (~2.4x) and csv-parse 14.67 MB/s.

**Known shortcoming:** Upstream marks this monorepo deprecated in favour of split cisv-core / cisv-cli / language-binding repos; the benchmark measures CLI row counting, not full parsing.

**How:** Vectorized byte scanning for delimiters/quotes/newlines using AVX-512 mask compares (or AVX2/SSE2 movemask + ctz, ARM NEON fallback) instead of a byte-at-a-time state machine. Input files are zero-copy memory-mapped with kernel read-ahead hints and read through an L3-sized ring buffer. A chunk-splitting API (mmap + split-at-row-boundaries) enables multi-threaded parallel parsing, described in the header as a '1 Billion Row Challenge technique'.

**Use it when:**
- Row-counting or bulk parsing of large CSVs on x86-64 with AVX-512 or AVX2 available
- Embedding a small C parser/writer directly into a C/C++ codebase rather than shelling out to a Python tool
- Node.js/Python/PHP apps that need faster synchronous CSV parsing than PapaParse/csv-parse for one-shot batch jobs
- Workloads needing early-exit row iteration (stop after N matching rows) without loading the whole file
- Multi-core boxes where parallel chunked parsing of one large file is worth the added complexity

**Skip it when:**
- Production systems: the whole monorepo is archived/deprecated by its own author, moved to separate cisv-core/cisv-cli/bindings repos with unclear activity
- CPUs without AVX2/AVX-512 (older x86, some cloud instance types) — falls back to SSE2/NEON/scalar with speed not benchmarked
- Anywhere `miller` is an option: the author's own table shows miller ~14x faster than cisv on the same 1M-row count
- Windows — unsupported (README lists it as 'planned... maybe')
- Teams needing a mature, community-supported CSV toolkit rather than a single-author experimental project (91 stars, author calls it 'still evolving')

**Integration:** source-drop / static lib (CMake or Makefile build) plus separate Node.js/Python/PHP native bindings · none for core C library; Node.js 14+, Python 3.7+, or PHP 7.4+ toolchains for the respective bindings · GCC 7+ or Clang 6+, CMake 3.14+ · x86-64 (AVX-512 or AVX2 preferred, SSE2 fallback), ARM64/NEON; Linux and macOS only, no Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick cisv only for a minimal, vendorable C library/CLI using raw SIMD intrinsics with no dependencies; zsv (same category) does the same mmap+SIMD row-counting approach but is faster in its own benchmarks, more actively maintained, and has broader language coverage, so prefer zsv unless you specifically want cisv's smaller C surface.

**Gotchas:**
- Repo is marked DEPRECATED in its own README; code has moved to split repos (cisv-core, cisv-cli, cisv-nodejs, cisv-python, cisv-php)
- Peak throughput requires AVX-512; on AVX2/SSE2/NEON hardware speed is unverified
- Author states the code changed during writing of the benchmark blog post, so published numbers may not match current source
- Row iterator's returned field pointers are only valid until the next call — no copy-out API mentioned for retention

**Status:** Abandoned/archived, and the monorepo itself declares itself deprecated in favor of split successor repos; MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but pick a maintained fork or successor repo before depending on it.

[repo](https://github.com/sanix-darker/cisv) · [benchmark](https://sanixdk.xyz/blogs/how-i-accidentally-created-the-fastest-csv-parser-ever-made)

##### DuckDB (CSV reader)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

In-process OLAP SQL engine that queries CSV files directly, beating pandas read_csv + groupby on large files.

**Beats:** pandas read_csv — A third-party, DuckDB-unaffiliated blog (duckdblab.org) reports that on one Ryzen 9 7950X / 64GB DDR5 / NVMe machine, DuckDB SQL run directly over a synthetic ~8GB/50M-row Nginx access-log CSV (date parsing, group-by status code, percentile calc) took ~3.8s and ~380MB RAM, versus a naive `pd.read_csv` + groupby at ~180s and ~4.2GB RAM — about 47x faster and 90% less memory. DuckDB was 'v1.5.x plus some v2.0 Preview features'; pandas version, compiler flags, and a benchmark script were not published.

**How:** It uses a vectorized, columnar execution engine (operates on batches of values rather than row-by-row Python objects) combined with a multi-threaded CSV scanner that reads and parses chunks of the file in parallel (`parallel=true` by default). A CSV "sniffer" auto-detects delimiter, quoting, header, and column types from a sample of the file before the full parallel scan, and query operators (filter/group-by/projection) push down into the scan instead of materializing the whole table first, which is what keeps memory low relative to a full `pd.read_csv` load.

**Use it when:**
- Query, filter, join, or aggregate CSV data larger than comfortably fits in a pandas DataFrame (tens of millions of rows / multi-GB files) without hand-writing chunked pandas code
- The workload is naturally SQL-shaped: group-bys, window functions, percentiles, or joins across multiple CSV/Parquet files
- You want to query CSV/Parquet (including gzip-compressed CSV) in place without a separate ETL/load step
- Single-machine job where you want multi-core throughput on the read+aggregate path without standing up Spark/Dask
- You already use pandas/Polars downstream and just want DuckDB as an accelerator for ingest+aggregate, then hand results back as a DataFrame

**Skip it when:**
- Pure scanning/row-counting/field-extraction with no aggregation — sibling tools like zsv and xan are reported to beat DuckDB's own CSV reader on those tasks
- Team is committed to pandas' imperative, method-chaining style and can't adopt SQL or a relational API
- CSV has very long lines/fields beyond the default 2MB max_line_size, or wildly inconsistent schemas across many files, without tuning the sniffer (max_line_size, sample_size, files_to_sniff)
- You need guaranteed constant memory regardless of input method: memory behavior currently differs between reading by filename (streams) and reading CSV via a pipe/stdin with the same query (open GH issue #25165 as of Sept 2026)
- Columns contain long numeric IDs — the sniffer has been reported to infer these as DOUBLE instead of HUGEINT/VARCHAR, silently losing precision unless types are pinned explicitly

**Integration:** shared lib / static lib / source-drop (single-file amalgamation) / language packages (pip, npm, etc.) · none required to build the core (vendors what it needs); optional extensions may pull their own deps · C++17-compliant compiler, CMake, Python 3 (build-time only, per README) · x86-64 and aarch64 on Linux/macOS/Windows, plus WebAssembly (DuckDB-Wasm) via language clients

**Vs siblings:** Pick DuckDB when the job is more than parsing — joins, group-bys, window functions, or percentiles across one or more CSV/Parquet files in a single SQL statement. For pure scanning, row-counting, or field extraction, siblings like zsv and xan are reported faster than DuckDB's own CSV reader and are lighter-weight if a full SQL engine isn't needed.

**Gotchas:**
- CSV type sniffer reported to infer long numeric ID columns as DOUBLE instead of HUGEINT/VARCHAR, causing precision loss unless column types are pinned explicitly (GH #22750, closed)
- Memory profile isn't uniform across input methods: reading a named CSV file streams in near-constant memory, but reading CSV from a pipe/stdin with the same query has been reported to retain the full projected columns in memory (GH #25165, open)
- Default max_line_size is 2,000,000 bytes and the sniffer samples a bounded prefix by default — very long lines or unusual multi-file schemas may need manual max_line_size/sample_size/files_to_sniff tuning
- The parallel CSV reader has had past correctness bugs combining ignore_errors=true with specific internal vector-size builds (GH #7755, closed) — the multi-threaded CSV path is intricate enough that staying on a current release matters

**Status:** Actively developed (repo pushed within the last day of this review, current dev branch v2.0-cyanoptera, 41.7k stars, MIT-licensed) with prebuilt packages for most languages and platforms — no maintenance risk; 'copyable' here just means querying a CSV via DuckDB is a few lines of SQL, not that DuckDB's own source is meant to be vendored.

[repo](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb) · [benchmark](https://duckdblab.org/en/post/duckdb-large-file-processing/)

##### Polars  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust DataFrame engine with lazy query optimization and SIMD execution; ~45x faster CSV writing than pandas.

**Beats:** pandas (CSV write path; independent benchmarks separately report CSV read speedups) — An official Polars blog post benchmarked reading 15 Parquet files (~800MB, NYC Yellow Tripdata) and writing the result to CSV on a MacBook Pro M3 (24GB RAM): Polars 0.20.30 is reported ~45x faster than pandas and ~3.5x faster than pyarrow on the CSV write step (ratios read from plots, no absolute pandas/pyarrow times or benchmark code given), and 0.20.30 itself is ~40% faster than 0.20.19 (8.975s vs 14.684s) due to PR #15576's per-datatype serializer.

**How:** The core engine is multi-threaded and vectorized (SIMD) over Arrow's columnar memory layout, with a lazy execution mode whose query optimizer applies predicate/projection pushdown so only needed data is read and computed. The specific CSV-writer speedup (0.20.19 to 0.20.30) came from PR #15576, which replaced generic per-value serialization with a dedicated serializer per datatype, cutting function-call overhead and type conversions during writing.

**Use it when:**
- Reading/writing large Parquet or CSV files (hundreds of MB to multi-GB) where pandas' single-threaded loops bottleneck
- Datasets larger than RAM, using the streaming engine (`collect(engine='streaming')`)
- Multi-core machines where a query (joins, group-by, filters) can be parallelized across threads and columns
- Teams willing to adopt the expression/lazy API instead of pandas indexing semantics
- Multi-language pipelines (Python/Rust/Node/R) that want to share Arrow memory zero-copy

**Skip it when:**
- Codebases tightly coupled to pandas' `.loc`/`.iloc`/index-based API - migrating is real engineering work, not a swap
- Row counts above ~4.2 billion (2^32) - the default build uses 32-bit indexing and needs a bigidx build
- Pre-2011 CPUs or CPUs without AVX2 - the default release build targets modern instruction sets; use the `LTS_CPU=1` build instead
- x86-64 Python installs running under Rosetta on Apple Silicon need special install handling per the docs
- Treating the 45x/3.5x numbers as proof of CSV *read* speed - this benchmark measures a Parquet-read + CSV-write pipeline on a first-party blog post with no published benchmark code or build flags, and pandas/pyarrow figures come from plots, not stated absolute times

**Integration:** crate (Rust workspace of polars-* crates) + prebuilt Python wheel / Node package / R package · none required beyond the language runtime for prebuilt packages; internally vendors its own Arrow implementation (polars-arrow) rather than depending on the reference Arrow crate · Rust edition 2024 (recent rustc, e.g. 1.85+) for building from source; Python >=3.10 for py-polars · x86-64 (AVX2 assumed by default release build; LTS_CPU=1 build for older CPUs), aarch64; optional NVIDIA GPU acceleration for query execution

**Vs siblings:** Most siblings in this category (xan, cisv, qsv, zsv, Sep, go-simdcsv, simd-csv, vroom, zsv-ruby) are single-purpose CSV parsers; DuckDB is the closest comparable full engine. Pick Polars when you need a full DataFrame/query engine (joins, group-by, lazy optimization, larger-than-RAM streaming) and are migrating off pandas, not just parsing CSV as fast as possible — for pure CSV-read throughput, a dedicated parser like zsv/qsv/DuckDB is the better-evidenced choice since this benchmark only covers Polars' CSV write path.

**Gotchas:**
- Default release binaries assume AVX2; pre-2011 CPUs need the separate LTS_CPU=1 build
- Default build indexes rows with 32-bit integers, capping datasets at ~4.2 billion (2^32) rows without a bigidx build
- Apple Silicon users running an x86-64 Python build under Rosetta need special installation handling (per the install guide)
- The quoted 45x/3.5x figures come from a plot in a first-party blog post with no benchmark code or build flags published, and measure Parquet-read+CSV-write, not a pure CSV-read microbenchmark

**Status:** Actively maintained — pushed to today, 39,859 stars, ~2,930 open issues on a large fast-moving repo; MIT-licensed and installable via `pip install polars` / `cargo add polars`, so vendoring is unnecessary.

[repo](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars) · [benchmark](https://pola.rs/posts/polars-in-aggregate-jun24/)

##### qsv  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

CLI data-wrangling toolkit that computes CSV summary stats far faster than pandas describe, no DataFrame required.

**Beats:** pandas read_csv / pandas .describe()-style stats — On a 124MB, 2.7M-row CSV, qsv's default `stats` finished in under 0.16s versus pandas computing comparable stats in 12s (75x faster), and `stats --everything` (48 measures) took 2s (6x faster); these are the maintainer's own numbers from an April 28, 2022 GitHub Discussion post, with no hardware or compiler flags disclosed for that specific comparison (a separate footnote's 22.4s/Ryzen 7 4800H figure is for a different, larger NYC-311 run with no pandas comparison).

**How:** `stats` streams the file once and computes its default statistic set (sum, min/max, mean, stddev, sparsity, etc.) in constant memory instead of materializing a DataFrame, and it multithreads per-column work once a `qsv index` (.idx) exists for the file. The non-streaming statistics that need the whole dataset (median, quartiles, mode, cardinality) use a memory-aware chunking algorithm rather than a naive full load. `stats` also assumes the CSV is well-formed and UTF-8, letting it skip repeated UTF-8 validation and bounds checks that a general-purpose parser like pandas' would perform.

**Use it when:**
- One-off or scripted CSV summary stats / type inference from shell pipelines, Makefiles, or CI, without spinning up Python or pandas.
- You can build a `qsv index` for the file first (or set QSV_AUTOINDEX_SIZE) to unlock multithreaded stats, frequency, split, and instant count/slice/sample.
- You need guaranteed, deterministic type inference per column rather than pandas' best-effort dtype guessing.
- Large CSVs (hundreds of MB to tens of GB) where you want the default 'streaming' stats in constant memory rather than a full in-memory DataFrame.
- Batch/ETL contexts where a standalone compiled CLI (or its MCP server) is an acceptable dependency.

**Skip it when:**
- You need the result as an in-memory DataFrame/array for further Python computation — qsv emits CSV/JSON text, not a DataFrame object.
- Your CSVs are malformed or non-UTF-8: `stats` explicitly assumes well-formed, valid UTF-8 input and warns of undefined behavior otherwise; run `qsv validate` first.
- You need the full 48-statistic 'advanced' set (median, quartiles, mode, cardinality) on very large files without accepting an extra chunked, higher-memory pass.
- Team is Python-only and can't add a separate compiled binary/CLI step to the pipeline.
- You want a reproducible, modern-hardware performance claim: the 75x/6x numbers are from an April 2022 maintainer GitHub Discussion post, not a benchmark suite, with no hardware or compiler flags given for that specific run.

**Integration:** source-drop · none for prebuilt binaries; building from source pulls in many optional, feature-gated crates (Polars, DuckDB-backed commands, Luau, geocoding databases, etc.) — the project's Cargo.toml notes `cargo install qsv` from crates.io is not currently supported · Rust 1.98 (edition 2024), per Cargo.toml and the README badge · Linux (x86_64 GNU/musl, aarch64 GNU), macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows (x86_64 MSVC, aarch64), plus IBM Power (PowerPC64 LE) and IBM Z (s390x); prebuilt x86_64 binaries deliberately skip CPU-specific optimizations to avoid SIGILL faults across CPU variants

**Vs siblings:** Pick qsv over xan, zsv, or DuckDB's CSV reader when you want one CLI with dozens of built-in wrangling verbs (join, dedupe, geocode, schema/JSON-Schema inference, Polars-backed SQL) beyond just fast parsing or stats. Pick zsv or xan instead when raw parse/read throughput is the goal — zsv's own darwin-arm64 shootout benchmarks it directly against qsv (and xsv, xan) and shows it ahead on parsing speed.

**Gotchas:**
- `stats` assumes a well-formed, UTF-8 CSV and skips validation for speed; malformed input is explicitly undefined behavior — run `qsv validate` first if unsure.
- Multithreading, instant `count`/`slice`/`sample`, and faster `stats`/`frequency`/`schema`/`split` only kick in once you build a `qsv index`; without one, stats runs single-threaded and streaming.
- Only the default 'streaming' statistics run in constant memory; median, quartiles, mode/antimode, and cardinality require loading more data (via a memory-aware chunker, not the naive whole file) and must be enabled explicitly (e.g. `--everything`).
- GitHub's UI reports the license as NOASSERTION; the repo's own LICENSE-MIT, COPYING, and Cargo.toml confirm MIT-only licensing since v21.1.1 (dual MIT/Unlicense in v21.1.1 and earlier).

**Status:** Actively maintained (commits as recently as today) and MIT-licensed since v21.1.1; ships as prebuilt binaries for all major OS/arch combinations or builds from a Rust 1.98 source tree, making it straightforward to vendor as a standalone CLI tool.

[repo](https://github.com/dathere/qsv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dathere/datapusher-plus/discussions/15)

##### simd-csv (Rust crate)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

SIMD-accelerated Rust CSV reader/writer family beating the csv crate on throughput, gains data-dependent.

**Beats:** csv crate (docs.rs/csv, i.e. BurntSushi/rust-csv, the de facto standard Rust CSV library) — First-party README table compares simd-csv's three reader modes (Splitter/split, ZeroCopyReader/zero_copy, Reader/copy) against the docs.rs `csv` crate (v1.3.1 in dev-dependencies) parsing 10 files (100MB-11GB) streamed from SSD on x86_64 with AVX2, no CPU model given. Reported gains range from ~1.0x on worst-case.csv (100MB, split mode) up to ~6.0x on tweets.csv (6.5GB, split mode), with most files in the ~1.5-4.8x range and quote-heavy/low-entropy files (quote-always.csv, range.csv) near 1.0-1.4x.

**How:** Hybrid design: a traditional state machine for CSV structure, combined with memchr-style SIMD string searching for structural characters (comma, newline, quote) instead of byte-by-byte scanning. Unquoted runs use an amortized move-mask scan that reuses a mask across multiple matches instead of restarting per match; quoted runs instead use memchr's unrolled routines directly, because the authors found wider AVX2 registers hurt performance there. ByteRecord stores fields as ranges over the raw byte slice (rather than pure offsets) so the copying Reader can copy large runs of unquoted bytes at once instead of field-by-field.

**Use it when:**
- Large CSV/TSV files (hundreds of MB to multi-GB) streamed from disk where parse throughput matters
- Data with large records/cells and mostly non-quoted content (README: bigger cells/records give bigger wins)
- Just need record or line counts / positions: Splitter or LineReader avoid cell-level work entirely
- x86_64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX2 auto-detected), aarch64 (NEON), or wasm (simd128) targets
- Willing to depend on a young Rust crate (memchr as only hard dependency) and adapt to a non-csv-crate API

**Skip it when:**
- QUOTE_ALWAYS-style or heavily-quoted data, or single-column/short-cell data: gains shrink to ~1.0-1.4x (quote-always.csv, range.csv, worst-case.csv)
- Need the csv crate's full feature set, serde integration, or maximum flexibility/ergonomics
- CSV with lone-CR (old Mac style) line endings: only CRLF and LF are recognized, and leading CR bytes are silently trimmed
- Data where fields may contain a stray opening quote mid-field: the parser has no 'beginning of field' concept and can merge/misalign subsequent fields
- Risk-averse production use of a 19-star, single-maintainer crate not yet used outside its own xan CLI ecosystem

**Integration:** crate · memchr 2.7.6 (required); simdutf8 0.1.5 (optional, only for the `str` feature) · Rust 1.81.0 (pinned in rust-toolchain.toml), edition 2021 · x86_64 (SSE2 always, AVX2 via runtime detection), aarch64 (NEON), wasm (simd128), scalar/SWAR fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Use simd-csv over the plain csv crate when writing Rust code that streams large, mostly-unquoted CSV/TSV from disk and you can tolerate its lower-level, non-drop-in API; use its sibling xan instead if you just want a ready-made CLI (xan is built by the same authors for the same use case) rather than a library to embed. The other siblings (go-simdcsv, Sep, zsv, cisv, zsv-ruby) target Go, .NET, C, Node and Ruby respectively and aren't relevant unless leaving the Rust ecosystem.

**Gotchas:**
- Mid-field opening quotes can corrupt output: the parser has no 'beginning of field' state, so quotes anywhere except a field's true start can merge subsequent fields/rows
- Only CRLF and LF line terminators are handled; lone CR is not, and leading CR characters are trimmed from record starts as a documented tradeoff
- In single-column CSV, an empty cell must be written as a quoted empty string ("") — an unquoted blank line is treated as a skipped empty line, not an empty record
- Wider AVX2 registers are deliberately avoided for unquoted-data scanning because the authors measured them as slower than the amortized memchr approach used

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-16, steady stream of open enhancement issues, no open bug-tagged issues found) but a tiny, single-maintainer project (19 stars); MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor/copy if the dependency risk is a concern.

[repo](https://github.com/medialab/simd-csv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/medialab/simd-csv#regarding-performance)

##### vroom  `R`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Lazy, ALTREP-backed delimited-file reader for R; indexes then reads on demand, beating base R's read.delim/readr/data.table.

**Beats:** R base read.delim (utils) — On a real 1.53GB/14.7M-row/11-column taxi-trip CSV, the tidyverse blog table reports vroom reading in 3.6s versus base R read.delim's 1m21.5s (~22.6x), and a full read+print+head+tail+sample+filter+summarise workflow at 7s versus 1m22.6s (~11.8x); the post gives no CPU or compiler flags. A newer benchmarks vignette (vroom 1.5.1, public code in inst/bench/taxi, EC2 m5.4xlarge/16 vCPUs) shows read.delim at 1m12.3s versus vroom 1.3s to read, still without compiler flags.

**How:** Memory-maps the input file (bundled mio C++ library) and scans it with multiple threads to build a byte-offset index of every delimited field, so no value is parsed before it's needed. Returned columns are R ALTREP objects (character columns lazy by default) that convert raw bytes to R values only on access; non-character materialization and file writing also run multi-threaded, and grisu3 provides fast double-to-string formatting when writing.

**Use it when:**
- Large local, uncompressed CSV/TSV/FWF files (hundreds of MB to multi-GB) read directly from disk, where memory-mapping applies
- Pipelines that only touch a subset of rows/columns after loading (select/filter before printing or string ops), so lazy character materialization pays off
- Existing readr users who want a faster, largely drop-in replacement without rewriting column-spec code
- Writing large delimited files, where parallel formatting plus async write beats base R's write functions
- R >= 4.1 environments, where ALTREP is fully supported by the runtime

**Skip it when:**
- Small files, where indexing overhead and R startup cost dominate and base read.delim/readr are already fast enough
- Workflows that immediately print, filter, or string-process every character column, since that forces materialization and shifts most of the 'read' cost to first access, hiding behind read-time-only benchmarks
- Remote or compressed sources (.gz/.bz2/.xz/.zip): vroom downloads to a temp file before mapping it, losing the mmap/lazy advantage
- Contexts needing embedded newlines inside quoted headers/fields, which force num_threads = 1 and remove the multi-threaded indexing speedup
- Situations requiring reproducible cross-hardware speedup numbers: the cited benchmarks give no compiler flags, and only the newer vignette names a CPU (EC2 m5.4xlarge)

**Integration:** module · R packages bit64, cli, glue, hms, lifecycle, rlang, tibble, tidyselect, tzdb, vctrs, withr (Imports); cpp11, progress, tzdb (LinkingTo, compile-time); bundled mio (header-only C++ mmap library) · R >= 4.1 (Depends, needed for full ALTREP support); C++ compiler to build from source (CRAN also ships binaries) · any platform R runs on (Windows/macOS/Linux, x86-64/aarch64) via mio's cross-platform mmap wrapper

**Vs siblings:** All catalogued siblings target C/Go/Rust/.NET/Ruby/Python CSV stacks; vroom is the only R-ecosystem entry, so pick it whenever the pipeline is already in R and you want readr-compatible syntax — its speed claim is against base R's read.delim, not against any sibling's baseline, so it isn't a substitute for those language-specific choices.

**Gotchas:**
- Only character columns use ALTREP lazy loading by default (VROOM_USE_ALTREP_CHR=true); numeric/integer/date ALTREP is opt-in via separate env vars, so headline read-time numbers can hide deferred character-materialization cost
- Reading from R connections or compressed/remote files downloads to a temp file first, forfeiting the mmap-based lazy-read advantage
- Embedded newlines inside quoted headers or fields require num_threads = 1, disabling the multi-threaded indexing that produces most of the speedup
- Repository moved from r-lib/vroom to tidyverse/vroom in April 2022; the r-lib URL still resolves via GitHub's redirect

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-06-09, current CRAN release 1.7.1, part of the core tidyverse); MIT-licensed (DESCRIPTION and LICENSE.md) and simple to depend on via CRAN or pak, despite GitHub's NOASSERTION license auto-detection.

[repo](https://github.com/r-lib/vroom) · [benchmark](https://tidyverse.org/blog/2019/05/vroom-1-0-0/)

##### xan  `Rust`  `Unlicense`  `active`  `Tier C`

CLI CSV toolkit with a SIMD parser and built-in expression language; faster single-threaded select than xsv, Polars, DuckDB.

**Beats:** BurntSushi/xsv and Python Polars/DuckDB CSV readers (independent comparison; xan itself targets csvkit-style CSV toolkits) — On zsv's own darwin-arm64 shootout (Apple M3 Pro, xan 0.54.1, csv crate-based xsv as baseline, 500000x20-row unquoted/sparse-quoted data, best-of-5), xan's `select` ran 0.077s/0.081s versus xsv's 0.189s/0.195s (~2.4x), beating single-threaded Polars (0.410s/0.408s) and default DuckDB v0.10.2 (0.110s/0.105s), but losing to zsv fast/compat in --parallel mode and to DuckDB with QUOTE='' on sparse-quoted data; the xan binary's compiler flags are not stated.

**How:** Core parsing goes through medialab/simd-csv, a separate SIMD-accelerated CSV parser crate, instead of a byte-at-a-time scalar reader like the csv crate xsv uses. Selected commands (e.g. the `parallel` subcommand and some stats/aggregation paths) multithread across cores. The moonblade expression language is evaluated directly by xan rather than by invoking an external scripting interpreter, cutting subprocess/interpreter overhead for row transforms.

**Use it when:**
- Ad hoc CLI exploration and filtering of large (GB-TB) CSV files where you'd otherwise reach for xsv or csvkit
- Unquoted or sparsely-quoted CSV where single-threaded select/count throughput matters (fastest single-threaded tool in the zsv shootout)
- Want stats, join, dedup, pivot, and format conversion in one CLI without leaving the shell for pandas/DuckDB
- Converting CSV to/from JSON, ndjson, Excel, Parquet, or numpy from the command line
- Already scripting with xsv and want a faster, more feature-rich drop-in CLI replacement

**Skip it when:**
- Need an embeddable Rust/Python library rather than a CLI binary; not documented as an embeddable API (use simd-csv or the csv crate directly instead)
- Data contains nonstandard-quoted CSV; xan produces incorrect output there per the wave3 verification pass
- Need the single fastest option regardless of thread count: zsv fast/compat with --parallel and DuckDB with QUOTE='' beat xan on the same benchmark
- Need a build with documented, reproducible compiler flags; the benchmarked xan binary's flags are unstated (evidence tier C)
- Want a minimal, small dependency footprint; xan bundles 60+ crates including Excel, Parquet, HTML, and Markdown parsers

**Integration:** crate (binary via cargo install; not designed as an embeddable library) · 60+ crates, including ahash, aho-corasick, csv, calamine (Excel), comrak (Markdown), docopt, jiff, and medialab/simd-csv for the fast CSV path · Rust 1.88.0, edition 2024 (per Cargo.toml) · x86_64 (Linux gnu/musl, macOS, Windows msvc), aarch64 (macOS, Linux gnu); ppc64le only via unofficial conda-forge build, not CI-built
