- Want CI confidence out of the box — an open 'Build fail' issue (#2) shows the bench/test build breaking against a newer clang/CMake/googlebenchmark combination

**Integration:** static lib · cpu_features (Google, ISA detection), fmt; googlebenchmark and googletest additionally for bench/tests only · C++20 (CMakeLists sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20), CMake 3.24+; clang recommended by the README, GCC also handled in CMakeLists · x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512 (ISA chosen per template instantiation at compile time); AArch64/NEON detection is present in demo.cpp but the sort call is unimplemented

**Vs siblings:** Pick this only if you specifically want an AVX2/AVX-512 partition-plus-bitonic-network vectorized quicksort port of .NET's VxSort for raw numeric arrays and don't need comparator/generic-type support; x86-simd-sort, BlockQuicksort, quadsort, and fluxsort all publish real std::sort or std::stable_sort comparisons and are more actively maintained, so prefer one of them when the baseline claim matters or adoption/maintenance risk is a concern.

**Gotchas:**
- ISA is selected at compile time via which header you include (vxsort.avx2.h vs vxsort.avx512.h) and the vxsort_targets_enable_*.h wrapper; using the wrong one for the running CPU is a caller error (the demo does its own cpu_features runtime check before choosing)
- Only built-in numeric types appear in the benchmark/test suite (i16/u16/i32/u32/f32/i64/u64/f64); no evidence of support for arbitrary structs, strings, or custom comparators
- Internally falls back to heap_sort past a depth limit and to a bitonic-network small-sort under 1024 elements — behavior isn't a single flat algorithm the way std::sort's introsort is, though this is invisible at the call site
- Open issue #2 shows the benchmark/test build breaking under newer clang/CMake due to a googlebenchmark C-dialect flag mismatch — unrelated to the sort code but relevant if you try to reproduce the published numbers

**Status:** Abandoned on its default branch since 2023-05-10 (later activity moved to an unrelated-history 'nextgen' branch); MIT-licensed and small/self-contained enough to vendor, but only 33 stars and an open build-fail issue against its bench/test harness.

[repo](https://github.com/damageboy/vxsort-cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/damageboy/vxsort-cpp#results-ryzen-3950x-38ghz)

##### x86-simd-sort (numpy/x86-simd-sort)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

AVX-512/AVX2 SIMD quicksort/select library beating std::sort on primitive arrays and key-derived struct sorts (object_qsort).

**Beats:** std::sort — Numbers come from x86-simd-sort's own README benchmark (benchmarks/bench-objsort.hpp, Google Benchmark, run with --benchmark_filter=*obj*), comparing object_qsort against std::sort on arrays of 3D Point structs (float or double x/y/z) sorted by one coordinate or by Manhattan, Euclidean, or Chebyshev distance from the origin, on an unspecified x86 processor with AVX-512 and no disclosed compiler or flags: up to ~5x faster for float (32-bit) keys and ~4x for double (64-bit) keys sorting by one coordinate, up to ~10x faster sorting by Euclidean distance.

**How:** Built-in-type routines vectorize quicksort partitioning using AVX-512 compressstore instructions (with an AVX2 fallback), based on two cited SIMD-partitioning papers, and drop to bitonic sorting networks on AVX-512/AVX registers for arrays below a size threshold (64-512 elements). object_qsort does not vectorize struct comparisons directly: it extracts each object's key into a separate array, sorts the resulting (key, index) pairs with the SIMD keyvalue_qsort, then permutes the original object array into place with a scalar cycle-following swap loop. Its speedup therefore comes from the primitive keyvalue sort plus, for expensive keys like Euclidean distance, auto-vectorized key computation, not from vectorizing the object comparisons themselves.

**Use it when:**
- Sorting arrays of built-in 16/32/64-bit ints, floats, or doubles (or key-value pairs) on x86-64 hardware with AVX2 or AVX-512, where std::sort's per-element comparator overhead dominates
- Sorting an array of structs by one scalar key -- a single member or a computed metric like Euclidean/Manhattan/Chebyshev distance -- via object_qsort's key-extraction lambda
- Need argsort/argselect/partial_qsort with built-in NaN placement control (nans_last) instead of hand-rolling NaN partitioning around std::sort/std::nth_element
- Batch or offline sorts where allocating O(N) extra memory for keys and an index array is acceptable
- Comfortable depending on code already proven at NumPy/PyTorch/OpenJDK vendoring scale rather than a smaller, newer project

**Skip it when:**
- Target hardware lacks AVX2/AVX-512, or is not x86-64 (no aarch64/ARM support)
- Sort key isn't reducible to one scalar of 32 or 64 bits -- object_qsort's key_func must return exactly float/double/(u)int32/64, not a multi-field comparator
- Memory-constrained settings: object_qsort needs O(N) extra space (a key array plus a uint32/64 index array) on top of the object array itself
- Need numbers independently verified on disclosed hardware/compiler: the object_qsort chart names only 'a processor with AVX-512', no CPU model, compiler, or flags, and the numbers are first-party
- Care about scaling on adversarial input distributions: an independent 2023 analysis (Voultapher sort-research-rs) found worse-than-O(N log N) scaling for the primitive AVX-512 qsort on a random_p5 pattern

**Integration:** header-only (src/x86simdsort-static-incl.h, compile-time AVX2/AVX-512 selection) or static/shared lib (Meson build under lib/, runtime CPUID dispatch) · none for the core routines; googletest and Google Benchmark (>=1.9.2) only if building the optional test/benchmark suite; OpenMP optional for parallelizing qsort/argsort/keyvalue_qsort · C++17; GCC 8+ (GCC 12+ required for _Float16/AVX-512FP16), Clang 8.0+, MSVC 2019 16.8+, or Intel icx · x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512 (exact subset varies: skylake-avx512 for 32/64-bit, icelake-client for 16-bit, sapphirerapids for _Float16); no aarch64/ARM

**Vs siblings:** A maintainer directly asked how this compares to vxsort-cpp (issue #12) and no comparison was ever produced, so there's no first-party head-to-head with that sibling. Pick x86-simd-sort over the other primitive-array sorters in this catalog (BlockQuicksort, Boost.Sort spreadsort, IPS4o, LearnedSort, fluxsort, quadsort, radix_sort) specifically when the workload is 'sort a struct by one field or a derived distance metric' via object_qsort, not a flat array of ints -- none of the other siblings' benchmarks target that struct/key-sort shape.

**Gotchas:**
- object_qsort's gain shrinks as sizeof(T) grows or the key gets cheap to compute relative to swap cost, since the final struct permutation is a scalar cycle-following swap loop, not SIMD
- object_qsort's key_func return type must be exactly 32 or 64 bits (float/double/int32/int64/uint32/uint64) or the call fails a static_assert at compile time
- For built-in-type routines, hasnan defaults to false; if the array actually contains NaNs and hasnan isn't set true, behavior is undefined
- GCC 16.0.1 with LTO enabled reportedly failed to build (issue #224, closed without a posted fix) when vendored into NumPy, due to an 'inlining failed: target specific option mismatch' error on an always_inline comparator

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-06-25); BSD-3-Clause. 'Copyable' fits since the src/ headers can be vendored standalone at compile time -- as NumPy, PyTorch, and OpenJDK already do -- while the runtime-dispatching library form requires a Meson build.

[repo](https://github.com/numpy/x86-simd-sort) · [benchmark](https://github.com/numpy/x86-simd-sort/blob/main/README.md)

#### string-search-and-hashing

##### Boost.Algorithm Boyer-Moore / Boyer-Moore-Horspool searchers  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only Boyer-Moore / Boyer-Moore-Horspool string searchers, ~4-5x faster than std::search on long patterns.

**Beats:** std::search — PR #25 (opened 2016 by Jeremy Murphy, still open/unmerged) republishes edited test/search_test2.cpp output on a 2,756,252-entry random 8-bit corpus: std::search 0.4848s vs boyer_moore_search 0.1171s (~4.1x) and boyer_moore_horspool_search 0.1076s (~4.5x) for a 105-entry pattern found mid-corpus, and std::search 1.028s vs boyer_moore_horspool_search 0.1825s (~5.6x) for a 91-entry not-found pattern; compiler, flags, CPU model, and standard library are not stated, and the PR author notes ~5-10% run-to-run variance.

**How:** Both algorithms precompute a bad-character skip table from the pattern (full Boyer-Moore adds a good-suffix table) so on a mismatch the search can jump ahead by more than one position instead of std::search's linear rescan. The skip table is a fixed-size array (O(2^CHAR_BIT) entries) for small numeric value types like unsigned char, or a boost::unordered_map/std::unordered_map otherwise, giving O(pattern length + alphabet size) preprocessing. Horspool drops the good-suffix table for cheaper preprocessing at the cost of slightly weaker worst-case skips.

**Use it when:**
- Long patterns (tens to hundreds of elements) searched against large corpora, the shape of the PR's benchmark (105/43/91-entry patterns over a 2.76M-entry corpus)
- The same pattern is searched repeatedly against many or large corpora: construct a boyer_moore/boyer_moore_horspool object once and reuse operator() to amortize the skip-table build
- Pre-C++17 toolchains, or any C++03/11/14 codebase that can take a Boost dependency but can't use std::boyer_moore_searcher
- Searching over random-access ranges of non-char element types with comparable (and ideally hashable) values, not just byte strings

**Skip it when:**
- Short, one-off pattern searches — the skip-table build can cost more than a plain linear scan for a single small search
- C++17+ code already reaching for std::boyer_moore_searcher/std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher, which is the same algorithm with no Boost dependency
- Forward-only or input iterators — both searchers require random-access iterators, unlike std::search
- Mixed-type pattern/corpus comparisons — a BOOST_STATIC_ASSERT requires identical value_type on both iterators
- Workloads wanting SIMD-level throughput on x86/ARM byte strings — this is a scalar algorithm; StringZilla or sse4-strstr target that instead

**Integration:** header-only · Boost.Config, Boost.Assert, Boost.StaticAssert, Boost.Range, Boost.Core, Boost.TypeTraits, Boost.Array, and Boost.Unordered (all header-only Boost libraries; part of full Boost distributions) · C++03 (README lists 'Properties: C++03, Header-only'; falls back to boost::unordered_map when BOOST_NO_CXX11_HDR_UNORDERED_MAP is defined, std::unordered_map otherwise) · any (portable C++, no SIMD or architecture-specific code observed in the headers read)

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over sse4-strstr or StringZilla when the workload needs a portable, non-SIMD, header-only implementation that works over arbitrary random-access element types (not just bytes) or that reuses a prebuilt search object across many corpora; pick StringZilla or sse4-strstr instead when the goal is maximum single-call byte-string throughput on x86/ARM via SIMD.

**Gotchas:**
- Random-access iterators are required for both corpus and pattern; forward/input iterators that std::search accepts will not compile
- Pattern and corpus iterators must share the same value_type, enforced at compile time via BOOST_STATIC_ASSERT
- Non-numeric or wide value types fall back to an unordered_map-based skip table, which is slower to build and probe than the fixed array table used for byte-like data
- The much larger Musser-Nishanov searcher proposed in the same PR #25 (still open/unmerged) had a reported segfault on large real-world corpora during development; that bug is in the unmerged code, not the mainline boyer_moore/boyer_moore_horspool searchers this benchmark measures

**Status:** Actively maintained mainline Boost.Algorithm code (develop branch last commit 2026-08-05), BSL-1.0 licensed and header-only, trivial to vendor a single header pair; the PR these benchmark numbers come from has sat open and unmerged since 2016 and proposes a different, unrelated Musser-Nishanov searcher.

[repo](https://github.com/boostorg/algorithm) · [benchmark](https://github.com/boostorg/algorithm/pull/25)

##### CityHash  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Non-cryptographic 64/128-bit string hash family beating Murmur2/Murmur3F, ~1.7-2.5x faster at 64 bytes.

**Beats:** MurmurHash2/MurmurHash3 (Murmur2, Murmur3F, Murmur3A) — widely-used non-cryptographic hash functions used in place of std::hash — Google's own README (MIT, ~2011-2013 numbers) reports CityHash64 v1.0.3 vs Murmur2/Murmur3F on a single core of a 2.67GHz Xeon X5550: 9ns vs 15ns/23ns at 64 bytes (~1.7x-2.5x faster), and CityHashCrc256 at 5-5.5 bytes/cycle vs Murmur3F's 2.4 bytes/cycle on long strings (~2.1x-2.3x faster); compiler and flags used for these specific numbers are not stated.

**How:** Short inputs (<=4, <=8, <=16, <=32, <=64 bytes) each get a dedicated fast path using register-width multiply/rotate mixing tuned to that length bucket, so most hash-table-key-sized strings finish in a handful of instructions. For long strings, CityHashCrc128/256 layer that same multiply-rotate mixing on top of the hardware CRC32 instruction (_mm_crc32_u64) as a cheap mixing primitive, reaching about 5-5.5 bytes/cycle versus ~2.4 bytes/cycle for pure-software Murmur3F.

**Use it when:**
- Fixed, fully-buffered byte strings (not streamed) used as hash-table keys, especially short strings in the 1-64 byte range
- x86-64 targets with SSE4.2 available, where CityHashCrc128/256 can use the CRC32 instruction for long-string throughput
- Codebases that want to vendor a tiny, frozen source drop (city.cc/city.h/citycrc.h) rather than add a package-manager dependency
- Need an MIT-licensed implementation with a stable, unchanging API (no upstream churn since 2013)
- Non-adversarial input, or input always hashed with a caller-supplied random seed via the *WithSeed variants

**Skip it when:**
- Need to hash data arriving in chunks/streams — no incremental API exists
- Want the fastest available long-string throughput on modern hardware — newer SIMD-tuned hashes (xxh3, rapidhash, komihash) beat it and are actively maintained
- Non-x86-64 or no-SSE4.2 platform and you wanted the CRC-based variants (CityHashCrc128/256 hard-require _mm_crc32_u64)
- Untrusted/adversarial keys going into a hash table without supplying a random seed — CVE-2012-6051 hash-flooding DoS applies to unseeded CityHash
- Want a maintained project — repo is archived by Google, last real release was v1.1.1 in June 2013

**Integration:** source-drop · none (stdint.h, utility); CRC variants additionally need an SSE4.2-capable CPU and compiler support for the _mm_crc32_u64 intrinsic · not documented precisely; header only uses uint32_t/uint64_t/std::pair, autoconf build dates to 2011-2013, no C++11-only constructs observed · little-endian x86/x86-64 primarily (CRC variants need SSE4.2); header states big-endian support is only lightly tested

**Vs siblings:** Pick CityHash mainly for legacy/reproducibility reasons (matching an existing on-disk hash or a 2011-era baseline); for new code, komihash, rapidhash, or t1ha in this catalog beat both CityHash and Murmur with active maintenance, and MUM/VMUM-V2 explicitly benchmarks itself against CityHash64 and wins.

**Gotchas:**
- No seed randomization by default: CityHash64/CityHash32 without a seed are vulnerable to a hash-flooding DoS (CVE-2012-6051); pass a random seed via the *WithSeed/*WithSeeds variants for adversarial input
- CRC-based variants (CityHashCrc128/256 in citycrc.h) require an SSE4.2 CPU and the _mm_crc32_u64 intrinsic; the autoconf build's --enable-sse4.2 flag must be set or citycrc.h isn't installed
- hash(a+b) cannot be derived from hash(a) and hash(b) for any function in this file (stated in the header) — no incremental combination of partial hashes (open issue #17)
- Big-endian support is explicitly called out in city.h as 'only lightly tested'

**Status:** Archived by Google; last commit 2022-07-19 was housekeeping, last real release was v1.1.1 in June 2013. MIT-licensed and small enough (3 source files) to vendor, but expect no further fixes — known issues such as CVE-2012-6051 and #46 (Windows byteswap.h detection) remain open.

[repo](https://github.com/google/cityhash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/google/cityhash/blob/master/README)

##### StringZilla  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only SIMD string kernels (search, hashing, sort, UTF-8) beating std::string::find and find_first_of.

**Beats:** std::string::find — README Performance table: finding the first occurrence of a ~5-byte random word, std::string::find (STL, GCC+glibc) hit 9.1 GB/s vs sz_find 21.0 GB/s (~2.3x) on an Intel Sapphire Rapids Xeon4, and 10.9 vs 37.1 GB/s (~3.4x) on Apple M5 Pro (Apple Clang+libc++). Splitting lines on \n/\r, std::string::find_first_of hit 1.1 GB/s vs sz_find_byteset 13.8 GB/s on Xeon4, and 4.1 vs 23.7 GB/s on M5 Pro.

**How:** Per-ISA SIMD kernels (SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 on x86, NEON/SVE/SVE2 on ARM, plus WASM SIMD128, RISC-V RVV, PowerPC VSX, LoongArch) selected at compile time or via a runtime dispatch table in the optional shared build. Needle-length-adaptive algorithm choice: brute-force SIMD comparisons at multiple needle offsets for short needles, Boyer-Moore-Horspool with a bad-character shift table and Raita-style character-anomaly detection for mid/long needles, and SWAR (64-bit word) fallback with no SIMD.

**Use it when:**
- Hot substring search over large text buffers where std::string::find shows up in a profile
- Splitting/tokenizing on multiple delimiter bytes (replacing find_first_of/strcspn) via sz_find_byteset
- Multi-language pipelines that need identical search/hash/sort kernels across C/C++/Python/Rust/Go/Swift/JS/C#/Java
- Unicode case-folding, segmentation, or normalization at C speed instead of ICU/ICU4X
- Apple Silicon or ARM server targets, where the README reports the widest gap over the system libc strstr

**Skip it when:**
- Multi-pattern literal matching: no Aho-Corasick automaton is shipped; README points to hyperscan or pyahocorasick instead
- Need a std::hash-compatible hasher: sz's hash is a separate AES-based non-standard function, not a std::hash specialization
- Building for i386 — currently broken (open issue #341)
- Need find_all() match offsets relative to the parent string — reported broken in open issue #278
- Very short, early-diverging comparisons (equality/order checks) — README itself says vectorization is 'almost useless' there
- Risk-averse adoption of sz::argsort right now — open crash report (#337) and an open UBSAN misaligned-write report (#279)

**Integration:** header-only · none (freestanding build available via SZ_AVOID_LIBC=1); optional precompiled shared library for runtime dispatch · C99 / C++11 minimum to compile; CI-validated on GCC 12+, Clang 16+, MSVC 2022, NVCC CUDA 12+ (GCC 10 and older fail STL insert conformance needed by the test suite) · x86-64 (SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 tiers), aarch64 (NEON/SVE/SVE2), WebAssembly (SIMD128 via wasm32-wasip1), RISC-V (RVV), PowerPC (VSX), LoongArch; i386 currently fails to build (issue #341)

**Vs siblings:** sse4-strstr is the closest sibling but covers only substring search as a single header with no bindings; pick StringZilla when you also need byte-set scanning, hashing, sorting, or non-C++ language bindings and can accept a larger, fast-moving dependency. Pick sse4-strstr instead when you want a small, frozen, single-purpose kernel to vendor with nothing else attached.

**Gotchas:**
- sz_find_byte_serial historically mis-compared bytes > 0x7F when compiled with -fsigned-char (issue #306, closed/fixed) — a signed-char caution sign for anyone pinning old versions
- find_all() results reportedly cannot recover the match's position within the parent string (open issue #278)
- sz::argsort has an open crash report (#337)
- UBSAN reports a misaligned-address write in a SWAR code path (open issue #279)

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-12, 3,563 stars, Apache-2.0); header-only core is easy to vendor ('copyable'), but several open bugs (i386 build failure, argsort crash, misaligned-write UBSAN report) mean trusting specific kernels rather than the whole surface unverified.

[repo](https://github.com/ashvardanian/StringZilla) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ashvardanian/StringZilla/blob/main/README.md)

### storage-and-data

#### caches

##### cachegrand  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Multi-threaded C key-value server speaking the Redis protocol (string commands only); out-scales single-threaded Redis on many-core Linux.

**Beats:** Redis — Vendor memtier_benchmark runs (128 B values, Gaussian keys over a 1M-key range, 25 connections per memtier thread, two load servers) on an AMD EPYC 7502P 32c/64t with bonded 2x25GbE and Ubuntu 22.04 measured cachegrand v0.2.1 at 935.6K GET ops/s per load node with 16 client threads against Redis 7.0.11's 71.1K with 1 client thread (about 13x). At equal single-thread load it was only 78.8K vs 71.1K (about 1.1x), and Redis was never run with more client threads or as multiple instances; both were built from source by the prep script (cachegrand as a CMake Release build, which is -O2, with t1ha2; Redis with a plain make), but the GCC version and the server configs are not published.

**Known shortcoming:** Own benchmark repo with no compiler/flags. tN is memtier client threads, not server workers, and Redis was run only at t1, so the 13.2x/31.5x at t16/t64 compare 16-64x more clients; at equal load it is ~1.11x.

**Known shortcoming:** Partial Redis compatibility (~53 string/key commands; no lists/hashes/sets/zsets/pubsub/MULTI/Lua/replication/cluster; Kafka/Memcache/WASM are plans). The win comes from threads, not the algorithm: at matched single-thread load it is ~1.1x, and with pipeline=64 at one thread Redis beats it on SET (386K vs 273K). The hash table is fixed-size (default 1M keys, no resize, 32-line probe cap) so inserts fail when full; the memory limit ignores key bytes (#439).

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: the default config has auth off and binds 0.0.0.0, and if Sentry reporting is enabled crash dumps go to the author's DSN. The benchmarked v0.2.1 had lock-free GETs, but main takes read spinlocks since PR #434 (2023-10) and was never re-benchmarked; expiry tests are commented out as broken (2024-12); last release v0.4.0 (2023-05). Needs io_uring, kernel 5.7+ and a high memlock limit.

**How:** It runs one pinned worker thread per core; each worker multiplexes connections as user-space fibers (hand-written x86-64/aarch64 context switch) over io_uring, so there is no thread per connection and few syscalls. All workers share one multi-producer/multi-consumer open-addressing hashtable that packs 14 32-bit slot IDs (filled bit, probe distance, 16-bit hash fragment) into each 64-byte cache line, a layout borrowed from Folly's F14. It probes at most 32 neighbouring lines and compares a whole line with two AVX2 compares; AVX-512F, AVX, NEON and scalar variants are chosen at startup through GNU ifunc. Writes take a small spinlock per 14-slot chunk, so contention is spread across the table instead of behind one global lock, and memory comes from mimalloc with optional 2 MB hugepages.

**Use it when:**
- String-only Redis workloads (GET/SET/MGET/INCR/EXPIRE on small values; the vendor test used 128 B) that need more throughput than one Redis process gives, where you would rather not shard across several Redis instances.
- Many concurrent client connections hitting a many-core Linux x86-64 or aarch64 server (kernel 5.7+ for io_uring) on which you can dedicate cores, pin NIC queues and grant hugepages and unlimited memlock.
- A cache with a known keyspace ceiling: the hashtable is sized up front from database.limits.hard.max_keys, which suits workloads whose maximum key count you can set in advance.
- Studying or vendoring a BSD-3-Clause C implementation of a cache-line-packed SIMD concurrent hashtable, fibers and io_uring networking.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything beyond Redis strings and keys: other data types, pub/sub, MULTI/EXEC, Lua/functions, replication and cluster mode are missing, and the transactions and cluster-mode issues are still open.
- Single-client or pipelined traffic. In the vendor data it is only about 1.1x Redis at one memtier thread without pipelining, and with pipeline=64 Redis 7.0.11 beat it on SET (386K vs 273K ops/s per load node).
- Production systems that need an active upstream. There has been no release since v0.4.0 (May 2023), the last commit was 2025-01-02, and the expiry tests for SET/SETEX/PSETEX/GETEX were commented out as broken in December 2024.
- Non-Linux hosts, older kernels, or sandboxes and containers that block io_uring or high memlock limits; io_uring is the only network backend.
- A keyspace that can grow past a preset limit. There is no online resize (storage_db hard-codes can_auto_resize = false), and the memory limit does not count key bytes (open issue #439).

**Integration:** standalone server binary (CMake build from source or the cachegrand/cachegrand-server Docker image); not a library · liburing, libnuma, libyaml/libcyaml, mbedTLS >= 2.28, libcurl, pcre2, json-c, liblzf, libatomic, mimalloc, t1ha/xxHash (several vendored under 3rdparty); hiredis only for tests; optional sentry · GCC (the build docs require gcc; the README's sample log shows gcc 11.3.0), CMake 3.16+, C11 (C++17 for tests and benches), Linux kernel 5.7+ · Linux only: x86-64 (runtime dispatch across AVX-512F/AVX2/AVX/scalar) and aarch64 (NEON)

**Vs siblings:** Dragonfly and KeyDB also serve the Redis protocol from many threads but cover far more of the command set and are maintained; Valkey is the maintained Redis fork. Pick cachegrand only for a GET/SET-only cache where its own data showing it ahead of Dragonfly v1.1.2 matters (about 1.4x GET and 1.25x SET at 64 memtier threads, about 3x GET with pipelining), or when you want a small BSD C hashtable and io_uring design to study or vendor.

**Gotchas:**
- The hashtable size is fixed at start: the next power of two of database.limits.hard.max_keys (default 1,000,000). Probing stops after 32 cache lines (448 slots), so once a neighbourhood fills, inserts fail instead of the table resizing.
- The skeleton config binds 0.0.0.0 and :: on 6379/6380 with require_authentication: false and max_clients: 100. If you turn on sentry, it uploads crash minidumps, which may contain stored data, to the author's sentry.io DSN by default.
- The hashtable doc and the v0.2.1 benchmark describe lock-free, fence-based GETs. Since PR #434 (Oct 2023) GETs take per-chunk read spinlocks, and current main has not been re-benchmarked.
- It needs high memlock and nofile ulimits (io_uring shares locked memory with the kernel) and preferably 2 MB hugepages. The performance docs also tell you to pin NIC IRQ/XPS queues per worker and disable irqbalance to approach the published numbers.

**Status:** Stale since 2025-01-02, with no release after v0.4.0 (May 2023), about 1k stars and one main author; it is BSD-3-Clause and builds with CMake, but treat it as a research-grade server, not a production Redis replacement.

[repo](https://github.com/danielealbano/cachegrand) · [benchmark](https://github.com/cachegrand/cachegrand-benchmarks)

##### Cachelot  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Single-threaded C++ LRU cache library plus a memcached-text-protocol server that fits 7-16% more data than Memcached in the same RAM.

**Beats:** memcached — The author's own chart (cachelot.io, circa 2016) fills Cachelot and Memcached, each capped at 2 GB, with the same shuffled random dataset over 10 runs and counts surviving key+value bytes. Cachelot keeps 91-94% of the budget vs 79.5% for Memcached on 10 B-1 KB values, 94-99% vs 86.7% on 1-4 KB, 93-97% vs 87.3% on 4 KB-1 MB, and 93-97% vs 86.9% on mixed sizes, which is 7-16% more stored data by the 10th run. Cachelot's figures fall slightly each run while Memcached's stay flat. No CPU, compiler, flags or Memcached version is given, and the script in the repo now uses 4 GB, not 2 GB.

**Known shortcoming:** The win is memory ('saves up to 15% RAM'; the chart shows 7-18% more data stored), not speed. Abandoned (last commit 2023-04).

**Known shortcoming:** The memory win (7-16% more stored bytes than Memcached, shrinking each run) comes only from a vendor chart with no Memcached version or hardware; no throughput/latency numbers. Single-threaded by design (even get() mutates the page LRU; stats are a global non-atomic struct). The binary protocol throws not_implemented; flush_all drops only expired items; exptime is always relative; 16-bit flags.

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: the -d/-l/-C options are parsed but ignored and it binds TCP and UDP on 0.0.0.0:11211 by default, a UDP amplification risk. Page-level LRU evicts a whole 1 MB page with a linear page scan. Abandoned since 2023-04; Boost dependency.

**How:** The memory gain comes from the allocator, not the index. One power-of-two arena is split into fixed pages (1 MB by default). Inside each page, items are variable-size blocks with an 8-byte header, kept on segregated free lists (power-of-two ranges each cut into 32 sub-classes, TLSF-style), and split or coalesced with their neighbours. Each item is stored close to its exact size, instead of being rounded up to a slab-class chunk as in memcached. Items keep the key and value inline behind a compact header (64-bit CAS stamp, 32-bit hash, length, expiry, 16-bit flags). The index is a Robin Hood open-addressing hash table with hashes stored in a separate array, FNV-1a 32-bit hashing and a 93% max load factor, and it grows by incremental two-table rehashing to avoid resize stalls. There are no locks anywhere.

**Use it when:**
- A memcached text-protocol cache that is memory-bound with mostly small values (10 B-1 KB): the vendor chart shows about 91-94% of a 2 GB budget holding live data vs about 79.5% for Memcached
- Embedding a hard-capped LRU cache inside a single-threaded event loop, or one instance per core/shard, where you want no malloc after startup and predictable memory use
- Resource-limited targets (the README lists 32-bit ARM and x86-64) where the cache must never exceed a fixed arena
- 'Consistent cache' use (-M / enable_evictions=false), where a full cache should return an error instead of silently evicting data
- C or FFI embedding through the provided C API (cachelot_set/get/add/cas-style calls and an eviction callback)

**Skip it when:**
- You need one multi-threaded process or concurrent readers. The author states it is not thread-safe by design, and even get() mutates the LRU state, so you must shard or put it behind a single worker queue
- You need full memcached compatibility: there is no binary protocol, no SASL/TLS, no meta commands and no 'stats <arg>'; flush_all and exptime semantics differ; flags are 16-bit
- You pick a cache for throughput or latency. The only published comparison is memory efficiency; the 'faster latency' claim has no numbers, and siblings such as Pelikan, MemC3 and Pogocache publish throughput data
- Hit ratio is sensitive to eviction precision. LRU is tracked per page (1 MB by default), and an eviction drops every item on the chosen page whatever their individual recency
- You need a maintained, security-reviewed daemon. The last commit was April 2023, the only CI config is a legacy .travis.yml (no GitHub Actions), and several CLI flags are silently ignored

**Integration:** static lib (libcachelot, mostly inline headers plus a few .cpp files) and a cachelotd server binary; Docker image cachelot/cachelot · Boost >= 1.53 (system, program_options and asio for the server, unit_test_framework for tests; the library itself uses Boost error_code/intrusive pieces); CMake · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); GCC, Clang or MSVC (VS 2022 via vcpkg for Boost on Windows) · x86-64 and 32-bit ARM; the README says it is tested on Alpine, CentOS 7, Ubuntu, macOS and Windows 10/11

**Vs siblings:** Pick Cachelot over Pelikan/Segcache, MemC3, Pogocache or Dragonfly only when RAM efficiency on a memcached-text workload, or an embeddable fixed-arena single-threaded LRU library, matters more than throughput; those siblings publish multi-threaded throughput wins over Memcached (for example Segcache at about 8x with 24 threads) and are better choices for a maintained, concurrent server.

**Gotchas:**
- flush_all only removes items that have already expired; unlike memcached, it does not invalidate live items. exptime is always taken as relative seconds, with no absolute-Unix-time rule for values over 30 days, so absolute expiries effectively never fire
- The server's -d (daemon), -l (listen), -C (no-cas) and socket-access flags are parsed but never applied (issue #15 confirms -d is unimplemented). TCP and UDP both bind to all interfaces on 11211 by default, and UDP memcached on a public interface is a known reflection-amplification vector, so pass -U 0 or firewall it
- Eviction works per page: touching an item promotes its whole page, and evicting a page frees every item on it after a linear scan of the page table. A smaller -P page gives finer eviction but also caps the maximum item size, because an item must fit in one page
- -m and -P must be powers of two. Library calls throw system_error (out_of_memory, key_too_long, item_too_big), and the pointer returned by do_get is valid only until the next Cachelot call

**Status:** Abandoned since the last commit on 2023-04-12, but the BSD-2-Clause library is small and self-contained apart from Boost, so it is easy to vendor; treat the cachelotd daemon as unhardened.

[repo](https://github.com/cachelot/cachelot) · [benchmark](https://cachelot.io/index.html#benchmarks)

##### Caffeine  `Java`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Concurrent in-process JVM cache using W-TinyLFU and buffered policy updates; beats ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava Cache and synchronized LinkedHashMap on multi-threaded throughput.

**Beats:** ConcurrentLinkedHashMap (LRU) — Only the author's own JMH GetPutBenchmark numbers exist. They date from about 2015 and an early Caffeine release, and the JVM version and flags are not stated. The run was on a 16-core Azure G4 Xeon E5-2698B v3 (hyperthreading off, Ubuntu 15.04). At 16 threads, bounded Caffeine did 382M ops/s on 100% reads vs 314M for ConcurrentLinkedHashMap (~1.2x) and 43M for Guava at concurrencyLevel 64; 279M vs 122M on 75/25 read/write (~2.3x); and 48M vs 40M on 100% writes (~1.2x). In the current benchmark source the cache is prepopulated for a 100% hit rate with ~11K Zipf-distributed keys against a 65,536-entry bound, so the runs measure hit and update bookkeeping, not eviction throughput. No C++ or stdlib comparison is involved.

**Known shortcoming:** Only first-party numbers from ~2015 (Azure G4, Ubuntu 15.04, early release), JVM version and flags unstated, no independent benchmark. The current GetPutBenchmark prepopulates ~11K Zipf keys against a 65,536-entry bound (100% hits, no eviction), so it measures hit/update bookkeeping, not eviction. Gain over ConcurrentLinkedHashMap is modest (~1.2x read-only and write-only, 2.3x at 75/25); the 7-9x ratios are against Guava (concurrencyLevel 64). CLHM is the same author's predecessor. Java, not C++. Writes slower than Guava under write floods with both expirations on (#1320); slow loads block other keys and eviction via ConcurrentHashMap bin locks (#672); mutable keys caused 100% CPU in 2.x (#1696).

**How:** It follows the BP-Wrapper idea: reads are recorded into striped, lossy ring buffers and writes into a bounded, growable MPSC queue, and a single thread replays them in batches under a try-lock. Readers therefore never contend on the LRU-list lock that ConcurrentLinkedHashMap-style and Guava-style caches take or segment. It decorates Java 8's ConcurrentHashMap (lock-free reads), uses relaxed memory ordering where the lock already provides visibility, and generates a separate class for each feature combination so unused per-entry fields are dropped. For compute/get-with-loader it checks for a present entry without locking before falling back to computeIfAbsent (1.58B vs 29.7M ops/s for plain ConcurrentHashMap on a single hot key in the author's server run). Hit rate comes from Window TinyLFU: a small LRU admission window, a segmented-LRU main space, a 4-bit Count-Min Sketch frequency filter, and hill climbing to size the window.

**Use it when:**
- Read-heavy, skewed (Zipf-like) lookups inside one JVM with many threads, where a synchronized LinkedHashMap LRU or Guava Cache is the contention point (author's 16-thread server run: 382M reads/s vs 43M for Guava at concurrencyLevel 64 and 13.6M for LinkedHashMap LRU).
- Mixed read/write traffic on a bounded cache: 75/25 read/write was 2.3x ConcurrentLinkedHashMap's throughput in the same run.
- Workloads where LRU hit rate suffers from scans, loops or shifting recency/frequency patterns: the author's trace simulations show W-TinyLFU near Belady's optimum and competitive with ARC and LIRS without keeping ghost entries.
- Services that need loading, async refresh, per-entry variable expiration (timer wheel, amortized O(1)) or stampede protection via AsyncCache, not just a bounded map.
- Existing Spring, Quarkus, Micronaut, Play or Guava-cache code: integrations exist, and CaffeinatedGuava provides an adapter for code written against Guava's cache interfaces.

**Skip it when:**
- State has to be shared across processes or hosts, or has to survive restarts: this is a per-JVM on-heap cache with no off-heap or persistence mode; use a networked cache (or put Caffeine in front of one as an L1).
- Write floods: writes go through a bounded buffer drained by one maintenance thread, and writers spin and then yield when it is full. In the author's own 100% write run, Caffeine (48.3M ops/s) is only ~1.2x ConcurrentLinkedHashMap and slightly below unbounded ConcurrentHashMap (50.6M). In issue #1320 a user's non-JMH test found writes slower than Guava when using merge() with both expiration modes enabled.
- Code that relies on strict LRU order or exact capacity: the policy is eventually consistent with the map, eviction runs once the maximum is crossed (Guava evicts before), and TinyLFU can reject newly inserted entries.
- Memory-tight caches that use weak or soft references: the author's measurements show 112 bytes per entry for weakKeys+weakValues vs 72 for Guava (it is 64 vs 64 for plain maximumSize).
- Java 8 runtimes (3.x needs Java 11; stay on 2.x) or Android/GWT, which the wiki says are not supported.

**Integration:** module (Maven Central jar com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine, about 1.06 MB for 3.3.0; JPMS module com.github.benmanes.caffeine) · jspecify 1.0.1 and error_prone_annotations 2.50.0, which are annotation-only jars declared 'requires static' in module-info; optional extra artifacts are caffeine-guava and caffeine-jcache · Java 11+ for 3.x (the build defaults to Java 11 as the release target); Java 8 needs the 2.x line · any JVM 11+; the wiki says Android/GWT are not supported

**Vs siblings:** Garnet, Pelikan/Segcache and KeyDB are networked Redis/Memcached-style servers shared by many clients. Pick Caffeine when the cache can live inside a single JVM process, which avoids a network hop and serialization per lookup, or use it as a near cache in front of one of them.

**Gotchas:**
- Loads and asMap().compute run inside ConcurrentHashMap's bin locks. A slow load can block other keys that hash to the same bin and can stall eviction (issue #672). A compute must not write to the same cache, which livelocks on Java 8 and throws IllegalStateException on 9+. The documented mitigations are AsyncCache or a larger initialCapacity.
- Mutating a key's equals/hashCode while it is cached corrupts state. In 2.x this could spin a CPU at 100% in a retry loop (issue #1696); since v3.1.2 it throws IllegalStateException instead.
- Expiration and eviction happen only during maintenance triggered by cache activity, and that maintenance runs asynchronously on the executor. Configure a Scheduler (e.g. Scheduler.systemScheduler()) if entries must expire promptly, and call cleanUp() or use a direct executor in tests.
- weakKeys(), weakValues() and softValues() switch comparisons to identity (==) instead of equals(). Weights are computed only on write and do not change afterwards.

**Status:** Actively maintained: v3.3.0 was released 2026-09-21, there are commits through 2026-09-25, and 1 issue is open. It is an Apache-2.0 Maven dependency and the default in-process cache of many JVM frameworks. The baseline, ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, is the same author's predecessor and has been in maintenance mode since Caffeine appeared.

[repo](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Benchmarks)

##### Ferrous  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

AI-written Rust Redis/RESP2 server; self-reported 0-8% over Valkey 8.0.4 on single commands, ~2x slower pipelined SET.

**Beats:** Valkey 8.0.4 — The README table is a single first-party redis-benchmark run against Valkey 8.0.4 on the same unnamed machine: 10,000 requests per command with the tool's default client count and payload, logs to /dev/null, and no CPU, OS, Rust version or Valkey settings stated. The public script covers the PING pipeline but not the SET pipeline. Ferrous leads by 0-8% on single commands and by 25% on 10-deep PING pipelines, Valkey leads by 94% on 10-deep SET pipelines, and PR #42's post-fix run (Nov 2025, Rust 1.89) puts Ferrous GET at 73,529 ops/s, below the README's Valkey GET figure of 74,626.

**Known shortcoming:** Mixed results vs Valkey (not a listed baseline): wins some operations and loses others.

**Known shortcoming:** maxmemory is parsed but never applied (MemoryManager::unlimited, eviction TODO), so the cache is unbounded. The README's 'multi-threaded/Tokio' claim is false: one loop polls each std::net socket without epoll and a WouldBlock flush sleeps up to 100 ms, stalling all clients. Pipelined SET: Valkey 588k vs 303k; post-fix GET 73,529 is below the README's Valkey 74,626; runs are 10k requests (~0.13 s, noise). Docs contradict each other; SCAN copies and sorts all keys every call; reads take a shard write lock; unsafe raw-pointer skiplist. No commits since 2025-11; not on crates.io; AI-written, 18 stars.

**How:** There is no distinctive algorithm behind the numbers. The README says 'multi-threaded' and 'Tokio-based', but Cargo.toml enables only tokio's rt and time features, and server.rs spawns no threads: one loop polls every non-blocking std::net socket in turn (no epoll/kqueue), reads up to 8 KB per connection, runs all complete frames and flushes the replies with a single write (TCP_NODELAY on), then yields when busy or sleeps 10 us to 1 ms when idle. Data sits in 16 FNV-1a-sharded std HashMaps per database behind RwLocks; reads skip LRU access-time bookkeeping, WATCH tracking is skipped when nobody is watching, and the release build uses LTO with codegen-units=1. Each benchmark run is 10,000 requests, about 0.13 s at ~76k ops/s, which is too short to separate a 0-8% margin from noise.

**Use it when:**
- You want a compact pure-Rust reference implementation of RESP2, Streams consumer groups, WATCH and Redis-style Lua scripting to read, fork or teach from.
- Local development or CI tests that need a Redis-compatible endpoint on port 6379, where the dataset fits in RAM and nothing needs evicting.
- Non-pipelined request/response traffic with small values and modest connection counts. This is the only workload where the README shows it level with or slightly ahead of Valkey.
- Experiments on AI-generated systems code, using the bundled redis-benchmark scripts (tests/performance) to re-measure against Valkey yourself.

**Skip it when:**
- As a bounded cache. The config parser reads maxmemory, but the server builds its storage with StorageEngine::new(), which hard-codes MemoryManager::unlimited(), and eviction is marked 'TODO: implement eviction'. Memory grows without limit.
- Pipelined or batched writes: the README's own table has Valkey at 588,235 vs Ferrous 303,030 ops/s for SET with 10-command pipelines.
- Many connections or multi-core scaling. One thread issues a read on every connection each loop, so loop cost grows with connection count, and there is no parallel command execution to compete with Dragonfly or KeyDB.
- Slow clients or large replies. When a socket buffer is full, Connection::flush() sleeps 10+20+30+40 ms (up to 100 ms) inside the only event-loop thread, which stalls every other client.
- Production, or anything that needs cluster, modules, HyperLogLog, bit ops, RESP3 or partial resync. The code is AI-generated, the repo has 18 stars and no filed issues, and its docs contradict the code.

**Integration:** source-drop (standalone server binary built with cargo build --release; not on crates.io, where the 'ferrous' name belongs to an unrelated 2016 test-matcher crate) · tokio (rt, time only), mlua 0.11 with vendored Lua 5.1 (needs a C compiler), crossbeam, crossbeam-epoch, futures, lazy_static, rand, uuid, sha1, hex, thiserror · Rust edition 2021 with no rust-version or toolchain pin. Main builds on Rust 1.89.0 after PR #42; older commits fail there on the now deny-by-default dangerous_implicit_autorefs lint. A C toolchain is needed for the vendored Lua. · Not documented. Networking uses only portable std::net non-blocking sockets; test scripts assume Linux with dnf (Fedora/RHEL).

**Vs siblings:** Rarely. Valkey itself (catalogued) is more complete and far faster on pipelined writes, and Dragonfly or KeyDB are the choices when you need multi-core throughput from a Redis-compatible server. Pick Ferrous only when you specifically want a small pure-Rust RESP2 server with Streams and Lua to study or fork.

**Gotchas:**
- The docs disagree with each other and with the code. ARCHITECTURE.md describes edge-triggered epoll, I/O and worker thread pools and a custom allocator, none of which the code has. VALIDATION.md reports pipelined SET at 316k vs ~280k (Ferrous ahead), while the README reports 303k vs 588k (Valkey ahead), and RELEASE_NOTES claims equal 769k pipelined throughput.
- Every SCAN call copies and sorts all keys in the database before returning a page. A full keyspace iteration therefore costs O(N log N) per page, and each call blocks all clients on the single loop thread.
- GET and LRANGE take the shard's write lock and clone the returned data. The expiry thread walks every key that has a TTL once per second instead of sampling. Sorted sets use a hand-written unsafe raw-pointer skiplist, which needed 26 compile fixes for Rust 1.89 (PR #42).
- The idle loop backs off to 1 ms sleeps after ~100 empty cycles, so the first request after a quiet spell can wait up to ~1 ms. Under load the loop spins with yield_now and burns a core.

**Status:** The record calls it active, but main has had no commits since 2025-11-05 (a Rust 1.89 build fix), about 11 months before this entry, and one bit-operations PR is still open. It is dual MIT/Apache-2.0 per Cargo.toml (GitHub shows MIT) and fine to borrow code from, but it is not a production Redis replacement.

[repo](https://github.com/iGentAI/ferrous) · [benchmark](https://github.com/iGentAI/ferrous/blob/main/README.md)

##### golang-fifo  `Go`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Go generic in-process cache implementing SIEVE and S3-FIFO eviction; about 16-18% fewer misses than hashicorp LRU, but no higher ops/sec.

**Beats:** lru-hashicorp / lru-groupcache — The author's go-cache-benchmark harness runs a Get-then-Set-on-miss loop over 7.5M Zipf(0.99) string keys drawn from 500K items. Results are single runs on an unnamed desktop, with go.mod at Go 1.22 and golang-fifo v0.1.3. They show SIEVE with 16-18% fewer misses than hashicorp/golang-lru v2 at 0.1%, 1% and 10% cache sizes, but lower QPS at 2-16 goroutines (for example 2.64M vs 3.05M ops/s at 16 goroutines with a 0.1% cache) and higher QPS only single-threaded (5.05M vs 4.65M). The README's headline 2.51M vs 2.06M QPS row comes from an older (2023-12-12) run of the same harness, which the later tables contradict. No CPU model, compiler flags or repeat runs are reported for any of these comparisons.

**Known shortcoming:** The win is hit ratio (+11 points at a 0.1% cache), not speed: the linked benchmark's newer 2024-03 results show SIEVE QPS below lru-hashicorp/groupcache at concurrency 2-16 (at 16: 2.64M vs 3.05M), faster only at concurrency 1 (~1.09x).

**Known shortcoming:** v0.1.5 replaced the reader lock with an exclusive Mutex on Get (race #21), and every QPS table predates it (the harness pins v0.1.3), so none measures shipping code. The repo ships only SIEVE and S3-FIFO (the other policies in the harness are third-party). S3-FIFO TTL likely keeps an int8 bucket overflow fixed only in SIEVE (PR #32, untested); Get ignores expiry until the sweeper runs; callbacks run under the mutex (re-entry deadlocks); no sharding (#24); O(n) worst-case eviction (#18); stale since 2025-05.

**How:** The gain is fewer misses, not cheaper operations. SIEVE (NSDI'24) keeps one FIFO list plus a 'visited' bit per entry. A hit only sets the bit, and eviction walks a hand from the tail toward the head, clearing bits until it finds an unvisited entry. On Zipf-like traffic this keeps popular items and drops one-hit wonders quickly. S3-FIFO (SOSP'23) uses a small FIFO holding 10% of capacity, a main FIFO with a 2-bit frequency counter, and a ghost list of recently evicted keys, so one-hit wonders are filtered out before they reach the main queue. The README's claim that SIEVE hits need only a reader lock is out of date. v0.1.5 (January 2024) moved every call to an exclusive sync.Mutex after a data-race report (issue #21), so hits now serialize just as hashicorp's LRU Get does.

**Use it when:**
- Go services with read-heavy, power-law (Zipf-like) key popularity, such as web or API response caching, where each miss costs a database or network round trip. In the author's harness SIEVE's hit rate beat hashicorp LRU's by about 11 points at a 0.1% cache and about 4 points at 10%.
- Caches that are small relative to the key space (roughly 0.1-1% of distinct items), where the hit-ratio gap over LRU is widest.
- Code already using hashicorp/golang-lru or groupcache/lru that wants a better eviction policy with little API churn and no runtime dependencies (standard library only).
- Single-goroutine or low-contention callers. At concurrency=1 the harness had SIEVE at about 1.09x lru-hashicorp's QPS.
- Cases needing one TTL for the whole cache plus an eviction callback that tells capacity evictions, expirations and explicit removals apart.

**Skip it when:**
- Throughput-bound, highly concurrent hot paths. Each cache uses one global mutex. In the author's harness SIEVE trailed both LRU baselines at 2-16 goroutines (0.66-0.87x lru-hashicorp QPS at 16 goroutines), golang-fifo's own S3-FIFO ran at about 0.6x, and otter and sharded freelru were much faster.
- Scan-heavy or looping access patterns. The README says SIEVE is not scan-resistant; S3-FIFO or TinyLFU-style admission handles these better.
- Workloads close to a 100% hit ratio. Both policies have O(n) worst-case eviction when every entry has been touched (issue #18, open since January 2024).
- Large or GC-sensitive caches. Every entry is a heap object plus a container/list element holding a boxed key (the README appendix shows 4 allocs/op), and the README says the library does not try to compete with bigcache or freecache.
- Cases needing Keys/Values iteration, Resize, GetOldest/RemoveOldest, per-entry TTL, cost- or byte-based sizing, or sharding. A sharded variant is still an open request (issue #24).

**Integration:** module · none at runtime (standard library container/list, sync, context, time); fortio.org/assert is used only by tests · Go 1.24 (go.mod 'go 1.24'; CI tests on 1.24.x). The code needs generics and the Go 1.21 min builtin. · any Go target (pure Go, no unsafe or assembly)

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued SIEVE and S3-FIFO entries are libCacheSim simulators and CacheLib prototypes, and Caffeine and W-TinyLFU target the JVM and C++. Pick this one when you need those eviction policies as an importable Go package with an LRU-like API. If your Go hot path is limited by lock contention rather than misses, the author's own harness points to otter or sharded freelru (not catalogued) instead.

**Gotchas:**
- No published throughput number measures the shipping code. The README table (2023-12-12) and the harness tables (March 2024, pinned to golang-fifo v0.1.3) both come from before v0.1.5 replaced the RWMutex with a Mutex. The harness was bumped to v1.2.0 in July 2025, but its README results were not re-run. Hit rates depend only on the algorithm and should carry over; QPS should not be assumed to.
- S3FIFO with TTL > 0 looks unsafe. Its addToBucket still computes the bucket index in int8 arithmetic, the same expression PR #32 fixed in SIEVE after an 'index out of range [-28]' panic, and no S3FIFO test calls Set after the cleanup counter passes 28. S3FIFO.New also skips SIEVE's size check, and S3FIFO.Purge leaves TTL bucket entries behind.
- Expiry is enforced only by the background sweeper, which cycles through 100 time buckets and ticks every ttl/100. Get does not check an entry's expiry time, so an expired value can be returned until its bucket is swept. TTL caches that are never Closed leak their sweeper goroutine.
- The eviction callback runs while the cache mutex is held, so calling the same cache from inside it will deadlock (sync.Mutex is not reentrant). SIEVE's Close/Purge fires the callback with EvictReasonRemoved for every remaining entry, while S3FIFO's Purge fires none.

**Status:** Stale: the last release, v1.2.0 on 2025-05-10, only bumped Go to 1.24, and sharding (#24), O(n) worst-case eviction (#18) and concurrency tests (#22) remain open. Still, it is MIT-licensed, about 700 lines with no runtime dependencies and easy to vendor, and pkg.go.dev lists a handful of importers, including redpanda-operator.

[repo](https://github.com/scalalang2/golang-fifo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/scalalang2/golang-fifo#benchmark-result)

##### IKV (Inlined Key-Value Store)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Embedded, eventually consistent Rust key-value store for ML features that serves reads in-process instead of calling a remote Redis.

**Beats:** Redis (AWS ElastiCache, Redis Cluster) — In the in-memory test, 16 Java threads read from IKV embedded in a c5.4xlarge and, through JedisCluster HGET, from a 16-shard ElastiCache Redis 7.1 cluster (cache.r5.xlarge) in the same AZ, on 1M docs with three 50 B fields. IKV averaged about 3 us (p99 about 5-6 us) versus about 320 us (p99 about 515-530 us) for Redis at 25K-100K QPS, and it also held 1M and 3M QPS. The tiered test (c5d.4xlarge local SSD, Zipfian, 6000 B docs, 16 IKV threads vs 1 Redis thread, different dataset sizes per system) gave IKV avg 118 us / p99 748 us at 1:4 memory:data, versus avg 225 / p99 349 us for in-memory single-shard Redis. No CPU model, compiler or flags were given, and most of the gap is the removed network hop.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~100x is mostly the removed network hop: an embedded store on c5.4xlarge vs a remote 16-shard ElastiCache r5.xlarge cluster, not a faster engine. The tiered '2x' is average only; IKV's p99 is worse (748 vs 349 us) (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: the Go and Python SDKs download and dlopen libikv from the S3 bucket 'ikv-binaries', which no longer exists and whose name can be re-registered by anyone, so installing the SDKs could load an attacker's binary; do not use the published SDKs. The vendor is gone (inlined.io flagged as malicious; docs and gateway have no DNS), so readers can't start without self-hosting or patching. Kafka TLS certificate checks are off; the mmap flush is commented out; JNI unwraps inputs. Eventual consistency, no TTL/eviction/Redis API, full key-to-offset table on each reader's heap, append-only with offline compaction. Core is a cdylib (no Rust API); prebuilt for linux x64/arm64 and mac arm64 only; v0.0.36, stale since 2024-05.

**How:** Reads never leave the process. The primary key is hashed with fxhash to one of 16 RwLock-guarded segments. There, an in-memory std HashMap maps the key to a per-field vector of offsets, and the value is sliced out of an append-only memory-mapped file (2-byte type tag, then fixed-width bytes or a varint length). When data exceeds RAM it spills through the OS page cache, which keeps skewed (Zipfian) reads on local SSD under a millisecond on average. Writes are applied asynchronously by a background Kafka consumer, so the read path pays nothing for replication or consensus.

**Use it when:**
- Read-heavy online ML feature serving (recommendation, search, ranking), where every app host can hold its partition locally and a few milliseconds of staleness is fine.
- Per-lookup budgets in single-digit microseconds that a same-AZ network round trip (about 300 us to ElastiCache in the vendor's test) cannot meet.
- Feature sets 2-4x larger than RAM with skewed access, on hosts with local NVMe. The vendor measured avg 53 us (1:2) and 118 us (1:4 memory:data) with sub-millisecond p99.
- Java, Go or Python services that would otherwise put a remote Redis or DynamoDB in front of static or slowly changing features.
- As an MIT-licensed reference design for an embedded read replica: hash index, append-only mmap and stream replay from a snapshot plus Kafka.

**Skip it when:**
- You need read-after-write consistency, atomic updates, TTL or eviction, or Redis data structures. IKV has none of these; reads are eventually consistent.
- You cannot run its data plane. The hosted IKV Cloud is gone, self-hosting is still marked 'coming soon' in the README, and the ikv-cloud code expects Kafka, S3 and a DynamoDB-backed Java gateway with no setup docs.
- Memory is tight or the fleet is large. Every reader holds the whole key-to-offset hash table on heap and a full copy of its partition. Old values are only reclaimed by an offline index-build compaction.
- Tail latency matters on tiered data: at 1:4 memory:data, IKV's p99 was 747.65 us against 348.88 us for in-memory single-shard Redis.
- You want production maturity or a Rust API. It stopped at v0.0.36, nearly all commits are by one developer, and the core crate is built only as a cdylib behind C/JNI entry points, with no Rust-facing API.

**Integration:** shared lib · Core (Rust): rdkafka (librdkafka with vendored OpenSSL), tokio, aws-sdk-s3, memmap2, protobuf, jni, fxhash, flate2/tar. Runtime: a Kafka topic per store, an S3 bucket for base-index snapshots, and a gRPC gateway for config and writes. Python SDK: boto3, cffi, grpcio, protobuf. · Rust 2021 edition (MSRV not documented); Python SDK requires Python 3.8+; Go and Java minimums not documented. · The SDK loaders only know prebuilt binaries for linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64 and macOS aarch64 (no Windows, no Intel Mac). 64-bit only: the offset table uses usize and is commented as 32-bit incompatible. The prebuilt binary bucket no longer exists, so you must build from source.

**Vs siblings:** Garnet, Dragonfly, KeyDB and Pogocache are shared network servers benchmarked on server throughput against Redis, and Caffeine is an in-process JVM heap cache you fill yourself. Pick IKV only if you want every app host to hold a stream-synced, disk-spillable read replica of a feature dataset and will run and maintain its Kafka/S3 data plane yourself. Otherwise a sibling is the safer choice.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'no network calls' claim covers steady-state reads only. Opening a reader fetches config over gRPC from gateway.inlined.io, may download a base-index tarball from S3 (region hard-coded to us-west-2), and blocks until its Kafka partition is consumed to the high watermark. All vendor endpoints are now dead, so readers cannot start without code changes or a self-hosted data plane.
- Supply-chain risk: the Go and Python SDKs list a public S3 bucket named ikv-binaries, download the highest-versioned libikv from it, and dlopen it. That bucket now returns NoSuchBucket, so anyone who re-creates the name could serve the code the SDKs load. Pin and build your own binary. Also, the README's inlined.io links now redirect to an unrelated site flagged as potentially malicious.
- The Kafka consumer sets enable.ssl.certificate.verification=false while it authenticates with the account passkey over SASL/SCRAM. In a self-hosted setup, override this with the kafkaprop_ config prefix.
- Durability and robustness are thin. mmap.flush() is commented out ('TODO(critical): this fails on macos'), so value bytes are synced only when the OS writes pages back. The JNI and C entry points unwrap() or expect() on inputs and config. A comment warns that a panic in the consumer thread is not surfaced.

**Status:** The project has been stale since v0.0.36 (2024-05-14) and is effectively orphaned. As of 2026-09-26, inlined.io redirects to an unrelated flagged site, docs.inlined.io and gateway.inlined.io do not resolve, and the SDKs' binary bucket is gone. Using it now means building libikv from source and self-hosting or patching out the data plane, though the MIT-licensed Rust index is small enough to study or vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store) · [benchmark](https://github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store#benchmarks--100x-faster-than-redis)

##### KeyDB  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Multithreaded C++ Redis 6.2 fork serving one keyspace from many event-loop threads; claims ~7x Redis 6 throughput under TLS.

**Beats:** Redis — KeyDB's own blog (Sept 2020) drove servers on an AWS m5.4xlarge from an m5.8xlarge with memtier_benchmark --tls --threads=32 and otherwise default settings: KeyDB with 16 server threads and TLS got close to 1M ops/s (about 800k with 8 threads) versus ~130k ops/s for single-threaded Redis 6.0 with TLS, which is 36% below non-TLS single-threaded Redis and 61% below non-TLS Redis with io-threads. CPU model, compiler, build flags and exact versions are not given, Redis was not sharded or run as several instances, and the 'up to 7x lower latency' claim has no table.

**Known shortcoming:** Dead in practice: last commit 2024-04, last release v6.3.4 (2023-10); the lead developer left Snap in early 2025 and pointed users to Valkey (#895); open deadlock/crash issues (#883, #743, #827). Stuck at Redis 6.2 (can't load Redis 7 dumps, #527). A global spinlock still serializes every command, so gains shrink for writes, hot keys and long EXEC/Lua. The benchmark used 16 server-threads (README recommends 4) against an unsharded Redis, with no CPU/compiler/flags; the '7x lower latency' claim has no data. Threading needs Linux SO_REUSEPORT; ARM startup assert (#856); FLASH is beta; multi-master consistency/crash reports (#366). An existing redis.conf 'io-threads' line silently maps to server-threads.

**How:** It runs the stock Redis ae event loop on N threads and pins each connection to one thread at accept() (spread with Linux SO_REUSEPORT plus active client balancing), so socket I/O, TLS and RESP parsing run in parallel. Command execution against the shared keyspace is still serialized by a single global lock: a fair ticket spinlock ('fastlock', with an x86-64 assembly fast path) that spins with pause/yield and falls back to a futex wait, and that uses otherwise wasted spin time to do incremental dict rehashing ('async rehash'). KEYS/SCAN, and optionally GET/MGET ('enable-async-commands') and in-process BGSAVE ('use-fork no'), read from copy-on-write MVCC snapshots of the database so they do not hold the global lock.

**Use it when:**
- A single Redis 6.x node that is CPU-bound on networking, TLS or protocol parsing (many connections, small GET/SET values) and you want more ops/s from one box without sharding into Redis Cluster or running one instance per core
- TLS-terminated Redis traffic: the benchmarked Redis 6 could not combine io-threads with TLS, while KeyDB does TLS on every server thread
- Existing Redis 6.x deployments on Linux (Redis 6 RDB files, modules, Lua) that want a binary swap and can tolerate a stale codebase
- You specifically need active-active (multi-master) replication or per-member hash/set expiry, which upstream Redis does not provide

**Skip it when:**
- New production deployments: no commits since April 2024, last release v6.3.4 (Oct 2023), the lead developer left Snap in early 2025 and told users to move to Valkey, and deadlock/crash issues (e.g. #883 replication deadlock, #743, #827) remain open
- Anything needing Redis 7+ commands or data: RDB_VERSION is 9, so Redis 7 dumps (RDB v10) fail to load (#527) and Redis 7 commands such as PEXPIRETIME are missing
- Write-heavy or hot-key workloads and long MULTI/EXEC or Lua: every command still runs under one global lock (transactions hold it for the whole EXEC), so parallelism is limited to I/O and parsing
- Non-Linux hosts, and ARM with caution: the threading model relies on Linux SO_REUSEPORT load balancing, and there are open ARM startup-assert reports (#856)
- Multi-master or FLASH setups you cannot babysit: FLASH is labelled experimental/beta, active replication has an open data-consistency report (#366), and HN users reported cluster-wide crashes and deadlocks in multi-master mode

**Integration:** standalone server binary (keydb-server, built with make; Docker image eqalpha/keydb); not a linkable library · Bundled in deps/: jemalloc, Lua, hiredis, linenoise, hdr_histogram, moodycamel concurrentqueue, cpp-statsd-client, memkind (optional), RocksDB submodule (FLASH only). System: OpenSSL (TLS on by default), libuuid, libcurl (MOTD, disable with NO_MOTD=yes), nasm (x86-64 spinlock), bz2/zstd/lz4/snappy for RocksDB builds; Makefile can link system jemalloc/RocksDB/hiredis instead · C++17 (-std=c++17 -fno-rtti) plus C11/C99 for the C files; GCC or Clang (Clang builds use libc++); GCC 13.1 build fixed in 6.3.4; minimum compiler versions not documented · Linux (tested); x86-64 gets the assembly spinlock, aarch64 builds exist but have open crash reports; FreeBSD compiles as of 6.3.4; macOS builds but README says only Linux is supported for the threading model

**Vs siblings:** No siblings catalogued yet.

**Gotchas:**
- server-threads should follow NIC queue count, not core count: the README recommends 4 (default 2) and warns more threads can be slower because the global lock is a spinlock, yet the headline TLS benchmark used 16 threads with affinity
- An existing redis.conf with 'io-threads 8' silently becomes 8 KeyDB server threads, since io-threads is an alias for server-threads
- KeyDB expects exclusive use of its cores (spinning waiters burn CPU), and keydb-benchmark/redis-benchmark are single-threaded and too slow to measure it; use memtier on separate cores
- multi-master-no-forward yes loses data unless every master is in a full mesh; enable-async-commands relaxes cross-client read-your-writes ordering and currently covers only GET/MGET

**Status:** Stale: last release v6.3.4 (Oct 2023) and last commit April 2024, and the lead developer, leaving Snap, recommended Valkey. The code is BSD-3-Clause and builds with make, but anyone adopting it maintains the fork themselves.

[repo](https://github.com/Snapchat/KeyDB) · [benchmark](https://docs.keydb.dev/blog/2020/09/29/blog-post/)

##### otter  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Caffeine-style concurrent Go cache (adaptive W-TinyLFU): 10-34x hashicorp/golang-lru throughput at 25-100% reads; slower on pure writes.

**Beats:** hashicorp/golang-lru — The numbers come from the project's own Go port of Caffeine's GetPutBenchmark: 8 goroutines (-cpu=8), with a 32,768-entry cache pre-filled from a scrambled Zipf over about 10.9K string keys, so every Get hits and every Set is an update with no eviction. Run once on an Apple M1 Pro (darwin/arm64) with an unrecorded Go toolchain, otter reached 106.4M ops/s at 100% reads vs 3.14M for hashicorp/golang-lru v2 (about 34x), about 27x at 75/25, 21x at 50/50 and 10x at 25/75, while golang-lru was about 1.4x faster at 100% writes (3.23M vs 2.32M ops/s).

**Known shortcoming:** No Go toolchain version stated (go.mod minimum only). The ~27x read-throughput lead shrinks with writes, and at 100% writes golang-lru is ~1.4x faster.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark flatters it: a 32,768-slot cache over ~10.9K Zipf keys means every Get hits, every Set updates and nothing is evicted; one M1 Pro run. Pure writes lose (2.32M vs golang-lru 3.23M ops/s; second-slowest of 8 caches). MaximumSize is soft with the async executor (#171 shows 1,027 entries at max 2; use the sync executor). Open bugs: drainBuffers mutex contention under Compute (#177); the loader runs more than once per key (#152, fix PR #184 open). Not a drop-in (renamed API, W-TinyLFU not LRU); Go 1.24+; no commits since 2025-12.

**How:** The hash table is a fork of puzpuzpuz/xsync's MapOf, a CLHT-style (Cache-Line Hash Table) design with 64-byte buckets of 5 entries and SWAR meta-byte probing, so Get does no memory writes and takes no locks. Policy bookkeeping follows BP-Wrapper: reads go into a lossy striped ring buffer (the stripe count grows when contention is detected) and writes into a bounded growable MPSC queue, and both are replayed in batches under one eviction mutex taken with TryLock, so readers never wait on the policy lock. By contrast, golang-lru takes an exclusive sync.RWMutex Lock on every Get to move the entry to the front. Eviction is adaptive W-TinyLFU (admission window plus segmented main space, a 4-bit count-min sketch and hill-climbing window sizing), expiry uses a hierarchical timing wheel, and node structs are code-generated per feature set so options you don't use add no per-entry memory.

**Use it when:**
- Read-heavy in-process caches shared by many goroutines on multi-core machines, where golang-lru's global lock on Get is the bottleneck (first-party: 34x at 100% reads, 27x at 75/25, 21x at 50/50).
- Bounded caches whose access pattern is unknown or shifts between recency- and frequency-biased, where the adaptive W-TinyLFU window beats plain LRU hit rates on the project's trace simulations (S3, DS1, P8, OLTP, Glimpse, mixed).
- When you want Caffeine's feature set in Go: per-entry variable TTL, loader dedupe to limit stampedes, background refresh-ahead, weight-based bounds, stats counters, and deletion callbacks.
- Generic keys of any comparable type (hashed with maphash.Comparable) and any value type, from hundreds to millions of entries (the eviction benchmark covers capacities from 100 to 1,000,000).

**Skip it when:**
- Pure-write or update-heavy workloads: at 100% writes otter measured 2.32M ops/s vs golang-lru's 3.23M, behind theine, ristretto, sturdyc, gcache and ttlcache too; the docs themselves list extreme write-heavy loads as the exception.
- When the size cap must hold at every instant (tiny caches, or entries that pin scarce resources): with the default async Executor, a tight Set loop pushed a MaximumSize=2 cache to 1,027 entries (issue #171). The maintainer's fix is a synchronous Executor, which moves the eviction work back onto the caller.
- Low-contention or single-goroutine use, or small insert-only caches. The gains come from contention; in the insert-only eviction benchmark golang-lru was faster at capacity 100 (266.6 vs 307.5 ns/op), though otter was faster at 10K and 1M.
- Hot paths built on Compute with slow callbacks: Compute holds a hash-table bucket lock while the function runs, and open issue #177 reports heavy mutex delay in drainBuffers under frequent Compute (v2.2.1, root cause not yet found).
- Toolchains older than Go 1.24, or projects that cannot track new Go releases: the README says only the two most recent Go minor versions are supported.

**Integration:** module · none at runtime beyond the Go standard library (the only direct requirement in go.mod is stretchr/testify, for tests); the slog logger plugin is a separate module (plugin/pslog) · Go 1.24 (go.mod `go 1.24.0`; uses maphash.Comparable and runtime.AddCleanup). Only the two newest Go minor versions are supported; CI runs Go 1.25.x, plus a 32-bit job on 1.24.x. · pure Go, so any GOOS/GOARCH in principle. CI runs Linux (ubuntu-latest) plus a 32-bit build; the GOARCH=wasm build was fixed in v2.3.0. Published benchmarks exist only for darwin/arm64 (Apple M1 Pro).

**Vs siblings:** go-sieve and golang-fifo also report large wins over golang-lru with SIEVE-style policies; pick otter when you also need Caffeine-style features (variable TTL, loader dedupe, refresh-ahead, weights, stats) and an adaptive policy that holds up on both recency- and frequency-biased traces. Caffeine itself is the JVM original that otter's design and benchmark are ported from.

**Gotchas:**
- Policy state is only eventually consistent with the map: eviction and expiry reordering run in batches on a goroutine started through the Executor (default `go fn()`), so EstimatedSize can exceed MaximumSize for a while. Pass a synchronous Executor if you need strict bounds, as the project's own hit-ratio simulator does.
- Get(ctx, key, loader) works like singleflight: under a burst of concurrent Gets the loader can still run more than once for the same key (issue #152). A fix PR (#184) has been open since 2026-06-25.
- Weights are computed once, on write, and never recomputed; they only decide whether the cache is over capacity, not which entry is evicted. Zero weight or an expiry of math.MaxInt64 is the documented way to pin an entry.
- When expiry is enabled, a cleanup goroutine ticks once per second. It is stopped by a runtime.AddCleanup finalizer or by an explicit StopAllGoroutines (needed under synctest, issue #158). SaveCacheTo/LoadCacheFrom use encoding/gob, so K and V must be gob-encodable.

**Status:** v2.3.0 was released 2025-12-22 and main's last commit is 2025-12-23, but the maintainer was still answering issues in 2026 and bug reports and a fix PR (#184) are open; Apache-2.0, pure Go with no runtime dependencies, and the README lists users including Grafana, Centrifugo and FrankenPHP.

[repo](https://github.com/maypok86/otter) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maypok86/otter/main/benchmarks/throughput/results/throughput.txt)

##### Pogocache  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Multithreaded C cache server speaking RESP, memcache, HTTP and Postgres; about 2x Redis and 1.2-2.3x memcached throughput (author-run).

**Beats:** Redis, Memcached — The only benchmark is the author's cache-benchmarks suite: memtier_benchmark with 256 connections over a local UNIX socket, 1-1024 B values, persistence off, server pinned to 16 cores of an AWS c8g.8xlarge (ARM64), median of 31 runs. At 8 threads and pipeline 1, Pogocache 1.2.0 did 3.08M GET/s and 2.95M SET/s vs 1.51M/1.67M for Redis 8.2.1 and 2.60M/1.27M for memcached 1.6.38, with GET p99 of 0.119 ms vs 0.207 ms and 0.191 ms. It beats Redis, Valkey, memcached and Dragonfly in every thread/pipeline cell (smallest margin: 1.07x over memcached on GET at 1 thread, pipeline 10). No compiler flags are stated, and the older README table (about 3.5x Redis) is stale.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~3.5x-over-Redis figure is a stale July 2025 run against Redis 8.0.2; the current author-run suite shows ~2.0x Redis 8.2.1 and ~1.18x memcached GET at 8 threads. No compiler or flags. Garnet beats it at pipeline depths 25/50 (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** Garnet wins GET in 34 of 36 pipelined cells. Strings only (no Redis data types, pub/sub, MULTI or Lua), no HA/replication, SELECT 0 only. maxmemory is enforced by polling RSS once a second (a third-party Raspberry Pi 4 test ran ~50% over the limit). memcache CAS is off by default (every cas fails without --cas yes). Embedded mode uses hash seed 0 and no memory limit. The benchmarked 1.2.0 was AGPL; MIT only from 1.3.1. Source commits sparse since 2026-01.

**How:** Keys are hashed with th64 (random seed per process) into one of 4096 shards by default. Each shard is an independent Robin Hood open-addressing table with 10-byte buckets (48-bit entry pointer, 24-bit hash fragment, 1-byte distance-to-bucket) guarded by its own compare-and-swap spinlock, so two threads rarely wait on the same lock. Each entry is one heap allocation (mimalloc by default) with keys packed at 6 bits per character ('sixpack'). Networking runs one epoll/kqueue loop per thread with connections assigned round-robin; each tick batches reads, command execution and writes, using io_uring to submit the batched reads/writes on Linux when enough sockets are ready, and low-memory eviction uses 2-random sampling instead of maintaining an LRU list.

**Use it when:**
- Plain string GET/SET caching (sessions, rendered pages, query results; the benchmark used 1 B-1 KB values) where you want more ops per core than Redis or memcached and don't need Redis data types.
- Request/response traffic with little or no pipelining (depth 1-10) from many connections. This is where the author's suite shows the largest margins: about 2x Redis at 8 threads, with GET p99 of 0.12 ms vs 0.21 ms for Redis.
- CPU- or cost-limited hosts: about 7.1K CPU cycles per operation vs about 10K for Redis and 13.4K for memcached in the author's perf runs.
- Replacing memcached for text-protocol clients when you also want TLS, a password, HTTP access and manual SAVE/LOAD snapshots in one binary on Linux or macOS.
- An in-process cache in C/C++: drop in pogocache.c for a thread-safe sharded map with TTLs, eviction/notify callbacks and CAS, with no network hop.

**Skip it when:**
- You need Redis beyond strings. There are no hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub, MULTI/EXEC, Lua, INFO/HELLO/CLIENT, or databases other than 0 (SELECT only accepts 0). Lists and other types are an open request (issue #14).
- You need replication, failover or clustering. None exist, and high availability has been 'in the works' since Aug 2025 (issue #20). Persistence is only a manual SAVE/LOAD or a save on clean shutdown via --persist.
- Deeply pipelined clients (depth 25-50). In the same suite Garnet beats it on GETs in 34 of 36 pipelined configurations, e.g. 29.5M vs 11.4M ops/s at 8 threads, pipeline 50.
- Strict memory caps. The limit works by polling process RSS once a second. A third-party test with 1 MiB values on a Raspberry Pi 4 hit a VmHWM of 3.3 GB against --maxmemory 2 GiB (about 50% over).
- Risk-averse production. It was first released in July 2025 by a single company/maintainer, and the only published throughput benchmark is the author's own.

**Integration:** source-drop: the server binary is built with make (static release builds and a Docker image exist); pogocache.c + pogocache.h are embeddable · The server build git-clones and statically links mimalloc 3.1.5, jemalloc 5.3.0, liburing 2.12 (Linux) and OpenSSL 3.5.2, which needs cmake, autotools and perl at build time. Each can be disabled with NOMIMALLOC/NOJEMALLOC/NOURING/NOOPENSSL=1. The embedded pogocache.c needs only the C standard library. · C11 (stdatomic.h, static_assert) plus GCC/Clang extensions (__thread, __builtin_ia32_pause, -flto=auto); minimum compiler versions not documented · 64-bit Linux and macOS (documented; CI on ubuntu-latest); x86-64 and aarch64 spin hints; benchmarked on ARM64 (AWS c8g); no Windows; the Makefile also has an Emscripten/WASM target
