- You want to ship or persist the filter. to_bin produces a 28-byte little-endian header plus the fingerprint array, and contain queries that binary in place without deserializing it.
- You are replacing Bloomex or Blex and lookup latency is the bottleneck. At 1M keys the author's benchmark shows about 6x and 9x faster lookups, and about 2.8x over the Rust-NIF erbloom (ratios derived).

**Skip it when:**
- The set changes. There is no insert or delete after finalize, so every update is a full rebuild. The rebuild needs roughly 32 bytes per key of transient C memory (derived from the key buffer plus populate's scratch arrays), on top of the Erlang list and the `sets` dedup copy.
- Default hashing on large sets. erlang:phash2/1 returns only 27-bit values (0..2^27-1), so any non-member whose phash2 value collides with a member's is a false positive. The derived effective rate is ~1.1% at 1M keys and ~7.8% at 10M, against 0.39% for the filter alone. Use `none` with a 64-bit hash instead.
- You need a false-positive rate below ~0.4%. Only fuse8 is exposed (no fuse16); exor_filter offers xor16.
- Filters come from untrusted sources. The NIF checks only that the binary length matches its ArrayLength field (its minimum-size check is 16 bytes, for a 28-byte header) and never validates the segment fields, so a crafted binary can drive out-of-bounds reads inside the VM.
- You need a maintained dependency. There has been a single 0.1.0 release (2021), and the vendored binaryfusefilter.h predates two upstream fixes: guards for 0-2-key sets (2021-08-21/22), and a construction retry path that did not reset its state or reseed (2022-03-23, commit ed27385).

**Integration:** module · None at runtime, because FastFilter's binaryfusefilter.h is vendored. Building needs make (gmake on FreeBSD) and a C99 compiler, run by a rebar3 pre-compile hook. · Erlang/OTP 24+ (per the README; it uses sets version 2), rebar3 or Mix, and a C99 compiler with __uint128_t (GCC or Clang) · rebar3 build hooks exist only for Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and Solaris, so there is no Windows build. It is 64-bit only in practice because it needs __uint128_t, and the macOS Makefile defaults target x86_64 only.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over exor_filter (same author, xor8/xor16 NIF) when you want the smaller binary fuse layout and fuse8's error rate is good enough; the xorfilter entry cites ~13% over the information-theoretic bound, against ~23% for xor filters. The shared benchmark's ~9% lookup edge over xor8 at 1M keys is confounded, because only fuse8 skipped phash2. Choose exor_filter for 16-bit fingerprints, a custom hash function or a lower-memory incremental build, and outside the BEAM use the upstream C header (xor_singleheader) or xorf/xorfilter directly.

**Gotchas:**
- NIF errors are stored in the record instead of being returned. new(List, none) only checks that some element is an integer (lists:any), so a mixed list or negative integers produce a #fuse8{} whose reference is {error, convert_to_uint64_t_error}. The first contain on that record raises case_clause. A negative integer key passed to contain on a `none` filter also raises case_clause.
- A serialized filter built with `none` must be queried with contain/4 (..., none) or reloaded with from_bin/2. contain/2 and contain/3 on a binary always apply phash2, which gives silent false negatives.
- The helper named over_100k matches on 10_001, so builds of more than 10,000 elements (not 100k, as its doc says) run on a dirty CPU scheduler. Smaller builds and every contain call run on normal schedulers; open issue #4 proposes a dirty contain for large filters.
- On macOS the Makefile's default CFLAGS and LDFLAGS hard-code `-arch x86_64`. An Apple Silicon (arm64) BEAM therefore needs those variables overridden before the NIF will load (inferred from the Makefile, not tested).

**Status:** Abandoned: there has been one hex release (0.1.0, 2021-08-08, ~300 downloads), the last commit was 2021-08-17, and in November 2024 the author wrote that it had been 'quite a while' since he last touched it. It is Apache-2.0 and about 1,150 lines of C and Erlang, so vendoring it is realistic, and the Zabrane/efuse_filter fork carries an unmerged update to the latest upstream header.

[repo](https://github.com/mpope9/efuse_filter) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mpope9/exor_bechmark#benchee-output)

##### Entry-Extensible Cuckoo Filter (E2CF)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Growable cuckoo filter that extends buckets into adjacent memory; paper: up to 82% less query time than Dynamic Cuckoo Filter.

**Beats:** State-of-the-art dynamic approximate-membership filters with filter-level extension (the paper's references suggest Dynamic Cuckoo Filter / Dynamic Bloom Filter; exact baselines are not named on the README or in the abstract) — The open-access HAL manuscript of the NPC 2020 paper (hal-03768761) names the baselines: DBF and the lab's own DCF, with m=2^22 buckets, b=4, α=0.9 and 16-bit fingerprints for E2CF and DCF, run on an Intel Xeon E5-2670 at 2.60GHz with 64 GB RAM over MAWI/WIDE traces and synthetic data, averaging five runs. It reports negative-query time up to 82% lower than DCF (85% vs DBF) with up to 32 sub-filters, instantaneous non-repeatable insert time up to 28% (45%) lower, cumulative insert time up to 22% (41%) lower, delete time up to 79% (84%) lower, and memory comparable to DCF. All results are plots with no tables, the compiler and flags are not stated, and the public repo (-O0 build, 12-bit fingerprints, no baseline) cannot reproduce them.

**Known shortcoming:** The baseline is unnamed dynamic filters (likely DCF/DBF), not a plain cuckoo filter; no baseline code in the repo and an -O0 build.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo differs from the paper: fingerprints are hard-coded at 12 bits whatever FPR is requested (~0.2% at 1 sub-filter, ~3% at 16). Won't build on OpenSSL >=1.1.0. Bugs: queryImpl's 12-bit miss path has no return (UB), insertItem always returns true (silent drops), the destructor deletes PtoCF[128] out of bounds, 7-byte buckets are accessed as unaligned 8-byte words. Growth is capped at ~16 sub-filters and compact() is declared but never defined.

**Known shortcoming:** The paper (HAL hal-03768761) compares against DBF and DCF with plot-only results (query -82% vs DCF at <=32 sub-filters, insert -28%); test.cpp is not a real benchmark (-O0, no baseline); not thread-safe; little-endian only.

**How:** The core technique is entry-level extension. When a partial cuckoo filter (PCF) k at level l splits, its odd-indexed buckets move to a new PCF numbered k+2^l, and the freed entries merge into the neighbouring even bucket, so a logical bucket at level l is 2^l physically adjacent 4-slot buckets. A query hashes once, picks the PCF by index mod 2^l, and scans each of its two candidate runs sequentially with a 64-bit SWAR match (hasvalue12, from the Stanford bit-twiddling hacks). DCF instead makes two small random bucket reads per sub-filter. Asynchronous extension (each PCF splits on its own once its load passes a threshold or a kick chain fails) keeps memory close to DCF's. Fine-grained splitting moves buckets lazily during inserts, tracked by a per-bucket flag (a 4-bit level field in the code), so there is no stop-the-world rehash. By the paper's own cost model (Eq. 4-5), query memory traffic still grows linearly with the number of PCFs s (s/8 to s/2 cache lines, vs 2s for DCF), so the gain is a smaller constant, not O(1) lookups.

**Use it when:**
- Research or teaching: you want a compact reference for entry-level extension to set against DCF and the Dynamic Bloom Filter (DBF), and you will write your own benchmark harness. The lab's CGCL-codes/DCF repo carries both the DCF and DBF code that the paper compared against.
- A deletable filter must grow several-fold from an unknown starting size, and lookup latency, not space, is the bottleneck. The paper's gains grow with the number of sub-filters (measured up to 32). With a single filter, E2CF is a plain cuckoo filter.
- Lookup streams dominated by absent keys (the paper uses MAWI/WIDE network-traffic traces), where DCF must probe every sub-filter before it can answer 'no'. At s=32 the paper shows E2CF ahead of DCF and DBF at every negative-query mix from 0% to 100%.
- Single-threaded x86-64 Linux code that can vendor about 1,200 lines of C++, fix it, and replace the per-operation OpenSSL SHA-1 with a fast non-cryptographic hash.

**Skip it when:**
- Any production use as-is. Reading the code shows correctness bugs: CuckooFilter::queryImpl has no return statement on the 12-bit miss path (undefined behaviour, which is risky once you add -O2). insertItem returns true even when an insert or victim relocation failed. The destructor deletes PtoCF[128], one element past the 128-slot array.
- Large or unbounded growth. Load-triggered splits happen only while countCF<16 and numCF+2^l<=16, kick-failure splits stop past slot 37, and the level is a 4-bit field in fixed 128-slot arrays. Beyond those limits, items are dropped while the call still reports success. Shrinking is not implemented: the paper describes merging sparse PCFs, but compact() has no definition.
- When you need a specific false-positive rate. The fingerprint is 12 bits whatever FPR you pass, because every branch of the constructor's size switch sets 12 (the paper's experiments used 16). Each level also doubles the entries scanned, so by the paper's Eq. 7 the rate is about 2^(l+1)*4/2^12: roughly 0.2% with one PCF and about 3% with 16. The repo's default config asks for 0.05%.
- Static or known-size sets. E2CF is only faster than other growable filters. A fixed cuckoo, Morton, Vacuum, Xor or BuRR filter sized for the peak is smaller or faster and better engineered.
- Multithreaded access, big-endian or strict-alignment targets, binary keys containing NUL bytes (keys are hashed up to strlen), or builds against OpenSSL 1.1.0 or newer.

**Integration:** source-drop (the makefile builds only the ./test driver; there is no library target, install step or package) · OpenSSL libcrypto (EVP SHA-1 in hashfunction.cpp, linked with -lssl -lcrypto), and it needs the pre-1.1.0 API: a stack-allocated EVP_MD_CTX and EVP_MD_CTX_cleanup · C++11 (makefile: /usr/bin/g++ -std=c++0x -Wall, with no -O flag) plus OpenSSL 1.0.x headers. The authors built on RHEL 6.2; the compiler version is not stated. · Little-endian only (the code carries 'Little-Endian' comments and packs 12-bit fingerprints with unaligned 16/32/64-bit type-punned loads and stores). Only tested on x86-64 Linux. It uses no SIMD, only 64-bit SWAR.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when the object of study is growable filters. It is the query-optimised successor to the sibling Dynamic Cuckoo Filter (DCF, same lab), and you would read the two side by side. For anything that ships, size a static filter for the peak and rebuild on growth: the efficient/cuckoofilter reference, Morton Filter (1.3-2.5x faster lookups than it) or Vacuum Filter if you need deletes, and Xor or BuRR for immutable sets.

**Gotchas:**
- It does not build against current OpenSSL as written. hashfunction.cpp declares EVP_MD_CTX on the stack and calls EVP_MD_CTX_cleanup, and OpenSSL 1.1.0 (Aug 2016) made EVP_MD_CTX opaque and removed that call (use EVP_MD_CTX_new/free/reset). Every operation also computes a full SHA-1 and allocates a std::string before any filter work.
- Buckets are 7 bytes (four 12-bit fingerprints plus a 4-bit level) but are read and written as unaligned 8-byte words. The last bucket's load runs one byte past the allocation. The split helper addBNewCF does *(uint64_t*)p &= 0xf0000000000000, which zeroes byte 7: the next bucket's level nibble and the low 4 bits of its first fingerprint.
- test.cpp is not a benchmark. It records insert time only every 20,000,000 inserts and never increments its false-positive counter, most Metric fields are uninitialised, and the shipped config is 100 items. That is why result/result.txt holds garbage. The repo has no DCF or DBF code to compare against.
- Headers leak: cuckoofilter.h does 'using namespace std;' and #defines MaxNumKicks 40, and EECuckooFilter.h relies on both (unqualified queue<int>). Split paths print to stdout with cout inside insert, and each CuckooFilter destructor frees the Bucket array but leaks the fingerprint storage.

**Status:** Abandoned: one code upload plus README edits on 2020-08-28/29, 3 stars, no issues or releases, one fork identical to upstream and the other no longer reachable. It is Apache-2.0 and about 1,200 lines of library code, so it can be vendored as a design reference, but it needs an OpenSSL 1.0.x toolchain or a hash patch plus the bug fixes above before it is usable.

[repo](https://github.com/CGCL-codes/E2CF) · [benchmark](https://github.com/CGCL-codes/E2CF#e2cf-the-entry-extensible-cuckoo-filter)

##### exor_filter (Erlang NIF, Xor Filter)  `Erlang`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Erlang/Elixir C NIF for static xor8/xor16 filters; 2.6-10x faster lookups than BEAM Bloom libraries in the author's benchmark.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — In the author's own Benchee run (exor_filter pinned to v0.5.2, a C NIF built with -O3 -std=c99 by an unnamed compiler, on Elixir 1.12.2 and OTP 24.0.5, on an Intel i5-7267U macOS laptop), 10,000 lookups per iteration took 1.55 ms for xor8 on a 1M-key filter, against 8.87 ms for Bloomex, 13.17 ms for Blex and 4.01 ms for the erbloom Rust NIF (about 5.7x, 8.5x and 2.6x), and 1.77 ms for xor16 at 10M against 15.24 ms (Bloomex) and 18.47 ms (Blex). The Bloom filters were configured at 10% or 1% FPR, the queried keys 1..10,000 are all members of the large filters, and the script builds its 'erbloom 10M' filter from only 10k keys, so the 2.2x erbloom-at-10M ratio is not like-for-like.

**Known shortcoming:** Ratios are derived; the Bloom baselines ran at FPR 0.1/0.01 vs xor8's ~0.39%, so FPRs are not matched; the NIF is C built with -O3 (compiler unnamed).

**Known shortcoming:** The default phash2 hash is only 27 bits (README says 60), adding ~0.7% FPR at 1M keys and ~7% at 10M. GPL-2.0+ EWAH files are compiled into the Apache-2.0 NIF (license risk). from_bin/contain size checks can overflow so a crafted binary causes an out-of-bounds read and node crash; incremental add seems to leak and is not dirty-scheduled (#21). Abandoned since 0.8.2 (2021-12); the same author's efuse_filter is faster.

**How:** It is a xor filter (Graf & Lemire): each key maps to 3 slots in a table of about 1.23n 8- or 16-bit fingerprints. A lookup is one murmur64 finalizer mix, three multiply-shift range reductions (Lemire's alternative to modulo), three loads and one XOR compare, so it always costs exactly 3 memory accesses. A Bloom filter probes k bits instead. Construction peels a random 3-hypergraph and retries with a new seed up to 100 times. On the BEAM, much of the gain also comes from doing the whole probe in one C NIF call on a native resource. Bloomex probes in pure Elixir and Blex probes over Erlang atomics. The benchmark's roughly 155 ns per lookup includes the Elixir loop, phash2 and NIF-call overhead, not just the C probe.

**Use it when:**
- An Erlang or Elixir service needs a read-mostly membership pre-check over a set that is built once, such as a blocklist, a seen-ID set, or a guard in front of a slow store or cache, and many processes query it.
- Lookup latency matters more than build time. The author's run shows about 1.5-1.8 ms per 10,000 lookups on 1M-10M-key filters, against 4-18 ms for Bloomex, Blex and erbloom.
- You want less memory per unit of accuracy than a Bloom filter: xor8 uses about 9.8 bits/key at a 2^-8 (~0.4%) FPR, and xor16 about 19.7 bits/key at a 2^-16 (~0.0015%) FPR.
- The set has up to about 20K keys with the default hash, or you can supply your own collision-free 64-bit hash (or pre-hashed uint64 keys) for larger sets.
- You need to ship a filter to another node or system. to_bin produces a flat binary that contain/2 can query directly without deserializing.

**Skip it when:**
- The set changes after construction. There is no add or delete on a finalized filter, so every change means rebuilding from the full key list. Blex and Bloomex support incremental puts.
- Large sets with the default hash. erlang:phash2/1 returns only 27 bits (0..2^27-1 per the Erlang docs), so every non-member that collides with a member is a false positive. By our arithmetic that adds about 0.7% FPR at 1M keys and about 7% at 10M, which swamps xor8's 0.4%.
- You need the best filter available on the BEAM today. The same author's efuse_filter (binary fuse filters, OTP 24+, almost API-compatible) beat xor8 and xor16 at every size in the same benchmark (though its rows used pre-hashed `none` keys, skipping phash2). The vendored xorfilter.h also predates the upstream binary fuse filters.
- Strict license policies or proprietary distribution. The NIF compiles in git's EWAH bitmap files (bitmap.c, ewah_bitmap.c, ewok.h), which are GPL-2.0-or-later, alongside the Apache-2.0 code.
- Production use that needs an actively maintained native dependency. It has had no release since 0.8.2 (2021-12-02) and has no CI (issue #19 open). It has no Windows build hook, and any NIF memory bug crashes the whole BEAM node, as the fixed double-free in issue #17 showed.

**Integration:** module (hex.pm/rebar3/mix package that compiles a C NIF shared library via make at build time) · No runtime deps. The build needs a C99 compiler, make (gmake on FreeBSD) and erl_interface (libei). It vendors xor_singleheader (Apache-2.0) and git's EWAH bitmap code (GPL-2.0+). · Erlang/OTP 23+ for 0.8.x (the README says to use v0.5.2 below OTP 23), plus a C99 compiler. Newer OTP releases are not tested or documented; the benchmark used OTP 24.0.5 and Elixir 1.12.2. · Linux, macOS (Apple Silicon since 0.8.2), FreeBSD and Solaris, per the rebar3 pre_hooks and Makefile. There is no Windows build hook. The code is endian-portable only for xor8 serialization.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when the code runs on the BEAM and you want a ready-made NIF rather than writing one. Outside Erlang/Elixir, use the C library it wraps (Xor Filter / xor_singleheader, which now also has smaller binary fuse filters) or xorf in Rust. On the BEAM, first consider the same author's efuse_filter, whose fuse8 rows beat xor8 in the same benchmark.

**Gotchas:**
- The README says the default phash2 hash 'uses 60 bits on a 64-bit system', but erlang:phash2/1 returns 0..2^27-1. Colliding members are silently deduplicated (usort), so there is an FPR floor of roughly n/2^27. With a custom fun or `none`, keys are not deduplicated, and construction returns {error, duplicates_in_hash_error} if any hashes repeat.
- The incremental builder is not dirty-scheduled, so a large finalize can block a normal scheduler (open issue #21). It supports only the default hash (open issue #15). add/2 mutates and returns the same resource. add_elements_to_bitset also overwrites filter->bitmap without freeing the previous EWAH bitmap, so each add appears to leak it.
- contain/2 and from_bin/1 accept raw binaries, and their size check multiplies an unchecked 64-bit blockLength read from the binary. A crafted binary can therefore pass validation and cause out-of-bounds reads that crash the node. Only query or deserialize binaries you produced. xor16 to_bin copies host-endian uint16s (a 'TODO endianness' in the source).
- Errors come back as {error, Atom} tuples rather than exceptions or false. For example, a custom hash that returns a negative number or one above 2^64 makes contain return {error, get_key_for_contains_error}, and contain on an unfinalized builder returns {error, unfinalized_filter_error}.

**Status:** Abandoned since 0.8.2 (2021-12-02), with 3 open issues including no CI and blocking incremental builds, and about 1,100 all-time hex downloads. The Erlang and xor code is Apache-2.0 but the bundled EWAH files are GPL-2.0+; at about 900 lines of NIF C it is small enough to fork, strip the EWAH builder from, and vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/mpope9/exor_filter) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mpope9/exor_bechmark#benchee-output)

##### fastbloom  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust Bloom filter crate: classic non-blocked layout, faster lookups than other Rust Bloom crates, plus a lock-free atomic variant.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — The author's Criterion microbenchmark on an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X measures per-lookup latency for u64 keys in a 64 KiB filter holding 45,000 items (about 8 hashes each). Each iteration repeats the same 10 query keys, the rustc version and flags are unstated, and perf.py reads Windows-style paths, suggesting a Windows build. fastbloom (with foldhash) took 1.36 ns per non-member check vs 5.16 ns for sbbf (xxh3) and 14.5-42.6 ns for SipHash-based crates, and 7.67 ns per member check vs 5.30 ns for sbbf and 27-122 ns for the rest. Insert throughput, multi-threaded runs and out-of-cache filters were not measured.

**Known shortcoming:** The '2-20x' is overstated: on its own chart the sbbf crate's member check (5.30 ns) beats fastbloom (7.67 ns); measured gains are ~3.8-31x for non-members and ~3.6-16x for members vs the rest. Only lookups are benchmarked (no inserts), and fastbloom used foldhash while the others used SipHash.

**Known shortcoming:** Flattering benchmark: the same 10 query keys repeated against a 64 KiB cache-hot filter, with foldhash vs SipHash rivals; no insert, multi-threaded or DRAM-resident numbers; rustc/flags unstated. Non-blocked design (k random probes per hit). Recent correctness fixes: FP blowup for filters >512 MiB until 0.16 (#22), atomic set() fixed in 0.14.1; 0.17 serde format breaks older versions; still 0.x with frequent breaking bumps.

**Known shortcoming:** Each filter gets a random SipHash key, so union/intersect require the same seed and this is not checked; the README's hash description is stale; tiny expected_items gives a huge k.

**How:** Each item is hashed once, to 64 bits. The other k-1 bit positions come from cheap double hashing (Kirsch-Mitzenmacher, 'Less hashing, same performance'): h2 = h1 * constant, then each next index is rotl(h1, 5) + h2, instead of k separate hash calls. Indexes are mapped to the bit array with Lemire's multiply-shift fast range reduction rather than modulo. contains returns on the first unset bit, so a non-member usually costs one hash and one or two memory probes. The bit array is a plain boxed u64 slice with no SIMD and no blocking; since 0.17 the author deliberately chose a non-blocked layout, trading member-check speed for accuracy and faster non-member rejection (issue #20).

**Use it when:**
- Rust services where most queries are misses, such as cache or disk-read avoidance or dedup pre-checks, since non-member checks are its strongest case (1.36 ns vs 5-43 ns for other crates on the author's benchmark).
- Filters that grow by incremental inserts at runtime and may need union or intersect, which a build-once xor or fuse filter cannot do.
- Many threads inserting and querying one filter: AtomicBloomFilter uses fetch_or on AtomicU64 words with no lock.
- Low false-positive targets per bit: the author's accuracy chart shows it tracking the classic-Bloom curve, well below the blocked sbbf and below bloom and bloomfilter at the same load.
- no_std or embedded targets with alloc: CI checks thumbv7em-none-eabi, and portable-atomic covers targets without native 64-bit atomics.

**Skip it when:**
- Workloads dominated by positive lookups: a member check touches k random words, and on the author's own chart the SIMD split-block sbbf is faster (5.30 ns vs 7.67 ns).
- Filters much larger than cache: non-blocked probes each risk a cache miss. The published numbers come only from a 64 KiB, cache-resident filter, and DRAM-scale behaviour is not measured.
- Static key sets built once: a xor or binary fuse filter (xorf) gives smaller filters and constant-probe lookups.
- Needs deletion or counting: not supported. A counting Bloom filter (issue #10) and xor filters (issue #7) are open requests.
- Cross-language or cross-version persisted filters: no C API, and 0.17 changed the algorithm, so serialized filters are incompatible with earlier versions.

**Integration:** crate · foldhash, siphasher, libm, portable-atomic (always); rand (default feature), serde and loom (optional features) · Rust 1.70 (rust-version in Cargo.toml; CI has an MSRV job on 1.70), edition 2021 · any Rust target, with no arch-specific or SIMD code; std and no_std+alloc, with thumbv7em-none-eabi checked in CI; tests run on ubuntu-latest

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over xorf when you need incremental or concurrent inserts rather than a build-once static set. Pick it over the Impala-style SIMD blocked Bloom (efficient/cuckoofilter) or a cuckoo filter when you are in Rust, misses dominate and you want classic-Bloom accuracy per bit without deletes. Choose a blocked Bloom when hits dominate or the filter lives in DRAM, and a cuckoo filter when you need deletion.

**Gotchas:**
- The default hasher is SipHash-1-3 with a random key per filter. Filters built separately cannot be unioned, intersected or compared unless both use .seed(&u128) or the same hasher, and union and intersect do not check this. Note also that the headline benchmark swapped in foldhash.
- Every probe is derived from one 64-bit hash, so a weak custom hasher (or raw values fed to insert_hash) degrades all k positions at once. The README says hashes are built from 32-bit halves, but the 0.17 code actually multiplies and rotates a single 64-bit hash.
- k comes from ln2 * bits / items, and the minimum size is 64 bits, so tiny expected_items gives huge k (issue #17: 354 hashes for 1 item when the minimum was 512 bits; expected_items(0) meant u32::MAX hashes before the clamp to 1). In 0.15-0.16, hashes(0) panicked; 0.17 clamps it to 1.
- Recent correctness fixes, so pin to 0.17 or later: AtomicBitVec::set returned the wrong value until 0.14.1, and filters above u32::MAX bits (about 512 MiB) mapped every index into a u32 range, causing mass false positives, until 0.16 (issue #22). The src/ tree has no unsafe code.

**Status:** Actively maintained (0.17.0 on 2026-03-01, maintainer still replying to issues in July 2026), MIT OR Apache-2.0, a small pure-safe-Rust crate with heavy real-world use (about 23.6M crates.io downloads, a dependency of quinn-proto, turso_core and libafl), but still 0.x with breaking releases every few months.

[repo](https://github.com/tomtomwombat/fastbloom) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tomtomwombat/fastbloom#speed)

##### GBF-NEON (Galois Bipartite Filter, Ribbon-filter variant)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Static uint64 filter using per-block GF(2) solves and NEON parity; ~2x faster negative queries than author's blocked Bloom.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — Only the author's src/bench_vs.cpp, run once on one Apple M2 (-O3 -march=native, compiler unstated) with 1M random uint64 keys, backs the claim. The timed loop covers only the 1M non-member queries, so '8.4 ns vs 16.4 ns' is amortized per-query time on an all-miss stream, not isolated latency or a mixed workload. The baseline is the author's scalar blocked Bloom (512-bit blocks, 8 double-hashed bits, 64-bit modulo, early-exit loop), not a library implementation. My re-simulation of its hashing reproduces the published 2.90% and 1.97% FPRs, while the same layout with independent bit positions gives about 2.5% and 0.40%. So GBF's FPR edge holds at about 8.3 bits/key, but the 12-bits/key Bloom row is about 5x worse than it should be. GBF's 30 ms build uses one thread per partition, against 4-7 ms of single-threaded Bloom inserts.

**Known shortcoming:** A hobby project (0 stars) whose baseline is its own blocked Bloom filter; -O3 -march=native with the compiler unstated. The author reports 7 of 8 tried ideas failed.

**Known shortcoming:** The 8.4 ns lookup is an all-miss stream; the author's own 50/50 mix is 20.2 ns, and the Bloom baseline is never timed on hits. The baseline is the author's branchy scalar Bloom with 64-bit modulo; with proper hashing the same layout gets 2.5%/0.40% FPR instead of 2.90%/1.97%, so the 12 bits/key comparison is ~5x too pessimistic.

**Known shortcoming:** Memory sawtooth from power-of-two block rounding (1M keys 8.52 bits/key, 1,015,809 keys 16.77); build throws with no retry and in simulation almost always fails for N<=8k with 16 partitions (75% at 32k). Fixed 0.78% FPR, static only, x86 performance never measured, POSIX only. The xor8 adapter maps buffer serialization to a file-path save (silent misuse) and load_mmap skips the size check. Three commits in two days, AI-built.

**How:** Memory is split into 64-byte blocks, each holding eight 64-bit columns. Each key is placed by 2-choice cuckoo hashing into one of two blocks inside a hash-selected partition (64 keys per block at most, about 62 targeted). Gaussian elimination over GF(2) then solves each block so that the parity of (key hash vector AND column j) reproduces the key's 8-bit fingerprint, retrying up to 256 per-block seeds. The author calls it a Ribbon-filter variant, but it is block-local dense elimination with cuckoo placement, not Ribbon's banded matrix. A query hashes to two block indices using bit masks (power-of-two sizing removes the modulo), prefetches both cache lines, and checks 8 AND-popcount parities per block. On aarch64 those parities are explicit NEON vcnt/vpaddl lanes, which the author measured at 1.5-3 ns faster than the scalar __builtin_parityll loop. GBF touches two cache lines per query versus the blocked Bloom's one. The Bloom baseline uses a 64-bit modulo and a branchy 8-probe loop, so part of the gap likely comes from that baseline's implementation rather than the structure.

**Use it when:**
- A read-only set of 64-bit keys (or keys you pre-hash to 64 bits) that is built once and queried many times on Apple Silicon or other aarch64 with NEON, where most lookups miss. The 8.4 ns figure comes from an all-negative query stream.
- Around 1M-key sets where about 0.8% FPR at about 8.5 bits/key suits you and you can size N just below a power-of-two boundary. Bits/key is lowest just under 62 x 2^k keys, for example 1,015,808 or 2,031,616.
- Filters built offline and shipped as files to same-architecture readers: save() plus load_mmap() maps the payload without copying.
- Studying or prototyping cache-line-local GF(2) filters. The core is a readable 649-line header with a libFuzzer harness and a 'what failed' design log (ARTICLE.md).

**Skip it when:**
- Sets that change, or targets other than about 0.78% FPR. There is no insert or erase, and the 8-bit fingerprint and 2-way probe are hard-coded, so lower FPR cannot be bought with more memory.
- Arbitrary or growing N when memory matters. The block count rounds up to a power of two, so bits/key follows a sawtooth between about 8.4 and 16.8. By the sizing code, 1,000,000 keys cost 8.52 bits/key but 1,015,809 keys cost 16.77 at the same about 0.78% FPR. The README's 'up to ~30%' over-allocation understates this.
- Small and mid-size sets built with the default thread count. There is no resize-and-retry: the constructor throws std::runtime_error and the C API returns false. In my re-simulation of the partitioning at worst-case sizes with 16 partitions (machines with 9-16 hardware threads), some partition exceeds its capacity, which guarantees failure, in essentially 100% of trials up to N=7,936. The rate is 96% at 15,872, 75% at 31,744 and 20% at 63,488, and 83% at N=992 with 4 partitions. The tests build small sets only with threads=1, and the fuzz harness de-duplicates keys and treats build exceptions as acceptable.
- Mixed hit/miss or positive-heavy lookups without your own benchmark. The author's own article measured 20.2 ns for a 50/50 mix (versus 6.5 ns all-positive), which it attributes to branch mispredicts. The Bloom baseline was never timed on positives or mixes.
- x86, Windows, or anything that needs a track record. x86 falls back to a scalar parity loop with no AVX2/AVX-512 path and has never been performance-measured (the CI logs have since expired). The code needs POSIX open/mmap and GCC/Clang builtins, so there is no MSVC. It is a 3-commit, 0-star weekend project.

**Integration:** header-only (src/gbf.hpp + src/hash.hpp); optional static lib gbf_c for the C API · none beyond the C++ standard library, pthreads (std::thread; CMake links Threads::Threads) and POSIX file/mmap calls · C++17 and CMake 3.16+. Needs GCC or Clang (__builtin_parityll, __builtin_prefetch). Compiler versions are not documented: CI built with ubuntu-latest gcc and clang, and the logs have expired. · aarch64 with NEON, measured only on an Apple M2. x86-64 Linux compiles and passes tests in CI using scalar parity, with no performance numbers. POSIX only; no Windows.

**Vs siblings:** Rarely. At its best-case N, GBF's 8.52 bits/key for 0.78% FPR is about 22% above the 7-bit minimum, roughly the Xor filter's 23% overhead cited in the BuRR entry, and it probes two cache lines instead of three with a parallel build. But xor_singleheader is mature, portable and has no size cliff, BuRR is far closer to the space minimum, and the Impala-derived SIMD blocked Bloom in efficient/cuckoofilter supports inserts with one cache line per query. Pick GBF only for a read-only uint64 set on aarch64 whose size you control, or as a small header to experiment with.

**Gotchas:**
- The xor8 adapter maps xor8_serialize/xor8_deserialize to gbf_filter_save/gbf_filter_load. In xor_singleheader those functions take a memory buffer (char*), but here they take a file path, so ported code compiles and silently treats the buffer as a filename. xor8_allocate's size argument is ignored, and populate copies the keys and builds with all hardware threads.
- The file format stores a magic number plus block and partition counts, but not WAYS and not the payload length. load_mmap() never checks the file size, so a truncated or untrusted file can be read out of bounds, and a GBF<3> file opened as GBF<2> silently gives false negatives. After load, key_count() and bits_per_key() return 0.
- The layout (partition count) depends on the build machine's hardware_concurrency unless you pass threads explicitly. The CMake gbf_headers INTERFACE target also pushes -O3 -march=native onto every target that links it, which yields non-portable binaries.
- The README's batch example does not compile, because std::vector<bool> has no data(); contains_batch needs a real bool array (bench.cpp casts a char buffer). fast_hash (a splitmix64-style mixer) is declared in the global namespace. The version labels disagree: v0.3 in bench_vs.cpp, v0.4 in gbf.hpp, v0.8 in comments, v1.0 in the README.

**Status:** Effectively a one-weekend drop: three commits on 2026-05-27/28 and nothing since, 0 stars, forks or issues, and the author says it was built in 24 hours and heavily AI-assisted. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to read and vendor, but not production-proven.

[repo](https://github.com/ElVec1o/GBF-NEON) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ElVec1o/GBF-NEON#head-to-head-vs-competent-blocked-bloom-buildbench_vs)

##### go-qfext (Facebook Quotient Filter for Go)  `Go`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go quotient filter that keeps full 64-bit hashes plus optional per-key integers; about 3.6x faster positive lookups than bits-and-blooms/bloom.

**Beats:** Bloom filter (bits-and-blooms/bloom v3 Go implementation) — The claim rests on one README go test -bench run on an Apple M1 MacBook Pro (Go version unstated, numbers from August 2021): positive Contains lookups took 20.43 ns/op unpacked and 30.95 ns/op packed, against 74.47 ns/op for bits-and-blooms/bloom v3.0.1 built with NewWithEstimates(273, 0.0001). That is about 3.6x and 2.4x faster, not the README's 'about 4 times'. The test set is 273 short strings (163 distinct), so both structures sit in L1 cache (Bloom about 0.65 KB with 14 probes, unpacked filter 4 KB), and the filter runs at a far lower false-positive rate than the Bloom filter it is compared with.

**Known shortcoming:** Go version unstated; the 3.6x/2.4x are derived from page data and the README's '4x' overstates them.

**Known shortcoming:** Weak benchmark: 163 unique keys (the table fits in L1), positive lookups only, and the Bloom filter set to 1e-4 FPR (14 probes per lookup). Memory-heavy: stores the full 64-bit hash with non-tunable FPR, about 77 bits/key packed vs ~19 for Bloom (the README's 1B-key example needs 9 GB). No delete or merge; the disk reader does one pread per slot and panics on I/O error (no mmap, issue #7 open since 2020).

**Known shortcoming:** Bugs: ReadFrom never checks read length, so filters over 1 GiB loaded from a file can silently truncate; disk mode always uses the built-in hash, so custom-hash filters answer wrongly; ReadFrom ignores the packed flag; the README example does not compile (package is named qf). Stale since 2021 apart from a 2025-09 cleanup.

**How:** It is a classic quotient filter. The top q bits of a 64-bit MurmurHash64A (seed 0, inlined) pick a home bucket, the remaining 64-q bits are stored as the remainder, and 3 metadata bits per slot (occupied, continuation, shifted) encode sorted runs in neighbouring slots, like linear probing. A lookup is one hash plus usually one or a few adjacent slot reads. In the benchmark's configuration (1e-4 FPR) a bits-and-blooms Bloom lookup instead runs two murmur3-128 passes and tests k=14 bit positions, each reduced modulo a non-power-of-two m. The unpacked mode keeps each slot in a whole uint64 so a slot read is plain array indexing; the packed mode bit-packs slots at 67-q bits to save memory, and it was about 50% slower in the README run.

**Use it when:**
- Go services that check many string or byte keys against a large set built offline (the README targets 'large models that are expensive to generate') and want essentially no false positives: the error rate is only the 64-bit hash-collision rate.
- You need a small integer per key (an ID, a class, a shard number) returned by the same probe. External storage added about 5 ns in the README run (25.59 vs 20.43 ns/op).
- Sets that grow incrementally to an unknown final size. The table doubles at 65% load and rehashes losslessly because the full hash is kept, with no need to size it up front.
- Replacing a map[string]struct{} used only for membership over many long keys. Slots hold hash bits, not the key bytes, but lookups were about 2.2x slower than a Go map in the README run (20.43 vs 9.37 ns/op).
- RAM-starved, read-mostly deployments that can accept slow lookups. OpenReadOnlyFromPath opened a 2 MB filter in about 9 µs (README) and serves lookups with pread instead of loading the file.

**Skip it when:**
- Memory-tight approximate filtering. The remainder width is fixed at 64-q bits and load stays between 32.5% and 65%, so the README's own 1-billion-key example needs 9 GB packed (about 77 bits/key), and the unpacked form uses a full 64-bit word per slot. By the bloom package's own sizing formula, a Bloom filter needs about 19 bits/key at 1e-4 FPR and about 10 bits/key at 1%.
- You need deletion, merging or counting: the filter has no Delete, Remove or Merge API.
- Disk-backed lookups on a hot path. Disk makes one pread per slot probed, allocates a buffer per read in packed mode, panics on I/O errors, and has no mmap option (issue #7, open since 2020). No Disk lookup timings are published, and the 'packed' disk benchmark helper ignores its packed argument.
- Large DRAM-resident sets, or workloads dominated by misses, where you need evidence. The only published numbers are positive lookups over 163 distinct keys in a 4 KB table.
- Teams that need an active upstream. After the August 2021 README update the only changes are a September 2025 unsafe/ASAN cleanup and a yaml bump, three issues from 2018-2020 have no replies, and pkg.go.dev lists a single importer (an internal Tencent BlueKing package).

**Integration:** module · none at runtime (the library imports only the Go standard library); go.mod also pulls aviddiviner/go-murmur, bits-and-blooms/bloom/v3 and testify for tests, and urfave/cli/v2 for the cmd tool · Go 1.20 (go.mod; the code uses unsafe.StringData and unsafe.SliceData) · any Go target: pure Go, no assembly or SIMD. The serialized format is little-endian, so big-endian hosts take a slower byte-swapping path, and the packed Disk reader's big-endian branch indexes raw[cnt*8:(cnt+1)*8] with cnt instead of i, so it looks broken.

**Vs siblings:** The closest Go sibling is ribbonGo, a static filter at about 7.3 bits/key. Pick go-qfext instead when keys arrive incrementally, you want an integer payload per key, or you need practically zero false positives and can afford roughly 10x the bits per key (about 77 vs 7.3). For C/C++ or counting workloads, the Counting Quotient Filter (splatlab/cqf) is the more complete quotient-filter implementation.

**Gotchas:**
- The package name is qf, not qfext. The README snippet calling qfext.New() compiles only with the import alias that example/example.go uses.
- Filter.ReadFrom ignores the header's BitPacked flag, and HashFn is never persisted. Build the receiving Filter with the same BitPacked and HashFn as the writer. OpenReadOnlyFromPath always uses the built-in murmur hash (the code has an 'XXX: handle variable hash functions' comment), so a filter built with a custom HashFn gives wrong answers from disk without any error.
- ReadFrom reads each vector with a single io.Reader.Read call and never checks the byte count. On Unix, Go's os.File.Read returns at most 1 GiB per call (internal/poll maxRW), so loading a multi-GB filter straight from an *os.File can be silently truncated. Use a reader that fills the whole buffer (io.ReadFull semantics), or use Disk.
- Packed vectors panic, rather than return an error, when a stored value is wider than BitsOfStoragePerEntry; unpacked vectors store it silently. Disk lookups also panic on read errors.

**Status:** Stale: essentially unchanged since 2021 apart from a September 2025 unsafe/ASAN cleanup and dependency bump, but it is MIT-licensed, standard-library-only and about 1,400 lines, so it is easy to vendor and patch.

[repo](https://github.com/facebookincubator/go-qfext) · [benchmark](https://github.com/facebookincubator/go-qfext#performance---compute)

##### pleat (Pleated Ribbon Filter, Rust)  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml and README; LICENSE plus LICENSE-APACHE present; GitHub detector reports MIT)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust ribbon-filter crate: about 7.6 bits/key at 0.8% FPR, less than Bloom, with cache-local 'pleated' construction.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — The crate's own Criterion benchmarks on an Intel i9-14900HX (rustc version and flags not stated) measure a homogeneous w=64, R=7 filter at about 7.6 bits/key with a measured 0.783% FPR. They also show pleated construction at 26.0 ns/key vs 60.4 for the crate's own arrival-order build at 10M 64-bit keys (2.3x), and slightly slower at 1M (26.1 vs 23.8). No Bloom filter is measured in the crate. The 'less memory than Bloom' claim is analytical, and the companion preprint's C++ measurements show pleated ribbon construction still slower than single-thread blocked-Bloom insertion.

**Known shortcoming:** The Bloom comparison is memory only and qualitative; build is slower than a single-threaded Bloom build (per the paper preprint).

**Known shortcoming:** No Bloom filter measured (memory win is analytical, ~7.6 vs ~10 bits/key at R=7); builds are slower than Bloom (paper ~24 vs 6.1-11.5 ns/key at 100M; the crate's 8 threads only 24.4 vs 26.0 at 10M); queries vs Bloom unmeasured (up to 112 B per probe). Build-once u64 API; fixed-seed hash lets chosen keys inflate FPR; 1 star, 21 downloads; the paper is an unreviewed preprint.

**How:** The memory win comes from the ribbon filter itself (Dillinger and Walzer; banded GF(2) linear system solved by on-the-fly Gaussian elimination). Homogeneous w=64 ribbon costs about 1.09*R bits/key. The companion preprint puts Bloom at about 44% over the minimum, which works out to roughly 10 bits/key at R=7 against 7.6 here. The speed contribution is 'pleating' (partition-instead-of-sort): one counting-sort pass buckets keys by start slot into 2^16-slot windows (about 768 KiB) before banding. That turns the dependent, cache-missing row-reduction chains of arrival-order banding into cache-local work, and because the banding solution is order-independent the output is bit-identical. from_keys_parallel splits the slot range across std threads and defers keys within 2^14 slots of a range boundary (plus any spills) to a sequential tail, following parallel BuRR.

**Use it when:**
- Static key sets rebuilt in bulk (immutable LSM/SST files, periodic snapshots, deduplication indexes) where filter RAM or disk size matters more than build CPU.
- Filters of about 10M+ 64-bit keys, where the banding table outgrows L3 and pleating pays off: 26.0 vs 60.4 ns/key at 10M in the crate's own benchmark.
- When you want the false-positive rate tunable in 1-bit steps (R from 1 to 32), e.g. R=7 at about 7.6 bits/key and 0.8% FPR, or R=10 at about 10.9 bits/key and 0.1%, rather than fixed 8/16-bit fingerprints.
- Rust services that persist filters and want a versioned, checksummed blob whose decoder rejects corrupt or mismatched input with typed errors (fuzzed and Miri-checked in CI).
- Multi-core build machines that want a parallel build they can check: from_keys_parallel output is bit-identical to the sequential build.

**Skip it when:**
- The key set changes or its final size is unknown. The filter is build-once, with no insert, delete, union or counting; use a Bloom, cuckoo or quotient filter.
- Build time must match Bloom. In the companion preprint's C++ harness, pleated ribbon is still about 24 ns/key at 100M keys against 6.1-11.5 ns/key for single-thread blocked-Bloom insertion, and it takes 16 threads (11.9 ns/key) to catch up. In this crate, 8 threads give only 24.4 vs 26.0 ns/key over single-thread pleated at 10M.
- Small filters, where the banding table fits in cache. At 1M keys pleated is slower than arrival order (26.1 vs 23.8 ns/key), and from_hashable always uses the pleated path.
- Lookup latency is the bottleneck. No Bloom query comparison is measured, and each probe reads up to 2*R u64 words (112 bytes at R=7) against one cache line for a blocked Bloom filter. The crate reports 17.4 ns scalar and 15.4 ns batched miss-dominated lookups at 10M keys (standard w=128: 24.2 ns).
- You need proven production maturity. It has 1 GitHub star, 21 crates.io downloads, 0 reverse dependencies and a single author, has had no commits since 2026-07-12, and its companion paper is an unreviewed preprint.

**Integration:** crate · xxhash-rust 0.8 (xxh3 feature) only; requires std (not no_std). The default feature 'parallel' uses std::thread with no extra crates. · Rust 1.87 (MSRV, built in CI), edition 2021 · Pure Rust, any target. CI runs tests on Linux, macOS and Windows plus i686-unknown-linux-musl (32-bit). The software prefetch in contains_batch is only compiled on x86_64; other architectures run batch queries without prefetch.

**Vs siblings:** Pick pleat over xorf (about 9 bits/key at 0.4% for BinaryFuse8) when you are in Rust and want a static filter with a tunable R and slightly less space (about 8.75 bits/key at R=8, derived from the crate's sizing formula), and your large rebuilds can use the pleated or parallel build. Choose BuRR or RocksDB Ribbon (C++) when you need sub-1% space overhead or a battle-tested production implementation, and fastbloom or Boost.Bloom when keys arrive incrementally or lookup and build speed matter more than bits/key.

**Gotchas:**
- The from_hashable/contains_hashable path hashes Rust Hash output with fixed-seed xxh3. The crate warns this is only reliable within the same process, target and toolchain, so do not persist such filters. For durable filters, hash a stable encoding to u64 yourself.
- The hash seed is fixed and non-cryptographic. SECURITY.md says an adversary who chooses the queried keys can inflate the false-positive rate, so keyed hashing is your job.
- Peak build memory is well above the final filter (derived from the source). A pleated w=64 build copies the whole key slice (8 B/key) and allocates about 1.09n u64 coefficient rows (about 8.7 B/key). StdRibbon allocates a u128 coefficient row plus a u32 result row per slot, re-bands every key on each seed retry (up to 64 seeds), and returns BuildError::NoSolvingSeed if none solves.
- Filter sizing is fixed by n and R at build time, and bits_per_key(n) needs you to pass n back in. An empty key set still produces a non-empty filter.

**Status:** A new single-author research release: repository created 2026-07-11, last main-branch commit 2026-07-12 with Dependabot PRs left open since, v0.1.0 on crates.io. It is dual MIT/Apache-2.0, tested byte-for-byte against the fastfilter_cpp reference kernel, fuzzed, Miri-checked and under a 90% coverage gate, so it is usable as a dependency or small enough (about 2.4k lines of Rust source, tests included) to vendor, but it has no track record of production use.

[repo](https://github.com/integrallis/pleat) · [benchmark](https://github.com/integrallis/pleat#readme)

##### rbloom  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust (PyO3) Bloom filter for Python with a set-like API; beats other PyPI Bloom packages on insert+lookup wall time.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — The README table comes from the in-repo benchmarks/compare.py: insert 10M float keys into Bloom(10_000_000, 0.01), then look all of them up, averaged over 5 timeit runs on an Apple M1 Pro. rbloom took 2.52 s, versus pybloomfiltermmap3 4.78 s (~1.9x), pybloom3 46.76 s (~18.6x), Flor 76.94 s (~30.5x) and bloom-filter2 165.54 s (~65.7x); ratios are derived from page data. The timings are whole-loop wall time including the Python interpreter loop. Flor and bloom-filter2 ran through a struct.pack-to-bytes fallback that adds per-key packing cost. Competitor versions are pinned in requirements.txt (pybloomfiltermmap3 0.6.0, pybloom3 0.0.3, flor 1.1.3, bloom-filter2 2.0.0), but the Python version, rustc version and wheel build flags are not stated. The table was last updated in the 2024-10-01 'Reflect benchmark changes' commit, and nothing was compared against a native C/C++ Bloom filter.

**Known shortcoming:** The large multiples are vs pure-Python Bloom libraries; vs the C-extension pybloomfiltermmap3 it is only ~1.9x (derived).

**Known shortcoming:** Python call overhead dominates (~126 ns/op derived) and there is no vectorized API (#23); a plain unblocked Bloom filter with no SIMD. p>0.5 gives k=0 so every membership test returns True (silently useless, untested); k is floored so FPR slightly exceeds the target.

**Known shortcoming:** Persistence is raw k+bits with no header/checksum, so a truncated file gives silent false negatives; the default hash cannot be saved/pickled; custom hashes are capped to signed i128 (#22). The GIL is never released; custom Python hashes can raise 'already borrowed' across threads; importing re-enables the GIL on free-threaded builds; no 3.13t/PyPy/musl wheels. CI runs no tests.

**How:** Each `add` or `in` makes one call into compiled Rust. The object is hashed once, with Python's `hash()` (an isize) or the user's `hash_func` (up to i128). That single hash seeds a 128-bit linear congruential generator (multiplier from L'Ecuyer 1999), which produces all k bit indices. This is the one-hash-many-indices trick, similar in spirit to Kirsch-Mitzenmacher double hashing. Bits live in a plain `Box<[u8]>`, each index is `x % m`, and lookups stop at the first zero bit. Sizing is textbook: m = -n ln p / ln^2 2 and k = floor(log2(1/p)). There is no blocking, SIMD, or GIL release, so the speedup comes from moving hashing and bit work out of interpreted Python, not from a better filter layout.

**Use it when:**
- Python code that needs a probabilistic 'seen before?' set over arbitrary hashable objects (str, tuples, floats, frozen dataclasses), such as URL or record dedup when a real `set` would not fit in RAM (about 9.6 bits per key at 1% FPR, derived from the sizing formula).
- Replacing pybloom3, Flor or bloom-filter2 in a loop-heavy Python pipeline: the README table shows 18-66x lower wall time than those three (derived from page data).
- Replacing pybloomfiltermmap3 when you don't need its mmap file backing: about 1.9x faster in the same table, and it installs from prebuilt abi3 wheels (the README reports pybloomfiltermmap3 failing to install on 3.11 and segfaulting on 3.10 in January 2023, but fine by October 2024).
- Building filters in several processes or shards and merging them with `|` / `update` or comparing them with `issubset`, as long as every filter uses the same deterministic custom `hash_func` object and the same (n, p) parameters.
- Deployments without a Rust toolchain on mainstream platforms: PyPI ships cp37-abi3 wheels for manylinux x86_64/i686/aarch64/armv7l/ppc64le/s390x, macOS x86_64/arm64 and Windows win32/amd64.

**Skip it when:**
- Throughput-critical bulk work: every operation pays Python call and interpreter-loop overhead. The README run works out to about 126 ns per operation (2.52 s / 20M ops, derived). A user in issue #23 measured 8.89M queries/s on an M4 Pro. There is no vectorized NumPy/Arrow insert or query API (issue #23 is open). From Rust, C or C++, use a native filter instead.
- You need deletion, counting, a real length, or auto-growth. It is a plain fixed-size Bloom filter: going past `expected_items` silently raises the FPR, and `approx_items` is an O(m) popcount over the whole bit array (issue #25 asks for O(1)).
- Large, memory-bound filters where cache misses dominate. The layout is unblocked, so each operation makes k independent random bit probes over the whole array. There is no blocked, SIMD, xor, or ribbon variant, so both space and probes per operation are worse than those designs.
- You need a file-backed, mmap-ed or zero-copy shared filter (pybloomfiltermmap3 does this), or you want to pickle it. Pickle is refused by design (issue #16). `save`/`load` work only with a user-supplied deterministic `hash_func`, because the built-in `hash()` is salted per process.
- Free-threaded CPython (3.13t+), multi-core parallel queries, PyPy, or musl/Alpine. The module does not declare `gil_used = false`, so per PyO3 docs a free-threaded interpreter turns the GIL back on at import. No 3.13t, PyPy or musllinux wheels are published, so those builds compile from source with Rust and maturin.

**Integration:** module · none at runtime; build from source needs PyO3 0.27 (main; the 1.5.4 release used 0.26) and maturin >=1.0,<2.0 · CPython 3.7+ (abi3-py37 wheels); source builds need Rust 1.74+ (PyO3 0.26/0.27 MSRV) and maturin 1.x · Prebuilt wheels: Linux (manylinux) x86_64, i686, aarch64, armv7l, ppc64le, s390x; macOS x86_64 and arm64; Windows x86 and x64. Other platforms, including PyPy, musl and free-threaded CPython, build from the sdist.

**Vs siblings:** Pick rbloom when your code is Python and you want a mutable, set-like filter over arbitrary Python objects from a pip-installable wheel. Every catalogued sibling is a C/C++/Rust/Go/GPU library with no Python API here. If you are writing Rust, fastbloom (one-hash-derived indices plus a lock-free AtomicBloomFilter) or xorf (static xor/binary-fuse filters, smaller and faster to query but built once) are better. efficient/cuckoofilter is the choice when you need deletions.

**Gotchas:**
- `false_positive_rate` above 0.5 gives k = floor(log2(1/p)) = 0 hash probes. Such a filter never sets a bit, so every `x in bf` is True and `bool(bf)` is always False. The tests construct Bloom(1140, 0.999) but never exercise membership on it. Because k is floored rather than rounded, p=0.01 uses 6 probes and p=0.001 uses 9, so the real FPR lands slightly above target (derived from the constructor arithmetic).
- The default `hash()` is salted per process and follows Python equality (1, 1.0 and True collide on purpose), so a default-hash filter can't be saved or shared across processes. A custom `hash_func` must return an int in [-2^127, 2^127-1]: unsigned 128-bit digests such as xxh3_128_intdigest raise OverflowError (issue #22). Each call to it costs a Python function call.
- The persistence format is 8 bytes of little-endian k followed by raw bits, with no magic number, stored length, n/p or checksum. A truncated or corrupted file loads silently with a different bit length. Every index is `% len`, so that shows up as false negatives rather than an error. `load_bytes` on fewer than 8 bytes hits a Rust slice panic, surfaced as PanicException. The hash function passed to `load` must match the one used to build the filter, and nothing checks this.
- Set operations and comparisons require the exact same hash-function object (identity, not equality) and identical (n, p). Otherwise they raise ValueError. The `rbloom.pyi` stub also declares `load_bytes` without `@classmethod`, which can confuse type checkers.

**Status:** MIT-licensed, a single 682-line lib.rs with 318 stars and a Zenodo DOI. Maintenance is low-cadence and bursty: the last PyPI release is 1.5.4 (2025-09-09, PyO3 0.26), the last commit (2025-11-23) only bumped PyO3 to 0.27 and is unreleased, and three feature requests (#22, #23, #25) are open. CI builds wheels but does not run tests/api_test.py.

[repo](https://github.com/KenanHanke/rbloom) · [benchmark](https://github.com/KenanHanke/rbloom#benchmarks)

##### Register-Blocked SIMD Bit-Pattern Bloom Filter (bloomfilter_benchmarks)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Benchmark header of AVX2 bit-pattern Bloom filters: 19-22x a naive Bloom filter's throughput on small filters, at ~6% FPR.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — On the author's nanobench harness (i9-9900K, g++ 12.2.0, -O3 -mavx2, random 64-bit hashes, 1% FPR target), naive Basic cost 57-58 cycles/op at 1K keys and 254-266 at 67M, while the AVX2 Patterned filter cost 2.9-3.1 at 1K-16K keys (19-20x; the blog says 2.5 cycles and 22x) and 25-30 at 67M (8.8-10.3x). The Patterned filter's 6.0-6.9% FPR against Basic's ~1% was measured on pre-fix code and with different memory per key.

**Known shortcoming:** Trades FPR for speed: the SIMD bit-pattern filter is faster than a classic Bloom filter at a higher false-positive rate; a benchmark project, not a packaged library; needs AVX2.

**Known shortcoming:** The published CSVs (2023) predate PR #1 (2024-07), which fixed the Patterned mask index (ANDed with an uninitialized variable) and Blocked Query (read the first 32 B, not the key's block); the fixed code was never re-benchmarked and the flat ~27-cycle blocked probe is an artifact. CSVs give 19-20x, not the blog's 22x, and only 8.8-10.3x at 67M keys.

**Known shortcoming:** Patterned ignores epsilon: 16 bits/key at all sizes (power-of-two round-up) vs 9.57 for basic Bloom, so ~1.7x memory and ~6x FPR (6.0-6.9%); the AVX2 register-blocked variant shares low hash bits between block index and bit position, the likely cause of its unexplained 7.4-9.8% FPR. Header-only, x86 AVX2 only; std::random_device mask table (not reproducible); the 8-hash batch reads past the end; int overflow above 2^28 keys; hashing not timed. The same design ships in Apache Arrow Acero's BlockedBloomFilter.

**How:** Register blocking (Lang et al., VLDB 2019; Putze et al., 2010) maps each key to one 64-bit word, so an insert or query is one memory access plus one AND/compare. Instead of computing k bit positions, the Patterned variant uses 10 hash bits to pick one of 1024 overlapping 57-bit masks (4-5 bits set) from a 136-byte table and 6 more bits to rotate it ('mask rotation'), with the remaining bits picking the block, so one 64-bit hash is enough. The AVX2 path handles 8 hashes per call, using _mm256_i64gather_epi64 to read the mask table and, on query, the filter words.

**Use it when:**
- You are writing your own filter for a hash join or columnar scan and want a short, readable reference for the register-blocked bit-pattern design. It uses the same layout as Apache Arrow Acero's BlockedBloomFilter: 57-bit masks, 4-5 bits set, 1024 masks, 6-bit rotation.
- Negative-heavy probe workloads on x86-64 with AVX2, where 5-7% false positives are acceptable because an exact check runs afterwards.
- Filters that stay in cache. The checked-in results show the largest gain over Basic (19-20x) at 1K-16K keys, which is 2-32 KB of filter, and only 8-10x at 4M-67M keys.
- Batch probing where the 64-bit hashes already sit in arrays whose length is a multiple of 8.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a target false-positive rate. PatternedSimdBloomFilter ignores eps: it always allocates max(512, 8n) bits, rounded up to the next power of two strictly above that. It measured 6.0-6.9% FPR when asked for 1%.
- Production use. This is benchmark code with no tests, no key hashing, no releases and no handling of batches that are not a multiple of 8. Its int sizing (8*n) overflows above about 2^28 (268M) keys.
- Targets without x86-64 AVX2, or MSVC. The header includes <immintrin.h> unconditionally, uses __builtin_clz, and has no NEON path and no runtime CPU dispatch.
- You need reproducible or shareable filters. Each instance seeds its mask table from std::random_device, so bit vectors differ between instances and processes. Arrow's version uses a fixed seed.
- Using SimdBloomFilter (the plain AVX2 register-blocked variant) as is. Its block index (h1 & (num_blocks-1)) and its bit positions ((h1 + i*h2) & 63) both use the low 6 bits of h1, so keys in the same block share a bit offset. That plausibly explains the 7.4-9.8% FPR the author says he could not explain.

**Integration:** header-only · None for bloom_filters.h beyond the standard library and <immintrin.h>. The bench/fpr harness bundles nanobench.h. · Not stated. Built with g++ 12.2.0 at -O3 -mavx2 with no -std flag, so GCC 12's default C++17. Needs GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_clz). · x86-64 only. The SIMD variants require AVX2 (gathers, variable shifts). No ARM/NEON and no runtime dispatch.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to study or copy the bit-pattern and mask-rotation trick in about 540 lines. For real use, Boost.Bloom's block<uint64_t,K> filters give the same one-word-per-key layout with FPR control and active maintenance, and the Impala-derived AVX2 blocked filter in efficient/cuckoofilter has been tested and benchmarked by independent researchers.

**Gotchas:**
- The published numbers predate bug fixes. Every CSV comes from the initial commit of 2023-05-30. PR #1 (July 2024) fixed two bugs. First, PatternedSimdBloomFilter ANDed the hash with its own uninitialized variable instead of the 10-bit mask-index mask. Second, BlockedBloomFilter::Query read the filter's first 32 bytes instead of the key's block. No results have been published for the fixed code. The Blocked probe cost stays flat at ~27 cycles at every size, which is an artifact of the Query bug. The Patterned filter's ~6% FPR is consistent with a near-constant mask index: 64 rotations with about 4 keys per word.
- Memory per key is not matched across variants. The Patterned sizing, 32 - __builtin_clz(m), doubles exact powers of two. At every benchmarked size (powers of 4) the Patterned filter therefore used 16 bits/key against Basic's 9.57, about 1.7x the memory for about 6x the FPR. A Hacker News commenter raised the equal-FPR question in 2023, and it got no reply.
- The SIMD Insert and Query always read 8 hashes with unaligned 256-bit loads. Pad the input to a multiple of 8, or they read past the end.
- Timings exclude hashing. The harness feeds pre-generated random 64-bit values as hashes, and the probe keys are fresh random values, so nearly all probes are negative lookups. Hashing real keys adds cost to every variant and narrows the speedup ratio.

**Status:** Stale (five commits, last on 2024-07-15, 21 stars, no tests or releases) but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as a reference to re-benchmark, while Apache Arrow Acero's BlockedBloomFilter is a production implementation of the same design with AVX2 dispatch, prefetching and folding.

[repo](https://github.com/save-buffer/bloomfilter_benchmarks) · [benchmark](http://blog.krassovsky.com/bloom_filter.html)

##### Ribbon Filter (ribbonGo)  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go static Ribbon filter (Dillinger-Walzer 2021) storing 7.3-7.5 bits/key at 0.78% FPR, below textbook Bloom and Xor sizes.

**Beats:** Bloom filter, xor filter — Only self-measurements from the repo's go test BenchmarkPaper_* suite with r=7 and sequential 8-byte integer keys, Go version and flags unstated. At w=128, build was 106.3 ns/key at 7.33 bits/key for n=1e6, and 384.7 ns/key at 7.51 bits/key for n=1e8, on an Apple M3 Pro. Queries at n=1e6 were 43.2/31.7 ns positive/negative, a warm-cache loop over 8192 cycled probes on an unnamed Xeon Platinum; no n=1e8 query numbers are published, and the README says only the query table was re-measured after the July 2026 storage-layout change. The Bloom (9.6 bits/key at 1%) and Xor figures are textbook constants, not benchmark runs, and FPRs are not matched: against a Bloom filter at the same 2^-7 FPR (about 10.1 bits/key by the README's 44% figure) the saving would be about 27%, not the quoted 23.6%.

**Known shortcoming:** The Bloom 9.6 bits/key comparison is a textbook constant, not a benchmark; FPRs are not matched (r=7 is about 0.78%).

**Known shortcoming:** Static only: no add/delete and no serialization (issue #23), so it cannot be persisted. At matched 2^-7 FPR a Bloom filter needs ~10.1 bits/key, so the saving is ~27%; the Bloom baseline is never benchmarked (#26). Duplicate keys or a 64-bit XXH3 collision (~3% at 1e9 keys) make all 256 seeds fail.

**Known shortcoming:** Real slot overhead is 4.7-45% (doc comments say 1.8-7.2%); w=32 at 1e8 keys is no better than Bloom; r<=8 gives an FPR floor of 0.39%; build needs ~25 B/key. The README benchmark command runs no benchmark; query numbers are warm-cache at n=1e6 only; the w<=64 build lacks prefetch (#42).

**How:** Each key is hashed once with XXH3 to 64 bits. That hash is cheaply remixed per seed into a start slot, a w-bit coefficient row and an r-bit fingerprint. The rows form a banded linear system over GF(2), solved by on-the-fly Gaussian elimination (the paper's 'Rapid Incremental Boolean Banding ON the fly') plus back-substitution, retrying with a new seed if banding hits a linear dependence. At w=128, RocksDB's empirical slot tables put the slot count only about 5-7% above n, so storage stays near the r-bits/key minimum. The README puts Bloom at about 44% overhead. The solution is stored in RocksDB's Interleaved Column-Major Layout. A query is one hash plus up to r shift/AND/POPCNT parity checks over two adjacent w-bit words, and it exits on the first mismatched column, so negatives are cheaper than positives.

**Use it when:**
- Go programs (no cgo) that build a filter once over a known, de-duplicated key set of about 1e6-1e8 keys and query it many times in the same process, for example per-snapshot or per-shard membership sets.
- Memory-bound cases at about 0.4-1% FPR. At w=128 the author measured 7.33 bits/key (n=1e6) and 7.51 (n=1e8). The textbook figures, from the README's own overhead percentages applied to 7 bits, are about 8.6 for Xor with 7-bit fingerprints and about 10.1 for Bloom at 2^-7. That is roughly 13-27% smaller.
- Relatively high FPR targets (r=1-8, so 50% down to 0.39%): the Ribbon paper says the design is most competitive for f >= 2^-7.
- Read-heavy services where build time of about 0.1-0.4 microseconds per key is acceptable and queries of about 30-45 ns (warm cache, n=1e6) are fast enough.

**Skip it when:**
- Sets that grow or change: there is no Add or Delete. Every change is a full rebuild costing 57-385 ns/key in the author's M3 Pro runs, with per-key cost rising at larger n.
- Filters that must be persisted or shipped, such as LSM table blocks or on-disk indexes. No serialization API exists (issue #23 is open). The hash is final XXH3, which the code notes is not byte-compatible with RocksDB's on-disk Ribbon blocks.
- FPR below about 0.39%: ResultBits is capped at 8. The Config comment lists r=10, but validateConfig panics above 8.
- Memory-tight build hosts. Construction holds 8 B/key of stored hashes plus 17 B/slot of banding arrays at w=128 (9 B/slot at w<=64), on top of the caller's key slice. The benchmark file warns of about 8 GB peak at n=1e8, including the test keys.
- Narrow widths at large n. w=32 at n=1e8 used 10.17 bits/key (45% slot overhead, from extrapolated non-RocksDB sizing constants), no better than a textbook Bloom at the same FPR. w=64 at n=1e8 (8.23 bits/key) is only about 4% under textbook Xor.

**Integration:** module · github.com/zeebo/xxh3 v1.1.0 (indirect: klauspost/cpuid/v2, golang.org/x/sys) · Go 1.24.2 per go.mod; CI runs tests on Go 1.25 · Any Go target: the library is pure Go, and the xxh3 dependency ships amd64 SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512 and arm64 NEON assembly with a generic fallback. Published numbers cover arm64 (Apple M3 Pro) and x86-64 (Xeon Platinum); CI runs on ubuntu-latest.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you need the smallest static filter at about 0.4-1% FPR in pure Go without cgo. If C/C++ is acceptable, BuRR (bumped Ribbon; the Ribbon paper reports load-balanced Ribbon below 1% overhead, against 4.7-7.3% here) or xor_singleheader (simpler, with published head-to-head benchmarks) are stronger picks. The cuckoo-family siblings (Vacuum, Windowed cuckoo) fit better if you need inserts after build.

**Gotchas:**
- Keys must be unique, and uniqueness really applies to the 64-bit XXH3 hash. Every seed retry remixes only the stored hash, and the bander rejects even consistent redundant equations. So a duplicate key, or two distinct keys whose 64-bit hashes collide (birthday odds of about n^2/2^65: about 3e-4 at 1e8 keys, about 3% at 1e9), fails every seed. Build then runs all MaxSeeds (default 256) banding attempts before returning ErrConstructionFailed.
- The Config doc comments quote the paper's asymptotic overheads (w=32 about 7.2%, w=64 about 3.6%, w=128 about 1.8%). Measured slot overhead is much higher: 31.8/12.0/4.7% at n=1e6 and 45.3/17.6/7.3% at n=1e8. That is because slot counts follow RocksDB's tables for a 5% per-seed failure rate and grow with log n.
- NewWithConfig and NewFromKeysWithConfig panic, rather than return an error, on an invalid CoeffBits or ResultBits. Keys are []string only; the pre-hashed build path (buildFromHashes) is unexported.
- The README's benchmark commands (-bench='BenchmarkRibbon...') match no benchmark function; the real ones are BenchmarkPaper_Build/Query_Positive/Query_Negative/Space, and -short skips n=1e8. The w<=64 build loop also lacks the prefetch load that the README credits with a 20-36% gain at scale (open issue #42); only the w=128 path has it.

**Status:** Active but young: created March 2026, v1.0.10 released 2026-07-18 after the ICML storage rewrite, 15 stars, 10 open issues including serialization (#23) and Bloom/Cuckoo/Xor benchmarks (#26). It is MIT-licensed, seven source files and one dependency, so easy to vendor, but not production-proven.

[repo](https://github.com/RibbonFilter/ribbonGo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/RibbonFilter/ribbonGo#benchmarks)

##### Windowed Cuckoo Filter (WindowFilter, implements 'Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters')  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Safe-Rust (2,2) windowed cuckoo filter: 12.8 bits/key at 2^-10 FPR, 12% under Bloom, 7-25% under cuckoo; slower inserts.

**Beats:** cuckoo filter, Bloom filter — In one run of the author's benchmark binary (100k string keys, 200k queries half present, target rate 2^-10, release build with thin LTO on unpinned stable Rust, CPU not stated), the windowed (2,2) filter used 1.596 bytes/key vs 1.803 for the author's own classic Bloom and 2.130 for the author's own (2,4) cuckoo; lookups tied with cuckoo (60.3 vs 61.2 ns) and beat Bloom (81.6 ns), while inserts were 2.8x slower than cuckoo (163 vs 59 ns). Most of the 25% memory gap to cuckoo is power-of-two rounding at n=100k, which leaves the cuckoo table at 76% load: against a well-sized cuckoo the code's parameters give about 7% (12/0.94 vs 13/0.95 bits per key), matching the paper's overhead factors of 1.272 vs 1.365.

**Known shortcoming:** Baselines are the author's own Bloom/cuckoo implementations; no CPU model; inserts 2.8x slower than cuckoo (162.97 vs 58.74 ns); 0 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** The '25% smaller than cuckoo' is mostly an artifact: its own cuckoo baseline rounds to a power of two (76% load at n=100k); against a well-sized cuckoo filter the gain is about 7% (matching the paper's 1.272 vs 1.365). Baselines are self-made (unblocked Bloom), cache-resident 100k keys, one run, no CPU stated; FNV string hashing dominates lookup time.

**Known shortcoming:** Inserts are 2.8x slower than cuckoo; no resize (~2% headroom); no dedup (a fifth copy fails after 10k kicks); a 160 KB rollback Vec per kicking insert. &str keys only, fixed hash seeds (unsafe for adversarial keys), no serialization. A one-day repo (18 commits on 2026-09-03), not on crates.io, 0 stars; the paper authors' own implementation is gitlab rahmannlab/cuckoo-filters (Python/numba).

**How:** The gain is in memory, not speed. It implements (2,2) windowed cuckoo hashing from Schmitz, Zentgraf and Rahmann (arXiv:2505.05847): each key has two candidate windows of two adjacent slots, neighbouring windows overlap by one slot, and the theoretical load threshold is 0.965 with only four candidate slots (vs 0.980 with eight slots for (2,4) buckets), so a 2^-k rate needs k+2 bits per slot instead of k+3 and the table is sized for 94% load. The second window is the first plus a fingerprint-derived offset modulo the window count (a signed offset instead of the classic XOR), so the table size need not be a power of two; each slot also stores a choice bit and a window-offset bit, which let an evicted fingerprint find its other window and count as extra match bits. Slots are bit-packed into a Vec<u64>, and lookups check the four slots one at a time: no SIMD, no bit-parallel matching, no prefetching.

**Use it when:**
- A Rust service needs a deletable 'definitely absent' pre-check in front of a disk, database or network lookup, the maximum key count is known, and bytes per key matter more than insert speed: about 12.8 bits/key at a 2^-10 rate vs 14.4 for a classic Bloom filter.
- Key counts that fall just above a power-of-two boundary, where a standard XOR-addressed cuckoo filter must round its bucket count up and can waste up to about 2x (the author's own cuckoo sits at 76% load for 100k keys).
- Read-mostly workloads: fill once or slowly, then query often. The author's run measured lookups on par with (2,4) cuckoo and faster than an unblocked Bloom filter, on a cache-resident 100k-key filter.
- Keys are already strings, or converting them to &str is cheap.
- You want a short, readable reference for the windowed layout (about 740 lines of library code including tests, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], no dependencies) that you can vendor and adapt.

**Skip it when:**
- Insert-heavy or streaming fills. Inserts were 2.8x slower than the author's (2,4) cuckoo (163 vs 59 ns) and 1.7x slower than Bloom. The paper's own implementation also shows windowed (2,2) inserting about 2x slower than bucketed (2,4), and about 10x slower than the Prefix filter (3.1 vs 33 M keys/s at 2^-8).
- Untrusted keys. The hash is FNV-1a plus a splitmix finalizer with fixed seeds, and the relocation RNG is a fixed-seed xorshift, so crafted keys can collide and force failed inserts; the README says it is for experiments and trusted input only.
- Unknown or growing key counts. There is no resizing: the table is sized for 94% load at the declared capacity, and the author's max-load run failed at 95.75%, which leaves only about 2% headroom before insert returns false.
- Static key sets known up front. At a 2^-10 rate, Xor filters (1.23x overhead, per the paper) and BuRR are smaller than this filter's ~1.28x and need no relocation.
- Production dependencies that need persistence, integer or byte keys, batch or SIMD lookups, concurrent inserts, or a maintained crate. None of these are provided; the crate is not on crates.io, has 0 stars, and all 18 commits landed within one day. Performance on DRAM-sized filters was never measured (the benchmark stops at 100k keys, about 160 KB).

**Integration:** crate (git dependency only; not published on crates.io) · none (std only; Cargo.lock lists no external packages) · Rust 1.85+, implied by edition 2024. No rust-version field; rust-toolchain.toml pins only the floating 'stable' channel. · any Rust std target: pure safe Rust (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]) with no SIMD or architecture-specific code; CI runs only on ubuntu-latest, and the benchmark hardware is not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you need a deletable filter in dependency-free safe Rust and can live with slow inserts; Vacuum Filter (a similar ~25%-smaller-than-cuckoo claim) and Morton Filter (1.3-2.5x faster lookups) are more heavily engineered C++, and Prefix Filter inserts about 10x faster but needs AVX-512. For key sets known up front, Xor Filter or BuRR is smaller.

**Gotchas:**
- Any insert whose four candidate slots are all full allocates a rollback log with Vec::with_capacity(max_kicks) before the first kick: 16-byte entries x 10,000 is about 160 KB per such insert at the default setting.
- Inserts are not deduplicated. Repeated inserts of one key each take a slot, and once the key's four candidate slots (three when its two windows are adjacent) all hold its copies, the next insert runs all 10,000 kicks and fails.
- delete on a key that was never inserted can remove another key's matching entry and create false negatives. The README warns about this, as with cuckoo filters in general.
- Bad parameters panic instead of returning errors: new asserts capacity > 0 and fpr_bits in 1..=30 (1..=29 for CuckooFilter). A fingerprint of 0 is remapped to 1 so that 0 can mean an empty slot, which slightly raises the false-positive rate (the paper makes the same trade).

**Status:** Listed as active, but it is a one-day project (18 commits on 2026-09-03, CI green, no issues, releases or crates.io publication) that is MIT-licensed, dependency-free and small enough to vendor, so treat it as a readable reference rather than a maintained library; for the full design (bit-parallel probes, prefetching, parallel subfilters), see the paper authors' MIT-licensed Python/numba code at gitlab.com/rahmannlab/cuckoo-filters.

[repo](https://github.com/EvanGruhlkey/WindowFilter) · [benchmark](https://github.com/EvanGruhlkey/WindowFilter#benchmark)

##### xor-filter (Java, komiya-atsushi)  `Java`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Small Java xor filter (8/16-bit) built on Guava Funnels; about 2x faster Long-key queries than Guava BloomFilter at equal FPR.

**Beats:** Bloom filter (Guava com.google.common.hash.BloomFilter) — This is first-party JMH (Gradle jmh plugin 0.5.0 defaults, time unit ms) on an undisclosed JVM and CPU. Each filter was built from 8,192 keys (every other of 16,384 pregenerated keys) and queried round-robin over all 16,384, so half the queries hit, everything stayed cache-resident, and hashing went through Guava 28.2 murmur3_128 for both filters. XOR8 did 17,458 vs 8,879 queries/ms against Guava BloomFilter at fpp 0.389% for boxed Long keys (1.97x) and 7,122 vs 5,318 for 20-character strings (1.34x). A separate 100,000-key run gave 9.84 vs 11.55 bits/key serialized (1.17x smaller). All ratios are derived from the README tables.
