- A duplicate singular sub-message field on the wire is rejected outright (ArenaDecodeError::RepeatedSingularMessage), not merged the way protoc merges two concatenated messages
- Enums always decode open, even proto2/editions-CLOSED enums — an unrecognized value arrives as a raw integer instead of routing to unknown fields
- Recursion-depth guards against pathological nesting are sized for an 8MB stack; Windows defaults to a 1MB stack, so untrusted deeply-nested input needs a larger linked stack (/STACK:8388608) to stay safely rejecting

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-14) and Apache-2.0-licensed, but a brand-new, 3-star project (created 2026-06-28) with no independent benchmark or adoption track record yet; it is copyable/vendorable since the consumer-facing output is generated header-only code, but treat the maturity as early.

[repo](https://github.com/VeaaC/rapidproto) · [benchmark](https://github.com/VeaaC/rapidproto/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md)

##### vtprotobuf (protoc-gen-go-vtproto)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

protoc plugin generating reflection-free Marshal/Unmarshal/Size/Equal/Clone helpers for Go protobuf APIv2; ~1.7x faster unmarshal than stock protoc-gen-go.

**Beats:** protoc — Per the author's 2021 Vitess blog post (Vicent Marti), a synthetic VReplication stress test replicating a large MySQL table between keyspaces measured 7.17 CPU-seconds of unmarshal overhead with stock protoc-gen-go (APIv2) vs 4.15 CPU-seconds with vtprotobuf's UnmarshalVT (~1.7x), falling to 0.63 CPU-seconds (~11x) when vtprotobuf's generated memory pooling is also used; the post gives no hardware, Go version, or compiler flags, and the repo ships no benchmark code to reproduce the numbers.

**How:** All (de)serialization logic is fully unrolled per-field at codegen time (ported from gogo/protobuf's approach to the APIv2 API), so there is no reflection walk over the message descriptor at runtime. SizeVT precomputes the exact encoded size so MarshalVT allocates its output buffer once. UnmarshalVTUnsafe casts wire bytes directly into string/[]byte fields instead of copying them. The optional generated sync.Pool-backed object pools (ResetVT/ReturnToVTPool/FromVTPool) let callers reuse whole message structs across unmarshal calls, avoiding allocation entirely, which is where most of the reported speedup comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Go services already on google.golang.org/protobuf (APIv2) with (de)serialization visible as CPU cost in profiles (RPC hot paths, replication/streaming row processing).
- gRPC, DRPC, or Twirp services that can install vtprotobuf's provided codec so all messages benefit without touching call sites.
- Teams that can explicitly opt into memory pooling per message type and manage single-owner reuse lifetime carefully, where most of the >10x gain reported by the author lives.
- Want reflection-free CloneVT/EqualVT/SizeVT even without wiring the whole RPC path.
- Comfortable checking in generated *_vtproto.pb.go files as part of the normal protoc build step.

**Skip it when:**
- Still generating APIv1/gogo code: vtprotobuf targets APIv2 only and is explicitly not compatible with APIv1-generated code per the README.
- Can't tolerate unsafe byte aliasing: UnmarshalVTUnsafe pins the entire input buffer alive via GC for the life of any string/bytes field taken from the message (open issue #167), which can silently balloon retained memory if a field is cached long-term.
- Messages are small or short-lived: the author's own post notes many protobuf messages are too small for pooling to help, and the ~1.7x codegen-only gain (no pooling) is the realistic floor.
- Need pooling correctness for repeated fields, maps, or nested messages: multiple open issues report pooled ResetVT/ReturnToVTPool bugs with repeated fields (#92) and note pooling only reaches the outer message, not nested children (#162, 'Recursive Pool Usage').
- Want a single drop-in replacement for proto.Marshal/Unmarshal with zero call-site changes and no RPC codec registration step.

**Integration:** source-drop · google.golang.org/protobuf (APIv2) required; optional integration deps on google.golang.org/grpc, storj.io/drpc, or github.com/twitchtv/twirp for the provided codecs · go.mod pins `go 1.26.4` to build the plugin/runtime as of the last commit; the `unique` string-interning field option additionally needs Go 1.23+ in consumer code · any (pure Go, no architecture-specific code in the repo tree)

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings (RapidProto, Zserio, FlatBuffers) are all C++ alternatives to protoc's C++ output; pick vtprotobuf instead whenever the stack is Go on google.golang.org/protobuf APIv2, since it optimizes protoc's existing Go codegen and wire format rather than replacing either.

**Gotchas:**
- UnmarshalVTUnsafe keeps the whole input wire buffer alive via GC for as long as any string/bytes field from the message is reachable (unsafe.String aliasing); documented as an open gap in issue #167, not yet in the README.
- UnmarshalVT on a non-zeroed message behaves like proto.Merge rather than a fresh Unmarshal; call Reset() first or use a freshly allocated message.
- Memory pooling is opt-in per message (`option (vtproto.mempool)` or `--go-vtproto_opt=pool=...`) and, as of issue #162, only pools the outer message — nested/child messages are still freshly allocated on each unmarshal.
- Returning a pooled repeated-field message has open correctness bugs (issue #92, generated ResetVT); verify pool behavior with your own message shapes before relying on it in production.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-02, 1118 stars, used in production by Vitess/PlanetScale and widely adopted in the Go gRPC ecosystem); BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor, but 'copyable' here means installing the plugin and wiring it into your protoc invocation, not literally copying a header.

[repo](https://github.com/planetscale/vtprotobuf) · [benchmark](https://vitess.io/blog/2021-06-03-a-new-protobuf-generator-for-go/)

##### Zserio  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Own-IDL C++/Java/Python serialization framework; bit-packed decode 1.2x-2.6x faster than protoc.

**Beats:** protoc — Per-decode time (protobuf ParseFromString vs zserio read, pre-serialized blob, JSON load/serialize untimed) on 4 schemas, gcc 11.3.0 CMake-Release build, Intel i7-9850H/Linux Mint 21.1: Zserio beat protoc-generated C++ by 1.17x-2.63x (addressbook 1.478 vs 1.731ms, apollo 0.244 vs 0.641ms, carsales 1.374 vs 2.053ms, simpletrace 0.221 vs 0.386ms); byte-aligned variants reached 2.05x and 2.22x. Benchmark is first-party (same org as Zserio, 6-star companion repo), evidence tier C.

**How:** Zserio packs fields at the bit level rather than byte level, and its default schemas carry no per-field tag IDs or explicit length prefixes the way protobuf's wire format does, so there is less to scan per field during decode. Byte-aligning fields (the '_align' schema variants) trades blob size for speed by removing bit-shift work, cutting decode time roughly another 40-45% versus the default schema on addressbook and carsales in this benchmark. No SIMD or algorithmic trick is documented; the win is wire-format layout, not a decode algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Designing a new wire format from scratch where blob size matters as much as decode speed
- Multi-language C++/Java/Python project willing to author .zs schemas instead of .proto
- Need built-in SQLite table serialization, JSON debug export, or generic reflection/services without hand-rolling them
- Functional-safety-conscious C++ codebase: C++11 runtime, >600 unit tests, ASan/UBSan clean, 99% line coverage
- Deserialize-heavy workloads (parse once, read many) where a 1.2x-2.6x per-decode win compounds

**Skip it when:**
- Already invested in protobuf schemas, tooling, or cross-org interop; migration cost likely exceeds the modest measured speedup
- Need protobuf-style forward/backward field compatibility; Zserio's compactness comes partly from dropping field IDs and lengths
- Team can't add a Java-based external compiler step (zserio.jar) to the build
- Need platforms beyond 64/32-bit Linux and 64-bit Windows; macOS/ARM are not in the stated Supported Platforms list
- Want a larger, independently verified speedup: siblings RapidProto (~7x) and vtprotobuf (~1.7x) show bigger measured wins over protoc

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the C++ runtime itself; bundled SQLite3 only if using the SQL-database extension; Java (JRE) needed at build time to run the zserio.jar code generator, not at runtime · C++11; gcc 7.5.0+ (11.4.0/7.5.0 tested), clang 11.0.0+ (14.0.6/21.1.8 tested), MinGW 7.5.0+, MSVC 2017+; CMake 3.15+ if using the bundled CMake helper · 64-bit Linux, 32-bit Linux, 64-bit Windows per README's Supported Platforms list; macOS/ARM not stated

**Vs siblings:** Pick Zserio when you want a full schema framework (SQLite mapping, JSON debug strings, services/pub-sub, one schema for C++/Java/Python) and can move off .proto. Pick RapidProto or vtprotobuf instead if you must keep .proto files and want a bigger measured decode speedup with less schema-language lock-in.

**Gotchas:**
- Byte-aligned (_align) and delta-packed (_packed) schema variants trade blob size against decode speed in opposite directions; pick per workload
- Compact wire format omits field tags/lengths, so schema-evolution/compatibility rules differ sharply from protobuf's
- Code generated by the zserio compiler inherits the license of the input .zs schema, separate from the BSD-3-Clause runtime license
- Open issue #577 'Consider to optimize C++ serialization performance' (still open) indicates maintainers see further headroom

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-17, frequent releases); BSD-3-Clause runtime, with generated code separately licensed under the input schema's license.

[repo](https://github.com/ndsev/zserio) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ndsev/zserio-protobuf-benchmarks)

## Copyleft

### compression-and-encoding

#### entropy-coders

##### CUHD / gpuhd (massively parallel Huffman decoding on GPUs)  `CUDA/C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

CUDA Huffman decoder (CUHD) that splits one unpartitioned bitstream across GPU threads by self-synchronization; reported 10x+ over zstd's CPU huff0.

**Beats:** Zstandard's CPU Huffman decoder (huff0) — Per WebSearch summaries of the peer-reviewed ICPP 2018 paper (not opened; ACM blocked here), GPU decoding on TITAN V, TITAN Xp and GTX 1080 was over an order of magnitude faster than Zstandard's CPU Huffman decoder, and one citing-work snippet puts CUHD at about 10 GB/s; no CPU model, compiler flags or dataset are known, and the comparison pits a GPU against a CPU.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the ICPP 2018 paper, known only from abstract snippets ('over one order of magnitude' vs zstd's CPU Huffman, no multiplier); the DOI page is unopened.

**Known shortcoming:** MAX_CODEWORD_LENGTH 11 is compile-time, symbols are uint8 and the stream format is its own llhuff (not huff0 or deflate compatible); the phase-2 sync loop relaunches until done (data-dependent pass count); auxiliary memory is about the size of the compressed input; the Makefile is hand-edited (cuda-9.1, sm_70); the repo has no results and the speedup is known only from snippets ('over one order of magnitude' vs zstd huff0, about 10 GB/s per a citing snippet).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Uses the self-synchronization property of Huffman codes: each thread starts decoding a small subsequence (4 x 32-bit units in the demo) at an arbitrary bit offset, and decoding from a wrong offset usually falls back into codeword alignment within a few codewords. Phase 1 synchronizes subsequences within a thread block, phase 2 is relaunched until every block boundary has synchronized, phase 3 is a Thrust exclusive scan over per-subsequence symbol counts to get output offsets, and phase 4 re-decodes and writes symbols in parallel. Each symbol is decoded by a single direct lookup in a 2^11-entry table using a two-word sliding window.

**Use it when:**
- You control both encoder and decoder and need to decode large (tens of MB and up) byte-symbol Huffman streams that already live on, or are headed to, an NVIDIA GPU.
- You cannot afford to add partition metadata (gap arrays, chunk offsets) to the stream format but still want GPU-wide parallel decode.
- Research or baseline use: it is the reference self-synchronization GPU Huffman decoder (ICPP 2018) that later work such as ipdps22-opthuffdec builds on and compares against.
- Throughput-bound pipelines where amortizing host-to-device transfers and kernel launches over a big buffer is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Decoding standard formats (deflate, zstd/huff0, JPEG): codeword length is capped at MAX_CODEWORD_LENGTH = 11 (compile-time) and the bit layout is CUHD's own 32-bit-unit format from its llhuff encoder.
- Alphabets larger than 256 symbols: SYMBOL_TYPE is std::uint8_t.
- Small inputs or latency-sensitive calls: the decode runs four kernel phases, a host round-trip per phase-2 iteration and a Thrust scan, plus PCIe copies.
- Codes or data that synchronize slowly: phase 2 is relaunched in a host loop until all sequences synchronize, so the number of passes is data-dependent and unbounded in the code.
- Production use that needs a maintained library, AMD/Intel GPUs, Windows or macOS: the README targets GNU/Linux and CUDA only, and there are no commits since 2019-02-02.

**Integration:** static lib · CUDA runtime and driver (libcudart, libcuda), Thrust (bundled with the CUDA toolkit); the bundled encoder/ subdirectory for encoding · README: GCC 5.4.0+ and CUDA SDK 8+; the Makefile compiles host code with -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native -Wall -Werror and device code with nvcc --std=c++11 -O3, so a GCC with C++17 support is needed in practice · GNU/Linux with an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 3.0+; ARCH in the Makefile defaults to 70 (Volta) and must be edited per GPU

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Huffman_coding_Gap_arrays when the stream format cannot carry a gap array, but prefer the optimized self-sync and gap-array variants in ipdps22-opthuffdec, which report faster decoding with CUHD as their baseline. For CPU decoding of standard Huffman, PIVCO-Huffman or FSE's Huff0 are the practical choices; for GPU entropy decoding with a newer design, the same author's multians (tANS) is the sibling.

**Gotchas:**
- Build is configured by hand-editing CUDA_INCLUDE, CUDA_LIB and ARCH in the Makefile (defaults point at /usr/local/cuda-9.1 and sm_70); there is no CMake or install target.
- The caller must know the exact uncompressed size up front to size CUHDOutputBuffer; the stream carries no length or table header.
- Auxiliary memory scales with input: one uint4 sync point (16 bytes) plus a 32-bit output count per subsequence, which is 16 bytes of input in the demo configuration (SUBSEQ_SIZE 4, 128 threads), so aux memory is roughly the size of the compressed input.
- The repository has no benchmark results; the demo only prints per-phase microsecond timings and checks the round trip on random binomially distributed bytes.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-02-02 (8 commits, 50 stars, no issues filed); LGPL-3.0, so static linking into closed-source code carries relinking obligations, and the code targets CUDA 8/9-era toolchains.

[repo](https://github.com/weissenberger/gpuhd) · [benchmark](https://doi.org/10.1145/3225058.3225076)

##### multians (massively parallel ANS decoding on GPUs)  `CUDA/C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

CUDA research decoder for a single unpartitioned tANS bitstream; paper claims up to 17x over 64 CPU threads.

**Beats:** 64-thread multicore CPU tANS decoder, a SIMD-based decoder and Zstandard's entropy codec — The ICPP 2019 paper's abstract, seen only as a search snippet, reports up to 17x over a 64-thread CPU decoder, up to 31x over a SIMD decoder and up to 39x over Zstandard's entropy codec. The GPU, CPU and compiler behind those numbers were not readable here because ACM DL is blocked. The repo prints only raw microsecond timings of GPU kernels against its own std::thread decoder on synthetic data and contains no zstd comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the ICPP 2019 paper (abstract snippet: up to 17x vs 64 CPU threads, 31x vs SIMD, 39x vs Zstandard's entropy codec); the repo demo compares only against its own multicore CPU decoder. LGPL-3.0, last commit 2019-07-26.

**Known shortcoming:** Open issue #1 (Nov 2020, unanswered): the build fails with 'src/multians_output_buffer.cc:28:49: error: invalid use of array with unspecified bounds'. Demo GPU timing leaves out H2D/D2H copies; the phase-2 sync loop has no iteration cap; max codeword length 11 is hard-coded in main.cc; no zstd comparison in the repo; the paper hardware is unreadable (ACM blocked).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It decodes speculatively and relies on self-synchronisation. Each GPU thread starts decoding a small subsequence of input units (SUBSEQUENCE_SIZE 4) at a guessed state and bit offset and records a sync point (unit, bit, state, symbol count). Phase 1 synchronises subsequences within a thread block and phase 2 repeats a cross-block kernel until every block's start matches the previous block's end state. A thrust::exclusive_scan over per-subsequence symbol counts then gives output offsets, and phase 4 decodes again and writes the output in parallel.

**Use it when:**
- Research or prototyping on GPU entropy decoding, especially as the baseline that later work such as Recoil compares against
- You already have large single-stream tANS data (radix 2, one table, up to 256 symbols) and an NVIDIA GPU, and you cannot change the encoder to add partitions
- Data already resident in GPU memory: the demo times only the decode kernels, not the PCIe copies
- Studying self-synchronising speculative decoding; the same author's CUHD/gpuhd applies the idea to Huffman

**Skip it when:**
- Decoding zstd or FSE frames: the bit layout comes from the repo's own toy encoder and has no zstd format compatibility
- Anything that needs multiple tables, adaptive models, more than 256 symbols, rANS or byte-wise renormalisation (README: single table, b = 2 only)
- Production code: 5 commits, no tests beyond the demo's equality check, untouched since 2019-07-26, and an open build-failure issue (#1, 2020) left unanswered
- CPU-only or non-NVIDIA targets: only a CUDA implementation exists (the README says an OpenCL port 'should be straightforward' but none exists)
- Small inputs or latency-bound paths: kernel launches, a host-side sync loop and the prefix scan dominate short streams

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA toolkit 9+ (nvcc, thrust), pthreads; GNU/Linux per README · C++14 (nvcc --std=c++14), CUDA SDK 9+, GPU compute capability 3.0+ · Linux x86-64 with an NVIDIA GPU; the Makefile hard-codes ARCH = 61 plus -arch=sm_70 and must be edited

**Vs siblings:** Pick multians over the CPU coders (FiniteStateEntropy, hypersonic-rANS, htscodecs) only when the data is a single unpartitioned tANS stream that must be decoded on a GPU. For new GPU ANS work, Recoil (rANS, CPU and GPU, decoder-adaptive splits) is newer, maintained and reports higher throughput than multians. CUHD/gpuhd is the Huffman equivalent from the same author.

**Gotchas:**
- Open issue #1 (Nov 2020): build fails with 'src/multians_output_buffer.cc:28:49: error: invalid use of array with unspecified bounds' on newer compilers; no fix in the repo
- Phase 2 is a do/while loop on the host that relaunches the kernel until all blocks report synchronised. It has no iteration cap, so a stream that synchronises slowly costs extra kernel launches and host round trips
- main.cc passes a hard-coded maximum codeword length of 11 to decode() and decodes output in reverse order (output_buffer->reverse() afterwards), matching the demo encoder only
- The demo's GPU timing covers decode kernels only: host-to-device copies of input and table, and the device-to-host copy of output, are outside TIMER_START/TIMER_STOP

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-07-26 with an open, unanswered build issue; LGPL-3.0, and the five main source files total about 1.7k lines, so vendoring is feasible, but expect to patch it for current CUDA/GCC.

[repo](https://github.com/weissenberger/multians)

#### general-lossless

##### lbzip2 (maintained fork)  `C`  `GPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier A`

Maintained fork of lbzip2, a parallel bzip2-compatible compressor; single-threaded it already beats bzip2 1.0.8 by about 1.3x to 1.8x.

**Beats:** bzip2 (bzip2 1.0.8) — lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.2 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar) measured lbzip2 2.6.5 -1 at 22.0 MB/s compress and 62.7 MB/s decompress versus bzip2 1.0.8 -1 at 13.5 and 41.1 MB/s, and -9 at 22.4 and 47.0 versus 12.7 and 35.5 MB/s at the same 25.75% ratio (1.6-1.8x compress, 1.3-1.5x decompress, derived from page data). The fork's own README adds about 8% faster compression and 9% faster decompression over lbzip2 2.5 on an Apple M5 Max (first-party); most of the gain over bzip2 comes from upstream lbzip2's design, and lzbench's multithreaded table does not include lbzip2.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on lzbench 2.4 (the maintainer ran the table; the lzbench CHANGELOG credits the integration to caius72). A maintained fork of kjn/lbzip2, which is not otherwise listed, so it stands.

**Known shortcoming:** CLI only with no library API (lzbench wraps the internal encode.h/decode.h); GPL-3.0-or-later; one maintainer, 1 star. The SSSE3 inverse-MTF path is used only when built with -march=native or x86-64-v2; --small is ignored; upstream issues #35 (permissions), #27 (-n with tar) and #29 (slow lbzcat) are not covered by the fork's changelog; lzbench's multithread table omits lbzip2.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The BWT is computed with divbwt, an induced-sorting suffix-array construction from Yuta Mori's libdivsufsort lineage, instead of bzip2's comparison-based block sort, so compression speed barely changes from -1 to -9 (22.0 vs 22.4 MB/s in lzbench 2.4) where bzip2 slows down. Huffman tables are built with length-limited minimum-redundancy coding (Larmore-Hirschberg, Moffat-Katajainen) and decoded table-driven (Liddell-Moffat). The fork adds a vectorised forward MTF (SSE2/NEON), an inverse MTF done with one byte shuffle (pshufb with SSSE3, vqtbl1q_u8 on AArch64), slice-by-8 CRC32 and four rotating frequency counters. On top of that, input blocks are compressed and decompressed in parallel across worker threads.

**Use it when:**
- You must produce or consume .bz2 files (archives, distro packages, legacy pipelines) and want them faster without changing the format.
- Multicore machines: the fork's README reports 220 MB compressing in 0.32 s on 18 cores versus 4.68 s single-threaded (Apple M5 Max), about 14.6x (derived from page data).
- Replacing bzip2 in shell pipelines or tar (tar -I lbzip2) on Linux, macOS or MSYS2.
- High levels (-9, 900k blocks) where bzip2 is slowest: lbzip2 keeps about 22 MB/s single-threaded versus 12.7 MB/s for bzip2 -9 on Silesia.

**Skip it when:**
- If you are free to choose the format: zstd, bzip3 or libbsc give better ratio and speed than any bzip2 implementation (bzip3 -5 reaches 22.29% and bsc -m0 23.26% on Silesia versus 25.75% for lbzip2 -9).
- In-process compression from C/C++: there is no supported library API; use libbz2 or an embeddable codec instead.
- Projects that cannot accept GPL-3.0-or-later code in the build or distribution.
- Native Win32 builds: only the MSYS2 POSIX runtime (needs msys-2.0.dll) is supported.
- Where long-term maintenance matters: the fork is one person's work since August 2026 (1 star, 0 forks); upstream kjn/lbzip2 is unmaintained.

**Integration:** command-line tool (built from source with CMake; Homebrew tap caius72/lbzip2) · POSIX threads and POSIX runtime (fork, sigaction, sysconf); no external libraries · C99 compiler, CMake 3.15+ · Linux (glibc, musl), macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows via MSYS2; SIMD paths for x86-64 (SSE2; SSSE3 only when enabled at compile time) and AArch64 NEON, scalar fallback elsewhere

**Vs siblings:** Pick lbzip2 over bzip3, libbsc or zstd only when the output must stay in bzip2 format; those siblings win on ratio and speed with their own formats. Compared with pigz or Rapidgzip it is the analogous parallel tool for the .bz2 rather than .gz ecosystem.

**Gotchas:**
- Like bzip2, it deletes the input file after compressing unless -k or -c is given.
- The SSSE3 inverse-MTF path compiles in only when the build already targets SSSE3 (-march=native or x86-64-v2); a default x86-64 build uses the slower branchy path.
- --small is accepted but ignored (main.c: 'For now --small is ignored'), so memory use is not reduced.
- Open upstream issues not listed as fixed in the fork's CHANGES.md: #35 (changes file permissions on files the user does not own), #27 (-n not working with tar) and #29 (lbzcat slower when the output file already exists).

**Status:** Active since August 2026 (2.6.5, last commit 2026-08-19) as the de facto maintained lbzip2 after Homebrew dropped the unmaintained upstream; GPL-3.0-or-later, CI on four platforms with 1111 tests, but a single maintainer.

[repo](https://github.com/caius72/lbzip2) · [benchmark](https://github.com/inikep/lzbench)

#### succinct-structures

##### 3star-rankselect (3* rank/select)  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Research rank/select bit vector with worst-case constant-time select at about 0.8 percent space overhead, far below SDSL, sux and pasta.

**Beats:** SDSL (sd_vector, mcl select), sux (rank9sel, simple_select), pasta flat rank/select, Poppy (benchmark script options) — Checked-in multibench_out logs (1e9 random bits at densities 0.5, 0.2 and 0.02, 2e7 dependent random select_1 queries, one run each, Clang 18.1.3 -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG, Intel Core i9-13900H) show m3 at 0.82 percent overhead and 95-96 ns per select, against pasta flat 3.58 percent, sux simple_select s1 2.34 percent, SDSL mcl about 23 percent and rank9sel about 50-56 percent, at 76-185 ns for those competitors; the space win (about 2.9x to 95x less overhead, derived from page data) is the result, not speed. The paper's 0.78 percent and 4.5x to 64.1x figures come from a search snippet of arXiv 2509.17819 (blocked here).

**Known shortcoming:** Raised C to A from the repo's multibench_out logs (i9-13900H, Clang 18.1.3, -O3 -march=native), but the win is space only (0.82% overhead vs 2.34-78.15%); select_1 is level or slower (m3 100.4 ns vs simple_s3 49.1 ns).

**Known shortcoming:** m3::access and m3::select_0 are stubs returning 0. Input is read from globals (bits/N_bits/N_words), so not a drop-in library. Macro typo CUSTOM_LO != 512 in rank_1 (should be CUSTOM_L0), so the 512-bit-L0 exclusion never applies (checked-in select-only runs unaffected). x86-64 AVX2+BMI2+LZCNT only, C++20, CMake 3.28. Logs confirm 0.82% overhead at 95-96 ns, level with or slower than SDSL mcl/rank9sel/simple_select at density 0.5 and ahead only at 0.02. Single-run logs; competitors cloned unpinned.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** first-party logs

**How:** It pairs a summary tree (per-superblock counters: 64 Ki-bit superblocks of 32 L0 blocks of 2048 bits, with 12-bit relative L0 counts unpacked with SSE/AVX2 shuffles and compared in SIMD) with a compressed three-level sample tree that stores positions of some 1-bits, which bounds select to a constant number of steps in the worst case. Blocks whose minority bits are rare are stored sparsely as 11-bit position lists and dense blocks verbatim, and the final in-word step uses PDEP/TZCNT. Prefetch hints and 2 MiB transparent huge pages (madvise) cut cache and TLB misses.

**Use it when:**
- Very large static bit vectors (around 1e9 bits and up) where the rank/select index must stay under 1 percent of the bits, e.g. succinct trees, FM-index or wavelet-tree building blocks under tight memory.
- Workloads that need worst-case constant select time, including adversarial or very uneven densities where sampling-based select (sux simple_select, SDSL mcl) can degrade.
- x86-64 machines with AVX2 and BMI2 (Haswell or Zen 2 and later) built with -march=native.
- As a reference design for engineering your own low-overhead select: the code exposes many compile-time variants (L0 size 512/1024/2048, tree strategies, prefetch and huge-page switches).

**Skip it when:**
- When select latency matters more than space: in the repo's own runs at 0.82 percent overhead select_1 took about 95-100 ns; at density 0.5 that is level with sux rank9sel (88 ns) and simple_select s1 (91 ns) and slower than SDSL mcl (about 81-85 ns) and simple_select s3 (about 49 ns at 7 percent overhead). It only pulls ahead at density 0.02, where pasta flat (144 ns) and SDSL mcl (185 ns) slow down.
- If you need select_0 or access: m3::select_0 and m3::access are stubs that return 0.
- Non-x86 targets (ARM, RISC-V) or x86 without AVX2/BMI2: the code includes x86intrin.h and uses _mm256_*, _pdep_u64 and _lzcnt_u64 unconditionally.
- Dynamic bit vectors: the index is built once (build_auxiliaries) over a static input.
- If you want a packaged dependency: there is no install target, no tests beyond the driver's validate mode, 15 commits, 5 stars.

**Integration:** source-drop · none for m3 itself beyond the repo's bv.hpp, alignedallocator.hpp, constants.hpp and Tree3.hpp; the benchmark driver also pulls vendored pasta and tlx and clones sdsl-lite, sux, rankselect and rankselect2 at HEAD · C++20 (std::popcount, constexpr std::string), CMake 3.28; logs show Clang 18.1.3 · x86-64 only, AVX2 + BMI2 + LZCNT required (built with -march=native); Linux (madvise MADV_HUGEPAGE via sys/mman.h)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over SPIDER (about 3.8 percent overhead), orzo and pasta flat when the index size must be under 1 percent and you only need rank_1/select_1; pick SPIDER, QuadRank/BiRank or splatlab's PTSelect when query speed or throughput is the priority, and LA-vector or h0_bv when the bit vector itself should be compressed.

**Gotchas:**
- m3::access(i) and m3::select_0(k) are unimplemented and silently return 0; calling them gives wrong answers rather than an error.
- Input is not passed in: m3 builds from the globals bits / N_bits / N_words (declared extern in bv.hpp, defined in bv.cpp), so extracting it into another project means rewiring those globals or editing the class.
- Macro typo in m3::rank_1: '#if REVERSE==2 && POP==2 && CUSTOM_LO != 512' tests CUSTOM_LO (letter O), which is undefined and evaluates to 0, so the intended exclusion for 512-bit L0 blocks never applies; it affects rank_1 only with CUSTOM_L0=512 (the 3.2 percent configuration) and was not exercised by the select-only checked-in runs. Run the driver's 'valid' job (compares every query against a naive structure) before trusting a non-default configuration.
- Benchmark caveats: single instance, single iteration per point, random uniform densities only (indep generator), FORCE_CRIT_PATH makes queries dependent (latency, not throughput), and competitors are cloned at their current heads, so reruns may not match the logs.

**Status:** Active (README edited 2026-09-15, code last changed 2025-09-21), MPL-2.0 so files can be vendored with file-level copyleft; research code from the KIT group (Kurpicz, Rigi-Luperti, Sanders) that needs extraction work before use outside its benchmark driver.

[repo](https://github.com/nrilu/3star-rankselect) · [benchmark](https://github.com/nrilu/3star-rankselect/tree/main/multibench_out)

### crypto-and-hashing

#### aead-and-ciphers

##### Tiaoxin-346  `C`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Tiaoxin-346, an AES-round AEAD with 3 AES rounds per 16 bytes in AES-NI C; 1.8-5.6x faster than SUPERCOP's AES-256-GCM, unmaintained.

**Beats:** AES-256-GCM — eBACS (supercop-20260627, page dated 2026-09-25) measured tiaoxinv2/nim, built with gcc 14.2.0 -march=native -O2, against SUPERCOP's fastest AES-256-GCM (Dolbeau's AES-NI intrinsics, Debian clang 19.1.7 -O2) on one Raptor Cove P-core of an Intel Core 5 210H. Median cycles/byte were 0.15 vs 0.70 on long+long encrypt (4.7x) and 0.28 vs 0.57 on decrypt/forgery (2.0x). Across all 15 sections the gain ranges from 1.8x (long+0 decrypt, 0.44 vs 0.81) to 5.6x (long+0 encrypt, 0.19 vs 1.07, a row flagged noisy).

**Known shortcoming:** CAESAR third-round candidate not in the final portfolio; code only in SUPERCOP. Decrypt gain is only ~2.0x (encrypt 0.15 vs 0.70 cycles/byte). GPL-2.0+.

**Known shortcoming:** CAESAR round 3 (v2.1), not a finalist; 128-bit key, so against AES-128-GCM it is 4.2x encrypt / 1.8x decrypt. Decrypt bug (also in the reference): `clen -= 16; if (clen < 0)` on an unsigned length never fires, so inputs under 16 bytes read/write out of bounds; aligned loads on caller buffers; memcmp tag check; plaintext released before verification. Nonce reuse gives master-key recovery in 30 queries (ePrint 2017/1147). AEGIS-128X2 is faster in every section.

**Independent measurement:** eBACS: Tiaoxin-346 0.15 vs AES-256-GCM 0.70 cycles/byte (nim, GCC 14.2 -O2).

**How:** The state is three shift registers of 3, 4 and 6 128-bit words (T3, T4, T6). Each 32-byte block feeds M0 into T3, M1 into T4 and M0^M1 into T6, costing 6 aesenc calls with no data dependencies between them. They pipeline through the AES-NI unit and hide its 7-8 cycle latency, which the spec cites as the reason for the wider state. Ciphertext comes from a cheap output function (6 XOR, 2 AND per 32 bytes), the code unrolls 128 bytes per loop iteration, and AD is absorbed with the same update but no output function. Decryption is slower because M1's recovery depends on the freshly recovered M0 before the state can absorb them (DECRYPTION_ROUND), which lengthens the critical path.

**Use it when:**
- Encrypt-heavy bulk AEAD on AES-NI x86 in a closed system where you control both ends: long+long encrypt 0.15 vs 0.70 cycles/byte (4.7x) and 1536+1536 encrypt 0.20 vs 0.82 (4.1x) against SUPERCOP's fastest AES-256-GCM.
- Authenticating large AD with little or no message: 0+long is 0.11-0.12 against 0.32-0.33 cycles/byte (about 2.7-2.9x), though eBACS flags these rows as noisy.
- Short messages despite the setup cost: initialization plus finalization is worth about 1120 bytes of message (per the spec), yet 64+64 still measures 1.25-1.33 against 4.70-5.13 cycles/byte (about 3.8x).
- As a research baseline for AES-round AEADs (AEGIS, Rocca, HiAE) or for cryptanalysis: weak-key distinguishers on 8-round Tiaoxin (ToSC 2021(2), ePrint 2021/187) and quantum hidden-shift state recovery (ToSC 2024, ePrint 2023/1306) both target it.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs a standardized or vetted AEAD. Tiaoxin was CAESAR round 3 only, has no library adoption, and a GitHub repository search finds only two 0-star repositories named tiaoxin. The only optimized code is GPL-2.0-or-later.
- Anywhere a nonce could repeat. The update and initialization are invertible, so recovering the state recovers the master key. Vaudenay and Vizar (ePrint 2017/1147) recover the key with 30 nonce-reusing queries, and Kales, Eichlseder and Mendel (ePrint 2017/1137) give an implemented nonce-misuse key recovery. For AES-GCM, reuse enables forgery and CPA decryption rather than key recovery.
- Decrypt-dominated traffic sized from the headline: decrypt and forgery are only 1.8-2.2x AES-256-GCM (long+long 0.28 vs 0.57, long+0 0.44 vs 0.81).
- When AEGIS is available. On the same page AEGIS-128X2 (0.11 cycles/byte long+long) beats Tiaoxin in every section, and AEGIS-128L decrypts faster (0.21 vs 0.28 long+long, 0.23 vs 0.44 long+0).
- CPUs without AES-NI. The only fallback is the table-lookup ref variant (sboxes.h), about 13.6x slower in SUPERCOP's timing column (21560 vs 1589 cycles) and exposed to classic T-table cache-timing leaks.

**Integration:** source-drop (tiaoxin-optimized.c/.h, encrypt.c and api.h; you supply crypto_aead.h or call tiaoxin_optimized_encrypt/decrypt directly) · none beyond libc (string.h, stdlib.h) and the SSE2/SSSE3/AES-NI intrinsic headers · GCC or clang with -maes -mssse3, or -march=native on an AES-NI CPU. eBACS's fastest build is gcc 14.2.0 -march=native -mtune=native -O2; Debian clang 19.1.7 builds are 4-10% slower, and clang -mcpu=native fails to compile (always_inline _mm_shuffle_epi8/_mm_aesenc_si128 without ssse3/aes). The designer used gcc 4.8.1 -O3 -msse2 -maes -mavx -march=native. · x86-64 with AES-NI and SSSE3 (nim variant; only amd64 results were checked). The ref variant is portable C with table-based AES.

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over libaegis only for the peak single-stream encrypt rate on a pre-VAES AES-NI core, where it beats AEGIS-128L (0.15 vs 0.21 cycles/byte long+long). AEGIS-128L wins on decrypt, AEGIS-128X2 wins everywhere on this Raptor Cove host, and libaegis is maintained and MIT-licensed. Against the MORUS-1280 and AEZ entries from the same mirror, Tiaoxin is 4.4x and 1.7x faster on long+long encrypt, and unlike MORUS it has no published break of the full cipher in the nonce-respecting setting.

**Gotchas:**
- Decrypt does 'clen -= 16; if (clen < 0) return -1;' on an unsigned long long, so the check never fires. A ciphertext shorter than 16 bytes wraps clen to about 2^64 and the loop reads c and writes m out of bounds. Check clen >= 16 before calling; the table-based ref variant has the same code.
- The load macro is _mm_load_si128, an aligned load, applied directly to the caller's key, nonce, AD, message and ciphertext pointers. Unaligned buffers are undefined behavior and can fault, so switch it to _mm_loadu_si128 when vendoring.
- The tag is checked with memcmp, which is not constant-time. Plaintext is written to m before verification and not wiped on failure, although the spec's security goals assume only 'false' is returned.
- The key is 128 bits (CRYPTO_KEYBYTES 16), so the AES-256-GCM baseline is not like-for-like. Against aes128gcmv1 on the same page the gain is 4.2x encrypt (0.15 vs 0.63) and 1.8x decrypt (0.28 vs 0.50). The exported tiaoxin_optimized_encrypt/decrypt symbols are unprefixed (flagged by eBACS as namespace violations) and collide with tiaoxinv1's identical names.

**Status:** Abandoned. The mirror is frozen at supercop-20160716 (its open issue #4 says to fetch SUPERCOP from bench.cr.yp.to instead), but the GPL-2.0-or-later nim file is about 16 KB and easy to vendor if copyleft and the bugs above are acceptable.

[repo](https://github.com/floodyberry/supercop) · [benchmark](https://bench.cr.yp.to/results-aead/amd64-freshwrap,big.html)

#### non-crypto-hashes

##### pengyhash  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Tiny multiply-free 64-bit ARX hash; its v0.2 beat xxHash64 bulk speed in rurban/smhasher, current v0.3 does not.

**Beats:** xxHash64 — rurban/smhasher's 262,144-byte bulk test on its reference Ryzen 5 3350G (logs normalized to 3 GHz; compiler and flags unstated) measured pengyhash v0.2 at 13,347 MiB/s against 11,177 MiB/s for xxHash64. That is ~19%, or ~9% against xxHash64's best alignment (12,263 MiB/s), since xxHash64 drops to 10,125 MiB/s at alignments 4-7. SMHasher3 on a Ryzen 9 3950X pinned at 3.5 GHz measured the current v0.3 at 12.47 GiB/s vs 13.02 GiB/s for XXH64, about 4% slower.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins on rurban/smhasher only (13,347 vs 11,177 MiB/s); SMHasher3 has it ~4% slower than XXH64 (12.47 vs 13.02 GiB/s). GPL-3.0.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~19% win over XXH64 is for v0.2; current v0.3 is ~4% slower than XXH64 in SMHasher3, and small keys are slow (89.81 vs 52.60 cycles). v0.3 has unsequenced-modification UB (s[1]/s[3], issue #2 open since 2023); license changed to GPL-3.0 in v0.3 (v0.2 was BSD-2). Seed applied only at finalization, giving 64-bit SeedBlockLen collisions on 16-31 byte keys. Abandoned since 2022-11.

**Independent measurement:** SMHasher3: pengyhash 12.47 vs XXH-64 13.02 GiB/s.

**How:** It uses no multiplications. The state is four 64-bit words updated with add-rotate-xor (ARX) steps, 32 input bytes per iteration, in two cross-coupled chains (s0/s1 and s2/s3), with every input word added twice per block. The last 0-31 bytes are packed into four words and mixed by six fixed finalization rounds, the only place the seed enters. There is no SIMD; speed comes from cheap scalar ALU ops and instruction-level parallelism.

**Use it when:**
- You want a very small, portable 64-bit hash with no multiplies, for example on cores where 64x64 multiplication is slow. The whole algorithm is about 25 lines of add, rotate and xor.
- Hashing medium-to-large buffers (KBs and up) where scalar XXH64-class throughput is enough: about 3.8 bytes/cycle for v0.3 in SMHasher3, about 4.7 for v0.2 in rurban/smhasher.
- You need the same output on little- and big-endian hosts. v0.3 assembles words byte by byte in little-endian order, and SMHasher3 registers it as endian-independent with identical LE/BE verification values.
- You must match hash values already produced by rurban/smhasher or the Fortran stdlib pengy_hash; that requires the v0.2 code (BSD-2-Clause), not the current repo.

**Skip it when:**
- Short keys such as hash-table strings or integers: SMHasher3 averages 89.81 cycles/hash on 1-31-byte keys (about 116 at 8-16 bytes), against 52.60 for XXH64 and 29.31 for wyhash. rurban/smhasher shows 74.79 vs 49.67 for xxHash64.
- Expecting to beat XXH64 with the code you download today: the current v0.3 runs about 4% slower than XXH64 in SMHasher3 (12.47 vs 13.02 GiB/s). xxh3 and wyhash are about 1.6-1.7x faster in bulk in the rurban table.
- Proprietary or permissively licensed products: v0.3 is GPLv3, unlike most peer non-crypto hashes. Only the older v0.2 is BSD-2-Clause.
- Seeded use that relies on the seed to separate hash families. The seed is mixed in only during finalization, and SMHasher3's SeedBlockLen test finds full 64-bit collisions on 16-31-byte keys (126 found where 0 are expected) when seed and key blocks vary together.
- Code that must be well-defined C: v0.3 has an unsequenced read and write of the same state word, reported in 2023 (issue #2) and unanswered, in a repo abandoned since November 2022.

**Integration:** source-drop · none (stdint.h, stddef.h) · C99 (stdint.h); no compiler versions documented · any (portable scalar C, no intrinsics); v0.3 output is endian-independent, v0.2 (memcpy loads) is not

**Vs siblings:** Rarely. SpookyHash (SpookyV2_64) matches its rurban bulk speed (13,401 vs 13,347 MiB/s), and xxHash (XXH3) and wyhash are about 1.6-1.7x faster in bulk and much faster on short keys, so pengyhash only wins if a tiny multiply-free ARX hash with endian-independent output (v0.3) is itself the requirement.

**Gotchas:**
- Undefined behavior in v0.3. Statements such as s[1] = (s[0] += (s[1] += V64(p+8)) + V64(p)) ^ rotl(s[1],14) read and modify s[1] without a sequence point (GCC -Wsequence-point), so the hash can change with the compiler's evaluation order. SMHasher3 ships a rewrite with explicit sequencing whose verification value (0x861A1254) matches the repo's own v0.3 log. Use that form.
- v0.2 and v0.3 give different hashes, and the published ~19% win over xxHash64 was measured on v0.2 (rurban/smhasher bundles v0.2, verification 0x1FC2217B; v0.3 is 0x861A1254). v0.2 also reads input with native-endian memcpy, so its values differ on big-endian machines, which the Fortran stdlib documents for its port.
- The license changed from BSD-2-Clause (v0.2) to GPLv3 (v0.3) in the same commit that changed the algorithm, so older attributions citing BSD for pengyhash.c at master (rurban issue #210, Fortran stdlib docs) now point at GPLv3 code.
- Every call runs six full finalization rounds regardless of length, so there is a fixed ~68-116-cycle cost per hash even for 1-byte keys (SMHasher3: 67.63 cycles at 1 byte).

**Status:** Abandoned: the last commit (v0.3 and the GPLv3 relicense) was November 2022, and a 2023 undefined-behavior report is unanswered. The two small files are trivial to vendor, but pick v0.2 (BSD-2-Clause) or SMHasher3's sequenced v0.3 rewrite deliberately, based on your license and output-compatibility needs.

[repo](https://github.com/tinypeng/pengyhash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/rurban/smhasher/blob/master/README.md)

#### signatures-kem

##### ENG25519 (Curve25519_AVX512IFMA)  `C`  `LGPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

AVX-512IFMA X25519/Ed25519 code plus an OpenSSL 1.1.1 ENGINE; beats OpenSSL's x86-64 Curve25519 code 3.3-12x on throughput.

**Beats:** OpenSSL 1.1.1 X25519 (x86-64 assembly, crypto/ec/asm/x25519-x86_64.pl) and Ed25519 (C implementation, crypto/ec/curve25519.c), extracted from OpenSSL_1_1_1-stable and compiled into the paper's benchmark harness; the TLS-level experiments use OpenSSL 1.1.1q — Warm-start cycle counts were measured with GCC 9.2.0 -O2 on an Alibaba Cloud Xeon Platinum 8369B (Ice Lake, Turbo on), against OpenSSL 1.1.1's X25519 assembly and Ed25519 C code extracted into the same harness. The results: batched X25519-KeyGen 60,479 cycles per 8 keys vs 90,809 per key (12.01x throughput); Ed25519 sign 24,723 vs 93,606 cycles (3.79x) and verify 81,506 vs 271,445 (3.33x); fixed-base scalar multiplication 8.06x. Against Faz-Hernandez's AVX2 code the margins shrink to 1.18x for sign and 1.33x for verify, and end-to-end TLS 1.3 handshakes improved only 25%.

**Known shortcoming:** Only X25519 key generation is 8-way batched; Ed25519 Sign (1x8) and Verify (1x2) are single-operation paths, and the Ed25519 baseline is OpenSSL's C code.

**Known shortcoming:** Needs AVX-512 IFMA (built with -march=native, no fallback); speedups are warm-start, cold runs are 1.6-3.8x slower without a warm-up thread. Built as an OpenSSL 1.1.1 ENGINE: the ENGINE API was deprecated in 3.0 and removed in 4.0.0 (Apr 2026). X25519 derive is Hisil et al.'s code (only 1.47x) and lacks the all-zero shared-secret check OpenSSL does. Against Faz-H AVX2 it is only 1.18x sign / 1.33x verify; never compared with Intel crypto_mb (#1). Stale since 2024-06.

**How:** Field elements mod 2^255-19 are stored in radix 2^51 (five limbs) to fit the 52-bit vpmadd52luq/vpmadd52huq multiply-add instructions, and field arithmetic runs 8x1-way: eight independent field elements across the eight 64-bit lanes of a zmm register. The paper's 'maximize transferable parallelism' idea carries that 8-way parallelism up the stack. KeyGen runs eight independent fixed-base scalar multiplications per call (8x1 -> 8x1 -> 8x1), Sign spreads one table-based fixed-base scalar multiplication over 8 lanes (8x1 -> 8x1 -> 1x8), and Verify uses a 2x4-way window-based double-point scalar multiplication (8x1 -> 2x4 -> 1x2, window width 5). The ENGINE's X25519-Derive is not the authors' code but a wrapper around Hisil et al.'s AVX-512F 4-way Montgomery ladder.

**Use it when:**
- TLS 1.3 servers whose throughput is limited by handshakes, running OpenSSL 1.1.1 on Intel Xeons with AVX-512IFMA (Ice Lake or newer) and using X25519 key exchange with Ed25519 certificates. The paper measured 25% more handshakes per second than stock X25519 (1,707 vs 1,366) and 24-41% higher DoT peak throughput.
- Bulk generation of ephemeral X25519 keypairs, where eight keypairs per call fits naturally (key pools, precomputed keypairs for session setup).
- Services that sign a lot of Ed25519 on AVX-512IFMA servers: about 24.7k cycles per signature, versus 93.6k for OpenSSL 1.1.1's C code.
- A reference design for AVX-512IFMA Curve25519 arithmetic, with CryptoLine-verified field routines, or for handling the cold start of AVX-512 units in latency-sensitive code.

**Skip it when:**
- CPUs without AVX-512IFMA, which includes AVX2-only parts, Cascade Lake and Cooper Lake Xeons (per the paper) and ARM. There is no fallback path, and the build uses -march=native.
- OpenSSL 3.x or 4.x stacks. The ENGINE API was deprecated in OpenSSL 3.0, and OpenSSL 4.0.0 (April 2026) removed engine support, so ENG25519 would have to be ported to the provider API.
- Workloads dominated by X25519 shared-secret derivation. The authors did not beat prior work there: the ENGINE's derive is Hisil et al.'s code at 61,867 cycles, only 1.47x OpenSSL 1.1.1.
- Clients or lightly loaded servers. Cold AVX-512 units made the primitives 1.6-3.8x slower in the paper's DoT test, and the fix is a helper thread that keeps the vector unit awake.
- Production code that needs maintained, audited crypto. This is a research artifact, stale since June 2024, with no releases. Only the field arithmetic is formally verified, and the authors never benchmarked it against Intel's own AVX-512IFMA multi-buffer crypto_mb Curve25519 code (issue #1).

**Integration:** shared lib (OpenSSL 1.1.1 ENGINE loaded via openssl.cnf); the raw primitives are a source-drop with no library target (their CMake builds only a benchmark executable) · OpenSSL 1.1.1 (1.1.1q recommended; needed for SHA-512 and the ENGINE API), CMake 3.10+; the DoT experiments also use unbound · GCC 9.2.0 tested (C with inline AVX-512IFMA intrinsics plus GNU assembler files), built with -O2 -mavx512ifma -march=native · x86-64 Linux with AVX-512IFMA required (Intel Cannon Lake/Ice Lake or later, not Cascade/Cooper Lake); tested on Ubuntu (20.04 recommended for the DoT experiments)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you specifically need faster X25519/Ed25519 for TLS 1.3 on AVX-512IFMA servers. UltrafastSecp256k1 targets secp256k1 ECDSA (Bitcoin-style signing), fasthqc/hqc is a post-quantum code-based KEM, and VecFalcon (same first author) speeds up Falcon post-quantum signing, so none of them substitutes for Curve25519.

**Gotchas:**
- X25519 keygen through the ENGINE does not compute a fresh key per call. It hands out keys from a pool held in OpenSSL secure heap: 128 X25519 keypairs refilled by 16 batch calls, and 8 for Ed25519. Each refill stalls roughly 0.22-0.33 ms, according to the paper.
- The ENGINE's X25519 derive never checks for an all-zero shared secret; its provider returns success unconditionally. The OpenSSL X25519() it replaces returns failure on an all-zero output.
- The published speedups are warm-start numbers (2,000 warm-up runs). Cold-start cost in real TLS traffic is 1.6-3.8x higher unless you run the authors' timer_warmup or heuristic_warmup helper pinned to the sibling hyperthread, which also works against the CPU's power saving.
- After the ENGINE's reference count drops to zero, the global lock is freed and never recreated, because the init is guarded by run_once. Re-initializing the ENGINE in the same process therefore fails.

**Status:** Stale research artifact (last commit June 2024, no releases, one open issue). It is LGPL-3.0, and the primitives are small enough to vendor, but the ENGINE is tied to an API that OpenSSL deprecated in 3.0 and removed in 4.0.

[repo](https://github.com/Ji-Peng/eng25519_artifact) · [benchmark](https://ji-peng.com/uploads/usenix_security2024/paper.pdf)

##### Falcon-Mitaka GPU (High Throughput Lattice-based Signatures on GPUs)  `CUDA`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Batched CUDA Falcon-512/Mitaka-512 sign and verify; the paper reports 8.8-18.5x sign and 105-149x verify throughput over CPU AVX2 Falcon.

**Beats:** Falcon NIST-submission AVX2-optimized CPU implementation (Fouque et al. [4]); Mitaka is compared only against its FP64 reference C. liboqs was not benchmarked. — The TPDS 2024 paper (Tables 5-6, CUDA 11, averaged over 30 runs, batch K=16,384) reports Falcon-512 at 27,908 sign/s and 1,913,380 verify/s on an RTX 3080, and 58,595 and 2,721,562 on an A100. Against the Falcon AVX2 CPU rates of 3,167 sign/s and 18,230 verify/s, that is 8.8x/105x (RTX 3080) and 18.5x/149x (A100); Falcon-1024 comes out at 5.35x/66x and 13.2x/114x. The CPU model, thread count and compiler for the AVX2 baseline are never stated. The paper's own 'vs AVX2' ratios are really against the FP64 reference, and its AVX2 Falcon-512 sign rate (3,167/s) is oddly below the FP64 reference's (3,587/s).

**Known shortcoming:** GPU vs CPU: the AVX2 baseline's compiler, flags, CPU and thread count are unstated. The paper's ratios do not match its own tables (7.78x/52.43x are vs the FP64 reference; 20.03x/29.51x are Mitaka vs FP64). Real Falcon-512 RTX 3080 vs AVX2 is 8.81x/104.96x (derived).

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark harness only: hard-coded keys/seeds/nonces, no keygen or API, no cudaFree or error checks. ffSampling seeds every block from slot 0, so real per-signature seeds would share sampler randomness; norm-failed signatures are not retried; Mitaka PRNG keys come from rand(). Small batches lose: K=32 on an RTX 3080 gives 2,000 signs/s (16 ms), below the CPU AVX2 3,167/s. Repo's Mitaka verify now uses an integer NTT (Nov 2023) while the paper measured FP64. Falcon-512 only, sm_86, GPL-3.0.

**Independent measurement:** TPDS 2024 tables: Falcon-512 on RTX 3080 vs AVX2 CPU 8.81x / 104.96x (derived).

**How:** The work is split coarse- then fine-grain. K signatures run as K CUDA blocks, and inside each block the polynomial work is spread over threads (N/4 threads for the shared-memory FFT, N/2 for the NTT mod 12289, N for coefficient-wise ops), with small kernels fused under COMB_KER. Falcon's recursive ffSampling is rewritten as an iterative loop over an explicit stack (ffSampling_fft_dyntree), which avoids CUDA dynamic parallelism. That loop still runs one thread per signature and dominates signing time (65.8% of Falcon-512 CPU signing time per the paper's Table 1). Mitaka's sampler is split into a bulk ChaCha20 random-byte phase (N threads per signature) and a per-coefficient discrete-Gaussian phase, so Mitaka signing is fully data-parallel. Falcon verification runs entirely on integer NTT kernels, which is why the verify gains are much larger than the sign gains.

**Use it when:**
- Server-side bulk Falcon-512 verification with thousands of pending signatures on an NVIDIA GPU: on the RTX 3080 the paper reports 1.07M verifies/s at K=1024 (0.95 ms per batch) and 1.91M/s at K=16,384, against 18,230/s for the AVX2 CPU code.
- Throughput-bound batch signing when latency of tens to hundreds of ms per batch is acceptable. On the A100, Falcon-512 reaches 58,595 signs/s at K=16,384 (280 ms per batch).
- Comparing Mitaka with Falcon for parallel hardware: Mitaka-512 signing is 2.7-2.8x faster than Falcon-512 at K=16,384 on the RTX 3080 and A100.
- Starting point for GPU FN-DSA/Falcon research (GPL-3.0): the iterative ffSampling, shared-memory FFT/NTT kernels and kernel-fusion patterns can be reused.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency-bound or small-batch signing. At K=32 on the RTX 3080, Falcon-512 signs only 2,000/s with 16 ms batch latency, below the paper's own CPU AVX2 figure of 3,167/s.
- Anything production-like. Keys, seeds and nonces are test vectors, there is no keygen or real API, failed norm checks are not retried, the Mitaka sampler keys come from libc rand(), and there are no CUDA error checks or cudaFree calls.
- Falcon-1024, Mitaka-1024 or FIPS 206 FN-DSA: only the 512 variants are in the repo, even though the paper benchmarks the 1024 variants.
- Consumer or inference GPUs with weak FP64. Falcon signing is FP64-bound, so the A100 signs about 2.1x faster than the RTX 3080 at K=16,384, and the paper notes FP64 runs at 1/32 of the int32 rate on the RTX 3080 and T4.
- Proprietary products that cannot accept GPL-3.0 copyleft, or settings that need side-channel review. The paper does not discuss constant-time or GPU timing leakage.

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA runtime (cudart) only · nvcc from CUDA 11.7 (Falcon Makefile) or CUDA 12.1 (Mitaka Makefile) with gcc as the host compiler; the paper lists CUDA 11 · NVIDIA GPUs. Both Makefiles hard-code -arch sm_86, and the README says it is tested on the RTX 3080 and A100; the paper also ran it on V100 and T4. No CPU fallback.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over GOLF when you need GPU Falcon code you can actually read and run. GOLF reports far higher Falcon throughput (420k sign/s on an RTX 4090), but no repository is catalogued for it. Pick VecFalcon instead when you care about per-signature latency on a CPU (SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON/RVV, 1.1-1.6x over c-fn-dsa); pick this one only for large GPU batches or to evaluate Mitaka.

**Gotchas:**
- ffSampling_fft_dyntree loads the sampler SHAKE state from scA[0..24] (batch slot 0) in every block instead of scA[bid*25+i]. With real per-signature seeds, every signature in a batch would draw the same sampler randomness; the harness hides this because all slots use the same seed.
- A signature that fails the norm bound is not regenerated. is_short_half_gpu/check_norm only set a flag or printf 'short half detected', whereas the reference implementation restarts sampling.
- The repo's Mitaka verify defaults to an integer NTT path added in November 2023 (FLOAT_VER is off), while the paper's Mitaka verify numbers used FP64 FFT, so re-runs will not match Table 5. Mitaka also allocates a BATCH×512×512-byte PRNG buffer, 256 MiB at BATCH=1024 and 4 GiB at 16,384.
- Reported throughput includes host-device copies. Falcon rebuilds the full basis (complete_private) and the LDL tree for every signature, with no expanded-key fast path.

**Status:** Stale: 9 commits, the last on 2023-11-14 (Mitaka integer verify), 5 stars and no issues. It is GPL-3.0 and small enough to copy as research code, but it needs a real API, key and nonce handling, and the RNG and retry bugs fixed before any real use.

[repo](https://github.com/benlwk/Falcon-Mitaka) · [benchmark](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/399.pdf)

### media-and-graphics

#### rasterizers-2d

##### Marlin renderer (Java 2D)  `Java`  `GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Java antialiasing shape rasterizer for Java 2D that replaced Pisces and Ductus; OpenJDK's default renderer since JDK 9.

**Beats:** OpenJDK 8 Pisces and Oracle JDK 8 Ductus (the Java 2D antialiasing rasterizers) — MapBench 0.4 (longer shared profile) on an Intel i7 4800 fixed at 2 GHz without HT or turbo, Oracle Java 8u60-ea with CMS and 2 GB heap: Marlin 0.5.6 rendered 9 serialized GeoServer maps with a mean per-test ratio of 2.29x against Oracle JDK 8 Ductus and 2.24x against OpenJDK 8 Pisces across 1, 2 and 4 threads; single-threaded the per-map geometric mean is about 1.18x over Ductus (range 1.00x to 1.42x) and 1.89x over Pisces, rising to about 3.7x over Ductus at 4 threads because Ductus does not scale (derived from page data). The summary Pct95 figures are arithmetic means over maps, so they are weighted toward the largest map (about 750 to 960 ms per op).

**Known shortcoming:** Java (language-filter mismatch). Tier A on the linked MapBench 0.5.6 summary (bourgesl/mapbench harness; Intel i7 4800 fixed at 2 GHz, JDK 1.8.0_60-ea-b05, full JVM flags): 228.90% vs Ductus and 223.85% vs Pisces, the JDK default rasterizers before JDK 9 (recognisable incumbents, not on the category list). The wiki 0.3 tables name no CPU.

**Known shortcoming:** The MapBench summary Pct95 is an arithmetic mean over maps weighted toward the 750-960 ms map; per-map single-thread geomeans are 1.18x versus Ductus (1.00-1.42x) and 1.89x versus Pisces, and the 4-thread 3.7x reflects Ductus serialisation (derived from page data). Historical result: Marlin is the OpenJDK 9+ default renderer, so the jar matters only for JDK 8 or for fixes newer than the bundled copy. Open bugs #35 and #38 (stroked curve cusps and offsets); the default master branch is stale (pom 0.7.0.1) and the live code is on the jdk branch.

**How:** It is a rewrite of the Pisces scanline rasterizer that avoids garbage: each rendering thread gets a reusable RendererContext (ThreadLocal or ConcurrentLinkedQueue, held by soft/weak/hard references) with pooled array caches, and edge data lives in off-heap memory managed through Unsafe. The scanline loop advances edge crossings with fixed-point DDA, keeps crossings almost sorted between scanlines and finishes with insertion sort, merge sort or a dual-pivot quicksort depending on size, and stores coverage as RLE or raw tiles with tile flags so empty tiles are skipped. Defaults are 256 subpixels in x and 8 in y (quality profile) and 128x64 tiles where large tiles are supported. Because contexts are per thread, it scales across cores where Ductus serialised rasterization through a native singleton.

**Use it when:**
- Server-side Java 2D rendering on many threads (map servers such as GeoServer, chart or report generation): the 0.5.6 MapBench run kept per-op time flat from 1 to 4 threads while Ductus per-op time rose about 4x.
- Applications still on OpenJDK 8 or Oracle JDK 8, where the default Pisces (about 1.9x slower single-threaded in MapBench, derived from page data) or Ductus is in use.
- OpenJDK 11, 17 or 21 deployments that want rasterizer fixes newer than the Marlin copy their JDK bundled (for example JDK 17 ships Marlin 0.9.1.4; the standalone jar is 0.9.4.9 with fixes such as JDK-8341381 and JDK-8277574).
- Workloads dominated by antialiased stroked and filled vector shapes (map layers, polylines, polygons) rather than images or text.

**Skip it when:**
- Native C or C++ code: it only runs inside a JVM as a Java 2D RenderingEngine; use a native rasterizer instead.
- If you are on a current OpenJDK and have no rendering bug to fix: you already run Marlin, so swapping in the jar brings fixes, not the historical 1.2x to 4x gains over Pisces or Ductus.
- Text rendering, image scaling or compositing bottlenecks: Marlin only produces shape coverage masks; blending and blits stay in the JDK pipeline.
- Very large stroked curves with cusps: open bug #35 (self-intersections in large stroked curves) and #38 (cubic offset computation) are unresolved.
- Thread-heavy web servers with default ThreadLocal contexts can hold one cached context per thread; the wiki suggests useThreadLocal=false (CLQ mode) to cap memory.

**Integration:** module (jar patched into the JDK; built into OpenJDK 9+) · none (Maven build, no third-party runtime dependencies); uses JDK-internal Unsafe and java.desktop internals · JDK 8 (0.9.4.7 jar via -Xbootclasspath/p), JDK 11 to 21 (0.9.4.8 jar), JDK 17 to 26 (0.9.4.9 jar, built with Java 17) · any platform with a HotSpot-style OpenJDK and Java 2D (pure Java; JDK 8 releases also targeted Oracle JDK 8)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Marlin only when your code draws through Java 2D Graphics2D on a JVM: Blend2D, AGG and Vello CPU are faster native options but need a different API and native integration, and ImageSharp.Drawing is the comparable choice on .NET. For a native C or C++ project, Blend2D is the stronger catalogued pick.

**Gotchas:**
- Releases are per JDK line (JDK 8, 11+, 17+); the JDK 8 branch use_Unsafe has not been maintained since 2024-01, and the default master branch still carries an old 0.7.0.1 pom, so take sources from the jdk branch or the release jars.
- Patching java.desktop replaces JDK-internal classes (sun.java2d.marlin); a JDK update can change internals the jar relies on, so match the jar to the supported JDK range in its release notes.
- Many tuning system properties (subpixel counts, tile sizes, profile=quality|speed, pixelWidth/pixelHeight for initial array sizes) change both speed and output; the published benchmarks used non-default settings for their time (tileSize_log2=5, useRef=soft).
- Later fixes have themselves caused regressions (JDK-8341381: random lines introduced by the JDK-8297230 fix, fixed in 0.9.4.9), so test rendering output after upgrading the jar.

**Status:** Active: release 0.9.4.9 for JDK 17 to 26 in late 2025 and 10 open issues, mostly quality enhancements; GPL-2.0 with Classpath exception, and since Marlin ships inside OpenJDK most users already have it, so the standalone jar matters mainly for JDK 8 and for newer fixes on older JDKs.

[repo](https://github.com/bourgesl/marlin-renderer) · [benchmark](https://bourgesl.github.io/marlin-0.5.6/longer_shared/perf_summary.htm)

##### JUCE software renderer (juce_graphics)  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

JUCE's CPU path rasterizer (EdgeTable + SWAR pixel blending); about 1.7x Skia and 2.9x Cairo single-threaded on M1 Pro.

**Beats:** Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo 1.18.4 — An independent run (Vello CPU author) of the Blend2D bl_bench harness on an Apple M1 Pro, single-threaded, SrcOver, 29 shape tests x 5 paint styles x 6 sizes (8x8 to 256x256), gives JUCE 8.0.8 a geometric-mean 1.68x Skia (1.64x without the non-equivalent StrokeRect tests) and 2.93x Cairo 1.18.4; my recomputation of the 2026-06-08 file matches (per style vs Skia: solid 1.48x, linear 1.94x, radial 1.78x, patterns 1.61-1.63x). Compiler, flags and the Skia version are not recorded, there is no x86 run, and output equivalence is not checked.

**Known shortcoming:** JUCE 8.0.8 software renderer at B on the same vello_chart data (1.68x Skia winning 84% of cells, 2.93x Cairo; 1.64x/2.90x without the StrokeRect tests, where JUCE's drawRect is four inner fills rather than a path stroke); its radial gradient has no focal point. Losses are the large solid and pattern rectangle fills (down to 0.31x). Licence AGPLv3 or commercial.

**Known shortcoming:** Recomputed from the vello_chart data: 1.68x Skia and 2.93x Cairo, but 0.41x Blend2D and 0.68x Vello CPU single-threaded (1.43x AGG, 3.09x Rust tiny-skia; derived from page data); JUCE loses on big rectangle and image fills. The measured 8.0.8 renderer takes precision shortcuts (blend divides by 256, gradient lookup table, sampled EdgeTable coverage), so the test is not output-equivalent, and JUCE 9.0.0 since reworked the software renderer (divide-by-255 blend, vectorised fills, image fills 2-4x faster per a search snippet), so the measured version is stale.

**How:** Paths are flattened (PathFlatteningIterator) into an EdgeTable: per-scanline lists of (x in 1/256 pixel, winding step) points, sampled at an adaptive number of sub-scanlines (256 / (1 + |dx/dy|) sub-steps, so steep edges cost one sample per scanline), then sorted and converted to 8-bit coverage spans. Spans are handed to templated per-fill callbacks (SolidColour, Gradient, ImageFill, TransformedImageFill) that write whole runs at once, with full-coverage runs taking a plain replace/blend loop. Pixels are blended SWAR-style, two 8-bit channels per 32-bit word (0x00ff00ff masks); gradients read a precomputed colour lookup table (up to 256 entries per colour stop, capped at 3x the gradient extent) indexed in fixed point. Translation-only transforms take separate fast paths (TranslationOrTransform, ImageFill vs TransformedImageFill).

**Use it when:**
- You already ship a JUCE app or audio plug-in and need CPU rendering (Linux, embedded, offscreen images) that is faster than Skia or Cairo would be.
- Stroke-heavy vector UI and charts: on the M1 Pro run strokes averaged 2.10x Skia (StrokeWorld 3.08x, StrokeFish 2.47x).
- Complex polygon and path fills at 32-256 px (FillPolyNZi40 solid 1.4-2.2x Skia at 32x32 and above) and gradient-filled shapes (linear-gradient cells 1.94x Skia, derived from page data).
- Your project is AGPLv3 or you hold a commercial JUCE licence.

**Skip it when:**
- Large solid or image rectangle fills and blits: JUCE 8.0.8 runs FillRectA solid at 0.31x Skia at 128x128 and 256x256, and aligned pattern blits at about 0.71x Skia (derived from page data).
- You want the fastest CPU rasterizer: Blend2D single-threaded is about 2.4x faster (JUCE 0.41x Blend2D) and Vello CPU single-threaded about 1.5x faster (JUCE 0.68x, faster in only 20% of cells), both derived from the same M1 Pro file.
- You need pixel parity with Skia or Cairo: coverage is approximate, 8.0.8 blends with a divide-by-256 shortcut, radial gradients in 8.0.8 have no focal point, and drawRect draws inside the bounds.
- Closed-source products without a commercial JUCE licence, or projects that want a small standalone library: juce_graphics pulls in juce_events and juce_core, plus freetype2 and fontconfig on Linux.
- Multi-threaded rendering: the renderer is single-threaded with no tiling or worker pool.

**Integration:** module · juce_events and juce_core (JUCE modules); freetype2 and fontconfig on Linux; Cocoa and QuartzCore frameworks on macOS · C++17, CMake 3.22+; Xcode 12.4, Visual Studio 2019, g++ 7 or Clang 6 · macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android (x86_64, x86, arm64; 32-bit Arm not regularly tested); portable C++ with no ISA requirement

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Blend2D or Vello CPU only when you are already inside JUCE: both are faster on the same M1 Pro harness and are standalone, permissively licensed libraries. Against AGG (1.43x AGG, derived from page data) and Skia or Cairo it is the faster option for strokes and complex paths, but it loses to Skia on large rectangle and image fills.

**Gotchas:**
- Graphics::drawRect fills four rectangles inside the shape bounds instead of stroking a centred path, so stroked rectangles look and cost differently from Skia or Cairo strokes (StrokeRectU measured 3.44x Skia for this reason).
- JUCE 8.0.8 PixelARGB::blend uses (0x100 - alpha) and >> 8 with clamping, a divide-by-256 approximation; JUCE 9 (HEAD) switched to a rounded divide-by-255 SWAR blend, so 8.0.8 output and speed are not those of the current release.
- The benchmark forces juce::SoftwareImageType and builds with USE_COREGRAPHICS_RENDERING=0; JUCE's native image types and window peers can use CoreGraphics or Direct2D instead, so in a normal macOS or Windows app you get this renderer only if you ask for it.
- EdgeTable sampling cost grows as edges get flatter (up to 256 sub-scanline samples per scanline for near-horizontal edges, since the step is clamped to 1-256), and coverage within a scanline is taken from one x sample per sub-step, not exact area.

**Status:** Actively developed (JUCE 9.0.3, last commit 2026-09-28, 8.9k stars); JUCE 9.0.0 lists 'Improved the performance of the software renderer' and, per search-result text from the JUCE 9 forum announcement (forum page not opened), refactored PixelARGB for vectorised fills with 2-4x faster image fills, so the 8.0.8 numbers, especially the losing image and rectangle fills, are likely out of date; copyable under AGPLv3 or the commercial JUCE licence.

[repo](https://github.com/juce-framework/JUCE) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LaurenzV/vello_chart/HEAD/data/arm/2026-06-08.json)

#### video-audio

##### libsoxr (SoX Resampler)  `C`  `LGPL-2.1-or-later`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

LGPL C audio resampler (the SoX engine) that ran 6.8-22x libsamplerate 0.2.2's throughput in a third-party streaming benchmark.

**Beats:** libsamplerate 0.2.2 (Secret Rabbit Code, SRC_SINC_MEDIUM_QUALITY and SRC_SINC_BEST_QUALITY converters) — The SampleRateTap author's harness (bench_compare.cpp, Google Benchmark, GCC 13.3 -O3, Ubuntu 24.04 packages soxr 0.1.3 and libsamplerate 0.2.2, unnamed shared Xeon at 2.10 GHz, median of 5, 2026-09-25) streams a float32 interleaved 997 Hz sine from 48 kHz to 48 kHz x (1 + 200 ppm) in 128-frame blocks, single-threaded, counting output frames. soxr HQ vs libsamplerate MEDIUM: 114.3 vs 5.2 (mono), 52.9 vs 4.8 (stereo) and 12.9 vs 1.9 (8-ch) Mframes/s; soxr VHQ vs BEST: 32.1 vs 1.6 (stereo). That is about 6.8-22x, derived from page data. Reading the harness found no flaw: soxr reads input in place while libsamplerate gets an extra 128-frame copy, which is negligible at these rates. The page's THD+N measurement covers VHQ (at the 24-bit format ceiling) but not HQ, so the HQ-to-MEDIUM quality pairing rests on vendor-stated stopbands.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on tap/SampleRateTap async/docs/COMPARISON.md, a shootout run by a competitor (Timothy Place; async/bench/compare/bench_compare.cpp, GCC 13.3 -O3, single thread, Ubuntu 24.04 packages, 'shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz' with no model, so not A): 52.9 vs 4.8 MB/s stereo, 114.3 vs 5.2 mono, 12.9 vs 1.9 8-channel, 32.1 vs 1.6 VHQ against libsamplerate 0.2.2. The ratio tested is near unity (1 plus 200 ppm), not 44.1 to 48 kHz; HQ vs MEDIUM are matched (about 120 dB, 91.3% vs 90% bandwidth), while VHQ vs BEST trades a narrower band (91.3% vs 97%) for more rejection. soxr's own repo and SourceForge wiki carry no comparison. Licence LGPL-2.1-or-later.

**Known shortcoming:** The int16 and int32 output paths carry a stale fe_test_invalid flag that corrupts samples (issue #11; PR #12 open since 2023-11; the float path is unaffected), and int16 dither is seeded with time(0), so output is non-deterministic (issue #8). Upstream CMake builds scalar on AArch64 (FindSIMD32 tries NEON only for '^arm'; the dofuuz fork claims over 2x from fixing it); the FFT-cache lock is a no-op without OpenMP; CMake 4 needs a minimum-version bump (issue #14); soxr_oneshot defaults to low quality. Latency 424-788 frames at HQ.

**How:** The README says the design follows Laurent de Soras' 'The Quest For The Perfect Resampler': Julius O. Smith's bandlimited interpolation combined with FFT-based oversampling. In cr.c a long, steep low-pass runs as overlap-save FFT convolution in large blocks (DFT sizes from 2^10 up to 2^17 by default). For the benchmarked near-unity ratio that block upsamples 2x, then a short polyphase FIR with polynomial-interpolated coefficients produces the fractional step, sized to a 400 kB coefficient budget. Rational ratios with small factors skip the coefficient interpolation, and power-of-two factors use half-band stages. CPUID at run time picks the SIMD engines on x86: HQ runs single precision with SSE and PFFFT (cr32s), and VHQ runs double precision with AVX and PFFFT (cr64s). libsamplerate instead does a per-sample time-domain sinc convolution.

**Use it when:**
- Offline or batch conversion at real ratios (44.1 to 48 kHz, 96 to 44.1 kHz, downsampling for ML front ends). python-soxr's README times 10 s of 48 to 44.1 kHz at 10.8 ms for soxr HQ against 223 ms for libsamplerate sinc_medium, and 14.5 ms for VHQ against 794 ms for sinc_best.
- Replacing libsamplerate SINC_MEDIUM or SINC_BEST in throughput-bound desktop or server code that can absorb about 10-20 ms of filter delay. In the third-party table HQ gets 52.9 vs 4.8 Mframes/s on stereo, and VHQ gets 32.1 vs 1.6 for BEST.
- Mixed-format pipelines that want one call to deinterleave, convert int16/int32/float64 to the engine's type, resample, apply gain and dither back to int16.
- Multichannel streams on spare cores: with num_threads = 0 and an OpenMP build, soxr processes channels in parallel (the default is 1 thread).
- Applications that need tunable quality, e.g. minimum-phase filters for lower pre-ringing, or 28-33-bit precision for mastering.

**Skip it when:**
- Live monitoring or other paths with a 1-2 ms budget. In the SampleRateTap measurement HQ holds back 424-788 frames (8.8-16.4 ms at 48 kHz) and VHQ 433 frames. The README itself quotes about 1000 output samples (about 20 ms) for HQ at 44.1/48 kHz. libsamplerate MEDIUM holds 46 frames and SampleRateTap 24.
- Upstream builds on AArch64 (Apple silicon, Graviton). FindSIMD32.cmake tries NEON flags only when the processor name starts with 'arm', and SSE flags otherwise, so 0.1.3 builds its scalar engines there. The dofuuz/soxr fork says it enables AArch64 optimization for an over 2x speed-up.
- Closed-source products that must link statically and cannot meet LGPL-2.1 relinking terms. r8brain-free-src is MIT and header-only.
- Projects that need a maintained upstream. The last release is 0.1.3 (2018-02-24). The GitHub mirror has 9 open issues and 6 open pull requests, including a distortion fix (PR #12, 2023), AArch64 support (PR #9, 2022) and a CMake minimum bump (issue #14) that newer CMake needs.
- Real clock-drift correction. soxr has a variable-rate mode but no ratio estimation, so an external servo must feed soxr_set_io_ratio. SampleRateTap recovers the clock itself.

**Integration:** shared lib (static via -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF); optional libsoxr-lsr with a libsamplerate-style API · none required beyond libm. Optional: OpenMP (multi-channel threading and the FFT-cache locks), the bundled PFFFT (BSD-like licence, on by default for the HQ SIMD engine), libavcodec as an alternative FFT, and libavutil for NEON detection on 32-bit ARM · C compiler with 64-bit integers; the library builds as -std=gnu89; CMake 3.1 per CMakeLists.txt (INSTALL says 3.0). CMake 4.x needs a minimum-version bump (issue #14; fixed in the dofuuz fork). · x86 and x86-64 with run-time selection between SSE (HQ) and AVX (VHQ) engines; 32-bit ARM NEON when libavutil is found or SOXR_USE_SIMD is set; scalar elsewhere, including AArch64 in upstream 0.1.3; Windows (MSVC, MinGW), Linux, macOS

**Vs siblings:** Pick soxr over r8brain-free-src for raw throughput when LGPL is acceptable: in the same SampleRateTap table it is 3.1-3.2x faster at the 120 dB tier and 1.7-2.3x faster at the 140 dB tier, with less delay than r8brain's default settings (VHQ 433 frames vs 1,700-1,782), all derived from page data. Pick r8brain for an MIT, header-only drop-in. LibFResample's numbers come from a different harness (libsamplerate 0.1.8 on a Phenom II), and zita-resampler (GPL) has only directional claims, so neither can be compared with soxr directly.

**Gotchas:**
- Integer output is risky in 0.1.3. The int16/int32 RINT_CLIP path tests fe_test_invalid() and writes a full-scale clip value when the FE_INVALID flag is set. Issue #11 and PR #12 (open since 2023-11) report a stale flag corrupting otherwise valid samples. The float32 output path used in the benchmark does not go through this check.
- int16 output is dithered with a seed built from time(0) and the object's address (soxr.c), so results differ from run to run (issue #8, open). The dofuuz fork makes int16 output reproducible and fixes a periodic-zeros dithering bug.
- soxr_oneshot() defaults to LQ quality, not the HQ default of soxr_create(), so pass an explicit quality spec. Streaming calls return a varying number of output frames, and soxr_delay() changes with the streaming state.
- Environment variables override the application's runtime spec: SOXR_NUM_THREADS, SOXR_COEFS_SIZE, SOXR_MIN_DFT_SIZE, SOXR_LARGE_DFT_SIZE and SOXR_USE_SIMD/SIMD32/SIMD64. Pin or clear them in benchmarks and deployments.

**Status:** Upstream has been abandoned since 0.1.3 (2018-02-24), but that release is still what Linux distributions ship, and the LGPL-2.1-or-later C sources build with CMake. For ARM64, CMake 4 or reproducible int16 output, use the maintained dofuuz/soxr fork (last commit 2026-06-27), which python-soxr bundles.

[repo](https://github.com/chirlu/soxr) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tap/SampleRateTap/blob/main/async/docs/COMPARISON.md)

### networking-and-servers

#### event-loops-io

##### uring_exec  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only liburing adapter for stdexec (std::execution) senders; beats Asio's io_uring backend on loopback TCP ping-pong.

**Beats:** Boost.Asio (io_uring backend) — Loopback TCP ping-pong on one AMD 5800H box (Linux 6.4.8, GCC 13.2 -O3, 16 KiB blocks, 5 s): a uring_exec echo server beat an Asio coroutine echo server built with ASIO_HAS_IO_URING and ASIO_DISABLE_EPOLL by 1.27x-3.46x across 2/4/8 threads and 10/100/1000 sessions (e.g. 4 threads/1000 sessions: 4.411 vs 1.275 GiB/s). The client was uring_exec's own ping in both cases, and there was one run per cell with no variance reported. A newer 10 s table in benchmarks/README adds Asio on epoll, which beats uring_exec at 10-100 sessions with 2+ threads.
