**Known shortcoming:** Beats Asio's io_uring backend (1.27-3.46x) but Asio on its default epoll backend beats uring_exec at low session counts (4 threads/100 sessions: 8.744 vs 3.226 GiB/s); the author says io_uring cannot beat epoll on the current kernel and calls the project effectively archived since 2025.

**Known shortcoming:** Loopback benchmark with uring_exec's own client; its run() loop busy-polls (keeps a core busy when idle) while Asio threads block; single runs, no variance. Against Asio on epoll it loses in 5 of 6 rows at 10-100 sessions with 2-8 threads (epoll 1.4-3.2x faster). No TLS or multishot/zero-copy; noexcept constructor terminates if io_uring is unavailable.

**How:** Each thread that calls run() lazily gets its own thread-local io_uring ring, created with IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER and IORING_SETUP_COOP_TASKRUN, and all rings share one kernel worker pool through IORING_SETUP_ATTACH_WQ. Operation states are immovable and intrusive, with a per-object vtable for type erasure, and the CQE user_data points straight at them, so the library itself does no per-I/O heap allocation. Work scheduled from other threads goes through lock-free CAS intrusive queues split into 16 buckets that run threads drain by round-robin plus random pick. The default run loop submits without blocking, harvests completions in batches with io_uring_peek_batch_cqe (64 per batch, up to 512 per step) and calls yield() when idle instead of sleeping in the kernel. The author gives no explanation of why this beats Asio.

**Use it when:**
- Your code base already uses stdexec/P2300 senders and you want Linux socket or file I/O as composable senders with stop-token cancellation and when_any timeouts.
- Many concurrent TCP connections (1,000-100,000) served by several threads on one box. The author's newer table has it beating Asio epoll there, e.g. 8 threads/10,000 sessions 6.662 vs 2.118 GiB/s.
- A single-threaded event loop: at 1 thread it beat both Asio backends at every session count in the author's table (e.g. 100 sessions: 4.026 vs 3.600 io_uring, 3.052 epoll GiB/s).
- You can give the event loop dedicated cores, because the default run loop polls and yields rather than blocking.
- As a small, readable reference (about 1,600 lines of headers) for mapping io_uring onto sender/receiver before writing your own.

**Skip it when:**
- Few connections spread over several threads. In 5 of the 6 rows with 10-100 sessions and 2-8 threads, Asio's default epoll backend was 1.4-3.2x faster in the author's own table (4 threads/100 sessions: 8.744 vs 3.226 GiB/s), and the author says io_uring cannot beat epoll on the current kernel.
- Production services that need a maintained dependency: the README calls it effectively archived since 2025, there is one author, the repo has only two test files and no CI config, and the build follows stdexec main, whose upstream changes have broken compilation (issue #2, the 2026-05 fix commit, a ~10x compile-time regression noted for ping_when_any).
- You need TLS, DNS or higher-level socket types. The API is raw file descriptors, and the author says in issue #3 that async OpenSSL is out of scope (workarounds: poll-based SSL or kTLS).
- You want advanced io_uring features: the sender list has no multishot accept/recv, provided buffer rings, registered files/buffers or zero-copy send.
- Non-Linux targets, kernels older than about 6.1 (the recommended minimum), or environments where io_uring is disabled. Also workloads that cancel every I/O, since per-operation cancellation adds overhead according to the benchmarks README.

**Integration:** header-only · stdexec (NVIDIA, tracked at main), liburing (link -luring, recent enough for io_uring_prep_futex_wait/bind), pthread; Asio only for the comparison benchmark · C++20; benchmarked with GCC 13.2; the benchmarks README says Clang also works (there is a clang-19 workaround commit) · Linux only (io_uring), kernel 6.1+ recommended; architecture support not documented (benchmarked on x86-64 AMD 5800H)

**Vs siblings:** Pick uring_exec when you specifically want io_uring exposed as std::execution senders. For a maintained C++20-coroutine io_uring runtime that aims to cover most io_uring features and also posts wins over epoll and Asio, Condy is the safer choice. At low connection counts, stock Asio on epoll (or PhotonLibOS, which edges out boost::asio in its own ping-pong) is faster than uring_exec according to the author's own data.

**Gotchas:**
- The default run() never blocks in the kernel. It calls io_uring_submit without waiting, peeks the CQ and calls std::this_thread::yield() when nothing moved, so each run thread keeps a core busy even when idle. run_policy{.waitable=true} switches to io_uring_submit_and_wait.
- An I/O sender submits its SQE to the thread-local ring of whichever thread calls start(). Hop onto the scheduler first (stdexec::schedule or starts_on, as every example does), or the operation sits in a ring that no run() loop drains.
- Thread-local rings are keyed by the io_uring_exec constructor's call site through a template lambda parameter. The header warns that constructing it repeatedly at one site (e.g. in a loop) reuses the same per-thread ring, so treat it as a long-lived singleton. The constructor is noexcept, but ring setup throws std::system_error on failure, which means std::terminate if io_uring is unavailable.
- async_read/async_write default to offset 0, so on a seekable file every call hits byte 0 unless you pass an offset. Errors arrive as set_error(exception_ptr to std::system_error), and -ECANCELED arrives as set_stopped.

**Status:** The author declares it effectively archived since 2025 (the last commit, 2026-05-01, only follows stdexec API renames); it is header-only and MPL-2.0, so it is easy to vendor, but you inherit stdexec churn yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/Caturra000/uring_exec) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Caturra000/uring_exec/blob/master/README.md)

#### http-servers-frameworks

##### Lwan  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

C HTTP/1.1 server and embeddable library; topped TechEmpower Round 10 JSON at ~5.8x Go net/http's throughput.

**Beats:** Go net/http — TechEmpower Round 10 (April 2015), Peak Hosting dual-Xeon E5 v2 servers (40 hyperthreads) over 10 GbE, JSON-serialization test: Lwan rev 49607add (CMake Release, compiler not stated) peaked at 2,200,066 req/s at 256 connections, #1 of 145, versus 379,662 req/s for TFB's Go 1.4.2 net/http + encoding/json entry (5.8x); the ratio was 1.7x at 8 connections. In the same round's plaintext test the gap was ~2.6x (2,075,046 vs 799,052 req/s, Lwan #7, far behind ULib's 6.9M), and Lwan's JSON handler then built a ccan/json DOM per request, so the win comes from the server core, not from JSON encoding.

**Known shortcoming:** The evidence is TechEmpower Round 10 (2015, Go 1.4.2 baseline), about 5.8x on JSON; no recent independent rounds are cited. No compiler or exact CPU model stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is TechEmpower Round 10 (April 2015, Go 1.4.2); the maintainer reported a big regression in later preview rounds (#291). The 5.8x is the 256-connection best case (1.7x at 8, 2.6x at 32); plaintext in the same round is ~2.6x. September 2026 fixed an out-of-bounds read in the URL decoder (#380), request desynchronization via stale pipelining state (#381, #382) and a WebSocket worker spin (#383); lost/stuck socket reports still open. HTTP/1.x only, TLS experimental (Linux, TLS 1.2), no chunked uploads, 40 KB default body cap, >4 KB pipelined requests fail (#218). Default CMake build is Debug; Release uses -march=native; no coroutine stack guard page. GPL-2.0-or-later.

**How:** One worker thread per online CPU, pinned using the sysfs thread_siblings topology, each with its own SO_REUSEPORT listening socket (with a CBPF steering filter where available) and its own edge-triggered epoll set; connection state lives in one preallocated array indexed by file descriptor. Every connection runs in a stackful coroutine switched by a hand-written x86-64/aarch64 swapcontext that skips floating-point registers and the signal mask, so handlers read like blocking code with no per-request thread or callback chain. The request parser dispatches on methods and headers by loading 2/4/8 bytes as integers (`STRING_SWITCH`), finds line ends with memchr/memmem, and decodes URLs with SSE/SWAR; idle keep-alive connections expire through a timeout queue driven by a timer wheel. Release builds add LTO and `-march=native`.

**Use it when:**
- Small, CPU-cheap HTTP/1.1 responses (JSON, plaintext, cached small files) at high connection counts, where per-request server overhead dominates; in Round 10 its lead over Go net/http grew from 1.7x at 8 connections to 5.8x at 256.
- Linux x86-64 or aarch64 hosts where you build from source for the target CPU and want one pinned worker per core.
- Embedding an HTTP endpoint in a C program via liblwan without a C++ runtime or an external event library.
- Config-only static file or Lua serving: files under 16 KiB are mmap-cached with precompressed deflate/gzip/Brotli/zstd variants, and larger files go out via sendfile.
- A fast backend stub or load target for benchmarking proxies and gateways (the README lists Kong, KrakenD and Istio using it this way).

**Skip it when:**
- You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3: Lwan is HTTP/1.x only (issue #17, open since 2014).
- You need production TLS: TLS is marked experimental, works only on Linux through kTLS (tls.ko plus mbedTLS), and supports TLSv1.2 only; the README suggests a separate terminator such as Hitch.
- Uploads without Content-Length or of large size: a request body with no Content-Length gets 400 (no chunked request bodies), POST/PUT bodies are capped at 40,960 bytes by default, and issue #218 (open) reports pipelined requests over 4 KB failing.
- An internet-facing edge that needs a hardened parser: September 2026 reports fixed request desynchronization via stale pipelined state (#381, #382), a WebSocket-FIN busy-spin that pinned a worker (#383), and an 8-byte out-of-bounds read in the SWAR URL decoder (#380); lost/stuck socket reports #348 and #353 remain open.
- Proprietary software that ships the binary: Lwan is GPL-2.0-or-later, so distributing a program linked with liblwan carries GPL obligations (the README notes that only serving over HTTP does not).

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (liblwan-static / liblwan.so with installed headers), or the standalone `lwan` server binary · Required: CMake 3.20+ (CMakeLists.txt; the README still says 2.8) and one of zlib, zlib-ng or libdeflate. Optional: Lua 5.4, Brotli, zstd, mbedTLS (kTLS), mimalloc/jemalloc/tcmalloc, SQLite and MariaDB client (samples only); libucontext on architectures other than x86-64/aarch64. · C compiler that accepts -std=gnu11 (GCC or Clang; uses GNU extensions, inline assembly and linker sections) · Linux x86-64 is primary (CI build, tests, static analysis, OSS-Fuzz); FreeBSD and OpenBSD x86-64 build (epoll emulated on kqueue); aarch64 has a native context switch; other CPUs fall back to libucontext, which fails on Apple Silicon macOS (issue #366). Windows not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Lwan over Drogon, Crow, Oat++, CWIST or Agoo-C when you want a pure-C HTTP/1.1 server with the widest measured margin over Go net/http (5.8x in TFB JSON versus ~1.5x for Crow in the catalog), and GPL plus no HTTP/2 is acceptable. If you need HTTP/2 or production TLS, Lwan is the wrong choice; look at H2O or a C++ framework instead.

**Gotchas:**
- The default CMake build type is Debug, which logs every request while holding a lock; benchmark only with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
- Release builds default to -march=native/-mtune=native (MTUNE_NATIVE=ON), so a binary can fail on other CPUs; pass -DMTUNE_NATIVE=OFF when packaging.
- Coroutine stacks are fixed-size (4x SIGSTKSZ, 8x with Brotli, page-rounded) and in release builds come from the heap with no guard page, so deep recursion or large stack buffers in handlers can silently overflow (see issue #130).
- At startup Lwan raises RLIMIT_NOFILE and preallocates max_file_descriptors (default 524288) x sizeof(struct lwan_connection); max_file_descriptors must be at least 10x threads. A crash when threads < online CPUs was fixed only on 2026-09-18.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-22; latest tag v0.7, June 2025; September 2026 security reports were fixed within days), GPL-2.0-or-later, built from source with CMake or pulled as GHCR container images and Alpine/Arch/NixOS packages.

[repo](https://github.com/lpereira/lwan) · [benchmark](https://www.techempower.com/benchmarks/results/round10/peak.json)

#### tls

##### wolfSSL  `C`  `GPL-3.0 (the LICENSING file lets certain listed projects, e.g. MariaDB and OpenVPN, use it under GPL-2.0 instead)`  `active`  `Tier B`

Embedded-first C TLS 1.3 library, not an OpenSSL fork, that beat every OpenSSL version in HAProxy's 64-core Graviton4 tests.

**Beats:** OpenSSL — HAProxy Technologies ran HAProxy 3.1-dev1 on a 64-core Graviton4 (AWS r8g.16xlarge, gcc 11.4, mid-2024) with wolfSSL 5.7.0 and with OpenSSL 1.1.1w, 3.0.x and 3.1-3.4-dev. At 64 threads wolfSSL handled 59.7k full RSA handshakes/s vs 48.3k for 1.1.1w, ~43k for 3.1+ and ~21k for 3.0.x, and ~150k end-to-end ticket resumptions/s vs 17.8k (1.1.1w with pthread locks), 23-28k (3.1+) and 1.6-3.7k (3.0.x). It was second to AWS-LC in both tests, and neither wolfSSL's build flags nor the test harness were published.

**Known shortcoming:** GPL-3.0 (commercial licence otherwise), so not freely copyable into proprietary code. Test scripts and flags for the HAProxy benchmark unpublished.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked on 5.7.0 (mid-2024) with unpublished configure flags; a plain ./configure leaves the SP and CPU assembly off, and --enable-haproxy is not implied by distro builds. Use >= 5.9.4 for three High-severity certificate-verification CVEs (one widened in OpenSSL-compatible builds); open ASan use-after-free with HAProxy's test suite (#10123). Only ticket resumption was measured; session-ID resumption uses a global cache under one rwlock. AWS-LC beat it in both tests.

**How:** Public-key math runs on wolfCrypt's 'SP' (single-precision) backend. This is generated code with a fixed size per key length (2048-bit RSA is 32 x 64-bit words) that does Karatsuba multiplication and Montgomery reduction in inline AArch64/x86-64 assembly (sp_arm64.c alone is ~7 MB). It is paired with ARMv8 Crypto Extension/NEON and AES-NI/AVX2/AVX-512 code for AES-GCM, SHA-2, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and X25519. For multi-core scaling, the manual says the library is 'thread safe by design' because it 'avoids global data', and reference counts use C11 <stdatomic.h> or GCC __atomic builtins (wc_port.h). In HAProxy's profiles, wolfSSL's resumption curve did not change between pthread locks and HAProxy's lightweight locks ('it clearly doesn't need locks'), while OpenSSL 1.1.1w and 3.x spent most of their CPU in pthread_rwlock calls and atomics.

**Use it when:**
- HAProxy, or another OpenSSL-API server that already has a wolfSSL port, taking many short-lived TLS connections on many cores, where OpenSSL 3.x lock and atomic contention caps throughput. At 64 threads HAProxy measured 59.7k vs ~43k RSA full handshakes/s (OpenSSL 3.1-3.4-dev) and ~150k vs 23-28k ticket resumptions/s.
- Workloads heavy on ticket resumption, such as a proxy re-encrypting to backends or clients that reconnect often, where you want linear scaling to 64 cores without special lock builds.
- Embedded, RTOS or kernel-module targets that need TLS 1.3/DTLS 1.3 in tens of kB. The repo ships ports for Zephyr, ESP-IDF, STM32, Renesas, NXP and others, custom allocators (wolfSSL_SetAllocators) and a static memory pool (WOLFSSL_STATIC_MEMORY).
- You need a FIPS 140-3 validated module and a vendor that sells commercial licenses and support contracts (HAProxy notes an LTS period is 'probably negotiable').
- Post-quantum TLS work: ML-KEM/ML-DSA with AVX-512/AArch64 assembly plus native Falcon and FrodoKEM, with no liboqs dependency as of 5.9.4.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a binary drop-in for libssl/libcrypto or exact OpenSSL behavior. The compatibility layer is a macro mapping, and HAProxy reports 'minor differences' and says deploying it 'requires a lot of testing and feature validation'.
- Proprietary distribution without buying a commercial license: the code is GPL-3.0, and GPL-2.0 is allowed only for a named list of projects (MariaDB, OpenVPN, U-Boot from Cisco, ...).
- You want the absolute top numbers on Graviton. AWS-LC (v1.32.0+30) beat it on full RSA handshakes (63.1k vs 59.7k/s), and AWS-LC built with C11 beat it by ~20% on resumption (183k/s).
- You depend on distro packages and automatic OS security updates. HAProxy found that the Debian/Ubuntu wolfSSL packages lacked the HAProxy options and CPU optimizations it needed, so it had to build and maintain wolfSSL by hand.
- You can't upgrade quickly. 5.9.4 (2026-09-25) fixed three High-severity certificate-verification CVEs, and one of them (CVE-2026-93302, trusted-peer CA check) widens to all CA loading in OPENSSL_COMPATIBLE_DEFAULTS builds, which --enable-haproxy, --enable-nginx, --enable-all and --enable-distro all turn on.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (autotools ./configure or CMake; also source-drop with user_settings.h for IDE/RTOS builds) · none beyond libc (optional hardware or crypto-callback ports; the liboqs dependency was removed in 5.9.4) · ANSI C (a C89 build is supported via --enable-c89); autoconf/automake/libtool for git checkouts or CMake 3.16+ (CMake support described as 'still under development'); asm is auto-enabled only for GNU-C-compatible compilers; the benchmark used gcc 11.4 · any C target; assembly for x86-64 (AES-NI/AVX2/AVX-512), AArch64 (ARMv8 crypto extensions/NEON), ARM32/Thumb-2/Cortex-M, RISC-V 64 and PPC32/64; Linux, Windows, macOS/iOS, Android, many RTOSes and a Linux kernel module

**Vs siblings:** Pick wolfSSL over AWS-LC when you need a small, embeddable or FIPS 140-3 stack across many CPUs and RTOSes, a vendor support contract, or good multi-core scaling from a default build (the AWS-LC versions tested needed CMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 to avoid lock collapse, since fixed upstream); pick AWS-LC for the highest Graviton numbers and an API descended from BoringSSL/OpenSSL. Tempesta FW is a complete web accelerator and DDoS-protection proxy rather than a library, so wolfSSL is the choice when you link TLS into your own server.

**Gotchas:**
- Speed depends on configure flags. The fixed-size SP assembly and the ARMv8/Intel assembly are off by default in a plain ./configure (--enable-sp, --enable-armasm and --enable-intelasm all default to disabled). You enable them with --enable-sp --enable-sp-asm, --enable-armasm/--enable-intelasm, or --enable-all-asm; configure.ac turns all-asm on automatically only under --enable-all/all-crypto on 64-bit GNU C. HAProxy did not publish the flags it used.
- The ABI depends on the build configuration. configure generates wolfssl/options.h, which you must include before any other wolfSSL header (or define WOLFSSL_USE_OPTIONS_H). Struct layouts vary with options and between releases (5.9.4 changed OcspRequest, so code that embeds it must be rebuilt).
- Unlike OpenSSL, a client verifies the server by default: without loaded CAs, connect fails with -188 (README Note 2). Static-key RSA/DH/PSK cipher suites are disabled unless you enable them with WOLFSSL_STATIC_* defines.
- The benchmark only measured ticket resumption. Session-ID resumption goes through the process-global SessionCache under one rwlock unless ENABLE_SESSION_CACHE_ROW_LOCK is defined (ssl_sess.c). Issue #10123, still open, reports an ASAN use-after-free when HAProxy's vtest suite runs against wolfSSL master.

**Status:** Actively maintained by wolfSSL Inc. (5.9.4 released and last commit 2026-09-25) under GPL-3.0 or a commercial license. It is production-usable, but you build it yourself with the right configure flags and must keep up with frequent security releases.

[repo](https://github.com/wolfSSL/wolfssl) · [benchmark](https://www.haproxy.com/blog/state-of-ssl-stacks)

#### websocket-grpc-rpc

##### wtx (gRPC server)  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust crate with its own HTTP/2 and gRPC stack. Its unary gRPC server served 3.7-5.5x grpc-go's req/s on HttpArena.

**Beats:** gRPC (grpc-go, official google.golang.org/grpc implementation) — HttpArena ran a unary GetSum gRPC call over plaintext h2c, driven by h2load with 256 and 1024 connections, 100 streams each, 5 s runs, best of 3. The machine was a Threadripper PRO 3995WX, with the server pinned to 32 cores plus their SMT threads. wtx 0.49 (nightly Rust, target-cpu=native) served 3,990,708 req/s against grpc-go v1.72.0 (Go 1.24, default grpc.NewServer) at 720,798 req/s with 256 connections (5.5x). With 1024 connections it served 3,620,970 against 969,718 (3.7x). Two limits apply: wtx used about 64 logical CPUs against grpc-go's 44, and the two results come from different run dates (grpc-go on 2026-04-12, wtx re-validated on 2026-08-24).

**Known shortcoming:** Rust. The wtx and grpc-go HttpArena runs were weeks apart, the author contributed the entry, and earlier wtx numbers were invalid (empty reply body, fixed in PR #1300). Several other entries (zix, cardigan, swerver) reach ~6.8-7.0M rps on the same board.

**Known shortcoming:** Unary gRPC calls only, with hand-written service definitions (#231) and third-party message codegen. The author calls it a free-time project that probably shouldn't be used in production (#452); no security audit, including its own TLS 1.3. An independent grpc_bench run (discussion #559, 2026-04, Xeon Gold 6548N, wtx 0.40) had it behind go_grpc (93,004 vs 117,082 req/s at 4 CPUs) and tonic, while an earlier run (#547, Ryzen 5900X) had it ahead, so the result depends on environment. HttpArena p99 is 69.9 ms at 256 connections vs a 6.55 ms average, and grpc-go's p99 field repeats its average, so tail latency cannot be compared. Returning () or a string type from a handler silently sends an empty body with grpc-status 0 (behind the invalid HttpArena results fixed in PR #1300). Needs nightly Rust; 7 breaking releases in 3 months (benchmarked 0.49, current 0.52.1). Plain HTTP/2 is slower than hyper (4.08M vs 6.97M req/s). Missing crypto feature fails at runtime, not build time.

**How:** Http2ServerFramework::run_in_threads uses a runtime-per-thread, shared-nothing design. It starts one single-threaded tokio LocalRuntime per available thread. Each runtime binds its own listener (SO_REUSEPORT is on by default) and runs its connection and stream tasks locally, so the hot path has no work-stealing and no cross-thread handoff. The HTTP/2 framing, HPACK and Huffman code are written in-house, and the response is built in the same buffer as the request, so a reply no larger than the request needs no new allocation. The benchmark binary also used target-cpu=native, thin LTO, codegen-units=1, panic=abort and wtx's optimizations-std feature (memchr, simdutf8, socket2).

**Use it when:**
- A Rust service whose hot path is small unary gRPC calls at very high request rates on a many-core Linux box. On HttpArena, wtx served 3.99M req/s against grpc-go's 0.72M with 256 h2c connections.
- Workloads with hundreds to thousands of connections, each carrying many concurrent streams. These spread well across the per-thread listeners; the benchmark used 256-1024 connections with 100 streams each.
- gRPC over TLS without a separate TLS stack: in HttpArena's unary-grpc-tls test, with wtx's own TLS 1.3, it reached 3.69M vs 0.70M req/s (256 connections) and 3.63M vs 0.93M (1024).
- Internal services, prototypes or benchmark rigs where you control the .proto files and both ends, and you can type the service routes by hand.
- Projects that want gRPC, HTTP/2, WebSocket and Postgres from one crate with a small dependency tree and fast builds. The README reports 2 required dependencies and a 6.53 s clean optimized build for the gRPC client.

**Skip it when:**
- You need server, client or bidirectional streaming RPCs. The gRPC module supports unary calls only.
- You need generated service stubs or the usual gRPC ecosystem. Services must be typed by hand; the macro for this is still open issue #231. Reflection, health checking and interceptor libraries are not documented.
- Production or security-sensitive systems. The README says wtx has had no security audit. In issue #452 (Nov 2025) the author calls it 'a fun project developed in my free-time that probably shouldn't be used in production' and advised a user to stay on tokio-tungstenite.
- Small CPU budgets or strict tail-latency targets. In grpc_bench's 2026-04-23 run (wtx 0.40, 1-4 server CPUs, 1000 clients), wtx trailed go_grpc (93,004 vs 117,082 req/s at 4 CPUs) and tonic, and its p90 stayed at about 42 ms. On HttpArena its p99 was 69.93 ms at 256 connections (average 6.55 ms), and it used 727 MiB of memory against grpc-go's 310.5 MiB.
- Teams that require stable Rust or a stable API. lib.rs enables nightly features, and crates.io lists 7 breaking minor releases (0.46 to 0.52) between 2026-05-16 and 2026-08-10.

**Integration:** crate · For the benchmarked gRPC server: tokio, quick-protobuf, hashbrown, foldhash, plus memchr, simdutf8 and socket2 through optimizations-std. pb-rs (or another generator) is needed at build time to generate message types. TLS or other crypto needs one backend feature: crypto-ring (ring), crypto-alr (aws-lc-rs), crypto-graviola or crypto-ruco (RustCrypto). · Rust nightly only. lib.rs uses #![feature(random, return_type_notation)] even though crates.io lists rust-version 1.96. The repo pins nightly-2026-09-03, the crate uses edition 2024, and HttpArena built wtx 0.49 with nightly-2026-06-27. · The core is no_std + alloc, and the README says it works on embedded devices with a heap allocator. Targets with 16-bit pointers are not supported. The multi-threaded server needs std; the executors are tokio, wtx's own std executor, and embassy-net. Benchmarks exist only for x86-64 Linux.

**Vs siblings:** Pick wtx when the service is written in Rust and must keep standard gRPC-over-HTTP/2 clients: its measured gain over grpc-go (3.7-5.5x) is larger than that of Kitex (1.5-1.7x) or rpcx (2.3-2.6x), both Go, though each was measured on a different harness. grpcxx is the closest C++ analogue that also speaks gRPC; brpc is the more mature C++ multi-protocol choice.

**Gotchas:**
- The response is built in the request buffer, and the handler's return type decides what happens to that buffer. ResFinalizer for () (and for &str, String and Vector) calls req.clear(). A handler that writes its reply into req.msg_data.body and returns () therefore sends an empty body with grpc-status 0. This bug invalidated wtx's own HttpArena entry until PR #1300; return StatusCode or VerbatimParams instead.
- If no crypto backend feature is selected, crypto calls panic or halt at runtime instead of failing the build. TLS and secure cookies need one of crypto-ring, crypto-alr, crypto-graviola or crypto-ruco.
- HTTP/2 has no HTTP/1.1 Upgrade path. Clients must use prior-knowledge h2c or ALPN over TLS. Stream prioritization and server push are not supported.
- The README warns that wtx assumes the summed length of any number of slices cannot overflow. On 32-bit targets, oversized input can overflow and cause unexpected behavior. The docs also flag PlaintextCtx (the TLS config used for plain h2c) as dangerous if misconfigured.

**Status:** Actively developed, almost entirely by one author (764 of about 790 non-bot commits; last commit 2026-09-08; 0.52.1 released 2026-08-14; about 70k crates.io downloads). The crate is MPL-2.0 and easy to depend on, but it is pre-1.0 with breaking releases every few weeks, nightly-only, unaudited, and its author does not recommend it for production.

[repo](https://github.com/c410-f3r/wtx) · [benchmark](https://www.http-arena.com/data.json)

### numerics-and-science

#### autodiff-and-ml-kernels

##### Optimizing DGEMM on Intel CPUs with AVX512F  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Step-by-step AVX-512 DGEMM tutorial whose final kernel roughly matches single-threaded Intel MKL on large square matrices.

**Beats:** Intel oneMKL DGEMM — On one Intel Xeon W-2255 core (GCC 7.3.0, -march=skylake-avx512, oneMKL 2021.1 beta sequential), the repo's plot shows kernel 18 at about 33-115 GFLOPS across square n=100..3000, behind MKL from n=200 to 1500 and about 2-8% ahead from n=1600 to 3000 (about 115 vs 110 GFLOPS at n=3000, read from the plot). No measurement of the parallel kernel 19 against MKL was found.

**Known shortcoming:** Win over MKL appears only in plots on cs.ucr.edu (unverified size); Makefile builds own kernels at -O0 against oneMKL 2021.1 beta; abandoned (last commit 2022-02-03).

**Known shortcoming:** Single core: ~10-20% slower than MKL for n=200..1500, ~2-8% faster only for n>=1600 (~115 vs 110 GFLOPS at 3000); harness links mkl_sequential with MKL_NUM_THREADS=1, so parallel kernel never measured against threaded MKL; alpha==0 or K==0 returns without scaling C by beta (breaks BLAS semantics); loose 1e-2 correctness tolerance; 3 runs, no warm-up.

**Independent measurement:** repo figures/Kernel18.png (single core vs MKL)

**How:** Goto/BLIS-style blocking (M=192, K=384, N=8640 blocks) with packing of A and B into 4096-byte-aligned buffers, and a 24x8 register-blocked micro-kernel in AVX-512 inline asm (vbroadcastsd + vfmadd231pd on zmm registers). It adds software prefetching (prefetcht0) on A, B and C, a tuned C-scaling routine, and 'discontinuous' packing of B meant to help the L2 hardware prefetcher. Kernel 19 parallelises over M with a shared packed-B buffer and OpenMP barriers.

**Use it when:**
- Learning or teaching how a BLIS/Goto-style DGEMM is built on AVX-512, one optimisation at a time
- Vendoring a small, readable FP64 GEMM micro-kernel into GPL-compatible code on Skylake-X/Cascade Lake-class CPUs
- Large square column-major FP64 GEMM (about n >= 1600), where kernel 18 was a few percent ahead of single-threaded MKL on a Xeon W-2255
- As a starting point for your own AVX-512 kernel tuning experiments

**Skip it when:**
- Small and mid-size matrices: in the repo's own plot kernel 18 trails MKL by roughly 10-20% for n=200..1500
- Any production BLAS need: only NN column-major DGEMM, no transposes, no other precisions or routines; use MKL, OpenBLAS or BLIS
- CPUs without AVX-512F (all AMD before Zen 4, most Intel client chips), or non-x86
- Closed-source or permissive-licence projects: GPL-3.0
- Multi-threaded claims: the harness links mkl_sequential and run.sh sets MKL_NUM_THREADS=1, so the parallel kernel 19 was never compared to threaded MKL

**Integration:** source-drop · OpenMP (kernel 19); Intel MKL only for the test harness and correctness reference · GCC with AT&T inline asm and -march=skylake-avx512 (tested with GCC 7.3.0); C11 aligned_alloc · x86-64 with AVX-512F only

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over llamafile tinyBLAS or TCL when you want FP64 GEMM on AVX-512 and readable, staged code to learn from; tinyBLAS targets FP16/BF16/quantised LLM matmuls and TCL targets tensor contractions on top of a BLAS.

**Gotchas:**
- If alpha==0 or K==0 the function returns without applying beta to C, unlike BLAS semantics (C = beta*C)
- Correctness check in the harness uses an absolute tolerance of 1e-2, which is loose
- Timing is 3 repetitions via gettimeofday with no warm-up; MKL's 7 GFLOPS at n=100 in the plot looks like a first-call artifact
- The Makefile builds everything at -O0; the hot path is inline asm so this matters less, but the C driver/packing code is unoptimised

**Status:** Abandoned since February 2022 and tutorial code, but GPL-3.0 and small (one ~670-line header per kernel), so it can be vendored by GPL projects; last tested compiler GCC 7.3.0.

[repo](https://github.com/yzhaiustc/Optimizing-DGEMM-on-Intel-CPUs-with-AVX512F) · [benchmark](https://github.com/yzhaiustc/Optimizing-DGEMM-on-Intel-CPUs-with-AVX512F)

##### XAD  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Operator-overloading C++ AD library whose adjoint tape beats Adept 2 and CppAD by 1.1-2.3x on quant-finance gradients.

**Beats:** CppAD, Adept 2, autodiff (C++ AD libraries), finite differences — In the vendor's ad-benchmarks repo (GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma, Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, Ubuntu 24.04, median of 10 iterations after warmup), open-source XAD tape-mode gradients took 40 ms (Heston MC), 8.4 ms (SABR), 2.6 s (XVA CVA) and 1.00 s (LIBOR swaption), against Adept 2 at 91 ms / 19 ms / 7.1 s / 1.15 s and CppAD at 268 ms / 32 ms / 8.0 s / 4.57 s. The commercial xad-codegen column (21 ms / 4.9 ms / 0.57 s / 0.31 s) cannot be reproduced from public code.

**Known shortcoming:** Vendor-run benchmark (Xcelerit sells XAD-Codegen); original headline numbers came from the closed commercial Codegen backend; open AGPL tape mode is only ~1.1-2.3x faster than Adept.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark harness pulls every library from main/master (numbers not tied to versions); XAD_ALLOW_INT_CONVERSION on by default can silently drop dependencies.

**How:** Adjoint AD by operator overloading onto a tape (the benchmark repo labels XAD tape-based, like CppAD, while Adept 2 uses expression templates with stack recording); the internal tape layout is not documented in the pages read. An optional JIT backend interface supports record-once/replay-many for Monte Carlo; the commercial xad-codegen backend compiles the recorded graph to AVX2 native code and is 2-5x faster than the tape in the vendor's runs. Compile-time options trade speed for memory (XAD_REDUCED_MEMORY, XAD_TAPE_REUSE_SLOTS), force inlining (XAD_USE_STRONG_INLINE) or remove thread-local tape overhead (XAD_NO_THREADLOCAL).

**Use it when:**
- Many-inputs/one-output gradients (risk sensitivities, calibration Jacobians) where finite differences cost O(N) primal runs; the vendor run shows about 70x over FD at 161 inputs
- Monte Carlo pricing and XVA-style workloads in existing double-based C++ code, including QuantLib (via QuantLibAAD)
- Projects that need higher-order derivatives, checkpointing for tape memory, or hooks for external (non-AD) functions
- Codebases already using Eigen that need AD through Eigen expressions
- AGPL-compatible projects, or teams willing to buy the commercial licence

**Skip it when:**
- Proprietary/closed-source distribution without a commercial licence: the library is AGPL-3.0
- If you expect the headline benchmark speeds for free: the fastest column is xad-codegen, a closed commercial add-on
- Small statically-known expression graphs where an expression-template-only library such as FastAD may be faster (not measured head-to-head here)
- Very long recordings on memory-tight machines: reverse-mode tapes grow with operation count unless you use checkpointing
- Tensor/ML-style workloads; XAD targets scalar operator-overloading AD, not batched tensor kernels

**Integration:** static lib · none (Eigen optional; xad-codegen optional and commercial) · C++11; GCC 7+, Clang 11+, Apple Clang 11+, Visual Studio 2019+; CMake 3.15.2+ · Linux, macOS, Windows; x86-64 with SSE2/AVX/AVX2/AVX512 selectable via XAD_SIMD_OPTION (default AVX), Apple M1 option on macOS

**Vs siblings:** Pick XAD over FastAD when you need a maintained, general-purpose AD with forward/reverse/higher-order modes, checkpointing, Eigen support and QuantLib integration; FastAD's own paper reports bigger margins over Adept on small expression benchmarks but is narrower in scope. The other siblings (DGEMM kernels, tinyBLAS, MNN, T-MAC, TCL, nanoinfer) are ML/linear-algebra kernels, not AD libraries.

**Gotchas:**
- Tape behaviour is fixed at build time through CMake options written into a generated Config.hpp; build your project and XAD with the same compiler and flags (the install guide warns about this)
- XAD_ALLOW_INT_CONVERSION is ON by default: real-to-int conversions compile silently and can drop dependencies from the derivative
- Moving from tape to xad-codegen requires rewriting data-dependent branches as xad::less(a,b).If(then,else) so the recorded graph is branch-free
- The benchmark harness pulls XAD, CppAD, Adept and autodiff from their main/master branches, so the numbers are not tied to fixed versions

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit September 2026) with a commercial backer (Xcelerit); usable as source under AGPL-3.0, with a paid licence for closed-source use and for xad-codegen.

[repo](https://github.com/auto-differentiation/XAD) · [benchmark](https://github.com/auto-differentiation/ad-benchmarks)

##### CoDiPack (operator-overloading AD, expression templates)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only C++17 operator-overloading AD with expression templates; peer-reviewed paper reports it beats ADOL-C and roughly matches Adept.

**Beats:** ADOL-C and Adept (other C++ operator-overloading AD tools); none of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) apply — Not reproduced here: the only evidence is the peer-reviewed ACM TOMS 45(4) 2019 paper, which per search-result text compares CoDiPack's tape types with Adept and ADOL-C on a coupled Burgers test and on SU2 with GCC and Intel compilers, finding CoDiPack faster and lighter than ADOL-C and close to Adept, with index tapes speeding up reverse interpretation. CPU model, compiler versions, flags and exact ratios were not seen because the paper hosts are blocked from this session.

**Known shortcoming:** Win over Adept is marginal (parity plus 5-15% less tape memory); no harness in the repo; paper (arXiv 1709.07229) not opened here.

**Known shortcoming:** Open #49: forward and reverse derivatives disagree (0 vs -14) through cancellation when a variable repeats in one statement; closed #46 is similar with no documented fix. README flag -DCODI_UseForcedInlines is stale (config.h 3.1.2 reads only CODI_ForcedInlines). Default types share one static tape, not thread-safe. Paper numbers unverified here.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Expression templates collapse each full right-hand-side statement into one tape entry instead of one entry per elementary operation. Two taping strategies are offered: Jacobian taping (stores the statement's partial derivatives, as Adept and dco/c++ do) and primal value taping (stores primal values and re-evaluates the statement's derivative from generated code during the reverse sweep, as ADOL-C does, but with expression templates). Index managers either hand out linear identifiers or reuse freed ones (the *Index types), which shrinks the adjoint vector; per search-result text of the TOMS paper, that smaller footprint is what makes the index-reuse tapes faster in the reverse interpretation.

**Use it when:**
- Gradients of large simulation codes (CFD, PDE solvers; the paper evaluates SU2) where tape memory, not only speed, limits what you can differentiate
- Existing double-based C++ code where you can substitute a type, and you want to trade memory for generality by switching among RealReverse, RealReverseIndex, RealReversePrimal and RealReversePrimalIndex without changing user code
- MPI or OpenMP parallel codes, via MeDiPack and the RealReverseIndexOpenMP / OpDiLib bindings
- Mixed workflows that need external functions, preaccumulation, tape editing, tape writing to disk or Enzyme-generated derivatives inserted into the tape (helper since v2.2.0)
- Open-source (GPL-3.0) projects, or teams willing to negotiate a different license with the RPTU group

**Skip it when:**
- Closed-source distribution without a separate license: CoDiPack is GPL-3.0
- When raw speed over Adept 2 is the goal: per search-result summaries the TOMS paper shows rough parity with Adept (a few percent less tape memory), and no public benchmark harness exists to check it
- Small statically known expression graphs, where FastAD's paper claims 2-10x over Adept (not measured against CoDiPack)
- Plain multithreaded code using the default types: the default active types share one static tape per type, so threads need the OpenMP-specific types
- Projects stuck on C++11/14: CoDiPack 3.x requires C++17 (use the 2.x series otherwise)

**Integration:** header-only · none (optional: Eigen, MPI via MeDiPack, OpenMP/OpDiLib, Enzyme) · C++17 for 3.x (CMake target sets cxx_std_17; 2.x for C++11); README says tested with GCC, Clang and Intel; CMake 3.12+ for the package config · any platform with a C++17 compiler; CI runs clang++ on Ubuntu; MSVC compile problems were reported and closed in issues 5, 16 and 29

**Vs siblings:** Pick CoDiPack over Adept 2 or XAD when you need primal-value tapes, index-reuse memory savings, MPI/OpenMP support or Enzyme integration for a large simulation code, and GPL-3.0 is acceptable; XAD has the stronger published head-to-head numbers (vendor-run) and Adept 2 a more permissive Apache-2.0 license. Enzyme and Clad avoid operator overloading altogether but need an LLVM/Clang toolchain.

**Gotchas:**
- Performance depends on inlining, and the README's recommended -DCODI_UseForcedInlines is stale: include/codi/config.h in 3.1.2 only reads CODI_ForcedInlines (default 0), so define that name to actually force inlining
- The *Index types do not support C-style memory operations such as memcpy on active values; RealReverse and RealReversePrimal do
- Open issue 49 (v2.3.2, clang 16): with a variable repeated in one statement and a 1e30 term, forward returns 0 and reverse -14 (or the reverse when operands are swapped); per-occurrence partials are summed in an order that loses the small term, and splitting the statement fixes it. Closed issue 46 shows a similar cancellation with no documented fix
- The static tape makes gdb output verbose; the README suggests 'set print static-members off'

**Status:** Actively maintained by the RPTU Scientific Computing group (v3.1.2 released 2026-07-13, regular feature releases since 2015); GPL-3.0 header-only, so easy to vendor for open-source projects but a licensing question for proprietary ones.

[repo](https://github.com/SciCompKL/CoDiPack) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.07229)

##### TTV (tlib tensor-times-vector library)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only C++17 mode-q tensor-times-vector product built on BLAS gemv/dot; beat Eigen Tensor, TBLIS and usually TCL in 2019.

**Beats:** Eigen Tensor (sequential in-place tensor-times-vector); also TBLIS and TCL — Bassoy's ICCS 2019 paper and the README plots compare TTV (OpenBLAS 0.2.20 gemv/dot, OpenMP, GCC 7.3 -Ofast -march=native) against TCL 0.1.1, TBLIS 1.0.0 and sequential Eigen 3.3.90 on a 10-core Core i9-7900X across 324 symmetric and 1296 asymmetric order-2 to 10 shapes: read off the plots, TTV is mostly 2-8x faster than TBLIS, between 0.3x and 35x of TCL (abstract: 6.1x average, 12.6x maximum over TCL) and peaks near 35 Gflop/s in single precision. The large Eigen ratios (up to about 900x) compare 20 parallel threads with single-threaded Eigen, and the comparison harness is not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim not reproducible from the repo: no benchmark harness (test/ has only gtest unit tests, misc/ only PNG plots); ICCS 2019 paper unreachable here (abstract snippet: 6.1x average, 12.6x max over TCL). Plots: Eigen 3-900x is sequential Eigen vs 10-core TTV (not like-for-like); TBLIS 1-17x; TCL 0.3-35x, so TTV is slower than TCL in some cases.

**Known shortcoming:** Wraps OpenBLAS/MKL gemv/dot, so it is not faster than BLAS itself; likely the wrong category (tensor-times-vector contraction, not blas-lapack); LICENSE.txt is LGPL-3.0 while the README badge says GPL.

**Known shortcoming:** README and wiki say to build with -DUSE_INTELBLAS but the code checks only USE_MKL, so that flag silently builds the non-BLAS fallback; complex types never hit BLAS; the first parallel call runs popen("lscpu"); parallel paths reset process-wide BLAS/OpenMP thread counts; Eigen ratios compare 20 threads with Eigen's 1; open #4/#5 link failures and failing tests on macOS/PowerPC.

**How:** Loops-over-GEMM (LOG): instead of transposing the tensor (the TTGT approach TCL uses), it views contiguous slices or larger subtensors of A in place as matrices and calls the BLAS sgemv/dgemv (or dot) on each, so no copy or extra memory is needed. Loop fusion collapses the outer loops into one, and OpenMP parallelizes across slices or subtensors, with a mode that splits cores between OpenMP threads and BLAS threads; for large tensors it reaches the BLAS gemv's own throughput. Without a BLAS it falls back to its own OpenMP-SIMD gemv loops.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated mode-q tensor-times-vector products (for example in higher-order power methods, tensor decompositions or multilinear PCA) on dense, contiguous tensors of order 2 to 10
- Float or double tensors on a multicore x86-64 Linux box where OpenBLAS, MKL or BLIS is already linked
- You must contract in place on first-order (column-major), last-order or permuted layouts without allocating a transposed copy
- You want a small, header-only dependency instead of a full tensor framework, or a numpy-callable TTV via ttvpy

**Skip it when:**
- General tensor-tensor contractions or tensor-times-matrix: use TCL or TBLIS (the same author's separate bassoy/ttm repo covers tensor-times-matrix)
- Strided views or sparse tensors: elements must be stored contiguously
- Complex or other non-float/double element types where speed matters: the BLAS path only calls sgemv/dgemv, and other types fall back to the built-in loops
- Non-Linux or non-GCC builds: CI runs only g++ on ubuntu-latest, core detection shells out to lscpu, and the two open issues (2023) report link failures and failing MatrixTimesVector tests on macOS/PowerPC
- Applications that set their own BLAS or OpenMP thread counts: the parallel paths reset them globally on each call

**Integration:** header-only · OpenMP headers (matrix_times_vector.h includes <omp.h> unconditionally); optional BLAS: OpenBLAS (-DUSE_OPENBLAS), Intel MKL (-DUSE_MKL, ILP64 in the shipped mkl.mk) or BLIS (-DUSE_BLIS); googletest for the tests; numpy for ttvpy · C++17 (if constexpr, inline variables, nested namespaces); tested with GCC only (paper runs: GCC 7.3; CI: current Ubuntu g++) · x86-64 Linux documented and CI-tested; other platforms not documented (open issue reports test failures on macOS PowerPC)

**Vs siblings:** Pick TTV over TCL when the contraction is specifically tensor-times-vector and you cannot afford TCL's transpose (TTGT) buffers; TCL stays the choice for general contractions and was faster than TTV in a few plotted cases. LIBXSMM and Fastor target small dense GEMM, not tensor-times-vector.

**Gotchas:**
- The README and wiki say to compile with -DUSE_INTELBLAS for MKL, but the headers only test USE_MKL; with -DUSE_INTELBLAS the code silently builds the non-BLAS fallback
- The README's policy names (tlib::execution::blas, tlib::slicing::large, tlib::tensor) predate the 2024 move to the tlib::ttv namespace; the code now uses tlib::ttv::execution_policy::par_blas, slicing_policy::subtensor and so on, so README snippets need adapting
- The first parallel call runs popen("lscpu ...") to count physical cores (cached in a function-local static); this spawns a shell, fails quietly where lscpu is absent (it then uses std::thread::hardware_concurrency) and may be unwelcome in sandboxed or setuid processes
- Validation errors (bad mode, shape, layout or stride, null pointers) throw std::runtime_error, so the low-level interface is not usable with exceptions disabled

**Status:** Maintained by a single author (last commit 2025-11-02 added a combined OpenMP/BLAS policy; 24 stars, no releases); LGPL-3.0 header-only code is easy to vendor but carries LGPL obligations, and the README badge wrongly says GPL.

[repo](https://github.com/bassoy/ttv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bassoy/ttv#experiments)

#### big-integer-arbitrary-precision

##### ECM-ELF (ECM stage 1, AVX-512 IFMA 8-curve batch backend)  `C/C++ (GitHub lists C as primary; the AVX-512 kernels are .cpp; CUDA and OpenCL backends also exist)`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

AVX-512 IFMA ECM stage 1 running 8 curves per core; 2.3-3x faster per curve than GMP-ECM on Mersenne numbers.

**Beats:** GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (ecm-zen3.exe, built on GMP, curve family -param 0); the same table also compares Prime95 v31.04b05 (GWNUM FFT) — On one pinned 3990 MHz Zen 5 core of a Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (MSVC Release, /arch:AVX512 on the IFMA files), stage 1 for param-0 curves on M4001 took 0.596 / 6.264 s per curve at B1 = 1e5 / 1e6 against 1.787 / 15.008 s for the prebuilt GMP-ECM 7.0.6 ecm-zen3.exe (3.0x and 2.4x), and a B1 = 1e6 sweep gives 2.26-2.54x for M1277 to M4001. Every input is a Mersenne number, where the code's fold reduction applies, and the Prime95 ratios come from a model anchored on a single measured M3001 run.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier A (MSVC /O2 /arch:AVX512, Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, exact commands public), but the baseline is a prebuilt public GMP-ECM binary (ecm-zen3.exe) with unknown build flags, accepted under the MKL-baseline precedent. Inputs are Mersenne numbers only, where the folded reduction alone is worth about 2x per the README.

**Known shortcoming:** The GMP-ECM baseline is unstable within the project's own docs: section 9.4 logs GMP-ECM 7.0.6 on the same machine at about 0.72 s/curve (M3001, B1=1e5) while section 10.4 has ecm-zen3.exe at 1.148 s/curve for the same case. General N likely gains nothing: section 19.4 gives 0.85 s/curve for a 2999-bit semiprime on the CIOS path (derived) and the Mersenne fold path is 1.8x faster than CIOS (section 19.8). The scalar fallback is much slower than GMP-ECM; only a Windows/MSVC build is documented.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** All curves in a batch share one exponent s = lcm(1..B1), so eight curves run in lock-step as the lanes of one zmm register per 52-bit limb (radix 2^52, vpmadd52lo/hi) with no divergence. For N = 2^k-1 a Mersenne fold domain replaces Montgomery CIOS reduction, cutting a modular multiply from n(4n+3) to 2n^2 madds (squaring about n(n-1)+2n), and the binary Montgomery ladder keeps the difference point affine so the differential add costs 3M+2S. Multiplication stays schoolbook: the dev doc measured Karatsuba slower at every size up to about 8000 bits and reports the multiply phase at 91-96% of the machine's madd throughput.

**Use it when:**
- Many ECM stage-1 curves on Mersenne numbers 2^k-1 below about 3700 bits, where the doc measures 2.26-2.54x per core over GMP-ECM 7.0.6 at B1=1e6 (M1277-M4001) and 3.0x at B1=1e5 on M4001.
- Small Mersenne inputs (M127 to M2203) where Prime95's smallest FFT length is oversized: the doc's model puts it 3.9x (M1277) to 32.7x (M127) ahead of Prime95 per curve.
- x86-64 machines with AVX512-F/DQ/IFMA, run with one thread per physical core and at least 8 curves per thread (128 curves to fill 16 cores).
- Pipelines that already hand stage 2 to Prime95 or GMP-ECM and want a faster stage 1 with interoperable save files, checkpoints and resume.

**Skip it when:**
- General (non-Mersenne) N: the fold domain is off and CIOS is used, which the doc measures 1.8x slower than the fold (section 19.8); section 19.4 gives about 0.85 s/curve for a 2999-bit semiprime at B1=1e5 on one thread (27.1 s for 32 curves), inside the doc's own GMP-ECM range for M3001 at that B1 (0.72-1.15 s/curve), so expect little or no gain (derived from page data; no general-N GMP-ECM comparison is published).
- Mersenne N above about 3760 bits: Prime95's GWNUM FFT wins per the doc's FFT-tier model (about 1.5x at 5755 bits, about 6x at 19701 bits).
- CPUs without AVX-512 IFMA: backend=simd exits with an error and backend=auto falls back to the scalar GMP mpn path, about 5.6 s/curve at M1277, B1=1e5 against 0.135 s for SIMD, far slower than GMP-ECM itself.
- When you need stage 2, P-1/P+1 or a linkable library: this is a stage-1 application only.
- Code that cannot take GPL-3.0, or a Linux/GCC build of the CPU path you need to trust: the documented desktop build is Windows/MSVC/vcpkg, and all published CPU timings are from one Windows laptop.

**Integration:** application (CMake-built ecm.exe / ecm_cuda.exe); the IFMA kernels are C++ source files with a C header (source-drop at best) · GMP, OpenSSL (Crypto and SSL) and an OpenCL ICD, all REQUIRED by CMakeLists.txt for the ecm target; CUDA toolkit plus CGBN for ecm_cuda; optional Pari/GP for --go; Dear ImGui, Direct3D 11 and NVML for the Windows GUI · CMake 3.20+; Visual Studio 2022 recommended (timed binary built with MSVC /O2 from build_vs18); CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD is commented out, so the minimum C++ standard is not documented; GCC/Clang get -mavx512f -mavx512ifma -mavx512dq on the IFMA files · x86-64 with AVX512-F/DQ/IFMA for the fast path (measured only on an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, Zen 5); Windows is the documented desktop build; the OpenCL path also targets Linux, macOS and Android

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over primefactors (whose own README says its GPU programs do not beat the CPU GMP-ECM path on hard inputs) and over generic batched Montgomery kernels such as the Truncated batch SIMD AVX512 code when the job is complete ECM stage 1 on Mersenne numbers with saves GMP-ECM and Prime95 can continue. For general N up to about 1000 bits, try AVX-ECM (bbuhrow/avx-ecm, BSD-2-Clause, not yet catalogued; its README claims 1.5-2.5x GMP-ECM throughput) first.

**Gotchas:**
- The unit of parallelism is an 8-curve task, so 8 curves use one thread however many cores exist; SMT adds about 10% on the big cores but costs 19% once the whole Zen 5c cluster is loaded, and the README advises leaving affinity unset.
- field=auto uses the fold only when N = 2^k-1 with k >= 64 and otherwise silently uses CIOS; field=mersenne errors on other N. Check the 'field layer :' log line before comparing timings.
- All published timings use hand-pinned clocks (3990 MHz on Zen 5 cores); the doc says the pinned single-thread runs are about 30% faster than earlier unpinned ones, so stock-clock results will differ.
- The GMP-ECM baseline itself varies: section 9.4 logs an earlier GMP-ECM 7.0.6 run on the same machine at about 0.72 s/curve for M3001 at B1=1e5, while section 10.4 measures 1.148 s/curve with ecm-zen3.exe for the same case.

**Status:** Active single-author project (264 commits, last commit 2026-10-02, no issues filed, 5 stars) under GPL-3.0, so usable as a tool but not vendorable into closed code; the benchmark numbers date from 2026-09-24 and were not re-run against HEAD.

[repo](https://github.com/AllogeneSSRD/ECM-ELF) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AllogeneSSRD/ECM-ELF/HEAD/docs/ECM_Montgomery_STAGE1.md)

##### Malachite  `Rust`  `LGPL-3.0-only`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-Rust port of GMP/FLINT integer algorithms; beats GMP (via rug) on sub-64-bit values and string parsing, not on large operands.

**Beats:** GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate) — In DRMacIver's public Criterion suite (rustc 1.92.0, Cargo default bench profile, Apple M2 Max), malachite-nz 0.9.1 beat rug 1.30.0 (GMP) on 10-bit operations (add, mul, gcd, extended gcd, pow, to_dec) and on hex/decimal parsing at all sizes up to 10^4 bits, but rug won add, sub, mul, div, pow and modular arithmetic from about 100-1,000 bits upward. The small-value wins come from avoiding rug's per-result heap allocation rather than from faster limb kernels.

**Known shortcoming:** Beats rug/GMP only at tiny operands and parsing; rug is faster from about 1000 bits; Rust only, no C++ API; license now LGPL-3.0-only.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked 0.9.1 may include a regression: issue #90 reports e to 1M digits at ~7000 ms on 0.7.0+ vs 800 ms on 0.6.1, closed 2026-06-18 (the day before 0.9.2) with the fix version undocumented; past panics on valid inputs (#55, #73, #86) closed; LGPL-3.0-only with static linking by default; no C API.

**How:** A Natural is an enum of Small(Limb) or Large(Vec<Limb>), so any value below 2^64 lives inline without a heap allocation, which is where it beats rug/mpz. For large operands it ports GMP's machinery: schoolbook, Toom-22/33/44/6h/8h and unbalanced Toom variants with GMP-style tuned thresholds (Toom-22 from 16 limbs on 64-bit), a small-prime FFT derived from Daniel Schultz's FLINT code plus Schonhage-Strassen from William Hart's FLINT code, GMP's divide-and-conquer and mu division with Newton inversion, and a subquadratic half-GCD. By-value operator overloads reuse the operand's buffer to avoid allocations in chains like &x + &y + &z.

**Use it when:**
- Rust code dominated by values under 64 bits that must not overflow (interpreters, exact counters, property-test shrinkers): 10-bit add 2.1 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, gcd 8.5 ns vs 20.9 ns, pow 5.1 ns vs 41.6 ns
- Parsing many decimal or hex strings: from_dec and from_hex beat rug at every size up to 10^4 bits (from_dec 8.37 us vs 11.51 us at 10^4 bits)
- Pure-Rust, no_std or wasm targets that need GMP-class asymptotics (Toom, FFT, half-GCD) without a C toolchain or GMP build
- Projects that want rationals and big integers with the same API family, or a num-bigint replacement via malachite-bigint (as RustPython does)

**Skip it when:**
- Operands above about 1,000 bits where raw speed matters: rug/GMP is faster on mul (8.28 us vs 4.52 us at 10^4 bits), div, pow and modular pow (250.90 ms vs 143.02 ms at 10^4 bits), and on every task in tczajka's suite (e to 10M digits 3.689 s vs 2.788 s)
- Values of 65-128 bits: they already allocate (ubig_add at 100 bits 18.7 ns vs dashu 3.7 ns), so dashu is faster there
- C or C++ codebases: there is no C API; call GMP directly
- Closed-source distribution without accepting LGPL-3.0-only terms; Rust links crates statically by default, so the LGPL relinking obligations apply (issue #52 asked for a permissive license; it remains LGPL-3.0-only)
- Arbitrary-precision floats in production: the README says malachite-float is not yet feature-complete

**Integration:** crate (use the malachite meta-crate; malachite-nz holds the integer code) · malachite-base, itertools, libm, wide; optional serde, pyo3 (enable_pyo3), rand-based 'random' feature · Rust 1.90 (rust-version for 0.9.x-0.12.0), edition 2024 · any Rust target; 64-bit limbs by default, 32_bit_limbs feature for u32 limbs; no_std supported (closed issue #97 reported std leaking in through wide under no-default-features)

**Vs siblings:** Pick malachite over ibig and dashu when operands grow past a few thousand bits or you need gcd, modular and rational arithmetic with GMP-derived algorithms (the report finds it usually second to rug at 1,000-10^4 bits); pick dashu instead for 65-128-bit values or a permissive license, and FLINT or GMP itself from C/C++.

**Gotchas:**
- Fast versions move quickly (0.9.1 in February 2026 to 0.12.0 in September 2026, minor-version bumps with API changes, e.g. issue #58 export incompatibility in 0.4.19+); pin versions
- Issue #90 reported e to 1M digits at about 7000 ms on 0.7.0 and newer vs 800 ms on 0.6.1; it was closed 2026-06-18, the day before 0.9.2, so the benchmarked 0.9.1 may carry that regression (fix version not documented)
- Past panics on valid inputs, all closed: extended_gcd 'mid > len' (#73), Natural::factorial assertion (#86), squaring 2^(2^25) (#55)
- Mixed operations with primitives are deliberately not implemented (no Natural + u64); convert with Natural::from, which is cheap below 2^64

**Status:** Very active (commits to 2026-09-30, 0.12.0 released 2026-09-20, about 2.8 million recent crates.io downloads for malachite-nz) and copyable as LGPL-3.0-only safe Rust; floats are still incomplete.

[repo](https://github.com/mhogrefe/malachite) · [benchmark](https://github.com/DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks/blob/main/benchmark-report.md)

##### Truncated batch SIMD AVX512 Montgomery multiplication  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Research C code doing 8 Montgomery multiplications or modexps at once with AVX512-IFMA; ~4-5x GMP/OpenSSL throughput.

**Beats:** GMP 6.2.0 (also OpenSSL 3.2.1) — On an i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake, Turbo off), GCC 9.4.0 -O3 -march=native, a batch of 8 truncated Montgomery multiplications ran 5.34x/4.86x/3.95x faster than 8 GMP 6.2.0 calls at 1024/2048/4096 bits, and batched fixed-window modexp ran 3.98x/3.71x/3.30x faster than OpenSSL 3.2.1 BN_mod_exp_mont_consttime. Against OpenSSL's IFMA consttimex2 path the gain is 1.75x (1024) and 1.38x (2048).

**Known shortcoming:** Batch of 8 SIMD ops vs 8 sequential GMP/OpenSSL calls; needs AVX512-IFMA; vs OpenSSL's IFMA path only 1.38-1.75x; modular arithmetic only, research code; stale (2024-09-19).

**Known shortcoming:** No library API, only benchmark programs; operand size fixed at compile time (script swaps size-specific source); conversion into batch format excluded from headline cycle counts; one laptop with Turbo Boost off.

**How:** Operands are held in radix 2^52 and word-sliced, so lane i of each 512-bit register holds one word of operand i; VPMADD52LUQ/HUQ then do eight 52x52-bit multiply-adds per instruction. The 'truncated' Montgomery reduction skips computing low-order product words that are known to cancel to zero, which the paper reports saves about 21% over the non-truncated variant. Schoolbook multiplication is used up to 4108 bits and Karatsuba (double Karatsuba at 4154 bits) above that. Each operand size gets its own code: a script includes a size-specific source file (e.g. sb512_1040.c) at build time.

**Use it when:**
- You have many independent modular multiplications or exponentiations with the same bit size, e.g. batched RSA/DH private-key operations or batch signature work, and can group them in eights.
- Your CPU has AVX512-IFMA (Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Zen 4 or later) and you want throughput, not single-operation latency.
- Operand sizes from 1024 to 4096 bits, where the paper measures 3.3-5.4x over GMP mpn_sec_powm and OpenSSL BN_mod_exp_mont_consttime.
- You are studying or prototyping IFMA Montgomery kernels and want a reference for the truncated-reduction trick.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a single modexp at a time: the speedup comes from 8-way batching, and a batch of one still costs a full batch.
- You already use OpenSSL 3's IFMA path (BN_mod_exp_mont_consttimex2): the margin falls to 1.75x at 1024 bits and 1.38x at 2048, and the 256-bit-vector batch-of-4 variant is only 1.05x faster at 2048 bits.
- You need general big-integer arithmetic (add, divide, GCD, arbitrary sizes): only Montgomery mul/sqr/modexp at compile-time-fixed sizes are provided.
- The CPU lacks AVX512-IFMA (older Intel, Zen 3 and earlier, ARM): the paper notes NEON has no 52-bit multiply-add equivalent and no fallback exists.
- You need GPL-incompatible licensing or a maintained API: GPL-3.0, 7 commits, no releases, benchmark mains rather than a library interface.

**Integration:** source-drop · GMP and OpenSSL libcrypto (linked by the benchmark Makefiles for baselines and tests); libm · GCC with AVX512-IFMA intrinsics (paper used GCC 9.4.0, -O3 -funroll-all-loops -march=native) · x86-64 with AVX512F + AVX512-IFMA required; Linux assumed (rdtsc/rdpmc benchmarking)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ctbignum or mp++ only for batched fixed-size modular exponentiation on AVX512-IFMA hardware, a case they do not vectorize; for general mpz-style arithmetic use mp++ or FLINT, and for small fixed-limb compile-time arithmetic use ctbignum.

**Gotchas:**
- Operand size is a compile-time macro (SIZE) and script.sh rewrites a source include per size, so each size needs a separate build.
- Converting between 64-bit limbs and the 52-bit sliced format costs extra; the paper reports conversion overhead separately, and it is not included in the headline cycle counts.
- Measured on a laptop with Turbo Boost off; AVX512 frequency effects on other CPUs are acknowledged but not characterized.
- The GMP baseline is eight sequential mpn calls; GMP has no batched API, so the comparison is throughput-vs-latency by design.

**Status:** Stale research code (last commit 2024-09-19, 3 stars) under GPL-3.0; copyable if GPL fits, but expect to extract kernels from benchmark mains yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/lea-gl/TruncatedBatchSIMDAVX512MontgomeryMultiplicationsModularExponentiation) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18129)

#### blas-lapack

##### Eigen  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++ template library for dense/sparse linear algebra; beats OpenBLAS at small-to-mid sizes without linking BLAS.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS — On an Intel Xeon Gold 6444Y (GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx512dq -mfma, single-threaded), Eigen's own kernels beat OpenBLAS 0.3.26's geometric-mean GFLOP/s on GEMV, DOT, TRSM, POTRF and SYEV across most size bands (roughly 1.1-4.9x), are near parity on large GEMM, and lose on GEEV and GESDD; against Intel oneMKL 2025.3, Eigen is generally slower at large sizes. The harness (Google Benchmark 1.8.3, median of 10 reps) is public but still an unmerged GitLab merge request (!2903), and frequency was not locked during the run.

**Independent measurement:** Eigen 5.0.1 reached 193.1 GFLOP/s on f32 matmul N=1024 (91% of the host's measured single-core FMA peak of 212.2, 1.42x a hand-written xsimd kernel, 1.85x Blaze), but lost fixed 4x4 multiplies to a naive triple loop (5.87 vs 3.20 ns, naive 1.83x) and 3x3 to hand-rolled xsimd (5.59 vs 2.26 ns, 2.5x). At N=64 hand-rolled xsimd also beat it 1.41x (187.4 vs 133.2 GFLOP/s), and the naive 4x4 win is gcc-specific (clang 18 leaves that loop scalar and Eigen wins there). (developer source, private repo; selection harness in docs/linear-algebra.md, gcc 13 -O3 -march=native, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, run 2026-09-03-third-party)

**Independent measurement:** Built without -march=native, Eigen fell from 193.1 to 34.6 GFLOP/s on f32 matmul N=1024 (5.6x loss), while OpenBLAS with runtime CPU dispatch went from 575.9 to 569.2. sizeof(struct{Eigen::Matrix4f; char;}) is 80/96/128 bytes under SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512, so translation units built with different arch flags silently disagree on layout. (developer source, private repo; selection harness in docs/linear-algebra.md, gcc 13, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, run 2026-09-03-third-party)

**How:** Expression templates fuse chained operations into a single loop at compile time, avoiding temporaries. Eigen's own GEMM kernel does three-level cache blocking -- mc x kc panels packed for L2/L3, mr x kc micro-panels kept in L1, and a register-blocked micro-kernel -- the same family of technique GotoBLAS/BLIS use, confirmed in the header comment of GeneralBlockPanelKernel.h. Kernels are explicitly SIMD-vectorized (SSE/AVX/AVX-512/NEON/etc.), and small fixed-size matrices get compile-time loop unrolling that skips packing overhead entirely, which is why Eigen's edge over OpenBLAS is largest at small sizes (DOT 4.9x, GEMV 2.2x at n<=16) and shrinks or reverses as size grows.

**Use it when:**
- Small and medium dense ops (roughly n<=1024) where OpenBLAS's dispatch/call overhead dominates -- GEMV and DOT measured 1.1-4.9x faster than OpenBLAS here
- You want a header-only dependency with no external BLAS/LAPACK to build, package, or version-pin
- Fixed-size or compile-time-sized linear algebra (small transforms, small solvers) where Eigen's unrolled kernels apply
- TRSM, POTRF, SYEV workloads at small/mid size, where Eigen beat OpenBLAS by 1.25-3.6x per this benchmark
- C++ codebases that want expression-template ergonomics instead of raw BLAS call signatures

**Skip it when:**
- Very large dense GEMM/SYRK (n in the 1500+ range) where Eigen is roughly at parity with OpenBLAS and often slower than oneMKL
- GEEV (nonsymmetric eigenvalues) -- measured at 0.45x OpenBLAS at 192-1024, and well behind oneMKL at large sizes
- GESDD (SVD) at mid-to-large sizes -- measured 0.6-0.9x OpenBLAS
- Large-scale multi-threaded numerics -- this benchmark and Eigen's own kernels are single-threaded; OpenMP only parallelizes some ops (dense GEMM, PartialPivLU, a few iterative sparse solvers), not the full LAPACK surface
- Storing fixed-size Eigen objects in STL containers or passing them by value without alignment care -- triggers runtime alignment assertions on SIMD builds

**Integration:** header-only · none (STL only); optional external BLAS/LAPACK backend for large-matrix offload · C++14 (target_compile_features cxx_std_14 in CMakeLists.txt); CMake 3.18+ only needed for the optional install/test build, not for using the headers · x86-64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 optional), aarch64/ARM NEON, PowerPC Altivec/VSX, MIPS MSA; this benchmark ran on AVX-512

**Vs siblings:** no siblings catalogued yet

**Gotchas:**
- Fixed-size vectorizable types (Vector4d, Matrix4d, Quaternionf, etc.) assert at runtime if misaligned -- avoid storing them by value in STL containers or passing by value without EIGEN_MAKE_ALIGNED_OPERATOR_NEW
- OpenMP thread count should match physical cores, not logical/hyperthreads -- oversubscription slows things down since Eigen's kernels already saturate a core
- Heavy expression-template usage increases compile times
- For very large dense problems, Eigen's own docs and this benchmark both point toward linking an external BLAS/LAPACK backend instead of relying solely on Eigen's kernels

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23) with a large downstream user base (ROS, TensorFlow, Ceres Solver, OpenCV, Blender); MPL-2.0, header-only, trivial to vendor.

[repo](https://gitlab.com/libeigen/eigen) · [benchmark](https://libeigen.gitlab.io/benchmarks/2026-09-xeon-gold-6444y-blas-lapack-avx512/)

##### GEMM_AVX2_FMA3  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Archived 2019 AVX2/FMA3 OpenMP sgemm_/dgemm_ for very large matrices, 2-6% faster than MKL 2019u4 on an i9-9900K.

**Beats:** Intel MKL 2019 update 4 — The author ran the bundled tester on an Intel Core i9-9900K (AVX offset 6, OMP_NUM_THREADS=8). The library was built with gcc -fopenmp -march=haswell -O2 (compiler version not stated) and timed against MKL 2019 update 4 linked statically with the GNU OpenMP layer, one call each per iteration with MKL first. At M=N=K=20000 it reached SGEMM 963-976 vs 944-951 GFLOPS and DGEMM 477-481 vs 466-469 GFLOPS (about 2-3%), and SGEMM at 45000 reached about 996 vs 943 GFLOPS (about 6%, derived from page data). Results matched MKL to about 1e-11 max absolute difference.

**Known shortcoming:** Margin only 2-6% (bench/dgemmtest.c, gcc -O2 -march=haswell, i9-9900K).

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness (code read): the driver splits N by omp_get_max_threads() and spin-waits for that many threads, so a smaller OpenMP team (nested call, OMP_DYNAMIC) hangs and leaves part of C uncomputed; int offsets overflow past ~2^31 elements; alpha=0,beta=0 scales C instead of zeroing (NaN survives).

**How:** It is a Goto-style blocked GEMM. For each 256-deep K slice, the master thread packs the full-height panel of A into a shared 4096-byte-aligned buffer. Each thread packs its own alpha-scaled 256x256 block of B and runs a hand-written AT&T-syntax assembly micro-kernel. The kernel holds a 12x4 (double) or 24x4 (float) tile of C in 12 ymm accumulators, broadcasts B, does 3 aligned A loads per k step, issues explicit prefetcht0/prefetcht1 for upcoming A, B and C, and handles edges with vmaskmov. N is split statically across OpenMP threads, and a hand-rolled spin barrier (synproc with a ~3 us delay loop) replaces OpenMP barriers around each shared A-panel refill.

**Use it when:**
- Very large single- or double-precision GEMMs (the author recommends dimensions above 2000; numbers are given for 20000 and 45000) on an AVX2/FMA3 x86-64 Linux machine, run with all physical cores
- Studying or reusing a compact (about 1,100 lines) Haswell-class GEMM with a full transpose-case driver and an assembly micro-kernel, under GPL-3.0
- Benchmarking another dgemm_/sgemm_ shared library against MKL: the bench harness dlopens any library that exports those symbols

**Skip it when:**
- Small or medium matrices, or tall-skinny shapes: every call does aligned_alloc of an M x 256 A panel, packs it on one thread, and splits N statically across threads, so overhead and load imbalance dominate below the large-square regime
- Code that must stay under a permissive license: it is GPL-3.0
- AVX-512 machines, AMD Zen, or anything that is not Linux/ELF: block sizes are tuned for a Coffee Lake i9-9900K, and the kernel is ELF-only AT&T assembly built with -march=haswell
- When you need the rest of BLAS, CBLAS, ILP64, complex types or input validation: use OpenBLAS, BLIS or MKL
- Production use: archived since 2019-08-27, 1 star, no tests beyond the MKL-comparison bench

**Integration:** shared lib (DGEMM.so / SGEMM.so via the Makefile) · OpenMP (libgomp); the bench programs need Intel MKL (VSL RNG and dgemm as reference) · GCC with -fopenmp and C11 aligned_alloc; compiler version not documented · x86-64 Linux with AVX2 and FMA3 (Haswell or later); tuned only on an Intel i9-9900K

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over cpu_gemm_opt or sgemm.c (salykova) when you need double precision and a standard Fortran dgemm_/sgemm_ entry point covering every transpose case for multi-threaded large matrices. Those two are sgemm teaching kernels measured against OpenBLAS. The author's successor GEMM_AVX2 adds per-CPU tuning headers (dgemm_tune.h, sgemm_tune.h) and claims to outperform MKL 2019u4 after tuning.

**Gotchas:**
- From reading gemm_driver.c (not tested): the driver splits N into omp_get_max_threads() chunks and spin-waits in synproc until that many threads check in. If the actual team is smaller (called from inside another parallel region with nesting off, OMP_DYNAMIC=true, or a thread limit), part of C is never computed and the call would spin forever. The barrier also uses plain non-atomic int reads, which works on x86 in practice but is a data race in C11 terms.
- Pointer offsets such as LDC*cchunks[tid] are computed in 32-bit int, so matrices with more than about 2^31 elements (beyond ~46000 x 46000) overflow. aligned_alloc results are not checked for NULL.
- No argument validation (no xerbla). With alpha=0 and beta=0, C is multiplied by 0 rather than zeroed, so NaN/Inf already in C survive, unlike reference BLAS.
- Prebuilt test binaries (sgemmtest, dgemmtest, *_new) ship in bench/ and must be chmod +x to run; per the README the older pair links MKL 2018 and the *_new pair MKL 2019. Build your own from bench/*.c rather than running opaque binaries.

**Status:** Archived on 2019-08-27 and GPL-3.0. It is small enough to vendor as a reference kernel, but it is a parity-plus result on one desktop CPU with known driver hazards; the author's later GEMM_AVX2 (updated 2020-03-23) and GEMM_AVX512F repos supersede it.

[repo](https://github.com/wjc404/GEMM_AVX2_FMA3) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wjc404/GEMM_AVX2_FMA3/HEAD/README.md)

##### Zynum  `Zig`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier A`

Zig BLAS 1-3 with CBLAS/Fortran ABI and SME kernels; about 2x OpenBLAS GEMM on Apple M5, roughly even with Accelerate.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS 0.3.34 (also Apple Accelerate) — The author's fresh-process interleaved sweep on an Apple M5 (10 logical CPUs, macOS 27.0, Zig 0.16.0, -Dcpu=baseline -Ddispatch=dynamic ReleaseFast) over 42 NN column-major shapes per s/d/c/zgemm shows median 2.15x OpenBLAS 0.3.34 (10 threads), with Zynum faster in 146 of 168 cases, and median 1.11x Accelerate (faster in 100 of 168), e.g. sgemm 1024^3 1999 vs 473 (OpenBLAS) and 1925 (Accelerate) GFLOP/s; correctness is sampled only.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarks were run from a dirty tree (199 of 203 file hashes match HEAD).

**Known shortcoming:** Runs 0.16-0.22x of Accelerate on small odd shapes (m ~31-129, k ~31-33); 32-bit BLAS ints only, no LAPACK; no x86 performance data; CBLAS silently ignores bad arguments.

**How:** One library carries separately compiled ISA tiers (baseline, SVE2, SME, SME2, SME2p1, AVX, AVX2+FMA, AVX-512) and picks one at load time from sysctl/HWCAP/CPUID, so a baseline build still reaches Apple M4/M5 SME streaming outer-product kernels, the likely source of its 2-4x lead over OpenBLAS's NEON code on M5. GEMM goes through a catalog/tuning/planner layer that chooses among packed-panel, direct, vector-edge (GEMV-like) and, for complex, 3-real-multiply or 4-real-multiply plane decompositions per shape. Work is split across a persistent std.Io thread pool by disjoint output tiles; an Apple AMX route exists but is off unless built with -Dapple-amx=true.

**Use it when:**
- Apple M4/M5-class Macs (SME/SME2) where you want a portable CBLAS/Fortran BLAS faster than OpenBLAS: median 2.15x GEMM GFLOP/s over OpenBLAS 0.3.34 across 168 cases on an M5
- Complex GEMM on Apple Silicon: cgemm and zgemm medians are 1.21x and 1.47x Accelerate in the published sweep (zgemm 1024^3: 598 vs 407 GFLOP/s)
- Medium-to-large square or rectangular GEMM (n of a few hundred to 1024) with all cores in use
- Zig projects that want a typed, bounds-checked BLAS API with no external dependencies

**Skip it when:**
- Small or irregular shapes (m, n about 31-129 with k about 31-33): Zynum runs at 0.16-0.22x Accelerate there, and m17_n2048_k257 sgemm is 107 vs 429 GFLOP/s (Accelerate) and 203 (OpenBLAS)
- Real sgemm/dgemm on macOS when Accelerate is available: medians are 0.92x and 0.99x of Accelerate
- x86-64 or Linux servers: AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 tiers exist but no native x86 performance numbers are published, and Windows correctness rows are pending
- Anything needing LAPACK, ILP64 (64-bit integer) BLAS, or a stable API: Level 1-3 only, 32-bit BLAS integers, 0.0.1-beta with dispatch policy subject to change
- Projects that cannot accept LGPL-3.0-or-later linking terms

**Integration:** shared lib · none at runtime (static and shared libraries are both built); Zig 0.16 to build; Python 3 for the benchmark tooling · Zig 0.16.0 (minimum_zig_version in build.zig.zon); any C or Fortran compiler for consumers · aarch64 macOS (benchmarked on Apple M5 with SME/SME2), aarch64 Linux (HWCAP detection, link-only CI row), x86-64 Linux and Windows (SSE2/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 tiers, no published performance)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Zynum over GEMM-only Apple kernels such as sme-gemm, MaxMulSK or apple-bottom when you need a whole BLAS 1-3 library with CBLAS and Fortran ABI and complex types, not one fast GEMM; pick Apple Accelerate itself for real sgemm/dgemm or small shapes on macOS, and OpenBLAS or BLIS on x86.

**Gotchas:**
- Default thread count is the full CPU count; set ZYNUM_MAXIMUM_THREADS before the first BLAS call (later changes are ignored)
- CBLAS entry points silently return without touching outputs on invalid enum/layout arguments instead of calling xerbla
- Do not compile Fortran callers with -fdefault-integer-8: the BLAS integer is 32-bit
- The benchmark manifest (source.json, measured 2026-09-21) marks the measured working tree dirty on top of base revision 6a989d0, so the timed code is identified by content hashes rather than a commit

**Status:** Weeks-old beta (0.0.1-beta, 42 commits, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-23) under LGPL-3.0-or-later; usable for evaluation, but expect API and dispatch changes and verify on your own hardware.

[repo](https://github.com/kaix-huang/Zynum) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kaix-huang/Zynum/HEAD/docs/assets/benchmarks/current/gemm.csv)

##### FT-BLAS  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research double-precision BLAS for AVX-512 Intel CPUs with built-in soft-error checks; paper reports small wins over OpenBLAS, BLIS, MKL.
