**Beats:** OpenBLAS, BLIS, Intel MKL — The peer-reviewed ICS '21 paper reports FT-BLAS (including its fault-tolerant variants) up to 22.14% faster than OpenBLAS, 21.70% faster than BLIS and 3.50% faster than Intel MKL across routines from all three BLAS levels, built with icc 19.0 -O3 on an Intel Xeon Gold 5122 (Skylake) and a Xeon W-2255 (Cascade Lake), with fault-tolerance overhead under 3% while errors were injected. These are best-case 'up to' figures, and the repository's test programs time only FT-BLAS itself, so the comparison is not reproducible from the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Code now public (GPL-3.0) but no benchmark code for the paper's numbers in the repo; abandoned (last commit 2023-02-28), 7 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: dgemm/dsymm/dtrmm/dtrsm wrappers return early when alpha==0, so C is not scaled by beta (or B not zeroed), breaking the BLAS spec; unsupported cases (dgemm supports only ColMajor NoTrans/NoTrans) call exit(-1) inside the library.

**Known shortcoming:** Fault-tolerance claim not reproducible from the repo: FT DGEMM's checksum verify/correct code is commented out and FT DDOT only prints and returns a truncated wrong result on a detected error; the repo has no harness comparing against OpenBLAS/BLIS/MKL; -march=skylake-avx512 hard-coded; GPL-3.0.

**How:** The non-FT kernels are Goto-style blocked GEMM (A/B packing into 4 KiB-aligned buffers, KC=384, 24x8 AVX-512 micro-kernel in inline assembly with software prefetch) and unrolled AVX2/AVX-512 assembly loops for level-1/2. For fault tolerance, the paper uses a hybrid scheme: dual modular redundancy (each FMA issued twice into separate registers and compared with vpcmpeqd/vmovmskpd) for memory-bound level-1/2, where the duplicate instructions hide behind memory stalls, and algorithm-based fault tolerance (row/column checksums of A, B and C) for level-3, with the checksum updates fused into the packing routines so they cost almost no extra memory traffic.

**Use it when:**
- Research or evaluation of soft-error-tolerant linear algebra on Intel Skylake-SP / Cascade Lake class CPUs with AVX-512.
- Studying or borrowing a compact, readable AVX-512 DGEMM (Goto blocking + 24x8 assembly micro-kernel) or DMR-in-assembly level-1 kernels as a starting point for your own code, under GPL-3.0 terms.
- Single-node, double-precision, column-major, non-transposed GEMM/DOT/AXPY workloads where you can test that your exact call shapes are supported.

**Skip it when:**
- As a production replacement for OpenBLAS, MKL or BLIS: many argument combinations are unimplemented (cblas_dgemm accepts only ColMajor NoTrans/NoTrans; dsymm only Left/Lower; dtrsm and dtrmm only Left/Lower/NoTrans) and the library calls exit(-1) on anything else.
- Code that relies on alpha == 0 semantics: the dgemm, dsymm, dtrmm and dtrsm wrappers return immediately when alpha is 0, leaving C unscaled by beta (or B not zeroed), which violates the BLAS specification.
- Anyone who needs the fault tolerance to actually protect results: in the released DGEMM the checksum comparison and correction code is commented out, and the fault-tolerant DDOT on a detected mismatch only prints a message and returns a truncated (wrong) dot product instead of recomputing.
- Non-AVX-512 CPUs, AMD/ARM machines, complex or most single-precision routines, or multithreaded BLAS: CMake hard-codes -march=skylake-avx512 and the DGEMM/DDOT sources contain no threading.
- Closed-source or permissively licensed products: the code is GPL-3.0.

**Integration:** static lib (CMake add_library without SHARED; builds libSrcFuncs plus test binaries) · none beyond libm and libpthread; CMake passes -fopenmp · C++11, CMake 3.17; GCC/Clang-style inline assembly (AT&T syntax) and AVX-512 intrinsics; the paper used icc 19.0 -O3 · x86-64 Linux with AVX-512F (Skylake-SP, Cascade Lake or newer Intel); -march=skylake-avx512 is hard-coded

**Vs siblings:** Pick FT-BLAS only when soft-error tolerance on x86 is the research question, since no catalogued sibling offers it; for plain speed on CPUs, BLASFEO or LibShalom (small matrices) and GEMMFIP or Eigen (general sizes) are complete, maintained and permissively licensed, and CLBlast is the GPU option.

**Gotchas:**
- Unsupported layout/transpose/side combinations and bad leading dimensions call printf then exit(-1) or exit(-2) from inside the library instead of returning an error code.
- Each DGEMM call allocates about 32 MB of packing buffers (384x1152 and 384x9216 doubles) and frees them on return, which hurts repeated small calls.
- The fault-tolerant DGEMM compares checksums against an absolute threshold of 1e-2 (in commented-out code), which would false-alarm on large-magnitude data and miss small errors if re-enabled.
- The top-level CMake overwrites CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS with CMAKE_C_FLAGS plus its own flags, so CXX flags passed by the user are dropped.

**Status:** Abandoned research code (last commit 2023-02-28, 7 stars, no releases); GPL-3.0 with an OpenBLAS license file included, usable for study or experiments but not production-ready.

[repo](https://github.com/yzhaiustc/ftblas) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.00897)

##### M4RI (dense GF(2) linear algebra: Method of the Four Russians, Strassen-Winograd, PLE elimination)  `C`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier B`

C library for dense matrix arithmetic over GF(2); 2008 paper shows 1.4-1.5x faster multiplication than Magma on Core 2.

**Beats:** Magma 2.14 (2.14-14 on the Core 2 Duo, 2.14-13 on the Opteron, per search snippets), the proprietary computer algebra system's asymptotically fast GF(2) matrix multiplication; GAP 4.4 also appears in the tables. None of the listed baselines (OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, Eigen, BLIS) apply because they do not operate on bit-packed GF(2) matrices. — Snippet only: search-engine summaries of the Albrecht-Bard-Hart paper (arXiv 0811.1714, ACM TOMS Algorithm 898) report M4RI-20080821 multiplying square GF(2) matrices 1.36-1.50x faster than Magma 2.14 on a 2.33 GHz Core 2 Duo (for example 1.504 s vs 2.210 s at n=10,000), built with GCC 4.3.1 -O2 -msse2, and at parity with Magma (within about 2%) on a 2.6 GHz Opteron. Those are 2008 numbers against a proprietary baseline that cannot be reproduced; the repo's bench/ programs time M4RI only, and the PLE paper (arXiv 1111.6549) claims gains over the previous fastest implementation without numbers on any page opened here.

**Known shortcoming:** Raised C to B on the peer-reviewed ACM TOMS Algorithm 898 (arXiv 0811.1714), seen only as search snippets (1.36-1.50x over Magma 2.14 on a Core 2 Duo; parity on an Opteron) because arxiv.org, ar5iv, wrap.warwick.ac.uk and malb.bitbucket.io were blocked. The baseline is Magma, not any listed BLAS; numbers are 2008-era.

**Known shortcoming:** Not thread-safe by default (global MMC and mzd caches unless --enable-thread-safe); open issue #10 says 64x64-class products are 'embarrassingly bad'; cache sizes are fixed at configure time, and issue #4's L3 misdetection gave random OpenMP failures (fixed in #37, Dec 2025). No AVX2, AVX-512, GFNI or NEON kernels (GFNI only proposed, issue #36). The only numbers remain the 2008 snippet-only Magma tables.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Bit-packing turns 64 GF(2) additions or multiplications into one XOR or AND, and multiplication uses the Method of the Four Russians (Kronrod's method, M4RM): Gray-code tables of all 2^k combinations of k rows of B (up to six tables at once) replace inner products with table lookups and row XORs. Above a cache-derived cutoff it recurses with Strassen-Winograd (O(n^2.807)); elimination uses the M4RI algorithm (O(n^3/log n)) and a block-iterative PLE decomposition that reuses the same tables. Block sizes and cutoffs come from L1/L2/L3 cache sizes detected at configure time, because the authors found memory traffic and data locality, not arithmetic, to be the bottleneck.

**Use it when:**
- Dense GF(2) matrices from hundreds to tens of thousands of rows and columns: cryptanalysis (linear systems from algebraic attacks, linearization), coding theory, Groebner-basis linear algebra over F2 (PolyBoRi-style)
- Rank, row echelon form, kernel or inverse of large bit matrices, where the O(n^3/log n) M4RI and PLE routines beat naive XOR elimination
- Products of large square or rectangular bit matrices, where M4RM plus Strassen-Winograd beats a hand-written word-parallel triple loop
- Linux x86-64 builds, the only platform the README promises to support; SSE2 code paths are used there
- Code already in the SageMath ecosystem, or code that needs the companion M4RIE library for GF(2^e), 2 <= e <= 10

**Skip it when:**
- Sparse GF(2) systems (LDPC, sieve matrices from factoring): dense bit-packed storage and O(n^2.807) work waste time; use a Wiedemann/Lanczos or structured-Gaussian-elimination code instead
- Many tiny products (64x64 times 64x1, 64x64 times 64x64, Nx64 times 64x64): open issue #10 calls M4RI's performance there 'embarrassingly bad'
- Fields other than GF(2), or floating-point BLAS work: it covers only F2 (GF(2^e) needs the separate M4RIE library)
- Proprietary or permissively licensed products: GPL-2.0-or-later is copyleft
- Windows (MSYS2/MinGW) or macOS deployments that need guaranteed support: the README calls these best effort that 'may disappear any time'; there are no AVX2/AVX-512/GFNI or NEON kernels (GFNI is only a proposal in open issue #36)

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (autotools: autoreconf, ./configure, make; pkg-config file m4ri.pc) · none required; libpng optional (PNG matrix I/O, on by default if found), OpenMP optional (--enable-openmp), PAPI optional for benchmarks; the bench/ suite vendors libcpucycles and needs python3 to build · C99 compiler (configure aborts without C99); headers wrap declarations in extern "C" for C++ (not under MSVC) · Linux supported (x86-64 with SSE2 paths, portable 64-bit-word code elsewhere); macOS and Windows MSYS2/MinGW64 best effort; CI builds on ubuntu-latest (with AddressSanitizer), macos-latest and windows-latest

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued blas-lapack siblings (OpenBLAS-class GEMMs, BLASFEO, Eigen, faer, fast-matmul) handle GF(2): emulating F2 with 0/1 floats and a mod-2 step costs 32-64x the memory and loses M4RM's table tricks. Pick M4RI whenever the field is GF(2) and the matrices are dense; it is the reference implementation in this niche.

**Gotchas:**
- Cache sizes and the Strassen cutoff (min(sqrt(4*L3), 4096)) and PLE cutoff are compiled in at configure time; a distro or cross-built binary is tuned for the build machine. Issue #4 reported L3 misdetection causing random failures with OpenMP on some systems; a fix ('Correct L3 Detection', #37) landed in December 2025, and --with-cachesize=L1:L2:L3 overrides detection.
- If the library was built with SSE2, client code must also be compiled with SSE2 enabled, or m4ri.h stops with #error.
- mzd_transpose does not work in place for square matrices (documented only in open issue #5); M4RI's solve_left corresponds to Sage's solve_right (issue #6); the PLUQ specification is flagged as unclear (issue #8, label bug).
- Allocation failure calls m4ri_die(), which prints and abort()s; there are no error codes. Windowed sub-matrices (mzd_init_window) share storage with their parent and need not be word-aligned.

**Status:** Actively maintained (tags 20251206, 20251207 and 20260122, last commit 2026-08-25, CI on Linux/macOS/Windows) and packaged by Debian, Fedora, Homebrew and SageMath; GPL-2.0-or-later, so usable as a linked library but copyleft.

[repo](https://github.com/malb/m4ri) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.1714)

#### fft

##### SFFT3 (3-D FFT built from FFTW 1-D transforms)  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

500-line OpenMP 3-D real FFT over FFTW 1-D plans; 1.2-1.3x faster than FFTW 3-D plans on large float volumes.

**Beats:** FFTW3 own 3-D routines (FFTW_PATIENT on the Ryzen table, FFTW_MEASURE on the i7 table) — The author's test_sfft3.c times SFFT3 against fftwf_plan_dft_r2c_3d/c2r_3d in one binary, single precision, one OpenMP thread per physical core, planning and padding excluded. Build: gcc -O3 -march=native -fopenmp -flto=auto; gcc and FFTW versions not stated. It won by 1.20x at 512^3 and 1.31x at 1024^3 on a Ryzen 7 3700X (both PATIENT) and by 1.01-1.10x at its winning sizes on an i7-6700K (both MEASURE), and lost at small sizes. The printed figure is the mean of one forward and one inverse transform, not the pair sum. The harness never renormalizes between round trips, so the timed data overflow to inf/NaN for both libraries alike.

**Known shortcoming:** Single precision only; larger workspace than FFTW; slower at 4 of 9 i7 sizes.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: with plan->scale=1, sfft3_execute_dft_c2r treats the padded array as dense M*N*P floats, scaling padding and leaving the tail unscaled. sfft3_create_plan calloc()s threads^2 x max(M*N*4, M*P*8) x 8 bytes (4 GiB virtual for 1024^3 on 8 threads). Harness flaws: the timed loop never renormalizes, so data overflow to inf/NaN for both libraries; warmup passes the r2c plan to fftwf_execute_dft_c2r. Reported time is the mean of one forward and one inverse; ratios still hold.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Row-column decomposition with cache-blocked transposes. For each XY plane it runs r2c along the contiguous X lines. It then copies a group of Y lines, sized to fit in L2, into a per-thread workspace through a 32x32 stack tile sized for L1. There it runs contiguous unit-stride FFTW 1-D c2c transforms and transposes the result back; the Z axis is done the same way over XZ planes. OpenMP parallelizes over planes with single-threaded FFTW plans, so every 1-D FFT runs on contiguous cache-resident data rather than strided memory.

**Use it when:**
- Large float 3-D real FFTs (about 256^3 and up) on multi-core x86 where FFTW's own 3-D plan is the bottleneck: 8-core Ryzen 3700X, both FFTW_PATIENT, 512^3 1.20x and 1024^3 1.31x (derived from README data)
- Codes already built around FFTW's padded in-place r2c/c2r layout that only need forward/inverse 3-D transforms, e.g. FFT convolution of large volumes
- As a starting point for your own 3-D driver: the author says switching the 1-D backend from FFTW needs relatively small changes
- GPL-compatible projects that already link FFTW

**Skip it when:**
- Small volumes: 64^3 and 128^3 were 1.54x and 1.50x slower than FFTW_PATIENT on the Ryzen, and 128^3 was 1.79x slower on the i7-6700K (derived from README data)
- Hardware you have not measured yourself: on the 4-core i7-6700K with FFTW_MEASURE it lost at 4 of 9 sizes (including 2100x2100x121) and won by only 1-10% elsewhere; the author does not expect the results to generalize
- Double precision, complex input, 1-D/2-D, out-of-place or batched transforms: only in-place float 3-D r2c/c2r exists
- Memory-tight or overcommit-disabled systems: it uses more workspace than FFTW's 3-D plans and, through a sizing bug, requests far more than it uses
- Production code: the author calls it an untested proof of concept with nothing more planned, and FFTW plus GPL-3.0 rule out closed-source use

**Integration:** source-drop · FFTW3 single precision (fftw3f via pkg-config; the makefile also links -lfftw3f_omp) and OpenMP · C11 with GNU extensions (makefile uses -std=gnu11; code uses VLAs and __attribute__((aligned))) plus OpenMP; built with gcc, and the README says clang also works · Any platform with FFTW3 and OpenMP. Its own code has no explicit SIMD; measured only on x86-64 Linux (Ryzen 7 3700X, i7-6700K).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over FFTW's own 3-D plans only for large float r2c volumes on multi-core x86, after measuring on your machine, and only if you can spare a per-thread plane buffer. Admiral reports a larger N-D margin over FFTW_MEASURE and PocketFFT avoids FFTW's GPL, so look at those first if you are not tied to FFTW.

**Gotchas:**
- Do not set plan->scale = 1: the normalization loop in sfft3_execute_dft_c2r treats the padded array as dense M*N*P floats. It scales padding slots and leaves the tail of the array unscaled. Keep the default (0) and normalize the real elements yourself.
- sfft3_create_plan calloc()s threads^2 x max(M*N*4, M*P*8) x 8 bytes (4 GiB of virtual memory for 1024^3 with 8 threads), while execution touches only about (M/2+1) x max(N,P) x 8 bytes per thread. This works only with lazy zero-page allocation.
- Release builds use -DNDEBUG, which removes the assert() checks on plan and workspace allocation, so an allocation failure crashes instead of reporting an error
- L1/L2 block sizes are compile-time macros (SFFT3_L1=64000, SFFT3_L2=512000 bytes) with no autotuning; the i7 results needed -DSFFT3_L2=256000

**Status:** Stale proof of concept (18 commits, last 2025-08-29, 0 stars, no issues; the author says nothing more is planned). GPL-3.0 and about 660 lines over FFTW, so easy to vendor into GPL code and fix yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/elgw/sfft3) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elgw/sfft3/HEAD/README.md)

##### FFTW++ (implicit dealiased convolutions on FFTW3)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier B`

C++ layer over FFTW3 whose implicitly/hybrid-dealiased convolutions beat explicit zero-padded FFT convolutions in 2D and 3D.

**Beats:** FFTW 3 with explicit zero-padded convolutions (and FFTW's MPI transpose for the distributed code) — The baseline is explicit zero padding run through the same FFTW plans (tests/timing.py has -r implicit/explicit run types for the hybridconv* tests), so the win is algorithmic rather than a faster FFT kernel. Per WebSearch summaries of the papers (not opened; hosts blocked), the 2011 SIAM paper reports compute savings of about a factor of two from data locality and memory 1/2^(d-1) of explicit padding in d dimensions, and the 2024 hybrid paper reports matching or beating explicit dealiasing in 1-D and greatly outperforming it in 2-D and 3-D; no CPU, compiler or result data are committed to the repository.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers only in papers (unreadable here); the 'up to 2x' comes from a search summary.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug fixed: issue #26, Hermitian convolution with A>B gave ~50% relative error until the 2026-08-12 fix; baseline is explicit padding through the library's own code; double precision only; plan creation writes wisdom3.txt to the working directory and errors call exit().

**How:** Implicit dealiasing (Bowman and Roberts, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2011) never transforms the padded zeros: it splits the padded transform into residue subtransforms and decouples work arrays from data arrays, so higher-dimensional convolutions need much less memory and gain data locality. Hybrid dealiasing (Murasko and Bowman, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2024) generalises this to arbitrary padding ratios, with explicit padding as a special case, and picks the subtransform size m, the number of residues processed at once D and in-place versus out-of-place by timing candidate configurations when the fftPad object is constructed. Multidimensional convolutions are decomposed into lower-dimensional ones, and the MPI code uses an adaptive hybrid OpenMP/MPI transpose instead of FFTW's MPI transpose.

**Use it when:**
- Pseudospectral PDE solvers (for example Navier-Stokes or turbulence codes) that evaluate quadratic nonlinearities as dealiased convolutions with the 2/3 or 1/2 padding rule, in 2-D or 3-D, where explicit zero padding costs memory and time.
- Large 3-D convolutions that barely fit in RAM: per the 2011 paper implicit padding asymptotically needs 1/2^(d-1) of the memory of explicit padding.
- Centered Hermitian-symmetric (real-field) spectral data, which has dedicated routines (fftPadHermitian, Convolution2/3 with Hermitian symmetrization helpers).
- Distributed-memory runs with MPI plus OpenMP where FFTW's own MPI transpose is the bottleneck.
- You want a small C++ RAII interface around double-precision FFTW3 with automatic wisdom and threading, regardless of convolutions.

**Skip it when:**
- Plain FFTs: the fft classes call FFTW plans directly, so there is no speedup over FFTW itself.
- Single precision, GPUs or non-FFTW back ends: everything is double-precision FFTW3 (no fftwf calls) on the CPU.
- Closed-source products without a commercial FFTW licence: FFTW++ is LGPL-3.0-or-later but links FFTW, which is GPL.
- 1-D convolutions where speed is the goal: the 2024 paper reports hybrid dealiasing only matching or modestly beating explicit padding in 1-D; the big gains are in 2-D and 3-D.
- Code that must not exit the process on error or write files: invalid parameters and failed plans call exit(), and planning reads and writes a wisdom file in the working directory.

**Integration:** static lib · FFTW3 double precision plus libfftw3_omp (CMake requires both), OpenMP; MPI for mpi/; optional Array class (Array.h is bundled); Python, C and Fortran wrappers optional · C++11 (CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake 3.15; flag sets for GCC, Clang, AppleClang, Intel and IBM XL · Linux and macOS documented in CMake; x86-64 builds use -msse2 -march=native and an SSE2 complex-multiply path (cmult-sse2.h) with a generic fallback; Windows builds have needed fixes (issue #17)

**Vs siblings:** Among the catalogued FFT entries it is the only CPU library aimed at dealiased convolutions for spectral solvers; pick FlashFFTConv instead for long 1-D convolutions in deep learning on NVIDIA GPUs, and FINUFFT when samples are nonuniform rather than needing a padded uniform convolution. For plain FFTs, a faster kernel such as Admiral or SFFT3 (3-D FFT built from FFTW 1-D transforms) matters more than this wrapper.

**Gotchas:**
- Constructing an fftPad object runs a timing search over subtransform sizes (repeated timed convolutions until the median stabilises within 2%), so construction is slow and the chosen m and D can differ between runs and machines; pass m, D and I to Application to pin them.
- Planner() loads and saves FFTW wisdom in a file named wisdom3.txt in the current working directory (written via a temporary wisdom3.txt_<pid> and renamed), and fftw::effort defaults to FFTW_MEASURE.
- Issue #26 (fixed 2026-08-12): Hermitian two-loop convolutions with more inputs than outputs (A > B, for example 15 to 3 channels) returned outputs with about 50% relative error; use a build from after that fix.
- The CMake flags are -Ofast -ffast-math -march=native, so default builds are not portable across CPUs and relax IEEE semantics; the vcpkg port is a 2019 snapshot that predates the hybrid convolution code entirely.

**Status:** Actively maintained (2,942 commits, last commit 2026-08-12 fixing issue #26, header version 3.04) by its University of Alberta authors; LGPL-3.0-or-later, but any binary that links FFTW falls under the GPL unless FFTW is licensed commercially.

[repo](https://github.com/dealias/fftwpp) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1008.1366)

##### KFR  `C++`  `GPL-2.0-or-later (dual commercial license)`  `active`  `Tier B`

C++20 SIMD DSP framework whose any-length FFT tracks or beats FFTW in vendor and LIGO/KAGRA benchmarks; GPL or paid license.

**Beats:** FFTW — The independent evidence is an LVK (LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA) proceedings paper (arXiv 2503.14292, Fig. 6): complex forward in-place FFTs on a local Osaka cluster show KFR 6.0.2 with higher MFlops than FFTW 3.3.10 (Clang), shown only as graphs, with no CPU model or planner flags and using a harness first written by KFR's author. KFR's own README graphs (KFR 3.0.5-rc, clang 7.0.1, AVX2, Windows) show roughly 1.3-3x FFTW 3.3.8 on powers of two, but its kfrlib/fft-benchmark harness plans FFTW with FFTW_ESTIMATE, which understates FFTW.

**Known shortcoming:** README graph is old (KFR 3.0.5-rc) and measures FFTW in FFTW_ESTIMATE mode, overstating the gap; independent LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA paper (arXiv 2503.14292) gives a graph only, no CPU model.

**Known shortcoming:** Vendor harness (kfrlib/fft-benchmark, libs/fftw/fftw.cpp at HEAD) still plans FFTW with FFTW_ESTIMATE, so its graphs overstate the gap to FFTW.

**Known shortcoming:** The LVK paper's benchmark harness was first written by KFR's author, so the tier-B measurement is not fully independent.

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #272: KFR 7.0.1 built with MSVC Release gave a ghost peak on a 2^19 r2c FFT (closed, labelled compiler bug); building the DFT module ran out of memory in vcpkg CI (#261).

**How:** Transforms run on KFR's own vec<T,N> SIMD layer (SSE2 to AVX-512, NEON, RVV) rather than relying on auto-vectorization, with multiarchitecture builds dispatching to the best kernel at runtime on x86. Power-of-two sizes use a four-step (DIF half plus DIT half, the 'sandwich') decomposition whose split is chosen from hard-coded per-architecture tables that switch layout once the data exceeds 32 KiB (AVX) or 128 KiB (Apple NEON). Other sizes use mixed-radix stages with fixed SIMD butterflies for radices 2-10 plus a generic butterfly, and Bluestein's algorithm where needed. There is no runtime measurement or wisdom phase, so plan creation is deterministic.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated fixed-size 1D FFTs (power-of-two or arbitrary, including primes) in float or double where FFTW's GPL is acceptable but its planning time or wisdom management is not
- Audio and real-time DSP pipelines that also need FIR/IIR filters, FFT convolution, sample-rate conversion and audio file I/O from one library
- Cross-platform builds (x86 SSE2-AVX-512, ARM/AArch64 NEON, RISC-V RVV, WebAssembly, iOS/Android) that want one FFT code base with runtime CPU dispatch on x86
- Real-time callbacks with a fixed power-of-two size: ngfft has no allocation and no scratch at execution time
- Projects that can pay for KFR's commercial license and want an FFT outside FFTW's licensing

**Skip it when:**
- Closed-source or permissively licensed products that will not buy a commercial license: KFR is GPLv2+ otherwise
- MSVC-only toolchains: the DFT module is off by default with MSVC, the docs warn of lower DFT performance, and a Release-mode MSVC build produced a wrong 2^19 real FFT (issue #272, labeled compiler bug)
- Multithreaded single large transforms: no internal threading is documented, and its own benchmark harness disables multithreading
- Strided, transposed or non-contiguous multidimensional data: MD plans require contiguous row-major tensors, and real MD transforms require an even last axis
- When you need proof that it beats a tuned FFTW (FFTW_MEASURE/PATIENT) on your CPU: the published comparisons use FFTW_ESTIMATE or do not state planner flags

**Integration:** static lib (DFT, DSP, IO and audio modules are compiled libraries via CMake; the SIMD/expression core is header-only); optional C API library · none beyond a C++20 standard library; CMake 3.16+ to build · C++20; Clang 16+, GCC 11+, MSVC 2022 (19.30+), Xcode 13+; Clang recommended for best performance · Windows, Linux, macOS, iOS, Android, WebAssembly; x86/x86-64 (SSE2-AVX-512), ARM/AArch64 (NEON), RISC-V 64 with RVV (VLEN >= 128, Linux, Clang); runtime dispatch only on x86

**Vs siblings:** Pick KFR over PocketFFT, PFFFT or muFFT when you want SIMD speed on arbitrary 1D lengths plus a full DSP toolkit and can accept GPL or a paid license; over FFTS because FFTS is unmaintained. Pick VectorFFT only for x86 double c2c work that wants an MIT license and an MKL-beating claim, and VkFFT for GPUs.

**Gotchas:**
- No transform is normalized: forward then inverse returns N times the input (2/N for the DCT pair)
- Real-spectrum layout depends on dft_pack_format (CCs default vs Perm); ngfft real transforms always use Perm, and irealdft infers an even length from the buffer size
- Building the DFT module is memory-heavy (vcpkg CI out-of-memory in issue #261); KFR_CLASSIC_FFT restores the pre-7.1 FFT path
- ngfft twiddle buffers must be cache-line aligned and outlive the plan; ngfft_twiddle_count returns SIZE_MAX for sizes unsupported on the active architecture

**Status:** Actively maintained (KFR 7.1.0 released 2026-08-18, about 1.9k stars, 18 open issues); usable as GPLv2+ code or under a paid commercial license, with prebuilt release packages and CMake integration.

[repo](https://github.com/kfrlib/kfr) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14292)

#### geometry-spatial

##### HXT parallel 3D Delaunay (in Gmsh)  `C++`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier B`

Gmsh's HXT module: OpenMP-parallel 3D Delaunay tetrahedralization in C, about 3x faster serially than CGAL, TetGen and Geogram.

**Beats:** CGAL 3D Delaunay triangulation (CGAL 4.12) — The HXT authors' paper (arXiv 1805.08831, published in IJNME 117(9):967-990, 2019 per the HXT README and the Gmsh manual) reports a serial kernel about 3x faster than CGAL, TetGen and Geogram (about 2 s vs about 6 s for 1M random points). In parallel it reports 10M points in 4.48 s vs 20.15 s for CGAL 4.12 on a 64-core Xeon Phi 7210, with CGAL not completing 10^8 points, and 3 billion tetrahedra in 53 s on a dual-socket EPYC 7551. Compiler and flags are not stated, the authors wrote HXT, and CGAL 4.12 (2018) is old.

**Known shortcoming:** No compiler or flags; authors are Gmsh developers; CGAL 4.12 baseline is old; repo is a mirror; venue unconfirmed by verifier.

**Known shortcoming:** Licence trap: tetMesh CMake always links tetBR, whose standalone copy is TetGen 1.5 'non-commercial use' code relicensed only for use inside Gmsh (source warns 'Using TetgenBR without Gmsh - please note the different licensing terms').

**Known shortcoming:** HXT_OMP_CHECK calls exit() on error inside a parallel region, killing the host process; uint32 vertex indices; Gmsh's default 3D algorithm is Delaunay (1), not HXT (10), so users must opt in.

**Independent measurement:** paper Fig. 11b: 10M points on 64-core Xeon Phi 4.48 s vs CGAL 4.12 20.15 s

**How:** Points are sorted along a Moore (closed Hilbert) space-filling curve with radix sort and inserted in BRIO rounds by the Bowyer-Watson kernel: walk to the containing tetrahedron, breadth-first search to dig the cavity with Shewchuk's adaptive orient3d/insphere predicates (Devillers-Teillaud symbolic perturbation breaks ties), then refill it, computing the new adjacencies in `omp simd` loops over aligned buffers. For parallelism each OpenMP thread owns a contiguous range of Moore indices. An insertion whose cavity touches a vertex outside the thread's range is deferred to a later round, which re-sorts along a randomly shifted Moore curve and lowers the thread count when the conflict ratio rises. Conflicts are avoided by these partition-ownership checks, not by per-element locks; the README lists Geogram-style point locks only as future work.

**Use it when:**
- Unconstrained 3D Delaunay of 10^6 to 10^9 points on a many-core shared-memory CPU: 10M points in 4.48 s on a 64-core Xeon Phi 7210 vs 20.15 s for CGAL 4.12, and 3 billion tetrahedra in 53 s on a dual-socket EPYC 7551 (paper)
- Volume tetrahedral meshing for FEM inside Gmsh, where Mesh.Algorithm3D=10 parallelises the meshing of a single volume (the default Delaunay algorithm does not)
- GPL-compatible open-source C or C++ codes that want a fast Delaunay kernel and can vendor C99 sources built as CMake object libraries
- Pipelines that need bit-identical meshes across thread counts: reproducible=1 reorders the output deterministically, at extra cost

**Skip it when:**
- Proprietary or closed-source products: HXT is GPL-2.0-or-later, and its exception only covers combining with Gmsh's own code
- Dynamic or specialised triangulations (vertex removal, incremental point location queries, weighted/regular or periodic Delaunay): CGAL has them, while HXT's single-point insertion API is commented out as 'NOT IMPLEMENTED YET'
- More than about 4.29 billion vertices: vertex indices are uint32_t (ghost vertex = UINT32_MAX), and '40+ bits nodes' is still a TODO in the README
- Robustness-first meshing of messy CAD or STL input: the Gmsh manual calls the default 'Delaunay' algorithm the most robust and the only one that makes hybrid meshes with pyramids. Search results list Gmsh tracker issues on HXT crashes in reshapeCavityIfNeeded, failures on discontinuous STL and runaway memory with size fields (not opened)
- An NVIDIA GPU is available and the point set fits in its memory: gDel3D is the GPU alternative

**Integration:** source-drop · OpenMP 4 (optional, with a serial fallback) and libm; tetMesh also needs HXT core, predicates (Shewchuk) and tetBR (TetGen/BR boundary recovery, C++). Full Gmsh optionally adds FLTK and OpenCASCADE. · C99 compiler plus a C++ compiler for tetBR, CMake 3.9+; the README builds with -march=native so that parts of tetMesh auto-vectorise · Any platform with a C99/OpenMP compiler. The paper ran on x86-64 (Core i7-6700HQ, Xeon Phi 7210, EPYC 7551). The standalone HXT CMake turns OpenMP off by default under MSVC, which makes it serial.

**Vs siblings:** Among the catalogued siblings only gDel3D also does 3D Delaunay, and it needs a CUDA GPU (4-10x over serial CGAL 4.2). Pick HXT for many-core CPUs, no NVIDIA GPU, or point sets too large for GPU memory. The other siblings (mesh booleans: Manifold, MeshLib, trueform; spatial indexes: nanoflann, rtree.c, KdBoxTree, THST) solve different problems.

**Gotchas:**
- An error inside the parallel insertion region calls exit() (the HXT_OMP_CHECK macro in hxt_tetDelaunay.c), so a failure kills the host process instead of returning an HXTStatus
- Licensing trap when extracting HXT from Gmsh: the standalone tetBR copy is TetGen 1.5 code headed 'redistributed for non-commercial use' and is relicensed only for use in Gmsh. The source emits the compile warning 'Using TetgenBR without Gmsh - please note the different licensing terms', and the tetMesh CMake always links tetBR.
- hxtDelaunay reorders mesh->vertices into Moore order, overwrites each vertex's 4th coordinate and deletes vertices it could not insert; use hxtDelaunaySteadyVertices when indices must stay stable. Multithreaded tetrahedron order is nondeterministic unless reproducible=1.
- Gmsh's default 3D algorithm is Delaunay (1), not HXT, so you must set Mesh.Algorithm3D=10 or -algo hxt to get this code path, including through gmsh::algorithm::tetrahedralize

**Status:** Gmsh is very active (mirror commits on 2026-09-28; the canonical repo is gitlab.onelab.info), but the HXT Delaunay file changes rarely: its last edits were 2025 warning fixes and a division-by-zero guard. It is GPL-2.0-or-later, so it can only be copied into GPL-compatible code.

[repo](https://github.com/live-clones/gmsh) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.08831)

##### ikd-Tree (incremental k-d tree)  `C++`  `GPL-2.0-only`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Incremental 3-D k-d tree for LiDAR SLAM maps: point/box updates without full rebuilds; per-scan time 1.03-2.1x below nanoflann and Boost R*-tree.

**Beats:** Boost.Geometry R*-tree, PCL octree and nanoflann dynamic k-d tree, each integrated into FAST-LIO2 (FAST-LIO2, IEEE T-RO 2022, Table III); also a static k-d tree rebuilt every scan (FAST-LIO, and the ikd-Tree preprint's PCL comparison) — In the peer-reviewed FAST-LIO2 paper (IEEE T-RO 2022, same group), the authors wired ikd-Tree, Boost.Geometry's R*-tree, PCL's octree and nanoflann's dynamic k-d tree into FAST-LIO2 and timed 18 sequences on an Intel i7-8550U (DJI Manifold 2-C), k=5, compiler not stated. Total per-scan time (updates plus kNN) was 1.03-1.34x lower than nanoflann, 1.26-2.09x lower than the R*-tree and 2.29-3.06x lower than the octree (derived from page data). The octree had the fastest updates in most sequences, and the main win over nanoflann is avoiding its multi-second update peaks. The baseline integration code (with emulated downsampling for the other trees) is not public.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is the FAST-LIO2 T-RO 2022 paper (PDF in hku-mars/FAST_LIO), Table III on an i7-8550U: total time 1.26-2.09x vs Boost.Geometry R*-tree, 2.3-3.1x vs PCL octree, only 1.03-1.34x vs nanoflann; the octree is faster at updates. GPL-2.0; abandoned since 2022.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: open #25 confirmed in code, point delete searches only one side of each split, so a point tying on the split coordinate can be missed. Security/robustness: #20 double free when Nearest_Search runs on several OpenMP threads (closed, no fix shown); open #37 segfault. The 1M-entry rebuild log ring buffer has no overflow check and adds ~44-64 MB to every tree object. GPLv2; abandoned since 2022, 24 open issues.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Each node stores its subtree's bounding cuboid, size and lazy 'deleted' labels, so box deletes and box re-adds mark whole subtrees in O(log n)-style traversals and push labels down later instead of touching every point. Points are inserted one at a time, and a subtree is rebuilt only when it violates an alpha-balanced criterion (child share outside 1-alpha_bal..alpha_bal) or an alpha-deleted criterion (invalid share above alpha_del), a scapegoat-tree style partial rebuild. Subtrees of 1,500 points or more are rebuilt on a second pthread while the main thread keeps updating and querying; updates made meanwhile go into an operation log that is replayed onto the new subtree before it is swapped in. k-NN uses bounding-box ('bounds-overlap-ball') pruning plus the max-distance cutoff that LiDAR odometry naturally supplies.

**Use it when:**
- LiDAR or LiDAR-inertial odometry and mapping that inserts a few thousand downsampled points per scan and runs small k-NN (FAST-LIO2 uses k=5) against a local map of 10^5-10^6 points
- Sliding-window or moving-map applications that need box-wise deletion of everything outside a region, which ikd-Tree does with lazy labels instead of per-point removes
- Real-time loops where worst-case update latency matters more than mean: in FAST-LIO2's Table III ikd-Tree's update peak stays at or under 214 ms while nanoflann's dynamic index peaks above 3 s on seven sequences
- Embedded x86 or ARM Linux robots already using PCL (the paper runs FAST-LIO2 on an i7-8550U and on a Cortex-A73 board)

**Skip it when:**
- Anything other than 3-D float points: x/y/z and per-axis node ranges are hard-coded (issue #26 asks about 2-D; issue #39 reports pcl::PointXYZL not working)
- Bulk loading or large batch inserts: Add_Points inserts point by point, and issue #36 reports 30,000-point inserts slower than PCL's kd-tree
- Commercial or permissive-license projects: GPLv2, and the README asks commercial users to contact the authors
- Code that needs a maintained dependency or exact deletes: last commit 2022-03-04, 24 open issues, including an open report (#25) that ties on the split coordinate make point lookups miss
- Pure insert-heavy workloads: in FAST-LIO2's comparison PCL's octree has the fastest incremental updates in most sequences; ikd-Tree wins on k-NN and total time

**Integration:** source-drop (ikd-Tree/ikd_Tree.h + ikd_Tree.cpp; FAST-LIO2 vendors its own copy) · PCL (the header includes pcl/point_types.h; Eigen::aligned_allocator arrives through it), POSIX threads (pthread, usleep). The demos need PCL 1.8+ · C++14 (the demo CMakeLists builds with -std=c++14 -pthread -O3); CMake 2.8+ · POSIX/Linux (pthread and unistd.h); Windows and macOS not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick ikd-Tree over nanoflann's dynamic index when you need bounded worst-case update latency, box deletion and on-tree downsampling for a single 3-D LiDAR map; nanoflann is BSD, header-only, any dimension and maintained. Pick PSI/SpaceTreeLib or Pkd-tree instead for large parallel batch updates on many-core servers, and PH-tree for a permissively licensed dynamic index with general key types.

**Gotchas:**
- Each KD_TREE object embeds a 1,000,000-entry operation-log ring buffer (MANUAL_Q, Q_LEN) by value, about 44 MB per tree for its own point type and about 64 MB for pcl::PointXYZI (derived from the header's struct layout), so construct it on the heap (KD_TREE::Ptr). The ring buffer's push has no overflow check, so more than 10^6 operations logged during one background rebuild would silently overwrite entries
- Deletes are lazy: deleted points stay in memory and in tree size until a rebuild, so memory and k-NN cost depend on rebuild timing (issue #42 reports memory not released after deleting the root). Delete_by_point descends one side only on strict less-than, which is why issue #25's tie case can miss a point
- The constructor starts a pthread and prints 'Multi thread started' to stdout; the destructor joins it (issue #43 reports a hang on destruction). Default parameters differ between the constructor (balance 0.6) and InitializeKDTree (balance 0.7)
- Only ikdTree_PointType, pcl::PointXYZ and pcl::PointXYZI are explicitly instantiated in ikd_Tree.cpp; other point types need an added 'template class' line (issue #30 reports an undefined reference to KD_TREE<POINT_TYPE>::~KD_TREE(), the symptom of a missing instantiation)

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-03-04 (24 open issues, several crash and correctness reports unanswered) and GPLv2-only, so vendor it knowingly; the copy inside FAST-LIO2 is the best-exercised version.

[repo](https://github.com/hku-mars/ikd-Tree) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hku-mars/FAST_LIO/HEAD/doc/Fast_LIO_2.pdf)

#### random-and-quasi-random

##### randp (AES-CTR Random Pool)  `C`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Linux C library with arc4random-style API backed by a thread-local 3-round-AES pool; 2-21x faster than glibc arc4random.

**Beats:** glibc arc4random / arc4random_buf / arc4random_uniform (glibc 2.36+ getrandom-based); also getentropy, RDRAND, RDSEED — In the author's Google Benchmark run of 2026-09-22 (i9-13980HX, Linux 7.2.6, glibc 2.44 with the getrandom vDSO, gcc 16.2.1, one thread, median of 5), filling 4 GiB in 256-byte calls took 247 ms with randp_bytes against 5211 ms with arc4random_buf (21.1x). One uint32 took 7.00 ns against 14.0 ns for arc4random, and a bounded uint32 (bounds cycling over 1..0x100000) took 7.19 ns against 23.6 ns for arc4random_uniform. Runs on glibc 2.40, before the vDSO, showed 27-43x; randp_bytes itself slowed from 199 ms (librandp 4.5, February 2026) to 247 ms (7.0), and the cause is not documented.

**Known shortcoming:** Security: the 'AES-CTR' generator runs only 3 AES rounds (3 keys x 1 aesenc), not AES-128, yet the README calls the output practically unpredictable; the comparison against ChaCha20-backed glibc arc4random is not like for like. No LICENSE file (MPL-2.0 SPDX headers only).

**Known shortcoming:** Published numbers cover the 128-bit AES-NI path only: librandp.a is built with config.mk -march=x86-64-v2 -maes, and -mvaes applies only to the benchmark C++ file, so the record's flags line is misleading. The 4 GiB test calls each function in 256-byte chunks. randp_bytes regressed from 199 ms (4.5) to 247 ms (7.0) with no documented cause. Keys and counter stay in memory, so a disclosure exposes outputs before and after up to the next reseed (256 KiB); fatal exit on mmap/madvise/getentropy failure; x86-64 Linux with GCC 14+ only; soname went 4.5 to 7.0 in 2026; the GitHub topic says CSPRNG while the README disclaims it.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The generator transforms a counter with three AESENC instructions under three independent random 128-bit round keys: no key schedule, no initial key whitening, no AESENCLAST, so far less work than the kernel getrandom path that glibc's arc4random wraps. The counter advances as two 64-bit Weyl sequences with odd per-lane increments. Output is produced 256 bytes at a time into a lock-free thread_local pool, so randp_u32 is a memcpy plus explicit_bzero with no syscall or vDSO call; bounded integers use Lemire's nearly divisionless multiply-and-reject method. A VAES/AVX2 path that generates two blocks per instruction exists, but the default config.mk build (-march=x86-64-v2 -maes) compiles the 128-bit AES-NI path.

**Use it when:**
- Linux x86-64 code that calls arc4random or arc4random_uniform in hot loops (shuffles, sampling, randomized algorithms, jitter, non-secret IDs): 7.0 ns versus 14.0 ns per uint32 and 7.19 ns versus 23.6 ns per bounded draw on the author's machine.
- Bulk filling of buffers with unpredictable-looking bytes where secrecy does not matter (test data, fuzz inputs, randomized padding): about 16 GiB/s on one thread versus about 0.8 GiB/s for arc4random_buf in 256-byte calls (both derived from page data).
- Multi-threaded or forking servers that want per-thread, lock-free randomness with no seeding code: the pool is thread_local and MADV_WIPEONFORK makes a forked child reseed before its first output.
- You want periodic automatic reseeding from the OS, which plain xoshiro/PCG-style generators do not do.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys, nonces, session tokens, salts, or anything an attacker gains from predicting: three AES rounds are not a cipher, there is no security proof, and the README makes no CSPRNG claim. Use getrandom/arc4random, or Randen if you need speed with a stated security argument.
- Reproducible simulations: there is no seed or stream API; it is always seeded from getentropy and reseeds every 256 KiB per thread.
- Anything other than Linux x86-64 with GCC 14+ and glibc 2.34+: non-x86-64 hits #error "Architecture not supported", clang is explicitly unsupported, and MADV_WIPEONFORK needs Linux 4.14+.
- Maximum raw throughput for statistics or Monte Carlo: the pool copy and wiping cost time, and the same author's raw aes_ctr_128 generator (prng-test-bench) is listed at 37.22 GiB/s per thread versus about 16 GiB/s for randp_bytes (different benchmarks).
- Long-lived production dependencies: 1 star, single author, the soname went from 4.5 (February 2026) to 7.0 (September 2026), and parameters and build options change frequently.

**Integration:** static lib, shared lib, or header-only (make randp-single.h amalgamation) · none beyond glibc 2.34+ (getentropy, explicit_bzero, C11 threads in libc) and Linux 4.14+ (mmap, MADV_DONTDUMP, MADV_WIPEONFORK); python3 to generate the single header; Google Benchmark for the benchmarks · GCC 14+ in C23 mode (clang and clang++ not supported); the C++ benchmarks use g++ -std=c++23 · Linux x86-64 only, AES-NI plus SSE4.1 required (optional VAES + AVX2 path)

**Vs siblings:** Pick randp over Randen when you want arc4random's seedless, per-thread, fork-safe API on Linux and can accept a reduced-round generator with no proof; pick Randen when you need its stated indistinguishability and backtracking resistance. For seeded simulation streams or raw speed, the same author's prng-test-bench aes_ctr_128 or testingRNG's aesctr skip randp's pool copy and wiping.

**Gotchas:**
- Despite the name, the defaults (3 keys x 1 round in src/aes_ctr_128_prng-defaults.h and aes_ctr_256_prng-defaults.h) give 3 AESENC rounds on a Weyl-sequence counter, not AES-128 in CTR mode. The parameters are compile-time constexpr values; the build-time override was removed on 2026-09-24, so changing them means editing the headers.
- Failures are fatal: an error from mmap, madvise (for example a kernel without MADV_WIPEONFORK), getentropy or tss_create calls err/errx and exits the process.
- The keys and counter sit in the per-thread page between reseeds, so a memory disclosure exposes outputs both before and after it up to the next reseed (256 KiB); wiping handed-out pool bytes does not prevent that. Each thread that calls randp also holds a 4 KiB mapping until it exits.
- There is no LICENSE file at the root (raw LICENSE returns 404); MPL-2.0 comes only from SPDX headers in each source file. The published numbers cover the 128-bit AES-NI path: benchmarks/Makefile adds -march=x86-64-v3 -mvaes only to the C++ benchmark file, while librandp.a is built with config.mk's -march=x86-64-v2 -maes.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-02, commits almost daily) but a 1-star single-author project. MPL-2.0 by SPDX headers only, and small enough to vendor through randp-single.h if you accept its Linux/x86-64/GCC-only scope.

[repo](https://github.com/planet36/randp) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/planet36/randp/HEAD/benchmarks/README.md)

##### RANLUX++ (sibidanov/ranluxpp)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

RANLUX recast as a 576-bit LCG with x86-64 assembly modmul; about 8x faster than classic RANLUX implementations.

**Beats:** std::ranlux (GCC libstdc++ RANLUX) in the repo README and tests/std_random_test.cxx; ROOT's TRandom1 (James' RANLUX implementation) in the independent ROOT measurement — A ROOT developer measured Sibidanov's assembly implementation at about 8 ns per number against about 62 ns for ROOT's TRandom1 RANLUX (single precision only) on one core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900, CentOS 8.2, GCC 8.3.1, 10 repetitions with under 1% standard deviation, flags not stated (about 7.8x, derived from page data). The README's own figure, 20 versus 198 clocks per float against GCC's std RANLUX on Haswell, is first-party, mixes CPUs and does not say whether ranlux24 or ranlux48 was timed.

**Known shortcoming:** Faster than ROOT's TRandom1 (RANLUX, ~8 ns vs ~62 ns) but still slower than MT (~3 ns); last commit 2018-01-17; COPYING and COPYING.LESSER exist (record said no license files).

**Known shortcoming:** ROOT's RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx lists fixes to this code: the modulo result is not always the smallest value, reading output straight from the LCG state biases the upper bits, and it uses 52 instead of 48 bits per double; ROOT's fixed portable version measured ~9 ns vs ~8 ns here, so the speed largely holds after the fixes. init() does not reset state or caches; Makefile builds everything with -mavx2. Randompack's MIT ranlux++ reportedly as fast or up to 2x faster (paper snippet only).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Classic RANLUX generates and throws away most of its subtract-with-borrow outputs to decorrelate them; the LCG view replaces all that skipping with a single 576x576-bit modular multiplication. That multiply is hand-written AT&T x86-64 assembly (schoolbook, 81 64x64 products) with mulx and adcx/adox variants picked by GCC function multiversioning, plus a reduction specialized to the sparse modulus: 155 cycles per modmul on Skylake per the README. One modmul yields 24 floats (24-bit) or 11 doubles (52-bit) unpacked directly from the state bits.

**Use it when:**
- HEP, lattice or other Monte Carlo codes that must use a RANLUX-family generator for its theoretical mixing guarantees and are bottlenecked by std::ranlux24/48 or James-style RANLUX (TRandom1)
- x86-64 Linux with GCC, where the assembly and function multiversioning build as shipped
- Many independent streams: seeds map to jumps of 2^96*seed states, and jump(n) skips n RANLUX numbers in O(log n) modmuls
- Research or testing that needs the RANLUX-to-LCG state mapping (getlcgstate / getranluxseq) or a fast reference to check another RANLUX++ port against

**Skip it when:**
- Throughput-first simulations: RANLUX++ is still slower than Mersenne Twister (ROOT measured TRandom3 at about 3 ns versus about 8 ns), and xoshiro/PCG/Philox are faster still
- Non-x86-64 targets, Windows/MSVC, or non-GCC toolchains: the assembly uses the System V register ABI and the dispatch relies on GCC target attributes; ROOT's portable RanluxppEngine (about 9 ns after tuning on the same Ryzen) or Randompack's MIT ranlux++ cover those cases
- Code that needs bit-exact RANLUX output or the full theoretical guarantees: ROOT's reimplementation documents fixes to this code (canonical modulo result, converting the LCG state back to RANLUX numbers to avoid a bias in the upper state bits, 48 rather than 52 bits per double)
- Projects that cannot accept LGPL-3.0-or-later or an unmaintained dependency (last commit 2018-01-17, 6 commits)
- Code that expects a std:: engine: there is no result_type/min()/max() interface, so <random> distributions cannot use it directly

**Integration:** static lib (Makefile builds libranlux++.a from C++ and GNU as assembly) · none beyond GCC and GNU as · GCC with function multiversioning (target("arch=...") overloads); C++11 delegating constructors plus GNU extensions (__attribute__, __builtin_expect, hex-float literals); exact GCC version not documented · x86-64 only (System V ABI assembly); the Makefile builds everything with -mavx2, so the shipped build needs an AVX2 CPU even though mul9x9mod has a generic fallback

**Vs siblings:** No other catalogued sibling is a RANLUX-family generator except Randompack, whose MIT-licensed ranlux++ engine is reported (per a search snippet of its paper) to be as fast as or up to 2x faster than this code; pick this repo only as the reference assembly on x86-64 Linux with GCC. If RANLUX-grade theory is not required, xoshiro, PCG or Philox siblings (e.g. benchmark-rngs PhiloxSIMD, simdrng) are several times faster.

**Gotchas:**
- Outputs are unpacked from the LCG state, not from the RANLUX base-2^24 sequence, so the numbers differ from std::ranlux24/48 and TRandom1 even when the states are equivalent; primitive() changes the multiplier to a^2048 + 13, which leaves RANLUX equivalence altogether
- init(seed) multiplies the current state instead of resetting to x_0, and it does not clear the float/double caches, so reseeding a used object does not reach the documented x_0*A^(2^96*seed) state (read from src/ranluxpp.cxx)
- Multiversion dispatch is keyed to arch=haswell/broadwell/skylake; GCC selects arch= versions by CPU model, so other CPUs (AMD Zen, newer Intel cores) likely run the generic mul path (inferred from src/mulmod.cxx, not documented)
- operator() reinterprets a uint32_t/uint64_t cache as float/double through pointer casts (a strict-aliasing violation) and is marked noinline, so per-call overhead is a real function call; getarray is the fast path

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2018 (6 commits) and LGPL-3.0-or-later; the algorithm lives on in ROOT 6.24+ (TRandomRanluxpp / RanluxppEngine, portable and with correctness fixes) and in Randompack's MIT reimplementation, which are the better choices for new code.

[repo](https://github.com/sibidanov/ranluxpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/root-project/web/blob/main/blog/_posts/2020-11-30-ranluxpp.md)

##### wrs (lorenzhs/wrs, parallel weighted random sampling and alias tables, ESA 2019)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research C++17 library of sequential and parallel alias tables and weighted samplers; reported 3-4x faster queries than GSL's gsl_ran_discrete.

**Beats:** GNU Scientific Library (GSL) alias table implementation — Search-result summaries of the ESA 2019 paper (not opened; arXiv and Dagstuhl are blocked here) report sequential alias-table queries about 4x faster than GSL 2.5 gsl_ran_discrete at n = 10^8 (an earlier summary says more than 3x) and construction 30% faster on an Intel 80-core/160-thread machine and 44% faster on an AMD 32-core/64-thread machine; the GSL comparison is run single-threaded (benchmark/run_seq.sh passes -t 1) against an allocation-free copy of GSL's preprocessing in wrs/gsl.cpp. Compiler version, CPU models and build type for those runs are not stated in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B (ESA 2019 paper; benchmark/alias.cpp runs the GSL alias table beside wrs), but the GSL numbers (queries about 3-4x faster than GSL 2.5; Vose construction 30% faster on Intel, 44% on AMD) are known only from search summaries because drops.dagstuhl.de and publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu were blocked. Build flags -march=native -flto with a default Debug build type. Paper-based retier to A still open.

**Known shortcoming:** The GSL query comparison is not like for like: the GSL path draws gsl_rng_mt19937 per call while wrs uses MKL/dSFMT block uniforms plus 2 MB huge-page tables (madvise); benchmark/alias.cpp itself says to use size_t rather than the default uint32 index for a fair GSL comparison, and gsl_alias shares one gsl_rng so GSL ran single-threaded (run_seq.sh -t 1). Linux x86-64 only (prebuilt asmlib libaelf64.a, madvise, -march=native); CMake defaults to Debug. The 3-4x GSL numbers remain snippet-only.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The table is stored as an array of structs {double p; uint32 alias} so a query touches one cache line, where GSL keeps F[] and A[] in separate arrays; the query picks between bucket and alias with a branchless index (candidates[rand >= p]) and reuses the fractional part of one uniform draw. Construction classifies small and large items into a single work array and pairs them in one sweep (Vose-style), and the parallel PSA variants split the item range with prefix sums so threads build disjoint table segments. Tables above 1 MB are allocated 2 MB-aligned with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE), and uniforms come from Intel MKL or dSFMT in blocks rather than one gsl_rng call per sample.

**Use it when:**
- Millions to hundreds of millions of static weights sampled many times (Monte Carlo, graph generators, particle resampling) on Linux x86-64.
- You can build the table once and run queries from many threads: sample(u) is const and takes the random number as an argument.
- Table construction itself is the bottleneck and you have a many-core NUMA box: PSA and multi_alias build in parallel and the paper reports near-linear scaling.
- You need a batch of k samples with replacement and only want counts per item: outsens returns multiplicities instead of k individual draws.
- You are studying or reimplementing alias-table algorithms and want a reference with GSL wired in for comparison.

**Skip it when:**
- Closed-source or permissively licensed products: the code is GPL-3.0.
- Weights that change between draws: alias tables must be rebuilt in O(n); no dynamic or update API exists.
- Non-Linux or non-x86-64 targets: it calls madvise, links a prebuilt x86-64 ELF static library (extlib/stocc/libaelf64.a) and compiles with -march=native.
- Production use expecting maintenance: 8 commits, last one 2020-12-09, no releases, no issues filed, research-oriented logging and benchmark scaffolding throughout.
- Small tables or few queries: for a handful of weights std::discrete_distribution or a linear or binary search over a prefix sum is simpler and the setup cost (thread pool, submodules) dominates.

**Integration:** static lib · tlx (author's fork, threadpool_init branch, git submodule), pthread, libatomic, Agner Fog's stocc with prebuilt asmlib libaelf64.a (vendored); optional Intel MKL (fast uniform generation), libnuma with hwloc and the Silo and Topo submodules (NUMA-aware pools), GSL (comparison only); googletest for tests · C++17, CMake 3.9.2+ (GCC or Clang; MSVC branch exists in CMake but untested here) · Linux x86-64 (madvise, prebuilt x86-64 asmlib, -march=native); NUMA optional

**Vs siblings:** No other alias-table or weighted-sampling library is catalogued in this category; the siblings (SFMT, Randen, xoshiro and Philox SIMD generators, Ziggurat samplers) produce uniform or normal variates and can feed wrs's sample(u), so pick wrs for discrete weighted draws and pair it with whichever uniform generator wins for your platform. For GPU work, ByteHamster/alias-table-gpu (same group, CUDA, GPL-3.0) ports PSA to the GPU.

**Gotchas:**
- Default index type is uint32_t; a table with more than 2^32-1 items needs wrs::alias<size_t>, and construct() on a too-large or wrong-sized input only logs an error and returns, leaving the table unusable without throwing.
- CMake defaults to a Debug build; pass -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, and run git submodule update --init first.
- Benchmark fairness: benchmark/alias.cpp says the wrs tables must be switched to size_t indices for a fair GSL comparison, and the GSL query path draws from gsl_rng_mt19937 while wrs uses MKL or dSFMT block generation plus huge-page tables, so part of the reported query gain is the RNG and allocator, not the table layout.
- Move construction and move assignment are deleted on wrs::alias; copies deep-copy the table.

**Status:** Abandoned research code (last commit 2020-12-09, dissertation version; ESA version under the esa tag), GPL-3.0, usable as a reference or vendored into GPL projects on Linux x86-64.

[repo](https://github.com/lorenzhs/wrs) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lorenzhs/wrs)

#### sparse-and-solvers

##### Spectra  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++/Eigen implicitly restarted Arnoldi/Lanczos eigensolver; ARPACK redesign, modestly faster than ARPACK-NG in the author's dense tests.

**Beats:** ARPACK (ARPACK-NG) — Using the repo's benchmark program (10 random dense matrices per size, 10 replicates, k=10, ncv 20/30, tol 1e-10, both sides using the same Eigen mat-vec), Spectra v1.0.0 vs ARPACK-NG 3.7.0 on an Intel Core i7-11800H (Clang 11.1.0 -O2 -march=native, single-threaded OpenBLAS 0.3.15) gave symmetric speedups of about 1.3-1.5x at n=100 and 1.15-1.2x at n=1000. The general solver was about 1.0-1.6x. These figures are read from bar charts.

**Known shortcoming:** Gain only about 1.0-1.6x (read off plot images) on small dense random matrices; repo Makefile says g++ -O2, not the benchmark page's Clang 11.1.0 -O2 -march=native.

**Known shortcoming:** Margins only 1.0-1.6x, measured on small dense random matrices. Open issues: #165 shift-invert generalized solve with k=128 unfinished after 10 min vs SciPy eigsh ~9 s; #133 repeated eigenvalue missed; #126/#172 shift-invert results disputed.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It implements the same algorithm as ARPACK: implicitly restarted Arnoldi, or Lanczos for symmetric and Hermitian problems (Lehoucq-Sorensen, ARPACK Users' Guide). The speed comes from C++ templating over Eigen rather than Fortran reverse communication, so the user operator is called inline. It also has its own small-matrix kernels: TridiagQR with a deflation test, a dedicated UpperHessenbergSchur for the projected Hessenberg matrix (SIMD-accelerated in 1.0.1) and Givens-based UpperHessenbergQR. In the benchmark both sides use the same Eigen mat-vec, so the measured gap is the restart and projection machinery alone.

**Use it when:**
- C++ code already using Eigen that needs a few extreme eigenpairs of a large sparse or matrix-free operator (spectral clustering, PCA, graph Laplacians, vibration modes) without linking Fortran ARPACK.
- Symmetric problems: the author's benchmark shows the symmetric solver faster than ARPACK-NG in every tested case (about 1.15-1.5x on n=100 and n=1000 random matrices, k=10).
- Matrix-free operators, where you implement perform_op() and never form A.
- Complex Hermitian or complex general matrices (HermEigsSolver, complex GenEigsSolver since 1.1.0/1.2.0) inside a header-only dependency.
- Code that wraps the same engine in R (RSpectra) or Python and wants one C++ core.

**Skip it when:**
- Shift-and-invert generalized problems with many requested eigenvalues: open issue #165 reports a SymGEigsShiftSolver run with k=128 that did not finish in 10 minutes, where SciPy eigsh (ARPACK) took about 9 s. Open issues #126 and #172 report shift-invert results differing from expected or MATLAB values.
- Large k or full spectra: nev must be at most n-1, and issue #182 asks to lift this limit; use a dense eigensolver (LAPACK/Eigen SelfAdjointEigenSolver) instead.
- Multi-threaded eigensolves: only your operator and Eigen's own kernels can be parallel (multithreading is requested in open issue #185).
- When you need a big speedup over ARPACK: the measured gains are 1.0-1.6x, the general solver is described as almost identical to ARPACK, and the numbers come only from small dense random matrices.
- Clustered or repeated eigenvalues with a tight ncv: open issue #133 reports SymEigsSolver missing one copy of a repeated eigenvalue at k=20, ncv=50, which reappears at k=25.

**Integration:** header-only · Eigen 3 (header-only; the optional CMake install finds a system Eigen or downloads Eigen 3.4.0 through CPM). Your own sparse factorization (Eigen, CHOLMOD and so on) if you use shift-and-invert. · C++11 (required since 1.0.0); CMake 3.10+ only for the optional install and tests · any platform Eigen supports; open issue #177 reports ctest failures on Fedora s390x and #139 reports test eigenvalues differing between macOS and Linux

**Vs siblings:** No other eigensolver is catalogued in this category. Spectra complements the sparse direct solvers listed here (for example CKTSO, BaSpaCho or a CHOLMOD-based operator): one of them can supply the factorization behind a SymEigsShiftSolver operator.

**Gotchas:**
- The constructor needs nev < ncv <= n, and the docs advise ncv >= 2*nev. Too small an ncv slows convergence and can miss eigenvalues.
- Always check info() == CompInfo::Successful. compute() returns the number of converged eigenvalues, which can be fewer than requested. Issue #158 reports a silent failure on a 2x2 matrix.
- Version 1.0.0 (2021) broke the API (enum classes, selection rule passed to compute() instead of as a template parameter, operators passed by reference); see MIGRATION.md when updating older code.
- In shift-and-invert mode the selection rule applies to 1/(lambda - sigma), and the quality of your shift-solve operator decides both accuracy and speed.

**Status:** Active (1.2.0 released 2025-06-29, last commit 2026-07-04, 38 open issues), MPL-2.0 like Eigen, header-only and packaged in vcpkg and Conan, so it is easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/yixuan/spectra) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yixuan/spectra/gh-pages/performance.md)

##### PanguLU  `C`  `AGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Distributed MPI+CUDA sparse LU direct solver using regular 2D sparse blocks; reports up to 11.7-18x over SuperLU_DIST on 128 GPUs.

**Beats:** SuperLU_DIST — Per the SC'23 paper's abstract (paper body not opened, so matrices, SuperLU_DIST version and flags are unknown), PanguLU reached up to 11.70x over SuperLU_DIST on 128 NVIDIA A100s and up to 17.97x on 128 AMD MI50s, and scaled 47.51x and 74.84x over one GPU. These are best-case maxima from the 2023 code, not typical ratios. An independent 2025 paper (Hu et al.) implies about 2.2x over SuperLU_DIST on one A100 (derived from the 1.50x and 3.32x geometric means in its abstract).

**Known shortcoming:** SC'23 abstract (via search): 11.70x and 17.97x over SuperLU_DIST, which is not a listed baseline; paper unreadable here.

**Known shortcoming:** Numerical robustness: no partial pivoting; pivots below 1e-16 are replaced by +1e-16; no iterative refinement; MC64 optional and unavailable for complex. Open #5: residual ~10 on some matrices. Closed #2: one A100 2-10x slower than the paper (cage12 578.7 s), unexplained. Errors call exit(1). make.inc defaults to sm_61. Repo has no AMD backend although the paper used MI50.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Instead of supernodal or multifrontal layouts, the matrix is cut into equal nb x nb blocks that stay sparse, which avoids the extra fill a dense supernode stores, and the blocks are mapped 2D block-cyclically over a p x q process grid. Each block task (GETRF, TSTRF, GESSM, SSSSM) adaptively picks a sparse or dense BLAS kernel on CPU or GPU, and a synchronisation-free communication scheme lets ranks start tasks as soon as their inputs arrive instead of waiting at level barriers. Version 5.0 adds a task aggregator for numeric factorization and a smaller GPU memory layout.

**Use it when:**
- Large unsymmetric sparse systems whose factors outgrow one node, on an MPI cluster with one NVIDIA GPU per rank, where you would otherwise run SuperLU_DIST
- Matrices whose factors are still fairly sparse inside blocks, so sparse block kernels beat SuperLU_DIST's dense supernodal kernels (an independent 2025 study on one A100 found PanguLU about 2.2x faster than SuperLU_DIST in numeric factorization, geometric mean, derived from its abstract)
- Many right-hand sides with a fixed matrix: factor once with pangulu_gstrf, then call pangulu_gstrs repeatedly
- Complex-valued or single-precision systems on GPUs (all four value types are supported, chosen at build time)

**Skip it when:**
- Ill-conditioned or hard-to-pivot matrices: numeric factorization does no partial pivoting and silently replaces pivots smaller than 1e-16 with 1e-16, MC64 static pivoting is optional and unavailable for complex values, and there is no iterative refinement; open issue #5 (2025, unanswered) reports relative residuals around 10 for some matrices and kernels
- Single-GPU use where newer solvers exist: Caracal (SC25) reports up to 94x over PanguLU on one A100, and the structure-aware irregular blocking paper reports 1.50x over PanguLU
- Reproducing the paper's numbers out of the box: closed issue #2 measured 2-10x slower factorization than the paper on one A100 40GB (cage12: 578.7 s numeric, 7.3 GFLOP/s) with no maintainer explanation
- Proprietary or SaaS products that cannot accept AGPL-3.0, which also covers network use
- AMD GPUs with the current code: the SC'23 paper ran on MI50, but the repo ships only CPU and CUDA platform backends

**Integration:** static lib · MPI (tested MPICH 4.3.0), OpenMP, BLAS for CPU kernels (tested OpenBLAS 0.3.26), CUDA for GPU (tested 12.9), optional METIS (32-bit index build); MC64 is built in · C compiler with OpenMP (gcc), mpicc, nvcc and GNU make; you edit make.inc and examples/Makefile by hand (it builds both libpangulu.a and libpangulu.so) · Linux clusters, x86-64 CPU-only or NVIDIA GPU; make.inc defaults to -gencode arch=compute_61 (Pascal), so edit it for newer GPUs such as the A100 (sm_80)

**Vs siblings:** Pick PanguLU over CKTSO, GSS or RSLAB when you need a distributed, multi-node GPU LU and SuperLU_DIST is your reference. For single-node circuit matrices CKTSO targets KLU-class workloads, and for SPD systems a Cholesky solver such as BaSpaCho or the task-based CHOLMOD is the better fit.

**Gotchas:**
- On errors such as a null options pointer, nb = 0 or a value-type mismatch, the library calls exit(1) inside the solver rather than returning a status
- The process grid is p x q, where p is the largest divisor of the rank count at or below its square root, so a prime number of ranks gives a 1 x P grid
- Missing structural diagonal entries are filled with 1e-8 before factoring, which perturbs the matrix you passed in
- Block size nb strongly affects speed and must be tuned per matrix (the example uses -nb 10 on a toy matrix; init falls back to 256 only when nb is negative)

**Status:** Active research code (v5.0.0, latest commit 2026-06-25, 38 commits, 51 stars), but AGPL-3.0, with an unanswered accuracy report (issue #5) and an unanswered performance-gap report (issue #2), so validate residuals on your own matrices before adopting it.

[repo](https://github.com/SuperScientificSoftwareLaboratory/PanguLU) · [benchmark](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3581784.3607050)

##### QPALM  `C`  `LGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Sparse C solver for convex and nonconvex quadratic programs; lower runtime geometric mean than OSQP on Maros-Meszaros, but less reliable.

**Beats:** OSQP — In the third-party qpbenchmark v2.3.0 run (2024-09-07, prebuilt Python wheels qpalm 1.2.3 and osqp 0.6.7.post0 via qpsolvers, Intel Core i7-6500U, no compiler flags applicable), QPALM's shifted geometric-mean runtime on the 138 Maros-Meszaros problems was 3.6/4.8/3.4/2.2 versus OSQP's 12.7/16.1/52.8/51.9 at default/high/low/mid accuracy, with PIQP = 1.0. Its success rates were 55.8/25.4/31.2/31.2%, and failures reported as 'solved' are timed at face value rather than at the 1000 s limit.

**Known shortcoming:** Its 'solved' return codes are correct on only 34-63% of problems, and success is 25-31% at non-default tolerances (8-13% on the sparse subset); qpbenchmark charges the 1000 s limit only when no solution returns, so wrong fast answers count at their real runtime; QP solver vs OSQP (off the baseline list); fork of Benny44/QPALM_vLADEL.

**Known shortcoming:** qpbenchmark timed QPALM 1.2.3; 1.3.0 (2026-08-26) later fixed scaling of the initial dual guess, the dual objective, and the Fortran interface returning a scaled solution (#9). These fixes concern warm starts, dual-objective reporting and Fortran, not the cold-start path qpbenchmark times, so the tier stays B. Open #7: computing the dual cost fails when the Hessian is rank deficient, so the 'solved' status is unreliable there.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It is a proximal augmented Lagrangian method whose inner subproblems are solved with a semismooth Newton method and an exact line search (sorting breakpoints of a piecewise quadratic), so each outer iteration takes few, accurate steps instead of the many cheap ADMM steps OSQP takes. The Newton systems are solved with the bundled LADEL sparse LDL factorization (AMD ordering), choosing between the KKT system and a Schur complement, and updated by low-rank row updates and downdates when constraints enter or leave the active set instead of refactorizing. For nonconvex Q it estimates the minimum eigenvalue with LOBPCG and a Gershgorin bound to set the proximal term.

**Use it when:**
- Sparse convex QPs at default or moderate tolerances (around 1e-6 to 1e-3) where OSQP needs too many ADMM iterations; in qpbenchmark its runtime geometric mean is 3.6 vs OSQP 12.7 at default settings and 2.2 vs 51.9 at mid accuracy.
- Nonconvex QPs where a stationary point is acceptable (for example subproblems inside SQP or nonlinear MPC); the README states this scope and the code has a dedicated path (LOBPCG minimum-eigenvalue estimate, compiled in by default with QPALM_NONCONVEX).
- Sequences of related QPs (MPC, branch and bound) where warm starts, bound and vector updates and the optional dual-objective termination limit can be used.
- Projects that need the same solver from C, C++, Python, Julia, Matlab and Fortran, with prebuilt binaries for Linux, Windows and macOS on x86-64 and ARM64.

**Skip it when:**
- When a correct 'solved' status matters: in qpbenchmark v2.3.0 its solved return codes matched the tolerance check on only 57/63/34/37% of Maros-Meszaros problems (default/high/low/mid), against 96-100% for ProxQP and PIQP.
- High-accuracy solves (1e-9): success rate 25.4% vs OSQP 26.1% on the full set and 8% vs 13% on the sparse subset, and its duality-gap geometric mean (1237362.9) is the worst in the table.
- When the fastest robust convex QP solver is the goal: PIQP is 2-5x faster than QPALM in the same table and solves 73-97% of problems.
- Closed-source static linking without LGPL obligations: the core, LADEL and LOBPCG are LGPL-3.0.
- Dense small QPs: the solver is built around sparse LDL factorization; no dense path is documented in the files read.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake 3.23+), plus PyPI wheel, Julia package and Matlab zip · LADEL (bundled, LGPL-3.0, includes AMD ordering); bundled LOBPCG and LAPACK pieces; Eigen3 only for the C++ interface · C11 compiler with stdatomic.h (MSVC needs /experimental:c11atomics); C++17 for the C++ interface; CMake 3.23 · Portable C; binaries for Linux, Windows and macOS on x86-64 and ARM64, wheels also for ARMv6/ARMv7

**Vs siblings:** Pick QPALM over PIQP and ProxQP (ProxSuite) only when the QP may be nonconvex or you need its Fortran, Julia or Matlab bindings; for convex QPs PIQP is faster and far more reliable in the same independent benchmark, and ProxQP has much better solved-status correctness. Against the OSQP baseline QPALM wins on runtime at all four settings but is not more accurate at high tolerance.

**Gotchas:**
- The default eps_abs and eps_rel are 1e-4 and verbose output is on by default; set tolerances explicitly before comparing against another solver.
- Check residuals yourself rather than trusting QPALM_SOLVED: the independent benchmark found many 'solved' answers that fail the stated tolerance, and qpbenchmark charges no time-limit penalty for them, which flatters the runtime figure.
- Version 1.3.0 (2026-08-26) fixed scaling of the initial dual guess, residual recomputation on time or iteration limits, the dual objective and the Fortran interface's unscaled solution; the qpbenchmark numbers are from 1.2.3, before these fixes. Issue #9 (solution variables returned scaled on HS21) is closed, while issue #7 (dual cost computation fails when the Hessian is rank deficient) is still open.
- The C++ Solver returns a solution view that is only valid while the Solver object is alive and unchanged; copy x and y into vec_t to keep them.

**Status:** Actively maintained by KU Leuven's optimization group (version 1.3.0 released 2026-08-26 with scaling and dual-objective fixes; the original Benny44/QPALM_vLADEL repo is unmaintained); LGPL-3.0 with prebuilt C/C++/Fortran libraries and PyPI wheels, so linking it is easy but vendoring into a closed binary carries LGPL obligations.

[repo](https://github.com/kul-optec/QPALM) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qpsolvers/maros_meszaros_qpbenchmark/main/results/maros_meszaros.md)

### parsing-and-text

#### parser-generators-and-combinators

##### PAPAGENO (PArallel PArser GENeratOr)  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Bison-style generator that emits pthreads-parallel operator-precedence parsers, up to 5.5x faster than Flex+Bison on ARM.

**Beats:** GNU Bison + GNU Flex (sequential LALR(1) parser/lexer) — The paper (Barenghi et al., preprint for Science of Computer Programming) benchmarks the PAPAGENO-generated parallel lexer/parser against the authors' own sequential Flex+Bison LALR(1) reference parser, both built with gcc 4.9.1 -O3 -march=native, on a 16-core quad-Opteron 8378 server and a 4x-Cortex-A15 Odroid-XU ARM board, over real-world JSON (2.7KiB-75MiB) and Lua (7KiB-35MiB) inputs. It reports up to 5.5x speedup on the ARM board and a separate maximum 7x speedup for parallel lexing alone vs. sequential Flex (not vs. the full Flex+Bison pipeline); the 16-core server JSON comparison (Fig. 13b) is a 3D plot with no stated exact peak number against Flex+Bison.

**How:** Exploits the OPG property that the shift/reduce decision between two adjacent terminals depends only on a fixed precedence relation, not on global parse state, so the input can be split into chunks and reduced independently on separate POSIX threads with no wasted re-computation when recombining partial trees. Lexing can likewise be split into an independent parallel pass (test/JSON_parallel_lexer). The README states throughput scales close to linearly with thread count on JSON workloads.

**Use it when:**
- Files large enough for parallelism to amortize thread overhead (paper shows real gains mainly on multi-MB inputs, up to 75MiB JSON / 35MiB Lua)
- A grammar that is already an Operator Precedence Grammar, or small enough to convert without exploding the rule set (e.g. arithmetic expressions, JSON)
- Batch/offline C parsing on multi-core x86_64 servers or ARM big.LITTLE boards where lexing/parsing is a proven bottleneck
- You can vendor and maintain generated C source yourself (Python 2.x generator, no upstream releases since 2015)

**Skip it when:**
- General LALR(1) or ambiguous/context-free grammars: converting real-world Lua to OPG+Fischer-normal-form blew productions up from 144 to 8547 plus required manual lexer transforms
- Small or streaming inputs (KB-scale) — paper reports negligible or negative speedup there from thread migration/NUMA overhead
- Anywhere you need Bison's GLR mode or ANTLR-style handling of ambiguous grammars — OPG is a strict LALR(1) subset
- Projects needing an actively maintained tool or Python 3 support: last commit 2015-04-20, generator is Python 2.x only, one unresolved GitHub issue
