- Many-core builds or very large sets. Most build time goes to BuRR, which has no parallel implementation, so the partitioned build scaled poorly on a 64-core AMD machine. Construction is in-memory only (an external-memory build is only sketched in the paper), and the paper tested up to 2x10^8 keys.
- Tiny sets, or MSVC/Windows/macOS targets. Below about 1M keys it no longer dominates (paper Appendix B). The 4-key README example segfaulted until a Nov 2024 fix (issue #4). CI covers only Linux GCC/Clang.

**Integration:** header-only API (CMake INTERFACE target) that links a compiled shared lib (SimpleRibbon, a BuRR wrapper); consumed via add_subdirectory with recursive git submodules · SimpleRibbon/BuRR (Apache-2.0, built as a shared lib), ips2ra, ByteHamster/Util (GPL-3.0; Elias-Fano on pasta-bit-vector, MurmurHash64) and tlx, all as git submodules; the CI also installs libtbb-dev · C++20, CMake 3.25+; CI tests GCC 11-14 and Clang 16-18 · Linux x86-64 in CI; the paper also ran it on an AMD Ryzen 3950X and an ARM Neoverse-N1. Uses GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_prefetch, __uint128_t). Windows/macOS/MSVC are not documented. -march=native is added only when SicHash is the top-level CMake project

**Vs siblings:** Pick SicHash over PTHash when build time matters at about 2 bits/key. The thesis measured 148-180 vs 268 ns/key at 100M keys, and the paper shows 3.27 vs 0.61 MKeys/s at 1.75 bits/key; the cost is slower lookups (about 65 vs 35-60 ns/query). Pick it over the RecSplit family (RecSplit, SIMDRecSplit, ShockHash) when query latency matters more than 0.3-0.7 extra bits/key: 64-66 vs 118-157 ns/query at 2.08-2.20 vs 1.49-1.81 bits/key.

**Gotchas:**
- Construction prints progress to std::cout by default; set `config.silent = true`. `spaceUsage()` on a minimal SicHash<true> always prints a 'Remap space' line.
- Keys must be std::string (hashed internally with MurmurHash64) or values you have already hashed. Raw integers passed to the uint64_t constructor trip a sanity check that throws invalid_argument. Every key collapses to one 64-bit hash, and there is no duplicate-key check, so duplicates or 64-bit collisions are not detected; the behavior is not documented.
- A loadFactor of 0.999 or more throws; use SicHash<true> to get a minimal PHF. For minimal PHFs, pick the minimalFanoLowerBits template argument (3/4/5 for load factor <0.89/<0.94/<0.97). Thresholds that are too aggressive throw logic_error after 65,536 seed retries in one bucket.
- A SicHash object can be neither copied nor moved: its BuRR members are move-only, it has a user-declared destructor and it owns a raw Elias-Fano pointer. Hold it through a pointer, as the author's MPHF-Experiments wrapper does. `writeTo()` dumps raw structs, and the format tag is checked only by assert(), so files are not portable across compilers or endianness and are not validated in release builds.

**Status:** The author still maintains it: last commit 2025-09-30, CI on GCC 11-14 and Clang 16-18, no open issues. Commits are sporadic, it has 20 stars, and GPL-3.0 plus the submodule-based CMake build limit vendoring to GPL-compatible projects.

[repo](https://github.com/ByteHamster/SicHash) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.01560)

##### SimdRecSplit / GpuRecSplit  `C++`  `GPL-3.0 WITH GCC-exception-3.1`  `active`  `Tier A`

SIMD, multicore and GPU construction of RecSplit minimal perfect hashes; single-threaded builds about 4x faster than BBHash at similar space.

**Beats:** BBHash — Paper Table 3 (arXiv 2212.09562v2) measures 10M random strings of length 10-50, single-threaded, with GCC 11.2 -O3 -march=native on an AVX-512 Intel i7-11700. SIMDRecSplit l=5,b=5 builds at 49 ns/key and 2.96 bits/key, against BBHash gamma=1.0 at 208 ns/key and 3.059 bits/key (about 4.2x, derived); BBHash gamma=5.0 matches the speed but needs 6.871 bits/key. The 50x/239x/5438x speedups over original RecSplit (SIMD 1 thread, 16 threads, RTX 3090) come from Table 1 (l=18, b=50, 5M random 128-bit keys), and there is no std baseline.

**How:** Rotation fitting splits a leaf's keys into two halves by one hash bit, then cyclically rotates one half's bit mask to fill the other's holes, so one hash evaluation tests up to m candidate bijections (up to 3x faster construction per the paper). The brute-force seed search is vectorized: each AVX2/AVX-512 lane (Vector Class Library) tests a different seed, and splitting counts use packed 8-bit counters. Independent buckets are radix-sorted with IPS2Ra and split across threads. On the GPU, each leaf or split runs as a CUDA thread block, and same-shaped trees are batched into one kernel.

**Use it when:**
- Static sets of millions of string keys on x86-64 with AVX2/AVX-512, when build time and space both matter (1.81 bits/key at 107 ns/key build, single-threaded, 10M keys).
- Very compact MPHFs (about 1.56-1.7 bits/key) that original RecSplit takes hours to build. For 5M keys at 1.56 bits/key, the paper reports about 2 minutes on the CPU and 5 s on an RTX 3090, against 1.5 hours for the original code.
- Multi-core offline builds: buckets are split across threads without changing the query layout, and the paper shows good scaling on 8-core and 64-core machines.
- You have an NVIDIA GPU and want the most space-efficient settings: GPURecSplit reaches 1.496 bits/key with l=24.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency-bound lookups: queries take 71-110 ns/key, against 20-35 ns for PTHash and 36-51 ns for BBHash (Table 3). Queries run on the CPU and walk a Golomb-Rice-coded tree.
- Non-x86 CPUs, or CPUs without AVX2/AVX-512. SIMDRecSplit is x86-only and falls back to slow emulated SIMD without AVX2. On an AVX2-only AMD EPYC, sequential SIMDRecSplit took 4.6x longer than on the AVX-512 Intel machine. On ARM, only the non-SIMD variant reportedly builds, and CI does not test it.
- Dynamic key sets, or input with possible duplicate keys. The structure is static, and duplicate keys make construction never return.
- Projects that cannot take GPL-3.0 (even with the GCC Runtime Library Exception), or that must ship portable binaries, because the CMake targets force -march=native onto consumers.
- GPURecSplit in a process that uses CUDA for other work (see gotchas). The GPU also gains little for space-inefficient settings, where host-device transfers dominate.

**Integration:** shared lib: header-only class templates, plus one small CMake-built shared library (Ips2raRecSplitSorter) that every target links. Consume it via git clone --recursive and add_subdirectory. · Git submodules: sux (ByteHamster fork), gcem, tlx, ips2ra, and vectorclass (SIMD only). System: Intel TBB, pthread and libatomic. The CUDA toolkit is needed for GPURecSplit. · C++20 and CMake 3.25+. CI uses GCC 10-13 on Ubuntu 24.04. The paper used GCC 11.2 and CUDA 11, and a Jan 2026 commit fixes a newer nvcc. · SIMDRecSplit: x86-64 only; the target needs SSE4.2, and full speed needs AVX2 or AVX-512 (tuned for AVX-512). GPURecSplit: NVIDIA GPU for construction, CPU for queries. Portable variant: reportedly builds on ARM. CI covers Linux only.

**Vs siblings:** On 10M string keys it builds 1.81 bits/key in 107 ns/key, against SicHash's 2.41 bits in 119 ns and PTHash's 3.31 bits in 199 ns, and it builds Sux RecSplit's ~1.8 bits/key 6.6x faster with about 7% slower lookups. Pick PTHash instead when lookups dominate (20-35 vs 71-110 ns), and ShockHash (1.489 bits/key, per the author) for space near the 1.44-bit bound.

**Gotchas:**
- Duplicate keys make the constructor loop forever, so deduplicate first. Leaf size is capped at 24, and the code comments say bucket size works with high probability only up to an average of about 2000 (MAX_BUCKET_SIZE=3000).
- The CMake targets set -march=native and -DSIMD as INTERFACE options, so your own target is compiled for the build machine's CPU.
- GPURecSplit calls cudaDeviceReset() at the end of construction and exit() on any CUDA error, which destroys other CUDA state in the process or the process itself.
- The output is not interchangeable. The functions differ from Sux RecSplit, and the portable variant differs from SIMD/GPU (a test checks those two for equivalence). Serialization is a raw native binary stream that checks only the leaf size.

**Status:** Active research code from KIT (last commit 2026-01-04 fixes nvcc compatibility; CI on GCC 10-13; 0 open issues, 16 stars), copyable as a git submodule plus add_subdirectory under GPLv3 with the GCC Runtime Library Exception, the same terms as libstdc++.

[repo](https://github.com/ByteHamster/GpuRecSplit) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09562)

##### MorphisHash  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Minimal perfect hash function that removes ShockHash's redundant cycle-orientation bits: 1.501 vs 1.523 bits/key at equal build time.

**Beats:** ShockHash — In the MPHF-Experiments harness (std::string keys) on 100M keys on an Intel Core i7-11700, bipartite MorphisHash-RS (n=52, b=n-4) measured 1.501 bits/key, 137 ns/query and 6,669 ns/key build vs bipartite ShockHash-RS (n=66) at 1.523 bits/key, 147 ns and 7,186 ns/key. At an equal 1.489 bits/key, it built in 8,085 vs 172,738 ns/key. The paper does not state the compiler or flags (the CMake default is Release with -march=native), and there is no std:: or CMPH baseline. The abstract's '20x less overhead' applies to one unpartitioned base case (under 0.1 vs about 2 bits total at b=n-6, with about 4x more seed tests), not to the bits/key of a full MPHF.

**How:** The gain is in space, not speed. As in bipartite ShockHash, each key gets two candidate positions, and a seed search samples random graphs until the graph is a pseudoforest, which can be oriented into a bijection. ShockHash then stores n bits of orientation in a retrieval structure and wastes about one bit per cycle, because every cycle has two valid orientations. MorphisHash writes the valid orientations as a GF(2) linear system Ay = d, substitutes a smaller b-bit retrieval vector (y = Hx, b < n), and solves AHx = d with Gaussian elimination only for seeds that pass the pseudoforest filter. The paper proves this saves Θ(ln n) bits per base case in expectation; a query reads the seed and the b-bit vector, takes the parity of a masked 128-bit hash and picks one of the two candidates.

**Use it when:**
- Static key sets that are built once and queried many times, where the size of the MPHF matters most (for example compressed indexes or k-mer tools), and single-core build costs of about 6-8 microseconds per key are acceptable.
- You want the space-optimized RecSplit-style trade-off. On 100M keys, MorphisHash-RS (n=52, ws=4) gives 1.501 bits/key with 137 ns queries and a 6,669 ns/key build, about 0.02 bits/key less than bipartite ShockHash-RS at the same build time.
- You need ShockHash-RS space (1.489 bits/key) without its build time: MorphisHash-RS builds at 8,085 ns/key vs 172,738 ns/key, about 21x faster, with similar queries (139 vs 131 ns).
- You want queries around 75 ns at about 1.54 bits/key: MorphisHash-Flat (n=88, ws=2) gives 1.541 bits/key vs 1.554 for bipartite ShockHash-Flat at the same query time.
- Your platform is Linux x86-64 with GCC 11-13 and CMake subprojects, and a GPL-3.0 (plus GCC Runtime Library Exception) dependency is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Space is the only priority: in the same Table 1, Consensus-RS reaches 1.447 bits/key at a similar build cost (6,733 ns/key), but its queries are slower (222 ns vs 137 ns).
- Query latency is the priority: PHOBIC answers in 49 ns vs 137 ns for MorphisHash-RS, at 1.749 bits/key.
- The key set changes or you need membership tests: there is no insert or delete, and non-member keys map to arbitrary valid slots unless you store keys or fingerprints yourself.
- You need a maintained production library: there is no save/load serialization API in the headers and no README usage docs; the repo has 3 stars, and the code last changed in April 2025.
- Your toolchain is MSVC or non-GCC: the code needs libstdc++ <experimental/simd>, __uint128_t, __builtin_parityll and glibc's __attribute_noinline__ macro, and CI only covers GCC 11, 12 and 13 on Ubuntu 24.04.

**Integration:** shared lib — header templates plus two CMake-built shared libraries (MorphisHash2Precompiled, Ips2raMorphisHashSorter); consume via add_subdirectory and link the MorphisHash target · sux, tlx, ips2ra (links Intel TBB, pthread and libatomic) and ByteHamster/Util (pulls in pasta bit_vector); all are git submodules except TBB, which must be installed · C++20, CMake 3.25+, GCC 11+ (CI tests GCC 11, 12 and 13) · x86-64 Linux is tested (paper uses an Intel Core i7-11700; top-level Release builds use -march=native). The GCC/glibc-specific code rules out MSVC. Other architectures are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick MorphisHash over ShockHash when you want ShockHash-RS space at about 1/21 of its build time, or slightly less space at the same build time. Pick ConsensusRecSplit instead when the last 0.05 bits/key matters more than queries 1.6x slower (1.447 bits/key, 222 ns vs 137 ns in the same table), and PTHash/PHOBIC or PtrHash when queries must be under about 50 ns and 1.7-3 bits/key is acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- Input keys must be distinct, and neither constructor checks this. Identical keys hash identically under every seed, so the while (true) seed search can never find a bijection.
- The library writes to stdout during construction ('Skipped seed because of floating point inaccuracy' from the seed-pairing function). The precompiled base-case dispatcher prints to stderr and calls exit(1) for leaf sizes or widths that were not compiled in (leaf sizes up to 106 and up to 7 below each).
- MorphisHashFlat allocates its rank-select structure with a raw new and has no destructor or copy/move handling, so it leaks and copies share the pointer. Construct it in place, as MPHF-Experiments does with new.
- All tuning is compile-time and barely documented. The paper's Pareto picks are ws=4 (b=n-4) for RS and ws=2 for Flat. MorphisHashFlat's template order is <k, ws, extraSeedBits>, while the MPHF-Experiments wrapper orders it <l, eb, ws>.

**Status:** The repo is stale research code, a fork of ByteHamster/ShockHash: the code last changed 2025-04-08, the README 2025-07-03, and its only release is a 'zenodo' archive tag (2025-11-13). It ships ShockHash's GPLv3 COPYING plus COPYING.RUNTIME (GCC Runtime Library Exception), so it can be vendored at a pinned commit with submodules, but expect to fix build and API rough edges yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/stefanfred/MorphisHash) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10161)

#### ordered-maps-trees

##### Flat-Map-RB-Tree (dro::FlatMap)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Header-only flat red-black tree map/set in a vector; 1.4-1.9x faster than std::map at scale.

**Beats:** std::map — On gcc 14.2.1 with libstdc++, -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, on an isolcpus-pinned Intel Core i5-9300H (4 cores), dro::FlatMap beat std::map at 10,000,000 int32 elements: insert 622ns vs 855ns, find 551ns vs 774ns, erase 627ns vs 916ns (~1.4-1.9x across sizes); numbers are from the repo's committed benchmarks/results/*.txt, not chart-reading.

**How:** Storing nodes in a vector keeps the tree cache-contiguous and lets the implementation prefetch the next probed level during binary search on insert/erase, cutting cache misses versus a pointer-chasing red-black tree. Rotations swap node and child slots in place rather than relocating via pointers, and erase swaps the deleted key with the in-order successor then moves it to the vector's end instead of freeing/reallocating a node.

**Use it when:**
- Insert/find/erase-heavy workloads on int32-like keys where std::map's per-node allocation dominates, especially at 1M-10M elements (1.4-1.9x measured gain).
- You can pick a MaxSize index type (uint8_t-uint64_t) matching your expected element count for space efficiency.
- Keys/values are default-constructible and you don't need pointer/reference stability across inserts/erases.
- You want ordered iteration plus a map-like API without accepting flat_map's insert/erase cost.

**Skip it when:**
- Find-dominated workloads at large sizes: boost::flat_map find is faster than dro::FlatMap by 1M elements (134ns vs 234ns), and folly::heap_vector_map overtakes dro on find from ~100K elements.
- Code that holds iterators across modifying operations: every insert/erase/clear invalidates ALL iterators, not just erased ones.
- Long-lived containers with heavy erase churn: erased slots stay allocated until shrink_to_fit() or destruction, so memory can grow unbounded between compactions.
- Key/value types that aren't default-constructible.
- Production use requiring maturity: project is self-labeled Beta Testing with ~50% test coverage and has no issue-tracker history to gauge stability (issue tracker is empty).

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only: <vector>, <stdexcept>, <concepts>, <type_traits>, etc.) · C++20 per README; repo's own CMakeLists.txt builds with C++23 · not documented (no architecture-specific intrinsics in the header; no platform restrictions stated)

**Vs siblings:** Pick over boost::container::flat_set/flat_map when insert/erase throughput matters more than find at scale (boost::flat_map degrades sharply on insert/erase, e.g. 146,200ns at 1M vs dro's 283ns), but pick boost::flat_map instead if find dominates. Versus fast-containers or frozenca/BTree (larger, more mature B-tree alternatives with wider verified gains), dro::FlatMap is a smaller header-only option but is explicitly beta with ~50% test coverage.

**Gotchas:**
- All iterators are invalidated by any modifying operation (insert/erase/clear/swap), not just iterators to erased elements as in std::map.
- erase() does not free memory; call shrink_to_fit() or destroy the container to reclaim space from erased slots.
- Key and Value types must be default-constructible in addition to copy/move-assignable.
- The MaxSize template parameter (an integral type) bounds max_size() and throws std::runtime_error if the container grows past it.

**Status:** Stale: last commit 2024-11-16, GPL-3.0, and the project self-labels 'Beta Testing' with ~50% coverage — usable as a copyable single header, but treat as unmaintained and verify against current libstdc++ before relying on it.

[repo](https://github.com/drogalis/contiguous-rb-tree-map) · [benchmark](https://github.com/drogalis/contiguous-rb-tree-map/blob/main/README.md)

#### sorting

##### BlockQuicksort  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

In-place Quicksort using block-buffered Hoare partitioning to avoid branch mispredictions; ~88% more elements/s than GCC std::sort on random ints.

**Beats:** std::sort — On GCC 4.8.4 (-O3 -march=native) on an Intel Core i5-2500K (4 cores, Ubuntu 14.04.4), the optimized BlockQuicksort variant needs ~45 ns/element vs ~85 ns/element for the repo's bundled copy of GCC 4.7.2's std::sort at n=2^28 on random 32-bit ints (~88% more elements sorted per second); smaller but still positive gains hold on 10-dim Vector and 21-field Record comparators for the mo-sqrt(n), duplicate-check variant, and std::sort wins on sorted/nearly-sorted input.

**How:** partition.h's hoare_block_partition_* functions compare a BLOCKSIZE=128 chunk of elements against the pivot into small fixed-size index buffers first, then do the swaps in a second, branch-free loop, so the CPU's branch predictor never has to guess the per-element comparison outcome during the swap phase. Pivot selection samples a median of ~sqrt(n) elements (median.h), and the qsort_double_pivot_check main loop (quicksort.h) adds a check for duplicate-heavy partitions adapted from Elmasry/Katajainen/Stenmark's Tuned Quicksort, falling back to insertion sort/std::partial_sort at small sizes like libstdc++'s introsort.

**Use it when:**
- Sorting large (n in the hundreds of millions) arrays of random 32-bit ints where per-element comparison is cheap and branch mispredictions dominate cost — the paper's largest reported gain (~88%) is at n=2^28.
- Multi-field comparators (the paper's 10-dim Vector / 21-field Record benchmarks) where smaller but still positive gains hold for the mo-sqrt(n),dc variant.
- Batch/offline throughput-oriented sorts where an unstable, in-place sort is acceptable and you're willing to hand-integrate a research header into your own call sites.
- As a reference implementation or benchmarking baseline for new sequential sort research — it's already used as the 'closest sequential competitor' in the IPS4o paper.
- Random or otherwise non-sorted input distributions; the paper itself reports std::sort wins on sorted/nearly-sorted input.

**Skip it when:**
- Need stability (equal elements keep relative order) — not stable, no stable variant provided.
- Sorted or nearly-sorted input — the input record's own claim notes std::sort wins there.
- Want a true drop-in replacement for std::sort with no call-site changes — this exposes sort() under its own namespace, not an overload of std::sort.
- Production/commercial use needing an actively maintained, permissively-licensed dependency — repo abandoned since Nov 2021 with two issues open and unanswered since 2019, and it's GPL-3.0 (the branch-avoidance technique itself has since been reimplemented under more permissive licenses in pdqsort and PPQSort).
- Want to just include one clean header — mixing more than one *.h++ interface file in the same translation unit causes duplicate-template-definition compile errors (open issue #6, unresolved).

**Integration:** source-drop · none external; each *.h++ variant needs matching repo-internal headers (quicksort.h, partition.h, median.h, insertionsort.h, rotations.h) included alongside it · C++11 (repo makefile: g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -march=native; benchmarked with GCC 4.8.4) · x86-64 only benchmarked (-march=native, Intel Core i5-2500K); portable C++11 templates with no explicit SIMD intrinsics observed — the branch-avoidance win depends on the compiler auto-vectorizing/optimizing the small fixed-size block-classification loop, so results are compiler- and arch-dependent

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over Boost.Sort/IPS4o/LearnedSort/etc. only when you specifically want the original peer-reviewed (ESA 2016 / JEA 2019) branch-avoidance partitioner — e.g. reproducing or benchmarking against it as IPS4o did — since the technique itself is now available in actively maintained, permissively-licensed form in pdqsort and PPQSort; for production sequential sorting prefer fluxsort or a pdqsort-family library instead of this abandoned GPL-3.0 repo.

**Gotchas:**
- Including more than one *.h++ interface header in the same translation unit triggers 'redefinition of template' errors from median.h (issue #6, open since 2019).
- Release-flag builds compile with -DNDEBUG, so the assert() sanity checks scattered through partition.h are stripped in the benchmarked configuration.
- The README recommends only blocked_double_pivot_check_mosqrt.h++ and blocked_simple.h++ out of ~40 header variants; a user asked in issue #5 (2019, still open) for clearer guidance on which variant to actually use.
- BLOCKSIZE (128) and pivot-sample-size constants are compile-time #defines tuned for the paper's int/Vector/Record types on one CPU; other key types or hardware may need retuning.

**Status:** Abandoned since its last commit on 2021-11-29, with two open issues unanswered since 2019, but classified 'copyable' — the source is small enough to vendor directly if your project's license tolerates GPL-3.0.

[repo](https://github.com/weissan/BlockQuicksort) · [benchmark](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/opus/volltexte/2016/6389/pdf/LIPIcs-ESA-2016-38.pdf)

##### LearnedSort  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

CDF-model-based sort for numeric arrays, ~4x faster than std::sort on random data, ~15-20x on sorted/duplicate data.

**Beats:** std::sort — On 50M double-precision keys via Google Benchmark (GCC 9.3.0-10ubuntu2, CMake Release with -O3 -march=native -mavx, Intel Xeon Gold 6150), LearnedSort ran ~1080-1150ms vs std::sort's ~4850-5030ms (~4.2-4.6x) across Uniform, Exponential, Mixture-of-Gaussians, Zipf-0.75, and TwoDups, and ~50-60ms vs std::sort's ~750-1000ms (~15-20x) on Sorted, ReverseSorted, and Identical -- all read off the README's bar chart (plots/perf_charts.png), which prints no exact numeric labels.

**How:** Builds a two-layer 'recursive model index' (RMI): a root linear model plus, by default, 1000 leaf linear models trained on a 1% sample of the keys, which together approximate the empirical CDF. Each key's model-predicted CDF value picks one of ~1000 buckets directly (O(1) per key instead of O(log n) comparisons), the array is partitioned into those buckets in one pass, and each bucket is finished with std::sort/insertion sort. Separately, sort() first does a linear is_sorted/is_reverse_sorted check and returns immediately if it hits, which is why Sorted/ReverseSorted/Identical inputs are ~15-20x faster than std::sort -- that path bypasses the CDF model entirely.

**Use it when:**
- Large batches (tens of millions+) of primitive numeric keys (double/int/long) with no attached payload
- Data from a reasonably smooth/well-behaved distribution (uniform, exponential, Gaussian mixture, Zipfian, moderate duplicates) where the RMI's CDF approximation is accurate
- One-off or batch/offline sorts where the model-training cost amortizes over a large input, not per-call microsorts
- You can vendor a small header-only GPL-3.0 dependency and your project tolerates copyleft
- x86-64 Linux/GCC builds with AVX and -march=native, matching the environment this was actually benchmarked on

**Skip it when:**
- Sorting records/structs with payloads or string keys -- explicitly unsupported per the README's Limitations section
- Small inputs -- below roughly fanout x threshold (1000 x 100 = 100,000 elements by default) it just calls std::sort, so there's no upside
- GPL-3.0 is unacceptable for the target codebase -- heavier copyleft than most sibling sort libraries in this catalog
- Need active maintenance -- no commits since August 2021, all filed issues closed, unmaintained academic prototype
- Sorted, reverse-sorted, or all-duplicate inputs where you want a general-purpose winner -- the project's own chart shows IS4o matching or beating LearnedSort there

**Integration:** header-only · none for the sort itself (STL only, include/learned_sort.h + rmi.h + utils.h); the repo's benchmark/test harness additionally pulls in Google Benchmark, Google Test, and several third-party sort implementations, but those aren't needed to call learned_sort::sort · C++20 (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20); benchmarked with GCC 9.3.0-10ubuntu2 · Only tested on Linux (RHEL 7, Ubuntu 20.04); Release flags include -march=native -mavx, so x86-64 with AVX is assumed. A Windows/MinGW-w64 GCC10 user hit a correctness bug (issue #16), since fixed

**Vs siblings:** Pick LearnedSort over IPS4o/BlockQuicksort/x86-simd-sort/radix_sort when you have large batches (10M+) of doubles or ints from a smooth distribution and accept GPL-3.0 plus an unmaintained codebase for the ~4x win; for sorted/duplicate-heavy or adversarial data, or if you need ongoing support, IS4o matches or beats it on those inputs per LearnedSort's own benchmark chart.

**Gotchas:**
- Automatically short-circuits to std::sort for inputs at or below ~fanout*threshold elements (100,000 by default) or when RMI training fails, so the learned path silently never runs on small inputs
- The huge Sorted/ReverseSorted speedups come from an explicit is_sorted()/is_reverse_sorted() linear-scan pre-check with early return, not from the CDF model doing work
- Historically had several correctness bugs specific to integer key types (slope underflow, int-division in RMI training, failures with many repeated keys) -- all filed as issues and fixed via PRs by mid-2021, but there's been no activity since to catch anything similar
- No payload/tuple or string-key support (README 'Limitations'); only bare numeric arrays are sortable

**Status:** Abandoned academic prototype: no commits since August 2021 and every filed issue is closed with no further activity, but it's a small header-only, GPL-3.0 library, so it's easy to vendor and freeze at the last known-good GCC 9/10 toolchain.

[repo](https://github.com/anikristo/LearnedSort) · [benchmark](https://github.com/anikristo/LearnedSort/blob/master/plots/perf_charts.png)

### storage-and-data

#### columnar-analytics

##### data.table (R)  `C`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

R's in-memory data.frame replacement with C/OpenMP radix grouping and joins; ~3-4x faster than pandas on db-benchmark groupby.

**Beats:** pandas — On db-benchmark (DuckDB Labs, batch 2025-02-10, AWS c6id.metal: Xeon Platinum 8375C, 128 cores, 250GB), data.table 1.16.99 dev with setDTthreads(0) against pandas 2.2.3 (pyarrow CSV reader, categorical ids) on 100M rows and 100 groups: 'sum v1 by id1' took 0.456-0.524s vs 1.525-1.528s (3.3x), and all 10 groupby questions were 4.2x faster by geometric mean (9/10 wins), recomputed from time.csv. No compiler or flags are published, and the 1B-row out-of-memory gap belongs to the original 125GB H2O node: on c6id.metal, pandas 2.2.2 finished 9-10 of 10 1B-row questions in 2024 (q1 ~17.2s vs data.table 5.1s in a later batch).

**Known shortcoming:** R, not C++; evidence is the H2O/DuckDB Labs db-benchmark (last H2O run 2021-06; ~3.3x vs pandas 2.2.3 on the DuckDB Labs fork).

**Known shortcoming:** At 1e7 rows with K=2 the lead drops to 1.65x; loses q7 (max-min not GForce-optimized in CRAN <=1.18.6.1). Not the fastest: DuckDB is ~9.8x and Polars ~2.3x faster on shared questions. Max 2^31-1 rows (#3957); default uses 50% of CPUs while the benchmark used all 128; GForce int64 sum with NA gave silent wrong results until 1.18.2.1 (#7571). R only; numbers from dev builds.

**How:** Ordering and grouping use forder.c, a parallel MSD byte-wise radix sort built on Terdiman/Herf float twiddling; it skips unused byte buckets, packs compressed keys across byte boundaries and splits skewed groups in parallel (an earlier version became base R's radix sort). 'GForce' rewrites simple j expressions (sum, mean, min, max, median, var, sd, prod, first, last, head, tail, .N) into C kernels (gsumm.c) that scatter rows into per-thread batches keyed by the high and low 16-bit halves of the group id and aggregate them in parallel, with no R evaluation per group. Joins are multi-column binary searches over sorted keys (bmerge.c), and := writes columns in place with no copy.

**Use it when:**
- You work in R and run grouped aggregations over roughly 10M to 1B+ in-memory rows. On db-benchmark it was 2.4-5.1x faster than pandas by geometric mean per dataset, and joins were 4.9-6.4x faster.
- Time-series or interval work that needs rolling (last observation carried forward, or nearest), non-equi or overlap-range joins, which pandas covers only partly (merge_asof).
- Memory-constrained pipelines where in-place column updates (:=, set*) avoid the copies that data.frame or dplyr would make.
- Production R code that needs a stable dependency: it depends on base R only, supports back to R 3.5.0 (2018), and keeps a careful API lifecycle.
- Fast CSV ingest and export via fread/fwrite (memory-mapped, multithreaded), even if the rest of your stack is not data.table.

**Skip it when:**
- Your stack is Python. There is no drop-in path from pandas, and the fastest single-node engines are elsewhere. On the same c6id.metal machine type (different batches), DuckDB was ~9.8x and Polars ~2.3x faster than data.table by geometric mean over the 6 groupby questions they share on 100M rows.
- Tables over 2^31-1 rows. There is no long-vector support (issue #3957, open since 2019), and fread can build a larger table that then fails on print or subset (#7438).
- j expressions that GForce cannot rewrite, such as arbitrary R functions or combined expressions, especially with many groups. These run single-threaded R code per group (#5200). It is the one db-benchmark groupby question where pandas wins: max(v1)-min(v2) by id3, 5.72s vs 5.04s.
- Many tiny queries in a loop. The R-level dispatch overhead of [.data.table can dominate on small inputs (#5636, #5650 report single-column/single-row subsets far slower than base R). At 10M rows with 2 id1 groups, the lead over pandas shrinks to 1.65x geomean and q1 is roughly a tie.
- Larger-than-RAM data. It is purely in-memory with no out-of-core or streaming execution.

**Integration:** module · none beyond base R (Imports only the base packages methods, stats, utils); OpenMP optional at build time · R >= 3.5.0 plus a C compiler to build from source (CRAN ships binaries); OpenMP needed for multithreading, and Apple clang lacks the runtime (install libomp or use LLVM/GCC per the Installation wiki) · any platform R/CRAN supports (Linux, macOS, Windows; x86-64 and arm64). Without OpenMP it runs single-threaded.

**Vs siblings:** Among catalogued pandas-beaters, pick data.table when you are in R and want an in-memory dataframe with ordered, rolling and non-equi joins and in-place updates, on CPU only. Pick chDB (embedded ClickHouse SQL) or cuDF.pandas (needs an NVIDIA GPU) to stay in Python, and DataFusion if you want an embeddable SQL engine; on db-benchmark DataFusion was ~6.9x faster than data.table on the shared groupby questions.

**Gotchas:**
- GForce only recognises its listed functions used standalone in j. In CRAN releases through 1.18.6.1, max(x) - min(x) is not optimised and falls back to per-group R evaluation. The unreleased 1.18.99 NEWS says arithmetic on GForce calls and type conversions such as sum(as.numeric(x)) now optimise.
- Default threads are 50% of logical CPUs. The benchmark called setDTthreads(0L), all 128 logical CPUs, so out-of-the-box runs on a big box use half the threads the published numbers used.
- := and set* modify in place, so any other variable that shares the table sees the change (use copy()). data.table sorts strings in C locale, which can differ from base R's order().
- Correctness regression: grouped sum() on an integer64 column containing NA gave silently wrong results under GForce until the fix in 1.18.2.1 (Jan 2026, #7571). Use 1.18.2.1 or later.

**Status:** Actively maintained (CRAN 1.18.6.1 published 2026-08-24, master commit 2026-09-10, NumFOCUS-sponsored), MPL-2.0; install from CRAN, though the benchmark numbers come from unreleased dev builds and pandas has not been re-run since Feb 2025.

[repo](https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table) · [benchmark](https://duckdblabs.github.io/db-benchmark/ (current DuckDB Labs continuation, report generated 2026-08-17; raw timings in https://github.com/duckdblabs/db-benchmark/blob/main/time.csv); original 2021 H2O run: https://h2oai.github.io/db-benchmark/)

#### embedded-kv

##### ArceKV (ElasticLSM + Arce)  `C++`  `GPL-2.0 (GitHub-detected; repo is a modified RocksDB tree that ships both LICENSE.Apache and LICENSE.leveldb, matching RocksDB's dual Apache-2.0/GPL-2.0 licensing)`  `active`  `Tier B`

RocksDB fork whose workload-driven compaction and write-stall policy (Arce) beats RocksDB leveling when read/write mixes shift.

**Beats:** RocksDB — In PVLDB 19(5):958-972 (2026), on an i9-13900K with 128 GB RAM capped to 75 GiB, NVMe/ext4, one flush and one compaction thread, and two 245.76M-operation compound workloads, ArceKV's average throughput was 2.00x and 1.41x that of 1-Leveling (RocksDB's default style, reimplemented on the RocksDB-based Moose framework) and 2.17x-2.92x that of Tiering and LazyLeveling; no compiler or flags are stated, and the abstract's '~3x' is measured against the slowest baseline. The prod README's own test (tmpfs, one thread, point reads plus inserts, uniform keys, 64 MB memtable, no compression, compared against RocksDB 9.5 leveled compaction with dynamic level bytes off) shows 2.87x lower total time at 10% reads, shrinking to 1.09x at 90%.

**Known shortcoming:** The default branch (prod) is an in-memory TikTok variant that does not match the paper; the on-disk code on the dev branch shows only 1.41x runtime. Paper gives no compiler or flags; venue is PVLDB 19(5) 2026.

**Known shortcoming:** Prod branch: the compaction controller is a raw pointer with a detached thread capturing 'this' (use-after-free if deleted); DB::Open blocks polling for the first state; compactioner is read without a null check; a README cmake typo gives a Debug build. Dev branch: a null controller creates a new default one per pick, running a grid search under the DB mutex; omp_set_num_threads(16) is process-wide.

**Known shortcoming:** The workload mix is supplied by the caller, not measured; the paper's Eigen SIMD and online statistics modules are absent from both branches; single compaction stream only. The abstract's ~3x is vs the slowest baseline; on disk (dev) insert latency is worse and compaction writes rise 54%.

**How:** Each candidate compaction gets an 'effectiveness score': M times its long-term benefit (runs removed x (range + FPR x point) lookup cost) minus a short-term penalty for the reads slowed and writes stalled while it runs. Only non-dominated candidates can win, meaning none removes more runs in less time. Write stalls are decoupled from level shape: in the prod code, writes slow once the count reaches a threshold c and stop at 4c. A background simulation over a windowed cost model (one window = memtable size / entry size updates) grid-searches (M, c) on 16 OpenMP threads and reruns when the average run count drifts more than 10%. In read-heavy phases this yields multi-level merges that cut runs faster than Leveling; in write-heavy phases it defers compaction more than Tiering.

**Use it when:**
- Reproducing or extending workload-aware LSM compaction research (against Moose, Ruskey, CAMAL, LazyLeveling) on a RocksDB code base with ~1 KB values, as in the paper (24 B keys, 1000 B values).
- Read/write mixes that shift over time (for example, write-heavy ingest followed by read-heavy serving), where you know or can measure the mix and pass it to the controller.
- Write-heavy to balanced phases where leveled RocksDB is stall-bound. The prod README's tmpfs table shows the largest gains at 10-40% reads (2.87x to 1.39x lower total time), mostly on the write side: 183.7 s vs 702.7 s of write latency at 10% reads.
- In-memory or tmpfs single-column-family stores with one compaction stream, which is the setup the prod branch was adapted to (a TikTok recommendation service) and the setup both repo harnesses test.
- Linux x86-64 with GCC and OpenMP available; the paper and README results are from an i9-13900K on Ubuntu 22.04.

**Skip it when:**
- Production systems that need a supported RocksDB: 1 star, no releases, and the default branch says it is not a faithful implementation of the paper.
- Steady read-dominated workloads. At 90% reads the prod gain is about 9% (438 s vs 479 s), and the paper shows ArceKV trailing 1-Leveling and Leveling right after an abrupt write-to-read shift (workload B to D).
- On-disk stores sensitive to insert latency or SSD wear. The dev README's on-disk run has higher insert latency (2.45 us vs 2.15 us) and 54% more compaction writes (426 GB vs 276 GB) than leveled compaction.
- Setups that rely on parallel compactions. Both branches assume one compaction decision stream: dev logs a warning when max_background_jobs or max_background_compactions is above 1 ('may lead to unstable run indexing'), and the paper's evaluation used one compaction thread.
- Workloads that need range filters or an up-to-date upstream: prod removed the range-filter policy and is pinned to RocksDB 9.5.

**Integration:** static lib (a full RocksDB source fork built with CMake; it replaces librocksdb instead of linking beside it) · prod: gflags, OpenMP (REQUIRED in CMakeLists; <omp.h> is included from a public header), and the grafite git submodule (SSH URL git@github.com:marcocosta97/grafite.git, pulling sux and sdsl-lite headers) included by table/block_based/filter_policy_internal.h. The tools/arce_bench harness also links TBB. dev: gflags, with OpenMP optional (WITH_OPENMP=ON by default, falls back to serial) and no submodules. RocksDB's usual optional compression libraries apply to both. · prod: C++17 (RocksDB 9.5 base), CMake 3.10+. dev: C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20, RocksDB 11.2 base). Compiler versions are not documented beyond 'gcc/g++'. · Tested only on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 22.04, i9-13900K). Other RocksDB platforms are not documented, and prod will not build on a toolchain without OpenMP.

**Vs siblings:** Pick ArceKV over Titan or DobLIX when the problem is compaction and write-stall policy under a read/write mix that changes over time with ~1 KB values: Titan targets large values through key-value separation, and DobLIX speeds up SST index lookups but gains only 1.04x on write-heavy loads. If you can leave RocksDB's format entirely and want bigger raw write gains from a maintained engine, pick SplinterDB, KVell or F2 instead.

**Gotchas:**
- prod: the AdaptiveCompactionController is a raw pointer in Options that the README example allocates with new and never frees. Its constructor spawns a detached thread that captures this and loops with 5 s sleeps, so deleting the controller while that thread is alive is a use-after-free. DB::Open also blocks in find_first_mc_when_ready(), polling once a second until the first tree state appears, and prints timings to stdout.
- prod: ColumnFamilyData::RecalculateWriteStallConditions (db/column_family.cc) reads comp_controller->compactioner without a null check, so column families that do not use the dynamic style depend on the optimizer removing that dead load. The stall check also compares the L0 file count against c and 4c, while the simulation models total runs. The README's cmake line '-CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release' is a typo; use -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, because RocksDB's CMakeLists makes a git checkout a Debug build by default.
- dev: if arce_compaction_controller is null, PickCompaction builds a fresh default controller on every call, so the (M, c) grid search reruns on every pick with a default update-only workload. Even with a controller, the search runs inside PickCompaction (which RocksDB calls with the DB mutex held), and both branches call omp_set_num_threads(16), which changes the OpenMP thread count for the whole process.
- The library does not measure the workload mix. You pass range/update/point proportions (prod: once, at construction; dev: via SetWorkloadProportions, which the dev harness calls at each phase change). The paper's online workload-statistics module and Eigen/SIMD score vectorization are not present in either branch.

**Status:** An active research artifact (last push 2026-04-29, 1 star, 0 issues, no releases), dual-licensed GPLv2/Apache-2.0 like RocksDB; using it means building the whole fork, with prod as the in-memory TikTok adaptation and dev as the on-disk port on RocksDB 11.2.

[repo](https://github.com/NTU-Siqiang-Group/ArceKV) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03565 (PVLDB 19(5): 958-972, 2026; https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol19/p958-liu.pdf))

##### SpanDB  `C++`  `GPL-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Modified RocksDB 6.x that writes WAL and top LSM levels to raw SPDK NVMe; up to 8.8x write throughput.

**Beats:** RocksDB — Per the FAST'21 paper, on a 2x20-core Xeon Gold 6248 server (CentOS 7.7) using SATA RAID5, P4510, P4610 and Optane P4800X drives as capacity/speed pairs, SpanDB beat vanilla RocksDB v6.5.1, which also wrote its WAL to the fast disk but through ext4. On a 512GB database of 1KB values with 20M Zipfian operations it was 7.6-8.8x faster on all-write YCSB, 2.6-4.0x on YCSB-A (1.7-2.4x uniform) and 1.03-1.66x on read-heavy B/E, with up to 50.3% more on LinkBench. Tests used sync WAL and no compression; compiler and flags are not stated, and the LinkBench driver is not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** The 8.8x is YCSB all-write only; read-heavy workloads gain 1.03-1.66x. Baseline RocksDB 6.5.1 on 2x Xeon Gold 6248; no compiler/flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Gains need the new Async* API, SPDK, root, hugepages and a whole NVMe drive per process, so it is only a partial drop-in. Spinning pinned cores use 94.5% vs 63.7% CPU. Frozen on RocksDB 6.x and SPDK v20.01 (5 commits, last 2023-08); open issues: warmup hang (#6), SPDK link failure (#9), core-count abort (#12); OOM report closed without reply (#13). The LinkBench driver is not in the repo.

**How:** WAL writes skip ext4 and use SPDK user-space polled NVMe I/O. The paper measured ext4 small-write latency at 6.8-12.4x SPDK's. RocksDB's single-leader group commit is replaced by 1-3 dedicated logger threads that write batched WAL entries into 4KB pages in parallel, allocating pages with CAS; the paper reports about 10x more logging bandwidth. Requests are handled in stages, SEDA-style: client threads drop requests into queues (ProLog/Log/EpiLog/Read), and core-pinned worker threads that spin instead of sleeping handle memtable work, flush and compaction, so no thread sleep/wakeup sits on the critical path. The top levels live in TopFS, a minimal file system over raw SPDK pages with its own hugepage cache. Which levels go there is decided at runtime by monitoring device bandwidth. Flush/compaction I/O is cut to 64KB and kept on separate NVMe queues so WAL writes keep priority.

**Use it when:**
- Write-heavy workloads that need a synchronous WAL (sync=true), where RocksDB's group commit through ext4 is the bottleneck. The paper measured 7.6-8.8x on all-write YCSB and 2.6-4.0x on Zipfian YCSB-A.
- Large databases (the paper tested 512GB-2TB) on cheap SATA or high-capacity NVMe drives, where you can add one small Optane-class or fast NVMe SSD owned by the KV process.
- Transactional or graph OLTP work that cannot drop the WAL, which is KVell's approach. On LinkBench (206GB, about 70% reads) the paper reports up to 50.3% more throughput and up to 41% lower latency.
- Research, or as a reference implementation of parallel WAL logging and a minimal file system over SPDK that you plan to port into your own RocksDB-based engine.
- Applications that can be rewritten around an issue-then-poll async loop and can give SpanDB dedicated pinned cores.

**Skip it when:**
- Read-dominated workloads. Read-heavy YCSB-B/E gained only 1.03-1.66x, and the paper says all-read workloads see little speedup plus slight overhead from asynchronous processing.
- Hosts where you cannot give one process a whole NVMe device. SPDK unbinds the drive from the kernel, so no other process or file system can use it, and the maintainer says one process cannot open two SpanDB databases (use column families; issue #14).
- CPU-constrained or shared machines. Server threads spin on pinned cores (94.5% CPU vs 63.7% for RocksDB on a 50%-write test) and the TopFS cache must sit in hugepages.
- Production use. The code is frozen on RocksDB 6.x and SPDK v20.01 with no upstreaming (issue #3). Issue reports include hangs at warmup with 100% CPU (#6, open), memory growth until the OOM killer (#13, closed without a reply), a compaction read-ahead overflow (#7) and link failures against SPDK/ISA-L (#9).
- Non-Linux platforms, or anyone who needs current RocksDB features and fixes. Setup is documented only for CentOS and Ubuntu, and SATA drives cannot be the SPDK speed disk.

**Integration:** shared lib (a patched librocksdb.so built from the full RocksDB tree with CMake; SPDK/DPDK are linked into the shared target) · SPDK v20.01.x built with --with-shared, plus its bundled DPDK (CMake fails unless the DPDK_LIB and DPDK_INCLUDE env vars are set); libnuma and TBB, both linked unconditionally; gflags, snappy, zlib, bzip2, lz4, zstd. At runtime: hugepages and an NVMe device bound to SPDK via scripts/setup.sh (root). · C++11 (README: GCC >= 4.8), CMake >= 3.5.1. The maintainers recommend CMake 3.5 for the YCSB harness because newer CMake fails (issue #10). · Linux x86-64 as tested (2x Xeon Gold 6248, CentOS 7.7) with Intel NVMe SSDs as the speed disk. ARM support is not documented beyond RocksDB's inherited build flags.

**Vs siblings:** Pick SpanDB over KVell when you need WAL durability and RocksDB transactions: KVell has no commit log, and the paper puts SpanDB at 96-140% of KVell's throughput with 2.3-21.6x lower latency. Pick it over MatrixKV when your fast tier is an NVMe SSD rather than byte-addressable NVM. For a production RocksDB replacement, maintained drop-ins such as Speedb or ToplingDB are safer bets.

**Gotchas:**
- The YCSB driver runs system("rm <data_dir>/*") and, in rocksdb mode, empties the log dir. The SpanDB run must be done as root with ulimit -n 100000. SST files migrated to the raw SPDK device disappear from the file system, which is expected (maintainer reply in issue #6).
- The harness hardcodes 40 cores and sets spandb_worker_num = cores - background cores - clients. With too many client threads this goes negative and aborts with std::bad_array_new_length (issue #12).
- Async calls can return Status::Busy when internal queues are full, and the caller must resubmit. On completion SpanDB stores a heap-allocated Status* into the caller's atomic slot, and the caller must delete it.
- HUGEMEM must be larger than topfs_cache_size (the harness sets 90), and the WAL device is addressed by PCIe address (traddr:0000:xx:00.0), not a path.

**Status:** Abandoned research prototype: 5 commits, code dropped in January 2021, last touched 2023-08-02. GitHub labels it GPL-2.0, and the RocksDB-derived files keep RocksDB's GPLv2/Apache-2.0 header. The SPDK WAL and TopFS code is worth studying or copying, but it is pinned to RocksDB 6.x and SPDK v20.01, with open build and hang reports.

[repo](https://github.com/SpanDB/SpanDB) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast21/presentation/chen-hao)

#### indexes

##### TidesDB  `C`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Embeddable transactional LSM key-value engine in C; the author's benchmark shows 4-5x RocksDB's iterator-seek throughput at about 3.5x the memory.

**Beats:** RocksDB — The TidesDB author's Dec 2025 benchtool run compared TidesDB v6.1.0 with RocksDB v10.7.5, both C libraries built with GCC -O3, on an i7-11700K with 48 GB RAM and a SATA SSD under Ubuntu 23.04: 8 threads, 16 B keys / 100 B values, no fsync. It measured iterator Seek() on 5M keys at 3.73M vs 893K ops/s random (4.17x), 8.87M vs 1.87M sequential (4.74x) and 3.56M vs 679K Zipfian (5.25x); 100-key scans were 2.41x faster and 1000-key scans 1.11x (a tie). Caveats: this is a first-party vendor result, the article's own conclusion quotes different figures (4.11x/4.58x/6.31x), and no C++ std baseline is involved.

**Known shortcoming:** Uses ~3.46x more RSS than RocksDB in the benchmark (851 vs 246 MB). The original benchtool repo now 404s; its code survives in a mirror (dhoard/tidesdb-benchtool).

**Known shortcoming:** Speedups were measured on v6.1.0 (2025-12); v10 changed the read path (B+tree key logs, whole-file Bloom removed, custom comparators removed) and cannot read 9.x files (upgrade means dump and reload); v10 keybench shows 2.4-4.4x RSS on 3 of 4 workloads. The article contradicts itself (body 4.17/4.74/5.25x vs conclusion 4.11/4.58/6.31x); vendor-run with fsync off (also the default). 1000-key scans tie; ~97% of commits from one maintainer; own C API, not a RocksDB drop-in.

**How:** The benchmarked v6.1.0 kept SSTable metadata resident until it was provably safe to free: sparse block indices, per-SSTable bloom filters (~10 bits/key), min/max keys and open file handles. Its partitioned CLOCK block cache (2 shards per core, lock-free hits, atomic refcounts) held already-deserialized key-log blocks, so a seek to hot data needed no syscall, decompression or parsing. The current v10 line changes the structure. Each SSTable's key log is a B+tree whose parsed nodes are cached and whose root stays pinned, whole-file blooms are replaced by partitioned range filters, and WiscKey-style key/value separation keeps values of 1 KiB and up out of the tree, which shortens it. Compaction follows Spooky (partitioned merges on the largest level's boundaries, Dynamic Capacity Adaptation).

**Use it when:**
- Seek-heavy or point-lookup-heavy workloads over small keys and values (16 B / 100 B in the benchmark) with a hot working set that fits in RAM: iterator Seek ran 4.2x (random), 4.7x (sequential) and 5.3x (Zipfian) faster than RocksDB 10.7.5 at 8 threads.
- Short range scans (about 100 keys) where positioning the iterator dominates the cost (2.41x faster than RocksDB at 100 random keys).
- Write-heavy ingest of values of 1 KiB and up where key/value separation pays: the author's v10.0.0 vs RocksDB 11.8.1 defaults run reports 2-10x faster seeding of a 10 GiB dataset and 2.5-5.4x lower write amplification.
- Embedded C/C++ services that want multi-column-family atomic transactions, MVCC snapshots, isolation levels up to serializable and XA two-phase commit in one library with no mandatory dependencies.
- Slow SATA-class storage under default RocksDB settings, where RocksDB's L0 write stalls dominate (the author's small-server median advantage was 3.8x, against 1.82x on NVMe).

**Skip it when:**
- Memory-constrained deployments (containers with ~2 GB limits, many instances per host). Peak RSS was 851 MB vs RocksDB's 246 MB in the seek benchmark, and 2.4-4.4x RocksDB's raw peak on three of four v10 keybench workloads. Filter directories are held outside the block-cache budget.
- Long range scans that need values. 1000-key ranges were a tie (1.11x, within variance per the author), there is no parallel value-log prefetch, and every separated value costs an extra read per entry.
- When you need RocksDB API compatibility, its tooling and ecosystem, or custom comparators. v10 removed comparators, so keys must be encoded to sort correctly by memcmp.
- When you need a stable on-disk format or a long-proven engine. Four major versions shipped between Dec 2025 (v6.1.0) and Sep 2026 (v10.0.0); 10.x cannot read 9.x files and migration is dump-and-reload. About 97% of commits come from one maintainer.
- Tight disk budgets. In the v10 keybench the store averaged about 2x its live data because of value-log retention, and the author says to size disks for the peak.

**Integration:** shared lib (static by default on Windows); CMake package TidesDB::tidesdb, public header <tidesdb/db.h> · none mandatory (C standard library + threads; xxHash bundled); optional Snappy, LZ4, Zstd, and optionally mimalloc/tcmalloc/jemalloc · C11 with atomics; CMake 3.12+; GCC 7+, Clang 6+, MSVC 2019 16.8+ (/experimental:c11atomics) · Linux (x86, x64, ARM64, PowerPC32, RISC-V64), macOS (x64, Apple Silicon), Windows (x86/x64, MSVC and MinGW), FreeBSD/OpenBSD/NetBSD/DragonFlyBSD/Illumos/Solaris x64; 32-bit and PowerPC targets need libatomic

**Vs siblings:** Pick TidesDB over TerarkDB (a RocksDB 5.18 fork that is drop-in for RocksDB) when you can adopt a new C API and want an actively maintained engine with MVCC transactions and key/value separation. Pick it over libmdbx or redb (B-tree engines) for write-heavy or large-value ingest and multi-column-family LSM workloads, accepting more RAM and format churn. Bourbon is a research artifact, not a library you would ship.

**Gotchas:**
- Durability is off by default (memtable_sync_mode = TDB_SYNC_NONE). Set TDB_SYNC_FULL or TDB_SYNC_INTERVAL if acknowledged commits must survive a crash. The headline benchmark also ran with sync disabled on both engines.
- TDB_ERR_LOCKED from a read means a source was busy (memtable rotation, file-descriptor budget exhausted) and you must retry. The docs call treating it as not-found a correctness bug. TDB_ERR_CONFLICT likewise needs a retry loop.
- Buffers the library returns must be freed with tidesdb_free, never free(). With a non-default allocator build, calling free() crashes.
- The benchmarked seek path belongs to an architecture that no longer exists (block-format key logs, whole-file bloom filters). An iterator-seek correctness bug (issue #490: seek returned too few keys after reopen, due to a wrong early exit) was found against v7.0.2 and fixed in Dec 2025, so re-benchmark your own workload on v10.

**Status:** Very active (v10.0.2 released 2026-09-24, pushed 2026-09-26) and MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft, fine to link from proprietary code), but effectively a one-maintainer project that breaks its on-disk format at each major release; the v6.1.0 design the headline numbers come from has since been replaced.

[repo](https://github.com/tidesdb/tidesdb) · [benchmark](https://tidesdb.com/articles/benchmark-design-range-seek-tidesdb610-rocksdb1075/)

##### FAST+FAIR (Failure-Atomic ShifT + Failure-Atomic In-place Rebalancing B+-Tree)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Crash-consistent persistent-memory B+-tree using failure-atomic in-place shifts; range scans 6-33% faster than FP-tree/wB+-tree (emulated PM).

**Beats:** wB+-tree, FP-tree, WORT and SkipList (single-threaded); FP-tree, B-link tree and SkipList (concurrent) — In the FAST'18 paper (g++ 4.8.2 -O3 single-threaded on a Xeon E7-4809 v3, with PM emulated by Quartz at 300 ns), range queries over 10M random 8-byte keys in 1 KB nodes were 6-27% faster than FP-tree, 25-33% faster than wB+-tree and up to 20x faster than SkipList. Inserts were on par with FP-tree and WORT, and WORT won inserts at higher write latency. Concurrent results were measured at -O0 and are self-scaling only (11.7x search, 12.5x insert at 16 threads versus 7.7x and 4.4x for FP-tree and B-link tree); the baseline implementations are not published in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo has no baseline code; the 1.61x is ARM only, the 2.2x is FP-tree's figure, 12.5x is at 16 threads and 20x is only vs a skip list; the LB+-tree and BzTree papers do not evaluate it. Requires persistent memory.

**Known shortcoming:** Open concurrency bugs: a key is lost on concurrent split (#5, confirmed by RECIPE; fix PR #4 unmerged), wrong-child search (#16), duplicate/unsorted range scans (#7). No real recovery: non-PMDK builds keep nodes in DRAM and PMDK builds segfault on pool reopen (#12). The concurrent build must use -O0 (no atomics or fences); readers are read-uncommitted.

**Known shortcoming:** License clash: LICENSE says GPL-3.0 but btree.h headers say UNIST non-commercial only. x86 asm only; int64 keys and unique non-null char* values only; no upsert; nodes never freed. On real Optane (RECIPE) it has the best range scans but P-ART is 1.6x faster write-heavy and P-HOT 1.5x read-heavy. Abandoned since 2020-06.

**How:** FAST (Failure-Atomic ShifT) inserts into a sorted node by shifting entries right one 8-byte store at a time. It flushes only when the shift crosses a cache-line boundary, and a transiently duplicated pointer marks an in-flight shift that readers skip, so no undo/redo log is needed. FAIR (Failure-Atomic In-place Rebalancing) splits and merges nodes in place using B-link-style sibling pointers, and later traversals tolerate a half-finished split and repair it lazily. Keys stay sorted in small nodes (512 B by default) that are scanned linearly. That keeps range scans sequential and prefetcher-friendly, and it lets readers run lock-free by scanning in the direction given by a per-node switch_counter (the paper found linear search beat binary search below 4 KB nodes).

**Use it when:**
- Reproducing or baselining persistent-memory index research on 8-byte integer keys: DPTree, APEX and RECIPE all benchmark against this code.
- Range-scan-heavy ordered index on PM with 64-bit integer keys: RECIPE's independent evaluation on real Optane DCPMM (16 threads, 64M keys) found FAST & FAIR beat P-ART, P-HOT, P-Masstree and P-BwTree on range scans.
- Studying or prototyping log-free failure-atomic B+-tree techniques: each variant is a single ~1,000-line header that is easy to read and modify.
- Read-mostly multi-threaded lookups where read-uncommitted visibility is acceptable: in the paper, lock-free search scaled about 11.7x from 1 to 16 threads on emulated PM.

**Skip it when:**
- Holding data you cannot lose. Known correctness bugs: concurrent internal-node splits can place a key in the wrong node so it is never found (issue #5/PR #4, confirmed by the RECIPE authors, fix unmerged), the lock-free inner-node search can follow the wrong child (#16), concurrent range scans can return duplicate or unsorted results (#7), and RECIPE lost keys after consecutive crashes during split and merge.
- Needing actual restart and recovery. single/ and concurrent/ keep nodes in volatile DRAM, and the PMDK variants segfault when reopening a pool that already holds data, because volatile lock pointers are stored inside persistent nodes (issue #12, open).
- String or variable-length keys, upserts, or NULL or duplicate values: keys are int64_t only, values must be unique non-null char* pointers (NULL is the end-of-node sentinel), and there is no update operation.
- Write-heavy or point-lookup-heavy workloads on real Optane: RECIPE measured P-ART up to 1.6x faster on write-heavy and P-HOT 1.5x faster on read-heavy YCSB, and 2.5-5x gaps with string keys. The catalogued DPTree and APEX also beat it.
- Non-x86 targets or commercial use: the code uses x86-only inline asm (rdtsc, pause, clflush, mfence), and the source headers restrict use to non-commercial research despite the GPL-3.0 LICENSE file.

**Integration:** source-drop · none for single/ (libc, -lrt -lm); pthread for concurrent/; libpmemobj (PMDK) for single_pmdk/ and concurrent_pmdk/ · C++11 with GNU inline asm; the Makefiles use g++ -std=c++11 and the paper used g++ 4.8.2. The code uses the `register` storage class, which C++17 removed. · x86-64 only (the ARM/non-TSO variant from the paper is not in the repo); Linux

**Vs siblings:** Pick FAST+FAIR over DPTree, APEX or LB+-Tree only when you want a simple sorted-leaf PM B+-tree baseline, or a range-scan-heavy 64-bit-integer workload, and can live with research-grade code. DPTree has up to 1.82x faster lookups and APEX up to 3.8x faster inserts than FAST+FAIR, while LB+-Tree targets real 3D XPoint. For DRAM-only ordered indexes, prefer ALEX, LIPP, HOT or ART, since FAST+FAIR's flushes are pure overhead there.

**Gotchas:**
- The concurrent Makefiles compile with -O0 on purpose. The paper says -O3 reorders memory operations the lock-free reads depend on, because the read path uses plain loads with no std::atomic or compiler fences, so turning on optimization can silently break correctness.
- btree.h defines globals (for example write_latency_in_ns) and non-inline member functions at namespace scope, plus `using namespace std;`. Include it in exactly one translation unit, or you get duplicate-symbol link errors.
- Every flush is clflush fenced by mfence on both sides, with an rdtsc spin loop for emulated write latency (CPU_FREQ_MHZ is hard-coded to 1994). Keep write_latency_in_ns at 0 on real hardware, and expect no clwb/clflushopt.
- Memory is never reclaimed: there is no btree destructor, merged nodes are only marked is_deleted, and concurrent deletes skip rebalancing entirely. btree_search_range writes into an unbounded caller buffer, and lookup misses print "NOT FOUND" to stdout.

**Status:** Abandoned research code: the last master commit was 2020-06-12 (the issue-13 branch was last touched in 2021-03), and bug-fix PRs #4 and #15 remain unmerged. The LICENSE file is GPL-3.0 but every btree.h header grants only a non-commercial research license from UNIST, so clear the licensing before any product use.

[repo](https://github.com/DICL/FAST_FAIR) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/fast18/fast18-hwang.pdf)

##### fast64 (FAST: Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, 64-bit)  `Rust`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Rust/C AVX-512 static search tree for sorted u32/u64 keys; about 10% faster lookups than STX B-Tree in SOSD.

**Beats:** B-tree (STX B-Tree) — On an Intel Xeon Gold 6230, the SOSD paper (Marcus et al., PVLDB 14(1)) ran 10M random lookups on a 32-bit version of the 200M-key amzn dataset: the fastest FAST variant took 435.33 ns per lookup at 102 MB, including last-mile binary search (its size matches a tree sampling every 16th key), against 482.11 ns at 166 MB for the fastest STX B-Tree variant, about 1.1x faster. No compiler or version is stated (SOSD's CMake uses -march=native -ffast-math, and build.rs compiles the C kernel with -march=native), and the 32x figure compares FAST at 40 threads with FAST at one thread, not with B-Tree.

**Known shortcoming:** The listed numbers are for 32-bit keys (SOSD's create_fast32), not 64-bit; compiler unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** A static read-only tree over sorted u32/u64 keys; lookup returns a bracketing pair (a search bound, not a map), with no inserts or found flag. About 1.1x vs the STX B-tree on 32-bit keys only; RMI, RadixSpline and PGM are faster and smaller in the same SOSD table.

**Known shortcoming:** The AVX-512 path is chosen on the build host (-march=native), so binaries are not portable; the non-AVX-512 path is an unbenchmarked scalar C fallback. Bugs: aligned allocations freed with the wrong alignment (UB, admitted in a comment); offsets cast to u32 silently truncate beyond ~2^31 keys; the shipped bench references a nonexistent Fast64 type and does not compile; the Rust struct is not Send/Sync. No README, not on crates.io, GPL-3.0.

**How:** Named after Kim et al.'s FAST (Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, SIGMOD 2010), the code builds a pointer-free B+-tree bottom-up in which every node is a 128-byte-aligned page: one 64-byte cache line of keys (8 u64 or 16 u32), then one line of child offsets, or of values at the leaves. Each level does a branch-free node search in C (one AVX-512 broadcast, one unsigned compare-to-mask and one popcount), and the count indexes straight into the offset line, so a lookup reads one page per level with fanout 8 for u64 keys or 16 for u32. The SOSD authors credit its multithreaded scaling to few cache misses and to AVX-512 overlapping compute with memory reads.

**Use it when:**
- Read-only, build-once lower-bound lookups over sorted, unique u64 or u32 integer keys where the value is an array position, for example a sparse index over a large sorted array followed by a last-mile binary search.
- x86-64 servers with AVX-512F, like the paper's Xeon Gold 6230, where you build and run on the same CPU model.
- Throughput-bound lookups across many threads. SOSD measured the highest relative scaling of any structure: 32x its single-thread throughput at 40 threads. Its latency barely changed with a memory fence between lookups.
- 32-bit keys. Each 512-bit compare covers 16 keys, and SOSD notes that tree structures gain from 32-bit keys while learned indexes do not.
- As a reproducible SIMD-tree baseline in index research, since it is the exact code behind SOSD's FAST numbers (SOSD pins its final commit, b3d15a9).

**Skip it when:**
- Any workload with updates. There is no insert or delete, so every change means a full rebuild, and SOSD found FAST's build among the slowest of the non-learned structures it tested.
- When a learned index or hash table fits. In the same SOSD table, RMI (180.90 ns, 48 MB), RadixSpline (266.58 ns, 4 MB) and PGM (326.48 ns, 14 MB) are all faster and smaller than FAST (435.33 ns, 102 MB). If order does not matter, the hash tables took 94-115 ns.
- CPUs without AVX-512F, non-x86 targets, or binaries that must be portable. Without AVX-512F you get an unbenchmarked scalar C fallback (a linear scan with early exit), and build.rs ties the binary to the build machine's CPU.
- When you need exact-match or membership answers, duplicate keys, arbitrary payload types, range iteration, or more than about 2.1 billion u64 keys (see gotchas).
- Proprietary or closed-source distribution (GPL-3.0), or when you need a maintained dependency: it has no README, no docs, no releases and no activity since April 2020.

**Integration:** crate (Cargo lib + staticlib with a C-ABI header fast64.h; git-only, not published on crates.io) · num 0.2 (Rust); cc build-dependency plus a C compiler for c/lookup.c; criterion and rand for dev only. SOSD builds it with `cargo build --release` and links target/release/libfast64.a. · Rust 2018 edition with a C compiler that accepts -march=native (GCC or Clang). MSRV not documented, and Cargo.lock is gitignored, so dependency versions float. SOSD's README targets Ubuntu 20.04 with clang and rustup stable. · x86-64. The AVX-512F SIMD path is chosen when build.rs detects avx512f on the build host (CPUID). Other x86-64 CPUs get a scalar C fallback. Non-x86 is not documented: build.rs uses an x86-only feature check. Windows/MSVC is not documented.

**Vs siblings:** RMI, RadixSpline and PGM-index all beat it on both latency and size in the same SOSD table, and ALEX, LIPP and HOT also accept inserts, so pick FAST only if you want a model-free comparison tree on AVX-512 hardware (nothing to tune except the sampling rate, and depth depends on key count, not key distribution). Its SOSD strengths are highly concurrent or fence-separated lookups: it scaled 32x at 40 threads and barely moved with fences that slowed RMI and RS by about 50%, though the learned indexes still had the better size/latency trade-off.

**Gotchas:**
- The SIMD path is picked at build time. build.rs checks avx512f on the machine running cargo and compiles lookup.c with -march=native. A binary built on an AVX-512 host can fault on a CPU without it, and cross-compiling picks the host's path, not the target's.
- It returns bounds, not matches. A query below the minimum key returns (0, min_val); a query at or above the maximum returns (max_val, T::MAX). Keys must already be sorted ascending (min and max are taken from the first and last element, and order is never checked). Duplicate-key behavior is not documented, and SOSD only runs the 64-bit wrapper on unique-key datasets.
- Unsafe memory handling. copy_to_aligned passes a 128-byte-aligned allocation to Vec, which frees it with T's smaller alignment; the source comment admits this, and it breaks Rust's allocator contract. Empty input or unequal key/value lengths panic (unwrap/assert_eq), and the C API has no error return. The build copies the input three times and allocates a small Vec per page, which helps explain the slow build.
- Child offsets are stored through `index as u32`, so a u64 tree whose leaf layer exceeds 2^32 slots (about 2^31 keys) silently truncates offsets. The bundled Criterion bench imports a nonexistent `fast64::Fast64` type and does not compile as shipped. fast64.h uses a bare extern "C" block and includes no <stdint.h>, so it only works from C++.

**Status:** Abandoned after 12 commits over 10 days (last 2020-04-23), with no README, releases or crates.io package and two outside Oct 2025 PRs (a C++23/Highway port and CI) closed unmerged; at about 500 lines of Rust and 150 of C it is easy to vendor, but GPL-3.0 copyleft applies and you would maintain it yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/RyanMarcus/fast64) · [benchmark](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

##### IBTree (Interpolating B-Tree, SOSD implementation)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Static B-tree using interpolation search inside nodes, from the SOSD benchmark; about 8% faster lookups than STX B+-tree.

**Beats:** B-tree (STX B-Tree, in-memory) — SOSD's PVLDB 14(1) Table 2 (fastest variant of each structure, 32-bit version of the 200M-key amzn dataset, 10M lookups in one harness that finishes with a search over the sorted array) reports IBTree at 446.55 ns per lookup and 9.0 MB against 482.11 ns and 166.0 MB for the STX B+-tree, about 8% faster, on an Intel Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz with 256 GB RAM. The build used SOSD's Release -march=native -ffast-math flags, but no compiler is named, no std:: container is compared, and the 64-bit datasets have only Pareto plots, not IBTree numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** The only numbers come from SOSD (PVLDB 14(1) Table 2) on 32-bit amzn keys; no compiler named; a SOSD competitor implementation rather than a standalone library.

**Known shortcoming:** Bulk-load only (no insert/delete, though the paper's Table 1 says updatable). No virtual destructor on the node base (UB; most of the tree leaks); a key above the max indexed reads values[count] (uninitialized or past the end); on skewed data one interpolation guess is followed by a linear walk of up to 255 slots with no binary fallback. Only ~8% faster than STX; RS/RMI/PGM/FAST are faster in the same table and the 18x memory gap reflects the fastest-variant pick. GPL-3.0 source drop in SOSD, abandoned.

**How:** Each inner and leaf node stores a slope, count / (last_key - first_key), so a lookup guesses the slot as slope * (key - first_key) in one linear-interpolation step. It then walks left or right one slot at a time to the exact lower bound, instead of binary-searching the node (the linear and std::lower_bound versions remain in the file, commented out). The idea is from G. Graefe, 'B-tree indexes, interpolation search, and skew', DaMoN '06 (DOI 10.1145/1140402.1140409), not a 2018 VLDB paper. When keys within a node are close to evenly spaced the guess lands near the target, so the walk is short, and the 256-way fanout keeps the tree shallow.

**Use it when:**
- Static, sorted 32- or 64-bit unsigned integer keys that are loaded once and then only read.
- Keys whose distribution is close to linear inside each 256-key node (smooth CDFs like SOSD's amzn), so the interpolation guess is nearly exact.
- A small sparse index over a large sorted array: index every Nth key and finish with a binary search in the returned window. The 9.0 MB variant beat STX's best 166 MB variant on 32-bit amzn.
- Index-structure research or benchmarking, as the 'B-tree plus interpolation, no learned model' baseline next to RMI, RadixSpline and PGM.
- You want a ~370-line template with no dependencies that you can vendor and modify, and GPL-3.0 is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Any workload with inserts, deletes or updates. The SOSD code only bulk-loads, even though the paper's Table 1 marks IBTree as supporting updates.
- Skewed or clustered keys inside a node, such as osm-like cell IDs. A bad guess is corrected by a linear walk of up to 255 slots per node, with no fallback to binary search.
- Latency is the priority. In the same Table 2, RMI (180.90 ns), RadixSpline (266.58 ns), PGM (326.48 ns) and FAST (435.33 ns) are all faster, and the hash tables are faster still for pure point lookups (RobinHash 93.69 ns, CuckooMap 114.50 ns).
- Non-numeric or composite keys such as strings or tuples. Interpolation needs key subtraction and conversion to double, and there is no comparator parameter.
- You need range scans, iteration, a 'not found' result, a maintained library, or a non-copyleft license. None of these is provided, the code is only exercised by SOSD's harness, and the license is GPL-3.0.

**Integration:** source-drop · The core interpolation_btree::BTree needs only the C++ standard library. The file itself does not include <vector>, <functional> or <cassert>; it gets them through SOSD's competitors/base.h -> util.h. The InterpolationBTree wrapper also needs SOSD's Competitor, KeyValue, SearchBound and util::timing. · Not documented. SOSD builds with CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17, but the header uses only C++11-level features. The maintainers built SOSD with g++-9 in an Ubuntu 18.04 container (issue #8), and the README installs clang on Ubuntu 20.04. · Any. The code is portable scalar C++ with no SIMD intrinsics. The paper's numbers were measured on x86-64 (Xeon Gold 6230) with SOSD's -march=native -ffast-math build.

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over RadixSpline, RMI or FAST (fast64) only when you want a plain comparison tree with no model tuning, no RMI code generation and no Rust/AVX-512 FAST library; on speed alone it loses, since RadixSpline is both faster (266.58 ns) and smaller (4.0 MB) in the same table. If you need updates, use PGM-index, ALEX or LIPP instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Destruction is broken. BTreeNodeBase has no virtual destructor, so `delete root` and `delete children[i]` go through base pointers. That is undefined behavior, the inner-node destructors never run, and nearly the whole tree leaks. Separately, the inner destructor loop runs i < count and would skip the last of the count+1 children anyway.
- Querying a key larger than the largest indexed key is undefined behavior. The leaf's early-exit path returns `count`, so Lookup reads values[count], which is uninitialized or past the end of a full 256-entry leaf. SOSD avoids this only because its wrapper always indexes the last key and it only queries existing keys.
- Lookup has lower-bound semantics and never reports a miss: it always returns some value. Node fanout (256) is hard-coded in private type aliases, nodes are allocated with plain new (no allocator parameter), and the internal asserts are compiled out in SOSD's Release (-DNDEBUG) build.
- The 9.0 MB vs 166.0 MB memory comparison reflects which sampling variant was fastest for each structure (both are tuned by indexing every Nth key), not an inherent 18x difference in compactness.

**Status:** Abandoned (the IBTree file last changed in a May 2021 reformat, SOSD's last commit was April 2022, and a maintainer wrote in March 2026 in issue #35 that the repo is not kept up to date), but it is a ~370-line GPL-3.0 header that is easy to copy, as long as you accept the copyleft and fix the destructor and out-of-range bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/learnedsystems/SOSD/blob/master/competitors/interpolation_btree.h) · [benchmark](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

##### MyRocks (RocksDB storage engine for MySQL)  `C++`  `GPL-2.0-only`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Meta's RocksDB (LSM-tree) storage engine for MySQL: ~4x smaller on disk, ~5x InnoDB's TPC-C tps when cache is tiny.

**Beats:** InnoDB B-tree storage engine (MySQL / Percona Server 5.7) — Percona's Vadim Tkachenko ran sysbench-tpcc (100 warehouses x 10 tables, 56 threads, 1-hour runs averaged over the last 1600 s, READ-COMMITTED, no FKs, ROW binlog with sync_binlog=10000, direct I/O on both engines) on packaged Percona Server 5.7.21-20. The box had 2x Xeon E5-2683 v3 (28 cores), 256GB RAM and a Samsung SM863 SSD, and the cache was swept from 5GB to 100GB. MyRocks averaged 4206 tps vs InnoDB's 849 at 5GB (~5x), the gap closed to 1.16x at 50GB, and InnoDB led from 60GB (~1.30x at 80-100GB). No compiler or build flags were given, and the binary was not built from this repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins only at low memory: InnoDB wins from 60 GB up and is ~30% faster at 100 GB (Percona tpcc); tested Percona Server 5.7.21's MyRocks build, not the facebook repo binary.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins only when data greatly exceeds RAM (4.95x at 5 GB cache down to 1.16x at 50 GB; InnoDB wins from 60 GB, ~1.30x at 80-100 GB). Missing foreign keys, fulltext/spatial, savepoints and gap locks (RR is snapshot isolation; row binlog only). Big transactions live in RAM (1M row-lock cap); many-row statements 7-10x slower than InnoDB (#194); large ALTER can OOM and the bulk_load workaround is non-atomic and skips unique checks; an ALTER to RocksDB can silently leave an empty table when the merge buffer is too small (Percona #1249). Periodic 1 s tps drops; RSS can outgrow the cache (#1269). The facebook repo is archived; real use is via Percona/MariaDB builds.

**Independent measurement:** Meta's UDB migration paper: 62.3% smaller and 75% fewer bytes written vs compressed InnoDB.

**How:** Every index is a key range in RocksDB, prefixed by a 4-byte index id. Keys are encoded in a memcmp-comparable ('mem-comparable') form, so the bytewise comparator orders them.
