The primary key maps to the full row (a clustered layout), and each secondary key embeds the PK. Writes go to a WAL and an in-memory MemTable and are later flushed and compacted into sorted, block-compressed SST files (leveled compaction; LZ4 on upper levels, ZSTD recommended at the bottom). That means no in-place page rewrites, no doublewrite buffer and no padding of compressed pages to 8KB. Non-unique secondary indexes are maintained with blind Put/SingleDelete and no read-before-write, and prefix bloom filters plus the block cache limit read amplification. In Percona's run this showed up as I/O. At a 5GB cache InnoDB wrote ~245k KB/s and spent 57% of its time in iowait, while MyRocks wrote ~87k KB/s and was CPU-bound (56% us + 11% sy). Derived from the page's tables, that is ~21 KB written per transaction for MyRocks at every cache size, vs ~288 KB for InnoDB at 5GB.

**Use it when:**
- OLTP on SSD where the dataset is several times larger than RAM. With a 90GB (InnoDB-sized) TPC-C dataset, MyRocks delivered 4.95x InnoDB's tps at 5GB of cache, 2.4x at 20GB and 1.16x at 50GB (ratios derived from the page's table).
- Storage cost or flash wear is the constraint. Meta's user database (UDB) migration cut instance size by 62.3% vs compressed InnoDB and bytes written by 75% (one replica set: 2187.4GB vs 824.4GB, 13.34 vs 3.42 MB/s written), at slightly lower CPU.
- Insert- or update-heavy tables with several non-unique secondary indexes, or loading new tables. rocksdb_bulk_load ingests SST files straight into the bottom level; Meta measured 2.2x (1 table) to 5.7x (20 parallel tables) InnoDB's load rate.
- Cloud instances where memory and IOPS are billed. Throughput barely changes from a 5GB to a 100GB cache (4206 to 4599 tps), so you can run small-memory instances.
- Your application already runs under READ-COMMITTED with row-based binlog, no foreign keys, and mostly PK or prefix lookups with forward range scans (Meta's social-graph pattern).

**Skip it when:**
- The working set fits in the buffer pool. InnoDB overtakes at 60GB (4757 vs 4571 tps) and is ~1.30x faster at 80-100GB (5985 vs 4617, 5961 vs 4599). MyRocks still reads ~13.7 KB per transaction at 100GB vs ~0.3 KB for InnoDB (derived), which is LSM read amplification.
- You need InnoDB features it lacks: FOREIGN KEY, fulltext and spatial indexes, SAVEPOINT, EXCHANGE PARTITION, transportable tablespaces, gap/next-key locks, statement or mixed binlog format, Group Replication, the Clone plugin, multi-valued indexes or table encryption (per the Meta wiki and Percona's current docs). Only READ-COMMITTED and REPEATABLE-READ are accepted (the source rejects the other levels).
- Big single transactions. All uncommitted changes stay in memory, and a transaction is capped by rocksdb_max_row_locks (default 1,048,576). Open issue #194 measures many-row statements at 7-10x InnoDB's time (for example, updating an indexed column on 1M rows took 99.5 s vs 12.4 s), and Percona warns that a large ALTER ... ENGINE=RocksDB can be OOM-killed unless you use bulk-load mode.
- You are sensitive to latency jitter. Percona saw periodic 1-second throughput drops it could not explain, the data directory swung from 20GB to 31GB between compactions, and the tuning wiki says compaction without a rate limiter can write 300-500MB/s and cause short stalls.
- You want an upstream that answers bugs. This repo is archived with 237 open issues and PRs, so you depend on Percona Server or MariaDB builds and their tuning expertise. Tuning also takes expertise: the wiki calls the defaults (4MB SST files, 4KB blocks) too small, and Percona's benchmark used settings supplied by Meta's MyRocks team.

**Integration:** module — a MySQL storage-engine plugin compiled into Meta's MySQL server fork (a static, mandatory rocksdb_se plugin by default; ROCKSDB_DYNAMIC_PLUGIN builds a loadable module). You deploy the whole server, or use the MyRocks packaged in Percona Server / MariaDB. · RocksDB (git submodule), Boost (submodule) and zlib. Optional: LZ4, ZSTD, Snappy, BZip2, jemalloc, liburing, TBB, folly/glog, and Faiss (submodule, only with WITH_FB_VECTORDB). Plus the usual MySQL build dependencies (OpenSSL, bison, ncurses, libaio). · fb-mysql-8.0.32: GCC 7.1+ or Clang 5+ (enforced in cmake/os/Linux.cmake), CMake 3.5.1+ (higher minimums on some platforms). The 5.6-era wiki lists gcc 4.9/5.4/6.1 and Clang 3.9 as internally verified. · POSIX only (the CMake hard-codes ROCKSDB_PLATFORM_POSIX; no Windows). Linux x86-64 is the tested target: the wiki officially supports CentOS 6.8/7.2 and Ubuntu 14.04-16.04 on a best-effort basis. Darwin build paths exist, and big-endian test failures are an open issue (#600).

**Vs siblings:** Pick MyRocks when you need a MySQL-compatible transactional SQL engine with replication, not an embedded store: TerarkDB and TidesDB are RocksDB-class key-value libraries, and redb and libmdbx are embedded B-tree KV stores, so each would need its own SQL layer. The only sibling that is also a write-optimized MySQL engine is TokuDB/PerconaFT; MyRocks is the one proven at Meta's UDB scale, and Percona's current docs (9.7 branch) still cover it.

**Gotchas:**
- REPEATABLE-READ is PostgreSQL-style snapshot isolation, not InnoDB's gap-lock RR. Locking reads do not block phantoms, and statement-based binlog on a source can diverge replicas. Percona Server 5.7 rejected SELECT ... FOR UPDATE under RR, which is why the benchmark ran READ-COMMITTED (the tuning wiki recommends RC anyway).
- rocksdb_bulk_load disables unique checks and enables commit-in-the-middle, so a bulk load is neither atomic nor duplicate-checked, and ingested key ranges must not overlap existing data. Open issue #1249 reports ALTER TABLE ... ENGINE=RocksDB from MyISAM finishing 'successfully' with an empty table when the merge buffer was too small (Percona 5.7). The fix was raising rocksdb_merge_buf_size.
- Scan direction is fixed per column family when the table is created. Forward scans are fast and backward scans are slow, unless you put the index in a 'rev:' family, which reverses the trade-off.
- Memory can exceed block cache plus memtables. Issue #1269 saw RSS grow from 95G to 120G after mass TTL compactions (resolved via TCMALLOC_RELEASE_RATE or by disabling TTL compaction). In issue #814 the server could not reopen RocksDB after an OOM kill. A maintainer blames a partially written WAL under rocksdb_wal_recovery_mode=1, and the tuning wiki sets it to 2.

**Status:** The public repo is archived (last commit 2025-01-27 on fb-mysql-8.0.32, 237 open issues and PRs), though Meta presented new MyRocks features at FOSDEM 2025 (Faiss vectors, Thrift NoSQL access, user-defined timestamps). It is a GPLv2 MySQL server fork with Oracle's linking exception, so in practice you consume it through Percona Server or MariaDB rather than vendoring code.

[repo](https://github.com/facebook/mysql-5.6) · [benchmark](https://www.percona.com/blog/2018/04/30/a-look-at-myrocks-performance/)

##### Wormhole (fast ordered index)  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Concurrent in-memory ordered KV index in C fusing hash table, trie and B+-tree; lookups beat B+-tree, skip list, ART, Masstree.

**Beats:** Skip list (extracted from LevelDB), STX B+-tree (fanout 128), Adaptive Radix Tree (libart from GitHub), Masstree (beta release) — The EuroSys'19 paper ran uniformly random point lookups on 8 keysets (Amazon review metadata, MemeTracker URLs, random 8B-1KB keys) on a 2x16-core Xeon E5-2697A v4 server (one NUMA node, hyper-threading off). The baselines were LevelDB's skip list, the STX B+-tree (fanout 128), libart ART and Masstree. At 16 threads Wormhole beat the best other index by 1.3-4.2x per keyset; single-threaded on Az1 it did 1.266 MOPS vs ART's 0.834. Three of the four baselines ran without locking on read-only workloads, and neither the compiler/flags nor the comparison harness is published.

**Known shortcoming:** The up-to 8.4/4.9/4.3/6.6x gains use the paper's default 16 threads; single-thread it is 1.266 vs 0.834 MOPS on the Az1 Amazon keyset; the repo has no harness against the baselines (LevelDB skiplist, STX B+tree, libart, Masstree).

**Known shortcoming:** For u64 keys, seek on absent keys is 2x slower than std::upper_bound (the author, #11) and uses 2-3x the space of a packed array; scans are only 1.05-1.59x over a B+tree with no prev() and are slow right after load (lazy leaf sort); inserts run at about skip-list speed and saturate at high thread counts; Cuckoo Trie has up to 50% faster lookups. lib.c constructors hijack SIGSEGV and hang the process 'waiting for GDB' unless built with -DNOSIGNAL (plus mlock and stderr noise); an idle wormhole reference blocks writers (deadlock risk). GPL-3.0 (relicense request #12 unanswered); no commits since 2022-04, no CI.

**How:** Leaves are B+-tree-style nodes of 128 keys linked in a sorted list. The internal nodes are replaced by a trie over the leaves' anchor keys (the MetaTrie), which is stored in a hash table (MetaTrieHT). A lookup runs a binary search over prefix length, hashing the key's prefixes incrementally with CRC32C and probing the table for the longest prefix match, so the cost is O(log L) in key length rather than O(log N) in key count. Table probes compare 16-bit hash tags with SSE or NEON before reading full keys. Inside a leaf, entries are ordered by tag so a point lookup jumps to a predicted slot (1-3 tag compares) instead of binary-searching (the paper's TagMatching, IncHashing, SortByTag and DirectPos). The paper's ablation says these raise the gain over the B+-tree from 1.26-2.25x for the base design to up to 4.9x. Concurrency uses per-leaf rwlocks, QSBR RCU and a second copy of the MetaTrieHT, so readers keep running while splits and merges update the trie.

**Use it when:**
- Point lookups on long or variable-length string or binary keys (tens to hundreds of bytes, e.g. URLs or composite item|user|time keys), where a B+-tree's O(log N) full-key comparisons dominate. On 82-byte MemeTracker URLs the paper still measured at least 1.7x over every rival.
- Very large DRAM-resident indexes (hundreds of millions of keys). Lookup cost follows anchor length, not key count, and the Cuckoo Trie authors measured nearly constant Wormhole lookup throughput from 10M to 640M keys.
- Read-mostly multi-threaded services that need a thread-safe ordered map with iterators, callable from C or C++ on Linux, FreeBSD or macOS on x86-64 or AArch64, without adding an external lock.
- Keys containing arbitrary bytes, including NULs, or keys longer than 255 bytes. Per the author's notes in issue #5, HOT's implementation cannot handle these (it uses null-terminated keys of at most 255 bytes).
- Workloads that need atomic read-modify-write (merge), in-place value updates or range deletes under concurrency.

**Skip it when:**
- Fixed-size integer keys. The planned 64-bit-integer specialization (issue #8) never shipped. In the author's own test in issue #11, seek() over 10M random u64 keys took 7.5 s for absent keys vs 3.8 s for std::upper_bound on a sorted array, and only tied on present keys. KV pairs are allocated individually, which the author estimates at 2-3x the space of a packed array.
- Scan-heavy workloads. The paper measured only 1.05-1.59x over the STX B+-tree for 100-key range scans. There is no reverse iteration (no prev() or seek-for-less-equal). Cuckoo Trie's authors saw low scan throughput right after loading, because leaves are sorted lazily.
- Insert-heavy or bulk-load-heavy use. In the paper, single-thread insert throughput only matches LevelDB's skip list and falls below the B+-tree and skip list on long URL keys. The Cuckoo Trie authors found Wormhole's insert throughput saturating at high thread counts.
- Keysets with long shared prefixes, such as zero-padded keys. Long anchors mean more hash probes: with 512-byte keys that share all but their last 4 bytes, lookups fell from about 78% to 40% of a cuckoo hash table's throughput.
- Products that cannot take a GPL-3.0 dependency, or that need an actively maintained one. There have been no commits since April 2022 and there is no CI. A January 2026 request to relicense (issue #12) has had no reply.

**Integration:** shared lib (make builds libwh.so) or source-drop (lib.c, kv.c, wh.c plus lib.h/kv.h/wh.h/ctypes.h) · pthread and libm; librt on Linux/FreeBSD and libexecinfo on FreeBSD. The Makefile links libbacktrace and liburing only if their headers are found. No other libraries. · C (the Makefile uses -std=gnu18) with Clang (default, and faster per the README) or GCC. Minimum versions are not documented. The author reported a 2-4% regression with Clang 9. The headers are wrapped in extern "C", and the author's issue #11 benchmark includes them from C++17. · Linux, FreeBSD, macOS. x86-64 with SSE4.2 required (AVX2 used if enabled), or AArch64 with NEON and the crc extension. Builds with -march=native by default. No Windows support.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Wormhole over HOT or ART Synchronized when keys are long, binary or variable-length and you need a complete thread-safe ordered map with deletes, range deletes and merge. The author's single-thread numbers in issue #5 put it ahead of HOT on string keysets (1.80 vs 1.27 MOPS on Amazon keys). Cuckoo Trie beat Wormhole by up to 50% on YCSB-C in its SOSP'21 paper, but its own README says it is not robust enough for use in real programs.

**Gotchas:**
- Linking lib.c installs process-wide constructors. Unless it is built with -DNOSIGNAL (make O=ns), a SIGSEGV, SIGFPE, SIGILL or SIGBUS anywhere in the host process prints a backtrace and then sleeps forever 'waiting for GDB' instead of crashing. Internal fatal errors (debug_die) do the same. It also tries to mlock() every mmap'd region and prints 'mlock disabled' to stderr when that fails.
- With the struct-kv APIs, the caller must keep each key's CRC32C hash current (kv_update_hash / kref_refill_hash32). Only debug builds assert this.
- Keys are compared as byte strings, so integer keys must be byte-swapped to big-endian (e.g. __builtin_bswap64) to sort numerically.
- The main tuning knobs are compile-time macros in wh.c and lib.c: keys per leaf (WH_KPN, default 128; 256 is 5-10% faster for point operations, 64 is better for scans), slab and hugepage size, and QSBR capacity. A split fails if 129 keys share a common prefix of 65,535+ bytes. In-place update callbacks must change only value bytes, or the index is corrupted.

**Status:** Abandoned since an April 2022 'minor sync' commit; a copy of wh.c also ships in the author's RemixDB, last pushed March 2023. It is GPL-3.0, which rules out permissive-license products, but at about 10k lines of plain C in three modules it is small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/wuxb45/wormhole) · [benchmark](http://web.archive.org/web/20211016045757/https://www.cs.uic.edu/~wuxb/papers/wormhole.pdf)

#### probabilistic-filters

##### Clubcard  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Rust exact-membership filter (partitioned two-level Ribbon cascade) that replaced Firefox CRLite's Bloom filter cascade at under half the size.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — This is a size-only comparison on Mozilla's production CRLite data. The 2024-08-29 snapshot (816M certificates, 795 issuers, 11.7M revoked) encodes to an 8.5 MB clubcard, versus 19.3 MB for Mozilla's own multi-level Bloom filter cascade, 56% smaller. The IEEE S&P 2025 paper reports issuer-partitioned clubcards averaging 54% smaller than the cascades for 2024-10-29 to 2024-11-11. There is no compiler or query-speed comparison. The crate docs also cite a preliminary build of 8.5 MB in 200 s versus 19.8 MB in 293 s for the cascade (Ryzen 3975WX, 64 GB).

**Known shortcoming:** The win is size (clubcards ~54-56% smaller than Bloom cascades for revocation sets), not lookup speed; designed for static certificate-revocation sets.

**Known shortcoming:** Batch build only and it must enumerate the whole universe U (exact only inside U); unstable API and format, serde required, non-deterministic builds (thread_rng). Weak on uniform unpartitioned sets (+10% over optimum vs ncrlite's +1.4%); part of the win comes from issuer partitioning (a sharded Bloom is ~13 MB vs 8.5 MB); size blows up near 50% block density. No query-speed benchmark (~10 us per clubcard query in the paper); epsilon hard-coded at 0.02.

**How:** It uses Mike Hamburg's two-level cascade (RWC 2022). A Ribbon approximate filter, a homogeneous GF(2) system with k = floor(log2(|U\R|/|R|)) columns, cuts U down to R plus about |R| false positives. A one-bit Ribbon retrieval function over those survivors then corrects them, for roughly (k+2)|R| bits in total, where a Bloom cascade needs many levels. Both systems are solved by Dillinger-Walzer Ribbon banded elimination with back-substitution (band 64*W bits, 256 in CRLite; epsilon 0.02). Each partition block (the issuer, in CRLite) gets its own ribbons, stitched into one matrix sorted by descending rank. Total size therefore tracks sum n_i*H(r_i/n_i), which falls below the unpartitioned bound when member density varies across blocks. Blocks denser than one half are encoded by their complement using an inverted flag.

**Use it when:**
- Static set membership over a universe you can list in full at build time, such as revoked certificates among all CT-logged certificates, when in-universe keys must never be false positives.
- Filters shipped to many clients where bytes matter more than build time or per-query nanoseconds. CRLite ships a roughly 4 MB snapshot every 45 days plus 12-hour deltas.
- Data with a natural partition whose member density varies a lot across blocks, such as issuer or expiry hour. In the README's example, partitioning by issuer lowers the information-theoretic bound from 11 MB to 7.6 MB.
- Replacing a CRLite-style multi-level Bloom filter cascade that you already rebuild in batches.
- Snapshot-plus-delta distribution. A clubcard for R2\R1 inside U2 zstd-compresses to about 26 kB per 6-hour WebPKI delta when the previous snapshot is used as the dictionary.

**Skip it when:**
- Online inserts or deletes. Construction is batch-only, and the exact stage must see every element of U, not just the members. For streaming use, pick a Bloom, cuckoo or quotient filter.
- An open or unknown key universe, such as arbitrary strings. Answers are only defined for items in U: unchecked_contains is undefined outside it, and contains is only as good as the in_universe predicate you write.
- Hot paths that need nanosecond lookups. The paper puts a CRLite query at about 10 microseconds per clubcard (one SHA-256 plus some memory accesses), and query cost grows linearly with the number of delta clubcards. The crate has no published query microbenchmarks.
- Unpartitioned sets of uniform density. In the paper's simulation (n=1M, r=10k), clubcards were 10% above the optimum while Westerbaan's ncrlite was 1.4% above. Without partitioning, the win over Bloom shrinks to the Ribbon part alone: the README estimates an issuer-sharded Bloom cascade at about 13 MB versus 8.5 MB.
- Projects that need a stable API or wire format, or need to avoid serde. The README says neither the API nor the serialization format is stable. The crate is 0.x, has one main author, and requires serde (issue #6 asking to make it optional was closed). Blocks near 50% density also blow up in size: the paper's hypothetical 180M-certificate issuer grows from 0.29 MB to 25.4 MB if half its certificates are revoked.

**Integration:** crate · serde with derive (required); rand 0.8 only with the `builder` feature; sha2 is a dev-dependency only, since you supply the hash yourself · Rust edition 2021 with no rust-version declared; the code uses let-else (Rust 1.65+) and const generics. The CRLite wrapper clubcard-crlite declares rust-version 1.85. · any: pure safe Rust with no SIMD and no unsafe outside tests. It is vendored in Firefox (third_party/rust/clubcard) and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS desktop.

**Vs siblings:** BuRR, RocksDB Ribbon, ribbonGo, xorf and xor_singleheader are approximate filters: they have a false-positive rate but need only the member keys. Pick Clubcard when you can enumerate the whole universe and need exact answers for every in-universe key, especially if a partition with uneven densities exists. For a general-purpose static approximate filter in Rust, xorf or a Ribbon implementation is simpler and has published speed numbers, which Clubcard does not.

**Gotchas:**
- Builds are not deterministic. Back-substitution fills free variables and the solution tail from thread_rng, so the same input gives different bytes each time. This matters for reproducible builds and binary diffing.
- You write the hash. AsQuery::as_query must return an Equation with s uniform in [0,m) and a[0]&1 == 1 (asserted). A weak hash causes insertion failures, which go into a per-block exceptions list that every query scans linearly.
- Answers are only exact for items inside U. When you combine a snapshot with deltas, merge the results in precedence order: member > non-member > no data > not in universe.
- Epsilon is hard-coded at 0.02. Bumped ribbon retrieval (#2), false-positive herding (#3) and a compact index encoding (#5, about 50 kB saved) are open TODOs. The README says 8.5 MB is 12% above the bound and that about 8% is reachable.

**Status:** Active but slow-moving: a single-author Mozilla crate at v0.3.4 (2026-07-31), MPL-2.0, about 1,300 lines including tests, vendored in Firefox and the default desktop CRLite backend since Firefox 137. Fine to depend on, but pin the exact version because the API and format are declared unstable.

[repo](https://github.com/mozilla/clubcard) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mozilla/clubcard#application-to-crlite-and-performance)

## Copyleft — Unverified claims (tier C/D)

### compression-and-encoding

#### entropy-coders

##### Recoil (parallel rANS decoding)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++20 rANS library that splits one interleaved stream for parallel decode on AVX2/AVX-512 CPUs and CUDA GPUs.

**Beats:** single-thread interleaved rANS, conventional fixed-partition parallel rANS, and the multians GPU ANS decoder (not zstd/lz4/zlib/brotli/xz) — Per search snippets of the ICPP 2023 paper (arXiv 2306.12141, not opened), CPU runs on a 16-core Xeon W-3245 compared AVX2 and AVX-512 single-thread, conventional fixed-partition and Recoil decoders, and GPU runs on an RTX 2080 Ti compared multians, conventional and Recoil CUDA decoders. Recoil matched conventional throughput (over 90 GB/s on the GPU) with lower partition overhead. The public harness (recoil-testscripts: gcc-10, CUDA 12.1, CMake Release with -O3 -march=native, ProbBits 11/16, multians built with NUM_STATES 1024/32768 from the lin-toto/multians fork) has no recorded numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: the harness is public (recoil-testscripts: gcc-10, CUDA 12.1, CMake Release) but the results xlsx is an empty template and the paper numbers ('over 90 GB/s on a Turing GPU') are snippet-only (arXiv blocked); baseline is single-thread/conventional rANS plus multians. GPL-3.0. Could reach B with paper access.

**Known shortcoming:** 'Active' is overstated: code dormant since 2023-06-26, the only later commit adds a LICENSE (2026-07-12, PR #3 by another contributor). The CPU split decoder is hard-wired to AVX2/AVX-512 with -march=native; the CUDA grid uses integer division splits/(NThreads/32) so trailing splits may go unlaunched (undocumented); kernel-only timing leaves out PCIe copies; the encoder buffers the whole input. Paper setup from snippets only: Xeon W-3245 and RTX 2080 Ti.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It uses interleaved rANS (32 lanes) with SIMD decoders (RansDecoder_AVX2_32x32, RansDecoder_AVX512_32x32) and a CUDA decoder in which each warp lane is one rANS state; lanes share the bitstream pointer through __ballot_sync/__popc. Parallelism comes from split points: the encoder stores the state of each interleaved coder near a cut, and a split decoder starts there and runs 'sync' decodes (syncRansOnce) until all 32 lanes are initialised. Unlike conventional fixed partitioning, it does not need fresh coder states and flushes per partition. A heuristic picks split points to balance symbol counts (HeuristicSymbolCount) or bitstream length (EqualBitstreamLength).

**Use it when:**
- Static-model or per-symbol-CDF rANS payloads (8- or 16-bit symbols, ProbBits 11 or 16) that one encoder writes and decoders of very different widths read, e.g. a 16-thread CPU and a GPU
- Bandwidth-sensitive delivery where split metadata should match the decoder: encode with many splits once, then reduce the split count per client
- GPU-resident bulk decode: the paper snippet reports over 90 GB/s on a Turing GPU (RTX 2080 Ti)
- Learned-image-compression style workloads with per-symbol distributions (the LIC examples 20-28)

**Skip it when:**
- Adaptive-model or context-mixing coding: the decoders take precomputed CDF/LUT offsets, with no adaptive model updates
- Non-x86 CPUs or CPUs without AVX2: RansSplitDecoder hard-wires the AVX2 or AVX-512 32x32 decoder, and the testscripts build.sh exits without AVX2
- Projects that cannot accept GPL-3.0 (copyleft for a header-only library means your binary is covered)
- Small inputs or single-threaded decode: hypersonic-rANS or htscodecs are simpler and faster per core, and Recoil's win is parallel scalability, not per-thread speed
- Production use without your own testing: no releases, no tests, no docs, last code change 2023-06-26

**Integration:** header-only · none for CPU (pthread used by examples); CUDA 12+ for the GPU decoder · C++20 (concepts, std::span), gcc 10+ or clang 14+, CMake 3.24+ for examples, CUDA 12+ · x86-64 with AVX2 (AVX-512 optional via -DAVX512) for the split CPU decoder; NVIDIA GPUs (CMake default CUDA arch 70) for CUDA

**Vs siblings:** Choose Recoil over multians when you control the encoder and want rANS with static or per-symbol CDFs, decoding on both CPU and GPU, and newer CUDA. The paper compares against multians on GPU and reports much higher throughput. Choose hypersonic-rANS or htscodecs instead for single-core CPU rANS speed or a maintained, permissively licensed codec, and torch_ans for PyTorch-integrated GPU rANS.

**Gotchas:**
- The CPU split decoder picks AVX2 or AVX-512 at compile time through the AVX512 macro; the CMake build also adds -march=native, so binaries are not portable across CPUs
- The CUDA decoder static_asserts NInterleaved == 32, and its grid is metadata.splits.size() / (NThreads / NInterleaved) with integer division, so split counts that are not multiples of the warps per block look like they leave trailing splits unlaunched (not documented)
- RansSplitDecoderCuda::decodeAll times only the kernel with CUDA events; bitstream and CDF pool are copied to the GPU in the constructor and the result is copied back afterwards, so lastDuration excludes PCIe transfers
- The encoder buffers all symbols and every intermediate state (symbolBuffer, intermediateStates) before flushSplits, so encode memory grows with input size; there is no streaming encode
- Decoding past the end throws DecodingReachesEndException, and buffer or offset mismatches throw std::runtime_error, so exceptions must be enabled on the CPU path

**Status:** The code has been dormant since 2023-06-26; the only later commit is a GPL-3.0 LICENSE added 2026-07-12 through PR #3 by another contributor. Usable research code with no open issues, but 'active' maintenance overstates it.

[repo](https://github.com/lin-toto/recoil) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lin-toto/recoil-testscripts)

##### TurboRC (Turbo Range Coder)  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

GPL C library of adaptive range coders, adaptive-CDF rANS and a BWT compressor that beats bzip2 on ratio everywhere and on speed on some files.

**Beats:** Other range/arithmetic and adaptive ANS coders (unnamed in the README; listed only on an external benchmark page); BWT section compares head-to-head with bzip2, bsc and bzip3 — The README's enwik8bwt table compares only TurboRC's own coders (for example 'ans auto' 116.76 MB/s encode and 202.27 MB/s decode at 24.85%; o0 range coder 88.20/88.54 MB/s at 23.33%); the 2026-10 BWT tables show TurboRC beating bzip2 on ratio everywhere and on both speeds on the NASA log (2.5x compress, 1.3x decompress, derived from page data), while trading wins with bsc. No CPU, compiler or flags are stated, and the '3x faster than the next fastest range coder' headline is backed only by an external sites.google.com page that is blocked here.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: the '3x faster' headline is unbacked in the README (its sites.google.com source is blocked); the BWT section's head-to-head gives NASA log 20e8 38.69/106.37 MB/s vs bzip2 15.71/83.16 but it is slower than bzip2 on enwik8 and Silesia. No CPU, compiler or flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Issue #7 ('Some errors in ans' on ARMv8) open since Dec 2023 with no reply; the default x86 build needs AVX; no CPU, compiler or flags for any table. bzip2 decompresses faster than TurboRC 20e8 on enwik8, Silesia and enwik9. The '3x faster' claim exists only on a blocked sites.google.com page. rcbwtenc accepts a thread count but the BWT path calls libsais single-threaded.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The range coder is written branchless (renormalization and bit coding without data-dependent branches) and offers 8/16/32-bit renormalization output; adaptive models are simple shift-based probability counters. The rANS path updates an adaptive CDF and is compiled three times (scalar, SSE, AVX2) with a runtime dispatcher (anscdfini), plus 2-way interleaved static CDF coders. The BWT pipeline uses libsais for the suffix array, optional 16-bit BWT, LZP and UTF-8 preprocessing, and QLFC (quantized local frequency coding) feeding the range coder instead of MTF plus Huffman as in bzip2.

**Use it when:**
- You need an adaptive (per-symbol updated) entropy coder, bitwise or multi-symbol, with context models or mixing, and want a fast tested implementation instead of writing your own range coder
- Coding integer streams (gamma, Rice, large-integer VLC, zigzag delta) or 8/16/32-bit data where adaptive range coding beats static Huffman or tANS on ratio
- A BWT compressor that outperforms bzip2 on ratio on every listed corpus and on speed on logs: NASA access log at level 20e8 gives 4.40% at 38.69/106.37 MB/s vs bzip2 5.8% at 15.71/83.16 MB/s
- Adaptive-CDF rANS when decode speed matters more than encode: 'ans auto' on enwik8bwt decodes at 202.27 MB/s vs 88.54 MB/s for the order-0 range coder at about 1.5 points worse ratio
- GPL-3.0 projects, or commercial projects willing to buy the offered commercial license

**Skip it when:**
- Static order-0 entropy coding at maximum throughput: README rANS/CDF rows are in the 100-630 MB/s range, while siblings hypersonic-rANS (about 3 GB/s enwik8 decode), FSE/Huff0 and pivco-huffman are an order of magnitude faster
- Proprietary code without a commercial license: GPL-3.0 applies to the library as well as the CLI
- When you need a documented stable container format or API reference: usage is 'see examples in turborc.c', raw codecs have no framing and the caller must keep the original length
- Fast BWT decompression on general text: bzip2 decompresses faster than TurboRC 20e8 on enwik8 (43.39 vs 36.21 MB/s), Silesia (52.14 vs 34.69) and enwik9 (46.46 vs 37.90), and bsc 0e0 is slightly faster on enwik8 and Silesia at a slightly larger size
- If you need independently reproduced numbers: no CPU, compiler or flags are given for the README tables and the '3x faster than the next fastest range coder' claim lives only on an external page

**Integration:** static lib · libsais (git submodule, clone with --recursive) for BWT; bundled libdivsufsort optional; pthread and libm on Linux · C; README lists GCC >= 4.6, Clang >= 3.2, Visual C++ 2022, MinGW-w64, Xcode >= 9 · x86-64 (default build uses -mavx -mpopcnt; make AVX2=1 adds -march=haswell), aarch64, RISC-V (rv64gcv), ppc64le, s390x, Apple M-series; 32 and 64-bit

**Vs siblings:** Pick TurboRC when you need adaptive or context-modelled coding (bitwise, order-1/2, mixing, integer VLC) or a ready BWT compressor; for static order-0 throughput, hypersonic-rANS, htscodecs, FSE/Huff0 or ryg_rans-style interleaved rANS are faster and more permissively licensed.

**Gotchas:**
- Output buffers must be at least inlen bytes; if the result equals inlen the input was incompressible and was copied verbatim, so the caller must record that and the original length
- Default x86-64 make adds -mavx, so a default build will not run on pre-AVX CPUs; pick SIMD level at build time
- Open issue #7 (Dec 2023, no maintainer reply) reports errors in the ans codecs on Linux ARMv8 with attached data; closed issue #2 was a level 25 decompression failure on enwik8 (2020); build failures on macOS were reported in #5 and #6 (closed)
- include/anscdf.h uses cdf_t, which is defined in include/turborc.h, so include turborc.h first

**Status:** Actively maintained (README updated 1 Oct 2026, last commit 2026-10-02) by a single author since 2013; GPL-3.0 with a commercial license on request, built via make or Visual Studio projects.

[repo](https://github.com/powturbo/Turbo-Range-Coder) · [benchmark](https://github.com/powturbo/Turbo-Range-Coder)

#### general-lossless

##### lrzip  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Command-line compressor that removes long-distance duplicates (rzip) before multithreaded LZMA; beats xz/7z on large redundant files.

**Beats:** xz and 7z (LZMA), plus bzip2 and gzip — Author's own 2012 tables, no compiler or flags, run on a 3 GHz quad-core Core2 with 8 GB, lrzip 0.612: on the 431 MB Linux 2.6.37 tarball the default mode compressed in 72 s versus 242 s for xz and 148 s for 7z at about the same size (14.9% versus 14.7-14.8%), and decompressed in 4.3 s versus 8.7 s for xz; on a 10 GB VM image it took 10m23s to reach 12.8% versus xz 50m58s at 21.2% (derived from page data). These compare multithreaded lrzip with the single-threaded xz of that era on old lrzip versions; the 2026 0.7.x releases with LZMA SDK 26.02 have no published benchmarks.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: all numbers are in doc/README.benchmarks dated 2012-07-07 (i7-3930K), including the 10 GB VM-image table; GPL-2.0.

**Known shortcoming:** CLI only (liblrzip removed in 0.650); GPL-2.0; CVEs on crafted .lrz input (CVE-2017-8844, CVE-2017-8846, CVE-2018-5747, CVE-2022-26291, CVE-2023-39741); the 2012 benchmarks compare multithreaded 0.612 against single-thread xz, and 0.7.x (2026, LZMA SDK 26.02) is unbenchmarked; 0.7.0 changed the format and its default encryption is unreadable by 0.6.x; 32-bit dropped.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The rzip stage keeps a hash table of tags computed by a rolling XOR-of-random-values hash over 31-byte windows (MINIMUM_MATCH), thinning entries by tag bit pattern as the table fills, so matches hundreds of MB to GB apart are replaced by short references before the backend runs. Because that stage shrinks the data, the much slower LZMA or ZPAQ backend has less to do, and the backend works on independent chunks in a thread per CPU. Each block is first test-compressed with LZ4 and skipped if incompressible; a 'sliding mmap' lets the window exceed RAM, at a large speed cost.

**Use it when:**
- Archiving large files (from about 100 MB up to many GB) with redundancy far apart: VM and disk images, tarballs of several source trees or versions, backups and database dumps.
- Multi-core machines with plenty of RAM where you want 7z/xz-class ratios in less wall time, or much better ratios when long-range duplication dominates (10 GB VM image: 12.8% versus 21.2% for xz in the author's table).
- Quick space savings on big files with -l (rzip plus LZO), which the author's tables show running at about gzip speed with better ratios on redundant data.
- As a preprocessor: -n writes rzip-reduced output that another compressor can then shrink faster.

**Skip it when:**
- Small or medium files (under about 10-50 MB per the README) or data without long-range repeats: the rzip pass adds little and plain xz -T0 or zstd is simpler.
- You need an embeddable library, streaming or random access, or a format other tools read: lrzip is a POSIX CLI with its own format, and the README says piped stdin/stdout loses window size and ratio on files larger than about 25% of RAM.
- Memory-constrained or shared production hosts: the README says it uses all available RAM by design, LZMA may request up to 25% of total RAM, and LZMA spawns its own threads on top of -p.
- Untrusted archives on older versions: CVEs on crafted .lrz files include heap overflows and use-after-free bugs (CVE-2017-8844, CVE-2017-8846, CVE-2018-5747, CVE-2022-26291, CVE-2023-39741 in libzpaq on 0.651); fixes continue in 2026 (heap overflow in clear_buffer() fixed 2026-09-21).
- 32-bit targets or native Windows: 32-bit support was removed in 0.7.0, and an open issue (#276) reports MSYS builds failing on PRIO_MIN.

**Integration:** CLI tool (standalone program; liblrzip removed in 0.650) · pthreads, libm, zlib, libbz2, liblzo2, liblz4 (testing only); embeds LZMA SDK 26.02 and libzpaq 7.15 · autoconf 2.71 or newer to bootstrap, a C and C++ compiler (gcc tested; README recommends -O2 -march=native, since an unoptimized build is about 3x slower) · 64-bit POSIX (Linux, macOS 10.5+ noted, Android build fixes); hardware AES and PCLMUL paths for encryption where the compiler supports them

**Vs siblings:** Pick lrzip over xz-beating siblings such as bzip3, libbsc, Kanzi or fast-lzma2 when the input is a single multi-GB file with long-distance duplication, since their windows or blocks are far smaller than lrzip's RAM-sized rzip window. For library use, streaming, or general files, zstd (with --long for long-range matching) is the safer default.

**Gotchas:**
- 0.7.0 introduced a new file format and AES-256-GCM encryption; archives encrypted with the new default cannot be read by lrzip 0.6.x (use --legacy-encrypt for that), and streamed large stdio archives are also incompatible.
- -U (unlimited window) can be much slower when the file is far larger than RAM; once a file is over about 5x the window, plain LZMA can compress smaller (README FAQ).
- -p 1 gives slightly better compression than the multithreaded default, so ratio and speed figures depend on thread count.
- ZPAQ mode (-z) decompresses as slowly as it compresses (2m08s versus 4.3s for the default on the kernel tarball).

**Status:** Actively maintained in 2026 (0.7.3 released 2026-09-14, security and performance commits to 2026-09-21, one open issue); GPL-2.0, so use it as an external tool rather than linking it into non-GPL code.

[repo](https://github.com/ckolivas/lrzip) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ckolivas/lrzip/HEAD/doc/README.benchmarks)

#### integer-bitpacking

##### NeaTS  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Research C++23 learned compressor for 64-bit integer time series with constant-time random access; paper claims xz-like ratios, faster decompression.

**Beats:** xz (and Brotli, Zstd, Lz4, Snappy; time-series codecs Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, TSXor, DAC (sdsl dac_vector), plus LeCo and ALP per the paper) — Not verified from an opened source: the ICDE 2025 paper (arXiv 2412.16266, blocked here) reportedly compares NeaTS with xz, Brotli, Zstd, Lz4 and Snappy run through Squash on fixed-size blocks (the harness sweeps 512 to 16384 values per block, default 1000) and with Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, TSXor, DAC, LeCo and ALP on 16 datasets, using a Xeon Gold 6140M and GCC 13.2.1 with no flags seen; search snippets say ratios close to xz and Brotli, up to 10x faster decompression and about 1000x faster random access. In the repo, the NeaTS timing code is real (50 full-decompression runs; 1e6 random accesses x 10 runs). Its biases mostly go against NeaTS (allocation and zero-fill of the output inside the timed loop; size_in_bits counts the starting-position Elias-Fano structure twice and adds sizeof(*this)), except that per-query random-access time is truncated to whole nanoseconds. The random-access gap over block codecs depends on the block size chosen for them.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C placeholder: the README carries no numbers; the comparison against xz, Brotli, Zstd, Lz4 and Snappy (52.77%/50.20% ratio vs Lz4/Snappy, 28.49% vs Zstd; Xeon Gold 6140M, GCC 13.2.1) lives in the ICDE 2025 paper (DOI 10.1109/ICDE65448.2025.00122, arXiv 2412.16266), blocked here and seen only in search snippets. Retier to B once the paper is readable.

**Known shortcoming:** Repo harness is not a baseline benchmark: benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp main() runs only squash_scan('lz4') with the other baseline calls commented out, main_simd.cpp's last 'Decompression speed' line times a raw SIMD copy, and CMake sets no C++ optimization level. GPL-3.0; last commit 2025-07-15 (stale); the co-author copy gvinciguerra/NeaTS is active through 2026-03-08 and carries a float-coefficient fallback fix.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher: possible correctness flaw behind the numbers: slopes are stored as float (T1=float) and out-of-range residuals are silently truncated; main_simd.cpp prints a mismatch count yet still prints the CSV ratio and speeds; co-author commit a85ae14 (gvinciguerra, 2026-03-08) adds a float-to-double fallback, so the float failure is real on some inputs (effect on the paper's numbers unknown, paper unread). Residual offsets are uint32, so more than 2^32 residual bits overflow into a heap overflow; CMake forces -mavx512f with no -O level; a copied or moved compressor leaves its sdsl rank_support pointing at the other object's storage. Harness biases mostly run against NeaTS (output allocation and zero-fill timed; size_in_bits double-counts starting_positions_ef), but random-access times are truncated to whole nanoseconds and block-codec baselines use 1000-value blocks by default.

**Independent measurement:** paper tables (blocked)

**How:** The series is cut into segments, and each segment is approximated by one of four function shapes (linear, exponential, quadratic, square root) whose maximum error fits a chosen residual width; a shortest-path style dynamic program over all (shape, width) pairs picks the partition that minimizes total bits. Each value is stored as its model prediction plus a fixed-width residual, so random access is an Elias-Fano predecessor search on segment starts (sux select), one model evaluation and one bit-field read, with no block to decompress. Full decompression evaluates the models over 8 lanes at a time with std::experimental::simd (AVX-512 on the paper's Skylake Xeon) and adds residuals that are unpacked one field at a time with BEXTR.

**Use it when:**
- Large, smooth or trending integer time series (sensor readings, prices, temperatures after fixed-point scaling) that you query by position many more times than you rewrite.
- Point lookups or short range scans on compressed data where block codecs (xz, Brotli, Zstd on 8 KB blocks) would have to decompress a whole block per query.
- Read-mostly archives where a slow, one-off compression pass is acceptable in exchange for ratios the paper reports as close to xz and Brotli.
- Research or prototyping on Linux x86-64 with GCC 13 or newer, ideally on an AVX-512 machine like the paper's Xeon Gold 6140M.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a production codec: the repo is research code with 13 stars, no tests, no install target, no release, its last commit was 2025-07-15, and its benchmark harness has most baseline calls commented out.
- Data is noisy or random: the piecewise models only pay off when segments follow a curve; otherwise residual width approaches the raw value width.
- Streaming or append workloads: the structure is built in one pass over the whole array and is static afterwards.
- Very large series: offsets into the residual bit array are 32-bit (x_t = uint32_t by default), so more than 2^32 residual bits (about 512 MiB of residuals) or 2^32 values overflow the counters, and writes then run past the allocated buffer.
- Portable binaries or non-x86 targets: this copy's CMake forces -march=native and -mavx512f, so binaries fail with illegal-instruction errors on CPUs without AVX-512, and <experimental/simd> requires libstdc++. The co-author's copy (gvinciguerra/NeaTS) drops these flags.

**Integration:** header-only (include/NeaTS.hpp plus include/*.hpp), but distributed as a CMake research project with example executables, not a packaged library · sdsl-lite and sux (both vendored in lib/); Squash 0.7 only for the Benchmark target · C++23 (uses <stdfloat> and std::to_underlying), GCC 13+ or Clang 16+ with libstdc++ (needs <experimental/simd>), CMake 3.22 · Linux x86-64; and-gue CMake forces AVX-512F (-mavx512f -march=native); BMI1 BEXTR is used when available, with a portable fallback; the co-author copy adds an aarch64 -mcpu=native branch

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over LeCo when the series has nonlinear trends (the paper, per search snippets only, reports 12.80% better ratio and 36.26% faster compression than LeCo) and you need per-element random access; prefer FastPFor, TurboPFor or Sprintz when you need a mature, fast, block-decoded codec for posting lists or streaming sensor data rather than random access into smooth series.

**Gotchas:**
- Lossless output is not guaranteed by construction: segment slopes are fitted in double but stored as float (default T1 = float), and residuals that then fall outside the chosen bit width are silently truncated. main_simd.cpp checks decompression and random access against the input, but on a mismatch it only prints an error count and still prints the CSV row of ratio and speeds. The co-author's March 2026 commit a85ae14 ('Use double precision if compression with float coefficients fails') adds verify-and-retry-with-double to the new neats_compress tool, which confirms that float coefficients can fail on real inputs. Check decompressed output against the input before trusting a result.
- A plain 'cmake ..' as in the README sets no C++ optimization level (only CMAKE_C_FLAGS carry -O9), so pass -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release before measuring anything.
- The rank supports (sdsl rank_support_v) hold raw pointers into the compressor's own bit vectors, and the class uses default copy and move, so a copied or moved compressor can point into another object's storage; load() here returns a fresh object by value (the co-author changed it to load in place in March 2026). Build or load it in place and do not copy it.
- The input is shifted by its minimum minus epsilon before compression and the decompressed output is not shifted back by the library; preprocess_data in algorithms.hpp does the shift and postprocess_data the inverse, so callers must keep the offset. Residual widths above 57 bits are unsupported (read_field reads 8 bytes at a byte offset).

**Status:** Stale research code (13 stars, last commit 2025-07-15, GPL-3.0); the co-author's copy gvinciguerra/NeaTS was updated through 2026-03-08 with portable build flags, float-to-double fallback, serialization fixes and compress/decompress command-line tools, and is the better starting point.

[repo](https://github.com/and-gue/NeaTS) · [benchmark](https://github.com/and-gue/NeaTS)

##### TurboPFor Integer Compression  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

GPL C library of SIMD bit packing, PFor, variable-byte and Elias-Fano integer codecs; README tables beat Simple-8b, FastPFor and VByte.

**Beats:** Simple-8b, FastPFor (FP_VByte/FP_SimdFastPFor), varint-style VByte — The author's icapp benchmark (single thread, CPU, compiler and flags not stated beside the 2019.11 tables) on 100M Zipfian integers (alpha 1.5, range 0-255, 128/256-value blocks) shows TurboPackV (SSE) encoding at 17,357 MB/s and decoding at 12,363 MB/s against Simple-8b's 848/3,832 and TurboVByte at 11,191/10,333 against FastPFor's VByte at 5,200/4,268; on gov2.sorted with delta coding TurboPackV runs 7,064/10,268 MB/s versus Simple-8b 836/3,296. Simple-8b packs slightly smaller than plain TurboPack on Zipf (24.0% versus 25.0%), while TurboPFor256 packs smaller than both (15.7%).

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: first-party README tables with no flags; the record's TurboPack scalar decode figure was 8876 (TurboFor) and is corrected to 10138. GPL-2.0.

**Known shortcoming:** No documented bounds checks; #133 p4nbound16 under-sizes the encode buffer by 2 bytes; #122 reports the fix for #60 (uninitialized registers) silently reverted; #130 memory corruption in vlccomp32, #135 fpx32 decode bug and #141 1+ MB of stack were all bulk-closed in Apr 2026 with no visible reply; the default x86 build needs AVX (-march=corei7-avx). Debian Code Search dropped the C library in Aug 2026 for a pure-Go SIMD port (Stapelberg blog, snippet only).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** TurboPFor picks a base bit width per block from a histogram of value bit lengths and an estimated cost, packs all values at that width, and stores the high bits of exceptions separately behind a 64-bit-word bitmap (hybrid mode can store them as variable bytes); decode unpacks the block and then adds exceptions back with pshufb shuffle tables indexed by 4- or 8-bit bitmap slices. TurboPackV/TurboPack256V are SSE/AVX2/NEON vertical (lane-interleaved) bit packers with delta, delta-of-1, FOR and zigzag fused into the unpack loop, so no second pass over the output is needed. The x86 build compiles AVX2 copies of the hot files and selects them at run time (cpuini/cpuisa), and fixed-width data supports direct access to one element (bitgetx32) without decoding the block.

**Use it when:**
- Inverted-index posting lists, docid/frequency/position arrays or column-store integer columns in blocks of 128 or 256 values, where decode speed and bits per integer both matter
- Sorted 32-bit ids: delta-fused SIMD unpack (TurboPackV256 about 11.9 GB/s decode on gov2.sorted) or TurboPFor256 (4.48 bits/int) depending on the size-versus-speed point
- Timestamps and other monotonic time series, where zigzag/delta-of-delta plus bit packing reached 0.008-0.2% of raw size in the README's ts.txt test
- Projects that can accept GPL-2.0, or buy the author's commercial license, on x86-64 (SSE4.1/AVX2), ARMv8 NEON or POWER9
- Random access to individual packed values without decompressing the block

**Skip it when:**
- Closed-source or permissively licensed products that will not buy a commercial license: the code is GPL-2.0; FastPFor, simdcomp, streamvbyte and MaskedVByte are Apache-2.0 or similar
- Decoding untrusted data: no bounds checks are documented beyond 'normally does not read outside the input buffers', a third-party analysis (Stapelberg 2019, snippet only) says it reads and writes as far as it needs and decode buffers need about 32 extra integers, and issue #133 showed p4nbound16 under-sizing an encode buffer by 2 bytes
- Code that needs a reviewable history: issue #122 reports a fix for uninitialized registers (#60) silently reverted, most commits have no message, and a batch of bug reports (#130 memory corruption in vlccomp32 on small inputs, #135 fpx32 decode bug, #141 1+ MB stack use) was closed in April 2026 with no visible reply
- Small stacks or embedded targets: issue #141 measured over 1 MB of stack because large switch blocks sum their frames, and the Windows ICCODEC build links with a 32 MB stack
- Pre-AVX x86 CPUs with the default makefile, which compiles the base objects with -march=corei7-avx (Sandy Bridge); riscv64 only gets the scalar generic path

**Integration:** static lib · none for libic.a (libm, librt on Linux for the benchmark); optional git submodules (zstd, lz4, Turbo-Range-Coder, bitshuffle and others) only for ICCODEC=1 and the icapp benchmark · C99-style C with GCC >= 4.6 or Clang >= 3.2 on x86-64, GCC >= 6.3 on aarch64, GCC >= 8 on ppc64le, Visual C++ >= VS2008 (makefile.vs) or the VS2022 project; GCC 14 build problems were reported in issue #134 · x86-64 (default build needs AVX via -march=corei7-avx, AVX2 paths dispatched at run time), aarch64 NEON including Apple M1, POWER9 Altivec, riscv64 scalar generic path (added June 2026); Linux, macOS, Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick TurboPFor when you want one library covering bit packing, PFor, varint, Elias-Fano and time-series transforms with the best size/speed points in its own tables (TurboPFor256 15.7% at 10.9 GB/s decode versus FP_SIMDOptPFor 16.3% at 2.7 GB/s) and GPL is acceptable; choose simdcomp or FastPFor for permissive licensing and conservative code, streamvbyte or MaskedVByte for a small, well-specified varint format, and ds2i for partitioned Elias-Fano indexes.

**Gotchas:**
- Size output buffers with the matching *bound function and pad inputs; low-level p4enc32 and similar calls are limited to 128/256 integers per call, and only the 'n' array variants handle arbitrary lengths
- Scalar, 128v (SSE/NEON) and 256v (AVX2) variants are separate function families; decode with the same family and integer width that encoded the data
- The library defines no stream header: you must store the element count and choose the codec yourself, and the README benchmark tables (2019.11) predate many later code changes
- Debian Code Search, the best-known user, replaced its cgo binding with a pure-Go SIMD port of the TurboPFor format in August 2026 (Stapelberg blog, WebSearch snippet only)

**Status:** Actively changed (commits through 2026-09-21, riscv64 path merged June 2026) but by one author with mostly unlabelled commits and reports of reverted fixes; GPL-2.0 with a paid commercial license, so 'copyable' only under copyleft terms.

[repo](https://github.com/powturbo/TurboPFor-Integer-Compression) · [benchmark](https://github.com/powturbo/TurboPFor-Integer-Compression)

#### succinct-structures

##### wavelet_forest  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier D`

Research code for the SPIRE 2024 wavelet-forest paper: per-block SDSL Huffman wavelet trees instead of one global tree.

**Beats:** SDSL Huffman-shaped wavelet tree (sdsl-lite), uncompressed bitvectors — No measurements are reachable: the README states qualitatively that the forest often beats an SDSL Huffman-shaped wavelet tree on access for ASCII and hex alphabets with uncompressed bitvectors, best near 0.5 MB blocks, citing the SPIRE 2024 paper (arXiv 2308.07809, blocked here); no compiler, flags or hardware are given, and the repo's own timer cannot reproduce a fair comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to D: no numbers; the SPIRE 2024 paper (arXiv 2308.07809) is blocked. The README describes tools that do not exist in the repo (gen_text, build_wf, bench_access); src/main.cpp's timing is flawed (the WT loop discards its result, the WF loop prints to stdout inside the timed region); the README says 'permissive' but the license is GPL-3.0. Last commit 2025-08-29, stale.

**Known shortcoming:** Build is broken (root CMakeLists lists main.cpp etc. while the files sit in src/ with no src/CMakeLists.txt). Block-size mismatch: the builder uses 1 MiB blocks while the timer indexes with 10,000,000, out-of-bounds UB. Off-by-one: uniform_int_distribution(0, size) can return wt.size(). random_device seed, not repeatable. Unfair timing (WT result discarded, WF prints inside the timed loop). Access only, no rank/select. GPL-3.0 although the README says permissive. Paper (arXiv 2604.11338) blocked here.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** no numbers in repo

**How:** Wavelet forest (block-partitioned wavelet tree, as used in fixed-block compression boosting): each block's tree has small bitvectors, so a root-to-leaf access descent stays inside one small region of memory instead of touching log(sigma) far-apart bitvectors of a global tree. Search-result snippets of the paper put it as a wavelet-tree descent usually causing about 4 cache misses where a forest may cause one. The effect needs texts much larger than the last-level cache.

**Use it when:**
- As a reference for reproducing or extending the 'Another Virtue of Wavelet Forests' experiments (access on byte alphabets, uncompressed bitvectors).
- When you already use SDSL wt_huff for access-heavy queries on multi-GB byte texts and want a few-dozen-line sketch of the block-partitioned alternative to re-implement.
- Large alphabets (hex, ASCII) where the README reports the forest most often ahead; block sizes around 0.5 MB are the README's suggested starting point.

**Skip it when:**
- As a library: there is no header, no API, no rank/select, no tests, and every program has hard-coded placeholder paths.
- When you need numbers to justify the switch: the repo has none and its timing program is not a fair comparison (see gotchas).
- Small texts that fit in cache (the generator's default is only 8 MB), or binary/DNA-sized alphabets, where the README itself reports little or no gain.
- GPL-incompatible projects: the LICENSE is GPL-3.0 despite the README calling it permissive.
- If you want a maintained fast wavelet structure: QWT (C++ or Rust) and faster-minuter's wt_fbb are complete libraries with rank/select.

**Integration:** source-drop · sdsl-lite (fetched at HEAD via FetchContent), libdivsufsort 2.0.1, malloc_count v0.7.1, CLI11 v1.9.0 (included but unused), optional OpenMP · C++17, CMake 3.22 (README says g++ 12+) · not documented; Linux and macOS OpenMP paths in CMakeLists.txt

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to study or reproduce the wavelet-forest locality idea; for a usable fast wavelet structure, QWT (C++ quad-wavelet-tree or Rust qwt) has numbers about 2x over SDSL and full access/rank/select, and faster-minuter's wt_fbb is the maintained fixed-block-boosting wavelet tree with the same block-partitioning idea.

**Gotchas:**
- The build is broken as checked in: the root CMakeLists.txt calls add_executable(wavelet_forest main.cpp) and likewise for randomFileGenerator.cpp and wavelet_engine.cpp, but those files live in src/ and there is no src/CMakeLists.txt, so configuration should fail on missing sources. The README's bin/gen_text, build_wt, build_wf and bench_access tools and CSV output do not exist.
- Inconsistent block size: wavelet_engine.cpp builds the forest with 1 MiB (1,048,576-symbol) blocks while main.cpp looks it up with block_size = 10,000,000, so forest[idx / 10000000][idx % 10000000] indexes past the end of a 1 MiB block (undefined behaviour, wrong answers) unless the user edits one of them.
- Off-by-one in the query generator: std::uniform_int_distribution<size_t>(0, size) is inclusive, so a query can hit position wt.size(), one past the end. Queries are seeded from std::random_device, so runs are not repeatable.
- Unfair timing in main.cpp: the wavelet-tree loop discards wt[i] (the compiler may drop the work), while the forest loop prints every result to std::cout inside the timed region; only 10,000 queries, one run, and no build type or -O flags set in CMakeLists.txt.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-08-29, 1 star, 0 issues), GPL-3.0 research code that does not build as checked in; treat it as a paper companion, not a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/AaronHong1024/wavelet_forest) · [benchmark](https://github.com/AaronHong1024/wavelet_forest/blob/master/src/main.cpp)

### crypto-and-hashing

#### aead-and-ciphers

##### stdx-go ChaCha20 (Go simd/archsimd)  `Go`  `MIT (per LICENSE.txt and GitHub detection); the README contradicts this, saying 'The code is licensed under AGPL-3.0 (see LICENSE.txt)'`  `active`  `Tier C`

Go ChaCha20 stream cipher written with experimental simd/archsimd (AVX2/AVX-512/NEON); claims 7.5x over x/crypto's scalar amd64 path.

**Beats:** golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20 (the Go project's x/crypto module, not the std library proper). It is pure-Go scalar on amd64: the package has assembly only for arm64, ppc64x, s390x and loong64. — The author's blog reports XORKeyStream on 1 MB at 7,517.67 MB/s against 1,005.23 MB/s for golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20 (about 7.5x). The CPU is named only as an AMD EPYC Zen5-family part, with Go 1.27, GOEXPERIMENT=simd and GOAMD64=v4. On an unnamed arm64 host the result is 1,349.27 against 1,390.28 MB/s, i.e. no gain. These page numbers were not re-verified because kerkour.com was not fetched, but the public bench_test.go matches the described setup: 64 B to 1 MB, with a fresh cipher per iteration for both sides. The amd64 baseline is x/crypto's pure-Go scalar fallback. Nothing was compared against OpenSSL, libsodium or existing SIMD Go ChaCha20 code such as aead/chacha20 (AVX2 assembly), which stdx-go itself vendors as crypto/chacha.

**Known shortcoming:** The 7.5x is SIMD against x/crypto/chacha20's pure-Go scalar code on amd64 (no assembly there); on arm64, where x/crypto has NEON assembly, there is no gain. Only the author's blog with a CPU family, no model (retiered B to C). README says 'NOT SAFE FOR PUBLIC USE'; license conflict (LICENSE.txt MIT vs README AGPL-3.0).

**Known shortcoming:** Needs Go 1.27 with the experimental GOEXPERIMENT=simd (unstable API); backend files lack the goexperiment build tag, so it likely does not build without it. Raw keystream only; SetCounter allows counter rollback (x/crypto panics); tail padded to a full 8/16-block batch. Untagged, 3 stars.

**How:** It generates many blocks at once with SIMD, written in Go's experimental simd/archsimd intrinsics rather than assembly. On amd64, the AVX-512 path computes 16 blocks (1 KiB) per iteration in a word-sliced layout, using VPROLVD rotates and a two-stage in-register transpose. The AVX2 path computes 8 blocks (512 B) in the column-major layout of the classic chachaAVX2_amd64.s: VPSHUFB byte shuffles do the 16- and 8-bit rotations, and the transpose is fused into the stores. arm64 uses a 4-block NEON path with VTBL rotations. The large amd64 gain exists mainly because x/crypto/chacha20 ships no amd64 assembly, so this is 8- to 16-way SIMD measured against one-block-at-a-time scalar Go.

**Use it when:**
- Pure-Go (no cgo) code on amd64 that XORs large ChaCha20 keystreams, roughly 4 KiB and up, where the 8- and 16-block batches are fully used. Examples: bulk file or stream encryption.
- AVX-512 x86 servers such as Zen4/Zen5, where the 16-block path engages for inputs over 256 bytes. The 7.5x headline at 1 MB was measured on an AMD EPYC Zen5-family CPU.
- Building your own ChaCha20-based construction when you can pin Go 1.27+ with GOEXPERIMENT=simd. The repo's own ChaCha20-BLAKE3 Go port does exactly this.
- Protocols that need the original DJB ChaCha20 (64-bit counter, 8-byte nonce), which x/crypto/chacha20 does not expose.

**Skip it when:**
- Production or security-sensitive code. The author calls the code not production-ready, the repo README says 'NOT SAFE FOR PUBLIC USE', and there are no tagged releases.
- arm64 (Graviton, Apple silicon). x/crypto already has NEON assembly there, and the author's own numbers put this package at about 97% of x/crypto's speed.
- When you need authenticated encryption. There is no ChaCha20-Poly1305 or XChaCha20 here, so use golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20poly1305 or one of the AEAD siblings.
- Builds that must stay on stable Go without experiments. simd/archsimd is still experimental in Go 1.27, and the release notes say its API is 'not yet considered stable', so a later Go release can break this code.
- Messages of 64 bytes or less. They take the portable scalar path on every architecture, and no gain is documented for them.

**Integration:** module (package github.com/skerkour/stdx-go/chacha20 inside the multi-package stdx-go module); vendoring the 7 non-test source files as a source-drop is more practical · Standard library plus the experimental simd/archsimd package (GOEXPERIMENT=simd). Tests and benchmarks also import golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20. Requiring the module pulls in stdx-go's go.mod, which has 25 direct requirements (pgx, minio-go, quic-go, wazero and others), though the chacha20 package itself imports none of them. · Go 1.27 (per go.mod), with GOEXPERIMENT=simd on amd64 and arm64. The blog run also used GOAMD64=v4; that detail was not re-verified. · amd64: runtime dispatch picks AVX-512 for inputs over 256 B, AVX2 for inputs over 64 B, and scalar otherwise. arm64: NEON for inputs over 64 B. Every other GOARCH uses portable scalar Go.

**Vs siblings:** All catalogued siblings are C or Rust AEADs (chacha20poly1305-simd, libaegis, the Rust ChaCha20-BLAKE3 and others), so pick this only when you need a raw ChaCha20 keystream in pure Go on amd64 without cgo. For an authenticated Go construction from the same author, use the repo's crypto/chacha20blake3, which wraps this package; for a standardized AEAD, stay with x/crypto/chacha20poly1305 or a sibling.

**Gotchas:**
- The amd64 and arm64 backend files import simd/archsimd with no goexperiment.simd build tag; only chacha20_test.go has one. Without GOEXPERIMENT=simd, the package should therefore fail to compile on those architectures instead of falling back to the scalar code.
- SetCounter lets you move the counter backward, while x/crypto's SetCounter panics on rollback to prevent accidental keystream reuse. Here, misuse silently reuses keystream.
- The tail of each call is always padded to a full SIMD batch. A 257-byte input on an AVX-512 CPU still computes 16 blocks (1 KiB) of keystream, and 65-511 bytes on AVX2 still computes 8 blocks, so gains at mid sizes are smaller than the 1 MB headline.
- The license is ambiguous: LICENSE.txt and GitHub say MIT, but the README says 'licensed under AGPL-3.0'. Settle this before vendoring.

**Status:** Actively developed: 15 commits to the chacha20 path from 2026-07-23 to 2026-08-24. It is untagged, has 3 stars, is self-described as not production-ready and depends on an experimental Go feature; it is small enough to vendor for experiments once the MIT-versus-AGPL license question is settled.

[repo](https://github.com/skerkour/stdx-go/tree/main/chacha20) · [benchmark](https://kerkour.com/golang-chacha20-encryption-simd-archsimd)

#### crypto-hashes

##### keccak-batch  `Rust`  `AGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust crate that hashes 2/4/8 equal-length inputs at once with SIMD Keccak-256; ~5.5x per hash over keccak-asm (README).

**Beats:** keccak-asm (assembly Keccak-256 backend behind Alloy's asm-keccak feature) and tiny-keccak scalar implementation — The crate's own perf example, run with cargo --release on an unnamed 'Zen-class AVX-512 part', measured 8-wide batched Keccak-256 at ~5.4x (64 B) and ~4-5x (4 KiB) per hash over its scalar path; open PR #15 names the maintainer's Zen 4 host as a Ryzen 9 7940HS and puts width-8 at ~3.5 us per 64 hashes. The tiny-keccak parity and keccak-asm comparisons (~1.3x over scalar; batch ~5.5x over keccak-asm) come from an unpublished same-binary harness; the public examples/perf.rs and benches/keccak.rs time only the crate's own scalar vs batch.

**Known shortcoming:** Created 2026-07-02, ~3.2k downloads. CPU given only as 'Zen-class'; the keccak-asm/tiny-keccak comparison exists only in README prose, not in perf.rs or the benchmark code.

**Known shortcoming:** README ratios do not compose (5.4x / 1.3x is ~4.2x, but it claims 5.5x over keccak-asm) and the external baselines come from an unpublished harness; hardware unnamed (PR #15 hints Ryzen 9 7940HS). Equal-length batches only (panics otherwise); single hashes run scalar; legacy Keccak-256 (0x01 padding), not SHA-3; aarch64 capped at 2-wide. AGPL; 1 star, 1 reverse dependency; MSRV 1.92.

**How:** It does not speed up a single Keccak-f[1600] permutation. It runs one independent state per SIMD lane: 8 states in AVX-512 zmm registers, 4 with AVX2, 2 with SSE2/NEON/wasm simd128. The permutation is written once, generic over a small Lane trait (xor, andnot, rotate, splat, load, store). The 25-lane state is passed by value and rho/pi is unrolled so LLVM can keep the lanes in vector registers. The maintainers' disassembly (PRs #7 and #15) shows the AVX-512 build already fuses chi/theta into vpternlogq and turns the rotates into immediate vprolq. Spilling from register pressure on the 25-lane state is the remaining bottleneck, and the gather/scatter transpose costs about 9%.

**Use it when:**
- Merkle/BMT levels, proof systems or sampling loops that hash many independent 64-byte (one-permutation) inputs in Ethereum/Swarm Keccak-256
- x86-64 servers with AVX-512F (8-wide, ~5.4x over the crate's scalar path at 64 B) or AVX2 (4-wide, ~3.1x at 64 B)
- Bulk hashing of equal-length blocks up to multi-KiB (README reports ~4-5x at 4 KiB, 8-wide)
- wasm with simd128 enabled at build time, where the 2-wide path took the 64-byte hash from ~379 ns to ~222 ns under wasmtime
- Rust code already generic over digest::Digest or alloy's Keccak256 shape that also needs a batch entry point

**Skip it when:**
- Single-message or latency-bound hashing: keccak256/Keccak256 run the scalar path, which the README puts at parity with tiny-keccak and ~1.3x slower than keccak-asm
- Inputs of mixed lengths: a batch absorbs in lockstep and panics on unequal lengths, so you must bucket inputs by length yourself
- FIPS-202 SHA3-256, SHAKE or other Keccak widths: only legacy-padded Keccak-256 with a 32-byte output is implemented
- Proprietary or closed-source products: AGPL-3.0-or-later copyleft, and there is no C/C++ API
- aarch64 servers looking for more than 2-wide: aarch64 is fixed at NEON width 2, and there is no SVE path or use of the ARMv8.2 SHA3 instructions

**Integration:** crate · digest 0.11 (optional, default-on feature 'digest'); otherwise none (std required: dispatch uses is_x86_feature_detected!, std::env and a std atomic) · Rust 1.92 (edition 2024) · x86-64 (SSE2 baseline 2-wide; AVX2 4-wide; AVX-512F+AVX2 8-wide, runtime-detected), aarch64 (NEON 2-wide), wasm32 (2-wide only with +simd128 at compile time, else scalar), other targets scalar

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over KangarooTwelve/XKCP when you must keep Ethereum/Swarm Keccak-256 output and want a native Rust crate. XKCP also ships parallel Keccak-p[1600] times2/times4 kernels, but in C. BLAKE3 or blake2_simd are faster choices only when you are free to change the hash function.

**Gotchas:**
- The detected width and the KECCAK_BATCH_NO_AVX512 / KECCAK_BATCH_NO_AVX2 caps are read once and cached per process, so set the env vars before the first hash
- keccak256_many::<1> is a compile error, but keccak256_many_into accepts a count of 0 or 1 and runs the scalar path
- The README numbers don't compose: ~5.4x over scalar divided by keccak-asm's ~1.3x over scalar gives ~4.2x, yet the README claims ~5.5x over keccak-asm
- AVX-512 kernels require only avx512f (plus avx2 for batch tails); on parts where AVX-512 downclocks, the README suggests capping to AVX2

**Status:** Active but very young: created 2026-07-02, one crates.io release (0.1.0, ~3.2k downloads, single reverse dependency nectar-primitives), last main commit 2026-07-24, README still says pre-release. AGPL-3.0-or-later limits use to copyleft-compatible projects.

[repo](https://github.com/nxm-rs/keccak-batch) · [benchmark](https://github.com/nxm-rs/keccak-batch/blob/main/README.md)

#### encoding

##### hx (binary-to-hex-simd, NEON table lookup)  `Rust`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Hobby Rust crate that hex-encodes bytes with an AArch64 NEON tbl lookup in inline asm, ~7.9x its own scalar loop.

**Beats:** naive byte-by-byte hex encoding — On an Apple M1 MacBook (on battery, not a quiet machine), nightly cargo bench over 12 MiB of random bytes measured the repo's own branchy scalar loop at 14.86 ms per iteration (0.79 GiB/s), the std::simd arithmetic version at 3.39 ms (3.46 GiB/s) and the NEON tbl asm at 1.88 ms (6.24 GiB/s). That is about 7.9x and 4.4x over scalar, with a best single run of 6.53 GiB/s. The rustc version and flags are not given, and nothing was compared against the hex crate, const-hex or std formatting.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline is the author's own naive scalar loop (7.9x derived); NEON table lookup on M1 only, noisy benchmark; nightly Rust with no rustc version stated.

**Known shortcoming:** NEON asm reads out of bounds (`ldp q0,q1,[src],#16` loads 32 bytes but advances 16, overrunning the input by 16 bytes) and writes registers declared input-only (UB per the Rust Reference). AArch64 asm has no cfg gate, and current nightly moved SimdPartialOrd, so it likely does not build unmodified. GPL-3.0, not on crates.io, uppercase only, one test vector; const-hex uses the same NEON tbl technique on stable Rust.

**How:** The neon_tbl loop takes 16 input bytes per iteration. It splits them into high-nibble and low-nibble vectors (ushr #4 and and 0x0F), interleaves those into output order with zip1/zip2, then runs two tbl.16b lookups against the 16-byte table "0123456789ABCDEF" held in a register, and writes all 32 output bytes with one stp. This is the standard SIMD shuffle-table hex encoder (pshufb on x86), hand-written as Rust inline asm; the first len % 16 bytes are converted scalar before the loop. The portable_simd variant computes digits arithmetically instead (a nibble >= 10 compare selects an offset of 'A'-10 or '0', which is then added) on std::simd u8x16 and interleaves the results. The baseline pushes two bytes per input byte into a Vec, with one branch per nibble.

**Use it when:**
- Learning material: about 100 lines that show a NEON tbl hex encoder, Rust inline asm (asm!, clobber_abi, post-indexed ldp/stp) and a cargo bench harness comparing it with std::simd and scalar code on the same 12 MiB input.
- Reproducing or extending the M1 experiment (0.79 -> 3.46 -> 6.24 GiB/s) on an AArch64 machine with a Rust nightly toolchain.
- As a sketch to port the five-instruction core (ushr/and/zip/tbl/stp) into your own code after fixing the over-read and asm-operand issues listed under gotchas, and only if GPL-3.0 is acceptable for the copied code.

**Skip it when:**
- Any production use. The sibling const-hex uses the same NEON technique (vqtbl1q_u8 lookup plus vzipq_u8) through intrinsics on stable Rust 1.64+, with runtime NEON detection, x86 SIMD paths, lower- and upper-case output, validated decoding and an MIT OR Apache-2.0 license.
- x86-64 or other non-AArch64 targets. neon_tbl.rs is compiled unconditionally and contains AArch64 asm, and to_ascii_hex picks the backend with cfg!() (both branches are compiled), so as written the crate should fail to build there even though a portable_simd fallback exists. This is inferred from the source and was not tested.
- Stable Rust, or a current nightly without edits. lib.rs needs #![feature(portable_simd)] and #![feature(test)], and portable_simd.rs imports std::simd::SimdPartialOrd, which current nightly docs list only under std::simd::cmp and the prelude. No toolchain is pinned and there is no Cargo.lock.
- Projects under MIT, Apache or other permissive licenses, because the code is GPL-3.0.
- When you need lower-case hex (what the hex crate and {:02x} produce), decoding, or an allocation-free API.

**Integration:** source-drop (an unpublished crate named hx; it could be used as a git dependency) · None at runtime. Dev-dependencies are fastrand 1.8 and lazy_static 1.4. Cargo.toml also declares a cc 1.0.78 build-dependency, but the tree has no build.rs; it is left over from a C extension removed in January 2023. · Rust nightly, edition 2021, with the portable_simd and test features. The nightly version is not pinned; the code comments date it to 2023-01-24. · In practice AArch64 with NEON only; benchmarked on an Apple M1. The portable_simd path is written for any target but cannot be reached on non-AArch64 targets while neon_tbl is compiled unconditionally.

**Vs siblings:** Only as a teaching reference. For real code pick const-hex (the same NEON tbl technique plus x86 SIMD and decoding on stable Rust, permissively licensed), or fast-hex (zbjornson) for C++ on AVX2. hx's only unique value is its side-by-side comparison of std::simd and hand-written NEON asm.

**Gotchas:**
- The asm loop loads with `ldp q0, q1, [src], #16`, which reads 32 bytes but advances only 16, and q1 is never used. The last iteration therefore reads 16 bytes past the end of the input slice. That is an out-of-bounds read that can fault when the input ends at a page boundary, and it also doubles load traffic.
- The asm post-increments the source and destination pointers and decrements the length counter in operands declared only as in(reg). The Rust Reference says registers not declared as outputs must hold the same value on exit, or behavior is undefined. The code only works when register allocation happens to overlap those inputs with clobber_abi("C") lateouts, which the Reference says code should not rely on.
- Test coverage is one 57-byte vector checked across all three implementations plus two 4-byte doc-tests, which never reach the SIMD loop. There are no fuzz, property, empty-input or unaligned-length tests.
- Every benchmark iteration includes allocating a fresh 24 MiB output String, the reported GiB/s counts input bytes, and there is only a single noisy laptop run with no rustc version or flags.

**Status:** Abandoned: 26 commits between 2023-01-22 and 2023-01-25, with 0 stars, forks, issues or PRs. It is GPL-3.0, unpublished, and needs nightly Rust (probably with edits) to build today, so treat it as a reference rather than a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/eddieantonio/binary-to-hex-simd) · [benchmark](https://github.com/eddieantonio/binary-to-hex-simd#readme)

##### Turbo-Base64  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

GPL-3 C base64 codec with SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512 VBMI/Neon kernels; author's tables beat Chrome's codec 7-11x, aklomp 11-70%.

**Beats:** base64 (RFC 4648 encode/decode) — These are the author's own tables, and the competitor harness is not published. On an i7-9700K with gcc 11.2 (2022), the AVX2 path encodes/decodes a 1 MB buffer at 29.1/29.7 GB/s, against 2.5/4.3 for Google Chrome's codec (about 11.4x/6.9x) and 26.2/22.5 for aklomp AVX2; the Ryzen 9 7950X AVX-512 VBMI figures (77.6/76.7 GB/s) have no external row. As a partial outside check, base64-turbo's criterion harness (upstream per-file flags, default partial-check build) measured it at 80.7/107.8 GiB/s at 64 KiB on Zen 5 EPYC 9R45, against 13.5/27.9 for Rust's base64 crate.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party numbers from a harness (xtb64.mak / xb64test.h) that is not public, with no compiler flags stated. Earlier ratio mixed 7950X numbers with an i7 Chrome row; corrected i7 1 MB figures: 29,086/29,748 MB/s vs Chrome 2,541/4,289 (~11.4x encode, ~6.9x decode).

**Known shortcoming:** GPL-3.0. Codec untouched since 2023-08 (2025-26 commits are contributor build fixes); open ASan issue #26 (encoder over-read/over-write) unanswered since 2024-09. Default build validates only part of the input (AVX2 main loop checks 1 of 4 vectors); the CMake FULLCHECK option is a no-op typo, only `make FULLCHECK=1` validates fully. Lazy CPU dispatch is not thread-safe. No base64url, whitespace or streaming. ClickHouse dropped it in 2023 (GPL, init race) for aklomp/base64.

**Independent measurement:** base64-turbo (hacer-bark) harness, Zen 5, 64 KiB: Turbo-Base64 80.7 / 107.8 GiB/s enc/dec.

**How:** The SIMD kernels follow Mula and Lemire's AVX2 base64 method (arXiv 1704.00605, cited in the source): pshufb splits 3-byte groups, mulhi/mullo shifts unpack 6-bit fields, and a pshufb offset table maps them to ASCII. Decode uses aqrit's hashed-LUT variant (avg_epu8 + two pshufb lookups), with maddubs/madd to pack 6-bit values back into bytes.
