The AVX-512 VBMI path does encode with vpermb + vpmultishiftqb, per Mula's AVX-512 notes. Loops are unrolled 128-256 bytes with software prefetch. By default only part of the input is validated (in the AVX2 main loop, 1 of every 4 32-byte vectors), which removes most of the check work. The fast scalar path (tb64x) uses an 8 KB 12-bit encode table and four 1 KB decode tables.

**Use it when:**
- x86-64 servers with AVX-512 VBMI (Ice Lake or later, Zen 4/5) moving 10 KB to multi-MB standard-base64 blobs, where GPL-3 or a commercial license is acceptable. The author's Ryzen 9 7950X table shows 77.6/76.7 GB/s at 1 MB, against 45.3/46.7 GB/s for its own AVX2 path. On Zen 5 in base64-turbo's harness it still leads at 10 MB (37.7/55.8 vs 29.4/45.7 GiB/s).
- AVX2-only machines where you want more than aklomp/base64 or fastbase64 give. On the author's i7-9700K, tb64v256 beats aklomp b64avx2 by 11%/32% (encode/decode) at 1 MB and 18%/70% at 50 KB.
- Apple M1 or other aarch64 targets built with clang: the M1 50 KB table shows 24.0/15.4 GB/s against aklomp's neon64 at 19.1/12.5.
- CPUs with no usable SIMD path (the RISC-V build is scalar only): the tb64x scalar codec runs 6.5/5.5 GB/s at 1 MB on the i7-9700K, against Chrome's scalar codec at 2.5/4.3.

**Skip it when:**
- You can't ship GPL-3 and won't buy a license. ClickHouse dropped it for aklomp/base64 in Sept 2023 (PR 54119) over GPL-3 and its non-thread-safe initialization, and accepted slower base64 in exchange.
- You need base64url (JWT, URLs), MIME/PEM line breaks, whitespace tolerance or forgiving decoding. None is supported, and tb64dec rejects any input over 20 bytes whose length is not a multiple of 4.
- You rely on the decoder to reject every malformed input. The default build checks only part of the input, so corrupted characters in the unchecked parts decode to garbage without an error. Full checking needs make FULLCHECK=1, and the CMake FULLCHECK option is broken (it defines DB64CHECK instead of B64CHECK).
- Memory-safety-sensitive code run under ASAN/fuzzers with exact-size buffers. Open issue #26 (Sept 2024, no reply) reports tb64enc reading past in+inlen and writing past tb64enclen(inlen) for inlen=94.
- You need independently reproducible cross-library numbers. The competitor harness (xtb64.mak, xb64test.h) is not in the repo, and the README tables were last updated in Aug 2023.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (make builds libtb64.a/libtb64.so; the CMake target is turbo::base64); a handful of .c files, so a source-drop also works · none (libc only) · C (no standard stated). The README lists GCC>=4.6 or Clang>=3.2 on x86, GCC>=6.3 or Clang>=6.0 on aarch64, Xcode>=9, VS2017 and ppc64le GCC>=8. The AVX-512 file needs -mavx512vbmi support; otherwise build with NAVX512=1. The CMake build needs 3.15+. · x86/x86-64 with runtime dispatch (scalar, SSSE3, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512 VBMI); aarch64 Neon and ppc64le Power9 Altivec chosen at compile time; s390x and big-endian are supported; RISC-V gets only the scalar plus generic v128 build

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over aklomp/base64 (BSD-2; ClickHouse's 2023 replacement) or the research codecs fastbase64/base64simd only when you need the last 10-70% of AVX2 throughput, or its AVX-512 VBMI path, on standard-alphabet data and GPL-3 or a commercial license is fine. In Rust, base64-turbo (0BSD, fully validated, base64url) ties it in cache and trails only on DRAM-sized buffers; simdutf is the choice for base64url or forgiving decoding.

**Gotchas:**
- Buffers: tb64enc does not write a trailing NUL, so allocate tb64enclen(n)+1 if you terminate the output yourself (issue #23). Open issue #26 shows it can also touch bytes past both buffer ends, so leave slack.
- Validation is partial unless you build with FULLCHECK=1 through make. A return of 0 means both 'invalid' and 'empty input'. Unpadded inputs of 20 bytes or fewer are decoded best-effort (ClickHouse PR 54119 notes this), while longer ones are rejected.
- tb64ini(0,1) turns on the short-string AVX2 mode (_tb64v256*). Its decoder skips most checks and may read up to 32 bytes past the input end, and a ClickHouse bug (PR 31797) had this path leaking the next string's bytes into encoded output. The mode is ignored on AVX-512 machines.
- On x86-64 the CMake build compiles the scalar core with -march=native, so the library it produces may not run on older CPUs; the makefile does not do this. README MB/s figures are counted on base64-text size for both encode and decode (issue #11), so raw-byte throughput is 0.75x.

**Status:** The codec itself has not changed since the Aug 2023 release. Later commits (2025-2026) are contributor build fixes for Apple Silicon and RISC-V, and the 2024 ASAN report is still unanswered. It is GPL-3 with a commercial license on request, and small enough to vendor if the license works for you.

[repo](https://github.com/powturbo/Turbo-Base64) · [benchmark](https://github.com/powturbo/Turbo-Base64#benchmark-incl-the-best-simd-base64-libs)

#### non-crypto-hashes

##### MuseAir (C++ port)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

GPL-3.0 C++20 header port of deprecated MuseAir v0.4-rc4. Ties wyhash in bulk, slower on short keys.

**Beats:** wyhash — The only performance data is the author's own SMHasher3 speed runs, shown as PNG charts, on an i7-12700K under Windows/MSYS with GCC 11.3.0 (flags not stated; GiB/s at a nominal 3.5 GHz). They show MuseAir at parity with wyhash v4.2 in bulk (about 33-34 GiB/s), BFast at about 42 GiB/s (about 1.2x, colour-ambiguous), and both slower than wyhash and rapidhash on 1-31-byte keys. The charts predate the current code and may not be of this port at all. SMHasher3's public results (MuseAir v0.3 bfast 8.64 bytes/cycle vs wyhash 6.98) come from a different, CC0 implementation of an older algorithm version.

**Known shortcoming:** C++ port of eternal-io/museair (listed separately). Its own chart shows it slower than wyhash/rapidhash on 1-31 byte keys and only about equal to wyhash in bulk (BFast ~42 vs ~34 GiB/s, read from chart); README's 33.2 GiB/s does not match the chart. GCC 11.3 MSYS, flags not stated. License is inconsistent (badge GNU, README MIT, LICENSE file GPL-3.0): treat as GPL-3.0.

**Known shortcoming:** Ports algorithm v0.4-rc4; the upstream CHANGELOG (Jul 2026) says all pre-v2 versions are compromised, and the port's 17-32 byte path has the same seed-free collision structure (code reading); v0.4-rc4 128-bit failed SMHasher3. Charts predate the 2026-02 rewrite and the log builds SMHasher3's own museair.cpp, so they may not measure this port. README claims asm/SIMD but the code has none. 7 stars, 4 commits, no CI or tests. Use eternal-io/museair v2 (CC0) instead.

**How:** The core is scalar 64x64->128-bit multiplication (__uint128_t, or _umul128 on MSVC x64) with no SIMD or assembly, despite the README's claims. Inputs over 96 bytes go through a six-word 'ring accumulator'. Each 16-byte step XORs two input words into adjacent state words, wide-multiplies them, and feeds the low/high halves into the next word, so the six multiplies per 96 bytes run in parallel through instruction-level parallelism. Standard mode adds the product into the state (+=); BFast overwrites it (=), which saves work but loses protection against 'blinding multiplication' (a zero multiplicand wiping state). Inputs of 32 bytes or less take a branchy short path with two to four wide multiplies, and 33-96 bytes take an unrolled partial-body path.

**Use it when:**
- You specifically want MuseAir v0.4-rc4 hash values in a C++20 codebase that can accept GPL-3.0, for example to match outputs from a system already pinned to that version.
- Bulk hashing of trusted, non-adversarial buffers of a few hundred bytes and up with the BFast variant. The author's i7-12700K chart shows about 42 GiB/s (at a nominal 3.5 GHz) against about 34 GiB/s for wyhash v4.2, though the chart's line colours are ambiguous and predate the current code.
- Portable scalar hashing on any 64-bit compiler with __uint128_t; there are no CPU-feature requirements such as AES-NI or AVX2.

**Skip it when:**
- Any new use. Upstream's CHANGELOG says a seed-independent trivial-collision flaw (eternal-io/museair#3, July 2026) means 'all previous versions of the algorithm are deprecated, and should be considered compromised'. The fixed algorithm is v2; this port is still on v0.4-rc4. The port's 17-32-byte short path has the flawed structure: the second 16 bytes pass through seed-free multiplies and are XORed into the state, so colliding pairs can be built for every seed.
- The 128-bit output. Upstream says the v0.4-rc4 128-bit variant 'had insufficient output diffusion and actually failed the SMHasher3 test suite', and the fix came in a later version.
- Hash-table keys and short strings (1-31 bytes). By the port's own chart, MuseAir and BFast take more cycles than wyhash and rapidhash at nearly every length: about 18.6 vs 15.1 at 1-4 bytes, 14.6 vs 11.0 at 12-16 bytes, and about 35-45 vs 27 at 17-31 bytes.
- Proprietary or permissively licensed products. The LICENSE file and the header are GPL-3.0, even though the README says MIT; upstream's own museair.cpp reference is CC0.
- Projects that need a maintained, tested dependency. The repo has 7 stars and 4 commits, no releases, no tests beyond a main.cpp verification-code check, and no CI (the README's CI badge points to a workflow that does not exist).

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only; <intrin.h> on MSVC x64) · C++20 (uses <bit> std::endian/std::rotl, [[likely]]); the demo CMakeLists needs CMake 3.10+. The repo topics say cpp17, but the code needs C++20. · Any 64-bit target with __uint128_t (GCC/Clang) or MSVC x64 _umul128; a 32x32 fallback exists for others. Big-endian needs the caller to pass ByteSwap=true. Only x86-64 Windows/MSYS results are shown.

**Vs siblings:** Rarely. For MuseAir itself, prefer the upstream eternal-io/museair (Rust crate 0.6.0 or its CC0 museair.cpp reference, both algorithm v2 with the collision fix). For short keys in C/C++, wyhash, rapidhash and a5hash are faster, and a5hash posts 26.91 SMHasher3 cycles against wyhash's 29.31. Pick this port only if you must reproduce v0.4-rc4 outputs from a C++20 header and GPL-3.0 is acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- The README contradicts the code in several places. It says MIT, but the LICENSE file is GPL-3.0. It mentions 'platform-specific assembly' and 'SIMD', but there is none. It describes BlindFast as trading 'accuracy'; in fact BFast gives up blinding-multiplication resistance, and upstream notes that 64-bit BFast has a fixed 8-byte prefix that makes bytes 9-16 irrelevant for 9-16-byte inputs.
- The benchmark charts were last updated in the June 2025 commit, before the February 2026 rewrite to 0.4-rc4. The SMHasher3 build log shown compiles SMHasher3's own hashes/museair.cpp, and nothing shows that this port's header was the code measured. The README's '33.2 GiB/s' also disagrees with the chart.
- ByteSwap is not auto-detected. The README example always uses hash<false>, so on big-endian hosts it produces different values from the little-endian reference unless you pass std::endian::native != std::endian::little, as main.cpp does.
- hash() and hash_128() are non-const, non-static member functions, so they cannot be called on a const MuseAir object. Correctness is checked only by self-generated verification codes in main.cpp, which the README does not cross-reference with upstream.

**Status:** Nominally active (last commit 2026-02-23), but a one-person GPL-3.0 port stuck on algorithm v0.4-rc4, which upstream deprecated as compromised in July 2026; small enough to vendor, but the upstream CC0 v2 code is the better starting point.

[repo](https://github.com/Twilight-Dream-Of-Magic/museair-cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Twilight-Dream-Of-Magic/museair-cpp)

### media-and-graphics

#### color-and-resampling

##### babl  `C`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

GIMP/GEGL's C pixel-format and matrix+TRC colour-space converter. GIMP claims up to 10x over LCMS2; no published benchmark backs it, and an lcms2 test found babl slower.

**Beats:** Little CMS 2 (lcms2) — The only claim is first-party and comes without methodology: the GIMP 2.10 release notes (gimp.org, blocked here; WebSearch snippet) say babl is 'up to 10 times faster than LCMS2 for the cases tested', and a search-result summary adds that GIMP uses babl for ICC matrix-based conversions because it is 'an order of magnitude faster' than lcms2. No cases, timings, hardware or code are published. The babl tree holds no lcms2 comparison (tools/babl-benchmark.c times babl fishes alone in MPx/s on 1 Mi-pixel buffers), and the one reachable rebuttal (Little CMS blog, 2019-10-02, snippet only) measured babl at 6.36 s against lcms2 at 3.59 s, roughly 1.8x slower (derived from snippet). Any advantage is plausible only on matrix+TRC RGB paths: CMYK in babl runs through lcms2 itself.

**Known shortcoming:** The 'up to 10 times faster than LCMS2 for the cases tested' claim exists only in the GIMP 2.10 release notes (blocked, snippet) with no timings or cases, and the babl tree has no lcms2 harness (tools/babl-benchmark.c is babl-only). The Little CMS project's rebuttal (snippet only) measured lcms2 3.59 s vs babl 6.36 s on 8-bit data, so the claim is disputed. LGPL-3.0-or-later.

**Known shortcoming:** The speed claim stays snippet-only (GIMP 2.10 'up to 10x'; the lcms blog measured lcms2 3.59 s against babl 6.36 s, so babl lost there). CMYK runs through lcms2 itself (double-precision CMYKA_DBL to scRGB with BPC); CLUT RGB profiles are refused unless BABL_ICC_INTENT_PERFORMANCE and the absolute and saturation intents are unimplemented, so any gain is matrix plus TRC only. The default 256^3 u8 LUT (64-256 MiB) is built after 32768 pixels and its malloc result is unchecked in babl-fish-path.c; the documented tolerance 0.000001 differs from the code's 0.0000047. GIMP issue #3764 (30 s sRGB to matrix ICC conversion) unread (gitlab.gnome.org blocked).

**How:** babl does not walk a general ICC pipeline. For RGB-to-RGB between spaces it multiplies the source RGB-to-XYZ and destination XYZ-to-RGB matrices once into a single float 3x3 (babl-rgb-converter.c), and linearises u8 input through 256-entry TRC tables. Conversions are 'fishes' built from chains of registered fast-path converters. At runtime babl times candidate chains (searching up to BABL_PATH_LENGTH steps, 3 by default) and keeps the fastest one whose error against its 64-bit floating-point reference stays under BABL_TOLERANCE (0.0000047 in code). The choices are cached on disk in ~/.cache/babl/babl-fishes. Hot converters are compiled several times, for x86-64-v2/v3/v4 (SSE4.1, AVX2/F16C/FMA, AVX-512) and for NEON, and dispatched at runtime. Once a fish with 8-bit-per-channel input has processed 32,768 pixels, babl replaces it with a full 256^3 (or 256^2) lookup table, enabled by default on little-endian hosts (BABL_LUT).

**Use it when:**
- GEGL or GIMP plug-ins, or any C program that converts pixel buffers between u8/u16/half/float encodings, alpha modes and RGB spaces in one call.
- Matrix+TRC RGB-to-RGB conversion (sRGB, Adobe RGB, ProPhoto, Rec2020, display profiles without CLUTs), where babl folds the profile pair into one 3x3 plus TRC tables.
- Long-running processes that convert many 8-bit images with the same format pair, where the automatic 256^3 lookup table pays off after its 32,768-pixel threshold.
- Interactive previews where you can trade accuracy for speed with babl_fast_fish("fast"/"glitch") or a BABL_TOLERANCE of 0.01-0.1 (docs).

**Skip it when:**
- CMYK or other CLUT-based ICC work: babl hands every CMYK profile to lcms2 itself (cmsCreateTransform with TYPE_CMYKA_DBL to and from a linear scRGB profile, double precision, BPC on), so it adds a step on top of lcms2 rather than beating it.
- RGB profiles whose A2B0/B2A0 CLUTs matter: babl_space_from_icc refuses them for relative colorimetric ('use lcms, accuracy desired and cluts are present') unless BABL_ICC_INTENT_PERFORMANCE is set, refuses explicit perceptual on CLUT profiles, and does not implement absolute colorimetric or saturation intents.
- Choosing it on speed alone against lcms2: the only timed head-to-head found, from the Little CMS project (2019), had lcms2 at 3.59 s against babl at 6.36 s, and lcms2 with the fast_float plugin at 1.7 s (snippet only).
- Memory-constrained hosts with BABL_LUT enabled: a single 8-bit RGBA fish can allocate 64 MiB (u8 out) or 256 MiB (float out) for its table, freed only after 5 minutes unused by default.

**Integration:** shared lib (meson build; extensions are loaded from BABL_PATH as shared objects at runtime) · none required for RGB/gray; lcms2 >= 2.8 (optional, meson with-lcms) for CMYK ICC profiles; threads; optional gobject-introspection and vapigen for bindings · meson >= 0.60; C compiler with C11 atomics (MSVC built with /std:c11 since 0.1.126); gcc/clang on Linux, BSD and macOS · x86-64 (runtime-dispatched v2/v3/v4 builds of SIMD extensions), aarch64 and 32-bit ARM NEON, i686, other little- and big-endian targets (LUTs disabled on big-endian); win32, Linux, BSDs, macOS; initial WASM support since 0.1.128

**Vs siblings:** Pick babl when you need GEGL-compatible pixel-format conversion (data type, alpha mode and matrix+TRC RGB space in one call) inside a C codebase. For ICC transforms with CMYK or CLUT profiles, use Little CMS 2 with its fast_float plugin (C) or moxcms (Rust); jsColorEngine covers the same ICC ground for JavaScript hosts.

**Gotchas:**
- The first use of a new format pair runs a timed path search, and the result is persisted to ~/.cache/babl/babl-fishes keyed on version, BABL_PATH_LENGTH and BABL_TOLERANCE, so first-run and cache-miss latency differ from steady state.
- The 256^3 LUT allocation in babl-fish-path.c (babl_fish_lut_process_maybe) is written to straight after malloc with no NULL check. Set BABL_LUT=0 where a 64-256 MiB allocation can fail.
- The docs give the default BABL_TOLERANCE as 0.000001, but the code uses 0.0000047. babl_fast_fish results are not singletons and leak unless the caller caches them (babl.h).
- LUT handling has had regressions: 0.1.102 disabled LUT code paths by default ('brown paper bag release'), 0.1.104 re-enabled them, 0.1.106 fixed 1bpp-to-4bpp LUTs, and 0.1.114 fixed a broken TRC cache for formula-based ICC TRCs and removed 'some broken conversions'.

**Status:** Actively maintained in GNOME GitLab (0.1.128 released 2026-08-07; commits since then through 2026-10-03 are build and CI changes, mirrored read-only to GitHub with 25 stars). It is LGPL-3.0-or-later and a core GIMP/GEGL dependency, so it is safe to link dynamically, but the speed claim against lcms2 is unsubstantiated.

[repo](https://github.com/GNOME/babl) · [benchmark](https://www.gimp.org/release-notes/gimp-2.10.html)

##### CompV  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

GPL C++ computer-vision library with hand-written x86/ARM assembly; first-party numbers show 3-11x over OpenCV colour conversion and bilinear resize.

**Beats:** OpenCV (cv::resize bilinear; cvtColor CV_RGB2GRAY, CV_YUV2RGB_I420, CV_RGB2HSV) — One first-party result file (last edited 2019) on an Intel Core i7-4790K iMac running Windows 8 reports 10,000 iterations at 1282x720: RGB24 to gray 449 vs 3086 ms (6.9x), YUV420P to RGB24 968 vs 5919 ms (6.1x), RGB24 to HSV 2137 vs 15709 ms (7.4x), YUV420P to HSV 3045 vs 32920 ms (10.8x), and 8-bit grayscale bilinear 1282x720 to 1064x597 1474 ms (8 threads, AVX2) vs 4148 ms (2.8x), all ratios derived from page data. OpenCV's version, build, harness and compiler flags are unpublished, and the CompV side computes lower-precision, differently defined outputs (7-bit limited-range gray, 5-bit YUV coefficients, 0-255 hue, 8-bit bilinear with acknowledged drift), so the rows are not like-for-like in output.

**Known shortcoming:** GPL-3.0. Result-file numbers (i7-4790K, 2017-2019) match and the CompV drivers are public (tests/image/chroma_conv.cxx, scale.cxx), but the OpenCV harness, version, IPP and thread settings are unpublished and outputs were never matched against OpenCV; scaling was measured on grayscale, HSV uses an approximate reciprocal, and the '50x' appears only in the repo description.

**Known shortcoming:** Compared outputs are not like-for-like with OpenCV: RGB24 to grey computes limited-range BT.601 luma ((33R+65G+13B)>>7)+16, so white gives 237 where OpenCV RGB2GRAY is full-range; YUV to RGB uses 5-bit coefficients (37/32); HSV hue spans 0-255 (OpenCV CV_RGB2HSV uses 0-180); the bilinear AVX2 path is hard-coded 8-bit fixed point and the maintainer's open issue #176 says shift 8 drifts (derived: the last column samples x 1278.9 instead of 1280.9, weights sum to 255/256 so white gives 253). The IPP build swaps the grey formula; 143 open issues.

**How:** Each kernel has a scalar C++ reference plus SSE2/SSSE3/SSE4.1/AVX2 intrinsics, YASM x86/x64 assembly and NEON32/NEON64 assembly, chosen at run time by CPU flags and buffer alignment, and rows are split across a custom thread dispatcher (8 threads in the published run). Much of the speed comes from low-precision fixed point: grayscale uses 7-bit coefficients (Y = ((33R+65G+13B)>>7)+16), YUV to RGB uses 5-bit coefficients (R = (37Y'+51V')>>5), bilinear scaling uses 8-bit fractional coordinates and weights so every product fits in 16-bit lanes (mullo/mulhi_epu16), and HSV uses lookup tables of reciprocals, with an optional approximate SSSE3 reciprocal. Results quoted in the comparison file were taken with assembler code and TBBMalloc or TCMalloc.

**Use it when:**
- A GPL-3.0 (or commercially licensed from Doubango) pipeline on 8-bit grayscale frames where CompV's own resize, threshold, Canny, FAST, CCL or MSER chain replaces several OpenCV calls.
- Studio-range BT.601 luma is acceptable or wanted: CompV's 'grayscale' from RGB is limited-range Y (16-235), the same as the Y plane of a YUV conversion, not OpenCV's full-range 0.299R+0.587G+0.114B.
- Real-time HD camera pipelines on x86 AVX2 or ARM NEON (Android, iOS, Raspberry Pi, Jetson) where a few levels of rounding error per pixel do not matter and multithreading across rows is available.
- Building pyramids or downscaled detection inputs, where the 8-bit fixed-point bilinear scaler's small geometric drift and slight darkening are tolerable.

**Skip it when:**
- When output must match OpenCV: CompV's RGB-to-gray is limited-range Y with truncation (white maps to 237, not 255), YUV-to-RGB uses 5-bit coefficients (1.156 instead of 1.164 for Y), HSV hue spans 0-255 (OpenCV CV_RGB2HSV uses 0-180), and bilinear resize is neither centre-aligned nor bit-exact.
- Quality-sensitive resizing: the bilinear scaler uses 8-bit fractional steps, which the maintainer's open issue #176 says 'produces drift'. For 1282x720 to 1064x597 the step is quantized to 1.203125 instead of 1.2049, so the last column samples source x 1278.9 instead of OpenCV's 1280.9 (derived from the code). Weights sum to 255/256, so a flat white image comes out at 253.
- Colour (RGB) resizing: CompVImageScaleBilinear::process returns NOT_IMPLEMENTED unless the input is 8u with one plane.
- Single-threaded use: the result file's own single-thread AVX2 bilinear time (5435 ms) is slower than OpenCV's 4148 ms; bicubic scaling and rotation have no result ('Shame!!'), and issue #167 says bicubic is slower than OpenCV.
- Proprietary products without a Doubango licence (GPL-3.0), or teams that need documentation and support: the README calls it an undocumented R&D project with 143 open issues and no releases.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake; also Visual Studio .sln and Xcode project) · YASM for x86/x64 assembly (CMake fails without it); bundled tbbmalloc sources and thirdparties headers; pthread/dl on Unix, Shlwapi/Winmm on Windows; optional Intel IPP (COMPV_HAVE_INTEL_IPP), CUDA, OpenCL, OpenGL and other GPU back ends in separate modules · C++11, CMake 3.10+, YASM; MSVC, GCC or Clang (Release builds use -O3) · x86 and x86-64 (SSE2 to AVX2/FMA, run-time dispatch) on Windows, Linux and macOS; ARM32/ARM64 NEON on Android, iOS, Raspberry Pi and Jetson

**Vs siblings:** Pick CompV over RGB2Y, DeltaCV or KLERP only when you want a whole GPL vision stack (scaling, thresholding, features, CCL) with ARM and x86 assembly from one vendor. For standalone conversions that must match OpenCV or a standard, KLERP (bilinear, matches OpenCV output) and libyuv, sparkyuv or yuvutils-rs (YUV) are permissive, documented and verifiable.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD and assembly paths are selected only when output pointers and strides are 16- or 32-byte aligned; unaligned buffers silently fall back to slower intrinsics or the scalar C++ path.
- The bilinear SIMD kernels are hard-coded for 8-bit fixed point; the source comment says a shift of 11 is correct but no SIMD code exists for it, so the drift in issue #176 (open since 2022-11-30) applies to the AVX2 path behind the published numbers.
- Builds with COMPV_HAVE_INTEL_IPP switch RGB24-to-gray to ippiRGBToGray (full range), which gives different output from the default build's limited-range formula.
- HSV conversion can use an approximate SSSE3 reciprocal, and its expected MD5 differs between x86 and ARM, so HSV output is not bit-identical across platforms.

**Status:** Code is still committed to (last commit 2026-09-20 per the verifier) and used in Doubango's commercial SDKs, but it is GPL-3.0, undocumented, has no releases and 143 open issues, so it is copyable mainly for GPL projects willing to vendor a large codebase.

[repo](https://github.com/DoubangoTelecom/compv) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DoubangoTelecom/compv/HEAD/speed_compare%20(core%20i7%20quad%404ghz).txt)

##### FFmpeg (libswscale and filters)  `C`  `LGPL-2.1-or-later (optional parts make the build GPL-2.0-or-later when configured with --enable-gpl, per LICENSE.md); libswscale and vf_convolution.c are LGPL`  `active`  `Tier C`

FFmpeg's libswscale and libavfilter (scale, crop, convolution) run the vips-bench crop/resize/sharpen job about 2.1x faster than ImageMagick 7.

**Beats:** ImageMagick 7.1.1 (magick, convert) — The libvips maintainers' Speed-and-memory-use table (AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04 packages, quickest real time of five runs, whole process including TIFF I/O) lists ffmpeg 7.1.1 at 2.06 s and 1338.36 MB peak against magick 7.1.1 at 4.41 s / 1500.52 MB and convert 4.44 s / 1499.29 MB, about 2.1x faster (derived from page data). Per the 7.1 code, the timed ffmpeg run is strip-TIFF decode, crop, swscale bicubic resize with RGB24 to YUV444P conversion, SSE4 3x3 sharpen on Y/Cb/Cr, and a PackBits YCbCr TIFF write, so it is not the same pixel pipeline as ImageMagick's RGB one.

**Known shortcoming:** libswscale resize at B on the libvips maintainers' wiki run (Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04 packages, 12 August 2025): ffmpeg 7.1.1 2.06 s vs ImageMagick magick 4.41 s. Work is not identical: ffmpeg.sh reads a strip TIFF and uses swscale's default SWS_BICUBIC while im7.sh reads a tiled TIFF, crops on load and uses -filter triangle; the test is IO-dominated. No flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered B to C (retier-10): the libvips wiki's 2.06 s row (dated 12 Aug 2025) cannot come from the committed vips-bench scripts, because ffmpeg.sh was first committed 2025-09-21 and benchmark.sh passed an '-o' option that ffmpeg 7.1 rejects until commit c4dbb24 (2026-04-12), with no re-run afterwards. The pipeline also does different work: FFmpeg's convolution filter is planar-only and tiffenc lacks GBRP, so it converts to limited-range YUV444P, sharpens Y, Cb and Cr and writes a PackBits YCbCr TIFF, not ImageMagick's RGB output.

**How:** libswscale (the 7.1 'legacy' backend) is a separable two-pass scaler. Each input line is converted to a planar intermediate (hand-written SIMD for packed RGB24 to Y/UV in x86 input.asm), filtered horizontally with precomputed per-pixel taps into 15-bit samples (hscale8to15 kernels specialised by filter size, AVX2 versions in scale_avx2.asm), then combined vertically from a ring buffer of lines (yuv2planeX, AVX2 yuv2yuvX). The scale filter hands swscale the filter graph's thread count, so it runs slice-threaded. The convolution filter is slice-threaded too, and for 8-bit 3x3 kernels on x86-64 it uses the ff_filter_3x3_sse4 assembly kernel. Master adds a new graph-based swscale with chained 'ops' SIMD kernels, a JIT and a Vulkan SPIR-V backend, but swscale.h says these backends are auto-selected only with SWS_UNSTABLE.

**Use it when:**
- Frames are already in an FFmpeg pipeline (decode, filter, encode) and you need resize, crop or format conversion without leaving libav*: libswscale is the standard choice there.
- Batch command-line jobs on many-core x86-64 boxes where ImageMagick 7 is the current tool and the format is something FFmpeg reads (strip TIFF, PNG, JPEG, video frames). In the libvips table, ffmpeg 7.1.1 took 2.06 s versus 4.41 s for magick on a 16-core Threadripper PRO 3955WX, with about 160 MB less peak memory (1338 MB versus 1500 MB).
- Pixel-format conversion between YUV and RGB families with many supported layouts (8-16 bit, planar and packed, alpha), where breadth matters more than the last factor of speed.
- Simple fixed-kernel sharpen or blur on 8-bit planar data: the convolution filter's SSE4 3x3 path plus slice threading is cheap to use from a filter string.

**Skip it when:**
- Still-image batch processing where speed and memory matter most. In the same table libvips (vips-c 8.18) took 0.57 s and 94 MB against ffmpeg's 2.06 s and 1338 MB, and GraphicsMagick 1.4 matched ffmpeg (2.05 s).
- High-quality resizing in a video pipeline: zimg's README reports a Lanczos FHD-to-UHD resize in 7.7 ms versus 15.2 ms for swscale 4.0.2 (i7-8565U), and libyuv-style converters beat swscale on YUV/RGB conversion.
- RGB-exact or colour-managed image work. Filters that accept only planar formats force hidden conversions, and with the vips-bench filter string the RGB image is converted to limited-range YUV 4:4:4 before the sharpen (see gotchas).
- Tiled TIFF input: the benchmark had to feed ffmpeg a strip TIFF because its TIFF decoder does not read tiled TIFF (benchmark.sh comment).
- Projects that cannot accept LGPL obligations, or builds configured with --enable-gpl (then GPL-2.0-or-later).

**Integration:** shared or static libraries (libswscale, libavfilter, libavutil, plus libavcodec/libavformat for file I/O) built with FFmpeg's configure/make, or the ffmpeg CLI · libswscale needs only libavutil. libavfilter's scale filter needs libswscale. Reading and writing TIFF needs libavcodec and libavformat. The x86 SIMD sources are NASM-syntax .asm files, so an assembler is needed at build time to get the fast paths. · Not documented in the files read this session (FFmpeg's configure script sets the requirements). · Any OS FFmpeg builds on. libswscale has SIMD directories for x86, aarch64, arm, loongarch, ppc and riscv, and master adds a Vulkan backend. On x86 the AVX2 horizontal scaler is skipped on CPUs flagged SLOW_GATHER (AMD family 0x19 and earlier, Intel Haswell-class), so the 3955WX in the benchmark ran the SSE-class hscale kernels.

**Vs siblings:** Pick FFmpeg when the data already lives in an FFmpeg decode/encode pipeline or you need its breadth of pixel formats. Pick libvips for still-image batch work (3.6x faster than ffmpeg in the same table with about a fourteenth of the peak memory, derived from page data). Pick zimg for higher-quality, faster resampling of video frames, and libyuv or yuv2rgb for raw YUV/RGB conversion.

**Gotchas:**
- Hidden format conversion: in release/7.1, convolution accepts only planar formats (no packed RGB24), and the TIFF encoder accepts RGB24, RGBA, gray, PAL8 and planar YUV but not GBRP. Format negotiation therefore picks YUV444P as the closest common format to the RGB24 input (pick_format with av_find_best_pix_fmt_of_2), and the encoder declares limited-range YUV. The vips-bench command sharpens Y, Cb and Cr planes and writes a YCbCr TIFF, not an RGB one. Insert format=gbrp before convolution and convert back to rgb24 explicitly if you need RGB output, and check the choice with -loglevel debug ('picking ... out of').
- Defaults differ from ImageMagick: the scale filter passes no flags, so libswscale uses its SWS_BICUBIC default. ffmpeg's TIFF encoder compresses with PackBits by default (compression_algo), while ImageMagick writes uncompressed TIFF here. Both add work on ffmpeg's side, so they do not inflate its result, but outputs are not byte-comparable.
- Speed depends on CPU generation and backend: the AVX2 gather-based hscale is disabled on Zen 1-3 and Haswell, and the new swscale ops/JIT backends in master are used only with SWS_UNSTABLE ('may be faster, slower, or produce different output').
- The GitHub repository is a read-only mirror. Its README says GitHub pull requests are ignored and patches go to the ffmpeg-devel mailing list, so do not look for bug reports or reviews there.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-03, libswscale major version 10 on master with a new frame-based API). LGPL-2.1-or-later unless built with --enable-gpl. Usable as libraries, but too large to vendor piecemeal.

[repo](https://github.com/FFmpeg/FFmpeg) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/libvips/libvips/Speed-and-memory-use.md)

##### jsColorEngine  `JavaScript (optional WebAssembly SIMD kernels)`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-JavaScript ICC colour engine with WebAssembly SIMD CLUT kernels; 3.1-3.6x faster than lcms-wasm on 8-bit LUT image transforms.

**Beats:** Little CMS 2 (lcms2 2.18 native built with gcc at -O2 and -O3; lcms-wasm = LittleCMS 2.16 compiled to WebAssembly) — The README 'Current figures' table (Ryzen 7 7700X, one thread, Node v24.16.0 on Windows 10, 1 MPx from a 5-photo corpus, GRACoL2006 and AdobeRGB1998, relative colorimetric, 8-bit) gives int-wasm-simd at 78.6-120.3 MPx/s. That is 3.1-3.6x lcms-wasm 1.0.5 (LittleCMS 2.16 built with Emscripten, flags not stated) and 1.8-2.2x native lcms2 2.18 (gcc 9.3.0 -O2/-O3 under WSL2, taskset -c 0). None of these README rows appears in any generated table. The frozen same-run snapshot bench/history/1.6.0 (2026-08-22: BenchResults.md plus native-content-O2/O3.txt) gives jsCE SIMD 112.2/113/81.2/81/110.6 MPx/s against best cached native lcms at 66.4/61.5/39.7/35.8/57.1, which is 1.69/1.84/2.05/2.26/1.94x (derived from page data). On photos lcms's cmsFLAGS_NOCACHE build is faster (72.8/65.6/40.1/35.8/61.5), so against lcms's best configuration the margin is 1.54-2.26x (derived from page data). The README's RGB-to-Lab 3.6x over lcms-wasm does not follow from any published lcms-wasm figure (120.3/35.9 = 3.35x; the 1.6.0 table says 3.2x).

**Known shortcoming:** JavaScript library with optional WebAssembly SIMD kernels (language-filter mismatch); neither ImageMagick nor stb_image_resize was tested. The native-C comparison (bench/lcms_c, gcc 9.3.0, -O2/-O3, Ryzen 7700X) is still being re-measured after issue #6, where the Little-CMS author pointed out wrong API calls; README figures differ from docs/BenchResults.md and LcmsComparison.md, and the 328 vs 119 MPx/s row compares the jsCE kernel with its own CLUT path, not with lcms.

**Known shortcoming:** The README table (120.3/119.3/78.6/80.8/115.9) matches no generated file; the frozen same-run snapshot bench/history/1.6.0/win32-x64-amd-ryzen-7-7700x-8-core (native-content-O2/O3.txt plus BenchResults.md, 2026-08-22) is the reproducible source and its native harness already runs flags=0 / NOCACHE. The README ratio against native uses cached lcms2 although NOCACHE is faster on photos: derived 1.6.0 ratios are 1.69-2.26x against cached and 1.54-2.26x against NOCACHE (README says 1.8-2.2x); the RGB to Lab 3.6x against lcms-wasm is not derivable (120.3/35.9 = 3.35x; the 1.6.0 table says 3.2x). The lcms_c README's fast_float '3-4x' claim is stale (old 256-colour generator); the pixelCache 'auto' default since 1.6.0 lifts flat-content figures.

**How:** When the transform is created, the whole profile chain is sampled into a u16 CLUT (33^3 for RGB input, 17^4 for CMYK input, the same grid sizes lcms2's _cmsReasonableGridpointsByColorspace picks by default). Each pixel is then evaluated with tetrahedral interpolation and Q0.16 weights, in hand-written WebAssembly (.wat). The SIMD is channel-parallel: the 3-4 output channels at each tetrahedron corner are loaded into one i32x4 vector (v128.load64_zero + i32x4.extend_low_i16x8_u), so all channels of a pixel are interpolated at once. There is one monomorphic kernel per (input dims x output channels x data format), picked at create(). Stock lcms2 interpolates with scalar code behind a general stage walker, so the project's own analysis puts the ~2x over native C down to 128-bit width, not a better algorithm. Since 1.5.5, RGB-to-RGB matrix-shaper pairs skip the CLUT and run a fused curve-3x3-curve kernel (328-331 MPx/s at int8 on photos).

**Use it when:**
- JavaScript or TypeScript code (Node, browsers, Electron, web workers, Adobe CEP panels) that converts images between ICC profiles and would otherwise install lcms-wasm.
- 8-bit photographic content of about 1 MPx or more, where one core sustains roughly 80-120 MPx/s on RGB/CMYK LUT workflows (Ryzen 7 7700X, Node 24).
- Soft-proofing or prepress previews in the browser or on a headless server where WebGL/WebGPU shaders are not an option.
- Folders of images on a multicore Node host: transformImages() peaked at 787 MPx/s on 8 workers (noise content, int kernel) with output byte-identical to the sequential path.
- Shipping a baked, content-signed LUT JSON (Transform.fromJSON) instead of the ICC profiles themselves.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ code bases: there is no native API. Use lcms2 (with the GPL3 fast_float plugin for matrix-shaper RGB) or moxcms from Rust.
- Work that needs bit-identical output to LittleCMS: the image path is within 1 LSB of lcms on 100% of samples but only 96.8-99.2% bit-exact. The f64 path (buildLut: false) is an order of magnitude slower.
- Matrix-shaper RGB-to-RGB at peak speed: lcms2 with fast_float reaches about 455 MPx/s (SSE2) against jsCE's 328-331 MPx/s fused kernel. WebAssembly SIMD is fixed at 128 bits, so AVX2/AVX-512 native code can always go wider.
- Memory-constrained parallel use: each worker holds its own copy of every LUT (about 1.4 MB for a 33-point CMYK LUT, about 11.5 MB across 8 workers, plus a WASM copy per worker), where lcms's threaded plugin shares one.
- Named-colour (ncl2), abstract or ColorSpace-class profiles and MPE-only profiles are unsupported. N-channel input is slow: 5CLR and 6CLR got only WASM-scalar LUT kernels in 1.6.0 (16.4 and 7.66 MPx/s), and 7-15CLR input has no LUT path at all, so it runs per pixel on the accuracy pipeline.

**Integration:** module (npm package jscolorengine; CommonJS source, or a UMD bundle of about 115 KB gzip with the WASM inlined) · none at runtime (canvas, esbuild, jest, utif and wabt are dev-only) · not documented (no engines field); the top tier needs a WebAssembly engine with 128-bit SIMD, and the dispatcher falls back to WASM scalar and then pure JS · any JavaScript host: Node, browsers, Electron, web workers, React Native, Adobe CEP; results quoted for x86-64 Windows and Apple M4

**Vs siblings:** Pick jsColorEngine when the code has to run inside a JavaScript or WebAssembly host. In C or C++, stay with Little CMS 2 plus the fast_float plugin, and in Rust use moxcms. babl is GEGL/GIMP's pixel-format converter rather than a general ICC CMYK engine.

**Gotchas:**
- lutMode 'auto' picks int-wasm-simd only for int8/int16 data with buildLut: true; every other combination resolves to the slow 'float' path. Check xform.lutMode after create().
- pixelCache defaults to 'auto' since 1.6.0. The in-kernel last-pixel memo gains up to 3.94x on flat colour, costs about 4% on noisy photos and runs 5-channel photos at 0.84x; set pixelCache: 0 for grainy input.
- Throughput depends on CLUT coverage. Buffers under about 1x the CLUT cell count (for example 64K px against a 17^4 CMYK grid) or synthetic gradients read up to 1.8x high. The project withdrew its pre-1.5 figures (about 210-216 MPx/s) because its noise generator produced only 256 distinct colours.
- Premultiplied-alpha pixels must be unpremultiplied first (alpha.unpremultiply). Before 1.6.1 (issue #9), profiles loaded from a Uint8Array view with a non-zero byteOffset, as embedded in TIFF or JPEG, were silently mis-parsed.

**Status:** Active, single maintainer: 1.6.1 shipped on 2026-09-10, the last commit is 2026-09-09 (195 commits) and no issues are open. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft and fine to vendor into JS applications, but the library is not usable from C++ without embedding a JS/WASM runtime.

[repo](https://github.com/glennwilton/jsColorEngine) · [benchmark](https://github.com/glennwilton/jsColorEngine/blob/main/README.md)

##### libvips  `C`  `LGPL-2.1-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

Demand-driven, horizontally threaded C image library; author's crop/resize/sharpen TIFF test: 7.8x faster than ImageMagick 7 convert, 16x less memory.

**Beats:** ImageMagick 7.1.1 (convert/magick) — The libvips author's vips-bench test (load a 10,000 x 10,000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 px per edge, 90% bilinear shrink, 3x3 sharpen, save; quickest real time of five warm-cache runs; RSS sampled with ps) on a 16-core Threadripper PRO 3955WX under Ubuntu 25.04 reports the vips.c program at 0.57 s and 94 MB peak against ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert at 4.44 s and 1499 MB (magick 4.41 s), with both given 16 threads. The ImageMagick side is the Ubuntu package at its default 16-bit quantum; the libvips side was an unreleased 8.18 development build of unknown compiler and flags, and outputs were not compared.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers are the libvips wiki table (vips-c 0.57 s and 94.28 MB vs ImageMagick convert 4.44 s and 1499.29 MB) measured with distro packages and no compiler flags; memory and single-thread ratios are derived from page data. Outputs differ: libvips integer convolution vs ImageMagick Q16.

**Known shortcoming:** Provenance flaw in the wiki table: the rows say libvips 8.18 and sat in the 15 Aug 2025 revision 112504a, but 8.18.0 was released 17 Dec 2025, so libvips was an unreleased git build (flags and Highway state unknown) rather than the Ubuntu package used for the others. im.sh and im7.sh run vipsheader twice inside the timed ImageMagick script; only real time is measured (vips-bench issue #7 open since 2017); exit status and output are never checked; the pipeline is 8-bit integer against ImageMagick's 16-bit quantum. 8.18.1 had an integer-convolution underflow (#4955), fixed in 8.18.2.

**How:** Pixels stream through the pipeline as small overlapping regions instead of whole images, so memory stays near the working set (94 MB peak for a 300 MB image in the table). Threading lives in the image I/O system: each worker gets its own light copy of the whole pipeline (horizontal threading, almost lock-free), and a separate write-behind thread overlaps output with compute. Hot kernels have Google Highway SIMD paths with runtime dispatch, chosen when Highway is present at build time: vips_reduce precomputes 16-bit fixed-point filter tables per sub-pixel position and uses a vector path for 3- and 4-band uchar images, and the integer convolution turns the mask into 8-bit mantissas with a shared exponent for a uchar vector path. Orc run-time code generation is the fallback when Highway is absent.

**Use it when:**
- Server-side batch or request-time processing of large images (thumbnails, resize, crop, sharpen, colour conversion) where peak memory per job matters, for example many concurrent jobs per box.
- Very large inputs (gigapixel TIFF, OpenSlide whole-slide images, image pyramids via dzsave) that do not fit comfortably in RAM.
- Multi-core machines where you want a whole load-process-save pipeline parallelised without writing threading code; the single-threaded row (VIPS_CONCURRENCY=1) was still 0.77 s against 4.44 s for 16-thread convert.
- Applications already on Node (sharp), Ruby on Rails (ActiveStorage), Python (pyvips) or Go that want a mature native engine through an existing binding.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a single fast in-memory resize kernel with no I/O: specialised resizers in this catalog beat libvips on that narrower task (see siblings).
- Scripts that depend on ImageMagick's command-line syntax, its format coverage or its specific filter behaviour: the vips CLI is a different language, and the vips CLI writes intermediate files to disc (the wiki warns of heavy disc traffic; vips-cli row 1.25 s vs 0.57 s for the C program).
- Random-access operations on formats with only sequential decoders (JPEG, PNG) at large sizes: libvips must decompress them fully to memory or a temporary file first, which costs time and space.
- Projects that cannot meet LGPL-2.1 linking obligations, or that must avoid the large attack surface of optional loaders such as ImageMagick or PDF libraries when handling untrusted files (the README itself warns about this).

**Integration:** shared lib (static possible with meson --default-library static); also distro packages and Windows binaries · Required: glib-2.0 (>= 2.52) and expat. Optional, picked up by pkg-config: libjpeg(-turbo/mozjpeg), libtiff, libpng or spng, libwebp, libheif, libjxl, OpenJPEG, lcms2, fftw3, cgif, libimagequant, pangocairo, librsvg, poppler or PDFium, OpenSlide, OpenEXR, cfitsio, matio, libraw, ImageMagick/GraphicsMagick, and Highway (preferred) or Orc for SIMD. · Meson (README says 0.56+, meson.build declares >= 0.55); C++14 required since 8.18.0, C sources built as gnu11, and the 8.19 ChangeLog formally raises the toolchain requirement to C11. Default meson buildtype is release. · Linux, macOS, other Unix-likes and Windows. SIMD through Highway runtime dispatch (x86-64 and ARM targets; big-endian Highway paths fixed in 8.18.1), else Orc, else plain C.

**Vs siblings:** Pick libvips for complete load-process-save pipelines on large images where memory and core usage matter: in the same table it beats Pillow-SIMD (1.51 s), GraphicsMagick (2.05 s), FFmpeg (2.06 s), OpenCV (3.15 s) and OpenImageIO (3.46 s). Pick fast_image_resize (which beats libvips 8.15.1 single-threaded on pure RGB8 resize kernels, e.g. Lanczos3 13.52 vs 17.31 ms) or Pillow-SIMD when you only need an in-memory resize inside Rust or Python.

**Gotchas:**
- Access mode matters: vips_image_new_from_file defaults to random access, which for JPEG/PNG-style formats means full decompression to memory (under about 100 MB) or to a temporary disc file. Pass access=VIPS_ACCESS_SEQUENTIAL for top-to-bottom pipelines. The benchmark uses uncompressed tiled TIFF, which libtiff can read randomly, the best case for libvips (jpg-vips-c: 0.82 s and 286 MB vs 0.57 s and 94 MB for tiled TIFF).
- Integer convolution on uchar images takes a vector path that rounds the mask to 8-bit mantissas with a shared exponent and only falls back to the exact C path if the mask's DC response is off by more than 2 levels. The benchmark mask (-1 x8, 16, scale 8) is exactly representable, but other masks can give slightly different results from the C path.
- Avoid 8.18.1: issue #4955 reports white artifacts from an underflow in integer convolution with a sharpening mask (introduced in 8.18.1, fixed in 8.18.2, 'convolution: avoid using unsigned accumulators').
- Error handling is a single -1/NULL return plus a process-global error buffer, so under concurrency the message in the buffer may not belong to the failure you just saw.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-02, 8.18.7 released 20 Sep 2026, 8.19 in development, OSS-Fuzz coverage and a steady stream of hardening fixes); LGPL-2.1-or-later, so link dynamically or meet the relinking terms if you ship it.

[repo](https://github.com/libvips/libvips) · [benchmark](https://github.com/libvips/libvips/wiki/Speed-and-memory-use)

##### Little-CMS fast_float plugin  `C`  `GPL-3.0-or-later for the fast_float plugin (plugins/fast_float source headers say 'version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later version'; COPYING.GPL3 in that directory; the plugin PDF says a paid alternative licence is available from the author). The lcms2 core in the same repo is MIT.`  `active`  `Tier C`

GPL-3.0 add-on for Little CMS 2 that swaps stock transforms for precomputed-table, SSE2 and 15-bit kernels; about 7x on one Lab-to-RGB float case.

**Beats:** Little CMS 2 (lcms2) stock transforms — One RawTherapee developer (issue #6016, Dec 2020) reported that the Lab-to-RGB output transform for a 45.6 MP export took 5312 ms with stock lcms2 and 754 ms with the plugin (about 7x). No CPU, thread count, compiler, flags or lcms2 commit are given. lcms2 since 2.11 skips plugins under cmsFLAGS_NOOPTIMIZE, which RawTherapee's lab2rgbOut still passes, so that run must have used locally modified RawTherapee code that was not published on the issue page as read here. The fast path for that case is the 51^3 tetrahedral Lab grid, an approximation of stock output whose error the testbed reports but does not bound.

**Known shortcoming:** Plugin licence is GPL-3.0-or-later (headers and COPYING.GPL3) while the Little-CMS core is MIT. The only numbers are issue #6016 (5312 vs 754 ms) with no methodology. The plugin trades accuracy for speed: its testbed allows a float difference of 0.005.

**Known shortcoming:** The only number needs an unpublished patched build (retier-18): RawTherapee's lab2rgbOut passes cmsFLAGS_NOOPTIMIZE and lcms2 2.11+ skips transform plugins under that flag; RawTherapee does not use the plugin (issue #6016 open, no cmsFastFloatExtensions call in its sources). The 7x path is a 51^3 tetrahedral Lab CLUT approximation (L clamped to 0..100, a/b to plus or minus 128). Autotools builds the plugin with -Ofast (isnan guards may vanish); SSE2 only, no NEON; past wrong-output bugs #272, #325 (about 100x off in 2.13.1) and #247 (Krita), and segfaults #236 and #260, all closed.

**How:** At transform creation the dispatcher tries, in order, 15-bit matrix-shaper, joined 8-bit curves, an SSE2 8-bit matrix-shaper (float matrix on 1.14 fixed-point shaper tables, chosen after a runtime cpuid check), a plain 8-bit matrix-shaper, joined float curves, a float matrix-shaper, 8-bit and 16-bit prelinearization plus tetrahedral CLUT, and float CLUTs for RGB, CMYK and Lab input. The float Lab-input path (fast_float_lab.c) resamples the whole Lab-to-device pipeline into a 51^3 float grid (33 with cmsFLAGS_LOWRESPRECALC, 66 with HIGHRESPRECALC), puts a sigmoid on the a*/b* axes, and evaluates each pixel with tetrahedral interpolation. Stock lcms2 instead runs every float pipeline stage per pixel (its own optimizers skip float formats). So the speedup comes from replacing exact evaluation with table lookups, not only from SIMD.

**Use it when:**
- You already use lcms2 and run float-to-float transforms (Gray, RGB, CMYK or Lab input) on large images, e.g. a raw developer's working-space-to-output step.
- 8-bit RGB or CMYK transforms on whole images, where the precomputed curve, matrix and tetrahedral tables pay off over millions of pixels.
- Pipelines that hold Photoshop 1.15 fixed-point data (TYPE_*_15) or need dithered 8-bit output to reduce banding.
- Your application is GPL-3.0-compatible, or you will buy the commercial licence the plugin PDF offers.
- You want speed and keep full ICC v4 profile support: profile parsing and pipeline construction are still done by lcms2.

**Skip it when:**
- Closed-source or MIT-only products that cannot accept GPL-3.0-or-later and will not buy the alternate licence. The lcms2 core is MIT; this plugin is not.
- Workflows that need bit-identical output to stock lcms2. The testbed accepts float differences up to 0.005 (EPSILON_FLOAT_TESTS) and 0.007 in another check. For the Lab float path, CheckLab2RGB only prints the maximum RGB distance and asserts no limit.
- Soft-proofing or gamut-check transforms (the dispatcher refuses cmsFLAGS_SOFTPROOFING), reversed-polarity (FLAVOR) formats, or transforms that later need cmsChangeBuffersFormat().
- Small per-call batches, e.g. one pixel per call or per-scanline calls. The PDF says creating the transform and starting a call are costly, and it recommends one cmsDoTransformLineStride() call over many lines.
- Unbounded or out-of-range float Lab input. The Lab kernel clamps L* to 0..100 and a*/b* to -128..128 before indexing the grid.

**Integration:** static or shared lib (liblcms2_fast_float), built from the plugins/fast_float directory of the lcms2 source tree; off by default in autotools, meson and CMake · lcms2 2.12 or newer (REQUIRED_LCMS_VERSION 2120), libm · C99 compiler (also compiles as C++ since 2.12); autotools, meson or CMake 3.16+; Visual Studio project in plugins/fast_float/VC2022 · Any platform lcms2 supports. The SSE2 8-bit matrix-shaper kernel is x86 only, with runtime detection, and CMS_DONT_USE_SSE2 disables it. Every other kernel is portable scalar C, and there are no NEON or AVX kernels.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over moxcms (Rust) or jsColorEngine (JS/WASM) when you are in C or C++, already depend on lcms2's full ICC v4.4 implementation, and want the speedup without changing your colour-management code. Pick babl only inside GEGL/GIMP. moxcms publishes reproducible numbers against lcms2, while this plugin has only one anecdotal number.

**Gotchas:**
- cmsFLAGS_NOOPTIMIZE silently disables the plugin. In lcms2 2.11, 2.12 and current master, AllocEmptyTransform calls transform plugins only when that flag is clear, and the plugin PDF does not mention this. RawTherapee's current lab2rgbOut creates its Lab_FLT-to-RGB_FLT transform with cmsFLAGS_NOOPTIMIZE | cmsFLAGS_NOCACHE.
- The autotools build compiles the plugin with -Ofast (plugins/fast_float/src/Makefile.am). That flag implies -ffast-math, under which the isnan() guards in fclamp, flerp and fclamp128 may be optimised away. The meson build does not add -Ofast.
- Past wrong-output and crash bugs in the plugin's issue history, all closed now: #272 (8-bit RGB to Lab with Optimize8BitRGBTransform), #325 (float sRGB to Lab off by about 100x in 2.13.1), #247 (Krita, broken or transparent tiles with cLUT display profiles), #236 and #260 (segfaults). Test your own profiles against stock lcms2 before switching.
- On aarch64 nothing is vectorised. PR #549 (March 2026) fixed an ARM64 compile failure in the SSE2 file, so older releases may not build there.

**Status:** Actively maintained in the lcms2 repo (last commit 2026-10-02; the ChangeLog says the formerly commercial plugin was open-sourced under GPL3 in 2.10). It is copyable under GPL-3.0-or-later or a paid licence, while the lcms2 core stays MIT. Correction to the record: RawTherapee does not ship it. Issue #6016 is still open, and RawTherapee's dev CMakeLists.txt, rtengine/iccstore.cc, rtengine/init.cc and rtgui/main.cc never call cmsFastFloatExtensions.

[repo](https://github.com/mm2/Little-CMS) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Beep6581/RawTherapee/issues/6016)

##### pngquant / libimagequant  `C`  `GPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

Lossy PNG palette quantizer (CLI plus libimagequant library); author claims its fast setting is 2.5-6x ImageMagick's quantizer.

**Beats:** ImageMagick's built-in colour quantization (an old ImageMagick 6-era version, not stated); no pngnq, Pillow quantize or other baseline numbers were found in the repo — The only comparison with the baseline is first-party and snippet-only: a 'fast and rough' libimagequant setting said to be 2.5 to 6 times faster than ImageMagick's then-current quantizer 'while still mostly winning in quality', from the author's proposal thread on the legacy ImageMagick forum (blocked; no images, versions, settings, compiler or hardware). The repo's own figure, speed 10 being about 8x faster than the default at about 5% lower quality, is a self-comparison, and the repo's bench file (benches/bench.rs) times only libimagequant on a private image (/Users/kornel/Desktop/canvas.png) with no baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** The 'ImageMagick 2.5 to 6 times' claim is snippet-only, tracing to the author's legacy ImageMagick forum thread (t=23340, blocked here), and compares pngquant's fast setting with ImageMagick's quantizer at different quality and dithering work; no pngnq or Pillow numbers exist anywhere. The 8x figure is speed 10 against pngquant's own default. The engine (libimagequant) is now Rust (pngquant 3) with a C CLI.

**Known shortcoming:** The ImageMagick 2.5-6x claim is snippet-only and first-party, measured on the old C libimagequant 2.x (the engine is now Rust) at speed 10 (no k-means, no feedback trials, no dither maps), so it is not equal work. Output is not deterministic (libimagequant #130: x86_64 versus aarch64 palettes of 111 versus 120 colours; dither chunk count follows available_parallelism); README and man page are stale (C99, OpenMP, default speed 3); open #424 (desaturated colours versus ImageMagick); benches/bench.rs has no baseline and uses a private image.

**How:** A histogram of 32-bit colours goes into a hash map (posterized to fewer bits at speeds 8-10 or past a million colours), then a variance-driven modified median cut builds the palette, refined by weighted k-means (Voronoi) iterations in a feedback loop. Nearest-colour search uses a vantage-point tree with a 'likely index' shortcut and a half-distance-to-nearest-neighbour early exit. The colour distance (premultiplied alpha, max of over-black and over-white error) is a 4-lane SSE, NEON or WASM simd128 routine. The speed knob trades work directly: speed 4 (default) runs 12 k-means iterations and 20 feedback trials over up to 1.7M histogram entries, speed 10 runs no k-means, no feedback loop, no dither or contrast maps and caps the histogram at 131,072 entries; k-means, remap and dithering run on rayon threads.

**Use it when:**
- Shrinking PNG assets for the web or apps where 8-bit palette plus full alpha is acceptable (README: often 60-80% smaller than 24/32-bit PNG).
- Real-time palette generation (map tiles, GIF frames) with --speed 10/11 or liq_set_speed(10), where the author says quality drops about 5% for about 8x the speed of the default.
- Batch pipelines that need a quality gate: --quality min-max plus --skip-if-larger rejects images that would degrade too much.
- C or Rust code that needs a palette quantizer with alpha-aware dithering, fixed palette colours, importance maps or remapping onto a background (GIF animation).
- GPL-3.0-or-later projects, or closed-source ones willing to buy the commercial licence.

**Skip it when:**
- Permissive-licence products that cannot take GPL-3.0-or-later and will not pay for the commercial licence.
- Pure C/C++ toolchains that cannot add Rust: since libimagequant 4 / pngquant 3 the engine is Rust (C ABI kept), so building needs cargo; the C99 code lives only on the unmaintained 2.x branch.
- Pipelines that need bit-identical output across machines: open libimagequant issue #130 shows palettes of 111 vs 120 colours for the same image on x86_64 and aarch64 at speeds 1-7, and dithered remapping splits large images into chunks by core count (see gotchas).
- When you need a quality or speed comparison against ImageMagick, Pillow or libvips you can trust: none is published in either repo, and open issue #424 reports desaturated colours from pngquant --nofs where ImageMagick's PNG8 output looked right.
- Images that must keep more than 256 colours, or 16-bit precision: output is 8-bit palette (the large_palettes feature goes to 2048 colours but not for remapping).

**Integration:** CLI binary (Rust main plus C rwpng.c/pngquant.c via the cc crate); library as Rust crate imagequant or static lib libimagequant_sys.a with libimagequant.h (cargo-c for a shared lib) · CLI: libpng (libpng-sys), zlib, optional Little CMS 2 (default feature) or Cocoa on macOS, getopts, rayon via imagequant. Library: arrayvec, rgb, rayon and thread_local (threads feature); no runtime deps for C users of the static lib. · Rust 1.67 for pngquant 3.0.4 (Cargo.toml rust-version; libimagequant says 1.65 in Cargo.toml and 1.70+ in its README), plus a C99 compiler for the CLI's C files · Any Rust target; SIMD colour distance on x86_64 (SSE), aarch64 (NEON) and wasm32 (simd128), scalar elsewhere; threads must be disabled for WASM; no_std build available without threads

**Vs siblings:** No catalogued sibling is a palette quantizer: the siblings resize, convert colour spaces or manage ICC profiles. Pillow can call libimagequant itself (its quantize method has a libimagequant option when Pillow is built against it), so use pngquant/libimagequant directly when you want the quality gate, the speed knob and alpha-aware dithering, and Pillow's own fast-octree mode only when speed matters more than colour fidelity.

**Gotchas:**
- Stale docs: the pngquant README still says C99, OpenMP and SSE, and pngquant.1 says the default speed is 3; the code (pngquant.c help, imagequant set_speed) uses 4, threading is rayon, and libimagequant's README says OpenMP 'has been dropped entirely'. The C file's version string still reads '(January 2022)'.
- Speed 11 exists only in the CLI: it maps to library speed 10 plus --nofs and fast PNG compression; liq_set_speed accepts 1-10.
- Dithered output depends on the machine: remap_to_palette_floyd splits images over about 1 MP into up to num_cpus() chunks (std::thread::available_parallelism, not RAYON_NUM_THREADS), and each chunk restarts error diffusion after two warm-up rows, so results can differ between machines with different core counts.
- The palette is refined during remapping (one more k-means pass), so read the palette after remap_into, not before; quality numbers can be -1 at high speeds unless a quality range is set.

**Status:** Active (pngquant last commit 2026-06-21, libimagequant 4.5.0 with commits on 2026-06-21 and a WASM SIMD path added 2026-02-11), dual-licensed GPL-3.0-or-later or commercial, so copyable under copyleft; the C 2.x branch is the only all-C option and is not maintained.

[repo](https://github.com/kornelski/pngquant) · [benchmark](https://jqmagick.imagemagick.org/discourse-server/viewtopic.php?t=23340)

#### image-codecs

##### fNBLI (NBLI lossless image codec)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-threaded AVX2 lossless codec for 8-bit gray and 24-bit RGB; 7.8x faster encode than Pillow PNG with 33% smaller files.

**Beats:** PNG encoded and decoded through Pillow 10.1.0's own PNG codec (PngImagePlugin over Pillow's zlib-based 'zip' codec, not libpng), optipng 0.7.7 for optimized PNG encoding, and libwebp lossless via Pillow 10.1.0 — The author's own Image-Compression-Benchmark ran the prebuilt fNBLI.exe v0.4 (compiler and flags unknown) once per image through os.system on an i7-12700H under Windows 10, single-threaded, with file I/O included and the round trip checked for losslessness. On CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.09 GB) fNBLI took 43.164 s to compress and 27.450 s to decompress, producing 1,337,587,020 bytes. Pillow 10.1.0's in-process PNG took 334.791 s and 33.677 s for 2,003,016,524 bytes (7.8x faster encode, 1.23x faster decode, 33% smaller, derived), and Pillow WebP lossless method 5 took 1112.134 s and 49.442 s.

**Known shortcoming:** Author-run shootout (CLIC2021: 43.164 s vs 27.450 s) with fNBLI.exe's compiler and flags unstated; the fNBLI source was published 2026-07-18 (src/fNBLI, commit 6561fc8, GPL-3.0). The Pillow PNG baseline is Pillow's own zlib codec rather than libpng, and Pillow runs in-process while fNBLI pays a per-file os.system start. Decode is slower than optipng's PNG (27.450 vs 26.625 s).

**Known shortcoming:** AVX2 and x86 only (intrinsics lack target attributes, so -mavx2 is required), and the bitstream depends on the encoder's CPU: AVX2-encoded files return NULL on non-AVX2 decoders; no macOS build (static_assert); no build recipe, and the shipped binary is not rebuilt from source. The decoder is unhardened: fNBLIdecompress takes no input length, crafted histogram codes can write past the 512-entry histogram and the 16,384-entry decode LUT (heap overflow), and the gathers over-read up to 3 bytes.

**How:** It uses a CALIC-style pixel pipeline. A reversible lifting colour transform (G as luma, R-G and B-G as chroma) feeds a gradient-adjusted predictor that blends a 6-tap linear predictor with the left or upper neighbour depending on edge direction. An activity measure quantized to 12 levels, times an 8-bit texture pattern, indexes CALIC-style bias-correction contexts. Residuals go through a two-pass static rANS coder: the encoder collects every (context, symbol) pair, normalizes one 512-symbol 14-bit histogram per coding context (24 in total), then codes in reverse. The speed comes from processing 16 image rows at once in a diagonal wavefront (each row 2 pixels behind the row above), with the predictor, context lookups (AVX2 gathers) and 16 interleaved rANS states running in AVX2 lanes. That gives data parallelism in one thread without changing the model, which the README presents as a 'parallel entropy encoding method that does not affect the compression ratio'.

**Use it when:**
- Archiving or caching large photographic RGB or gray images that only your own software reads, where you want JPEG-XL-e7-class size (1,337.6 MB vs 1,337.1 MB on CLIC2021) at 62x the encode speed and 9x the decode speed (derived).
- Replacing PNG in an internal pipeline where PNG encode time dominates: 7.8x faster encode than Pillow's default PNG and 102x faster than optipng -o2 (derived), with 30-33% smaller files.
- Single-core x86-64 workers with AVX2 (Haswell or newer) processing images with at least 18 rows, 32 columns and 4,096 pixels, up to 32000x32000. Smaller images take the scalar path.
- Research or benchmarking of fast context-modelling lossless coders: the source is short (about 2,800 lines) and shows a vectorized wavefront plus interleaved rANS design.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that must be read by browsers, OS image viewers or other tools: .fnbli is a private format with no spec, a 4-byte magic and no version field, and no alpha, palette or 16-bit support.
- Decode-bound workloads: decoding is no faster than optimized PNG (27.45 s vs 26.63 s for optipng -o2 output on CLIC2021). QOI, QOIR and Zpng decode faster still, at much larger sizes.
- Untrusted input: fNBLIdecompress takes no input length, and the rANS and histogram decoders read and write without bounds checks (a crafted repeat code or histogram can write past the 512-entry histogram or the 16,384-entry decode table), so treat it as unsafe on hostile files.
- Non-x86 or pre-AVX2 targets: the vector code is AVX2 intrinsics only. A file encoded on an AVX2 machine uses the 16-row layout, and fNBLIdecompress returns NULL on a CPU without AVX2. SupportAVX2.h static_asserts unless building for Linux or Windows, so macOS does not build.
- Closed-source or permissive-license products: GPL-3.0.

**Integration:** source-drop (no build system; compile src/fNBLI/*.cpp with ../FileIO.h and src/imageio for the CLI), or the prebuilt fNBLI.exe / Linux fNBLI binaries · none for the codec; the CLI uses the bundled imageio (PNM, uPNG) sources · C++17 (static_assert without message) with GCC or Clang; uses __attribute__((aligned(32))) and AVX2 intrinsics without target attributes, so it needs -mavx2. Exact compiler version not documented · x86-64 with AVX2 (Haswell or later) on Linux or Windows; a scalar path exists for small images and non-AVX2 encoders, but a GCC/Clang build with -mavx2 is AVX2-only anyway

**Vs siblings:** Pick fNBLI over HALIC (same harness: 22.2 s encode, 28.4 s decode, 1,473.5 MB) when about 9% smaller files are worth roughly 2x slower encoding at equal decode speed and you want source code (HALIC is closed). Pick it over QOI, QOIR or Zpng when size matters more than speed: those encode 1.7-2.3x faster and decode 1.1-1.45x faster, but their files are 31-70% larger (derived from CLIC2021). Pick the libjxl fast_lossless/JPEG-XL route or CharLS instead when you need a standard format.

**Gotchas:**
- The bitstream depends on the encoding CPU: an image with at least 18 rows, 32 columns and 4,096 pixels, encoded where AVX2 is present, uses the 16-row wavefront layout and can only be decoded where AVX2 is present. Without AVX2 the encoder silently takes the slower serial path.
- Memory: the encoder allocates about 2.1x the raw image size plus 4 MB (output buffer and symbol stack share one uint16 buffer), and the decoder builds a 768 KB lookup table. The decompress input must be 2-byte aligned or it returns NULL.
- The AVX2 gathers read 4 bytes per element from uint8 and int16 tables and from the caller's pixel buffer, so they read up to 3 bytes past the end of the image and table allocations. This is harmless in practice, but AddressSanitizer or Valgrind will flag it unless buffers are padded.
- CRC32 is optional (-x; crc32 != 0 in the API), uses a slow 4-bit table, and is off in the benchmarked command, so corruption is otherwise undetected. The README's NBLI link points to ./src_NBLI, but the source lives in src/NBLI and src/fNBLI.

**Status:** There are five commits in total: v0.4 dates from October 2024, and the source was opened on 2026-07-18 (commit 6561fc8, no binary rebuilt). The repo has 98 stars, no open issues or PRs and no releases, so it is effectively a finished research artifact under GPL-3.0. It is small enough to vendor, but with no build recipe, tests or format spec.

[repo](https://github.com/WangXuan95/NBLI) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark/HEAD/README.md)

##### Grok JPEG 2000 codec  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0-only`  `active`  `Tier C`

AGPL C++23 JPEG 2000 (Part 1 and HTJ2K) codec. Its GDAL driver beats OpenJPEG on tiled, region and S3 reads.

**Beats:** OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000); also Kakadu (proprietary, via GDAL JP2KAK) — A first-party README table times gdal_translate decodes with the JP2Grok, JP2KAK (Kakadu 8.4.1) and JP2OpenJPEG (2.5.4) drivers on an unnamed '8 core / 16 thread' CPU under Fedora 42, with Grok 20.0.0 built by GCC 15.2. Those details were in the October 2025 README and were removed later. Results: Spot 6 26624x26624 12-bit lossless with TLM, local 26.92 s vs OpenJPEG 52.09 s; the same file on MinIO 35.17 s vs 85 s; an 8000x8000 region of a Pleiades 16-bit lossy file 0.74 s vs 4.28 s. The local-storage OpenJPEG cell was 34.91 s (1.30x) until commit ac33404 (2026-02-26, 'README: update benchmark number') changed only that cell to 52.09 s (1.94x), with no re-run of the Grok or Kakadu cells and no explanation.

**Known shortcoming:** AGPL-3.0-only. First-party GDAL driver table (Grok 20.0 vs OpenJPEG 2.5.4 and Kakadu 8.4; OpenJPEG is not a listed baseline) with no CPU model or flags; benchmark/results.txt holds only 'xx' placeholders. No independent numbers found (encode.su and fastcompression.com blocked here).

**Known shortcoming:** Commit ac33404 (2026-02-26, 'README: update benchmark number') changed only the OpenJPEG local cell from 34.91 s to 52.09 s without re-running the Grok or Kakadu cells or giving a reason, moving the local ratio from 1.30x to 1.94x. The October 2025 README gave an 8-core/16-thread CPU and GCC 15.2 with MinIO at 20 ms while results.txt says 50 ms and one 'MinIO' command reads a local file. The default decoder is now the Rust 'Mercury' path (lossy output shifts by 1 LSB, #425); GDAL 3.13.2 fixed a JP2Grok CopyTileData region-offset bug; vendors the OpenJPH HT coder; OpenJPEG BSD-2 lineage.

**How:** Code-block (T1) decoding and the per-tile pipeline run on a Taskflow work-stealing pool, and the inverse 5/3 and 9/7 lifting wavelets use Google Highway SIMD kernels with an int16 fast path for low-precision data. HTJ2K blocks go through a vendored copy of OpenJPH's BSD-2 HT block coder, with SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512 variants. For the GDAL workflows that were measured, most of the gain comes from I/O: TLM/PLT markers let it fetch and decode only the tiles and packets inside the window, AdviseRead-driven async decode overlaps packet parsing with T1, and cached tile-part offsets and compressed chunks avoid re-walking the codestream or re-fetching from S3. Newer builds also route eligible full-resolution decodes through 'Mercury', a Rust streaming engine (bounded SPSC rings, O(window) buffering). Its README reports ~10.9 s and ~63 MB RSS versus ~14.4 s and multiple GB for the classic pipeline on one HiRISE image.

**Use it when:**
- GDAL pipelines that read large tiled JPEG 2000 satellite or aerial products (Spot, Pleiades) from local disk or S3/MinIO, especially windowed reads of files with TLM markers.
- Remote (S3/HTTP) reads where request count and latency dominate: the first-party network-storage run is 35 s vs OpenJPEG's 85 s, a gap that comes from fetch strategy rather than entropy-decoding speed.
- You need an open-source codec that both reads Part 1 (EBCOT/MQ) files and reads and writes HTJ2K, with multi-threaded decode, and AGPL terms are acceptable.
- Server-side region or overview extraction where the caller can pass the read window up front (AdviseRead in GDAL, or a decode window in the C API).

**Skip it when:**
- Proprietary or permissively licensed products, or network services you cannot open-source: the library is AGPL-3.0-only (no 'or later'). OpenJPEG (BSD-2) or OpenJPH (BSD-2, HTJ2K only) avoid that.
- If you need a codec-only speed claim: the published numbers are end-to-end gdal_translate timings dominated by I/O, caching and region selection, and no single-image decode throughput against OpenJPEG is published.
- Older toolchains: the build sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23, and INSTALL.md asks for GCC 12+, Clang 16+ or MSVC 2022 and CMake 3.20+ (CMakeLists requires 3.21).
- Code that needs a stable decoder: releases arrive every few days (v20.4.5 to v20.4.14 in September 2026 alone), the default decode path changed to the Rust Mercury engine in August 2026, and that change shifts lossy 9/7 output by plus or minus 1 LSB (issue #425).
- Whole-image decode of huge single-tile files on memory-limited hosts: the pre-2025 README showed Grok 9.7.8 using 16.6 GB against Kakadu's 0.05 GB on a HiRISE image (13.74 s vs 9.02 s). Mercury targets this case, but only for eligible streams.

**Integration:** shared lib by default (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS ON), static optional; CMake package and pkg-config; Debian, AUR and Homebrew packages; SWIG Python/C#/Java and Rust bindgen bindings · git submodules Highway, Taskflow (maintainer's fork), spdlog, CLI11; lcms2 (built by default); libcurl for S3/HTTP reads; libtiff, libpng and libjpeg for the command-line tools (built by default); optional Rust toolchain (cargo, rust-version 1.87) for the Mercury fast path; a private, off-by-default CUDA/Metal GPU plugin submodule · C++23; GCC 12+, Clang 16+, MSVC 2022 per INSTALL.md (CMakeLists only rejects GCC < 10); CMake 3.21 · Linux x86-64 and AArch64, Windows, macOS, WebAssembly (Emscripten); runtime SIMD dispatch through Highway; s390x big-endian test failures fixed in issue #418

**Vs siblings:** Pick Grok over OpenJPH when you must read ordinary Part 1 JPEG 2000 or want multi-threaded and region decode of large tiled files; Grok embeds OpenJPH's HT block coder anyway. OpenJPH stays the permissive (BSD-2), dependency-free choice for HTJ2K-only work. CharLS and HALIC are different formats (JPEG-LS, custom) and do not read JPEG 2000 archives.

**Gotchas:**
- Builds differ silently: the Mercury fast path is compiled in only when a working cargo is found at configure time, and otherwise mercury_fastpath.cpp compiles to a no-op. GRK_MERCURY=0 forces the classic pipeline. Mercury rejects HT, BYPASS and RESTART code-block modes, tile-part POC, region and reduced-resolution decodes, and falls back to the classic path for them.
- In GDAL the JP2Grok driver decodes asynchronously only when the caller calls AdviseRead first. Without it the driver falls back to synchronous per-swath decode, which the driver docs call 'much slower, especially when decompressing over the network'.
- The early JP2Grok driver had correctness fixes after release: GDAL 3.13.1 scaled overview coordinates (#14516) and fixed the overview tile-cache strategy, and GDAL 3.13.2 fixed 'CopyTileData was using tile origin as region offset'. Use GDAL 3.13.2 or later.
- Recent correctness issues, all now closed: #420, nondeterministic decoded samples with 4+ threads on macOS arm64 (v20.3.10); #442, rate control silently writes an empty image when an ICC profile exceeds the first layer's byte budget; #427, LTO with AVX-512 constant initialisers.

**Status:** Very active (last commit 2026-10-03, v20.4.14 on 29 Sep, ~1,000 commits, OSS-Fuzz and 2,000+ tests, upstream GDAL driver since 3.13). Copyable only under AGPL-3.0-only, and the LICENSE file shows the code incorporates OpenJPEG's BSD-2 work.

[repo](https://github.com/GrokImageCompression/grok) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GrokImageCompression/grok/HEAD/README.md)

##### oss-nvjpg  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

C++20 driver for the Tegra X1 NVJPG hardware JPEG decoder; README shows 3-4x lower latency than libjpeg-turbo on the A57 cores.

**Beats:** libjpeg-turbo — First-party README table: one image decoded to an RGB surface, averaged over 1000 iterations, on a Tegra X1 with its Cortex-A57 at max 2.091 GHz; NVJPG 2.036 ms vs libjpeg-turbo 6.127 ms for a 70 KiB 720x1080 file and 15.997 vs 66.341 ms for a 1.6 MiB 3200x1800 file (about 3.0x and 4.1x, derived from page data). The table was already in the README by 2021-02-08, before the Horizon port (2021-03-08), the hardware-definition corrections and both 2025 fixes, so it was measured on the early Linux build and never re-run; the timing harness, libjpeg-turbo version and build, NVJPG clock rate and timed region are not published (the shipped examples time one render plus wait, i.e. scan copy plus hardware decode, after header parsing).

**Known shortcoming:** Different hardware: the Tegra X1 NVJPG block (likely a Nintendo Switch per the Makefile) against software libjpeg-turbo on its Cortex-A57 cores; the README table is the only evidence, the examples time one NVJPG render and never call libjpeg-turbo, and no flags or libjpeg-turbo version are given. Stale since 2025-06-18.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (2026-10-04): the README table (NVJPG 2.036 vs libjpeg-turbo 6.127 ms, 15.997 vs 66.341 ms, about 3.0x and 4.1x derived from page data) was in the README by 2021-02-08, before the Horizon port, hardware-definition corrections and both 2025 correctness fixes, and was never re-run; harness, libjpeg-turbo build, NVJPG clock and timed region are unpublished. Security: the parser (lib/image.cpp) is unsafe on untrusted files: parse_dht reads up to 4080 symbols into a 162-byte array and indexes 4-entry tables with a 4-bit id, parse_dqt likewise, table ids from SOF/SOS are never range-checked, parse_dqt computes precision as info >> 8 on a uint8_t (always 0, so 16-bit tables are misread), and Image(path) leaks the file descriptor. History: 1-based component-id assumption until 16c10a3 (2025-06-09, issue #1), infinite loop on non-JPEG input until PR #2. Tegra X1 only (libnx or L4T kernel); GPL-3.0; stale since 2025-06-18.

**Independent measurement:** first-party README table
