**How:** The CPU only parses the JPEG headers, copies the entropy-coded scan data into a DMA buffer and fills a 0xb2c-byte picture-info block (Huffman and quantization tables, sampling, pitches); Huffman decoding, IDCT, chroma upsampling, YUV-to-RGB conversion (fixed-point BT.601, BT.709 or full-range JFIF kernels) and power-of-two downscaling (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) all run in the NVJPG hardware. Work is submitted as a Host1x command buffer and completion is signalled by a syncpoint fence, and Decoder::initialize(num_ring_entries) keeps a ring of submission slots so the CPU can parse and queue the next image while the hardware decodes. The speedup comes from dedicated silicon, not from a better software algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Nintendo Switch homebrew (devkitA64, libnx) that loads many baseline JPEG icons, thumbnails or screenshots and wants the Cortex-A57 cores free; the Switch menu sphaira uses it (issue #1).
- Tegra X1 boards running NVIDIA's L4T kernel, where /dev/nvhost-nvjpg, /dev/nvhost-ctrl and /dev/nvmap exist and you need lower per-image decode latency than libjpeg-turbo on the A57 (README: about 3x on a 720x1080 file, about 4x on 3200x1800).
- Pipelines that hand the decoded image straight to the GPU: Surface::to_deko3d wraps the output buffer as a deko3d texture without a copy.
- Thumbnail generation where hardware downscale by 2, 4 or 8 and hardware YUV-to-RGB conversion replace CPU passes.

**Skip it when:**
- Any hardware other than the Tegra X1: it programs the NVJPG engine directly, and on Linux it needs NVIDIA's downstream nvhost/nvmap UAPI, not mainline host1x.
- Progressive, arithmetic-coded or lossless JPEGs, CMYK or other 4-component files, and files whose component ids are 4 or higher (Adobe-style 'R','G','B' ids) all return an error.
- Untrusted input: the header parser does not bound DHT symbol counts or table ids (see gotchas), so a malformed file can write past fixed-size arrays.
- Workloads that read decoded pixels back on the CPU: surfaces are allocated non-CPU-cacheable, which suits GPU consumers but makes CPU reads slow.
- Projects that cannot take GPL-3.0 code, or that need active maintenance: the only changes since 2022 are two 2025 fixes prompted by one downstream user.

**Integration:** static lib (meson default_library=static, or libnvjpg.a from the devkitA64 Makefile) · Linux: NVIDIA L4T kernel device nodes /dev/nvmap, /dev/nvhost-ctrl, /dev/nvhost-nvjpg (SDL2 only for the examples). Switch: libnx (nvdrv and mmu services), deko3d optional for the texture-export path and examples. · C++20 (gnu++20; uses concepts, requires-clauses and the GNU case-range extension), so GCC with GNU extensions; devkitA64 for Switch, meson for Linux · aarch64 Tegra X1 only (Nintendo Switch under Horizon with libnx, or Tegra X1 under NVIDIA L4T Linux)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libjpeg-turbo, jpeg-nitro or zenjpeg only when you are on Tegra X1 (Switch or L4T) with trusted baseline JPEGs and want the decode off the CPU; those siblings are portable CPU decoders, and GPUJPEG targets CUDA GPUs, not the X1's NVJPG block.

**Gotchas:**
- Parser memory safety (lib/image.cpp): parse_dht reads sum(codes) symbols, up to 4080, into a 162-byte array and indexes 4-entry table arrays with a 4-bit id (up to 15); parse_dqt does the same for quantization ids; table ids from SOF and SOS are never range-checked. parse_dqt also computes precision as `info >> 8` on a uint8_t, which is always 0, so 16-bit quantization tables are misread. Image(path) opens a file descriptor that is never closed, and a short read() is not detected.
- History: component ids were assumed 1-based until commit 16c10a3 (2025-06-09, issue #1: a 4:4:4 Switch icon decoded to garbage), and parse() could loop forever on non-JPEG input until PR #2 (2025-06-18). In that PR the author says his FFmpeg 'envideo' hwaccel (averne/FFmpeg, envideo_mjpeg.c) 'handles surface formats correctly, aborts on some hardware issues', which this library does not.
- The scan-data buffer defaults to 5 MiB per ring entry (Decoder::initialize capacity 0x500000); larger scans fail with ENOMEM until Decoder::resize is called. Output pitch is aligned to 256 bytes, so rows are not tightly packed.
- On Switch, nj::initialize() temporarily sets __nx_applet_type to LibraryApplet to obtain nvdrv:a/s/t, and on Linux NJ_TRY_ERRNO tests errno without clearing it first, so a stale errno from an earlier unrelated call makes initialize fail.

**Status:** Stale since 2025-06-18 (23 commits, 19 stars, no open issues or PRs); about 1.5k lines of GPL-3.0 C++20 that can be vendored, but it only runs on Tegra X1 with libnx or NVIDIA's downstream L4T kernel, and its parser should not see untrusted files.

[repo](https://github.com/averne/oss-nvjpg) · [benchmark](https://github.com/averne/oss-nvjpg)

##### PZP (Portable Zipped PNM)  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zstd-compressed PNM container in a single C header; loads palette-friendly label maps about 2.3x faster than PNG via cv2.imread.

**Beats:** libpng (PNG decode through OpenCV cv2.imread) — First-party scripts/compare_load_speed.py run on 500 COCO val2017 panoptic label maps (3-channel uint8, files encoded with USE_COMPRESSION, USE_RLE and USE_PALETTE): best of 3 passes after one warm-up, PNG through cv2.imread (OpenCV's libpng, version unstated) took 1141.2 ms against PZP through ctypes and libpzp.so at 500.6 ms (2.28x), with files 4.1 MB versus 2.0 MB; libpzp.so used gcc -O3 -mavx2 -march=native, and no CPU model, OpenCV, libpng, zstd or gcc version is recorded.

**Known shortcoming:** A format comparison (zstd-compressed PNM against deflate PNG through cv2.imread), not a faster PNG decoder; harness scripts/compare_load_speed.py (best of 3, pixel check on 10 pairs) with libpzp.so built -O3 -mavx2 -march=native and no CPU model; 3-channel data skips the SIMD RLE path.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e97, 2026-10-04): the README's 2.28x load figure is stale: it was measured by 2026-03-21 (bc7a2b8) on code with checksum verification on every read, no ZSTD_DCtx reuse, scalar 3-channel reconstruction and no header bounds checks; since 2026-03-29 the 3-channel path is AVX2 de-interleaved, checksum verification is off by default (PZP_VERIFY_CHECKSUM=0) and zstd frames are written without a content checksum, so the measured code is not the current code. Bug outside the benchmark: the decoder rejects payloads above 100,000,000 bytes while the encoder has no cap, so 16-bit RGB above about 16.7 MP or 8-bit RGB above about 33 MP writes but never reads back. libpzp.so is built -march=native with no runtime dispatch. First commit 2025-02-01.

**Independent measurement:** first-party harness

**How:** Decoding is one zstd (or LZ4) call into a single buffer, using a per-thread reused ZSTD_DCtx, followed by an in-place left-delta prefix sum and a palette table lookup; there is no chunk parsing, no per-row filter selection and no zlib inflate. Under -DINTEL_OPTIMIZATIONS the prefix sum is an AVX2 Kogge-Stone scan with explicit cross-lane carry; since the 2026-03-29 commit 3-channel images are de-interleaved with SSSE3 shuffles, scanned per plane and re-interleaved (doc/performance.md still says 3-channel falls back to scalar, which was true of the code that produced the published numbers). Palette mode is compressed at zstd level 19, so label maps with few distinct values per channel shrink well and decode fast.

**Use it when:**
- Training-data pipelines that re-read the same images many times (segmentation label maps, masks, depth maps) and can afford a one-time conversion from PNG.
- 8-bit or 16-bit grayscale/RGB images with few distinct values per channel, where USE_PALETTE plus USE_RLE gives both a smaller file and a faster load than PNG.
- Python data loaders on Linux x86-64 with AVX2 that today call cv2.imread on PNG and are bound by decode time; PZP.read returns a numpy array directly.
- Storing short image sequences or depth streams where the inter-frame delta and multi-frame container (with delays, metadata and audio) are useful.
- When LZ4 is acceptable for larger files in exchange for faster decode on a ramdisk or NVMe.

**Skip it when:**
- You need interoperability: no browser, image editor or standard library reads .pzp, and the format is at v0.03 with a layout change in 2026 (PZP0 to PZP1 frames).
- Photographs or high-entropy images: the only published number is for COCO panoptic label maps, the README's own best case; no photo, fpng, libspng, Wuffs or QOI comparison exists.
- Large frames: the decoder rejects any frame whose uncompressed payload exceeds 100,000,000 bytes (for example 16-bit RGB above about 16.7 megapixels or 8-bit RGB above about 33 megapixels), while the encoder has no such limit, so such files write but do not read back.
- Untrusted input with integrity needs: read-time checksum verification is off by default (PZP_VERIFY_CHECKSUM=0) and zstd frames are written without a content checksum, whereas PNG checks CRC32 and Adler-32.
- GPL-3.0 is incompatible with your product, or you need a portable prebuilt library: libpzp.so is built with -march=native and AVX2 with no runtime dispatch.

**Integration:** header-only (pzp.h, all functions static) plus an optional shared lib (libpzp.so) and a pip-installable Python ctypes package · libzstd and liblz4 (system packages); optional OpenZL v0.3.0 built from source with PZP_USE_OPENZL=1; Python bindings work without numpy (raw bytes) and return numpy arrays when it is installed; the CLI reads only binary PNM (P5/P6) input · C11 (uses _Thread_local); built and documented with gcc only; toolchain version not documented · Header: any little-endian target with zstd and lz4 (multi-byte header fields are copied in native byte order). libpzp.so as built by the Makefile: x86-64 with AVX2 and the build machine's -march=native; setup.py names .dylib/.dll but the Makefile only builds libpzp.so

**Vs siblings:** Pick PZP over Zpng or QOI when your data is palette-like label maps or 16-bit depth and you want a Python numpy reader, palette and inter-frame modes in one container; pick fpng, libspng or the PNG-compatible siblings when files must stay PNG, and QOI or QOIR when you want a permissively licensed format with third-party benchmark numbers.

**Gotchas:**
- The 2.28x figure was published in the README by 2026-03-21 (commit bc7a2b8) and measured on that code, which verified a checksum on every read, created a fresh zstd context per call, ran 3-channel delta reconstruction as a scalar loop and did not bounds-check header fields; current code differs in all four respects, so the number is unmeasured for today's build (likely conservative for speed).
- Palette mode always compresses at zstd level 19 (non-palette at level 1), so encoding label maps is slow; plan for a write-once, read-many workflow.
- The palette is per channel (up to 256 values each), not per colour, so an RGB map with many distinct colours but few values per channel still benefits, while one with near-full channel ranges does not.
- doc/c-api.md lists pzp_compress_combined as returning void; it now returns int (1 on success, 0 on failure) and no longer exits the process on write errors.

**Status:** Active single-author project (initial commit February 2025, burst of work since March 2026, last commit 2026-09-29, 2 stars, 132 commits, one closed issue about the license); GPL-3.0, small enough to vendor, and the author vendors it into the DataLoader of the RGBToPoseDetect2D project.

[repo](https://github.com/AmmarkoV/PZP) · [benchmark](https://github.com/AmmarkoV/PZP/blob/HEAD/doc/performance.md)

##### TinyTIFF  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Small C library that appends fixed-size uncompressed frames to a multi-page TIFF with less per-frame overhead than libTIFF.

**Beats:** libTIFF (libtiff 3.8.2 and 4.6.0) — The author's tinytiffwriter_speedtest writes 64x64 16-bit greyscale frames and a frame-size sweep, timing each frame with QueryPerformanceCounter and reporting a trimmed mean in ms per frame. Against libTIFF 4.6.0 on a Ryzen 7 5800H (Windows 11, SSD, 64-bit Release, compiler not stated), TinyTIFF was 1.6-2.8x faster for 10 to 100,000 frames and 1.5-5.1x faster across frame sizes; against libTIFF 3.8.2 on a Ryzen 5 3600 (Windows 10, hard disk, 32-bit Release), the gap grew with frame count to 2421x at 100,000 frames, but TinyTIFF was slower from 1024x1024 upward.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party harness tests/tinytiffwriter_speedtest with .ods result sheets; CPUs named but compiler and flags not. SSD run with libTIFF 4.6.0 gives 1.51-5.15x (both sides uncompressed, stripped), but libTIFF writes about 8 KB strips and the timed path includes a copy loop, so the comparison is not configuration-matched. The HDD run (libTIFF 3.8.2, up to 2421x) also shows TinyTIFF slower at 1024x1024 and above (0.19x), and the 1,000,000-frame row is about 8.2 GB, past the 4 GB TIFF limit, so it is not a valid-file comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** The 1,000,000-frame SSD row (3.10x) is invalid on both sides: the SSD sheet was committed 2024-04-30 on pre-fix code whose 32-bit ftell broke offsets past 2 GB (issue #23; the writer now checks TINYTIFF_MAX_FILE_SIZE since 54e8391 of 2024-05-08 but still writes IFDs and skips pixels past the limit), while libTIFF 4.6.0 refuses classic writes past 4 GB and prints from its error handler inside the timed loop, and the harness ignores every return value. The HDD frame-size sweep varies the frame count (10,000 down to 50), so the 289-3674x ratios are a frame-count effect; the RAW reference is opened in text mode. Code bugs not behind the numbers: writeImagePlanarReorder is wrong for samples above 8 bits (sample index used as byte offset; likely issue #32); open reader memory-safety report #35 has no maintainer reply.

**How:** All frames share one shape, so the writer reserves a fixed IFD block per frame (500 bytes, at most 20 entries plus space for rational and array values), assembles it in a reused memory buffer, and issues two fwrite calls per frame: the IFD, then the pixels as a single strip in host byte order, with no copy or byte swap. The next-IFD pointer is computed arithmetically from the known frame size, so the writer never seeks back or walks the directory chain; it seeks only at close to end the chain and fill in the ImageDescription. libTIFF 3.8.2's per-frame time grows with the number of directories already written, consistent with walking the IFD chain to link each frame, while libTIFF 4.6.0 caches the last directory offset (tif_lastdiroff in TIFFLinkDirectory) and stays flat. Against current libTIFF the remaining gain (1.5-5x on the author's SSD) comes from libTIFF's per-frame tag serialisation, its roughly 8 KB TIFFDefaultStripSize strips, and the harness's strip-copy loop, not from a different I/O technique.

**Use it when:**
- Streaming fixed-size camera or microscope frames (8-64-bit integer or float, greyscale or RGB(A)) into one uncompressed multi-page TIFF that ImageJ/Fiji or libTIFF will read later, as long as the file stays under 4 GB.
- Many small frames, where per-frame overhead dominates: on the author's SSD run against libTIFF 4.6.0, 64x64 16-bit frames took 0.018-0.022 ms vs 0.05-0.06 ms per frame (2.6-2.8x) for 100 to 10,000 frames, and 128x128 to 512x512 frames were 3.1-5.1x faster.
- Code still linked against old libTIFF 3.x, whose per-frame write time grows with frame count (205.8 ms vs 0.085 ms per 64x64 frame at 100,000 frames on the author's hard-disk run).
- Projects that want a small C dependency with no zlib, libjpeg or libTIFF behind it, for both writing and reading simple stacks.

**Skip it when:**
- Output that can exceed 4 GB. There is no BigTIFF; libTIFF 4.x opened with mode "w8" writes BigTIFF. Builds without ftello64/_ftelli64 detected at configure time are limited to 2 GB. Issue #23 (files over 2 GB fail to open in ImageJ, Nov 2023) is still open, although release 4.0.0.0 (May 2024) improved 2-4 GB handling.
- Compressed (LZW, Deflate, JPEG), tiled, palette or pyramidal TIFF, frames that change size or type within a file, or rich metadata (OME-XML, per-frame tags). The writer emits a fixed tag set with resolution 1/1 and a single ImageDescription of at most 1024 characters, and only in the first frame.
- Large frames, where the disk is the bottleneck. On the SSD the gain shrinks to 1.5-2.1x from 1024x1024 upward. On the author's 2020 hard-disk run TinyTIFF was slower than libTIFF 3.8.2 at 1024x1024 (22.28 vs 4.21 ms per frame), 2048x2048 and 4096x4096.
- Reading untrusted TIFF files. Issue #35 (June 2026, no maintainer reply) reports a reproducible memory-safety bug reachable through TinyTIFFReader_open on malformed input; two earlier security reports (#19, #20) were closed in April 2024.
- Projects that cannot accept LGPL-3.0. Issue #16 asks for BSD or dual licensing and is still open.

**Integration:** static or shared lib (CMake; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults to ON; targets TinyTIFF::TinyTIFF and the header-only TinyTIFF::TinyTIFFXX C++ helpers in tinytiff_tools.hxx); vcpkg port 'tinytiff' · none (libTIFF only for the optional comparison tests) · C core (pure C since 3.0.0.0; no C standard pinned in CMake), CMake 3.10+; C++ only for the .hxx helpers and tests · Windows (MSVC CI) and Linux (CI); stdio file I/O, with an optional WinAPI path; writes files in host byte order; the reader byte-swaps opposite-endian files

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued image-codecs siblings writes TIFF; they are PNG, JPEG, QOI or texture codecs, all of which compress. Pick TinyTIFF when you need an uncompressed multi-page TIFF stack that scientific tools open directly, and one of the PNG/QOI encoders (fpng, fpnge, QOI) when the frames are standalone images and size on disk matters.

**Gotchas:**
- Check every TinyTIFFWriter_writeImage return value. When the next frame would push the file past the size limit (0xFFFFFFFE minus 1 KB with 64-bit ftell, otherwise 2 GB), the writer has already written and linked that frame's IFD before it returns false without the pixels. On close the chain therefore ends in a frame whose strip lies beyond the end of the file, and every further call appends another data-less IFD.
- TinyTIFFWriter_writeImagePlanarReorder (interleaved input, planar output) is wrong for samples wider than 8 bits. In tinytiffwriter.c the source index sampidx counts samples but is used as a byte offset into the input, so 16-, 24-, 32- and 64-bit samples are copied from the wrong bytes (derived from reading the code). Issue #32 ('Cannot write RGB images', open) uses this path. The planar-to-chunky direction indexes bytes correctly.
- Without large-file support detected, TINYTIFF_MAX_FILE_SIZE is defined as (2*1024*1024*1024-1), an int expression that overflows, so that build's limit depends on the compiler.
- Issue #21 (RGBA writes missing the alpha channel) is open. Frames must all match the shape given to TinyTIFFWriter_open; there is no per-frame size or type.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit was on 2024-05-22 (release 4.0.1.0 followed on 2024-05-23), and issues #23, #32 and #35 have no maintainer reply. It is small and dependency-free, but LGPL-3.0, so link it as a library or accept the LGPL terms if you vendor it.

[repo](https://github.com/jkriege2/TinyTIFF) · [benchmark](https://github.com/jkriege2/TinyTIFF)

##### zenjpeg  `Rust`  `AGPL-3.0 or commercial (dual-licensed)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Safe pure-Rust JPEG encoder/decoder; progressive decode 1.35x libjpeg-turbo, baseline about 6% slower single-threaded.

**Beats:** libjpeg-turbo (mozjpeg-sys 2.2 with nasm_simd, C+NASM) — First-party zenbench runs on a Ryzen 9 7950X under WSL2, cargo bench with the release profile (debug=true, no LTO, default target, runtime SIMD dispatch, rustc version unrecorded), against mozjpeg v4's libjpeg-turbo-derived decoder through mozjpeg-sys 2.2 with nasm_simd (C built by cc-rs at the Cargo profile's opt level with no -march; C compiler version unrecorded), read one scanline per call with default ISLOW IDCT and fancy upsampling, on 10 CID22 512x512 photos re-encoded by mozjpeg-rs at Q85 4:2:0: baseline 73.8 vs 78.1 MiB/s (0.94x) with defaults, 80.4 MiB/s with box upsampling, progressive 46 vs 34 MiB/s (1.35x); no committed result file or commit hash backs these CID22 figures. The 2.5x to 7.5x parallel figures (Feb 2026 synthetic set, commit 39f012f) compare multi-threaded zenjpeg with single-threaded libjpeg-turbo; single-threaded on the same set zenjpeg was only 1.05x to 1.07x faster.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). Bench code public (zenjpeg/benches/decode_zenbench.rs) but rustc unpinned and mozjpeg-sys C flags unstated. Single-thread like-for-like: baseline decode 0.94x (slower), progressive 1.35x faster, and the default Jpegli IDCT is not pixel-exact (exact IDCT costs about 37%). The headline 2.5-7.5x is rayon multi-threading against single-threaded C on synthetic images, a comparison the repo's own bench rules forbid.

**Known shortcoming:** decode_zenbench.rs counts compressed input bytes for MiB/s; the lane labelled 'zenjpeg LibjpegCompat (Libjpeg IDCT)' only sets Triangle upsampling, so the default configuration runs under the wrong label; load_or_generate_pixels logs 'loaded' even for synthetic pixels; CLAUDE.md says the parallel table ran on an 8-thread system despite the 7950X claim. The C side is mozjpeg v4 via mozjpeg-sys cc-rs at the Cargo profile's opt level with no -march, release profile debug=true and no LTO. BENCH-AUDIT.md notes BGRA output 47% slower than RGB at 4096x4096 single-threaded; open issue #215 (decode_into InternalError on baseline 4:2:0 with RST markers).

**How:** Baseline JPEGs go through a streaming single-pass decoder: Huffman decode, IDCT, chroma upsampling and YCbCr-to-RGB run per MCU row with no coefficient buffer, using fused AVX2 upsample+color-convert kernels, partial dequantization driven by the coefficient count, and a DC-only fast path. Progressive decode, the one clear single-thread win, comes from fused per-scan AC loops with a combined 9-bit Huffman+value lookup and a u64 nonzero-coefficient bitmap per block walked with trailing_zeros during AC refinement (callgrind: 415M vs 580M instructions for zune-jpeg at 2048x2048). The default IDCT is a jpegli-style integer IDCT rather than libjpeg's ISLOW, SIMD is dispatched at runtime through archmage tokens (AVX2/FMA, AVX-512, NEON, SIMD128), and with --features parallel images carrying restart markers are split by restart segment across a rayon pool.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services that decode many progressive JPEGs (mozjpeg-style web images): 46 vs 34 MiB/s single-threaded on CID22 512x512 Q85 4:2:0, and 0.60x to 0.69x of mozjpeg's time on the Feb 2026 synthetic 256 to 4096 px set.
- Latency-bound decode of large baseline JPEGs that carry restart markers (DRI) on a multi-core box, with the parallel feature: 3.05 ms vs 15.8 ms single-threaded libjpeg-turbo at 2048x2048 (multi-thread vs one thread).
- Untrusted-input pipelines that want a memory-safe decoder with max_pixels/max_memory caps, cooperative cancellation and Strict to Permissive error policies.
- Bounded-memory decode of very large images through the scanline reader (the wave-parallel path caps its buffer at 6 MB at 4096x4096).
- Pure-Rust jpegli-quality encoding where a C++ toolchain is unwanted; the project's own note puts the encoder about 15 to 20% slower than C++ jpegli at matched quality.

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ projects: there is no C API, so you would write and maintain an extern "C" shim, and the code is AGPL-3.0-only unless you buy Imazen's commercial licence.
- Throughput servers that already decode one image per core: single-thread baseline decode is 0.94x of libjpeg-turbo with the default upsampling, and the parallel speedups need restart markers that most camera and web JPEGs lack.
- When output must be pixel-identical to libjpeg-turbo: the default IDCT differs and the default Triangle upsampling is only within max_diff 3; the pixel-exact Libjpeg IDCT is documented as adding about 37% overhead, which would put baseline decode well behind C (not measured in the README).
- BGRA or RGBA output at large sizes until re-measured: the repo's BENCH-AUDIT.md found the streaming path emits RGB and then swizzles, measuring 4096x4096 single-thread Bgra 47% slower than Rgb and the imageflow BGRA bench 9 to 19% behind mozjpeg's JCS_EXT_BGRA (later sink-path work added a garb swizzle).
- Code that needs a stable API: the crate is 0.x (0.9.0 in the repo while the README still says 0.8) and the README calls the decoder API prerelease with breaking changes expected.

**Integration:** crate · Pure-Rust crates only (archmage, magetypes, garb, zenyuv, zenpixels, zencodec, zenanalyze, enough, memchr, aligned-vec, bytemuck, imgref, rgb, tinyvec, thiserror, whereat, linear-srgb); optional rayon (parallel), moxcms (color management), ultrahdr crates; no C dependencies · Rust 1.93 (MSRV, edition 2024); rust-toolchain.toml pins the stable channel only · x86-64 (AVX2/FMA and AVX-512 by runtime dispatch, no target-cpu flags needed), aarch64 NEON, wasm32 SIMD128 (build with -C target-feature=+simd128), scalar fallback elsewhere; CI covers Linux, macOS and Windows on x86-64 and ARM64 plus i686

**Vs siblings:** Pick zenjpeg over libjpeg-turbo-rs (pure-Rust libjpeg-turbo port claiming 0.77x to 0.93x of libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2's baseline decode time) when progressive decode, jpegli-class encoding, bounded-memory streaming or safety limits matter more than baseline libjpeg-compatible speed; pick jpeg-nitro (C) or plain libjpeg-turbo for C++ code, and mozjpeg-rs (same author) if you only need a mozjpeg-compatible encoder.

**Gotchas:**
- With --features parallel, a single decode() call fans out over every rayon thread when restart markers are present; in a server that already parallelizes across images set num_threads(1) to avoid oversubscription.
- Open issue #215 (2026-10-02): decode_into() fails with 'internal error: coefficient data unavailable (streaming decode consumed entropy data)' on some baseline 4:2:0 JPEGs with restart markers (1024x768 with 11 RST, 2048x2048 photos with 31 RST), while decode() on the same bytes works.
- The headline baseline numbers use non-pixel-exact defaults: the Jpegli integer IDCT plus Triangle upsampling within max_diff 3; the NearestNeighbor 1.03x figure uses a cheaper box upsample than libjpeg-turbo's fancy h2v2.
- Bench-harness issues in zenjpeg/benches/decode_zenbench.rs, none of which change the README ratios: throughput is MiB/s of compressed JPEG input, not decoded pixels; the lane labelled 'zenjpeg LibjpegCompat (Libjpeg IDCT)' only sets Triangle upsampling (the default), so it re-runs the default config under a wrong label; and load_or_generate_pixels logs 'loaded' even when it falls back to synthetic pixels. CLAUDE.md attributes the 4096 parallel scaling to 'an 8-thread system' although the stated CPU is a 16-core Ryzen 9 7950X, so the thread count of the parallel table is unclear.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-28, about 2,600 commits, 15 stars, 20 open issues, 7 open PRs) with frequent correctness fixes in 2026; usable as source only under AGPL-3.0 or with a paid (or $1 startup) commercial licence, and the decoder API is still prerelease.

[repo](https://github.com/imazen/zenjpeg) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/imazen/zenjpeg/HEAD/README.md)

#### rasterizers-2d

##### ctx (2D vector rasterizer and terminal by Oyvind Kolas)  `C`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later (renderer, ctx.h); GPL-3.0-or-later (ctx terminal), per COPYING on the mirror's dev branch`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Portable C 2D vector rasterizer (HTML5-canvas-style API, one generated header) that wins many heats against cairo and Qt6 but loses most to Blend2D.

**Beats:** Cairo (with pixman); Qt6 also compared; Blend2D is faster than ctx in the same tournament — Snippet only: the ctx.graphics/performance/ 'rasterizer tournament' (blocked here) runs Blend2D-style tests (FillRectU, FillRectRot, StrokeButterfly, StrokeLine and others at 8x8-256x256, SrcOver/SrcCopy, Solid/Pattern) for ctx, Blend2D (static), cairo and Qt6 (Debian packages), built with clang on an AMD Ryzen AI 7 445 locked at 2.0 GHz. Quoted heats, where higher appears to be better because the snippet calls Blend2D's 33.3 the better FillRectRot result: FillRectU-256x256-SrcCopy-Pattern_NN ctx 52.1, Blend2D 16.7, Qt6 14.9, cairo 5.6; StrokeButterfly-8x8-SrcOver-Solid ctx 17.1, Blend2D 10.5, cairo 6.5, Qt6 5.2; FillRectRot-256x256-SrcOver-Solid Blend2D 33.3, ctx 31.9, Qt6 7.4, cairo 6.7. Units, run counts and the ctx benchmark backend are not readable from here.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers are snippet-only: the tournament page https://ctx.graphics/performance/ is blocked (snippets confirm 259/61/1/3 wins against Blend2D, Qt6, Cairo and AGG with clang, Debian cairo and qt6 packages, Ryzen AI 7 445 at 2.0 GHz), and the 1.25x/5x-over-Cairo figures come from older author posts (pippin.gimp.org, Patreon), not the tournament. The GitHub mirror has no benchmark code (tests/test-size measures binary size) and was last updated 2024-10-01; the canonical repo is git at https://ctx.graphics/.git/. Licence LGPL-3.0-or-later for the renderer, GPL-3.0-or-later for the terminal.

**Known shortcoming:** src/x86-64-level.c checks AVX2 and BMI on cpuid leaf 2 instead of leaf 7, so the x86-64-v3 code path is picked by accident and probably never on AMD (slows ctx; no inflation). Segments past the edge-list cap (4096 or 16384) and beyond 253 active edges are silently dropped; -ffinite-math-only is global; the test target ends in '; true'; aarch64 builds generic only. Search snippets of the blocked tournament page give conflicting win counts (259/61/1/3 versus 259/226/154/130), and blend2d-testing/bench has no ctx backend, so the harness cannot be verified.

**How:** The rasterizer is a scanline active-edge-list design in fixed point (edge multiplier 2048, CTX_SUBDIV 8). Its anti-aliasing is adaptive: a scanline where no edge starts, ends or crosses gets each edge as a linear coverage ramp in one pass, and coverage can be applied straight to the destination row ('allow_direct' via ctx_rasterizer_apply_grads). Only complex scanlines are vertically oversampled, with 3, 5 or 15 sub-scanlines chosen from the steepest edge slope. Compositing is specialized per pixel format, paint type and full-coverage case (for example ctx_RGBA8_source_over_normal_full_cov_fragment), with fast fill_rect and stroke_rect paths (config.h credits CTX_FAST_FILL_RECT with a 15-20% win on larger rectangles) and a 256-entry gradient cache. There are no hand-written intrinsics. The Makefile compiles the same C three times (generic, x86-64-v2 with SSE4.2, x86-64-v3 with AVX2/FMA, all with -ftree-vectorize) and picks one at runtime with CPUID. ARMv7 gets a NEON build checked through /proc/self/auxv.

**Use it when:**
- Embedded or microcontroller UIs that need anti-aliased vector drawing straight into RGB565, RGB332 or 1-8 bit gray framebuffers from one C source drop, with compile-time knobs (config.h) that trade features for ROM and RAM.
- Desktop or server C code that today renders with cairo's image surface and spends most of its time on gradient, pattern or partially transparent fills. Older author posts (snippet only) claim 1.25x on partially transparent and 5x on gradient fills versus cairo/pixman in 8-bit mode, and in the tournament ctx won FillRectU-256x256-SrcCopy-Pattern_NN at 52.1 versus cairo's 5.6 (snippet only).
- Pipelines that need CMYK or 32-bit float, colour-managed rendering (babl-backed CTX_ENABLE_CM) rather than only 8-bit RGBA.
- Record-and-replay or remote rendering: the drawlist and text protocol let one process record and another render, with tile hashing (CTX_HASH_ROWS x CTX_HASH_COLS) so the cb/fb backends redraw only changed tiles across up to CTX_MAX_THREADS (8) render threads.

**Skip it when:**
- Maximum CPU raster throughput is the goal. Blend2D took 259 first places in the same tournament (snippet only), and its JIT pipelines beat ctx in most heats.
- Opaque solid fills against cairo/pixman. The older author posts (snippet only) say cairo is still faster for opaque fills in 8-bit mode.
- Very complex paths or wide canvases. A path's edge list is capped at CTX_MAX_EDGE_LIST_SIZE (defaults to 4096 segments, 16384 in the stock ctx.c), and ctx_drawlist_add_single() silently returns 0 for segments past the cap. Active edges per scanline stop at CTX_MAX_EDGES-2 (253). config.h says CTX_SUBDIV 8 limits framebuffer width to 4095 px.
- You need analytic (area-coverage) anti-aliasing like the AGG-derived rasterizer in Blend2D. ctx approximates complex scanlines with 3, 5 or 15 vertical samples (CTX_ANTIALIAS_FAST/GOOD/FULL), so steep crossings get coarser coverage.
- Proprietary static linking or a stable, versioned API. The renderer is LGPL-3.0-or-later and the terminal GPL-3.0-or-later. The mirror has no releases (CTX_VERSION=0.0.0 in the Makefile) and no README, and the only reachable copy is an unofficial mirror last updated 2024-10-01.

**Integration:** source-drop: single header ctx.h (define CTX_IMPLEMENTATION in one file). The mirror holds the split sources in src/, and `make ctx.h` concatenates them in src/index order. The upstream site is where the Makefile's updateweb target copies a prebuilt ctx.h. The Makefile also builds libctx.so/libctx.a with the multi-pass SIMD objects. · None for the core renderer beyond libm and pthreads. Optional: SDL2, babl (colour management), HarfBuzz, libcurl, ALSA, libdrm, plus vendored stb_truetype/stb_image in deps/. · C compiler with GNU extensions (inline-asm cpuid, __restrict__, #pragma GCC optimize). No minimum version is documented. The build is configure.sh + GNU make, and the tournament used clang (snippet). · x86-64 (runtime pick of generic, x86-64-v2 or x86-64-v3 builds), ARMv7 (NEON build when auxv reports it), AArch64 and other CPUs as a generic auto-vectorized build (configure.sh sets HAVE_SIMD=0 for aarch64), WebAssembly (with or without simd128, single-threaded), and microcontrollers via config.h. Linux is the main host. Other OSes are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick ctx over Blend2D when you need plain C, CMYK or float/colour-managed targets, tiny-framebuffer formats (RGB565, GRAY1) or a record/replay protocol and can accept the LGPL. Blend2D is faster in most tournament heats and Zlib-licensed, so it wins for pure x86-64/AArch64 throughput. Pick ThorVG for SVG/Lottie loading, and AGG if you want exact-area coverage in a small permissive codebase.

**Gotchas:**
- CPU dispatch bug in src/x86-64-level.c (mirror, 2024-10-01): after checking that the maximum CPUID leaf is at least 7, ctx_x86_64_level() runs cpuid(2, 0) and tests the AVX2, BMI1 and BMI2 bits in EBX. Leaf 2 holds cache/TLB descriptors on Intel and is reserved on AMD; those bits belong to leaf 7 subleaf 0. Selection of the x86-64-v3 (AVX2/FMA) build is therefore accidental, and CPUs where those bits read zero fall back to the x86-64-v2 build. This can only slow ctx down. Whether the newer upstream code used in the tournament fixes it is unknown.
- The whole library is compiled with -ffinite-math-only, -fno-signed-zeros, -fno-trapping-math and -fno-math-errno (top-level Makefile CFLAGS), and the ARMv7 NEON object adds -ffast-math. NaN or infinite coordinates and colours are undefined behaviour under these flags, so validate input from untrusted drawings.
- Over-limit geometry fails silently. Segments past the edge-list cap are dropped and edges past 253 active per scanline wait, which gives missing or wrong coverage rather than an error. Raise CTX_MIN_EDGE_LIST_SIZE/CTX_MAX_EDGE_LIST_SIZE before including ctx.h if you draw big paths.
- ctx_new_for_framebuffer() renders on the calling thread. The threaded, tile-hashed rendering is in the cb/fb/sdl backends, so pick the backend before comparing speed with Blend2D's multi-threaded mode.

**Status:** The facsimiles/ctx mirror is stale (last commit 2024-10-01, 8 stars, no releases) while upstream at ctx.graphics is evidently newer. The renderer is LGPL-3.0-or-later and vendorable as one header; the terminal is GPL-3.0-or-later.

[repo](https://github.com/facsimiles/ctx) · [benchmark](https://ctx.graphics/performance/)

##### Fast UI Draw (FastUIDraw)  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Intel's archived GPU-only C++ canvas (OpenGL/GLES); author's clip-heavy demo ran about 5-8x Skia GL's frame rate in 2016.

**Beats:** Skia (OpenGL backend), Cairo (CPU renderer and OpenGL backend), Qt — The only numbers are first-party and known only from search snippets of Kevin Rogovin's XDC 2016 slides. In the painter-cells demo, frame rate normalized to Cairo's CPU image surface was FastUIDraw 9.33 vs Skia GL 1.91 at 25x12 cells and 11.11 vs 1.36 at 50x25 cells, on an unnamed Intel-GPU laptop, which is about 4.9x and 8.2x over Skia GL (derived from snippet data). Contrary to the record's caveat, the Qt, Cairo (xlib, image, GL) and Skia GL ports and the run scripts are public on the repo's with_ports_of_painter-cells branch (last updated 2018-12-20). The scripts ran 1920x1080 or 1920x1200 fullscreen, swap_interval 0, 25x12 cells, a 4000x2000 table, table and cells rotating and clipped, and images from /usr/share/games/blobwars/gfx. The Skia port's Makefile gives gn args (is_official_build=true, clang) and a tested Skia commit, 01979132133e. Two limits remain: the hardware is unnamed, and the branch's 2018-era Skia API (GrContext::MakeGL) is newer than the 2016 runs. The ports are also not fully equivalent. The Skia port calls SkCanvas::drawText on UTF-8 strings every frame, while FastUIDraw draws pre-formatted GlyphSequences. The Cairo port pre-lays out cairo_glyph_t arrays, and the Qt port was given QGlyphRun 'to make the comparison more fair'. That makes the Skia GL ratio somewhat favorable to FastUIDraw.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers exist only in search snippets of the blocked x.org XDC 2016 slides and abstract (normalised to Cairo CPU: FastUIDraw 9.33 against Skia GL 1.91 at 600 cells and 11.11 against 1.36 at 1250 cells, 4.9-8.2x over Skia GL derived from snippet data) on an unnamed Intel-GPU laptop; the Qt, Cairo and Skia ports used are not public. Archived 2023-01-07 with the last code commit on 2019-12-20.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e109, 2026-10-05): the Qt, Cairo and Skia painter-cells ports are public on branch with_ports_of_painter-cells (2018-12-20) with example-benchmark.sh, bench.sh (typo 'vlank_mode=0'), Skia gn args and Skia commit 01979132133e, correcting the verifier; still C because CPU and GPU are unnamed, the numbers are snippet-only and the ports postdate the 2016 runs. Fairness flaw: the Skia port calls drawText every frame while FastUIDraw, Cairo and Qt pre-lay glyphs, so the Skia GL ratio favours FastUIDraw. Issue #19: Mesa SWR 1.9 fps vs Cairo 32.7; issue #49: about 7x nanovg's CPU load, no fix. Archived 2023-01-07.

**Independent measurement:** first-party XDC 2016 slides (snippet)

**How:** Everything is drawn by one uber-shader. Per-item state (transform, clip equations, brush, shader IDs) is packed into a data store, a texture buffer object by default, and each vertex reads a header from it. Canvas state changes therefore do not become GL state changes, and the README says only a blend-mode change forces a new pipeline state, so a frame needs only a handful of draw calls. Rectangle clip-in uses hardware clip planes (gl_ClipDistance by default). Clip-out and path clips use the depth buffer as an occluder (depth test GL_GEQUAL, z incremented per item), so changing the clip costs little more than drawing one occluding shape. Path tessellation, stroking geometry and glyph data are built once and reused, and images and glyphs live in GPU atlases so they cause no draw breaks.

**Use it when:**
- UI or canvas scenes on desktop-class GPUs that change clip and transform state very often (many nested, clipped, rotating widgets per frame), which is the painter-cells workload behind the published numbers.
- Linux or Windows (MinGW) apps that already own a GL 3.3 or GLES 3.0 context and want a 2D layer that issues very few draw calls.
- Intel GPUs from Ivy Bridge on with recent Mesa or Intel Windows drivers, which the README says have every extension needed for all blend modes at full speed.
- Studying or forking a GPU canvas design: uber-shader with packed data store, depth-buffer clipping, and custom shader chaining, all MPL-2.0.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything needing support or security fixes: Intel archived the repo on 2023-01-07 and accepts no patches. The last code commit is 2019-12-20, and questions about maintenance and Chromium integration (#61, #50) were never answered.
- Machines without a real GPU driver: issue #19 measured 1.9 fps with Mesa's SWR software rasterizer against 32.7 fps for Cairo on an i3-4160 at 1280x1280.
- Many short-lived or freshly built paths per frame. Issue #49 reported about 7x the CPU load of nanovg (around 29% CPU) on a line-drawing test at gcc 7.4 -O3, and it was closed without a recorded fix. The fast path assumes geometry is tessellated once and reused.
- macOS (system GL headers unusable and the GL there is deprecated), WebGPU, Vulkan or Metal targets: there are only GL and GLES backends.
- When you need Skia-level text shaping, color management, PDF or SVG output, or a CPU fallback: none of these is provided.

**Integration:** shared lib (libFastUIDraw plus libFastUIDrawGL or libFastUIDrawGLES, release and debug variants, pkg-config files and a fastuidraw-config script) · FreeType; Khronos GL/GLES headers (glcorearb.h, khrplatform.h) supplied by the user; flex and perl at build time; SDL2 and SDL2_image for demos only; doxygen for docs · C++11 (-std=c++11), GNU Make, g++ (clang said to work); release libraries build at -O3 -fstrict-aliasing · Linux and MinGW32/64 under MSYS2 per README; macOS only with copied Khronos headers ('Yes, this is a hack'); needs GL 3.3 or GLES 3.0, and blend modes beyond Porter-Duff need framebuffer fetch or fragment-shader interlock or ordering

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Pathfinder 3 or vger only if you need a full canvas feature set (clip-out by path, advanced blend modes, custom shaders) on GL and can live with an archived C++ codebase. For CPU rendering or maintained projects, Blend2D, Skia or ThorVG are the safer choices, and Rive Renderer and Vello are the maintained GPU-side options.

**Gotchas:**
- Debug and release libraries must not be mixed; the README tells you to take matching flags from pkg-config or fastuidraw-config.
- Benchmark mode (num_frames) times the gap between draw_frame calls, which includes buffer swap. Vsync is only disabled if you pass swap_interval 0 or set vblank_mode=0 on Mesa. The ports branch's bench.sh echoes vblank_mode=0 but actually runs with a misspelled 'vlank_mode=0'.
- Images not on the atlas become bound textures when bindless texturing is missing, which breaks batching. The demo itself warns 'large performance impact expected'.
- The first frames compile the uber-shader in the GL driver. Skip them (num_skip_frames) before timing anything.

**Status:** Abandoned: archived by Intel on 2023-01-07 with a discontinuation notice (last code change 2019-12-20). It is MPL-2.0 and copyable, but it is a large GL-specific codebase you would have to own outright.

[repo](https://github.com/intel/fastuidraw) · [benchmark](https://www.x.org/wiki/Events/XDC2016/Program/fast_ui_draw.pdf)

##### tdewolff/canvas  `Go`  `MIT (Fribidi component is LGPL)`  `active`  `Tier D`

Pure-Go vector drawing library (paths, booleans, text, raster/PDF/SVG/EPS output); claims 2x over Inkscape/Cairo, no published numbers.

**Beats:** Inkscape and Cairo (named in the README as 'existing solutions'; which Cairo-based tool was run, e.g. rsvg-convert or CairoSVG, is not stated on any readable page) — Nothing measured is verifiable: the README asserts at least 2x over 'existing solutions' and larger images than Inkscape and Cairo for one extreme SVG (an end-to-end SVG-to-raster conversion of score.svg from issue #280), but the linked comment does not render, and no Go version, flags, hardware, tool versions or harness exist in the repo or in tdewolff/canvas_benchmarks, which covers only polygon booleans. Treat it as a directional, first-party claim made on a since-replaced rasterizer backend.

**Known shortcoming:** Go (language-filter mismatch). Downgraded C to D: the only claim is README line 29 ('at least twice as fast' than Inkscape and Cairo) pointing to issue #280 comment 1995990038, which never rendered here; no number, machine or harness anywhere, and canvas_benchmarks tests polygon booleans only. The wording fits the old x/image/vector backend; the default renderer switched to the pure-Go scanx on 2025-02-06 (#334), so the claim describes superseded code. MIT with LGPL FriBidi; 1.8k stars, active.

**Known shortcoming:** The README's assembly claim is stale: the default rasteriser has been the pure-Go srwiley/scanx since 2025-02 (no .s files; the scanx README calls itself beta software with known bugs); issue #280 comment 1995990038 remains unreadable here. Code-reading bugs, untested and not behind numbers (there are none): ToScanxScanner does not implicitly close open subpaths so fills may lose coverage; RenderImage with sRGB gamma-converts the caller's image in place and panics on non-draw.Image inputs (image.YCbCr); open #348 (SetCoordRect scaling). In canvas_benchmarks iOverlay takes 0.0368 s against canvas 0.2563 s at 87,721 segments.

**How:** The raster backend (renderers/rasterizer) flattens Béziers and arcs to line segments at a tenth-of-a-pixel tolerance, converts them to 26.6 fixed point and feeds them to srwiley/scanx, a Go port of FreeType's 'smooth' area/coverage accumulation scanner that writes spans straight into an image.RGBA; it replaced golang.org/x/image/vector in February 2025 after issue #334 reported x/image/vector as 500-1000x slower for many rounded rectangles. The README's 'highly optimized with ASM' wording dates from the x/image/vector era: scanx is plain Go with no assembly files, and rasterizer.go itself carries a TODO for an ASM version. Path booleans use a Bentley-Ottmann sweep with snap rounding (Hobby, Hershberger) for numerical stability.

**Use it when:**
- Go services that need one scene rendered to several outputs (PNG plus PDF/SVG/EPS) without cgo or an external Cairo/Inkscape install.
- Server-side charts, maps and documents in Go (it ships go-chart and gonum/plot renderers and OpenStreetMap/Natural Earth examples) where text quality and bidi/complex scripts matter.
- Very large raster outputs from Go: the rasterizer accepts any image up to MaxInt32 pixels (it panics above that), allocated as one image.RGBA at 4 bytes per pixel.
- Robust polygon boolean operations on messy GIS data in pure Go, where it is comparable to Clipper2 in the author's own benchmark.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need a measured rasterization speedup: the only claim (at least 2x over 'existing solutions' on one extreme SVG, issue #280 comment 1995990038) has no readable number, machine or harness, and if measured it was on the x/image/vector backend that is no longer the default.
- Raster throughput-critical paths: C/C++ rasterizers in this category (Blend2D, ThorVG, tiny-skia) publish measured wins over Cairo or Skia, and gradient fills here go through a per-pixel color callback while sRGB output does a per-pixel At()/SetRGBA pass (marked 'TODO: parallelize').
- Fast polygon booleans: in the author's canvas_benchmarks union(Europe, Chile) at 87,721 segments takes 0.2563 s against 0.0368 s for iOverlay (about 7x slower, derived from page data; no hardware stated).
- Production code that cannot tolerate panics or rough edges: the README says the library 'inevitably must have a great amount of bugs', path-intersection panics recur in the issue tracker (#272, #280, #287, #306, #313), and #348 (SetCoordRect not scaling paths in the rasterizer) is open.
- Projects needing an old Go toolchain or a small module graph: go.mod requires Go 1.26 and lists Fyne, Gio, go-gl, gonum/plot, go-chart and AVIF/WebP encoders as direct requirements.

**Integration:** module · Go module github.com/tdewolff/canvas; the raster path uses srwiley/scanx (2019 pseudo-version, self-described beta), srwiley/rasterx and golang.org/x/image; text uses go-text/typesetting and benoitkugler/textprocessing (native Go or CGO HarfBuzz/FriBidi). The root go.mod also requires Fyne, Gio, go-gl, gonum/plot, go-chart, go-avif and go-webp for the optional backends. FriBidi is LGPL. · Go 1.26 (go.mod 'go 1.26.0') · any Go target for the pure-Go raster/PDF/SVG/EPS paths; HTML Canvas via WASM; OpenGL, Gio and Fyne backends need their own platform support

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over stilus (also Go, with measured wins over x/image/vector) when you need the whole pipeline (text layout, booleans, PDF/SVG/EPS output), not only a fast scanline fill; pick Blend2D, ThorVG or tiny-skia when raster speed is the requirement, since they publish measured results against Cairo or Skia and canvas does not.

**Gotchas:**
- The README's ASM claim is stale: the default rasterizer has used pure-Go scanx since February 2025, and scanx's own README warns 'Scanx is beta software. There are known bugs being worked on.'
- From reading the code (not tested): Path.ToScanxScanner, the default fill path, emits no implicit closing edge for open subpaths (ToVectorRasterizer closes the last one), and scanx's Start() does not close the previous contour, so filling an open subpath can lose coverage; close fill paths explicitly.
- From reading rasterizer.go: with a non-linear color space (e.g. SRGBColorSpace), RenderImage gamma-decompresses the source image in place when no rotation or shear margin is added, so the caller's image (and the canvas layer that references it) is modified, and a source that is not a draw.Image (e.g. *image.YCbCr from JPEG decoding) hits an unchecked type assertion and panics.
- Errors surface as panics: FromImage panics on a zero-sized raster and on images over MaxInt32 pixels, and path-intersection panics have been reported repeatedly.

**Status:** Active (1.8k stars, 124 forks, 21 open issues, last commit 2026-09-23) and MIT-licensed apart from the LGPL FriBidi component; the README asks for funding and leaves production readiness to the user's judgment.

[repo](https://github.com/tdewolff/canvas) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tdewolff/canvas)

#### video-audio

##### KNLMeansCL  `C++ (OpenCL)`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

OpenCL non-local means denoiser plugin for AviSynth(+) and VapourSynth; one user anecdote shows it about 2.5-3x faster than HandBrake's CPU NLMeans.

**Beats:** HandBrake NLMeans (CPU non-local means filter); not FFmpeg nlmeans or nlmeans_opencl — The only comparison is a 2017 HandBrake feature request (issue 839, CvH): about 17-20 fps whole-encode speed with HandBrake's built-in CPU NLMeans versus 50-55 fps with KNLMeansCL on the same file (about 2.5-3.2x), with no hardware, resolution, filter settings or versions. Because the issue asks HandBrake to add KNLMeansCL, the faster run cannot have been inside HandBrake, so the two numbers come from different, unstated pipelines. The wiki Benchmark page gives absolute fps only (v1.0.2, 1080p, d=1 a=2 s=4, Core i5-4690 with Radeon RX 480, Windows 10).

**Known shortcoming:** The only number is a HandBrake issue 839 quote of whole-encode fps (50-55 against 17-20 for HandBrake's CPU NLMeans), GPU against CPU with no setup given, and the wiki Benchmark page has no baseline; off the category baselines; GPL-3.0; abandoned since 2023-01-05.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e128, 2026-10-05): tier C stands. Measurement flaw: HandBrake issue 839 asks for KNLMeansCL to be added, so the 50-55 fps run was outside HandBrake, with different unstated pipelines and whole-encode fps; the wiki fps have no baseline. Possible bug (code reading, untested): the last d frames read stale temporal slots t-k that were never uploaded (k_end clamped while the loop runs to k_start) in NLMVapoursynth.cpp and NLMAvisynth.cpp, so out-of-order requests may blend an unrelated frame; not behind the throughput numbers. Per-frame re-upload of 2d+1 frames plus a blocking clFinish; global setlocale change (issue 43); macOS flashing (issue 56, fix only in unmerged PR 60); PRs 59 and 61 unmerged; Boost in meson unused; ocl_x below s gives out-of-bounds local reads.

**Independent measurement:** user-reported fps (HandBrake issue 839)

**How:** Implements the Goossens et al. (ACIVS 2010) GPU NLMeans scheme: for each search offset q it builds a per-pixel squared-difference image (nlmDistance), box-filters it into patch distances with separable horizontal and vertical kernels that tile through __local memory (O(s) per pixel per pass instead of O(s^2)), turns them into weights (native_exp for the Welsch mode) and accumulates. Weights are symmetric, so only half the (2a+1)^2(2d+1) window is computed and each distance image serves both p+q and p-q. Frame size, radii and channel layout are baked into the kernel as -D constants at build time with -cl-fast-relaxed-math, and work-group shapes are picked per vendor from CL_DEVICE_MAX_WORK_GROUP_SIZE.

**Use it when:**
- AviSynth+ or VapourSynth encode scripts that need NLMeans denoising and have an otherwise idle GPU while x264/x265 keep the CPU busy.
- AMD or Intel GPUs where CUDA-only denoisers (for example BM3DCUDA) are not an option; OpenCL 1.2 covers AMD, Intel and NVIDIA.
- Chroma-only or 4:2:0 denoising at 1080p: the wiki's RX 480 table shows the UV planes of 4:2:0 at up to 67 fps versus about 25 fps for 8-bit luma.
- Workflows that compute weights on a prefiltered reference clip (rclip) and apply them to the original.

**Skip it when:**
- HandBrake- or FFmpeg-only pipelines: it is a frame-server plugin and cannot be loaded there (HandBrake issue 839 requesting it is closed); use FFmpeg nlmeans_opencl or av-denoise instead.
- Apple Silicon or macOS AMD GPUs: issue 56 (flashing pink/green frames on M1, open since 2023-05-02) is only fixed in unmerged PR 60 (2026-04-10).
- CPU-only machines: it needs an OpenCL CPU runtime (issues 51 and 57 report device_type='cpu' failures), and search snippets of the Doom9 thread (forum blocked here) put TNLMeans level with it on a weak CPU.
- 4:4:4, RGB or float clips at high resolution: the wiki table drops to about 9 fps at 1080p on an RX 480, and clips above 8192x8192 are refused.
- Projects that need maintained binaries: the last tagged release is v1.1.1, master (1.1.1e) last changed on 2023-01-05, and issue 58 (2025-11-27) asks for a new build.

**Integration:** shared lib (AviSynth/AviSynth+ and VapourSynth plugin) · OpenCL 1.2 ICD and a vendor runtime; VapourSynth API 3 headers (VapourSynth.h, VSHelper.h) or AviSynth+ headers; meson.build also requires Boost filesystem/system although no source file includes Boost; Windows builds need the Visual C++ 2015 redistributable · C++11 (meson cpp_std=gnu++11), OpenCL 1.2 (0.6.11 is the last release for OpenCL 1.0/1.1) · Windows, Linux, macOS; any OpenCL 1.2 GPU, CPU or accelerator (wiki lists AMD HD 5800+, Intel HD 2500+, NVIDIA GT 640+); maximum 8192x8192

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over av-denoise when the pipeline is AviSynth+ or VapourSynth rather than FFmpeg and you need temporal NLMeans on a non-NVIDIA GPU; pick VapourSynth-BM3DCUDA instead when you have NVIDIA hardware and want BM3D quality, since KNLMeansCL publishes no head-to-head numbers against either.

**Gotchas:**
- Possible stale-frame bug at the end of a clip (from reading NLMVapoursynth.cpp and NLMAvisynth.cpp, not tested): uploads cover frames n+k_start..n+k_end with k_end clamped to the clip end, but the symmetric loop still reads the future slot t-k for every k down to k_start = -min(d, n). For the last d frames those slots hold whatever an earlier request uploaded. In strict sequential order that is the last frame repeated; under out-of-order requests (seeking, multithreaded vspipe) it is an unrelated frame, which would blend into the output.
- Each output frame re-uploads all 2d+1 input frames, issues 4 to 7 kernel launches per search offset (about 37 offsets at the defaults a=2, d=1) and ends with a blocking clFinish, so there is no overlap of transfer and compute across frames; one instance per GPU stays single-stream.
- Driver-specific breakage is fixed only in unmerged PRs: macOS buffer-fill sync (PR 60), Radeon compiler crash from unused nlmUnpack image arguments (PR 59), AUTO device fallback on runtimes that return CL_INVALID_VALUE (PR 61). Mesa OpenCL is not recognised (issue 55).
- Manual ocl_x/ocl_y/ocl_r overrides are not checked against s: the horizontal and vertical kernels need block width and height of at least s, or their __local buffer reads go out of bounds (the auto-selected blocks are at least 8 and s is limited to 8).

**Status:** Abandoned upstream (last commit 2023-01-05, three driver-fix PRs from 2026-04-10 unmerged), GPL-3.0, so it is fine as a plugin but cannot be vendored into permissively licensed code; the pinterf fork carries later AviSynth+ work.

[repo](https://github.com/Khanattila/KNLMeansCL) · [benchmark](https://github.com/HandBrake/HandBrake/issues/839)

##### libfoxenflac  `C`  `LGPL-2.1-or-later`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Tiny C99 FLAC decoder with no libc and no heap use; author claims about 25% faster than the flac CLI.

**Beats:** flac command-line reference decoder application (Xiph flac, built on libFLAC); no comparison against libFLAC's API, FFmpeg or dr_flac is published — The only speed evidence is one 2018 README sentence: about 25% faster than the flac command-line decoder on x86_64, with no file, machine, compiler, flags, flac version (likely 1.3.2, the release current then) or timing method, and no harness in the repo. That baseline does different work: flac -d always enables MD5 checking (FLAC__stream_decoder_set_md5_checking(..., true) in src/flac/decode.c) and writes a WAV file, while libfoxenflac computes no MD5 and may or may not have had CRCs enabled (FX_FLAC_NO_CRC). So the figure compares a stripped decoder with a full CLI pipeline, not library against library.

**Known shortcoming:** One README sentence (2018-08-05): 25% faster than the flac CLI application on x86_64, with no machine, compiler, flags or benchmark code, and nothing against the libFLAC API, FFmpeg or dr_flac. The CLI likely verifies MD5 and writes a file while libfoxenflac never computes MD5, so the work may differ. Licence LGPL-2.1-or-later.

**Known shortcoming:** The 25% claim compares unlike work: the flac reference application always verifies MD5 (src/flac/decode.c) and writes WAV, while libfoxenflac computes no MD5 and its CRC checking may be off (FX_FLAC_NO_CRC). The decoder hot loop is scalar (unary Rice read one bit per call, per-byte CRC callback, generic int64 LPC loop) against libFLAC's word-wise CLZ Rice, word CRC16 and order-specialised LPC, so a library-versus-library win is unlikely. 32-bit FLAC (FLAC 1.4.0+, RFC 9639) is rejected (fx_flac_sample_sizes_[7] = -1) although the README claims all FLAC features; tests cover the IETF subset only; an undersized instance drops frames silently; README build paths are stale.

**How:** Mostly by doing less, not by clever kernels: there is no MD5 computation, no file or WAV output, no allocation and no metadata parsing beyond STREAMINFO. The hot loops are plain C: a 64-bit MSB-first bit buffer refilled one byte at a time, Rice residuals whose unary prefix is read one bit per call, CRC-8/CRC-16 updated per byte through a table-driven callback, and a generic int64-accumulator LPC restore loop for every order; no SIMD and no count-leading-zeros tricks. libFLAC's current decoder, by contrast, reads Rice blocks word-wise with count-leading-zeros (plus a BMI2 variant), updates CRC-16 over whole words and has order-specialised LPC restore with 32-bit accumulation when safe. A compile-time switch FX_FLAC_NO_CRC (off by default, under #if 0) drops all CRC checks, which the source says makes the decoder 'significantly faster'.

**Use it when:**
- Microcontrollers, bare-metal firmware or WASM builds that must decode FLAC with no C runtime and no malloc (8.8 KiB of WebAssembly per the README).
- Streaming playback where FLAC bytes arrive in arbitrary chunks (network, DMA buffers) and you want a push-style decoder with no callbacks.
- 16- or 24-bit, 1-8 channel Subset files, where the integration tests compare every sample against the flac reference decoder; 48 kHz stereo needs only about 40 KiB of decoder state.
- Projects that want to vendor two source files (src/foxen-flac.c and src/foxen-flac.h) instead of building libFLAC.

**Skip it when:**
- As a desktop or server throughput choice: there are no published numbers against libFLAC's library API, FFmpeg or dr_flac, and the bit-at-a-time Rice loop is simpler than libFLAC's word-wise count-leading-zeros reader. The author calls the code 'not optimized' and says ARM6 performance is 'significantly worse'.
- 32-bit FLAC (written by FLAC 1.4.0 and later, defined in RFC 9639): sample-size code 7 maps to -1 in fx_flac_sample_sizes_, so every frame header is rejected, and 33-bit side channels cannot fit the int32 buffers. The README's 'Supports all FLAC features' predates 32-bit FLAC.
- Seeking, cue sheets, tags, pictures or ReplayGain: none of these are implemented, and seeking is explicitly out of scope.
- When you need integrity verification of the decoded audio: the STREAMINFO MD5 is exposed but never computed.
- Proprietary static linking without LGPL obligations: the licence is LGPL-2.1-or-later (since March 2025), so vendoring the .c file into closed code brings relinking terms.

**Integration:** source-drop (two files) or Meson-built static/shared library · none (only assert.h, stddef.h, stdint.h, stdbool.h); the FX_FLAC_ALLOC_* convenience macros call malloc · C99 compiler; Meson for the tests; MSVC 19.28 (Visual Studio 2019) fixes merged in PR #7; Emscripten for WASM · any: x86_64, ARM (Arduino support merged Feb 2025), WebAssembly; plain C with no SIMD

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Symphonia or rusty_flac when the target is C or C++ with no runtime and no heap (MCU, WASM, kernel-like code) and footprint matters more than speed; those Rust siblings publish measured decode-speed tables against FFmpeg, which libfoxenflac does not. go-flac is an encoder and does not compete.

**Gotchas:**
- Output samples are left-justified to fill the whole int32 (decoded value shifted left by 32 minus bit depth); shift right by (32 - FLAC_KEY_SAMPLE_SIZE) to get native PCM.
- Errors after the metadata are not reported: a CRC mismatch, a reserved value, or a frame whose block size or channel count exceeds what the instance was sized for makes the decoder silently resynchronise to the next frame, so an undersized FX_FLAC_ALLOC_SUBSET_FORMAT_DAT() instance drops audio without an error.
- The integration test (test_flac_integration.c) only checks 16- and 24-bit files against flac -d and skips other bit depths with 'we're probably fine'; the runner covers the IETF flac-test-files subset/ directory but not uncommon/ (which holds the 32 bps, changing-bitdepth and 768 kHz files).
- README build notes look stale: it says to add flac.c and flac.h (the files are src/foxen-flac.c/.h) and its emcc command names subprojects/libfoxenbitstream, whose code is now copied into foxen-flac.c.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-03-29, a README fix, after the Feb 2025 Arduino support PR and the March 2025 relicence), 84 stars and no open issues, but it is small, dependency-free and LGPL-2.1-or-later, so it is easy to vendor for embedded or WASM decoding as long as 32-bit FLAC is not needed.

[repo](https://github.com/astoeckel/libfoxenflac) · [benchmark](https://github.com/astoeckel/libfoxenflac)

##### Nelux (NeLux)  `C++ (Python package with PyTorch tensor output)`  `AGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

FFmpeg-backed Python video reader returning PyTorch tensors; parallel RGB conversion outruns torchcodec and ffmpeg-CLI rgb24 pipes.

**Beats:** FFmpeg CLI piped decode (ffmpeg-rgb24 subprocess; ffmpeg-nvdec subprocess for the GPU path); torchcodec also compared — First-party, Windows 11 on an i9-13900K + RTX 3090, nelux 0.10.1/0.11.0 build (compiler and flags not recorded) over FFmpeg 8.x, H.264 to RGB uint8, 600 frames (300 at 4K): default reader 3393 / 2563 / 539 fps at 720p / synthetic 1080p / synthetic 4K vs torchcodec 2924 / 1589 / 367 and an ffmpeg -vf format=rgb24 subprocess 2273 / 1102 / 254. The ffmpeg rows include process start-up while nelux is timed after reader construction, convert_workers=0 brings nelux to torchcodec parity, and the rows are single 0.18-0.6 s runs taken on a build that still had the convert-pool RAM leak.

**Known shortcoming:** Decoding is FFmpeg's libavcodec, so the win over the ffmpeg CLI comes from parallel swscale colour conversion plus the subprocess start-up counted in the ffmpeg timings (ffmpeg -f null at 720p runs 2906 fps against Nelux's 3394 with RGB output); the CLI baseline is whatever ffmpeg is on PATH (8.0.1-gyan in perf_findings) while the wheel pins TAS-FFMPEG 8.1.2; the README's 'default' row is really the prefetch/fanout row; the NVDEC baseline does no RGB conversion.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e117, 2026-10-05): the benchmarked 0.10.1/0.11.0 build had a default convert-pool host-RAM leak of about one frame per decoded frame (CHANGELOG 0.12.5); tests/output/thread_modes.json shows it (nelux default RSS 1532 / 3769 / 7353 MB vs torchcodec 673 / 732 / 1095 MB at 720p / 1080p / 4K), so the README's 'RSS essentially identical' claim, taken from a cumulative in-process high-water mark, is invalid. fps were never re-measured after the leak fix, pooled buffers, FFmpeg 9.0.2 or the new convert-worker default clamp(hw - decode threads, 1, 8) (README still says min(hw, 16)); the 1080p/4K clips are synthetic testsrc2. Tier C stands (numbers from a build later fixed for a correctness bug); the decoder is FFmpeg's, so the entry could fold under FFmpeg.

**Independent measurement:** first-party results.json

**How:** Decoding is stock libavcodec with frame threading (num_threads=0 lets FFmpeg pick), so no codec work is faster than FFmpeg. The gain is a pool of convert worker threads that run the per-frame libswscale YUV-to-RGB conversion in parallel, with a sequence-keyed reorder map and bounded in-flight backpressure so conversion no longer serialises behind decode; current code also recycles 64-byte-aligned output buffers wrapped with from_blob instead of allocating a tensor per frame. On NVDEC, a CUDA NV12/P010-to-RGB kernel converts on the GPU and the tensor never leaves the device. The README itself says that with convert_workers=0 fps, CPU and RSS land within about 2% of torchcodec.

**Use it when:**
- Feeding a PyTorch training or inference loop from H.264/HEVC files at 1080p or above, where single-threaded RGB conversion is the bottleneck and the machine has idle cores (first-party: 1.6x torchcodec at 1080p, 1.47x at 4K).
- NVDEC decode straight into cuda:0 tensors with the colour conversion done on the GPU, avoiding a host round-trip.
- Replacing ffmpeg subprocess pipes in Python (decode, process, NVENC or x264 encode, audio passthrough) with an in-process library, especially for many short clips where process start-up dominates; reconfigure() reuses a reader across files.
- ML work that needs per-block motion vectors from FFmpeg's decoder side data (CPU path only).

**Skip it when:**
- CPU-limited hosts or multi-worker DataLoaders: the default mode used 874-1656% CPU against torchcodec's 344-502% for the published gains, and with convert_workers=0 it is only torchcodec-speed.
- When raw decode speed is the problem: every CPU row is FFmpeg's libavcodec, so it cannot beat ffmpeg's own decoder; the ffmpeg -f null decode-only run was faster than nelux at 4K (735 vs 539 fps).
- Closed-source or hosted products: NeLux is AGPL-3.0 and the bundled FFmpeg is GPL-2.0-or-later (libx264, libx265 linked).
- Environments off its narrow matrix: Python 3.13+, a wheel built per PyTorch minor (currently 2.14), CUDA 13 wheels need compute capability 7.5+ (Pascal/Volta need a source build), macOS is CPU-only.
- Versions before 0.12.5 on long CPU runs: the default convert pool leaked roughly one decoded frame of host RAM per frame.

**Integration:** Python wheel: pybind11 C++20 extension (shared lib) with FFmpeg shared libraries bundled · PyTorch (must be imported first; wheel tied to one torch minor), numpy, bundled TAS-FFMPEG 9.0.2 (GPL); CUDA 13 runtime from the CUDA torch wheel for NVDEC/NVENC. Source builds: scikit-build-core, CMake, Ninja, vcpkg, MSVC 18 on Windows · Python 3.13+, C++20 (MSVC 18 on Windows), CMake + Ninja; CUDA 13 for published GPU wheels · Windows x64 and Linux x86_64 (manylinux_2_28+) with CPU + NVDEC/NVENC; macOS arm64 14+ CPU only

**Vs siblings:** Pick NeLux over video_reader-rs when the consumer is PyTorch (including CUDA tensors from NVDEC) and spare cores can absorb the parallel RGB conversion. It does not decode H.264 faster than libavcodec, so if decode itself is the bottleneck, edge264 or rivet-h26x (faster H.264/H.265 decoders than libavcodec in their own benchmarks) are the relevant siblings.

**Gotchas:**
- The README's 'RSS is essentially identical' line is not supported by its own data. In the in-process comprehensive run every decoder shares one Python process and RSS climbs down the rows (601 MB to 2597 MB at 720p, 4864 MB to 9264 MB at 4K), so it is a running high-water mark, not per-decoder. The per-subprocess thread_modes.json shows nelux default at 1532 / 3769 / 7353 MB against torchcodec 673 / 732 / 1095 MB, which matches the convert-pool host-RAM leak (about one decoded frame retained per frame) that the changelog fixed in 0.12.5, after the published numbers were taken.
- Defaults have drifted from the docs and the benchmark: README and changelog say convert_workers=None means min(hw, 16), but current Decoder.cpp uses clamp(hw - decode threads, 1, 8) (8 on a 24-thread CPU) with an in-flight cap of clamp(64 MB / frame, 4, 16), and FFmpeg is now 9.0.2; the published fps were never re-measured on these.
- import torch must come before import nelux; on Windows another package's avcodec DLL of the same soname can win the load, so check nelux.__ffmpeg_version__ reports '9.0.2-tas'.
- Several wrong-output bugs were fixed in 2026 (decode_batch used BT.601 regardless of colour space, #58; NVDEC set_range returned frames offset from the keyframe, #57; set_range with start>0 aborted the process, #60; unchecked CUDA launches gave silent black frames, #69), so pin a recent release.

**Status:** Very active (0.20.0 in pyproject.toml, last commit 2026-09-28, releases every few weeks), installable with pip on Windows, Linux and macOS, but AGPL-3.0 with GPL FFmpeg inside, and the benchmark tables date from 0.11.0 (May 2026) while the decode pipeline and defaults have changed since.

[repo](https://github.com/NevermindNilas/Nelux) · [benchmark](https://github.com/NevermindNilas/Nelux)

##### OpenVVC  `C`  `LGPL-2.1`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

INSA Rennes' lightweight C decoder for H.266/VVC; matches Fraunhofer VVdeC's speed in an independent study while using about half the memory.

**Beats:** VTM reference decoder and Fraunhofer VVdeC — Snippet only: search summaries of the authors' arXiv 2205.12217 paper (blocked) give about 37 fps FHD and 12 fps UHD single-threaded, 249 fps FHD and 75 fps UHD on average multi-threaded, and above 290 fps FHD and 90 fps UHD at best on an unnamed multi-core x86 platform (compiler and flags not visible), with VVdeC slightly faster single-threaded and OpenVVC scaling better. The independent JRTIP 2023 embedded study (also snippet only) found speed and energy on par with VVdeC (real-time FHD on 8 cores, HD on 4) and VVdeC using about 2x the memory, so the confirmed advantage is memory, not decode speed; the 34,000x MMSys 2023 figure is an end-to-end pipeline result driven by the encoder.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers exist only in snippets of blocked papers (arXiv 2205.12217, MMSys 2023); the 290/90 fps figures were not found in any snippet, and the 34,000x is a whole-pipeline figure including the encoder. An independent JRTIP 2023 study rates its speed comparable to VVdeC, with VVdeC needing twice the memory. Last commit 2022-03-22, abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** CI/conf.vmd5 marks 72 of 238 JVET conformance streams as failing (WPP, SLICES_A, SUBPIC, TILE_B-G, WP, LMCS_A/B, 4:4:4). rcn.c enables SIMD only when bitdepth == 10, so 8-bit runs scalar C; configure puts -msse4.1 -mavx2 into the global CFLAGS, so binaries may not run on CPUs without AVX2. Dead since 2022-03-22 with issues #17, #16 and #7 unanswered. The paper's figures (290/90 fps peak, 249/75 average, 37/12 single-thread FHD/UHD; VVdeC slightly faster single-threaded) remain snippet-only with CPU and flags not visible.

**How:** Written from scratch in C rather than derived from the C++ VTM reference, with SIMD kernels for the reconstruction stages: SSE4.1 for transforms, intra (angular, DC/planar, MIP, CCLM), motion compensation, DMVR, BDOF/PROF, ALF/CC-ALF, SAO, deblocking and dequantization, plus AVX2 versions of MC, ALF, SAO, MIP, DMVR, BDOF/PROF and intra angular (5,374 lines in x86/rcn_mc_avx2.c alone), selected at run time with __builtin_cpu_supports. On Arm the same SSE code is translated through a vendored SIMDe, plus hand-written AArch64 assembly for MC and DC/planar. Parallelism combines frame-level threads (several pictures in flight) with entry (tile) threads; both default to the core count.

**Use it when:**
- You need a small, LGPL-2.1 C library to play or analyse 10-bit 4:2:0 VVC main-profile streams (JVET CTC-style random-access or all-intra) and want lower memory than VVdeC: the independent JRTIP 2023 study measured VVdeC needing about 2x OpenVVC's memory.
- Embedded or mobile Arm decoding (Linux, Android, macOS, iOS build support) where memory footprint matters and real-time HD on 4 cores or FHD on 8 cores is enough, per the same study.
- Research on VVC decoder parallelism or energy, where a compact C codebase with separate 8-bit and 10-bit DSP templates is easier to modify than VVdeC's C++.
- Feeding VVC into an FFmpeg-based pipeline through the OpenVVC FFmpeg fork, as in the authors' uvg266 + uvgRTP + OpenVVC live 4K intra toolkit.

**Skip it when:**
- General-purpose or untrusted VVC playback: 72 of the 238 JVET conformance streams in CI/conf.vmd5 are commented out as failing, including WPP_A/B, SLICES_A, SUBPIC_A to E, TILE_B to G, WP_A/B (weighted prediction), LMCS_A/B, DMVR_A, SCALING_A to C, GDR, FIELD, PALETTE, ACT, BDPCM and all 4:4:4 streams; the project site lists WPP, subpictures, 4:0:0/4:2:2/4:4:4 and 12-bit as unsupported and slices and multi-tile as partial.
- 8-bit content when speed matters: every SIMD init in rcn.c is guarded by bitdepth == 10, so 8-bit streams run the scalar C templates only.
- Anything that needs maintenance or security fixes: the last commit on master is 2022-03-22, issue #17 (June 2026) asking whether it is still maintained has no reply, and issue #7 on decoding corrupted files was never answered; no fuzzing or error-resilience work is documented.
- When FFmpeg's native VVC decoder (FFVVC, the subject of a FOSDEM 2024 talk seen in search results) or VVdeC is an option: both avoid the out-of-tree FFmpeg fork OpenVVC needs; their speed and conformance were not checked in this pass.
- Builds on a fresh macOS toolchain or Linux/ARM64 without some effort: issues #16 (configure failure on a MacBook, April 2025) and #15 (ARM64 build and test request) are open with no maintainer response.

**Integration:** shared lib (libovvc.so via libtool) and static lib, with pkg-config file libopenvvc.pc and the dectest example binary · POSIX threads (required); optional SLHDR library (slhdr_cwrap via pkg-config, enabled automatically if found, --disable-slhdr to skip); SIMDe headers are vendored under libovvc/arm/simde · C compiler (configure probes gcc, then clang), autoconf, automake and libtool; Windows only through Cygwin or MSYS2; no C standard level documented · x86 and x86-64 (SSE4.1 and AVX2 kernels for 10-bit), AArch64 and 32-bit Arm (SIMDe-translated SSE code plus AArch64 assembly), Linux, macOS, Windows (Cygwin/MSYS2), Android, iOS (build support added March 2022)

**Vs siblings:** No other VVC decoder is catalogued; VVenC (the Fraunhofer encoder) and uvgRTP are pipeline partners rather than competitors. Pick OpenVVC over the uncatalogued VVdeC or FFmpeg's native VVC decoder only when memory footprint on 10-bit 4:2:0 content outweighs conformance coverage and maintenance.

**Gotchas:**
- configure appends -msse4.1 and -mavx2 to the global CFLAGS whenever the compiler accepts them, so every source file, not only the kernels behind the __builtin_cpu_supports checks, may be compiled with AVX2 code; a binary built this way is not safe to ship to CPUs without AVX2 unless you override CFLAGS or pass --disable-simd.
- The README changelog stops at v1.0.0 and says only 8-bit bitstreams were added, yet VERSION reads 1.1.0 and the library builds both 8-bit and 10-bit DSP templates, with all SIMD on the 10-bit path; trust the code and CI/conf.vmd5, not the README, for what is supported.
- OVDEC_NB_ENTRY_THREADS parallelises tiles only (per ovdec.h), so single-tile streams get no intra-picture speedup and scale only through frame threads; the frame-thread count is capped at the entry-thread count.
- The CI conformance script and README test command download bitstreams from openvvc.insa-rennes.fr and nasext-vaader.insa-rennes.fr, which may not stay online now that the project is idle.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-03-22 (2,197 commits, 133 stars, open issues unanswered) but LGPL-2.1 and plain C, so it can be vendored for 10-bit 4:2:0 decoding if you accept the conformance gaps listed in its own CI file.

[repo](https://github.com/OpenVVC/OpenVVC) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12217)

##### pedalboard  `Python (C++17/JUCE core)`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Spotify's Python audio-effects and audio-file library on a JUCE C++17 core; first-party claims of beating pySoX, SoxBindings and librosa.load.

**Beats:** pySoX (Python wrapper that runs the SoX command-line program), SoxBindings (Python bindings to libsox) and librosa.load (audio file reading) — The README's 300x (vs pySoX) and 4x (vs librosa.load) figures have no published method, corpus or machine; PR #85 first claimed up to 20x versus librosa.load 'without resampling', and a later commit 'tempered' the claim. The only public numbers are a third-party notebook (iCorv/pedalboard_with_tfdata: Python 3.8.11, pedalboard version and hardware not recorded) on LJ Speech at 22.05 kHz with six default-parameter effects. There SoxBindings took 38.1-130.8 s and pedalboard 10.8-32.2 s (2.4-6.3x, derived from page data). However, pedalboard ran with tf.data num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE while SoxBindings ran serially (the notebook says soxbindings does not allow multi-threading). No single-thread, like-for-like measurement exists behind the README's 'even when only using one thread' wording.

**Known shortcoming:** Python with a C++17/JUCE core via pybind11 (language-filter mismatch); weak category fit (audio effects, no resampling). README compares only pySoX (which spawns a SoX subprocess), SoxBindings and librosa.load, with no FFmpeg and no machine; the 300x and 4x are first-party.
