The cited SoxBindings notebook (iCorv) ran Pedalboard in parallel (tf.data AUTOTUNE) against serial SoxBindings, contradicting the README's 'one thread', and a single Pedalboard chain was slower there (357.2 s vs 305.2 s).

**Known shortcoming:** The iCorv chain row shares one Pedalboard across tf.data AUTOTUNE workers and the per-plugin std::mutex in process.h serialises it, which is the only row lost to SoxBindings (357.2 against 305.2 s); float64 input is cast to float32. Linux wheels up to 0.9.21 were built -march=native and SIGILL on old CPUs (#454, PR #511); AVX is now required. No C++ API; GPL-3.0.

**How:** The work runs in compiled C++ inside one process. pySoX instead launches the SoX program per transform, and most of the 300x figure is that overhead. process.h copies the array once into a juce::AudioBuffer<float>. It then runs every plugin in place over 8192-sample blocks (DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE) with the GIL released (py::gil_scoped_release), so several Python threads can use separate cores. The DSP is JUCE's dsp module (for example juce::dsp::Reverb, a Freeverb-style design) plus Rubber Band for pitch and time stretching. Rubber Band's FFTs use vendored FFTW with AVX codelets on Linux and vDSP on macOS. The extension builds as a CMake Release with -O3 and interprocedural optimisation, and Linux x86 wheels target -mavx. File reads decode through JUCE readers, including a patched MP3 decoder, straight into the output buffer with the GIL released.

**Use it when:**
- ML data augmentation in Python (tf.data, PyTorch DataLoader threads) that applies built-in effects to many clips. The GIL is released during processing, so threads scale across cores without multiprocessing, provided each thread owns its own plugin instances.
- Replacing pySoX code that runs the sox command line once per transform. Most of the claimed 300x is removed subprocess and temporary-file overhead, so short clips gain the most.
- Reading, transcoding or resampling large files from Python in constant memory: chunked AudioFile.read(), resampled_to() with O(1) memory, and WAV/FLAC/OGG/MP3 encoding without FFmpeg.
- Batch rendering through third-party VST3 or Audio Unit plugins from a Python script on macOS, Windows or Linux.

**Skip it when:**
- C++ projects. The core is a pybind11 extension (pedalboard_native) with no C++ API or standalone library, so use JUCE's dsp classes or Rubber Band directly.
- Closed-source or permissively licensed products. pedalboard is GPL-3.0 and statically bundles JUCE (GPLv3 or commercial), the VST3 SDK, Rubber Band and FFTW (GPLv2+), and LAME (relicensed to GPLv3 here).
- Pipelines that must match SoX output. The effects are JUCE algorithms, not SoX ports, and the SoxBindings comparison ran each library's own effect at default parameters, so the outputs differ.
- float64 processing. process() casts float64 input to float32 (astype) and always returns float32.
- x86-64 CPUs without AVX. Linux x86-64 wheels require AVX, and Linux wheels up to 0.9.21 were built with -march=native and could crash with SIGILL on import on older CPUs (issue #454, fixed by PR #511 in September 2026).

**Integration:** module (Python C++ extension, platform wheels on PyPI; vendored C/C++ dependencies compiled in statically) · numpy at runtime. Bundled and statically linked: JUCE 6, VST3 SDK, Rubber Band, FFTW 3 (Linux only), LAME/mpglib, libgsm, dr_wav, pybind11. A Linux source build also needs freetype and ALSA development packages. · Python 3.10+ (requires-python >=3.10; tested 3.10-3.15). Building from source needs C++17, CMake 3.18+, scikit-build-core >=0.5 and pybind11 >=2.9. · Linux x86-64 (AVX required) and aarch64 (manylinux and musllinux wheels); macOS x86-64, arm64 and universal2; Windows amd64

**Vs siblings:** No catalogued sibling offers a Python effect chain or plugin host, so pick pedalboard for effects and for file I/O and encoding from Python. audioFlux is the catalogued choice for spectral feature extraction against librosa. libsoxr or r8brain-free-src are the C/C++ choices when the job is resampling throughput and quality rather than effects.

**Gotchas:**
- A Pedalboard or plugin shared across threads serializes on its mutex. Build one chain per worker. The iCorv notebook's 'Pedalboard Chain' row shared one board across tf.data AUTOTUNE workers, and it is the only row where pedalboard lost to SoxBindings (357.2 s vs 305.2 s).
- reset=True is the default, so each call clears delay lines and reverb tails. Chunked or streaming processing needs reset=False (README quick start). Plugins with latency get compensated output that is padded and then trimmed.
- Every call copies the input array into a JUCE buffer and copies the result back, and float64 input costs an extra conversion. For very short clips the copies and Python call overhead are a large share of the time.
- MP3 frames and duration are estimates until the file has been read through (exact_duration_known is False), so the length can change during reading.

**Status:** Actively maintained by Spotify: v0.9.25 released 2026-09-09, last commit 2026-09-23, 6.3k stars, 85 open issues and 58 open PRs. It is easy for Python users (pip wheels), but GPL-3.0 and not reusable as a C++ library.

[repo](https://github.com/spotify/pedalboard) · [benchmark](https://github.com/spotify/pedalboard)

##### rkvdec-vdpu383 HEVC/H.264 read-cache fix  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Linux kernel patch that turns on the RK3576 VDPU383 decoder's read caches, cutting mainline HEVC/H.264 hardware decode time several-fold.

**Beats:** Mainline Linux rkvdec-vdpu383 HEVC and H.264 backends (upstream driver without read-cache configuration); vendor MPP stack as reference — These are first-party numbers on an RK3576 running Armbian 7.0.1-edge-rockchip64, decoding one unnamed 1080p clip. Measured time per frame runs from the decode kick to the hardirq: HEVC ~12 ms cache-off vs 1.70 ms cache-on (~7x), H.264 8.7 ms vs 3.6 ms (~2.4x). The timer is published as the sibling driver's vp9_time module parameter (ktime_get at the kick, hardirq timestamp, mean printed every 100 frames), so the values are per-frame means, not per-clip totals. The kick timestamp is taken before the cache writes, so the cache-on time also includes seven MMIO writes. The clip, frame count and run count are not published. The author's own code comments give different figures for the same comparison (HEVC 4.6 ms cache-off vs MPP 1.15 ms, '~4x'/'~5x'), so read the ratio as roughly 2-7x, not as a precise number.

**Known shortcoming:** Off-category: a Linux kernel driver change measuring hardware-decoder throughput on one SoC (RK3576, kernel 7.0.1-edge-rockchip64, 1080p, MMIO-to-completion timing: HEVC about 12 ms to 1.70 ms, H.264 8.7 ms to 3.6 ms) with no clip, harness or run count. The README contradicts itself (the table says equal to the vendor MPP stack while the residual section says about a 1.9x gap remains for HEVC), and the patch is a hunk sketch with elided paths, so git am fails.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e123, 2026-10-05): the timer lives in the sibling rkvdec-vdpu383-av1 source (vp9_time parameter, ktime from kick to hardirq, mean over 100 frames), so the numbers are per frame. The author's own figures disagree: README about 12 ms to 1.70 ms (about 7x, '= MPP'), a driver comment of 2026-06-27 gives HEVC cache-off 4.6 ms vs MPP 1.15 ms (about 4x), and the module help says 'about 5x', so the ratio is uncertain; C at best. The upstream rk3576.dtsi already carries the 'cache' register window (0x27b00600), so the verifier's device-tree caveat is mostly moot, but the upstream driver never maps it (confirmed in torvalds master). The sibling driver is heavily experimental and its AV1 backend has a documented nondeterminism bug; no upstream submission found. Possible but unmeasured: the same cache gap on RK3588 VDPU381.

**Independent measurement:** first-party in-driver timer

**How:** The VDPU383 has three reference read caches (CACHE0/1/2) in a dedicated register window at 0x27b00600 on RK3576. Mainline Linux (torvalds master, checked 2026-10-05) maps only the 'link' and 'function' windows, so these caches are never configured and every reference read goes to DRAM. The patch writes CACHEABLE|READ_ALLOC|LINE_64 (0x13) to each cache's config register, clears all three, and sets MAX_READS to 0x1c before setting DEC_E. These are the values the author captured from a register-write trace of the vendor MPP driver. It only changes how the hardware fetches memory: the README reports HEVC output byte-identical with the cache off and on.

**Use it when:**
- You decode HEVC or H.264 on an RK3576 board (Radxa ROCK 4D, Armbian edge kernels) through mainline V4L2 stateless decoding and hardware decode time limits frame rate or power.
- You maintain a downstream kernel built on Collabora's merged VDPU383 support and want the cheapest throughput gain before tackling AFBC or link-mode pipelining.
- You are comparing mainline against the vendor BSP/MPP stack on the same silicon and need to remove a known non-silicon gap first.
- You want a tiny, auditable change: seven register writes plus one optional ioremap, gated by a runtime module parameter.

**Skip it when:**
- Any SoC other than RK3576: the patch touches only the VDPU383 backends. RK3588 (VDPU381) also has a 'cache' window in the upstream DT and its upstream backend does not configure it either, but nobody has tested or measured a port.
- You need a fix that git am can apply: the patch file uses elided paths ('drivers/.../rkvdec.c') and tells you in prose to add a struct field, so you must port it by hand or take the much larger experimental sibling driver.
- You need vendor-stack throughput: the README itself reports a ~1.9x residual against MPP after the fix, attributed to missing AFBC reference compression and link-mode pipelining.
- You need upstream-supported code: the patch has not been accepted into mainline. A search found no linux-media submission of the cache fix, only the merged VDPU381/383 series and a May 2026 H.264 deblocking bug thread.
- You need CPU or software decoding, or another codec: VP9/AV1 on this chip live in the sibling out-of-tree driver.

**Integration:** source-drop (kernel patch sketch); buildable as the out-of-tree rockchip-vdec.ko module from the sibling rkvdec-vdpu383-av1 repo · Linux kernel with Collabora's rkvdec VDPU383 HEVC/H.264 backends (merged early 2026); DT node exposing reg-name 'cache' (upstream rk3576.dtsi already does) · Kernel build tree; developed against Armbian 7.0.1-edge-rockchip64 (kernel headers, KBUILD_MODPOST_WARN=1 for the out-of-tree build) · Rockchip RK3576 (VDPU383) only, aarch64

**Vs siblings:** Every catalogued sibling decoder (edge264, rivet-h26x, rusty_h265, dav1d) is a CPU decoder racing libavcodec. Pick this patch only when you already use the RK3576 hardware decoder through mainline V4L2 and want it to run at closer to its real speed. On any other platform, or for portable software decoding, use edge264 (H.264) or rivet-h26x/rusty_h265 (HEVC).

**Gotchas:**
- Mapping is optional: if the DT lacks reg-name 'cache', the driver silently keeps the old cache-off behaviour. The sibling module logs 'rkvdec: cache window mapped/ABSENT' at probe, so check dmesg. Upstream rk3576.dtsi already lists 'link', 'function', 'cache' (0x27b00600, size 0x100), so the verifier's DT caveat matters only for older or downstream DTs.
- The author's own numbers disagree. README and patch: HEVC ~12 ms to 1.70 ms (~7x, '= vendor MPP'), H.264 8.7 to 3.6 ms. The sibling driver's 2026-06-27 code comment: HEVC 4.6 ms cache-off vs MPP 1.15 ms (~4x). Module help text: '~5x throughput fix'. The H.264 comment: '~5x pure-HW-decode-time gap vs MPP'.
- The sibling driver that carries the fix is a heavily instrumented development module, about 167 KB of rkvdec.c against 51 KB upstream, with dozens of A/B module parameters. Its AV1 backend has a documented non-deterministic decode bug (docs/NONDETERMINISM_BUG.md: about half of runs wrong). Lift only the cache hunk into production kernels.
- Stale comment in the sibling rkvdec.c: it says 'Default off for the A/B', but the code sets hevc_cache = 1.

**Status:** A one-off GPL-2.0 drop (three commits, all 2026-06-28, 1 star, no issues or PRs) that has not been submitted or accepted upstream. The change is small enough to port by hand into any kernel carrying the merged VDPU383 backends.

[repo](https://github.com/SympleNZ/rkvdec-vdpu383-h264-hevc) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SympleNZ/rkvdec-vdpu383-h264-hevc)

##### Shine (fixed-point MP3 encoder)  `C`  `LGPL-2.0-only`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Small fixed-point C MP3 (Layer III) encoder that runs about 2-4x faster than LAME by skipping most of LAME's quality work.

**Beats:** LAME 3.100 (M1 Pro run) and LAME 3.99.5 (outdated Raspberry Pi run) CLI, 128 kbps CBR, qval=3, joint stereo with psychoacoustic model — The only numbers are first-party pasted CLI runs from the README: on an M1 Pro (2022-12-30) stock LAME 3.100 -b 128 (qval=3, joint stereo, psychoacoustic model) reports 88.773x realtime by CPU time while shineenc reports 318.0x for a 318 s file, which is 318 s divided by a 1 s reading of whole-second time() wall clock that also includes WAV open and file writes, so Shine's real speed is only bounded to more than about 1.8x LAME's. The code shows Shine skips the psychoacoustic model, block switching, bit reservoir, noise shaping and mid/side, so the ratio compares much less work against LAME at qval=3; the fair comparison (LAME -q 9 or -f) was never run.

**Known shortcoming:** README Apple M1 Pro figures (LAME 3.100 at 88.773x realtime vs Shine 318.0x, about 3.6x derived) are single runs with no script or compiler, and shineenc times with time() at 1-second resolution (src/bin/main.c), so 318.0x means 318 s of audio in 1 s and the true ratio is only bounded at about 1.8x or more; the LAME figure is CPU time, Shine's is wall clock. Fixed-point encoder with no psychoacoustic model and plain stereo against LAME qval=3 joint stereo; quality never measured (issue #27 open since 2017); open bugs #24 (full-scale distortion), #37 (final frame truncated), #39 (padding bit at 32 kHz/48 kbps). Raspberry Pi run (model unnamed, outdated): about 2.0x. Last commit 2023-01-01, abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** The speed comes from skipped work (code-confirmed): calc_xmin is always 0 (no psychoacoustic model or noise shaping), long blocks only, the bit reservoir is off (ResvMax fixed at 0), and mode_ext is always 0 (-j sets the header only, no mid/side), while the LAME baseline at qval 3 does far more work and a fair LAME -q 9 or -f run was never made; timing is whole-second time() wall clock including WAV open and I/O. Bug at HEAD: shine_flush drops up to 31 cached bits (issue #37, PR #38 unmerged). js/package.json declares LGPL-2.0-only.

**How:** Mostly by doing far less work than LAME, not by a cleverer algorithm. calc_xmin() sets the allowed distortion to zero for every band and the outer loop only binary-searches the global quantizer step (bin_search_StepSize, then the inner rate loop), so there is no psychoacoustic model and no scalefactor noise shaping; only long blocks are coded (no block switching), the bit reservoir is off (ResvMax is fixed at 0, so each granule gets mean_bits and the rest is stuffing), and mode_ext is always 0, so -j only sets the joint-stereo header with no mid/side coding. What remains is a direct-form 32-band polyphase analysis filter and a direct 18x36 MDCT in Q31 fixed point (32x32-to-64-bit multiplies; ARMv6 SMMUL/SMULL and MIPS32 inline asm, plain C int64 elsewhere including AArch64), a 10,000-entry x^(3/4) lookup table for quantization, and loops unrolled by 7.

**Use it when:**
- CPUs without an FPU or with weak floating point (ARMv5/armel, MIPS32, microcontrollers): the fixed-point core needs only integer multiplies (issue #29 reports use on STM32).
- Live streaming or transcoding many channels at once (Liquidsoap, FFmpeg -c:a libshine) where CPU per stream matters more than MP3 quality at a given bitrate.
- Constant-bitrate MP3 at 128 kbps or higher where the result only has to decode everywhere (voice, monitoring, previews) and transparency is not required.
- In-browser or Node MP3 encoding through the wasm build; its README reports 46x to 99x realtime on a 5.57 s file in Chrome 108, Firefox 108, Safari 16.2 and Node 19 (first-party, December 2022).

**Skip it when:**
- Music archiving or any use where quality per bit matters: no psychoacoustic model, no block switching (pre-echo on transients), no bit reservoir and no mid/side stereo, and no quality measurement exists (issue #27 open since 2017).
- Full-scale or clipping-prone input: issue #24 (open since 2017, no reply) reports the output level wobbling on full-amplitude sines, and the README warns the encoder 'may not be exempt of bugs'.
- Bit-exact or strictly valid final frames: issue #37 and the unmerged PR #38 report a truncated last frame, and at HEAD shine_flush() returns only whole 32-bit words, so up to 31 bits left in the bitstream cache are never written.
- VBR/ABR, 24-bit or float input, or LAME-style presets: none are implemented; input is int16 only and bitrate is fixed per encoder.
- Projects needing an active upstream: last commit 2023-01-01, 11 open issues and 5 open PRs (three are dependabot bumps) with no maintainer replies on the bug reports.

**Integration:** shared lib or static lib (autotools libshine), or source-drop of the nine src/lib/*.c files · libm only (sin/cos/pow at init, log in calc_scfsi, sqrt in the out-of-table quantize path); no other libraries · C99-era C with GCC-style extensions (statement expressions and inline asm in the ARM and MIPS multiply headers, __attribute__((unused))); Makefile.am adds -O2 -funroll-loops -fsigned-char; Windows needs third-party build files (open PR #40, issue #45) · any with a 64-bit integer multiply; hand-written multiplies for 32-bit ARM (non-Thumb) and MIPS32 only; big-endian via SHINE_BIG_ENDIAN from configure; wasm via emscripten

**Vs siblings:** Pick Shine over SuperLAME (multi-threaded LAME at LAME quality) when the target has no FPU, only one core per stream, or needs a tiny dependency-free encoder; pick SuperLAME, or glint's LAME 3.100 numbers, whenever MP3 quality at a given bitrate matters.

**Gotchas:**
- Each encode call needs exactly shine_samples_per_pass() samples per channel; the caller pads the last block (shineenc zero-pads), and the returned buffer is only valid until the next call.
- shineenc ignores the WAV data-chunk length (wave.c 'TODO: respect data chunk length'), so trailing chunks after the PCM data are encoded as audio; the library itself is unaffected.
- Joint stereo (-j or JOINT_STEREO) only changes the header: mode_ext is always 0, so channels are coded as plain left/right.
- Issue #39: the padding bit can be wrong at some rate/bitrate pairs (32 kHz/48 kbps reported) because slot accounting uses double arithmetic with truncation in layer3.c.

**Status:** Abandoned (last commit 2023-01-01, open correctness issues #24, #37, #39 unanswered) but small, dependency-free and LGPL (COPYING is the GNU Library GPL v2 text; js/package.json declares LGPL-2.0-only), so it is copyable as a library or vendored source if LGPL obligations are acceptable.

[repo](https://github.com/toots/shine) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/toots/shine/HEAD/README.md)

##### SuperFast Codecs (fre:ac multi-threaded codec drivers)  `C++`  `GPL-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

fre:ac encoder drivers that run several Opus/AAC/MP3/Speex encoder instances on overlapping chunks to use multiple cores for one output file.

**Beats:** fre:ac's regular single-threaded codec drivers: libopus (Opus), FAAC and Core Audio AAC in the initial release; FDK-AAC, LAME and Speex drivers added later — In the author's own PDF, fre:ac converts one file in single-file mode about 3x faster with four SuperFast threads than with the regular single-threaded FAAC and Opus drivers (chart readings about 2.9-3.2x at 4 threads and 4.5-4.8x at 8). In multi-file mode the gain is only about 1-10%. Charts have no units, the only machine detail is 'a 6 core CPU', and no compiler, OS, codec version or script is given; LAME, FDK-AAC, Core Audio and Speex have no published numbers here.

**Known shortcoming:** fre:ac SuperFast drivers: the speedup is parallel codec instances (about 3x at 4 threads, 4.5-4.8x at 8 threads, derived from PDF charts covering only FAAC and Opus; no y-axis unit, machine only '6 core CPU'), with overlap frames adding work, output not bit-identical to the single-instance encoder, no quality or bitrate data, and LAME's bit reservoir repacked. Last commit 2020-12-10.

**Known shortcoming:** The charted FAAC and Opus numbers come from the 2017 128/8 prototype (block/overlap) while the repo's Opus driver is now 256/24 and was not re-measured; workers reuse one encoder across blocks without reset (stale state), contrary to the record's 'fresh state' caveat. Archived-code bugs by reading: the LAME mono path passes the block start as buffer_l every frame (repeats the first frame; fixed in BoCA), flush advances framesToProcess minus overlap so input shorter than the overlap gives a negative memmove (fixed in BoCA), and the Opus overlap 24*960/frameSize ignores the sample rate and exceeds the 256-frame block at 8-16 kHz with 5-10 ms frames (loop runs backwards; still in BoCA). fre:ac 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 fixed SuperFast crashes and CBR MP3 issues; issue #3 reports random superopus failures. MSIVST/SuperLAME (also listed) derives its repacker from this code.

**How:** High-level data parallelism over encoder instances, the 'split into fragments' approach that LAME MT abandoned because it cannot be bit-identical. Opus blocks are 256 frames with an overlap of max(24, ceil(24*960/frameSize)) frames, FAAC 128 frames with 8, and LAME 128 frames with 4*1152/frameSize; the overlap frames re-adapt encoder state and their packets are discarded. Worker encoders are not reset between blocks (Opus and FAAC reuse one handle per worker; LAME flushes with lame_encode_flush_nogap after each block), so each block starts from stale state left by that worker's previous block. For MP3 a serial repacker unpacks frames, rebuilds the bit reservoir across seams and makes the worker re-encode, after feeding dummy frames to fill the reservoir, when a frame does not fit. Even at one thread, decoding and encoding run on separate threads, which the PDF credits for a small gain.

**Use it when:**
- Encoding one long input (an album joined into one file, an audiobook, a long recording) to Opus or AAC on a 4-16 thread desktop, where stock fre:ac drivers use a single core.
- Batch jobs with fewer output files than cores; mainline fre:ac only engages SuperFast when the number of output files is at most half the logical CPUs.
- 48 kHz input to Opus (or input already at the MP3 output rate for LAME), the paths where the chunking runs in parallel without a serial resampler in front.
- As a design template for parallelizing any codec with constant frame sizes and interceptable packets; use the BoCA mainline source, not this archived copy.

**Skip it when:**
- You need output bit-identical to a single-threaded encode, or a quality guarantee: seams differ, and the only quality evidence is the author's difference-signal plots, with no listening test or objective metric.
- Many files at once: multi-file mode gains only about 1-10% because per-file parallelism already fills the cores.
- Non-48 kHz Opus input or LAME with resampling: the Opus resampler stays single-threaded, and the LAME driver disables SuperFast when the input rate differs from the MP3 output rate.
- Vorbis, FLAC or WMA: the author says block-size switching or closed packet APIs make the method unworkable for them.
- Code from this archived repo as is: it predates fixes shipped in fre:ac 1.1.1/1.1.2 (a SuperFast crash and several CBR MP3 issues) and has the short-input and mono-MP3 bugs listed under gotchas.

**Integration:** shared lib (BoCA encoder components loaded by fre:ac) · smooth class library, BoCA component framework, plus the codec libraries loaded at run time (libopus/libogg, FAAC/mp4v2, FDK-AAC, LAME, Speex, Core Audio on Windows/macOS) · not documented (GNU make with BoCA's Makefile-commands; C++ with the smooth framework) · Windows, macOS, Linux and FreeBSD builds were published (x86-64 and i686; macOS universal binary includes PPC)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it, through BoCA mainline, when you need multi-core encoding of one stream with the stock libopus, FAAC/FDK-AAC or LAME. SuperLAME is a standalone CLI that ports this LAME driver and repacker and publishes numbers with a named CPU (Ryzen 7 5800X3D), so it is the better-documented choice for MP3 alone. The faster single-threaded codecs (opus-pure, libopus-rs, ruopus) speed up each instance and could be combined with this chunking.

**Gotchas:**
- Archived LAME driver, mono input: lame_encode_buffer gets samplesBuffer (the block start) as the left channel for every frame, so mono MP3 output repeats each block's first frame. BoCA mainline passes the per-frame offset. Found by code reading, not run.
- Archived Opus, FAAC and LAME drivers advance by framesToProcess - overlap even on the final flush, so an input shorter than the overlap (under about 0.48 s for Opus at 20 ms frames) makes framesProcessed negative and the memmove runs out of bounds. Mainline uses (flush ? 0 : overlap). Found by code reading.
- The Opus overlap formula uses 960 (a 20 ms frame at 48 kHz) at every sample rate, so the overlap is 72/256 frames at 16 kHz and 144/256 at 8 kHz (28% and 56% of the work discarded), and with 5-10 ms frames at 8-16 kHz it exceeds the 256-frame block (e.g. 288 at 8 kHz/10 ms), which drives the block loop backwards with negative offsets. Still present in BoCA mainline; found by code reading.
- The published numbers come from the 2017 proof of concept (128-frame blocks, 8-frame overlap); the repo's Opus driver now uses 256/24 and was not re-measured. Issue #3 reports intermittent 'Could not process file' errors with superopus only (2018 alpha build), closed without a fix when the repo was archived.

**Status:** Archived 2020-12-11 and superseded by enzo1982/BoCA, where SuperFast is on by default and later fixes landed. GPL-2.0 and tied to the BoCA/smooth frameworks, so it is only copyable as a design or into GPL code.

[repo](https://github.com/enzo1982/superfast) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enzo1982/superfast/master/doc/SuperFast%20Codecs.pdf)

##### SuperLAME  `C++`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

Multithreaded MP3 encoder CLI that runs many LAME r6531 instances on chunks; beats single-threaded LAME on wall time, not per core.

**Beats:** LAME (stock single-threaded libmp3lame 3.101 beta) — First-party only, on a Ryzen 7 5800X3D (Zen 3, 8C/16T, Windows 11) using the clang 21.1.6 -O3 -march=znver3 engine. docs/COMPARISON_REPORT.md (2026-06-29, before v1.1.0) times 16-thread SuperLAME against a single-threaded lame.exe built from the same patched LAME r6531 (its flags unstated) on four commercial albums: VBR -V2 5.84-6.17x and CBR 320 1.49-4.73x. The v1.1.0 fix took the 44-minute CBR 320 album from 7.19 to 3.85 s at 16 threads, but no stock-LAME run was repeated on v1.1.x, and the timing method for the June table is not documented, so the README's '~8x' rests on SCALING_NOTES (about 28 s against about 3.6 s, mode unstated, pre-v1.1.0).

**Known shortcoming:** Multithreaded LAME front end, not a faster codec: four CPU-dispatched LAME r6531 builds plus fre:ac/BoCA SuperFast parallel chunks and a repacker; the baseline is the same LAME core single-threaded, so the win is 16 threads against 1, and its own -t1 run is about 1.5x slower than stock LAME. docs/COMPARISON_REPORT.md: VBR -V2 5.84-6.17x, CBR 320 1.49-4.73x (pre-v1.1.0); SCALING_NOTES about 28 s vs 3.6 s. No public stock-LAME script, baseline flags unstated, test albums commercial.

**Known shortcoming:** The built-in timer (main.cpp, t0 at line 1335) covers encode plus repack only and excludes WAV read, resample and write, while the June table's timing method is undocumented, so the multithreaded side may omit I/O that stock LAME pays; there is no stock-LAME rerun on v1.1.x and the README's 'about 8x' rests on pre-v1.1.0 SCALING_NOTES (mode unstated); the '-t1 1.5x slower' and 'plateau at 2 workers' notes are stale (pre-v1.1.0 15.6 ms sleep-poll stalls). 'Bit-identical to stock LAME' is untested: regression.ps1 never runs stock lame.exe and the znver3 and SSE2 builds already differ (FMA rounding, below -50 dB); the baseline phase2 lame.exe flags are unknown and the build needs a config.h not in the repo. FrameChainValid checks headers only. v1.0.1 lost 6.6% of audio on resampled outputs and v1.1.1 lost frames at CBR 8-56 (the -V2 and CBR 320 rows are unaffected).

**How:** Chunk-level thread parallelism (Robert Kausch's fre:ac/BoCA 'SuperFast' technique): workers encode overlapping blocks (128 frames, overlap 4*1152/frameSize = 4 MPEG-1 frames) and flush with lame_encode_flush_nogap; a single serial SuperRepacker then unpacks each frame's main data, rewrites main_data_begin, zero-fills surplus reservoir, re-picks VBR bitrate indices, enlarges earlier frames (padding or bitrate) when the reservoir runs short, and asks a worker to re-encode with dummy frames when a frame still does not fit. Since v1.1.0 worker handoffs use condition variables instead of a 1 ms sleep-poll that Windows rounded to ~15.6 ms, which made MT encodes 1.8-1.9x faster. The LAME core is unchanged apart from per-CPU builds (-O3 -march=znver3 etc.); per thread SuperLAME is no faster than LAME.

**Use it when:**
- Turning one long file (album, audiobook, DJ mix) into an MP3 as fast as possible on a many-core x86-64 Windows machine, where single-file latency matters more than total CPU spent.
- VBR -V2 encodes: the largest measured gains (5.84-6.17x with 16 threads against single-threaded LAME in the June 2026 report).
- You want LAME r6531 with the maikmerten q4 CBR/ABR quality patch, plus native FLAC/24-bit/hi-res input and a complete Xing/Info tag even when writing to stdout.
- Hi-res or FLAC sources that need resampling to an MP3 rate: r8brain resampling is parallelized and done up front.

**Skip it when:**
- Batch conversion of many files: one stock LAME process per file keeps every core busy with no seam overlap or serial repacker (SuperLAME's own docs recommend one process per file; v1.1.0 reports only ~61% parallel efficiency at 16 threads).
- You need output that is byte-identical to a reference LAME encode: multithreaded output differs at chunk seams (ST-vs-MT decoded difference -45 to -87 dB in the June report), and single-thread output matches only a LAME built with the same -march flags.
- Linux, macOS or ARM: build scripts target clang with x86_64-windows-msvc and all tests are PowerShell; no non-Windows build is documented and the engines are x86-64 only.
- Streaming or memory-constrained encoding: the whole input, its float copy and the output MP3 are held in RAM (about 1-2 GB practical input), and nothing is written until the encode finishes.
- CBR on dense, loud material: the June report measured only 1.49x (Static-X) and 2.02x (American Head Charge) at CBR 320, because the repacker needs more seam retries in CBR.

**Integration:** CLI application (prebuilt Windows .exe in releases) or source-drop of the C++17 frontend; not a library · LAME trunk r6531 plus patches (q4 clamp, ID3v2.4 synchsafe sizes), libmpg123 >= 1.26 (1.33.6 used), r8brain-free-src (header-only), dr_flac (vendored); build needs clang/LLVM 21 with llvm-ar, llvm-nm and llvm-objcopy, plus CMake and NASM for mpg123. build/build_dispatch.sh also reads a LAME config.h from build/phase4-znver3/, which is not in the repository. · C++17; clang/LLVM 21 (tested 21.1.6) targeting x86_64-windows-msvc; MSVC cannot build the SIMD paths · x86-64 Windows (tested on Windows 11, Zen 3); CPUID picks a znver5, znver4 (AVX-512), znver3 (AVX2/FMA) or SSE2 engine; znver4/znver5 engines are built but never run, and Intel CPUs are untested

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over fre:ac's SuperFast drivers (enzo1982/superfast), which use the same technique, when you want a standalone LAME-style CLI with FLAC/hi-res input and the post-2018 BoCA repacker fixes, rather than a full converter GUI. Pick it over Shine when you need LAME quality and have many cores; Shine is a fixed-point encoder aimed at weak or embedded CPUs and trades quality for speed.

**Gotchas:**
- The speed and realtime figures SuperLAME prints come from a timer that covers only encode and repack (main.cpp starts it after input read and resampling and stops before the file write), whereas stock LAME's time includes reading the WAV; compare whole-process wall time or use --bench, which reports wall and CPU clocks.
- The self-heal safety net (FrameChainValid, which re-encodes single-threaded if the MT stream is broken) only walks frame headers; a repacker error that leaves headers intact but corrupts main_data_begin chaining would not trigger it.
- The regression suite never compares against a stock lame.exe: it checks ST against MT (<= -40 dB) and znver3 against SSE2 (<= -50 dB, the two differ by FMA-contraction rounding), so 'bit-identical to stock LAME' holds only for a LAME built the same way.
- Files under about 300 MB become cache-resident and give flat, misleading thread-scaling timings (the project's own warning); docs/SCALING_NOTES.md and CONTRIBUTING.md still describe a plateau at about 2 workers and a -t1 1.5x slower than LAME, figures that predate the v1.1.0 sleep-poll fix.

**Status:** Active (v1.1.1 released 2026-08-21, 21 commits, 3 stars, one closed issue, no pull requests), maintained by one person on a best-effort basis; GPL-2.0-or-later because it combines LGPL LAME and mpg123 with GPL code ported from fre:ac/BoCA, so it is copyable only under GPL terms.

[repo](https://github.com/MSIVST/SuperLAME) · [benchmark](https://github.com/MSIVST/SuperLAME/blob/master/docs/COMPARISON_REPORT.md)

##### Symphonia  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure, safe-Rust audio demuxing and decoding library; beats single-threaded libavcodec on FLAC, ALAC, MP1/MP2, high-bitrate MP3.

**Beats:** FFmpeg libavcodec native decoders (FLAC, ALAC, MP1, MP2, MP3, AAC-LC, Vorbis, ADPCM), single-threaded, built as the static 'ffbench' example from a pdeljanov/FFmpeg fork — BENCHMARKS.md (first-party, 2023-02-03) times whole-process hyperfine runs (30 after 3 warmups) of symphonia-play --decode-only (rustc 1.67.0, target-cpu=native) against a statically linked FFmpeg ffbench example (plain ./configure, compiler unstated) on an i7-4790K, an M1 Pro and a Pi 4B, using one or two unpublished files per codec. Symphonia needs 0.45-0.84x FFmpeg's time for MP1/MP2/FLAC/ALAC/320 kbps MP3 on x86 and M1 but loses on AAC-LC and Vorbis. From the code, ffbench uses default decoder options (one thread) and discards frames, and decode-only mode decodes with verification off and gapless trimming on, logging and skipping decode errors; PCM/WAV rows, where an FFmpeg developer reported Symphonia 1.5-2x slower in issue #179, are not in the table.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust (language-filter mismatch). BENCHMARKS.md ratios against FFmpeg's decoders match and ffbench.c confirms FFmpeg ran single-threaded, but FFmpeg's compiler and the input files are unstated, so C; Symphonia loses the ADPCM rows and wins 10 of 16 rows on the Raspberry Pi.

**Known shortcoming:** Whole-process timings with decode-only skipping decode errors and gapless on; the PCM/WAV rows disappeared after issue #179, where an FFmpeg developer reported Symphonia 1.5-2x slower there; the table predates the v0.5.4 and 0.6 speedups, so it is stale. No C API; open isomp4 fuzz panics #559 and #560.

**How:** The decoders are written so LLVM can auto-vectorize them: the FLAC LPC predictor is a const-generic function specialised for maximum orders 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 32, so the common subset orders run fixed-length i64 multiply-accumulate loops. AAC, Vorbis and MP3 compute the IMDCT through an N/2-point complex FFT, backed by rustfft's SSE/AVX/NEON kernels when the default opt-simd features are on. The README warns that speed depends strongly on the rustc version and target CPU because it relies on these LLVM optimisations.

**Use it when:**
- Rust applications decoding FLAC, ALAC, MP1/MP2 or 320 kbps MP3 on x86-64 or Apple silicon, where the published table shows 0.45-0.84x of single-threaded FFmpeg's decode time.
- Services that parse untrusted media and want memory safety: symphonia-core is #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and the project fuzzes its demuxers.
- Players needing gapless playback and tag reading in one dependency (FLAC, MP3, Vorbis, ALAC, ADPCM, PCM gapless; WAV, AIFF and OGG gapless demuxing).
- Builds that want to avoid linking FFmpeg: MPL-2.0, a handful of pure-Rust dependencies, and per-codec feature flags to keep the binary small.

**Skip it when:**
- AAC-LC or Vorbis heavy workloads: 1.10-1.27x and 1.05-1.24x FFmpeg's time in the 2023 table; 128 kbps MP3 is at parity to 7% slower.
- Low-power ARM such as a Raspberry Pi 4: margins shrink to 0.81-0.96 and 16-bit FLAC is 4% slower than FFmpeg.
- Opus, HE-AAC, WavPack, video, encoding or resampling: not implemented (Opus and HE-AAC only through third-party adapters that wrap libopus and libfdk-aac).
- C or C++ codebases: there is no C API, so you need a Rust toolchain and your own FFI shim; libavcodec, dr_flac or minimp3 integrate directly.
- Multi-threaded decoding of one FLAC or ALAC stream: Symphonia decoders use one thread, while FFmpeg can frame-thread those codecs (BENCHMARKS.md footnote).

**Integration:** crate · lazy_static, log, smallvec, bitflags, bytemuck, num-complex; rustfft (optional, pulled in by the default opt-simd features) · Rust 1.85, edition 2024 (0.6.x); 0.5.x needs Rust 1.53 · any Rust target; SIMD FFT paths for x86 SSE/AVX and ARM NEON; benchmarked on x86-64 (i7-4790K), Apple M1 Pro and Cortex-A72 (Raspberry Pi 4B)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Symphonia when you want one safe-Rust library that both demuxes and decodes many formats. For a single codec, rusty_flac (FLAC against FFmpeg 8.1.2) or minimp3/nanomp3 (MP3, from C or Rust) are narrower and easier to embed from C/C++.

**Gotchas:**
- Default features enable only royalty-free formats (FLAC, Vorbis, ADPCM, PCM, WAV, OGG, MKV): AAC, ALAC, MP1/MP2/MP3, ISO/MP4, AIFF and CAF need the aac, alac, mpa, isomp4, aiff, caf or all features. The README table lists opus and wavpack as default features, but they are neither in Cargo's default list nor implemented.
- 0.6.0 (2026-05-15) is a breaking API redesign with MSRV 1.85; 0.5 code needs the migration guide.
- Safe Rust prevents memory corruption but not panics: open fuzzing reports #559 (index out of bounds on a fragmented MP4 trun) and #560 (unreachable!() on an lpcm sample entry), both in the isomp4 demuxer, so isolate or catch_unwind when parsing hostile files.
- The published numbers use RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native; a generic distribution build was not measured and may be slower, since the decoders rely on auto-vectorisation.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v0.6.1 on 2026-08-13, about 15.7 million crates.io downloads), MPL-2.0 and usable as a crate today. The benchmark table predates the v0.5.4 'major optimizations for AAC, FLAC, MP3, and Vorbis' and the 0.6.0 decoding speedups, so current ratios are unmeasured.

[repo](https://github.com/pdeljanov/Symphonia) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pdeljanov/Symphonia/main/BENCHMARKS.md)

##### VapourSynth-BM3DCUDA  `C++ (CUDA, HIP, AVX2)`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

BM3D/V-BM3D denoiser for VapourSynth on CUDA, AVX2, HIP and SYCL; no published number against VapourSynth-BM3D.

**Beats:** VapourSynth-BM3D (original CPU plugin) and FFmpeg bm3d; no comparison against either found — The only first-party numbers are self-comparisons. R2.13 times its own CUDA (T4), HIP (Radeon Pro V520) and AVX2 (32-core Hygon 7390, Sapphire Rapids, EPYC Zen4, all on Windows Server 2022) builds at 1920x1080 GrayS/YUV444PS, for example 342/152/208/598/674 fps at radius 0 basic, with no script, parameters beyond radius/chroma/final, or CPU compiler flags (current CI builds the CPU DLLs with clang -mtune=<arch> -ffast-math -mavx2 -mfma). The V520 column came from a build whose own notes say output 'may be broken'. Third-party numbers: AmusementClub/vapoursynth-nssfactory PR #23 times bm3dcuda at 636 fps on an RTX 5080 (1080p gray) as the baseline for a faster port. A Doom9 post, seen only as a search snippet, gives 165.55 fps at radius 0 against a single-threaded 'BM3D_cpu' at 22 fps on an i7-8700, but the GPU and which CPU filter was used are unstated. Nothing measures it against VapourSynth-BM3D or FFmpeg bm3d.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the R2.13 table times only its own CUDA, HIP and AVX2 backends (T4 342.23 fps, EPYC Zen 4 CPU build 674.37 fps) with no number against VapourSynth-BM3D or FFmpeg bm3d in the README, releases or 25 issues, no bench script and the CPU compiler unstated; it is not the same work as VapourSynth-BM3D (no coefficient normalisation, a ps_num quality regression, non-bitwise-identical output; issues #31 and #33); the HIP release was disabled in R2.17.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e125, 2026-10-05): D stands; no bug behind the CUDA/AVX2 numbers, but the R2.13 V520 (bm3dhip) column was measured on a build the author's own notes say 'may be broken' (#23 open). The CPU build uses _mm256_rcp_ps approximate reciprocals plus -ffast-math in the CI DLLs; no Kaiser window, no th_mse, group size fixed at 8, so the output is not the same work as VapourSynth-BM3D. Bug: cpu_source/cpuid.h cpu_supports_avx2() returns 1 when the AVX/OSXSAVE bits are absent, so a pre-AVX CPU passes the check and then faults. Open #8 hang on non-power-of-two block_step, #31 host RAM leak, #17. Third-party: nssfactory PR #23 on an RTX 5080 measured bm3dcuda 636 fps vs nss_cuda 732 fps; PR #35 rolling mode 1.7-2.7x over the project's own legacy path.

**Independent measurement:** first-party README timings; third-party nssfactory PR

**How:** It implements BM3D (Dabov et al. 2007) with fixed 8x8 blocks and a fixed group of 8, so one 3D group is 8x8x8 floats. The CPU build holds that group in 64 AVX2 registers, runs an 8-point DCT taken from FFTW's genfft codelets with FMA, does exhaustive SSD block matching, and keeps a sorted top-8 candidate list in one vector register, updated with permutevar and blend. Reciprocals use the approximate _mm256_rcp_ps, and the Windows release CPU DLLs are built with clang -ffast-math, one DLL per -mtune target. The CUDA kernel gives each reference block 8 lanes of a warp (4 blocks per warp), reduces SSD and maintains the top-8 list with warp shuffles, transposes through shared memory, and aggregates with float atomicAdd. Each frame runs as a CUDA Graph on pinned host buffers, with up to 4 concurrent resource sets when fast=True. The _rtc build compiles the kernel with NVRTC at filter creation, baking width, stride, sigma and the search parameters in as constants, and the R2.17 rolling BM3Dv2 path keeps temporal accumulators on the GPU instead of shipping 2*(2r+1) intermediate planes to the CPU.

**Use it when:**
- VapourSynth encode chains that already run in 32-bit float and want BM3D or V-BM3D on an NVIDIA GPU (compute capability 5.0+): R2.13 lists 342 fps on a T4 for 1080p GrayS at radius 0, and a third-party harness (AmusementClub/vapoursynth-nssfactory PR #23) measured 636 fps on an RTX 5080 at 1080p gray.
- Many-core AVX2 servers with no GPU: in the R2.13 table, bm3dcpu on a 32-core EPYC Zen4 (674 fps at radius 0) or Sapphire Rapids (598 fps) beats the T4 in every row.
- Temporal denoising on CUDA through BM3Dv2's rolling mode (R2.17). PR #35 reports 1.7x to 2.7x over the old temporal path at radius 1-4 (RTX 5080, 640x360 GrayS); use rolling_chunk=16 for linear renders.
- When you need bit-reproducible GPU output (set extractor_exp >= 3) or want to experiment with other transforms (Haar, WHT, Bior1.5) and block costs (SAD, ZSSD, ZSAD) through the _rtc build.

**Skip it when:**
- When results must match VapourSynth-BM3D or the reference MATLAB BM3D. This plugin has no Kaiser window, no coarse prefiltering, no th_mse early cut-off, a group size fixed at 8 (issue #19 is open) and no coefficient normalization, so the same sigma does not give the same strength.
- When you need proof that it beats the CPU plugin or FFmpeg's bm3d filter: every first-party table times only its own backends. The only third-party GPU number found compares it with another CUDA port, which was faster (nss_cuda 732 vs bm3dcuda 636 fps).
- On AMD GPUs: the HIP build is disabled in R2.17, issue #23 (artifacts on an RX 6900 XT) and issue #33 (plugin fails to load with Adrenalin 26.5.1+) are open, and R2.13's own notes say HIP output frames 'may be broken'.
- In integer or 16-bit pipelines (input must be 32-bit float), in AviSynth (only requested, in open issues #7 and #26), or with large ps_num, which the README says can lower quality because duplicate temporal candidates are not merged.
- Long UHD encodes on Linux without watching memory: open issue #31 reports host RAM growing until OOM-kill at 3840x2160 (RTX 5060 Ti, Ubuntu 24.04, CUDA 13.0).

**Integration:** shared lib (VapourSynth plugin DLL/.so per backend) · VapourSynth API 3 headers; CUDA toolkit and driver 450+ for bm3dcuda (NVRTC, statically linked by default, for bm3dcuda_rtc); ROCm/HIP for bm3dhip; Intel oneAPI SYCL for bm3dsycl; none for bm3dcpu · CMake 3.20; C++17 (CPU build, CUDA kernel), C++20 (CUDA/RTC/HIP/SYCL host code); CUDA 11.5+ for the static-NVRTC RTC build; CI uses CUDA 12.8 (Linux) and 13.4.2 (Windows) · x86-64 with AVX2+FMA (bm3dcpu); NVIDIA GPUs sm_50+ (sm_35 with a manual build); AMD RDNA wave32 GPUs (HIP, currently disabled); Intel gen12lp+ GPUs (SYCL); Linux, Windows, macOS build fix merged (PR #25), Linux arm64 workflow present

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over KNLMeansCL or av-denoise when you want BM3D's transform-domain filtering, with its own CUDA, AVX2 and SYCL backends, rather than NLMeans. av-denoise's README claims about 1.3x the speed of V-BM3D on HIP, and KNLMeansCL is OpenCL NLMeans, so neither runs the same algorithm, and none of the three has been timed against the same incumbent.

**Gotchas:**
- GPU output is non-deterministic by default (float atomicAdd aggregation); only extractor_exp >= 3 (pre-rounding) makes it bitwise reproducible, and CPU and CUDA outputs never match bit for bit. The CPU build also uses ~12-bit approximate reciprocals for weights, Wiener coefficients and the final division.
- With radius > 0, legacy BM3D() returns an intermediate clip of height*2*(2r+1) rows; feeding it anywhere except bm3d.VAggregate gives garbage, and unprocessed planes in that path are undefined.
- Open issue #8: the CUDA build hangs for non-power-of-2 block_step (3, 5, 6, 7) on an RTX 2070 Super; the kernel still uses the full-warp __syncwarp(membermask) logic the reporter blamed.
- cpu_source/cpuid.h cpu_supports_avx2() returns 1 when CPUID lacks the AVX or OSXSAVE bits, so on a pre-AVX CPU the creation-time check passes and bm3dcpu would fault with an illegal instruction instead of the intended 'requires AVX2-capable cpu' error.

**Status:** Active (R2.17 on 2026-09-26 with a contributed rolling BM3Dv2 and CUDA 13.4.2; HIP release paused). The GPL-2.0 plugins are built by CI workflows for Windows and Linux, so they are easy to adopt in a VapourSynth chain, but GPL rules out vendoring into closed code.

[repo](https://github.com/WolframRhodium/VapourSynth-BM3DCUDA) · [benchmark](https://github.com/WolframRhodium/VapourSynth-BM3DCUDA/releases/tag/R2.13)

##### zita-resampler  `C++`  `GPL-3.0-or-later`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Real-time-safe polyphase windowed-sinc audio resampler (fixed and variable ratio); claims to beat libsamplerate, with no published numbers.

**Beats:** libsamplerate (Secret Rabbit Code), named in the library docs as the comparison — Nothing was measured: the docs say only that at its highest quality zita 'will be faster than most similar libraries providing the same quality, e.g. libsamplerate'. The SSE2 'factor of at least 2' is against its own scalar build, and test/speedtest.cc (44.1 to 48 kHz, input frames per second, CLOCK_REALTIME) times zita alone, with no baseline, hardware or results.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the docs name libsamplerate but give no numbers, and the only benchmark code (test/speedtest.cc) times zita-resampler alone; the SSE2 'factor of at least 2' is against its own scalar build. The GitHub record is a 2021 import of upstream 1.8.0 (digital-stage, 8 commits, not a fork) whose CMakeLists.txt uses ignored variables and never defines ENABLE_SSE2, so a CMake build gets the scalar path without -O2. Canonical upstream is kokkinizita.linuxaudio.org (Fons Adriaensen, 1.11.2 as of 2025-06-04, blocked here). GPL-3.0-or-later.

**Known shortcoming:** Still no numeric comparison anywhere (SampleRateTap COMPARISON.md unchanged; lastique's src_test covers only speex and soxr), so tier D stands. The filter targets only 60 dB at Nyquist, so 'same quality as libsamplerate' is a relaxed claim. The digital-stage CMake ignores flags (issue #2 open), sets no ENABLE_SSE2 or -O2 and builds no tests; the SSE2 path drops the 1e-20 denormal guard with no FTZ/DAZ; VResampler's 3-argument setup rejects ratios below 1/16 although the docs say 1/64; the Windows port PR #1 has been unmerged since 2021.

**How:** It is a constant-bandwidth polyphase FIR: only the output samples are computed, using a precomputed table of np+1 phases x hlen taps of a sinc times a 3-term cosine window (0.384 + 0.5 cos + 0.116 cos 2x). The filter's symmetry halves the table: each output uses phase ph and the mirrored phase np-ph. Input is deinterleaved into one contiguous delay line per channel, so each output is a pair of straight dot products; in 1.8.0 these use SSE2 4-wide multiply-adds when ENABLE_SSE2 is defined, which the docs say cuts CPU load by at least 2x against the library's own scalar build. The filter is deliberately short: it is dimensioned for only 60 dB attenuation at Nyquist and lets the transition band and aliasing sit above 20 kHz for standard rates, with hlen 16-96 giving a CPU range of about 1:6. VResampler linearly interpolates coefficients between 120 fixed phases once per output frame, so the extra cost is shared across channels.

**Use it when:**
- Inside a JACK or other real-time audio callback: process() and reset() are documented RT-safe (no allocation), while setup() is not.
- Bridging two sound cards or network streams whose clocks drift: VResampler::set_rratio (0.95-16 of the configured ratio) with set_rrfilt smoothing is what zita-ajbridge/zita-njbridge are built on.
- Standard-rate conversion (44.1/48/88.2/96/192 kHz) of multichannel float audio where inaudible aliasing above 20 kHz is acceptable and hlen 32-48 is enough per the author's listening tests.
- Linux audio projects that are already GPL and want a small 4-file library with distribution packages and a stable, padded class layout (reserved _dummy[8] members).

**Skip it when:**
- When you need measured throughput: no published zita versus libsamplerate, libsoxr or r8brain timing exists, while soxr and r8brain-free-src have third-party tables showing 6.8-11x over libsamplerate.
- When you need deep stopband rejection or full-band transparency (mastering, measurement, 120 dB-class SRC): the filter targets 60 dB at Nyquist, so 'same quality as libsamplerate' depends on that relaxed definition.
- Closed-source or permissively licensed products: GPL-3.0-or-later.
- Integer, double-precision or planar (non-interleaved) buffers, or ratios outside 1/64-64 (Resampler also needs b <= 1000); there is no NEON path in 1.8.0, and the docs only promise ARM NEON for a future release.
- Building this digital-stage copy with its CMakeLists.txt as is: the flags go into CMAKE_CXXFLAGS_FLAGS and CMAKE_CPPFLAGS_FLAGS, which CMake ignores, and ENABLE_SSE2 is never defined, so you get the scalar path with no -O2 unless you set flags yourself (open issue #2 since 2024-01-24).

**Integration:** shared or static lib (4 .cc files, easy source-drop) · pthreads (table registry mutex); nothing else · Plain C++ (no modern-standard features); the SSE2 path needs GCC or Clang (it subscripts __m128 as S[0]) and posix_memalign; this copy's CMake needs 3.16 · Linux and other POSIX systems; x86 SSE2 path optional; MSVC/Windows needs a port (unmerged PR #1 from 2021 swaps in pthreads4w); no ARM SIMD in 1.8.0

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over libsoxr or r8brain-free-src when you need a tiny, RT-safe, push/pull API with built-in smooth variable-ratio drift correction inside a GPL Linux audio app; pick libsoxr, r8brain-free-src or LibFResample when you want a resampler whose speed advantage over libsamplerate has actually been measured, or when you need a permissive licence or 120 dB stopbands.

**Gotchas:**
- No automatic edge padding: prefill inpsize()/2 - 1 zeros to align first input and output, and append zeros at the end, or the output starts late and is truncated (documented, but easy to miss when coming from libsamplerate's src_simple).
- The scalar path adds and removes a 1e-20 bias to keep the accumulator out of denormals, but the SSE2 path does not and the library never sets FTZ/DAZ: set them in your audio thread when signals decay to silence.
- Docs and code disagree on limits: setup() accepts hlen down to 8 (docs say 16-96), and VResampler's 3-argument setup rejects ratios below 1/16 even though the class documents 1/64; set_rratio silently clamps to 0.95-16.
- Downsampling scales the filter length by 1/r (hl = ceil(hlen/r)), so CPU per output frame and table size grow with the decimation ratio (e.g. 192 kHz to 44.1 kHz at hlen 96 gives about 418 taps per half-filter, derived from resampler.cc).

**Status:** The digital-stage copy has been frozen at upstream 1.8.0 since 2021-03-10 (8 commits, 35 stars), with an open CMake-flags bug and an unmerged Windows port. Upstream by Fons Adriaensen has moved on (1.11.2 in nixpkgs per the record), so use a distribution package or the upstream tarball rather than this copy; GPL-3.0-or-later.

[repo](https://kokkinizita.linuxaudio.org/linuxaudio/zita-resampler-doc/quickguide.html) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/digital-stage/zita-resampler/main/docs/resampler.html)

### networking-and-servers

#### tls

##### Tempesta FW (Tempesta TLS)  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Linux-kernel TLS 1.2 server stack in the Tempesta FW proxy; 6-83% more handshakes/s than Nginx+OpenSSL in vendor tests.

**Beats:** OpenSSL — The authors' NetDev 0x14 (2020) paper ran TLS 1.2 ECDHE-ECDSA P-256 handshakes against Tempesta FW on Linux 5.7 and Nginx 1.19.1 + OpenSSL 1.1.1d, using tls-perf and wrk; on a 1-vCPU KVM guest (i7-6500U host, no vAPIC), Tempesta reached 2,180 vs 1,545 handshakes/s with 307 vs 1,340 ms average latency. On bare-metal Xeon E3-1240v5 limited to one physical core (2 hyperthreads) with 10GbE, it gained 83% on resumption but only 6% on new sessions (7,921 vs 7,426), with worse average, p95 and max latency; compiler and build flags are not given.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party NetDev paper; on bare metal Nginx/OpenSSL had lower average and 95th-percentile latency, and Tempesta showed tail-latency spikes up to +3000%. In-kernel TLS tied to Tempesta FW, not a drop-in library. No compiler or flags stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Not a drop-in for OpenSSL: an out-of-tree kernel module inside the Tempesta FW reverse proxy with no OpenSSL-compatible API. TLS 1.2 server-side only (TLS 1.3 open, #1031), secp256r1 and AES-GCM/CCM only (no ChaCha20). Needs a patched kernel, x86-64 with SSE4.2/BMI2/ADX, 8 GB RAM and huge pages. Mixes constant-time and non-constant-time code with RDRAND randomization. Self-described Beta.

**How:** The handshake runs in SoftIRQ right after the TCP handshake, with a zero-copy state machine on skbs, so there are no user/kernel context switches, socket syscalls or extra copies. Hot paths make no heap allocations: each cipher suite has a precomputed 'MPI profile' that is copied in one shot, and temporary big integers come from per-CPU page pools. P-256 uses hand-written x86-64 BMI2/ADX Montgomery arithmetic (after Gueron-Krasnov) in Jacobian coordinates, with fixed-base comb tables (window 7) for m*G, RDRAND randomization in place of full constant-time table scans, and the Linux crypto API for AES-GCM/CCM. The paper reports 40x the original mbed TLS port's rate (2,180 vs 51 handshakes/s), but raw ECDSA/ECDHE op/s stay below OpenSSL's, so the gain over Nginx comes from where the code runs, not from faster math.

**Use it when:**
- Dedicated x86-64 Linux edge servers where full or resumed TLS handshakes/s is the bottleneck, for example short-lived HTTPS connections or TLS handshake floods (DDoS), and you can replace Nginx/HAProxy with Tempesta FW
- Traffic dominated by session resumption through RFC 5077 session tickets: the paper measured 35,263 vs 19,203 conn/s (+83%) against Nginx/OpenSSL on bare metal
- Small VMs without virtual APIC, where fewer VM exits matter: on a 1-vCPU KVM guest, the paper measured +41% handshakes/s and 77% lower average latency
- ECDSA P-256 certificates with ECDHE P-256 and AES-GCM suites, serving HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (the only ALPN protocols supported)
- Deployments that want private and session keys held in non-swappable kernel memory, away from the application's address space

**Skip it when:**
- You need TLS 1.3, X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, P-384 or client-side TLS: only TLS 1.2 server-side with AES-GCM/CCM on secp256r1 is supported, and TLS 1.3 (issue #1031) is still open
- You need a library to link into your own application or into Nginx/HAProxy: there is no OpenSSL-compatible API, and the kernel TLS socket API (issue #1433) is only a proposal
- Bare-metal services that care about tail latency: in the paper, Nginx/OpenSSL had 50-170% lower average and p95 latency for new sessions, and Tempesta's max latency was up to 30x worse (28,262 vs 925 ms) under load
- Non-x86-64 hardware (ARM/Graviton), CPUs without BMI2/ADX, or managed kernels: the product needs a patched kernel (linux-6.12.12-tfw for 0.9/master, 5.10.35-tfw for 0.8), at least 8 GB RAM, 2 MB huge pages and an RSS-capable NIC
- RSA-certificate workloads (the docs say RSA isn't performance-optimized), or teams that cannot accept a Beta, GPLv2 in-kernel TLS stack that enlarges the kernel TCB

**Integration:** module · Patched Linux kernel (tempesta-tech/linux-6.12.12-tfw for 0.9/master, linux-5.10.35-tfw for release-0.8); Linux crypto API for symmetric ciphers and hashes; build packages listed in the install docs include gcc, g++, libboost-all-dev, libssl-dev, libelf-dev, flex, bison and dwarves · not documented (no GCC version given); Ubuntu 24.04 is the preferred build and run environment; needs kernel headers and 35-40 GB of disk for the kernel build · x86-64 Linux only; SSE4.2, BMI2 and ADX are required by the Makefile. AVX2 is listed as required in the docs, and the Makefile warns not to use builds without it in production. Needs RDRAND and huge-page support.

**Vs siblings:** AWS-LC and wolfSSL are user-space libraries that link into HAProxy or Nginx, support TLS 1.3 and ARM, and scale across many cores (their benchmarks use a 64-core Graviton4). Pick Tempesta only when you can replace the whole HTTPS proxy on dedicated x86-64 Linux and TLS 1.2 ECDSA-P-256 handshake cost per core is your limit, since its gain comes from kernel placement and its own crypto is slower than OpenSSL's.

**Gotchas:**
- Side-channel protection mixes constant-time code with non-constant-time code plus RDRAND randomization (as in mbed TLS) rather than OpenSSL's constant-time-everywhere approach. A CRYPTO_CONST_TIME build flag exists. On SRBDS-affected Intel CPUs, the microcode mitigation cuts RDRAND to about 3% of its original speed, and the requirements page says the mitigation is needed in public clouds.
- Curve25519 source (tls/ec_25519.c) is present but marked 'slow and incomplete' and is not in the supported-curve list; secp256r1 is the only ECDHE curve offered.
- Heavy public-key math runs in SoftIRQ with kernel_fpu_begin/end. The paper links this to tail-latency spikes and packet drops under heavy load on bare metal.
- The master branch is a development (unstable) branch. The README says to use release-0.8 for a stable version, and the project calls itself Beta.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-25; Ubuntu 24 package release 0.8.2 in October 2025) but still self-described Beta; GPL-2.0 kernel module deployed as a complete reverse proxy, not a TLS library you can vendor into another program.

[repo](https://github.com/tempesta-tech/tempesta) · [benchmark](https://netdevconf.info/0x14/pub/papers/35/0x14-paper35-talk-paper.pdf)

#### websocket-grpc-rpc

##### Lightstream  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust/Python Arrow-table transport over raw TCP, QUIC, HTTP/2 and WebSocket; 1.06-1.71x Arrow Flight throughput between AWS hosts.

**Beats:** Apache Arrow Flight (gRPC/HTTP2) — The project's own ECS rig ran 2x AWS i3en.12xlarge in one cluster placement group (50 Gbit/s): RAM-resident 1M-row tables in 4 shapes, warm median of 5 runs, Lightstream's parallel protocol over plaintext TCP vs arrow-flight 59.2 DoGet over tonic/HTTP/2 (8 MiB windows, default 2 MiB slicing, dictionary Resend), built with unpinned Rust nightly --release. Lightstream led in all 16 cells by 1.06x-1.71x, but its 1-stream cells (1.108-1.109 GiB/s, about 9.5 Gbit/s) sit at AWS's ~10 Gbps per-flow cap and its 16-stream cells (5.75-5.79 GiB/s, about 49.4-49.7 Gbit/s) sit at the link limit, so the ratios mostly show how far Flight falls short of the network ceiling; Lightstream's timing also includes a global reorder that Flight does not do.

**Known shortcoming:** Lightstream's results sit at the network ceilings (1 stream ~9.5 Gbit/s = AWS per-flow cap; 16 streams ~49.5 Gbit/s = the 50 Gbit/s link), so the ratios mostly show how far Flight falls short of the link; no CPU-per-byte data. Framing differs: run.sh defaults to 8 MiB batches (its header comment says 0) while Flight slices at 2 MiB; the table doesn't say which was used. The benchmark image patches minarrow to a sibling checkout and uses an unpinned nightly. Lightstream pays for a global reorder Flight doesn't; latency chart is single-stream only. Nightly-only (allocator_api, portable_simd). Not a Flight drop-in: minarrow Table API, no Flight wire compatibility, parallel writer is plaintext TCP only (max 256 connections, u32 frames, 2 GiB virtual reservation per decoder). One maintainer, 41 stars, 938 downloads, 0.1-0.4 yanked; 0.7.0 can't read back Parquet-with-nulls from earlier releases. Doc errors (missing benchmarks/ path, 'cargo install' for a library).

**How:** Each table goes on the wire as Arrow IPC inside a 5-byte TLV frame ([u8 tag][u32 LE length]) directly over TCP, skipping gRPC/HTTP/2 framing, protobuf FlightData wrapping and arrow-flight's default 2 MiB batch slicing. Buffers are minarrow 64-byte-aligned Vec64, and the receive path reads socket bytes straight into decoder-managed buffers from a reused per-stream arena, so steady-state decode does no per-batch allocation (per source comments). Parallel mode opens one TCP connection per stream, feeds them round-robin through bounded tokio channels (depth 8), decodes each connection on its own task, and restores global order by pulling connections in the same rotation, with no sort. The project publishes no profile that attributes the gain to any one of these parts.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk transfer of multi-MiB Arrow batches between Rust or Python services on a LAN/cluster, especially over one connection, where the published gain is largest (1.18x-1.71x at 1 stream).
- You need one globally ordered table stream spread across several parallel TCP connections and do not want to write the merge yourself.
- You want Arrow tables and typed Protobuf/MessagePack side messages on the same connection instead of hand-rolled adjacent-bytes framing.
- You want one API to swap between TCP, UDS, QUIC, WebSocket, HTTP/2, stdio, Arrow IPC/Parquet files and mmap, and can build on nightly Rust or use the Python wheels.

**Skip it when:**
- You need Flight ecosystem interop (Flight SQL, DoPut/DoExchange, existing Flight clients/servers, GetFlightInfo endpoint discovery); Lightstream is not wire-compatible with Flight.
- Your build must use stable Rust: the crate needs nightly (allocator_api, portable_simd via minarrow/vec64), and rust-toolchain.toml pins only channel = "nightly", no date.
- The link is already the bottleneck: at 8-16 streams the published lead shrinks to 1.06x-1.26x, because both systems approach the 50 Gbit/s limit.
- Small request/response RPC or general service APIs; this is a bulk columnar transport, not an RPC framework.
- Production-critical paths that need a mature project: one maintainer, 41 stars, 0 issues ever filed, versions 0.1-0.4.x yanked on crates.io, and 0.7.0 cannot read Parquet files with nulls written by earlier releases.

**Integration:** crate (also Python package lightstream-io) · tokio, futures-*, flatbuffers, minarrow 0.18, vec64, tracing, log; optional per feature: quinn, h2/http/bytes, tokio-tungstenite, wtransport, tokio-rustls (ring), prost, rmp-serde, zstd, snap, simd-json, tokio-uring · Rust nightly (edition 2024; unpinned nightly channel); no stable MSRV. Python >=3.9 for the wheels. · CI runs Linux x86-64, macOS x86-64/arm64 and Windows x86-64 (Windows without uds/mmap); io_uring and vmap64 are Linux-only; PyPI also ships manylinux aarch64 wheels. Published benchmarks are Linux x86-64 only.

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings (DRPC, fRPC, brpc, rpcx, cmd-stream) are general RPC frameworks benchmarked on small-message QPS against gRPC, and none carries Arrow tables natively. Pick Lightstream when the payload is bulk Arrow columnar data or you need ordered multi-connection streaming; pick DRPC, fRPC or brpc for many small request/response calls.

**Gotchas:**
- Ordered mode stalls on the slowest connection: a lagging stream holds back every table behind it (documented on SortBehaviour::Ordered), with 8 buffered frames per connection.
- LightstreamParallelWriter caps at 256 connections (each connection announces its index as one byte), and each frame's payload length is a u32, so a single frame must stay under 4 GiB; split big tables into views.
- Each streaming decoder reserves 2 GiB of virtual address space (tunable via LIGHTSTREAM_ARENA_CAPACITY); many parallel streams add up under strict overcommit or ulimit -v.
- LightstreamParallelWriter::connect opens plain TcpStreams from a SocketAddr, and that file has no TLS variant; TLS exists on the single-connection TCP/WebSocket/HTTP/2 writers (tls feature) and in QUIC. The Rust README's 'cargo install lightstream' is wrong for a library crate; use cargo add.

**Status:** Active (v0.7.0 released 2026-09-19; one maintainer, 7 self-merged PRs, 0 issues) and MPL-2.0 with file-level copyleft, so it is fine to link as a dependency, but it is pre-1.0, nightly-only and still making format-breaking changes.

[repo](https://github.com/SpaceCell/lightstream) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SpaceCell/lightstream/blob/main/rust/README.md)

### numerics-and-science

#### autodiff-and-ml-kernels

##### TCL (Tensor Contraction Library)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Multithreaded C++ tensor contraction library (TTGT over BLAS + HPTT); up to 18x over the best of Eigen Tensor, NumPy, ITensor and Tensor Toolbox.

**Beats:** Eigen Tensor, Tensor Toolbox, NumPy, ITensor — The author measured 1000 random contractions on a 2-socket Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 (Haswell-EP, 24 threads) against the fastest of Eigen Tensor, Tensor Toolbox, NumPy and ITensor for each case; TCL was faster on every case, up to 18x at low arithmetic intensity, falling toward parity as GEMM dominates. Compiler and flags for the run are not stated; first-party only.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party only; speedup vs the best of Eigen/Tensor Toolbox/NumPy/ITensor with no per-library figures; compiler and flags not stated; unmaintained since 2019-08-22 (README points to cuTENSOR).

**Known shortcoming:** Not thread-safe for concurrent calls (global MemoryBroker assertion under OpenMP, issue #3, unfixed); TTGT needs extra memory for transposed tensors; Makefile builds with -march=native.

**How:** It uses the Transpose-Transpose-GEMM-Transpose (TTGT) approach: operands are permuted with HPTT, a high-performance tensor transposition library, into layouts that turn the contraction into one large GEMM on a tuned BLAS (BLIS, MKL, OpenBLAS). The speedup comes mostly from fast transpositions, so it is largest for low-arithmetic-intensity contractions where transposes dominate.

**Use it when:**
- CPU dense tensor contractions with many index permutations (quantum chemistry, tensor networks) where Eigen Tensor or numpy.einsum is the bottleneck
- Low-arithmetic-intensity contractions (small contracted dimensions), where the README reports the largest gains (up to 18x)
- Multicore x86 servers with a multithreaded BLAS and pinned threads (benchmark: 2-socket Haswell-EP, 24 threads)
- Python code using einsum that can call tcl.tensorMult instead

**Skip it when:**
- Concurrent contractions from several threads: a global MemoryBroker is not thread-safe (issue #3, assertion failure under OpenMP)
- Memory-constrained runs: TTGT needs auxiliary buffers for the transposed tensors (README limitation); GETT, which avoids them, was never added
- GEMM-dominated (high arithmetic intensity) contractions, where speedup falls toward 1x because any BLAS-backed library hits peak
- Projects needing maintenance or GPU support: abandoned since 2019; the author points to NVIDIA cuTENSOR
- Sparse or symmetric tensors: dense contractions only

**Integration:** shared lib · HPTT, a BLAS (BLIS by default in the Makefile; MKL/OpenBLAS/ATLAS), OpenMP · C++11; tested with g++ 5.1.0 and icpc 17.0.2 · x86-64 Linux as tested; Makefile builds with -march=native

**Vs siblings:** It is the only general tensor-contraction entry in the category; pick it over hand-rolled transposes plus a GEMM kernel (e.g. the AVX-512 DGEMM sibling) when contractions have arbitrary index orders, and prefer T-MAC or llamafile for quantized LLM matmul instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Plain Makefile with -march=native: you must edit HPTT_ROOT/BLIS_ROOT paths, and the binary is not portable to other CPUs
- Set thread affinity (KMP_AFFINITY/taskset) and OMP_NUM_THREADS, and link Python against a multithreaded BLAS, or performance suffers (README)
- Index strings define the contraction; layout defaults to column-major, so row-major callers must pass useRowMajor
- LGPL-3.0: static linking into closed-source code carries relinking obligations

**Status:** Abandoned (last commit 2019-08-22, README says no longer maintained), LGPL-3.0; small enough to vendor but expect to fix the thread-safety bug yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/springer13/tcl) · [benchmark](https://github.com/springer13/tcl)

##### Clad (Clang-plugin source-transformation AD)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

Clang-plugin source-transformation AD for C++ generating derivative source code; no published timing against other AD tools.

**Beats:** Enzyme (LLVM-level AD, run through Clad's own use_enzyme backend); Tapenade planned; none of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) apply — Nothing measured: the repo's benchmark/ directory contains Google Benchmark comparisons of Clad against its own Enzyme backend, Tapenade (memory), vector forward mode, Hessians and a GPT-2 training run (built -O3 -ffast-math), but no committed results, hardware or compiler versions. The only numbers seen are snippet-level reports of RooFit gradients (5.5x faster minimization at about 1,000 parameters) versus finite differences, which is not another AD tool.

**Known shortcoming:** No numbers against an AD baseline; kept because ROOT uses it. ACAT 2022 snippets show 5.5-29x only versus finite differences.

**Known shortcoming:** Open wrong-derivative bugs with no diagnostic: #2082 reference members give a 2x gradient, #2075 forward mode drops output tangents, #2099 reverse mode drops pointer casts; #2114 OpenMP reverse race gives a different wrong gradient each run. Silently falls back to finite differences unless -DCLAD_NO_NUM_DIFF. No virtual methods. No published performance results.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Source transformation: the derivative is plain C++ that the compiler optimizes together with the primal, so there is no operator-overloading or tape-interpretation overhead at run time. In reverse mode a to-be-recorded (TBR) analysis decides which overwritten values must be pushed on a clad::tape, so statements like y = y + x*i store nothing, and activity analysis skips inactive variables. Release 2.5 recomputes counted-loop trip counts in the reverse sweep and accumulates broadcast-read adjoints in registers; 2.3 added a tape that can offload to disk.

**Use it when:**
- Gradients of self-contained numeric C++ kernels (likelihoods, cost functions, physics formulas) with many inputs and one output, where you control the source and compile with upstream Clang 14-23
- When you want to read, debug or ship the derivative as source code (dump(), -fgenerate-source-file) instead of a runtime tape
- ROOT/RooFit users: Clad is the AD engine behind RooFit's code-generation path; the ACAT 2022 paper and ROOT blog report a 5.5x faster minimization for about 1,000 parameters versus numerical gradients (search-result snippets, pages blocked here)
- Interactive work in Jupyter through xeus-cpp/clang-repl (conda-forge packages)
- Floating-point error estimation of a function, which operator-overloading AD libraries do not offer

**Skip it when:**
- If you need evidence that it beats another AD tool: the repo ships Google Benchmark sources (Enzyme, Tapenade memory, vector mode, Hessians, GPT-2) but publishes no results
- Code that calls functions defined in other translation units or binary-only libraries, uses virtual methods (unsupported per issue 2176), exceptions, goto or reference data members
- GCC, MSVC or Apple Clang builds: the plugin only loads into the exact upstream Clang it was built against
- OpenMP-parallel reverse sweeps: open issue 2114 reports a race that gives a different wrong gradient on each multithreaded run
- Teams that cannot absorb an evolving tool: 144 open issues, several of them wrong-derivative reports opened in September 2026

**Integration:** shared lib · LLVM/Clang 14.0.x-23.2.x development libraries (plugin clad.so plus the clad/Differentiator headers); optional Enzyme backend built via -DCLAD_ENABLE_ENZYME_BACKEND; conda-forge package available · Upstream Clang 14 to 23 (same version Clad was built against); README says Clad needs C++14 features and its examples compile with -std=c++17 · Linux and macOS with upstream LLVM (Apple Clang disables plugins); Windows via WSL2 per README; CUDA device code partly supported (issue 2172)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Clad over CoDiPack, XAD or Adept 2 when your code is self-contained C++ compiled with upstream Clang and you want compiler-optimized derivative source without an active type; pick the operator-overloading tools for code spread across libraries, virtual dispatch or GCC/MSVC builds. Pick Enzyme instead when you need multi-language or LLVM-IR-level AD with published speedups (Enzyme reports 4.5x over AD on unoptimized IR); Clad's own Enzyme backend exists mainly for cross-validation.

**Gotchas:**
- If Clad cannot differentiate a function it silently falls back to numerical (finite-difference) differentiation; compile with -DCLAD_NO_NUM_DIFF to make that an error
- Integer and char variables are differentiated like reals and lossy casts are not warned about, which the README says can give incorrect derivatives
- Open wrong-derivative bugs without diagnostics: reference data members double the gradient (issue 2082), forward mode drops output-parameter tangents (2075), reverse mode drops pointer casts (2099)
- The caller must allocate and zero gradient and Hessian storage; stale values are accumulated into

**Status:** Very active (release 2.5 on 28 September 2026, last commit 2026-09-30, 2,128 commits) and LGPL-3.0, but correctness bugs are still being filed at a steady rate, so validate derivatives against finite differences before relying on them.

[repo](https://github.com/vgvassilev/clad)

#### big-integer-arbitrary-precision

##### FLINT  `C`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

C number-theory library on top of GMP; FLINT 3 (with Arb) computes pi about 2x faster than GMP and does integer matmul far faster.

**Beats:** GMP (Chudnovsky pi, mpz matrix multiplication) — On an 8-core Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U (Zen 3), FLINT's arb_const_pi computed 100 million digits of pi in 31.6 s versus 62.1 s for GMP-chudnovsky (about 2x), and in 9.34 s on 8 threads (about 6.6x). A 100x100 fmpz_mat_mul took 0.0000678/0.00235/0.0456 s at 10/100/1000-bit entries versus 0.0122/0.0172/0.159 s for naive GMP mpz loops. The numbers are first-party and no compiler or flags are given.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party numbers only, compiler and flags not given; naive matmul slower than GMP at 100 and 1000 bits. License LGPL-3.0-or-later confirmed from README.

**Known shortcoming:** API is fmpz_t, not a drop-in for mpz_t; AVX2 must be enabled at build time (--enable-avx2). Note: issue #2852 slowdown was a -g0 unoptimised build, not a real regression (at -O3 fft_small ~3x faster than GMP on Zen 5).

**Independent measurement:** Arb (merged into FLINT) ARITH 2019 peer-reviewed paper: dot product/matmul vs MPFR fma, Table I

**How:** Large integer and polynomial multiplication goes through fft_small, a truncated number-theoretic transform over several word-size primes in double precision with Chinese remaindering (van der Hoeven's approach), vectorised for AVX2 or NEON and multithreaded. Matrix multiplication (fmpz_mat_mul) uses multimodular reduction with BLAS-backed modular products instead of naive mpz loops. arb_const_pi uses binary splitting with FLINT's multiplication. The inline small-integer fmpz form avoids heap allocation for word-size entries.

**Use it when:**
- Integer matrices and polynomials with small to medium entries, where fmpz_mat_mul is roughly 180x (10-bit) to 3.5x (1000-bit) faster than naive GMP loops
- Huge single multiplications or constants (pi, e, special functions) at millions of digits, especially with flint_set_num_threads
- Computer algebra and number theory: factorization, finite fields, number fields, rigorous ball arithmetic (Arb)
- x86-64 with AVX2 or ARM64 with NEON, where fft_small is enabled

**Skip it when:**
- Element-by-element mpz-style code: FLINT's own naive fmpz matmul is no faster than GMP at 100/1000 bits (0.0213 vs 0.0172 s, 0.163 vs 0.159 s)
- When you need a drop-in mpz_t/mpz_class replacement; the API is fmpz_t and you must rewrite calls
- Projects that cannot accept LGPL-3.0-or-later (dynamic linking or relinkable objects required)
- Platforms without AVX2/NEON, where fft_small is unavailable and large multiplies fall back to slower paths
- Header-only or no-dependency setups: it needs GMP 6.2.1+ and MPFR 4.1.0+ plus an autotools build
