**Integration:** shared lib · GMP >= 6.2.1, MPFR >= 4.1.0; optional BLAS for matrix multiplication · C compiler (GCC/Clang); autotools on Unix, CMake on Windows · Linux/Unix, macOS, Windows (CMake, MinGW64); fft_small needs x86-64 AVX2 (--enable-avx2) or aarch64 NEON

**Vs siblings:** Pick FLINT over mp++ or ctbignum when operands are large or the work is matrix, polynomial or constant computation; those two win on fixed small limb counts and per-operation overhead. Pick it over DoT or the AVX-512 Montgomery code when you need a maintained, licensed library instead of research kernels.

**Gotchas:**
- Build with optimisation: issue #2852 reported fft_small 10x slower than GMP on Zen 5, but the cause was CFLAGS=-g0 overriding configure's -O flags; with -O3 it was about 3x faster than GMP
- AVX2 is not on by default; pass --enable-avx2 on x86-64 to get fft_small
- fmpz_t is an array-of-one type; index arrays with pointer arithmetic, and pair fmpz_init with fmpz_clear (memory from flint_malloc must be freed with flint_free)
- Multithreading is off until you call flint_set_num_threads(n); the 8-thread pi and matmul figures need it

**Status:** Actively developed (3.7.0-dev, commits in late September 2026) under LGPL-3.0-or-later by Fredrik Johansson and Albin Ahlbäck; mature and production-grade.

[repo](https://github.com/flintlib/flint) · [benchmark](https://flintlib.org/applications.html)

##### GNU MPFR with CUDA/CGBN backend (gnu-mpfr-cgbn)  `C`  `LGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

MPFR 4.2.1 with a CUDA/CGBN backend: bit-identical batched mul/div/sqrt/fma, 18-30x over one CPU core, 115-284x device-resident.

**Beats:** MPFR 4.2.1 scalar functions (GMP 6.3.0) on one CPU core — First-party wall-clock measurements (tests/cgbnbench) on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell with CUDA 13.2, MPFR 4.2.1, GMP 6.3.0 and GCC 14.3.1, against scalar MPFR in a loop on one core of an unnamed CPU in the same machine: batch peaks of 18-30x at n = 1024 (div 30.4x, sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits) and resident peaks of 115-284x at n = 16384 (fma 284x at 8192 bits). Host CFLAGS and the CPU model are not stated, and a multi-core MPFR baseline was not measured.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline is one CPU core; at n=1 it is about 3x-1570x slower than CPU MPFR (derived from page data); CPU model and CFLAGS missing (host GCC 14.3.1, tests/cgbnbench.c); LICENSE file GPL-3.0 while sources say LGPL-3.0+; not upstream MPFR though it carries FSF/INRIA copyright headers; single commit (2026-09-12).

**Known shortcoming:** At 16 CPU cores the 18-30x batch peaks would drop to about 1-2x (derived); div/sqrt above 32768 bits still go to the GPU and lose to the CPU; the auto-offload threshold is a plain process-wide global; the device mutex exists only if pthread.h is found.

**How:** Significands are packed left-aligned into fixed-width CGBN integers (a ladder of 13 widths from 128 to 65536 bits) and each element is computed by a cooperative group of 4-32 GPU threads per instance, so thousands of independent operations run in parallel. The kernels form the exact (2x or, for fma, 3x width) result with CGBN integer arithmetic and round it on the device; exponent range and flags are applied back on the host. Batches are staged through page-locked buffers in chunks of up to 32 MiB, and device-resident vectors skip the PCIe round trip entirely, which is where the 100x-plus factors come from.

**Use it when:**
- Many independent MPFR operations of one precision between 4096 and 16384 bits, in batches of a few thousand: the README calls this the sweet spot (resident mul 230x at 4096 bits, div 157x at 16384, n = 16384).
- Chains of operations that can stay on the GPU (vec_mul, vec_fma, vec_div ... then one vec_get): resident fma reaches 284x at 8192 bits.
- One-shot batches of about 1024 or more mul, div, sqrt or fma at 2048-32768 bits where data must round-trip each call: batch div 30.4x and sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 4.9x at 4096 bits (n = 1024).
- Code that must keep MPFR's exact semantics (rounding modes, ternary values, exception flags) while moving bulk arithmetic to an NVIDIA GPU.

**Skip it when:**
- Single operations or small batches: n = 1 is always slower (launch floor about 6.5 us resident, 16 us with transfers), and batch mul at 128-512 bits stays at or below 1.8x even at n = 16384.
- Batched addition or subtraction with transfers: every add batch cell is 0.7x or less; add only pays on resident data between other operations.
- Division or square root above 32768 bits: CGBN switches to a much slower algorithm (div 71x, sqrt 163x slower per instance from 32768 to 40960 bits) and the backend still sends them to the GPU, where they lose to the CPU.
- Precision above 65536 bits, transcendental functions (exp, log, sin and others are not offloaded), batches with mixed result precisions, or hosts without an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA.
- When you can spread scalar MPFR over many CPU cores: all ratios are against one core, so a 16-core run at linear scaling would cut the 18-30x batch peaks to about 1-2x (derived from page data).

**Integration:** shared lib · GMP 5.0.0+ with GMP_NUMB_BITS a multiple of 32, CUDA toolkit with nvcc (developed against 13.2) and libcudart, the header-only CGBN tree (README links the author's fork steleman/nvidia-cgbn), libstdc++, pthreads (optional, for the device mutex) · nvcc from CUDA 13.2 as tested (older toolkits not documented); host GCC 14.3.1 in the design PDF; GPU compute capability 3.5 or later · NVIDIA GPUs only (sm_35+; tested on an RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell, sm_120); build instructions are Linux/autotools (gmake), other OSes not documented; static and shared libmpfr both supported

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over raw CGBN or midint-arithmetic-division when you need correctly rounded MPFR floating point (all rounding modes, flags) rather than fixed-width integers, and over APFP when the hardware is an NVIDIA GPU rather than an FPGA and the work is element-wise batches rather than 512-bit matrix multiply.

**Gotchas:**
- Cost follows the width rung, not the precision asked for: a 33000-bit operand does 40960-bit work, and one bit above 40960 moves it to 49152.
- If the result elements in a batch do not all share one precision, or it exceeds 65536 bits, the call silently runs on the CPU; the return value (elements done on the device) is the only signal.
- Device-vector arithmetic runs in MPFR's extended exponent range; emin/emax checks and exception flags only happen in mpfr_cgbn_vec_get.
- Widths above 32768 bits use CGBN beyond its documented maximum (checked against GMP by tests/cgbn-verify); MPFR_RNDF is evaluated as MPFR_RNDZ with a meaningless ternary value.

**Status:** One 'Initial Github commit' on 2026-09-12 (3 stars, 0 forks, 0 issues) with a detailed README, design PDF and correctness tests; LGPL-3.0-or-later sources inside a stock MPFR 4.2.1 tree, so it is usable, but it is a personal fork with no upstream MPFR release carrying it found.

[repo](https://github.com/steleman/gnu-mpfr-cgbn) · [benchmark](https://github.com/steleman/gnu-mpfr-cgbn)

##### mp++  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

C++ multiprecision integer/rational/float types over GMP with inline small-value storage; 4-8x faster than raw GMP on 1-limb operands.

**Beats:** GMP (mpz_t) — First-party mp++ 2.0.0 benchmark page compares integer<1>/<2> to GMP (via Boost gmp_int), Boost cpp_int, FLINT fmpzxx and native ints on 3e7-element vectors: on 1-limb unsigned values mp++ is ~4x faster than GMP for dot product, >7x for multiply-add and ~8x for division (FLINT similar on division). Compiler, flags and CPU are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** No compiler, flags or CPU stated on the benchmark page; the 4-8x gains over GMP apply only to 1-limb operands.

**Known shortcoming:** Fast paths only for 1- and 2-limb values, larger operands fall through to GMP; requires GMP and CMake build (not header-only).

**Independent measurement:** first-party benchmark page

**How:** Small-buffer (small-value) optimisation: values up to SSize 64-bit limbs live inline in the object with no heap allocation, and only spill to a GMP mpz_t when they grow past SSize. Hand-written primitives for SSize 1 and 2 (add, mul, addmul, div, shift, gcd) avoid GMP's general-purpose call and allocation overhead on tiny operands.

**Use it when:**
- Computer algebra / polynomial coefficient arithmetic where most integers fit in 64 or 128 bits but must not overflow.
- Large vectors of mostly-small arbitrary-precision integers (dot products, multiply-add, division, sort) where GMP's per-object heap allocation dominates.
- You want a modern C++ wrapper over GMP/MPFR/MPC with one consistent API, including arbitrary-precision special functions via FLINT/Arb.
- Code that must interoperate with existing mpz_t-based libraries without copying.

**Skip it when:**
- Large operands (many limbs): arithmetic defers to GMP, so expect no speedup and a small wrapper cost.
- You need fixed-width wide integers (uint256/uint512): explicitly a non-goal; use Boost.Multiprecision fixed cpp_int.
- Dependency-free or header-only builds: GMP is mandatory and the library is built with CMake.
- Projects needing an actively maintained dependency: last commit 2024-12-10 (2.0.0).

**Integration:** shared lib (static via MPPP_BUILD_STATIC_LIBRARY) · GMP 5+ (required); optional MPFR 3+, GNU MPC, FLINT 3+, libquadmath, Boost (serialization/benchmarks), fmt 6.2+ · C++11 (uses C++14/17/20 features when available), CMake 3.12; tested on GCC, Clang, MSVC · Linux, Windows, macOS, FreeBSD; x86 and ARM

**Vs siblings:** no siblings catalogued yet

**Gotchas:**
- Choice of SSize is a compile-time tradeoff: larger SSize bloats every object; optimised fast paths exist only for SSize 1 and 2.
- Promotion to dynamic storage is automatic but demotion back to static storage requires an explicit demote() call.
- mpz_view references internal data and is invalidated by modifying the integer; assigning from an aliasing mpz_t is not allowed.
- Binary serialization format is platform-specific, not for long-term storage.

**Status:** Stale since mp++ 2.0.0 (2024-12-10) with 9 open issues, but MPL-2.0, on conda-forge and mature enough to use as a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/bluescarni/mppp) · [benchmark](https://bluescarni.github.io/mppp/integer_benchmarks.html)

##### wjr (WJR big integer and utility library)  `C++`  `LGPL-2.1`  `active`  `Tier D`

x64-tuned C++17 big-integer library with GMP-style mpn kernels, Toom-Cook and FFT multiplication; has a GMP harness but publishes no numbers.

**Beats:** GMP (mpn_* low-level functions in the repo's own benchmark) — Nothing was measured publicly: benchmarks/src/biginteger.cpp pairs wjr_* and gmp_* Google Benchmark cases (mpn_add_n, mpn_mul, mpn_tdiv_qr, mpn_get_str and others) at 4 to 1024 limbs, built Release with -march=native, but no result files, tables or CPU models are published and the weekly CI on ubuntu-24.04 runners builds without GMP by default.

**Known shortcoming:** Verifier rejected as not notable at tier D: 7 stars and no published numbers against any baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** Still no numbers vs GMP. CMake forces -march=native. FFT/mulmod sources keep GMP comments and macros but carry only a wjr 2025 header under LGPL-2.1 while GMP is LGPLv3+/GPLv2+, so licence provenance is a risk. README TODO: unique_stack_allocator broken in shared-library builds.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Small and medium sizes use hand-tuned x64 kernels (optional NASM assembly modules, intrinsics guarded by WJR_HAS_* macros) for carry-propagating add/sub and multiply-accumulate. Larger products switch through Toom-2 to Toom-5 thresholds (toom22 to toom55, plus unbalanced toom32/42/43/53/63) and then to a Schönhage-Strassen FFT with mulmod_bnm1 and mulmod_bknp1 wrapping, whose sources keep GMP's mpn_mul_fft structure, comments and macro names through a gmp-helper.hpp shim. Temporary limbs come from a stack allocator (unique_stack_allocator) instead of malloc.

**Use it when:**
- You want a GMP-style integer class in C++17 on x86-64 without linking libgmp, and are willing to benchmark it yourself first.
- Operand sizes of a few to roughly a thousand 64-bit limbs, which is the range the repository's own benchmark sweeps (4 to 256 limbs for most kernels, up to 1024 for mul_n and sqr).
- Code that already uses WJR's JSON or string modules, where the big-integer type comes for free.
- Studying a modern C++ restructuring of GMP's mpn algorithms (Toom, FFT, division, radix conversion).

**Skip it when:**
- You need evidence: there are no published results against GMP anywhere in the README, docs, issues or CI summaries; the CI benchmark only compares to its own previous run.
- Non-x64 targets or AMD-specific tuning: the README says most optimizations are x64-only and AMD has not been tested or tuned.
- Code that relies on exceptions: the README says exception handling is poorly supported.
- Shared-library builds: the README TODO list says unique_stack_allocator under a dynamic library still needs fixing.
- You need gcd, integer square root, rationals or floats: none of these appear in the biginteger header (GMP, FLINT or Boost.Multiprecision cover them).

**Integration:** static lib · fmt (git submodule in third-party/); optional NASM for x64 assembly; GMP only for the comparison benchmarks and tests · C++17, 64-bit, CMake; CI tests Clang 17-20, GCC 9 and 11-14 on Linux and MSVC/Clang on Windows · x86-64 Linux and Windows (main optimizations); other 64-bit targets via generic fallbacks

**Vs siblings:** Pick wjr over Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int or libzahl only if you need GMP-scale algorithms (Toom-Cook, FFT) in a C++ class without libgmp and can verify speed yourself; mp++ or FLINT are the safer choices when linking GMP is acceptable and you want measured, maintained speedups.

**Gotchas:**
- The top-level CMakeLists.txt adds -march=native for every GCC/Clang build, so binaries built this way are tied to the build machine's CPU.
- C++20 is disabled by default (WJR_DISABLE_CXX_20=ON); -DWJR_DISABLE_EXCEPTIONS=ON compiles with -fno-exceptions.
- License provenance: the FFT and mulmod files (src/biginteger/detail/fft.cpp, mulmod_bknp1.cpp) carry GMP's comments and macros but only a 2025 wjr copyright header, while the repository is LGPL-2.1; GMP itself is LGPLv3+/GPLv2+, so check provenance before redistributing.
- To get GMP numbers you must configure with -DWJR_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON, -DWJR_BENCHMARK_PROFILE=all and libgmp installed; the CI 'all' profile runs 1 repetition at 0.03 s minimum time.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-08-27, 1,150 commits) by one maintainer with 7 stars and no issues filed; LGPL-2.1, so it is usable via dynamic or relinkable linking, but treat it as unproven.

[repo](https://github.com/wjr-z/wjr)

#### blas-lapack

##### GEMM_AVX512F (wjc404; AVX-512F SGEMM/DGEMM)  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Hand-written AVX-512F SGEMM/DGEMM with a Fortran-ABI entry point; claims 99% of one-thread MKL, which is parity, not a win.

**Beats:** Intel MKL single-thread SGEMM/DGEMM — The only performance statement is the README line 'able to reach 99% MKL 1-thread performance after tuning'. It gives no GFLOPS, matrix sizes, MKL version, compiler or CPU, and the repo contains no GEMM benchmark (AVX512_CPUTEST.c only measures peak FMA throughput and latency); the tune headers say the parameters were tuned on a Xeon Platinum 8269CY. Read literally, it is a 1% deficit against single-threaded MKL: parity, not a win.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster: the only claim is '99% of MKL 1-thread after tuning', with no benchmark code, sizes, MKL version or CPU. Historical value: the author upstreamed dgemm_kernel_16x2_skylakex.c into OpenBLAS (2020-02-03). Last commit 2022-05-22, abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** beta=0 multiplies C by zero instead of overwriting, so NaN in C survives. The thread count comes from omp_get_max_threads() with a spin barrier, so nesting or OMP_DYNAMIC can hang (inferred from code, not tested). ELF/System V assembly only. Upstream confirmed: wjc404's OpenBLAS commits 'AVX512 16x2 DGEMM kernel' (2020-02-03) and 'AVX512 STRMM kernel' (2020-02-16) match changelog 0.3.8/0.3.9.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It uses Goto-style blocking. Each thread packs its own B block, with alpha folded into the packed copy. A is packed once per K block into a buffer that all threads share. A GNU-assembler micro-kernel (src/kernel/gemm_kernel.S) keeps GEMM_UNROLL_M_VEC x GEMM_UNROLL_N zmm accumulators live, by default 3x8 = 24 registers (a 48x8 tile for SGEMM, 24x8 for DGEMM), and updates them with vbroadcastss/sd plus vfmadd231ps/pd. The software-prefetch distances (prefetcht0/t1) into packed A and B come from the L2/L3 latency and FMA-unit parameters in sgemm_tune.h and dgemm_tune.h, and AVX512_CPUTEST.c measures FMA throughput and latency to help set them. Threads split N into equal column chunks and meet at a spin barrier around each shared A pack.

**Use it when:**
- Reading a complete, small AVX-512 GEMM (assembly micro-kernel, packing, prefetch-distance arithmetic, OpenMP driver) in under 2,000 lines.
- Experimenting with register-tile and cache-block parameters on an AVX-512 Xeon: change the tune headers, rebuild, and compare against your own MKL or OpenBLAS runs.
- A GPL-3.0-compatible project that wants a self-contained sgemm_/dgemm_ without a full BLAS and accepts roughly MKL single-thread speed as the best case.
- Tracing where OpenBLAS's SkylakeX DGEMM and STRMM kernels came from (the author committed them upstream in 2020).

**Skip it when:**
- If you want to beat MKL or OpenBLAS: the only claim is 99% of one-thread MKL, with no numbers, sizes, CPU or MKL version, and the repo has no GEMM benchmark program.
- Code that cannot be GPL-3.0.
- CPUs without AVX-512F, or non-ELF platforms: the kernels are System V AMD64 assembly (.type @function, stack red zone), so Windows and macOS builds are not supported as written.
- Multi-threaded production use: thread 0 packs A alone while the others spin, and the one issue (#1, 2020) reports that the OpenMP .so is less efficient than the serial sgemm.c. Plain OpenBLAS already contains the author's upstreamed kernels and is maintained.
- Anything that needs maintenance or other BLAS routines: last commit 2022-05-22, GEMM only, no tests and no argument checking.

**Integration:** shared lib · OpenMP (gcc -fopenmp); nothing else · GCC with -mavx512f and the GNU assembler (AT&T-syntax .S); C11 aligned_alloc; exact GCC version not documented · x86-64 with AVX-512F, ELF / System V ABI (Linux); default parameters tuned on a Xeon Platinum 8269CY

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to study or retune an AVX-512 GEMM kernel. The same author's GEMM_AVX2_FMA3 at least publishes numbers against MKL 2019 (2-3% faster at 20000^3 on 8 threads), FT-BLAS claims up to 3.5% over MKL, and stock OpenBLAS already ships this author's SkylakeX DGEMM and STRMM kernels.

**Gotchas:**
- beta=0 multiplies C by zero (C_MULT_BETA) instead of overwriting it, so NaN or Inf already in C survive; reference BLAS lets callers pass an unset C when beta is zero.
- The thread count comes from omp_get_max_threads(). For the single-thread setting the 99% claim refers to, set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1.
- Tuning is compile-time only, by editing sgemm_tune.h and dgemm_tune.h; gemm_set_parameters.h silently clamps out-of-range values (for example GEMM_UNROLL_N is capped at 24/GEMM_UNROLL_M_VEC).
- aligned_alloc and malloc results are not checked, nothing returns early when m, n or k is 0, and the assembly defines a global symbol with the generic name timedelay (used by the spin barrier).

**Status:** Abandoned since 2022-05-22 (82 commits, 15 stars, one open 2020 issue) and GPL-3.0, so vendoring it brings copyleft. Its lasting value is upstream: the author's OpenBLAS commits include 'AVX512 16x2 DGEMM kernel' (2020-02-03) and 'AVX512 STRMM kernel' (2020-02-16), matching the AVX512 DGEMM kernel added in OpenBLAS 0.3.8 and the SkylakeX STRMM kernel in 0.3.9.

[repo](https://github.com/wjc404/GEMM_AVX512F) · [benchmark](https://github.com/wjc404/GEMM_AVX512F)

##### batmat (batched small-matrix linear algebra)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

C++20 SIMD kernels for batches of same-shape small matrices (gemm, syrk, trsm, trtri, Cholesky); claims wins over per-matrix MKL, OpenBLAS and BLASFEO, with no published numbers.

**Beats:** Intel MKL and OpenBLAS (per-matrix BLAS/LAPACK calls via the BLAS interface), BLASFEO — Nothing measured is published. The README says batmat beats Intel MKL, OpenBLAS and BLASFEO below about 100x100, especially for triangular and symmetric matrices. The repo's Google Benchmark harness (one core via taskset -c 0, OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, batch depth 8, sizes 1 to 1024) times batmat against per-matrix LAPACK/BLAS through guanaqo, per-matrix BLASFEO and Eigen LLT, but no CPU, compiler flags or result files are given. In the BLAS path the potrf loop calls PauseTiming/ResumeTiming around a copy for every matrix, which adds timer overhead to the baseline at tiny sizes. The Cyqlone paper abstract (search snippet only) says the batched routines 'significantly outperform BLAS and BLASFEO' for optimal-control-sized matrices, with no figures seen.

**Known shortcoming:** Verifier rejected as not notable at tier D: 3 stars and a speed claim without numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim has no numbers; baseline is per-matrix LAPACK/BLAS, not MKL compact. The BLAS potrf baseline loop calls PauseTiming/ResumeTiming for every matrix, adding timer overhead to the baseline at tiny n. potrf has no info code (NaN on non-positive-definite input). gemmt/trmm/potrf have no cache blocking; cache sizes are hard-coded.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Batch-wise vectorization: each SIMD lane holds a different matrix, so even a 3x3 Cholesky uses full vectors and has no horizontal shuffles or per-call dispatch overhead, and independent lanes expose instruction-level parallelism. Fully unrolled register-blocked micro-kernels (3x3 accumulator tiles on AVX2, 5x5 on AVX-512, 4x4 on NEON) are reached through compile-time lookup tables indexed by the remainder size, and several operations are fused (syrk+potrf, gemm with diagonal scaling). The Cholesky kernel computes sqrt and an rsqrt (hardware estimate plus Newton steps on AVX2 float and AVX-512) in parallel, so the pivot division leaves the critical path. Larger gemm calls fall back to BLIS-style cache tiling with packing of A and B.

**Use it when:**
- Stage-wise structured problems such as Riccati recursions, multiple-shooting optimal control (its main user is the Cyqlone solver), batched Kalman filters or many small least-squares systems, where you have at least one SIMD width (4 or 8 doubles) of same-shape matrices per operation
- Matrices below roughly 100x100 (the README's L2-cache bound), especially triangular and symmetric work (potrf, syrk+potrf, trsm, trtri), where per-matrix BLAS/LAPACK calls are dominated by call overhead and poor vector utilization
- x86-64 builds with AVX2 or AVX-512 enabled through compiler flags and GCC 14+, Clang or ICX, where you control the toolchain and can ship ISA-specific binaries (Cyqlone ships separate AVX2 and AVX-512 builds)
- Code that can keep data in batmat's interleaved layout across a whole algorithm, so the cost of converting to and from ordinary column-major storage is paid once

**Skip it when:**
- Single matrices, or batches whose matrices have different sizes: the layout needs one shape per batch and pads the batch depth up to a multiple of the batch size
- Medium and large matrices: cache sizes are hard-coded (48 KiB L1, 512 KiB L2, 16 MiB L3, 8 cores, marked TODO), and gemmt, trmm and potrf have no cache blocking, so MKL or OpenBLAS are the better choice above about 100x100
- When you need a measured speedup: no result files, CPU model or numbers are published, and the harness compares batched kernels with per-matrix LAPACK/BLAS calls (MKL or OpenBLAS through guanaqo), per-matrix BLASFEO and Eigen LLT, not with MKL's compact/batched API
- MSVC, Apple Clang or locked-down toolchains: the SIMD layer needs libstdc++'s <experimental/simd> or the GSI-HPC simd library, the build uses Conan with recipes from the author's own remote, and CI covers only GCC 16 on Ubuntu x86-64
- Input that may not be positive definite: potrf returns void with no LAPACK-style info code, and pivots go unchecked into sqrt/rsqrt, so failures show up as NaN or inf (an optional regularization argument adds to the diagonal)

**Integration:** static lib · guanaqo (the author's utility library, from his Conan remote); optional OpenMP (off by default) and GSI-HPC/simd; benchmarks also need Google Benchmark, hyhound, a BLAS/LAPACK (MKL in the dev profile), and optionally BLASFEO and Eigen · C++20 (concepts, designated initializers, ranges); GCC 14+ per README, Clang (older versions need -o with_gsi_hpc_simd=True) or Intel ICX; CMake 3.24+; Conan recommended. Shared library is a Conan option · x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512, ARM NEON (register sizes tuned on a Cortex-A53), generic fallback; the ISA is fixed at compile time from __AVX512F__/__AVX2__/__ARM_NEON with no runtime dispatch. Default instantiation is double only, with vector lengths 1, 4 and 8 on x86

**Vs siblings:** Pick batmat over BLASFEO when you have many same-size matrices to process in lockstep rather than one small matrix at a time; BLASFEO has published per-matrix wins and a stable C API. cbk is the sibling with measured wins over MKL's compact (batched) kernels, the fair baseline batmat has not been publicly measured against, so prefer cbk's evidence if the routines you need overlap and batmat's C++20 API and fused Cholesky variants if they do not.

**Gotchas:**
- Dimension checks use BATMAT_ASSERT, which throws std::logic_error even in release builds, while kernel-level BATMAT_ASSUME conditions become [[assume]]/unreachable (undefined behavior if violated) under NDEBUG unless BATMAT_VERIFY_ASSUMPTIONS is on
- Results differ from LAPACK in the last bits: micro-kernels are built with -ffp-contract=fast, and Cholesky inverse pivots use rsqrt estimates refined by Newton steps (two for double and one for float on AVX-512, one for float on AVX2)
- SIMD flags come from your Conan profile; without them you get the generic 3x3 path. float support requires BATMAT_DTYPES to include it (default is double only), and every dtype/vector-length/storage-order combination is a separate instantiation, so build time and binary size grow
- Structure is explicit: potrf writes only the tril() part of the output, and the README example zeroes triu(L) with la::fill first. LGPL-3.0-or-later, and the Conan default is a static library, which brings LGPL relinking obligations

**Status:** Active but pre-1.0 (v0.0.24, last commit 2026-06-15, 743 commits, 3 stars, single maintainer); LGPL-3.0-or-later and copyable, but in practice tied to the author's Conan ecosystem (guanaqo, custom recipes), so expect API churn.

[repo](https://github.com/tttapa/batmat) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tttapa/batmat)

##### TTM / TLIB(TTM) (in-place tensor-times-matrix via loops-over-GEMM)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier D`

Header-only C++17 mode-q tensor-times-matrix product on top of BLAS; paper claims it beats Eigen, LibTorch and MKL batched GEMM.

**Beats:** Eigen (Tensor module) and LibTorch tensor-matrix products, plus Intel MKL batched GEMM; the paper reports parity with TBLIS — Nothing in the repository measures TTM against another library: example/measure.cpp times only TTM's own variants, and the README says only that large tensors reach peak GEMM performance. Per search-engine summaries of the two peer-reviewed papers (neither could be opened here), the Journal of Computational Science 2025 article reports a median 2.47 TFLOPS on a Xeon Gold 5318Y and 2.93 TFLOPS on an EPYC 9354, 2.57x over MKL batched GEMM for large slices and 6.21% (average) to 334.31% (best case) over LibTorch and Eigen; the ICCS 2024 conference version reports a median 1.37 double-precision TFLOPS on a Xeon Gold 6248R with MKL and at least 14.05% on average, up to 3.79x, over LibTorch and Eigen; compiler, flags and library versions are unknown.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to D: no reachable page shows numbers. The claimed comparison lives in the peer-reviewed Journal of Computational Science 2025 article (vol. 87, 102568), blocked here, and example/measure.cpp times only TTM's own variants with no Eigen, LibTorch, MKL or TBLIS run. Paper-access retier candidate (likely B). Last commit 2025-03-24, stale.

**Known shortcoming:** Each call resets process-wide BLAS threads and OpenMP nesting; unsupported policy tags print to cout and leave C unwritten; batched_gemm is a no-op without MKL; popen(lscpu) runs at static initialization; the MKL setup is ILP64; wiki policy names are stale and the CPP-Interfaces wiki page 404s. PyPI 'ttmpy' is an unrelated package. The ICCS 2024 paper (LNCS 14832; snippet: median 1.37 double-precision TFLOPS on a Xeon Gold 6248R with MKL, average at least 14.05% and up to 3.79x over LibTorch/Eigen) was blocked; retier candidate to B.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Loops-over-GEMM (LoG): instead of transposing the tensor into a matrix (TTGT), it walks the free modes and hands each 2-D slice or larger q-order subtensor directly to BLAS gemm/gemv, so there is no copy and no extra memory. Eight policy combinations (sequential, multithreaded BLAS, OpenMP parallel-for or taskloop over slices with single-threaded BLAS, nested loop plus threaded BLAS, MKL gemm_batch; slice vs subtensor slicing; none/outer/all loop fusion) cover different shapes. The default 'combined' path is a runtime heuristic: if the outer loop count is at least the core count it runs an OpenMP loop over subtensors, else an OpenMP loop over 2-D slices if that gives enough work, else one multithreaded BLAS call per subtensor.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated mode-q products of a dense 3rd-order-or-higher tensor with a matrix (Tucker/HOSVD, HOOI, tensor-train sweeps), float or double, on a multicore x86-64 Linux box with MKL, OpenBLAS or BLIS/AOCL already linked.
- Tensors stored in an arbitrary or row-major/column-major permuted layout where you do not want to pay for a transpose or a second buffer the size of the tensor.
- Large tensor slices, where the author reports reaching near-peak GEMM throughput and the largest margin over MKL's batched GEMM.
- Prototyping from Python with NumPy arrays when you can build the ttmpy extension yourself and want to replace np.einsum/tensordot for this one contraction.

**Skip it when:**
- General tensor contractions (more than one contracted index, tensor-tensor products): TTM does only tensor-times-matrix; use TBLIS or TCCG/GETT.
- Integer, half, bfloat16 or complex element types, strided or non-contiguous views: only contiguous float and double are supported.
- Windows, macOS or builds without a separate BLAS: CI is Ubuntu only, the build files are GNU make fragments with Ubuntu and TUHH cluster paths, and core detection shells out to lscpu through popen.
- Code that needs strict control of global threading state: every call resets the BLAS library's thread count (openblas_set_num_threads, mkl_set_num_threads or bli_thread_set_num_threads) and may turn on nested OpenMP.
- Production projects that need a support track record: 5 stars, one author, no releases, last commit March 2025, and the speed claims are not reproducible from the repo.

**Integration:** header-only · A CBLAS: Intel MKL (selected with -DUSE_MKL, configured as ILP64), OpenBLAS (-DUSE_OPENBLAS) or BLIS/AOCL (-DUSE_BLIS); OpenMP 4.5+; pybind11 and NumPy for the optional Python wrapper; GoogleTest for the unit tests. The shipped openblas.mk expects OpenBLAS under $HOME/local and blis.mk a static libblis-mt.a under /usr/local, so paths usually need editing. · C++17 for the library and examples (g++ -O3 -std=c++17 -fopenmp); the unit tests build with -std=c++2a; CI uses g++ on ubuntu-latest · x86-64 Linux is the only tested target (GitHub Actions on Ubuntu with MKL and OpenBLAS); other platforms not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick TTM over TBLIS or TCCG/GETT when your only contraction is a single-mode tensor-times-matrix and the tensor layout varies at runtime: it needs no packing buffers and reuses your tuned BLAS, while TBLIS (per the paper's abstract, on par for most shapes) and TCCG cover general contractions. Pick Eigen's Tensor module only if you need its expression templates and no BLAS dependency.

**Gotchas:**
- Unsupported parallel/slicing/fusion tag combinations hit a generic template that prints 'This type of ttm is not yet defined' to std::cout and returns without writing C; the batched_gemm policy compiles to a no-op for the general case unless built with USE_MKL.
- The wiki's policy names (threaded_gemm_t, omp_forloop_t, omp_forloop_and_threaded_gemm_t) and its claim that the high-level interface uses function 3 do not match the current tags.h (parallel_blas_t, parallel_loop_t, parallel_loop_blas_t, combined_t) or the operator*, which uses the combined heuristic.
- Each translation unit that includes the header runs popen("lscpu ...") twice during static initialization to count physical cores, falling back to std::thread::hardware_concurrency.
- The shipped mkl.mk and ttmpy/setup.py link MKL statically with the ILP64 interface (-DMKL_ILP64); mixing with LP64 MKL elsewhere in the process breaks. 'pip install ttmpy' from PyPI installs an unrelated package (TTMPy 0.1 'toolbelt'); the wrapper must be built from the repo's ttmpy folder.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-03-24, no releases, no issues ever filed) and a single-author research code, but LGPL-3.0 and header-only, so vendoring the include/tlib folder is easy; the README badge says GPL while LICENSE.txt is LGPL-3.0.

[repo](https://github.com/bassoy/ttm) · [benchmark](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877750325000456)

#### fft

##### dft_simd (vertical-SIMD FFTW codelets)  `C++`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

Recipe and test code that runs FFTW genfft codelets on AVX2/AVX-512 vectors, 8 or 16 short DFTs per call; beats FFTW on bulk short transforms.

**Beats:** FFTW 3 (planner/execute API with its SSE/AVX codelets, single and 8-transform advanced interface) — The author's gtest programs time 2^24 (AVX2) or 2^25 (AVX-512) single-precision real-to-complex transforms on one core against FFTW plans made with FFTW_MEASURE. On an AMD EPYC 9474F (2025; compiler and FFTW build not stated) the fixed-stride AVX2 codelet took 79 ms vs 858 ms for FFTW at N=60 (10.8x) and 7,270 ms vs 12,136 ms at N=1024 (1.67x, derived from page data); the AVX-512 codelet took 10,610 ms vs 24,657 ms (2.3x). In 2018 the N=60 codelet ran in 379 ms (207 ms fixed stride) vs 1,912 ms for the best FFTW plan on an i5-5287U with Apple LLVM 9.0.0, and 220 ms vs 2,194 ms on a Xeon E5-2650 v4 with GCC 4.8.5.

**Known shortcoming:** GPL-2.0-or-later; packing is not timed; the AVX512 test runs 2^25 transforms against 2^24 for AVX2.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: in dft_simd_1024_avx512.cpp the DK macro fills a 16-lane __m512 constant with only 8 values, so lanes 8-15 get zero twiddles and half of each call's transforms are wrong; the test prints only lane 0, so the bug is unseen (timing likely unaffected); 2025 EPYC run names no compiler or FFTW build.

**How:** 'Vertical' SIMD: each vector lane carries a different transform, so the codelet runs the exact scalar FFTW algorithm with no shuffles or horizontal combines, while FFTW's own SIMD codelets vectorise within a single transform and run partly scalar at small N. genfft codelets are fully unrolled straight-line code (the N=60 codelet is 374 adds and 154 multiplies), so with the size fixed at compile time there is no planner or loop overhead. Hard-coding the stride in the WS() helper removes the scalar address arithmetic that otherwise delays the vector pipelines; on the author's 2018 laptop this cut the N=60 time from 379 ms to 207 ms. Optional 2x unrolling uses a std::pair of vectors to fill pipelines when strides are variable.

**Use it when:**
- Millions of independent short real DFTs of one fixed size, such as digitised detector waveforms (the author's case: 60-sample Cherenkov-telescope traces), where an 8x-10x gain over FFTW at N=60 matters
- x86-64 with AVX2+FMA or AVX-512 when you control the data layout and can store samples lane-interleaved (sample i of 8 or 16 waveforms in one vector)
- Single-precision r2c/c2r at sizes up to about 1024, where the published gain over FFTW shrinks to roughly 1.7x (AVX2) and 2.3x (AVX-512) on an EPYC 9474F
- Projects already GPL-compatible that can add an OCaml genfft step to the build to emit codelets for their own sizes and types (double-precision __m256d is mentioned as possible but untested)

**Skip it when:**
- A single large transform or variable sizes: there is no planner, and the README itself says long codelets grow as N log N and overflow the cache; the N=1024 codelet is already 700 KB of C with 1,370 stack variables
- Data stored one waveform after another: the published timings do not include transposing into or out of the lane-interleaved layout, and FFTW given that layout (TransposedEight) was the slowest aligned FFTW case
- Non-x86 targets: only AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 shims exist; the OpenCL path is a naive single-work-item experiment that was slower than the CPU codelet on an Iris 6100
- Permissive-license products: the code is GPL-2.0-or-later (inherited from FFTW's generator), with only the README under CC-BY-SA-4.0
- Production code needing tests of numerical output: the programs print lane 0 of the first result and never compare against FFTW

**Integration:** source-drop · FFTW 3 (for the comparison tests and for genfft, which needs OCaml with ocamlbuild, unix and num to regenerate codelets); bundled googletest 1.8.0; OpenCL optional · C++11, CMake 3.5+; .travis.yml builds with GCC 4.9-7 and Clang 3.9-5.0; 2018 timings used Apple LLVM 9.0.0 and GCC 4.8.5; compiler for the 2025 runs not documented · x86-64 with AVX+FMA (AVX2 for the 8-lane tests) or AVX-512F (16-lane test); CMake forces -march=native

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over FFTW-beating libraries such as Admiral or KFR only when the workload is a huge batch of identical short transforms and you can store data lane-interleaved; for anything else (one big FFT, many sizes, an FFTW-like API) Admiral, KFR or PocketFFT are real libraries, and VectorFFT is the catalogued library option benchmarked at small sizes (N=2 to 4,096 against MKL).

**Gotchas:**
- Correctness bug in dft_simd_1024_avx512.cpp: its DK macro initialises a 16-lane __m512 constant with only 8 values, so lanes 8-15 of every twiddle constant are zero and half of the 16 transforms per call give wrong results; only lane 0 is printed, so the test does not show it. Timing is probably unaffected (same instruction stream), but copy the macro with 16 initialisers
- FFTW's FNMA/FNMS meanings are swapped relative to Intel's intrinsics; the shims map FNMA to _mm*_fnmsub_ps and FNMS to _mm*_fnmadd_ps, and getting this wrong silently corrupts results
- The r2cf codelet leaves Ci[0] (and Ci[N/2] for even N) untouched; the caller must zero them, and strides apply when indexing them
- The FFTW_DESTROY_INPUT flag is set on every FFTW plan, and both sides re-transform the same in-cache buffer, so the comparison is of hot-cache compute only

**Status:** A research note with test code by one author (LLR/Ecole Polytechnique), 79 commits from March 2018 to November 2025 and no issues filed; small enough to copy, but GPL-2.0-or-later, and you must regenerate codelets with genfft for any size other than 60 or 1024.

[repo](https://github.com/sfegan/dft_simd) · [benchmark](https://github.com/sfegan/dft_simd)

##### tcFFT  `CUDA/C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Research FP16 FFT kernels that run radix-16 butterflies on NVIDIA tensor cores; beats cuFFT half precision on V100/A100.

**Beats:** NVIDIA cuFFT (half precision) — The tcFFT paper (arXiv 2104.11471, IEEE CLUSTER 2021) reports average speedups of 1.29x-3.24x on V100 and 1.10x-3.03x on A100 over cuFFT 11.0 FP16 for batched 1D and 2D C2C FFTs; the repo's paired speed binaries time repeated in-place forward transforms with gettimeofday for at least 4 s per size, built by nvcc with -std=c++11 for sm_70/sm_80 and no explicit -O flag. The digit-reversal permutation is excluded from the tcFFT timing, and the host CPU and exact CUDA version are not stated in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Half precision only; CUDA version only '11.0 or higher', CPU unnamed; Makefile sets no explicit -O flag; 4 commits, abandoned (2021-05-21).

**Known shortcoming:** Unequal benchmark: tcFFT's input is put into digit-reversed order on the host outside the timed loop while cuFFT is timed on natural-order input, so the 1.29x-3.24x speedups are an upper bound.

**Known shortcoming:** Accuracy: sums in FP16; open issue #5 reports error 1.9 for tcFFT vs 0.0185 for cuFFT FP16 on an RTX 3090 with the repo's own test; issue #2 reports NaN output.

**Known shortcoming:** Crashes: sizes outside its fixed table run with uninitialized plan fields; 2D with Nx=1024 calls a never-set function pointer. The code never selects its A100 kernels, so how the paper's A100 runs were made is undocumented. GPL-3.0, no inverse transform, abandoned since May 2021.

**How:** Cooley-Tukey with radix 16: each radix-16 DFT stage is written as a 16x16 complex matrix product against the DFT matrix, split into four real FP16 WMMA mma_sync calls (real/imag parts) on tensor cores. Several radix-16 stages plus a final radix-2 or radix-4 step are fused into one kernel (256-, 512- or 1024-point 'mergings') that keeps data in shared memory, so a 2^27-point transform needs only three global-memory passes. Twiddle multiplication and the small radix-2/4 tails run as ordinary half2 CUDA-core arithmetic.

**Use it when:**
- Large batches of forward FP16 complex FFTs whose size is exactly one of the hard-coded lengths (for example 1M batches of 256/512/1024 points) on a V100 or A100.
- Throughput-bound pipelines that already tolerate FP16 error (mixed-precision ML or signal pre-processing) and can produce input in the library's digit-reversed order for free.
- As a reference design if you are writing your own tensor-core FFT kernels; the code is about 2,600 lines of CUDA in two files.
- Reproducing or extending the CLUSTER 2021 tcFFT paper's experiments.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything needing accuracy: it accumulates in FP16 (half accumulator fragments), and open issue #5 reports a mean relative error of 1.9 for tcFFT versus 0.0185 for cuFFT FP16 on an RTX 3090 with the repo's own accuracy test; issue #2 reports NaN output after tcfftExec.
- Any size not in the switch table, inverse transforms, real-to-complex, 3D, FP32/FP64 or non-power-of-two lengths: none exist (issue #1 asked for sizes beyond 1k; the inverse is requested in #2 and unanswered).
- Production code: four commits in May 2021, no error checking on CUDA calls, no plan destructor (device twiddle buffers leak), five open/closed bug reports with no maintainer replies.
- Closed-source or permissively licensed products: the code is GPL-3.0.
- Non-NVIDIA GPUs or GPUs older than Volta: the Makefile builds sm_70 and sm_80 only and the kernels use nvcuda::wmma.

**Integration:** source-drop · CUDA >= 11.0 runtime (cuda_fp16/mma.h); the header also includes cublas_v2.h; FFTW >= 3.3.8, cuFFT and OpenMP only for the test/benchmark binaries · nvcc from CUDA 11.0+, -std=c++11; host compiler with OpenMP for the harness · NVIDIA tensor-core GPUs, Makefile targets sm_70 (V100) and sm_80 (A100); Linux Makefile only

**Vs siblings:** Pick tcFFT over VkFFT or TurboFFT only for batched forward FP16 transforms at its exact sizes where tensor-core throughput matters more than accuracy; VkFFT (FP16/32/64, any size, inverse, Vulkan/CUDA/HIP/OpenCL, MIT) and TurboFFT (FP32/FP64, fault tolerance) are maintained, general libraries and the safer choice otherwise.

**Gotchas:**
- Unsupported sizes fall through 'default: break' in tcfftCreate, leaving n_radices/n_mergings uninitialized; tcfftExec then launches with garbage values. In 2D, Nx = 1024 selects plan.layer_1[2], a function pointer that tcfftCreate never sets.
- The repo benchmark permutes the input into digit-reversed order on the host inside setup(), outside the timed loop, while cuFFT is timed on natural-order input; a real user has to pay for that permutation (an extra full read and write of the array) somewhere, so the published speedups are an upper bound.
- The *_A100 kernel variants in tcfft_half.cu and tcfft_half_2d.cu are never bound by tcfftCreate (tcfftExec is commented '// V100'); how the paper's A100 runs selected them is not documented.
- Small sizes launch N*batch/(n_cont*RADIX) blocks (n_cont = 32, 16, 8 for 256, 512, 1024), so batch counts that are not a multiple of 32/16/8 leave trailing transforms unprocessed; test.sh only says the batch 'should bigger than 32 for short sizes'.

**Status:** Abandoned research code (four commits, May 2021, no maintainer replies to issues); GPL-3.0 and small enough to vendor, but treat it as a reference implementation rather than a library.

[repo](https://github.com/rox906/tcFFT) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11471)

##### AOCL-FFTW (AMD-optimized FFTW)  `C`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier D`

AMD's AOCL build of FFTW 3.3.10 with Zen-tuned kernels, copies, transposes and planners; vendor claims beating stock FFTW, no published numbers.

**Beats:** FFTW 3.3.10 (upstream MIT/FFTW release it is derived from) — Nothing measured: the README and release notes only list optimisations (SIMD kernels, copy routines, 256-bit kernel selection, MPI transpose, faster planning) with no baseline numbers, compiler setup or hardware. The only figures seen are third-party search snippets (GFFT, ICPP 2023) comparing against AOCL-FFTW rather than measuring AOCL-FFTW against FFTW, and an open user issue says stock FFTW 3.3.10 was faster.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: no numbers anywhere reachable; an independent ICPP 2023 paper (GFFT, search snippet) found it only 'comparable' to FFTW on EPYC; kept as AMD's official AOCL build; GPL-2.0-or-later; a vendor fork of the FFTW baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** No numbers anywhere. Open issue #24 (no AMD reply): stock FFTW 3.3.10 with --enable-float --enable-avx2 --enable-avx512 was faster; #19: very slow vs MKL on Genoa. configure enables --enable-amd-opt only on an AuthenticAMD build host and silently ignores it otherwise (also under --enable-debug). App-opt layer forces FFTW_PATIENT and reads/writes ./wis.dat. Open build bugs: GCC+CMake+threads (#26), static-lib duplicate symbols (#27).

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The README credits improved SIMD kernels, a planner rule that prefers 256-bit AVX2 kernels (kernel/ifftw.h only allows 128-bit AVX2 kernels below size 1024), AVX2 intrinsic versions of the cpy2d and cpy2d_pair copy routines used by rank-0 and buffered plans, and an optional cache-tuned in-place transpose (Toms513-based) for large sizes. MPI FFTs get a block-based in-place transpose that overlaps memcpy with MPI communication. Planning time drops with a hash-table 'fast planner'; the Top-N planner stores the best three plans in wisdom to cut run-to-run variance; the application layer forces FFTW_PATIENT plans but caches them in an in-memory hash and a wisdom file so re-planning is cheap. Release 4.0 added AVX-512 DFT kernels and AVX-512 copy/transpose routines.

**Use it when:**
- HPC codes already built on FFTW 3 (Quantum ESPRESSO, VASP-style plane-wave codes) running on AMD EPYC Zen 1-5 nodes, where relinking costs nothing and you can A/B test
- Distributed in-place 3-D FFTs with fftw_mpi on Open MPI, where the AMD MPI transpose (--enable-amd-mpifft, optionally --enable-amd-mpi-vader-limit with btl_vader_eager_limit=65536) targets the transpose step
- Applications that plan the same sizes repeatedly and suffer from FFTW_PATIENT planning time or run-to-run plan variation (fast planner, Top-N planner, app layer with wisdom)
- Sites that standardise on the AOCL stack (Spack amdfftw, AOCC) and want one vendor-supported FFTW build

**Skip it when:**
- When you need a measured win: no repository page publishes a single number, issue #24 (Aug 2025, open, no AMD reply) reports stock FFTW 3.3.10 built with --enable-float --enable-avx2 --enable-avx512 was faster than this library built as the README says, and issue #19 reports it 'very slow' against MKL FFT on a Genoa machine
- Intel or non-x86 CPUs: --enable-amd-opt only takes effect when configure runs on an AuthenticAMD host, and the kernels and flags target Zen; there is no ARM or POWER work beyond upstream FFTW
- Thread-parallel single-node FFTs where performance matters: a search snippet of the ICPP 2023 GFFT paper (not opened) reports GFFT averaging 9.87x over AOCL-FFTW at 16 threads on EPYC, against 1.18x single-threaded
- Projects that cannot accept GPL-2.0-or-later: the source is GPL like FFTW, and the verifier found Spack linking an AMD EULA for the prebuilt AOCL binaries
- Builds with GCC through CMake with threads: issue #26 (open) shows the default ENABLE_AVX2 build failing because -mavx2 is not added, plus a link-order error

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (autotools or CMake); prebuilt AOCL binaries from AMD · none for the serial library; MPI (Open MPI assumed by the vader options) for MPI FFTs; OpenMP or pthreads for threaded builds · C compiler with AVX2/FMA; GCC 9+ to get -march=znver2, AOCC 4.0 / Clang 14+ for the dynamic dispatcher (configure errors out on older Clang); MSVC or Clang via CMake on Windows · x86-64 Linux and Windows; AMD optimisations only on AMD Zen (Naples, Rome, Milan, Genoa, Zen 5 via AMD_ARCH=znver1..znver5); dynamic dispatcher is Linux-only (CMake stops with a fatal error on Windows); quad precision not available on Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick AOCL-FFTW when you must keep the exact FFTW API and MPI/wisdom features on AMD EPYC and want the vendor-supported build; KFR, Admiral or VectorFFT have published single-node wins over FFTW or MKL but require a different API, so use them for new code where speed is measured.

**Gotchas:**
- configure reads /proc/cpuinfo: if it does not run on an AuthenticAMD machine (CI runner, Intel login node) or --enable-debug is set, --enable-amd-opt is silently ignored and you get plain FFTW 3.3.10
- --enable-amd-app-opt overrides the caller's planner flags to FFTW_PATIENT, imports wisdom from ./wis.dat and exports new plans to ./wis.dat in the current working directory, and allocates a scratch copy of the input array during planning
- Do not combine --enable-amd-opt with --enable-generic-simd128/256; the 256-bit-only switch (AMD_OPT_PREFER_256BIT_FPU) is incompatible with wisdom
- Static libraries have had duplicate-symbol problems (issues #22 closed, #27 open, Mar 2026) and a 5.1 shared-library segfault on dlopen from Python (issue #23, closed)

**Status:** Active as AMD's AOCL component (releases 3.0.1 to 5.3; last commit 2026-05-19), but 5.2 and 5.3 say 'No major change', open build issues get no maintainer replies, and the code is GPL-2.0-or-later like FFTW.

[repo](https://github.com/amd/amd-fftw) · [benchmark](https://github.com/amd/amd-fftw/blob/HEAD/README_AMD.md)

##### eFFT (event-based FFT)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier D`

Header-only C++17/Eigen incremental 2D FFT for event cameras; updates an exact spectrum per event instead of rerunning FFTW.

**Beats:** FFTW (fftw_plan_dft_2d, full N x N 2D FFT recomputed after every event or event packet) — No comparative numbers are published in the repo or on any reachable page. benchmarks/efft_benchmark.cpp (Google Benchmark, -O3 -march=native -ffast-math for eFFT) pits eFFT against an FFTW 2D transform rerun after every event or packet with FFTW_ESTIMATE | FFTW_NO_SIMD in double precision (a deliberately weak baseline), and CI runs it without committing results. The only figures seen are absolute eFFT times from the TPAMI abstract snippet, with no CPU named.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded C to D: paired FFTW benchmark code exists but no numbers are published anywhere reachable (abstract snippet gives absolute times only). The FFTW baseline is deliberately crippled (FFTW_ESTIMATE, FFTW_NO_SIMD, double vs float).

**Known shortcoming:** update(Stimuli&) reorders the caller's vector and shifts its row/col in place; initialize(matrix) overwrites its argument; events set pixels only to 0 or 1; no power-of-two check on N; complex float only, no inverse transform; GPLv3. The TPAMI paper (pubmed blocked, snippet only) gives absolute times and says FFTW SIMD was disabled 'for fair comparison'.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It stores every intermediate matrix of a 2D radix-2x2 decimation-in-time FFT in a quadtree (log2 N + 1 levels). An event changes one leaf, so only the matrices on that leaf's root path are recomputed. A level of size n costs about n^2 butterfly outputs, so one event costs roughly (4/3) N^2 complex operations, against about N^2 log2 N for a full FFT; this ratio is derived from reading the code, not measured. Events that do not change a pixel's state stop the recomputation, and packet updates partition the events by row and column parity so each shared ancestor matrix is recomputed once per packet, not once per event.

**Use it when:**
- Event-camera (DVS) pipelines that need the full 2D spectrum after every event or small packet, e.g. frequency-domain registration or filtering on 64x64 to 256x256 windows.
- Sparse binary frames where a few pixels toggle between consecutive transforms and you would otherwise rerun a full 2D FFT at each step.
- Packets of tens to thousands of events at 128x128; the TPAMI abstract (seen only as a search snippet) reports under 1 microsecond per event for packets over 40 events and under 0.5 microsecond for packets over 200.
- GPL-compatible C++ or Python projects (pip install efft, nanobind bindings) that already use Eigen.

**Skip it when:**
- General FFTs of dense or fully changing data: every update still rewrites the full N x N root matrix, so a from-scratch FFT (FFTW, PocketFFT, KFR) is the right tool.
- Non-binary pixel values: update() can only set a pixel to 0 or 1; arbitrary intensities enter only through initialize(matrix).
- Non-power-of-two or non-square frames, 1D or 3D transforms, inverse transforms or double precision: none is supported (complex float only; issue #1 asked for IFFT code).
- Memory-tight targets: the tree holds (log2 N + 1) x N^2 complex floats plus an N(N+1) twiddle table, about 5 MB at N=256, spread over roughly (4N^2)/3 separately heap-allocated Eigen matrices (figures derived from the code).
- Proprietary or permissively licensed codebases: GPLv3 copyleft.

**Integration:** header-only · Eigen >= 3.4 (Eigen 5 handled); optional FFTW3 >= 3.3.8 with -DEFFT_USE_FFTW3 for ground-truth checks; GTest and Google Benchmark for tests and benchmarks; nanobind for the Python package · C++17, CMake >= 3.20 · any with C++17 and Eigen; CI builds and tests on Ubuntu, Windows (MinGW-w64 GCC via MSYS2) and macOS

**Vs siblings:** Pick eFFT when the input changes sparsely between transforms and you need the full exact spectrum each time. MPSFT and the SFFT library target sparse spectra, PFT and Auto-MPFT compute only a few output coefficients, and SpFFT handles sparse 3D plane-wave input; for ordinary one-shot 2D FFTs, FFTW, PocketFFT or KFR are the choice.

**Gotchas:**
- update(Stimuli&) reorders the caller's vector and right-shifts its row/col fields in place, so the packet is unusable afterwards (the tests copy it first); initialize(matrix) likewise overwrites its argument with the transform.
- Within one packet, duplicate events on a pixel resolve to 'on' if any of them is on, regardless of order; it is not last-event-wins.
- No bounds or size checks: row and col are effectively taken modulo N, and no static_assert enforces a power-of-two N.
- Precision is single-precision float. The tests accept a Frobenius-norm difference from FFTW (double) below 0.001 after single events and below 0.1 after packets, for N up to 256.

**Status:** Active: 57 commits, last commit 2026-09-22, a TPAMI 2024 and a JORS 2026 paper, a PyPI package (efft 1.0.5) and a Docker image; it is a single small header that is easy to vendor, but GPLv3 limits that to GPL-compatible projects.

[repo](https://github.com/raultapia/efft) · [benchmark](https://github.com/raultapia/efft/blob/main/benchmarks/efft_benchmark.cpp)

##### SFFT library (ETH Zurich optimized sparse FFT, versions 1-3)  `C++`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

ETH Zurich's SSE-optimized C++ build of MIT's sparse FFT (sFFT v1-v3) for k-sparse spectra; no published win over FFTW.

**Beats:** FFTW — No benchmark exists in the repository: README.txt, CHANGELOG.txt and doc/*.rst give no numbers, and the --develop tools (sfft-timing, sfft-timing_many, sfft-instruction_count) time or count only the SFFT call with no FFTW harness. Any faster-than-FFTW claim rests on the unopened Schumacher 2013 ETH thesis and Schumacher/Pueschel SiPS 2014 paper, whose search snippets reportedly show 2-5x over the MIT reference sFFT and roughly FFTW parity at large n.

**Known shortcoming:** No numbers in the repo; sfft-timing times SFFT only (no FFTW harness). Thesis, spiral.net and ETH research-collection blocked here; a search snippet says 2-5x over the MIT reference code and roughly equal to FFTW for large n, so faster-than-FFTW is unproven. Docs call it experimental, not a drop-in replacement ('be prepared to find bugs'). Abandoned since 2015; mirror of the spiral.net 0.1.0 release.

**Known shortcoming:** Build broken on modern compilers (open #3: 'complex_t has not been declared'; fft.h defines complex_t as C99 double complex and sfft.h uses tr1::unordered_map). sfft_exec zeroes all n output entries every call (O(n) cost); header and docs disagree on the output type. v1 and v2 plans share global WITH_COMB/ALGORITHM1 flags, so mixing them in one process is unsafe.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The sFFT algorithms (Hassanieh, Indyk, Katabi, Price) permute the spectrum pseudo-randomly, apply flat-window (Gaussian/Dolph-Chebyshev) filters to hash frequencies into B buckets, run small FFTW transforms on the buckets, and then locate and estimate the large coefficients by voting over several loops; v3 does this in O(k log n) for exactly sparse signals. Schumacher's 2013 ETH thesis added a plan/execute split, SSE2 intrinsics for the filter and permutation loops (about 140 _mm_ calls in the v3 source), batched in-place FFTW calls, an interleaved data layout, fixed loop counts in v3 and optional Intel IPP vector math.

**Use it when:**
- Exactly sparse, noise-free spectra (v3) where n is large (the tuned tables go up to 2^24 points) and k is tiny relative to n, for example k=50 at n=4,194,304.
- Many same-size sparse transforms that can share one plan and run in parallel through sfft_exec_many on x86 with OpenMP.
- Research or algorithm comparison where you need a tuned reference sFFT implementation rather than the original MIT code.
- Noisy signals only if your (n, k) is one of the 20 pairs the usage docs list for v1/v2 (n = 2^13..2^24 with k=50, or n=4,194,304 with k from 50 to 4,000).

**Skip it when:**
- Dense or moderately sparse spectra: it is not a general FFT, and the README says it is 'NOT intended to be used as a drop-in replacement for the FFT library of your choice'.
- Any setting that needs a demonstrated speedup: the repo has no FFTW comparison, and the only figures seen (search snippets of the thesis) suggest parity with FFTW at large n, not a clear win.
- Noisy signals with v3, or v1/v2 with an (n, k) outside the tuned table: parameters fall back to defaults and n is silently floored to a power of two.
- Non-x86 targets, Windows or MSVC: SSE intrinsics are mandatory, intrinsics.h errors out on compilers other than GCC/ICC, and the docs say it was tested only on Linux with GCC 4.4/4.7 and ICC 13+.
- Production or closed-source code: experimental, abandoned since 2015, open build-failure issues, and GPL-2.0-or-later.

**Integration:** static lib + shared lib (libsfft.a / libsfft.so, waf build); optional Python ctypes wrapper · FFTW 3, OpenMP (libgomp), libm, librt, Intel IPP by default (--without-ipp disables it); the waf configure step also checks for valgrind even without --develop · Documented for GCC 4.4/4.7 and Intel C++ 13+ (ICC 12 does not work); uses std::tr1::unordered_map and C99 'double complex' through <complex.h>, so modern C++11+ default modes may fail (open issue #3: 'complex_t has not been declared') · x86/x86-64 with SSE2 (built with -march=native -ffast-math by default); Linux only tested

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over MPSFT only when you specifically need the classic MIT sFFT v1-v3 algorithms on power-of-two sizes; MPSFT publishes timings against FFTW (19.4 ms vs 225.3 ms at N about 2^22, S=64) and handles prime sizes. For anything dense, FFTW, PocketFFT or KFR remain the right choice; Auto-MPFT covers the partial-transform case.

**Gotchas:**
- sfft_exec in this repo writes a dense length-n output array and zeroes all n entries on every call, an O(n) memory pass that undercuts the sublinear point of v3; the docs/usage.rst still describe an unordered_map output, so docs and header disagree.
- sfft_v1_make_plan sets the global WITH_COMB=false and sfft_v2_make_plan sets it true, but sfft_v1 execution does not reset it, so creating a v2 plan after a v1 plan changes how the v1 plan runs.
- Default build flags are -O3 -ffast-math -march=native, so binaries are not portable to older CPUs and IEEE semantics are relaxed.
- Inputs must come from sfft_malloc (16-byte aligned _mm_malloc) because the SSE kernels use aligned loads.

**Status:** Abandoned: a 2015 GitHub import (12 commits, last 2015-06-03) of the 2013 spiral.net 0.1.0 release plus a BSD-licensed Python ctypes wrapper; the library itself is GPL-2.0-or-later, and three issues about build errors, Windows and cross-compiling are open without replies.

[repo](https://github.com/davidediger/sfft)

#### geometry-spatial

##### Bonxai  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++17 sparse, unbounded VDB-style voxel grid; first-party preliminary numbers show 4.5-22x faster inserts and iteration than Octomap.

**Beats:** Octomap (octree-based 3D occupancy map) — The README's preliminary Google Benchmark block (bonxai_core/benchmark, PCD clouds table_scene_mug_rgb at 1 cm or room_scan at 5 cm; which one, and the compiler and CPU, are not stated) reports Create 1165 vs 25522 us, Update 851 vs 3824 us and IterateAllCells 124 vs 698 us against Octomap (about 21.9x, 4.5x and 5.6x, derived from page data). Per point, Bonxai only stores a uint32, while Octomap runs OcTree::updateNode, a probabilistic log-odds update. The like-for-like full-mapping harness (bonxai_map/benchmark/benchmark_kitti.cpp, ProbabilisticMap vs OcTree::insertPointCloud on KITTI) and a NanoVDB harness exist, but no results from them are published.

**Known shortcoming:** Not like for like: the Octomap benchmark does log-odds updateNode while Bonxai does a plain setValue. No CPU, flags or dataset stated. Octomap is not a category baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** Open #71 (2026-09-28) reports memory-safety bugs including a heap-use-after-free reproduction via rootMap().erase; the move-grid part was fixed the same day and erase is now only documented. An older double-free with leaf_bits>=4 is fixed. benchmark_nanovdb.cpp and benchmark_kitti.cpp exist with no published results.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It implements a shallow OpenVDB-style hierarchy (Museth, 'VDB', ACM TOG 2013): a root hash map from block key to an inner grid (default 4^3 bitmask-indexed slots) whose slots point to dense leaf grids (default 8^3 values plus an occupancy bitmask), so a lookup is one hash probe and two array indexes instead of an octree descent. The root map is a custom CoordMap (open addressing, linear probing over 16-byte buckets, values that never move), Accessors cache the last root/inner/leaf so spatially coherent writes skip the hash, leaf blocks for trivial types come from a pooled block allocator, and iteration walks set bits in the masks.

**Use it when:**
- Robotics or 3D-mapping code that inserts many points per scan into a sparse voxel map and finds Octomap's per-point insertion too slow.
- Storing custom per-voxel payloads (TSDF values, colours, counters, small structs) without a fixed map boundary.
- Spatially coherent access patterns (scan lines, neighbouring voxels) where the accessor cache avoids most root-map lookups.
- Fast full-map traversal (forEachCell) for publishing or exporting the map.
- Projects that want a small vendorable core: the README says the core data structure is under 1,000 lines and header-only.

**Skip it when:**
- Very sparse clouds where memory matters: the README says Bonxai can use 20-40% more memory than Octomap there.
- You need multi-resolution queries, octree pruning or Octomap's file formats and ecosystem tools; Bonxai is a single-resolution grid.
- Concurrent writers: VoxelGrid is not thread-safe for writes.
- Safety-critical code without testing: the author calls it a project built 'mostly for fun and for educational purposes', still under development, and memory-safety bugs in accessors and the leaf pool were being fixed as recently as September 2026 (issue #71 open).
- Decisions based on the published speedup: the README numbers are labelled preliminary, give no compiler, CPU or dataset, and compare a plain value store against Octomap's probabilistic update.

**Integration:** header-only (bonxai_core, CMake INTERFACE target Bonxai::bonxai_core); bonxai_map and bonxai_ros are optional built components · none for the core; bonxai_map needs Eigen3 (and is only built when PCL is found); benchmarks need Google Benchmark, PCL and octomap (NanoVDB for its comparison); LZ4 optional; bonxai_ros needs ROS 2 (rclcpp, tf2, pcl_conversions) · C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17), CMake 3.10 · portable C++17 with no SIMD intrinsics in the core (GCC/Clang and MSVC attribute macros present); ROS 2 Humble/Jazzy support in bonxai_ros

**Vs siblings:** Pick Bonxai when you need a sparse voxel map that stores values per cell (an Octomap or occupancy-grid replacement). ikd-Tree, nanoflann and PH-tree answer nearest-neighbour or range queries over points, and small_gicp's voxel grid only downsamples clouds for registration.

**Gotchas:**
- Erasing roots or clearing the map through rootMap() frees nodes that accessors may have cached; the header says to recreate accessors afterwards (issue #71 shows a heap-use-after-free reproduction for that pattern). clear() and releaseUnusedMemory() are handled by an epoch counter.
- Moving a VoxelGrid broke its pooled leaves until the 2026-09-28 fix commit ('a moved VoxelGrid keeps its pooled leaves and invalidates accessors'); use a recent main.
- Older code double-destroyed LeafGrid and double-freed Mask::words_ when leaf_bits >= 4 (fixed per an in-source comment), so non-default grid shapes are less battle-tested.
- The default CMake build type is RelWithDebInfo, so set Release explicitly before benchmarking.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-28, 879 stars, 1 open and 24 closed issues), MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft, so the header-only core can be vendored into proprietary code if changes to its files are shared).

[repo](https://github.com/facontidavide/Bonxai) · [benchmark](https://github.com/facontidavide/Bonxai)

##### DGtal QuickHull  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

Exact-integer QuickHull for convex hulls in any dimension, inside DGtal; authors claim over 2x faster than CGAL convex_hull_3.

**Beats:** CGAL convex_hull_3 (Cartesian and Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel) — The only comparison is one sentence repeated in QuickHull.h and the module docs: 'generally more than twice faster than CGAL convex_hull_3' for the Cartesian and EPICK kernels, with no CGAL numbers, point sets, CGAL version, compiler or hardware given, and no CGAL benchmark in the repository. The docs' own DGtal-only timings (MacBook Pro, 2.7 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7) are 7.9 s total for 1e7 random lattice points in a radius-1000 ball, of which 3.2 s is the Quickhull core and 4.2 s is duplicate removal.

**Known shortcoming:** Claim is one '>2x vs CGAL convex_hull_3' sentence with no CGAL numbers (C/D border); its own docs say Delaunay mode is 5-10x slower than CGAL.

**Known shortcoming:** The >2x vs CGAL claim has no CGAL numbers and no CGAL benchmark in the repo; DGtal's own docs say Delaunay via the lifted hull is 5-10x slower than CGAL. Overflow is reported only as a status (InvalidRidge/InvalidConvexHull), not an error. Needs C++20, Boost headers, zlib and Eigen.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It implements Barber et al.'s Quickhull (1996): start from a full-dimensional simplex, assign each point to one facet it lies above, repeatedly take the furthest point of a facet, find visible facets through neighbour links, build the horizon ridges, cone new facets to the point, merge coplanar facets and reassign the outside points. Geometry is delegated to a kernel that uses exact integer arithmetic (int64 by default, optional BigInteger) for facet normals, intercepts and above/on tests, so there is no floating-point filtering or exact-arithmetic fallback cost. Coplanar facets are merged instead of triangulated, which keeps the facet count low on lattice inputs where coplanarity is common.

**Use it when:**
- 3D convex hulls of integer or voxel/lattice point sets (digital geometry, voxelized shapes) where you want exact, robust results without CGAL's licence or kernel machinery
- Hulls in 4D-6D or higher of lattice points, which convex_hull_3 does not cover; the docs give the int64 coordinate limits per dimension (about 1.5e6 in 3D, 4e4 in 4D, 5e3 in 5D, 1.2e3 in 6D)
- Floating-point points that may be snapped to a rational grid: the rational kernel rounds x * precision to integers, and the docs report 1e7 points in a radius-1000 ball (precision 1024) in about 7.9 s total on a 2.7 GHz quad-core i7 MacBook Pro
- You need polygonal (merged coplanar) facets, for example lattice polytopes or H-representations, rather than a triangulated hull
- Projects already using DGtal for digital topology or geometry, where the hull comes at no extra dependency cost

**Skip it when:**
- Delaunay triangulation: the same docs say the lifted-hull Delaunay is 5-10x slower than CGAL's point-location method (1M lattice points in 2D took about 20.7 s), so use CGAL, Delaunay32 or gDel3D/HXT instead
- Incremental or dynamic hulls with point insertion and removal: the docs say it is not tailored for that
- Large coordinates or high dimensions with default int64: overflow is possible past the documented bounds, is reported only as an InvalidRidge or InvalidConvexHull status, and switching to BigInteger costs about 25x (35x when both coordinate and internal types are BigInteger)
- When you need a measured speedup: the '2x faster than CGAL' line has no published CGAL timings, point distributions, compiler or benchmark program
- Small dependency footprint or permissive licence: it ships inside the LGPL-3.0 DGtal library, which needs C++20, CMake 3.20, Boost headers, zlib and Eigen

**Integration:** header-only · DGtal headers (DGtal 2.x is 'almost header only'), Boost headers (fetched via CPM at CMake time), zlib and Eigen as required DGtal build dependencies; the QuickHull core itself uses only DGtal kernel types and the standard library · C++20 compiler, CMake 3.20 (DGtal 2.0+); Visual Studio supported per README · any (portable C++, no SIMD); CI covers Linux, macOS and Windows; Python wheels are published to PyPI, though whether QuickHull is exposed there is not documented

**Vs siblings:** No sibling entry is a dedicated 3D convex hull: pgl beats CGAL on convex_hull_2 in the plane only, and gDel3D or HXT target 3D Delaunay, where DGtal's lifted method is 5-10x slower than CGAL. Pick DGtal QuickHull for exact integer hulls in 3D or more dimensions, especially if you already use DGtal; pick Delaunay32, gDel3D or HXT for triangulations.

**Gotchas:**
- Facets are not simplicial: a facet can be any planar polygon (or higher-dimensional cell), so code expecting CGAL's triangle mesh must triangulate the facets itself
- Roughly half of total time goes to duplicate removal (a sort over the input, 4.2 s of 7.9 s for 1e7 points); pass remove_duplicates = false to setInput only if your input is known to be duplicate-free
- Choose CoordinateInteger and InternalInteger to fit your coordinate range and dimension; overflow is not an exception but a bad status (InvalidRidge or InvalidConvexHull) that you must check
- The rational kernels round coordinates to multiples of 1/precision, so distinct real points can collapse into one vertex, and too large a precision overflows int64

**Status:** Actively maintained (DGtal 2.1 released and 2.1.1 in development, last commit 2026-09-23, 398 stars, SGP 2016 Software Award), LGPL-3.0, with QuickHull present since DGtal 1.2; there are no QuickHull-specific issues, but you must take the whole DGtal library to use it.

[repo](https://github.com/DGtal-team/DGtal) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DGtal-team/DGtal/HEAD/src/DGtal/geometry/tools/QuickHull.h)

##### GeoDesk (libgeodesk)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Embedded C++20 query engine over memory-mapped OpenStreetMap GOL files; claims 50x faster queries than an SQL database.

**Beats:** SQL-based geospatial databases (README says 'SQL'; PostgreSQL/PostGIS is implied but not named) — Only first-party README slogans exist: queries 'typically 50 times faster than SQL', GOL build '20 times faster than an import into an SQL database', and GOL files 20% to 50% larger than the source PBF and under a tenth of SQL storage, with no hardware, compiler, dataset or named database. The repo's Catch2 benchmark times 1,000 containing() queries on Western European admin areas and a count of all US buildings, GeoDesk only, with no SQL baseline.

**Known shortcoming:** README slogans only ('50x faster than SQL', database unnamed); benchmark_main.cpp has no SQL baseline and hard-coded d:\ paths.

**Known shortcoming:** The 50x/20x README ratios have no methodology and cannot be reproduced. Open #43: incomplete area relations in regional extracts match as false positives. #34: Linux build/link failures (GCC 14.3, Clang 19) and a segfault when the .gol file is missing. Borderline category: an OSM feature store, not a geometry library.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** The GOL file is memory-mapped (clarisma::FreeStore over MemoryMapping) and queried in place, with no row decoding or ORM layer. Data is partitioned into a tile pyramid walked depth-first against the query box (TileIndexWalker), and each tile holds separate spatial indexes for nodes, ways, areas and relations, each an R-tree whose branches carry a bitmask of indexed tag keys so branches lacking the queried keys are skipped before any bounding-box test. Tag queries are compiled into matchers, strings are interned in a global string table, and tiles are scanned in parallel by a thread-pool of TileQueryTask workers.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated tag-plus-area queries over OSM extracts (country or planet) from a C++ program, where running and importing into PostGIS is the alternative.
- Desktop or batch tools that need OSM relation semantics (route members, multipolygon areas, parent relations) without an SQL schema.
- Low-ops deployments: a single read-mostly file, no database server, any 64-bit Windows, Linux or macOS machine.
- Region-scoped workflows that can download pre-made tiles instead of processing a full planet PBF.

**Skip it when:**
- Non-OSM geometry: it indexes only GOL-encoded OSM features, not your own polygons or point clouds; use TG, GEOS or an R-tree library for those.
- When you need the claimed speedup proven: the README ratios (50x queries, 20x import, under one tenth of SQL storage) have no methodology, hardware, dataset or named database, and the repo's only benchmark times GeoDesk alone against hard-coded local Windows paths.
- Heavy transactional writes or arbitrary SQL joins and aggregates; the engine is a read-mostly query API.
- Toolchains without solid C++20 support or projects that cannot accept LGPL-3.0 linking terms; an open issue (#34) lists GCC 14.3 / Clang 19 install and link failures on Linux.
- Regional extracts where area relations may be incomplete: open bug #43 says such relations can still match as areas (false positives).

**Integration:** static lib · gtl (greg7mdp, fetched by CMake); optional GEOS and GDAL/OGR; Catch2 for tests; Java 16+ for the separate gol build tool · C++20, CMake 3.14+ · 64-bit Windows, Linux, macOS

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when the data is OpenStreetMap and the alternative is an osm2pgsql/PostGIS import; TG or GeoToolbox are better when you need fast predicates or indexes over your own geometries rather than an OSM feature store.

**Gotchas:**
- Builds a static library by default (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS forced OFF in CMakeLists.txt); shared builds need GEODESK_SHARED handling.
- RelWithDebInfo builds strip NDEBUG (-U NDEBUG), so assertions stay on; benchmark with Release.
- Without the GOL tool (Java) you cannot create GOL files from .osm.pbf; an open issue (#36) asks for in-process conversion.
- Open todo issues note missing guards for truncated files (#40) and extremely large GOQL queries (#42), and a reported segfault when a .gol file is not found (#34).

**Status:** Actively developed by one main author (last commit 2026-09-28, 186 commits, 20 stars) with Java and Python siblings; LGPL-3.0-only, so check the license's relinking terms before shipping the default static build inside a closed-source product.

[repo](https://github.com/clarisma/libgeodesk) · [benchmark](https://github.com/clarisma/libgeodesk)

##### Hob3l  `C`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

C command-line tool that turns SCAD/CSG models into layered STL for 3D printing, 50-350x faster than OpenSCAD's CGAL render.

**Beats:** OpenSCAD with CGAL rendering (CGAL Nef polyhedron 3D CSG) converting SCAD/CSG to STL — First-party `time` wall-clock runs from the README: OpenSCAD's CGAL 3D CSG render vs Hob3l at 0.2 mm layers on two Prusa i3 MK3 parts and two of the author's own models (45.2 s vs 0.82 s, 2m42s vs 1.24 s, 53.4 s vs 0.61 s including a 23 MB STL write, and 4m30s vs 0.75 s). No CPU, compiler, flags or OpenSCAD version is stated, the outputs differ in kind (layered vs solid), and per GitHub's blame view the timings date from October 2018, before the April 2023 'replace core by robust integer arithmetics' rewrite.

**Known shortcoming:** No hardware or versions; layered output, not like-for-like with full 3D CSG; author admits memory leaks; stale.

**Known shortcoming:** Speed timings date from Oct 2018, before the April 2023 core rewrite to robust integer arithmetic, so they are not reproducible on current code.
