There is no block index, so a lookup that reaches an SSTable scans its key log linearly.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or forking a compact LSM: about 2.8k lines in one file plus small pager, T-tree, Bloom and trie-filter packages, MPL-2.0 and easy to vendor.
- Small Go datasets that mostly stay in the memtable, with small records (key plus value under roughly 100 bytes so each serialized record fits one 128-byte page), where losing up to ~256 ms of acknowledged writes on a crash is acceptable.
- Single-process, write-mostly tools that want built-in helpers like PrefixSearch, LongestPrefixSearch or DeleteByPrefix without writing iterator code.

**Skip it when:**
- Workloads that overwrite or delete keys and expect the latest value back. From the code, Get scans each level's SSTables oldest-first and returns the first hit, and mergeTables keeps duplicate keys instead of dropping superseded versions, so once two versions are on disk the older one can win. No test overwrites a key across flushes.
- Records over 128 bytes. The pager splits any record larger than the 128-byte page into up to 128 chunks, each written as its own 144-byte page with a separate stat, seek and write, so a ~1 KB value takes ~116 pages (~16 KB on disk). Past 16 KiB a chunk no longer fits its page and copy() truncates it, which corrupts the value. This comes from reading pager.go; I did not run it.
- Read-heavy data larger than the memtable. A Get that misses the memtable deserializes every klog record of each candidate SSTable, and Bloom filters are off in the README's example config.
- Concurrent services. One global sync.Mutex (not an RWMutex) serializes every read, write and scan, and flush plus recursive compaction run inline in the caller's Put.
- Strict durability or real ACID. Fsync happens only in the background; a flush truncates the WAL without first fsyncing the new SSTable; and a transaction writes one WAL record per op with no commit marker, so a crash mid-commit can replay a partial transaction.

**Integration:** module · github.com/klauspost/compress (S2/Snappy), go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver (BSON record encoding), github.com/zeebo/xxh3, github.com/cespare/xxhash/v2; no cgo · Go 1.24 (go.mod); CI workflow uses Go 1.23 · Pure Go, so in principle any Go target; CI tests only ubuntu-latest and no platform support is documented

**Vs siblings:** Badger is the mature Go implementation of the same WiscKey key-value-separation idea, and Pogreb is the Go option for read-heavy point lookups. Pick Starskey over them only when you want a small, readable LSM to study or fork, not for data you can't afford to lose or read back stale.

**Gotchas:**
- Delete is Put(key, 0xDEADBEEF), so storing that exact 4-byte value makes a key read as deleted. Range also returns the raw tombstone bytes for keys deleted but not yet flushed, because memtable range results are not tombstone-filtered.
- Transactions are weaker than the README's 'fully serializable' claim. Txn.Put's rollback writes a tombstone instead of restoring the old value. Txn.Delete on a memtable-resident key re-puts its current value instead of a tombstone. Txn.Get reads outside the DB lock, so Update read-modify-write can lose updates. A failed Commit calls Rollback while still holding the non-reentrant DB mutex, which deadlocks.
- Most OptionalConfig knobs are ignored: the memtable always uses the package-level TTreeMin/TTreeMax, every pager uses the package-level PageSize, and Bloom filters use the package-level BloomFilterProbability. Passing any OptionalConfig leaves BackgroundFSync at its zero value (false), which turns off fsync entirely (only transaction commits still fsync) rather than making writes synchronous.
- An unset Permission defaults to decimal 750 (octal 01356), not 0750. Logging: true calls log.SetOutput on Go's global logger, sending the whole process's log output into the DB's .log file. Without it, the engine writes every open, flush and compaction line to the standard logger.

**Status:** Single-maintainer project with no commits since 2025-03-19 (latest tag v0.1.9) and no open issues. It is MPL-2.0 and small enough to vendor, but the correctness problems above make it a study codebase rather than a production store, despite the author calling it production-ready in issue #48.

[repo](https://github.com/starskey-io/starskey) · [benchmark](https://github.com/starskey-io/bench#starsky-benchmarker)

##### VortexDB  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Hobby C++17 WiscKey-style key-value store with nested sub-databases; beats LevelDB only on small-value new-key inserts.

**Beats:** LevelDB — The author ran an unpublished C++ chrono harness with 10,000 keys on an i5-12450HX laptop (Windows 11, NVMe, single-channel RAM) against LevelDB v1.23 and SQLite v3.51.3 (synchronous=OFF, in-memory journal), with the benchmark's compiler and flags not stated. VortexDB won only small-value (~8 B key, ~10 B value) new-key inserts, ~550k vs ~188k ops/s (~2.9x; ~536k vs ~186k with a 100k memtable), and lost updates, read hits, read misses and range scans to LevelDB, plus every operation with 1 KB values.

**Known shortcoming:** Loses 4 of 5 operations to LevelDB (with 1 KB values it loses all 5, writes included); the harness is unpublished; the README badge says MIT while LICENSE says AGPL.

**Known shortcoming:** The only win is 10k-key small-value new inserts (~550k vs ~188k ops/s); it loses to LevelDB on updates, read hits, misses, scans and all 1 KB operations. Its cuckoo filter can give false negatives (fixed 10k buckets, re-insert on every put, fingerprints dropped after 500 kicks, non-reversible alt index), so existing keys can read as missing. get() mutates shared state under a shared lock (concurrent readers race) and reopens the file on every memtable hit.

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: unauthenticated SAVE/LOAD commands on 0.0.0.0:8080. No fsync; CRC32 written but never checked; compaction deletes the old value log before the rename; SST chunk names collide within one second. MEMTABLE_LIMIT is hard-coded (the benchmark needed source edits); Winsock-only, no build system or tests; AGPL while the README says MIT.

**How:** It uses WiscKey key/value separation: each put appends the entry to a 64 KB user-space buffer in front of 5 MB value-log segments and inserts a pointer into an in-memory std::map, so new-key ingest is buffered sequential appends with no compaction work during the run. A single global cuckoo filter (4 slots per bucket, 8-bit fingerprints) rejects most lookups of absent keys before the memtable or any SSTable is searched. Writes are pushed to the OS only with ofstream::flush; there is no fsync anywhere in the source.

**Use it when:**
- Reading or teaching a compact (about 2,000 lines) WiscKey-style engine: value log, sparse-index SSTables, cuckoo filter, heap-based merging iterator, stop-the-world compaction.
- Windows desktop prototypes that want a filesystem-like hierarchical key namespace (root/users/configs) with a text TCP protocol and shell, where losing data is acceptable.
- One-shot bulk loads of tens of thousands of new small keys (~8-byte keys, ~10-byte values) in one process, the only case where the author measured a win (~550k vs ~188k ops/s for LevelDB), and only if reads afterwards don't matter.

**Skip it when:**
- Read-heavy workloads: in the author's small-value test, read hits took 0.063 ms vs LevelDB's 0.0008 ms and range scans 6.58 ms vs 0.17 ms.
- Values of ~1 KB or more, which is where WiscKey is supposed to help: it lost every operation to LevelDB, including new writes (45,709 vs 95,153 ops/s).
- Update-heavy workloads: overwriting a key that is still in the memtable forces a VLog buffer flush plus a VLog read, and small-value updates ran at 49,465 ops/s vs LevelDB's 188,215.
- Anything that needs durability or integrity. There is no fsync. A CRC32 is written with every entry but never checked on read. compact() deletes the old VLog segments before renaming the new one. The memtable index (.idx) is saved only on flush or shutdown, and VLog replay runs only when the loaded index is empty.
- Linux/macOS, concurrent readers, or production use: the server and shell need Winsock2, and the repo has no build system, tests, releases or filed issues (3 stars, one author).

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the engine (C++17 standard library incl. std::filesystem and std::shared_mutex); ws2_32 (Winsock2) for server.cpp/main.cpp · C++17; README names MSVC (Visual Studio 2019+) or MinGW g++ -std=c++17 · Windows (only documented platform; server is Winsock2). The engine files use only standard headers, but no non-Windows build is documented.

**Vs siblings:** Only for learning or a Windows toy project, since it is the only one of these with a nested sub-database namespace. For faster writes behind LevelDB's own include/ API pick HyperLevelDB, and for production WiscKey-style key/value separation pick Titan (a C++ RocksDB plugin) or Badger (Go).

**Gotchas:**
- The cuckoo filter can give false negatives, which makes get() report an existing key as missing. It is fixed at 10,000 buckets x 4 slots and is never resized. Every put, updates included, adds another fingerprint. A fingerprint is dropped after 500 failed kicks, and the alternate-bucket formula ((i ^ h(fp)) % 10000) is not reversible for a non-power-of-two table. del() of a key that was never stored can also erase a colliding key's fingerprint. The benchmark used only 10,000 keys.
- Every memtable read hit calls invalidate() on its VLog segment. That closes and reopens the file handle and walks the 2,000-entry LRU cache to evict that file's entries, which is why hot reads (0.059 ms) are barely faster than cold ones. Each range or prefix scan also deletes the writer and clears the whole cache.
- get() returns the string "ERROR: Key not found." instead of a status. Any key containing '/' is treated as a path and auto-creates a child database, so such keys can't be stored as plain keys. All files go into the process's current working directory as raw struct/size_t dumps.
- MEMTABLE_LIMIT is a hard-coded const of 100,000, so the 1k and 10k benchmark runs needed source edits. compact() names each 100k-key SSTable chunk with a one-second timestamp, so two chunks written in the same second overwrite each other. The TCP server parses each 1,024-byte recv() as one command, so larger SETs get split. SAVE and LOAD, which copy and delete files, are served with no authentication on 0.0.0.0:8080.

**Status:** The code is from an April 2026 burst of commits (the only later one, in May 2026, changed the license), with no tests, build files, releases or issues, and it is AGPL-3.0 even though the README badge and footer still say MIT, so vendoring its ~2,000 lines brings AGPL obligations.

[repo](https://github.com/AmeeteSh-A/VortexDB) · [benchmark](https://github.com/AmeeteSh-A/VortexDB#-benchmarking--performance-analysis)

#### indexes

##### Adaptive Radix Tree (rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++11 adaptive radix tree for C-string keys; 1.5-2.4x faster than std::map<std::string> in author's microbenchmark.

**Beats:** std::map (red-black tree, libstdc++) -- the closest stdlib ordered-index analog to the assignment's B-tree baseline — The author's picobench table (README, Nov 2018) was built with CMake Release -O3 -DNDEBUG; compiler, standard library and CPU are not stated. It ran 1.6M operations on random 64-bit (insert/delete) or 32-bit (query) integers formatted as decimal strings, with key-string construction inside every timed loop. Against std::map<std::string,int>, ART was 1.5x faster on uniform lookups, about 2x on insert/delete/mixed and 2.4x on base-64-encoded keys, while std::unordered_map beat ART by 1.4-1.9x on lookups and deletes. An earlier 16M-key run (Oct 2018 README, older code) showed smaller margins on delete (1.07x) and insert (1.65x), and the README heading still says '16M keys'. The numbers predate the Nov 2025 correctness fixes.

**Known shortcoming:** Keys are to_string'd u64, so the baseline is std::map<std::string>; picobench harness; -O3 -DNDEBUG with no compiler or CPU.

**Known shortcoming:** The '16M keys' heading is a leftover; the 2018 16M run shows only 1.07x (delete) and 1.65x (insert) over std::map, and all numbers predate the 2025-11 bug fixes. std::unordered_map is 1.4-1.9x faster on lookup/delete. Needs signed char (the aarch64 fix is a CMake flag not exported to consumers); bytes >= 0x80 sort before ASCII, unlike std::map<std::string>. Code-reading bugs (not run): node_256::shrink out-of-bounds read, node_48 grow/shrink drops byte 0x7F, del() throws on sibling bytes >= 0x80, begin(key) may loop forever, begin() on an empty tree dereferences null, shallow copies double-free. C-string keys only, single-threaded, GPL-3.0; dormant 2022 until an AI-agent fix burst in 2025-11.

**How:** It is a byte-wise radix trie (8-bit span), so a lookup costs O(key length) byte steps instead of O(log n) full std::string comparisons down a red-black tree. Inner nodes adapt to their child count using the paper's Node4/Node16/Node48/Node256 layouts, which keeps nodes small and cache-friendly. On x86, Node16 is searched with SSE2 (_mm_cmpeq_epi8 + movemask + ctz); other architectures use a scalar binary search. Paths are compressed pessimistically: each node keeps its whole compressed path in a heap array, leaves keep the remaining key suffix, and matching uses std::mismatch. It omits the paper's hybrid 8-byte inline prefix, pointer tagging and concurrency, and nodes use virtual dispatch.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded, in-memory ordered map with ASCII/text keys (decimal IDs, identifiers, paths) where std::map<std::string> insert/lookup is a measured hotspot and you still need sorted iteration.
- Workloads around 1-2M keys with insert-heavy or mixed insert/delete traffic: the author's run shows about 2x over std::map on insert and mixed, and parity with std::unordered_map on insert.
- Skewed (Zipf) lookups on short string keys, where it matched std::unordered_map (1.005x) while keeping keys ordered.
- GPL-3.0-compatible projects, or as a small, readable reference ART (~1.75k lines of headers plus a written report) to study or adapt.
- x86-64 Linux with GCC/Clang, the only configuration exercised by CI (ubuntu-22.04).

**Skip it when:**
- Pure point lookups or deletes with no need for ordering: in the same benchmark std::unordered_map was 1.9x faster on uniform lookups (230 vs 444 ns/op) and 1.45x faster on deletes.
- Binary keys, keys containing NUL bytes, non-ASCII/UTF-8 keys, or native integer keys: the API is strlen-based and high bytes (>=0x80) are handled through signed-char arithmetic with several defective code paths (see gotchas).
- Any concurrent use: the author's report says the implementation 'dictates single threaded usage'. There is no locking, OLC or ROWEX.
- Production-critical or proprietary code: it is GPL-3.0, and serious bugs stayed open for years before being fixed in a Nov 2025 burst of PRs (node_16->node_48 growth made children unreachable, a one-byte overflow in set(), a crash iterating a single-element tree, an aarch64 crash). Node48/Node256 growth and shrink are not exercised by tree-level tests.
- Memory-constrained deployments: every node carries a vtable pointer and a separately heap-allocated prefix. The repo publishes no memory comparison against std::map (make bench-mem profiles ART only).

**Integration:** header-only · none (doctest, picobench and a zipf generator are git submodules used only by tests/benchmarks) · C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); CMake 3.12 for the bundled build. Uses GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_ctz) on x86. Supported compiler versions are not documented. · x86/x86-64 (SSE2 Node16 path, CI on ubuntu-22.04). Other architectures fall back to scalar code but need -fsigned-char (Linux aarch64 crashed per issue #17). Windows/MSVC not documented or tested.

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings are learned indexes over sorted numeric keys benchmarked against STX B+-tree (CARMI, PGM-index) and persistent on-disk KV engines (libmdbx, redb, TerarkDB). Pick this ART when you need a mutable, in-process, in-memory ordered map keyed by variable-length text strings and can accept GPL-3.0; pick PGM/CARMI for mostly static numeric key sets and a sibling KV store when you need durability.

**Gotchas:**
- Assumes signed char: Node48/Node256 index with 128 + partial_key. The aarch64 fix (issue #17) only adds -fsigned-char to this project's CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS and is not exported by the INTERFACE target, so your own code on unsigned-char targets must add -fsigned-char. Even then, iteration order puts bytes 0x80-0xFF before ASCII, unlike std::map<std::string>, which compares as unsigned char.
- Keys are C strings: "aa" and "aa\0" are the same key (a test documents this after issue #21). prefix_len_ is uint16_t, so keys of 64 KiB or more would be truncated (from code reading). Because get() returns T{} for a missing key, art<int> cannot tell 0 from absent, so store pointers or a sentinel-bearing type.
- art has a raw root pointer and a destructor but no user-defined or deleted copy operations, so copying a tree (for example passing it by value) makes a shallow copy and a double free (from code reading). del() and ~art() never free stored values, so pointer values are yours to manage.
- Code-reading defects in untested paths (not executed here):
- node_256::shrink loops partial_key 0..255 over children_[128+k], which reads past the array and skips bytes >=0x80.
- node_48 grow/shrink loops stop at 126 and drop a child keyed 0x7F.
- del() finds the lone sibling with next_partial_key(0) and can throw std::out_of_range when that sibling's byte is >=0x80.
- begin(key) hits `continue` without advancing when the seek key sorts below a leaf's suffix, e.g. tree {"b"} with begin("a"), which looks like an infinite loop.
- begin() on an empty tree dereferences a null root.
Tests cover only decimal/hex keys and seeks to keys already in the tree.

**Status:** Dormant from June 2022 until a Nov 2025 burst of mostly Copilot-agent bug-fix PRs and release 6.0 (last commit 2025-11-24, 0 open issues, 174 stars); header-only and small enough to vendor into GPL-3.0 code, but treat it as study-grade rather than a hardened production container.

[repo](https://github.com/rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree) · [benchmark](https://github.com/rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree#benchmark-results)

##### TokuDB / PerconaFT Fractal Tree Index  `C++`  `GPL-2.0 and AGPL-3.0 per README (GitHub reports AGPL-3.0); locktree and omt portions also Apache-2.0; separate PATENTS file`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Fractal Tree (Bε-tree) transactional key-value library behind TokuDB/TokuMX; beat MongoDB 2.2's B-tree indexes on out-of-RAM inserts.

**Beats:** MongoDB's default B-tree index (MMAPv1 storage engine) — In Tokutek's 2012 vendor blog, MongoDB v2.2.RC0 loaded documents that each carried a 100-element array under a multikey index, so each insert meant 100 index operations. After 3.5M documents, stock MMAPv1 B-tree indexes had dropped to 2.11 inserts/s against 1,124.36 inserts/s for Tokutek's Fractal-Tree-indexed build. The machine was a Sun x4150 (2x Xeon 5460, 16 GB RAM, 4x10K SAS in RAID 0 behind a 256 MB write-back cache, Ubuntu 10.04, ext4). The figure is a single end-of-run 'exit velocity' point in a disk-bound regime, not an average, and no compiler flags are given. On HN a commenter noted that the stock curve had decayed to near zero, so the ratio depends on where the run stopped.

**Known shortcoming:** The 532x is an end-of-run 'exit velocity' point from a 2012 Tokutek MongoDB prototype vs the old MMAP B-tree; licensing is GPL-2.0 plus AGPL-3.0 with Apache-2.0 parts and a PATENTS file.

**Known shortcoming:** The stock MongoDB curve decayed to near zero, so the 532x depends on where the run stopped (one disk-bound end point, no flags). Not a MongoDB drop-in: a Berkeley-DB-style C API, with the MongoDB side needing the dead TokuMX fork or the old PSMDB engine. Stale since 2023-11 with issues off and 28 unmerged PRs (fsync errors #410, out-of-locks crash #443, TSan races #396, 4K sectors #385); TokuDB was dropped from Percona Server 8.0.28. Loses in RAM, on sequential keys and on read-before-write; Percona's 2015 iiBench found RocksDB 'overall better'. 64-bit Linux only; refuses to start with transparent huge pages on; bundled xz is a 2009 beta; the patent grant ends if you challenge the patents.

**How:** Every dictionary is a Fractal Tree, which is Tokutek's industrial Bε-tree (the buffered B-tree / cache-oblivious streaming B-tree family from Bender, Farach-Colton and Kuszmaul). Each internal node keeps one message buffer per child, ordered by key and message sequence number. Inserts, deletes (as tombstones) and upserts enter as messages near the root and are flushed down in batches to the fullest child, so one node I/O moves many updates instead of one random leaf read-modify-write per key. Nodes are large and compressed (4 MB default, fanout 16, leaves split into 128 KB basement nodes for partial reads, QuickLZ by default), and a promotion heuristic sends runs of sequential inserts straight to the rightmost leaf. In the benchmark, the 100-entry multikey index most likely outgrew 16 GB RAM, which forced MongoDB's B-tree into random disk reads per index entry. The fractal tree avoids those reads, though the blog post itself gives no cause.

**Use it when:**
- Insert, delete or update-heavy workloads with several secondary indexes whose combined size is far beyond RAM on HDDs or bandwidth-limited SSDs, with random, high-cardinality keys. That is the regime of the 532x run and of Percona's 'up to two orders of magnitude' claim.
- Blind updates such as counters, timestamps or balance deltas, written as DB->update upsert callbacks so no read-before-write is needed. The Bε-tree authors say upserts can speed updates up by one to two orders of magnitude.
- An embedded transactional C/C++ key-value store with a Berkeley DB-like API, compressed on-disk nodes (QuickLZ, zlib, LZMA or Snappy) and hot index builds, on 64-bit Linux, where GPLv2/AGPLv3 is acceptable.
- Keeping an existing TokuDB, TokuMX or Percona-FT deployment running, or studying a production-grade Bε-tree with checkpointing, logging and a range-lock manager.

**Skip it when:**
- Data or indexes that fit in RAM, or mostly sequential keys. Percona's docs say fractal trees only 'match B-trees' on sequential data. In Percona's own 2015 iiBench run (1B rows, 3 indexes, one SSD), WiredTiger's B-tree was fastest while data fit in memory, and RocksDB was 'overall better' than PerconaFT as data grew.
- Read-before-write patterns such as unique-key checks and query-modify-insert. These run at point-query speed, which is no better than a B-tree, and every lookup must also apply pending messages buffered along the root-to-leaf path.
- New projects that need an active upstream. The last commit was 2023-11-28 and GitHub issues are disabled. 28 PRs sit unmerged, including fsync error handling (#410, 2018), a crash when out of locks (#443), ThreadSanitizer-found data races (#396) and filesystems with non-512-byte sectors (#385). Percona dropped TokuDB as of Percona Server for MySQL 8.0.28-19 (2022-05-12).
- Targets other than 64-bit Linux. 32-bit is unsupported, macOS and FreeBSD only 'may work' (macOS CI jobs were allowed to fail), and the cycle timer has #error for anything but x86, aarch64 and POWER. The s390x/RISC-V port PR is unmerged, and the TSan PR notes an x86 memory-model bias in the code.
- Projects that need a permissive license. The core is GPLv2/AGPLv3 (only locktree and omt are Apache-2.0), and the PATENTS grant can be terminated if you challenge the patents.

**Integration:** shared lib · zlib (system). Bundled in third_party: xz 4.999.9beta (LZMA), Snappy 1.1.2 and QuickLZ source. CMake >= 2.8.12. Valgrind is optional for tests. · C++11 (-std=c++11) and C99. CI covered GCC 4.8-10 and Clang 4-10 on Ubuntu 18.04 (Travis). CMake 2.8.12+. · 64-bit Linux (CentOS, Debian, Ubuntu supported). macOS 10.8 and FreeBSD 'may work'. No 32-bit. Timer code exists only for x86-64, aarch64 and POWER.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over MyRocks, the LSM engine for MySQL that is still maintained, or over TidesDB and redb only if you specifically want an embeddable Berkeley DB-style transactional library with upsert messages for index-heavy, far-larger-than-RAM random writes, and you accept inheriting maintenance. The in-memory siblings (ALEX, HOT, Wormhole, the learned indexes) target a different, RAM-resident regime and are not substitutes.

**Gotchas:**
- It refuses to start when Linux transparent huge pages are enabled, because they break its memory accounting and can overcommit. TOKU_HUGE_PAGES_OK=1 overrides this, but the README says to use it only for testing with a small cache.
- Under lock-memory pressure, DB->put can return TOKUDB_OUT_OF_LOCKS, and callers must handle it. The pending-lock retry path crashes in that case (PS-4328), and the fix is still an unmerged PR (#443).
- Deletes are tombstone messages, so deleted rows and their space linger until the messages are flushed to the leaves. Compression failures assert instead of returning error codes (compress.h). The bundled xz is a 2009 beta.
- The README build steps are stale (a jemalloc checkout, CMake 2.8.9, gcc47): CMakeLists.txt now requires 2.8.12 and no longer references jemalloc. The core is built with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti, while the ftcxx wrapper throws ft_exception. TokuDB on-disk formats differ across MySQL variants, so moving between them takes a dump and reload.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit (2023-11-28) was a license fix, issues go to Percona's Jira rather than GitHub, and Percona dropped TokuDB from Percona Server 8.0.28-19 in 2022. The source can still be vendored and builds with CMake under GPLv2/AGPLv3 plus a patent grant, but you own all maintenance.

[repo](https://github.com/percona/PerconaFT) · [benchmark](http://web.archive.org/web/20150725021440/http://www.tokutek.com:80/2012/11/532x-multikey-index-insertion-performance-increase-for-mongodb-with-fractal-tree-indexes/)

#### message-queues-logs

##### Mino  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

C++20 shared-memory pub/sub framework passing slab handles over SPSC rings; beat Protobuf+ZeroMQ in author's six-process pipeline benchmark.

**Beats:** ZeroMQ — The author ran a 2-round saturation test on an 8-vCPU Debian 13 KVM guest (CPU model undisclosed, bazel -c opt, C++20, compiler for this build not stated) with six processes and five hops, where every stage validates and copies the full payload. Mino SHM had mean p50 end-to-end latency of 1.8 ms vs 10.6 ms for Protobuf over ZeroMQ ipc:// PUSH/PULL at 256 B, 0.98 vs 1.97 ms at 64 KiB and 13.7 vs 26.9 ms at 1 MiB; a separate 50-message smoke run gave Mino loopback TCP 0.855 ms p50 vs 10.33 ms for ZeroMQ (which used ipc://, because all six roles shared one boot), and all percentiles include queueing delay.

**Known shortcoming:** Serialization confound: the ZeroMQ baseline runs Protobuf over ipc:// at each hop while Mino SHM passes zero-copy handles with no codec. The 12x network figure is one 50-message smoke run; KVM with no CPU model and an unpinned compiler. Solo developer, 2 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark commit predates the zero-copy hop, so each stage still makes two payload copies; the win comes from skipping Protobuf and socket syscalls, not zero-copy. The 12x 'network' figure is loopback TCP vs ZeroMQ ipc:// at saturation (queue-dominated), where Cyclone DDS (0.97 ms) is close to Mino (0.855 ms). The gap shrinks with size (30x at 256 B to 1.35x at 1 MiB); Fast DDS wins 64 KiB throughput and Cyclone beats Mino TCP across two hosts for small messages.

**Known shortcoming:** Polling busy-yields (burns a core); the futex/park wakeup in the design doc is not in the code. /dev/shm sizing can SIGBUS; the SHM layout ABI has changed incompatibly (v3 vs v7). Linux x86-64 only, Bazel-only, no releases, two months old; LGPL static linking carries a relink obligation.

**How:** The control path and the data path are separate. A cache-line-aligned SPSC index ring keeps the producer and consumer cursors on separate cache lines and needs no CAS. It carries ShmHandle offsets into a central slab allocator that uses fixed-size classes and a sharded atomic bitmap, so allocate and free are O(1). Frames are generated with a fixed layout, so a same-host hop needs no Protobuf-style encode/parse and no socket syscall, and subscribers spin on the ring with yield instead of blocking in the kernel. In the benchmarked commit (c977bd1), each forwarding stage still copied the payload out and into a new slab, so the measured win comes from skipping serialization and socket I/O. True zero-copy forwarding (the 'exclusive hop', TakeExclusive -> PublishLocal) landed later in a1b76c3, and docs/benchmarks has no end-to-end numbers for it.

**Use it when:**
- Linux x86-64, several processes on one host in a fixed pipeline (robotics or autonomous-driving stages, sensor fusion) where Protobuf+ZeroMQ encode/parse per hop dominates latency.
- Small, frequent messages (about 256 B): 5.8x lower saturated p50 than Protobuf+ZeroMQ on the KVM run. The author's earlier paced 100 Hz run on an i9-9900KS gave 19 us vs 586 us p50 end to end over five hops.
- Typed fixed-layout messages up to about 1 MiB where you want deterministic O(1) slab allocation and explicit crash recovery of leases, pins and allocation journals (SimpleNode::Recover(), a journal-backed Subscriber).
- Systems that need one C++ API and one IDL for same-host SHM and a cross-host TCP bridge, with optional TLS 1.3 mTLS or frame AEAD.
- Teams that already build with Bazel/Bzlmod and C++20 and control every process that attaches to the segment.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything other than Linux x86-64 in production. AArch64 is unqualified (cross-build/QEMU only), and macOS is only for compiling and non-persistent-SHM tests.
- When you need ZeroMQ's feature set: REQ/REP, ROUTER/DEALER, bindings for many languages, brokerless TCP across hosts as the primary path. Mino is C++-only pub/sub and work queues.
- Cross-host throughput. In the author's one-round two-host run, Mino TCP did 28.2k msg/s at 256 B vs Cyclone DDS's 51.5k. In the one-host six-process smoke, Mino TCP (0.855 ms p50) was only slightly ahead of Cyclone DDS (0.97 ms).
- Large payloads. The advantage shrinks to about 2x saturated (1.35x paced) at 1 MiB, and Fast DDS had higher 64 KiB throughput (3571 vs 2925 msg/s).
- Production-critical use today. The project is about 2 months old, has one author and no releases, every ADR is ACCEPTED but none VALIDATED or FROZEN, the hardware and clean-ref qualification gates are open, and September commits are still fixing CI race conditions.

**Integration:** static lib (Bazel/Bzlmod targets built from source; no CMake, no releases) · OpenSSL 3.5.5 (source-built via BCR, production TLS), spdlog 1.15.3, toml++ 3.4.0; minoc codegen for IDL types; ZeroMQ, Protobuf, Fast DDS and Cyclone DDS are benchmark-only · C++20, Bazel 7.4.1; CI uses GCC 12 and hermetic Clang/LLVM 18.1.8 · Linux x86-64 only for production (ADR-0001); requires lock-free 64-bit atomics; AArch64 and macOS not qualified

**Vs siblings:** Pick Mino over TCPSHM, the other ZeroMQ-beater here and a small point-to-point connection library with sub-microsecond SHM round trips, when you need topic-based multi-process pipelines with IDL-typed messages, MPSC or broadcast fan-out, crash recovery and one API that bridges to TCP across hosts. Pick Zenoh instead when you need a mature, multi-language, routed pub/sub rather than a young C++/Linux-only single-host pipeline.

**Gotchas:**
- Segments are sized as ring capacity x maximum payload. 1 MiB x 64 slots needs about 768 MiB, and the author's smoke run hit SIGBUS on a 64 MiB /dev/shm. Newer code fails closed via posix_fallocate, and the pipeline benchmark falls back to a file-backed mapping.
- Waiting burns CPU. Subscriber::Poll loops on std::this_thread::yield() and a kBlock publisher spins with a pause instruction. The design doc lists spin-then-park and futex wait strategies, but code search found no futex use in the source.
- Shared-memory layouts are still changing. SimpleNode manifest v3 and SharedHostDomain v3 (MINOSHD3) cannot open older segments, and writable secondary attach needs region layout v7, so upgrades mean recreating segments.
- No isolation among processes attached to the same RW region; the trust boundary is UID/GID/namespace. LGPL-3.0 plus Bazel static linking means you must ship relinkable objects if you distribute.

**Status:** Actively developed by one author (152 commits since 2026-07-26, last on 2026-09-13), with no releases and 2 stars. It is LGPL-3.0 and builds only with Bazel, so treat it as a candidate to evaluate rather than a dependency to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/bkcarlos/Mino) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bkcarlos/Mino/blob/master/docs/benchmarks/kvm-2026-08-25/REPORT.md)

##### RabbitMQ  `Erlang`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Erlang multi-protocol broker; unbatched per-message delivery gave ~2.5x lower median latency than Kafka at 500 msg/s.

**Beats:** Apache Kafka — In a personal benchmark repo (i-safonoff/broker-tradeoffs), one Python publisher and one consumer at a fixed 500 msg/s of 256-byte persistent, confirmed messages gave RabbitMQ 4 classic queues (pika blocking client) a p50 of 2.6 ms vs 6.5 ms for Kafka (cp-kafka 7.8.0 image, single KRaft node, acks=1, linger.ms=5, confluent-kafka client), with p99.9 tied at 11.1 vs 11.0 ms; both ran in Docker Desktop on an unspecified Apple Silicon laptop with 4 CPU/4 GB per broker and RF=1. At 2,000 and 8,000 msg/s the single pika publisher topped out near 1,100 msg/s, so those RabbitMQ rows measure load-generator backlog, while Kafka kept up at 4.4 and 3.4 ms p50.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is a 0-star personal benchmark repo on unnamed Apple Silicon; Kafka's latency floor comes from linger.ms=5, and pika with publisher confirms tops out at ~1.1k msg/s while Kafka wins at 2k/8k msg/s.

**Known shortcoming:** The harness skews latency (the RabbitMQ consumer polls basic_get with a 2 ms sleep while Kafka long-polls with linger.ms=5); the win holds only at 500 msg/s because one pika publisher caps at ~1,100 msg/s; classic queues only, RF=1, unpinned rabbitmq:4 image. SECURITY: 83 GHSAs from 2026-05 to 09 (2 critical, 20 high), with public patches only for the latest series; 4.3.0 removed CQv1 and Mnesia (breaking).

**How:** The latency win comes from not batching: each publish goes on the wire at once (listener sockets default to TCP_NODELAY), a direct exchange routes it with a hash lookup, and it lands in a per-queue Erlang process that keeps up to 2,048 messages in memory for a short queue. Persistent messages in a durable classic queue (CQv2) are appended to a per-queue segment store if under the 4,096-byte embedding threshold, or to the shared per-vhost message store if larger. fsync is a group commit: the queue syncs as soon as its mailbox drains, or on a 200 ms timer under load, and only then sends publisher confirms. The benchmark's median gap is mostly Kafka's producer waiting out linger.ms=5 for a batch, which the benchmark page itself calls a tunable dial rather than a broker limit.

**Use it when:**
- Work queues at modest rates (hundreds of msg/s per queue, small payloads) where median end-to-end latency matters more than p99.9: 2.6 ms vs Kafka's 6.5 ms p50 at 500 msg/s with 256 B persistent, confirmed messages.
- Per-message routing through exchanges and bindings, plus built-in retry, delay and dead-letter handling that Kafka leaves to the application.
- Absorbing a spike by starting more competing consumers on a queue, with no partition count planned in advance.
- Mixed-protocol estates: AMQP 0-9-1 and 1.0, MQTT 5.0 devices and STOMP or WebSocket clients on one broker.
- Cases where Kafka's low-rate floor is its linger.ms batching delay and you can't or won't trade throughput to set linger.ms=0.

**Skip it when:**
- Fan-out to many independent readers on classic queues: each reader is a full copy. 8 readers held 176,000 messages vs Kafka's 22,000, and publish rate fell 37% vs 13%. Streams would avoid the copies but were not benchmarked.
- Per-key ordering under parallel consumers: 11.5% of same-key messages were reordered with 8 competing consumers, vs 0% for Kafka, unless you rebuild partitioning with the consistent-hash exchange.
- Replaying history after a bug: an acknowledged classic-queue message is gone.
- High sustained confirmed publish rates from a synchronous client. One pika publisher with per-message confirms capped at ~1,100-1,500 msg/s, against 415,767 msg/s for one Kafka producer in the same suite. The docs also say confirm latency under constant load can reach a few hundred ms.
- Data safety or HA on classic queues: they are non-replicated since 4.0. Quorum queues or streams are the replicated options, and neither was measured here.

**Integration:** standalone server (Erlang/OTP release; distro packages, Docker image, Kubernetes operator); applications use a protocol client library · Erlang/OTP runtime. Bundled Erlang deps: Ranch, Ra (Raft), Khepri (metadata store), Osiris (streams), Cowboy (HTTP), Seshat (metrics). Plus a client library per protocol (the benchmark used pika). · Erlang/OTP 27.0+ (4.3.6 supports OTP [27.0, 29.0)); source builds use GNU Make 4 and Elixir 1.17-1.20 for the CLI tools · Linux (Debian/Ubuntu, RPM distros, openSUSE), Windows 10 and Windows Server, macOS; FreeBSD and Solaris run unofficially; not z/OS or hosts with under 100 MB RAM

**Vs siblings:** NATS JetStream's catalogued result is a lower p50 (0.5 ms vs Kafka's 7.2-7.8 ms, from a different harness), and LavinMQ speaks only AMQP 0-9-1 and MQTT 3.1.x, so pick RabbitMQ when you need exchange-based routing, dead-lettering and delays, AMQP 1.0/MQTT 5.0/STOMP, or replicated quorum queues and streams. For high-rate log workloads, the Kafka-replacement siblings (Redpanda, AutoMQ, Pulsar) target that case and this entry does not.

**Gotchas:**
- The benchmark harness skews both sides. Its RabbitMQ consumer polls with basic_get and sleeps 2 ms whenever all four lane queues are empty, while the Kafka consumer long-polls (fetch.min.bytes=1, fetch.wait.max.ms=10). The harness also sets Kafka's linger.ms=5 explicitly. So neither p50 is a broker constant.
- Confirms for persistent messages wait for fsync, and fsync is group-committed (on queue idle, or on a 200 ms timer). Waiting for one confirm at a time serialises every publish on a round trip; use asynchronous or streamed confirms, or several publishers.
- 4.3.0 is a breaking release. It removed CQv1, so declaring x-queue-mode or x-queue-version=1 now fails. It removed Mnesia in favour of Khepri, so a majority of cluster nodes must be up. It rejects transient non-exclusive queues by default. In-place upgrades are only supported from 4.2.x.
- Security churn: 83 GitHub security advisories were published May-Sep 2026 (2 critical, 20 high; e.g. pre-auth decompression bombs, OAuth/JWKS flaws, topic-wildcard routing blowup). Fixes land in current patch releases, and COMMUNITY_SUPPORT.md says patch releases for series out of community support are not public for non-paying users, so stay on the latest series.

**Status:** Actively maintained by Broadcom's RabbitMQ team (4.3.6 released 2026-09-14, last push 2026-09-26) with an MPL-2.0 core that is free to deploy, but community support and public patch releases cover only the latest release series.

[repo](https://github.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server) · [benchmark](https://github.com/i-safonoff/broker-tradeoffs/blob/main/docs/02-latency.md)

### toolchain-and-build

#### build-systems

##### ccache  `C++`  `GPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

Compiler cache that skips re-running GCC/Clang/MSVC on unchanged source, reusing prior object output.

**Beats:** Uncached compilation (same compiler command run without ccache); the page does not involve Make/Ninja and does not name the compiler — First-party ccache.dev page reports median-of-100-runs, single-file cache-hit timings on an Intel Core i5-4690K with SSD (compiler unnamed, ccache 3.7.1): compiling ccache.c (-g -O2 -MD) was 145.39x/137.81x/28.33x faster than an uncached compile in direct/depend/preprocessor mode, and compiling the header-heavy c++_includes.cc (-MD) was 29.10x/29.32x/5.09x faster. These are cache-hit-only, single-file numbers against a plain uncached compile, not end-to-end project build speedups, and the same page shows cache misses running 0.83-0.98x (slightly slower) than uncached.

**How:** In direct mode it hashes the raw, unpreprocessed source plus its `#include`d headers (using mtime/ctime plus content hashes) to form a cache key, skipping the preprocessor pass entirely on a hit. Preprocessor mode falls back to running cpp and hashing its output when direct mode is unsafe (e.g. macros like __TIME__). Depend mode derives the key from the compiler's -MD/-MMD dependency list. Hashing uses BLAKE3 and results are stored zstd-compressed, so a hit is a hash computation plus a file copy instead of a full parse/codegen/link.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated local or CI rebuilds of the same C/C++/CUDA/Objective-C tree where most translation units are unchanged (branch switches, re-running CI on similar commits)
- Toolchains already on GCC, Clang, MSVC, or NVCC on Linux, macOS, or native Windows (mingw-w64), where masquerading as the compiler via symlink or PATH prefix is acceptable
- Shared build farms or multi-developer teams that want cross-machine hits via ccache's Redis or HTTP remote storage backends
- Header-heavy C++ files where preprocessing dominates wall time and hit rate is expected to be high

**Skip it when:**
- True cold/clean builds or CI that wipes the cache every run — the vendor's own numbers show cache misses at 0.83-0.98x (i.e. slightly slower) than an uncached compile
- Source using __TIME__, __DATE__, or __TIMESTAMP__, which forces the slower preprocessor-mode fallback unless you opt into `sloppiness=time_macros`
- Build flags that defeat the cache key: most -Xpreprocessor uses, -Wp options other than -MD/-MMD/-D/-U, or filesystems with coarse mtime granularity that make ccache disable caching as a race-condition safeguard
- Windows setups needing more than mingw-w64 parity — MSYS2 and other Unix-likes are only partially supported, and MSVC-style compilers don't get full direct-mode support
- Situations demanding fully reproducible, audited benchmark numbers — the vendor's own performance page never names the compiler used

**Integration:** source-drop · Required: BLAKE3, fmt, tl-expected, xxhash, Zstandard (bundled or auto-downloaded if not found locally). Optional: cpp-httplib and hiredis for HTTP/Redis remote storage, doctest for tests. · CMake 3.15+ to build; C++20 compiler (GCC 11+, Clang 12+, AppleClang 10+) plus a C99 compiler. Note: the benchmarked version (3.7.1) predates this and had much looser requirements. · Linux and macOS (Level A, regularly tested on Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 and macOS 14); native Windows via mingw-w64 (Level A); Windows/MSYS2 and other Unix-likes (Level B, partial)

**Vs siblings:** No direct siblings — Mill, Buck2, tup, and xmake are build-graph orchestrators, while ccache caches individual compiler invocations underneath any of them. Use ccache alongside those tools when the bottleneck is redundant single-file recompiles rather than build-graph scheduling or dependency tracking.

**Gotchas:**
- __TIME__/__DATE__/__TIMESTAMP__ in source disables direct mode and forces the slower preprocessor-mode path
- If an included header's mtime is newer than the time ccache started, it disables caching entirely for that compile as a race-condition safeguard (tune with sloppiness=include_file_ctime,include_file_mtime)
- Default cache size cap is 5 GB with no file-count limit; old entries are evicted silently once the cap is hit
- Direct mode has compiler-option restrictions (most -Xpreprocessor uses and non-dependency -Wp options force preprocessor mode)

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-19; current release targets C++20/CMake 3.15+), GPL-3.0-or-later, and easy to obtain via package managers or source build — it's the de facto default compiler cache bundled in many Linux distros and CI images.

[repo](https://github.com/ccache/ccache) · [benchmark](https://ccache.dev/performance.html)

##### tup  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

File-based build tool that beats Make's incremental-rebuild scanning via a persistent Linux-only file monitor and per-command sandboxing.

**Beats:** Make — On tup's own synthetic C-project generator (log-scale graphs, N up to 100k files / ~200k with headers, make run as `make -rR`, no CPU/OS/compiler flags stated), tup reports ~0s no-op checks and ~0.1s single-file rebuilds versus make's figures of roughly 20-30 minutes at 100k files; tup's cold/initial build is itself 5-30% slower than make, and tup's own file monitor took up to 2min:30s to cold-start at 200k files.

**How:** Speed comes from a persistent background 'monitor' process (inotify on Linux) that watches the filesystem so tup never has to stat/walk the whole tree like make does on every invocation; state lives in an embedded SQLite database rather than being recomputed each run. Per-command FUSE sandboxing produces an exact dependency graph (not user-declared globs), so a change dirties only the affected graph nodes -- turning no-op and single-file rebuild checks into near O(changed files) instead of O(all files).

**Use it when:**
- Large Linux C/C++ trees (tens of thousands of files) where make's per-invocation directory scan/stat dominates the edit-compile-test loop.
- Teams willing to run a persistent `tup monitor` daemon in the background and keep it warm.
- Projects that want undeclared-dependency errors caught automatically via file-access tracing instead of hand-maintained header dependency lists.
- GPL-2.0-compatible projects that can vendor the tool as-is (it already bundles Lua, PCRE2 and SQLite3, no external runtime deps).

**Skip it when:**
- Clean/cold builds: tup measured 5-30% slower than make across sizes on the vendor's own benchmark.
- macOS/Windows, or Linux without FUSE: the fast-path monitor is inotify/Linux-specific, the OSX shim has an open unresolved issue since 2014, and FUSE-based sandboxing broke on libfuse3 3.17.1 as recently as 2025 (issue #518).
- Teams needing Makefile compatibility, mainstream IDE integration, or a large plugin ecosystem -- 1.3k stars versus make's ubiquity.
- Build outputs generated dynamically/implicitly -- tup requires every output declared up front; undeclared writes are errors, which is a real migration cost.
- One-off or CI-only cold builds where the monitor never warms up -- most of the claimed win depends on a hot monitor and hot OS cache.

**Integration:** source-drop (build tup itself from source via bootstrap.sh; not header-only) · none required to vendor -- bundles Lua, PCRE2, SQLite3 in-tree; needs libfuse on Linux for command sandboxing · not documented precisely -- plain C, built via its own bootstrap.sh/tup; Windows build via build-win32.sh (MinGW) · Linux (full speed: inotify monitor + FUSE sandbox), macOS (dllinject/ldpreload shim, no monitor -- open issue since 2014), Windows (dllinject-based tracing)

**Vs siblings:** Pick tup over xmake/Mill/Buck2/ccache when the specific pain is make's linear directory-scan overhead on a huge Linux C/C++ tree during interactive edit-rebuild, and you can run a persistent monitor daemon and rewrite the build in Tup's DAG syntax; xmake is the closer choice for a faster Make-compatible generator without changing build files, and ccache if the bottleneck is recompilation itself rather than dependency scanning.

**Gotchas:**
- Near-zero no-op/rebuild times require `tup monitor` already running; without it tup falls back to scanning, and a third-party benchmark (issue #268) found it slower than make/ninja.
- libfuse3 ABI changes have broken tup's build-command file sandboxing before (3.17.1, reported 2025).
- Monitor cold-start took 2min:30s at 200k files in the vendor's own benchmark (2.5s once cache is hot).
- All build outputs must be declared explicitly; undeclared writes are treated as errors, not warnings.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-30, closed a race-condition crash as recently as July 2026) but niche -- 1,262 stars, 168 open issues; GPL-2.0 and copyable/vendorable, though its FUSE-based build sandboxing has broken on newer libfuse3 as recently as 2025.

[repo](https://github.com/gittup/tup) · [benchmark](http://gittup.org/tup/make_vs_tup.html)

#### compilers-frontends

##### TinyCC (tcc)  `C`  `LGPL-2.1`  `active`  `Tier C`

Tiny self-hosting C compiler/JIT that compiles about 9x faster than gcc -O0, trading away optimization.

**Beats:** GCC — On Fabrice Bellard's own tcc benchmark page, compiling the Links web browser (76,936 source lines, but 1,950,947 lines / 67.2MB actually compiled due to repeated header inclusion) on a 2.4GHz Pentium 4: TinyCC 0.9.22 finished in 2.27s (859,000 lines/s, 29.6MB/s) versus GCC 3.2 at -O0 in 20.0s (98,000 lines/s, 3.4MB/s), about a 9x wall-clock advantage. Both compilers ran with no comparable optimization flags enabled (tcc has none), and the hardware/compiler versions are roughly 2003-2005 era.

**How:** It skips almost everything gcc's pipeline does beyond translation: no real optimizer (tcc has no flag comparable to -O1/-O2/-O3), a single fast pass from source straight to machine code, and its own integrated preprocessor/assembler/linker avoid forking out to separate cc1/as/ld processes. It also natively supports 6 target architectures (i386, x86-64, ARM, AArch64, RISC-V64, plus legacy TMS320C67xx) with a simple, non-SSA-optimizing code generator per target. The cost of skipping optimization is codegen roughly at gcc -O0/-O1 quality.

**Use it when:**
- Tight edit-compile-run development loops where compiler latency, not runtime speed, dominates iteration time
- Ad hoc 'C scripting' -- running a .c file directly via a #!tcc -run shebang instead of compiling a real binary
- Embedding a C compiler/JIT inside another program (via libtcc) for runtime code generation, e.g. compiling small C snippets to native code and calling them in-process
- Bootstrapping or rescue environments where binary size matters (GNU Mes uses tcc to bootstrap a build from source)
- Local/CI dev builds of large C codebases where a project bundles tcc for fast iteration and uses a real compiler for release builds (this is how the V language uses it)

**Skip it when:**
- Producing optimized release binaries -- there is no optimization pass comparable to gcc -O1/-O2/-O3, so generated code is measurably slower
- Code relying on full C11 or the broader GNU C extension surface -- tcc covers 'many' C11 features and GNU extensions, not all of them (not documented as 100% coverage)
- C++ code -- tcc is a C compiler only
- Toolchains that depend on gcc/clang-specific features such as LTO, sanitizers, or vendor-specific builtins not implemented by tcc
- Programs combining the -b bounds checker with signal handlers or fork() in a multi-threaded process -- the docs call this out as a known incompatibility because the bounds-checking code uses locks

**Integration:** source-drop / standalone compiler binary (CLI, gcc-like flags); optional static and shared libtcc library for embedding as an in-memory JIT · none required to build (self-hosting: ./configure && make, or make test); optional -lpthread when using the -pthread flag · Any ANSI C (C89) host compiler to bootstrap from source, or tcc itself; as a language target it implements ISO C99, many ISO C11 features, and GNU C extensions (inline asm, _Thread_local, __attribute__((cleanup)), _Static_assert, asm goto, stdatomic) · x86 (i386), x86-64, ARM, AArch64, RISC-V64, legacy TMS320C67xx; Linux/BSD (ELF), native macOS x86-64 (Mach-O), Windows (PE, see tcc-win32.txt), Android (position-independent executables)

**Vs siblings:** Pick tcc over zapcc or MIR/c2m when you want a mature, widely-deployed, general-purpose C compiler and embeddable JIT rather than a narrower research/prototype tool: zapcc is an abandoned Clang fork focused on incremental C++ template caching, and MIR/c2m is a newer, more experimental C-to-MIR JIT (bigger claimed speedup, less production track record). Neither zapcc nor cg_clif target C the way tcc does (zapcc is C++-only via Clang, cg_clif is a Rust backend), so for straight C dev-loop speed or in-process C JITing, tcc is the direct fit.

**Gotchas:**
- The -b bounds checker is incompatible with signal handlers (checking is disabled inside them) and interacts badly with fork() in multi-threaded programs, per tcc-doc.texi -- both stem from locking inside the bounds-checking runtime
- Bound-checked code (-b) is not included in shared libraries; the main executable must itself be built with -b for the checker to take effect
- Codegen quality sits around gcc -O0/-O1; don't compare tcc binaries' runtime speed to an optimized gcc/clang build
- -std=version only distinguishes c11/gnu11 (sets __STDC_VERSION__ to 201112) from everything else (199901); it isn't a fine-grained standards switch like gcc's

**Status:** Actively maintained: this GitHub mirror tracks the upstream repo.or.cz mob development branch and was pushed 2026-09-22; current in-tree version is 0.9.28rc. LGPL-2.1, small self-contained C source tree, easy to vendor -- matches its 'copyable' usability rating.
